as3-explainer-validator.name: AS3 declaration explainer
as3-explainer-validator.blurb: Paste the JSON you POST to /mgmt/shared/appsvcs/declare and it reads it back: whether it is a full AS3 request or an ADC-only declaration, the schemaVersion and metadata, and the Tenant to Application to resource tree with every class explained, while checking the structural rules F5 documents. Runs entirely in your browser.
as3-explainer-validator.inputLabel: An AS3 request or ADC declaration (JSON)
as3-explainer-validator.inputPlaceholder:
Paste an AS3 declaration, for example:
{ "class": "AS3", "action": "deploy", "declaration": { "class": "ADC", "schemaVersion": "3.0.0", "MyTenant": { "class": "Tenant", "MyApp": { "class": "Application", "service": { "class": "Service_HTTP", "virtualAddresses": ["10.0.0.1"] } } } } }
as3-explainer-validator.runsLocally: Parsed in your browser. Nothing you paste is uploaded.
as3-explainer-validator.empty: Paste an AS3 request or an ADC declaration to see its structure explained and checked.
as3-explainer-validator.scopeNote: A structure explainer and sanity checker, not a full JSON-Schema validator: it checks the documented structural rules and explains the classes, but a declaration that passes here can still be rejected by AS3 itself. It never contacts a BIG-IP.

kind.as3Request: This is a full AS3 request (class AS3)
kind.adcOnly: This is an ADC-only declaration (class ADC, no AS3 wrapper)
kind.notAs3: This is not an AS3 or ADC declaration

finding.parseError: That looks like JSON but could not be parsed
finding.notAs3: The top-level object has no class of AS3 or ADC, so this is not an AS3 declaration. An AS3 request starts with class AS3; an ADC declaration starts with class ADC.
finding.adcOnly: This is an ADC-only declaration (no AS3 wrapper), so the action and persist options are not available. Wrap it in a class AS3 object to use them.
finding.missingSchema: The ADC declaration has no schemaVersion. AS3 requires it, and it is decoupled from the AS3 release version.
finding.noTenant: The declaration has no Tenant. A declaration must contain at least one object with class Tenant, which becomes a BIG-IP partition.
finding.emptyTenant: Tenant {tenant} has no Application. Each tenant must contain at least one object with class Application.
finding.emptyApp: Application {app} in tenant {tenant} has no resources. An application must contain at least one ADC resource, for example a Service or Pool.
finding.templateMismatch: Application {app} in tenant {tenant} uses template {template}, which requires a matching {needs} object named service (formerly serviceMain), but none was found.
finding.invalidName: The name "{name}" in {where} is not a valid AS3 name: names are 1 to 64 characters, alphanumeric or underscore, and must start with a letter.

as3-explainer-validator.unknownClass: (class not in this tool's catalogue; still shown)

share.carries: The link carries the declaration with every passphrase, key and token replaced by {redacted}; names, addresses and iRules go as pasted.
share.redacted: {n, plural, =0 {Nothing in it needed replacing.} one {One value is replaced.} other {# values are replaced.}}
share.blocked: No link: this text is not valid JSON and names “{name}”, so its secrets cannot be found safely; fix the JSON first.

base64.name: Base64, Base32, Hex & Percent Codec
base64.blurb: Encode text to Base64, URL-safe Base64, Base32, hexadecimal, or percent-encoding, and decode any of them back. Tolerant of missing padding and whitespace, and it flags binary (non-UTF-8) results. Runs entirely in your browser.
base64.runsLocally: Encoding and decoding run locally. Nothing you paste leaves your browser.

decodeErrors.invalid-characters: That input contains characters outside the selected codec's alphabet.
decodeErrors.invalid-length: That input is not a valid length for the selected codec.
decodeErrors.invalid-escape: That input has a malformed percent-escape (a % not followed by two hex digits).

base64.decodedBytes: Decoded {bytes, plural, one {# byte} other {# bytes}}.
base64.notUtf8: Decoded {bytes, plural, one {# byte} other {# bytes}}, but the result is not valid UTF-8 text (likely binary).
base64.layersOptionTitle: {n, plural, =1 {Single pass (no extra layers)} other {Apply the codec # times: n-encode, or peel # layers when decoding}}

share.carries: The link carries the text in the box as typed, with the direction, the codec and the layers.
share.caution: Encoded text often hides a password or a token (HTTP Basic is base64 of user:password), so check what you send.

cert-renewal-planner.blurb: Work out a TLS certificate's validity, whether it fits the CA/Browser Forum 47-day schedule, and the renewal cadence it implies - all offline.
cert-renewal-planner.runsLocally: Everything runs in your browser; nothing is uploaded.
cert-renewal-planner.maxForPhase: Maximum for its issuance date: {max} days.
cert-renewal-planner.overByText: {days, plural, one {{days} day} other {{days} days}} over the {max}-day maximum for its issuance date - a public CA would not issue it.
cert-renewal-planner.renewalsValue: About {n} renewals per year at this validity.
cert-renewal-planner.daysRemaining: {days, plural, one {{days} day} other {{days} days}} until it expires.
cert-renewal-planner.expiredText: Expired {days, plural, one {{days} day} other {{days} days}} ago.
cert-renewal-planner.renewByText: Renew by {date} (about {lead, plural, one {{lead} day} other {{lead} days}} before expiry)
cert-renewal-planner.renewByDue: {days, plural, one {{days} day} other {{days} days}} from now
cert-renewal-planner.dcvText: Domain control validation (DCV) data can be reused for {days} days.
cert-renewal-planner.siiText: Organization identity (OV/EV SII) can be reused for {days} days.
cert-renewal-planner.scheduleIntro: Public TLS maximums key off the certificate's issuance date:
cert-renewal-planner.projectionIntro: Renewals per certificate per year, as the caps tighten:
cert-renewal-planner.note_overCap: This validity exceeds the {max}-day maximum for its issuance date.
cert-renewal-planner.note_future47: Compliant today, but longer than the eventual 47-day cap - expect more frequent renewals as the schedule advances.
cert-renewal-planner.note_publicOnly: These caps apply to publicly trusted TLS certificates only. Private or internal PKI (public key infrastructure) is not governed by SC-081v3.
cert-renewal-planner.note_automate: At these cadences, automate issuance and renewal with ACME (RFC 8555) and ARI (RFC 9773); manual renewal does not scale.
cert-renewal-planner.err_empty: Enter both the issue and expiry dates.
cert-renewal-planner.err_order: The expiry date must be after the issue date.

cidr.name: CIDR / Subnet Calculator
cidr.blurb: Break down any IPv4 CIDR block into network and broadcast addresses, usable host range, host count, and netmask, and see which IANA special-purpose range it falls in. The other modes carve variable-length subnets (VLSM) out of a parent block, summarize prefixes into a supernet, and find overlaps and gaps. Runs entirely in your browser.
cidr.title: CIDR Calculator
cidr.description: Compute the network and broadcast addresses, usable host range, host count, and netmask of an IPv4 CIDR block, with the IANA special-purpose range it falls in; plan VLSM subnets, summarize prefixes into a supernet, and find overlaps and gaps. Runs locally in your browser.
cidr.runsLocally: Runs locally. Nothing is sent to any server.
cidr.bitsNote: The highlighted bits identify the network - the rest address hosts within it.

results.lastAddressNoBroadcast: Last address (no directed broadcast on a /31 or /32)

errors.empty: Enter a CIDR block to calculate.
errors.invalid: That does not look like a valid CIDR block. Try a format like 192.168.1.0/24.

modeDesc.subnet: Analyse a single IPv4 CIDR block: network, broadcast, mask, host range, and the special-purpose ranges it falls in or overlaps.
modeDesc.vlsm: Carve variable-length subnets from a parent block to fit a list of host counts.
modeDesc.supernet: Summarize a list of prefixes into the smallest set of covering blocks.
modeDesc.overlap: Find overlaps and containment between prefixes, plus gaps within an optional scope.

vlsm.maskedNote: The parent {typed} has host bits set, so it was masked to {parent}; the plan is carved from {parent}.
vlsm.orderNote: Requests are placed largest block first, not in the order entered, so every block starts on a multiple of its own size.
vlsm.noFree: No free space left in the parent.

supernet.label: Prefixes to aggregate
supernet.singleExtra: Adds {extra, plural, one {{extra} extra address} other {{extra} extra addresses}} beyond the inputs.

overlap.label: Prefixes to check
overlap.noGaps: No gaps in the given scope.

err.ipv4: Not a valid IPv4 address. Use four octets 0-255, like 192.168.1.0.
err.octet: An octet is out of range (each must be 0-255).
err.prefix: The prefix length must be between 0 and 32.
err.tooMany: Too many entries. Trim the list and try again.
err.noReqs: Add at least one subnet requirement with a host count.
err.noPrefixes: Enter at least one prefix, one per line.
err.zeroHosts: A subnet requirement asks for 0 hosts. Every subnet needs at least 1 host: correct the count or remove the row.

cidr.rfcNote: /31 and /32 reserve nothing: every address is usable (RFC 3021).
cidr.reservedNote: The first address is the network and the last is the broadcast; both are reserved, so usable = total − 2.
cidr.classifyPartial: Partly special-purpose: {special} of {total} addresses fall in the ranges listed below; the rest are in no special-purpose range.
cidr.classifyNone: No special-purpose range (globally routable unicast space).
cidr.classifyNote1: [1] Registry footnote: several protocols have been granted exceptions to this rule (for examples, see RFC 8029 and RFC 5884).
cidr.classifyNote2: [2] Registry footnote: not usable unless by virtue of a more specific reservation.
cidr.classifyFlagsNote: The flags are the registry's. Source and Destination: whether an address from the range is valid as the source or the destination of a datagram that transits two devices. Forwardable: whether a router may forward such a datagram between external interfaces. Globally reachable: whether it is forwardable beyond a specified administrative domain.
cidr.classifySource: Rows from the IANA IPv4 Special-Purpose Address Space registry (updated 2025-10-09) and, for 224.0.0.0/4, the IANA IPv4 Multicast Address Space registry, both read 2026-10-19. The registry notes that a listed range is not guaranteed to be routable in any particular local or global context.
cidr.legacyHandoff: This page was opened by an older link that carried the block in its query string (?input=), so that one request did reach the site's host before anything ran here. The calculation itself is local, and the address now keeps the block after the #, which no request carries.

share.carries: The link carries the block you calculated, and nothing else.

cipher.name: Cipher Suite Decoder
cipher.blurb: Enter a TLS cipher suite, as an IANA name, an OpenSSL or GnuTLS name, or a hex code point, to break it into its key exchange, authentication, cipher, mode, and MAC, with a plain-language security read-out and the official IANA recommendation. Runs entirely in your browser against a bundled copy of the IANA registry.
cipher.runsLocally: Decoding runs locally against a bundled copy of the IANA TLS Cipher Suite registry. Nothing is sent anywhere.
cipher.notInRegistryNote: This name parsed structurally but was not found in the bundled IANA registry snapshot, so its code point and cross-names are not shown.

errors.empty: Enter a cipher suite to decode.
errors.format: That is not a cipher suite. Enter an IANA name (TLS_...), an OpenSSL name, or a hex code point such as 0x1301.
errors.unknown: That is a valid code-point format, but it is not an assigned cipher suite in the IANA registry.

reasons.nullCipher: NULL cipher: the traffic is not encrypted at all.
reasons.anon: Anonymous key exchange: the peer is not authenticated, so it gives no protection against an active man-in-the-middle.
reasons.export40: Export-grade 40-bit key: trivially brute-forced, a relic of 1990s export rules.
reasons.rc4: RC4 stream cipher: a biased keystream makes it broken, and RFC 7465 prohibits it for TLS.
reasons.singleDes: Single DES with a 56-bit key: brute-forceable in hours.
reasons.rc2: RC2: an obsolete 40/64-bit cipher that is not safe for modern use.
reasons.tripleDes: 3DES has a 64-bit block, which exposes it to the Sweet32 birthday attack (CVE-2016-2183). RFC 8429 deprecates it.
reasons.md5Mac: MD5 MAC: MD5 is cryptographically broken.
reasons.cbcMac: CBC with an HMAC-SHA1 or MD5 MAC uses MAC-then-encrypt, which is exposed to padding-oracle attacks such as Lucky13; on TLS 1.0, CBC's predictable initialization vectors also allow BEAST.
reasons.ccm8: CCM_8 truncates the authentication tag to 8 bytes, weakening integrity. IANA does not mark it Recommended.
reasons.noFs: No forward secrecy: with a static key exchange, one compromised long-term key can decrypt past sessions. Modern guidance requires ECDHE or DHE.
reasons.legacyCipher: {value} is a legacy cipher that is deprecated for TLS.
reasons.aead: AEAD cipher (authenticated encryption): confidentiality and integrity in one primitive, with no separate MAC to misuse.
reasons.fs: Forward secrecy: an ephemeral key exchange keeps past traffic safe even if the long-term key is later compromised.
reasons.tls13: TLS 1.3 suite: only modern AEAD ciphers, with the key exchange negotiated separately and always ephemeral.
reasons.ianaD: IANA marks this suite "D" (discouraged): it SHOULD NOT or MUST NOT be used, depending on the situation.
reasons.ianaN: IANA does not mark this suite "Recommended": it has limited applicability or has not been through the IETF consensus process.
reasons.signalling: Signalling suite (SCSV): not an actual cipher, it carries a protocol signal such as fallback protection or renegotiation info.

groups.title: Key-exchange groups
groups.intro: TLS negotiates the actual key-agreement group separately from the cipher suite, in the supported_groups extension. As "harvest now, decrypt later" drives the move to post-quantum key agreement, the hybrid groups below pair a classical curve with ML-KEM.
groups.foot: X25519MLKEM768 is the hybrid most browsers now send by default.

share.carries: The link carries the cipher suite as typed.

csr-decoder.name: CSR decoder
csr-decoder.blurb: Decode a PKCS#10 certificate signing request to read its subject, public key, requested SANs and extensions, and attributes - entirely in your browser.
csr-decoder.inputLabel: Certificate signing request (PEM, base64, or hex)
csr-decoder.runsLocally: Everything runs in your browser; the CSR is never uploaded.
csr-decoder.notCertNote: A CSR is a request, not a certificate. It has no serial number, no issuer, and no validity dates - only what the requester is asking a CA to certify.
csr-decoder.noSubject: No subject name (this CSR relies on requested SANs).
csr-decoder.err_empty: Paste a certificate signing request to decode.
csr-decoder.err_format: That does not look like a PEM, base64, or hex CSR.
csr-decoder.err_der: The DER structure could not be parsed.
csr-decoder.err_structure: This parses as DER but is not a PKCS#10 certification request.

share.carries: The link carries the box as pasted: the request and anything else in it.
share.blockedPrivateKey: No link: the box also holds a private key, so remove that block to share the request.
share.blockedChallenge: No link: this request carries a challenge password in clear, and a link would carry it too.

curl-command-builder.name: curl command builder
curl-command-builder.blurb: Pick any of the 27 protocols curl speaks, fill in protocol-aware fields, and get the exact command with every flag explained and safety warnings surfaced. The inverse of the curl command explainer: that one reads a command, this one writes it.

ui.passNote: Leaving the password empty makes curl prompt for it at run time, keeping it out of your shell history.
ui.insecure: Skip TLS verification (-k), with a warning
ui.err_host: Enter a host to build the command.
ui.err_path: Enter a local file path for the file:// URL.
ui.windowsNote: Quoting targets POSIX shells (bash, zsh). cmd.exe and PowerShell quote differently; run these as written in Git Bash or WSL.
ui.privacy: Runs entirely in your browser. Nothing you type is sent anywhere and no request is ever executed.

http.name: HTTP
http.desc: The web's transfer protocol. curl speaks HTTP/0.9 through HTTP/3 and gives you full control over method, headers, body, cookies, and authentication.

https.name: HTTPS
https.desc: HTTP inside TLS: the same request model with the transport encrypted and the server authenticated by certificate.

ws.name: WebSocket
ws.desc: A bidirectional, TCP-like channel set up over a plain HTTP request. The ws scheme is the cleartext flavour.

wss.name: WebSocket Secure
wss.desc: The same bidirectional WebSocket channel established over HTTPS, so the whole session runs inside TLS.

ftp.name: FTP
ftp.desc: The classic File Transfer Protocol: downloads, uploads, and directory listings. Starts in cleartext; the session can upgrade to TLS.

ftps.name: FTPS
ftps.desc: FTP with an implicit TLS layer from the first byte. Historically awkward through firewalls because of its separate data connections.

sftp.name: SFTP
sftp.desc: The SSH File Transfer Protocol carried over SSH version 2: one encrypted connection for both commands and data.

scp.name: SCP
scp.desc: The classic SSH copy protocol over SSH version 2. Plain file-copy semantics; SFTP is the richer sibling.

tftp.name: TFTP
tftp.desc: Trivial FTP over UDP: tiny, unauthenticated, cleartext by design. The firmware and network-boot workhorse.

smb.name: SMB
smb.desc: Windows file sharing. curl supports SMB version 1 for uploading and downloading files on a share.

smbs.name: SMBS
smbs.desc: SMB wrapped in TLS: the same version 1 file semantics with the transport encrypted.

file.name: Local file
file.desc: Local file access through a URL, no network at all. Handy for testing pipelines with real curl syntax.

smtp.name: SMTP
smtp.desc: Mail submission: uploading a message to an SMTP server means sending it. The envelope sender and recipients are set with dedicated flags.

smtps.name: SMTPS
smtps.desc: SMTP with implicit TLS from the first byte, conventionally on port 465.

pop3.name: POP3
pop3.desc: Retrieve mail from a POP3 server: downloading means fetching a message. Starts cleartext and can upgrade with STLS.

pop3s.name: POP3S
pop3s.desc: POP3 inside implicit TLS on port 995.

imap.name: IMAP
imap.desc: Read mail and mailboxes on an IMAP server; the URL selects the mailbox and message. Starts cleartext, can upgrade to TLS.

imaps.name: IMAPS
imaps.desc: IMAP inside implicit TLS on port 993.

mqtt.name: MQTT
mqtt.desc: The IoT publish-subscribe protocol, version 3. Downloading a topic subscribes to it; posting data publishes on it.

mqtts.name: MQTTS
mqtts.desc: MQTT carried inside TLS, conventionally on port 8883.

ldap.name: LDAP (Lightweight Directory Access Protocol)
ldap.desc: Directory lookups: the URL encodes the base DN, attributes, scope, and filter in one line.

ldaps.name: LDAPS
ldaps.desc: LDAP inside implicit TLS on port 636.

dict.name: DICT
dict.desc: The dictionary server protocol: a URL like /d:word looks the word up on the server.

gopher.name: Gopher
gopher.desc: The pre-web document protocol, still alive in niches. Retrieves menus and documents.

gophers.name: GopherS
gophers.desc: Gopher over TLS, a modern extension to the old protocol.

rtsp.name: RTSP
rtsp.desc: The Real Time Streaming Protocol: curl supports RTSP 1.0 downloads for talking to streaming media servers.

telnet.name: Telnet
telnet.desc: An interactive cleartext session: curl sends what it reads on stdin and prints what the server returns. Useful for poking raw TCP services.

opt.headOnly: -I asks for headers only (a HEAD request); no body is transferred.
opt.method: -X sets the request method explicitly; curl only needs it when the method cannot be inferred.
opt.httpVersion: Pins the HTTP version instead of letting curl negotiate one.
opt.header: -H adds one request header exactly as written.
opt.user: -u sends credentials; with no password given, curl prompts for it.
opt.data: -d sends this data as the request body: on HTTP it implies POST, on MQTT it publishes to the topic.
opt.dataUrlencode: --data-urlencode sends the data URL-encoded, safe for arbitrary characters.
opt.form: -F builds a multipart/form-data body; a leading @ uploads the file at that path.
opt.upload: -T uploads the given local file to the URL (PUT on HTTP, STOR on FTP, the message on SMTP).
opt.cookie: -b sends the given cookie string, or reads cookies from a file.
opt.cookieJar: -c writes the cookies received during the transfer to this file.
opt.proxy: -x sends the transfer through this proxy.
opt.resolve: --resolve pins host:port to a specific address, bypassing DNS for that name.
opt.cacert: --cacert verifies the server against this CA bundle instead of the system store.
opt.connectTimeout: --connect-timeout caps how long establishing the connection may take, in seconds.
opt.maxTime: --max-time caps the whole transfer duration, in seconds.
opt.retry: --retry retries a transient failure this many times, with backoff.
opt.followRedirects: -L follows HTTP redirects to the final location.
opt.compressed: --compressed asks for a compressed response and transparently decompresses it.
opt.listOnly: -l asks for a names-only listing (FTP directory or mailbox).
opt.outputRemote: -O saves the download under its remote file name.
opt.outputFile: -o saves the download to the given file name.
opt.include: -i includes the response headers in the output.
opt.verbose: -v narrates the whole exchange, including connection and TLS details.
opt.silent: -s silences the progress meter and error output.

warn.insecure: -k disables TLS certificate verification: the connection is encrypted but the peer is not authenticated. Fine against a lab box, dangerous anywhere else.
warn.cleartext: This protocol starts in cleartext: everything, including any credentials, crosses the network unencrypted unless the session upgrades to TLS.
warn.passOnCli: The password is part of the command line: it can land in shell history and show in the process list. Prefer -u user alone and let curl prompt, or use a .netrc file.
warn.dataDefaultCt: With -d and no Content-Type header, curl sends application/x-www-form-urlencoded. If this body is JSON, add a Content-Type: application/json header.
warn.considerSslReqd: This protocol can upgrade to TLS (STARTTLS style). Consider adding --ssl-reqd so the transfer fails rather than continue in cleartext.
warn.telnetInteractive: telnet: opens an interactive session; curl sends what it reads on stdin and prints what the server returns.
warn.smbV1: curl speaks SMB version 1, which many modern servers disable. Expect this to work mainly against legacy shares.

share.carries: The link carries the form with the password and every token or cookie value replaced by {mark}; the rest goes as typed.
share.redacted: {n, plural, =0 {Nothing in it needed replacing.} one {One value is replaced.} other {# values are replaced.}}
share.blocked: No link: the command still holds a key, token or password ({label}) that cannot be replaced safely. Put a placeholder in its place, then share again.

cvss-vector-decoder.name: CVSS vector decoder
cvss-vector-decoder.blurb: Paste a CVSS v3.1 or v3.0 vector and get the score computed and mapped to a severity, with every metric spelled out. Local and offline; nothing is sent anywhere.
cvss-vector-decoder.privacy: The vector is scored in your browser. Nothing is uploaded.
cvss-vector-decoder.notCvss: Paste a CVSS v3.0 or v3.1 vector string to decode it.
cvss-vector-decoder.parseError: That does not parse as a CVSS vector ({detail}).
cvss-vector-decoder.unsupportedVersion: This is a CVSS {version} vector. This decoder computes CVSS v3.0 and v3.1 only. CVSS v4.0 uses a different scoring model, and CVSS v2 is retired.

warnings.title: Notes
warnings.no-version-prefix: No CVSS version prefix was found. Scored as CVSS v3.1; add a CVSS:3.1/ or CVSS:3.0/ prefix to be explicit.
warnings.duplicate-metric: A metric appears more than once. The last value given was used.
warnings.incomplete-base: Some mandatory base metrics are missing, so no score can be computed. All eight of AV, AC, PR, UI, S, C, I, and A are required.

diff.emptyState: Paste text in both boxes to compare them.
diff.tooLarge: These inputs are too large to diff in the browser. Try comparing smaller sections.

share.carries: The link carries both texts as pasted and the two options; a text holding a credential gets none.
share.caution: Compared texts can be private: read both before you send the link.

dig-output-explainer.name: dig output explainer
dig-output-explainer.blurb: Paste real dig output and get a decoded, explained breakdown: the header and flags, the EDNS OPT pseudo-section, every record in each section, and the query stats. Parsed entirely in your browser, nothing is resolved or sent anywhere.

input.label: Paste dig output
input.placeholder:
; <<>> DiG 9.18.1 <<>> example.com A
;; ->>HEADER<<- opcode: QUERY, status: NOERROR, id: ...

dig-output-explainer.privacy: Parsed entirely in your browser. Nothing is resolved or sent anywhere.
dig-output-explainer.notDig: This does not look like dig output. Paste the full text dig prints, including the ;; ->>HEADER<<- line.

warnings.title: Worth noticing
warnings.nonzero-rcode: The status is not NOERROR, so this is not a normal successful answer. See the status meaning above.
warnings.truncated-tc: The TC (truncated) flag is set: the UDP answer did not fit and is incomplete. dig normally retries over TCP.
warnings.noerror-nodata: Status is NOERROR but there are no answer records (NODATA): no data of this type at this name. Usually the name exists without this type; a zone using compact denial of existence (RFC 9824) also answers this way for a name that does not exist.
warnings.looks-like-query: The QR flag is not set, so this looks like a query rather than a response.
warnings.dnssec-requested-not-validated: DNSSEC was requested (the DO flag is set) but the AD flag is not, so the resolver did not return validated data.
warnings.ttl-units: dig printed the TTLs in units (+ttlunits: s, m, h, d, w). Each is converted to seconds and shown both ways.
warnings.ttl-absent: Some records were printed without a TTL column (+nottlid). The TTL is still in the message; dig just did not print it, so it cannot be shown here.

header.title: Header
header.negativeTtlHelp: A negative answer may be cached for the TTL of the SOA in the AUTHORITY section, which the authoritative server sets to the minimum of the SOA's own TTL and its MINIMUM field (RFC 2308, section 5): here min({soaTtl}s, {minimum}s) = {ttl}s. A cache counts it down from there.

opt.title: EDNS (OPT pseudo-section)
opt.help: EDNS(0) extends DNS over UDP: it advertises a larger UDP payload size and carries flags such as DO (DNSSEC OK) and options like COOKIE.

share.carries: The link carries the dig output as pasted, and nothing else.
share.caution: The output can name internal hosts, addresses and the resolver you asked: read it before you send the link.

do-explainer-validator.name: DO declaration explainer + validator
do-explainer-validator.blurb: Paste the JSON you POST to /mgmt/shared/declarative-onboarding and it reads it back: whether it is a DO request wrapper or a bare Device declaration, the top-level options, and the Common tenant's class-objects grouped by the phase DO onboards them in, with every class named and explained. It also checks the structural rules F5 documents and flags the gotchas that bite in production, from the DO 1.36 allowService default change to a root user missing its oldPassword. DO is the sibling of AS3: DO does the L1-L3 onboarding, AS3 the L4-L7 services.
do-explainer-validator.inputLabel: A DO declaration (Device JSON) or a class DO request wrapper
do-explainer-validator.runsLocally: Decoding runs locally in your browser. Nothing you paste leaves this page.
do-explainer-validator.empty: Paste a DO declaration to see it explained.
do-explainer-validator.scopeNote: This is a structure explainer and sanity checker, not a full JSON-Schema validator. It never contacts a BIG-IP or BIG-IQ and nothing you paste leaves the browser. A declaration that passes here can still be rejected by DO itself.
do-explainer-validator.clusterNote: This declaration includes clustering classes, so it onboards one member of a high-availability pair or group.
do-explainer-validator.walkOrderNote: Grouped by the phase DO effectively onboards them in: licensing and provisioning gate the modules, system identity is foundational, networking builds the data plane, then clustering joins the box to its peers.
do-explainer-validator.unknownClass: (class not in this tool's catalogue, but still reported)

req.noDeclaration: no declaration found in the wrapper

finding.notDo: This is not a DO declaration. Paste a Device declaration, or a class DO request wrapper.
finding.deviceOnly: This is a bare Device declaration, as POSTed straight to a BIG-IP (a class DO wrapper with a targetHost is used against a BIG-IQ).
finding.missingSchema: No schemaVersion. A DO declaration should declare the schemaVersion it targets.
finding.noCommon: No Common tenant found. A DO declaration must contain a single tenant named Common.
finding.tenantNotCommon: The tenant is named "{name}", but DO requires the tenant to be named Common.
finding.emptyCommon: The Common tenant has no onboarding objects.
finding.hostnameConflict: hostname is set on both Common and a System class. They are mutually exclusive; set it in one place only.
finding.rootOldPassword: The root user "{name}" has no oldPassword. Changing the root password requires its existing oldPassword.
finding.allowServiceDefault: The self IP "{name}" sets no allowService. Since DO 1.36 the default changed from `default` to `none`, so it now allows no services unless you set them explicitly.
finding.asyncNote: async is true, so DO returns a 202 with a task id immediately; poll the task with GET until it completes.

share.carries: The link carries the declaration with every password, key, token and community replaced by {redacted}; names and addresses go as pasted.
share.redacted: {n, plural, =0 {Nothing in it needed replacing.} one {One value is replaced.} other {# values are replaced.}}
share.blocked: No link: this text is not valid JSON and names “{name}”, so its secrets cannot be found safely; fix the JSON first.

class.Authentication: remote authentication configuration (RADIUS, TACACS+, LDAP, or Active Directory)
class.ConfigSync: the config-sync self IP used to propagate configuration across the device group
class.DbVariables: arbitrary BIG-IP database (sys db) variables set by name and value
class.DeviceCertificate: the device's own management certificate and key
class.DeviceGroup: a device group and its members (sync-failover or sync-only); the owner creates it, members join
class.DeviceTrust: device-trust settings that add this box to the trust domain (ignored on the owner itself)
class.DNS: DNS name servers and search domains (configuring this disables DHCP for DNS)
class.FailoverMulticast: the multicast address used for failover heartbeat
class.FailoverUnicast: the unicast address(es) used for failover heartbeat
class.FirewallPolicy: an AFM firewall policy (a DO-onboarded policy object)
class.GSLBGlobals: global BIG-IP DNS (GTM) settings for onboarding
class.License: a BYOL licence (regKey or a BIG-IQ licensePool); omit it for PAYG images that are already licensed
class.ManagementRoute: a route on the management network
class.MirrorIp: the primary/secondary mirroring addresses for connection mirroring
class.NTP: NTP servers and the system timezone (configuring this disables DHCP for NTP)
class.Provision: module provisioning levels (ltm, gtm, asm, apm, afm, avr, and so on: dedicated, nominal, minimum, or none)
class.RemoteAuthRole: a remote (RADIUS/TACACS/LDAP/AD) authentication role, ordered by lineOrder
class.Route: a TMM route (name it `default` for the default route)
class.RouteDomain: a route domain (an isolated L3 address space), referenced elsewhere by its id
class.RouteMap: a route map applied to routing protocols
class.RoutingAccessList: a routing access list of permit/deny address entries
class.RoutingBGP: BGP routing configuration (neighbours, local AS, address families)
class.RoutingPrefixList: a routing prefix list of permit/deny entries
class.SelfIp: a self IP on a VLAN, with its allowService port-lockdown and traffic group
class.SnmpAgent: SNMP agent settings (contact, location, allowed clients)
class.System: system-level settings: hostname, CLI/console inactivity timeouts, autoPhonehome, autoCheck
class.TrafficControl: global traffic control tunables (acceptIpOptions, timeouts, and related settings)
class.TrafficGroup: a traffic group of floating objects that fail over together
class.Trunk: a link-aggregation trunk of physical interfaces
class.Tunnel: a network tunnel (for example a VXLAN overlay)
class.User: a user account, its role, shell, and partition access (root requires its existing oldPassword)
class.VLAN: a VLAN and its tagged/untagged interfaces (the object name becomes the VLAN name)

epoch.name: Unix time converter
epoch.blurb: Type a Unix timestamp - seconds, milliseconds, microseconds, or nanoseconds, detected automatically - or an ISO-8601 date, and read it back in every common format. All in your browser.
epoch.runsLocally: Converted in your browser. Nothing is sent anywhere.
epoch.scopeNote: Pure date math. The unit is guessed from the number's size; correct it if needed.
epoch.err_empty: Enter a timestamp or date to begin.
epoch.err_invalid: That is not a Unix timestamp or an ISO-8601 date.
epoch.err_outOfRange: That timestamp is outside the representable date range.

share.carries: The link carries the timestamp or date as typed; the relative time comes from the opener's clock.

note.beforeEpoch: This instant is before 1970-01-01 (the Unix epoch), so the timestamp is negative.
note.parsedUtc: Parsed as a date; a value with no time zone was read as UTC.
note.parsedZone: Parsed as a date with an explicit time zone.
note.readAs: Read as {unit} ({digits, plural, one {{digits} digit} other {{digits} digits}}).
note.y2038: This is close to 2038-01-19T03:14:07Z, where a signed 32-bit seconds counter overflows (the Year 2038 problem). 64-bit systems are unaffected.
note.yearRange: The year falls outside the usual 4-digit range; double-check the unit was detected correctly.

f5-afm-rule-context.name: AFM rule-context & match explainer
f5-afm-rule-context.blurb: Walk a packet through AFM's documented context order and watch the semantics that decide real outcomes: accept passes one context and the traffic is processed again at the next, only accept-decisively ends the walk, ICMP rules at a virtual server or self IP are ignored, and staged policies log without enforcing. A lone policy gets the redundant-and-conflicting audit the system itself defines.
f5-afm-rule-context.inputLabel: Contexts + policies + a packet, a lone policy, or "contexts" / "actions"
f5-afm-rule-context.runsLocally: Runs locally in your browser. Nothing you paste leaves this page.
f5-afm-rule-context.postureNote: Explains and simulates documented processing; nothing here probes or touches any device.

share.carries: The link carries the box as typed; a paste that sets a password, passphrase or secret gets none.
share.caution: A firewall policy names your addresses, contexts and virtual servers: read it before you send the link.
share.blocked: No link: the paste sets “{name}”, which no link may carry; remove that line to share the rest.

global.name: global
global.text: First in the processing order; applies to all traffic the system processes. A policy enforced here runs before anything narrower sees the packet.

routeDomain.name: route-domain
routeDomain.text: Second: the route domain the traffic belongs to. Between the global sweep and the per-listener contexts.

edge.name: virtual / self-ip
edge.text: Third and last of the policy contexts: the virtual server the packet targets, or the self IP for traffic to the system's own addresses. The manual's ICMP restriction lives here: ICMP/ICMPv6 rules cannot be created in these contexts, and one arriving via a rule list is ignored.

management.name: management port
management.text: Processed separately from all of the above and cannot take a policy; rules are configured inline on the management context itself.

accept.name: accept
accept.text: The packet passes THIS context and is processed again at the next one. Accept is a ticket to the next checkpoint, not through the whole building.

acceptDecisively.name: accept-decisively
acceptDecisively.text: The packet is permitted and no further context processing is performed (the DevCentral overview's own wording). The one action that ends the walk with a yes.

drop.name: drop
drop.text: Silently discarded. The walk ends; the client hears nothing.

reject.name: reject
reject.text: Discarded loudly: a TCP RST when the protocol is TCP, an ICMP unreachable otherwise.

why.unsupported: uses {criteria}: outside this tool's evaluated subset

finding.redundant: {rule} is fully covered by {earlier} with the same action; the manual's Redundant state.
finding.conflictingAccept: {rule} is covered by {earlier} but carries a different action ({action} vs {earlierAction}); the manual notes accept and accept-decisively are treated as conflicting even though both accept. {earlier} matches first, so {rule} never fires.
finding.conflicting: {rule} is covered by {earlier} but carries a different action ({action} vs {earlierAction}). {earlier} matches first, so {rule} never fires.

err.empty: Paste contexts + policies + a packet line for the walk, a single `security firewall policy` for the audit, or "contexts" / "actions" for the reference cards.
err.packetIp: packet: src/dst must be IPv4 addresses.
err.ruleList: policy {policy}: rule-list {ruleList} is referenced but not defined in the paste. Include its stanza (order matters: define rule-lists before policies).
err.noPacket: No packet line found. Add: packet src A.B.C.D[:port] dst E.F.G.H[:port] proto tcp|udp|icmp [vlan NAME]
err.noContexts: No context declarations found. Add lines like: context global '{' policy P1 '}'
err.bothEdges: Both a virtual and a self-ip context are declared, but a packet traverses one or the other. Keep the one this packet targets.
err.policyUndefined: context {kind} {name}: policy {policy} not defined in the paste.

note.contexts: Order per the Policies and Implementations manual: global, route domain, then virtual server or self IP; management port separate.
note.actions: Accept continues to the next context (the manual's processed-again-at-the-next-context sentence); only accept-decisively ends the walk.
note.stops: Rule {rule}: {reasons}. The walk stops honestly here rather than guessing past a criterion it cannot compute.
note.staged: STAGED match: the manual's staging semantics, the match is logged but connectivity is unaffected; the walk continues as if this policy were absent.
note.accept: accept: this context is passed and the traffic is processed again at the next context (the manual's own sentence).
note.decisivelyAtEdge: accept-decisively at the last policy context: same outcome as accept here; its distinctive skip-ahead power matters at global and route-domain.
note.icmpSkipped: ICMP/ICMPv6 rule(s) {rules} skipped: the manual states such rules on a {kind} context are ignored (arrive via rule list or not).
note.stagedNoMatch: Staged policy, no match: nothing logged, nothing affected.
note.noMatch: No rule matched in this context; the walk continues.

obs.icmpRule: Rule {rule} matches {protocol}: remember the manual's restriction, on a virtual server or self IP context such a rule is ignored; ICMP rules belong at global or route-domain.
obs.unsupported: Rule {rule} uses {criteria}: recognized, reported, not evaluated by this tool.
obs.order: Order walked per the manual: global, then route domain, then the virtual server or self IP context; management port rules are processed separately and take no policies.

final.permitted: PERMITTED at {context} by {rule} (accept-decisively): no further context processing is performed.
final.rejectedTcp: REJECTED at {context} by {rule}: TCP RST returned.
final.rejectedIcmp: REJECTED at {context} by {rule}: ICMP unreachable returned.
final.defaultAccept: No terminal match in any context: the declared default-action accept permits the traffic.
final.defaultOther: No terminal match in any context: the declared default-action {action} disposes of it.
final.noDefault: No terminal match in any context, and no default-action declared: the disposition falls to the box's Default Firewall Action (ADC vs Firewall mode); declare `default-action accept|drop|reject` to resolve the walk, or see the paired article for the mode split.

f5-apm-session-variable-reference.name: APM session-variable reference
f5-apm-session-variable-reference.blurb: The Session Variables chapter as a pattern-aware lookup: paste session.ad.last.attr.memberOf and it resolves against the chapter's own templates, paste an mcget expression and every reference inside is explained with the secure audit riding along, the classic empty-value trap named exactly: a bare mcget on session.logon.last.password reads back empty, because secure variables require -secure.
f5-apm-session-variable-reference.inputLabel: A variable, an expression, a family, or "variables"
f5-apm-session-variable-reference.runsLocally: Runs locally in your browser. Nothing you paste leaves this page.

share.carries: The link carries the box as typed, and nothing else.

err.empty: Paste a session variable (session.ad.last.attr.memberOf), a branch-rule expression with mcget, a %'{'session.x'}' embedding, a family name (ssl, ad, logon...), or "variables" for the catalogue.
err.unknown: "{text}" is not a session variable, expression, or family. Try session.logon.last.username, a family like ssl, or "variables".

family.ad: Active Directory auth and query results, plus one variable per retrieved attribute.
family.assigned: What the session was granted: webtop, resources by type, bandwidth policies.
family.client: What APM learned about the client: UI mode, platform, capabilities, IP.
family.custom: Variables you create with Variable Assign.
family.endpoint: Endpoint inspection: files, processes, registry, machine certs, disk encryption, Windows info.
family.ldap: LDAP auth and query results, plus one variable per retrieved attribute.
family.localdb: Local database reads, group membership for LocalDB lookups.
family.logon: What the logon flow captured: username, password (secure), domain, UPN, CAPTCHA tracking.
family.otp: One-time passwords: generated value, TTL, expiry, verification result.
family.policy: The policy's own verdict and endings: result, redirect URL, webtop, decision boxes.
family.radius: RADIUS auth results and retrieved attributes.
family.ssl: The presented client certificate, field by field.
family.sso: The SSO-side credential cache that SSO Credential Mapping fills and SSO methods consume.

note.attrBinding: $attr_name resolved to "{value}": per the chapter, each retrieved attribute is converted to a separate session variable, so the tail is whatever the query returned.
note.debug: Debug surfaces: the Current Sessions report displays all session variables for a session, and sessiondump allkeys (or sessiondump sid for one session) is the CLI view.
note.embedding: %'{'...'}' embedding: the syntax that expands a session variable inside configuration text, message boxes, and agent fields; the chapter's own OTP message example uses %'{'session.otp.assigned.val'}'.
note.exprScope: Expressions parsed for variable references only; Tcl evaluation is out of scope by design.
note.liveView: Live-session view: the Current Sessions report shows every variable APM collected; sessiondump sid '<'id> is the CLI equivalent.
note.nameBinding: $name resolved to "{value}": the agent's configured name, or the string last for the most recent agent of that type.
note.notVendored: Not in the vendored core. The full reference is the Session Variables chapter of the Visual Policy Editor manual (linked in this tool's sources); custom and agent-created names are unbounded by design.
note.secureMismatch: SECURE MISMATCH: this is a secure variable read WITHOUT -secure. Secure-variable semantics, F5's own wording: the value is stored encrypted in the session db, is not displayed in the session report UI, is not logged by the logging agent, and requires the -secure flag for both mcget and access::session data get/set. A bare mcget here yields nothing, the classic empty-value trap.
note.secureUnneeded: -secure used on a variable the reference does not mark secure; harmless if the variable was stored secure by a custom action, otherwise unnecessary.
note.vendored: Vendored core of the official Session Variables chapter (Visual Policy Editor manual), source-pinned and access-dated; the chapter itself is the exhaustive list.

obs.anatomy: Naming anatomy, per the chapter: hierarchical nodes separated by periods, session, then a type, then the agent name or the string last, then agent-specific nodes like attr or result, then the attribute name.
obs.populatedDiscipline: Populated-by discipline: a variable is only as real as the action that fills it; the Per-Request references repeat it per family, an AD Query for session.ad.*, an LDAP Query for session.ldap.last.attr.memberOf, RADIUS Auth or Acct for the class attribute.

engine.secure: Secure-variable semantics, F5's own wording: the value is stored encrypted in the session db, is not displayed in the session report UI, is not logged by the logging agent, and requires the -secure flag for both mcget and access::session data get/set.

session_ad_name_attr_attr_name.meaning: A user attribute retrieved during the AD query; the chapter's own sentence, each retrieved attribute is converted to a separate session variable (memberOf, primaryGroupID, lastLogon, and whatever else the query returned).
session_ad_name_attr_attr_name.quirk0: The Per-Request Policy reference's canonical branch rule reads exactly this family: expr '{' [mcget '{'session.ad.last.attr.memberOf'}'] contains "CN=Administrators" '}'.

session_ad_name_attr_group_attr_name.meaning: A group attribute retrieved during the AD query, one variable per attribute.

session_ad_name_authresult.meaning: Active Directory authentication result: 0 failed, 1 passed.
session_ad_name_authresult.populatedBy: AD Auth action ($name is the agent name or last).

session_ad_name_queryresult.meaning: Active Directory query result: 0 failed, 1 passed.

session_assigned_bwc_dynamic.meaning: Name of the assigned dynamic bandwidth control policy (.static for the static one).

session_assigned_resources_na.meaning: Space-delimited names of assigned Network Access resources (siblings: .at app tunnels, .pa portal access, .rd remote desktops, .saml SAML resources).

session_check_machinecert_last_result.meaning: Machine Cert Auth result: 0 neither cert nor key found, 1 both found, 2 cert without key, -2 various errors (nothing received, bad format, missing CA profile, Linux client).
session_check_machinecert_last_result.quirk0: The chapter's own note: the Machine Cert Auth action is not supported on Linux.

session_check_software_last_hd_item_1_st.meaning: Hard-disk encryption check: 0 not all drives encrypted, 1 all drives encrypted.
session_check_software_last_hd_item_1_st.quirk0: The chapter's honesty gem sits on this row's sibling: session.check_software.last.hd.state is an unused session variable that always shows 0.

session_client_activex.meaning: Whether the client can run ActiveX controls: 0 no, 1 yes.

session_client_jailbreak.meaning: Whether a mobile device reports jailbroken or rooted: 0 no, 1 yes.

session_client_js.meaning: Whether the client can execute JavaScript: 0 no, 1 yes.

session_client_platform.meaning: Client platform from HTTP headers: Android, ChromeOS, iOS, Linux, MacOS, and the Windows family strings.

session_client_type.meaning: Client type from HTTP headers: portalclient, or Standalone for the Edge Client.

session_custom_attr_name.meaning: Your own variables: F5's lab shows Variable Assign creating session.custom.mynewvar, with APM using the word after session as the container.

session_decision_box_last_result.meaning: Decision box outcome: 1 the user chose option 1, 0 the user chose option 2 (the fallback branch).

session_ldap_name_attr_attr_name.meaning: A user attribute retrieved during the LDAP query, one variable per attribute; LDAP Group Lookup compares against session.ldap.last.attr.memberOf.
session_ldap_name_attr_attr_name.populatedBy: LDAP Query action (the reference notes it is required to populate this).

session_localdb_groups.meaning: Groups read from a local database instance; the LocalDB Group Lookup default expression reads it, and the name is user-specifiable in the Local Database action.
session_localdb_groups.populatedBy: Local Database action (the same variable name must be used in the action and the lookup).

session_logon_captcha_tracking.meaning: A bitmask used when CAPTCHA is enabled: bit 0 tracks logon attempts by IP address, bit 1 by user name.
session_logon_captcha_tracking.quirk0: The chapter's own caution: should not be used by external modules; intended for very specific purposes.

session_logon_last_domain.meaning: The logon domain; the SSO Configuration Guide notes the NTLM Domain setting defaults to this variable.
session_logon_last_domain.populatedBy: Logon Page or domain-aware logon agents.

session_logon_last_password.meaning: The password the logon flow captured, stored as a secure variable.
session_logon_last_password.populatedBy: Logon Page in the access policy.
session_logon_last_password.quirk0: Reading it in an expression requires mcget -secure; a bare mcget yields nothing, the classic empty-value trap.

session_logon_last_upn.meaning: The user principal name; F5's own lab example populates it by extracting the UPN from a presented client certificate with a Variable Assign action.
session_logon_last_upn.populatedBy: Variable Assign, certificate attribute extraction, or logon agents.

session_logon_last_username.meaning: The username the logon flow captured; the classic left side of the SSO credential wiring.
session_logon_last_username.populatedBy: Logon Page (or another logon agent) in the access policy.

session_otp_assigned_expire.meaning: Internally used expiration timestamp, seconds since 1970-01-01 00:00:00 UTC.

session_otp_assigned_ttl.meaning: OTP time-to-live in seconds, configurable as the OTP timeout.

session_otp_assigned_val.meaning: The generated one-time password value; the chapter's own message example embeds it as One-Time Passcode: %'{'session.otp.assigned.val'}'.

session_policy_result.meaning: The access policy's outcome: allowed, access_denied, or redirect, per the ending reached.
session_policy_result.populatedBy: The policy ending (Allowed, Denied, or Redirect).

session_policy_result_redirect_url.meaning: The URL specified in a Redirect ending.

session_policy_result_webtop_network_acc.meaning: The resource automatically started for a network access webtop.
session_policy_result_webtop_network_acc.populatedBy: Allowed ending with a network access webtop.

session_policy_result_webtop_type.meaning: The assigned webtop's type: network_access or web_application.

session_radius_name_attr_attr_name.meaning: A user attribute retrieved during RADIUS authentication, one variable per attribute; RADIUS Class Lookup compares against session.radius.last.attr.class.
session_radius_name_attr_attr_name.populatedBy: RADIUS Auth or RADIUS Acct action.

session_ssl_cert_exist.meaning: Whether a client certificate exists: 0 no, 1 yes.

session_ssl_cert_valid.meaning: Certificate validation result: OK or an error string.

session_sso_token_last_password.meaning: The password SSO methods consume; the Form Based method's password source defaults to exactly this variable.

session_sso_token_last_username.meaning: The username SSO methods consume; SSO Credential Mapping feeds it from the logon variables.

session_ui_charset.meaning: Character set used in the session.

session_ui_lang.meaning: Language in use in the session, for example en.

session_ui_mode.meaning: UI mode from HTTP headers: 0 Full Browser, 6 Pocket PC, 7 Standalone (clientless), 8 ActiveSync, 9 Mobile Browser, 10 Citrix Receiver.
session_ui_mode.quirk0: The chapter's own nuance: UI mode does not map directly to client type; when BIG-IP Edge Client uses a web browser component to establish the session, ui.mode is 0 (Full Browser).

session_user_access_mode.meaning: Enables direct access to a Citrix resource from the webtop; example value local.

session_user_clientip.meaning: The client's IP address as APM sees it; F5's lab uses mcget '{'session.user.clientip'}' as its message-box example.

session_windows_check_file_name_item_0_e.meaning: True if all checked files exist on the client.

session_windows_check_file_name_item_0_m.meaning: MD5 value of a checked file.

session_windows_check_process_name_resul.meaning: Windows Process check result: 0 failure, 1 success, -1 invalid check expression.

session_windows_check_registrys_name_res.meaning: Windows Registry check result: 0 failure, 1 success, -1 invalid check expression.

session_windows_info_os_name_platform.meaning: The client's Windows platform string (Win7, Win8, WinXP, Win2003, WinLH, and so on).

f5-apm-sso-explainer.name: APM SSO method explainer
f5-apm-sso-explainer.blurb: The eight SSO (single sign-on) methods APM's own chapter defines, each card carrying the verdict that decides outages: a misconfigured SSO object for any non-form method can disable SSO for every method in that user's session; Form Based and Forms - Client Initiated are the only exempt ones. Kerberos ships its full prerequisite list, including the line worth framing: APM Kerberos SSO does not need or use a keytab file.
f5-apm-sso-explainer.inputPlaceholder: kerberos · ntlmv2 · forms · fbci · basic · saml · oauth · methods
f5-apm-sso-explainer.runsLocally: Runs locally in your browser. Nothing you type leaves this page.

share.carries: The link carries the method name as typed, and nothing else.

err.empty: Name an SSO method (for example "kerberos", "ntlmv2", "forms", "fbci", "basic", "saml", "oauth"), or type "methods" for the full catalogue.
err.unknown: "{input}" is not in the curated method table. Type "methods" to see the eight the chapter defines.

form-based.credentials: Cached username + the password source, which defaults to session.sso.token.last.password.
form-based.mechanism: APM constructs and sends the application's own logon form POST on the user's behalf, using cached credentials. The Start URI decides when it fires: a request URI matching it triggers the SSO; a blank Form Action means the original request URL is used for the POST.
form-based.name: Form Based
form-based.prereq0: The application form's field names (username and password parameters), discoverable with browser dev tools.
form-based.prereq1: The Start URI of the application's logon page.
form-based.quirk0: One of only two methods the chapter exempts from the session-wide SSO disable when another method's object is misconfigured.

forms-client-initiated.credentials: The Configuration Guide's own detail: the password parameter is assigned a password token rather than the actual user password; APM redeems the token server-side when the submission arrives. The real password never sits in the page.
forms-client-initiated.mechanism: APM detects the request for the logon page (a URI, header, or cookie configured for matching), lets the application serve its own form, then inserts generated JavaScript into that page; the script assigns the form values and auto-submits.
forms-client-initiated.name: Forms - Client Initiated
forms-client-initiated.prereq0: Detection criteria for the logon page (URI, header, or cookie).
forms-client-initiated.prereq1: The form's parameter names for the script to fill.
forms-client-initiated.quirk0: The second of the two exempt methods; the token indirection is the design, not an implementation accident.

http-basic.credentials: Cached username + password (the password travels to the backend, base64-encoded, on every request; that is the method's nature, not a defect).
http-basic.mechanism: The SSO plug-in uses the cached user identity and sends each request with an Authorization header carrying the Basic token: the base64 encoding of username, colon, password.
http-basic.name: HTTP Basic
http-basic.prereq0: Cached credentials populated by the access policy (Logon Page or equivalent, then SSO Credential Mapping).
http-basic.quirk0: Base64 is encoding, not encryption: the transport to the backend must be trusted or TLS-protected, because the credential is fully recoverable from the header.

kerberos.credentials: A user identity (UPN or username + realm), not a password: which is exactly why its natural front doors are methods where the password never travels in clear text, client certificates and NTLM among the chapter's own examples.
kerberos.mechanism: Transparent authentication of users to Windows web application servers (IIS) joined to an Active Directory domain: APM obtains service tickets on the user's behalf via constrained delegation.
kerberos.name: Kerberos (constrained delegation)
kerberos.prereq0: A delegation account in Active Directory, one per server realm, dedicated to delegation with a non-expiring password.
kerberos.prereq1: The delegation account's SPN, entered as the Account Name in SPN format (for example HTTP/apm4.my.host.lab.mynet.com).
kerberos.prereq3: The manual's own words: APM Kerberos SSO does not need or use a keytab file. If a keytab appears in a Kerberos SSO design, something else is being configured.
kerberos.prereq4: Servers in multiple realms: one delegation account in the primary realm with Resource-Based Constrained Delegation granted on the trusted realms, per the 17.1 guidance.
kerberos.quirk0: The delegation account is the identity doing the asking; its health and its SPN registration are where Kerberos SSO troubleshooting starts.

ntlmv1.credentials: Cached username + password used to answer the server's challenge; the password itself does not cross the wire to the backend.
ntlmv1.mechanism: The chapter's own description: NTLM employs a challenge-response mechanism for authentication, where users can prove their identities without sending a password to a server.
ntlmv1.name: NTLMv1
ntlmv1.prereq0: Cached credentials; the NTLM Domain setting defaults to the session.logon.last.domain variable.
ntlmv1.quirk0: Superseded by NTLMv2 in most estates; present for backends that still negotiate v1.

ntlmv2.credentials: Cached username + password answering the challenge; no password on the wire to the backend.
ntlmv2.mechanism: The same challenge-response mechanism, in the protocol's updated version.
ntlmv2.name: NTLMv2
ntlmv2.prereq0: Cached credentials; domain defaults from session.logon.last.domain.
ntlmv2.quirk0: Documented and worth memorizing: if an HTTP 401 response from the server includes more than one WWW-Authenticate: NTLM header, NTLMv2 SSO fails, and the manual calls this expected behaviour. A 401 should carry exactly one such header.

oauth-bearer.credentials: An issued token; the access policy's OAuth machinery obtains and refreshes it.
oauth-bearer.mechanism: SSO by presenting an OAuth bearer token to the backend rather than replaying cached passwords.
oauth-bearer.name: OAuth Bearer
oauth-bearer.prereq0: An OAuth configuration issuing the token the backend accepts.
oauth-bearer.quirk0: Listed by the chapter among the methods whose misconfigured object disables session-wide SSO.

saml.credentials: An assertion about the authenticated identity; no password replay.
saml.mechanism: SSO by SAML assertion: APM as IdP (or broker) issues the assertion the backend service provider consumes.
saml.name: SAML
saml.prereq0: The SAML federation objects (IdP/SP services) the assertion flow requires.
saml.quirk0: Also on the chapter's session-wide-disable list; the two form methods remain the only exempt ones.

note.condensed: Mechanisms condensed faithfully from the APM Single Sign-On Methods chapter and the method-specific guides; every card carries its isolation verdict because the blast radius is the operational headline.
note.nameLimit: One small documented bound for completeness: an SSO configuration name is limited to 225 characters including the partition name.

obs.exempt: {name} is one of the two exempt methods: a broken SSO object elsewhere in the session does not disable it.
obs.isolation: The SSO Methods chapter's blast-radius paragraph: a misconfigured SSO object for HTTP Basic, NTLMv1, NTLMv2, Kerberos, OAuth Bearer, or SAML can disable SSO for ALL authentication methods in that user's session; Form Based and Forms - Client Initiated are the only two methods not disabled when another method's object is broken.
obs.plumbing: Credentials plumbing, common to all methods: access-policy agents populate the session variables SSO consumes; the classic wiring is a Logon Page (or a password-less front door) followed by SSO Credential Mapping, feeding session.logon.last.* into session.sso.token.last.*.
obs.poisons: {name} sits on the poisons side of the split: misconfigure its object and every method's SSO in that user's session can go dark, the two form methods excepted.

f5-awaf-declarative-policy-explainer.name: AWAF declarative-policy explainer
f5-awaf-declarative-policy-explainer.blurb: Paste a BIG-IP Advanced WAF (web application firewall) declarative security policy (JSON) and get a section-by-section, plain-language reading grounded in F5's published schema, with security callouts that read the values: transparent enforcement means monitor-only, plus signature staging, Data Guard off, and cookies missing Secure or HttpOnly. Runs entirely in your browser.
f5-awaf-declarative-policy-explainer.runsLocally: Runs entirely in your browser. Nothing you paste is uploaded or leaves the page.
f5-awaf-declarative-policy-explainer.empty: Paste a declarative WAF policy above to see it explained.
f5-awaf-declarative-policy-explainer.notRecognized: This does not look like a declarative WAF policy

share.carries: The link carries the policy as pasted; a policy holding a credential gets none.
share.caution: A policy can name internal hosts, URLs and addresses: read it before you send the link.
share.maybeSecret: {more, plural, =0 {Line {line} may hold a secret ({label}): check it, and any internal names, before you send the link.} one {Line {line} ({label}) and one more line may hold secrets: check them, and any internal names, before you send the link.} other {Line {line} ({label}) and # more lines may hold secrets: check them, and any internal names, before you send the link.}}

Replace it with a placeholder, then share again.} one {No link: line {line} ({label}) and one more line hold credentials. Replace them with placeholders, then share again.} other {No link: line {line} ({label}) and # more lines hold credentials. Replace them with placeholders, then share again.}}

antivirus.on: On: HTTP file uploads are sent for antivirus inspection.

detail.blockingSettings: {count, plural, one {{count} violation setting} other {{count} violation settings}} present; {blocked} marked to block (block enforced only in blocking mode).
detail.bruteForce: {count, plural, one {{count} brute-force configuration} other {{count} brute-force configurations}} present.

caseInsensitive.off: Case-sensitive: element matching respects letter case.
caseInsensitive.on: Case-insensitive: URLs, file types, and parameters are matched without regard to case.

detail.cookies: {count, plural, one {{count} cookie} other {{count} cookies}} defined.
detail.cookiesWeak: {count, plural, one {{count} cookie} other {{count} cookies}} defined. {weak, plural, one {{weak} enforced cookie} other {{weak} enforced cookies}} set without the Secure and/or HttpOnly attribute.

dataGuard.off: Explicitly off in this policy: responses are not masked by Data Guard.

enforcement.blocking: Blocking: requests that trigger a block-configured violation are rejected.
enforcement.transparent: Transparent: this policy is monitor-only. Violations are detected and logged, but no request is blocked, regardless of per-violation block flags.

detail.filetypes: {count, plural, one {{count} file type} other {{count} file types}} defined.

general.both: new entities stay in staging for {days, plural, one {{days} day} other {{days} days}} before they can be enforced; X-Forwarded-For is trusted for the client IP, so only genuinely trusted upstream proxies should be allowed to set it.
general.days: new entities stay in staging for {days, plural, one {{days} day} other {{days} days}} before they can be enforced.
general.xff: X-Forwarded-For is trusted for the client IP, so only genuinely trusted upstream proxies should be allowed to set it.

detail.name: Named "{name}".
detail.parameters: {count, plural, one {{count} parameter} other {{count} parameters}} defined.

passive.on: On: attached via FastL4, so traffic is inspected but cannot be modified or blocked inline.

policyBuilder.off: Auto-apply is OFF: learned changes are suggested, not applied automatically.
policyBuilder.on: Auto-apply is ON: the Policy Builder can commit learned changes automatically.

protocolIndependent.off: Off: URLs are configured without regard to HTTP vs HTTPS.
protocolIndependent.on: On: HTTP and HTTPS URLs are treated as distinct.

signatureStaging.off: Signature staging is OFF: signatures are enforced immediately (subject to enforcement mode).
signatureStaging.on: Signature staging is ON: matched signatures are logged for review but do not block yet.

flag.dataGuardOff: Data Guard is explicitly disabled: sensitive data in responses is not masked by this policy.
flag.passive: Passive/FastL4 mode: the policy inspects but cannot block or modify traffic inline.
flag.staging: Attack signatures are in staging: matched signatures are logged but do not block yet.
flag.transparent: Policy is in transparent (monitor-only) mode: nothing is blocked, even violations flagged to block.
flag.xff: The policy trusts X-Forwarded-For for the client IP; make sure only trusted proxies can set it.

reason.empty: No input. Paste a declarative WAF policy JSON.
reason.noSections: This JSON has no recognizable WAF policy sections. Expected a declarative policy like '{' "policy": '{' "enforcementMode": ..., "template": ... '}' '}'.
reason.notObject: This JSON is not an object, so it is not a WAF policy.

antivirus.label: Antivirus (ICAP)
antivirus.summary: ICAP antivirus inspection of HTTP file uploads.

applicationLanguage.label: Application language
applicationLanguage.summary: The character encoding for the web application. It determines how the policy processes character sets. The default is auto-detect.

behavioral-enforcement.label: Behavioural enforcement
behavioral-enforcement.summary: Behavioural and DoS enforcement, including which violation classes and signature accuracy levels may block.

blocking-settings.label: Blocking settings
blocking-settings.summary: Defines the policy's block, alarm, and learn behaviour across violations, evasion techniques, HTTP-protocol compliance, and web-services security.

brute-force-attack-preventions.label: Brute-force protection
brute-force-attack-preventions.summary: Brute Force Protection configuration. A default entry applies to all login URLs unless a specific entry exists for a given login page.

caseInsensitive.label: Case sensitivity
caseInsensitive.summary: Whether the policy treats microservice URLs, file types, URLs, and parameters as case sensitive. When enabled, the system stores these elements in lowercase.

character-sets.label: Character sets
character-sets.summary: Which characters are allowed in each context (URL, parameter name and value, headers, JSON, XML, and so on).

cookie-settings.label: Cookie length limits
cookie-settings.summary: The maximum combined length of a cookie header name and value that the system processes.

cookies.label: Cookies
cookies.summary: Cookie entities. Allowed cookies may be changed by the client; enforced cookies may not. Per-cookie security attributes cover HttpOnly, Secure, and SameSite.

csrf-protection.label: CSRF protection
csrf-protection.summary: Cross-Site Request Forgery protection, including token expiration and whether it applies only over SSL.

csrf-urls.label: CSRF-protected URLs
csrf-urls.summary: The specific URLs to which CSRF protection is applied.

data-guard.label: Data Guard
data-guard.summary: Data Guard prevents responses from exposing sensitive information by masking it, covering credit-card numbers, US Social Security numbers, and custom patterns.

database-protection.label: Database protection
database-protection.summary: Database security integration for the policy.

deception-response-pages.label: Deception response pages
deception-response-pages.summary: Response pages used by the deception feature.

description.label: Description
description.summary: A free-text description of the policy.

disabled-action-items.label: Disabled action items
disabled-action-items.summary: Policy-Builder suggestions that have been explicitly dismissed.

disallowed-geolocations.label: Disallowed geolocations
disallowed-geolocations.summary: Countries that may not access the web application.

enablePassiveMode.label: Passive mode
enablePassiveMode.summary: Passive Mode lets the policy attach to a Performance L4 (FastL4) virtual server. With FastL4, traffic is analysed but is not modified in any way.

enforcementMode.label: Enforcement mode
enforcementMode.summary: How the system handles a request that triggers a violation. In blocking mode, traffic is blocked when it causes a violation configured for blocking. In transparent mode, traffic is not blocked even when a violation is triggered.

filetypes.label: File types
filetypes.summary: File types categorize request URLs by extension. They form an allow or deny list, imply per-type length limits, and decide whether response signatures are checked for that type.

fullPath.label: Full path
fullPath.summary: The full name of the policy including its BIG-IP partition.

general.label: General settings
general.summary: Several advanced policy settings. Notable ones are the enforcement readiness (staging) period, whether the policy trusts the X-Forwarded-For header for the client IP, and how it masks sensitive data in requests.

graphql-profiles.label: GraphQL profiles
graphql-profiles.summary: GraphQL payload profiles, with their defense attributes and sensitive data.

header-settings.label: Header length limits
header-settings.summary: The maximum combined length of an HTTP header name and value that the system processes.

headers.label: Headers
headers.summary: Header entities the policy defines, with their per-header checks.

host-names.label: Host names
host-names.summary: The host names the policy applies to.

ip-intelligence.label: IP intelligence
ip-intelligence.summary: Reputation-based blocking by IP intelligence category (for example anonymous proxies, scanners, or known bad actors).

json-profiles.label: JSON profiles
json-profiles.summary: JSON payload profiles, with their defense attributes, metacharacter overrides, sensitive data, and validation files.

json-validation-files.label: JSON validation files
json-validation-files.summary: JSON schema files used to validate JSON payloads.

login-enforcement.label: Login enforcement
login-enforcement.summary: Which URLs require prior authentication, plus logout URLs.

login-pages.label: Login pages
login-pages.summary: URLs a request must pass through to reach authenticated URLs. Used to prevent forceful browsing and to enable session tracking.

methods.label: HTTP methods
methods.summary: The HTTP methods the policy permits, with any act-as mappings.

microservices.label: Microservices
microservices.summary: Per-microservice definitions, each able to override violations, evasions, and HTTP-protocol checks.

name.label: Policy name
name.summary: The unique, user-given name of the policy. It cannot contain spaces or special characters beyond dot, dash, colon, and underscore.

navigation-parameters.label: Navigation parameters
navigation-parameters.summary: Parameters used to track navigation through the application.

open-api-files.label: OpenAPI files
open-api-files.summary: OpenAPI/Swagger definition files that drive the policy's allowed URLs and parameters.

parameters.label: Parameters
parameters.summary: The parameters the policy permits in requests, with their data types and staging state.

policy-builder-central-configuration.label: Policy Builder learning location
policy-builder-central-configuration.summary: Defines where the Policy Builder learns from and related central configuration.

policy-builder-cookie.label: Policy Builder: cookies
policy-builder-cookie.summary: Policy Builder learning behaviour for cookies.

policy-builder-filetype.label: Policy Builder: file types
policy-builder-filetype.summary: Policy Builder learning behaviour for file types.

policy-builder-header.label: Policy Builder: headers
policy-builder-header.summary: Policy Builder learning behaviour for headers.

policy-builder-parameter.label: Policy Builder: parameters
policy-builder-parameter.summary: Policy Builder learning behaviour for parameters, including dynamic parameters.

policy-builder-redirection-protection.label: Policy Builder: redirection
policy-builder-redirection-protection.summary: Policy Builder learning behaviour for redirection protection.

policy-builder-server-technologies.label: Policy Builder: server technologies
policy-builder-server-technologies.summary: Policy Builder learning behaviour for server technologies.

policy-builder-sessions-and-logins.label: Policy Builder: sessions and logins
policy-builder-sessions-and-logins.summary: Policy Builder learning behaviour for sessions and logins.

policy-builder-url.label: Policy Builder: URLs
policy-builder-url.summary: Policy Builder learning behaviour for URLs.

policy-builder.label: Policy Builder
policy-builder.summary: Automatic Policy Builder settings: how the system learns from live traffic to tighten or loosen the policy, and whether it applies those changes automatically.

protocolIndependent.label: Protocol independent
protocolIndependent.summary: Whether the policy distinguishes HTTP from HTTPS URLs. When enabled it treats them separately; when disabled it configures URLs without a specific protocol, so the same URL is not stored twice.

redirection-protection-domains.label: Redirection domains
redirection-protection-domains.summary: The allowed redirection domains for open-redirect protection.

redirection-protection.label: Redirection protection
redirection-protection.summary: Open-redirect protection: the set of domains the application is allowed to redirect to.

response-pages.label: Response pages
response-pages.summary: The blocking and login response pages returned to clients when a request or response is blocked.

sensitive-parameters.label: Sensitive parameters
sensitive-parameters.summary: Parameters whose values are hidden in logs and interfaces (shown as asterisks). 'password' is sensitive by default.

server-technologies.label: Server technologies
server-technologies.summary: The server-side applications, frameworks, web servers, or operating systems configured in the policy, so it can adapt to the checks needed for each technology.

session-tracking-statuses.label: Session tracking statuses
session-tracking-statuses.summary: The current tracked-session statuses (for example blocked or under investigation).

session-tracking.label: Session tracking
session-tracking.summary: Tracks client sessions and users to detect and act on anomalies, with block-all, delayed blocking, and logging controls.

signature-requirements.label: Signature requirements
signature-requirements.summary: Minimum attack-signature set requirements for the policy.

signature-sets.label: Signature sets
signature-sets.summary: The attack-signature sets assigned to the policy, with their block and alarm state.

signature-settings.label: Signature settings
signature-settings.summary: Global settings for attack signatures, including whether new and updated signatures go into staging. Staging matches signatures in a learn-only mode without enforcing them, so you can review before they can block.

signatures.label: Signature overrides
signatures.summary: Per-signature overrides applied to the policy.

ssrf-hosts.label: SSRF hosts
ssrf-hosts.summary: Host definitions used for Server-Side Request Forgery protection.

template.label: Base template
template.summary: The base template the policy is built from. The template supplies the default protections; everything else in the policy is an adjustment on top of it. Common templates include POLICY_TEMPLATE_RAPID_DEPLOYMENT, POLICY_TEMPLATE_FUNDAMENTAL, POLICY_TEMPLATE_COMPREHENSIVE, and POLICY_TEMPLATE_API_SECURITY.

threat-campaign-settings.label: Threat-campaign settings
threat-campaign-settings.summary: Global settings for F5 Threat Campaigns, which detect specific, curated real-world attack campaigns.

threat-campaigns.label: Threat campaigns
threat-campaigns.summary: The individual Threat Campaign entries and their enforcement state.

urls.label: URLs
urls.summary: Explicit and wildcard URL entities the policy knows about, each with its own protection settings.

webhooks.label: Webhooks
webhooks.summary: Webhook targets the policy notifies on events.

websocket-urls.label: WebSocket URLs
websocket-urls.summary: WebSocket URL entities, with cross-origin enforcement and metacharacter checks.

whitelist-ips.label: IP exceptions
whitelist-ips.summary: IP addresses with special treatment, such as always-trusted or always-blocked sources and per-IP policy behaviour.

xml-profiles.label: XML profiles
xml-profiles.summary: XML payload profiles, including web-services security (WSS) configuration and SOAP methods.

xml-validation-files.label: XML validation files
xml-validation-files.summary: XSD/WSDL files used to validate XML payloads.

engine.templateNote: A declarative WAF policy lists only its adjustments on top of a base template. Anything not shown here keeps the template's default, so an absent section means "template default", not "disabled".

f5-awaf-evasion-explainer.name: AWAF evasion-technique explainer
f5-awaf-evasion-explainer.blurb: Type a sub-violation name or "evasions" for F5's eight evasion sub-violations explained, each with its default and the encoding trick it catches, or paste the evasions block of a declarative WAF (web application firewall) policy to read each one back as enabled or disabled with the Multiple-decoding pass count. Grounded in F5 K7929; runs entirely in your browser.

{ "blocking-settings": { "evasions": [ { "description": "Multiple decoding", "enabled": true, "maxDecodingPasses": 3 } ] } }
