f5-awaf-evasion-explainer.empty: Type "evasions" for F5's eight sub-violations, a single name, or paste an evasions block to read it back.
f5-awaf-evasion-explainer.nameMiss: That is not one of F5's eight evasion sub-violations. Try "evasions" for the full list.
f5-awaf-evasion-explainer.passesDefault: Multiple-decoding passes: not set, so the default of {value} applies.
f5-awaf-evasion-explainer.bridgeNote: Several of these are the same decode operations this toolbox performs: %u, bare-byte and the %XX in Bad unescape are the Base64/Percent codec's territory, and Multiple decoding is repeated percent-decoding. The related tool on each card lets you see the decode by hand.

notes.notName: That is not JSON and not a known sub-violation name.
notes.parseError: That looks like JSON but could not be parsed
notes.noBlock: This JSON has no evasions array. Paste the evasions block, or a policy whose blocking-settings contains one.
notes.allDefault: No evasion sub-violation was explicitly set here, so every one takes its template default (all eight are Enabled by default).
notes.disabled: Disabled here: {names}. A disabled sub-violation means that normalization or check is skipped, so its evasion trick can slip past the signatures.
notes.passesRange: Multiple-decoding passes is {value}, outside the schema's 2-to-5 range. The system would reject or clamp this value.
notes.passesRaised: Multiple-decoding passes is raised to {value} (default is 3). More passes catch deeper nested encoding but cost slightly more processing.
notes.unknownEntry: An evasions entry has an unrecognized description ({description}); it is not one of F5's eight sub-violations.
notes.learnGated: Learning is disabled on the parent "Evasion technique detected" violation, so per the schema these sub-violations are not learned even when a request triggers them.

pct-u.name: %u decoding
pct-u.what: Performs Microsoft %u-style Unicode decoding on the URI and parameters, so a character written as %u00XX is resolved to what it really is before the signatures see it.
pct-u.catches: Attacks hidden behind Microsoft %u Unicode escapes, a classic way to write a metacharacter so a naive filter misses it.

apache-ws.name: Apache whitespace
apache-ws.what: Detects the whitespace bytes ASCII 9, 11, 12 and 13 in the URI, control characters some servers treat as separators.
apache-ws.catches: Requests that smuggle payloads past a filter using unusual whitespace that the origin server tolerates.

bad-unescape.name: Bad unescape
bad-unescape.what: Detects illegal hex encoding, a percent sign not followed by two valid hex digits (for example %RR).
bad-unescape.catches: Malformed percent-escapes crafted so the WAF and the server disagree on what the sequence decodes to.

bare-byte.name: Bare byte decoding
bare-byte.what: Detects higher-ASCII bytes, raw values above 127 sent unescaped in the request.
bare-byte.catches: Non-ASCII bytes injected directly to represent characters a signature is watching for, without the encoding that would reveal them.

dir-traversal.name: Directory traversals
dir-traversal.what: Detects path-traversal patterns such as ../ that walk up the directory tree.
dir-traversal.catches: Attempts to escape the intended path and reach files elsewhere on the server, the core of a path-traversal attack.

iis-backslash.name: IIS backslashes
iis-backslash.what: Normalizes the backslash \ to a forward slash /, the way IIS treats the two as equivalent in a path.
iis-backslash.catches: Payloads that use \ where the signatures expect /, relying on the server to fold them together after the WAF has looked.

iis-unicode.name: IIS Unicode codepoints
iis-unicode.what: Decodes IIS-specific %u code-point mappings from the Windows-1252 code page.
iis-unicode.catches: The IIS Unicode-escape evasions that famously let attackers write traversal and metacharacters in a form only IIS would decode.

multi-decode.name: Multiple decoding
multi-decode.what: Decodes the URI and parameter values repeatedly, up to the configured number of passes, so payloads hidden under several layers of encoding are unwrapped before inspection.
multi-decode.catches: Double- and triple-encoded payloads, where a value is percent-encoded more than once so a single-pass decoder never reveals the real characters.

f5-awaf-false-positive-triage.name: AWAF false-positive triage
f5-awaf-false-positive-triage.blurb: The flip side of the poisoning estimator: relax a genuine Advanced WAF (web application firewall) false positive correctly, with scope, and stop before relaxing a real attack. Pick a violation category, its average violation rating, and whether it is enforced, staged, or transparent, and get F5's rating-based verdict and the scoped fix. Runs entirely in your browser.
f5-awaf-false-positive-triage.runsLocally: Computed in your browser. Nothing is sent.
f5-awaf-false-positive-triage.scopeNote: A deterministic model of F5's documented triage behaviour, not a probe. Read the violation, rating, and enforcement state from the request in Security > Event Logs > Application > Requests. It never contacts a BIG-IP.

cat.meta-char: Illegal meta character (in parameter, value, or URL)
cat.length: Illegal length (URL, query, POST data, request)
cat.xml-json-signature: Signature in XML or JSON payload

triage.likely-attack: Likely a real attack - do not relax

action.accept-if-confirmed: If you confirm it is legitimate, apply the scoped fix below (or accept the learning suggestion).
action.investigate-first: Examine the request in the event log first; a rating of 3 can go either way.
action.clear-do-not-relax: Clear the learning suggestion without changing the policy. Relaxing this would open a hole.

f5-awaf-false-positive-triage.remediationHeading: Scoped remediation (if it is a confirmed false positive)

rem.disableSignatureScoped: Disable the specific signature on the specific URL or parameter only, never for the whole policy.
rem.allowEntityBypass: Add the URL or parameter as an allowed entity so the check is bypassed just there.
rem.potentialFpDetection: Enable Potential False Positive Detection so the system learns request similarity and treats requests like the majority as benign, flagging outliers.
rem.stageSignature: Put the signature (back) into staging so it logs but does not block while you gather more traffic.
rem.allowMetaChar: Add the character to the allowed meta-characters of that parameter, value, or URL character set.
rem.addAllowedParameter: Add the parameter as an allowed parameter with the correct value type and length.
rem.addAllowedUrl: Add the URL to the allowed URLs.
rem.addAllowedFileType: Add the file type to the allowed file types.
rem.raiseLength: Raise the relevant length limit (URL, query string, POST data, or request) to fit legitimate traffic.
rem.markFileUploadParam: Add an explicit parameter with Value Type 'User-input value' and Data Type 'File Upload' so uploaded binary content is not scanned as text.
rem.attachContentProfile: Attach an XML or JSON content profile so the structured payload is parsed and signatures apply appropriately, rather than to raw bytes.
rem.allowCookieNotEnforced: Only if the application legitimately modifies the cookie, allow that specific cookie as not-enforced.
rem.investigateCookie: Cookie violations are usually real tampering; confirm the application actually changes the cookie before relaxing anything.
rem.adjustHttpComplianceSubcheck: Adjust the specific HTTP compliance sub-check only, if the deviation is legitimate for this application.
rem.urlOverride: Use a Microservices or URL-level override to relax the check for that one host and URL.

note.ratingBlocks: A rating of 4 or 5 blocks the request even when every detected violation has its Block flag off, because the combined rating marks it as a likely attack.
note.staged: This signature or entity is in staging: it logs but does not block. Treat the 'false positive' as a learning signal, validate over one to two weeks, then enforce.
note.transparent: The policy is in Transparent mode, so it blocks nothing. This is logged, not blocked; the fix matters for when you move to Blocking.
note.discipline: The rule that governs all of this: relax the policy only where a false positive actually occurred, never where a real attack caused the violation.
note.scopeIt: Always scope the fix to the specific URL or parameter. Disabling a signature or violation policy-wide trades one false positive for a blind spot everywhere else.
note.potentialFp: For attack-signature false positives, Potential False Positive Detection is the lightest-touch option: it lets the system decide by traffic similarity instead of you hand-disabling signatures.
note.unlearnable: Some rating-5 violations are unlearnable (for example Null in request): the policy will never relax them, so there is nothing to accept.

share.carries: The link carries the three choices (category, rating and state), and nothing else.

f5-awaf-learning-poisoning-estimator.name: AWAF automatic-learning poisoning estimator
f5-awaf-learning-poisoning-estimator.blurb: How many requests does an attacker need to drill a hole through your BIG-IP Advanced WAF (web application firewall) policy when the Policy Builder is left in Automatic learning against untrusted traffic? Enter your Loosen thresholds and the attacker's resources; it computes the minimum sources, requests, and time to force one automatic relaxation, and gates on the rules that make it impossible. Runs entirely in your browser.
f5-awaf-learning-poisoning-estimator.runsLocally: Computed in your browser. Nothing is sent.
f5-awaf-learning-poisoning-estimator.scopeNote: A deterministic model of F5's documented Policy Builder behaviour, not a probe. It never contacts a BIG-IP. Read your policy's real Loosen thresholds from Security > Application Security > Policy Building > Learning and Blocking Settings.

f.attackerTrusted: Attacker's IPs are in the Trusted IP list
f.ratingFactorHint: F5 requires more for higher ratings but does not publish the curve; set your own (1 = model only the threshold)

verdict.learning-disabled: Safe: learning is Disabled - the policy never changes itself.
verdict.manual: Safe: Manual mode - a human must accept every relaxation, so there is no automatic hole to drill.
verdict.unlearnable: Safe: a rating-5 violation is unlearnable - the Policy Builder never auto-relaxes it, no matter how much traffic arrives.
verdict.trusted-only-blocked: Safe: loosening is restricted to trusted traffic, so an untrusted attacker cannot reach the Loosen path.
verdict.insufficient-sources: Out of reach: the attacker does not control enough distinct sources to meet the Loosen threshold.
verdict.drillable: Drillable: this configuration can be relaxed automatically. Minimum attacker effort:

f5-awaf-learning-poisoning-estimator.insufficientDetail: The Loosen rule needs {need} distinct sources; the attacker controls {have}. Raising this threshold is one of the mitigations below.

note.autoEnforce: In Automatic mode, a suggestion that reaches a 100% learning score is accepted and enforced with no human in the loop - including suggestions that disable a violation or widen an entity.
note.unlearnable: The most severe violations (for example Null in request, unparsable content, bad HTTP version) are unlearnable: no suggestion is ever created and the rating is fixed at 5, so the control cannot be laundered away this way.
note.ratingCost: At rating {rating}, F5 slows learning and requires more different sources and sessions before it relaxes. The higher the rating, the more expensive the poisoning.
note.trustedOneSession: Trusted clients relax the policy with as little as one session; untrusted traffic needs many more distinct sources over a period. That asymmetry is the anti-poisoning design.
note.emptyTrusted: If the Trusted IP list is empty, the system treats all traffic as untrusted - so an empty list does not make you safe, it makes the untrusted thresholds the only defence.
note.attackerTrusted: These IPs are trusted, so the fast trusted-traffic rules apply - this is why you must never place untrusted-reachable ranges in the Trusted IP list.
note.lowerBound: This request count is a documented lower bound (one distinct hit per required source/session). A real campaign needs more, because the pattern must recur to raise the score.

mit.manual: Set Learning Mode to Manual (or Disabled) so no suggestion is applied without a human accepting it. This is the clean default for production.
mit.trustedOnly: Loosen only from trusted traffic where the option exists (Track Site Changes), and build policies from a known-good Trusted IP range rather than live untrusted traffic.
mit.raiseThresholds: Raise the untrusted Loosen thresholds (different sources, sessions, time spread) so untrusted traffic effectively never relaxes the policy during the learning period.
mit.keepOut: Never put internet-reachable or attacker-reachable ranges in the Trusted IP list - trusted traffic relaxes the policy with a single session.
mit.disableAfter: Once the policy is built and stable, disable automatic policy building (or Track Site Changes) so the policy stops learning from live traffic.

f5-awaf-learning-poisoning-estimator.untrustedActiveNote: This scenario loosens from untrusted traffic in Automatic mode - the exact configuration to avoid on an internet-facing policy.

share.carries: The link carries all eleven settings of the form as the estimate reads them, and nothing else.

f5-awaf-learning-suggestion-interpreter.name: AWAF learning-suggestion interpreter
f5-awaf-learning-suggestion-interpreter.blurb: Ties the poisoning estimator and the false-positive triage together. Characterize a Traffic Learning suggestion and it tells you whether accepting it loosens or tightens the policy, whether a loosening is a false-positive fix or a security relaxation, and whether Automatic learning is about to enforce it for you. Runs entirely in your browser.
f5-awaf-learning-suggestion-interpreter.inputLabel: The learning suggestion you are weighing up
f5-awaf-learning-suggestion-interpreter.runsLocally: Computed in your browser. Nothing is sent.
f5-awaf-learning-suggestion-interpreter.scopeNote: A deterministic model of F5's documented learning behaviour, not a probe. Read the action, learning score, and average violation rating from the Traffic Learning screen. It never contacts a BIG-IP and does not depend on the exact REST suggestion JSON.

action.add-entity: Add a valid entity (URL / parameter / file type / cookie)
action.add-meta-char: Allow a meta-character on an entity
action.relax-attribute: Relax an entity attribute (e.g. longer length)
action.disable-signature: Disable or relax an attack signature
action.remove-wildcard: Remove a wildcard, add explicit entities

assessment.add-legitimate: Adding a legitimate entity the policy had not learned
assessment.fp-fix: Loosening that resolves a genuine false positive
assessment.likely-relaxing-attack: This loosening would relax a real attack

note.scoreRatingInverse: The learning score rises as the violation rating falls, so the lowest-rated suggestions (the most likely false positives) reach auto-accept fastest. That is by design, and it is also exactly what an attacker feeding low-rated violations drives up.
note.autoEnforce: In Automatic learning, a suggestion that reaches a 100% learning score is accepted and enforced automatically, with no human step.
note.poisoningVector: This is the poisoning vector: a relaxing loosening from untrusted traffic climbing towards auto-accept in Automatic mode. Model how far it is with the poisoning estimator, and consider Manual learning or trusted-only loosening.
note.discipline: Relax the policy only where a false positive occurred, never where a real attack caused the violation. The violation rating is how you tell the two apart.
note.enforceCheckFp: Enforcing moves the entity from staging to blocking, so confirm it has generated no false positives during staging before you accept.
note.tighteningSafe: Tightening increases the policy's specificity, so accepting it generally improves security rather than weakening it.
note.manualHuman: In Manual learning a human must accept every suggestion, so nothing is enforced without your review.
note.scoreNearAccept: At a {score}% learning score this suggestion is close to being accepted; check it deliberately rather than letting it through.

share.carries: The link carries the five choices that describe the suggestion, and nothing else.

f5-awaf-policy-diff.name: AWAF policy-diff hole checker
f5-awaf-policy-diff.blurb: Paste a before and an after declarative WAF (web application firewall) policy and it classifies every security-relevant change as a relaxation or a tightening, then answers the question that matters after tuning: did this open a hole? It flags relaxations that widen protection beyond a single entity apart from a properly-scoped single-entity allow. Runs entirely in your browser.
f5-awaf-policy-diff.inputLabel: Two declarative WAF policies to compare
f5-awaf-policy-diff.beforePlaceholder:
Paste the earlier policy JSON, e.g.
{ "policy": { "enforcementMode": "blocking", "data-guard": { "enabled": true } } }
f5-awaf-policy-diff.afterPlaceholder:
Paste the later policy JSON, e.g.
{ "policy": { "enforcementMode": "transparent", "data-guard": { "enabled": false } } }
f5-awaf-policy-diff.runsLocally: Compared in your browser. Neither policy is uploaded.
f5-awaf-policy-diff.scopeNote: A deterministic diff of the security-relevant sections F5's declarative policy schema defines. It reads enforcement mode, signature staging, X-Forwarded-For trust, Data Guard, CSRF, per-violation block flags, per-evasion enablement, and the URL / parameter / file-type entities. It never contacts a BIG-IP.
f5-awaf-policy-diff.empty: Paste a before and an after policy to see which changes opened a hole and which stayed scoped.
f5-awaf-policy-diff.parseError: One of the two inputs is not valid JSON. Check both policies and try again.
f5-awaf-policy-diff.notPolicy: One of the inputs does not look like a declarative WAF policy (expected a policy object, optionally wrapped in a "policy" key).

verdict.opened-hole: This opened a hole: a policy-wide relaxation is present
verdict.scoped-only: Scoped changes only: the widenings stay entity-scoped
verdict.no-change: No security-relevant change between the two policies

f5-awaf-policy-diff.summary: {wide, plural, one {{wide} policy-wide relaxation} other {{wide} policy-wide relaxations}}, {scoped, plural, one {{scoped} scoped widening} other {{scoped} scoped widenings}}, {tight, plural, one {{tight} tightening} other {{tight} tightenings}}.
f5-awaf-policy-diff.policyWideHeading: Policy-wide relaxations (these widen beyond a single entity)
f5-awaf-policy-diff.scopedHeading: Scoped widenings (single-entity - the normal false-positive fix)

label.enforcementToTransparent: Enforcement switched to Transparent: the whole policy stops blocking, regardless of per-violation block flags.
label.enforcementToBlocking: Enforcement switched to Blocking: the policy now enforces its block flags.
label.sigStagingOn: Signature staging turned on: signatures log but no longer block until enforced.
label.sigStagingOff: Signature staging turned off: signatures now enforce.
label.trustXffOn: X-Forwarded-For trust turned on: the policy now trusts a client-supplied header for the source IP, which is spoofable.
label.trustXffOff: X-Forwarded-For trust turned off: the policy no longer trusts the client-supplied header.
label.dataGuardOff: Data Guard turned off: responses are no longer masked for sensitive data leakage.
label.dataGuardOn: Data Guard turned on: responses are masked for sensitive data.
label.wildcardAdded: Wildcard {type} added: {name} - this matches many, not one entity.

f5-awaf-request-log-triage.name: AWAF request-log triage
f5-awaf-request-log-triage.blurb: Paste an ASM request-log entry (syslog key-value or CEF) and it extracts the policy, the support ID for log correlation, the request status, the violation rating, the client IP, method, and URI, classifies each violation, and gives F5's rating-based verdict, then bridges to the false-positive triage tool. Runs entirely in your browser.
f5-awaf-request-log-triage.inputLabel: An ASM request-log entry (syslog key-value or CEF)
f5-awaf-request-log-triage.inputPlaceholder:
Paste a line like:
ASM:policy_name="prod",violations="Attack signature detected,Illegal meta character in parameter value",violation_rating="2",support_id="5268275531735896872",request_status="blocked",ip_client="192.0.2.9",method="GET",uri="/search"
f5-awaf-request-log-triage.runsLocally: Parsed in your browser. Nothing you paste is uploaded.
f5-awaf-request-log-triage.empty: Paste an ASM request-log line (key-value or CEF) to parse it and triage its violations.

verdict.likely-fp: Rating says: likely a false positive
verdict.likely-attack: Rating says: likely a real attack
verdict.no-rating: No violation rating in this log

note.noRating: This log has no violation_rating field (older versions omit it). Open the request in Security > Event Logs > Application > Requests to read its rating, then triage from there.
note.ratingAttack: The violation rating is {rating}. A 4 or 5 is most likely a real attack and blocks even with Block flags off, so clear any learning suggestion rather than relaxing the policy.
note.ratingFp: The violation rating is {rating}. A 1 or 2 is usually a genuine false positive, so if you confirm the request is legitimate you can apply the scoped fix in the false-positive triage tool.
note.ratingInvestigate: The violation rating is {rating}. A 3 is ambiguous; examine the request in the event log before you decide.
note.unparsed: This does not look like an ASM request-log line. Paste a syslog key-value line (starting with ASM:) or a CEF line (containing |F5|ASM|).
note.supportIdOpaque: The support ID is a correlation reference for finding this exact request in the event log. It does not encode the violations, so it cannot be decoded into them; this tool reads them from the log line instead.
note.bridge: Take each violation above into the false-positive triage tool with its category and the rating to get the scoped remediation.

share.caution: The copy keeps the client address and the URI: check them before you send the link.
share.maybeSecret: The copy may hold a secret ({label}): check it before you send the link.

share.blockedUnparsed: No link: this is not an ASM log line, so there are no fields to copy.
share.blockedCopy: No link: a copy of the fields would not read the same as the line, so none is offered.

f5-awaf-signature-accuracy-risk.name: AWAF signature accuracy/risk interpreter
f5-awaf-signature-accuracy-risk.blurb: Read an attack signature's published Accuracy and Risk and it tells you how false-positive-prone it is, how damaging a real match would be, and the tuning move. F5 defines accuracy as false-positive susceptibility, so low accuracy means many false positives. Runs entirely in your browser.
f5-awaf-signature-accuracy-risk.runsLocally: Computed in your browser. Nothing is sent.
f5-awaf-signature-accuracy-risk.scopeNote: A deterministic model of F5's documented signature properties, not a per-ID database. Read Accuracy, Risk, and Systems from the signature's own entry under Security > Options > Application Security > Attack Signatures. It never contacts a BIG-IP.

system.in-stack: Yes - a system my app runs
system.not-in-stack: No - a system my app does not run

quadrant.reliable-high-stakes: Reliable and high-stakes - do not relax

rec.fp-prone-low-stakes: This is the prime relax candidate. Low accuracy means frequent false positives and low risk means little is lost if you relax it, so disabling it on the specific URL or parameter (or leaving it in staging) is reasonable once you have confirmed a false positive.
rec.fp-prone-dangerous: Investigate the actual request before you relax anything. Low accuracy makes false positives likely, but the potential damage means a genuine match must not be waved through. Do not blindly disable this one.
rec.reliable-high-stakes: Do not relax this. High accuracy means a match is very likely a genuine attack, and the potential damage is severe. Treat matches as real and keep it enforcing.
rec.reliable-low-stakes: Reliable but low-stakes. Matches are trustworthy, so relax only with a confirmed false positive, and even then scope it to the specific URL or parameter.

accuracyFp.low: F5 defines accuracy as a signature's susceptibility to false positives, and a Low accuracy signature has a high likelihood of false positives.
accuracyFp.medium: F5 defines accuracy as a signature's susceptibility to false positives, and a Medium accuracy signature has some likelihood of false positives.
accuracyFp.high: F5 defines accuracy as a signature's susceptibility to false positives, and a High accuracy signature has a low likelihood of false positives.

note.systemNotInStack: This signature targets a system your application does not run, so it is pure noise here. Rather than disable it one policy at a time, scope your signature set to your actual systems (for example only the databases, web servers, and languages you use).
note.systemUnknown: Confirm whether this signature's system applies to your stack; a signature for a system you do not run only generates false positives.
note.staged: This signature is in staging: it logs but does not block. Treat any false positive as a learning signal, and enforce it only once you are confident it is clean.
note.transparent: The policy is in Transparent mode, so it blocks nothing. This is logged, not blocked; the accuracy and risk matter for when you move to Blocking.
note.highAccuracyLever: If low-accuracy false positives are frequent, let accuracy guide which signatures you enforce. Accuracy is a documented signature property and a signature-set filter criterion, so a signature set weighted towards higher-accuracy signatures produces fewer false positives, because F5 defines accuracy as false-positive susceptibility.
note.disciplineHighRisk: Because this signature guards against a damaging attack, do not disable it just because it is false-positive-prone. Check the actual request first; the cost of relaxing a real match here is high.
note.scopeIt: Scope any change to the specific URL or parameter, or filter the signature set. Disabling a signature policy-wide trades one false positive for a blind spot everywhere else.

share.carries: The link carries the four choices that describe the signature, and nothing else.

f5-bigip-license-explainer.name: F5 BIG-IP licence explainer
f5-bigip-license-explainer.blurb: Paste your /config/bigip.license, full file or a fragment, and get a plain-language reading: management flavour, licensing dates with the K7727 upgrade verdict, Registration Key and platform, active and optional modules, constraints, and feature tokens. Runs entirely in your browser.
f5-bigip-license-explainer.inputPlaceholder: Paste the contents of /config/bigip.license here, the full file or any fragment.
f5-bigip-license-explainer.runsLocally: Parsed entirely in your browser. Nothing is uploaded, and key or signature values are never displayed.
f5-bigip-license-explainer.verifyNote: Field meanings follow the cited F5 articles; confirm licensing decisions against F5 documentation or support.

errors.notRecognized: That text does not look like a BIG-IP licence. Expected markers such as active module, Registration Key, or the licence file header.

dates.k7727Blocked: Branches from {label} need a service check date of {date} or later, so a licence reactivation would come first.

platform.heading: Platform and keys
platform.regKeyOdd: This registration key does not match the published 5-5-5-5-7 shape.
platform.decodedUnknown: Platform ID not in the vendored map; check F5 K9476, the hardware and software compatibility matrix.

modules.optionalNote: Listed as licensable but dormant until licensed; provisioning may be possible while the feature stays inactive.

constraints.exvNote: Per F5 K42091606, the permitted BIG-IP range is read from the BIG-IP-style entries; F5's own example also lists low entries (5.*.* to 8.*.*) alongside them, below the K7727 table's 9.2.0 floor, without labelling what they refer to.
constraints.ceiling: Highest BIG-IP entry: {glob}. Version ceilings map to Version Plus SKU generations, per F5 K15643.

tokens.heading: Feature and limit tokens
tokens.count: {n, plural, one {# token found} other {# tokens found}}; values shown exactly as written.

validation.heading: Validation material
validation.privacy: Presence and length only; the values themselves are never displayed.

f5-bigip-persistence-cookie.name: BIG-IP persistence-cookie decoder
f5-bigip-persistence-cookie.blurb: Decode an F5 BIGipServer persistence cookie into the backend pool member's IP and port, or encode one from an address and port. Runs entirely in your browser.
f5-bigip-persistence-cookie.inputPlaceholder: Paste a cookie value, a name=value pair, or a full Set-Cookie line. Example: 1677787402.20480.0000
f5-bigip-persistence-cookie.runsLocally: Decoded in your browser. The cookie is never sent anywhere.

errors.empty: Enter a BIGipServer cookie value to decode.
errors.unrecognized: This does not match any known BIG-IP persistence cookie format. Check that you pasted the cookie value, not just the name.

encodeErrors.address: Enter a valid IPv4 or IPv6 address.
encodeErrors.routedomain: Route domain must be a number between 0 and 65535.

reasons.INFO_DISCLOSURE: This cookie exposes a backend pool member's IP address and port to anyone who can read the response. Enable cookie encryption on the persistence profile to prevent this.
reasons.INTERNAL_ADDRESS: The decoded address is {value}, confirming an internal pool member and revealing part of your internal topology.
reasons.ROUTE_DOMAIN: The pool member sits in route domain {value}.
reasons.ENCRYPTED: This cookie is AES-encrypted. The pool member cannot be recovered without the BIG-IP's key, which is the recommended secure configuration.

f5-bigip-persistence-cookie.disclosureNote: Decoding uses only the public encoding scheme (F5 K6917). It confirms what any client can already read from the cookie; the fix is to encrypt the persistence cookie.
f5-bigip-persistence-cookie.encryptedNote: An encrypted persistence cookie is the recommended configuration. There is nothing to decode without the key, and that is by design.

encode.resultNote: This is the value a BIG-IP would set for that pool member using the default (unencrypted) encoding.

share.carries: {mode, select, encode {The link carries the address, port and route domain you typed, and nothing else.} other {The link carries the cookie the page decoded, name and value, never the rest of the line.}}
share.caution: It names a pool member's address and port, usually internal: check it before you send the link.

f5-bigip-tcpdump-builder.name: BIG-IP tcpdump builder
f5-bigip-tcpdump-builder.blurb: Assemble a BIG-IP-correct tcpdump command from structured choices: the TMM interface syntax, flow detail, snaplen, file output, and a BPF filter. It formats the command for you to run; it captures nothing.
f5-bigip-tcpdump-builder.runsLocally: The command is assembled in your browser. Nothing is captured, run, or sent anywhere.
f5-bigip-tcpdump-builder.ifaceHint: 0.0 captures on every TMM. You can also name a VLAN, a tunnel, or a self-IP.
f5-bigip-tcpdump-builder.detailHint: Adds the F5 noise/flow trailer to each packet. Higher detail prints flow and peer-flow information.
f5-bigip-tcpdump-builder.bothSidesHint: Capture the client-side and server-side flows of the same connection.
f5-bigip-tcpdump-builder.nameResHint: -n and -nn keep the capture fast and avoid reverse lookups that can stall it.
f5-bigip-tcpdump-builder.countHint: Optional. Leave blank to capture until you stop it with Ctrl-C.
f5-bigip-tcpdump-builder.fileNameHint: Required when sending a capture to F5 Support. Save under /var/tmp or /shared/tmp.
f5-bigip-tcpdump-builder.filterHint: Standard tcpdump/BPF syntax: host, net, port, src/dst, tcp/udp, and / or / not.

warnings.unfiltered-all-tmm: Capturing on 0.0 is not rate-limited. Add a filter (host or port) or a packet count (-c) so the capture file stays bounded.
warnings.snaplen-zero-modern: On BIG-IP 15.x and later, -s0 maps to the default snap length of 262144 bytes (kept for compatibility), so it still captures whole packets.
warnings.hex-with-writefile: -X only affects on-screen output. It has no effect when you also write a binary file with -w.
warnings.colon-in-iface-name: An interface name must not contain a colon on BIG-IP. The colon is reserved for the TMM detail suffix.

share.carries: The link carries every field of the form you set, and nothing else.
share.caution: The interface and the filter can name internal addresses: check them before you send the link.

f5-cipher-string-expander.runsLocally: Parsed in your browser. Nothing is uploaded.

f5-cipher-string-expander.ruleExpands: Pre-built rule {name} uses the cipher string:

SSLV2.label: SSL 2.0
SSLV2.note: An obsolete, broken protocol. It should never be enabled.

SSLV3.label: SSL 3.0
SSLV3.note: A deprecated protocol vulnerable to POODLE. Disable it.

TLSV1.label: TLS 1.0
TLSV1.note: A deprecated protocol; most compliance regimes now require it off.

TLSV1_1.label: TLS 1.1
TLSV1_1.note: A deprecated protocol; disable it in favour of TLS 1.2 and 1.3.

TLSV1_3.label: TLS 1.3
TLSV1_3.note: The newest protocol version; note BIG-IP manages its suites separately.

DTLSV1.label: DTLS 1.0
DTLSV1.note: Datagram TLS 1.0, the UDP analogue of TLS 1.0; deprecated.

DTLSV1_2.label: DTLS 1.2
DTLSV1_2.note: Datagram TLS 1.2, the UDP analogue of TLS 1.2.

ECDHE.label: Ephemeral ECDH key exchange
ECDHE.note: Elliptic-curve ephemeral key exchange; provides forward secrecy.

DHE.label: Ephemeral DH key exchange
DHE.note: Finite-field ephemeral key exchange; provides forward secrecy but is slower than ECDHE.

EDH.label: Ephemeral DH key exchange
EDH.note: An alias for DHE; provides forward secrecy.

ECDH.label: Static ECDH key exchange
ECDH.note: Static elliptic-curve key exchange; no forward secrecy.

DH.label: Static DH key exchange
DH.note: Static finite-field key exchange; no forward secrecy.

ECDHE_RSA.label: ECDHE with RSA authentication
ECDHE_RSA.note: Ephemeral ECDH key exchange authenticated by an RSA certificate; forward secrecy.

ECDHE_ECDSA.label: ECDHE with ECDSA authentication
ECDHE_ECDSA.note: Ephemeral ECDH key exchange authenticated by an ECDSA certificate; required when offering an ECDSA cert only.

DHE_RSA.label: DHE with RSA authentication
DHE_RSA.note: Ephemeral DH key exchange authenticated by RSA; forward secrecy.

RSA.label: RSA
RSA.note: RSA key exchange or authentication. As a key exchange method (not ECDHE/DHE) it does not provide forward secrecy.

DSS.label: DSS
DSS.note: Authentication with a DSA certificate; rarely used today.

ADH.label: Anonymous DH
ADH.note: Anonymous Diffie-Hellman: no certificate, no authentication. It allows man-in-the-middle attacks and must be disabled.

AECDH.label: Anonymous ECDH
AECDH.note: Anonymous elliptic-curve DH: no authentication; disable it.

AES.label: AES
AES.note: AES bulk encryption (both 128 and 256, CBC and GCM unless narrowed).

AES-GCM.label: AES-GCM
AES-GCM.note: AES in Galois/Counter Mode: an AEAD cipher, the preferred bulk choice.

AES-CBC.label: AES-CBC
AES-CBC.note: AES in CBC mode; functional but lacks the AEAD properties of GCM.

CHACHA20-POLY1305.label: ChaCha20-Poly1305
CHACHA20-POLY1305.note: An AEAD stream cipher, strong and fast on devices without AES hardware.

CAMELLIA.label: Camellia
CAMELLIA.note: A block cipher comparable to AES; uncommon and not hardware-accelerated on most platforms.

3DES.label: Triple DES
3DES.note: A slow 64-bit-block cipher vulnerable to Sweet32. Avoid it.

DES.label: DES
DES.note: Single DES: broken by brute force. Never enable it.

RC4.label: RC4
RC4.note: A stream cipher with known biases, prohibited by RFC 7465. Disable it.

NULL.label: Null cipher
NULL.note: No encryption at all. Only ever appropriate for testing; never in production.

IDEA.label: IDEA
IDEA.note: A legacy block cipher; uncommon and not recommended.

SEED.label: SEED
SEED.note: A legacy Korean block cipher; uncommon.

SHA.label: SHA-1 MAC
SHA.note: HMAC-SHA1 for message authentication. Acceptable as a TLS MAC, though SHA-1 is retired for certificates.

SHA256.label: SHA-256 MAC
SHA256.note: HMAC-SHA256, or the PRF hash for newer suites.

MD5.label: MD5 MAC
MD5.note: HMAC-MD5: MD5 is broken and must not be used.

AEAD.label: AEAD
AEAD.note: Authenticated encryption (GCM or ChaCha20-Poly1305) where the cipher provides its own integrity.

DEFAULT.label: DEFAULT
DEFAULT.note: The BIG-IP default cipher set for this TMOS version. F5 recommends appending to it rather than replacing it.

NATIVE.label: NATIVE
NATIVE.note: Cipher suites implemented natively by TMM (as opposed to the removed COMPAT/OpenSSL stack).

ALL.label: ALL
ALL.note: Every cipher suite TMM supports, including weak ones; narrow it before use.

COMPAT.label: COMPAT
COMPAT.note: The OpenSSL compatibility stack, REMOVED in TMOS 13.0+. If present it is replaced with NONE and affected connections fail.

HIGH.label: HIGH
HIGH.note: Cipher suites with long keys; F5 recommends including HIGH alongside disabling ADH.

MEDIUM.label: MEDIUM
MEDIUM.note: Medium-strength cipher suites; review what this admits.

EXPORT.label: EXPORT
EXPORT.note: Deliberately weakened export-grade ciphers (FREAK/Logjam). Always exclude.

EXP.label: EXPORT
EXP.note: Shorthand for EXPORT: deliberately weakened ciphers. Always exclude.

ENULL.label: eNULL
ENULL.note: Ciphers with no encryption. Exclude them.

ANULL.label: aNULL
ANULL.note: Ciphers with no authentication (anonymous). Exclude them.

NONE.label: NONE
NONE.note: No ciphers. A profile resolving to NONE cannot complete a handshake.

sort.STRENGTH: Re-sort the ciphers selected so far by key length (strongest first).
sort.SPEED: Asks for a re-sort by encryption speed, which F5 says is no longer supported: on BIG-IP 14, DEFAULT:@SPEED returned the same list as DEFAULT. Check with tmm --clientciphers on your version.

literal.label: Literal cipher suite
literal.note: A fully-named cipher suite, taken as-is.

unknown.note: Not a recognized BIG-IP cipher keyword.

set.delete: Removes {list} from the list so far (it may be re-added later).
set.lower: Lowers the priority of {list}, moving it towards the end.

pos.pfs: Includes an ephemeral key exchange (ECDHE or DHE), so connections get forward secrecy.
pos.excludes: Explicitly excludes {list}, which is good hardening.

concern.all: ALL admits every supported suite, including weak ones; pair it with exclusions or narrow it.
concern.noPfs: No ephemeral key exchange is explicitly required, so non-forward-secret RSA key exchange may be selected; consider leading with ECDHE.

err.empty: Enter an F5 cipher string or a pre-built rule name.

f5-dos-vector-explainer.name: AFM DoS-vector & profile explainer
f5-dos-vector-explainer.blurb: Every AFM DoS vector explained in F5's own words, with the threshold mechanics spelled out and the configuration cross-checked: the silent mitigation-below-detection inversion, automatic-mode semantics, policing without detection, and the SYN-cookie interplay. Defensive configuration only.
f5-dos-vector-explainer.inputLabel: security dos device-config / profile stanzas, a vector name, or "vectors"
f5-dos-vector-explainer.runsLocally: Runs locally in your browser. Nothing you paste leaves this page.
f5-dos-vector-explainer.defensiveNote: This tool explains defensive configuration. It never generates traffic of any kind.

share.carries: The link carries the box as typed; a paste that sets a password, passphrase or secret gets none.
share.caution: DoS thresholds show what your protections let through: read them before you send the link.
share.blocked: No link: the paste sets “{name}”, which no link may carry; remove that line to share the rest.

err.empty: Paste a security dos device-config stanza and/or security dos profile stanzas, a single vector name (for example "tcp-half-open"), or the word "vectors" for the catalogue.
err.noStanzas: No security dos device-config or security dos profile vector stanzas found. Paste them as tmsh lists them, a vector name, or type "vectors".
err.noStanzasParser: No security dos device-config or security dos profile vector stanzas found (parser: {message}). Paste them as tmsh lists them, a vector name, or type "vectors".
err.unknownVector: "{text}" is not in the curated vector catalogue. Type "vectors" to list it.

field.allow-upstream-scrubbing: advertise the attacked destination for upstream scrubbing
field.auto-threshold: automatic mode: detection thresholds adjust to observed traffic; mitigation limits are driven by measured stress
field.blacklist-category: the IP Intelligence category offenders are added to
field.blacklist-detection-seconds: how long an IP must offend before blacklisting
field.blacklist-duration: how long the IP stays blocked
field.ceiling: the maximum the automatic mode may set for the internal rate limit
field.default-internal-rate-limit: the mitigation ceiling: programmed in hardware where the platform has DoS hardware, otherwise enforced in software; bad packets are always dropped regardless; infinite disables the limit
field.detection-threshold-percent: relative detection: compares the 1-minute average against a dynamically learned 1-hour average; an increase by this percent declares an attack; infinite disables it
field.detection-threshold-pps: absolute detection: attack declared when the current rate (a 1-minute average) reaches this value; infinite disables detection
field.enforce: the packet-drop action of DoS detection for this attack type
field.floor: the minimum the automatic mode may set for detection-threshold-pps (0 = no floor)
field.packet-types: which packet types this sweep/flood vector classifies
field.per-dst-ip-detection-pps: attack detection threshold (pps) per destination IP
field.per-dst-ip-limit-pps: attack mitigation threshold (pps) per destination IP
field.per-source-ip-detection-pps: bad-actor detection rate for a single source IP
field.per-source-ip-limit-pps: bad-actor allowed rate for a single source IP
field.rate-increase: relative detection: percent increase over the learned average that declares an attack
field.rate-limit: the mitigation ceiling for this vector; traffic above it is dropped
field.scrubbing-detection-seconds: how long the destination must be attacked before scrubbing (default 10)
field.scrubbing-duration: how long the destination is scrubbed (default 900)
field.simulate-auto-threshold: logs what automatic mode would have detected or mitigated; the reference scopes it to manual mode only
field.threshold-sensitivity: how much padding automatic and behavioural DoS apply to thresholds (low/medium/high; default medium)

note.catalog: Names and descriptions reproduce the tmsh security dos device-config reference's vector table, sys-db tunables included; the grouping is this tool's organization. Vector sets vary by version and provisioning.
note.sensitivity: threshold-sensitivity {value}: how much padding automatic and behavioural DoS apply when adjusting thresholds (default medium).

obs.auto: auto-threshold is enabled: per F5's DDoS training material, the system adjusts the DETECTION thresholds to observed traffic patterns, while the MITIGATION rate limits are always dynamic, driven by measured system or protected-object stress. Anomalous traffic without stress raises alerts but does not block.
obs.autoManual: Manual detection thresholds are also present on this vector. Under automatic mode the automatic values govern; the floor and ceiling attributes are the supported way to bound what automatic mode may choose.
obs.autoSimulate: simulate-auto-threshold is set while auto-threshold is enabled; the reference scopes the simulation option to manual mode only.
obs.badActorNoRates: bad-actor is enabled but neither per-source-ip threshold is set here; per-source detection needs its rates to act on.
obs.dbVar: The boundary this vector enforces is tunable: sys db {dbVar}.
obs.detectOnly: state detect-only: the vector detects and reports but does not drop. Visibility without action.
obs.enforceOff: enforce is disabled: detection still counts and reports, but the packet-drop action for this attack type is off. Monitoring, not mitigation.
obs.inversion: {limitKey} ({limit}) sits BELOW {detKey} ({det}). Rate limiting engages before an attack is ever declared: traffic between the two values is silently dropped with no attack log. F5's SYN-cookie troubleshooting series warns about exactly this arrangement - the system does warn at configuration time, and then drops quietly.
obs.learnOnly: state learn-only: the vector contributes to baselines without alerting or acting.
obs.noPacketTypes: No packet-types list on this sweep/flood vector in the paste; the vector classifies the packet types that list selects.
obs.perSourceInversion: per-source-ip-limit-pps ({limit}) sits below per-source-ip-detection-pps ({det}): the same inversion as above, per offending source.
obs.policing: Both detection thresholds are infinite (detection disabled) while a finite rate limit is set: the vector limits traffic without ever raising an attack event. Deliberate for pure policing; surprising if you expected logs.
obs.ratesNoBadActor: per-source-ip thresholds are set but bad-actor is not enabled on this vector; the per-source rates ride the bad-actor feature.
obs.simulate: simulate-auto-threshold: the system logs what automatic mode would have detected or mitigated, without acting. A dry run for auto-thresholding, valid exactly here, in manual mode.
obs.stateDisabled: state disabled: this vector neither detects nor mitigates.
obs.stateUnknown: state "{state}" is outside the documented set (mitigate, detect-only, learn-only, disabled); shown as written.
obs.uncurated: "{name}" is outside this tool's curated catalogue (the tmsh reference's vector table as reproduced here). The threshold mechanics below still apply; the identity line does not. Vector sets vary by version and module provisioning.

parser.tooDeep: The configuration nests deeper than the parser allows.
parser.unbalanced: The configuration has an unbalanced brace.

bad-ext-hdr-order.desc: IPv6 extension headers in the packet are out of order.

bad-icmp-frame.desc: Bad ICMP frames (the reference points at the written documentation for the classification reasons).

bad-igmp-frame.desc: Bad IGMP frames (the reference points at the written documentation for the classification reasons).

bad-ipv6-hop-cnt.desc: Bad IPv6 hop count: terminated packet with count == 0. Dropped when the rate hits the rate limit.

bad-ipv6-ver.desc: Bad IPv6 version: the IP version in the IPv6 packet is not 6.

bad-tcp-flags-all-clr.desc: Bad TCP flags: all TCP header flags cleared.

bad-tcp-flags-all-set.desc: Bad TCP flags: all flags set.

bad-ttl-val.desc: Bad IP TTL value (TTL == 0 for IPv4).

bad-udp-hdr.desc: Bad UDP header (the reference points at the written documentation for the classification reasons).

bad-ver.desc: Bad IP version 4: the IPv4 version in the IP header is not 4.

dns-oversize.desc: DNS packet larger than the tunable maximum DNS frame size.

ether-mac-sa-eq-da.desc: Ethernet MAC source address equals the destination address.

ext-hdr-too-large.desc: IPv6 extension header size too large.

fin-only-set.desc: TCP header with only the FIN flag set.

flood.desc: A Flood is an attack where multiple (typically many) endpoints initiate network traffic to a single subnet or receiving endpoint.
flood.note0: The packet-types list selects which packet types this vector classifies.

hdr-len-gt-l2-len.desc: Header length > L2 length: no room in the L2 packet for the IPv4 header (including options).

hdr-len-too-short.desc: Header length too short: IPv4 header length in the IP header is less than 20 bytes.

hop-cnt-leq-one.desc: IPv6 hop count at or below the tunable minimum when the packet needs to be forwarded.

icmp-frame-too-large.desc: Packets larger than the maximum ICMP frame size.

ip-bad-src.desc: The IP address is a broadcast or multicast address.

ip-err-chksum.desc: IP error checksum: IPv4 header checksum error.

ip-len-gt-l2-len.desc: IP length > L2 length: total length in the IPv4 header is greater than the L3 part length in the L2 packet.

ip-opt-frames.desc: IP option frames: IPv4 packets with options.

ip-other-frag.desc: The total IPv4 fragments' size has exceeded the reassembly queue or the maximum IP packet size.

ip-short-frag.desc: IPv4 fragments whose payload size is less than the minimum IPv4 fragment size.

ipv6-atomic-frag.desc: IPv6 frame with a fragment extension header, but the MF and offset fields are both 0.

ipv6-bad-src.desc: IPv6 source address is a multicast address, or the IPv6 source or destination is an IPv4-mapped IPv6 address.

ipv6-other-frag.desc: The total IPv6 fragments' size has exceeded the reassembly queue or the maximum IP packet size.

ipv6-short-frag.desc: IPv6 fragments whose payload size is less than the minimum IPv6 fragment size.

l2-len-ggt-ip-len.desc: L2 length >> IP length: the L2 packet length is much greater than the payload length in IPv4.

l4-ext-hdrs-go-end.desc: No L4: extended headers go to or past the end of the frame.

land-attack.desc: Land attack: IP source address equals IP destination address. Both v4 and v6 are counted.

no-l4.desc: No L4: no L4 payload for IPv4.

opt-present-with-illegal-len.desc: TCP option present with illegal length.

payload-len-ls-l2-len.desc: Payload length '<' L2 length: payload length in the IPv6 header is less than the L3 part length in the L2 packet.

sweep.desc: A Sweep is an attack where a single endpoint initiates network traffic to a large number of receiving endpoints or subnets.
sweep.note0: The packet-types list selects which packet types this vector classifies; bad-actor per-source detection is its natural companion.

tcp-ack-flood.desc: TCP packets with the ACK flag set (for non-existing flows).

tcp-bad-urg.desc: TCP packets with the URG flag set but a URG pointer of 0.

tcp-half-open.desc: Embryonic (half-open) TCP connections: SYN received, handshake not completed.
tcp-half-open.note0: The device-level vector behind AFM's SYN-cookie response. F5's troubleshooting series states the precedence plainly: AFM Device DoS has preference over the LTM global SYN cookie, so when this vector's rate limit sits at or below the LTM global-syn-challenge-threshold, the AFM vector triggers first.
tcp-half-open.note1: Incompatible neighbour: per-VLAN hardware-syncookie (net vlan) is documented as not compatible with the DoS device configuration.

tcp-hdr-len-gt-l2-len.desc: TCP header length > L2 length: no room in the packet for the TCP header (including options).

tcp-hdr-len-too-short.desc: TCP header length too short: the offset field in the TCP header is less than 20 bytes.

tcp-opt-overruns-tcp-hdr.desc: TCP option overruns the TCP header.

tcp-psh-flood.desc: TCP header with PUSH flag set.

tcp-rst-flood.desc: TCP header with only the RST flag set.

tcp-syn-flood.desc: TCP header with only the SYN flag set.
tcp-syn-flood.note0: This is the classic SYN-flood counter. Its close relative tcp-half-open counts embryonic connections instead of raw SYN packets, and is the vector whose mitigation answers with SYN cookies - see the SYN-flood article for the whole LTM/AFM interplay.

tcp-syn-oversize.desc: TCP data-SYN with a packet length above the tunable maximum (128 bytes by default).

tcp-synack-flood.desc: TCP header with only the SYN and ACK flags set.

tcp-window-size.desc: TCP non-RST packet with a window size below the tunable minimum.

too-many-ext-hdrs.desc: Too many extended headers: more than 4 by default.

ttl-leq-one.desc: TTL less than or equal to the tunable minimum, for IPv4 forwarding.

udp-flood.desc: UDP Flood. The UDP flood vector counts any UDP packets that either match the UDP Port Inclusion List or do not match the UDP Port Exclusion List.
udp-flood.note0: The port lists live in their own object: tmsh modify security dos udp-portlist.

f5-gslb-decision-flow.name: GSLB decision-flow explainer
f5-gslb-decision-flow.blurb: The BIG-IP DNS two-tier global server load balancing (GSLB) decision, explained: pool selection at the wide IP, then the preferred, alternate and fallback chain inside the pool, with the grammar validated and the manual's rules cross-checked.
f5-gslb-decision-flow.inputLabel: gtm wideip / gtm pool stanzas, a method name, or "methods"
f5-gslb-decision-flow.runsLocally: Runs locally in your browser. Nothing you paste leaves this page.
f5-gslb-decision-flow.undocumentedToken: Not a documented token for this tier.
f5-gslb-decision-flow.poolTierTitle: Pool tier: the preferred / alternate / fallback methods

share.carries: The link carries the box as typed; a paste that sets a password, passphrase or secret gets none.
share.caution: Wide IP and pool names identify your infrastructure: read the paste before you send the link.
share.blocked: No link: the paste sets “{name}”, which no link may carry; remove that line to share the rest.

err.empty: Paste gtm wideip and/or gtm pool stanzas, a method name (for example "quality-of-service"), or the word "methods" for the full catalogue.
err.noStanzas: No gtm wideip or gtm pool stanzas found. Paste them (tmsh list gtm wideip a '<'name> / gtm pool a '<'name>), a method name, or type "methods".
err.noStanzasParser: No gtm wideip or gtm pool stanzas found (parser: {message}). Paste them (tmsh list gtm wideip a '<'name> / gtm pool a '<'name>), a method name, or type "methods".
err.unknownMethod: "{text}" is not a documented GTM load-balancing method. Type "methods" to list the catalogue.

completion-rate.behavior: Selects the virtual server that currently maintains the least number of dropped or timed-out packets during a transaction between a data centre and the client LDNS.
completion-rate.note0: The metric is measured on the path to the requesting LDNS, which is exactly the data that is missing when the preferred method fails - hence the grammar keeps it out of the alternate tier.

cpu.behavior: Selects the virtual server that currently has the most CPU processing time available to handle name resolution requests.

drop-packet.behavior: Does nothing with the packet, and simply drops the request.
drop-packet.note0: The manual's stated use: most often selected as the Alternate method, to make sure the system does not hand out an address for an unavailable resource.

fallback-ip.behavior: Returns the IP address that you specify (the pool's fallback-ip) as the answer to the query.
fallback-ip.note0: The address is not monitored for availability; the manual scopes this method to disaster recovery, and to the Fallback tier specifically.

fewest-hops.behavior: Selects the virtual server in the data centre that has the fewest router hops from the Local DNS.

global-availability.behavior: Distributes requests to the virtual servers in the pool in the order in which they are listed: the first available resource keeps receiving requests until it becomes unavailable.
global-availability.note0: The manual adds the pairing rule: selecting the next resource in the list only happens when the Fallback method is set to None.

kilobytes-per-second.behavior: Selects the virtual server currently processing the fewest kilobytes per second.

least-connections.behavior: Selects the virtual server on the Local Traffic Manager that currently hosts the fewest connections.
least-connections.note0: The count lives on the LTM that hosts the virtual server - a server-side statistic, not a path measurement.

lowest-round-trip-time.behavior: Selects the virtual server with the fastest measured round trip time between a data centre and the client LDNS.

none.behavior: Skips the tier. As an alternate: jump straight to the fallback method. As a fallback: use the next pool; with no more pools, the result is the same as return-to-dns.
none.note0: The manual completes the cascade: with multiple pools all exhausted, the system returns an aggregate of ALL pool members' addresses using BIND.

packet-rate.behavior: Selects the virtual server currently processing the fewest packets per second.
packet-rate.note0: Measured, yet admitted as an alternate: the packets-per-second statistic is server-side, so it survives the missing-path-metrics situation that usually causes the preferred method to fail.

quality-of-service.behavior: Calculates an overall score for each virtual server from current performance information, then distributes requests based on those scores.
quality-of-service.note0: The score blends weighted factors; the pool's qos-* coefficients set the weights (defaults: rtt 50, lcs 30, hit-ratio 5, kbps 3, packet-rate 1, the rest 0).

ratio.behavior: Distributes requests among the pool's virtual servers using a weighted Round Robin: each member receives requests in proportion to its ratio weight.

return-to-dns.behavior: Immediately returns the request to the Local DNS for resolution.
return-to-dns.note0: This is the DEFAULT fallback-mode: unless configured otherwise, a pool whose preferred and alternate methods both fail hands the query back.

round-robin.behavior: Distributes requests in a circular, sequential pattern among the virtual servers in the pool. The default preferred and alternate mode.

static-persistence.behavior: Consistently maps an LDNS IP address to the same available virtual server for the duration of a session.

topology.behavior: Uses proximity-based load balancing: topology records score the candidates and the best score wins.
topology.note0: The record sorting and scoring mechanics have their own tool and article; see the topology longest-match scorer.

virtual-server-capacity.behavior: Builds a list of the virtual servers weighted by capacity and picks from it: the servers with the greatest capacity are picked most often, but over time all are returned.
virtual-server-capacity.note0: The tmsh reference's alternate-mode text describes this token with the Virtual Server Score wording (a user-defined ranking); the preferred-mode text carries the real weighted-by-capacity semantics. A documented copy quirk worth knowing when reading the man page.

virtual-server-score.behavior: Assigns requests to virtual servers based on a user-defined ranking system.
virtual-server-score.note0: The Load Balancing manual restricts it to pool members controlled by LTM systems - the score is an LTM-side ranking.

note.catalog: Pool-tier grammar per the tmsh gtm pool a reference: 18 preferred tokens; 12 admitted as alternate; all 18 plus none admitted as fallback. Wide-IP tier per the gtm wideip a reference.

obs.altNotAllowed: alternate-mode {token} is outside the tmsh grammar for the alternate tier. The reference admits only: drop-packet, fallback-ip, global-availability, none, packet-rate, ratio, return-to-dns, round-robin, static-persistence, topology, virtual-server-capacity, virtual-server-score - the manual's rule that the alternate can be only static, expressed as a token list (the measured exceptions all use server-side statistics, never the LDNS path).
obs.altUndocumented: "{token}" is not a documented alternate-mode token.
obs.dynamicRatio: dynamic-ratio enabled: instead of the single best-metric member taking everything, the metrics are treated as ratios and every member serves in proportion - the manual's example: RTTs of 50 and 100 microseconds mean the faster member answers twice as often, not always.
obs.dynamicRatioScope: dynamic-ratio is enabled, but the reference scopes it to these preferred modes: completion-rate, fewest-hops, kilobytes-per-second, least-connections, lowest-round-trip-time, quality-of-service, virtual-server-capacity, virtual-server-score. With {gui} preferred, the option has no documented effect.
obs.fallbackIpDefault: A tier resolves with the Fallback IP method, but fallback-ip is "{ip}" (the unset default). The method answers with exactly this address; as configured, the disaster-recovery answer is empty.
obs.fallbackIpMissing: A tier resolves with the Fallback IP method, but fallback-ip is not set. The method answers with exactly this address; as configured, the disaster-recovery answer is empty.
obs.fallbackIpUnused: fallback-ip is set to {ip}, but no tier uses the Fallback IP method, so the address is never returned.
obs.fbDefaulted: No fallback-mode is set, so the documented default applies: return-to-dns. Preferred and alternate both failing hands the query back to the requesting LDNS.
obs.fbIgnoresAvailability: Fallback resolves with {gui}, and the fallback tier ignores the availability status of the resource - the manual is explicit that this exists so the system always returns a response. An answer from this tier can point at a member that monitors consider down.
obs.fbUndocumented: "{token}" is not a documented fallback-mode token.
obs.gaPairing: Global Availability walks its ordered list to the next resource only when the Fallback method is None (the manual's pairing rule). With a different fallback configured here, exhaustion goes to the fallback tier instead of down the list.
obs.manualResume: manual-resume is enabled: a member that goes down stays out of rotation until someone re-enables it by hand, even after its monitors recover.
obs.prefNone: The preferred tier's grammar does not admit "none"; the tmsh reference lists it only for alternate-mode and fallback-mode.
obs.prefUndocumented: "{token}" is not a documented load-balancing-mode token. Type "methods" for the catalogue.
obs.qosZero: A tier uses Quality of Service but every configured qos-* coefficient is 0: the score has nothing to weigh. The defaults weigh rtt 50, lcs 30, hit-ratio 5, kbps 3 and packet-rate 1.
obs.ratioUnusedMany: {count} members carry a ratio weight, but no tier uses the Ratio method, so the weights never apply.
obs.ratioUnusedOne: {count} member carries a ratio weight, but no tier uses the Ratio method, so the weights never apply.
obs.topologyBothTiers: Topology runs at both tiers (wide IP {wideips} and this pool), and this pool's fallback is {fallback}. The Load Balancing manual's warning applies: set each pool's Fallback to None in this arrangement, or the system can send a request to a pool with no available members and fall back to BIND; with None, an empty pool passes the request to another pool instead.
obs.verifyOff: verify-member-availability is disabled: the system does not verify member availability before answering (the default is enabled).
obs.wipDefault: No pool-lb-mode is set, so pool selection runs Round Robin - the documented default.
obs.wipGaNoOrder: Global Availability follows the order of the pool list; no explicit order values are set here, so the listed order is the priority order.
obs.wipRandom: pool-lb-mode random: described in the v13 wideip reference but absent from the current syntax line - version-dependent; verify on your version before relying on it.
obs.wipRatioNoWeights: pool-lb-mode is ratio, but none of the attached pools carries a ratio value on this wide IP; without weights there is no proportion to follow.
obs.wipSinglePool: pool-lb-mode is relevant only when multiple pools are configured (the reference's own scoping); with a single pool the selection tier has nothing to choose between.
obs.wipUndocumented: "{mode}" is not a documented pool-lb-mode. The wideip reference lists: global-availability, ratio, round-robin, topology (and the v13 text also describes random).

parser.tooDeep: The configuration nests deeper than the parser allows.
parser.unbalanced: The configuration has an unbalanced brace.

setting.dynamic-ratio: disabled: best metric wins outright; enabled: metrics become ratios and every member serves in proportion
setting.failure-rcode: the RCODE returned when failure-rcode-response is enabled
setting.failure-rcode-response: answer failures with a DNS RCODE instead of falling through
setting.fallback-ip: the address the Fallback IP method returns; not monitored for availability
setting.last-resort-pool: the pool used when every configured pool is exhausted
setting.load-balancing-decision-log-verbosity: the built-in way to watch this decision flow happen: pool-selection, pool-traversal, pool-member-selection, pool-member-traversal
setting.manual-resume: enabled: a member that went down stays out until re-enabled by hand
setting.max-answers-returned: how many available virtual servers a response lists (default 1)
setting.persistence: pin an LDNS to its previous answer for ttl-persistence seconds
setting.verify-member-availability: whether member availability is verified before sending a connection (default enabled)

tier.alternate: Tried when the preferred method fails. The grammar admits only methods that need no LDNS path metrics; per the manual, the alternate method can be only static.
tier.fallback: Tried when preferred and alternate both fail. To ensure the system returns a response, the fallback method IGNORES the availability status of the resource.
tier.preferred: Tried first. May be static or dynamic; a dynamic method here is the usual reason the chain advances - the manual notes a preferred-method failure usually means the proper metrics could not be acquired.

wipMethod.global-availability: Repeatedly selects the FIRST pool in the list for as long as it is available; only when it becomes unavailable does the next pool in the list take over.
wipMethod.random: Selects a pool in no pattern or order. Described in the v13 wideip reference; absent from the current syntax line - a version-dependent token.
wipMethod.ratio: Selects a pool based on the ratio assigned to the pool on this wide IP.
wipMethod.topology: Selects a pool based on topology information in the incoming LDNS request.

cmp.globals: Global variables in use ({globals}): per the CMP Compatibility page, global variables are not CMP-compatible, the validator catches the global form as of v10, and the virtual server is demoted from CMP, putting every connection for it on a single TMM. The documented alternative for shared static values is the static:: namespace.
cmp.ruleInitKeys: Key material handled in RULE_INIT: the compatibility page warns that when keys are generated in RULE_INIT, every TMM gets its own key, so requests cannot be decrypted successfully across TMM instances. Derive or share keys in a CMP-aware way instead.

cmp.stats: STATS:: usage: the compatibility page notes statistics profiles are not fully CMP-compatible; each TMM instance keeps a separate instance of the profile, with cumulative counts shown in the GUI and SNMP.

event.CACHE_REQUEST: Triggered when the system receives a request for a cached object.
event.CACHE_RESPONSE: Triggered immediately prior to sending a cache response.
event.CLIENTSSL_CLIENTCERT: Triggered when the system adds an SSL client certificate to the client certificate chain.
event.CLIENTSSL_CLIENTHELLO: Triggered when the system has received the client's SSL ClientHello message.
event.CLIENTSSL_DATA: Triggered each time new SSL data is received from the client while the connection is in "collect" state.
event.CLIENTSSL_HANDSHAKE: Triggered when a client-side SSL handshake is completed.
event.CLIENTSSL_PASSTHROUGH: Triggered when SSL receives plaintext data and enters passthrough mode.
event.CLIENTSSL_SERVERHELLO_SEND: Triggered when the system is about to send its SSL ServerHello message on the clientside connection.
event.CLIENT_ACCEPTED: Triggered when a client has established a connection.
event.CLIENT_CLOSED: Fired at the end of any client connection, regardless of protocol.
event.CLIENT_DATA: Triggered each time new data is received from the client while the connection is in "collect" state.
event.DNS_REQUEST: Triggered when the system receives a DNS request.
event.DNS_RESPONSE: Triggered when the system responds to a DNS request.
event.FLOW_INIT: Triggered once for TCP and unique UDP/IP flows, after packet filters.
event.HTML_COMMENT_MATCHED: Raised when an HTML comment is encountered.
event.HTML_TAG_MATCHED: Raised when an HTML tag is encountered.
event.HTTP_PROXY_CONNECT: Triggered when proxy chaining is in use through the HTTP proxy connect profile.
event.HTTP_PROXY_REQUEST: Triggered when a virtual server has proxy-mode explicit.
event.HTTP_PROXY_RESPONSE: Triggered when the response from the remote HTTP proxy is received.
event.HTTP_REJECT: Triggered when HTTP aborts the connection.
event.HTTP_REQUEST: Triggered when the system fully parses the complete client HTTP request headers.
event.HTTP_REQUEST_DATA: Triggered when an HTTP::collect command has collected the specified amount of request data.
event.HTTP_REQUEST_RELEASE: Triggered when the system is about to release HTTP data on the serverside of the connection.
event.HTTP_REQUEST_SEND: Triggered immediately before an HTTP request is sent to the server-side TCP stack.
event.HTTP_RESPONSE: Triggered when the system parses all of the response status and header lines from the server response.
event.HTTP_RESPONSE_CONTINUE: Triggered whenever the system receives a 100 Continue response from the server.
event.HTTP_RESPONSE_DATA: Triggered when an HTTP::collect command has collected the specified amount of response data.
event.HTTP_RESPONSE_RELEASE: Triggered when the system is about to release HTTP data on the clientside of the connection.
event.LB_FAILED: Triggered when the system fails to select a pool or a pool member, or when a selected resource is unreachable.
event.LB_QUEUED: Serverside event triggered when a connection limit is hit at the pool or pool member level.
event.LB_SELECTED: Triggered when the system selects a pool member.
event.NAME_RESOLVED: Triggered after a NAME::lookup command has been issued and a response has been received.
event.PERSIST_DOWN: Triggered when persistence dictates that a connection would be sent to a pool, pool member, or node which has been marked down.
event.RULE_INIT: Triggered when an iRule is added or is modified.
event.SA_PICKED: Triggered after source translation is completed.
event.SERVERSSL_CLIENTHELLO_SEND: Triggered when the system is about to send its SSL ClientHello message.
event.SERVERSSL_DATA: Triggered when new SSL data is received from the target node after SSL::collect has been issued.
event.SERVERSSL_HANDSHAKE: Triggered when a server-side SSL handshake is completed.
event.SERVERSSL_SERVERCERT: Triggered when the system finishes the server certificate verification.
event.SERVERSSL_SERVERHELLO: Triggered when the system has received the server's SSL ServerHello message.
event.SERVER_CLOSED: Triggered when the server side connection closes.
event.SERVER_CONNECTED: Triggered when a connection has been established with the target node.
event.SERVER_DATA: Triggered when new data is received from the target node after TCP::collect has been issued.
event.SERVER_INIT: Triggered when BIG-IP has been configured to collect options and the serverside TCP SYN is sent.
event.SIP_REQUEST: Triggered when the system fully parses a complete client SIP request header.
event.SIP_RESPONSE: Triggered when a SIP response is received from the server.
event.STREAM_MATCHED: Triggered when a stream expression matches.
event.USER_REQUEST: Triggered by the TCP::notify request command.
event.USER_RESPONSE: Triggered by the TCP::notify response command.
event.WS_CLIENT_FRAME: Raised to indicate the start of a WebSocket frame received from the client.
event.WS_REQUEST: Raised when certain headers are present in the client request.
event.WS_RESPONSE: Raised when certain headers are present in the server response.

order.analysis: {event} appears {count} times. Per the priority reference (default 500, lower runs first, same priority runs in insertion order), the evaluation order here is: {order}. Across multiple iRules on one virtual, same-priority blocks run in the order the rules are listed on the virtual.

rule.cmpVerdict: CMP verdict: this rule demotes its virtual server from clustered multiprocessing as written (global variables). Demotion means every connection for the virtual is handled by a single TMM; the fix the compatibility page names is static:: for shared statics, or the table/session commands' documented patterns for shared mutable state.

f5-irules-event-order.name: iRules event-order explainer
f5-irules-event-order.blurb: Pick the profile stack on a BIG-IP virtual server - client-SSL, HTTP, server-SSL, pool - and see the order the common iRule events fire, from CLIENT_ACCEPTED to CLIENT_CLOSED, as a timeline and a list. All in your browser.
f5-irules-event-order.runsLocally: Computed in your browser. Nothing is sent anywhere.
f5-irules-event-order.scopeNote: A model of documented F5 behaviour for a Standard virtual server. It never contacts a BIG-IP.
f5-irules-event-order.conditionalNote: These fire only under specific conditions: a TCP::collect or HTTP::collect, a load-balancing failure, or a 100 Continue response.

share.carries: The link carries the five profile switches as set, and nothing else.

ev.CLIENT_ACCEPTED: A client connection is established. On a Standard virtual server this is when the TCP three-way handshake completes; on FastL4 it fires on the initial SYN.
ev.CLIENTSSL_CLIENTHELLO: The client's TLS ClientHello has been received, before the handshake is processed. Useful for SNI-based decisions.
ev.CLIENTSSL_HANDSHAKE: The client-side TLS handshake has completed successfully.
ev.HTTP_REQUEST: The system has fully parsed the complete client HTTP request headers.
ev.LB_SELECTED: The system has selected a pool member for the connection.
ev.SERVER_CONNECTED: The server-side connection to the selected pool member has been established.
ev.SERVERSSL_HANDSHAKE: The server-side TLS handshake has completed successfully.
ev.HTTP_REQUEST_SEND: Immediately before the HTTP request is sent to the server-side TCP stack. Runs in the server-side context.
ev.HTTP_RESPONSE: The system has parsed all of the response status and header lines from the server response.
ev.SERVER_CLOSED: The server-side connection has been closed.
ev.CLIENT_CLOSED: The client-side connection has been closed.
ev.CLIENT_DATA: After a TCP::collect on the client side has gathered the requested data. Common on raw TCP virtual servers with no HTTP profile.
ev.HTTP_REQUEST_DATA: After an HTTP::collect has gathered the specified amount of request payload.
ev.LB_FAILED: Instead of LB_SELECTED, when the system fails to select a pool or member, or the selected resource is unreachable.
ev.SERVER_DATA: After a TCP::collect on the server side has gathered the requested data.
ev.HTTP_RESPONSE_CONTINUE: Before HTTP_RESPONSE, whenever the server sends a 100 Continue interim response.
ev.HTTP_RESPONSE_DATA: After an HTTP::collect has gathered the specified amount of response payload.

note.fastl4: FastL4 is a packet-based fast path, not a full TCP proxy. Most L7 and SSL events do not fire; CLIENT_ACCEPTED triggers on the initial SYN. This model shows the Standard (full-proxy) sequence - treat the HTTP and SSL rows as not applicable under FastL4.
note.serverssl-no-pool: A server-SSL profile only takes effect once there is a server-side connection. With no pool, the server-side events (including SERVERSSL_HANDSHAKE) never fire.
note.http-no-pool: With an HTTP profile but no pool, HTTP_REQUEST still fires (the request is parsed on the client side), but there is no server to forward to - typical of an iRule that answers directly with HTTP::respond.
note.serverssl-no-clientssl: Server-SSL without client-SSL means the BIG-IP terminates plaintext from the client and initiates TLS to the pool - a less common 'encrypt on the way out' design.
note.priority: Within a single event, multiple iRules run by priority (default 500, lowest number first); the priority command overrides that. This ordering is across events, not within one.
note.provisioning: Availability also depends on provisioning: module events (APM ACCESS_*, ASM/Advanced WAF (web application firewall), bot defense) only fire when that module is provisioned. And CLIENT_DATA, SERVER_DATA, HTTP_REQUEST_DATA, and HTTP_RESPONSE_DATA need an explicit TCP::collect or HTTP::collect first.
note.json-sse: Not placed in this sequence: the JSON events (JSON_REQUEST, JSON_RESPONSE and their error and missing variants) and SSE_RESPONSE were introduced in BIG-IP 21.0.0 and need a JSON or SSE profile on the virtual server along with the HTTP profile.
