note.strategies: Strategy semantics verbatim from the ltm policy-strategy reference; the precedence head reproduces the built-in table's ordering, and user-defined strategies exist precisely for organizations whose idea of specificity differs.

reason.conditions: conditions map onto {reads} operands (http-uri, http-header, http-cookie selectors in the policy grammar)
reason.headerWrite: header rewriting maps onto the http-header replace/insert action the x-forwarded-for example uses
reason.log: logging maps onto the log write action, tcl: substitution included, as the examples show
reason.pool: pool selection maps onto the forward-to-pool action
reason.reset: connection rejection maps onto the forward reset action the shellshock example uses
reason.verify: {cmd}: plausibly covered by policy conditions/actions on current versions, but not demonstrated in the sources this tool verified; check your version's condition and action lists before migrating

strategy.all-match: Executes the actions for all conditions that match, continuing evaluation as traffic flows.
strategy.best-match: For situations when multiple conditions match simultaneously; allows the more specific match to win. Equal condition counts fall through to the strategy's precedence table, where a lower ordinal is more significant.
strategy.first-match: Terminates the matching engine on the first condition that matches and executes that rule's actions. When multiple rules match simultaneously, the rule's ordinal breaks the tie, lower value first.

summary.expressible: {count, plural, one {{count} block maps} other {{count} blocks map}} cleanly onto the verified policy grammar. The payoff the sources describe: LTM Policy is the highly performant layer that, unlike iRules, does not require programming, and none of the iRule CMP-demotion hazards exist inside a policy.
summary.irule: {count, plural, one {{count} block belongs} other {{count} blocks belong}} in iRules, for the named blockers on each card. That is what iRules are for.
summary.mechanics: Migration mechanics per the Getting Started manual: build the policy as a draft, publish it, then attach the published policy to the virtual server; the vendor ships its examples in both policy and iRule form for exactly this comparison.
summary.verify: {count, plural, one {{count} block looks} other {{count} blocks look}} expressible but lean on conditions or actions the verified sources did not demonstrate; confirm them against your version's policy condition and action lists before migrating.

f5-l4-profile-explainer.name: LTM L4 protocol profile explainer
f5-l4-profile-explainer.blurb: The protocol-profile decision in cards: full-proxy tcp with every feature, the living f5-tcp-* four that F5 continually updates (read-only, tuned via child profiles) versus the frozen legacy -optimized trio, FastL4's PVA packet path with the loose pair for asymmetric routing, and FastHTTP's narrow-but-fast HTTP case with its complete when-to-use criteria list and K8024 as required reading.
f5-l4-profile-explainer.inputPlaceholder: fastl4 · fasthttp · f5-tcp-progressive · tcp-wan-optimized · legacy · profiles
f5-l4-profile-explainer.runsLocally: Runs locally in your browser. Nothing you type leaves this page.

err.empty: Name a profile (for example "fastl4", "fasthttp", "f5-tcp-progressive", "tcp-wan-optimized", "legacy"), or type "profiles" for the full table.

note.roadmap: Stanza parsing with a per-option audit (the OneConnect tool's pattern) is this tool's documented roadmap enhancement.
note.spine: The decision spine in one line: full-proxy tcp for features, FastL4 for the packet path when little or no L4/L7 processing is required, FastHTTP for the narrow HTTP case that clears every criterion on its list.

obs.fasthttp: Pairing: the Performance (HTTP) virtual server type; the operations guide sends every deployment to K8024 first, and this card's when-to-use list is that reading in criterion form.
obs.fastl4: Virtual-server pairing per the operations guide: Performance (Layer 4), Forwarding (Layer 2), and Forwarding (IP); the Performance type is the one F5 recommends when little or no L4/L7 processing is required.
obs.legacy: The vendor's own mapping: f5-tcp-wan, f5-tcp-lan, and f5-tcp-mobile are the updated versions of this trio; new work belongs on the living family, and these remain for configurations that depend on their frozen values.
obs.living: The living contract, from F5's own announcement: the four f5-* profiles and the default tcp are living, continually updated with best practices; brand-new features appear in f5-tcp-progressive immediately and in the more conservative living profiles after a couple of releases; all five are read-only, so tuning means a child profile, where the custom flag pins a setting against future pushes.

f5-tcp-lan.name: f5-tcp-lan
f5-tcp-lan.quirk0: Benchmark claim from the announcement: throughput at least as high, and often better, than the default tcp profile for its link type.
f5-tcp-lan.story: The living, updated version of tcp-lan-optimized: all settings adapted to LAN-grade links, without enabling the very newest features. The profiles reference pairs it with LAN-based or highly interactive traffic behind a standard virtual server.
f5-tcp-lan.tradeoff0: Link-type-tuned: on the side of a virtual server that faces a WAN, a LAN profile gives WAN traffic LAN behaviour, so split-profile virtual servers (LAN inside, WAN outside) exist for exactly this.
f5-tcp-lan.when0: Server-side profiles on fast, low-loss data-center links.
f5-tcp-lan.when1: Interactive LAN traffic where latency dominates.

f5-tcp-mobile.name: f5-tcp-mobile
f5-tcp-mobile.quirk0: The legacy mobile pair carries the reference's sizing note: for files under 1 MB, tcp-mobile-optimized generally beats mptcp-mobile-optimized.
f5-tcp-mobile.story: The living, updated version of tcp-mobile-optimized, tuned for cellular client behaviour: variable latency, radio-state-driven loss patterns, and battery-conscious pacing.
f5-tcp-mobile.tradeoff0: Mobile tuning on fixed-line clients trades throughput for resilience those clients do not need.
f5-tcp-mobile.when0: Client-side profiles where the population is predominantly mobile.

f5-tcp-progressive.name: f5-tcp-progressive
f5-tcp-progressive.quirk0: Living and read-only, tuned via child profiles like the rest of the five.
f5-tcp-progressive.story: The announcement's own definition: a general-use profile, like the tcp default, but containing the very latest features for early adopters. New generally-applicable TCP features land here first, immediately; the conservative living profiles receive them a couple of releases later.
f5-tcp-progressive.tradeoff0: Early-adopter posture by design: features arrive here before the conservative profiles, which is the point and the risk in one sentence.
f5-tcp-progressive.when0: A modern default for mixed or unknown client populations when you want current TCP behaviour without hand-tuning.
f5-tcp-progressive.when1: F5's published benchmark criterion: equal or higher throughput than the default tcp profile across all representative network types.

f5-tcp-wan.name: f5-tcp-wan
f5-tcp-wan.quirk0: Same living benchmark claim, for WAN link types.
f5-tcp-wan.story: The living, updated version of tcp-wan-optimized, adapted to slower, lossier wide-area links. The reference's classic example: clients arrive over a WAN generally slower than the BIG-IP-to-server path, and a WAN-tuned client side lets the system accept data efficiently while server resources stay available.
f5-tcp-wan.tradeoff0: Same link-type caveat as its LAN sibling, mirrored.
f5-tcp-wan.when0: Client-side profiles for internet or WAN-facing virtual servers.
f5-tcp-wan.when1: Anywhere round-trip time and loss, not bandwidth, bound performance.

fasthttp.name: FastHTTP
fasthttp.quirk0: The OneConnect-style reuse is built in rather than layered on, which is why the OneConnect article on this site is its natural companion reading.
fasthttp.story: The profiles reference's definition: a configuration tool designed to speed up certain types of HTTP connections, combining selected features from the TCP Express, HTTP, and OneConnect profiles into a single profile optimized for the best possible network performance. It pairs with the Performance (HTTP) virtual server type, and its signature benefit is connection reuse: the system can transform or add the HTTP Connection header to keep server-side connections open.
fasthttp.tradeoff0: Every criterion above is a limitation read backwards: SSL termination, compression, caching, full iRules, or source-IP preservation each disqualify FastHTTP, and the standard virtual server with tcp+http (+OneConnect where wanted) is the answer instead.
fasthttp.tradeoff1: The operations guide's verdict, worth quoting in reviews: possibly the fastest way to pass HTTP traffic under certain circumstances, with specific requirements and limitations, and K8024 is the required pre-deployment reading.
fasthttp.when0: The reference's own criteria, all of them: you do not need remote server authentication, SSL traffic management, or TCP optimizations; nor compression, pipelining, or RAM Cache.
fasthttp.when1: You do not need to maintain source IP addresses (translation to a BIG-IP-owned address is part of the design).
fasthttp.when2: You want fewer connections opened to servers, and the servers support keep-alive (HTTP/1.1, or HTTP/1.0 with Keep-Alive; IIS by default).
fasthttp.when3: Basic iRule support suffices: CLIENT_ACCEPTED, SERVER_CONNECTED, and HTTP_REQUEST are the reference's own event examples.

fastl4.name: FastL4
fastl4.quirk0: pva-acceleration: full | none | partial | dedicated (man page); dynamic offload adds packet-count thresholds and an offload state of embryonic or establish.
fastl4.quirk1: The loose pair, defaults disabled: loose-initialization accepts any TCP packet rather than requiring a SYN, loose-close closes on the first FIN from either side; together they are the asymmetric-routing survival kit.
fastl4.quirk2: tcp-timestamp-mode and tcp-wscale-mode default to preserve: the pass-through posture in two option defaults.
fastl4.quirk3: late-binding: an iRule reads a Layer 7 FIX packet to select the pool, then the ePVA carries the stream at hardware latency; the man page requires a FIX profile on the Performance (Layer 4) virtual server for it.
fastl4.story: Not a TCP proxy: a packet-path profile. The profiles reference states its purpose, assigning a Fast L4 profile lets the Packet Velocity ASIC (PVA) hardware, where the platform supports it, process some or all of the Layer 4 traffic, raising performance and throughput for L4 routing and switching. It pairs with Performance (Layer 4), Forwarding (Layer 2), and Forwarding (IP) virtual servers, and dynamic offload can hand established flows to ePVA hardware mid-connection.
fastl4.tradeoff0: Minimal L7 information is available, the guide's words, so load-balancing decisions are limited in scope: no HTTP profile, no content-aware features, and iRule events are the L4 set (the event-order explainer on this site flags exactly which).
fastl4.tradeoff1: One flow, not two stacks: client and server see essentially the same TCP conversation, with the profile's IP/TCP field modes (TTL, DF, timestamp, window-scale) governing what is preserved or rewritten.
fastl4.when0: The operations guide's own clause: when little or no L4 or L7 processing is required.
fastl4.when1: Stateless or semi-stateless forwarding: Forwarding (IP) virtual servers require FastL4 options for it.
fastl4.when2: Steering traffic to inspection devices (firewall, IDS), with address and port translation disabled per the guide.

legacy.name: The legacy trio (tcp-lan-optimized, tcp-wan-optimized, tcp-mobile-optimized)
legacy.quirk0: mptcp-mobile-optimized adds Multipath TCP for reverse-proxy mobile fronts; the reference's own sizing note says tcp-mobile-optimized is generally better below 1 MB.
legacy.quirk1: These are not read-only like the living five, which is exactly how configurations drifted before the child-profile discipline existed.
legacy.story: The pre-13.0 tuned family, frozen where it stood when the living profiles arrived. The announcement is explicit that f5-tcp-wan, f5-tcp-lan, and f5-tcp-mobile are their updated versions; the legacy names still ship (the 21.0 profiles reference lists both families side by side) so existing configurations keep working unchanged.
legacy.tradeoff0: Frozen means frozen: best-practice updates F5 pushes to the living profiles never arrive here.
legacy.when0: Existing deployments that depend on the exact frozen values and change control that forbids behavioural drift.
legacy.when1: Nothing new: for new work the living family is the vendor's own upgrade path.

tcp.name: tcp (the full-proxy default)
tcp.quirk0: Living and read-only: modifying it means creating a descendant profile, which also aids troubleshooting by making local tuning explicit.
tcp.story: The standard virtual server's baseline: two independent TCP stacks, one facing the client and one facing the servers, each negotiated and tuned separately. Every LTM feature that reads or rewrites traffic rides on this full proxy. Since the 13.0 reorganization it is also one of the five living profiles: F5 updates its best practices over releases, and it is read-only, tuned via child profiles.
tcp.tradeoff0: Full proxying costs more CPU per connection than FastL4's packet-by-packet path; that cost buys every feature the platform has.
tcp.when0: Any virtual server that needs L7 features: HTTP profiles, SSL termination, full iRules, WAF, compression, caching.
tcp.when1: When client-side and server-side link characteristics differ and each stack should be tuned to its own side.

f5-lb-method-chooser.name: LB-method chooser
f5-lb-method-chooser.blurb: Paste an ltm pool and get its load-balancing method explained in F5's own terms, with cross-checks against the rest of the pool, or answer two questions and get a sourced recommendation. All in your browser.
f5-lb-method-chooser.inputLabel: Pool config, a method name, or "methods"
f5-lb-method-chooser.runsLocally: Processed in your browser. Nothing is sent.
f5-lb-method-chooser.catalogHeading: The 19 documented modes, in the tmsh reference's order
f5-lb-method-chooser.capacityRatio: Different, and I can state the proportion
f5-lb-method-chooser.capacityMeasured: Different, and I want it measured for me
f5-lb-method-chooser.reactLabel: What should the method react to?

share.carries: {part, select, panel {The link carries your two answers in Help me choose, and nothing from the box.} other {The link carries the text in the box as typed, not your Help me choose answers.}}
share.caution: Pool and member names can identify your servers: check them before you send the link.

dynamic-ratio-member.weighs: ratio weights the system keeps recomputing from server measurements
dynamic-ratio-member.behavior: Like Ratio, but the weights come from continuous monitoring of the servers and are therefore continually changing, instead of being set by hand.
dynamic-ratio-member.chooseWhen: Pool members differ in capacity and you want the weights measured, not guessed: the system keeps them current as server performance moves.
dynamic-ratio-member.caveat0: The weights need something to measure: server-side performance monitoring must be in place for the ratios to be meaningful. K14129 shows how to view the weight the system computed.
dynamic-ratio-member.oneLiner: Ratio weights the system keeps recomputing from server measurements.

dynamic-ratio-node.weighs: system-computed, continually changing ratio weights, counted per node across every pool
dynamic-ratio-node.behavior: The node-scope twin of Dynamic Ratio (member): weights come from continuous monitoring and change on their own; the accounting follows the server across all pools it belongs to.
dynamic-ratio-node.chooseWhen: Same measured-capacity case as the member form, when servers are shared across multiple pools and should be weighted by their whole load.
dynamic-ratio-node.caveat0: Node scope means a busy server in another pool lowers this one's share here too - that is the point, but it surprises people reading a single pool's config.
dynamic-ratio-node.oneLiner: System-computed, continually changing ratio weights, counted per node across every pool.

fastest-app-response.weighs: response speed, tracked as outstanding Layer 7 requests
fastest-app-response.behavior: Passes a new connection based on the fastest response of all currently active nodes in the pool. Per K6406 the underlying count is the number of outstanding Layer 7 requests to a member.
fastest-app-response.chooseWhen: The vendor's own suggestion: particularly useful where nodes are distributed across different logical networks, so path speed differs as much as server speed.
fastest-app-response.caveat0: It counts outstanding Layer 7 requests (K6406), so the virtual server has to be processing traffic at Layer 7 for the count to mean anything.
fastest-app-response.oneLiner: Response speed, tracked as outstanding Layer 7 requests.

fastest-node.weighs: response speed per node, measured across all pools the server is in
fastest-node.behavior: Passes a new connection based on the fastest response of a server counted across all pools of which it is a member - the node-scope form of Fastest.
fastest-node.chooseWhen: The cross-network case again, when the same servers sit in several pools and their responsiveness should be judged on their total work.
fastest-node.caveat0: Same Layer 7 dependency as the application form: the outstanding-request count (K6406) needs L7 processing to exist.
fastest-node.oneLiner: Response speed per node, measured across all pools the server is in.

least-connections-member.weighs: open connections right now, counted within this pool
least-connections-member.behavior: Passes a new connection to the member with the fewest current connections in the pool, measured at the moment the request arrives (K6406).
least-connections-member.chooseWhen: Servers of similar capability - the vendor's stated best fit. Because it counts what is open right now, it also absorbs uneven connection durations that trip Round Robin.
least-connections-member.caveat0: With OneConnect enabled, idle connections are excluded: only active connections count in the selection (K6406).
least-connections-member.caveat1: It counts BIG-IP-to-member connections only, not whatever else the server is doing.
least-connections-member.caveat2: A freshly recovered member has zero connections and would take a flood; the tmsh reference calls slow-ramp-time particularly useful with exactly this mode (default 10 seconds).
least-connections-member.oneLiner: Open connections right now, counted within this pool.

least-connections-node.weighs: open connections right now, counted across every pool the server is in
least-connections-node.behavior: Passes a new connection to the node with the fewest current connections out of all pools of which it is a member.
least-connections-node.chooseWhen: Similar-capability servers that appear in several pools, when the fair count is the server's total connections rather than this pool's slice.
least-connections-node.caveat0: The same OneConnect and slow-ramp notes as the member form apply; the count is just taken per node.
least-connections-node.oneLiner: Open connections right now, counted across every pool the server is in.

least-sessions.behavior: Passes a new connection to the member that currently has the least number of persistent sessions.
least-sessions.chooseWhen: Session-heavy applications where balance should follow sessions rather than raw connections, and persistence is already in play.
least-sessions.caveat0: It only works when the virtual server references a persistence profile of a type that tracks persistence connections (K42275060) - without one there is nothing to count.

observed-member.weighs: a per-second ratio the system computes from recent Layer 4 connection counts
observed-member.behavior: Ranks members by connection count and gives a greater share to those with a better balance of fewest connections. Unlike Least Connections, which measures only at the moment of load balancing, Observed tracks Layer 4 connections over time and turns them into a ratio, reassigned every second (K6406).
observed-member.chooseWhen: The vendor's wording: works well in any environment, but may be particularly useful where member performance varies significantly - it smooths where Least Connections reacts instant by instant.
observed-member.caveat0: The smoothing is also lag: a member that just got slow keeps its good ratio for a moment.
observed-member.oneLiner: A per-second ratio the system computes from recent Layer 4 connection counts.

observed-node.weighs: the same per-second connection-based ratio, counted per node across pools
observed-node.behavior: The node-scope twin of Observed (member): the over-time connection ratio follows the server across all pools it belongs to.
observed-node.chooseWhen: The Observed case when servers are shared across pools.
observed-node.caveat0: Same smoothing-versus-lag trade as the member form.
observed-node.oneLiner: The same per-second connection-based ratio, counted per node across pools.

predictive-member.weighs: the Observed ranking plus its trend - improving or declining
predictive-member.behavior: Uses the Observed ranking, then analyses the trend of that ranking over time: members with better rankings that are currently improving, rather than declining, receive a higher proportion of connections (K6406).
predictive-member.chooseWhen: The vendor states it plainly: this mode works well in any environment. Reach for it when you want Observed's smoothing plus a preference for members getting healthier.
predictive-member.caveat0: Trend analysis makes it the least predictable mode to reason about by hand - which is fine, until someone asks why a specific request went where it did.
predictive-member.oneLiner: The Observed ranking plus its trend - improving or declining.

predictive-node.weighs: the Observed-node ranking plus its trend
predictive-node.behavior: The node-scope twin of Predictive (member): trend-weighted ranking, counted per node across every pool.
predictive-node.chooseWhen: The Predictive case when servers are shared across pools.
predictive-node.caveat0: Same reasoning-by-hand caveat as the member form.
predictive-node.oneLiner: The Observed-node ranking plus its trend.

ratio-least-connections-member.weighs: your ratio weight combined with each member's active connection count
ratio-least-connections-member.behavior: Weights the selection by the ratio defined on each member (an unset ratio counts as 1) together with the number of connections each member has active; available since LTM 11.0.0 (K6406).
ratio-least-connections-member.chooseWhen: Mixed-capacity servers where you can state the difference as a ratio but still want live connection counts respected.
ratio-least-connections-member.caveat0: It is the exception to the ratio rule: outside this mode (and its node twin), member ratios only apply under a ratio method (K6406).
ratio-least-connections-member.oneLiner: Your ratio weight combined with each member's active connection count.

ratio-least-connections-node.weighs: the node's ratio weight combined with its active connection count
ratio-least-connections-node.behavior: The node-scope twin: the ratio defined for the member's node, combined with the node's active connections (unset ratio counts as 1).
ratio-least-connections-node.chooseWhen: The Ratio Least Connections case when weighting belongs to the server as a whole.
ratio-least-connections-node.caveat0: The ratio consulted is the node's, so it must be set on the node object, not the pool member.
ratio-least-connections-node.oneLiner: The node's ratio weight combined with its active connection count.

ratio-member.weighs: a fixed ratio weight you define per pool member
ratio-member.behavior: Each member receives connections over time in proportion to the ratio weight you define for it within the pool.
ratio-member.chooseWhen: Known, stable capacity differences: say a 4-CPU box next to 2-CPU boxes. You state the proportion once and the split follows it.
ratio-member.caveat0: Static by design - it never notices a member struggling.
ratio-member.caveat1: K11870: the ratio method costs more CPU than Round Robin; the cheapest mode is still Round Robin.
ratio-member.oneLiner: A fixed ratio weight you define per pool member.

ratio-node.weighs: a fixed ratio weight you define per node, across all pools
ratio-node.behavior: Each machine receives connections in proportion to a ratio weight defined for it across all pools of which the server is a member.
ratio-node.chooseWhen: The Ratio case when the proportion belongs to the server everywhere, not to one pool's member entry.
ratio-node.caveat0: Set the weight on the node object; a member-level ratio is a different knob.
ratio-node.oneLiner: A fixed ratio weight you define per node, across all pools.

ratio-session.weighs: sessions over time, proportioned by a ratio weight per member
ratio-session.behavior: The number of sessions each machine receives over time is proportionate to a ratio weight you define per member - the session-counting sibling of Ratio.
ratio-session.chooseWhen: Session-oriented traffic where you want a stated proportion of sessions, not connections. K42275060 adds one sharp detail: pending sessions count as active sessions.
ratio-session.caveat0: Pending sessions count as active (K42275060), so bursts of half-open sessions shape the split.
ratio-session.oneLiner: Sessions over time, proportioned by a ratio weight per member.

round-robin.weighs: nothing - only whose turn it is
round-robin.behavior: Passes each new connection to the next server in line, eventually distributing connections evenly across the pool. It is the default mode.
round-robin.chooseWhen: The vendor's own advice twice over: it works well in most configurations, especially when the machines are roughly equal in processing speed and memory - and by default the BIG-IP will use it.
round-robin.caveat0: Even distribution of connections is not even distribution of load when requests differ wildly in cost.
round-robin.oneLiner: Nothing - only whose turn it is.

weighted-least-connections-member.weighs: each member's connection count as a percentage of its connection-limit
weighted-least-connections-member.behavior: Passes a new connection to the member handling the lowest percentage of its specified maximum concurrent connections - the connection-limit acts as the capacity statement.
weighted-least-connections-member.chooseWhen: Different but quantified capability limits, in the reference's words: you know each box's ceiling and want load spread as a fraction of it.
weighted-least-connections-member.caveat0: The reference is explicit: this mode requires a connection-limit value on all members of the pool. A member left at the default 0 breaks the arithmetic.
weighted-least-connections-member.oneLiner: Each member's connection count as a percentage of its connection-limit.

weighted-least-connections-node.weighs: each node's connection count as a percentage of the node's connection-limit
weighted-least-connections-node.behavior: The node-scope twin: the lowest percentage of the node's specified connection limit wins the next connection.
weighted-least-connections-node.chooseWhen: The quantified-capacity case when the ceiling belongs to the server across all pools.
weighted-least-connections-node.caveat0: Requires a non-zero connection-limit on all nodes used by the pool's members (K42275060 / the tmsh reference) - and node limits live on the node objects, which a pool paste does not show.
weighted-least-connections-node.oneLiner: Each node's connection count as a percentage of the node's connection-limit.

unknown.behavior: This token does not appear in the tmsh ltm pool reference's load-balancing-mode list.
unknown.chooseWhen: Use one of the 19 documented tokens; type "methods" for the catalogue.

setting.notDocumented: not a documented mode token; see the method list
setting.absent: defaults to round-robin per the tmsh reference
setting.slowRamp: seconds a just-up member takes to reach a full share of new traffic
setting.minActive: members that must be up to confine traffic to a priority group
setting.ipw: whether persistence-selected connections are discounted from the algorithm's accounting

obs.unknownMode: "{mode}" is not a load-balancing-mode the tmsh reference documents. The 19 documented tokens are listed in the method catalogue (type "methods").
obs.defaultMode: No load-balancing-mode is set, so this pool runs Round Robin - the documented default.
obs.pluralQuirk: The token is spelled with the plural, exactly as the tmsh reference's SYNTAX block spells it - the same page's OPTIONS text uses the singular. Both mean Least Connections (member).
obs.ratiosIgnored: Member ratio weights are set ({list}) but {method} does not use them: per K6406, members configured with a ratio must reference a ratio load-balancing method for the ratios to apply.
obs.wlcNoLimitOne: Weighted Least Connections (member) requires a connection-limit on all members of the pool, but {names} has none (the default 0). The percentage-of-limit arithmetic has nothing to divide by.
obs.wlcNoLimitMany: Weighted Least Connections (member) requires a connection-limit on all members of the pool, but {names} have none (the default 0). The percentage-of-limit arithmetic has nothing to divide by.
obs.wlcNode: Weighted Least Connections (node) requires a non-zero connection-limit on all nodes used by the pool's members. Node limits live on the ltm node objects, which this pool stanza does not show - verify them there.
obs.leastSessions: Least Sessions only works when the virtual server references a persistence profile of a type that tracks persistence connections (K42275060). The pool alone cannot satisfy that - check the virtual.
obs.slowRampDefault: slow-ramp-time is not set, so the default of 10 seconds applies. The tmsh reference calls slow ramp particularly useful with least-connections: a member that just came up has zero connections and would otherwise take a flood.
obs.slowRampZero: slow-ramp-time is 0: a member that just came up starts with zero connections and Least Connections will send it a burst of new traffic immediately. The reference singles out this pairing as the one slow ramp helps most.
obs.ipwYes: ignore-persisted-weight yes: connections that arrive via persistence are not counted as picks, so they stop influencing this mode's accounting - useful when persistence concentrates returning clients and the ratios start chasing that concentration.
obs.ipwOutOfScope: ignore-persisted-weight is set, but the reference scopes its effect to the observed, predictive, ratio, and ratio-least-connections modes - it does not change {method}.
obs.priorityGroups: Priority groups are in use ({groups}) with min-active-members {min}: traffic stays confined to the highest-priority group while at least {min} of its members are active - an active member being up and below its connection limit. {method} then balances within the group that is receiving traffic.
obs.priorityNoMin: Members carry priority-group values, but min-active-members is 0 (or unset), so no priority-based activation threshold is in force - the reference ties confinement to a priority group to that minimum.

err.empty: Paste an ltm pool stanza, a method name (for example "least-connections-member"), the word "methods" for the full list, or "choose capacity=... react=..." for a recommendation.
err.unknownMethod: "{text}" is not a documented load-balancing mode. Type "methods" to list the 19 tokens the tmsh reference documents.
err.noPoolsParser: No ltm pool stanzas found (parser: {parser}). Paste the pool (tmsh list ltm pool '<'name>), a method name, or type "methods" for the catalogue.
err.noPools: No ltm pool stanzas found. Paste the pool (tmsh list ltm pool '<'name>), a method name, or type "methods" for the catalogue.

note.catalog: 19 modes, in the tmsh reference's order. Static modes ignore live server state; dynamic modes react to it.

parser.unbalanced: The configuration has an unbalanced brace.
parser.tooDeep: The configuration nests deeper than the parser allows.

why.measured: You asked for capacity that is measured rather than declared: that is Dynamic Ratio by definition - weights from continuous monitoring of the servers, continually changing.
why.ratioSession: Session-counted balance with a declared proportion is exactly Ratio (session): sessions over time, proportioned by the ratio you set - remembering that pending sessions count as active.
why.leastSessions: Balancing by session count is Least Sessions: the member with the fewest persistence-table entries takes the next connection.
why.response: Reacting to response speed is Fastest: the fastest-responding active node takes the connection - the vendor suggests it especially where nodes sit on different logical networks.
why.trend: Reacting to the trend - preferring members that are improving over those declining - is Predictive, built on the Observed ranking. The vendor's own words: works well in any environment.
why.wlc: Live connection counts scaled by declared ceilings is Weighted Least Connections: the member at the lowest percentage of its connection-limit wins.
why.rlc: Live connection counts combined with a declared proportion is Ratio Least Connections: the ratio weight and the active-connection count decide together (LTM 11.0.0 and later).
why.lc: Equal servers reacting to live load is Least Connections: the member with the fewest open connections at that moment takes the next one - the vendor's stated best fit for similar-capability servers.
why.ratio: Declared capacity with no live reaction is Ratio: each member receives connections in proportion to the weight you set, and nothing else moves it.
why.connlimitStatic: Connection limits only shape load balancing through Weighted Least Connections, which reacts live. If you truly want no live reaction, state the same proportions as Ratio weights instead.
why.roundRobin: Roughly equal machines and no need to react is the textbook Round Robin case - the vendor's default, recommended when the equipment is roughly equal in processing speed and memory.

prereq.measured: Server-side performance monitoring must exist for the system to have something to measure (see K14129 for viewing the computed weight).
prereq.sessions: The virtual server must reference a persistence profile of a type that tracks persistence connections (K42275060) - otherwise there are no sessions to count.
prereq.response: The count behind it is outstanding Layer 7 requests (K6406), so the virtual must process traffic at Layer 7.
prereq.wlc: Every member of the pool needs a non-zero connection-limit - the reference states the requirement outright.
prereq.lc: Pair it with slow-ramp-time so a freshly recovered member is not flooded; the reference calls the pairing particularly useful (default 10 seconds).

alt.measuredNode: when the same servers sit in several pools and should be weighted by their total load
alt.sessionsRatio: when members should carry stated proportions of the sessions
alt.responseNode: when the same servers appear in several pools and speed should be judged across them
alt.trendObserved: when the per-second smoothed ratio is enough and the trend preference is not wanted
alt.trendNode: when the trend should follow servers across every pool they belong to
alt.wlcNode: when the ceiling belongs to the server across all pools (limits set on the node objects)
alt.rlcNode: when the ratio belongs to the node rather than the pool member
alt.lcNode: when the same servers serve several pools and the fair count is their total
alt.lcObserved: when instantaneous counts feel too twitchy and a per-second smoothed ratio fits better
alt.ratioNode: when the proportion belongs to the server across all pools
alt.ratioDynamic: if you later want those weights measured instead of maintained by hand
alt.connlimitWlc: if reacting to live counts scaled by those limits is actually acceptable
alt.rrLc: if uneven connection durations start skewing the even split

f5-oneconnect-source-mask.name: OneConnect source-mask explainer
f5-oneconnect-source-mask.blurb: Paste a one-connect profile for the full option audit with the man page's own semantics and defaults, or simulate a mask against real client IPs and watch the reuse groups form. The marquee demonstration: SNAT translates first, so a single SNAT address collapses every client into one reuse group no matter how narrow the mask.
f5-oneconnect-source-mask.inputLabel: A one-connect profile, a mask simulation, or "settings"
f5-oneconnect-source-mask.runsLocally: Runs locally in your browser. Nothing you paste leaves this page.

share.carries: The link carries the text in the box as typed, and nothing else.

sourceMask.all: The manual's own words: a mask of 0.0.0.0 causes the system to share reused connections across all clients. Maximum reuse, zero client separation on the server side.
sourceMask.host: A host mask (all 1s in binary): the system shares only those reused connections originating from the same client IP address. Per-client reuse pools.
sourceMask.other: The system applies this mask to the source address to determine reuse eligibility: clients whose addresses share the same masked value ({mask}) form one reuse group, exactly like a subnet mask groups hosts.

explain.maxAge: Maximum age, in seconds, of a connection in the reuse pool; older connections are removed from the pool. {value, plural, one {{value} second} other {{value} seconds}}.
explain.maxAgeDefault: Maximum age, in seconds, of a connection in the reuse pool; older connections are removed from the pool. {value} seconds (the default: one day).
explain.maxReuse: Maximum number of times a server connection can be reused before it is retired. {value} reuses.
explain.maxSize: Maximum number of connections held in the reuse pool; when full, a finishing server connection simply closes instead of parking. {value, plural, one {{value} connection} other {{value} connections}}. Note the pool lives per TMM: F5's own lab article shows the configured value dividing across TMM instances, so on a multi-core box each TMM keeps its share.

limit.strict: The manual's warning, condensed: the TCP connection limit is honoured with no exceptions, so idle connections prevent NEW connections until they expire, even when they could have been reused. The page itself says this is not a recommended configuration except in very special cases with short expiration timeouts.
limit.idle: Idle connections are dropped as the TCP connection limit is reached; during the drop-and-establish overlap the limit may be briefly exceeded, per the manual.
limit.none: The historical handling: simultaneous in-flight requests and responses count towards the connection limit, and there may be more TCP connections open than in-flight requests, particularly (the manual notes) with SNAT pools and narrow source masks.

idle.disabled: Disabled (the default): idle flows follow the protocol profile's timeout.
idle.value: Overrides how long a connection may sit idle before its flow is eligible for deletion ({value}). Man-page quirk, flagged honestly: the SYNTAX block declares disabled|enabled while the description speaks of a number of seconds; real configurations carry an integer here.

share.enabled: Enabled: the manual's semantics verbatim in spirit, connections may be shared not only within a virtual server but among similar virtual servers (those differing only in destination address) that use the same OneConnect and internal network profiles.
share.disabled: Disabled (the default): reuse stays within the virtual server.

explain.defaultsFrom: Parent profile: inherits every unset value from {parent}.
explain.appService: Owned by application service {service}; strict-updates on the service would lock this profile.

obs.snatOrder: The ordering both K7208 and K5911 state: the system performs SNAT translation on the source address FIRST, then applies the OneConnect source mask to the TRANSLATED address to determine reuse eligibility. The mask never sees the client's real IP when SNAT is in play.
obs.maskUnset: source-mask is unset, so the default 0.0.0.0 applies: reused connections are shared across ALL clients (the manual's own description of that value). If the application derives anything from the server-side connection's identity, requests from different clients will arrive over the same connection; the HTTP profile's X-Forwarded-For insertion is the standard companion.
obs.snatImplication: Reasoned implication of that ordering (not a quote): with a single SNAT address on the virtual, every client translates to the same source, so ANY mask, however narrow, yields exactly one reuse group. A narrow mask only separates clients when the translated addresses differ (SNAT pool, or no SNAT).
obs.strict: limit-type strict carries the manual's own warning: idle connections will prevent new TCP connections until they expire, even if they could otherwise be reused; not recommended except in very special cases with short expiration timeouts.
obs.limitNone: limit-type none (the historical handling) counts in-flight requests towards pool-member connection limits, and the manual notes more TCP connections may be open than in-flight requests, particularly with SNAT pools and narrow source masks.
obs.sharePools: share-pools enabled widens reuse beyond one virtual server: similar virtuals (differing only in destination address) that share this OneConnect and the same internal network profiles can hand connections to each other, per the manual.
obs.stats: Statistics honesty, from F5's own lab article: the Current Idle counter includes every idle server-side connection whether or not it is eligible for reuse under this mask, and max-size divides across TMM instances rather than being one global pool. Read `tmsh show ltm profile one-connect` with both in mind.
obs.nonContiguous: Non-contiguous mask: the bitwise AND still applies, but this is a highly unusual configuration worth double-checking.
obs.singleSnat: With the single SNAT address {snat}, every listed client translates to that one source before the mask is applied: the simulation below therefore shows ONE group regardless of the mask. That is the K7208/K5911 ordering doing exactly what it says.
obs.oneGroup: All listed clients fall in the same reuse group: any of them may be handed an idle connection previously used by another.
obs.groups: {count} reuse groups: connections park and are reclaimed only within a group.

note.settings: Defaults and semantics from the tmsh reference v17.
note.uncurated: "{key}" is outside this tool's curated option table; the man page is the reference.

err.empty: Paste an `ltm profile one-connect` stanza, a mask simulation ("mask 255.255.255.0 ips 10.1.1.5 10.1.1.99 10.1.2.7 [snat 192.0.2.10]"), or the word "settings".
err.notMask: "{mask}" is not a mask. Use dotted (255.255.255.0) or prefix (/24) form.
err.snatNotIp: snat "{snat}" is not an IPv4 address.
err.noStanza: No `ltm profile one-connect NAME '{' ... '}'` stanza found, and the input is not a mask or "settings".

f5-packet-filter-explainer.name: BIG-IP packet-filter explainer
f5-packet-filter-explainer.blurb: Paste net packet-filter rules for the ordered first-match walk with the man page's own semantics, shadow detection, and the platform context every filter decision sits inside. Add a sim: line and an honest three-state simulator answers which rule matches your packet.
f5-packet-filter-explainer.inputLabel: net packet-filter stanzas, optional sim: line
f5-packet-filter-explainer.inputPlaceholder:
net packet-filter spoof_blocker {
    order 5
    action discard
    vlan external
    rule "(src net 172.19.255.0/24)"
}
sim: tcp src 172.19.255.7 dst 172.19.254.80 dport 443 vlan external
f5-packet-filter-explainer.runsLocally: Runs locally in your browser. Nothing you paste leaves this page.
f5-packet-filter-explainer.postureNote: Explains and simulates your own filter walk; the configuration is parsed, never executed.
f5-packet-filter-explainer.walkTitle: Evaluation order (single global list, lowest order first)

share.carries: The link carries the packet filters and the sim: line as pasted.
share.caution: Filter rules show which networks and hosts get through: check them before you send the link.

err.empty: Paste net packet-filter stanzas (tmsh list net packet-filter output). Add a line "sim: tcp src 10.0.0.5 dst 172.19.254.80 dport 443 vlan external" to simulate a packet through the walk.

issue.badAction: action "{action}" is not one of accept | continue | discard | reject.
issue.noOrder: order is missing; the man page marks it required, greater than 0, and unique across the single global list.
issue.noAction: action is missing; the man page gives it no default, you must specify one.
issue.noRule: rule expression attribute is missing; it is mandatory (though it may be empty).
issue.duplicateOrder: order {order} duplicates rule "{prior}"; the man page requires orders to be unique across the single global list.
issue.unreachableVlan: Unreachable: rule "{name}" (order {order}) earlier in the walk matches ALL packets on vlan {vlan} with terminal action {action}.
issue.unreachableAll: Unreachable: rule "{name}" (order {order}) earlier in the walk matches ALL packets on all VLANs with terminal action {action}.

note.emptyRule: Empty expression: per the man page, an empty rule matches ALL packets. Combined with a terminal action, everything after this rule (within its VLAN scope) is unreachable.
note.allVlans: No vlan attribute: the rule applies to all VLANs.

context.masterSwitch: Master switch: packet filtering is DISABLED by default; with the global Packet Filtering setting off, no packet filter settings or rules operate and the BIG-IP system allows all traffic by default.
context.trusted: Trusted exemptions (net packet-filter-trusted) process BEFORE rule list evaluation; per the reference it is impossible to override this option and mask out traffic with a packet filter rule.
context.exemptions: Default protocol exemptions: ARP is always accepted, and so are the important IPv4 ICMP types UNREACH, SOURCEQUENCH, REDIRECT, and TIMEXCEED, unless those global settings were cleared.
context.established: Established connections are NOT filtered by default; the Filter Established Connections option is off, so rules see connection-initiating traffic. F5 notes enabling it does not typically enhance security and can impact performance.
context.unhandled: Packets matching no rule take the global Unhandled Packet Action, default Accept, and F5 warns about changing it before your accept rules are complete.
context.management: The management interface is not affected by any packet filter configuration, per the man page's own management-access example.
context.incoming: Packet filters apply to incoming traffic only, and per the chapter they are unrelated to iRules; FLOW_INIT in the iRules event list fires after packet filters.

outcome.arp: ARP is exempt by default (Always accept ARP is enabled unless cleared): the packet is accepted before any rule runs.
outcome.stops: Simulation stops honestly at rule "{name}": its expression is outside the evaluated BPF subset, so every verdict after it would be a guess. Everything above this rule is deterministic.
outcome.accept: Rule "{name}" (order {order}) matches first with terminal action accept: the packet is accepted and evaluation stops.
outcome.discard: Rule "{name}" (order {order}) matches first with terminal action discard: the packet is dropped silently and evaluation stops.
outcome.reject: Rule "{name}" (order {order}) matches first with terminal action reject: the packet is dropped and a reject is sent (ICMP type 3 code 13 if Send ICMP Error on Packet Reject is enabled, protocol-dependent otherwise).
outcome.unhandled: No terminal rule matched: the packet takes the global Unhandled Packet Action, default Accept.

step.vlanSkip: rule scoped to vlan {vlan}, packet on {packetVlan}.
step.outsideSubset: expression uses primitives outside this simulator's evaluated subset; consult the rule on-box.
step.noMatch: expression evaluates false for this packet.

f5-persistence-method-explainer.name: Persistence-method explainer
f5-persistence-method-explainer.blurb: Paste BIG-IP persistence profiles and virtual servers and get the method behind each, its failure modes, and the primary-to-fallback chain, all in your browser.
f5-persistence-method-explainer.inputPlaceholder: Paste ltm persistence profiles and ltm virtual servers with their persist and fallback-persistence settings.
f5-persistence-method-explainer.runsLocally: Parsed in your browser. Nothing is uploaded.
f5-persistence-method-explainer.emptyState: No persistence profiles or virtual-server persistence found. Paste a persistence profile or a virtual with a persist setting.

share.carries: The link carries the profiles and virtual servers with any cookie encryption pass phrase, or other secret value, replaced by {mark}.
share.redacted: {n, plural, =0 {Nothing in it needed replacing, so the link carries it as pasted.} one {One value is replaced.} other {# values are replaced.}}
share.irules: {n, plural, one {The iRule goes as pasted: check it for hard-coded tokens or passwords.} other {The # iRules go as pasted: check them for hard-coded tokens or passwords.}}

cookie.label: Cookie persistence
cookie.keysOn: an HTTP cookie that encodes the chosen pool member
cookie.howItWorks: BIG-IP ties the client to a pool member through an HTTP cookie. In Insert mode it adds the cookie to the response and reads it back on later requests, so no server-side persistence record is needed. In Rewrite mode the server emits a placeholder cookie that BIG-IP overwrites. In Passive mode the server itself sets the specially formatted cookie and BIG-IP only reads it. In Hash mode BIG-IP load-balances on a hash of a server-set cookie.
cookie.goodFor: HTTP, or HTTPS that BIG-IP decrypts, where unique per-client identification is wanted without per-client state on the device.
cookie.caveat0: Requires an HTTP profile on the virtual server; it cannot work on non-HTTP traffic or on HTTPS that is passed through undecrypted.
cookie.caveat1: It depends on the client accepting and returning cookies; a client that strips cookies will not persist, which is the classic reason to pair it with a source-address fallback.
cookie.caveat2: Insert mode stores the mapping in the client cookie, so it leaves no entry in the persistence table; do not expect to see it with show persistence records.

field.cookie-name: The cookie name BIG-IP inserts or reads. A default insert-mode name looks like BIGipServer'<'pool>.
field.method: The cookie mode: insert, rewrite, passive, or hash.
field.cookie-encryption: Whether the cookie value is encrypted (required, preferred, or disabled). Encryption hides the encoded backend address.
field.always-send: Whether the cookie is re-sent on every response rather than only the first.
field.expiration: The cookie lifetime; a session cookie lives only for the browser session.
field.match-across-services: For cookie profiles this applies to the Cookie Hash method only.

source-addr.label: Source address affinity persistence
source-addr.keysOn: the client source IP address (with a configurable mask)
source-addr.howItWorks: BIG-IP records which pool member served a given client source address and sends later connections from that address to the same member. With the default mask of 255.255.255.255 each address gets its own record; a coarser mask groups a subnet into one record.
source-addr.goodFor: Any protocol, including non-HTTP, when clients have stable, distinct source addresses.
source-addr.caveat0: It breaks when many users share one address, as behind NAT, a proxy, or a VPN gateway: they all map to the same member and load distribution collapses.
source-addr.caveat1: A mask of 255.255.255.255 creates one record per client address, which can grow the persistence table; a coarser mask trades precision for fewer records.
source-addr.caveat2: A client whose source address changes mid-session loses persistence.

field.match-across-services: Share the record across virtuals that use the same virtual address.
field.match-across-virtuals: Share the record across virtuals with different virtual addresses.
field.match-across-pools: Allow a record to direct traffic to any pool that holds it (can override the virtual's pool).
field.timeout: Seconds a record is kept after its last use.
field.hash-algorithm: How the source address is hashed when selecting a member.
field.mask: The netmask applied to the source address; coarser masks group clients into shared records.

dest-addr.label: Destination address affinity persistence
dest-addr.keysOn: the destination IP address of the packet
dest-addr.howItWorks: Also called sticky persistence, this sends all requests for a given destination address to the same pool member, regardless of which client sent them. It supports both TCP and UDP.
dest-addr.goodFor: Load balancing caching or proxy servers, where sending the same destination to the same cache maximizes hit rate.
dest-addr.caveat0: It persists by destination, not client, so it does not pin an individual user; it pins a target.
dest-addr.caveat1: As with source affinity, the mask decides how finely destinations are grouped into records.

field.timeout: Seconds a record is kept after its last use.
field.mask: The netmask applied to the destination address.
field.match-across-services: Share the record across virtuals using the same virtual address.

ssl.label: SSL persistence
ssl.keysOn: the SSL/TLS session ID exchanged in the handshake
ssl.howItWorks: BIG-IP observes the SSL session ID, which is sent in cleartext during the handshake, and maps it to the chosen pool member. When the client reconnects presenting the same session ID, BIG-IP returns it to the same member, even if the client's IP address has changed.
ssl.goodFor: HTTPS that is not decrypted on BIG-IP, and other SSL-based services (FTPS, LDAPS, SMTPS, IMAPS), especially when clients have translated or changing IP addresses.
ssl.caveat0: It works only with TLS 1.2 and earlier; TLS 1.3 made the session ID obsolete, so it cannot be relied on there.
ssl.caveat1: Even on TLS 1.2, modern clients may use other resumption mechanisms or not reuse the session ID consistently, which weakens it.
ssl.caveat2: A common design is SSL persistence as the primary with source-address affinity as the fallback for when no valid session ID is presented.

field.timeout: Seconds a record is kept after its last use.
field.match-across-services: Share the record across virtuals using the same virtual address; member addresses must match across those virtuals.
field.match-across-virtuals: Share the record across virtuals with different virtual addresses.

universal.label: Universal persistence
universal.keysOn: any value extracted from the traffic by an iRule expression
universal.howItWorks: Universal persistence lets you persist on any sequence of bytes from a request or response, defined with an iRule (UIE) expression, such as a JSESSIONID, a custom header, or a field in the payload. The extracted value itself becomes the persistence key.
universal.goodFor: Stateful applications whose session identifier is not a cookie or an address, where you need full control over what to key on.
universal.caveat0: It requires an iRule (or a rule reference on the profile) to define the value; without one it has nothing to persist on.
universal.caveat1: BIG-IP must be able to see the value, so for encrypted traffic it must terminate TLS first.

field.rule: The iRule whose persist uie expression supplies the value to key on.
field.timeout: Seconds a record is kept after its last use.
field.match-across-services: Share the record across virtuals using the same virtual address.
field.match-across-virtuals: Share the record across virtuals with different virtual addresses.

hash.label: Hash persistence
hash.keysOn: a hash of a chosen value, rather than the value itself
hash.howItWorks: Hash persistence works like universal persistence, except the persistence key is a hash of the data instead of the raw data. The hash can be built from values such as source IP, destination IP, and destination port, which spreads persistence more evenly across members.
hash.goodFor: Even distribution when keying on a value that would otherwise cluster, while still pinning each client consistently.
hash.caveat0: A hash is not guaranteed unique per session, so two distinct values can collide onto the same member.
hash.caveat1: Like universal, custom hashing usually relies on an iRule to define the input.

field.rule: The iRule that supplies the value to be hashed.
field.hash-algorithm: The algorithm used to hash the selected value.
field.timeout: Seconds a record is kept after its last use.

msrdp.label: Microsoft RDP persistence
msrdp.keysOn: the Microsoft Remote Desktop Protocol session token
msrdp.howItWorks: BIG-IP tracks RDP sessions between client and server so a reconnecting client returns to the same session host.
msrdp.goodFor: Load balancing Remote Desktop session hosts.
msrdp.caveat0: It is specific to RDP and relies on the routing token; it has no meaning for other protocols.

field.timeout: Seconds a record is kept after its last use.
field.has-session-dir: Whether a Session Directory or Broker is in use, which changes how the token is read.

sip.label: SIP persistence
sip.keysOn: a SIP header, by default the Call-ID
sip.howItWorks: BIG-IP persists SIP traffic by a SIP header value so all messages in a call reach the same server.
sip.goodFor: Load balancing SIP servers that process call signalling.
sip.caveat0: It applies to SIP signalling only and depends on a SIP profile being present.

field.sip-info: The SIP header used as the persistence key (Call-ID by default).
field.timeout: Seconds a record is kept after its last use.

howItWorks.unknown: This persistence type is not in the explainer's knowledge base yet, but its fields are shown below.

chain.both: Primary persistence is {primary}; when it yields no record, BIG-IP falls back to {fallback}.
chain.same: The primary and fallback resolve to the same method, which defeats the purpose of a fallback; they should differ.
chain.sslSource: This is the recommended pairing for SSL persistence: source-address affinity catches clients that present no reusable session ID.
chain.cookieSource: This is a common pairing: source-address affinity catches clients that refuse cookies.
chain.primaryOnly: Primary persistence is {primary} with no fallback configured; clients the primary cannot match are load-balanced normally.
chain.fallbackOnly: A fallback persistence is set but no primary persistence is configured on this virtual.

parser.unbalanced: The configuration has an unbalanced brace.
parser.tooDeep: The configuration nests deeper than the parser allows.

f5-service-check-date.name: F5 service check date
f5-service-check-date.blurb: Enter a BIG-IP version to get the minimum service check date its licence must carry, or enter a service check date to see the newest version you can upgrade to. Based on F5's published License Check Date table (K7727); runs entirely in your browser.
f5-service-check-date.runsLocally: This runs locally against a bundled copy of F5's License Check Date table (K7727). Nothing is sent anywhere.
f5-service-check-date.verifyNote: For production upgrade planning, always confirm against F5 K7727 or the target system's /etc/version_date file.

errors.empty: Enter a BIG-IP version or a service check date.
errors.format: That is not a BIG-IP version or a service check date. Enter a version like 17.1.3 or a date like 20230611.
errors.unknownVersion: That version is not in F5's License Check Date table.
errors.licenseNoDate: Found a Service check date label in the pasted text, but no date next to it. Check the paste or enter the date directly.

version.heading: Minimum service check date
version.forVersion: To upgrade to {label}, the licence's service check date must be:
version.majorMinorNote: The check applies to the major.minor branch, so every maintenance and point release within {label} shares this date.
version.consequence: If the service check date is earlier than this, the system still boots after the upgrade but does not load its configuration until you reactivate the licence.

date.heading: Upgrade eligibility
date.newestReachable: Newest version you can upgrade to
date.withinNote: Any maintenance or point release within {label} is included.
date.none: No version in the table is reachable with this service check date. Reactivate the licence to obtain a newer service check date.
date.allReachable: This service check date reaches the newest version in the table; nothing is blocked.
date.blockedHeading: Newer branches you cannot reach yet
date.blockedHint: Each needs the licence's service check date to be on or after the date shown. Reactivate the licence first.
date.needsDate: needs a service check date of {date} or later

f5-service-check-date.pasteHint: You can also paste your /config/bigip.license contents or the tmsh show sys license output; the service check date is picked out automatically.

share.carries: {licence, select, yes {The link carries only the service check date line read from your licence, never the licence itself.} other {The link carries the version or the date as typed, and nothing else.}}

f5-service-check-date.pickDateLabel: Or pick a service check date
f5-service-check-date.pickVersionLabel: Or pick a version from K7727

f5-ssl-profile-explainer.name: F5 SSL profile explainer
f5-ssl-profile-explainer.blurb: Paste a tmsh client-ssl or server-ssl profile and get its role, the TLS protocol matrix, and a security read covering chain, renegotiation, SNI, OCSP (Online Certificate Status Protocol), and mutual TLS - all in your browser.
f5-ssl-profile-explainer.runsLocally: Parsed in your browser. Nothing is sent anywhere.
f5-ssl-profile-explainer.scopeNote: Decodes a pasted profile block. It never contacts a BIG-IP.
f5-ssl-profile-explainer.err_empty: Paste an SSL profile to begin.
f5-ssl-profile-explainer.err_noHeader: Expected a line like: ltm profile client-ssl /Common/name ...
f5-ssl-profile-explainer.err_noBody: No opening brace was found in the profile.
f5-ssl-profile-explainer.err_tooLong: That input is too large to parse.
f5-ssl-profile-explainer.err_invalid: That does not look like a client-ssl or server-ssl profile.
f5-ssl-profile-explainer.clientNote: A client-ssl profile terminates the client's TLS at the BIG-IP. The connection on to the pool member is re-encrypted only if a server-ssl profile is applied; with none, that leg is cleartext (SSL offload).
f5-ssl-profile-explainer.serverNote: A server-ssl profile lets the BIG-IP open a fresh TLS connection to the pool member (re-encryption). The client side is handled by a separate client-ssl profile.

share.carries: The link carries the profile with every passphrase value replaced by {redacted}; names and hosts stay.
share.redacted: {n, plural, =0 {It holds no passphrase value.} one {One passphrase value is replaced.} other {# passphrase values are replaced.}}

field.alpn: ALPN negotiation is configured - required for the virtual server to negotiate HTTP/2 over TLS.
field.caFileClient: The trusted-CA bundle used to validate CLIENT certificates for mutual TLS.
field.caFileServer: The trusted-CA bundle used to validate the BACKEND server certificate.
field.certKeyChain: Modern identity binding. Each entry pairs a server certificate with its private key and an intermediate chain bundle. Multiple entries let one profile serve, for example, both an RSA and an ECDSA certificate, picked per client capability.
field.cipherGroup: A cipher GROUP is in use: the negotiated suites come from the named group's allow/restrict cipher rules, not the legacy ciphers string. The ciphers string is ignored when a group is set.
field.ciphers: The legacy cipher STRING. Expand it with the F5 cipher-string expander to see the exact ordered suite list it resolves to. DEFAULT tracks F5's recommended modern set for the TMOS version.
field.legacy: Legacy single cert/key/chain binding (pre cert-key-chain). It works, but cert-key-chain is preferred and is required to serve multiple certificate types from one profile.
field.ocspOff: OCSP stapling is off; clients that check revocation must reach the CA's OCSP responder on their own.
field.ocspOn: The BIG-IP staples a fresh OCSP response into the handshake (RFC 6066/6961), so clients need not contact the CA themselves - faster and more private. Requires an OCSP Stapling profile.
field.options: Protocol and behaviour flags. Each no-'<'version> flag DISABLES that version; a version is enabled when its flag is absent. dont-insert-empty-fragments turns off the empty-fragment countermeasure, a zero-length record before each CBC record (a legacy BEAST workaround).
field.peerIgnore: No peer certificate is requested (the default). No mutual TLS.
field.peerRequest: The peer certificate is REQUESTED but optional - the handshake still completes if none is presented. Often paired with an iRule or APM that inspects the result.
field.peerRequireClient: Mutual TLS is ENFORCED: clients must present a valid certificate chaining to the trusted CA, or the handshake fails.
field.peerRequireServer: The backend server MUST present a valid certificate; the BIG-IP rejects the connection otherwise.
field.renegOff: Mid-connection renegotiation is OFF. This blocks client-initiated renegotiation, removing a class of DoS and the insecure-renegotiation risk. Common and safe for most virtual servers.
field.renegOn: Mid-connection renegotiation is ON. Combined with secure-renegotiation, this controls whether the peer must support RFC 5746.
field.secRenegRequest: request only: secure renegotiation is requested but not enforced. A peer that does not support RFC 5746 is still allowed to renegotiate, which is weaker.
field.secRenegRequire: The peer must support secure renegotiation (RFC 5746) to renegotiate, but the initial handshake is still allowed from peers without it. A reasonable default.
field.secRenegStrict: Strongest: the peer must support secure renegotiation (RFC 5746) even on the INITIAL handshake. Connections from peers without the extension are rejected.
field.serverName: The FQDN this profile serves. When several SSL profiles share a virtual server, the BIG-IP picks the profile whose server-name matches the client's SNI (RFC 6066).
field.sniDefault: This is the DEFAULT SSL profile: it answers when the client sends no SNI, or no other profile's server-name matches. Exactly one profile per virtual server should be the SNI default.
field.sniRequire: Clients that do not send an SNI extension are REJECTED. Strict, but it can break very old clients.
field.ticketOff: Session tickets are off; resumption relies on the server-side session cache instead.
field.ticketOn: Stateless session resumption via tickets (RFC 5077) is on - faster reconnects without server-side session cache.

backendNotValidated.detail: This server-ssl profile encrypts to the pool but does not validate the server's certificate (no peer-cert-mode require + ca-file). The backend leg is encrypted but not authenticated.
backendNotValidated.title: Backend server certificate is not validated

chainPresent.detail: An intermediate chain is attached, so the BIG-IP sends the certificates needed for clients to build a path to a trusted root.
chainPresent.title: Chain bundle present

customCiphers.detail: This is a hand-built cipher string. Expand it to confirm it excludes NULL, EXPORT, RC4, and other weak suites, and that ordering is sane.
customCiphers.title: Custom cipher string

noCert.detail: A client-ssl profile with no cert/key cannot present an identity to clients. Bind a certificate and key (via cert-key-chain).
noCert.title: No certificate configured

noChainCkc.detail: No chain bundle is set on any cert-key-chain entry. If your certificate is not signed directly by a root, clients that lack the intermediate will fail to build the path. Attach the intermediate CA bundle as the chain.
noChainCkc.title: No intermediate chain configured

noChainLegacy.detail: chain is none. If the certificate is not signed directly by a trusted root, attach the intermediate CA bundle as the chain, or clients missing it will fail validation.
noChainLegacy.title: No intermediate chain configured

noIssues.detail: Nothing in the recognized settings raised a security flag. Always confirm against your own policy.
noIssues.title: No issues flagged

noTls.detail: Every protocol is disabled by options; the profile cannot complete a handshake.
noTls.title: No TLS version is enabled

oldTls.detail: {proto} is permitted ({flag} is absent). It is deprecated (RFC 8996) and fails most compliance baselines - add {flag} unless a legacy client truly requires it.
oldTls.title: {proto} is not disabled

peerNoCa.detail: peer-cert-mode requests/requires a certificate, but no ca-file (trusted CA) is set. Validation cannot anchor to a trust source. Set the trusted CA bundle.
peerNoCa.title: Peer validation without a trusted-CA bundle

secRenegRequest.detail: Renegotiation is permitted even for peers without RFC 5746. Prefer require (or require-strict), or disable renegotiation entirely.
secRenegRequest.title: secure-renegotiation is request, not require

serverPref.detail: cipher-server-preference lets the BIG-IP choose the cipher from its own ordered list, not the client's.
serverPref.title: Server cipher preference is set

sslv3.detail: no-sslv3 is absent, so this profile permits SSLv3. SSLv3 is broken (POODLE, CVE-2014-3566) - add no-sslv3 to options. On current TMOS it may already be blocked at the system level, but make it explicit.

ltm_virtual.summary: A virtual server: the listening IP and port that clients connect to, and the front door that ties together a pool, profiles, persistence, and iRules.

field.destination: The IP address and port the virtual server listens on (the virtual address plus service).
field.mask: The netmask applied to the destination, defining whether this is a host or network virtual server.
field.pool: The default pool of backend members this virtual sends traffic to.
field.ip-protocol: The L4 protocol the virtual accepts (tcp, udp, or sctp).
field.profiles: The profiles attached to the virtual; these decide the L4/L7 behaviour (TCP, HTTP, SSL, OneConnect, and so on).
field.rules: The iRules attached to the virtual, run in order on connection events.
field.persist: The persistence profile that keeps a client pinned to the same pool member.
field.fallback-persistence: The persistence method used when the primary method has no match.
field.source-address-translation: How the source IP is translated towards the backend (automap, a SNAT pool, or none).
field.translate-address: Whether the destination address is translated to a pool member (enabled) or passed through.
field.translate-port: Whether the destination port is translated to the pool member's port.
field.source: The client source address range the virtual will accept (0.0.0.0/0 means any).
field.vlans: The VLANs the virtual listens on, when restricted.
field.vlans-enabled: Marks the listed VLANs as the only ones the virtual accepts traffic from.
field.vlans-disabled: Marks the listed VLANs as excluded; the virtual accepts all others.
field.connection-limit: The maximum concurrent connections; 0 means unlimited.
field.auth-pam-idle-timeout: Idle timeout for PAM authentication, when used.
field.description: A free-text description of the object.
field.security-log-profiles: The security logging profiles attached to this virtual.
field.fw-enforced-policy: An AFM firewall policy enforced on this virtual.

ltm_pool.summary: A pool: a group of backend members that the virtual server load-balances across, with a health monitor deciding which members are eligible.

field.members: The backend members (address and port) in the pool.
field.monitor: The health monitor (or monitor rule) that marks members up or down.
field.load-balancing-mode: The algorithm used to pick a member (round-robin, least-connections-member, ratio, and so on).
field.slow-ramp-time: Seconds over which a newly available member is eased back into rotation.
field.service-down-action: What to do with connections when the chosen member is down (none, reset, reselect, drop).
field.allow-nat: Whether NAT connections are allowed to pool members.
field.allow-snat: Whether SNAT connections are allowed to pool members.
field.reselect-tries: How many times to try another member when one fails.
field.min-active-members: The minimum number of up members before the pool itself is considered down.
field.description: A free-text description of the object.

ltm_node.summary: A node: a backend host by IP address, independent of port. Pool members reference nodes, and a node monitor can mark the whole host up or down.

field.address: The IP address of the backend host.
field.monitor: The health monitor applied at the node (host) level.
field.session: Administrative state controlling whether the node accepts new connections (user-enabled or user-disabled).
field.ratio: The ratio weight used by ratio load-balancing modes.
field.connection-limit: The maximum concurrent connections to this node; 0 means unlimited.
field.description: A free-text description of the object.

ltm_monitor.summary: A health monitor: the probe BIG-IP uses to decide whether a pool member or node is available.

field.send: The request string the monitor sends to the member.
field.recv: The response string the monitor expects to mark a member up.
field.recv-disable: A response string that marks a member as disabled rather than down.
field.timeout: Seconds without a successful probe before the member is marked down.
field.destination: The address and port probed; '*:*' means the member's own address and port.
field.time-until-up: Seconds a member must stay healthy before being marked up.
field.cipherlist: The cipher list used by an HTTPS monitor.
field.username: The username an authenticated monitor sends.

ltm_profile.summary: A profile: a reusable bundle of protocol or feature settings (TCP, HTTP, SSL, OneConnect, FastL4, and so on) that a virtual server attaches to shape traffic.

field.defaults-from: The parent profile this one inherits its unset settings from.
field.key: The private key paired with the certificate (SSL profiles).
field.cert-key-chain: The certificate, key, and chain bundle used by an SSL profile.
field.ciphers: The cipher string or group governing which TLS ciphers are offered or accepted.
field.cipher-group: A named cipher group governing TLS cipher selection.
field.options: Protocol options toggled on the profile (for SSL, things like no-tlsv1.1).
field.server-name: The SNI server name for a server-side SSL profile.
field.sni-default: Whether this SSL profile is the default when no SNI matches.
field.insert-xforwarded-for: Whether an HTTP profile inserts the X-Forwarded-For header.
field.idle-timeout: Seconds of inactivity before a TCP connection is closed.
field.source-mask: The mask applied when OneConnect reuses server-side connections.
field.redirect-rewrite: How an HTTP profile rewrites redirects (none, all, matching, nodes).

ltm_persistence.summary: A persistence profile: the method BIG-IP uses to keep a given client pinned to the same pool member across connections.

field.defaults-from: The parent persistence profile this one inherits from.
field.cookie-name: The cookie name used by cookie persistence.
field.cookie-encryption: Whether the persistence cookie is encrypted (required, preferred, or disabled).
field.expiration: How long a persistence record is kept.
field.match-across-services: Whether persistence is shared across virtuals on the same address.
field.match-across-virtuals: Whether persistence is shared across different virtual addresses.
field.hash-algorithm: The hashing algorithm for hash persistence.
field.timeout: Seconds a persistence record is kept after the last use.

ltm_rule.summary: An iRule: a Tcl program run on connection events (such as HTTP_REQUEST or CLIENT_ACCEPTED) to inspect and steer traffic. The body below is Tcl, not tmsh configuration, and is shown verbatim.

ltm_snatpool.summary: A SNAT pool: a set of translation addresses BIG-IP uses as the source when translating client connections towards the backend.

field.members: The translation IP addresses in the SNAT pool.

ltm_snat.summary: A SNAT: maps client source addresses to a translation address or SNAT pool for outbound or inbound flows.

field.origins: The client source addresses this SNAT applies to.
field.source-port: Whether the source port is preserved or changed.
field.translation: The translation address used as the new source.
field.snatpool: The SNAT pool providing translation addresses.

ltm_data-group.summary: A data group: a named list or map (of addresses, strings, or integers) that iRules and policies look up at runtime.

field.type: The data-group value type (string, ip, or integer).
field.records: The entries in the data group, optionally with associated data.

net_self.summary: A self IP: an address BIG-IP owns on a VLAN, used as the source for health checks and SNAT and as the gateway-facing interface for a subnet.

field.address: The self IP address and prefix length.
field.vlan: The VLAN this self IP lives on.
field.allow-service: Which services this self IP answers (default, all, none, or a specific list).
field.traffic-group: The traffic group that owns this self IP for HA failover (floating self IPs).

net_vlan.summary: A VLAN: a layer-2 broadcast domain on BIG-IP, carrying one or more tagged or untagged interfaces.

field.interfaces: The physical or trunk interfaces assigned to the VLAN, tagged or untagged.
field.mtu: The maximum transmission unit for the VLAN.

net_route.summary: A static route: a destination network and the gateway or interface BIG-IP uses to reach it.

field.network: The destination network and prefix (default means 0.0.0.0/0).
field.interface: The egress interface, when the route points at one instead of a gateway.

net_route-domain.summary: A route domain: an isolated routing table identified by an ID, letting overlapping address spaces coexist on one BIG-IP.

field.id: The numeric route-domain identifier (appended to addresses as %id).
field.vlans: The VLANs that belong to this route domain.
