warnings.title: Worth a look
warnings.allow-all-policy: This policy allows all requests. Every request that reaches it is permitted, with no further checks.
warnings.allow-all-rule: A rule allows every request (ALLOW with no conditions). It matches everything that reaches it, so any rule below it is never evaluated. This is the common catch-all pattern, but confirm it is intentional.
warnings.no-rules: The rule list is empty. With no rules to match, requests fall through and the default is to deny.
warnings.expired-rule: A rule has an expiration timestamp in the past. It still exists in the config but is no longer applied.
warnings.case-sensitive-exact: An exact-value matcher has no LOWER_CASE or UPPER_CASE transformer, so the comparison is case-sensitive. '/Admin' will not match '/admin'.
warnings.inverted-matcher: A matcher is inverted (invert_matcher). It matches when the condition is NOT met, which is easy to misread.

algorithm.title: How the rules are evaluated
algorithm.FIRST_MATCH: First match: rules are evaluated top to bottom until one matches. That rule's action is applied and evaluation stops.
algorithm.DENY_OVERRIDES: Deny overrides: all DENY rules are evaluated before any ALLOW rule, so a matching DENY wins over a matching ALLOW.
algorithm.ALLOW_OVERRIDES: Allow overrides: all ALLOW rules are evaluated before any DENY rule, so a matching ALLOW wins over a matching DENY.
algorithm.defaultDeny: If no rule matches, the request does not match this policy and the next policy in the set is evaluated. If nothing allows it, the request is denied.

rule.matchesEverything: No conditions: this rule matches every request that reaches it.

logic.andAll: All of the following must be true (AND):

sourceList.allow_list: A request is allowed if its source matches any of the following:

hash-preimage-finder.name: Hash Preimage Finder
hash-preimage-finder.blurb: Watch a bounded, local brute-force search recover a weak hash input in seconds, or run out of keyspace on anything with real entropy. No wordlist, no table, just your browser. A demonstration of why fast, unsalted hashes fail.
hash-preimage-finder.hashPlaceholder: Paste an MD5, SHA-1, or SHA-256 hash
hash-preimage-finder.detectHint: Paste a hex hash; the algorithm is detected from its length.
hash-preimage-finder.notDetected: Not a recognized hash. Expected 32 (MD5), 40 (SHA-1), or 64 (SHA-256) hex characters.
hash-preimage-finder.brokenNote: cryptographically broken; never use for new work
hash-preimage-finder.keyspaceBeyond: (search stops at {cap}; larger keyspaces are the point, they are infeasible)
hash-preimage-finder.foundIn: Recovered in {attempts, plural, one {{attempts} attempt} other {{attempts} attempts}}, {ms} ms. A secret this weak offers no protection once the hash leaks.
hash-preimage-finder.exhaustedSub: The entire keyspace was searched with no match. Widen the alphabet or length, or, more likely, the input has more entropy than a short brute force can reach.
hash-preimage-finder.budgetSub: The search hit its budget with far more keyspace remaining (this alphabet and length span {n} candidates). This is exactly why length and randomness defeat brute force: the work grows faster than any attacker can keep up with.

teach.head: This is why weak hashes fall, and how storage is actually protected
teach.intro: A fast hash of a low-entropy input is trivially reversible by enumeration, as you just saw. Real password storage defends against this in three layers.

salt.title: Salting defeats precomputed tables
salt.body: A unique random salt per password makes every stored hash different, even for identical passwords. That is what breaks lookup services like CrackStation: a precomputed table would need rebuilding for every salt, so it becomes useless.

kdf.title: Slow KDFs defeat brute force
kdf.body: bcrypt, scrypt, Argon2, and PBKDF2 are deliberately slow and tunable. Making each guess cost milliseconds instead of nanoseconds cuts an attacker's rate by six orders of magnitude or more, turning a seconds-long crack into millennia.

algo.title: Algorithm and length matter
algo.body: MD5 and SHA-1 are collision-broken and, like SHA-256, far too fast for storing secrets. Use a purpose-built password hash, and give secrets enough length and randomness that no keyspace search can reach them.

hash-preimage-finder.disclaimer: Everything runs locally in your browser. Nothing you paste is uploaded. This tool exists to demonstrate hash weakness and is bounded so it can only recover trivially weak inputs.

share.caution: Anyone who opens it can run the same search: send hashes of test values, never of a real password.

hmac.name: HMAC Generator (SHA-256/384/512)
hmac.blurb: Compute a keyed HMAC over a message with your secret key, shown as hex and Base64, via the browser's native Web Crypto. The same construction the JWT verifier uses for HS256. Your key never leaves your browser.

struct.heading: How HMAC is built
struct.note: HMAC hashes the message twice. The key is XORed with a fixed inner pad before the first hash and with an outer pad before the second, and this two-pad construction is what prevents length-extension attacks. The key is first reduced to the hash's block size.

note.gzip: iQuery is an XML protocol sent gzip-compressed over TCP 4353; iqdump shows it decompressed and in the clear so you can read the exchange.

big3d.body: big3d is the agent that answers iQuery. It runs on BIG-IP DNS and on the LTM (and pre-21.0 Link Controller) systems that DNS probes, listening on TCP 4353 on all self IPs and the management IP. It performs the monitor probes and returns availability and metric data to gtmd. Its version must be the same as, or newer than, the BIG-IP DNS software; big3d_install upgrades it on older peers so the whole mesh is compatible.
big3d.title: The big3d agent

gtmd.body: gtmd is the BIG-IP DNS process that drives GSLB. It opens the iQuery connections, monitors both the availability of BIG-IP systems and the integrity of the network paths between the systems hosting a domain and the LDNS servers that resolve it, and writes connection-status changes to /var/log/gtm. When a big3d connection is established or lost, gtmd logs it (and can raise an SNMP trap on a box state change).
gtmd.title: The gtmd agent

iqdump.body: iqdump lets you view the raw iQuery data between systems and check the path plus SSL authentication from a BIG-IP DNS to another mesh device. Syntax: iqdump '<'ip> '<'syncgroup> (the sync-group name is optional; use the -s switch to name a non-default group). It streams until you press Ctrl-C. The remote software version is reported in the version XML stanza. If the path or SSL auth is broken, iqdump fails and reports an error. The tmsh equivalent is `tmsh show /gtm iquery all`, and DNS > GSLB > Servers shows each server's iQuery status.
iqdump.title: The iqdump command

mesh.body: The set of long-lived iQuery connections among BIG-IP DNS devices and between BIG-IP DNS and BIG-IP LTM devices is called the iQuery mesh. All BIG-IP DNS devices are iQuery clients: each one's gtmd connects to the big3d on every BIG-IP server in the configuration. A device closer to a monitor target is elected to run the probe and shares the result across the mesh, so a unified view matters: if devices are not all connected to the same peers, monitor responsibility can disagree and objects can flap (marked down then up repeatedly).
mesh.title: The iQuery mesh

metrics.body: BIG-IP DNS uses iQuery to determine the availability status of objects (such as a virtual server on a remote BIG-IP) and to gather the load-balancing metrics that dynamic GSLB methods need. Because DNS must answer as clients see the network, iQuery probes have to follow the same network path as DNS clients; otherwise BIG-IP DNS can return an answer that is healthy on a private path but wrong for real clients. A common mismatch: a virtual server shows offline (red) on BIG-IP DNS but available (green) on the LTM because the virtual-server names on the two systems do not match.
metrics.title: What iQuery carries (availability + metrics)

overview.body: iQuery is F5's proprietary, XML-based protocol (sent gzip-compressed) that BIG-IP DNS (formerly GTM) uses to communicate with other BIG-IP systems. The gtmd agent on BIG-IP DNS connects to the big3d agent on itself and on every BIG-IP defined in its configuration, to learn object availability, gather load-balancing metrics, exchange sync-group state, and carry configuration synchronization. It is not a client protocol like DNS; it is the control-plane conversation between BIG-IP devices.
overview.title: What iQuery is

port.body: iQuery runs over TCP port 4353. big3d listens on 4353 on all self IPs and on the management IP. For the mesh to form, port 4353 must be open through any firewall between the BIG-IP DNS, LTM, and (pre-21.0) Link Controller devices in the sync group. The setup scripts that establish trust additionally need SSH (port 22) open to the target devices.
port.title: TCP port 4353

trust.body: iQuery communication is encrypted with SSL, and the devices authenticate each other with certificate-based authentication; they must exchange certificates and share a configuration sync group before they can share data. Trust is bootstrapped from the CLI with bigip_add (same-version BIG-IP peers), big3d_install (upgrades big3d on older peers), or gtm_add (joins an existing DNS sync group). Each exchanges SSL certificates over SSH. With a third-party CA, the mesh can also trust a shared root placed under /config/gtm/server.crt and /config/big3d/client.crt without running those scripts.
trust.title: SSL trust and the setup scripts

vlan.body: A BIG-IP system sends iQuery communications only on the VLAN on which it receives incoming iQuery messages. This is why the self IP addresses you assign to a server object matter: gtmd attempts an iQuery connection to every self IP listed for a BIG-IP-type server, and the path those addresses take determines which VLAN carries the traffic. Using a single, well-chosen self IP per server keeps the path predictable; extra IPs add paths and complexity.
vlan.title: iQuery and VLANs

xml.big3d: The big3d agent build string on the remote system. big3d must be the same version as, or newer than, the BIG-IP DNS software; big3d_install upgrades it on older peers.

xml.version: The BIG-IP software version reported by the remote system in the version XML stanza (here {value}). Use it to confirm the peer's version and that big3d is at least as new as this BIG-IP DNS.

reasons.MISSING_REQUIRED_CLAIM: Missing required claim {value}. An ID token must contain iss, sub, aud, exp, and iat.
reasons.ALG_NONE: The token uses alg none, meaning it is unsigned. An unsigned ID token proves nothing and must be rejected.
reasons.ALG_SYMMETRIC: Signed with {value}, a symmetric (HMAC) algorithm. ID tokens from a public provider normally use an asymmetric algorithm like RS256 or ES256 so the relying party can verify with the public key.
reasons.ALG_UNKNOWN: Signed with {value}, an algorithm this tool does not recognize. Confirm it is an expected, strong algorithm.
reasons.SIGNED_ASYMMETRIC: Signed with {value}, an asymmetric algorithm. The relying party verifies it against the provider's public key from the JWKS.
reasons.NO_NONCE: No nonce claim. The nonce binds the token to the authentication request and protects against replay. It should be present when the request sent one.
reasons.MULTI_AUD_NO_AZP: The token has multiple audiences but no azp (authorized party). With more than one audience, azp should name the client the token is for.
reasons.DISCOVERY_ALG_NONE: The provider advertises the none signing algorithm for ID tokens, which would allow unsigned tokens. This should not be offered.
reasons.DISCOVERY_NO_PKCE: No code_challenge_methods_supported. The provider does not advertise PKCE, which is recommended for the authorization code flow.
reasons.DISCOVERY_NO_PKCE_S256: PKCE is advertised but without the S256 method. S256 is the recommended code challenge method.

flow.heading: Authorization code flow
flow.s1: Redirect the user to the provider with scope=openid
flow.s2: Provider authenticates the user and gets consent
flow.s3: Provider redirects back with an authorization code
flow.s4: Relying Party exchanges the code at the token endpoint
flow.s5: Provider returns an ID token plus an access token
flow.s6: Relying Party validates the ID token signature against the JWKS
flow.s7: Relying Party may call UserInfo with the access token

regex.redosBody: This pattern nests an unbounded quantifier inside another (the (a+)+ shape), which can be slow or hang on some inputs. Run it against a short string first.
regex.noMatches: No matches in the test text.
regex.tooLong: The test text is too long to run; shorten it and try again.
regex.portIntro: This tester runs only ECMAScript, through your browser's JavaScript engine. The rows below are a static comparison: for each construct in your pattern whose support or meaning differs, they say how ECMAScript, PCRE2 and Tcl Advanced Regular Expressions (AREs) treat it. Same means supported with the meaning in the row's title.
regex.portNone: No construct from this view's list appears in the pattern. That is not proof that it ports: the note below says what the view does not check.
regex.portTooLong: The pattern is longer than {limit} characters, so the portability view does not read it.
regex.portWhereHeading: Where each flavour runs, as the vendors document it:
regex.portWhereEcmascript: ECMAScript: this tester, through your browser's JavaScript engine (ECMA-262 2026 with its browser annex). Engines adopt a new edition at their own pace, so the compile status above is what this browser accepts.
regex.portWherePcre2: PCRE2: NGINX regular-expression locations (~ and ~*), map and server_name. NGINX uses the PCRE2 library from 1.21.5 unless it is built with the original PCRE library, which this view does not compare.
regex.portWhereTcl: Tcl ARE: BIG-IP iRules regexp and regsub. F5 states that the iRules command set was developed from Tcl 8.4.6 (K6091), and neither command is on its list of disabled Tcl commands (K36322151).
regex.portWhereAsm: BIG-IP ASM attack and bot signatures: F5's signature syntax names three regular-expression options. pcre is based on PCRE syntax, but which PCRE library and version is not stated by F5; re2 uses the RE2 syntax F5 recommends, which this view does not compare; ipp, for bot signatures only, uses an Intel-based engine whose syntax is not stated by F5.
regex.portScope: Scope: a reading of the pattern's syntax against ECMA-262 2026, the PCRE2 manual and the Tcl 8.4 re_syntax manual (the Tcl 8.6 and 9.0 manuals change none of these rules except the \w note). It never runs the pattern in PCRE2 or Tcl, and it does not check engine limits (quantifier bounds, pattern size, the lookbehind limit beyond its default), performance or backtracking, options a product sets for you (NGINX's ~*, a signature's modifiers, PCRE2 UTF or UCP mode), or constructs outside its list, such as subroutines, conditionals, comments, \K, \G, \R, \X and hexadecimal or octal escapes.

lookbehindFixed.name: Lookbehind, fixed length
lookbehindFixed.es: Supported: an ECMAScript lookbehind takes any pattern, fixed or variable in length.
lookbehindFixed.pcre2: Supported: every top-level alternative matches a single length (alternatives may differ, up to 65,535 characters each).
lookbehindFixed.tcl: Not supported: Tcl AREs have lookahead only, (?= and (?!, and the Tcl 8.6 and 9.0 manuals add no lookbehind.

lookbehindBounded.name: Lookbehind, variable length with a maximum
lookbehindBounded.es: Supported: an ECMAScript lookbehind takes any pattern, fixed or variable in length.
lookbehindBounded.pcre2: Supported differently: PCRE2 10.43 and later accept it while each branch stays within a limit the calling program sets, 255 characters by default (this one reaches {max}); earlier releases, and the pcre2_dfa_match() function, accept only fixed-length branches.
lookbehindBounded.pcre2Over: Not supported by default: a branch may match up to {max} characters, above the default limit of 255 that the calling program can raise; releases before 10.43 accept only fixed-length branches.
lookbehindBounded.tcl: Not supported: Tcl AREs have lookahead only, (?= and (?!, and the Tcl 8.6 and 9.0 manuals add no lookbehind.

lookbehindUnbounded.name: Lookbehind with no maximum length
lookbehindUnbounded.es: Supported: ECMAScript places no length limit on a lookbehind.
lookbehindUnbounded.pcre2: Not supported: a PCRE2 lookbehind needs a known maximum length, and unlimited repetition such as * or + inside one is rejected.
lookbehindUnbounded.tcl: Not supported: Tcl AREs have lookahead only, (?= and (?!, and the Tcl 8.6 and 9.0 manuals add no lookbehind.

lookaheadGroups.name: Lookahead holding a group or a backreference
lookaheadGroups.es: Supported: a group inside a lookahead captures as it does anywhere else, and backreferences work there.
lookaheadGroups.pcre2: Supported: a group inside a lookahead captures as it does anywhere else, and backreferences work there.
lookaheadGroups.tcl: Supported differently: parentheses inside an ARE lookahead never capture, so they take no number and the groups after them are numbered differently.
lookaheadGroups.tclBackref: Not supported: an ARE lookahead may not contain a backreference.

namedGroup.name: Named capturing group
namedGroup.es: Supported: this is the only spelling ECMAScript accepts.
namedGroup.pcre2: Supported: PCRE2 also accepts two other spellings of a named group, and NGINX documents all three.
namedGroup.pcre2NonAscii: Supported differently: outside UTF mode PCRE2 accepts only ASCII letters, digits and underscores in a group name, so this name needs UTF mode.
namedGroup.tcl: Not supported: Tcl AREs have no named groups; use a plain group and its number.

namedGroupAlt.name: Named group in the Python or quoted spelling
namedGroupAlt.es: Not supported: ECMAScript accepts only the angle-bracket spelling and rejects this one as an invalid group.
namedGroupAlt.pcre2: Supported: PCRE2 accepts the Perl quoted spelling and the Python spelling as well as the angle-bracket one.
namedGroupAlt.tcl: Not supported: Tcl AREs have no named groups; use a plain group and its number.

namedBackref.name: Backreference to a named group, angle-bracket spelling
namedBackref.es: Supported, for a group named in the same pattern.
namedBackref.pcre2: Supported; PCRE2 also accepts four other spellings.
namedBackref.tcl: Not supported: AREs have no named groups, and \k is not an ARE escape, so the expression is an error.

backrefPcreOnly.name: Backreference in a PCRE2-only spelling
backrefPcreOnly.es: Not supported: ECMAScript writes a backreference only as a backslash and a number, or as \k with a name in angle brackets. A browser rejects this spelling, or, with no named group in the pattern and neither u nor v set, reads it as plain letters and text.
backrefPcreOnly.pcre2: Supported: PCRE2 accepts the Perl, Python and .NET spellings of a named backreference, and \g with a number, a signed relative number or a name.
backrefPcreOnly.tcl: Not supported: an ARE refers to a group only as a backslash and its number, and this spelling is an error.

inlineFlagsScoped.name: Inline modifiers scoped to a group
inlineFlagsScoped.es: Supported from ECMAScript 2025 on, for the letters i, m and s only. An engine that predates that edition rejects it; the compile status above shows what this browser does.
inlineFlagsScoped.esLetters: Not supported: ECMAScript modifier groups take only the letters i, m and s, each at most once and with no caret, so {letters} is rejected.
inlineFlagsScoped.pcre2: Supported: the options apply inside the group only.
inlineFlagsScoped.pcre2Letters: Not supported: {letters} has a letter or a combination PCRE2 does not accept in an option setting.
inlineFlagsScoped.tcl: Not supported: a Tcl ARE takes embedded options only as a bare group of letters at the very start of the expression, with no scoped form.

inlineFlagsGlobal.name: Inline options for the rest of the pattern
inlineFlagsGlobal.es: Not supported: ECMAScript has only the scoped form that ends in a colon, so a bare option group is an invalid group.
inlineFlagsGlobal.pcre2: Supported: the options apply from here to the end of the enclosing group, or of the pattern at top level.
inlineFlagsGlobal.pcre2Letters: Not supported: {letters} has a letter or a combination PCRE2 does not accept in an option setting.
inlineFlagsGlobal.tclSame: Supported at the very start of the expression, where these letters mean the same: i is case-insensitive matching and x the expanded syntax.
inlineFlagsGlobal.tclDiffers: Supported differently: at the start of an ARE, Tcl reads these letters its own way. m is an old synonym for n, newline-sensitive matching (the dot and negated brackets stop at newlines, ^ and $ match at them); s is the default non-newline-sensitive mode; b, e and q switch the rest to basic, extended or literal syntax.
inlineFlagsGlobal.tclNotStart: Not supported here: Tcl accepts embedded options only at the very start of the expression.
inlineFlagsGlobal.tclLetters: Not supported: Tcl option letters are b, c, e, i, m, n, p, q, s, t, w and x, with no hyphen to turn one off and no caret, so {letters} is rejected.

possessive.name: Possessive quantifier
possessive.es: Not supported: a quantifier cannot follow another, so the pattern is a syntax error.
possessive.pcre2: Supported: the extra + makes the quantifier possessive, the short form of an atomic group: what it matched is never given back.
possessive.tcl: Not supported: an ARE atom takes a single quantifier, so the second one is an error.

atomicGroup.name: Atomic group
atomicGroup.es: Not supported: ECMAScript has no atomic groups and rejects this as an invalid group.
atomicGroup.pcre2: Supported: once the group has matched, the engine does not backtrack into it.
atomicGroup.tcl: Not supported: AREs have no atomic groups, and this is not ARE syntax.

anchorStart.name: Start of the string, whatever the mode
anchorStart.es: Not supported: a browser reads \A as the letter A when neither u nor v is set, and rejects it as an invalid escape when either is.
anchorStart.pcre2: Supported: the start of the subject, in multiline mode too.
anchorStart.tcl: Supported: matches only at the beginning of the string, whatever the newline mode.

anchorEndNewline.name: End of the string, or before a final newline
anchorEndNewline.es: Not supported: a browser reads \Z as the letter Z when neither u nor v is set, and rejects it as an invalid escape when either is.
anchorEndNewline.pcre2: Supported: the end of the subject, or just before a newline that ends it.
anchorEndNewline.tcl: Supported differently: \Z matches only at the very end of the string, because AREs give a trailing newline no special treatment.

anchorEnd.name: Very end of the string
anchorEnd.es: Not supported: a browser reads \z as the letter z when neither u nor v is set, and rejects it as an invalid escape when either is.
anchorEnd.pcre2: Supported: the very end of the subject, never before a final newline.
anchorEnd.tcl: Not supported: \z is not an ARE escape, so the expression is an error; the ARE escape for the very end is \Z.

dollar.name: End anchor
dollar.es: Supported: the end of the input; with the m flag, also before each line terminator (LF, CR, U+2028, U+2029).
dollar.pcre2: Supported differently: by default $ also matches just before a newline at the very end, so a validator ending in $ accepts one trailing newline unless the application sets PCRE2_DOLLAR_ENDONLY; in multiline mode it matches before any newline.
dollar.tcl: Supported: the end of the string by default; newline-sensitive matching (the -line switch, or n at the start) adds the position before each newline.

dot.name: Dot and newlines
dot.es: Supported: any character except the line terminators LF, CR, U+2028 and U+2029, unless the s flag is set.
dot.pcre2: Supported differently: any character except a newline as the newline convention defines it, LF alone in a default build, so a lone CR matches; the s option (PCRE2_DOTALL or (?s)) lets it match newlines too.
dot.tcl: Supported differently: by default the dot matches every character, newline included; the -line or -linestop switches, or n or p at the start, stop it at newlines.

posixClass.name: POSIX bracket class
posixClass.es: Not supported: ECMAScript has no POSIX classes. It reads the brackets, colons and letters as ordinary members of the set, and without the v flag the first closing bracket ends the class.
posixClass.pcre2: Supported: by default the class covers ASCII characters only; when PCRE2_UCP is set, Unicode properties replace several of the classes.
posixClass.pcre2Unknown: Not supported: the name is not a PCRE2 class name, which is an error.
posixClass.tcl: Supported differently: Tcl's only locale is the Unicode locale, so the class is defined by Unicode rather than by ASCII.
posixClass.tclUnknown: Not supported: Tcl knows twelve class names (alpha, upper, lower, digit, xdigit, alnum, print, blank, space, punct, graph, cntrl) and no negated form.

posixWordEdge.name: Start or end of a word, POSIX bracket form
posixWordEdge.es: Not supported: ECMAScript has no POSIX forms and reads the brackets and symbols as ordinary characters.
posixWordEdge.pcre2: Supported to help migrations: PCRE2 converts it to a word boundary with a lookahead or lookbehind for a word character, and advises against it in new patterns.
posixWordEdge.tcl: Supported, though the manual deprecates it in favour of the constraint escapes \m and \M.

quoteLiteral.name: Quoted literal text
quoteLiteral.es: Not supported: a browser reads \Q and \E as the letters Q and E when neither u nor v is set, and the text between them as pattern syntax.
quoteLiteral.pcre2: Supported: everything between \Q and \E is literal, inside a character class or out.
quoteLiteral.tcl: Not supported: \Q is not an ARE escape, so the expression is an error; Tcl can instead make a whole expression literal by starting it with three asterisks and an equals sign.

unicodeProperty.name: Unicode property escape
unicodeProperty.esU: Supported differently: with the u or v flag only, and with stricter names. A script needs Script=, sc=, Script_Extensions= or scx= before it, and names must be written exactly as the specification lists them.
unicodeProperty.esNoU: Not supported here: without the u or v flag a browser reads it as a plain letter followed by literal text.
unicodeProperty.pcre2: Supported in a build with Unicode support (the default): names match loosely, ignoring case, spaces, hyphens and underscores, and a script name may stand alone.
unicodeProperty.tcl: Not supported: \p is not an ARE escape, so the expression is an error; the POSIX bracket classes are the nearest form.

unicodePropertyShort.name: One-letter Unicode property without braces
unicodePropertyShort.es: Not supported: ECMAScript requires the braces. Without the u or v flag a browser reads this as two plain letters, and with either it rejects it.
unicodePropertyShort.pcre2: Supported: a one-letter general category may drop the braces.
unicodePropertyShort.tcl: Not supported: \p is not an ARE escape, so the expression is an error; the POSIX bracket classes are the nearest form.

lazy.name: Lazy quantifier
lazy.es: Supported: as few repetitions as the rest of the pattern allows.
lazy.pcre2: Supported: as few repetitions as the rest of the pattern allows.
lazy.tcl: Supported differently: Tcl reports the longest or shortest overall match, and a whole branch takes the preference of its first quantified atom, so a pattern mixing lazy and greedy quantifiers can match a different stretch than ECMAScript or PCRE2.

wordBoundary.name: Word boundary
wordBoundary.es: Supported: word characters are A to Z, a to z, 0 to 9 and the underscore, plus characters that case-fold into them when i is used with u or v.
wordBoundary.pcre2: Supported: word characters are ASCII by default and follow Unicode properties when PCRE2_UCP is set.
wordBoundary.tcl: Supported differently: in an ARE \b is the backspace character. The word boundary is \y, with \m for the start of a word and \M for the end.

nonWordBoundary.name: Not a word boundary
nonWordBoundary.es: Supported: a position that is not a word boundary.
nonWordBoundary.pcre2: Supported: a position that is not a word boundary.
nonWordBoundary.tcl: Supported differently: in an ARE \B is another way to write a backslash. The non-boundary is \Y.

wordClass.name: Word-character shorthand
wordClass.es: Supported: the ASCII letters, digits and underscore, plus characters that case-fold into them when i is used with u or v.
wordClass.pcre2: Supported: ASCII letters, digits and underscore by default; Unicode letters, numbers, non-spacing marks and connector punctuation when PCRE2_UCP is set.
wordClass.tcl: Supported differently: \w is [[:alnum:]_], and the classes come from Tcl's only locale, the Unicode locale, rather than from ASCII; the Tcl 8.6 and 9.0 manuals also add connector punctuation.

classNegatedShorthand.name: Negated shorthand inside brackets
classNegatedShorthand.es: Supported: \D, \S and \W work inside a character class.
classNegatedShorthand.pcre2: Supported: \D, \S and \W work inside a character class.
classNegatedShorthand.tcl: Not supported: an ARE rejects \D, \S and \W inside a bracket expression; write the set another way, for example [^[:alnum:]_] for \W on its own.

tclWordConstraint.name: Tcl word constraint
tclWordConstraint.es: Not supported: a browser reads it as a plain letter when neither u nor v is set, and rejects it when either is.
tclWordConstraint.pcre2: Not supported: PCRE2 rejects an unrecognized letter escape at compile time; \b and \B are its word assertions.
tclWordConstraint.tcl: Supported: \m matches at the start of a word, \M at the end, \y at either and \Y anywhere else.

quantifierOmittedMin.name: Quantifier with no lower bound
quantifierOmittedMin.es: Not supported: a browser reads it as literal text when neither u nor v is set, and rejects it when either is.
quantifierOmittedMin.pcre2: Supported from PCRE2 10.43 on, as zero to n repetitions; earlier releases read it as literal text.
quantifierOmittedMin.tcl: Not supported: in an ARE a brace not followed by a digit is a literal brace, so this is literal text.

share.carries: The link carries the pattern, the flags and the test text as typed; a credential in them stops it.
share.caution: Test text is often real data: read it before you send the link.
share.maybeSecret: {field, select, input {The pattern} other {Line {line} of the test text}} may hold a secret ({label}){more, plural, =0 {} one {, and one more place may too} other {, and # more places may too}}: check before you send the link.
share.blockedSecret: No link: {field, select, input {the pattern} other {line {line} of the test text}} holds a credential ({label}){more, plural, =0 {} one {, and one more place does} other {, and # more places do}}. Replace it with a placeholder, then share again.

saml-decoder.name: SAML Decoder
saml-decoder.blurb: Paste a SAML Response or assertion (raw, base64, or URL-encoded) and decode its issuer, status, subject, conditions, audience, and attributes, with signature and weak-algorithm checks. Hardened against XXE.
saml-decoder.inputPlaceholder: Paste a SAML Response, an assertion, or the base64 SAMLResponse value
saml-decoder.runsLocally: Decoding runs locally in your browser. Nothing is sent anywhere.
saml-decoder.encryptedNote: {n, plural, one {{n} encrypted assertion} other {{n} encrypted assertions}} detected. Decrypting requires the service provider's private key and is out of scope for this decoder.
saml-decoder.notVerifiedNote: This tool decodes and explains structure only. It does not verify signatures, validate the message, or decrypt encrypted content.

errors.empty: Paste a SAML message to decode.
errors.not-decodable: This does not look like XML or base64. Paste a SAML Response, an assertion, or its base64 form.
errors.deflated: This decodes to compressed (DEFLATE) bytes, which is the HTTP-Redirect binding. Paste the raw XML or the base64 HTTP-POST form instead.
errors.doctype-forbidden: This message contains a DOCTYPE or entity declaration, which a SAML message must not have. It is rejected to prevent XML external entity (XXE) attacks.
errors.not-xml: The input could not be parsed as XML.
errors.no-saml: This is XML, but not a recognizable SAML message.
errors.malformed: The XML is malformed (an unclosed or mismatched tag).
errors.too-large: The message is too large to decode here.
errors.too-deep: The XML is nested too deeply to decode.
errors.too-many-nodes: The XML has too many elements to decode.

reasons.SIGNED_RESPONSE: The response is signed at the top level.
reasons.SIGNED_ASSERTION: An assertion signature is present ({value} signed).
reasons.UNSIGNED: Nothing in this message is signed. Its authenticity cannot be established, so it must be treated as untrusted until a signature is added and verified.
reasons.WEAK_SIG_ALGO: The signature uses {value}, a weak algorithm. Prefer RSA-SHA256 or stronger.
reasons.WEAK_DIGEST_ALGO: The signature digest uses {value}, a weak hash. Prefer SHA-256 or stronger.
reasons.ENCRYPTED_ASSERTION: {value, plural, one {{value} assertion is} other {{value} assertions are}} encrypted. This tool reports their presence but does not decrypt them.
reasons.STATUS_NOT_SUCCESS: The response status is {value}, not Success. The login did not succeed.
reasons.NO_CONDITIONS: An assertion has no Conditions element, so it carries no validity window or audience restriction.
reasons.NO_AUDIENCE_RESTRICTION: An assertion has Conditions but no AudienceRestriction, so it is not bound to a specific service provider.
reasons.BEARER_NO_NOTONORAFTER: A bearer SubjectConfirmation has no NotOnOrAfter, so the confirmation does not expire. This weakens replay protection.
reasons.BEARER_NO_RECIPIENT: A bearer SubjectConfirmation has no Recipient, so it is not bound to the intended endpoint.
reasons.MULTIPLE_ASSERTIONS: The message contains {value} assertions. Confirm your service provider processes the one it expects, since multiple assertions can be used in wrapping attacks.

flow.heading: Web browser SSO (SP-initiated)
flow.s1: A user requests a protected resource at the service provider
flow.s2: The SP builds an AuthnRequest and redirects the browser to the IdP
flow.s3: The IdP receives the AuthnRequest over the Redirect binding
flow.s5: The IdP issues a signed Response carrying an Assertion
flow.s6: The browser POSTs the SAMLResponse back to the SP's ACS
flow.s7: The SP checks the signature, conditions, and audience
flow.s8: The SP establishes a session and grants access

share.carries: The link carries the message as pasted; one with a signed or encrypted assertion gets none.
share.caution: A SAML message names your IdP and SP, and a subject can name a person: check it before you send the link.
share.blockedAssertion: {encrypted, select, yes {No link: this message holds an encrypted assertion, which the service provider can open and accept as a sign-in. Share one without it.} other {No link: this message holds a signed assertion, which signs its subject in until it expires. Share one without it.}}

secure-headers.name: Secure Headers Analyser
secure-headers.blurb: Paste an HTTP response and get a graded breakdown of its security headers, cookie flags, and cross-origin policy, checked against OWASP, RFC 6797, CSP Level 3, and RFC 6265bis.
secure-headers.inputPlaceholder:
HTTP/2 200
strict-transport-security: max-age=63072000; includeSubDomains; preload
content-security-policy: default-src 'self'; object-src 'none'
x-content-type-options: nosniff
set-cookie: id=abc; Secure; HttpOnly; SameSite=Lax
secure-headers.runsLocally: Analysis runs locally in your browser. Nothing is sent anywhere.

errors.empty: Paste an HTTP response or a block of headers to analyse.
errors.no-headers: No headers found. Paste a response with header lines like 'Header-Name: value'.

reasons.HSTS_MISSING: No Strict-Transport-Security header. Browsers may use plain HTTP, leaving the first request open to downgrade attacks.
reasons.HSTS_MAXAGE_ZERO: max-age is {value}, which disables HSTS. Set a positive max-age such as 31536000 (one year).
reasons.HSTS_MAXAGE_LOW: max-age is only {value, plural, one {{value} second} other {{value} seconds}}, under the recommended six-month minimum.
reasons.HSTS_MAXAGE_OK: max-age is {value} seconds, acceptable but below the one-year baseline.
reasons.HSTS_MAXAGE_STRONG: max-age is {value} seconds (one year or more), the recommended baseline.
reasons.HSTS_SUBDOMAINS: includeSubDomains is set, extending HTTPS enforcement to every subdomain.
reasons.HSTS_NO_SUBDOMAINS: includeSubDomains is not set, so subdomains are not covered.
reasons.HSTS_PRELOAD: preload is set, making the host eligible for the browser HSTS preload list.
reasons.CSP_MISSING: No Content-Security-Policy. The main defence-in-depth control against cross-site scripting is absent.
reasons.CSP_HAS_DEFAULT_SRC: A default-src directive is set, giving every resource type a baseline policy.
reasons.CSP_NO_DEFAULT_SRC: No default-src directive, so resource types without their own directive are unrestricted.
reasons.CSP_HAS_OBJECT_SRC: object-src is set, restricting legacy plugin content.
reasons.CSP_HAS_BASE_URI: base-uri is set, preventing base-tag injection.
reasons.CSP_FRAME_ANCESTORS: frame-ancestors is set, the modern control against framing and clickjacking.
reasons.CSP_UNSAFE_INLINE: Uses 'unsafe-inline', which permits inline scripts or styles and largely defeats the XSS protection of CSP.
reasons.CSP_UNSAFE_EVAL: Uses 'unsafe-eval', which permits eval() and similar dynamic code execution.
reasons.CSP_WILDCARD: A wildcard '*' source allows content from any origin, weakening the policy.
reasons.CSP_RO_ABSENT: No report-only policy is set. This is optional and used to stage a CSP before enforcing it.
reasons.CSP_RO_ONLY: A report-only CSP is present but there is no enforced Content-Security-Policy. Report-only does not protect the page.
reasons.CSP_RO_WITH_ENFORCED: A report-only CSP is present alongside the enforced policy, useful for testing changes.
reasons.XCTO_MISSING: No X-Content-Type-Options. Browsers may MIME-sniff responses, risking content being run as script.
reasons.XCTO_NOSNIFF: Set to nosniff, which stops MIME-type sniffing.
reasons.XCTO_INVALID: Unexpected value “{value}”. The only valid value is nosniff.
reasons.XFO_MISSING: No X-Frame-Options. Without it, or CSP frame-ancestors, the page can be framed for clickjacking.
reasons.XFO_DENY: Set to DENY, preventing the page from being framed by any site.
reasons.XFO_SAMEORIGIN: Set to SAMEORIGIN, allowing framing only by same-origin pages.
reasons.XFO_ALLOWFROM_DEPRECATED: Uses ALLOW-FROM, which is obsolete and ignored by modern browsers. Use CSP frame-ancestors instead.
reasons.XFO_INVALID: Unexpected value “{value}”. Use DENY or SAMEORIGIN.
reasons.REFERRER_MISSING: No Referrer-Policy. The browser default applies, which may leak full URLs to other origins.
reasons.REFERRER_WEAK: Set to “{value}”, which still sends the origin or more to other sites.
reasons.REFERRER_UNSAFE_URL: Set to unsafe-url, which sends the full URL, including path and query, to every destination.
reasons.PERMISSIONS_MISSING: No Permissions-Policy. Powerful features such as camera, microphone, and geolocation are not restricted.
reasons.PERMISSIONS_PRESENT: Present, restricting access to powerful browser features.
reasons.COOP_MISSING: No Cross-Origin-Opener-Policy. The page shares a browsing-context group with cross-origin openers.
reasons.COOP_SAME_ORIGIN: Set to same-origin, isolating the page from cross-origin windows.
reasons.COOP_ALLOW_POPUPS: Set to same-origin-allow-popups, isolating the page while keeping popups it opens.
reasons.COOP_UNSAFE_NONE: Set to unsafe-none, which provides no opener isolation.
reasons.COEP_ABSENT: No Cross-Origin-Embedder-Policy. This is optional and required only for cross-origin isolation.
reasons.COEP_PRESENT: Set to “{value}”, requiring embedded resources to opt in.
reasons.CORP_ABSENT: No Cross-Origin-Resource-Policy. This is optional and limits who may embed this resource.
reasons.CORP_SAME_ORIGIN: Set to same-origin, the tightest setting.
reasons.CORP_SAME_SITE: Set to same-site, allowing same-site embedding.
reasons.CORP_CROSS_ORIGIN: Set to cross-origin, allowing any site to embed this resource. Make sure that is intended.
reasons.CACHE_ABSENT: No Cache-Control header. Set no-store on responses that carry sensitive data.
reasons.CACHE_RESTRICTED: Caching is restricted (no-store, no-cache, or private), appropriate for sensitive responses.
reasons.CACHE_PERMISSIVE: Caching is permissive. Make sure the response contains no sensitive data.
reasons.CORS_WILDCARD: Access-Control-Allow-Origin is '*', letting any site read the response. This is safe only for public, credential-free data.
reasons.CORS_WILDCARD_CREDENTIALS: Access-Control-Allow-Origin is '*' together with credentials. This exposes credentialed data to any origin, a serious misconfiguration.
reasons.CORS_NULL_ORIGIN: Access-Control-Allow-Origin is 'null', which several contexts can forge. Avoid the null origin.
reasons.CORS_SPECIFIC_ORIGIN: Access-Control-Allow-Origin allows “{value}”. Confirm that origin is trusted.
reasons.CORS_CREDENTIALS_TRUE: Access-Control-Allow-Credentials is true, so the response may carry cookies cross-origin. Pair this only with a specific, trusted origin.
reasons.XPCDP_ABSENT: No X-Permitted-Cross-Domain-Policies. OWASP recommends setting it to none.
reasons.XPCDP_NONE: Set to none, the hardened value.
reasons.XPCDP_ALL: Set to all, the most permissive value. Prefer none.
reasons.CLEAR_SITE_DATA_PRESENT: Clear-Site-Data is set (“{value}”), telling the browser to clear site data. Use it on logout endpoints.
reasons.FEATURE_POLICY_DEPRECATED: Feature-Policy is deprecated. Migrate to Permissions-Policy.
reasons.HPKP_DEPRECATED: HTTP Public Key Pinning is deprecated and removed from browsers. Remove this header.
reasons.EXPECT_CT_OBSOLETE: Expect-CT is obsolete (“{value}”). Certificate Transparency is enforced by default, so remove it.
reasons.XSS_PROTECTION_LEGACY: X-XSS-Protection is “{value}”. The legacy auditor is gone from modern browsers. Remove it, or set it to 0, and rely on CSP.
reasons.XSS_PROTECTION_DISABLED_OK: X-XSS-Protection is 0, which correctly disables the obsolete auditor.
reasons.SERVER_VERSION_DISCLOSED: Server reveals version detail (“{value}”), helping attackers target known flaws. Minimize it.
reasons.SERVER_PRODUCT_DISCLOSED: Server names the product (“{value}”). Consider removing or minimizing it.
reasons.XPOWEREDBY_PRESENT: X-Powered-By reveals the stack (“{value}”). Remove it.
reasons.XASPNETVERSION_PRESENT: X-AspNet-Version reveals the runtime version (“{value}”). Remove it.
reasons.XASPNETMVCVERSION_PRESENT: X-AspNetMvc-Version reveals the framework version (“{value}”). Remove it.
reasons.COOKIE_COUNT: {value, plural, one {{value} cookie} other {{value} cookies}} set.
reasons.COOKIE_WEAK_COUNT: {value, plural, one {{value} cookie has} other {{value} cookies have}} weak attributes.
reasons.COOKIE_SECURE: Secure is set, so the cookie is sent only over HTTPS.
reasons.COOKIE_NO_SECURE: Secure is not set, so the cookie can be sent over plain HTTP.
reasons.COOKIE_HTTPONLY: HttpOnly is set, hiding the cookie from JavaScript.
reasons.COOKIE_NO_HTTPONLY: HttpOnly is not set, so script can read the cookie and an XSS flaw could steal it.
reasons.COOKIE_SAMESITE_STRICT: SameSite=Strict, the strongest cross-site request protection.
reasons.COOKIE_SAMESITE_NONE: SameSite=None with Secure, allowing cross-site sending.
reasons.COOKIE_SAMESITE_NONE_INSECURE: SameSite=None without Secure. Browsers reject this and it is insecure. Add Secure.
reasons.COOKIE_NO_SAMESITE: No SameSite attribute. Set Lax or Strict for cross-site request resistance.
reasons.COOKIE_HOST_PREFIX_OK: The __Host- prefix requirements are met (Secure, Path=/, and no Domain).
reasons.COOKIE_HOST_PREFIX_VIOLATION: The __Host- prefix requires Secure, Path=/, and no Domain. Those conditions are not all met.
reasons.COOKIE_SECURE_PREFIX_OK: The __Secure- prefix requirement is met (Secure is set).
reasons.COOKIE_SECURE_PREFIX_VIOLATION: The __Secure- prefix requires Secure, which is not set.
reasons.OVERALL_INFO_LEAK: {value, plural, one {{value} header discloses} other {{value} headers disclose}} server or stack details.
reasons.OVERALL_WEAK_COOKIES: {value, plural, one {{value} cookie has} other {{value} cookies have}} weak attributes.
reasons.OVERALL_CORS_RISK: A cross-origin (CORS) policy exposes data to other sites.
reasons.OVERALL_POOR: Several core security headers are missing.

ssrf-url-classifier.name: SSRF URL classifier
ssrf-url-classifier.blurb: Paste a URL and see where it actually points: loopback, a private or link-local range, a cloud metadata endpoint, CGNAT, any block of the IANA special-purpose registries, or the public internet. Decimal, octal and hex IP obfuscation is decoded, so is an IPv4 address hidden inside an IPv6 one (IPv4-mapped, IPv4-compatible, NAT64, 6to4, Teredo); dangerous schemes and embedded credentials are flagged, and an SSRF risk level is shown. It never resolves DNS and never sends the request.
ssrf-url-classifier.privacy: Everything is computed in your browser. This tool never resolves DNS and never sends the request; it classifies the address purely from the text you paste.

categoryDesc.loopback: The host itself (127.0.0.0/8 or ::1). A server fetching this reaches its own local services.
categoryDesc.private: An RFC 1918 private range (10/8, 172.16/12, 192.168/16) or IPv6 ULA. Typically internal infrastructure.
categoryDesc.link-local: A link-local address (169.254.0.0/16 or fe80::/10), reachable only on the local segment.
categoryDesc.cloud-metadata: A cloud instance metadata endpoint (IMDS). Reaching it can expose credentials and instance data.
categoryDesc.cgnat: Carrier-grade NAT (network address translation) shared address space (100.64.0.0/10). Not public, but not classic private either.
categoryDesc.reserved: A reserved or special-use range (documentation, benchmarking, multicast, broadcast, future use).
categoryDesc.public: A public, routable address on the internet.
categoryDesc.internal-name: A hostname with an internal suffix (.internal, .local, .corp). Not a public name.
categoryDesc.unresolved: A hostname whose address is only known after a DNS lookup, which this tool does not perform.

facts.title: What you pasted
facts.embeddedBlock: Block of the embedded IPv4 address (IANA)

flags.title: Flags
flags.obfuscated: The host is written in {form} form, which decodes to {ip}. This is a common way to slip an internal address past a filter that only blocks dotted-decimal.
flags.scheme: The {scheme}:// scheme is a non-HTTP fetch that escalates SSRF, for example local-file read or protocol smuggling to another service.
flags.userinfo: Credentials are embedded in the URL (user:pass@host). The real host may ignore them while a naive filter is fooled into reading the wrong part as the host.
flags.embedded: This IPv6 address is {embedding} and carries the IPv4 address {ip}. It is rated by {ip}: a filter that checks only the IPv6 form lets that target through.
flags.embeddedLayout: 64:ff9b:1::/48 leaves the translation prefix length to the operator (RFC 8215), so the tool read the address with the RFC 6052 /96, /64, /56 and /48 layouts and shows the /{length} reading: the most internal one, or the /96 reading when none points inside. The /48 is not globally reachable, so a public reading is still rated reserved.
flags.ipv4Compatible: The IPv4-compatible format is deprecated (RFC 4291 section 2.5.5.1), and the IPv4 address inside it must be a globally unique unicast address. A stack that still accepts the format reaches the carried address, so the tool rates it by that address.
flags.teredo: A Teredo address carries two IPv4 addresses: the server {server} in bits 32 to 63, and the client {client}, stored with every bit inverted in the last 32 bits (RFC 4380 section 4). Both are rated, and the more internal one, {ip}, decides.
flags.anycastService: {prefix} is a special-purpose anycast service address: {name} ({rfc}). The topologically nearest node that holds the address answers it, and that node can be a middlebox on your own network path. {reachable, select, yes {The IANA registry marks it globally reachable, so it rates public; an allow-list should still name it explicitly.} other {The IANA registry marks it not globally reachable.}}
flags.specialPublic: {prefix} is "{name}" ({rfc}), a special-purpose block that the IANA registry marks globally reachable, so it rates public. It is named here so that an allow-list can decide on it explicitly.
flags.noReach: {prefix} is "{name}" ({rfc}). The IANA registry gives this deprecated block no Globally Reachable value, so it is not rated public.

defenses.title: Defences
defenses.allowlist: Prefer an allow-list of exact hosts over a block-list; block-lists miss encodings and new ranges.
defenses.blockRanges: Reject loopback, private, link-local, CGNAT, and metadata ranges for both IPv4 and IPv6.
defenses.resolveThenCheck: Resolve the hostname first, then check every resulting address, to catch DNS that points at an internal IP.
defenses.noRedirects: Disable or re-validate redirects; a public URL can 302 to an internal one.
defenses.schemes: Allow only http and https; reject file, gopher, dict, ftp, and similar schemes.

struct.heading: How a PRI splits into facility and severity
struct.note: A single PRI integer carries both fields. Dividing by 8 gives the facility, and the remainder gives the severity, so PRI 134 is facility 16 and severity 6. Encoding runs the other way: facility × 8 + severity.

telemetry-streaming-explainer.name: Telemetry Streaming (TS) explainer
telemetry-streaming-explainer.blurb: Paste the JSON you POST to /mgmt/shared/telemetry/declare and it reads it back: it confirms the top-level Telemetry class, reads the optional Controls, and walks every class-object grouped by its role in the telemetry pipeline: the data sources that produce telemetry (system pollers, event listeners), the consumers that forward it out (Splunk, Azure, AWS, DataDog, Prometheus, and the rest of the catalogue), and the grouping and endpoint classes. It flags the pipeline gaps that make a declaration succeed but do nothing. TS is the third F5 Automation Toolchain extension: AS3 and DO configure the box, TS observes it.
telemetry-streaming-explainer.inputLabel: A TS declaration (the JSON you POST to /mgmt/shared/telemetry/declare)
telemetry-streaming-explainer.runsLocally: Decoding runs locally in your browser. Nothing you paste leaves this page.

telemetry-streaming-explainer.scopeNote: This is a structure explainer and sanity checker, not a full JSON-Schema validator. It never contacts a BIG-IP and nothing you paste leaves the browser. A declaration that passes here can still be rejected by TS itself. Note: F5 has placed Telemetry Streaming in maintenance mode; it remains supported with critical and security fixes, with no deprecation planned.
telemetry-streaming-explainer.walkOrderNote: Grouped by each class's role: data sources produce telemetry (system pollers collect statistics, event listeners ingest logs), consumers forward it to an external system, and the supporting classes group and extend the rest. A working declaration needs at least one source and at least one consumer.

finding.noSource: No data source. Add a Telemetry_System (with a systemPoller) or a Telemetry_Listener, or the declaration collects nothing to forward.
finding.noConsumer: No consumer. Add a Telemetry_Consumer (push) or Telemetry_Pull_Consumer (pull), or the telemetry has nowhere to go.
finding.systemWithoutPoller: The Telemetry_System "{name}" has no systemPoller (and no iHealthPoller). To collect metrics, a Telemetry_System must define systemPoller.

finding.namespacesPresent: This declaration uses Telemetry_Namespace: pollers, listeners, and consumers inside a namespace operate as an isolated unit and only see each other.

class.Controls: optional top-level controls for logging and debugging (logLevel, debug, and the beta memoryMonitor); the class value must always be Controls
class.Telemetry_System: a target system to poll; define a systemPoller inside it to collect and normalize device, virtual-server, pool, and pool-member statistics on an interval, and optionally an iHealthPoller
class.Telemetry_System_Poller: a standalone (referenced) system poller, e.g. to pull statistics from an additional BIG-IP by host/username/passphrase
class.Telemetry_Listener: an event listener on TCP and UDP (default port 6514) that ingests logs and events the BIG-IP publishes (LTM request logs, AFM/ASM security logs)
class.Telemetry_Consumer: a push consumer that forwards telemetry to an external system; the type selects the target (Splunk, Azure Log Analytics, AWS CloudWatch/S3, Graphite, Kafka, ElasticSearch, DataDog, Generic HTTP, OpenTelemetry, and more)
class.Telemetry_Pull_Consumer: a pull consumer that exposes telemetry for an external system to scrape on demand rather than pushing (e.g. the Prometheus pull consumer); added in TS 1.11
class.Telemetry_Namespace: a namespace that groups a set of pollers, listeners, and consumers so they operate as an isolated unit (objects inside a namespace only see each other)
class.Telemetry_Endpoints: a reusable set of custom TMSH/REST endpoints a system poller can query, for statistics beyond the default output
class.iHealth_Poller: an iHealth poller (referenced form) that creates a QKView, uploads it to the F5 iHealth Service, and fetches the analysis; must be attached to a Telemetry_System
class.unknown: a class not in this tool's catalogue (reported as-is)

totp-hotp.name: TOTP / HOTP Generator & Validator
totp-hotp.blurb: Generate and check time-based (TOTP, RFC 6238) and counter-based (HOTP, RFC 4226) one-time passwords - the codes behind authenticator apps and hardware tokens such as FortiToken. SHA-1/256/512, configurable digits and step. Computed locally with Web Crypto; your secret never leaves your browser.
totp-hotp.runsLocally: Computed in your browser. Your secret is never sent anywhere.
totp-hotp.secretError: That secret could not be decoded with the selected encoding. Check the value and the Base32 / Hex / ASCII toggle.
totp-hotp.validMatch: Match - this code is valid right now.
totp-hotp.validNoMatch: No match for the current parameters.
totp-hotp.validWindowNote: Real validators usually accept the adjacent steps too; this check allows +/-1 step of clock drift.
totp-hotp.explainNote: HMAC the 8-byte moving factor under your secret, take the low nibble of the last byte as an offset, read 4 bytes there as a 31-bit number, then take that modulo 10^digits. That is RFC 4226 dynamic truncation; TOTP just feeds the time step in as the counter.

url-inspector.blurb: Dissect any URL into its named parts: scheme, host, port, path, query parameters, and fragment. Decodes percent-escapes and internationalized hosts, and flags credentials and other issues. Runs entirely in your browser.

errors.empty: Enter a URL to inspect.

reasons.RELATIVE_REFERENCE: This is a relative reference, not an absolute URL: it has no scheme and no host.
reasons.NO_SCHEME: No scheme is present, so this URL is not absolute.
reasons.CREDENTIALS_IN_URL: This URL embeds a username and password. Credentials in a URL are easily logged, cached, and shared, and should be avoided.
reasons.USERINFO_PRESENT: This URL includes a userinfo component (a username before the host).
reasons.PLAINTEXT_SCHEME: The {value} scheme is not encrypted in transit. Anything sent over it can be read on the network.
reasons.NON_DEFAULT_PORT: The port {value} is not the default for this scheme.
reasons.REDUNDANT_DEFAULT_PORT: The port {value} is the default for this scheme and can be omitted.
reasons.IDN_HOST: The host is internationalized and stored in punycode; the Unicode form is shown above. Watch for look-alike characters in untrusted links.
reasons.UPPERCASE_SCHEME: The scheme contains uppercase letters. Schemes are case-insensitive and are normally written in lowercase.
reasons.UPPERCASE_HOST: The host contains uppercase letters. Host names are case-insensitive and are normally written in lowercase.
reasons.PERCENT_ENCODED: This URL contains percent-encoded characters, which have been decoded in the breakdown above.
reasons.PLUS_IN_QUERY: The query contains a plus sign. Under form encoding (application/x-www-form-urlencoded) a plus means a space; under strict RFC 3986 it is a literal plus. The values above keep it literal.

url-inspector.note: Components are shown exactly as written, without normalization. Parsing follows RFC 3986; the query is split on & and =, and each part is percent-decoded.

security.title: Security analysis
security.doctype-present: A DOCTYPE is present. The DOCTYPE is the gateway to XML entity attacks; a hardened parser disables it entirely.
security.external-dtd: The DOCTYPE references an external DTD. A parser that fetches it can be steered to attacker-controlled content.
security.external-entity: An external entity is declared (SYSTEM or PUBLIC). Resolving it would read a local file or make a network request: the classic XXE vector.
security.parameter-entity: A parameter entity is declared. Parameter entities are used to build blind and out-of-band XXE payloads.
security.entity-expansion: Entities reference other entities. Chained expansion can grow exponentially and exhaust memory, the billion laughs denial of service.

errors.multiple-roots: Multiple root elements ({detail}). XML must have exactly one.

arg.count: Stop automatically after {count, plural, one {{count} packet} other {{count} packets}}. Ctrl+C stops earlier.
arg.count0: Packet count 0 means capture until you stop it with Ctrl+C. Set a number to auto-stop after that many packets.
arg.filter: BPF-style filter, matched against every packet. ''{filter}' selects only traffic that matches. Because neither src nor dst is fixed on a bare host/port, both directions are captured.
arg.filterNone: No filter: every packet on the interface is captured. Because it is unfiltered, expect a lot of output; add host/port/proto to narrow it.
arg.iface: Capture only on interface {iface}. Naming a physical interface (rather than 'any' or a VLAN interface) is what lets a verbose 6 capture keep the real Ethernet header and VLAN tag.
arg.ifaceAny: Capture on all interfaces. Note that on 'any' the link layer is Linux cooked capture (SLL), not Ethernet, so the real Ethernet header and any VLAN tag are not shown.
arg.verboseIfacePcap: Verbosity {level}: {help}. Interface names are shown (verbose 4-6). Full Ethernet-level output can be converted to a .pcap for Wireshark with Fortinet's fgt2eth.pl script.
arg.verboseNoIface: Verbosity {level}: {help}. Interface names are NOT shown at this level; use 4, 5, or 6 to see which interface each packet used.
arg.verboseNoIfacePcap: Verbosity {level}: {help}. Interface names are NOT shown at this level; use 4, 5, or 6 to see which interface each packet used. Full Ethernet-level output can be converted to a .pcap for Wireshark with Fortinet's fgt2eth.pl script.

note.lowVerbose: At verbosity 1-3 the interface name is not printed. If you need to see which interface each packet used (especially with 'any'), use 4, 5, or 6.
note.noArgs: No arguments found after 'diagnose sniffer packet'.
note.noCount: No packet count given. On the device this means the sniff runs until you press Ctrl+C.
note.noVerbose: No verbosity level found. FortiOS expects a level 1-6 after the filter.
note.notSniffer: This does not start with 'diagnose sniffer packet'. Decoding the remaining tokens as best-effort positional arguments; the first token is treated as the interface.
note.offload: If expected packets never appear, the session may be hardware-offloaded (NP/SoC). The kernel sniffer cannot see offloaded sessions; temporarily set 'set auto-asic-offload disable' in the matching firewall policy while troubleshooting.
note.relativeTs: The timestamp is relative to the start of the sniff. For captures you run in parallel on multiple interfaces or SSH sessions, use 'a' (absolute UTC) or 'l' (absolute local) so the lines can be correlated.
note.sshFlood: An unlimited, unfiltered capture over SSH can flood your own session with the very traffic your SSH connection generates. Add a filter (or exclude 'not port 22') and/or a packet count.
note.vlanStripped: On the 'any' interface (and on VLAN interfaces), the VLAN tag is stripped from the output at verbose 3/6. To capture the VLAN tag, run the sniffer on the underlying physical interface and match on the tag, e.g. "ether[14:2]=0x00db" for VLAN 219.

ref.count: Number of packets before stopping. 0 (or omitted) captures until Ctrl+C.
ref.filter: BPF-style expression in single quotes, e.g. 'host 10.0.0.1 and tcp port 443'. Use none for no filter.
ref.interface: Interface to capture from, e.g. port1 or wan1, or 'any' for all interfaces.
ref.note: Type or build a command, or paste an existing 'diagnose sniffer packet ...' line to have each argument explained.
ref.tsformat: a = absolute UTC, l = absolute local, omitted = relative to sniff start.
ref.verbose: Verbosity 1-6. 1-3 add more payload; 4-6 additionally print interface names.

a.detail: yyyy-mm-dd hh:mm:ss.ms in UTC (no time zone). Use for parallel captures so lines from different sessions can be correlated.
a.label: absolute UTC

l.detail: yyyy-mm-dd hh:mm:ss.ms in the FortiGate's local time. Also safe for parallel captures.
l.label: absolute local

rel.detail: seconds since the sniff started (ss.ms). The default when the argument is omitted; not suitable for correlating parallel captures.
rel.label: relative

verb.3: print header and data from Ethernet of packets (if available)
verb.4: print header of packets with interface name
verb.5: print header and data from IP of packets with interface name
verb.6: print header and data from Ethernet of packets (if available) with interface name

helper.convert_addr: Packs a dotted IPv4 address into a single 32-bit number. Pure arithmetic.
helper.dateRange: True within a date range. The bounds are ordered.
helper.dnsDomainIs: True when the host ends in the given domain suffix. Pure string comparison; no DNS.
helper.dnsDomainLevels: Returns the number of dots in the host. Pure string operation.
helper.dnsResolve: Resolves a hostname to a dotted IP string. Consults DNS and can block.
helper.dnsResolveEx: Microsoft IPv6 extension of dnsResolve. Consults DNS; Chromium-only.
helper.isInNet: True when the host's IP is in the given subnet (pattern + mask). If a hostname is passed, it is resolved via DNS first, so this can block.
helper.isInNetEx: Microsoft IPv6 extension of isInNet (CIDR prefix form). May consult DNS; Chromium-only.
helper.isPlainHostName: True when the host has no dots, i.e. an unqualified single-label name. The classic way to send intranet short names DIRECT.
helper.isResolvable: Tries to resolve the host and returns true on success. This consults DNS and can block; use it sparingly.
helper.isResolvableEx: Microsoft IPv6 extension of isResolvable. Consults DNS; Chromium-only.
helper.localHostOrDomainIs: True on an exact hostname match, or when only the unqualified name is given and it matches. Pure string comparison.
helper.myIpAddress: Returns the machine's own IP. Unreliable on multi-homed hosts and may fall back to a loopback address like 127.0.0.1; treat its result with caution.
helper.myIpAddressEx: Microsoft IPv6 extension of myIpAddress; may return a semicolon-separated list of addresses. Supported by Chromium, not by Firefox.
helper.shExpMatch: Shell-glob match (* and ?, and [chars] in some browsers). This is NOT a regular expression; regex syntax will not work here.
helper.sortIpAddressList: Microsoft helper that sorts a list of IPs by preference. Pure; Chromium-only.
helper.timeRange: True within a time-of-day range. The bounds are ordered.
helper.weekdayRange: True within a weekday range. Note that the bounds are ordered, so the order of the two days matters.

lint.alert: alert() only writes to the browser console; it does not affect proxy selection and is a debugging aid.
lint.bracesExtra: Unbalanced curly braces ({n} extra closing). The function body will not parse.
lint.bracesOpen: Unbalanced curly braces ({n} unclosed). The function body will not parse.
lint.dns: Uses DNS-consulting helper(s): {names}. These force a DNS lookup on every call and can block; MDN recommends ordering cheaper string checks (isPlainHostName, dnsDomainIs) first so DNS is only consulted when nothing else has decided.
lint.dynamic: The file appears to use eval, new Function, XMLHttpRequest, or fetch. A PAC file should be pure decision logic; dynamic code or network calls are unusual and a security and reliability concern.
lint.entry: FindProxyForURL(url, host) entry point is present.
lint.httpsPath: Modern Chromium-based browsers strip the path and query from https:// URLs before calling the PAC, so matching on the path of an HTTPS URL (via the url argument) may not work as written.
lint.myIp: myIpAddress() can be unreliable: on multi-homed machines it may return an unexpected interface, and it can fall back to a loopback address such as 127.0.0.1.
lint.netskope: This looks like a Netskope Cloud Explicit Proxy steering file: it points traffic at a goskope.com explicit-proxy host, typically eproxy-'<'tenant>.goskope.com on port 8081. Bypasses (identity-provider hosts, plain hostnames) are returned DIRECT so they skip the proxy, and Netskope uses cookie surrogates for user identity. Replace the tenant placeholder with your real tenant and ensure the Netskope root CA is trusted for TLS inspection.
lint.noDirect: No DIRECT appears in any return string. If every listed proxy is unreachable, the browser has no direct-connection fallback and may block traffic; a trailing DIRECT is the usual safety net.
lint.noEntry: No FindProxyForURL(url, host) function was found. A PAC file must define exactly this entry point; browsers call it for every request.
lint.noReturn: No return statement was found. FindProxyForURL must return a proxy string (or null for no proxy).
lint.shExp: shExpMatch uses shell-glob wildcards (* and ?), not regular expressions. Patterns like .*\.example\.com will not behave as a regex here.
lint.unknownKeyword: Return string(s) contain something that is not a PAC directive keyword: {found}. Only DIRECT, PROXY, SOCKS, SOCKS4, SOCKS5, HTTP, and HTTPS are valid.

part.direct: Connect straight to the destination with no proxy.
part.http: Send the request to the HTTP proxy at {at} (newer keyword; Firefox-era addition).
part.https: Send the request to the HTTPS (TLS) proxy at {at} (newer keyword).
part.proxy: Send the request to the HTTP proxy at {at}.
part.socks: Send the request through the SOCKS server at {at}.
part.socksN: Send the request through the {kw} server at {at}.
part.unknown: Not a recognized PAC directive keyword. A return string part must begin with one of {keywords}.

ref.direct: Connect straight to the destination, no proxy.
ref.newer: Newer keywords for a specific proxy type. Semicolon-separated parts are tried left to right as failover.
ref.paste: Paste a PAC file (a FindProxyForURL(url, host) function) to have its proxy directives, helper functions, and structure explained. This tool reads the file; it never runs it.

exos-config-explainer.name: ExtremeXOS config explainer
exos-config-explainer.blurb: Paste an ExtremeXOS (EXOS / Switch Engine) configuration and it explains each command in plain English, summarizes the VLANs (tag, tagged and untagged ports, IP addresses), and groups the commands by category. Never touches a switch.
exos-config-explainer.runsLocally: Runs locally in your browser. Nothing you paste leaves this page.
exos-config-explainer.inputPlaceholder:
create vlan engineering tag 100
configure vlan engineering add ports 1:1, 1:2 tagged
configure vlan engineering ipaddress 10.1.1.1/24
enable ipforwarding

share.carries: {state, select, blocked {The link carries the configuration with each password, community, shared secret and key replaced by {mark}.} other {{n, plural, =0 {The link carries the configuration as pasted: nothing in it needed replacing.} one {The link carries the configuration with its one secret value (a password, community, shared secret or key) replaced by {mark}.} other {The link carries the configuration with its # secret values (passwords, communities, shared secrets, keys) replaced by {mark}.}}}}
share.caution: The copy still names addresses, VLANs, ports and hosts: read it before you send the link.
share.blockedSecret: No link: line {line} holds a key, token or password ({label}) that cannot be replaced safely. Put a placeholder in its place, then share again.
share.revealLabel: {n, plural, one {Include the replaced value in the link} other {Include the # replaced values in the link}}

account.create: Creates a local account "{name}" with role {role} (EXOS roles are typically admin or user).
account.createNoRole: Creates a local account "{name}" with no role given (EXOS roles are typically admin or user).

l3.default: Adds a default route via next hop {gw} (the gateway of last resort).
l3.forwardOn: Enables IP routing (forwarding) so the switch routes between its Layer 3 VLAN interfaces.

lag.lacp: Creates a link aggregation group (LAG) with master port {master}, using LACP. In EXOS a LAG is called a "sharing" group and is referenced by its master port.
lag.membersLacp: Creates a link aggregation group (LAG) with master port {master} and members {members}, using LACP. In EXOS a LAG is called a "sharing" group and is referenced by its master port.
lag.membersStatic: Creates a link aggregation group (LAG) with master port {master} and members {members} (static). In EXOS a LAG is called a "sharing" group and is referenced by its master port.
lag.static: Creates a link aggregation group (LAG) with master port {master} (static). In EXOS a LAG is called a "sharing" group and is referenced by its master port.

note.noForwarding: One or more VLANs have IP addresses but no 'enable ipforwarding' command was seen. Without it, the switch will not route between those VLAN interfaces.
note.noVerbs: None of these lines begin with an EXOS verb (create, configure, enable, disable, delete, unconfigure). This may be a configuration for a different platform, such as Cisco IOS or VOSS.
note.none: No EXOS commands were recognized. Make sure this is an ExtremeXOS configuration (lines beginning with create, configure, enable, disable, delete, or unconfigure).
note.read: Read {count, plural, one {{count} command line} other {{count} command lines}}.
note.readVlans: Read {count, plural, one {{count} command line} other {{count} command lines}} and {vcount, plural, one {{vcount} VLAN} other {{vcount} VLANs}}.
note.untagged: Remember that an untagged port can belong to only one VLAN. Adding an untagged port to a new VLAN requires first removing it from the Default VLAN.

ports.label: Sets a text label on port(s) {plist}.

ref.flat: EXOS has no interface sub-modes. Every line is a self-contained command that begins with one of these verbs acting on a named object, which is why a config reads as a flat list rather than nested blocks.
ref.paste: Paste an ExtremeXOS (EXOS / Switch Engine) configuration to have each command explained, the VLANs summarized, and the commands grouped by category. This tool reads the config; it never touches a switch.

stp.addVlan: Adds a VLAN (and its ports) to spanning-tree domain "{domain}".

verb.configure: Sets a property on an existing object. The workhorse verb; often abbreviated to 'config'.
verb.create: Creates a new object (a VLAN, account, STP domain, and so on).
verb.disable: Turns a feature or object off.
verb.enable: Turns a feature or object on (routing, a port, sharing, a protocol).
verb.unconfigure: Resets part of the configuration to its default.

vlan.addTagged: Adds port(s) {plist} to VLAN "{name}" as tagged. Tagged ports carry the 802.1Q tag and can belong to many VLANs (a trunk).
vlan.addUntagged: Adds port(s) {plist} to VLAN "{name}" as untagged. Untagged ports can belong to only one VLAN; they must first be removed from the Default VLAN.
vlan.create: Creates VLAN "{name}" (untagged until a tag is set).
vlan.ip: Assigns IP address {addr} to VLAN "{name}", making it a routed (Layer 3) interface. Routing between VLAN interfaces still needs "enable ipforwarding".

f5-irules-runtime-calculator.name: iRules runtime calculator
f5-irules-runtime-calculator.blurb: Turn iRule timing statistics into real runtime, CPU cost per request, and maximum requests per second.
f5-irules-runtime-calculator.timingLabel: iRule timing output (from tmsh show ltm rule field-fmt)
f5-irules-runtime-calculator.timingPlaceholder: Paste the field-fmt event blocks (avg-cycles, min-cycles, max-cycles, total-executions), or lines of the form: HTTP_REQUEST 729 total 0 fail 0 abort | Cycles (min, avg, max) = (3693, 3959, 53936)
f5-irules-runtime-calculator.overrideHint: Leave blank to use cores x clock, exactly as the spreadsheet does. Enter a platform-specific figure to override it.
f5-irules-runtime-calculator.downloadNote: Prefer a spreadsheet? Download the branded, offline-ready workbook with the same four tables, live formulas, and a guided walkthrough:

share.carries: The link carries the timing output and the three numbers as typed.

note.avgReliable: Average is the reliable column. Maximum is inflated because the first run of a freshly edited rule includes one-time compile-time optimization, and OS scheduling adds overhead at least once per tick; timing also carries a roughly 70 to 100 cycle margin of error. Push a large, representative load (ten thousand or more requests) and clear the stats once after the first hit.
note.coresXClock: Cycles per second is cores x clock (cores x MHz x 1,000,000), exactly as the DevCentral spreadsheet computes it from /proc/cpuinfo. Supply a platform-specific figure in the override to use a different basis.
note.cmpDemotion: These figures assume the work spreads across all cores (CMP). If the rule modifies a global variable it is demoted to a single core; recompute with cores = 1 for that case.
note.noneRecognised: No timing lines were recognized. Paste the output of tmsh show ltm rule '<'name> field-fmt (blocks with avg-cycles / min-cycles / max-cycles / total-executions), or lines of the form: HTTP_REQUEST 729 total 0 fail 0 abort | Cycles (min, avg, max) = (3693, 3959, 53936).

f5-irules-performance-linter.name: iRules performance linter
f5-irules-performance-linter.blurb: Paste an iRule; it flags F5-documented performance anti-patterns line by line, with severity, cause, and fix. The big one: global variables demote CMP. Local, no network.
f5-irules-performance-linter.irPlaceholder: Paste an iRule to scan for documented performance anti-patterns
f5-irules-performance-linter.summaryClean: No high-confidence anti-patterns found. This scan is not a substitute for measurement.
f5-irules-performance-linter.catGlobalDetail: Global variables demote the virtual server to a single TMM instance (CMP demotion), so one core handles all of its traffic. They have been deprecated since v10, and the old data-group-as-global form raises a runtime error and resets the client on v11 and later.
f5-irules-performance-linter.catGlobalFix: Use the CMP-safe static:: namespace for shared constants, ordinary local variables for per-connection data, or the class command for data groups. Never prefix a data group name with two colons.
f5-irules-performance-linter.catExprDetail: Without braces, Tcl substitutes and re-parses the expression and can double-substitute; bracing lets the bytecode compiler optimize it.
f5-irules-performance-linter.catExprFix: Wrap the expression in curly braces after expr.
f5-irules-performance-linter.catMatchclassDetail: matchclass and findclass were deprecated in v10; the class command offers better functionality and performance.
f5-irules-performance-linter.catMatchclassFix: Use class match or class search.
f5-irules-performance-linter.catRegexTitle: Regular expression in the data path
f5-irules-performance-linter.catRegexDetail: regexp and regsub cost materially more than fixed string work.
f5-irules-performance-linter.catRegexFix: When the match is a prefix, suffix, exact value, or simple glob, use string, scan, switch -glob, or a data group instead.

f5-release-cadence-calendar.name: F5 release cadence calendar
f5-release-cadence-calendar.blurb: F5 moved to a monthly security cadence in July 2026. This computes the upcoming hardened-release and security-notification dates so you can plan patch windows. Local, no network.
f5-release-cadence-calendar.inDays: in {n, plural, one {# day} other {# days}}
f5-release-cadence-calendar.daysAgo: {n, plural, one {# day} other {# days}} ago
f5-release-cadence-calendar.note1: Every date is a third Wednesday: that month's hardened release ships, and the previous month's security notification is published one month after the release it covers.
f5-release-cadence-calendar.note2: These are the scheduled dates. F5 also issues out-of-band security alerts and engineering hotfixes for urgent issues at any time, and retains flexibility to adjust notification timing.
