f5-bigd-thread-calculator.name: BigD thread calculator
f5-bigd-thread-calculator.blurb: Enter your vCPU count (and whether the system is hyperthreaded) to get the BigD thread count BIG-IP 21.1 derives automatically, per F5's documented formulas, plus the bigd.numprocs override cap and the 15,000-monitor ceiling.
f5-bigd-thread-calculator.inputPlaceholder: 8 r10900, 16 r4800, 22 velos, 8 ht, or just 6
f5-bigd-thread-calculator.runsLocally: Runs entirely in your browser: two documented formulas, no network, no clock.
f5-bigd-thread-calculator.threadsFloor: {floor, plural, one {{floor} thread} other {{floor} threads}} ({exact} exact)
f5-bigd-thread-calculator.fractionNote: F5 documents the formula but not a rounding rule for fractional results; the exact value and its whole-thread floor are both shown. The running system's own count is authoritative.
f5-bigd-thread-calculator.zeroNote: At 2 vCPUs the documented formula yields 0; bigd still runs as a single multi-threaded instance, so treat this edge as "minimal threading" rather than "no bigd".

config.heading: Override and ceiling
config.numprocsNote: bigd.numprocs sets the thread count by hand but is capped at the number of available vCPUs; its default 0 means the count is calculated automatically with the formula above.

f5-bigd-thread-calculator.verifyNote: Formulas verbatim from F5's BIG-IP 21.1.0 release notes (BigD enhancements for large-scale configurations). For sizing beyond 5,000 monitor instances, F5's 21.0 notes point to In-TMM monitors.

errors.empty: Enter a vCPU count, optionally followed by ht or normal.
errors.format: Could not read that. Try a count plus a type, like "8 ht" or "16 normal".
errors.range: The vCPU count must be a whole number between 1 and 1024.

platform.heading: Platform:
platform.htNote: This platform is hyperthreaded: each Intel core appears as two vCPUs, so the hyperthreaded formula applies to the vCPU count the tenant sees.
platform.normalNote: This platform does not use hyperthreading: it counts physical CPU cores only, so the normal formula applies.
platform.veNote: Virtual Edition inherits whatever the hypervisor exposes. Check inside the guest (lscpu: "Thread(s) per core", 2 means hyperthreaded) and pick the matching formula; both are shown.
platform.rseriesAmbiguous: rSeries splits down the middle: r5000/r10000/r12000 are hyperthreaded, r2000/r4000 are not. Enter the model (e.g. r10900, r4800) and the right formula is selected.
platform.not21x: Context only: this platform cannot run BIG-IP 21.x, and the multi-threaded BigD with these formulas is a 21.1 feature. It stays on 17.x with the classic bigd.
platform.overridden: Your explicit ht/normal choice overrides this platform's documented default (useful when hyperthreading is disabled in firmware).

E-APP-1.action: Read the application's own logs on the members that served failing requests, at the failure timestamps.

E-APP-2.action: Reproduce against a backend member directly, bypassing the fronting layer, and compare.

cmd.load-balancer: curl to the member IP:port with the Host header set - isolates app vs LB

E-APP-3.action: Check the health of the app's own dependencies (database, cache, queue, downstream APIs) for the same window.

E-ASY-1.action: Trace the path in BOTH directions and overlay them; asymmetry itself is normal, asymmetry through stateful devices is the suspect.

E-ASY-2.action: Compare policy/NAT rules on the diverging legs; look for the flow in each device's session table.

E-ASY-3.action: If ECMP is in play, pin a test flow to each member (vary source port) and map which member fails.

E-CAP-1.action: Compare interface, CPU, memory, and connection-count graphs at the incident hour against the same hour on a known-good day.

E-CAP-2.action: Look for drops, retransmits, or queue growth on the path devices during the window.

cmd.load-balancer: tmsh show sys performance; tmsh show ltm virtual '<'vs> - watch conns and drops

E-CAP-3.action: Check whether a growth event (new site, campaign, batch job) coincides with symptom onset.

E-CHG-1.action: Pull the exact change record: what was changed, where, and the precise timestamps.

E-CHG-2.action: Diff the changed configuration against the last known-good version.

cmd.generic: diff against your config backup / git history
cmd.load-balancer: tmsh show sys config-diff (or compare UCS archives)

E-CHG-3.action: Establish first-error time from logs and compare it to the change window, not to when users reported.

E-CHG-4.action: If a safe rollback path exists, test the rollback in a maintenance window rather than debating it.

E-CLI-1.action: Reproduce from a second machine and from a different network (e.g. a phone hotspot); note which combination fails.

E-CLI-2.action: Compare the affected client's resolver, proxy, and VPN settings against a working client's.

E-CLI-3.action: Temporarily rule the endpoint security stack in or out in line with your organization's policy.

E-DNS-1.action: Resolve the name against the client's configured resolver AND directly against an authoritative server; compare answers and TTLs.

E-DNS-2.action: Check when the record last changed and whether the failure window matches a TTL expiry after that change.

E-DNS-3.action: Verify the resolver itself is reachable and answering from the affected client network.

cmd.load-balancer: if a GSLB/wide-IP answers this name, check pool member availability and last resort behaviour

E-EXT-1.action: Pull the provider's status history and maintenance calendar for the exact window; open a ticket referencing your circuit/service IDs.

E-EXT-2.action: Correlate: do OTHER services from the same provider show the same degradation shape?

E-IDN-1.action: Check the identity provider's status and its logs for the affected window and client set.

E-IDN-2.action: Compare NTP-synced time on every token validator; skew beyond the allowed window silently invalidates good tokens.

E-IDN-3.action: Decode a failing token and verify audience, issuer, expiry, and the signing key id against current metadata.

cmd.load-balancer: if an access policy fronts the app, read its per-session logs for the failing branch

E-MTU-1.action: Probe the path with do-not-fragment pings at increasing sizes to find the largest that passes.
E-MTU-1.cmd: ping -M do -s 1472 '<'host> (Linux) / ping -f -l 1472 (Windows), then step down

E-MTU-2.action: Trace the path and list every tunnel, VPN, or encapsulation layer on it; check each hop's MTU.

E-MTU-3.action: Verify whether ICMP 'fragmentation needed' is being filtered anywhere on the path - PMTUD depends on it arriving.

E-PBK-1.action: Read per-member health and error counters, not the aggregate; averages hide one bad member.

cmd.load-balancer: tmsh show ltm pool '<'pool> members - status, cur conns, total fails per member

E-PBK-2.action: Correlate failing user sessions to the specific member that served them (persistence records, logs, response headers).

E-PBK-3.action: Drain the suspect member and watch the error rate; a controlled drain is evidence, not remediation.

E-PRV-1.action: Walk the path end to end in order: name resolves -> address routes -> firewall permits -> service listens -> TLS presents -> health checks pass. Stop at the first broken link.

E-PRV-2.action: Verify the request actually arrives at the service (packet capture or connection logs at the destination).

cmd.load-balancer: check the virtual server's stats for the test's packets; zero conns means it never arrived

E-PRV-3.action: Compare against a working sibling service's provisioning as a reference checklist.

E-SHD-1.action: List what every affected service actually shares (device, circuit, provider, IdP, database) - draw it, don't assume it.

E-SHD-2.action: Check provider/platform status pages and maintenance notices for the exact window.

E-SHD-3.action: Test one path that deliberately bypasses the suspected shared element.

E-TLS-1.action: Run a raw handshake against the affected endpoint and read the verdict: expiry, chain completeness, SAN match, negotiated protocol and cipher.

cmd.load-balancer: openssl s_client to the virtual server AND to a pool member - the two TLS legs are separate

E-TLS-2.action: Check certificate notBefore/notAfter against the fault onset time; certificates expire without any change being made.

E-TLS-3.action: Confirm which side terminated: client-facing certificate vs backend re-encryption use different material and fail independently.

cmd.load-balancer: compare client-ssl and server-ssl profile chains and options

H-APP-BACKEND.rationale: Transport succeeding while the application errors moves the domain up the stack: the app process, its configuration, or a dependency behind it (database, queue, downstream API).
H-APP-BACKEND.supports0: Application logs at the serving member show errors matching the window
H-APP-BACKEND.supports1: Bypassing the intermediary and hitting a member directly reproduces the error
H-APP-BACKEND.supports2: A dependency (DB, queue, API) reports degradation in the window
H-APP-BACKEND.title: Application or backend dependency
H-APP-BACKEND.weakens0: Direct-to-member requests succeed while only the fronted path fails (suspect the intermediary instead)

H-ASYMMETRIC-PATH.rationale: One path working while another fails points at divergence between them: routing asymmetry, an ECMP hash bucket, a policy or NAT rule on one leg, or a stateful device seeing only half the flow.
H-ASYMMETRIC-PATH.supports0: Traceroutes in each direction take different paths
H-ASYMMETRIC-PATH.supports1: Failures map to one ECMP member or one firewall of a pair
H-ASYMMETRIC-PATH.supports2: A stateful device logs half-open or out-of-state drops
H-ASYMMETRIC-PATH.title: Asymmetric path or policy divergence
H-ASYMMETRIC-PATH.weakens0: Both directions traverse identical, healthy paths

H-CAPACITY-SATURATION.rationale: Slowness that tracks load - time of day, growth trend, or an event - points at a saturated resource: link, CPU, memory, connection table, or a queue in between.
H-CAPACITY-SATURATION.supports0: Utilization graphs at the incident hour sit at or near a ceiling
H-CAPACITY-SATURATION.supports2: Connection counts or queue drops climb with the symptom
H-CAPACITY-SATURATION.title: Capacity or saturation ceiling
H-CAPACITY-SATURATION.weakens0: Resources sit far below limits during the symptom window
H-CAPACITY-SATURATION.weakens1: Symptom occurs equally at negligible load

H-CHANGE-REGRESSION.rationale: Onset aligned with a known change is the strongest single signal in fault isolation: the change is a hypothesis to test first, not a culprit to assume.
H-CHANGE-REGRESSION.supports0: Fault onset timestamp matches the change record within minutes
H-CHANGE-REGRESSION.supports1: Rolling the change back in a test path clears the symptom
H-CHANGE-REGRESSION.supports2: Only surfaces touched by the change are affected
H-CHANGE-REGRESSION.title: Regression from the recent change
H-CHANGE-REGRESSION.weakens0: Log evidence shows the symptom predates the change
H-CHANGE-REGRESSION.weakens1: Unchanged, unrelated systems show the same symptom

H-CLIENT-LOCAL.rationale: A single affected user makes the client environment - its resolver, proxy, cache, security agent, or network segment - the cheapest domain to eliminate first.
H-CLIENT-LOCAL.supports0: A second machine on the same network reproduces cleanly
H-CLIENT-LOCAL.supports1: The same user succeeds from a different machine or network
H-CLIENT-LOCAL.title: Client-local environment
H-CLIENT-LOCAL.weakens0: Multiple independent clients on different networks show the same failure

H-DNS-RESOLUTION.rationale: When a service works by IP but not by name, or lookups fail outright, the resolution chain (client resolver, forwarder, authoritative, record content, TTL) is the domain to test before anything else.
H-DNS-RESOLUTION.supports0: Direct-to-IP access works while the name fails
H-DNS-RESOLUTION.supports1: dig against the configured resolver and the authoritative server disagree
H-DNS-RESOLUTION.supports2: Failures correlate with a recent zone or record change, or a TTL expiry
H-DNS-RESOLUTION.title: Name-resolution path
H-DNS-RESOLUTION.weakens1: Resolution returns correct, fresh records from every vantage point

H-EXTERNAL-PROVIDER.rationale: Provider maintenance - announced or otherwise - is a fault domain you verify against their record, not against your own configuration.
H-EXTERNAL-PROVIDER.supports0: Provider status page or maintenance calendar matches the window
H-EXTERNAL-PROVIDER.supports1: Circuits or services from the same provider degrade together
H-EXTERNAL-PROVIDER.title: External provider or maintenance window
H-EXTERNAL-PROVIDER.weakens0: Provider confirms clean health and paths avoiding them fail identically

H-IDENTITY-CHAIN.rationale: Authentication failures usually live in the chain, not the app: the IdP, clock skew breaking token validation, expired signing material, or an audience/issuer mismatch after a change.
H-IDENTITY-CHAIN.supports0: IdP status or logs mark errors in the window
H-IDENTITY-CHAIN.supports1: Validator clock skew exceeds token tolerance
H-IDENTITY-CHAIN.supports2: Tokens inspected show wrong audience/issuer or expired signing keys
H-IDENTITY-CHAIN.title: Identity and token chain
H-IDENTITY-CHAIN.weakens0: Tokens validate cleanly end-to-end and the same credentials work on a sibling app

H-PARTIAL-BACKEND.rationale: Intermittent failures hitting some users while others sail through is the signature of one bad member in a pool or ECMP set: whoever hashes to it, hurts.
H-PARTIAL-BACKEND.supports0: Failures correlate to one specific member when per-member stats are read
H-PARTIAL-BACKEND.supports1: Draining the suspect member clears the symptom
H-PARTIAL-BACKEND.supports2: Health monitors flap on exactly one member
H-PARTIAL-BACKEND.title: One unhealthy member behind a balanced service
H-PARTIAL-BACKEND.weakens1: Symptom persists with the suspect member drained

H-PATH-MTU.rationale: Small transactions succeeding while large transfers hang is the classic MTU signature, usually introduced by a tunnel, VPN, or encapsulation added somewhere on the path.
H-PATH-MTU.supports0: Pings with DF set succeed at 1400 bytes and fail near 1500
H-PATH-MTU.supports1: A tunnel or overlay was recently introduced on the path
H-PATH-MTU.supports2: TCP sessions establish, then stall on the first large segment
H-PATH-MTU.title: Path MTU / fragmentation behaviour
H-PATH-MTU.weakens1: Full-size DF probes traverse the path cleanly

H-PROVISIONING-GAP.rationale: A brand-new service that has never worked is a provisioning checklist, not a fault: some link in DNS, addressing, routing advertisement, firewall policy, certificate, or health-check config was never completed.
H-PROVISIONING-GAP.supports0: The service has never worked from the affected vantage point
H-PROVISIONING-GAP.supports1: A checklist walk finds a concrete missing element
H-PROVISIONING-GAP.supports2: It works from one network segment but was never opened from another
H-PROVISIONING-GAP.title: Incomplete provisioning of the new path
H-PROVISIONING-GAP.weakens0: The service demonstrably worked before from the same vantage point (then this is a change/regression question instead)

H-SHARED-DEPENDENCY.rationale: When everyone is affected at once, the fault domain is whatever everyone shares: a core device, a circuit, a provider, an identity provider, or a common backend.
H-SHARED-DEPENDENCY.supports0: Independent services with only the shared element in common fail together
H-SHARED-DEPENDENCY.supports1: Provider or platform status reporting matches the window
H-SHARED-DEPENDENCY.supports2: The shared device's own health or logs mark the onset
H-SHARED-DEPENDENCY.title: Shared upstream dependency
H-SHARED-DEPENDENCY.weakens0: Paths bypassing the suspected shared element fail identically

H-TLS-PKI.rationale: TLS failures cluster around a small set of testable causes: expiry, incomplete chain, name mismatch, protocol/cipher mismatch, and - on terminating proxies - a client-side leg that differs from the server-side leg.
H-TLS-PKI.supports0: openssl s_client shows expiry, chain, or SAN problems directly
H-TLS-PKI.supports1: Failures began at a certificate's notAfter instant with no other change
H-TLS-PKI.supports2: Only clients enforcing newer/older protocol versions fail
H-TLS-PKI.title: TLS handshake and certificate chain
H-TLS-PKI.weakens0: Plain-TCP or cleartext checks to the same endpoint also fail
H-TLS-PKI.weakens1: Handshake completes cleanly from every client profile

md.method: This worksheet structures hypotheses to TEST, ranked by deterministic rules over the described situation. It is not a diagnosis; evidence decides. Generated locally in the browser - nothing was uploaded.
md.residualCoherent: These leftovers agree with each other on {id}: {observations}. Unexplained observations that cohere are the signature of a SECOND, separate fault - consider testing it as one rather than folding it into the first.
md.residualIntro: The leading hypothesis does not account for these reported observations:
md.residualNoCommon: They share no common alternative, so this is more likely noise or detail the rule set does not model than a second fault.
md.residualUncovered: - {value} (no rule in this engine covers it)
md.title: Fault hypothesis worksheet

rule.R-APP-5XX: 5xx is the server side declaring its own failure; the serving app's logs are primary evidence.
rule.R-APP-TCPOK: Transport succeeds and the application errors - the domain moves up the stack to the app and its dependencies.
rule.R-ASYM-PATH: Divergent behaviour between two paths is observed - test the divergence itself.
rule.R-AUTH-SYMPTOM: Authentication-shaped failures put the identity chain (IdP, clocks, tokens, signing material) in primary scope.
rule.R-CAP-GROWTH: A known growth event moves capacity ceilings into scope on its own.
rule.R-CAP-TOD: Slowness tracking time of day is the load-following signature of a saturated resource.
rule.R-CHG-ALIGN: Onset is reported as 'since a change' and an internal change is on record - alignment of the two is the strongest isolation signal.
rule.R-CHG-DEPLOY-5XX: Server-side 5xx after a software deploy reinforces the regression hypothesis specifically at the application layer.
rule.R-CHG-PRESENT: A config/software/network change is on record even though onset wasn't reported as change-aligned - worth testing the timeline before dismissing it.
rule.R-DNS-BYNAME: Working by IP while failing by name isolates the fault to the resolution path almost by definition.
rule.R-DNS-FAILS: Observed lookup failures put the resolution chain directly in scope.
rule.R-EXT-ALIGN: Onset aligned with the provider's maintenance window strengthens the case for verifying their record first.
rule.R-MTU-LARGE: Size-dependent failure (small OK, large stalls) is the classic path-MTU signature.
rule.R-MTU-NETCHANGE: A network change alongside size-dependent failure suggests a new tunnel/encapsulation on the path.
rule.R-NEWSVC: A service that has never worked is a provisioning walk, not a regression hunt.
rule.R-PARTIAL-5XX: Partial 5xx (not a full outage) is consistent with a subset of members erroring.
rule.R-PARTIAL-INTERMIT: Some users failing while others succeed on the same service is the one-bad-member signature behind a balanced pool.
rule.R-PROVIDER-MAINT: Known provider maintenance in the window must be verified against their record before deeper internal digging.
rule.R-PROVIDER-TIMEOUTS-SITE: Site-wide timeouts are consistent with that site's upstream circuit or provider path degrading.
rule.R-SCOPE-EVERYONE: Everyone down at once points at whatever everyone shares.
rule.R-SCOPE-ONEUSER: A single affected user makes the client environment the cheapest domain to eliminate first.
rule.R-SCOPE-SITE: One whole site affected points at that site's shared elements: its uplink, its edge devices, its local services.
rule.R-TLS-CERTCHANGE: Certificate or key material changed recently; the TLS legs touched by it are a primary test target.
rule.R-TLS-ERRORS: Handshake errors are observed - the TLS/PKI domain must be tested directly.
rule.R-TLS-SILENT-EXPIRY: TLS errors with 'nothing changed' fits the silent-expiry pattern: certificates expire without anyone changing anything.

warn.W-NOCHANGE: 'Nothing changed' is a hypothesis, not a fact. Verify it against the change record, deployment logs, and provider maintenance calendars before trusting it - most faults follow a change somebody didn't mention.
warn.W-OUTAGE-ONEUSER: 'Total outage' scoped to one user usually means 'total for that user' - confirm whether anyone else is affected before treating it as an outage.
warn.W-SPARSE-CLUES: No layer clues selected. The ranking below leans on scope/timing alone; two minutes spent gathering one concrete observation (does it work by IP? does TLS handshake?) will sharpen it considerably.

change-window-runbook-builder.name: Change Window Runbook Builder
change-window-runbook-builder.blurb: Describe a planned change in six structured fields; a fixed rule set assembles an ordered runbook across six phases - with the risks the plan carries and readiness cautions about the input. Advisory structure to review and adapt, never an approval.

form.heading: Describe the change (quick mode)
form.changeType: What kind of change is this?
form.safeguards: What is already in place? (all that apply)

change-window-runbook-builder.runsLocally: Runs entirely in your browser. The free-text notes flow only into the exported runbook - they never influence which steps appear, and nothing is uploaded.
change-window-runbook-builder.emptyState: Describe the change above and the runbook appears here - phased, with the risks it carries, live as you refine.

notes.heading: Optional detail for the export (does not affect the runbook)
notes.hint: These lines are copied verbatim into the runbook's Change summary so a change ticket starts complete.

results.heading: Your runbook
results.framing: Assembled by deterministic rules over what you described - a proposal to review and adapt, not an approval. Work the phases in order; check off steps as you go.
results.whyIntro: Every rule that fired, with its reason. The runbook is the sum - inspectable, never an oracle.

budget.heading: Rollback time budget (optional)
budget.hint: Minutes left in the window, and how long the rollback and the check after it take, from a rehearsal of this change. The tool only does the arithmetic.
budget.verify: Verification after the rollback, in minutes
budget.invalid: Enter all three as whole minutes from 0 to 1440 to see the budget.
budget.fits: The rollback still fits: {margin} min of margin after reserving {needed} min.
budget.noMargin: No margin left: the {needed} min the rollback needs fill the window exactly.
budget.exceeds: The rollback no longer fits: it is {short} min short of the {needed} min it needs.

share.carries: The link carries the form, the time budget and your notes as typed, not your ticks; a note holding a credential gets none.
share.caution: Your notes can name hosts, the change ticket and the back-out owner: read them before you send the link.
share.maybeSecret: “{field}” may hold a secret ({label}): check it before you send the link.
share.blockedSecret: No link: “{field}” holds what looks like a credential ({label}). Put a placeholder in its place, then share again.

budget.exceeds: the rollback no longer fits the window
budget.noMargin: no margin left: start the rollback now if the change is not confirmed
budget.rehearsal: - Times should come from a rehearsal of this change; the margin is arithmetic, not a guarantee.

md.method: This runbook is assembled by deterministic rules over the described change - a proposal to review and adapt, not an approval and not a guarantee. A human runs it and signs off. Generated locally in the browser; nothing was uploaded.
md.title: Change window runbook

RK-BROAD-BLAST.label: Broad blast radius
RK-BROAD-BLAST.note: Many services or users share this path; a small mistake is a large incident.

RK-BUSINESS-HOURS.label: Change during business hours
RK-BUSINESS-HOURS.note: Users are active; impact is felt immediately. Prefer a maintenance window if the change allows.

RK-CERT-OUTAGE.label: Certificate change affects every TLS client
RK-CERT-OUTAGE.note: A wrong chain or mismatched key breaks the handshake for everyone at once; verify the pair and chain before install.

RK-DNS-TTL.label: DNS change propagates over TTL
RK-DNS-TTL.note: The old answer lingers in caches for the TTL; a mistake is not undone instantly.

RK-EMERGENCY.label: Emergency change, compressed process
RK-EMERGENCY.note: Speed raises the error rate; slow down on the irreversible steps even when the clock is loud.

RK-HARD-REVERSE.label: Hard to reverse
RK-HARD-REVERSE.note: Rollback is slow or lossy; treat the pre-change verification as the real safety net.

RK-NO-BACKUP.label: No backup recorded
RK-NO-BACKUP.note: Without a fresh, verified backup there is nothing to roll back to. Take one first.

RK-ONEWAY.label: One-way change: no clean rollback
RK-ONEWAY.note: Prevention beats back-out here; verify twice and have a forward-fix ready.

RK-PROD-CRITICAL.label: Business-critical production
RK-PROD-CRITICAL.note: The cost of an outage is high; keep the blast radius and the window as tight as possible.

RK-ROLLBACK-UNTESTED.label: Rollback not tested
RK-ROLLBACK-UNTESTED.note: A written but untested back-out often fails when it is finally needed.

RK-SHARED-INFRA.label: Shared infrastructure
RK-SHARED-INFRA.note: Other services ride this device or link; confirm what else is affected before you start.

rule.R-BACKUP-STEP: A reversible change needs a fresh backup up front, explicit back-out steps that restore it, and a fresh post-change backup at the end.
rule.R-BASE-SPINE: Every change gets the operational spine: scope it, baseline it, confirm approval, apply, verify against the baseline, watch, and close out with a defined rollback trigger.
rule.R-BROAD-BLAST: A wide blast radius means a small mistake is a large incident; the affected surface must be listed before you start.
rule.R-BUSINESS-HOURS: Changing during business hours means users feel impact immediately; notify them and move in small, reversible steps.
rule.R-CERT-ROTATION: A certificate rotation breaks every TLS client at once if the pair or chain is wrong; stage and verify the material before install, then test the handshake end to end.
rule.R-COMMS-NOTIFY: No pre-change notice is marked as sent; the affected stakeholders and users need one before the window.
rule.R-DNS-CHANGE: A DNS change propagates over the record TTL rather than instantly; plan the timing and verify resolution from more than one vantage point.
rule.R-DNS-PRESET: A DNS-flavored change still propagates over TTL; the old answer lingers in caches, so a mistake is not undone instantly.
rule.R-EMERGENCY-NOW: An emergency change compresses the process but is still a recorded change; capture the reason and get expedited approval.
rule.R-FAILOVER-MAINT: A failover or maintenance change turns on a healthy peer: confirm HA state, drain the node before touching it, and restore it to service afterwards.
rule.R-FIREWALL-DIFF: A firewall change is easy to get subtly wrong; review the diff, move in small steps, and verify both that intended traffic passes and unintended traffic is still blocked.
rule.R-HARD-REVERSE: Reversal is slow or lossy, so the back-out steps must be written out and the pre-change verification carries the safety.
rule.R-LB-HA-AWARE: On a load balancer, a config or software change should respect the HA pair: confirm the peer and change one unit at a time.
rule.R-MAINT-WINDOW: A scheduled window needs its bounds confirmed and a check that no conflicting change shares it.
rule.R-NO-BACKUP-WARN: The change is reversible but no backup is recorded yet; without one there is nothing to roll back to.
rule.R-ONEWAY: There is no clean rollback, so the plan leads with prevention and a forward-fix rather than a back-out.
rule.R-PROD-CRITICAL: Business-critical production raises the cost of any slip: confirm the blast radius and stand up a bridge with named roles.
rule.R-ROLLBACK-UNTESTED: A rollback is possible but not marked as tested; an untested back-out often fails when it is finally needed.
rule.R-SCALE-CAPACITY: A capacity change adds or resizes members incrementally and verifies each takes traffic before the next.
rule.R-SHARED-INFRA: Shared infrastructure carries other services; confirm what else rides this device and move in small, checked increments.
rule.R-SOFTWARE-UPGRADE: A software upgrade should land on one node first and be verified there before it rolls across the rest.

S-AP-APPROVAL.text: Confirm the change is approved (change ticket in the approved state, or the emergency equivalent) before you touch anything.

S-AP-BRIDGE.text: For a high-impact change, open a bridge or a chat channel and name who is running the change, who is watching monitoring, and who makes the rollback call.

S-AP-FREEZE.text: Confirm no conflicting change is running on the same systems in this window - check the change calendar.

S-AP-NOTIFY.text: Send the pre-change notice to the stakeholders and the affected users: what, when, expected impact, and how long.

S-CO-CLOSE.text: Close the change ticket with what was actually done, any deviations from the plan, and anything to watch over the next day.

S-CO-CONFIRM.text: Confirm success against the baseline one more time, then send the all-clear to the same people you notified.

cmd.load-balancer: tmsh save sys config; save a fresh post-change UCS archive

S-CO-SAVE.text: Persist the new configuration and take a fresh backup of the post-change state, so the new good state is the one that restores next time.

cmd.dns: edit the record/zone; increment the SOA serial; reload the zone
cmd.firewall: apply the policy change; commit only after reviewing the diff
cmd.load-balancer: make the change; tmsh save sys config once verified

S-EX-APPLY.text: Apply the change itself, following the exact steps you wrote in pre-flight - read them, do not improvise at the keyboard.

cmd.load-balancer: import the cert/key/chain; update the client-ssl profile; the change takes effect on new connections
cmd.tls-pki: install the new cert and chain; reload the service that serves it

S-EX-CERT-INSTALL.text: Install the staged certificate and chain, bind it where it is used, and be ready to check every service that presents it.

S-EX-DNS-TTL.text: Remember DNS change is not instant: it propagates over the record's TTL, so plan the timing around it and lower the TTL ahead of a cutover if you can.

cmd.load-balancer: set the pool member to disabled (allow existing connections to finish) before the change

S-EX-DRAIN.text: Drain connections from the node before changing it, rather than dropping active sessions.

cmd.load-balancer: change the standby (or one pool member) first; verify; then fail over / proceed

S-EX-ONE-NODE-FIRST.text: Apply the change to one node first, verify it there, and only then roll it across the rest - never all members at once.

S-EX-SEQUENCE.text: Work in small, reversible increments where possible, and after each one pause to confirm it did what you expected before moving on.

cmd.dns: back up the zone files / export the zone before editing
cmd.firewall: export the running configuration and confirm the file downloads
cmd.generic: export or snapshot the current config and verify the file opens
cmd.load-balancer: save sys config; save a UCS archive (tmsh save sys ucs pre-change.ucs)

S-PF-BACKUP.text: Take a fresh configuration backup of every device you will touch and confirm it is readable before you start.

cmd.dns: record current resolution answers and TTLs for the names in scope
cmd.load-balancer: tmsh show sys performance; note virtual-server and pool member status
cmd.tls-pki: record current certificate notAfter and chain for the endpoints in scope

S-PF-BASELINE.text: Capture a health baseline now - the metrics and a few known-good probes you will re-check afterwards - so 'working' has a definition.

S-PF-BLAST.text: Confirm the blast radius: list what shares this device or path and could be affected beyond the intended target, and decide whether that is acceptable for this window.

cmd.generic: verify the new key/cert pair and chain offline before install
cmd.tls-pki: openssl x509 -noout -modulus -in new.crt | openssl md5; compare to the key modulus; openssl verify -untrusted chain.pem new.crt

S-PF-CERT-STAGE.text: Stage the new certificate and its full chain, and verify the key matches and the chain is complete, before installing anything.

S-PF-EMERGENCY-NOTE.text: This is an emergency change: capture the reason it cannot wait and get whatever expedited approval your process allows, even if retroactive - an emergency change is still a recorded change.

cmd.firewall: confirm the HA peer is healthy and in sync before touching either unit
cmd.load-balancer: tmsh show cm failover-status; confirm the standby is in sync

S-PF-HA.text: If this runs on a high-availability pair or cluster, confirm the peer is healthy and will carry the load, and know which unit you are acting on.

S-PF-MAINT-WINDOW.text: Confirm you are inside the approved maintenance window and that the people who need to be available are.

S-PF-SCOPE.text: Write down exactly what is changing, on which systems, and the precise start and end you expect - the same words go in the change ticket.

S-RB-ONEWAY.text: This change is hard to reverse: there is no clean rollback, so the plan must lead with prevention - extra verification before and during, and a forward-fix plan for when back-out is not an option.

cmd.dns: restore the previous record/zone; increment the SOA; reload
cmd.firewall: restore the exported configuration; confirm the previous policy is active
cmd.load-balancer: restore the pre-change UCS / config; verify the virtual server serves the old behaviour

S-RB-STEPS.text: Write the back-out steps explicitly - restoring from the backup you took, in order - so rollback is a procedure to follow, not a decision to make under pressure.

S-RB-TESTED.text: Confirm the rollback has actually been tested, not just written - an untested back-out is a hope, not a plan.

S-RB-TRIGGER.text: Decide the rollback trigger BEFORE you start: the specific signal (error rate, failed probe, elapsed time with no success) that means you back out rather than push on.

cmd.dns: resolve the names in scope from a client and from the authoritative server; compare
cmd.firewall: test that the intended traffic passes and the unintended traffic is still blocked
cmd.load-balancer: test through the virtual server end to end; watch pool member and connection stats
cmd.tls-pki: openssl s_client to the endpoint; confirm the new chain, SAN, and expiry

S-VF-FUNCTIONAL.text: Test the actual user-facing function through the changed path, not just the device's own status.

S-VF-REPEAT-BASELINE.text: Re-run the exact baseline checks you captured in pre-flight and compare - the change is verified when the known-good probes pass again, not when the command returned zero.

cmd.load-balancer: re-enable the pool member; confirm it returns to the active pool and passes health checks

S-VF-RESTORE-STATE.text: Re-enable anything you drained or disabled during the change, and confirm it takes traffic normally.

S-VF-WATCH.text: Watch monitoring and error rates for a defined soak period before you call it done - some failures only show under real traffic a few minutes in.

warn.W-BUDGET-EXCEEDED: The remaining window ({remaining} min) no longer holds the rollback ({rollback} min) plus the verification after it ({verify} min): it is {short} min short. The stop criterion has already passed; back out now or agree an extension, rather than finishing the change late.
warn.W-BUDGET-NO-MARGIN: The rollback ({rollback} min) plus its verification ({verify} min) exactly fill the remaining window ({remaining} min). There is no margin left: if the change is not confirmed healthy now, this is the moment to start the rollback.
warn.W-CRITICAL-BUSINESS-HOURS: This is a business-critical system and the window is business hours. If the change can wait for a maintenance window, that is the safer plan.
warn.W-NO-APPROVAL: The change is not marked as approved. Confirm approval before you begin; this runbook does not approve anything.
warn.W-NO-BACKUP: No backup is marked as taken. A reversible change still needs a fresh, verified backup before you start - there is otherwise nothing to roll back to.

incident-timeline-rca-builder.blurb: RCA stands for root cause analysis - the disciplined walk from an incident's symptoms back to the conditions that allowed it. Enter an incident's events as a small timeline and mark the contributing-factor domains you observed; a fixed rule set orders the timeline, derives the milestone spans, and structures candidate contributing factors with the evidence for each. It never names a root cause - candidates to investigate, not a verdict.

clock.heading: Clock check (optional)
clock.hint: When events come from different sources, enter each one's logged time and its source's clock offset in milliseconds, on one shared scale. The offset uses NTP's sign: the reference clock minus the source's clock, so a source running 100 ms fast has an offset of -100. The uncertainty is what is still unknown after the correction.
clock.incomplete: Fill all three fields with whole milliseconds, the uncertainty 0 or more, for each event you want checked.

capacity-saturation.confirm0: Utilization at the incident window sat at or near a ceiling
capacity-saturation.confirm2: A growth or event (campaign, batch, new site) coincided with onset
capacity-saturation.rationale: If the incident tracked load or growth, a saturated resource (link, CPU, memory, connection table, queue) is a domain to investigate.
capacity-saturation.ruleOut0: Resources sat well below limits throughout the window
capacity-saturation.ruleOut1: The symptom occurred at negligible load
capacity-saturation.title: Capacity or saturation

configuration-error.confirm0: The running configuration differs from the intended or last-known-good version
configuration-error.confirm1: Correcting the configuration cleared the symptom
configuration-error.rationale: A wrong or drifted configuration is a domain to test, distinct from the act of change: config can be wrong without a recent change (drift, a latent error surfaced by conditions).
configuration-error.ruleOut0: The configuration matches the intended version exactly
configuration-error.ruleOut1: The symptom persisted after the configuration was corrected
configuration-error.title: A configuration error

dependency-failure.confirm0: A dependency's own health signals degraded in the same window
dependency-failure.confirm1: The affected service recovered when the dependency did
dependency-failure.confirm2: Errors point at calls to the dependency specifically
dependency-failure.rationale: If a downstream service, database, or shared component degraded, the incident may be a symptom of its failure rather than of the affected service itself.
dependency-failure.ruleOut0: Every dependency stayed healthy through the window
dependency-failure.ruleOut1: The service failed even on paths that do not touch the dependency
dependency-failure.title: A failed dependency

expired-credential.confirm0: A certificate or credential's expiry instant matches the symptom onset
expired-credential.rationale: Certificates and credentials expire on their own schedule with no change made; if the timeline shows TLS or auth failures, this is a domain to check against expiry instants.
expired-credential.ruleOut0: All relevant certificates and credentials were valid through the window
expired-credential.ruleOut1: The failure was not authentication or handshake related
expired-credential.title: An expired certificate or credential

external-provider.confirm0: The provider's status history shows an incident overlapping your window
external-provider.confirm1: Your symptom cleared when theirs did
external-provider.rationale: If a provider (cloud, transit, DNS, upstream API) had an incident in the same window, the contributing factor may be theirs; the evidence is their status history, checked against your timeline.
external-provider.ruleOut0: The provider reported healthy throughout the window
external-provider.ruleOut1: The symptom appeared on paths that do not traverse the provider
external-provider.title: An external provider

human-process-gap.confirm0: A defined step was skipped or a runbook was ambiguous at the decision point
human-process-gap.confirm1: The same gap has contributed to a prior incident
human-process-gap.rationale: Sometimes the contributing factor is in the process - a missed step, an unclear runbook, a handoff that dropped - and naming it is how the process improves, not how blame is assigned.
human-process-gap.ruleOut0: The process was followed as written and the outcome still occurred
human-process-gap.title: A process or human-factors gap

monitoring-gap.confirm0: The symptom began well before any alert fired or a human noticed
monitoring-gap.confirm1: No monitor covered the failing signal
monitoring-gap.rationale: If the timeline shows a long gap between symptom onset and detection, the monitoring itself is a domain to investigate - not as the cause of the incident, but as why it ran longer than it needed to.
monitoring-gap.ruleOut0: An alert fired promptly at or near symptom onset
monitoring-gap.ruleOut1: Detection was immediate and the delay was elsewhere
monitoring-gap.title: A detection or monitoring gap

recent-change.confirm0: The change record's timestamp sits just before the first symptom event in the timeline
recent-change.confirm1: Rolling the change back cleared the symptom
recent-change.confirm2: Only surfaces the change touched were affected
recent-change.rationale: A change close to the symptom onset is the most common contributing factor and the first to test against the timeline - alignment is a hypothesis to confirm, not a verdict.
recent-change.ruleOut0: The first symptom event precedes the change
recent-change.ruleOut1: Unchanged, unrelated systems showed the same symptom
recent-change.title: A recent change

unknown-still.confirm0: The evidence needed to distinguish the remaining candidates has not yet been collected
unknown-still.rationale: An honest RCA scaffold names what is still not understood. Leaving this open is a finding, not a failure: it marks the evidence still owed before the review can close.
unknown-still.ruleOut0: Evidence has confirmed one of the other candidates and closed the question
unknown-still.title: Still unknown

RK-LONG-DETECT-GAP.label: Long gap before detection
RK-LONG-DETECT-GAP.note: Several events passed between the symptom beginning and it being detected; the monitoring-gap candidate is worth investigating.

RK-NO-CHANGE-EVENT.label: No change recorded in the timeline
RK-NO-CHANGE-EVENT.note: If a change contributed, adding it to the timeline lets its alignment be reasoned about; if none, that is itself a finding.

rule.R-CHANGE-IN-TIMELINE: The timeline records a change; its alignment with the symptom onset is a candidate to test even though it was not listed as an observed factor.
rule.R-DETECT-GAP: Several events passed between the symptom beginning and detection; the monitoring/detection domain is a candidate for why the incident ran as long as it did.
rule.R-NO-CHANGE: No change is recorded in the timeline; if one contributed, adding it lets its alignment be reasoned about, and if none did, that absence is itself a finding.
rule.R-NO-DETECT: No detection milestone is recorded, so detection time cannot be reasoned about; add when the incident became known.
rule.R-NO-RESOLVE: No resolution milestone is recorded, so the incident duration is unbounded; add when service was restored.
rule.R-OBSERVED-FACTORS: Each contributing-factor domain you observed is surfaced as a candidate to investigate, with the evidence that would confirm or rule it out.
rule.R-STILL-UNKNOWN: No contributing factor was observed and none is implied by the timeline yet, so the scaffold names the question as still open - the evidence to close it is still owed.

warn.W-CHANGE-AFTER-SYMPTOM: The change is ordered after the symptom began. If the change did not precede the symptom, it is unlikely to be a contributing factor - check the ordering against your records.
warn.W-CLOCK-CONTRADICTS: Corrected for each source's offset, the clocks put these pairs the other way round from your order: {pairs}. Either the order or a source's offset is wrong; recheck both before the timeline is used as evidence.
warn.W-CLOCK-ORDER-UNSUPPORTED: Corrected for each source's offset, the possible times overlap or touch for: {pairs}. The clocks alone cannot establish that order; keep it only if other evidence supports it, such as one transaction identifier seen in both records.
warn.W-MULTI-CONFIRMED: More than one factor is marked confirmed. Incidents often have several contributing factors; make sure each confirmation rests on its own evidence rather than a single assumption.
warn.W-SPARSE: The timeline has very few events. A useful RCA usually needs at least the change (if any), the symptom onset, detection, and resolution.

change-blast-radius-mapper.blurb: Describe what you are changing and its structure; a fixed rule set maps the blast radius as concentric tiers (target, co-located, downstream, human) populated with what could be affected, plus severity-tagged risks and containment measures. It maps what could be affected, never asserts what will break.

share.carries: The link carries the form and your notes as typed, not your ticks; a note holding a credential gets none.
share.caution: Your notes can name the target host, customers or the change ticket: read them before you send the link.

share.blockedSecret: No link: “{field}” holds what looks like a credential ({label}). Put a placeholder in its place, then share again.

band.contained: No high or medium factors surfaced from what you described. The reach appears contained - still confirm against the real environment.
band.moderate: Medium-severity factors are present. The reach is more than the target alone; apply the containment measures below.
band.wide: At least one high-severity factor is present. Treat the reach as wide: lean on containment, sequence carefully, and prefer a maintenance window.

contain.C-COMMS: Send targeted comms to the downstream owners and, if customer-facing, to customers, so the impact is expected rather than discovered.
contain.C-DRAIN: Drain sessions from the target before the change so live connections finish rather than drop.
contain.C-FAILOVER-FIRST: Fail over to the healthy peer and change the standby first, keeping the active path untouched until the change is proven.
contain.C-ISOLATE-NEIGHBOURS: Confirm what else shares this device and, where possible, move the change to a time those neighbours can tolerate too.
contain.C-LOWER-TTL: Lower the record's TTL ahead of the change so a bad answer expires from caches quickly instead of lingering.
contain.C-MAINT-WINDOW: Move the change into a maintenance window so the human surface is smallest when the reach is widest.
contain.C-ONE-NODE: Change one node first and verify it there before rolling across the rest, so a mistake costs one unit, not the service.
contain.C-RESTORE-REDUNDANCY: Restore the degraded peer to health before changing anything, so there is a safety net during the change.
contain.C-STAGE-VERIFY-CERT: Stage and verify the new key, certificate, and full chain offline before installing, so no client meets a broken handshake.

item.I-CO-HA-PEER: The HA peer or cluster members - a change that desyncs or fails over affects them, and a change made while the peer is degraded has no safety net.
item.I-CO-SAME-DEVICE: Other services running on the same device or appliance - a device-wide fault (reboot, resource exhaustion, a bad global config) hits them too.
item.I-CO-SAME-PLATFORM: Other tenants on the same shared platform or cluster node - blast can cross tenant boundaries when the platform layer is touched.
item.I-CO-SHARED-CPU: Neighbours sharing the target's CPU, memory, or connection table - a change that spikes resource use can starve them.
item.I-DS-CACHED-ANSWERS: Anything caching the target's answers (resolvers, CDNs, clients) - for a DNS or config change, stale answers linger for the TTL after you change the record.
item.I-DS-DEPENDENTS: Services that call or depend on the target - if it degrades, they see it as their own failure and may page their own owners.
item.I-DS-EVERY-FLOW: Every flow that traverses the target in the traffic path - an in-path change affects transit, not just endpoints, so the reach is everything that passes through.
item.I-DS-EVERY-TLS-CLIENT: Every client that completes a TLS handshake with the target - a wrong key or chain breaks all of them at once, not gradually.
item.I-DS-TRANSITIVE: The dependents' own dependents - blast can propagate a second hop when many things depend on the target, so the reach is wider than the direct callers.
item.I-HU-CUSTOMER: Customers and any external SLA - customer-facing impact is visible outside the organization and may carry contractual weight.
item.I-HU-EVERYONE: Effectively the whole user base - when everything depends on the target, the human surface is everyone at once.
item.I-HU-ONCALL: The on-call and support surface - a wide change during load means more pages, more tickets, and more people pulled in.
item.I-HU-USERS: The end users behind the affected services - the people who feel the impact and open the tickets.
item.I-TGT-CONFIG-STATE: The target's own persisted state and configuration - the thing your backup must capture before you start.
item.I-TGT-DIRECT: The service or object being changed directly - it is expected to be affected; the point is that this is the intended surface.
item.I-TGT-SESSIONS: Any live sessions or connections currently terminating on the target - they may drop if not drained first.

RK-CUSTOMER-FACING.label: Customer-facing reach
RK-CUSTOMER-FACING.note: Impact is visible outside the organization and may carry SLA weight; comms matter more here.

RK-DNS-TTL-LINGER.label: DNS answers linger for the TTL
RK-DNS-TTL-LINGER.note: The old answer stays cached downstream for the record's TTL; the change is not undone the instant you fix the record.

RK-EVERYONE.label: Reaches the entire user base
RK-EVERYONE.note: The human surface is everyone at once; the cost of a slip is maximal.

RK-EVERYTHING-DEPENDS.label: Everything depends on the target
RK-EVERYTHING-DEPENDS.note: The downstream tier is effectively the whole estate; treat this as a maximum-blast change.

RK-HA-DEGRADED.label: HA peer already degraded
RK-HA-DEGRADED.note: The safety net is compromised before you start; a change now risks losing the last healthy unit.

RK-HEAVILY-SHARED.label: Heavily shared hardware or platform
RK-HEAVILY-SHARED.note: A device-wide fault crosses into many co-located services; the radius is much wider than the target alone.

RK-IN-PATH.label: In the live traffic path
RK-IN-PATH.note: Everything passing through is exposed, not just the endpoints; an in-path change has an inherently wide reach.

RK-MANY-DEPENDENTS.label: Many downstream dependents
RK-MANY-DEPENDENTS.note: Failure propagates to many callers and possibly their callers; the reach is wider than the direct target.

RK-NO-REDUNDANCY.label: No redundancy (standalone)
RK-NO-REDUNDANCY.note: There is no peer to carry load; any interruption is a full interruption of the target.

RK-SOME-SHARED.label: Some shared hardware or platform
RK-SOME-SHARED.note: A few co-located services could be caught by a device-wide fault; confirm what else rides this device.

RK-TLS-ALL-CLIENTS.label: Certificate change affects every TLS client
RK-TLS-ALL-CLIENTS.note: A wrong key or chain breaks the handshake for all clients simultaneously; verify the pair and chain before install.

rule.R-BASE-TARGET: Every change has a target tier: the object being changed and the persisted state your backup must capture.
rule.R-CERT-TARGET: The target is a certificate, so every TLS client is downstream and a wrong key or chain breaks all of them at once.
rule.R-CUSTOMER: The reach is customer-facing, so customers and any SLA are on the human surface and comms carry more weight.
rule.R-DNS-TARGET: A DNS record (or DNS-flavored change) propagates over the TTL, so caches downstream hold the old answer until it expires.
rule.R-EVERYONE: The reach is the entire user base, so the human surface is everyone at once and the on-call load rises with it.
rule.R-EVERYTHING-DEPENDS: Effectively everything depends on the target, so the downstream tier is the whole estate, including dependents of dependents - a maximum-blast change.
rule.R-FEW-DEPENDS: A few services depend on the target, so they belong in the downstream tier and their owners should be told.
rule.R-HA-DEGRADED: The HA peer is already degraded, so the safety net is compromised before you start; restore it to health first.
rule.R-HA-PAIR: There is an HA peer or cluster, so the peer/members are in the co-located tier - and you can fail over and change the standby first to keep the active path untouched.
rule.R-HEAVILY-SHARED: The target sits on heavily shared hardware or a shared platform, so a device-wide fault reaches many co-located services and even other tenants.
rule.R-IN-PATH: The target is in the live traffic path, so live sessions on it are at risk and every flow that traverses it is exposed - drain before touching it.
rule.R-MANY-DEPENDS: Many things depend on the target, so failure propagates to many callers and possibly their callers; the reach is wider than the direct target.
rule.R-SESSIONS-LB: A load balancer terminates connections, so its live sessions are at risk even when you would not call the change 'in-path' - drain them first.
rule.R-SOME-SHARED: Some services share the target's device, so a device-wide fault could catch them; confirm what else rides it.
rule.R-STANDALONE: The target is standalone with no peer to carry load, so any interruption is a full interruption - shrink the human surface with a maintenance window.
rule.R-USERS-NARROW: There is a bounded set of users behind the target; they belong on the human surface even when the reach is narrow.

warn.W-DEGRADED-PEER: You marked the HA peer degraded. Changing now risks losing the last healthy unit; restoring the peer first is usually the safer sequence.
warn.W-MAX-BLAST: In the traffic path and everything depends on it: this is close to a maximum-blast change. Weight the plan heavily towards containment and a maintenance window.
warn.W-SHARED-EVERYONE: Heavily shared and reaching everyone: a device-wide fault here has an unusually wide human surface. Confirm exactly what else rides this device before proceeding.

RK-NO-IMPACT.note: Impact sets the severity the vendor assigns; stating it up front avoids being graded lower than the situation warrants.

RK-NO-PROBLEM.label: No problem statement collected
RK-NO-PROBLEM.note: A case with no clear problem statement is the slowest kind to triage; write it before opening.

RK-NO-REPRO-CAP.label: Intermittent with no capture staged
RK-NO-REPRO-CAP.note: An intermittent problem is hard to catch; stage the capture now so the next occurrence is recorded rather than missed.

RK-SEV1-THIN.label: Sev1 with a thin packet
RK-SEV1-THIN.note: A down-severity case with little collected will still stall on the first request for data; gather the essentials even under pressure.

rule.R-BASE-CORE: Every escalation needs the core: a problem statement, the exact error, a timeline, the business impact, and exact versions - the questions a support engineer asks first.
rule.R-DIAG-BUNDLE: The vendor's diagnostic bundle and the affected configuration are near-universal first requests; attaching them up front skips a round trip.
rule.R-DNS-VENDOR: A DNS escalation needs the query logs from the failing lookups so the vendor can see the actual resolution path.
rule.R-HAPPENED-ONCE: The problem happened once, so the logs from that window are the primary record; collect them before they roll over.
rule.R-HIGH-SEV: A high-severity case benefits from a topology sketch and a capture so the vendor can act on structure and evidence rather than description.
rule.R-INTERMITTENT: The problem is intermittent, so a capture and logs must be staged now to catch the next occurrence rather than miss it.
rule.R-NO-DIAG: No diagnostic bundle is collected; the vendor will ask for it first.
rule.R-NO-IMPACT: No business impact is stated; impact sets the severity the vendor assigns, so stating it up front matters.
rule.R-NO-PROBLEM: No problem statement is collected yet; a case without one is the slowest to triage.
rule.R-REPRODUCIBLE: The problem is reproducible, so exact reproduction steps are the highest-value artifact - a case the vendor can reproduce moves fastest.
rule.R-SEV1-THIN: This is a down-severity case with little collected; it will stall on the first request for data unless the essentials are gathered.
rule.R-TLS-VENDOR: A TLS/PKI escalation needs a handshake capture so the vendor can read the exact negotiation and certificate exchange.

section.to-collect: To collect before opening the case

warn.W-NOTHING-TRIED: Nothing has been tried yet. Vendors triage faster when you show what you already ruled out; a quick config review or KB search before escalating often helps - and occasionally resolves it.
warn.W-SEV1-NO-IMPACT: This is a Sev 1 with no business impact stated. For a down case the impact statement is what justifies the severity; include it so the case is graded correctly.
warn.W-WORKAROUND-NOTE: A workaround is in place. State it explicitly in the packet, including what it masks, so the vendor knows the current behaviour is not the raw fault.

ja4-fingerprint-decoder.name: JA4 / JA3 TLS fingerprint decoder
ja4-fingerprint-decoder.blurb: Decode a JA4 TLS client fingerprint or a JA3 fingerprint into its fields, compute the hashed JA4 from raw values, or compute a JA3 MD5. It auto-detects which you paste. All in your browser.
ja4-fingerprint-decoder.runsLocally: Computed in your browser. Nothing is uploaded.
ja4-fingerprint-decoder.extCountDesc: Extensions offered including SNI and ALPN, ignoring GREASE.
ja4-fingerprint-decoder.cipherHashDesc: First 12 hex of the SHA-256 of the sorted cipher list. One-way; it cannot be reversed to the ciphers.
ja4-fingerprint-decoder.extHashDesc: First 12 hex of the SHA-256 of the sorted extensions plus signature algorithms. One-way.
ja4-fingerprint-decoder.anatomyNote: A JA4 has three parts joined by underscores: JA4_a is human-readable (transport, TLS version, SNI, cipher count, extension count, ALPN); JA4_b is a truncated SHA-256 of the sorted cipher list; JA4_c is a truncated SHA-256 of the sorted extensions plus the signature algorithms. GREASE values are ignored throughout.
ja4-fingerprint-decoder.ja3ExtCountDesc: Extensions, in the order the client sent them.

share.carries: The link carries the fingerprint as pasted, and nothing else.

alpn.marker: ALPN marker "{alpn}" (first+last character of the first ALPN value)

err.ja3Empty: Enter a JA3 string or a JA3 MD5.
err.ja3Fields: A JA3 string has five comma-separated fields: SSLVersion,Ciphers,Extensions,EllipticCurves,EllipticCurvePointFormats.
err.ja4Empty: Enter a JA4 fingerprint or a raw JA4_r value.
err.ja4Hex: JA4_b and JA4_c must each be 12 lowercase hex characters (a truncated SHA-256). If you have the raw cipher and extension lists, paste those instead to compute them.
err.ja4Sections: A hashed JA4 has three underscore-separated sections: JA4_a_JA4_b_JA4_c.
err.ja4aLength: The JA4_a section (before the first underscore) must be exactly 10 characters, e.g. t13d1516h2.

note.cap99: Cipher count is capped at 99 by the spec.
note.computed: Computed from raw (unhashed) values. GREASE was ignored; ciphers and extensions were sorted; SNI and ALPN were removed from the extension hash.
note.ja3Md5: This is a 32-character MD5, the JA3 hash itself. It is one-way and cannot be decoded back to the ClientHello fields. Paste the JA3 string (the comma-separated field list) to see the fields and recompute the hash.
note.ja3Md5Of: The JA3 fingerprint is the MD5 of this exact string. GREASE values should already be excluded, per the JA3 specification.
note.ja3Version: SSLVersion {ver} is not one of the common values; showing it as-is.
note.oddShape: JA4_a does not match the usual shape (transport, 2-char version, d/i, 2-digit counts, ALPN); decoding it positionally anyway.
note.oneWay: JA4_b and JA4_c are truncated SHA-256 hashes and cannot be reversed to recover the cipher or extension lists.

oui-lookup.name: OUI / MAC vendor lookup
oui-lookup.blurb: Look up the manufacturer behind a MAC address, and read whether it is unicast or multicast and universally or locally administered. All in your browser.
oui-lookup.runsLocally: Looked up in your browser against an embedded IEEE snapshot. Nothing is uploaded.
oui-lookup.ouiDesc: The first 24 bits identify the manufacturer.
oui-lookup.ouiOnlyDesc: You entered a bare OUI (the manufacturer prefix).
oui-lookup.multicastDesc: A group address (the I/G bit is set).
oui-lookup.universalDesc: Globally unique, assigned from an OUI.
oui-lookup.localDesc: Locally administered (the U/L bit is set); no vendor.
oui-lookup.ipv4GroupsLabel: The 32 IPv4 groups that share this MAC
oui-lookup.ipv4GroupsDesc: RFC 1112 section 6.4 copies only the low 23 bits of the group address into the MAC. A group address has 28 significant bits, so 5 bits are lost and these 32 groups map to the same MAC.
oui-lookup.ipv6Low32Label: Low 32 bits of the IPv6 group
oui-lookup.ipv6Low32Desc: RFC 2464 section 7: 33-33 followed by the last four octets of the IPv6 multicast address.
oui-lookup.bridgeFilteredNote: IEEE RA: frames sent to 01-80-C2-00-00-00 to 01-80-C2-00-00-0F are not relayed by MAC bridges conforming to IEEE 802.1D.
oui-lookup.vridOutOfRange: VRID 0 is outside the 1 to 255 range that RFC 9568 defines.

err.empty: Enter a MAC address or OUI.
err.hex: That is not valid hex. Use a MAC address, optionally separated by colons, hyphens, or dots.
err.length: A MAC is 12 hex digits (16 for EUI-64) and an OUI is 6; got {count}.

note.local: This is a locally administered address (the U/L bit is set): it was assigned by software, not by a manufacturer, so it has no OUI vendor.
note.multicast: The I/G bit is set, so this is a multicast (group) address rather than a single interface.
note.notInSnapshot: This OUI is not in the IEEE MA-L snapshot. It may be unassigned, newer than the snapshot, or from the MA-M / MA-S registries this tool does not yet include.

voss-fabric-id.runsLocally: Decoded in your browser. Nothing is uploaded.

bmac.group: The I/G bit is set (a group address); a node system-id / B-MAC should be an individual (unicast) address.
bmac.local: The U/L bit is set: this is a locally administered address, which matches Extreme's SPBM guidance to use 02 as the first octet of the system-id.
bmac.universal: The U/L bit is clear (universally administered). Extreme's SPBM guidance is to use a locally administered address (first octet 02) for the system-id / B-MAC.

voss-exos-translator.name: VOSS / EXOS command translator
voss-exos-translator.blurb: A side-by-side reference between VOSS (Fabric Connect / SPBM) and EXOS. Search a task or command to see how each CLI expresses it - and where EXOS has no equivalent.
voss-exos-translator.searchPlaceholder: e.g. i-sid, nickname, vlan, fabric attach
voss-exos-translator.hint: A reference, not a config generator. EXOS does not run SPBM; it joins a fabric as a Fabric Attach edge.

config-mode.note: EXOS has no separate enable / configure-terminal step; configuration commands run straight from the top prompt.

create-vlan.note: In VOSS the VLAN stays local to the edge; the fabric carries the service by its I-SID (see the Layer 2 VSN row).

fabric-attach.note: VOSS runs the FA Server; EXOS runs the FA Proxy/Client. FA rides LLDP, and the Server auto-provisions the I-SID from the edge VLAN. The sharing/grouping line is only for a LAG uplink.

fabric-core.concept: Build the SPBM fabric core (area, nickname, B-VLANs, system-id)
fabric-core.note: No equivalent: EXOS does not support SPBM. It joins the fabric through Fabric Attach instead of becoming a fabric node.

fabric-uplink.note: No equivalent: VOSS runs IS-IS only on fabric NNI links. On EXOS the uplink to the fabric is a Fabric Attach port (see the Fabric Attach row).

l2vsn.note: EXOS does not create I-SIDs. As a Fabric Attach edge it signals the VLAN on its uplink, and the VOSS FA Server provisions the matching I-SID into the fabric.

l3vsn.concept: Layer 3 VSN (a routed service across the fabric)
l3vsn.note: No equivalent: EXOS does not run L3 VSN. To exchange IP routes with the fabric, redistribute OSPF, BGP, or RIP across the boundary.

verify.note: On VOSS you verify the I-SID in the fabric; on EXOS you verify the Fabric Attach state and the VLAN.

vlan-ports.note: VOSS ports are slot/port form (1/1); EXOS uses a port list. Use tagged instead of untagged for a trunk / uplink port.

f5xc-rate-limit-calculator.name: F5XC rate-limit calculator
f5xc-rate-limit-calculator.blurb: Turn an F5 Distributed Cloud rate-limiter configuration into its effective rate, burst ceiling, and exact leaky-bucket behaviour - including why Disabled is not a bypass and how a Block lockout holds.
f5xc-rate-limit-calculator.runsLocally: Calculated in your browser. Nothing is uploaded.
f5xc-rate-limit-calculator.behaviorLeakyBucket: Enforcement is a leaky bucket: when the bucket overflows, the load balancer returns HTTP 429.
f5xc-rate-limit-calculator.behaviorDisabled: Mitigation Action Disabled still returns 429 on overflow. It only means no extra lockout timer is applied - Disabled is not a bypass.
f5xc-rate-limit-calculator.behaviorBlock: Mitigation Action Block adds a lockout of {secs, plural, one {{secs} second} other {{secs} seconds}}: after the bucket overflows the user is blocked for the full lockout even if the bucket drains, and can send again only once the timer expires.
f5xc-rate-limit-calculator.behaviorOverMax: This lockout exceeds F5's maximum blocking time of 48 hours (172800 seconds).
f5xc-rate-limit-calculator.overshootCaveat: Counting is distributed per Regional Edge / proxy, so you may briefly see more requests than the limit before enforcement converges (K000157944). Layered Server URL and API endpoint rules are evaluated first-match, in the order configured.

errors.min-number: Number must be an integer of at least 1.
errors.min-periods: Periods must be an integer of at least 1.
errors.per-period: Per Period must be Seconds, Minutes, or Hours.
errors.min-burst: Burst Multiplier must be at least 1 (default 1).
errors.block-lockout: Block mitigation needs a lockout duration of at least 1.

summary.Low: TLS 1.0 with non-PFS ciphers and weak algorithms. Includes every High and Medium cipher plus four static-RSA suites.

f5xc-tls-security-level-mapper.cumulativeNote: Includes every higher level's ciphers, plus {n} added at this level.

f5xc-tls-security-level-mapper.gotchaWeak: The static-RSA suites here have no forward secrecy and are what scanners flag as weak ciphers (K000148079).

f5xc-lb-algorithm-chooser.name: F5XC load-balancing algorithm chooser
f5xc-lb-algorithm-chooser.blurb: A short questionnaire recommends an F5XC origin-pool load-balancing algorithm - with the BIG-IP equivalent, caveats, and where to set it - and explains the XC model where consistent hashing IS the persistence method.
f5xc-lb-algorithm-chooser.title: Load-balancing algorithm chooser
f5xc-lb-algorithm-chooser.q1: Do sessions need to stick to the same origin server?
f5xc-lb-algorithm-chooser.q3dyn: Is the origin pool dynamic (autoscaling / Kubernetes pods)?
f5xc-lb-algorithm-chooser.prompt: Answer the questions above to see a recommended algorithm.

round-robin.label: Round Robin
round-robin.rationale: Sends requests to origins in turn, spreading load evenly. The simplest choice when origins have similar capacity and requests are short.
round-robin.config: Origin pool > Load Balancing Algorithm > Round Robin.

least-active-request.label: Least Active Request
least-active-request.rationale: Sends each request to the origin with the fewest in-flight requests. Better than Round Robin when request costs vary or connections are long-lived.
least-active-request.config: Origin pool > Load Balancing Algorithm > Least Active Request.

random.label: Random
random.rationale: Picks an origin at random. Statistically even across very large pools and avoids the synchronized stepping Round Robin can show.
random.bigip: (no direct equivalent; approximates Round Robin at scale)
random.config: Origin pool > Load Balancing Algorithm > Random.

source-ip-stickiness.label: Source IP Stickiness
source-ip-stickiness.rationale: Consistent-hashing on the client source IP, so a given client keeps landing on the same origin. In XC this hashing algorithm IS the persistence - there is no separate profile.
source-ip-stickiness.config: Origin pool > Load Balancing Algorithm > Source IP Stickiness.

cookie-stickiness.label: Cookie Based Stickiness
cookie-stickiness.rationale: Consistent-hashing on a cookie value, so a client carrying that cookie keeps landing on the same origin. The hashing algorithm is itself the persistence.
cookie-stickiness.config: Origin pool > Load Balancing Algorithm > Cookie Based Stickiness (or use Load Balancer Override to set the cookie name, TTL, and path per route).

ring-hash-custom.label: Ring Hash (custom hash policy)
ring-hash-custom.rationale: Consistent-hashing on a hash policy you define - typically an application header carrying a session ID. Ideal for microservices that pass their own session token.
ring-hash-custom.config: Origin pool > Load Balancing Algorithm > Ring Hash, then define the hash policy (header / cookie / source IP).

lb-override.label: Load Balancer Override
lb-override.rationale: Defers the choice to the HTTP load balancer so you can set stickiness per route or per domain, rather than one setting for the whole pool.
lb-override.config: Origin pool > Load Balancing Algorithm > Load Balancer Override, then set Advanced Options > Load Balancing Control per route (Cookie or Source IP).

caveat.no-persistence: This algorithm does not keep a client on the same origin. If the app needs sticky sessions, choose a consistent-hashing option instead.
caveat.least-uneven-cost: Best when requests differ in cost or run long; for uniform, short requests Round Robin is simpler.
caveat.random-large-pool: Evenness is statistical, so it shows best across large pools; small pools may look lumpy.
caveat.dynamic-no-persistence: Your pool is dynamic, but this algorithm does not persist - a scaling event will freely reshuffle clients, which is fine only if the app is stateless.
caveat.low-client-diversity: If many clients share a source IP (behind NAT or a proxy), hashing on source IP concentrates them on one origin and load becomes uneven.
caveat.cookie-params: You will set the cookie name, TTL, and path; the client must return that cookie for stickiness to hold.
caveat.custom-header-session: Pick a header whose value is stable per session (a session ID), not something that changes per request.
caveat.per-route-control: Set the stickiness under each route's Advanced Options > Load Balancing Control - different routes or domains can differ.
caveat.dynamic-hash-good: Good fit for a dynamic pool: consistent hashing remaps the fewest clients when origins are added or removed.

f5xc-lb-algorithm-chooser.teachingNote: On BIG-IP the load-balancing method and the persistence profile are two separate settings on the virtual server. XC folds them together: the consistent-hashing algorithms (Source IP Stickiness, Cookie Based Stickiness, Ring Hash) ARE the persistence method, and Round Robin, Least Active Request, and Random do not persist at all. There is no separate persistence profile object - to vary persistence per route, use Load Balancer Override.

resolution.none: No load balancer domain matches {host}, and there is no Default load balancer - this hostname would not be picked up.

warn.auto-cert-conflict: Both *.{base} and the apex {base} are configured - F5 advises against mixing a wildcard and its apex across load balancers when using automatic certificates.
warn.dup-exact: The exact domain {domain} is claimed by more than one load balancer ({lbs}) - only one can win.
warn.multi-default: More than one Default load balancer is configured ({lbs}) - only one is allowed per advertise policy (IP + port).
warn.ambiguity: {host} matches {a} and {b} with equal specificity - this is ambiguous and should be avoided.
warn.wildcard-cert-multilabel: {host} routes via the wildcard {domain}, but a wildcard TLS certificate covers a single label - a multi-label host like this may route yet fail certificate validation.

f5xc-domain-sni-match-resolver.teachingNote: XC matches the hostname (from SNI on HTTPS, or the Host header on HTTP) to the most specific domain across all load balancers sharing an IP and port. An exact FQDN wins over a wildcard, and a wildcard like *.foo.com covers subdomains but not the apex foo.com - to serve the apex, add it as its own domain. One load balancer per advertise policy can be the Default, catching anything unmatched.

finding.op-skip-verify: TLS to the origin skips server verification - the connection is encrypted but the origin certificate is not validated, so a man-in-the-middle could impersonate the origin.
finding.op-no-sni: SNI is disabled on the connection to the origin - origins that host multiple names may return the wrong certificate or site.
finding.op-cleartext: TLS to the origin is disabled - traffic from XC to the origin is sent in cleartext.
finding.op-no-healthcheck: No health check is referenced - the pool relies on implicit health only, with no active probe.
finding.op-single-origin: The pool has a single origin server - there is no redundancy if it fails.
finding.lb-no-waf: No WAF (app_firewall) is attached to this load balancer - application-layer attacks are not inspected.
finding.lb-cleartext: This load balancer has a plain-HTTP listener with no HTTPS - client traffic is unencrypted.
finding.lb-no-redirect: HTTPS is configured but HTTP-to-HTTPS redirect is off - clients arriving over HTTP are not upgraded.
finding.lb-route-waf-off: Route {index} disables the WAF (web application firewall) - requests matching it skip application-firewall inspection.
finding.lb-route-shadow: Route {index} is a catch-all but is not last - later routes after it can never match (first-match wins).
finding.lb-wildcard-apex: Both *.{base} and the apex {base} are configured - F5 advises against mixing a wildcard and its apex when using automatic certificates.
finding.waf-monitoring: The WAF is in monitoring mode - it detects and logs attacks but does not block them.
finding.waf-tc-off: Threat campaigns are disabled - known active-exploit campaigns are not detected.

bigip-ltm-lb-simulator.name: BIG-IP LTM load balancing simulator
bigip-ltm-lb-simulator.blurb: Configure pool members, pick a load balancing method and a request count, and see where the next N connections land.
bigip-ltm-lb-simulator.runsLocally: Simulated in your browser. Nothing is uploaded.

reason.fastest: Fastest routes to the member with the quickest response time. That depends on live latency measurements, so it cannot be simulated deterministically from configuration alone.
reason.observed: Observed assigns a ratio every second based on current connection counts. It depends on live, changing metrics, so it cannot be simulated deterministically from configuration alone.
reason.predictive: Predictive extends Observed with performance trends (whether a member is improving or declining). It depends on live trend data, so it cannot be simulated deterministically.
reason.dynamic-ratio: Dynamic Ratio sets ratios from real-time performance metrics, often gathered by SNMP. It depends on live metrics, so it cannot be simulated deterministically.

bigip-ltm-lb-simulator.resultTitle: Where the next N connections land
bigip-ltm-lb-simulator.summaryLine: {requests, plural, one {{requests} request} other {{requests} requests}} across {active, plural, one {{active} active member} other {{active} active members}} ({standby} on standby).

note.standby: Members in a lower priority group are on standby and receive no traffic while the active group meets the priority group activation threshold.
note.lc-fresh: Least Connections is simulated from a fresh connection table (this tool takes no current-connection count), so it starts even, like Round Robin. On a live system it favours members with fewer active connections.
note.cookie-fallback: Least Sessions uses the persistence-record count as its metric. Note: with cookie-based persistence, BIG-IP falls back to Round Robin.

ja3-tls-fingerprint.permutedNote: The extensions are not in ascending order, so this JA3 will change if the client permutes its extension order (JA3 churn). Use JA3N, which sorts them, or JA4 for a stable fingerprint.
ja3-tls-fingerprint.stableNote: The extensions are already in ascending order, so JA3 and JA3N match here. Modern browsers that randomize extension order would still churn the JA3.
ja3-tls-fingerprint.greaseNote: GREASE values were found and excluded before hashing (RFC 8701): {values}.

err.version: The first field (TLS version) must be a decimal integer, e.g. 771 for TLS 1.2.

packet-capture-plan-builder.name: Packet Capture Plan Builder
packet-capture-plan-builder.blurb: Command builders answer how to capture; this answers where, why, and what it would mean. Describe the path and the symptom; a 35-rule original registry designs a phased capture plan: ranked points on named boundaries, expected observations, an interpretation matrix with supports and weakens decided before collection, and sync/authorization discipline. It plans captures - it never ingests them.
