R-AC-SINGLE.0: Request access to at least one more point across the nearest boundary - phase 2 of this plan depends on it.

R-AC-UNKNOWN.0: Establish WHO can capture WHERE (and with what approval) before scheduling any window.

R-ARCH-EW.0: Confirm SPAN/mirror or tap availability on the east-west segment (and its packet-drop behaviour under load) before scheduling.

R-ARCH-UNKNOWN.0: Map the path first: list every hop, its owner, and where addresses or TLS change - then rebuild this plan against the real path.

R-BASE-AUTHZ.0: Confirm capture authorization for every point in this plan (owner sign-off where the interface is not yours).
R-BASE-AUTHZ.1: Agree retention and access control for the capture files before collection starts.

R-INT-MULTI.0: Enumerate the intermediaries IN ORDER (client -> ... -> server) and note at which of them addresses or TLS change - the phase-2 pairs depend on that order.

R-SY-LOSS.0: Compare interface drop/error counters at each hop alongside the captures - counters localize cheaply before packets confirm.

R-TC-MIXED.0: Pin down the 5-tuple (or at least protocol and port) of the affected flow before capture - unfiltered captures on busy links bury the evidence.

R-TC-SENSITIVE.0: Prefer header-length snaplen and bounded duration; store captures with restricted access and redact before any sharing.

R-TM-CHANGE.0: Capture the same points in a known-good window (rollback or a healthy peer) as the comparison baseline - one failing capture proves little without its pair.

R-TM-LOCATION.0: Plan the same capture points at one FAILING site and one WORKING site - the comparison is the evidence; a single-site capture is only half of it.

R-TM-SYNC.0: Synchronize clocks (NTP) on every capture host and record the offset before starting.
R-TM-SYNC.1: Run overlapping ring-buffer captures at all points until the symptom reproduces - never sequential windows.

P-CLIENT.means: The client-side truth to compare against the server side, packet for packet.
P-CLIENT.observe: The flow as the client sends and receives it

P-SERVER.means: Present here but absent effects at the client localizes the return path; absent here localizes the forward path.
P-SERVER.observe: The flow as the server sees it

P-MIRROR.means: The neutral third view that arbitrates when the two endpoints disagree.
P-MIRROR.observe: The segment's traffic at a SPAN/mirror or tap

P-FW-IN.means: Present outside, absent inside: the device dropped it - policy, NAT exhaustion, or inspection. Match flows by ports and TCP sequence numbers, not by addresses.
P-FW-IN.observe: The flow after enforcement and translation (addresses rewritten)

P-FW-OUT.means: Arrival here proves the network delivered it to the boundary.
P-FW-OUT.observe: The flow before enforcement and translation

P-LB-BACK.means: Failures here with a healthy front side localize to member selection, member health, or the server segment.
P-LB-BACK.observe: The balancer's own connections to pool members (often from a SNAT address)

P-LB-FRONT.means: Separates 'client cannot reach the VIP' from everything behind it.
P-LB-FRONT.observe: Client connections to the VIP: SYN, handshake, and any resets

P-PROXY-BACK.means: A healthy front with a failing back localizes to the origin or the proxy's upstream policy - and the two sessions will NOT share ports or sequence numbers.
P-PROXY-BACK.observe: The proxy-to-origin session (new source address, often new TLS)

P-PROXY-FRONT.means: Separates client-side failures from anything the proxy does upstream.
P-PROXY-FRONT.observe: The client-to-proxy session, including TLS handshake if the proxy terminates it

P-CLIENT.means: Separates 'agent/tunnel never built' from policy applied inside the service.
P-CLIENT.observe: The client's tunnel or proxy session establishment (and the SNI it offers)

P-EGRESS.means: Traffic bypassing the tunnel here, while policy assumes steering, is a steering fault - not a provider fault.
P-EGRESS.observe: What actually leaves the site (tunneled, or direct on bypass)

P-VPN-INNER.means: The only place near the gateway where the actual conversation is visible.
P-VPN-INNER.observe: The application flow in clear, entering/leaving the tunnel

P-VPN-OUTER.means: Healthy, symmetric ESP with an absent inner flow localizes to selectors/routing at a gateway; absent ESP localizes to the underlay or IKE.
P-VPN-OUTER.observe: ESP or UDP/4500 between the gateways - and nothing else of the flow

P-FW-IN.means: Correlate to the pre-NAT capture by ports, TCP sequence numbers, and timing - never by IP addresses.
P-FW-IN.observe: Post-translation addressing of the same flow

P-FW-OUT.means: One half of the correlation pair.

P-RESOLVER.means: A resolution failure ends the investigation before any packet-path work; an unexpected address redirects it.
P-RESOLVER.observe: The DNS query and its answer: NXDOMAIN, timeout, or an unexpected address

P-CLIENT.means: An alert names the layer; silence after ClientHello points at the path or a device eating the handshake.
P-CLIENT.observe: ClientHello (with SNI) and whatever answers it: ServerHello, an alert, or silence

P-CLIENT.means: The first packet where the two diverge names the layer to investigate.
P-CLIENT.observe: The failing client's flow, side by side with a working client's capture of the same operation

P-CLIENT.means: Where the chain stalls is where the evidence should focus next.

P-RESOLVER.means: An IdP-side DNS or reachability failure explains an 'application' login failure without the application being at fault.
P-RESOLVER.observe: Resolution of the identity provider's name, separately from the application's

C-ASYM-RETURN.candidate: The forward path works and the return path takes a different, failing route
C-ASYM-RETURN.supports: Requests arrive at the server and responses leave it, but those responses never appear at the client-side capture - the return leg is dropping them.
C-ASYM-RETURN.weakens: Responses never leave the server at all, or the forward leg itself is incomplete - the asymmetry story collapses.

C-CHANGE-ALIGNED.candidate: The change altered on-the-wire behaviour at a specific boundary
C-CHANGE-ALIGNED.supports: The before/after pair at one boundary differs exactly where the change plausibly acts (new resets, new path, new TLS parameters) while other boundaries match.
C-CHANGE-ALIGNED.weakens: Before and after captures are materially identical at every planned point - the change's wire effect is elsewhere or absent.

C-DELAY-SPLIT.candidate: The delay is server-side (first-byte), not network transit
C-DELAY-SPLIT.supports: Request leaves the client and arrives at the server with ordinary transit time, but the first response byte lags at the SERVER capture itself.
C-DELAY-SPLIT.weakens: The request-to-arrival gap between the two captures carries the delay - transit (or a middle device) owns it instead.

C-ERROR-ORIGIN.candidate: An intermediary, not the origin, is generating the error status
C-ERROR-ORIGIN.supports: The origin-side capture shows no matching request reaching the origin (or a different status leaving it) while the client receives the error - the device in between wrote it.
C-ERROR-ORIGIN.weakens: The origin-side capture shows the same request arriving and the same error status leaving the origin itself.

C-IDENTITY-SIDEFLOW.candidate: The failure is in the identity side-flow, not the application path
C-IDENTITY-SIDEFLOW.supports: The redirect to the IdP is observed but the IdP leg fails (DNS, TCP, TLS, or an error response on the IdP host) while direct application requests succeed.
C-IDENTITY-SIDEFLOW.weakens: The full redirect chain completes and the application itself then errors - the identity leg is exonerated.

C-LB-SPLIT.candidate: The fault sits behind the VIP (member side), not in front of it
C-LB-SPLIT.supports: Clean, completed handshakes at the VIP front while the member-side capture shows failures, retransmissions, or no corresponding member connection.
C-LB-SPLIT.weakens: The front-side capture already shows the failure (no SYN-ACK from the VIP, resets from the VIP address) - then the balancer or the path to it is implicated instead.

C-RST-ORIGIN.candidate: A middle device, not the server, is originating the resets
C-RST-ORIGIN.supports: The RST appears on the client side but the server-side capture shows no corresponding RST leaving the server (or shows the session healthy) - TTL and timing of the RST further separate a nearby middlebox from the far endpoint.
C-RST-ORIGIN.weakens: The server-side capture shows the server itself sending the RST for that exact session (sequence numbers match).

C-TLS-BOUNDARY.candidate: The failure sits at a TLS boundary (handshake, certificate, SNI, or ALPN mismatch at one termination point)
C-TLS-BOUNDARY.supports: A capture on the client side of the terminator shows the handshake failing (alert visible, or handshake never completes) while the terminator's upstream side shows either no attempt or a separately healthy session.
C-TLS-BOUNDARY.weakens: Handshakes complete cleanly at every termination point in the plan - the failure then lives above TLS (application) or below it (transport), not at the boundary.

C-UPSTREAM-LOSS.candidate: The traffic is lost between two adjacent capture points
C-UPSTREAM-LOSS.supports: The flow (or its retransmissions) is present at the upstream point and absent at the next one downstream, within a synchronized window.
C-UPSTREAM-LOSS.weakens: The flow appears at both points - the loss, if any, is further along; move the pair and repeat.

md.title: Packet capture plan

P-CLIENT.where: On the client itself (or its access switch port)

P-EGRESS.where: At the outbound egress / SSE tunnel head

P-FW-IN.where: Inside interface of the firewall (after enforcement/NAT)

P-FW-OUT.where: Outside interface of the firewall (before enforcement/NAT)

P-LB-BACK.where: Server side of the load balancer (traffic to pool members)

P-LB-FRONT.where: Client side of the load balancer (traffic to the VIP)

P-MIRROR.where: A SPAN/mirror or tap on the east-west segment

P-PROXY-BACK.where: Origin side of the proxy or WAF

P-PROXY-FRONT.where: Client side of the proxy or WAF

P-RESOLVER.where: Between the client and its DNS resolver

P-SERVER.where: On the server itself (or its access switch port)

P-VPN-INNER.where: Inner (cleartext) side of the VPN gateway

P-VPN-OUTER.where: Outer (encrypted) side of the VPN gateway

dns.P-RESOLVER: Command family: tcpdump/tshark 'port 53' near the client, and query logging on the resolver, together cover both halves of the resolution leg.

firewall.P-FW-IN: Command family: the INSIDE-zone on-box capture, plus the device's session/flow table for the same tuple, pairs with the outside view.
firewall.P-FW-OUT: Command family: most firewalls expose an on-box packet capture per interface/zone; capture the OUTSIDE zone here and pair it with the inside capture.

load-balancer.P-LB-BACK: Command family: capture on the server-side VLAN/interface of the ADC, or on the member itself, to see the balancer-originated (often SNATed) session.
load-balancer.P-LB-FRONT: Command family: on BIG-IP, tcpdump on interface 0.0 sees both sides of the proxy in one capture (with p-flags for peer flows); other ADCs expose equivalent VIP-side capture.

tls-pki.P-CLIENT: Command family: a client-side tcpdump/tshark of the handshake plus the browser/openssl s_client view of the presented chain covers transport and certificate evidence together.

rule.R-AC-SINGLE: Single-point access with an intermediary present cannot localize loss - the plan says so out loud.
rule.R-AC-UNKNOWN: Unknown capture access makes scheduling premature.
rule.R-ARCH-DIRECT: A direct path is localized by comparing the two endpoints.
rule.R-ARCH-EW: East-west traffic rarely crosses a natural capture boundary; create one with a mirror/tap, and capture the endpoints.
rule.R-ARCH-FWNAT: A firewalled/NATted path is localized by pairing captures across the enforcement boundary.
rule.R-ARCH-LB: A load-balanced path has two conversations: client-to-VIP and LB-to-member. Capture both sides of the balancer.
rule.R-ARCH-PROXY: A proxied path is TWO TCP sessions; the proxy's two sides are separate conversations that must be captured separately.
rule.R-ARCH-SSE: An outbound SSE/proxy path is localized between the client agent/tunnel and the egress the provider sees.
rule.R-ARCH-UNKNOWN: An unknown or mixed path cannot be planned with confidence; establish the path first.
rule.R-ARCH-VPN: A site-to-site VPN path has an encrypted outside and a cleartext inside; only the inner side shows the application flow.
rule.R-BASE-AUTHZ: Capture authorization, retention, and access control are the operator's responsibility on every plan.
rule.R-INT-FW: A firewall in the path adds an enforcement boundary worth pairing across.
rule.R-INT-LB: A load balancer among the intermediaries adds the VIP/member boundary even off the LB archetype.
rule.R-INT-MULTI: Multiple intermediaries mean multiple boundaries; the plan must name their order before two-point comparisons mean anything.
rule.R-INT-NAT: Address translation breaks address-based matching; pair across the NAT and match by ports and sequence numbers.
rule.R-INT-PROXY: A proxy/WAF among the intermediaries adds the two-session boundary even off the proxy archetype.
rule.R-INT-UNKNOWN: An unknown middlebox inventory undermines every between-points inference.
rule.R-INT-VPN: A VPN gateway among the intermediaries adds the outer/inner boundary even off the VPN archetype.
rule.R-SY-CONNFAIL: Connection-establishment failures begin before the connection: resolution first, then the SYN's journey.
rule.R-SY-HTTPERR: An HTTP error is generated WHERE the request is decrypted and processed; the capture must sit where that status is visible.
rule.R-SY-LATENCY: Latency decomposes into client think-time, network transit, and server first-byte - two synchronized points separate them.
rule.R-SY-LOSS: Packet loss is proven by pairwise comparison: the same flow, two points, one delta.
rule.R-SY-ONEWAY: One-way traffic is a return-path problem until proven otherwise; capture BOTH directions at two points.
rule.R-SY-RESET: A reset has an ORIGINATOR; captures on both sides of the nearest stateful device reveal which side manufactured it.
rule.R-SY-TIMEOUT: For timeouts, ABSENCE is the evidence: the last point where packets are seen bounds the loss.
rule.R-SY-TLSFAIL: A TLS failure is best observed where the handshake actually happens - on the client side of whichever hop terminates it.
rule.R-TC-DNS: DNS-class traffic makes the resolver leg a first-phase point in its own right.
rule.R-TC-MIXED: A mixed/unknown traffic class needs the flow defined before filters mean anything.
rule.R-TC-SENSITIVE: TLS, HTTP, and mixed classes can carry secrets; the plan must minimize exposure by construction.
rule.R-TM-CHANGE: Change-aligned symptoms want BEFORE/AFTER evidence pairs, not just a single failing capture.
rule.R-TM-CLIENT: Client-specific symptoms are localized fastest by differential capture: one failing client, one working one.
rule.R-TM-LOCATION: Location-specific symptoms mean path-specific captures: pair a failing site with a working one.
rule.R-TM-SYNC: Non-constant symptoms with multi-point plans demand synchronized clocks and overlapping windows.
rule.R-TR-AUTHRED: An authentication redirect creates a SECOND flow (to the IdP) whose failure masquerades as an application failure.
rule.R-TR-TLS: Mid-path TLS termination splits the path into separate TLS worlds; transport evidence must not be presented as payload evidence.

warn.W-INT-UNKNOWN: The intermediary inventory is unknown. Every unlisted middlebox is a boundary the plan cannot see - enumerate the path's devices before trusting any two-point comparison.
warn.W-PATH-UNKNOWN: The path itself is not established. A capture plan built on an unknown path risks observing the wrong boundary entirely - map the hops and their owners first, then plan the captures.
warn.W-SENSITIVE: This traffic class can carry credentials, tokens, cookies, or user content. Truncate capture length (snaplen) to headers where possible, cap duration, control file access, and redact before sharing.
warn.W-SINGLE-POINT: Only one side of the path is reachable while an intermediary sits between the endpoints. Absence of packets at a single point cannot localize where they were lost - it can only prove they did not arrive there.
warn.W-SYNC: The symptom is not constant and more than one capture point is in play: without clock synchronization and overlapping windows, multi-point comparison will mislead rather than localize.
warn.W-TLS-CLAIMS: TLS terminates mid-path: transport evidence and decrypted application evidence are different things. A capture on the encrypted side can prove handshake and flow behaviour, never payload content - do not let the plan's readers claim otherwise.

R-AUTH-IDP.0: Model the IdP leg's own path (resolution, TLS, reachability) as seriously as the application's.

R-BASE-MODEL.0: Confirm each modelled hop with its owner: does the device exist, in this position, doing what the model says?
R-BASE-MODEL.1: Mark every confirmed hop and keep the unconfirmed ones visibly provisional.

R-ENF-UNKNOWN.0: For each middlebox: establish whether it ENFORCES, LOGS, both, or neither - and where those logs live.

R-RES-MULTI.0: Map which client populations use which resolution mechanism - the split may BE the symptom pattern.

R-RES-SPLIT.0: Resolve the name from an internal AND an external vantage and record both answers side by side.

R-RES-STATIC.0: Compare the static entry against the authoritative record before trusting any path conclusion.

R-RET-POLICY.0: Trace the RETURN route explicitly (routing table, policy rules, SD-WAN decisions) - do not mirror the forward assumption.

R-TLS-E2E.0: Note in the model: mid-path devices see transport only; any application-content claim must come from an endpoint.

R-TLS-PLAIN.0: Record that content is observable at every hop - and treat captures accordingly (exposure discipline applies).

R-TLS-REENC.0: For each TLS segment, record which certificate is presented and which name is expected - per segment, not per path.

R-TR-DNAT.0: Record the pre- and post-rewrite address pairs so captures and logs on both sides can be correlated.

R-TR-SNAT.0: Identify where the original client identity survives (header, log field) past the rewrite point - if nowhere, say so in the model.

FD-CONNECTOR.candidate: The access agent or connector layer, not the destination, gates the failure
FD-CONNECTOR.supports: The agent or connector is down, misrouted, or version-broken for the failing population, and bypassing it (where sanctioned) restores access.
FD-CONNECTOR.weakens: The agent path is confirmed healthy for the failing population - enrolment, tunnel, and steering all verified.

FD-IDENTITY-SIDEFLOW.candidate: The identity side-flow (IdP leg), not the application path, is failing
FD-IDENTITY-SIDEFLOW.supports: The redirect to the IdP is observed but the IdP leg fails - its own DNS, TLS, clock skew, or token validation - while direct application access works.
FD-IDENTITY-SIDEFLOW.weakens: The full redirect chain completes and tokens validate; the application itself then errors.

FD-IDENTITY-VISIBILITY.candidate: Source rewriting hides the real client from backend policy and logs
FD-IDENTITY-VISIBILITY.supports: Backend logs show the SNAT or proxy address where the client should be, and per-client policy behaves as if all traffic were one client.
FD-IDENTITY-VISIBILITY.weakens: An identity-preserving header or log field carries the original client end to end, and policy keys on it.

FD-REGISTRY.candidate: Service-discovery registry health, not the service, drives the failures
FD-REGISTRY.supports: Registry lookups fail, lag, or return deregistered instances while the service itself answers when addressed directly.
FD-REGISTRY.weakens: Discovery returns fresh, correct instances promptly - the registry is exonerated.

FD-RESOLUTION-DRIFT.candidate: Static or hosts-file resolution has drifted from the real service address
FD-RESOLUTION-DRIFT.supports: The static entry differs from the authoritative record, and traffic goes to the stale address.
FD-RESOLUTION-DRIFT.weakens: The static entry matches the authoritative answer - drift is not in play.

FD-RESOLUTION-SPLIT.candidate: Inside and outside resolve the name differently (split-horizon divergence)
FD-RESOLUTION-SPLIT.supports: The same name returns different addresses from an internal and an external resolver, and the failing population maps to one of the views.
FD-RESOLUTION-SPLIT.weakens: Both views return the same records, or the failing population does not correlate with resolver view at all.

FD-RETURN-POLICY.candidate: Policy routing or multiple exits steer returns somewhere the model does not expect
FD-RETURN-POLICY.supports: Return traffic exits through a different edge than assumed (routing table, policy route, or SD-WAN decision confirms it).
FD-RETURN-POLICY.weakens: The return route is confirmed identical to the assumption at every decision point.

FD-SILENT-MIDDLEBOX.candidate: A middlebox in the path acts on the flow without appearing in any log the team watches
FD-SILENT-MIDDLEBOX.supports: Behaviour changes across a device whose enforcement and logging status nobody can state; its counters or captures reveal decisions no log records.
FD-SILENT-MIDDLEBOX.weakens: Every device in the path has confirmed enforcement AND logging status, and the logs account for the observed behaviour.

FD-STATEFUL-ASYM.candidate: An asymmetric return path is breaking stateful devices mid-flow
FD-STATEFUL-ASYM.supports: Forward traffic takes one path while returns take another, and a stateful device on only one of them drops the unseen half.
FD-STATEFUL-ASYM.weakens: Forward and return demonstrably traverse the same devices, or no stateful device sits on either leg.

FD-TLS-SEGMENT.candidate: One specific TLS segment - not TLS in general - carries the failure
FD-TLS-SEGMENT.supports: Handshakes complete on every segment except one, whose certificate, SNI, or cipher story differs at that boundary.
FD-TLS-SEGMENT.weakens: Every segment's handshake completes cleanly with the expected identities - the failure lives above or below TLS.

FD-TUNNEL-SELECTORS.candidate: Tunnel selectors or routing at a VPN gateway exclude part of the traffic
FD-TUNNEL-SELECTORS.supports: The affected traffic never appears inside the tunnel while other traffic between the same sites does - selectors, interesting-traffic ACLs, or routes carve it out.
FD-TUNNEL-SELECTORS.weakens: The affected flows are confirmed entering and leaving the tunnel at both gateways.

FD-TWO-SESSION.candidate: The proxy's two sessions diverge: the client-side conversation is not the origin-side conversation
FD-TWO-SESSION.supports: The client-side session is healthy while the proxy's own upstream session fails (or carries different parameters), or vice versa.
FD-TWO-SESSION.weakens: Both sessions are observed healthy and parameter-consistent end to end.

FD-UNKNOWN-PATH.candidate: The path itself is not established; any localization is premature
FD-UNKNOWN-PATH.supports: Attempts to name the hop owners, addresses, or order come back inconsistent or blank - the model cannot be confirmed.
FD-UNKNOWN-PATH.weakens: Each hop, its owner, and where addresses or TLS change are confirmed - the model stops being a guess and this domain dissolves.

effect.dnat: Destination address rewritten: the dialed address is not the answering address.
effect.proxy-source: Upstream session originates at the proxy with its own source identity.
effect.snat: Source address rewritten: downstream devices see the rewrite point, not the client.

rule.R-ARCH-FED: An identity-federated application carries a second flow to the IdP whose failures masquerade as application failures.
rule.R-ARCH-PROXY: A proxied path is two sessions; their divergence is its own failure domain.
rule.R-ARCH-UNKNOWN: An unknown or mixed archetype makes the whole chain provisional.
rule.R-ARCH-VPN: A site-to-site tunnel adds gateway pair semantics: selectors decide what enters, and only the inner side shows the conversation.
rule.R-AUTH-AGENT: An agent or connector in the auth path is a component whose health gates everything behind it.
rule.R-AUTH-IDP: An IdP redirect adds DNS, TLS, clock, and token dependencies OUTSIDE the primary path - a whole side-flow with its own failure modes.
rule.R-AUTH-UNKNOWN: Unknown authentication flow may hide an entire side-flow from the model.
rule.R-BASE-MODEL: A map assembled from selections is a proposed model, not discovered topology - it must be verified before it is trusted.
rule.R-ENF-UNKNOWN: In quick mode no intermediary's enforcement or logging status is established - none of them may be assumed to have observed or controlled the flow.
rule.R-ORDER-ASSUMED: With two or more middleboxes the chain uses a canonical assumed order; the real insertion order must be verified.
rule.R-RES-MULTI: Multiple resolution mechanisms mean the answer can depend on who asks - document which population uses which.
rule.R-RES-SD: With service discovery, the registry's health is part of the path.
rule.R-RES-SPLIT: Split-horizon DNS means inside and outside may resolve the same name differently - the divergence itself is a failure domain.
rule.R-RES-STATIC: Hosts-file or static resolution drifts silently as services move.
rule.R-RES-UNKNOWN: Unknown resolution leaves the model's very first hop unestablished.
rule.R-RET-ASYM: A known-asymmetric return with stateful or rewriting devices in the path is a standing failure domain, not a curiosity.
rule.R-RET-POLICY: Policy routing and multiple exits steer returns by rules the forward model never sees.
rule.R-RET-UNKNOWN: An unknown return path alongside stateful or rewriting devices is the classic silent breaker.
rule.R-TLS-E2E: End-to-end TLS means no mid-path device can see or generate application content - claims otherwise contradict the model.
rule.R-TLS-ONCE: A single mid-path termination still creates two evidence worlds: encrypted before it, exposed at it.
rule.R-TLS-PLAIN: Plaintext on the wire makes every hop a full-content observer - an evidence convenience and an exposure fact, both worth recording.
rule.R-TLS-REENC: Terminate-and-re-encrypt splits the path into TLS segments with separate certificate, SNI, and cipher stories - each boundary is its own domain.
rule.R-TLS-UNKNOWN: Unknown TLS behaviour leaves certificate identity and payload visibility unmodeled.
rule.R-TR-DNAT: Destination rewriting means the address the client dialed is not the address the server answers on - correlate flows by ports and sequence, not addresses.
rule.R-TR-PROXYSRC: A proxy-originated source means the upstream conversation is a NEW session bearing the proxy's identity.
rule.R-TR-SNAT: Source rewriting means backend policy and logs may never see the original client identity.
rule.R-TR-UNKNOWN: Unknown address transformation undermines every log correlation the model would otherwise support.

resolution.default: Name resolution happens before the first packet of the primary flow.
resolution.sd: Service discovery: the registry's health and freshness are part of this path.
resolution.split: Split-horizon: the answer depends on which view the client reaches - model both.
resolution.title: Resolution side-flow
resolution.unknown: Resolution mechanism unknown - this side-flow is unverified.

tls.clientSide: Client-side TLS segment: the certificate presented HERE is what the client judges.
tls.endToEnd: One TLS world end to end: mid-path devices see transport only.
tls.final: Final TLS segment to the server.
tls.segmentN: TLS segment {n}: separate identity and cipher story.

warn.W-AUTH-UNKNOWN: The authentication flow is unknown. If a redirect or agent is involved, an entire side-flow is missing from this model.
warn.W-ENF-UNKNOWN: The modelled intermediaries have unverified enforcement and logging status. Do not assume any of them observed or controlled the flow - or that their absence from a log means the flow bypassed them.
warn.W-ORDER-ASSUMED: Two or more middleboxes are modelled: the chain shown uses a canonical assumed order. Verify the REAL insertion order - conclusions that depend on order inherit this assumption.
warn.W-PATH-UNKNOWN: The path archetype itself is unknown or mixed. Everything downstream of this selection is provisional - establish the real chain before acting on the model.
warn.W-RES-UNKNOWN: How the name resolves is unknown. Resolution is part of the path; until it is established, the client may not even be talking to the modelled destination.
warn.W-RET-UNKNOWN: The return path is unknown while stateful or rewriting devices are modelled - asymmetry would break them silently. Treat the return leg as unverified.
warn.W-TLS-NODES: Multiple TLS terminations were declared, but the modelled path has fewer than two nodes capable of terminating - the TLS story and the path story disagree; reconcile them.
warn.W-TLS-UNKNOWN: Where TLS terminates is unknown. Certificate identity, payload visibility, and evidence boundaries all hinge on it.
warn.W-TOPOLOGY-SENSITIVE: This map and its export describe internal topology. Keep it local, prefer abstract labels, and share deliberately.
warn.W-TR-UNKNOWN: Whether addresses are rewritten is unknown. Every between-points comparison and every log correlation depends on knowing this - establish it first.

baseline.verified: Both sides are captured and verified - the comparison stands on real state.
baseline.weaker: At least one side of this comparison is weaker than a verified capture - the gate reflects it.

R-AFTER-NONE.0: Capture the after across the SAME dimension set, same method, same vantage as the baseline.

R-AFTER-PARTIAL.0: List the dimensions with NO after-capture - they are open items, not passes.

R-AFTER-UNVERIFIED.0: Verify the after-capture: right target, right scope, complete content.

R-BASE-DECLARED.0: Verify each declaration against the actual capture: does the 'before' really exist, verified, where you think it is?

R-BEFORE-ASSUMED.0: Capture a real baseline NOW and treat today's state as the reference for the future, not as proof about the past.

R-BEFORE-MEMORY.0: Capture a real baseline NOW - it cannot rescue this comparison, but it is the 'before' the next one deserves.

R-BEFORE-NONE.0: Capture the full dimension set NOW: today's capture is the baseline every future comparison will thank you for.

R-BEFORE-UNVERIFIED.0: Open the baseline capture and verify it: right target, right scope, complete content.

R-CHURN-HIGH.0: Judge fast-churn dimensions by rates and NEW classes, never by raw before/after inequality.

R-CTX-DRIFT.0: Record the baseline's capture date and re-baseline on every approved change - drift is measured against the last KNOWN-GOOD, not the oldest file.

R-CTX-MIGRATION.0: Capture the after on the NEW target and freeze the OLD target's final state - the fallback depends on both existing.

R-CTX-POSTCHANGE.0: List the differences the change was SUPPOSED to make - every other difference is a finding.

R-CTX-POSTINCIDENT.0: Compare against the pre-incident baseline, not the mid-incident state - and note where no pre-incident capture exists.

R-CTX-ROLLBACK.0: Verify the rollback path itself: the artifact to restore exists, is the right version, and its application procedure is rehearsed.

R-SCOPE-CLUSTER.0: Compare per-member (same identity before and after) AND check members against each other for divergence.

R-SCOPE-HA.0: Capture BOTH members - status, sync state, config epoch - not just the active.

R-SCOPE-POPULATION.0: Capture the aggregate AND a named exemplar per role - the exemplar is where differences become explainable.

R-SVC-VS-STATE.0: Pair at least one service-tier dimension (end-to-end probe, auth transaction) with the component dimensions - and record BOTH verdicts.

R-WIN-EXTENDED.0: For each difference, ask: could ordinary drift over this window explain it? Attribute before you attribute-to-the-change.

DIM-AUTH-FLOW.meaning: Auth can break while everything below it stays green - this dimension catches it.
DIM-AUTH-FLOW.record: A full test-principal login: redirect chain, token issuance, and the claims received.
DIM-AUTH-FLOW.title: Authentication transaction

DIM-CAPACITY-HEADROOM.meaning: A headroom step-change after a change outlives the validation window - it is tomorrow's incident.
DIM-CAPACITY-HEADROOM.record: CPU, memory, and table utilization (connections, routes, sessions) at comparable load.
DIM-CAPACITY-HEADROOM.title: Capacity headroom

DIM-CERT-CHAIN.meaning: A changed chain is either the intended renewal or the wrong cert now in production - never noise.
DIM-CERT-CHAIN.record: The certificate chain each endpoint presents, with expiry dates.
DIM-CERT-CHAIN.title: Presented certificates

DIM-CONFIG-STATE.meaning: Any difference is a real configuration change - intended or not. Attribute every line.
DIM-CONFIG-STATE.record: The full running configuration (or its hash) from the same export path both times.
DIM-CONFIG-STATE.title: Configuration state

DIM-CONTROL-ADJ.meaning: A missing or flapped adjacency explains reachability changes no data-plane counter will.
DIM-CONTROL-ADJ.record: Routing neighbours and their states, with learned-prefix counts per neighbour.
DIM-CONTROL-ADJ.title: Control-plane adjacencies

DIM-ERROR-COUNTERS.meaning: Rates matter, absolutes mislead: compare per-interval deltas, and expect movement on a live system.
DIM-ERROR-COUNTERS.record: Drops, resets, retransmits, denies - the same counters, with the time they were read.
DIM-ERROR-COUNTERS.title: Error counters

DIM-HA-SYNC.meaning: A healthy active with a broken standby is a change that passed validation and a failover that will not.
DIM-HA-SYNC.record: Sync status, config epoch, and failover counters on EVERY member - not just the active.
DIM-HA-SYNC.title: HA / cluster sync state

DIM-LOG-ERRORCLASS.meaning: A brand-new error class after a change is a finding at any volume; familiar noise at familiar volume is not.
DIM-LOG-ERRORCLASS.record: The SET of distinct error classes in the window - not the volume.
DIM-LOG-ERRORCLASS.title: New log error classes

DIM-NEIGHBOR-TOPOLOGY.meaning: A neighbour that moved or vanished re-frames every other difference as possibly topological.
DIM-NEIGHBOR-TOPOLOGY.record: LLDP/CDP neighbours and the ARP/MAC entries for the affected segments.
DIM-NEIGHBOR-TOPOLOGY.title: Neighbour topology

DIM-OBJECT-STATUS.meaning: A member that changed state is a finding even when the aggregate still serves.
DIM-OBJECT-STATUS.record: Operational status of the managed objects: pool members, interfaces, tunnels, peers - as a list, not a count.
DIM-OBJECT-STATUS.title: Managed-object status

DIM-POLICY-HITS.meaning: A policy that stopped (or started) matching is the change's real effect showing itself.
DIM-POLICY-HITS.record: Hit counts on the policies the change touched, plus the default/deny rule.
DIM-POLICY-HITS.title: Policy hit counters

DIM-RESOLUTION-ANSWERS.meaning: An answer change moves traffic somewhere else entirely - upstream of every other dimension.
DIM-RESOLUTION-ANSWERS.record: What the relevant names resolve to, from each view that matters (internal, external).
DIM-RESOLUTION-ANSWERS.title: Resolution answers

DIM-SERVICE-PROBE.meaning: The service tier's own verdict - the dimension that keeps green components from being mistaken for a working service.
DIM-SERVICE-PROBE.record: The same scripted request from the same vantage: status, latency, and the identity presented.
DIM-SERVICE-PROBE.title: Service response, end to end

DIM-SESSION-COUNTS.meaning: Reads as load context, not pass/fail - a cliff or a void is the signal, not ordinary movement.
DIM-SESSION-COUNTS.record: Concurrent sessions and new-connection rate, same counter, same sampling method.
DIM-SESSION-COUNTS.title: Session / connection counts

expected-drift.supports: A difference here is EXPECTED under the declared churn: only rate cliffs, voids, or brand-new classes count as findings.
expected-drift.weakens: Neither a match nor a difference here settles anything on its own - this dimension is context, not verdict, at this churn level.

read-with-care.supports: A difference here is a lead, not a verdict: normal operation can move this dimension, so corroborate with a stable dimension before treating it as the change's effect.
read-with-care.weakens: A match here is comforting but not conclusive - the dimension could have moved and returned within the window.

should-match.supports: Any difference here is a material finding: this dimension should not move on its own under the declared conditions - attribute it fully before concluding anything.
should-match.weakens: An exact match here genuinely supports 'no unintended change' for this dimension - it is the kind of evidence the gate can lean on.

gap.afterPartial: The after-capture does not cover the full dimension set.
gap.baselineNotCapture: The baseline is not a capture (memory / assumption).
gap.churnUnknown: Expected churn is undeclared - fast dimensions are uncalibrated.
gap.windowImmediate: Time-dependent effects have not had their window.

R-AFTER-NONE.reason0: The after-state has not been captured yet.

R-AFTER-PARTIAL.upgrade0: Completing the after-capture across the dimension set raises the gate.

R-BEFORE-ASSUMED.reason0: The baseline is an assumption of health.

R-BEFORE-UNVERIFIED.reason0: The baseline exists but is unverified.
R-BEFORE-UNVERIFIED.upgrade0: Verifying the baseline capture raises the gate.

R-BEFORE-VERIFIED.upgrade0: Keep capturing verified baselines on a cadence - the next comparison inherits this one's discipline.

R-CHURN-FROZEN.reason0: A freeze is declared: differences in ANY dimension are findings.

R-CTX-POSTINCIDENT.upgrade0: A pre-incident baseline located and verified for every dimension raises what this comparison can conclude.

R-CTX-ROLLBACK.downgrade0: An unverified rollback artifact turns 'roll back' from a decision into a second incident.
R-CTX-ROLLBACK.reason0: The decision context is rollback: the gate speaks to whether the evidence justifies rolling back, staying, or holding ready.

R-SVC-VS-STATE.reason0: Any 'continue' is conditional on a service-tier dimension agreeing with the component tier.

R-WIN-IMMEDIATE.upgrade0: Re-capture after an operational window (hours, spanning real load) to let time-dependent effects surface.

gate.defaultDowngrade: Any dimension found different where the expectation is should-match drops the verdict until it is attributed.
gate.defaultReason: The declared evidence classes support this tier - conditional on the checklist and the service-tier pairing.

rule.R-AFTER-NONE: No after-capture yet: the comparison has one side - the gate can only say what to capture and wait.
rule.R-AFTER-PARTIAL: A partial after-capture means validation completeness is itself a finding: what was not captured cannot be declared unchanged.
rule.R-AFTER-UNVERIFIED: An unverified after-capture carries the same risks as an unverified baseline - wrong target, wrong scope, truncated.
rule.R-BASE-DECLARED: The report is gated on declared state classes, never on ingested data - the declarations themselves must be verified.
rule.R-BEFORE-ASSUMED: Assumed-healthy is not a baseline - it is the hypothesis the comparison was supposed to test.
rule.R-BEFORE-MEMORY: A from-memory baseline caps the conclusion: differences against recollection are stories, not evidence.
rule.R-BEFORE-NONE: With no baseline there is nothing to compare against - the honest output is a capture plan, not a comparison.
rule.R-BEFORE-UNVERIFIED: A baseline captured but never verified may be the wrong device, the wrong partition, or a truncated export - verify it before trusting deltas against it.
rule.R-BEFORE-VERIFIED: A captured and verified baseline is the strongest position this comparison can start from.
rule.R-CHURN-FROZEN: Under a freeze, even fast dimensions should hold still - any drift is sharp evidence precisely because churn was excluded.
rule.R-CHURN-HIGH: On a high-churn target, fast-moving dimensions are EXPECTED to differ - reading their movement as regression is the classic false alarm.
rule.R-CHURN-UNKNOWN: Unknown churn means fast dimensions can be neither dismissed nor trusted - calibrate before concluding from them.
rule.R-CTX-DRIFT: A drift check is only as honest as the baseline's age - a stale golden state turns drift detection into archaeology.
rule.R-CTX-MIGRATION: A cutover has TWO targets: the new platform's after must be captured, and the old platform's state preserved for the fallback window.
rule.R-CTX-POSTCHANGE: Post-change validation compares the intended delta against everything else: intended differences confirmed, unintended differences hunted.
rule.R-CTX-POSTINCIDENT: Recovered is not restored: the honest baseline is the PRE-incident capture, not the mid-incident state everyone stared at.
rule.R-CTX-ROLLBACK: A rollback decision needs one more comparison: the rollback path itself is a change, with its own before, after, and blast radius.
rule.R-CTX-UNKNOWN: An unknown comparison context leaves the gate ranking evidence without knowing which decision it feeds.
rule.R-SCOPE-CLUSTER: In a cluster, compare the same member to itself - cross-member comparison confuses drift with divergence.
rule.R-SCOPE-HA: An HA pair is TWO devices: a healthy active with a broken standby is a validation pass and a failover failure.
rule.R-SCOPE-POPULATION: A service population needs an aggregate view plus a named exemplar - aggregates hide the one member that broke.
rule.R-SCOPE-UNKNOWN: With unknown scope, 'the same state' has no defined meaning.
rule.R-SVC-VS-STATE: Green components are not a working service, and unchanged configuration is not health - the two tiers must BOTH be compared.
rule.R-TARGET-UNKNOWN: An unknown target class falls back to the generic dimension catalogue - class-specific dimensions may be missing from the plan.
rule.R-WIN-EXTENDED: Over an extended window, unrelated drift accumulates - attribute each difference before charging it to the change.
rule.R-WIN-IMMEDIATE: An immediate window has not let convergence, caches, or slow consumers speak - a clean picture now upgrades nothing.
rule.R-WIN-UNKNOWN: With an unknown window the report cannot say whether time-dependent effects have had their chance.

warn.W-AFTER-INCOMPLETE: The after-state is incomplete or unverified. Validation completeness is part of the conclusion: what was not captured cannot be declared unchanged.
warn.W-BASELINE-WEAK: The baseline is memory or assumption, not a capture. Differences against it are stories, not evidence - the gate is capped until a real baseline exists.
warn.W-CHURN-UNKNOWN: Expected churn is unknown: fast-moving dimensions cannot be calibrated, so their differences can be neither dismissed nor trusted.
warn.W-CTX-UNKNOWN: The comparison context is unknown - the gate can rank evidence quality but cannot tailor the decision it feeds.
warn.W-DECLARED-STATES: This report is gated on DECLARED state classes, not on data this tool has seen. You declare the states, the tool gates the conclusion - verify the declarations against the actual captures.
warn.W-GREEN-NOT-DONE: Never label a change successful on green components alone: at least one service-tier dimension (end-to-end probe, auth transaction) must agree before any conclusion above 'observe' is honest.
warn.W-SCOPE-UNKNOWN: The scope is unknown: whether one device or a population is being compared changes what 'the same state' even means.
warn.W-TARGET-UNKNOWN: The target class is unknown - the dimension catalogue falls back to the generic set; class-specific dimensions may be missing.
warn.W-WIN-IMMEDIATE: The observation window is immediate. Convergence, cache expiry, session re-establishment, and slow consumers have not spoken yet - a clean immediate picture upgrades nothing.
warn.W-WIN-UNKNOWN: The observation window is unknown - the report cannot say whether time-dependent effects have had their chance to appear.

p0f-signature-explainer.name: p0f passive TCP/IP signature explainer
p0f-signature-explainer.blurb: Decode a p0f v3 SYN fingerprint into its eight fields and see what each reveals about the sender's OS, network path, and stack.
p0f-signature-explainer.runsLocally: Runs locally. The signature you paste never leaves your browser.

share.carries: The link carries the signature as typed, and nothing else.

err.empty: Paste a p0f v3 TCP signature, e.g. 4:64:0:*:mss*20,7:mss,sok,ts,nop,ws:df,id+:0
err.fields: A p0f v3 signature has 8 colon-separated fields (ver:ittl:olen:mss:wsize,scale:olayout:quirks:pclass); found {count}.
err.version: The version field must be 4, 6, or * (found "{ver}").

mean.mssAny: varies with the sender's link; used to guess the network type
mean.olayout: the order of TCP options - one of the strongest signals
mean.olen: {n, plural, one {{n} byte} other {{n} bytes}} of IP options / IPv6 extension headers

opt.eol: explicit end-of-options marker, sometimes followed by padding bytes (eol+N)
opt.mss: advertises the largest TCP payload the sender will accept; tied to the interface MTU
opt.nop: a single padding byte used to align later options to word boundaries; its count and position are themselves a fingerprint
opt.sack: carries selective-ACK blocks (unusual in a SYN)
opt.ts: enables RTT measurement and PAWS; its presence and position vary by stack
opt.unknownNote: not a recognized p0f option token
opt.ws: the shift applied to the window field, allowing windows above 64 KB

os.exactWhy: Initial TTL {ttl}, option layout {layout}, and quirks {quirks} match p0f's documented signature for this family.
os.familyWhy: The option layout is not an exact database entry, but the initial TTL near {initial} points to {fam}.
os.noMatchWhy: The field shape does not match a bundled reference signature; p0f would fall back to a generic family or report unknown.

quirk.0_plus: the IP 'must be zero' field is non-zero
quirk.ack_minus: the ACK field is zero while the ACK flag is set
quirk.ack_plus: the ACK field is non-zero while the ACK flag is clear
quirk.df: the IP Don't-Fragment bit is set
quirk.ecn: an explicit congestion-notification flag is set
quirk.exws: the window-scale factor is excessive (greater than 14)
quirk.flow: the IPv6 flow label is non-zero
quirk.id_minus: DF is not set yet the IP ID field is zero
quirk.id_plus: DF is set and the IP ID field is non-zero (many modern stacks)
quirk.opt_plus: there is non-zero data in the options padding
quirk.seq_minus: the TCP sequence number is zero
quirk.ts1_minus: the first timestamp value is zero
quirk.ts2_plus: the second timestamp is non-zero in a SYN
quirk.uptr_plus: the urgent pointer is non-zero while the URG flag is clear

ttl.note: An initial TTL near {initial} is characteristic of {src}. Because each router decrements TTL, a mismatch between this value and the OS a User-Agent claims is a classic proxy or NAT signal: the packet carries the proxy's stack TTL, not the client's.
ttl.noteHops: An initial TTL near {initial} is characteristic of {src}. Because each router decrements TTL, a mismatch between this value and the OS a User-Agent claims is a classic proxy or NAT signal: the packet carries the proxy's stack TTL, not the client's. The "+{hops}" records the observed hop distance.
ttl.unparsed: The initial TTL could not be parsed.

win.fixed: A fixed window of {n, plural, one {{n} byte} other {{n} bytes}}.
win.fixed65535: A fixed window of 65535 bytes. 65535 is the classic 16-bit maximum advertised by Windows before scaling.
win.mss: The window is expressed as {mult} times the MSS - a stack that sizes its receive window from the segment size (typical of Linux, whose initial window is often 10 or 20 times MSS).
win.mtu: The window is expressed relative to the interface MTU.
win.wild: The window size is wildcarded, so it varies and is excluded from the match.

user-agent-entropy-analyzer.bitsDisclaimer: Bit estimates are illustrative, from published fingerprinting research - not a live measurement of any population.

share.carries: The link carries the User-Agent as typed; a paste holding a cookie, token or password gets none.
share.maybeSecret: Line {line} may hold a secret ({label}): check it before you send the link.
share.blockedSecret: No link: line {line} holds a credential ({label}). Paste the User-Agent alone, then share again.

err.empty: Paste a User-Agent string, e.g. Mozilla/5.0 (Windows NT 10.0; Win64; x64) AppleWebKit/537.36 (KHTML, like Gecko) Chrome/120.0.0.0 Safari/537.36
err.notUa: That does not look like a User-Agent string. A UA usually starts with "Mozilla/5.0" and carries product/version tokens.

note.arch: coarse architecture hint; being folded into Client Hints
note.browser: the product family; a handful of browsers dominate, so this alone is low-entropy
note.clientHints: Modern browsers are moving identifying detail out of the User-Agent and into User-Agent Client Hints: Sec-CH-UA, Sec-CH-UA-Platform, Sec-CH-UA-Mobile and friends. A site must actively request the high-entropy hints (full version, model, platform version) via Accept-CH, which makes the collection visible in headers instead of implicit in one string.
note.device: desktop vs phone vs tablet, inferred from tokens
note.engine: the rendering engine is largely implied by the browser
note.frozen: This string is in the reduced/frozen form: the minor version reads 0.0.0 and platform detail is capped, so the UA itself leaks less. The detail did not vanish - it moved to Client Hints a site has to ask for.
note.full: This string carries full version and platform detail. On the current web that detail is increasingly available only through the reduced UA plus Client Hints; a fully detailed classic UA is itself a mild signal.
note.os: OS family plus version narrows the field
note.versionFull: the full version can be distinguishing, especially just after a release
note.versionReduced: reduced to a frozen value, so it carries little entropy by design

http-header-order-fingerprint.runsLocally: Runs locally. The headers you paste never leave your browser.
http-header-order-fingerprint.missingIntro: A browser would normally send these:

share.carries: The link carries the header block with every credential, cookie value and secret parameter replaced by {mark}; names and order stay.
share.redacted: {n, plural, =0 {Nothing in it needed replacing.} one {One value is replaced.} other {# values are replaced.}}
share.blockedSecret: No link: line {line} holds a key, token or password ({label}) that cannot be replaced safely. Put a placeholder in its place, then share again.
share.blockedCopy: No link: the copy would read differently from the block. Remove the credentials yourself, then share again.

casing.lower: All header names are lowercase, which is how HTTP/2 carries them on the wire - consistent with an HTTP/2 capture.
casing.mixed: Mixed casing across header names, which itself can distinguish a hand-built or library request from a browser.
casing.title: All header names are Title-Cased, the HTTP/1.1 convention. On the wire HTTP/2 lowercases them, so Title-Case here suggests an HTTP/1.1 capture or a tool that rewrites casing.

err.empty: Paste a raw HTTP request header block (a request line and one "Name: value" per line).
err.line: Line {line} is not a valid header ("Name: value" expected): {text}
err.none: No headers found. Include at least one "Name: value" line.

hint.chromium: The header order closely matches the Chromium sequence and Sec-CH-UA client hints are present.
hint.firefox: The order matches Gecko's sequence, with Fetch Metadata but no Sec-CH-UA (Firefox does not send UA client hints).
hint.lib: The User-Agent names {tool}, a non-browser HTTP client; its header set and order match a library, not a browser.
hint.minimal: No browser-only headers and an order that does not match a known browser; treat as a library or custom client.
hint.modern: Browser-only headers are present, but the order does not cleanly match one engine - possibly reordered by a proxy.
hint.script: Common browser headers are missing ({missing}) and no Sec-Fetch/Sec-CH headers appear - the signature of a non-browser client.
hint.scriptLabel: Likely a script or HTTP library (curl, requests, Go, etc.)

pos.accept: Accept - the exact default value and position is browser-characteristic
pos.host: Host - browsers and libraries differ on whether it leads; HTTP/2 carries it as the :authority pseudo-header
pos.other: ordinary header; its slot in the sequence still contributes to the order fingerprint
pos.secCh: a User-Agent Client Hint - only browsers that support Client Hints emit these, and only after a site requests them
pos.secFetch: a Fetch Metadata header - emitted by modern browsers, rarely reproduced by scripts
pos.userAgent: User-Agent - its position relative to Accept differs between Chromium and Gecko

bigip-dns-gslb-simulator.memberTierTitle: Member tier - which virtual server resolves
bigip-dns-gslb-simulator.memberDynamicNote: One or more pools use a dynamic member method; those members show 0 because their selection needs live metrics.
