agent-mediated-buying.changed: Projected: software evaluating vendors, comparing terms, and transacting on a company's behalf.
agent-mediated-buying.enabled: If it holds, procurement cycles compress from weeks to hours, and vendor discovery stops being a human activity.
agent-mediated-buying.source: Gartner projects that by 2028, 90% of business-to-business buying will be intermediated by AI agents, routing over 15 trillion US dollars of spend through agent exchanges.
agent-mediated-buying.title: Agent-intermediated business purchasing

agents-in-apps.changed: Projected: software that carries out multi-step work rather than waiting to be operated step by step.
agents-in-apps.enabled: If it holds, routine process work shifts from being performed to being supervised.
agents-in-apps.source: Gartner projects 40% of enterprise applications will integrate task-specific AI agents by the end of 2026, up from under 5% in 2025. Gartner also projects that over 40% of agentic AI projects could be abandoned by 2027 on governance and return-on-investment failures. Field surveys in 2026 report high adoption but only around one in ten deployments running in production.
agents-in-apps.title: Task-specific AI agents inside enterprise applications

agents-in-ops.changed: Projected: infrastructure changes proposed and executed by software under human policy rather than human hands.
agents-in-ops.enabled: If it holds, operations work moves towards defining guardrails and reviewing decisions instead of making changes.
agents-in-ops.source: Gartner (Predicts 2026: AI Agents Will Transform IT Infrastructure and Operations, published 4 December 2025) projects adoption rising from under 5% in 2025 towards a majority by 2029, and human-in-the-loop involvement in IT operations workflows falling from 95% in 2025 to 40% by 2028.
agents-in-ops.title: Agentic operations in IT infrastructure

ai-act-annex1.changed: AI inside medical devices, machinery, vehicles and similar regulated products comes under the AI Act's high-risk regime.
ai-act-annex1.enabled: Regulatory coverage of AI that arrives inside a physical product rather than as software you choose to install.
ai-act-annex1.source: Regulation (EU) 2024/1689, Annex I obligations scheduled for 2 August 2027; the provisionally-agreed Digital Omnibus would move this to 2 August 2028 if adopted.
ai-act-annex1.title: EU rules for AI embedded in regulated products

ai-act-gpai.changed: Providers of large general-purpose models took on documentation and transparency duties in the EU.
ai-act-gpai.enabled: Regulatory attention on the model itself, not only on the application built from it.
ai-act-gpai.title: EU obligations for general-purpose AI models begin

ai-act-high-risk.changed: Systems used for recruitment, credit scoring, education, law enforcement and similar face conformity assessment, registration, and human-oversight duties.
ai-act-high-risk.contestedNote: Actively moving. The Digital Omnibus on AI reached provisional trilogue agreement on 7 May 2026 to defer Annex III obligations to 2 December 2027, and product-embedded Annex I obligations to 2 August 2028. That agreement is NOT yet law: until it is formally adopted and published in the Official Journal, 2 August 2026 remains the operative legal date and should be planned for.
ai-act-high-risk.enabled: The most operationally demanding tier of AI regulation, and the clearest test of whether the framework is workable.
ai-act-high-risk.source: Regulation (EU) 2024/1689, Annex III high-risk obligations scheduled for 2 August 2026.
ai-act-high-risk.title: EU AI Act high-risk obligations

ai-act-prohibitions.changed: Certain AI uses became illegal in the EU outright, with penalties up to 35 million euro or 7% of global turnover.
ai-act-prohibitions.enabled: The first binding line between AI that may be built and AI that may not, anywhere in the world.
ai-act-prohibitions.source: Regulation (EU) 2024/1689, prohibitions and AI-literacy obligations applicable 2 February 2025.
ai-act-prohibitions.title: EU AI Act prohibitions apply

arpanet.changed: Nothing, for almost everyone. Four university nodes could exchange data over leased lines.
arpanet.enabled: A network built to survive the loss of any node, which is why no one can switch the internet off today.
arpanet.title: ARPANET carries its first packets

broadband.changed: The internet stopped being a place you went to and started being a thing that was simply on.
broadband.enabled: Media, software delivery, and real-time services that a metered, occupied phone line could never carry.
broadband.title: Broadband replaces dial-up

cloud.changed: Starting something no longer required buying servers or waiting months for a data centre.
cloud.enabled: A two-person company renting the same class of infrastructure as a bank, and paying by the hour.
cloud.title: Cloud turns infrastructure into a purchase

creator-platforms.changed: Anyone could publish to a potential audience of millions with a phone and no gatekeeper.
creator-platforms.enabled: New livelihoods and new reach, plus a recommendation layer that now decides what most people see.
creator-platforms.title: Distribution stops being the barrier

delivery-platforms.changed: Meals, rides, and groceries arrived by app, and waiting became a tracked progress bar.
delivery-platforms.enabled: Convenience at scale, alongside a labour model whose employment status is still being litigated worldwide.
delivery-platforms.title: On-demand delivery becomes ordinary

ecommerce.changed: A shop stopped needing to be somewhere you could walk to during opening hours.
ecommerce.enabled: Selection beyond what a local shelf could hold, and sellers reaching customers with no shopfront at all.
ecommerce.title: Buying online becomes possible

egov.changed: Taxes, licences, and records became forms you submit rather than queues you join.
egov.enabled: Service at population scale without proportional staff, and a new class of exclusion for those without access.
egov.title: Government services move online

ehr.changed: Your history stopped living in a folder in one building.
ehr.enabled: Care that follows the patient between providers, and a permanent argument about who may read it.
ehr.title: Medical records go digital

forced-remote.changed: Offices closed and knowledge work moved home in weeks, using capability that had existed for years.
forced-remote.enabled: Hiring detached from geography, and a permanent renegotiation of what an office is actually for. The clearest example that transformation is usually blocked by assumption rather than by technology.
forced-remote.title: Remote work stops being a request

gdpr.changed: Consent, access, and erasure became rights with penalties attached rather than policies you hoped for.
gdpr.enabled: A template copied worldwide, and the first credible answer to 'what happens if they misuse my data'.
gdpr.title: GDPR makes data protection enforceable

lgpd.changed: Brazilian residents gained enforceable rights over their personal data, with a national authority behind them.
lgpd.enabled: Data protection anchored in Brazilian law rather than borrowed from abroad, alongside the Marco Civil's earlier guarantees.
lgpd.source: Lei 13.709/2018 (LGPD), in force from 2020; ANPD as supervisory authority.
lgpd.title: Brazil's LGPD takes effect

llm-assistants.changed: Drafting, summarizing, translating, and explaining became things you could ask for in ordinary words.
llm-assistants.enabled: Software that responds to intent rather than to syntax, for people who never learned the syntax.
llm-assistants.title: Language models become everyday tools

marketplaces.changed: Small sellers reached national customers without building distribution of their own.
marketplaces.enabled: A one-person business with global reach, and a new dependence on the platform that grants it.
marketplaces.title: Marketplaces absorb the long tail

mobile-payments.changed: Paying stopped requiring a card, and eventually stopped requiring a wallet at all.
mobile-payments.enabled: Payments for people a card network never reached, and merchants with no terminal.
mobile-payments.title: The phone becomes the wallet

online-banking.changed: Checking a balance or moving money stopped requiring a queue and a counter.
online-banking.enabled: Financial admin at any hour, and the slow decline of the branch network that had defined retail banking.
online-banking.title: Banking leaves the branch

personal-computer.changed: Computing stopped being something you requested from a department and became something on your own desk.
personal-computer.enabled: Individual authorship of documents, models, and software, without asking permission from a mainframe operator.
personal-computer.title: The personal computer reaches the desk

physical-agent-data.changed: Projected: robots, vehicles, and sensors producing trajectory data at a scale that dwarfs today's digital telemetry.
physical-agent-data.enabled: If it holds, the data-protection and networking problems of the next decade are physical rather than web-shaped.
physical-agent-data.source: Gartner data and analytics predictions (announced 11 March 2026) project that by 2029, AI agents will generate ten times more data from physical environments than all digital AI applications combined.
physical-agent-data.title: Agents generating more data from the physical world than from the digital one

pix.changed: Transfers between any two people or businesses settled in seconds, free for individuals, at any hour.
pix.enabled: A national instant-payment rail built by the central bank rather than by card networks, adopted at a speed that surprised nearly everyone and became a reference case internationally.
pix.title: Brazil launches PIX instant payments

remote-capable.changed: Laptops and VPNs made it possible to work away from the office, for those permitted to.
remote-capable.enabled: The technical precondition for remote work, sitting unused for fifteen years because the culture said no.
remote-capable.title: Work becomes technically portable

smartphone.changed: The phone stopped being a phone. Access became continuous rather than a thing you sat down for.
smartphone.enabled: Location-aware, always-available services, and the first computing most of the world ever owned.
smartphone.title: The smartphone puts the internet in a pocket

streaming.changed: Watching stopped being something that happened at a time somebody else chose.
streaming.enabled: On-demand everything, the collapse of the broadcast schedule, and eventually the fragmentation of the audience.
streaming.title: Streaming replaces the schedule

telemedicine.changed: A consultation stopped requiring travel, a waiting room, and a day off work.
telemedicine.enabled: Access for remote and immobile patients, following regulatory change that had been debated for a decade and moved in weeks.
telemedicine.title: Telemedicine becomes normal practice

web-public.changed: Finding information stopped requiring you to know where it lived, or to own the right reference book.
web-public.enabled: Publishing to a global audience with no printing press, no distributor, and no permission.
web-public.title: The web becomes public

fortigate-policy-lookup-explainer.name: FortiGate policy lookup explainer
fortigate-policy-lookup-explainer.blurb: Paste a FortiGate policy list and a packet, and see which policy matches, why each earlier policy did not, and which policies below the match can never take effect as ordered.
fortigate-policy-lookup-explainer.emptyState: Paste a policy list and a packet line to see which policy wins.
fortigate-policy-lookup-explainer.runsLocally: Runs entirely in your browser. Nothing is uploaded.
fortigate-policy-lookup-explainer.pastePlaceholder:
config firewall policy ... end

packet: srcintf=port1, dstintf=port2, srcaddr=LAN, dstaddr=WebSrv, service=HTTPS
fortigate-policy-lookup-explainer.implicitDeny: No policy matched. This traffic meets the implicit deny at the end of the list.

share.carries: The link carries the box with each password, key, community and ENC value as a numbered mark such as {mark}; a private key or token gets none.
share.caution: A policy list names your interfaces, addresses and objects: read it before you send the link.
share.redacted: {n, plural, =0 {Nothing in it needed replacing, so the link carries it as pasted.} one {One value is replaced.} other {# values are replaced.}}
share.maybeSecret: {more, plural, =0 {Line {line} may hold a secret ({label}): check it, and any internal names, before you send the link.} one {Line {line} ({label}) and one more line may hold secrets: check them, and any internal names, before you send the link.} other {Line {line} ({label}) and # more lines may hold secrets: check them, and any internal names, before you send the link.}}
share.blockedSecret: {more, plural, =0 {No link: line {line} holds a key, token or password ({label}) that cannot be replaced safely. Put a placeholder in its place, then share again.} one {No link: line {line} ({label}) and one more line hold keys, tokens or passwords that cannot be replaced safely. Put placeholders in their place, then share again.} other {No link: line {line} ({label}) and # more lines hold keys, tokens or passwords that cannot be replaced safely. Put placeholders in their place, then share again.}}

detail.covered: This policy also matches but is broader than policy {id} above it, which is the normal shape of a catch-all. Nothing to fix.
detail.disabled: Policy is disabled, so it is never consulted.
detail.noMatch: The {label} did not match: policy has {policyHas}, packet has {packetHas}.
detail.shadowed: This policy is at least as specific as policy {id} above it and also matches, so as ordered it can never take effect for this traffic. Move it above policy {id}.

note.coveredMany: {count} broader policies below the match would also match ({ids}). That is the normal shape of a catch-all and is not a fault.
note.coveredOne: {count} broader policy below the match would also match ({ids}). That is the normal shape of a catch-all and is not a fault.
note.explicitDeny: Policy {id} matched and its action is DENY, so the traffic is dropped by an explicit rule rather than by the implicit deny.
note.implicitDeny: No policy matched, so this traffic meets the implicit deny at the end of the list. By default that drop is not logged, which is why traffic can disappear with no policy showing a hit.
note.names: Matching here compares object NAMES, not resolved addresses: a pasted policy list does not carry the address-object definitions, so supply the object name (or 'all') rather than an IP.
note.noPacket: No packet was supplied, so the policies are listed without a lookup. Add a line like: packet: srcintf=port1, dstintf=port2, srcaddr=all, dstaddr=WebServer, service=HTTPS
note.shadowedMany: {count} policies are shadowed for this packet: {ids}. They would match, but a policy above already won, so they can never take effect as ordered.
note.shadowedOne: {count} policy is shadowed for this packet: {ids}. It would match, but a policy above already won, so it can never take effect as ordered.

ref.every: Every criterion must match: incoming interface, outgoing interface, source address, destination address, service, schedule, and user where configured.
ref.firstMatch: FortiOS evaluates firewall policies top to bottom and stops at the FIRST policy whose criteria all match.
ref.hitCounter: A policy that matches nothing shows a hit counter that never increments. Nothing warns you.
ref.implicitDeny: At the end of the list is an implicit deny, and by default it is not logged.
ref.paste: Paste a policy list and add a line such as: packet: srcintf=port1, dstintf=port2, srcaddr=all, dstaddr=WebServer, service=HTTPS

warn.capped: Only the first {max} policies were parsed.
warn.noPolicies: No policies were recognized in the input.
warn.noRows: No policy rows were recognized in the table.

fortigate-session-table-explainer.name: FortiGate session table explainer
fortigate-session-table-explainer.blurb: Paste diagnose sys session list output and have it read back: which policy admitted the flow, what was translated on each leg, and whether the far side ever replied.
fortigate-session-table-explainer.emptyState: Paste session output to have it decoded.
fortigate-session-table-explainer.runsLocally: Runs entirely in your browser. Nothing is uploaded.
fortigate-session-table-explainer.pastePlaceholder: session info: proto=6 proto_state=01 duration=125 expire=3590 ...
fortigate-session-table-explainer.howToRead: How to read a FortiGate session
fortigate-session-table-explainer.trafficHint: Counters in each direction. Outbound traffic with zero reply means the packets left and nothing came back.
fortigate-session-table-explainer.timersHint: How long the session has existed, when it expires, and the configured idle timeout.
fortigate-session-table-explainer.gwyHint: The next-hop gateway chosen for each direction.
fortigate-session-table-explainer.noDocumentedMeaning: No documented meaning is asserted for this value.

share.carries: The link carries the sessions as pasted; a box holding a credential gets none.
share.caution: Session output names internal addresses, ports, NAT translations and sometimes users: read it before you send the link.
share.maybeSecret: {more, plural, =0 {Line {line} may hold a secret ({label}): check it, and any internal names, before you send the link.} one {Line {line} ({label}) and one more line may hold secrets: check them, and any internal names, before you send the link.} other {Line {line} ({label}) and # more lines may hold secrets: check them, and any internal names, before you send the link.}}
share.blockedSecret: {more, plural, =0 {No link: line {line} holds a credential ({label}). Replace it with a placeholder, then share again.} one {No link: line {line} ({label}) and one more line hold credentials. Replace them with placeholders, then share again.} other {No link: line {line} ({label}) and # more lines hold credentials. Replace them with placeholders, then share again.}}

find.allowErr: A non-zero allow_err count means packets were permitted despite an error condition, which is worth investigating rather than ignoring.
find.bothWays: Traffic has flowed in both directions, so the path works in both directions and the policy permitted it.
find.dnat: Destination NAT is present, so a VIP matched. Remember the ordering: destination translation happens BEFORE the routing lookup and before policy evaluation, which is why the policy destination must be the VIP object.
find.expiring: This session expires in {seconds, plural, one {{seconds} second} other {{seconds} seconds}} and is about to be removed from the table, which is why a second look may not find it.
find.noNat: No translation on any leg: this session was routed without NAT.
find.noReply: NOTHING CAME BACK. The FortiGate forwarded traffic in the original direction and has seen no reply packets. The session exists and the policy permitted it, so this is not the firewall blocking the traffic: look at routing beyond this device, at the destination host, or at a filter further along the path.
find.offloaded: The session is offloaded to hardware. Offloaded traffic does not traverse the CPU path, so a packet sniffer on the device will not show it unless offload is disabled for the test.
find.policy: Policy {policy} admitted this session. That is the authoritative answer to which rule matched, and it beats reading the policy list.
find.policy0: policy_id=0 means no ordinary firewall policy admitted this session; it is typically local traffic to the FortiGate itself or an implicitly handled flow.
find.replyOnly: Reply traffic only, with nothing in the original direction. That usually means the session was created by traffic this device did not see the start of, or the directions are the reverse of what you assumed.
find.snat: Source NAT is present, applied AFTER the policy matched. The translated tuple in brackets is what the far side sees.

flag.dirty: session is flagged for re-evaluation against the policy set
flag.local: session terminates on the FortiGate itself rather than passing through
flag.may_dirty: session may be re-evaluated if the policy set changes
flag.ndr: no dirty routing: the route is not re-checked on every packet
flag.npu: session is offloaded to the network processor
flag.synced: session has been synchronized to the HA peer

hook.dnatTo: Destination NAT: {dst} was rewritten to {translated}, which is a VIP doing its work.
hook.snatTo: Source NAT: the source {src} was rewritten to {translated} on the way out.

note.deadMany: {count} of {total} sessions have outbound traffic and no reply. That is the signature of a path that works in one direction only.
note.deadOne: {count} of {total} session has outbound traffic and no reply. That is the signature of a path that works in one direction only.
note.raw: Fields whose full value tables are vendor documentation are shown raw rather than guessed at.

ref.authoritative: The session table is the authoritative record of what the FortiGate did: which policy admitted the flow, what was translated, and whether the far side replied.
ref.hooks: hook=post dir=org act=snat carries the post-NAT source; hook=pre dir=reply act=dnat carries the pre-NAT destination.
ref.paste: Paste the output of `diagnose sys session list` (filter it first with `diagnose sys session filter dst '<'address>` so you get the session you mean).
ref.policyId: policy_id names the rule that actually matched, which settles arguments the policy list alone cannot.
ref.statistic: The most useful field is the statistic line. org traffic with reply=0 means the packets left and nothing came back, which is not the firewall blocking anything.

state.tcp01: TCP established: the handshake completed and the session is open.
state.tcpOther: TCP state pair {raw}. The two digits are the connection state in the original and reply directions; consult Fortinet's session-state documentation for the full table.
state.udp00: UDP one-way: the FortiGate has seen traffic in the original direction only. Nothing has come back.
state.udp01: UDP two-way: traffic has been seen in both directions.

warn.capped: Only the first {max} sessions were parsed.
warn.noBlocks: No session blocks were recognized. Each session starts with a line beginning 'session info:'.

fortigate-ha-failover-simulator.name: FortiGate HA failover simulator
fortigate-ha-failover-simulator.blurb: Describe an FGCP cluster and see which unit becomes primary, which criterion decided it, and who would be primary if override were toggled.
fortigate-ha-failover-simulator.emptyState: Describe a cluster to run the election.
fortigate-ha-failover-simulator.runsLocally: Runs entirely in your browser. Nothing is uploaded.
fortigate-ha-failover-simulator.pastePlaceholder:

cmp.age: {winner} has been in the cluster longer (age {a} vs {b}). Higher age wins, and with override disabled age is compared BEFORE priority.
cmp.failedMany: {winner} has {n} failed monitored interfaces against {loser}'s {m}. Fewer wins, and this is compared before everything else.
cmp.failedOne: {winner} has {n} failed monitored interface against {loser}'s {m}. Fewer wins, and this is compared before everything else.
cmp.serial: Everything else tied, so the serial number decides: {a} over {b}. This exists only to make the election deterministic.

find.ageBeatsPriority: {highest} has the highest priority ({priority}) and is NOT primary. That is not a fault: with override DISABLED, which is the default, FGCP compares age before priority, and {primaryName} has been in the cluster longer. The default exists so a flapping unit cannot repeatedly seize and lose the role, because each seizure is a disruption.
find.byFailed: The election was settled by monitored interface health, which is compared before every other criterion. Fix the down interface and the comparison moves on to the next criterion.
find.bySerial: Every other criterion tied, so the serial number decided. That is deterministic but arbitrary: if you want a specific unit preferred, set a priority rather than relying on this.
find.counterOff: With override DISABLED instead, {other} would be primary. That single setting is what decides this cluster's outcome.
find.counterOn: With override ENABLED instead, {other} would be primary. That single setting is what decides this cluster's outcome.
find.noCounter: Toggling override would not change the outcome for this cluster, so the override setting is not what is deciding it here.
find.notPrimary: {highest} has the highest priority and is not primary, decided on {criterion}. Priority is only consulted after that criterion.
find.override: Override is ENABLED, so priority is compared before age. The preferred unit reclaims the primary role as soon as it returns, which is usually what people want and does mean a failback disruption each time it comes back.

ref.describe: Describe the cluster and this tool runs the election and shows which criterion decided it.
ref.lineMemberA: member: name=FGT-A, serial=FG100A, priority=200, age=120, failed=0
ref.lineMemberB: member: name=FGT-B, serial=FG100B, priority=128, age=8600, failed=0
ref.order: FGCP elects the primary by comparing, in order: failed monitored interfaces (fewer wins), age (higher wins), priority (higher wins), then serial number.
ref.overrideOff: With override DISABLED, which is the default, age is compared BEFORE priority. A rebooted unit therefore stays secondary even with a higher priority.
ref.overrideOn: With override ENABLED, priority is compared before age, so the preferred unit reclaims the role when it returns, at the cost of a failback disruption.

issue.auth: Authentication method mismatch: {nameA} uses {authA}, {nameB} uses {authB}. Phase 1 fails on identity before any proposal is considered.
issue.intersects: {name} intersects on {values}. The lists differ but that is fine: a tunnel needs one common proposal, not identical lists.
issue.lifetime: {phase} lifetimes differ ({la} vs {lb}). This is NOT a failure: the shorter value wins, so the effective lifetime is {shorter} seconds. Very different values only mean rekeys at awkward intervals.
issue.mode: IKEv1 mode mismatch: {nameA} is {modeA}, {nameB} is {modeB}. Main and aggressive mode cannot interoperate.
issue.noCommon: No common {name}. {nameA} offers {offerA}; {nameB} offers {offerB}. Proposals must INTERSECT, so add a value both sides accept.
issue.pfsOffOn: Perfect forward secrecy is disabled on {nameA} and enabled on {nameB}. Phase 2 fails, and the log message does not usually say PFS, which is why this one costs time.
issue.pfsOnOff: Perfect forward secrecy is enabled on {nameA} and disabled on {nameB}. Phase 2 fails, and the log message does not usually say PFS, which is why this one costs time.
issue.selectorLocal: Selector mismatch: {nameA} local is {aSrc} but {nameB} remote is {bDst}. These must match EXACTLY and are compared crossed, because one peer's local subnet is the other's remote. A subnet against a supernet is a mismatch, not an approximation.
issue.selectorRemote: Selector mismatch: {nameA} remote is {aDst} but {nameB} local is {bSrc}. These must match exactly.
issue.selectorsOk: Selectors are mirrored correctly: each peer's local subnet is the other's remote.
issue.version: IKE version mismatch: {nameA} is {versionA}, {nameB} is {versionB}. The peers cannot negotiate at all across versions.

note.onlySupplied: Only the fields you supplied are compared. A field present on one side and absent on the other is treated as not stated rather than as a disagreement.

ref.describe: Describe both peers, one block each:
ref.failures: Phase 1 failures are identity or proposal. Phase 2 failures are selectors, transforms or PFS.
ref.intersect: Proposals INTERSECT: the lists do not have to be identical, they only need one value in common.
ref.lifetimes: Lifetimes do NOT need to match. The shorter value wins.
ref.linePhase1: phase1: version=ikev2, encryption=aes256, hash=sha256, dhgroup=14, auth=psk, lifetime=86400
ref.linePhase2: phase2: encryption=aes256, hash=sha256, pfs=enable, dhgroup=14, src=10.1.0.0/16, dst=10.2.0.0/16
ref.mirrored: Selectors are mirrored: one peer's local subnet is the other's remote, and they must match exactly.
ref.phases: Phase 1 authenticates the peers and protects the negotiation; phase 2 negotiates the security associations and the selectors.

verdict.none: No fatal disagreement was found in what you supplied. If the tunnel still does not pass traffic, remember that a tunnel which reports up and carries nothing is missing a ROUTE or a FIREWALL POLICY, not an IPsec setting.
verdict.phase1: PHASE 1 WOULD FAIL. The peers cannot establish the protected channel, so phase 2 is never attempted. Expect no phase 2 in the logs at all.
verdict.phase2: PHASE 1 WOULD SUCCEED AND PHASE 2 WOULD FAIL. The peers authenticate and then disagree about what to protect, which is the signature of a selector, transform or PFS problem.

warn.firstTwo: Only the first two peers were compared.
warn.needTwo: Two peers are needed to compare. Each starts with a line like: peer: name=SiteA

detail.down: Withdrawn: the route is down, so it is not in the forwarding table. This is what link health monitoring does, and it is what lets a floating backup take over when the path beyond the interface fails.
detail.ecmpMany: Installed, longest matching prefix (/{len}), and tied on priority {priority} with {others} other routes. Traffic is load shared across them by ECMP.
detail.ecmpOne: Installed, longest matching prefix (/{len}), and tied on priority {priority} with {others} other route. Traffic is load shared across them by ECMP.
detail.floating: NOT INSTALLED. Distance {distance} lost to distance {min} for the same prefix, so this route is absent from the forwarding table rather than merely deprioritized. It is a floating backup: it appears only when the lower-distance route is withdrawn.
detail.lessSpecific: Installed and in the table, but a more specific route (/{len}) also matches {destination}. Longest prefix wins at forwarding time, so this route is used only for destinations the longer prefix does not cover.
detail.priorityLost: Installed, but priority {priority} lost to priority {minPrio} among the routes with the longest matching prefix.
detail.selected: Installed, longest matching prefix (/{len}), and lowest priority ({priority}). This is the route traffic to {destination} takes.

note.ecmp: Several routes tied completely, so ECMP load shares across them. The default hash is source-IP based, which keeps a given source on a consistent path - per-packet sharing across paths of different latency causes reordering.
note.floatingMany: {count} routes are configured but NOT in the forwarding table, having lost the distance comparison. A route you cannot find in `get router info routing-table all` did not fail to save; it lost on distance.
note.floatingOne: {count} route is configured but NOT in the forwarding table, having lost the distance comparison. A route you cannot find in `get router info routing-table all` did not fail to save; it lost on distance.
note.scope: This models the routing table only. A policy route is consulted BEFORE the table and overrides it, and SD-WAN rules select a member before the table is reached.
note.unroutable: No installed route covers {destination}. The packet would be dropped as unroutable.

ref.distance: DISTANCE decides which route is INSTALLED. Routes to the same destination compete, the lowest distance wins, and the loser is absent from the table rather than merely deprioritized.
ref.lineRoute1: route: prefix=0.0.0.0/0, gw=192.0.2.1, dev=wan1, distance=10, priority=0
ref.lineRoute2: route: prefix=10.2.0.0/16, gw=10.1.1.1, dev=port3, distance=10, priority=0
ref.longest: Forwarding takes the LONGEST matching prefix among installed routes. True ties on prefix, distance and priority are load shared by ECMP.
ref.policyRoute: A policy route is consulted BEFORE the routing table and overrides it. If the table says one thing and traffic does another, look for a policy route first - this tool models the table, not policy routes.
ref.priority: PRIORITY decides which of several ALREADY-INSTALLED routes is preferred. It never resurrects a route that lost on distance.
ref.samePrefix: Same prefix and same distance means both install and priority chooses. Different distances means one installs and the other is a floating backup.

degraded.application-control: Without decryption it can still identify some applications from handshake metadata such as SNI, so coverage is partial rather than absent. Many applications are not distinguishable that way.
degraded.web-filter: Without decryption it can filter by hostname from SNI, but not by URL path or page content, so a per-path policy does not apply.

detail.blindCert: BLIND. The traffic is encrypted and the policy uses certificate inspection, so there is no payload to examine. The profile is attached and configured and does nothing. Deep inspection is what this profile needs.
detail.blindNone: BLIND. The traffic is encrypted and the policy uses no SSL inspection, so there is no payload to examine. The profile is attached and configured and does nothing. Deep inspection is what this profile needs.
detail.degradedCert: The traffic is encrypted and the policy uses certificate inspection, so the payload is never decrypted. {note}
detail.degradedNone: The traffic is encrypted and the policy uses no SSL inspection, so the payload is never decrypted. {note}
detail.denied: The policy DENIES this traffic, so it never reaches any security profile. Nothing inspects what was blocked, and attaching profiles to a deny policy has no effect.
detail.effectiveDeep: Effective. The policy permits the traffic, the payload is readable because deep inspection is in force, and {inspection} mode supports it.
detail.effectivePlain: Effective. The policy permits the traffic, the payload is readable because the traffic is not encrypted, and {inspection} mode supports it.
detail.unknown: Not a profile this tool models.

flow.antivirus: In flow mode the file is scanned as it streams rather than buffered whole, so very large files and deeply nested archives are where coverage thins. Check the oversize-file action: the default passes them, which leaves the biggest downloads uninspected.
flow.dlp: Data loss prevention depends on seeing complete objects, so proxy mode is the stronger position.

note.blindMany: {count} profiles are attached and blind for the same reason: the payload is never decrypted. Switching this policy to deep inspection is the single change that fixes all of them - and it is a real decision, because deep inspection means terminating TLS, which has certificate-trust, privacy and performance consequences.
note.blindOne: {count} profile is attached and blind because the payload is never decrypted. Switching this policy to deep inspection is the single change that fixes it - and it is a real decision, because deep inspection means terminating TLS, which has certificate-trust, privacy and performance consequences.
note.certNotWeaker: Certificate inspection is not a weaker form of deep inspection; it is a different thing. It validates the certificate and reads the handshake, and never decrypts the body.
note.coverage: This models COVERAGE, not detection: it answers whether a profile can see the traffic, never whether it would catch a particular threat.

ref.certInspection: Certificate inspection validates the certificate and reads the handshake. It does NOT decrypt the payload, so AntiVirus, IPS, DLP and file filter have nothing to examine.
ref.chain: A security profile only acts when every precondition above it holds: the policy must permit the traffic, SSL inspection must decrypt it, the inspection mode must support the feature, and only then does the profile act.
ref.degrade: Application control and web filter degrade rather than go blind: SNI still identifies some hosts, but not URL paths or page content.
ref.secondStep: Most reports that a profile is not working resolve at the second step. The traffic is HTTPS, the policy carries certificate inspection rather than deep inspection, and there is nothing to read.

warn.modeUnknown: Did not recognize mode "{value}"; expected flow or proxy. Assuming flow.
warn.noProfiles: No profiles listed. Add a line like: profiles: antivirus, ips, application-control
warn.sslMissing: No ssl setting supplied; assuming certificate inspection, which is the common default and the usual cause of a blind profile.
warn.sslUnknown: Did not recognize ssl "{value}"; expected none, certificate or deep. Assuming certificate.

detail.moved: ORDER CHANGED in an order-sensitive section. Before: {before}. After: {after}. First match wins here, so moving an object changes what the device does even though no setting changed.
detail.sectionRemovedMany: The entire section was removed, along with {n} objects.
detail.sectionRemovedOne: The entire section was removed, along with {n} object.

note.insensitive: Structural comparison: an object that moved within an order-INSENSITIVE section is not reported, because it changes nothing.
note.moved: An order change in an order-sensitive section is a behaviour change with no setting change, which is exactly the edit a line diff buries and a reviewer misses.
note.none: No structural differences. The two configurations describe the same objects with the same settings; any textual difference is formatting or ordering in a section where order does not matter.

ref.nested: Nested config blocks inside an object are parsed, and their settings are prefixed so they cannot collide with a same-named setting on the parent.
ref.order: For most sections the order of objects is irrelevant and is ignored. For firewall policy and its relatives, order IS the behaviour, so a reordering there is reported as a real change even when no setting differs.
ref.paste: Paste two configurations separated by a line containing only --- , or use the labels BEFORE: and AFTER: on their own lines.
ref.structure: This compares STRUCTURE, not text. A block that moved is not reported as a deletion plus an insertion, and a setting that changed is one line naming the old and new value.

warn.noSections: No configuration sections were recognized. Expected `config '<'section>` blocks.
warn.noSides: Could not find two sides. Separate them with a line containing only --- , or label them BEFORE: and AFTER: on their own lines.

err.action: action must be accept, drop, or inline:'<'layer>
err.noOrdered: at least one ordered layer is needed
err.ruleOutside: a rule must follow a "layer" line
err.svc: svc must be a port number or "any"
err.testNeeds: test needs src=, dst= and a numeric svc=

find.cleanupNoLog: the cleanup rule has track set to none, which defeats its only purpose: it exists to make the implicit drop visible.
find.noCleanup: no explicit cleanup rule. Unmatched traffic still drops, but silently - add any/any/any drop with logging as the last rule so you can see what is being refused.
find.noLog: rule {pos} ("{name}") has track set to none, so its matches leave no evidence.
find.shadow: rule {pos} ("{name}") is unreachable: rule {abovePos} ("{aboveName}") above it already matches everything it would.

step.accept: rule {pos} ("{name}") accepts. In an ordered layer that means PROCEED TO THE NEXT LAYER, not allowed.
step.acceptLast: rule {pos} ("{name}") accepts, and this is the LAST ordered layer - so the connection is allowed.
step.cleanup: no rule in "{layer}" matched, so the implicit cleanup rule dropped the connection. It logs NOTHING - which is why an explicit cleanup rule with drop and log is added as the last rule.
step.drop: rule {pos} ("{name}") drops. A drop in any layer ends evaluation - no later layer is consulted.
step.dropSilent: rule {pos} ("{name}") drops with track set to none, so the connection fails and NOTHING appears in the logs.
step.inline: rule {pos} ("{name}") matched, so evaluation continues INSIDE the inline layer "{layer}". The parent rule is a gate, not a decision.

find.dup: "{raw}" repeats "{prev}" from earlier in the file. NGINX would reject a duplicate exact or prefix location outright; a duplicate regex is simply unreachable.
find.dupPredicate: "{raw}" repeats "{prev}" from earlier in the file. Predicates are tried in file order and a cacheable variable is evaluated once per request, so the later block can never be reached.
find.noCatchAll: There is no "location /" catch-all. Requests matching nothing fall through to the server block, which is fine if that is intended.
find.noValue: {pattern} has no value here, so "{raw}" is treated as not matching. Add a line such as "variable {pattern} 1" to test the request as NGINX would see it with that value.
find.predicates: Predicate locations ("location $variable") need nginx 1.31.5 or later. They are tried after the regular expressions, so a matching regex still wins, and a "^~" prefix skips them.
find.stolen: "{raw}" can be taken over by "{stealer}": that regular expression matches the prefix itself, and regexes beat prefix matches. Add "^~" to the prefix block if it should win.

step.exact: "{raw}" is an exact match for {uri}. NGINX stops here - no prefix block, no regular expression and no predicate is even considered.
step.fallback: With no regular expression matching, the longest prefix match "{raw}" wins after all.
step.fallbackPredicates: With no regular expression and no predicate matching, the longest prefix match "{raw}" wins after all.
step.longest: Of the prefix locations that match, the LONGEST is "{raw}". Length decides this round, not the order the blocks are written in.
step.longestBeats: Of the prefix locations that match, the LONGEST is "{raw}" - it beats {others} on length, not on position in the file.
step.noExact: No exact ("=") location matches {uri}, so the search continues.
step.noPredicate: None of the {count, plural, one {{count} predicate location} other {{count} predicate locations}} has a variable that is neither empty nor "0" for this request.
step.noRegex: None of the {count, plural, one {{count} regular expression location matches} other {{count} regular expression locations match}} {uri}.
step.nothing: Nothing matches {uri}. In a real server this falls through to the server-level configuration, and typically returns 404.
step.predicate: No regular expression matched, so predicate locations are tried in file order. "{raw}" is the first whose variable is neither empty nor "0" ({pattern} = "{value}", from {from}), so it wins. Predicate locations exist from nginx 1.31.5.
step.predicateBeats: No regular expression matched, so predicate locations are tried in file order. "{raw}" is the first whose variable is neither empty nor "0" ({pattern} = "{value}", from {from}), so it wins - beating the longest prefix "{prefix}". Predicate locations exist from nginx 1.31.5.
step.priority: "{raw}" carries "^~", which means: stop here and do NOT try the regular expressions. That modifier is not a priority boost, it is an early exit - and it is the fix when a regex block keeps stealing traffic from a prefix block.
step.priorityPredicates: "{raw}" carries "^~", which means: stop here and do NOT try the regular expressions or the predicate locations. That modifier is not a priority boost, it is an early exit - and it is the fix when a regex block keeps stealing traffic from a prefix block.
step.regex: "{raw}" is the FIRST regular expression in file order that matches, so it wins.
step.regexBeats: "{raw}" is the FIRST regular expression in file order that matches, so it wins - beating the longest prefix "{prefix}". This is the step where writing order matters, and it is why a regex further down a file can quietly take over from a prefix block written above it.

nginx-proxy-pass-rewriter.name: NGINX proxy_pass rewriter
nginx-proxy-pass-rewriter.blurb: One trailing slash decides whether your backend sees /app/page or /page. Paste the directive and see both answers side by side.
nginx-proxy-pass-rewriter.inputLabel: location, proxy_pass and a request URI
nginx-proxy-pass-rewriter.privacy: Computed in your browser. The upstream name is never resolved or contacted.

share.carries: The link carries the box as typed; a box holding a credential gets none.
share.caution: The upstream names a backend host or address: check it before you send the link.
share.maybeSecret: {more, plural, =0 {Line {line} may hold a secret ({label}): check it, and any internal names, before you send the link.} one {Line {line} ({label}) and one more line may hold secrets: check them, and any internal names, before you send the link.} other {Line {line} ({label}) and # more lines may hold secrets: check them, and any internal names, before you send the link.}}
share.blockedSecret: {more, plural, =0 {No link: line {line} holds a credential ({label}). Replace it with a placeholder, then share again.} one {No link: line {line} ({label}) and one more line hold credentials. Replace them with placeholders, then share again.} other {No link: line {line} ({label}) and # more lines hold credentials. Replace them with placeholders, then share again.}}

err.line: expected a location, proxy_pass, or request line
err.slash: the request URI must start with "/"

expl.passthrough: proxy_pass has NO URI part - nothing after the host - so the ORIGINAL request URI is passed through unchanged, location prefix included. The backend sees {backendUri}.
expl.rejectedNamed: NGINX refuses this configuration. A named location has no literal prefix to replace, so proxy_pass may not carry a URI part here. Drop everything after the host, or use a rewrite to build the path you want.
expl.rejectedRegex: NGINX refuses this configuration. A regular-expression location has no literal prefix to replace, so proxy_pass may not carry a URI part here. Drop everything after the host, or use a rewrite to build the path you want.
expl.replaced: proxy_pass HAS a URI part ("{uriPart}"), so the part of the request that matched the location prefix ("{stripped}") is REPLACED by it. {requestUri} becomes {backendUri}.
expl.variable: The proxy_pass value contains a variable, so it is resolved per request and NGINX does NOT perform the prefix substitution. The path is used as written. This is the exception people trip over when they add a variable to an otherwise working proxy_pass and the path silently changes.
expl.variableOriginal: The proxy_pass value contains a variable, so it is resolved per request and NGINX does NOT perform the prefix substitution. The path is used as written, which here means the original request URI. This is the exception people trip over when they add a variable to an otherwise working proxy_pass and the path silently changes.

find.doubled: The location "{location}" does not end in a slash while proxy_pass carries a URI part. The replacement is literal, so the leftover slash from the request is kept and the backend receives a DOUBLED slash. Matching trailing slashes on both sides is the usual fix.
find.joined: The location ends in a slash but the proxy_pass URI part does not, so the rest of the request path is appended to the URI part with no slash between them. Matching the slashes on both sides removes the ambiguity.
find.resolver: Because the value contains a variable, NGINX also resolves the upstream name at request time rather than at startup, which means a resolver directive is usually required and a name that fails to resolve becomes a runtime error rather than a config error.

note.addSlash: Add a single trailing slash and the location prefix is stripped instead.
note.rejected: Without the URI part it is legal, and the original request URI is passed through unchanged.
note.removeUri: Remove the URI part and the location prefix is kept instead.

nginx-proxy-cache-decision.name: NGINX cache decision explainer
nginx-proxy-cache-decision.blurb: Two different questions: will this response be stored, and will a later request be served from it. Paste the directives and the exchange to see both answers and why.
nginx-proxy-cache-decision.inputLabel: Cache directives, the request, and the upstream response
nginx-proxy-cache-decision.placeholder:
proxy_cache zone1
proxy_cache_valid 200 10m

request GET /a

response 200
nginx-proxy-cache-decision.privacy: Decided in your browser. Nothing is fetched and no upstream is contacted.
nginx-proxy-cache-decision.storedYes: STORED - this response is written to the cache
nginx-proxy-cache-decision.storedNo: NOT STORED - this response never reaches the cache
nginx-proxy-cache-decision.servedYes: SERVED - a later matching request gets it from cache
nginx-proxy-cache-decision.servedNo: NOT SERVED - a later request goes upstream
nginx-proxy-cache-decision.storeHeading: Why it is or is not stored
nginx-proxy-cache-decision.serveHeading: Why it is or is not served

share.carries: The link carries a copy of the box with cookie values and credentials replaced; a credential left elsewhere gets none.
share.replaced: {n, plural, =0 {Nothing in it needed replacing.} one {# value is replaced by [redacted].} other {# values are replaced by [redacted].}}
share.maybeSecret: {more, plural, =0 {Line {line} may hold a secret ({label}): check it, and any internal names, before you send the link.} one {Line {line} ({label}) and one more line may hold secrets: check them, and any internal names, before you send the link.} other {Line {line} ({label}) and # more lines may hold secrets: check them, and any internal names, before you send the link.}}
share.blockedSecret: {more, plural, =0 {No link: line {line} holds a credential ({label}). Replace it with a placeholder, then share again.} one {No link: line {line} ({label}) and one more line hold credentials. Replace them with placeholders, then share again.} other {No link: line {line} ({label}) and # more lines hold credentials. Replace them with placeholders, then share again.}}
share.blockedCopy: No link: a copy with those values replaced would not decide the same, so none is offered.
share.revealLabel: {n, plural, one {Include the replaced value in the link} other {Include the # replaced values in the link}}
share.carriesRevealed: The link carries the box as typed, every cookie value and credential included.
share.revealedCaution: Cookie values are often live sessions and Authorization values are credentials: send the link only to someone you would show the exchange to.

err.validArgs: proxy_cache_valid needs a status and a time

rule.entry: an entry exists under this key
rule.lifetime: a lifetime is known for this status

serve.bypass: proxy_cache_bypass is "{value}", so this request skips the cache LOOKUP and goes upstream. Note it still STORES the result - that is the difference from proxy_no_cache, which prevents storing.
serve.entry: A later request producing the key "{computedKey}" finds this entry.
serve.method: {method} is served from cache when an entry matches.
serve.noBypass: proxy_cache_bypass is unset or zero, so a lookup happens.
serve.noEntry: This response was not stored, so there is nothing under "{computedKey}" to find.
serve.noMethod: {method} is not a cached method, so it always goes upstream.
serve.off: With no proxy_cache zone there is nothing to serve from.

store.ccAllows: Upstream Cache-Control is "{cc}", which does not prevent storage.
store.ccBlocks: Upstream sent Cache-Control: {cc}, which prevents storage. The origin is telling you not to cache this.
store.ccIgnored: Upstream says "{cc}", but Cache-Control is in proxy_ignore_headers, so NGINX overrides the origin's instruction and stores it.
store.cookie: The response carries Set-Cookie, so NGINX will NOT store it. This default assumes the response is user-specific, and it is the reason a login page or a personalized page is never cached by accident.
store.cookieIgnored: The response sets a cookie, but Set-Cookie is in proxy_ignore_headers, so NGINX stores it anyway. This is the setting that turns a per-user response into a shared one.
store.freshness: No proxy_cache_valid for {status}, but the response carries its own freshness header, which supplies the lifetime.
store.noCache: proxy_no_cache is "{value}", which is non-empty and non-zero, so this response is not stored.
store.noCacheUnset: proxy_no_cache is unset or evaluates to zero.
store.noLifetime: Nothing gives {status} a lifetime: no matching proxy_cache_valid and no freshness header from upstream. Without a lifetime NGINX has nothing to store it under.
store.noMethod: {method} is not in proxy_cache_methods ({methods}). The default is GET and HEAD only, so a {method} is never cached unless you add it deliberately.
store.noZone: No proxy_cache directive, so caching is OFF entirely. Every other directive here is inert until this is set - this is the most common reason nothing is ever cached.

warn.cookieRequest: The REQUEST carries a Cookie and the cache key ignores it. NGINX excludes cookied RESPONSES from storage by default, but it does NOT exclude cookied REQUESTS from being served a shared entry - so a logged-in user can receive another user's cached page. If responses vary per user, the key must vary too.
warn.defaultKey: Using the default key {key}. $request_uri includes the query string, so query variations are distinct entries - which is safe, and also means a cache-busting parameter defeats the cache entirely.
warn.poisoning: Set-Cookie is being ignored while the cache key does not vary by cookie. That combination stores a per-user response under a key every user shares, which is the classic cache-poisoning-by-configuration mistake.
warn.query: The cache key does not include the query string, but this request has one. Two requests differing only in their query would share a cache entry, so one would be served the other's response.

extreme-spbm-multicast-mac.name: SPBM multicast address builder
extreme-spbm-multicast-mac.blurb: SPBM group addresses are computed, not learned. Build one from a nickname and an I-SID, or paste a line from the multicast FIB and get back whose tree it is.
extreme-spbm-multicast-mac.macLabel: Group address from the multicast FIB
extreme-spbm-multicast-mac.privacy: Arithmetic in your browser. Nothing is resolved or looked up.
extreme-spbm-multicast-mac.resultBuild: The address every node will compute

share.carries: {job, select, decode {The link carries the address as typed, and nothing else.} other {The link carries the nickname and the I-SID as typed, and nothing else.}}

checkpoint-nat-proxy-arp.name: Check Point NAT reachability checker
checkpoint-nat-proxy-arp.blurb: Why a correct-looking NAT (network address translation) delivers nothing. Works out whether anything will answer ARP for the translated address, which is usually where the traffic disappears.
checkpoint-nat-proxy-arp.methodManual: Manual rule in the NAT rule base
checkpoint-nat-proxy-arp.privacy: Arithmetic in your browser. No ARP is sent and no gateway is contacted.
checkpoint-nat-proxy-arp.verdictArrives: YES - nothing here stops it at layer 2
checkpoint-nat-proxy-arp.verdictBlackHole: NO - the packet never reaches the gateway

share.carries: The link carries every field of the form as set, and nothing else.

check.publish: Does this NAT publish an address for inbound traffic?
check.subnet: Is the translated address inside a subnet the gateway is connected to?

err.prefix: A prefix length must be between 0 and 32; got {prefix}.

find.hide: If inbound connections were the goal, hide NAT is the wrong type: it is one-way by design. Static NAT is what publishes a host.
find.merge: Check Global Properties has 'Merge manual proxy ARP configuration' enabled, or the automatic entries and your manual ones will not coexist.
find.route: Check that the upstream router actually has a route for this address pointing at the gateway. A translated address outside every connected subnet reaches the firewall only because someone routed it there.
find.silent: The policy will install cleanly and the rule base will look right. The failure is one layer below: the upstream router ARPs for the address, gets no answer, and the packet is never sent. A capture on the outside interface shows ARP requests with no reply - and no traffic at all in the firewall logs, because nothing ever arrived to be logged.

publish.no: No. Hide NAT translates the source of outbound connections. There is no inbound service to reach, so nothing needs to answer ARP on its behalf.

engine.remedy: Add a proxy ARP entry for {natIp} on the gateway, mapping it to the MAC of the interface at {gatewayIp}, then reinstall policy. On Gaia this is the local.arp file under $FWDIR/conf, or the equivalent in the Gaia configuration.

subnet.no: No. {natIp} is outside {network}/{prefix}. Nobody on this segment will ARP for it, so proxy ARP is not the question - an upstream device has to ROUTE it to the gateway.
subnet.yes: Yes. {natIp} falls inside {network}/{prefix}, which is the interface at {gatewayIp}. Something on that segment will ARP for it.

who.automatic: Automatic NAT adds the proxy ARP entry itself at policy install, because Automatic ARP configuration is enabled in Global Properties.
who.automaticOff: This is automatic NAT, but Automatic ARP configuration is switched OFF in Global Properties - so nothing is created, and the entry has to be added by hand exactly as if the rule were manual.
who.manual: Nobody. MANUAL NAT DOES NOT CREATE PROXY ARP ENTRIES. This is the single most common reason a correct-looking manual NAT rule black-holes traffic.

netskope-dlp-match-predictor.name: DLP match predictor
netskope-dlp-match-predictor.blurb: Why a DLP (data loss prevention) rule fired, or did not. Separates the three stages that fail separately: candidates found, checksum passed, threshold reached.
netskope-dlp-match-predictor.placeholder: Paste the text you expect the rule to match, or the text that surprised you by matching.
netskope-dlp-match-predictor.privacy: Everything stays in this browser. Nothing you paste is transmitted, stored or logged.

share.carries: The link carries stand-ins with each number's length, separators and checksum result, never your text or digits.
share.arrived: These numbers are stand-ins from a shared link: the same length, separators and checksum result as the sender's, never their digits.
share.blockedNone: No link: nothing in the text has the shape of a number this page checks, and the link never carries the text.
share.blockedCopy: No link: stand-ins for these numbers would not read the same, so none is offered.

err.threshold: A threshold is a whole number of matches, at least 1; got {threshold}.

explain.belowMany: {matches} valid matches against a threshold of {limit}. The identifier worked; the rule is set to require more before it acts.
explain.belowOne: {matches} valid match against a threshold of {limit}. The identifier worked; the rule is set to require more before it acts.
explain.checksumMany: {count} strings had the right shape and none passed the checksum. The engine does not count these, which is exactly the behaviour that makes people think DLP "missed" something.
explain.checksumOne: {count} string had the right shape and did not pass the checksum. The engine does not count it, which is exactly the behaviour that makes people think DLP "missed" something.
explain.firesMany: {matches} valid matches meets the threshold of {limit}, so the rule fires.
explain.firesOne: {matches} valid match meets the threshold of {limit}, so the rule fires.
explain.noCandidates: Nothing in the text has the shape of a {label}, so the checksum never runs and the rule cannot fire. If you expected a hit, check for formatting the pattern does not accept.

find.blunt: Raising a threshold is a blunt way to cut false positives, because it also delays the true ones. A proximity keyword or a narrower channel usually costs less accuracy.
find.length: A valid card here is not sixteen digits. Card numbers run from thirteen to nineteen, and rules written around a fixed length miss the rest.
find.rejectedMany: {n} candidates looked right and failed the checksum. That gap is why raising or lowering a threshold rarely fixes a tuning complaint: the count the rule sees is not the count a person reading the document would make.
find.rejectedOne: {n} candidate looked right and failed the checksum. That gap is why raising or lowering a threshold rarely fixes a tuning complaint: the count the rule sees is not the count a person reading the document would make.

reason.invalid: Fails the checksum, so the engine does not treat it as this identifier at all - however much it looks like one.
reason.repeated: A repeated-digit sequence. The arithmetic may work but these are never issued, so the engine rejects them.

ognl-injection-decoder.name: OGNL injection decoder
ognl-injection-decoder.blurb: Paste an OGNL payload you found in a WAF (web application firewall) or application log and read what it was trying to do. Separates a sandbox escape from an execution call, names the advisory family the shape is consistent with, and always states what it did not determine. Decodes only - it never evaluates the payload and holds no templates.
ognl-injection-decoder.runsLocally: Runs entirely in your browser. Nothing is uploaded and nothing in the payload is executed.
ognl-injection-decoder.empty: Paste a payload from a log entry. URL-decode it first if it arrived encoded.

memberAccess.id: the member-access family (S2-045, S2-046, S2-057 and others)
memberAccess.vector: wherever the application evaluated attacker-controlled input
memberAccess.what: A group of issues sharing one shape: reach OGNL's own restriction object, disable it, then call whatever you like. Apache's fixes repeatedly tightened what an expression may touch.

s2045.what: The Jakarta multipart parser evaluated the Content-Type header when it failed to parse it. Widely exploited in 2017 and the flaw behind several very large breaches.

s2057.what: Namespace and result values were evaluated as expressions when certain configuration was in use, making a URL path an execution vector.

caveat.absence: Absence of a recognized construct is not absence of risk. Payloads are routinely URL-encoded, double-encoded or split across parameters; decode first, then read.
caveat.families: Advisory families are reported as consistent with the payload's shape, not as identification. Several share a shape, and a payload proves what was attempted rather than what was present.
caveat.syntax: This reads syntax. It cannot tell you whether the request was blocked, whether the application evaluated it, or whether it succeeded - those answers are in the WAF event and the application log, not in the payload.

actionContext.label: action context access
actionContext.meaning: #context reaches the map holding the request, response and session objects, which is how a payload gets from expression evaluation to writing output the attacker can see.

altDelimiter.label: alternative expression delimiter
altDelimiter.meaning: $'{'...'}' is evaluated in some contexts where %'{'...'}' is not. Its presence suggests the sender was trying more than one evaluation path.

defaultMemberAccess.label: default member access reference
defaultMemberAccess.meaning: A permissive member-access object exposed as a constant, used to replace a restrictive one in a single assignment.

delimiter.label: OGNL expression delimiter
delimiter.meaning: In Struts, %'{'...'}' marks a value that should be evaluated as an OGNL expression rather than treated as text. Its presence in a header or parameter is the whole basis of this class of attack: the payload is only dangerous if something evaluates it.

memberAccess.label: member-access manipulation
memberAccess.meaning: #_memberAccess is the object that enforces OGNL's restrictions on what an expression may reach. Writing to it is an attempt to disable the sandbox rather than to work within it.

multipart.label: multipart content type
multipart.meaning: A Content-Type value. Characteristic of the 2017 file-upload parser flaw, where the header itself was evaluated when parsing failed.

ognlInternals.label: OGNL internals referenced by class name
ognlInternals.meaning: Naming OGNL's own context, class resolver or type converter is a way of reaching the machinery that decides what is permitted, rather than using it.

outputCapture.label: output capture
outputCapture.meaning: Reads the output of a started process so it can be sent back in the response.

processBuilder.label: ProcessBuilder
processBuilder.meaning: An alternative route to starting a process, used where a direct Runtime call is filtered.

processExec.label: process execution
processExec.meaning: Starts an external command. This is the point at which an expression stops reading the application and starts running things on the host.

redirectPrefix.label: redirect prefix
redirectPrefix.meaning: Struts result prefixes that were themselves evaluated as expressions, making the destination of a redirect an execution vector.

responseObject.label: response object access
responseObject.meaning: Reaching the response is how results are returned. A payload that reads something and cannot return it has learned nothing.

runtimeHandle.label: runtime handle
runtimeHandle.meaning: Obtains the JVM's Runtime object, whose purpose here is a single method: starting an operating system process.

staticMethodAccess.label: static method access flag
staticMethodAccess.meaning: Setting this to true permits calling static Java methods from an expression. Without it, the runtime call below is refused; with it, the expression can reach the whole class library.

systemProperty.label: system property read
systemProperty.meaning: Reads JVM properties such as the OS name or user. Frequently a probe rather than an attack: it produces evidence that the expression evaluated at all.

summary.both: This has both halves of a working attempt: something that tries to disable the expression sandbox, and something that tries to run a command. Treat it as a genuine exploitation attempt rather than a scan, and establish whether the request was blocked and what the application did with it.
summary.empty: Nothing to read. Paste a payload from a log entry.
summary.escape: Sandbox manipulation without an execution call. Often the first stage of a two-part attempt, or a probe checking whether expressions evaluate at all before anything expensive is sent.
summary.execution: An execution primitive is present without an obvious sandbox escape. On a patched runtime the call would be refused, which makes this more likely a scanner working through a list than a payload tailored to this target.
summary.none: No OGNL constructs recognized. This may be an unrelated string, an encoded payload that needs decoding first, or a form this tool does not know.
summary.probe: Expression syntax is present but nothing reaches beyond it. Most commonly a probe testing whether input is evaluated - which is worth knowing, because the answer determines whether anything else matters.

ognl-injection-decoder.placeholder: Paste the value your WAF or application logged. URL-decode it first if it arrived encoded.
ognl-injection-decoder.caveatsTitle: What this does not tell you
ognl-injection-decoder.privacy: Read locally in your browser. Nothing is sent anywhere, and nothing in the payload is evaluated: the tool recognizes syntax and describes it.

pingfederate-ognl-explainer.name: PingFederate OGNL expression explainer
pingfederate-ognl-explainer.blurb: Reads an expression from an attribute mapping or an issuance criterion and explains it construct by construct, then flags what breaks in production rather than in testing: attributes read without a null check, static Java calls, and criteria that never actually compare anything. Parses only - it never evaluates the expression.
pingfederate-ognl-explainer.runsLocally: Runs entirely in your browser. The expression is parsed and described, never evaluated.
pingfederate-ognl-explainer.empty: Paste an expression from an attribute mapping or an issuance criterion.

share.carries: The link carries the expression as typed and where it is used; one holding a credential gets none.
share.caution: Expressions name real attributes and sometimes real groups: read it before you send the link.
share.blocked: No link: line {line} holds a credential ({label}); replace it with a placeholder to share the expression.

diag.long: This is long for an expression. Long expressions are hard to review and harder to hand over, and the logic in them is invisible to everyone without the expression role - which includes most of the people who will one day be debugging it.
diag.noNullMany: Reads {count} attributes ({attrs}) with no null check. If any of them is ever absent the expression fails at runtime, and directories are less consistent than the accounts used to test them.
diag.noNullOne: Reads an attribute ({attrs}) with no null check. If it is ever absent the expression fails at runtime, and directories are less consistent than the accounts used to test them.
diag.notBoolean: An issuance criterion should evaluate to true or false, and nothing here looks like a comparison. A criterion that returns a value rather than a boolean will not behave as intended.
diag.passThrough: This maps one attribute straight through with no transformation. That is legitimate, and it is usually also achievable without an expression at all - which is worth preferring, because a mapping anyone can read beats an expression only the expression role can edit.
diag.static: Calls a static Java method. This is supported and sometimes the right answer, and it is also why expression authoring is a separate administrative role: the same construct that formats a date can reach a great deal more.

expects.criterion: A boolean. The criterion permits issuance when the expression evaluates true, and denies it otherwise.
expects.criterionEmpty: A boolean. The criterion permits issuance when the expression is true.
expects.mapping: A value for the mapped attribute, which is sent onward in the assertion or token.
expects.mappingEmpty: A value for the mapped attribute.

rule.caseNorm: Case normalization, usually applied to an email address or username before it is compared or sent onward.
rule.conditional: A conditional. The value before the colon is used when the test is true and the value after it when false - which is how a default is supplied for an attribute that may be missing.
rule.contextRef: A context reference. Reaches something outside the attribute set itself, which widens what the expression depends on and therefore what can change underneath it.
rule.get: Reads the attribute named in the quotes from the incoming set. Returns null if the attribute is absent, which is the single most common cause of an expression failing in production but not in test - test directories tend to be tidier than real ones.
rule.mapLiteral: A map literal. Used to translate one set of values into another - directory group names into application role names, for example - without a chain of conditionals.
rule.membership: A membership or pattern test. In an issuance criterion this is usually the whole decision; in a mapping it is usually feeding a conditional.
rule.nullCheck: An explicit null check. Present in every expression that survives contact with real directory data, because absent is not the same as empty and both occur.
rule.projection: A projection or selection over a collection: transform every element, or keep the ones matching a test. The usual way to handle multi-valued attributes such as group membership.
rule.staticCall: A static Java method call. Legitimate and sometimes necessary here, and also the construct that makes expression authoring a privileged operation: static access is the difference between reading attributes and reaching the class library.
rule.stringManip: String manipulation. Frequently used to strip a domain from a username, cut a prefix from a group name, or tidy whitespace that a directory has been carrying since 2004.
rule.toString: Converts the value to a string. Needed because attribute values arrive as objects, and calling a string method on one without this fails at runtime rather than at save time.

context.issuance-criterion: Issuance criterion: returns true or false

pingfederate-ognl-explainer.nothingRecognised: Nothing recognized. That may mean the expression uses a construct this tool does not know, or that what was pasted is not an expression at all.
pingfederate-ognl-explainer.privacy: Read locally in your browser. The expression is parsed and described, never evaluated, which is the same reason the product itself puts expression authoring behind its own administrative role.

portal.jumpLede: Skip the signposting and go to the index below: every tool, filterable by vendor and category.
portal.hubsLede: One page per platform, gathering its tools, articles and certification material in a single place. The way in if you already know which vendor you are working on.
portal.guidesLede: Walkthroughs of the protocols and mechanisms themselves, with no exam attached. Read these to understand the thing rather than to pass something.
portal.examsLede: Objective by objective for each exam, showing what is covered here and, honestly, what is not.

f5os-restconf-path-explainer.name: F5OS RESTCONF path explainer
f5os-restconf-path-explainer.blurb: Paste an F5OS RESTCONF path and get it decoded segment by segment: the YANG module prefix, the container hierarchy, list keys such as tenant=tenant1, and the module:node prefixing convention. It also explains the port 8888 /restconf versus port 443 /api duality from F5OS 1.8. Local and offline.

reference.title: Modules this tool can describe
reference.intro: A finite list. If a path uses a module that is not here, the structure is still decoded and the description is withheld rather than guessed.

share.carries: The link carries the path or address as typed; an address with a password before its @ gets none.
share.caution: A full address names your platform's management host and port: read it before you send the link.
share.blocked: No link: the address holds a password before the @; remove it to share the path.

err.empty: Nothing to decode: paste an F5OS RESTCONF path.

module.f5-system-image: F5OS platform images on the controller itself
module.f5-system-partition: chassis partitions on VELOS - a group of blades presented as one system
module.f5-system-slot: slot assignment: which blade belongs to which partition or tenant
module.f5-tenant-images: the tenant image inventory available to launch instances from
module.f5-tenants: tenants: the guest BIG-IP instances a VELOS or rSeries system hosts
module.f5-utils-file-transfer: file import and export operations on the platform
module.openconfig-interfaces: physical and logical interfaces, their configuration and counters
module.openconfig-lacp: link aggregation control protocol groups and members
module.openconfig-platform: hardware inventory: chassis components, slots, transceivers
module.openconfig-system: system-level configuration and state: hostname, clock, DNS, AAA, logging

note.apiAlias: The /api root is the F5OS 1.8+ alias for /restconf on the standard HTTPS port.
note.port443: Port 443 with the /api prefix is the F5OS 1.8+ arrangement, equivalent to the original listener on 8888 under /restconf.
note.port8888: Port 8888 is the original F5OS RESTCONF listener. From F5OS 1.8 the same API is also reachable on the standard HTTPS port under /api, so a path written against 8888 and one written against 443 can address the identical resource.
note.prefixing: Note the module:node prefixing convention: a module prefix appears when the path crosses into that module's tree, and the nodes beneath it are written bare. A prefix reappearing mid-path means the path has crossed into a different module.
note.query: A query string was present and has been set aside. RESTCONF query parameters such as depth, fields and content qualify the request; they do not change which resource the path identifies.
note.rpc: This is an RPC path rather than a datastore path: it invokes an operation rather than reading or writing a node.
note.unknownModule: Unrecognized module prefix: {modules}. The structure is still decoded; only the description of what the module governs is withheld.
note.unknownModules: Unrecognized module prefixes: {modules}. The structure is still decoded; only the description of what the module governs is withheld.

seg.listKey: Selects one entry from the "{node}" list, the one whose key is "{key}". In RESTCONF a list entry is addressed by its key in the path itself rather than by a query parameter.
seg.moduleKnown: The node "{node}", qualified by the YANG module "{module}" ({governs}).
seg.moduleUnknown: The node "{node}", qualified by the YANG module "{module}". That module is not in this tool's table, so nothing is claimed about what it governs.
seg.nodeInherited: A container or leaf named "{node}", inside the module qualified earlier in the path. Only the FIRST node of a module needs the module prefix; the nodes below it inherit it.

warn.noNodes: No addressable nodes were found after the API root.
warn.notApi: The path does not begin with /restconf or /api, so this may not be an F5OS API path. The segments below are decoded on the assumption that it is.
warn.rootResource: The root resource is "{resource}". F5OS paths normally address /data for the configuration and state datastore, or /operations for RPCs.

icontrol-rest-path-explainer.name: iControl REST path explainer
icontrol-rest-path-explainer.blurb: Paste an iControl REST URL and get it decoded: the TMOS module, the collection, the tilde-encoded partition and folder path with its tmsh equivalent, sub-collections such as pool members, and the query options. Local and offline; it never contacts a device.

reference.title: Modules this tool can describe
reference.intro: A finite list. If a path uses a module that is not here, the structure is still decoded and the description is withheld rather than guessed.

share.carries: The link carries the path with any auth token masked and any password or header credentials replaced by {mark}.
share.redacted: {n, plural, =0 {It holds no credential, so the link carries the path as typed.} one {One value is replaced.} other {# values are replaced.}}

err.empty: Nothing to decode: paste an iControl REST path.

module.analytics: AVR: statistics collection profiles and reports
module.apm: Access Policy Manager: access profiles, policies, SSO, connectivity
module.asm: Application Security Manager: WAF policies, signatures, learning suggestions
module.auth: authentication of administrators: users, roles, partitions, remote auth sources
module.cm: configuration management: devices, device groups, trust domains, failover
module.gtm: Global Traffic Manager, now DNS: wide IPs, pools, data centres, servers, topology
module.ltm: Local Traffic Manager: virtual servers, pools, monitors, profiles, iRules, persistence
module.net: networking: VLANs, self IPs, route domains, trunks, tunnels, ARP
module.pem: Policy Enforcement Manager: subscriber policies and classification
module.security: AFM, ASM and DoS configuration: firewall rules, policies, protection profiles
module.sys: system: files, licences, provisioning, NTP, DNS resolvers, database variables, iApps
module.vcmp: virtual clustered multiprocessing: guests and their resource allocation

note.members: Pool members are a sub-collection. They are not returned with the pool unless expandSubcollections is set, which is the usual reason a script sees a pool with no members.
