note.noPartition: The object name carries no partition. The device resolves it in the caller's current partition, which is why the same request can succeed for one administrator and return a 404 for another.
note.shared: The /mgmt/shared tree is the shared worker space - iApps LX, file transfer, licensing and similar - rather than the TMOS configuration tree under /mgmt/tm.
note.tilde: The tilde is a folder separator. A URL already uses the slash for its own structure, so iControl REST encodes the partition and folder path with tildes instead - which is why ~Common~web_pool means /Common/web_pool.

option.expandSubcollections: When true, inlines sub-collections such as pool members instead of returning links to them. Convenient and expensive: it can multiply the response size.
option.filter: Filters a collection server-side. Commonly used as partition eq Common to restrict results to one partition.
option.options: Passes tmsh-style options through, for example options=recursive.
option.select: Returns only the named properties instead of the whole object. The single most effective way to reduce a large response.
option.skip: Skips this many items, used with $top to page through a large collection.
option.top: Returns at most this many items from a collection.
option.unknown: Not a query option this tool recognizes. It is passed through as typed and nothing is claimed about its effect.
option.ver: Pins the response to a specific TMOS version's schema.

warn.notMgmt: The path does not begin with /mgmt, so this may not be an iControl REST path. It is decoded below on the assumption that it is.
warn.root: The root after /mgmt is "{root}". The configuration tree is /mgmt/tm and the shared worker space is /mgmt/shared.

fortios-flow-debug-builder.name: FortiOS debug flow builder
fortios-flow-debug-builder.blurb: Assembles the ordered `diagnose debug flow` sequence a FortiGate needs to trace a session: the clean-state reset, the filter, the display options, the packet-count trace and the enable, with the cleanup commands that matter more than the setup. Local and offline; it generates text and contacts nothing.
fortios-flow-debug-builder.formLabel: What do you want to trace?

fields.proto: Protocol (tcp, udp, icmp or a number)

share.carries: The link carries every field of the form as typed, and both switches.
share.caution: The filters name hosts, ports and a VDOM of your network: check them before you send the link.

err.noFilter: Set at least one filter. An unfiltered debug flow on a production firewall traces every session it sees, which is the fastest way to make a console unusable.

note.lineNumbers: Function line numbers in the output are not stable across FortiOS versions. Match on the function name, never on the line number.
note.offload: Traffic offloaded to hardware does not pass through the code this traces. On platforms with NP or SP processors a correct filter can produce nothing at all while traffic is plainly flowing - the session is being handled in silicon. Disabling offload for a test changes what you are measuring, so treat it as a deliberate step rather than a fix.
note.order: Fortinet's administration guide shows `diagnose debug enable` FIRST, before the filter. This sequence puts it last. Both work, and the difference matters on a busy firewall: enabling output before the filter is set means everything is traced until the filter lands.

warn.bigCount: A trace count of {count} on a busy interface can produce more output than a console session can usefully display. Start smaller and repeat if you need to.
warn.notAddress: "{val}" does not look like an address. It is passed through as typed.
warn.proto: Protocol "{proto}" is not a name this tool knows or a number. It is passed through as typed.

why.addr: Matches this address as either source or destination. The usual starting point.
why.cleanClear: Clears the filter so the next person starts clean.
why.cleanDisable: Stops debug output. Do this even if the trace count has been exhausted.
why.configVdom: Filters apply within a virtual domain. Enter the one that owns the traffic.
why.enable: Turns the output on. Last on purpose: with the filter already set, output starts narrow instead of arriving for everything.
why.functionName: Includes the kernel function name in each line, which is what turns the output from a wall of text into a readable path through the packet flow.
why.iprope: Reveals the internal iprope rule checks - the tables traffic is matched against, including local-in policy. Off by default and frequently the thing you actually needed.
why.port: Matches this port as either source or destination.
why.proto: Restricts the trace to protocol {num}. FortiOS wants the number, not the name.
why.protoNamed: Restricts the trace to protocol {num} ({raw}). FortiOS wants the number, not the name.
why.resetClear: Clears any filter left behind. A leftover filter silently narrows your trace to somebody else's problem.
why.resetDisable: Stops any debug output already running from an earlier session.
why.resetReset: Returns all debug settings to their defaults, so what follows is the only thing in effect.
why.showFilter: Run with no arguments, this PRINTS the filter now in effect. Check it before starting the trace - it is the one step that catches a typo before it costs you a reproduction.
why.timestamp: Prefixes each line with a timestamp, which matters when correlating with a packet capture or a log.
why.traceStart: Arms the trace for {count} PACKETS. This is a packet count, not a duration - a busy interface can exhaust it in under a second.

icontrol-rest-stats-decoder.name: iControl REST stats decoder
icontrol-rest-stats-decoder.blurb: Paste an iControl REST stats response and get it flattened into one line per statistic. It unwraps the entries, nestedStats, value and description envelopes, reduces the URL keys to the objects they name, and combines 64-bit counters that arrive split into high and low halves. A pure local transform; nothing is fetched.
icontrol-rest-stats-decoder.placeholder: Paste the response from a /stats endpoint

share.carries: The link carries the stats response as pasted, and nothing else.

note.combined: "{key}" arrived split into .high and .low halves and has been combined. F5 splits 64-bit counters this way because JSON numbers cannot carry them safely.
note.objects: {count} objects are present in this response. A collection endpoint returns every member, which is why a pool's stats and each of its members' stats can arrive together.
note.totals: Counters here are totals since the last reset, not rates. The response carries no interval, so a rate cannot be derived from a single sample - take two and divide by the time between them.

err.empty: Nothing to decode: paste an iControl REST stats response.
err.notObject: The response parsed, but it is not an object.
err.noEntries: No `entries` object at the top level. iControl REST stats responses always carry one - this looks like a configuration response rather than a stats response.

warn.noStats: The response carried an `entries` object but no statistics were found inside it.

sse-architecture-explainer.name: SSE / SASE single-pass architecture explainer
sse-architecture-explainer.blurb: Describe a request (where it is going, how it is steered, whether the device is managed, whether TLS is decrypted) and see the single pass: which SSE services engage, which are pillars and which are cross-cutting, and what a chain of separate appliances would have done instead. SSE (security service edge) is the security half of SASE (secure access service edge). Deterministic and offline.

share.carries: The link carries every field of the form, and nothing else.

because.adaptiveManaged: Device posture is known, so policy can be more permissive with justification rather than simply refusing.
because.adaptiveUnmanaged: The device is unmanaged, which is the case where isolation and read-only outcomes earn their keep - access without the data landing on the endpoint.
because.appId: This is the step that distinguishes a corporate tenant of a service from a personal one. Without it, policy can only speak about domains, and 'allow the company account but not the personal account' is not expressible.
because.casb: The destination is a software-as-a-service application, where the useful unit of control is the ACTIVITY rather than the address.
because.casbNot: Not engaged: no software-as-a-service application is involved.
because.dlp: DLP is NOT a pillar. It runs inside the same pass and receives whatever the pillars decrypted, which is why one data profile covers web, software-as-a-service and private applications alike.
because.dlpBlind: Cannot run meaningfully: without decryption there is no content to classify.
because.dlpNothing: Little to do: this request carries no payload worth classifying.
because.fw: The request is on a non-web port, which the web-facing services do not govern.
because.fwNot: Not engaged: this is web or application traffic.
because.notTls: The flow is not TLS, so there is nothing to decrypt.
because.pop: The architectural claim worth checking in any SSE product is whether every location runs full compute, or whether some are thin nodes that only resolve DNS and forward. A thin node means a detour to somewhere that can actually inspect.
because.swg: The destination is web traffic, which is what a secure web gateway governs.
because.swgNot: Not engaged: this request is not to the general web.
because.threat: Also cross-cutting, and running in the same pass on the same decrypted stream rather than after a re-encryption.
because.threatLimited: Limited without decryption: the verdict rests on reputation and metadata rather than on content.
because.tlsNotPermitted: TLS is present but policy does not permit decryption here. Everything below that needs payload visibility is limited to what the handshake and the metadata reveal.
because.tlsOnce: Decryption happens ONCE for the whole pass. In a chain of separate appliances each device decrypts and re-encrypts, and that repetition is most of the latency people blame on inspection.
because.ztna: A private application is being reached. The broker connects the user to that application alone, rather than placing them on a network the way a virtual private network does.
because.ztnaNot: Not engaged: no private application is involved.

contrast.decrypt: Chained appliances decrypt and re-encrypt at every hop. A single pass decrypts once and hands the same stream to every engine.
contrast.latency: Chained appliances add their latencies together, and each one is a place the chain can break. A single pass adds its engines in parallel within one traversal.
contrast.policy: Chained appliances each hold their own policy. A single engine holds one policy, so 'block this data leaving' does not need writing four times in four dialects.

err.noRequest: Describe the request: at least a destination and a steering method.

note.privateApp: Private application access is normally brokered through the endpoint agent, because the broker needs to know the user rather than the site.
note.singlePass: Single-pass is an architectural claim, not a bundling claim. Several products are sold as converged and are four engines behind one invoice - the question to ask is whether the payload is decrypted once or once per engine.
note.unmanaged: On an unmanaged device the interesting policy outcomes are not allow and block. Remote browser isolation and read-only access let work continue while keeping data off an endpoint nobody controls.

steer.client: The endpoint agent steers selected traffic to the nearest point of presence. It is the only method that carries device posture and user identity with the flow.
steer.dns: DNS steering points a name at the service edge. It is the lightest touch and the least specific: it cannot distinguish two applications behind one address.
steer.gre: A tunnel like IPsec but unencrypted, used where the path is already trusted and throughput matters more than confidentiality on that hop.
steer.ipsec: A tunnel from the site's edge device. It steers everything from that site, and it knows the site rather than the user - identity has to come from somewhere else.
steer.proxyChain: An existing on-premises proxy forwards to the service edge. Useful during a migration; the first proxy is still in the path and still yours to operate.

warn.dns: DNS steering cannot distinguish two applications that share an address, and it carries no user identity. It is a coarse instrument - useful for coverage, insufficient for activity-level policy.
warn.noDecrypt: Without decryption, every stage below application identification is working from metadata. A policy written as though content were visible will not do what its author believes.

what.adaptive: The verdict can be more than allow or block: coach the user, isolate the session in a remote browser, require step-up authentication, or permit a read-only view.
what.appId: Protocol, host and path are examined to identify the application, and often the specific instance and the activity.
what.casb: Application, instance and activity are matched against policy - upload, download, share, post.
what.dlp: Content is classified against the data profile.
what.fw: Ports and protocols outside web traffic are evaluated.
what.pop: The request arrives at an edge location running the complete inspection stack.
what.steering: Traffic reaches the service edge by {steering}.
what.swg: URL category, risk and web policy are evaluated.
what.threat: Files and content are scanned, with sandboxing where the verdict is uncertain.
what.ztna: The user is brokered to one private application, and to nothing else.

fabric-connect-spb-explainer.name: Fabric Connect / SPB explainer
fabric-connect-spb-explainer.blurb: Give an I-SID, a nickname or a role and get the Shortest Path Bridging vocabulary sorted: which backbone VLAN carries the service and why, what an L2VSN and an L3VSN actually bind to, what a B-VLAN is and is not, and the difference between a backbone edge bridge and a backbone core bridge. Deterministic and offline.

share.carries: The link carries every field of the form as typed, and nothing else.

err.nothing: Give at least an I-SID, a nickname or a role to explain.
err.range: An I-SID is a 24-bit value: {min} to {max}. "{isid}" is outside that range.

fact.bcb: Nothing service-specific is configured here. A BCB forwards on B-MAC alone and never sees a customer MAC address. Adding a service to the fabric does not touch it at all - which is the operational claim SPB is actually making.
fact.beb: Services are provisioned here. A BEB is where a customer VLAN or VRF meets an I-SID, and where MAC-in-MAC encapsulation is added and removed.
fact.bvlanEven: Even I-SIDs are carried on one backbone VLAN and odd ones on the other, so the two shortest-path trees each carry roughly half the services. {isid} is even, so it rides {carriedBy}. This is the default distribution rather than a rule of the standard - a deployment can assign differently, and checking which tree a service is actually on is the first step when one service behaves differently from its neighbours.
fact.bvlanOdd: Even I-SIDs are carried on one backbone VLAN and odd ones on the other, so the two shortest-path trees each carry roughly half the services. {isid} is odd, so it rides {carriedBy}. This is the default distribution rather than a rule of the standard - a deployment can assign differently, and checking which tree a service is actually on is the first step when one service behaves differently from its neighbours.
fact.bvlans: The transport instance. A B-VLAN is NOT a VLAN in the usual sense: it does not flood unknown, broadcast or multicast traffic. It forwards only on B-MAC tables that IS-IS has provisioned from shortest-path trees, so there is no spanning tree and no blocked link.
fact.isid: The service identifier, carried in the 802.1ah backbone header. Twenty-four bits, so roughly sixteen million services against a VLAN tag's four thousand - which is the reason a fabric can give every service its own identifier rather than rationing them.
fact.nickname: A short unique identifier for this node, used in multicast addressing so that a tree can be named without carrying a full system identifier. Unique across the fabric, and unrelated to the IS-IS system id, which is separate and also unique.

note.edgeOnly: Provisioning happens at the edge only. Adding a service means configuring the two or more BEBs where it appears; every core bridge between them is untouched, because they forward on backbone MACs and know nothing about the service.
note.isis: IS-IS here is a link-state protocol carrying Ethernet reachability rather than IP routes. It is the same protocol family used for IP routing, doing a different job, and 802.1aq currently defines only Level 1.
note.lowIsid: Low I-SID values are legal but confusing in practice: a number that looks like a VLAN ID invites the assumption that it is one. Many deployments start their I-SIDs above 10000 deliberately, and several encode the VLAN into the I-SID - 20010 for VLAN 10, for instance - so the mapping is readable at a glance.
note.macHidden: The customer MAC is hidden. 802.1ah MAC-in-MAC encapsulation means core bridges learn backbone MACs only, so the core's forwarding table is sized by the number of fabric nodes rather than by the number of end stations.

service.l2vsn: A Layer 2 Virtual Services Network: this I-SID is associated with an edge VLAN. Two sites configure the same I-SID against their local VLAN and they are in the same broadcast domain, with nothing configured in between.
service.l3vsn: A Layer 3 Virtual Services Network: this I-SID is associated with a VRF rather than a VLAN. It carries routed traffic for one routing instance across the fabric - the equivalent of an IP VPN, provisioned at the edge only.
service.multicast: Multicast over SPB uses source-specific trees built by IS-IS. Enable it globally and turn on IGMP at the edge; there is no PIM, no rendezvous point and no multicast routing protocol to design.
service.unknown: The service type was not given. An I-SID bound to a VLAN is a Layer 2 service; bound to a VRF it is a Layer 3 service. The number alone does not say which.

warn.nickname: "{nk}" is not in the x.xx.xx nickname form. A nickname is twenty bits written as three dotted groups, and it must be unique in the fabric - a duplicate is one of the few configuration errors here that breaks things far from where it was typed.
warn.sameBvlan: The two backbone VLANs are the same value. The pair exists so that services can be distributed across two shortest-path trees; with one, there is nothing to distribute across.

f5-eth-trailer-decoder.name: F5 Ethernet trailer decoder
f5-eth-trailer-decoder.blurb: Paste the F5 Ethernet trailer that a BIG-IP appends to packets captured with the tcpdump noise flags, and get each field explained: direction, slot and TMM, the virtual server, flow and peer identifiers, and the device's own RST cause. It detects a TLS provider section and deliberately decodes none of it, because from v15 that section carries session secrets. Local and offline.
f5-eth-trailer-decoder.placeholder: Paste the F5 Ethernet Trailer section from Wireshark, or the raw trailer bytes as hex

tls.title: A TLS provider section is present
tls.body: From BIG-IP v15 the trailer can carry TLS session secrets, and Wireshark will turn them into keylog entries and decrypt the capture. This tool reports that the section is there and decodes none of it. Treat the file accordingly: F5 documents that the trailer never leaves the device on the wire, which is true and is about the wire. The file is a different question, and sending this capture to a vendor, a ticket or a colleague sends the session keys with it.

share.carries: The link carries the trailer text as pasted; TLS secrets and raw bytes never go.
share.blockedTls: No link: the trailer holds TLS session secrets (a TLS section, a secret or a keylog line).
share.blockedBytes: No link: bytes past the trailer's header can hold packet data or TLS secrets; share the Wireshark text view instead.

err.empty: Nothing to decode: paste the trailer bytes, or the F5 Ethernet Trailer section from Wireshark.
err.nothing: Nothing recognizable found. Paste either the raw trailer bytes as hex, or the F5 Ethernet Trailer section as Wireshark displays it.

field.direction: Which way the packet was going relative to the device. Present at the lowest noise level because it is the first thing that disambiguates a capture: the same connection appears twice, once on each side, and without this the two look like duplicates.
field.flow: The device's identifier for this side of the connection. Unique only within a slot and TMM combination, and REUSED over time - so the same flow ID can appear on unrelated packets earlier or later in one capture.
field.peer: The identifier for the other side of the same connection: the server-side flow when this is the client side, and the reverse. Filtering on f5ethtrailer.anyflowid rather than flowid returns BOTH halves, which is almost always what you actually want.
field.slot: The blade that handled the packet, on a chassis. On an appliance it is constant and uninteresting; on a VIPRION or VELOS it tells you which blade to look at when only some traffic misbehaves.
field.tmm: The Traffic Management Microkernel instance that handled the packet. Each TMM owns its own connections, so a problem confined to one TMM behaves like an intermittent problem until you notice the pattern.
field.vip: The virtual server the packet matched, where one applied. An empty value on traffic you expected to be proxied is itself the answer: nothing matched.

note.magic: The magic 0xf5deb0f5 marks the start of the F5 trailer. Anything before it in the frame is the packet proper; anything after is the device talking about that packet.
note.mediumFields: Most of the medium-level fields beyond flow, peer and RST cause are meaningful to F5 support rather than to you. That is not a criticism of the format - it is diagnostic instrumentation for the people who wrote the code.
note.noise: Noise levels are set on the tcpdump command line by suffixing the interface: :n for low, :nn for medium, :nnn for high, with -s0 so frames are not truncated. Higher levels add fields rather than replacing them.
note.rst: The RST cause is the single most useful field in the trailer. A reset seen in a capture without it tells you a connection died; with it, the device tells you why it killed the connection itself.

rst.flow-expired: The connection was idle beyond its timeout and the device removed it. If this appears on traffic the application believes is alive, the idle timeout and the application's keepalive interval disagree.
rst.no-flow-found: A packet arrived for a connection the device has no record of. Usually a late packet on a flow that has already been torn down, or traffic arriving on a path that did not carry the handshake.
rst.no-local-listener: No virtual server was listening on that address and port. The commonest cause of a reset that surprises somebody: the traffic arrived, the device looked for a listener, and there was not one.
rst.unknown: The device's own reason for sending the reset. This tool does not carry an explanation for this particular cause and will not invent one - the string is the thing to search F5's documentation for.

warn.noMagic: No 0xf5deb0f5 magic found in those bytes. Either this is not an F5 trailer, or the capture was taken somewhere other than on the BIG-IP itself - the trailer only exists in files written by tcpdump running on the device.
warn.tlsFile: Treat the capture file accordingly. F5 documents that the trailer never leaves the device on the wire, which is true and is about the wire - the FILE is a different question. Sending this pcap to a vendor, a ticket or a colleague sends the session keys with it.
warn.tlsPresent: A TLS provider section is present in this trailer. From BIG-IP v15 that section carries SESSION SECRETS, and Wireshark will convert them into keylog entries and decrypt the capture. This tool reports its presence and decodes none of it.

fortigate-policy-match-order.name: FortiGate policy match-order explainer
fortigate-policy-match-order.blurb: Paste an ordered FortiGate policy list and, optionally, a packet, and see which policy wins and why. It walks the list top-down showing the first field that ruled each policy out, names the policies that can never be reached because something broader sits above them, and applies the virtual-IP matching rules that ordering alone does not solve. Local and offline.
fortigate-policy-match-order.policiesHint: One per line: id | incoming interface | outgoing interface | source | destination | service | action | flags. Flags are optional and may include vip, match-vip and disabled.
fortigate-policy-match-order.policiesPlaceholder: 10 | port1 | port2 | all | all | ALL | accept
fortigate-policy-match-order.packetHint: incoming interface | outgoing interface | source | destination | service

shadow.title: Policies that can never be reached

share.carries: The link carries the policies and the packet line as typed; a field holding a credential gets none.
share.caution: Policies name your interfaces, address objects and services: check them before you send the link.
share.maybeSecret: {field, select, packet {The packet line may hold a secret ({label}): check it before you send the link.} other {Line {line} of the policies may hold a secret ({label}): check it, and any internal names, before you send the link.}}
share.blockedSecret: {field, select, packet {No link: the packet line holds a credential ({label}). Replace it with a placeholder, then share again.} other {No link: line {line} of the policies holds a credential ({label}). Replace it with a placeholder, then share again.}}

err.noPolicies: Give at least one policy. The list is the thing being reasoned about.

note.direction: Each direction needs its own policy. Traffic being permitted from A to B says nothing about B to A - Fortinet documents this plainly and it still catches people, because most communication is two-way and the policy list is not.
note.idNotPosition: The policy ID is an identifier, not a position. Policy 3 can sit below policy 47, and renumbering changes nothing about evaluation order. The order of the rows is what matters, which is what the GUI's By Sequence view shows.
note.implicitDeny: Nothing matched, so the packet reaches the implicit deny: incoming any, source any, outgoing any, destination any, action deny. Its only editable setting is whether violations are logged - and turning that on is usually the fastest way to see what is actually arriving.
note.pairView: A policy using any as an interface, or several interfaces at once, breaks the Interface Pair View - the GUI switches itself to By Sequence, because the policies can no longer be grouped by a single pair.
note.vip: A policy with a virtual IP applied is matched differently from an ordinary policy and takes priority over one. Ordering alone does not block a source from reaching a VIP.

shadow.why: Policy {earlier} at position {position} covers every field this one matches, and sits above it. Nothing can reach policy {later}: any packet it would match is decided earlier.

step.disabled: Disabled, so it is skipped entirely - it is not a deny, it is absent.
step.match: MATCH. Every field covers the packet, so this policy decides the outcome and evaluation stops here - nothing below is consulted.
step.noMatch: No match: the {field} is "{policyValue}" and the packet has "{packetValue}".

warn.acceptMatchVip: Policy {id} is an accept policy with match-vip set. FortiOS does not permit that combination - match-vip applies to deny policies only.
warn.noMatchVip: There is a policy with a VIP and no deny policy carrying match-vip. To stop a specific source reaching that VIP, the deny policy needs match-vip enabled and must sit above it. New deny policies have match-vip on by default; an accept policy cannot have it at all.

netskope-steering-explainer.name: Netskope steering-method explainer
netskope-steering-explainer.blurb: Describe the situation - managed device or not, on a site or roaming, whether the certificate bundle can be installed - and see which steering method fits: the endpoint client, an IPsec or GRE tunnel, an explicit proxy, or chaining from a proxy you already run. Every method lists what it costs, chosen or not. Deterministic and offline.

flags.needUserIdentity: Policy needs the user, not just the site
flags.existingProxy: An on-premises proxy already in place

methods.title: The methods, and what each costs

share.carries: The link carries your seven answers, and nothing else.

cost.chainFirst: The first proxy is still in the path and still yours to run, patch and troubleshoot. Two proxies fail in more ways than one.
cost.chainPhase: Treat it as a phase rather than a destination, and record what would end it.
cost.clientDeploy: It has to be deployed and kept current on every device, which is an endpoint-management problem before it is a security one.
cost.clientTamper: Steering exceptions live on the client, so a device that has been tampered with is a device whose exceptions you no longer control.
cost.greClear: Unencrypted on that hop, so it belongs only where the path is genuinely trusted.
cost.greIdentity: Same identity gap as IPsec: it knows the site.
cost.proxyOnly: It steers what is configured to use it, and nothing else. An application that ignores proxy settings is simply not steered, and nothing will tell you so.
cost.proxyPerApp: It is a per-application or per-system setting, which means it is a per-application or per-system failure.
cost.tunnelIdentity: It knows the site, not the person. User identity has to come from somewhere else - commonly the client deployed alongside it purely to provision certificates and identify the user.
cost.tunnelTwo: Build at least two tunnels to different data planes. One tunnel is a single point of failure for an entire site.

err.noSituation: Describe the situation: at least whether the device is managed.

note.bypassVsNoDecrypt: A steering bypass and a do-not-decrypt rule are different things. The first means the traffic never reaches the service; the second means it arrives and is not opened. Certificate-pinned applications usually need the first, and confusing them produces a policy that looks applied and never ran.
note.nonWeb: Traffic beyond ports 80 and 443 needs the steering configuration set to all traffic rather than web traffic. Non-standard ports declared as web are sent to the proxy and are NOT inspected by the cloud firewall - so declaring a port as web when it carries something else quietly removes it from firewall policy.
note.privateApps: Private application access is a separate steering decision from web traffic, and the client is normally where it lands, because the broker needs to know the user rather than the site.
note.thirdArrangement: There is a third arrangement worth knowing: deploy the client alongside the tunnel not to steer, but to provision certificates and supply user identity. The tunnel carries the traffic, the client answers who the user is.
note.visibility: Steering decides what the edge can see. Everything downstream - inspection, data protection, policy - is limited by what arrived, and a connected client or an established tunnel is one checkpoint rather than proof that a particular request was inspected.

warn.clientDisables: The client and a tunnel are both viable here, and that is where the surprise lives: the client detects other steering methods and by default DISABLES ITSELF when it finds IPsec, GRE or an explicit proxy. Running both is not automatically belt and braces - it is one of them, decided by a setting. Choose deliberately, and if the intent is for the client to keep steering, that has to be configured.
warn.identity: User identity is required and the client is not available. A tunnel identifies the site; identity must come from an explicit proxy with authentication, from an identity provider integration, or from the client deployed for identity alone.
warn.noCert: Without the Netskope root and intermediate certificates on the endpoint, there is no TLS inspection and no SAML authentication. Traffic still arrives and policy still runs - on metadata. Any rule written as though content were visible will not do what its author believes, and it will look correct in the console.

why.client: The endpoint agent is the recommended method for end-user traffic, and the only one that carries user identity and device posture with the flow rather than inferring them. It follows the user off the corporate network, which a tunnel from a site cannot do.
why.clientUnmanaged: An agent cannot be installed on a device the organization does not manage. That is not a limitation of the product; it is what unmanaged means.
why.explicitProxy: Point the browser or the operating system at the service and traffic goes there without an agent or a tunnel. It is the method for legacy and regulated environments, and for cases where policy-based routing cannot be configured.
why.gre: The same site-level steering as IPsec without the encryption overhead, for a path that is already private. Choose it over IPsec on throughput grounds, not on convenience grounds.
why.ipsec: A tunnel from the site steers everything leaving it, including devices that will never run an agent - printers, appliances, contractor laptops. It also preserves the user's private address, which is what makes address-based policy and detailed logging possible. IPsec encrypts the hop, which matters when the path to the edge is not already trusted.
why.proxyChain: The proxy already in place forwards to the service edge. This is a migration method: it lets the estate move without touching every endpoint on the same day.
why.proxyChainNone: There is no existing proxy to chain from. Introducing one to enable this would be adding a hop in order to have a hop.
why.tunnelNoSite: A tunnel steers a site. It cannot follow a user who is not at that site.

terminal-stack-explainer.name: Terminal, shell, TTY and console explainer
terminal-stack-explainer.blurb: Paste what `tty` printed - /dev/pts/3, /dev/tty2, /dev/ttyS0, /dev/tty, /dev/console, or “not a tty” - and see which layer you are actually looking at, what is holding the other end, and what that implies for signals, job control and what happens when the window closes. Local and offline.
terminal-stack-explainer.inputHint: Run `tty` in a shell and paste what it prints, or pick one of the examples.

words.title: The four words, in one line each
words.terminal: A program that draws characters and sends keystrokes - or, once, a machine that did. It has no idea what a command is.
words.shell: A process like any other, reading lines and running programs. The kernel gives it no special status whatsoever.
words.tty: The kernel object between the two, doing line editing, echo, and turning Ctrl+C into a signal. This is where the behaviour lives.
words.console: A particular terminal: the one attached to the machine itself, and where the kernel prints when nothing else exists yet.

share.carries: The link carries the device path or tty output as typed, and nothing else.

extreme-switch-os-mapper.name: Extreme Universal switch OS-name mapper
extreme-switch-os-mapper.blurb: ExtremeXOS is Switch Engine and VOSS is Fabric Engine - but only on Universal hardware, and the image files and boot menus still use the old names. Give a model series or an OS name and see which applies, the version the rename landed at, and the caveats that come with the series. It states plainly that changing persona deletes the configuration. Local and offline.
extreme-switch-os-mapper.inputLabel: A model series or an OS name

naming.title: The two renamings
naming.body: Same operating systems, renamed on Universal hardware: Switch Engine from 31.6, Fabric Engine from 8.6. There are no feature or functional differences arising from the rename, and older non-Universal models keep the original names.

families.title: Universal hardware
families.intro: The series the new names apply to. Anything not on this list keeps EXOS and VOSS.

share.carries: The link carries the model or OS name as typed, and nothing else.

5320.0: Fabric Engine support begins at 8.6 on this series.

5420.0: Ran VOSS 8.4 and 8.5 before the rename; Fabric Engine from 8.6.
5420.1: Upgrading from an older ExtremeXOS to Switch Engine 31.6 CHANGES THE SNMP SysObjectID. Monitoring that identifies the device by that value will stop recognizing it, and nothing looks wrong from the console.

5520.0: Ran VOSS 8.2.5 through 8.5 before the rename; Fabric Engine from 8.6.
5520.1: Same SysObjectID change as the 5420 when upgrading to Switch Engine 31.6.

5720.0: Fabric Engine support begins at 8.7 on this series.
5720.1: Uses the GRUB boot menu rather than the space-bar prompt.

7520.0: Stacking is supported when running Switch Engine and NOT when running Fabric Engine. If the design depends on stacking, the persona choice is already made for you.
7520.1: Uses the GRUB boot menu rather than the space-bar prompt.

7720.0: Uses the GRUB boot menu rather than the space-bar prompt.

err.empty: Give a model series such as 5520, or an OS name such as VOSS.

note.bootMenu: The boot-menu question is worth memorizing because Switch Engine is chosen by answering no: when the switch asks "Would you like to change the switch OS to VOSS? [y/N/q]", answering N keeps Switch Engine and y moves to Fabric Engine.
note.exos: ExtremeXOS and Switch Engine are the same operating system. If a document, an image filename or a boot menu says EXOS, it is not out of date in any way that matters - the file names and the boot menus still use the old names.
note.notUniversal: The {named} is not in this tool's Universal list. Non-Universal models keep the ORIGINAL names - EXOS and VOSS - and the rename does not apply to them. That is the commonest reason a search for "Switch Engine" plus a model number returns nothing useful.
note.preprovision: Persona can also be pre-provisioned centrally, so a switch collects its intended OS on first boot rather than being chosen at the console. That is the difference between a site visit and a delivery.
note.universal: This is Universal hardware, so it carries the new names: what used to be called EXOS is Switch Engine here, and what used to be called VOSS is Fabric Engine.
note.voss: VOSS and Fabric Engine are the same operating system. The ACLI grammar, the Fabric Connect behaviour and the Avaya lineage are all unchanged by the renaming.

value.dual: yes - either OS can run on it

warn.destructive: Changing persona is destructive. Extreme's own release notes state that changing the network operating system DELETES all configuration files, debug information, logs, events and statistics belonging to the previous one. Treat it as a rebuild with a fresh configuration, not as a migration.

f5os-tenant-config-explainer.name: F5OS tenant config explainer
f5os-tenant-config-explainer.blurb: Paste an f5-tenants:tenants block, from the CLI or from RESTCONF, and get it read back plainly: the configured / provisioned / deployed lifecycle and what each state means, the image and platform it belongs to, blades and VLANs, and the memory allocation checked against F5's published minimum of (3.5 × 1024 × vCPU) + 512. Local and offline.
f5os-tenant-config-explainer.placeholder: Paste the tenant configuration as the CLI prints it, or the RESTCONF JSON

share.carries: The link carries the tenant block as typed, and nothing else.
share.caution: The block names the tenant's management address, gateway and VLANs: read it before you send the link.

err.empty: Nothing to decode: paste an f5-tenants:tenants block, as the CLI prints it or as RESTCONF returns it.
err.nothing: Nothing recognizable found. This expects an f5-tenants block containing fields such as running-state, vcpu-cores-per-node and memory.

field.appliance-mode: Restricts the tenant's administrators from reaching a shell. It hardens the tenant and it also removes a diagnostic route, which is worth deciding deliberately rather than inheriting from a template.
field.cryptos: Whether the tenant is given access to the platform's crypto and compression hardware. It can only be changed while the tenant is in the configured or provisioned state.
field.gateway: Default gateway for the tenant management address.
field.image: The tenant image bundle. The filename carries the BIG-IP version and, on a chassis, ALL-VELOS rather than ALL-F5OS - so an image built for one platform will not deploy on the other, and the filename is the fastest way to notice.
field.mgmt-ip: Out-of-band management address for the tenant itself, separate from the platform's own. A tenant is reached here, not through the chassis address.
field.mgmt-vlan: VLAN for tenant management traffic, where the platform separates it.
field.nodesMany: The blades within the chassis partition this tenant runs on. More than one means the tenant spans blades, which is a VELOS arrangement - rSeries is an appliance and has none.
field.nodesOne: The node this tenant is scheduled on. On VELOS this is a blade within the chassis partition; on rSeries there is a single node.
field.prefix-length: Mask for the tenant management address.
field.storage: Disk allocated to the tenant, in gigabytes.
field.tenant-auth-support: Can only be changed while the tenant is NOT deployed.
field.type: The tenant type. BIG-IP is the usual answer; the field exists because F5OS is a platform layer rather than a BIG-IP feature.
field.vlans: VLANs presented to the tenant from the platform. The tenant sees these and nothing else, which is the actual boundary between tenants on shared hardware.

note.aboveMin: Memory is {memory} MB against a minimum of {min} MB - {above} MB above it. That is legitimate, and worth knowing was a decision rather than a default.
note.deployedChange: To change vCPU or memory on a deployed tenant, move it back to provisioned first, make the change, then return it to deployed. It is not a live operation, and treating it as one is how a maintenance window becomes an outage.
note.imageF5os: The image name contains ALL-F5OS, the appliance-platform build.
note.imageVelos: The image name contains ALL-VELOS, so it is built for the chassis platform and will not deploy on rSeries.
note.minMemory: F5 publishes the minimum memory as (3.5 × 1024 × vCPU) + 512, so {vcpu} vCPU requires at least {min} MB. More than the minimum can be configured deliberately.
note.rseries: This looks like rSeries: an appliance rather than a chassis. There are no chassis partitions and no blades, vcpu-cores-per-node moves in multiples of four with a default of four, and the default memory is 12288 MB.
note.vcpuNotMultiple: A vCPU count of {vcpu} is valid on VELOS. On rSeries the value must be a multiple of four, so this configuration is chassis-shaped - which matters if it is being copied between platforms.
note.velos: This looks like VELOS: a chassis, with chassis partitions and blades. Each blade offers up to 22 vCPUs, around 95 GB of memory and roughly 600 GB of disk to tenants, so partition capacity is what limits how many tenants fit.

state.configured: Configured: the tenant is defined and no resources have been assigned. Nothing is running and nothing is reserved.
state.provisioned: Provisioned: the platform has assigned the tenant to its nodes and created its virtual disks, and the image is installed. It is ready to deploy and it is not running.
state.unknown: No running-state was found in this block. The field is what tells the platform what you WANT the tenant to be doing.

warn.belowMin: Memory is {memory} MB and the published minimum for {vcpu} vCPU is {min} MB. This allocation is BELOW the minimum.
warn.vcpuNoMemory: A vCPU count is present with no memory value. When expanding a tenant, both must be changed together - raising vCPU alone leaves the tenant below its new minimum.

fortios-cli-config-explainer.name: FortiOS CLI config explainer
fortios-cli-config-explainer.blurb: Paste a FortiOS config block and get the structure as a tree with every verb explained. It flags the trap that costs the most: `set` on a multi-value field REPLACES the whole list, so setting one source address on a policy that had four silently removes three. It also catches unclosed blocks and reminds you that `end` is what commits. Local and offline.
fortios-cli-config-explainer.placeholder:
config firewall policy
    edit 10
        set action accept
    next
end

share.carries: The link carries the block with each password, key, community and ENC value as a numbered mark such as {mark}; a private key or token gets none.
share.caution: A configuration names your interfaces, addresses, objects and users: read it before you send the link.
share.redacted: {n, plural, =0 {Nothing in it needed replacing, so the link carries it as pasted.} one {One value is replaced.} other {# values are replaced.}}
share.maybeSecret: {more, plural, =0 {Line {line} may hold a secret ({label}): check it, and any internal names, before you send the link.} one {Line {line} ({label}) and one more line may hold secrets: check them, and any internal names, before you send the link.} other {Line {line} ({label}) and # more lines may hold secrets: check them, and any internal names, before you send the link.}}
share.blockedSecret: {more, plural, =0 {No link: line {line} holds a key, token or password ({label}) that cannot be replaced safely. Put a placeholder in its place, then share again.} one {No link: line {line} ({label}) and one more line hold keys, tokens or passwords that cannot be replaced safely. Put placeholders in their place, then share again.} other {No link: line {line} ({label}) and # more lines hold keys, tokens or passwords that cannot be replaced safely. Put placeholders in their place, then share again.}}

err.empty: Nothing to explain: paste a FortiOS configuration block.
err.noVerbs: No FortiOS configuration verbs found. This expects a block using config, edit, set, next and end.

explain.abort: Leaves the block DISCARDING the changes. The counterpart to end, and the one to reach for when you are unsure.
explain.append: Adds to {field} without disturbing what is already there. This is the safe half of the set/append pair.
explain.appendNoField: Adds to a list field without disturbing what is already there. This is the safe half of the set/append pair.
explain.config: Opens {rest}. If this names a table, the entries inside are reached with edit; if it names a single object, set applies directly.
explain.delete: Removes {rest}. There is no confirmation and no undo within the session.
explain.edit: Enters the table entry "{rest}" - AND CREATES IT if it does not already exist. This is not a lookup that fails on a typo: a mistyped name makes a new object, which is why a stray entry usually traces back to a keystroke rather than to a decision.
explain.end: Closes the block AND COMMITS it. This is the line that makes the change real.
explain.next: Closes this table entry and STAYS IN THE TABLE, ready for the next edit. It does not leave the block and it does not commit.
explain.purge: Removes EVERY entry in the current table. Rarely what was meant, and never reversible from the session.
explain.set: Assigns {field}. A set replaces whatever was there.
explain.setList: Sets {field}. THIS REPLACES THE WHOLE LIST. Anything previously in {field} and not named here is removed, silently and successfully. Use append to add to it instead.
explain.setNoField: Assigns a field. A set replaces whatever was there.
explain.unknown: Not a FortiOS configuration verb this tool recognizes. It is shown in place and nothing is claimed about it.
explain.unset: Returns {field} to its default. Not the same as setting it empty - the default may be a value.
explain.unsetNoField: Returns the field to its default. Not the same as setting it empty - the default may be a value.

note.nextEnd: next and end are not interchangeable. next closes an entry and stays in the table; end closes the table and commits. A block that uses end where next was meant leaves the table early, and the remaining edits apply somewhere else entirely.
note.noEnd: There is no end in this block. Nothing here has been committed - end is the line that makes a change real, and abort is the line that discards it.
note.show: show displays only what differs from the defaults; show full-configuration displays everything. A field missing from a config block is not necessarily unset - it may simply be at its default.

warn.purge: Line {line}: purge removes every entry in the table, not one.
warn.setList: Line {line}: "set {field}" replaces every value in {field} rather than adding to it. If the intent was to add, the command is append.
warn.unclosed: {count, plural, one {{count} block was} other {{count} blocks were}} opened and never closed: {path}. An unclosed block has not been committed, and pasting it into a live device leaves the session somewhere unexpected.

network-os-comparer.name: Network operating system comparer
network-os-comparer.blurb: Fourteen network operating systems - IOS, IOS XE, IOS XR, NX-OS, Junos, Junos Evolved, EOS, TMOS, F5OS, EXOS, VOSS, FortiOS, PAN-OS and Gaia - with lineage, what each runs on, how components share state, where the planes divide, and what an upgrade costs. Pick one for a full profile or two to see them axis by axis. Every entry lists weaknesses as well as strengths.
network-os-comparer.pick: Choose a system, and a second one to compare

share.carries: {mode, select, compare {The link carries the two systems you chose, and nothing else.} other {The link carries the system you chose, and nothing else.}}

base.label: What it runs on
base.why: Determines what tooling exists, what can be installed beside it, and how much of the platform an engineer can inspect directly.

configModel.label: How changes are applied
configModel.why: Immediate means a mistake is live. Candidate-and-commit means a mistake is an abandoned edit - the difference between an incident and an afternoon.

differentiator.label: The distinguishing idea
differentiator.why: Every one of these was designed to solve something. Naming it explains the rest of the design.

planes.label: Control and forwarding
planes.why: Decides whether traffic keeps moving while the control plane is rebuilt, and whether the tools you reach for are looking at the path the packets take.

stateModel.label: How state is shared
stateModel.why: The best single predictor of what happens when a component fails. Shared memory means a fault spreads; a state store means a restarted process can resume.

upgrade.label: What an upgrade costs
upgrade.why: The gap between a maintenance window and a process restart is the gap between planning a change and simply making it.

err.same: Pick two different systems - comparing one with itself says nothing.

eos.base: An UNMODIFIED Linux kernel. Not a fork, not a patched tree - the same kernel, so the tooling is the ordinary Linux tooling.
eos.configModel: Immediate, with configuration sessions available for staged changes.
eos.differentiator: State is separated from the processes that produce it. That single decision is why an agent can be restarted, upgraded or replaced without the rest of the system noticing.
eos.planes: Control plane processes above Linux, forwarding in merchant silicon.
eos.stateModel: SysDB: a central in-memory state database with publish and subscribe. Processes do not talk to each other at all - they publish state and subscribe to what they care about. A restarted agent gets the current state from SysDB and continues.
eos.strength0: Process restart is genuinely routine rather than an emergency measure.
eos.strength1: An unmodified kernel means standard Linux tools work as documented.
eos.strength2: One software train across the portfolio.
eos.upgrade: Individual agent restart; in-service upgrade on supported hardware.
eos.weakness0: The publish-subscribe model is a different mental model to learn, and reasoning about who published what takes practice.
eos.weakness1: Merchant silicon means hardware capability is bounded by what the chosen chipset does.

exos.base: Linux, with networking functions as modular userspace processes.
exos.configModel: Immediate, with scripting and on-box Python available.
exos.differentiator: Modularity from early on, and an unusual willingness to let the switch run scripts of its own.
exos.lineage1: renamed Switch Engine on Universal hardware from 31.6
exos.planes: Control plane in software, forwarding in ASICs.
exos.stateModel: Independent modules with process-level restart, so a failed protocol does not take the switch.
exos.strength0: Process restart without taking the switch down.
exos.strength1: On-box scripting and automation that predates the fashion for it.
exos.strength2: Consistent across a broad hardware range.
exos.upgrade: Process restart for many changes; image upgrade with the usual reboot for the rest.
exos.weakness0: Smaller community than the market leaders, so third-party material is thinner.
exos.weakness1: The Switch Engine renaming means documentation exists under two names, which complicates searching.

f5os.base: A Linux platform layer with container orchestration, hosting BIG-IP tenants rather than serving traffic itself.
f5os.configModel: Immediate, over a CLI and RESTCONF interface driven by YANG models.
f5os.differentiator: F5OS is not a traffic operating system at all. It is the layer that decides which BIG-IPs exist, and confusing it with the BIG-IP inside is the commonest mistake people make with VELOS and rSeries.
f5os.planes: The platform owns the hardware and presents VLANs and resources to tenants; each tenant has its own data plane.
f5os.stateModel: Platform and tenant are separate. The platform allocates; the tenant runs its own TMOS.
f5os.strength0: Tenants are genuinely separated, with their own resources and their own lifecycle.
f5os.strength1: Model-driven interfaces throughout, so automation is a first-class path.
f5os.strength2: Platform and tenant versions are decoupled.
f5os.upgrade: Platform and tenants upgrade independently, which is the point of separating them.
f5os.weakness0: Another layer to learn, with its own CLI, its own API and its own failure modes.
f5os.weakness1: Changing a tenant's resource allocation is not a live operation, which surprises people expecting virtualization to behave like a hypervisor.

fortios.base: A proprietary operating system with a Linux-derived foundation, built around Fortinet's own silicon.
fortios.configModel: Immediate, with the config/edit/set/next/end grammar. `end` commits.
fortios.differentiator: Custom silicon in the mainstream price range. The offload engine is what allows inspection at throughputs that general-purpose CPUs would not reach at that cost.
fortios.planes: The silicon is the story: network processors, content processors and system-on-chip units offload flows from the CPU. Traffic offloaded to hardware does not traverse the software path at all, which is why a correct debug can show nothing while traffic flows.
fortios.stateModel: Integrated rather than distributed - the security functions share a session table and a policy engine.
fortios.strength0: Very strong price to throughput ratio, because the work is done in hardware.
fortios.strength1: One console for a wide portfolio, from firewalls to switches to access points.
fortios.strength2: Extremely wide deployment, so the material and the community are deep.
fortios.upgrade: Image upgrade with reboot; HA pairs upgrade in sequence.
fortios.weakness0: Offload makes diagnosis harder: the packet you are looking for may never reach the code you are watching.
fortios.weakness1: Feature behaviour can differ between models depending on which silicon is present.

gaia.base: Linux, unifying two earlier operating systems that Check Point maintained in parallel.
gaia.configModel: Immediate on the gateway, with policy installed from a separate management server.
gaia.differentiator: Management is a separate product from the gateway. Policy is written centrally and installed, which is a three-tier arrangement rather than a device you configure.
gaia.lineage0: IPSO, from the Nokia appliance line
gaia.planes: Acceleration paths sit beside the full inspection path, so an established connection can be handled faster than the first packet was.
gaia.stateModel: Software blades on a shared platform, with state synchronized between cluster members.
gaia.strength0: Central management across many gateways is the design rather than an add-on.
gaia.strength1: A unified operating system, which was a genuine consolidation of two divergent lines.
gaia.strength2: Long history in stateful inspection - Check Point largely invented the category.
gaia.upgrade: Image upgrade; cluster members upgrade in sequence.
gaia.weakness0: The three-tier model means more infrastructure to run before the first rule exists.
gaia.weakness1: Two lineages merged means some inherited inconsistencies persist in places.

ios-xe.base: A Linux kernel, with IOS itself running on top as a single daemon - IOSd.
ios-xe.configModel: Immediate, preserving the classic IOS operational model deliberately.
ios-xe.differentiator: The familiar CLI kept, the architecture underneath replaced. It is the compatibility answer: existing knowledge and existing scripts continue to work while the failure domain shrinks.
ios-xe.planes: Control plane in IOSd and platform processes; forwarding in hardware, with the platform layer between them.
ios-xe.stateModel: IOSd remains a monolith internally, but system functions were lifted out of it into separate Linux processes. A failure in one of those does not take the kernel with it; a failure inside IOSd still takes IOSd.
ios-xe.strength0: Existing IOS knowledge transfers almost entirely.
ios-xe.strength1: Process isolation for platform functions, and multi-core scheduling.
ios-xe.strength2: Containers and on-box applications become possible because there is a real Linux underneath.
ios-xe.upgrade: Sub-packages can be upgraded individually, and later releases add containerized services alongside.
ios-xe.weakness0: IOSd is still a monolith, so the biggest single failure domain was reduced rather than removed.
ios-xe.weakness1: Two layers to reason about when something goes wrong - the Linux side and the IOSd side.

ios-xr.base: Originally the QNX real-time microkernel; later releases moved to a 64-bit Linux foundation.
ios-xr.configModel: Candidate and commit. Changes are made against a copy, checked, then committed - so a half-finished edit is an abandoned candidate rather than a live outage.
ios-xr.differentiator: A different code base from IOS, not a rework of it. The CLI resembles IOS and the operational model does not: the two-stage commit changes what a mistake costs.
ios-xr.planes: Strict separation, and designed for distributed forwarding across many linecards from the outset.
ios-xr.stateModel: Fully distributed. Components run as independent protected processes that can be restarted individually, and they communicate by message passing rather than by sharing memory.
ios-xr.strength0: Process-level restartability, so a protocol defect is a restarted process rather than a lost router.
ios-xr.strength1: Commit model catches errors before they are live, and supports rollback.
ios-xr.strength2: Built for scale: many linecards, many routes, many protocol instances.
ios-xr.upgrade: Individual packages, and process restart without a reboot for many changes.
ios-xr.weakness0: The learning curve is real - the CLI's familiarity is partly a trap, because the operational model beneath it is not IOS.
ios-xr.weakness1: Complexity is the price of the distribution: more moving parts, more to understand when diagnosing.

ios.base: No host operating system. IOS is the operating system, running directly on the hardware as a single binary image.
ios.configModel: Immediate. A command takes effect as it is entered; there is no candidate configuration to review.
ios.differentiator: The one everybody learned first, and the reason every other vendor's CLI looks vaguely like it. Its architecture is the baseline the others were designed to escape.
ios.planes: Routing and forwarding are distinct functions in software. Protocols build the RIB, which is processed into the FIB that forwarding consults.
ios.stateModel: Shared globals. Every process runs in ONE address space with no memory protection, so any process can corrupt any other's data. The scheduler is run-to-completion and non-preemptive: a running process keeps the CPU until it makes a kernel call.
ios.strength0: Small, fast and predictable on the hardware it was written for.
ios.strength1: The most widely known command set in the industry, which is a genuine operational asset.
ios.strength2: Decades of documented behaviour, so almost any symptom has been seen before by somebody.
ios.upgrade: Replace the whole image and reboot. There is no partial upgrade without redundant supervisors.
ios.weakness0: No memory protection: a defect in one feature can corrupt another's data and bring the box down.
ios.weakness1: A non-preemptive scheduler means a badly behaved process can starve everything else, including routing protocols.
ios.weakness2: Upgrades are all-or-nothing and require a reboot.

junos-evolved.base: A Linux kernel natively, with direct access to Linux utilities rather than through an emulation layer.
junos-evolved.differentiator: The state store is the point. In classic Junos a restarted daemon rebuilds; here it retrieves, which is a different guarantee entirely.
junos-evolved.planes: Node-based rather than Routing Engine centric. The system means all nodes - routing engines, forwarding complexes and the rest - not just the control processor.
junos-evolved.stateModel: A distributed data store. Processes publish state to it rather than to each other, and a restarted process retrieves its state from the store - even when it comes back on a different node. State is eventually consistent at the transport layer, causally consistent at the application layer.
junos-evolved.strength0: State survives process restart, and survives the process moving to another node.
junos-evolved.strength1: Native Linux, so containers and modern telemetry are first-class rather than bolted on.
junos-evolved.strength2: The node-based model matches how large systems are actually built.
junos-evolved.upgrade: Each software version is stored separately, so installing one does not disturb another.
junos-evolved.weakness0: A second platform to know alongside classic Junos, with real behavioural differences.
junos-evolved.weakness1: Eventual consistency is a correct engineering choice and it means the answer to what is the state right now is more nuanced than on a system with one copy of it.

junos.base: FreeBSD. Because that is a Unix, there is a real Unix shell underneath with the ordinary Unix tools available.
junos.configModel: Candidate and commit, with rollback and configuration comparison built in. This was Junos's signature from the beginning and much of the industry has since followed.
junos.differentiator: One operating system, one source tree, across routing, switching and security. The consistency is the product as much as any individual feature.
junos.lineage2: ScreenOS security folded in after the NetScreen acquisition
junos.planes: The RE/PFE split is the design's organizing idea, and it is why the control plane can be rebuilt or fail over while forwarding continues.
junos.stateModel: Routing Engine centric: the RE holds the control plane and the Packet Forwarding Engine does the forwarding, with a defined boundary between them. Daemons are separate processes.
junos.strength0: The commit model, with rollback and a readable diff before anything is applied.
junos.strength1: A single consistent operating system across very different hardware.
junos.strength2: A genuine Unix underneath, so ordinary tools and scripting are available.
junos.upgrade: Unified releases across the portfolio; in-service upgrade on supported platforms.
junos.weakness0: The configuration hierarchy is unfamiliar to engineers arriving from an IOS-shaped world, and the transition takes real effort.
junos.weakness1: Two architectures now coexist - FreeBSD-based Junos and Linux-based Junos Evolved - and knowing which one is in front of you matters.

nx-os.base: Linux, with networking features as modular processes above it.
nx-os.configModel: Immediate, in the IOS tradition, though the feature-enable model changes what is running.
nx-os.differentiator: It came from storage. The SAN heritage shows in its attitude to modularity and to features that are absent until asked for, which is unusual in a switch operating system.
nx-os.lineage0: SAN-OS, written for MDS storage switches
nx-os.planes: Control plane in software, forwarding in ASICs, with the data centre fabric as the design target.
nx-os.stateModel: Modular processes with individual restart, and features started only when configured.
nx-os.strength0: Features not enabled are not running, which reduces both attack surface and memory use.
nx-os.upgrade: In-service upgrade on supported platforms; individual process restart.
nx-os.weakness0: The feature-enable model surprises engineers who expect a command to exist before it has been switched on.
nx-os.weakness1: Similar-looking CLI to IOS with different behaviour in places, which is its own kind of trap.

pan-os.base: A Linux-derived operating system with a hard split between control and data plane, frequently on separate processors.
pan-os.configModel: Candidate and commit. Changes accumulate and are committed as a set, and the commit is a visible operation with its own duration.
pan-os.differentiator: Application identity as the primary policy object rather than port numbers. The whole design follows from deciding that the question is which application, not which port.
pan-os.planes: Single-pass parallel processing: a packet is classified once, and application identification, user identification, content inspection and policy all run against that single pass rather than in a chain of engines each redoing the work.
pan-os.stateModel: The planes are genuinely separate, with their own resources. Management load does not compete with traffic handling, which is the point of the arrangement.
pan-os.strength0: Policy expressed in terms of applications and users reads closer to intent than port-based rules.
pan-os.strength1: Single-pass avoids the latency of chaining separate inspection engines.
pan-os.strength2: The commit model makes review possible before anything is live.
pan-os.upgrade: Image upgrade with reboot; HA pairs upgrade in sequence.
pan-os.weakness0: Commits take time, and on a large configuration that time is operationally significant.
pan-os.weakness1: Application identification requires enough of the flow to classify it, which has implications for very short connections.

tmos.base: Linux for management and control, with the Traffic Management Microkernel - TMM - as a separate real-time process handling traffic.
tmos.configModel: Immediate through tmsh, with declarative layers such as AS3 available above it.
tmos.differentiator: A full proxy, not a router. TMOS terminates connections and creates new ones, which is a different relationship with traffic from anything that forwards it.
tmos.planes: The important detail: TMM BYPASSES the Linux network stack entirely. Traffic does not traverse Linux networking on its way through the device, which is why Linux tools show you the management plane and not the traffic.
tmos.stateModel: Two worlds. Linux runs management, and TMM runs the data path with its own memory, its own scheduling and its own network stack.
tmos.strength0: The full-proxy model allows inspection and manipulation that a forwarding device cannot do.
tmos.strength1: TMM's dedicated stack gives predictable performance independent of the Linux side.
tmos.strength2: iRules make behaviour programmable at the point of traffic handling.
tmos.upgrade: Software volumes, allowing a new version to be installed beside the running one and booted into.
tmos.weakness0: Two worlds to understand, and Linux tooling answers questions about the wrong one - a persistent source of confusion.
tmos.weakness1: The device is in the connection path by design, so it is a failure domain rather than a bystander.

voss.base: Linux, with an ACLI command grammar inherited from the Avaya and Nortel line.
voss.configModel: Immediate, in the ACLI style inherited from the Avaya and Nortel line - which is a genuinely different grammar from EXOS on the same Universal hardware, so a two-persona estate means two command sets to know.
voss.differentiator: The fabric. Services are provisioned only at the edge and the core is untouched, because the core forwards on backbone MACs and does not know the services exist.
voss.lineage3: renamed Fabric Engine on Universal hardware from 8.6
voss.planes: Its distinguishing feature is above the plane split: Shortest Path Bridging means forwarding is computed by IS-IS rather than learned, with no spanning tree and no blocked links.
voss.stateModel: Modular processes; the fabric control plane is IS-IS carrying Ethernet reachability.
voss.strength0: Adding a service touches only the edge switches it appears on.
voss.strength1: No spanning tree, and every link carries traffic.
voss.strength2: A mature lineage - this technology has been in production for a long time under three different owners.
voss.upgrade: Image upgrade; the fabric itself tolerates node loss by design.
voss.weakness0: The vocabulary is a barrier: I-SID, B-VLAN, BEB, BCB and L2VSN all arrive at once.
voss.weakness1: An ACLI grammar distinct from EXOS on the same hardware, so a two-OS estate means two command sets.

shared.commit: Both use a candidate-and-commit configuration model, so a half-finished change is an abandoned edit on either.
shared.linux: Both run on Linux, which means the difference between them is what they built ON it rather than what they built on.
shared.vendor: Both are {vendor} systems, which usually means shared tooling and a shared support path even where the architectures differ.

http-request-translator.name: HTTP request translator
http-request-translator.blurb: Paste a raw HTTP/1.1 request and get the equivalent curl, fetch, HTTPie, Python and PowerShell. Nothing is sent and no request is run.
http-request-translator.privacy: Parsed in your browser. The request is never sent, and nothing leaves the page.

err.notARequest: That does not start with a request line. A request begins with a method, a target and a version - for example: GET /users HTTP/1.1

warn.not-a-request-line: The first line is not a request line.
warn.unknown-method: That method is not one of the standard ones. It may still be valid for the server that answers it.
warn.odd-version: The version token does not look like HTTP/1.1.
warn.header-without-colon: A header line had no colon and was skipped.
warn.no-host: There is no Host header, so the absolute URL had to be guessed. Origin-form requests need one.
warn.content-length-mismatch: Content-Length does not match the body length. Servers and proxies may disagree about where this message ends.
warn.chunked-body: The body is chunked. It is passed through as pasted rather than decoded.
warn.cleartext: This request is plain http, so headers and body travel in the clear.
warn.carries-authorization: This request carries an Authorization header. Treat the paste as a credential.
warn.carries-cookie: This request carries a Cookie header, which is usually a live session.

share.redacted: {n, plural, =0 {Nothing in it needed masking.} one {One value is masked.} other {# values are masked.}}
share.blocked: No link: line {line} holds a key, token or password ({label}) that cannot be replaced safely. Put a placeholder in its place, then share again.

dhcp-option-43.blurb: Build the vendor-specific option 43 value a wireless controller actually expects. One option number, four incompatible encodings.
dhcp-option-43.runsLocally: Runs entirely in your browser. A controller address is internal topology and never leaves this page.

notes.string-not-hex: This vendor expects a plain string, not hex. Entering a hex value here is a common and silent failure: the access point reads it, cannot parse an address out of it, and simply never joins.
notes.not-option-43: This vendor does not use option 43 for controller discovery by default. It reads option {option} instead, which carries the controller address directly. Fortinet documents that another option number can be used if the access points are configured to match.
notes.vendor-class-required: Option 43 alone is not enough. The access point only asks for vendor-specific information when option 60 matches, so the DHCP server must also send option 60 as: {vci}
notes.ascii-not-binary: This vendor spells the address out as text, one byte per character, dots included. That is the opposite of the Cisco convention and the single most common error here: 10 as a binary byte is 0a, but as text it is 31 30.

errors.empty: Enter at least one controller address.
errors.unknown-vendor: That vendor profile does not exist.
errors.bad-address: That is not a valid IPv4 address. Check for a missing octet, a value above 255, or a leading zero, which some DHCP servers read as octal.
errors.too-many: This vendor takes a single controller address in this option.
errors.value-too-long: The value exceeds the 255 bytes a single DHCP option can carry. Use fewer controller addresses.

share.vendorNotCarried: The vendor is not in the link: it opens on {first}, so tell the reader to choose {vendor}.

panos-policy-evaluation-order.name: PAN-OS policy evaluation order
panos-policy-evaluation-order.blurb: Put a Panorama rulebase into the order PAN-OS actually evaluates it, trace a flow to the deciding rule, and find the rules that never fire because something above them already matched.
panos-policy-evaluation-order.rulesPlaceholder:
shared-pre | block-tor | deny | from=any to=any app=tor
local | web-out | allow | from=trust to=untrust app=web-browsing
panos-policy-evaluation-order.runsLocally: Runs entirely in your browser. A rulebase names your zones, subnets and users, and none of it leaves this page.
panos-policy-evaluation-order.traceLabel: Trace a specific flow through the rulebase
panos-policy-evaluation-order.noShadowing: No rule is fully shadowed by a rule above it.
panos-policy-evaluation-order.shadowedBy: never fires: {rule} above it already matches everything it would.
panos-policy-evaluation-order.crossesLayer: This crosses layers, from {from} down to {to}, so it cannot be seen or fixed from the firewall alone.
panos-policy-evaluation-order.actionDiffers: The two rules disagree about what to do, so the outcome is not what the shadowed rule intended.

notes.intrazone-default-allow: Nothing matched, and the source and destination zones are the same, so intrazone-default applies and it ALLOWS. This is the asymmetry that surprises people: only traffic between different zones is denied by default.
notes.interzone-default-deny: Nothing matched, and the zones differ, so interzone-default applies and denies the traffic.

errors.empty: Enter at least one rule.
errors.bad-rule: A rule needs at least layer, name and action, separated by pipes.
errors.bad-layer: The layer must be one of shared-pre, dg-pre, local, dg-post or shared-post.
errors.bad-action: That is not a PAN-OS action. Use allow, deny, drop, reset-client, reset-server or reset-both.
errors.no-traffic: Describe the flow you want traced.
errors.too-many-rules: That is more rules than this tool will reason about at once.

f5-irules-number-notation.name: iRules number notation converter
f5-irules-number-notation.blurb: Type a value as it appears in an iRule (010, 0x1F, 08, 1e3) and see how Tcl 8.4 reads it: integer or double, the base, the same value in other notations, and why 010 == 8 is true while 010 eq 8 is false. Local, no network.
f5-irules-number-notation.valueLabel: Value, as written in the iRule

special.inf: an infinity, read by the C library
special.nan: not-a-number, read by the C library
special.hex: a hexadecimal floating-point value, read by the C library

f5-irules-number-notation.noCanonical: No numeric reading: Tcl keeps the text as it is

note.whitespace: Spaces around the digits are accepted when the number is held in a value. Inside an expression they are only separators.
note.wrapped64: The value lies between 2 to the power 63 and 2 to the power 64 minus 1. Tcl 8.4 accepts it but stores it as a signed 64-bit integer, so it wraps around to <c>{value}</c>.
note.octal: A leading 0 makes Tcl read the digits as octal (base 8): <c>{text}</c> is {value} in decimal.
note.octal-not-decimal: This is the classic iRules surprise: a value that looks decimal, such as a zero-padded code or time, is octal because of its leading 0.
note.hex: 0x makes Tcl read the digits as hexadecimal (base 16): <c>{text}</c> is {value} in decimal.
note.outside32: The value does not fit in 32 bits. Tcl 8.4 integers are as wide as the C long of the platform it was built for; this tool uses 64 bits, and a 32-bit build would read the value differently.
note.double: A double is never an integer to Tcl, even when it is a whole number: <c>3.0</c> keeps its decimal point when printed, and integer-only operators such as <c>%</c> refuse it.
note.twelve-digits: Tcl 8.4 prints doubles with 12 significant digits (tcl_precision defaults to 12), so the printed form can hide the rest of the value. Compare the exact value below.
note.c-library: This is an infinity or a not-a-number, read by the C library's strtod. Held in a value it can be compared, but any arithmetic on it fails; written as a literal in an expression it is refused.
note.invalid-octal: <c>{text}</c> starts with 0, so Tcl tries octal, and 8 and 9 are not octal digits. Arithmetic refuses it; comparisons fall back to comparing text.
note.too-large: The integer needs more than 64 bits, so Tcl 8.4 refuses it: integer value too large to represent.
note.int-garbage: It starts like an integer but other characters follow, so it is not a number.
note.empty: An empty string is not a number. Arithmetic refuses it; comparisons treat it as text.
note.float-range: The value is outside the range of a double (too large, or so small it underflows), so Tcl refuses it.
note.not-number: Not a number: arithmetic refuses it, and comparisons such as == fall back to comparing text.

f5-irules-number-notation.formsWrite: How to write it in an iRule

double.roundTrip: Shortest form that reads back to the same double
double.exact: Exact value of the binary double

f5-irules-number-notation.literalNote: A literal is read when the expression is compiled, so a bad one (such as 08) stops the whole expression before anything in it runs.
f5-irules-number-notation.variableNote: A value is read only when an operator needs a number. If it cannot be read, arithmetic fails at that point, and comparisons quietly compare text instead.

probeWhy.num: Numeric when both sides read as numbers; otherwise the text is compared.

f5-irules-number-notation.probesNote: In these expressions <c>$x</c> holds <c>{text}</c> and <c>$y</c> holds <c>{other}</c>, both set as plain values.
