f5-irules-expression-lab.name: iRules expression lab
f5-irules-expression-lab.blurb: Evaluate an expression the way expr and if do in an iRule and see every step: how each operand was read, numeric or text comparison, precedence, where && stopped, and == next to eq. Tcl 8.4 or iRules mode. Local, no network.
f5-irules-expression-lab.sampleTitle: Sample request (what the iRules commands return)
f5-irules-expression-lab.sampleNote: In this sample HTTP::method returns GET and the User-Agent header is curl/8.0. Nothing is sent anywhere.

stageNote.setup: The variables are set by ordinary Tcl commands, so quoting works exactly as in an iRule.
stageNote.parse: Tcl could not read the expression, so nothing in it ran. The caret marks where reading stopped.
stageNote.compile: Tcl 8.4 checks literals when it compiles an expression, so this stops the whole expression before any part of it runs.
stageNote.run: The parts drawn below ran before the error; the rest did not.

f5-irules-expression-lab.groupingNote: Every operator with its operands in parentheses. Tcl applies the higher-precedence operator first, whatever the spacing.

exprNote.lit-int: A whole number written in the expression, {base, select, 8 {in octal (it starts with 0)} 16 {in hexadecimal (it starts with 0x)} other {in decimal}}.
exprNote.lit-bool: A boolean word written in the expression.
exprNote.lit-double: A floating-point number written in the expression.
exprNote.braced: Text in braces is taken literally: nothing inside it is substituted.
exprNote.lone-dollar: A <c>$</c> with no variable name after it is just the character <c>$</c>.
exprNote.cmd: Runs the command in brackets; its result becomes the operand.
exprNote.quoted: Text in double quotes, with nothing inside to substitute.
exprNote.quoted-subst: Text in double quotes: the variables and commands inside it are substituted first.
exprNote.ternary: The condition is {branch, select, then {true, so the value after <c>?</c> is used} other {false, so the value after <c>:</c> is used}}; the other branch is never evaluated.
exprNote.bitnot: <c>~</c> flips every bit of an integer.
exprNote.uplus: Unary <c>+</c> requires a number and leaves it as it is.
exprNote.lnot: <c>!</c> gives 1 for a false operand and 0 for a true one.
exprNote.short-circuit: <c>{op}</c> stopped here: the left side is {left, select, true {true} other {false}}, which already decides the result, so the right side never ran.
exprNote.logic: Both sides ran: {left, select, true {true} other {false}} <c>{op}</c> {right, select, true {true} other {false}}.
exprNote.streq: <c>{op}</c> compares the two values as text, character by character. Numbers are never converted.
exprNote.f5-op: <c>{op}</c> is one of the operators F5 adds to iRules. It compares the values as text.
exprNote.mod: The remainder of {a} divided by {b}. It takes the sign of the divisor.
exprNote.shl: Shift left by {count, plural, one {{count} bit} other {{count} bits}}.
exprNote.shr: Shift right by {count, plural, one {{count} bit} other {{count} bits}}; the sign bit is copied in from the left.
exprNote.arith: <c>{op}</c> on {mode, select, int {integers} other {floating-point numbers, because at least one operand is a double}}: {a} {op} {b}.
exprNote.intdiv: {floored, select, true {Integer division rounds down, towards negative infinity: {a} / {b} gives the floor of the exact quotient, not the value truncated towards zero.} other {Integer division keeps the whole part of {a} / {b}.}}
exprNote.cmp-same: Both sides are the very same value, so they are equal without any conversion.
exprNote.cmp-string: Compared as text because {why, select, empty {one side is an empty string} left_text {the left side is not a number} right_text {the right side is not a number} left_bad_int {the left side looks like an integer but is not a valid one (a leading 0 followed by 8 or 9, for example)} right_bad_int {the right side looks like an integer but is not a valid one (a leading 0 followed by 8 or 9, for example)} other {one side is not a number}}. Character codes decide the order, so every upper-case letter sorts before every lower-case one.
exprNote.cmp-number: Compared as {mode, select, int {integers} other {floating-point numbers}}: {left} and {right}.
exprNote.canon: The result is a number, so Tcl returns it in canonical form: <c>{from}</c> becomes <c>{to}</c>.
exprNote.canon-none: The result <c>{text}</c> is not a number, so it is returned exactly as it is.

platform.int-overflow: The exact result does not fit in 64 bits, and Tcl 8.4 wraps it around without an error.
platform.shift-count: A shift count outside 0 to 63 is undefined in C. x86 processors use only the low 6 bits of the count, which is what is shown here.
platform.int-range-32: The result does not fit in 32 bits. A build of Tcl 8.4 with 32-bit integers would give a different answer.
platform.libm: This value comes from the platform's C math library and can differ in the last digits from one system to another.

compareWhy.num: Numbers when both sides read as numbers; otherwise text.

f5-irules-string-workbench.name: iRules string workbench
f5-irules-string-workbench.blurb: Run a Tcl 8.4 string command (range, first, map, match, compare, trim and more) and see the result on a character ruler: what was searched, matched, returned or replaced, and how indexes like end-1 or 010 were read. Local, no network.

opHelp.bytelength: Counts the bytes of Tcl's internal UTF-8 form.
opHelp.tolower: Lower-cases the string, or only the characters from first to last.
opHelp.toupper: Upper-cases the string, or only the characters from first to last.
opHelp.range: Returns the characters from first to last, both included. Indexes can be integers, <c>end</c>, or <c>end-N</c>.
opHelp.index: Returns one character, or an empty string when the index is outside the string.
opHelp.first: Returns the index where the needle first appears, or -1. A start index makes the search begin later.
opHelp.last: Returns the index where the needle last appears, or -1. A last index makes the search end earlier.
opHelp.map: Replaces each key with its value in one pass from left to right. At each position the first key in the list that matches wins.
opHelp.match: Glob matching: <c>*</c> matches any run of characters, <c>?</c> one character, <c>[abc]</c> one of a set. Returns 1 or 0.
opHelp.compare: Returns -1, 0 or 1 by comparing character codes, so upper case sorts before lower case.
opHelp.equal: Returns 1 when the two strings are identical, 0 otherwise.
opHelp.trim: Removes the given characters (white space by default) from both ends.
opHelp.trimleft: Removes the given characters (white space by default) from the start.
opHelp.trimright: Removes the given characters (white space by default) from the end.
opHelp.replace: Replaces the characters from first to last with the new string, or removes them when no new string is given.
opHelp.repeat: Returns the string repeated count times.

f5-irules-string-workbench.readInt: {base, select, 8 {an octal integer (leading 0)} 16 {a hexadecimal integer} other {a decimal integer}}
f5-irules-string-workbench.mapTitle: The single pass of string map

note.bytes-differ: Characters outside ASCII take more than one byte in Tcl's internal UTF-8, so the byte count is larger than the character count.
note.empty-span-unchanged: The first and last indexes select no characters, so the string comes back unchanged.
note.range-empty: The last index is before the first, so the result is empty.
note.index-out-of-range: The index is outside the string, so the result is an empty string, not an error.
note.empty-needle: An empty needle is never found: the result is -1.
note.last-whole-match: With a last index, only matches that end at or before it count.
note.map-one-pass: Each replacement is final: the text it inserts is never scanned again, so one pass cannot chain replacements.
note.compare-codes: Characters are compared by their codes, one by one: every upper-case letter comes before every lower-case one.
note.trim-set: The characters to remove are a set, not a word: each character in it is removed from the ends, in any order.
note.replace-unchanged: The indexes select nothing inside the string, so it comes back unchanged.
note.octal-index: An index written with a leading 0 is octal: <c>010</c> means index 8.
note.end-prefix: Tcl 8.4.6 accepts any prefix of <c>end</c> on its own (<c>e</c>, <c>en</c>), but not with an offset (<c>e-1</c> is an error).

share.carries: The link carries the subcommand and its fields as typed, with -nocase when ticked.

f5-irules-scan-explainer.name: iRules scan explainer
f5-irules-scan-explainer.blurb: Give a value and a scan format and see each %d, %s or %[^&] line up against the characters it took, the variable it filled, and exactly why scanning stopped. Explains the -1 result and the Tcl 8.4 quirks. Local, no network.
f5-irules-scan-explainer.varsPlaceholder: hours minutes (leave empty for a list)
f5-irules-scan-explainer.resultCount: {n, plural, =0 {No variable received a value: the first conversion did not match.} one {One variable received a value.} other {# variables received a value.}}
f5-irules-scan-explainer.resultMinusOne: The input ran out before the first conversion, so scan returns -1 rather than 0.
f5-irules-scan-explainer.resultInline: No variable names were given, so scan returns the converted values as a list.
f5-irules-scan-explainer.rulerTitle: The value, as the format consumed it
f5-irules-scan-explainer.rulerTruncated: Only the first 400 characters are drawn.

conv.i: integer in the base its prefix shows (0 octal, 0x hexadecimal)
conv.c: one character, stored as its code
conv.n: count of input consumed so far (uses no input)

dirKind.space: white space: skips any amount, including none

f5-irules-scan-explainer.width: (at most {n, plural, one {{n} character} other {{n} characters}})
f5-irules-scan-explainer.int32Cell: outside 32 bits: stored through a C int

stopped.format-end: Every directive in the format ran.
stopped.mismatch: Scanning stopped at a character the directive could not use. The variables after it were not set by this scan.
stopped.no-chars: Scanning stopped because the <c>%[...]</c> set matched no characters.
stopped.input-end: The input ran out before the format did.

note.minus-one: -1 means the input ended before the first conversion; 0 means a conversion was tried and failed. Check for both when a value may be empty.
note.n-bytes: Tcl 8.4.6 counts bytes of its internal UTF-8 for <c>%n</c>, although the manual says characters: each character outside ASCII counts 2 or 3.
note.i-prefix: <c>%i</c> takes the base from the prefix, like an integer in an expression: 0 means octal, 0x hexadecimal. Use <c>%d</c> for zero-padded decimal values such as times.
note.int32: Tcl 8.4.6 stores integer conversions through a C int, so a value outside 32 bits comes back changed (the <c>l</c> modifier does not help here). To keep a large number intact, scan it as text with <c>%[0-9]</c> and let <c>expr</c> read it.
note.inline: With no variable names, scan returns a list of the converted values (an empty element for a conversion that did not happen).

share.carries: The link carries the value, the format and the variable names as typed.

f5-irules-script-stepper.name: iRules script stepper
f5-irules-script-stepper.blurb: Run a short iRule snippet one command at a time and see what each command received after substitution, what it returned and which variables changed. The quickest way to understand quotes, braces, append, concat, incr and the branch if or switch took. Local, no network.
f5-irules-script-stepper.sampleTitle: Sample request (what the iRules commands return)
f5-irules-script-stepper.sampleNote: These are the answers the iRules commands give in this tool. Nothing is sent anywhere: pool, HTTP::redirect and similar actions are recorded, not performed.

code.break: Ended with break outside a loop:
code.continue: Ended with continue outside a loop:

f5-irules-script-stepper.stepsTitle: {n, plural, one {One command} other {# commands}}, in the order they started
f5-irules-script-stepper.stepsNote: An indented command ran inside the one above it: in its body, or in brackets while its words were being built (so it finished first).

exprNote.lit-int: A whole number written in the expression, {base, select, 8 {in octal (it starts with 0)} 16 {in hexadecimal (it starts with 0x)} other {in decimal}}.
exprNote.lit-bool: A boolean word written in the expression.
exprNote.lit-double: A floating-point number written in the expression.
exprNote.braced: Text in braces is taken literally: nothing inside it is substituted.
exprNote.lone-dollar: A <c>$</c> with no variable name after it is just the character <c>$</c>.
exprNote.cmd: Runs the command in brackets; its result becomes the operand.
exprNote.quoted: Text in double quotes, with nothing inside to substitute.
exprNote.quoted-subst: Text in double quotes: the variables and commands inside it are substituted first.
exprNote.ternary: The condition is {branch, select, then {true, so the value after <c>?</c> is used} other {false, so the value after <c>:</c> is used}}; the other branch is never evaluated.
exprNote.bitnot: <c>~</c> flips every bit of an integer.
exprNote.uplus: Unary <c>+</c> requires a number and leaves it as it is.
exprNote.lnot: <c>!</c> gives 1 for a false operand and 0 for a true one.
exprNote.short-circuit: <c>{op}</c> stopped here: the left side is {left, select, true {true} other {false}}, which already decides the result, so the right side never ran.
exprNote.logic: Both sides ran: {left, select, true {true} other {false}} <c>{op}</c> {right, select, true {true} other {false}}.
exprNote.streq: <c>{op}</c> compares the two values as text, character by character. Numbers are never converted.
exprNote.f5-op: <c>{op}</c> is one of the operators F5 adds to iRules. It compares the values as text.
exprNote.mod: The remainder of {a} divided by {b}. It takes the sign of the divisor.
exprNote.shl: Shift left by {count, plural, one {{count} bit} other {{count} bits}}.
exprNote.shr: Shift right by {count, plural, one {{count} bit} other {{count} bits}}; the sign bit is copied in from the left.
exprNote.arith: <c>{op}</c> on {mode, select, int {integers} other {floating-point numbers, because at least one operand is a double}}: {a} {op} {b}.
exprNote.intdiv: {floored, select, true {Integer division rounds down, towards negative infinity: {a} / {b} gives the floor of the exact quotient, not the value truncated towards zero.} other {Integer division keeps the whole part of {a} / {b}.}}
exprNote.cmp-same: Both sides are the very same value, so they are equal without any conversion.
exprNote.cmp-string: Compared as text because {why, select, empty {one side is an empty string} left_text {the left side is not a number} right_text {the right side is not a number} left_bad_int {the left side looks like an integer but is not a valid one (a leading 0 followed by 8 or 9, for example)} right_bad_int {the right side looks like an integer but is not a valid one (a leading 0 followed by 8 or 9, for example)} other {one side is not a number}}. Character codes decide the order, so every upper-case letter sorts before every lower-case one.
exprNote.cmp-number: Compared as {mode, select, int {integers} other {floating-point numbers}}: {left} and {right}.
exprNote.canon: The result is a number, so Tcl returns it in canonical form: <c>{from}</c> becomes <c>{to}</c>.
exprNote.canon-none: The result <c>{text}</c> is not a number, so it is returned exactly as it is.

platform.int-overflow: The exact result does not fit in 64 bits, and Tcl 8.4 wraps it around without an error.
platform.shift-count: A shift count outside 0 to 63 is undefined in C. x86 processors use only the low 6 bits of the count, which is what is shown here.
platform.int-range-32: The result does not fit in 32 bits. A build of Tcl 8.4 with 32-bit integers would give a different answer.
platform.libm: This value comes from the platform's C math library and can differ in the last digits from one system to another.

stepNote.append-creates: The variable did not exist, so <c>append</c> created it.
stepNote.lappend-creates: The variable did not exist, so <c>lappend</c> created it as a list.
stepNote.catch: The script inside ended with code {code} (0 ok, 1 error, 2 return, 3 break, 4 continue); <c>catch</c> returns that code instead of letting an error stop everything.
stepNote.class-longest: {count, plural, one {{count} entry} other {{count} entries}} matched; with starts_with or ends_with, class match returns the longest one, <c>{name}</c>.
stepNote.class-match: {hit, select, true {The data group entry <c>{name}</c> matched (operator {op}).} other {No entry in the data group matched (operator {op}).}}
stepNote.concat: <c>concat</c> trimmed the white space at both ends of each argument, dropped empty ones, and joined the rest with single spaces.
stepNote.cut-count: A number as terminator is a length: up to {count, plural, one {{count} character} other {{count} characters}}, fewer when the string ends first.
stepNote.cut-terminator: Stopped just before <c>{terminator}</c>, found at index {at}.
stepNote.cut-terminator-absent: <c>{terminator}</c> does not appear after the start point, so the rest of the string is returned.
stepNote.expr-unbraced: <c>expr</c> received several words: Tcl joins them with spaces and substitutes the result again, so a value holding <c>[</c> or <c>$</c> runs as code. Brace the expression (F5 K57410758).
stepNote.findstr-found: The search string starts at index {at}; the result begins {skip, plural, one {{skip} character} other {{skip} characters}} after that.
stepNote.foreach: Ran the body once per element: {iterations} in all.
stepNote.getfield: Split into {count, plural, one {{count} field} other {{count} fields}}; field {field} is returned (fields count from 1).
stepNote.domain: The name has {labels, plural, one {{labels} label} other {{labels} labels}}; the last {count, plural, one {{count} is} other {{count} are}} returned (<c>domain</c> counts from the right, and 1 is the last label).
stepNote.if-branch: A condition was true, so the body after it runs and the rest are skipped.
stepNote.if-else: No condition was true, so the <c>else</c> body runs.
stepNote.if-none: No condition was true and there is no <c>else</c>: nothing runs and <c>if</c> returns an empty string.
stepNote.incr-octal: The variable holds <c>{text}</c>, which <c>incr</c> reads as an octal integer because of the leading 0.
stepNote.switch-list: The patterns and bodies are given as one braced list.
stepNote.switch-match: The value matched the pattern <c>{pattern}</c> ({mode} matching){fallthrough, select, true {; its body is a dash, so the next body runs} other {}}.
stepNote.switch-none: No pattern matched and there is no <c>default</c>: <c>switch</c> returns an empty string.
stepNote.when: <c>when {event}</c>: on a BIG-IP this body runs each time the event fires; here it runs once, with the sample request.

undocumented.skip-past-end: F5's pages do not say what <c>{cmd}</c> returns when the skip goes past the end of the string. The tool assumes an empty string; check on a BIG-IP before relying on it.
undocumented.negative-skip: F5's pages do not cover a negative skip count for <c>{cmd}</c>. The tool starts at the beginning of the string; check on a BIG-IP before relying on it.
undocumented.count-format: The count <c>{text}</c> is not written as plain decimal digits. Tcl reads it as an integer (a leading 0 means octal, 0x hexadecimal), but F5 does not say how findstr and substr read it.
undocumented.count-zero: F5's rule says a number as terminator returns that many characters, which would make 0 return nothing, yet F5's own substr example with 0 returns the rest of the string. The tool follows the example. A contributor note on F5's API reference page reports that 0 did not work for them on 11.5.4 and 11.6.0, so check on your version.
undocumented.count-negative: F5's pages do not cover a negative count. The tool returns the rest of the string; check on a BIG-IP before relying on it.
undocumented.empty-terminator: F5's pages do not cover an empty terminator. The tool returns the rest of the string; check on a BIG-IP before relying on it.
undocumented.terminator-absent-findstr: F5's findstr page does not say what happens when the terminator is absent (its substr page says the rest of the string is returned). The tool assumes the same for findstr.
undocumented.findstr-not-found: F5's pages do not say what findstr returns when <c>{search}</c> is not in the string. The tool assumes an empty string. F5 calls findstr equivalent to string range with string first, but that equivalent returns the whole string here, so the two cannot both be right; check on a BIG-IP before relying on it.
undocumented.substr-no-terminator: The terminator is optional in F5's syntax, but the page does not say what happens without it. The tool returns the rest of the string; check on a BIG-IP before relying on it.
undocumented.getfield-empty-split: F5's pages do not cover an empty separator. The tool treats the whole string as field 1.
undocumented.getfield-empty-field: Two separators in a row make an empty field here. F5's pages do not show this case.
undocumented.getfield-out-of-range: There are {count, plural, one {{count} field} other {{count} fields}} and field {field} was asked for. F5's pages do not say what getfield returns then; the tool assumes an empty string.
undocumented.domain-count: F5's page shows <c>domain</c> only with counts of 1 or more. For {count}, the tool assumes an empty string; check on a BIG-IP before relying on it.
undocumented.domain-empty-label: The name has an empty label (a leading, trailing or doubled dot). F5's page has no example of this for <c>domain</c>.
undocumented.class-contains-multiple: {count} entries contain the value. F5 documents that starts_with and ends_with return the longest match, but not which entry contains returns; the tool takes the first one in the order the data group lists them.

share.carries: The link carries the fields as typed, the sample request only in iRules mode; a key or credential in them stops it.
share.caution: A script can name internal hosts, pools and data groups: read it before you send the link.

f5-irules-string-extract.name: findstr, substr and getfield explainer
f5-irules-string-extract.blurb: Run F5's findstr, substr or getfield on your string and see the match, the skip, the terminator and the result marked on a ruler, next to the plain Tcl that does the same job. Cases F5 does not document are flagged. Local, no network.

syntax.findstr: <c>findstr string search ?skip? ?terminator?</c> finds the search string, skips that many characters from the start of the match, then returns up to the terminator: a length, or text to stop before.
syntax.substr: <c>substr string skip ?terminator?</c> starts at index skip (0 is the first character), then returns up to the terminator: a length, or text to stop before.
syntax.getfield: <c>getfield string separator field</c> splits at every occurrence of the separator (one character or a string) and returns that field, counting from 1.

f5-irules-string-extract.rulerTruncated: Only the first 400 characters are drawn.

note.findstr-found: The search string starts at index {at}; the result begins {skip, plural, one {{skip} character} other {{skip} characters}} after that.
note.cut-count: A number as terminator is a length: up to {count, plural, one {{count} character} other {{count} characters}}, fewer when the string ends first.
note.cut-terminator: Stopped just before <c>{terminator}</c>, found at index {at}.
note.cut-terminator-absent: <c>{terminator}</c> does not appear after the start point, so the rest of the string is returned.
note.getfield: Split into {count, plural, one {{count} field} other {{count} fields}}; field {field} is returned (fields count from 1).
note.split-chars: Plain Tcl's <c>split</c> treats every character of <c>{sep}</c> as a separator of its own, so it is not an equivalent here: getfield splits at the whole string.

The tool follows the example. A contributor note on F5's API reference page reports that 0 did not work for them on 11.5.4 and 11.6.0, so check on your version.
