f5-irules-string-extract.equivalentTitle: The same job in plain Tcl

equivalentNote.findstr: F5 describes two-argument findstr as equivalent to this. The tool runs it in the same Tcl 8.4 engine to check.
equivalentNote.substr: string range takes a last index rather than a length or a stop text, so this is the closest plain Tcl, run here to check.
equivalentNote.getfield: split makes a list and lindex picks one element, counting from 0 where getfield counts from 1.

share.carries: The link carries the command, the string and its fields as typed.

f5-irules-conditional-builder.name: iRules if / switch / class builder
f5-irules-conditional-builder.blurb: Describe one decision as rules and get it written as an if / elseif chain, a switch and a class match with its tmsh data groups, then see which pool each picks for a test value. Shows where first match and longest match disagree. Local, no network.
f5-irules-conditional-builder.shadowed: Rule {rule} can never be chosen by if or switch: rule {by} comes first and matches every value rule {rule} matches.

note.class-multiple-groups: The rules use more than one comparison, so the class form needs one data group per comparison, looked up in the order the comparisons first appear.
note.class-longest-vs-first: class match with starts_with or ends_with returns the longest matching entry, whatever the order of the rules (F5's class reference). if and switch take the first rule that matches, in order.
note.case-sensitive: The value is compared as it is, so case matters: Curl would not match curl. Tick lower case to compare without case, and write the rule values in lower case.
note.uppercase-never-matches: A rule value has upper-case letters, but the request value is lower-cased first, so that rule can never match.
note.unmatched-brace: A rule value has a brace without its partner, so the code writes it with a backslash in front. Tcl counts the braces inside a braced body even between double quotes, so a lone one there would break the rule.
note.tmsh-quoted: A record name has characters other than letters, digits and _ . / : -, so the tmsh text puts it in double quotes. That quoting has not been tried on a BIG-IP: after creating the data group, list it in tmsh and check the record.
note.path-stops-at-query: The test value has a question mark, which starts the query string. HTTP::path returns only the part before it, and that part is what the rules compare.

formNote.if: Conditions are tested from the top; the first true one wins.
formNote.switch: Patterns are tested from the top; the first match wins. The -- keeps a value that starts with a dash from being read as an option (F5 K15650046).
formNote.class: Each lookup returns the matching entry's value, here the pool name. The data groups must exist on the BIG-IP; their tmsh definitions are below.

unavailable.glob: class match has no glob comparison, so rules that use a glob pattern cannot become a data group lookup.
unavailable.empty: There are no rules to put in a data group.

share.carries: The link carries the whole decision as typed: rules, pools, data group and test value.

f5-irules-style-checker.name: iRules style checker
f5-irules-style-checker.blurb: Paste an iRule and read it against the DevCentral iRules Style Guide: indentation, braces, comments, braced expressions, switch --, event priorities, static:: names and more, plus a real Tcl 8.4 syntax check. Parsed, never run. Local, no network.

preset.thread-points: == on text, break in a switch
preset.array-and-keyword: Array variable, if glued to a brace

f5-irules-style-checker.clean: No findings: it follows the guide on every point the checker reads.
f5-irules-style-checker.counts: {error, plural, one {# error} other {# errors}}, {warning, plural, one {# warning} other {# warnings}}, {info, plural, one {# note} other {# notes}}.
f5-irules-style-checker.stats: {lines, plural, one {{lines} line} other {{lines} lines}}; the longest has {longest, plural, one {{longest} character} other {{longest} characters}}.

E1.tab: A tab character. The guide asks for 4-space indents and no tabs.
E1.indent: Indented by {spaces, plural, one {{spaces} space} other {{spaces} spaces}}, which is not a multiple of 4.

E2.main: {length} characters long. The guide aims for 100 columns, 120 at most.

E3.crlf: A Windows line ending (carriage return). The guide asks for Unix line feeds.
E3.trailing: White space at the end of the line.
E3.non-ascii: {glyph} ({char}), column {col}{count, plural, =1 {} other {, one of # on this line}}: a character outside ASCII. The guide asks for ASCII files; inside a quoted log message it is harmless, anywhere else check it.
E3.no-final-newline: The file does not end with a line feed.
E3.dash: {name} ({char}), column {col}{count, plural, =1 {} other {, one of # on this line}}: a dash that is not the ASCII hyphen-minus. Tcl reads it neither as an option dash nor as a minus sign; a switch with an en dash before its value takes the dash as the value and silently matches nothing.
E3.lookalike: {glyph} is {name} ({char}), column {col}{count, plural, =1 {} other {, one of # on this line}}: it looks like {ascii} but is a different character, so Tcl does not treat it as {ascii}.

R1.invisible: {name} ({char}), column {col}{count, plural, =1 {} other {, one of # on this line}}: an invisible character. Tcl reads it as part of the text around it, so after a closing brace the rule will not load, and on a line of its own it runs as a command that does not exist. Delete it.
R1.space: {name} ({char}), column {col}{count, plural, =1 {} other {, one of # on this line}}: it looks like a space, but Tcl separates words only on ASCII white space, so the words on either side run together. Type an ordinary space.
R1.quote: {name} ({char}), column {col}{count, plural, =1 {} other {, one of # on this line}}: a typographic quote. Tcl does not treat it as a quote, so it does not hold words together. Type a straight quote.

R2.main: {chars} characters ({bytes} bytes as UTF-8). F5 K9204 limits an iRule to 65,520 characters, and BIG-IP refuses to save or load a longer one; split it into several iRules, or move data into data groups.

R4.main: A brace alone on its own line. Put the opening brace at the end of the line before it.
R4.else-line: else or elseif starts a new line. Keep the closing brace, else and the opening brace on one line.

R6.eol: An end-of-line comment. Put comments on their own line, at the indent of the code.
R6.no-space: A comment with no space after the hash. The guide writes comments as hash, space, text, and keeps hash-then-text for commented-out code.
R6.switch-comment: A comment between switch patterns. Tcl reads it as a pattern, which breaks the switch; put comments inside a body.

R7.main: {count} commands on one line. Write one command per line.

R8.main: A single-line if. Spread it over several lines, even for a debug log.

R9.main: State stored as {value}. Store it as 0 or 1.

R10.main: One of F5's word operators (and, or, not). Use the Tcl operators &&, || and !, with parentheses to make the grouping plain.

R11.main: A closing brace followed directly by an opening one. Leave a space between them.
R11.keyword-brace: {word} is a single word to Tcl, not the keyword followed by a brace, so this line fails when it runs (an invalid command name, or extra words in the if). Put a space before the brace.

R12.main: An expression that is not braced: {word}. An unbraced expression is substituted twice (an injection risk, F5 K57410758) and cannot be compiled ahead; brace it.

R13.main: A variable in an expression without a space on each side.

R14.main: A variable in an expression written without braces around its name. The guide writes the name in braces after the dollar sign.

R15.main: {command} without -- before its value. A value that starts with a dash would be read as an option (F5 K15650046).

R16.main: The event {event} has no priority. The guide asks for one on every event; the default is 500.

R17.main: A table entry without a timeout or lifetime. F5 then applies a default timeout of 180 seconds and an indefinite lifetime; set them on purpose.

R18.main: static::{name} has no prefix. Prefix static:: names, for example with the rule's name, so two rules cannot collide.

R19.main: A static:: debug flag. The guide warns these lead to log storms; keep the flag in a variable set per connection instead.

R20.commented-code: Commented-out code. Remove it before the rule goes to production.

syntax.main: Tcl 8.4 cannot parse this: {message}. The rule will not load.

D1.main: {op} with the text {text}. == and != compare as numbers whenever both sides look like numbers (in Tcl 8.4, 10 == 012 is true, 012 being octal); for text use {suggest}. Raised in the guide's comment thread; F5's How To Write Fast Rules also asks you to compare strings to strings.

D2.outside-loop: {cmd} with no loop around it. switch is not a loop, so its arms never need {cmd} to stop, and outside a loop Tcl 8.4 turns it into an error: invoked "{cmd}" outside of a loop. Remove it; to leave the event early, use return.
D2.leaves-loop: {cmd} in a switch arm leaves the enclosing loop, not just the switch: in Tcl, switch is not a loop. If you only meant to end the arm, remove it; an arm never runs into the next one.
D2.return-arm: return leaves the whole event (F5's return page: it exits the currently executing event), not just the switch. An arm never runs into the next one, so no return is needed to end it.

limit.array: {ref} is an array variable. Tcl accepts it, but this tool does not model arrays, so it was read as a plain variable and the rest of the rule was still checked.

f5-irules-style-checker.limits: The checker reads structure and text, never runs the rule. Where it cannot be sure (for example whether a line starting with a hash is code or a comment missing its space) the finding is a note, not a warning. D1 and D2 come from the guide's comment thread, and characters are named from the Unicode Character Database 18.0.0.

share.carries: The link carries the iRule as pasted; an iRule holding a key or credential gets none.
share.caution: An iRule can name internal hosts, pools and data groups: read it before you send the link.
share.maybeSecret: {more, plural, =0 {Line {line} may hold a secret ({label}): check it, and any internal names, before you send the link.} one {Line {line} ({label}) and one more line may hold secrets: check them, and any internal names, before you send the link.} other {Line {line} ({label}) and # more lines may hold secrets: check them, and any internal names, before you send the link.}}
share.blockedSecret: {more, plural, =0 {No link: line {line} holds a key or credential ({label}). Replace it with a placeholder, then share again.} one {No link: line {line} ({label}) and one more line hold keys or credentials. Replace them with placeholders, then share again.} other {No link: line {line} ({label}) and # more lines hold keys or credentials. Replace them with placeholders, then share again.}}

f5-bigip-index-base-finder.name: BIG-IP zero-or-one finder
f5-bigip-index-base-finder.blurb: Zero or one? Look up where each Tcl command, iRules command, configuration object, API and on-box tool on a BIG-IP starts counting, with F5's own wording and the date each source was read, then translate a position into every command's own number and run it. Local, no network.
f5-bigip-index-base-finder.modeLabel: What do you want to do?
f5-bigip-index-base-finder.lookupIntro: Every place on a BIG-IP found to count from 0 or from 1, with what is counted, how to reach the first and the last, what comes back when nothing is there, and the sources. Filter by where counting starts, or search.

thumb.1: Tcl positions count from 0, and <c>end</c> is the last index, the length minus one.
thumb.2: F5's field-style numbers count from 1: <c>getfield</c> fields, <c>URI::path</c> depths, LTM policy path-segment indexes, the legacy <c>matchclass</c>.
thumb.3: Counters return 1 for the first item: <c>HTTP::request_num</c>, <c>table incr</c>.
thumb.4: Many zeros are values, not positions: route domain 0, port 0, connection-limit 0, <c>SSL::verify_result</c> 0, and tcpdump's 0.0.
thumb.5: Lower goes first almost everywhere (event priority, policy ordinals, BIG-IP DNS order, syslog severity), except pool priority groups, where higher wins.
thumb.6: In an <c>if</c>, 0 is false and every other number is true, -1 included: compare an index with <c>>= 0</c> instead of testing it, and store your own flags as 0 or 1, as the DevCentral iRules Style Guide asks.

f5-bigip-index-base-finder.searchPlaceholder: getfield, path, route domain, tcpdump, priority...
f5-bigip-index-base-finder.noResults: Nothing matches. Try fewer words, or clear the filters.

baseHelp.right: Counted back from the end: end, end-1, or the last N.
baseHelp.mixed: Both bases meet in the same place.
baseHelp.value: Not a position: 0 means something (default, no limit, all, success, equal).
baseHelp.count: Not a position, though it is easy to mistake for one.

confidence.verified: Stated by the Tcl manual and run in tclsh 8.4.6
confidence.example: Shown only by an example on the source page

f5-bigip-index-base-finder.translateIntro: Ask the way people count, where 1 is the first. Each command below gets the number it needs, runs in the Tcl 8.4.6 teaching engine, and sits next to the off-by-one version.

question.field: The Nth field after a split
question.segment: The Nth segment of a path
question.label: The last N labels of a host name
question.element: The Nth element of a Tcl list

f5-bigip-index-base-finder.answerNone: No single answer: the commands disagree.

form.split-lindex-forgot: split, then lindex, forgetting the empty element
form.lrange-end: split, lrange from the end, join
form.lindex-end: only that label (lindex from the end)
form.lrange-end-n: lrange from the end, one label too many

tnote.split-multichar: <c>split</c> treats each character of {sep} as a separator, while <c>getfield</c> splits on the whole string, so the two can give different fields.
tnote.leading-separator: The value starts with the separator, so the first field is empty: field 1 for <c>getfield</c>, element 0 after <c>split</c>.
tnote.leading-slash: The path starts with a slash, so <c>split</c> makes an empty element 0 and <c>getfield</c> an empty field 1: each command needs one more than you might expect.
tnote.getfield-leading-assumed: F5's getfield page has no example where the string starts with the separator. The tool assumes field 1 is the empty text before it, as <c>split</c> does; check on a BIG-IP before relying on it.
tnote.query-in-path: The value has a question mark: a path taken from <c>HTTP::uri</c> includes the query string. Use <c>HTTP::path</c> to cut segments without it.
tnote.right-rows-disagree: Commands that should answer the same question disagree here: read the notes before choosing one.
tnote.lrange-list: <c>lrange</c> returns a list, so an element with spaces or braces comes back quoted, while <c>lindex</c> returns the element itself.
tnote.found-at-zero: Found at index {index}, the very first position (position {position} for people). An <c>if</c> on the index reads 0 as false and skips the body.
tnote.found: Found at index {index} (position {position} for people). Any index above 0 is true in an <c>if</c>, so the trap only shows at 0 and -1.
tnote.not-found: Not found: -1. An <c>if</c> on the index reads -1 as true and runs the body anyway.

undocumented.skip-past-end: F5's pages do not say what <c>{cmd}</c> returns when the skip goes past the end of the string. The tool assumes an empty string; check on a BIG-IP before relying on it.
undocumented.negative-skip: F5's pages do not cover a negative skip count for <c>{cmd}</c>. The tool starts at the beginning of the string; check on a BIG-IP before relying on it.
undocumented.count-format: The count <c>{text}</c> is not written as plain decimal digits. Tcl reads it as an integer (a leading 0 means octal, 0x hexadecimal), but F5 does not say how findstr and substr read it.
undocumented.count-zero: F5's rule says a number as terminator returns that many characters, which would make 0 return nothing, yet F5's own substr example with 0 returns the rest of the string. The tool follows the example. A contributor note on F5's API reference page reports that 0 did not work for them on 11.5.4 and 11.6.0, so check on your version.
undocumented.count-negative: F5's pages do not cover a negative count. The tool returns the rest of the string; check on a BIG-IP before relying on it.
undocumented.empty-terminator: F5's pages do not cover an empty terminator. The tool returns the rest of the string; check on a BIG-IP before relying on it.
undocumented.terminator-absent-findstr: F5's findstr page does not say what happens when the terminator is absent (its substr page says the rest of the string is returned). The tool assumes the same for findstr.
undocumented.findstr-not-found: F5's pages do not say what findstr returns when <c>{search}</c> is not in the string. The tool assumes an empty string. F5 calls findstr equivalent to string range with string first, but that equivalent returns the whole string here, so the two cannot both be right; check on a BIG-IP before relying on it.
undocumented.substr-no-terminator: The terminator is optional in F5's syntax, but the page does not say what happens without it. The tool returns the rest of the string; check on a BIG-IP before relying on it.
undocumented.getfield-empty-split: F5's pages do not cover an empty separator. The tool treats the whole string as field 1.
undocumented.getfield-empty-field: Two separators in a row make an empty field here. F5's pages do not show this case.
undocumented.getfield-out-of-range: There are {count, plural, one {{count} field} other {{count} fields}} and field {field} was asked for. F5's pages do not say what getfield returns then; the tool assumes an empty string.
undocumented.domain-count: F5's page shows <c>domain</c> only with counts of 1 or more. For {count}, the tool assumes an empty string; check on a BIG-IP before relying on it.
undocumented.domain-empty-label: The name has an empty label (a leading, trailing or doubled dot). F5's page has no example of this for <c>domain</c>.
undocumented.class-contains-multiple: {count} entries contain the value. F5 documents that starts_with and ends_with return the longest match, but not which entry contains returns; the tool takes the first one in the order the data group lists them.

tcl-string-index.rule: <c>string index</c> counts characters from 0: index 0 is the first character, <c>end</c> the last, and <c>end-1</c> the one before it. An index below 0, or at the length or beyond, returns an empty string, not an error.

tcl-string-range.rule: <c>string range</c> takes a first and a last index, both counted from 0 and both included: <c>string range $s 0 2</c> returns three characters. A first index below 0 is read as 0, and a last index past the end is read as <c>end</c>.
tcl-string-range.trap: Because the last index is included, the result has last minus first plus one characters. The first N characters are <c>string range $s 0 N-1</c>, not N.

tcl-string-first.rule: <c>string first</c> and <c>string last</c> return the index where the text starts, counted from 0, or -1 when it is not there. The optional start index of <c>string first</c> (and last index of <c>string last</c>) uses the same numbering.
tcl-string-first.trap: In an <c>if</c>, 0 is false and every other number is true. So <c>if [string first ...]</c> skips the body when the text is at the very start (index 0) and runs it when the text is missing (-1). Test <c>[string first ...] >= 0</c> instead.

tcl-string-compare.counts: a comparison result, not a position
tcl-string-compare.rule: <c>string compare</c> returns -1, 0 or 1: 0 means the two strings are equal, -1 that the first sorts before the second, and 1 that it sorts after.
tcl-string-compare.trap: Read as a condition, 0 is false: <c>if [string compare $a $b]</c> runs when the strings are different. For equality use <c>string equal</c> or the <c>eq</c> operator, which give 1 when the strings are equal.

tcl-truth.rule: In an <c>if</c> condition, and wherever <c>expr</c> reads a value as true or false, 0 is false and every other number is true, -1 included. Tcl also accepts the words true, yes and on, and false, no and off, in upper or lower case and shortened, as long as the short form is not ambiguous: <c>n</c>, <c>t</c> and <c>of</c> work, while <c>o</c> is an error. The DevCentral iRules Style Guide asks you to store state only as 0 or 1.
tcl-truth.trap: <c>string is true</c> and <c>string is false</c> follow different rules from <c>if</c>: they accept only 0, 1 and the words, so <c>string is true -1</c> returns 0 although <c>if</c> treats -1 as true. Without <c>-strict</c> they also return 1 for an empty string, which <c>if</c> rejects with an error.

tcl-string-other.rule: <c>string replace</c> takes first and last indexes like <c>string range</c>; <c>string wordstart</c> and <c>string wordend</c> take an index and return one; <c>string is</c> with <c>-failindex</c> stores the index of the first character that failed. All count from 0, and the index arguments accept <c>end</c>.

tcl-end-keyword.rule: <c>end</c> is the last index, which is the length minus one, and <c>end-1</c> is the one before it. It works in <c>string index</c>, <c>string range</c>, <c>string replace</c>, <c>lindex</c>, <c>lrange</c>, <c>linsert</c>, <c>lreplace</c> and <c>lsort -index</c>.
tcl-end-keyword.trap: <c>end</c> is not the length: in a 4-character string, <c>end</c> is 3. <c>end-0</c> is the same as <c>end</c>.

tcl-lindex.rule: <c>lindex</c> counts elements from 0: index 0 is the first element and <c>end</c> the last. A negative index, or one at the number of elements or beyond, returns an empty string.

tcl-lrange.rule: <c>lrange</c> returns the elements from first to last, counted from 0 and both included: <c>lrange $l 0 1</c> is the first two. A first index below 0 is read as 0, and a last index past the end as <c>end</c>.

tcl-lsearch.rule: <c>lsearch</c> returns the index of the first matching element, counted from 0, or -1 when nothing matches. <c>-start</c> takes an index in the same numbering.
tcl-lsearch.trap: The same trap as <c>string first</c>: a match at index 0 is false in an <c>if</c>, and no match (-1) is true. Compare the result with -1.

tcl-list-edit.rule: <c>linsert</c>, <c>lreplace</c> and <c>lset</c> take indexes counted from 0. <c>linsert</c> at 0 (or below) puts the new elements first, and at <c>end</c> (or past the end) appends them.

tcl-lsort-index.rule: <c>lsort -index</c> sorts a list of lists by one element of each sublist, counted from 0: <c>-index 1</c> sorts by the second element. <c>end</c> and <c>end-N</c> are allowed.

tcl-split.rule: <c>split</c> makes a list, and <c>lindex</c> counts it from 0. When the string starts with the separator, the first element is the empty text before it.
tcl-split.trap: A path starts with a slash, so <c>split /api/v2/users /</c> gives four elements, the first one empty: the first segment, api, is element 1, not 0.

tcl-regexp-indices.rule: With <c>-indices</c>, <c>regexp</c> stores each match as a pair of indexes, the first and the last character, counted from 0 and both included. A group that took no part in the match gets -1 -1. <c>-start</c> takes an index in the same numbering.

tcl-regexp-groups.rule: Capture groups count from 1, in the order their opening parentheses appear: the first sub-match variable of <c>regexp</c> holds group 1, and <c>regsub</c> writes it as <c>\1</c>. Group 0 is the whole match: the match variable of <c>regexp</c>, and & or <c>\0</c> in <c>regsub</c>.
tcl-regexp-groups.trap: Group numbers start at 1 while string positions start at 0: in the same <c>regexp -indices</c> call, group 1 can report position 0.

tcl-positional.rule: In <c>format</c> and <c>scan</c>, a position specifier such as <c>%2$s</c> picks an argument (or a variable) by number, and 1 is the first. When one specifier is positional, all of them must be.

tcl-scan-count.rule: <c>%n</c> stores how much of the input <c>scan</c> has read so far, so it equals the index where the rest of the string starts and can feed <c>string range</c>.
tcl-scan-count.trap: In Tcl 8.4.6 that amount is counted in bytes of UTF-8, not characters: after a character such as é it runs ahead of <c>string range</c> (the scan explainer shows it).

tcl-clock-zero.rule: These <c>clock format</c> fields start at 0: %w is the weekday with Sunday 0, %H the hour from 00 to 23, %M and %S from 00 to 59, and %U and %W the week of the year from 00 (in tclsh 8.4.6, 1 January 1970, a Thursday, is week 00 for both).

tcl-clock-one.rule: These <c>clock format</c> fields start at 1: %u is the weekday with Monday 1 and Sunday 7, %d and %e the day of the month, %j the day of the year from 001, %m the month from 01, %I the 12-hour clock from 01, and %V the ISO 8601 week from 01.
tcl-clock-one.trap: %w and %u number the same day differently: Sunday is 0 for %w and 7 for %u, while Monday is 1 for both.

tcl-binary-at.rule: In <c>binary scan</c>, @ moves the cursor to an absolute byte position, and position 0 is the first byte. A position past the end leaves the cursor after the last byte.

tcl-levels.rule: <c>info level</c> is 0 at the top (the global level) and 1 inside a proc called from there. <c>uplevel</c> and <c>upvar</c> take a relative level, where 1 (the caller) is the default, or an absolute one written with #: #0 is the global level.

tcl-rand.rule: <c>rand()</c> returns a value between 0 and 1, never 1 itself, so <c>int(rand()*N)</c> is a whole number from 0 to N-1: exactly the <c>lindex</c> positions of a list with N elements.

f5-getfield.rule: <c>getfield</c> splits a string on a character or a string and returns one field. F5's page: the field number is 1 indexed, so field 1 is the text before the first separator.
f5-getfield.trap: When the string starts with the separator, field 1 is the empty text before it, so the first segment of a path is field 2. F5's page has no example with a leading separator; the translator flags it.

f5-substr.rule: <c>substr</c> starts at an index counted from 0: F5's page says the skip count is the index of the first character returned, where 0 is the first character. The terminator is either a length or a text to stop before.
f5-substr.conflict: F5's rule says a numeric terminator returns that many characters, so 0 would return nothing, yet the published example with 0 returns the rest of the string, and the API page marks that line as not working on 11.5.4 and 11.6.0.

f5-findstr.rule: <c>findstr</c> finds the search text, then skips a number of characters counted from the first character of the match: 0, the default, returns the match itself. To start right after the search text, skip its length.
f5-findstr.trap: <c>substr</c> counts its skip from the start of the string and <c>findstr</c> from the start of the match, although F5's substr page says the two use these arguments in the same way.

f5-domain.rule: <c>domain</c> returns the last N labels of a dotted name, counted from the right: in F5's example, 1 gives com and 2 gives domain.com. A count larger than the number of labels returns the whole name.
f5-domain.trap: For a name such as www.sub.my.domain.co.uk, 2 returns co.uk, not the organization's name (F5's own example).

f5-uri-path.rule: <c>URI::path</c> with a start (and an end) depth returns part of the directory path, and depth 1 is the first directory: F5's page says the range needs start >= 1, and its example shows that 0 raises a Tcl error.
f5-uri-path.conflict: F5's example contradicts itself: a comment says the depth is 3 where the output shows 2, a start of 3 returns / while a start of 4 returns /path/to/, and the tmsh copy of the page leaves those lines out.

f5-request-num.rule: <c>HTTP::request_num</c> counts the HTTP transactions on the current connection including the current one, so the first request returns 1. <c>HTTP2::requests</c> counts the same way for the HTTP/2 session and returns 0 when HTTP/2 is not active.

f5-http-header.rule: <c>HTTP::header at</c> returns the name of the header at a zero-based index, so 0 is the first header line. Asking for the value of a header that is not there returns an empty string.
f5-http-header.trap: When a header appears more than once, <c>HTTP::header value</c> works on the last one, while <c>SIP::header</c> without an index returns the first. <c>HTTP::header values</c> returns them all.

f5-payload.rule: The payload commands take a byte offset counted from 0: F5's HTTP::payload page says that to replace the whole payload the offset should be 0, and the TCP, UDP and SSL payload pages show the same base in their examples.
f5-payload.result: the collected TCP payload is now empty (F5's example)

f5-tcp-offset.rule: Despite its name, <c>TCP::offset</c> is not a position: F5's page says it returns the number of bytes currently held in memory by <c>TCP::collect</c>.
f5-tcp-offset.trap: Use it as a length, not as the offset of the last byte: with N bytes held, the last one is at offset N minus 1.
f5-tcp-offset.result: the number of bytes collected so far

f5-ssl-cert.rule: <c>SSL::cert</c> and <c>SSL::cert issuer</c> take an index from 0: F5's page says zero denotes the first certificate in the chain the peer sent and one the next. <c>SSL::cert count</c> is the total, so the last index is the count minus 1.
f5-ssl-cert.conflict: One of F5's examples has the comment "Check if there is more than one client cert" above a test for a count greater than 0, which means at least one.
f5-ssl-cert.result: the first certificate the peer sent (F5's examples use it as the client's own certificate)

f5-ssl-extensions.rule: <c>SSL::extensions -index</c> returns the N-th extension, zero-indexed in F5's words, and <c>SSL::extensions count</c> is how many arrived.
f5-ssl-extensions.trap: F5's own example loops from 0 and prints the number plus one for people: count from 0 in code and from 1 in messages.
f5-ssl-extensions.result: the first extension received, as bytes

f5-class-index.rule: With <c>-index</c>, <c>class match</c> and <c>class search</c> return entry indexes, and <c>class element</c> takes one; F5's example lists the first three matches as 0 1 2. Without an option, <c>class match</c> returns 1 for a match and 0 for none.
f5-class-index.trap: F5 warns that these indexes are not guaranteed to stay the same when the data group changes, even between events.
f5-class-index.conflict: An example comment on F5's page calls lindex $element 1 the key, but in the name and value pair that index is the value.

f5-matchclass.rule: The legacy <c>matchclass</c> returns the matching row's index counted from 1, and 0 when nothing matches, so the result works as a condition. F5's page adds that lindex counts from 0, hence the minus 1 in its example.
f5-matchclass.conflict: The same page states that no match returns 0, yet its example tests the result against -1.
f5-matchclass.result: the matching row of the old list-style data group

f5-tmm-cmp.rule: <c>TMM::cmp_unit</c> returns the number (0-x) of the CPU, the TMM instance, running the rule, and F5's example calls 0 the first TMM instance. <c>TMM::cmp_group</c> returns the group (0-x), which is always 0 on platforms other than a chassis. <c>TMM::cmp_count</c> is how many TMMs run.

f5-sip-index.rule: <c>SIP::route</c> and <c>SIP::record-route</c> take a numeric zero-based index (or the word top), and <c>SIP::via</c> takes a zero-based index too, according to the tmsh copy of its page. Without an index, <c>SIP::via</c> returns the first Via.
f5-sip-index.result: the protocol part of the first Via header

f5-diameter-avp.rule: <c>DIAMETER::avp</c> picks the Nth AVP with a given code by a zero-based index, and leaving the index out works exactly like index 0, the first one.

f5-radius-avp.rule: F5's <c>RADIUS::avp</c> examples read repeated attributes with index 0, 1, 2 and so on, and stop at the first empty result. The page never states the base in words.
f5-radius-avp.result: the first matching vendor-specific attribute, as a string

f5-message-field.rule: <c>MESSAGE::field value</c> takes an optional index that F5's page calls 0-based. A field that is not there returns an empty string, and the order of repeated fields depends on the protocol.
f5-message-field.result: the first Via field of the message

f5-name-response.rule: <c>NAME::response address</c> takes an index from 0 to 15 inclusive; without one it returns the list of up to 16 records, and null when none came back. F5 deprecated it in version 15.1 in favour of the RESOLVER and DNSMSG commands.
f5-name-response.result: the first address returned by NAME::lookup

f5-json-array.rule: The <c>JSON::array</c> commands, which F5 lists as introduced in BIG-IP 21.0.0, count positions from 0: inserting at an index equal to the size appends, and removing slides the later values down by one. The page never writes the base in words.
f5-json-array.result: the first value of the array

f5-dns-lists.rule: <c>RESOLV::lookup</c> and <c>DNSMSG::section</c> return Tcl lists, so <c>lindex</c> 0 is the first item; F5's RESOLV::lookup page uses exactly that to get a single address.
f5-dns-lists.conflict: F5's DNSMSG::record example stores lindex $answer 1 in a variable named first_rr, but index 1 is the second record.
f5-dns-lists.result: the first address the lookup returned

f5-whereis.rule: <c>whereis</c> returns a Tcl list with the continent, the country and the state, in that order, so F5's example reads the continent with <c>lindex</c> 0 and the country with <c>lindex</c> 1.

f5-member-lists.rule: <c>active_members -list</c> returns a Tcl list of address and port pairs for the active members, and <c>members -list</c> covers every member, so <c>lindex</c> 0 is the first pair in the list.
f5-member-lists.trap: F5's pages do not say in what order the members come, so the first pair is not a particular member: do not build logic on a position.

f5-table-incr.rule: <c>table incr</c> starts a missing key at 0, adds 1 unless told otherwise, and returns the value after adding, so the first call returns 1.

f5-stats-fields.rule: F5's page says the fields of a Statistics profile are numbered from 1 to 32, but <c>STATS::incr</c> takes the field's name, not its number.
f5-stats-fields.result: the hits field of the my_stats profile goes up by 1

f5-priority.rule: An event's priority runs from 0 to 1000 inclusive and defaults to 500, and lower numbers run first, so priority 0 runs before the higher numbers on that event. The DevCentral iRules Style Guide asks for a priority on every event, with 500 when you have no other starting point.
f5-priority.conflict: The same F5 page also says a priority can be assigned between 1 and 1000.
f5-priority.result: this HTTP_REQUEST body runs before the ones at the default 500

f5-mr-clone-id.rule: <c>MR::message clone -count</c> numbers the new clones from the previous clone count plus 1, so the first clone of a message gets ID 1; the original has no clone ID (an empty string).
f5-mr-clone-id.conflict: F5's page describes clone_count as the number of clones including the original, and in the same sentence says it returns 0 when there are no clones.
f5-mr-clone-id.result: two clones, with clone IDs 1 and 2 for a message that had none

f5-mr-instance.rule: <c>MR::connection_instance</c> returns text in the form instance of total, and F5's page says incoming connections return 0 of 1: the instance counts from 0.

f5-ssl-verify-result.counts: a result code, not a position
f5-ssl-verify-result.rule: <c>SSL::verify_result</c> returns 0 for X509_V_OK, which F5's table describes as the operation was successful; the other numbers are verification error codes.
f5-ssl-verify-result.trap: Read as a condition, success is false: <c>if [SSL::verify_result]</c> runs when verification failed. Compare with 0 to say what you mean.

f5-lb-server.counts: a priority value and a route domain
f5-lb-server.rule: <c>LB::server priority</c> returns 1 when the pool member has no priority configured, and <c>LB::server route_domain</c> returns null when the route domain is 0, the default.
f5-lb-server.conflict: The pool member setting itself, priority-group, defaults to 0 in the tmsh reference, so the 1 that LB::server reports for an unconfigured member does not match the configured default. Not tested on a BIG-IP.

cfg-route-domain.rule: Route domain 0 is the default: F5's routing guide says that with no route domains created every route belongs to route domain 0, and that an address without a %ID uses the partition's default route domain, or route domain 0 in Common. The tmsh reference adds that when no route is found, the system searches route domain 0.
cfg-route-domain.result: a pool member on 10.10.10.30, port 80, in route domain 2

cfg-priority-group.rule: A pool member's priority-group runs from 0 to 65535 and defaults to 0, and higher numbers get traffic first, so 0 is the lowest group: its members receive traffic only when every member in the higher groups is unavailable. A min-active-members of 0 turns priority group activation off.
cfg-priority-group.trap: Here the bigger number wins, the opposite of event priority, LTM policy ordinals and GTM order, where the lower number goes first.

cfg-ratio.rule: Ratio weights default to 1 for LTM pool members, and the AS3 schema gives 1 as the default for GSLB (global server load balancing) pool members too; it allows 0 to 100 for an LTM pool member.

cfg-zero-limits.rule: In these fields 0 is not a size, it means no limit: a connection-limit of 0 allows unlimited connections on virtual servers, pool members and route domains, a queue-depth-limit of 0 means no limit, and reselect-tries 0 means the system does not try another pool member.

cfg-port-zero.rule: Port 0 on a virtual server means every port: F5 describes a default wildcard virtual server as one that uses port 0 and handles traffic for all services. The tmsh examples write the port as any.
cfg-port-zero.result: a virtual server on 11.11.11.12 for every port

cfg-policy-numbers.rule: Inside an LTM policy rule, conditions and actions are numbered 0, 1 and so on, as F5's tmsh example shows. Rules carry an ordinal: the lower value comes first, and DevCentral's article on matching strategies says 0 is the default and is not shown.
cfg-policy-numbers.conflict: The iControl REST reference describes the ordinal as a positive integer, while the default is 0.
cfg-policy-numbers.result: the first condition of the rule

cfg-policy-index.rule: In an LTM policy condition, path-segment index and unnamed-query-param index count from 1, and negative values count from the right.
cfg-policy-index.trap: The first segment of /api/v2 is index 1 in a policy and element 1 after split in Tcl, for different reasons: the policy counts from 1, while Tcl counts from 0 and has an empty element before the leading slash.
cfg-policy-index.result: the condition looks at the second segment of the Referer path

cfg-policy-precedence.rule: The precedence table of an LTM policy strategy starts at 1, and a lower value is a higher precedence: best-match uses it to decide which matching condition is the most specific.
cfg-policy-precedence.result: the highest precedence in the table

cfg-gtm-order.rule: In BIG-IP DNS, a wide IP's pools and a pool's members carry an order that starts at 0: F5's lab creates the first pool with order 0, and the AS3 schema defaults memberOrder to 0. Global Availability takes the first pool in the list for as long as it is available.

cfg-vlan-tag.rule: A VLAN tag runs from 1 to 4094: the range starts at 1. The tmsh reference also accepts 4096, a special tag that is not used in the packet processing path and helps with virtual-wire configuration.

cfg-traffic-group.rule: Every BIG-IP comes with traffic-group-1, the floating group that new floating objects join by default, and traffic-group-local-only: the floating group is numbered from 1. A traffic group's unit ID is between 1 and 15.

cfg-apm-acl-order.rule: acl-order places an APM ACL (access control list) in the list of ACLs, and a lower number sits higher in the list.
cfg-apm-acl-order.conflict: The tmsh reference describes acl-order 3 as the third ACL in the list, which counts from 1, while F5's Ansible module documentation says the lowest number, 0, is the topmost, which makes 3 the fourth.
cfg-apm-acl-order.result: MyACL's place in the list of ACLs

plat-interfaces.rule: BIG-IP interfaces are named slot.port, such as 1.1, 1.2 and 2.1 in F5's examples, so both numbers start at 1. On a VIPRION the blade's slot comes first, as in 1/1.2 (slot 1, interface 1.2), and the management interface is named mgmt.

plat-f5os-ports.rule: On F5OS, rSeries ports are numbered from 1.0 to the last port (10.0 on the r5000 series, 20.0 on the r10000 series). On VELOS a bundled port is 1/1.0, and the same port unbundled into four is 1/1.1 to 1/1.4.
plat-f5os-ports.trap: The .0 is not a port 0: on VELOS it marks a port that is not split, and the split parts are .1 to .4.
plat-f5os-ports.result: the first port of an rSeries appliance

plat-slots.rule: VIPRION slots count from 1: F5's LCD article says the slot ID is counted from 1, so blade 2 is 2, and tmsh lists cluster members 1 to 8. On an appliance the same LCD commands use slot 0.
plat-slots.trap: In vCMP, a guest's slots setting is a number of slots (greater than zero, default 1), not a slot number.
plat-slots.result: clears the level 0 LCD warnings of slot 0, an appliance

plat-volumes.rule: Software volumes are named HDX.Y (MDX.Y on RAID, CFX.Y on compact flash), where X is the disk and Y the volume on it; F5's examples start at HD1.1 and MD1.1.
plat-volumes.result: reboots into the first volume of the first disk

plat-tmm-ids.rule: TMM instances are numbered from 0: tmsh shows Sys::TMM: 0.0 to 0.7 on an eight-TMM platform, and the processes start at tmm.0. With HTSplit only even IDs are used: the 10th TMM has the ID 18.

api-rest-skip.rule: In iControl REST paging, $skip is how many objects to skip, so the first page is $skip=0 (F5's bug note fetches the first 100 pools that way), and $top is how many to return.

api-rest-page-index.rule: The paging fields of an iControl REST response count from 1: in DevCentral's example the first page reports pageIndex 1 and startIndex 1.
api-rest-page-index.trap: So the same first page is $skip=0 in the request and startIndex 1 in the response.

api-soap-sysloglevel.rule: The iControl SOAP Log::SyslogLevel values sit one above the syslog numbers: LOG_LEVEL_EMERG is 1 and LOG_LEVEL_DEBUG 8, with 0 for an unknown level. ASM::SeverityName on the same site uses the syslog numbers, EMERG 0 to DEBUG 7.
api-soap-sysloglevel.trap: Converting between them is off by one: a SyslogLevel value minus 1 is the syslog severity.

log-severity.rule: Syslog severities run from 0, the most severe (emerg), to 7 (debug). In a BIG-IP log line, the digit between the colons after the message code is the severity, with 0 being the highest.
log-severity.trap: A bigger number is less severe: 3 (err) is worse than 6 (info).

log-facility.rule: BIG-IP uses the syslog facilities local0 to local7, and local0 is BIG-IP's own: F5 maps it to /var/log/ltm, where iRule messages logged with local0 land. The local-syslog default facility is local0.

cap-tcpdump-00.counts: an interface name, not a number
cap-tcpdump-00.rule: In tcpdump on a BIG-IP, 0.0 is not interface number 0: it means all TMM interfaces at once. It does not capture the management interface and is not rate-limited, so use filters.

cap-ethtrailer.rule: The F5 Ethernet trailer in a capture records the chassis slot and the TMM that handled each packet, and F5's Wireshark example for TMM0 on Slot1 reads slot == 1 and tmm == 0: slots count from 1, TMMs from 0.
cap-ethtrailer.result: packets handled by the first TMM on the first blade

share.carries: {mode, select, translate {The link carries the question, the value and its inputs.} other {The link carries your search words and filters.}}

ascii-table.name: ASCII table explorer
ascii-table.blurb: All 128 ASCII codes in every notation, with their names from RFC 20 to Unicode 18.0.0, how to write each one in C, JSON, JavaScript, Python, Tcl, HTML and URLs, and a look-up that tells you when a character is not ASCII at all.
ascii-table.runsLocally: Runs in your browser. Nothing you type leaves the page.
ascii-table.lookupLabel: Look up a code, a character or a name
ascii-table.lookupHelp: Reads decimal, hexadecimal (0x41 or 41h), octal (0o101), seven or eight binary digits, RFC 20 column/row (4/11), U+0041, HTML references, percent-encoding, backslash escapes, caret notation, control abbreviations and names, Unicode names, or the character itself.
ascii-table.unknownTitle: Nothing here reads as a code, a character or a name.
ascii-table.unknownBody: Try a number (65, 0x41, 0o101), a position (4/1), U+0041, a reference (A), an escape, caret notation (^A), or a name (LF, line feed).
ascii-table.outsideNoName: This code point has no name.
ascii-table.outsideBytes: ASCII stops at 127 (0x7F). This one needs {n} bytes in UTF-8.

outsideHidden.invisible: It is invisible: it takes up no space on screen.
outsideHidden.space: It is a space, but not the ASCII space (32).
outsideHidden.quote: It is a typographic quotation mark, not the ASCII quote it resembles.
outsideHidden.dash: It is a dash, not the ASCII hyphen-minus (45).
outsideHidden.lookalike: Its compatibility form is ASCII text.

ascii-table.outsideAsciiMeant: If you meant the ASCII character, it is <c>{ch}</c>, code {code}: in HTML write <c>{ref}</c> or the character itself.
ascii-table.outsideInspect: See every property of this code point in the Unicode inspector.
ascii-table.columnRowHelp: Bits b7 b6 b5 give the column, b4 to b1 the row.
ascii-table.bitsHelp: Each button flips one bit and jumps to the code it lands on. b6 (value 32) separates upper and lower case; b7 (value 64) separates a control from the character it is paired with in caret notation.

class.CC: Communication control: controls or helps the transmission of information over networks.
class.FE: Format effector: controls layout or position on a printer or display.
class.IS: Information separator: divides data logically, in a hierarchy of four.
class.none: Control without a class in RFC 20.

ascii-table.noteAgree: RFC 20 note 3: do not use this position in international interchange without agreeing on it first.
ascii-table.notePound: RFC 20 note 4: where # is not needed, the pound sterling sign may take this position.
ascii-table.noteDelStrict: RFC 20: in the strict sense, DEL is not a control character. Unicode classes it as a control (Cc).
ascii-table.noteGcPo: UAX #44 notes that @, #, % and & have long been classed as Other_Punctuation, although Western typography does not use them as punctuation.

c0.rfc: The all-zeros character, defined to fill time or space on a medium. C ends every string with it, so a NUL inside data cuts the text short in C code.

c1.rfc: Start of Heading: opens a heading, the address or routing information sent before a message's text. An STX ends the heading.

c2.rfc: Start of Text: opens the text that is to travel to its final destination as one unit. It also closes a heading opened by SOH.

c3.rfc: End of Text: closes the text that STX opened.
c3.today: Typed as Ctrl-C at a Linux terminal, it is the interrupt character: the terminal sends SIGINT to the program (termios(3)).

c4.rfc: End of Transmission: closes a transmission that may have held several texts and their headings.
c4.today: Typed as Ctrl-D, it is the end-of-file character: pending input goes to the program at once, and at the start of a line the program reads end of file (termios(3)).

c5.rfc: Enquiry: asks a remote station to answer, for example with its identity ("Who Are You") or its status.
c5.today: On DEC's VT102 terminal it triggered an answerback message (console_codes(4)).

c6.rfc: Acknowledge: a receiver's positive answer to a sender.

c7.rfc: Bell: calls for human attention, and may set off an alarm or attention device.
c7.today: The Linux console beeps when it receives it (console_codes(4)).

c8.rfc: Backspace: moves the printing position one place back on the same line.
c8.today: The Linux console moves back one column, never past the start of the line (console_codes(4)); Ctrl-H is one of the usual erase characters at a terminal (termios(3)).

c9.rfc: Horizontal Tabulation: moves the printing position to the next of a series of preset positions on the line; on punched cards, the skip function.
c9.today: The Linux console goes to the next tab stop, or to the end of the line if there is none (console_codes(4)).

c10.rfc: Line Feed: moves the printing position to the next line. Sender and receiver may agree that it also means New Line (NL): the first position of the next line.
c10.today: The Linux console gives a line feed, and a carriage return as well when new-line mode is set (console_codes(4)). POSIX ends every line of a text file with the newline character, which C writes as \n: LF on ASCII systems.

c11.rfc: Vertical Tabulation: moves the printing position to the next of a series of preset lines.
c11.today: The Linux console treats it as a line feed (console_codes(4)).

c12.rfc: Form Feed: moves the printing position to the first preset line of the next form or page.
c12.today: The Linux console treats it as a line feed (console_codes(4)).

c13.rfc: Carriage Return: moves the printing position to the first position of the same line.
c13.today: The Linux console returns to the start of the line (console_codes(4)). SMTP and HTTP/1.1 end their lines with CR followed by LF (RFC 5321, RFC 9112).

c14.rfc: Shift Out: the codes that follow are read outside the standard character set, until a Shift In.
c14.today: The Linux console switches to its G1 character set (console_codes(4)).

c15.rfc: Shift In: the codes that follow are read with the standard table again.
c15.today: The Linux console switches back to its G0 character set (console_codes(4)).

c16.rfc: Data Link Escape: changes the meaning of a few characters that follow it, to carry extra controls in data communication networks.

c17.rfc: Device Control 1: controls an ancillary device, chiefly switching it on or off.
c17.today: Typed as Ctrl-Q, it is the start character: output stopped by Ctrl-S resumes (termios(3)). DEC's VT102 used it as XON, to resume transmission (console_codes(4)).

c18.rfc: Device Control 2: controls an ancillary device, chiefly switching it on or off.
c18.today: Typed as Ctrl-R, Linux terminals use it to reprint unread input (termios(3); not in POSIX).

c19.rfc: Device Control 3: controls an ancillary device, chiefly switching it on or off.
c19.today: Typed as Ctrl-S, it is the stop character: output halts until Ctrl-Q (termios(3)), so a terminal that seems frozen after Ctrl-S needs a Ctrl-Q, not a restart. DEC's VT102 used it as XOFF (console_codes(4)).

c20.rfc: Device Control 4: controls an ancillary device; when one single stop control is needed, this is the one to use.

c21.rfc: Negative Acknowledge: a receiver's negative answer to a sender.
c21.today: Typed as Ctrl-U, it is the kill character: it erases the input typed since the start of the line (termios(3)).

c22.rfc: Synchronous Idle: sent by a synchronous link when there is nothing else to send, so both ends keep or regain synchronism.
c22.today: Typed as Ctrl-V, Linux terminals use it as literal next: the next key loses any special meaning (termios(3); not in POSIX).

c23.rfc: End of Transmission Block: ends a block of data for communication purposes; the blocks need not match how the data is processed.
c23.today: Typed as Ctrl-W, Linux terminals use it to erase the last word (termios(3); not in POSIX).

c24.rfc: Cancel: the data sent with it is in error or should be disregarded.
c24.today: The Linux console aborts an escape sequence in progress (console_codes(4)).

c25.rfc: End of Medium: marks the physical end of the medium, or the end of the part of it that is used or wanted.

c26.rfc: Substitute: takes the place of a character found to be invalid or in error.
c26.today: Typed as Ctrl-Z, it is the suspend character: the terminal sends SIGTSTP (termios(3)). The Linux console also aborts an escape sequence when it receives it (console_codes(4)).

c27.rfc: Escape: a prefix that changes the meaning of a limited number of characters after it, to extend the code.
c27.today: At the Linux console it starts an escape sequence, and ESC [ is the Control Sequence Introducer, which begins the sequences that set colours and move the cursor (console_codes(4)).

c28.rfc: File Separator: the most inclusive of the four information separators (FS, GS, RS, US), used to divide data in a hierarchy.
c28.today: Typed as Ctrl-\, it is the quit character: the terminal sends SIGQUIT (termios(3)).

c29.rfc: Group Separator: the second of the four information separators, inside a file and above a record.

c30.rfc: Record Separator: the third of the four information separators, inside a group and above a unit.

c31.rfc: Unit Separator: the least inclusive of the four information separators.

c32.rfc: Space: a normally non-printing graphic character that separates words. It is also a format effector: it moves the printing position one place forward.

c127.rfc: Delete: used mainly to erase unwanted characters on punched paper tape. Its seven bits are all ones. RFC 20 adds that, strictly speaking, DEL is not a control character.
c127.today: It is one of the usual erase characters at a Linux terminal, removing the character before the cursor (termios(3)); the Linux console ignores it when received (console_codes(4)).

ascii-table.writeHelp: Inside a string literal of each language, or in HTML and a URL.

escNote.c-octal: C: octal escapes take at most three digits, so they cannot swallow the next character; a hexadecimal escape such as \x1B keeps reading every hex digit that follows.
escNote.json-must: JSON: quotation mark, reverse solidus and the controls 0 to 31 must be escaped (RFC 8259, section 7).
escNote.json-solidus: JSON: the solidus may be written as \/ but need not be.
escNote.json-del: JSON: DEL (127) is not among the characters that must be escaped, so it may appear as it is.
escNote.js-nul: JavaScript: \0 is NUL only when no digit follows it.
escNote.tcl-quoted: Tcl: needs the backslash inside a quoted word; inside braces nothing is substituted.
escNote.tcl-octal: Tcl 8.4 (and iRules): written in octal because \x reads every hexadecimal digit that follows and keeps only the last two, so "\x1Bfoo" is not ESC followed by foo.

htmlNote.null: HTML: a reference to 0 is a parse error and becomes U+FFFD, the replacement character.
htmlNote.control: HTML: a reference to this control is a parse error (the character is still inserted).

urlClass.unreserved: Unreserved in RFC 3986: it never needs percent-encoding.
urlClass.gen-delim: A general delimiter in RFC 3986: encode it when it is data, not syntax.
urlClass.sub-delim: A sub-delimiter in RFC 3986: encode it when it is data, not syntax.
urlClass.other: Not allowed as itself in a URI: always percent-encode it.

ascii-table.wsHelp: Which definitions count this code as white space, measured in each implementation on 2026-10-03.
ascii-table.caretHelp: <c>{caret}</c>: the control is <c>{pair}</c> with bit b7 cleared (64 subtracted).
ascii-table.caretDelHelp: <c>^?</c>: DEL is written as the question mark with bit b7 set (64 added).
ascii-table.otherCaseHelp: <c>{other}</c>, one bit away: upper and lower case differ only in b6 (value 32).
ascii-table.digitHelp: {value}: the digits are 48 (0x30) plus their value.
ascii-table.confusableHelp: UTS #39 gives it the same prototype, <c>{prototype}</c>, as: {others}
ascii-table.tableHelp: Laid out as RFC 20 draws it: eight columns by sixteen rows. Pick a code to see it above.
ascii-table.textLabel: Paste text to see every character's code
ascii-table.textPlaceholder: Paste a line from a config, an iRule, an email...
ascii-table.textSummary: {total, plural, one {# character} other {# characters}}: {ascii} ASCII, {outside} outside ASCII.
ascii-table.textTruncated: Only the first 2,000 characters are shown.
ascii-table.compareHelp: The same ten codes, seven definitions. JSON leaves out VT and FF, WHATWG leaves out VT, Tcl ends a command at LF instead of separating words, and Python also counts the four information separators.

share.carries: The link carries the value in the look-up box, not the text in Text to codes.

unicode-inspector.name: Unicode inspector
unicode-inspector.blurb: See what is really in a piece of text: every code point with its name, and the characters that hide or deceive, from zero-width spaces and Trojan Source bidirectional controls to Cyrillic letters posing as Latin. Look up any code point, find one by name, clean a text and write it as escapes in eight languages.
unicode-inspector.runsLocally: Runs in your browser. Nothing you paste leaves the page.
unicode-inspector.textPlaceholder: Paste a line of code, a URL, a user name, a config file...
unicode-inspector.summary: {cps, plural, one {# code point} other {# code points}}, {units, plural, one {# UTF-16 unit} other {# UTF-16 units}}, {bytes, plural, one {# UTF-8 byte} other {# UTF-8 bytes}}, {lines, plural, one {# line} other {# lines}}; {outside} outside ASCII.
unicode-inspector.truncated: Only the first 10,000 code points are read.
unicode-inspector.verdictClean: Nothing hides here: no invisible, bidirectional, control, unusual line-break or lookalike characters.
unicode-inspector.verdictFound: {n, plural, one {# code point needs} other {# code points need}} a look.
unicode-inspector.openBidiLine: Line {line}: <c>{controls}</c> still open at the end of the line. Everything after them on that line can be displayed in an order different from the order a compiler or parser reads it, which is the Trojan Source pattern (CVE-2021-42574).
unicode-inspector.mixedWord: <c>{word}</c> (line {line}, column {col}) mixes {scripts}: no single writing system uses all its letters (UTS #39 mixed-script detection).
unicode-inspector.revealTitle: The text, with every hidden character shown
unicode-inspector.revealHelp: Each character that needs a look is drawn as a tag with its code point; hover or focus it for the name.
unicode-inspector.cleanHelp: Choose what to change. Folding lookalikes also changes genuine words in other scripts, so it is off by default.

cleanOpt.asciiSpaces: Use ASCII spaces and line feeds

unicode-inspector.cleanChanges: {removed} removed, {spaces, plural, one {{spaces} space or line break} other {{spaces} spaces or line breaks}}, {punctuation, plural, one {{punctuation} quote or dash} other {{punctuation} quotes or dashes}}, {folded} lookalikes replaced.
unicode-inspector.escapeHelp: Every character outside printable ASCII as an escape, and the characters each language reserves escaped too. Each form was decoded back by its own language when this tool was built.

escUnavailable.tcl: Tcl 8.4, and so iRules, has no escape for a character beyond U+FFFF, and Tcl 8.4.6 reads its four UTF-8 bytes as four characters.
escUnavailable.url: A lone surrogate has no UTF-8 form, so it cannot be percent-encoded.
escUnavailable.html: A lone surrogate cannot appear in HTML.
escUnavailable.css: CSS turns an escaped 0 or surrogate into U+FFFD.
escUnavailable.c: A lone surrogate cannot be written in a C string.

unicode-inspector.cpLabel: A code point, a character or a name
unicode-inspector.cpPlaceholder: U+00E9, é, 0xE9, é, \u00e9, zero width space, BOM
unicode-inspector.cpHelp: Reads U+XXXX, hexadecimal, decimal, the character itself, HTML references, backslash escapes, percent-encoding, and any Unicode name or alias.
unicode-inspector.cpUnknown: Nothing here reads as a code point or a name.
unicode-inspector.encNoUtf8: none: UTF-8 cannot encode a surrogate code point

htmlNote.null: HTML: a reference to 0 is a parse error and becomes U+FFFD.
htmlNote.surrogate: HTML: a reference to a surrogate is a parse error and becomes U+FFFD.
htmlNote.c1: HTML: a reference to U+0080 to U+009F is a parse error, and 27 of the 32 are replaced by the Windows-1252 character (the reference to U+0085 gives an ellipsis).
htmlNote.control: HTML: a reference to this control is a parse error (the character is still inserted).
htmlNote.noncharacter: HTML: a reference to a noncharacter is a parse error.

unicode-inspector.cNote: C: a universal character name cannot name a character below U+00A0 other than $, @ and `, nor a surrogate (C11, 6.4.3).
unicode-inspector.tclNote: Tcl 8.4 and iRules: \u takes one to four hexadecimal digits, so nothing beyond U+FFFF has an escape.
unicode-inspector.cssNote: CSS: end the escape with a space when a hexadecimal digit or a space follows it.

bidi.label: Bidirectional control
bidi.help: Changes the order in which the text around it is displayed. Right-to-left text needs it; in code it can make a line read differently from how it runs (UTS #55).

invisible.label: Invisible
invisible.help: Default_Ignorable_Code_Point: where it is not supported it is simply not rendered at all.

control.label: Control
control.help: A control code, not text. Most tools drop it, show a box or stop on it.

line-break.label: Line break other than LF or CR
line-break.help: An editor may start a new line where a language does not, or the reverse: UTS #55 shows a null check hidden this way.

surrogate.label: Lone surrogate
surrogate.help: Half of a UTF-16 pair. Not a character, and UTF-8 cannot encode it.

noncharacter.label: Noncharacter
noncharacter.help: Permanently reserved for internal use and never assigned to a character.

private-use.label: Private use
private-use.help: Its meaning is defined by private agreement, so fonts and systems differ.

unassigned.label: Unassigned
unassigned.help: No character has this code point in Unicode 18.0.0.

replacement.label: Replacement character
replacement.help: U+FFFD: often the mark of a conversion error upstream, where bytes could not be decoded.

space.label: Non-ASCII space
space.help: A space that is not the ASCII space (32): splits, trims and comparisons may not treat it as one.

quote.label: Typographic quote
quote.help: A quotation mark that is not the ASCII quote a parser expects.

dash.label: Non-ASCII dash
dash.help: A dash that is not the ASCII hyphen-minus (45).

confusable.label: Confusable with ASCII
confusable.help: UTS #39 lists it as visually confusable with the ASCII text shown.

compat-ascii.label: Styled ASCII
compat-ascii.help: Its compatibility decomposition is ASCII: a fullwidth, ligature or similar form of ordinary text.

combining.label: Combining mark
combining.help: Attaches to the character before it.

format.label: Format character

charset-equivalency.name: Charset converter and mojibake fixer
charset-equivalency.blurb: Turn text into bytes and bytes into text in fourteen charsets, from UTF-8, UTF-16 and UTF-32 to windows-1252, IBM 850 and EBCDIC, with every ill-formed byte replaced exactly as a browser replaces it. Paste a hex dump, escapes, %XX or Base64, compare what every charset makes of the same bytes, and turn garbled text such as cafÃ© back into what it was.
charset-equivalency.runsLocally: Runs in your browser. Nothing you paste leaves the page.

policy.html: Write an HTML reference, as a browser form does

charset-equivalency.bomLabel: Start with a byte order mark (UTFs only)
charset-equivalency.encSummary: {cps, plural, one {# character} other {# characters}} became {bytes, plural, one {# byte} other {# bytes}} in {charset}.
charset-equivalency.encBom: The first {n, plural, one {# byte} other {# bytes}} ({bytes}) are the byte order mark, U+FEFF.
charset-equivalency.encLone: {n, plural, one {# lone surrogate} other {# lone surrogates}} in the text became U+FFFD, as a browser's TextEncoder does.
charset-equivalency.encUnencodable: {charset} cannot hold {n, plural, one {# character} other {# characters}} of this text.

encPolicy.replace: Each was written as ?, the replacement most converters use; the original character is not in the bytes.
encPolicy.html: Each was written as a decimal HTML reference such as €. A browser does this when a form is submitted in a charset that cannot hold what was typed, and the server cannot tell it from someone typing those characters.
encPolicy.strict: Strict mode writes nothing when a character does not fit.

charset-equivalency.readBackHelp: What each charset makes of the same bytes. The row of the charset they were written in is the text itself; every other row is the mojibake that a wrong guess produces. Controls and replacement characters are shown as tags.

charset-equivalency.sniffLabel: Let a byte order mark decide the charset

parseError.odd-hex: An odd number of hex digits: the digit at position {at} has no partner.
parseError.bad-char: Position {at} holds something that is neither a hex digit nor a separator.
parseError.bad-escape: The escape at position {at} is not one this tool reads: \x with hex digits, octal \NNN up to \377, or \n, \t, \r and the other C escapes.
parseError.bad-base64: Not Base64: the character at position {at}, or the length, does not fit the alphabet of RFC 4648.
parseError.unrecognised: Not recognized as hex, a hex dump, escapes, percent-encoding or Base64. If it is one of them, choose it under Written as.
parseError.too-long: Too long: this tool reads up to 64 KiB of bytes.

charset-equivalency.utf8Literals: Characters beyond ASCII in the box were taken as their UTF-8 bytes.
charset-equivalency.urlSafe: This Base64 uses the URL-safe alphabet (- and _ instead of + and /, RFC 4648 section 5).

guess.bom: A byte order mark at the start says {charset}.
guess.ascii: Every byte is ASCII, so every ASCII-compatible charset reads the same text (shown as US-ASCII).
guess.utf8-valid: The bytes are well-formed UTF-8 and include characters beyond ASCII, which rarely happens by chance: read as UTF-8.
guess.zeros: The zero bytes fall where ASCII text in {charset} puts them: read as {charset}.
guess.ebcdic: 0x40, the EBCDIC space, is common, there are no ASCII spaces, and most bytes are above 0x80: EBCDIC, read as {charset}.
guess.none: No single answer: these bytes are not well-formed UTF-8 and show no other pattern. Compare the readings below.

charset-equivalency.bomFound: The data starts with a {charset} byte order mark ({n} bytes), which is not part of the text.
charset-equivalency.bomOverride: The data starts with a {charset} byte order mark, which overrides the charset chosen, as in a browser: the WHATWG Encoding Standard treats a byte order mark as more authoritative than a label.
charset-equivalency.decSummary: {cps, plural, one {# character} other {# characters}} from {bytes, plural, one {# byte} other {# bytes}} in {charset}.
charset-equivalency.truncatedBytes: Only the first 64 KiB were decoded.
charset-equivalency.decErrors: {n, plural, one {# ill-formed sequence was} other {# ill-formed sequences were}} replaced with U+FFFD.
charset-equivalency.decClean: Every byte decoded; nothing was replaced.

error.continuation: A continuation byte (0x80 to 0xBF) where a character should start: its sequence lost its first byte, or the data is not UTF-8.
error.overlong-lead: 0xC0 or 0xC1, which could only start a two-byte form of an ASCII character, a form UTF-8 forbids.
error.invalid-lead: A byte from 0xF5 to 0xFF, which never appears in UTF-8.
error.overlong: A longer form of a code point that has a shorter one (E0 followed by 80 to 9F, or F0 followed by 80 to 8F).
error.surrogate: ED followed by A0 to BF: a surrogate, U+D800 to U+DFFF, which UTF-8 cannot carry.
error.too-large: F4 followed by 90 to BF: beyond U+10FFFF, the last code point.
error.truncated: The sequence was cut short by a byte that cannot continue it; the bytes taken so far became one U+FFFD and that byte was read again.
error.truncated-end: The data ends in the middle of a character.
error.unpaired-lead: A leading surrogate (D800 to DBFF) not followed by a trailing one.
error.unpaired-trail: A trailing surrogate (DC00 to DFFF) with no leading surrogate before it.
error.odd-byte: One byte left over: UTF-16 needs two bytes per code unit.
error.utf32-invalid: A four-byte unit that is a surrogate or beyond U+10FFFF.
error.utf32-incomplete: One to three bytes left over: UTF-32 needs four bytes per unit.
error.not-ascii: A byte of 0x80 or more, outside the seven bits of US-ASCII.

evidence.looks: Weaker evidence: every byte decodes in these charsets, so this reading is chosen only because it looks more like ordinary text.

browser.no: Browsers do not decode {charset}: the WHATWG Encoding Standard does not define it.
