chmod-permission-calculator.name: chmod permission calculator
chmod-permission-calculator.blurb: Type a file mode as octal (4755), as ls shows it (-rwsr-xr-x) or as chmod clauses on a base (g+s,o-rwx) and read it every other way: the bits, who may do what, what setuid, setgid and the sticky bit mean for a file or a directory, the commands that reach it, the umask that would create it, and a trace of each clause. From POSIX.1-2024 chmod and ls and coreutils 9.11 chmod(1); nothing leaves the browser.
chmod-permission-calculator.modeHint: Octal (one to five digits), an ls string (nine characters, or ten with the type letter), or chmod clauses separated by commas. A clause with no class (+x) is applied under the umask, as chmod does.
chmod-permission-calculator.baseHint: What the clauses are applied to. Blank means 644 for a file and 755 for a directory. On a directory, a numeric mode of up to four digits keeps its set-user-ID and set-group-ID bits, as GNU chmod does.
chmod-permission-calculator.umaskHint: Bits set here are left alone by + and - when no class is named. Blank means 022.

form.symbolic: Read as chmod clauses on the base.

chmod-permission-calculator.gridTitle: The twelve bits (click one to flip it)

directory.execute: enter it and reach entries by name

setuid.name: setuid
setuid.file: On execution the process takes the file owner's effective user ID. Shown as s (or S without execute) in the owner's third slot.
setuid.directory: No portable meaning on a directory; some systems ignore it. Shown as s or S in the owner's third slot.

setgid.name: setgid
setgid.file: On execution the process takes the file's group as its effective group ID. Shown as s (or S without execute) in the group's third slot.
setgid.directory: New entries created inside take the directory's group instead of the creator's (most systems). Shown as s or S in the group's third slot.

sticky.name: sticky
sticky.file: On a regular file the bit has no portable meaning today; some older systems used it to keep the program text in swap. Shown as t or T in the last slot.
sticky.directory: Restricted deletion: an entry can be removed or renamed only by its owner, the directory's owner or a privileged user. /tmp is the classic case. Shown as t (or T when others cannot search) in the last slot.

flag.no-permissions: No permission bit is set: nobody can read, write or execute it, including the owner (who can still change the mode).
flag.all-permissions: Every permission bit is set: anyone on the system can read, write and execute it.
flag.world-writable-file: Others can write this file: anyone on the system can change its contents.
flag.world-writable-dir-no-sticky: Others can create and remove entries in this directory, and without the sticky bit they can remove entries they do not own.
flag.world-writable-dir-sticky: Others can create entries here, and the restricted deletion flag keeps them from removing what they do not own (the /tmp pattern).
flag.setid-world-writable: A set-user-ID or set-group-ID file that others can write: anyone could replace its contents and run them with the file's privileges.
flag.setuid-without-execute: set-user-ID is set but the owner cannot execute the file: ls shows a capital S, and the bit does nothing until an execute bit is set.
flag.setgid-without-execute: set-group-ID is set but the group cannot execute the file: ls shows a capital S in the group slot.
flag.setuid-file: A set-user-ID program: it runs with the owner's effective user ID. Keep it unwritable by anyone but the owner.
flag.setgid-file: A set-group-ID program: it runs with the file's group as its effective group ID.
flag.setuid-directory: set-user-ID on a directory has no portable meaning; some systems ignore it.
flag.setgid-directory: set-group-ID on a directory: new entries inherit the directory's group, the usual setting for a shared project directory.
flag.sticky-directory: The restricted deletion flag is set: entries can be removed only by their owner or the directory's owner.
flag.sticky-file: The sticky bit on a regular file has no portable meaning today; some older systems used it to keep the program text in swap.
flag.sticky-no-search: The restricted deletion flag is set but others cannot search the directory, so ls shows a capital T.
flag.owner-execute-without-read: The owner can execute but not read: a script cannot be run this way (the interpreter has to read it); a compiled program can.
flag.group-execute-without-read: The group can execute but not read: a script cannot be run this way; a compiled program can.
flag.other-execute-without-read: Others can execute but not read: a script cannot be run this way; a compiled program can.
flag.owner-write-without-read: The owner can write but not read: the file can be overwritten and appended to, not read back.
flag.group-write-without-read: The group can write but not read.
flag.other-write-without-read: Others can write but not read.
flag.owner-list-without-search: The owner can list the directory's names but not enter it: names are visible, their contents and attributes are not reachable.
flag.group-list-without-search: The group can list names but not enter the directory.
flag.other-list-without-search: Others can list names but not enter the directory.
flag.owner-less-than-others: The owner has less than the group or others. Legal, and almost always a mistake, because the owner is still the one who can change the mode.

chmod-permission-calculator.umaskYes: A umask of {umask} creates this mode from the default a program asks for ({def}).

umaskNo.special-bits: No umask creates this mode: the special bits never come from a umask.
umaskNo.needs-execute: No umask creates this mode for a file: programs ask for 666, so execute bits are never set by creation alone.

chmod-permission-calculator.traceTitle: Clause by clause, from {base} under umask {umask}

note.x-skipped: X granted nothing: the target is a file with no execute bit.
note.s-with-o: s with only o named changes nothing (POSIX).
note.umask-applied: No class named: bits set in the umask were left alone.
note.permcopy: The permissions of one class copied to another.
note.gnu-dir-preserves-special: A numeric mode on a directory keeps its set-user-ID and set-group-ID bits unless written as 00755, -6000 or =755 (chmod(1)).
note.gnu-numeric-operator: A numeric mode with a leading =, + or - (GNU chmod): = sets exactly, + adds, - removes.

error.too-long: Too long ({at} characters; the limit is 64).
error.octal-digit: {at} is not an octal digit (0 to 7).
error.octal-too-long: An octal mode has at most five digits: {at}.
error.octal-range: An octal mode is at most 7777: {at}.
error.ls-position: Not a valid ls string: {at}. Each class takes r w x (or -), with s or S allowed only in the owner's and group's third slot and t or T only in the last one.
error.symbolic-perm: {at} is not a permission letter (r w x X s t) or a class to copy from (u g o).
error.symbolic-no-operator: No operator in {at}: a clause needs +, - or =.
error.base-unreadable: The base mode could not be read: {at}. Use octal or an ls string.
error.umask-unreadable: The umask could not be read: {at}. Use octal, for example 022.

chmod-permission-calculator.limits: The calculator knows the mode bits, not the file system: it cannot see ownership, access control lists, capabilities, mount options or the mandatory access control that may override these bits. The GNU-specific behaviours (a directory keeping setuid and setgid under a numeric mode; =755, +x and -w with a number) are modelled as chmod(1) from coreutils 9.11 describes them; other implementations may differ.

share.carries: The link carries the mode as typed, the kind, and the base and umask when filled in.

cert-chain-builder.name: Certificate chain builder
cert-chain-builder.blurb: Paste a leaf and its intermediates in any order and get the chain a server should send: the end entity first, each issuer after the certificate it signed, the root optional. Links are made by key identifier or by name, RFC 5280's rules are checked along the way (cA, keyCertSign, pathLenConstraint, validity, windows), missing and extra certificates are named, and each signature is verified in your browser. Nothing is fetched.
cert-chain-builder.runsLocally: Runs in your browser. Nothing is sent anywhere and nothing is fetched, not even the URLs the certificates name.
cert-chain-builder.asOfChosen: Validity is judged at 00:00 UTC on {date}. Clear the date to use the clock.
cert-chain-builder.asOfClock: Validity is judged at this moment, {instant}. Set a date to ask about another day.

verdict.anchor-omitted: Chain ends at a CA whose issuer is not here

verdictBody.complete: {n, plural, one {{n} certificate} other {{n} certificates}}, from the end entity to a self-signed root, every link made and every rule of RFC 5280 checked here satisfied.
verdictBody.complete-with-warnings: {n, plural, one {{n} certificate} other {{n} certificates}}, from the end entity to a self-signed root, every link made; the warnings below are worth reading before you deploy it.
verdictBody.anchor-omitted: {n, plural, one {{n} certificate} other {{n} certificates}}, sound as far as they go; the last one was issued by {missing}, which is not in the input. If {missing} is a root in your clients' trust stores, this is the normal chain to send (a trust anchor may be omitted). If it is an intermediate, clients that do not already hold it will fail.
verdictBody.incomplete: The path stops at the end entity: its issuer, {missing}, is not in the input, and no client can build the chain from what is here. Add the intermediate certificates.
verdictBody.invalid: A rule of RFC 5280 path validation is broken along the path; a conforming client will reject this chain. The errors below say where.
verdictBody.unreadable: No certificate could be read from the input. Paste PEM blocks, each between BEGIN CERTIFICATE and END CERTIFICATE lines.

cert-chain-builder.pathTitle: The chain, in the order a server sends it
cert-chain-builder.pathNote: "Send" is the position in the chain a TLS server sends (RFC 9846 section 4.5.1, formerly RFC 8446 section 4.4.2: the end entity first, each following certificate directly certifying the one before it). Signatures are verified by this browser's WebCrypto against the issuer's key shown in the table; a self-signed root is checked against its own key, which proves consistency, not trust.
cert-chain-builder.missingTitle: The issuer that is not here
cert-chain-builder.missingBodyCa: The last certificate on the path was issued by {name}. That issuer is not in the input. A trust anchor is normally not sent in the chain, so if clients hold it, nothing is missing; if it is itself an intermediate, add it.
cert-chain-builder.missingBodyLeaf: The end entity was issued by {name}, which is not in the input. Every client needs that intermediate (and anything above it) to build the chain; a server that sends only the leaf fails on clients without an AIA fetch.
cert-chain-builder.missingAki: The end entity names its issuer's key by this identifier:
cert-chain-builder.missingAia: The certificate says where the issuer can be downloaded (Authority Information Access, caIssuers); nothing is fetched here:

findingTitle.cert-unreadable: A block could not be read
findingTitle.no-end-entity: Every certificate is issued by another
findingTitle.subject-predates-issuer: Subject issued before its issuer's certificate
findingTitle.root-omitted: Trust anchor not in the input
findingTitle.order-differs: Pasted order differs from the chain order
findingTitle.weak-key: Key smaller than the Baseline Requirements allow
findingTitle.end-entity-is-ca: End of the path is a CA

finding.input-empty: Paste one or more PEM certificates.
finding.input-too-long: The input is longer than {detail} characters and was not read.
finding.input-no-certificates: No block between BEGIN CERTIFICATE and END CERTIFICATE lines was found.
finding.input-too-many: More than {detail} certificate blocks; paste the chain, not the store.
finding.cert-unreadable: Block {detail} (position:reason) is not a readable DER certificate and was skipped; the chain was built from the others.
finding.duplicate-certificate: #{at} is byte for byte the same certificate as #{other}; the copy was ignored.
finding.single-self-signed: #{at} ({cn}) is self-signed and alone: there is no chain to build. A self-signed certificate is its own root; clients trust it only if told to.
finding.no-end-entity: Every certificate here is the issuer of another, which real chains never produce; the path was built from #{at} ({cn}) so you can see why.
finding.multiple-end-entities: {detail} certificates are end entities nobody here issues. The path was built from #{at} ({cn}); the others are listed as extra. Paste one chain at a time.
finding.target-is-ca: #{at} ({cn}) is a CA certificate and nothing here is issued by it, so the chain was built from it. That is fine for checking an intermediate bundle; a server chain starts at an end entity.
finding.issuer-not-found: #{at} ({cn}) was issued by {detail}, which is not in the input.
finding.issuer-matched-by-name-only: #{at} ({cn}) was linked to #{other} ({otherCn}) by matching names, because one of them carries no key identifier. RFC 5280 allows it; a key identifier would make the link unambiguous.
finding.issuer-name-matches-key-differs: #{at} ({cn}) names an issuer with the same name as #{other} ({otherCn}), but its Authority Key Identifier does not match that certificate's Subject Key Identifier: a different key under the same name, usually a rolled-over CA. #{other} is not the issuer; the real one is missing.
finding.multiple-issuer-candidates: #{at} ({cn}) has {detail} possible issuers in the input (a cross-signed CA, or two certificates for the same key). #{other} ({otherCn}) was chosen because its validity covers the subject's; the alternatives are listed as extra.
finding.issuer-not-ca: #{at} ({cn}) issued #{other} but its basicConstraints says cA FALSE. RFC 5280 section 4.2.1.9: a key that is not a CA MUST NOT be used to verify certificate signatures.
finding.issuer-no-basic-constraints: #{at} ({cn}) issued #{other} but, as a version 3 certificate, has no basicConstraints extension at all; a conforming client treats it as not a CA (RFC 5280 section 6.1.4 step k).
finding.issuer-missing-keycertsign: #{at} ({cn}) issued #{other} but its keyUsage extension does not assert keyCertSign (RFC 5280 section 6.1.4 step n).
finding.pathlen-exceeded: #{at} ({cn}) is one intermediate too many: a CA above it (#{other}) carries pathLenConstraint {detail}, the number of non-self-issued intermediates allowed below it (RFC 5280 section 4.2.1.9).
finding.issuer-expires-before-subject: #{at} ({cn}) expires on {detail}, before the certificate it issued (#{other}) does. On that date the chain stops validating even though the leaf has not expired; the usual remedy is a renewed intermediate.
finding.subject-predates-issuer: #{at} ({cn}) was valid from before {detail}, the start of the issuer certificate #{other} it is linked to. That happens when a CA is cross-signed later than it issued; a client that enforces the order of dates (few do) would object.
finding.root-included: #{at} ({cn}) is a self-signed root. Servers normally leave it out of the chain they send (RFC 9846: a trust anchor MAY be omitted); the copy below offers both forms.
finding.root-omitted: The chain ends at #{at} ({cn}), issued by {detail}, which is not here. If that is a root your clients hold, this is the chain to send.
finding.order-differs: The certificates were pasted in a different order from the chain. Send them as {detail} (input positions, end entity first); the copy below is already in that order.
finding.extra-certificate: #{at} ({cn}) is not on the path from the end entity and is not sent.
finding.weak-signature: #{at} ({cn}) is signed with {detail}. The Baseline Requirements no longer permit SHA-1 or MD5 signatures in publicly trusted certificates, and clients reject them.
finding.weak-key: #{at} ({cn}) carries an {detail} key; the Baseline Requirements require RSA moduli of at least 2048 bits.
finding.end-entity-is-ca: The path was built from #{at} ({cn}), a CA certificate; a server chain starts at an end entity.
finding.end-entity-no-san: #{at} ({cn}) has no subjectAltName; browsers match the host name against subjectAltName only, so a server certificate without one is not accepted.
finding.revocation-pointers: {detail, plural, one {{detail} certificate} other {{detail} certificates}} on the path name a CRL (certificate revocation list) or an OCSP (Online Certificate Status Protocol) responder. A validator checks revocation there; this page lists the pointers and does not contact them.

cert-chain-builder.pemNote: Re-encoded from the certificates' bytes, 64 columns, in chain order. Paste it where your server expects the certificate chain (a combined file for most servers; a separate chain object on platforms that keep the leaf apart).
cert-chain-builder.certsTitle: The {n, plural, one {{n} certificate} other {{n} certificates}}, in detail
cert-chain-builder.limits: Not done here, and done by a validator: no trust store is consulted (a complete chain here is complete, not trusted); the host name is not matched against the subjectAltName; name constraints, policy constraints and extended key usage are not evaluated along the path; revocation is not checked. Signatures are verified here by WebCrypto for RSA (PKCS#1 v1.5 and PSS), ECDSA on P-256, P-384 and P-521, and Ed25519 where the browser supports it; anything else reads as not checked.

share.carries: The link carries the certificates as pasted and the validity date, if you set one.
share.blockedPrivateKey: No link: the box also holds a private key, so remove that block to share the chain.

bits-bytes.name: Bits, bytes and throughput
bits-bytes.blurb: A size in every unit of both conventions with the bit count written out (1.5 GB is 12 000 000 000 bits and 1.397 GiB; read the 1024 way it would be 7.37 % more), a rate in bits and bytes per second and per minute, hour and day, and any two of size, rate and time giving the third, with the protocol efficiency of TCP over Ethernet applied if you ask. The connection table answers for a modem, T1, E1 and every Ethernet speed at once. Exact arithmetic; nothing is rounded until it is printed.
bits-bytes.inputsLabel: Any one quantity, or any two
bits-bytes.inputsHint: Write them the way you would say them: 1.5 GB, 700 MiB, 10K, 8 bits; 100 Mbit/s, 12.5 MB/s, 1 Gbps; 90 s, 2h 30min, 1 day. One field is explained on its own; two give the third (with all three, the time is recomputed from size and rate). b is a bit, B a byte; k and M are 1000s, Ki and Mi are 1024s.
bits-bytes.effHint: Line rate counts every bit on the wire as payload. The presets count only the payload of full 1500-byte frames: 1460 of 1538 bytes on the wire for TCP over IPv4 (94.93 %), 1440 of 1538 for TCP over IPv6, 1472 of 1538 for UDP over IPv4; headers from RFC 791, RFC 8200 and RFC 9293, the frame, preamble and gap from RFC 2544 Appendix B.
bits-bytes.runsLocally: Runs in your browser. Nothing is sent anywhere.

error.unreadable-size: The size could not be read. Try 1.5 GB, 700 MiB, 10K or 8 bits.
error.unreadable-rate: The rate could not be read. Try 100 Mbit/s, 12.5 MB/s or 1 Gbps.
error.unreadable-time: The time could not be read. Try 90 s, 2h 30min or 1 day.
error.need-two: Give two of the three to derive the third.
error.zero-rate: A rate of zero moves nothing; there is no transfer time.
error.zero-time: A time of zero has no rate.
error.efficiency-range: Efficiency is a percentage above 0 and up to 100, or one of the presets.
error.empty: Type a size, a rate or a time.

transfer.sizeNote: {bits, plural, one {{bits} bit} other {{bits} bits}} of payload, at {eff} % efficiency.

presetNote.line-rate: Every bit on the wire counted as payload.
presetNote.tcp-ipv4-ethernet-1500: TCP over IPv4 over Ethernet, full 1500-byte frames: 1460 payload octets per 1538 on the wire (14-byte header and 4-byte FCS, 8 bytes of preamble, 12 of inter-frame gap), 94.93 %. Real transfers also lose to acknowledgements, slow start and loss; this is the ceiling.
presetNote.tcp-ipv6-ethernet-1500: TCP over IPv6 over Ethernet, full 1500-byte frames: 1440 payload octets per 1538 on the wire (the IPv6 header is 40 bytes), 93.63 %.
presetNote.udp-ipv4-ethernet-1500: UDP over IPv4 over Ethernet, full 1500-byte frames: 1472 payload octets per 1538 on the wire (an 8-byte UDP header), 95.71 %.

note.ambiguous-kb: A capital prefix with a lower-case b (Kb, Mb, Gb) was read as bits, which is what the symbol says. Some product sheets write bytes that way; if that is what you meant, write the capital B.
note.bare-k-is-1024: A bare K, M or G with no unit was read as a power of 1024 of bytes, the way ls -h and du -h print sizes. Write kB or KiB to be explicit.
note.si-on-bytes: An SI prefix on bytes (kB, MB, GB, TB) means a power of 1000, as the prefixes mean everywhere else and as disk and network makers use them. Some operating systems label powers of 1024 with the same letters; the line below shows both readings.
note.iec-binary: An IEC binary prefix (Ki, Mi, Gi, Ti) means a power of 1024 and nothing else; this reading is unambiguous.
note.bits-per-second: The rate was written in bits per second, as link speeds are.
note.bytes-per-second: The rate was written in bytes per second, as file transfers are reported; multiplied by eight for the link.

bits-bytes.otherReading: Read as decimal (the SI meaning): {decimal}. Read as binary (the 1024 convention some systems still label with the same letters): {binary}. The gap is {gap} %.
bits-bytes.rounded: rounded to six decimals; the exact value does not terminate
bits-bytes.rateTitle: The rate, per second and over time
bits-bytes.perTime: At this rate: {minute} a minute, {hour} an hour, {day} a day.
bits-bytes.lineageTitle: A row of the 2004 calculator's connection table
bits-bytes.linksNote: Nominal rates: ITU-T V.90 for the modem, ITU-T G.704 for T1 and E1, IEEE 802.3-2022 for Ethernet. The rows marked 2004 were in the connection table of the bits-and-bytes calculator on nutzmann.net in 2004 and ntz.com.br in 2013, the oldest ancestor of the tools here. Times are at the efficiency chosen above; a real link also carries acknowledgements and retransmissions.
bits-bytes.limits: The arithmetic is exact (BigInt decimals) and rounded only when printed, to six decimals. Not modelled: TCP window and round-trip limits, loss, compression, and the difference between a link's nominal rate and what a provider actually delivers. The two-readings line shows what a label means under each convention; which one a given operating system uses is that system's documentation to state.

share.carries: The link carries the size, the rate, the time and the efficiency as typed.

dig-command-builder.name: dig command builder
dig-command-builder.blurb: Say what to look up, where to ask and how, and get one copy-pasteable dig command with every token explained, the combinations the manual calls redundant or contradictory flagged, and a summary of what the query will carry: transport, port, RD, DO, CD, EDNS and cookie. The inverse of the dig output explainer. Runs nothing; built in your browser from the BIND 9 manual and the DNS RFCs.
dig-command-builder.inputsHint: Fill in what you know; everything else keeps dig's default and is not written. The command updates as you type. Nothing is run here.

ui.name: Name
ui.questionNote: A is dig's default type and IN its default class, so neither is written. With -x, dig derives the PTR name itself and the name, type and class fields are not used. ANY, AXFR and IXFR are query types dig accepts in the type field.
ui.trace: +trace: iterate from the root, following referrals
ui.nssearch: +nssearch: find the zone's name servers and show each one's SOA
ui.norecurse: +norecurse: clear the RD bit (ask only what this server knows)
ui.dnssec: +dnssec: set the DO bit, ask for the DNSSEC records
ui.cd: +cd: set the CD bit (do not validate for me)
ui.ignore: +ignore: no TCP retry when a UDP answer is truncated
ui.nsid: +nsid: ask the server to identify itself
ui.noedns: +noedns: send no OPT record at all
ui.qr: +qr: also print the query as sent
ui.keyNote: Only a key file is offered. dig also has -y, which takes the shared secret on the command line; the manual says to use -k instead, because the secret would show in ps output and in the shell's history.
ui.empty: Type a name, or an address for a reverse lookup.
ui.shellNote: Written for a POSIX shell (tokens that need it are single-quoted). In Windows cmd.exe, quote with double quotes instead.
ui.privacy: Built entirely in your browser from the intent above. Nothing is resolved, sent or stored.

transportNote.udp: dig's default: UDP to port 53, retrying over TCP when the answer comes back truncated (unless +ignore). Type ANY and ixfr=N default to TCP, and AXFR always uses TCP.
transportNote.tcp: +tcp: the query goes over a TCP connection to port 53 from the start.
transportNote.tls: +tls: DNS over TLS; the port defaults to 853 (RFC 7858).
transportNote.https: +https: DNS over HTTPS (RFC 8484); the port defaults to 443 and the endpoint to /dns-query, with the query in an HTTP POST.

findingTitle.transfer-needs-server: A transfer with no server named

finding.empty: Type a name, or an address for a reverse lookup.
finding.bad-name: "{value}" is not a name dig can look up: labels are letters, digits, hyphens and underscores, separated by single dots (a lone asterisk is accepted as a wildcard label).
finding.name-too-long: The name is longer than 253 characters; RFC 1035 limits a name to 255 octets on the wire.
finding.label-too-long: One label is longer than 63 characters, RFC 1035's limit for a label.
finding.unknown-type: "{value}" is not a record type in the IANA registry. Use a mnemonic (A, AAAA, MX, TXT, CAA...) or TYPEnn with the number.
finding.bad-type-number: "{value}": a TYPEnn number must be 0 to 65535.
finding.ixfr-needs-serial: An incremental transfer needs the SOA serial of the copy you hold; dig writes it as ixfr=N.
finding.bad-serial: "{value}" is not a serial: an integer from 0 to 4294967295.
finding.bad-reverse: "{value}" is neither an IPv4 nor an IPv6 address, which is what -x takes.
finding.bad-server: "{value}" is not a server dig can be pointed at: a host name, an IPv4 address or an IPv6 address, with no port, path or scheme (the port goes in -p).
finding.bad-port: "{value}" is not a port: an integer from 1 to 65535.
finding.bad-source: "{value}" is not a source: an IPv4 or IPv6 address of this machine, with an optional #port.
finding.bad-bufsize: "{value}" is outside the range the manual gives for +bufsize, 0 to 65535.
finding.bad-subnet: "{value}" is not a client subnet: an IPv4 or IPv6 address with an optional /prefix-length, or 0.
finding.bad-timeout: "{value}" is not a timeout in whole seconds.
finding.bad-tries: "{value}" is not a number of tries.
finding.bad-retry: "{value}" is not a number of retries.
finding.bad-endpoint: "{value}" is not an endpoint path: it starts with / and has no spaces.
finding.bad-keyfile: "{value}" is not a file path this builder will write into a command: no spaces or shell metacharacters.
finding.ipv-mismatch: -{family} restricts dig to one address family, and {server} is a literal of the other; dig would have nowhere to send the query. Drop the restriction or change the server.
finding.bufsize-under-512: A value lower than 512 MUST be treated as equal to 512 by the receiver (RFC 6891, section 6.2.3), so {value} advertises 512. DNS Flag Day 2020 recommends 1232 as the minimum safe size.
finding.noedns-conflict: +dnssec, +trace, +bufsize, +nsid and +subnet travel in the EDNS OPT record (RFC 6891; the DO bit is RFC 3225), so the query must carry one. +noedns was not written.
finding.any-minimal: A server may answer an ANY query with a subset of its records or a synthesized HINFO record rather than everything it holds (RFC 8482). Ask for the types you need.
finding.transfer-needs-server: No @server: dig would send the transfer request to the resolvers in /etc/resolv.conf. A zone transfer is answered by a server that holds the zone, so name one with @server (RFC 5936).
finding.timeout-min: The manual: an attempt to set the timeout below 1 is silently set to 1.
finding.tries-min: The manual: tries less than or equal to zero are silently rounded up to 1.
finding.reverse-ignores-name: With -x, dig builds the PTR name from the address and sets the type and class itself; the name, type and class fields are not used.
finding.q-disambiguates: "{value}" is also a type or class mnemonic, and dig reads bare words on the command line as types and classes before names (the manual notes the IN and CH top-level domains). -q names the query explicitly.
finding.type-default: A is dig's default type and is not written.
finding.port-default: Port {port} is the transport's default, so -p is not written.
finding.server-brackets: dig takes an IPv6 literal bare after the @; the brackets are a URL habit and were removed.
finding.axfr-tcp: AXFR queries always use TCP (the manual; RFC 5936). The server must be willing to transfer the zone to you.
finding.tcp-default-for-type: For {type} dig already uses TCP, so +tcp changes nothing; it is kept because you asked for it.
finding.ignore-no-udp: +ignore stops the retry over TCP after a truncated UDP answer; over TCP, TLS or HTTPS there is no such retry, so it has no effect.
finding.trace-server-root-only: With +trace, @server affects only the initial query for the root name servers; the referrals are followed to the servers they name.
finding.trace-sets-dnssec: +trace sets +dnssec itself (and +cookie), to emulate a name server's own queries; writing +dnssec again is harmless.
finding.redundant-norecurse: +trace and +nssearch disable recursion themselves; +norecurse adds nothing here.
finding.bufsize-large: RFC 6891 suggests 4096 octets as a starting point and warns that advertising an architectural limit invites fragmentation; {value} is above that.
finding.bufsize-default: +bufsize=0 advertises a 0-byte EDNS UDP buffer, which the receiver treats as 512 (RFC 6891, section 6.2.3); it does not restore the default. The manual gives that job to +bufsize with no value. dig's default is 1232 bytes in every BIND release from 9.18.0; it was 4096 before, and still is in the 9.16 branch's dig.
finding.subnet-zero: A source prefix length of 0 tells the resolver not to use your address when answering (RFC 7871); +subnet=0 is the short form.
finding.identify-needs-short: +identify shows the answering server's address only when +short is in use; it was not written.
finding.tsig-keyfile: The query is signed with the key in the file. The server has to know the same key name, algorithm and secret (a key statement in BIND's named.conf).

eff.title: What the query will carry
eff.question: Question
eff.iterative: dig iterates from the root itself (+trace)
eff.bufsizeDefault: advertising dig's default size, 1232 bytes in BIND 9.18 and later
eff.noOpt: (no OPT record, so no DO bit and no options)
eff.note: Derived from the manual's stated defaults and interactions, not from running dig: RD set by default, cleared by +norecurse, +trace and +nssearch; DO set by +dnssec or +trace; EDNS version 0 by default; the cookie on by default and off with +nocookie or +noedns; type ANY and ixfr=N over TCP by default, AXFR always.

explain.server: @server: ask this name server instead of the ones in /etc/resolv.conf. A host name is resolved first; an IPv4 or IPv6 address is used as is.
explain.norc: -r: do not read $'{HOME}'/.digrc, so the command behaves the same on every machine.
explain.source: -b address[#port]: send the query from this local address (and port).
explain.port: -p port: send to this port instead of the transport's default.
explain.keyfile: -k keyfile: sign the query with TSIG or SIG(0) using the key read from this file.
explain.reverse: -x address: a reverse lookup. dig builds the in-addr.arpa (IPv4) or ip6.arpa (IPv6, one nibble per label) name and queries PTR in class IN.
explain.qname: -q name: the name to look up, given explicitly because the bare word would also read as a type or class.
explain.name: The owner name to look up.
explain.type: The record type (dig's default, A, is omitted).
explain.type-axfr: AXFR: a full zone transfer, always over TCP.
explain.type-ixfr: ixfr=N: an incremental zone transfer, every change since the serial N you hold.
explain.type-any: ANY: every record type the server chooses to return (it may answer minimally).
explain.class: The query class: CH (Chaosnet) or HS (Hesiod); IN is the default and is omitted.
explain.tls: +tls: DNS over TLS; port 853 by default.
explain.https: +https[=endpoint]: DNS over HTTPS; port 443 and /dns-query by default.
explain.trace: +trace: iterative queries from the root name servers, following referrals and showing each server's answer; sets +dnssec and +cookie, disables recursion.
explain.nssearch: +nssearch: find the zone's authoritative name servers and show the SOA each one holds; disables recursion.
explain.norecurse: +norecurse: clear the RD bit, so the server answers only from what it has.
explain.dnssec: +dnssec: set the DNSSEC OK (DO) bit in the OPT record, asking for the RRSIG and other DNSSEC records.
explain.cd: +cd: set the CD (checking disabled) bit, asking the resolver not to validate.
explain.noedns: +noedns: send no OPT record (no EDNS at all).
explain.bufsize: +bufsize=B: advertise this UDP payload size in the OPT record (0 advertises 0 bytes; +bufsize with no value restores dig's default, 1232).
explain.nocookie: +nocookie: do not send the DNS COOKIE option (on by default).
explain.nsid: +nsid: include the NSID option, asking the server to identify the instance that answers.
explain.subnet: +subnet=addr/prefix: send the EDNS Client Subnet option; 0 means do not use my address.
explain.ignore: +ignore: accept a truncated UDP answer instead of retrying over TCP.
explain.timeout: +timeout=T: wait this many seconds for each answer (default 5).
explain.tries: +tries=T: try the query this many times in total (default 3).
explain.retry: +retry=T: retry this many times after the first attempt (default 2).
explain.short: +short: print only the answer data, one record per line (global: applies to every lookup on the line).
explain.identify: +identify: with +short, also print the address and port of the server that answered.
explain.answer: +answer: ...then turn the answer section back on. Order matters: query options apply in sequence.
explain.yaml: +yaml: print the response in a detailed YAML form.
explain.multiline: +multiline: print records such as SOA and DNSKEY over several lines with comments.
explain.ttlunits: +ttlunits: print TTLs in s, m, h, d and w rather than seconds.
explain.qr: +qr: also print the query message as it is sent.

share.carries: The link carries the form as filled in, so it opens on the same command.

python-playground.name: Python playground
python-playground.blurb: Real CPython 3.14 in your browser, for the arithmetic of networks: subnets, masks, EUI-64, DNS headers in struct, HMAC, latency statistics, transfer times. A 13.5 MB engine downloads once, when you say so; nothing you type leaves the page.

explainer.title: A WebAssembly tool
explainer.runs: What runs: {engine} {version}, which is CPython {python} compiled to WebAssembly by the Pyodide project, under the {licence} licence. It is a real interpreter, not an imitation of one.
explainer.origin: Where it comes from: the same origin as this page, pinned by version and by SHA-256 digest at build time. No third-party server is contacted at run time.
explainer.cost: What the first use costs: about {mb} MB, downloaded only when you press the button that names the size. Your browser caches it; the second visit costs nothing.
explainer.leaves: What leaves the page: nothing. The program and its input stay in a Web Worker on your device. The interpreter has no network and no processes; the page policy would refuse them anyway.
explainer.checks: What the site's own checks cover: the harness around the engine, the examples (re-run through the real engine at every build), the preflight and the limits. The interpreter's own behaviour is its project's.

python-playground.codeHint: Python 3.14 standard library only; no packages in this version. Up to {max} characters. The value of the last expression is shown as the result, as in a REPL.
python-playground.stdinLabel: Standard input (what input() and sys.stdin read, one line per line)
python-playground.stdinPlaceholder: Lines for input() or sys.stdin, if the program reads any
python-playground.loading: Downloading the engine: {pct}% of about {mb} MB, then starting Python
python-playground.loadFailed: The engine could not be loaded. Offline, a blocked download or an unsupported browser are the usual causes; the examples stay readable.
python-playground.blocked: Fix the items marked as errors; the program is not sent to the engine while any remain.
python-playground.noResult: Finished; the last statement produced no value.
python-playground.outputTruncated: Output was cut at {max} characters per stream.
python-playground.timedOut: Stopped after {seconds} s, the wall-clock limit. The engine was restarted; press Run to try again.
python-playground.stopped: Stopped. A fresh engine is starting from the cached files; press Run when it is ready.

findingTitle.import-distribution: Package not loaded in this version
findingTitle.input-no-stdin: input() with an empty stdin box

finding.empty: The editor holds no code, only blank lines or comments.
finding.too-long: The program is {chars} characters; the limit is {max}. Shorten it, or split the work.
finding.stdin-too-long: The stdin box holds {chars} characters; the limit is {max}.
finding.line-cut: {lines, plural, one {{lines} line exceeds} other {{lines} lines exceed}} {max} characters. The engine still runs them; only this preflight reads them cut.
finding.import-unavailable: {module} is part of the Python standard library but not of this WebAssembly build: the engine says "{error}". Nothing on the page can supply it.
finding.import-distribution: {module} exists for Pyodide as the package {package}, but packages are not loaded in this version ({version}): the import will raise ModuleNotFoundError. The standard library is what is available.
finding.import-unknown: {module} is neither in the standard library nor in the Pyodide distribution, so it cannot be imported here; the import will raise ModuleNotFoundError.
finding.import-relative: {module} is a relative import, which needs a package to be relative to; a program run here is a single module and the import will fail.
finding.import-pyodide: {module} is the bridge between Python and the JavaScript side of the Worker. It works, but it reaches a Worker scope with no document, and the page policy allows this origin only.
finding.network: The program uses the network ({modules}). The engine runs in a Worker with no sockets, and the page's connect-src policy allows this origin only: connections raise an error.
finding.processes: The program starts processes ({modules}). Emscripten does not support processes; subprocess, os.system and multiprocessing raise OSError 138.
finding.threads: Threads are available but run cooperatively inside one WebAssembly instance; CPU-bound threads do not run in parallel here.
finding.zoneinfo: zoneinfo finds no time zone database in this build (no system tzdata and no tzdata package loaded): ZoneInfo(...) raises ZoneInfoNotFoundError. Use datetime.timezone with a fixed offset instead.
finding.pip: pip and micropip are not available in this version: packages are off, so nothing can be installed. The standard library is what is available.

finding.input-stdin: The program reads standard input; the box supplies {lines, plural, one {{lines} line} other {{lines} lines}}, one per read, then end of file.

expect-script-explainer.name: Expect script explainer
expect-script-explainer.blurb: Paste an Expect script and read what it would do, command by command: what it spawns, what it waits for, what it types, when it hands over to you. Then the dialogue it conducts and the findings: a password in clear text, a timeout left at the default or set to never, a pattern that matches too soon, a send without the return the program waits for, a braced block Expect reads as one pattern, a script that ends before the program has answered. Parsed with the site's Tcl parser (Tcl 8.4's rules plus Tcl 8.5's argument expansion), never run; every rule cites the expect(1) manual or the Expect 5.45.4 source.
expect-script-explainer.scriptPlaceholder: Paste an Expect script (spawn, expect, send...)
expect-script-explainer.syntaxBad: Tcl cannot read all of it.
expect-script-explainer.clean: No findings on the points the explainer checks.
expect-script-explainer.counts: {error, plural, one {# error} other {# errors}}, {warning, plural, one {# warning} other {# warnings}}, {info, plural, one {# note} other {# notes}}.
expect-script-explainer.facts: {lines, plural, one {# line} other {# lines}}, {commands, plural, one {# command} other {# commands}}.
expect-script-explainer.timeoutAt: Timeout at the first expect: {t, select, default {the default, 10 seconds} infinite {infinite (-1)} other {{t} seconds}}.
expect-script-explainer.handsOver: Hands the keyboard to the user (interact).
expect-script-explainer.waitsEof: Waits for the program to end (eof).
expect-script-explainer.endsNoEof: Never waits for the program to end.

E1.send: A secret typed in clear text: right after a password prompt the script sends {preview}, written in the file. Anyone who can read the script can read the password. Take it from the command line (lindex $argv), from the environment ($env(NAME)), or ask for it with stty -echo and expect_user.
E1.variable: A secret stored in the script: {variable} is set to {preview}. Take it from the command line (lindex $argv) or from the environment ($env(NAME)) instead.

E2.infinite: set timeout -1 is an infinite timeout (expect(1)). An expect whose pattern never arrives waits forever, and so does whatever runs the script. Give it a number and a timeout handler.
E2.default: No timeout was set before this expect, so the default of 10 seconds applies (expect(1)). Slow logins and long commands need more; say what you mean with set timeout.

E3.flush: The pattern {pattern} matches whatever is in the buffer, at once: expect(1) says the pattern "*" (and -re ".*") will flush the output buffer without reading any more output from the process. The script does not wait for the prompt here.
E3.short: A one-character pattern, {pattern}. Patterns are unanchored and match anywhere in the output, so a banner or an earlier line that contains this character ends the wait early. Match more of the prompt, and anchor a regexp with $ (expect(1) encourages it when you can describe the end of the string).
E3.dollar: The pattern "$" alone. In Expect's glob matcher a $ that ends the pattern anchors it to the end of the buffer, and the search never tries the end position itself (exp_glob.c, 5.45.4), so "$" matches only an empty buffer, at once, before anything is read, and never matches text already waiting. It does not wait for a shell prompt. Write the prompt with what comes before it: -ex "$ " or -re '{'\$ $'}'.
E3.anchor: A regexp that is only an anchor, {pattern}: it matches the empty string at once, at the start or the end of whatever the buffer holds, so the expect returns without waiting for anything. Name the end of the prompt instead, for example -re '{'\$ $'}'.

E4.main: The script's last act is a send. When the script ends, Expect closes the connections to its spawned processes (expect(1)), so whatever the program prints in answer is never read, and the program may not have finished. End with expect eof, an expect for the final prompt, or interact.

E5.none: No return at the end of the string. Characters are sent at once, but a program with line-buffered input will not read them until a return character, written \r, arrives (expect(1)). The program is left waiting for the end of the line.
E5.braced: A braced string: Tcl substitutes nothing between braces (Tcl(n)), so {text} is sent with its backslash and dollar sign as ordinary characters. The program never receives a return, and a $name is sent as a name. Use double quotes.

E6.main: The string ends with a newline (\n), not a return. expect(1) names \r as the return character a line-buffered program waits for; whether a program accepts a bare newline depends on its terminal settings. Write \r.

E7.main: {count, plural, one {One expect waits} other {# expects wait}} on a pattern with no timeout handler. When the pattern does not arrive in time, expect(1) executes an implicit null action: the expect returns silently and the script carries on as if it had matched, typing commands at a program that is not where the script thinks it is. Add a timeout pattern that reports and exits.

E8.main: exp_continue outside an expect body. It tells the enclosing expect to keep waiting (expect(1)); here there is none to continue, and the script errors.

E9.command: Square brackets inside a quoted pattern: Tcl performs command substitution on {pattern} before Expect sees it, so the bracketed text runs as a command and the script errors (the braced form of expect substitutes too, expect(1)). Brace the pattern: -re '{...}'.
E9.variable: A $variable inside a quoted regexp: Tcl substitutes it before Expect reads the pattern, {pattern}. Here the substitution looks intended; if the dollar sign was meant as the end-of-line anchor, brace the pattern.

E10.main: ssh is spawned with StrictHostKeyChecking at its default, ask (ssh_config(5)): on a host whose key is not yet known, ssh asks the user to confirm before connecting, and nothing in the script answers a (yes/no) question. The first run against a new host waits for an answer until the timeout. Answer the question in an expect block, or pass -o StrictHostKeyChecking=accept-new.

E11.main: sleep {seconds}: a fixed wait where expect would wait for the event itself. Too short on a slow day, wasted on a fast one. Wait for the prompt or for eof instead.

E12.main: log_user 0 hides the dialogue from stdout and nothing turns it back on (log_user 1, expect(1)). Fine for a quiet script; a surprise when something goes wrong and there is nothing to read.

E13.main: set timeout after the first expect (line {firstExpectLine}), which therefore ran on the default of 10 seconds (expect(1)). Move the set timeout above it.

E14.main: Nothing is spawned: the script never starts a program, so expect and send have nothing to talk to. Expect scripts begin with spawn (or attach to an existing spawn_id).

E15.main: stty -echo with no stty echo afterwards. The password-reading idiom in expect(1) turns echo back on as soon as the password has been read; leave the terminal as you found it.

E16.main: close without wait. close does not call wait (expect(1)), so the spawned process is not reaped; call wait after close.

E17.main: A send straight after spawn, before any expect. expect(1): it is a good idea to precede the first send to a process by an expect, which waits for the process to start, while send cannot; if the first send completes before the process starts running, the data may be ignored.

E18.main: set timeout inside a procedure: variables written there are local unless a global command has been issued (expect(1)), so this value applies only to the expects inside this procedure. Add global timeout if the whole script should use it.

syntax.main: Tcl cannot parse this: {message}. The script stops here when run; the commands before it are explained above.

E19.oneline: A braced expect block written on one line. Expect 5.45.4 reads one braced argument as patterns and bodies only when a newline comes before its first non-blank character (expect.c); here none does, so the whole block is one glob pattern, {pattern}, which the output almost never contains. None of the arms inside runs, not even the timeout arm: the expect waits for the timeout and the implicit null action follows. Put a newline after the opening brace, or write expect -brace '{...}'.
E19.firstline: The first pattern of this braced expect block sits on the brace's line. Expect 5.45.4 reads one braced argument as patterns and bodies only when a newline comes before its first non-blank character (expect.c), so the whole block, every line of it, is one glob pattern, {pattern}, which the output almost never contains. None of the arms inside runs, not even the timeout arm: the expect waits for the timeout and the implicit null action follows. Move the first pattern to the next line, or write expect -brace '{...}'.

E20.main: A pattern that begins with a dash, {pattern}. expect reads every word that starts with "-" as a flag, by its full name or a unique abbreviation, and this one is {kind, select, ambiguous {an abbreviation of several flags} other {not a flag it knows}}, so the command fails with "{kind, select, ambiguous {ambiguous} other {bad}} flag" and the script stops. expect(1): any pattern beginning with "-" should be protected; write -gl, -ex or -- before it.

explain.shebang: Runs under {interpreter}: the first line names the interpreter; to Tcl it is a comment.
explain.spawn: Starts {program}{hasArgs, select, yes { with {args}} other {}} as the current process{noecho, select, yes {, without echoing the command line} other {}}. From here, expect reads its output and send types at it.
explain.expect: {variant, select, expect_before {Registers patterns tried before the patterns of every later expect} expect_after {Registers patterns tried after the patterns of every later expect} expect_user {Waits for keystrokes from the user} other {Waits for the program's output to match}}: {n, plural, one {one pattern} other {# patterns}}{timeout, select, none {} other {, with its own timeout of {timeout} seconds}}.
explain.send: Types {text} at {target, select, process {the program} user {the user, on stdout} error {the user, on stderr} other {the terminal}}{ending, select, cr {, ending with a return} lf {, ending with a newline} other {, with no return at the end}}{pace, select, slow {, slowly} human {, with human-like pauses} other {}}.
explain.setTimeout: Sets the timeout for every following expect to {how, select, infinite {never (-1): an expect can wait forever} seconds {{value, plural, one {{value} second} other {{value} seconds}}} other {the value of {value}}}.
explain.set: Sets {name} to {value}{argv, select, yes { (argument {index} of the command line)} other {}}.
explain.global: Declares {names} global inside this procedure, so writing it changes the script's variable.
explain.interact: Hands the keyboard to the user: keystrokes go to the program and its output comes back, until the user or the program ends it.
explain.expContinue: Keeps the enclosing expect waiting for the next match instead of returning.
explain.logUser: {on, select, yes {Shows the dialogue on stdout again.} other {Stops showing the dialogue on stdout (the script still reads it).}}
explain.logFile: {hasArgs, select, yes {Records a transcript of the session in {args}.} other {Stops recording the transcript.}}
explain.close: Closes the connection to the program; most programs see end-of-file and exit.
explain.wait: Waits for the spawned process to terminate, so the system can release it.
explain.exit: Ends the script{code, select, none {} other { with status {code}}}; every connection to a spawned process is closed.
explain.sleep: Pauses for {seconds, plural, one {{seconds} second} other {{seconds} seconds}}, whatever the program is doing.
explain.stty: {mode, select, off {Turns the terminal's echo off: what the user types is not shown.} on {Turns the terminal's echo back on.} other {Changes the terminal modes: {args}.}}
explain.proc: Defines the procedure {name}{hasParams, select, yes { with the parameters {params}} other {}}; its body runs when it is called.
explain.control: {name, select, if {Branches: the commands inside run when the condition holds.} foreach {Loops over a list, running the commands inside for each element.} while {Loops while the condition holds.} for {A counted loop over the commands inside.} switch {Picks the first arm whose pattern matches the value.} other {A Tcl {name}.}}
explain.puts: Prints {text} for the user (stdout, or the channel named first).
explain.matchMax: Sets the buffer expect matches against to {value} bytes (the default is 2000).
explain.expInternal: {on, select, yes {Turns on Expect's internal diagnostics on stderr.} other {Turns Expect's diagnostics off.}}
explain.catch: Runs the commands inside and catches any error they raise.
explain.other: {name} with {argc, plural, =0 {no arguments} one {one argument} other {# arguments}}: a Tcl command the explainer passes over.

special.eof: end-of-file: the program closed its output
special.full_buffer: the buffer filled (match_max) with no match
special.null: a NUL byte, when nulls are allowed

expect-script-explainer.limits: The explainer reads the script's text and never runs it. It reads expect's arguments as Expect 5.45.4 does, and it follows the bodies of expect, if, foreach, while, for, switch, catch and proc in source order, so it cannot know which branch a run takes, how many times a loop runs or whether a procedure is ever called. Patterns and strings that depend on a variable are shown as written. Every fact about Expect comes from expect(1) or the Expect 5.45.4 source, cited under Sources.
expect-script-explainer.expansionNote: {n, plural, one {Line} other {Lines}} {lines} {n, plural, one {uses} other {use}} the argument expansion '{*}' of Tcl 8.5 and later: when the script runs, the word's value is split into several arguments; the explainer reads it as one word.

share.carries: The link carries a copy of the script, each password rule E1 finds replaced by the bullets shown here.
share.caution: A script names hosts, users and commands: read it before you send the link.
share.maybeSecret: {more, plural, =0 {Line {line} may hold a secret ({label}): check it, and any internal names, before you send the link.} one {Line {line} ({label}) and one more line may hold secrets: check them, and any internal names, before you send the link.} other {Line {line} ({label}) and # more lines may hold secrets: check them, and any internal names, before you send the link.}}
share.blockedSecret: {more, plural, =0 {No link: line {line} holds a credential ({label}). Replace it with a placeholder, then share again.} one {No link: line {line} ({label}) and one more line hold credentials. Replace them with placeholders, then share again.} other {No link: line {line} ({label}) and # more lines hold credentials. Replace them with placeholders, then share again.}}
share.redacted: {n, plural, =0 {Nothing in it needed replacing.} one {# password is replaced by bullets.} other {# passwords are replaced by bullets.}}
share.blockedEscaped: No link: the password on line {line} is written with escape sequences, so it cannot be replaced safely.
share.blockedCopy: No link: a copy with the passwords replaced would not read the same, so none is offered.

err.tooLong: The script is longer than {max} characters.

http-message-decoder.name: HTTP message decoder
http-message-decoder.blurb: Paste a raw HTTP/1.1 request or response and read it decoded: the request line or status line against the IANA registries, every field filed under the part of the specification that defines it, the framing decision RFC 9112 makes for the body (which of its eight rules applies, Content-Length against the bytes present, Transfer-Encoding overriding it, the chunks decoded one by one with their trailers), and the credentials and cookies the message carries, surfaced and masked. The decode-only half of an interception proxy's inspector: it never sends, replays or tampers.
http-message-decoder.messagePlaceholder: Paste a request or a response, start line first (CRLF or LF line endings)

preset.post-form-basic: POST with Basic auth and cookies
preset.duplicate-host-space-colon: Two Hosts, a space before a colon

http-message-decoder.clean: No findings on the points the decoder checks.
http-message-decoder.counts: {error, plural, one {# error} other {# errors}}, {warning, plural, one {# warning} other {# warnings}}, {info, plural, one {# note} other {# notes}}.
http-message-decoder.facts: {lines, plural, one {# line} other {# lines}}, {headers, plural, one {# field line} other {# field lines}}, line endings {ending, select, crlf {CRLF} lf {LF only} mixed {mixed CRLF and LF} other {none}}, {octets, plural, =0 {no body} one {# octet of body} other {# octets of body}}.
http-message-decoder.urlSchemeNote: the scheme is not in the message; shown as http
http-message-decoder.framingTitle: How the body is framed (RFC 9112, Section 6.3)

rule.0: The start line was not read as HTTP, so no framing rule applies.
rule.1: Rule 1: a response to HEAD, or a 1xx, 204 or 304 response, ends at the empty line after the fields, whatever the fields say. It cannot carry a body.
rule.2: Rule 2: a 2xx response to CONNECT turns the connection into a tunnel right after the empty line; Content-Length and Transfer-Encoding are ignored.
rule.3: Rule 3: both Transfer-Encoding and Content-Length are present, so Transfer-Encoding overrides Content-Length. RFC 9112 says such a message might indicate an attempt to perform request smuggling or response splitting and ought to be handled as an error.
rule.4: Rule 4: a Transfer-Encoding field is present. With chunked as the final coding, the body ends where the chunks say; in a response with another final coding, it ends when the server closes; in a request, a server answers 400.
rule.5: Rule 5: Content-Length is present without Transfer-Encoding but is not a single valid number, so the framing is invalid and the recipient MUST treat it as an unrecoverable error (400 in a request, 502 from a proxy).
rule.6: Rule 6: a valid Content-Length without Transfer-Encoding defines the body length in octets. If the connection closes before that many octets arrive, the message is incomplete.
rule.7: Rule 7: a request with neither Transfer-Encoding nor Content-Length has a body of length zero.
rule.8: Rule 8: a response with neither Transfer-Encoding nor Content-Length is read until the server closes the connection.

delimiter.none: no body: the empty line ends the message

http-message-decoder.chunksTitle: {n, plural, =0 {No data chunks} one {# chunk} other {# chunks}}
http-message-decoder.lastChunkNo: The last-chunk (size 0) never arrives: the body is incomplete.
http-message-decoder.decodedLength: Decoded content: {n, plural, one {# octet} other {# octets}}.
http-message-decoder.fieldsTitle: {n, plural, one {# field} other {# fields}}, by what they are for

handoff.method: Compare this method with the others
handoff.jwt: Decode the Bearer token as a JWT (paste it there; it is not carried in the link)
handoff.replay: Translate the request to curl, fetch and others

H1.unrecognised: The first line is neither a request line (method, target, version) nor a status line (version, three-digit code, reason). The rest was not read as HTTP.
H1.extra-words: {count, plural, one {One extra word} other {# extra words}} on the request line after the version. RFC 9112: request-line = method SP request-target SP HTTP-version.

H2.missing: An HTTP/1.1 request without a Host field. RFC 9112, Section 3.2: a client MUST send a Host header field in all HTTP/1.1 request messages, and a server MUST respond with 400 (Bad Request) to one that lacks it.
H2.duplicate: {count} Host field lines. RFC 9112, Section 3.2: a server MUST respond with 400 (Bad Request) to any request message that contains more than one Host header field line.
H2.not-first: Host is field {position}, not the first. RFC 9110, Section 7.2: a user agent that sends Host SHOULD send it as the first field in the header section.

H3.space-before-colon: Whitespace between the field name {name} and the colon. RFC 9112, Section 5: no whitespace is allowed there, and a server MUST reject such a request with 400 (Bad Request).
H3.no-colon: A line in the header section with no colon: not a field line. A recipient cannot parse it as name: value.

H4.main: {name} continues on the next line (obsolete line folding). RFC 9112, Section 5.2: a sender MUST NOT generate it outside message/http, and a server MUST either reject with 400 or replace each fold with spaces. The decoder joined the lines with one space.

H5.main: {count, plural, one {One bare CR} other {# bare CRs}} (a CR not followed by LF). RFC 9112, Section 2.2: a sender MUST NOT generate one outside the content, and a recipient MUST consider the element invalid or replace each bare CR with a space.

H6.main: Both Transfer-Encoding ({codings}) and Content-Length ({length}) are present. Transfer-Encoding overrides, and RFC 9112 says such a message might indicate an attempt to perform request smuggling or response splitting and ought to be handled as an error; an intermediary that forwards it MUST first remove Content-Length.

H7.invalid: Content-Length is not a decimal number: {values}. RFC 9110, Section 8.6: Content-Length = 1*DIGIT. Without Transfer-Encoding the framing is invalid and a server MUST respond 400 and close.
H7.differ: Content-Length values that differ: {values}. RFC 9112, Section 6.3, rule 5: unless every value in the list is the same, the message framing is invalid and the recipient MUST treat it as an unrecoverable error.
H7.repeated: Content-Length repeated {count} times with the same value, {value}. RFC 9110, Section 8.6: a recipient MAY either reject the message or replace the list with a single instance of the value, since this likely indicates a duplicate generated upstream.

H8.shorter: Content-Length declares {declared, plural, one {{declared} octet} other {{declared} octets}} but {actual, plural, one {{actual} was} other {{actual} were}} pasted. RFC 9112, Section 6.3, rule 6: a recipient that does not receive the declared number of octets MUST consider the message incomplete and close the connection (a paste may simply have lost its body).
H8.longer: Content-Length declares {declared, plural, one {{declared} octet} other {{declared} octets}} but {actual, plural, one {{actual} was} other {{actual} were}} pasted: {extra} more. A recipient reads exactly {declared} and treats the rest as the start of the next message, which is how a desynchronized connection begins.

H9.request-not-chunked: Transfer-Encoding ({codings}) in a request without chunked as the final coding. RFC 9112, Section 6.3, rule 4: the body length cannot be determined reliably; the server MUST respond with 400 (Bad Request) and close the connection.
H9.response-read-to-close: Transfer-Encoding ({codings}) in a response without chunked as the final coding: the body is read until the server closes the connection.
H9.stacked: Codings before chunked: {codings}. The chunks frame the message; the data inside them is still encoded with those codings and is shown as it is.

H10.bad-size: A chunk-size line that is not hexadecimal. RFC 9112, Section 7.1: chunk-size = 1*HEXDIG, optionally followed by chunk extensions.
H10.truncated: The chunk's data ends before its size says. The paste is incomplete, or the size is wrong.
H10.missing-crlf: The chunk's data is not followed by CRLF. RFC 9112, Section 7.1: chunk = chunk-size [ chunk-ext ] CRLF chunk-data CRLF.
H10.no-last-chunk: The last-chunk (a size of 0) never arrives, so the body never ends. A recipient keeps waiting.
H10.leftover: {octets, plural, one {One octet follows} other {# octets follow}} the end of the chunked body. A recipient reads them as the start of the next message on the connection: the request-smuggling shape when a front end framed the message by Content-Length instead.

H11.main: Transfer-Encoding in an HTTP/1.0 message. RFC 9112, Section 6.1: a recipient MUST treat the message as if the framing is faulty, even if a Content-Length is present, and close the connection after processing the message.

H12.main: A body of {octets, plural, one {{octets} octet} other {{octets} octets}} follows the fields, but the request has neither Content-Length nor Transfer-Encoding. RFC 9112, Section 6.3, rule 7: the body length is zero, so a server reads the pasted body as the beginning of the next request.

H13.main: A body of {octets, plural, one {{octets} octet} other {{octets} octets}} after a {code} response. RFC 9112, Section 6.3, rule 1: this response is terminated by the first empty line after the fields and cannot contain a message body; a recipient reads the body as the start of the next response.
H13.content-length-forbidden: Content-Length in a {code} response. RFC 9110, Section 8.6: a server MUST NOT send Content-Length in any response with a 1xx or 204 status code.

H14.basic: Basic credentials for the user-id {userId}: RFC 7617 forms them as user-id, a colon and the password, Base64-encoded, and says the scheme is not a secure method of user authentication, nor does it in any way protect the entity, which is transmitted in cleartext. Anyone holding this message holds the password. The decoder shows the user-id only.
H14.bearer: A Bearer token. Whoever holds this message can present it until it expires; the value is masked here.
H14.bearer-jwt: A Bearer token shaped like a JWT (three base64url parts). Whoever holds this message can present it until it expires; the value is masked here and can be read in the JWT decoder.
H14.other: Credentials with the {scheme} scheme. RFC 9110, Section 11.1: the scheme name is a case-insensitive token; the value is masked here.

H15.sent: {count, plural, one {One cookie is sent} other {# cookies are sent}}: {names}. Values are masked; whoever holds this message holds the session.
H15.prefix: {name} carries the {prefix} prefix but not what it promises. rfc6265bis, Section 4.1.3: __Secure- requires the Secure attribute; __Host- requires Secure, Path=/ and no Domain attribute. A user agent rejects the cookie.
H15.no-secure: {name} has no Secure attribute: a user agent may send it over plain HTTP. rfc6265bis: when a cookie has the Secure attribute, the user agent will include it only if the request is transmitted over a secure channel.
H15.no-httponly: {name} has no HttpOnly attribute: scripts on the page can read it.
H15.no-samesite: {name} has no SameSite attribute. rfc6265bis: the cookie is subject to a default enforcement mode that is equivalent to Lax.
H15.samesite-unknown: {name} has SameSite={value}, which is not Strict, Lax or None; it is treated as the default, Lax.
H15.none-without-secure: {name} has SameSite=None without Secure. rfc6265bis requires Secure with SameSite=None; user agents reject or ignore the cookie.
H15.both-ages: {name} has both Max-Age and Expires. rfc6265bis: the Max-Age attribute has precedence and controls the expiration date of the cookie.
H15.expires-format: {name} has an Expires value that is not an HTTP-date: {value}.

H16.unknown: {method} is not in the methods table (the RFC 9110 methods, PATCH, QUERY and the WebDAV methods). A server that does not implement it answers 501 (Not Implemented) or 405 (Method Not Allowed).
H16.case: {method} is written in a case other than {canonical}. Methods are case-sensitive tokens; a server would not recognize it.

H17.differs: The reason phrase sent, {sent}, differs from the registry's, {registry}. RFC 9110: reason phrases are only recommendations and a client SHOULD ignore the reason-phrase content.
H17.absent: No reason phrase (the registry's is {registry}). RFC 9112 allows it: status-line = HTTP-version SP status-code SP [ reason-phrase ].

H18.not-three-digits: {code} is not a three-digit status code (RFC 9112: status-code = 3DIGIT).
H18.out-of-range: {code} is outside 100 to 599. RFC 9110, Section 15: all valid status codes are within that range, and a client that receives an invalid one SHOULD process the response as if it had a 5xx status code.
H18.unassigned: {code} is not in the IANA status code registry. RFC 9110, Section 15: a client MUST treat an unrecognized status code as the x00 status code of its class, here {klass}00.

H19.obsolete: {name} uses the obsolete {format} date format. RFC 9110, Section 5.6.7: a recipient MUST accept all three HTTP-date formats, but a sender MUST generate IMF-fixdate (Sun, 06 Nov 1994 08:49:37 GMT).
H19.invalid: {name} is not an HTTP-date: {value}. RFC 9110, Section 5.6.7 defines IMF-fixdate and the two obsolete formats a recipient must accept; nothing else.

H20.main: {name} appears {count} times. RFC 9110, Section 5.3 lets a recipient combine repeated field lines into one comma-separated list only for fields defined as lists; {name} is not one, so the message is ambiguous.

H21.name-not-token: The field name {name} is not a token (RFC 9110, Section 5.1: field-name = token). A recipient rejects the line.
H21.nul-in-value: The value of {name} contains a NUL character. RFC 9110, Section 5.5: a recipient MUST either reject the message or replace each such character with a space.

H22.main: {count, plural, one {One field name} other {# field names}} with the X- prefix: {names}. RFC 6648 (BCP 178) deprecates the prefix for new names and says implementations MUST NOT make assumptions about a parameter's status from it; these fields mean whatever the sender and receiver agree.

H23.main: {name} is {status, select, deprecated {deprecated} other {obsoleted}} in the IANA field name registry ({reference}). It still parses, but current specifications no longer define its behaviour.

H24.invalid: {target} is not one of the four request-target forms (origin-form /path, absolute-form scheme://host/path, authority-form host:port, asterisk-form *).
H24.authority-not-connect: An authority-form target (host:port) with {method}. RFC 9112, Section 3.2.3: the authority-form of request-target is only used for CONNECT requests.
H24.asterisk-not-options: An asterisk-form target with {method}. RFC 9112, Section 3.2.4: the asterisk-form of request-target is only used for a server-wide OPTIONS request.
H24.connect-not-authority: CONNECT with the target {target}. RFC 9112, Section 3.2.3: CONNECT uses the authority-form, host:port.
H24.absolute: An absolute-form target, {target}: the form a client sends to a proxy. RFC 9112, Section 3.2.2: a server MUST accept the absolute-form in requests even though most HTTP/1.1 clients will only send it to a proxy.

H25.main: The version token is {version}. RFC 9112, Section 2.3: HTTP-version = HTTP-name "/" DIGIT "." DIGIT, with HTTP-name case-sensitive; a request line without a version is HTTP/0.9, which has no fields at all.

H26.main: {method} defines a meaning for enclosed content, but the request carries neither Content-Length nor Transfer-Encoding. RFC 9110, Section 8.6: a user agent SHOULD send Content-Length in such a request, even when the value is 0.

H27.close: Connection: {options}. The sender will close the connection after this message; a persistent connection is not expected.
H27.keep-alive: Connection: {options}. An HTTP/1.0-era request for a persistent connection; HTTP/1.1 connections persist by default.
H27.upgrade: Connection: {options}. The message asks to switch protocols (see Upgrade); the Connection field names the hop-by-hop fields intermediaries must strip.
H27.other: Connection: {options}. RFC 9110, Section 7.6.1: the listed names are hop-by-hop fields an intermediary MUST remove before forwarding, along with Connection itself.
H27.expect-continue: Expect: {options}. The client waits for a 100 (Continue) interim response before sending the body.

H28.lf: Lines end with LF alone. RFC 9112, Section 2.2: the line terminator is CRLF, but a recipient MAY recognize a single LF as a line terminator and ignore any preceding CR. Pasted text often loses its CRs; this is noted, not counted against the message.
H28.mixed: Lines end with a mixture of CRLF and LF. A recipient that accepts a single LF reads them all; one that does not may misread the header section.

http-message-decoder.limits: The decoder reads the message as text and never sends it. Octet counts are UTF-8 counts of the pasted text, so a body with binary content or a different charset measures differently on the wire. The scheme of a request's URL is not in an HTTP/1.1 message (http is assumed), and whether a response answers a HEAD request cannot be known from the response alone. Field values are shown as written; only credentials and cookies are masked. Facts come from RFC 9112, RFC 9110, RFC 9111, the IANA registries, rfc6265bis-22, RFC 7617 and RFC 6648, cited under Sources.

share.carries: The link carries the message with every credential, cookie and body secret masked, lengths kept; the rest goes as pasted.
share.redacted: {n, plural, =0 {Nothing in it needed masking.} one {One value is masked.} other {# values are masked.}}
share.blocked: No link: line {line} holds a key, token or password ({label}) that cannot be replaced safely. Put a placeholder in its place, then share again.

err.tooLong: The message is longer than {max} characters.

color-contrast-format.name: Colour contrast & format
color-contrast-format.blurb: Two colours in any CSS notation (named, hex, rgb, hsl, hwb, lab, lch, oklab, oklch, color()) and out come the WCAG contrast ratio with pass or fail at every level (AA and AAA, normal and large text, user interface components), a live preview, each colour converted to every notation with its relative luminance, and the nearest foreground that would pass each failing level. Pure arithmetic from the WCAG formulas and the CSS Color Level 4 sample code; nothing leaves the browser.
color-contrast-format.pairLabel: Two colours, in any CSS notation
color-contrast-format.ratioSentence: contrast ratio, from relative luminances {lighter} (lighter) and {darker} (darker).
color-contrast-format.compositedNote: The foreground has an alpha of {alpha}, so it was composited over the background first; the colour measured is {hex}. WCAG defines contrast between opaque colours; the composite is what the display shows.
color-contrast-format.previewNormal: Body text at the usual size: the 4.5:1 rule applies here (7:1 for AAA).
color-contrast-format.previewLarge: Large text, 18 point or 14 point bold: 3:1 (4.5:1 for AAA).
color-contrast-format.previewUi: A control's outline or a chart line: 3:1 against what is next to it.

note.hex-short: A short hex form, expanded by replicating each digit to {expanded}.
note.legacy-commas: Legacy comma-separated syntax, still valid; CSS Color Level 4 prefers space-separated components with a slash before alpha.
note.rgb-clamped: A component outside 0 to 255 (or 0% to 100%) was clamped, as the specification does at parsed-value time.
note.out-of-gamut: The colour lies outside the sRGB gamut. The hex, rgb(), hsl() and hwb() forms and the luminance use the colour clipped to the gamut; lab(), lch(), oklab(), oklch() and XYZ keep the unclipped value.

color-contrast-format.fixesIntro: For each level the pair misses, the nearest foreground that reaches it, found by moving the foreground's lightness in OKLCH (its hue and chroma kept, chroma reduced only when the result would leave the sRGB gamut). Lighter and darker are both shown when both exist.
color-contrast-format.formulaLuminance: Each sRGB channel (0 to 1) is linearized: c / 12.92 when c is at most 0.04045, else ((c + 0.055) / 1.055) ^ 2.4. The relative luminance is L = 0.2126 R + 0.7152 G + 0.0722 B, 0 for black and 1 for white.
color-contrast-format.formulaRatio: The contrast ratio is (L1 + 0.05) / (L2 + 0.05) with L1 the lighter luminance and L2 the darker: ({lighter} + 0.05) / ({darker} + 0.05) = {ratio}. It runs from 1:1 to 21:1.
color-contrast-format.thresholds: WCAG 2.2 Success Criteria: 1.4.3 Contrast (Minimum), Level AA, asks 4.5:1 for text and 3:1 for large-scale text; 1.4.6 Contrast (Enhanced), Level AAA, asks 7:1 and 4.5:1; 1.4.11 Non-text Contrast, Level AA, asks 3:1 for user interface components and graphical objects. Large-scale text is at least 18 point, or 14 point bold. Incidental text and logotypes are exempt.
color-contrast-format.limits: The ratio is WCAG's formula over sRGB, which is what the criteria require; it is not a perceptual model, and two colours that pass can still be hard to read for some readers. Colours outside the sRGB gamut are clipped before measuring, since the criteria are defined for displayable colours. Alpha on the background is ignored (it is treated as opaque). The named colours, notations and conversions are CSS Color Level 4's; the sources are cited under Sources.

error.empty: No {which, select, foreground {foreground} other {background}} colour given.
error.bad-hex: The {which, select, foreground {foreground} other {background}} colour is not a hex colour of 3, 4, 6 or 8 digits.
error.unrecognised: The {which, select, foreground {foreground} other {background}} colour is not a notation this tool reads: a named colour, #hex, rgb(), hsl(), hwb(), lab(), lch(), oklab(), oklch() or color().
error.bad-alpha: The {which, select, foreground {foreground} other {background}} colour's alpha is not a number or percentage.
error.arity: The {which, select, foreground {foreground} other {background}} colour's function needs three components.
error.bad-component: A component of the {which, select, foreground {foreground} other {background}} colour is not a number, percentage or angle of the kind that function takes.
error.bad-space: The {which, select, foreground {foreground} other {background}} colour names a color() space this tool does not convert; it reads srgb, srgb-linear, display-p3, display-p3-linear, xyz, xyz-d50 and xyz-d65.

share.carries: The link carries the two colours as typed, and nothing else.

css-specificity-calculator.name: CSS specificity calculator
css-specificity-calculator.blurb: Paste one or more CSS selectors, or a whole stylesheet, and read each selector's specificity as the (A, B, C) triple of Selectors Level 4, every simple selector named with the column it adds to, the selectors ranked the way the cascade ranks them with ties called out, and the special cases spelled out: :where() counts for nothing, :is(), :not() and :has() take their most specific argument, :nth-child(of) adds its argument, the universal selector adds nothing, a repeated class counts twice, a legacy single-colon pseudo-element counts as one. With the reminder of the five things the cascade checks before specificity.
css-specificity-calculator.selectorsLabel: Selectors (one per line, or comma-separated, or a stylesheet)
css-specificity-calculator.tiesNote: {n, plural, one {One tie} other {# ties}}: order of appearance decides there.
css-specificity-calculator.columns: A counts ID selectors; B counts class selectors, attribute selectors and pseudo-classes; C counts type selectors and pseudo-elements. The universal selector counts for nothing. Specificities compare column by column, A first (Selectors Level 4).
css-specificity-calculator.tieRule: equal specificity: among these, the last declaration in document order wins (CSS Cascade Level 5, order of appearance).

note.universal: the universal selector is ignored when counting (Selectors Level 4).
note.where-zero: the specificity of :where() is replaced by zero, whatever its arguments.
note.is-max: the specificity of :is() is that of the most specific selector in its argument list.
note.not-max: the specificity of :not() is that of the most specific selector in its argument list; the negation changes nothing.
