ruleName.M39: CSP meta not a child of head

finding.M1: No title element. HTML 4.2.2: "The title element represents the document's title or name. Authors should use titles that identify their documents even when they are used out of context, for example in a user's history or bookmarks, or in search results."
finding.M2: {n} title elements. HTML 4.2.2: "There must be no more than one title element per document." The first one is read.
finding.M3: The title element is empty; it identifies nothing out of context.
finding.M4: No meta name=description. HTML 4.2.5.1 defines it as "a free-form string that describes the page. The value must be appropriate for use in a directory of pages, e.g. in a search engine"; Google: "In some situations, this description is used in the snippet shown in search results."
finding.M5: meta name={what} appears {n} times. HTML 4.2.5.1 allows it once: for description, "There must not be more than one meta element where the name attribute value is an ASCII case-insensitive match for description per document"; application-name once per language; color-scheme once per document.
finding.M7: No character encoding declaration. HTML 4.2.5.4: "If an HTML document does not start with a BOM, and its encoding is not explicitly given by Content-Type metadata, and the document is not an iframe srcdoc document, then the encoding must be specified using a meta element with a charset attribute or a meta element with an http-equiv attribute in the Encoding declaration state." "A character encoding declaration is required ... even when all characters are in the ASCII range".
finding.M8: {which, select, late {The declaration ends at byte {bytes}. HTML 4.2.5.4: "The element containing the character encoding declaration must be serialized completely within the first 1024 bytes of the document."} other {The declared encoding is "{what}". HTML 4.2.5.4: "The Encoding standard requires use of the UTF-8 character encoding and requires use of the "utf-8" encoding label to identify it"; the declaration "specifies an encoding label using an ASCII case-insensitive match for "utf-8"". Google: "We recommend using Unicode/UTF-8 where possible."}}
finding.M9: {n} character encoding declarations. HTML 4.2.5.4: "there can only be one meta-based character encoding declaration per document." The first one is read.
finding.M10: No meta name=viewport. MetaExtensions: it "provides a way for documents to specify ... the size, zoom factor, and orientation of the viewport"; Google: "Presence of this tag indicates to Google that the page is mobile friendly."
finding.M11: The viewport says {what}, which keeps the user from zooming. WCAG 2.2 SC 1.4.4 Resize Text (Level AA): "Except for captions and images of text, text can be resized without assistive technology up to 200 percent without loss of content or functionality."
finding.M12: No link rel=canonical. RFC 6596: "The canonical link relation specifies the preferred IRI from resources with duplicative content." Without one, applications choose the representative URL themselves.
finding.M13: {n} canonical links. RFC 6596 speaks of "the preferred IRI", one; which of several an application honours is not defined.
finding.M14: The canonical href "{what}" is relative. RFC 6596 allows it (the target "MAY: Specify a relative IRI"); it is resolved against the page's own URL, which this inspector does not have.
finding.M15: og:url is "{what}" and the canonical link is "{which}". ogp.me calls og:url "The canonical URL of your object that will be used as its permanent ID in the graph"; two different canonical URLs for one page are worth a second look.
finding.M16: Open Graph is present but {n, plural, one {one required property is missing: {what}} other {# required properties are missing: {what}}}. ogp.me: "The four required properties for every page are: og:title, og:type, og:image, og:url".
finding.M17: og:image "{what}" has no og:image:alt. ogp.me: "A description of what is in the image (not a caption). If the page specifies an og:image it should specify og:image:alt."
finding.M18: {what} appears before any {which} it could belong to. ogp.me: "Put structured properties after you declare their root tag." It attaches to nothing.
finding.M19: og:locale is "{what}". ogp.me: "Of the format language_TERRITORY. Default is en_US."
finding.M20: {which, select, name {{what} is written with name= rather than property=. ogp.me's markup is property=; the inspector reads it as Open Graph anyway, as many consumers do.} type {{what} is not one of ogp.me's global types (website, article, book, profile, the music.* and video.* types, payment.link) and is not a CURIE with a colon. ogp.me: "Any non-marked up webpage should be treated as og:type website."} other {{what} is not a property ogp.me lists (core, optional, structured or a vertical type's). Consumers ignore what they do not know.}}
finding.M21: No Open Graph properties. ogp.me: "Any non-marked up webpage should be treated as og:type website"; a share then falls back to the title and whatever the consumer scrapes.
finding.M22: twitter:* properties are present but there is no twitter:card. MetaExtensions registers twitter:card as "The card type, which will be one of "summary", "photo", "app", or "player"."
finding.M23: {which, select, common {twitter:card is "{what}", a type in common use that the MetaExtensions registry does not list (it names summary, photo, app and player). X's own card documentation is not published any more (checked 2026-10-05), so no current normative source is quoted.} other {twitter:card is "{what}", which is not one of the four types the MetaExtensions registry names (summary, photo, app, player) nor a type in common use.}}
finding.M24: {what} is not among the twitter:* names registered in MetaExtensions. It may still be read by X; the registry is the only published list the inspector can cite.
finding.M25: JSON-LD block {n} is not valid JSON: {what}. JSON-LD 1.1 section 7: a data block is JSON "in a script element with the type attribute set to application/ld+json"; a consumer that cannot parse it reads nothing.
finding.M26: JSON-LD block {n} has no @context. JSON-LD 1.1: the context (3.1) maps the short names in the document to IRIs; without it, "name" and "@type" values are not terms of any vocabulary.
finding.M27: {count, plural, one {One node} other {# nodes}} in JSON-LD block {n} {count, plural, one {has} other {have}} no @type. JSON-LD 1.1: "A node type specifies the type of thing that is being described"; consumers such as search engines act on typed nodes.
finding.M28: JSON-LD block {n} contains "'</script'" or "'<'!--". JSON-LD 1.1 section 7.2: authors "should avoid using character sequences in scripts embedded in HTML which may be confused with a comment-open, script-open, comment-close, or script-close"; escape them.
finding.M29: A script of type {what} contains "@context" and looks like JSON-LD; JSON-LD 1.1 section 7 reads data blocks from "a script element with the type attribute set to application/ld+json" only.
finding.M30: {which}: {what}. Google: "Do not show this page, media, or resource in search results."
finding.M31: Conflicting rules for {which}: {what}. Google: "In the case of conflicting robots rules, the more restrictive rule applies."
finding.M32: {which}: {what} is no longer used by Google Search (its documentation says so for noarchive, nocache and nositelinkssearchbox, "as the feature no longer exists").
finding.M33: {which}: "{what}" is not a rule in Google's published list (all, noindex, nofollow, none, nosnippet, indexifembedded, max-snippet, max-image-preview, max-video-preview, notranslate, noimageindex, unavailable_after). Other crawlers may define their own.
finding.M34: {what, select, several {A meta element with more than one of name, http-equiv, charset and itemprop.} other {A meta element with none of name, http-equiv, charset, itemprop (or RDFa's property).}} HTML 4.2.5: "Exactly one of the name, http-equiv, charset, and itemprop attributes must be specified."
finding.M35: meta {what} has no content attribute. HTML 4.2.5: "If either name, http-equiv, or itemprop is specified, then the content attribute must also be specified."
finding.M36: meta name="{what}" is neither a standard metadata name (HTML 4.2.5.1) nor a name registered in the WHATWG MetaExtensions wiki that this inspector knows. HTML 4.2.5.2: "Anyone can create and use their own extensions to the predefined set of metadata names"; registering is encouraged.
finding.M37: {what, select, redirect {meta refresh: after {seconds} s, go to {url}.} other {meta refresh: reload every {seconds} s.}} HTML 4.2.5.3: "This pragma acts as a timed redirect." Google: "it is not supported by all browsers and can be confusing to the user. We recommend using a server-side 301 redirect instead."
finding.M38: A Content-Security-Policy is delivered in a meta element. HTML 4.2.5.3: "This pragma enforces a Content Security Policy on a Document." The policy itself is read by the CSP evaluator (meta delivery ignores frame-ancestors, report-uri and sandbox).
finding.M39: The CSP meta element is not a child of head. HTML 4.2.5.3: "If the meta element is not a child of a head element, return." It enforces nothing.
finding.M40: http-equiv={what}. HTML 4.2.5.3: "This feature is non-conforming" (content-language: "Authors are encouraged to use the lang attribute instead"; set-cookie: "has no effect. User agents are required to ignore this pragma").
finding.M41: X-UA-Compatible is "{what}". HTML 4.2.5.3: the content "must have a value that is an ASCII case-insensitive match for the string "IE=edge"".
finding.M42: {what, select, empty {The root element's lang attribute is empty.} other {No lang attribute on the root element.}} HTML 4.1.1: "Authors are encouraged to specify a lang attribute on the root html element, giving the document's language. This aids speech synthesis tools to determine what pronunciations to use, translation tools to determine what rules to use, and so forth."
finding.M43: {n, plural, one {One meta element sits} other {# meta elements sit}} outside head. Document metadata belongs in head (HTML 4.2.1); Google notes it "will respect robots meta tags in the body section of an HTML document as well", which says nothing about other consumers.
finding.M44: {what, select, title {One title element with text.} description {One description.} charset {UTF-8 declared once, within the first 1024 bytes.} canonical {One canonical link.} opengraph {The four required Open Graph properties are present.} jsonld {JSON-LD block {n} is valid JSON with a @context and every node typed.} other {In order.}}
finding.M45: {n, plural, one {One hreflang alternate} other {# hreflang alternates}}; {what, select, xdefault {an x-default is among them} other {no x-default among them}}. link rel=alternate with hreflang is the HTML link type "alternate" (4.6.7) with the language of the alternate; which pages should list which alternates is the consumer's documentation, not the standard's.
finding.M46: {which} is "{what}", a relative URL. ogp.me describes og:url as "The canonical URL of your object" and og:image as "An image URL"; a consumer must resolve a relative one against the page URL, which the inspector does not have, and not every consumer does.

syslog-message-parser.name: Syslog message parser
syslog-message-parser.blurb: Paste one syslog message, or a TCP frame carrying one, and read every field named in the order its RFC names them: the PRI opened into facility and severity, the RFC 5424 header, the structured data element by element, the message; or the BSD form of RFC 3164 with its TIMESTAMP, HOSTNAME, TAG and CONTENT. Whatever is non-compliant is said in the RFC's own words. Nothing is sent anywhere.
syslog-message-parser.inputLabel: The message (one line, as received; a trailing newline or a leading octet count is read as framing)
syslog-message-parser.placeholder: <165>1 2003-10-11T22:14:15.003Z mymachine.example.com evntslog - ID47 [exampleSDID@32473 iut="3"] An application event log entry...

grammar.bsd: BSD syslog message (the form RFC 3164 describes).
grammar.unknown: Not a syslog message: no PRI at the start.

framing.octet-counting: TCP octet counting (RFC 6587): the frame declares {declared, plural, one {{declared} octet} other {{declared} octets}} and carries {actual}.
framing.non-transparent: TCP non-transparent framing (RFC 6587): the message ends with the LF trailer.

syslog-message-parser.lengthLine: {octets, plural, one {# octet} other {# octets}} ({chars, plural, one {# character} other {# characters}}).
syslog-message-parser.truncated: The input was cut at 8,192 characters.
syslog-message-parser.fieldsTitle: The fields, in the RFC's order

field.PRI: Facility × 8 + Severity in angle brackets; three to five characters (RFC 5424 §6.2.1).
field.VERSION: The protocol version; this RFC's is 1 (§6.2.2).
field.TIMESTAMP: RFC 3339 form: date, T, time, optional fraction of up to six digits, Z or an offset; or the NILVALUE (§6.2.3).
field.HOSTNAME: The originator: FQDN, static IP address, hostname or dynamic IP address, in that order of preference; 1 to 255 printable US-ASCII characters (§6.2.4).
field.APP-NAME: The device or application that originated the message; 1 to 48 characters (§6.2.5).
field.PROCID: A change in its value indicates a discontinuity in reporting (often the process ID); 1 to 128 characters (§6.2.6).
field.MSGID: The type of message; 1 to 32 characters (§6.2.7).
field.STRUCTURED-DATA: Zero or more elements, each [SD-ID param="value" ...]; the NILVALUE when none (§6.3).
field.MSG: Free-form text; UTF-8 when it starts with the BOM, otherwise of unknown encoding (§6.4).
field.HEADER: The header as far as it could be read.
field.TAG: The name of the program or process; alphanumeric, at most 32 characters, ended by the first other character (RFC 3164 §4.1.3).
field.CONTENT: The details of the message, free-form (RFC 3164 §4.1.3).
field.bsd-TIMESTAMP: "Mmm dd hh:mm:ss" in local time: no year, no zone; a day under 10 is written with a leading space (RFC 3164 §4.1.2).
field.bsd-HOSTNAME: The hostname as the device knows itself, or its IP address (RFC 3164 §4.1.2).

finding.pri-missing: no PRI at the start of the message
finding.pri-leading-zero: leading zero in the PRI: only the value 0 may start with 0 (RFC 5424 §6.2.1)
finding.version-not-1: a VERSION other than 1; this RFC defines 1 (§6.2.2)
finding.header-short: fewer header fields than the grammar requires
finding.timestamp-not-rfc3339: not the RFC 3339 form the RFC requires (§6.2.3)
finding.timestamp-lowercase-tz: T and Z must be upper case (§6.2.3)
finding.timestamp-leap-second: a 60th second: leap seconds must not be used (§6.2.3)
finding.sd-missing: structured data neither an element nor the NILVALUE (§6.3)
finding.sd-id-bad-chars: characters not allowed in an SD-ID (§6.3.2)
finding.sd-id-unregistered-no-pen: a name that is neither IANA-registered nor private with an enterprise number (§6.3.2)
finding.sd-param-unclosed: a parameter value with no closing quote (§6.3.3)
finding.sd-value-unescaped-bracket: a ] inside a value must be escaped (§6.3.3)
finding.sd-param-unknown-for-iana-id: a parameter the IANA SD-ID does not define (§7)
finding.sd-id-duplicate: the same SD-ID twice in one message (§6.3.2)
finding.msg-no-space: no space between the structured data and the MSG (§6)
finding.msg-non-ascii-without-bom: non-ASCII characters without the UTF-8 BOM: the encoding is unknown (§6.4)
finding.length-over-2048: over 2048 octets: beyond what receivers should accept (§6.1)
finding.length-over-480: over 480 octets: beyond what every receiver must accept (§6.1)
finding.bsd-month-unknown: not one of the twelve month abbreviations (RFC 3164 §4.1.2)
finding.bsd-tag-missing: no TAG at the start of the message part (RFC 3164 §4.1.3)
finding.bsd-no-header: no valid HEADER: a receiver treats everything after the PRI as the message (RFC 3164 §4.3)
finding.frame-length-mismatch: the octet count differs from the message's length (RFC 6587 §3.4.1)

syslog-message-parser.bsdTimestampParts: local time; the year and the zone are not in the message
syslog-message-parser.bomNo: No BOM: the encoding is not declared.
syslog-message-parser.sdTitle: Structured data: {n, plural, one {# element} other {# elements}}

timeQuality.tzKnown: whether the originator knows its time zone (0 or 1)
timeQuality.isSynced: whether the originator is synchronized to a reliable external time source (0 or 1)
timeQuality.syncAccuracy: the accuracy in microseconds, when synchronized

origin.ip: an IP address of the originator
origin.software: the software that generated the message, at most 48 characters

meta.sequenceId: an integer the originator increments per message, 1 to 2147483647
meta.sysUpTime: the originator's uptime in hundredths of a second (SNMP sysUpTime)
meta.language: the BCP 47 language tag of the MSG

limits.rfc5424: Length: {octets, plural, one {{octets} octet} other {{octets} octets}}. Every receiver must accept 480; every receiver should accept 2048 (RFC 5424 §6.1).
limits.bsd: Length: {octets, plural, one {{octets} byte} other {{octets} bytes}}. A BSD syslog packet must be 1024 bytes or less (RFC 3164 §4.1).

syslog-message-parser.transports: Transports: UDP port 514 (RFC 5426); TCP with octet counting or a trailer (RFC 6587); TLS on TCP port 6514 (RFC 5425).

log-level-mapper.name: Log level mapper
log-level-mapper.blurb: Pick a level in one logging system (syslog, the Linux kernel, Cisco IOS, Junos, Windows Event Log, .NET, Python, java.util.logging, Log4j 2, OpenTelemetry) and read its nearest equivalent in every other, with each system's own number and words, where the match is exact and where it is only the nearest rung. The bridge is OpenTelemetry's SeverityNumber, the one scale defined to hold the others. Nothing is sent anywhere.
log-level-mapper.levelLabel: The level (a name, or the system's own number)

error.unknown-level: {system} has no level named or numbered {level}.

log-level-mapper.sentinel: A sentinel, not a message level: it has no place on the severity scale and no equivalent elsewhere.
log-level-mapper.equivalentsTitle: The nearest level in every other system
log-level-mapper.nearest: {n, plural, one {# step} other {# steps}} away
log-level-mapper.tie: a tie: the mapping is not one-to-one
log-level-mapper.scaleNote: Distances are in SeverityNumber steps (1 to 24). Each ladder is placed on the scale by its own documentation or by OpenTelemetry's example mapping (Data Model Appendix B); where two rungs of a system are equally near, both are shown.
log-level-mapper.laddersTitle: Every ladder, on the one scale
log-level-mapper.colRungs: levels, most severe first, each with its own number and its SeverityNumber
log-level-mapper.laddersNote: Sources: RFC 5424 Table 2; the Linux kernel's printk documentation; the Cisco IOS command reference (logging buffered); Juniper's Junos syslog reference; the Windows event manifest schema; the .NET LogLevel enum; the Python logging documentation and the table of the OpenTelemetry SDK (software development kit) for Python itself; the Java SE 21 Level class; the Log4j 2 manual; the OpenTelemetry Logs Data Model and its Appendix B. All read on 2026-10-05; the full list is under Sources below the tool.

share.carries: The link carries the system and the level as typed, and nothing else.

cisco-ios.caveat: Syslog's numbers with Cisco's keywords; the command reference maps each to its LOG_* constant; the default buffered level is generally 7.

dotnet.caveat: 0 is the least severe; None (6) is a filter value, not a message level.

jul.caveat: Numbers grow with severity; CONFIG sits between INFO and FINE; OFF and ALL are the integer extremes, not levels.

junos.caveat: Names only on Juniper's page, in syslog's order from emergency to info; "any" selects every level and "none" disables logging; there is no named debug rung.

log4j2.caveat: A lower priority number is more severe (FATAL 100, TRACE 600); OFF (0) and ALL (Integer.MAX_VALUE) are filters, not levels.

otel.caveat: The scale the others are placed on: 24 values in six ranges of four; 0 is unspecified.

printk.caveat: Eight levels named and numbered like syslog's severities, written as strings in the message prefix; placed on the scale by that correspondence of name and number. KERN_DEFAULT (no prefix) and KERN_CONT ("c") are not levels.

python.caveat: Numbers grow with severity in steps of ten; NOTSET (0) means "inherit"; any integer is a legal level, and the OpenTelemetry SDK for Python maps the tens exactly (10 DEBUG, 20 INFO, 30 WARN, 40 ERROR, 50 FATAL) and the values between to the range's second, third and fourth steps.

syslog.caveat: 0 is the most severe; eight levels, three of them (Emergency, Alert, Critical) above most other ladders' top.

windows.caveat: 1 is the most severe; 0 (LogAlways) is not a level; custom levels 16 to 255 are provider-defined.

dotnet.Critical: an unrecoverable application or system crash, or a catastrophic failure that requires immediate attention
dotnet.Error: the current flow of execution is stopped due to a failure
dotnet.Information: the general flow of the application
dotnet.None: not used for writing log messages
dotnet.Trace: the most detailed messages; may contain sensitive application data
dotnet.Warning: an abnormal or unexpected event in the application flow

otel.FATAL: a fatal error such as an application or system crash (21 to 24)
otel.TRACE: fine-grained debugging, typically disabled by default (1 to 4)
otel.WARN: not an error but likely more important than informational (13 to 16)

python.CRITICAL: a serious error, indicating that the program itself may be unable to continue running
python.DEBUG: detailed information, typically only of interest to a developer
python.ERROR: the software has not been able to perform some function
python.INFO: confirmation that things are working as expected
python.NOTSET: ancestor loggers are consulted to determine the effective level
python.WARNING: something unexpected happened, or a problem might occur in the near future

windows.Critical: an abnormal exit or termination event
windows.Informational: a non-error event such as an entry or exit event
windows.Warning: a warning event such as an allocation failure

rpki-origin-validation.name: Route origin validation calculator
rpki-origin-validation.blurb: Paste a route (prefix and origin AS) and the VRPs you have, and get its RFC 6811 state (Valid, Invalid or NotFound) with the reason VRP by VRP: which VRPs cover it, which match, and why the others fail. AS 0 and maxLength are handled as the RFCs state them, IPv4 and IPv6 alike, and nothing is fetched.
rpki-origin-validation.vrpsLabel: VRPs (Validated ROA Payloads): one per line, or a SLURM JSON file
rpki-origin-validation.formatHelp: Each line holds a prefix, an optional maxLength and the AS, in that order; the AS may be asplain (AS64496 or 64496) or asdot (AS1.10). The maxLength may also follow the prefix after a hyphen (203.0.113.0/24-26, as RFC 9319 writes it). Without a maxLength only the exact prefix is authorized. An AS written with its AS prefix may stand anywhere on the line (AS64496,192.0.2.0/24,24). A # starts a comment. You can also paste RFC 8416 SLURM JSON: its prefixAssertions are read as the VRPs.
rpki-origin-validation.runsLocally: Runs in your browser and fetches nothing: no RPKI repository, no validator, no route collector. The verdict holds for the VRPs you paste and for no other list.

errors.route-empty: Enter a route: a prefix and its origin AS, such as 192.0.2.0/24 AS64496.
errors.route-format: A route is a prefix and its origin AS separated by a space, such as 192.0.2.0/24 AS64496, or NONE for the origin value RFC 6811 calls NONE.
errors.prefix-format: That is not a prefix: write address/length, with a length of at most 32 for IPv4 or 128 for IPv6.
errors.host-bits: The address has bits set beyond the prefix length (192.0.2.1/24 names a host, not a prefix): write the network address, such as 192.0.2.0/24.
errors.origin-format: That is not an AS number: write it in asplain (AS64496 or 64496) or in asdot (AS1.10), the notations of RFC 5396.
errors.origin-as0: A route whose origin is AS 0 is malformed: RFC 7607 section 2 says a BGP speaker MUST NOT originate or propagate one, so it never reaches validation. AS 0 belongs in a ROA, not in a route.
errors.as-range: AS numbers run from 0 to 4294967295 (four octets); in asdot each half runs from 0 to 65535.
errors.vrps-empty: Enter at least one VRP: a prefix, an optional maxLength and an AS, one per line.
errors.vrp-format: A VRP line holds one prefix, an optional maxLength and one AS, such as 192.0.2.0/24 24 AS64496.
errors.maxlength-range: maxLength must be at least the prefix length and at most 32 for IPv4 or 128 for IPv6 (RFC 9582 section 4.3.2.2).
errors.too-many: That is more than this tool reads at once: at most 20000 VRPs or 1000000 characters, and 200 characters for the route.
errors.slurm-format: The JSON is not a SLURM file, an object with prefixAssertions or an array of prefix assertions (RFC 8416 section 3.4.1), or an assertion lacks its prefix or its asn.
errors.slurm-member: The JSON uses a member RFC 8416 does not define: an assertion carries prefix and asn, and optionally maxPrefixLength and comment (sections 3.1 and 3.4.1).
errors.request-format: The request must be an object with a route and a vrps member.

Valid.label: Valid.
Valid.why: {matching, plural, one {# VRP matches} other {# VRPs match}} this route, which means covering the prefix, allowing its length within maxLength and naming the route's origin as the AS (RFC 6811 section 2).

Invalid.label: Invalid.
Invalid.why: {covering, plural, one {# VRP covers} other {# VRPs cover}} this prefix and none matches the route, so the route is Invalid (RFC 6811 section 2). The table says why each covering VRP fails.

NotFound.label: NotFound.
NotFound.why: No VRP in the list covers this prefix, so origin validation has nothing to say about it (RFC 6811 section 2). NotFound is not a pass: no ROA in the list speaks for this address space.

table.heading: VRP by VRP ({count, plural, one {# VRP} other {# VRPs}})
table.implied: (no maxLength given: the exact prefix only)
table.viaMaxLength: Matched through the maxLength range: the route is longer than the VRP prefix.
table.rule: RFC 6811 section 2: a VRP covers a route when its prefix length is no longer than the route's and the two prefixes agree on every bit of the VRP's length; it matches when it covers, the route's length is no more than the VRP's maxLength and its AS is the route's origin. Valid: at least one VRP matches. Invalid: at least one covers and none matches. NotFound: none covers.

match.label: Match
match.why: covers, /{length} is within maxLength {maxLength}, and AS{asn} is the origin.

wrong-as.label: Another AS
wrong-as.why: covers, but it authorizes AS{asn}, not this origin.

too-specific.label: Too specific
too-specific.why: covers, but /{length} is longer than its maxLength {maxLength}.

wrong-as-and-too-specific.label: Another AS, too specific
wrong-as-and-too-specific.why: covers, but it authorizes AS{asn} and only up to /{maxLength}.

as0.label: AS 0
as0.why: covers, but a VRP with AS 0 can never be matched (RFC 6811 section 2): the holder states the space should not be routed (RFC 6483 section 4).

origin-none.label: Origin NONE
origin-none.why: covers, but a route whose origin is NONE cannot be matched by any VRP (RFC 6811 section 2).

not-covering.label: Does not cover
not-covering.why: the route's prefix is outside this VRP, or shorter than it.

other-family.label: Other family
other-family.why: an IPv4 VRP and an IPv6 route, or the reverse: never compared.

notes.heading: Notes
notes.as0-only: Every VRP that covers this prefix names AS 0. RFC 6483 section 4 reads such a ROA as the holder's statement that the prefix "and any more specific prefix, should not be used in a routing context", and RFC 7607 section 2 says a BGP speaker MUST NOT originate or propagate a route with AS 0 in its AS_PATH.
notes.as0-overridden: An AS 0 VRP also covers this prefix, but another VRP matches, so the route is Valid: RFC 6483 section 4 gives an AS 0 ROA "a lower relative preference than any other ROA that has a routable AS as its subject".
notes.origin-none: The origin is NONE: RFC 6811 section 2 uses that value when the AS_PATH ends in a segment that is not AS_SEQUENCE, AS_CONFED_SEQUENCE or AS_CONFED_SET. Such a route can be Invalid or NotFound, never Valid.
notes.duplicates-removed: {count, plural, one {# duplicate VRP was} other {# duplicate VRPs were}} counted once: the same prefix, maxLength and AS twice add nothing (RFC 8416 section 3.4.1 sends the set excluding duplicates).
notes.slurm-filters-not-applied: The SLURM file holds {filters, plural, one {# prefixFilter} other {# prefixFilters}}, not applied here: filters remove VRPs that came from RPKI validation, and RFC 8416 section 3.2 says "Locally Added Assertions MUST NOT be removed by output filtering". Only the file's prefixAssertions are compared.
notes.valid-via-maxlength: Every match comes through a maxLength range: the route is more specific than the VRP prefix, and the VRP's maxLength allows it.

maxLength.heading: maxLength wider than the prefix (RFC 9319)
maxLength.item: VRP {index}: {prefix} with maxLength {maxLength} for AS{asn} authorizes {count, plural, one {{count} prefix} other {{count} prefixes}}, every prefix inside it from its own length to /{maxLength}.
maxLength.rfc9319: RFC 9319 (BCP 185) recommends minimal ROAs, holding "only those IP prefixes that are actually originated by an AS in BGP", and says operators "SHOULD avoid using the maxLength attribute in their ROAs, since its inclusion will usually make the ROA non-minimal" (section 5). It explains that prefixes a ROA authorizes but its AS does not announce are vulnerable to what it calls a forged-origin sub-prefix hijack (sections 1, 3 and 4). Whether that applies to these prefixes depends on what the AS really announces, which this tool cannot see.

share.carries: The link carries the Route and the VRP list as typed, and nothing else.

cgn-port-blocks.name: CGN port blocks and MAP port sets
cgn-port-blocks.blurb: Divide one public IPv4 address among subscribers: port blocks per address and per pool (RFC 7768), RFC 7422 deterministic mapping with its forward and reverse lookup, and the MAP-E and MAP-T port set of a PSID (RFC 7597), with the log volume that blocks remove.
cgn-port-blocks.title: Port blocks and port sets
cgn-port-blocks.runsLocally: Runs in your browser: integer arithmetic over the inputs, no network and no clock (times are inputs).

modeDesc.blocks: How many blocks fit on one address, how many subscribers a pool holds when each keeps all its blocks on one address (RFC 6888 REQ-2), and how much per-session logging the blocks remove (RFC 7768).
modeDesc.deterministic: RFC 7422 algorithm 0 (Sequential): remove the reserved ports R, give each inside address 1/(C+D) of the rest, and keep the remainder as the dynamic pool. Look up an inside address, or reverse an outside address, port and time.
modeDesc.map: The MAP port field is A, then the PSID, then j (RFC 7597 section 5.1, used unchanged by MAP-T): give the offset a, the PSID length k and a PSID to list its ranges, or a port to find the PSID that owns it.

blocks.pool: Public pool (prefix, range, address or count)
blocks.inside: Or the inside prefix or range

deterministic.outside: Outside range O (address, prefix or range)
deterministic.compressionRatio: Compression ratio C (blank: I / O rounded up)

errors.json: The request must be a JSON object that names its mode.
errors.mode: Choose a mode: blocks, deterministic or map.
errors.field: A required field is missing or has the wrong type.
errors.address: An address is not a valid IPv4 address (four octets from 0 to 255, without leading zeros).
errors.prefix: A prefix length must be from 0 to 32.
errors.range: An address range runs backwards: give the lower address first.
errors.count: An address set must hold at least 1 address and at most a /8.
errors.port-range: The usable ports must be a range such as 1024-65535, running forwards inside 0 to 65535.
errors.reserved: The reserved list R takes ports and ranges separated by commas, such as 0-1023,5004,5060.
errors.block-size: The block size must be at least 1 and no larger than the usable ports of one address.
errors.blocks-per-subscriber: One subscriber's blocks must fit on one address: RFC 6888 REQ-2 keeps a subscriber on one external address.
errors.subscribers: The subscriber count must be a whole number of at least 1.
errors.ratio: C must be a whole number of at least 1, and C times O must cover every inside address; D must be 0 or more.
errors.no-ports: C + D is larger than the number of candidate ports, so no inside address would get a port.
errors.time: Times are UTC to the second, written as YYYY-MM-DDTHH:MM:SSZ.
errors.window: The configuration window ends before it starts.
errors.map-bits: a and k are whole numbers with a + k at most 16, the width of the port field.
errors.psid: The PSID must be from 0 to 2^k - 1 (decimal, or hexadecimal with 0x).
errors.port: A port must be from 0 to 65535.

blocks.pairedNote: Each subscriber's blocks are counted on one address: RFC 6888 REQ-2 makes a CGN use the same external address for all of a subscriber's sessions, and REQ-4 asks for a configurable per-subscriber port limit, here the block size times the blocks per subscriber.
blocks.leftoverNote: Left over on each address: {ports, plural, one {{ports} port} other {{ports} ports}} that no whole block covers, and {blocks, plural, one {{blocks} block} other {{blocks} blocks}}, too few for another full subscriber share.
blocks.systemExcluded: The usable range {first}-{last} leaves out the System Ports 0-1023 (RFC 6335 section 6), which RFC 7422 says a CGN should at least remove.
blocks.systemIncluded: The usable range {first}-{last} includes System Ports (0-1023, RFC 6335 section 6). RFC 7422 says a CGN should at least remove them, and RFC 6269 calls 1024-65535 safe for outgoing source ports.
blocks.fits: The pool holds them: {needed} of its {have, plural, one {{have} address} other {{have} addresses}} {needed, plural, one {is} other {are}} needed.
blocks.doesNotFit: The pool is too small: {needed, plural, one {{needed} address is} other {{needed} addresses are}} needed and it has {have}. Use smaller blocks, fewer blocks per subscriber, or more addresses.
blocks.logHeading: Log volume per subscriber per day
blocks.logNote: The per-session row uses RFC 7422 section 1: about {connections} connections per household per day and {bytes}-byte messages. RFC 7768 section 2 says blocks reduce log generation by a factor equal to the block size, here {factor}; the block row divides by that factor, so it is computed, not measured.

det.reservedNote: Reserved ports R: {list} ({ports, plural, one {{ports} port} other {{ports} ports}}), removed first (RFC 7422 section 2, step 1).
det.systemPortsWarning: Some System Ports (0-1023) are left as candidates; RFC 7422 says a CGN should at least remove them.
det.dynamicRanges: Dynamic pool on each outside address: {ranges}. Blocks given out from it must be logged (step 4).
det.leftoverNote: With D = 0 the dynamic pool is disabled, yet the division leaves {ports, plural, one {{ports} port} other {{ports} ports}} over: the remainder of the candidate ports divided by C.
det.overflowNote: M = {m}: a subscriber may take {extra, plural, one {{extra} more port} other {{extra} more ports}} from the dynamic pool, enough for {users} subscribers at their full overflow at once.
det.maxBelowBlock: M is smaller than the pre-allocated block, so the block alone exceeds the maximum per user.
det.unusedSlots: {slots, plural, one {{slots} block on the last outside address is} other {{slots} blocks on the last outside address are}} held by no inside address.
det.loggingNone: D = 0: no translation logging, which RFC 7422 notes limits the connections power users can open. Only the configuration record is kept (section 3).
det.loggingDynamic: D > 0: pre-allocated ports are not logged, dynamically assigned blocks must be (step 4), and the configuration record is kept (section 3).
det.forwardNotInside: {inside} is not in the inside range I.
det.reverseHeading: Reverse: outside address, port and time

reverse.deterministic: {address} port {port} is in the block of {inside} ({ranges}): found by arithmetic, without the translation logs.
reverse.dynamic: {address} port {port} is in the dynamic pool ({ranges}): only the dynamic block log can say who held it at that time.
reverse.reserved: Port {port} is reserved (in R): no subscriber is mapped to it.
reverse.unassigned: {address} port {port} is in a block ({ranges}) that no inside address holds.
reverse.not-in-pool: {address} is not in the outside range O.

det.outsideWindow: The time {time} falls outside the window in which this configuration was in force: use the configuration record for that time.
det.insideWindow: The time {time} falls inside the window in which this configuration was in force.
det.reverseNext: RFC 7422 section 2.3 then correlates the inside address with the DHCP or PPP lease records for that time, and accurate clocks are vital (RFC 6269 section 12).

missing.inside-prefix: the inside range as a prefix
missing.outside-prefix: the outside range as a prefix or one address

det.tableOmitted: The table is shown for up to 256 inside addresses and this plan has {rows}; use the forward and reverse lookups.

map.layout: The 16-bit port is A ({a, plural, one {{a} bit} other {{a} bits}}), then the PSID ({k, plural, one {{k} bit} other {{k} bits}}), then j ({m, plural, one {{m} bit} other {{m} bits}}). Every CE that shares the address must use the same a and k (RFC 7597 section 5.1).
map.excluded: With a > 0, A must be larger than 0, so ports 0-{last} belong to no CE, which keeps out the System Ports 0-1023.
map.excludedPartial: With a > 0, A must be larger than 0, so ports 0-{last} belong to no CE; with this offset some System Ports (up to 1023) stay in the port sets. RFC 7597 sets a = 6 by default to exclude 0-1023.
map.offsetZero: With a = 0 each port set is one contiguous range and nothing is excluded; RFC 7597 Appendix B.1 keeps low ports out by allowing only PSIDs from {psid} up, which leaves 0-1023 unassigned.
map.lostRange: Its range in the excluded A = 0 block, {range}, is the 2^m ports the section 5.1 formula subtracts.
map.includesSystem: This port set includes System Ports (0-1023).
map.reverseExcluded: Port {port} has A = 0: with a > 0 it belongs to no CE's port set.
map.reverseOwner: Port {port} belongs to PSID {psid} ({hex}): A = {aValue}, j = {j}.

share.carries: The link carries the open tab and the values typed in it; the other tabs stay out.

routing-table-explainer.name: Routing table explainer
routing-table-explainer.blurb: Paste the output of ip route, netstat -rn or route print to read every route field by field, see which default route wins, and ask which route a destination would use, by longest prefix and then metric.

input.label: Routing table output (ip route, netstat -rn, route print)
input.placeholder:
default via 192.0.2.1 dev eth0
192.0.2.0/24 dev eth0 proto kernel scope link src 192.0.2.2

routing-table-explainer.privacy: Parsed in your browser: the text never leaves this page, and no route is changed or queried.

iproute2.name: Linux iproute2 (ip route)
iproute2.note: One route per line: an optional type, the destination (default stands for 0/0 or ::/0), then keyword and value pairs such as via, dev, proto, scope, src, metric and table, as ip-route(8) defines them.

netstat-linux.name: Linux net-tools (netstat -rn, route -n)
netstat-linux.note: The Kernel IP routing table: Destination with Genmask gives the prefix, and the Flags column says whether a gateway is used, with the columns route(8) describes under OUTPUT. netstat -r prints what route -e prints (netstat(8)).

netstat-bsd.name: BSD or macOS netstat -rn
netstat-bsd.note: Routing tables, then one section per family (Internet: and Internet6:). Each route is a destination and a gateway, and the Flags letters say how the route is used (FreeBSD netstat(1), Apple netstat.1).

windows.name: Windows route print
windows.note: An Interface List, then an IPv4 and an IPv6 route table, each with Active Routes (in use) and Persistent Routes (stored configuration). On-link in the Gateway column means no next-hop router.

unknown.name: Not recognized
unknown.note: No line looked like ip route, netstat -rn or route print output, so every line is listed below as not understood.

warnings.no-routes: No route was found in the text.
warnings.truncated: Only the first 5000 lines were read.
warnings.line-too-long: A line longer than 2000 characters was kept as not understood.
warnings.netstat-linux-ipv6: The Kernel IPv6 routing table is listed as not understood: route(8) describes the IPv4 columns only. Paste the output of ip -6 route instead.

defaults.title: Default routes
defaults.none: No default route (prefix length 0) in this table: a destination that matches no other route has nowhere to go.

reasons.single: Only one default route here, so it carries everything that no longer prefix matches.
reasons.lowest-metric: Several default routes have the same prefix length (zero), so the metric decides: the lowest value wins.
reasons.equal-metric: Several default routes share the lowest metric, so these rules alone cannot name one.
reasons.no-metric: These default routes carry no comparable metric, so no winner can be named from this text.

defaults.notConsulted: This table is not reached by the three default policy rules (local, main, default): it is used only when an ip rule points to it.
defaults.notConsultedWindows: These are Persistent Routes: stored configuration that fills the table when TCP/IP starts, not the routes in use, which are listed under Active Routes.

table.title: Routes
table.help: Each row is one route as printed. Select a row number to read its fields one by one.

reading.title: Route #{n}, line {line}, field by field
reading.destDefault: The default route: prefix length zero, so it contains every {family} address and loses to any longer prefix that also contains the destination (RFC 1812, section 5.2.4.3).
reading.destHost: A host route: {prefix} is one single address.
reading.destNetwork: A network prefix: an address matches when its first {len, plural, one {{len} bit} other {{len} bits}} equal those of {prefix}.
reading.destUnparsed: Not an address with a length (a name, an abbreviation or a redacted value): shown as printed and left out of lookups.
reading.hopVia: Handed to the router {gw}, which must itself be reachable on a connected link.
reading.hopOnLink: No next-hop router: the destination is reached directly on {iface}.
reading.hopMultipath: A multipath route with {count} next hops, listed below.
reading.hopByType: None: this route type does not forward to a next hop (see Type).
reading.srcHelp: The source address to prefer when sending to the destinations covered by the route prefix (ip-route(8)).
reading.weightHelp: A weight reflects the hop's relative bandwidth or quality (ip-route(8), nexthop).
reading.unparsedHelp: These tokens are kept exactly as printed, and no meaning is guessed for them.

interfaces.netstat-linux: Iface: the interface to which packets for this route will be sent (route(8)).
interfaces.netstat-bsd: Netif: the network interface used for the route (netstat(1)).
interfaces.windows-ipv4: Interface: the address of the local adapter used when a datagram is forwarded (Microsoft Learn, The IP routing table).
interfaces.windows-ipv6: If: the interface index; the Interface List names the adapter.

metrics.iproute2: metric: a 32-bit number; among routes of equal prefix length, lower values are preferred (ip-route(8)).
metrics.iproute2-none: No metric printed. In the capture behind this tool's examples, a route that ip route printed without a metric read Metric 0 in route -n, so such a route is compared as 0.
metrics.netstat-linux: Metric: the distance to the target, usually counted in hops (route(8)); among equal prefixes the lower value wins.
metrics.netstat-linux-none: No Metric column: netstat -rn prints MSS, Window and irtt instead, and route -n prints the metric.
metrics.netstat-bsd-none: BSD netstat prints no metric, so routes of equal prefix length cannot be ranked from this text.
metrics.windows: Metric: the cost of using the route; when several routes lead to the same destination, the lowest metric is selected (Microsoft Learn, The IP routing table). Persistent Routes may read Default.

types.unicast: The route entry describes real paths to the destinations covered by the route prefix (ip-route(8)).
types.local: The destinations are assigned to this host: the packets are looped back and delivered locally.
types.broadcast: The destinations are broadcast addresses: the packets are sent as link broadcasts.
types.multicast: A special type used for multicast routing, not present in normal routing tables.
types.throw: A control route for policy routing: when it is selected, the lookup in this table ends as if no route were found and the next rule is tried; without policy routing the packet is dropped with ICMP net unreachable.
types.unreachable: The packets are discarded and ICMP host unreachable is generated; local senders get EHOSTUNREACH.
types.prohibit: The packets are discarded and ICMP communication administratively prohibited is generated; local senders get EACCES.
types.blackhole: The packets are discarded silently; local senders get EINVAL.
types.nat: A Route NAT entry, which ip-route(8) says is no longer supported since Linux 2.6.
types.anycast: Listed by ip-route(8) as not implemented.
types.reject: The reject flag is set: host or net unreachable (netstat(1); the ! flag of route(8)).

tables.main: The main table (ID 254): by default all normal routes are inserted here.
tables.local: The local table (ID 255): routes for local and broadcast addresses, maintained by the kernel.
tables.default: The default table (ID 253), consulted last by the default rules and empty unless filled.
tables.other: Any other table is consulted only when a policy rule (ip rule) points to it.

protocols.kernel: Installed by the kernel during autoconfiguration (ip-route(8)).
protocols.boot: Installed during the bootup sequence; a routing daemon that starts purges it. ip assumes boot when no protocol is given.
protocols.static: Installed by the administrator to override dynamic routing; routing daemons respect it.
protocols.redirect: Installed because of an ICMP redirect.
protocols.other: Not one of the fixed values: such tags are free for daemons and administrators, and the kernel does not interpret them (rtnetlink(7)).

scopes.host: A route on the local host; ip assumes it for local routes.
scopes.link: A route on this link; ip assumes it for direct unicast and broadcast routes.
scopes.global: A global route; ip assumes it for all gatewayed unicast routes.
scopes.site: An interior route in the local autonomous system (rtnetlink(7)).
scopes.other: A numeric or locally named scope, kept as printed.

flags.RTF_BROADCAST: The route represents a broadcast address.
flags.RTF_LLINFO: Valid protocol to link address translation.
flags.RTF_XRESOLVE: External daemon translates protocol to link address.
flags.RTF_PRCLONING: Protocol-specified generate new routes on use.
flags.RTF_IFSCOPE: Route is associated with an interface scope.
flags.RTF_IFREF: Route is holding a reference to the interface.
flags.RTF_MULTICAST: The route represents a multicast address.
flags.RTF_WASCLONED: Route was generated as a result of cloning.
flags.RTF_PROXY: Proxying; cloned routes will not be scoped.
flags.RTF_GLOBAL: Route to a destination of the global internet (policy hint).
flags.LINUX_R: R: reinstate route for dynamic routing.
flags.LINUX_D: D: dynamically installed by daemon or redirect.
flags.LINUX_M: M: modified from routing daemon or redirect.
flags.unknown: No manual read for this tool lists this letter, so it is shown as printed.

nhflags.onlink: Pretend that the next hop is directly attached to this link, even if it does not match any interface prefix (ip-route(8)).
nhflags.pervasive: A next-hop flag listed in ip-route(8) under NHFLAGS.

attrs.pref: The IPv6 route preference of RFC 4191: low, medium or high.
attrs.mtu: The MTU along the path to the destination.
attrs.nhid: Uses the nexthop object with this id as the next hop.
attrs.expires: A route option listed in ip-route(8) under OPTIONS (expires TIME).
attrs.advmss: The MSS to advertise to these destinations when establishing TCP connections.
attrs.Refs: The current number of active uses of the route (netstat(1)).
attrs.Use: BSD: the number of packets sent using the route (netstat(1)). Linux: the count of lookups for the route (route(8)).
attrs.Expire: The route's timeout: it is deleted if the host does not respond in time (FreeBSD Handbook).
attrs.Ref: The number of references to this route, not used in the Linux kernel (route(8)).
attrs.MSS: The default maximum segment size for TCP connections over this route.
attrs.Window: The default window size for TCP connections over this route.
attrs.irtt: The initial round trip time, which the kernel uses to guess the best TCP parameters.
attrs.other: A per-route option listed in ip-route(8) under OPTIONS, kept as printed.

notes.host-route-no-length: Printed without a length: ip assumes a full-length host route (ip-route(8)).
notes.default-family-from-context: default with no address on its line: its family is taken from the other routes.
notes.non-contiguous-mask: The netmask is not a run of ones followed by zeros, so it gives no prefix length; the route is left out of lookups.
notes.destination-not-an-address: The destination is not an address with a length (a name, an abbreviation or a redacted value), so the route is left out of lookups.
notes.network-without-length: A network printed without a length and without the H flag: its length cannot be read from this text.
notes.gateway-link: {gw} names an interface, not a router: this is a direct route.

lookup.title: Which route does this destination use?
lookup.label: Destination address (IPv4 or IPv6)
lookup.rules: Basic match keeps every route whose prefix contains the address, longest match keeps the longest of them, and among equal lengths the lowest metric wins (RFC 1812, section 5.2.4.3; ip-route(8)).

errors.bad-address: Enter one IPv4 or IPv6 address, without a length or a zone.
errors.bad-request: That request could not be read.

actions.nat: a Route NAT entry, no longer supported.
actions.tie: Several routes share the longest prefix and the lowest metric, so these rules cannot name one.
actions.no-route: No route contains this address: the packet is discarded as unreachable.

decidedBy.only-candidate: Only one route contains the address.
decidedBy.longest-prefix: Several routes contain it, and the longest prefix wins.
decidedBy.lowest-metric: Several routes of the same, longest length contain it, and the lowest metric wins.

outcomes.no-match: Nothing here, so the next table is consulted.
outcomes.throw: A throw route won: the lookup leaves this table as if nothing matched.
outcomes.tie: Undecided: equal length and equal metric.

skipped.policy-rule-only: {section} was not consulted: only a policy rule reaches it.
skipped.persistent-store: {section} was not consulted: persistent routes are configuration, not routes in use.

lookup.unusable: Left out because the destination is not an address with a length: {list}.
lookup.throwNoRoute: A throw route ended the lookup in its table and no later table matched; without policy routing the packet is dropped with ICMP net unreachable (ip-route(8)).

interfaceList.title: Interface List
interfaceList.help: Windows numbers its adapters, and the If column of the IPv6 table refers to these numbers.

unparsed.title: Lines not understood
unparsed.help: Kept exactly as pasted: nothing is dropped silently.

share.carries: The link carries the table as pasted and, if you typed one, the destination.
share.caution: A routing table names internal addresses, gateways and interfaces: read it before you send the link.

tools.metaDescription: Networking and security tools that compute in your browser: subnet and IPv6 calculators, certificate and token decoders and more, found by what you paste or what you need to do, each with its own documentation.

xml-formatter.name: XML Formatter & Validator
xml-formatter.blurb: Check that an XML document is well-formed, with the line, column and reason when it is not, then pretty-print it with two spaces, four spaces or tabs, or minify it. Text, CDATA sections, comments, processing instructions and xml:space="preserve" content are kept as written; no entity is expanded and nothing is fetched. Runs in your browser.
xml-formatter.inputPlaceholder: Paste an XML document to check and format, such as a SAML message or a configuration file.
xml-formatter.runsLocally: Checked and formatted in your browser: nothing is sent anywhere, no entity is expanded and no DTD is fetched.
xml-formatter.excerptLabel: The line where the document fails, with a caret under the column

errors.empty: The box holds only white space: there is no XML document to check.
errors.too-large: The document is longer than {max} characters, the most this tool reads.
errors.too-deep: Elements are nested more than {max} levels deep, the most this tool reads.
errors.illegal-character: The character {char} is not allowed anywhere in an XML 1.0 document (section 2.2).
errors.bad-xml-declaration: The XML declaration is malformed. It reads <?xml version="1.0"?>, optionally with encoding and then standalone, in that order, and the version is 1. followed by digits (section 2.8).
errors.misplaced-xml-declaration: An XML declaration may only be the very first thing in the document, with nothing before it, not even a line break or a space (sections 2.6 and 2.8).
errors.bad-pi: A processing instruction starts with a target name, followed by white space or ?>; the target cannot be xml in any mix of cases (section 2.6).
errors.unterminated-pi: This processing instruction is never closed with ?>.
errors.unterminated-comment: This comment is never closed with -->.
errors.comment-double-hyphen: A comment may not contain two hyphens in a row, and may not end with three hyphens before the > (section 2.5).
errors.unterminated-cdata: This CDATA section is never closed with ]]>.
errors.cdata-outside-root: A CDATA section may only appear inside an element, not before or after the root (section 2.7).
errors.bad-doctype: The document type declaration is malformed: after <!DOCTYPE come white space, the root element's name, an optional SYSTEM or PUBLIC identifier in quotes, an optional internal subset in square brackets, and > (section 2.8).
errors.unterminated-doctype: The document type declaration is never closed.
errors.bad-internal-subset: The internal DTD subset may hold only markup declarations (<!ELEMENT, <!ATTLIST, <!ENTITY, <!NOTATION), comments, processing instructions, parameter-entity references and white space. A parameter-entity reference may not appear inside a declaration there, and an entity declaration must follow its grammar (sections 2.8 and 4.2).
errors.misplaced-doctype: The document type declaration must come once, before the root element (section 2.8).
errors.unknown-markup: Unrecognized markup: inside a document, <! starts only a comment, a CDATA section or the document type declaration.
errors.bad-start-tag: Malformed start tag: a name, an attribute, > or /> was expected here (section 3.1). For a literal less-than sign in text, write <.
errors.bad-attribute: Malformed attribute: an attribute is a name, an equals sign and a value in single or double quotes, separated from the previous one by white space (section 3.1).
errors.duplicate-attribute: The attribute {name} appears twice in the same tag (section 3.1, Unique Att Spec).
errors.lt-in-attribute: An attribute value may not contain a literal less-than sign; write < (section 3.1).
errors.unterminated-tag: This tag is never closed with > or />.
errors.bad-end-tag: Malformed end tag: after the element name only white space and > may follow (section 3.1).
errors.mismatched-end-tag: The end tag {found} does not match the open element {expected} (section 3.1, Element Type Match).
errors.unexpected-end-tag: The end tag {found} has no open element to close.
errors.unclosed-element: The element {name} opened here is never closed.
errors.bad-reference: An ampersand must start a reference such as &, & or & (sections 2.4 and 4.1). For a literal ampersand, write &.
errors.illegal-char-reference: The character reference {ref} names a character that XML 1.0 does not allow (section 4.1, Legal Character).
errors.undeclared-entity: The entity {ref} is not declared. Without a declaration, only &, <, >, ' and " may be used; HTML names such as   are not XML (section 4.1, Entity Declared).
errors.unparsed-entity-reference: The entity {ref} is an unparsed entity (declared with NDATA): it may be named in an ENTITY attribute, never referenced in text (section 4.1, Parsed Entity).
errors.external-entity-in-attribute: The entity {ref} is an external entity, and an attribute value may not refer to one (section 3.1, No External Entity References).
errors.cdata-end-in-text: The sequence ]]> may not appear in text; write ]]> (section 2.4).
errors.text-outside-root: Text is not allowed outside the root element: only comments, processing instructions and white space may come before or after it (sections 2.1 and 2.8).
errors.multiple-roots: A second top-level element starts here, but a document has exactly one root element (section 2.1).
errors.no-root: The document has no root element (section 2.1).

notes.bom-removed: A byte order mark (U+FEFF) at the start was removed: it marks the encoding and is not part of the document's text.
notes.line-endings-normalised: Carriage returns were read as line feeds, as section 2.11 of the XML 1.0 Recommendation requires of every processor, so the output uses LF line breaks only.
notes.doctype-kept: The document type declaration is copied exactly as written. No entity was expanded and no external DTD was fetched; the declarations inside it, beyond entity declarations, were not checked.
notes.entities-unchecked: The DOCTYPE names an external DTD or uses parameter entities, which this tool never reads, so entity names not declared in the internal subset were accepted as written.
notes.xml-space-invalid: An xml:space attribute has a value other than default or preserve. Section 2.10 gives such values no meaning, so the attribute was ignored for formatting and kept as written.

xml-formatter.whatChanged: Only white space between elements was changed: text, CDATA sections, comments, processing instructions, attribute values, references and anything under xml:space="preserve" are exactly as you pasted them, and the spacing inside tags was tidied. A schema can still give meaning to white space a formatter treats as layout.
xml-formatter.signedNote: Do not reformat a signed document, such as a signed SAML assertion: canonicalization keeps the white space in character content, so the digest of a reformatted document no longer matches its signature.
xml-formatter.statMixed: Elements with text, kept as written: {n}

secrets.what: It looks for: PEM private key blocks (RFC 7468, OpenSSL, OpenSSH); Authorization headers with Bearer or Basic credentials; AWS access key IDs (AKIA, ASIA); JWTs; passwords in URLs; FortiOS set ... ENC values and set password lines; tmsh password, passphrase and encrypted-password; Cisco password and secret lines; and JSON, YAML, shell, Python and Tcl assignments whose name ends in password, passphrase, secret, token, psk or a key such as api_key. A masked value becomes eight bullets, whatever its length.
secrets.notComplete: This is not a complete secret scanner. It does not know every vendor's formats, it cannot tell a real secret from an example, and a secret it does not look for stays in the image: read the image before you publish it.
