tomlError.too-large: The file is too large to read.
tomlError.too-deep: Arrays, inline tables or dotted keys are nested too deeply (more than 100 levels, or more than 128 key parts).
tomlError.bom: The file starts with a byte order mark (U+FEFF). Python's tomllib refuses it, so this parser does too.
tomlError.bad-character: A control character, or a broken UTF-16 surrogate, where TOML allows none.
tomlError.bare-cr: A carriage return without a line feed after it: TOML accepts only LF or CRLF line ends.
tomlError.expected-key: Expected a key, a table header or a comment here.
tomlError.expected-equals: A key must be followed by = and a value.
tomlError.expected-newline: Something follows the value or header on the same line; each key = value pair needs its own line.
tomlError.newline-in-string: A single-line string runs into the end of the line; use a multi-line string (three quotes) or \n.
tomlError.control-in-string: A control character inside a string must be written as an escape.
tomlError.bad-escape: An escape TOML 1.0.0 does not define (\b, \t, \n, \f, \r, \", \\, \uXXXX and \UXXXXXXXX are the ones it does).
tomlError.bad-unicode-escape: A \u or \U escape needs 4 or 8 hexadecimal digits and must name a Unicode scalar value.
tomlError.bad-number: Not a valid TOML number (leading zeros, misplaced underscores or a bad exponent, for example).
tomlError.bad-date-time: Not a valid TOML date or time.
tomlError.bad-value: Not a TOML value: strings need quotes, and true and false are lower case.
tomlError.unterminated-array: An array is not closed with ].
tomlError.expected-array-comma: Array values must be separated by commas.
tomlError.unterminated-inline-table: An inline table is not closed with a brace.
tomlError.inline-table-newline: An inline table must stay on one line in TOML 1.0.0.
tomlError.inline-table-trailing-comma: TOML 1.0.0 does not allow a comma after the last pair of an inline table.
tomlError.expected-inline-comma: The pairs of an inline table must be separated by commas.
tomlError.bad-header: A table header must be closed by ] or, for an array of tables, ]].
tomlError.dotted-redefines-table: A dotted key adds to {key}, a table already defined elsewhere.
tomlError.immutable: {key} is an inline table or a static array, which cannot be extended afterwards.
tomlError.not-a-table: {key} already holds a value that is not a table.

finding.toml-1-1: Uses TOML 1.1.0 syntax from line {line, number}: {features}. Python's tomllib reads it only from Python 3.15 on; in Python 3.11 to 3.14 it reads TOML 1.0.0 only, so tools built on those versions refuse the file.
finding.unknown-top-level: The top-level table {key} is not defined: the specification reserves every table other than [build-system], [project], [dependency-groups] and [tool] for future use. Tool settings belong under [tool].
finding.wrong-type: Expected {want}; the value is of type {got}.
finding.no-build-system: No [build-system] table: build front-ends use requires = ["setuptools"] and the legacy setuptools build (PEP 517).
finding.bs-requires-missing: The [build-system] table has no requires key, which is mandatory in the table.
finding.bs-requirement-invalid: Not a valid dependency specifier: {code} (character {at, number}).
finding.bs-backend-missing: No build-backend: front-ends fall back to the legacy setuptools behaviour (running setup.py, or the setuptools.build_meta:__legacy__ back-end).
finding.bs-backend-invalid: {value} is not an object reference: module names separated by dots, optionally followed by : and attribute names, with no spaces.
finding.bs-backend-path-outside: {value} leaves the source tree; backend-path directories must stay inside it.
finding.bs-unknown-key: {key} is not one of the keys [build-system] defines (requires, build-backend, backend-path).
finding.no-project: No [project] table: the metadata comes from the build back-end's own configuration.
finding.unknown-project-key: {key} is not a [project] key. Back-ends must refuse keys the specification does not define; tool settings belong under [tool].
finding.name-missing: [project] has no name. The name must always be given statically.
finding.name-dynamic: name is listed in dynamic. The name must never be dynamic.
finding.name-invalid: Not a valid project name: {problem} (character {at, number}).
finding.name-not-normalized: Normalized, the name is {normalized}; tools compare names in this form.
finding.version-missing: [project] has no version and dynamic does not list it: the version must be given statically or listed in dynamic.
finding.version-not-normalized: The normal form is {normalized}; the specification says to prefer already-normalized versions.
finding.version-local: The version has a local label (after +); PyPI does not accept local versions.
finding.static-and-dynamic: {key} is given here and also listed in dynamic. Back-ends must refuse this for {key}, which is not a list or table they may extend.
finding.static-and-dynamic-extensible: {key} is given here and listed in dynamic: allowed since PEP 808 (May 2026) for lists and tables; the back-end may add entries but must not change or remove these.
finding.dynamic-unknown: dynamic lists {key}, which is not a [project] key that can be dynamic.
finding.description-multiline: The description has more than one line; it is a one-line summary, and tools may refuse it.
finding.readme-suffix: {file} does not end in .md or .rst, so the content type cannot be known; tools must raise an error unless they know the suffix.
finding.readme-both: The readme table has both file and text; they are mutually exclusive.
finding.readme-neither: The readme table has neither file nor text.
finding.readme-content-type-missing: The readme table has no content-type, which is required in the table form.
finding.readme-content-type-unsupported: {value} is not text/plain, text/x-rst or text/markdown, the content types core metadata defines.
finding.readme-charset: charset={charset}: only UTF-8 is defined (tools may support others).
finding.readme-variant: variant={variant}: core metadata names GFM and CommonMark for text/markdown; others are read as GFM.
finding.requires-python-invalid: Not a valid version specifier set: {code}.
finding.license-invalid: Not a valid SPDX licence expression: {code}.
finding.license-not-canonical: Valid. With the SPDX list's case, it is written {canonical}; tools should normalize the case.
finding.license-deprecated-id: {id} is deprecated on the SPDX License List.
finding.license-table: The table form of license is deprecated (PEP 639); write an SPDX licence expression and list the files in license-files.
finding.license-table-both: The license table has both file and text; they are mutually exclusive.
finding.license-classifier-with-expression: A licence expression and License :: classifiers are both given; build tools may refuse that.
finding.license-files-empty: license-files is an empty array: the project ships no licence files.
finding.person-empty: A person needs a name, an email or both.
finding.person-unknown-key: {key}: a person table has only name and email.
finding.person-name-comma: {name} contains a comma, which a name must not.
finding.person-email-invalid: {email} does not look like an email address (only the basic shape is checked).
finding.url-label-long: The label {label} has {length, number} characters; Project-URL labels are limited to 32.
finding.url-no-scheme: {url} has no scheme (such as https:), so it is not a URL a browser can open.
finding.entry-point-reference: {value} is not an object reference (module, or module:object).
finding.entry-point-name: The entry point name {name}: a name must not contain =, start with [ or begin or end with white space; letters, digits, underscores, dots and hyphens are recommended.
finding.entry-points-group-name: {group} is not a valid group name (word characters separated by dots).
finding.entry-points-nested: {name} is a nested table; entry point groups are only one level deep.
finding.requirement-invalid: Not a valid dependency specifier: {code} (character {at, number}).
finding.requirement-strict-pin: {clause} pins one exact version; that is strongly discouraged for published projects.
finding.requirement-arbitrary: {clause} uses ===, arbitrary equality, which is heavily discouraged.
finding.requirement-direct-url: A direct reference ({url}); public index servers should not allow such dependencies.
finding.requirement-url-semicolon: The URL contains a ; with no space before it, so it is read as part of the URL, not as the start of a marker.
finding.requirement-url-unverified: The direct reference cannot be checked: {issue}.
finding.requirement-extra-name: The extra {extra} is compared normalized, as {normalized}.
finding.requirement-parenthesized: The version is written in parentheses, the old style the grammar still accepts.
finding.extra-invalid: {extra} is not a valid extra name.
finding.extra-not-normalized: {extra} is not in the form core metadata requires for Provides-Extra; normalized it is {normalized}.
finding.extra-clash: {extra} and {other} are the same extra once normalized.
finding.self-extra-unknown: The project refers to its own extra {extra}, which optional-dependencies does not define.
finding.self-reference: The project depends on itself with extras ({extras}): a self-referential extra, which most package managers support.
finding.import-name-invalid: {value} is not an import name: dotted Python identifiers, optionally followed by ; private.
finding.import-name-both: {name} is in both import-names and import-namespaces; tools must raise an error.
finding.group-name-invalid: {group} is not a valid group name.
finding.group-duplicate: {group} and {other} are the same group once normalized; tools should report it as an error.
finding.group-item-invalid: Neither a dependency specifier nor a table with exactly one key, include-group. Tools should refuse it when the group is used.
finding.group-include-unknown: The include names {target}, which is not a group in this file.
finding.group-cycle: The includes form a cycle: {cycle}. Includes must not.
finding.group-matches-extra: {group} has the same name as an extra; the specification advises against it.
finding.tool-not-table: tool.{name} is not a table; each tool keeps its settings in a sub-table of [tool].

text-encryption.name: Text Encryption with a Passphrase (AES-GCM)
text-encryption.blurb: Encrypt your own text with your own passphrase and decrypt it again, entirely in your browser: PBKDF2-HMAC-SHA-256 with 600,000 iterations derives an AES-256 key, and AES-GCM seals the text into one self-describing string. A wrong passphrase or an altered string gives nothing back. Nothing is stored or sent.
text-encryption.textPlaceholder: Type or paste the text you want to protect.
text-encryption.encryptedPlaceholder: Paste a string that starts with aesgcm1. (made by this tool)
text-encryption.runsLocally: Encrypted and decrypted in your browser with the Web Cryptography API. The text and the passphrase are never sent, never stored and never put in the address; the page holds them only while it is open.
text-encryption.mismatch: The two passphrases differ. Text encrypted with a mistyped passphrase cannot be recovered, so Encrypt waits until they match.
text-encryption.examplePassphraseNote: This is the Example's passphrase, "Password", the test password published in RFC 7914 (section 11). Anyone can read it there, so it protects nothing: never use it for real text.

facts.length: {n, plural, one {# character} other {# characters}} ({bytes, plural, one {# byte} other {# bytes}} in UTF-8)
facts.edgeWhitespace: It starts or ends with white space, which is easy to leave out when you type it again.
facts.prepared: It contains a non-ASCII space or a decomposed accent. Before the key is derived, every non-ASCII space becomes an ordinary space and accents are composed (RFC 8265), so the same passphrase typed on another keyboard still works.
facts.noScore: No strength score: a guesser tries likely passphrases first (words, names, dates, quotations, leaked passwords), and this page cannot know how likely yours is. NIST counts length as a primary factor (SP 800-63B-4, appendix A) and says passphrases shorter than 20 characters are usually considered weak (SP 800-132, appendix A.1). Anyone holding the string can keep guessing offline, as fast as their hardware allows.

text-encryption.notAStringTitle: Not a string this tool can read

fields.sizesValue: salt {salt} bytes, IV {iv} bytes, ciphertext {ciphertext, plural, one {# byte} other {# bytes}}, tag {tag} bytes

stats.saltIv: salt {salt} bytes and IV {iv} bytes, both random
stats.sizes: text {text, plural, one {# byte} other {# bytes}}, sealed {sealed, number} bytes (with the {tag}-byte tag)
stats.textBytes: text {n, plural, one {# byte} other {# bytes}}

notes.passphrase-prepared: The passphrase was prepared as RFC 8265 says (non-ASCII spaces to ordinary spaces, accents composed) before the key was derived.
notes.whitespace-removed: Spaces and line breaks in the pasted string were removed before reading it; they are never part of the format.

text-encryption.freshEveryTime: Encrypting the same text with the same passphrase again gives a different string, because the salt and the IV are new each time. Each of those strings decrypts with the passphrase.
text-encryption.lengthShows: Encryption hides the content, not the size: the string's length shows roughly how long the text is.
text-encryption.authenticatedNote: The 128-bit tag verified, so this is exactly the text that was encrypted with this passphrase, and the string's version, iteration count, salt and IV are as they were written.

errors.empty-text: There is no text to encrypt.
errors.text-too-large: The text is larger than {maxBytes, number} bytes in UTF-8, the most this page encrypts or decrypts.
errors.lone-surrogate: {field, select, text {The text contains an unpaired surrogate code unit, which UTF-8 cannot represent, so the text would not come back unchanged.} passphrase {The passphrase contains an unpaired surrogate code unit, which UTF-8 cannot represent.} other {The input contains an unpaired surrogate code unit, which UTF-8 cannot represent.}}
errors.passphrase-too-long: The passphrase is longer than {maxChars, number} characters, the most this page accepts.
errors.bad-salt-length: The salt is not 16 bytes (128 bits) long.
errors.bad-iv-length: The IV is not 12 bytes (96 bits) long.
errors.iterations-out-of-range: The iteration count is outside {min, number} to {max, number}. NIST SP 800-132 (section 5.2) recommends at least {min, number} and calls {max, number} appropriate for especially critical keys.
errors.input-too-large: The pasted text is longer than {maxInput, number} characters, the most this page reads.
errors.bad-format: An encrypted string has five fields separated by dots: aesgcm1, the iteration count, the salt, the IV and the ciphertext. This text does not.
errors.unknown-version: The first field is not aesgcm1, the only format this tool writes and reads.
errors.bad-iterations: The second field must be the iteration count, in decimal digits with no leading zero.
errors.bad-encoding: The {field, select, salt {salt} iv {IV} ciphertext {ciphertext} other {encoded}} field is not base64url without padding (RFC 4648, section 5): only A to Z, a to z, 0 to 9, - and _ may appear, and the last character must leave no stray bits.
errors.too-short: The ciphertext field is shorter than the {tag}-byte tag, so it cannot hold a ciphertext.
errors.auth-failed: Either the passphrase is not the one used to encrypt, or the string was changed after it was made (one character is enough). AES-GCM gives back all of the text or none of it, so nothing is shown.
errors.not-utf8: The tag verified, but the content is not UTF-8 text. This tool never writes such a string.
errors.no-crypto: This page has no Web Cryptography API: browsers offer it only in secure contexts, such as pages served over HTTPS. Nothing was encrypted or decrypted.
errors.crypto-error: The browser's Web Cryptography API refused the operation. Nothing was encrypted or decrypted.

share.carries: The link carries only the encrypted string, never the passphrase or the text. Send the passphrase another way.
share.arrived: This string came from a shared link. A link never carries the passphrase: type the one you were given separately, then press Decrypt.

tcpdump-filter-explainer.name: tcpdump command and filter explainer
tcpdump-filter-explainer.blurb: Paste a tcpdump command or a capture filter and read every option and every primitive in plain words: the hidden defaults made explicit, how and, or and not group, byte-offset tests decoded, and errors placed where libpcap would stop.

input.label: tcpdump command or capture filter
input.placeholder: e.g. tcpdump -nn -i eth0 'tcp port 443 and host 192.0.2.10', or just: not port 22

tcpdump-filter-explainer.privacy: Parsed entirely in your browser: nothing is captured, run, resolved or sent.

refused.empty: Paste a tcpdump command or a filter expression.
refused.tooLong: The input is longer than 4096 characters.

summary.title: What was read
summary.versions: Explained against the releases tcpdump.org offers, read on 27 October 2026: tcpdump {tcpdump} (stable) for the options, and libpcap {libpcapStable} (stable) and {libpcapTesting} (testing) for the filter, each from its own manual page and source code. Where they differ, the explanation says which does what; the development versions (tcpdump {tcpdumpDev}, libpcap {libpcapDev}) are mentioned only where they differ again.

from.afterDoubleDash: the words after --, joined with spaces

snmp-counter-wrap-calculator.name: SNMP counter wrap and rate calculator
snmp-counter-wrap-calculator.blurb: How long a Counter32 or Counter64 takes to wrap at an interface speed and load, the longest poll interval that cannot miss a wrap, whether RFC 2863 requires 64-bit counters at that speed, and the rate from two readings of one counter, with exact 64-bit arithmetic.
snmp-counter-wrap-calculator.runsLocally: Runs locally in your browser. Nothing is sent anywhere.
snmp-counter-wrap-calculator.speedLabelOptional: Interface speed (optional: it enables the checks)
snmp-counter-wrap-calculator.speedHint: A number and a unit, with a point for decimals: 100M, 2.5 Gb/s, 10G. A bare number is bit/s, as ifSpeed reports it; ifHighSpeed reports units of 1,000,000 bit/s, so an ifHighSpeed of 10000 is 10000M or 10G.
snmp-counter-wrap-calculator.sizeHint: Blank means 84: the smallest Ethernet frame with its preamble and gap, the fastest a packet counter can move. Enter your average packet size for a typical load.
snmp-counter-wrap-calculator.emptyWrap: Enter or pick the interface speed and the time to wrap appears; add a poll interval for a verdict on it. Example fills a 10 Gb/s port at 40 % polled every 300 s.
snmp-counter-wrap-calculator.emptyRate: Enter two readings of the same counter and their times; add the interface speed to check whether the rate can be trusted. Example fills two Counter64 readings 300 s apart.

dur.daysH: {d, plural, one {# day} other {# days}} {h} h

poll.heading: Poll interval
poll.neverMiss: Never misses a wrap, even at line rate
poll.noneHint: Enter a poll interval for a verdict on it.

rfc.heading: RFC 2863 at this speed
rfc.notRequired: not required; 32-bit counters MUST be supported

snmp-counter-wrap-calculator.notesHeading: Why, and how the tool counts
snmp-counter-wrap-calculator.learn: The arithmetic in context, with the rest of SNMP: SNMP on network devices.

rate.heading: Rate
rate.lineMax: Most the interface can count in this interval

share.carries: The link carries the mode, the counter and this mode's fields as typed; the other mode's fields stay here.

err.unsafeNumber: Send counter values above 9007199254740991 as JSON strings: a JSON number that large has already lost digits.
err.tooLong: A field is longer than this tool reads ({max} characters).
err.width: The counter width must be 32 (Counter32) or 64 (Counter64).
err.kind: Say what the counter counts: octets or packets.
err.speedEmpty: Enter the interface speed, for example 10 Gb/s.
err.speedBytes: "{value}" reads as bytes per second (a capital B). Enter the interface speed in bits per second, for example 10 Gb/s.
err.speedBad: "{value}" is not a speed this tool reads. Write a number with a point for decimals and a unit, for example 100 Mb/s, 2.5 Gb/s or 10G.
err.speedZero: The interface speed must be above zero.
err.utilBad: "{value}" is not a percentage. Enter the utilization as a number above 0 and at most 100, with a point for decimals, for example 40.
err.utilRange: Utilization must be above 0 and at most 100 percent; "{value}" is outside that range.
err.sizeBad: "{value}" is not a packet size. Enter whole octets from 1 to 65535, for example 84.
err.pollBad: "{value}" is not a poll interval. Write a number of seconds, or a number and a unit (ms, s, min or h), with a point for decimals, for example 300 or 5 min.
err.pollZero: The poll interval must be above zero.

valueBad.first: "{value}" is not a counter reading (first): a counter value is a whole number written with digits only, or the snmpget output line that carries it (for example IF-MIB::ifHCInOctets.1 = Counter64: 1234).
valueBad.second: "{value}" is not a counter reading (second): a counter value is a whole number written with digits only, or the snmpget output line that carries it (for example IF-MIB::ifHCInOctets.1 = Counter64: 1234).

valueRange.first: "{value}" is more than a Counter{width} can hold (at most {max}): check the counter width.
valueRange.second: "{value}" is more than a Counter{width} can hold (at most {max}): check the counter width.

err.timeUnit: The time unit must be s (seconds) or ticks (sysUpTime, in hundredths of a second).

timeEmpty.first: Enter the time of the first reading.
timeEmpty.second: Enter the time of the second reading.

ticksBad.first: "{value}" is not a sysUpTime value (first reading): write hundredths of a second as a whole number from 0 to 4294967295, or paste the snmpget output line for sysUpTime.0 (for example SNMPv2-MIB::sysUpTime.0 = Timeticks: (586731977) 67 days, 21:48:39.77).
ticksBad.second: "{value}" is not a sysUpTime value (second reading): write hundredths of a second as a whole number from 0 to 4294967295, or paste the snmpget output line for sysUpTime.0 (for example SNMPv2-MIB::sysUpTime.0 = Timeticks: (586731977) 67 days, 21:48:39.77).

timeBad.first: "{value}" is not a time in seconds (first reading): write seconds as a number with a point for decimals, for example 1793616304 or 0.
timeBad.second: "{value}" is not a time in seconds (second reading): write seconds as a number with a point for decimals, for example 1793616304 or 0.

err.zeroInterval: Both readings carry the same time, so there is no interval and no rate.
err.ticksBackwards: The second sysUpTime is lower than the first: either the agent was re-initialised between the readings, which restarts its counters and makes any delta meaningless, or sysUpTime passed 4294967295 hundredths of a second (about 497 days) and went round. The tool does not guess which.
err.negativeInterval: The second reading's time is earlier than the first: enter the readings in the order they were taken.
err.mode: Choose a mode: wrap (time to wrap and poll interval) or rate (rate from two readings).
err.json: The request body is not valid JSON: send one JSON object that names its mode, wrap or rate.

widthMismatch.first: The first reading says Counter{lineWidth}, but the counter width is set to {width} (Counter{width}): the tool does not change the width for you. Set the width to {lineWidth} if that is the counter you polled, or paste a Counter{width} reading.
widthMismatch.second: The second reading says Counter{lineWidth}, but the counter width is set to {width} (Counter{width}): the tool does not change the width for you. Set the width to {lineWidth} if that is the counter you polled, or paste a Counter{width} reading.

notCounter.first: The first reading has the type {type}, which is not a counter: this tool computes rates from Counter32 and Counter64 readings, such as ifInOctets or ifHCInOctets.
notCounter.second: The second reading has the type {type}, which is not a counter: this tool computes rates from Counter32 and Counter64 readings, such as ifInOctets or ifHCInOctets.

ticksInSeconds.first: The time of the first reading is a sysUpTime line (Timeticks, hundredths of a second), but the times are set to seconds: set them to sysUpTime ticks to use it.
ticksInSeconds.second: The time of the second reading is a sysUpTime line (Timeticks, hundredths of a second), but the times are set to seconds: set them to sysUpTime ticks to use it.

band.low: RFC 2863, section 3.1.6: "For interfaces that operate at 20,000,000 (20 million) bits per second or less, 32-bit byte and packet counters MUST be supported."
band.mid: RFC 2863, section 3.1.6: "For interfaces that operate faster than 20,000,000 bits/second, and slower than 650,000,000 bits/second, 32-bit packet counters MUST be supported and 64-bit octet counters MUST be supported."
band.high: RFC 2863, section 3.1.6: "For interfaces that operate at 650,000,000 bits/second or faster, 64-bit packet counters AND 64-bit octet counters MUST be supported."

use64.octets: RFC 2863 requires 64-bit octet counters on an interface of this speed: poll ifHCInOctets and ifHCOutOctets (Counter64) instead of the 32-bit ifInOctets and ifOutOctets.
use64.packets: RFC 2863 requires 64-bit packet counters on an interface of this speed: poll the ifHC packet counters (ifHCInUcastPkts, ifHCOutUcastPkts and their multicast and broadcast siblings, Counter64) instead of the 32-bit ones.

note.singleValue: A single counter value means nothing on its own: "Counters have no defined "initial" value, and thus, a single value of a Counter has (in general) no information content" (RFC 2578, sections 7.1.6 and 7.1.10). Only the difference between two readings of the same counter carries information.
note.margin: The margin is the tool's choice, not a standard's: half the line-rate wrap time, so that one lost poll (a request that timed out) still leaves less than one wrap between the two readings that remain.
note.lineRateOctets: Line rate here is the interface speed divided by 8: an interface cannot count more octets per second than its bits carry, so the line-rate figures are the fastest the counter can move.
note.packetSize: Packet counters move fastest with the smallest packets. The packet rate here assumes each packet takes {octets} octets of line time; on Ethernet the smallest frame takes 84 (64 octets of frame, an 8-octet preamble and a 12-octet gap, RFC 2544 Appendix B).
note.belowEthernetMinimum: {octets} octets is less than the 84 octets of line time the smallest Ethernet frame takes, so on Ethernet the real packet rate cannot be this high. RFC 2863's own example counts 64-byte packets this way, without the preamble and the gap.
note.wrapAssumed: The second reading is lower than the first. Unless the counter had a discontinuity, the only explanation is a wrap: it reached {max}, went back to zero and counted on, so the delta is 2^{width} minus the first reading plus the second.
note.rareWrap64: A Counter64 takes years to go round even at the fastest interface speeds, so a lower second reading is far more likely a discontinuity (an agent restart or a counter reset) than a wrap: check ifCounterDiscontinuityTime before trusting this delta.
note.noSpeed: Enter the interface speed to check whether the counter could have gone round more than once in this interval.
note.discontinuity: A counter discontinuity makes the delta meaningless. Interface counters can jump "at re-initialization of the management system, and at other times as indicated by the value of ifCounterDiscontinuityTime" (RFC 2863): read ifCounterDiscontinuityTime with every poll, and discard the pair if it changed between the two readings.
note.ticks: sysUpTime counts "hundredths of a second" since the agent's management system "was last re-initialized" (RFC 3418), and TimeTicks are kept "modulo 2^32" (RFC 2578), so it goes round after about 497 days (RFC 2579).

poll.safe: Polling at this interval cannot miss a wrap, even at line rate, and a single lost poll still spans less than one wrap.
poll.noMargin: This interval cannot miss a wrap at line rate, but one lost poll doubles the gap between readings, and a doubled gap could hide a wrap: the tool's margin is half the line-rate wrap time.
poll.burst: At the stated load the counter goes round less than once between polls, but a burst towards line rate could take it round a full cycle, and the delta would then be wrong without any sign.
poll.wraps: At the stated load the counter goes round at least one full cycle between polls, so the deltas are wrong and no rate computed from them can be trusted: poll more often, or use a 64-bit counter.

rate.okChecked: The readings give a usable rate: at the interface speed the counter cannot go round a full cycle in this interval.
rate.okUnchecked: The second reading is higher than the first, so no wrap is assumed. Without the interface speed the tool cannot rule out a full cycle between them.
rate.wrapImpossible: The second reading is lower, but at the interface speed the counter could not have gone round to it in this interval: a wrap cannot explain it. A discontinuity (an agent restart or a counter reset) is the likely cause, and the delta is meaningless.
rate.exceedsSpeed: The delta is more than the interface could count in this interval even at its full speed, so the two readings do not belong together: look for a counter discontinuity, a different interface or counter, or the wrong counter width.
rate.multipleWraps: At the interface speed this counter can count a full cycle (2^{width}) or more in this interval, so it may have gone round more often than the readings show: the delta may be short by a multiple of 2^{width}, and this rate cannot be trusted.

acl-first-match-evaluator.name: ACL first-match evaluator
acl-first-match-evaluator.blurb: Paste a Cisco IOS or IOS XE IPv4 access list and describe a packet: see which entry matches first, the field that ruled out every entry above it, or the implicit deny, with shadowed and redundant entries flagged and every wildcard shown as a prefix.

input.label: Access list (Cisco IOS or IOS XE, IPv4)
input.help: Numbered access-list lines, or an ip access-list standard or extended block with or without sequence numbers. Lines the tool does not read are listed below with the reason.
input.placeholder:
ip access-list extended MGMT-PROTECT
 10 permit tcp 10.1.10.0 0.0.0.255 10.1.99.0 0.0.0.255 eq 22
 20 deny ip any 10.1.99.0 0.0.0.255
 30 permit ip any any

acl-first-match-evaluator.privacy: Read in your browser: nothing you paste or type is sent anywhere.

scope.text: Reads Cisco IOS and IOS XE IPv4 syntax only. Other platforms end a list differently: Juniper EX discards, Extreme Switch Engine and Fabric Engine permit by default.
scope.link: Why, with the sources: the ACL (access control list) article

lists.label: List to evaluate
lists.help: The text holds several lists; the walk and the lint read the one chosen.

packet.title: Test packet
packet.ackrst: ACK or RST set (part of an established connection)
packet.help: Protocol: tcp, udp, icmp, igmp, gre, esp, eigrp, ospf, pim or a number from 0 to 255. Ports count for TCP and UDP only. The opening SYN of a connection has neither ACK nor RST.
packet.none: Fill in the test packet to see which entry decides it; the lint below reads the list without one.

walk.title: First match, entry by entry
walk.help: Entries in the order the device tests them, up to the first match; each one above it shows the first field that ruled it out.

lint.title: Lint
lint.none: Nothing to flag: no entry is shadowed or redundant, and every wildcard is contiguous.

entries.title: Entries of {list} ({kind}), in the order tested

share.carries: The link carries the access list as pasted and the test packet as typed; a list holding a credential gets none.
share.caution: An access list names internal networks and hosts and what may reach them: read it before you send the link.
share.blockedSecret: No link: line {line} holds a credential ({label}). Put a placeholder in its place, then share again.

err.tooLong: The text has {count} characters; the most this tool reads is 65,536.
err.tooManyLines: The text has {count} lines; the most this tool reads is 4,000.

issue.accessGroup: ip access-group applies a list to an interface; v1 reads the list, not where it is applied.
issue.action: An entry starts with permit or deny, or is a remark.
issue.address: {token} is not an IPv4 address in dotted-decimal form; host names are not read.
issue.duplicateEntry: The same entry as {seq}, apart from its sequence number: Cisco makes no change.
issue.dynamic: Dynamic, reflexive and evaluate entries are outside v1.
issue.establishedNotTcp: established is valid for TCP only (Cisco: the flag and established keywords are not valid for UDP).
issue.fragmentsL4: fragments cannot be combined with ports or established: Cisco refuses it on an entry with Layer 4 information.
issue.icmpType: {token}: ICMP and IGMP message types are outside v1.
issue.ipAccessListOther: ip access-list {word} is not a list definition this tool reads; v1 reads standard and extended IPv4 lists.
issue.nameForm: A list name starts with a letter, or is a number in the range of its list type.
issue.noCommand: A no command removes configuration; v1 reads the list as written and does not apply removals.
issue.numberRange: List number {number} is not an IPv4 standard (1 to 99, 1300 to 1999) or extended (100 to 199, 2000 to 2699) list.
issue.objectGroup: Object groups are outside v1: the tool cannot see their members.
issue.outsideList: An entry outside any list: no ip access-list line above it opens one.
issue.portMissing: {op} needs {count, select, 2 {two port numbers} other {a port number}}.
issue.portName: {token} is not a {proto} port name in Cisco's IOS XE 17.18.1 data model; write the port number.
issue.portNoNumber: {token} is listed by Cisco as a {proto} port name, but no source read for this tool gives its number; write the number.
issue.portNotAllowed: Ports follow tcp or udp only; this entry's protocol is {proto}.
issue.portNumber: Port {token} is out of range: a port is a number from 0 to 65535.
issue.portPlace: {token} is out of place: a port test comes right after the source or the destination it tests.
issue.portWrongProto: {token} is a {other} port name: Cisco reads TCP port names only with tcp and UDP port names only with udp.
issue.protocolName: Protocol {name}: Cisco accepts this keyword, but no source read for this tool gives its protocol number; write the number instead.
issue.protocolNumber: Protocol {token} is out of range: a protocol number runs from 0 to 255.
issue.protocolUnknown: {token} is not a protocol keyword this tool reads (ip, tcp, udp, icmp, igmp, gre, esp, eigrp, ospf, pim) or a number from 0 to 255.
issue.rangeOrder: range {from} {to}: the first port is greater than the second, and the sources read do not say what the device does with that.
issue.seqDuplicate: Sequence number {seq} is already used in list {list}: Cisco refuses the entry with Duplicate sequence number.
issue.seqExceeded: The next sequence number would pass 2147483647: Cisco refuses the entry with Exceeded maximum sequence number.
issue.seqOnNumbered: Numbered access-list lines take no sequence number; give one inside ip access-list {kind} {name}.
issue.seqRange: A sequence number runs from 1 to 2147483647.
issue.showOutput: This is a show access-lists heading; paste the configuration lines (access-list or ip access-list) instead.
issue.standardExtra: A standard entry tests the source address only; {token} belongs in an extended list.
issue.unknownLine: Not an access-list line this tool reads.
issue.unreadOption: {token} tests something the test packet does not carry (precedence, ToS, DSCP, time ranges, IP options, TTL, TCP flags other than established); v1 does not read it.
issue.wildcardRequired: An extended entry needs a wildcard after {address} (or host before it, or any instead).

lint.hashOrder: Entry {seq} names a single host in a standard list. Cisco looks host entries up in a hash table before the other entries, so it is tested before entry {before} although its sequence number is higher.
lint.ignoredBits: Entry {seq}: the {field} address {address} has bits set where the wildcard {wildcard} ignores them, so it matches the same addresses as {base} {wildcard}.
lint.longRemark: The remark on line {line} has {count} characters; Cisco's IOS XE 17.18.1 data model allows 1 to 100.
lint.neverMatches: Entry {seq} can never match an unfragmented packet: its port test {written} admits no port.
lint.nonContiguous: Entry {seq} uses the non-contiguous wildcard {wildcard} on its {field} ({written}): legal, since Cisco says wildcard bits set to 1 need not be contiguous, but no prefix length can express it, and its {count} addresses do not form one block.
lint.redundant: Entry {seq} is redundant: entry {by} is tested before it and matches every packet it would, with the same action ({byAction}), so removing it changes nothing.
lint.redundantImplicit: Entry {seq} denies only packets the implicit deny at the end would deny anyway, since no later entry permits any of them; it changes no verdict, though its counter shows the traffic.
lint.redundantImplicitLog: Entry {seq} denies only packets the implicit deny at the end would deny anyway, since no later entry permits any of them; it changes no verdict and is there for its {log}.
lint.redundantLater: Entry {seq} is redundant: entry {by}, tested later, matches every packet it would with the same action ({action}), and no entry between them decides any of those packets otherwise.
lint.redundantUnfragmented: Entry {seq} is redundant for every unfragmented packet: entry {by} is tested before it and matches all of them with the same action ({byAction}). It still decides non-initial fragments, which Cisco does not test against a deny entry with ports or established.
lint.shadowed: Entry {seq} can never match: entry {by} is tested before it and matches every packet it would, with the opposite action ({byAction}). It is shadowed.
lint.shadowedUnfragmented: Entry {seq} is shadowed for every unfragmented packet: entry {by} is tested before it and matches all of them with the opposite action ({byAction}). It still decides non-initial fragments, which Cisco does not test against a deny entry with ports or established.
lint.standardReach: List {list} is a standard list: its entries test the source address only, so each one decides for everything those sources send, whatever the destination, protocol or port.

note.hashOrder: This standard list names single hosts after other entries. Cisco looks host entries up first, so the walk tests them first, ahead of their sequence numbers.
note.listMissing: There is no list {wanted} in the text, so the first list, {first}, is read.
note.log: Entry {seq} has {log}: Cisco logs the first packet that matches it, then a count of matches every 5 minutes.
note.noList: No access list was found: paste access-list lines, or an ip access-list standard or extended block with its entries.
note.portsIgnored: Ports are read only for TCP and UDP, so the ports typed play no part for protocol {proto}.
note.scope: This reads Cisco IOS and IOS XE IPv4 access lists only. Other platforms end a list differently: Juniper EX discards what no term matched, and Extreme Switch Engine and Fabric Engine permit it by default.
note.standardPacket: A standard list reads the packet's source address only: the protocol, the destination and the ports played no part.
note.unreadEntries: Entry lines not read: {count} (listed below). If the device holds any of them, the verdict may differ: it covers only the entries that were read.

packet.destination: The packet's destination address is an IPv4 address in dotted-decimal form, such as 10.1.99.10.
packet.port: The packet's {which} is a number from 0 to 65535.
packet.protocol: The packet's protocol is tcp, udp, icmp, igmp, gre, esp, eigrp, ospf, pim or a number from 0 to 255.
packet.source: The packet's source address is an IPv4 address in dotted-decimal form, such as 10.1.10.25.

step.destination: No match on the destination address: {address} is outside {written}.
step.destinationPort: No match on the destination port: the entry wants {written} and the packet's destination port is {port}.
step.established: No match on established: the entry matches only TCP segments with ACK or RST set, and this packet has neither (the opening segment of a connection).
step.fragments: No match on fragments: the entry applies only to non-initial fragments, and the test packet is not a fragment.
step.match: Match: every field the entry tests covers the packet, so this entry decides and no later entry is read.
step.matchStandard: Match: {address} is inside {written}, and a standard entry tests nothing else, so this entry decides and no later entry is read.
step.protocol: No match on the protocol: the entry matches {entry} and the packet is {packet}.
step.source: No match on the source address: {address} is outside {written}.
step.sourcePort: No match on the source port: the entry wants {written} and the packet's source port is {port}.

verdict.deny: Entry {seq} matches first and denies the packet.
verdict.empty: List {list} has no entries. Cisco documents that an interface with an empty access list applied to it permits all traffic.
verdict.implicitDeny: No entry matches, so the packet meets the implicit deny at the end of the list and is denied: Cisco documents that if no conditions match, the packet is dropped, because each access list ends with an unwritten deny statement.
verdict.permit: Entry {seq} matches first and permits the packet.

vrrp-timer-calculator.name: VRRP timer, virtual MAC and election calculator
vrrp-timer-calculator.blurb: Skew_Time and the time a Backup waits before it declares the Active Router down, with the arithmetic shown, for VRRPv3 (RFC 9568) and VRRPv2 (RFC 3768); who wins the election, who takes over when it fails and what happens when it comes back, with preemption on or off; and the virtual MAC address for any VRID, exactly.
vrrp-timer-calculator.runsLocally: Runs locally in your browser. Nothing is sent anywhere.

inputs.timers: One router's priority and the interval
inputs.election: The routers of one virtual router

vrrp-timer-calculator.priorityHint: 1 to 254 for a Backup (100 by default), 255 for the router that owns the virtual address. 0 is never configured: an Active Router sends it when it shuts down.

intervalHint.v3: Centiseconds from 1 to 4095, or a time with a unit: 100, 1 s, 250 ms. Blank is the default, 100 cs (1 s).
intervalHint.v2: Whole seconds from 1 to 255: VRRPv2 has no sub-second interval. Blank is the default, 1 s.

vrrp-timer-calculator.routersHint: Two to eight routers. The primary address is the router's own interface address on the LAN (for IPv6, its link-local address); it breaks a tie between equal priorities. A blank name reads R1, R2 and so on.
vrrp-timer-calculator.vridHint: The Virtual Router Identifier, a whole number from 1 to 255.

empty.timers: Enter or pick a priority and the timers appear; the interval is optional. Example fills the course lab's Backup: priority 100 at 1 s.
empty.election: Enter at least two routers with a priority and a primary address. Example fills the course lab's two core switches, priorities 110 and 100.
empty.mac: Enter a VRID and the virtual MAC appears. Example fills the course lab's VRID 10.

timers.summary: A Backup at priority {p} declares the {role} down {down} after the last ADVERTISEMENT it heard, and takes over {skew} after a clean shutdown.
timers.summaryOwner: Priority 255 is the address owner: it becomes the {role} at once and never waits as a Backup, so its timers below apply only if a second router claims 255.
timers.heading: The arithmetic ({rfc}, section 6.1)

failover.heading: When a Backup at this priority takes over

election.tableNote: Priority first, then the higher primary address. The timers are those each router would wait as a Backup; the owner never waits.

time.window: Between {from} and {to} after the failure, depending on when it falls between two ADVERTISEMENTs

mac.summary: The virtual MAC of VRID {vrid} for {family}:
mac.heading: Virtual Router MAC address

vrrp-timer-calculator.learn: The Learn article First-hop redundancy: VRRP, HSRP, and the gateway that is a fiction works these timers step by step and has an election lab that plays failures and returns in order.

share.carries: The link carries the mode, the VRRP version and the fields of the mode shown, as typed.
share.caution: Router names and primary addresses describe a private network: read them before you send the link.

err.tooLong: A field is longer than this tool reads (64 characters).
err.version: Choose VRRP version 3 (RFC 9568) or version 2 (RFC 3768, obsoleted by RFC 5798 and now RFC 9568, still found on older equipment).
err.priorityEmpty: Enter the router's priority, a whole number from 1 to 255.
err.priorityBad: "{value}" is not a priority: enter a whole number from 1 to 255.
err.priorityZero: Priority 0 is never configured: RFC 9568 reserves it for the Active Router to indicate it is relinquishing responsibility for the Virtual Router. The Active Router sends it in its last ADVERTISEMENT when it shuts down, and the Backups then take over after Skew_Time (sections 5.2.4 and 6.1). Enter 1 to 254 for a Backup, or 255 for the address owner.
err.priorityRange: Priority {value} does not exist: the field is 8 bits, 1 to 254 for routers backing up the Virtual Router and 255 for the address owner (RFC 9568, sections 5.2.4 and 6.1).

intervalBad.v3: "{value}" is not an advertisement interval: enter whole centiseconds from 1 to 4095, or a time with a unit, such as 100, 1 s or 250 ms.
intervalBad.v2: "{value}" is not an advertisement interval: enter whole seconds from 1 to 255, such as 1.

err.v2Unit: "{value}" is a sub-second unit, and VRRPv2 counts the advertisement interval in whole seconds (RFC 3768, section 5.3.7); centisecond intervals are VRRPv3's (RFC 9568, section 5.2.7). The two versions' arithmetic does not mix: enter whole seconds, or choose VRRPv3.
err.v2Zero: The advertisement interval cannot be zero: an ADVERTISEMENT every 0 seconds is no interval. RFC 3768 states no range in words; this tool reads 1 to 255 seconds, the values its 8-bit Adver Int field can carry (sections 5.1 and 5.3.7).
err.v2Whole: "{value}" is not a whole number of seconds: the VRRPv2 Adver Int field carries whole seconds (RFC 3768, sections 5.1 and 5.3.7); for a sub-second interval choose VRRPv3.
err.v2Range: "{value}" is more than the VRRPv2 Adver Int field can carry: it is 8 bits of whole seconds, at most 255 (RFC 3768, section 5.1).
err.intervalZero: The advertisement interval cannot be zero: verified erratum 8301 to RFC 9568 makes the range 1 to 4095 centiseconds, because a zero interval makes Skew_Time and Active_Down_Interval zero and every Backup times out at once.
err.intervalFraction: "{value}" is not a whole number of centiseconds: VRRPv3 carries the interval as whole centiseconds (RFC 9568, section 5.2.7).
err.intervalRange: "{value}" is longer than VRRPv3 can carry: the interval field is 12 bits of centiseconds, 1 to 4095, at most 40.95 seconds (RFC 9568, section 5.2.7, and verified erratum 8301).
err.addressBad: "{value}" is not an IPv4 or IPv6 address this tool reads (write it without a prefix length or a zone).
err.vridEmpty: Enter the VRID, a whole number from 1 to 255.
err.vridBad: "{value}" is not a VRID: enter a whole number from 1 to 255, in decimal.
err.vridZero: VRID 0 does not exist: a Virtual Router Identifier is 1 to 255, with no default (RFC 9568, sections 1.7 and 6.1), so 00-00-5E-00-01-00 is not a VRRP address.
err.vridRange: "{value}" is more than a VRID can be: the field is 8 bits, 1 to 255 (RFC 9568, sections 5.1 and 6.1).
err.family: Choose the address family: ipv4 or ipv6.
err.routersList: Send the routers as a list of objects, each with a priority and an address.
err.routersCount: Enter from 2 to 8 routers: an election needs at least one Backup.
err.nameBad: "{value}" is not a router name this tool reads: use up to 32 letters, digits, dots, hyphens or underscores, without spaces.
err.ownerPriority: The address owner's priority MUST be 255 (RFC 9568, section 5.2.4), not {value}.
err.reserved255: Priority 255 is reserved for the router that owns the virtual address (RFC 9568, section 6.1): mark this router as the owner, or give it 1 to 254.
err.nameDup: Two routers are called "{value}": give each router its own name.
err.familyMix: The routers' addresses mix IPv4 and IPv6. A Virtual Router is IPv4 or IPv6, never both: the two families are always separate Virtual Router instances (RFC 9568, Abstract).
err.v2Ipv6: VRRPv2 is for IPv4 only (RFC 3768, section 1.2: "This protocol is intended for use with IPv4 routers only"); IPv6 needs VRRPv3 (RFC 9568). The two versions do not mix in one calculation: choose VRRPv3, or use IPv4 addresses.
err.notLinkLocal: "{value}" is not a link-local address. For IPv6 the primary address that breaks a tie is the link-local address ADVERTISEMENTs are sent from (RFC 9568, sections 1.7 and 5.1.2.1), in fe80::/10 (RFC 4291, section 2.5.6).
err.addressDup: {first} and {second} have the same primary address, {value}: two routers on one LAN cannot share it, and the tie-break needs them to differ.
err.twoOwners: {first} and {second} both claim to own the virtual address. Only one router SHOULD have priority 255 (RFC 9568, section 8.3.2): as published, an owner discards every ADVERTISEMENT it receives, so two owners both stay Active (section 7.1), and verified erratum 8298 changes that check so that the higher primary address wins. The outcome depends on which text an implementation follows, so the tool does not guess: keep one owner.
err.preempt: Preempt_Mode is on or off (true or false).
err.macV2Ipv6: VRRPv2 is for IPv4 only (RFC 3768, section 1.2), so it has no IPv6 virtual MAC: the 00-02 block belongs to VRRPv3 (RFC 9568, section 7.3). Choose VRRPv3 for IPv6.
err.mode: Choose a mode: timers, election or mac.
err.json: The request body is not valid JSON: send one JSON object that names its mode: timers, election or mac.

terms.v3: RFC 9568 calls the forwarding router the Active Router and the waiting time Active_Down_Interval; RFC 5798, which it obsoletes, and RFC 3768 before it said Master and Master_Down_Interval, as many routers' output still does.
terms.v2: RFC 3768 calls the forwarding router the Master and the waiting time Master_Down_Interval; RFC 9568, which obsoletes RFC 5798 and through it RFC 3768, renamed them Active Router and Active_Down_Interval.

defaultInterval.v3: No interval entered: the default, 100 centiseconds (1 second), is used (RFC 9568, section 6.1).
defaultInterval.v2: No interval entered: the default, 1 second, is used (RFC 3768, section 6.1).

learned.v3: A Backup computes its timers from the interval the Active Router advertises (Active_Adver_Interval), which starts as its own Advertisement_Interval (RFC 9568, sections 6.1 and 6.4.2); a receiver SHOULD check that the two match (section 7.1).

match.v2: VRRPv2 routers of one VRID must share the interval: a router discards an ADVERTISEMENT whose Adver Int differs from its own (RFC 3768, section 7.1).

note.subSecond: Sub-second intervals are allowed, but RFC 9568 warns that queueing delay longer than the interval can make a Backup promote itself and fall back, a process that "can repeat many times per second, causing a significant disruption of traffic"; it suggests giving VRRP packets priority on egress queues (section 2.5).
note.owner: Priority 255 belongs to the address owner, which becomes the {activeRole} at once when it starts and preempts any lower priority whatever Preempt_Mode says ({rfc}, sections 6.1 and 6.4.1). It waits on these timers only if it ever runs as a Backup, which takes a second router claiming 255, and only one SHOULD (RFC 9568, section 8.3.2).
note.failover: After a silent failure a Backup takes over when its {downTimer} fires, one {down} after the last ADVERTISEMENT it heard, so the takeover comes between one interval less than the {down} and the full {down} after the failure itself, depending on where in the interval the failure falls. After a clean shutdown the {activeRole} sends an ADVERTISEMENT with priority 0 and the Backup takes over after Skew_Time ({rfc}, sections 6.4.2 and 6.4.3). Propagation and processing delays are not included.

skew.v2: In VRRPv2, Skew_Time does not grow with the interval: it is (256 - Priority) / 256 of a second whatever the interval (RFC 3768, section 6.1). In VRRPv3 it is the same fraction of the interval (RFC 9568, section 6.1).

note.exact: The RFC sets no rounding: every value here is exact (a whole number of 256ths of the interval's unit), and each implementation keeps its timers at its own resolution.
note.model: The calculation assumes that every router has the same advertisement interval and the same Preempt_Mode, that they start together, and that ADVERTISEMENTs arrive without delay. Tracking, preemption delays and other vendor features are outside the RFC and outside this calculation.
note.preemptDefault: Preempt_Mode was not given: the default, True (on), is used ({rfc}, section 6.1).
note.ownerPreempts: The owner preempts even with Preempt_Mode off: "the router that owns the IPvX address associated with the Virtual Router always preempts, independent of the setting of this flag" (RFC 9568, section 6.1).
note.compare: A tie between Active Routers goes to the higher primary address, compared as an unsigned integer in network byte order (RFC 9568, section 6.4.3).
note.ipv6Primary: For IPv6 the primary address is the link-local address ADVERTISEMENTs are sent from (RFC 9568, section 1.7), so it is the one compared in a tie, as an unsigned 128-bit number.

mac.layout: 00-00-5E is the IANA's Organizationally Unique Identifier; the next two octets, {block}, are the block assigned to VRRP for {familyName}, and the last octet is the VRID in hexadecimal ({rfc}, section 7.3).

use.ipv4: The Active Router sends its ADVERTISEMENTs from this address and answers ARP requests for the virtual IPv4 address with it, never with its own physical MAC, so hosts keep the same gateway MAC whichever router is active; after a takeover, switches learn it on the new router's port (RFC 9568, sections 7.2 and 8.1.2).
use.ipv6: The Active Router sends its ADVERTISEMENTs from this address and answers Neighbor Solicitations for the virtual IPv6 address with it, never with its own physical MAC, so hosts keep the same gateway MAC whichever router is active; after a takeover, switches learn it on the new router's port (RFC 9568, sections 7.2 and 8.2.2).

dest.ipv4: ADVERTISEMENTs are sent to 224.0.0.18, IP protocol 112, with a TTL of 255 (RFC 9568, section 5.1.1; the same in RFC 3768, section 5.2).
dest.ipv6: ADVERTISEMENTs are sent to ff02::12, Next Header 112, with a Hop Limit of 255, from the router's link-local address (RFC 9568, section 5.1.2).

mac.v2: VRRPv2 uses the same IPv4 block, 00-00-5E-00-01 followed by the VRID (RFC 3768, section 7.3).
mac.notations: The three forms are the same 48 bits written three ways: hyphens, as RFC 9568 writes it; colons; and three dotted groups of four hexadecimal digits.

start.owner: {name} owns the virtual address (priority 255): it sends an ADVERTISEMENT and becomes the {activeRole} at once, and every other router starts as a Backup ({rfc}, section 6.4.1).
start.tie: No router owns the virtual address, so every router starts as a Backup. {list} share the highest priority, {p}: their timers fire together and each of them turns {activeState}. One that hears an ADVERTISEMENT of the same priority from a higher primary address returns to Backup, so {name}, with the highest address, stays the {activeRole} ({rfc}, sections 6.4.1 and 6.4.3).
start.elected: No router owns the virtual address, so every router starts as a Backup with its {downTimer} running. {name} has the highest priority, {p}, and so the shortest {down}: its timer fires first and it becomes the {activeRole}. The others hear its ADVERTISEMENT, of a higher priority than theirs, and stay Backup ({rfc}, sections 6.4.1 and 6.4.2).

failure.tie: If {active} fails silently, {list} share the highest remaining priority, {p}: their timers fire together, each of them turns {activeState}, and {name}, with the higher primary address, stays the {activeRole} ({rfc}, sections 6.4.2 and 6.4.3).
failure.one: If {active} fails silently, the Backups stop hearing ADVERTISEMENTs. {name}, with the highest remaining priority, {p}, has the shortest {down}: its {downTimer} fires one {down} after the last ADVERTISEMENT it heard, and it becomes the {activeRole} ({rfc}, section 6.4.2).

shutdown.tie: If {active} shuts down cleanly, it sends an ADVERTISEMENT with priority 0. {list} share the highest remaining priority, {p}, and so the same Skew_Time: each of them turns {activeState} at the same moment, and {name}, with the higher primary address, stays the {activeRole} ({rfc}, sections 6.4.2 and 6.4.3).
shutdown.one: If {active} shuts down cleanly, it sends an ADVERTISEMENT with priority 0, and every Backup sets its timer to its own Skew_Time. {name}, with the highest remaining priority, {p}, has the shortest skew and becomes the {activeRole} ({rfc}, sections 6.4.2 and 6.4.3).

return.owner: When {name} comes back, it owns the virtual address: it becomes the {activeRole} at once and {current} returns to Backup, whatever Preempt_Mode says ({rfc}, sections 6.1 and 6.4.1).
return.preempts: When {name} comes back, it starts as a Backup. Preempt_Mode is on and its priority, {p}, is higher than {current}'s, {pc}, so it discards {current}'s ADVERTISEMENTs; its own {downTimer} fires one {down} after it starts, it becomes the {activeRole}, and {current}, hearing a higher priority, returns to Backup ({rfc}, sections 6.4.2 and 6.4.3).
return.noPreempt: When {name} comes back, it starts as a Backup. Its priority, {p}, is higher than {current}'s, {pc}, but Preempt_Mode is off: it resets its timer on every ADVERTISEMENT from {current} and stays Backup, and {current} stays the {activeRole} ({rfc}, section 6.4.2).
return.equal: When {name} comes back, it starts as a Backup with the same priority as {current}, {p}. A Backup resets its timer on any ADVERTISEMENT of equal or higher priority, and the primary address breaks a tie only between routers that are already {activeState}, so {name} stays Backup and {current} stays the {activeRole}, with or without preemption ({rfc}, sections 6.4.2 and 6.4.3).

verdict.owner: {name} is the {activeRole}: it owns the virtual address.
verdict.tie: {name} is the {activeRole}: it shares the highest priority, {p}, and has the highest primary address.
verdict.priority: {name} is the {activeRole}: it has the highest priority, {p}.

warn.samePriority: {list} have the same priority, {p}. RFC 9568 asks for different priorities, with "sufficient differences" so that Backups do not turn Active together (section 8.3.2); between them, the primary address decides only once both are Active.

multicast-mac-mapper.name: Multicast group to MAC mapper
multicast-mac-mapper.blurb: The Ethernet MAC address of an IPv4 or IPv6 multicast group, with the bits that reach it and the ones that do not, where the group sits in IANA's registries and the 32 IPv4 groups that share each MAC; and the reverse, from a 01-00-5E or 33-33 MAC to the groups behind it.
multicast-mac-mapper.runsLocally: Runs locally in your browser. Nothing is sent anywhere.
multicast-mac-mapper.inputHint: An IPv4 group (224.0.0.0 to 239.255.255.255) or an IPv6 group (ff00::/8) gives its MAC; a MAC in colon (01:00:5e:01:01:01), hyphen (01-00-5E-01-01-01) or Cisco dot (0100.5e01.0101) notation gives the groups behind it.
multicast-mac-mapper.empty: Type a group to see its MAC address, or a MAC to see the groups behind it. The Example fills 233.252.0.1, the group the Learn article works through bit by bit.

headline.v6reverse: <m>{mac}</m> carries any IPv6 group ending in {low}

bits.v4caption: 1110 marks every group; the next five bits ({lost}) are lost; the last 23 ({kept} in hex) follow 01-00-5E, and the MAC's fourth octet always begins with a 0 bit.
bits.v4reverseCaption: Every candidate is 1110, then five bits the MAC does not carry (shown as ?), then the 23 bits it does carry ({kept} in hex).
bits.v6group: The address, hex digit by hex digit
bits.v6caption: The first 96 bits are lost; the last 32 ({low}) follow 33-33.

scope4.local-expansion: Kept for the Local Scope to grow into
scope4.organisation-expansion: Kept for the Organization Local Scope to grow into

sameMac.heading: Other addresses IANA names on this MAC

v6r.heading: The groups behind this MAC
v6r.candidates: Addresses IANA names with these last 32 bits

multicast-mac-mapper.learn: The mapping in context, with IGMP, snooping and PIM: Multicast: what it costs to not flood.
multicast-mac-mapper.related: SPBM's backbone group addresses are computed another way, by the <spbm>SPBM multicast address builder</spbm>; other group MACs, such as the IEEE reserved ones, are read by the <oui>OUI / MAC vendor lookup</oui>.

share.carries: The link carries the address in the field, as typed, and nothing else.

v4.snooping: A switch that keeps its multicast table by MAC address cannot tell these 32 groups apart, and one that keeps it by IP address can: IGMP snooping switches "may maintain forwarding tables based on either MAC addresses or IP addresses", and IP is preferred "because the mapping between IP multicast addresses and link-layer multicast addresses is ambiguous" (RFC 4541, section 2.1.2). Its questionnaire asks the same of 224.1.2.3 and 239.129.2.3, which share a MAC (section 4).
v4.host: A host that joins one of them can receive frames for the others: a network interface "may deliver up packets destined to more addresses" than it joined, and the IP layer discards datagrams for groups the host does not belong to "without generating any error report or log entry" (RFC 1112, sections 7.2 and 7.3).
v4.mapping: RFC 1112 maps a group "by placing the low-order 23-bits of the IP address into the low-order 23 bits of the Ethernet multicast address 01-00-5E-00-00-00 (hex)" (section 6.4). Every group begins with 1110 (section 4), so the five bits after those four never reach the MAC.
v4.ssmLinkLayer: RFC 4607 warns that "SSM destinations in 232.0.0.0/24 and 232.128.0.0/24 use the same link-layer addresses as the reserved IP multicast group range 224.0.0.0/24" (section 9).
v4.collision: Because "there are 28 significant bits in an IP host group address, more than one host group address may map to the same Ethernet multicast address" (RFC 1112, section 6.4): 2^5 = 32 groups share each MAC.

block.localControl: Local Network Control Block (224.0.0.0/24): IANA says multicast routers "should not forward any multicast datagram with destination addresses in this range, regardless of its TTL", and snooping switches must forward packets to these addresses "on all ports" unless they are IGMP (RFC 4541, section 2.1.2).
block.internetwork: Internetwork Control Block (224.0.1.0/24): protocol control traffic that "MAY be forwarded through the Internet" (RFC 5771, section 5).
block.adhoc: AD-HOC block: addresses IANA assigns to applications that fit neither control block; they "MAY be globally routed" (RFC 5771, section 6). The registry names each assignment; this tool names the block.
block.testNet: MCAST-TEST-NET (233.252.0.0/24) is "for use in documentation and example code", and its addresses "MUST NOT appear on the public Internet" (RFC 5771, section 9.2; RFC 6676, section 2).
block.reserved: IANA lists this range as RESERVED (RFC 5771, section 3).
block.sdp: SDP/SAP Block (224.2.0.0/16): addresses "explicitly for use by SDP/SAP" that "MUST NOT be used for other purposes" (RFC 5771, section 7).
block.dis: DIS Transient Groups (224.252.0.0/14), as IANA's registry lists them (RFC 2365, section 6.3).
block.ssm: Source-Specific Multicast Block (232.0.0.0/8): a receiver subscribes to a channel (S,G), one source and this group (RFC 4607, section 1); IANA reserves 232.0.0.1 to 232.0.0.255 for its own allocation and leaves the rest to "local host allocation".
block.glop: GLOP Block (RFC 3180, section 3): 233.X.Y.0/24 belongs to the autonomous system whose 16-bit number is 256 x X + Y, so this group is in the /24 of AS {as}.
block.glopDoc: AS 64496 to 64511 are reserved for documentation, so their GLOP prefixes, 233.251.240.0/24 to 233.251.255.0/24, are for examples (RFC 6676, section 2.2).
block.ubm: Unicast-prefix-based (RFC 6034, section 3): shifting the group left by 8 bits gives {prefix}, inside the unicast space of the organization that may use this group.
block.admin: Administratively Scoped Block (239.0.0.0/8): "for local use within a domain" (RFC 5771, section 10); packets to these groups "do not cross configured administrative boundaries", and the addresses "are not required to be unique across administrative boundaries" (RFC 2365, section 3).

scope.local: IPv4 Local Scope (239.255.0.0/16): "the minimal enclosing scope" (RFC 2365, section 6.1).
scope.localExpansion: 239.253.0.0/16 and 239.254.0.0/16 are kept for the Local Scope to grow into and "should not be utilized until the 239.255.0.0/16 space is no longer sufficient" (RFC 2365, section 6.1.1).
scope.organisation: IPv4 Organization Local Scope (239.192.0.0/14): "the space from which an organization should allocate sub-ranges when defining scopes for private use" (RFC 2365, section 6.2).
scope.organisationExpansion: 239.0.0.0/10, 239.64.0.0/10 and 239.128.0.0/10 "are unassigned and available for expansion" of the Organization Local Scope and "should be left unassigned until the 239.192.0.0/14 space is no longer sufficient" (RFC 2365, section 6.2.1).
scope.adminOther: RFC 2365 names no scope for this part of 239.0.0.0/8; it is administratively scoped like the rest of the block (section 4).

relative.local: Relative address {offset} of the Local Scope: the top /24 of every scope "is reserved for relative assignments", counted down from its highest address, 239.255.255.255 (RFC 2365, section 9).
relative.organisation: Relative address {offset} of the Organization Local Scope: the top /24 of every scope "is reserved for relative assignments", counted down from its highest address, 239.195.255.255 (RFC 2365, section 9).

v4r.mapping: The top bit of the fourth octet is 0, so this is the IPv4 mapping: IANA gives 01-00-5E-00-00-00 to 01-00-5E-7F-FF-FF to IPv4 multicast (RFC 9542, section 2.1.3). Its last 23 bits are the group's low-order 23 bits (RFC 1112, section 6.4); the five bits after 1110 are not carried, so any of these 32 groups could be the one.

v6.collision: Every IPv6 multicast address with the same last 32 bits maps to this MAC: 2^(112 - 32) for each flags and scope value, "more than 1.2e24" (RFC 4541, section 3), and 2^88 in all. RFC 3307 keeps group IDs within 32 bits so that they "will generate unique link-layer addresses within a given multicast scope" (section 2); the same group ID in another scope, such as ff02::101 and ff05::101, shares the MAC.
v6.snooping: Because of that overlap, RFC 4541 recommends that "IPv6 address based forwarding is preferred to MAC address based forwarding" in MLD snooping switches (section 3).

gid.permanent: The last 32 bits, the group ID, are in 0x00000001 to 0x3FFFFFFF, the range IANA assigns to permanent addresses, which have T = 0 and P = 0 (RFC 3307, section 4.1).
gid.service: The last 32 bits, the group ID, are in 0x40000000 to 0x7FFFFFFF, for permanent group IDs that name a service "regardless of the upper 96 bits of the multicast address" (RFC 3307, section 4.2).
gid.dynamic: The last 32 bits, the group ID, are in 0x80000000 to 0xFFFFFFFF, for dynamic allocation (RFC 3307, section 4.3); IANA's Dynamic Multicast Group IDs registry (RFC 10028) lists this value under "{row}".

v6.mapping: RFC 2464 sends a packet for an IPv6 multicast address to "the Ethernet multicast address whose first two octets are the value 3333 hexadecimal and whose last four octets are the last four octets" of the address (section 7): the first 96 bits never reach the MAC.
v6.zone: The zone index "%{zone}" is set aside: zone identifiers "have purely local meaning within the node in which they are defined" (RFC 9844, section 1; the form is RFC 4007's, section 11), so the group and its MAC are the same without it.
v6.t1: T = 1: a non-permanently-assigned ("transient" or "dynamically" assigned) multicast address (RFC 4291, section 2.7).
v6.t0: T = 0: a permanently-assigned ("well-known") multicast address, assigned by IANA (RFC 4291, section 2.7).
v6.x: The highest flag bit (X) is set: RFC 7371 keeps it "for future assignment" (section 4.1.1) and requires that "Implementations MUST treat flag bits as separate bits" (section 3).
v6.scope1: Interface-Local scope "spans only a single interface on a node and is useful only for loopback transmission of multicast" (RFC 4291, section 2.7).
v6.notOnLink: Addresses in ff00::/15 "should never appear in packets on the link", and no MLD message is sent for them (RFC 4541, section 3).
v6.scopeF: Scope F is reserved: nodes "should not originate" packets to it, and such a packet "must be treated the same as packets destined to a global (scop E) multicast address" (RFC 4291, section 2.7).
v6.scopeUnassigned: An unassigned scope: these "are available for administrators to define additional multicast regions" (RFC 4291, section 2.7).
v6.allNodes: ff02::1 is the link-local all-nodes address: no MLD message is ever sent for it, so snooping switches should forward it "on all ports" (RFC 4541, section 3).
v6.documentation: ff0X::db8:0:0/96 is "allocated for documentation purposes", with T = 0 (RFC 6676, section 3).
v6.solicited: A solicited-node address, formed by "taking the low-order 24 bits of an address (unicast or anycast)" (RFC 4291, section 2.7.1): every unicast or anycast address ending in {low24} shares it, and so does its MAC.
v6.ssmIana: An SSM address (P = 1, T = 1, plen = 0: RFC 4607, section 1) in ff3x::4000:0001 to ff3x::7fff:ffff, the range reserved for IANA allocation (section 4.3).
v6.ssmDynamic: An SSM address (P = 1, T = 1, plen = 0: RFC 4607, section 1) in ff3x::8000:0000 to ff3x::ffff:ffff, the range for dynamic allocation by hosts (section 1).
v6.ssmPrefix: Its network prefix field is not zero: RFC 4607 asks that SSM addresses be allocated within ff3x::/96, while "a system should treat all of FF3x::/32 as SSM addresses" (section 1).
v6.prefix: Unicast-prefix-based (P = 1, RFC 3306, section 4): plen and the network prefix field give {prefix}, the unicast prefix of the network that owns the group.
v6.rp: Embedded RP (R = 1, RFC 3956, section 4, as updated by RFC 7371): copying the first plen bits of the network prefix and putting the RIID in the last 4 bits gives the Rendezvous Point {rp}.

v6r.mapping: The first two octets are 33-33, the IPv6 mapping (RFC 2464, section 7; RFC 9542, section 2.3.1): the last four octets are the group's last 32 bits, and the first 96 bits are not carried, so any IPv6 multicast address ending in {low} could be the one.
v6r.allNodes: ff02::1, the link-local all-nodes address, maps here: no MLD message is ever sent for it, so snooping switches should forward it "on all ports" (RFC 4541, section 3).
v6r.solicited: A solicited-node address maps here: {group}, formed from "the low-order 24 bits of an address (unicast or anycast)" (RFC 4291, section 2.7.1), so every unicast or anycast address ending in {low24} has this solicited-node address, and it maps to this MAC.
v6r.none: IANA's IPv6 multicast registry names no address that ends in these 32 bits.

v4.base: 224.0.0.0 "is guaranteed not to be assigned to any group" (RFC 1112, section 4).
v4.ssmZero: 232.0.0.0 "is reserved, and it must not be used as a destination address" (RFC 4607, section 4.3).
v4.sharesLocalControl: This MAC is also the mapping of {group}, in the Local Network Control Block, which snooping switches must forward on all ports (RFC 4541, section 2.1.2). RFC 4541's questionnaire asks whether a switch forwards frames to 01:00:5E:00:00:01 to 01:00:5E:00:00:FF on all ports (section 4); one that does floods this group with it.

v4r.localControl: One of these groups, {group}, is in the Local Network Control Block, which snooping switches must forward on all ports (RFC 4541, section 2.1.2). RFC 4541's questionnaire asks whether a switch forwards frames to 01:00:5E:00:00:01 to 01:00:5E:00:00:FF on all ports (section 4); one that does floods the other 31 groups with it.

v6.pWithoutT: P = 1 with T = 0: "If P = 1, T MUST be set to 1" (RFC 3306, section 4).
v6.rWithoutPT: R = 1 without both P and T: an embedded-RP address "MUST have the P-bit and T-bit both set to 1" (RFC 3956, section 4, as updated by RFC 7371, section 4.2.3), so no RP is read from it.
v6.scope0: Scope 0 is reserved: "Nodes must not originate a packet to a multicast address whose scop field contains the reserved value 0; if such a packet is received, it must be silently dropped" (RFC 4291, section 2.7).
v6.reservedAddress: ff00:: to ff0f:: "are reserved and shall never be assigned to any multicast group" (RFC 4291, section 2.7.1).
v6.ff2: Bits 17 to 20 (ff2) are not zero: they "MUST each be sent as zero and MUST be ignored on receipt" (RFC 7371, section 4.1.1).
v6.rsvd: With R = 0, the four bits before plen "MUST be sent as zero and MUST be ignored on receipt" (RFC 3956, section 3).
v6.ssmInvalid: An SSM address whose last 32 bits are 0x00000000 to 0x3FFFFFFF: RFC 4607 calls ff3x::0000:0000 to ff3x::3fff:ffff "invalid IPv6 SSM addresses", and "a router or host MAY choose to drop" packets sent to them (section 1).
v6.ssmReserved: ff3x::4000:0000 "is also reserved", kept as an invalid SSM destination that can serve as a null value (RFC 4607, section 4.3).
v6.plen: plen is {plen}, more than 64: "plen" higher than 64 "MUST NOT be used, as that would overlap with the high-order bits of multicast group-id" (RFC 3956, section 4), and the network prefix field holds 64 bits (RFC 3306, section 4).
v6.riid0: The RIID is 0, which "must not be used, as using it would cause ambiguity with the Subnet-Router Anycast Address" (RFC 3956, section 6.3).
v6.rpExcluded: The RP this gives, {rp}, falls in a range routers must refuse: "At least fe80::/10, ::/16, and ff00::/8 MUST be excluded" (RFC 3956, section 4).

mac.unicast: {mac} is a unicast MAC address: its group bit, the lowest bit of the first octet, is 0 (RFC 9542, section 2.1.1). Neither RFC 1112's mapping nor RFC 2464's gives a unicast address.
mac.broadcast: FF-FF-FF-FF-FF-FF is the broadcast address, not the mapping of an IP multicast group: IPv4 groups map into 01-00-5E-00-00-00 to 01-00-5E-7F-FF-FF (RFC 1112) and IPv6 groups into 33-33-00-00-00-00 to 33-33-FF-FF-FF-FF (RFC 2464).
mac.ianaUpperOne: {mac} has the 25th bit set (the top bit of the fourth octet), so it is not an IPv4 mapping: RFC 1112 puts a group's low-order 23 bits after 01-00-5E with that bit 0, and IANA gives only 01-00-5E-00-00-00 to 01-00-5E-7F-FF-FF to IPv4 multicast (RFC 9542, section 2.1.3). IANA's registry lists {first} as "{usage}".
mac.ianaUpper: {mac} has the 25th bit set (the top bit of the fourth octet), so it is not an IPv4 mapping: RFC 1112 puts a group's low-order 23 bits after 01-00-5E with that bit 0, and IANA gives only 01-00-5E-00-00-00 to 01-00-5E-7F-FF-FF to IPv4 multicast (RFC 9542, section 2.1.3). IANA's registry lists {first} to {last} as "{usage}".
mac.otherGroup: {mac} is a group MAC address outside the two IP multicast mappings, 01-00-5E-00-00-00 to 01-00-5E-7F-FF-FF for IPv4 (RFC 1112) and 33-33-00-00-00-00 to 33-33-FF-FF-FF-FF for IPv6 (RFC 2464), so no IP group maps to it.

err.tooLong: The input is longer than this tool reads ({max} characters).
err.empty: Enter an IPv4 or IPv6 multicast group, or a multicast MAC address.
err.lines: Enter one address, on one line.
err.malformed: "{value}" is not an IPv4 group, an IPv6 group or a MAC address in a notation this tool reads. Write a group as 239.1.1.1 or ff02::1, and a MAC as 01:00:5e:01:01:01, 01-00-5E-01-01-01 or 0100.5e01.0101.
err.prefix: "{value}" has a prefix length: enter one group address, without "/".
err.zone: "{value}" has an empty or unreadable zone index after "%": write it with letters, digits, ".", "_" or "-", or leave it out.

v6.malformed: "{value}" is not an IPv6 address: write eight groups of up to four hex digits separated by colons, with "::" at most once for a run of zero groups, for example ff02::1.
v6.notMulticast: {value} is not an IPv6 multicast address: those begin with the octet ff, binary 11111111 (RFC 4291, section 2.7).

v4.octet: "{value}" is not an IPv4 address: each of the four numbers must be from 0 to 255.
v4.leadingZero: "{value}" has a number with a leading zero, which some systems read as octal: write each number without leading zeros, for example 239.1.1.1.
v4.unicast: {value} is not a multicast group: IPv4 groups begin with the bits 1110, from 224.0.0.0 to 239.255.255.255 (RFC 1112, section 4), and this address is below that range.
v4.classE: {value} begins with the bits 1111, which RFC 1112 reserves "for future addressing modes" (section 4): it is not a multicast group.

stp-election-calculator.name: Spanning tree election calculator
stp-election-calculator.blurb: The root bridge, every root port, every designated port and the ports left as alternate or backup in a small switched network you describe in a few lines, each step with the comparison that decided it; and the long (802.1t) and short (802.1D-1998) path costs by link speed, with each vendor's documented default.
stp-election-calculator.runsLocally: Runs locally in your browser. Nothing is sent anywhere.

grammar.bridge: <c>bridge SW1 32768 00-00-5E-00-53-01</c>: a name, a priority (a multiple of 4096 from 0 to 61440) and a MAC address; end the line with <c>short</c> or <c>long</c> to give that bridge its own path cost method.
grammar.link: <c>link SW1:1 SW2:1 1G</c>: two ports and a speed (10M, 100M, 1G, 10G, 25G, 40G, 50G, 100G, 1T or 10T), or <c>cost 4000</c> in place of the speed; three or more ports make a shared segment.
grammar.port: <c>port SW1:2 priority 64</c> or <c>port SW1:2 cost 4000</c>: a port priority (a multiple of 16, 128 by default) or a cost for that port alone.
grammar.vlan: <c>vlan 10</c> adds the VLAN ID to every priority (the system ID extension); <c>priority-format 802.1d</c> reads the 16-bit priorities of 802.1D-1998. A # starts a comment.
grammar.limits: Up to 16 bridges, 32 links, 8 ports on a segment, 128 ports, 80 lines and 4000 characters.

stp-election-calculator.speedHint: A number and a unit: 100M, 1G, 40 Gb/s or 1T. The tool knows only the speeds a document read for it gives a cost for.

empty.election: Describe a switched network, one statement per line, or press Example for the course's six-bridge example (chapter 2.4, slide 259).
empty.cost: Type or pick a link speed to see its long and short path costs, the documents that give them, and each vendor's default method.

stp-election-calculator.learn: The election, the costs and the timers are explained in the Learn article Spanning tree in one article, whose lab runs four switches.
stp-election-calculator.puzzle: Practise on the daily Spanning Tree puzzle: the same rules, a new network every day.
