share.carries: The link carries the mode, the path cost method and the topology, or the speed, as typed.
share.caution: Bridge names and MAC addresses can describe a real network: read them before you send the link.

step1.heading: 1. Root bridge: the lowest bridge ID

step2.heading: 2. Root ports: each bridge's best path to the root

step3.heading: 3. Designated ports: one on every segment

step4.heading: 4. Every port
step4.none: No port discards: the topology has no loop.

cost.tableHeading: Path costs by speed; the speed asked for names its documents

note.fast: Above 10 Gb/s the documents read agree less: the short values come from MikroTik's table (and, at 40 Gb/s, Huawei's), and some long ones from one or two vendors; each value lists the documents that give it.
note.mixed: Whatever the method, every switch in one network should use the same one: a short-cost switch advertises root path costs thousands of times smaller than a long-cost neighbour, and the tree bends towards it.
note.scales: The long values are the 32-bit ones of 802.1t, kept in 802.1D-2004 (1 to 200,000,000, RFC 4188 dot1dStpPortPathCost32); the short ones are 802.1D-1998's 16-bit values (1 to 65,535, dot1dStpPortPathCost). Both fall as the speed rises, "in inverse proportion to the speed of the attached LAN".

cost.verdictNoShort: {speed}: long (32-bit) cost {long}; no document read gives a short (16-bit) cost for it.

err.bridgeCount: The topology declares {count} bridges; the tool elects among {min} to {max}.
err.bridgeDup: A bridge called {name} is already declared on line {first}.
err.bridgeMethod: {name}: "{value}" is not a path cost method; write long or short after the MAC address, or nothing.
err.bridgeName: "{name}" is not a bridge name: start with a letter, then up to 15 letters, digits, dots, hyphens or underscores.
err.bridgeShape: A bridge line is the word bridge, a name, a priority and a MAC address (bridge SW1 32768 00-00-5E-00-53-01), then optionally long or short for that bridge's path cost method.
err.costShortBridge: {bridge} uses short path costs, whose range is 1 to 65535 (RFC 4188, dot1dStpPortPathCost; Extreme: "the path cost range setting is 1 to 65,535" on 802.1D-1998 bridges), so it cannot take cost {value}.
err.disconnected: The topology is not connected: {outside} cannot reach {inside} over any link. Each separate part would elect its own root, so the tool computes one connected network at a time.
err.empty: Describe the topology: one bridge line per switch (bridge SW1 32768 00-00-5E-00-53-01: a name, a priority and a MAC address) and one link line per cable (link SW1:1 SW2:1 1G: two ports and a speed).
err.endpoint: "{value}" is not a port: write the bridge's name, a colon and the port number, such as SW1:24.
err.format: Write priority-format 802.1t (a priority in steps of 4096 with the system ID extension, the default) or priority-format 802.1d (the 16-bit priority of 802.1D-1998, 0 to 65535).
err.json: The request body is not valid JSON: send one JSON object that names its mode, election or cost.
err.keyword: "{word}" is not a statement this tool reads: start each line with bridge, link, port, vlan or priority-format (a # starts a comment).
err.lineTooLong: the line is longer than {max} characters.
err.linkCost: "{value}" is not a port path cost: write a whole number from 1 to 200000000 (RFC 4188, dot1dStpPortPathCost32).
err.linkCount: The tool reads at most {max} links.
err.linkPorts: A link joins 2 to {max} ports (more than two is a shared segment); this one lists {count}.
err.linkShape: A link line is the word link, two ports and a speed (link SW1:1 SW2:1 1G), or two ports and a typed cost (link SW1:1 SW2:1 cost 4000); list more than two ports for a shared segment.
err.mac: {name}: "{value}" is not a MAC address; write six octets with colons or hyphens (00-00-5E-00-53-01), three dotted groups (0000.5e00.5301) or twelve hexadecimal digits.
err.macDup: {second} has the same MAC address as {first}, {mac}. The bridge address is the part of the bridge ID that makes it unique (RFC 4188, dot1dBaseBridgeAddress: "referred to in a unique fashion"), so two bridges never share it, and with equal priorities their bridge IDs would be the same.
err.method: Choose the path cost method: long (the 32-bit values of 802.1t and 802.1D-2004) or short (the 16-bit values of 802.1D-1998).
err.mode: Choose a mode: election or cost.
err.noLinks: The topology has bridges but no link lines: write one link line per cable, such as link SW1:1 SW2:1 1G.
err.portCost: {value}: the port path cost must be a whole number from 1 to {max}.
err.portCostTwice: {value} already has a cost on this line.
err.portCount: The tool reads at most {max} ports in all.
err.portNumber8021d: {value}: the port number must be from 1 to 255, the one octet of an 802.1D-1998 port ID (RFC 4188, dot1dStpPortPriority).
err.portNumber8021t: {value}: the port number must be from 1 to 4095, the twelve bits of an 802.1t port ID (IEEE 802.1Q YANG, port-id).
err.portPriority8021d: {value}: an 802.1D-1998 port priority is one octet, 0 to 255 (RFC 4188, dot1dStpPortPriority).
err.portPriority8021t: {value}: a port priority is a multiple of 16 from 0 to 240 (RFC 4188, dot1dStpPortPriority: "0-240, in steps of 16").
err.portPriorityTwice: {value} already has a priority from line {first}.
err.portShape: A port line is the word port, a port and a priority (port SW1:2 priority 64), a cost (port SW1:2 cost 4000), or both pairs.
err.portTwice: {bridge}:{number} is already on the link of line {first}: a port attaches to one segment.
err.portUnknown: {value} is not on any link line; a port line sets a port that a link uses.
err.priority8021d: {name}: priority {value} does not fit the two octets of an 802.1D-1998 bridge priority (0 to 65535, RFC 4188).
err.priority8021t: {name}: priority {value} is not a multiple of 4096 from 0 to 61440. With the system ID extension the priority keeps only four bits (RFC 4188, dot1dStpPriority: "0-61440, in steps of 4096"). For a bridge that uses the 16-bit priority of 802.1D-1998, add the line priority-format 802.1d.
err.priorityNotNumber: {name}: "{value}" is not a bridge priority; write a whole number.
err.speedEmpty: Type a link speed, such as 1G, 100M or 40G.
err.speedForm: "{value}" is not a speed: write a number and a unit, such as 100M, 1G or 10G, or write the word cost and a number.
err.speedFormCost: "{value}" is not a speed: write a number and a unit, such as 100M, 1G, 40 Gb/s or 1T.
err.speedNoShort: {bridge} uses short path costs, and no document read for this tool gives a short cost for {speed} (they give one up to 100 Gb/s). Type a cost on this link, or use long costs.
err.speedTooLong: A speed is at most {max} characters, such as 100 Mb/s.
err.speedUnknown: No document read for this tool gives a port path cost for {value}; the speeds it knows are {list}. Write the word cost and the number your switches use instead.
err.speedUnknownCost: No document read for this tool gives a port path cost for {value}; the speeds it knows are {list}. A switch at another speed still has a cost: read it with its own show command.
err.tooLong: The topology is {length} characters long; the tool reads at most {max}.
err.tooManyLines: The topology has {count} lines; the tool reads at most {max}.
err.unknownBridge: {value} names a bridge, {name}, that no bridge line declares.
err.vlan: Write vlan followed by a VLAN ID from 1 to 4094; its number becomes the system ID extension of every bridge ID.
err.vlanWith8021d: A vlan line needs the 802.1t priority format: the 802.1D-1998 bridge ID has two octets of priority and no system ID extension to carry the VLAN (RFC 4188, dot1dStpPriority).

engine.name: {value}

note.bridgeMethod: A bridge line that ends in long or short uses that method for its own ports' speeds; the cost a port adds is always its own bridge's.
note.format8021d: priority-format 802.1d: bridge priorities are the two octets of 802.1D-1998 (0 to 65535), port priorities one octet and port numbers one octet (RFC 4188).
note.methodDefault: No path cost method was chosen, so link speeds use the long (32-bit) values; choose short for 802.1D-1998 bridges.
note.methodLong: Link speeds use the long (32-bit) path costs of 802.1t, kept in 802.1D-2004: 2000000 for 10 Mb/s down to 2000 for 10 Gb/s.
note.methodShort: Link speeds use the short (16-bit) path costs of 802.1D-1998: 100 for 10 Mb/s, 19 for 100 Mb/s, 4 for 1 Gb/s and 2 for 10 Gb/s.
note.model: The tool computes the stable result every bridge agrees on. It does not model timers and convergence, the proposal and agreement handshake, edge ports, link types, topology changes, MSTP regions and instances, failed links, or BPDU Guard, Root Guard and Loop Guard.
note.noVlan: No vlan line: the system ID extension is 0, as in a single RSTP tree (Arista's manual gives the VLAN number for Rapid-PVST, the instance number for MST and 0 for RST). Add a vlan line (vlan 10) to compute one VLAN's tree as Cisco's Rapid PVST+ does.
note.shared: A link line with more than two ports is a shared segment, as through a hub: one port on it is designated and every other port on it hears that one.
note.states: Root and designated ports forward. Alternate and backup ports are "placed in the discarding state" in RSTP (Juniper); classic 802.1D calls the same state blocking (RFC 4188, dot1dStpPortState).
note.vlan: VLAN {vlan} is added to every priority as the 12-bit system ID extension, as in Cisco's per-VLAN trees ("a 12-bit extended system ID value equal to the VLAN ID"): a bridge at priority 32768 has the priority field {example}.

block.alternate: {port} is an alternate port: {sender} is designated on its segment and {bridge} already reaches the root through {rootPort}, so it discards, a ready second path if {rootPort} fails.
block.backup: {port} is a backup port: the better BPDU it hears comes from {sender}, another port of {bridge} on the same segment, so it discards and stands by for that designated port.

dp.bid: {segment}: {bridge} and {otherBridge} both reach the root at {cost}; {bridge}'s bridge ID, {bid}, is the lower (against {otherBid}), so {port} is designated.
dp.cost: {segment}: {bridge} reaches the root at {cost}, less than {otherBridge} at {otherCost}, so {port} is designated.
dp.portId: {segment}: two ports of {bridge} are on this segment, {port} and {other}; {port} has the lower port ID, {pid} against {otherPid}, and is designated.
dp.root: {segment}: {bridge} is the root, at root path cost 0, so its port {port} is designated.

root.mac: {root} is the root bridge: its priority field, {field}, ties with {next}'s, and its MAC address, {mac}, is the lower, so its bridge ID, {bid}, is the lowest.
root.priority: {root} is the root bridge: its bridge ID, {bid}, is the lowest, and its priority field, {field}, is lower than the next bridge's, {next} ({nextField}), so the MAC address is not needed.

rp.cost: {bridge}: {port} has the lowest root path cost, {cost} ({sender} advertises {senderCost}, and {port} adds {portCost}); the next best, {other}, would cost {otherCost}. {port} is the root port.
rp.only: {bridge} hears another bridge on one port only, {port}: it is the root port, at root path cost {cost} ({sender} advertises {senderCost}, and {port} adds {portCost}).
rp.receivingPort: {bridge}: {port} and {other} hear the same port, {sender}, at cost {cost}, on a shared segment. Their own port IDs decide: {ownPid} against {otherPid}, so {port} is the root port.
rp.senderBid: {bridge}: {port} and {other} both reach the root at cost {cost}. The BPDU on {port} comes from {senderBridge}, bridge ID {senderBid}, lower than {otherBridge}'s, {otherBid}, so {port} is the root port.
rp.senderPort: {bridge}: {port} and {other} both hear {senderBridge} at cost {cost}. {senderBridge} sends to {port} from port ID {senderPid} and to {other} from {otherPid}; the lower sender port ID wins, so {port} is the root port.

vendor.arista: "1 gigabit interfaces have a default cost of 20000" and 10 gigabit ones 2000; no method setting appears in the manual read, only spanning-tree cost on the interface.
vendor.aruba: Long values by speed (10 Mbps 2,000,000 to 1 Tbps 20); the AOS-CX page read gives no command to change the method, only spanning-tree cost on the port (1 to 200,000,000).
vendor.cisco: The documents disagree. The Catalyst 9300 command reference (17.18 and 26.x) gives spanning-tree pathcost method a "Command Default" of short, and the configuration guides and the IOS XE 17 STP guide say "The short path cost method is the default STP path cost method used"; yet the guides' default-configuration tables list the long values (20000 for 1 Gbps), and the command reference's own show spanning-tree examples print "Configured Pathcost method used is long" and a port path cost of 20000. Read a switch's method with show spanning-tree summary, and pin it on every switch: spanning-tree pathcost method long, the change Cisco's case 225591 made.
vendor.extreme-fe: spanning-tree mstp pathcost-type sets the default path cost type to 16 or 32 bits; "The default is 32 bits."
vendor.extreme-se: Long values by default since ExtremeXOS 11.6 (2,000,000 for 10 Mb/s down to 2,000 for 10 Gb/s; ExtremeXOS 11.5 and earlier used 100, 19, 4 and 2). There is no method switch: to match an 802.1D-1998 bridge, Extreme's advice is to type the old value on the port, 19 instead of 200,000 for 100 Mb/s.
vendor.huawei: "By default, the IEEE 802.1t is used to calculate the path cost": the long values. stp pathcost-standard switches to dot1d-1998 (the short values) or to Huawei's own legacy scale (20 for 1 Gb/s, 2 for 10 Gb/s), and changing it puts every port's typed cost back to the default. Huawei's table gives one less for full duplex at 10 and 100 Mb/s (1,999,999 and 199,999 long, 99 and 18 short) and lower costs for aggregated links, so a Huawei port at those speeds can differ from the table here.
vendor.juniper: "The link cost is determined by the link speed", with no method statement in the pages read; the example output of show spanning-tree interface prints 20000 on a ge- (1 Gb/s) interface and 2000 on an xe- (10 Gb/s) one.
vendor.mikrotik: port-cost-mode on the bridge, long or short, "Default: long"; RouterOS before 7.13 gave every port 10 whatever its speed.

engine.verdict: {root} is the root bridge. Forwarding: root ports {rootPorts}, designated ports {designatedPorts}. Discarding: alternate ports {alternates}, backup ports {backups}.

warn.groupMac: {name}'s MAC address, {mac}, has the group (multicast) bit set: "If it is zero, the MAC address is unicast" (RFC 9542, section 2.1.1), and a bridge's own address is a unicast one. The election still compares it as a number.
warn.mixed: Path cost methods are mixed: short on {short}, long on {long}. A short-cost bridge advertises a root path cost thousands of times smaller, so paths through it look cheapest whatever their speed: Extreme warns that "an 802.1D-1998 compliant bridge could become the most favorable transit path", and Cisco's case 225591 fixed a root inconsistency by changing a switch from short to long. Set one method on every switch.
warn.rootByMac: Every bridge has priority {priority}, so the lowest MAC address chose the root, {root}, by accident rather than design. The course's advice is to lower the intended root's priority on purpose (4096, for example).

lacp-hash-and-state-reader.name: LACP member link and state reader
lacp-hash-and-state-reader.blurb: Which member of a link aggregation group carries a flow, for the one hash an implementation publishes in full (the Linux bonding driver's), with every step, what a failed member moves and how a run of flows spreads; Cisco's documented split shows why 2, 4 and 8 members share evenly. And the LACP actor and partner state flags read bit by bit, with the timers and a verdict for the pair.
lacp-hash-and-state-reader.runsLocally: Runs locally in your browser. Nothing is sent anywhere.

inputs.state: The state values, as a LACPDU or a show command gives them

policyHint.l2: Reads the last byte of each MAC address and the EtherType; the IP addresses only set the EtherType, IPv4 or IPv6.
policyHint.l23: Reads the last byte of each MAC address, the EtherType and both IP addresses.
policyHint.l34: Reads both IP addresses and the TCP or UDP ports; the MAC addresses are not read.
policyHint.vlan: Reads the VLAN tag and the source MAC address only.

lacp-hash-and-state-reader.membersHint: 2 to 8. Counted from 0 in the order they joined the bond; in 802.3ad mode, only those of the active aggregator.
lacp-hash-and-state-reader.spreadToggle: Spread: vary one field over a run of flows
lacp-hash-and-state-reader.spreadHint: From the value typed upward, one step each: 1 to 4096 flows.

empty.link: Enter the member count and the fields the policy reads. Example fills a two-member bond, as the course's lab bundles two cables, carrying the first flow of the Learn article's lab.
empty.state: Enter the actor's state, and the partner's if you have it. Example fills 0x3F on both ends: active, fast rate, in the bundle.

down.heading: If a member goes down
down.own: its own member: moves to member {m}

spread.heading: {count} flows, varying the {field}
spread.even: Even: no member carries more than one flow more than another.
spread.uneven: Uneven: the busiest member carries {max} flows, the quietest {min}.
spread.first: The first flows land on members: {list}

cisco.heading: Cisco's documented split for {n} ports (Catalyst 6500/6000)
cisco.even: Even: every port takes the same share of the 8 values.
cisco.uneven: Uneven: 8 values do not divide by this many ports, so some ports take twice the share of others even with random addresses.

vendors.heading: Not computed: the hash is not published
vendors.cisco: Cisco Catalyst 9300 (IOS XE 17.18): the load-balance methods and the src-mac default are documented, not the function.
vendors.juniper: Juniper Junos: the fields depend on the EtherType and the hash also uses internal values, such as the source port ID and device ID.
vendors.arista: Arista EOS: the hashing inputs vary by switch platform; the function is not described.
vendors.aruba: HPE Aruba AOS-CX: l2-src-dst, l3-src-dst and l4-src-dst are documented, not the function.
vendors.extreme: Extreme Switch Engine: xor, crc-16 and crc-32 are named, not how the fields are laid out for them.
vendors.huawei: Huawei VRP (S5700 and S6700, V200R025C00): load-balance takes dst-ip, dst-mac, src-ip, src-mac, src-dst-ip (the default), src-dst-mac or an enhanced profile, and applies to outgoing traffic only, so the two ends of a link may use different modes. The hash factors vary with the packet type and the model: Layer 2 packets fall back to their source and destination MAC addresses; the S5736-S hashes src-dst-ip with the TCP or UDP source and destination ports whatever is configured, with one mode for the whole switch; on the S5731-H, S5731-S, S5731S-S, S5731S-H, S5732-H, S6730-H, S6730S-H, S6730-S and S6730S-S, whichever of the six basic modes is configured, packets are load balanced based on their physical-layer source port numbers. The function is not given, so nothing is computed: <c>display eth-trunk load-balance</c> shows the hash factors a switch uses.
vendors.mikrotik: MikroTik RouterOS: the policies are described in words with a pointer to the Linux documentation; a bond offloaded to the switch chip hashes there, with no formula given.

formatHint.octet: As the LACPDU carries it: 0x3D as Cisco's show lacp prints it, 61 as Linux prints it in /proc/net/bonding, or 0b00111101.
formatHint.snmp: dot3adAggPortActorOperState or PartnerOperState as SNMP returns it: one octet in hexadecimal, bit 0 in the high-order bit.
formatHint.extreme: Eight positions in the order A T G S C D F E, a hyphen for a bit not set, as Extreme Switch Engine prints them.
formatHint.arista: A or P, S or L, G or I, s+ or s-, and any of C, X, D and d, as Arista EOS prints them.
formatHint.huawei: The PortState column of Huawei's display eth-trunk: eight characters of 0 and 1, Bit 1 first. Paste the whole output, or type the actor's and the partner's PortState.

lacp-hash-and-state-reader.partnerHint: The partner's state as this end reports it: what it last received, or its defaults when Defaulted is set.

timers.heading: Timers
timers.actorTimeout: This end gives up on the partner
timers.partnerTimeout: The partner gives up on this end
timers.none: not periodically: both ends are passive
timers.needsPartner: at the rate the partner asks for (add its state)

state.huaweiOrder: PortState {ps} as printed, Bit 1 first; written the usual way, bit 7 first: 0b{bin}, {hex}.

lacp-hash-and-state-reader.learn: The Learn article Link aggregation and LACP explains bundles, LACP and why one flow never runs faster than one member, with a hashing lab.

share.carries: The link carries the mode and its fields as typed; in link mode only the fields the policy reads.
share.caution: MAC and IP addresses and ports can describe hosts on a private network: read them before you send the link.
share.cautionDisplay: A pasted display eth-trunk output names the switches' system IDs (MAC addresses) and interfaces: read it before you send the link.

err.mode: Choose a mode: link (which member carries a flow) or state (read LACP state flags).
err.json: The request body is not valid JSON: send one JSON object that names its mode, link or state.
err.tooLong: A field is longer than this tool reads (64 characters).
err.policy: Choose a transmit hash policy the Linux bonding driver documents and this tool computes: layer2, layer2+3, layer3+4 or vlan+srcmac. encap2+3 and encap3+4 can read the inner headers of a tunnel, which this tool does not take.
err.byteOrder: Choose the processor's byte order: little (little-endian) or big (big-endian).
err.membersEmpty: Enter how many members can transmit, a whole number from 2 to 8.
err.membersBad: "{value}" is not a member count: enter a whole number from 2 to 8.
err.membersRange: The tool reads 2 to 8 members: with one there is nothing to choose, and eight is as far as it goes.
err.srcMacEmpty: Enter the source MAC address: this policy reads it.
err.dstMacEmpty: Enter the destination MAC address: this policy reads it.
err.macBad: "{value}" is not a MAC address: write six octets in hexadecimal, as 00:00:5e:00:53:0a, 00-00-5E-00-53-0A or 0000.5e00.530a.
err.srcIpEmpty: Enter the source IP address: this policy reads it (for layer2, it sets the EtherType).
err.dstIpEmpty: Enter the destination IP address: this policy reads it (for layer2, it sets the EtherType).
err.ipBad: "{value}" is not an IPv4 or IPv6 address this tool reads (write it without a prefix length or a zone).
err.familyMix: The source and destination addresses mix IPv4 and IPv6: one packet carries one family.
err.protocol: Choose the transport protocol: tcp or udp. layer3+4 reads the ports of unfragmented TCP and UDP only.
err.srcPortEmpty: Enter the source port: layer3+4 reads it.
err.dstPortEmpty: Enter the destination port: layer3+4 reads it.
err.portBad: "{value}" is not a port: enter a whole number from 0 to 65535.
err.vlanBad: "{value}" is not a VLAN ID: enter a whole number from 1 to 4094, or leave it blank for an untagged frame (the IEEE 802.1 MIBs do not permit 0 and 4095 as VLAN identifiers).
err.priorityBad: "{value}" is not a priority: enter a whole number from 0 to 7.
err.priorityNoTag: A priority travels in a VLAN tag: enter the VLAN ID too, or leave the priority blank.
err.spreadField: {policy} does not read {field}, so varying it would move nothing: choose a field the policy reads.
err.spreadFieldBad: Choose the field to vary: srcPort, dstPort, srcIp, dstIp, srcMac, dstMac or vlan.
err.spreadCount: "{value}" is not a flow count: enter a whole number from 1 to 4096.
err.spreadVlan: To vary the VLAN, start from a VLAN ID: an untagged frame has none.
err.spreadOverflow: That run of values goes past the last {field} there is: start lower or count fewer.
err.format: Choose how the values are written: octet, snmp, extreme, arista or huawei.
err.actorEmpty: Enter the actor's state: the value for the end whose output you are reading.
err.octetBad: "{value}" is not a state octet: write it in hexadecimal with 0x (0x3D, as Cisco prints it), in decimal (61, as Linux prints it in /proc/net/bonding) or in binary with 0b (0b00111101).
err.octetHex: "{value}" looks hexadecimal: write it with 0x in front (0x{value}), so it is not read as decimal.
err.octetRange: "{value}" is more than one octet can hold: a state is 0 to 255 (0x00 to 0xFF).
err.snmpBad: "{value}" is not an SNMP BITS value of one octet: write two hexadecimal digits, with or without 0x (0xBC), or binary with 0b.
err.extremeBad: "{value}" is not an Extreme flags string: write eight positions, each its letter or a hyphen, in the order A T G S C D F E (A-GSCD-- is an active member in the bundle).
err.aristaBad: "{value}" is not an Arista state: write A or P, S or L, G or I, s+ or s-, and any of C, X, D and d, each once (ALGs+CD is an active member in the bundle).
err.octetBits: "{value}" is eight characters of 0 and 1: for the PortState that Huawei's display eth-trunk prints (Bit 1 first), choose the huawei format; for an octet in binary, written bit 7 first, put 0b in front.
err.huaweiBad: "{value}" is not a Huawei PortState: write the eight characters display eth-trunk prints, each 0 or 1, Bit 1 first (10111100 is an active member in the bundle).
err.huaweiBoth: Paste the display eth-trunk output or type the PortState values, not both.
err.displayLong: The pasted output is longer than this tool reads (8192 characters, or 96 lines that are not blank).
err.displayRows: No member rows were found in the pasted output: paste display eth-trunk from an Eth-Trunk in LACP mode, with its Local table (port, Status, PortType, PortPri, PortNo, PortKey, PortState, Weight) and, if you have it, its Partner table.
err.displayRowBad: The row for {port} does not read as a member row of display eth-trunk: after the port name come Status (Selected, Unselect or ForceFwd), PortType, PortPri, PortNo, PortKey, a PortState of eight characters 0 or 1, and Weight.
err.displayPartnerBad: The Partner row for {port} does not read as one: after the port name come the system priority, the system ID (as 00e0-fc6e-bb11), PortPri, PortNo, PortKey and a PortState of eight characters 0 or 1.
err.displayTwice: {port} has two rows in the same table: paste one display eth-trunk output at a time.
err.displayOrphan: The Partner table has a row for {port}, which the Local table does not list: paste the whole display eth-trunk output.
err.displayPort: "{value}" is not a member port in the pasted output: choose one of the ports its Local table lists.

0.set: Active: the port takes part in the protocol whatever its partner's setting, and sends LACPDUs on its own.
0.clear: Passive: the port does not send LACPDUs unless its partner is active.

1.set: Short timeout: the port asks its partner for a LACPDU every second, and gives up on it after 3 seconds without one.
1.clear: Long timeout: the port asks its partner for a LACPDU every 30 seconds, and gives up on it after 90 seconds without one.

2.set: Aggregatable: the link can join an aggregation.
2.clear: Individual: the link can operate only as an individual link.

3.set: In sync: the link is allocated to the correct link aggregation group, the group is associated with a compatible aggregator, and its identity is consistent with the system ID and key transmitted.
3.clear: Out of sync: the link is not, or not yet, in the right aggregation.

4.set: Collecting: frames received on the link are passed to the aggregator.
4.clear: Not collecting: the receive function of the link is not enabled for the aggregation.

5.set: Distributing: the aggregator may send frames on the link.
5.clear: Not distributing: distribution of outgoing frames on the link is disabled.

6.set: Defaulted: the port is using partner information configured by default, not information received in a LACPDU.
6.clear: Not defaulted: the partner information in use was received in a LACPDU.

7.set: Expired: the port's receive machine is in the Expired state, because no LACPDU arrived before its timer ran out.

verdict.bundled: Bundled: both ends are aggregatable, in sync, collecting and distributing, and each is using what it heard from the other.
verdict.bundledThisEnd: This end is bundled: aggregatable, in sync, collecting and distributing, on partner information received in a LACPDU. Add the partner's state to read the other direction.
verdict.notBundled: Not fully bundled: the findings below say why.
verdict.notBundledThisEnd: This end is not bundled: the findings below say why.

f.bothPassive: Both ends are passive (LACP_Activity clear on each): neither sends a LACPDU until it hears one, so none are exchanged and the aggregation does not form. Juniper: "If both links are in passive mode, they won't exchange LACP packets"; Cisco: a port in the passive mode "cannot form an EtherChannel with another port that is also in the passive mode". Set at least one end to active.
f.actorExpired: This end is Expired: no LACPDU arrived before its timeout ran out. If none arrives before the timer runs out again, it moves to Defaulted (Juniper, show lacp interfaces). While Expired, the Linux driver treats the partner as asking for the short timeout, so it sends every second.
f.actorDefaulted: This end is Defaulted: it has received no LACPDU in time and is using partner information configured by default (Juniper), so the partner values beside it are those defaults, not what the far end said. Check that the far end runs LACP on this link and that at least one end is active.
f.partnerExpired: The partner reports Expired: LACPDUs from this end stopped reaching it before its timeout ran out.
f.partnerDefaulted: The partner reports Defaulted: it has received no LACPDU from this end in time and uses default information for it, so LACPDUs from this end are not reaching it.
f.actorIndividual: This end's link is individual (Aggregation clear): it can operate only as an individual link and does not join the aggregation.
f.partnerIndividual: The partner's link is individual (Aggregation clear): the far end will not aggregate it.
f.actorOutOfSync: This end is out of sync: the link is not in the right aggregation. Synchronization means the link is in the correct group and the group's identity matches the system ID and key transmitted (Juniper), so compare the system IDs and keys: ports form one aggregation when they have "the same actor system ID, actor key, partner system ID, and partner key" (HPE Aruba). A member cabled to another switch, or to a port of another group there, shows a different partner system ID or key from the other members.
f.partnerOutOfSync: The partner reports out of sync: on the far end this link is not in the right aggregation. Compare the system IDs and keys of the members on both ends.
f.actorNotForwarding: This end is in sync but not both collecting and distributing: it is still being attached to the aggregator, or waiting for the partner (the mux state in show lacp interfaces says which).
f.partnerNotForwarding: The partner is in sync but not both collecting and distributing: on the far end the link is still being attached.
f.timeoutsDiffer: The two ends ask for different timeouts. Each sends at the rate its partner asks for and times its partner out by its own setting, so a silent failure is noticed after a different time in each direction. LACP still works.

state.order: Bit 0 is LACP_Activity and bit 7 is Expired, the order of the Actor_State and Partner_State fields of a LACPDU as IEEE 802.1AX's MIB module and the Linux driver give it; the hexadecimal and decimal forms read the octet with bit 0 as its lowest bit, 0x01.
state.snmp: Read through SNMP, dot3adAggPortActorOperState and dot3adAggPortPartnerOperState are BITS values: the first bit, LACP_Activity, is the high-order bit of the octet (RFC 3417, section 8), so the octet appears bit-reversed there.
state.timers: Each end asks its partner for LACPDUs every second (short timeout) or every 30 seconds (long), and gives up on the partner after three intervals without one, 3 or 90 seconds (Juniper; Cisco, lacp rate; the Linux driver). Both ends passive means no periodic LACPDUs at all.
state.actor: The actor is the end whose output you are reading; the partner values are what it last received from the far end, or its defaults when Defaulted is set.
state.standard: IEEE 802.1AX-2020 is offered through the IEEE GET Program behind an IEEE account and was not read: the bit names come from its published MIB module, and the meanings from Juniper's documentation and the Linux driver.
state.snmpRead: You entered SNMP BITS values: each was reversed into the octet the LACPDU carries before it was read.
state.extremeRead: You entered Extreme Switch Engine flags: A, T, G, S, C, D, F and E are bits 0 to 7, a hyphen a bit not set (configure sharing, show lacp member-port).
state.aristaRead: You entered Arista EOS letters: A or P, S or L, G or I and s+ or s- give bits 0 to 3; C, D, d and X set Collecting, Distributing, Defaulted and Expired.
state.huaweiRead: You entered Huawei PortState strings, as display eth-trunk prints them: each was read from Bit 1, its first character, which is bit 0 of the octet.
state.huaweiTrunks: The pasted output holds more than one Eth-Trunk: only the first with member rows is read. Paste display eth-trunk with a trunk's number to read another.
state.huaweiDisplay: From the pasted display eth-trunk output, the Local table gives each member's own PortState (the actor) and the Partner table the partner's, matched by port name; the bits, timers and findings are for the member read in detail.
state.huaweiOrder: Huawei prints PortState as eight characters that read left to right from Bit 1 to Bit 8: Bit 1 is LACP_Activity, the octet's lowest bit (0x01), and Bit 8 is Expired, its highest (0x80). An octet is usually written the other way round, bit 7 first, so 10111100 as printed is 0b00111101, which is 0x3D; it is the same eight digits as the SNMP BITS value written in binary.
state.huaweiTable: Huawei's table describes Bit 1 as whether the member interface is an Actor, with a fixed value 1: it sits where the IEEE 802.1AX MIB module puts LACP_Activity, so it is read as Activity here. Huawei words Bits 5 and 6 as whether the interface can receive and can send LACPDUs, where the MIB module names Collecting and Distributing. By default an Eth-Trunk member interface uses the long timeout, 90 seconds.

link.linux: This is the Linux bonding driver's transmit hash, as the kernel's bonding HOWTO gives it and drivers/net/bonding/bond_main.c computes it. Each end chooses the member only for what it sends: the switch picks the member for the return traffic with its own hash, which is not computed here.
link.policyDefault: No policy given: layer2, the driver's default, is used.
link.order: The driver reads the IP addresses and the ports as the processor holds them in memory: a little-endian processor reads their bytes in the reverse order of the header, so its hash differs from the HOWTO's formula read most significant byte first, which is what a big-endian processor computes. The member changes with it only when the member count is not a power of two: the two folds of bond_ip_hash leave in the lowest byte the XOR of the word's four bytes, which their order does not change, and a modulo by 2, 4 or 8 reads only bits from that byte. Which fields count, the folds, the shift and the modulo are the same.
link.orderNone: This policy reads single bytes, or builds its numbers byte by byte, so little-endian and big-endian processors get the same result.
link.members: Members are numbered from 0 in the order they joined the bond, counting only those that can transmit (in 802.3ad mode, those of the active aggregator); the driver picks the member at position hash modulo count (bond_update_slave_arr, bond_xmit_3ad_xor_slave_get).
link.ifDown: When a member goes down, the list is rebuilt without it and the modulo runs over one member fewer, so flows on members that stayed up can move too.
link.layer2: layer2 reads only the last byte of each MAC address and the EtherType, so all traffic between two MAC addresses, such as every flow sent to the default gateway, uses one member.
link.layer23: layer2+3 keeps each pair of hosts on one member: two connections between the same two addresses always share it.
link.layer34: layer3+4 reads the ports of unfragmented TCP and UDP only: fragments and other protocols hash without ports, and the HOWTO warns that a conversation with both fragmented and unfragmented packets can be striped over two members. The last shift drops the lowest bit, so two ports that differ only in their last bit usually hash alike.
link.vlan: vlan+srcmac XORs the tag's whole tag control information, priority included (the driver reads vlan_tci, not only the VLAN ID), and counts an untagged frame as 0. It reads nothing of the destination, so every flow from one MAC address in one VLAN uses one member.
link.ipv6: For IPv6, each address is first folded to 32 bits by XORing its four 32-bit words (ipv6_addr_hash).
link.cisco: Cisco publishes the spread, not the hash: on the Catalyst 6500/6000 its proprietary hash gives one of 8 values and each port accepts some of them, so only 2, 4 or 8 ports split traffic evenly, "even with random addresses" (document 12023). The split below is that table, not a computation of Cisco's hash.
link.notPublished: Cisco's current Catalyst switches, Juniper, Arista, HPE Aruba, Extreme, Huawei and MikroTik's switch chips document which fields they hash, not the function, so the member they pick for a flow is not computed here; IEEE 802.1AX's own MIB module calls the description of the distribution algorithm vendor specific.

status.Selected: Selected: Huawei defines a member interface in this state as active.
status.Unselect: Unselect: Huawei defines a member interface in this state as inactive.
status.ForceFwd: ForceFwd: Huawei defines a member interface in this state as one that can forward Layer 2 traffic.

lacp-hash-and-state-reader.displayHint: Paste the whole output: the Local table gives each member's PortState and Status, the Partner table what it received. Or leave this blank and type the PortState values below.
lacp-hash-and-state-reader.displayReading: The pasted output is being read, so the PortState fields are not used: clear it to type values instead.

huawei.heading: The pasted display eth-trunk
huawei.hashNote: The Hash arithmetic line is shown as printed: Huawei does not publish the hash function, so nothing is computed from it.

lacp-hash-and-state-reader.orderExplain: A 32-bit value takes four bytes: a big-endian processor stores its most significant byte at the lowest address, a little-endian one its least significant. Of the Linux architectures Debian lists, amd64, arm64, ppc64el, riscv64 and loong64 are little-endian; s390x, ppc64, mips and sparc64 are big-endian. The driver XORs the addresses and the ports as raw words loaded from the header, so the two give different hashes for the same flow, and the member can differ only when the member count is not a power of two: Big-endian and little-endian.

vlan-tag-and-trunk-calculator.name: 802.1Q tag decoder and trunk VLAN calculator
vlan-tag-and-trunk-calculator.blurb: Decode an 802.1Q tag or a frame's start: TPID, PCP with its traffic type, DEI and VID with the bits laid out, stacked 802.1ad tags and the EtherType that follows, named from IANA's list. Or paste the trunk lines of both ends, in Cisco IOS XE, Junos, AOS-CX, RouterOS, Switch Engine, Fabric Engine, Arista EOS or Huawei VRP syntax, and see which VLANs cross, which one end drops, and where the native VLANs disagree.

inputs.tag: Octets in hexadecimal: a tag, or a frame's start
inputs.trunk: The trunk port's lines at each end

vlan-tag-and-trunk-calculator.hexHint: Two hexadecimal digits an octet, with spaces, colons, hyphens or dots between them (a capture tool's hex view pastes as it is). Auto reads octets that start with 0x8100, 0x88A8 or 0x9100 as a tag, and anything else of 14 octets or more as a frame's start: destination MAC, source MAC, then tags.
vlan-tag-and-trunk-calculator.trunkHint: Paste only the trunk port's lines, as the switch shows them; other interface lines are listed as not read. A bare list such as 10,20,30-40 also works. Junos and Switch Engine VLAN names are resolved from their set vlans and create vlan lines. Huawei VRP lists VLANs with spaces and to (10 to 30).

end.inUnconfirmed: not confirmed by the vendor pages
end.heading: End {end}: {vendor}
end.readCaption: The lines read, and what each one does

vlan-tag-and-trunk-calculator.runsLocally: Runs in your browser: nothing you paste leaves this page.

empty.tag: Paste the octets of a tag or of a frame's start, or press Example for the course lab's voice VLAN.
empty.trunk: Paste the trunk port's lines of each end, or press Example for the course lab's Cisco and Junos ends.

vlan-tag-and-trunk-calculator.learn: The Learn articles VLANs and 802.1Q trunking and The Ethernet frame, field by field explain the tag, the native VLAN and the allowed list, and the VLAN article has a trunk lab.

share.carries: The link carries the octets as typed (tag), or both ends' vendor and lines as typed (trunk).
share.cautionTag: A frame's octets include two MAC addresses, which identify devices: read them before you send the link.
share.caution: Interface and VLAN names describe a private network: read the lines before you send the link.

bits.title: The tag's 32 bits
bits.note: Octet by octet, most significant bit first: two octets of TPID, then the TCI, whose first three bits are the PCP ({pcp}), the next one the DEI ({dei}), and the last twelve the VID ({vid}).

dei.1: 1: drop eligible where the port uses DEI

vid.null: The null VLAN ID: priority only

decodings.caption: PCP {pcp} under the four PCP selections

mac.heading: Addresses
mac.groupLink: The multicast group to MAC mapper reads a group MAC back to the IP groups behind it.

next.heading: After the tags
next.name: Name
next.afterValue: {n, plural, one {# octet} other {# octets}} after it

fate.unconfirmed: not confirmed by the vendor pages
fate.heading: VLAN by VLAN, both ways
fate.note: A tagged frame is placed in the VLAN its tag names when the receiving end carries that VLAN; an untagged frame is placed in the receiving end's native VLAN (its PVID). Runs of VLANs with the same fate share a row.

tag.empty: Enter the octets in hexadecimal: a tag (81 00 00 0a) or a frame's start, destination and source MAC first.
tag.long: The text is {n} characters long; the decoder reads at most {max}.
tag.char: "{c}" is not a hexadecimal digit: write the octets with 0 to 9 and a to f, separated by spaces, colons, hyphens or dots.
tag.odd: The text holds {n, plural, one {{n} hexadecimal digit} other {{n} hexadecimal digits}}, an odd number: every octet is two digits.
tag.octets: That is {n} octets; the decoder reads at most {max}, which is far more than a frame's MACs, tags and EtherType take.
tag.start: Choose where the octets start: auto, tpid or mac.
tag.short: {n, plural, one {{n} octet that does not start} other {{n} octets that do not start}} with 0x8100, 0x88A8 or 0x9100: too short for a frame's start (6 + 6 octets of MAC, then 2 of type) and not a tag.
tag.frameShort: A frame's start needs at least 14 octets (destination MAC, source MAC, then 2 octets of type); these are {n}.
tag.many: More than {max} tags in one stack: the decoder stops there.
tag.cut: The tag that starts at octet {at} is cut short: a TPID is followed by two octets of TCI.
tag.notTag: The octets start with {value}, which is not 0x8100, 0x88A8 or 0x9100: choose "Destination MAC" if they are a frame's start.

vid.form: "{tok}" is not a VLAN ID: VLAN IDs are whole numbers from 1 to 4094.
vid.zero: "{tok}": write VLAN IDs without leading zeros.
vid.0: VLAN 0 is the null VLAN ID, for priority-tagged frames only: it is never configured as a VLAN (P802.1ad/D2.4, Table 9-2).
vid.4095: VLAN 4095 (FFF) is reserved for implementation use and is never configured or transmitted (P802.1ad/D2.4, Table 9-2); the IEEE YANG vlanid range is 1 to 4094.
vid.big: {v} is beyond the 12-bit VID: VLAN IDs run from 1 to 4094.
vid.fe: {v}: Fabric Engine configures VLAN IDs 1 to 4059 and reserves 4060 to 4094 for internal use (Fabric Engine 9.4 User Guide, Add or Remove Ports in a VLAN).
vid.max: {v} is above {max}, the highest VLAN ID this syntax takes.

list.empty: "{text}" has an empty item between commas.
list.atom: "{atom}" is not a VLAN ID or a range such as 30-40.
list.order: The range {atom} runs backwards: write the lower VLAN ID first.

end.empty: End {end}: paste the trunk port's lines in {vendor} syntax, or a VLAN list such as 10,20,30-40.
end.long: End {end}: {n} characters; at most {max} are read.
end.lines: End {end}: {n} lines; at most {max} are read. Paste only the trunk port's lines.
end.none: End {end}: no {vendor} trunk line was read. A line such as "{hint}", or a VLAN list such as 10,20,30-40.
end.missing: End {end} is missing: give its vendor and its lines.

line.long: the line is {n} characters long; at most {max} are read.

err.mode: Choose a mode: tag or trunk.
err.json: The request body is not valid JSON: send one JSON object that names its mode: tag or trunk.

next.length: {value} is a length, {n, plural, one {{n} octet} other {{n} octets}}, not an EtherType: an IEEE 802.3 frame whose data starts with LLC (DSAP, SSAP, control) (RFC 9542, section 3).
next.neither: {value} is neither a length (below 0x05DD) nor an EtherType (0x0600 and above) (RFC 9542, section 3).
next.llc: {value} is the LLC encapsulation EtherType, used in place of a length as a "length indication" of nonspecific length (RFC 9542, section 3).
next.unlisted: {value} is an EtherType that IANA's list does not name; the IEEE Registration Authority keeps the full public list (IANA, IEEE 802 Numbers).
next.named: {value} is the EtherType IANA's list describes as "{name}".

name.c: C-TAG, an 802.1Q Customer VLAN tag (TPID 0x8100; IANA: "Customer VLAN Tag Type (C-Tag, formerly called the Q-Tag)").
name.s: S-TAG, an 802.1Q Service VLAN tag, introduced by 802.1ad and incorporated into 802.1Q in 2011 (TPID 0x88A8).
name.junos: 0x9100: the TPID Juniper's bridging page says Junos switches support for Q-in-Q. It is not an IEEE 802.1Q tag type and IANA's list does not name it.

tag.vid0: VID 0 is the null VLAN ID: the tag carries only priority information, no VLAN identifier (P802.1ad/D2.4, Table 9-2). A port places such a priority-tagged frame in its PVID (IEEE8021-Q-BRIDGE-MIB, ieee8021QBridgePvid), and Junos reserves VLAN ID 0 "for tagging the priority of frames".
tag.vid1: VID 1 is the default PVID, the VLAN untagged frames are placed in on a port nobody has changed (P802.1ad/D2.4, Table 9-2; the IEEE YANG pvid default 1).

dei.s: DEI is 1: in an S-TAG this bit has always been the drop eligible bit (P802.1ad/D2.4, section 9.7). A port that uses DEI marks the frame drop eligible; one that does not ignores the bit on receipt (IEEE YANG, use-dei).
dei.c: DEI is 1. The bit is now the Drop Eligible Indicator (IEEE YANG, use-dei: a port that uses it marks the frame drop eligible, one that does not ignores it on receipt); in the C-TAG of 2004 it was the CFI, the Canonical Format Indicator (P802.1ad/D2.4, section 9.6).

note.autoTpid: Read as a tag because the octets start with {tpid}; choose "Destination MAC" if they are the start of a frame.
note.docMac: These are documentation MAC addresses (RFC 9542, section 2.1.4: 00-00-5E-00-53-00 to -FF and 01-00-5E-90-10-00 to -FF).
note.endAfterTags: The octets end after the last tag, so the EtherType that follows is not in them.
note.after: {n, plural, one {{n} octet after the EtherType or length is} other {{n} octets after the EtherType or length are}} not decoded.
note.pcp: The traffic type is the one P802.1ad/D2.4 Table G-2 gives for the priority the PCP decodes to under the default 8P0D selection; HPE Aruba's AOS-CX QoS guide lists the same eight today. A port set to 7P1D, 6P2D or 5P3D decodes some values differently (Table 6-5).
note.vlan1: VLAN 1 crosses this trunk. It is the default PVID of every 802.1Q port (P802.1ad/D2.4, Table 9-2), so devices nobody configured land in it; the VLAN article explains why trunks are often built without it.
note.assume: The tool compares the configuration lines only: it assumes every VLAN in them exists on both switches, the link is up and a trunk at both ends, and nothing else (pruning, spanning tree, VLAN registration) removes a VLAN.

warn.sourceGroup: The source address has the M bit set, which makes it a group address (RFC 9542, section 2.1.1); a frame's source is normally an individual address, so check where these octets start.
warn.vid4095: Tag {i} carries VID 4095 (FFF), which 802.1Q reserves for implementation use: it shall not be "transmitted in a tag header" (P802.1ad/D2.4, Table 9-2), and Junos reserves it too.
warn.order: Tag {i} is an S-TAG inside a C-TAG: provider bridging puts the S-TAG outside and the customer's C-TAG inside (P802.1ad/D2.4, section 9.7).
warn.cc: Tags {o} and {i} are both C-TAGs (0x8100). 802.1ad stacks a C-TAG inside an S-TAG (0x88A8); two C-TAGs is also the shape of the double-tagging case the VLAN article describes.
warn.9100: 0x9100 is read with the 802.1Q TCI layout (PCP, DEI, VID) because Juniper names it beside 0x8100 and 0x88A8 as a TPID; the page names the value, not its layout.
warn.emptyEnd: End {end} carries no VLAN at all.
warn.native: Native VLAN mismatch: end A puts untagged frames in VLAN {a}, end B in VLAN {b}, so untagged frames cross between the two VLANs at layer 2. Cisco's guide warns that when the native VLANs of the two ends differ, "spanning-tree loops might result", and asks to make sure "the native VLAN for an IEEE 802.1Q trunk is the same on both ends".
warn.untaggedDropped: End {s} sends VLAN {v} untagged, and end {r} drops untagged data frames ({vendor}).
warn.nothing: No VLAN arrives in the same VLAN in both directions.
warn.nativeNotCarried: End {end} ({vendor}): its native VLAN {v} is not among the VLANs it carries, so no frame crosses untagged at this end in either direction; the end's reading says why.

verdict.untagged: An untagged frame: no 802.1Q tag; the type field reads {value}.
verdict.tags: Tags: {n}; the outermost has VID {vid} and PCP {pcp}; then {next}.
verdict.trunk: Same VLAN in both directions: {carried}. Only from A to B: {aOnly}. Only from B to A: {bOnly}. Into another VLAN: {crossed}. Not confirmed by the vendor pages read: {unconfirmed}.

cisco.all: All VLANs, 1 to 4094 (all "specifies all VLANs from 1 to 4094").
cisco.spaces: Cisco's guide says: "Do not enter any spaces between comma-separated VLAN parameters or in hyphen-specified ranges."
cisco.add: Adds {list} (add "adds the defined list of VLANs to those currently set").
cisco.except: Every VLAN except {list} (except "lists the VLANs that should be calculated by inverting the defined list").
cisco.noAllowed: Back to the default list, all VLANs ("The no form of the allowed vlan command resets the list to the default list").
cisco.native: The native VLAN is {v}: frames of VLAN {v} leave untagged, and untagged arrivals go to VLAN {v}.
cisco.noNative: The native VLAN goes back to VLAN 1, the default.
cisco.vlan1: Cisco IOS XE: "VLAN 1 is the default VLAN on all trunk ports"; it can be removed from the allowed list, and the interface "continues to send and receive management traffic" (17.18 VLAN guide).
cisco.100x: VLANs 1002 to 1005 are in this list, but on a Catalyst 9300 they are the default Token Ring and FDDI VLANs: "reserved for Token Ring and FDDI VLANs", and the device "does not forward FDDI, FDDI-Net, TrCRF, or TrBRF traffic" (17.18 VLAN guide).
cisco.nativeOut: The native VLAN {v} is not in the allowed list. Cisco's pages read (the 17.18 command reference and VLAN guide, every sentence on the native VLAN) say the allowed list is for traffic "in tagged format" and the native VLAN is for "sending and receiving untagged traffic", but not whether a native VLAN missing from the list is carried; the tool marks VLAN {v} as not confirmed. Adding it to the allowed list removes the doubt.

bare.set: Read as the allowed list typed alone: {list}.
bare.add: Read as VLAN members typed alone: {list}.
bare.tagged: Read as the port's tagged VLANs typed alone: {list}.

junos.name: VLAN {name} is VLAN ID {v}.
junos.form: "{value}": vlan members takes one VLAN, or several between [ and ].
junos.all: vlan members all: the Junos pages read do not say which VLANs "all" stands for on a switch with ELS, so the tool does not guess; list the VLAN IDs.
junos.unknown: VLAN name "{name}" has no "set vlans {name} vlan-id N" line here: add it, or write the VLAN ID.
junos.noNative: No native-vlan-id: a Junos trunk with ELS "recognizes untagged control packets, but it does not recognize untagged data packets" (Juniper, bridging and VLANs), so untagged data frames arriving here are dropped.
junos.nativeOut: native-vlan-id {v} is set, but VLAN {v} is not in the VLAN members. Juniper: "The logical interface on which untagged packets are to be received must be configured with the same VLAN ID as the native VLAN ID", so untagged data frames are dropped until VLAN {v} is added to the members.

aruba.all: All VLANs: "all the VLANs currently configured on the switch and any new VLANs that are configured in the future".
aruba.form: AOS-CX writes the list as "a single ID, or a series of IDs separated by commas (2, 3, 4), dashes (2-4), or both (2-4,6)", without spaces in the list.
aruba.set: The allowed VLANs become {list} (after "all", or as the first list: "To only allow specific VLANs on the trunk, issue the vlan trunk allowed command specifying only specific VLANs").
aruba.add: Adds {list} ("Multiple VLAN IDs can be assigned to a trunk interface").
aruba.lastRemoved: AOS-CX: "When the last VLAN is removed from a trunk interface, the interface continues to operate in trunk mode, and will trunk all the VLANs currently defined on the switch".
aruba.native: The native VLAN is {v}; "the switch automatically executes the vlan trunk allowed all command", so a list must come after this line.
aruba.tag: VLAN {v} is tagged too: "Incoming packets that are untagged are dropped except for BPDUs" and "Egress packets are tagged".
aruba.noTag: The native VLAN is untagged again.
aruba.noNative: The native VLAN goes back to VLAN 1 (the no form "assigns VLAN ID 1 as its native VLAN").
aruba.allMeans: AOS-CX "all" means every VLAN configured on the switch, now and later; the tool counts 1 to 4094, so read this end's list as "every VLAN that exists on this switch".
aruba.tagOut: VLAN {v} is the tagged native VLAN but is not in the allowed list, so it is not carried: HPE Aruba's vlan trunk native page assigns a native VLAN "and then" removes it "from the list of allowed VLANs. (Only allow VLAN 10 on the trunk.)"
aruba.nativeOut: The native VLAN {v} is not in the allowed list, so it is not carried: frames of VLAN {v} are neither sent nor accepted untagged. HPE Aruba's vlan trunk native page gives this as an example: "Assigning native VLAN ID 20 to trunk interface 1/1/2 and then removing it from the list of allowed VLANs. (Only allow VLAN 10 on the trunk.)" Add VLAN {v} to the allowed list to carry it.

mt.tagged: The port is a tagged member of {list} ("Interfaces ... that transmit frames with a VLAN tag").
mt.both: Line {n} has both tagged= and untagged=; the tool reads the trunk port as the tagged one.
mt.untagged: The port is an untagged member of {list}: these frames leave without a tag.
mt.pvid: The port's PVID is {v}: "Port VLAN ID (pvid) specifies which VLAN the untagged ingress traffic is assigned to".
mt.tagOnly: frame-types=admit-only-vlan-tagged: the port admits only tagged frames, and it is not added as an untagged member of its PVID.
mt.conflict: End {end}: VLAN {v} is both a tagged and an untagged member of the port.
mt.pvidTagged: End {end}: the PVID {v} is also listed as tagged; RouterOS adds a port "as untagged" for its PVID when frame-types admits untagged frames.
mt.auto: With frame-types at its default, admit-all, the port is "automatically added as untagged" for its PVID, VLAN {v} (RouterOS 7.24, Bridge VLAN Table).
mt.manyUntagged: The port leaves untagged in {n} VLANs ({list}); RouterOS warns that several untagged VLANs on one port can send "tagged packets ... as untagged packets through the wrong access port". Untagged frames coming back are all placed in the PVID, VLAN {pvid}.
mt.assume: The tool reads every bridge VLAN entry here as one that lists the trunk port; paste only the entries for that port. RouterOS drops a VLAN that is not in the bridge VLAN table ("VLANs that don't exist in the bridge VLAN table are dropped").

exos.tagRange: Tag {v}: Switch Engine takes tags from 2 to 4094 ("tag 1 is assigned to the default VLAN, and tag 4095 is assigned to the management VLAN").
exos.noTag: VLAN {name} is created without a tag here; Switch Engine: "If the VLAN is untagged, the ports cannot be tagged". Add "configure vlan {name} tag N".
exos.unknown: VLAN name "{name}" has no "create vlan {name} tag N" line here: add it, or write the VLAN ID.
exos.autoOn: Untagged ports may move straight from one untagged VLAN to another (auto-move on or inform).
exos.autoOff: Auto-move off: "you cannot directly move untagged ports from untagged VLANs without first removing the port VLAN configuration".
exos.createdId: VLAN {v} is created by its ID.
exos.name: VLAN {name} has tag {v}.
exos.created: VLAN {name} is created without a tag.
exos.tagged: The port is a tagged member of VLAN {v}.
exos.conflict: the port is still untagged in VLAN {u} and auto-move is off: "Untagged ports can only be a member of a single VLAN", and the switch answers "Protocol conflict when adding untagged port". Delete the port from that VLAN first.
exos.moved: The port becomes the untagged member of VLAN {v} and leaves VLAN {u}: with auto-move at its default, inform, the switch reports "Port # untagged has been auto-moved".
exos.untaggedDefault: The port is the untagged member of VLAN {v} (untagged is the default when neither keyword is given).
exos.untagged: The port is the untagged member of VLAN {v}.
exos.both: End {end}: VLAN {v} is both the untagged and a tagged VLAN of the port.
exos.default: The port is still in the Default VLAN (tag 1), untagged: Default "initially contains all ports" and "is untagged on all ports" (Switch Engine 33.7.1). The course removes it with configure vlan Default delete ports.
exos.noUntagged: The port is untagged in no VLAN; the Switch Engine pages read do not say what it does with an untagged frame that arrives, so the tool marks those frames as not confirmed.

fe.option: the option {o} is not read: the Fabric Engine pages read do not say how it changes what the port carries.
fe.oneVid: Fabric Engine's vlan members add and remove take one VLAN ID, from 1 to 4059; write one line per VLAN.
fe.zero: default-vlan-id 0: the command reference gives the range 0 to 4059 but does not say what 0 means, so the tool does not guess.
fe.untag: The default VLAN leaves untagged (untag-port-default-vlan "Untags the default VLAN for the port").
fe.noUntag: The default VLAN leaves tagged again.
fe.encap: Tagging on (encapsulation dot1q: "Enable tagging on the ports before configuring Untagged VLANs").
fe.vlan1: Fabric Engine: "VLAN ID 1 is the default VLAN and you cannot create or delete VLAN ID 1." Whether this port is still a member of VLAN 1 is not in these lines; add vlan members add 1 if it is.
fe.3500: VLANs 3500 to 3998 are in this list: Fabric Engine reserves them too when the vrf-scaling and spbm-config-mode boot flags are on.
fe.nativeOut: The default VLAN {v} is untagged but the port is not a member of it here; the Fabric Engine pages read do not say whether it is then carried, so the tool marks VLAN {v} as not confirmed.
fe.untagNoDefault: untag-port-default-vlan is on but no default-vlan-id is set in these lines; the tool does not guess the default VLAN.
fe.noNative: Every VLAN leaves this port tagged (untag-port-default-vlan is off, its default). The Fabric Engine pages read do not say what the port does with untagged frames that arrive, so the tool marks those frames as not confirmed.

type.4: Video, under 100 ms latency and jitter
type.5: Voice, under 10 ms latency and jitter

arista.notTrunk: switchport mode {mode}: the tool reads trunk ports (switchport mode trunk).
arista.mode: Trunk switching mode: "The interface may be a member of multiple VLANs, as configured by the switchport trunk allowed vlan command".
arista.all: All VLANs, 1 to 4094 ("By default, interfaces handle tagged traffic for all VLANs").
arista.set: The allowed list becomes {list}: the VLANs for which the trunk "handles tagged traffic".
arista.noAllowed: Back to all VLANs: the no and default forms restore the default list, all.
arista.native: The native VLAN is {v}: in trunk mode "Untagged traffic is associated with the interface's native VLAN", and its frames leave untagged unless egress priority tagging sends "priority tagged Ethernet frames in place of untagged frames".
arista.tag: native vlan tag: the "interface drops all untagged frames"; Arista's page does not say whether the native VLAN's own frames then leave tagged.
arista.noNative: Back to VLAN 1, untagged: the no and default forms "restore vlan 1 as the trunk mode native VLAN" by removing the switchport trunk native vlan command.
arista.noMode: No switchport mode trunk line here: Arista's default switching mode is access, and the tool reads these lines as a trunk port's.
arista.tagNative: VLAN {v}, the native VLAN, is in the allowed list, but with native vlan tag Arista's page says only that the "interface drops all untagged frames": not whether VLAN {v}'s own frames then leave tagged, so the tool marks VLAN {v} as not confirmed in that direction.
arista.nativeOut: The native VLAN {v} is not in the allowed list. Arista's manual has no sentence on this case; its own example, an allowed list of 6-10, prints "Trunking Native Mode VLAN: 1 (inactive)", and the tool reads that as: VLAN {v} is not carried, so no frame of it is sent or accepted untagged. Add VLAN {v} to the allowed list to carry it.

huawei.form: Huawei writes the VLANs separated by spaces, with to for a range (10 to 30), at most ten items in one command.
huawei.ten: {n} items in one command: port trunk allow-pass vlan takes at most ten; write the rest on another line, which adds to this one.
huawei.notTrunk: port link-type {type}: the tool reads trunk ports (port link-type trunk).
huawei.trunk: The port is a trunk (port link-type trunk).
huawei.onlyVlan: port trunk allow-pass only-vlan applies only to an interface negotiated as a trunk: it "configures VLANs allowed by the interface that is configured as a trunk interface through LNP negotiation", after port link-type negotiation. On a static trunk (port link-type trunk), use port trunk allow-pass vlan.
huawei.all: All VLANs, 1 to 4094 (all "Adds a trunk interface to all VLANs").
huawei.add: Adds {list}; allow-pass lines add up: "the interface is added to all the specified VLANs".
huawei.pvid: The default VLAN (PVID) is {v}; a later port trunk pvid vlan line replaces it. The command "only specifies the default VLAN of a trunk interface but does not add the trunk interface to the default VLAN".
huawei.undoPvid: The PVID goes back to VLAN 1: "The undo port trunk pvid vlan command restores the default VLAN of a trunk interface to the default setting", and "By default, VLAN 1 is the default VLAN of trunk interfaces".
huawei.noType: No port link-type trunk line here: the default link type is negotiation-desirable (negotiation-auto on the S5736-S), and the tool reads these lines as a trunk port's.
huawei.vlan1: VLAN 1 is allowed on this trunk: "By default, a trunk interface is in VLAN 1"; undo port trunk allow-pass vlan 1 removes it, as the course does.
huawei.exist: Huawei: "If a specified VLAN does not exist, the configuration does not take effect", and a PVID that names a VLAN that does not exist puts untagged packets in VLAN 1. The tool cannot see which VLANs exist on the switch and counts every VLAN these lines name.
huawei.pvidOut: The PVID {v} is not among the allowed VLANs. Huawei: "A trunk interface forwards frames with the default VLAN ID only after it is added to the default VLAN using the port trunk allow-pass vlan command", and an untagged frame is discarded "if the default VLAN ID is denied by the interface" (Table 4-2). Add port trunk allow-pass vlan {v}.

ospf-cost-and-adjacency-checker.name: OSPF cost and adjacency checker
ospf-cost-and-adjacency-checker.blurb: Each interface's OSPF (Open Shortest Path First) cost from the reference bandwidth by each vendor's documented rule, the speeds that collapse to the same cost and the smallest reference that tells them apart; and, for two neighbouring interfaces, every mismatch, the packet each side drops under RFC 2328 or RFC 5340, and the neighbour state each side stalls in.
ospf-cost-and-adjacency-checker.runsLocally: Runs locally in your browser. Nothing is sent anywhere.

inputs.cost: A vendor and the interface speeds
inputs.adjacency: The two ends of one link

ospf-cost-and-adjacency-checker.linksHint: One to eight speeds with a unit, separated by commas: 100M, 1G, 2.5G, 10G, 1544k.

reference.mbps: {vendor} divides the reference by the interface speed. Type the reference as its CLI takes it, in whole Mbit/s (100000 is 100 Gbit/s), or with a unit; blank uses the default, {def}.
reference.bps: {vendor} divides the reference by the interface speed. Type the reference in bits per second (10000000000), or with a unit (10g); blank uses the default, {def}.
reference.unset: {vendor} gives every Ethernet interface a cost of {cost} while auto-cost reference-bandwidth is not configured: leave the reference blank for that, or type the rate as the command takes it, in whole Mbit/s (1 to 4294967), to see the costs once it is set.

hint.table: {vendor} takes each interface's default cost from a table by speed: there is no reference bandwidth to set.

unknown.no-default: {vendor}: the documentation read states no default cost, so the tool computes none.

cost.smallestHeading: The smallest reference that tells them apart

basis.below-one-undocumented: faster than the reference: not documented
basis.not-configured: auto-cost not configured: the Ethernet default

ospf-cost-and-adjacency-checker.sameKeyHint: The key itself is never asked for: only whether both sides hold the same one.
ospf-cost-and-adjacency-checker.scenariosLabel: The course lab and its breakages

tableHint.v2: Address/prefix is the interface address with its length (10.0.12.1/30). A Key ID applies to Keyed-MD5 and HMAC-SHA only. A blank Router ID or priority is left out of the checks that need it.
tableHint.v3: OSPFv3 has no address field: the Hello carries no mask and the source need not share a subnet. An SA ID applies to the Authentication Trailer (HMAC-SHA) only.

state.none: no neighbour: every Hello is dropped
state.Init: Init: Hellos arrive but never list it
state.either: ExStart or Exchange, depending on the Router IDs

findings.heading: What differs, in the order the routers check it ({n})

drops.both: Each side drops the other's packets.
drops.bothDd: Each side ignores the other's Database Description packets.
drops.none: No packet is dropped for this.

ospf-cost-and-adjacency-checker.notReached: Not reached yet: an earlier mismatch stops the routers before this check.
ospf-cost-and-adjacency-checker.learn: The Learn article OSPF: the map, the math, and area 0 explains the cost trap and every neighbour state, with an FRRouting lab.

empty.cost: Pick a vendor and enter the interface speeds. Example fills Junos at its default reference with 100 Mbit/s, 1 Gbit/s and 10 Gbit/s.
empty.adjacency: Fill in both ends of the link. Example fills the course lab's uplink with a different Hello on the uplink router, as its step 8 asks.

share.carries: The link carries the mode and its fields as typed: never a key, which the tool never asks for.
share.caution: Router IDs, addresses and labels describe a private network: read them before you send the link.

err.tooLong: A field is longer than this tool reads ({max} characters).
err.vendor: Choose a vendor: cisco-ios-xe, juniper-junos, arista-eos, aruba-aos-cx, extreme-switch-engine, extreme-fabric-engine, huawei-vrp, mikrotik-routeros or frr.
err.speedBad: "{value}" is not an interface speed this tool reads: write a number and a unit, such as 100M, 1G, 2.5G, 10 Gbit/s or 1544k.
err.speedFraction: "{value}" is not a whole number of bits per second.
err.speedRange: "{value}" is outside what this tool reads: 1 kbit/s to 10 Tbit/s.
err.speedDup: {value} appears twice: the same speed always gets the same cost, so enter each speed once.
err.referenceBad: "{value}" is not a reference bandwidth: type it as {vendor} takes it (a bare number is {unit}), or with a unit, such as 10G.
err.referenceGrid: "{value}" is not a value {vendor} accepts: its reference bandwidth is set in {unit}.
err.referenceRange: "{value}" is outside the range {vendor} documents: {min} to {max} {unit}.
err.noReference: {vendor} has no reference bandwidth in the documentation read, so there is nothing to set: leave the reference blank.
err.nameBad: "{value}" is not a router label this tool reads: use up to 32 letters, digits, dots, hyphens or underscores, without spaces.
err.routerId: "{value}" is not a Router ID: write it in dotted decimal, such as 10.255.0.1 (a 32-bit number, RFC 2328 section 1.2).
err.areaEmpty: Enter the Area ID: dotted decimal, such as 0.0.0.0, or a decimal number, such as 0.
err.area: "{value}" is not an Area ID: it is a 32-bit number (RFC 2328 appendix A.3.1), written in dotted decimal or as a decimal from 0 to 4294967295.
err.areaType: Choose the area type: normal, stub or nssa.
err.backboneStub: Area 0 cannot be a stub area: "The backbone cannot be configured as a stub area" (RFC 2328 section 6).
err.backboneNssa: Area 0 cannot be an NSSA: "The backbone is always a Type-5 capable area" (RFC 3101 section 1.3).
err.network: Choose the network type: broadcast, point-to-point, nbma or point-to-multipoint.
err.addressEmpty: Enter the interface address with its prefix length, such as 10.0.12.1/30: OSPFv2 checks the subnet and the Network Mask (RFC 2328 sections 8.2 and 10.5).
err.address: "{value}" is not an IPv4 address with a prefix length, such as 10.0.12.1/30.
err.addressV3: OSPFv3 has no Network Mask in its Hellos and no subnet check (RFC 5340 sections 4.2.2 and 4.2.2.1): leave the address out.
err.hello: "{value}" is not a HelloInterval: whole seconds from 1 to 65535 (a 16-bit field).

dead.v2: "{value}" is not a RouterDeadInterval: whole seconds from 1 to 4294967295 (a 32-bit field in OSPFv2).
dead.v3: "{value}" is not a RouterDeadInterval: whole seconds from 1 to 65535 (a 16-bit field in OSPFv3).

err.mtu: "{value}" is not an interface MTU: whole bytes from 1 to 65535 (the 16-bit Interface MTU field of a Database Description packet).

auth.v2: Choose OSPFv2 authentication: none, simple, md5, hmac-sha-1, hmac-sha-256, hmac-sha-384 or hmac-sha-512 (RFC 2328 appendix D, RFC 5709).
auth.v3: Choose OSPFv3 authentication: none, an Authentication Trailer algorithm (hmac-sha-1, hmac-sha-256, hmac-sha-384 or hmac-sha-512, RFC 7166) or ipsec (RFC 4552). OSPFv3 has no simple password or MD5 (RFC 5340 section 2.6).

keyId.v2: "{value}" is not a Key ID: a whole number from 0 to 255 (8 bits, RFC 5709 section 3.2).
keyId.v3: "{value}" is not an SA ID: a whole number from 0 to 65535 (16 bits, RFC 7166 section 3).

err.keyIdUnused: A Key ID applies only to cryptographic authentication: leave it blank for none, simple or ipsec.
err.priority: "{value}" is not a Router Priority: a whole number from 0 to 255 (8 bits, RFC 2328 appendix C.3).
err.instance: "{value}" is not an Instance ID: a whole number from 0 to 255 (8 bits).
err.version: Choose OSPF version 2 (RFC 2328, IPv4) or 3 (RFC 5340, IPv6).
err.sameKey: Same key is true or false.
err.nameDup: Both routers are called "{value}": give each its own label.
err.mode: Choose a mode: cost or adjacency.
err.json: The request body is not valid JSON: send one JSON object that names its mode: cost or adjacency.

smallest.range: No reference bandwidth within {vendor}'s documented range gives every interface its own documented cost below 65,536.
smallest.limit: The search for a reference that gives every interface its own cost stopped after 200,000 candidates without one; speeds this close together need a reference far above the fastest.
smallest.found: The smallest reference bandwidth that gives every interface its own documented cost is {ref}. A larger reference can merge two costs again, and the slowest interface's cost must stay at or below 65,535; Juniper's user guide suggests a reference "based on a multiple of the highest speed interface".

note.formula: {vendor} computes cost = reference bandwidth / interface bandwidth, with a default reference of {def}; a cost set on the interface by hand overrides it.

truncate.cisco: Cisco's own examples keep the integer part of the quotient: a 64 kbit/s link gets 1562 (100,000,000 / 64,000 = 1562.5) and a T1 at 1544 kbit/s gets 64 (64.77), so the tool truncates.

atOrAbove.one: {vendor} documents a cost of 1 for an interface at or above the reference bandwidth.
atOrAbove.cisco: An interface at or above the reference costs 1 on Cisco: the auto-cost example "changes the cost of the FDDI link to 10, while the gigabit Ethernet link remains at a cost of 1" at a reference of 1000, so a gigabit link, ten times faster than the default reference of 100 Mbit/s, costs 1 there too; the ip ospf cost list gives "ATM-- Default cost is 1", and RFC 2328 forbids 0 (appendix C.3).

mustMatch.frr: FRRouting's documentation says the reference bandwidth "MUST be consistent across all routers within the OSPF domain".
mustMatch.other: The {vendor} pages read do not say that the reference bandwidth must match on every router; FRRouting's documentation says it "MUST be consistent across all routers within the OSPF domain", because each router advertises its own interface costs and every router adds them up as one scale.

table.switchEngine: Switch Engine does not divide a reference by the speed: "automatic", the default, takes the cost from the OSPF metric table (10 Mbit/s 10, 100 Mbit/s 5, 1 Gbit/s 4, 2.5 and 5 Gbit/s 3, 10, 25, 40 and 50 Gbit/s 2, 100 Gbit/s 1), which configure ospf metric-table changes.
table.fabricEngine: Fabric Engine does not divide a reference by the speed: ip ospf default-cost sets one default per Ethernet speed (10 Mbit/s 100, 100 Mbit/s 10, and 1 for 1, 10, 25, 40 and 100 Gbit/s), and a VLAN interface defaults to 1.

note.rfc: RFC 2328 does not tie cost to bandwidth: the interface output cost is a configured number that "must always be greater than 0" (appendix C.3), carried in a 16-bit metric (appendix A.4.2), so 1 to 65535. The bandwidth formulas and tables are each vendor's own.
note.order: Each router checks a received packet in a fixed order: the IP-level tests and the OSPF header (Area ID, authentication) for every packet, then the Hello's own fields, then, only between routers that become adjacent, the Database Description exchange (RFC 2328 sections 8.2, 10.5 and 10.6). The first failure decides, but every mismatch is listed here, because fixing one reveals the next.
note.v3: In OSPFv3, neighbours are identified by Router ID on every link type, the Hello has no Network Mask, and the source address need not be on the link's subnet, because "IPv6 OSPF runs per-link instead of per-IP-subnet" (RFC 5340 sections 4.2.2 and 4.2.2.1).
note.noRid: A Router ID was not given, so the checks that need both (equal IDs, and who becomes Leader in ExStart) are reported only as far as they can be.
note.noPriority: A Router Priority was not given: the checker assumes at least one side can be Designated Router (priority above 0).
note.sameKey: The checker never asks for a key: it asks only whether the two keys are the same, and a share link never carries one.
note.vlink: Virtual links, NBMA neighbour lists, more than one key per interface and multiple areas on one link are outside this checker.

huawei.rule: Huawei's ospf cost and bandwidth-reference pages give the rule: "Cost of the interface = Bandwidth reference value/Interface bandwidth. The integer of the calculated result is the cost of the interface. If the calculated result is smaller than 1, the cost is 1." The reference is set per OSPF process with bandwidth-reference, 1 to 2147483648 Mbit/s, default 100 Mbit/s; ospf cost sets 1 to 65535 by hand, and a loopback interface defaults to 0.
huawei.trunk: Eth-Trunk interfaces, as Huawei's two pages write it: ospf cost says "No default cost is configured for trunk interfaces, because a trunk interface has multiple member interfaces that are in constant change", and bandwidth-reference says that when it runs on an Eth-Trunk interface, "the bandwidth of the Eth-Trunk interface is equal to the total bandwidth of all its member interfaces". The tool reads each speed as one interface.

arista.unset: auto-cost reference-bandwidth is not configured: "When this parameter is not set, the default cost for Ethernet interfaces is the default ip ospf cost value of 10", so every Ethernet interface costs 10 whatever its speed. Type a rate (1 to 4294967, whole Mbit/s) in the reference field to see the costs once the command is set.
arista.rule: With auto-cost reference-bandwidth configured, EOS computes "ospfv2-cost = (auto-cost value * 1 Mbps) / interface bandwidth"; "The switch uses a minimum ospfv2-cost of 1. The switch rounds down all non-integer results." Its own example: a 10 Gbit/s interface costs 1 at a rate of 100 and 5 at 59000.
arista.interfaces: The formula is documented for Ethernet interfaces only: the ip ospf cost page gives port channel and VLAN interfaces a default of 10.

aruba.vlan: "For VLAN interfaces the link speed value is taken as 1 Gbps (if the OSPFv2 interface cost is not explicitly set)": enter 1G for a VLAN interface.

dead20.huawei: {list}: on a Huawei VRP switch (S5700/S6700 V200R025C00) a dead interval below 20 s does not take effect as set: "the actual dead interval of an OSPF neighbor is not shorter than 20s" (ospf timer dead; ospf timer hello says the same of a Hello below 5 s), unless ospf timer hello is given its conservative keyword.

warn.belowOne: {list}: faster than the reference, so the formula gives less than 1. RFC 2328 requires a cost greater than 0 (appendix C.3), and the {vendor} pages read do not say what such an interface costs, so the tool does not guess: raise the reference to at least the fastest speed, or set the cost by hand.
warn.fraction: {list}: the quotient is not a whole number, and the {vendor} pages read do not say how it is rounded, so the tool gives the two whole numbers around it instead of a cost.
warn.aboveMax: {list}: the quotient is above 65,535, the largest cost a router-LSA can carry (RFC 2328 appendix A.4.2: a 16-bit metric); the {vendor} pages read do not say what is advertised then.
warn.notInTable: {list}: not a speed the {vendor} table lists, so the pages read give no default cost for it.
warn.noDefault: {vendor}: the interface-template page lists cost as "Interface cost expressed as link state metric" with no default and no reference bandwidth, and the other OSPF pages read state none, so the tool computes no cost.
warn.shared: {list} all cost {cost}: OSPF sees them as equal and cannot prefer the faster one.
