warn.possible: {first} and {second} may share a cost: their possible costs overlap and the rounding is not documented.
warn.deadShort: {side}: a RouterDeadInterval of {dead} s is not longer than its HelloInterval of {hello} s, so the neighbour can be declared down between two Hellos; RFC 2328 says it "should be some multiple of the HelloInterval (say 4)" (appendix C.3).
warn.simple: {side}: a simple password travels in clear: "Anyone with physical access to the network can learn the password" (RFC 2328 appendix D.2).
warn.md5: {side}: Keyed-MD5 is kept for compatibility; RFC 5709 makes HMAC-SHA-256 the algorithm implementations MUST support (section 3).
warn.unset: With every Ethernet interface at 10, OSPF counts hops: a path through {count} interfaces of any speed costs the same as {count} of any other. Configure auto-cost reference-bandwidth, or set ip ospf cost on each interface, to make speed count.

aruba.disagree: The AOS-CX 10.16 pages disagree. reference-bandwidth says that "If the OSPFv2 interface cost is not explicitly set, then the cost of all the OSPFv2 interfaces is recalculated based on the reference bandwidth and link speed of the interface", default 100000 Mbps; the ip ospf cost page says "Default: 1". The tool computes the reference-bandwidth reading, and neither page states rounding or a minimum: check the cost the switch shows before relying on either.

verdict.oneUnknown: The cost of {speed} is not documented for {vendor}.
verdict.distinct: Every one of the {n} interfaces gets its own cost, so OSPF can tell each speed from the others.
verdict.shared: Some of the {n} interfaces share a cost, so OSPF cannot tell those speeds apart.
verdict.unknown: Not every cost is documented for {vendor}, so the tool cannot say whether all {n} interfaces are told apart.
verdict.none: No neighbour forms: each router drops every Hello the other sends, so neither lists the other, not even in Init.
verdict.stalled: The adjacency stalls: {a} sees {b} as {viewA}, and {b} sees {a} as {viewB}.
verdict.unused: Both reach Full, but the two ends describe the link differently, so the shortest-path calculation does not use it.
verdict.full: Nothing checked here differs: these two interfaces can reach Full.
verdict.fullNote: These two interfaces can reach Full; read the note on what differs.

both.hellos: each router drops the other's Hellos
both.packets: each router drops the other's packets

f.ownAddress: Both interfaces have the address {addr}. Each router takes the other's packets, sent from its own address, for its own: "Locally originated packets should not be passed on to OSPF" (RFC 2328 section 8.2), so neither hears the other.

area.v2: Area ID: {a} is in area {areaA} and {b} in area {areaB}. "The Area ID found in the OSPF header must be verified" against the receiving interface's area, and the packet is discarded (RFC 2328 section 8.2; the backbone case applies only to virtual links, which this checker does not model). Every packet is dropped, Hellos included, so no neighbour appears.
area.v3: Area ID: {a} is in area {areaA} and {b} in area {areaB}. "The Area ID and Instance ID found in the OSPF header must be verified", and a packet that matches neither the link's area nor a virtual link "should be discarded" (RFC 5340 section 4.2.2). No neighbour appears.

f.subnet: Subnet: {who}. With the Area ID matching, "the packet's IP source address is required to be on the same network as the receiving interface", checked by masking both addresses with the receiving interface's mask, a comparison that "should not be performed on point-to-point networks" (RFC 2328 section 8.2). {a} is {addrA} and {b} is {addrB}.

instance.v2: Instance ID: {a} uses {instA} and {b} uses {instB}. "Received packets with an Instance ID not equal to one of the configured OSPFv2 Instance IDs on the receiving interface MUST be discarded" (RFC 6549 section 3.1, which defines the field and its default of 0; a router without RFC 6549 reads those 8 bits as part of the AuType).
instance.v3: Instance ID: {a} uses {instA} and {b} uses {instB}. The Instance ID is checked with the Area ID and a packet that matches no interface instance "should be discarded" (RFC 5340 sections 2.4 and 4.2.2); RFC 5838 reserves 0 to 31 for IPv6 unicast, 64 to 95 for IPv4 unicast.

authType.v2: Authentication type: {a} uses {authA} (AuType {tA}) and {b} uses {authB} (AuType {tB}). "The AuType specified in the packet must match the AuType specified for the associated interface" (RFC 2328 section 8.2, as verified erratum 3734 corrects it), so every packet is discarded in both directions.

v3.ipsec: Authentication: {a} uses {authA} and {b} uses {authB}. With IPsec enabled, "OSPFv3 packets that are not protected with AH or ESP MUST be silently discarded" (RFC 4552 section 3); the other side does not take the IPsec-protected packets as OSPF, whose Next Header must be 89 (RFC 5340 section 4.2.2). Every packet is dropped in both directions.
v3.trailer: Authentication: {a} uses {authA} and {b} uses {authB}. A router with the Authentication Trailer configured drops "Hello and Database Description packets with the AT-bit clear" (RFC 7166 section 4.6); the trailer side omits the OSPFv3 header checksum (section 4.2), which the other side verifies (RFC 5340 section 4.2.2), unless it runs the transition mode of RFC 7166 section 5. Expect no neighbour on either side.

key.simple: Simple password: the passwords differ. The 64-bit authentication field "must be equal to the 64-bit password" configured for the receiving interface (RFC 2328 appendix D.5.2), so every packet fails and is discarded in both directions.
key.crypto: Key: Key ID {k} uses {auth} on both sides, with different keys. The digest computed with the receiver's key does not match the one received, so "the OSPF packet is discarded" (RFC 2328 appendix D.5.3, step 3c; RFC 5709 section 3.4) in both directions. The key itself never crosses the wire (appendix D.3).
key.v3: Key: SA ID {k} uses {auth} on both sides, with different keys, so the authentication data differs and "the packet MUST be discarded" (RFC 7166 section 4.6) in both directions.
key.ipsec: IPsec keys: the two sides hold different keys, and "OSPFv3 packets that fail the authentication checks MUST be silently discarded" (RFC 4552 section 3), in both directions.

keyId.v2: Key ID: {a} signs with Key ID {kA} and {b} with Key ID {kB}. The receiver looks for its own key "having Key ID equal to that specified in the received OSPF packet" and, "If the key is not found", discards the packet (RFC 2328 appendix D.5.3, step 1), so with one key on each side every packet is dropped in both directions.
keyId.v3: SA ID: {a} uses {kA} and {b} uses {kB}. "If the SA is not found ... the OSPFv3 packet is dropped" (RFC 7166 section 4.6), so with one SA on each side every packet is dropped in both directions.

algorithm.v2: Algorithm: Key ID {k} is {authA} on {a} and {authB} on {b}. "The cryptographic algorithm/mode in use is indicated implicitly by the KeyID" (RFC 5709 section 3.4), so each receiver computes the digest with its own algorithm, the digests differ, and "the OSPF packet is discarded" (RFC 2328 appendix D.5.3, step 3c) in both directions.
algorithm.v3: Algorithm: SA ID {k} is {authA} on {a} and {authB} on {b}. Each SA ID specifies the authentication algorithm and the key (RFC 7166 section 3), so the computed data does not match the received data and "the packet MUST be discarded" (section 4.6) in both directions.

f.mask: Network Mask: {a} sends {maskA} and {b} sends {maskB}, so {who}: the mask "must be checked against the values configured for the receiving interface. Any mismatch causes processing to stop and the packet to be dropped", except that "on point-to-point networks and on virtual links, the Network Mask in the received Hello Packet should be ignored" (RFC 2328 section 10.5).

hello.v2: HelloInterval: {a} sends every {hA} s and {b} every {hB} s. The HelloInterval in a received Hello "must be checked against the values configured for the receiving interface. Any mismatch causes processing to stop and the packet to be dropped" (RFC 2328 section 10.5), in both directions: no neighbour appears on either side.
hello.v3: HelloInterval: {a} sends every {hA} s and {b} every {hB} s. OSPFv3 keeps the HelloInterval check of RFC 2328 section 10.5, "Any mismatch causes processing to stop and the packet to be dropped" (RFC 5340 section 4.2.2.1 lists only the differences), in both directions: no neighbour appears on either side.

dead.v2: RouterDeadInterval: {a} advertises {dA} s and {b} {dB} s. Like the HelloInterval, it is checked against the receiving interface and "Any mismatch causes processing to stop and the packet to be dropped" (RFC 2328 section 10.5), in both directions.
dead.v3: RouterDeadInterval: {a} advertises {dA} s and {b} {dB} s. OSPFv3 keeps the check of RFC 2328 section 10.5 (RFC 5340 section 4.2.2.1), so Hellos are dropped in both directions.

areaType.nssa: Area type: {a} has area {area} as {typeA} and {b} as {typeB}. "both the N-bit and the E-bit found in the Hello packet's option field" must match the receiving area, and "A mismatch in the options causes processing of the received Hello packet to stop and the packet to be dropped" (RFC 3101 section 2.1), in both directions.
areaType.stub: Area type: {a} has area {area} as {typeA} and {b} as {typeB}. "If AS-external-LSAs are not flooded into/throughout the area (i.e, the area is a "stub") the E-bit must be clear in received Hello Packets, otherwise the E-bit must be set. A mismatch causes processing to stop and the packet to be dropped" (RFC 2328 section 10.5), in both directions.

f.noDr: Router Priority: both {a} and {b} send priority 0, and "A router whose Router Priority is set to 0 is ineligible to become Designated Router" (RFC 2328 appendix C.3). On a {net} network routers become adjacent only with the Designated Router and the Backup Designated Router, so with neither elected "the state of the neighbor communication stops at 2-Way" (section 10.4).
f.oneSided: {tries} always tries to become adjacent on its {netT} interface, but {stays}, on a {netS} interface with both priorities 0, elects no Designated Router and stays at 2-Way, where Database Description packets "should be ignored" (RFC 2328 sections 10.4 and 10.6): {tries} waits in ExStart.
f.routerId: Router ID: both routers use {rid}. A Router ID "uniquely identifies the router within an Autonomous System" (RFC 2328 section 1.2), and ExStart ends only when the neighbour's Router ID is larger or smaller than the router's own (section 10.6); with equal IDs neither case matches, every Database Description packet is ignored, and both stay in ExStart.

tail.unknown: Where the other side stops depends on the Router IDs: with the higher one it stays in ExStart as Leader, with the lower one it becomes Follower and moves to Exchange; give both Router IDs to see which.
tail.leader: {large} has the higher Router ID, so it insists on being Leader and ignores {small}'s initial packet: both stay in ExStart.
tail.follower: {large} has the lower Router ID, so it accepts {small}'s initial packet as Follower and moves to Exchange, while {small} keeps rejecting its replies and stays in ExStart.

mtu.main: MTU: {small} has {mtuS} bytes and {large} {mtuL}. "If the Interface MTU field in the Database Description packet indicates an IP datagram size that is larger than the router can accept on the receiving interface without fragmentation, the Database Description packet is rejected" (RFC 2328 section 10.6; the same in OSPFv3, RFC 5340 section 4.2.2): {small} rejects {large}'s. Hellos carry no MTU, so the two reach 2-Way and the problem shows only after it. {tail}

network.mixed: Network type: {a} runs {netA} and {b} runs {netB}. No Hello field carries the network type, so none of the receive checks catches it. The two then describe the link differently in their router-LSAs: a point-to-point side as a Type 1 link to the neighbour's Router ID (RFC 2328 section 12.4.1.1), a broadcast or NBMA side as a Type 2 link to the Designated Router's network (section 12.4.1.2). The shortest-path calculation skips a link whose far end "does not have a link back" (section 16.1, step 2b), so even when both reach Full, no route uses this link.
network.p2pLike: Network type: {a} runs {netA} and {b} runs {netB}. Both describe the link as a Type 1 link to the other's Router ID (RFC 2328 sections 12.4.1.1 and 12.4.1.4), so the shortest-path calculation can use it; the addresses are advertised differently (a stub link for the subnet or the neighbour's address on point-to-point, a host route for its own address on Point-to-MultiPoint), and only the Point-to-MultiPoint side checks the Network Mask (section 10.5).
network.bcastNbma: Network type: {a} runs {netA} and {b} runs {netB}. Both elect a Designated Router and describe the link as a transit network (RFC 2328 section 12.4.1.2), but the NBMA side sends Hellos only to neighbours configured on it (section 9.5.1), so whether they meet depends on that configuration and on the implementation.

mtu.cisco: Cisco IOS XE: ip ospf mtu-ignore disables the check ("OSPF MTU mismatch detection is enabled" by default, and the check "is performed when neighbors exchange DBD packets"), Cisco IOS IP Routing: OSPF Command Reference.
mtu.fabricEngine: Extreme Fabric Engine 9.4: ip ospf mtu-ignore enable lets the switch "accept OSPF database description (DBD) packets with a different MTU size"; the same page says incoming DBD packets are dropped "if their MTU is greater than 1500 bytes".
mtu.others: The Juniper OSPF User Guide, the Switch Engine command reference, the RouterOS interface-template page, the FRRouting OSPFv2 page and the Arista EOS OSPFv2 chapter read here document no setting to ignore it.
mtu.huawei: Huawei VRP (S5700/S6700 V200R025C00): "By default, an interface adds the MTU 0 (not the actual MTU) in DD packets to be sent and does not check the MTUs in received DD packets", so a Huawei side left at its default neither rejects the other's packets nor sends a size the other could reject (RFC 2328 section 10.6 rejects only a larger one). ospf mtu-enable sends the actual MTU and checks "whether the MTU in a received DD packet is greater than the local MTU"; then "If the interface MTU settings of the local and remote ends are different, an OSPF neighbor relationship cannot enter the Full state", and configuring it restarts the OSPF process.

hello.huawei: Huawei VRP (S5700/S6700 V200R025C00): ospf timer hello defaults to 10 s on point-to-point and broadcast interfaces and 30 s on NBMA and point-to-multipoint ones; when the Hello is set and the dead interval is not, "the dead interval of an OSPF neighbor is four times the value of hello interval", so a Hello changed on a Huawei side changes its dead interval too.

dead.huawei: Huawei VRP (S5700/S6700 V200R025C00): ospf timer dead defaults to 40 s on point-to-point and broadcast interfaces and 120 s on NBMA and point-to-multipoint ones (range 1 to 235926000 s), and to four times the Hello when only the Hello is set.

radius-packet-decoder.name: RADIUS packet decoder
radius-packet-decoder.blurb: Paste the hex of a RADIUS (Remote Authentication Dial-In User Service) packet as a capture shows it and read its Code, Identifier, Length and Authenticator and every attribute in its data type, named from IANA's registries, with vendor attributes, EAP and VLAN assignment explained; hidden passwords are explained, never decrypted, and a short comparison sets RADIUS beside TACACS+.
radius-packet-decoder.runsLocally: Decoded in your browser: nothing is sent anywhere, and no shared secret is ever asked for.
radius-packet-decoder.inputHint: Plain hex, bytes separated by spaces, colons, hyphens or dots, 0x prefixes, or a hex dump with offsets as Wireshark copies it (the ASCII column is ignored). Copy the RADIUS layer, not the whole frame: a pasted Ethernet frame or IP packet is recognized and refused with the octet where RADIUS starts.
radius-packet-decoder.empty: Paste a packet, press Example, or pick one of the RFCs' own packets above.

headline.packet: {name} (Code {code}), Identifier {id}, Length {length}: {n, plural, one {# attribute} other {# attributes}}.
headline.attributes: {octets, plural, one {{octets} octet} other {{octets} octets}} read as attributes: {n, plural, one {# attribute} other {# attributes}}.

header.heading: Header
header.lengthPadding: of the {octets} octets given; the last {padding} are padding

auth.request-md5: Request Authenticator: an MD5 with the shared secret
auth.response: Response Authenticator: an MD5 with the shared secret

attrs.heading: {n, plural, one {# attribute} other {# attributes}}
attrs.none: No attributes: the packet ends after its header.

eap.heading: EAP packet in {n, plural, one {# EAP-Message attribute} other {# EAP-Message attributes}}

radius-packet-decoder.noSecret: Nothing here is checked cryptographically: the Authenticators, Message-Authenticator and the hidden attributes depend on the shared secret, which this tool never asks for. If the packet came over RADIUS/1.1 (TLS with the ALPN name "radius/1.1", RFC 9765, Experimental), octets 5 to 20 are a Token and reserved octets instead of the Authenticator, and the octets alone do not say which applies.
radius-packet-decoder.learn: The packet, the attributes, 802.1X and accounting step by step: <r>RADIUS end to end</r>; the device-administration side: <x>TACACS+ for device administration</x>.

compare.heading: RADIUS and TACACS+ side by side
compare.intro: What the two protocols' own documents say, as chapter 4.6 of the course presents them: RADIUS for network access, TACACS+ for device administration.

transport.label: Transport and ports
transport.radius: UDP: port 1812 for authentication (RFC 2865, section 3), 1813 for accounting (RFC 2866, section 3) and 3799 for Disconnect and CoA requests (RFC 5176, section 2.3).
transport.tacacs: TCP: server port 49 (RFC 8907, section 3.4). Cisco's tech note 13838 draws the same line: "RADIUS uses UDP while TACACS+ uses TCP."

protected.label: What is protected
protected.radius: Only the hidden attributes: User-Password and Tunnel-Password are XORed with MD5 of the shared secret (RFC 2865, section 5.2; RFC 2868, section 3.5), and the Authenticators and Message-Authenticator authenticate the packet (RFC 2865, section 3; RFC 3579, section 3.2). Every other attribute is sent as it is, which is why this decoder reads it without the secret; Cisco's tech note 13838 says the same of the Access-Request: "The remainder of the packet is unencrypted."
protected.tacacs: The whole body, XORed with an MD5 pad built from the shared secret; the 12-byte header is not (Cisco's tech note 13838: TACACS+ "leaves a standard TACACS+ header"). Where Cisco says the body is encrypted, RFC 8907 calls it obfuscation, not encryption: it provides "no meaningful integrity, privacy, or replay protection" (sections 4.5 and 10.1).

aaa.label: Authentication, authorization, accounting
aaa.radius: Authentication and authorization in one exchange: the server authenticates the user and returns "all configuration information necessary for the client to deliver service" (RFC 2865, section 1); accounting is separate, on its own port (RFC 2866). Cisco's tech note 13838 puts it as "RADIUS combines authentication and authorization."
aaa.tacacs: Three separate exchanges, "essentially ... a suite of three protocols", which allows authorization and accounting "of individual commands in a session" (RFC 8907, section 1); in Cisco's tech note 13838, TACACS+ separates authentication, authorization and accounting.

use.label: Typical use
use.radius: Network access: a Network Access Server (NAS), such as a switch port or an access point, admits a user or a device (RFC 2865, section 1); 802.1X carries EAP inside RADIUS (RFC 3579; RFC 3580).
use.tacacs: Device administration: "authenticating access to network devices, providing central authorization of operations, and auditing of those operations" (RFC 8907, section 1).

tls.label: Over TLS
tls.radius: RADIUS over TLS on TCP 2083 (RFC 6614, Experimental); RADIUS/1.1 drops the MD5 methods over TLS (RFC 9765, Experimental).
tls.tacacs: TACACS+ over TLS 1.3 on TCP 300 (RFC 9887, Proposed Standard, December 2025), which makes the obfuscation obsolete.

status.label: Status of the specification
status.radius: RFC 2865 is a Draft Standard; RFC 2866 (accounting) is Informational.
status.tacacs: RFC 8907 (September 2020) is Informational: it documents the protocol as deployed.

compare.sources: From RFC 2865, 2866, 2868, 3579, 3580, 5176, 6614, 8907, 9765 and 9887, the RFC Editor's index and IANA's port registry, read on 8 November 2026, and Cisco's tech note 13838, Compare TACACS + and RADIUS (updated 30 June 2025), read in a browser on 8 November 2026 because the site refuses automated reads.

share.carries: The link carries the packet with its hidden passwords, keys, challenge responses and secret-based authenticators replaced by zeros.
share.caution: The copy still shows user names, NAS and client addresses, MAC addresses and session identifiers of a private network.
share.copyExample: This is one of the RFCs' published examples, octets and shared secret printed in the RFC, so the link carries it as typed.
share.copyNothing: Nothing in it needed zeroing, so the link carries it as typed.
share.copyZeroed: {n, plural, one {One field is zeroed; the page that opens the link marks it.} other {# fields are zeroed; the page that opens the link marks each one.}}

err.notText: Paste the packet as text: hexadecimal digits.
err.tooLong: The text is longer than this tool reads ({max} characters).
err.empty: Paste a RADIUS packet in hexadecimal, as a capture shows it: plain hex, bytes separated by spaces or colons, or a hex dump with offsets.
err.tooMany: These are more than {max} octets ({octets} so far): a RADIUS packet is at most 4096 octets (RFC 2865, section 3), and this tool reads no more.
err.dumpLine: Line {line} does not begin with an offset, but the first line did: in a hex dump every line begins with the offset of its first byte (the format text2pcap reads).
err.dumpOffset: Line {line} begins with offset {found}, but {expected, plural, one {{expected} byte} other {{expected} bytes}} came before it: a hex dump's offsets count the bytes (the format text2pcap reads).
err.dumpBytes: Line {line} has an offset but no bytes after it.
err.ether4: These octets begin with an Ethernet header (EtherType 0x0800, RFC 894), then an IPv4 header carrying UDP (protocol 17: RFC 791, IANA's Protocol Numbers) from port {src} to port {dst} (RFC 768). The RADIUS packet starts at octet {offset}: copy only the RADIUS layer, or delete the first {offset} octets.
err.ether6: These octets begin with an Ethernet header (EtherType 0x86DD, RFC 2464), then an IPv6 header with Next Header 17, UDP (RFC 8200, IANA's Protocol Numbers), from port {src} to port {dst} (RFC 768). The RADIUS packet starts at octet {offset}: copy only the RADIUS layer, or delete the first {offset} octets.
err.ipv4: These octets begin with an IPv4 header carrying UDP (protocol 17: RFC 791, IANA's Protocol Numbers) from port {src} to port {dst} (RFC 768). The RADIUS packet starts at octet {offset}: copy only the RADIUS layer, or delete the first {offset} octets.
err.ipv6: These octets begin with an IPv6 header with Next Header 17, UDP (RFC 8200, IANA's Protocol Numbers), from port {src} to port {dst} (RFC 768). The RADIUS packet starts at octet {offset}: copy only the RADIUS layer, or delete the first {offset} octets.
err.tacacs: These octets are not a RADIUS packet: the first octet, {first}, is not a Code IANA assigns, and the first 12 read as a TACACS+ header (RFC 8907, section 4.1): version {version}, type {type} ({typeName}), seq_no {seq}, flags {flags}, session_id {session}, body length {length}, which is the number of octets that follow. A TACACS+ body is obfuscated with the shared secret (section 4.5), so this tool does not decode it; the comparison below sets the two protocols side by side.
err.tacacsPartial: These octets are not a RADIUS packet: the first octet, {first}, is not a Code IANA assigns, and the first 12 read as a TACACS+ header (RFC 8907, section 4.1): version {version}, type {type} ({typeName}), seq_no {seq}, flags {flags}, session_id {session}, body length {length}, though {given} octets follow. A TACACS+ body is obfuscated with the shared secret (section 4.5), so this tool does not decode it; the comparison below sets the two protocols side by side.
err.attrHeader: Attribute {index} would start at octet {offset}, but only one octet is left: an attribute needs at least a Type and a Length octet (RFC 2865, section 5). The packet is malformed.
err.attrLength: Attribute {index} at octet {offset}, {label}, has Length {length}. An attribute's Length counts its Type and Length octets, so it is at least 2 (RFC 2865, section 5): the packet is malformed, and RFC 2865 has an Access-Request with an invalid attribute Length answered with an Access-Reject, and a reply with one treated as an Access-Reject or silently discarded.
err.rfc2865erratum6486: Attribute {index} at octet {offset}, {label}, has Length {length}, which runs {over, plural, one {{over} octet} other {{over} octets}} past the end of the packet at octet {end}. These are the octets of RFC 2865's example in section 7.3 as published: its last attribute, State, says 0x10 where 10 octets (0x0a) follow, and verified erratum 6486 corrects it to 0x0a.
err.attrOverrun: Attribute {index} at octet {offset}, {label}, has Length {length}, which runs {over, plural, one {{over} octet} other {{over} octets}} past the end of the packet at octet {end} (RFC 2865, section 5): the packet is malformed. The capture may be cut short, or the Length field of the packet or of the attribute is wrong.
err.short: These are {octets, plural, one {{octets} octet} other {{octets} octets}}; a RADIUS packet has at least 20: Code (1), Identifier (1), Length (2) and the Authenticator (16) (RFC 2865, section 3). If they are attributes without the header, choose Attributes only.
err.lengthSmall: The Length field says {length}, below the minimum of 20 (RFC 2865, section 3): the header alone takes 20 octets.
err.lengthLarge: The Length field says {length}, above the maximum of 4096 (RFC 2865, section 3).
err.truncated: The Length field says {length} octets, but only {octets} were given: the packet is shorter than its Length, and a receiver MUST silently discard it (RFC 2865, section 3). The capture may be cut short.
err.mode: Choose packet (a whole RADIUS packet) or attributes (attributes only, without the 20-octet header).
err.json: The body is not valid JSON: send the hex itself, or one JSON object with "input" (the hex) and an optional "mode" (packet or attributes).
err.token: Line {line}: "{token}" is not hexadecimal. Bytes are pairs of hex digits, separated by spaces, colons, hyphens or dots, or run together; a 0x prefix is allowed.
err.oddToken: Line {line}: "{token}" has an odd number of hex digits; write every byte as two digits (05, not 5).

attr.size: A value of data type {dataType} is {want} octets (RFC 8044, section {section}); this one has {got}, so it is an invalid attribute (RFC 6929, section 2.8) and is shown as octets.
attr.empty: The value is empty: text and string values of length zero MUST NOT be sent (RFC 8044, sections 3.4 and 3.5; RFC 2865, section 5), and the fixed-size types cannot be empty, so it is an invalid attribute (RFC 6929, section 2.8).
attr.utf8: The value is not well-formed UTF-8, which a text value must be (RFC 8044, section 3.4; RFC 3629), so it is an invalid attribute (RFC 6929, section 2.8) and is shown as octets.
attr.enumUnknown: {value} is not a value IANA lists for this attribute; RFC 8044 (section 3.2) says an enum outside its defined values SHOULD be treated as an invalid attribute.
attr.enumNoList: IANA's RADIUS Types registry lists no value names for this attribute, so the number is shown as it is.
attr.timeEarly: A date before 2017 is likely to mean a configuration error or a clock without the correct time (RFC 8044, section 3.3).
attr.tlv: The value does not divide into TLVs whose TLV-Length is 3 to 255 (RFC 8044, section 3.13), so it is an invalid attribute (RFC 6929, section 2.8) and is shown as octets.
attr.prefixSize: An ipv6prefix value is 2 to 18 octets (RFC 8044, section 3.10); this one has {got}, so it is an invalid attribute (RFC 6929, section 2.8).
attr.prefixLen: Prefix-Length {plen} is above {max}, so the value MUST be treated as an invalid attribute (RFC 8044, section {section}).
attr.prefixShort: Prefix-Length {plen} needs {need, plural, one {{need} octet} other {{need} octets}} of prefix, and only {got} follow, so the prefix cannot be read and the attribute is invalid (RFC 8044, section {section}; RFC 6929, section 2.8).
attr.reserved: The Reserved octet is {value}; RFC 8044 says it is always zero (section {section}).
attr.prefixBits: Bits beyond the prefix length are set; RFC 8044 says they MUST be zero (section {section}).
attr.prefixZero: The address is 0.0.0.0, for which RFC 8044 says the Prefix-Length MUST be 32 (section 3.11).
attr.experimental: Type {type} is in the range IANA keeps for experimental use (192 to 223): its meaning is local to whoever uses it, so the value is shown as octets.
attr.implementation: Type {type} is in the range IANA keeps for implementation-specific use (224 to 240): its meaning is up to the implementation, so the value is shown as octets.
attr.reservedType: Type {type} is reserved in IANA's registry, so the attribute is invalid (RFC 6929, section 2.8) and is shown as octets.
attr.unassigned: IANA's registry assigns no attribute of Type {type}; RFC 6929 (section 2.8) recommends treating an attribute of unknown Type as an invalid attribute, so it is shown as octets.
attr.userPasswordSize: A User-Password String is 16 to 128 octets, a multiple of 16 (RFC 2865, section 5.2); this one has {got}, so it is an invalid attribute (RFC 6929, section 2.8).
attr.userPassword: Hidden: the password, padded with zeros to a multiple of 16 octets, is XORed 16 octets at a time with MD5 of the shared secret and the Request Authenticator, then of the shared secret and the previous 16 octets (RFC 2865, section 5.2). These {octets} octets hold a password of {min} to {octets} octets; reading it needs the shared secret, which this tool never asks for.
attr.chapSize: A CHAP-Password has Length 19, a CHAP Ident and a 16-octet response (RFC 2865, section 5.3); this one has {length}, so it is an invalid attribute (RFC 6929, section 2.8).
attr.chap: CHAP Ident {ident}, then the 16-octet CHAP response of the user (RFC 2865, section 5.3). The challenge it answers is the CHAP-Challenge attribute when the packet has one, otherwise the Request Authenticator.
attr.tunnelPasswordSize: A Tunnel-Password is a Tag, a two-octet Salt and a String that is a multiple of 16 octets, since the plaintext is padded to one before it is encrypted (RFC 2868, section 3.5); these {got} octets do not divide that way, so it is an invalid attribute (RFC 6929, section 2.8).
attr.tunnelPassword: Encrypted: Tag {tag}, Salt 0x{salt}, then {octets} octets holding the password's length, the password and padding, XORed with MD5 of the shared secret, the Request Authenticator of the Access-Request and the Salt (RFC 2868, section 3.5). Reading it needs the shared secret, which this tool never asks for.
attr.saltBit: The Salt's most significant bit is 0, but RFC 2868 (section 3.5) says it MUST be set.
attr.tagRange: Tag 0x{tag} is not 0x00 (unused) or 0x01 to 0x1F, the valid values (RFC 2868, section {section}).
attr.maSize: A Message-Authenticator has Length 18, a 16-octet HMAC-MD5 (RFC 3579, section 3.2); this one has {length}, so it is an invalid attribute (RFC 6929, section 2.8).
attr.ma: An HMAC-MD5 of the whole packet, keyed with the shared secret and computed with these 16 octets set to zero (RFC 3579, section 3.2). A receiver that holds the secret recomputes it and silently discards the packet when it does not match; this tool has no secret, so it cannot check it.
attr.taggedSize: {name} has Length 6, a Tag and a three-octet Value (RFC 2868, section {section}); this one has {length}, so it is an invalid attribute (RFC 6929, section 2.8).
attr.taggedEmpty: {name} has a Tag but no String, which RFC 2868 says must be present (section {section}), so it is an invalid attribute (RFC 6929, section 2.8).
attr.vsaSize: A Vendor-Specific attribute has Length 7 or more: Type, Length, a four-octet Vendor-Id and at least one octet of String (RFC 2865, section 5.26); this one has {length}, so it is an invalid attribute (RFC 6929, section 2.8).
attr.vsaHigh: The Vendor-Id's high-order octet is {value}; RFC 2865 (section 5.26) has it 0, with the Private Enterprise Number in the low three octets, and RFC 8044 (section 3.14) says a vsa that does not match its format SHOULD be treated as an invalid attribute.
attr.vendorUnknown: Private Enterprise Number {pen} is not one of the vendors this tool names; IANA's Private Enterprise Numbers registry gives its owner.
attr.vendorOffline: {vendor}'s configuration guides are no longer published online, so its sub-attributes are shown by number.
attr.vendorNotRead: This tool has no sub-attribute list from {vendor}'s documentation, so its sub-attributes are shown by number.
attr.vsaOctets: The String does not divide into vendor type, vendor length and value fields, the format RFC 2865 says it SHOULD use (section 5.26), so it is shown as undistinguished octets.
attr.redacted: Redacted in this link: {octets, plural, one {{octets} octet of this value was replaced by zeros when the link was made, so it is not the original} other {{octets} octets of this value were replaced by zeros when the link was made, so they are not the originals}}.

sub.mppe: Encrypted session key: Salt 0x{salt}, then the key's length, the key and padding, XORed with MD5 of the shared secret, the Request Authenticator and the Salt (RFC 2548, sections 2.4.2 and 2.4.3). Reading it needs the shared secret, which this tool never asks for.
sub.size: The vendor's documentation gives this sub-attribute four octets; it has {got}.
sub.untyped: The vendor's table gives this sub-attribute's name but not its data type: the octets are shown, as text when they are printable.
sub.unlisted: Vendor type {type} is not in the list this tool has from {vendor}'s documentation.
sub.msSecret: This Microsoft sub-attribute carries a challenge response, an encrypted password or key material (RFC 2548); it is shown as octets.
sub.avpairMandatory: Cisco's protocol:attribute sep value format: protocol {protocol}, attribute {attribute}, value {value}; the separator "=" makes it mandatory ("*" would make it optional).
sub.avpairOptional: Cisco's protocol:attribute sep value format: protocol {protocol}, attribute {attribute}, value {value}; the separator "*" makes it optional ("=" would make it mandatory).
sub.hexHuawei: Huawei's table types this sub-attribute hex: its octets are shown as they are.
sub.hwPrivilege: Privilege level {level} of an administrator, such as a Telnet user: Huawei's table gives HW-Exec-Privilege the range 0 to 15.
sub.hwPrivilegeHigh: Level {level} is outside the range 0 to 15 that Huawei's table gives HW-Exec-Privilege, and the table says a level "greater than or equal to 16 is ineffective".
sub.sizeHuaweiInteger: Huawei's table types this sub-attribute integer, which RADIUS writes as four octets, most significant first (RFC 2865, section 5); it has {got}.
sub.sizeHuaweiIpaddr: Huawei's table types this sub-attribute ipaddr: four octets are read as an IPv4 address and sixteen as an IPv6 address; it has {got}.
sub.unlistedHuawei: Vendor type {type} is not in Huawei's table of proprietary RADIUS attributes (Table 1-11 of the S5700 and S6700 V200R025C00 configuration guide), so it is shown as octets.
sub.hwFramedIpv6: Huawei's table describes HW-Framed-IPv6-Address as the "IPv6 address to be configured for the user": an address, not a prefix.
sub.dhcpRead: Read as DHCP options, as Huawei's table describes this value: "DHCP Option, encapsulated in Type-Length-Value (TLV) format".
sub.dhcpBad: Huawei's table describes this value as DHCP options in Type-Length-Value form, but the option starting at octet {at} of the value needs {need, plural, one {{need} octet} other {{need} octets}} and only {left} remain, so the value is shown as octets.
sub.dhcpOnly82: Option {code} is not Option 82, and Huawei's table says "Only Option 82 can be delivered."
sub.dhcp82Short: Option 82 has length {length}, but RFC 3046 (section 2.0) gives the Relay Agent Information option a minimum length of two, since at least one sub-option must be present, so its value is shown as octets.
sub.dhcp82Bad: Option 82's value does not divide into the sub-options of RFC 3046 (section 2.0): the sub-option starting at octet {at} of the option's value needs {need, plural, one {{need} octet} other {{need} octets}} and only {left} remain, so the value is shown as octets.
sub.dhcp82Unknown: Sub-option {code} of Option 82 is not one RFC 3046 defines (section 2.0 assigns 1, Agent Circuit ID, and 2, Agent Remote ID), so its value is shown as octets.

ext.size: This extended attribute has Length {length}; its format needs at least {min}: Type, Length, Extended-Type{flags} and one octet of data (RFC 6929, sections 2.1 and 2.2), so it is an invalid attribute (section 2.8).
ext.moreLength: The More flag is set, but the Length is {length}, not 255: with More set the Length MUST be 255 (RFC 6929, section 2.2), so the fragmented attribute is invalid.
ext.moreMissing: The More flag is set, but the next attribute is not a fragment with the same Type and Extended-Type, so the fragmented attribute is an invalid attribute (RFC 6929, section 2.2).
ext.evsSize: An Extended-Vendor-Specific value is at least 6 octets, a four-octet Vendor-Id, a Vendor-Type and data (RFC 8044, section 3.17); this one has {got}, so it is an invalid attribute (RFC 6929, section 2.8).
ext.evsData: The vendor defines what its Vendor-Type means and how its data is encoded (RFC 8044, section 3.17); the data is shown as octets, and as text when it is printable.
ext.fragments: Reassembled from {n} fragments: the More flag is set on every fragment but the last, and the data is their Ext-Data fields joined in order (RFC 6929, section 2.2).
ext.reserved: Extended-Type {ext} is reserved (241 to 255 are, RFC 8044 section 3.15), so the attribute is invalid (RFC 6929, section 2.8).
ext.unassigned: IANA's registry assigns nothing at {id}; RFC 6929 (section 2.8) recommends treating an attribute of unknown Extended-Type as an invalid attribute.
ext.truncation: The T (Truncation) flag is set: this chunk is intentionally truncated and continues in a later one (RFC 8044, section 3.16).
ext.fragmentOf: A later fragment of attribute {first}: its data is read there.

warn.eapSplit: The EAP-Message attributes are not consecutive: when there are several, they MUST be in order and consecutive (RFC 3579, section 3.1). The EAP packet below joins them in the order they appear.
warn.eapShort: The EAP-Message data is {octets, plural, one {{octets} octet} other {{octets} octets}}, shorter than an EAP header: Code, Identifier and a two-octet Length (RFC 3748, section 4).
warn.eapCode: EAP Code {code} is not one IANA's EAP registry assigns; RFC 3748 (section 4) has EAP packets with codes it does not define silently discarded.
warn.eapLength: The EAP Length says {length}, but the EAP-Message attributes hold {octets, plural, one {{octets} octet} other {{octets} octets}}: an EAP message with a Length larger than the octets received MUST be silently discarded (RFC 3748, section 4).
warn.eapPadding: The EAP Length says {length}, and the EAP-Message attributes hold {octets, plural, one {{octets} octet} other {{octets} octets}}: octets beyond the Length are padding and are ignored (RFC 3748, section 4).
warn.mustNot: {label} is present, but {rfc}'s table of attributes (section {section}) says it MUST NOT be in this packet type.
warn.atMostOne: {label} appears {n} times, but {rfc}'s table of attributes (section {section}) allows at most one in this packet type.
warn.exactlyOne: This packet type needs exactly one {label} ({rfc}, table of attributes in section {section}); it has {n}.
warn.reqNas: An Access-Request MUST contain a NAS-IP-Address or a NAS-Identifier (RFC 2865, section 4.1), or a NAS-IPv6-Address (RFC 3162, section 2.1); this one has none of them.
warn.reqCredential: An Access-Request MUST contain a User-Password, a CHAP-Password or a State (RFC 2865, section 4.1), or another kind of authentication information such as EAP-Message (RFC 3579); this one has none of them.
warn.reqKinds: An Access-Request MUST NOT contain more than one of User-Password, CHAP-Password, ARAP-Password and EAP-Message (RFC 3579, section 3.3, Note 1); this one has {list}.
warn.reqNoMa: This Access-Request has no Message-Authenticator. RFC 2865 as published does not ask for one, and RFC 3579 makes it optional without EAP-Message (section 3.2): the requirement comes from CVE-2024-3596 and from draft-ietf-radext-deprecating-radius, an Internet-Draft (revision 10 of 3 July 2026), not an RFC. RFC 2865 erratum 9034 records it for readers, "Access-Request packets MUST contain a Message-Authenticator attribute", with the status Held for Document Update (since 26 August 2026), not Verified.
warn.eapNoMa: This packet carries EAP-Message but no Message-Authenticator: one MUST protect every Access-Request, Access-Challenge, Access-Accept and Access-Reject that contains an EAP-Message, and a receiver SHOULD silently discard the packet without it (RFC 3579, section 3.1).
warn.acctNas: An Accounting-Request MUST contain a NAS-IP-Address or a NAS-Identifier, or both (RFC 2866, sections 4.1 and 5.13); this one has neither.
warn.acctResponse: RFC 2866 (section 5.13) says no attributes should be in an Accounting-Response except Proxy-State and possibly Vendor-Specific; this one has {list}.
warn.statusNoMa: A Status-Server packet MUST include a Message-Authenticator, without which it could be trivially spoofed (RFC 5997, section 3); this one has none.
warn.vlanRange: Tunnel-Private-Group-ID "{group}" is not a VLAN ID: RFC 3580 (section 3.31) carries a VLAN ID from 1 to 4094 as its decimal string.
warn.codeUnassigned: Code {code} is not assigned in IANA's RADIUS Packet Type Codes registry; a receiver silently discards a packet with an invalid Code (RFC 2865, section 3).
warn.codeReserved: Code {code} is reserved in IANA's RADIUS Packet Type Codes registry; a receiver silently discards a packet with an invalid Code (RFC 2865, section 3).
warn.acctMax: An accounting packet is at most 4095 octets (RFC 2866, section 3); this one's Length is 4096.
warn.padding: {n, plural, one {{n} octet follows} other {{n} octets follow}} the end the Length field gives ({length}): RFC 2865 (section 3) has them treated as padding and ignored, so they are not decoded.
warn.invalidAttr: Attribute {index}, {label}, is an invalid attribute; RFC 6929 (section 2.8) says a receiver SHOULD silently discard it, and MUST NOT discard the whole packet for it.

note.authRequest: In an Access-Request the Authenticator is the Request Authenticator, a 16-octet random number that SHOULD be unpredictable and unique over the lifetime of a shared secret; it is also the input that hides User-Password (RFC 2865, section 3).
note.authStatus: In a Status-Server packet the Authenticator is a 16-octet random Request Authenticator, made as in an Access-Request (RFC 5997, section 3).
note.authResponse: In a reply the Authenticator is the Response Authenticator: MD5 over the Code, Identifier, Length, the request's Request Authenticator, the reply's attributes and the shared secret (RFC 2865, section 3). Checking it needs the request and the shared secret; this tool asks for neither.
note.authAcctRequest: In an Accounting-Request the Request Authenticator is MD5 over the Code, Identifier, Length, 16 zero octets, the attributes and the shared secret (RFC 2866, section 3); checking it needs the shared secret, which this tool never asks for.
note.authAcctResponse: In an Accounting-Response the Authenticator is the Response Authenticator: MD5 over the Code, Identifier, Length, the request's Request Authenticator, the reply's attributes and the shared secret (RFC 2866, section 3).
note.authDynRequest: In a Disconnect-Request or a CoA-Request the Request Authenticator is computed as for an Accounting-Request, and the request goes to UDP port 3799 (RFC 5176, section 2.3).
note.authDynResponse: In a Disconnect-ACK, Disconnect-NAK, CoA-ACK or CoA-NAK the Authenticator is the Response Authenticator, over the reply and the request's Request Authenticator (RFC 5176, section 2.3).
note.authOther: This tool does not know how the Authenticator of Code {code} is formed; it shows the 16 octets as they are.
note.example: These are the octets of an example in {rfc}, section {section}, which the RFC computed with the shared secret "{secret}".
note.exampleNoSecret: These are the octets of an example in {rfc}, section {section}.
note.erratum1469: RFC 2865 verified erratum 1469: this example's text says Framed-Routing None (0), but its octets carry 2, Listen for routing packets; the decoder reads the octets.
note.erratum6486: These are the octets as RFC 2865 verified erratum 6486 corrects them: State's Length is 0x0a, where the RFC as published printed 0x10.
note.rfc6929: RFC 6929 says its examples show the format of the attributes, not a consistent meaning: read against IANA's registry as it stands, some of them are invalid attributes.
note.rfc5997reply: RFC 5997's text calls this reply an Accounting-Response (5), but its first octet is 02, Access-Accept. Its Response Authenticator is the MD5 the RFC describes taken over Code 5 with the RFC's shared secret, so the 02 is the misprint; the RFC Editor listed no erratum on it on 2026-11-08.
note.vlanTagged: VLAN assignment as RFC 3580 describes it (section 3.31): Tunnel-Type VLAN (13), Tunnel-Medium-Type 802 (6) and Tunnel-Private-Group-ID "{group}", all with Tag {tag}.
note.vlan: VLAN assignment as RFC 3580 describes it (section 3.31): Tunnel-Type VLAN (13), Tunnel-Medium-Type 802 (6) and Tunnel-Private-Group-ID "{group}".
note.vlanName: Tunnel-Private-Group-ID "{group}" is not a number: RFC 3580 (section 3.31) carries a VLAN ID from 1 to 4094 as its decimal string; whether a switch also accepts a VLAN name is up to the switch.
note.eap: The NAS passes the EAP packet through without understanding the method (RFC 3579, section 3.1): the conversation inside is between the supplicant and the server.
note.codeExperimental: Code {code} is in the range IANA keeps for experimental use (250 to 253).
note.attributesMode: Attributes only: there is no header, so the checks that depend on the packet type and the Authenticator are not made.
note.redactedAuthenticator: Redacted in this link: the Authenticator is 16 zero octets, since the original is an MD5 with the shared secret, against which a reader could test guesses of the secret offline.
note.redactedPadding: Redacted in this link: {n, plural, one {the {n} octet after the Length is zero, since this tool does not read it and cannot tell what it held} other {the {n} octets after the Length are zeros, since this tool does not read them and cannot tell what they held}}.

bit-numbering-and-order.name: Bit numbering and bit order
bit-numbering-and-order.blurb: Every bit of a value with its weight and its number under LSB 0, MSB 0 and 1-based numbering, the field you name as bits i to j, the value bit-reversed and in the order a link sends it, a printed bit string read in the order it was printed, and a MAC address in canonical and bit-reversed form, with the I/G and U/L bits named. Layouts for the LACP state, the TCP flags, the DNS flags, the ToS octet and the 802.1Q tag.
bit-numbering-and-order.runsLocally: Runs locally in your browser. Nothing is sent anywhere.

inputHint.value: Hexadecimal needs 0x and binary 0b; plain digits are decimal, and a minus sign gives the two's complement bits.
inputHint.printed: Only 0s and 1s, in the order the device printed them; single spaces, underscores or dots between groups are fine.
inputHint.mac: Hyphens, colons, Cisco dots (1234.5678.9abc) or twelve hex digits.

layoutHint.none: No layout: just the bits and their numbers.
layoutHint.lacp: 8 bits: the Actor_State or Partner_State octet of the Link Aggregation Control Protocol (LACP), LACP_Activity to Expired.
layoutHint.macOctet: 8 bits: the first octet of a Media Access Control (MAC) address, with the I/G, U/L, Y and Z bits.
layoutHint.tcpFlags: 8 bits: the fourteenth octet of the TCP header, CWR to FIN.
layoutHint.dnsFlags: 16 bits: the second word of the DNS header, QR to RCODE.
layoutHint.tos: 8 bits: the IPv4 Type of Service octet (the IPv6 Traffic Class), DSCP and ECN.
layoutHint.vlanTci: 16 bits: the tag control information of an 802.1Q tag, priority, DEI and VLAN ID.

bit-numbering-and-order.fieldHint: Optional: give bits i to j in the numbering above to get the field's mask, shift and value; leave the second blank for one bit.

empty.value: Type a value, or press Example for the DNS answer flags 0x81A0.
empty.printed: Type the bits as printed, or press Example for Huawei's PortState 10111100.
empty.mac: Type a MAC address, or press Example for RFC 2469's 12-34-56-78-9A-BC.

bit-numbering-and-order.learn: Least and most significant bit explains the numberings, the order on a wire and the cases these layouts come from; Big-endian and little-endian covers byte order.
bit-numbering-and-order.related: Related tools: the <lacp>LACP member link and state reader</lacp> decodes the state octets in full, the <oui>OUI lookup</oui> names a MAC address's vendor, the <mcast>multicast group to MAC mapper</mcast> maps groups to group addresses, and the <vlan>802.1Q tag decoder</vlan> reads whole tags.

err.json: The request body is not valid JSON: send one JSON object that names its mode: value, printed or mac.
err.tooLong: A field is longer than this tool reads ({max} characters).
err.empty: Type a value first.

err.bareHex: "{value}" looks hexadecimal: write it with 0x in front (0x{value}), so it is not read as decimal.
err.macInValue: "{value}" looks like a MAC address: choose the MAC address mode to read it.
err.tooWide: The value has more than 64 bits; this tool reads 1 to 64.
err.width: "{value}" is not a width: write a whole number of bits from 1 to 64.
err.fit: The value needs {need, plural, one {{need} bit} other {{need} bits}}, more than the width of {width}: widen it or check the value.
err.negativeFit: {value} does not fit {width, plural, one {{width} bit} other {{width} bits}} as a two's complement number, which holds {min} to {max}.
err.layout: Choose a layout: none, lacp, mac-octet, tcp-flags, dns-flags, tos or vlan-tci.

note.lsb0: LSB 0 numbers the bits from the least significant, so bit k weighs 2 to the power k: Intel's "Bit positions are numbered from right to left. The numerical value of a set bit is equal to two raised to the power of the bit position", and the Linux kernel's BIT(n), which is 1 shifted left n times.
note.msb0: MSB 0 numbers them from the most significant, as the RFC diagrams do: "the bit labeled 0 is the most significant bit", so the octet drawn 1 0 1 0 1 0 1 0 is 170 (RFC 791, Appendix B).
note.one: 1-based numbering counts from 1 at the least significant bit: SNMP places a BITS value in "bits 8 (high order bit) to 1 (low order bit)" of each octet (RFC 3417, section 8), and Huawei's display eth-trunk numbers its PortState Bit 1 to Bit 8.
note.inferredHex: No width was given: {width} bits, four for each hexadecimal digit typed, leading zeros included.
note.inferredBin: No width was given: {width, plural, one {{width} bit} other {{width} bits}}, one for each binary digit typed, leading zeros included.
note.inferredDec: No width was given: {width} bits, the smallest of 8, 16, 32 and 64 that holds the decimal value.
note.sign: The most significant bit is set, so read as a two's complement signed number the value is negative. Intel: "The sign bit is located in bit 7 in a byte integer, bit 15 in a word integer, bit 31 in a doubleword integer, and bit 63 in a quadword integer".
note.parity: Parity counts the ones: with even parity a link adds the bit that makes "an even number of logic 1s in the data and parity bits", with odd parity the bit that makes the count odd (TI TL16C550D UART).
note.wire: On an Ethernet link each octet goes least significant bit first: "the physical order of bit transmission within an octet on an IEEE [802.3] link is from the lowest order bit to the highest order bit (i.e., the reverse of the IETF's ordering)" (RFC 9542). The octets are taken in the order written, most significant first, as network byte order sends a number (RFC 791); a UART and PPP send each octet least significant bit first too. An I2C bus sends most significant bit first: "Data is transferred with the Most Significant Bit (MSB) first" (NXP UM10204, 3.1.5), and so does an SPI bus unless set otherwise.
note.reverse: Reversing the bits of each octet in place is the bit swap RFC 2469 describes between canonical and Token Ring addresses; reversing the whole width also reverses the order of the octets, and that part is byte order, not bit order.
note.printedMsb: The string was read most significant bit first, the order numbers are written in. Read least significant bit first, the same string is another value: a misread order changes the number without any error.
note.printedLsb: The string was read least significant bit first: its first character is bit 0 of the value. Read most significant bit first, as numbers are usually written, the same string is another value.
note.field: The field is GENMASK({hi}, {lo}) in the Linux kernel's LSB 0 terms, "a contiguous bitmask starting at bit position @l and ending at position @h": shift right by {lo}, then keep {span} bits.
note.fieldBit: One bit: BIT({lo}) in the Linux kernel's terms; it is {state}.

mac.canonical: Canonical form maps "The first bit of each byte that appears on the LAN" to "the least significant (i.e., right-most) bit of each byte in memory", which "puts the group address indicator ... in the least significant bit of the first byte"; Ethernet and 802.3 hardware work this way (RFC 2469).
mac.reversed: Token Ring, and some FDDI hardware, mapped the first bit to the most significant bit instead ("MSB format", "non-canonical form"), so an adapter held the address with every octet bit-reversed: RFC 2469's 12-34-56-78-9A-BC is 48-2C-6A-1E-59-3D there.
mac.typedReversed: You entered the bit-reversed form: the canonical address is each octet with its bits reversed.
mac.bits: The I/G bit is "The least significant bit of Octet 0" and the U/L bit "the second least significant bit" (IEEE RA); Ethernet sends each octet least significant bit first (RFC 9542), so the I/G bit is the first bit of the address on the wire.
mac.slap: A local address may follow the IEEE 802 Structured Local Address Plan, whose Y and Z bits split the local space into four quadrants (RFC 9542, section 2.1.1); the plan is optional.
mac.bridges: Bridges between Token Ring and Ethernet had to "perform bit swaps of the addresses in the address fields of ARP packets" (RFC 2469, section 3.2): reading one form as the other names a different station, with other I/G and U/L bits, as the misread line shows.

lacp.note: IEEE 802.1AX numbers the Actor_State and Partner_State bits 0 (LACP_Activity) to 7 (Expired), and the Linux driver's masks put LACP_Activity at 0x01 and Expired at 0x80, so 802.1AX's bit k weighs 2 to the power k (LSB 0). Huawei's display eth-trunk prints the same eight bits as Bit 1 to Bit 8, Bit 1 (LACP_Activity) first, so its PortState string reads least significant bit first, and SNMP's BITS form puts LACP_Activity in the high-order bit.

mac-octet.note: The IEEE RA names "The least significant bit of Octet 0 (the I/G bit)" and "the second least significant bit of Octet 0 (the U/L bit)"; RFC 9542 draws the octet MSB 0, with M (I/G), X (U/L), Y and Z in positions 7, 6, 5 and 4. Ethernet sends the I/G bit first.

tcp-flags.note: This is the TCP header's fourteenth octet. IANA's TCP Header Flags registry numbers its bits 8 (CWR) to 15 (FIN), counting from the most significant bit of the 16 bits that begin with the Data Offset, while the Linux kernel defines TCPHDR_FIN as BIT(0) and TCPHDR_CWR as BIT(7). AE, IANA's bit 7, is the lowest bit of the octet before.

dns-flags.note: This is the DNS header's second 16-bit word. RFC 1035 draws it MSB 0 ("the bit labeled 0 is the most significant bit"), and IANA's DNS Header Flags registry follows it: AA is bit 5, AD bit 10, CD bit 11. Under LSB 0 the same AA is bit 10, and RD (IANA's bit 7) is bit 8.

tos.note: The IPv4 ToS octet (the IPv6 Traffic Class) holds the DSCP in bits 0 to 5 of RFC 2474's MSB 0 drawing and ECN in "Bits 6 and 7" (RFC 3168): the DSCP is the octet shifted right by 2, ECN its two lowest bits.

vlan-tci.note: The 802.1Q TCI as the Linux kernel masks it: VLAN_PRIO_MASK 0xe000 with VLAN_PRIO_SHIFT 13 for the priority, VLAN_CFI_MASK 0x1000, "Canonical Format Indicator / Drop Eligible Indicator", and VLAN_VID_MASK 0x0fff for the VLAN ID.

doc.tcp: bit {i} in IANA's registry, BIT({k}) in Linux
doc.dnsBit: bit {p} in RFC 1035 and IANA's registry
doc.tosDscp: bits 0 to 5 of RFC 2474's DS field

mac.x: universal/local: 0 for an address under an IEEE-assigned prefix, 1 for a local one
mac.y: the SLAP's Y bit, which with Z picks the quadrant of a local address
mac.rest: the rest of the first octet, part of the prefix or of the local address
