privacy_page.title: Your data, and what this site does with it
privacy_page.lede: A plain-language account of exactly what this website does and does not do with your information. It is written to be accurate rather than merely reassuring, because under regulations like the GDPR and Brazil's LGPD it is the accurate disclosure that matters.
privacy_page.short1: The site's own code sets no cookies, shows no advertising, and adds no third-party trackers or fingerprinting; nothing it runs follows you across the web. Cloudflare, which hosts the site, runs a bot check of its own that may place up to two cookies, explained under Hosting and server logs. The site does count requests at the server, in aggregate, and that counting is described in full below. With your yes, and only then, its pages also tell the server what you use (a tool, a game, a search), as Interest counts below describes.
privacy_page.short2: It does not sell, share, or build profiles of its visitors, and it asks you for nothing in order to read it.
privacy_page.short3: The catalogue's interactive tools run entirely in your browser: what you paste or type into them stays on your device. The one exception is the red room (/dev/out), whose tools send a query when you press Ask or Enter, or test data when you press Start on the speed test, straight from your browser to the official service they name; nothing goes to this site's servers.
privacy_page.short4: Only seven things involve data at all, and each is explained below: a handful of preferences, one short reading trail and My desk, saved in your own browser; what Cloudflare does as the host when it serves a page (its connection logs, a log of each request that reaches the site's Worker, a bot check that may set up to two cookies, and the error reports your browser may send it when a request fails); the aggregate request counts kept at the site's own server; the results of the daily puzzles and daily runs you finish in /dev/fun and /arcade, posted to a public scoreboard unless you switch sharing off; the interest counts, which your browser sends only if you said yes; the encrypted copy of My desk, only if you make a sync code, which the site cannot read; and any message you choose to send by email.
privacy_page.controllerBody: This is the personal website of Rodolfo Nützmann (ronutz.com). For any privacy question, or to exercise any of the rights described below, write to {email}. Enquiries are handled directly by Rodolfo Nützmann, as the data controller.
privacy_page.noTrackTitle: No cookies set by the site's code, no third-party analytics, and what is counted instead
privacy_page.noTrackBody:
The site's own code sets no cookies. It uses no third-party analytics service (such as Google Analytics or Plausible), no advertising network, no social-media tracking pixels, and no device fingerprinting, and none of its own scripts reports anything about you; they send three things only: the result of a daily puzzle or daily run you finish in /dev/fun or /arcade, to the public scoreboard, unless you switch that off (see Game scores below); only if you said yes when asked, the interest counts, which name what was used and never who used it (see Interest counts below); and, only if you make a sync code, an encrypted copy of My desk that the site cannot read (see My desk below). The one thing on the page that does not come from the site's code is Cloudflare's bot check, a script and up to two cookies of Cloudflare's own, explained under Hosting and server logs below.

What the site does keep is a count, made at its own server as it answers each request. Two separate records are written, and they are deliberately kept apart so that neither can be matched to the other. The first records the address asked for and whether a page was found there, the language, the visiting country as your network reports it, whether the request came from a person or from a known crawler, and, for a person, the coarse class of device (phone or tablet, desktop or laptop, or other). The second records only a referring address, when your browser sends one and a page was served, and carries nothing else at all - no page, no country, no time correlation with the first.

The counting code never writes your IP address. It never writes your browser's user agent or the network your connection comes from either; they are read only to decide whether the request came from a person or a crawler (a browser on a cloud or hosting provider's network counts as a machine) and, for a person, which class of device sent it, and what is kept is a label such as "search engine", "monitoring tool" or "phone or tablet". No identifier of any kind is used, so there is no visitor to profile, no session to reconstruct, and nothing to share.
privacy_page.browserTitle: What is stored in your browser
privacy_page.browserBody: A few small things, all in your browser's local storage, none of them sent to this site or to anyone else except as Game scores below describes, each clearable through your browser at any time: your visual theme (ronutz-theme); the language you last used, so the bare domain can send you back to it (ronutz-lang); whether glossary hints are shown (ronutz-glossary-hints); any keyboard shortcuts you rebound (ronutz-shortcuts); whether the search box starts empty each time you open it (ronutz-search-fresh); the cards-or-list density you chose on an index page (ronutz:view:*); the Guided or Directory reading you chose on the Learn and Tools pages (ronutz:hub:*); the last six pages you opened, so the home page can offer them again under "Continue where you left off", with a button that forgets them (ronutz:recent:v1); on two dev-room pages only, a motion switch and a practice score (ronutz-mb-motion, ronutz:subnet-drill:stats); and, in the /dev/fun and /arcade games, each game's streak, scores, settings, progress and daily puzzles from the last seven days, whether each daily puzzle was solved (kept for 400 days), the 14 earlier puzzles played most recently, the Meeting Bingo card in play, whether finished daily puzzles go to the public scoreboard, the initials you gave it and the random number each round of the last two days was sent with (ronutz:fun:v1); a game's "Reset my stats" button clears its streak and scores, and old daily puzzles drop out after seven days. One session-only flag (ronutz.privPreview) exists for the author's private preview of unpublished pages and is never set for a reader. Your answer to the interest counts' question is kept the same way (ronutz:interest:v1). My desk (/desk) keeps the items you save, the ones you mark as read or done (with the day of each mark, never a time), your reading paths, its layout and settings, your notes and, if you turn on sync, your sync code (ronutz:desk:v1); it holds the names of the site's pages, not their titles. If you sync, the last synced copy of the things listed under My desk is kept too, with the time of that sync to the minute, so the next sync can tell which side changed (ronutz:portable:base). The games also keep the day this browser last published a round to the scoreboard (ronutz:fun:posted-day), so that the board can count each browser once a day without knowing which; the day itself is never sent, only whether a round is the first of its day (see Game scores below). Nothing else about you is stored on your device.
privacy_page.hostingBody: The site is delivered through Cloudflare, which provides its hosting and content delivery. As with any website, loading a page means your device connects to a server, and Cloudflare, acting as the hosting provider, processes basic connection data, including your IP address and standard request details, in order to deliver the pages to you and to protect the site against abuse and attack. This processing is necessary to operate and secure the site (a legitimate interest under GDPR Article 6(1)(f), and the corresponding bases under LGPD Articles 7 and 10). How long Cloudflare keeps this data is set by Cloudflare's own policies, not by this site's code, and it is not used here to identify or track you.
privacy_page.toolsTitle: The tools run in your browser
privacy_page.toolsBody: The decoders and calculators on this site, for JWTs, IP addresses, certificates and the rest, compute entirely within your browser. The values you enter are processed on your own device and are never sent to a server. When one page hands a value to a tool, for example the home page's CIDR box opening the full calculator, the value travels after the # in the address (#input=...): browsers never send that part in a request, so the host does not receive it, but it stays in your address bar and history, and anyone you share the address with can read it. Some tools also offer a Share results button: it builds such a link only when you press it, says first exactly what the link will carry, and never changes your address bar; where a tool's input can hold secrets, the link carries a derived form instead, such as an encrypted string without its passphrase or a copy with its secrets masked. The Global Cat Distribution System, one of the /dev/fun toys, offers the same kind of link for its answer: it is made only when you press Copy, and it carries the name you typed, and the city if you gave one, after the #. Older links that carried the value in the query string (?input=) sent it to the host with that page request, as every query string is sent; such a link still opens the tool, which then moves the value after the # so it is not sent again. The one exception to local computation is the red room (/dev/out), whose tools exist to ask a live service: when you press Ask, or Enter in the field, your query goes from your browser directly to the official service named on screen, a domain registry for example, and this site's servers never see it; the speed test likewise exchanges test data with Cloudflare's speed test service only when you press Start. That service receives the query or the test data and the usual connection details, under its own terms. The programmatic interface (an API) documented on this site follows the same rule, stateless and logging no query or request body; ronutz.com does not serve it. One tool also offers a link that carries a value out: under a file's digests, the Hash tool links that file's SHA-256 to VirusTotal's report on it, and only if you follow the link does your browser send the hash, never the file, to VirusTotal, under VirusTotal's own terms.
privacy_page.contactBody: The contact form does not submit to any server. Instead it opens a pre-filled message in your own email application, which you then send yourself from your own account, so nothing passes through a third party. If you do write, whether through the form or directly, I receive the information you include, such as your name, email address and message, and use it only to reply to you. I keep it only for as long as needed to deal with your enquiry, do not use it for marketing, and do not share it.
privacy_page.intlBody: Because Cloudflare operates a global network, the connection-level processing described above may take place on servers located outside your own country, including outside Brazil and the European Economic Area. Where personal data is handled internationally in this way, it is processed under the safeguards offered by the provider concerned.
privacy_page.childrenBody: This site is intended for a professional, general audience. It is not directed at children and does not knowingly collect personal data from them.
privacy_page.rightsBody: Depending on where you live, you have rights over your personal data, including to access it, to have it corrected or deleted, to object to or restrict its processing, to request a copy in a portable form, and to be told how it is handled. To exercise any of these, simply write to {email}. Because so little personal data is ever processed here, in practice there is usually very little to act on, but the channel is always open.
privacy_page.rightsGdpr: If you are in the European Economic Area or the United Kingdom, you also have the right to lodge a complaint with your local data protection supervisory authority.
privacy_page.rightsLgpd: If you are in Brazil, you hold the rights set out in Article 18 of the LGPD, and may also contact the national data protection authority (the ANPD).
privacy_page.changesBody: If this notice changes, the revised version will be published on this page and the date below will be updated. Material changes will not be applied retroactively.

revisions.r20261013: The Portuguese notice re-read beside the English, and a lost qualifier restored.
revisions.r20261007: The visitor count records whether a page was found; the user agent and network reads are explained; the Guided or Directory choice joins the list of stored values; the local-first promise is scoped to the catalogue, with the red room named as the exception.
revisions.r20261006: The search box's reopen preference joins the list of stored values.
revisions.r20261005: Every key the site writes to the browser is listed, including the language last used, the keyboard shortcut bindings and the trail of recently opened pages.
revisions.r20260703: Why preferences live only on this device, and nowhere else.
revisions.r20261025: How a value handed from one page to a tool travels (after the # in the address, never in a request), what older ?input= links sent, that the certification hub keeps its search there too, and that Enter sends a red-room query just as Ask does.
revisions.r20261026: Where the code that counts can be read, how long the store keeps the counts (from Cloudflare's own documentation), and that Cloudflare, not this site's code, sets how long its connection data is kept.
revisions.r20261026b: What Cloudflare does as the host is set out: its Workers Logs (what a record holds and for how long), its bot check (the script it adds to each page and the two cookies it may set) and the network error reports a browser may send it. The statements about cookies are scoped to the site's own code, which sets none.
revisions.r20261027speed: The speed test joins the red room: what it sends (test data, to Cloudflare's speed test service), and when (only when you press Start), stated beside the lookups' Ask and Enter.
revisions.r20261027share: The Share results button is described: it builds a link only when pressed, says what the link carries, and carries a derived form where a tool's input can hold secrets.
revisions.r20261027hash: The Hash tool's link to VirusTotal is set out: a file's SHA-256 reaches VirusTotal only if you follow that link, and the file itself never leaves your device.
revisions.r20261028address: The contact address is now shown by a button that reveals it in your browser; the notice no longer writes it in any form a harvester could read.
revisions.r20261102cookie: The language menu no longer writes a cookie. Until this revision, changing language with it also saved the chosen language in a cookie named NEXT_LOCALE, kept for a year, which nothing on the site read; the language stays where it always worked, in your browser's storage, and a visit now removes a cookie left from before.
revisions.r20261103fun: The /dev/fun games join the list of stored values: each game's streak, scores, settings, progress and last seven days of daily puzzles, and the Meeting Bingo card in play, in one key; a game's "Reset my stats" button clears its streak and scores.
revisions.r20261103catlink: The Global Cat Distribution System's share link is described: it is made only when Copy is pressed, and it carries the name, and the city if one was given, after the #.
revisions.r20261105earlier: The /dev/fun games also keep whether each daily puzzle was solved (for 400 days) and the 14 earlier puzzles played most recently, for the list of earlier puzzles every daily game now offers.
revisions.r20261108scores: The public scoreboard of the /dev/fun and /arcade games is set out under Game scores: what a finished daily puzzle sends unless sharing is switched off, what each row keeps and never keeps, that rows are kept for 400 days, and how to have one removed.
revisions.r20261112interest: The interest counts are new: with your yes, and only then, the pages tell the site's server what you use (a tool, a game, an article read to its end, a share, a search), in notes that name the thing and never you. What a note holds, the one case that carries words you typed, how long the counts and the daily totals are kept, and where the choice is changed are set out in a section of their own.
revisions.r20261112desk: My desk: its key in this browser (ronutz:desk:v1), the optional encrypted sync (what the server holds, for how long, and what it cannot read), and the count sent when an item is saved; what moves to another browser by sync, file or link, and what stays with each browser (ronutz:portable:base among them); and, for a setting changed in two browsers, the latest change wins, by change times kept in this browser and inside the encrypted copy (ronutz:portable:times), unless you choose in Settings to keep this browser's value (ronutz:portable:no-times).
revisions.r20261112browsers: Game scores: the first round a browser publishes on a puzzle day carries one yes or no saying so, decided from the day of its last published round, which that browser keeps (ronutz:fun:posted-day) and never sends; the server keeps only that bit on the round, and the daily sum is shown as unique browsers (browsers, not people) and kept in the daily totals.

privacy_page.prefsTitle: Theme, language, and what this site remembers
privacy_page.prefsBody: Your preferences, your reading trail, My desk, the two dev-room values and the games' scores, settings and progress are stored only in this browser's localStorage, on your device; the theme is applied before first paint on your next visit. There is no cookie and no account, and no server sees any of it, with one exception you control: unless you switch sharing off, the result of a daily puzzle you finish goes to the public scoreboard described under Game scores. If you make a sync code, an encrypted copy of My desk also goes to the site's server, which cannot read it (see My desk below). None of it can follow you: a private window, cleared site data, or a different browser or device starts you back at the defaults by design. Your language works in two layers: it lives in the address itself (/en/ and /pt-BR/ are different pages, so bookmarking or sharing a URL in your language keeps it), and the last language you used is also remembered in this browser, so that a visit to the bare domain lands on it rather than on the default. The certification hub's find field and its retired switch also live in the address, after the # (#q=...), a part your browser never sends in a request, so the words you search for do not reach the server; they do stay in your history, and a shared address shares them. An older link with ?q= sent its words with that one request; the hub then moves them after the #. That is the whole trade: with no accounts and no tracking, preferences can only live where you can see and delete them.
privacy_page.shortcutsBody: The site has a handful of single-key shortcuts for quick navigation, active on every page. Press b for the boss key, which hides whatever you are reading behind a convincing 1980s work application until you press any key or click; t jumps to the Tools index; l to the Learn index; m opens the Mega Brain console; and z opens Meeting Bingo. These are deliberately inert whenever you are typing: if the focus is in a text field, a paste box, a search input, or any editable area, the keystroke belongs to that field and the shortcut does nothing, so nothing you type is ever swallowed. They are also ignored when a modifier key is held, so your browser's own combinations such as Ctrl+T for a new tab are never shadowed. The shortcuts run entirely in your browser, add no tracking, and are purely a convenience you can ignore.
privacy_page.noTrackSource: This section describes what the code does, and the code is public: the counting is done by <analytics>worker/analytics.ts</analytics>, the Stats page is served by <stats>worker/stats.ts</stats>, and the two separate datasets are bound in <config>wrangler.jsonc</config>. The counts are kept in Cloudflare's Workers Analytics Engine, which stores what is written to it for three months (<retention>Cloudflare's documentation</retention>, read {date}). What Cloudflare itself processes as the host is outside this code, and is described under Hosting and server logs below.
privacy_page.metaDescription: What happens to your information here: what is counted, what your browser stores, what the tools do with what you paste, who is responsible, and your rights under the GDPR and Brazil's LGPD.
privacy_page.hostingLogs: Every page request passes through the site's Worker, the small program that runs at Cloudflare in front of the pages, and so do the requests a page makes for the visitor counts it displays; the scripts, styles and search index, among other files, are served without it. Cloudflare's Workers Logs may keep a record of each of these requests in the site's Cloudflare account. Cloudflare describes each record as holding the request, the response and related metadata, and names among its fields the method and the full address, query string included, the response status, the processing time the Worker used and the visiting country (<logs>Workers Logs</logs> and <fields>its query fields</fields>, read {date}). Cloudflare publishes no complete list, so this notice does not claim that your IP address is left out. Cloudflare turns this logging on by default for new Workers, and the site's configuration does not turn it off. A record is kept for up to seven days: three days on Cloudflare's free Workers plan and seven on its paid plan, and seven on both from 1 December 2026 (<pricing>Cloudflare's pricing</pricing>). The site's own code adds nothing to these records, because the Worker writes no log lines of its own, which a build check verifies. The part of an address after a #, where a tool receives a value handed to it, is never sent in a request, so it never reaches them.
privacy_page.hostingBots: Cloudflare also runs bot protection in front of the site, to tell people from automated traffic, and two parts of it reach your browser; neither comes from the site's code. First, Cloudflare adds a small script of its own to each page, loaded from the site's address under <c>/cdn-cgi/challenge-platform/</c>; it runs in the background and gives Cloudflare signals from your browser that help it judge whether a person is using it. Cloudflare calls this <jsd>JavaScript Detections</jsd>. Second, Cloudflare may place up to two cookies: <c>__cf_bm</c>, which expires after 30 minutes without activity, and <c>cf_clearance</c>, which stores the result of that check and is tied to the device it was issued to; Cloudflare's default lifetime for it is 30 minutes (<clearance>Clearance</clearance>, <passage>Challenge Passage</passage>). Cloudflare describes both as strictly necessary for its bot protection. Apart from timing information, the contents of <c>__cf_bm</c> are encrypted and readable only by Cloudflare, and a separate <c>__cf_bm</c> is issued for each site because, Cloudflare states, it does not track anyone from site to site or from session to session. Cloudflare also states that cookie data may be processed in its data centre in the United States (<cookies>Cloudflare's cookie documentation</cookies>, read {date}).
privacy_page.hostingNel: Cloudflare also adds two headers of its own to every response, <c>NEL</c> and <c>Report-To</c>, which set up Network Error Logging: they ask a browser that supports it to report requests to the site that fail. As read on {date}, they ask for every failed request to be reported and none of the successful ones (<c>success_fraction</c> 0.0), and the browser keeps that instruction for seven days. If a request fails, such a browser may later send a short report straight to Cloudflare at <c>a.nel.cloudflare.com</c>, not to the site: the address it was loading and the referring page, the request method and protocol, the stage at which it failed and the type of error, the status code, the server address and how long it took. Cloudflare states that it derives the network, country and metro area from the IP address the report comes from, keeps that address in memory only while it processes the report, does not log it, and does not share reports with third parties (<nel>Network Error Logging</nel>, read {date}; what the headers mean is set out in the <spec>W3C specification</spec>). The site's own code neither sets these headers nor receives or reads the reports.
privacy_page.gamesBody: The daily puzzles in /dev/fun and the arcade games' daily runs in /arcade have a public scoreboard. When you finish a daily puzzle on its own day, your browser sends the round to the site's server, unless you have switched "Share my results on the public board" off (in each daily game and on the scores page; the choice is kept in this browser). Practice rounds, earlier puzzles and rounds of any other day are never sent. What is sent is the part of the game's own saved round that the server needs to check it against the day's puzzle (the board, the answers or the picks, and the clock), your initials if you gave them, and a random number made for that one submission, which lets your browser change that round's initials on the same day and does nothing else. With the first round your browser publishes on a puzzle day it also sends one yes or no saying so, and with every later round that day a no. To know which round is the first, your browser keeps the day of its last published round (ronutz:fun:posted-day), written only after the server has stored the round; that day is never sent and never moves to another browser.
privacy_page.gamesStored: For each round the server stores the game, the puzzle's day, the mode, whether it was solved, the score it works out itself and the parts the game shows (such as checks, hints or wrong answers), your initials (three characters, or ??? when none were given), the country Cloudflare attaches to the request (two letters, or nothing), that random number, and the date it arrived, in UTC. It never stores your IP address, your browser's user agent or any other request header, a cookie, an account, any identifier of your browser or device, or any time finer than the day. Because nothing links one round to another, the board cannot recognize anyone from one day to the next, and it counts no streaks. The code is public: <scores>worker/scores.ts</scores> stores and reads the rounds, <verify>src/lib/fun/verify.ts</verify> checks them, and <schema>migrations/0001_fun_scores.sql</schema> defines the table. The server also stores that yes or no on the round, and only on a round it stores for the first time. It is the same for the first round of the day from any browser, so it does not say which browser sent a round and links no round to another. Adding up, day by day, the rounds marked yes gives how many browsers published at least one round: the unique browsers shown on the scores page (/dev/fun/scores) and the Stats page (/stats). They are browsers, not people: a phone and a laptop count as two, and a private window or cleared site data counts again. Each day's sum is also kept in the site's daily totals for 760 days, so the count outlasts the rounds' 400 days; migrations/0004_fun_first_today.sql adds the column.
privacy_page.gamesKept: Rounds are kept in a Cloudflare D1 database for 400 days from the day they arrived, then deleted; the deletion runs as new rounds are written. The boards are public: anyone can read a day's players, average, median, histogram and top ten (initials, country and score), and the countries with at least three rounds.
privacy_page.gamesRemoval: To have a round removed, use the <contact>contact page</contact> and give its game, its day and the initials it was posted with; with no identifier, that is the only way to find it, and a round posted as ??? may not be told apart from others of the same day. Your record in this browser is not affected either way, and switching sharing off stops any further round being sent.
privacy_page.interestTitle: Interest counts, only with your yes
privacy_page.interestBody: The site asks whether it may count what you use, and counts nothing of the kind unless you say yes. With a yes, your browser sends the site's own server a short note when you work with a tool (the first time you type or press a button in it on a visit to its page), start or finish a game, read an article or a glossary entry to its end after at least twenty seconds on the page, use Share, save an item to My desk, follow a link to Red Education, or run a search. Each note names what kind of thing was done, the part of the site, the item (a tool's or an article's name as its address spells it), the page's language and, for two kinds, one fixed word: for a game, won or lost; for a share, whether the address was copied, the system's share sheet was used or a tool's results were shared. A search's note says whether the search found anything, and a followed link's note names, in place of an item, the kind of page the link was on.
privacy_page.interestWords: One kind of note can carry words you typed. A search that found nothing, with no filter narrowing it, sends its words, because those words are the list of what the site lacks. They are sent only when they are a few plain words: at most four words and forty characters, no more than four digits in all, nothing but letters, digits and a few signs, and no word with more than one dot or more than one slash. A search that does not fit is counted as an empty search with no words at all; that is how an email address, an IP address, a web address written with its scheme, a path or a subdomain, a long number, a key or a sentence is left out. The same check runs in your browser before sending and at the server before anything is kept. The words are never published: the public figures count searches and do not list them.
privacy_page.interestNever: The site's own code sends a note with credentials left out, so no cookie travels with it. A note carries no identifier of any kind, nothing typed into a tool, no address of the page beyond the item's name, and no country or device. The server reads the same request headers it reads to tell a person from a crawler, drops a note that comes from automation, and keeps none of those headers; it never writes your IP address or your browser's user agent. The notes go into a third record, apart from the two described under the request counts, with nothing in common that would let one be matched to another. Like every request that reaches the site's Worker, the one that carries a note may be recorded in Cloudflare's Workers Logs, as Hosting and server logs describes below: its address is the same for every note (/api/e) and has no query string, and the note itself travels in the body of the request. The code is public: <shape>the rules for what a note may hold</shape>, <client>the page's side</client>, <events>the server's side</events> and <check>the check that runs at every build</check> to hold the code to this section.
privacy_page.interestKept: The notes are kept in Cloudflare's Workers Analytics Engine for three months, like the request counts. Once a day the server adds the previous day up and keeps the totals in the site's database: pages served to people per address, the interest counts per kind and item (the kept words of empty searches among them), and a few whole-site figures. Those daily totals are sums; they describe the site's pages and never a visit. They are kept for 760 days, about 25 months, and then deleted.
privacy_page.interestChoice: The choice is yours and can be changed at any time on the <settings>Settings page</settings>; it is one value in your browser's storage, like the other preferences. If your browser sends Global Privacy Control or Do Not Track, the site takes that as a no: it does not ask, and it sends nothing even if a yes was stored earlier. This counting rests on your consent (GDPR Article 6(1)(a); LGPD Article 7, I), and withdrawing it is the same switch.
privacy_page.deskBody: My desk (/desk) is a page of your own: the items you save, the ones you mark as read or done, your reading paths, the page's layout and settings, and the notes you write. It exists only because you use it: nothing is kept before you save, mark or arrange something. All of it stays in this browser's local storage under one key, ronutz:desk:v1, as the names of the site's pages (such as learn:acme-protocol) with the day of each mark, never titles and never a time finer than a day; to show titles, the page loads a list of the site's items, a file on this site, and sends nothing with that request. Nothing on the desk reaches this site, with two exceptions you control: saving an item sends one interest count, only if you said yes to the interest counts (see Interest counts above); and the encrypted sync described below, only if you turn it on. On the Settings page, under Use this on another browser, you can take the desk, with the other things listed below, to another browser: by pairing with a QR code or a link, by typing the sync code, or without the server, as a file or as a link that carries it after the # (a part of an address your browser never sends). You can also empty it there.
privacy_page.deskSync: The sync is off until you make a sync code on the Settings page. The code is 20 random bytes made by your browser and shown to you as 32 letters and digits; the site never receives it. From it your browser derives two things: a name for your copy (the first half of a SHA-256 hash of the code, the Secure Hash Algorithm, which cannot be turned back into the code) and an encryption key, made from the code, that never leaves the browser. Your browser gathers the desk and the other things that move with it (listed below), compresses them with gzip and encrypts them with that key, using AES-GCM (the Advanced Encryption Standard in Galois/Counter Mode) with a 256-bit key, and the site's own code sends the server only the copy's name and the encrypted copy, with credentials left out, so no cookie travels with them. Notes are left out unless you tick Include notes. On another device the same code finds the copy, and that browser decrypts it and merges it with its own: saved items and read marks are combined (a removal wins only when it is the later), and for each path, and for the layout and settings, the newer version is kept. Without the code nobody, this site included, can read the copy, and a lost code cannot be recovered. The pairing QR code and link on the Settings page carry the code after the # of the address, which a browser never sends; whoever has them can read and change the synced copy, so show them only to your own devices. Your browser keeps the last synced copy, and the time of that sync to the minute, in its own storage (ronutz:portable:base), so the next sync can tell a change made here from one made elsewhere; the time is never sent.
privacy_page.deskSyncKept: The copy is kept in the site's one database, Cloudflare D1, as one row that holds only the copy's name, the encrypted copy, its version number, its size, the day it was last read or written, the day of the latest write and the number of writes on that day. There is no IP address, no user agent and no cookie in it and no time finer than a day, and the site's own code writes no log of it. A copy may be at most 98,304 bytes (a request at most 140,000 bytes), one copy accepts at most 300 writes a day (UTC), and only pages of this site may send one. The daily clean-up deletes a copy that has been neither read nor written for more than 365 days; Delete the copy on the server, on the Settings page, deletes it at once, and Stop syncing this browser forgets the code in this browser only. Like every request that reaches the site's Worker, a sync request may be recorded in Cloudflare's Workers Logs (see Hosting and server logs below): its address carries the copy's name, and the encrypted copy travels in the request's body. When the database is not available the server says so (sync is not available right now), and the desk keeps working in your browser.
privacy_page.deskSyncSource: The code is public: the server's side, the table, the browser's side, the encryption and the check run at every build.
privacy_page.deskPortable: What moves to another browser, and what stays. By sync, file or link these move: My desk (ronutz:desk:v1; its notes only if you include them, and never the sync code kept in it); the games' results, streaks, best scores, settings and progress (ronutz:fun:v1, without the public scoreboard choices, which stay with each browser); the last pages you opened (ronutz:recent:v1); the subnet drill's score (ronutz:subnet-drill:stats); and your settings: the theme (ronutz-theme), the language (ronutz-lang), glossary hints (ronutz-glossary-hints), the motion switch (ronutz-mb-motion), rebound shortcuts (ronutz-shortcuts), and the density and reading choices of index pages (ronutz:view:*, ronutz:hub:*). When two browsers differ, records are combined (results and marks from both sides, the longer streak and the better score), and for a setting changed in both browsers between two syncs, the latest change wins: to tell which came last, each browser notes the minute each of your settings last changed (ronutz:portable:times), kept in that browser and sent only inside the encrypted copy, which only your own browsers can read, never the server. On the Settings page you can choose instead to keep the value of the browser in use and record no change times (a choice kept as ronutz:portable:no-times); the stored times are then deleted, and an older copy without times is merged the same way. A browser that pairs takes the other browser's settings, except those it changed more recently itself. These never move: your answer to the interest counts (ronutz:interest:v1), because a consent belongs to the browser it was given in; how the search box opens (ronutz-search-fresh), a habit of one device; the last synced copy (ronutz:portable:base), which each browser needs for its own merging; and what is kept for one session only: the author's preview flag (ronutz.privPreview), the operator's key for the private dashboard (ronutz:intel:key) and a flag that stops a crashed page reloading itself twice (ronutz:crash-reload). The day your browser last published a scoreboard round (ronutz:fun:posted-day) never moves either: each browser counts once a day as itself. A check run at every build fails if the site's code stores anything under a name missing from these two lists.

about.role: Senior Technical Instructor at Red Education
about.lede: Network and security training, delivered by a professional who has spent half of a thirty-year career on the hands-on side - implementation and troubleshooting - and the other half studying, designing, and teaching resilient, secure network communications.

now.title: What I do
now.body: I deliver official, certified instructor-led training across security and networking platforms. There are hands-on labs on real systems, and for people who already know the fundamentals and came to practice, that is exactly the point: real environments to work in. For groups newer to a technology, the time goes first into building the foundations the topic rests on, so the hands-on work makes sense and people leave understanding why things behave the way they do, not just which buttons to press. Both are equally valuable, and the balance shifts with who is in the room. Teaching and technical enablement have been part of my work since the late 1990s, on a career that began on the implementation side in 1996.
now.teachesValue: Virtual and on-site instructor-led training, globally, in any time zone
now.permitsValue: German and Brazilian citizen: the European Union, and wherever either passport is accepted without a visa; a valid United States visa
now.offersValue: Executive-level technical advisory for mission-critical decisions, alongside official instructor-led training

platforms.body: Being an authorized instructor for these vendors means I can teach each one properly and compare them honestly.
platforms.f5: BIG-IP across the full instructor-led curriculum: LTM, DNS, Advanced WAF (ASM), APM, AFM, SSL Orchestrator, automation, and troubleshooting.
platforms.fortinet: Fortinet certified training across the NSE 4, 5 and 6 levels.
platforms.extreme: Extreme Networks switching, SD-WAN, and API and automation tracks, across installation, configuration, management, and troubleshooting.

path.title: The path here
path.intro: My career began on the vendor and implementation side in 1996 and widened from there into systems audits and design, technical and sales enablement - three decades in enterprise networking, two of them hands-on before I focused fully on training. That depth and range is the reason the training lands: I have built, broken, and fixed these systems in production.
path.cabletron: Network engineer and certified instructor. Non-Ethernet and Ethernet networks, campus networks, IP routing. Cabletron was then Cisco's largest reseller, through the OEM line that put Cisco IOS and Cisco routing inside its own hubs, and I was one of the experts for that line: I went out to customers with feature explanations and configuration examples drawn from the internal documentation CDs Cabletron periodically sent its offices. We called them the "Jeopardize" discs, after the stern warning on each one that distributing the CD or its confidential contents would seriously jeopardize one's job.
path.riverstone: Product support engineer and knowledge-base coordinator in California. Gigabit Ethernet, metropolitan area networks, IP routing, BGP. Third-level escalation, customer scenario recreation, and regression testing.
path.cisco: Network consulting engineer in Brasília, acting as the single point of contact for two of Brazil's federal customers: SERPRO, the government's data-processing agency, and ECT-Correios, the national postal service. Escalation and customer-satisfaction management.
path.enterasys: Network engineer and instructor. Enterprise networks, IP routing, user access control and NAC, IDS and IPS.
path.juniper: Channel support engineer and instructor for enterprise switches and firewalls. Technical sales enablement and Junos-SRX operations training.
path.implementation: Deploying and integrating security and network platforms for end customers, mostly under contracts held by resellers and occasionally direct. Juniper SSG, SRX, EX and Secure Access - the line that became MAG and then Pulse Secure - alongside Cisco ASA, Palo Alto Networks next-generation firewalls, and Extreme Networks Summit and BlackDiamond switches.
path.f5channel: Channel-facing sales and pre-sales engineering for F5, providing technical enablement, proof-of-concept execution, and partner training across distribution. Secondary work in the same years covered FireEye, McAfee, VMware, Ixia and Keysight, and Pulse Secure.
path.rededucation: Authorized training instructor delivering official certified courses across F5, Fortinet, Extreme Networks, and Netskope to organizations worldwide. Teaching has been part of the job since 1997, at every role since: internetworking at Cabletron, routing at Riverstone, switching and network access control at Enterasys, JUNOS at Juniper, and vendor enablement across the distribution years. What changed in 2020 is that it became the whole job - F5 courses as a fixed contractor to an authorized training centre in Brazil, widening in 2021 to Extreme Networks delivery on demand for authorized partners in Brazil and Poland, and settling at Red Education, contracted from 2021 and full-time from September 2023.
path.rededucationWhere: Full-time instruction · Red Education from 2021 (full-time September 2023)
path.ironport: Channel development and pre-sales technical consulting for IronPort's C-Series e-mail security appliances: late 2004 with IronPort's own São Paulo operation, then through 2005 with a Cisco and IronPort reseller, from RFPs and installation to customer support. IronPort was acquired by Cisco in 2007.
path.cylk2020: Solutions consulting and pre-sales through CYLK, the São Paulo security integrator, while full-time instruction with its sister company InLearn began: F5 application delivery and security, Palo Alto Networks firewalls, Fortinet, Tenable vulnerability management, CyberArk privileged access and Corvil network analytics, as proofs of concept, designs and customer training. All six hold a mark here, and each has its chapter in the career record.
path.implementationWhere: Implementation · via CYLK, TDec and direct engagements

origins.title: Where it started
origins.body: Before the formal career, there was the curiosity. Through the early 1990s I was importing and assembling computers, running and using bulletin board systems, and working across DOS, Unix, Linux, Netware, early Ethernet, X.25, and dial-up internet. By 1995 that hands-on work had become a first formal role building an electronic-data-interchange system. The thread from then to now is the same: take something genuinely complex, make it work, and make it make sense to someone else. Those have never been separate phases - the teaching started in 1997 and has run alongside every role since.

approach.title: How I teach
approach.body: I chose to specialize in training because it combines deep technical knowledge with the part of the work I enjoy most: explaining complex concepts simply. The strongest sessions connect each concept to the job the learner actually has to do, so the content has somewhere to land. Real-world examples, real labs, and a focus on understanding over memorization.
approach.short: I chose to specialize in training because it joins deep technical knowledge to the part of the work I enjoy most: explaining complex concepts simply.

advise.title: How I advise
advise.body: Thirty years of first-hand experience with decisions that carry business or mission consequences: which technology to adopt, what to enable, what to improve, and what the adoption will actually cost in practice rather than on the slide. What I bring to a board or a steering committee is a structured, methodical and independent analysis - the diagnosis, the options, the cautions, the risks, and what each one would take to carry out. Independent is the operative word: I hold authorized instructor status across four platforms and no sales quota on any of them, so the recommendation is not the product of a commission. The impact is for the business to tell, and I would rather be judged on that than on the deck.

why.title: Why ronutz exists
why.body: The tools I wanted while teaching did not exist in a form I could trust: calculators that compute instead of guessing, explanations that cite the vendor's own page, and a record of the industry I lived through that someone else can check. So I built them, in the open, from documentation read live, with nothing a reader types leaving the browser in the catalogue's tools; the two red room lookups that do query a registry say so before they ask, and ask only on the reader's word. The site began as the classroom's companion and grew into a workbench, a knowledge base and a record of the industry; it is free because the knowledge in it was never mine alone.
