teach.title: An instructor who built these systems before teaching them.
teach.lede: Most technical training is delivered by people who learned the material to teach it. This is the opposite: three decades of building, breaking, and fixing real networks and security systems, distilled into training that connects every concept to how it actually behaves in production.
teach.s1Title: Why this matters in a classroom
teach.s1Body: There is a difference between explaining how a feature is supposed to work and explaining why it behaves the way it does at three in the morning when something critical is down. The first comes from a manual. The second comes from having been there. Since 1996, the work was implementation: designing networks and standing them up, then troubleshooting them under pressure and being the person called to resolve the critical availability and security incidents that halt a business, for vendors and for some of the largest organizations in Brazil. That depth is what every student receives: an engineer who has lived inside these systems explaining how they truly work.
teach.s2Body: Deep technical knowledge is necessary but not sufficient. The rarer skill is translating it: taking something genuinely complex, web application firewalls, identity federation, traffic management, SD-WAN, and making it click for someone encountering it for the first time. Students consistently single out the real-world examples and the clear, structured didactics, the ability to put each concept in the context of the work they actually do. Teaching has been a thread through this entire career, present in nearly every role since 1997, and the full-time focus since 2020.
teach.s3Body: Technical skill is built by doing, so every course has hands-on labs on real systems, backed by managed lab environments where practice always has somewhere real to happen. For people who already know the fundamentals and came to get their hands on the technology, that is exactly what they are here for, and it is time well spent. For those newer to it, the time goes first into the foundations the labs rest on, so the hands-on work makes sense rather than being followed by rote. Both are equally valuable, and the balance simply shifts with the room. The format adapts to the audience: virtual instructor-led training delivered globally, in-person when that serves better, in English or Portuguese. Either way, people should leave with something real and useful in hand and a real understanding of why it works.
teach.s4Body: F5 DevCentral MVP for three consecutive years, in 2022, 2023, and 2024. F5 certifications held since 2015, and instructor authorization across F5, Extreme Networks, Fortinet and Netskope. Delivery is truly global, reaching Asia-Pacific including Australia, New Zealand, Singapore, the Philippines, India and Bangladesh, Europe including the United Kingdom, the Netherlands, Belgium, Germany, Poland, Switzerland and Norway, the Middle East and Africa including the United Arab Emirates and Ghana, Latin America including Brazil, Mexico and Colombia, and North America including Canada and the United States, through Red Education, a premier global authorized training centre for the main cybersecurity and enterprise networking vendors.

teach.heroBody: I began teaching alongside engineering work. The examples, the failure modes and the operational questions I bring into a course come from years spent designing, deploying and troubleshooting the systems being discussed, and you can inspect how I explain things, in hundreds of articles and tools, before you book anything.
teach.routesTitle: Who I teach, and where to start
teach.routesLede: Three kinds of reader arrive here with three different questions. Each has its own door.
teach.route1Title: I know which course I need
teach.route1Body: An engineer or administrator who has already picked the course. The catalogue lists every course I currently teach; each course page gives the duration, the prerequisites, an outline summary linked to the vendor's own, the certification it relates to or a plain note that it is not exam-specific, and the next course, with a request link that goes to Red Education.
teach.route2Title: I need to train a team
teach.route2Body: A manager with six, fifteen or forty engineers, mixed experience levels, a time zone and a date. A private class can be shaped around the group and run in your working hours; the two engagements Red Education published further down show what that looks like.
teach.route3Title: I know the capability we need, not the course
teach.route3Body: A new BIG-IP operations team, F5 administrators moving into WAF, a FortiGate team that keeps calling support, engineers moving to SASE. Start from the outcome; choosing the sequence is part of what I do.
teach.catalogueBody: These are the official courses I deliver today, by platform: the exact set, kept current, not a representative sample. When a course leaves my delivery portfolio it leaves this list; when one joins, it appears here.
teach.catalogueNote: Each course page links the vendor's own outline and shows the day it was last checked, with the courseware version where the vendor publishes one; the vendor remains the authoritative source for its own programme.
teach.redCatalogueTitle: Looking beyond my own teaching portfolio?
teach.redCatalogueBody: Red Education delivers a far broader catalogue across networking, cybersecurity, cloud and adjacent technologies through its global instructor community, and can assemble several instructors around one requirement. If the course you need is not on this page, it is very likely there.
teach.howLede: The official curriculum defines what the course must cover. My role is to connect it to the mechanisms underneath, the operational consequences, and the kinds of problems engineers meet when the system is actually running. Three principles do most of the work.
teach.how1Body: A feature is explained by what it does to the packets, the sessions and the state, not by the position of a checkbox, because the engineer who understands the mechanism can reason about a situation the slide never showed.
teach.how2Body: Hands-on labs are a core part of the technical courses I deliver, in the official lab environment provided for the curriculum. They are there to test understanding, not to imitate a recipe: the point is to see the system behave, break it, and explain what happened.
teach.how3Body: The same curriculum needs very different emphasis depending on who is sitting there. Experienced groups move quickly into application and troubleshooting; newer groups spend the first hours on the foundations the labs rest on. Questions from your own environment are welcome, and often the best part of the day.
teach.howPractitioner: Since 1996 the work was implementation: designing networks and standing them up, troubleshooting them under pressure, and being the person called when a critical availability or security incident halted a business, for vendors and for some of the largest organizations in Brazil. That is where the examples come from.
teach.liveTitle: Why live technical training still matters
teach.liveLede: Information is no longer scarce. Vendor documentation, self-paced courses, videos and AI can explain almost any feature on demand; they are excellent learning tools, I use them myself, and they have changed what live instruction has to contribute.
teach.liveBody: The value of a live instructor is somewhere else: noticing why someone has misunderstood a mechanism, asking the next question, changing the explanation, connecting one feature to the rest of the system, answering the question behind the question, and working through what happens when the clean example stops matching the real system. Explanations have become abundant; that raises the bar for what a classroom should add, and it is exactly where three decades of engineering practice matter.
teach.liveLadder: On this site the ladder is visible: read an article, explore a tool, work through a study guide, then sit in a course where the explanation adapts to you. Training is the step between understanding something yourself and applying senior judgement to a decision, which is what advisory is for.

colophon_page.title: How this was built
colophon_page.lede: Most websites do not explain themselves. This one does, because how it was made is part of what it is: a deliberate experiment in building well, with unusual collaborators, and a record worth keeping.
colophon_page.concordBody1: This site was designed and built through a protocol called CONCORD: a structured collaboration between one person and three different AI systems, each in a distinct role. It is a working method, with its own governance, its own decision record, and a single human accountable for every choice that shipped.
colophon_page.concordBody2: The premise is simple. Different AI models have different strengths, and a hard problem benefits from more than one perspective held in tension. So the work was divided by role, and one person sat at the centre, relaying between them, ratifying what was sound, and rejecting what was not.
colophon_page.concordBody3: CONCORD was not adopted from anywhere. It was designed by Rodolfo Nützmann for this project, out of a practical need: how to draw on several AI systems at once, each genuinely strong at something different, without surrendering the single thread of human accountability that real work requires. The answer was to give each system a defined seat, keep them from negotiating with one another, and route every exchange through one person who held the whole picture. That arrangement has an older name. The AI systems are agents: they act on direction and on someone else's behalf. PRIME is the principal: the party who actually decides, who exercises the judgment, and who carries both the consequences and the name.
colophon_page.concordBody4: It began informally, as a way of dividing the work, and hardened over the build into a named method: fixed seats, a single overriding rule that nothing ships without PRIME ratifying it, and a written record of why each choice was made. The name states the aim: concord, agreement reached on purpose through a process, not whatever an unsupervised tool happens to produce.
colophon_page.concordPrincipal: The leverage is the agents'. The accountability is the principal's, and it does not transfer.
colophon_page.mech1Gloss: Each seat puts forward options within its own remit.
colophon_page.mech2Gloss: PRIME carries proposals between seats; they never negotiate directly.
colophon_page.mech3Gloss: PRIME accepts what is sound and rejects what is not. Nothing ships otherwise.
colophon_page.mech4Gloss: A standing set of house rules bounds every output, in every seat.
colophon_page.mech5Gloss: A written decision log keeps the reasoning behind each choice.
colophon_page.mech6Gloss: Context, the house rules, and that log persist as files, carried from one session to the next, so the method outlives any single conversation.
colophon_page.rolePrimeBody: The principal, and the sole ratifier. Every decision, every line that shipped, passed through one human who held the full picture and bore final responsibility. The agents proposed; PRIME disposed.
colophon_page.roleAnvilBody: The chief engineer seat. Architecture, code, content structure, and the build itself, turned from intention into a working, tested, deployable site.
colophon_page.roleScoutBody: The strategy and positioning seat. The questions of what this is, who it is for, and how it should present itself to the world.
colophon_page.rolePrismBody: The design seat. The visual language, the typography, the colour, and the feel of the thing, shaped into a coherent system.
colophon_page.seatsModelNote: AI model versions as of June 2026; the engineering seat's as of November 2026.
colophon_page.principlesBody: A few principles held throughout, and they are visible if you know where to look.
colophon_page.p1Body: The catalogue's tools calculate answers locally and deterministically. They do not call a server with your input, and they do not approximate: what runs in your browser stays in your browser. The red room is the declared exception, a few tools whose job is to ask a live service, and they say so before you press Ask, Enter or Start. The oldest tools have a lineage: a bits-and-bytes calculator, an IP addressing calculator and a cabling pinout were already on nutzmann.net in 2004 and on ntz.com.br in 2013, and the Internet Archive still has them.
colophon_page.p2Body: The deterministic logic each catalogue tool runs is the whole of the tool. There is no hidden server step and no account, and none of the values you enter is reported anywhere; what the site counts is the request for each page, in aggregate, as the <privacy>Privacy page</privacy> sets out. Everything on the main floor runs in your browser.
colophon_page.p3Body: Every part of the codebase is commented and documented, not as an afterthought but as a standing rule. The build is meant to be legible, to its maintainer and to anyone who inherits it.
colophon_page.p4Title: Built to last and to travel
colophon_page.p4Body: The site is a static export: fast, cacheable, and rendered by no server at request time; a small Worker in front of the pages sends an address without a language to its English page and keeps the aggregate request count. It is structured for many languages from the ground up, so it can speak to a global audience without being rebuilt.
colophon_page.stackBody: For those who care about such things, the technical foundation, stated plainly.
colophon_page.stackFrameworkV: Next.js 15 and React 19, exported as a fully static site
colophon_page.stackI18nV: next-intl, with {count} locales and right-to-left support
colophon_page.stackDesignV: A skinnable, token-based theme engine; the default theme is Obsidian
colophon_page.stackTypeV: Inter for prose, JetBrains Mono for data and codes
colophon_page.stackEngineV: A deterministic compute layer that runs entirely in the browser
colophon_page.stackSearchV: Static, client-side full-text search; no search server
colophon_page.codeSynth: The code is 100% synthesized by Claude.
colophon_page.vibeBody1: It is a fair question, and worth answering plainly. Vibe coding is a term the AI researcher Andrej Karpathy coined in early 2025 for a way of building software where you describe what you want to a language model, accept what it writes without reading it closely, and steer by results rather than by the code itself. He framed it as giving in to the vibes and forgetting that the code even exists, and was clear that it suited quick, throwaway projects more than systems people depend on.
colophon_page.vibeBody2: By that definition, part of this site was built that way, and it is worth owning rather than hiding. The application's surface, the framework wiring, the components, the styling, the plumbing that holds the pages together, was produced quickly with an AI engineer and steered by outcome and by a fixed set of house rules, not typed out by hand line by line. For that layer, where a mistake is visible and easily corrected, speed was the point.
colophon_page.vibeBody3: The parts that matter most are held to a different standard. Everything that computes your data is verified, not vibed: each tool's core is checked against the published standard it implements, the relevant RFCs and specifications, and its output is confirmed against independent references before it ships. As a widely cited line from the programmer Simon Willison puts it, code you have reviewed, tested, and understood is not vibe coding at all. Karpathy himself now calls the disciplined version agentic engineering: keeping the leverage of AI without conceding the quality of the result. That is the line this project draws. Fast where speed is free, rigorous where it counts, and one human accountable for all of it.
colophon_page.closingBody: Building software with AI collaborators is new enough that the honest thing is to be transparent about it. Nothing here was published without a human deciding it should be. The AIs were instruments, capable ones, but instruments. The judgment, the accountability, and the name on the work are human.
colophon_page.standardsLede: Every tool here implements a published specification, not a guess. The decoders and calculators are built against the documents that define their formats, and pinned to the test vectors those documents publish, so each answer is checked against the source of truth rather than against itself.
colophon_page.specsBody: JSON Web Tokens follow RFC 7519, with signatures and algorithms in RFC 7515 and 7518; PKCE is RFC 7636; Base64 and its siblings are RFC 4648; UUIDs are RFC 9562 (which obsoleted RFC 4122 in 2024 and ships its own test vectors); HMAC is RFC 2104, over the SHA family standardized in FIPS 180-4 and FIPS 202; X.509 certificates are RFC 5280; IPv4 is RFC 791 and CIDR notation is RFC 4632; IPv6 addressing and its canonical text form are RFC 4291 and RFC 5952; and the cipher-suite decoder is driven by the official IANA TLS Cipher Suites registry, cross-referenced with the TLS 1.3 and 1.2 specifications (RFC 9846 and 5246), the registry-update rules that set the "Recommended" column (RFC 8447), and the RC4 prohibition (RFC 7465). Where a registry is the authority, its data is vendored directly rather than retyped.
colophon_page.vectorsBody: Each tool ships with a set of golden vectors: known inputs paired with known-correct outputs, taken from the relevant RFCs and standards bodies. They run on every build, so a refactor that quietly changes an answer fails the build instead of shipping.
colophon_page.owaspBody: The security tools are defined against OWASP's frameworks rather than assembled ad hoc. The cryptographic and TLS tools map onto the Cryptographic Failures and Security Misconfiguration areas of the OWASP Top 10 and the matching checks in the Application Security Verification Standard; the token tooling follows OWASP's guidance for inspecting and validating JWTs. OWASP's prevention cheat sheets also set hard rules for what gets built next: any XML or SAML handling added here is required to be hardened against XXE before it ships.
colophon_page.redblueBody: The same decode-and-explain that lets a red-teamer read a captured token lets a blue-teamer understand what their own stack is emitting. The platform deliberately sits on the analysis side of that line: it identifies, decodes, converts, and explains, and it stops short of forging, injecting, or defeating controls. That boundary is a design decision, not an oversight; these tools exist to teach and to diagnose, not to weaponize.
colophon_page.localBody: Every catalogue tool runs in the browser. It calls a pure function: given the same input it returns the same output, holds no state, and sends none of your input to a server. A value handed from one page to a tool travels after the # in the address, which browsers never put in a request. The red room's tools are the declared exception, live lookups and a speed test that name the service they use and send nothing until you press Ask, Enter or Start. The browser security policy every page carries lets scripts connect only to this site, and only the red room's tools may also reach the services they use: any host over HTTPS for the two registry lookups, which follow IANA's bootstrap files, the five named resolver hosts for the DNS-over-HTTPS lookup, the one Pwned Passwords host for the password check, and the one Cloudflare speed test host for the speed test; a build check fails if that changes. The site's own code sets no cookies and uses no third-party analytics. The <privacy>Privacy page</privacy> sets out in full its aggregate request counting and what Cloudflare adds as the host: request logs, a bot check that may set up to two cookies, and network error reports.
colophon_page.limitsBody1: This site runs as a single Cloudflare Worker serving static assets, and that platform has hard, published limits worth being honest about. A Worker version may carry at most 20,000 static files on the free plan and 100,000 on the paid plan (raised from 20,000 in September 2025, and only when deploying with Wrangler 4.34 or newer), with no single file over 25 MiB. Requests for static assets themselves are free and unlimited; only invocations of the Worker script, such as the API, are metered.
colophon_page.limitsBody2: Those numbers matter because this architecture multiplies content deliberately. Every rendered page ships as roughly three files: its HTML, the framework's navigation payload, and a search-index fragment, across all sixteen languages, and the English and Portuguese pages add machine-readable Markdown twins. In practice one tool costs about fifty files and a tool with its companion article about a hundred, so the current site stands at a little over eighteen thousand files. Under the paid ceiling that leaves room for hundreds more tools; the build is measured against these limits, and if the toolbox ever truly outgrows a single Worker, the expansion path is already mapped: splitting routes across additional Workers, each with its own allowance, and ultimately object storage with no count limit at all.
colophon_page.wordDef: 1. A note, traditionally at the end of a book, recording how it was made: who produced it, where, and with which tools and typefaces.
colophon_page.wordExt: 2. By modern extension, a page on a website that explains how the site was built. In other words: this page.
colophon_page.wordEty: From the Greek kolophōn, via Latin: summit, finishing touch.
colophon_page.fableNote: A note on Fable 5. It is the seat's intended engine, but only for a limited window on the current plan; after that it becomes pay-per-use, and the added cost means it will see little use here. In practice it also falls back to Claude Opus 4.8 for most of this work: ARSENAL's subject is network and application security, and the safeguards on Fable 5 route security-related requests to Opus 4.8, catching this content (sometimes as a false positive) because Fable 5 is currently gated from handling those subjects. So most of what stands here was built on Opus 4.8. As of November 2026, the seat runs on Claude Opus 5.5.
colophon_page.p5Body: Good ideas are adopted here wherever they come from: a reader's note, an outside review, a vendor's documentation, a standard, another site's habit worth having. Each one arrives with its source named, in the <changelog>changelog</changelog> entry that adopts it and in the page that carries it, so the trail from idea to origin is never lost. Two response headers say the same thing to anyone who reads headers: <clacks>X-Clacks-Overhead</clacks> carries <pratchett>Terry Pratchett</pratchett>'s name in the overhead, as thousands of sites have since 2015, and <collective>X-Collective</collective> states the method in six words. Resistance is futile; attribution is mandatory.

api.title: API
api.lede: The catalogue's tools run in your browser and keep your data on your device. Each one is also built to run as a small, deterministic HTTP API, the programmatic counterpart to the browser tools. That API is fully implemented and documented here, but this site does not serve it. The reference below is a specification browser, not a live endpoint.
api.privacyTitle: What this means for your data
api.privacyBody: By design, the API would receive only the input you send it, compute a result, and return it: stateless, logging no query values or request bodies. Since the API is not served here, nothing you enter on this page is sent anywhere; the try-it panels below only show you the request you would make.
api.engineTitle: The same engine as the browser
api.engineBody: Every endpoint runs the same pure function the in-browser tool runs, so the API and the browser return byte-identical results.
api.specBody: The full contract is published as OpenAPI 3.1. Download it, point your own tooling at it, or read the reference below.
api.authValue: None by design. The API is specified as a public, read-only interface. It is not currently served from this site (see below).
api.loadError: The specification could not be loaded.
api.tryItHint: This builds the exact request URL you would call, but sends nothing: the API is not served from this site.
api.swaggerLoadError: Swagger UI could not be loaded.
api.servedTitle: Why the API is documented but not served here
api.servedBody: Running a public API means paying for compute on every call, with a bill that grows with usage in ways a single maintainer cannot cap safely. This site is deliberately free and predictable to run, so it serves the browser tools (which compute on your own device, at no cost to the host) and keeps the API dormant rather than risk unbounded cost. The endpoints are real and the contract is stable; what is switched off is the hosted execution. If you need the API today, the engine is open and can be run yourself.
api.swaggerCaveat: This is the standard Swagger UI rendering of the specification. It is a documentation browser only: there are no "try it out" controls, because the API is not served from this site.
api.servedOnTitle: The API is served locally on this origin
api.servedOnBody: Local API processing is switched on. The same-origin Worker serves each endpoint using the in-house engines, returning the same deterministic, byte-identical results as the browser tools. It is stateless and logs no query values or request bodies. If you would rather keep everything on your own device, the browser tools remain the zero-egress default.
api.selfHostTitle: Self-hosting: turn the toolbox into your API
api.selfHostBody: Everything needed to consume these tools as an Application Programming Interface (API) ships in the open-source repository, and the path from download to serving is deliberately short. One: download the source - github.com/ronutz/arsenal, Apache-2.0 licensed. Two: switch the API on - open src/config/apiSurface.ts and flip the single API_PROCESSING switch from 0 to 1; that one value drives both the Worker that serves the endpoints and every API badge in this interface, so the two can never disagree. Three: compile and deploy - npm install, npm run build, and publish to your own Cloudflare Workers account with the adapter already wired into the repository. Four: call the endpoints documented in the reference below - now answered by your deployment, on your domain, under your control.
api.selfHostBody2: That is the whole design: self-hosting plus a flip of a switch makes this an API toolbox. The same deterministic engines that power these pages answer the endpoints - tools that compute, never guess - and the switch works in both directions: set API_PROCESSING back to 0, redeploy, and the surface returns to documented-but-not-served, endpoints answering 404, badges neutral.

contributeIdeas.title: Share an idea
contributeIdeas.lede: ronutz is built to grow, and the clearest signal for where it should go comes from the people using it. Found a bug, a mistake, or an inaccuracy? Want a tool that isn't here yet? See a better way to handle something, or a result you'd word differently? Send it, every kind of input is welcome.
contributeIdeas.sendBody: Bugs, mistakes, and inaccuracies of any kind: a tool that misbehaves, a wrong result, an error in a Learn article, or anything that simply looks off. Feature requests for tools that already exist. Ideas for new tools the toolbox should have. Corrections and additions to the Learn articles, like a clearer explanation, a better source, or a topic that is missing. Or simply a different angle on a problem. Rough is fine; a sentence is enough to start a conversation.
contributeIdeas.toolTitle: If you're proposing a new tool
contributeIdeas.toolBody: Tools here are small, self-describing modules: a manifest that says what the tool is and where its correctness comes from, one pure function that does the work, and a set of golden vectors, the fixed input-and-output pairs that prove it. A good fit computes locally and deterministically (the same input always yields the same output, with no clock, network, or randomness in the result), keeps anything sensitive on the device, and pins its correctness to a cited source such as an RFC rather than to opinion. You don't need to build any of that to propose one: just describe what it should compute, an example, and the source it rests on.
contributeIdeas.fitRule: One test decides which floor a tool belongs on. The main floor holds tools a computer can work out just from what you type, by following a fixed, published rule, entirely in your browser. The green room takes tools that run the same way but whose form is still settling. The red room is for the rare tool whose whole job is to ask a live service, a domain registry for example: it names the official service on screen and sends nothing until you press Ask, Enter or Start. Anything that needs to sign you in or remember you fits none of them.
contributeIdeas.fitYesBody: decoding or explaining something you paste in (a token, a certificate, a config, command output), converting between formats, calculating from a standard or formula, or generating from a rule, like a UUID, a hash, or a command line.
contributeIdeas.fitNoBody: anything that needs an account, a login, or saved data; anything that probes or scans a system that is not yours; or anything whose answer is not fixed by a published standard. A live lookup (querying a live DNS server, asking a registry who holds a domain) does not fit the main floor, but may fit the red room, under its rules.
contributeIdeas.fitUnsure: Not sure which side your idea falls on? Send it anyway and say what it should do. I will tell you honestly whether it fits, and why.
contributeIdeas.emailBody: Email is the channel. Tell me what you found or what you'd like, with enough detail to act on: an example, a link, the exact wording, whatever fits. If it makes the site better, it gets built.
contributeIdeas.roadmapCheck: It's worth checking the roadmap first, to see what's already planned or shipped and avoid duplicates:
contributeIdeas.disclaimerIntro: In the interest of total honesty: these tools are built with CONCORD, my AI-assisted build process, and it runs on real, recurring costs. Three paid AI subscriptions carry it, one for each working seat.
contributeIdeas.disclaimerSeatAnvil: ANVIL, the engineering seat, runs on Claude from Anthropic, and this is the load-bearing one: it does the actual building, so it has to sit on one of Claude's Max tiers for there to be enough capacity to design, write, and test new tools at all.
contributeIdeas.disclaimerSeatScout: SCOUT, the strategy and brand seat, runs on ChatGPT Plus from OpenAI.
contributeIdeas.disclaimerSeatPrism: PRISM, the design seat, runs on Google AI Pro.
contributeIdeas.disclaimerInfra: On top of the three seats, a Cloudflare Workers plan keeps the site served, and the domains renew once a year for a fee of their own.
contributeIdeas.disclaimerTotal: All in, it comes to roughly USD 150 to USD 250 a month, depending mostly on which Claude tier the engineering seat is running that month.
contributeIdeas.disclaimerCadence: When the tooling is funded, tools get built. When it is not, building simply pauses until it is, which is why new tools tend to arrive in bursts rather than on a fixed schedule. You can read how the seats work, and who sits in each, on <colophon>the colophon</colophon>.
contributeIdeas.disclaimerBody2: If you would like to help it along, <coffee>buy me a coffee</coffee>. Every contribution goes into a single reserve spent on nothing but keeping that toolchain running: the three subscriptions, the hosting, and the domains. No cut, no surprises.
contributeIdeas.disclaimerStatus: Right now: the tooling is funded and new tools are actively being built.

license_page.lede: ronutz.com is open source. Its code is licensed under the Apache License 2.0, and its written content under Creative Commons Attribution 4.0 (CC BY 4.0). You may use, modify, and redistribute both, including commercially, provided you give appropriate credit to Rodolfo Nützmann (ronutz.com), link to the licence, and indicate any changes. ronutz.com remains the canonical, maintained source.
license_page.materialsHeading: Open course materials: the CC0 exception
license_page.materialsBody: The course materials offered under Open materials (the editable deck with its speaker notes, as PPTX) are released under the licence each datasheet states, and the datasheet governs its own files whatever the site-wide badges in the footer say. Where that licence is CC0 1.0, the material is dedicated to the public domain: copy it, adapt it, translate it and teach from it, commercially or not, with no attribution required. Credit is appreciated, never required.
license_page.thirdBody: This site stands on open-source work. The site itself is built with Next.js and React and shipped as a static export; internationalization uses next-intl; the Learn content is rendered with next-mdx-remote, gray-matter, remark-gfm, and js-yaml; the HTML structure explainer parses with parse5 (and its dependency entities, BSD-2-Clause); search is powered by Pagefind; and the red room's speed test runs Cloudflare's measurement engine, @cloudflare/speedtest. These are provided under the MIT License, except next-mdx-remote (Mozilla Public License 2.0) and entities (BSD-2-Clause). The API reference embeds Swagger UI, under the Apache License 2.0. Each component stays under its own licence, and the full notices ship alongside the source.
license_page.sourceBody: The full source is on GitHub. Issues and pull requests are welcome; ronutz.com remains the canonical, maintained deployment.

languageStatus.title: Translation status
languageStatus.explainBody: English is the source: written with AI in International English (en-001), with Oxford spelling (British spelling with -ize, as ISO and the United Nations write it) and dates and numbers in a form readers everywhere know. Brazilian Portuguese is written with AI too and reviewed gradually, and so are the interface and the tools in Spanish, German, French and Italian; the rest of the Spanish, German, French and Italian sites is machine-translated. Other languages join the list once their interface, tools and games are written in them. Each language is marked by how far along it is: blue once it covers the whole site, yellow while newer content is still in English and catching up. No language is reviewed by a person yet, so every one of them carries a short notice, English included, and you are welcome to help improve any of them.

roadmap.title: What's on the roadmap
roadmap.lede: The tools we're planning and considering for the toolbox. This page is generated from the live build catalogue, so it's always current: a tool appears here the moment it's queued and moves into the shipped count the moment it ships. No dates, just direction and rough priority.
roadmap.intentTitle: Built for more than a browser tab
roadmap.intentIntro: The code behind this toolbox is already open source. Two directions build on that, both intentions rather than promises.
roadmap.intentApi: The tools already run behind a small, versioned internal API. Opening that up as a hosted service, so the same deterministic engines answer a request and not just fill a browser tab, is a direction rather than a dated plan.
roadmap.intentOpen: Each tool is a self-contained, documented module, and the source is public. A packaged self-host path, dropped straight into your own build and CI pipelines and running inside your own environment with nothing leaving it, is the direction that openness makes possible.
roadmap.intentClose: What makes them possible is that the tooling has been built from the ground up expecting them: deterministic cores, no hidden state, a clean API surface, machine-readable docs.
roadmap.ideaBody: Every tool here started the same way: someone needed a small, specific thing and could not find it at the worst possible moment, the digital cousin of being one console cable short at 2am with the maintenance window closing. If the one you are reaching for is not here yet, propose it. Worth a scroll through the list first, though, in case that exact adapter is already on my bench half-built.
roadmap.metaDescription: The tools planned and under consideration for the ronutz.com toolbox, generated from the live build catalogue.
roadmap.ceiling: Growth here has a measured ceiling, not a vague one. The hosting platform caps how many static files one Worker may carry, and this site's own arithmetic - roughly a hundred files per tool-and-article pack, across sixteen languages - is checked against that cap on every build. Today there is room for hundreds more tools, and the expansion path beyond a single Worker is already designed, so the roadmap below is constrained by judgment, not by hosting.

SASE adds the network itself, usually as a software-defined wide area network (SD-WAN). Every tool and article on them, gathered in one place.

access-points.metaDescription: A daily logic puzzle: place one wireless access point in every row, column and zone of an office floor, with no two touching. New floor every day.
access-points.title: Access Points
access-points.tagline: One per row, one per column, one per zone. Zero interference.
access-points.intro: The office needs wireless coverage and the budget stretches to exactly one access point per row, per column and per zone. Put two side by side and they shout over each other, so none may touch.
access-points.cardBlurb: Cover every zone of the floor with one access point each, none touching. A new floor every day.
access-points.checksUsed: {n, plural, one {# check (+{s} s)} other {# checks (+{s} s)}}
access-points.sizeLine: {n}×{n} floor · {level, select, gentle {gentle} medium {medium} tricky {tricky} other {hard}}
access-points.sayClash: Access point at row {r}, column {c} clashes with another one.
access-points.sayMarkedMany: {n, plural, one {# cell marked.} other {# cells marked.}}
access-points.sayChecked: {n, plural, =0 {Check: nothing wrong so far.} one {Check: # cell is wrong.} other {Check: # cells are wrong.}} {s} seconds added.

rules.goal: Place one wireless access point in every row, every column and every zone of the floor.
rules.one: Each row, each column and each zone (lettered A, B, C and so on, with walls between them) holds exactly one access point.
rules.touch: No two access points may touch, not even at a corner: they would interfere.
rules.tap: Tap a cell to cycle: empty, × (no access point here), access point. A quick double tap or a long press places an access point at once. With a mouse, drag across cells to mark them all with ×; on a touch screen a swipe scrolls the page and marks nothing.
rules.keys: Keyboard: arrow keys move, Space or Enter cycles, A places an access point, X marks, Backspace empties.
rules.check: Your time is your score. Check marks the wrong cells and adds {s} seconds each time you use it.
rules.week: A new floor every day at 00:00 Coordinated Universal Time (UTC), the same for everyone, with exactly one solution that reasoning alone can reach. Monday is a gentle 6×6; the floors grow to 8×8 and ask for more reasoning towards the weekend.
rules.auto: The switch under the floor, off at first, marks every cell an access point rules out with a smaller red ×: its row, its column, its zone and the eight cells around it. Remove the access point and those marks go with it; your own × stay. Switching it on adds {s} seconds to your time, once per floor; switching it off again gives nothing back.

access-points.shareChecks: {n, plural, =0 {no checks} one {# check (+{s} s)} other {# checks (+{s} s)}}

hint.mistake: {n, plural, one {The highlighted cell does not fit the only answer: empty it before going on.} other {The # highlighted cells do not fit the only answer: empty them before going on.}}
hint.single: Only one cell of {kind, select, row {row {k}} column {column {k}} other {zone {zone}}} can still take an access point: row {r}, column {c}.
hint.confine: {ownerKind, select, row {Row {o}} column {Column {o}} other {Zone {oz}}} only has room for its access point in {keyKind, select, row {row {k}} column {column {k}} other {zone {kz}}}, so the rest of that {keyKind, select, row {row} column {column} other {zone}} can be marked ×.
hint.group: {ownerKind, select, row {Rows {owners}} column {Columns {owners}} other {Zones {owners}}} only have room for their access points in {keyKind, select, row {rows {keys}} column {columns {keys}} other {zones {keys}}}, so the rest of those {keyKind, select, row {rows} column {columns} other {zones}} can be marked ×.
hint.lookahead: An access point at row {r}, column {c} would leave {kind, select, row {row {k}} column {column {k}} other {zone {zone}}} with nowhere to put its own, so that cell can be marked ×.
hint.answer: No rule settles the next step from here, so this one comes straight from the answer: the cell at row {r}, column {c} holds an access point.

origins.p1: One piece in every row and every column, none threatening another: the oldest puzzle of this kind is the eight queens problem, which the German chess enthusiast Max Bezzel posed in 1848 under the pen name "Schachfreund". Franz Nauck put the number of solutions at 92; set rotations and reflections aside and 12 distinct ones remain.
origins.p2: Its closest relative is Star Battle, a Dutch puzzle style that Hans Eendebak created for the 2003 World Puzzle Championship in Arnhem: every row, column and region holds the same number of stars, and stars may not touch, not even diagonally. GM Puzzles notes that the idea likely arose from an earlier puzzle by Tim Peeters called Cattle. Krazydad's Star Battles have run in the print edition of The New York Times as Two Not Touch since 20 April 2020.
origins.p3: LinkedIn launched Queens on 1 May 2024 with two other daily games: one queen in each row, column and colour region, and no two touching. GM Puzzles calls it a simplified version of Star Battle, and Thomas Snyder provided its first puzzles. Access Points plays by the same rules, with access points in place of queens.

access-points.autoMarkPaid: Mark the cells each access point rules out (+{s} s already added)
access-points.autoMarkOnCost: Auto-mark on: {s} seconds added to your time, once for this floor.

bit-balance.metaDescription: A daily 6×6 logic puzzle of zeros and ones: three of each in every row and column, no run of three, and every equal or different sign obeyed.
bit-balance.title: Bit Balance
bit-balance.tagline: Three zeros, three ones, never three in a row.
bit-balance.intro: A six by six register that has to balance: every row and every column carries three 0s and three 1s, no bit repeats three times in a line, and the signs between cells tell you which neighbours match.
bit-balance.cardBlurb: Fill a 6×6 grid with bits: three of each per line, no runs of three, every sign obeyed. New grid every day.
bit-balance.checksUsed: {n, plural, one {# check (+{s} s)} other {# checks (+{s} s)}}
bit-balance.sizeLine: 6×6 grid · {level, select, gentle {gentle} medium {medium} tricky {tricky} other {hard}}
bit-balance.sayChecked: {n, plural, =0 {Check: nothing wrong so far.} one {Check: # cell is wrong.} other {Check: # cells are wrong.}} {s} seconds added.

rules.goal: Fill every cell with a 0 or a 1.
rules.balance: Each row and each column holds three 0s and three 1s.
rules.run: No more than two equal bits may sit next to each other, across or down.
rules.signs: A = between two cells means they hold the same bit; a × means they hold different bits. Given bits are fixed.
rules.tap: Tap a cell to cycle: empty, 0, 1. Keyboard: arrow keys move, 0 or 1 sets, Space or Enter cycles, Backspace empties. A broken rule shows at once, in red with a !.
rules.check: Your time is your score. Check marks the wrong bits and adds {s} seconds each time you use it.
rules.week: A new grid every day at 00:00 Coordinated Universal Time (UTC), the same for everyone, with exactly one solution. Early in the week the basic rules carry you through; towards the weekend there are fewer clues and you will need to try a bit and see what breaks.

bit-balance.shareChecks: {n, plural, =0 {no checks} one {# check (+{s} s)} other {# checks (+{s} s)}}

hint.mistake: {n, plural, one {The highlighted bit does not fit the only answer: empty it before going on.} other {The # highlighted bits do not fit the only answer: empty them before going on.}}
hint.sign: {sign, select, equal {An = sign ties the cell at row {r}, column {c} to the {b} next to it, so it is {b} too.} other {A × sign means the cell at row {r}, column {c} differs from the {b} next to it, so it is {w}.}}
hint.pair: Two {b}s sit side by side in {lk, select, row {row {li}} other {column {li}}}, so the cell next to them, row {r}, column {c}, must be {w}.
hint.gap: The cell at row {r}, column {c} sits between two {b}s in {lk, select, row {row {li}} other {column {li}}}, so it must be {w}.
hint.count: {lk, select, row {Row {li}} other {Column {li}}} already has three {b}s, so {n, plural, one {its last empty cell is} other {its # empty cells are}} {w}.
hint.trial: If the cell at row {r}, column {c} were {b}, the rules would soon break in {lk, select, row {row {li}} other {column {li}}}, so it must be {w}.
hint.answer: No rule settles a cell from here, so this one comes straight from the answer: the cell at row {r}, column {c} is {w}.

origins.p1: Balancing two symbols across a grid is a well-travelled puzzle family. PeterFrank, founded by Peter De Schepper and Frank Coussement, published its first Binairo in the summer of 2009 in Belgium's largest newspaper. Conceptis credits the Italian puzzle author Adolfo Zanellati with inventing the same concept, Tic-Tac-Logic, notes that PeterFrank invented a similar puzzle at the same time, and gives Takuzu as its name in the French publications Le Figaro and Ludojeux.
origins.p2: Classic Binairo asks for as many zeros as ones in every row and column, no more than two of the same number next to each other, and no two rows or columns with exactly the same content. Martin Kool's 0h h1, a little logic game by Q42, plays the same rules with coloured tiles.
origins.p3: LinkedIn introduced Tango on 7 October 2024: three suns and three moons in each row and column, an equals sign between cells that must hold the same symbol and an X between cells that must differ. GM Puzzles, which built it together with LinkedIn, says Binary and Binairo-type games were on the list of ideas it evolved from. Bit Balance follows Tango's rules, signs included, with 0s and 1s for suns and moons.

patch-path.metaDescription: A daily logic puzzle: run one patch cable across the panel from port 1 to the last port, through every cell once, reaching the ports in order.
patch-path.title: Patch Path
patch-path.tagline: One cable, every cell once, every port in order.
patch-path.intro: Somebody numbered the ports and left you one very long patch cable. Run it from port 1 to the last port through every cell of the panel, exactly once, plugging into the ports in order.
patch-path.cardBlurb: Run one cable through every cell of the panel, ports in order, around the cable ducts. New panel every day.
patch-path.checksUsed: {n, plural, one {# check (+{s} s)} other {# checks (+{s} s)}}
patch-path.sizeLine: {n}×{n} · {ports} ports{ducts, plural, =0 {} one { · # duct} other { · # ducts}} · {level, select, gentle {gentle} medium {medium} tricky {tricky} other {hard}}
patch-path.boardLabel: Patch panel, {n} by {n}. Next port: {next} of {ports}. Use the arrow keys to run the cable.
patch-path.progressDone: {k} of {total} cells covered · every port reached
patch-path.sayHead: Cable at row {r}, column {c}: {k} of {total} cells.
patch-path.sayChecked: {n, plural, =0 {Check: nothing wrong so far.} one {Check: # cell is off the route.} other {Check: # cells are off the route.}} {s} seconds added.

refuse.last: The last port has to be the final cell: cover every other cell first.
refuse.wall: A cable duct is in the way.
refuse.far: Pick a cell next to the end of the cable.
refuse.used: The cable already runs through that cell.

rules.goal: Run one cable from port 1 to the highest-numbered port.
rules.order: It passes through every cell exactly once, moving up, down, left or right, and reaches the ports in number order.
rules.ducts: Thick bars between cells are cable ducts: the cable cannot cross them.
rules.draw: Drag from port 1 to run the cable, and drag back over it to pull it back: a drag over any cell of the cable cuts it back to that cell, or, with Careful pull-back switched on under the panel, only along its last cells, so brushing an earlier stretch leaves it alone; press any cell of the cable to cut it there. You can also click the cells next to the end of the cable, one at a time. On a touch screen, a drag that starts on the end of the cable or on a cell beside it (or on port 1) draws, and the page does not move while it does; a swipe anywhere else scrolls the page, and a tap cuts or extends the cable.
rules.keys: Keyboard: focus the panel, then the arrow keys extend the cable (an arrow back along it pulls it back) and Backspace removes the last step.
rules.check: Your time is your score. Check marks where the cable leaves the route and adds {s} seconds each time you use it.
rules.week: A new panel every day at 00:00 Coordinated Universal Time (UTC), the same for everyone, with exactly one route. Monday is a 6×6 with plenty of ports; from Thursday the panel is 7×7, ducts turn up on some days, and the weekend panels have the fewest ports.

hint.start: The cable starts at port 1, in row {r}, column {c}.
hint.only: Only one way on is open from the end of the cable: {dir}, to row {r}, column {c}.
hint.forced: The cell at row {r}, column {c} can only be reached from here: if the cable went anywhere else, that cell would be left a dead end. Go {dir}.
hint.forcedPort: Port {p} can only be reached from here: if the cable went anywhere else, the port would be left a dead end. Go {dir}.

why.split: going {dirs} would cut the free cells in two

hint.ruledOut: {reasons}, so the cable goes {dir}, to row {r}, column {c}.
hint.answer: No rule settles this step quickly, so it comes straight from the answer: the cable goes {dir}, to row {r}, column {c}.

origins.p1: LinkedIn introduced Zip on 18 March 2025. GM Puzzles, which helps design and edit it, gives the rules: draw a path through all cells, moving horizontally or vertically between adjacent squares, never crossing itself or a wall, starting at 1, passing the other numbers in ascending order and ending at the highest. Patch Path keeps those rules, with ports for the numbers and one long cable for the path.
origins.p2: Nikoli's Numberlink is a cousin: it connects pairs of the same numbers with continuous lines instead of threading one numbered path.
origins.p3: Underneath is graph theory. A path that visits every cell exactly once is a Hamiltonian path, and the earliest example is the knight's tour in chess; the first known tour is believed to be the work of al-Adli ar-Rumi, a philosopher who lived in Baghdad in the ninth century.

mode.carefulOn: On: a drag pulls the cable back only along its last cells, so passing over an earlier stretch leaves it alone.
mode.carefulOff: Off (classic): dragging over any cell of the cable cuts it back to that cell.

phish-or-legit.metaDescription: A daily round of 15 links and email senders: phish or legit? Every answer names the tell, from homoglyphs and punycode to the userinfo trick.
phish-or-legit.title: Phish or Legit
phish-or-legit.tagline: Fifteen links. Two buttons. No clicking through.
phish-or-legit.intro: Judge each link or sender the way you would in your inbox, then see the tell: a Cyrillic letter, an xn-- name, a brand parked on someone else's domain. Every brand here is invented, and none of the addresses is a link.
phish-or-legit.cardBlurb: Fifteen links and senders a day. Spot the homoglyph before it spots you.
phish-or-legit.rule1: Each card shows a link as a preview or an address bar shows it, or an email's From line, with the brand it claims to be and that brand's real domain. Decide: Phish or Legit.
phish-or-legit.rule2: Press Phish or Legit, use the left and right arrow keys, or swipe the card left (phish) or right (legit). Every answer names the tell and explains it.
phish-or-legit.rule3: Daily: the same 15 cards for everyone on a day in Coordinated Universal Time (UTC). 100 points a right answer, up to 100 more for a run of right answers, and 10 or more right keeps your streak of days going.
phish-or-legit.rule4: Practice goes on as long as you like. The speed run gives you 60 seconds, and each wrong answer costs 3 of them.
phish-or-legit.rule5: Every real domain here ends in .example, a name set aside for documentation (Request for Comments 2606), so nothing on these cards points at anyone real.
phish-or-legit.inRow: {n, plural, one {# in a row} other {# in a row}}
phish-or-legit.keysHint: Keys: left arrow for phish, right arrow for legit, Enter for the next card. On a touch screen, swipe the card.
phish-or-legit.keysHintSpeed: Left arrow for phish, right arrow for legit, or swipe the card.
phish-or-legit.dailyDetail: {points, plural, one {{points} point} other {{points} points}}; best run {streak} in a row.
phish-or-legit.speedIntro: Cards come one after another with a one-line verdict and no pause; the full explanations wait for the end. A wrong answer costs 3 seconds.
phish-or-legit.speedDetail: {wrong} wrong, {points, plural, one {{points} point} other {{points} points}}.
phish-or-legit.shareSpeed: Phish or Legit speed run: {correct} right in 60 s

origins.p1: Merriam-Webster dates the first known use of phishing to 1996: a respelling of fishing, with the ph probably taken from phreaking, the fraud of dodging the bill for telephone calls. Koceilah Rekouche, who wrote AOHell, a mid-1990s hacking tool aimed at America Online (AOL), says in his own account that the word was coined there.
origins.p2: The look-alike letter has a paper of its own. In "The Homograph Attack" (Communications of the ACM, February 2002), Evgeniy Gabrilovich and Alex Gontmakher registered a homographed microsoft.com spelt with the Russian letters с and о. Internationalized domain names are written in the Domain Name System (DNS) as Punycode (RFC 3492, March 2003), each label marked by the ACE prefix xn-- (RFC 3490).
origins.p3: Jigsaw's Phishing Quiz is a well-known exercise of the same kind.

phish-or-legit.startNote: Press Start to see the first card. The clock counts only while a card waits for your answer; reading the explanation is free.
phish-or-legit.rule6: The daily round and practice are timed: the clock counts while a card waits for your answer and stops while you read the explanation, so the time measures deciding, not reading. The daily round starts with Start, and its time is kept with your answers.

log-detective.metaDescription: A new incident hidden in a web or SSH log every day: find the attacker, the first malicious request and the line where it worked.
log-detective.title: Log Detective
log-detective.tagline: Sixty lines of noise. One intruder.
log-detective.intro: Every day, a fresh excerpt from a web server's access log or a Secure Shell (SSH) server's authentication log. Most of it is ordinary traffic; somewhere in it, one address is up to no good. Read it the way an analyst would.
log-detective.cardBlurb: One incident a day, hidden in a log that looks like the real thing.
log-detective.rule1: Answer three questions: which address is the attacker, which line is its first malicious request, and on which line the attack succeeded (a sign-in that worked, a file, a table or a hidden page that came back, a command that ran).
log-detective.rule2: Pick the address from the list. For the two line questions, tap a line, or move through the log with the arrow keys, and confirm it. One try each; if you miss, the right answer is shown.
log-detective.rule3: Web lines are in the combined log format: client address, time, request, status, size, referrer, user agent. SSH lines are the messages sshd itself writes, in syslog form. Every address comes from the ranges set aside for documentation.
log-detective.rule4: The same case for everyone on a day in Coordinated Universal Time (UTC). Your score is your right answers and your time; two or more right keeps your streak of days going. Practice brings a new case whenever you like.

q.first: Which line is the attacker's first malicious request?
q.success: On which line did the attack succeed?

log-detective.pickLine: Tap a line in the log, then confirm it.
log-detective.listHint: In the log: up and down arrows move, Page Up and Page Down jump ten lines, Enter confirms.
log-detective.headline: {right} of 3 in {time}
log-detective.alreadyDone: You closed today's case earlier; a new one opens at 00:00 UTC.

cred-stuffing.name: Credential stuffing
cred-stuffing.what: {ip} sent {count} sign-in attempts to /login in a burst, each answered 401, until one was answered 302 on line {success}: a redirect into an account. That is leaked username and password pairs tried until one works. The attack began on line {first}.
cred-stuffing.log: Every sign-in, success and failure, with the account name and the address: the access log alone shows only the address and the status. The Open Worldwide Application Security Project (OWASP) Logging Cheat Sheet lists authentication successes and failures among the events to always log.
cred-stuffing.alert: Many failed sign-ins from one address in a short time, and above all a success right after them. Rate-limit the sign-in page and ask for a second factor.

ssh-brute.name: Secure Shell (SSH) brute force
ssh-brute.what: {ip} tried root and names that are not accounts at all (sshd logs Invalid user for those), {count} failed passwords in all, until Accepted password for {user} on line {success}. A service account with a guessable password was the way in. The attack began on line {first}.
ssh-brute.log: sshd at its default LogLevel, INFO, already records every failed and accepted sign-in with the address and port. Send those lines off the host, so an intruder who gets in cannot erase them.
ssh-brute.alert: An Accepted line from an address that has just failed many times, and any password sign-in to a service account. Better still: PasswordAuthentication no, and keys only.

traversal.name: Path traversal
traversal.what: {ip} first downloaded an ordinary file, then from line {first} put ../ sequences into the file parameter. {count} tries were refused before a percent-encoded one (%2e%2e%2f is ../) came back 200 on line {success}, carrying {path}.
traversal.log: The whole request line with its query string, as the combined format does, and the size of every answer: a 200 of the wrong size from a download page is the evidence.
traversal.alert: ../ in any parameter, plain or encoded, and above all one answered 200. The fix is in the code: map names to an allow list of files instead of joining paths.

dotfile.name: A probe for secrets
dotfile.what: From line {first}, {ip} asked for files that should never be public. {count} misses (404) came first, then {path} came back 200 on line {success}. A .env file holds keys and passwords; .git/config describes the repository and where it lives.
dotfile.log: The 404s as well as the 200s, with their paths: the misses are what show a probe for what it is.
dotfile.alert: Any 200 for a path that starts with a dot, other than /.well-known/. Better: deploy without dot-files, block them at the web server, and change every secret that was exposed.

sqli.name: SQL injection
sqli.what: {ip} viewed a product, then on line {first} added a quote and got a 500: the database query (SQL, Structured Query Language) broke. It tested true and false conditions, counted {count} columns, and on line {success} a UNION SELECT from the {path} table came back 200 at about fifty times the page's usual size.
sqli.log: Query strings and response sizes, and the application's database errors: the 500 after a single quote is the first sign.
sqli.alert: Quotes or SQL keywords in parameters, a run of 500s from one address, and an answer far larger than that page ever sends. The fix is parameterized queries.

webshell.name: A web shell upload
webshell.what: {ip} opened the upload form like anyone else, but what it sent on line {first} was a script. On line {success} {path}?cmd=id answered 200: the server ran it, and {count} more commands followed.
webshell.log: Each upload with the stored file's name and type (the access log shows only POST /upload), and every request into the uploads folder.
webshell.alert: Any request for a script in a folder that should only hold pictures, and any parameter called cmd. Never let the uploads folder run code.

scan-admin.name: A scan that finds a panel
scan-admin.what: From line {first}, {ip} asked for {count} well-known admin and sign-in paths, every one a 404, until {path} answered 200 on line {success}; the very next request tried to sign in to it.
scan-admin.log: The 404s with their paths, counted per address: one address with many misses in a minute is a scanner.
scan-admin.alert: Many 404s from one address, then a 200 on an admin path from that same address. Keep admin panels off the public internet, behind a virtual private network (VPN) or an allow list of addresses.

log-detective.alreadyDoneEarlier: You already closed this day's case.

origins.p1: In August 1986 a persistent intruder attacked the computers of Lawrence Berkeley Laboratory (LBL), and Clifford Stoll set out to trace him. Stoll later told C-SPAN that it began with accounts just seventy-five cents off, traced to someone who had used about nine seconds of computer time without paying.
origins.p2: He wrote the hunt up as "Stalking the Wily Hacker" in Communications of the ACM in May 1988 and told the whole story in The Cuckoo's Egg (Doubleday, 1989).
origins.p3: The web server excerpts follow the Apache HTTP Server's Combined Log Format, which Apache's documentation describes as exactly the Common Log Format with two more fields, the Referer and the User-agent. Spotting one figure in a crowd of ordinary ones is also the game of Martin Handford's Where's Wally?, whose first book reached the UK in 1987.

prefix-of-the-day.metaDescription: A daily subnetting puzzle: one IPv4 address and prefix length, six tries to find its network, broadcast, mask and usable hosts. A new puzzle at 00:00 UTC.
prefix-of-the-day.title: Prefix of the Day
prefix-of-the-day.tagline: One address, one prefix, six tries.
prefix-of-the-day.intro: Every day at 00:00 UTC (Coordinated Universal Time) there is a new IPv4 (Internet Protocol version 4) address with its prefix length, the same for everyone. Find the network address, the broadcast address, the subnet mask and the usable hosts; the arrows tell you which way to go.
prefix-of-the-day.cardBlurb: The daily subnetting puzzle: network, broadcast, mask and hosts in six tries.
prefix-of-the-day.rule1: Each try fills in four facts about the block the address belongs to: its network address, its broadcast address, the subnet mask (dotted, such as 255.255.240.0, or as a prefix length, /20 or just 20) and the number of usable hosts.
prefix-of-the-day.rule2: After a try every field is marked: a tick when it is right, an up arrow when the answer is higher than what you typed, a down arrow when it is lower. Addresses and masks are compared as 32-bit numbers. You have six tries.
prefix-of-the-day.rule3: The week gets harder: Monday stays on octet boundaries such as /24 and /16, Sunday sits in the middle of an octet, and the weekend brings the odd /31 or /32.
prefix-of-the-day.rule4: A /31 is a point-to-point link with two usable addresses (RFC 3021, where RFC stands for Request for Comments) and a /32 is a single host. Neither has a broadcast address, so type the last address of the block there (for a /32, the address itself), as the CIDR (Classless Inter-Domain Routing) calculator shows it.
prefix-of-the-day.rule5: The daily puzzle counts for your streak. Practise below as long as you like; it does not count.
prefix-of-the-day.tier2: Tuesday, easy: a bit or two past an octet
prefix-of-the-day.tier4: Thursday, medium: deeper inside the octet
prefix-of-the-day.tier5: Friday, tricky: short and long prefixes
prefix-of-the-day.tier6: Saturday, hard: odd boundaries, the odd /31

prefix-of-the-day.errMask: Subnet mask: type a dotted mask whose ones are contiguous, such as 255.255.240.0, or a prefix length from 0 to 32, such as /20.
prefix-of-the-day.errHosts: Usable hosts: type a whole number.

prefix-of-the-day.whyNone: The prefix ends just before octet {octet} ({value}, {binary} in binary): all its bits are host bits, so the network address has 0 from there on and the broadcast address 255.
prefix-of-the-day.whyAll: A /32 keeps all 32 bits: octet 4 ({binary}) belongs to the network too, so the block is this one address.

origins.p1: The daily format comes from Wordle. Josh Wardle limited players to one game per day and released it to the rest of the world in October 2021; players have six tries, and The New York Times bought the game in January 2022.
origins.p2: The arithmetic is Classless Inter-Domain Routing (CIDR), set out in September 1993 in RFC 1519, "an Address Assignment and Aggregation Strategy" by V. Fuller, T. Li, J. Yu and K. Varadhan. RFC 4632 replaced it in August 2006 and writes the legacy "Class C" network 192.168.99.0 as the prefix 192.168.99.0/24, the address-and-length notation of each day's puzzle.

aggregate.metaDescription: Slide IPv4 prefixes together and summarize them: two tiles merge only when they are siblings. A daily challenge and endless free play.
aggregate.title: Aggregate
aggregate.intro: A sliding-tile game about route summarization. Every tile is a real IPv4 (Internet Protocol version 4) prefix inside one private /16. Slide them together: two blocks of the same length merge into their parent only when they sit side by side and aligned. Equal length is not enough.
aggregate.cardBlurb: Slide prefixes together; only true siblings summarize. How large a block can you build?
aggregate.rule1: Use the arrow keys, swipe on the board, or press the arrows below it: every tile slides as far as it can that way.
aggregate.rule2: Two tiles that meet merge only when they are siblings: the same length, next to each other in the address space and aligned, so together they are exactly their parent. 10.0.0.0/26 and 10.0.0.64/26 make 10.0.0.0/25; 10.0.0.64/26 and 10.0.0.128/26 do not, because no /25 starts at .64.
aggregate.rule3: A tile made by a merge waits for the next move before it merges again, and the tiles nearest the wall go first. After every move that changes the board, a new /26 or /27 appears.
aggregate.rule4: Each merge scores the size of the block it makes (a /25 is 128 addresses). Build a /24, then a /23, then a /22. The round ends when no move changes the board.
aggregate.rule5: The daily challenge drops the same tiles for everyone who plays the same moves that UTC (Coordinated Universal Time) day. Its first finished round counts for your streak; replay it as often as you like to raise your best score. Free play deals new tiles every round, and a reload picks it up where you left it.
aggregate.boardLabel: Board of prefixes. Use the arrow keys to slide the tiles.
aggregate.boardHelp: Use the arrow keys while the board is on screen; on a touch screen, swipe on it.
aggregate.overDetail: Score {score} in {moves, plural, one {# move} other {# moves}}.
aggregate.replayNote: Today's challenge is already counted; replays can only raise your best score.

aggregate.livePairs: {n, plural, =0 {No sibling pairs on the board right now.} one {One sibling pair, numbered 1 on both its tiles.} other {# sibling pairs, each numbered on both its tiles and ringed in its own pattern.}}
aggregate.replayNoteEarlier: This challenge was already played; replays of an earlier puzzle count towards no score.

origins.p1: The movement is the one from 2048, which Gabriele Cirulli released in March 2014: the tiles slide together, and when two tiles with the same number touch, they merge into one. His page credits 1024 by Veewo Studio and calls 2048 conceptually similar to Threes by Asher Vollmer, the iOS puzzle he made with Greg Wohlwend, which made its debut on 6 February 2014.
origins.p2: The rule that only siblings merge is route aggregation. RFC 1519 showed it in 1993, describing a block of network numbers as one "supernetted" route, 192.24.0.0 with mask 255.248.0.0, and RFC 4632 describes a provider that advertises a single aggregate route for the larger block, with no explicit route needed for each end site.

five-clues.metaDescription: A daily IT category puzzle: up to five clues, the hardest first, and you name what links them. Fewer clues, better score.
five-clues.title: Five Clues
five-clues.tagline: What do they have in common?
five-clues.intro: Every day at 00:00 UTC (Coordinated Universal Time) there is a new hidden category from networking, security, systems or the web. The clues are members of it, revealed one at a time and hardest first; name the category with as few as you can.
five-clues.cardBlurb: Name the IT category behind up to five clues. The fewer you need, the better.
five-clues.rule1: The first clue is the hardest. Type what you think links the clues and press Guess; a wrong guess reveals the next clue.
five-clues.rule2: Answers are forgiving: case, accents and punctuation do not matter, one typo in a long answer is fine, and English or Portuguese both count. A guess that is only part of the answer, such as DNS (Domain Name System) for DNS record types, is marked close and costs nothing.
five-clues.rule3: Not sure? Next clue reveals one without a guess, but it counts as a clue used. Your score is the number of clues you needed, from 1 to 5. Each clue spent without the answer adds a nudge under the box: how many words the answer has, where its members are listed, then its shape with the first letter of each word.
five-clues.rule4: Every clue is checked against the document that lists it (an RFC, or Request for Comments; an IANA, or Internet Assigned Numbers Authority, registry; a manual page or a vendor's documentation), linked at the end. Practice below replays the last 30 days and a few warm-ups.
five-clues.noteEmpty: Type a guess, or press Next clue to see another one.
five-clues.noteClose: Close: {guess} is part of it. Be more specific; no clue used.
five-clues.won: {n, plural, one {Got it with # clue} other {Got it with # clues}}
five-clues.practiceIntro: Warm-ups: puzzles written for practice, never a daily one. The ones you have played are marked ✓ or ✗. Practice does not touch your streak; earlier daily puzzles are under Earlier puzzles, above.
five-clues.practiceBest: {n, plural, one {Best practice round: # clue} other {Best practice round: # clues}}
five-clues.statusPracticeLost: Played in practice, not solved yet

origins.p1: Naming a hidden link from clues revealed one at a time, with more points for fewer clues, is a round of Only Connect, the quiz that began on BBC Four on 15 September 2008 with Victoria Coren Mitchell as host: 5, 3, 2 or 1 points after the first, second, third or final clue.
origins.p2: Television played with categories long before that. The $10,000 Pyramid began in 1973, hosted initially by Dick Clark; in its bonus round, the Winner's Circle, one player describes six categories to a partner within 60 seconds by listing things that belong to them.
origins.p3: The New York Times turned grouping into a daily game with Connections, which launched in beta in June 2023: 16 words to sort into four groups.

first-match.metaDescription: Order Cisco IOS access-list entries, then send a wave of packets through them: the first match decides, the implicit deny catches the rest. Twenty levels and a daily level.
first-match.title: First Match
first-match.tagline: The first entry that matches decides. Nothing below it gets a say.
first-match.intro: An access control list (ACL) on a Cisco router is read from the top, one entry at a time, and the first entry a packet matches permits or denies it; a packet that matches nothing meets the implicit deny at the end. Read the policy, pick the entries that implement it, put them in the right order and send the traffic.
first-match.cardBlurb: Order access-list entries against a wave of packets. Twenty levels, a daily level, and the implicit deny always waiting at the bottom.

rules.r1: Read the policy. Pick entries from the hand (each goes to the bottom of your list), then put them in order with the arrows.
rules.r2: Press Send traffic. Each packet is tested against your entries from the top: the first match permits or denies it, and nothing below is read. A packet that no entry matches is denied by the implicit deny.
rules.r3: Some cards are traps: too broad, the wrong port, the port on the wrong side of the address, a subnet mask where a wildcard belongs, or a deny that hides a permit. Packets are TCP (Transmission Control Protocol), UDP (User Datagram Protocol) or ICMP (Internet Control Message Protocol).
rules.r4: A level is passed when every packet gets the verdict the policy asks for. Fewer entries score more: par is the shortest list that works.
rules.r5: The daily level changes at 00:00 UTC (Coordinated Universal Time) and gives you six waves. Keys: Tab to an entry; the arrows move between entries, Shift with an arrow moves the entry, Delete removes it.
rules.r6: Stuck on a level? After {waves} waves, Hint shows one entry of a shortest list in its place, with the reason, for {cost} points off the level's score. The daily level has no hints.
