l01.title: The implicit deny
l01.policy: Web (HTTP, TCP 80) to the server 10.0.0.10 from anywhere. Nothing else.
l01.lesson: Every Cisco access list ends with an unwritten deny, so a list that only permits what the policy allows needs no deny at all.

l02.title: Port and host
l02.policy: Web (HTTP, TCP 80) and secure web (HTTPS, TCP 443) to 10.0.0.10 from anywhere. Nothing else.
l02.lesson: Leave out the port and an entry matches every TCP port; write any as the destination and it matches every server. Each field left out widens the entry.

l03.title: Order matters
l03.policy: Web (TCP 80) to 10.0.0.10 from anywhere, but the host 203.0.113.66 is banned from everything. Nothing else.
l03.lesson: After the first match no later entry is read, so the deny for one host must sit above the permit that would otherwise let it in.

l04.title: Shadowed
l04.policy: Secure Shell (SSH, TCP 22) to the jump host 10.0.0.20 only from the admin host 10.1.20.5. Web (TCP 80) to 10.0.0.10 from anywhere. Nothing else.
l04.lesson: A broad deny above a permit shadows it: the permit can never match. Specific entries go above general ones.

l05.title: Wildcards are not masks
l05.policy: SSH (TCP 22) to 10.0.0.20 from the network 10.1.20.0/24. Nothing else.
l05.lesson: In a wildcard a 0 bit must match and a 1 bit is ignored, so a /24 is 0.0.0.255. Write the subnet mask 255.255.255.0 instead and the entry matches any address that ends in .0.

l06.title: One host, one protocol
l06.policy: Domain Name System (DNS) over UDP port 53 to 10.0.0.53 from anywhere. Nothing else.
l06.lesson: host 10.0.0.53 is short for 10.0.0.53 0.0.0.0, exactly one address, and domain is Cisco's name for port 53. UDP 53 and TCP 53 need separate entries.

l07.title: The wrong side
l07.policy: Web (TCP 80) to 10.0.0.10 from anywhere. Nothing else.
l07.lesson: A port test belongs to the address it follows: after the source it tests the source port, after the destination the destination port. Anyone can send from port 80, so eq 80 after any lets them all in.

l08.title: gt and lt
l08.policy: TCP to 10.0.0.30 on any port above 1023, from the build network 10.1.30.0/24. Nothing else.
l08.lesson: gt 1023 means 1024 and up: gt and lt never include the port they name, while range includes both of its ends.

l09.title: Range
l09.policy: UDP ports 16384 to 32767 on the voice gateway 10.0.0.40, from the phone network 10.1.40.0/24. Nothing else.
l09.lesson: range is inclusive: range 16384 32767 matches both ends and every port between them, and nothing outside.

l10.title: Not equal
l10.policy: Every TCP port on the lab server 10.0.0.50 except Telnet (TCP 23), from the lab network 10.1.50.0/24. Nothing else.
l10.lesson: neq matches every port except the ones it names, so one entry does the work of a deny followed by a permit.

l11.title: Several ports, one entry
l11.policy: Mail to 10.0.0.25 from anywhere on TCP ports 25, 587 and 993. Nothing else. One entry can do it.
l11.lesson: In IOS XE an eq test takes up to 10 ports, so eq 25 587 993 is a single entry. A range would let in every port between.

l12.title: Blocks of eight
l12.policy: Web (TCP 80) and secure web (TCP 443) to the web farm 10.0.0.8 to 10.0.0.15, from anywhere. Nothing else.
l12.lesson: 10.0.0.8 0.0.0.7 is the block from .8 to .15: a wildcard of 7 covers eight addresses starting at a multiple of eight. 0.0.0.8 is another thing entirely: it ignores a single bit.

l13.title: Nested exceptions
l13.policy: Web (TCP 80) to 10.0.0.10 from anywhere, except the network 198.51.100.0/24, which is banned from everything; but its host 198.51.100.7, a partner, may use the web server. Nothing else.
l13.lesson: Exceptions stack from the narrowest: the partner's permit first, then the deny for its network, then the general permit.

l14.title: ICMP is not IP
l14.policy: The monitoring host 10.1.20.9 may send ICMP (Internet Control Message Protocol) messages, such as ping, to anything in 10.0.0.0/24. Web (TCP 80) to 10.0.0.10 from anywhere. Nothing else.
l14.lesson: The icmp keyword matches ICMP alone, while ip matches every protocol, TCP and UDP included.

l15.title: Established
l15.policy: The users on 10.1.60.0/24 browse out freely. On the way back in, let through only TCP replies: segments with acknowledgement (ACK) or reset (RST) set. Nothing else.
l15.lesson: established matches TCP segments with the ACK or RST bit set, so replies come back in, while an opening SYN (synchronize) from outside does not.

l16.title: The empty list
l16.policy: Migration night: every packet to 10.0.0.0/24 must get through. Fewest entries wins.
l16.lesson: A list with no entries has no implicit deny to reach: Cisco documents that an interface with an empty access list applied permits all traffic.

l17.title: Replies, the right way
l17.policy: Let TCP replies (ACK or RST set) back in to the users on 10.1.60.0/24, and SSH (TCP 22) to the jump host 10.0.0.20 from 10.1.20.0/24. Nothing else.
l17.lesson: gt 1023 lets in anyone who opens a connection to a high port; established admits only segments carrying ACK or RST, which no opening SYN does.

l18.title: Wildcards with gaps
l18.policy: SSH (TCP 22) to 10.0.0.20 from the admin hosts at .5 in four labs: 10.1.0.5, 10.1.1.5, 10.1.2.5 and 10.1.3.5. Nothing else. One entry can do it.
l18.lesson: Wildcard bits set to 1 need not be contiguous: 10.1.0.5 0.0.3.0 ignores two bits of the third octet and matches .5 in all four labs.

l19.title: Deny in the middle
l19.policy: Web and secure web (TCP 80 and 443) to 10.0.0.10 from anywhere except 203.0.113.0/24. SSH (TCP 22) to 10.0.0.20 from 10.1.20.0/24. DNS (UDP 53) to 10.0.0.53 from anywhere, 203.0.113.0/24 included. Nothing else.
l19.lesson: A deny only has to sit above the permits it overrides: here it goes below the DNS entry and above the web entry.

l20.title: Everything at once
l20.policy: SSH (TCP 22) to the jump host 10.0.0.20 from 10.1.20.0/24 and from the on-call laptop 192.0.2.44. The monitor 10.1.20.9 may send ICMP to anything in 10.0.0.0/24. Web (TCP 80) to 10.0.0.10 from anywhere except 192.0.2.0/24. Nothing else.
l20.lesson: Every lesson at once: the host exception above its network's deny, the deny above the general permit, and nothing wider than the policy.

origins.p1: Reading a rule list from the top and stopping at the first match is an old idea. In March 1989 Jeffrey C. Mogul of Digital Equipment Corporation's Western Research Laboratory described screend, which controls the datagrams that flow through a Unix-based gateway, in WRL Research Report 89/4, a preprint of his paper for the Summer 1989 USENIX Technical Conference. For each packet its rules are searched in the order they appear, and if none matches, a default action applies, normally rejection.
origins.p2: Cisco IOS access control lists (ACLs) read the same way: the first entry a packet matches decides whether it is permitted or denied, and every list ends with an unwritten, implicit deny. So the order matters as much as the entries: a broad permit near the top hides everything below it.
origins.p3: As a puzzle, First Match belongs with the programming games in which a few instructions, put in the right order, make a machine do the right thing, such as Zachtronics' TIS-100 and Tomorrow Corporation's Human Resource Machine.

spanning-tree.metaDescription: A daily IEEE 802.1D puzzle: find the root bridge, every root port, every designated port and the ports that block. Easy and hard, with practice rounds.
spanning-tree.title: Spanning Tree
spanning-tree.tagline: One root, one path each, no loops. Find them before a broadcast storm does.
spanning-tree.intro: The Spanning Tree Protocol (STP) of IEEE 802.1D (the Institute of Electrical and Electronics Engineers standard for bridges) keeps a switched network with redundant links free of loops. The switches elect a root bridge, every other switch picks its best port towards it, every link gets one designated port, and every remaining port blocks. Work it out the way the switches do.
spanning-tree.cardBlurb: Elect the root bridge, pick the root ports and the designated ports, block the rest. A new network every day, easy or hard.

rules.r1: Step 1: click the root bridge, the switch with the lowest bridge ID. A bridge ID is a priority followed by a MAC (media access control) address: the lower priority wins, and with equal priorities the lower MAC address.
rules.r2: Step 2: on every other switch, mark its root port, the port with the lowest root path cost (the link costs added up from the root). On a tie: the lowest sender bridge ID, then the lowest sender port ID, then the lowest receiving port ID.
rules.r3: Step 3: on every link, mark the designated port: the end whose switch has the lower root path cost; on a tie, the lower bridge ID; then the lower port ID.
rules.r4: Step 4: every port left over blocks. Once the last designated port is marked, the board marks them for you, and the loops are gone.
rules.r5: A port ID reads priority.number (128.2 is priority 128, port 2), and lower wins. Every MAC address here starts 0000.5e00.53, the block set aside for documentation, so the last two digits decide. The clock starts when you press Start; each mistake adds 10 seconds to the score. The daily puzzles change at 00:00 UTC (Coordinated Universal Time).

spanning-tree.boardLabel: The switched network: switches, links with their costs, and a port at each end of each link
spanning-tree.idsNote: Priority, then MAC address. The diagram shows the priority and the last four digits of the MAC address. R marks a root port, D a designated port, B a blocked port.

why.rootPrio: {root} has a lower bridge ID than {other}: {rootBid} against {otherBid}. The priority is compared first, and the lower one wins.
why.rootMac: {root} has a lower bridge ID than {other}: {rootBid} against {otherBid}. The priorities are equal, so the lower MAC address decides.
why.rpOnRoot: {sw} is the root bridge, so it has no root port: every port of the root is designated.
why.rpIsDesignated: On that link {sw} sends the better BPDU (bridge protocol data unit) towards {far}, so {port} is the designated port there and cannot be the root port.
why.rpCost: {sw} reaches the root at cost {costRight} through {right} and at cost {costPort} through {port}: the lowest root path cost wins.
why.rpSenderBid: Both ports reach the root at cost {cost}. The BPDU on {right} comes from {senderRight} ({bidRight}), lower than {senderPort} ({bidPort}) on {port}: the lowest sender bridge ID wins.
why.rpSenderPort: Both ports reach the root at cost {cost} through {sender}, which sends on {pidRight} towards {right} and on {pidPort} towards {port}: the lowest sender port ID wins.
why.rpReceiving: Same cost ({cost}), same sender ({sender}) and same sender port: the lowest receiving port ID wins, {right} over {port}.
why.dpCost: {swRight} is {costRight} from the root and {swPort} is {costPort}: the end with the lower root path cost is designated, {right}.
why.dpBid: Both ends are {cost} from the root. {swRight} has the lower bridge ID ({bidRight} against {bidPort}), so {right} is designated.
why.dpPort: Same switch, same cost: the lower port ID is designated, {pidRight} over {pidPort}.

origins.p1: Radia Perlman worked out the spanning tree algorithm at Digital Equipment Corporation (DEC) and published it in September 1985, in "An Algorithm for Distributed Computation of a Spanning Tree in an Extended LAN" at SIGCOMM '85: bridges that know only their neighbours compute, between them, a subset of the network that reaches every local area network (LAN) yet has no loops. The paper also carries a short poem of hers, "Algorhyme", which puts the algorithm in rhyme; the scan of the paper, in the sources, shows it.
origins.p2: The Institute of Electrical and Electronics Engineers (IEEE) approved 802.1D-1990, the bridge standard that carries the protocol, on 31 May 1990. The Rapid Spanning Tree Protocol (RSTP) followed as 802.1w in 2001 and was incorporated into 802.1D-2004.
origins.p3: In 2011 RFC 6325, the base specification of Routing Bridges (RBridges), with Perlman as first author, opened its introduction with a sequel, "Algorhyme V2" by Ray Perlner, which answers the first poem's tree with a graph of least-cost paths. Both poems are in the documents listed below.

whack-a-bug.metaDescription: Sixty seconds, nine panes of code, bugs that pop up for a moment. Squash them, leave the features alone, chain hits for a multiplier. A new daily run every UTC day.
whack-a-bug.title: Whack-a-Bug
whack-a-bug.tagline: Squash the bugs. Leave the features alone.
whack-a-bug.intro: Bugs crawl out of the code for a moment at a time. Hit them before they vanish, but mind the features: hitting one costs points, because it is not a bug, it is a feature. The daily run is the same 60 seconds for everyone; practice rounds never run out.
whack-a-bug.cardBlurb: Sixty seconds of bugs to squash and features to leave alone. A daily run and endless practice.
whack-a-bug.rule1: A round lasts 60 seconds. Bugs pop up in the nine panes and vanish again; hit each one before it goes.
whack-a-bug.rule2: Green parcels are features. Hitting one costs {penalty} points and breaks your combo.
whack-a-bug.rule3: A golden bug is rare and worth five times as much.
whack-a-bug.rule4: Every five hits in a row raise the multiplier, up to ×4. Tapping an empty pane, hitting a feature or letting a bug get away resets it.
whack-a-bug.rule5: Tap or click a pane, or press the key shown on it: Q W E, A S D, Z X C, or 7 8 9, 4 5 6, 1 2 3 on the number pad.
whack-a-bug.rule6: The daily run is the same for everyone on a UTC day and counts once, from the moment it starts: leave or reload mid-round and it ends with the score it had. Switching to another tab pauses the round, and a 3-2-1 countdown brings it back. Practise as often as you like. The pace picks up as the minute goes on.
whack-a-bug.dailyDone: Today's run is in. Practise as much as you like; the next daily run starts at 00:00 UTC.
whack-a-bug.keysHint: Keys: Q W E / A S D / Z X C, or the number pad.
whack-a-bug.featureHit: It's not a bug, it's a feature. −{penalty}
whack-a-bug.sayEnd: Time's up. {score, plural, one {{score} point} other {{score} points}}, {acc}% accuracy.
whack-a-bug.resultDetail: {hits, plural, one {# bug squashed} other {# bugs squashed}}, {features, plural, one {# feature broken} other {# features broken}}, {acc}% accuracy, best combo {combo}.
whack-a-bug.resultInterrupted: The run was left mid-round, so it ended there.
whack-a-bug.sayPaused: The round paused while the tab was hidden. It goes on in {seconds, plural, one {# second} other {# seconds}}.
whack-a-bug.dailyDoneEarlier: This day's run is in. Practise as much as you like.

origins.p1: Whack-a-mole began in Japan: Kato Seisakusho built Mogura Taiji, and TOGO released it in 1975. It reached the United States in 1977, where Aaron Fechter of Creative Engineering named it Whac-A-Mole; Bob's Space Racers, which has always made and sold the original game, credits its invention to two carnival operators, Gerald Denton and Donny Anderson.
origins.p2: Bugs are older than computers. In March 1878 Thomas Edison wrote to William Orton, president of Western Union, that he had found a "bug" in his apparatus. In 1947 engineers on Harvard's Mark II taped a moth into the log book as the "first actual case of bug being found"; the page is kept at the Smithsonian's National Museum of American History, and the log book was probably not Grace Hopper's.
origins.p3: And the thing you must not hit: the Jargon File lists "That's not a bug, that's a feature!" as a common catchphrase.

exit-the-editor.metaDescription: An escape room in a fake terminal: thirteen programs, from vim in Insert mode to a frozen ssh session, each to be left cleanly, the way its own manual says.
exit-the-editor.title: Exit the Editor
exit-the-editor.tagline: Every program has a way out. It is in the manual.
exit-the-editor.intro: Each level traps you in a program: vim, less, man, nano, Emacs, top, Python's interactive prompt, a frozen ssh session, tail -f, telnet, tmux and git commit's editor, then a final boss that stacks four of them. Leave each one cleanly. The programs answer the way their documentation says they do, including to the classic wrong guesses. A daily escape brings one of them back each day, in a new scene.
exit-the-editor.cardBlurb: Thirteen programs to leave cleanly, in a fake terminal. Yes, vim is one of them.
exit-the-editor.rule1: Click or tap the terminal, then type. On a phone, the key row gives Esc, Ctrl, Tab, the arrows, ~, : and Enter; Ctrl stays down for the next key you press.
exit-the-editor.rule2: A level is cleared when the program exits cleanly. Leaving the wrong way (a suspended program, a killed backup, an aborted commit) restarts the level.
exit-the-editor.rule3: Hints appear on their own after a few wrong tries, free; the Hint button shows the next one sooner, for {perHint} points.
exit-the-editor.rule4: A level scores {max} points, less {perKey} for each keystroke beyond the shortest way out, {perHint} for each hint you ask for and {perSecond} for each second after the first {free} (the clock starts when you press Start), but never less than {floor}. Levels unlock in order, and your progress stays in this browser.
exit-the-editor.levelDone: {score} pts{medal, select, under { · Under par} par { · Par} other {}}
exit-the-editor.ctrlArmed: Ctrl is held for the next key.
exit-the-editor.allDone: Every program left cleanly. The manuals were right all along.
exit-the-editor.clearedDetail: {keys, plural, one {# keystroke} other {# keystrokes}} in {time}: {score, plural, one {{score} point} other {{score} points}}. Total {total}.{medal, select, under { Under par: a medal for that.} par { Bang on par: a medal for that.} other {}}
exit-the-editor.sayCleared: Level cleared: {name}, {score, plural, one {{score} point} other {{score} points}}{medal, select, under {, under par} par {, at par} other {}}.
exit-the-editor.shareSummary: Levels {cleared}/{total} · {keys, plural, one {# keystroke} other {# keystrokes}} · {time}

fail.suspended: Suspended, not exited: Ctrl-Z stopped the program, and it is still there in the background. Try again.
fail.emptyCommit: The editor closed, but git aborted the commit: the message was empty. Write a line, save, then quit.
fail.killedJob: You got out, but the backup died with the pane. The point was to leave it running.
fail.stoppedJob: Ctrl-Z stopped the backup instead of leaving it running.
fail.closedSession: You left by ending the session, and everything in it ended too. Detach instead.
fail.interruptedJob: Ctrl-C reached the backup and stopped it. You are still inside tmux, at the shell in the same pane; the job was meant to keep running.

vim.brief: You were typing release notes in vim and the file has unsaved changes. Leave vim, saving or not: your choice.
vim.hint1: Typing quit only adds the word to the file: you are in Insert mode, as the bottom line says.
vim.hint2: Esc returns to Normal mode. Commands for the editor itself start with a colon.
vim.hint3: Esc, then :wq and Enter to save and quit, or :q! and Enter to quit without saving.

less.brief: You opened a log with less. Close it.
less.hint1: Ctrl-C only interrupts what less is doing; it does not end it.
less.hint2: less takes single-letter commands, and its own help is on h.

man.brief: You looked something up with man. The page is shown by a pager: leave it.
man.hint1: The bottom line tells you how, in brackets.
man.hint2: In the help screen, q closes the help, not the page.

nano.brief: nano is open on a to-do list. Get out, and if you typed something, decide whether to keep it.
nano.hint1: The two lines at the bottom are the shortcuts. ^ means Ctrl.
nano.hint2: Esc is a prefix in nano, and :q is just text here.
nano.hint3: Ctrl-X. If it asks whether to save the modified buffer, answer Y (then Enter) or N.

emacs.brief: Emacs started with no file, so you are in the *scratch* buffer. Leave Emacs.
emacs.hint1: Ctrl-G cancels whatever is half typed; it does not exit.
emacs.hint2: Exiting takes a two-key sequence, so that it is hard to type by accident. Both keys use Ctrl.

top.brief: top is showing the processes. Stop watching.
top.hint1: Letters in top change the display: e, i and t are toggles.
top.hint2: The two most important keys in top are help and quit.

python.brief: You are at Python's interactive prompt (version 3.12). Leave it.
python.hint1: In 3.12, typing exit on its own only tells you how to exit.
python.hint2: exit is a function, or you can send an end of file.
python.hint3: Type exit() and Enter, or press Ctrl-D on an empty line.
python.after: Since Python 3.13, the new interactive shell also takes plain exit and quit, no brackets needed. In 3.12, as here, they only tell you how to leave.

ssh.brief: Your Secure Shell (SSH) session to 203.0.113.10 has frozen: nothing you type reaches the server. Close the connection from your end.
ssh.hint1: Everything you type, Ctrl-C included, goes to the frozen server. Only the ssh client's own escape sequences act locally.
ssh.hint2: The escape character is ~, and it is only recognized right after a newline.

tail.brief: tail -f is following a log and will never stop on its own. Stop it.
tail.hint1: Letters you type are only echoed by the terminal; tail is not reading them.
tail.hint2: The terminal's interrupt character sends the running program a signal to stop.

telnet.brief: telnet is connected to a service that never answers. Leave telnet.
telnet.hint1: Typed lines are sent to the remote end, which ignores them, quit included.
telnet.hint2: telnet told you its escape character when it connected.
telnet.hint3: Ctrl-] for the telnet> prompt, then quit (q is enough) and Enter.

tmux.brief: A backup is running inside tmux on web01. Leave tmux without stopping it.
tmux.hint1: Ctrl-C would reach the backup and kill it.
tmux.hint2: tmux commands start with a prefix key, Ctrl-B by default.

git.brief: git commit opened its editor, vim here. Make the commit: write a message, save, quit.
git.hint1: Quitting without a message aborts the commit; lines starting with # do not count.
git.hint2: Press i to insert, type a message, then Esc.
git.hint3: i, a message, Esc, then :wq and Enter.

boss.brief: Over ssh, inside tmux, you were reading a manual page, and git commit is next. Get all the way back to your laptop: close the page, make the commit, detach tmux, then drop the connection when it freezes.
boss.hint1: One program at a time: each way out leads to the next program.
boss.hint2: After the commit, the shell in tmux is not your laptop: exiting it would end the session.
boss.hint3: q; i, a message, Esc, :wq and Enter; Ctrl-B d; then Enter, ~ and . to drop the frozen connection.

exit-the-editor.readScreen: Read the screen aloud (for screen readers)
exit-the-editor.rule5: Each level has a par: the keystrokes of its shortest documented way out, shown on its card and in its header. Leave in exactly par for the ⛳ Par medal; find a shorter way that still leaves cleanly and it is the 🐦 Under par medal. Your fewest keystrokes count, so a slower clear later never takes a medal away.
exit-the-editor.rule6: The daily escape is one trap a day, the same for everyone on a UTC (Coordinated Universal Time) day: a program from the levels, in a new scene. Your attempt starts when you press Start and counts once. A reload picks it up where you left it, with the clock still running; leaving the wrong way sets the trap again, and your keystrokes and the clock carry on. Get out to keep your streak.

daily.man: man is showing a page, {where, select, end {scrolled down to its end} other {at its first line}}. The pager has it: leave the pager.

daily.python: You are at Python's interactive prompt (version 3.12){history, select, exit {, where exit on its own has just told you how to leave} sys {, with sys already imported} math {, after a quick sum} other {}}. Leave it.
daily.ssh: Your Secure Shell (SSH) session to {host} froze {when, select, after {right after you pressed Enter} other {while you were typing}}: nothing reaches the server. Close the connection from your end.
daily.tail: tail -f is following {file} and will never stop on its own. Stop it.

origins.p1: In August 2012 a Stack Overflow user asked how to exit Vim. Five years later Stack Overflow counted over a million developers who had got stuck in Vim and needed that answer: during peak traffic hours on weekdays, about 80 people per hour.
origins.p2: Bill Joy created vi at Berkeley in 1976, as the visual mode of a line editor called ex, and it was included in the first Berkeley Software Distribution (BSD), released in 1978. Bram Moolenaar released Vim, the "Vi IMitation", on 2 November 1991 and was its lead developer for more than 30 years.
origins.p3: The format is the escape room, a video game genre that Toshimitsu Takagi's Crimson Room (2004) is often credited with popularizing: you are locked in, and the way out is somewhere in what you can see.

incident-commander.metaDescription: An idle game about running a service: buy servers and resilience, answer incidents with the right call, decide whether to approve releases without review, and write the post-mortem.
incident-commander.title: Incident Commander
incident-commander.tagline: Keep it up. Keep it fast. Write it down.
incident-commander.intro: Your service earns a credit for every ten requests it serves. Spend the credits on servers, caching and resilience; when an incident pops up, pick the right response before users notice. It keeps running while you are away, at half pace, for up to eight hours.
incident-commander.cardBlurb: An idle game about keeping a service up: incidents, on-call, and the approve-without-review switch.
incident-commander.rule1: Requests come in, your servers serve what they can, and every request served earns credits. Each release brings more users, so capacity has to keep up.
incident-commander.rule2: Incidents arrive at random, more or less often depending on your setup; the first arrives within the first {minutes, plural, one {minute} other {# minutes}} of a run, and they come more often early on. Each offers three responses and one is right: the right one fixes it quickly, a wrong one costs 20 seconds. Monitoring notices sooner, runbooks fix faster, and on-call engineers take some on their own.
incident-commander.rule3: Uptime counts the requests that incidents fail, shown as nines: 99.9% is three nines. Spare capacity absorbs part of an incident.
incident-commander.rule4: Approve without review ships a release every 20 seconds instead of every 50, but far more of them are bad deploys. Each level of the staging environment halves that risk.
incident-commander.rule5: Write the post-mortem once a run has earned enough: the setup starts again, and every lesson learned adds 10% to income for good. The service keeps earning while the tab is closed, at half the rate, for up to {hours} hours.
incident-commander.overloaded: Over capacity: {n, plural, one {{n} request per second is} other {{n} requests per second are}} being turned away.
incident-commander.undetected: Something is failing, and nothing has noticed what yet. Monitoring would.
incident-commander.onCallFixing: The on-call engineer is on it: about {s} s.
incident-commander.locked: That did not help. Next call in {s} s.
incident-commander.approveTradeoff: Reviewed: a release every {reviewedEvery} s, {reviewedRisk}% of them bad. Without review: every {approvedEvery} s, {approvedRisk}% of them bad. Every release brings more users; every bad deploy costs reputation.
incident-commander.approveCount: This run: {features, plural, one {# release} other {# releases}}, {bad, plural, one {# bad deploy} other {# bad deploys}}.
incident-commander.setupLine: Incidents are noticed after about {detect} s; an on-call engineer takes {onCall}% of them.
incident-commander.pmExplain: Once this run has earned {target, plural, one {{target} credit} other {{target} credits}}, write the post-mortem: the setup starts again from scratch, and the lessons learned stay.

servers.name: Servers
servers.effect: Each one serves 6 requests per second.

loadBalancer.name: Load balancer
loadBalancer.effect: +20% capacity per level, and it routes around part of every failure.

caching.name: Caching
caching.effect: +15% capacity per level. Cache stampedes come with it.

cdn.name: Content delivery network (CDN)
cdn.effect: +20% capacity per level; each level absorbs a quarter of a traffic flood.

autoscaling.name: Autoscaling
autoscaling.effect: +10% capacity per level; softens a region outage.

monitoring.name: Monitoring and alerting
monitoring.effect: Incidents are noticed 40% sooner per level; certificate and disk alerts prevent some.

onCall.name: On-call engineers
onCall.effect: Each one may take an incident on their own.

runbooks.name: Runbooks
runbooks.effect: Fixes take 30% less time per level.

staging.name: Staging environment
staging.effect: Halves the chance of a bad deploy per level, and catches memory leaks.

chaos.name: Chaos drills
chaos.effect: Every failure hurts 10% less per level: fewer leaks, gentler region outages.

tls.title: Expired certificate
tls.desc: Browsers refuse the site: the Transport Layer Security (TLS) certificate's validity period ended overnight.
tls.a0: Renew the certificate and reload the web server
tls.a2: Tell users to click through the browser's warning

disk.title: Disk full
disk.desc: Writes are failing on the application servers: the log partition is at 100%.
disk.a0: Rotate and compress the logs to free space

dnsTtl.title: Users reach the old server
dnsTtl.desc: The Domain Name System (DNS) record now points at the new server, but its time to live (TTL) is a day, so resolvers keep handing out the old answer.
dnsTtl.a0: Keep the old server answering until the TTL runs out, and lower TTLs before the next move
dnsTtl.a1: Flush the DNS cache on your own laptop
dnsTtl.a2: Switch the old server off at once

bgp.title: Route leak
bgp.desc: A network you do not control is announcing your prefixes through the Border Gateway Protocol (BGP), and traffic is going the wrong way.
bgp.a0: Get your upstream providers to filter the leaked routes

ddos.title: Traffic flood
ddos.desc: A distributed denial-of-service (DDoS) attack is filling the links with junk requests.
ddos.a0: Turn on the CDN's flood protection and rate-limit at the edge
ddos.a1: Block the attacking addresses by hand, one at a time

badDeploy.title: Bad deploy
badDeploy.desc: The release that just went out returns errors on half the pages.
badDeploy.a0: Roll back to the previous release
badDeploy.a1: Push a quick fix straight to production, unreviewed

memLeak.title: Memory leak
memLeak.desc: The application's memory use climbs until the system kills it, again and again.
memLeak.a0: Restart it on a schedule to buy time, then capture a heap profile

stampede.title: Cache stampede
stampede.desc: A popular entry expired and thousands of requests are rebuilding it at once.
stampede.a0: Serve the stale copy while a single request refreshes it

dbLock.title: Database lock
dbLock.desc: Queries pile up behind one transaction that holds a lock and never finishes.
dbLock.a0: Find the blocking session and end it
dbLock.a2: Add an index right now, on the live table

region.title: Cloud region outage
region.desc: The cloud provider's region your service runs in is down.
region.a0: Fail over to the standby region
region.a1: Restart the instances in the failed region

alwaysDns.title: It's always DNS
alwaysDns.desc: Nothing can reach the database: its name stopped resolving after a change to the internal zone.
alwaysDns.a0: Query the record and fix the zone

origins.p1: Incident command started on the fire line. The FIRESCOPE project grew out of the tragic 1970 wildland fire season in Southern California, when over 700 homes were destroyed and 16 lives lost; the United States Congress chartered it in 1972, and its work included the Incident Command System (ICS).
origins.p2: Google's Site Reliability Engineering (SRE) book says the company's incident management system is based on the Incident Command System, calls blameless postmortems a tenet of SRE culture, and describes the Wheel of Misfortune, a disaster role-play that resembles a tabletop role-playing game, as a way to prepare engineers for on-call.
origins.p3: The engine that keeps earning while you are away comes from idle games. Progress Quest, first released in 2002, needs no interaction at all; Cookie Clicker came out on the web in 2013; and Universal Paperclips (2017), by Frank Lantz, took its theme from a thought experiment popularized by the philosopher Nick Bostrom.

packet-stack.metaDescription: Headers fall into a four-column well. Steer each into its layer and set its field, so the EtherType names the IP version, the Protocol number names TCP or UDP and the port names the application: a full row that reads as a real frame is delivered. A new daily run every UTC day.
packet-stack.title: Packet Stack
packet-stack.tagline: Every header names the next one. Stack them right and the frame goes out.
packet-stack.intro: A frame on the wire is a stack of headers: Ethernet, then the Internet Protocol (IP), then the Transmission Control Protocol (TCP) or the User Datagram Protocol (UDP), then the payload, and each header says what follows it. Here the headers fall. Steer each one into its column and set its field (the EtherType, the Protocol number or the destination port) so that every full row reads as a frame a receiver would accept. The daily run is the same sixteen frames for everyone; practice never runs out.
packet-stack.cardBlurb: Falling headers: stack Ethernet, IP, TCP or UDP and the payload into frames a receiver would accept. A daily run and endless practice.
packet-stack.rule1: Each block is one header or the payload, and its column is its layer, left to right: Ethernet, IP, TCP or UDP, payload. A full row is one frame.
packet-stack.rule2: Every header names the block to its right. The EtherType names the IP version (0x0800 IPv4, 0x86DD IPv6); the Protocol number, called Next Header in IPv6, names the transport (6 TCP, 17 UDP); and the destination port names the application (TCP 80 HTTP, TCP 443 HTTPS, UDP 53 DNS and so on). Change field cycles the value while the block falls.
packet-stack.rule3: Look right before you set a field: the block it has to name is either beside the landing spot already or waiting in the queue under Next. Building a frame from the payload outwards, as a real stack does, means every field is set knowing what it carries.
packet-stack.rule4: A frame whose every header names the next is delivered: 100 points, plus 25 for each earlier frame in the streak, up to 200. A full row that breaks the chain is dropped, as a receiver would drop it, and stays at the bottom of the well; four frames delivered in a row clear the oldest dropped one.
packet-stack.rule5: The run ends when every block has landed, or when a block has no room to appear. Blocks fall faster every three rows.
packet-stack.rule6: Keys: Left and Right move the block, Up or X changes its field (Z goes back), Down moves it one row, Space drops it, 1 to 4 send it to a column and P pauses. On a touch screen, tap a column to steer the block there, tap its own column to drop it, or use the buttons.
packet-stack.rule7: The daily run is the same for everyone on a UTC day and counts once, from the moment it starts: leave or reload and it waits, paused, where you left it. Switching to another tab pauses it too, and the well stays hidden until the 3-2-1 count brings it back.
packet-stack.boardLabel: The well: four columns, Ethernet, IP, TCP or UDP, and payload

origins.p1: Packet Stack borrows a mechanic, not a game: blocks fall into a well, the player steers them, and a full row clears. A mechanic is a way of playing, and United States copyright law expressly excludes "any idea, procedure, process, system, method of operation" from protection, as the United States Copyright Office's Circular 33 quotes it; a particular game's name, art and look are another matter, so this one has its own, taken from the frame on the wire.
origins.p2: The rows follow the rule a receiver applies. Request for Comments (RFC) 894, of April 1984, requires the type field of an Ethernet frame carrying an IP datagram to hold the value hexadecimal 0800, and RFC 2464, of December 1998, sets 86DD for IPv6. RFC 9542, of April 2024, says what the field is for: Ethernet's protocol identifiers, the EtherType among them, indicate near the beginning of a frame what the frame contains, and a device cannot, in general, safely process anything in the frame past an EtherType it does not understand. EtherTypes are assigned by the Registration Authority of the Institute of Electrical and Electronics Engineers (IEEE); the Internet Assigned Numbers Authority (IANA) keeps a list of them, where 0806 is the Address Resolution Protocol (ARP).
origins.p3: Inside the frame, the IPv4 header's Protocol field, defined in RFC 791 of September 1981, indicates the next level protocol, and IPv6's Next Header (RFC 8200) uses the same values: IANA's Protocol Numbers registry gives 6 to TCP, 17 to UDP, 1 to the Internet Control Message Protocol (ICMP) and 58 to ICMP for IPv6. Ports are a step further: IANA's port registry lists the services, and each protocol's own document says which transport it runs over: DNS on UDP and TCP port 53 (RFC 1035), the Network Time Protocol (NTP) on UDP port 123 (RFC 5905), Secure Shell (SSH) on port 22 over TCP (RFC 4253), HTTP on TCP port 80 and, over Transport Layer Security (TLS), on TCP port 443 (RFC 9110), and syslog on UDP port 514 (RFC 5426).
origins.p4: The four columns are the internet's own layers as RFC 1122, of October 1989, lists them: application, transport, internet and link. The same document requires every host on a 10 Mb/s Ethernet to send and receive packets in RFC 894's encapsulation, the frame these blocks build.

ttl.metaDescription: Steer a packet across a network where every router takes one off its Time to Live (TTL). Reach each host before the TTL runs out: twelve packets a day, traceroute as a game.
ttl.title: TTL
ttl.tagline: Every router takes one. Zero is the end.
ttl.intro: Steer a packet to its host. Each router it passes is a hop: its TTL (Time to Live) drops by one and its trail grows by one, and the router that takes the TTL to zero discards the packet and sends back an ICMP (Internet Control Message Protocol) Time Exceeded message, the answer traceroute maps a path with. Twelve packets a day, each leaving with a TTL one higher than the last.
ttl.cardBlurb: Steer a packet through routers that each take one off its Time to Live, and reach the host before zero. A daily run and practice.
ttl.rule1: Steer the packet with the arrow keys or W A S D, a swipe, a tap on either side of it, or the arrows under the board. It never stops moving.
ttl.rule2: Packet 1 leaves with TTL 1, packet 2 with TTL 2, and so on up to packet 12, the way traceroute raises its probes' TTL one at a time.
ttl.rule3: Each router you enter forwards the packet and takes one off its TTL: +{hop} points, and the trail grows by one. The router that takes the TTL to zero discards the packet, and the run ends. At TTL 1 the router turns red: it would be the last.
ttl.rule4: Reach the host to deliver the packet: +{delivery} points. A host accepts a packet at any TTL, even 1. The next packet leaves from that host with a fresh TTL and no trail.
ttl.rule5: Run into your own trail and you have made a routing loop; leave the board and there is no route. Either ends the run.
ttl.rule6: The daily run is the same network for everyone on a UTC day and counts once, from the moment it starts. A reload or a hidden tab pauses it, and Resume carries on where it stopped; P or Escape pauses it too. Practise as often as you like. The packets move faster as the run goes on.
ttl.rule7: The IPv4 (Internet Protocol version 4) and IPv6 (version 6) buttons under the board switch the names: IPv6 calls the same field Hop Limit and answers with ICMPv6 (the ICMP of IPv6) Time Exceeded, type 3 instead of 11.

origins.p1: The Time to Live (TTL) field comes from RFC 791 (Request for Comments 791), the Internet Protocol's specification of September 1981. It was set in seconds, but since every module that processes a datagram must take at least one off it, the RFC says the TTL "must be thought of only as an upper bound on the time a datagram may exist"; its intention is "to cause undeliverable datagrams to be discarded". The registry of the IANA (Internet Assigned Numbers Authority) gives 64 as the current recommended default.
origins.p2: RFC 1812, the requirements for IPv4 (Internet Protocol version 4) routers, of June 1995, makes it a hop count: "When a router forwards a packet, it MUST reduce the TTL by at least one", and the router that takes it to zero must discard the packet and send an ICMP (Internet Control Message Protocol) Time Exceeded message, code 0, to the source; RFC 792 numbers that message type 11. The hop count, RFC 1812 adds, is what keeps routing problems from "causing packets to loop infinitely in the network". A host, by contrast, must not discard a datagram "just because it was received with TTL less than 2" (RFC 1122).
origins.p3: IPv6 (Internet Protocol version 6) renamed the field: RFC 8200 records that the IPv4 "Time-to-Live" field "was renamed 'Hop Limit' in IPv6". Its ICMPv6 Time Exceeded message, type 3 in RFC 4443, "indicates either a routing loop or too small an initial Hop Limit value", the same two things that end a run here.
origins.p4: Traceroute turns the rule into a map. RFC 1393, of January 1993, describes it: a packet goes out with a TTL of 1, the first hop answers that the TTL expired, then the packet goes again with a TTL of 2, and so on until the destination is reached, the source of each answer recorded as one hop of the path. The FreeBSD manual credits the program to Van Jacobson, "from a suggestion by Steve Deering"; the Linux one still says "We start our probes with a ttl of one and increase by one", up to 30 hops by default.
origins.p5: The addresses on the board are the blocks set aside for documentation: 192.0.2.0/24, 198.51.100.0/24 and 203.0.113.0/24 (RFC 5737) and, in the IPv6 view, 2001:db8::/32 (RFC 3849). By RFC 5737, none of the three should appear on the public Internet.

rule-inspector.metaDescription: A daily shift at a firewall desk: fifteen connections to permit or deny against a policy that tightens every round. The first match decides, a state table remembers, the implicit deny waits at the end, and the audit shows every wrong call.
rule-inspector.title: Rule Inspector
rule-inspector.tagline: Fifteen connections. One policy. The first match decides.
rule-inspector.intro: An office's edge firewall, a queue of connections and a policy that gets stricter as the shift goes on. Read the rules from the top, remember the connections the policy has already let open, and leave the rest to the implicit deny. The audit at the end shows every wrong call and the rule that decides it.
rule-inspector.cardBlurb: Permit or deny each connection at the firewall desk, against a policy that tightens every round. The audit is waiting.
rule-inspector.rule1: Connections reach the office's edge firewall one at a time. Each card shows what the firewall reads: the direction, the protocol with its Internet Assigned Numbers Authority (IANA) number, the addresses and ports, and the flags of a Transmission Control Protocol (TCP) packet. Permit or deny it with the buttons, A or the left arrow, D or the right arrow.
rule-inspector.rule2: The firewall works in the same order every time. First the state table: a reply to a connection the policy has already let open this round passes, and a TCP packet that is not a bare SYN with no open connection behind it is dropped. Then the rules, from the top: the first rule that matches decides. Then the implicit deny, for anything no rule matches.
rule-inspector.rule3: A shift has three rounds of five connections. Before the second and the third, a change tightens the policy: the notice shows the rules it inserts, and the clock stops while you read it.
rule-inspector.rule4: No verdicts during the shift: the audit at the end shows every wrong call and what decided it. {pass} of {total} right passes and keeps your streak; on the public board, the time breaks ties.
rule-inspector.rule5: Today's shift is the same for everyone on a day in Coordinated Universal Time (UTC). Practice shifts are new every time and stay in this browser.
rule-inspector.rule6: The internet and the office's public servers use the documentation blocks of Request for Comments (RFC) 5737 (192.0.2.0/24, 198.51.100.0/24 and 203.0.113.0/24), as examples should; a real edge would filter them too. The office network is 10.20.0.0/24, private-use space from RFC 1918.

origins.p1: Rule Inspector borrows a familiar game formula: an inspector at a desk, a queue that keeps coming, a rulebook that grows stricter by the day, and someone checking the inspector's work afterwards. Here the queue is network connections, the rulebook is a firewall policy, and the check is the audit.
origins.p2: Reading rules from the top and stopping at the first that matches is as old as packet filtering. In March 1989 Jeffrey C. Mogul of Digital Equipment Corporation's Western Research Laboratory described screend, which screens the datagrams crossing a Unix gateway: its rules are evaluated in the order they appear, so specific exceptions go before a general rule, a default action (normally rejection) covers the rest, and both directions of a path take a rule each. The Internet Engineering Task Force (IETF) model for access control lists (RFC 8519, 2019) says the same of every vendor's lists: the actions of the first matching entry apply and the entries after it are not processed. Juniper writes the end out: every firewall filter on its EX Series switches ends with an implicit deny.
origins.p3: A rule for each direction is what a stateful filter saves. Request for Comments (RFC) 6092 (2011), written for home gateways, describes one: when an inside host opens a Transmission Control Protocol (TCP) flow with a SYN, or sends a User Datagram Protocol (UDP) packet out, the filter allocates a state record and forwards the flow's packets by it, and it refuses packets that match no active flow and do not conform to a rule that may create one. RFC 9293, the current TCP specification, opens every connection with the three-way handshake that starts with a SYN.
origins.p4: The numbers on the cards are the registries' own. The Internet Assigned Numbers Authority (IANA) keeps the protocol numbers (TCP 6, UDP 17, ESP, the Encap Security Payload, 50), the service names and port numbers (ssh on 22, https on 443, isakmp on 500; clients use the Dynamic Ports from 49152 to 65535, which are never assigned) and the IPv4 special-purpose address registry that RFC 6890 set up in 2013. The anti-spoofing rule refuses as sources from the internet the blocks that registry marks as not globally reachable: the three private-use blocks of RFC 1918 (1996), the shared address space of RFC 6598, loopback, link local and the rest. RFC 5737 (2010) set aside 192.0.2.0/24, 198.51.100.0/24 and 203.0.113.0/24 for documentation, which is why they stand in for the internet here, and asks that packet filters drop them.

spoof.title: Anti-spoofing at the edge
spoof.why: Addresses from private-use and other special-purpose blocks cannot be real sources on the internet, and neither can the office's own public block. Both rules go on top, so they are read before every permit.

ssh.title: SSH only from the admins' network
ssh.why: Secure Shell (SSH) to the public servers was open to the whole internet. A permit for the admins' network and a deny for everyone else go in just above the old rule, which first match now never reaches for SSH.

http.title: Plain HTTP closed
http.why: The web server answers on HTTPS only from now on. A deny goes in just above the old HTTP permit, which stays in the list until the next clean-up but is never read for port 80 again.

dns.title: DNS only through the resolver
dns.why: Workstations were asking outside Domain Name System (DNS) servers directly. A permit for the office resolver and a deny for every other inside host go in above the old rule.

smb.title: File sharing and remote desktop blocked outbound
smb.why: Nothing in the office should reach file sharing (microsoft-ds, port 445) or remote desktop (ms-wbt-server, port 3389) on the internet. A deny goes in above the broad outbound permit.

blockhost.title: A reported host blocked
blockhost.why: One internet host was reported for attacking the office. A deny for that address goes on top, so nothing below can let it in.

settings_page.title: Settings
settings_page.lede: Personalize how the site behaves. Everything here is saved on this device only - there are no accounts and no server, so your choices never leave your browser.
settings_page.shortcutsBody: Rebind any shortcut key to a different action. Pick an action from each menu; the change applies immediately. Some keys may be fixed by the site administrator, in which case they are shown locked. Press ? anywhere on the site to see the current shortcuts at a glance.
settings_page.persistNote: Saved on this device only. Clearing site data or using another browser or device restores the defaults.
settings_page.themeLangBody: Theme and language are set from the controls in the header. Your theme is remembered on this device; your language is remembered too, and a return visit to the site's home sends you to your preferred language. An explicit link in a specific language is always honoured as-is.
settings_page.readingBody: Inline glossary hints add a subtle dashed underline to the first mention of a technical term in an article. Hover or tap it for a short definition, with a link to the full glossary entry. This is a device-only preference.
settings_page.hintToggleDesc: Underline glossary terms in articles and tool docs: the first mention of each term, every mention, or none.
settings_page.interestBody: With your yes, the site counts what you use: a tool worked with, a game started or finished, an article or glossary entry read to its end, a share, a link followed to Red Education, and whether a search found anything. A search that finds nothing also sends its words, when they are a few plain words. The counts name the thing used and never you: the site's own code sends them with no cookie, no identifier and nothing typed into a tool. They show which parts of the site deserve more work.
settings_page.interestOn: On: counts are sent from this browser.
settings_page.interestBrowserNo: Your browser sends Global Privacy Control or Do Not Track, which the site reads as a no: nothing is sent, whatever this switch says.
settings_page.interestMore: What is counted, and what never is
settings_page.deskBody: Your desk (/desk) lives in this browser. Keep a copy as a file, move it with a link, or sync it between your devices with a code only you hold.

bossScreens.metaDescription: Browse the vintage work-app screens the boss key can summon, and open any one fullscreen.
bossScreens.title: Boss-Key Screens
bossScreens.intro: Press the boss key anywhere (or B) and the page hides behind one of these vintage work apps. Here they all are: open any screen to see it full screen, then browse the rest with the left and right arrow keys, or by swiping sideways on a touch screen.

blurb.amiga: Kickstart's insert-disk screen: the animated hand offering a Workbench floppy, the friendliest boot in computing.
blurb.amipro: Samna's Amí was the first fully functional Windows word processor, a year ahead of Word for Windows. Lotus bought Samna in 1990; the colourful SmartIcons were its signature.
blurb.aol: For millions the internet WAS the blue screen and the friendly voice: You've Got Mail. Quantum, the company behind Q-Link, renamed its service America Online in 1989, and later mailed the world a floppy.
blurb.apple1: Wozniak's first: no OS, just the 256-byte WozMon. Press Reset and it prints a backslash and a blinking cursor, ready for hex.
blurb.appleii: The enhanced //e that ran a generation of US schools. Its ROM shows Apple //e, then the Applesoft ] prompt.
blurb.appleii1977: The original. No autostart: it comes up in Wozniak's monitor at a * prompt; Ctrl-B enters Integer BASIC and its > prompt.
blurb.appleiic: Apple's compact, portable II. With no disk it beeps, shows Apple //c, then Check Disk Drive; Ctrl-Reset drops to BASIC.
blurb.appleiigs: The 16-bit II: colour, sound, and the friendly Check Startup Device screen where the Apple logo slides side to side.
blurb.appleiiplus: The Apple II Plus with Applesoft in ROM: the plain Apple ][ banner and the ] prompt where countless first programs ran.
blurb.at286: The AT and its POST: a memory count marching upward before the operating system loads.
blurb.atari800xl: Atari's 8-bit workhorse: a deep blue screen, Atari BASIC's READY, and colours that slowly cycle to spare your TV.
blurb.bbcmicro: Acorn's machine that taught Britain to code, from its terse grey banner and BASIC prompt.
blurb.bsod: The Blue Screen of Death: Windows' STOP error, arguably the most recognized screen in PC history.
blurb.c64: The best-selling home computer ever. Boots to a blue BASIC V2 prompt; here it types a little program by itself.
blurb.clipper: Nantucket's dBASE compiler, the small-business workhorse: millions of DOS apps between 1985 and 1992, and Summer '87 stayed in use for a decade.
blurb.coco: The CoCo: Microsoft Color BASIC in black-on-green, the OK prompt waiting on a TV set.
blurb.commander: The twin-panel DOS file manager that defined orthodox file management, in unmistakable blue.
blurb.compuserve: The first big consumer online service, from Columbus, Ohio: forums, email and stock quotes behind a numbered menu and a lone ! prompt, long before the web.
blurb.cp300: Brazil's compact TRS-80 Model III clone. No disks, straight to cassette BASIC: Cass?, Memory Size?, then READY.
blurb.cp400: Brazil's TRS-80 Color clone (a CoCo 2 inside): Extended Color BASIC in black-on-green, the OK prompt waiting.
blurb.cp500: Brazil's TRS-80 Model III clone, in green phosphor. A reserva-de-mercado icon that ran BASIC and DOS 500.
blurb.cpc464: Unmistakable bright yellow on blue: Locomotive BASIC greeting you with Ready on a built-in cassette machine.
blurb.dbase: The database that ran 1980s business, driven from its famous dot prompt.
blurb.dbase2: Ratliff's Vulcan from JPL, renamed by Ashton-Tate marketing (there was never a dBASE I). The dot prompt that started the xBase world, on CP/M first.
blurb.esxi: The bare-metal hypervisor's yellow-and-grey console (the DCUI): host version, CPU and memory, and just two keys, F2 to configure and F12 to shut down. Released 17 April 2018.
blurb.expert: Gradiente's Brazilian MSX. Standard MSX BASIC, a detached keyboard, and a soap-opera-famous look.
blurb.harvard: SPC's Harvard Presentation Graphics let a DOS PC mix text, charts and clip art into slide shows; version 2.0 gave it the famous name.
blurb.hotbit: Sharp/Epcom's Brazilian MSX. The other national MSX, booting MSX BASIC with Portuguese accents.
blurb.ibmpc: The machine that set the standard. Cassette BASIC in ROM: the IBM Personal Computer BASIC banner.
blurb.lotus: The IBM PC's killer app and the archetypal boss-key screen: a spreadsheet that looks like real work.
blurb.macfinder: The desktop that taught the world the metaphor: menu bar, icons, and a Trash in the corner. System 7 (1991) finally let the Trash keep what you dropped in it.
blurb.macintosh: Susan Kare's friendly boot: a blinking floppy with a question mark, then the smiling Happy Mac and Welcome to Macintosh.
blurb.mosaic: The browser that showed the masses a picture and a link on the same page. Built at NCSA by Andreessen and Bina; its team went on to make Netscape.
blurb.msworks: Unveiled 14 September 1987 for DOS: word processor, spreadsheet, database and communications in one program that ran in 256 KB.
blurb.msx1: The Microsoft/ASCII home standard: the logo scrolls up, then MSX BASIC and its Ok prompt.
blurb.msxturbor: The last, fastest MSX (Japan only). The logo assembles from the sides, then MSX BASIC 4.0 on its R800 CPU.
blurb.multimate: The Wang word processor reborn on a PC, keyboard template and all. Ashton-Tate paid about USD 20 million for it in December 1985.
blurb.netware: The LAN era's heartbeat: MONITOR.NLM on the server console, utilization ticking about once a second, cache buffers healthy above Novell's 40% rule.
blurb.norton: Peter Norton's blue toolkit; the Disk Doctor rescued many a floppy.
blurb.oblivion: The ANSI art scene's darling: OBV/2's one-of-a-kind interface made underground boards beautiful. Freeware from 1997; v2.40 closed out the decade.
blurb.os2warp: IBM's object-oriented Workplace Shell, better DOS than DOS and a rock-solid multitasker. Warp 3 (1994) was its best shot at the desktop, LaunchPad and all.
blurb.pc386: A tricked-out 386 clone: the AMIBIOS POST counting memory, cache and turbo lit, Hit DEL for SETUP.
blurb.pcboard: Clark Development's high-end DOS BBS. The modem dials Salt Air, the carrier locks at 2400 bps, and the v15.22 node banner answers a caller.
blurb.profwrite: SPC's friendlier answer to WordPerfect: pfs:Write's successor with pull-down menus and context help, beloved by offices that just wanted letters typed.
blurb.remoteaccess: Andrew Milner's shareware giant from Australia, running multiple nodes under DESQview when few could. Its FrontDoor-styled sysop console sits waiting for a caller.
blurb.sidekick: Kahn's USD 49.95 TSR that popped over whatever you were doing on Ctrl-Alt: notepad, calculator, calendar, dialer, ASCII table. A million copies in three years.
blurb.sniffer: The DOS protocol analyser that named a whole category, and Wireshark's ancestor. Three-panel Miller-column menus over a blue screen; first sold December 1986.
blurb.snifferconficker: A decoded capture in the Sniffer's three-pane view: a TCP SYN scan to port 445, the SMB flow Conficker rode via MS08-067. Header bytes only, no exploit payload.
blurb.snifferhttp420: A full HTTP decode in the Sniffer: Twitter's non-standard 420 Enhance your calm rate-limit response, headers and JSON body and all, the way the analyser would show it.
blurb.snifferiloveyou: An SMTP decode of the LoveLetter worm's mail envelope: the ILOVEYOU subject line and its infamous attachment name. Mail headers only, no script.
blurb.sniffermirai: A decoded Telnet session to port 23, the credential-guessing vector the Mirai botnet used against IoT devices. Connection metadata only, no credential list.
blurb.sniffermorris: A decoded capture showing the fingerd (port 79) and sendmail (port 25) flows the 1988 Internet Worm rode. Protocol headers only, no exploit code.
blurb.snifferpetya: A decoded SMB flow to port 445, the EternalBlue / MS17-010 vector NotPetya shared with WannaCry. Header bytes only, no exploit payload.
blurb.snifferstuxnet: A decoded SMB print-spooler flow to port 445, one of the vectors (MS10-061) Stuxnet used to reach Siemens WinCC systems. Headers only, no payload.
blurb.snifferwannacry: A decoded SMB flow to port 445, the EternalBlue / MS17-010 vector WannaCry rode across flat networks in May 2017. Header bytes only, no exploit payload.
blurb.telegard: Born of leaked WWIV code and ancestor of Renegade: the hobbyist sysop's free workhorse, shown in its final Telegard 3.09/g2 form.
blurb.ti99: Texas Instruments' 16-bit home computer: the cyan title screen, TEXAS INSTRUMENTS HOME COMPUTER, press any key to begin.
blurb.tk82c: Microdigital's ZX81 clone, where many Brazilians (this one's author included) first learned to program: a blank screen and one inverse K.
blurb.tk90x: Brazil's ZX Spectrum clone, where many Brazilians first typed real programs in colour. It boots paper-white with its own name, TK90X - Color Computer, over a colour test bar.
blurb.tk95: The TK90X's successor in a Plus/4-style case with a better keyboard. Its power-on screen shows a colour band field and its name in full: Microdigital TK95.
blurb.trs80: Radio Shack's all-in-one. Cass? then Memory Size?, then Level II BASIC and its READY prompt.
blurb.turbopascal: Borland's beloved blue IDE that taught a generation to program, compiler and editor in one.
blurb.unitron: Brazil's faithful Apple II Plus clone with a Portuguese ROM: the Apple ][ banner and ] prompt, made under market reserve.
blurb.vic20: The friendly computer and the C64's older sibling: CBM BASIC V2 with 3583 bytes free.
blurb.videotexto: Brazil's videotex: TELESP's ANTIOPE-based service in São Paulo, 1982, home micros as terminals at 1200/75 bps, the index painting line by line in eight colours.
blurb.visicalc: The first spreadsheet, on the Apple II. The original boss screens imitated exactly this budget grid.
blurb.wfw311: The grey-chrome Program Manager that ran offices worldwide, now with peer networking baked in. Codenamed Snowball, it shipped 8 November 1993.
blurb.wordperfect: The near-blank blue writing screen that ruled DOS word processing, with just a status line in the corner.
blurb.wordstar: The word processor of the CP/M and early DOS era, remembered for its Ctrl-key command menus.
blurb.xtreegold: The gilded XTree: pull-down menus, Norton-style split panes and, from 2.0, ZIP archives handled in place.
blurb.xtreepro: Executive Systems' tree view grew up: multiple drives, more speed, and the single-letter command rows that made hard disks navigable.
blurb.zx81: Minimalism itself: a blank screen and a single inverse K cursor waiting in the corner.
blurb.zxspectrum: The machine that built the UK bedroom-coder scene. A blank white screen and one line: © 1982 Sinclair Research Ltd.
blurb.zxspectrum128: The 128K's start menu: Tape Loader, 128 BASIC, Calculator, 48 BASIC, over the AY chip's three-channel sound and that rainbow ident.
blurb.zxspectrum2a: Amstrad's black-cased +2A: a +3 with a cassette deck instead of the disk, so its menu still reads +3 BASIC. The last Spectrum made.
blurb.zxspectrum3: Amstrad's +3 added a 3-inch floppy and +3DOS to the Spectrum line. Loader, +3 BASIC, Calculator, 48 BASIC, and drive M: for the RAMdisk.
blurb.defrag: Microsoft's DOS 6 defragmenter, a cut-down Norton SpeedDisk: the whole drive as a grid of blocks, shuffled before your eyes.
blurb.copyiipc: Central Point's legendary disk backup utility that copied what others could not, track by patient track.

copyEditor.title: Copy editor
copyEditor.lede: View and edit every UI string on the site, one language at a time. Pick a language, search for the text you want, edit it in place, then export the result.
copyEditor.caveat: This is a workbench, not a live editor. The site is static with no server, so changes here cannot be saved back to the live site. Export the updated file (or just the changed keys), commit it into src/i18n/messages/, and redeploy to publish.
