guide.title: How to use ronutz
guide.lede: A practical guide to the whole site: the five worlds it is organized into, how each one works and where to start in it, then the reference material, the tools one line each, common tasks with the tools that get them done, and the manual for the features that cut across everything.
guide.datasheetIntro: The essentials in one panel. These figures are generated from the site itself at build time, so they always match what is actually published.

ds.privacyValue: Stays in your browser, except a red-room lookup you send
ds.techValue: Next.js, exported as a static site with a web app manifest
ds.costValue: Free to use; the first useful answer is never behind a paywall

guide.quickrefIntro: Every general-purpose tool, grouped by category. This list is generated from the live registry, so it is always complete. Tools tied to a specific vendor live on that vendor's page.
guide.usageIntro: Common tasks, and the tools that get them done. Follow the tools in order for each task.

inspect-a-token.title: Inspect a token you received
inspect-a-token.desc: Decode a JSON Web Token to read its claims, then decode any Base64 fields inside it.

plan-a-subnet.title: Plan an IP subnet
plan-a-subnet.desc: Work out network ranges, masks and host counts for IPv4, see which special-purpose range a block falls in, and carve a parent block into variable-length subnets with the free blocks left over; then read an IPv6 address or prefix the same way, with its special-use type and its size.

size-bfd-timers.title: Size BFD timers and check what is on the wire
size-bfd-timers.desc: Work out the interval each direction of a BFD session really runs at, how long each side waits before declaring the path down and whether Echo may run, with the RFC section behind every number; decode a captured BFD Control packet to compare, and plan where to capture UDP 3784 when only one end comes up.

work-with-a-certificate.title: Work with a TLS certificate
work-with-a-certificate.desc: Decode a certificate to see its fields, check a signing request, and plan the renewal date.

set-up-app-login.title: Set up sign-in for an app
set-up-app-login.desc: Understand an OpenID Connect flow, add PKCE for a public client, and add a one-time-password second factor.

read-a-dns-answer.title: Read a DNS answer
read-a-dns-answer.desc: Make sense of the output from dig, and from nslookup, line by line: TTLs printed in units read back in seconds, how long a negative answer may be cached, and whether the answer came from a server authoritative for the name.

verify-data-integrity.title: Verify data integrity
verify-data-integrity.desc: Compute a hash of some data, or an HMAC when a shared secret is involved.

debug-a-saml-login.title: Debug a SAML single sign-on
debug-a-saml-login.desc: Decode a SAML response to read its assertions and conditions, then inspect the X.509 certificate that signed it.

map-a-jwks-to-tokens.title: Match a token to its signing key
map-a-jwks-to-tokens.desc: Read a JWKS key set to see the keys it publishes, then decode a JSON Web Token to find the key that signed it.

understand-a-tls-connection.title: Understand a TLS connection
understand-a-tls-connection.desc: Decode the negotiated cipher suite, inspect the server certificate, and review the response security headers.

harden-a-web-response.title: Harden a web response
harden-a-web-response.desc: Audit a site's HTTP security headers, then inspect the URL those headers protect.

assess-ssrf-risk.title: Assess a URL for SSRF risk
assess-ssrf-risk.desc: Classify whether a URL could reach an internal target, then inspect its parts in detail.

score-a-vulnerability.title: Score a vulnerability
score-a-vulnerability.desc: Decode a CVSS vector string into its metrics to understand how severe a finding really is.

convert-and-tidy-config.title: Convert and tidy a config
convert-and-tidy-config.desc: Convert a config between JSON and YAML, then format the result so it is easy to read.

compare-two-files.title: Compare two files
compare-two-files.desc: Normalize two JSON blobs with the formatter, then diff them to see exactly what changed.

reproduce-an-http-request.title: Reproduce an HTTP request
reproduce-an-http-request.desc: Break a URL into its parts, then translate the call into curl, fetch, or another client.

identify-an-unknown-hash.title: Identify an unknown hash
identify-an-unknown-hash.desc: Look up a digest against known values, then recompute a hash to confirm the match.

read-a-syslog-line.title: Read a syslog line
read-a-syslog-line.desc: Decode a syslog PRI value into its facility and severity.

build-and-test-a-regex.title: Build and test a regex
build-and-test-a-regex.desc: Write a regular expression and test it against sample text as you go.

read-an-f5os-path.title: Read an F5OS path, then the declaration behind it
read-an-f5os-path.desc: Decode an F5OS RESTCONF path segment by segment to see which module, tenant and node it addresses, then read the AS3 declaration that configures the service running inside that tenant.

read-a-bigip-object-path.title: Decode a BIG-IP object path, then its statistics
read-a-bigip-object-path.desc: Paste an iControl REST URL to see the module, collection and tilde-encoded object with its tmsh equivalent; flatten the object's stats response into readable lines; then use the F5OS explainer for the platform layer underneath.

trace-a-session-on-a-fortigate.title: Work out why a FortiGate is not passing that traffic
trace-a-session-on-a-fortigate.desc: Check which policy actually matches the packet and whether the rule you expected is even reachable, then build the diagnose debug flow sequence to watch it happen on the device.

understand-an-sse-pass.title: Understand what one request meets in an SSE platform
understand-an-sse-pass.desc: Describe a request and walk the single pass: which services engage, which are pillars and which are cross-cutting, and what a chain of separate appliances would have done instead.

make-sense-of-an-spb-fabric.title: Make sense of an SPB fabric configuration
make-sense-of-an-spb-fabric.desc: Paste an I-SID, a nickname or a role and get the Shortest Path Bridging vocabulary sorted: which backbone VLAN carries the service, what the service actually binds to, and what changes between an edge bridge and a core bridge.

read-what-the-bigip-wrote-in-the-capture.title: Find out why the BIG-IP reset that connection
read-what-the-bigip-wrote-in-the-capture.desc: Paste the F5 Ethernet trailer from a capture taken on the device and read the RST cause, the slot and TMM that handled the packet, and the flow identifiers - plus a warning if the trailer carries TLS session secrets.

choose-how-traffic-reaches-the-edge.title: Decide how traffic should reach the service edge
choose-how-traffic-reaches-the-edge.desc: Choose the steering method for a situation and see what it costs, then trace what a specific flow will actually do once that configuration is in place.

work-out-which-terminal-layer-you-are-in.title: Work out which terminal layer you are actually in
work-out-which-terminal-layer-you-are-in.desc: Paste what tty printed and see whether you are on a pseudoterminal, a virtual console or a real serial line - and what that means for signals, job control and what happens when the window closes.

work-out-which-extreme-os-you-have.title: Work out which Extreme OS name applies to your switch
work-out-which-extreme-os-you-have.desc: Check whether a model carries the new Switch Engine and Fabric Engine names or the original EXOS and VOSS, see the caveats that come with the series, then translate a task between the two command sets.

size-and-read-an-f5os-tenant.title: Read an F5OS tenant configuration and check its sizing
size-and-read-an-f5os-tenant.desc: Paste the tenant block to see its lifecycle state, its platform and whether the memory allocation meets F5's published minimum, then decode the RESTCONF path you would use to change it.

read-a-fortios-config-block.title: Read a FortiOS config block before you paste it
read-a-fortios-config-block.desc: See the structure as a tree, find out whether any set command is about to replace a list rather than add to it, and check whether the policy it configures can even be reached.

compare-two-network-operating-systems.title: Understand how two network operating systems differ
compare-two-network-operating-systems.desc: See lineage, what each runs on, how state is shared and where the planes divide - and what each of those predicts about behaviour when something fails.

work-out-why-awaf-blocked-a-request.title: Work out why AWAF blocked a request
work-out-why-awaf-blocked-a-request.desc: Start from the request log entry, decide whether the block was a false positive, weigh how much to trust the signature that fired, then compare the policy against the version that behaved.

write-an-irule-that-behaves.title: Write an iRule that behaves
write-an-irule-that-behaves.desc: Check which event your logic belongs in before writing it, confirm the commands are legal in that context, then lint for the patterns that cost CPU and estimate what the rule will actually spend.

work-an-incident-to-escalation.title: Work an incident from first symptom to escalation
work-an-incident-to-escalation.desc: Turn a symptom into testable hypotheses, reason the traffic path, plan a capture that will answer the question, build the timeline as you go, and hand the vendor a packet that does not come back asking for more.

plan-and-verify-a-change.title: Plan a change and prove it worked
plan-and-verify-a-change.desc: Map what the change can reach before you make it, write the runbook with its rollback, then compare health before and after. The third step is the one most often skipped.

fingerprint-an-unknown-client.title: Fingerprint an unknown client
fingerprint-an-unknown-client.desc: Read the TLS handshake as JA3 and JA4, compare the HTTP header order against what the claimed browser sends, and measure whether the user agent string is as common as it pretends to be.

get-an-access-point-onto-its-controller.title: Get an access point onto its controller
get-an-access-point-onto-its-controller.desc: Build the DHCP option 43 value in the encoding your access point vendor actually expects, and plan the cable run that gets power and data to where the AP is going.

cut-a-value-out-of-a-request.title: Cut a value out of a request
cut-a-value-out-of-a-request.desc: Check whether the command you picked counts from 0 or from 1, cut the value with findstr, substr or getfield beside the plain Tcl that does the same, try the string commands on your exact input, and read a structured value with scan.

work-out-what-tcl-does-with-a-value.title: Work out what Tcl does with a value
work-out-what-tcl-does-with-a-value.desc: See how Tcl 8.4 reads a number as written (010 is octal, so it equals 8), how expr and if evaluate a condition step by step with == next to eq, then run the snippet one command at a time and watch each substitution.

turn-a-routing-decision-into-an-irule.title: Turn a routing decision into an iRule
turn-a-routing-decision-into-an-irule.desc: Write the decision as rules and get it as an if chain, a switch or a class match with its data group, check the code against the DevCentral iRules Style Guide, then lint it for the patterns that cost CPU.

find-what-is-hiding-in-a-string.title: Find what is hiding in a string
find-what-is-hiding-in-a-string.desc: Paste the text into the Unicode inspector to see every code point, with invisible characters, bidirectional controls, unusual line breaks and lookalikes flagged; compare against the ASCII the text should have held; and run an iRule through the style checker, which reports the same characters in Tcl.

write-a-character-in-any-language.title: Write a character in any language
write-a-character-in-any-language.desc: Look up an ASCII code in any notation and copy its escape for C, JSON, JavaScript, Python, Tcl, HTML or a URL; for anything beyond ASCII, take the escapes and UTF-8 bytes from the Unicode inspector; then encode the bytes as hex, Base64 or percent-encoding.

fix-garbled-text.title: Fix text that came out garbled
fix-garbled-text.desc: Paste the garbled text into the charset converter's Fix mojibake mode to find the charset that misread it and get the original back; if you have the raw bytes, read them in Bytes to text and compare every charset side by side; then check the result for hidden characters in the Unicode inspector.

check-a-route-against-its-roas.title: Check a route against its ROAs
check-a-route-against-its-roas.desc: Paste a route and the VRPs your validator exports, or a SLURM file, to get its RFC 6811 state with the reason VRP by VRP; then work the covering prefixes with the CIDR or IPv6 calculator.

size-a-cgn-pool.title: Size a carrier-grade NAT pool, or trace an abuse report
size-a-cgn-pool.desc: Work out how many subscribers a public pool holds with port blocks, lay out an RFC 7422 deterministic mapping and reverse an address, port and time to the inside address, read the port set of a MAP PSID, then check the inside and pool prefixes with the CIDR calculator.

read-a-routing-table.title: Read a routing table
read-a-routing-table.desc: Paste the output of ip route, netstat -rn or route print to read each route field by field, see which default route wins and which route a destination takes, then check one prefix's arithmetic in the CIDR calculator.

check-a-servers-tls-from-the-command-lin.title: Check a server's TLS from the command line
check-a-servers-tls-from-the-command-lin.desc: Paste an openssl s_client command and what it printed to see what was really checked and what the output proves, put the certificates it showed in the order a server should send them, then decode the one that matters.

script-a-device-login-safely.title: Script a device login safely
script-a-device-login-safely.desc: Build an Expect script from the connection, the device profile and the commands, with no password in the file and nothing secret in the logs, then read any Expect script command by command before it runs.

share-a-config-snippet-without-leaking-s.title: Share a config snippet on a slide without leaking secrets
share-a-config-snippet-without-leaking-s.desc: Turn code, configuration or terminal output into a picture for a slide or a ticket: the secrets check masks keys, tokens and passwords before anything is drawn, and the alt text it writes is the code itself.

find-why-a-scripted-monitor-marks-a-memb.title: Find out why a Scripted monitor marks a member down
find-why-a-scripted-monitor-marks-a-memb.desc: Check the send and expect file against F5's rules, capture the monitor's conversation with the pool member on the BIG-IP, then paste it as a transcript to see which line fails and why.

carry-a-regex-into-nginx-or-an-irule.title: Carry a regex into NGINX or an iRule
carry-a-regex-into-nginx-or-an-irule.desc: Test the pattern and see what changes between JavaScript, PCRE2 and Tcl, then check which NGINX location it wins for a URI, or what a regexp costs in an iRule.

check-and-tidy-an-xml-document.title: Check and tidy an XML document
check-and-tidy-an-xml-document.desc: Find out whether the document is well-formed and where it breaks, pretty-print or minify it, then read its tree, its DOCTYPE and its entities for the attack surface they open.

start.b: Open any tool, paste or type your input, and the result appears immediately. There is no sign-in and nothing to install. Most tools include an Example button that fills in sample input, and a Clear button that resets the fields. Below each tool you will find related Learn articles that explain the underlying concept.

privacy.b: The catalogue's tools run entirely in your browser, so the values you enter are not transmitted anywhere. When one page hands a value to a tool, it travels after the # in the address, a part browsers never put in a request, although it stays in your history and in any address you share. The red room's tools, the one exception, send a query only when you press Ask or Enter, or test data only when you press Start on the speed test, and only to the official service they name. Every page carries a browser security policy that lets its scripts connect only to this site, with the red room's tools alone also allowed to reach the services they use (any registry over HTTPS for the two registry lookups, five named resolvers for the DNS-over-HTTPS lookup, one named host each for the password check and the speed test), and a build check fails if that policy is loosened anywhere else. Your theme, the language you last used and a few other preferences are remembered in your browser only and never sent anywhere. The <privacy>Privacy page</privacy> names each of them and says exactly what is and is not kept, including the aggregate count of page requests.

api.b: Each tool's logic is also documented as an API, with a machine-readable specification you can read on the API page. The API is documented for reference; whether requests are served depends on the site's current configuration, which the API page states plainly.

languages.b: The interface is available in several languages; switch using the language control in the header. English is the source, written with AI; Brazilian Portuguese is written with AI too and reviewed gradually, and so are the interface and the tools in Spanish, German, French and Italian; the rest of the Spanish, German, French and Italian sites is machine-translated. Where a phrase has not yet been translated for a given language, the English text is shown for that phrase so nothing is ever missing.

offline.b: Pages are not stored for offline use: there is no service worker, so a page you have not opened needs a connection. On a catalogue tool's page that has finished loading, the calculation itself makes no request, so it keeps working if the connection drops; a few tools fetch their engine or a data table from the site the first time you run them, and need the connection for that. The site publishes a web app manifest, so a browser that supports installing web apps can add it to your home screen or desktop; it still loads its pages over the connection.

source.b: The project is open source. The code is licensed under Apache 2.0 and the written content under CC BY 4.0. You can read the source, report an issue, or suggest a tool from the repository, which is linked in the footer and on the License page.

learning.b: Two learning aids sit alongside the tools. The Glossary defines the acronyms, terms, and jargon the tools and articles use, from protocol names to attack backronyms, each with a short definition and a fuller explanation. And in the Learn articles and tool documentation, the first mention of a term carries a subtle dashed underline: hover or tap it for a quick definition without leaving the page, with a link to the full glossary entry. If you find the underlines distracting, turn them off under Settings, in the Reading section.

beyond.b: The site is more than the calculators. The Learn library holds articles that explain the concepts the tools operate on. The Vendors pages gather the vendor-specific tools and reference material for platforms like F5, along with the corporate history behind the names. And the Certifications area offers study guides and reading paths for people working towards a certification. All of it is reachable from the header.

guide.mapIntro: Everything on ronutz lives in one of five worlds, the same five the footer of every page, the colophon and the sitemap use. The counts are computed from the site itself when it is built, so they are the figures of the pages they point at.
guide.howIntro: One section per surface: what it is for, how to use it, and the two or three places to start. The sections below this one are the reference: the datasheet, every tool on one line, the common tasks, and the manual.

tools.p1: Every tool in the catalogue computes in your browser and sends none of your input anywhere (the <privacy>Privacy page</privacy> sets out what does travel): paste or type the input and the result appears, with an Example button that fills a known-good input and a Clear button beside it. The tools index opens three ways in: paste what you have, and the box lines up the tools that recognize the shape of what you pasted; choose by what you need to do (decode, understand, compute, build, check); or follow a workflow that takes one thing from tool to tool, a CIDR to a firewall rule, a certificate to the headers a browser enforces.
tools.p2: The index has three floors, stated on the page: the main floor, where every tool has a fixed shape and golden test vectors; the green room, for tools whose form is still settling; and the red room, the one place a tool can send your input out, to the official service named on screen, and only when you ask. Each tool has a documentation page, readable as a web page or as Markdown, and the same logic is described as an API with a machine-readable specification.

learn.p1: The Learn library is the explanation behind the tools: articles grouped by subject, in the same taxonomy the tools use, each citing the documentation it was written from and linking the tools that compute what it describes. The hub can be read two ways, Guided or Directory. Guided asks what you want to do (understand a subject, learn something in order from the start, prepare for an exam, work with a particular platform, find a definition fast) and sends you to the right door; Directory lists every article by subject in reading order.
learn.p2: Around the articles sit the Article series, subjects told in order from an opener through their parts; the Stories, longer pieces that argue a point; The Practice, about the work rather than the technology (triage, escalation, change, the human side); the Glossary, with a definition for every term the articles and tools use; and the People, the engineers and authors behind the protocols. In any article, the first mention of a technical term carries a dashed underline you can hover or tap for a short definition; that hint can be switched off in Settings.

guides.p1: A study guide is a reading path: the articles to read, in order, with one sentence saying what you will understand at the end, grouped into families (protocols and foundations, identity and security, application delivery, vendor platforms). Each path opens on its first article, and every article in it links back to the path, so you can leave and return without losing your place.
guides.p2: The certification guides are the same material arranged against a vendor exam: the exam's own code and objectives, with the articles and tools that cover each objective. They are reading plans, not exam dumps; where an objective has no coverage yet the guide says so in its place, and a build check fails if one is left silent, which is how the gaps stay visible when the exams change.
guides.p3: The page opens with the training series: fundamentals in order, one level at a time, each a set of modules with a stated outcome, its parts in reading order and the tools to practise on, and a page of its own that starts it. That makes five ways to read in order, each with its own job: a training series takes one level of a curriculum, module by module; an article series tells one subject from its opener through its parts; a reading path gathers published articles towards one understanding; a certification guide maps one exam's objectives to the articles that cover them; a story argues one case across several pieces.

hubs.p1: A vendor hub is one page per vendor family that gathers everything the site holds for it: the tools that decode or compute that vendor's formats, the articles grounded in its documentation, its place on the industry record and its lineage of acquisitions and renames. If you work on one platform all day, its hub is the page to bookmark.
hubs.p2: Where the author teaches a vendor's official courses, the hub says so and links the training page, which routes to Red Education; where he does not, the hub says nothing about teaching, by rule. Naming a vendor on this site is never a claim of a relationship with it.

industry.p1: The industry record is a chronology of the organizations that built networking and security, in the order their stories begin, each with its founding year, its sources and, where it applies, who bought whom and for how much. Six ways in sit before the list: follow a company, follow a lineage, explore an era, the Brazilian ecosystem, where the author's own path crossed it, and the people. Each is a filtered view with its own address, so it can be shared.
industry.p2: The career chapters are the author's own record, one chapter per company he worked inside or alongside, with the credentials of each; the people timeline runs from the voltaic pile to the present. A method page states the rules every entry follows (what counts as a source, what founded means, how an acquisition is recorded, what is done with an uncertain date) and names the build checks that enforce them. A correction route on the contact page is one click from every entry.

search.p1: The search field in the header, or Ctrl K, opens a dialog that searches tools, articles, guides and pages at once; the pills under the field narrow it to one kind. A hub's own field searches only that hub's world, and a section's field (The Practice, The Roles) only that section, with an Only in pill that one click widens again. Search runs in your browser against an index built with the site: the words you type are not sent anywhere, although the browser fetches from the site the parts of the index those words fall in.
search.p2: A handful of single-key shortcuts work on every page: press ? to see them, and rebind any of them in Settings. The human sitemap lists every page by world, for the times a map beats a search box.

privacy.h: Privacy and what stays on your device
privacy.p1: The site's own code sets no cookies and runs no third-party analytics or trackers; Cloudflare, which hosts the site, runs a bot check that may set up to two cookies of its own. Your theme, your language, your shortcut bindings, the glossary-hint preference and a short reading trail live in your browser's local storage, on your device only, and are never sent anywhere; clearing site data restores the defaults. The <privacy>Privacy page</privacy> lists every key the site writes, by name, what the server counts in aggregate, and what Cloudflare records and sets as the host.
privacy.p2: Pages are not stored for offline use (there is no service worker), so a page you have not opened needs the connection. On a catalogue tool's page that has loaded, the calculation itself makes no request; a few tools fetch their engine or a data table from the site the first time they run. A value handed from one page to a tool travels after the # in the address, a part your browser never sends; the <privacy>Privacy page</privacy> says what that does and does not hide. The stats page shows what is most read, from the aggregate counts; the colophon says how the site is built and what every number on it is computed from.

devOther.empty: No residents yet. The first tool that defies the definitions for a reason other than network egress moves in here - green walls, honest label.

subnetDrill.metaDescription: Timed subnetting practice: network and broadcast addresses, usable hosts, masks, prefix sizing, and containment, generated fresh each round with a remembered streak. Runs entirely in your browser.
subnetDrill.name: Subnetting drill
subnetDrill.blurb: Randomized CIDR practice with difficulty tiers and a streak your browser remembers.
subnetDrill.why: This tool lives in the green room because it GENERATES exercises (randomness) and REMEMBERS your streak (state) - two things the catalogue's fixed input-to-output tools do not do. The math it quizzes is the site's own CIDR engine.
subnetDrill.about1: Pick a difficulty and each round deals ten fresh questions drawn from a new random seed, so no two rounds repeat. The subnet arithmetic is computed by the same engine behind the CIDR tool, so every canonical answer is exactly what that tool would produce.
subnetDrill.about2: Your current streak, best streak, and lifetime score are kept in your browser's local storage and never leave it. Clear them any time with Reset; nothing here is uploaded or tracked.
subnetDrill.runsLocally: Everything - the questions, the grading, the score - happens in your browser. Nothing is generated on or sent to a server.

pcap.metaTitle: PCAP analyser - read a capture in your browser
pcap.metaDescription: Drop a .pcap or .pcapng and get an L2-L4 summary, conversation and top-talker tables, and first-tier anomaly flags - computed entirely in your browser, nothing uploaded.
pcap.name: PCAP analyser
pcap.blurb: Drop a capture and read it locally: protocols, conversations, talkers, and anomaly flags - nothing uploaded.
pcap.why: This tool lives in the green room because its input is a BINARY FILE, not the paste/form text the catalogue's tools take. That is an input contract the catalogue cannot hold yet; the day it can, this tool graduates to the main floor.
pcap.about1: Drop a capture file and it is read into memory and dissected in your browser: the container format (classic pcap in either byte order, including the nanosecond variant, and pcapng), then Ethernet through IPv4/IPv6 and TCP/UDP/ICMP - enough for the overview, the conversation and top-talker tables, and a first tier of anomaly flags stated as observations, not verdicts.
pcap.about2: This first version dissects layers 2 through 4. Application-payload parsing (DNS, TLS, HTTP details) is a deliberate future pass, not a hidden gap - the tool tells you the depth it reached. Files are capped at 50 MB because a browser is for triage, not multi-gigabyte forensics; larger captures are refused rather than freezing the tab.
pcap.dropHint: or click to choose a file - it never leaves your browser
pcap.runsLocally: The file is read into memory and dissected entirely in your browser. Nothing is uploaded; there is no server round-trip at all.
pcap.depthNote: This summary covers layers 2-4. Application-payload dissection (DNS/TLS/HTTP contents) is a future pass.

flags.highRst: {rst, plural, one {# RST packet} other {# RST packets}}, a high share of the capture: connections are being reset often.
flags.truncated: The file ended mid-record; the last packet was incomplete and parsing stopped there.
flags.singleConversation: The whole capture is a single conversation - a targeted capture, or a filter left applied.

errors.format: This does not look like a pcap or pcapng file (unrecognized magic).
errors.unsupported: That capture format is not supported yet.

fingerprint.metaTitle: Self-fingerprint inspector - what this page can read about you
fingerprint.metaDescription: See the browser and device signals a tracker could read to fingerprint you - user agent, screen, canvas and WebGL hashes, fonts, timezone and more - computed entirely in your browser and shown only to you.
fingerprint.name: Self-fingerprint inspector
fingerprint.blurb: The signals a tracker could read to identify your browser, shown only to you and computed only here.
fingerprint.why: This tool lives in the green room because its input is your BROWSER AND DEVICE - the output legitimately differs for every visitor, so there is no fixed correct answer for golden vectors to assert. It is the privacy thesis made visible.
fingerprint.intro: Click below and this page computes, in your browser, the signals a fingerprinting script would read. This tool sends none of it anywhere - the reading is shown only to you.
fingerprint.runsLocally: Every signal is computed in your browser and displayed here only. Nothing is uploaded, stored, or compared against anyone else.
fingerprint.entropyNote: About {n} of these signals are individually high-entropy - the more of them a tracker can read, the more uniquely they identify you. This is a rough indicator, not a precise bit count.
fingerprint.footer: Reload the page to discard this reading; the tool computed it in this tab and sent it nowhere.
fingerprint.about1: Fingerprinting does not need cookies. A script can combine your user agent, screen geometry, installed fonts, and the exact way your GPU renders a hidden canvas into an identifier that follows you across sites without any stored ID. This tool computes those same signals so you can see the surface for yourself.
fingerprint.about2: This tool runs locally and shows the reading only to you - it uploads and retains nothing. But that is a fact about the tool, not about the signals, and the difference is the real lesson. Your user agent and the other HTTP request headers, along with your TLS handshake (the basis of JA3 and JA4), are already sent to every server you connect to; passive fingerprinting is just servers reading what you send. Whether a given server keeps it is up to that server. The other signals here - the canvas and WebGL hashes, the font probe, the screen metrics - are not in the request at all; they sit in your browser until a script on a page you load reads them and sends them back. So the surface splits in two: what you broadcast on every connection, and what a script can collect if you let its page run.

webserial.metaTitle: WebSerial console - a browser terminal for console cables
webserial.metaDescription: A serial terminal in your browser for network gear: connect a USB console adapter, pick a baud rate, and read and send lines - all local, Chromium-only, nothing uploaded.
webserial.name: WebSerial console
webserial.blurb: A serial terminal in your browser - console into a switch or firewall over a USB adapter, nothing installed.
webserial.why: This tool lives in the green room because it uses the browser's serial hardware-permission API and holds a LIVE session - there is no fixed input and output to golden-vector. The catalogue's tools are pure functions; a live console is not.
webserial.runsLocally: This talks only between your browser and the connected device. Nothing is uploaded; the session lives in this tab and is gone on reload unless you download it.
webserial.unsupported: This browser does not support the Web Serial API.
webserial.unsupportedHint: Web Serial is available in Chromium-based browsers (Chrome, Edge, Opera) on desktop. Open this page there to use the console.
webserial.connectError: Could not open that port. Another program may be holding it, or the connection was cancelled.
webserial.consolePlaceholder: Session output will appear here once you connect to a port.
webserial.linePlaceholder: Type a command and press Enter
webserial.about1: Console access usually means installing a terminal program and hunting for the right COM port. The Web Serial API lets a browser talk to a USB-to-serial adapter directly, so you can console into a switch, router, or firewall from a locked-down machine with nothing installed - pick the baud rate, click connect, and the browser shows its own device picker.
webserial.about2: The console is Chromium-only and permission-gated by design: the browser, not this page, decides which device you grant access to. Nothing that scrolls by is stored or sent; the scrollback lives in memory and is discarded on reload unless you download it.
webserial.pasteHint: Paste a config block and send it line by line, with a delay so the console does not drop lines.
webserial.logStarted: Disk log started - every line is written to the chosen file as it arrives.
webserial.logStopped: Disk log stopped and file closed.
webserial.logUnsupported: Real-time disk logging needs the File System Access API (Chromium browsers - the same family Web Serial requires).
webserial.interactiveHint: Keys go to the device: Enter = line ending, Backspace = 0x7F, arrows = ANSI. Click outside to release.

devOut.metaDescription: The red room of ronutz.com: live lookups and a speed test against the real internet (RDAP registration data, the holder of an AS number, whether a password has appeared in a data breach, the bandwidth and latency of your connection), with the rules of engagement stated out loud. Your query or test data goes browser-direct to the official service named on screen; nothing is sent to ronutz.com servers.
devOut.title: /dev/out
devOut.intro: The main site's thesis is tools that compute, never guess: local, deterministic, zero egress. The tools in this room cannot keep that promise, because their whole job is to ask the live internet a question. So they live here, behind red walls, with the differences written on the door.

notice.title: How this room differs from the rest of the site
notice.p1: Tools here send something out of the browser: a query built from your input or, for the speed test, test data. Nothing is sent while you type or when a page opens: press Ask, or Enter in the field, to send the query displayed on screen, or Start to begin the speed test. What is sent goes directly from your browser to the official service named there (the registry or service that answers it), never to ronutz.com servers, which see nothing in this version. That service receives the query or the test data and the usual connection details, and its own privacy terms apply.
notice.p2: Results are the live world, not a computation. They come from third parties, can change between two identical queries or two runs, can be rate-limited or unavailable, and carry no golden-vector guarantee - the tested, deterministic parts here are the local computation (input parsing, registry routing, hashing, the speed test's plan and the formatting of its numbers), the construction of the query and the parsing of the response, and the tool shows which service it will ask, and exactly what, before anything is sent.
notice.p3: Everything else still holds. No account, no tracking by us, no ads, open source. The third party you query will see your request (that is how asking works) - its own terms and privacy policy apply to that hop, and each tool links the exact endpoint so you can inspect it.
notice.p4: The deep-red background is the marker: same darkness as the rest of the site, different hue, different rules. When the walls are red, you are in the room where packets leave.
notice.lead1: What leaves your browser, and when

rdapLookup.name: RDAP lookup
rdapLookup.blurb: WHOIS, the modern way: domain, IP, or AS number in, the official registry's structured answer out - asked directly from your browser, with the registry named before anything is sent.
rdapLookup.sends: a domain, an IP address or an AS number
rdapLookup.to: the official registry for it, named before sending

asnLookup.name: ASN lookup
asnLookup.blurb: Who holds an AS number: special-purpose ASNs answered locally with their RFC, real ones fetched browser-direct from the owning RIR - with the registry named before anything is sent.
asnLookup.sends: an AS number (special-purpose ones are answered locally, nothing sent)
asnLookup.to: the RIR that holds it, named before sending

pwnedPasswords.name: Pwned Passwords check
pwnedPasswords.blurb: Has a password appeared in a data breach? It is hashed on your device, and only the first five characters of its SHA-1 hash are sent, to the Pwned Passwords service of Have I Been Pwned, when you press Ask or Enter.
pwnedPasswords.sends: the first five characters of the password's SHA-1 hash
pwnedPasswords.to: the Pwned Passwords service of Have I Been Pwned

speedTest.name: Speed test
speedTest.blurb: Download and upload bandwidth, latency and jitter, idle and under load, measured from your browser against Cloudflare's speed test service with its open-source engine, when you press Start. Results logging is switched off: the numbers stay on the page.

dohLookup.name: DNS-over-HTTPS lookup
dohLookup.blurb: Ask a public resolver one DNS question over HTTPS, browser-direct: the query is built and shown byte by byte on your device, the resolver is named before anything is sent, and the answer is decoded with its flags and DNSSEC state.
dohLookup.sends: one DNS query, shown byte by byte first
dohLookup.to: the resolver you pick: Cloudflare, Google, Quad9, DNS.SB or Control D

rdap.metaTitle: RDAP lookup - WHOIS, the modern way
rdap.metaDescription: Query the official RDAP registries for a domain, IP address, or AS number, browser-direct. Deterministic routing from vendored IANA bootstrap snapshots; explicit-egress design: nothing leaves until you press Ask or Enter.
rdap.inputLabel: Domain, IP address, or AS number
rdap.nothingLeaves: Nothing is sent while you type: typing only computes, locally, which registry would answer. Press Ask, or Enter in this field, to send the displayed query directly to that registry; its privacy terms apply.
rdap.willAsk: This {kind} query would ask {registry} directly from your browser:
rdap.notFoundBody: The registry answered 404: no object by that name in its database. For a domain, that usually means it is not registered (or the registry does not publish it over RDAP).
rdap.httpErrorBody: That status comes from the registry, not from this site. It may be rate limiting, maintenance, or a query it will not serve. The same query from your own terminal:
rdap.netErrorTitle: The query could not complete from the browser
rdap.netErrorBody: Either the network failed, or the registry does not allow browser-direct queries (no CORS header: some registries, RIPE among them as of 2026-07-08, do not send one), or this page was served with a security policy other than the one it ships with, which the browser console reports as a Content Security Policy violation. This is a known limit of the browser-direct design: nothing was silently proxied. Run the identical query from your own terminal:
rdap.bootstrapNote: Registry routing is deterministic: it walks vendored snapshots of the four IANA RDAP bootstrap files (RFC 9224), vendored {vendored}; the dns table's own publication stamp is {dns}. The live answer, by design, is not deterministic, which is why this tool lives in the red room.

errors.empty: Enter a domain, an IP address, or an AS number.
errors.format: Could not read that as a domain, IP address, or AS number.
errors.noEndpoint: IANA's bootstrap registry publishes no RDAP endpoint for that - honest answer: this tool cannot ask anyone about it.

rdap.about1: RDAP is WHOIS rebuilt on HTTPS and JSON (RFCs 7480, 9082, 9083): the same registry data, structured, with consistent field names and honest redaction notices instead of free-form text. This tool resolves which registry is authoritative using vendored snapshots of IANA's bootstrap files (RFC 9224), builds the exact query URL, shows it, and only sends it when you press Ask or Enter: directly from your browser to the registry, never through ronutz.com. A special-purpose AS number or IP address (documentation, private, loopback, link-local, shared address space, multicast and the other IANA special-purpose blocks) is explained here and never sent.
rdap.about2: The deterministic layers (input classification, IDN punycode conversion, bootstrap routing, URL construction, response parsing) are golden-vector-tested like every tool on the main site. The one thing that cannot be pinned is the registry's live answer - which is exactly why this tool lives here and not at /tools.
rdap.timeoutTitle: The registry did not answer within 12 seconds
rdap.timeoutBody: The request was abandoned after 12 seconds without an answer. The registry may be slow or busy, or the path to it congested; nothing was proxied, and this says nothing about the name, address or number you asked about. The same query from your own terminal:
rdap.unreadableTitle: The registry answered HTTP {status}, but not with JSON
rdap.unreadableBody: An answer arrived, but its body could not be read as an RDAP JSON document, so nothing is shown as a result. The same query from your own terminal shows what came back:

cat.noFlag: special-purpose, with no Globally Reachable value

specialIp.row: The IANA {registry} Special-Purpose Address Space registry lists {prefix} as "{name}" ({rfc}).
specialIp.multicast: {range} is the multicast range, which IANA lists in a registry of its own.
specialIp.embedded: This IPv6 address carries the IPv4 address {ipv4}.
specialIp.why: Because the address is special-purpose, it is answered here from the IANA registry instead of being sent to a regional registry: there is no Ask, and nothing left the browser.
specialIp.source: The rows come from the IANA IPv4 and IPv6 Special-Purpose Address Space registries as the SSRF URL classifier carries them (read 2026-10-19; registries updated 2025-10-09).

asn.metaTitle: ASN lookup - who holds an AS number
asn.metaDescription: Type an AS number and see, before anything is sent, which regional registry would answer. Special-purpose ASNs (private, documentation, AS_TRANS, AS0) are explained locally with their RFC and never leave the browser; real ones are fetched browser-direct from the owning RIR when you press Ask or Enter.
asn.nothingLeaves: Nothing is sent while you type: typing only computes, locally, what kind of number this is and which registry would be asked. Press Ask, or Enter in this field, to send the displayed query directly to that registry; its privacy terms apply. Special-purpose numbers are answered here and never sent.
asn.willAsk: This would ask {registry} (browser-direct, never through ronutz.com):
asn.notFoundTitle: The registry has no object for this number
asn.notFoundBody: An HTTP 404 from the RIR means no autnum object is registered there for this number. That is the registry's honest answer, relayed unchanged.
asn.httpErrorBody: Shown verbatim rather than interpreted. You can run the same query from your own machine:
asn.netErrorTitle: The browser could not complete the request
asn.netErrorBody: This is a network failure, a registry that does not send CORS headers to browsers (RIPE, as of 2026-07-08, does not), or a page served with a security policy other than the one it ships with (the browser console names a Content Security Policy violation in that case). The page cannot tell the first two apart by design. The same query from your own machine:
asn.redirectNote: The bootstrap registry redirected this number to {host} - a national registry answering on the RIR's behalf. The browser followed the redirect; the answer above is theirs.
asn.provenance: Routing is decided locally against a vendored copy of the IANA RDAP bootstrap (asn.json publication {asnPub}, vendored {vendored}); special-purpose classification against the IANA Special-Purpose AS Numbers registry (accessed {specialAccessed}). Live answers come from the registries themselves and carry no golden-vector guarantee.
asn.about1: An Autonomous System number identifies a routing domain on the internet, and five regional registries hold the records of who each one belongs to. This tool classifies your input locally, and only for globally-assignable numbers builds the one URL that would answer - the owning RIR's RDAP autnum endpoint - showing it to you before anything is sent.
asn.about2: Two whole classes of answer never touch the network: special-purpose numbers (AS0, AS112, AS_TRANS, documentation and private ranges, the two reserved ends of the space) are explained with their RFC right here, and numbers falling in bootstrap gaps are reported as unallocated. An honest tool refuses to pretend a lookup where none exists.

special.body: This is a special-purpose AS number, set aside by {rfc}. No regional registry holds a delegation for it, so there is nothing to ask and no query will be made.
special.noEgress: Answered entirely locally - zero bytes left the browser.

unallocated.title: not delegated to any registry
unallocated.body: This number falls in a gap of the IANA bootstrap file: no RIR currently serves RDAP for it, which usually means the block is unallocated or not yet delegated. That is the answer; no query will be made.

errors.empty: Type an AS number.
errors.format: Not an AS number - accepted forms: AS15169, as 15169, the bare number, or dotted asdot notation such as 1.10.
errors.range: Beyond the 32-bit AS number space (the maximum is 4294967295).
errors.dotRange: In dotted notation (asdot or asdot+, RFC 5396) each part is a 16-bit value: the part before the dot and the part after it must each be 0 to 65535.
errors.dotEmpty: In dotted notation (asdot or asdot+, RFC 5396) both parts are needed: a number before the dot and a number after it, as in 1.10.

asn.dotted: {input} is dotted notation: {high} × 65536 + {low} = {asplain}. The registry lookup uses the asplain number.
asn.timeoutTitle: The registry did not answer within 12 seconds
asn.timeoutBody: The request was abandoned after 12 seconds without an answer. The registry may be slow or busy, or the path to it congested; nothing was proxied, and this says nothing about the number. The same query from your own machine:
asn.unreadableTitle: The registry answered HTTP {status}, but not with JSON
asn.unreadableBody: An answer arrived, but its body could not be read as an RDAP JSON document, so nothing is shown as a result. The same query from your own machine shows what came back:

pwned.metaTitle: Pwned Passwords check - has a password appeared in a breach
pwned.metaDescription: Check a password against the breached-password corpus of Have I Been Pwned without sending it: your browser hashes it with SHA-1, shows the five characters that would be sent before anything leaves, and compares the answer on your device when you press Ask or Enter.
pwned.nothingLeaves: Nothing is sent while you type: your browser hashes the password with SHA-1 here, on this device. Press Ask, or Enter in this field, to send only the first five characters of that hash to {host}, the Pwned Passwords service of Have I Been Pwned; its privacy terms apply. The password and the other 35 characters of the hash are never sent, stored or put in the page address.
pwned.noCrypto: This page cannot hash here: browsers offer Web Crypto only on pages served over HTTPS. Nothing has been hashed or sent.
pwned.keptValue: The password and the other 35 characters of the hash, which are compared here.
pwned.keptMasked: The 35 characters are masked while the password is hidden: the full SHA-1 of a common password can be looked up.
pwned.willAsk: This would ask {host} (browser-direct, never through ronutz.com):
pwned.foundTitle: Found: this password has been seen {count, plural, one {# time} other {# times}} in data breaches
pwned.foundBody: Its hash suffix is in the answer the service returned, so this password has appeared in at least one data breach, and passwords from earlier breaches are among the first that attackers try. Do not use it, and change it wherever it is used.
pwned.notFoundTitle: Not found: this password does not appear in Pwned Passwords
pwned.notFoundBody: Its hash suffix is not in the answer, so the password is not among those the service has loaded from breaches. That does not make it a strong password, only one not seen in those breaches.
pwned.rangeStats: The service answered prefix {prefix} with {lines, plural, one {# line} other {# lines}}: {real, plural, one {# hash} other {# hashes}} and {padded, plural, =0 {no padding} one {# padding line with a count of 0, discarded} other {# padding lines with a count of 0, discarded}}. The comparison was made on this device.
pwned.refusedTitle: The answer could not be read as a range of hashes
pwned.refusedBody: Nothing is shown as a result. The same request from your own machine shows what came back:

refused.empty: The body was empty, and every prefix has entries.
refused.tooLarge: The body was longer than the 2,000,000-character limit for a range answer.
refused.malformedLine: Line {line} is not a 35-character hexadecimal suffix, a colon and a count.
refused.duplicate: Line {line} repeats a hash that already had a count.

pwned.httpErrorBody: Shown verbatim rather than interpreted. The service documents HTTP 200 for every prefix, so this is not an answer about the password. The same request from your own machine:
pwned.netErrorTitle: The browser could not complete the request
pwned.netErrorBody: This is a network failure, a block on the way (a firewall, a proxy or a browser extension), or a page served with a security policy other than the one it ships with (the browser console names a Content Security Policy violation in that case). The service sends CORS headers to every origin (measured on 2026-10-26), so a missing one is unlikely. Nothing was proxied. The same request from your own machine:
pwned.timeoutTitle: The service did not answer within 12 seconds
pwned.timeoutBody: The request was abandoned after 12 seconds without an answer; nothing was proxied, and this says nothing about the password. The same request from your own machine:
pwned.unreadableTitle: The service answered HTTP {status}, but the body could not be read
pwned.unreadableBody: An answer arrived but could not be read as text, so nothing is shown as a result. The same request from your own machine:
pwned.provenance: Hashing (Web Crypto SHA-1 over the password's UTF-8 bytes), the split into five sent and 35 kept characters, the reading of the answer and the comparison run on this device and are pinned by golden vectors. The endpoint, the padding header and the answer's format follow the service's API documentation, read {accessed}. The live answer carries no golden-vector guarantee.
pwned.about1: Pwned Passwords is the corpus of passwords that Have I Been Pwned has collected from data breaches, each stored as the SHA-1 hash of the password's UTF-8 bytes. Its range search applies k-anonymity: a client sends only the first five characters of a hash and receives every suffix in the corpus that begins with them, each with the number of times it has been seen, so the comparison happens on the client and the service cannot tell which password, among all those sharing the prefix, was checked.
pwned.about2: This page asks with padding on, the Add-Padding: true header the documentation describes: the service then adds lines with a count of 0, so that the size of the encrypted answer does not give the prefix away to someone watching the traffic, and this page discards those lines before comparing. Because a custom header needs the service's permission, the browser first sends a CORS preflight to the same address, carrying the same five characters and nothing more. The request carries no cookies and no Referer header, is never cached, and is sent once, when you press Ask or Enter. The documentation warns that checking while a password is still being typed can let someone who sees the requests arriving at the service work the password out; this page sends nothing while you type.
pwned.about3: The email search of Have I Been Pwned is not offered here. Searching by address needs an API key that comes with a subscription, its k-anonymity range mode included, and the service asks that such a key is never used from a browser page, where every visitor could read it; the direct search would also send the whole address. Pwned Passwords needs no key, has no rate limit according to its documentation, and accepts requests from any website, which is why it can run here.
pwned.attributionNote: The service sets no licence or attribution requirement on the Pwned Passwords API and welcomes attribution, which is given here.

speed.metaTitle: Speed test - bandwidth, latency and jitter, measured from your browser
speed.metaDescription: Measure download and upload bandwidth, latency and jitter, idle and under load, with Cloudflare's open-source speed test engine, run from your browser against speed.cloudflare.com only when you press Start. Packet loss is left out, results logging is switched off, and the numbers stay on the page.
speed.planHostValue: {host}, Cloudflare's speed test service, reached straight from your browser and never through ronutz.com
speed.planRequestsValue: {latency} empty requests to time the round trip, up to {downloads} downloads of {downMin} to {downMax} and up to {uploads} uploads of {upMin} to {upMax}, in {steps} steps, plus an empty request every {throttleMs} ms while a download or upload runs
speed.planVolumeValue: {down} down and {up} up. Each direction stops growing once even the quickest request of a size takes longer than a second, so a slower connection moves less.
speed.planLoggingValue: Off. By default the engine reports each finished test to {url}; this page switches that off, so the results stay here.
speed.planNotMeasuredValue: Packet loss, which needs a TURN server, and no grade or score (both explained below).
speed.willSend: Start sends, browser-direct and never through ronutz.com:
speed.privacy: Nothing is sent until you press Start. Then your browser exchanges test data with {host}, Cloudflare's speed test service, and with nothing else: empty requests, downloads, and uploads filled with the character 0. Cloudflare sees your IP address, as any server you connect to does, and this site's address without the page (the Origin and Referer headers); no cookie is sent. Cloudflare's own privacy statement for its speed test applies, and is summarized below. The results are not reported to anyone: they stay on this page, and leaving it forgets them.
speed.loadingNote: Loading the engine's code from this site. Nothing has been sent to the speed test service yet.
speed.stoppedAt: Stopped at step {index} of {total} ({what}); nothing more is sent.
speed.stoppedBeforeSend: Stopped before the engine started: nothing was sent to the speed test service.
speed.progressNote: Larger sizes in a direction are skipped once even the quickest request of a size takes longer than {seconds, plural, one {# second} other {# seconds}}, so the bar can jump and the test can end before the last step.

step.latency: {count, plural, one {# empty request} other {# empty requests}} to time the round trip
step.download: {count, plural, one {# download} other {# downloads}} of {size}
step.upload: {count, plural, one {# upload} other {# uploads}} of {size}

speed.resultsRunning: Measuring: the values update as requests complete
speed.resultsStopped: Stopped before the end: these values are incomplete
speed.resultsStay: These values exist only on this page: nothing is sent anywhere, and leaving or reloading the page forgets them.

fail.loadTitle: The test engine could not be loaded
fail.loadBody: Its code is a separate file from this site, fetched when you press Start, and that download failed: the connection may be offline, or the site may have been updated since this page was opened (reloading the page fixes that). Nothing was sent to the speed test service.
fail.rateLimitedTitle: The speed test service asked the test to slow down (HTTP 429)
fail.rateLimitedBody: The engine waited and retried three times, as long as the service's Retry-After header asked, and then stopped. No values are shown: an interrupted run is not a measurement. Try again later.
fail.httpTitle: The speed test service answered with HTTP {status}
fail.httpBody: The engine stops on any answer other than success, and no values are shown: an interrupted run is not a measurement.
fail.networkTitle: The browser could not reach the speed test service
fail.networkBody: This is a network failure, a block on the way (a firewall, a proxy or a browser extension), or a page served with a security policy other than the one it ships with (the browser console names a Content Security Policy violation in that case). The service answers requests from every website (measured on 2026-10-27), so a missing CORS header is unlikely. No values are shown.

speed.defsTitle: What each number means (the engine's definitions)

defs.bandwidth: Bandwidth in bits per second. Each request's rate is its size in bits divided by its duration, without the server's own processing time; requests shorter than {minMs} ms are left out, and the value shown is the {percentile}th percentile of the rest (a high value among them, not the average).
defs.latency: The round trip of an empty request while nothing else transfers: the time from sending the request to the first byte of the final answer (an interim 1xx answer does not count), without the server's own processing time. The value shown is the median.
defs.jitter: The average difference between consecutive round trips, so it needs at least two.
defs.loaded: The same round trip and jitter, measured by empty requests sent every {throttleMs} ms while downloads or uploads run, counting only sizes whose requests take at least {minMs} ms and keeping the last {maxPoints}.
defs.units: Rates in bits per second with SI prefixes (1 Mbit/s is 1,000,000 bit/s), times in milliseconds, sizes in SI bytes (1 MB is 1,000,000 bytes).

speed.provenance: The plan, its totals, the progress line, the formatting and the reading of the engine's values run on this device and are pinned by golden vectors, which also check that the plan and every setting quoted here are the engine's own. The engine is @cloudflare/speedtest {version}; its README and code were read on {accessed}. The measurements themselves carry no golden-vector guarantee.
speed.about1: The engine is @cloudflare/speedtest, the open-source code that makes the measurements of Cloudflare's own speed test at speed.cloudflare.com, run here in your browser. It sends requests to Cloudflare's network and reads their timings from the browser's Resource Timing interface, which a browser exposes for another site's requests only when that site allows it; the service does, for every website (its Timing-Allow-Origin: * header, measured on 2026-10-27).
speed.about2: By default the engine reports each finished test to Cloudflare; its README says the results are collected "for the purpose of calculating aggregated insights regarding Internet connection quality". The engine's configuration documents a switch for this report (logAimApiUrl: "Set to null to disable"), and this page sets it, as well as the per-measurement log, which is already off by default. Nothing about your result is sent: the numbers exist only on this page.
speed.about3: Cloudflare's privacy statement for its speed test, written for speed.cloudflare.com, says that Cloudflare receives the IP address you connect from, uses it to estimate your location at country and city level and to identify your network's Autonomous System Number, shares anonymized measurement information such as that location and network with measurement partners but not your IP address, and truncates the address it receives to /24 for IPv4 or /48 for IPv6 (read on 2026-10-27). This page sends no results, so what Cloudflare receives from it is the test traffic itself. The answers to the download requests carry, in their headers, the IP address Cloudflare saw and its estimate of your country, city, postal code, coordinates and network, which this page neither reads nor shows; they also carry a Network Error Logging policy, so a browser that supports it may report every failed request to the service, and about one in a hundred successful ones, to Cloudflare at a.nel.cloudflare.com (both measured on 2026-10-27). That instruction comes from Cloudflare's headers, not from this page, and the reports go to Cloudflare, never to ronutz.com.
speed.about4: Packet loss is not measured. The engine measures it by sending UDP packets through a WebRTC relay (a TURN server) and counting those that do not come back, and the README of this version says that "Packet loss is opt-in: it is not part of the default measurements, and it needs your own TURN server configuration." This site runs no TURN server, so the plan has no packet-loss step, and no WebRTC connection is opened.
speed.about5: Nor does the page grade the connection. The engine can turn its measurements into Cloudflare's Aggregated Internet Measurement scores, from bad to great for streaming, gaming and video calls, but packet loss is an input to all three, and the README of this version says that without a packet-loss measurement "packet loss is left out of the scores, so they come out lower than for a connection measured with under 5% loss." The point thresholds also live in the engine's code, not in Cloudflare's published description of the scores. So the page shows the measurements and their definitions, and leaves the judgement to you.
speed.about6: The numbers describe the path between your browser and the Cloudflare data centre that answers, at the moment of the test and with whatever else your connection carried at the same time; they say nothing about any other destination.
