doh.metaTitle: DNS-over-HTTPS lookup - ask a public resolver, read the wire format
doh.metaDescription: Build a DNS query in wire format, see its bytes and the exact RFC 8484 GET or POST before anything is sent, then ask Cloudflare, Google, Quad9, DNS.SB or Control D from your browser and read the decoded answer: response code, header flags, sections with TTLs, EDNS options and the DNSSEC state the resolver reports.
doh.about1: DNS over HTTPS (RFC 8484) carries one DNS message, in the binary wire format of classic DNS, inside an HTTPS exchange. With GET the query rides in the URL as the dns parameter, in base64url without padding, and the answer comes back as application/dns-message with a successful HTTP status, whatever the DNS response code.

aboutQuery.lead: What this page puts in the query.
aboutQuery.body: ID 0, which RFC 8484 recommends so that equal queries share an HTTP cache entry; RD; AD, so that the resolver reports what it validated; and, as you choose, CD and an EDNS(0) record with the DO bit and padding to a multiple of 128 octets (RFC 8467). The octets and the exact URL show before anything is sent.

aboutWhy.body: A web page can read another site's answer only when that site allows it with a CORS header. On 2026-10-27 Cloudflare, Google, Quad9, DNS.SB and Control D each answered a DoH GET with access-control-allow-origin: * and each documents its endpoint; several other public resolvers left that header out, so a web page cannot read their answers (dig and curl can).

aboutGet.body: A GET whose only extra header is Accept needs no CORS preflight, and RFC 8484 calls GET friendlier to many HTTP caches. A POST carries the query unchanged as its body, but its Content-Type, application/dns-message, makes the browser ask the resolver first with an OPTIONS request. On 2026-10-27 Cloudflare, DNS.SB and Control D allowed it and Google and Quad9 did not, so POST is offered for those three.

aboutSees.body: The name and type you ask about, your IP address and the usual connection details, under its own privacy terms; to answer, it may ask the zone's own servers about the name. The request carries no cookies and no Referer header, bypasses the browser's cache, and is sent once, when you press Ask or Enter; a POST's preflight, sent just before it, carries no part of the query.

aboutDnssec.body: HTTPS hides the question from the network path, not from the resolver. RFC 8484 calls DoH and DNSSEC independent protocols, each solving a different problem: the AD bit shown here is the resolver's statement, not a validation done on this page.

doh.inputLabel: Name to look up (or an IP address, for PTR)
doh.resolverIs: {service} is {operatedBy}; this page connects to {host} and nowhere else.

resolverNote.cloudflare: Its FAQ says 1.1.1.1 validates DNSSEC and does not send client IP information (EDNS Client Subnet) to authoritative servers; its privacy page commits to keeping no source IP address in non-volatile storage, beyond a sample of at most 0.05% of traffic for troubleshooting and attack mitigation, and to deleting its logs within 25 hours (read 2026-10-27).
resolverNote.google: Google's security page says Google Public DNS validates DNSSEC; its EDNS Client Subnet guidelines describe the resolver sending partial client IP address information to authoritative servers that support it; its privacy page describes temporary logs with the IP address, deleted within 24 to 48 hours, and permanent logs without it (read 2026-10-27).
resolverNote.quad9: This is Quad9's recommended service: its page lists malware blocking and DNSSEC validation, and for a malicious host the resolver "refuses to answer with the IP address"; its privacy policy says Quad9 does not collect or record users' IP addresses (read 2026-10-27).
resolverNote.dnssb: Its DoH page lists this endpoint as the global CDN one, with no logging and DNSSEC enabled; its FAQ says DNS.SB validates DNSSEC, sends no EDNS Client Subnet and blocks or filters no domains except for legal requirements; its privacy policy says it does not record the domains queried, the IP address or the time of a query (read 2026-10-27).
resolverNote.controld: This is the Unfiltered resolver of Control D's free DNS, "Nothing blocked" in its own words: its Free DNS Resolvers page lists this endpoint and says the free resolvers store no logs (no individual browsing history, timestamps or query logs), but does not say whether they validate DNSSEC; its answers for example.com, a signed name, carried AD when probed on 2026-10-27. Its privacy policy covers Control D's website and platform in general (read 2026-10-27).

doh.ednsSwitch: EDNS(0), with the query padded to a multiple of 128 octets
doh.cdSwitch: Checking disabled (CD bit): ask the resolver not to validate
doh.nothingLeaves: Nothing is sent while you type or choose. Ask, or Enter in the name field, sends the request shown below once, from your browser straight to {host}, never through ronutz.com{method, select, POST {; for a POST, your browser sends the preflight shown first} other {}}.

invalid.nonAscii: Only ASCII is accepted: enter an internationalized name as its A-label (the xn-- form). Nothing is sent.
invalid.badCharacter: The label "{label}" holds a character other than letters, digits, hyphen and underscore (a lone * is allowed, as a wildcard). Nothing is sent.
invalid.emptyLabel: The name has an empty label (two dots in a row, or a leading dot). Nothing is sent.
invalid.labelTooLong: The label "{label}" is longer than 63 characters, the most a DNS label holds (RFC 1035, section 2.3.4). Nothing is sent.
invalid.nameTooLong: The name is longer than 255 octets in wire form, the most a DNS name holds (RFC 1035, section 2.3.4). Nothing is sent.
invalid.addressNeedsPtr: This is an IP address: choose the PTR type to look up the name it points back to (the page builds the in-addr.arpa or ip6.arpa name for you). Nothing is sent.

doh.planHeaderValue: ID 0 (RFC 8484 asks for 0, so that equal queries share an HTTP cache entry), opcode QUERY, flags {flags}
doh.planEdnsOn: an OPT record: payload size 4096, {dnssec, select, yes {DO set (DNSSEC records wanted)} other {DO clear}}, and the Padding option filling the query to a multiple of 128 octets (RFC 8467)
doh.planEdnsOff: none: no OPT record, so no DO bit, no padding and no Extended DNS Error in the answer
doh.rawQuery: What the query holds: its fields and its {count} octets
doh.rawQueryNote: These octets are the DNS message itself. A GET carries them in the dns parameter, in base64url without padding; a POST sends them unchanged as its body (RFC 8484, section 6). AD is set in the query so that the resolver reports what it validated (RFC 6840, section 5.7).
doh.willAsk: This would ask {host} (browser-direct, never through ronutz.com):
doh.httpNote: RFC 8484 uses a successful HTTP status for every DNS answer, NXDOMAIN and SERVFAIL included, so the DNS response code below is what says whether the question succeeded. The request bypassed the browser's cache, so the TTLs below are as the resolver sent them.
doh.noQuestion: The answer carries no question section (QDCOUNT 0), which RFC 9619 tells middleboxes not to treat as malformed; nothing else in it contradicts the question asked.
doh.pointers: {count, plural, =0 {No name in this answer uses compression.} one {One compression pointer in this answer points a name back to an earlier one (RFC 1035, section 4.1.4).} other {# compression pointers in this answer point names back to earlier ones (RFC 1035, section 4.1.4).}}

qr.clear: this message is a query, not a response.

aa.set: authoritative answer: the data comes from a server authoritative for the zone. A recursive resolver sets it only for names it serves itself, such as its own discovery records.
aa.clear: not authoritative: the resolver answered from its cache or from what it asked the zone's servers on your behalf, which is normal for a recursive resolver.

tc.set: truncated: the message is incomplete and records may be missing. Over HTTPS a message may be up to 65,535 octets (RFC 8484, section 6), so a resolver rarely needs this.
tc.clear: not truncated: the message is complete.

rd.set: recursion desired, copied from the query: this page asked the resolver to resolve the name fully.
rd.clear: not copied back, although this page set recursion desired in the query.

ra.set: recursion available: the resolver resolves names on behalf of this client.
ra.clear: recursion not available: the resolver says it does not recurse for this question, so the answer comes only from data it holds itself.

ad.set: authentic data: the resolver says it validated every RRset in the answer and authority sections with DNSSEC (RFC 4035, section 3.2.3).
ad.clear: not marked authentic: the zone is not signed, the resolver did not validate the answer, or the query set CD.

cd.set: checking disabled, copied from the query: the resolver was asked not to validate, and should return the data even if it would fail validation (RFC 4035, section 3.2.2).
cd.clear: checking enabled: the resolver was free to validate; what each resolver documents about DNSSEC is on its card, under Resolvers offered.

doh.dnssecTitle: DNSSEC, as the resolver reports it

dnssec.validated: Validated: the resolver set AD, its statement that it checked the signatures from a trust anchor down to this answer. It is the resolver's word, carried over an authenticated HTTPS connection: RFC 8484 (section 9) leaves it to the client to validate answers itself or to trust the resolver's AD bit.
dnssec.notValidated: Not validated: AD is clear. Either the zone is not signed, which makes the answer insecure rather than failed, or the resolver did not validate this answer. Turn on DNSSEC records (DO) to see whether signatures come back.
dnssec.checkingDisabled: Checking disabled: this query set CD, so the resolver was told not to validate, and AD says nothing either way. Without CD, a resolver must answer SERVFAIL for data that fails validation; with CD, it should return the data (RFC 4035, section 3.2.2). Asking twice, with and without CD, tells a validation failure apart from other failures.
dnssec.servfailHint: SERVFAIL with checking enabled. A validating resolver answers SERVFAIL when data fails validation (RFC 4035, section 3.2.2), but SERVFAIL has other causes too, such as authoritative servers that cannot be reached. Ask again with Checking disabled (CD): if the data then arrives, validation is the likely cause. An Extended DNS Error, when the resolver sends one, names the reason.

doh.signatures: {count, plural, =0 {No RRSIG records in the answer and authority sections} one {One RRSIG record in the answer and authority sections} other {# RRSIG records in the answer and authority sections}}{asked, select, yes {; the query set DO, asking for them.} other {; the query did not set DO, so a resolver normally leaves them out.}}
doh.dnssecLab: DNSSEC end to end, with the chain-of-trust lab
doh.digBuilder: dig command builder, which also writes the dig +https form

negative.nxdomain: A resolver may cache this negative answer for {ttl, plural, one {{ttl} second} other {{ttl} seconds}}: the smaller of the TTL ({soaTtl}) and the MINIMUM field ({minimum}) of the SOA record of {isRoot, select, yes {the root zone} other {the zone {zone}}} (RFC 2308, section 5).
negative.nodata: The response code is NOERROR, but the answer section holds no {type} record. A resolver may cache this negative answer for {ttl, plural, one {{ttl} second} other {{ttl} seconds}}: the smaller of the TTL ({soaTtl}) and the MINIMUM field ({minimum}) of the SOA record of {isRoot, select, yes {the root zone} other {the zone {zone}}} (RFC 2308, section 5).

doh.compactDenial: Compact denial of existence: an NSEC record in the authority section lists the NXNAME type, which says this name does not exist at all, although the response code is NOERROR. Zones signed on the fly can answer for a nonexistent name this way, as if it existed with no data (RFC 9824).
doh.truncated: TC is set: this message is incomplete, so a missing record proves nothing.
doh.ednsNote: The payload size matters only to DNS over UDP: a DoH server must ignore it in a query (RFC 8484, section 6), and a message over HTTPS arrives whole either way.
doh.paddingNote: The resolver added {padding, plural, one {{padding} octet} other {{padding} octets}} of padding (RFC 7830), so that the encrypted answer's size says less about the question; RFC 8467 recommends padding answers to a multiple of 468 octets, and this one is {size, number} octets.
doh.ednsDropped: No OPT record: this page sent one, and the resolver answered without EDNS(0), so it reported no DO bit, no padding and no Extended DNS Error. RFC 6891 (section 6.1.1) says a compliant responder includes an OPT record when the query carried one.
doh.ednsNotAsked: No OPT record: this page sent none (EDNS(0) is off), and RFC 6891 (section 7) says a responder must not include one then.

note.nullMx: A null MX: preference 0 and the root as the exchange say that this domain accepts no mail (RFC 7505).
note.caaCritical: The critical flag (128) is set: a certification authority must not issue for the name if it does not understand this property's tag (RFC 8659, section 4.1).
note.keySep: Secure Entry Point flag set (flags 257): by convention the key the parent zone's DS record points at, commonly called the KSK. RFC 4034 (section 2.1.1) calls the flag a hint: validators must not change their behaviour because of it.
note.keyZone: Zone key without the Secure Entry Point flag (flags 256): commonly called a ZSK, the key that signs the zone's other records.
note.keyRevoked: The REVOKE flag is set: a resolver that sees it in a self-signed DNSKEY set must no longer use this key as a trust anchor (RFC 5011).
note.nxname: The type list includes NXNAME: this record says that the name does not exist (compact denial of existence, RFC 9824).
note.optOut: The Opt-Out flag is set: this NSEC3 record may cover unsigned delegations (RFC 5155, section 3.1.2.1).
note.aliasMode: Priority 0 is AliasMode: the record aliases the service to its target name (RFC 9460, section 2.4.2).
note.ttlTopBit: The TTL arrived with its top bit set, which RFC 2181 (section 8) says to read as zero.

doh.malformedRecord: This record's data does not have the shape its type defines, so it is shown in the generic form of RFC 3597 (\# and its length, then the octets in hex) instead of being guessed at.

summary.aliasOnly: An alias (CNAME), with no {type} record at its end

doh.signedBy: {count, plural, one {One signature} other {# signatures}} (RRSIG) by {isRoot, select, yes {the root zone} other {{signer}}}, key tag {tag}, valid until {until}
doh.wireTitle: The answer is not a well-formed DNS message

wire.tooShort: It is shorter than the 12 octets of a DNS header.
wire.tooLarge: It is longer than the 65,535 octets a DNS message over HTTPS may have (RFC 8484, section 6).
wire.truncatedName: A name runs past the end of the message (at octet {offset}).
wire.badLabelType: A label uses a reserved label type (at octet {offset}).
wire.badPointer: A compression pointer does not point back before the name it belongs to (at octet {offset}); a pointer forward, or onto itself, could make a reader loop.
wire.tooManyPointers: A name follows more than 127 compression pointers (at octet {offset}).
wire.nameTooLong: A name is longer than 255 octets (at octet {offset}).
wire.truncatedRecord: A question or record runs past the end of the message (at octet {offset}).
wire.trailingBytes: Octets are left over after the last record the header counts (from octet {offset}).
wire.optNotRoot: An OPT record is owned by a name other than the root (at octet {offset}).
wire.optOutsideAdditional: An OPT record sits outside the additional section (at octet {offset}).
wire.multipleOpt: The message carries a second OPT record (at octet {offset}).
wire.badOption: An EDNS option runs past the end of its OPT record (at octet {offset}).

doh.wireBody: Nothing is shown as an answer. The same request from your own machine, saving the binary answer to answer.bin:
doh.mismatchTitle: The message does not answer this question

mismatch.notResponse: QR is clear: it is a query, not a response.
mismatch.opcode: Its opcode is not QUERY, the only one this page sends.
mismatch.id: Its ID is not 0, the ID this page sent.
mismatch.multipleQuestions: It carries more than one question, which RFC 9619 says must be treated as an incorrectly formatted message.
mismatch.otherQuestion: Its question is not the one this page asked: the name, the type or the class differs.

doh.httpErrorBody: Shown verbatim, not interpreted. Under RFC 8484 (section 4.2.1), a response with a non-successful HTTP status carries no answer to the DNS question; a DNS failure such as NXDOMAIN or SERVFAIL would have come with a successful status. The same request from your own machine, saving the answer to answer.bin:
doh.notDnsTitle: The resolver answered HTTP {status} with something other than a DNS message
doh.notDnsBody: Its Content-Type was {type}; this page reads application/dns-message only (RFC 8484, section 6), so nothing is shown as an answer. The same request from your own machine, saving the answer to answer.bin:
doh.tooLargeTitle: The answer is larger than a DNS message can be
doh.tooLargeBody: More than 65,535 octets were announced or delivered, so the answer was not read. The same request from your own machine, saving the answer to answer.bin:
doh.netErrorTitle: The browser could not complete the request
doh.netErrorBody: This is a network failure, a block on the way (a firewall, a proxy or a browser extension), or a page served with a security policy other than the one it ships with (the browser console names a Content Security Policy violation in that case). All five resolvers sent the CORS header a browser needs when probed on 2026-10-27, and the three offered with POST passed its preflight, so a missing one is unlikely. Nothing was proxied. The same request from your own machine, saving the binary answer to answer.bin:
doh.timeoutTitle: The resolver did not answer within 12 seconds
doh.timeoutBody: The request was abandoned after 12 seconds without an answer; nothing was proxied, and this says nothing about the name. The same request from your own machine, saving the binary answer to answer.bin:
doh.unreadableTitle: The resolver answered HTTP {status}, but the body could not be read
doh.unreadableBody: An answer arrived but could not be read, so nothing is shown as a result. The same request from your own machine, saving the binary answer to answer.bin:
doh.provenance: Building the query and decoding the answer run on this device and are pinned by golden vectors, among them dig's own encoding of the same queries and its decoding of 28 recorded answers. The endpoints, their CORS behaviour and their privacy terms were read and probed on {accessed}; the live answer carries no golden-vector guarantee.

doh.preflightName: CORS preflight, sent by your browser first
doh.preflightNote: It carries no part of the query. The POST follows only if the answer has a 2xx status, an access-control-allow-origin that admits the page, and content-type among the headers its access-control-allow-headers lists (WHATWG Fetch); for later POSTs the browser may reuse that answer for as long as access-control-max-age allows, 5 seconds when the resolver sends none.

glossary.title: Glossary
glossary.tagline: The field's terms, acronyms, expressions, jargon, and lore - defined, sourced, and linked to the tools that compute them.
glossary.disputedNote: A popular version of this story is inaccurate - see the note above.

the-hacker-manifesto.def: A short 1986 essay, written after its author's arrest, that became the defining statement of hacker curiosity.
the-hacker-manifesto.context: Published in Phrack under the handle The Mentor, it frames hacking as a hunger to understand rather than to harm, and its line about being judged for curiosity resonated widely. It remains the most quoted text in hacker culture, for better and worse.
the-hacker-manifesto.depth:
The Conscience of a Hacker was written in 1986 by Loyd Blankenship, under the handle The Mentor, shortly after his arrest, and published in Phrack. It is short, adolescent in tone, and has been reprinted more than almost anything else in the culture.

Its argument is about curiosity meeting institutions. The narrator describes being bored by school that rewards memorization, finding a computer that responds to what he actually does, and discovering a world of people who care about the same things. The famous line, that his crime is curiosity, positions the whole text as a defence of exploration against a society that reads exploration as trespass.

It deserves to be taken seriously and read critically, and both at once. The account of what draws people to computers is genuinely true and explains a great deal about the field's culture. The framing of unauthorized access as pure intellectual inquiry elides real harm to real people, which the text simply does not engage with, and the romanticism has been used since to excuse things that were not curiosity at all. It is a primary document of a culture, not a settled ethics.

the-gnu-manifesto.def: Richard Stallman's 1985 call to build a free Unix-compatible operating system that anyone could share and change.
the-gnu-manifesto.context: It launched the GNU Project and articulated the free-software ethic - that users should be free to run, study, modify, and redistribute software. The tools it produced, combined years later with the Linux kernel, became the operating system running much of the internet.
the-gnu-manifesto.depth:
Richard Stallman published the GNU Manifesto in 1985 to explain why he was building a free replacement for Unix. The argument is not that software should be inexpensive; it is that a user who cannot read, modify and share the software running their machine is subject to whoever can.

The reasoning is deliberately about power rather than economics. Proprietary software creates a dependency in which the user must ask permission to fix or understand a tool they rely on, and the manifesto treats that as an ethical problem before a practical one. The GPL implements the position: it grants freedoms and requires that anyone redistributing preserves them, which is why it is called copyleft, and it uses copyright law against the outcome copyright normally produces.

Its influence is easier to see forty years on than the argument itself. GNU tools plus the Linux kernel became the operating system of the internet, and the licence created the conditions for an enormous commons. The permissive licences that later dominated deliberately dropped the reciprocity requirement, which is a genuine philosophical disagreement rather than a simplification, and it is still live every time a company builds on open source without contributing back.

the-cathedral-and-the-bazaar.def: Eric Raymond's 1997 essay contrasting closed, top-down development with open, community-driven development.
the-cathedral-and-the-bazaar.context: The 'cathedral' is software built quietly by a small anointed group; the 'bazaar' is the noisy, open Linux model where anyone can contribute and releases are frequent. It popularized open-source development to a business audience and coined Linus's Law about many eyes making bugs shallow.
the-cathedral-and-the-bazaar.depth:
Eric Raymond's 1997 essay contrasted two development models: the cathedral, where code is crafted by a small group and released finished, and the bazaar, where development happens in public with frequent releases and many contributors. Linux was the evidence that the second could work.

Its practical claims became standard practice. Release early and release often, treat users as co-developers, and the line about many eyeballs making bugs shallow all entered the vocabulary through this essay, and it substantially influenced how businesses came to see open source. It also helped coin open source as a term deliberately separate from free software, framing the practice as a superior development method rather than an ethical position, which is the split with the GNU tradition that has never closed.

Read now, its central optimism needs the corrections that experience supplied. The bazaar produces excellent results where enough motivated, capable people show up, and it produces abandoned repositories and unmaintained critical infrastructure where they do not, which Heartbleed demonstrated. The essay describes a mechanism accurately and understates how much depends on the conditions that let the mechanism run.

kevin-mitnick.def: The American hacker whose social engineering of telephone and technology companies made him the most notorious computer intruder of the 1990s; a fugitive from 1992, arrested in North Carolina in 1995 and released in 2000, he spent the rest of his life as a penetration tester, author and teacher of security awareness, and died in 2023.
kevin-mitnick.context: Mitnick broke into corporate networks largely by manipulating people rather than machines, became a fugitive, and was arrested in 1995 after a high-profile hunt. He later reinvented himself as a security consultant and author, making 'the human is the weakest link' a lasting lesson.
kevin-mitnick.depth:
Why he matters. Kevin Mitnick was the defining computer criminal of the American 1990s and then, for more than two decades, one of the best-known teachers of what he had done. His importance to security lies less in any technical exploit than in what his career showed: that the controls of large telephone and technology companies could be walked around by someone who telephoned the right employee with the right story. In March 2000, six weeks out of federal prison, he told a United States Senate committee that his access to Motorola, Nokia, AT&T and Sun had depended on the willingness of people to bypass policies and procedures that had been in place for years, that verification by voice mail and fax was the weak link, and that comprehensive user training mattered more than new policy. Security awareness training has made the same argument ever since.

Beginnings and the first conviction. He was born on 6 August 1963 and grew up in the Los Angeles area, reaching computers through the phone phreaks. By his own testimony he was largely self-taught, and in 1985 he graduated in computer systems and programming from a technical college in Los Angeles whose administrators, finding that he was hacking their machines, asked him to design security enhancements instead. In 1979, at 16, he got into the Ark, the Digital Equipment Corporation (DEC) system used to develop the RSTS/E operating system, by telephoning DEC as a member of its development team. His first national attention came from obtaining manuals for Pacific Bell's COSMOS (Computer Systems for Mainframe Operations); the Associated Press (AP) recorded that he was first arrested at 17 for walking into a Pacific Bell office and taking manuals and door-lock codes, and spent a year in a rehabilitation centre. In 1988 he pleaded guilty in federal court to hacking into DEC computers, stealing proprietary software and using unauthorized access devices, and was sentenced to twelve months in prison and three years of supervised release.

The fugitive years. Near the end of that supervised release he hacked into Pacific Bell voice-mail computers together with a previously convicted associate; a warrant was issued and he went underground in 1992. The Department of Justice's account of the next two and a half years describes unauthorized access to dozens of networks, cloned cellular phones used to hide his location, proprietary software stolen from some of the country's largest cellular telephone and computer companies, intercepted passwords and private e-mail read. His own account of one target shows the method. At Motorola he persuaded operations staff to read him, again and again, the code on a security token that changed every 60 seconds together with the static PIN (personal identification number), then had an account enabled for him, then talked a reluctant engineer out of his password by claiming to be looking at a form on which it was recorded. Against AT&T he set up a borrowed voice mailbox and a fax relay so that a manager's secretary faxed him the password of a DataKit controlling dial-up access to the company's network. A file of some 20,000 credit card numbers copied from the provider Netcom was found on his computer, but the AP found no evidence that he ever used any of them.

The hunt and the arrest. The pursuit made him a media figure before it made him a defendant. A New York Times cover story on 4 July 1994 by John Markoff, co-author of the 1991 book Cyberpunk, called him the world's most wanted cybercriminal, a label Mitnick told the Senate was fictitious and which, he said, grew into the false claim that he had been on the Federal Bureau of Investigation's (FBI) Ten Most Wanted list; asked by the AP, the FBI denied it. On Christmas Day 1994 the workstations of Tsutomu Shimomura, a researcher at the San Diego Supercomputer Center, were entered by Internet Protocol (IP) source address spoofing and Transmission Control Protocol (TCP) sequence number prediction against the trust of the remote shell services, followed by the hijacking of an open connection through a loadable kernel STREAMS module, as Shimomura documented on Usenet on 25 January 1995. Federal agents captured Mitnick in Raleigh, North Carolina, in February 1995 with Shimomura's assistance, and he made his first appearance in federal court there on 15 February; he was carrying cloned cellular phones, more than a hundred cloned phone codes and several pieces of false identification. Markoff's book Takedown told the story of the hunt, and Mitnick, who said Markoff had single-handedly created the myth of Kevin Mitnick, filed a defamation suit that delayed the film made from it.

Plea, sentence and the argument over money. He spent four years as a pretrial detainee, without bail, a bail hearing or, he said, the ability to see the evidence against him. The government's original indictment had 25 counts. On 26 March 1999 Judge Mariana R. Pfaelzer accepted his plea to seven: four counts of wire fraud, two of computer fraud and one of illegally intercepting a wire communication. On 9 August 1999 she sentenced him to 46 months, which with an earlier 22-month sentence for possessing cloned cellular phones and violating supervised release made 68. The Department of Justice named Motorola, Novell, Fujitsu, Sun Microsystems, Nokia Mobile Phones and the University of Southern California, whose computers had been used to store the stolen programs, and put the losses in the millions of dollars. The numbers are where the case was really fought. The indictment's figure of 80 million dollars and the victims' later claim of about 290 million were built largely from research and development costs; under the plea Mitnick stipulated to 5 to 10 million; prosecutors asked for 1.5 million dollars in restitution and the judge ordered 4,125 dollars, a token amount she was sure he could pay. Ira Winkler, who put the real damage nearer 1.5 million, called the 80 million figure absolutely ridiculous.

Release and the conditions. He left the federal prison at Lompoc, California, on 21 January 2000, having served, by his own count, 59 months and 7 days after 180 days of good-time credit. For three years of supervised release, under conditions the Ninth Circuit had already upheld against his challenge on 20 May 1998, he could not without his probation officer's approval possess computers, software, modems, cellular telephones or any device able to reach a network, a landline telephone excepted, nor work in the computer or telecommunications business. His lawyers asked the court what counted as a computer and were not told. Christopher Painter, one of his prosecutors, used the case in a 2001 Department of Justice bulletin to show how far such conditions can go when a defendant's history justifies them; the plea also barred Mitnick from profiting from his story for seven years. The restrictions were eased over time, and he was not allowed back online until December 2002.

The second career. By the time he testified to the House Financial Services Committee on 3 April 2003 he had co-founded an information security firm and, with William L. Simon, written The Art of Deception for Wiley, a book on the con-man techniques intruders use and how companies can defend against them. The Art of Intrusion followed in 2005, the memoir Ghost in the Wires in 2011 and The Art of Invisibility, with Robert Vamosi, in 2017. From 2003 he ran his own penetration-testing firm, and from 2011 he was the business partner of Stu Sjouwerman at KnowBe4, the security awareness training vendor where he was chief hacking officer and part owner. He died of pancreatic cancer in Las Vegas on 16 July 2023, aged 59.

The disputes. The record supports more than one reading. The lead prosecutor, David Schindler, called his conduct a concerted, deliberate and in some instances mean-spirited attempt to steal information and trick victims, not a benign, inquisitive search; Mitnick, on release, said his were simple crimes of trespass driven by curiosity about how phone networks worked, and in 2005 told CNN he had made really stupid mistakes he regretted. The solitary confinement shows how the legend fed the case: his own firm says he spent eight and a half months of his five years in solitary, his business partner told the AP nine, and both attribute it to the fear that he could start a nuclear war by whistling into a pay phone. He always denied the story, partly behind the film WarGames, that he had broken into the North American Aerospace Defense Command (NORAD). A grassroots Free Kevin campaign protested his years in jail without trial, and some supporters defaced websites, The New York Times among them; the defence lawyer Jennifer Granick said prosecutors had used him as a warning to others, and the AP judged in 2023 that the case had taught the public to tell serious computer crime from youthful troublemaking. The lesson he drew himself, that verification is the weak link and a helpful employee will bypass a control that has stood for years, is the one the profession kept.

the-414s.def: A group of Milwaukee teenagers who broke into dozens of computer systems in 1983 and put hacking on front pages.
the-414s.context: Named after their area code, they accessed systems including a cancer centre and Los Alamos National Laboratory, mostly through default and guessed passwords. Their case helped spur the first US computer-crime laws and fixed the young 'hacker' in the public imagination.
the-414s.depth:
The 414s were a group of teenagers in Milwaukee, named for their area code, who in 1983 accessed dozens of computer systems including Los Alamos National Laboratory and a cancer treatment centre. They used default passwords and dial-up connections, and mostly they were exploring.

The technical bar was low by design of the era. Systems shipped with well-known default credentials, security was assumed to come from obscurity and the cost of long-distance calls, and nobody expected teenagers to be systematically dialling number ranges. The damage was minimal and one incident, deleting billing records at the cancer centre, was consequential enough to make the point that intent and impact are different things.

Their importance is legislative. The case arrived in Congress in the same period that WarGames put the scenario in cinemas, hearings followed, and the resulting attention contributed directly to the Computer Fraud and Abuse Act. That statute, drafted in response to curious teenagers, became the instrument used against everyone since, and its breadth has been criticized ever since, which is what happens when a law is written from a news cycle rather than from a settled understanding of the activity.

log4shell.def: The 2021 vulnerability in the ubiquitous Log4j logging library that let a logged string execute arbitrary code.
log4shell.context: Because Log4j is embedded in countless Java applications, a crafted string in something as innocent as a username or user agent could trigger remote code execution almost anywhere. Its reach and severity made it one of the most serious and widespread flaws ever disclosed.
log4shell.depth:
Log4Shell was a vulnerability in Log4j, a Java logging library, where a specially formatted string in any logged text would cause the library to fetch and execute remote code through JNDI lookup. The exploit string was short enough to fit in a username, a chat message, or a device name.

The severity came from the combination of trivial exploitation and near-universal presence. Anything that logged user input was potentially vulnerable, which is essentially everything, and Java runs a large fraction of enterprise backends. Proof of concept exploitation required no authentication and no unusual conditions, and within days people were changing their phone names to exploit strings to see what would call home.

The lasting consequence was about supply chain visibility rather than about Java. Organizations discovered they could not answer whether they used Log4j, because it arrived as a transitive dependency inside products they had bought, and vendors took weeks to say which of their own products were affected. That gap is what drove software bills of materials from a compliance idea into something regulators now expect, and the honest position is that most organizations still could not answer the question quickly today.

heartbleed.def: The 2014 OpenSSL flaw that let attackers read chunks of a server's memory, including keys and passwords.
heartbleed.context: A missing bounds check in the TLS heartbeat extension let a client ask for more data than it sent and receive whatever happened to be adjacent in memory. It was one of the first bugs with a logo and a name, and it forced a global scramble to patch servers and rotate secrets.
heartbleed.depth:
Heartbleed was a missing bounds check in OpenSSL's implementation of the TLS heartbeat extension. A client could claim its message was sixty-four kilobytes long while sending one byte, and the server would return that byte plus whatever happened to be adjacent in memory: session keys, credentials, private keys, other users' requests.

Two properties made it exceptionally serious. It left no trace, because a heartbeat is a legitimate message and nothing about the exchange looked anomalous in logs, so nobody could establish whether they had been exploited. And it had been present for roughly two years in software running a large share of the internet's HTTPS, which meant every affected key had to be treated as compromised and every certificate reissued.

It also changed how the industry funds its foundations. OpenSSL at the time was maintained by a very small number of people on almost no money, despite being load-bearing for global commerce, and the discovery that this was normal rather than exceptional led to the Core Infrastructure Initiative and its successors. Heartbleed is the reason "given enough eyeballs, all bugs are shallow" is now quoted with a caveat.

shellshock.def: Shellshock is the family of six vulnerabilities disclosed in GNU Bash between 24 September and 5 October 2014, led by CVE-2014-6271: Bash executed commands that followed a function definition imported from an environment variable, so any service that put untrusted data into the environment of a Bash process could be made to run code.
shellshock.context: Bash can pass shell functions to child shells through environment variables, and when it imported them it did not stop at the end of the definition, whatever the variable was called. That turned an obscure feature into remote code execution wherever outside data reached Bash's environment across a privilege boundary: CGI (Common Gateway Interface) scripts on web servers, which receive every request header as an environment variable, OpenSSH's ForceCommand, DHCP (Dynamic Host Configuration Protocol) client scripts and more. Stéphane Chazelas reported it on 12 September 2014, coordinated disclosure followed on 24 September, and the first fix proved incomplete; five more CVE identifiers and six upstream patches followed within two weeks. The feature dated from August 1989, so the flaw had shipped for 25 years in a shell present on almost every Unix-like system.
shellshock.depth:
What it is. Shellshock is not one bug but a cluster in GNU Bash, the Bourne-Again Shell, disclosed in the last week of September 2014. The National Vulnerability Database (NVD) describes the first, CVE-2014-6271, as Bash through version 4.3 processing trailing strings after function definitions in the values of environment variables, which allows remote attackers to execute arbitrary code; Florian Weimer of Red Hat, announcing it on the oss-security list on 24 September, put it in one line: trailing code in function definitions was executed, independent of the variable name. The original name proposed by its finder, Stéphane Chazelas, was bashdoor; the press settled on Shellshock. Unlike most of that year's headline flaws, the core issue was not memory corruption: the parser did exactly what it was built to do, on input nobody had expected to come from a stranger.

How it worked. Bash lets a script export a shell function so that child Bash processes inherit it. Before the fix, the function travelled in an ordinary environment variable named after the function, whose value began like a function definition, with a pair of empty parentheses and an opening brace. A starting Bash scanned its environment for such values and parsed them as definitions, and it did not stop at the closing brace: whatever followed was executed as a command, at startup, before the script itself ran. Because any variable name worked, the attacker did not need to know which variable a program used; it was enough to control the value of any variable that reached a Bash process.

Why it reached so far. Environment variables are a common way to hand data from one program to another, and much of that data comes from outside. The CGI specification, RFC (Request for Comments) 3875, tells a web server to present each request header to the script as a meta-variable named HTTP_ followed by the header name, and on Unix those meta-variables are environment variables; a CGI script written in Bash, or one that called a shell to run a command where Bash was the system shell, therefore parsed request headers as possible function definitions. The NVD lists the vectors the analysts found: the ForceCommand feature of OpenSSH's sshd, Apache httpd's mod_cgi and mod_cgid modules, scripts run by Dynamic Host Configuration Protocol (DHCP) clients, which pass server-supplied options in the environment, and any other case in which the environment is set across a privilege boundary from Bash's execution. The pre-disclosure notice Weimer later posted names the concrete carriers: with Apache httpd, the Host header (as REMOTE_HOST), any other header value (as an HTTP_ variable) and the protocol string (as SERVER_PROTOCOL), with the method, path and query string possible in other CGI implementations; and, for OpenSSH, variables accepted through AcceptEnv, TERM or SSH_ORIGINAL_COMMAND. That last NVD phrase is the general lesson: the danger was not Bash alone but every place where one side of a boundary filled the environment and the other side started a shell.

The disclosure. Chazelas, in his own timeline on oss-security, found the bug on the morning of 12 September 2014 (UK time) and that afternoon reported it to the Bash maintainer, Chet Ramey, and to the security contacts of Debian, Red Hat, Ubuntu and Mandriva, with the SSH and HTTP header vectors. Ramey's first patch came the same day and was easily bypassed; several iterations followed on the closed list. On 16 September Weimer proposed the schedule: early notice to other Unix and Linux vendors on the 22nd, selected infrastructure providers such as content delivery networks on the 23rd, and public disclosure on the 24th at 14:00 UTC (Coordinated Universal Time). Ramey had patches for every Bash release back to 3.0 by 16 September. The courtesy notice to organizations with network filtering capabilities asked them to prepare protection but not yet to distribute intrusion detection or prevention signatures; someone passed it to the press before the date, and Weimer then posted it in full. On 24 September the upstream patch bash43-025 was published, crediting Chazelas, and CVE-2014-6271 went public.

The patch chain. The first fix was not the last, and the order matters for anyone who audits versions. CVE-2014-7169, published on 25 September, covered malformed definitions that bash43-025 still processed; Tavis Ormandy is credited on bash43-026. On 27 September bash43-027, reported by Weimer, made the structural change: exported functions now travel in variables whose names carry the prefix BASH_FUNC_ and the suffix %%, so Bash no longer decides from a variable's contents alone whether to treat it as a function, and an HTTP header can no longer be mistaken for one. Bash43-028, also from Weimer, fixed two buffer overflows in the parser triggered by many here-documents or deeply nested loops, which the NVD records as CVE-2014-7186 and CVE-2014-7187; bash43-029 and bash43-030, reported by Michal Zalewski and released by 5 October, fixed an uninitialized here-document delimiter and a case where nested command substitution still executed trailing code, matching the NVD descriptions of CVE-2014-6277 and CVE-2014-6278. Six identifiers were published between 24 and 30 September. Every one scores 10.0 under version 2 of the Common Vulnerability Scoring System (CVSS); CVE-2014-6271 and CVE-2014-7169 score 9.8 under version 3.1.

How old it was. In the first days Chazelas and Ramey said the feature arrived in Bash 1.13, and that figure spread; Chazelas later found it already in 1.05, whose ChangeLog records the exporting of functions added on 5 August 1989 and release 1.03 on 1 September 1989, and on 12 October 2014 Ramey confirmed that the feature went into Bash in early August 1989 and first shipped in bash-1.03. The flaw had therefore been in every release for 25 years, in a program installed on almost every Linux and Unix system and read by a great many people. Some vendor advisories still carry the early version ranges: Fortinet's, for example, describes Bash 1.14.0 through 4.3.

Where it showed up, and what vendors did. Bash was embedded in appliances as well as servers. Fortinet's advisory FG-IR-14-030 of 25 September 2014 listed FortiAnalyzer, FortiManager and FortiAuthenticator (where exploitation required authentication) and FortiDB as affected, adding 32-bit FortiWLC wireless controllers in 2021, and offered network protection while the firmware followed: an intrusion prevention system (IPS) signature, Bash.Function.Definitions.Remote.Code.Execution, in FortiGate IPS update 5.552, an antivirus signature, and a FortiWeb web application firewall (WAF) signature, 090420001, for HTTP requests carrying crafted environments. That pattern, a signature in front within a day and the real fix in each product later, is the usual shape of an appliance response, and it is one reason the disclosure schedule warned infrastructure providers a day before the public. The United States Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency (CISA) later placed CVE-2014-6271 and CVE-2014-7169 in its Known Exploited Vulnerabilities (KEV) catalogue on 28 January 2022, and CVE-2014-6278 on 2 October 2025.

What it taught. Four lessons have outlived it. First, a feature can be the vulnerability: exporting functions and passing headers as environment variables were each reasonable, and the flaw lived in the join between them, which is why the same shape returned in Log4Shell in 2021. Second, the fix that matters is structural: the BASH_FUNC_ naming change removed the class, where the first patches only closed instances. Third, assume the first patch is not the last; anyone who patched on 24 September and stopped was exposed to the follow-ups. Fourth, know where interpreters sit in the data path, including the shell behind a CGI script, a DHCP hook or an appliance's management interface. Coming five months after Heartbleed, published on 7 April 2014, it ended the comfortable assumption that old, foundational and widely read open-source code had been made safe by its age.

The numbers worth remembering. Reported on 12 September 2014; disclosed on 24 September at 14:00 UTC; six CVE identifiers (CVE-2014-6271, 7169, 7186, 7187, 6277 and 6278) between 24 and 30 September; bash43-025 to bash43-030 between 24 September and 5 October; the BASH_FUNC_ prefix and %% suffix from bash43-027; CVSS 10.0 under version 2; the feature added on 5 August 1989 and shipped in bash-1.03; 25 years in the code.

stuxnet.def: Stuxnet is the Windows worm, found in 2010, that carried code to reprogram Siemens programmable logic controllers (PLCs) at Iran's Natanz uranium enrichment plant and damage its centrifuges while showing operators normal readings: the first publicly disclosed cyberweapon, and the first known to have broken machinery.
stuxnet.context: It spread on USB (Universal Serial Bus) drives and local networks through four Windows flaws that were unpatched at the time and an older one, used drivers signed with certificates stolen from two hardware makers, Realtek and JMicron, and stayed inert on almost every machine it reached; only a Siemens Step 7 installation driving a particular set of frequency converters or cascade valves triggered its payload, which altered the controller's logic and replayed recorded values to the monitoring screens. Symantec counted about 100,000 infected hosts by September 2010, some 60 per cent of them in Iran, and the Institute for Science and International Security linked it to the replacement of about 1,000 centrifuges at Natanz. The New York Times reported in 2012 that it was part of a joint United States and Israeli programme code-named Olympic Games; no government has acknowledged it on the record. It moved cyber sabotage from scenario to precedent and showed every industrial operator that isolation is crossed by people and their laptops.
stuxnet.depth:
What it was. Symantec's analysis, the W32.Stuxnet Dossier, states the goal plainly: to reprogram industrial control systems (ICS) by modifying code on programmable logic controllers (PLCs) so that they work as the attackers intended, most likely outside their specified limits, and to hide those changes from the operator. To get there it carried an unusual arsenal: exploits for flaws Microsoft had not yet fixed, a Windows rootkit, what Symantec called the first ever PLC rootkit, antivirus evasion, process injection and hooking code, several ways to spread, peer-to-peer updates within a local network and a command and control (C&C) interface. It is not a general-purpose attack on any industrial plant: on almost every machine it infected it did nothing beyond spreading, and its payload ran only where it found a specific Siemens configuration. Nor was it an internet scanning worm in the style of the early 2000s; it travelled on removable drives, file shares and engineering project files.

How it was found. On 17 June 2010 VirusBlokAda, an antivirus company based in Belarus, found two samples that could infect a fully patched Windows 7 machine when someone merely viewed an infected USB (Universal Serial Bus) drive in Windows Explorer; Brian Krebs made it public on 15 July. Symantec's timeline then runs quickly: Microsoft's security advisory on 16 July and VeriSign's revocation of the Realtek Semiconductor certificate that had signed the driver; on 17 July ESET found a new driver signed with a JMicron Technology certificate, revoked on 22 July; on 19 July Siemens said it was investigating reports of malware infecting its WinCC supervisory systems; on 2 August Microsoft shipped MS10-046, rated Critical for all supported Windows, for the shortcut flaw (CVE-2010-2568), which ran code as soon as the icon of a crafted shortcut was displayed. The Print Spooler fix, MS10-061, followed on 14 September, and the Task Scheduler elevation fix, MS10-092 (CVE-2010-3338), on 14 December. The earliest sample of the version found in 2010 dates from June 2009, and in 2013 Symantec described an older one, Stuxnet 0.5, submitted to a public scanning service on 15 November 2007, with C&C domains registered on 3 November 2005, which had stopped spreading on 4 July 2009. The 1.x versions were set to stop infecting after 24 June 2012.

How it spread and gained control. Symantec lists the routes: shortcut files on removable drives (the LNK flaw); the Windows Print Spooler flaw and the Server service flaw already fixed in 2008 as MS08-067, the same one Conficker used, to move across a local network; network shares; WinCC database servers, entered with a password hard-coded in the Siemens software (CVE-2010-2772, which the National Vulnerability Database records against WinCC and PCS 7); and Step 7 project files, infected so that opening the project ran the worm. To gain administrator rights it used two further unpatched flaws, one in the Win32k.sys keyboard layout handling on Windows XP and 2000 (later MS10-073) and the Task Scheduler flaw on Vista, 7 and Server 2008. In all it used four Microsoft vulnerabilities unpatched at the time, which Ralph Langner noted can each fetch hundreds of thousands of dollars on the open market, plus drivers signed with stolen certificates so that newer Windows would load them as legitimate.

What it looked for, and what it did. On machines running Step 7, Stuxnet hooked the software's communication library and infected two families of Siemens controller. For the S7-315-2, it required a Profibus communications processor, the CP 342-5, talking to at least 33 frequency converter drives made by Fararo Paya in Tehran or by Vacon in Finland, the drives that set the speed of a motor. The attackers expected those drives to run between 807 and 1,210 hertz; after about thirteen days of counting normal operation, the code set the maximum frequency to 1,410 hertz, then to 2 hertz, then to 1,064 hertz, and over again. During the sabotage it recorded the drives' previous operating frequencies and played them back to WinCC through hooked functions, so the monitoring systems believed everything was normal, and it took over organization block OB35, a watchdog, so that a graceful shutdown could not run even if operators noticed. For the S7-417 the code expected six groups of 164 peripherals, which Symantec read as six cascades of 164 centrifuges; it recorded 21 seconds of input values and blocked the real outputs while its own ran. Langner, who analysed the controller code independently, describes the S7-417 as running the cascade protection system, the valves and pressure sensors of up to six cascades, and calculated that the later attack brought rotors from 63,000 to 120 revolutions per minute (rpm) and back.

Two attacks, not one. In 2013 Symantec and Langner both described the older variant: an attack on the protection system rather than the drives, closing valves so that pressure rose inside the centrifuges, which Langner called an overpressure attack. Symantec found Stuxnet 0.5 partly built on the platform behind Flamer, while later versions used a different one. Langner's reading is that the second variant, deployed in 2009, was simpler but much noisier: it self-replicated to any Windows machine, not only those with Siemens software, and its zero-days and stolen certificates made it far easier to identify as malicious, while the first had looked almost like a legitimate Siemens project.

Targets and damage. Symantec's data, from the infection records each sample carried, showed five organizations, all with a presence in Iran, attacked in waves between June 2009 and May 2010, and about 100,000 infected hosts by 29 September 2010, roughly 60 per cent in Iran; new Iranian infections stopped reporting from 22 August 2010, most likely because Iran blocked the C&C servers. The Institute for Science and International Security reported on 22 December 2010 that Iran had decommissioned and replaced about 1,000 IR-1 centrifuges at the Natanz Fuel Enrichment Plant in late 2009 or early 2010, more breakage than expected, and quoted President Ahmadinejad acknowledging that software had created problems for a limited number of centrifuges and the head of Iran's atomic energy organization, Ali Akbar Salehi, saying on 23 November 2010 that malware had reached Iran but had been caught. The New York Times reported in 2012 that the last attacks of the series temporarily took out nearly 1,000 of the 5,000 centrifuges Iran had spinning.

Who, and how it got out. David Sanger's account in The New York Times on 1 June 2012, based on unnamed American, European and Israeli officials, said the programme was code-named Olympic Games, begun under President Bush and accelerated by President Obama, that the worm was developed by the United States and Israel, and that it became public in the summer of 2010 because a programming error let it escape Natanz. Langner disputed that last point in 2013: in his reading, contractors who served Natanz and other clients carried infected laptops from site to site, and since the worm reported each victim's Internet Protocol (IP) address and hostname to its C&C servers, the attackers expected the spread and watched it. No government has acknowledged the operation on the record; the attribution rests on that reporting and on the analysis, and careful practice is to state both the attribution and its status.

What defenders took from it. First, isolation is crossed by people: Langner calls the contractors with legitimate access the royal road into hard targets, and notes that most industrial facilities depend on such contractors, good at engineering and weak at security. Second, the instruments can lie: a plant whose screens show recorded values needs checks that do not depend on the same controller, and Langner observes that the speed changes should have been audible to experienced staff without ear protection. Third, trust anchors fail: two stolen code-signing certificates let kernel drivers load cleanly, and both were revoked within days of discovery. Fourth, vendor credentials embedded in industrial software are vulnerabilities, as CVE-2010-2772 recorded. And the Windows side did not age out quickly: the United States Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency (CISA) added the shortcut flaw, CVE-2010-2568, to its Known Exploited Vulnerabilities (KEV) catalogue on 15 September 2022, twelve years after the patch.

The numbers worth remembering. Four Windows flaws unpatched at the time plus MS08-067; about 100,000 infected hosts and some 60 per cent in Iran by September 2010; at least 33 frequency converters running between 807 and 1,210 hertz, driven to 1,410, 2 and 1,064 hertz; six cascades of 164 centrifuges; about 1,000 IR-1 centrifuges replaced at Natanz; the earliest variant in the wild by November 2007; the version found in 2010 dated from June 2009 and set to stop on 24 June 2012.

wannacry.def: WannaCry, also called WannaCrypt, is the ransomware worm that spread across the world on 12 May 2017 through EternalBlue, a leaked National Security Agency (NSA) exploit for a Windows Server Message Block version 1 (SMBv1) flaw Microsoft had patched two months earlier, encrypting hundreds of thousands of computers in a day; the United States and United Kingdom attributed it to North Korea.
wannacry.context: It used the EternalBlue exploit against Server Message Block (SMB) on TCP (Transmission Control Protocol) port 445 to spread from machine to machine with nobody clicking anything, encrypting files and demanding 300 dollars in bitcoin. Within hours it had reached hospitals of the United Kingdom's National Health Service (NHS), carmakers' factories, a telecom operator in Spain and German railway station displays. A researcher who registered a domain hard-coded in the malware stopped new infections from detonating that same evening, almost by accident; estimates of the total cost ran from hundreds of millions to billions of dollars. The flaw had been fixed in Microsoft's bulletin MS17-010 on 14 March 2017, 59 days earlier, which makes WannaCry the standard case of the gap between a patch existing and a network being patched.
wannacry.depth:
What it was, and what it was not. Microsoft's analysis of 12 May 2017 listed its names, WannaCrypt, WannaCry, WanaCrypt0r, WCrypt and WCRY, and explained why it was different: ransomware usually arrives through email or social engineering and stays on the machine where a user ran it, while this one carried publicly available exploit code for a patched Server Message Block (SMB) flaw, which gave ordinary ransomware the behaviour of a worm. Microsoft also said it had found no evidence of the initial entry vector; an infected email and an unpatched machine exposed to the internet were the two likely routes, and early press reports of spam attachments were never confirmed. The exploit worked only against unpatched Windows 7, Windows Server 2008 and older systems, so Windows 10 was not affected. It was criminal software in form, a ransom screen and bitcoin wallets, but its payment design was so poor that paying rarely bought anything back.

The flaw and the patch. Microsoft's bulletin MS17-010, rated critical and published on 14 March 2017, fixed six vulnerabilities in the Server Message Block version 1 (SMBv1) server, catalogued as Common Vulnerabilities and Exposures (CVE) entries CVE-2017-0143 to CVE-2017-0148: five allowed remote code execution and one, CVE-2017-0147, information disclosure. At release none was listed as publicly disclosed or exploited. The CVE identifier most catalogues attach to EternalBlue is CVE-2017-0144, published on 17 March 2017 and added by the Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency (CISA) to its Known Exploited Vulnerabilities (KEV) catalogue on 10 February 2022; Microsoft's own WannaCry analysis cited CVE-2017-0145, a sibling in the same bulletin. The exploit itself became public a month after the patch, in the Shadow Brokers dump of 14 April 2017, a group that said it had stolen the tools of the Equation group; Microsoft's president Brad Smith wrote two days after the outbreak that the exploits had been stolen from the National Security Agency (NSA), and compared the leak to the United States military having some of its Tomahawk missiles stolen.

How it worked. Cisco Talos described the chain on the first day. The worm scanned heavily over TCP (Transmission Control Protocol) port 445, both on the local network and across the internet, used ETERNALBLUE to exploit the SMB flaw and then implanted the DOUBLEPULSAR backdoor, another leaked tool, to install the ransomware; where DOUBLEPULSAR was already present it used it directly. Before doing anything else it made a Hypertext Transfer Protocol (HTTP) request to a long, keyboard-mashed domain: if the request failed, infection continued; if it succeeded, the program exited. On encryption it walked every lettered drive, network shares and removable media included, encrypted files with the extensions on its list using 2048-bit RSA (Rivest-Shamir-Adleman) keys according to Talos, renamed them with a .WNCRY suffix, deleted the Windows shadow copies with vssadmin and WMIC (Windows Management Instrumentation Command-line) so that local recovery failed, and installed a Tor client to reach its command servers on .onion addresses. Kaspersky found ransom notes in 28 languages, Portuguese among them; one sample asked for 600 dollars where the first payments had been about 300, with a countdown after which the demand rose.

The day itself. Cisco's resolvers saw the first lookups of the hard-coded domain at 07:24 Coordinated Universal Time (UTC) on Friday 12 May, and its honeypots an uptick in scanning shortly before 09:00 UTC. Talos named Telefónica in Spain, the United Kingdom's National Health Service (NHS) and FedEx in the United States among the first victims. Within hours Kaspersky had recorded more than 45,000 attacks in 74 countries, mostly in Russia; Avast reported more than 126,000 infections the next day, 60 per cent of them in Russia, followed by Ukraine and Taiwan. Renault halted production at several sites, including Sandouville in France and its Dacia plants in Romania, Nissan's plant in Sunderland was affected, and Deutsche Bahn station displays showed the ransom screen. Brazil was among the first 74 countries. That afternoon the Brazilian headquarters of Telefônica/Vivo in São Paulo told staff to switch off their computers and leave the building; the Court of Justice of São Paulo asked employees to shut down, and its website, the Regional Labour Court's and the state Public Prosecutor's Office's went off the air; the state's data processing company, Prodesp, told staff to switch off, and the federal one, Serpro, reported no attack but activated its contingency plan.

The kill switch. Marcus Hutchins, who wrote as MalwareTech, registered the domain that afternoon as routine: tracking botnets, he had registered several thousand such domains in the previous year, pointing them at a sinkhole, a server that captures malicious traffic so that the spread can be counted. He learned what he had done from a post by the researcher Darien Huss saying that sinkholing the domain stopped execution, and confirmed it by making the lookup fail on a test machine, whereupon the sample encrypted his files. His own reading was that the check was not a deliberate off switch but a badly thought-out anti-analysis technique: some sandboxes answer for any domain, so malware that gets a reply from a domain that should not exist assumes it is being watched and exits, and WannaCry did this with a single hard-coded name. The National Audit Office (NAO) dates it to the evening of 12 May, after which WannaCry stopped locking devices. Machines that had already been encrypted stayed encrypted, which is why the NHS trusts hit early in the day, in the north and the Midlands, suffered most, and why Cisco saw lookups to the domain still climbing to a peak of just over 1,400 nearly ten hours after the first.

The NHS. The NAO's investigation of 27 October 2017 found that the NHS was not the specific target. NHS England declared a major incident at 16:00 on 12 May; at least 80 of England's 236 trusts were affected, 34 of them infected and locked out of devices and the rest disrupted or shutting systems down as a precaution, together with 603 primary care and other organizations, including 595 general practitioner (GP) practices. NHS England identified 6,912 cancelled appointments and estimated about 19,494 in all, and five accident and emergency departments had to divert patients. No NHS organization paid the ransom. Most infected devices ran Windows 7, a supported system that simply had not been patched, although NHS Digital had issued alerts to apply the fix on 17 March and 28 April; machines still on Windows XP were a minority, but some were embedded in equipment such as magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) scanners that only their vendors could update. Managing internet-facing firewalls would also have protected trusts. The Comptroller and Auditor General called it a relatively unsophisticated attack that basic information technology (IT) security practice would have prevented. In October 2018 the Department of Health and Social Care put the cost to the NHS at about 92 million pounds: 19 million in lost output and 73 million in IT support during and after the attack.

The ransom and the money. Check Point found on 14 May that the three bitcoin addresses had received more than 33,000 dollars and that not a single victim had reported getting files back: unlike competing ransomware, which gives each victim a unique identifier and wallet, WannaCry had no reliable way to tie a payment to a payer. In early August 2017 about 140,000 dollars were withdrawn from the wallets. Damage estimates spread widely: four days after the outbreak the risk-modelling firm Cyence put potential global losses at 4 billion dollars, while others predicted hundreds of millions.

Attribution. Symantec found tools used exclusively by the Lazarus group on machines infected with earlier WannaCry versions that could not yet spread over SMB, and code shared with Lazarus malware. On 19 December 2017 the United Kingdom said its National Cyber Security Centre (NCSC) judged it highly likely that North Korean actors known as the Lazarus Group were behind the campaign, and the White House homeland security adviser Thomas Bossert made the American attribution the same day, describing the attack as reckless and noting that paying had not unlocked computers. On 6 September 2018 the United States Department of Justice announced charges, filed under seal on 8 June, against Park Jin Hyok, a programmer for Chosun Expo Joint Venture, which it described as a North Korean government front, for a conspiracy that included creating the WannaCry 2.0 malware, the attack on Sony Pictures Entertainment in 2014 and the theft of 81 million dollars from Bangladesh Bank in 2016.

Microsoft's response and the argument it reopened. Microsoft took the unusual step of publishing fixes for systems it no longer supported, Windows XP, Windows 8 and Windows Server 2003, and Brad Smith used the event to press for what Microsoft had called in February a Digital Geneva Convention, including a requirement that governments report vulnerabilities to vendors instead of stockpiling them. WannaCry and EternalBlue became the reference case in that argument, about whether an agency that finds a flaw should keep it or disclose it.

What lasted. Variants kept circulating after the original was contained: in August 2018 Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Company (TSMC) said a WannaCry variant, introduced on 3 August during the installation of software on new equipment, had halted production at its Taiwan plants for two days. The protocol under it has been retired step by step: Microsoft's documentation says SMBv2 superseded SMBv1 from 2007, that SMBv1 was publicly deprecated in 2014, that it has not been installed by default since Windows 10 and Windows Server version 1709, and that Windows 11 ships with neither its server nor its client. The defensive lessons are the ones Talos and the NAO wrote down in 2017: apply MS17-010 everywhere, find and remove SMBv1, block TCP ports 139 and 445 from the internet at the firewall, isolate what cannot be patched, and keep backups the malware cannot reach. The fix existed for 59 days before the outbreak; every machine WannaCry encrypted was one on which it had not been applied.

the-iloveyou-virus.def: The 2000 email worm whose 'ILOVEYOU' subject line tricked millions into infecting their own machines.
the-iloveyou-virus.context: Opening the attached 'love letter' ran a script that overwrote files and mailed itself to the victim's entire address book, spreading around the globe in hours. Its social hook, not any technical brilliance, is what made it one of the most damaging worms of its time.
the-iloveyou-virus.depth:
ILOVEYOU spread in May 2000 as an email attachment with a subject line promising affection, and reached millions of machines in days. It overwrote files, harvested passwords, and mailed itself to everyone in the victim's address book, which is why it moved faster than anything before it.

The technical trick was social rather than clever. The attachment was a script whose real extension was hidden by a Windows default that concealed known file types, so a file that looked like a text document was executable. The virus did not defeat a security control; it exploited an interface decision made for tidiness, and the interaction between a cosmetic default and an executable file format was the whole vulnerability.

Its lasting effect was on defaults rather than on antivirus. Mail systems began stripping executable attachments, scripting hosts were restricted, and the assumption that a user's judgement is the last line of defence lost credibility in a way that produced real architectural change. The other legacy is the recognition that a message from a known contact carries trust that the content has not earned, which is still the mechanism behind most successful phishing.

the-turing-test.def: Alan Turing's 1950 proposal to judge machine intelligence by whether it can converse indistinguishably from a human.
the-turing-test.context: Rather than ask 'can machines think', Turing reframed it as an imitation game: if a human judge cannot reliably tell the machine from a person by text alone, the question is answered pragmatically. It set the terms for decades of debate about artificial intelligence.
the-turing-test.depth:
Turing's 1950 paper proposed replacing the unanswerable question of whether machines can think with an operational one: can a machine's responses be distinguished from a human's by an interrogator communicating through text. He called it the imitation game, and framed it explicitly as a way to sidestep definitions nobody could agree on.

The test has been criticized continuously and productively. Searle's Chinese Room argues that behaviour indistinguishable from understanding is not understanding, and the practical objection is that the test rewards deception rather than intelligence, since a system optimized to pass is optimized to seem human, which includes pretending to be worse at arithmetic than it is.

What large language models did was collapse the test's usefulness rather than settle it. Systems now produce text that convinces many people in casual conversation, and the reaction has largely been to conclude that the test was measuring the wrong thing rather than to accept the result. Turing anticipated some of this and would probably have found it interesting: the paper is more careful and more provisional than its reputation, and it was always about what we can observe rather than about what is really happening inside.

ada-lovelace.def: The 19th-century mathematician often called the first programmer for her notes on Babbage's Analytical Engine.
ada-lovelace.context: In 1843 she translated a paper on Charles Babbage's proposed machine and added notes far longer than the original, including what is often described as the first published algorithm intended for a computer. She also grasped that such a machine could manipulate symbols, not just numbers - an insight ahead of its time.
ada-lovelace.depth:
Ada Lovelace's notes on Charles Babbage's Analytical Engine, published in 1843, contain what is generally regarded as the first published algorithm intended for a machine: a method for computing Bernoulli numbers. Her notes ran to roughly three times the length of the paper she was translating.

The more consequential contribution is conceptual. Babbage saw a calculator; Lovelace saw that if the machine could manipulate symbols according to rules, and if numbers could represent things other than quantity, then it could operate on anything expressible in symbols, including music. That leap from arithmetic to general symbol manipulation is the idea computing is built on, and nobody else made it for a century.

Her assessment of limits has aged just as interestingly. She wrote that the engine could originate nothing and could only do what we know how to order it to perform, a position Turing later named Lady Lovelace's objection and argued against directly. That exchange, conducted across a hundred years, is still the shape of the argument about what machines can do, which is a remarkable thing for notes appended to a translation.

the-eniac-programmers.def: The six women who programmed the ENIAC in the 1940s, largely uncredited for decades.
the-eniac-programmers.context: Working without programming languages or manuals, they configured the room-sized machine by physically rewiring it and setting switches, effectively inventing hands-on programming as they went. Their contribution went unrecognized for years, and their story reshaped the history of who built early computing.
the-eniac-programmers.depth:
The six women who programmed ENIAC, among them Kay McNulty, Betty Jennings, Betty Snyder, Marlyn Meltzer, Fran Bilas and Ruth Lichterman, worked without programming languages, manuals or precedent, because none existed. They configured the machine physically, by setting switches and connecting cables, from an understanding of the mathematics and the hardware together.

Their obscurity was structural rather than accidental. Hardware was considered the achievement and programming was classified as clerical work, an assumption that mapped onto who was assigned to do it. They were not introduced at the 1946 public demonstration, several were assumed by attendees to be models posing with the equipment, and the standard histories omitted them for decades.

Recovering the record matters for more than fairness. Their work included techniques the field later reinvented, notably systematic debugging and the practice of stepping through execution to find where behaviour diverges from intent. The broader point is that the boundary between important and clerical work was drawn before anyone knew what programming would become, and a great deal of subsequent history follows from where that early line was placed.

the-streisand-effect.def: When an attempt to hide or suppress information ends up drawing far more attention to it.
the-streisand-effect.context: It is named for a 2003 lawsuit in which Barbra Streisand tried to remove an aerial photo of her home from an obscure coastal survey, which then went viral because of the suit. On the internet, trying to bury something is often the surest way to spread it.
the-streisand-effect.depth:
In 2003 Barbra Streisand sued a photographer over an aerial image of her home, part of a coastal erosion survey. The photograph had been downloaded six times before the lawsuit, two of those by her own lawyers. The publicity generated by the suit brought hundreds of thousands of views, and Mike Masnick named the pattern.

The mechanism is simple and reliable. An attempt to suppress information signals that the information matters, motivates people to find and copy it, and converts a document nobody was looking at into a story. Once copies exist across many jurisdictions and archives, removal becomes impossible in practice however clear the legal right might be.

Its relevance to security is direct and frequently ignored. Legal threats against researchers who disclose vulnerabilities reliably produce more attention to the vulnerability, not less, and the same applies to takedown demands against leaked documents. The practical conclusion is unwelcome to lawyers and correct: once information is public, the decision is not whether it spreads but whether you participate in the conversation about it, and suppression as a strategy has a documented failure mode named after the person who demonstrated it.

moores-law.def: The observation that the number of transistors on a chip roughly doubles every couple of years.
moores-law.context: Gordon Moore noted the trend in 1965, and it held for decades as a self-fulfilling roadmap the whole industry planned around. It is slowing as physics intrudes, but it remains the reference point for talking about the pace of computing progress.
moores-law.depth:
