the-answer-42.def: The number a supercomputer gives, after 7.5 million years, as the Answer to Life, the Universe, and Everything.
the-answer-42.context: In Douglas Adams's novel, Deep Thought computes 42 but notes the real problem is that nobody knows what the Question was. It has become a running in-joke across programming culture, hidden in Easter eggs from Google's calculator to countless default values and test fixtures.
the-answer-42.depth:
In The Hitchhiker's Guide to the Galaxy, the computer Deep Thought calculates for seven and a half million years and reports that the answer to the ultimate question of life, the universe and everything is 42. Nobody knows what the question was, which is the joke and also the point.

Douglas Adams said repeatedly that he chose the number because it was ordinary and unremarkable, and that the theories about binary representations, ASCII values and base thirteen were all wrong. The elaborate explanations people constructed are more revealing than the number: a culture that finds meaning in numeric patterns will construct a pattern from anything, and Adams found this funnier than any of the theories.

It became a genuine convention in computing, appearing as a default value, a test constant, a port number and a status code in more codebases than anyone could count. That is a small demonstration of how technical culture works: a shared reference becomes shorthand, and using it signals membership more efficiently than explaining anything. The substantive lesson underneath, that an answer without its question is useless, is one most analytics dashboards would benefit from.

boil-the-ocean.def: To attempt something so broad or ambitious that it is doomed by its own scope.
boil-the-ocean.context: Used as a warning in planning: 'let's not boil the ocean' means pick a tractable slice instead of trying to solve everything at once. The image is deliberately absurd - you cannot heat an entire ocean, so do not scope work as if you could.
boil-the-ocean.depth:
Boiling the ocean is attempting something so ambitious in scope that it cannot succeed, and the phrase is usually deployed as a warning in a planning meeting. The rewrite that will fix everything, the migration that moves all systems at once, the standard that will unify every team's tooling.

The failure is not ambition, it is the absence of intermediate value. A project that delivers nothing until it delivers everything has no way to learn, no way to demonstrate progress to the people funding it, and no safe point to stop at if circumstances change. Since circumstances always change, the outcome is a large investment abandoned partway, which is worse than either finishing or never starting.

The alternative is not thinking smaller, it is sequencing. The same ambitious end state, decomposed so each step is independently useful and independently revertible, gets further because it survives changes in priority and produces evidence along the way. If a plan cannot be decomposed that way, that is usually a sign the plan is not yet understood rather than a sign the work is inherently monolithic.

drink-the-kool-aid.def: To adopt a belief or technology with uncritical, group-driven enthusiasm.
drink-the-kool-aid.context: Often said of teams that embrace a framework or methodology as dogma, past the point of honest evaluation. The phrase has a dark origin in the 1978 Jonestown deaths, so it carries an edge of warning about blind conviction even when used lightly in tech.
drink-the-kool-aid.depth:
Drinking the Kool-Aid means accepting a belief system uncritically, and the phrase has a genuinely grim origin in the 1978 Jonestown mass murder-suicide, which is worth knowing given how casually it is used in business settings. Many who died were coerced or were children, and the flippant usage sits uncomfortably against that.

In technology it describes uncritical adoption: the framework that will solve everything, the methodology applied without regard to context, the vendor pitch repeated internally as though it were an assessment. The tell is not enthusiasm but the absence of stated limits. Someone who genuinely understands a technology can describe where it fits badly, and someone who cannot describe that has usually adopted a position rather than reached one.

There is a defensible inverse, though. Committing to a chosen approach and using it properly beats perpetual hedging, and a team that treats every decision as provisional never gets the benefit of any of them. The distinction is whether the commitment came after the evaluation or instead of it, which is a question about process rather than about how strongly anyone believes.

bus-factor.def: The number of people who would have to be hit by a bus before a project stalls for lack of knowledge.
bus-factor.context: A bus factor of one means a single person holds critical, undocumented knowledge - a serious risk. Teams raise it deliberately through documentation, pairing, and code review so that no component depends on exactly one irreplaceable head.
bus-factor.depth:
The bus factor is the number of people who would have to be hit by a bus before a project is in serious trouble, and the morbid framing is the point: it forces an uncomfortable question that politer language lets people avoid. A bus factor of one means a single person's absence stops the work.

What makes it useful is that it measures something organizations systematically fail to see. The person who is the bus factor is usually productive, reliable and trusted, so nothing looks wrong. The risk is invisible precisely because the system is working, and it only materializes when they take leave, change teams, or resign, at which point the knowledge turns out to have been in one head and nowhere else.

Raising it is unglamorous and cheap compared to the alternative. Documentation that describes why rather than what, pair work on the systems only one person touches, rotating who handles which incident, and deliberately sending the expert on holiday to find out what breaks. The last one is the honest test: a team that cannot function while someone is away has already discovered its bus factor, it just has not admitted it.

happy-path.def: The default scenario where everything is valid and nothing goes wrong.
happy-path.context: Code that only handles the happy path works in the demo and breaks in production, where inputs are malformed and services time out. Good engineering spends most of its effort on the unhappy paths - the errors, edges, and failures the happy path ignores.
happy-path.depth:
The happy path is the execution route where everything works: valid input, available dependencies, sufficient permissions, no timeouts. It is the path demos follow, the path most tests cover, and the path that represents the smallest fraction of what production actually does.

Everything interesting lives off it. The disk fills, the token expires mid-request, the upstream returns a 200 with an empty body, the user pastes a name with an emoji in it. Systems are judged by how they behave in those cases, and the difference between a mature system and a fragile one is rarely happy-path behaviour, which is usually identical in both.

The practical discipline is to enumerate deliberately rather than reactively. What happens when this call fails, when it succeeds slowly, when it succeeds twice because the client retried, when the response is well-formed and wrong. Most production incidents are unhandled paths that were entirely predictable in advance, and the reason they were not handled is that nobody scheduled the fifteen minutes it takes to write them down before writing the code.

code-smell.def: A surface sign in code that hints at a deeper design problem, without being a bug itself.
code-smell.context: Long methods, duplicated logic, and giant classes are classic smells: the code runs, but something is off and likely to cause pain later. Kent Beck coined the term and Martin Fowler popularized it as a prompt to consider refactoring, not an automatic verdict.
code-smell.depth:
A code smell is a surface indication that usually corresponds to a deeper problem, and the metaphor is doing careful work: a smell is not a bug, it is a hint that something may be wrong. Kent Beck coined the term and Martin Fowler popularized it in the refactoring literature, deliberately choosing a word that implies suspicion rather than proof.

The classic catalogue is worth knowing because it gives names to things everyone recognizes. Long methods, large classes, long parameter lists, duplicated code, feature envy where a method is more interested in another class than its own, and shotgun surgery where one change requires edits in a dozen places. Naming them turns a vague unease during review into a specific observation someone can act on.

The failure is treating the catalogue as a rulebook. A long method that reads clearly and does one thing is fine, and mechanically breaking it into six small ones can make the logic harder to follow. Smells are prompts for investigation, not violations, and a codebase optimized to eliminate every smell is optimizing for a metric rather than for the humans who have to read it.

yagni.def: The principle that you should not build functionality until it is actually required.
yagni.context: A staple of Extreme Programming, YAGNI pushes back on speculative generality - the features and abstractions added 'just in case' that add cost and rarely get used. Build for today's real need and let tomorrow's requirements, when they arrive, drive tomorrow's code.
yagni.depth:
You aren't gonna need it is an extreme programming principle, and it is a claim about probability and cost rather than about ambition. Most speculative features are never used, every one of them must be maintained and understood by everyone who reads the code afterwards, and building for imagined requirements usually produces the wrong abstraction because the requirement, when it arrives, is not shaped the way you guessed.

The economics are the argument. Code that is not written has no bugs, needs no tests, and does not constrain future design. Adding a feature later, when the requirement is real and specific, is often cheaper than adapting a generic mechanism built for a guess, and it is always more likely to fit.

The honest boundary is that YAGNI applies to features, not to structural decisions. It is not an argument against security, error handling, or choosing an architecture that can accommodate growth, and it is frequently misused as one. Some decisions are genuinely expensive to reverse, and for those the correct instinct is the opposite: think ahead. The skill is telling the two apart, and the rough test is whether the thing is easy to add later or has to be designed in from the start.

worse-is-better.def: The observation that a simpler, less complete design often wins over a more correct but complex one.
worse-is-better.context: Richard Gabriel argued that Unix and C spread precisely because they favoured implementation simplicity over completeness, unlike richer designs that were harder to build and port. The phrase is now shorthand for the uncomfortable truth that the technically superior solution does not always win.
worse-is-better.depth:
Worse is better is Richard Gabriel's 1989 argument that a simpler design with worse behaviour often wins over a more correct one, and it is genuinely uncomfortable because he was arguing against his own preferences. The comparison was the MIT approach, which prioritizes correctness and completeness even at the cost of implementation complexity, against the New Jersey approach behind Unix and C, which prioritizes simplicity of implementation above all.

The claim is about propagation rather than quality. A simple implementation is easier to port, easier to understand, and easier to build on, so it spreads faster and gets improved by more people, while the correct design is still being finished. Half a solution that ships and adapts beats a whole solution that arrives late, and the ecosystem effects compound.

Unix and C are the evidence, and the argument is not a comfortable one to accept. Gabriel himself kept revisiting it and wrote both sides. The useful reading is not that quality does not matter, but that adoption is a real force with its own dynamics, and a design that ignores how software actually spreads is optimizing for a judgement nobody will be around to make.

cattle-not-pets.def: The mindset that servers should be disposable and interchangeable, not lovingly maintained individuals.
cattle-not-pets.context: A pet server has a name, gets nursed back to health when sick, and is irreplaceable; cattle are numbered, identical, and simply replaced when one fails. The analogy captures the shift to immutable, automated infrastructure where you rebuild rather than repair.
cattle-not-pets.depth:
Cattle not pets describes the shift from servers that are individually named, cared for and nursed back to health, to instances that are numbered, identical and replaced rather than repaired. The pet is a machine with a personality and a hostname someone chose; the cattle is one of forty that can be destroyed without ceremony.

The operational consequence is what matters. If a server is cattle, its configuration exists in a repository rather than in its filesystem, its state lives somewhere else, and rebuilding it is routine rather than an event. That property is what makes automated recovery, autoscaling and immutable deployment possible at all, and the cultural shift is harder than the technical one because it means giving up the diagnostic satisfaction of fixing a machine.

The honest limit is that not everything is cattle. Stateful systems, databases with real data in them, and the appliances that terminate your traffic are not disposable, and treating them as though they were produces confident destruction of things nobody can rebuild. The useful reading is not that pets are wrong, but that most machines were pets by accident rather than by decision, and being deliberate about which is which is the actual discipline.

premature-optimization.def: Tuning code for speed before you know it matters, at the cost of clarity and time.
premature-optimization.context: Knuth's line - 'premature optimization is the root of all evil' - warns against contorting code for performance gains that profiling has not shown you need. The full quote allows for the critical few percent that do matter; the point is to measure first, then optimize the part that actually moves the needle.
premature-optimization.depth:
Premature optimization is the root of all evil is the most misquoted line in software, and the damage comes from the truncation. Knuth wrote that we should forget about small efficiencies about ninety-seven percent of the time, and then immediately added that we should not pass up our opportunities in that critical three percent. The sentence is an argument for measurement, not against performance work.

The mangled version has been used to justify a great deal of genuinely slow software. It gets deployed against thinking about complexity at design time, against choosing an appropriate data structure, against caring how many round trips a page makes. None of that is what Knuth meant: the target was hand-tuning arbitrary lines of code on intuition before knowing where time is actually spent.

The distinction is between optimization and design. Choosing an algorithm whose complexity suits the expected input size is design, and doing it late is expensive because it changes the shape of everything around it. Rewriting a loop to save instructions before profiling is optimization, and doing it early is usually waste. Measure first, optimize what the measurement identifies, and do not confuse either with the architectural decisions that have to be made before there is anything to measure.

chestertons-fence.def: The principle that you should not remove something until you understand why it was put there.
chestertons-fence.context: The parable: do not tear down a fence across a road just because its purpose is not obvious, because someone had a reason you may not see. In code, it is the caution against deleting the strange line, the odd check, or the legacy workaround before you learn what quietly depends on it.
chestertons-fence.depth:
Chesterton's fence is the argument that you should not remove something until you know why it was put there. The original passage describes a fence across a road: the reformer says it serves no purpose and should go, and the reply is that if you do not know why it exists, you are not yet qualified to remove it. Find the reason first, then remove it if the reason is gone.

In software this is the mysterious configuration line, the check that appears redundant, the sleep call in the middle of an initialization routine. Someone put it there, probably at three in the morning, probably after an outage. It looks like noise because the incident it prevents has not happened since it was added, which is what a working fix looks like from the outside.

The principle has a real counterweight, and stating only the first half turns it into an argument for never changing anything. Sometimes the fence was built for a reason that no longer exists, sometimes nobody remembers and nobody can find out, and a codebase that never removes anything accumulates until it cannot be reasoned about at all. The discipline is proportional investigation: spend effort finding the reason in proportion to what the fence costs and what removing it risks.

footgun.def: A feature or API so easy to misuse that it invites you to shoot yourself in the foot.
footgun.context: C's manual memory management, implicit type coercion, and mutable global state are classic footguns: powerful, occasionally necessary, and quick to cause self-inflicted damage. Calling something a footgun is a warning that the default, obvious use is also the dangerous one.

sneakernet.def: Moving data by physically carrying storage media instead of using a network.
sneakernet.context: Walking a hard drive across the building - in your sneakers - can beat the network for sheer bulk, which is why 'never underestimate the bandwidth of a station wagon full of tapes' is a standing joke. Cloud providers formalized it with truck-scale data-transfer appliances for moving petabytes that would take months over the wire.

fud.def: A tactic of spreading fear, uncertainty, and doubt to undermine a competitor or idea.
fud.context: Classically aimed at buyers - implying a rival's product is risky or unproven to freeze a decision - the term dates to 1970s mainframe sales. In security it also describes vendor marketing that overstates threats to sell a fix.

anycast.def: Anycast assigns one IP (Internet Protocol) address to servers in many places and lets ordinary routing deliver each packet to one of them, normally the one nearest in routing terms rather than in distance.
anycast.context: With anycast, the network's own routing sends each client to the closest advertising site, spreading load and shrinking latency; it is the backbone of the DNS (Domain Name System) root, public resolvers and CDN (content delivery network) edges. The same address, many places, and the routing decides which one each client gets, which suits short, self-contained exchanges far better than long stateful sessions.
anycast.depth:
What it is. Anycast gives one IP (Internet Protocol) address to several servers in different places and lets ordinary routing decide which one a packet reaches. The idea was written down in Request for Comments (RFC) 1546, Host Anycasting Service (November 1993), by Craig Partridge, Trevor Mendez and Walter Milliken of Bolt Beranek and Newman (BBN), as an experimental service rather than a protocol. Its definition still holds: a stateless, best-effort delivery of a datagram to at least one, and preferably only one, of the hosts that serve the anycast address. The motivation was to find a server without caring which one: instead of consulting a list of archie servers and choosing one, a user would reach the nearest, and DNS (Domain Name System) resolvers would no longer need configured server addresses. Anycast is neither multicast, which copies a packet to every member of a group, nor load balancing in the usual sense: nothing inspects the packet or measures the servers, and the choice is made entirely by the routing tables between client and server.

How it is built. IPv4 has no anycast address class, so in practice the same unicast prefix is announced from every site, by BGP (Border Gateway Protocol) across the internet or by an interior protocol inside one network. RFC 4786 (December 2006, Best Current Practice 126, by Joe Abley and Kurt Lindqvist) is the operating manual. It notes that the routing system makes the node selection on the client's behalf, which is why nearest means preferred by routing policy and path length, not nearest on a map. Because the global BGP system does not reliably propagate host routes, each site announces a covering prefix short enough to survive common import filters, often a /24 for IPv4. A global node announces that prefix to its transit providers for the whole internet; a local node restricts it to a regional catchment with communities such as NO_EXPORT or NOPEER. IPv6 formalized part of the idea: RFC 4291 takes anycast addresses from the unicast space, syntactically indistinguishable from it, and predefines one, the Subnet-Router anycast address, the subnet prefix with an all-zero interface identifier, which every router must answer for the links it is attached to.

Why it suits DNS and strains TCP (Transmission Control Protocol). RFC 1546 already saw the problem: if a client sends two datagrams to an anycast address, the second may reach a different server from the first, so stateful protocols need some extra mechanism. RFC 4786 turns it into a design rule: the routing system's choice ought to stay stable for substantially longer than the transaction, which suits single-packet exchanges such as DNS over UDP (User Datagram Protocol) and is harder for bulk downloads or media streams. The Internet Architecture Board's RFC 7094 (January 2014) is blunter: unmodified stateful transports such as TCP fail probabilistically, but possibly catastrophically, under normal routing dynamics, because a session that lands on a node without its state is reset. It records that an anycast session at the 46th IETF (Internet Engineering Task Force) meeting in November 1999 reached no firm conclusion about TCP, and calls UDP the lingua franca of anycast. In practice TCP over anycast works where routes are stable and sessions short, and long-lived sessions are better moved to a unicast address after an anycast first contact, as RFC 4786 suggests.

The DNS runs on it. RFC 3258 (April 2002) described how an authoritative operator can serve one named server from many locations to reach under-served parts of the topology and cut query latency. The root zone is the best-known case: root-servers.org lists 13 root server identities, the letters A to M, run by 12 independent organizations, served on 11 November 2026 by 2,046 operational instances. The popular claim that there are 13 root servers confuses identities with machines, and taking one letter offline would mean taking down every instance announcing it. AS112 (RFC 7534, May 2015) uses anycast as a sink: queries for the reverse zones of private-use addresses that leak onto the public internet are answered by nodes anywhere that announce 192.175.48.0/24 and 2620:4f:8000::/48, among them the servers BLACKHOLE-1 and BLACKHOLE-2.IANA.ORG at 192.175.48.6 and 192.175.48.42, and the project is named after the autonomous system number assigned to it, 112.

Tying the route to the service. A node that announces the prefix while its service is down attracts traffic and drops it. RFC 4786 therefore recommends coupling the two, so that availability of the service triggers the route advertisement and failure triggers its withdrawal. F5 implements this on BIG-IP DNS as IP Anycast route health injection: with the Route Advertisement setting enabled on a DNS listener and ZebOS dynamic routing licensed, the system adds or removes the listener's route according to its availability, and zebos cmd sh ip route shows the advertised route with code K; F5 presents it as a way to blunt DDoS (distributed denial of service) attacks and cut DNS latency. The same coupling explains Meta's outage of 4 October 2021: its DNS servers were built to withdraw their BGP advertisements when they could not reach the data centres, and when the backbone failed every location did so at once, leaving servers that were still running unreachable from anywhere. Health-based withdrawal protects against one failed site; it needs a guard against all sites deciding they are unhealthy together.

Security and operations. RFC 4786 lists anycast's defensive value: each node sinks attack traffic from its own catchment, so a widely distributed attack is spread across all nodes instead of concentrated on one. It also lists the costs. More nodes mean more systems to monitor and patch, and an unauthorized party can announce the same prefix and capture requests; since the legitimate service is already visible from many origins in the routing system, a rogue node is harder to spot, which is why the RFC recommends protocols with robust authentication or integrity protection, DNSSEC (DNS Security Extensions) among its examples. Troubleshooting adds a variable, which instance answered, and RFC 4786 points to mechanisms built into protocols, such as the DNS Name Server Identifier (NSID) option of RFC 5001, as better than relying on a traceroute taken after the problem has moved.

Where it was retired. Not every service suits anycast. 6to4 relays were reachable through the anycast prefix 192.88.99.0/24 of RFC 3068, but experience showed the mechanism unsuitable for widespread use in anycast mode, since a client had no control over which relay, of whatever quality, it reached. RFC 7526 (May 2015, BCP 196) moved RFC 3068 to Historic, recommended that future products not support 6to4 anycast, and ruled that 192.88.99.0/24 must not be reassigned. The lesson generalizes: anycast works when every instance gives an equivalent answer and the conversation is short, and fails when instances differ in what they can do or the client needs the same one twice.

baz.def: The third metasyntactic placeholder, following foo and bar.
baz.context: When an example needs more than two placeholder names, "baz" comes next, then "qux". Like foo and bar, its lineage is recorded in RFC 3092.
baz.depth:
Baz is the third placeholder, arriving after foo and bar when an example needs another arbitrary name, and it is followed by qux and then by increasingly disputed conventions that no one agrees on.

Its etymology is the most contested of the set and probably reflects a truth about all of them: baz most likely emerged simply because two placeholders were not always enough and the sequence needed continuation. The Jargon File records the usage without settling the origin, and RFC 3092 documents the family while treating the derivations as folklore rather than fact.

Where it earns a mention of its own is in what happens past qux. There is no agreed fifth, and examples that need one reveal the author's background: quux marks a Lisp lineage, corge and grault come from a different tradition, and many people simply switch to numbered names. That is a small ethnographic signal in otherwise anonymous documentation, and it is the sort of thing that makes placeholder names worth a glossary entry rather than a footnote.

beaconing.def: The regular, automated check-ins a compromised host makes to its command server.
beaconing.context: Malware beacons to ask "any orders?" on an interval. That rhythm, even when the traffic is encrypted and disguised, is a strong detection signal: humans and normal apps do not phone the same unfamiliar host on a metronome.

bgp.def: Border Gateway Protocol (BGP) is the path-vector routing protocol that autonomous systems (ASes), the independently run networks of the internet, use to tell one another which Internet Protocol (IP) prefixes they can reach and through which chain of ASes. Its current version, BGP-4, is specified in RFC (Request for Comments) 4271.
bgp.context: Each autonomous system (AS) runs Border Gateway Protocol (BGP) sessions over TCP (Transmission Control Protocol) port 179 with its neighbours and announces the prefixes it originates or is willing to carry, each tagged with the list of ASes the route has crossed. A router keeps one best path per prefix, chosen first by local policy and only then by a fixed tie-break order, so the path traffic takes reflects business relationships (customer, peer, provider) as much as distance. Because the base protocol believes what a neighbour announces, filtering, RPKI (Resource Public Key Infrastructure) origin validation and declared peering roles carry the work of keeping hijacks and route leaks from spreading.
bgp.depth:
What it is, and what it is not. Border Gateway Protocol (BGP) version 4 is defined in Request for Comments (RFC) 4271 (January 2006), which obsoletes RFC 1771. It exchanges reachability between autonomous systems (ASes), sets of routers under one technical administration, and each route carries the list of ASes it has traversed, which is enough to build a graph of AS connectivity, prune routing loops and apply policy at the AS level. BGP is not an interior gateway protocol (IGP): it discovers no neighbours, measures no links and computes no shortest path. It supports only destination-based forwarding, so one AS cannot use it to make a neighbour carry traffic along a route other than the one that neighbour uses itself.

Sessions and messages. BGP runs over TCP (Transmission Control Protocol) port 179 and so needs no retransmission or sequencing of its own. Messages have a 19-octet header and a 4,096-octet maximum, raised to 65,535 by RFC 8654 (October 2019) for all but OPEN and KEEPALIVE when both sides advertise the capability. There are four types: OPEN (1), UPDATE (2), NOTIFICATION (3) and KEEPALIVE (4). Each side uses the smaller of the two hold times proposed in OPEN, which must be zero or at least 3 seconds; the suggested default is 90 seconds, with keepalives every third of it. The state machine runs Idle, Connect, Active, OpenSent, OpenConfirm, Established, and Active misleads: it means the speaker is still trying to acquire a peer by listening for a TCP connection, not that the session works. Once Established, each side sends what its export policy allows and afterwards only changes; there is no periodic refresh, and an error closes the session with a NOTIFICATION.

What a route carries. An UPDATE withdraws prefixes, announces prefixes and attaches path attributes. RFC 4271 defines seven: ORIGIN (type code 1), AS_PATH (2) and NEXT_HOP (3), all well-known mandatory; MULTI_EXIT_DISC, the MED (4); LOCAL_PREF (5), used inside an AS; ATOMIC_AGGREGATE (6); and AGGREGATOR (7). Each AS prepends its own number to AS_PATH towards external peers, and a route whose AS_PATH contains an AS loop is excluded from selection, which is how BGP keeps loops out. RFC 1997 (August 1996) added communities, 32-bit policy tags with well-known values such as NO_EXPORT (0xFFFFFF01); RFC 4760 (January 2007) lets sessions carry IPv6 and other address families; and RFC 6793 (December 2012) widened AS numbers to four octets, with AS_TRANS, 23456, standing in for them on paths encoded for older two-octet speakers.

How the best path is chosen. Local policy sets a degree of preference first (inside the AS, the LOCAL_PREF), and only routes tied on it reach the fixed tie-break: fewest ASes in AS_PATH (an AS_SET counts as one), lowest ORIGIN, lower MED but only between routes from the same neighbouring AS, a route from external BGP (EBGP) before one from internal BGP (IBGP), lowest interior cost to the NEXT_HOP, lowest BGP Identifier, lowest peer address. Path length is a tie-breaker, not the objective, which is why traffic often follows a commercially preferred route over a shorter one. A route learned from one internal peer must not be passed to another unless the speaker acts as a route reflector, so IBGP needs a full mesh, route reflectors or confederations.

Where it came from. RFC 4271 credits experience with the Exterior Gateway Protocol (EGP) of RFC 904 in the NSFNET (National Science Foundation Network) backbone. Kirk Lougheed of Cisco and Yakov Rekhter of IBM's T.J. Watson Research Center published BGP as RFC 1105 in June 1989. The Washington Post, telling the story in 2015, has them sketching it on three ketchup-stained napkins over lunch at an engineering conference in Austin in January 1989, the 'three-napkins protocol', and quotes Rekhter: security 'wasn't even on the table'. BGP-2 (RFC 1163, June 1990) and BGP-3 (RFC 1267, October 1991) followed, and BGP-4, first published as RFC 1771 in March 1995, dropped address classes in favour of prefixes and aggregation, the support Classless Inter-Domain Routing (CIDR) needed.

The table it carries. Geoff Huston's annual review for APNIC (Asia Pacific Network Information Centre), published on 8 January 2026, counted between 1,040,000 and 1,050,000 IPv4 entries in the default-free zone, 5 per cent up on the year, about 242,000 IPv6 entries, up 9 per cent, and some 77,900 ASes in IPv4. RFC 7454 (BCP 194, February 2015) notes that IPv4 prefixes longer than /24 and IPv6 prefixes longer than /48 are generally neither announced nor accepted, and recommends a maximum-prefix limit on every session: below the full table for a peer, so that a peer suddenly leaking the full table is shut down, and above it for a full-table upstream, to protect router memory.

Trust is the weak point. RFC 4271 requires support for TCP MD5 (Message Digest 5) signatures, and RFC 7454 prefers the TCP Authentication Option (TCP-AO) and recommends TTL (time to live) security, the Generalized TTL Security Mechanism (GTSM), but these protect the session, not the truth of what it carries. On 24 February 2008, in the reconstruction by the RIPE NCC (Réseaux IP Européens Network Coordination Centre), Pakistan Telecom (AS17557) announced 208.65.153.0/24 from 18:47 UTC and its upstream PCCW Global (AS3491) propagated it; more specific than YouTube's own 208.65.152.0/22, it won by longest prefix match until YouTube announced two /25s at 20:18 and PCCW withdrew the route at 21:01. A leak is the other failure: RFC 9234 (May 2022) defines it as propagation against the assumed relationships, such as from one transit provider to another, and lets neighbours declare roles in OPEN (provider, customer, peer, route server, route server client), with an Only to Customer (OTC) attribute that stops a route travelling back up.

The defences in the standards. RFC 8212 (July 2017) changed the default: without an explicit import or export policy, nothing is accepted from or sent to an EBGP peer. Route origin validation, RFC 6811 (January 2013), checks each route against Validated ROA (Route Origin Authorization) Payloads derived from the Resource Public Key Infrastructure (RPKI) and labels it Valid, Invalid or NotFound, leaving the treatment of Invalid to local policy. The RFC calls it a partial answer, since only the origin AS is checked, and warns that dropping Invalids turns the validation database into a denial-of-service target.

Not every outage is an attack. Meta's engineering post of 5 October 2021 explains the previous day: a command meant to assess global backbone capacity took down every backbone connection, a bug in the audit tool failed to stop it, and the DNS (Domain Name System) servers, designed to withdraw their BGP advertisements when they cannot reach the data centres, did exactly that and became unreachable while still running.

In practice. Fortinet's basic FortiGate example configures config router bgp (set as, set router-id, then set remote-as for each neighbour) and checks it with "get router info bgp neighbors" and "get router info bgp network". F5 BIG-IP runs BGP4 in the ZebOS bgpd daemon, enabled per route domain and configured through run /util imish in tmsh; F5's guide notes that the self IP port lockdown must admit TCP 179, that equal-cost multipath stays off until bgp max-paths is set, and that route health injection advertises virtual addresses with redistribute kernel.

bikeshedding.def: Spending disproportionate discussion on a trivial detail while an important, complex decision passes with little scrutiny.
bikeshedding.context: The name comes from C. Northcote Parkinson's 1957 illustration: a committee approves a nuclear plant quickly but argues for hours over the colour of the bike shed, because everyone has an opinion on the shed and few can weigh the reactor. It is the standing hazard of every design review.
bikeshedding.depth:
Bikeshedding is the observation that a committee will approve a nuclear power plant with little discussion and then argue for hours about the colour of the bicycle shed. Parkinson called it the law of triviality: the time spent on an agenda item is inversely proportional to its cost, because trivial items are the ones everyone feels qualified to have an opinion about.

The mechanism is not stupidity, which is why it is worth understanding rather than mocking. Nobody wants to admit they cannot evaluate the reactor design, so the reactor passes on the authority of whoever presented it. The bike shed is different: everyone has seen a shed, everyone can picture a colour, and participating costs nothing. Attention flows to where competence feels available.

The term entered software culture through a 1999 message on a FreeBSD mailing list, and it has been a standard piece of engineering vocabulary since. Naming it is most of the cure: in a design review, noticing aloud that the group has spent forty minutes on a variable name and four on the concurrency model tends to redirect the room without anyone needing to be told they are wasting time.

blast-radius.def: How far the damage spreads when one component fails or is compromised.
blast-radius.context: Blast radius is a design lens: architect so a single failure, a bad deploy, a breached account, is contained rather than cascading. Minimizing it, through isolation, segmentation, and limits, is why changes are staged and privileges are scoped.
blast-radius.depth:
Blast radius is the question to ask before a change, not during the incident review afterwards: if this goes wrong, what else goes with it? The image is an explosion's reach, and cloud operators use the phrase alongside the more formal scope of impact: Amazon Web Services (AWS) wrote after its February 2017 storage outage that it had been refactoring Amazon S3 (Simple Storage Service) into smaller cells to reduce blast radius, and its builders' library presents shuffle sharding as a way to limit it. The same idea runs through security, where Microsoft's zero trust guidance tells designers to assume breach, expecting attackers to be inside already and focusing controls on limiting the impact of a breach. In both senses it is a property of the structure around a component, not of the change or the attack itself, and it is distinct from likelihood: a small chance of a failure that reaches everything can matter more than a likely one that reaches nothing.

The size is rarely visible from the change ticket. A configuration that touches one virtual server has a small radius; one that touches a shared profile, a route domain, or a certificate used by forty services has a large one. On F5 BIG-IP the documentation spells out why shared objects travel: custom profiles inherit setting values from their parent, and editing a default profile, which F5 does not recommend, changes what every custom profile later created from it inherits. The Access Policy Manager manual goes further and states a radius outright: a misconfigured single sign-on object for HTTP (Hypertext Transfer Protocol) Basic, NTLM (NT LAN Manager), Kerberos or OAuth Bearer can disable single sign-on for every method in the user's session when that resource is reached, while the two form-based methods are the only exceptions.

Simple changes with large radii cause the worst outages, which is why difficulty and consequence have to be judged separately. On 28 February 2017, at 9:37 AM Pacific time, an authorized S3 engineer following an established playbook ran a command to remove a small number of servers from a billing subsystem in the US-EAST-1 region; one input was mistyped, a much larger set was removed, and it included servers for the index subsystem, which holds the metadata and location of every S3 object in the region, and the placement subsystem. GET, LIST and DELETE requests recovered at 1:18 PM and PUT at 1:54 PM, and until 11:37 AM AWS could not even update its own health dashboard, which depended on S3. The fixes were about radius rather than skill: the tool now removes capacity more slowly and refuses to take any subsystem below its minimum, other tools were audited for the same safeguard, and partitioning of the index subsystem into smaller cells was brought forward.

Shared dependencies carry the largest radii, and identity and endpoint software are the most shared of all. On 15 March 2021 an automated key-rotation job removed one signing key that Azure Active Directory (Azure AD) still needed; once the changed metadata was published at about 19:00 UTC (Coordinated Universal Time), applications that trusted Azure AD stopped accepting tokens signed with that key, and recovery ran until 09:25 UTC the next day as caches refreshed. On 19 July 2024 a CrowdStrike content update for the Windows sensor, Channel File 291, supplied 21 input fields where the sensor expected 20; the out-of-bounds read crashed the machines that received it, an estimated 8.5 million Windows devices according to Microsoft, under one per cent of the total but concentrated in enterprises running critical services. CrowdStrike's remedies were radius controls: deployment rings that content must pass before production, customer control over when content is applied, and bounds checking in the interpreter.

Architecture can bound the radius in advance. AWS's bulkhead or cell pattern, named after the watertight compartments of a ship, runs several independent copies of a workload that share no state, each handling a slice of requests chosen by a partition key such as customer ID behind a thin routing layer; with 10 cells serving 100 requests, a failure leaves 90 per cent of requests unaffected, and it contains bad deployments and poison-pill requests as well as hardware faults. Shuffle sharding goes further: with eight workers split into four fixed shards a problem reaches a quarter of customers, but assigning each customer to one of the 28 possible pairs of workers cuts the overlap to 1/28; Amazon Route 53 gives every domain four of 2,048 virtual name servers, about 730 billion combinations, so an attack on one domain spares the others.

In security the radius of a breach is whatever the compromised identity, host or key can reach. Least privilege, which Microsoft frames as only the access needed for the shortest time required, segmentation and microsegmentation, separate administrative accounts and short-lived scoped credentials all shrink it, and the signing key of an identity provider is the clearest case of a component whose radius is everything that trusts it.

Practically, thinking in blast radius changes what you do rather than just how nervous you feel. It decides whether you stage the change on one node or one cell and verify before rolling on, whether you need a maintenance window, whether rollback is one command or a restore, whether a tool should refuse inputs above a threshold, and whether anybody outside your team needs to know. Those decisions should follow from the radius, not from the calendar. Neighbouring terms divide the work: the attack surface is what can be reached from outside, a single point of failure is a component whose radius is the whole service, a canary release is a deliberately tiny radius for the first exposure, and concentration risk is the same idea at the level of suppliers. Worth remembering: 90 per cent of requests safe with ten cells, 1/28 with shuffle sharding over eight workers, and one mistyped input in 2017 for a region's storage.

blue-team.def: The defenders: the people and tooling that detect, respond to, and recover from attacks.
blue-team.context: The blue team is the standing defence, monitoring, hardening, hunting, and responding, the counterpart the red team is testing. Most of the work is unglamorous and continuous: the alerts that fire, the logs that get read, the drills that get run.

bohrbug.def: A solid, reproducible bug that behaves the same way every time you run it.
bohrbug.context: The counterpart to the heisenbug, named after the deterministic Bohr atom. A bohrbug is the good kind of hard: it does not hide from observation, so once you find the input that triggers it, it triggers every time.
bohrbug.depth:
A bohrbug is the opposite of a heisenbug and, mercifully, the common case. It is deterministic: the same input produces the same failure every time, it survives a debugger, and it does not care whether anyone is watching. The name comes from the Bohr atom, solid and predictable, in contrast to Heisenberg's uncertainty.

Its virtue is that it is tractable. A reproducible bug can be bisected, minimized to a small case, fixed and then proven fixed by a regression test that fails before and passes after. The whole apparatus of software testing is built for this class, which is why bohrbugs are the ones that get closed and heisenbugs are the ones that get reopened.

The useful reflex is to try converting one into the other. When a fault is intermittent, effort spent finding the input that makes it deterministic is usually better spent than effort spent catching it in the act, and much of debugging skill is exactly this: narrowing conditions until an unpredictable failure becomes a predictable one. The taxonomy also includes mandelbugs, whose causes are so complex the behaviour looks chaotic, and schrödinbugs, which work fine until someone reads the code and realizes they never should have.

botnet.def: A network of compromised machines controlled as one, often for attacks or spam: each infected device (a bot, or zombie) runs software that takes instructions from the operator's command-and-control (C2) infrastructure, without its owner's knowledge.
botnet.context: Each infected device (a "bot" or "zombie") answers to a common command-and-control, letting an operator wield thousands of machines at once, most infamously to launch DDoS (distributed denial of service) floods. The owners usually have no idea their device has enlisted. Today the same machinery also sells initial access to ransomware gangs, rents out residential Internet Protocol (IP) addresses as proxies and hides state-sponsored intrusions behind home routers, which is why the defensive work has moved from blocking floods to taking command servers away from their owners.
botnet.depth:
What it is exactly. The word joins robot and network. The Internet Engineering Task Force's recommendations on bots in internet service provider (ISP) networks, Request for Comments (RFC) 6561 of March 2012, defines a bot as a program installed on a system so that it performs a task or set of tasks automatically, or semi-automatically, typically under the command and control of a remote administrator, the bot master; bots are also called zombies, and are usually installed without the user's full understanding, hidden inside other software or under false pretences. A botnet is a concerted network of such bots able to act on remotely generated instructions. The RFC notes that there are good bots too, in games and Internet Relay Chat (IRC), and excludes them; the term in security always means the malicious kind. MITRE's ATT&CK knowledge base, which catalogues adversary behaviour, files it as sub-technique T1584.005: adversaries may build a botnet by compromising many third-party systems, rent one from a booter or stresser service, or take over somebody else's by redirecting its bots to their own command servers. A botnet is not a kind of malware; it is what a malware campaign produces. Conficker was a worm whose purpose was a botnet, Mirai a worm-like program that built one, and Emotet an email-borne Trojan that turned victims into one.

What botnets are used for. RFC 6561's list is long and still accurate: identity theft, spam (by email, instant messaging and internet telephony), harvesting email addresses, distributed denial-of-service (DDoS) attacks, keylogging, fraudulent Domain Name System (DNS) redirection, hosting proxies and illegal content, fast-flux hosting, man-in-the-middle attacks and click fraud. The last decade has made three uses dominant. Botnets sell initial access: Emotet and Qakbot spread through spam with malicious attachments or links and then delivered other malware, ransomware above all; the US Department of Justice names Conti, ProLock, Egregor, REvil, MegaCortex and Black Basta among the ransomware groups that used Qakbot as their way in. Botnets sell addresses: 911 S5 rented out compromised home computers as residential proxies so that criminals could hide behind ordinary household IP addresses, and the Justice Department links its addresses to about 560,000 fraudulent unemployment insurance claims during the pandemic. And botnets hide state operations: ATT&CK records Volt Typhoon using end-of-life Cisco and NETGEAR small office and home office (SOHO) routers implanted with the KV Botnet malware, and another cluster, Quad7, using compromised SOHO routers for password spraying. The DDoS botnet, which made the word famous, is now one use among several.

How machines are recruited. The RFC's list of infection vectors covers almost every weakness in the field: unpatched operating systems, software vulnerabilities including zero-days, weak or absent passwords, malicious web sites, unpatched browsers, inherently insecure protocols, protocols deployed with their security switched off, and social engineering. Each famous botnet leaned on one. Conficker, from November 2008, infected Windows computers that had not installed the MS08-067 patch Microsoft had released weeks earlier, and its second version added removable storage devices. Mirai logged in to cameras and recorders over telnet with a built-in list of 62 default credentials and held 200,000 to 300,000 devices at a time. Emotet and Qakbot arrived as email. 911 S5 was bundled into free virtual private network (VPN) applications and into pay-per-install packages that came with pirated software. In every case the owner, in the Justice Department's recurring phrase, typically did not know the machine was infected.

Command and control, and its evolution. A botnet is only as useful, and only as vulnerable, as its command channel. RFC 6561 describes the arc: early bots used IRC, which was easy to shut down once the command server was identified; bot masters then moved to peer-to-peer (P2P) architectures, to Hypertext Transfer Protocol (HTTP) and other resilient channels, and to encryption, which made bots far harder to pick out of ordinary traffic and pushed defenders towards anomaly detection and behavioural analysis. Two DNS techniques became signatures of the period. Fast flux binds a domain to many addresses with very short time-to-live (TTL) values, so that it resolves to a changing set of proxies running on compromised hosts while the real server stays hidden. Domain generation algorithms (DGAs) let each bot compute the day's rendezvous domains for itself: early Conficker generated 250 pseudo-random domains a day, and its C version, from April 2009, 50,000 a day across some 110 top-level domains, of which each bot tried 500, while also using peer-to-peer updates. Researchers broke the algorithm quickly, but the author signed his updates, so registering a domain was not enough to hijack the botnet; the defenders could only deny him the domains.

How defenders find bots. RFC 6561 is still the best short guide for network operators, and it says its methods apply to campus and enterprise networks as well as ISPs. Detection draws on flow analysis of specific traffic (to mail servers, for example), aggregate traffic data, feeds from other ISPs and organizations, such as lists of the provider's addresses reported for sending spam, and complaints from customers and other users. It should combine several data points to avoid false positives, try to classify the bot so as to judge the threat and the remedy, keep tracking it because botnets change their capabilities, and protect the personal data it touches. Notification options range from email, telephone, post, instant message and Short Message Service (SMS) to browser notices and the walled garden, in which an infected customer's access is restricted to remediation resources until the machine is cleaned. Inside an enterprise the same logic applies to egress: a compromised host is a problem for its owner and a weapon for someone else, so outbound flows, DNS queries for fast-flux and generated domains, and connections to known command servers are where bots show themselves. ATT&CK is frank about the limit: the building of a botnet happens outside the target organization's visibility, so detection has to focus on the stages it touches, such as phishing or denial of service.

Taking botnets down. Since 2008 the answer to large botnets has been coordinated action against their command channels. Against Conficker, an informal coalition of Microsoft, the Internet Corporation for Assigned Names and Numbers (ICANN), domain registry operators, antivirus vendors and academic researchers, later called the Conficker Working Group, registered or blocked the generated domains before the author could use them, 250 a day and then, organized in under three weeks, the domains of the C variant across about 110 top-level domains. Its own report counts its biggest success as preventing the author from gaining control of the botnet, while admitting that infections, estimated at more than five million and concentrated in Asia, particularly India, and in Brazil, persisted for years. The model since has been seizure plus a law enforcement payload. In January 2021 police in several countries, working with the Federal Bureau of Investigation (FBI), gained lawful access to Emotet's servers and replaced its update with a file that cut infected computers off from their controllers without removing malware already installed, after about 1.6 million infections in under ten months. In August 2023 the FBI redirected Qakbot's traffic through its own servers, which told more than 700,000 infected computers to download an uninstaller, and seized about 8.6 million dollars in cryptocurrency. In May 2024 a US, Singaporean, Thai and German operation dismantled 911 S5, which the FBI called likely the world's largest botnet ever, with more than 19 million IP addresses in nearly 200 countries, and arrested its alleged administrator. Non-profit and private partners such as the Shadowserver Foundation and Microsoft appear in almost every one of these releases.

Neighbours, and the numbers worth keeping. A botnet is the resource; command and control (C2) is its nervous system; DDoS, spam, proxying and initial access are its products; booters and stressers are the shops that rent DDoS capacity to anyone. Its scale has moved with the devices: millions of Windows desktops for Conficker and 911 S5, hundreds of thousands of cameras and routers for Mirai, end-of-life routers for a state actor who needs addresses rather than bandwidth. The defensive lesson has been the same since RFC 6561: bots are found by watching what machines send, not what they receive, and they are beaten by taking away the channel through which they are told what to do.

brute-force.def: A brute-force attack tries every possible value of a password, key or other secret, or every value in a chosen list of likely ones, until one is accepted; its cost depends only on how many candidates there are and how fast each can be tested.
brute-force.context: A brute-force attack simply exhausts the space, every password, every key, whereas a dictionary attack tries likely candidates first, and password spraying and credential stuffing are its variants against many accounts at once. The decisive split is online versus offline: guessing against a live login is limited by the service, which can count failures and slow or lock the account, while guessing against a stolen hash or a captured ciphertext runs at the attacker's own hardware speed. Strong, high-entropy secrets win by making the space too large to search in any useful time; rate limiting and lockouts make each online guess costly, and salted, deliberately slow password hashing does the same offline. MITRE's ATT&CK knowledge base catalogues it as technique T1110, and the United States National Institute of Standards and Technology (NIST) caps online attempts at 100 consecutive failures per account.
brute-force.depth:
Brute force is the attack that needs no cleverness: enumerate candidates, test each, stop at the first that works. Its cost is the size of the search space multiplied by the cost of one test, divided by the number of tests that can run in parallel, and nothing else. That makes it the baseline against which every secret is measured. A key or password chosen uniformly from 2 to the power n possibilities has n bits of entropy, as the entry on entropy explains, and an attacker who must try them all needs 2 to the power n tests in the worst case and about half that on average. Every additional bit doubles the work, so the defender's levers are few and clear: enlarge the space, make each test more expensive, or limit how many tests the attacker may run.

The family has several members, and the names matter in an incident report. Pure exhaustive search tries every value in a defined space, every 56-bit key or every eight-character string from a given alphabet. A dictionary attack tries a list of likely values first, common passwords, leaked passwords, words with predictable substitutions, because people do not choose uniformly. ATT&CK, the MITRE Corporation's public knowledge base of adversary tactics and techniques, files all of them under technique T1110, Brute Force, in the Credential Access tactic, with four sub-techniques as read on 12 November 2026: T1110.001 Password Guessing against a live service, T1110.002 Password Cracking against acquired hashes, T1110.003 Password Spraying, which tries one or a few common passwords against many accounts so as to stay under each account's lockout threshold, and T1110.004 Credential Stuffing, which replays username and password pairs leaked from other breaches. The weakness on the defender's side has its own number in MITRE's Common Weakness Enumeration (CWE): CWE-307, Improper Restriction of Excessive Authentication Attempts, a product that does not stop many failed logins in a short time.

Online and offline guessing are different problems. Online, every guess is a login attempt the service can see, count and refuse, so the rate is the defender's to set. NIST (the United States National Institute of Standards and Technology), in SP 800-63B-4, the authentication volume of its Digital Identity Guidelines published in July 2025, requires a verifier to disable an authenticator after no more than 100 consecutive failed attempts on one account, and explains the number: it balances the chance of a correct guess, for instance 100 tries against a six-digit one-time code, against the cost of account recovery. It allows waits that grow as the limit approaches, from 30 seconds up to an hour, and bot-detection challenges, so that the legitimate user is not locked out by the attacker. Offline, the attacker holds a password hash or a ciphertext and tests candidates on their own hardware, as fast as it runs, with no one counting. There the only defences are the size of the space and the cost of each test, which is why NIST requires passwords to be stored salted and hashed with a password hashing scheme that takes a cost factor, and a salt of at least 32 bits, so that each guess is expensive and precomputed tables such as rainbow tables are useless, as the entries on salt and on rainbow tables describe.

Keys show the arithmetic at its starkest. The Data Encryption Standard (DES) had a 56-bit key, 2 to the power 56 possibilities. In July 1998 the Electronic Frontier Foundation (EFF) built a machine for well under 250,000 US dollars out of custom chips, 35,868 search units each testing 2.5 million keys per second, about 90 billion keys a second in all; it started on 13 July and found the key of RSA Laboratories' DES Challenge II-2 after 56 hours, on 15 July. That settled the argument about DES. A 128-bit key, as in AES-128 (the Advanced Encryption Standard), has 2 to the power 72 times as many possibilities as DES, so the same hardware would need roughly 2 to the power 72 times as long; this is why exhaustive search is not the threat to modern symmetric keys, and why attacks go instead after the weakest secret in the chain, which is usually a human password or a key derived from one.

Passwords are where brute force still succeeds, because human choices are small and skewed. NIST's current guidance answers with length and blocklists rather than composition rules: at least 15 characters for a password used as the only factor and at least 8 when it is part of multi-factor authentication (MFA), support for at least 64, a check of every new password against a list of common, expected and compromised values, and no other composition requirements. Because online guessing is already throttled, NIST notes, a blocklist only needs to remove the values an attacker would try first. Defenders who see one source trying many passwords on one account are looking at guessing; one source trying one password on many accounts is spraying; many sources each trying one valid-looking pair are stuffing, and lockouts counted per source address do nothing against the last two.

The controls are found at every layer. OWASP (the Open Worldwide Application Security Project) recommends counting failed logins per account, not per source address, choosing a threshold, an observation window and a lockout duration, considering an exponential lockout that starts at a second and doubles, and guarding against the denial of service that lockout itself creates, since an attacker can lock out other people's accounts on purpose; it treats CAPTCHA as defence in depth only, because many are solved automatically. ATT&CK's own mitigations for T1110 are lockout policies, with the same warning that too strict a policy becomes a denial of service, MFA, password policies that follow NIST, and resetting accounts known to appear in breached credential sets. On Linux, pam_faillock locks an account by default after 3 consecutive failures within 900 seconds, for 600 seconds. On Windows, the Account lockout threshold policy accepts 0 to 999, with 0 meaning never, and Microsoft's security baselines treat 10 as an acceptable starting point. FortiOS locks out an administrator after three failed attempts by default, for 60 seconds, adjustable with admin-lockout-threshold and admin-lockout-duration. ATT&CK also notes that adversaries combine brute forcing with External Remote Services as part of initial access, and with password policy and account discovery once inside, which is why exposed management interfaces and remote access services deserve the strictest limits.

The numbers worth keeping: n bits of entropy means 2 to the power n candidates; 56 hours for 56-bit DES in 1998; 100 consecutive failures as NIST's ceiling for online attempts; 15 characters for a single-factor password; a salt of at least 32 bits; and T1110 with its four sub-techniques. Brute force is also the measure behind most other entries: a key derivation function exists to make each guess slower, a salt exists to stop one computation serving many victims, and rate limiting exists to keep online guessing online.

bug-bounty.def: A program that pays researchers for responsibly reporting security flaws.
bug-bounty.context: Bug bounties put responsible disclosure on a formal footing: a defined scope, rules, and rewards turn would-be adversaries into paid allies. They do not replace internal security, but they widen the set of eyes looking for what you missed.

cargo-cult-programming.def: Copying code or rituals that seem to work without understanding why, in the hope the result follows.
cargo-cult-programming.context: The phrase adapts Richard Feynman's "cargo cult science": going through the motions and expecting the outcome to appear. In code it looks like pasting a config, an incantation, or a boilerplate class because it worked somewhere else, without grasping what it does. The cure is understanding, not more copying.
cargo-cult-programming.depth:
Cargo cult programming is copying the form of something that worked without understanding why it worked. The configuration block gets pasted in because a search result had it, the flag is set because a colleague sets it, and the code is correct in appearance and hollow in mechanism.

The name comes by way of Feynman's 1974 Caltech address, where he described cargo cult science as work with all the outward apparatus of rigour and none of the substance. The metaphor is drawn from post-war Pacific islands and is worth handling carefully, since it patronizes the people it describes; the software usage has drifted far from the anthropology and mostly names a failure of curiosity rather than a failure of intelligence.

What makes it worth naming is that it is invisible from the outside. Working code and cargo cult code look identical until conditions change, and then the copied thing fails in a way nobody can diagnose because nobody ever knew what it did. The test is simple and uncomfortable: can you explain what this line does and what breaks without it. If not, you have not written it, you have transcribed it.

chain-analysis.def: Tracing cryptocurrency flows across a public blockchain to follow the money.
chain-analysis.context: Because most blockchains are public and permanent, transactions can be clustered and followed, which is how investigators unwind laundering despite mixers. It is the defender's and regulator's side of the same ledger the darkweb relies on.

cia-triad.def: The three core goals of information security: confidentiality, integrity, and availability.
cia-triad.context: Confidentiality keeps data from the wrong eyes, integrity keeps it from being altered, and availability keeps it reachable when needed. Almost every security control serves one of these three, and they often trade off against each other.

cidr.def: Classless Inter-Domain Routing (CIDR) writes an IP (Internet Protocol) network as an address plus a prefix length, such as 10.0.0.0/8, and allocates and routes address space in blocks of any power-of-two size instead of the old fixed classes.
cidr.context: Classless Inter-Domain Routing (CIDR), RFC (Request for Comments) 4632, replaced the rigid class A, B and C system with a slash number saying how many leading bits are the network. It lets blocks be sized to need and lets many adjacent networks be announced as one prefix, which is what kept the global routing table manageable, and it is the notation behind almost every subnet, firewall rule, ACL (access control list) and cloud network decision.
cidr.depth:
What it is. Classless Inter-Domain Routing (CIDR) is two things at once, an address allocation plan and the notation that goes with it. The current statement is Request for Comments (RFC) 4632 (August 2006, Best Current Practice 122, by Vince Fuller and Tony Li), which obsoletes RFC 1519. In CIDR notation a prefix is a 32-bit IPv4 address followed by a slash and a decimal from 0 to 32 giving the number of significant bits: the legacy class B network 172.16.0.0 with mask 255.255.0.0 becomes 172.16.0.0/16, and the class C network 192.168.99.0 becomes 192.168.99.0/24. Any power-of-two block from 1 to 2^32 addresses can be described. CIDR is not the same thing as subnetting: RFC 950 (August 1985) introduced subnet masks to divide a classful network internally, and RFC 1817 (August 1995) describes CIDR as the generalization of variable-length subnet masks (VLSM) together with the elimination of classes altogether.

What it replaced. RFC 791 had divided the address space into classes by leading bits: class A (0), 128 networks of 16,777,216 addresses; class B (10), 16,384 networks of 65,536; class C (110), 2,097,152 networks of 256, of which 254 are usable hosts; 1110 later became multicast. In the late 1980s demand for class B networks grew at what looked like an exponential rate, and in November 1991 the Internet Engineering Task Force (IETF) formed the ROAD (Routing and Addressing) group, which met in January 1992 and named three problems: class B exhaustion, since class C was too small and class B too large for most organizations; routing tables growing beyond what software, hardware and people could manage; and eventual exhaustion of the 32-bit space. The first two were expected to become critical between 1993 and 1995.

The response. Supernetting was proposed in RFC 1338 (June 1992), and CIDR was published as RFC 1518 and RFC 1519 in September 1993. It was meant as a three-to-five-year measure while a permanent architecture was built; RFC 4632 notes dryly that CIDR has far outlasted its anticipated lifespan. It slowed both routing table growth and address consumption, but did not try to solve exhaustion: the Number Resource Organization announced on 3 February 2011 that the IANA (Internet Assigned Numbers Authority) free pool was fully depleted, each Regional Internet Registry (RIR) having received its final /8. Routing protocols had to carry prefix lengths: RFC 1817 counts OSPF (Open Shortest Path First), version 2 of RIP (Routing Information Protocol), Integrated IS-IS and E-IGRP among the interior protocols that support CIDR and BGP-4 (Border Gateway Protocol 4) as the exterior one, and lists the original RIP, BGP-3, EGP (Exterior Gateway Protocol) and IGRP as protocols that do not.

Allocation follows topology. IANA allocates /8 blocks to the RIRs; they allocate smaller blocks to local registries and providers, RFC 4632's examples being a /15 for a large provider and a /21 for a smaller one, and providers assign to customers. Allocate means delegating space for further delegation; assign means numbering hosts directly. A single-homed site numbered from its provider's block needs no route of its own, because the provider announces one aggregate. Two cases punch holes in that: a multi-homed site, which every provider must announce explicitly, and a site that changes provider without renumbering. Legacy class C space that could not be aggregated, known as the swamp, was estimated at about 15,000 routes in 2006.

Longest match and the null route. RFC 4632's first rule is that forwarding is done on a longest-match basis: when prefixes overlap, the most specific wins, which is how a re-homed customer's /24 can coexist with its old provider's aggregate and also how a more-specific hijack captures traffic. The second rule is that a router that announces an aggregate must discard packets matching the aggregate but none of its more specific routes, with the null interface as next hop, because otherwise unreachable addresses inside the aggregate would loop. The RFC warns about the side effect: traceroute then shows the drop inside the aggregating network, even when the real fault is that another network stopped announcing the more specific prefix.

The arithmetic. A prefix of length n contains 2^(32 minus n) addresses, so each extra bit halves the block: /32 is a single host route, /24 holds 256 addresses, /16 65,536, /8 16,777,216, and /0 is the default route. On a conventional subnet the first address names the network and the last is the broadcast address, leaving 2^(32 minus n) minus 2 for hosts; RFC 3021 (December 2000) made /31 usable on point-to-point links, where both addresses are hosts. Two aligned CIDR blocks either do not overlap at all or one contains the other, so an overlap test is a single containment check. RFC 4632 records that prefixes shorter than /8 have never been allocated, although 128.0.0.0/1 and 192.0.0.0/2 have been seen in routing tables through operator error.

IPv6 and the cloud. IPv6 kept the notation: RFC 4291 writes prefixes as ipv6-address/prefix-length, and RFC 7608 (July 2015, BCP 198) requires that forwarding not restrict prefix length by design, handling any length up to /128 in increments of 1. Cloud networks turn CIDR into hard constraints. Amazon's VPC (virtual private cloud) guide allows an IPv4 VPC block between /16 (65,536 addresses) and /28 (16), forbids overlap with blocks already associated, rules out ranges such as 0.0.0.0/8, 127.0.0.0/8, 169.254.0.0/16 and 224.0.0.0/4, and does not allow an existing block to be resized, which is why the first prefix chosen for a VPC deserves the most thought.

cipher-suite.def: The named combination of algorithms a TLS (Transport Layer Security) connection agrees on, identified by a two-byte value: up to TLS 1.2 the key exchange, authentication, bulk cipher and integrity check; in TLS 1.3 only the authenticated cipher and the hash used for key derivation.
cipher-suite.context: A cipher suite names the algorithms both sides settle on during the handshake, each one registered with a two-byte value by the Internet Assigned Numbers Authority (IANA). Up to TLS (Transport Layer Security) 1.2 the name spells out the key exchange, the server authentication, the bulk cipher and the integrity algorithm, as in TLS_ECDHE_RSA_WITH_AES_128_GCM_SHA256. TLS 1.3 cut the suite down to an authenticated encryption with associated data (AEAD) cipher and a hash, as in TLS_AES_128_GCM_SHA256, and negotiates key exchange and signatures separately. Which suites a server allows, and in which order, decides how strong and modern its connections are.
cipher-suite.depth:
What it is on the wire. The Transport Layer Security (TLS) 1.2 specification, Request for Comments (RFC) 5246 of August 2008, defines a cipher suite as two bytes, uint8 CipherSuite[2], standing for a whole combination of algorithms. The client lists the suites it supports in its ClientHello, most preferred first; the server picks one or, if nothing is acceptable, answers with a handshake failure alert. A server must ignore values it does not recognize, and that rule is what GREASE (Generate Random Extensions And Sustain Extensibility, RFC 8701, January 2020) relies on: it reserves 16 values from 0x0A,0x0A to 0xFA,0xFA that clients advertise so peers keep handling unknown values correctly. A suite is not the protocol version and not the certificate; it is the algorithm agreement that both have to fit.

Reading a TLS 1.2 name. RFC 5246 says each suite fixes a key exchange algorithm, a bulk encryption algorithm with its key length, a message authentication code (MAC) algorithm and a pseudorandom function (PRF), and the names spell the parts out in order, which makes them look intimidating when they are in fact self-describing. TLS_ECDHE_RSA_WITH_AES_128_GCM_SHA256, value 0xC0,0x2F, is Elliptic Curve Diffie-Hellman Ephemeral (ECDHE) key exchange, a server authenticated by an RSA (Rivest-Shamir-Adleman) certificate, the Advanced Encryption Standard (AES) with a 128-bit key in Galois/Counter Mode (GCM), and SHA-256 (Secure Hash Algorithm, 256-bit) as the hash. TLS_RSA_WITH_AES_128_CBC_SHA, 0x00,0x2F, the suite RFC 5246 made mandatory to implement, is RSA key transport, AES in cipher block chaining (CBC) mode and HMAC-SHA1 (a hash-based message authentication code over SHA-1). OpenSSL calls the first one ECDHE-RSA-AES128-GCM-SHA256.

TLS 1.3 changed the shape on purpose. RFC 8446 (August 2018) pruned every legacy symmetric algorithm, leaving only authenticated encryption with associated data (AEAD), removed static RSA and Diffie-Hellman so that every public-key exchange gives forward secrecy, and took key exchange and authentication out of the suite. A TLS 1.3 suite, named TLS_AEAD_HASH, fixes only the record cipher and the hash used with the HMAC-based key derivation function (HKDF); the key exchange group travels in the supported_groups and key_share extensions and the signature scheme in signature_algorithms, chosen independently. There are five suites, 0x13,0x01 to 0x13,0x05: TLS_AES_128_GCM_SHA256, which every implementation must support, TLS_AES_256_GCM_SHA384 and TLS_CHACHA20_POLY1305_SHA256, which it should, and two using AES in CCM mode (counter mode with a CBC-MAC). The families do not mix: a 1.3 suite cannot be used for TLS 1.2, nor the reverse. RFC 9846 (July 2026) republished TLS 1.3 with the same five suites and obsoleted both RFC 8446 and RFC 5246.

The registry and its verdicts. The Internet Assigned Numbers Authority (IANA) keeps the TLS Cipher Suites registry, with a Recommended column: N means a suite has not been through the consensus of the Internet Engineering Task Force (IETF), has limited applicability or serves specific uses, not that it is broken; Y marks the ones endorsed; and D, added by RFC 9847 in December 2025, means discouraged, SHOULD NOT or MUST NOT. The registry warns against implementing its suites blindly and keeps CCM_8 at N for its truncated authentication tag. On 11 November 2026 the other four TLS 1.3 suites and TLS_ECDHE_RSA_WITH_AES_128_GCM_SHA256 were Y, while the once-mandatory TLS_RSA_WITH_AES_128_CBC_SHA, the Rivest Cipher 4 (RC4) suites and Triple DES (3DES) were D.

What the IETF says to allow. Best Current Practice (BCP) 195, now RFC 9325 (November 2022), forbids NULL encryption, RC4, already banned in every TLS version by RFC 7465 of February 2015, and anything under 112 bits of security, including the 40- and 56-bit export suites. It discourages anything under 128 bits, which catches 3DES, whose 168-bit key gives an effective 112 against meet-in-the-middle attacks; requires support for and preference of forward secrecy; and recommends four TLS 1.2 suites, ECDHE with RSA or ECDSA (Elliptic Curve Digital Signature Algorithm) authentication and AES-128 or AES-256 in GCM. RFC 10015 (July 2026) tightened TLS 1.2 further: static RSA key transport and finite-field Diffie-Hellman, ephemeral or not, are now MUST NOT. Its reasons are concrete: RSA key exchange has no forward secrecy and keeps producing variants of Daniel Bleichenbacher's 1998 attack, such as DROWN (2016) and ROBOT (2018); finite-field groups are often 1,024 bits against a discrete logarithm record of 795; and reused keys feed the Raccoon timing attack of 2020. RFC 9851, also July 2026, froze TLS 1.2 apart from urgent security fixes, exporter labels and Application-Layer Protocol Negotiation (ALPN) identifiers.

Configuring it. The two generations are set separately.
