OpenSSL takes a cipher list for TLS 1.2 and below, strings joined by colons in which an exclamation mark removes suites for good, a minus sign removes them so a later string can add them back, a plus sign moves them to the end and @STRENGTH sorts by key length, plus a separate ciphersuites list for TLS 1.3, by default TLS_AES_256_GCM_SHA384:TLS_CHACHA20_POLY1305_SHA256:TLS_AES_128_GCM_SHA256; openssl ciphers -v -stdname shows what a string really selects. On F5 BIG-IP the DEFAULT string is a subset of NATIVE, the full set the system supports, cipher rules combined in cipher groups (allow, restrict, exclude, in order) build the string, and tmm --clientciphers prints what a string expands to. DEFAULT has meant different things in different versions, so a profile left on it can change behaviour at upgrade time, and expanding a string into its resulting list before deploying it is worth the thirty seconds.

Order is policy, and the trade never goes away. The client states a preference; RFC 9325 notes that servers usually need their order set explicitly to prefer strong suites, and asks clients to offer TLS_ECDHE_RSA_WITH_AES_128_GCM_SHA256 first and servers to prefer it over weaker suites wherever it appears. Too permissive, and vulnerable options stay alive for clients that should have been upgraded years ago; too strict, and real users on old devices are locked out. Most of the protocol attacks of the 2010s exploited weak or obsolete options left on for compatibility, from RC4 to export-grade keys and Bleichenbacher oracles, which is why TLS 1.3 removed the options rather than patching around them.

Neighbours and numbers. Forward secrecy is a property of the key exchange, which only some TLS 1.2 suites give; and in TLS 1.3 the group and the signature scheme are negotiated beside the suite, which is where post-quantum key exchange arrives: X25519MLKEM768, a hybrid of X25519 and ML-KEM-768 (Module-Lattice-Based Key-Encapsulation Mechanism), is supported group 4588 in the IANA registry, not a cipher suite. Worth remembering: two bytes per suite, five TLS 1.3 suites from 0x13,0x01, four recommended TLS 1.2 suites, 112 bits as the floor and 128 as the target.

circuit-breaker.def: A pattern that stops calling a failing dependency for a while, so one outage does not drag everything down.
circuit-breaker.context: Like its electrical namesake, a software circuit breaker trips after too many failures and fails fast instead of piling up doomed requests, then periodically tests whether the dependency has recovered. It contains the blast radius of a downstream failure.

collision.def: When two different inputs produce the same hash output.
collision.context: Every hash has collisions in theory, since it maps infinite inputs to finite outputs, but a secure one makes finding a useful pair computationally infeasible. When a hash's collision resistance breaks (as happened to MD5 and SHA-1), it is retired for security use.
collision.depth:
A hash collision is two different inputs producing the same digest. Collisions always exist because a hash maps an unbounded input space onto a fixed-size output; the security question is whether anyone can find one on purpose, and for a strong function of sufficient output length the answer is no within any practical budget.

The distinction that matters operationally is between a collision, where the attacker chooses both inputs, and a preimage, where they must match a digest that already exists. Collisions are far cheaper, which is why MD5 and SHA-1 are broken for signatures, where an attacker can prepare two documents in advance, while being harder to abuse where the target value was fixed by someone else. Chosen-prefix collisions closed most of that remaining gap.

control-plane.def: The part of a network device or distributed system that decides how traffic or work should be handled (routing and signalling protocols, scheduling, distribution of configuration) and programs the data plane, which does the per-packet or per-request work at speed. A third plane, management, configures and monitors both.
control-plane.context: The control plane decides where things go (routes, configuration, scheduling) while the data plane does the actual forwarding at speed. Separating them is a core design idea across networking, Kubernetes and service meshes, and it sets the failure mode that matters most: whether traffic keeps flowing while the control plane is down, slow or under attack.
control-plane.depth:
Inside a router. The Internet Engineering Task Force's Forwarding and Control Element Separation (ForCES) requirements, Request for Comments (RFC) 3654 of November 2003, state the classic split. A network element has forwarding-plane components, built on application-specific integrated circuits (ASICs), network processors or general-purpose processors, which handle all data-path operations, and control-plane components, typically on general-purpose processors, which run routing and signalling protocols such as the Routing Information Protocol (RIP), Open Shortest Path First (OSPF) and the Resource Reservation Protocol (RSVP) and dictate forwarding behaviour by writing forwarding tables, per-flow quality of service (QoS) tables and access control lists (ACLs). RFC 3654 names the two logical halves the control element (CE) and the forwarding element (FE). RFC 6192 (March 2011) adds the definition engineers use when filtering: the control plane handles packets addressed to the device itself and packets it originates, while the forwarding plane receives a packet, looks up the next hop and sends it out; forwarding is usually done in ASICs at very high packet rates, control in software on a general-purpose CPU (central processing unit).

How many planes. RFC 7426, written by the Internet Research Task Force's Software-Defined Networking Research Group in January 2015, lists five: the forwarding plane, the resources that forward traffic; the operational plane, the resources that run each device; the control plane, the functions that instruct devices how to process and forward packets; the management plane, the functions that monitor, configure and maintain devices; and the application plane, the software that programs network behaviour. It separates control from management on three axes. Timescale: the control plane updates often, in milliseconds, while the management plane works in minutes, hours or days. Persistence: control-plane state such as computed routes is ephemeral, management state such as configuration persists across reboots. Locality: the control plane has traditionally run on each device and been distributed, the management plane centralized; software-defined networking (SDN), by logically centralizing control in a controller, muddles that last distinction. RFC 7426 names ForCES and OpenFlow as examples of control-plane southbound interfaces, and records that controllers such as NOX and Beacon speak OpenFlow.

Protecting it. Because the control plane runs in software on one general-purpose processor, the cheapest way to break a router is not to fill its links but to flood the traffic it must process itself. RFC 6192's method is to identify every legitimate kind of control-plane traffic (routing sessions, management, monitoring) and install a filter in the forwarding plane that drops, or rate-limits to an acceptable level, everything else destined to the router; the filter applies only to traffic addressed to the device, never to transit traffic. The same reasoning explains Bidirectional Forwarding Detection (BFD): RFC 5880 defines a Control Plane Independent bit that a system sets when its BFD runs in the forwarding plane and keeps working through control-plane disruptions, so that a neighbour can tell whether a lost BFD session means a dead path or a busy CPU.

On security appliances. A FortiGate makes the split per session. According to Fortinet's hardware acceleration guide, packets that initiate a session go to the CPU, which applies policy and decides whether the session meets the fast-path requirements; if it does, the CPU hands the session key, or the Internet Protocol Security (IPsec) security association (SA), and the firewall action to a network processor (NP), which then matches and forwards the following packets itself. Features the NP cannot perform, intrusion prevention among them, keep a session on the CPU. On BIG-IP, the Traffic Management Microkernel (TMM) is the data plane and daemons such as MCPd, mergeD and the BigD health monitor make up the control plane. F5's 21.1 release notes describe moving control-plane components to 64-bit, raising BigD to 15,000 control-plane monitors with a thread formula that assumes TMM takes half the hyperthreaded cores, and warn that MCPd restarts interrupt the data path and affect TMM: the separation is real, but not total.

In Kubernetes and service meshes. Kubernetes uses the networking vocabulary for its own architecture. Its control plane components manage the overall state of the cluster: kube-apiserver exposes the Kubernetes Hypertext Transfer Protocol (HTTP) application programming interface (API), etcd is the consistent and highly available key-value store for all API server data, kube-scheduler assigns unbound Pods to nodes, kube-controller-manager runs the controllers that implement API behaviour, and an optional cloud-controller-manager integrates with a cloud provider. Node components (the kubelet, the optional kube-proxy and the container runtime) keep the Pods running. Istio splits a service mesh the same way: a data plane of Envoy proxies deployed as sidecars, which mediate all communication between microservices and report telemetry, and a control plane that configures those proxies.

In the cloud, and the failure that matters. Amazon's Builders' Library defines a control plane as the machinery for making changes (adding, deleting and modifying resources) and propagating them, and the data plane as the daily business of those resources: for Amazon Elastic Compute Cloud (EC2), launching an instance is control plane, routing its packets and serving its disk reads is data plane, and the data plane is far simpler. Its design rule, static stability, is that the system keeps working when a dependency is impaired, even if it sees no updates. The incident Amazon Web Services (AWS) suffered on 7 December 2021 shows why. Congestion on the devices joining AWS's internal network, which hosts monitoring, internal Domain Name System (DNS) resolution, authorization and parts of the EC2 control plane, to the main network made the EC2 APIs for launching and describing instances fail from 7:33 AM Pacific Standard Time (PST), with launches recovering only by 2:40 PM PST, while running instances were unaffected. The data plane held; anything whose recovery depended on creating resources did not. The practical rule for any design is the same on a router, an appliance or a cluster: the data plane must keep forwarding on its last good state when the control plane is gone, and nothing in the recovery path should require the control plane to be healthy.

cors.def: Cross-Origin Resource Sharing (CORS) is the header protocol, now defined in the Fetch Standard, by which a server tells browsers that a script loaded from another origin may read its response and, for requests beyond what an HTML form could send, may send the request at all.
cors.context: By default the same-origin policy stops a script from one origin (scheme, host and port) from reading responses from another; Cross-Origin Resource Sharing is how a server opts in to specific cross-origin access, with response headers such as Access-Control-Allow-Origin. For anything beyond the simplest requests, the browser first asks permission with a preflight: an OPTIONS request the server must answer correctly before the real one is sent. Misunderstanding that two-step exchange is behind a large share of blocked-by-CORS errors in development. CORS relaxes a browser restriction rather than protecting the server, and a simple cross-origin POST still reaches the server whatever the answer says.
cors.depth:
CORS is a browser mechanism, and understanding that one fact resolves most confusion about it. The Fetch Standard of the WHATWG (Web Hypertext Application Technology Working Group), where it now lives, says the protocol exists to allow sharing responses across origins and to allow more versatile fetches than an HTML form can make; it is layered on top of HTTP, and it has to be opt-in so that data in responses behind a firewall, on intranets, does not leak, and so that responses to requests carrying credentials are not shared by accident. It does not protect the server; it protects users from having their credentials silently used by a site they did not intend to authorize. The same-origin policy blocks cross-origin reads by default, and CORS is the controlled exception a server can grant. It is not authentication, not a firewall rule and not a defence against cross-site request forgery (CSRF), and it is not Content Security Policy (CSP), which restricts what a page may load rather than who may read a server's answers.

Everything turns on the origin. RFC (Request for Comments) 6454, The Web Origin Concept, by Adam Barth, December 2011, defines an origin as the scheme, host and port of a URI (uniform resource identifier), and two URIs share an origin only when all three match: https://example.com and http://example.com are different origins, so are ports 443 and 8443 on the same host, and so is a subdomain. The Fetch Standard now supersedes the RFC's semantics for the Origin header. A serialized origin has no trailing slash and no path, which is why a server that answers https://app.example/ instead of https://app.example fails a check that looks identical to a person.

A CORS request is simply an HTTP request with an Origin header, although browsers also send Origin on every request whose method is neither GET nor HEAD, so its presence alone does not prove CORS is in play. Requests that stay within what a form could always send go straight out: the safelisted methods GET, HEAD and POST, a few safelisted headers whose values are no longer than 128 bytes, and a Content-Type of application/x-www-form-urlencoded, multipart/form-data or text/plain. The server's response then decides whether the calling script may read it, through Access-Control-Allow-Origin, which carries either the literal origin of the request or an asterisk, Access-Control-Allow-Credentials, and Access-Control-Expose-Headers, which lists response headers the script may see beyond the safelisted few. Anything else, such as a PUT or DELETE, a JSON (JavaScript Object Notation) content type, an Authorization header or a custom header, needs permission first.

The preflight is what surprises developers. Before the real request the browser sends OPTIONS with Access-Control-Request-Method, and Access-Control-Request-Headers when headers outside the safelist are involved, and proceeds only if the answer, with an ok status such as 200 or 204, lists the method and headers in Access-Control-Allow-Methods and Access-Control-Allow-Headers. Access-Control-Max-Age says how many seconds the answer may be cached, 5 by default; browsers cap it, Firefox at 24 hours and Chromium at 2 hours since version 76, after 10 minutes before that. A preflight never carries credentials, so an endpoint that demands authentication for OPTIONS fails every preflight, however correct the rest of its configuration. That is why a failing request that never appears in the server's logs with the expected method is usually a preflight that was refused or mishandled, often by a proxy, a web application firewall (WAF) or an authentication layer in front of the application.

Credentials are where CORS becomes dangerous. When a script asks for credentials, cookies and HTTP authentication included, the response can be shared only if Access-Control-Allow-Origin names the exact origin, never the wildcard, and Access-Control-Allow-Credentials is the literal value true, which is case-sensitive. The Fetch Standard says plainly that sharing responses and allowing requests with credentials is rather unsafe, and that extreme care is needed to avoid the confused deputy problem. The dangerous misconfiguration is reflecting the requesting origin while allowing credentials. The specification forbids the wildcard together with credentials for good reason, and echoing back whatever origin asked achieves the same effect while evading the check: any site can then make authenticated requests to the server and read the answers, which is the vulnerability CORS exists to prevent rather than a way to satisfy it. Two cousins of the same mistake are allowing the origin null, which MDN Web Docs warns against because data: and file: resources and sandboxed documents all serialize as null, and matching allowed origins by prefix or substring instead of comparing the whole serialized origin exactly against a list. MITRE catalogues the class as CWE-942 (Common Weakness Enumeration), a permissive cross-domain policy with untrusted domains, and its mitigations are to keep the policy restrictive and avoid wildcards.

What CORS does not stop matters as much as what it does. A simple cross-origin POST is delivered without asking, and the server acts on it before any browser decides whether the calling script may read the reply, so state-changing endpoints still need their own CSRF defences. The Fetch Standard adds that any work the server performs might still leak through side channels such as timing, and that a server wishing to refuse explicitly can answer 403 without the CORS headers. Tools other than browsers, such as curl or a script on a server, ignore CORS entirely: it binds browsers on behalf of their users, not clients in general.

Caching adds a quieter failure. If Access-Control-Allow-Origin varies with the request, rather than being the asterisk or one fixed origin, the response must carry Vary: Origin. The Fetch Standard explains why: without it, a response fetched by an ordinary navigation, without the header, can be cached and later reused for a CORS request, which then fails; and a shared cache or content delivery network can hand a response that allowed one origin to a page from another. The fix belongs in the same place as the policy: Vary: Origin whenever the answer depends on the Origin header.

The standard has moved house once. Cross-Origin Resource Sharing became a World Wide Web Consortium (W3C) Recommendation on 16 January 2014, edited by Anne van Kesteren, formerly of Opera Software, and produced by the Web Application Security and Web Applications working groups; its acknowledgements credit Brad Porter, Matt Oshry and R. Auburn with editing earlier versions. On 2 June 2020, under the memorandum of understanding between the W3C and the WHATWG, it became a Superseded Recommendation, kept for reference while new implementations follow the Fetch Living Standard, last updated on 19 October 2026 at the time of reading.

In practice CORS is configured wherever the response headers are written: in the application or framework, in the web server, or in a proxy in front of it. F5 BIG-IP Application Security Manager (ASM), documented for version 17.5, has an HTML5 Cross-Domain Request Enforcement setting on each URL with four modes: Disabled, which passes the server's headers unchanged; Remove all CORS headers, so the browser refuses cross-origin access; Replace CORS headers, which substitutes the allowed origins, methods and headers configured on the device; and Enforce on ASM, which F5 recommends for maximum security, where the device checks the Origin against its own list and raises an Illegal cross-origin request violation when the header is missing or appears more than once. Testing a preflight needs nothing more than curl: curl -i -X OPTIONS -H 'Origin: https://app.example' -H 'Access-Control-Request-Method: PUT' followed by the resource URL shows exactly which Access-Control headers the server, or whatever sits in front of it, returns.

The neighbours are easy to mix up. The same-origin policy is the default wall; CORS is the door a server may open in it; CSP is a list of what a page may load and run; CSRF is the attack that sends a request on a user's behalf whether or not the response can be read. The numbers worth remembering are three for the origin (scheme, host, port); GET, HEAD and POST as the safelisted methods and three safelisted content types; a 5-second default preflight cache, capped at 7,200 seconds in Chromium and 86,400 in Firefox; no wildcard with credentials; and 16 January 2014 and 2 June 2020 for the W3C Recommendation and its supersession.

credential-stuffing.def: Automated login attempts using username and password pairs stolen from other breaches.
credential-stuffing.context: Because people reuse passwords, a set leaked from one site is tried en masse against many others. It is not guessing; it is replaying known-good pairs, which is why unique passwords and multi-factor authentication defeat it.
credential-stuffing.depth:
Credential stuffing is not password guessing. The attacker already has real username and password pairs, harvested from somebody else's breach, and is simply trying them against your service on the reasonable assumption that people reuse. Success rates are low per attempt and enormous in aggregate, which is why it is run at scale rather than targeted.

The formal definitions. The Open Worldwide Application Security Project (OWASP) catalogues it as automated threat OAT-008: mass log-in attempts used to verify the validity of stolen username and password pairs, whether taken directly from another application, bought in a criminal marketplace or picked up from public dumps, and distinct from OAT-007, credential cracking, because nothing is guessed. Its list of synonyms shows how many names the same thing goes by: account checking, credential replay, login stuffing, password list attack. MITRE ATT&CK files it as sub-technique T1110.004 of Brute Force, under the Credential Access tactic, and notes two things a network engineer should keep in mind: the services commonly targeted are not only web logins but management services on well-known ports, among them Secure Shell (SSH) on TCP 22, Telnet on 23, the File Transfer Protocol (FTP) on 21, Server Message Block (SMB) on 139 and 445, the Lightweight Directory Access Protocol (LDAP) on 389, Kerberos on 88, the Remote Desktop Protocol (RDP) on 3389, database listeners on 1433, 1521 and 3306, remote desktop sharing on 5900 and HTTP management on 80 and 443, plus single sign-on, cloud and federated applications; and stuffing is risky for the attacker because it can trigger lockouts. OWASP's prevention cheat sheet draws the line between the three relatives: brute force tests many passwords against one account, credential stuffing tests pairs breached elsewhere, and password spraying tests one weak password against many accounts.

This defeats most defences aimed at brute force. The passwords are correct, so complexity rules do not help. Attempts come from distributed residential proxies, so per-IP rate limiting sees a trickle. Each individual login looks entirely legitimate because, from the authentication system's perspective, it is: valid credentials, correctly presented. OWASP adds the mechanics: the toolkits used for stuffing have built-in support for proxy networks that spread requests across very large numbers of addresses, so both IP blocklists and rate limits can stay below their thresholds even during a high-volume attack, and correlating login traffic with intelligence about proxies and hosting-provider address ranges is needed to see the campaign as a whole.

Where the pairs come from, and how long they last. F5 Labs, which took over the series Shape Security published as the Credential Spill Report, traced the life of stolen credentials in its 2021 Credential Stuffing Report. The number of spill incidents nearly doubled between 2016 and 2020 while the average spill shrank from 63 million to 17 million records; plaintext password storage accounted for the most spilled credentials, with the long-discredited MD5 still common; and the median time for an organization to discover a spill was 120 days, the average 327, often after the data had already surfaced on criminal forums. Stolen pairs pass through five stages: a slow and quiet phase in which sophisticated attackers use them in stealth, a ramp-up of about a month as they circulate, a blitz once the spill is public and amateurs race to use them before users change passwords, a drop-off, and reincarnation as the pairs are repackaged into new collections. One such compilation, Collection X, appeared for sale in early 2019 and accounted for nearly 33 per cent of the logins F5 traced across Shape's customers, and the same credentials also turned up in legitimate human logins, most often at banks.

Cases that set the standard. OWASP's attack page records the early chain: after the Sony and Gawker breaches of 2011, two-thirds of the users present in both data sets turned out to use the same password on each; Dropbox said in 2012 that usernames and passwords stolen from unrelated services had been used in attempts to log in to sites across the internet, Dropbox among them; and the 2014 intrusion at JPMorgan Chase was traced to credentials from a third-party site for a charity race. The regulatory benchmark is 23andMe. The UK Information Commissioner's Office fined it 2.31 million pounds on 17 June 2025 after a credential stuffing attack that ran from April to September 2023 with credentials from unrelated breaches and reached the data of 155,592 UK residents, from names and birth years to family trees and health reports. The regulator's findings read as a list of the standard controls: no mandatory multi-factor authentication, no secure password protocols, no unpredictable usernames, no extra verification before raw genetic data could be downloaded, and no effective monitoring. The response was part of the failure: a claim in August 2023 that data on more than 10 million users had been stolen was dismissed as a hoax, and a full investigation began only in October.

How it is detected. Behaviour, not correctness, gives it away. F5 Labs gives two numbers to watch: legitimate human login success rates run between 60 and 80 per cent depending on the industry, so a sudden fall of 10 to 15 per cent suggests that someone is testing credentials that do not exist, and a rise in password reset requests can be reconnaissance for an attack; it also suggests checking login, reset and account creation for the daily rhythm of human users, while warning that capable attackers time their traffic to business hours. ATT&CK's detection strategy DET0460 describes the log patterns for each platform: many failures with distinct username and password pairs from one source in a short window, against remote desktop, SSH, cloud identity providers or the authentication logs of routers and firewalls. On the web, OWASP describes device fingerprinting from headers and JavaScript, and connection fingerprinting with JA3, HTTP/2 fingerprints and header order, which looks at how the client connects rather than what it claims to be; a login whose user agent says mobile browser and whose TLS fingerprint says scripting library is suspect. All client-supplied signals can be spoofed, so these layers are combined, and each should produce metrics of its own.

What actually works is making the password insufficient. Multi-factor authentication breaks the economics outright, since a valid pair no longer completes a login; OWASP calls it by far the best defence and cites Microsoft's analysis that it would have stopped 99.9 per cent of account compromises, and recommends at least requiring it for administrators and as a step-up for suspicious logins. Beyond that, detection shifts to behaviour rather than correctness, looking at velocity across accounts, device and client fingerprints, and impossible travel. Checking credentials against known-breached corpora at registration and at reset closes the loop, because the fastest way to survive a reused password is to refuse it. Special Publication (SP) 800-63B-4 of the National Institute of Standards and Technology (NIST), published in July 2025, makes that mandatory for verifiers: a new or changed password SHALL be compared against a blocklist that includes passwords from previous breach corpuses, no other composition rules may be imposed, periodic changes may not be required but a change must be forced on evidence of compromise, and consecutive failed attempts on one account are capped at 100. Have I Been Pwned's Pwned Passwords service is the common way to run the check without disclosing the password: the client hashes it with SHA-1 and sends only the first five characters of the hash, a k-anonymity model, and the service handled more than 18 billion requests a month when read. OWASP's further measures are cheaper and weaker: CAPTCHAs (Completely Automated Public Turing tests to tell Computers and Humans Apart) only for risky logins, since solving services exist; usernames that are not the email address; a multi-step login flow that breaks single-request tools without enabling user enumeration; and JavaScript challenges that force the attacker into a real browser, with an accessibility cost. ATT&CK's own mitigations add one more: proactively reset accounts known to appear in breached credentials.

Neighbours. Brute force is the parent technique and password spraying the sibling; Have I Been Pwned and Pwned Passwords are where defenders and users check exposure; multi-factor authentication (MFA) is the control that defeats it, and passkeys, which never send a reusable secret, remove the material it works on. Botnets and residential proxies supply the traffic, rate limiting and CAPTCHAs slow it, and TLS and browser fingerprinting, such as JA4, help tell the scripts from the people. The numbers worth keeping: 100 consecutive failures as NIST's ceiling per account, 60 to 80 per cent as a normal login success rate, and five hexadecimal characters of a SHA-1 hash as all a breached-password check needs to send.

csp.def: Content Security Policy (CSP): a policy a website sends to the browser, normally in the Content-Security-Policy response header, declaring which scripts, styles, frames and other resources a page may load and run, so that the browser refuses injected content and blunts attacks such as cross-site scripting (XSS).
csp.context: A Content Security Policy (CSP) lets a site declare which sources of scripts, styles and other content are allowed, so that a script injected into the page is refused by the browser even when the injection itself succeeded. Mozilla proposed it in 2009, Content Security Policy Level 2 became a W3C (World Wide Web Consortium) Recommendation in December 2016, and Level 3 is still a Working Draft that browsers largely implement. A policy is a list of directives such as script-src, object-src and frame-ancestors, each with source expressions: hosts, schemes, the keywords 'self' and 'none', and per-response nonces or hashes. It is a strong second line of defence behind proper output encoding, not a replacement for it, and its value depends on the policy: an allowlist with 'unsafe-inline' or a broad CDN (content delivery network) host protects almost nothing, while a nonce-based strict policy blocks most injected script.
csp.depth:
A Content Security Policy (CSP) is a set of rules a server hands to the browser about the page it is serving. It does not remove an injection flaw in the application; it limits what injected markup can do once it reaches the browser. Brandon Sterne of Mozilla introduced the idea publicly on 19 June 2009, after a year of work, with an argument that still holds: cross-site scripting (XSS) is possible because the browser grants every piece of content in a response the same privilege, so script the developer wrote and script an attacker smuggled in run with the same rights. A policy separates them by origin, by nonce or by hash. The Open Worldwide Application Security Project (OWASP) describes it as defence in depth, to be deployed on top of correct output encoding and never as the only defence against XSS, and that is the right mental model: encoding prevents the injection, CSP contains the injections that encoding missed.

The specification grew in three stages. Early implementations used prefixed headers, X-Content-Security-Policy in Firefox and in the preview of Internet Explorer 10 and X-WebKit-CSP in Chrome, and CSP 1.0, edited by Brandon Sterne and Adam Barth, reached W3C (World Wide Web Consortium) Candidate Recommendation on 15 November 2012; it was closed as a Working Group Note on 19 February 2015 in favour of its successor. Content Security Policy Level 2, edited by Mike West, Adam Barth and Dan Veditz, became a W3C Recommendation on 15 December 2016, and the header has been supported across the main browsers since August 2016. Content Security Policy Level 3, edited by Mike West and Antonio Sartori of Google, remains a Working Draft, most recently published on 27 October 2026, although browsers implement most of it. Level 3 added 'strict-dynamic' and 'unsafe-hashes', deprecated report-uri in favour of report-to, and let 'self' match the https and wss forms of the page's own origin.

A policy is a semicolon-separated list of directives. Fetch directives control where resources may come from: script-src, style-src, img-src, connect-src, font-src, frame-src and others, with default-src as the fallback for any fetch directive left out, script-src as the fallback for script-src-elem and script-src-attr, and child-src for frame-src and worker-src. That fallback is a classic misreading: once script-src is present, default-src no longer governs scripts at all. Document directives such as base-uri and sandbox constrain the page itself, navigation directives such as form-action and frame-ancestors constrain where it may submit and who may frame it, and frame-ancestors is what OWASP calls the replacement for the older X-Frame-Options header. Each directive takes source expressions: host and scheme sources, the quoted keywords 'self', 'none', 'unsafe-inline' and 'unsafe-eval', and the quoted forms 'nonce-' or 'sha256-' followed by a base64 value. The policy normally travels in the Content-Security-Policy response header; it can also be placed in an HTML meta element, but a meta policy cannot carry frame-ancestors, sandbox or report-uri, cannot be report-only, and does not apply to anything the parser has already met before it. When a response carries several policies, the browser enforces every one of them, so a second header can only tighten what the first allows.

The large-scale evidence on allowlists is discouraging. In a study presented at the ACM (Association for Computing Machinery) Conference on Computer and Communications Security in Vienna in 2016, Lukas Weichselbaum, Michele Spagnuolo, Sebastian Lekies and Artur Janc of Google examined 26,011 unique policies on 1,680,867 hosts and found bypasses in 94.72 per cent of them. Fourteen of the fifteen domains most often allowed for scripts hosted unsafe endpoints that let an attacker step around the policy, so 75.81 per cent of policies were defeated by their own allowlists, and 99.34 per cent of hosts with a CSP gained no protection against XSS from it. The other common failure is the one the policy author chooses: allowing 'unsafe-inline', which most existing sites need at first because their markup is full of inline handlers and style attributes, removes essentially all protection against the attack the policy was meant to stop.

Nonces and hashes are the way out, and they require changing how the application emits markup rather than adding a header. A nonce policy names a random value in script-src and the same value in the nonce attribute of every legitimate script element; an injected script cannot know it. The specification requires a fresh value every time a policy is sent, recommends at least 128 bits from a cryptographically secure generator, and warns that a leaked or reused nonce makes bypassing the policy trivial, because a nonce overrides the directive's other restrictions. A hash policy lists the SHA-256 (Secure Hash Algorithm), SHA-384 or SHA-512 digest of each permitted inline script, which suits static pages. When either is present, 'unsafe-inline' in the same directive is ignored, which lets one policy degrade safely in older browsers. The 'strict-dynamic' keyword, proposed in the 2016 paper, lets a trusted script load its own dependencies without listing every host. The strict policy recommended on web.dev is accordingly three directives: script-src with a nonce or hashes and 'strict-dynamic', object-src 'none' to shut out plugins, and base-uri 'none' so that an injected base element cannot redirect relative script paths. Trusted Types, enforced with require-trusted-types-for, extend the same idea to the DOM (Document Object Model) sinks where client-side XSS happens.

Deployment has a safe path that is worth using. The Content-Security-Policy-Report-Only header enforces nothing and sends a violation report for everything the policy would have blocked, so the breakage can be seen before it happens, which for a large existing site is invariably more than expected. Reports go to the endpoint named by report-to, defined in a Reporting-Endpoints header, or to the deprecated report-uri, and MDN advises sending both until report-to is supported everywhere. The realistic sequence is report-only, fix the inline code the reports reveal, tighten, and only then enforce, keeping a report-only copy of the next, stricter policy running beside the enforced one. Network equipment takes part in this. A reverse proxy, load balancer or web application firewall (WAF) can add the header to every response; FortiWeb, for example, inserts Content-Security-Policy together with X-Frame-Options, X-Content-Type-Options and Referrer-Policy as the first layer of its client-side security module. A static allowlist inserted that way works, but a nonce cannot be: it must be generated per response and must match the markup, so it belongs in the application, or in a component that rewrites both header and body, and never in a cached page served unchanged to many users.

CSP is easily confused with its neighbours. CORS (Cross-Origin Resource Sharing) works in the opposite direction: it is how a server tells the browser which other origins may load its resources, a relaxation of the same-origin policy, whereas CSP is how a page restricts what it will load and run. HSTS (HTTP Strict Transport Security) forces HTTPS for a host, and the upgrade-insecure-requests directive merely tells the browser to treat a site's insecure HTTP URLs as if they were HTTPS, for sites with many legacy links. None of them fixes the application. The points worth remembering: 2009 for Mozilla's proposal, Level 2 a Recommendation since 15 December 2016, Level 3 a Working Draft, 128-bit single-use nonces, 'unsafe-inline' cancels the protection unless a nonce or hash is present, and 94.72 per cent of the allowlist policies measured in 2016 could be bypassed.

csrf.def: An attack that tricks a logged-in user's browser into making an unwanted request.
csrf.context: Cross-Site Request Forgery abuses the fact that browsers attach cookies automatically: a malicious page can cause your authenticated browser to perform an action you did not intend. Anti-CSRF tokens and same-site cookies are the usual defences.
csrf.depth:
Cross-site request forgery makes a victim's browser send an authenticated request the victim did not intend, exploiting the fact that cookies are attached to a request automatically regardless of what caused it. The attacker cannot read the response, which is why CSRF is about actions rather than data theft: transfers, password changes, permission grants.

Anti-forgery tokens work because they require something the attacker cannot obtain from a third-party page, and the SameSite cookie attribute closes most of the class by default in modern browsers. The trap is treating that default as complete: SameSite=Lax still permits top-level navigations, cross-origin API endpoints authenticated by cookie remain exposed, and any endpoint that performs a state change on GET is vulnerable regardless of what the cookie policy says.

cve.def: A Common Vulnerabilities and Exposures (CVE) identifier, such as CVE-2021-44228, is the unique public name the CVE Program gives one publicly disclosed vulnerability; the CVE Record published with it by a CVE Numbering Authority (CNA) describes the flaw, the affected products and versions, and references.
cve.context: A Common Vulnerabilities and Exposures (CVE) identifier gives everyone one name for one flaw, so advisories, scanners, patches and threat reports can refer to the same thing unambiguously. It reads CVE, the year it was reserved or made public, and a sequence of four or more digits; the record behind it is written by one of the more than 500 CVE Numbering Authorities (CNAs). It is a name, not a verdict: severity comes from CVSS (Common Vulnerability Scoring System), extra analysis from NIST's (National Institute of Standards and Technology) National Vulnerability Database (NVD), and proof of exploitation from CISA's (Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency) Known Exploited Vulnerabilities (KEV) catalogue.
cve.depth:
What it is, and what it is not. The Common Vulnerabilities and Exposures (CVE) Program states its mission as identifying, defining and cataloguing publicly disclosed vulnerabilities, with one CVE Record for each. The identifier is the shared name and the record is the minimum shared description, so that two people or two tools can be sure they mean the same flaw. Naming is the whole job. Among the myths the program lists about itself is that it assigns severity scores: it does not, and a CVE number says nothing about exploitability or whether a given system is affected. In June 2026 it also restated the unit of naming: one identifier must not cover several distinct vulnerabilities that can be understood, exploited, fixed or acted on independently.

Why it was needed. On 8 January 1999 David E. Mann and Steven M. Christey of MITRE wrote Towards a Common Enumeration of Vulnerabilities, presented that month at a workshop on vulnerability databases at Purdue University. Their problem was operational: every scanner and intrusion detection system carried its own vulnerability database and none used a common name. Their example was a 1991 flaw allowing access to NFS (Network File System) file systems through guessable file handles, called nfs-guess in the ISS X-Force database, NFS file handle guessing check in CyberCop Scanner 2.4, and covered, with other problems, by CERT Advisory CA-91.21; matching them meant reading vague prose by hand. A working group that became a 19-member editorial board produced 321 original records, and the list went public in September 1999. NIST (National Institute of Standards and Technology) recommended it to US agencies in Special Publication 800-51 in 2002, and the ITU-T (International Telecommunication Union Telecommunication Standardization Sector) adopted it as Recommendation X.1520 in 2011.

Anatomy and lifecycle. An identifier is the prefix CVE, a year and a sequence number of four or more digits with no upper limit: CVE-1999-0067, CVE-2019-12345 and CVE-2021-7654321 are the program's own examples. The year is when the ID was reserved or the flaw made public, never when it was discovered. A record moves through three states. Reserved is the first: the ID exists and can be used to coordinate a fix before disclosure, but nothing is public. Published means the CNA has supplied at least a description, the affected products and versions, and references. Rejected means the ID must not be used, though the record stays on the list so that anyone holding it learns it is void. Records are JSON (JavaScript Object Notation) documents; format 5.2.0, released on 29 October 2025, can carry Package URL identifiers for software components. CVE-2021-44228 shows the pattern: Apache, the CNA for its own code, reserved it on 26 November 2021 and published it on 10 December 2021, describing Log4j2 2.0-beta9 through 2.15.0.

Who assigns them. CVE Numbering Authorities (CNAs) are vendors, researchers, open source projects, CERTs (computer emergency response teams), hosted services, bug bounty providers and consortia, each allowed to assign IDs within its own scope. On 31 March 2026 there were 502: 499 CNAs and 3 CNAs of last resort, from 42 countries, against 23 in 2016, when the program decided to federate assignment; the list passed 300,000 records in 2025. Roots manage groups of CNAs, and ENISA (the European Union Agency for Cybersecurity) became one on 20 November 2025. The share of records published by the CNAs of last resort, CISA (Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency) and MITRE, fell from 35% in 2021 to 5% in 2026, which means vendors increasingly name their own flaws.

The volume. The program's quarterly snapshots count 321 published records in 1999, 40,077 in 2024, 48,244 in 2025, and 72,812 in the first three quarters of 2026 alone, with 105,782 IDs reserved in 2026; its own posts attribute the acceleration partly to AI-assisted research and automation. Downstream analysis has not kept pace. NIST's National Vulnerability Database (NVD) enriches records with severity scores and product lists; it built a backlog from early 2024, and on 15 April 2026, citing a 263% rise in submissions between 2020 and 2025 and nearly 42,000 records enriched in 2025, NIST switched to risk-based enrichment. Records in CISA's Known Exploited Vulnerabilities (KEV) catalogue, with a target of one business day, software used by the US federal government and critical software under Executive Order 14028 come first; the rest are listed as lowest priority, backlogged entries published before 1 March 2026 moved to not scheduled, and NIST no longer routinely adds its own score when the CNA has supplied one. An identifier existing does not mean anyone has analysed it.

Governance and funding. MITRE runs the program under a contract sponsored by CISA, and in April 2025 that nearly ended: the contract was due to expire on 16 April, MITRE warned the CVE Board the day before, and CISA exercised the option period of the $57.8 million contract on the evening of 15 April, carrying it to 16 March 2026, while board members announced a nonprofit CVE Foundation to reduce dependence on a single sponsor. In March 2026 the contract was reported renegotiated, and in September 2026 a CISA white paper declared a quality era for the program, with government sponsorship and the CNAs of last resort among six lines of effort.

Using it well. A CVE is a join key, not a risk rating. Severity comes from CVSS (Common Vulnerability Scoring System), maintained by FIRST (Forum of Incident Response and Security Teams), whose version 4.0 names its variants CVSS-B, CVSS-BT, CVSS-BE and CVSS-BTE precisely so that a bare base score is not mistaken for the whole picture; exploitation evidence comes from KEV; applicability comes from checking versions and configuration against the record. A reserved ID may already appear in an advisory with no public record behind it, a rejected one should be dropped from scanners and tickets, and a year in the identifier is not the age of the bug. Counting the CVEs a product has accumulated rewards vendors who stay silent, which is why the number alone measures disclosure practice at least as much as code quality.

cvss.def: The Common Vulnerability Scoring System (CVSS): the open standard of the Forum of Incident Response and Security Teams (FIRST) that rates the severity of a vulnerability as a score from 0.0 to 10.0, published together with a vector string recording the metric values behind it.
cvss.context: The Common Vulnerability Scoring System (CVSS) combines factors, how a vulnerability is exploited and what it impacts, into a number and a vector string, so that teams can compare and prioritize. It is maintained by the Forum of Incident Response and Security Teams (FIRST); version 3.1 is still the one most advisories carry, and version 4.0 has been current since November 2023. It measures inherent severity, not a specific organization's risk, which also depends on exposure and context; the Exploit Prediction Scoring System (EPSS) and the Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalogue of the Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency (CISA) supply the likelihood and the evidence that CVSS deliberately leaves out.
cvss.depth:
The Common Vulnerability Scoring System (CVSS) exists so that two organizations reading the same vulnerability disclosure arrive at comparable severity numbers rather than arguing from instinct. It is owned and managed by the Forum of Incident Response and Security Teams (FIRST), incorporated as FIRST.Org, Inc., a non-profit based in the United States, which licenses it freely on two conditions worth knowing: attribution, and that anyone publishing scores gives both the score and the vector so others can see how it was derived. The vector string encodes how an attack is delivered, how complex it is, what privileges and user interaction it needs, and what it costs in confidentiality, integrity and availability; the score falls out of that arithmetic.

The standard has a history of correcting itself. The CVSS v2 documentation cites a 2004 paper for the National Infrastructure Advisory Council (NIAC) by Mike Schiffman, Gerhard Eschelbeck, David Ahmad, Andrew Wright and Sasha Romanosky as the origin of version 1, and FIRST's own history of v2 admits that v1 was never put through mass peer review and showed significant issues in production. The CVSS Special Interest Group (SIG) began work on version 2 in April 2005, NIST (the National Institute of Standards and Technology) statisticians reviewed the formulas for rounding, clustering and many-to-one problems, voting ended on 1 June 2007, and version 2 was released that month, written up by Peter Mell, Karen Scarfone and Sasha Romanosky. Version 3.0 introduced the Scope metric. Version 3.1 added no metrics or values; it redefined the Roundup function so that implementations on different hardware and languages stop disagreeing over floating-point residue, which moved fewer than 7 per cent of environmental metric combinations up by 0.1 and fewer than 1 per cent down, and it rewrote the text to say that CVSS measures severity, not risk. Version 4.0 was first published on 1 November 2023, with corrections on 9 November 2023 and 18 June 2024.

Version 3.1 has three metric groups. The Base group describes the vulnerability itself and assumes the reasonable worst case: Attack Vector (AV), which is Network, Adjacent, Local or Physical; Attack Complexity (AC), Low or High; Privileges Required (PR), None, Low or High; User Interaction (UI), None or Required; Scope (S), Unchanged or Changed, which raises the score when the impact crosses into components outside the vulnerable one's security authority; and the three impacts, Confidentiality (C), Integrity (I) and Availability (A), each High, Low or None. The vector begins with the label CVSS:3.1 and lists each metric by its code, so CVSS:3.1/AV:N/AC:L/PR:H/UI:N/S:U/C:L/I:L/A:N reads as reachable over the network, low complexity, high privileges needed, no user interaction, scope unchanged, low confidentiality and integrity impact, no availability impact. The Temporal group adjusts for things that change over time: Exploit Code Maturity, Remediation Level and Report Confidence. The Environmental group adjusts both to a particular deployment, through security requirements and modified versions of the Base metrics that reflect local mitigations. Scores map optionally to a qualitative scale: None at 0.0, Low from 0.1 to 3.9, Medium from 4.0 to 6.9, High from 7.0 to 8.9 and Critical from 9.0 to 10.0. The specification is explicit that Base scores are usually produced by the product's maintainer or a third party on its behalf, that only Base scores are typically published, and that consumers should supplement them with Temporal and Environmental scores of their own.

Version 4.0 rebuilt the system around four groups: Base, Threat, Environmental and Supplemental. Attack Requirements (AT) joins Attack Complexity to capture preconditions in the target's deployment; User Interaction becomes None, Passive or Active; Scope disappears, replaced by separate impact metrics for the vulnerable system, Confidentiality (VC), Integrity (VI) and Availability (VA), and for subsequent systems, Confidentiality (SC), Integrity (SI) and Availability (SA), where human safety can now register. The old Temporal group shrinks into a single Threat metric, Exploit Maturity, whose default when no threat intelligence is available is Attacked, the worst case. The Supplemental metrics, Safety, Automatable, Provider Urgency, Recovery, Value Density and Vulnerability Response Effort, add context without changing the score. Scores must now say what went into them: CVSS-B for Base alone, CVSS-BT, CVSS-BE or CVSS-BTE as Threat and Environmental metrics are added, and the specification notes that providers such as the NVD (National Vulnerability Database) typically publish only CVSS-B. The arithmetic changed character too: the SIG grouped the 15 million possible CVSS-BTE vectors into 270 equivalence sets, had experts rank them, kept the qualitative boundaries compatible with version 3.x, and now scores a vector from a lookup table of MacroVectors with interpolation inside each one, rather than from a closed formula.

The NVD shows how much depends on who scores. Its records carry the score of the CVE (Common Vulnerabilities and Exposures) Numbering Authority (CNA) that published the vulnerability beside NIST's own. For CVE-2021-26855, the Microsoft Exchange Server flaw, Microsoft's CVSS 3.1 vector ends A:N and scores 9.1, while NVD's ends A:H and scores 9.8; the older CVSS 2 score in the same record is 7.5. For CVE-2024-3400 in Palo Alto Networks PAN-OS, the vendor and NVD agree on 10.0, with Scope Changed. The same records now carry evidence CVSS does not hold: the date each CVE entered the Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalogue of the Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency (CISA), 3 November 2021 and 12 April 2024 respectively, and for CVE-2024-3400 a decision record in CISA's Stakeholder-Specific Vulnerability Categorization (SSVC) noting active exploitation, automatable, total technical impact.

The most common misuse is treating the base score as a priority. The base score describes the vulnerability in the abstract, deliberately ignoring the environment: whether the affected service is exposed to the internet, whether compensating controls exist, whether the asset matters. That is what the temporal and environmental metrics (threat and environmental in version 4.0) are for, and they are the parts most teams skip. FIRST's own text goes further, listing factors that are outside CVSS altogether, such as the number of customers on a product line, monetary losses, threats to life or property and public sentiment, and recommending a risk assessment that considers exposure and threat. So a 9.8 on an internal system behind three layers of access control can genuinely deserve less urgency than a 6.5 on a public endpoint handling payment data. Reading the vector rather than the number is what makes that judgement possible, and it is the difference between a patching queue that reflects risk and one that reflects arithmetic.

Two complements fill the gap CVSS leaves on purpose. The Exploit Prediction Scoring System (EPSS), also run by FIRST, is a data-driven machine-learning model that estimates the probability that a published CVE will be exploited in the wild within the next 30 days, publishing a probability between 0 and 1, with a percentile, every day for every CVE; its first version was developed in 2018 and 2019 and described by Jay Jacobs, Sasha Romanosky and colleagues in 2021, and FIRST now runs version 5. On 10 November 2026 it gave CVE-2024-3400 a probability of 0.99999 and CVE-2021-26855 0.99996. CISA's Known Exploited Vulnerabilities (KEV) catalogue is evidence rather than prediction: a vulnerability enters it only with an assigned CVE, reliable evidence of active exploitation (scanning, research or proof-of-concept code alone do not count) and clear remediation guidance, and Binding Operational Directive 22-01 obliged federal civilian agencies to fix listed flaws within prescribed timeframes until BOD 26-04 revoked and replaced it on 10 June 2026 with deadlines tiered by risk. Severity from CVSS, likelihood from EPSS and observed exploitation from KEV answer three different questions, and version 4.0's Exploit Maturity metric is the place where the second and third are meant to flow back into the first.

data-minimization.def: Collecting and keeping only the personal data you actually need, for only as long as you need it.
data-minimization.context: A core privacy principle: data you never collect cannot leak, be subpoenaed, or be misused. It is also the design instinct behind privacy-first tools, compute locally, keep nothing you do not have to.

ddos.def: Distributed denial of service (DDoS): an attack that overwhelms a service with traffic or requests from many sources at once, usually a botnet or a crowd of abused reflectors, so that legitimate users cannot be served.
ddos.context: A distributed denial of service (DDoS) floods a target from many machines at once, typically a botnet of compromised devices or innocent servers tricked into reflecting traffic, which makes it hard to stop by filtering any one address. It aims at availability, taking a service offline, rather than at stealing data. The flood can fill the link, exhaust the state tables of firewalls and servers, or repeat expensive application requests, and mitigation relies on absorbing or scrubbing it upstream of the bottleneck.
ddos.depth:
NIST (the National Institute of Standards and Technology) defines a distributed denial of service (DDoS) as a denial of service technique that uses numerous hosts to perform the attack. That distribution is the whole difficulty: blocking the origin is the obvious defence, and it fails because there are too many origins and most of them are innocent machines, either compromised devices in a botnet or legitimate servers tricked into answering someone else. Attacks fall into three families with different answers. Volumetric attacks saturate the link, so nothing behind it matters. Protocol attacks exhaust state, the connection tables of servers, firewalls and load balancers. Application-layer attacks issue requests that are individually legitimate and collectively ruinous, because each one costs the server far more than it costs the sender. Cloudflare calls an attack hyper-volumetric above 1 Tbps (terabit per second), 1 Bpps (billion packets per second) or 1 Mrps (million requests per second).

The state-exhaustion family has a documented birth. Request for Comments (RFC) 4987 (W. Eddy, August 2007) records that the TCP (Transmission Control Protocol) SYN (synchronize) flood was first publicized in 1996, with a description and a tool in Phrack magazine; that by September 1996 it had been seen in the wild against one provider's mail servers, causing well-publicized outages; and that CERT issued Advisory CA-1996-21. The attack was serious because it targets end-host resources, which take fewer packets to deplete than a network. The answers came fast: Dave Borman implemented a SYN cache at BSDi in October 1996, and SYN cookies go further by allocating no state at all for half-open connections, encoding what they need in the sequence number of the SYN-ACK and rebuilding it from the final ACK (acknowledgement). Firewalls apply the same idea as thresholds. On a FortiGate, denial-of-service (DoS) policies are checked before security policies, so an attack is dropped before it can trigger more expensive inspection, and the predefined tcp_syn_flood anomaly has a recommended threshold of 2,000 packets per second to one destination, with 5,000 concurrent sessions for the session-count anomalies.

The largest volumetric attacks depend on reflection and amplification. The Internet Architecture Board's RFC 4732 (November 2006) describes the attack amplifier: the attacker sends traffic carrying the victim's spoofed source address to a third party, which sends larger responses to the victim. Its first example, the smurf attack, sent an ICMP (Internet Control Message Protocol) echo request to a subnet broadcast address so that every host replied to the victim; the RFC notes that routers now usually drop such packets. DNS (Domain Name System) reflection replaced it, with queries chosen so the answer is much bigger than the question, the largest answers being those that carry DNSSEC (DNS Security Extensions) signatures. Even TCP can amplify, through SYN-ACK retransmissions to a spoofed source. Christian Rossow's measurements, presented at NDSS (the Network and Distributed System Security Symposium) in February 2014, put numbers on the multiplier with a bandwidth amplification factor (BAF), the ratio of UDP (User Datagram Protocol) payload bytes sent to the victim to payload bytes sent by the attacker, headers excluded: NTP (Network Time Protocol) monlist averaged 556.9 and reached 4,670; CharGen 358.8; QOTD (Quote of the Day) 140.3; DNS 28.7 to 64.1 on open resolvers and 54.6 to 98.3 on authoritative servers; SSDP (Simple Service Discovery Protocol) 30.8; SNMPv2 (Simple Network Management Protocol version 2) 6.3. On 27 February 2018 Cloudflare reported memcached on UDP port 11211 beating them all: a 15-byte request triggered 134 KB, a factor of 10,000, and in practice up to 750 kB, a factor of 51,200, with 260 Gbps of inbound reflected traffic at peak.

Botnets provide the other half of the scale. On 13 December 2017 the United States Department of Justice announced that Paras Jha, 21, Josiah White, 20, and Dalton Norman, 21, had pleaded guilty in the District of Alaska on 8 December to conspiracy to violate the Computer Fraud and Abuse Act by operating Mirai, which they created in the summer and fall of 2016 from IoT (internet of things) devices such as wireless cameras, routers and digital video recorders, hundreds of thousands of them at its peak. Jha posted the source code on a criminal forum that autumn, and other criminals have used Mirai variants since. A decade later the pattern holds at a larger size. Cloudflare's report of 3 December 2025 described Aisuru, an estimated 1 to 4 million infected hosts, behind record attacks of 29.7 Tbps and 14.1 Bpps, with slices of it rented as botnets-for-hire for a few hundred to a few thousand dollars; its report of 5 February 2026 recorded 31.4 Tbps from the Aisuru-Kimwolf botnet, made mostly of infected Android TVs, in an attack that lasted 35 seconds, HTTP (Hypertext Transfer Protocol) floods above 200 million requests per second, and 47.1 million DDoS attacks over 2025, more than double the year before. Its first-half 2026 report counted 935 network-layer attacks above 1 Tbps in six months, 805 of them in the second quarter, and named Brazil the largest source country, with 14.9 per cent of attack traffic over the half and 21.4 per cent in the second quarter. Every record is the largest any company had disclosed at the time, which is a measure of what was reported, not of everything that happened.

Most attacks are nothing like the records. In the same first half of 2026, 96.62 per cent of the network-layer attacks Cloudflare mitigated stayed under 500 Mbps and 90.60 per cent ended within ten minutes, which is still more than most links and servers can take, and over before a human has finished reading the alert. That is why the defence has to be automatic and upstream of the bottleneck, and why mitigation is generally a service rather than a device: a firewall on a saturated link is behind the problem it is meant to solve, however good its rules. Capacity is the argument; Cloudflare cites 500 Tbps of network capacity. Operators without that capacity have a blunter tool, documented in RFC 5635 (W. Kumari and D. McPherson, August 2009): remote triggered black hole (RTBH) filtering uses BGP (Border Gateway Protocol) to send a discard route for the target, often next-hopped to an address such as 192.0.2.1, to every edge router, which protects the rest of the network by dropping attack and legitimate traffic alike, so that, in the RFC's own words, the impact of the attack on the target is complete. Combined with unicast reverse path forwarding (uRPF) it can drop by source instead.

Amplification only works because some networks let forged traffic out, and that is the reason source address validation matters even to operators who will never be a target. RFC 2827, published in May 2000 as BCP 38 (Best Current Practice 38) by P. Ferguson and D. Senie, asks every provider to filter traffic entering from its customers so that it carries only source addresses from their legitimately advertised prefixes. It is candid about its limits, doing absolutely nothing against floods from valid addresses, and about its benefits: a network that applies it cannot be the launch point for a spoofed attack, and attacks from inside it can be traced to their true source. RFC 4732 makes the dependency explicit, noting that DNS reflection can only be used by an attacker able to spoof the victim's address. RFC 3704 (BCP 84, March 2004) extended the practice to multihomed networks with strict, feasible-path and loose reverse path forwarding, the uRPF modes routers expose today. The numbers worth remembering are the asymmetries: 4,670 for NTP monlist, 51,200 for memcached, and a single filter on a customer edge that removes a network from every reflection attack at once.

dead-drop.def: A method of passing information without the parties ever meeting.
dead-drop.context: Borrowed from spycraft, a digital dead drop leaves data in an agreed location for later pickup, decoupling sender and receiver in time. Named here for the concept only; the point is that separation in time defeats surveillance that watches for two parties meeting.

debugging.def: The systematic process of finding and fixing the cause of a defect in software or of unexpected behaviour in a system; on network devices, also the verbose diagnostic tracing switched on to observe that behaviour.
debugging.context: Debugging is detective work: reproduce, isolate, form a hypothesis, test it, repeat. The word is tangled with the 1947 moth, but the practice is much older, and techniques from rubber-duck explaining to a bisecting search are its everyday tools.
debugging.depth:
The method has a name. Google's site reliability engineering (SRE) book, in its chapter on effective troubleshooting by Chris Jones, describes it as an application of the hypothetico-deductive method: from a set of observations and an understanding of how the system should behave, propose a cause, test it, and repeat. The same chapter lists the ways sessions go wrong: looking at symptoms that are not relevant or misreading what a metric means, which produces wild goose chases; not knowing how to change the system, its inputs or its environment safely enough to test a hypothesis; preferring exotic explanations to common ones, against the medical rule to think of horses, not zebras, when you hear hoofbeats; and chasing correlations that are coincidences or that share a hidden cause. Its example of the last is packet loss and failing disks in one cluster, both caused by a power problem, neither causing the other; its case study is a latency increase that correlated neatly with a datastore call until static images, which never touched the datastore, turned out to be slow as well.

Narrowing the search. The chapter recommends working through a layered system from one end to the other, or, when that is too slow, bisection: split the system in half, establish which half is healthy, and repeat. It also gives the most productive first question, what touched it last, because a working system tends to keep working until something acts on it, such as a configuration change or a shift in load. Version control turns both ideas into a tool. git bisect performs a binary search over history between a commit known to be bad and one known to be good, asking at each step whether the checked-out revision has the bug; with git bisect run it executes a test script at every step and reads the result from its exit code, 0 for good, any value from 1 to 127 except 125 for bad, and 125 for a revision that cannot be tested and should be skipped. Because each step halves the range, about ten tests find the culprit among a thousand commits.

Debuggers. When the question is what a program is doing inside, a debugger answers it directly. GDB, the debugger of the GNU project (GNU, a recursive acronym for GNU's Not Unix, launched by Richard Stallman in 1983), was originally written by Stallman too, and describes its purpose as letting you see what is going on inside another program while it executes, or what it was doing at the moment it crashed, and lists four things it does: start the program with whatever affects its behaviour, stop it on specified conditions, examine its state when stopped, and change things in it to test a correction and move on to the next bug. A core dump read in a debugger turns a crash in production into a stack trace and the values of the variables at the instant of failure, which is often the whole investigation.

The bugs that hide. Jim Gray, in Why Do Computers Stop and What Can Be Done About It? (Tandem Computers, June 1985), named the two kinds that shape debugging strategy. Bohrbugs, like the Bohr atom, are solid and easily found by standard techniques; Heisenbugs go away when you look at them, because the act of observing, a debugger, an extra log line, a changed timing, perturbs the situation just enough. He argued that most production software faults are of the second kind, and in one measured period of a fail-fast spooler only one of 132 software faults recurred when the work was retried by a backup process; the rest vanished. That is both why retrying works as a recovery strategy and why it is dangerous as a debugging one: a fault that disappears on retry has not been fixed, only hidden, and the evidence is usually in the timing and the logs captured before the retry, not in a reproduction afterwards.

Debugging on network devices. On routers, firewalls and load balancers debug is also a mode the operator switches on, and it costs resources the device needs for forwarding. FortiOS 7.6 traces how the firewall handles a packet with a sequence of commands: diagnose debug flow filter narrows the trace by address, source or destination address and port, protocol or virtual domain; diagnose debug enable turns output on; diagnose debug flow show function-name enable adds the internal function names; diagnose debug flow trace start followed by a number captures that many packets, and trace stop ends it. Fortinet's guide warns not to run it longer than necessary because it generates a significant amount of data, forwarded as event logs when the unit reports to FortiAnalyzer or FortiCloud, and notes that traffic offloaded to NP6 or NP7 network processors never reaches the trace, so a session that looks invisible may simply be in hardware. Cisco's long-standing note on debug commands is blunter: a router prioritizes console output ahead of its other functions, excessive debugs to the console can make it hang, debugs should be run only under the direction of technical support, output belongs in the logging buffer, and the way to stop them is no debug all or undebug all, since turning off terminal output leaves the debug running and still consuming the router's resources. Filter first, bound the count, log to a buffer, and stop explicitly.

Where the word comes from, and why the date is disputed. The Smithsonian's National Museum of American History holds the log book of the Harvard Mark II, transferred from the Naval Surface Warfare Center, in which engineers taped a moth with the note first actual case of bug being found; it dates the book to 1947, says Grace Hopper was on the team although the book was probably not hers, and credits her and her colleagues with popularizing computer bug and debug. The word was already old: the museum notes that Thomas Edison spoke of bugs in electrical circuits in the 1870s, which is the joke the log entry depends on. The US Naval History and Heritage Command's caption for its photograph of the same page dates the entry 9 September 1945 and places the moth in relay number 70 of panel F. Two public institutions disagree about the year; the event is the same, and the record was kept because someone thought a log entry was worth writing.

What good debugging looks like in practice. Reproduce before changing anything, and write down the exact steps, versions and inputs; change one variable at a time so that each test answers one question; record negative results, which the SRE chapter calls conclusive because they settle something certain about the system; prefer the explanation that accounts for all the observations, not the first one that accounts for some; and when a fix works, confirm it explains the original symptom rather than merely making it stop. The common failure is not a lack of tools but a hypothesis accepted before the evidence for it existed.

defense-in-depth.def: Layering multiple independent controls so that if one fails, others still stand.
defense-in-depth.context: Defense in depth assumes any single control can be bypassed, so it stacks them, network, host, application, identity, forcing an attacker to defeat several in a row. No layer is perfect; the strength is in the overlap.
defense-in-depth.depth:
Defense in depth assumes your controls will fail, and asks what happens next. Any single mechanism, a firewall rule, an authentication check, an input validator, will eventually be bypassed, misconfigured, or found to have a flaw disclosed on a Tuesday. Layering means the failure of one is survivable rather than terminal.

The idea is borrowed from fortification, and the analogy is worth taking seriously because it includes the part people skip: layers must be different in kind, not merely repeated. Three firewalls from the same vendor sharing a common vulnerability are one layer wearing three hats. Genuine depth mixes prevention with detection, network controls with identity controls, and automated enforcement with human review, so a single class of mistake cannot defeat all of them at once.

The cost is honest and worth stating. Every layer adds latency, expense, and operational surface, and layers that nobody monitors are decoration. The discipline is deciding which failures you are actually defending against, then building the smallest set of genuinely independent controls that survive those failures, rather than accumulating products because each one seemed prudent in isolation.

devsecops.def: A culture and practice of building security into development and operations, not bolting it on.
devsecops.context: DevSecOps extends DevOps by making security a shared, automated responsibility across the pipeline rather than a gate at the end. The family, DevOps, SecOps, NetOps, SRE, all share one instinct: break down the walls between building, running, and securing.

digital-signature.def: A digital signature is a value computed from data with a signer's private key that anyone holding the matching public key can check, proving that the data has not changed since it was signed and that it was signed by whoever controls that private key.
digital-signature.context: A signature is produced with a private key and verified with the public key, so it proves both origin and integrity to anyone, not just to a partner who shares a secret, which is what separates it from an HMAC (hash-based message authentication code). Most schemes sign a hash of the message, but signing is not encrypting the hash with the private key: RSA (Rivest-Shamir-Adleman) keeps its signature operations separate from its encryption operations, and ECDSA (Elliptic Curve Digital Signature Algorithm) and EdDSA (Edwards-curve Digital Signature Algorithm) encrypt nothing at all. It is how software updates, certificates, documents, DNSSEC (Domain Name System Security Extensions) records and TLS (Transport Layer Security) handshakes prove they are authentic and untampered. What it proves is possession of a key, not the honesty or intent of the person behind it, and its strength is the weakest of the algorithm, the hash and the protection of the private key.
digital-signature.depth:
What it is. NIST (the National Institute of Standards and Technology) defines a digital signature, in FIPS (Federal Information Processing Standard) 186-5 and in its post-quantum standards, as the result of a cryptographic transformation of data that, properly implemented, lets a verifier check origin authentication, data integrity and signatory non-repudiation. FIPS 186-5 calls it the electronic analogue of a written signature: the signatory generates it with a private key that only the key pair owner may use, the verifier checks it with the corresponding public key, and the approved algorithms are designed so that someone without the private key cannot produce a valid signature on a different message. Non-repudiation, in the standard's terms, means that integrity and origin can be verified by a third party as coming from the entity in possession of the private key, which is exactly what a shared-key MAC (message authentication code) such as HMAC (hash-based message authentication code) cannot offer, since either holder of the key could have computed the tag.

What it is not. The common description, hash the message and encrypt the digest with the private key, is wrong in general and only loosely true of one algorithm. RFC (Request for Comments) 8017, which specifies RSA (Rivest-Shamir-Adleman), defines signature primitives that use the same modular exponentiation as its encryption primitives but names them separately because they are intended for different purposes, and it builds signature schemes with their own padding. ECDSA (Elliptic Curve Digital Signature Algorithm) and EdDSA (Edwards-curve Digital Signature Algorithm) involve no encryption at all, and FIPS 186-5 notes that for EdDSA the message is not even hashed before it enters the signing process. A signature is also not a certificate: a certificate is itself a signed statement binding a public key to a name, and the signature on a document only becomes evidence about a person once something like that binding exists.

The approved algorithms. FIPS 186-5, published on 3 February 2023 and superseding FIPS 186-4 of 2013, approves three techniques. RSA signatures follow RFC 8017 (PKCS #1 version 2.2, November 2016, Kathleen Moriarty as editor with Burt Kaliski, Jakob Jonsson and Andreas Rusch), which requires RSASSA-PSS in new applications and keeps RSASSA-PKCS1-v1_5 only for compatibility, while noting that no attacks against it are known, and recommends against using one RSA key pair in more than one scheme. ECDSA is specified in FIPS 186-5 itself, with a deterministic variant from RFC 6979; each signature needs a new secret number k, which must be protected like the private key.
