EdDSA follows RFC 8032 (Simon Josefsson and Ilari Liusvaara, January 2017), a variant of Schnorr's signature system on Edwards curves that needs no random number per signature, is more resilient to side channels, uses 32-byte public keys and 64-byte signatures for Ed25519 (57 and 114 for Ed448), needs no point validation thanks to complete formulas, and in its pure form survives collisions in its hash function. DSA (Digital Signature Algorithm) is no longer specified and may only verify signatures made earlier.

The hash underneath. Every scheme except PureEdDSA signs a digest, so the signature is only as unforgeable as the hash is collision-resistant: two documents with the same digest share every signature made over either. On 23 February 2017 researchers from CWI Amsterdam and Google announced the first practical SHA-1 (Secure Hash Algorithm 1) collision, two PDF files with identical hashes, after nine quintillion SHA-1 computations, and illustrated the risk with two insurance contracts with drastically different terms; Google had argued for years that SHA-1 should no longer sign TLS (Transport Layer Security) certificates. This is why signature algorithm identifiers always name the hash as well, as in rsa_pss_rsae_sha256 or ecdsa_secp256r1_sha256.

Where engineers meet it. In TLS 1.3, specified since July 2026 in RFC 9846, the server proves possession of its certificate's key with CertificateVerify, a signature over the whole handshake transcript, and every implementation must support rsa_pkcs1_sha256 for certificates, rsa_pss_rsae_sha256 for CertificateVerify and certificates, and ecdsa_secp256r1_sha256; the PKCS #1 version 1.5 values refer solely to signatures inside certificates and are not defined for handshake messages. The certificate chain itself is a series of signatures by certification authorities; JSON Web Tokens use RS256 or ES256; DNSSEC (Domain Name System Security Extensions) signs zone data; firmware and software updates are code-signed. Verification code is a target in its own right: CVE-2020-0601, published on 14 January 2020, was a flaw in how Windows CryptoAPI validated elliptic-curve certificates that let an attacker sign a malicious executable with a spoofed code-signing certificate so that it appeared to come from a trusted source.

What goes wrong. A stolen private key signs as well as the real owner, and nothing in the signature reveals the difference, which is why keys for code and certificate authorities live in hardware security modules and why revocation exists. A weak per-signature secret leaks the key: SEC 1 (Standards for Efficient Cryptography 1) records that an attacker who learns only the five most significant bits of the ECDSA ephemeral key over a few hundred signatures can compute the private key, and RFC 8032 lists freedom from per-signature randomness as an advantage of EdDSA for that reason. A weak hash allows substitution, as above. And a valid signature says nothing about intent: it shows that the data was signed by whoever held the key, not that the content is safe or that a person read it.

In law. Legal systems treat signatures in levels, and the cryptographic kind sits at the top. Brazil's Lei 14.063 of 23 September 2020 classifies electronic signatures as simple, which merely identify the signer or attach data, advanced, which use certificates not issued by ICP-Brasil or other means accepted by the parties and must be uniquely linked to the signer, under the signer's exclusive control and such that any later change is detectable, and qualified, which use a digital certificate under the Medida Provisória 2.200-2 of 24 August 2001, the instrument that instituted ICP-Brasil (Infraestrutura de Chaves Públicas Brasileira), and carry the highest reliability. Article 10 of that Medida Provisória is what gives them weight: statements in electronic documents produced with ICP-Brasil certification are presumed true in relation to their signatories, while other means of proving authorship and integrity remain allowed. The law also requires that the means of signing can be revoked or cancelled when its security is compromised, the legal mirror of certificate revocation.

After quantum computers. NIST IR (Interagency Report) 8547, final in October 2026, deprecates ECDSA, EdDSA and RSA signatures after 2030 and disallows them after 2035, and under OMB (Office of Management and Budget) Memorandum M-26-15 the United States government's high value assets and high impact systems must adopt post-quantum signatures by 31 December 2031. The replacements are larger. FIPS 204 (13 August 2024) specifies ML-DSA (Module-Lattice-Based Digital Signature Algorithm), whose smallest set, ML-DSA-44, has a 1,312-byte public key and a 2,420-byte signature, against 64 bytes for an Ed25519 signature; FIPS 205 specifies SLH-DSA (Stateless Hash-Based Digital Signature Algorithm), with 32-byte public keys but signatures of 7,856 to 17,088 bytes at its lowest security category. NIST's draft SP (Special Publication) 800-230, open for comment until 12 June 2026, adds six SLH-DSA parameter sets with smaller signatures and faster verification for signing software, firmware and certificates, at the price of a hard limit of 2 to the 24th signatures per key. Certificate chains, which carry several signatures and public keys each, feel the size first; the post-quantum cryptography entry covers the programme.

Numbers worth remembering: three approved families in FIPS 186-5 (RSA, ECDSA, EdDSA); 64-byte Ed25519 signatures and 32-byte keys; RSASSA-PSS required for new RSA applications; 23 February 2017 for the SHA-1 collision; 2030 and 2035 for the deprecation and disallowance of classical signatures; 2,420 bytes for an ML-DSA-44 signature; and simple, advanced and qualified as Brazil's three legal levels.

dns.def: The distributed, hierarchical naming system that maps names such as example.com to addresses and other typed data.
dns.context: Applications reach it through the operating system's stub resolver, which hands queries to a recursive resolver; that server answers from its cache or asks authoritative servers. When a name resolves wrongly or not at all, the useful first question is which of those layers holds the answer.
dns.depth:
What it is, and what it is not. The Domain Name System (DNS) is a distributed database, not a server and not a file. RFC (Request for Comments) 1034 and RFC 1035, written by Paul Mockapetris of the Information Sciences Institute (ISI) in November 1987, define its three parts: a tree-structured name space whose nodes carry resource records, name servers that hold the data for parts of the tree, and resolvers that extract it for clients. A label holds 0 to 63 octets, the empty label is the root, and a full name may not exceed 255 octets. Authority is cut into zones, each served by redundant name servers, and every record carries a type, a class and a time to live (TTL), so one name can hold addresses, mail exchangers, text and keys.

Where it came from. Before DNS, the Network Information Center (NIC) kept every host name in one file, HOSTS.TXT, which every host fetched over File Transfer Protocol (FTP); RFC 1034 notes that distributing each version cost bandwidth proportional to the square of the number of hosts. Mockapetris's first specification, RFC 882 and 883, appeared in November 1983. RFC 1034 and 1035 obsoleted them and are still the core, updated rather than replaced by later RFCs such as 2181, 2308, 4033 and 7766.

How a name resolves. In RFC 9499's terms, the operating system's stub resolver cannot perform all resolution itself, so it sends the question, with the Recursion Desired (RD) bit set, to a recursive resolver. The recursive resolver answers from its cache or starts at the root and follows referrals down the tree until a server authoritative for the zone answers. The root is published under 13 identifiers, A to M, run by 12 independent organizations; root-servers.org counted 2,046 operational instances on 11 November 2026. RFC 9499 also names the policy-implementing resolver, which changes answers on purpose, for instance to block malware, sometimes without telling the user.

The message. Every message has a header of six 16-bit fields, then the question, answer, authority and additional sections. The header holds a 16-bit identifier (ID) that pairs a reply with its query, the QR bit (query or response), a 4-bit Opcode, the flags AA (Authoritative Answer), TC (truncation), RD and RA (Recursion Available), and a 4-bit response code (RCODE) in which 2 is SERVFAIL, 3 is NXDOMAIN (a name error, meaningful only from an authoritative server) and 5 is REFUSED. The AA bit is the first thing to read when troubleshooting: an authoritative server sets it and a cached answer does not, so asking the authority and the resolver the same question with dig shows whether the zone or a stale cache is wrong.

Ports, sizes and transport. Servers use port 53 over the User Datagram Protocol (UDP) and the Transmission Control Protocol (TCP). RFC 1035 caps a UDP message at 512 bytes; a longer answer is truncated with TC set, the signal to retry over TCP, where each message carries a two-byte length prefix. Because RFC 1123 said only that resolvers SHOULD support TCP, some implementers treated it as optional; RFC 7766 (March 2016) requires every general-purpose implementation, the stub included, to support both. EDNS(0), the Extension Mechanisms for DNS (RFC 6891, April 2013, Internet Standard 75), lets each pair of hosts advertise a larger UDP size in an OPT pseudo-record, type 41, negotiated hop by hop; it exists because DNS Security Extensions (DNSSEC) signatures and multiple Internet Protocol version 6 (IPv6) addresses outgrew 512 bytes. Fragmented UDP is lost or spoofed too often, so DNS Flag Day (1 October 2020) set a default of 1,232 bytes: the 1,280-byte maximum transmission unit (MTU) that IPv6 requires, less 48 bytes of IPv6 and UDP headers. A firewall that blocks TCP port 53 therefore breaks every answer above that size.

Caching. The TTL is a 32-bit count of seconds set by the zone's administrator; caches count it down, zero forbids caching, and RFC 1034 advises lowering it before an anticipated change and restoring it afterwards. Negative answers are cached too. RFC 2308 (March 1998) separates NXDOMAIN, no such name, from NODATA, the name exists without the type asked, and takes their lifetime from the lower of the zone's start of authority (SOA) MINIMUM field and the SOA record's own TTL, adding that one to three hours suits a resolver's ceiling and more than a day causes trouble. Hence the new record that stays invisible: someone asked before it existed, and the resolver is serving the cached negative answer.

Poisoning. Classic DNS accepts the first matching answer, so an off-path attacker who guesses the 16-bit ID and the source port can plant a forgery in a resolver's cache; a well-randomized ID alone needs about 32,768 attempts on average. In 2008 Dan Kaminsky of IOActive showed how practical this was, and the CERT Coordination Center (CERT/CC) published Vulnerability Note VU#800113, CVE-2008-1447 (Common Vulnerabilities and Exposures), on 8 July 2008. The fix was per-query source port randomization, about 16 more bits to guess, later recommended by RFC 5452 (January 2009), but the note said only DNSSEC fully prevents poisoning. DNSSEC, introduced by RFC 4033 (March 2005), signs the data so that a validating resolver can check origin and integrity; it provides no confidentiality.

Encrypting the question. Privacy came separately, and only for the leg from stub to recursive resolver. DNS over Transport Layer Security (DoT, RFC 7858, May 2016) uses TCP port 853. DNS over HTTPS (DoH, RFC 8484, October 2018; HTTPS is Hypertext Transfer Protocol Secure) carries application/dns-message by GET or POST, and its authors note that the default port 443 and mixing with other HTTPS traffic deter on-path interference and traffic analysis. DNS over QUIC (DoQ, RFC 9250, May 2022) uses UDP port 853. None of the three authenticates the records, and the resolver still sees every name asked.

In practice. On Linux, glibc reads /etc/resolv.conf: up to three nameserver lines (MAXNS), tried in order, a default timeout of 5 seconds (capped at 30) and 2 attempts; ndots, default 1, decides when a name is tried as absolute before the search list is appended, so a short name can work in one office and fail in another with no server at fault. In application delivery DNS steers traffic: F5 BIG-IP DNS, named Global Traffic Manager (GTM) until version 11.x, answers for a wide IP by choosing the best available pool and then the best virtual server in it, and the TTL of those answers decides how fast clients follow a failover.

When it goes wrong. On 4 October 2021 Facebook vanished after a maintenance command took its backbone down; its DNS servers, built to withdraw their Border Gateway Protocol (BGP) advertisements when they cannot reach the data centres, did so, and the rest of the internet could no longer find them. Read the layers in order: the stub's configuration and search list, the recursive resolver's cache and policy, the parent zone's delegation, then the authoritative data.

dns-over-https.def: DNS over HTTPS (DoH) carries Domain Name System (DNS) queries and responses inside HTTPS (Hypertext Transfer Protocol Secure), standardized in Request for Comments (RFC) 8484 in October 2018, so that devices on the path between a client and its resolver can neither read nor alter them.
dns-over-https.context: Classic DNS (Domain Name System) travels in plaintext on port 53, so anyone on the path can see which names a device looks up and can forge or change the answers. DNS over HTTPS (DoH) maps each query and response into an ordinary HTTPS (Hypertext Transfer Protocol Secure) exchange on port 443, protected by TLS (Transport Layer Security) and mixed with web traffic; its sibling DNS over TLS (DoT) does the same on a dedicated port, 853. It protects the channel, not the data: the resolver still sees every query, and DNSSEC (DNS Security Extensions) is still what proves an answer genuine. It also stirs debate, because a client that sends its queries to an outside DoH resolver bypasses the network-level DNS filtering and logging that schools, families and enterprises rely on.
dns-over-https.depth:
DNS over HTTPS (DoH) is defined by Request for Comments (RFC) 8484, published in October 2018 on the Internet Engineering Task Force (IETF) Standards Track by Paul Hoffman of ICANN (the Internet Corporation for Assigned Names and Numbers) and Patrick McManus of Mozilla. It maps each Domain Name System (DNS) query and response pair into one HTTP (Hypertext Transfer Protocol) exchange over an https URI (Uniform Resource Identifier), and so inherits the confidentiality and server authentication of TLS (Transport Layer Security). The RFC insists it is more than a tunnel: it uses HTTP content negotiation, caching, redirection, proxying, authentication and compression. It names two use cases, keeping on-path devices from interfering with DNS and letting web applications reach DNS through browser interfaces consistent with CORS (Cross-Origin Resource Sharing), and it covers the hop from a stub resolver to a recursive resolver, not resolution between servers. It is not DNSSEC (the DNS Security Extensions): the RFC states that HTTPS protects the transport but not the integrity of the DNS data, that the two are independent and fully compatible, and that a client either validates itself or trusts the AD (Authentic Data) bit set by its DoH server.

The mechanics are deliberately plain. A client is configured with a URI template, such as https://dnsserver.example.net/dns-query with a variable named dns, and a DoH server must implement both methods. With GET, the binary DNS message goes in the dns query parameter encoded as base64url without padding, which caches well; the RFC's own example request for www.example.com is the string AAABAAABAAAAAAAAA3d3dwdleGFtcGxlA2NvbQAAAQAB. With POST, the message is the request body with the media type application/dns-message, which is usually smaller. Clients should send an Accept header, and should set the DNS identifier (ID) to 0 in every query, because HTTP already pairs request and response and a varying ID would make identical queries cache separately. HTTP/2 is the minimum recommended version, because classic UDP (User Datagram Protocol) DNS is unordered and low in overhead and HTTP needs multiplexing, reordering and header compression to compete; RFC 7540, which the RFC cites, has since been replaced by RFC 9113 (June 2022). A DNS message carried this way can be up to 65,535 bytes. The BIND (Berkeley Internet Name Domain) dig tool speaks DoH: +https queries port 443 by POST at the default endpoint /dns-query, and +https-get uses GET.

Because DoH is HTTP, HTTP caches can hold its answers, and RFC 8484 sets the rules. The freshness lifetime of a response must not exceed the smallest TTL (time to live) in its answer section, and equal to it is recommended; a client must subtract the Age header, so an answer with a TTL of 600 seconds that a cache has held for 250 has 350 left; a server that tailors answers to a client should prevent shared reuse with max-age 0 or a Vary header. The behaviour is easy to see. On 12 November 2026 at 12:58 UTC (Coordinated Universal Time) a GET to Google Public DNS at dns.google/dns-query with the RFC's example message returned HTTP/2 status 200, media type application/dns-message, a 65-byte message with ID 0 and two address records for www.example.com with a TTL of 300 seconds, and the header Cache-Control: private, max-age=300; Cloudflare's endpoint answered the same query with the same media type. Google documents that dns.google/dns-query implements RFC 8484 with GET and POST, while dns.google/resolve is a separate JSON (JavaScript Object Notation) interface, GET only, that is not part of the standard.

Finding and trusting the server is the hard part. RFC 8484 says the client chooses its DoH server by configuration and must not switch to a URI it learned any other way, such as through HTTP/2 server push or an unsolicited answer. It cannot use its DoH server to resolve that server's own name, so the RFC suggests resolving it once as part of configuration, using an IP (Internet Protocol) address in the URI with a certificate for that address, or resolving it over ordinary DNS while still authenticating the connection with HTTPS. It also warns of a deadlock: if checking the server's certificate needs an OCSP (Online Certificate Status Protocol) or AIA (Authority Information Access) fetch that itself needs DNS, the check can never finish, so DoH servers should staple their certificate status. Discovery was standardized five years later. RFC 9461 (November 2023) maps DNS servers to SVCB (service binding) records and adds a dohpath key carrying the URI template; RFC 9462, Discovery of Designated Resolvers (DDR), lets a client ask its unencrypted resolver for the SVCB records of _dns.resolver.arpa to find the encrypted resolvers that resolver designates; RFC 9463, Discovery of Network-designated Resolvers (DNR), announces them in DHCPv6 (Dynamic Host Configuration Protocol for IPv6, Internet Protocol version 6) option 144, DHCPv4 option 162 and IPv6 Router Advertisement option type 144.

Browsers moved first, and their choices shaped the debate. Firefox began enabling DoH by default for users in the United States on 25 February 2020, sending queries to Cloudflare, with NextDNS as the other trusted resolver on offer. Mozilla's escape hatch is a canary domain, use-application-dns.net: if the operating system's resolver answers it with any code other than NOERROR, or with NOERROR and no address records of type A or AAAA, Firefox leaves default DoH off, a signal a network that filters DNS can send on purpose; it does not apply to users who turned DoH on themselves, and Mozilla describes it as temporary until a standard exists. Chrome 83, announced on 19 May 2020, took the other route, a same-provider upgrade: Chrome keeps a list of DNS providers that offer DoH and switches to the DoH service of the provider the user already has, falls back to ordinary DNS if that fails, and turns Secure DNS off when it detects Windows parental controls or enterprise policies. In Windows the DNS client supports DoH from Windows Server 2022; it ships with a list of known DoH servers (Cloudflare, Google and Quad9), accepts more with Add-DnsClientDohServerAddress and its DohTemplate, AllowFallbackToUdp and AutoUpgrade parameters, and offers Allow, Prohibit and Require DoH by Group Policy, with a warning not to require DoH on domain-joined computers, because Active Directory depends on DNS and the Windows Server DNS Server service does not answer DoH queries.

The objection from network operators is written into the standard itself. Section 10 of RFC 8484 states that filtering or inspection systems that rely on unsecured DNS will not function where DoH is used, and the use of port 443, shared with every other HTTPS connection, is precisely what makes it hard to tell apart and block. The National Security Agency (NSA) guidance of January 2021, Adopting Encrypted DNS in Enterprise Environments, describes a browser sending DoH through the enterprise gateway on port 443 straight to an outside resolver, bypassing the enterprise resolver's logging and blocking, and recommends that enterprises use only designated enterprise resolvers, which should themselves support encrypted DNS, and disable and block all other encrypted resolvers; if the enterprise resolver cannot do DoH yet, it should still be used and encrypted DNS blocked. The attacker's side was visible early: in July 2019 Qihoo 360's Netlab described the Godlua backdoor for Linux, which kept its command and control address in DNS TXT records, on GitHub and on Pastebin, and used DNS over HTTPS to fetch it out of sight of plaintext DNS monitoring.

Firewalls answer by decrypting or by policy. FortiOS documents that before version 7.0 DoT and DoH traffic passed silently through its DNS proxy, and that from 7.0 the proxy daemon (WAD) hands their queries to the DNS proxy so the DNS filter profile applies, but only with full SSL (Secure Sockets Layer) deep inspection and, in Fortinet's example, a policy in proxy inspection mode; FortiOS 7.4.1 extended this to DNS over QUIC and DNS over HTTP/3 with set quic enable in the deep inspection profile. Where decryption is not allowed, the usual controls are the ones the NSA describes: a designated resolver that itself speaks DoH, policies pushed to browsers and operating systems, the canary domain for unmanaged Firefox installations, and blocking of known public DoH endpoints by address or category, which can never be complete because anyone can run a DoH server on any HTTPS host.

Encryption hides the content but not the shape of the traffic. RFC 8484 notes that session-level encryption has well-known weaknesses against traffic analysis, which DNS makes acute because query and response sizes are distinctive, and points to HTTP/2 padding and to the EDNS(0) (Extension Mechanisms for DNS) Padding option. RFC 8467 (Experimental, October 2018) turns Daniel K. Gillmor's measurements into a policy: clients pad queries to a multiple of 128 octets and servers pad responses to a multiple of 468, a size chosen so that three blocks still fit a typical MTU (maximum transmission unit). The RFC also lists what DoH adds to the privacy picture: HTTP cookies and the fingerprint of a client's header fields can correlate its queries, and the client's IP address still identifies it to the resolver unless something hides it. Oblivious DNS over HTTPS (ODoH, RFC 9230, June 2022, an experimental independent submission by authors from Apple, Fastly and Cloudflare) splits the roles between a proxy that sees the client and a target that sees only an encrypted query, so that no single server knows both.

DoH has two close neighbours. DNS over TLS (DoT, RFC 7858, May 2016) runs the classic DNS wire format over TLS on TCP (Transmission Control Protocol) port 853, which makes it easy to recognize and therefore easy to allow or block; DNS over QUIC (DoQ, RFC 9250, May 2022) uses QUIC on UDP port 853 with the ALPN (Application-Layer Protocol Negotiation) token doq. All three give the same protection on the path and the same exposure at the resolver; DoH differs in hiding among web traffic and in fitting the HTTP machinery that browsers, CDNs (content delivery networks) and proxies already run. The numbers worth remembering are port 443 for DoH and 853 for DoT and DoQ, the media type application/dns-message, ID 0, a cache lifetime no longer than the smallest TTL, padding blocks of 128 and 468 octets, and the discovery codes 144 and 162.

end-to-end-encryption.def: Encryption where only the communicating endpoints can read the messages, not the servers in between.
end-to-end-encryption.context: With E2EE the keys live on the devices, so the provider relaying the messages cannot read them, unlike transport encryption, which protects data only in transit between each hop. It is the standard for private messaging, and the reason lawful-access debates keep recurring.

entropy.def: A measure of unpredictability, counted in bits; in security, the amount of real randomness behind a key, token or password, which decides how many guesses an attacker needs.
entropy.context: High entropy means an attacker cannot narrow down the possibilities, which is why keys must come from a good random source, not a predictable one. Weak entropy (a poor random generator, a low-variety password) quietly undermines otherwise strong cryptography. It is counted in bits: a value chosen uniformly from 2 to the power n possibilities has n bits, however long it looks. Cryptography uses the conservative measure, min-entropy, which considers only the most likely outcome, and operating systems collect it from hardware and timing noise to seed a cryptographically secure pseudorandom number generator (CSPRNG).
entropy.depth:
Entropy is the measure of unpredictability, and in practice it is the thing that fails when cryptography fails. A key generated from a weak source is weak regardless of its length, and the failure is invisible because the output still looks random to anyone inspecting it. The measure comes from Claude Shannon's paper A Mathematical Theory of Communication, published in the Bell System Technical Journal in July and October 1948. For outcomes with probabilities p1 to pn he defined H as minus the sum of each probability multiplied by its logarithm, called it the entropy of the set of probabilities and remarked that it has the form of the H in Boltzmann's H theorem in statistical mechanics; with logarithms to base 2 the unit is the binary digit, or bit, a word he credits to J. W. Tukey. A value drawn uniformly from 2 to the power n possibilities therefore has n bits of entropy, and anything that makes some outcomes likelier than others leaves it with less.

Shannon's figure is an average, and an average can flatter a bad generator. Request for Comments (RFC) 4086, Randomness Requirements for Security (June 2005, by D. Eastlake, J. Schiller and S. Crocker, Best Current Practice 106, obsoleting RFC 1750), gives the standard example: a generator that outputs zero half of the time and a uniformly random 128-bit value otherwise has 64 bits of Shannon entropy, yet an adversary who simply tries zero breaks half of its keys. Cryptography therefore works with min-entropy, the negative base-2 logarithm of the probability of the single most likely outcome, which for that generator is 1 bit. The United States National Institute of Standards and Technology (NIST) defines it the same way, as a worst-case measure of unpredictability and a lower bound on entropy, and it is the measure its random bit generation standards use. The same RFC carries the warning that explains most real failures: statistically tested randomness is not the unpredictability that security needs. A 128-bit key expanded from an 8-bit seed passes for random and holds 8 bits of information, because the adversary has only 256 seeds to try.

Entropy belongs to the process that chose a value, not to the value. A four-digit PIN (personal identification number) drawn at random has the base-2 logarithm of 10,000, about 13.3 bits; eight characters drawn at random from the 95 printable ASCII (American Standard Code for Information Interchange) characters have about 52.6 bits; a password that a person invented has only what an attacker's model of people leaves it, far less than its length suggests. A strength meter is therefore an estimate, since it scores a string and cannot see the generator. RFC 4086 works an example from the defender's side: to hold an online guesser, limited to 500,000 tries, below a one-in-a-thousand chance of success, a password needs about 29 bits, which three words taken at random from a list of 1,000 supply; one in a million needs 39 bits and one in a billion 49, about 10 bits for each factor of 1,000.

Computers are deterministic, so entropy has to be harvested from something physical. NIST Special Publication (SP) 800-90B, of January 2018, models an entropy source as three parts: a noise source, an optional conditioning component and health tests. The noise source, which the document calls the root of security for the whole generator, is either physical (dedicated hardware) or non-physical (system data such as timings and memory contents, or human input such as mouse movements); if it fails, no other component can compensate. Conditioning is a deterministic function that reduces bias. The health tests run at start-up, continuously and on demand, and the two approved continuous tests are the Repetition Count Test, which catches a source stuck on one value, and the Adaptive Proportion Test. Validation estimates min-entropy from at least 1,000,000 raw samples. The entropy source then seeds a deterministic random bit generator (DRBG) built from a hash function or a block cipher, specified in SP 800-90A Revision 1 (June 2015), and SP 800-90C (September 2025) describes how the two are assembled into complete generators. The division of labour is the point: a few hundred unpredictable bits, stretched by sound cryptography, serve for any amount of output, and RFC 4086 judges that even the highest security system is unlikely to need keying material of much over 200 bits.

Modern operating systems solve this with a kernel pool seeded from hardware sources, and the practical rule is to use the system's random device rather than a language's general-purpose random function, which is fast, deterministic and not for keys. On Linux the kernel gathers entropy from device drivers and other environmental noise to seed a cryptographically secure pseudorandom number generator (CSPRNG). The getrandom system call, available since Linux 3.17, draws from it and blocks only until the pool has been initialized; /dev/urandom never blocks, which means that very early in boot it can return output from an uninitialized generator; and /dev/random, which used to block whenever the kernel's entropy estimate ran low, is called a legacy interface by its own manual page. In January 2020 LWN.net reported Andy Lutomirski's patch set removing the blocking pool, on the argument that the kernel's generator is good enough even for key generation. The file /proc/sys/kernel/random/entropy_avail shows the kernel's estimate in bits. The manual's sizing advice is worth keeping: a 3072-bit RSA (Rivest-Shamir-Adleman) key has an effective strength of 128 bits and needs only 128 bits of seed, and since no primitive in use promises more than 256 bits of security, a program that reads more than 32 bytes at a time is probably not well designed.

The same split appears in every environment. On Windows the call is BCryptGenRandom, whose default provider follows the counter-mode DRBG of NIST SP 800-90. In Python the random module is a Mersenne Twister with a period of 2 to the power 19937, minus 1, which its documentation calls completely unsuitable for cryptographic purposes; the secrets module reads the operating system's source instead, and its documentation treats 32 bytes as enough for a token. A long period is not entropy: the whole future output of such a generator follows from its internal state, and that state can be worked out from enough of its past output.

The recurring cause is predictable conditions at generation time. In January 1996 Ian Goldberg and David Wagner, then doctoral students at the University of California, Berkeley, showed that Netscape's browser seeded the generator behind its Secure Sockets Layer (SSL) keys from the time of day, the process identifier and the parent process identifier: at most 47 bits of unknowns behind a key advertised as 128 bits, and only about a million possibilities, tested in some 25 seconds on a workstation of the day, for an attacker with an account on the same machine. In May 2008 a bug was found in the OpenSSL package shipped by Debian that had left keys with only 15 bits of entropy for two years, so that each key size could yield just 294,912 distinct keys. Its record in the Common Vulnerabilities and Exposures (CVE) list, CVE-2008-0166, covers OpenSSL 0.9.8c-1 up to the versions before 0.9.8g-9 on Debian-based systems and says plainly that the random number generator generates predictable numbers.

Embedded devices and virtual machines that generate keys at first boot, before any real environmental noise has accumulated, have produced large populations of duplicate or factorable keys, discoverable by scanning public keys alone. The reference study is Mining Your Ps and Qs, by Nadia Heninger, Zakir Durumeric, Eric Wustrow and J. Alex Halderman (USENIX Security Symposium, August 2012). Scanning the public IPv4 (Internet Protocol version 4) address space, they collected 5.8 million unique TLS (Transport Layer Security) certificates from 12.8 million hosts and 6.2 million unique SSH (Secure Shell) host keys from 10.2 million hosts. They found that 0.75 per cent of the TLS certificates shared keys because of insufficient entropy at generation. They obtained the RSA private keys of 0.50 per cent of the TLS hosts and 0.03 per cent of the SSH hosts, because pairs of public moduli shared a prime factor that a greatest common divisor computation exposes, and the Digital Signature Algorithm (DSA) private keys of 1.03 per cent of the SSH hosts, because signatures had been made with insufficient randomness. The vulnerable hosts were overwhelmingly headless or embedded devices, from 54 manufacturers, and the cause the authors reproduced was a boot-time entropy hole: a window after start-up in which Linux's urandom could be entirely predictable, and in which the device generated its long-term keys. The paper also cites the virtual machine variant, in which a machine reset to a snapshot repeats random values it has already used.

Entropy is easily confused with its neighbours. Key length is a ceiling on entropy, not a guarantee of it. A nonce has to be unique and a salt unique per record, and neither has to be secret; a key, a session token or a password reset link has to be unpredictable, which takes entropy from a CSPRNG. A DRBG adds no entropy, it only stretches its seed, and a hash function adds none either, so the digest of a guessable input is guessable. The numbers worth remembering are few: 256 bits, or 32 bytes, is what both the Linux manual and Python's documentation treat as enough for any one secret; 15 bits was the whole Debian keyspace; 47 bits stood behind Netscape's 128-bit keys; and 29 bits is what RFC 4086 computes for a modest online guessing threat. The question that follows from all of it is where a secret's bits came from, not how long it is: which call produced them, on which machine, and how soon after boot.

ephemeral-key.def: A short-lived key, or key pair, generated for one run of a cryptographic process, typically one key exchange, and destroyed once that run is over, so that nothing kept afterwards can recreate what it protected.
ephemeral-key.context: Ephemeral key exchange, the E in DHE and ECDHE (finite-field and elliptic-curve Diffie-Hellman ephemeral), is the mechanism behind forward secrecy: because each side's private key exists for one conversation and is never stored, a later theft of long-term keys has nothing to work on. The National Institute of Standards and Technology (NIST) makes the rules explicit: an ephemeral private key is used in exactly one key-establishment transaction, destroyed as soon as possible, and never backed up or archived. Its opposite is a static key, meant for many runs over a long period, such as a certificate key that signs handshakes. The property is a discipline, not a label: software that quietly reuses an ephemeral key across connections, as several TLS (Transport Layer Security) servers did for years, keeps the name and loses the protection. In signatures the word has a second sense, the per-signature secret of DSA (Digital Signature Algorithm) and ECDSA (Elliptic Curve Digital Signature Algorithm), whose reuse or even partial leakage can reveal the signing key.
ephemeral-key.depth:
What it is, exactly. The glossary of the National Institute of Standards and Technology (NIST) defines an ephemeral key as a cryptographic key generated for each execution of a cryptographic process, such as key establishment, that meets the other requirements of its key type, for example being unique to each message or session, and sets it against the static key, intended for use over a relatively long period and typically in many runs of a key-establishment scheme. NIST Special Publication (SP) 800-57 Part 1 Revision 5 (May 2020) lists private and public ephemeral key-agreement keys as the short-term halves of key pairs used in a single key-establishment transaction to establish symmetric keys and, optionally, other material such as initialization vectors. The ephemeral key is not the session key. In a Diffie-Hellman exchange the ephemeral key pair produces a shared secret, a key derivation function turns that secret into the session keys, and then the ephemeral private key should be gone; what protects old traffic is that disappearance, not the shortness of the keys' life on paper.

The rules. SP 800-56A Revision 3 (April 2018), section 5.6.3.3, is the most precise statement anywhere: an ephemeral private key shall be used in exactly one key-establishment transaction; after its use it shall be destroyed as soon as possible, and protected until then; it shall not be backed up or archived; and the key pair should be generated as close to its time of use as possible, ideally just before the public key is sent. The same document classifies its schemes by how many ephemeral key pairs take part. In C(2e) both parties generate one, which suits interactive protocols such as Transport Layer Security (TLS); in C(1e) only the initiator does, which suits store-and-forward uses such as encrypting to a recipient's published key; in C(0e) there are none, and the result depends only on static keys. The categories explain at a glance which schemes can offer forward secrecy and for whom.

Where ephemeral keys live in protocols. In TLS 1.3, specified since July 2026 in RFC (Request for Comments) 9846, every key exchange is ephemeral, and the revision added a rule its predecessor lacked: clients and servers MUST NOT reuse a key share for multiple connections. Because RFC 8446 had permitted reuse, a receiver must still tolerate it from a peer, so the rule binds senders only. In IKEv2 (Internet Key Exchange version 2), RFC 7296 states that achieving perfect forward secrecy requires each endpoint, when a connection closes, to forget not only its keys but any information that could recompute them; it also allows an endpoint to reuse a Diffie-Hellman exponential across several setups for performance, either renewing it periodically, at the cost of less than perfect forward secrecy, or tracking which connections used it and deleting it only when the last one closes, and calls the choice private because it does not affect interoperability. In IPsec (Internet Protocol Security) the phase 2 PFS (perfect forward secrecy) setting, set pfs enable with a set dhgrp list on a FortiGate, is what makes each child security association run a fresh exchange. WireGuard zeroes all ephemeral private keys and symmetric session keys if no new keys have been exchanged within three times its REJECT_AFTER_TIME, and the initiator starts a new handshake once a session key reaches REKEY_AFTER_TIME. In the Signal Protocol's X3DH (Extended Triple Diffie-Hellman, revision of 4 November 2016), the sender generates a new ephemeral key pair for every run, and the recipient publishes one-time prekeys in advance, which the server hands out once and deletes, an ephemeral key prepared for a conversation that has not started yet.

How long a session key may live. An ephemeral exchange protects the session; it does not refresh it. RFC 4253 recommends that Secure Shell (SSH) change its keys after each gigabyte of data or each hour of connection, whichever comes first, with a full new exchange, and warns that the re-exchange is a public-key operation that should not be performed too often. TLS 1.3 takes a cheaper path: a KeyUpdate message derives the next application traffic secret from the current one with the label traffic upd, and implementations SHOULD delete the previous secret, so traffic already sent stays out of reach of anyone who later captures the current keys. No new Diffie-Hellman exchange is involved, so the protection runs only forward from the original handshake, which is why long-lived tunnels still rekey with a fresh exchange.

What goes wrong: reuse. The commonest failure is an ephemeral key that is not ephemeral. OpenSSL's advisory of 28 January 2016 explained that its SSL_OP_SINGLE_DH_USE option, which forces a new Diffie-Hellman key for each handshake, was not on by default, so a server using ephemeral Diffie-Hellman could reuse the same private exponent for the life of its process; combined with groups whose primes were not safe, that allowed CVE-2016-0701, in which an attacker who completed multiple handshakes could recover the exponent. OpenSSL 1.0.2f switched the option on by default. The Raccoon attack of 2020 also required reuse: its authors note it works only against servers that reuse Diffie-Hellman public keys, statically or by recycling ephemeral ones, which they observe was already bad practice because it gives up forward secrecy. Both show the same thing: the security argument rests on the destruction of the private value, and a cache that keeps it for performance turns every session sharing it into one target. RFC 10015 (Nimrod Aviram, July 2026) drew the conclusion for TLS 1.2: public key reuse, whether through static suites or reused ephemeral keys, can lead to timing side channels, as Raccoon showed for finite-field Diffie-Hellman and invalid curve attacks for elliptic curves, and since implementations in practice fail to apply every mitigation, it forbids finite-field Diffie-Hellman and discourages static ECDH (elliptic-curve Diffie-Hellman) in TLS 1.2 altogether.

What goes wrong: static on purpose. Some operators want the opposite. ETSI (European Telecommunications Standards Institute) TS 103 523-3, Enterprise Transport Security (version 1.3.1, August 2019), runs the TLS 1.3 handshake unchanged except that the server uses a static Diffie-Hellman key pair for each curve, shareable with authorized middleboxes so they can decrypt sessions, and announces itself with visibility information in the server certificate. The specification is explicit that this gives no per-session forward secrecy: anyone holding the static private key can decrypt every session made with it, and forward secrecy for those sessions begins only when every copy of that key is destroyed. It describes the relaxation as deliberate. A standard TLS 1.3 client cannot tell such a server from an ordinary one by the handshake alone, which is the argument for treating ephemeral keys as a policy to verify rather than a property to assume.

The second sense: signatures. In DSA (Digital Signature Algorithm) and ECDSA (Elliptic Curve Digital Signature Algorithm), each signature uses a fresh random number, which SEC 1 (Standards for Efficient Cryptography 1, version 2.0, May 2009) calls an ephemeral elliptic curve key pair, k and the point R. Its secrecy matters even more than in key exchange. FIPS (Federal Information Processing Standard) 186-5 requires a new secret number for each signature and, if it is computed in advance, protection equal to that of the private key, and SEC 1 notes that an attacker who learns only the five most significant bits of the ephemeral private key across a few hundred signatures can compute the private key, a result due to Howgrave-Graham and Smart. Deterministic generation and EdDSA (Edwards-curve Digital Signature Algorithm), covered under ECDSA and digital signatures, remove the dependence on a good random source at signing time.

Numbers worth remembering: one key-establishment transaction per ephemeral private key; C(2e), C(1e) and C(0e) for the three families of schemes; one gigabyte or one hour between SSH rekeys; three times REJECT_AFTER_TIME before WireGuard zeroes its ephemeral keys; and five leaked bits in a few hundred ECDSA signatures as enough to lose the signing key.

exit-node.def: The final Tor relay, where traffic leaves the network towards its destination.
exit-node.context: The exit sees the traffic as it re-enters the normal internet, which is why exit operators take on extra responsibility and why end-to-end encryption still matters even over Tor. The exit knows the destination but not the original source.

exit-scam.def: When an operator suddenly shuts down and disappears with users' funds.
exit-scam.context: A recurring pattern in unregulated marketplaces: build trust, accumulate deposits, then vanish. Named here to explain the fraud dynamic; the lesson generalizes to any custodial service where trust is doing all the work with no recourse behind it.

exploit.def: Code or a technique that turns a vulnerability into actual unintended behaviour, such as running the attacker's code, reading memory that should be private or skipping a check. As a verb, to exploit a flaw is to use it that way.
exploit.context: A vulnerability is the weakness; an exploit is what takes advantage of it, the working key cut for a specific broken lock. A weaponized exploit is one packaged for reliable, easy use, the stage scoring systems call functional or high maturity. It usually carries a payload: the thing that runs once the door is open. The gap between a flaw being known and an exploit existing, and between an exploit existing and it being used against you, is the clock every patch programme races.
exploit.depth:
Weakness, key and load. The three words are often blurred, and the difference matters when deciding what to do. A vulnerability is a property of the target; an exploit is the input, sequence or program that drives the target into behaviour its designers never intended; the payload is what the attacker does with that behaviour once it happens, opening a shell, writing a file, installing an implant. The technique for exploiting a public-facing application (T1190) in MITRE ATT&CK, MITRE's knowledge base of adversary behaviour, is deliberately broad about the weakness: a software bug, a temporary glitch or a misconfiguration. Its examples run from web servers and databases to services such as SMB (Server Message Block) and SSH (Secure Shell), device management protocols such as SNMP (Simple Network Management Protocol) and Smart Install, and edge appliances that cannot run host-based defences; ATT&CK also tracks exploitation for client execution and for stealth as separate techniques, because the same act serves different goals.

The classic mechanism. The worm released on 2 November 1988, described in Request for Comments (RFC) 1135, already used two kinds of exploit: a debugging feature left enabled in sendmail, a logic flaw, and an input longer than fingerd expected, a memory-corruption flaw. The second kind was explained to a generation by Aleph One's 'Smashing The Stack For Fun And Profit', file 14 of Phrack issue 49, dated 8 November 1996: on many C implementations, writing past the end of an array on the stack overwrites the saved return address, so a crafted input can make the routine return into code the attacker supplied. The article listed the flaws of the moment (syslog, splitvt, sendmail 8.7.5, the Linux and FreeBSD mount commands, the Xt library, at), and the technique became the template for decades of remote code execution. Memory corruption is now one family among many; for websites and databases ATT&CK points to the Open Web Application Security Project (OWASP) Top 10 and the Common Weakness Enumeration (CWE) Top 25 as the lists of the most common weaknesses.

Maturity, as scoring systems measure it. Version 3.1 of the Common Vulnerability Scoring System (CVSS), maintained by FIRST (the Forum of Incident Response and Security Teams), grades Exploit Code Maturity as Unproven (no code, or theoretical), Proof-of-Concept (works in some situations and may need substantial modification by a skilled attacker), Functional (works in most situations) and High (functional autonomous code, or delivery by a worm or virus); a weaponized exploit is the last two. CVSS v4.0 renamed the metric Exploit Maturity and changed the question from code to evidence: Attacked (attempts or toolkits have been reported), Proof-of-Concept and Unreported, with Not Defined treated as Attacked, the worst case, and a recommendation to feed it from several threat intelligence sources, automatically. Version 4.0 also says what makes an exploit hard. Attack Complexity is High when the attacker must evade exploit mitigations, its examples being address space layout randomization (ASLR) and data execution prevention (DEP), or must first obtain a target-specific secret; Attack Requirements captures conditions of the deployment, such as a race, that make success occasional.

From fix to exploit. A patch documents the flaw it fixes. In 2008 Brumley, Poosankam, Song and Zheng generated working exploits automatically from patched binaries, sometimes within minutes, which is why exploits for publicly fixed flaws (often called n-days) follow releases closely. Vendors now reason the same way about what they publish. F5 wrote on 13 August 2026 that artificial intelligence (AI) models can reason from a diff, a partial description or a version range to a working attack chain, and that attackers chain several low-severity issues into one path, which is why it paused regular security notifications and asked customers to judge exposure by reachability and criticality rather than by a single CVSS score.

How often, and how fast. Google's Threat Intelligence Group counted 75 zero-day vulnerabilities, flaws exploited before a patch existed, exploited in the wild in 2024, against 98 in 2023 and 63 in 2022; the share aimed at enterprise products rose from 37 to 44 per cent, and the 20 security and networking flaws among them made up more than 60 per cent of enterprise zero-day exploitation. Known flaws are faster still: Fortinet cited FortiGuard research putting exploitation of known vulnerabilities at an average of 4.76 days after public disclosure, in a year with more than 40,000 vulnerabilities recorded. Two public signals turn this into priorities. The Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency's (CISA) Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalogue lists flaws with evidence of exploitation, 1,779 of them in its 10 November 2026 version. FIRST's Exploit Prediction Scoring System (EPSS) is a machine-learning model that publishes, every day and for every Common Vulnerabilities and Exposures (CVE) entry, the probability from 0 to 1 that it will be exploited in the wild in the next 30 days.

Public exploits. The Exploit Database is a CVE-compliant public archive of exploits and proofs of concept, kept for penetration testers and vulnerability researchers and deliberately a repository of working code rather than advisories; frameworks such as Metasploit package exploits as modules with payloads attached. Their existence is the core of a long argument: publication lets defenders verify exposure and test detection, and lowers the skill an attacker needs, which is exactly the effect the CVSS maturity scale scores. Practitioners treat a public, reliable exploit for an exposed service as the trigger for emergency patching or mitigation, whatever the base score says.

The law draws the line at intent. In Brazil, Law 12,737 of 30 November 2012 added article 154-A to the Penal Code, the crime of invading another person's computing device, and its first paragraph applies the same penalty to whoever produces, offers, distributes, sells or spreads a device or computer program with the intent of permitting that invasion. Law 14,155 of 27 May 2021 rewrote the article, dropping the requirement that a security mechanism be violated and raising the penalty to one to four years of reclusão. The paragraph on tools did not change; what separates a researcher's proof of concept from a crime tool in that text is the purpose for which it is made and passed on, and authorization for testing is what makes the act itself lawful.

Neighbours. Proof of concept, a demonstration that a flaw is real; shellcode, the small machine-code payload classic memory exploits deliver; exploit kit, a packaged toolkit that simplifies exploitation, which CVSS v4.0 counts as evidence for the Attacked value; zero-day and n-day, by whether a fix existed at the time; remote code execution, the outcome the classic stack overflow was built to reach; and virtual patching, the controls that block a known exploit while the fix waits for its window.

five-hundred-mile-email.def: A classic sysadmin tale of an email system that mysteriously could not send mail farther than about 500 miles.
five-hundred-mile-email.context: Trey Harris's story turns out to have a real cause: a broken config defaulted a network timeout to near zero, so only servers close enough to answer within a few milliseconds ever connected, and a few milliseconds of light-speed round trip works out to roughly 500 miles. It is the perfect parable for why the absurd-sounding symptom deserves a real root-cause hunt.
five-hundred-mile-email.depth:
The 500-mile email is the best debugging story the profession has, because the absurd premise turns out to be literally correct. A statistics department reported that email would not send further than about 500 miles, the sysadmin's first reaction was that this is not how anything works, and the complaint was accurate.

The chain is genuinely beautiful. A mail server had been upgraded and its configuration file was written for a newer version, so the parser silently defaulted the connection timeout to zero rather than failing. A timeout of effectively zero meant the SMTP connection had to complete within the round trip time, and light in fibre plus switching delay works out to roughly the distance the users had measured. Speed-of-light latency became a business rule by accident.

The reason it endures is not the punchline. It is that the user's report was precise, the sysadmin's disbelief was reasonable, and the truth was underneath both. A story where the ridiculous complaint is correct is a permanent argument for taking reports seriously and for following a causal chain all the way down instead of stopping at the point where it stops making sense.

foo-bar.def: The canonical placeholder names in programming examples, used when the specific name does not matter.
foo-bar.context: "foo" and "bar" are metasyntactic variables: stand-ins that let an example focus on structure rather than naming. Their history is documented in RFC 3092, which traces the pairing to MIT and to the wartime slang FUBAR. When you need a third and fourth, "baz" and "qux" follow.
foo-bar.depth:
Foo and bar are the placeholder names every programmer reaches for, and their history is genuinely contested. The most cited derivation runs through FUBAR, the military acronym, though foo appears independently in American cartoons of the 1930s well before that usage spread, and the Jargon File treats the connection as probable rather than settled.

Their function matters more than their etymology. A placeholder name has to be obviously meaningless, so that nobody reading an example mistakes it for something significant, and foo has the useful property of carrying no domain associations at all. RFC 3092 exists specifically to document the terms, which is a fair indication of how deep into the culture they run.

The practical argument against them is worth making anyway. In documentation, foo and bar are cognitive overhead: a reader has to hold two arbitrary tokens in memory while following the logic, where names like user and order carry their own meaning and free attention for the actual point. Placeholders are honest in a language specification and lazy in a tutorial, and knowing which document you are writing decides which to use.

forward-proxy.def: A proxy that works for the client side: it receives the outbound requests of a set of clients and makes them to origin servers on their behalf, the opposite of a reverse proxy, which stands in front of the servers.
forward-proxy.context: The mirror image of a reverse proxy: a forward proxy represents the user going out to the internet, adding filtering, caching, logging or anonymity, while a reverse proxy represents the servers to whoever arrives. A corporate web proxy, a cloud secure web gateway and a personal privacy proxy are all this shape. The Hypertext Transfer Protocol (HTTP) standard calls it simply a proxy, a forwarding agent chosen by the client, and keeps the word gateway for the reverse kind. It is explicit when the client is configured to send its requests to it, by hand, by a Proxy Auto-Config (PAC) file or by an agent, and transparent, or intercepting, when the network redirects traffic to it without the client knowing. Encrypted traffic crosses it as an opaque tunnel opened with the CONNECT method, unless the proxy re-signs server certificates in order to decrypt and inspect it.
forward-proxy.depth:
The documentation of the Apache web server gives the plain definition: an ordinary forward proxy is an intermediate server that sits between the client and the origin server; the client sends its request to the proxy naming the origin server as the target, the proxy fetches the content and returns it, and the client must be specially configured to use it. The Hypertext Transfer Protocol (HTTP) specification itself, Request for Comments (RFC) 9110 of June 2022, never says forward. It names three intermediaries: a proxy, a message-forwarding agent chosen by the client, usually through local configuration rules; a gateway, also known as a reverse proxy, which acts as an origin server towards the client; and a tunnel, a blind relay. It adds that proxies are often used to group the requests of an organization through a common intermediary for security services, annotation services or shared caching. The deployment guide for F5 SSL Orchestrator draws the line by direction: a forward proxy handles outbound traffic, a finite set of internal users reaching an unlimited number of external resources, and a reverse proxy the opposite.

On the wire, a client that knows it is using a proxy changes the request line. HTTP/1.1 (RFC 9112) requires the absolute form of the target: GET http://www.example.org/pub/WWW/TheProject.html HTTP/1.1, where a request sent straight to the server would carry only the path. The proxy either answers from a valid cache or makes the same request on the client's behalf, to the origin server or to the next proxy in a chain, and it must rebuild the Host field from the target and ignore the one it received. Every proxy must add a Via field to each message it forwards, which is how loops are detected and how a chain shows itself. A proxy that wants to know who is asking answers 407 Proxy Authentication Required with a Proxy-Authenticate challenge, and the client repeats the request with Proxy-Authorization; unlike the 401 exchange with a website, these fields apply only to the next proxy and are consumed there. The 305 Use Proxy status code defined by earlier versions of HTTP is deprecated.

HTTPS, which is HTTP over Transport Layer Security (TLS), cannot be forwarded that way, because the proxy would have to read it. The client instead sends CONNECT with the authority form of the target, only host and port, as in CONNECT server.example.com:443, and there is no default port. Any successful 2xx answer means the proxy switches to tunnel mode and blindly relays bytes in both directions, so TLS is negotiated end to end through it and the proxy sees a host name, a port and a volume of data. RFC 9110 warns that a tunnel to arbitrary servers is a risk: a CONNECT to port 25 could trick the proxy into relaying spam, so proxies should restrict the method to a limited set of known ports. The same idea has since been extended beyond the Transmission Control Protocol (TCP): RFC 9298 (August 2022) proxies the User Datagram Protocol (UDP) in HTTP with the connect-udp token, and RFC 9484 (October 2023) proxies whole Internet Protocol (IP) packets with connect-ip, which is enough to build a remote access virtual private network (VPN) on an HTTP proxy.

Explicit and transparent describe how the traffic reaches the proxy. An explicit proxy is the one the standard defines, chosen by the client. A transparent proxy is one the client did not choose: RFC 9110 calls it an interception proxy, says it filters or redirects outgoing TCP port 80 packets, is commonly found on public access points and inside corporate firewalls, and is indistinguishable at the protocol level from an on-path attacker. The taxonomy in RFC 3040 (January 2001) recommended the name interception proxy precisely because transparent proxy already meant something else in HTTP, a proxy that does not modify the messages. The F5 guide lists the practical differences. In an explicit request the destination address of the packets is the proxy itself and the proxy performs the Domain Name System (DNS) resolution; in a transparent deployment the destination is the real remote address, the client resolves the name itself, and the traffic arrives through a gateway setting, policy-based routing or WCCP (listed in RFC 3040 as the Web Cache Control Protocol). Squid's configuration reference notes one consequence: its intercept and tproxy modes disable authentication on the port, because a client that does not know about the proxy cannot answer a 407.

The forward proxy is as old as the firewall. In May 1994 Ari Luotonen and Kevin Altis described how the web server developed at CERN, cern_httpd, could run as a proxy that provides access to the Web for people on closed subnets who can only reach the internet through a firewall machine, relaying HTTP, Gopher, WAIS (Wide Area Information Servers) and FTP (File Transfer Protocol), with caching as a brand new feature that made it useful even to people with full internet access. HTTP/1.0, RFC 1945 of May 1996, already defined the proxy and noted its use as a client-side portal through network firewalls. The same year RFC 1928 standardized SOCKS version 5, a general framework for crossing a firewall that is not tied to HTTP: the client connects to TCP port 1080 and asks for a CONNECT, a BIND or a UDP ASSOCIATE. Squid, the best-known open-source proxy, descends from the Harvest Cache Daemon of the early 1990s (the other fork became NetApp's NetCache), was funded by a grant from the United States National Science Foundation and normally listens on port 3128.

In configuration the ports give it away. F5 notes that the common explicit proxy ports are 8080 and 3128. A FortiGate turns its explicit web proxy on under config web-proxy explicit, with 8080 as the incoming HTTP port in Fortinet's example, enables it on the interface that listens, applies config firewall proxy-policy rules to it, and can serve the Proxy Auto-Config (PAC) file itself. Netskope's Cloud Explicit Proxy steers browsers with a PAC file to a tenant proxy on port 8081, identifies the user through Security Assertion Markup Language (SAML) 2.0 and a cookie, accepts only HTTP and HTTPS, and requires the traffic to the identity provider to bypass the proxy, or the login can never complete. On a host, curl takes the proxy with -x or --proxy, treats it as an HTTP proxy unless a scheme such as socks5h says otherwise (the h asks the proxy to resolve the name), and reads the environment variables http_proxy, HTTPS_PROXY, ALL_PROXY and NO_PROXY; http_proxy is the one that exists only in lower case.

Seeing inside TLS requires the proxy to stop being a tunnel. F5's guide states the consequence precisely: in a forward proxy the remote resource owns the encryption keys, so the proxy must re-issue, in its word forge, a local copy of the server certificate, and every client must trust the local certificate authority that signs those copies. Squid describes its equivalent mode, ssl-bump, as becoming the man-in-the-middle. The practice has a measured cost. A study presented at the Network and Distributed System Security (NDSS) Symposium in 2017 by Zakir Durumeric and colleagues, using data from Mozilla, Cloudflare and e-commerce sites, found more than an order of magnitude more interception than previously estimated, and concluded that nearly all the middleboxes and client-side security products examined reduced connection security and many introduced severe vulnerabilities. The policy input is shrinking as well: TLS Encrypted Client Hello, RFC 9849 of March 2026, encrypts the server name, which it calls the most sensitive information left in clear in TLS 1.3, and notes that managed enterprises may have to disable it by group policy or intercept and decrypt instead.

Two failures recur. The first is the open proxy. Apache ships with ProxyRequests off and warns that a forward proxy must be secured before it is enabled, because otherwise any client can reach arbitrary hosts through the server while hiding its identity, which is dangerous both for the network that runs it and for the internet at large. The second is the lost client address: the origin server sees the proxy, not the user. The non-standard X-Forwarded-For field and its standard successor, the Forwarded field of RFC 7239 (June 2014), exist to disclose the original address, and the same RFC observes that a proxy whose purpose is anonymity will simply not send them. A forward proxy can therefore serve opposite goals with the same mechanics: a corporate proxy identifies and logs every user, and a privacy proxy exists so that the destination cannot.

forward-secrecy.def: A property of a key agreement protocol: if long-term keys are compromised later, the session keys of earlier sessions stay secret, so traffic recorded before the theft cannot be decrypted with the stolen key.
forward-secrecy.context: With forward secrecy, each session negotiates a fresh ephemeral key that is thrown away afterwards, so compromising the server tomorrow cannot decrypt recordings of today's traffic. TLS (Transport Layer Security) 1.3 requires it of every public-key key exchange, which is why stealing a server's private key no longer unlocks captured sessions. It does not protect recordings against a later break of the key exchange itself, the "harvest now, decrypt later" risk from quantum computers that hybrid post-quantum key exchange is meant to close.
forward-secrecy.depth:
What it is, exactly. The Internet Security Glossary, Request for Comments (RFC) 4949 of August 2007, defines perfect forward secrecy for a key agreement protocol as the property that compromise of long-term keying material does not compromise session keys previously derived from it, and admits that the area is muddled: experts did not agree, and the literature in practice defines the term by describing Diffie-Hellman-Merkle key agreement. The word "perfect" is why many documents, RFC 9325 among them, now say forward secrecy, or PFS for short. It is not post-compromise security: RFC 9846, the July 2026 text of TLS (Transport Layer Security) 1.3, stresses that it limits leakage in one direction only, so a key stolen at time T2 does not expose keys from an earlier T1, while protection after a compromise needs a fresh asymmetric key exchange. Nor does it stop a thief who holds the signing key from impersonating the server to future clients.

How it works. Each side generates a fresh Diffie-Hellman key pair for the connection, the shared secret becomes the session keys, and everything is erased when the session ends; the long-term key only signs the exchange, so stealing it later yields nothing about the traffic. RSA (Rivest-Shamir-Adleman) key transport is the opposite: the client encrypts the premaster secret under the server's public key, so whoever later obtains the private key can decrypt every recorded handshake, which RFC 10015 sums up as no forward secrecy by construction. The erasure is part of the property. The Internet Key Exchange version 2 (IKEv2) standard, RFC 7296 of October 2014, says that once a connection closes each endpoint must forget not only its keys but anything that could recompute them, and RFC 9846 adds that key shares, shared secrets and derived keys left lying around simply become new long-term keys to protect.

Where the idea came from. The term "perfect forward secrecy" is credited to C. G. Günther, in a paper given at EUROCRYPT '89 and published in 1990, and it was developed by Whitfield Diffie, Paul van Oorschot and Michael Wiener in "Authentication and authenticated key exchanges" (June 1992), the Station-to-Station paper that RFC 9846 still cites for the property. On the web it stayed optional for two decades. On 22 November 2011 Adam Langley announced that Google had made forward secrecy the default for Gmail, search, Docs and Google+ using ECDHE_RSA, chosen over finite-field Diffie-Hellman Ephemeral (DHE) for speed, warning that traffic recorded today could be decrypted once a server key was broken later. Heartbleed (Common Vulnerabilities and Exposures entry CVE-2014-0160, public on 7 April 2014) made the point concrete: it leaked server private keys, and the advisory noted that forward secrecy should protect past communications from that retrospective decryption. TLS 1.3, RFC 8446 of August 2018, removed static RSA and static Diffie-Hellman so that every public-key exchange provides it.

TLS 1.2 is where the choice is still made. There it depends on the cipher suite: names starting TLS_ECDHE_ or TLS_DHE_ use Elliptic Curve Diffie-Hellman Ephemeral (ECDHE) or finite-field DHE and are forward secret; TLS_RSA_ and the static TLS_DH_ and TLS_ECDH_ suites are not. Best current practice, RFC 9325 (November 2022), says implementations must support and prefer forward-secret suites, and RFC 10015 (July 2026) made static RSA and finite-field Diffie-Hellman, ephemeral or not, MUST NOT, which leaves ECDHE as the forward-secret exchange for TLS 1.2.

Where it leaks anyway. Performance shortcuts are the usual culprit. RFC 9325 warns that reusing Diffie-Hellman exponents, in some cases for only a few hours, lets an attacker who later reaches the host decrypt earlier connections. Session tickets in TLS 1.2 are encrypted with a server key, so it asks that ticket keys change regularly, for example weekly, that old ones be destroyed, that tickets live about half as long as their key, and that sessions older than two rotation periods not be resumed. In TLS 1.3 a resumption using only the pre-shared key (the psk_ke mode) is not forward secret, so servers should choose psk_dhe_ke and answer with a key_share; zero round-trip time (0-RTT) early data carries no forward secrecy guarantee at all; and a KeyUpdate gives forward secrecy for earlier traffic only if the old key is actually deleted.

What it changes in operations. Passive decryption with a copy of the server's key stops working. The Wireshark documentation states that an RSA private key decrypts only when the chosen suite is not (EC)DHE and the version is TLS 1.2 or older, never TLS 1.3, while a key log file written by the client or server through the SSLKEYLOGFILE variable always works; OpenSSL reads that variable directly from version 3.4. Monitoring and inspection that relied on loading server keys into a sensor therefore has to move inline, as a proxy, or obtain per-session secrets. IP Security (IPsec) has its own switch: on a FortiGate, phase 2 PFS forces a new Diffie-Hellman exchange whenever the key lifetime expires, Diffie-Hellman groups 1, 2, 5 and 14 to 32 are offered and Fortinet recommends 15 to 21 and 28 to 32, mirroring the optional Diffie-Hellman exchange IKEv2 allows when it creates each child security association.

The limit worth knowing. Forward secrecy protects recordings against theft of long-term keys, not against a break of the key exchange itself. RFC 9954 (July 2026) describes retroactive decryption, also known as harvest-now-decrypt-later: if a cryptographic assumption falls to a quantum computer or another breakthrough, anyone who recorded handshakes and traffic can decrypt them. RFC 10024 (August 2026) is blunt that a passive observer with a cryptographically relevant quantum computer can recover the ephemeral scalar of an elliptic curve Diffie-Hellman exchange, which is why it defines hybrid groups such as X25519MLKEM768 that combine ECDHE with the post-quantum ML-KEM (Module-Lattice-Based Key Encapsulation Mechanism). Authentication is different: a signature cannot be broken retroactively, so the urgency sits with key exchange.

Numbers and neighbours. TLS 1.3 has been forward secret for every public-key exchange since August 2018; RFC 9325 suggests rotating ticket keys about weekly; a passive Wireshark capture with an RSA key works only for TLS 1.2 or older without (EC)DHE. Ephemeral keys are the mechanism, ECDHE the usual implementation, the cipher suite the place TLS 1.2 shows whether it is present, and post-quantum hybrid key exchange the next step for traffic that must stay confidential for years.

fubar.def: Slang for something broken beyond any reasonable repair.
fubar.context: "Fouled Up Beyond All Recognition" is the WWII sibling of SNAFU, and one of the threads RFC 3092 follows to explain where "foobar" in code came from. In practice it labels the state past which you stop patching and start over.
fubar.depth:
FUBAR is Second World War military slang, expanded politely as fouled up beyond all recognition, and it names a state past repair rather than a state of difficulty. It arrived in technical use alongside SNAFU, and the pair mark two genuinely different positions on a scale.

The distinction is operationally useful. SNAFU is the chronic condition: things are broken, everyone knows, work continues. FUBAR is the judgement that repair is no longer the right strategy, and that continuing to fix is spending effort on something that should be replaced. Recognizing which one you are in changes what you should do next, and teams frequently keep repairing long past the point where the answer was rebuild.

That the vocabulary comes from soldiers is fitting rather than incidental. Both terms encode a particular relationship with institutional failure: clear-eyed about it, unable to fix it from below, and coping through naming it precisely. Anyone who has worked in a large technical organization recognizes the posture immediately, which is why terms invented for a war have outlived every machine they were first applied to.

gdpr.def: The General Data Protection Regulation, Regulation 2016/679 of the European Union: the general law on processing personal data in the Union and the wider European Economic Area, in force since 24 May 2016 and applicable since 25 May 2018, which also reaches organizations outside Europe that target or monitor people in the Union.
gdpr.context: The General Data Protection Regulation (GDPR) sets the rules for handling personal data: a lawful basis for every processing operation (consent is one of six), purpose limits, rights of access, correction, erasure and portability, security duties and a 72-hour clock for notifying breaches, with fines of up to 20 million euros or 4% of worldwide annual turnover. It applies to any organization established in the European Union (EU) and to organizations elsewhere that offer goods or services to, or monitor the behaviour of, people who are in the Union, which is why companies with no European office found themselves in scope. Brazil's LGPD (Lei Geral de Proteção de Dados Pessoais) is closely modelled on it, and since January 2026 the European Commission and Brazil recognize each other's protection as adequate.
gdpr.depth:
What it is. The General Data Protection Regulation (GDPR) is Regulation 2016/679 of the European Union (EU), adopted by the European Parliament and the Council on 27 April 2016, published in the Official Journal on 4 May 2016, in force since 24 May 2016 and applicable since 25 May 2018, the day it repealed the Data Protection Directive adopted in 1995 by the European Community (EC), 95/46/EC. Being a regulation, it is one law for the whole Union rather than a set of national transpositions, which is the point the European Commission makes for it: a single text in place of fragmented national systems. It has been incorporated into the European Economic Area (EEA) Agreement, so it also applies in Norway, Iceland and Liechtenstein. It is one of three instruments that implement the right to data protection in Article 8 of the Charter of Fundamental Rights: the Law Enforcement Directive (LED), 2016/680, covers processing by police and criminal justice authorities, and Regulation 2018/1725 covers the Union's own institutions. The GDPR is the one that reaches companies, and its influence comes as much from that reach as from its content.

Who is in scope. Article 3 sets two tests. The first is establishment: the Regulation applies to processing in the context of the activities of an establishment of a controller or processor in the Union, regardless of whether the processing itself takes place there, so a European subsidiary cannot escape it by running its database in another continent. The second is targeting: a controller or processor with no establishment in the Union is covered when it offers goods or services to data subjects who are in the Union, whether or not they pay, or monitors their behaviour as far as it takes place there. The criterion is presence in the Union, not citizenship or residence. Companies with no European office therefore found themselves in scope, and many chose to apply the European rules everywhere rather than run two systems.

The vocabulary that reaches a system. Personal data, in Article 4, is any information relating to an identified or identifiable natural person, and the definition names location data and an online identifier among the identifiers, which is why access logs, device identifiers and telemetry are usually in scope.
