PKCE was designed against the authorization code interception attack on public clients, for example through communication between apps on the same device: the client invents a code_verifier of 43 to 128 characters, sends its SHA-256 (Secure Hash Algorithm) hash, base64url-encoded, as the code_challenge with method S256, and must present the verifier when it redeems the code. RFC 9700 now requires PKCE for public clients, recommends it for confidential ones and requires every authorization server to support it. Client credentials, usable only by confidential clients, is for machine-to-machine work with no user present; the device grant serves smart TVs, consoles and printers that lack a browser or a keyboard. The implicit grant, which returned the access token directly from the authorization endpoint in the URL fragment, should not be used: such tokens leak through Referer headers, browser history and logs, can be replayed, and cannot be bound to the client. The resource owner password credentials grant must not be used at all, because it hands the user's password to the client.

RFC 9700 adds the rules learned from real attacks: redirect URIs compared by exact string match, except for loopback ports in native apps; refresh tokens for public clients bound to the sender or rotated on every use; access tokens sender-constrained with mutual TLS or DPoP, so a stolen token is useless without the client's key; no open redirectors; and defences against mix-up attacks, in which a client talking to several authorization servers is tricked into sending a code or token meant for an honest server to one the attacker controls. Native apps must send the user to an external user-agent, normally the system browser, and never to an embedded one (RFC 8252), so the app never sees the password typed into the authorization server.

Tokens are credentials, and they are stolen like credentials. On 15 April 2022 GitHub reported that an attacker had used stolen OAuth user tokens issued to two integrators, Heroku and Travis CI, to download private repositories from dozens of organizations including npm, an investigation that began on 12 April; GitHub said the tokens were not obtained through any compromise of GitHub itself. Bearer tokens held by a third party are exactly the asset OAuth creates, which is why lifetimes, scopes and revocation per application matter. Most OAuth vulnerabilities are not flaws in the specification but the wrong flow, or a missing check, used confidently.

In infrastructure the same roles appear in products. F5 BIG-IP Access Policy Manager (APM) can act as an OAuth 2.0 client and resource server, relying on an external authorization server such as a social or enterprise provider, or as the authorization server itself, issuing authorization codes, access tokens and refresh tokens and answering token introspection; doing both needs two virtual servers with separate host names. Numbers worth remembering: RFC 6749 and 6750 (October 2012), a code lifetime of 10 minutes at most, verifiers of 43 to 128 characters, S256 as the only acceptable PKCE method, and RFC 9700 (January 2025) as the current rulebook.

observability.def: How well you can understand what a system is doing internally from the signals it emits: a property borrowed from control theory, where a system is observable if its internal state can be inferred from its outputs.
observability.context: Often summarized as logs, metrics and traces, observability is about being able to ask new questions of a running system without shipping new code, especially when something breaks in a way nobody anticipated. The idea comes from Rudolf Kálmán's control theory work of 1960, where a system is observable if its internal state can be worked out from its outputs; software borrowed the word for systems instrumented well enough that the answer to a novel question is already in the telemetry. It is what turns a mystery outage into a diagnosable one, and OpenTelemetry, a Cloud Native Computing Foundation (CNCF) project since 2019, is now the common way to produce the signals.
observability.depth:
The word is older than software operations. In control theory, observability is a measure of how well the internal states of a system can be inferred from knowledge of its external outputs, a concept introduced by the Hungarian-American engineer Rudolf E. Kálmán (1930 to 2016) for linear dynamic systems, in his paper On the General Theory of Control Systems, published in 1960 in the first volume of the proceedings of the International Federation of Automatic Control, and developed in his Mathematical Description of Linear Dynamical Systems of 1963. For a linear system observability and controllability are mathematical duals, and Kálmán's name is attached to the Kalman filter, a state observer that estimates what cannot be measured from what can. University lecture notes state the property in a sentence: some states are observable if they can be determined unambiguously from input and output measurements. For a linear time-invariant system the test is algebraic: stack the output matrix C on C times A, C times A squared and so on up to the power n minus one, and the system is observable exactly when that observability matrix has rank n, the number of states. The notes' own example is a reactor whose input is the rod position, whose output is power and one of whose states is the rod temperature: if the temperature cannot be recovered from the power, the plant is not observable, and the cure is to add a sensor. That is the whole software meaning in miniature: when you cannot work out what a system is doing from what it emits, you instrument it.

The software sense keeps the idea and widens it. The OpenTelemetry project's primer says observability lets you understand a system from the outside by letting you ask questions about it without knowing its inner workings, that it lets you handle novel problems, the unknown unknowns, and answer why something is happening, and that this requires the application to be properly instrumented, emitting traces, metrics and logs, to the point where developers do not need to add more instrumentation to troubleshoot an issue. Monitoring is the narrower, older practice. Google's site reliability engineering (SRE) book defines it as collecting, processing, aggregating and displaying real-time quantitative data about a system, distinguishes white-box monitoring, built on metrics the internals expose, from black-box monitoring, which tests externally visible behaviour as a user would, and names the four golden signals for a user-facing system: latency, traffic, errors and saturation. Monitoring tells you that a known thing broke; observability is about being able to investigate the thing nobody predicted, which is the situation every real incident presents. The same chapter adds a point that applies to any layered network: one person's symptom is another person's cause, so slow database reads are a symptom for the database team and a cause for the people running the website in front of it.

The three signals are conventional and complementary, and OpenTelemetry describes each. Metrics are aggregations of numeric data over a period, such as error rate, processor utilization or request rate; they are cheap and good at showing that something changed. Logs are timestamped messages emitted by services and components, not necessarily tied to any request; they carry detail and context but cost storage, are hard to query at scale, and become far more useful when correlated with a trace and a span. Traces record the path a single request takes through multiple services: a trace is made of spans, each a single unit of work with a name, timing data and attributes, and the first is the root span that represents the request from start to finish. Tracing is the only practical way to find where latency actually accumulates in a distributed system. Each answers a question the others answer badly. OpenTelemetry also carries baggage, contextual data passed between signals, and lists events and profiles, a record of resource use at the code level, as under development. Service level indicators (SLIs) and objectives (SLOs) sit on top: a good indicator measures the service from the user's side, such as how fast a page loads.

OpenTelemetry has become the common plumbing. It describes itself as an observability framework and toolkit for generating, exporting and collecting telemetry, open source and vendor- and tool-agnostic so that the same instrumentation can feed open-source backends such as Jaeger and Prometheus or commercial ones, and explicitly not an observability backend itself: storage and visualization are left to other tools. It was formed by merging two earlier projects, OpenTracing and OpenCensus, which had been trying separately to solve the lack of a standard for instrumenting code and sending telemetry. The Cloud Native Computing Foundation (CNCF) accepted it on 7 May 2019, moved it to the Incubating maturity level on 26 August 2021 and to Graduated on 11 May 2026. Underneath, the World Wide Web Consortium (W3C) Trace Context Recommendation of 23 November 2021 standardizes how a request carries its identity between vendors: a traceparent header holding a 16-byte trace identifier for the whole trace and an 8-byte parent identifier for the calling span, with all-zero values forbidden.

Network and application delivery gear now speaks the same language. F5's BIG-IP Telemetry Streaming added an OpenTelemetry Exporter consumer, experimental in version 1.23 and supported from 1.27, which sends BIG-IP telemetry to an OpenTelemetry Collector or any application programming interface (API) that speaks the OpenTelemetry Protocol (OTLP), so load balancer statistics can land in the same backend as the application's own traces. The older network signals map onto the same three families: interface counters polled over the Simple Network Management Protocol (SNMP) are metrics, syslog is logs, and flow records are the network's closest equivalent of request-level detail, although without a trace identifier they cannot be joined to an application request. A load balancer or proxy in the request path is also where trace context is most often lost or mangled, which is worth checking before blaming the tracing backend.

The failure mode is collecting all three and understanding none. High cardinality is the usual technical cause: Prometheus warns that every unique combination of label key-value pairs represents a new time series, and tells users not to put high-cardinality dimensions such as user identifiers, email addresses or other unbounded sets into labels, because a label with unbounded values multiplies series until the system storing them becomes the outage. The organizational cause is instrumenting comprehensively rather than deliberately, which produces dashboards nobody reads and bills nobody expected. Observability also costs people: Google's SRE book notes that even with shared infrastructure, a team of 10 to 12 engineers typically has one or two members whose main job is building and maintaining the monitoring for their service. Instrumenting for the questions actually asked during incidents produces less data and more answers, and Kálmán's test still applies: if the state you need cannot be reconstructed from what the system emits, more dashboards will not help; another sensor will.

off-by-one.def: The classic error of counting one too many or one too few, especially at the boundaries of a loop or range.
off-by-one.context: Also called a fencepost error (ten posts hold nine panels, not ten), it is the bug that lives at < versus <=, or at the first and last element. It is so common it is practically a rite of passage, which is why boundary cases get their own tests.
off-by-one.depth:
The off-by-one error is the bug that lives at less-than versus less-than-or-equal, at the first index and the last, at the boundary rather than in the logic. It is also called a fencepost error, from the observation that ten fence posts hold nine panels, which is the same confusion in a form people find intuitive.

Its persistence is not carelessness, it is that boundaries are genuinely where the mental model is thinnest. The middle of a loop is easy to reason about because it is the same every time; the beginning and end are special cases that require holding a slightly different picture, and every conversion between zero-based and one-based counting is an opportunity to hold the wrong one.

The security dimension is why it matters beyond correctness. A buffer written one byte past its end is a classic memory corruption primitive, and a bounds check that uses the wrong comparison is a vulnerability rather than a nuisance. That is why the defences are structural rather than attentional: languages with bounds checking, iterators that make the boundary implicit, and tests written specifically for the empty case, the single element, and the exact limit.

onion-routing.def: A privacy technique that wraps traffic in layers of encryption and bounces it through several relays.
onion-routing.context: Each relay peels one layer and learns only the next hop, so no single node knows both who you are and where you are going, the idea behind Tor. It is legitimate privacy technology used by journalists, activists, and ordinary people; the "dark web" is one use among many.
onion-routing.depth:
Onion routing hides who is talking to whom by wrapping a message in layers of encryption, one per relay in the path. Each relay peels its own layer, learns only the previous and next hop, and forwards. No single relay ever knows both the origin and the destination, which is the entire design goal.

The property this buys is unlinkability rather than secrecy of content. The first relay knows who you are but not where you are going; the last knows the destination but not who asked. That separation only holds while the relays are independent, which is why an adversary who can observe both ends of a circuit, or who runs enough relays, can correlate timing and volume to defeat it. Traffic analysis, not cryptanalysis, is the realistic attack.

The practical consequences are usually misunderstood. The exit relay sees whatever the destination sees, so unencrypted traffic leaving the network is readable by whoever runs that exit. Latency is a design consequence rather than a defect, since traffic takes a deliberately indirect path. And the technology itself is neutral: it is used by journalists, people under censorship, and criminals alike, which is why discussing it accurately matters more than discussing it approvingly or disapprovingly.

opsec.def: The discipline of protecting the small pieces of information that together reveal too much.
opsec.context: Operations security is about controlling metadata and habits, not just secrets: a username reused, a timestamp, a photo's location. A single item is harmless; the aggregate deanonymizes. For defenders and researchers alike, good OPSEC is mostly consistency.

owasp.def: The Open Worldwide Application Security Project (OWASP): a non-profit foundation and open community, launched in 2001, that produces free application security standards, guidance and tools, best known for the OWASP Top 10.
owasp.context: The Open Worldwide Application Security Project (OWASP) is best known for the OWASP Top 10, its periodically updated awareness list of the most critical web application security risks, but it also publishes the Application Security Verification Standard, the cheat sheets and a long list of tools. It is a common reference point when deciding what a WAF (web application firewall) policy, a penetration test or a secure-coding review should cover, and a frequent shorthand in contracts and audits, which is where its awareness lists are most often stretched beyond their purpose.
owasp.depth:
The Open Worldwide Application Security Project (OWASP) describes itself as a 501(c)(3) nonprofit foundation that works to improve the security of software. Its own history dates the project's launch to 1 December 2001 and its incorporation as the OWASP Foundation, Inc., a United States nonprofit, to 21 April 2004; secondary accounts credit Mark Curphey with starting it. The foundation elected its first board in 2011 and today counts more than 250 chapters, more than 100,000 community members and more than 275 active projects, all of them, with its documents and forums, free and open to anyone. The name changed in 2023: the W used to stand for Web, and in February 2023 the board voted to make it Worldwide, a recognition that its work had long since spread beyond web applications to APIs (application programming interfaces), mobile, supply chains and, from 2025, a flagship project on the security of generative artificial intelligence (AI), the Gen AI Security Project, which grew out of its Top 10 list for large language model applications.

OWASP is the open community behind the Top 10, the Application Security Verification Standard (ASVS), the testing guide, the cheat sheets and a long list of tools. The Top 10 is the piece everyone knows and the piece most often misused. OWASP calls it a standard awareness document for developers and web application security, representing a broad consensus about the most critical risks to web applications. It was started in 2003 as a starting point for secure development, and its own maintainers write that it has grown into a pseudo standard used as a baseline for compliance, education and vendor tools. It is an awareness document describing the categories most commonly found, not a checklist that constitutes a security programme when completed.

The 2025 edition, the eighth according to heise's review, was presented as a first release candidate at OWASP's Global AppSec USA conference, held in Washington, D.C., in the first week of November 2025, and the project page now lists it as the current version, with 2021 and 2017 before it. It reads: A01 Broken Access Control, A02 Security Misconfiguration, A03 Software Supply Chain Failures, A04 Cryptographic Failures, A05 Injection, A06 Insecure Design, A07 Authentication Failures, A08 Software or Data Integrity Failures, A09 Security Logging and Alerting Failures, and A10 Mishandling of Exceptional Conditions. The changes say a lot about the decade. Server-side request forgery (SSRF), its own category A10 in 2021, has been folded into Broken Access Control, which stays first with 40 mapped CWEs (Common Weakness Enumerations) found on average in 3.73 per cent of tested applications. Security Misconfiguration climbs from fifth to second because more application behaviour now lives in configuration. Software Supply Chain Failures widens the old Vulnerable and Outdated Components to the whole build and distribution chain and was overwhelmingly voted a top concern by practitioners even though it is hard to see in test data. Injection, which until 2017 led the list, falls to fifth, outside the top three for the first time in the list's history.

How the list is made explains how it should be read. The 2025 data covered more than 2.8 million applications and 589 distinct CWEs, against about 30 in 2017 and almost 400 in 2021; the team grouped 248 of them into ten root-cause categories, capped at 40 each. It counts prevalence, the share of applications with at least one instance, and deliberately ignores frequency, because automated scanners report every instance while manual testers report a flaw once. Exploit and impact weights come from the CVSS (Common Vulnerability Scoring System) scores of about 220,000 CVEs (Common Vulnerabilities and Exposures) mapped to CWEs. And two of the ten places are not from data at all: the authors call the list data-informed but not blindly data-driven, because test data looks at the past, so the community survey promotes risks that tools cannot yet measure, as it did for SSRF in 2021. The 2017 edition rested on 23 contributors covering about 114,000 applications plus a survey of more than 500 people. Anyone whose security requirements are literally the Top 10 has adopted a list of what other people found rather than an analysis of what they themselves are exposed to.

The more useful artefacts are the less famous ones. The ASVS exists, in the project's words, to normalize the coverage and level of rigour of web application security verification with a commercially workable open standard, and it names three uses: as a metric for how far an application can be trusted, as guidance for the people building security controls, and in procurement, as a basis for verification requirements written into contracts. Its requirements are graded and testable and carry stable identifiers; the current version, 5.0.0, was published on 30 May 2025, and OWASP asks that references include the version, as in v5.0.0-1.2.5, the requirement that operating system calls be protected against command injection. The cheat sheets answer specific implementation questions with current guidance rather than folklore; the server-side request forgery prevention sheet, with its split between allowlistable and arbitrary destinations, is a good example of the genre.

OWASP's tools have a history of outgrowing it. ZAP, the web application scanner Simon Bennetts launched in 2010 and soon brought into OWASP, became one of its best-known projects. On 1 August 2023 Bennetts announced that ZAP was joining the Linux Foundation's new Software Security Project as a founding project, which would pay him and Ricardo Pereira to work on it full time; since a project can only be in one foundation, ZAP left OWASP, and he wrote that OWASP had struggled to support and invest in big projects. OWASP's own blog, on 2 August 2023, congratulated the core team, Rick Mitchell included, and noted that ZAP had been part of OWASP for thirteen-odd years. ZAP's own pages date the departure to August 2023 on one page and September 2023 on another. On 24 September 2024 ZAP announced that Checkmarx would employ all three project leaders and that the scanner would be known as ZAP by Checkmarx, still controlled by the ZAP Core Team, open source and licensed under Apache 2.0; it now says it is not part of any foundation, and that any reference to OWASP ZAP is out of date. The episode is a useful caution for anyone choosing tools by the OWASP label: the foundation hosts and promotes projects, but their funding and their maintainers are their own.

path-mtu-discovery.def: How a sender finds the smallest MTU along the whole route, not just the first hop: packets go out marked Don't Fragment and shrink when an ICMP Fragmentation Needed reply comes back, which over-filtered networks silently break.
path-mtu-discovery.context: PMTUD (RFC 1191) probes the path and shrinks packets to fit its narrowest link, avoiding fragmentation end to end. When firewalls block the ICMP messages it relies on, it fails silently: the classic MTU black hole, where a connection opens but hangs on large transfers.
path-mtu-discovery.depth:
Path MTU discovery finds the largest packet a path will carry by sending packets marked do-not-fragment and listening for the ICMP message that reports one was too big. The mechanism is correct and it fails constantly, because those ICMP messages are widely blocked by firewalls configured on the belief that ICMP is dangerous.

When the report never arrives the sender learns nothing and keeps retransmitting the same oversized packet, which produces the classic symptom: the connection establishes, small requests succeed, and anything large hangs indefinitely. That is why MSS clamping exists as standard practice on tunnels, and why blocking ICMP wholesale is one of the most common self-inflicted network faults.

IPv6 makes this more consequential because routers do not fragment, so the sender must get this right or the packet simply does not arrive. That is why blocking ICMPv6 breaks IPv6 far more thoroughly than blocking ICMP breaks IPv4, and why the standard advice to permit the packet-too-big message is not a suggestion. MSS clamping remains the practical workaround where the path cannot be fixed.

payload.def: The part of a message, or of an attack, that carries what matters. In networking it is the data a protocol unit carries after its headers; in offensive security it is the code that runs on the target once an exploit has opened the way.
payload.context: If the exploit is how you get in, the payload is what you do next: run a shell, install a beacon, encrypt files. The same word appears benignly in networking for the data portion of a packet; context tells you which meaning is in play.
payload.depth:
One idea, two trades. The NIST (National Institute of Standards and Technology) glossary records both readings in its own documents: in SP (Special Publication) 800-113 the payload is the information passed down from the previous layer, and in SP 800-38C it is the input to the CCM mode (Counter with Cipher Block Chaining-Message Authentication Code) that is both authenticated and encrypted. What unites them, and the attacker's sense too, is the cargo as opposed to the vehicle: the headers, the framing or the exploit exist to deliver it.

Payload in packets. Encapsulation makes each layer's payload the next layer's whole unit. RFC (Request for Comments) 894 (April 1984) puts the IP (Internet Protocol) header and data in the Ethernet data field, with a minimum of 46 octets, padded with zeros that are not part of the IP packet, and a maximum IP datagram of 1500 octets. The IPv4 header is at least five 32-bit words, 20 octets (RFC 791, September 1981), and so is the TCP (Transmission Control Protocol) header, which is why RFC 8200 computes the TCP maximum segment size (MSS) as the maximum packet size minus 40 octets over IPv4 and minus 60 over IPv6: 1460 and 1440 bytes of payload in a 1500-byte packet. Without an MSS option a TCP sender must assume 536 bytes for IPv4 and 1220 for IPv6 (RFC 9293). The IPv6 Payload Length field is a 16-bit count of everything after the fixed header, extension headers included, so in IPv6 payload means the rest of the packet, not only the transport data.

Payload in tokens and ciphers. In JSON Web Signature (JWS, JSON being JavaScript Object Notation), RFC 7515 (May 2015), the JWS Payload is the sequence of octets to be secured, also called the message; a JSON Web Token (JWT), RFC 7519 of the same month, carries its claims set there. JWS secures content with signatures or MACs (message authentication codes) and serializes the payload as base64url, so anyone holding a signed token can read its claims; confidentiality needs the separate JSON Web Encryption (JWE) specification. In authenticated encryption modes such as CCM, by contrast, the payload is the part that is encrypted as well as authenticated.

Payload in attacks. The exploit and the payload are separate pieces of work, and Metasploit's documentation shows the separation clearly. Singles are fire-and-forget, useful when the target has no network access, as with a file-format exploit delivered on a removable drive. Stagers are small stubs that set up communication and pass execution to the next stage, which solves two problems: size limits in the exploit, and the coupling of a payload to one transport. Stages, loaded by the stager into memory it allocated, can be arbitrarily large and written in a language such as C. Names spell out the pieces, as in windows/x64/meterpreter/reverse_tcp: platform, architecture, the Meterpreter stage and the reverse TCP stager, with the connect-back address and port embedded in the stager.

Where the archetype came from. In Phrack 49, dated 8 November 1996, Aleph One's Smashing The Stack For Fun And Profit asked what to run once the return address had been overwritten, and answered that in most cases the attacker wants the program to spawn a shell, placing that code in the very buffer being overflowed. The term shellcode, for a payload whose original job was to start a shell, comes from that pattern; payloads in current tooling go further and load an agent such as the Meterpreter stage, a beacon to a command-and-control server or an encryption routine.

Payloads and defenders. Detection mostly reads payloads: Suricata's payload keywords inspect the content of the payload of a packet or stream, and its content keyword matches raw bytes, any of the 256 values. Encryption hides that content from network sensors, which is why devices such as a FortiGate in deep inspection mode decrypt, inspect and re-encrypt traffic. Web application firewall logs record attack payloads too, and reading them answers the first incident question: what was the attacker trying to make the server do. Two habits help: decode before judging, because payloads arrive percent-encoded, base64-encoded or compressed; and remember that a blocked payload says nothing about whether a different one, through the same flaw, was let through.

pentest.def: An authorized simulated attack that finds weaknesses before a real attacker does.
pentest.context: A penetration test is offensive security with permission: a scoped, sanctioned attempt to breach a system so the findings can be fixed. Distinct from a vulnerability scan, it chains weaknesses the way an adversary would, and ends in a report, not a compromise.

pepper.def: A secret value added alongside the salt when hashing passwords.
pepper.context: Where the salt is unique but stored with the hash, a pepper is a single secret kept apart, in code or an HSM (hardware security module), so that a stolen database alone is not enough to attack the hashes. It is defence in depth layered on top of salting.

phishing.def: Tricking someone, usually by email, text message, phone call or a counterfeit website, into revealing credentials or other sensitive data, approving a payment, or running malware, by impersonating a person or organization they trust.
phishing.context: Phishing weaponizes trust rather than code: a message that looks legitimate lures the target into clicking, logging in, or paying. "Spear phishing" is tailored to one person; "whaling" targets executives. It remains one of the most reliable ways in, because it attacks the human, not the firewall.
phishing.depth:
NIST (National Institute of Standards and Technology) defines phishing as a technique for acquiring sensitive data through a fraudulent solicitation by email or on a website, in which the perpetrator masquerades as a legitimate business or reputable person; SP (Special Publication) 800-63B-4, which once called it verifier impersonation, adds that it does not matter how the victim reached the impostor, by email or by a search result. The Anti-Phishing Working Group (APWG) adds the second half that the word now covers: social engineering that leads people to counterfeit sites, and technical subterfuge that plants malware to steal credentials directly. Merriam-Webster dates the word to 1996, a respelling of fishing with the ph probably taken from phreaking, the older abuse of the telephone network. Phishing persists because it attacks the person rather than the system, and no patch closes that; the defence has to work on a tired human at the end of a long day, not on a well-rested one reading a security bulletin.

The variants are named by target and channel. Mass phishing goes to millions of inboxes; spear phishing, in the UK National Cyber Security Centre's (NCSC) words, uses information about the company or the employee, much of it from the organization's own website and social media, to make the message persuasive; whaling is spear phishing aimed at a big phish, such as a board member with access to valuable assets. Smishing arrives by SMS (Short Message Service), vishing by voice call, and APWG has tracked millions of emails a day carrying QR (Quick Response) codes that lead to phishing sites. Business email compromise (BEC) skips malware entirely: the attacker impersonates an executive, a supplier or a colleague and simply asks for a payment to be redirected, which no attachment scanner will catch, because nothing in the message is malicious except its intent.

The scale is measured two ways, and both are large. APWG counts unique phishing sites reported by its members and the public: 1,069,681 in the second quarter of 2026, up 10.1 per cent from 971,181 in the first, with 425,808 in June alone, the highest monthly figure since April 2023, and SaaS (software as a service) and webmail the most attacked sector at 29.1 per cent. The FBI's (Federal Bureau of Investigation) Internet Crime Complaint Center (IC3) counts victim reports: in 2025 phishing and spoofing was again the most reported crime type, with 191,561 complaints (193,407 in 2024, 298,878 in 2023), yet only $215.8 million in losses was booked under that heading, because phishing is the way in and the money is lost under other names. BEC alone accounted for 24,768 complaints and $3,046,598,558 in losses, out of $20.877 billion across 1,008,597 complaints.

The sophistication has moved well past bad grammar. Targeted messages reference real projects and real colleagues and arrive at plausible moments, and the IC3 report describes chat generators producing official-sounding emails that mimic a chief executive, and voice cloning used to request wire payments; it logged 22,364 complaints involving artificial intelligence (AI), with $893 million in losses, more than $30 million of it in BEC. APWG's BEC data for the second quarter of 2026 shows the average wire-transfer request at $61,732, up 45 per cent in a quarter, with one group using fake invoices and a spoofed reply chain between a supplier and an executive to lend the request credibility. Channels are shifting as well: APWG recorded smishing up 40 per cent and vishing up 20 per cent between the first and second quarters of 2026.

Multi-factor authentication (MFA) raised the bar without ending credential phishing. In July 2022 Microsoft described an adversary-in-the-middle (AiTM) campaign that had targeted more than 10,000 organizations since September 2021: a proxy built from open-source kits such as Evilginx2 relayed the real sign-in page, captured the password and the session cookie, and replayed the cookie, so the second factor was bypassed rather than broken. NIST draws the line precisely in SP 800-63B-4: authenticators whose output the user types, one-time passwords and out-of-band codes, are not phishing-resistant because the typed value is not bound to the session, and approval-only push prompts are no longer acceptable because of authentication fatigue attacks. Phishing resistance requires cryptographic authentication with channel binding, as in client-authenticated TLS (Transport Layer Security) used by PIV (Personal Identity Verification) cards, or verifier name binding, as in WebAuthn (Web Authentication) with FIDO2 (Fast Identity Online 2) authenticators, which choose their secret by the authenticated domain name and so will not sign in to a lookalike domain however convinced the user is.

Mail authentication protects your own domain name and not much more. DMARC (Domain-based Message Authentication, Reporting, and Conformance) lets the owner of the domain in the From field publish what receivers should do with mail that fails SPF (Sender Policy Framework) and DKIM (DomainKeys Identified Mail) alignment and request reports; first published as Informational RFC (Request for Comments) 7489 in March 2015, it became a Standards Track protocol in RFC 9989 in May 2026. The NCSC recommends it because it stops phishers spoofing your exact domain, and asks receivers to honour senders' quarantine and reject policies. Its own scope statement lists what it does not do: display-name attacks, where a trusted name sits in front of an unrelated address, and anything about a lookalike domain registered by the attacker, which authenticates perfectly well as itself.

The defences that work reduce what a successful attempt achieves rather than trying to make people infallible. The NCSC splits them into four layers: make it hard for mail to reach users, help users identify and report it, protect the organization from the effects of what gets through, and respond quickly. It states that no training package, phishing simulations included, can teach users to spot every phish, that punishing people for clicking on simulated emails starts to resemble entrapment, and that the useful metric is how many reported a phish, not only how many clicked. Process controls carry much of the weight against BEC: important requests, payment changes above all, should be verified through a second channel such as a phone call to a known number. A reporting culture in which people are thanked for flagging rather than blamed for clicking turns staff into an early-warning system, since punishment produces silence rather than safety.

Neighbouring terms differ in method. Social engineering is the parent category; pretexting builds a false story, often by phone; typosquatting registers the lookalike domains that phishing links point at; credential stuffing replays passwords already leaked elsewhere and needs no lure at all; AiTM is the relay technique that defeats non-phishing-resistant MFA.

pii.def: Any data that can identify a specific person, on its own or combined with other data.
pii.context: Personally Identifiable Information covers the obvious (name, national ID) and the combinable (a birth date plus a postcode). Regulations like GDPR are built around protecting it, and data minimization is the discipline of not collecting what you do not need.

pki.def: The certification authorities, policies, software and procedures that issue, distribute, validate and revoke public key certificates, so that a stranger's public key can be trusted to belong to the name written on it.
pki.context: Public key infrastructure (PKI) answers the question "is this key really theirs?" by having a trusted certification authority (CA) sign a certificate that binds a public key to a name. Whoever relies on the certificate checks the signature, the dates and the revocation status, and follows the chain of issuers up to a trust anchor it already holds. It is the chain of trust behind the padlock in a browser and the machinery that makes Transport Layer Security (TLS) usable at internet scale. The same machinery, run privately, issues the certificates behind virtual private networks (VPNs), Wi-Fi authentication, smart cards and service-to-service mutual TLS.
pki.depth:
A public key infrastructure (PKI) answers a question that cryptography alone cannot settle: a signature can prove that someone controls a private key, but not that the key belongs to the organization named beside it. PKI supplies that binding through certificates issued by authorities whose own keys are already trusted, so trust becomes transitive rather than personal. The United States National Institute of Standards and Technology (NIST) defines it as a framework established to issue, maintain and revoke public key certificates. The Internet Security Glossary, Request for Comments (RFC) 4949, calls it a system of certification authorities, optionally with registration authorities and other supporting servers, that performs certificate, archive, key and token management for a community of users. Both definitions make the same point: PKI is not an algorithm or a file format but an organization with procedures, and a certificate says who was vouched for, never that the holder behaves well.

The model assumed by the Internet Engineering Task Force (IETF) in RFC 5280, of May 2008, has five kinds of component. An end entity is the user or system named as the subject of a certificate. A certification authority (CA), the standards' term for what most people call a certificate authority, signs certificates. A registration authority (RA) is an optional system to which a CA delegates management functions. A CRL issuer generates and signs certificate revocation lists (CRLs), and a repository stores certificates and CRLs and distributes them. Two documents described in RFC 3647 surround them: the certificate policy (CP), a named set of rules that says which community and class of application a certificate suits, and the certification practice statement (CPS), the CA's own account of how it issues, manages, revokes and renews. In the usual hierarchy a root CA certifies subordinate CAs, often called intermediates, and those issue to end entities; the rules for public CAs require the CA's private key to live in a hardware module validated to level 3 of Federal Information Processing Standards (FIPS) 140-2 or 140-3, or to an equivalent Common Criteria evaluation.

Whoever relies on a certificate validates a certification path: the end-entity certificate signed by one CA, then zero or more CA certificates signed by other CAs, ending at a trust anchor already held. For each certificate RFC 5280 requires a valid signature under the issuer's key, a current validity period, a status of not revoked and an issuer name that matches the certificate above. Extensions restrain what a CA may do. The cA boolean in basic constraints says whether a key may verify certificate signatures at all, pathLenConstraint caps how many intermediate CA certificates may follow, and name constraints fence the names a subordinate may certify. The standard states that the selection of a trust anchor is a matter of policy, and that is the whole difference between a public and a private PKI: the mathematics is identical, the list of anchors is not. On the command line, openssl verify checks a chain against chosen anchors, while openssl s_client with the -showcerts option only prints what a server sent, which its documentation warns is not a verified chain.

The idea is older than the web. In November 1976 Whitfield Diffie and Martin Hellman proposed placing each user's enciphering key in a public directory beside a name and address, and noted that this public file had to be protected from unauthorized modification. In 1978 Loren Kohnfelder's bachelor's thesis at the Massachusetts Institute of Technology (MIT), Towards a Practical Public-Key Cryptosystem, supervised by Leonard Adleman, first described digital certificates and, by his own account, the foundations of PKI. The format came from the International Telecommunication Union (ITU): X.509 was first published in 1988 as the authentication framework of the X.500 directory (version 1), was revised in 1993 (version 2) and gained extensions in version 3, completed in June 1996; the edition in force dates from October 2019. The first internet design, Privacy-Enhanced Mail (PEM) in RFC 1422 of 1993, prescribed one rigid hierarchy under an Internet Policy Registration Authority, and RFC 5280 records that the attempts to deploy it showed the first two certificate versions to be deficient. The internet profile followed as RFC 2459 (January 1999), RFC 3280 (April 2002) and RFC 5280, still the reference.

The trust store is where this gets uncomfortable. A browser and an operating system ship with a list of root authorities the user did not choose, an arrangement RFC 4949 calls a trust-file PKI, and any authority on the list can issue a certificate for any name. The rules those authorities follow are the Baseline Requirements of the CA/Browser Forum, where certificate issuers vote beside four certificate consumers: Apple, Google, Microsoft and Mozilla. That is a large amount of delegated trust, and the history includes authorities that were compromised, careless or coerced. In 2011 an intruder in the Dutch CA DigiNotar issued 531 fraudulent certificates for 344 domain names, Google's among them; DigiNotar's logs showed about 300,000 Online Certificate Status Protocol (OCSP) requests from addresses in Iran, a measure of how many users had been intercepted, and the company filed for bankruptcy on 20 September 2011. ENISA, the European Union Agency for Cybersecurity, drew the structural conclusion: the security of Hypertext Transfer Protocol Secure (HTTPS) equals the security of the weakest CA. In 2017 Chrome's security team reported that Symantec's PKI business, which ran the Thawte, VeriSign, Equifax, GeoTrust and RapidSSL brands, had issued numerous certificates that broke the Baseline Requirements, and announced that Chrome 70 would remove trust in that infrastructure altogether.

Certificate Transparency (CT) exists because detection turned out to be more achievable than prevention. RFC 6962, published as an experimental protocol by three Google engineers in June 2013 and revised as version 2.0 in RFC 9162 (December 2021), has certificates submitted to public, append-only logs that anyone can audit, and a log answers each submission with a signed certificate timestamp (SCT). Chrome refuses a publicly trusted TLS (Transport Layer Security) certificate that does not carry enough of them: embedded SCTs from at least two distinct logs when the certificate lives 180 days or less, three when it lives longer, from at least two different log operators. A mis-issued certificate can still be created, but no longer quietly.

Revocation is the weakest joint. A CA can publish a CRL or answer OCSP queries (RFC 6960, June 2013), but ENISA already noted in 2011 that clients often skip the check or give no clear warning when it fails. The industry's answer has been to depend on it less. Since 15 March 2024 the Baseline Requirements make OCSP optional and CRLs mandatory, and Let's Encrypt scheduled the shutdown of its OCSP responders for 6 August 2025, arguing that every OCSP query tells the CA which site a given address is visiting. Lifetimes are shrinking so that a bad certificate dies on its own: ballot SC-081v3, proposed by Apple and passed in April 2025 with no vote against, cuts the maximum validity of a public TLS certificate from 398 days to 200 on 15 March 2026, 100 on 15 March 2027 and 47 on 15 March 2029. At that cadence renewal has to be automatic, which is what the Automatic Certificate Management Environment (ACME), RFC 8555 of March 2019, provides.

Private PKI inverts the trade. Running an authority for internal services means no external party can issue for those names and no public log records their existence, at the cost of distributing the root to every client that must trust it. The Baseline Requirements say outright that they do not address enterprises operating a PKI for internal purposes whose root is not distributed by an application software supplier, so the 47-day schedule does not bind an internal CA. On Windows the usual tool is Active Directory Certificate Services (AD CS), a server role with root and subordinate CAs, web enrolment, an Online Responder for status queries and a Network Device Enrollment Service for routers without a domain account; Microsoft lists smart card sign-in, secure wireless, virtual private networks (VPNs), Internet Protocol Security (IPsec) and Secure/Multipurpose Internet Mail Extensions (S/MIME) among its uses. TLS inspection is a private PKI too: a FortiGate doing deep inspection re-signs each server certificate with its Fortinet_CA_SSL certificate or with a CA certificate the administrator uploads, and browsers warn until that CA is imported as trusted.

Not every PKI is a marketplace of competing roots. Brazil's national infrastructure, ICP-Brasil (Infraestrutura de Chaves Públicas Brasileira), is a single-root hierarchy in which the National Institute of Information Technology (ITI, Instituto Nacional de Tecnologia da Informação) acts as root authority and accredits and audits everyone below it, much as the PEM designers intended in 1993. At the other extreme is the web of trust of Pretty Good Privacy (PGP), which RFC 4949 describes as an architecture where each user defines their own trust anchors through personal relationships, usually with no public repository at all. The choice between a public and a private PKI, like the choice among these models, is really a choice about whom to depend on, and neither answer is free.

pod.def: The smallest deployable unit in Kubernetes: one or more containers that share networking and storage.
pod.context: A pod groups containers that belong together and run on the same node, sharing an IP and volumes, a common pattern being an app container plus a sidecar. Kubernetes creates, replaces, and scales pods rather than individual containers.

post-quantum-cryptography.def: Post-quantum cryptography (PQC) is public-key cryptography built on mathematical problems that no known quantum algorithm solves efficiently, running on ordinary computers and networks, designed to replace RSA (Rivest-Shamir-Adleman), Diffie-Hellman and elliptic-curve algorithms before a large quantum computer can break them.
post-quantum-cryptography.context: A capable quantum computer running Shor's algorithm would break the public-key cryptography in use today, RSA (Rivest-Shamir-Adleman), Diffie-Hellman and elliptic curves, so post-quantum cryptography (PQC) develops replacements that resist it; symmetric ciphers and hashes are only modestly affected. The urgency comes from harvest now, decrypt later: data encrypted today can be recorded and decrypted once such a machine exists, which is why key exchange moves first. NIST (the National Institute of Standards and Technology) published the first standards on 13 August 2024: FIPS (Federal Information Processing Standard) 203, ML-KEM (Module-Lattice-Based Key-Encapsulation Mechanism), for key establishment, and FIPS 204 and 205, ML-DSA (Module-Lattice-Based Digital Signature Algorithm) and SLH-DSA (Stateless Hash-Based Digital Signature Algorithm), for signatures; HQC and Falcon are being standardized as backups and companions. NIST IR (Interagency Report) 8547 deprecates the classical algorithms after 2030 and disallows them after 2035. In practice the change ships as hybrids, X25519MLKEM768 in TLS (Transport Layer Security) and mlkem768x25519-sha256 in SSH (Secure Shell), so that a session stays safe if either half holds. PQC is not quantum key distribution, which needs special hardware and provides no authentication.
post-quantum-cryptography.depth:
What it is, and what it is not. Post-quantum cryptography (PQC) is ordinary software cryptography, keys and messages exchanged over existing networks, whose security rests on problems such as finding short vectors in structured lattices, decoding random linear codes or inverting hash functions, for which no efficient quantum algorithm is known. It is not quantum cryptography. The UK National Cyber Security Centre (NCSC), in a white paper of 5 August 2025, points out that quantum key distribution (QKD) provides no authentication, so it must be combined with PQC or with pre-shared symmetric keys that do not scale; it calls PQC the best mitigation to the quantum threat and says the NCSC will not support QKD for government or military applications and that elsewhere it should not be relied upon alone. Nor does PQC replace all cryptography: it replaces the public-key part, key establishment and signatures.

The threat. In a paper first presented at the Symposium on Foundations of Computer Science in November 1994, Peter Shor showed that a quantum computer can factor integers and compute discrete logarithms in polynomial time, the two problems beneath RSA (Rivest-Shamir-Adleman), finite-field Diffie-Hellman and every elliptic-curve scheme, ECDH (elliptic-curve Diffie-Hellman), ECDSA (Elliptic Curve Digital Signature Algorithm) and EdDSA (Edwards-curve Digital Signature Algorithm) included. Lov Grover's algorithm of 1996 speeds up unstructured search only quadratically, examining N possibilities in about the square root of N steps, which is why NIST (the National Institute of Standards and Technology) states in IR (Interagency Report) 8547 that its approved symmetric primitives with at least 128 bits of classical security are believed to meet its lowest post-quantum security category, while the few 112-bit symmetric standards will be disallowed in 2030. No quantum computer able to do this exists yet, but IR 8547 names the reason not to wait: harvest now, decrypt later, in which adversaries collect encrypted data today in order to decrypt it once quantum technology matures. Forward secrecy does not help, because the recorded key exchange itself is what a quantum computer would break.

The standards. NIST opened its competition in December 2016 and, after three rounds, selected CRYSTALS-Kyber for key establishment and CRYSTALS-Dilithium, Falcon and SPHINCS+ for signatures; all but SPHINCS+ rest on structured lattices. On 13 August 2024 it published three of them as FIPS (Federal Information Processing Standards). FIPS 203 specifies ML-KEM (Module-Lattice-Based Key-Encapsulation Mechanism) in three sets, ML-KEM-512, 768 and 1024, with encapsulation keys of 800, 1,184 and 1,568 bytes, ciphertexts of 768, 1,088 and 1,568 bytes and a 32-byte shared secret. FIPS 204 specifies ML-DSA (Module-Lattice-Based Digital Signature Algorithm), with public keys of 1,312 to 2,592 bytes and signatures of 2,420 to 4,627 bytes. FIPS 205 specifies SLH-DSA (Stateless Hash-Based Digital Signature Algorithm), whose security rests only on hash functions: public keys of 32 bytes at the lowest category, signatures of 7,856 or 17,088 bytes. SP (Special Publication) 800-227 (September 2025) gives the rules for using key-encapsulation mechanisms, and NIST already lists errata to be fixed in FIPS 203 and 204. A key-encapsulation mechanism is not Diffie-Hellman: one side encapsulates a fresh secret to the other's public key, which changes how protocols are built around it.

Backups, casualties and what is still open. New mathematics breaks in public. SIKE, an isogeny-based scheme that had reached NIST's fourth round, fell to Wouter Castryck and Thomas Decru of KU Leuven, whose paper received on 30 July 2022 recovers keys from SIDH (Supersingular Isogeny Diffie-Hellman) and breaks the level-1 parameter set SIKEp434 in about ten minutes on a single core. Rainbow, one of three finalist signature schemes, fell to Ward Beullens of IBM Research Zurich, whose paper of 25 February 2022 recovers a level-1 secret key in about 53 hours on a laptop. That is why NIST hedges across mathematical families. From the fourth round, which also included BIKE and Classic McEliece, it selected HQC (Hamming Quasi-Cyclic), a KEM (key-encapsulation mechanism) whose security reduces to decoding a random linear code, on 11 March 2025 as the only further key-establishment algorithm to standardize, and Falcon, as FN-DSA, is also in the standardization pipeline. For signatures it reopened the field in September 2022, asking especially for schemes not based on structured lattices and for short signatures with fast verification: 40 first-round and 14 second-round candidates led, on 14 May 2026, to nine in the third round, SQIsign, HAWK (since withdrawn by its team), MQOM, SDitH, MAYO, QR-UOV, SNOVA, UOV and FAEST. Its draft SP 800-230, open for comment until 12 June 2026, adds SLH-DSA parameter sets with smaller signatures for software, firmware and certificate signing, capped at 2 to the 24th signatures per key.

The timeline. NIST IR 8547, published in its final form in October 2026 by Dustin Moody, Ray Perlner, Andrew Regenscheid, Angela Robinson and David Cooper, deprecates quantum-vulnerable public-key cryptography after 2030 and disallows it under NIST standards after 2035, the target that National Security Memorandum 10 had set for the federal migration. It also records stricter deadlines for the United States government's most sensitive systems: under Executive Order 14412 and OMB (Office of Management and Budget) Memorandum M-26-15, high value assets and high impact systems must adopt post-quantum key establishment by 31 December 2030 and post-quantum signatures by 31 December 2031, and agencies must support TLS (Transport Layer Security) 1.3 by 2 January 2030. During the transition NIST allows hybrids through SP 800-56C: a classical shared secret Z and a second secret T are concatenated and fed to an approved key derivation function, and it intends to let Z come from FIPS 203 as well.

Where engineers meet it. TLS moved first, because harvest now, decrypt later targets key exchange. RFC (Request for Comments) 10024 (August 2026) defines three hybrid groups for TLS 1.3, X25519MLKEM768, SecP256r1MLKEM768 and SecP384r1MLKEM1024, each pairing a classical curve with ML-KEM so that the session holds if either component does; the X25519MLKEM768 client share is 1,216 bytes against 32 for X25519 alone, and the key exchange entry covers its codepoints and deployment. OpenSSH made the hybrid mlkem768x25519-sha256 its default key agreement in version 10.0 (9 April 2025); version 10.6 (6 October 2026) enabled the hybrid ssh-mldsa44-ed25519 signature algorithm and an sshd WarnWeakCrypto option, on by default, that logs any key agreement that is not post-quantum safe, and 10.6p2 (5 November 2026) accepts it for certificate authorities. In IKEv2 (Internet Key Exchange version 2), IANA (Internet Assigned Numbers Authority) has assigned key exchange method numbers 35 to 37 to ML-KEM-512, 768 and 1024. WireGuard offers an optional pre-shared key mixed into its handshake for post-quantum resistance.

What goes wrong. Size is the first surprise: an ML-DSA-44 signature is 2,420 bytes against 64 for Ed25519, and certificate chains carry several signatures and public keys, so handshakes and certificate chains grow by kilobytes. Inventory is the second: IR 8547 asks organizations to find where vulnerable algorithms are used before they can replace them, and long-lived devices and firmware signing keys are the hard cases. New algorithms are the third: SIKE and Rainbow show that fresh schemes can fail outright, which is the argument for hybrids now and for algorithm agility always. Implementation is the fourth, as it was for RSA and ECDSA: side channels and careless randomness break good mathematics. And the opposite error is common too: the belief that a quantum computer breaks all encryption, covered under the quantum-breaks-everything myth, leads to discarding AES (Advanced Encryption Standard) and SHA-2 (Secure Hash Algorithm 2), which NIST keeps.

Numbers worth remembering: 1994 for Shor's algorithm; 13 August 2024 for FIPS 203, 204 and 205; 11 March 2025 for HQC; 14 May 2026 for the nine third-round signature candidates; 2030 and 2035 for deprecation and disallowance; 1,184 bytes for an ML-KEM-768 encapsulation key and 1,216 for an X25519MLKEM768 client share; 2,420 bytes for an ML-DSA-44 signature; 128-bit symmetric keys as still sufficient.

privilege-escalation.def: Turning limited access into greater access, ideally administrator or root.
privilege-escalation.context: Attackers rarely land where they want to be; privilege escalation is the step from a foothold to real control. "Vertical" gains higher rights on one host; "horizontal" (lateral movement) spreads sideways to other accounts or machines. Least privilege exists to make this step hard.

public-key-cryptography.def: Cryptography built on key pairs: a public key that anyone may hold and a private key that only its owner holds, so that two parties can establish secret keys, encrypt and verify signatures without first sharing a secret. Also called asymmetric cryptography.
public-key-cryptography.context: In asymmetric cryptography one key of a pair applies a protection and the other removes or verifies it, and knowing the public key does not reveal the private one. Published by Whitfield Diffie and Martin Hellman in 1976, and found earlier in secret at GCHQ (Government Communications Headquarters), it removed the need to exchange a secret key before communicating, and it underpins TLS (Transport Layer Security), digital signatures and PKI (public key infrastructure). It is slow next to symmetric ciphers, so in practice it sets up a symmetric key and proves identities, while the bulk of the data is encrypted symmetrically.
public-key-cryptography.depth:
NIST (the United States National Institute of Standards and Technology) states the idea precisely in Special Publication 800-57 Part 1 Revision 5 (May 2020): asymmetric-key algorithms, commonly known as public-key algorithms, use two related keys, a public key that may be known by anyone and a private key that should be under the sole control of the entity that owns the pair, and although the two are related, knowledge of the public key cannot be used to determine the private key. One key applies a cryptographic protection and the other removes or verifies it. The services are two: digital signatures, which give source, identity and integrity authentication, and key establishment, by key agreement (both sides contribute to a shared secret) or key transport (one side encrypts a key to the other). The everyday description, that what one key locks only the other can unlock, fits textbook RSA (Rivest, Shamir, Adleman) encryption, but not a Diffie-Hellman agreement or an ECDSA (Elliptic Curve Digital Signature Algorithm) signature, neither of which encrypts anything.

The public record begins with Whitfield Diffie and Martin Hellman's New Directions in Cryptography, published in the November 1976 issue of the IEEE (Institute of Electrical and Electronics Engineers) Transactions on Information Theory. They defined a public key cryptosystem as one in which enciphering and deciphering are governed by distinct keys, such that computing the deciphering key from the enciphering key is computationally infeasible (their example was a computation of 10 to the power 100 instructions), so that each user can place an enciphering key in a public directory and anyone can write to anyone without having met. They also proposed public key distribution, the exchange now named after them, by which two users agree on a key over an open channel; noted that Ralph Merkle had independently found a partial solution of a different form; described one-way authentication, the digital equivalent of a written signature; and left open the problem of finding trap-door one-way functions that would make a full public key cryptosystem practical.

Ronald Rivest, Adi Shamir and Leonard Adleman at MIT (the Massachusetts Institute of Technology) supplied one in A Method for Obtaining Digital Signatures and Public-Key Cryptosystems, Communications of the ACM (Association for Computing Machinery), volume 21, number 2, 1978. A message, represented as a number, is raised to a public power and reduced modulo a public number that is the product of two large secret primes; decryption uses a secret exponent that only someone who knows the primes can compute, so the security rests on the difficulty of factoring the modulus, for which they recommended about 200 digits. The paper names both consequences that still define the field: no courier is needed to deliver keys, and a message signed with the private key can be verified by anyone with the public key and cannot later be disowned. It also anticipated hybrid use, suggesting that the public-key system bootstrap a session key for the NBS (National Bureau of Standards) cipher, the Data Encryption Standard, which might be faster for the bulk of the traffic. The British signals agency had been there first: an IEEE Milestone dedicated in Cheltenham on 5 October 2010 records that at GCHQ (Government Communications Headquarters), by 1975, James Ellis had proved that a symmetric secret key was unnecessary and Clifford Cocks with Malcolm Williamson had shown how public-key cryptography could be achieved, work that was kept secret until 1997.

Every public-key scheme rests on a mathematical problem believed to be hard: factoring large integers for RSA, discrete logarithms in finite fields for classic Diffie-Hellman and DSA (the Digital Signature Algorithm), discrete logarithms on elliptic curves for ECDH (Elliptic Curve Diffie-Hellman), ECDSA and EdDSA (the Edwards-curve Digital Signature Algorithm), and, in the newest standards, problems on lattices and the security of hash functions. The problems scale differently, which is why key sizes differ so much. NIST's table of comparable strengths sets 112-bit security at RSA 2048 or an elliptic curve of 224 to 255 bits, 128-bit security, the level of AES-128 (the Advanced Encryption Standard with a 128-bit key), at RSA 3072 or a curve of 256 to 383 bits, 192-bit at RSA 7680 or 384 to 511 bits, and 256-bit at RSA 15360 or 512 bits and more, and it treats strengths below 112 bits as no longer approved. That is the arithmetic behind the move to elliptic curves: the RSA modulus grows far faster than the curve for each step of strength.

Because the operations are slow next to symmetric ciphers, public-key cryptography is used where only it can do the job and then hands over. In TLS (Transport Layer Security) 1.3, specified in RFC (Request for Comments) 9846 of July 2026, the server is always authenticated, by asymmetric cryptography such as RSA, ECDSA or EdDSA signatures or by a pre-shared key, and the session keys come from an asymmetric key exchange, Diffie-Hellman on elliptic curves or, increasingly, a key-encapsulation mechanism, after which all application data is protected with a symmetric cipher. SSH (Secure Shell), IPsec (Internet Protocol Security) key exchange, signed software updates and signed tokens follow the same division of labour. NIST adds a discipline that implementations often break: a single key should be used for only one purpose, since using one key pair for two processes may weaken both and widens the damage when it leaks.

The weak point is not the mathematics but the binding between a public key and its owner. The RSA paper states its own assumption plainly, that the intruder cannot modify or insert messages, and Diffie and Hellman required that the public directory itself be protected. An attacker who can substitute a public key in transit can read or sign in the victim's name without breaking anything, which is why public-key cryptography arrives together with a way of vouching for keys: certificates signed by certification authorities in a PKI (public key infrastructure), webs of trust among users, or a key fingerprint recorded on first contact and checked thereafter. Most real failures sit here or in the handling of private keys: keys generated with poor randomness, private keys copied onto too many machines, and certificates trusted for longer or more broadly than intended.

The longer horizon is quantum computing. Peter Shor described in 1995 polynomial-time algorithms for prime factorization and discrete logarithms on a quantum computer, and NIST's Interagency Report (IR) 8547, Transition to Post-Quantum Cryptography Standards, published in final form in October 2026, states that RSA, ECDSA, EdDSA and elliptic-curve key establishment are all vulnerable to Shor's algorithm on a cryptanalytically relevant quantum computer. Encrypted traffic recorded today can be read once such a machine exists, the "harvest now, decrypt later" threat, so key establishment is the urgent part. NIST will deprecate quantum-vulnerable public-key cryptography after 2030 and disallow it under its standards after 2035, and the replacements are themselves public-key algorithms: ML-KEM (Module-Lattice-Based Key-Encapsulation Mechanism) in FIPS (Federal Information Processing Standard) 203 of 13 August 2024, the signature schemes ML-DSA (Module-Lattice-Based Digital Signature Algorithm) and SLH-DSA (Stateless Hash-Based Digital Signature Algorithm) in FIPS 204 and 205, and the algorithm HQC, selected as an alternative key-encapsulation mechanism. The idea of 1976 survives the transition; the hard problems underneath it change.

purple-team.def: Red and blue working together, so every offensive finding immediately improves the defence.
purple-team.context: Rather than a separate group, purple teaming is a way of running an exercise: attackers and defenders share knowledge in real time, turning each successful technique into a new detection. It trades the drama of a surprise test for faster learning.

pwned.def: Slang for having been completely defeated or, in security, compromised: a system or account that is pwned is under someone else's control. The verb is pwn, usually pronounced pone; Merriam-Webster gives it as a respelling of own, probably from a typing slip, first used in 1999.
pwned.context: From a likely typo of "owned" (the p sits beside the o on a QWERTY keyboard), "pwned" spread through gaming culture and back into the security world it borrowed from, where crackers had long said a machine was owned, or 0wned, once a root exploit gave the attacker everything. It is immortalized in Have I Been Pwned, the service that checks whether your address appears in known breaches, and in the industry's own institutions: the Pwn2Own exploitation contest and the Pwnie Awards, both from 2007.
pwned.depth:
The word and its forms. Pwn is a transitive verb (pwns, pwning, pwned) meaning to dominate and defeat someone or something, with pwnage as the noun. Merriam-Webster lists it as slang, a written form usually read aloud as pone, and gives the etymology as a respelling of own, probably originally from a typing error, p and o being adjacent letters on the QWERTY keyboard, with a first known use in 1999. Its Wordplay column, written while the word was still on the watch list, notes the second sense that matters to this field, gaining illegal access to something such as a computer or, in one of its examples, a car, and records that the word entered the dictionary in September 2022. Pronunciation has never settled: pone is the dictionary's reading, and the radio programme A Way with Words heard from a caller in 2008 who had first learned it as poon before being corrected by a Counter-Strike player.

Where it came from, and the security word underneath. The typo story is the one dictionaries accept; in 2008 A Way with Words called it the correct story and rejected the claims of particular games, Counter-Strike among them, to have invented it. The more interesting history is the word it misspells. The Jargon File, version 4.4.7 of 29 December 2003, has an entry for owned with two senses. The first is cracker slang, often written 0wned: the condition of a machine cracked by a root exploit, so that the attacker can do anything with it. The second belongs to gamers and Internet Relay Chat (IRC): to be dominated or humiliated, the sense in which a player owns a game, and it lists the spelling variants 0wned, 0wn0r3d and even pwn0r3d, adding that hackers do not use that second sense. So the sequence is not that security borrowed a gamers' typo: the intrusion sense of owned was already there, the gaming sense grew beside it, and the misspelling travelled back into security as the informal word for total compromise.

Pwned against compromised. The formal vocabulary is narrower and more careful. In the glossary of the National Institute of Standards and Technology (NIST), compromise is defined, after the Committee on National Security Systems, as a judgment based on the preponderance of the evidence that a disclosure of information to unauthorized persons or a violation of a system's security policy has occurred, and NIST's key-management publications use it for the unauthorized disclosure, modification, substitution or use of keys and other security-related data. Compromise admits degrees and states a finding. Pwned, in the Jargon File's sense, claims the end state: the attacker can do anything. In an incident report the slang is therefore a summary, not a finding; the work is to say which accounts, which privileges, which hosts, how long and with what persistence, because a mailbox read once and a domain controller held for months are both pwned in conversation and very different in remediation.

The breach sense. Have I Been Pwned widened the word again. Troy Hunt launched it on 4 December 2013, after the Adobe breach, because in analysing breaches he kept finding the same accounts exposed again and again, people having their accounts pwned over and over; the site's own description is a free resource for anyone to assess whether an online account has been compromised or pwned in a data breach. That is a weaker claim than root on a server: an address listed in a breach means data about the account was exposed, which often includes a password or its hash, not that anyone has logged in. The distinction matters when the result reaches users, since the right response is to change that password everywhere it was reused and turn on a second factor, and the service's companion, Pwned Passwords, exists so that sites can refuse passwords already in criminal hands.

The industry's own institutions. Two fixtures of the research calendar took the word as their name. Pwn2Own, run by what is now Trend Micro's Zero Day Initiative, began at the CanSecWest conference in Vancouver in 2007, when Dino Dai Zovi won a MacBook and 10,000 dollars by compromising it at a time when Apple's machines had an aura of invincibility; it has grown to three events a year paying more than 1 million dollars per event, with the overall winner named Master of Pwn, and the 2025 Berlin event alone paid 1,078,750 dollars for 28 unique zero-day vulnerabilities, which are disclosed to the vendors. The Pwnie Awards, whose winners' archive begins in 2007, are an annual ceremony for the achievements and failures of security researchers, judged by researchers and earlier winners, with categories such as Lamest Vendor Response and Most Epic Fail, and for years an award for Mass 0wnage or Epic 0wnage, which went to Stuxnet in 2011 and the Shadow Brokers dumps in 2017; the 2012 Most Epic Fail went to F5's static root SSH (Secure Shell) key. Education adopted it too: pwn.college, the Arizona State University platform, powers much of that university's cybersecurity curriculum.

Why the slang survived. What pwned adds over compromised is completeness and tone. Compromised is clinical and admits degrees; pwned means the attacker has it, entirely, and the informality carries a hint of the humiliation a serious breach involves for the people who were meant to prevent it. That register is why it survived into professional use despite looking like a typo, and why a breach-notification service and a vendor-funded exploit contest could both put it in their names without losing credibility.

What the word says about the field. Its migration is worth noting for what it reveals. Much of the security vocabulary came from the offensive side, because that is where the culture was strongest and most verbal, from 0wned and leet spelling to the lamer and the script kiddie, and defenders inherited the language of the people they defend against. The inheritance is mostly harmless and occasionally revealing: a profession that describes its failures in the attacker's slang is one whose self-image was formed partly by the other side, and the Pwnie Awards' habit of honouring both excellent research and lame vendor responses on the same stage is the culture keeping score of itself.

qos.def: Techniques that prioritize some network traffic over others to meet performance needs.
qos.context: Quality of Service lets a network favour latency-sensitive traffic, a voice call, a video stream, over bulk transfers, so the important packets are not stuck behind the big ones. It matters most where bandwidth is contended and delay hurts.

rabbit-hole.def: An investigation that keeps pulling you deeper, well past where you meant to stop.
rabbit-hole.context: Borrowed from "Alice in Wonderland", going down a rabbit hole is chasing a problem or a curiosity through layer after layer. It can be productive or a trap; the skill is noticing which one you are in.
rabbit-hole.depth:
Going down a rabbit hole is following a chain of investigation far past the point that serves the original purpose. The phrase is from Alice in Wonderland, and its technical use captures something specific: each step is individually justified, and the aggregate is a day spent somewhere unrelated to the task.

It is the close cousin of yak shaving and differs in an important way. Yak shaving is a chain of prerequisites you must clear to get back to the work; a rabbit hole is a chain of curiosity that does not have to be cleared at all. The yak is blocking you. The rabbit hole is interesting.

That difference is why the response is different. Yak shaving needs a stack so you can climb back out; rabbit holes need a timebox and a note. The honest complication is that rabbit holes are also where a lot of genuine understanding comes from, and an engineer who never follows one learns only what was necessary. The discipline is not avoidance, it is knowing which one you are in, and deciding deliberately rather than looking up three hours later.

race-condition.def: A bug where the outcome depends on the unpredictable timing of concurrent operations.
race-condition.context: When two things touch shared state at once, order decides the result, and the wrong order corrupts data or opens a security hole (the TOCTOU class: time-of-check to time-of-use). Because timing is involved, race conditions often behave as heisenbugs.

rainbow-table.def: A precomputed lookup that reverses unsalted password hashes quickly.
rainbow-table.context: Instead of hashing guesses live, an attacker precomputes hashes for huge numbers of passwords and looks yours up. Salting defeats this entirely: a unique salt per password means the attacker's giant table matches nobody, forcing them back to slow per-target work.

red-team.def: A group that plays the adversary to test an organization's defences realistically.
red-team.context: A red team goes beyond a pentest: it emulates a real threat actor's goals and patience, testing people and processes as well as technology, often without the defenders knowing. It exists to answer "could a determined attacker get in", not just "is this box patched".
red-team.depth:
What it is exactly. The definition that the glossary of the National Institute of Standards and Technology (NIST) takes from CNSSI 4009-2022, a publication of the Committee on National Security Systems (CNSS), is a group of people authorized and organized to emulate a potential adversary's attack or exploitation capabilities against an enterprise's security posture, with the objective of improving security by demonstrating the impact of successful attacks and by showing what works for the defenders, the blue team, in an operational environment. NIST's Special Publication (SP) 800-53 Revision 5 defines the exercise in the same spirit: a simulated adversarial attempt, reflecting real-world conditions, to compromise the organization's missions or business processes and so assess its security capability as a whole. The operative words are emulate, objective and whole. A red team pursues a goal an attacker would want, such as reaching payment systems or a director's mailbox, by whatever path a real adversary might take, including people and physical access, and measures whether the organization noticed and responded. It is not a vulnerability scan, which lists weaknesses; not a penetration test, which finds and chains weaknesses within an agreed scope and ends in a report of them; and not a purple team, which is a way of running the same work collaboratively with the defenders.

Where the name comes from. The idea is older than computers.
