A 2016 review of Micah Zenko's book Red Team: How to Succeed by Thinking Like the Enemy (Basic Books, 2015) traces it to the sixteenth-century advocatus diaboli, the devil's advocate whose role was to argue against a canonization, and dates the term itself to the Cold War, when teams playing the red enemy were set against blue friendly forces to war-game strategies and plans. Zenko, then a senior fellow at the Council on Foreign Relations, examined seventeen case studies across the military, intelligence, security and business, set out six best practices and described what happens when red team findings are ignored; the Council on Foreign Relations' guide to the book argues that the 2014 theft of more than twenty million US government personnel records could have been avoided with red teaming. The colours stuck in security: red attacks, blue defends, and purple is the two working together.

How an engagement is run. The TIBER-EU framework of the European Central Bank (ECB), published in May 2018 for threat intelligence-based ethical red-teaming, is the most detailed public template. It names five teams. The blue team is the tested entity's own people, whose prevention, detection and response are tested without their foreknowledge; a threat intelligence provider surveys the possible threats and carries out reconnaissance on the entity; the red-team testers mount the simulated attack on its critical functions; a small control team inside the entity, the only people there who know a test is under way, leads and manages it; and the authority's TIBER cyber team oversees the test so that other authorities can recognize it. The phases run from initiation and scoping through threat intelligence, red-team planning, testing and reporting, to a blue team report, a remediation plan, a test summary report and an attestation, with separate guidance for purple-teaming in the testing or closure phase. The ECB is explicit that the outcome is not a pass or a fail: the test exists to reveal strengths and weaknesses and for its learning effect.

Regulators who require it. Finance led. The Bank of England, the Prudential Regulation Authority and the Financial Conduct Authority have used CBEST, their threat intelligence-led assessment, since 2014 to test systemically important firms and financial market infrastructures, and run it across borders with other regulators. TIBER-EU, developed by the ECB with the national central banks of the European Union, was updated in 2024 to align fully with the regulatory technical standards for threat-led penetration testing (TLPT) under the Digital Operational Resilience Act (DORA), and has been adopted in more than twenty jurisdictions, from Germany, France and Italy to Norway and Iceland, as well as by ECB Banking Supervision. The framework itself says it can be used in any critical sector, not only finance.

What it borrows from the adversary. A red team needs the same infrastructure an attacker uses: a way in, a command-and-control (C2) channel to drive compromised hosts, and the tradecraft to stay unseen. MITRE ATT&CK was born in that setting: it was created to categorize adversary behaviour for structured emulation exercises in MITRE's FMX research environment, used by the emulation team to build scenarios and by the defenders to measure progress. The overlap has a cost. Cobalt Strike, introduced in 2012 as an adversary simulation platform and acquired by Fortra, then HelpSystems, in 2020, became so popular with criminals in cracked legacy copies that Microsoft, Fortra and the Health Information Sharing and Analysis Center obtained a US court order on 31 March 2023 to seize domains and take that infrastructure offline. Red team tools are also targets: the theft of FireEye's red team tools, which F5 Labs set beside the SolarWinds Orion compromise as the twin shocks of that winter, was answered by FireEye publishing free detection rules for its own tools in Snort, YARA, ClamAV and HXIOC formats.

What it is for, from the defenders' side. The UK National Cyber Security Centre (NCSC) describes red team exercises as authorized, non-destructive simulated attacks whose output is a report, and notes that ideally a security operations centre (SOC) would detect all of the red team's activity; where it does not, the exercise shows where to improve. That is the real measure. A red team that gets in proves very little that a penetration test could not; one that gets in, achieves its objective and is never noticed has found something no scanner could, and one that is caught on the second day has tested the detection and response chain that the rest of the security budget pays for. The findings feed detection engineering directly, and a purple team exercise, where the same techniques are replayed with the SOC watching, is the fastest way to turn them into rules.

What goes wrong. The first failure is relabelling: a scoped penetration test sold as a red team, with no threat intelligence behind it and no measure of detection. The second is ignoring the result, the pattern Zenko's case studies return to. The third is risk to production: the NCSC warns that testing on live systems can change how they work or stop them working, which is why rules of engagement, a control team and an agreed way to halt the test matter as much as the attack plan. The fourth is the false negative read as a pass: a red team that failed to get in has shown that one team, with one plan and a fixed budget of time, did not succeed, not that a patient adversary could not.

Neighbours. The blue team is the defence being tested; the purple team runs the same work in the open; a penetration test is the narrower, scoped assessment; a tabletop exercise rehearses the response without any attack at all. TTPs and MITRE ATT&CK are the vocabulary red teams use to describe what they will emulate, Metasploit and C2 frameworks are among their tools, and social engineering is often their way in.

redos.def: A denial-of-service caused by a regular expression that takes catastrophically long on certain input.
redos.context: Some regex patterns backtrack exponentially on crafted strings, so a single request can pin a CPU, turning an innocent validation into a ReDoS vulnerability. The fix is safer patterns or a linear-time regex engine.

regex.def: A regular expression (regex) is a pattern in a compact notation that describes a set of strings, which an engine uses to test, search, extract or replace text.
regex.context: A regular expression describes a set of strings, used to validate, search, extract or split text. It is powerful and terse to the point of being famously write-only, and the name covers a family of dialects rather than one language: the same pattern can mean different things, or fail to compile, in POSIX (Portable Operating System Interface) tools, PCRE (Perl Compatible Regular Expressions), JavaScript and RE2. Poorly written patterns can also be slow enough on crafted input to be a denial-of-service risk (see ReDoS, regular expression denial of service).
regex.depth:
What it is, in theory and in practice. In the theoretical sense a regular expression denotes a regular language, the kind of set a finite automaton can recognize; the idea goes back to Stephen Kleene's RAND memorandum RM-704, Representation of Events in Nerve Nets and Finite Automata, of 15 December 1951. Deterministic and nondeterministic finite automata (DFA and NFA) and regular expressions are equivalent in power, and that equivalence is what makes fast matching possible. The regex of everyday tools is larger. A backreference such as \1 matches the exact text an earlier group captured, so (cat|dog)\1 matches catcat and dogdog but not catdog; as Russ Cox points out, expressions with backreferences are no longer regular, and matching them is NP-complete.

How it reached programmers. Ken Thompson introduced regular expressions to programmers in his implementation of the QED editor for CTSS (Compatible Time-Sharing System), and Dennis Ritchie followed in his QED for GE-TSS. Thompson's paper Regular expression search algorithm, in Communications of the ACM (Association for Computing Machinery) in June 1968, compiled the expression into machine code that simulated an NFA by tracking every state reachable at once. By the late 1970s regular expressions ran through the Unix tools ed, sed, grep, egrep, awk and lex. PCRE (Perl Compatible Regular Expressions), a library of C functions with the same syntax and semantics as Perl apart from a few differences, lives on as PCRE2, a revised interface written by Philip Hazel of the University Computing Service in Cambridge.

The POSIX (Portable Operating System Interface) dialects. IEEE (Institute of Electrical and Electronics Engineers) Std 1003.1-2024, the current POSIX base specification, defines Basic Regular Expressions (BRE), used by most utilities, and Extended Regular Expressions (ERE), used by some. In a BRE, groups are written with escaped parentheses and back-references \1 to \9 refer to them; bracket expressions accept character classes such as [:alpha:] and [:digit:] that hold in every locale. POSIX matching is leftmost-longest: of the matches that begin earliest in the string, the longest wins, and each subpattern, from left to right, takes the longest string it can, so the ERE (wee|week)(knights|night) matches all ten characters of weeknights. Issue 8 adds minimal (shortest-match) repetition and a REG_MINIMAL flag. Perl later added non-greedy operators (??, *? and +?), so the same pattern can capture different text in different engines.

Backtracking against automata. A backtracking engine, the kind Cox found in Java, Perl, PHP, Python and Ruby, tries one path through the pattern at a time and backs up on failure. An automaton-based engine follows all paths in parallel: an NFA with n states can only be in n states at a step, even though there may be 2 to the power n paths. Cox's 2007 measurement makes the gap concrete: matching a? repeated n times followed by a repeated n times against a string of n letters a, Perl needed over sixty seconds at 29 characters, while a Thompson-style NFA took twenty microseconds. RE2, in production at Google since 2006, guarantees match time linear in the length of the input, and Go's regexp package, which uses RE2 syntax, promises the same, a property it notes most open source implementations do not offer. The price is features: RE2 refuses backreferences and look-around assertions, because only backtracking solutions are known for them, and has no possessive quantifiers.

What the backtracking dialects add. PCRE2 supports lookahead, written (?= and (?!, and lookbehind, written (?<= and (?<!, which test what surrounds a position without consuming it; named groups, written with the name in angle brackets after (? in Perl's syntax or after (?P in Python's, with names of up to 128 code units; and an extended mode, the x option, that ignores white space and treats # as the start of a comment, so a long pattern can be laid out and annotated like code. Atomic groups, written (?>...), and possessive quantifiers, written with an extra plus as in \d++foo, lock up what they have matched so that a later failure cannot backtrack into them. JavaScript has its own flags, among them u and its upgraded form v for Unicode. A pattern copied from one engine into another is a common source of matching that is subtly wrong rather than an outright error.

ReDoS (regular expression denial of service). When a backtracking engine meets a pattern with many ways to divide the same input and an input that ultimately fails, the number of paths explodes. The OWASP (Open Worldwide Application Security Project) page on ReDoS calls such patterns evil regexes: a repeated group containing its own repetition, or alternatives that overlap, as in (a+)+$ and (a|aa)+$. For ^(a+)+$, the input aaaaX has 16 possible paths and sixteen letters a followed by X has 65,536, doubling with every extra letter. PCRE2's own documentation shows (\D+|<\d+>)*[!?] taking a long time to fail on a long run of a characters, and failing quickly once the first alternative is made atomic. Engines offer brakes: PCRE2's match limit, 10 million by default, ends a runaway match with PCRE2_ERROR_MATCHLIMIT, and .NET offers time-outs and, since .NET 7, a RegexOptions.NonBacktracking mode with linear-time matching. Microsoft is explicit that these guard against accidents, not malicious patterns, and that patterns must never be built from untrusted input.

The outage that made the point. On 2 July 2019 Cloudflare deployed, at 13:42 UTC (Coordinated Universal Time), a change to a WAF (web application firewall) managed rule for cross-site scripting detection. The rule contained a regular expression ending in .*(?:.*=.*) that backtracked enormously; CPUs (central processing units) serving HTTP (Hypertext Transfer Protocol) and HTTPS (HTTP Secure) traffic across the network went to nearly 100 per cent, and visitors to Cloudflare sites saw 502 errors for 27 minutes. The WAF ran on Lua using PCRE, which had no protection against a runaway expression. Cloudflare inspected all 3,868 managed rules for similar patterns and planned performance profiling of every rule in its test suite and a move to RE2 or the Rust regex engine, both of which have run-time guarantees.

In network and security products. F5's DevCentral guidance on iRules is that the regexp, regsub and matches_regex commands are fairly CPU intensive, and that the equals, contains, starts_with and ends_with operators or glob matching do the same job significantly faster when the pattern is simple. FortiGate shows the other trap, the confusion between glob and regex: in its web content filter the regex forti*.com matches fortiii.com but not fortinet.com, because the star repeats the preceding character instead of standing for any text, and an unanchored URL (Uniform Resource Locator) filter entry such as fa matches every URL that contains those two letters. The habits that follow: anchor, escape literal dots, prefer a literal or glob match when it is enough, use an atomic group or a linear-time engine for untrusted input, and test in the engine that will run the pattern.

replay-attack.def: Capturing a valid message and sending it again to produce an unauthorized effect.
replay-attack.context: In a replay attack the adversary need not decrypt anything, just resend a captured, still-valid request, like replaying an authentication token. Nonces, timestamps, and one-time values defeat it by making each message good only once.

responsible-disclosure.def: Reporting a vulnerability privately to the vendor and giving them time to fix it before going public.
responsible-disclosure.context: Also called coordinated disclosure, it balances two goods: users get a patch, and the flaw does not become a public weapon on day one. Practices vary on the deadline, but the principle is give the fix a head start over the exploit.

reverse-proxy.def: An intermediary that receives client requests as if it were the origin server and forwards them to one or more back-end servers, returning their responses as its own; the HTTP (Hypertext Transfer Protocol) standards call it a gateway.
reverse-proxy.context: A reverse proxy is the public face in front of the real servers: it can terminate Transport Layer Security (TLS), balance load, cache, and host a web application firewall (WAF), while the back ends stay hidden. Clients talk only to it, which is what makes it such a natural control point.
reverse-proxy.depth:
What it is, in the standard's words. HTTP (Hypertext Transfer Protocol) Semantics, Request for Comments (RFC) 9110 of June 2022, names three kinds of intermediary: proxy, gateway and tunnel. A gateway, "a.k.a. reverse proxy", acts as an origin server on its outbound side, towards the user agent, but translates the requests it receives and forwards them inbound to another server or servers; the same definition stood in RFC 7230 of June 2014, which RFC 9110 and RFC 9112 replaced. Every requirement on an origin server applies to that outbound side, while towards the back end it may speak any protocol it likes. A proxy, by contrast, is chosen by the client, usually through local configuration. That is the whole distinction: a forward proxy acts for the client and a reverse proxy acts for the server, and confusing the two makes documentation unreadable. The Apache HTTP Server documentation puts it practically: a reverse proxy appears to the client just like an ordinary web server, needs no client configuration, and decides where to send each request.

Why so much collapses onto it. RFC 9110 lists the classic reasons: encapsulating legacy or untrusted services, improving performance through "accelerator" caching, and partitioning or load balancing a service across machines; it also notes that content delivery networks (CDNs) are built on gateway caching. Apache adds publishing a server that sits behind a firewall and bringing several servers into one Uniform Resource Locator (URL) space. Transport Layer Security (TLS) termination, compression, request routing, header manipulation, rate limiting and web application firewalling join them because every request already passes through the same point. Consolidating them there is efficient, and it also makes the reverse proxy both the most useful and the most dangerous device in the path.

Two connections, not one. The client's Transmission Control Protocol (TCP) connection ends at the proxy and a second one starts towards the back end, so anything carried only by the first must be recreated deliberately. NGINX shows the defaults plainly: the client's Host and Connection fields are not passed; with HTTP/1.x it sends Host as $proxy_host, the name in proxy_pass, and Connection: close, so a back end that routes by virtual host sees the wrong name unless proxy_set_header Host $host is configured; a field set to an empty string is not sent at all; and proxy_http_version has defaulted to 1.1 only since NGINX 1.29.7, having been 1.0 before, which matters for keepalive to the back end. RFC 9110 also defines the Via field so that intermediaries can mark their passage, track forwards and avoid request loops.

The client's address is the first casualty. Behind a reverse proxy, and especially behind SNAT, which F5's documentation expands as secure network address translation, the back end sees the proxy as the client. The de facto fix is X-Forwarded-For: Apache's mod_proxy_http adds it with X-Forwarded-Host and X-Forwarded-Server and warns that each may already hold several comma-separated values. On F5 BIG-IP the HTTP profile has three proxy modes, Reverse (the default), Explicit and Transparent, and an option to insert the client address precisely for the SNAT case; it is off by default, and an F5 DevCentral walkthrough notes that BIG-IP does not sanitize headers the client already sent, it adds one more. RFC 7239 (June 2014) standardized the idea as Forwarded, with by, for, host and proto parameters, and is explicit that the field cannot be relied upon: any node, the client included, can write it, so only values added by proxies the server trusts mean anything, and the chain before the first trusted proxy means nothing.

Reading its errors. RFC 9110 gives two status codes that only an intermediary should produce. 502 Bad Gateway means the proxy received an invalid response from the server it forwarded to; 504 Gateway Timeout means it received no timely response. Either one says the client reached the proxy and the fault, or the wait, is behind it: a refused or reset back-end connection, a back end speaking the wrong protocol or TLS where plain HTTP was expected, or a proxy timeout shorter than the application's slowest request.

The subtle risk is disagreement about what a request means. A proxy usually sends many clients' requests over the same back-end connection, so proxy and back end must agree exactly where each request ends. When the proxy parses a request one way and the origin server another, the gap is exploitable: HTTP request smuggling, first documented by C. Linhart, A. Klein, R. Heled and S. Orrin of Watchfire in June 2005, hides a second request inside the first, typically by sending both Content-Length and Transfer-Encoding. James Kettle of PortSwigger revived the technique as "HTTP Desync Attacks" on 7 August 2019, presented at Black Hat and DEF CON, and later work showed that a front end speaking HTTP/2 to clients but downgrading to HTTP/1.1 towards the back end reopens the problem. RFC 9112 (June 2022) now says that when both length fields arrive, Transfer-Encoding wins, the message ought to be treated as an error, and an intermediary that forwards it must first remove Content-Length. Anywhere two implementations must agree on parsing, assume attackers will look for the seam.

Neighbours. A load balancer is a reverse proxy when it terminates HTTP; a layer 4 TCP proxy relays bytes and never parses requests; a CDN is a distributed reverse proxy cache; a web application firewall (WAF) is a policy engine that usually runs inside one; a forward proxy works for clients; and an interception proxy, which RFC 9110 warns is indistinguishable at protocol level from an on-path attacker, is something else again. The numbers worth remembering are few: RFC 9110 and RFC 9112 of June 2022 as the current HTTP texts, 502 and 504 as the two gateway errors, and RFC 7239 of June 2014 for Forwarded.

root-cause.def: The underlying reason a failure happened, beneath its visible symptoms: the condition that, if changed, would have prevented it and will prevent it from recurring. In complex systems it is usually several contributing causes rather than one.
root-cause.context: Root cause analysis (RCA) asks "why" past the first answer, with techniques such as the Five Whys, the Ishikawa fishbone diagram or a fault tree, until it reaches a condition that, if fixed, prevents recurrence. The discipline is resisting the tempting symptom-level fix that leaves the real cause in place. The counter-discipline, argued by safety researchers such as Richard Cook and by John Allspaw in operations, is resisting the single tidy cause: in complex systems failures need several contributors at once, and where an analysis stops says as much about the analysts as about the system.
root-cause.depth:
Root cause analysis (RCA) is the search for the condition beneath a failure's symptoms whose correction would prevent it from happening again. The distinction it draws is between the trigger and the reason: a link went down, a process crashed, a certificate expired, and each of those is an answer to the first question, not the last. Google's site reliability engineering (SRE) book builds the term into its definition of a postmortem, a written record of an incident, its impact, the actions taken to mitigate or resolve it, the root cause or causes, and the follow-up actions to prevent recurrence, and its reviewers ask of every draft whether the root cause was sufficiently deep. The plural in that sentence matters, and the rest of the story is about it.

The best-known method is the Five Whys, credited to Taiichi Ohno (1912 to 1990), who with Eiji Toyoda's backing helped establish the Toyota Production System and the basic framework of Just-in-Time. Ohno's own example, retold in countless training decks, is a machine that stopped: the fuse blew because of an overload; the overload came from a bearing that was not lubricated sufficiently; the lubrication pump was not pumping enough; its shaft was worn and rattling; and the shaft was worn because no strainer was fitted and metal scrap got in. The fix is the strainer, not a new fuse. Mark Graban pointed out in 2026 that the classic chain is really seven whys once its compressed steps are unpacked, and that a version on a Toyota website continued further: the filter had been removed to repair another robot because the stockroom had none, because the reorder point was set too low. Knowing when to stop is the whole skill. Graban quotes Tracey Richardson's test, deep enough when a countermeasure addresses the root cause and every symptom above it, too far when the problem's context has changed, and Jeff Liker's aim of a controllable cause that will make an impact.

The fishbone, or Ishikawa, diagram, named after its creator Kaoru Ishikawa and counted among the seven basic quality tools, adds breadth where the Five Whys is a single line. The problem is written at the head of a horizontal spine, category ribs branch from it, and a team brainstorms causes under each by asking why it happens, then why again for sub-causes. Ishikawa's generic categories are the 6 Ms: materials, machinery (including software), methods, measurement, manpower and mother nature, the environment, with money sometimes added as a seventh. For an outage the ribs translate readily into change, configuration, hardware, software, people, monitoring and supplier, and the diagram's value is that it forces a team to look in every direction before settling on the first plausible branch.

Fault tree analysis (FTA) works the other way, from the failure down, and is the method engineers use before anything has broken. The Fault Tree Handbook with Aerospace Applications of NASA (National Aeronautics and Space Administration), version 1.1 of August 2002, describes it as a deductive technique: specify an undesired state of the system, the top event, then find all realistic ways it can occur, drawing the parallel and sequential combinations of hardware failures, human errors and software errors as a tree of logic gates. An OR gate means the output occurs if one or more inputs occur; an AND gate means it occurs only if all of them do. The tree's minimal cut sets are the smallest combinations of basic events that produce the top event, and any minimal cut set with a single event is a single point of failure, the weak link to fix first; a cut set of identical components, such as identical valves, shows a common-cause failure that can defeat redundancy, which is the fault-tree reading of two high-availability firewalls running the same firmware bug. The handbook is candid about the limits: a fault tree is not a model of all possible failures, only of those the analyst judged realistic for one top event, and it is qualitative even when quantified. Its history runs from the aerospace and missile programmes of the early 1960s, where the method originated, through an early Apollo estimate of mission success so low that NASA set quantitative risk analysis aside until after the Challenger accident in 1986, to the nuclear industry after Three Mile Island in 1979 and the Nuclear Regulatory Commission's own Fault Tree Handbook, NUREG-0492, in 1981.

The strongest critique comes from safety science. Richard Cook's How Complex Systems Fail, a short treatise from the University of Chicago's Cognitive Technologies Laboratory dated 1998 to 2000, sets out why: complex systems are heavily defended, so catastrophe requires multiple failures and single point failures are not enough; they always contain latent failures and run in degraded mode; and post-accident attribution to a root cause is therefore fundamentally wrong, because each contributor is insufficient alone and only their combination produced the accident. Analyses that name one root cause, Cook writes, reflect less a technical understanding of failure than a social and cultural need to blame specific, localized forces, and hindsight makes the events before an accident look more obvious than they were to the people living through them.

John Allspaw carried the argument into web operations in 2014 with The Infinite Hows, a critique of the Five Whys as tunnel-visioned into a linear and simplistic account of how work gets done. Asking why produces first stories, which tend to end at a person and a judgement; asking how produces second stories about the tools, dashboards, pressures and conditions people were working with. He quotes Sidney Dekker's line that cause is something we construct, not find, and Nancy Leveson's observation that the selection of an initiating event is arbitrary: the chain stops where the analysts' stopping rule says, often at an event that is familiar, at the first point where something can be corrected, or at a cause that is politically acceptable. Human error is the most convenient such stop. The practical consequence is not to stop analysing, but to treat root cause as plural and provisional, and to record contributing factors with the evidence for each.

Google's postmortem culture is the operational form of that view. Its SRE book calls blameless postmortems a tenet of the discipline: a postmortem must identify the contributing causes without indicting any individual or team, assuming everyone acted with good intentions on the information they had. The practice came from healthcare and avionics, where mistakes can be fatal, and the reasoning is blunt: you cannot fix people, but you can fix the systems and processes that gave them incomplete or incorrect information, and an atmosphere of blame drives incidents under the rug. For a network or security engineer the methods fit different moments. A Five Whys chain suits a linear equipment fault, a fishbone a team brainstorm, a fault tree the design review that finds the single point of failure before it fails, and a contributing-factor analysis the incident in a system complex enough that no single fix would have prevented it. In every case the discipline from the old definition still holds: do not settle for the symptom-level fix that leaves the real cause in place, and do not settle for the one convenient cause that leaves the others there either.

rpki.def: Resource Public Key Infrastructure (RPKI): a hierarchy of certificates and signed records, following the way addresses are allocated, that lets routers check whether an autonomous system is authorized to announce a given address block in the Border Gateway Protocol (BGP).
rpki.context: Resource Public Key Infrastructure (RPKI), described in Request for Comments (RFC) 6480, attaches cryptographic proof of who may originate which prefixes, so a router can reject bogus Border Gateway Protocol (BGP) announcements. It is the main defence against route hijacks, accidental or malicious. The holder of an address block publishes a Route Origin Authorization (ROA); validating software checks the signatures and hands routers a plain list; each router marks a route Valid, Invalid or NotFound, and dropping the Invalid ones is a policy the operator has to configure. It checks the origin of a route, not its path.
rpki.depth:
Resource Public Key Infrastructure (RPKI) lets an address holder publish a signed statement of which autonomous system (AS) is authorized to originate its prefixes, so a router can reject an announcement that contradicts it. It is the first meaningful defence against the routing hijacks that the trust model of the Border Gateway Protocol (BGP) otherwise permits. Request for Comments (RFC) 6480, written by Matt Lepinski and Stephen Kent of BBN Technologies in February 2012, describes three elements: the public key infrastructure itself, digitally signed routing objects, and a distributed repository that holds both. The certificates follow the existing allocation hierarchy, with the Internet Assigned Numbers Authority (IANA) at the root, the five regional internet registries (RIRs) below it and national or local registries below them. They are X.509 certificates carrying the RFC 3779 extensions that list address blocks and AS numbers, and they attest to holdings, not to identity: in the RFC's words the RPKI provides authorization, but not authentication. Each relying party chooses its own trust anchors; in practice these are the RIRs, each reached through a Trust Anchor Locator (RFC 8630).

The object that matters day to day is the Route Origin Authorization (ROA), whose current profile is RFC 9582 (May 2024, replacing RFC 6482). A ROA names a single AS and a list of prefixes, each with an optional maxLength. Without maxLength the AS is authorized for the exact prefix only; the RFC's example is 203.0.113.0/24 with maxLength 26, which authorizes the /24, either /25 and any /26 inside it, but not a /27. A prefix legitimately announced by several networks needs a ROA for each, and a ROA for AS 0 declares that a prefix should not be routed at all (RFC 6483). The advice on maxLength has hardened: RFC 7115 asks for ROAs as precise as the announcements actually made, and RFC 9319 (October 2022) recommends avoiding maxLength except in specific cases, citing measurements of June 2017 in which 84 per cent of the prefixes in ROAs that used it were open to a forged-origin sub-prefix hijack.

Routers do no cryptography. Every certification authority publishes its certificates, revocation lists, manifests and ROAs at a repository, fetched with rsync, which RFC 6481 made mandatory, or with the RPKI Repository Delta Protocol (RRDP, RFC 8182, July 2017) over HTTPS (Hypertext Transfer Protocol Secure). Relying-party software such as Routinator from NLnet Labs downloads the lot, verifies every chain back to a trust anchor and reduces the result to a list of Validated ROA Payloads (VRPs), each a prefix, a maximum length and an origin AS. Routers pull that list over the RPKI-to-Router protocol (RFC 6810 of January 2013, version 1 in RFC 8210 of September 2017), on TCP (Transmission Control Protocol) port 323, or 324 over TLS (Transport Layer Security). RFC 7115 is blunt about the consequence: the router trusts the cache, so caches belong close to the routers, more than one of them, over protected transport. Local exceptions are written in SLURM (Simplified Local Internet Number Resource Management) files (RFC 8416), which filter or add entries without touching the global data.

The check itself is RFC 6811 (January 2013), and it has two tests. A route is covered by a VRP when the VRP's prefix is the same as the route's or less specific; it is matched when it is covered, its length does not exceed the maximum length, and its origin AS, the rightmost AS in the AS_PATH, equals the VRP's. No covering VRP gives NotFound; at least one match gives Valid; covered but never matched gives Invalid. The state alone changes nothing: RFC 6811 forbids excluding a route because of it unless the operator configures that, and RFC 8481 (September 2018) repeated the rule after vendors got it wrong. RFC 7115 explains what the policy has to be. NotFound must be accepted for a long time yet, and accepting Invalid at a low preference is often the same as treating it as Valid, because a more specific Invalid route wins by longest match whatever its preference. On Cisco IOS XE the pieces are bgp rpki server tcp for the cache and bgp bestpath prefix-validate allow-invalid for the exception, and the state can be passed to internal peers in an extended community (the announce rpki state option).

Its limits are worth stating precisely. Origin validation confirms who announced a prefix, not that the path is genuine, so a hijack that forges a plausible path, ending in the authorized AS, can still succeed; path validation is a separate and much less deployed problem. BGPsec (RFC 8205, September 2017) signs the path at every AS, and Autonomous System Provider Authorization (ASPA) records each network's providers in the RPKI, but on 12 November 2026 the ASPA profile was still an Internet-Draft in last call. Route leaks, in which a route is passed on in violation of the business relationship, are addressed by the roles of RFC 9234, not by ROAs. The Cloudflare incident of 27 June 2024 showed both gaps at once: the Brazilian network Eletronet (AS267613) originated 1.1.1.1/32, Invalid against Cloudflare's ROA, and several networks accepted it all the same, one Tier 1 provider as a blackhole route; at the same moment Nova (AS262504) leaked 1.1.1.0/24 with Cloudflare's AS13335 still at the origin, a route no origin check could fault. The resolver became unreachable from more than 300 networks in 70 countries.

The incidents that built the case are older. On 24 February 2008 Pakistan Telecom (AS17557) announced 208.65.153.0/24, a more specific piece of YouTube's 208.65.152.0/22; PCCW Global (AS3491) passed it on, and from 18:47 UTC (Coordinated Universal Time) YouTube's traffic went to Pakistan. On 24 June 2019 more specific routes produced by a BGP optimizer at DQE Communications (AS33154) reached Verizon (AS701) through a customer and spread; Cloudflare noted that its prefixes were signed for a maximum length of 20, so any network validating origins would have dropped the leaked routes.

Adoption is uneven, and a ROA only protects where the receiving network actually checks. Signing has become the norm: on 1 May 2024 the majority of IPv4 (Internet Protocol version 4) routes were covered by ROAs for the first time, and the monitor of the National Institute of Standards and Technology (NIST) counted 71.29 per cent of 1,274,930 IPv4 prefix-origin pairs Valid on 11 November 2026, with 27.19 per cent NotFound and 1.52 per cent Invalid, against 12.51 per cent Valid in April 2019. Filtering is harder to measure; Cloudflare's Is BGP safe yet? list names the networks that drop Invalid routes, the Tier 1 carrier Sparkle (AS6762) being its newest entry, on 3 February 2026, and the Mutually Agreed Norms for Routing Security (MANRS) include publishing routing information in the RPKI among their actions. In Brazil NIC.br, the national registry, opened RPKI to operators in December 2019 with NLnet Labs' Krill and without a hosted service: each operator runs its own certification authority, signed by NIC.br's, which is signed by the registry for Latin America and the Caribbean (LACNIC), and may publish through NIC.br's repository. There were 25 such installations and over 100 ROAs after one week.

The operational risk is self-inflicted. A ROA that omits an AS that really announces the prefix, or one that expires, turns the holder's own routes Invalid in every network that filters, which is why RFC 7115 asks for ROAs for every legitimate origin and for tools that warn before a ROA or certificate expires. RPKI is a real improvement and not a solution, which is the honest description of most incremental security in a system nobody can redesign.

rubber-duck-debugging.def: Debugging by explaining your code, line by line, to an inanimate object.
rubber-duck-debugging.context: Popularized by "The Pragmatic Programmer", the trick works because articulating the problem out loud forces you to make your assumptions explicit, and the wrong one usually surfaces mid-sentence. The duck is optional; the explaining is the point.
rubber-duck-debugging.depth:
Rubber duck debugging is explaining your problem, line by line, to an inanimate object, and the reason it works is not mystical. Articulating a system forces you to convert a vague internal model into explicit sequential statements, and the gaps you have been skipping over become audible the moment you have to say them out loud.

The name comes from The Pragmatic Programmer, where a programmer carried a duck and talked to it. The object is irrelevant and that is the point: a colleague works too, at the cost of their time, which is why experienced engineers apologize mid-sentence and walk away having answered themselves. The listener contributes nothing and is essential anyway.

The version worth internalizing is that this is an argument for writing. A bug report you write carefully often solves itself before you submit it, and a design document forces the same explicitness the duck does, at greater length and with a record. If you find yourself repeatedly solving problems the instant you start describing them, the lesson is not that ducks are magic. It is that your model was never as complete as it felt.

runbook.def: A documented, step-by-step procedure for carrying out a specific operational task or handling a known situation, written so that someone other than its author can follow it, and increasingly run as code.
runbook.context: A good runbook turns tribal knowledge into steps anyone on call can follow at 3 a.m.: preconditions, exact commands, the output to expect, checks, and the way back. The operational guidance of Amazon Web Services (AWS) defines it as a documented process to achieve a specific outcome, at its simplest a checklist, and sets it beside the playbook, the guide for investigating an incident and finding its cause. It is the difference between a calm, repeatable change and improvisation under pressure.
runbook.depth:
The Well-Architected guidance of Amazon Web Services (AWS) gives the plainest definition: a runbook is a documented process to achieve a specific outcome, a series of steps that someone follows to get something done, and at its simplest a checklist to complete a task. The same text traces the habit to the early days of aviation and lists what a runbook should hold beyond the steps: the desired outcome, the tools and permissions needed, how to handle errors and exceptions, and when and to whom to escalate. Runbooks belong in one central place, under version control, and updating them is part of change management rather than an afterthought. Its anti-patterns are recognizable in any operations team: relying on memory to complete each step, deploying changes manually without a checklist, different people performing the same process with different steps and different outcomes, and runbooks drifting out of sync with the systems and automation they describe. A runbook is not a policy, which says what must be true, nor a plan, which says who does what in a crisis; it is the procedure that makes one specific task come out the same every time.

The word sits next to playbook, and the two are used loosely enough to cause confusion. AWS draws the line by purpose: a runbook achieves an outcome, while a playbook is a step-by-step guide used to investigate an incident, scope its impact and identify a root cause, with an escalation plan for when no cause is found; when it finds one, the playbook should point to the runbook that resolves it. Google's site reliability engineering (SRE) books use playbook for the on-call guide attached to an alert, giving its severity and impact, debugging suggestions and actions that mitigate and resolve it, and say that whenever an alert is created a corresponding playbook entry usually is too. In security incident response, NIST (National Institute of Standards and Technology) Special Publication (SP) 800-61 revision 3, published in April 2025, says many organizations create playbooks as part of documenting their procedures, that playbooks provide actionable steps for people to perform in various scenarios, and that putting procedures in playbook form can make them more usable, citing the response playbooks of the United States Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency (CISA) as examples. Ansible uses playbook for something else again, an automation file written in YAML (YAML Ain't Markup Language). What matters in a team is to agree which word means what.

The case for writing them down is measured, not sentimental. In the introduction to Google's Site Reliability Engineering book, Benjamin Treynor Sloss writes that humans add latency to recovery, and that thinking through and recording the best practices ahead of time in a playbook produces roughly a threefold improvement in mean time to repair (MTTR) compared with winging it: the hero who knows everything does work, but a practiced on-call engineer armed with a playbook works much better. He adds the limit in the same breath: no playbook, however comprehensive, replaces engineers who can think on the fly, which is why Google pairs playbooks with exercises such as the Wheel of Misfortune, which prepares engineers to react to on-call events. The same chapter estimates that roughly 70 per cent of outages are due to changes in a live system, which is why the runbook around a change matters as much as the change.

The value of a runbook is in being followable by someone who was not there when it was written, and that is a higher bar than it sounds: a runbook written by the expert usually omits exactly the steps the expert no longer notices performing. The test is whether someone else has executed it, ideally in a drill rather than an incident. NIST makes the same point for incident procedures: they can be tested or exercised periodically to verify their accuracy and used to train new staff, and while no organization can write a procedure for every situation, it should cover the most common incident types and the processes that may be urgently needed in an emergency, with redeploying the organization's primary authentication platform as its example. An unexecuted runbook is a documented intention, and the failure mode is discovering mid-outage that it names a hostname that changed, a credential nobody holds, or a step whose output no longer looks like the example.

Runbooks decay with the systems they describe. Google's SRE workbook puts it bluntly: details in playbooks go out of date at the same rate as the production environment changes, so with daily releases a playbook may need updating on any given day. Its authors record a real disagreement about form, some SREs keeping entries general so that they change slowly (one entry for every high error-rate alert on remote procedure calls, read with an architecture diagram), others writing step-by-step entries to reduce human variability and drive down MTTR, and advise each team at least to agree on the minimal structured details every entry must have. They also ask that each alert have its entry, that pages link to the relevant monitoring consoles, and that the on-call engineer update the entry with fresh information whenever the corresponding page fires. Runbooks that are rehearsed and edited after use stay correct; runbooks that are written and filed decay silently.

The end state of a good runbook is often to stop being read by people. The same workbook says that if a playbook is a deterministic list of commands the on-call engineer runs every time a particular alert fires, it should be automation instead, and Google defines the work such lists represent as toil: manual, repetitive, automatable, tactical, without enduring value, and growing linearly with the service, with an advertised goal of keeping it below half of each engineer's time. AWS gives the same direction in its own terms, start with runbooks that are short and frequently used, script their steps, and expect most runbooks to be automated in some way over time, and for playbooks start by automating the discovery steps of low-risk incidents. The platforms use the word literally: an AWS Systems Manager Automation runbook is a sequence of steps, each built around a single action, whose output can feed a later step, and Azure Automation runs runbooks written in PowerShell 7.6, 7.4 or 5.1, in Python 3.10 or as graphical workflows. Automation does not remove the need for the written version; it moves it into code review, and keeps the human runbook for the cases the automation does not handle.

The cost of the missing runbook is on public record. The United States Securities and Exchange Commission's order on Knight Capital describes a deployment of new trading code that began on 27 July 2012 in stages; a technician did not copy the code to one of the eight servers of its order router, no second technician reviewed the deployment, and Knight had no written procedures that required such a review. On 1 August 2012 the forgotten server sent millions of orders into the market over 45 minutes and Knight lost more than 460 million dollars. The Commission's own conclusion is the argument for runbooks in one sentence: a written procedure requiring a simple double-check of the deployment could have identified that a server had been missed. For a network or security change the same discipline applies to everything wrapped around the commands: what is verified before anything is touched, the order of steps, the signal that means stop, and a way back that was written down and tested before it was needed.

salt.def: A salt is a value, unique per record and usually random, combined with a password or other input before it is hashed or passed to a key derivation function, so that identical inputs give different results and work precomputed for one cannot be reused on another. It is stored in the clear beside the hash.
salt.context: Salting means two people with the same password get different hashes, which defeats rainbow tables and makes precomputation useless; the attacker has to guess each record separately. A salt need not be secret, only unique; a secret companion value kept away from the database is called a pepper. The United States National Institute of Standards and Technology (NIST) now requires at least 32 bits, chosen to avoid collisions and stored with each hash, and modern password hashing schemes such as bcrypt, scrypt, Argon2id and PBKDF2 (Password-Based Key Derivation Function 2) take the salt as a parameter, which most libraries generate automatically.
salt.depth:
A salt is what stops an attacker from cracking a thousand passwords for the price of one. The glossary of the United States National Institute of Standards and Technology (NIST) defines it, in its password guidance, as a non-secret value used in a cryptographic process, usually to ensure that the results of computations for one instance cannot be reused by an attacker. Without a salt, identical passwords hash to identical values, so one table of precomputed hashes maps hashes back to passwords across every account and every breached database at once. The same glossary records other uses of the word, which share the idea of making one computation distinct from the next: the salt of the RSASSA-PSS (Rivest-Shamir-Adleman Signature Scheme with Appendix, Probabilistic Signature Scheme) signature scheme, and the salt of a key derivation, a byte string that may be secret or not and serves as the key of a message authentication code (MAC). What a salt is not matters as much: it is not a secret, it is not a pepper, and it does not make a weak or fast hash strong.

The idea is older than most of the field. Robert Morris and Ken Thompson of Bell Laboratories described it in Password Security: A Case History, in the Communications of the ACM (Association for Computing Machinery) of November 1979. When a Unix password was first set, the password program read a 12-bit random number from the real-time clock, appended it to the password and stored both this salt and the 64-bit result of the encryption in the password file; at login the salt was read back and appended again. They were exact about the effect. Salting did not make finding any individual password harder, starting from scratch, but it multiplied by 4,096, 2 to the power 12, the work of testing one guess against a large collection of passwords, because each password now had 4,096 encrypted versions. The same scheme slowed each guess by iterating the DES (Data Encryption Standard) algorithm 25 times. Today's crypt(5) manual still lists it as descrypt, the original method of Unix V7, and judges that with only 4,096 salts, passwords truncated to 8 characters and cheap DES, any passphrase it hashed can be recovered.

Adding a unique random value to each password before hashing destroys the economy of precomputation, and the crypt(5) manual lists three separate effects. A guess can no longer be hashed once and checked against every account; the computation has to be repeated for each one. Two accounts with the same passphrase can no longer be spotted without cracking one of them. And tables of precomputed hashes need an entry for every possible salt, which makes them impractically large. Precomputation had become very efficient. Philippe Oechslin's rainbow tables (CRYPTO 2003), refining the time-memory trade-off Martin Hellman described in 1980, cracked 99.9 per cent of all alphanumeric Windows LanManager password hashes, a space of 2 to the power 37, in 13.6 seconds using 1.4 GB of tables; the method only works, as Oechslin wrote, when the hashing scheme uses the same plaintext and method for every password, which is exactly what a salt prevents. The cost of skipping it is on the record: LinkedIn's 2012 breach, which surfaced in May 2016 with 164,611,595 accounts, held passwords stored as SHA-1 (Secure Hash Algorithm 1) hashes without salt, and according to Have I Been Pwned the vast majority were cracked within days.

What a salt does not do is just as important. As Morris and Thompson noted, it does not make one password harder to find: the salt is stored beside the hash, in plain view, and the design assumes the attacker has it. Its value lies entirely in being unique per record, which pushes the attacker back to attacking each account individually; the Open Worldwide Application Security Project (OWASP) puts it as cracking time that grows in direct proportion to the number of hashes. A salted fast hash still falls quickly to a dictionary run against one account. That is why NIST's 2025 revision of its authentication guidelines, Special Publication (SP) 800-63B-4, requires passwords to be salted and hashed with a password hashing scheme that takes three inputs, the password, the salt and a cost factor, sets the cost as high as practical, and warns that offline attackers can compute many billions of hashes per second. OWASP's current minimums are Argon2id with 19 MiB of memory, two iterations and one degree of parallelism; scrypt with a cost parameter of 2 to the power 17, block size 8 and parallelism 1; bcrypt with a work factor of at least 10 and its 72-byte password limit; or, where FIPS 140 (Federal Information Processing Standard 140) compliance is required, PBKDF2 (Password-Based Key Derivation Function 2) with HMAC-SHA-256 and at least 600,000 iterations.

The standards agree on size and storage. SP 800-63B-4 requires a salt of at least 32 bits, chosen to minimize collisions between stored hashes so that no two accounts share one, and requires the salt and the hash to be stored for each password, together with a reference to the scheme and its cost factor so that hashes can be migrated later. Request for Comments (RFC) 8018, the PKCS #5 (Public-Key Cryptography Standards number 5) specification of password-based cryptography (January 2017), asks for at least eight octets and explains the arithmetic: a 64-bit salt gives up to 2 to the power 64 keys per password, and by the birthday paradox collisions become significant only after about 2 to the power 32 keys. It also suggests that a salt can carry a non-random octet saying what the derived key is for, so that a salt taken from one operation cannot be replayed into another. RFC 9106 on Argon2 (September 2021) recommends 16 bytes, unique per password, calls 128 bits sufficient for all applications and 64 acceptable under space constraints. The crypt formats used in /etc/shadow write the salt into the stored string itself, which consists of a prefix, options, the salt and the hash: bcrypt ($2b$) uses 128 bits, sha512crypt ($6$) 6 to 96 bits with a default of 5,000 rounds that the manual calls too low for modern hardware, md5crypt ($1$) 6 to 48 bits, and yescrypt ($y$) up to 512 bits with 128 or more recommended. The manual's rule is the simple one: choose the salt at random for each user.

A pepper, by contrast, is a secret kept outside the database, and the two are complementary rather than alternatives. SP 800-63B-4 says verifiers should add an iteration of keyed hashing or encryption with a secret key known only to the verifier, generated by an approved random bit generator, stored separately from the hashed passwords and preferably used inside a hardware security module (HSM) or a trusted execution environment; while that key stays secret, brute force against a stolen password file is impractical. OWASP describes the same value as a pepper, shared by all stored passwords rather than unique to each, not public, kept in a secrets vault or HSM, and adds that on its own a pepper provides no additional security characteristics: it is defence in depth on top of salting and slow hashing, and changing it means rehashing at the next login.

Beyond passwords, salts appear wherever a key is derived. HKDF, the HMAC-based (hash-based message authentication code) Extract-and-Expand Key Derivation Function of RFC 5869 (May 2010, H. Krawczyk and P. Eronen), takes an optional salt, a non-secret random value that, unlike the input keying material, can be reused; if none is given, it uses a string of zeros as long as the hash output. The RFC stresses that a salt adds significantly to the strength of the construction, that ideally it is random and as long as the hash output, and that even a weaker salt still helps; the second version of the Internet Key Exchange (IKEv2) derives its salt from public nonces exchanged by the two peers. PBKDF2 does the same for keys derived from passphrases, and the RSA-PSS signature scheme randomizes each signature with a salt of its own. In all of these the salt separates one derivation from another; it never replaces the secret.

Network equipment shows the same history in its password types. Cisco's guidance on protecting secrets, updated in March 2026, says type 7 is a reversible cipher with a publicly known key and must be treated as plain text, that type 5 (MD5, Message Digest 5) should not be used and is converted to type 9 automatically from IOS XE 16.12, and recommends the salted, iterated types: type 8, PBKDF2 with SHA-256 (the 256-bit Secure Hash Algorithm), an 80-bit salt and 20,000 iterations, and the preferred type 9, scrypt with an 80-bit salt. On Linux, the same reading of a shadow entry applies: the characters between the second and third dollar signs are the salt, which is why two users with the same password still have different lines.

The pitfalls repeat. One salt shared by every record is not a salt in the sense that matters: it blocks generic tables but lets an attacker build one table for the whole site and still shows which accounts share a password, the exact properties a per-record value exists to remove. Salts that are too short collide, which RFC 8018's birthday arithmetic quantifies, and the original Unix salt drawn from a clock is a reminder that uniqueness, not secrecy, is the requirement. A salted but fast hash, such as the SHA-1 and MD5 schemes of many leaked databases, is still cheap to attack account by account. The numbers worth remembering are 12 bits and 4,096 variants in 1979, at least 32 bits for NIST, 64 bits for PKCS #5, 128 bits for Argon2 and bcrypt, and 2 to the power 37 LanManager hashes inverted in 13.6 seconds by a rainbow table in 2003.

serverless.def: A model where you run code without managing servers, and pay only while it runs.
serverless.context: Serverless (often functions as a service, like AWS Lambda) hides the machines entirely: the platform provisions, scales, and bills per invocation. "Serverless" is a slight misnomer, servers still exist, you just do not operate them.

service-mesh.def: A dedicated layer that manages service-to-service communication inside a cluster.
service-mesh.context: A service mesh (such as Istio or Linkerd) moves retries, encryption, routing, and observability out of application code and into sidecar proxies, giving uniform control over east-west traffic. It trades some complexity for consistency across many services.

shellcode.def: A small, self-contained piece of machine code an exploit runs, classically to open a shell.
shellcode.context: Shellcode is written to be compact and position-independent because it executes in whatever cramped space the exploit gives it. The name is historical, its job today may be anything, but the craft, tiny code that runs from nowhere, is the same.

shift-left.def: Moving testing, security, and quality checks earlier in the development process.
shift-left.context: Shifting left means catching problems while they are cheap, at design and commit time, rather than in production. In security it puts scanning and threat modelling into the pipeline; the whole idea is that the earlier you find a defect, the less it costs to fix.
shift-left.depth:
Shift left is the argument that quality and security work should happen earlier in the development timeline, where the diagram conventionally runs left to right from design to production. The economics behind it are real: a design flaw caught in a review costs a conversation, the same flaw caught in production costs an incident, a patch and a postmortem.

The implementation is where it goes wrong. Shifting left is often interpreted as moving the same gates earlier without moving the capability, so developers inherit security scanning they were never trained to interpret, on tools chosen by someone else, producing findings they cannot action. The work moved left; the expertise did not follow it, and the result is alert fatigue arriving at a new address.

The version that works treats it as enablement rather than delegation. That means tools integrated where developers already work rather than in a separate portal, defaults that are secure so the easy path is the right one, findings that explain the fix rather than naming the category, and a security team that stays available for the judgement calls. Shifting left without shifting support is just relocating the bottleneck onto people with less context.

sidecar.def: A helper container that runs alongside a main application to add capabilities without changing it.
sidecar.context: The sidecar pattern attaches concerns like proxying, logging, or TLS termination as a neighbour container, so the app stays focused on its own job. It is the building block of the service mesh, where the sidecar handles all network traffic.

slo.def: A concrete target for how reliable a service should be, like 99.9% of requests succeeding.
slo.context: A Service Level Objective turns "be reliable" into a measurable goal, and the gap between it and perfection becomes an error budget you can spend on change. It gives teams a shared, honest way to balance new features against stability.

smishing.def: Phishing carried out over SMS text messages.
smishing.context: Smishing is phishing's mobile cousin: a text posing as your bank or a delivery service, luring you to a fake site or a malicious app. "Vishing" is the voice-call equivalent. The channel changes; the social-engineering play does not.

snafu.def: Wartime slang for a situation that is a mess, yet routinely so.
snafu.context: The acronym spells out to "Situation Normal, All Fouled Up" (the polite version), coined in the US military in World War II. Its bite is the word "normal": the chaos is expected, which is exactly why it still fits operations work.
snafu.depth:
SNAFU is military slang from the Second World War, standing for situation normal, all fouled up in the printable version, and the sharpness is entirely in the first two words. It does not describe a disaster. It describes the ordinary state of affairs, in which things are broken and everyone proceeds anyway.

That is why it transferred so cleanly to technology operations. Anyone who has run infrastructure recognizes the sentiment immediately: there are always open incidents, deferred upgrades and known-bad workarounds, and the system runs regardless. Calling that situation normal is not cynicism, it is accuracy, and pretending otherwise is how organizations end up surprised by conditions they had documented for years.

It sits alongside FUBAR in the same lineage, and the pair mark a scale. SNAFU is the baseline, chronic and survivable. FUBAR is the state past recovery, where the correct response is to stop repairing and start replacing. Knowing which one you are actually in is a genuinely useful judgement during an incident, and the vocabulary a generation of soldiers invented for it has outlasted the machines it was first applied to.

soc.def: The team and facility responsible for continuously monitoring and defending an organization's security: a security operations centre (SOC) watches for attacks that get past preventive controls, investigates what it finds and coordinates the response.
soc.context: A security operations centre (SOC) watches the alerts, investigates incidents and coordinates response, often around the clock, usually fed by a SIEM (security information and event management) platform that aggregates logs. It is where the blue team's continuous work actually lands. The United Kingdom's National Cyber Security Centre (NCSC) states the purpose without decoration: prevention is not always possible, so the SOC limits the damage by detecting and responding to the attacks that get through. It can be staffed in house, bought from a managed security service provider (MSSP) or split between the two, and it should be sized to the threat the organization actually faces. The same three letters also name the System and Organization Controls (SOC) reports of the American Institute of Certified Public Accountants, such as SOC 2: audit reports on a service organization's controls, which are a different thing altogether.
soc.depth:
What it is, and what it is not. The United Kingdom's National Cyber Security Centre (NCSC) opens its guidance on building a security operations centre (SOC) by noting that SOCs vary widely in scope, that most are responsible for detecting and responding to cyber attacks, and that many also take on vulnerability assessment, compliance activities and system configuration. The function is the point, not the room: a SOC is a set of people with defined services, data and procedures, whether they sit together on a watch floor, work a rota from home or work for a provider. It is not a product, although products are sold under its name. It is not a network operations centre (NOC), which watches availability and performance; the SOC watches for an adversary, and a fault a NOC closes as resolved can be the very event the SOC needed to see. Nor is it everywhere the same thing as the computer security incident response team (CSIRT): in some organizations the SOC detects and hands over, in others the same people run the response. The National Institute of Standards and Technology (NIST) reflects that variety in Special Publication (SP) 800-61 Revision 3, its incident response recommendations of April 2025: incident handlers may be on staff, on contract (its example is outsourcing a security operations centre to a managed security service provider, MSSP) or available when needed from a parent organization, a services firm or law enforcement, and many organizations combine all three.

The other SOC. The American Institute of Certified Public Accountants (AICPA) uses the same letters for System and Organization Controls (SOC), a suite of services that certified public accountants provide on the system-level controls of a service organization or the entity-level controls of other organizations. A SOC 2 report is the document a customer asks a cloud or software provider for before signing, and when the AICPA's page was read in November 2026 it had proposed 2027 SOC 2 Trust Services Criteria out for comment. The two meet in practice, since an auditor examining a provider may test whether it monitors and responds to security events, but one is an attestation and the other is an operational team; in a contract, a security questionnaire or a job advertisement, the context decides which is meant.

What it does. The NCSC lists the services a SOC may offer, such as threat intelligence, content development (the detection logic itself), threat hunting and incident response, and organizes its guidance in five parts: the operating model, onboarding of systems and log sources (using attack trees to decide which logs are worth collecting), detection, threat intelligence, and incident response and management. The operating model starts from the threat profile, and the NCSC suggests the scale of threat actor sophistication in Structured Threat Information Expression (STIX) 2.1 for it, which runs from actors with little understanding to professional and state actors who develop new vulnerabilities and can affect the supply chain; detecting an attack by an actor at the Innovator level is far harder than one at the Expert level, and the guidance says plainly that it is acceptable to start with a lower capability and mature. Next come the most critical assets and their business context, so that monitoring can be prioritized, and a baseline of normal operation, built with the information technology operations team and the system designers, that enumerates user and data flows and how the security controls are meant to work.

Data and tooling. Indications of an attack are rarely isolated events on one component, so the NCSC calls a single platform where analysts can see and query the logs of every onboarded system invaluable; in most SOCs that platform is a security information and event management (SIEM) system, fed by firewalls, intrusion prevention, endpoint detection and response (EDR) agents, identity providers and cloud services. On it, use cases can be temporal (actions over a period) or spatial (actions across the estate). A concrete example of the raw material: a FortiGate whose intrusion prevention system (IPS) sensor is set to scan outgoing connections to botnet sites writes a log with the event type botnet and the message Botnet C&C Communication when a host reaches a known command-and-control address, and that is the kind of event a SOC ingests, enriches and triages. The NCSC notes that many SOCs give analysts runbooks so that they react promptly, and that this is contentious, because each alert should merit its own investigation by a capable analyst; security orchestration, automation and response (SOAR) platforms push the same idea further by automating enrichment and the repeatable steps of a response.

Why it became continuous. NIST's April 2025 revision explains why the old model gave way. Its 2012 predecessor drew incident response as a circular life cycle performed by a separate team, at a time when incidents were relatively rare, narrow in scope and usually handled within a day or two. Today, it says, incidents occur frequently, cause far more damage and can take weeks or months to recover from, so incident response has to be integrated across the organization's operations and lessons shared as soon as they are identified. A SOC is that integration made permanent. MITRE codified the practice in a book on the subject in 2014 and published the second edition, '11 Strategies of a World-Class Cybersecurity Operations Center' by Kathryn Knerler, Ingrid Parker and Carson Zimmerman, as a free download on 31 March 2022, adding material on operationalizing threat-oriented defence with cyber threat intelligence and on telling the SOC's story through metrics. NIST's glossary now cites the term from several of its publications, among them SP 800-53 Revision 5, SP 800-82 Revision 3 and SP 800-61 Revision 3.

What goes wrong. The most common failure is volume. Bushra Alahmadi, Louise Axon and Ivan Martinovic of the University of Oxford surveyed 20 SOC practitioners, who confirmed high false-positive rates requiring manual validation, then interviewed 21; their paper at USENIX Security 2022 found that most so-called false positives were benign triggers, true alarms explained by legitimate behaviour in the environment, and that the tedium of validating them leads to alarm burnout and, eventually, desensitization. The best-known consequence is Target in 2013: the US Senate Commerce Committee's majority staff report of 26 March 2014 records that the company's FireEye system raised urgent alerts with each installation of the data exfiltration malware between 30 November and 3 December, that the security team neither reacted nor allowed the software to delete the malware automatically, and that an alert with the generic name malware.binary could have been read as a false positive if the system alarmed frequently. The NCSC adds a quieter failure: a baseline taken from a system that is already compromised will include the attacker's traffic as normal, and the attack may never be detected.

Keeping it honest. The NCSC's prescription is the minimum number of alerts, so that each one that fires can be properly investigated; triage feedback that refines the detection logic; allow lists that are strictly bounded by object and time, so that they do not become a permanent hole in monitoring; and a lifecycle with regular reviews of the alerts that fire most, with the SOC cautiously open to removing those that mostly raise false positives. A use case that has never fired is not necessarily invalid, which is why the guidance recommends testing the SOC with red team exercises, where an authorized team simulates a non-destructive attack, and purple team exercises, where the same work is done alongside the SOC to close gaps as they are found. It also warns that the catalogue of detections must itself be protected, because in an attacker's hands it is a map of what will not be seen. Outsourcing moves the work but not the decisions: NIST places high-impact response actions, such as shutting down or rebuilding critical services, with the organization's leadership.

Neighbours. The blue team is the defensive role in exercises; the SOC is where that role works every day. Detection engineering produces the rules the SOC runs, alert fatigue is what happens when they are not maintained, and dwell time, the interval from compromise to detection, is the most honest single measure of how well the whole arrangement works. Incident response may live inside the SOC or next to it, and a post-incident review is where its lessons are turned into changes. MITRE ATT&CK, which the NCSC recommends for reasoning about coverage alongside threat modelling, gives the SOC, its tooling and its testers one vocabulary for adversary behaviour.

soc2.def: A report in the System and Organization Controls suite of services of the AICPA (American Institute of Certified Public Accountants), in which a CPA (certified public accountant) examines a service organization's controls relevant to security, availability, processing integrity, confidentiality or privacy.
soc2.context: The AICPA describes System and Organization Controls not as a standard but as a suite of service offerings that CPAs may provide on the controls of a service organization, and it promulgates the professional standards for those engagements. A SOC 2 report evaluates controls against the Trust Services Criteria (security, availability, processing integrity, confidentiality and privacy) and is commonly requested by customers before trusting a vendor with their data. It is evidence of process, not a one-time certificate of perfection.

social-engineering.def: Manipulating people, rather than technology, to gain access or information.
social-engineering.context: It is the technique that no patch closes, because the vulnerability is a human decision rather than a line of code. In threat-intelligence terms it is the classic attack vector and one of the most common techniques in any actor's tactics, techniques and procedures (TTPs): pretexting (inventing a believable role), phishing and its targeted cousins, baiting and tailgating are all procedures under it. The defence is correspondingly human: awareness training, verification habits, and processes that do not depend on any one person choosing correctly under pressure, which is why security is a process rather than a product.
social-engineering.depth:
What the term covers. The National Institute of Standards and Technology (NIST) carries several definitions in its glossary. The narrow one, from Special Publication (SP) 800-82, is an attempt to trick someone into revealing information, such as a password, that can be used to attack systems or networks. The broad one, from the Digital Identity Guidelines, is the act of deceiving an individual into revealing sensitive information, obtaining unauthorized access or committing fraud by associating with the individual to gain confidence and trust. The control catalogue SP 800-53 adds the element that matters most in practice, getting someone to take an action, and lists the family: phishing, pretexting, impersonation, baiting, quid pro quo, thread-jacking, social media exploitation and tailgating. It separates all of these from social mining, which is collecting information about an organization to support a later attack. Social engineering is therefore a method and not a kind of malware or a single channel: MITRE ATT&CK states that all forms of phishing are electronically delivered social engineering, and the same deception works by telephone, at a reception desk or in a chat window.

How the frameworks file it. ATT&CK long spread the subject over several techniques. Phishing (T1566) delivers something, with sub-techniques for an attachment, a link, a third-party service and voice; Phishing for Information (T1598) differs in that the aim is to collect data from the victim, not to run code; Multi-Factor Authentication Request Generation (T1621) is the bombardment with push prompts, text messages and calls until a tired user accepts one, known as MFA (multi-factor authentication) fatigue. On 14 April 2026 ATT&CK added a technique of its own, Social Engineering (T1684): influencing users to take actions that result in unauthorized access, approval of changes, disclosure of sensitive information or execution of the adversary's instructions while minimizing technical indicators. Its two sub-techniques are Impersonation (T1684.001, the address to which the former T1656 now redirects) and Email Spoofing (T1684.002), and its description names the scenarios of the moment: executive, vendor and help desk pretexts, including voice interactions enabled by artificial intelligence (AI), aimed at password resets, MFA changes and financial approvals.

Why it works. The MITRE description lists the levers plainly: a convincing narrative, a reference to current events or to the victim's role, and urgency, including threats of repercussions for not complying. Robert Cialdini's catalogue of persuasion gives them names that fit almost every case: reciprocity, scarcity, authority, consistency, liking, social proof and unity. A pretext of authority plus scarcity of time is the standard pair, and the Brazilian banking federation's booklet on the subject notes the third ingredient, that the caller is always polite, cordial and friendly. Context does the rest. In the Twitter case of 2020 the callers were believed because employees working remotely really were having trouble with the virtual private network (VPN), and because the callers used personal information about the employees they phoned.

Where the term comes from. Its best-known popularizer is Kevin Mitnick. Testifying to the United States Senate Committee on Governmental Affairs on 2 March 2000, weeks after his release from prison on 21 January, he described his first line of attack as what he called a social engineering attack, which really means trying to manipulate somebody over the phone through deception, and said he was so successful with it that he rarely had to go towards a technical attack. He called the human element the weakest link in the security chain. His first book, The Art of Deception, subtitled Controlling the Human Element of Security and carrying a foreword by Steve Wozniak, came out in October 2002.
