The reason given is the broadcast storm: one broadcast to a closed User Datagram Protocol (UDP) port could make every machine on the segment send back a Destination Unreachable, and on a large Ethernet the collisions could make the network useless for a second or more.

What goes wrong: unicast that behaves like broadcast. Unknown unicast flooding is the classic layer 2 fault that looks like a traffic problem and is really a table problem. Cisco's note on unicast flooding in campus networks names three causes. Asymmetric routing: return traffic takes a different path, the switch on the outbound path never sees the remote host transmit, its entry ages out while the router still holds an ARP entry for the same host, and every frame towards that host is flooded until it speaks again; the fix is to bring the router's ARP timeout and the switches' aging time close to each other. Spanning tree topology changes: each topology change notification shortens the aging time, so a port that flaps keeps flushing the table; the fix is PortFast on ports facing end devices, and finding the flapping port. And table overflow, sometimes deliberate in a MAC flooding attack, after which new addresses cannot be learned; the fix is port security. Broadcast, unknown unicast and multicast are flooded the same way, which is why storm control and overlay designs treat them as one class; RFC 7432, the Ethernet virtual private network (EVPN) specification of February 2015, calls it BUM (broadcast, unknown unicast or multicast) traffic.

Why unicast does not scale to audiences. Unicast cost grows with the number of receivers: the sender, or something near it, emits one copy per receiver, so a stream watched by a million people is a million streams leaving the origin. Multicast was designed to let the network make the copies instead, with the same best-effort delivery as unicast in RFC 1112's words, at the price of group state in every router and switch on the path. Across the public internet the industry mostly took the other route and kept unicast, moving the copies closer to the viewers in content delivery networks (CDNs). Inside a local area network the trade sometimes runs backwards: the Linux bridge can convert multicast to unicast per port, copying a packet once for each host that has joined the group and rewriting the destination to that host's MAC address, a feature its documentation intends for links such as Wi-Fi, where unicast frames are more reliable or more efficient than group frames.

Anycast is unicast with a twist. RFC 4291 takes anycast addresses from the unicast space and makes them syntactically indistinguishable from unicast; only the nodes that share one are configured to know. From the sender's side an anycast packet is an ordinary unicast packet, and the network delivers it to whichever holder its routing considers nearest. RFC 1546, written by C. Partridge, T. Mendez and W. Milliken at BBN in November 1993, spells out the consequence: anycasting is stateless, and the network has no obligation to deliver two successive packets to the same host. A User Datagram Protocol query can treat an anycast address exactly like a unicast one, which is why the Domain Name System (DNS) uses it so widely; the Transmission Control Protocol (TCP) is stateful, and if routing changes in the middle of a conversation the next segment can reach a different server that knows nothing of the connection. The numbers worth keeping are short: one bit at layer 2, three IPv6 address types and no broadcast, 2000::/3 for global unicast today, and one copy per receiver whenever the audience is more than one.

vlsm.def: Using different subnet sizes within the same network, sized to each segment's need.
vlsm.context: Variable-Length Subnet Masking abandons one-size-fits-all masks: a point-to-point link gets a tiny /30 while a user LAN gets a roomy /24, so addresses are not wasted. It depends on classless routing to carry the varied prefixes.
vlsm.depth:
VLSM means subnetting a network with masks of different lengths, so each subnet is sized to what it actually holds. Before it, every subnet in a network shared one mask, which forced the same allocation on a point-to-point link with two hosts and a floor with two hundred.

The waste was enormous and it compounded. A link needing two addresses consumed a block sized for the largest subnet in the plan, and across a large network that arithmetic ran into thousands of unusable addresses. Variable-length masks let a point-to-point link take a two-address block while a user floor takes what it needs, which is most of why IPv4 lasted as long as it did.

The design discipline it demands is allocation order. Assign the largest subnets first from the top of the range and work downward, because filling small blocks in first fragments the space and leaves no contiguous room for the large ones. That same ordering makes summarization possible later, since aggregating routes requires the blocks beneath a summary to be contiguous, and a network subnetted in whatever order requests arrived usually cannot be summarized at all.

vpn.def: A private network built across a shared or public one, usually as an encrypted, authenticated tunnel between two endpoints, so that remote users or whole sites communicate as if they were directly connected.
vpn.context: A virtual private network (VPN) wraps a connection so that it appears to originate from the VPN's endpoint, and is used to reach private corporate resources, to join sites, or to shield traffic on untrusted networks. It moves trust rather than removing it: whoever uses it trusts the VPN operator instead of the local network.
vpn.depth:
What the term covers. In the Internet Engineering Task Force's (IETF) own vocabulary, RFC (Request for Comments) 4026 of March 2005, virtual private network (VPN) is a generic term for using public or private networks to create groups of users that are separated from other users and communicate as if they were on a private network; encryption is explicitly an optional extra, outside the scope of the IETF's VPN working groups. That is why a service provider can sell a VPN with no cryptography in it at all: a BGP/MPLS IP VPN (Border Gateway Protocol over Multiprotocol Label Switching, RFC 4364, February 2006) keeps customers apart by routing. In enterprise and consumer use the word means something narrower, an encrypted and authenticated tunnel, in two shapes: remote access, one user's device to a network, and site-to-site, one network to another.

IPsec. The standards-track answer is Internet Protocol Security (IPsec), the security architecture for the Internet Protocol (IP) set out in RFC 4301 (December 2005). Its Encapsulating Security Payload (ESP, RFC 4303) is IP protocol 50. In transport mode it protects the next-layer protocol of a packet; in tunnel mode it protects a whole tunnelled IP packet, which is how two security gateways join sites, with one tunnel for all traffic or a separate one per connection. Keys and parameters are negotiated by the Internet Key Exchange (IKE), version 2 in RFC 7296 (October 2014, Internet Standard 79), on UDP (User Datagram Protocol) port 500; when a network address translator sits in the path, IKE and ESP move to UDP port 4500, with ESP encapsulated in UDP as RFC 3948 (January 2005) specifies. RFC 8221 (October 2017) sets the algorithm floor: AES-GCM and AES-CBC (Advanced Encryption Standard in Galois/Counter and cipher block chaining modes) MUST be implemented, ChaCha20-Poly1305 SHOULD, triple Data Encryption Standard (DES) SHOULD NOT and single DES MUST NOT. NIST (the National Institute of Standards and Technology) publishes the operational guide, SP 800-77 Revision 1, of June 2020.

The other tunnels. The Point-to-Point Tunneling Protocol (PPTP), documented in RFC 2637 (July 1999) by Ascend Communications and Microsoft, carried Point-to-Point Protocol (PPP) frames in an enhanced Generic Routing Encapsulation (GRE) header. Transport Layer Security (TLS) VPNs, sold as SSL (Secure Sockets Layer) VPNs, carry the tunnel inside a TLS session instead, which is what lets them use the web's own port. WireGuard, by Jason A. Donenfeld, takes the opposite design: it encapsulates IP packets over UDP with a fixed set of primitives, the Noise protocol framework, Curve25519, ChaCha20, Poly1305 and BLAKE2, and is meant to be implemented in very few lines of code and easily audited, in contrast to what its site calls the behemoths of IPsec and OpenVPN. It began on Linux and is now cross-platform.

The remote-access security model. The classic design authenticates a user once and then places the device on a network segment, so location quietly becomes the authorization decision: whoever gets through, with a phished password or a stolen laptop, inherits everything the segment can reach. NIST SP 800-207 (August 2020) describes zero trust as the refusal of exactly that, no implicit trust based solely on network location, and zero trust network access (ZTNA) products broker access per application instead. Split tunnelling is the other recurring decision. NIST SP 800-46 Revision 2 (July 2016) describes it as sending only traffic for the organization's resources through the tunnel: it improves efficiency and reduces load, but the organization can no longer examine or protect the rest, and a device with two active interfaces can end up bridging a trusted and an untrusted network, so NIST suggests disabling it on untrusted networks such as hotspots.

The gateway as target. A remote-access concentrator is an authentication service exposed to the whole internet, and attackers treat it that way. Two Ivanti Connect Secure flaws, CVE-2023-46805, an authentication bypass, and CVE-2024-21887, a command injection, chained together to run arbitrary commands; the US Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency (CISA), in Emergency Directive 24-01, required Ivanti's mitigation by 22 January 2024 and disconnection of affected products by 2 February, then factory reset and rebuild, rotation of certificates, keys and passwords, and treatment of domain accounts as compromised. Vendors have drawn conclusions: starting with FortiOS 7.6.3, Fortinet replaced SSL VPN tunnel mode on all FortiGate models with IPsec VPN, which can be configured to use Transmission Control Protocol (TCP) port 443.

Routing, the quiet weak point. Most clients steer traffic into the tunnel with routes, and routes can be outranked. CVE-2024-3661 (Common Vulnerabilities and Exposures), published on 6 May 2024, showed that a hostile Dynamic Host Configuration Protocol (DHCP) server on the local network can push classless static routes through option 121 that send traffic meant for a route-based VPN out of the physical interface instead, where it can be read or altered. Every tunnel also adds headers, so the usable maximum transmission unit (MTU) inside it shrinks; a path that drops the Internet Control Message Protocol (ICMP) messages announcing that leaves large packets failing silently inside an otherwise healthy tunnel.

The consumer meaning. A commercial VPN app routes traffic through servers the provider controls, so it changes the apparent origin of the traffic and, in the words of the US Federal Trade Commission (FTC) in February 2018, shifts trust from the local networks to the VPN app provider. Researchers the FTC cited, who examined almost 300 VPN apps, found that some did not use encryption and some shared data with third parties for advertising. That is a real change in who can watch, and not the same thing as anonymity.

waf.def: A filter placed in front of web applications that inspects Hypertext Transfer Protocol (HTTP) requests and responses and blocks those that match application-layer attacks, such as injection and cross-site scripting.
waf.context: A web application firewall (WAF) sits in front of an app and looks inside the Hypertext Transfer Protocol (HTTP), stopping injection, cross-site scripting and similar attacks that a network firewall cannot see. It is protection at layer 7, tuned to the shape of web requests rather than ports and addresses.
waf.depth:
What it is. NIST (the National Institute of Standards and Technology), in SP 800-41 Revision 1 of 2009, describes web application firewalls (WAFs) as specialized application firewalls that reside in front of the web server to detect the many ways attackers exploit the Hypertext Transfer Protocol (HTTP), a technology it called relatively new, facing threats that change frequently, and often considered very different from traditional firewalls. In practice a WAF runs as a reverse proxy that terminates the Transport Layer Security (TLS) session so that it can read requests, as an engine inside the web server, or as a cloud service in front of the origin, and in each case it needs the decrypted traffic. It decides on methods, URLs, parameters, headers and bodies, not on addresses and ports, and it does not fix anything in the application behind it.

Where it came from. ModSecurity, which OWASP (the Open Worldwide Application Security Project) now calls the standard open-source WAF engine, started in 2002 as an Apache module, was extended to Nginx and Microsoft's Internet Information Services (IIS), and in version 3 became a library, libmodsecurity, that web servers call through separate connectors; it passed from Trustwave to OWASP in February 2024. The OWASP Core Rule Set (CRS) is the free rule collection written for it and for compatible WAFs. Much of the commercial market was created by compliance. Requirement 6.4.1 of the Payment Card Industry Data Security Standard (PCI DSS) let an organization either assess its public web applications or put an automated solution in front of them; in version 4, requirement 6.4.2, effective from 31 March 2025, says that for public-facing web applications an automated technical solution to detect and prevent web-based attacks must be deployed, and the old either-or requirement, 6.4.1, is superseded.

How it decides. A negative security model, in OWASP's wording, defines what is disallowed and implicitly allows everything else: signatures for Structured Query Language (SQL) injection, cross-site scripting (XSS), path traversal and the like. A positive model defines what is allowed, URLs, parameter names, types and lengths, and rejects everything else, which is stronger and far more work to keep current as the application changes. CRS shows how a modern negative model avoids blocking on a single weak match: each rule only adds to an anomaly score, 5 for a critical match, 4 for an error, 3 for a warning and 2 for a notice, and after all request rules have run the transaction is denied if the total reaches the threshold, 5 by default for requests and 4 for responses. Paranoia levels 1 to 4 set how aggressive the rules are: at level 1 they hardly ever raise a false alarm, at level 4 they detect almost every attack, and each step up buys detection with false positives.

Operating one. The difficulty is almost entirely tuning. A policy that blocks nothing is theatre; a policy that blocks a checkout page gets switched off by the first team it hurts. Products build the caution in. On F5 BIG-IP, new attack signatures are always placed in staging, by default for seven days, during which a match is recorded but not enforced, and nothing is blocked at all unless the policy's enforcement mode is Blocking. The work in between is reading logs and telling an attack from an unusual but valid request, then writing the narrowest exception that removes the false positive. CRS distinguishes exclusions applied once at configure time, such as SecRuleRemoveById, which take effect when the engine starts or reloads, from runtime exclusions written as SecRule with a ctl action, which apply per transaction at a small computational cost; its own examples keep a rule protecting everything except the one parameter that trips it, and it strongly discourages editing the rule files themselves.

What it can and cannot see. Pattern matching suits the classes of attack that leave marks in the request: injection is A05 in the OWASP Top 10:2025. The category at the top of that list, A01, Broken Access Control, usually arrives as a perfectly well-formed request for someone else's object, which a filter that knows nothing of the application's authorization rules has no reason to stop. That is the honest framing of a WAF: it buys time between the disclosure of a flaw and the release of the fix, which is what virtual patching means, and it raises the cost of noisy attacks; it does not make the code correct.

Evasion. Attackers know the WAF is there. On 14 December 2021 Cloudflare reported that Log4Shell (CVE-2021-44228, in the Common Vulnerabilities and Exposures list) had been probed on 1 December, eight days before public disclosure, that the first attempt after disclosure came nine minutes after it, and that once WAF rules matched the plain lookup string, payloads moved to nested lookups such as lower, which lowercases a letter, and to the :- default-value syntax, which builds the word one character at a time. In December 2022 Noam Moshe of Claroty's Team82 showed that SQL written with JavaScript Object Notation (JSON) syntax passed WAFs from Palo Alto Networks, F5, Amazon Web Services, Cloudflare and Imperva, because the databases understood JSON and the WAFs did not parse it; the vendors added JSON support to their SQL inspection. The general lesson is the one RFC (Request for Comments) 9112 gives for request smuggling: when two pieces of software disagree about what a request means, the disagreement is the vulnerability, so a WAF has to decode and parse traffic exactly as the application behind it does.

wizard.def: A person with deep, almost intuitive mastery of a system.
wizard.context: In hacker usage a wizard is someone who understands a system so thoroughly they can fix what no one else can, the person you escalate to when the manual runs out. It carries genuine respect, and a hint of the arcane.
wizard.depth:
The four senses. The Jargon File, the lexicon hackers have kept of their own slang since the 1970s, gives the word four meanings in its last version, 4.4.7 of 29 December 2003. Used transitively, a wizard is a person who knows how a complex piece of software or hardware works, who groks it, and especially someone who can find and fix bugs quickly in an emergency. The File draws the line against its parent word carefully: someone is a hacker if they have general hacking ability, but a wizard with respect to something only if they have specific, detailed knowledge of that thing, and a good hacker could become a wizard for something given time to study it. Used intransitively, the word means someone with extremely high-level hacking or problem-solving ability. The third sense is about power rather than knowledge: a person permitted to do things forbidden to ordinary people, one who has wheel privileges on a system. The fourth is a Unix expert, especially a Unix systems programmer, a usage established enough that Unix Wizard was a recognized job title at some corporations and to most headhunters.

The neighbouring titles. Hacker culture ranks expertise with a small set of words, and the differences are instructive. A guru, in the File's definition, has not only wizard skill but a history of being a knowledge resource for others, which is why a team's go-to person is called the house guru. The British lord high fixer, borrowed from Gilbert and Sullivan, is the person in an organization who knows the most about some aspect of a system. A net.god earned the title on Usenet, by long visibility or by running one of the original backbone sites; a demigod has a world-wide reputation and a major role in a design or tool known to more than half the hacker community, the File naming Ken Thompson, Dennis Ritchie, Richard Stallman, Larry Wall, Linus Torvalds, James Gosling and Guido van Rossum. A true-hacker is defined by competence and helpfulness to other hackers. Most useful to an operations team is the wizard hat, the notional headgear worn by whoever is the wizard in a particular context, with the implication that it is a transferable role: the File's example is someone wearing the TCP/IP wizard hat while a colleague is on vacation. Treating wizardry as a hat rather than a person is the difference between a team with expertise and a team with a single point of failure.

The vocabulary of magic. Wizard sits inside a whole lexicon that describes knowledge as sorcery, and the lexicon is precise about how much is understood. To grok, from Robert Heinlein's Stranger in a Strange Land, is to understand so intimately that the knowledge becomes part of one's identity. Heavy wizardry is code or design that trades on intimate knowledge of a particular operating system, language or interface, writing device drivers being the File's example, and it shows up in source comments announcing that heavy wizardry begins here. Deep magic trades on arcane theoretical knowledge instead; cryptography and signal processing are still the File's examples. A black art is a collection of unpublished, ad hoc techniques, and the File traces the path the field follows: very-large-scale integration (VLSI) chip design and compiler optimization began as black arts, became deep magic as theory developed and, once textbooks were written, merely heavy wizardry. At the other end, an incantation is an obscure command that must be learned from a wizard, voodoo programming is using a system by guess or cookbook without understanding it, and waving a dead chicken is a ritual performed over crashed software so that others feel enough effort was spent. The arc from black art to textbook is the arc that documentation, training and good tooling exist to speed up.

Wizards with privileges. The third sense has a history of its own in games and systems. Wizard mode, from the game Rogue, is a special access mode of a program, usually passworded, that gives some users godlike privileges. On multi-user dungeons (MUDs) the wizards are the administrators, the only players who can toad a player, exiling them permanently, or use the FOD command, the finger of death. In BSD (Berkeley Software Distribution) Unix the equivalent is the wheel group, security group zero, to which root belongs, and some vendors modified Unix so that only members of wheel could become root. For a security engineer the overlap of the two meanings is the point worth keeping: the person who understands the system best is very often the person holding its most powerful account, and a hidden, passworded wizard mode is exactly the kind of feature an audit or a penetration test looks for.

The Wizard Book. One book carries the title. Structure and Interpretation of Computer Programs, by Hal Abelson, Jerry Sussman and Julie Sussman, published in 1984 by the press of the Massachusetts Institute of Technology (MIT) and used in introductory courses there, is called the Wizard Book because of the wizard on its jacket, and is one of the bibles of the Lisp and Scheme world. MIT Press's own companion site for the book opens by quoting that entry from the second edition of The New Hacker's Dictionary.

Where the dictionary came from. The File itself is part of the story of the word. Raphael Finkel began it at Stanford in 1975 from the jargon of the MIT and Stanford artificial intelligence laboratories and the other old communities of the ARPANET (Advanced Research Projects Agency Network); Mark Crispin copied it to MIT in 1976; Guy Steele edited a version into The Hacker's Dictionary in 1983; and after a seven-year hiatus Eric S. Raymond revived it in 1990, its versions becoming The New Hacker's Dictionary from MIT Press in 1991, 1993 and 1996. The File's advice about its central word applies with more force here: it is better to be described as a hacker by others than to describe oneself that way. Wizard is a title conferred by people who have watched someone fix the unfixable, never one claimed on a business card. The Internet Engineering Task Force's own glossary, RFC (Request for Comments) 1983 of August 1996, records only the parent word, a person who delights in having an intimate understanding of the internal workings of a system, computers and computer networks in particular.

Not the setup wizard. The same word names a user interface, and the two senses point in opposite directions. Microsoft's Windows design guidelines describe a wizard as a sequence of pages for a multi-step task, with choice pages that gather input, a commit page that performs an action Back or Cancel cannot undo, and an optional progress page, and they add drily that despite that wonderful, whimsical name, wizards are not really a special form of user interface. A setup wizard exists so that someone who is not a wizard can complete a task once; it encodes one expert's choices and hides them. That is convenient on day one and costly on the day something breaks, because the configuration the wizard wrote is configuration nobody on the team chose line by line, and the person who can read it back and explain it is, in the first sense of the word, the wizard.

xkcd-workflow.def: xkcd comic 1172, "Workflow" (11 February 2013), in which an update stops the processor overheating when the spacebar is held down and a user complains that it broke his workflow; the standing joke for the rule that any observable behaviour, however accidental, ends up being depended on by somebody.
xkcd-workflow.context: Randall Munroe's comic shows a changelog with a single fix and the user it hurts: he held the spacebar in place of the control key and had Emacs read the processor's rising temperature as a keypress, so he asks for an option to re-enable spacebar heating. Hyrum Wright's page links it as the obligatory illustration of Hyrum's law (all observable behaviours of a system will be depended on by somebody), and Software Engineering at Google cites it in its section on the law. Engineers quote it whenever a change to a system's output, timing or defaults is proposed, and network engineers meet it every time a device upgrade rewords the command-line output their scripts parse.
xkcd-workflow.depth:
The comic is xkcd number 1172, "Workflow", published by Randall Munroe on 11 February 2013. It shows the changelog of version 10.17 of some piece of software, with one change: the processor no longer overheats when the spacebar is held down. Below it, a long-time user complains that the update broke his workflow. He holds the spacebar in place of the control key, and he has configured Emacs to read the rapid rise in temperature as a control keypress. The administrator calls this horrifying; the user insists that his setup works and asks for an option to re-enable spacebar heating. The title text escalates in the voice of an outraged forum post, suggesting that children may be holding down the spacebar to keep warm in winter, so the update is murdering them.

The joke works because both sides are right. The maintainer fixed something genuinely broken: a processor that overheats is a defect by any standard. The user built on observed behaviour, which is the only thing a user can observe; nobody promised him that holding the spacebar would warm the chip, but it did, every time, and repeatability is what people build on. The comic is therefore about the cost of a change to the people downstream of it, which is usually not the interesting question of whether the old behaviour was correct, but of who depends on it and what happens to them when it goes.

It is the standard illustration of Hyrum's law. Hyrum Wright states it on his own page: with a sufficient number of users of an API (application programming interface), it does not matter what you promise in the contract, because all observable behaviours of your system will be depended on by somebody. He credits Titus Winters with naming it, calls it the Law of Implicit Interfaces, and states the consequence plainly: given enough use, there is no such thing as a private implementation. The interface of a popular system, he writes, reaches much deeper than its authors think, and consumers often do not notice that they depend on it. His page links the comic under the heading Obligatory XKCD.

Software Engineering at Google, whose first chapter was written by Titus Winters and edited by Tom Manshreck, gives the law its own section and cites the comic in a footnote to the line that sums it up: given enough time and enough users, even the most innocuous change will break something. Its worked example is the iteration order of a hash table. The order was never part of any contract, yet code comes to depend on whatever order it observes; meanwhile there are good reasons to change it, among them defending against hash-flooding attacks, which favour unpredictable iteration, and research into better hash functions and containers, which may iterate differently. Code that relies on the order is harmless in a script that runs once and a liability in software meant to last, because sooner or later changing the order becomes worth doing. The chapter also notes that the dependency can travel across a network: a remote procedure call can end up depending on the order in which values were serialized.

Large platforms have turned the user's side of the comic into policy. On 23 December 2012, replying about a media-subsystem change in Linux 3.8-rc1 that made user-space programs misbehave, Linus Torvalds wrote to the subsystem's maintainer, Mauro Carvalho Chehab, in capitals: WE DO NOT BREAK USERSPACE. His argument was that when a kernel change breaks a program that used to work, the bug is in the kernel, and kernel developers do not blame the program. Microsoft went further, for commercial reasons. Joel Spolsky, in "How Microsoft Lost the API War" (13 June 2004), retells a story he heard from one of SimCity's developers: the game used memory immediately after freeing it, which happened to work under DOS (Disk Operating System) and crashed under Windows, so Windows developers disassembled the game, found the bug and added code that detects SimCity and switches the memory allocator into a mode where freed memory can still be used. That is spacebar heating kept on purpose, for one customer, because the customer mattered more than the tidiness of the fix.

For network and security engineers the comic describes a daily hazard. Scripts that log in to a firewall or a load balancer and parse its command-line output depend on spacing, column order and wording that no vendor promised to keep; an upgrade that adds a column or rewords a status line breaks them exactly as the update broke the user's Emacs. Monitoring that keys on the text of a log message, automation that relies on the order in which a device lists its objects, and integrations that lean on an undocumented default all belong to the same family. The defences follow from Wright's argument: prefer the interfaces a vendor documents and versions, such as structured APIs and NETCONF, over screen-scraped output; pin and test the versions that automation runs against; and, on the producing side, avoid creating new accidental guarantees, making unspecified behaviour visibly unreliable rather than quietly consistent. In practice the comic is quoted whenever someone proposes changing what a system's output looks like, and its neighbour, xkcd 1205, "Is It Worth the Time?", when someone proposes automating the task in the first place.

xss.def: An attack that injects malicious script into a web page so it runs in other users' browsers.
xss.context: Cross-Site Scripting exploits a page that reflects or stores untrusted input without escaping it, letting an attacker's JavaScript run with the victim's session. Output encoding and a Content Security Policy are the standard defences; it is a perennial OWASP Top 10 entry.
xss.depth:
Cross-site scripting is the browser executing attacker-supplied script in the context of a site the user trusts, which means it inherits that site's cookies, session and permissions. The three shapes are stored, where the payload is saved and served to every visitor, reflected, where it rides in a request and comes back in the response, and DOM-based, where the page's own JavaScript writes untrusted data into a dangerous sink and the server never sees it.

The defence is contextual output encoding rather than input filtering, because the same string is safe in HTML text, dangerous in an attribute and differently dangerous inside a script block. Blocklists of tags and keywords fail because the encoding surface is enormous. Content Security Policy is the useful second layer, and it only works if the page is not already using unsafe-inline, which is the setting that removes the protection.

yak-shaving.def: The chain of unrelated sub-tasks you must finish before you can do the thing you actually set out to do.
yak-shaving.context: You want to fix one bug, but first you must update a library, which needs a newer runtime, which needs a config change, and suddenly you are shaving a yak. The term comes from the MIT AI Lab in the 1990s. Naming it is useful: it is the cue to ask whether the detour is really necessary.
yak-shaving.depth:
Yak shaving is the recursive descent from the task you meant to do into the unrelated prerequisite of the prerequisite. You sit down to fix a typo, which needs a newer library, which needs a runtime upgrade, which needs the package manager repaired, which needs a certificate renewed, and at some point you are shaving a yak with no memory of why.

The phrase comes from a Ren and Stimpy episode by way of MIT, where it was adopted to describe exactly this pattern of nested prerequisites. What makes it a genuinely useful term rather than a joke is that it names something real about technical work: the distance between intent and the current activity can grow arbitrarily long, and nobody notices while it is happening because each individual step is justified.

The practical discipline is a stack rather than an escape. Write down what you were originally doing before descending, so the way back exists, and set a limit on the descent before starting rather than discovering it at midnight. Sometimes the yak genuinely must be shaved. The failure is not shaving it, it is forgetting there was ever a reason.

zero-day.def: A vulnerability unknown to the vendor, with zero days available to have patched it.
zero-day.context: A zero-day is dangerous precisely because no fix exists yet: defenders have had zero days of warning. The term stretches to the exploit that uses such a flaw. Once the vendor learns of it and ships a patch, the clock starts and it is no longer a zero-day.
zero-day.depth:
A zero-day is a vulnerability the vendor has had zero days to fix, and the term is used loosely enough to be worth pinning down. Strictly it means no patch exists. The glossary of the United States Committee on National Security Systems, carried by the National Institute of Standards and Technology (NIST), defines a zero-day attack as one that exploits a previously unknown hardware, firmware or software vulnerability. Google's Threat Intelligence Group (GTIG), which publishes the yearly count most often quoted, uses an operational test: a vulnerability maliciously exploited in the wild before a patch was made publicly available. The word covers the flaw and also the exploit code written for it. Colloquially people apply it to anything being exploited before organizations have deployed the fix, which is a different and much more common situation with a name of its own: an n-day, a vulnerability first exploited after its patch is available.

The name is older than the meaning. According to Kim Zetter's account in Wired, the expression apparently originated in the days of bulletin board systems, when it counted the days since a new program had been released to the public: zero-day software was software not yet released, coveted by those who wanted to be first to have it. The count later moved to the vendor's side, the number of days the software maker has known of the hole, which is why the forms 0-day and 0day survive from that scene.

Its value to an attacker comes precisely from the absence of a signature to detect or a patch to apply, which is why zero-days are hoarded, sold and, by the actors who pay most for them, used sparingly against high-value targets instead of being sprayed widely. Zetter described three markets in 2014: a black market among criminals, a white market of bug bounty programmes and security firms, and a grey market in which researchers and contractors sell to governments, with prices from 5,000 dollars to several hundred thousand. Using one publicly burns it, since disclosure follows detection and a fix follows disclosure, so the economics push towards restraint until the target justifies the loss. GTIG's review of 2025 shows who the buyers are: for the first time it attributed more zero-days to the customers of commercial surveillance vendors than to state-sponsored espionage groups, among which groups linked to the People's Republic of China were the most prolific, with at least ten. Restraint is not universal, though. The same review attributes nine zero-days to financially motivated groups, two of them in operations that ended in ransomware.

How long an unused zero-day stays secret has been measured once in public. The RAND Corporation study Zero Days, Thousands of Nights, by Lillian Ablon and Andy Bogart, published on 9 March 2017, found an average life expectancy of 6.9 years for zero-day exploits and their vulnerabilities: a quarter did not survive 1.51 years and a quarter lived more than 9.5. For a given stockpile, about 5.7 per cent had been found and disclosed by someone else after a year, and once a vulnerability was in hand a working exploit took a median of 22 days to develop. Those figures frame the policy argument about government stockpiles. The United States charter for its Vulnerabilities Equities Process, dated 15 November 2017, sets out how agencies decide between telling the vendor and temporarily restricting knowledge of a newly discovered flaw for intelligence, law enforcement or military use, and states that in the vast majority of cases disclosure is clearly in the national interest. The cost of the exceptions was shown the same year: Microsoft's president wrote on 14 May 2017 that the exploits used by the WannaCrypt worm had been drawn from exploits stolen from the National Security Agency (NSA), for a flaw Microsoft had patched only on 14 March, and compared the loss to having Tomahawk missiles stolen.

The reference case for a zero-day used as intended is Stuxnet. Symantec's dossier lists zero-day exploits among its components, including a print spooler flaw fixed in Microsoft bulletin MS10-061 and two privilege escalation flaws; Zetter counts five zero-day exploits in all, four of them still unpatched when the worm was discovered. Spending that many on one operation was unheard of at the time, and it is the measure of what the target was worth to the attacker.

The yearly counts are stable and their composition is not. GTIG tracked 90 zero-days exploited in the wild in 2025, against 78 in 2024, a record 100 in 2023 and 63 in 2022; it describes a range of 60 to 100 over the past five years, and revises earlier totals as old incidents come to light (it first published 75 for 2024 and 98 for 2023). What has moved is the target. In 2025, 43 of the 90, or 48 per cent, were in enterprise technologies, the highest share recorded, and 21 of those were in security and networking products. The 2024 analysis named the products: Ivanti Cloud Services Appliance, Palo Alto Networks PAN-OS, Cisco Adaptive Security Appliance and Ivanti Connect Secure, the virtual private network (VPN) gateway. The reasons it gives are structural. Such devices sit at the edge, hold high privileges, connect to everything, and usually cannot run endpoint detection and response (EDR) agents, so a compromise there is both broad and hard to see.

A zero-day stays one only for its first victims. Mandiant examined 138 vulnerabilities disclosed in 2023 that were exploited: 97 were first exploited as zero-days and 41 as n-days, a ratio of 70 to 30 where earlier years had shown about 62 to 38. Its average time-to-exploit fell from 63 days in 2018 and 2019 to 44, then 32, then five days in 2023. Of the n-days, 12 per cent were exploited within a day of the patch, 29 per cent within a week and 56 per cent within a month. Disclosure policies are built around the same clock: Google's Project Zero gives a vendor 90 days and publishes details 30 days after the patch, but cuts the deadline to 7 days when a flaw is already being exploited in the wild, and the Zero Day Initiative allows 120 days.

The defensive conclusion is unwelcome but freeing. You cannot patch what has no patch, so resilience has to come from elsewhere: reduced attack surface, segmentation so that one compromise is not total, detection that keys on behaviour instead of known signatures, and an incident process that works. Between disclosure and the vendor's fix there is one more instrument, the virtual patch, which the Open Worldwide Application Security Project (OWASP) defines as a security policy enforcement layer that prevents the exploitation of a known vulnerability: a rule on a web application firewall or an intrusion prevention system that stops the attack in transit while the code itself is unchanged. It works only once the flaw is known, so it narrows the window after disclosure and does nothing during the true zero-day period. For the security and networking appliances that now account for 21 of the 90 zero-days of a year, the practical measures follow from GTIG's diagnosis: keep management interfaces off the internet, send the device's logs somewhere it cannot alter them, and treat the appliance itself as a host that can be compromised.

Meanwhile the statistic that matters most concerns ordinary flaws. Verizon's 2026 Data Breach Investigations Report puts the share of breaches that start with the exploitation of a software vulnerability at 31 per cent, ahead of stolen passwords. The catalogue of Known Exploited Vulnerabilities kept by the Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency (CISA) held 1,779 entries on 10 November 2026, the first added on 3 November 2021, each with a required action and a due date, and 361 of them flagged as used in ransomware campaigns. It is commonly said that the overwhelming majority of breaches use vulnerabilities that were patched months earlier. Neither Verizon's figure nor Mandiant's establishes that proportion, and Mandiant's show that the first exploitation of a patched flaw now usually comes within weeks, not months. The order of priorities it argues for stands all the same: an organization worried about zero-days while running unpatched software has its risks ordered wrongly.

The numbers worth remembering: 90 zero-days in 2025, inside a 60 to 100 band; 48 per cent of them in enterprise products; 6.9 years of average secret life and 5.7 per cent a year of independent rediscovery; 22 days to build an exploit; five days of average time-to-exploit in 2023; 90 plus 30 days at Project Zero, 7 when exploitation is under way, 120 at the Zero Day Initiative; and 1,779 known exploited vulnerabilities waiting for anyone who has not patched.

zero-trust.def: A security model in which no user, device or network location is trusted by default: every request for a resource is authenticated and authorized on its own, against identity, device state and context, and granted only the least privilege it needs.
zero-trust.context: Zero trust replaces the old "trusted inside, hostile outside" perimeter with continuous verification of identity, device, and context for every access, inside the network or not. "Never trust, always verify" is the slogan; least privilege and microsegmentation are how it is built.
zero-trust.depth:
What it is, and what it is not. The vendor-neutral definition is Special Publication (SP) 800-207, Zero Trust Architecture, published by the National Institute of Standards and Technology (NIST) in August 2020: a collection of concepts for making accurate, least-privilege, per-request access decisions in the face of a network viewed as compromised, with no implicit trust granted for network location or device ownership. A zero trust architecture (ZTA) is an enterprise's plan for applying them. It is not a single architecture but a set of guiding principles, not achievable by wholesale replacement of infrastructure, and not quick: NIST expects most enterprises to run a hybrid of zero trust and perimeter for an indefinite period. A product supplies a component; the inventory of identities and the policy of who should reach what must come from the enterprise.

The failure it answers. Perimeter security treated inside as trusted, which held until laptops left the building, applications moved to other people's data centres and one phished credential bought the whole interior. NIST calls this an implicit trust zone, like an airport boarding area where everyone past the checkpoint is trusted alike. Zero trust moves decision and enforcement next to each resource and shrinks those zones, so location proves nothing, access is granted per resource rather than per network, and a compromised session yields one application instead of a subnet to move laterally across.

The idea is older than the name. NIST traces it to the US military's "black core" work on securing individual transactions and to the Jericho Forum, which publicized de-perimeterization in 2004; its Commandments (version 1.2, May 2007) require that all devices be capable of maintaining their security policy on an untrusted network. John Kindervag of Forrester Research named the model in "No More Chewy Centers", dated 14 September 2010, mocking the motto of a network like an M&M, crunchy outside and chewy in the centre. His three concepts, secure access regardless of location, strict least privilege, and inspecting and logging all traffic, flipped "trust but verify" into "verify and never trust". In 2014 Rory Ward and Betsy Beyer described Google's BeyondCorp, which removed the privileged intranet and moved corporate applications onto the internet.

SP 800-207 states seven tenets. Every data source and service is a resource; all communication is secured regardless of location; access is granted per session with least privilege, and access to one resource grants nothing on another; access is decided by dynamic policy over identity, application, device state and behavioural and environmental attributes; the enterprise monitors the security posture of every asset; authentication and authorization are dynamic and enforced before access; and the enterprise collects all the telemetry it can to improve.

Three logical components do the work. The policy engine (PE) decides to grant, deny or revoke access, running enterprise policy and inputs such as continuous diagnostics and mitigation (CDM) and threat intelligence through a trust algorithm. The policy administrator (PA) executes the decision, opening or closing the path and issuing session credentials; together they form the policy decision point (PDP), on a control plane separate from the data plane. The policy enforcement point (PEP) sits in the data path, as one gateway or as a client agent plus a resource gateway. NIST names three ways to build it: enhanced identity governance; micro-segmentation, with next-generation firewalls, switches or host agents as PEPs; and software defined perimeters (SDP), with the PA as network controller.

Policy turned it into a deadline. After Executive Order 14028 of May 2021, the Office of Management and Budget (OMB) memorandum M-22-09 of 26 January 2022 gave US federal agencies until the end of fiscal year 2024 to adopt phishing-resistant multi-factor authentication (MFA), such as Personal Identity Verification (PIV) cards or FIDO2 and Web Authentication (WebAuthn); to encrypt internal Domain Name System (DNS) and Hypertext Transfer Protocol (HTTP) traffic; and to have users log into applications rather than networks, treating every application as internet-accessible. The Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency (CISA) published version 2 of its Zero Trust Maturity Model on 11 April 2023: five pillars (Identity, Devices, Networks, Applications and Workloads, Data), three cross-cutting capabilities (Visibility and Analytics, Automation and Orchestration, Governance) and four stages, from Traditional through the new Initial to Advanced and Optimal.

Between services, it becomes identity. SP 800-207A (September 2023) applies the model to cloud-native applications: identities instead of Internet Protocol (IP) addresses and subnets, enforced by application programming interface (API) gateways, service mesh sidecar proxies and the Secure Production Identity Framework for Everyone (SPIFFE). Each service holds a short-lived identity checked per connection with mutual Transport Layer Security (mTLS), connections may last as little as 15 to 30 minutes, and the end user travels to every hop as a token such as a JSON (JavaScript Object Notation) Web Token (JWT).

In products the PEP is usually a proxy. Zero trust network access (ZTNA) publishes applications, not networks. On a FortiGate, FortiClient EMS tags endpoints by posture and, as the ZTNA certificate authority, issues their client certificates; the access proxy, a reverse proxy for Hypertext Transfer Protocol Secure (HTTPS) or a forwarder for other Transmission Control Protocol (TCP) traffic, admits a session only when both match the policy. Netskope Private Access publishers sit beside the applications, initiate all traffic outbound to TCP port 443 and must never accept inbound connections from the internet.

What goes wrong is concentration. NIST's threat list starts with the decision process: whoever controls the PE's rules, or a compromised PA, can open access that should not exist. Denial of service against the PEP, PE or PA, or an outage of a hosted PE, can stop the whole enterprise. Stolen credentials still reach what they are authorized for, so MFA and contextual policy narrow the damage without closing it. Meanwhile the perimeter stays a target: CISA's Emergency Directive 24-01 gave agencies until 22 January 2024 to mitigate an authentication bypass and a command injection in Ivanti Connect Secure and Policy Secure gateways, then ordered every instance disconnected by 2 February.

Neighbours. Least privilege is the rule it enforces, micro-segmentation one way to build its PEPs, and the remote-access virtual private network (VPN), which authenticates once and grants a route into a network, the model it replaces. Zero trust does not remove trust; it stops inferring it from location and relocates it to the identity system and the policy engine, which become the components to defend first.

the-first-email.def: Ray Tomlinson sent the first networked electronic mail between two ARPANET machines in 1971, choosing @ to separate user from host.
the-first-email.context: Tomlinson was adapting his SNDMSG program at BBN when he picked the at sign, an underused character that read naturally as 'user at host'. He later admitted he could not remember the content of the first message, guessing it was something like QWERTYUIOP. The convention he chose in an afternoon still addresses every mailbox on Earth.
the-first-email.depth:
Ray Tomlinson sent the first network email in 1971, between two machines sitting next to each other on ARPANET, and later said he could not remember what the message contained because it was a test rather than an occasion. He also chose the @ sign to separate the user from the host.

The reason it mattered is that messaging already existed but only within a single machine. Users of a shared computer could leave each other notes; what Tomlinson did was make the recipient's location part of the address, which turned a local convenience into a network service. That is a small change in the code and a categorical change in what the network was for.

The consequence nobody planned is what the network became. ARPANET was built to share expensive computing resources, and within a few years the dominant traffic was people talking to each other, which was not in the design documents at all. That pattern repeats: the web was built to share physics papers, SMS was a diagnostic channel, and the thing a network is actually used for is discovered rather than specified.

alohanet.def: The 1971 University of Hawaii radio network whose random-access scheme became the ancestor of Ethernet's collision handling.
alohanet.context: Norman Abramson's team needed to link campuses across islands, so ALOHAnet let stations transmit whenever they had data and simply retransmit after collisions. That 'try, collide, back off' idea is the direct intellectual ancestor of Ethernet's CSMA/CD: Robert Metcalfe studied ALOHA closely before sketching Ethernet at Xerox PARC. Wireless networking, in a sense, came before wired LANs.
alohanet.depth:
ALOHAnet, built at the University of Hawaii in 1971, connected computers across islands using radio rather than cable, and had to solve a problem wired networks could avoid: many stations sharing one channel with no way to coordinate who transmits.

Its answer was radical and worked. Stations transmit whenever they have something to send, detect collisions by the absence of an acknowledgement, wait a random interval, and retry. The randomness is the whole trick, since two stations that collide and then retry after fixed delays will collide again forever. Slotted ALOHA improved efficiency by aligning transmissions to time boundaries, roughly doubling throughput.

That mechanism is the direct ancestor of Ethernet. Metcalfe cited ALOHAnet explicitly, and carrier sense multiple access with collision detection is ALOHA plus listening before transmitting. Modern Wi-Fi uses collision avoidance rather than detection, because a radio cannot easily listen while transmitting, but the random backoff is the same idea. A network built to cross water between islands produced the contention algorithm underneath most local networking since.

blue-box.def: The phone-phreaking device that generated the 2600 Hz tone and signalling frequencies to seize control of the long-distance network.
blue-box.context: In-band signalling meant the phone network trusted tones any caller could produce; a toy whistle from Cap'n Crunch cereal famously hit 2600 Hz, earning John Draper the name Captain Crunch. Steve Wozniak and Steve Jobs built and sold blue boxes before founding Apple, and Wozniak later said there would have been no Apple without them. The lesson outlived the hardware: never trust control signals carried in the data channel.
blue-box.depth:
A blue box generated the tones that controlled AT&T's long distance switching, allowing whoever held one to place calls the billing system never saw. The technique came from the same in-band signalling weakness that the 2600 Hz whistle exploited, and the box automated it.

The devices matter historically because of who built them. Steve Wozniak and Steve Jobs made and sold blue boxes before Apple, and Wozniak has been explicit that the confidence of building something that controlled the phone network was a precondition for believing they could build a computer company. A substantial part of early Silicon Valley passed through phone phreaking first.

The vulnerability was closed by moving signalling out of band, into a separate channel users cannot reach, which is the correct architectural fix and the one that generalizes. The historical interest is in the culture rather than the technique: a generation learned that large opaque systems are comprehensible if you are curious and persistent enough, which is the disposition the security field still selects for and occasionally prosecutes.

green-card-spam.def: The April 1994 Usenet mass-posting by two immigration lawyers that made commercial spam a household problem.
green-card-spam.context: Laurence Canter and Martha Siegel crossposted a 'Green Card Lottery' ad to thousands of Usenet newsgroups at once, ignoring every community norm of the pre-commercial Internet. The furious backlash, cancelbots, and press coverage that followed effectively founded anti-spam culture. Where the 1978 ARPANET message was a one-off, this was the moment spam became an industry.
green-card-spam.depth:
In April 1994 two immigration lawyers posted an advertisement for green card lottery services to essentially every Usenet newsgroup simultaneously. It was not the first unsolicited commercial message on the network, but it was the first mass cross-posting, and it is generally treated as the moment spam became an industry rather than an incident.

What made it a turning point was the reaction and its failure. The community responded with the tools it had, which were social: outrage, complaint to the upstream provider, and eventually retaliatory floods. The senders were disconnected, obtained new access, and publicly reported that the campaign had been profitable. That last part is the whole story: a business model was demonstrated, and social disapproval was shown to be an insufficient control against one.

Everything downstream follows. Cancelbots, then filtering, then reputation systems, then authentication, then the concentration of mail into a few providers large enough to run all of it at scale. The 1978 DEC message began the argument about norms; the 1994 posting ended it, by proving that the economics did not care.

trojan-room-coffee-pot.def: The Cambridge coffee machine whose monitoring camera became the world's first webcam.
trojan-room-coffee-pot.context: In 1991, researchers at the University of Cambridge Computer Laboratory pointed a camera at the shared coffee pot so nobody would trek to an empty one; when the image went onto the young web in 1993 it became the first webcam, watched by millions worldwide. The feed ran for a decade until the pot was switched off in 2001 and auctioned on eBay to a German news site. The purest origin story in computing: laziness, correctly applied.
trojan-room-coffee-pot.depth:
In 1991 researchers at Cambridge pointed a camera at a coffee pot and served the image over their local network, so that people on other floors could see whether coffee existed before walking to the room. In 1993 it was connected to the web and became the first webcam.

The problem it solved was mundane and completely real. The pot was in one room, the people were not, and the walk was wasted whenever the pot was empty. That is the entire motivation, and the fact that it became internationally famous says more about the novelty of live images on a network than about the coffee.

Its afterlife is the interesting part. Hundreds of thousands of people watched a coffee pot in another country for no reason beyond the fact that they could, which was the first widely shared demonstration that the network collapses distance in a way that feels different from reading a document. When the machine was finally switched off in 2001, it was covered as news, and the pot was auctioned. Every remote monitoring system and every doorbell camera descends from it.

the-evil-bit.def: The April Fools' RFC proposing that malicious packets simply set a header bit to declare themselves evil.
the-evil-bit.context: Steve Bellovin's RFC 3514 (1 April 2003) defines a security flag in the IPv4 header: benign packets set it to 0, attack packets must set it to 1, and firewalls need only drop the marked ones. It is the field's favourite satire of every product that promises to detect intent from the wire. Whenever someone proposes trusting the sender's self-declaration, an engineer will ask if it checks the evil bit.
the-evil-bit.depth:
RFC 3514, published on 1 April 2003, proposes using a spare bit in the IPv4 header to indicate malicious intent: attackers set the evil bit, firewalls check it, security is solved. It is written entirely in specification language, complete with requirements about how compliant implementations must behave.

The joke is a critique with a precise target. Security cannot be delegated to the party being defended against, and any scheme that depends on an attacker honestly declaring themselves is not a control. Stated that plainly it is obvious, and the RFC exists because the assumption keeps reappearing in real designs.

It has aged into a genuinely useful reference. Client-side validation trusted by the server, authorization decisions based on a header the client controls, and rate limiting keyed on an identifier the caller supplies are all the evil bit with a different name, and they ship regularly. When reviewing a design, asking whether a check depends on the attacker cooperating is a fast way to find this class of flaw, and having a canonical joke to point at makes the conversation shorter than an explanation would.

640k-quote.def: The famous line '640K ought to be enough for anybody', attributed to Bill Gates, who has repeatedly denied ever saying it.
640k-quote.context: No primary source has ever surfaced for the quote, and Gates has publicly denied it more than once, noting that nobody involved in the PC's memory limits thought them permanent. The 640 KB ceiling itself was real, an artifact of the original IBM PC memory map, which is why the line felt plausible enough to stick. It survives as the canonical parable about underestimating future requirements, pinned to a man who never said it.
640k-quote.depth:
The claim that Bill Gates said 640K ought to be enough for anybody is the most repeated quotation in computing history, and there is no evidence he said it. Gates denied it repeatedly and with visible irritation, no contemporaneous source has ever been produced, and the earliest attributions appear years after the supposed remark.

The reason it persists is that it feels true. The 640K limit was real, it came from the IBM PC's memory map reserving the upper portion of the first megabyte for hardware, and a generation of users genuinely fought it. Attaching a famous name to a shared frustration produces a story that explains the annoyance and assigns it a culprit, which is more satisfying than an architectural decision nobody remembers making.

It belongs with the room 404 story and the first computer bug as a case study in how technical folklore forms. A memorable quotation, a plausible speaker, endless repetition, and eventually the repetition becomes the source. The useful habit it argues for is asking where a famous quotation was first recorded, because the answer is often that nobody knows, and the people best positioned to deny it have been denying it for decades.

y2k.def: The two-digit-year defect that threatened date logic worldwide at the 1999 to 2000 rollover, and the remediation effort that largely defused it.
y2k.context: Decades of software stored years as two digits to save memory, so 00 could sort before 99 and break everything from interest calculations to embedded controllers. Hundreds of billions of dollars in global remediation later, the rollover passed with only scattered failures. Y2K became the field's standing lesson in the preparedness paradox: when prevention works, it looks afterwards like the danger was never real.
y2k.depth:
The defect. The year 2000 problem came from storing years as two digits, a decision that was entirely rational when storage cost real money and the systems involved were not expected to last two decades. Early business data processing on 80-column punched cards wrote a date in six digits, two each for month, day and year, a shortcut said to have saved as much as twenty dollars per date-sensitive record; COBOL (Common Business-Oriented Language) programs carried the format, and IBM's System/360, marketed from 1964, made it the industry norm. When the century rolled over, arithmetic on those dates would produce results that were wrong in ways ranging from cosmetic to catastrophic: 00 minus 99 is a negative age, 00 sorts before 99, and a test written as year greater than 99 never fires. A second, quieter trap sat in the calendar. A year divisible by 100 is a leap year only if it is also divisible by 400, so 2000 was one and 1900 was not, and code that applied only the century exception got 29 February 2000 wrong. Some systems also used 9999 as a placeholder for an unknown date, which made 9 September 1999, written 9/9/99, a date to watch.

Who saw it coming. Bob Bemer, one of COBOL's developers, noticed the problem in 1958 while working on genealogical software and published warnings in 1971 and 1979 that changed nothing. A book on the subject, Computers in Crisis by Jerome and Marilyn Murray, appeared in 1984, and the problem was being discussed on Usenet in January 1985. The alarm that worked was Peter de Jager's three-page article Doomsday 2000 in Computerworld in 1993; de Jager estimated that year that fixing it worldwide would cost 50 to 75 billion dollars. The name Y2K, with K for kilo, is attributed to the Massachusetts programmer David Eddy, in an e-mail of 12 June 1995; he recalled that it competed with CDC, for century date change, and FADL, for faulty date logic.

How it was fixed. Three techniques were used. Date expansion rewrote programs, files and databases to carry four-digit years: the cleanest answer and the most expensive, because it touched entire systems and every interface between them. Date windowing kept two-digit years and inferred the century when needed, for example reading 00 to 19 as 2000 to 2019 and 20 to 99 as 1920 to 1999; it needed only small patches and was far cheaper to test. Date compression packed the date into a 14-bit binary number so that record layouts did not change. Windowing was never meant to be permanent, and in January 2020 some windows closed: parking meters in New York City stopped accepting credit cards, point-of-sale units failed, some utilities printed bills dated 1920, and the video game WWE 2K20 crashed until a patch the same day. A fix with a pivot year is a fix with an expiry date, and somebody has to remember it.

What it cost. Estimates depend on who counted what. The United States Senate's special committee on the problem, in its final report of 29 February 2000, put United States spending at about 100 billion dollars, 8.5 billion of it inside the federal government, figures attributed to the Department of Commerce; one analyst estimate put United States spending at 134 billion dollars before the date and another 13 billion fixing problems in 2000 and 2001, and the worldwide total has been put at 308 billion. Other accounts give ranges from 200 to 600 billion. De Jager's 1993 estimate had been far too low.

What actually happened is the most misunderstood part. Very little broke, and the popular conclusion was that the threat had been exaggerated. The alternative explanation is that hundreds of thousands of people spent several years and enormous sums finding and fixing the affected code, and the quiet rollover was the result rather than the refutation. The failures that were recorded are instructive. At 19:00 Eastern time on 31 December 1999 a ground station at Fort Belvoir, Virginia, stopped processing data from five reconnaissance satellites because of a patch meant to prevent a Y2K fault; a contingency plan restored a limited service within three hours, and full function returned late on 2 January. Radiation monitoring equipment at Japan's Shika nuclear plant failed seconds after midnight; officials said there was no risk to the public and no excess radiation was found. In Sheffield an unfixed date calculation produced wrong ages for pregnant women and 154 incorrect Down syndrome risk assessments before it was found on 24 May. And in Brazil, computers at the Port of Santos upgraded for Y2K in July 1999 could not read about 20,000 three-year customs registrations created by the old system; once the problem surfaced on 10 January each registration could be fixed in minutes, and a computer at Viracopos airport briefly halted cargo unloading with the same fault. Many problems were absurd rather than dangerous, such as a 91,000-dollar late fee on a video rental in New York or a 105-year-old man called to kindergarten.

The control group that is not there. The usual defence of the spending holds that those who invested less suffered more; the record does not show that cleanly. In January 2000 Slate noted that Italy and Paraguay spent little and appeared to have fared as well as the United States; the experts' reply, that spending followed dependence on computers and Paraguay ran its water and power largely by hand, does not explain Italy, which had plenty of computers and a lagging effort. Essential services also ran uninterrupted in Russia, described as both technically sophisticated and largely unprepared, and about a third of small American businesses made no preparations at all. The Senate committee itself called the low level of disruption abroad somewhat surprising and offered four reasons: poor information about other countries' dependence and readiness, remediation in the last two months of 1999 that nobody had counted, the influence of multinational companies on their host countries, and contingency plans, including manual operation and staff on standby, that worked better than expected. The fear about embedded chips shrank under testing: estimates of failure among the billions of embedded controllers fell from 2 to 3 per cent to about 0.001 per cent by late 1999, and a review of commercial aircraft found no essential date-sensitive systems. None of this settles the question, because the world in which the money was not spent does not exist to be measured.

That leaves it as the canonical example of the prevention paradox: work that succeeds produces an absence of events, an absence of events looks like an absence of risk, and the people who did the work get blamed for alarmism. Anyone arguing for preventive investment is arguing against that dynamic, and Y2K is the reference case in both directions depending on who is citing it. The Senate committee judged the effort justified and listed what it left behind: renovated infrastructure, system documentation created for the first time, and the discovery by many organizations that their inventory of information technology was inaccurate or absent. Its neighbour is the Year 2038 problem, when signed 32-bit Unix time overflows at 03:14:07 UTC (Coordinated Universal Time) on 19 January 2038: unlike Y2K it is a limit of the field's width rather than of a formatting convention, and it is being handled with decades of notice. The numbers worth remembering: two digits, 1958 for the first warning, 1993 for the alarm, 100 billion dollars in the United States, 2000 as a leap year, and 2020 as the year the cheapest fixes began to expire.

melissa-virus.def: The March 1999 Word-macro virus that mailed itself to the first 50 Outlook contacts and buried corporate email worldwide.
melissa-virus.context: David L. Smith released Melissa on 26 March 1999, hiding it in a Word document; each opened copy mass-mailed itself onward, and the exponential flood forced companies including Microsoft to shut off outbound email. Smith, who named it after a dancer, was traced within days and sentenced to prison. Melissa marked the moment email itself became the malware transport of choice.
melissa-virus.depth:
Melissa arrived in March 1999 as a Word document containing a macro, which mailed itself to the first fifty entries of the victim's address book. The volume of mail it generated was enough to force major organizations to shut down their mail systems entirely, which was the actual damage.

What it demonstrated was that document formats are executable. A macro language embedded in an office suite for automation is a programming environment attached to a file type that everyone treats as data, and that gap between how a file is perceived and what it can do had not been widely internalized. Documents were things you opened without thinking, and Melissa is where that stopped being safe.

The response shaped a decade of enterprise policy: macros disabled by default, prompts before enabling, signed macros for legitimate internal tools, and eventually blocking macro-enabled documents from the internet entirely. That last change came more than twenty years later, which is a reasonable measure of how long it takes to remove a capability that some part of a business genuinely depends on.

code-red.def: The July 2001 IIS worm that defaced sites with 'Hacked By Chinese!' and infected hundreds of thousands of servers in hours.
code-red.context: Code Red exploited a buffer overflow in Microsoft IIS, spread with no file on disk, defaced English-language sites, and pointed a coordinated flood at the White House's address. CAIDA measured more than 359,000 infected hosts in under fourteen hours, the first hard data on how fast an Internet worm could really move. The eEye researchers who dissected it named it after the Code Red flavour of Mountain Dew they were drinking.
code-red.depth:
Code Red spread through a buffer overflow in Microsoft's web server in July 2001, defaced pages with a message, and was programmed to launch a denial of service attack against a fixed IP address belonging to the White House. The address was changed before the attack date, which blunted it.

Its interesting property was that it lived in memory only and left nothing on disk, so a reboot cleaned an infected machine, which then usually became reinfected within minutes because the underlying flaw was still there. That produced a peculiar dynamic where the population appeared to fluctuate rather than grow, and where administrators believed they had fixed something they had merely interrupted.

The hardcoded target is the part worth remembering. Malware that names a specific fixed destination is trivially defended against once discovered, and the lesson attackers took was to use dynamic target selection, which is why later families use algorithmically generated domains and peer-to-peer coordination. Defensive success against one generation is reliably an education for the next, which is the pattern of the whole field.

sql-slammer.def: The 376-byte worm that fit in a single UDP packet and infected most of its 75,000 victims within ten minutes on 25 January 2003.
sql-slammer.context: Slammer lived only in memory and network packets, never touching disk: one hand-optimized 376-byte payload fired at UDP port 1434, doubling its footprint roughly every 8.5 seconds at the peak. Bank ATMs failed, much of South Korea lost connectivity, and routers collapsed under the scanning load, all from a hole Microsoft had patched six months earlier. It remains the canonical proof that patch latency, not attacker brilliance, is what burns the Internet down.
sql-slammer.depth:
SQL Slammer, in January 2003, was 376 bytes, fitted in a single UDP packet, required no connection, and doubled its infected population roughly every eight seconds. It reached essentially every vulnerable machine on the internet within about ten minutes, faster than any human response was possible.

The speed came from the design. Because it used a connectionless protocol and needed no handshake, each infected host could spray packets as fast as its network interface allowed, with no waiting. The damage was mostly collateral: the traffic volume saturated links and took down networks, including bank cash machines and at least one emergency call system, for organizations that were not running the vulnerable database at all.

Two lessons stuck. A patch had been available for six months, so the exposure was a patching problem rather than an unknown vulnerability, which is the same finding that most breach statistics still produce. And it demonstrated that automated propagation can outrun human incident response entirely, which is the argument for defences that act at machine speed and for network segmentation that limits how far something can get.

conficker.def: Conficker, also called Downadup or Kido, is the Windows worm family first seen on 20 November 2008 that spread through the MS08-067 Server service flaw, removable drives and weak share passwords, built one of the largest botnets on record, and made the domain generation algorithm (DGA) a standard topic in malware analysis.
conficker.context: Microsoft had patched MS08-067 out of its regular cycle on 23 October 2008 and warned that the flaw could be used for a wormable exploit; a month later Conficker was scanning TCP (Transmission Control Protocol) port 445 for the machines that had not applied it. Instead of a fixed command server it computed, each day, a list of rendezvous domains from the date (250 for the first variants, 50,000 candidates across 110 top-level domains for Conficker C), and fetched signed updates from whichever one its authors registered. Defenders answered with the Conficker Working Group: Microsoft, ICANN, registries, antivirus vendors and researchers who registered or blocked the names in advance, while Microsoft offered a 250,000-dollar reward for information about the authors, who were never publicly identified. Infection estimates ran from 5 to 15 million, the botnet was barely used, and infected machines, many of them equipment nobody could patch, kept calling home for years.
conficker.depth:
What it was. Conficker is a family of Windows worms, named Downadup and Kido by some vendors, of which the Conficker Working Group (CWG) counts five variants, A to E. SRI International dates the first to 20 November 2008; CAIDA's network telescope saw scanning on Transmission Control Protocol (TCP) port 445 jump after midnight UTC on 21 November, matching the first reports. Its distinctive design was not a payload but a secure update channel: in SRI's words, its main purpose was to give its authors a binary updating service that allowed instant control of millions of PCs, protected so that nobody else could take it over. The CWG's own summary calls it malware intended to create a botnet. It is not a virus that damaged files, and for most of its life it did little with the access it held.

The flaw. Microsoft published security bulletin MS08-067 on 23 October 2008 for a privately reported vulnerability (CVE-2008-4250) in the Server service, the component behind Windows file and printer sharing, triggered by a crafted remote procedure call (RPC) request. On Windows 2000, XP and Server 2003 an attacker needed no authentication and the rating was Critical; on Vista and Server 2008 only authenticated users could reach the vulnerable code and the rating was Important. Unusually, the bulletin said it was possible the flaw could be used in the crafting of a wormable exploit, and that Microsoft knew of limited, targeted attacks. The National Vulnerability Database (NVD) records an overflow during path canonicalization, exploited in the wild by the Gimmiv.A trojan that October, and scores it 10.0 under version 2 of the Common Vulnerability Scoring System (CVSS) and 9.8 under version 3.1. SRI notes that the attack crossed host firewalls on machines that had file and print sharing enabled. The patch lag was the opening: the CWG cites a Qualys estimate that 30 per cent of Windows computers were still unpatched in January 2009, and millions of counterfeit copies of Windows could not get the update at all.
