The Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency (CISA) lists CVE-2008-4250 in its Known Exploited Vulnerabilities (KEV) catalogue with a date added of 20 May 2026, a measure of how long such flaws stay in use.

How it spread. Conficker A scanned random addresses for port 445, used Universal Plug and Play (UPnP) to ask the local firewall to open a high port as a backdoor from which new victims fetched the binary, and looked up its own public address and a geolocation database; CAIDA describes three scanning patterns, the local network, the neighbouring /24 networks of hosts it had infected, and random addresses. Conficker B, from late December 2008, added copying itself to removable drives as an autorun.inf file and spreading over network shares, the admin and IPC shares, by trying a list of more than 240 common passwords, which is why it travelled so well inside enterprises that had patched their perimeter but not their passwords. Conficker A also carried a check that made it exit on machines with a Ukrainian keyboard layout and skipped Ukrainian addresses, one of the clues SRI explored in its analysis.

The rendezvous algorithm. Rather than contact fixed servers that could be seized, each infected machine computed a fresh list of domain names every day from the current date in Coordinated Universal Time (UTC), which B obtained from the date headers of major search engines, and tried them over the Hypertext Transfer Protocol (HTTP) on port 80. Conficker A generated 250 names across five top-level domains (TLDs), .com, .net, .org, .info and .biz; B used eight, adding .ws, .cn and .cc. Anything it downloaded had to be encrypted with RC4 and carry an RSA signature, with a 1024-bit key in A and a 4096-bit key in B, so that defenders who registered a domain could watch the botnet but not command it; B also switched its hash from SHA-1 to MD6, a candidate published by Ron Rivest's group only weeks before. Conficker C, analysed by SRI in March 2009, kept as little as 15 per cent of B's code, added a peer-to-peer channel that needed no domains at all, and from 1 April 2009 drew 500 queries a day from 50,000 candidate names spread over 110 TLDs; it also disabled security services and Windows updates on the host.

The response. On 12 February 2009 Microsoft announced a coordinated effort with the Internet Corporation for Assigned Names and Numbers (ICANN) and Domain Name System (DNS) operators to disable the domains Conficker would use, naming among its partners NeuStar, VeriSign, CNNIC, Afilias, the Public Interest Registry, AOL, Symantec, F-Secure, ISC, Georgia Tech, the Shadowserver Foundation, Arbor Networks and Support Intelligence, and offered a 250,000-dollar reward for information leading to the authors. The informal group, at first nicknamed the Conficker Cabal, became the Conficker Working Group. Its lessons-learned report, written for the US Department of Homeland Security, calls the effort an unprecedented act of coordination: blocking 250 names a day was already new, and Conficker C forced it to organize in under three weeks with registries in more than 100 countries to block 50,000. The registrations had a second use, which CAIDA describes: every machine that queried a sinkholed domain was counted, so the defence doubled as a census.

What it was used for. Very little, as far as anyone could see. Conficker A tried to download a file from a site linked to the Antivirus XP fake security product. Conficker C updated nearly a million machines despite the blocking. Conficker E, released on 7 April 2009, installed the Waledac spam bot and the SpyProtect 2009 fake antivirus on machines already running C, then removed itself on 3 May and reverted to C, which the CWG reads as a sign that access was being rented to a criminal group. The CWG counts its biggest success as preventing the authors from taking control of the botnet and its biggest failure as the inability to clean infected computers; it could not say whether the author was one person or many, nor whether they were criminals or a state.

Scale, and the long tail. Counts depend on method. SRI's census to March 2009 found more than 4.7 million addresses for A and 6.7 million for B, but estimated the active populations at under 1 million and 3 million and judged press figures likely too high. The CWG reported that a year after release 5 to 13 million computers, from about 6 million addresses, were infected with A or B, with C down to 300,000 to 400,000 addresses by December 2009 from more than a million in April; F-Secure had estimated 15 million at the peak. The infections that lasted were in places patching could not reach. At Beth Israel Deaconess Medical Center in Boston, John Halamka recalled in 2012 that in 2009 Conficker had hit a Philips obstetrical workstation, a GE radiology workstation and nuclear medicine applications that could not be patched because of regulatory restrictions; they had to be shut down, cleaned and isolated from the network. Infected relics in industrial systems and other unmanaged machines kept calling home long after the headlines.

What defenders changed. Removable media was one fix: Microsoft stopped Windows 7 from running programs automatically from USB (Universal Serial Bus) drives, backported the change to XP and Vista in August 2009 and, on 8 February 2011, pushed it through Windows Update as KB971029, noting that four of the ten most common malware families at the end of 2010 still spread through AutoRun. The DNS was another: the CWG credits its success chiefly to the cooperation of ICANN and the country-code registries, which its report calls a model for cyber defence, with processes now in place to make future coordination easier. The rest is familiar. Block TCP 445 at the perimeter and between segments; do not rely on a host firewall when file sharing is enabled; replace weak administrator and share passwords, which B's 240-word list exploited; and close the gap between a patch and its installation. A former programme manager at the Microsoft Malware Protection Center made the comparison ten years later: WannaCry and NotPetya succeeded for the same reason, a known patch not applied.

The numbers worth remembering. MS08-067 on 23 October 2008; the first variant on 20 November 2008; TCP port 445; 250 domains a day over five TLDs for A and eight for B; 50,000 candidates over 110 TLDs, 500 queried, for C from 1 April 2009; more than 240 passwords in B's list; a 250,000-dollar reward; 5 to 13 million infected a year after release; KB971029 in Windows Update from 8 February 2011.

therac-25.def: The radiation therapy machine built by Atomic Energy of Canada Limited (AECL) whose software faults, a data-entry race condition among them, delivered massive overdoses to six patients between 1985 and 1987, killing three: the founding case study of software safety.
therac-25.context: Between 1985 and 1987 the Therac-25 gave at least six patients radiation overdoses, three of them fatal, after its makers removed hardware interlocks and trusted software that harboured race conditions triggered by fast operator input. Nancy Leveson and Clark Turner's investigation, published in IEEE Computer in 1993, became required reading: the failures were systemic, not a single bug, and reused code carried assumptions the new machine no longer honoured. Every 'the software will catch it' argument since has had to answer to Therac-25.
therac-25.depth:
What the machine was. The Therac-25 was a computer-controlled medical linear accelerator made by AECL, a Canadian Crown corporation, after the Therac-6 and Therac-20, which AECL had built with the French company CGR around a DEC PDP-11 minicomputer. It put the market's convenience in one box: it could treat either with a low-current electron beam scanned over the tumour by magnets, or with X-rays, produced by firing a beam of about 100 times the current into a tungsten target and passing the result through a flattening filter. A turntable carried the magnets, the target and filter, and a mirror for a third position, field light, used to aim the beam with visible light; microswitches told the computer where the turntable was. The machine went on sale in late 1982, a million-dollar device among the first of a generation of computer-controlled machines, and eleven were installed, six in Canada and five in the United States. Its software was written by one person over several years in PDP-11 assembly language, as an evolution of the Therac-6 software.

The design decision underneath. In most accelerators, hard-wired electromechanical interlocks made it physically impossible to reach X-ray beam intensity unless the target was in place, and the Therac-20's software, in a phrase the case literature repeats, merely added convenience to existing hardware that was capable of standing alone. In the Therac-25 both the position of the target and the intensity of the beam were controlled by the computer alone: AECL moved safety functions from hardware into software and did not duplicate some of them. It also reused modules from the earlier machines. Their software had worked for years, but partly because the hardware interlocks around it had been quietly catching its errors, and those interlocks had no way of reporting that they had fired, so nobody knew the errors were there.

The accidents. The first known overdose was on 3 June 1985 at the Kennestone Regional Oncology Center in Marietta, Georgia; the second on 26 July 1985 at the Ontario Cancer Foundation in Hamilton, where the machine paused with the message H-tilt and the operator pressed the key to proceed five times; the third in December 1985 at Yakima Valley Memorial Hospital in Washington state. Then came two at the East Texas Cancer Center in Tyler, which had treated more than 500 patients with the machine over two years without incident: on 21 March 1986 and on 11 April 1986, both after the operator typed X for X-ray, corrected it to E for electrons and started the treatment, and both ending with the message Malfunction 54. Both Tyler patients died, the second on 1 May 1986. The last accident was again at Yakima, on 17 January 1987, when a patient prescribed a total of 86 rad received an estimated 8,000 to 10,000 rad and died that April. Contemporary reports put the overdoses in Texas and Georgia at 17,000 to 25,000 rad to very small areas of the body, against roughly 1,000 rad that can be fatal to the whole body. Patients described the beam as an intense electric shock or a burning heat, and in several cases staff told them that what they felt was impossible.

The bugs. The Tyler fault was a race between the operator and the software. If an experienced operator selected X-ray mode by mistake, moved the cursor up to change it to electron mode and pressed Enter, all within about eight seconds of the first keystroke, the edit was not fully processed: the turntable moved to the electron position, but the beam was left at X-ray intensity, so a high-current beam reached the patient with no target or flattener in the way, while the screen showed the corrected prescription. The hospital's physicist, Fritz Hager, and the operator reproduced Malfunction 54 by practising fast data entry until they could produce it at will; AECL said it could reproduce the error only by following their instructions. The second Yakima accident had a different cause: the software set a flag by incrementing it rather than by assigning a fixed non-zero value, so every so often the counter overflowed to zero and a safety check was skipped, letting the beam fire with the turntable in the field-light position. Neither fault was exotic. Both were the kind that ordinary testing rarely reaches, because they needed an unusual timing or an unlucky count.

Why it took so long. The interface trained operators to ignore it. Errors appeared as the word MALFUNCTION and a number from 1 to 64 that the manual did not explain; a therapist at one site reported up to 40 diagnostic messages a day, most of them harmless; and the machine distinguished errors that halted it from errors that only paused it, letting the operator continue with a single key, P, even after some that endangered the patient. AECL's failure analysis did not consider the software, which was assumed free of bugs, and its testing concentrated on hardware. When hospitals reported injuries, the company replied that overdoses were impossible: after the first Yakima injury it sent a two-page letter saying neither machine failure nor operator error could cause one. An earlier hardware-based diagnosis of the Ontario accident led, at the Canadian government's request, to a redesign of the turntable position circuit with redundant switches, which did not touch the software faults. After Tyler, a physicist in Chicago, Frank Borger, found a similar fault in the Therac-20, where it only blew fuses, because that machine's hard-wired circuits stopped the beam.

What changed. After the Tyler accidents the machines were not withdrawn; warnings and a temporary fix were circulated, and the fix did not prevent the second Yakima accident. After the January 1987 accident, users were advised, though not ordered, to stop routine use until fixes approved by the Food and Drug Administration (FDA) were installed, and the main effect of those fixes was to restore safety features that worked independently of the computer; Ethics Unwrapped dates the FDA's shutdown to 6 February 1987, and the machine was recalled in 1987 for an extensive redesign of its safety features, software and mechanical interlocks. AECL had stopped selling therapy machines in 1985, and in 1988 its medical division was dissolved, with Theratronics International taking over maintenance of the installed machines. The FDA restructured its reporting requirements for radiation equipment and began to regulate software in medical devices. The international standard that now governs the life cycle of medical device software, IEC 62304, was first published in May 2006 and amended in 2015.

What the case established. Software in a safety-critical role is a different discipline, not a cheaper implementation of the same one. Leveson and Turner's account, An Investigation of the Therac-25 Accidents, IEEE Computer volume 26, number 7, July 1993, pages 18 to 41, is still taught because the failures were organizational as much as technical: overconfidence in reused code, safety analysis that left the software out, reports of injury dismissed as impossible because the software said so. Leveson's warning against the naive assumption that reusing software, or buying it off the shelf, makes a system safer because the code has been exercised extensively is the lesson that travels furthest; she returned to the case in The Therac-25: 30 Years Later, in the November 2017 issue of the same journal. Jonathan Jacky, writing in 1994, put the engineering rule in one line: the failure of a single component should never by itself be capable of causing an accident, which rules out designs whose safety depends entirely on one computer without hard-wired interlocks.

Why it belongs in a networking glossary. The same three mistakes recur in every field that automates control. Removing an independent safeguard because the new controller is smarter is the decision behind every single point of failure; a control plane that reports what it was told rather than what the hardware did is the operator's screen at Tyler; and a console that cries wolf forty times a day teaches people to press proceed, which is alert fatigue by another name. Defence in depth, in a firewall policy or in a radiation room, means a second mechanism that does not share the first one's assumptions, and Therac-25 is the case that shows what happens when the second one is taken away.

ariane-5.def: The 1996 maiden launch destroyed by an integer overflow in software reused from Ariane 4.
ariane-5.context: Thirty-seven seconds after liftoff on 4 June 1996, a 64-bit velocity value overflowed a 16-bit conversion inside inertial-alignment code inherited from Ariane 4, where the flight profile made the overflow impossible; on the faster Ariane 5 it was not. The exception took down both redundant units running identical code, the rocket veered and self-destructed, and roughly half a billion dollars of vehicle and payload fell into the Atlantic. The Lions report made it the eternal case study on reusing code outside its validated envelope.
ariane-5.depth:
On 4 June 1996 the maiden flight of Ariane 5 veered off course thirty-seven seconds after launch and destroyed itself, losing the rocket and its four scientific satellites. The cause was a conversion of a 64-bit floating point value to a 16-bit signed integer that overflowed, in code inherited from Ariane 4.

Three details make it exemplary rather than merely expensive. The code was doing something only meaningful before launch and had no function at all in flight, so the calculation that killed the rocket was not needed. The value overflowed because Ariane 5 flew a genuinely different trajectory with larger horizontal velocity, which the Ariane 4 assumption had ruled out. And the exception that resulted was handled by shutting down the inertial reference unit, which the backup unit, running identical software, had already done for the identical reason.

The lesson the inquiry drew was about reuse, not arithmetic. Code proven correct in one environment carries its assumptions with it, and inheriting it without revalidating those assumptions is inheriting an unstated specification. Redundancy that runs the same software is redundancy against hardware failure only, which is why design diversity exists and why it is expensive enough that people keep deciding they do not need it.

mars-climate-orbiter.def: The 1999 Mars probe lost because one team's software spoke pound-force seconds and the other expected newton seconds.
mars-climate-orbiter.context: On 23 September 1999 the orbiter hit the Martian atmosphere far too low and was destroyed: ground software from Lockheed Martin reported thruster impulse in imperial pound-force seconds while JPL's navigation expected metric newton seconds, and months of tiny trajectory errors compounded silently. NASA's mishap board turned it into the definitive parable of interface contracts. Units are part of the type; the universe does not do implicit conversion.
mars-climate-orbiter.depth:
The Mars Climate Orbiter was lost on 23 September 1999 because one team supplied thruster impulse figures in pound-seconds while the receiving software expected newton-seconds. The spacecraft approached far lower than intended and did not survive the atmosphere.

The interesting failure is not the units. It is that this was a well-known category of error with a well-known defence, and the defence was not applied at the interface between two organizations. Within each team the units were consistent and correct; the mismatch lived in the handoff, which is precisely where nobody's checklist ran and everybody assumed the other side had been explicit.

That pattern generalizes well beyond spacecraft. Interfaces between teams are where specifications go unstated, because inside a team the shared context makes them invisible, and the cost of writing them down feels higher than the cost of assuming. Typed quantities that carry their units, explicit contract tests at boundaries, and review that focuses on handoffs rather than on components are the responses, and they are all unglamorous work that nobody schedules until something is lost.

eternalblue.def: EternalBlue is the codename of a National Security Agency (NSA) exploit for a remote code execution flaw in the Server Message Block version 1 (SMBv1) server of Windows, fixed by Microsoft as MS17-010 on 14 March 2017 and published by the Shadow Brokers on 14 April 2017; within weeks it was spreading WannaCry and then NotPetya.
eternalblue.context: The flaw sat in the oldest dialect of Windows file sharing, reachable on TCP (Transmission Control Protocol) port 445 by an unauthenticated attacker sending crafted packets, and the exploit turned it into code execution inside the kernel of unpatched machines, usually followed by the DoublePulsar backdoor from the same leak. The Washington Post reported that the NSA used it for more than five years and warned Microsoft only after learning it had been stolen. The patch came a month before the leak, yet WannaCry on 12 May 2017 and NotPetya on 27 June 2017 found millions of machines without it, and the exploit kept working on unpatched networks for years after the headlines. The case changed defaults (current Windows no longer installs SMBv1), pushed Microsoft to patch long-unsupported systems, and became the standard example in the argument over whether governments should keep the flaws they find or disclose them so that everyone is protected.
eternalblue.depth:
What it is, and what it is not. EternalBlue is an exploit, working attack code, not the vulnerability itself. The flaw it uses is in the Server Message Block version 1 (SMBv1) server of Windows, and Microsoft fixed it in security bulletin MS17-010, published on 14 March 2017 and rated Critical for every supported release of Windows. The bulletin fixed six related flaws at once: five remote code execution vulnerabilities (CVE-2017-0143, CVE-2017-0144, CVE-2017-0145, CVE-2017-0146 and CVE-2017-0148) and one information disclosure (CVE-2017-0147). It described the attack as an unauthenticated attacker sending a specially crafted packet to an SMBv1 server, listed no mitigating factors, and offered a single workaround: disable SMBv1. Microsoft's analysis of NotPetya maps EternalBlue to CVE-2017-0144 and its sibling EternalRomance to CVE-2017-0145, while its analysis of WannaCrypt cites CVE-2017-0145, so the dependable reference is the bulletin rather than any one Common Vulnerabilities and Exposures (CVE) number. The National Vulnerability Database (NVD) record for CVE-2017-0144 lists Windows Vista SP2 through Windows 10 version 1607 and Windows Server 2016 as affected. Nor is EternalBlue the backdoor that usually came with it: DoublePulsar, from the same leak, is the implant the exploit left in the kernel to receive further code.

How it worked, as Microsoft described it. Microsoft's June 2017 analysis of the WannaCrypt propagation code, which borrowed EternalBlue and DoublePulsar directly, gives the chain at the level a defender needs. The exploit sprays the target's kernel memory with packets carrying a first-stage shellcode, then overwrites a function pointer so that control reaches it, which means code execution inside the kernel. The shellcode installs DoublePulsar by patching the dispatch table the SMBv1 driver uses for Transaction2 requests; later SMB packets, XOR-encoded, deliver the payload, which is finally started through kernel asynchronous procedure calls. Microsoft noted that this code worked only on older systems such as Windows 7 and Windows Server 2008 without MS17-010: from Windows 8 and Windows Server 2012 the hardware abstraction layer's memory is no longer executable, the Windows 10 Creators Update randomized the predictable addresses in it, the Fall Creators Update made the SMBv1 dispatch tables read-only, and virtualization-based security on Windows 10 can catch the processor register change the shellcode depends on. The leak's own list, as Ars Technica reported it, called EternalBlue a remote exploit over SMB and NetBIOS over TCP (NetBT) for Windows XP to Windows 2012. Kernel memory corruption is fragile, and The Washington Post reported that the NSA had to improve the tool because it tended to crash its targets, which earned it the nickname EternalBlueScreen.

Who built it and how it got out. The Washington Post, citing former employees of the National Security Agency (NSA), reported in May 2017 that the agency had used EternalBlue for more than five years, that one of them called the intelligence it produced unreal and another compared its use to fishing with dynamite, that some officials had discussed whether the flaw was dangerous enough to reveal to Microsoft, and that the agency warned Microsoft only after learning the tool had been stolen. The group calling itself the Shadow Brokers had begun dumping NSA tools in August 2016. On Friday 14 April 2017, the start of the Easter weekend, it published close to 300 megabytes including compiled exploits for Windows (EternalBlue, EternalRomance, EternalChampion, EternalSynergy and others) and Fuzzbunch, a framework for launching them that Ars Technica compared to Metasploit. In a post dated the next day, Microsoft said most of the exploits fell into vulnerabilities already patched, listed EternalBlue as addressed by MS17-010, and said three others did not reproduce on supported platforms. The bulletin had recorded the flaws as neither publicly disclosed nor exploited when it shipped, and named no finder. The patch therefore came first: 31 days before the leak, 59 days before WannaCry and 105 days before NotPetya.

WannaCry. The first mass use came on Friday 12 May 2017. Microsoft's analysis shows that WannaCry, which it calls WannaCrypt, borrowed the EternalBlue exploit and the DoublePulsar backdoor to spread as a worm, and the UK Foreign Office later put its reach at 300,000 computers in 150 countries. In England the National Audit Office (NAO) found that at least 81 of the 236 National Health Service (NHS) trusts were affected, with 603 primary care and other NHS organizations including 595 general practices; NHS England identified 6,912 cancelled appointments and estimated more than 19,000 in all, and five acute trusts diverted emergency patients. Its findings are the useful part for engineers: NHS Digital had issued critical alerts to patch in March and April 2017, every infected organization had unpatched or unsupported Windows, and managing internet-facing firewalls would have protected them whether they had patched or not. The spread stopped when a researcher registered a domain the code looked up, which acted as a kill switch; he wrote that he had not known it at the time. On 13 May Microsoft took what it called the highly unusual step of releasing the fix for Windows XP, Windows 8 and Windows Server 2003, platforms then in custom support only. The United Kingdom attributed WannaCry to North Korea's Lazarus Group on 19 December 2017, its National Cyber Security Centre judging that highly likely, and on 6 September 2018 the US Department of Justice charged Park Jin Hyok, alleging that he worked for a North Korean government front company, Chosun Expo, in a conspiracy that included creating WannaCry 2.0.

NotPetya. Six weeks later the exploit was used again, as one of several ways to spread. Microsoft's analysis of 27 June 2017 traced the first infections to the updater of M.E.Doc, Ukrainian tax-accounting software, counted more than 12,500 machines in Ukraine that encountered the malware, and listed EternalBlue (CVE-2017-0144) and EternalRomance (CVE-2017-0145) for unpatched machines alongside credential theft and remote execution with PsExec or WMIC for patched ones. Benjamin Delpy, author of the Mimikatz credential tool, summed up the combination for Wired: infect the computers that are not patched, take the passwords from them, and use those to infect the ones that are. Wired lists Maersk, the pharmaceutical company Merck, FedEx's TNT Express and Saint-Gobain among the multinationals it crippled; on 15 February 2018 the White House attributed NotPetya to the Russian military and called it the most destructive and costly cyberattack in history, with billions of dollars of damage across Europe, Asia and the Americas. Between the two outbreaks the victims ran from hospitals to shipping lines and manufacturers.

The afterlife. The exploit outlived both outbreaks. ESET reported in May 2018 that attempts to use it had fallen to hundreds of detections a day after WannaCry, began climbing again from September 2017 and in mid-April 2018 passed the peaks of 2017; it named cryptocurrency miners, the Satan ransomware and an espionage campaign against hotel Wi-Fi networks by the group it calls Sednit among later users. In the United States the Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency (CISA) added CVE-2017-0144 to its Known Exploited Vulnerabilities (KEV) catalogue on 10 February 2022, with the required action to apply the vendor's updates, and marks it as known to have been used in ransomware campaigns. The NVD scores the flaw 9.3 under version 2 of the Common Vulnerability Scoring System (CVSS) and 8.8 under version 3.1, whose vector records low privileges as required where the bulletin speaks of an unauthenticated attacker.

What defenders changed. On Windows the decisive change was removing the protocol. Microsoft's documentation says SMBv2 superseded SMBv1 in 2007 and that SMBv1 was publicly deprecated in 2014; since Windows 10 version 1709 and Windows Server version 1709 it is no longer installed by default, Windows Server 2019 and later contain neither the SMBv1 client nor the server after a clean installation, and Windows 10 Home and Pro remove the client by themselves if it goes unused for 15 days, a one-time operation an administrator can reverse. Removing it also removes the Computer Browser service, which needed SMBv1 to fill the Network node in Explorer, and that is usually the first thing users notice. On the network the advice in Microsoft's NotPetya guidance still stands: block SMB on TCP ports 445 and 139 at the perimeter, and between segments that have no need to share files, so that one infected host cannot reach the rest. Detection caught up too: the open Emerging Threats rule set for Suricata carries signatures named for EternalBlue probes, echo requests and heap spraying, and others for EternalRomance, EternalChampion and DoublePulsar's installation traffic, which is how an intrusion detection system (IDS) still flags a scanner sweeping a network for unpatched hosts.

The equities argument. EternalBlue is the reference case in the argument over the vulnerabilities equities process, by which a government decides whether to tell a vendor about a flaw it has found or keep it for intelligence, military or law enforcement use. Microsoft's president Brad Smith wrote on 14 May 2017 that the attack showed why the stockpiling of vulnerabilities by governments was such a problem, compared the theft to the US military having some of its Tomahawk missiles stolen, and repeated Microsoft's call for a Digital Geneva Convention requiring governments to report vulnerabilities to vendors rather than stockpile, sell or exploit them. On 15 November 2017 the White House published the charter of the Vulnerabilities Equities Policy and Process (VEP). It sends newly discovered, not publicly known vulnerabilities to an interagency Equities Review Board, which aims to decide by consensus whether to disclose or restrict them; disclosure is to happen when possible within seven business days, restricted vulnerabilities are reassessed every year until they are disclosed, become public or are otherwise mitigated, and an annual report is promised. The charter also states the other side: that the government did not create these vulnerabilities, that a policy of immediate disclosure would still leave others for adversaries to find, and that exploiting a vulnerability is at times the only way to understand a much bigger threat. What EternalBlue contributed to that debate was a case nobody had to imagine: a retained exploit for software on a large share of the world's computers, stolen, published and turned against hospitals and companies within weeks, by actors the United Kingdom and the United States later named as North Korean and Russian. Stockpiles leak, and the cost of a leak falls on everyone who runs the software.

The numbers worth remembering. MS17-010 on 14 March 2017; the Shadow Brokers release on 14 April; WannaCry on 12 May; NotPetya on 27 June; six CVEs in one bulletin, five of them remote code execution; TCP port 445, with 139 for NetBT; SMBv1 off by default from Windows 10 and Windows Server version 1709; the VEP charter on 15 November 2017; and CVE-2017-0144 in the KEV catalogue from 10 February 2022.

postels-law.def: 'Be conservative in what you do, be liberal in what you accept from others' - the robustness principle from the TCP specification.
postels-law.context: Jon Postel wrote the maxim into the 1980 TCP specification, and it shaped a generation of interoperable protocol implementations. Decades later the field partially recanted: tolerating malformed input lets errors and attacks hide, so modern guidance (including RFC 9413) argues for stricter validation. The law endures as the axis of one of protocol engineering's longest-running debates.
postels-law.depth:
Be conservative in what you send, be liberal in what you accept. Jon Postel wrote it into the early TCP specification, and it is probably the most consequential single sentence in the design of the internet, because it let independently written implementations interoperate before anyone had conformance test suites.

The modern reassessment is that the second half caused enormous long-term harm. Accepting malformed input means the malformed input becomes normal: senders never learn they are broken, receivers accumulate compensating code, and after twenty years the de facto protocol is whatever the most popular implementations happen to tolerate. HTML is the canonical example, where liberal parsing produced years of incompatible error recovery before HTML5 finally specified exactly how to handle broken markup.

Security made the argument sharper. Every leniency is a place where two implementations may disagree about what a message means, and request smuggling, certificate parsing bugs and a long list of injection classes all live in exactly that gap. Current practice leans the other way: specify strictly, reject early, and fail loudly, which is why newer protocols define parsing precisely rather than leaving room for kindness.

metcalfes-law.def: The value of a network grows with the square of its number of connected users.
metcalfes-law.context: Attributed to Ethernet co-inventor Robert Metcalfe and popularized in the 1990s, the law captures why networks tip: each new node adds links to every existing node. Economists have argued the true exponent is gentler (Odlyzko proposed n log n), but the qualitative point survived every critique. It is the one-line explanation for network effects, platform lock-in, and why the fax machine only mattered once everyone had one.
metcalfes-law.depth:
Metcalfe's law states that a network's value grows with the square of the number of connected users, because value comes from possible connections rather than from nodes. Two telephones make one link; twelve make sixty-six. Robert Metcalfe formulated it for Ethernet, and it became the standard justification for network effects generally.

The mathematics is also its weakness, and that is worth stating rather than repeating the law uncritically. Not all connections have equal value, and most have none: you will never contact the overwhelming majority of people on any large network. Later analyses proposed slower growth curves precisely because the square overstates things, and the dot-com era's more enthusiastic valuations leaned on the unqualified version.

What survives is the shape rather than the exponent. Networks genuinely do get disproportionately more valuable as they grow, which is why the incumbent is hard to displace and why a technically superior competitor with fewer users loses anyway. That dynamic explains messaging apps, social platforms, and why interoperability standards matter so much: they let a small network borrow the value of a large one instead of having to become it.

murphys-law.def: 'Anything that can go wrong will go wrong' - engineering's oldest planning assumption.
murphys-law.context: The name traces to Captain Edward Murphy and the 1949 rocket-sled tests at Edwards Air Force Base, though participants told conflicting versions of who said what, and the sentiment predates them all. In operations it is not pessimism but method: design for the failure mode, because given enough deployments it will occur. Every redundancy, backup, and chaos drill is Murphy's law taken seriously.
murphys-law.depth:
Anything that can go wrong will go wrong. The attribution is to Edward Murphy, an engineer on rocket sled tests in 1949, and the original context matters: it was not fatalism, it was a design principle. If a component can be installed backwards, someone will install it backwards, so design it so it cannot be.

That reading is the useful one and the one usually lost. Murphy's law is an argument for defensive engineering, not a shrug. It is why connectors are keyed, why dangerous commands ask for confirmation, and why a good API makes the correct usage the easy one. The pessimism is instrumental: assume the failure mode will happen and remove the possibility rather than the intention.

In operations it maps directly to blast radius thinking. The certificate will expire on a holiday, the disk will fill during the incident, the runbook will be on the system that is down. Each of those is a specific thing that can go wrong, and each has a preventable version, which is why writing them down before they happen is the whole discipline. Fatalism does nothing; enumeration does a great deal.

parkinsons-law.def: 'Work expands so as to fill the time available for its completion.'
parkinsons-law.context: Cyril Northcote Parkinson opened his 1955 Economist essay with the line, drawn from watching bureaucracies grow regardless of workload. Engineers meet it in every padded estimate and every sprint that fills exactly to its deadline. His same book gave the field the law of triviality, better known here as bikeshedding.
parkinsons-law.depth:
Work expands to fill the time available for its completion. Parkinson published it in 1955 as satire about the British civil service, and it has survived because it describes something real about how estimates and effort interact.

The mechanism is not laziness. Given more time, people add polish, explore alternatives, hold more meetings about the approach, and raise the standard of what counts as finished. Each of those is defensible individually, and the aggregate is a task that consumed its budget regardless of what the budget was. This is the same author who gave us the law of triviality, which is where bikeshedding comes from, and the two are related observations about how organizations spend attention.

The practical use is deadline design rather than deadline pressure. Shorter timeboxes genuinely produce faster completion for well-understood work, which is the honest core of the law. It is a bad principle to apply universally, though: for work whose scope is genuinely unknown, a tight deadline does not compress the work, it compresses the quality, and the difference between those two outcomes is invisible until much later.

peter-principle.def: In a hierarchy, people rise to their level of incompetence.
peter-principle.context: Laurence J. Peter's 1969 satire observed that promotion rewards performance in the current job, not aptitude for the next one, so employees climb until they reach a role they do poorly, and stay there. Tech companies built dual career ladders largely to blunt it, letting great engineers advance without becoming managers. The satire has since accumulated empirical support in studies of sales-force promotions.
peter-principle.depth:
The Peter principle observes that people are promoted based on performance in their current role until they reach a level where they are no longer competent, and there they remain. Laurence Peter published it in 1969, and its bite is that the mechanism requires nobody to behave badly: each promotion is a reasonable reward for demonstrated success.

Technology has an especially clean example. The strongest engineer is promoted to manage engineers, which is a different job requiring different skills, and the organization loses its best practitioner while gaining a manager who may be uncomfortable and unsupported. The failure is structural, not personal, and blaming the individual misreads it entirely.

The correction the industry landed on is the dual ladder: a technical track with genuine seniority, compensation and influence that does not route through people management. It works when the levels are real and fails when the technical track is decorative, which is easy to check by asking whether anyone on it can affect a decision the management track disagrees with. The other half of the fix is treating management as a skill to be trained rather than a prize for having been good at something else.

sturgeons-law.context: Science-fiction author Theodore Sturgeon coined it in the 1950s defending his genre: critics judged SF by its worst examples, though ninety percent of everything, in any field, is equally poor. Engineers reach for it when evaluating plugin ecosystems, npm search results, and conference submissions. The corollary matters more than the law: judge a field by its best ten percent.
sturgeons-law.depth:
Ninety percent of everything is crap. Theodore Sturgeon coined it defending science fiction from critics who judged the genre by its worst examples, and his point was comparative rather than cynical: ninety percent of literature, film and music is also poor, so singling out one field is unfair.

Applied to technology it is a useful corrective in both directions. Ninety percent of libraries, frameworks, conference talks and blog posts are unremarkable, which means encountering bad examples of something says almost nothing about the category. It also means that time spent filtering is not wasted time, it is the actual work of finding the ten percent.

The uncomfortable half is that it applies to your own output too. Most code anyone writes is ordinary, most ideas do not survive contact with implementation, and the ones that do are usually not the ones that felt most promising. That reading turns the law from a complaint into permission: producing a great deal of ordinary work is the normal path to the small amount that is not, and expecting every attempt to be excellent mostly prevents attempting.

kerckhoffs-principle.def: A cryptosystem must remain secure even if everything about it, except the key, is public knowledge.
kerckhoffs-principle.context: Auguste Kerckhoffs stated it in 1883 for military ciphers, and Claude Shannon compressed it into 'the enemy knows the system'. It is the formal argument against security through obscurity: designs leak, insiders defect, hardware gets captured, and only the key can be cheaply replaced. Every open cipher competition, from AES to the post-quantum process, is Kerckhoffs's principle institutionalized.
kerckhoffs-principle.depth:
Kerckhoffs's principle holds that a cryptographic system should remain secure even if everything about it except the key is public knowledge. Auguste Kerckhoffs stated it in 1883, for military ciphers, and it has survived every technology change since because the reasoning is about people rather than mathematics.

The argument is that secrets leak. Algorithms are reverse-engineered from the devices that implement them, disclosed by employees, or rediscovered independently, and a design whose security depends on staying hidden fails permanently the first time any of that happens. A key can be rotated in an afternoon; an algorithm cannot. So the sensible place to concentrate secrecy is the thing you can cheaply replace.

The practical consequence is public review, and the evidence is one-sided. Every widely used modern cipher was published, attacked for years, and adopted because the attacks failed; the proprietary alternatives that avoided scrutiny have a long history of falling quickly once examined. Security through obscurity fails as a foundation, though it remains reasonable as a thin extra layer over something that would hold anyway.

linus-law.def: 'Given enough eyeballs, all bugs are shallow.'
linus-law.context: Eric Raymond coined the phrase in The Cathedral and the Bazaar and named it for Linus Torvalds, as the core argument for open source's quality advantage. Heartbleed became its standing counterexample: the code was open for years, but almost nobody was actually looking. The modern reading adds the missing clause: eyeballs must be funded, qualified, and pointed at the code.
linus-law.depth:
Given enough eyeballs, all bugs are shallow. Eric Raymond formulated it in The Cathedral and the Bazaar and named it after Linus Torvalds, and it became the standard argument for why open source produces secure software.

The evidence has complicated it considerably. Heartbleed sat in OpenSSL for two years, in code that everyone could read and almost nobody did, and Shellshock survived in bash for decades. The law assumes eyeballs actually look, and looking at cryptographic C is difficult, unpaid, and unrewarding, so availability of source and review of source turn out to be very different things.

What survives is the conditional. Open source enables review, and where review genuinely happens the effect is real: widely used, well-funded projects with dedicated security attention do find and fix problems faster. Where it does not happen, being open provides no protection while providing attackers the same source. The industry's response was to stop assuming and start funding, which is why initiatives to pay for audits of critical infrastructure exist at all.

goodharts-law.def: 'When a measure becomes a target, it ceases to be a good measure.'
goodharts-law.context: Economist Charles Goodhart observed the effect in 1975 monetary policy; anthropologist Marilyn Strathern gave it the crisp modern phrasing. Engineering lives it daily: optimize ticket-close counts and quality dies, optimize line coverage and tests stop asserting, optimize velocity and estimates inflate. Any metric worth managing by is worth gaming, so pair every target with the behaviour it is supposed to proxy.
goodharts-law.depth:
When a measure becomes a target, it ceases to be a good measure. Charles Goodhart wrote it about monetary policy, and the mechanism generalizes to anything measured: the moment people are rewarded for a number, they optimize the number, and its correlation with the thing you actually cared about weakens.

Software supplies endless examples. Measure test coverage and you get tests that execute code without asserting anything. Measure tickets closed and issues get split, or closed as works-as-designed. Measure lines of code and you get verbosity; measure velocity and estimates inflate quietly until the chart looks healthy. In each case nobody is cheating exactly, they are responding to the incentive that was set.

The uncomfortable conclusion is that there is no metric immune to this, only metrics not yet load-bearing enough to distort. Partial defences exist: use several measures that are hard to game simultaneously, treat metrics as prompts for conversation rather than as verdicts, and keep the number away from compensation. The most reliable safeguard is asking what behaviour this measure would produce if someone optimized it ruthlessly, before publishing it.

two-hard-things.def: 'There are only two hard things in Computer Science: cache invalidation and naming things.'
two-hard-things.context: The line is attributed to Netscape engineer Phil Karlton, and its endurance comes from being true: both problems are about keeping a name or a copy faithful to a changing reality. The community's favourite corollary adds a third: off-by-one errors. Quote it whenever a stale cache and a misleading variable name conspire in the same incident.
two-hard-things.depth:
There are only two hard things in computer science: cache invalidation and naming things. The joke is Phil Karlton's, and the popular version adds off-by-one errors as a third item that arrives second, which is a better joke and a worse quotation.

Both halves are serious. Cache invalidation is hard because it demands knowing when something elsewhere changed, which is a distributed knowledge problem wearing a performance optimization's clothes, and almost every caching bug is really a question about whose responsibility it was to say the data was stale. The failures are also the worst kind: intermittent, environment-dependent, and invisible in testing where caches are usually cold or disabled.

Naming is hard for a different and more interesting reason. A name is a compressed description of a decision, so choosing one forces you to know exactly what the thing is, and the difficulty of naming is usually a signal that the concept is not clean. That is the practical value hidden inside the joke: when a name will not come, the problem is often the design rather than the vocabulary.

nerd-snipe.def: Presenting someone an irresistibly interesting problem, derailing whatever they were supposed to be doing.
nerd-snipe.context: The term comes from xkcd #356, where a physicist is stopped in his tracks (fatally, in the comic) by an infinite-resistor-grid puzzle placed in the road. Engineers use it both as accusation and confession: a well-aimed puzzle in a chat channel can burn an afternoon of a whole team. Consider it the denial-of-service attack that targets curiosity.

rtfm.def: The support-culture retort telling an asker the answer is already in the documentation.
rtfm.context: Canonized by the Jargon File, RTFM carries hacker culture's core covenant: respect for other people's time, and the expectation that you search before you ask. The polite expansion uses 'fine'; everyone knows the original. Modern communities soften it into 'let me link you the docs', but the underlying norm, do your homework first, is unchanged.

lgtm.def: The code-review approval stamp: looks good to me.
lgtm.context: LGTM is how a reviewer signs off a change, and entire review tools adopted it as the approval keyword. It also names the failure mode: a rubber-stamp LGTM on a thousand-line diff means nobody actually read it. The two-character review is both the grease of high-velocity teams and the epitaph on many an incident postmortem.

token-ring.def: Token Ring is the local area network (LAN) technology, developed by IBM and standardized by the Institute of Electrical and Electronics Engineers as IEEE 802.5, in which a circulating three-octet token grants the right to transmit. IBM championed it against Ethernet.
token-ring.context: Stations on a logical ring pass a token; only the holder transmits, so there are no collisions and latency is predictable under load, which is exactly what the shared Ethernet of the era could not promise. It ran at 4 and then 16 Mbit/s, with 100 Mbit/s and 1000 Mbit/s successors that arrived too late (802.5t-2000 and 802.5v-2001 of the Institute of Electrical and Electronics Engineers, IEEE), and it owned IBM-centric enterprises through the mid-1990s before the economics of switched Ethernet ended the war. Physically it was wired as a star through multistation access units, and beyond one ring it relied on source-route bridging. The IEEE 802.5 working group is disbanded and its standards are withdrawn. Technically elegant and commercially defeated, it remains networking's great counterfactual.
token-ring.depth:
What it is. Token Ring is a physical and data link layer technology for local area networks (LANs) whose access method is token passing: a station may transmit only while it holds the token. The name covers two things that are largely but not wholly the same, IBM's product and the standard of the Institute of Electrical and Electronics Engineers (IEEE). The IEEE record is clear about the dates: IEEE/ANSI 802.5-1985 was published on 29 April 1985, a second edition was approved on 2 June 1989, and the last consolidated text is ISO/IEC 8802-5:1998. That text defines the frame format with its delimiters, addressing and priority stacks, the media access control (MAC) protocol, symbol encoding and latency buffering, and attachment at 4 and 16 Mbit/s over shielded twisted pair, for commercial and light industrial environments. It was never the only token-passing LAN: ARCNET, the token bus of IEEE 802.4 and the Fiber Distributed Data Interface (FDDI) used similar mechanisms, and Proteon and Apollo sold their own rings from 1981.

Where it came from. Cisco's troubleshooting guide dates IBM's development to the 1970s, and the design work is credited to Werner Bux and Hans Müller at the IBM Zurich Research Laboratory. IBM launched the product on 15 October 1985, at 4 Mbit/s over shielded twisted pair, with attachments for its personal computers, midrange systems and mainframes, and argued that it was superior to Ethernet under load, a claim that was debated at the time. In February 1988, Request for Comments (RFC) 1042 still described the standard as specifying single rings at 1 and 4 Mbit/s, with source routing between rings as a vendor extension on its way into an addendum. The 16 Mbit/s rate followed at the end of the decade, and by November 1990 RFC 1191 listed a maximum transmission unit (MTU) of 17,914 octets for 16 Mbit/s IBM Token Ring beside 4,464 for the 4 Mbit/s standard.

How it works. When nobody is sending, a token of three octets (start delimiter, access control, end delimiter) circulates from station to station. A station with data seizes it, turns it into a frame and sends; each station repeats the frame to the next; the destination copies it and sets the address-recognized and frame-copied bits in the frame status octet at the end; the frame returns to its sender, which removes it and releases a new token; where early token release is supported, the new token goes out as soon as the frame has been sent. Collisions cannot happen, and the wait for the token is bounded by the number of stations and the time each may hold it. The frame carries a start delimiter, access control and frame control octets, 6-octet destination and source addresses, the data, a 4-octet frame check sequence (FCS), an end delimiter and the frame status. The access control octet holds three priority bits, the token bit, a monitor bit and three reservation bits, which give eight priority levels: a station can reserve the next token at its priority. Signalling is differential Manchester, and the delimiters are recognizable because they contain deliberate code violations. Frame size is limited by time, not by a constant: with a token-holding time of 9 milliseconds, a 4 Mbit/s ring allows 4,508 octets, which leaves 4,464 for an Internet Protocol (IP) datagram, and there is no minimum size at all.

The ring looks after itself. One station is the active monitor, chosen by a contention in which the highest address wins; every other station is a standby monitor ready to take over. The active monitor supplies the master clock, inserts a 24-bit delay so that a whole token always fits on the ring, makes sure exactly one token exists and removes frames that circulate without an owner. Every 7 seconds a ring poll lets each station learn its nearest active upstream neighbour, which is the information a fault report needs. A station that detects a serious fault, such as a cable break, sends beacon frames, which define a failure domain: the reporting station, its nearest active upstream neighbour and everything in between. The stations in that domain run diagnostics, and the ring tries to reconfigure around the failure. Joining is a five-phase procedure: a lobe test that loops 2,000 frames through the cable, physical insertion by a voltage that opens a relay in the access unit, a duplicate address check, participation in the ring poll, and a request for parameters. Every station must also run at the same ring speed, 4 or 16 Mbit/s, which Cisco lists among the classic media problems.

Wiring and bridging. The ring is logical. Physically, each station connects by a lobe cable to a multistation access unit (MAU), such as the IBM 8228, a passive box of relays that needs no power; the ring runs out to each station and back, so the building is wired as a star. The original cable was IBM Type 1, a heavy 150-ohm shielded twisted pair with a genderless IBM Data Connector, and later installations used unshielded twisted pair and the familiar 8-position modular plug. Rings were joined by source-route bridges: the sender puts the path in a Routing Information Field of up to 18 octets, a two-octet control field and up to eight two-octet route designators, flagged by the top bit of the source address, and discovers the path with all-routes broadcasts. Bridging to Ethernet exposed a second difference. Token Ring transmits each octet most significant bit first, so its adapters present addresses bit-reversed with respect to the canonical Ethernet form; RFC 2469 warns implementers about it, and RFC 1469 shows the result for IP multicast, which Token Ring maps to a single functional address written 03-00-00-20-00-00 in canonical form and C0-00-00-04-00-00 on the ring.

Why it lost, and how it ended. Each adapter needed a specialized processor and licensed firmware, and an interface is said to have cost about three times its Ethernet counterpart; Ethernet then moved to cheap unshielded twisted pair and to switches, and a switched full-duplex link has no collisions to avoid. The 802.5 group answered in kind. Dedicated Token Ring (802.5r, approved on 16 September 1997) added switching and a full-duplex mode; the High-Speed Token Ring projects were approved on 13 November 1997 and produced 100 Mbit/s in IEEE Std 802.5t-2000 and 1000 Mbit/s in IEEE Std 802.5v-2001, approved on 4 May 2001, for which no products ever reached the market. The working group's own site, last modified in March 2004, says it is in hibernation; the IEEE 802 committee now lists it as disbanded, the IEEE lists the amendments as withdrawn in September 2008, and in May 2012 a commit by Paul Gortmaker deleted all remaining Token Ring support from the Linux kernel.

What is left of it. An engineer still meets Token Ring in three places. The numbers 17,914 and 4,464 sit in the plateau table that Path MTU Discovery implementations inherited from RFC 1191. The tcpdump filter manual still warns that expressions on fields beyond the Token Ring header do not handle source-routed frames correctly, and Cisco IOS documentation still describes show interfaces tokenring. And the non-canonical address format survives in old captures and documentation, where a MAC address that looks wrong is often just written the other way round. The argument it lost is worth remembering precisely: Token Ring did not fail on determinism, it failed when switching gave Ethernet the same absence of collisions at a fraction of the price.

martian-packet.def: A packet whose source or destination address could not legitimately appear where it did, as if it arrived from Mars.
martian-packet.context: Router requirements (RFC 1812) use the term for addresses that are impossible in context: loopback ranges on the wire, reserved space, or a source that claims to be inside your own network arriving on an outside interface. Linux kernels log them when rp_filter catches spoofed traffic. Martians overlap with bogons but add the directional test: not just 'this prefix should not exist here' but 'this packet could not have come from there'.

smurf-attack.def: The classic amplification DDoS (distributed denial of service): ICMP echo requests sent to a broadcast address with the victim forged as the source.
smurf-attack.context: Every host on the abused network answers the ping, so one spoofed packet returns a crowd of replies to the victim; the name comes from smurf.c, the 1997 exploit tool. The defence reshaped defaults: routers stopped forwarding directed broadcasts (codified in RFC 2644) and networks learned to filter spoofed sources. Smurf is the ancestor every modern reflection attack, from DNS to NTP amplification, is measured against.

xerox-parc.def: The Palo Alto research lab that invented the modern computer's furniture, and famously let others sell it.
xerox-parc.context: Xerox's Palo Alto Research Center produced, in one astonishing 1970s run, the graphical user interface, the laser printer, Ethernet, object-oriented Smalltalk, and the Alto workstation that tied them together. Apple and Microsoft commercialized the GUI; 3Com commercialized Ethernet; Xerox kept the printers. PARC became the standing parable about the distance between inventing the future and owning it, and its alumni seeded half of this site's other stories, from Ethernet to Juniper's founder.
xerox-parc.depth:
Xerox PARC in the 1970s produced the graphical user interface, the mouse as a mainstream device, WYSIWYG editing, laser printing, object-oriented programming in Smalltalk and Ethernet. The Alto workstation combined most of it into a machine that looks recognisably modern in photographs taken fifty years ago.

The standard telling is that Xerox failed to commercialize any of it and Apple and Microsoft took the ideas. That is roughly true and unfairly simple. Xerox did commercialize the laser printer, which earned the company more than the rest was ever likely to, and the Alto's economics in 1973 were genuinely impossible: the machine cost more than a house to build. A copier company declining to bet itself on desktop computing was not obviously wrong at the time.

What the story actually illustrates is that invention and distribution are separate capabilities. PARC had extraordinary researchers and a parent company whose sales force, incentives and customers were organized around a different business entirely. Ideas do not travel from a lab to the world on merit; they travel through an organization that is built to carry them, and building that is a different problem from having the idea.

eliza.def: Joseph Weizenbaum's 1966 chatbot whose users confided in a pattern-matching script, naming the ELIZA effect.
eliza.context: ELIZA's DOCTOR script parodied a Rogerian therapist by reflecting the user's words back as questions, and Weizenbaum was disturbed to find people, including his own secretary, treating it as a confidant. The ELIZA effect, our readiness to attribute understanding to systems that merely manipulate symbols, is named for it. Every generation of conversational software since has re-run the experiment at larger scale.
eliza.depth:
Joseph Weizenbaum wrote ELIZA in the mid-1960s as a pattern-matching program that reflected a user's statements back as questions, imitating a particular style of psychotherapy. It had no model of meaning at all, and it worked by rearranging the words it was given.

What disturbed Weizenbaum was the reaction. People who knew exactly how simple it was formed attachments to it, disclosed personal matters, and asked to be left alone with it. His own secretary, who had watched him build it, asked him to leave the room. He spent much of the rest of his career arguing against the uses people wanted to put such systems to, becoming one of computing's earliest and most serious internal critics.

The ELIZA effect is the name for that tendency: attributing understanding to a system that produces plausible language. It is not a historical curiosity. Every generation of conversational software has reproduced it, the gap between fluency and comprehension is easier to bridge in the reader's mind than in the system, and Weizenbaum's central point was that the willingness to be convinced is a property of people rather than a property of the program.

the-crypto-wars.def: The long argument, fought hardest in the United States in the 1990s and reopened ever since, over whether strong cryptography could be exported, had to be escrowed with the government, or could be used freely at all.
the-crypto-wars.context: The United States government classed strong cryptography as a munition, proposed the key-escrowed Clipper chip in 1993, and investigated Phil Zimmermann for three years after PGP (Pretty Good Privacy) spread onto the internet; activists answered by printing source code in books, on the argument that no government could easily ban the export of a book, and the courts went on to hold source code to be speech protected by the First Amendment. Export rules were largely relaxed by January 2000, and the browser's padlock is the peace dividend. Every later proposal for lawful-access backdoors, from going dark to client-side scanning to the United Kingdom's secret notice to Apple, reopens the same trench lines.
the-crypto-wars.depth:
What the phrase covers. The crypto wars are not one event but a recurring dispute with a fixed shape: a government wants assured access to communications and stored data, and cryptographers answer that a system built to be readable by an authorized party is a system built to be readable. In the American 1990s the government used three instruments, export controls that treated encryption as a weapon, a proposal for escrowed keys, and prosecutions or the threat of them; its opponents used published code, lawsuits and demonstrations. The dispute is distinct from ordinary lawful interception of unencrypted traffic and from targeted hacking by the state; it is about whether the cryptography itself must be weakened or fitted with a second door.

Encryption as a munition. Until late 1996 encryption products sat in Category XIII of the United States Munitions List, regulated by the State Department under the Arms Export Control Act and the International Traffic in Arms Regulations (ITAR), the same regime as weapons. Executive Order 13026 of 15 November 1996 moved them to the Commerce Department's Commerce Control List, but on harder terms than other dual-use goods: it set aside the export law's foreign-availability provisions, so that comparable products sold abroad no longer obliged the government to lift controls, made the Justice Department a voting member of the export review board, and said controls could promote a key recovery management infrastructure. Even the federal standard for Clipper itself, FIPS (Federal Information Processing Standard) 185 of February 1994, reminded implementers that its devices were subject to the ITAR.

PGP, the investigation and the book. Phil Zimmermann published Pretty Good Privacy (PGP) free on the internet in 1991, by his account racing to get it out before software of that kind became illegal to publish: Senate Bill 266, the 1991 anti-crime bill, carried a sense-of-Congress resolution that communications providers should give the government the plaintext of traffic. When PGP spread worldwide he became the target of a three-year criminal investigation for violating export restrictions, which the government dropped in early 1996. In the meantime the MIT (Massachusetts Institute of Technology) Press published PGP Source Code and Internals (1995), the entire C source as a printed book designed to be scanned back in with optical character recognition (OCR) software; Zimmermann's preface explains the reasoning, that it would be politically difficult to forbid the export of a book anyone could find in a library, and that the State Department had already granted a commodity jurisdiction for Bruce Schneier's book Applied Cryptography.

Code as speech. Daniel J. Bernstein, then a graduate student at Berkeley, wanted to publish an encryption algorithm he called Snuffle, its source code and a paper explaining it; the regulations required him to submit his ideas for review, register as an arms dealer and obtain a licence. The Electronic Frontier Foundation (EFF) sued on his behalf in February 1995. On 15 April 1996 Judge Marilyn Hall Patel of the Northern District of California found no meaningful difference between computer language and German or French, the first ruling that code is speech, and after four years and one regulatory change the Ninth Circuit Court of Appeals held that software source code is speech protected by the First Amendment and the rules preventing its publication unconstitutional.

Escrow and the key-length ceiling. The government's positive offer was the Clipper chip, announced on 16 April 1993: a classified cipher designed by the National Security Agency (NSA), with a copy of each device key held by two escrow agents, which met massive public opposition, was shown by Matt Blaze in August 1994 to be bypassable, and was dead by 1996. The same years kept exportable encryption weak. The EFF says the government long pressed industry to limit encryption to the 56-bit Data Encryption Standard (DES) or weaker without saying how easy it was to break, and on 17 July 1998 its DES Cracker, built for less than 250,000 dollars, won RSA Laboratories' DES Challenge II in less than three days; on 19 January 1999, working with distributed.net and nearly 100,000 personal computers, it solved DES Challenge III in 22 hours and 15 minutes. The weak export grades outlived the rules that required them: in 2015 the FREAK and Logjam attacks on Transport Layer Security (TLS) turned export-grade cryptography still present in implementations into live vulnerabilities, and Matthew Green counted them among government-access mechanisms that blew back, with nearly a third of secure websites affected.

The settlement of 2000. An interim final rule of the Bureau of Export Administration, effective 14 January 2000 and implementing a White House policy announced the previous September, allowed the export of any encryption commodity or software to individuals, firms and other non-government end users in every destination, and of retail encryption products to all end users, except in seven states the government listed as supporting terrorism. Unrestricted encryption source code, the open-source case, could be exported once the exporter had notified the bureau of its internet location, with no obligation on later users. That is the legal ground under worldwide HTTPS (Hypertext Transfer Protocol Secure), strong VPNs (virtual private networks) and every open-source cryptographic library a network engineer deploys.

The engineering objection. The technical case against escrow was never about privacy alone, and it is the part that keeps being relevant. A mechanism that allows authorized access is a mechanism: it must be implemented in every device and maintained in every version, its key store is a target holding the keys to everything, and nothing in the mathematics distinguishes the authority it was built for from anyone who obtains the same access. Blaze's 1994 result showed the second half of the problem, that an escrow scheme can also fail in the other direction and let a determined user keep the encryption while discarding the escrow. When the argument returned in 2015, many of the authors of a 1997 study on key recovery reconvened for Keys Under Doormats (a technical report of MIT's Computer Science and Artificial Intelligence Laboratory, CSAIL, 6 July 2015) and concluded that the damage exceptional access could cause was greater than twenty years earlier: it would force designers to reverse forward secrecy, and in a world of millions of apps and global services new access requirements were likely to introduce unanticipated, hard-to-detect flaws.

Later rounds. The EFF counts the National Security Agency's covert efforts to insert backdoors into cryptographic standards from 2000 onward, a stated wish in 2010 to legislate key escrow, and decades of Federal Bureau of Investigation (FBI) warnings that communications were going dark as continuations of the same fight. In October 2021 a group of cryptographers including Blaze, Whitfield Diffie and Ronald Rivest published Bugs in our Pockets on client-side scanning, the proposal to analyse content on the device before it is encrypted, and argued that it neither guarantees crime prevention nor prevents surveillance and creates serious security and privacy risks for everyone. In the United Kingdom the argument became secret: in February 2025 it was reported that the Home Office had issued Apple a technical capability notice requiring access to iCloud data, Apple withdrew its end-to-end encrypted Advanced Data Protection from new British users, the Investigatory Powers Tribunal published a judgment on 7 April 2025 rejecting the government's claim that no information about the case should be public, the first notice was reported withdrawn in October 2025 and replaced with one aimed at British users, Apple filed a new claim in August 2026, and the substantive hearing of the challenge brought by Privacy International and Liberty is listed for December 2026. Anyone meeting the current version benefits from knowing it is the fourth or fifth iteration of the same question, not a new one.

the-l0pht-testimony.def: The 1998 Senate hearing where seven hackers testified they could take down the Internet in thirty minutes.
the-l0pht-testimony.context: In May 1998 the members of the Boston hacker collective L0pht appeared before a US Senate committee under their handles, Mudge, Weld Pond, Space Rogue and the rest, and told the senators the Internet's core protocols were so fragile the group could disable it in about half an hour. It was the moment hacker expertise entered the policy room as testimony rather than threat. Several of them, notably Mudge, went on to senior roles in government and industry security.
the-l0pht-testimony.depth:
In 1998 the members of L0pht, a Boston hacker collective, testified before a United States Senate committee under their handles rather than their names, and told the senators they could take down the internet in thirty minutes. The claim was about routing vulnerabilities, and it was broadly credible.

What makes the moment historically significant is the venue. A legislature invited people it could reasonably have prosecuted, and listened. That established a channel between the security research community and policymakers that had not previously existed, at a point when neither side had any established way to talk to the other, and several of those present went on to shape government security practice directly.

The specific warning was about the routing system's dependence on mutual trust, which is the same fragility that RPKI addresses partially today. Twenty-eight years later the honest assessment is that the vulnerability class they described has been mitigated rather than removed, and that the more durable outcome of the testimony was institutional: it made the idea of consulting hackers about security normal rather than scandalous.

room-641a.def: The secure room, number 641A, in AT&T's facility at 611 Folsom Street in San Francisco, where from 2003 fibre-optic splitters copied the internet traffic of AT&T's peering links into equipment controlled by the National Security Agency (NSA); revealed in 2006 by the retired AT&T technician Mark Klein.
room-641a.context: In 2006, retired AT&T technician Mark Klein disclosed documents describing a secure room at the Folsom Street facility where optical splitters duplicated the traffic on backbone fibres carrying AT&T's exchanges with other networks into analysis equipment in a room only staff cleared by the National Security Agency (NSA) could enter. The revelation became the core evidence of the Electronic Frontier Foundation's (EFF) lawsuit Hepting v. AT&T and, years before the leaks of 2013, put bulk interception of domestic traffic on the public record. It remains the concrete image behind the phrase upstream collection.
room-641a.depth:
The room. Klein's sworn declaration of 28 March 2006 gives the details. The Folsom Street facility occupied three floors of a building then operated by SBC Communications. On a tour in January 2003 he saw a new room nearly finished next to the room holding the 4ESS long-distance telephone switch; AT&T's documents called it the SG3 Secure Room, it was room number 641A, and it measured about 24 by 48 feet. Regular technicians, who had keys to every other door, were not allowed in: entry needed a physical key and a code on an electronic keypad, and to Klein's knowledge only employees cleared by the National Security Agency (NSA) had them. When the room's air conditioner leaked through the floor onto equipment below, the problem waited days for the one cleared technician to arrive.

How the copy was made. Klein, who oversaw the WorldNet internet room on the 7th floor, explained the physics in the declaration: unlike copper, fibre does not leak a signal that can be picked up without touching the circuit, so to monitor it one has to cut into the fibre and divert part of the light; a splitter divides the light between two fibres, each weaker but carrying the same information. AT&T procedures dated 13 and 24 January 2003 told technicians how to insert optical splitters into live Common Backbone circuits, at OC3 (Optical Carrier 3), OC12 and OC48 rates, by replacing existing cross-connects in the fibre patching complex; the splitters sat in a cabinet on the 7th floor, at aisle 177, bay 04, cabled down to the room on the 6th. From February 2003 the circuits split were AT&T's peering links with sixteen other networks and exchange points, among them UUNET, Level 3, Sprint, Qwest, Global Crossing, Verio, Telia and the MAE-West (Metropolitan Area Ethernet West) and PAIX (Palo Alto Internet Exchange) exchange points. An equipment list for the room named Sun servers, Juniper M40e and M160 backbone routers and a Narus STA 6400 semantic traffic analyser, and Klein learned that similar splitter cabinets were going into Seattle, San Jose, Los Angeles and San Diego.

Why the peering links matter. A splitter on a peering link copies everything AT&T exchanged with another network, so the selection was by circuit, not by person, and it took domestic traffic as readily as foreign. The Electronic Frontier Foundation's (EFF) summary of the expert declaration of J. Scott Marcus, a former senior adviser for internet technology at the Federal Communications Commission, drew the inference: the San Francisco evidence was consistent with a national deployment at 15 to 20 similar sites or more, which implied that a substantial fraction, probably well over half, of AT&T's purely domestic traffic was diverted, into equipment suited to capturing and analysing large volumes of data.

The witness. Klein worked for AT&T for more than 22 years, from November 1981, in New York and then California, moved to Folsom Street in October 2003 and retired in May 2004. When The New York Times reported in late 2005 that the NSA was spying inside the United States, he realized he had seen how it was being done; in early 2006 he walked into the EFF's office in San Francisco and asked whether they cared about privacy, bringing more than a hundred pages of AT&T schematics and tables. He also briefed journalists, congressional staff and senators, AT&T threatened to sue him and did not, and he told the story in a book, Wiring Up the Big Brother Machine... And Fighting It. He died on 8 March 2025 in Oakland, aged 79.

In court. The EFF had filed Hepting v. AT&T on 31 January 2006, on behalf of AT&T customers, and Klein's evidence became its core. More than 50 similar suits followed and were combined in a single proceeding; the government intervened, and the court rejected its first attempt to dismiss on state secrets grounds in 2006.
