The law does not forbid sophistication; it prices it, in future-you's debugging capacity at 3 a.m. Code review's most useful question is Kernighan's law in interrogative form: will we understand this in six months?
kernighans-law.depth:
Debugging is twice as hard as writing the code in the first place, so if you write the code as cleverly as possible you are, by definition, not smart enough to debug it. Brian Kernighan's formulation is a warning aimed specifically at capable programmers, since the incapable ones were never going to write the clever version.

The reasoning is about cognitive headroom rather than skill. Writing code, you hold the whole intent in your head and every line makes sense as you produce it. Debugging, you arrive without that context, often months later and possibly not as the same person, and you have to reconstruct the intent from the artefact. Clever code is exactly the code whose intent is hardest to reconstruct.

The practical consequence is a preference for boring solutions, which is genuinely difficult to sustain because clever code is more satisfying to write and looks more impressive in review. The reframe that helps is that you are not writing for the compiler or the reader today, you are writing for whoever debugs this at three in the morning during an incident, and their available intelligence at that moment is substantially lower than yours right now.

greenspuns-tenth-rule.def: 'Any sufficiently complicated C or Fortran program contains an ad hoc, informally-specified, bug-ridden, slow implementation of half of Common Lisp.'
greenspuns-tenth-rule.context: Philip Greenspun's quip (there are no rules one through nine) observes that large programs inevitably grow the dynamic features their language lacks: configuration interpreters, object systems, garbage collection, all reinvented badly. It is the classic argument for choosing expressive tools instead of rebuilding them by accident. The corollary is widely quoted: this includes Common Lisp implementations themselves.
greenspuns-tenth-rule.depth:
Any sufficiently complicated C or Fortran program contains an ad hoc, informally specified, bug-ridden, slow implementation of half of Common Lisp. Philip Greenspun's rule is a joke with a serious claim: large programs converge on the same set of capabilities regardless of the language they started in.

The observation holds up. Big C codebases grow dynamic dispatch tables, reference counting, a configuration language that acquires conditionals, and eventually something that evaluates expressions at runtime. Each addition is a reasonable local response to a real need, and the aggregate is an interpreter nobody designed, specified or tested as one.

The useful reading is not that everyone should use Lisp. It is that these capabilities are what complex systems require, so the choice is whether to get them from a well-tested implementation or to accrete them accidentally. The accidental version is the one described in the rule: ad hoc because no one designed it, informally specified because it was never written down, and bug-ridden because it was never the thing anyone was building.

atwoods-law.def: 'Any application that can be written in JavaScript, will eventually be written in JavaScript.'
atwoods-law.context: Jeff Atwood coined it in 2007 as a half-joke about the web platform's gravity; then Node took JavaScript to servers, Electron took it to the desktop, and React Native took it to phones, and the joke became a roadmap. The law is really about reach: the runtime installed everywhere wins, quality arguments notwithstanding. Its spiritual successor is already circulating: anything that can be compiled to WebAssembly, will be.
atwoods-law.depth:
Any application that can be written in JavaScript will eventually be written in JavaScript. Jeff Atwood's 2007 formulation was a prediction, and it has aged into an unremarkable description of reality.

The prediction came true through a mechanism worth naming: the browser was the only universal runtime, so anything that ran there ran everywhere without installation. Node put the same language on the server, Electron put it on the desktop, and React Native put it on phones. The language did not win on merit, it won on reach, which is the same dynamic that decided TCP/IP over technically superior alternatives.

WebAssembly complicates the sequel and is worth watching for that reason. It makes the browser a target for other languages, which removes the structural reason JavaScript won, and the honest question is whether reach or merit dominates when both are available. Atwood's law described an era in which there was no choice; whether it describes the next one is genuinely undecided.

poes-law.def: Without a clear marker of intent, parody of extreme views is indistinguishable from the views themselves.
poes-law.context: Nathan Poe formulated it on a creationism forum in 2005, and the Internet promptly proved it general: absent a winking emoji, someone will take the satire straight, and someone else will mistake the sincere post for satire. It is a genuine constraint on online communication, moderation, and now on datasets scraped from the web, where irony arrives unlabeled. Every community relearns it the day their in-joke escapes containment.
poes-law.depth:
Without a clear indicator of intent, a sufficiently extreme parody is indistinguishable from sincere belief, and someone will always take it seriously. Poe's law originated in a creationism forum in the mid-2000s and generalized immediately, because the phenomenon is not specific to any subject.

The mechanism is about the range of real opinion rather than about writing quality. Once genuine positions cover a sufficiently wide spectrum, any parody must be extreme enough to sit outside it, and there is no outside: whatever you invent, someone holds it sincerely. That is why satire dates so badly and why a joke read six months later, out of its original context, reliably reads as earnest.

Its practical relevance is in moderation and detection. A content system attempting to distinguish parody from advocacy is attempting something the law says is impossible from text alone, which is why platforms rely on labels, account history and context signals instead. It is also the reason that sarcasm markers keep being reinvented, from the emoticon onward: the underlying problem is that written text carries no tone, and every medium eventually needs a convention for supplying it.

cobra-effect.def: An incentive that worsens the problem it was meant to solve, named for a colonial bounty on cobras that created cobra farms.
cobra-effect.context: The story runs that British Delhi paid per dead cobra, enterprising residents bred them, and cancelling the bounty released the stock, leaving more cobras than before; the tale's documentation is thin but the mechanism is everywhere. Pay per bug found and bugs get planted; reward closed tickets and tickets get split; bounty vulnerabilities carelessly and you fund a grey market. It is Goodhart's law with fangs: the measure did not just decouple from the goal, it attacked it.
cobra-effect.depth:
The cobra effect names an incentive that makes the problem worse. The story is that a colonial administration in Delhi offered a bounty for dead cobras, people bred cobras to collect it, and when the scheme was cancelled the now-worthless snakes were released, leaving more cobras than before.

The anecdote's historical basis is thin, and the effect it names is thoroughly documented elsewhere, which is worth saying plainly rather than repeating the story as fact. Bounty schemes that create farming, targets that create gaming and metrics that create the behaviour they measure are all the same shape, and it is closely related to Goodhart's law: this is what happens when the measure becomes a target and someone can manufacture the measure.

In technology the pattern is everywhere. Paying per bug found produces bugs written to be found, rewarding tickets closed produces tickets split in half, and a security programme measured by vulnerabilities remediated will quietly favour trivial findings over hard ones. The defence is to ask, before publishing any incentive, what the cheapest way to satisfy it would be, and then assume somebody will find that way.

wheelers-law.def: 'All problems in computer science can be solved by another level of indirection', with the folk corollary: except too many levels of indirection.
wheelers-law.context: Attributed to Cambridge pioneer David Wheeler, co-inventor of the subroutine, the aphorism names the field's universal move: interpose a layer, a pointer, a proxy, a virtual machine, and the incompatible becomes compatible. The unofficial corollary carries the bill, since every layer adds latency, opacity, and a new place for abstractions to leak. Modern stacks are Wheeler's aphorism applied a few dozen times, followed by observability tools sold to see through the result.
wheelers-law.depth:
All problems in computer science can be solved by another level of indirection, attributed to David Wheeler, who is said to have added the crucial second half: except for the problem of too many levels of indirection.

The first half is genuinely true and is the most reusable idea in the field. Virtual memory is indirection between addresses and storage, DNS is indirection between names and addresses, an interface is indirection between a caller and an implementation, and a load balancer is indirection between a service and the machines providing it. Each one turns a rigid coupling into something that can change without coordination.

The second half is why systems become incomprehensible. Every layer costs performance, and more importantly costs understanding: a request that passes through eight abstractions is a request whose failure could originate in eight places, and debugging it requires holding all eight models simultaneously. That is the real limit, and it is cognitive rather than computational, which is why the useful discipline is asking what an additional layer buys before adding it, rather than assuming that another one is free.

clarkes-third-law.def: 'Any sufficiently advanced technology is indistinguishable from magic.'
clarkes-third-law.context: Arthur C. Clarke's third law was written about prophecy and progress, but engineering adopted it as a diagnosis: when users, or engineers, cannot see the mechanism, they reason about the system with superstition instead of models. That is where cargo-cult fixes, ritual reboots, and 'it works, don't touch it' come from. The working corollary for practitioners: any technology distinguishable from magic is insufficiently advanced, and any team treating its own stack as magic is insufficiently informed.
clarkes-third-law.depth:
Any sufficiently advanced technology is indistinguishable from magic. Arthur C. Clarke's formulation is usually quoted admiringly, and it is worth reading as a warning as well, because the state it describes is one where users cannot reason about a system at all.

The practical version appears constantly in support work. A user who cannot distinguish a network problem from an application problem from a device problem is in exactly the position Clarke described, and their model of the system is therefore ritual: this sequence of actions worked last time. That is not ignorance, it is the rational response to a system that offers no visible causality, and it makes accurate reporting impossible.

Which suggests a design obligation rather than a boast. Systems that expose some legible model of what they are doing, error messages that describe the actual condition, and interfaces whose behaviour can be predicted from a simple mental model all reduce the magic. That matters most in security, since a person who cannot tell normal from abnormal has no chance of noticing an attack, and the industry has spent a great deal of effort making its systems more magical rather than less.

dogfooding.def: Using your own product internally, so its failures bite you before they bite customers.
dogfooding.context: The phrase's tech usage is commonly traced to 1980s Microsoft, where a manager's 'Eating our own Dogfood' email pushed teams onto their own unfinished server software. Dogfooding shortens the feedback loop no survey can: the builders feel the latency, hit the edge cases, and cannot close the ticket on themselves. Its known failure mode is monoculture, since a company of power users eats a diet no customer eats; dogfood accordingly, then still test with strangers.
dogfooding.depth:
Dogfooding is running your own product in earnest, and the crude name is the point: nobody claims it is pleasant. The phrase entered software at Microsoft in the late 1980s and stuck because it names an accountability that marketing language cannot.

What it produces is not testing but consequence. A bug that annoys your users is a ticket; a bug that stops your own team from shipping is an emergency, and the priority sorts itself out without anyone arguing about severity levels. It also surfaces the things testing never finds, because tests exercise features while daily use exercises workflows, and the friction lives between features rather than inside them.

The limits deserve stating. Internal users are not representative: they have context, permissions, tolerance and access to the people who wrote the thing, so they route around problems that would stop a real customer cold. Dogfooding therefore catches a specific class of failure very well and systematically misses the onboarding experience, which is the one that decides whether anyone becomes a user at all.

backhoe-fade.def: Telecom's dry name for total signal loss caused by construction equipment digging through the fibre.
backhoe-fade.context: Radio engineers speak of rain fade; fibre operators, with gallows humor, of backhoe fade: the abrupt, physical severing of a buried cable by an excavator that never called before digging. It is a leading cause of major outages, which is why serious designs demand physically diverse paths, in separate trenches, ideally on separate sides of the road. The term encodes a career's worth of wisdom: your redundancy is only as real as the geography between the two cables.

magic-number.def: An unexplained constant buried in code, or the signature bytes that identify a file format.
magic-number.context: The term carries two related meanings: the anti-pattern (a bare 86400 or 0.85 whose significance lives only in the author's head, cured by named constants) and the file signature (the leading bytes, like PNG's or the 0xCAFEBABE of Java class files, that tell tools what they are reading; the Unix file command is a museum of them). Both senses are about the same thing, meaning encoded without explanation. One is a bug waiting; the other is a convention working.

wetware.def: The humans in the system, named as if they were another component alongside hardware and software.
wetware.context: Jargon File vintage, the word frames people as the third platform in the stack: the one that ships with fatigue, habits, and social trust preinstalled. Security uses it soberly, since phishing and social engineering are attacks on wetware that no patch fixes, only training and design that assumes human error. The term's half-joke carries the discipline's most serious lesson: the perimeter includes everyone with a badge and an inbox.

pebkac.def: Helpdesk code for 'the problem exists between keyboard and chair': the user.
pebkac.context: Alongside siblings like the ID-10T error (read it aloud) and PICNIC (problem in chair, not in computer), PEBKAC let support staff diagnose the human in front of witnesses. Modern usability doctrine inverted the verdict: if enough users hit the same wall, the wall is the defect, and 'user error' usually names a design that invited it. The acronym survives as both a joke and a confession about how systems used to blame their operators.

tldr.def: Too long; didn't read: the complaint that became the standard label for a summary.
tldr.context: Born on forums as a dismissal of walls of text, TL;DR flipped polarity: writers now preempt it by opening with a TL;DR section, and the abbreviation means the summary itself. Engineering culture institutionalized the move in RFC abstracts, executive summaries, and incident reports where the first three lines must carry the payload. It is attention economics compressed into five letters and a semicolon that most people omit.

eol.def: End of life: the date after which a product receives no fixes, no patches, and no vendor sympathy.
eol.context: Vendors publish staged sunsets, end of sale, end of software maintenance, end of support, and the final EOL, after which running the product means running unpatchable known vulnerabilities. Auditors treat EOL software as a standing finding, attackers treat it as a standing invitation, and half the industry's worst incidents trace to fleets past their dates. Tracking the dates is unglamorous and decisive, which is exactly the kind of work a tool should do for you.

air-gap.def: Isolation of a system or network by giving it no physical connection to any other and no automated logical one, so that data crosses only when a person carries it, under human control: the security control made of literal absence.
air-gap.context: Air-gapped networks protect classified systems, industrial control and backups by making sure no cable or radio link reaches them; data crosses only on media a person carries and checks. Stuxnet is the canonical proof of the limits: it reached Windows engineering stations that were never connected to an untrusted network by riding removable drives, and every espionage framework known to have attacked an air-gapped network has used USB (Universal Serial Bus) drives the same way. Researchers keep demonstrating exotic exfiltration through sound, heat and blinking LEDs (light-emitting diodes), at bit rates that matter only once malware is already inside. The gap raises the attacker's cost enormously without reducing the defender's need for discipline: the moment convenience wins one exception, the gap is a story told to auditors.
air-gap.depth:
What it is, and what it is not. The Internet Security Glossary, RFC (Request for Comments) 4949, written by Robert W. Shirey and published by the IETF (Internet Engineering Task Force) in August 2007, defines an air gap as an interface between two systems at which they are not connected physically and any logical connection is not automated, so that data is transferred through it only manually, under human control. Its example is two computers on opposite sides of a room with a person carrying a disk between them; when the two sit in different security domains, the crossing becomes an upgrade or downgrade operation, a deliberate decision to admit or release data. The glossary of NIST (the US National Institute of Standards and Technology) carries the same wording through the Committee on National Security Systems instruction CNSSI 4009-2022. The definition excludes more than it includes. A firewall, a VLAN (virtual local area network), a VRF (virtual routing and forwarding) instance or a private circuit separates traffic logically but is still an automated connection, and so is a cellular modem left in a cabinet for vendor support. The informal name for the manual crossing is sneakernet.

Where it is used. Classified and military networks keep classification levels physically apart. Operational technology (OT) keeps controllers, and the engineering stations that program them, away from enterprise and internet traffic: Symantec's W32.Stuxnet Dossier (version 1.4, February 2011) notes that PLCs (programmable logic controllers) are often programmed from Windows computers not connected to the internet or even to the internal network. Backups are the third case. The UK's National Cyber Security Centre (NCSC) wrote in August 2019 that it had seen ransomware encrypt not only the original data but the connected USB (Universal Serial Bus) and network drives holding the backups, and connected cloud storage as well, and set out an offline rule: at any given time at least one backup should be offline, which means connecting a backup only when necessary and never having all of them connected at once. NIST's guide to OT security, SP (Special Publication) 800-82 Revision 3 of September 2023, adds a humbler use: incident response plans kept on paper or on an offline, air-gapped system, so that the attack being handled cannot reach them.

Why it leaks. An isolated system still needs software updates, signatures, project files and configuration, and it produces logs and results that someone wants elsewhere; every one of those crossings is a channel. Stuxnet, found in 2010, is the reference case. Symantec's analysis describes it replicating through removable drives by exploiting the Windows shortcut flaw that allowed automatic execution, spreading across a LAN (local area network) through the Print Spooler, and using removable drives to cover the last hop to a Field PG, the Windows computer used to program the controllers, which is never connected to an untrusted network; the authors speculated that the first infection arrived through a contractor or an insider, on a removable drive. Two years earlier, in 2008, an infected flash drive inserted into a US military laptop at a base in the Middle East put code on a network run by US Central Command that spread undetected on both classified and unclassified systems. William J. Lynn III disclosed it in Foreign Affairs in September 2010 as the most significant breach of US military computers ever, countered by an operation called Buckshot Yankee. The worm, Agent.BTZ, took the Pentagon about fourteen months to clean up, and the response included banning USB drives and disabling the Windows autorun feature.

What attackers actually do. In December 2021 Alexis Dorais-Joncas and Facundo Muñoz of ESET reviewed every malicious framework publicly reported against air-gapped networks: seventeen by their count, four of them first seen in the first half of 2020 alone. All were built for espionage, all targeted Windows, and all used USB drives as the physical medium to carry data in and out. More than three quarters used malicious shortcut (.lnk) or autorun files on those drives, either for the first compromise of an isolated machine or to move inside the isolated network, and Microsoft had patched more than ten critical shortcut-related remote code execution flaws in Windows over the previous ten years. The authors split the frameworks into connected ones, operated remotely through an internet-facing machine that relays commands and stolen data by way of the drive, and offline ones that depend on a human asset on the ground. They found no case of actual or suspected use of a covert physical channel, and their advice follows from that: defend first against what known malware has done, before spending on the theoretical bypasses.

The covert channels. The theoretical bypasses are real research, much of it by Mordechai Guri, Yuval Elovici and colleagues at Ben-Gurion University of the Negev. AirHopper (2014) turned a computer's video output into an FM (frequency modulation) radio signal received by a nearby mobile phone at 1 to 7 metres, carrying 13 to 60 bytes per second. BitWhisper (2015) passed bits between two adjacent computers through heat and their built-in thermal sensors, at 0 to 40 centimetres and 1 to 8 bits per hour. Fansmitter (2016) modulated fan noise to defeat the practice of removing speakers from secure machines, the so-called audio gap, reaching a smartphone at up to eight metres and 900 bits per hour. xLED (2017) blinked the status LEDs (light-emitting diodes) of switches and routers for a camera to record, at 10 bit/s to more than 1 kbit/s per LED. Every one of them presupposes malicious code already running on the isolated side, which is the part the USB drive supplies. Their value to a defender is the reminder that isolation is a property of every emanation, not only of cables, which is why classified environments add bans on wireless interfaces and limits on electromagnetic leakage, TEMPEST measures and Faraday cages among them.

Its engineered neighbours. Few environments can live on sneakernet alone, so the standards describe controlled crossings instead. A unidirectional gateway, or data diode, combines hardware that lets data flow from one network to another but is physically unable to send anything back with software that replicates databases and emulates protocol servers on the far side; NIST SP 800-82r3 gives the common placement as the boundary between the operational and enterprise networks, letting traffic leave OT but not enter it. By the RFC 4949 definition it is not an air gap, because the connection is automated, but it removes the inbound path that a firewall rule could quietly reopen. A guard, in RFC 4949's terms, is a system trusted to mediate transfers between two systems that operate under different security policies, the idea behind what governments buy as cross-domain solutions. Where traffic must flow both ways, the same NIST guide describes a DMZ (demilitarized zone) architecture between the corporate and OT networks, so that nothing passes directly between them. NIST's own verdict is blunt: as OT systems are increasingly connected to IT (information technology) networks, relying on traditional measures such as air gaps is not enough, and devices with no business need to communicate should simply not be connected.

How it fails in practice. Because the definition is binary, the useful audit is concrete. Which machines on the isolated side have a wireless interface, a second network card, a modem or a cellular router; which laptops visit both sides; where the transfer station is, who uses it, what it scans and what it records; whether autorun and shortcut handling are locked down on every isolated host; and whether the backup described as offline can be reached with any credential an attacker might hold. The NCSC's warning about cloud backups generalizes: storage that cannot be unplugged has to be disconnected logically, through identity and access control, which makes it a different control with a different failure mode, not an air gap. The gap raises the attacker's cost a great deal, and the price of each exception is that the system is no longer air-gapped at all, whatever the network diagram says.

broadcast-storm.def: The meltdown where broadcast frames multiply through a switching loop until the network drowns in its own traffic.
broadcast-storm.context: Ethernet frames carry no time-to-live, so one redundant cable between switches lets every broadcast circulate forever while being reflooded out every port, saturating links and switch processors within seconds. Spanning Tree Protocol exists to break such loops, and storm control to cap the damage; the classic incident remains someone helpfully plugging both wall jacks 'for redundancy'. It is the layer 2 reminder that redundancy without a control plane is just a loop.
broadcast-storm.depth:
What it is. A switch forwards a broadcast, and any multicast or unknown unicast it cannot place, out of every port except the one it arrived on. That is how a LAN (local area network) finds things, and it is harmless as long as there is exactly one path between any two points. Put a loop in the topology and every flooded copy comes back to be flooded again. The specification of TRILL (Transparent Interconnection of Lots of Links), RFC (Request for Comments) 6325, names the root of the problem: the Ethernet header contains no hop count or TTL (time to live) field, so nothing in the frame ever ends its journey. One broadcast becomes a permanent resident, every new broadcast joins it, and in a mesh with several loops each copy spawns more on every pass. Wikipedia's article uses the older name broadcast radiation for the accumulation of broadcast and multicast traffic, notes that a packet which sets one off is sometimes called a Chernobyl packet, and gives the simplest possible cause: both ends of a single patch cable plugged into the same switch.

What it does. Links fill first, then everything that has to look at the traffic. Cisco's spanning tree troubleshooting guide warns that a high rate of broadcast or multicast on the VLAN (virtual local area network) the switch itself is managed on can overwhelm its CPU (central processing unit) and its ability to process bridge protocol data units (BPDUs), and that a massive loss of BPDUs makes blocked ports move to forwarding. That is the vicious circle of a storm: the flood starves the protocol that was supposed to prevent the loop, the protocol opens more paths, and the flood grows. Because copies of the same frames arrive from several directions, switches also keep relearning the same source addresses on different ports, the pattern the mac-flapping entry describes, and with the forwarding tables churning even ordinary unicast starts to be flooded. Every attached host has to process every broadcast too, which is why a storm feels like a total outage rather than a slow network.

Causes other than a cable. Most storms are loops: a cable between two wall jacks, a small unmanaged switch that closes a ring, a link that turns unidirectional so that a blocked port stops hearing BPDUs, which Cisco calls a common cause of bridging loops. But Cisco's storm control guide also lists protocol-stack errors, configuration mistakes and denial-of-service attacks, while noting elsewhere that a single host is unlikely to bring a network down with broadcasts alone. The best-known attack is Smurf: echo requests sent to a broadcast address with the victim's address forged as the source, so every host on the abused network replies to the victim. RFC 2644 (Best Current Practice 34, August 1999) answered it by changing what routers do by default: networks that accepted directed broadcasts from outside had become Smurf amplifiers, so the option to receive them must now be off unless an administrator turns it on. Wireless networks have their own variant, a spoofed disassociation sent to the broadcast address. And a flat network can drown in legitimate multicast with no loop at all.

A named case. On 13 November 2002 at 13:45 the network of Beth Israel Deaconess Medical Center stopped carrying traffic, and clinicians could no longer order medications or tests electronically. John Halamka, who led its information systems and approved changes during the outage himself, later published a candid post-mortem. The core was a switched layer 2 design, a reasonable architecture for 1996, in which a flood in one part of the network reached every other part; the trigger was a researcher's file-sharing application exchanging hundreds of gigabytes by multicast; the network was too saturated to diagnose; and configuration changes approved during the outage caused further spanning tree recalculations and more traffic. Fixing the structural problems took two days. His lessons read like a design checklist: a routed core with switched access layers in separate VLANs, out-of-band tools so that the network is not needed to diagnose the network, change control, and, in a crisis, backing out one's own changes before adding new ones.

Prevention. The first line is a loop-free topology kept that way by protocol: spanning tree and its rapid variants, link aggregation instead of parallel independent links, Shortest Path Bridging, and in metro rings protocols such as ERPS (Ethernet Ring Protection Switching) and EAPS (Ethernet Automatic Protection System). The second is keeping edge ports honest. Cisco warns that PortFast on a port that leads to a switch or hub can stop spanning tree from detecting a loop and cause broadcast storms, and pairs it with BPDU guard, which error-disables a PortFast port the moment a BPDU arrives, closing the two-wall-jacks case. The third is storm control, which does not find the loop but survives it. On a Catalyst 9300 it is disabled by default; when configured, the switch counts broadcast, multicast or unicast packets received on a port in each 1-second interval and compares the count with a rising threshold set as a percentage of bandwidth, in bits per second or in packets per second, blocking that traffic until it drops below the falling threshold; the default action is to filter, and the port can instead be error-disabled or an SNMP (Simple Network Management Protocol) trap sent. Wikipedia's summary is fair: storm control limits the intensity of the storm so that the operator can still reach the equipment to fix the cause. The fourth is size: smaller layer 2 domains, separated by routing, cap the blast radius of whatever does go wrong.

When one is under way. Cisco's guidance is practical. The signs are links running at abnormal utilization, processor load on the switches and, in a capture taken on a saturated link, the same packets appearing over and over. To stop an active loop, use console or out-of-band access, disable one suspected redundant path at a time and check connectivity after each change. Then find out why the protocol let it happen: a PortFast port with no BPDU guard, a unidirectional fibre, a switch that had stopped processing BPDUs, or a change that someone made five minutes earlier.

Numbers worth remembering: zero hop count in an Ethernet header, one patch cable to cause a storm, a 1-second storm control interval, RFC 2644 of 1999 for directed broadcasts, and two days for a hospital network to recover in 2002.

two-generals-problem.def: The proof that two parties on an unreliable channel can never be certain they agree to act together.
two-generals-problem.context: Two generals must attack simultaneously and can communicate only by messengers who may be captured; whichever confirmation is sent last, its sender cannot know it arrived, so no finite protocol reaches certain agreement, a result formalized in the 1970s. It is the bedrock impossibility beneath distributed transactions, exactly-once delivery, and every retry loop with idempotency keys. Its harder sibling, the Byzantine generals, adds traitors; real systems settle for probably-agreed, which is what timeouts and acknowledgements actually buy.
two-generals-problem.depth:
Two armies must attack simultaneously to win and can communicate only by messengers who may be captured. The first general sends a time, and cannot know it arrived. The second acknowledges, and cannot know the acknowledgement arrived. No finite sequence of messages produces certainty on both sides, and the problem is provably unsolvable.

It is not a puzzle, it is a boundary condition on distributed systems, and it means that guaranteed agreement over an unreliable channel is impossible rather than merely difficult. Every real system therefore works around it rather than solving it, and knowing that changes what you look for in a design.

The practical consequences are everywhere. Exactly-once delivery does not exist; what exists is at-least-once delivery plus idempotent processing, which produces the same observable result and is a genuinely different mechanism. A payment system cannot be certain a charge succeeded, so it reconciles. TCP does not guarantee the peer received your last message, only that it acknowledged earlier ones. Any design that assumes certainty about a remote party's state is assuming something the mathematics says it cannot have.

kalpana.def: The Sunnyvale startup that shipped the first multiport Ethernet switch in 1990 and, four years later, became one of Cisco's most consequential acquisitions.
kalpana.context: Founded in the late 1980s by Vinod Bhardwaj and Larry Blair and named after Bhardwaj's wife (Kalpana means 'imagination' in Sanskrit), the company introduced the seven-port EtherSwitch in 1990, inventing Ethernet switching and with it the modern LAN: dedicated bandwidth per port instead of a shared, collision-prone medium. It followed with full-duplex Ethernet and EtherChannel link aggregation. Cisco completed its acquisition on 7 December 1994, for about 200 million dollars, and Kalpana's switching lineage runs straight into this site's Cisco and Riverstone histories, where a Kalpana engineer later co-founded Yago. Sources put the founding anywhere from 1987 to 1990; the 1990 first-switch milestone is the fixed point.
kalpana.depth:
Kalpana was the company that built the first Ethernet switch, and the product changed what Ethernet fundamentally was. Before it, a network was a shared medium where every station heard everything and collisions were normal; after it, each port had a dedicated path and the collision domain shrank to a single link.

The consequences were larger than a performance improvement. Full duplex became possible because there was no longer contention to avoid, aggregate capacity stopped being a fixed number divided among users and started scaling with the number of ports, and the CSMA/CD mechanism that defines Ethernet in every textbook became vestigial on modern networks. The name and the frame format survived; the access method did not.

Its commercial history is the ordinary one for that era: acquired by Cisco in the mid-1990s and absorbed. The pattern is worth noticing, because switching was the change that let Ethernet defeat Token Ring, FDDI and every other contender, and the company that made it possible exists now only as a footnote. Being first to a foundational idea and being the one who profits from it are different achievements.

bit.def: A bit (binary digit) is the smallest unit of digital data, a single choice between 0 and 1, and also the unit in which information itself is measured.
bit.context: The word is a contraction of 'binary digit', coined by John Tukey in a Bell Labs memo dated 9 January 1947. His colleague Claude Shannon gave it its enduring meaning in 'A Mathematical Theory of Communication' (1948), the paper that founded information theory and the first to put 'bit' in print, crediting Tukey. Shannon's insight was that any message, from text to a photograph to a song, could be measured and transmitted as a number of bits, independent of the physical medium that carries it. Bytes, files, addresses, keys and protocols all follow from that one idea.
bit.depth:
Two meanings in one word. To the National Institute of Standards and Technology (NIST) glossary a bit is simply a binary digit, 0 or 1, the meaning every engineer uses when counting the bits in a field or an address. Information theory uses the same word as a unit of measurement: one bit is the information gained by learning the value of a variable that is 0 or 1 with equal probability, a unit also called the shannon. The two differ in practice. A stored binary digit can carry less than one bit of information when its value is predictable, and that difference is exactly what compression removes.

Where the word came from. John Tukey contracted binary digit to bit in a Bell Labs memo dated 9 January 1947. Claude Shannon put it into the literature in A Mathematical Theory of Communication, published in the Bell System Technical Journal in July and October 1948 and renamed The Mathematical Theory of Communication for the 1949 book. Shannon chose a logarithmic measure of information and wrote that with base 2 the resulting units may be called binary digits, or more briefly bits, a word suggested by J. W. Tukey. His examples are an engineer's: a device with two stable positions, such as a relay or a flip-flop circuit, stores one bit, N such devices store N bits because they have 2 to the power N states, and adding one relay doubles the number of possible states. The idea of binary storage is older than the word: punched cards for looms go back to Basile Bouchon and Jean-Baptiste Falcon in 1732 and to Joseph Marie Jacquard in 1804.

Information, not digits. Shannon's measure of the information produced by a source is its entropy, H, the negative sum of each probability times its logarithm, which reaches one bit for a fair binary choice and less for a biased one. The ratio of a source's entropy to the maximum it could have with the same symbols is its relative entropy, which Shannon identifies as the maximum compression possible in the same alphabet, and one minus that ratio is the redundancy. Applied to language, it gave one of the paper's best-known results: ordinary English, counting statistical structure over about eight letters, is roughly 50 per cent redundant, meaning that half of what we write is determined by the structure of the language and half is chosen freely. Redundancy is what a compressor removes, which is why text stored at eight bits per character shrinks so much.

Symbols and prefixes. The bit is not an International System of Units (SI) unit. The International Electrotechnical Commission (IEC), in IEC 60027 and IEC 80000-13, gives its symbol as bit, as in kbit; IEEE 1541, a 2002 standard of the Institute of Electrical and Electronics Engineers (IEEE), recommended a lower-case b, which is common; the upper-case B means byte. The NIST tables make the multiples explicit: 1 kbit is 1,000 bits, 1 Kibit is 1,024 bits, and 1 B is 8 bits. Transmission rates use the decimal prefixes, so a link of 100 Mbit/s moves at most 12.5 million bytes a second before any protocol overhead, and a download shown in megabytes per second looks eight times slower than the rate on the contract.

Order and significance. Inside a byte or a field, which bit is first must be stated. The internet's convention is in Request for Comments (RFC) 791: in its diagrams the bit labelled 0 is the most significant, so 10101010 represents 170, and in a multi-octet field the leftmost bit is the most significant of the whole field.

Bits as a measure of strength. Because each bit doubles the number of possible values, sizes are quoted in bits: an IPv4 address is a 32-bit number and an IPv6 address a 128-bit one, and cryptographic strength is stated the same way. NIST Special Publication (SP) 800-57 Part 1, revision 5 (May 2020), defines an algorithm that provides X bits of security as one that takes, on average, 2 to the power X-1 times the cost of one trial encryption to break by trying every key. Its comparison table puts a 2048-bit RSA key at 112 bits of security, AES-128 (the Advanced Encryption Standard with a 128-bit key) and 3072-bit RSA at 128, and AES-256 and 15,360-bit RSA at 256, and it no longer approves strengths of 80 bits or less for applying protection, with the caveat that the estimates will change significantly once quantum computing becomes practical. The key size and the security strength are different numbers: an RSA key needs thousands of bits to match what a symmetric key gives with 128.

Numbers worth remembering: 1947 for the word and 1948 for the theory; one bit per fair binary choice; 8 bits to a byte; 1,000 bits in a kbit against 1,024 in a Kibit; 32 and 128 bits for IPv4 and IPv6 addresses; 112 bits as the minimum security strength NIST approves for new protection; and one more bit for twice the work of an exhaustive search.

byte.def: A byte is the group of bits a computer handles as one unit: today eight bits, called an octet where exactness matters, and the basic unit of memory addressing and storage size.
byte.context: Werner Buchholz coined 'byte' in 1956 while designing IBM's 7030 Stretch supercomputer, deliberately respelling 'bite' so it could never be mistaken in print for 'bit'. Early machines used bytes of many sizes, and six-bit and nine-bit bytes were common into the 1960s; the eight-bit byte became the norm with IBM's System/360, announced in 1964. The mastication theme stuck, so half a byte is a nibble. One eight-bit byte holds 256 values, enough for a character of the Latin alphabet, which is why it became the natural unit for memory, files and addresses.
byte.depth:
What it is, exactly. Everyday usage and the standards agree that a byte is eight bits, and the International Electrotechnical Commission's (IEC) standard on information quantities, IEC 80000-13, codified that meaning with the symbol B. Programming languages are more careful. The C standard, ISO/IEC 9899:2024, defines a byte as the addressable unit of data storage large enough to hold any member of the basic character set, and requires only that CHAR_BIT, the number of bits in a byte, be at least 8. Network specifications sidestep the question by counting octets: Request for Comments (RFC) 791, the Internet Protocol specification of September 1981, gives an address as four octets (32 bits), and the IEC standard gives the octet its own symbol, o, which is how French speakers write ko and Mo.

Where the word came from. Werner Buchholz, on the IBM team designing the 7030 Stretch, IBM's first transistorized supercomputer, used the word in Stretch Memo No. 39G of 11 June 1956, describing a shift matrix that converted a 60-bit word into characters, or bytes as we have called them, of 1 to 6 bits each. Stretch addressed memory to the bit and had variable field length instructions with the byte size encoded in the instruction, so a byte was then whatever size a field needed. The spelling was a deliberate mutation of bite, to avoid confusion with bit, and the joke survives in the nibble, four bits, conveniently one hexadecimal digit. In 1962 Buchholz described a byte as a group of bits used to encode a character, or the number of bits transmitted in parallel to and from input-output units. He received the Computer Pioneer Award of the Institute of Electrical and Electronics Engineers (IEEE) in 1990.

Why eight won. For a decade the size followed the machine. Six-bit character codes were common, nine-bit bytes ran on 36-bit computers, and memory words of 12, 18, 24, 30, 36, 48 or 60 bits held a whole number of six-bit bytes. IBM's System/360, launched on 7 April 1964 to replace five incompatible product lines with one compatible family, pioneered the eight-bit byte, and its eight-bit Extended Binary Coded Decimal Interchange Code (EBCDIC) made the choice concrete; the prominence of the System/360 did the rest. The ARPANET already took eight bits for granted in 1969: Vint Cerf's RFC 20 put 7-bit American Standard Code for Information Interchange (ASCII) into an 8-bit byte whose high-order bit is always 0.

Inside the byte. Eight bits give 2 to the power 8, 256 distinct values, 0 to 255 when read as an unsigned number and exactly two hexadecimal digits when written down, which is why packet dumps are printed as pairs of hex digits. The order of bits and bytes is a convention that has to be stated. RFC 791's appendix on data transmission order is the internet's: octets are sent in the order they are read in English, in a diagram the bit labelled 0 is the most significant, the pattern 10101010 is 170, and when a multi-octet quantity is transmitted the most significant octet goes first. That is big-endian network byte order. Most processors, x86 and most ARM implementations among them, are little-endian, which is why the Berkeley sockets interface provides htons and htonl to convert host values to network order and ntohs and ntohl to convert them back.

Kilo, or kibi. A kilobyte meant 1,000 bytes to some and 1,024 to others for decades, so in December 1998 the IEC approved separate names for powers of two, published as Amendment 2 to IEC 60027-2 in January 1999 and folded into its second edition in November 2000: kibi (Ki, 2 to the power 10), mebi (Mi, 2 to the power 20), gibi (Gi, 2 to the power 30), tebi (Ti, 2 to the power 40) and upwards. They are not part of the International System of Units (SI), and the symbol is Ki with a capital K. IEC 80000-13 now carries them, and its second edition, published in February 2025, added new binary prefixes. The gap grows with size: 1 MB is 1,000,000 bytes and 1 MiB is 1,048,576, 1 GiB is 1,073,741,824 bytes, about 7.4 per cent more than 1 GB, and 1 TiB is about 10 per cent more than 1 TB.

Where the two kinds of kilo meet. Storage media, from hard drives and flash storage to optical discs, are sold in decimal units; macOS and iOS have reported capacity in decimal units since the releases that followed Mac OS X 10.5 and iOS 10, while Microsoft Windows reports binary multiples with the decimal symbols. A drive sold as 1 TB therefore shows up in Windows as roughly 931 GB without a single byte missing, a confusion that has reached court: Western Digital settled a lawsuit over it and added explicit disclaimers. Memory capacity is quoted with the binary convention, so 16 GB of memory is 16 GiB in strict notation.

Bytes are not bits. Network speeds are counted in bits per second with a lower-case b, and storage and file sizes in bytes with an upper-case B, so a factor of eight separates the two figures before any protocol overhead. Confusing Mb with MB, or MB with MiB, is the usual source of a support case that reads it should be faster.

Numbers worth remembering: 1956 for the word, 1964 for the eight-bit standard, 8 bits and 256 values per byte, 4 bits in a nibble, at least 8 bits for a C byte, most significant octet first on the wire, 1,024 for kibi against 1,000 for kilo, and 1998 for the IEC prefixes.

tcp-ip.def: The internet protocol suite, named after two of its protocols, the Transmission Control Protocol (TCP) and the Internet Protocol (IP): a layered family split in the late 1970s from a single 1974 design, which became the common language of the internet.
tcp-ip.context: Vint Cerf and Bob Kahn described one Transmission Control Program in 1974; by 1978 it had been cut in two, Transmission Control Protocol (TCP) for reliable ordered delivery and Internet Protocol (IP) for addressing and forwarding, so that applications that did not want reliability could skip it. The two were published as RFC (Request for Comments) 793 and RFC 791 in September 1981, and on 1 January 1983, the ARPANET (Advanced Research Projects Agency Network) flag day, the network's hosts were to leave the older NCP (Network Control Program) for TCP/IP at once, the moment often taken as the start of the modern internet. Its design keeps the network simple and stateless and puts reliability in the hosts, and its openly distributed, free-to-implement specifications let it outlast the proprietary networks of IBM, Digital and Xerox.
tcp-ip.depth:
What the name covers. TCP/IP is the usual name for the internet protocol suite, taken from two of its protocols, the Transmission Control Protocol (TCP) and the Internet Protocol (IP), but it covers the whole family and the architecture behind it; it is sometimes called the DoD model, after the United States Department of Defense that funded and adopted it. The host requirements, Request for Comments (RFC) 1122 and RFC 1123, both edited by R. Braden and published in October 1989, together form Internet Standard STD 3 and are still in force. They say a host must implement the layered set of protocols comprising the Internet protocol suite, typically at least one protocol from each layer, and RFC 1122 names four: a link layer for whatever network the host is attached to; the internet layer, home of IP, ICMP (Internet Control Message Protocol) and IGMP (Internet Group Management Protocol); the transport layer, with TCP as the reliable, connection-oriented, flow-controlled service and UDP (User Datagram Protocol) as the connectionless datagram service; and the application layer, with user protocols such as Telnet, FTP (File Transfer Protocol) and SMTP (Simple Mail Transfer Protocol) and support protocols such as DNS (Domain Name System), whose requirements are in RFC 1123.

The architecture is in the assumptions. RFC 1122 states them plainly: the internet is a network of networks, and two hosts on the same network use the same protocols they would use across the world; gateways, the RFC's word for IP routers, keep no connection state and forward each datagram independently, so redundant paths can be used around failures; all the state needed for end-to-end flow control and reliability lives in the hosts, so it is lost only if an end point fails; and routing complexity belongs in the gateways, not the hosts. IP itself is a connectionless datagram service with no end-to-end delivery guarantees: datagrams may arrive damaged, duplicated, out of order or not at all, and the layers above recover when they need to. These rules go back to Bob Kahn's early thinking as the Internet Society's history records it: each network had to stand on its own and need no internal changes to join; communication was best effort, with retransmission from the source; the black boxes joining networks, later called gateways and routers, would retain no information about the flows passing through them; and there would be no global control at the operations level. The consequence an engineer meets every day is that the core promises nothing about loss, order or delay, and whatever needs a guarantee builds it at the edge.

Where it came from. Kahn had arrived at the Defense Advanced Research Projects Agency (DARPA) in 1972 with the idea of open-architecture networking, and in the spring of 1973 he asked Vint Cerf, then at Stanford, to work on the detailed design with him. A first written version circulated at Sussex University as INWG 39, a paper of the International Network Working Group (INWG) in September 1973, and the refined paper, 'A Protocol for Packet Network Intercommunication', appeared in IEEE Transactions on Communications, volume COM-22, number 5, in May 1974. It describes a single transmission control program (TCP) in each host and a GATEWAY between networks, and it already contains decisions that still shape IP: a gateway may fragment a packet too large for the next network, and reassembly is the destination host's job, because reassembly in gateways would bring buffering problems, potential deadlocks and the need for every fragment to pass through the same gateway. DARPA then let three implementation contracts, to Stanford (Cerf), BBN (Bolt Beranek and Newman, with Ray Tomlinson) and University College London (Peter Kirstein), and within about a year three independent implementations could interoperate.

Why it became two protocols. The first TCP implementation offered only virtual circuits, which suited file transfer and remote login, but work on packet voice in the 1970s showed that some losses should be left to the application rather than corrected; the original TCP was reorganized into a simple IP for addressing and forwarding and a separate TCP for flow control and recovery, and UDP was added for applications that wanted IP's basic service directly. Jon Postel argued for the split in Internet Experiment Note (IEN) 2 on 15 August 1977, which opens 'We are screwing up in our design of internet protocols by violating the principle of layering' and proposes a hop-by-hop internet protocol, an end-to-end host protocol and a defined interface between them. By June 1978 the two had separate specifications, IEN 40 for TCP version 4 and IEN 41 for the Internetwork Protocol version 4, revised as IEN 55 and IEN 54 that September; RFC 791 still says the version field of the header it describes is 4.

The standards and their status. UDP was published as RFC 768 in August 1980, and IP as RFC 791, ICMP as RFC 792 and TCP as RFC 793 in September 1981, all by Postel. RFC 791 and RFC 792 together remain STD 5 and RFC 768 is STD 6. RFC 793 was obsoleted in August 2022 by RFC 9293, which gathers the changes made to TCP piecemeal over four decades, obsoletes six later documents along with RFC 793 (among them RFC 879 and RFC 6691 on the maximum segment size), updates the TCP parts of RFC 1122 and is now STD 7.

The flag day. RFC 801, Postel's NCP/TCP Transition Plan of November 1981, records that the Department of Defense had recently adopted IP and TCP as standards for all its packet networks, and sets the goal of a complete switch of the ARPANET (Advanced Research Projects Agency Network) from the Network Control Program (NCP) to IP/TCP by 1 January 1983. Every host organization was to begin its implementation by 1 January 1982; relay hosts would carry Telnet, file transfer and mail between NCP-only and TCP-only hosts in the meantime; most hosts were to be TCP-capable by July 1982 and the last NCP conversion complete by November 1982; and in January 1983 NCP would be removed from service and the relays would end. The Internet Society's history, written in 1997 by participants including Cerf, Kahn and Postel, calls it a flag-day style transition that required all hosts to convert simultaneously or be left to ad hoc mechanisms, planned over several years and surprisingly smooth, remembered in buttons reading 'I survived the TCP/IP transition'. The same history dates the adoption of TCP/IP as a defence standard to 1980, says the transition permitted the network to be split into MILNET for operational needs and ARPANET for research, and credits DARPA's funding of TCP/IP in Berkeley Unix (BSD) releases as one of the key elements in its spread. It also records that vendors of the early 1980s often treated TCP/IP as an add-on to their own proprietary networking, while the Department of Defense required it in many of its purchases.

Four layers, not seven. The Open Systems Interconnection (OSI) Basic Reference Model, in its current text ITU-T (International Telecommunication Union, Telecommunication Standardization Sector) Recommendation X.200, approved on 1 July 1994 and published identically by the International Organization for Standardization and the International Electrotechnical Commission (ISO/IEC) as 7498-1, defines seven layers: physical, data link, network, transport, session, presentation and application. RFC 1122 maps the internet suite onto it explicitly: the internet application layer essentially combines OSI's presentation and application layers and is not subdivided further, an internet host corresponds to an OSI end system and a gateway to an intermediate system, and the datagram IP was the model for OSI's Connectionless Network Protocol. There is no session layer, and the link layer is whatever the attached network defines, which is why the field speaks in OSI numbers, layer 2, layer 3, layer 7, about protocols designed in four. Layering is a tool rather than a law: RFC 3439 (December 2002) has a section titled 'Layering Considered Harmful', observing that a layer may need information from two layers down, such as lower-layer packet sizes, which is the problem maximum segment size clamping and path maximum transmission unit (MTU) discovery exist to solve.

The robustness principle. RFC 1122 applies Postel's rule to every layer, 'Be liberal in what you accept, and conservative in what you send', and pairs it with the instruction to assume the network is filled with malevolent entities sending packets designed to have the worst possible effect. RFC 9413 (June 2023) revisits the first half: tolerating unexpected input is no longer considered best practice in all scenarios, because when implementations silently accept faulty input the errors become entrenched, other implementations must tolerate them in turn, and a flaw can end up as a de facto standard; the remedy it argues for is active maintenance of protocols and their specifications.

Where the design was bent. The architecture assumed a stateless core; the network that grew filled with what RFC 3234 (February 2002) calls middleboxes, a term it credits to Lixia Zhang: any intermediary device performing functions other than the normal, standard functions of an IP router on the path between source and destination. Its catalogue runs from network address translation (NAT) and firewalls to proxies, caches and load balancers, all of which keep the per-connection state RFC 1122 said gateways would not, and it warns that protocols designed without considering middleboxes may fail in their presence, that middleboxes bring new failure modes, and that diagnosis becomes harder. QUIC, standardized as RFC 9000 in May 2021, is the current generation's answer: its packets travel in UDP datagrams, in the RFC's words to better facilitate deployment in existing systems and networks, and it authenticates the entirety of each packet and encrypts as much of each as is practical, leaving the path little to inspect or rewrite. The trade the original design made still holds: anyone can build a network or an application without asking the network's permission, competitors that put intelligence in the network offered stronger guarantees but could not be extended without the operator, and the price is that loss, ordering and delay remain the endpoints' problem.

ip.def: The best-effort, connectionless delivery layer that addresses and routes packets across interconnected networks, the thin waist every internet application stands on.
ip.context: The Internet Protocol (IP) does one job and refuses the rest: it gives every host an address, routes each datagram hop by hop towards it, and fragments packets to fit each link, but it promises nothing about order, duplication, or arrival. That deliberate minimalism, formalized in Request for Comments (RFC) 791 (September 1981, edited by Jon Postel), is what let the internet scale across wildly different networks; reliability was pushed up to the Transmission Control Protocol (TCP) and left out entirely by the User Datagram Protocol (UDP). The design traces to Cerf and Kahn's 1974 paper, and its addressing is the 'IP address' the whole world now quotes.
ip.depth:
The Internet Protocol (IP) is the network layer of the internet suite. It carries datagrams from a source host to a destination host, each identified by a fixed-length address, across any number of interconnected networks, and it fragments and reassembles datagrams when a network can only carry small packets. Its specification, Request for Comments (RFC) 791, is explicit about what it leaves out: no acknowledgements end to end or hop by hop, no error control for data beyond a header checksum, no retransmissions and no flow control. Errors travel back in the Internet Control Message Protocol (ICMP), which every IP module implements, and everything else belongs to the protocol carried inside, named by the 8-bit Protocol field: 1 for ICMP, 6 for the Transmission Control Protocol (TCP), 17 for the User Datagram Protocol (UDP), 50 for the Encapsulating Security Payload (ESP), in the registry kept by the Internet Assigned Numbers Authority (IANA).

IP began as half of something else. RFC 801 dates to 1973 the start of work on a single host-to-host protocol for the ARPANET, the network of the Advanced Research Projects Agency, and for the newer packet radio and satellite networks. Vinton Cerf and Robert Kahn's 1974 paper in IEEE (Institute of Electrical and Electronics Engineers) Transactions on Communications described one transmission control program that both crossed networks through gateways and kept the end-to-end connection; addressing and routing were later split out so that host protocols other than TCP could share the layer below. RFC 791, edited by Jon Postel at the Information Sciences Institute and published in September 1981 for the Defense Advanced Research Projects Agency (DARPA), says it draws on six earlier editions. RFC 801 (November 1981) planned the ARPANET's move from the Network Control Protocol (NCP) to IP and TCP, and the cutover happened on 1 January 1983. The Version field reads 4; the IANA registry lists 6 for IP version 6 (IPv6) and marks versions 5, 7, 8 and 9 as reserved and historic.

The IP version 4 (IPv4) header is 20 octets without options and at most 60, because the 4-bit Internet Header Length (IHL) counts 32-bit words. After Version and IHL come the Type of Service octet, which RFC 2474 (December 1998) superseded with the Differentiated Services field and its 6-bit code point (DSCP); a 16-bit Total Length, so no datagram exceeds 65,535 octets; a 16-bit Identification; three flag bits, among them Don't Fragment (DF) and More Fragments (MF); a 13-bit Fragment Offset counted in units of 8 octets; an 8-bit Time to Live (TTL); Protocol; a Header Checksum, recomputed at every hop because the TTL changes; the 32-bit source and destination addresses; and options. RFC 791 measured TTL in seconds but required every module to decrement it by at least one, so in practice it is a hop limit that discards looping datagrams.

Two sizes are written into the specification. Every host must accept a datagram of 576 octets, whole or in fragments, a figure chosen to fit a 512-octet data block plus 64 octets of headers and the origin of TCP's default Maximum Segment Size (MSS) of 536; and every module must forward 68 octets without further fragmentation, a maximal 60-octet header plus the minimum 8-octet fragment. A router facing a datagram larger than the next link's Maximum Transmission Unit (MTU) fragments it, unless DF is set; then it drops it and returns ICMP type 3, code 4, fragmentation needed and DF set, the signal Path MTU Discovery (RFC 1191, November 1990) uses to find the smallest MTU on a path. RFC 8900 (September 2020) sets out why fragmentation is now considered fragile: only the first fragment carries port numbers, so stateless firewalls must admit or drop the rest blindly; at high rates the 16-bit Identification repeats, and misassembled datagrams can slip past the TCP and UDP checksums; and filtered or lost ICMP messages create path MTU black holes.

The 32-bit address was first divided by class. RFC 791 gave class A a 7-bit network number, class B 14 bits and class C 21 bits. RFC 4632 tells what followed: as organizations joined in the late 1980s, class B space ran out fastest, because class C's 254 hosts were too few and class B's 65,534 too many for most, and routing tables grew beyond what routers and people could handle. The Internet Engineering Task Force (IETF) formed its Routing and Addressing group in November 1991, and the result was Classless Inter-Domain Routing (CIDR), first RFC 1519 (September 1993) and now RFC 4632 (August 2006), which replaces classes with a prefix length and keeps forwarding on a longest-match basis. Private ranges and address translation bought time, but on 3 February 2011 the Number Resource Organization (NRO) announced that IANA had allocated its last five /8 blocks, each 1/256 of the IPv4 space, one to each Regional Internet Registry (RIR), leaving no free pool at the top.

IPv6, now RFC 8200 (July 2017, Internet Standard 86, obsoleting RFC 2460 of December 1998), keeps the same best-effort service and changes the packet: 128-bit addresses; a fixed 40-octet header of Version, Traffic Class, a 20-bit Flow Label, Payload Length, Next Header and Hop Limit; extension headers in place of options; no header checksum; fragmentation only by the source, never by routers on the path; and a minimum link MTU of 1,280 octets.

IP authenticates nothing: the source address is whatever the sender writes. RFC 2827 (May 2000), Best Current Practice (BCP) 38, answers denial-of-service attacks with forged sources through ingress filtering at the network edge, so that a network forwards only packets whose source addresses belong behind it. Fragments carry their own attacks, described in RFC 1858 (October 1995): the tiny fragment attack forces TCP header fields into a second fragment so that filter rules never match them, and the overlapping fragment attack sends an innocuous first fragment that passes the filter and a later one that overwrites the TCP header, the destination port for instance, during reassembly.

In practice, ip addr and ip route on Linux show a host's addresses and its forwarding table, and ping -M do -s 1472 sends a 1,500-octet IPv4 packet with DF set (1,472 data bytes, 8 of ICMP header, 20 of IP header), the quickest path MTU test: if the full size fails and smaller sizes pass, something on the path is dropping fragments or the ICMP that should report them. On a link, IP rides in Ethernet frames with EtherType 0x0800, IPv6 with 0x86DD, and the Address Resolution Protocol (ARP) with 0x0806 maps IPv4 addresses to link addresses.

Numbers worth remembering: version 4, a 20-octet minimum header, 32-bit addresses, 65,535 octets per datagram at most, 576 octets every host must accept, 68 octets every router must forward unfragmented, fragments counted in 8-octet units, a default TTL of 64 on Linux (net.ipv4.ip_default_ttl), protocol 6 for TCP and 17 for UDP, and 1,280 octets as the IPv6 minimum MTU.

udp.def: The minimal transport that wraps a packet with just ports and a checksum and sends it with no handshake, no ordering, and no retransmission: fire and forget.
udp.context: Jon Postel defined the User Datagram Protocol (UDP) in Request for Comments (RFC) 768 on 28 August 1980 as the thinnest possible layer over the Internet Protocol (IP), an eight-byte header carrying source and destination ports, a length, and an optional checksum. It guarantees nothing about delivery or duplicates, which is exactly why latency-sensitive and query-response traffic prefers it: its first users were the internet name service and trivial file transfer, and its descendants carry the Domain Name System (DNS), the Dynamic Host Configuration Protocol (DHCP), voice over IP (VoIP), gaming, and the QUIC transport under modern HTTP (Hypertext Transfer Protocol). Where the Transmission Control Protocol (TCP) is a phone call, UDP is a postcard.
udp.depth:
The User Datagram Protocol (UDP) is the thinnest transport the internet has, and almost nothing about it has changed since Jon Postel's three-page Request for Comments (RFC) 768, dated 28 August 1980. That note defines UDP to make a datagram mode of packet-switched communication available over the Internet Protocol (IP): a procedure for programs to send messages to other programs with a minimum of protocol mechanism, transaction oriented, with delivery and duplicate protection not guaranteed. Applications that need ordered, reliable streams are told to use the Transmission Control Protocol (TCP) instead. UDP is IP protocol 17 (21 in octal, as the RFC adds).

The header is 8 octets: a 16-bit source port, optional and set to zero when unused; a 16-bit destination port; a 16-bit length covering header and data, so never less than 8; and a 16-bit checksum. The checksum is the one's complement of the one's complement sum over a pseudo-header (source and destination addresses, protocol and UDP length), the header and the data, the same procedure TCP uses, and the pseudo-header is what protects against misrouted datagrams. In IP version 4 (IPv4) the checksum is optional: all zeros means none was computed, and a computed zero is sent as all ones. IP version 6 (IPv6, RFC 8200) makes it mandatory and has receivers discard datagrams with a zero checksum, with one exception, tunnel encapsulations that enable a zero-checksum mode under RFC 6936. There is no sequence number, acknowledgement, window or connection state, so each send becomes one IP datagram and the receiver gets the whole message or nothing; message boundaries survive, which a TCP byte stream does not offer.

Size is left to the application. The 16-bit length allows 65,535 octets including the header, or 65,507 octets of payload over IPv4 once the 20-octet IP header is counted, but anything larger than the path's Maximum Transmission Unit (MTU) is fragmented by IP, with every fragility that brings. RFC 8085, the UDP usage guidelines (March 2017, Best Current Practice (BCP) 145), says applications should avoid IP fragmentation, use the path MTU the IP layer knows or discover it themselves, and otherwise stay within 576 bytes for IPv4 and 1,280 for IPv6. Linux does path MTU discovery for UDP by default and returns EMSGSIZE when a write exceeds the known path MTU. The Domain Name System (DNS) wrote a stricter limit into its specification: RFC 1035 (November 1987) restricts messages carried by UDP to 512 bytes, which is why larger answers needed extensions or a retry over TCP.

UDP also leaves congestion control to the application. RFC 8085 says applications should perform congestion control over all the UDP traffic they send, and one that cannot keep a round-trip estimate, because the destination never answers, should send no more than one datagram every 3 seconds. Middleboxes add a second burden, because there is no handshake or close for them to watch, only a timer. RFC 4787 (January 2007, BCP 127) requires a Network Address Translation (NAT) mapping for UDP to last at least two minutes and recommends five, yet RFC 8085 records that a significant fraction of deployed middleboxes use shorter timeouts, and it allows keep-alives no more often than once every 15 seconds, the interval inherited from Interactive Connectivity Establishment (ICE). When nothing listens on the destination port, the host returns an Internet Control Message Protocol (ICMP) destination unreachable, code 3, port unreachable (RFC 792, September 1981), so a scan that gets no reply at all cannot tell an open port from a filtered one.

What UDP lacks is what its users want. RFC 768 names its first major uses as the Internet Name Server and the Trivial File Transfer Protocol (TFTP). A query and answer that fit in one datagram, as in DNS on port 53, the Network Time Protocol (NTP) on 123 or the Dynamic Host Configuration Protocol (DHCP) on 67 and 68 (registered as bootps and bootpc), would pay a full round trip for a TCP handshake before asking anything. Real-time voice and video prefer a lost packet to a late one, since a retransmitted sample arrives after the moment it belonged to. New transports are built on UDP because it passes through existing networks: QUIC, RFC 9000 (May 2021), carries its packets in UDP datagrams, in its own words, to better facilitate deployment in existing systems and networks, and HTTP/3, version 3 of the Hypertext Transfer Protocol (RFC 9114, June 2022), runs on QUIC. RFC 9114 tells clients to fall back to TCP-based HTTP when UDP is blocked, which is why a firewall that drops UDP on port 443 breaks no browsing but quietly removes HTTP/3.

The missing handshake is also UDP's security problem. Nothing proves that a datagram came from its source address, so an attacker can send a small request carrying the victim's address to any server that answers with something larger, and the server does the attacking. Memcached on UDP port 11211 was the extreme case: in February 2018 Cloudflare measured a 15-byte request producing a 750 kB response, an amplification of about 51,200 times, and on 28 February 2018 GitHub was fully unavailable from 17:21 to 17:26 Coordinated Universal Time (UTC) under a memcached attack that peaked at 1.35 Tbit/s and 126.9 million packets per second. The defences sit on both sides: ingress filtering, so that networks do not emit spoofed sources (BCP 38, RFC 2827), and services that do not answer small unauthenticated UDP requests with large responses, or are not reachable from the internet at all.

In practice, ss -uan on Linux lists UDP sockets with numeric addresses; there is no state to read beyond whether a socket is bound or connected. On a stateful firewall or load balancer a UDP flow is only a pair of addresses and ports with an idle timer, so a long silence ends a flow the application still considers alive, and the next datagram may be dropped or sent to a different backend. Syslog (port 514, registered for UDP only), the Simple Network Management Protocol (SNMP) on 161 and 162, the Internet Security Association and Key Management Protocol (ISAKMP) on 500 and IPsec NAT traversal on 4500, as the Internet Assigned Numbers Authority (IANA) registry names them, are the UDP services an infrastructure engineer meets most often after DNS, NTP and DHCP.

Numbers worth remembering: protocol 17, an 8-octet header, a minimum length of 8, 65,507 octets of payload at most over IPv4, a checksum optional in IPv4 and mandatory in IPv6, 512 bytes for classic DNS over UDP, two minutes as the minimum NAT mapping lifetime, and 15 seconds as the shortest recommended keep-alive interval.

analog-vs-digital.def: The distinction between a continuous signal that varies smoothly and a discrete one built from countable steps, and the boundary the whole digital age is spent crossing.
analog-vs-digital.context: An analog quantity, a voltage or a groove in vinyl or a sound wave, takes infinitely many values along a continuum; a digital one is quantized into a finite set, ultimately bits. Converting between them is sampling and quantization, and the Nyquist-Shannon theorem sets exactly how often you must sample to reconstruct a bandlimited signal without loss, the mathematical bridge from the continuous world to the discrete one. The line is blurrier than it looks: 'organic' reality is often discrete at bottom (DNA is a four-symbol code; charge and energy come in quanta), while 'digital' systems are physically analog underneath (a transistor is a voltage we agree to read as 0 or 1). So the honest answer to whether organic can be digital, or digital organic, is that the labels describe how we choose to read a signal, not a hard fact about the signal itself: the same reality can be continuous to one instrument and discrete to another.

inter-frame-gap.def: The mandatory idle time between Ethernet frames, 96 bit times, that gives every receiver a beat to reset before the next frame arrives.
inter-frame-gap.context: IEEE 802.3 requires transmitters to leave at least 96 bit times of silence between frames: 9.6 microseconds at 10 Mb/s, 0.96 at 100 Mb/s, 96 nanoseconds at gigabit, always the same 12 byte times regardless of speed. The gap exists so receiving hardware can finish processing one frame, resynchronize, and arm for the next. It is also why line-rate arithmetic never matches the naive frame size: every frame on the wire really costs its length plus 8 bytes of preamble plus 12 bytes of gap, which is how a 64-byte minimum frame becomes the famous 84 bytes, and 10 Gb/s becomes 14.88 million packets per second.

split-horizon.def: A distance-vector routing rule: never advertise a route back out the interface you learned it from.
split-horizon.context: Documented in RFC 1058, the 1988 RIP specification, split horizon breaks the simplest routing loop: without it, two neighbours can advertise a dead route back and forth, counting the metric up towards infinity while traffic ping-pongs. The stricter variant, split horizon with poison reverse, does advertise the route back but with an infinite metric (16 in RIP), which kills the loop faster at the cost of bigger updates. The idea outlived RIP: iBGP applies its own split-horizon rule, refusing to re-advertise a route learned from one iBGP peer to another, which is exactly why iBGP needs a full mesh or route reflectors. Not to be confused with split brain, an unrelated high-availability failure that happens to share the adjective.
split-horizon.depth:
The rule survives inside link-state protocols wherever they pass summaries instead of maps. Between OSPF areas only summaries and external routes travel, and FRRouting's documentation draws the conclusion that routing between areas is distance vector, not link state. RFC 2328 then applies the old rule: an area border router does not originate a summary of a route back into an area when the route's next hops lie in that same area, which the RFC calls the logical equivalent of split horizon. OSPF also forces inter-area routing into a star, with area 0 as the hub.

IS-IS meets a similar loop between its levels: a prefix leaked from Level 2 down into a Level 1 area could be picked up by another router and advertised back up into the backbone.
