RFC 1195's answer was to allow advertising only upward; RFC 5305 records the later remedy for leaking, the up/down bit, set to 1 when a prefix travels down so that it may only continue down the hierarchy.

multicast.def: Delivery of one IP (Internet Protocol) datagram to a host group, a set of hosts named by a single address, with the network making the copies.
multicast.context: Defined in RFC (Request for Comments) 1112 (August 1989): a sender transmits once to a group address, in 224.0.0.0/4 for IPv4 or ff00::/8 for IPv6, routers forward it towards networks with members, and hosts report membership with IGMP (Internet Group Management Protocol), or MLD (Multicast Listener Discovery) in IPv6. OSPF (Open Shortest Path First) uses 224.0.0.5 and 224.0.0.6, multicast DNS (Domain Name System) 224.0.0.251, and market data feeds have registered groups.
multicast.depth:
The model. Request for Comments (RFC) 1112 (August 1989), by Steve Deering of Stanford University, defines IP (Internet Protocol) multicast around the host group: a set of zero or more hosts identified by one destination address, whose membership is dynamic, which a host may join or leave at any time and which anyone may send to without being a member. Delivery is best effort, as for unicast. The sender transmits once and the network makes copies only where paths to members diverge. That separates multicast from its neighbours: broadcast reaches every host on one link whether it wants the packet or not and stops at the router, while anycast delivers to one member of a group, the nearest. RFC 1112 grades hosts as level 0 (no multicast), level 1 (can send but not receive) and level 2 (full support), and notes that there is no multicast address, or any other, for all hosts on the Internet.

The IPv4 address plan. Group addresses run from 224.0.0.0 to 239.255.255.255, the old class D; 224.0.0.0 is never assigned and 224.0.0.1 is all hosts on the link. The IANA (Internet Assigned Numbers Authority) registry, last updated on 6 November 2026, divides the range into blocks. 224.0.0.0/24, the Local Network Control Block, holds link-local protocol groups: 224.0.0.2 all routers, 224.0.0.5 and 224.0.0.6 for OSPF (Open Shortest Path First), 224.0.0.9 for version 2 of RIP (Routing Information Protocol), 224.0.0.13 for PIM (Protocol Independent Multicast), 224.0.0.18 for VRRP (Virtual Router Redundancy Protocol), 224.0.0.22 for IGMP (Internet Group Management Protocol) and 224.0.0.251 for multicast DNS (Domain Name System). 224.0.1.0/24, the Internetwork Control Block, holds routed groups such as 224.0.1.1 for NTP (Network Time Protocol) and, since 1998, Nasdaq market data feeds from 224.0.1.91. 232.0.0.0/8 is reserved for source-specific multicast; 233/8 is GLOP, where RFC 3180 (September 2001) embeds a 16-bit autonomous system number in the middle two octets to give every autonomous system a /24; and 239.0.0.0/8 is administratively scoped, with RFC 2365 (July 1998) defining 239.255.0.0/16 as the local scope and 239.192.0.0/14 as the organization local scope, multicast's private address space.

IPv6 and the scope field. IPv6 multicast addresses begin with FF (FF00::/8), and RFC 4291 builds scope into the address itself with a 4-bit field: 1 interface-local, 2 link-local, 4 admin-local, 5 site-local, 8 organization-local and E global. FF02::5 and FF02::6 are therefore OSPFv3's link-scoped groups and ff02::d is all PIM routers. On Ethernet, RFC 2464 (December 1998) maps an IPv6 group to the MAC (media access control) address 33-33 followed by the last four octets of the group.

Frames and switches. RFC 1112 maps an IPv4 group to Ethernet by copying its low-order 23 bits into 01-00-5E-00-00-00. A group address has 28 significant bits, so 5 bits are lost and 32 groups share every MAC address; 224.0.0.1, 225.0.0.1 and 239.128.0.1 all become 01-00-5E-00-00-01, which means a group in 239.128.0.0/24 is indistinguishable at layer 2 from link-local control traffic in 224.0.0.0/24. A switch forwards a multicast frame out of every port in its VLAN (virtual local area network) unless it learns otherwise, and RFC 4541 (May 2006), the informational guide to IGMP and MLD (Multicast Listener Discovery) snooping, notes how much bandwidth that flooding wastes. Snooping switches watch membership reports to forward each group only where it is wanted, but RFC 4541 still requires non-IGMP traffic to 224.0.0.X to go out on all ports, and snooping depends on a querier on the segment: without one, membership entries age out and the group is either flooded or cut off, depending on the switch.

Membership: IGMP and MLD. Hosts report membership to their local routers with IGMP, IP protocol 2, in IPv4, and with MLD in IPv6. The current versions became Internet Standards in March 2025: IGMPv3 as RFC 9776 (STD 100), obsoleting RFC 3376 of October 2002 and backward compatible with it, and MLDv2 as RFC 9777 (STD 101), obsoleting RFC 3810. Version 3 added source filtering, so a host can ask for a group only from listed sources (INCLUDE) or from all but listed sources (EXCLUDE). Every IGMP message is sent with an IP TTL (time to live) of 1 and a Router Alert option; general queries go to 224.0.0.1 and version 3 reports to 224.0.0.22. The defaults are a Robustness Variable of 2, a Query Interval of 125 seconds and a Query Response Interval of 10 seconds. RFC 9776 also corrected, under erratum 6725, the Group Membership Interval after which a router decides a group has no members: Robustness Variable times Query Interval plus twice the Query Response Interval, 270 seconds with the defaults, where RFC 3376 had added only one, 260 seconds.

Routing between networks. The first multicast routing protocol, DVMRP (Distance Vector Multicast Routing Protocol), RFC 1075 (November 1988, Waitzman, Partridge and Deering), was experimental, derived from RIP (Routing Information Protocol), and built trees by truncated reverse path broadcasting and pruning. The protocol in use today is PIM-SM, PIM in Sparse Mode, RFC 7761 (March 2016, STD 83, obsoleting RFC 4601). It is protocol independent because it uses the unicast routing table, whatever filled it, to check where traffic should come from; it builds a shared tree per group rooted at a Rendezvous Point (RP), and can switch receivers to a shortest-path tree per source; its messages are IP protocol 103 sent to ALL-PIM-ROUTERS, 224.0.0.13 or ff02::d. Source-specific multicast, RFC 4607 (August 2006), removes the RP altogether: a receiver names both the source and the group, a channel written (S,G), within 232/8 or FF3x::/32, which requires IGMPv3 or MLDv2 on the host (RFC 4604).

Scope by TTL and by design. RFC 1112 tells hosts to send multicast with a TTL of 1 unless the application asks for more, so that sending beyond one network requires an explicit choice; an application that works on its own VLAN and fails across a router has usually left that default in place. The IANA registry says multicast routers should not forward 224.0.0.0/24 whatever its TTL, FF02:: groups are link scoped by definition, and administratively scoped groups stay inside a boundary that the operator configures.

What goes wrong. Most multicast faults are membership faults, not routing faults. A segment without an IGMP querier lets snooping entries expire, and receivers that worked for a few minutes go silent. A host still speaking IGMPv2 cannot express a source filter, so source-specific multicast fails for it. Overlapping MAC addresses make a switch flood a group that should have been pruned. A missing or unreachable Rendezvous Point leaves PIM-SM receivers with no shared tree. And because a sender needs no membership and receives no acknowledgement, a source can transmit perfectly into a network that delivers nothing, so verification has to happen at the receiver: is the host joined, has the router seen the report, and does the multicast routing table hold state for that group.

broadcast.def: One-to-all delivery inside a network segment: a frame or packet addressed so that every host must receive and process it.
broadcast.context: On Ethernet the destination FF:FF:FF:FF:FF:FF reaches every station in the segment; in Internet Protocol version 4 (IPv4), Jeffrey Mogul's Request for Comments (RFC) 919 (October 1984) set the conventions, 255.255.255.255 as the limited broadcast that routers never forward, and the highest address of each subnet as its directed broadcast. The who-has question of the Address Resolution Protocol (ARP) rides on it, as does discovery in the Dynamic Host Configuration Protocol (DHCP), which is why a host with no address at all can still ask for one. Because routers stop broadcasts, the broadcast domain ends where the router begins, and that boundary is most of the reason subnets and virtual LANs (VLANs) exist. Internet Protocol version 6 (IPv6) dropped broadcast entirely and does everything with multicast groups instead.
broadcast.depth:
Broadcast is one-to-all delivery inside a bounded domain: a single transmission that every station in the domain must receive and pass up its stack. It exists at two layers. On Ethernet it is a destination address of all ones, FF:FF:FF:FF:FF:FF, which every interface accepts; the least significant bit of its first octet is the group bit, so broadcast is the one group address that every station belongs to. In Internet Protocol version 4 (IPv4) it is a set of addresses meaning 'all hosts', which the sender maps onto the link-layer broadcast. The devices a broadcast reaches form the broadcast domain. A bridge or switch floods broadcast frames out of every port in the same virtual local area network (VLAN), the Linux bridge doing so by default on every port, and a router does not forward them, so the domain ends at the first routed interface.

The IPv4 conventions are Jeffrey Mogul's, in Request for Comments (RFC) 919, Broadcasting Internet Datagrams, and RFC 922 on broadcasting with subnets, both of October 1984. RFC 919 chose all ones in the host field to mean all hosts, because that number is unlikely to belong to a real host, and defined 255.255.255.255 as a broadcast on the local hardware network that must not be forwarded, for hosts that do not yet know their own network number. It also warned that a broadcast imposes a cost on every host that hears it, so it should be used only when it is the best solution to a problem. RFC 1812 (June 1995) sets the router rules: limited broadcasts must not be forwarded; a directed broadcast addresses a whole network prefix with all ones in the host part, 192.0.2.255 for 192.0.2.0/24; 0.0.0.0 is an obsolete form of the limited broadcast; and the all-subnets-directed broadcast of RFC 922, not well defined once addressing became classless, is deprecated.

Broadcast solves the bootstrap problem of reaching something whose address is not yet known. The Address Resolution Protocol (ARP), David Plummer's RFC 826 (November 1982), broadcasts its request to every station on the cable to ask which one owns an IP address, and only the owner replies. The Dynamic Host Configuration Protocol (DHCP), RFC 2131 (March 1997), begins with a DHCPDISCOVER broadcast on the local subnet from a client that sends with source address 0, because it has none yet. Servers answer at the client's hardware address, or by broadcast to 255.255.255.255 if the client sets the BROADCAST flag, and a DHCPNAK on the same subnet is always broadcast, because the client may hold the wrong address or mask. Routers do not forward these broadcasts, so a relay agent on each subnet carries them across to a server elsewhere, and the server replies to the relay's address, recorded in the giaddr field, on the DHCP server port, User Datagram Protocol (UDP) port 67.

Hosts handle broadcasts defensively. RFC 1122 (October 1989) forbids sending an Internet Control Message Protocol (ICMP) error about a datagram addressed to an IP broadcast or multicast address, or received as a link-layer broadcast, so that one malformed broadcast cannot draw an error from every host on the segment at once.

Directed broadcast became a weapon all the same. The CERT Coordination Center's advisory CA-1998-01 (5 January 1998) described the smurf attack, named after one of its exploit programs: forged ICMP echo requests, carrying the victim's address as their source, sent from outside to a network's directed broadcast address, so that potentially every machine on that intermediary network replies to the victim at once. RFC 2644 (August 1999), Best Current Practice (BCP) 34, noted that directed broadcasts on the internet backbone appeared to consist entirely of malicious attacks and reversed the old default of RFC 1812: routers must now block both the receipt and the forwarding of network-prefix-directed broadcasts unless an administrator enables them.

At layer 2 the danger is the broadcast storm. An Ethernet frame carries no hop count, so in a switching loop that spanning tree has not broken, flooded broadcasts circulate and multiply until the loop is cut, and a single faulty host can fill every link in the domain. Storm control limits the damage: on a FortiSwitch it measures broadcast, unknown unicast and unknown multicast traffic in packets per second and drops the excess above a configured rate, and it is disabled by default. Keeping broadcast domains small, with each VLAN carrying one subnet of sensible size, is the structural answer.

Internet Protocol version 6 (IPv6) has no broadcast at all. RFC 4291 (February 2006) states that its function is superseded by multicast: ff02::1 reaches all nodes on a link, and Neighbor Discovery, RFC 4861 (September 2007), resolves addresses by sending its solicitation to the target's solicited-node multicast address, built from the low-order 24 bits of the target address, so a resolution request interrupts only the few nodes that share those bits instead of every host on the link.

In practice, the tcpdump filter ether broadcast isolates the broadcast frames on a segment, usually ARP, DHCP and service discovery, and their rate is a fair measure of how large and noisy a broadcast domain has become. The numbers worth keeping: FF:FF:FF:FF:FF:FF on Ethernet; 255.255.255.255, never forwarded; the all-ones host address as a subnet's directed broadcast; source 0.0.0.0 for a DHCP client without an address; UDP ports 67 and 68; and ff02::1 as IPv6's nearest equivalent.

collision-domain.def: The stretch of shared network in which two devices transmitting at once garble each other: one collision domain, one conversation at a time.
collision-domain.context: On coaxial Ethernet the whole cable was a single collision domain, and hubs and repeaters only stretched it further: every added station raised the odds that two would speak at once and both would have to back off. Bridges and then switches broke the domain apart, giving each port its own, which is the entire commercial story of Kalpana's 1990 EtherSwitch. Full-duplex links finished the job by removing contention altogether, so on modern switched Ethernet a collision domain is a single cable with one device per end. The concept survives in exams and in the contrast that still matters daily: switches split collision domains, but only routers (or VLANs) split broadcast domains.

bum.def: Switching shorthand for the three traffic types a switch cannot deliver to a single known port and therefore floods: broadcast, unknown unicast, and multicast.
bum.context: A switch forwards a frame out one port only when its MAC table says where the destination lives; broadcasts never qualify, multicasts map to groups rather than ports, and an unknown unicast is simply a destination the table has not learned yet. All three get flooded to every port in the VLAN, which is harmless at small scale and a scaling problem at large scale. The term earns its keep in overlay networks: VXLAN fabrics must decide how to carry BUM traffic across the underlay, by ingress replication or by a multicast underlay, and storm-control features exist to rate-limit BUM before a loop or a chatty host turns flooding into a broadcast storm.

csma-cd.def: Classic Ethernet's channel etiquette: listen before you talk, talk only when the wire is quiet, and if two stations collide anyway, stop, jam, and retry after a random backoff.
csma-cd.context: Metcalfe and Boggs described the scheme in their July 1976 CACM paper on Ethernet, and IEEE 802.3 standardized it: a station senses the carrier, transmits when idle, keeps listening while sending, and on detecting a collision emits a jam signal so everyone notices, then waits a random interval chosen by binary exponential backoff before trying again. The 64-byte minimum frame exists for it, sized so a transmission lasts at least one round trip across the maximum segment and collisions are always detected in time. It is also the losing side of the great 1980s argument with Token Ring's deterministic turn-taking. Switched, full-duplex Ethernet retired the contention entirely, so CSMA/CD survives in the framing, the minimum frame size, and the exams.
csma-cd.depth:
In full duplex the whole scheme is switched off. Cisco's troubleshooting note puts the two worlds side by side: on a shared, half-duplex segment 'Collisions are not bad; they are essential to correct Ethernet operation', while 'In full-duplex Ethernet, collision detection is disabled'.

What survives in operations is the late collision. A collision 'detected by a station after it has sent the 512th bit of its frame' counts as late, because by then every station should already have heard the frame; Cisco lists the usual causes as incorrect cabling, too many hubs and faulty network cards. On a modern switched network, a late-collision counter that moves almost always means one thing instead: one end of the link is running half duplex and the other full, the duplex mismatch.

csma-ca.def: Wi-Fi's channel etiquette: a radio cannot hear a collision while it is transmitting, so stations work to avoid collisions up front with waits, random backoff, and per-frame acknowledgements.
csma-ca.context: IEEE 802.11 adopted collision avoidance because detection is physically off the table on radio: a transmitter drowns out its own receiver, and the hidden node problem means two stations can both be audible to the access point yet deaf to each other. So a station waits for the medium to go idle plus a spacing interval, counts down a random backoff, transmits, and treats a missing acknowledgement as a collision to retry. The optional RTS/CTS exchange reserves the air in advance, taming hidden nodes at the cost of overhead. The contrast with CSMA/CD is the classic exam question: Ethernet detected collisions after the fact, Wi-Fi spends effort so they mostly never happen.

sase.def: Secure access service edge (SASE): Gartner's 2019 name for converging the wide area network (WAN) and its security stack into one cloud-delivered service, applied at points of presence as close as possible to users, branches and applications, with policy driven by identity rather than by the address of a data centre.
sase.context: Coined by Gartner analysts Neil MacDonald, Lawrence Orans and Joe Skorupa in 'The Future of Network Security Is in the Cloud' (30 August 2019) and pronounced 'sassy', SASE (secure access service edge) bundles SD-WAN (software-defined wide area network) with a secure web gateway, a CASB (cloud access security broker), zero trust network access and firewall as a service, delivered from distributed points of presence and driven by identity rather than by the address of a data centre. The pitch: stop backhauling a remote workforce through headquarters appliances and put both the network path and its inspection where the users and the software as a service (SaaS) applications already are. Within two years the term had reorganized how vendors described their products, and in 2021 Gartner carved out the security half under its own name, security service edge (SSE), for buyers who wanted the protection without coupling it to the SD-WAN decision.
sase.depth:
What it is, and what it is not. Secure access service edge (SASE) is an analyst firm's market definition, not a protocol and not a product. The idea is to deliver wide area network (WAN) functions and security controls as a cloud service directly to the source of a connection, a user, a device, a branch or a workload, rather than to a data centre, so that traffic is inspected near where it starts instead of being carried to a building first. In the usual description it combines a software-defined WAN (SD-WAN) with network security functions: a secure web gateway (SWG), a cloud access security broker (CASB), zero trust network access (ZTNA), firewall as a service, data loss prevention (DLP) and malware inspection, delivered from points of presence (PoPs) placed near users, offices and cloud services. Policy follows identity, real-time context and compliance rules rather than the position of a firewall. SASE is not the same thing as its security half, security service edge (SSE), which has its own entry, nor is it SD-WAN with a new label: the definition requires both halves, operated as one service.

Where the term came from. Gartner analysts introduced it in a networking hype cycle and market trends report dated 29 July 2019 and described it at length in a report of 30 August 2019, The Future of Network Security Is in the Cloud, by Neil MacDonald, Lawrence Orans and Joe Skorupa. Vendors quoted it within weeks. Netskope's summary of 30 September 2019 gave the pronunciation, 'sassy', and two of the report's claims: that SASE would be as disruptive to network and network security architectures as infrastructure as a service (IaaS) had been to data centre design, and that by 2024 at least 40 per cent of enterprises would have explicit strategies to adopt it, up from less than 1 per cent at the end of 2018. Not every analyst agreed it was anything new. In November 2019 IDC and IHS Markit described it as neither a new market, technology nor product but an integration of existing technology under a single point of management; IHS Markit's Clifford Grossner doubted that enterprises would want all their SD-WAN and security functions from one vendor, and Gartner replied that chaining functions from several vendors yields inconsistent services, poor manageability and high latency. Forrester describes a similar converged stack under its own name, Zero Trust Edge.

The argument behind it. The traditional design carried branch and remote traffic over the WAN to one or a few corporate data centres, inspected it there with appliances and sent it on to the internet. Once users worked from anywhere and applications moved to software as a service (SaaS) and public clouds, that backhaul added latency in order to protect a perimeter that no longer contained much. SASE moves both the path and the inspection to the edge: each site or user connects to the nearest PoP, the security functions run there, and traffic continues to the internet, to SaaS or across the provider's backbone to another site. The characteristics usually listed follow from that: convergence of WAN and security functions; a cloud-native service with the elasticity of any cloud; a globally distributed fabric of PoPs, which have to be more numerous than those of a typical public cloud and backed by extensive peering; identity as the main input to policy, with location, time of day, device posture and data sensitivity as further context; and support for every kind of edge, from an SD-WAN device in a branch to an agent or clientless web access for a mobile user and tunnels from cloud networks.

How it is put together. Mechanically, a SASE service is the SSE cloud (proxies, firewalls and brokers in each PoP) plus the means of getting traffic into it and between sites. Branches arrive through an SD-WAN appliance that builds tunnels to the nearest PoP and can break traffic out locally; users arrive through an agent or a browser; data centres and cloud networks arrive through tunnels or direct interconnection. Vendors contract with several backbone and peering partners to carry traffic between PoPs, and many claim a single-pass design in which traffic is decrypted once and inspected by several policy engines instead of being chained through separate services. How traffic is steered to the security cloud, and what single-pass inspection means in practice, are covered in the SSE entry; what SASE adds is that the WAN edge and the security edge are configured, monitored and supported as one service.

The closest thing to a standard. Because the term belongs to an analyst firm, the attempt to pin it down came from the industry association MEF, originally the Metro Ethernet Forum and now the Mplify Alliance. On 13 December 2022 it announced the industry's first SASE standard, MEF 117, SASE Service Attributes and Service Framework, dated October 2022, together with a Zero Trust Framework for MEF Services, MEF 118. MEF 117 does not say how a product must work. It specifies the service attributes a provider and a subscriber agree on, covering security functions, policies and connectivity, and defines the behaviour of a SASE service as it is visible to the subscriber whatever the implementation. Its revision, Mplify 117.1 of June 2025, supersedes it. In that text a SASE Edge is a logical set of network and security functions located between the subscriber-facing interface and the underlying connectivity service; it can sit in a cloud, on the subscriber's premises or in the provider's network, in one device or spread across several, and each session has a subject edge and a target edge. The security functions come from MEF 138 plus definitions of its own for application identity and access management, data integrity, proxy, CASB and remote browser isolation, and its informative examples run from a SASE in a box on the customer's premises to a service delivered only from the cloud. That vocabulary is useful in a contract precisely because it describes outcomes rather than brand names.

How the market sorted itself. In 2021 Gartner defined the security subset as SSE, and buyers could then modernize inspection without waiting for a WAN refresh, or buy the two halves from two vendors. The single-vendor option got its own analysis: Gartner published a Magic Quadrant for Single-Vendor SASE in 2023 and 2024, renamed it the Magic Quadrant for SASE Platforms on 9 July 2025 (by Jonathan Forest, Neil MacDonald and Dale Koeppen), and published the next edition on 28 July 2026. Netskope noted in August 2024 that the Single-Vendor SASE report recognized only nine participants and placed it among the Leaders in both that report and the SSE one. Palo Alto Networks, with Prisma Access, announced a place among the Leaders of both reports for the fourth consecutive year in August 2026. Fortinet, a Leader in the 2025 SASE Platforms report, described its approach as secure SD-WAN, ZTNA and threat protection under a single operating system, FortiOS, and one licence. Gartner's own disclaimer, reproduced in every one of those announcements, is the reading to keep: the quadrant is an opinion, not a statement of fact. MEF, quoting the Dell'Oro Group's forecast of July 2022, expected SASE-related technologies to exceed US$13 billion by 2026.

Where the seams show. Vendors differ mostly in which half they came from, and it shows: networking vendors bolt security onto a WAN product, security vendors bolt connectivity onto an inspection cloud, and the seams are visible in whichever half was added second, in the policy model, the logging or the support boundary. Netskope's own retrospective of 2024 put it plainly from the vendor side: for years the industry could deliver pieces of what a SASE platform should look like, but most offerings were incomplete or poorly integrated, and many customers saw SASE as conceptual, even theoretical. The practical test is not the label but whether one policy, written once against an identity, governs a branch user on SD-WAN and the same user on a laptop at home, and whether the logs of both arrive in one place.

Two cautions. Single-vendor SASE gives one policy model and one support relationship, and it also gives a dependency whose outage is your outage and whose coverage is your ceiling: when the provider's PoPs or its control plane fail, both the network path and its security fail together, which is the reason to know how sites and users fall back and what they fall back to. The SSE entry records one such outage. And the term is marketing before it is architecture, drawn differently by every vendor, so an evaluation should ask which specific controls run where, in which PoPs, on which traffic, and how policy is expressed, not which acronym appears on the datasheet. MEF 117 and its revision are a ready-made checklist for that conversation, because they list what a provider and a subscriber must agree on.

Neighbours and dates. SSE is the security half and SD-WAN the networking half; ZTNA is the function that replaces the remote-access VPN (virtual private network) inside it; zero trust is the principle it is meant to apply; Zero Trust Edge is Forrester's near-synonym; and network as a service is the neighbouring idea of buying the WAN itself as a subscription. The dates worth keeping are 29 July and 30 August 2019 for the coinage, 2021 for SSE, October 2022 for MEF 117 and June 2025 for its revision, and 9 July 2025 for the rename of the single-vendor Magic Quadrant to SASE Platforms.

sse.def: Gartner's 2021 name for the security half of SASE (secure access service edge): secure web gateway, cloud access security broker (CASB) and zero trust network access delivered as one cloud service, with the networking left out.
sse.context: When SASE (secure access service edge) proved to be two purchases wearing one acronym, Gartner split it in 2021: security service edge (SSE) names the cloud-delivered security stack (secure web gateway, cloud access security broker, zero trust network access, with firewall as a service and data protection in practice), while the SD-WAN (software-defined wide area network) networking half stays a separate decision. The split let security teams modernize inspection and access control without waiting for a WAN refresh, and SSE promptly got its own Gartner Magic Quadrant. The three letters are heavily overloaded outside this field, and context is everything: in web development SSE means Server-Sent Events, and in processors it means Streaming SIMD Extensions, neither of which will secure anyone's SaaS (software as a service) traffic.
sse.depth:
Security service edge (SSE) is the name for delivering security controls from a cloud instead of from appliances in a building, and it exists because the assumptions appliances were built on stopped holding. When users work anywhere and applications live in someone else's data centre, backhauling traffic to an office to inspect it adds latency to protect a perimeter that no longer contains anything. Gartner's market definition is an offering that secures access to the web, to cloud services and to private applications regardless of where the user is, which device is used or where the application is hosted. Its list of mandatory features is more revealing than the definition: an identity-aware forward proxy with decryption, management and data planes that are primarily cloud-delivered, in-line protection of data in software as a service (SaaS) and private applications, out-of-band protection of SaaS data through application programming interfaces (APIs), access control for devices with and without an agent, and integration with external identity providers.

The term is a subdivision of another one. Gartner analysts coined secure access service edge (SASE) in 2019, in a report by Neil MacDonald, Lawrence Orans and Joe Skorupa titled The Future of Network Security Is in the Cloud, as the combination of cloud-delivered security services with wide area network (WAN) capabilities. In 2021 the firm defined the security subset as SSE; the arithmetic vendors repeat is that SSE plus a software-defined WAN (SD-WAN) equals SASE. One vendor glossary dates the introduction to 2022, which is the year of the first Magic Quadrant for the category. None of this is a standard: there is no Request for Comments (RFC) and no conformance test, only an analyst firm's market definition. The parent term drew that criticism from the start, when the analyst firms IDC and IHS Markit described SASE in November 2019 as neither a new market nor a new technology but an integration of existing ones under a single point of management.

The category usually bundles a secure web gateway (SWG) for outbound web traffic, zero trust network access (ZTNA) for private applications, a cloud access security broker (CASB) for SaaS, and often firewall as a service, data loss prevention (DLP), sandboxing and browser isolation. The argument for buying them together is a single policy model and a single enforcement point, instead of four consoles that disagree. ZTNA is the piece that replaces the remote access VPN (virtual private network): the user is never placed on the network and reaches one application at a time. The principle behind it is the one the United States National Institute of Standards and Technology (NIST) set out in Special Publication 800-207 in August 2020: no implicit trust is granted because of network location or ownership of the device, and authentication and authorization happen before a session to a resource is established.

Mechanically an SSE is a very large forward proxy with points of presence (PoPs) around the world, and most of the engineering is in getting traffic to it. The usual ways are an agent on the device, tunnels from offices with IPsec (Internet Protocol Security) or GRE (Generic Routing Encapsulation), and a proxy auto-config (PAC) file for machines that cannot run the agent. Netskope's explicit proxy, for example, receives browsers on port 8081, identifies the user through the identity provider, and requires the identity provider's own traffic to bypass the service. At the edge, traffic is decrypted once and passed through every engine in a single pass; that is the claim to test, since one vendor says of first-generation platforms that they route traffic through multiple disjointed inspection points. Decryption also means that the provider sees the content in clear, which is a matter of trust as much as of technology. What cannot be steered in line, such as data already stored in a SaaS application, is reached out of band through the application's API.

The market is tracked in a Gartner Magic Quadrant published every year since 2022. The fifth edition is dated 29 July 2026 and was written by John Watts, Thomas Lintemuth, Theo de Feligonde and Jonathan Forest; a companion Magic Quadrant for SASE Platforms appeared the day before. By the vendors' own announcements, Netskope has been a Leader in every edition, Zscaler from 2022 to 2026, and Palo Alto Networks, with Prisma Access, for four consecutive years; Cloudflare was named a Visionary in both 2026 reports and Fortinet a Challenger in the SASE Platforms report. A quadrant position describes an analyst's view of vision and execution, not how a given policy behaves on a given flow.

Two honest caveats belong with the enthusiasm. Concentrating inspection in one provider makes that provider a dependency on the critical path of everything, so their outage is your outage and their coverage is your coverage. On 18 November 2025 a fault in Cloudflare's network began at 11:20 UTC (Coordinated Universal Time); among the services affected was Access, its ZTNA product, where authentication failed for most users until a rollback began at 13:05, while sessions already established kept working. Nobody locked out that morning had a policy problem. And the acronyms are marketing before they are architecture: SSE, SASE and their neighbours are drawn differently by every vendor, so the useful question in an evaluation is which specific controls run where, not which three letters appear on the datasheet.

The letters have two older owners. In web development SSE is Server-Sent Events, section 9.2 of the HTML (HyperText Markup Language) Living Standard: a page creates an EventSource object and the server pushes messages to it over HTTP (Hypertext Transfer Protocol) with the text/event-stream media type. In processors SSE is Intel's Streaming SIMD (single instruction, multiple data) Extensions, introduced in the Pentium III family to extend the earlier MMX model to single-precision floating point in 128-bit registers, and followed by SSE2 in the Pentium 4 and Xeon. A log line, a job advertisement or a search result that says SSE can mean any of the three, and only the security one has a proxy in it.

strata.def: Palo Alto Networks' name for its founding network-security family: the next-generation firewalls and everything that manages and subscribes to them.
strata.context: When Palo Alto Networks regrouped its portfolio into three platform brands in 2019, Strata became the home of the original business: PA-Series hardware firewalls, VM-Series virtual and CN-Series container firewalls, Panorama management, and the subscription services layered on top (Threat Prevention, URL Filtering, WildFire, DNS Security, and kin). The name signals the layered, on-path enforcement model the company was built on, in contrast to its two younger siblings: Prisma for cloud-delivered security and Cortex for security operations. In vendor conversations, 'Strata' is simply shorthand for the firewall estate.

prisma.def: Palo Alto Networks' cloud-security family, announced in May 2019: securing cloud workloads, cloud access, and the WAN that reaches them.
prisma.context: Prisma bundles the company's cloud bets under one brand: Prisma Cloud, the code-to-cloud platform assembled from acquisitions such as RedLock, Twistlock, and PureSec; Prisma Access, the cloud-delivered SASE (secure access service edge)/SSE service; and Prisma SD-WAN (software-defined wide area network), the former CloudGenix, acquired in 2020. Announced in May 2019, three months after Cortex, it completed the three-family structure alongside Strata. The name earns a glossary entry because it collides constantly outside this context: Prisma is also a popular open-source TypeScript ORM, and neither product will do the other's job.

cortex.def: Palo Alto Networks' security-operations family, announced in February 2019: detection, response, and automation for the SOC (security operations centre).
cortex.context: Cortex arrived in February 2019 as an AI-based security platform together with Cortex XDR (extended detection and response), the product that pushed 'XDR' into the industry vocabulary as detection and response across endpoint, network, and cloud telemetry rather than endpoint alone. The family grew by acquisition and iteration: Cortex XSOAR from Demisto (2019) for orchestration and automation, Cortex Xpanse from Expanse (2020) for attack-surface management, and Cortex XSIAM (2022) as the AI-driven SOC platform folding those capabilities together. In practice the name marks the operations side of the house, where Strata enforces and Prisma covers the cloud.

vlan.def: A virtual local area network (VLAN): a logical layer 2 broadcast domain carved out of a physical switched network, isolating traffic without separate hardware.
vlan.context: Defined by IEEE (Institute of Electrical and Electronics Engineers) 802.1Q, which marks each frame on a trunk with a 4-octet tag carrying a 12-bit virtual local area network (VLAN) identifier; with the values 0 and 4095 set aside, that leaves 4094 usable VLANs. Access ports carry one VLAN untagged, trunks carry many tagged, and traffic between VLANs has to cross a router or firewall, which is what makes the VLAN boundary the natural place to enforce policy.
vlan.depth:
A virtual local area network (VLAN) is a broadcast domain defined in the configuration of switches rather than in their cabling. Ports and frames are assigned a VLAN identifier, and a VLAN-aware bridge learns addresses, forwards and floods separately within each VLAN, so hosts in different VLANs cannot exchange frames at layer 2 at all and must go through a router or firewall. F5's documentation for BIG-IP gives the working definition: a logical subset of hosts on a local area network (LAN) that operate in the same IP (Internet Protocol) address space, and in practice one VLAN usually carries one IP subnet. The standard is IEEE (Institute of Electrical and Electronics Engineers) 802.1Q, first issued as 802.1Q-1998, Virtual Bridged Local Area Networks, published in 1999, and current as IEEE 802.1Q-2022, Bridges and Bridged Networks, approved in September 2022.

On a link that carries several VLANs, every frame carries a 4-octet tag inserted after the source address. It begins with a 16-bit Tag Protocol Identifier (TPID), the EtherType 0x8100 for a customer VLAN tag, followed by 3 bits of priority with values 0 to 7, 1 bit that 802.1Q has used since 2011 as the Drop Eligible Indicator (DEI), formerly the Canonical Format Indicator (CFI), and a 12-bit VLAN identifier (VID). Twelve bits give 4,096 values, of which 1 to 4094 name VLANs: VID 0 marks a frame that carries only a priority, and the top value, 4095, is not used for a VLAN, which is why Request for Comments (RFC) 3580 and BIG-IP's documentation alike bound a VLAN number to 1 through 4094. The tag lengthens the largest Ethernet frame by 4 octets, a change IEEE 802.3ac-1998 made room for.

Ports come in two kinds. An access port belongs to one VLAN and carries its frames untagged, so the end device never sees a tag; a trunk carries many VLANs, each frame tagged with its VID, and joins switches to each other, to routers, hypervisors and appliances. A trunk may also carry one VLAN untagged, its native VLAN, and both ends must agree on which one that is, just as they must agree on every tag: BIG-IP's documentation says the tag of a VLAN on a BIG-IP interface must match the tag on the connected switch port, and an interface joins several VLANs as a tagged interface. On Linux, ip link add link eth0 name eth0.10 type vlan id 10 creates a tagged subinterface, and the protocol option selects 802.1Q or 802.1ad tagging.

Two extensions stretch the model. Service providers stack tags: an outer service tag, EtherType 0x88A8, which the IANA (Internet Assigned Numbers Authority) registry lists under IEEE 802.1Q as the S-Tag and Linux calls 802.1ad, carries a customer's own 802.1Q-tagged frames across the provider network. Membership can also follow the user instead of the port: after IEEE 802.1X authentication, a RADIUS (Remote Authentication Dial-In User Service) server returns Tunnel-Type 13 (VLAN), Tunnel-Medium-Type 802 and the VLAN number as Tunnel-Private-Group-ID, encoded as a string, as RFC 3580 (September 2003) describes, and the switch places the port in that VLAN.

Four thousand VLANs is a generous ceiling for a campus and a tight one for a data centre. RFC 7348 (August 2014), which defines Virtual eXtensible Local Area Network (VXLAN), opens with exactly that argument: the 12-bit VLAN ID served data centres that needed fewer than 4094 VLANs, but virtualization and multi-tenancy put the limit under pressure, and spanning tree led many operators to use even fewer. VXLAN carries Ethernet frames inside outer IP and UDP (User Datagram Protocol) headers and names each segment with a 24-bit VXLAN Network Identifier, allowing up to 16 million segments.

A VLAN is a segmentation tool, not a security control by itself. It separates broadcast domains and forces traffic between segments through a routed boundary where policy can be enforced, but only as long as the switches hold the line, and the classic VLAN hopping methods show where they fail. In switch spoofing, a port left in a dynamic trunking mode lets an attacker negotiate a trunk with the Dynamic Trunking Protocol (DTP) and see every VLAN. In double tagging, an attacker on a trunk's native VLAN sends a frame with two tags; the first switch strips the outer one, and the next delivers the frame into the VLAN named by the inner tag, a one-way attack because replies cannot return the same way. The defences are configuration: access ports set statically, DTP disabled, a native VLAN that no user occupies, and unused ports shut down. In September 2022 the CERT Coordination Center's Vulnerability Note VU#855201, credited to Etienne Champetier, showed that frames with stacked VLAN 0 headers and IEEE 802.2 Logical Link Control (LLC) and Sub-Network Access Protocol (SNAP) headers could slip past layer 2 inspections such as IP version 6 (IPv6) Router Advertisement Guard and dynamic ARP (Address Resolution Protocol) inspection, under the identifiers CVE-2021-27853, CVE-2021-27854, CVE-2021-27861 and CVE-2021-27862.

Most VLAN faults are mismatches. A VID allowed on one end of a trunk and not the other, a native VLAN that differs between the two ends, or an access port in the wrong VLAN all produce the same symptom, hosts that cannot reach their gateway, and a capture on a tagged interface, or one filtered with an expression such as vlan 17, shows whether frames carry the tag that was expected. The numbers worth keeping: a 4-octet tag; TPID 0x8100, or 0x88A8 for the service tag; 3 bits of priority; 12 bits of VID; VLANs 1 to 4094; and 16 million VXLAN segments.

trunk-port.def: A switch port that carries several virtual local area networks (VLANs) at once, each frame tagged with its VLAN ID so the far end can sort them back out.
trunk-port.context: The opposite of an access port, which belongs to exactly one virtual local area network (VLAN) and carries untagged frames. On a trunk every VLAN but one, the native VLAN, travels with a four-byte IEEE (Institute of Electrical and Electronics Engineers) 802.1Q tag, so one cable between two switches, or between a switch and a server, firewall or hypervisor, can carry hundreds of separate layer 2 networks. The word itself is vendor language: on F5 BIG-IP a trunk is a link aggregation group, not a tagged port.
trunk-port.depth:
What the standard calls it. IEEE (Institute of Electrical and Electronics Engineers) 802.1Q never needed the word trunk. It describes every bridge port with the same few settings, which its YANG (Yet Another Next Generation) data model spells out: for each VLAN (virtual local area network) ID, the set of ports that are members of that VLAN and the subset that send it untagged; for each port, a PVID (port VLAN ID), the VLAN given to untagged frames that arrive, 1 by default; the acceptable frame types, admit all frames (the default), admit only VLAN-tagged frames, or admit only untagged and priority-tagged frames; and ingress filtering, off by default, which drops frames for VLANs the port is not a member of. In that model a trunk port is simply a port that belongs to many VLANs and is in the untagged set of at most one, and an access port is a member of a single VLAN, untagged, with its PVID set to it. Reading a vendor's configuration through those four settings is the quickest way to compare two platforms that use different words for the same thing. The standard itself is 802.1Q-2022, available at no cost through the IEEE GET Program.

On the wire. The tag is four bytes inserted after the source address. Its first two bytes are the Tag Protocol Identifier (TPID) 0x8100, which IANA (Internet Assigned Numbers Authority) lists as the Customer VLAN Tag, formerly the Q-Tag and originally assigned to Wellfleet; then come a 3-bit priority (the 802.1p user priority), a 1-bit flag that Cisco's frame-format note calls the Canonical Format Indicator, and the 12-bit VLAN identifier (VID). A tagged Ethernet frame can therefore reach 1,522 bytes, four more than the untagged maximum, which is why equipment that never expected tags can count tagged full-size frames as oversized (the baby-giant entry covers the consequences). The native VLAN is the exception: Cisco states plainly that 802.1Q does not tag frames on the native VLAN. Before 802.1Q, Cisco trunks used Inter-Switch Link (ISL), a proprietary scheme that wrapped the whole original frame in 30 bytes of encapsulation instead of inserting a tag; a current Catalyst 9300 offers 802.1Q on every Ethernet interface.

On real equipment. On a Cisco Catalyst 9300 running IOS XE 17.12 a port becomes a trunk with switchport mode trunk, and the Dynamic Trunking Protocol (DTP) can also negotiate one: the default mode of every Ethernet interface is dynamic auto, which becomes a trunk if the neighbour is set to trunk or desirable, and switchport nonegotiate stops the port sending DTP frames at all. A new trunk carries all VLANs from 1 to 4094 and uses VLAN 1 as native; VLAN 1 can be removed from a trunk while management traffic continues to flow, and VTP (VLAN Trunking Protocol) pruning applies by default to VLANs 2 to 1001, never to the extended range from 1006. Juniper's switches start every port in access mode; their trunk interfaces usually accept only tagged packets, recognize untagged control frames such as LACP (Link Aggregation Control Protocol) and LLDP (Link Layer Discovery Protocol), and accept untagged data only when a native VLAN is configured. On Linux a VLAN-aware bridge describes a trunk with bridge vlan add, where pvid marks the VLAN that untagged arrivals join and untagged marks the VLAN sent without a tag; a host or a firewall terminates a trunk instead with VLAN subinterfaces, created by ip link add link eth0 name eth0.100 type vlan id 100, with the protocol set to 802.1Q or, for an outer service tag, 802.1ad. And on F5 BIG-IP the word trunk means a group of interfaces that acts as one interface for link aggregation, so a BIG-IP trunk may itself carry tagged VLANs: aggregated and trunked in Cisco's sense at the same time.

What goes wrong. The two ends must agree on three things: which VLANs are allowed, which one is native, and whether the link is a trunk at all. Cisco warns that a native VLAN that differs between the two ends of an 802.1Q trunk might cause spanning-tree loops; even without a loop, untagged frames from one VLAN arrive in another. A VLAN allowed at one end and not the other simply disappears across that link while every other VLAN works, which makes the fault look like a routing or server problem. A port left in dynamic auto turns into a trunk for any neighbour that asks for one, which is fine between switches and dangerous on a port facing a desk. And a capture taken on a host often shows no tags at all: the Wireshark project notes that drivers commonly strip the tag before the capture library sees the frame, and recommends a mirror port feeding a capture interface that is not itself a VLAN member when the tags matter.

Hardening. Cisco's campus design guide describes the double-tagging attack, in which an attacker on the native VLAN sends a frame with two 802.1Q tags so that the first switch strips the outer one and the second delivers the frame into the VLAN of the inner one; the attack is one-way and requires knowing the native VLAN. Its mitigations are the standard checklist for every trunk port: set the native VLAN to an unused ID or tag it, disable trunking on ports connected to hosts, hard-set trunks on with negotiation off, and prune every VLAN the far end does not need. The trunk and native-vlan entries carry the detail.

Numbers worth remembering: a 4-byte tag, TPID 0x8100, a 12-bit VID with VLANs 1 to 4094 usable on a Catalyst trunk, 1,522-byte tagged frames, native VLAN 1 and PVID 1 by default, dynamic auto as the Catalyst's default port mode, and 30 bytes for the ISL encapsulation that 802.1Q replaced.

spanning-tree.def: The Layer 2 protocol that blocks redundant switch links to prevent loops, keeping exactly one active path between any two points.
spanning-tree.context: Prevents switching loops by computing a loop-free tree across a redundant mesh and blocking the links outside it. Ethernet has no time-to-live field, so a loop is fatal rather than merely inefficient. Radia Perlman's 1985 algorithm became IEEE (Institute of Electrical and Electronics Engineers) 802.1D, now part of IEEE 802.1Q; its rapid version, RSTP (Rapid Spanning Tree Protocol), and its multiple-instance version, MSTP (Multiple Spanning Tree Protocol), keep the same idea and converge faster or carry several trees.
spanning-tree.depth:
Why it exists. A switched network needs redundant links so that one failure does not isolate anything, and Ethernet cannot survive them. As the specification of TRILL (Transparent Interconnection of Lots of Links), RFC (Request for Comments) 6325, puts it, the Ethernet header contains no hop count or time to live (TTL) field, which is dangerous whenever a loop forms: a frame circulates indefinitely, and a broadcast multiplies on every pass until the network is a solid wall of copies. The answer came from Radia Perlman at Digital Equipment Corporation (DEC). Her manager asked for something that could simply be plugged together, with no configuration, and would still settle on a single loop-free topology, using memory that did not grow with the network. In her account to Network World he set the puzzle on a Friday afternoon; she had the solution that night, wrote it up in about 25 pages on the Monday and Tuesday, and spent the rest of the week on a poem, Algorhyme, that opens her 1985 conference paper and that engineers still recite. She has also said that she always considered bridging a kludge, Ethernet being meant for talking to neighbours and routing being layer 3's job.

How it works. Every bridge has an identifier: a configurable priority followed by its MAC (media access control) address. On a Cisco Catalyst 9300 the priority occupies the two most significant bytes, defaults to 32768 and carries the VLAN (virtual local area network) number as an extended system ID, and when priorities tie the lowest MAC address wins, which with factory defaults often hands the root to the oldest switch in the building. Perlman described the comparison as three fields read as one multi-precision number, the best root ID heard, the cost to reach it and the sender's own ID, smaller being better, so every bridge converges on the lowest ID as root while storing only one message, about 50 bytes, per port. Each other bridge then picks the port with the lowest cost to the root as its root port, one bridge on each segment owns the designated port, and every remaining port blocks. The messages are bridge protocol data units (BPDUs), sent to the bridge group address 01-80-C2-00-00-00 every hello time, 2 seconds by default. Classic 802.1D moves a port through blocking, listening, learning and forwarding, with a maximum age of 20 seconds and a forward delay of 15, so a topology change costs from about 30 to 50 seconds. That was acceptable when the alternative was a broadcast storm and unacceptable by the time anyone ran voice over it.

RSTP. The rapid version, 802.1w, began as a supplement to 802.1D-1998 meant to keep spanning tree's plug-and-play behaviour while discarding the long reconfiguration time, and it was incorporated into 802.1D-2004, approved on 9 February 2004. It collapses the port states to discarding, learning and forwarding, splits the old blocking role into alternate (another path to the root, ready to take over) and backup (a second port on the same segment), and replaces timers with a proposal and agreement handshake between neighbours, which in Cisco's words does not rely on any timers. Every bridge sends BPDUs at each hello whether or not it hears the root, and a neighbour is considered lost after three missed BPDUs, about 6 seconds. The handshake needs point-to-point links, and a full-duplex port is assumed to be one; edge ports, which correspond to Cisco's PortFast, go straight to forwarding and cause no topology change when they flap. When a non-edge port does move to forwarding, the change is propagated and bridges flush the MAC addresses they learned on the affected ports. An RSTP port facing an old 802.1D bridge falls back to 802.1D on that port.

MSTP and the per-VLAN variants. One tree for the whole network means every VLAN follows the same path and the blocked links carry nothing. 802.1s, a supplement to 802.1Q folded into its 2005 revision, lets VLAN bridges run multiple spanning trees, mapping groups of VLANs to a small number of instances so that different VLANs use different physical paths and the blocked links start earning their keep. Switches belong to the same multiple spanning tree (MST) region only when they share a 32-byte region name, a two-byte revision number and the same 4096-entry VLAN-to-instance table, and the internal spanning tree, instance 0, makes the whole region look like a single bridge from outside. Cisco reached the same need earlier and differently: Per-VLAN Spanning Tree (PVST) ran one tree per VLAN over its own Inter-Switch Link (ISL) trunks, PVST+ did the same over 802.1Q, and Rapid PVST+ added RSTP's behaviour and is the default mode on the Catalyst 9300, which supports up to 300 such instances, or 65 in MST mode. Per-VLAN trees are simple to reason about and expensive at scale; Cisco's own MST guide calls 1,000 instances for two logical topologies a waste of CPU (central processing unit) cycles on every switch, and a thousand VLANs means a thousand state machines. Since 802.1Q-2014, approved on 3 November 2014 and superseding 802.1D-2004, spanning tree, RSTP and MSTP all live in 802.1Q.

The guards tell you where it hurts. PortFast exists because a printer does not need thirty seconds of listening and learning, and Cisco limits it to ports with a single end station, warning that on a port leading to a switch or hub it can stop spanning tree from detecting a loop and so cause broadcast storms. BPDU guard exists because PortFast on a port somebody later plugs a switch into is how an afternoon is lost: a BPDU arriving there puts the port in the error-disabled state. BPDU filtering, Cisco notes, is the same as disabling spanning tree on the interface. Root guard blocks a port, in a root-inconsistent state, when a switch beyond it would become root, because a small switch under a desk should not win an election it technically qualifies for. Loop guard keeps alternate and root ports from becoming designated after a unidirectional link failure, when a blocked port stops hearing the BPDUs that were keeping it blocked, which is the failure that turns redundancy into an outage. Every one of these is a patch over the same fact: the protocol trusts what it hears, and a network is full of things that can stop being heard.

The successors. Perlman herself went on to co-author TRILL, published as RFC 6325 in July 2011, whose RBridges apply link-state routing to bridging; its introduction lists what it was replacing: blocked ports that concentrate traffic, forwarding along whatever path the tree leaves rather than the shortest, no hop count, and VLANs that can partition when the tree reconfigures. The IEEE answer, Shortest Path Bridging (802.1aq), was approved on 29 March 2012 and folded into 802.1Q-2014. Neither displaced spanning tree in the enterprise, because a protocol that has run in every switch for three decades is not replaced by a better one, only by a different architecture, which is what a modern leaf-and-spine fabric with routing to the host actually is. Spanning tree did not lose. It was outlived, and it is still switched on by default, as Rapid PVST+ on a Catalyst 9300 for instance, as the safety net under whatever replaced it.

Numbers worth remembering: hello 2 seconds, maximum age 20, forward delay 15, 30 to 50 seconds for classic convergence, three missed hellos (about 6 seconds) for RSTP, default priority 32768, BPDUs to 01-80-C2-00-00-00, and 1985 for the paper.

arp.def: Address Resolution Protocol (ARP), RFC (Request for Comments) 826, is how an IPv4 (Internet Protocol version 4) host finds the hardware address, normally the Ethernet MAC (media access control) address, behind a neighbour's IP address on the same link: it broadcasts a request naming the IP address and caches the reply.
arp.context: Every IPv4 (Internet Protocol version 4) packet to a neighbour on an Ethernet or Wi-Fi segment, including every packet sent through the default gateway, first needs the next hop's MAC (media access control) address, and Address Resolution Protocol (ARP) supplies it on demand from a short-lived cache. It has no authentication: any host can answer, and an unsolicited packet updates an existing entry, which is what makes ARP spoofing on a LAN (local area network) so easy. IPv6 replaced it with Neighbor Discovery.
arp.depth:
What it is, and what it is not. Address Resolution Protocol (ARP) maps a protocol address to a hardware address on one link. David C. Plummer published it as Request for Comments (RFC) 826 in November 1982 for the DEC, Intel and Xerox 10 Mbit/s Ethernet, generalized for other media, because the addresses of the protocols sharing that cable (16 bits for CHAOS, 32 for the DoD Internet, 8 for Xerox PUP) bore no relation to the 48-bit Ethernet address a frame needs. In practice it resolves IPv4 (Internet Protocol version 4) next hops to MAC (media access control) addresses. It works only on the local segment: to reach a remote host, a sender resolves its gateway's address, never the remote host's. It is not used by IPv6, whose Neighbor Discovery (RFC 4861, September 2007) corresponds to ARP, ICMP (Internet Control Message Protocol) Router Discovery and ICMP Redirect combined.

The packet. An ARP message travels directly in an Ethernet frame with EtherType 0x0806, as the IANA (Internet Assigned Numbers Authority) registry of IEEE (Institute of Electrical and Electronics Engineers) 802 numbers records. The fields are hardware type (16 bits), protocol type (16), hardware address length (8), protocol address length (8), opcode (16), then the sender's hardware and protocol addresses and the target's hardware and protocol addresses. For Ethernet and IPv4 the values are hardware type 1, protocol type 0x0800, lengths 6 and 4, which makes the ARP payload 28 bytes. IANA's ARP registry lists opcode 1 as REQUEST and 2 as REPLY, alongside 3 and 4 for Reverse ARP (RFC 903, June 1984, EtherType 0x8035) and 8 and 9 for Inverse ARP. A request is broadcast with the target hardware address left unset, since that is the unknown; the owner swaps the fields, fills in its own addresses and sends the reply straight back to the requester's hardware address.

How a receiver updates its table. RFC 826 spells out the reception order, and it explains most of ARP's behaviour. If the sender's protocol address is already in the receiver's table, its hardware address is updated from the packet, and only then does the receiver check whether it is the target; a new entry is added only if it is. The opcode is looked at last, on the assumption that if A talks to B, B will soon talk to A, and a newer hardware address always supersedes an older one. Plummer also rejected periodic broadcasting: 100 workstations announcing themselves every 10 minutes would already mean a packet every 6 seconds, mostly into tables that would never use it. ARP therefore resolves on demand, and RFC 826 lets the sender drop the packet that triggered the request.

Rules added later. RFC 1122 (October 1989) made the cache safer and the first packet less likely to be lost. An implementation must flush out-of-date entries, with a timeout that should be configurable; it must prevent ARP flooding, with a recommended maximum of 1 request per second per destination; and it should keep at least the latest packet queued for an unresolved address and send it once the address resolves, because otherwise the first packet of every exchange is lost. The RFC adds that the spread of proxy ARP had made cache invalidation necessary, since entries go wrong more often when a gateway answers for other hosts. Proxy ARP itself is documented in RFC 1027 (October 1987), written at the University of Texas at Austin, where a gateway answered ARP for hosts on other subnets so that more than a hundred hosts across ten buildings could be split into subnets without being reconfigured.

The cache on a real host. Linux keeps ARP in its neighbour table, which ip neigh shows with a Neighbour Unreachability Detection state per entry: reachable, stale (valid but suspicious), delay, probe, incomplete (not yet resolved), failed (probes exhausted) or permanent. The arp(7) manual (man-pages 6.19) gives the defaults: an entry is valid for a random time between half and one and a half times base_reachable_time, 30 seconds, and is extended by positive feedback such as a TCP (Transmission Control Protocol) acknowledgement; a stale entry waits delay_first_probe_time, 5 seconds, then gets ucast_solicit unicast probes, 3, before a new broadcast; and gc_thresh3, 1,024 by default, is the hard maximum number of entries, a limit a large flat subnet or a busy router can hit.

Gratuitous ARP and conflict detection. RFC 5227 (July 2008), by Stuart Cheshire, updates RFC 826 with IPv4 Address Conflict Detection and names two special requests. An ARP Probe is broadcast with an all-zero sender IP address, so that no cache is polluted if the address turns out to be taken, and the probed address as target. An ARP Announcement has the same address as both sender and target, the gratuitous ARP of common usage, and tells every listener to update its table. The constants are fixed: wait up to 1 second, send 3 probes, then 2 announcements 2 seconds apart, and defend an address no more than once every 10 seconds. Failover depends on the announcement: an F5 BIG-IP that becomes active sends gratuitous ARPs to claim its addresses, and F5 bug 932825 records a rare case, fixed in 15.1.1 and 16.1.0, in which other traffic left first and destabilized IPsec tunnels after failover.

No authentication, by design. Nothing in an ARP packet proves who sent it, and the update rule means any packet naming an address already in a table rewrites that entry. RFC 5227's own security section puts it bluntly: it is easy for a host to answer all ARP requests with its own hardware address and so claim every address on the network. This is ARP spoofing, or cache poisoning: an attacker claims the gateway's IP address, traffic flows through it, and nothing appears broken. The fix has to live where frames are switched. Cisco's Dynamic ARP Inspection (DAI) intercepts ARP on untrusted ports and drops packets whose IP-to-MAC binding does not match the DHCP (Dynamic Host Configuration Protocol) snooping binding database; it is enabled per VLAN (virtual local area network) with ip arp inspection vlan, uplinks are marked with ip arp inspection trust, untrusted interfaces are limited to 15 ARP packets per second by default, statically addressed hosts need an ARP access list or a static binding, and show ip arp inspection reports the drops.

Reading the table. The ARP table is the quickest way to split a layer 2 fault from a layer 3 one. An incomplete or failed entry means no one answered: the target is down, in another VLAN, or not on that segment at all. One MAC address behind many IP addresses is normal for a router or a proxy-ARP gateway, and suspicious anywhere else. A gateway whose MAC address changes is either a failover, which should coincide with gratuitous ARPs from the new active unit, or an attack. And an entry that resolves while traffic still fails points up the stack, to routing, filtering or the application, because ARP has done its part.

dhcp.def: Dynamic Host Configuration Protocol (DHCP) gives an IPv4 (Internet Protocol version 4) host its address and settings, such as subnet mask, router and DNS (Domain Name System) servers, usually on a time-limited lease.
dhcp.context: Request for Comments (RFC) 2131 states its aim plainly: clients should require no manual configuration. The first lease takes four messages, known as DORA (Discover, Offer, Request, Acknowledgement) from Microsoft's guides, and a Windows client that gets no valid address is likely to fall back to an APIPA (Automatic Private IP Addressing) address in 169.254.0.0/16.
dhcp.depth:
Where it came from. Dynamic Host Configuration Protocol (DHCP) grew out of the Bootstrap Protocol (BOOTP), published as Request for Comments (RFC) 951 in September 1985 by Bill Croft of Stanford and John Gilmore of Sun, which reserved UDP (User Datagram Protocol) port 67 for the server and 68 for the client. Ralph Droms published the first DHCP specification as RFC 1531 in October 1993; the current text is RFC 2131 (March 1997), with the options in RFC 2132. DHCP kept the BOOTP message format and relay behaviour on purpose, so the two interoperate, and every DHCP options field still begins with BOOTP's magic cookie, 99.130.83.99. RFC 2131 defines three allocations: automatic (a permanent address), manual (an administrator's choice, merely delivered by DHCP) and dynamic, a lease for a limited time and the only kind that lets addresses be reused. It is an IPv4 protocol: DHCPv6 is a separate protocol, RFC 8415 (November 2018), on UDP 546 for clients and 547 for servers and relays, reached through the multicast address ff02::1:2.

The exchange. The message type travels in option 53: DHCPDISCOVER (1), DHCPOFFER (2), DHCPREQUEST (3), DHCPDECLINE (4), DHCPACK (5), DHCPNAK (6), DHCPRELEASE (7) and DHCPINFORM (8). A client with no address broadcasts with source 0.0.0.0. Where the server sends its answer depends on three fields: to the relay in giaddr if that is set, to ciaddr if the client already has an address, to the broadcast address if the client set the broadcast bit, and otherwise as a unicast to the client's hardware address and the offered address. Before handing out a reused address, a server should probe it, for example with an ICMP (Internet Control Message Protocol) echo; the client should probe the address it receives, for example with ARP (Address Resolution Protocol), and must send DHCPDECLINE if it is already in use. Microsoft's troubleshooting guidance reads a capture the same way: if DISCOVER, OFFER, REQUEST and ACK all appear, the exchange worked.

The options. RFC 2132 numbers the settings: 1 subnet mask, 3 router, 6 domain name servers, 43 vendor-specific information, 50 requested address, 51 lease time, 54 server identifier, 55 parameter request list, 58 and 59 the renewal (T1) and rebinding (T2) times, 60 vendor class identifier and 61 client identifier; codes 128 to 254 are left for site-specific use. Later RFCs kept adding. RFC 3442 (December 2002) defined option 121, classless static routes, and ruled that a client receiving both option 121 and the router option must ignore the router option, which surprises anyone who configured only a default gateway and finds it ignored.

The lease clock. Lease times are relative seconds, so client and server need no synchronized clocks. At T1, by default half the lease, the client enters RENEWING and unicasts a DHCPREQUEST to the server that issued the address; at T2, by default 87.5 per cent, it enters REBINDING and broadcasts to any server; if the lease expires first, it must stop using the address. RFC 2131 asks for some random fuzz around T1 and T2 so that clients do not all renew at once. A client that cannot reach its server keeps working until expiry, which is why a server outage shorter than half the lease often goes unnoticed, and why a long outage shows up all at once.

Relays. A broadcast does not cross a router, so a relay agent on the client's subnet forwards it to configured servers, writing the address of the receiving interface into giaddr; the server uses that address to choose the pool and sends its reply back to the relay. Microsoft's guides call relay agents IP Helpers. RFC 3046 (January 2001), written for public access networks behind cable modems, added option 82, Relay Agent Information: the relay inserts it, the server echoes it verbatim, and the relay strips it before the reply reaches the client. Its sub-options, Agent Circuit ID (1) and Agent Remote ID (2), tell the server which port and which subscriber the request came from, information the server may use for its address assignment policy.

Security. RFC 2131 is frank: DHCP in its current form is quite insecure. Unauthorized servers are easy to set up and can hand out wrong or duplicate addresses, spoofed routers and spoofed name servers, after which an attacker can go further; a malicious client can claim every address in a dynamic pool and starve the legitimate ones. RFC 3118 (June 2001) defined an authentication option, but the everyday defence is on the switch. As Cisco's documentation notes, enabling DHCP snooping on a switch makes every interface untrusted until an uplink is explicitly trusted, and the binding database that snooping maintains is the same one Dynamic ARP Inspection validates ARP packets against.

The client is attack surface too. CVE (Common Vulnerabilities and Exposures) 2018-1111, published on 17 May 2018, was a command injection in the NetworkManager integration script of the DHCP client in Red Hat Enterprise Linux 6 and 7 and Fedora 28: a malicious DHCP server, or anyone able to spoof one on the local network, could run commands as root (CVSS 7.5). CVE-2024-3661, published on 6 May 2024 and known as TunnelVision, turned option 121 against virtual private networks (VPNs): routes pushed by DHCP can make traffic that a VPN expected to protect leave over the physical interface, where an attacker on the same network can read, disrupt or possibly modify it (CVSS 7.6). Both are reminders that every option a client accepts is input from whoever answered first.

Troubleshooting. Microsoft's checklist covers each hop of the path: on the server, that the DHCP Server service is running and that the scope for the client's subnet still has leases; on the network, that routers or VLAN (virtual local area network) switches have relay agents configured; on the client, that no firewall blocks UDP 67 and 68. A Windows client that gets no valid address is likely to configure an APIPA (Automatic Private IP Addressing) address, which is the IPv4 link-local range of RFC 3927 (May 2005), 169.254/16, valid only on the directly connected link. An address in that range is therefore a symptom, not a configuration: the client asked and nobody answered, so the next step is a capture to see which of the four messages is missing.

ospf.def: Open Shortest Path First (OSPF) is the Internet Engineering Task Force's (IETF) link-state interior routing protocol: every router in an area holds the same map of routers, links and costs, and computes its own shortest-path tree from it with Dijkstra's algorithm.
ospf.context: Open Shortest Path First (OSPF) runs directly over IP (Internet Protocol) as protocol 89. Routers find neighbours with Hello packets, synchronize a link-state database by flooding link-state advertisements (LSAs), and each runs the shortest-path-first calculation on that shared map, so all of them reach consistent answers after a change. Areas bound the flooding, with area 0 as the backbone through which all inter-area traffic passes. OSPFv2 (RFC 2328, Request for Comments) carries IPv4; OSPFv3 (RFC 5340) carries IPv6.
ospf.depth:
What it is. Open Shortest Path First (OSPF) is a link-state interior gateway protocol (IGP) for routing inside one autonomous system. Version 2, for IPv4, is Request for Comments (RFC) 2328 (April 1998, Internet Standard 54), by John Moy. It runs directly over IP (Internet Protocol) as protocol 89, with no TCP (Transmission Control Protocol) or UDP (User Datagram Protocol) underneath. Routers do not trade routes, as distance-vector protocols do: each describes its own links in link-state advertisements (LSAs), flooding gives every router in an area an identical database, and each router runs Dijkstra's algorithm over that database to build a shortest-path tree with itself as the root. Identical inputs give consistent answers, which is what makes OSPF's convergence predictable: after a change, every router recomputes from the same map.

Packets and neighbours. RFC 2328 defines five packet types: Hello (1), Database Description (2), Link State Request (3), Link State Update (4) and Link State Acknowledgment (5). Hellos go to AllSPFRouters, 224.0.0.5, and the designated routers also listen on AllDRouters, 224.0.0.6; both are sent with an IP time to live (TTL) of 1 because they must never be forwarded. The RFC's sample HelloInterval for a local area network is 10 seconds and RouterDeadInterval should be a multiple of it (say four), and both must match on every router of a common network, as must the area and the authentication. A neighbour moves through Down, Attempt, Init, 2-Way, ExStart, Exchange, Loading and Full. On broadcast and NBMA (non-broadcast multi-access) networks a Designated Router (DR) and a Backup (BDR) are elected by Router Priority, priority 0 being ineligible, and every other router becomes adjacent only to those two; a router that comes up accepts an existing DR whatever its own priority, so the DR is stable rather than predictable.

The MTU (maximum transmission unit) trap. Database Description packets carry the sender's Interface MTU, and if it indicates a datagram larger than the receiver can accept without fragmentation, the packet is rejected. The neighbours then sit in ExStart or Exchange. Cisco's technote describes the Database Description packets being retransmitted until the adjacency is torn down with Too many retransmissions, and calls the interface command ip ospf mtu-ignore a check-disabler, not a fix: it does not change the size of real packets, so the proper solution is the correct MTU on both ends. Fortinet's troubleshooting tip gives the FortiGate equivalents, "get router info ospf neighbor" and "get router info ospf interface" to see the state and MTU, and set mtu-ignore enable under config ospf-interface, with the same warning that it may not help when OSPF packets themselves exceed the receiver's MTU.

LSAs and areas. Router-LSAs (type 1) are originated by every router, network-LSAs (2) by the DR of a transit network, summary-LSAs (3 for IP networks, 4 for autonomous system (AS) boundary routers) by area border routers, and AS-external-LSAs (5) by AS boundary routers. The backbone is area 0, usually written 0.0.0.0; it contains every area border router, carries all inter-area routing, and must be contiguous, if necessary through virtual links that the protocol treats as unnumbered point-to-point backbone links. A stub area receives no AS-external-LSAs and reaches external destinations through a default route only, which shrinks its database; the not-so-stubby area of RFC 3101 (January 2003, obsoleting RFC 1587) adds the ability to import external routes in a limited way, as type-7 LSAs. Each LSA is refreshed every 30 minutes (LSRefreshTime), flushed at 1 hour (MaxAge), and originated no more often than every 5 seconds (MinLSInterval).

Cost. RFC 2328 leaves the metric to the operator: an interface output cost, greater than zero, carried in a 16-bit field of the router-LSA, so up to 65,535. Implementations derive a default from bandwidth. Extreme Networks' SLX-OS reference states it plainly: cost is the reference bandwidth divided by the egress interface bandwidth, the default reference is 100 Mbps, the configurable range is 1 to 4,294,967 Mbps, and a result below 1 is rounded up to 1. With the default, every link of 100 Mbps or faster costs 1, and 1, 10 and 100 Gbit/s paths tie.
