The fix is a higher reference bandwidth (auto-cost reference-bandwidth on Cisco-style command lines), set identically on every router, or explicit per-interface costs, which override the computed value.

Where it came from. Moy's first OSPF specification was RFC 1131, published in October 1989 as a Proposed Standard and available only in PostScript. OSPF version 2 followed as RFC 1247 in July 1991, and the version in use today is RFC 2328. IPv6 has its own protocol, OSPF for IPv6 or OSPFv3, now RFC 5340 (July 2008, obsoleting RFC 2740). It is not a patch on version 2: addressing semantics were removed from the packets and basic LSAs, new LSAs carry IPv6 prefixes, the protocol runs per link rather than per IP subnet, an Instance ID allows several instances on one link, the multicast groups become FF02::5 and FF02::6, and authentication was removed from the protocol in favour of IPv6's Authentication Header and Encapsulating Security Payload (ESP).

Security. RFC 2328 offers null authentication, a simple cleartext password and cryptographic authentication with keyed MD5 (Message Digest 5). RFC 5709 (October 2009) added HMAC (Hash-based Message Authentication Code) with the SHA (Secure Hash Algorithm) family, SHA-1 to SHA-512, instead of being forced to use keyed MD5. Authentication protects against a rogue or misconfigured router joining the area and injecting LSAs, which, in a protocol where every router trusts the shared database, would be believed everywhere in the area at once.

In practice. F5 BIG-IP runs OSPFv2 in the ZebOS ospfd daemon (IPv4 only) and OSPFv3 in ospf6d (IPv6 only), enabled per route domain. F5's routing guide notes that on the standby unit of a pair the system raises the OSPF interface cost to the maximum, 65,535 for OSPFv2, and ages out its external type 2 LSAs, so that neighbours prefer the active unit; it also advises enabling OSPF on the active device first and then synchronizing. Across vendors the first checks are the same: the neighbour state (Full, or 2-Way between two routers that are neither DR nor BDR, which is normal), matching hello and dead intervals, area and area type, authentication and MTU, and then the database itself.

static-route.def: A route entered by hand rather than learned from a routing protocol: a destination prefix and a next hop or exit interface that stay in the table until someone removes them, absolute, silent, and exactly as correct as the person who typed it.
static-route.context: A static route never adapts: it stays in the routing table whether or not its next hop still works, unless something such as BFD (Bidirectional Forwarding Detection) or a link monitor withdraws it. That makes static routing ideal for stub sites, default routes and backup paths, and it scales beautifully to about a dozen routes; beyond that, dynamic routing exists for a reason. Its weight against other sources is set by administrative distance, 1 by default on Cisco and FRRouting and 10 on FortiGate, which is also how a floating static route waits behind a dynamic one.
static-route.depth:
What the standards say. RFC (Request for Comments) 1812, the IPv4 router requirements of June 1995, says a router SHOULD let the operator define a static route to a destination given as a network prefix, SHOULD allow a metric on it, MUST let the operator choose which static routes are propagated through a routing protocol and which are not, and SHOULD make it configurable whether a static route is preferred over a dynamic one. For hosts, RFC 1122 (October 1989) makes a table of static routes an optional extra, each entry possibly flagged to say whether ICMP (Internet Control Message Protocol) Redirects may override it, and names the cost plainly: static routes are set up by administrators to override the normal automatic routing for exceptional situations, but any static routing information is a potential source of failure as configurations change or equipment fails.

How a router weighs it. Among routes to the same destination the longest prefix wins first, whatever its source; only between equally specific routes from different sources does the router compare trustworthiness. RFC 1812 calls that administrative preference: a value from 0 to 254, lower preferred, with 255 meaning never use the route, and it warns that preferences configured inconsistently between neighbours can create routing loops. Vendors call it administrative distance. Cisco's defaults are 0 for connected routes, 1 for static, 20 for external BGP (Border Gateway Protocol), 90 for internal EIGRP (Enhanced Interior Gateway Routing Protocol), 110 for OSPF (Open Shortest Path First), 115 for IS-IS (Intermediate System to Intermediate System), 120 for RIP (Routing Information Protocol), 170 for external EIGRP and 200 for internal BGP, with 255 never installed. FRRouting also defaults static routes to 1, configurable from 1 to 255. FortiGate defaults them to 10 and adds a second number, priority (1 by default, lower preferred): two routes of equal distance and equal priority are installed together as ECMP (equal-cost multipath), a lower distance alone wins, and with equal distance the lower priority is preferred.

Floating static routes. RFC 1812 already described the use case: a primary static route over one interface and a secondary over another, with failover when the primary interface fails. The usual form today is a floating static route, configured with a higher administrative distance than the route it backs up, so it stays out of the table while the primary exists and is installed only when the primary disappears; Cisco's example keeps a static route at distance 250 hidden behind an OSPF route at 110. The catch is in the word disappears. A floating static only takes over when the better route is actually removed, and Cisco documents the case where it never was: the primary's next hop stayed resolvable through another, broader static route, so the primary remained installed, traffic went nowhere and the backup never floated in.

Next hops, interfaces and recursion. A static route needs its next hop to be reachable, normally through a connected prefix; if the next hop is not directly connected, the router resolves it recursively through another route, which is powerful and is exactly how the failure above happens. Cisco recommends specifying both the next hop and the outgoing interface, and warns against pointing a route at a multi-access interface such as Ethernet without a next hop, because the router then treats every destination in the prefix as directly connected and performs ARP (Address Resolution Protocol) for each one. FRRouting's nexthop tracking decides whether a next hop may resolve through the default route with ip nht resolve-via-default, which its documentation says is enabled by default in the traditional profile. On Linux, ip route add without a protocol tag marks the route as proto boot, which a routing daemon purges on start; proto static marks a route installed by the administrator, which daemons respect and may even advertise, and onlink tells the kernel to treat a next hop as attached even when no interface prefix covers it.

When the next hop dies but the link does not. A static route is withdrawn when its interface goes down; nothing withdraws it when the neighbour behind a still-up interface stops forwarding, which is the common case on Ethernet hand-offs, provider switches and firewall clusters. BFD (Bidirectional Forwarding Detection, RFC 5880, June 2010) exists to detect faults in the path between two forwarding engines quickly and independently of any routing protocol: each side sends control packets, for single-hop sessions to UDP (User Datagram Protocol) port 3784 under RFC 5881, and declares the session down after the remote detect multiplier times the agreed interval passes without one. RFC 5882 then says that when the remote system is known or presumed to run BFD and the session is not up, appropriate action SHOULD be taken, such as withdrawing a static route, and that it SHOULD NOT be taken if the peer does not support BFD.

The vendor implementations. FRRouting writes it as ip route followed by the prefix, the gateway and bfd, installing the route in the RIB (routing information base) only while the session is up, and lists BFD session down among a static route's inactive reasons. Extreme Networks' Switch Engine documentation states the problem directly: static routes never age out and without BFD remain operationally active, which can create a black hole; BFD for static routes has been available since ExtremeXOS 12.5.3 (enable iproute bfd for the gateway, then configure iproute add with bfd for the route), and since ExtremeXOS 30.3 a strict mode keeps a protected route down after a reboot while its BFD session is still initializing. FortiGate offers bfd per static route, and its link monitor or SD-WAN (software-defined wide area network) health checks withdraw static routes by default when they fail, unless link-monitor-exempt is enabled. F5 BIG-IP takes a different approach for gateways: a net route can point at a gateway address, an interface, a blackhole or a pool, which sends traffic to multiple load-balanced gateways and lets ordinary pool health monitoring decide which ones are used.

Discard routes and summaries. A static route to Null0, blackhole or reject (FRRouting accepts all three; reject answers with an ICMP Destination Unreachable while blackhole drops silently) is how a router that advertises a summary avoids forwarding traffic for unused parts of it back towards a default route; Linux has the same blackhole route type, and BIG-IP and FortiGate both offer a blackhole option on their static routes. Paired with the longest-match rule, a discard route for the aggregate catches only what no more specific route claims.

What goes wrong. Static routes fail silently, so the classic faults are a next hop that died behind an up interface, a floating route that never floats because the primary resolves recursively, a typo that sends a prefix the wrong way with nothing to correct it, a route redistributed into a dynamic protocol without the filter RFC 1812 asks for, and asymmetric return paths where only one direction was configured. Firewalls add one more: a FortiGate drops traffic whose return route fails its reverse path check, which is one reason its priority setting exists, letting a route stay active for the return direction while another carries the forward traffic.

default-route.def: The route of last resort, 0.0.0.0/0 in IPv4 (Internet Protocol version 4) and ::/0 in IPv6: a prefix of length zero that matches every destination and is used only when no more specific route claims the packet, the packet's way out of the building.
default-route.context: On a host the default route is what most people call the default gateway: one router on the local network that receives everything not addressed to an on-link destination. Inside an enterprise it is usually a static route or a default injected by the routing protocol towards the internet edge, and an OSPF (Open Shortest Path First) stub area is reached through one by design. At the top of the internet there famously is none: routers in the default-free zone hold a route for every reachable prefix in their BGP (Border Gateway Protocol) table instead.
default-route.depth:
What it is. RFC (Request for Comments) 1812, the June 1995 requirements for IPv4 (Internet Protocol version 4) routers, defines the default route as a route to all networks for which there are no explicit routes, and by definition the route whose prefix length is zero. A zero-length prefix constrains no bits, so it matches every destination; forwarding prefers the longest match, so it loses to every other route that also matches. RFC 4632, the CIDR (Classless Inter-Domain Routing) plan of August 2006, lists 0.0.0.0/0 in its prefix table as the default route, covering 4,294,967,296 addresses, and says that every implementation must accept it. IPv6 (Internet Protocol version 6) writes it ::/0, as RFC 4191 does in its examples, and the Linux ip route command accepts the keyword default as a spelling of either 0/0 or ::/0.

Why it always loses. The order is older than CIDR. RFC 1812's historical appendix describes how, once default routes, subnets and host routes coexisted, consensus settled on a hierarchy: host routes over subnet routes, subnet routes over network routes and network routes over default routes, later generalized as longest match. Administrative preference between sources only breaks ties inside that rule, so in RFC 1812's own example a static default route is never preferred over a dynamic route to a specific network, even on a router whose policy otherwise prefers static routes. When nothing at all matches, RFC 1812 requires the router to discard the packet and return an ICMP (Internet Control Message Protocol) Destination Unreachable; a router that holds a default never reaches that branch, so for unknown destinations any unreachable message comes from further along the path.

How hosts learn it. It can be typed in by hand. DHCP (Dynamic Host Configuration Protocol) delivers it in option 3, the Router option of RFC 2132, a list of routers on the client's subnet in order of preference. RFC 3442 (December 2002) added option 121, Classless Static Routes, and a client that receives both must ignore option 3, which is why the RFC asks administrators to put the default router in both. ICMP Router Discovery (RFC 1256, September 1991, edited by Steve Deering) let IPv4 routers advertise themselves with a preference level for hosts choosing a default router. In IPv6 that job belongs to the Router Advertisement: its 16-bit Router Lifetime, in seconds, puts the sender on the host's Default Router List when it is non-zero, the sending rules cap it at 9,000 seconds, and a lifetime of zero means the router is not a default router at all. RFC 4191 (November 2005) added a two-bit preference, High, Medium (the default) or Low, for hosts that hear several.

How routers learn and spread it. RFC 1812 notes that a router serving leaf networks with only one path in and out can simply send them a default, and requires that a router can be told whether to advertise all routes or only a default on each interface. RIP (Routing Information Protocol) represents it with the address 0.0.0.0. OSPF (Open Shortest Path First, RFC 2328) describes an external default with an AS-external-LSA (a link state advertisement for destinations outside the autonomous system) whose Link State ID and network mask are both 0.0.0.0, and in a stub area the area border routers advertise a default in summary-LSAs that are flooded throughout the area but no further. In IS-IS (Intermediate System to Intermediate System, RFC 1195), a level 1 router sends traffic for destinations outside its area to the nearest level 2 router that reports itself attached in its level 1 link state packets, and a level 2 router that has lost the backbone stops reporting itself attached, so its area routes around it.

How it is configured. On Cisco IOS, ip route 0.0.0.0 0.0.0.0 followed by a next hop installs a static default and requires IP routing to be enabled; show ip route then reports it as the gateway of last resort, with an asterisk marking candidate defaults. The similar-looking ip default-gateway applies only when IP routing is disabled and the device behaves as a host, and if both ip default-network and a static 0.0.0.0 route are configured, the static route takes precedence. On a FortiGate, config router static with set dst 0.0.0.0/0, set gateway and set device creates one, and an interface addressed by DHCP or PPPoE (Point-to-Point Protocol over Ethernet) installs its own default with a distance of 5 unless that is changed. On Linux, ip route add default via 192.0.2.1 does the same, and ip route get followed by an address prints the route exactly as the kernel will use it, which settles most arguments about which default wins.

How it fails. Quietly. A wrong or dead default leaves the local subnet working, because on-link destinations never touch the gateway, while everything else vanishes into a black hole, so a host that reaches its neighbours and nothing beyond them points first at its default. It is also a prize for an attacker on the same link. RFC 2131 warns that unauthorized DHCP servers are easily set up and can send incorrect routing information, spoof routers included. RFC 4861 describes a node that advertises itself as a default router and forges Router Advertisements with a Router Lifetime of zero on behalf of the legitimate routers, drawing every packet to itself; Neighbor Unreachability Detection will not notice as long as the rogue router answers its probes. RA-Guard (RFC 6105, February 2011) answers that with filtering in the layer 2 switches.

Where it must not go. RFC 4632 asks that 0.0.0.0/0 be advertised to another routing domain only when a router is explicitly configured to do so, never as an unconfigured default option, to protect against accidental advertisement. A router that advertises an aggregate must not follow its own default, or any less specific route, for addresses inside that aggregate that it cannot reach, or packets bounce between the two networks in a forwarding loop; RFC 4632 says this is usually done by installing a discard or null route for every aggregate advertised, and calls the default route a special case of the same rule. On Linux that is a blackhole route, which discards silently, as opposed to an unreachable route, which discards and returns an ICMP host unreachable.

Where there is none. At the top of the hierarchy the default disappears: routers in what operators call the default-free zone (DFZ) carry no default and instead hold an explicit route for every reachable prefix. Geoff Huston's RFC 3221 (December 2001) measured the global routing table from a point in the default-free part of the exterior routing domain, and the IAB (Internet Architecture Board) workshop held in Amsterdam on 18 and 19 October 2006, reported in RFC 4984, named the growth of the DFZ routing table, driven by multihoming, traffic engineering and policy routing, as a scaling problem growing at a potentially alarming rate. Everything below that zone, from a home router to a branch firewall, gets by with one line that says where everything else goes.

administrative-distance.def: The trust ranking a router applies when two routing sources offer the same prefix: the lower value wins, so with Cisco's defaults a connected route (0) beats a static route (1), which beats external Border Gateway Protocol (BGP) at 20, which beats Open Shortest Path First (OSPF) at 110.
administrative-distance.context: A local tie-breaker, not a protocol field: it never leaves the router, and two vendors may rank the same sources differently. Cisco calls it administrative distance (AD), Juniper route preference and Extreme relative route priority; the router requirements of 1995 called it administrative preference. It is consulted only when exactly the same prefix arrives from more than one source, after each protocol has chosen its own best path by metric; a route with a longer prefix is a different destination and wins on its own account. Raising the distance of a static route above that of a routing protocol turns it into a floating backup.
administrative-distance.depth:
Request for Comments (RFC) 1812, the 1995 requirements for Internet Protocol version 4 (IPv4) routers, writes route selection as pruning rules applied in order: basic match, then longest match, then the metric, which is compared only between routes from the same routing domain, and only then vendor policy. Administrative distance (AD) is that vendor policy, so it never overrides prefix length: a /24 from a less trusted source still beats a /16 from a more trusted one, and a metric never settles a tie between two different protocols. The same RFC suggests the mechanism, which it calls administrative preference: each route gets an integer from 0 to 255, zero the most preferred and 254 the least, with 255 meaning that the route should never be used. It also warns that the policy is not safe, since it can easily be misused to create routing loops: no protocol checks that the preferences configured on one router are consistent with those of its neighbours.

The need appeared as soon as a router had more than one source of routes. Appendix E of RFC 1812 tells it as history: first static routes made it possible to hold a static and a dynamic route to the same destination, and the router needed a policy to prefer one; then exterior gateways spoke an exterior protocol and an interior one at once, and the consensus was to prefer interior routes. In both cases the policy was only a tie-breaker for when longest match did not decide. The reason a separate number is needed is that metrics are not comparable: each protocol, the Routing Information Protocol (RIP) or Open Shortest Path First (OSPF) for instance, measures a path in its own way, which is why the RFC compares metrics only inside one routing domain.

Cisco's document on the subject, revised on 20 July 2026, places it precisely. Each routing protocol first selects its best candidate with its own metric and path selection algorithm; the routing table then compares the candidates for the same destination prefix by AD, which is used only when multiple routing sources advertise the same prefix; and the winner is installed if its next hop can be resolved. Longest prefix match is not part of route installation and is applied later, during packet forwarding, where neither AD nor metrics are evaluated. The value is local and is not advertised in routing updates. Cisco's route selection note makes the consequence concrete: 192.168.32.0/26 from Enhanced Interior Gateway Routing Protocol (EIGRP), 192.168.32.0/24 from RIP and 192.168.32.0/19 from OSPF are different destinations, all three are installed, and a packet for 192.168.32.100 follows the RIP route although RIP has the worst distance of the three.

The defaults are the numbers engineers memorize, and they are not universal. Cisco: connected 0, static 1, EIGRP summary 5, external Border Gateway Protocol (BGP) 20, internal EIGRP 90, Interior Gateway Routing Protocol (IGRP) 100, OSPF 110, Intermediate System to Intermediate System (IS-IS) 115, RIP 120, Exterior Gateway Protocol (EGP) 140, on-demand routing 160, external EIGRP 170, internal BGP 200, and 255 for an unknown source, which is not installed at all. FRRouting says care has been taken to choose the same distances as other routing suites: kernel and connected routes 0, static 1, external BGP 20, EIGRP 90, OSPF 110, IS-IS 115, RIP 120, internal BGP 200. Junos OS calls the value route preference and allows 0 to 4,294,967,295: directly connected 0, static 5, OSPF internal 10, IS-IS internal 15 and 18 by level, RIP 100, OSPF external 150 and BGP 170, internal or external alike. ExtremeXOS calls it relative route priority on yet another scale: direct 10, blackhole 50, static 1100, external BGP 1700, internal BGP 1900, OSPF intra-area 2200 and inter-area 2300, IS-IS 2350, RIP 2400, OSPF external 3200 and 3300. FortiOS uses 0 to 255, with 10 as the usual distance of a static default route.

The disagreement that matters is between BGP and the interior protocols. A router with Cisco's defaults prefers an external BGP route (20) to the same prefix learned from OSPF (110); Junos OS, as Juniper's own documentation points out, chooses the OSPF route (10) over the BGP one (170). A network that mixes vendors, or that mixes FRRouting with Junos, can therefore choose different exits for the same prefix on different routers without any misconfiguration. Administrative distance should also not be confused with BGP local preference, which is a path attribute carried between the routers of one autonomous system and where the highest value wins, nor with the Linux route metric, an arbitrary 32-bit preference in which lower is better and which the kernel keeps alongside a protocol field recording who installed the route.

Route tables print the pair. FRRouting shows distance and metric in brackets: [110/20] is an OSPF route at distance 110 and metric 20, an IS-IS route leads with 115, [20/0] is an external BGP route and [1/0] a static one, and the detailed view spells it out as distance 110, metric 20. Cisco's show ip route uses the same format, [administrative distance/metric], and FortiOS explains [20/0] as an administrative distance of 20 out of a range of 0 to 255. FRRouting's distance table starts with kernel and connected routes at 0 and static routes at 1, treats 255 as do not install, and has one oddity worth knowing: for a kernel route it did not create, it reads the top byte of the kernel metric as the distance and the lower three bytes as the metric. A FortiGate separates the routing database, which lists every learned route, from the routing table that holds only the winners, and when distances are equal it compares a second number, priority, before falling back to equal-cost multipath (ECMP).

Raising the distance turns a route into a fallback. FRRouting's static routes take an optional distance from 1 to 255, and its documentation shows both uses: a second next hop at distance 200 that is promoted only when the primary is gone, and a route to Null0 at 255 so that, if the real next hops become unreachable, traffic for the prefix is dropped instead of following a less specific route such as the default. Cisco's example is the floating static route ip route 10.0.0.0 255.255.255.0 172.16.1.200 250, which stays out of the table while OSPF holds the prefix at 110 and appears when OSPF loses it. Fortinet recommends the blackhole variant for the same reason, so that traffic meant for a tunnel that is down does not leave by the default route, and notes that its IPsec (Internet Protocol Security) wizard creates one.

What goes wrong is usually a default nobody looked at or a change nobody coordinated. On a FortiGate a default route learned through the Dynamic Host Configuration Protocol (DHCP) arrives with distance 5 and silently takes precedence over a static default route at 10. Changing distances with Cisco's distance command, or the order of ExtremeXOS priorities, is allowed, and both vendors attach a warning: Extreme recommends it only to those aware of the possible consequences, and Cisco lists them as asymmetric routing, suboptimal routing, routing loops and traffic black holes, adding that there are no general guidelines because every network differs. The numbers worth remembering for an exam and for a mixed network are few: 0, 1, 20, 90, 110, 115, 120, 170, 200 and 255 on Cisco and FRRouting, and 170 for all BGP on Junos.

longest-prefix-match.def: The forwarding rule that, among all the routes whose prefix contains a packet's destination address, the one with the longest prefix (the most specific) wins: /32 beats /24 beats /0, regardless of protocol, metric or administrative distance.
longest-prefix-match.context: Longest prefix match (LPM) is how an Internet Protocol (IP) router, host or cloud route table chooses when several routes cover the same destination: a host route beats a subnet route, a subnet route beats an aggregate, and the default route, whose prefix length is zero, is used only when nothing else matches. It is what lets a default route and a specific exception coexist with no explicit priority, what makes Classless Inter-Domain Routing (CIDR) aggregation work, and also the reason a leaked /25 can hijack traffic away from the legitimate /24: the lookup asks which prefix is most specific, never who is entitled to announce it. Administrative distance and metrics only choose between routes to the same prefix, so they never override a longer match.
longest-prefix-match.depth:
Longest prefix match (LPM) is the rule a router applies to every packet it forwards: of all the routes whose prefix contains the destination address, use the one with the most prefix bits. The requirements for Internet Protocol version 4 (IPv4) routers, Request for Comments (RFC) 1812 of June 1995, state it as an obligation: routers must use the most specific matching route, the longest matching network prefix, when forwarding traffic. The same document writes the lookup as pruning rules applied in order to the forwarding information base (FIB). Basic match keeps only the routes whose significant bits equal the same bits of the destination; longest match then keeps, of those, the ones with the largest prefix length. For a packet to 10.144.2.5 and routes to 10.144.2.0/24, 10.144.0.0/16 and 10.0.0.0/8, only the /24 survives. A host route therefore wins first, network prefixes follow in order of decreasing length, and the default route, by definition the route whose prefix length is zero, comes last. If nothing matches, the packet is discarded and an Internet Control Message Protocol (ICMP) destination unreachable message is generated.

What the rule does not do is rank routing protocols, and the order of the entries in the table never matters. In RFC 1812 the metric is compared only after longest match, and only between routes from the same routing domain; vendor policy, where administrative distance lives, comes last. Cisco's route selection note shows the effect with three routes from three protocols: 192.168.32.0/26 from Enhanced Interior Gateway Routing Protocol (EIGRP), 192.168.32.0/24 from Routing Information Protocol (RIP) and 192.168.32.0/19 from Open Shortest Path First (OSPF). Because the prefix lengths differ they are treated as different destinations and all three are installed. A packet to 192.168.32.1 follows the /26; a packet to 192.168.32.100, outside the /26, follows the RIP /24, although RIP has the least trusted administrative distance of the three (120, against 90 and 110). Distance and metric choose which route to a given prefix is installed; longest match chooses, packet by packet, among the prefixes that were.

The rule is older than its name. Appendix E of RFC 1812 describes a classic model, predating the Internet Protocol (IP), in which a router ran one routing protocol and looked for an exact match on the network part of the address. Default routes, subnets and host routes then made several entries match at once, and the consensus was a hierarchy: host routes over subnet routes, subnet routes over network routes, network routes over the default. Variable-length subnet masks generalized that hierarchy into choosing a route by preferring longest match, and the appendix notes that its sanctity remained unquestioned even as static routes and exterior protocols arrived: a policy between sources was only ever a tie-breaker. Classless Inter-Domain Routing (CIDR) then made it a requirement of the whole internet. RFC 1338 proposed supernetting in June 1992; RFC 1519, the CIDR standard of September 1993, ruled that routing to all destinations must be done on a longest-match basis only; and RFC 4632, which replaced it in August 2006 as Best Current Practice (BCP) 122, opens its rules with the sentence that forwarding in the internet is done on a longest-match basis.

Aggregation depends on the rule and is constrained by it. A provider can announce one aggregate for many customers because a customer that needs different treatment simply announces a more specific prefix, which wins wherever it is heard; for the same reason a multihomed network must always be announced explicitly and cannot hide inside one provider's aggregate. RFC 4632 adds a second rule: a router that generates an aggregate must discard packets that match the aggregate but none of its more specific routes, in practice a route to the null interface, or a forwarding loop appears when part of the block is unreachable. More specifics are also the everyday tool of traffic engineering, and the global table shows it. RFC 4632 counted about 75,000 base aggregates and some 85,000 more specific entries in March 2005; Geoff Huston's annual report counted about 1,050,000 IPv4 prefixes in January 2026, 544,000 of them more specifics, with /24, /23 and /22 together making up 84 per cent of the table, and 241,800 prefixes in the IP version 6 (IPv6) table.

Doing this for every packet is a hardware problem. Huston's arithmetic: a line card carrying 10 Tbit/s has about 70 nanoseconds per packet, a densely packed binary tree of a million entries needs some 20 decisions on average, and at 10 nanoseconds per memory access that is far too slow. High-speed routers therefore hold the table in ternary content-addressable memory (TCAM), which searches its entire contents in a single memory cycle and is a very expensive component of a line card, so the size of the table is something bought with the router. In software the usual structure is a trie. The Linux kernel's IPv4 table is an LC-trie, a trie with path compression and level compression based on the 1999 paper by Stefan Nilsson and Gunnar Karlsson on IP address lookup; each leaf keeps its routes sorted by prefix length, and when the first descent fails the lookup backtracks, shortening the key one step at a time until it finds the longest matching prefix. On Linux, ip route get followed by an address prints the route the kernel would use, and the fibmatch option shows the table entry that matched; on a FortiGate, get router info routing-table details followed by the address does the same.

Products state the rule almost in the same words and differ in what surrounds it. Fortinet's documentation for FortiOS 7.6 says the most specific route always takes precedence and that administrative distance only breaks a tie between equal prefixes, but the look-up runs in two steps, policy-based routes first and the forwarding table second, so a policy route can pre-empt a longer match. Microsoft Azure selects routes for a subnet by the longest prefix match algorithm and, when several routes carry the same prefix, prefers a user-defined route to a Border Gateway Protocol (BGP) route and a BGP route to a system route; its documented exception is that system routes for the virtual network itself, for peerings and for service endpoints are preferred even when BGP routes are more specific. Anything that evaluates rules in order is a different mechanism: in a Cisco access control list (ACL) traffic is compared to the entries in the order they occur until one matches, with an implicit deny at the end, while in a routing table position means nothing.

The same indifference to anything but length is a security problem between networks. The security considerations of RFC 4632 describe it directly: traffic can be hijacked by advertising a prefix more specific than the aggregate normally advertised for a destination, and CIDR makes this somewhat worse because longest-match routing causes all traffic to prefer the more specific route. An autonomous system (AS) that announces a longer prefix than the legitimate holder wins on every router that accepts the announcement. The best-known case is 24 February 2008. YouTube, AS36561, announced 208.65.152.0/22; at 18:47 UTC (Coordinated Universal Time) Pakistan Telecom, AS17557, began announcing 208.65.153.0/24, its upstream PCCW Global, AS3491, passed the announcement on, and within about two minutes the route had spread as far as it would and YouTube's traffic was being redirected to Pakistan. YouTube answered at 20:07 by announcing the same /24, which only produced a tie for BGP path selection to settle, and at 20:18 with 208.65.153.0/25 and 208.65.153.128/25, which won by longest match on every router that received them. PCCW withdrew the Pakistani routes at 21:01. The analysis by the RIPE Network Coordination Centre shows how few routers heard the /25s: 21 of its route collector peers, against 105 for the /24.

That is the practical limit of the rule on the internet: operators filter prefixes they consider too specific. RFC 7454, BCP 194 of February 2015, records the convention that IPv4 prefixes longer than /24 and IPv6 prefixes longer than /48 are generally neither announced nor accepted, which makes the /24 the usual floor both for a hijack and for the more specific announcement that answers one. Nothing in the algorithm asks whether the announcer is entitled to the address space, and that is exactly the gap the Resource Public Key Infrastructure (RPKI) was built to close: under RFC 6811 (January 2013) a router compares each BGP route with signed Route Origin Authorizations (ROAs) and marks it Valid, Invalid or NotFound, so a more specific prefix from the wrong origin, or one longer than the maximum length in the ROA, can be rejected before longest match ever sees it. RFC 9319, BCP 185 of October 2022, warns about what remains. A loose ROA such as 192.168.0.0/16 with a maximum length of 24 authorizes every /24 inside the block; an attacker announces an unused one with the legitimate origin forged at the end of the path, the route is Valid, and longest-prefix-match routing ensures it is always preferred over the legitimate /16. The advice is minimal ROAs that list only the prefixes actually announced; measurements from June 2017 cited there found 84 per cent of the prefixes in ROAs that used the maximum length attribute exposed in this way.

The phrase has a second, unrelated use. RFC 6724 (September 2012), the default address selection algorithm for IPv6, has a rule named Use longest matching prefix: among the candidate source addresses of a host it prefers the one that shares the most leading bits with the destination, and a matching rule orders destination addresses. That is a tie-breaker between a host's own addresses, applied before any packet exists, and it does not consult the routing table. Longest prefix match proper is the lookup that happens afterwards, at every hop, for every packet.

lacp.def: Link Aggregation Control Protocol (LACP): the IEEE (Institute of Electrical and Electronics Engineers) 802.1AX protocol, first published as 802.3ad, by which the two ends of parallel Ethernet links agree which links form one logical link and keep checking that every member still works, so the bundle is negotiated rather than hoped for.
lacp.context: Standardized by the IEEE (Institute of Electrical and Electronics Engineers) in 802.3ad in 2000 and in 802.1AX since 2008. Each member link exchanges LACP data units (LACPDUs) that carry both ends' identity, key and state, and a link carries traffic only when both ends agree it belongs to the same group; a member that stops hearing its partner is taken out. A bundle without negotiation, the static mode Cisco calls on, is how you get one-sided port channels and mystery outages. LACP decides membership, not distribution: which member carries a given flow is a hash, described in the link aggregation entry.
lacp.depth:
What it is, and what it is not. Link aggregation groups parallel full-duplex links into one logical link; the Link Aggregation Control Protocol (LACP) is the part that lets the two ends agree on the group and notice when a member fails. It does not carry user traffic and does not decide how frames are spread across members, which is a hash computed independently at each end (the link aggregation entry covers the group, the hash and the vendor names). The work began in the IEEE (Institute of Electrical and Electronics Engineers) 802.3 Trunking Study Group and was approved as IEEE 802.3ad-2000 at the March 2000 meeting of the IEEE Standards Board, published as part of 802.3; it later moved to 802.1AX, whose 2020 edition, a revision of 802.1AX-2014, was approved on 30 January 2020. Vendor documentation still says 802.3ad almost everywhere: Cisco's own guide states that LACP is defined in IEEE 802.3ad and contrasts it with the Port Aggregation Protocol (PAgP), which is Cisco-proprietary, runs only on Cisco devices and does not interoperate with LACP.

On the wire. LACPDUs belong to the Slow Protocols, EtherType 0x8809 in the IANA (Internet Assigned Numbers Authority) registry, and are sent to the multicast address 01-80-C2-00-00-02, which bridges do not forward. A subtype octet separates LACP (1) from the Marker protocol (2), whose protocol data units (PDUs) carry a requester's port, system and transaction identifier and are echoed back as a marker response. The Linux kernel's structure for an LACPDU shows the layout: a version, an Actor information TLV (type-length-value element) of 20 octets with the system priority, the system MAC (media access control) address, the key, the port priority, the port number and one state octet; a Partner information TLV of the same shape, holding what the actor currently believes about the far end; a Collector information TLV of 16 octets carrying the collector's maximum delay; a terminator; and 50 reserved octets, 110 octets in all. Because every LACPDU carries both views, each end can check that the other has heard it correctly: agreement is seeing yourself reflected accurately in your partner's message.

The state octet. Eight flags, from the least significant bit: LACP_Activity (0x01, set for an active port), LACP_Timeout (0x02, set when the port wants the short timeout and therefore fast transmissions), Aggregation (0x04, the link may join a group rather than stay individual), Synchronization (0x08, the port is attached to the right aggregator), Collecting (0x10) and Distributing (0x20), the permissions to receive and send user traffic, Defaulted (0x40, no LACPDU received, so the partner information is administrative defaults) and Expired (0x80, the receive machine timed out). A healthy active member on fast timers therefore shows 0x3F, the six low bits set, and on slow timers 0x3D; a port stuck with Synchronization clear, or with Defaulted set, is the first thing to look for. Wireshark exposes each flag as a field, from lacp.actor.state.activity to lacp.actor.state.expired, with the same set under lacp.partner.state.

Who decides. Each end has a system identifier made of a system priority and a MAC address, and each port has a port priority and number. Cisco's Catalyst 9300 defaults both priorities to 32768 and compares system priority, then system ID, then port priority, then port number, numerically lower values winning; the system that wins decides which links are active, and on that platform eight links can be active with up to eight more in hot standby, shown with an H flag in show etherchannel summary. The Linux bonding driver uses different defaults, a system priority of 65535 and a port priority of 255, and builds its port key from the duplex (bit 0), the speed (bits 1 to 5) and ten user-defined bits, which is why a port running at a different speed cannot join the same aggregate. Links join one group only when they share a key at each end and lead to the same partner system, so a cable patched to the wrong switch shows up as a partner identity that does not match.

Timers and machines. A port transmits periodically, every second on fast timers or every 30 seconds on slow ones, and declares its partner gone after three intervals without a LACPDU, 3 seconds or 90 seconds; the rate is a request made of the partner, carried in the LACP_Timeout flag, and the Linux driver asks for slow by default. The protocol also caps transmission at three LACPDUs a second, waits 2 seconds before attaching ports so that several can join together, and runs a churn detector with a 60-second timer that flags a port whose partner never reaches agreement. Behind this sit the state machines of the standard: a receive machine (initialize, port disabled, LACP disabled, expired, defaulted, current), a periodic transmission machine, and a mux machine that moves a port from detached through waiting and attached to collecting and distributing. A port in active mode starts the exchange; a passive one only answers, so two passive ends never form a group, and Linux's lacp_active option, on by default, turns a bond into a speak-when-spoken-to member when switched off.

What goes wrong. A static bundle, Cisco's mode on, has no protocol at all: both ends must be configured identically, and Cisco warns that a misconfigured group can cause packet loss or spanning-tree loops, because nothing tells either end that a member leads somewhere else; the result is traffic silently dropped on the mismatched member. With LACP the same mistake keeps the link out of the group. One side on and the other in LACP is a mismatch too: the LACP side hears nothing, and on Cisco its ports go to the suspended state, or to standalone where that mode is enabled. Slow timers let a member that fails without losing light keep receiving traffic for up to 90 seconds; fast timers cut that to 3. And LACP has no authentication. The Linux bonding documentation points out that LACPDUs cannot be sniffed, since they go to a link-local address that switches do not forward, but that most of their values are predictable or are simply the host's MAC address, so another machine in the same layer 2 domain could spoof LACPDUs, join a host's aggregate from the switch's point of view and receive a share of its traffic; it recommends setting a random actor system address, a random system priority and a user port key.

The expectation it does not meet. Four one-gigabit links do not make one four-gigabit link for a single flow. Frames of one conversation must stay in order, so the sender hashes addresses (and, optionally, ports) and keeps each flow on one member; a bundle raises aggregate capacity across many flows and does nothing for one large transfer, which is why a backup job across a bundle runs at member speed and surprises someone every year. In practice LACP is verified with show lacp internal and show etherchannel summary on Cisco, with the file /proc/net/bonding/bond0 on Linux, and in Wireshark with the display filter lacp. The numbers worth keeping are EtherType 0x8809, destination 01-80-C2-00-00-02, subtype 1, 110-octet LACPDUs, 1 or 30 seconds between them, 3 or 90 seconds to time out, at most three a second, 0x3F and 0x3D for healthy states, and 32768 as Cisco's default priorities.

vrrp.def: VRRP and Cisco's HSRP: routers on a LAN share one virtual gateway address and MAC, so the default gateway outlives a router.
vrrp.context: Hosts point at a virtual address held by whichever router is currently active; RFC 9568, the VRRP standard since April 2024, renamed the old Master the Active Router. Election runs on priority, the address owner at 255 always wins, and on failover the new Active Router announces the virtual MAC so switches and hosts follow it.
vrrp.depth:
VRRP's virtual MAC is 00-00-5E-00-01-XX for IPv4 and 00-00-5E-00-02-XX for IPv6, XX being the VRID in hexadecimal, from IANA's OUI, with a VRID of 1 to 255. The Active Router answers ARP and Neighbor Solicitations with that address, never its own, and sources its advertisements from it so that bridges learn where it is. Advertisements go to 224.0.0.18 or ff02::12 as IP protocol 112 with TTL 255, every 100 centiseconds by default.

A Backup declares the Active Router down after three advertisement intervals plus a skew of (256 minus priority) times the interval over 256: about 3.6 seconds at the default priority of 100, and under 4 seconds at the default interval whatever the priority. Preemption is on by default. Authentication was removed because misconfigured secrets elected several Active Routers and no authentication stops a hostile node from acting as a second one; the TTL 255 check keeps attacks local.

HSRP is Cisco's protocol, published as RFC 2281 in March 1998 with Informational status, not as a standard. It uses UDP port 1985 to 224.0.0.2 with TTL 1, the virtual MAC 00-00-0C-07-AC-XX, XX being the group number, recommended Hello and hold times of 3 and 10 seconds, and preemption only when configured; Cisco's version 2 moves to 224.0.0.102 and groups 0 to 4095. Neither protocol watches the uplink, so vendors add tracking, which lowers a router's priority when an interface or route it depends on fails.

vrf.def: VRF (virtual routing and forwarding): several independent routing and forwarding tables on one router, each bound to its own interfaces, so that overlapping or unrelated networks never mix; RFC (Request for Comments) 4364, which made the idea standard for provider VPNs (virtual private networks), reads the same initials as VPN routing and forwarding.
vrf.context: A VRF (virtual routing and forwarding instance) is the routing sibling of the VLAN (virtual local area network) idea: virtualize the table, not just the broadcast domain. Each instance has its own routes, its own default route and its own interfaces, and a packet is looked up only in the table of the interface it arrived on, so two customers, an old and an acquired network, or production and management can all use 10.0.0.0/8 on the same device. Providers built the idea into BGP/MPLS (Border Gateway Protocol over Multiprotocol Label Switching) VPNs (virtual private networks), where route distinguishers keep the copies apart; without MPLS it is called VRF-lite, and on BIG-IP the same thing is a route domain. Separation is a routing property, not encryption.
vrf.depth:
A VRF (virtual routing and forwarding instance) gives a router several independent routing tables, so the same address space can exist more than once on one device without collision. RFC (Request for Comments) 4364 describes it from the provider's side: each provider edge router maintains a number of separate forwarding tables, one of them the default forwarding table and the others VPN (virtual private network) routing and forwarding tables, VRFs. Every attachment circuit towards a customer is associated, by configuration, with one VRF (occasionally with a set of them), and a packet arriving on that circuit has its destination looked up in that VRF and nowhere else; the RFC calls it the packet's ingress VRF. A packet that arrives on a circuit with no VRF is looked up in the default table, which the RFC suggests thinking of as the public routes, with the VRFs holding the private ones. The terminology RFC for provider VPNs, RFC 4026 (March 2005), puts it in one line: a VRF is a per-site forwarding table, consulted only for packets that arrived from a site associated with it. It is the mechanism behind provider VPNs (virtual private networks) and behind any design that must keep tenants, environments or acquired networks separate while sharing hardware.

What a VRF is not helps place it. It is not a VLAN (virtual local area network), which separates broadcast domains at Layer 2; it separates routing at Layer 3, and the two are usually combined, a VLAN per tenant mapped into a VRF per tenant. It is not a full virtual router either: RFC 4026 defines a virtual router as an emulation of a physical router, with its own independent routing and forwarding tables, and treats it as a separate style of provider VPN, whereas a VRF is a table and its interfaces inside one router. On Linux the distinction is drawn in layers: network namespaces separate devices, VLANs on interfaces within a namespace provide Layer 2 separation, and VRF devices provide Layer 3 separation, and VRFs can be nested inside namespaces.

The initials have two readings, and both are correct. RFC 2547, published by Eric Rosen of Cisco Systems and Yakov Rekhter in March 1999 as an informational document, described BGP/MPLS VPNs (virtual private networks carried over the Border Gateway Protocol and Multiprotocol Label Switching), and its standards-track successor RFC 4364 (February 2006) spells VRF as VPN routing and forwarding. RFC 4659 (September 2006) extended the method to IPv6 customers. Later documents use the other reading: RFC 9135 (October 2021), on integrated routing and bridging in Ethernet VPN (EVPN) data centres, defines an IP-VRF as a virtual routing and forwarding table for IP routes, an instantiation of a Layer 3 VPN, and the Linux kernel documentation uses virtual routing and forwarding as well.

Inside an MPLS (Multiprotocol Label Switching) provider network the hard part is not keeping the tables apart on one router but keeping them apart across all of them, since many customers use the same private prefixes. RFC 4364 solves it with a new address family: a VPN-IPv4 address is 12 bytes, an 8-byte route distinguisher (RD) followed by the 4-byte IPv4 address, so that BGP can carry several completely different routes to the same prefix, one per VPN, and never treats VPN-IPv4 and IPv4 addresses as comparable. The RD is a 2-byte type field and a 6-byte value; type 0 puts a 2-byte autonomous system (AS) number before a 4-byte assigned number, type 1 a 4-byte IP address before a 2-byte number, and type 2 a 4-byte AS number before a 2-byte number. An RD is simply a number, the RFC insists, carrying no information about the route's origin or the VPNs it belongs to; which VRFs import a route is decided by Route Target attributes, BGP extended communities attached on export and matched on import. Connectivity follows from the routes a VRF holds: if a site's VRF contains only routes to sites with which it shares a VPN, the provider edge simply has no way to deliver its packets anywhere else. In the data plane, BGP distributes an MPLS label with each VPN route; the ingress provider edge pushes that label and then encapsulates the packet again, with another MPLS label or an IP or GRE (Generic Routing Encapsulation) tunnel header, so that it crosses the backbone to the right egress, and the core routers never need to know the VPN routes at all.

Without MPLS the same mechanism is called VRF-lite: several VRFs on one router or switch, each with its own interfaces, used for segmentation inside an enterprise or a data centre. The Linux kernel implements exactly that, its documentation names multi-tenancy, where each tenant needs its own routing tables and at the very least different default gateways, as one use case, and the setup is short: ip link add vrf-blue type vrf table 10 creates a VRF device bound to routing table 10, ip link set dev eth1 master vrf-blue enslaves an interface, and the interface's connected and local routes move into that table. Because a VRF works only at Layer 3 and above, Layer 2 tools such as the Link Layer Discovery Protocol (LLDP) keep working without being run per VRF. Sockets are where it surprises people: by default a listening socket that is not bound to a VRF serves only the default VRF, so a daemon that answers on every interface before the change goes silent on VRF interfaces after it, unless it is bound to the VRF or the tcp_l3mdev_accept and udp_l3mdev_accept sysctls are enabled, both off by default; the kernel documentation also warns that enabling them can hand VRF traffic to an unbound socket that lacks options such as TCP MD5 (Message Digest 5) keys.

Firewalls and application delivery controllers carry the same idea under their own names. FortiOS assigns interfaces to numbered VRFs within each virtual domain; release 7.6.1 extended the range from 0 to 251 to 0 to 511, allowing up to 512 VRFs per VDOM (virtual domain), its routing table output begins with Routing table for VRF=0, and the traffic the firewall originates itself, DNS (Domain Name System) lookups, FortiGuard updates, SNMP (Simple Network Management Protocol), NTP (Network Time Protocol), syslog and FortiAnalyzer logging, uses VRF 0 unless a vrf-select setting points it elsewhere. F5 BIG-IP calls the concept a route domain: each has a numeric ID, objects in it carry the ID after a percent sign, so 10.10.10.30%2 is a node in route domain 2, route domain 0 is the default and its addresses go unsuffixed, cross-routing between domains is restricted by default, a child domain can be given a parent whose routes it searches when it finds none of its own, and dynamic routing protocols and BFD (Bidirectional Forwarding Detection) are enabled per route domain.

What a VRF does not do is provide security by itself. RFC 4364 is precise about the claim: provider VPNs of this kind are meant to give security equivalent to a Layer 2 backbone such as Frame Relay, so that, in the absence of misconfiguration or deliberate interconnection of different VPNs, systems in one VPN cannot reach systems in another; it adds that the method neither encrypts data nor detects tampering, and that the guarantee depends on backbone routers refusing labelled packets and labelled VPN routes from untrusted links and peers. Separation is a routing property, and a route leaked between VRFs, a shared services block reachable from several of them, or a firewall configured to bridge them all reconnect what the design intended to isolate. Where VRFs mark security zones, the policy between them belongs on a firewall that inspects the traffic crossing over.

VRFs also multiply operational complexity in a specific way: every diagnostic command needs to name the table, and a command run in the wrong VRF reports a truthful answer about the wrong network. On Linux, ip route show vrf blue, ip neigh show vrf blue and ip addr show vrf blue are the per-VRF forms, the vrf keyword having arrived in iproute2 version 4.7; a plain ip route shows only the default table. The same trap waits in the device's own traffic: a FortiGate whose DNS servers live in a tenant VRF fails its lookups from VRF 0 until vrf-select is set, and a BIG-IP pool member written without its %ID suffix belongs to route domain 0, not to the tenant the administrator had in mind. Most VRF incidents are not failures of the mechanism but answers to the right question asked in the wrong table.

mpls.def: Multiprotocol Label Switching (MPLS) forwards packets on short labels instead of IP (Internet Protocol) lookups: the edge pushes a label, each hop swaps it, and the label is popped before the exit. It is the machinery under most carrier services.
mpls.context: An edge router classifies a packet once, pushes a label, and the core simply swaps labels along a pre-built label-switched path (LSP), so no core router needs the internet's routing table: the BGP-free core (BGP, Border Gateway Protocol). Labels can stack, which is the whole trick: an inner label meaning 'this customer's VPN (virtual private network)' rides under an outer label meaning 'this path across the backbone'. That stack is how Layer 3 VPNs (RFC 4364; RFC, Request for Comments) keep thousands of customers' overlapping address spaces apart on one network, and how traffic engineering pins flows to explicit paths. Labels historically came from LDP (Label Distribution Protocol) or RSVP-TE (Resource Reservation Protocol with traffic engineering extensions); Segment Routing now encodes the path in the packet and retires that signalling. MPLS (Multiprotocol Label Switching) took the virtual-circuit ideas of ATM (Asynchronous Transfer Mode) and left the cells behind, and while SD-WAN (software-defined wide area network) reshaped the enterprise edge, the carrier core underneath still speaks labels.
mpls.depth:
The idea. Multiprotocol Label Switching (MPLS) separates classifying a packet from forwarding it. RFC (Request for Comments) 3031, the architecture published in January 2001 by Eric Rosen, Arun Viswanathan and Ross Callon, starts from conventional forwarding, in which every router re-examines the network layer header and assigns the packet to a forwarding equivalence class (FEC), normally by longest match on the destination. In MPLS that assignment is made once, as the packet enters the network, and encoded as a short, fixed-length label; every later hop uses the label as an index into a table that gives the next hop and a new label, replaces the old one and forwards, without looking at the IP (Internet Protocol) header again. The RFC lists the advantages: label forwarding can be done by switches unable to analyse network layer headers at adequate speed; the ingress can classify on information that is not in the header, such as the port the packet arrived on; forwarding can depend on which router the packet entered by; classification can grow as complex as needed without burdening the routers that only forward; and a packet can be forced along a route chosen explicitly at the edge.

Speed was the first argument, and it did not last. MPLS forwards on a label rather than on a destination address, and the original justification was speed on hardware that found longest-prefix matching expensive; Wikipedia records that this goal is no longer relevant, because forwarding based on application-specific integrated circuits (ASICs) and ternary content-addressable memory (TCAM) handles plain IPv4 (IP version 4) as fast as labelled packets. MPLS thrived anyway, because the labels turned out to be useful for something else entirely. Because a label stands for a path rather than a destination, an operator can route traffic along a chosen route instead of the shortest one, reserving capacity and steering around congestion; and because labels stack, one shared backbone can carry many customers' private networks without any of them seeing each other, which is what an MPLS VPN (virtual private network) service really is.

The label stack entry. RFC 3032, published with the architecture, defines a 32-bit entry inserted between the link layer header and the network layer header: a 20-bit label value, a 3-bit field first called EXP and renamed Traffic Class (TC) by RFC 5462 in February 2009, a bottom-of-stack bit S set on the last entry, and an 8-bit time to live (TTL). Each label therefore costs 4 octets of maximum transmission unit (MTU). Twenty bits give 1,048,576 values, which is also the range of the Linux kernel's platform_labels setting (0 to 1048575; the default of 0 disables MPLS forwarding). No field says what is underneath: as RFC 3032 puts it, the label stack contains no field that identifies the network layer protocol, so the router that pops the last label must know it from the label itself. On Ethernet, EtherType 0x8847 marks MPLS and 0x8848 MPLS with an upstream-assigned label. Values 0 to 15 are special and, under RFC 7274, never to be made available for ordinary allocation: 0 is the IPv4 Explicit NULL, 1 the Router Alert, 2 the IPv6 (IP version 6) Explicit NULL and 3 the Implicit NULL, which a router may advertise but which never appears on the wire; IANA (the Internet Assigned Numbers Authority) also lists 7 as the Entropy Label Indicator, 13 as the Generic Associated Channel label, 14 as OAM (operations, administration and maintenance) Alert and 15 as the Extension label, and since RFC 9994 of June 2026 label 4 marks an MPLS Network Action sub-stack, which carries network actions and ancillary data inside the label stack itself.

Push, swap, pop. The ingress label switching router (LSR) pushes, transit LSRs swap, and the label is popped at the end of the label-switched path (LSP). Usually it is popped one hop early. RFC 3031 calls this penultimate hop popping: once the next-to-last router has decided to send the packet to the egress, the top label has no further function, and removing it spares the egress a second lookup, first of the label and then of what lies beneath. A router requests it by advertising the Implicit NULL label, so that its upstream neighbour, which would otherwise swap in a new label, pops the stack instead. Stacking makes hierarchy: an outer label carries the packet across the backbone to the egress router, and the inner label, untouched in transit, tells the egress what to do with it.

Where labels come from. The Label Distribution Protocol (LDP), now RFC 5036 of October 2007 (obsoleting RFC 3036), lets each router bind labels to the prefixes its interior gateway protocol (IGP) already knows; neighbours find each other with Hello messages on UDP (User Datagram Protocol) port 646 and exchange labels over TCP (Transmission Control Protocol) sessions on port 646, so LDP paths simply follow the IGP's shortest paths. RSVP-TE, the traffic engineering extensions to the Resource Reservation Protocol in RFC 3209 of December 2001, signals LSP tunnels along explicit routes, which is what lets an operator place traffic deliberately. Segment Routing changes the model: RFC 8402 (July 2018) describes it as source routing, in which the ingress steers a packet through an ordered list of instructions called segments, keeping per-flow state only at the ingress; RFC 8660 (December 2019) carries those segments as MPLS labels, each node's identifier an index into a Segment Routing Global Block (SRGB) that the IGP advertises. The core keeps forwarding labels as before, but no longer has to run a separate label signalling protocol or hold state for every tunnel.

What it is used for. The best-known service is the IP VPN of RFC 4364 (February 2006, obsoleting RFC 2547), built on the Border Gateway Protocol (BGP) and MPLS: each provider edge router keeps a separate VPN routing and forwarding instance (VRF) per customer; BGP carries customer routes as 12-byte VPN-IPv4 addresses, an 8-byte Route Distinguisher in front of the IPv4 (IP version 4) prefix, so that overlapping customer address spaces stay distinct; Route Targets decide which VRFs import which routes; and in the data plane the customer packet travels under two labels, a tunnel label to the egress provider edge and a VPN route label that selects the customer's VRF there. The same stack carries Layer 2 services, point-to-point pseudowires and multipoint Virtual Private LAN (local area network) Service (VPLS). Extreme Networks' Switch Engine, for instance, offers LDP, RSVP-TE, VPLS, Virtual Private Wire Service (VPWS), hierarchical VPLS and Layer 3 VPNs on switches whose ASICs support MPLS, under an MPLS feature pack licence, and warns that it has no graceful restart, so any restart of the MPLS process re-signals every connection.

Where it came from. MPLS took the virtual-circuit ideas of ATM (Asynchronous Transfer Mode) and Frame Relay, which already moved cells and frames on labels, and left the cells behind. Wikipedia's chronology runs from Toshiba presenting its Cell Switch Router ideas at an IETF (Internet Engineering Task Force) birds-of-a-feather session in 1994, through George Varghese and Girish Chandranmenon's paper on threaded indices at ACM SIGCOMM in 1995, to 1996, when Ipsilon proposed IP Switching (defined only over ATM) and Cisco proposed Tag Switching with its Tag Distribution Protocol, later renamed label switching and handed to the IETF; the IETF formed the MPLS working group in 1997, and the first MPLS RFCs followed in 2001.

What trips people up. Traceroute across MPLS depends on TTL handling, which RFC 3443 (January 2003) formalizes as three models: in the Uniform model the IP TTL is copied into the label and back, so every LSR appears as a hop; in the Pipe and Short Pipe models the whole LSP appears as a single hop. Linux exposes the choice as net.mpls.ip_ttl_propagate, 1 for Uniform (the default) and 0 for Pipe. RFC 4950 (August 2007) adds an MPLS label stack object to ICMP (Internet Control Message Protocol) messages, which is how a traceroute can print the labels of each hop. Every label adds 4 octets, so a VPN packet with two labels needs 8 octets more MTU in the core than the customer sees, and a deeper stack needs more. Packet filters need the same care: in tcpdump and libpcap each mpls keyword shifts the decoding offsets by 4 octets, one label at a time. On the business side, MPLS's position in the enterprise wide area network (WAN) is genuinely contested. SD-WAN (software-defined wide area network) made resilient connectivity over ordinary internet links possible at a fraction of the price, and plenty of enterprises have migrated away; what an MPLS service still sells is a contractual performance guarantee instead of best-effort delivery, which matters for latency-sensitive traffic and much less for a workload already sitting in a public cloud. The carrier core underneath, as the new MPLS Network Action work shows, is still being built on labels.

gre-tunnel.def: Generic Routing Encapsulation: wraps one packet inside another so traffic can cross networks that could not route it natively - a tunnel, without encryption.
gre-tunnel.context: Pair it with IPsec when confidentiality matters; GRE alone is an envelope, not a safe.

ipsec.def: IPsec (Internet Protocol Security) is the IETF (Internet Engineering Task Force) suite that encrypts and authenticates traffic at the IP layer, used by most site-to-site VPNs (virtual private networks); the keys and security associations it uses are negotiated by IKE (Internet Key Exchange).
ipsec.context: Two modes: transport mode protects the payload of the original packet, tunnel mode wraps the whole packet in a new one, and site-to-site virtual private networks (VPNs) between gateways live in tunnel mode. The protocol that carries the data is almost always ESP (Encapsulating Security Payload, Internet Protocol number 50); the keys come from IKE (Internet Key Exchange) on UDP (User Datagram Protocol) port 500, or 4500 when NAT (network address translation) sits in the path.
ipsec.depth:
Internet Protocol Security (IPsec) protects traffic at the network layer, and that is what separates it operationally from Transport Layer Security (TLS). TLS protects one connection between two applications that both know they are using it. IPsec protects everything between two endpoints, transparently, including protocols that have no security of their own, which is why it underpins site-to-site virtual private networks (VPNs). Its architecture, RFC (Request for Comments) 4301, written by Stephen Kent and Karen Seo of BBN Technologies in December 2005, says so plainly: it addresses security only at the IP layer, and the same machinery can build one encrypted tunnel for all traffic between two security gateways or a separate one for each Transmission Control Protocol (TCP) connection. The first architecture document, RFC 1825 by Randall Atkinson of the Naval Research Laboratory, dates from August 1995; RFC 2401 replaced it in November 1998, and RFC 4301 replaced that. The RFC also fixes the spelling: IPsec, every other capitalization deprecated.

There are two data protocols. The Authentication Header (AH), IP protocol 51, gives integrity and data-origin authentication, with optional anti-replay; the Encapsulating Security Payload (ESP), IP protocol 50, gives the same and adds confidentiality. Implementations must support ESP and may support AH, which was downgraded because ESP can also run with integrity alone; ESP with encryption but no integrity is not recommended. AH also protects the outer IP addresses, which makes it inherently incompatible with network address translation (NAT). Each protocol runs in transport mode, protecting mainly the next-layer protocol, or tunnel mode, applied to a whole IP packet inside a new one, the mode gateways use.

The unit of state is the security association (SA), and it is one-way: two-way traffic needs a pair, one in each direction. An SA is identified by a 32-bit Security Parameters Index (SPI) and carries a sequence number counter, 64-bit by default with 32-bit allowed, behind an anti-replay window. RFC 4301 defines three databases: the Security Policy Database (SPD), which decides whether each packet is protected, bypassed or discarded; the Security Association Database (SAD), which holds the live SAs; and the Peer Authorization Database (PAD), which ties authenticated peers to what they may negotiate. On the wire an ESP packet carries the SPI and sequence number as two 4-byte fields, then the payload (with any initialization vector), 0 to 255 bytes of padding, a pad length byte, a next header byte and the integrity check value.

It is really two things working together, and conflating them causes most confusion: IKE (Internet Key Exchange) negotiates, authenticating the peers and establishing the keys, and ESP then encrypts and protects the packets. IKE version 1 (RFC 2409, November 1998, with the Internet Security Association and Key Management Protocol (ISAKMP) and the IPsec domain of interpretation in RFCs 2408 and 2407) was obsoleted by IKEv2 in December 2005; the current IKEv2 is RFC 7296 (October 2014), Internet Standard 79. In April 2023 RFC 9395 moved IKEv1 to Historic, noting that it was vulnerable to amplification attacks and had seen no new work for at least a decade. IKEv2 normally needs four messages: IKE_SA_INIT negotiates the parameters and exchanges nonces and Diffie-Hellman values; IKE_AUTH carries the identities, proves knowledge of the secrets and sets up the first Child SA, the one that protects user traffic. Later CREATE_CHILD_SA exchanges add or rekey SAs, and INFORMATIONAL exchanges delete SAs and report errors; an empty INFORMATIONAL request is the liveness check behind dead peer detection. IKE uses User Datagram Protocol (UDP) port 500; when NAT is detected it moves to 4500, where ESP is wrapped in UDP (RFC 3948, January 2005) and IKE messages start with a non-ESP marker of four zero bytes.

When a tunnel fails, the useful first question is which phase failed. The IKEv1 words phase 1 and phase 2 survive in every firewall's interface and map onto the IKE SA and the Child SA. A phase 1 failure means the peers could not agree on parameters or prove their identities: a proposal, Diffie-Hellman group, pre-shared key, certificate or identity mismatch. A phase 2 failure means they agreed on who they are and not on what to protect: usually traffic selectors, which FortiGate calls proxy IDs, that do not mirror each other, or a different transform set. On a FortiGate, diagnose vpn ike gateway list shows phase 1 per gateway, with SPIs, the agreed proposal, lifetime and dead peer detection counters, and diagnose vpn tunnel list shows phase 2, with proxy IDs, SA details, traffic counters and offload flags.

Algorithm choice is now written down rather than guessed. RFC 8221 (October 2017) requires, for ESP, the Advanced Encryption Standard (AES) in Galois/Counter Mode (GCM) with a 16-byte tag and AES in cipher block chaining (CBC) mode, recommends ChaCha20-Poly1305, says triple DES (3DES) should not be used and forbids the Data Encryption Standard (DES) and Blowfish; for integrity, the hash-based message authentication code HMAC-SHA2-256-128 (SHA being the Secure Hash Algorithm) is a MUST, HMAC-SHA1-96 is MUST- (expected to lose that status) and HMAC-MD5-96, built on Message Digest 5, is forbidden. RFC 8247 (September 2017) does the same for IKEv2: Diffie-Hellman group 14, a 2,048-bit modular exponential group, is required, group 19, a 256-bit elliptic curve group, recommended, groups 2 and 5 should not be used and group 1, 768 bits, must not. Those group numbers are exactly what peers must agree on in phase 1.

The classic operational trap is fragmentation. Encapsulation adds a new IP header, the ESP header, padding and an integrity check value, so the usable maximum transmission unit (MTU) inside the tunnel shrinks. Path MTU discovery (PMTUD) depends on routers returning Internet Control Message Protocol (ICMP) Fragmentation Needed messages, and RFC 2923 (September 2000) records that firewalls are often configured to suppress all ICMP; the result is a black hole in which a connection opens, starts, then hangs on bulk data while small control packets keep working. That signature, small things work and big things fail, points at MTU and maximum segment size (MSS) far more often than at the tunnel itself. RFC 4459 (April 2006) lists the remedies: fragment and reassemble at the tunnel endpoints, signal the sources through PMTUD, or keep the backbone MTU above 1,500 bytes; it calls MSS clamping, in which the tunnel endpoint lowers the MSS in TCP handshakes, a hack that works only for TCP and does nothing for UDP.

Numbers to remember: ESP is IP protocol 50 and AH 51 (a filter allowing only TCP and UDP blocks native ESP), IKE runs on UDP 500 and 4500, the SPI is 32 bits, sequence numbers are 64 bits by default, ESP padding runs from 0 to 255 bytes, and an IKEv2 tunnel needs four messages to carry its first packet.

acl.def: An access control list (ACL) is an ordered set of permit and deny rules that a router, switch or firewall evaluates top-down against each packet, acting on the first rule that matches, usually with an implicit deny waiting at the end; the same name covers the per-object permission lists of operating systems and file systems.
acl.context: First match wins, which is why rule order is the whole game: a broad entry above a narrow one makes the narrow one unreachable, and the list's last line, written or implied, decides everything nothing else matched. A network ACL (access control list) is normally stateless, judging each packet alone by addresses, protocol, ports and sometimes TCP flags, so replies need their own permission; that is what separates it from stateful inspection, and also why it can run in switching hardware at full speed. The words are older than packet filtering: in an operating system or file system, an ACL is attached to an object and lists who may do what to it.
acl.depth:
Two senses of one idea. The Internet Security Glossary, RFC (Request for Comments) 4949 of August 2007, defines an access control list (ACL) as a mechanism that implements access control for a system resource by enumerating the system entities permitted to access it and stating, implicitly or explicitly, the access modes granted to each; it names ACLs and tickets as the two basic mechanisms of access control, and explains that in an access control matrix, with a row per subject and a column per object, each column is the ACL of an object and each row is the capability list of a subject. NIST (the US National Institute of Standards and Technology) carries the same definition in its glossary, beside one derived from an ISO (International Organization for Standardization) draft, 10181-2: a list of entities, together with their access rights, authorized to access a resource. Networking borrowed the name for packet filtering, where the subject becomes a packet described by its header fields, the object becomes an interface or a path through a device, and the access modes shrink to permit and deny, sometimes with logging, counting or rate limiting attached.

The network ACL, as standardized. The IETF (Internet Engineering Task Force) gave the network sense a vendor-neutral model in RFC 8519, a Standards Track data model written in the YANG modelling language, by M. Jethanandani, S. Agarwal, L. Huang and D. Blair (March 2019). It defines an ACL as a user-ordered set of rules used to filter traffic on a networking device, each rule an ACE (access control entry) with a group of match criteria, covering packet headers and metadata such as the input interface or the packet length, and a group of actions, from logging and rate limiting to dropping or simply forwarding. The decisive sentence is short: actions on the first matching ACE are applied with no processing of subsequent ACEs. The RFC also leaves a gap on purpose, since what happens when no ACE matches appears only in its example of a vendor's proprietary extension, with a default action of drop. RFC 9899 (December 2025) extends the model with defined sets, so that one rule can match a whole group of addresses or ports instead of one entry per value, and with matches on TCP (Transmission Control Protocol) flags, fragments, IPv6 extension headers, MPLS (Multiprotocol Label Switching) headers and VLANs (virtual local area networks).

Order is the behaviour. Because evaluation stops at the first match, the sequence of entries is the policy, and reading the list as a set of independent statements is the root of most ACL bugs.
