Juniper documents it for its EX switches: terms are evaluated in order, the first term whose conditions all match has its action taken and evaluation ends, and a matching term with no action accepts the packet. Cisco's guide for Catalyst 9000 switches says the first match decides whether the switch accepts or rejects the packet. The most common mistake follows directly: a broad rule placed above a narrower one makes the narrower one unreachable, and the policy reads correctly and does not do what it says. Platforms help with numbering. Amazon's network ACLs number their rules from 1 to 32766, evaluate them from the lowest number up, stop at the first match, and AWS (Amazon Web Services) recommends numbering in steps of 10 or 100 so that a rule can later be inserted between two others; Cisco IOS lists carry sequence numbers for the same reason.

What happens at the end. The second most common mistake is forgetting what the end of the list does, and the answer is a vendor default, not a law. Cisco states that the end of every ACL contains an implicit deny for all packets that matched nothing, and Juniper that every firewall filter ends with an implicit deny equivalent to a final term whose action is discard. Extreme Networks' Fabric Engine does the opposite: an ACL has a default action that applies when no entry matches, and its default mode is permit. Edge cases differ again. Cisco's Catalyst guide notes that a MAC (media access control) ACL applied to a Layer 2 interface but never defined makes the device act as if no ACL were applied and permit all packets, and in Windows an object with no DACL (discretionary access control list) at all grants full access to everyone while one with an empty DACL denies everything. A list moved between platforms without an explicit final rule can therefore change from deny-all to permit-all without a single error, which is a textbook silent failure; writing the last rule explicitly, and logging it, removes the ambiguity.

Stateless by default. A network ACL judges each packet on its own, with no memory of the request a reply belongs to, unless the platform says otherwise. AWS puts it plainly for network ACLs: they are stateless, so a rule allowing inbound traffic does not automatically allow the responses, in contrast to security groups, which are stateful. Return traffic therefore needs its own rule, and the rule set has to be reasoned about in both directions, including the ephemeral port range clients use. Cisco's extended lists offer the keyword established, which matches TCP segments with the ACK (acknowledgement) or RST (reset) flag set; it approximates return traffic for TCP only, admits any crafted packet with those flags, and does nothing for UDP (User Datagram Protocol). The same guide notes that Catalyst switches do not support dynamic or reflexive access lists. Tracking real connections is what stateful inspection does, and it is why firewalls moved past the ACL.

Cisco's dialect, and where lists attach. In Cisco IOS XE, standard IPv4 lists match the source address only and are numbered 1 to 99 or 1300 to 1999; extended lists match protocol, source and destination addresses and ports and are numbered 100 to 199 or 2000 to 2699; either kind can instead carry a name. Addresses are written with wildcard masks, in which a 0 bit must match and a 1 bit is ignored. A Catalyst switch accepts one router ACL per direction of a Layer 3 interface, one VLAN map per VLAN and, on a Layer 2 interface, one IP and one MAC access list, and on ingress it applies the port ACL first, then the VLAN map, then the router ACL. Other platforms use other words for the same object: Juniper calls it a firewall filter made of terms, AWS a network ACL attached to subnets, and FortiOS an ACL policy (config firewall acl, or acl6 for IPv6) that acts as a targeted blocklist on an interface.

Why ACLs survive. Statelessness is also the strength: with nothing to remember, an ACL can be compiled into the forwarding hardware. ESnet (the Energy Sciences Network), the US Department of Energy's network for science, recommends router ACLs rather than stateful firewalls in front of high-throughput science data transfers precisely because ACLs are usually implemented in the router's forwarding hardware and typically do not compromise performance. FortiOS offloads its ACL policies to the switch fabric so that they use no CPU (central processing unit) time, on supported models and on switch-fabric ports only. The cost is capacity rather than speed: hardware tables are finite and shared with other features, so long lists run out of space before they slow anything down, which is one reason RFC 9899's defined sets exist. ACLs therefore remain the tool for infrastructure protection, anti-spoofing at the edge, coarse filtering at line rate and segmentation inside switches, with stateful firewalls behind them for everything that needs to know about connections.

The file-system ACL. On hosts the older sense is everywhere. POSIX (Portable Operating System Interface) ACLs on Linux extend the owner, group and other permission bits with entries for named users and groups (the tags ACL_USER_OBJ, ACL_USER, ACL_GROUP_OBJ, ACL_GROUP and ACL_OTHER), plus ACL_MASK, which caps the rights any named user or group entry can grant. Windows attaches to every securable object a security descriptor that can hold two lists of access control entries: the DACL, which allows or denies access and whose entries the system checks in sequence until the requested rights are all granted or one is denied, and the SACL (system access control list), which records access attempts for auditing. The vocabulary is shared with the network sense, and so is the lesson: an ACL is only as correct as its order, its default and the reviewer's patience.

stateful-firewall.def: A firewall that tracks connections, allowing return traffic automatically for sessions it saw begin - judging flows, not lone packets.
stateful-firewall.context: The contrast is the stateless packet filter, which evaluates every packet as a stranger.

dmz.def: A demilitarized zone (DMZ) is a network segment placed between an untrusted network, usually the internet, and an internal one, holding the hosts that must be reachable from outside, so that outside traffic ends there and anything heading further inward has to cross a second, stricter policy.
dmz.context: The name comes from the military buffer strip between two armies, and the logic is the same: neither side's ground. A DMZ (demilitarized zone) exists because some services, such as a public web server, a mail relay, a reverse proxy or a VPN (virtual private network) concentrator, must accept connections from strangers, and anything that does will one day be compromised. Putting those hosts in their own segment means that the compromise of a DMZ host hands the attacker the DMZ, not the interior: connections from the DMZ inwards are denied by default and opened only for named flows, such as one web server to one database on one port. The pattern is old and coarse, but it was the first segmentation most networks ever had, and it survives under other names in cloud public subnets and in the zone that separates industrial networks from the enterprise.
dmz.depth:
What it is, and what the standards call it. RFC (Request for Comments) 2647, David Newman's firewall benchmarking terminology of August 1999, defines the demilitarized zone (DMZ) as a network segment or segments located between protected and unprotected networks: rather than connecting the two directly, firewalls and possibly public resources such as HTTP or FTP (File Transfer Protocol) servers sit on the DMZ, which is also called a perimeter network. The glossary of NIST (the US National Institute of Standards and Technology), quoting the Committee on National Security Systems instruction CNSSI 4009-2022, adds the purpose: to enforce the internal network's policy for external information exchange and to give external, untrusted sources restricted access to releasable information while shielding the internal networks. The Internet Security Glossary of the IETF (Internet Engineering Task Force), RFC 4949 (August 2007), dislikes the name: it lists demilitarized zone as a deprecated synonym for buffer zone, because the military metaphor mixes concepts in a potentially misleading way, and describes a buffer zone as a small, separate, isolated LAN (local area network) connected to both the private and the public network, with a firewall on one or both connections. Practitioners also say screened subnet. The metaphor is the strip created by the Korean Armistice Agreement of 1953, about 250 kilometres long and 4 wide, which belongs to neither army.

Where it came from. The DMZ grew up around the bastion host. RFC 4949 defines that as a strongly protected computer, inside or part of a firewall, that is the only host, or one of very few, directly reachable from the other side, so that only it needs hardening; services such as DNS (Domain Name System) and SMTP (Simple Mail Transfer Protocol) relay naturally through it. In the example network of Cheswick and Bellovin's Firewalls and Internet Security, whose first edition appeared in 1994, Net 1, the DMZ net, is inhabited solely by a gateway machine, with very limited connections permitted between it and the outside world and, separately, between it and the internal networks. The shape has not changed: a segment that strangers may reach, a policy towards the outside and a different, tighter policy towards the inside.

The two classic layouts. In the three-legged design one firewall has at least three interfaces, outside, inside and DMZ, and every policy lives on one device, which is cheap and simple and makes that firewall a single point of failure that must carry all traffic to both zones. In the back-to-back design a front-end or perimeter firewall admits only traffic destined for the DMZ and a back-end or internal firewall admits only traffic from the inside to the DMZ, so an attacker must defeat two devices; some designs use two vendors so that one flaw cannot open both, at a higher cost to buy and run. NIST is cooler about stacking than the folklore: its firewall guide, SP (Special Publication) 800-41 Revision 1 by Karen Scarfone and Paul Hoffman (September 2009), says that putting one firewall behind another may serve a goal in some environments but that multiple layers of firewalls can in general be troublesome. The same guide notes that many hardware firewalls simply have an interface called DMZ, that there is no single technical definition of one, and that what matters is that traffic between the DMZ and the protected side still crosses the firewall and its policy.

The policy that makes it a DMZ. A segment is only a DMZ if the rules say so. From the internet, only the published services reach the DMZ hosts that offer them. From the DMZ inwards, the default is deny, opened flow by flow (the web server to the application tier on one port, the mail relay to the internal mail server), because the DMZ host is the one most likely to be taken over. From the inside, administration reaches the DMZ through defined paths. From the DMZ outwards, egress is limited too, since a compromised web server that can open any connection to the internet is a ready-made command channel. NIST adds two traps. A NAT (network address translation) rule that pinholes a port straight to an inside host can quietly defeat a policy that all public HTTP servers live on the DMZ, and an organization with an edge DMZ should decide service by service which outward-facing systems belong there and which stay inside. Logs that show the translated rather than the private address hide which host did what.

The industrial DMZ. Operational technology (OT) gave the DMZ its most rigorous modern form. NIST SP 800-82 Revision 3 (September 2023) tells operators to implement a DMZ to separate the OT environment from the enterprise network so that any communication between the enterprise and the operations management level goes through services within the DMZ, such as replicated historians, update and file-transfer servers, rather than directly between the two networks. It also says why the DMZ itself needs watching: it connects to outside environments, so its services must be monitored and protected to keep an attacker from pivoting into OT without detection. The rule of thumb that follows is that no single connection crosses from enterprise to control network; both terminate in the DMZ.

Two other things called DMZ. The DMZ host on a home or small-office router is not a DMZ at all. TP-Link's own documentation says so: strictly speaking not a true DMZ, it is a host on the internal network with all UDP (User Datagram Protocol) and TCP (Transmission Control Protocol) ports open and exposed except those otherwise forwarded, totally exposed to the internet, and useful mainly to pass everything to another firewall or NAT device behind it; it is a less secure alternative to port forwarding. At the other extreme, the Science DMZ promoted by ESnet (the Energy Sciences Network), the US Department of Energy's high-performance network for science, is a segment at or near a campus or laboratory perimeter whose equipment, configuration and security policy are tuned for bulk scientific data transfer rather than for enterprise systems, with dedicated data transfer nodes and continuous performance measurement. ESnet recommends, in a note dated 15 January 2025, that stateful firewalls not be used to protect it because of their effect on throughput, and that router ACLs (access control lists), enforced in forwarding hardware, be used instead, while the institutional firewall keeps protecting business and end-user systems.

What it does and does not protect. The DMZ's promise is containment of the first compromise, and it holds only if the inward rules are narrow and watched. Its limit is that it is one coarse boundary: inside the DMZ, every host can usually reach every other, and inside the internal network, everything trusted the firewall to have done its job. That is the gap that segmentation inside the estate, microsegmentation and zero trust were built to close. The pattern itself has moved rather than disappeared. In a VPC (virtual private cloud), AWS (Amazon Web Services) calls a subnet with a direct route to an internet gateway a public subnet and one without it a private subnet, which is the DMZ and the interior expressed in routing tables, with security groups doing the job of the firewall rules between them.

snmp.def: Simple Network Management Protocol (SNMP): the long-standing standard for reading device health and counters by polling, for changing settings, and for receiving notifications (traps and informs) when something changes.
snmp.context: A manager polls an agent on User Datagram Protocol (UDP) port 161 and the agent sends notifications to port 162; what it can read or set is defined in management information bases (MIBs), trees of numbered objects such as interface counters, routes and system descriptions. Versions 1 and 2c authenticate with a community string sent in clear text, which the Internet Engineering Task Force (IETF) itself calls fundamentally insecure; version 3 adds real authentication and encryption. Default communities such as public and private still turn up in audits, and attackers still use them.
snmp.depth:
What it is. Simple Network Management Protocol (SNMP) is how most network equipment is monitored: a manager, the monitoring system, sends requests to an agent on the device, and the agent answers with values from its management information base (MIB) or sends a notification of its own when something happens. Request for Comments (RFC) 3417 suggests that agents listen on User Datagram Protocol (UDP) port 161 and that notification receivers listen on UDP port 162, and requires every implementation to accept messages of at least 484 octets. The operations, in the current definition of RFC 3416, are Get, GetNext and GetBulk to read, Set to write, the unacknowledged SNMPv2-Trap and the acknowledged InformRequest for notifications, and Response and Report. Its ubiquity is its strength; its version history is the problem.

Where it came from. SNMP grew out of the Simple Gateway Monitoring Protocol, RFC 1028 of November 1987, written by J. Davin, J. Case, M. Fedor and M. Schoffstall. RFC 1067 of August 1988 specified SNMP itself, and the version 1 that everyone implemented is RFC 1157 of May 1990, by the same four authors. The data model followed: MIB-II, RFC 1213 of March 1991, defined the system group, the interfaces table and the groups for the Internet Protocol (IP), the Internet Control Message Protocol (ICMP), the Transmission Control Protocol (TCP) and UDP that every agent still exposes. Version 2 produced several competing security frameworks; the one that shipped widely, community-based SNMPv2 or SNMPv2c, was published as an experimental RFC 1901 in January 1996 and kept version 1's community strings while adding the version 2 operations such as GetBulk and, as RFC 3584 on coexistence notes, the Counter64 type that version 1 never carries. Version 3, the set of RFC 3411 to RFC 3418 of December 2002, is the full Internet Standard number 62 (STD 62).

The security problem, in the standard's own words. RFC 3410, the SNMPv3 introduction, states that SNMPv1 and SNMPv2c messages support only trivial authentication based on plain-text community strings and, as a result, are fundamentally insecure; when SNMPv3 became a full Standard, SNMPv1 (formerly STD 15) and SNMPv2c were declared Historic to send a clear message about which framework to use. A community string is a password in the sense that a doormat key is a lock: it crosses the network in every request, anyone on the path can read it, and well-known defaults such as public are the first values any scanner tries. A read-only community is often dismissed as harmless, and it is not. MIB-II alone exposes the system description, every interface, the IP addresses, the device's IP routing table (ipRouteTable), its IP-to-physical address mappings (ipNetToMediaTable) and its TCP connections: a complete inventory of the device and its neighbours, which is precisely the reconnaissance an intruder would otherwise have to work for.

What version 3 adds. SNMPv3 separates the message from its security. The User-based Security Model (USM) of RFC 3414 authenticates each message with a hashed message authentication code (HMAC), originally HMAC-MD5-96 or HMAC-SHA-96, and encrypts it with the Data Encryption Standard (DES) in cipher block chaining mode, CBC-DES; RFC 3826 of June 2004 added the Advanced Encryption Standard (AES) in 128-bit cipher feedback mode, and RFC 7860 of April 2016 added HMAC with SHA-2. RFC 3411 defines three security levels: noAuthNoPriv, authNoPriv and authPriv, and only the last both authenticates and encrypts. Access control is the View-based Access Control Model (VACM) of RFC 3415, which grants each group access through MIB views built from subtrees. For networks that prefer existing key management, RFC 6353 of July 2011 runs SNMP over Transport Layer Security (TLS) and its datagram form, Datagram Transport Layer Security (DTLS). Version 3 has been widely available for two decades and is still unevenly deployed, because version 2c works and changing it touches every device and every monitoring system at once.

A named incident. In April 2023 the United Kingdom's National Cyber Security Centre, the US National Security Agency (NSA), the Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency (CISA) and the Federal Bureau of Investigation (FBI) described how APT28, which they attribute to Russian military intelligence, used SNMP against Cisco routers worldwide in 2021. Weak community strings, including the default public, gave access to router information, and further SNMP requests enumerated interfaces; the routers accepted SNMP v2, which sends community strings unencrypted. On some routers APT28 then exploited the Common Vulnerabilities and Exposures (CVE) entry CVE-2017-6742, an SNMP vulnerability Cisco had announced and patched on 29 June 2017, to install the Jaguar Tooth malware, which exfiltrated device information over the Trivial File Transfer Protocol (TFTP) and opened an unauthenticated backdoor. The advisory's advice is the hardening list in brief: allow SNMP only from known management hosts, disable SNMP v1 and v2c, use SNMPv3, and patch.

Counters and arithmetic. Most of what SNMP is used for is reading counters and dividing the difference by the polling interval, which only works if the counter has not wrapped in between. A 32-bit octet counter wraps after 2^32 bytes, about 4.3 GB, which at 10 Gbit/s takes under four seconds. RFC 2863, the Interfaces Group MIB of June 2000, therefore requires 64-bit octet counters (ifHCInOctets and its siblings) on interfaces faster than 20 Mbit/s and 64-bit packet counters as well at 650 Mbit/s or faster, because its authors had computed that a 32-bit packet counter wraps in about 57 minutes with minimum-size packets back to back at 650 Mbit/s. Polling a 32-bit counter on a fast link produces graphs that look plausible and are wrong.

On the devices. Vendors ship SNMP with conservative defaults and expect them to be changed. F5 BIG-IP's snmpd accepts requests only from 127 (the local host) until allowed-addresses is set, its default community public is read-only and limited to the local host, and SNMPv3 users are configured with an authentication protocol and a privacy protocol. The checklist is the same everywhere: SNMPv3 with authPriv, unique credentials per device, an access list naming the pollers, no write access unless something needs it, and notifications sent to a collector that is actually watched. The numbers worth remembering are UDP 161 and 162, the three security levels, and the 20 Mbit/s and 650 Mbit/s thresholds for 64-bit counters.

syslog.def: The standard way for devices and programs to send timestamped, severity-tagged event messages to a central collector, from debug chatter to emergencies, over User Datagram Protocol (UDP) port 514 or, better, over Transport Layer Security (TLS).
syslog.context: Request for Comments (RFC) 5424 formalized in 2009 what Berkeley Software Distribution (BSD) Unix had improvised: every message carries a priority that encodes a facility (the subsystem) and a severity, a timestamp, a hostname and free text. Severity 0 is Emergency and 7 is Debug, so the most urgent messages have the lowest numbers, and both ends of the scale get ignored at three in the morning. Classic syslog travels over the User Datagram Protocol (UDP) without acknowledgement or authentication; Transport Layer Security (TLS) on port 6514 fixes delivery and confidentiality, and on many devices it ships switched off.
syslog.depth:
What it is. Syslog is the lowest common denominator of machine logging, and its longevity comes from being simple enough that everything implements it. Request for Comments (RFC) 3164 of August 2001, written by C. Lonvick, was not a design but a description: it set out the observed behaviour of a protocol originally developed on the University of California's Berkeley Software Distribution (BSD) implementations and since ported to operating systems and devices of every kind, and it credits Eric Allman as the original inventor and author of the syslog daemon and protocol. RFC 5424 of March 2009, by R. Gerhards, replaced that description with a standard, The Syslog Protocol, and obsoletes RFC 3164. A message carries a priority, a timestamp, a hostname and text; that is nearly the whole idea, which explains both why it is universal and why parsing it consistently is harder than it looks.

The priority value. Every message begins with a number in angle brackets that encodes two things at once. RFC 5424 computes it as the facility multiplied by 8 plus the severity, and gives two examples: a kernel message (facility 0) of severity Emergency (0) is <0>, and a local use 4 message (facility 20) of severity Notice (5) is <165>. Reading it back is arithmetic, not inspection: the severity is the remainder after dividing by 8 and the facility is the quotient, so <134> is facility 16, local0, at severity 6, Informational. There are 24 facilities, from 0 kernel messages, 1 user-level, 2 mail, 3 system daemons and 4 security/authorization to 16 to 23, local0 to local7, which network devices use for themselves; and 8 severities: 0 Emergency, 1 Alert, 2 Critical, 3 Error, 4 Warning, 5 Notice, 6 Informational and 7 Debug. The ordering is the trap. Lower numbers are more urgent, so a filter written the intuitive way, keeping severity 4 and above, keeps Warning and everything less important and silently drops the messages that mattered.

Two formats on the wire. The BSD format of RFC 3164 has a timestamp in local time written Mmm dd hh:mm:ss, with no year and no time zone, followed by a hostname and a tag, and the whole packet must be 1024 bytes or less. RFC 5424 adds a version number (1), a full date and time with a T between them, a hostname of up to 255 characters, an application name, a process identifier and a message identifier, any of which may be the nil value, a hyphen; then structured data, named parameters in square brackets that a parser can read without guessing; then the message, optionally UTF-8 marked with a byte order mark. Receivers must accept messages of 480 octets and should accept 2048. A collector therefore sees both formats from different sources, often on the same port, and a parser that assumes one will mangle the other.

Transport, and why it matters. Classic syslog is the User Datagram Protocol (UDP) to port 514, and RFC 5426 of March 2009, which standardizes it, is frank about the consequences: datagrams are lost in congestion and nothing retransmits them, there is no congestion control, arrival order is not a reliable guide to the order of events, and the transport provides neither sender authentication nor protection against forged messages. It allows UDP only on managed networks where the path has been provisioned for syslog and says that Transport Layer Security (TLS) should be used everywhere else. The irony is operational: messages are most likely to be lost exactly when a device is under the stress you most want recorded. Legacy syslog over the Transmission Control Protocol (TCP) spread without a standard; RFC 6587 of April 2012 records it as Historic, with two framing methods, octet counting and non-transparent framing, the second with inherent problems. The standard secure path is RFC 5425, syslog over TLS on TCP port 6514, whose cipher suites RFC 9662 updated in October 2024: TLS_ECDHE_RSA_WITH_AES_128_GCM_SHA256 is now mandatory and preferred, TLS 1.2 remains mandatory and TLS 1.3 should be supported and preferred. RFC 5848 of May 2010 adds signatures to the messages themselves, so that integrity survives relays.

On real systems. On Linux, logger is the quickest test: logger -n 192.0.2.10 -d -p local3.info sends one UDP message with facility local3 and severity info, the default otherwise being user.notice, and --rfc5424 or --rfc3164 picks the format; -T uses TCP to the syslog-conn port, often 601. F5 BIG-IP sends to the remote-servers listed under sys syslog, with a remote-port of 514 unless changed. FortiOS configures remote logging under config log syslogd setting, where mode is udp by default, legacy-reliable for RFC 3195 or reliable for RFC 6587 over TCP, the port is 514, the format can be the default, CSV, CEF, RFC 5424 or JSON, the facility defaults to local7, and encryption (enc-algorithm) is disabled until someone turns it on. Each default is reasonable on its own; together they send logs unauthenticated, unencrypted and unacknowledged until someone changes them.

What goes wrong. Besides inverted severity filters and loss under load, three failures recur. Time: a BSD timestamp has no year and no zone, and RFC 5426 notes that messages from hosts whose clocks are not synchronized cannot be ordered, so log correlation without the Network Time Protocol (NTP) is guesswork. Size: a stack trace or a long web address is truncated at 1024 or 2048 bytes, or dropped. Trust: anyone who can reach UDP 514 can write convincing entries into the record, a reason to accept syslog only from known senders and to prefer TLS with certificates. The reason to care is that logs are the evidence for an incident that has not happened yet: a gap in them is discovered at the worst possible moment. The numbers worth keeping are UDP 514, TCP 6514, facility times 8 plus severity, 0 is the most urgent, 24 facilities, 1024 and 2048 bytes, and 2009 for RFC 5424.

netflow.def: Flow telemetry: routers export who-talked-to-whom records (addresses, ports, bytes, duration) so you can see traffic patterns without capturing packets.
netflow.context: Cisco's original; IPFIX is the IETF standard descendant, sFlow the sampling cousin.

port-mirroring.def: Copying a port's or VLAN's traffic to another port so an analyser or IDS (intrusion detection system) can watch without sitting inline.
port-mirroring.context: SPAN mirrors locally, RSPAN across switches, ERSPAN across routed networks - each hop adds ways to drop packets silently.

jumbo-frames.def: Ethernet frames carrying more than the standard 1500-byte payload, typically 9000: fewer headers per gigabyte, and misery when one hop in the path disagrees.
jumbo-frames.context: The 1500-byte limit is a 1980 economic decision that outlived its reasons; jumbos raise full-frame wire efficiency for TCP (Transmission Control Protocol) from about 94.9% to 99.1% and, historically more important, cut per-packet processor and interrupt work. The catch is agreement: every device in the layer 2 domain must accept the size, because a mismatch in MTU (maximum transmission unit) does not degrade politely: it black-holes. That is why jumbos thrive on controlled paths (storage, replication, overlay underlays inside the data centre) and die crossing the internet.
jumbo-frames.depth:
What they are, and what they are not. A jumbo frame is an Ethernet frame whose payload exceeds the 1,500 bytes the standard allows, almost always configured as an MTU (maximum transmission unit) of 9,000 bytes. It is a convention, not a standard. When the IEEE (Institute of Electrical and Electronics Engineers) 802.3 working group last enlarged the frame, in 802.3as-2006, its objectives said to maintain the maximum data field length of 1,500 octets and to grow the frame only for prefix and suffix fields; David Law's 2011 summary of the result lists 1,518-octet basic frames, 1,522-octet frames with an 802.1Q tag and 2,000-octet envelope frames, with the note that jumbo frames are not supported. So the maximum a given switch or network card accepts is whatever its vendor chose, and two devices that both 'support jumbo frames' can still disagree by a few hundred bytes. A frame a few bytes over 1,518 because of a tag or a label is a baby giant, a different and smaller problem; and other link layers were never bound by 1,500 at all, 802.11 carrying up to 2,304 bytes and FDDI, the "Fiber Distributed Data Interface" ring, about 4,352.

Why 1,500. The number dates from the first Ethernet specifications around 1980. Ben Cartwright-Cox's history of it quotes an email from Ethernet's original designer: packet buffer memory had a part in the choice, and a longer maximum, had it raised the cost of interface cards, might have kept Ethernet from being widely accepted. The 1980 Ethernet paper also weighed the efficiency of large packets against the time one station could hold a shared segment. Those reasons have gone, memory is cheap and links are switched and full duplex, but the internet as a whole settled on 1,500 because every Ethernet in a path had to carry it.

What they buy. Each frame on the wire costs 38 bytes besides its payload: a 7-byte preamble and 1-byte start-of-frame delimiter, a 14-byte header (two 6-byte addresses and a 2-byte type), a 4-byte frame check sequence and the 96-bit (12-byte) gap between frames. TCP (Transmission Control Protocol) over IPv4 (Internet Protocol version 4) without options leaves 1,460 bytes of data in a 1,500-byte packet, so a full standard frame carries 1,460 useful bytes for every 1,538 sent, 94.9 per cent; at 9,000 bytes the figure is 8,960 for 9,038, 99.1 per cent. The larger gain, historically, was per-packet work: six times fewer frames for the same data means fewer interrupts, header lookups and protocol passes. Modern hosts recover much of that without jumbo frames, because segmentation offloads let the stack hand the network card one large segment that the card cuts into wire-sized frames, and receive offload stitches arriving frames back together; that is why, on ordinary mixed traffic, the gain is usually negligible, while storage networks and backup traffic, long streams of full-sized frames, are where jumbo frames earn their keep. Cartwright-Cox's rough estimate for one large exchange point shows the stakes at internet scale: at least a fifth of the packets were maximum size, and their headers alone accounted for about 246 Gbit/s at peak, against roughly 41 Gbit/s had they been jumbo frames.

How they fail. Every device in the layer 2 path must accept the size, hosts, switch ports, VLAN (virtual local area network) interfaces, hypervisor switches, firewalls and router interfaces alike, and one left at the default silently drops the oversized frames. A switch has no way to say why: the only mechanism for reporting a packet too big is Path MTU Discovery, defined in RFC (Request for Comments) 1191 of November 1990, in which a router that cannot forward a datagram with the Don't Fragment (DF) bit set discards it and returns an ICMP (Internet Control Message Protocol) 'fragmentation needed and DF set' message. Within one layer 2 domain there is no router to send it. The result is a network that passes small packets and pings, completes TCP handshakes, and then stalls on real transfers, a symptom that looks like an application fault and is reported as one.

Finding the mismatch. The diagnostic converts the mystery into a number: send a ping with a large payload and fragmentation forbidden. On Linux, ping -M do -s 8972 sends 8,972 data bytes, which with the 8-byte ICMP header and 20-byte IPv4 header make exactly 9,000; with -M do the kernel refuses locally if its own interface MTU is smaller, and -M probe skips that local check. On Windows the equivalent is ping -f -l 8972. Walk the path one device at a time, lowering the size until replies return, and the largest size that passes, plus 28, is the effective MTU of the path.

Where they belong. Jumbo frames thrive on paths one team controls end to end: storage, replication, and the underlay beneath overlays. The VXLAN (Virtual eXtensible Local Area Network) specification, RFC 7348, says tunnel endpoints must not fragment VXLAN packets, allows the far end to silently discard fragments, and recommends that the MTU across the physical network be raised to accommodate the encapsulation, which adds outer Ethernet, IP (Internet Protocol) and UDP (User Datagram Protocol) headers and its own 8-byte header to every frame; a jumbo underlay is the usual way to keep a 1,500-byte MTU inside the overlay. They die crossing the internet: some transit carriers run a 9,000-byte MTU, but most do not, and any path that crosses one 1,500-byte link is a 1,500-byte path.

Numbers worth remembering: 1,500 bytes standard payload and 9,000 typical jumbo; 1,518, 1,522 and 2,000 octets for the standard's basic, tagged and envelope frames; 38 bytes of per-frame overhead; 94.9 against 99.1 per cent efficiency for TCP; and 8,972 as the ping size that tests a 9,000-byte MTU.

duplex-mismatch.def: One end at full duplex, the other at half: the link works, slowly and with late collisions. It was the classic 'the network is weird' root cause of the 2000s.
duplex-mismatch.context: Usually born from one side hard-coded and the other autonegotiating; the auto-negotiation side falls back to half duplex. The link comes up, pings and small transfers pass, and throughput collapses only under load, which is why it hides so well. Cisco still ranks it among the most common causes of performance problems on 10/100 Mb/s links, and the counters on the two ends, read together, give it away.
duplex-mismatch.depth:
What it is. A duplex mismatch is a twisted-pair Ethernet link whose two ends disagree about whether they may transmit and receive at the same time. One end runs full duplex and sends whenever it has a frame; the other runs half duplex, carrier sense multiple access with collision detection (CSMA/CD), and treats anything it receives while transmitting as a collision. Nothing in the protocol notices the disagreement. A patent Network Appliance filed in May 2000 and was granted in August 2005, for a method of detecting the condition automatically, describes the gap plainly: the Ethernet standard has no logic to detect and resolve such parameter mismatches, so finding one is manual work that means inspecting the configuration at both ends, which often belong to different teams or organizations.

How one is made. The mechanism is auto-negotiation's fallback. A port set to negotiate that hears nothing from a fixed-speed neighbour uses parallel detection, which can sense the speed from the signal but, in the University of New Hampshire InterOperability Laboratory's words, can never parallel detect to a full duplex link, so it assumes half duplex. Fix one end at 100 Mb/s full duplex, leave the other on auto, and the mismatch has been built on purpose. Cisco lists the other ways in: someone reconfigures one side of a link and forgets the other; after a reset, negotiation leaves the two partners with different settings; and some hardware cannot negotiate at all in certain set-ups, its example being a WS-6748-GE-TX module connected to a network tap. Modular SFP (small form-factor pluggable) and GBIC (gigabit interface converter) ports do not negotiate either, so the habit of hard-coding spreads from them to copper ports where it does harm.

What it looks like. The symptoms split by side. On the half-duplex end, frames from the full-duplex partner arrive while it is still sending, so it counts collisions, including late collisions, and Cisco's signature adds a rapid increase of frame check sequence (FCS) and alignment errors there; on the full-duplex end, which never expects collisions, the frames the other side aborted arrive as runts and FCS errors. Every damaged frame is lost, and the loss falls on whichever protocol carries the data, usually TCP (Transmission Control Protocol), which retransmits and slows down. Light traffic rarely overlaps in time, so the link stays up, ping succeeds and a short test passes; a file transfer or backup, with data flowing one way and acknowledgements the other, collides constantly and crawls. Because both directions are in use at once only under load, the fault hides until load arrives.

Reading the counters. The counters tell you which end is half duplex and which is full. On Cisco switches the interface counters to check are alignment and FCS errors, collisions and late collisions, runts and CRC (cyclic redundancy check) errors, and the rule that settles the question is Cisco's own: collisions must not be seen on interfaces configured as full duplex. On Linux, ip -s -s link show prints the same information under other names. The kernel defines tx_window_errors, shown as window, as transmission errors due to late collisions, those after the first 64 bytes of a frame and the equivalent of the IEEE (Institute of Electrical and Electronics Engineers) 802.3 counter aLateCollisions; rx_crc_errors as the 802.3 frame check sequence errors; rx_frame_errors as alignment errors; and collisions as collisions during transmission. Late collisions on one side and FCS errors on the other, rising together with traffic, are the fingerprint.

Letting the protocols tell you. Discovery protocols carry each end's view of the link to the other. Cisco Discovery Protocol (CDP) compares duplex settings and logs %CDP-4-DUPLEX_MISMATCH when they differ, though Cisco stresses that CDP reports the problem and does not fix it. The vendor-neutral Link Layer Discovery Protocol (LLDP) carries an IEEE 802.3 MAC/PHY (media access control and physical layer) element with the auto-negotiation support and state and the operational speed and duplex, so comparing the two neighbours' advertisements, with lldpcli on Linux or a switch's LLDP neighbour detail, shows the disagreement without touching the far end. The Network Appliance patent took an active approach instead: it induces traffic from the partner and checks whether a substantial share of the resulting collisions are late ones.

Fixing and preventing it. The rule is about pairs: both ends on auto-negotiation, or both fixed to the same speed and duplex, never one of each. Cisco's advice is to leave auto-negotiation on for devices compliant with 802.3u, the Fast Ethernet standard that defined it. From 1000BASE-T on the question mostly answers itself, because the IEEE 802.3 working group's interpretation 2-07/05 confirms that all 1000BASE-T physical layers shall support auto-negotiation, which there decides not only duplex but which end is the clock master; selecting 1000BASE-T still requires negotiation, and the interpretation's way to fix the speed is to keep negotiating while advertising only 1000BASE-T. After a correction, clear the counters on both ends and watch them under real load, since a quiet link proves nothing.

Where it still lives. Faster links have largely removed the problem: speeds from 10 Gb/s up are full duplex only, as the duplex entry explains. The mismatch survives where 10 and 100 Mb/s copper survives, in printers, building management controllers, industrial and medical devices, out-of-band management ports and old servers whose configuration someone hard-coded years ago, and in any change window where one end of a link is reconfigured and the other is not. Numbers worth remembering: late collisions are those after the first 64 bytes, collisions on a full-duplex port are always wrong, parallel detection always lands on half duplex, and the fix is always applied to both ends.

poe.def: Power over Ethernet (PoE): the switch, or a midspan injector, sends direct current (DC) down the same twisted pairs as the data, so phones, cameras and wireless access points need no mains outlet. IEEE 802.3af (2003), 802.3at (2009) and 802.3bt (2018) define it.
poe.context: The power sourcing equipment (PSE) supplies the power and the powered device (PD) draws it, after a detection and classification exchange that tells each side what the other can do. Type 1 (802.3af) provides up to 15.4 W at the PSE and 13 W at the device; Type 2 (802.3at) 30 W and 25.5 W, both over two pairs; 802.3bt adds Type 3, 60 W and 51 W, and Type 4, 90 W and 71.3 W, using all four pairs for Class 5 and above. The difference between the two figures is what the cable is allowed to lose, and the heat that power puts into a bundle of cables is why ANSI/TIA-568.2-E now carries an annex on power delivery over twisted pair.
poe.depth:
Three standards. The Institute of Electrical and Electronics Engineers (IEEE) 802.3af task force finished its work with the approval of IEEE Std 802.3af-2003 by the IEEE Standards Board in June 2003. Its successor, 802.3at, was approved in September 2009, and 802.3bt, which brought power over all four pairs, was approved by the IEEE Standards Association Standards Board on 27 September 2018.

Types and classes. The Ethernet Alliance's overview of 802.3bt sets out the ladder. Eight classes are defined by the power the power sourcing equipment (PSE) must supply: 4, 7, 15.4 and 30 W for Classes 1 to 4, then 45, 60, 75 and 90 W for Classes 5 to 8, against 3.84, 6.49, 13, 25.5, 40, 51, 62 and 71.3 W available at the powered device (PD). Types 1 and 2 deliver power over two pairs only; Types 3 and 4 may use two or four, and Class 5 and higher always use four. The generations interoperate: a Type 2 PSE powers a Type 1 device, and a Type 2 device on an older Type 1 PSE recognizes it and limits itself to 13 W. The newer types also require full hardware classification, which makes the negotiation more robust, and a PSE has a total power budget as well as a per-port one, so the number of devices that can run at full class depends on the switch, not only on the port.

The cable carries the cost. Current flowing in copper warms it, which is why PoE became a cabling question as well as a switching one. According to Siemon, ANSI/TIA-568.2-E of 2024 brought the guidance on power delivery into the cabling standard as Annex H, with installation and design requirements covering cable categories, cable types and operating conditions, including pathways and bundling. That is the practical lesson: with the higher classes, how many cables share a bundle and a pathway, and how warm that space runs, are design inputs alongside the category of the cable.

sfp.def: Small Form-factor Pluggable: the swappable module that gives a switch port its physical medium - copper or fibre, short reach or long haul.
sfp.context: SFP+ carries 10G, QSFP bundles four lanes; the port is a socket, the transceiver is the decision.
sfp.depth:
An SFP is a contract as much as a module: a cage shape, an electrical interface and a management interface that let any compliant optic fill any compliant port. The management side is the specification SFF-8472, whose second address, A2h, 'is used to access measurements of transceiver temperature, internally measured supply voltage, TX bias current, TX output power, received optical power'. That is digital optical monitoring, read on Cisco IOS with 'show interface transceiver' and on Junos with 'show interfaces diagnostics optics'.

The reading worth learning is received power. Set against the receiver sensitivity in the module's data sheet, it is the link's loss budget measured instead of estimated, so a link whose margin is shrinking shows it there before it starts dropping frames. Not every module supports the diagnostics; the data sheet says which.

lldp.def: Link Layer Discovery Protocol (LLDP), defined in IEEE (Institute of Electrical and Electronics Engineers) 802.1AB: each port of a device announces who it is, which port it is and what it can do to the device at the other end of the cable, turning 'what is on the other end?' into a show command.
lldp.context: Link Layer Discovery Protocol (LLDP) is the vendor-neutral successor to Cisco Discovery Protocol (CDP) and the other proprietary discovery protocols it borrowed from, standardized by the IEEE (Institute of Electrical and Electronics Engineers) as 802.1AB. Every port sends periodic one-way advertisements to a multicast address that bridges do not forward, so what a switch learns is exactly what sits at the far end of each link, kept in a management information base (MIB) readable from the command line or over SNMP (Simple Network Management Protocol). IP (Internet Protocol) phones and other media endpoints extend it as LLDP-MED (Media Endpoint Discovery) for voice VLANs (virtual local area networks), location and Power over Ethernet (PoE) hints.
lldp.depth:
What it is. Link Layer Discovery Protocol (LLDP) is specified in IEEE (Institute of Electrical and Electronics Engineers) 802.1AB, Station and Media Access Control Connectivity Discovery, which the IEEE summarizes as a protocol and a set of managed objects for discovering the physical topology from adjacent stations in IEEE 802 LANs (local area networks). The first edition, 802.1AB-2005, was approved on 20 March 2005 after a project that started in September 2002; it was revised in 2009 and again in 2016, when the edition approved on 29 January 2016 became the one most equipment cites. Two amendments followed in December 2021: 802.1ABcu added a YANG (Yet Another Next Generation) data model for configuration and status, and 802.1ABdh added a way to carry a set of TLVs (type-length-value elements) too large for a single frame across several. The newest edition, 802.1AB-2026, was approved on 25 September 2026 and published on 6 November 2026. The 2016 text can be downloaded at no cost through the IEEE GET Program. LLDP was modelled on the proprietary discovery protocols that came first, Cisco Discovery Protocol (CDP) and Extreme Discovery Protocol (EDP) among them, and Paul Congdon's 2002 drafts even had a protocol header with a version field; the final standard dropped the header and simply mandates certain TLVs.

On the wire. An LLDP data unit (LLDPDU) travels in an Ethernet frame with EtherType 0x88CC, the value IANA (Internet Assigned Numbers Authority) lists for IEEE 802.1AB, or over other 802 networks behind a SNAP (Subnetwork Access Protocol) header carrying the same EtherType. The usual destination is 01-80-C2-00-00-0E, an address in the range the IEEE reserves for protocols confined to a single LAN, so a bridge conforming to 802.1D-2004 does not forward it, and the frame is sent untagged. The body is a chain of TLVs, and four are mandatory, in this order: Chassis ID (type 1), Port ID (type 2), Time To Live (type 3) and End of LLDPDU (type 0). The optional ones carry the port description, the system name and description, the system capabilities (bridge, router, wireless access point and so on) and a management address. Organizationally specific TLVs extend the set: the IEEE 802.1 group's port VLAN ID and VLAN names, the IEEE 802.3 group's MAC/PHY (media access control and physical layer) configuration and status (auto-negotiation support, the operational speed and duplex), power via the media dependent interface (MDI) and link aggregation, and the TIA's (Telecommunications Industry Association) LLDP-MED set.

How it behaves. LLDP talks and never asks. Allied Telesis puts it plainly: advertisements do not solicit responses and received advertisements are not acknowledged, and the protocol is one hop, reaching only devices connected directly or through a hub or repeater. Each port can be set to transmit, to receive or both. By default a port advertises every 30 seconds and puts a Time To Live of 120 seconds in its frames, the transmit interval multiplied by a holdtime multiplier of 4; a receiver keeps the neighbour's entry in its remote systems MIB until that time runs out, so a neighbour that vanishes silently lingers for up to two minutes. A port on which LLDP is disabled by command sends a final shutdown LLDPDU with a Time To Live of 0, which tells the neighbour to delete the entry at once. A transmission delay of 2 seconds stops a burst of changes from producing a burst of frames, and a reinitialization delay of 2 seconds spaces disabling and re-enabling. LLDP runs on physical ports, not on the aggregated link or the VLAN interface above them, and the Allied Telesis guide notes two interactions worth knowing: a port blocked by spanning tree still sends and receives LLDP, while a port blocked by 802.1X authorization does not. Changes in the neighbour table can raise the SNMP notification lldpRemTablesChange.

LLDP-MED. Media Endpoint Discovery is the extension for phones and other endpoints, specified in ANSI/TIA-1057-2006 (ANSI being the American National Standards Institute) rather than by the IEEE. Its network policy TLV tells a phone which VLAN ID, user priority and Differentiated Services Code Point (DSCP) to apply to voice traffic, so a phone plugged into an ordinary data port tags its own voice frames while the computer behind it stays untagged. Its other TLVs carry capabilities, extended power management for PoE (Power over Ethernet) devices, inventory (hardware, firmware and software revisions, serial number, manufacturer, model and asset ID) and location, in coordinate, civic address or Emergency Location Identification Number (ELIN) form, the last a number used by emergency call services, typically 10 digits in North America. Cisco's Catalyst 9300 enables every LLDP-MED TLV as soon as LLDP itself is on, and advises switching off LLDP's power management TLV on interfaces where CDP already negotiates power.

On real equipment. On a Cisco Catalyst 9300 running IOS XE 17.12 LLDP is disabled by default, globally and per interface: lldp run turns it on, lldp transmit and lldp receive set the direction per port, and "show lldp neighbors", with detail, lists what was learned, with a 30-second timer, a 120-second holdtime and a 2-second reinitialization delay as defaults. On Linux, lldpd, an implementation under the ISC (Internet Systems Consortium) licence, now at version 1.0.23, speaks LLDP and also CDP, EDP, Nortel's SONMP (SynOptics Network Management Protocol) and the Foundry Discovery Protocol (FDP), advertises MAC/PHY, power, link aggregation and LLDP-MED TLVs, and answers "lldpcli show neighbors detail" or SNMP queries. In Wireshark the display filter is lldp and the capture filter ether proto 0x88cc. Because the 802.3 TLV carries the auto-negotiation state and the operational speed and duplex, comparing the two ends' advertisements is one of the quickest ways to confirm a suspected duplex mismatch.

What goes wrong. The information that helps an administrator map a network is handed to anyone on the wire: system names, software descriptions, management addresses and port names, sent unauthenticated to whatever is plugged in. The common practice is to keep LLDP on infrastructure links and on access ports that need LLDP-MED, and to stop transmitting on ports that face untrusted or external networks. The receive side is attack surface too, because every discovery daemon parses frames that any station on the segment can craft: the CVE (Common Vulnerabilities and Exposures) record CVE-2023-41910, published on 5 September 2023, describes an out-of-bounds heap read in lldpd before 1.0.17, triggered by a crafted CDP packet. Operationally, the 120-second Time To Live means a neighbour table can describe a device unplugged two minutes ago, and a port that hears more than one neighbour usually has an unmanaged switch or a hub behind it.

Neighbours and numbers. LLDP is not IPv6 Neighbor Discovery, which works at layer 3 and resolves addresses, and it is not CDP, though the two often run side by side on the same switch. The figures worth keeping are EtherType 0x88CC, destination 01-80-C2-00-00-0E, four mandatory TLVs (types 1, 2, 3 and 0), a 30-second interval, a multiplier of 4 and a 120-second Time To Live, a 2-second delay between frames, and a Time To Live of 0 for goodbye.

ecmp.def: Equal-cost multipath (ECMP): when a router holds several routes to one destination that tie on cost, it installs them all and spreads traffic across their next hops, normally per flow by hashing header fields rather than per packet, so each flow keeps its order on a single path.
ecmp.context: ECMP (equal-cost multipath) is the routing table's built-in load sharing. OSPF (Open Shortest Path First) and IS-IS (Intermediate System to Intermediate System) produce it naturally when shortest paths tie, BGP (Border Gateway Protocol) only when multipath is switched on, and static routes when several share distance and priority. The forwarding plane picks a next hop by hashing the fields that identify a flow, the source and destination addresses and often the ports and protocol of the five-tuple, so per-flow hashing keeps the packets of one connection in order on one path. The costs come from the same design: elephant flows can still make one path unfairly heavy, a change in the set of next hops moves flows that were in progress, and a member that silently drops traffic hides behind the paths that work.
ecmp.depth:
Equal-cost multipath (ECMP), in the words of RFC (Request for Comments) 2992, is a routing technique for routing packets along multiple paths of equal cost, where the forwarding engine identifies the paths by next hop and has to decide, packet by packet, which one to use. It is a property of the routing table, not a separate protocol: the routing protocol or the static configuration supplies several best routes to one prefix, and the forwarding plane spreads traffic over them. It is not link aggregation, which bundles parallel links between two neighbours at Layer 2 under one logical interface, although the two share the same hashing machinery and RFC 7424 treats them together as the standard ways of scaling capacity. It is not unequal-cost load sharing either, which a few protocols and platforms offer as weighted ECMP or variance, and it is not a load balancer in the application sense: nothing in ECMP looks at server health or connection counts.

In OSPF (Open Shortest Path First), equal cost is a by-product of the shortest-path calculation. RFC 2328 says that when several equal-cost routes to a destination exist they are all discovered and used, and that traffic is distributed equally among them. Each vertex in the calculation carries a list of next hops rather than one; when a second path to a vertex ties with the one already found, its next hops are added to the set instead of replacing it, every destination beyond inherits both, and network vertices must be taken before router vertices when distances tie so that all equal-cost paths are found. A footnote concedes that, strictly speaking, the result is then no longer a tree. The standard also lets an implementation keep only a fixed number of equal-cost routes per destination. FRRouting is generally compiled with a 64-way limit and prints the extra next hops as further via lines under the same prefix in show ip route; FortiGate caps the set with ecmp-max-paths in config system settings, where a value of 1 disables ECMP altogether.

Ties are fragile. In a six-router example, raising one link's metric from 1 to 20 moved three destinations off one first hop and ended their split, and a link failure collapses the pairs to a single next hop. The opposite trap comes from OSPF's reference bandwidth. The cost of an interface is the reference bandwidth divided by the interface's bandwidth, rounded up to 1 when the result is smaller, and the reference is 100 Mbit/s by default on platforms such as Extreme's SLX-OS, so every link of 100 Mbit/s or faster costs 1 and paths tie on hop count rather than on speed: a 1 Gbit/s path and a 100 Gbit/s path of the same length become equals, and ECMP faithfully sends them the same share. Raising the reference bandwidth consistently on every router in the domain is what restores the difference.

BGP (Border Gateway Protocol) is the opposite case: its decision process exists to select one best path, so multipath has to be enabled and the meaning of equal defined. RFC 7938, which describes BGP-only data centre fabrics, says that most BGP implementations treat paths as equal for ECMP if they match up to and including step (e) of the decision process in RFC 4271, the interior cost to the next hop. In those fabrics ECMP is the fundamental load-sharing mechanism of the Clos topology: the number of paths between two leaf devices equals the number of devices in the middle stage, and a fabric built from 64-port switches needs a fan-out of 32. The same RFC discusses ECMP across neighbours in different autonomous systems and weighted ECMP for paths of unequal capacity. FortiOS follows the same rule for BGP, aggregating paths that tie through the RFC 4271 tie-breakers including the interior gateway protocol (IGP) metric, without evaluating the last two conditions (lowest router identifier and lowest peer address), and only once ebgp-multipath or ibgp-multipath is enabled, both being off by default.

How the next hop is chosen matters more than the routing. RFC 2991 (November 2000) explains why naive per-packet schemes such as round-robin are harmful: paths with different MTUs (maximum transmission units) make the path MTU change packet by packet and defeat path MTU discovery; paths with different latencies reorder packets, and when three or more packets arrive before a late one TCP enters fast retransmit and resends data that was never lost; and ping and traceroute become unreliable or simply wrong. The remedy is to keep every packet of a flow on the same path, a flow being whatever the router hashes: destination only, source and destination, or those plus protocol and ports. Including transport ports spreads traffic better but has its own trap, since IP fragments after the first carry no port numbers. Its companion, RFC 2992, analyses three hashing methods by how many flows move when a next hop is added or removed. Modulo-N, a hash taken modulo the number of next hops, is fast but moves (N-1)/N of all flows. Hash-threshold, in which a CRC16 (16-bit cyclic redundancy check) key is mapped onto equal regions of the key space (four next hops get 65,536 divided by 4 values each), moves between a quarter and a half of them. Highest random weight moves only 1/N, at roughly N times the lookup cost. RFC 7938 recommends consistent hashing for the same reason, noting that it costs extra TCAM (ternary content-addressable memory) in hardware; FRRouting's resilient next-hop groups, built from hash buckets, are an implementation of the idea.

What gets hashed is configuration, and the defaults differ. On Linux, the net.ipv4.fib_multipath_hash_policy sysctl selects 0, Layer 3 (source and destination addresses, plus the flow label for IPv6), which is the default; 1, Layer 4, the standard five-tuple; 2, Layer 3 or the inner Layer 3 header when one is present; or 3, a custom set of fields chosen in fib_multipath_hash_fields. FortiGate's v4-ecmp-mode defaults to source-ip-based, in which every session from one source address takes the same path; the alternatives are source-dest-ip-based, weight-based (where weights of 80 and 20 send 80 and 20 per cent of sessions) and usage-based, which fills one interface up to a threshold and spills over to the next. FortiOS considers ECMP only after policy routes, and only among routes with the same destination and costs (for static routes, the same distance and priority) from the same protocol. A source-only hash puts all of one heavy user's traffic on one link, which is often exactly what an administrator did not expect.

Hashing works well only under conditions that real traffic often breaks. RFC 7424 (January 2015) lists them: the flows must hash fairly uniformly, each flow's rate must be much smaller than the link capacity, and rates must not differ dramatically. Long-lived large flows, which it puts at more than about 5 per cent of a link's bandwidth, IPsec tunnels across a provider backbone or storage backups in a data centre, defeat it, and the RFC describes routers that recognize such flows and place them deliberately. Tunnels make the problem worse because they hide the inner flows behind one outer header; the answers are to put entropy where transit routers can see it, through the IPv6 flow label (RFC 6438, November 2011) or MPLS (Multiprotocol Label Switching) entropy labels flagged by an Entropy Label Indicator (RFC 6790, November 2012), or to hash on the inner header as Linux's policy 2 does. Stacking hashes has its own failure: RFC 7938 warns that hierarchical ECMP, Layer 3 ECMP over Layer 2 link aggregation, raises the risk of flow polarization because less entropy is left for the second stage.

Spreading traffic can hide failures. RFC 9764 (April 2025) notes that BFD (Bidirectional Forwarding Detection) control packets may travel only along links that are up, so a session can stay Up while some component links drop traffic, and that no general-purpose BFD mechanism exercises every path of a multihop ECMP set; for a link aggregation group, RFC 7130 (February 2014) runs one micro-BFD session per member instead. Error messages can be misrouted too. RFC 7690 (January 2016) describes the case of anycast services behind ECMP: an ICMPv6 (Internet Control Message Protocol for IPv6) Packet Too Big message about a server's flow is addressed to the shared anycast address, hashes on its own outer headers, and usually reaches a different server from the one that needs it, so path MTU discovery fails; the mitigation is to hash on the flow quoted inside the ICMP payload. Each router also hashes on its own, so the return direction of a connection need not mirror its forward path, which is harmless for stateless routers and a problem the moment a stateful firewall sits on only one of them.

leaf-spine.def: The modern data-center fabric: every leaf switch connects to every spine, giving any two servers the same short predictable path.
leaf-spine.context: Replaced the three-tier core/distribution/access design as east-west traffic overtook north-south.

vxlan.def: Virtual Extensible LAN (VXLAN; LAN, local area network) carries Ethernet frames across a routed IP (Internet Protocol) network by encapsulating them in UDP (User Datagram Protocol), with a 24-bit segment identifier that allows about 16 million segments instead of the 4,094 usable VLANs (virtual local area networks) of IEEE (Institute of Electrical and Electronics Engineers) 802.1Q.
vxlan.context: Virtual Extensible LAN (VXLAN) is the overlay under most cloud and modern data-centre fabrics. A VXLAN tunnel endpoint (VTEP), in a hypervisor or a switch, wraps each Ethernet frame in a VXLAN header carrying the segment's VXLAN Network Identifier (VNI), then in UDP (User Datagram Protocol) to port 4789 and an outer IP (Internet Protocol) header, so any routed network can carry Layer 2 segments between racks or sites. The format says nothing about how endpoints find each other: the original specification flooded through IP multicast and learned from traffic, and production fabrics now usually run EVPN (Ethernet virtual private network) in BGP (Border Gateway Protocol) as the control plane. The cost is 50 bytes or more per packet and an underlay maximum transmission unit (MTU) raised to match.
vxlan.depth:
What it is. Virtual Extensible LAN (VXLAN) is specified in RFC (Request for Comments) 7348, published in August 2014 as an Informational document through the Independent Submission stream, under the title 'A Framework for Overlaying Virtualized Layer 2 Networks over Layer 3 Networks'. The problem it named was the multi-tenant data centre: the VLAN (virtual local area network) limit of 4,094 is inadequate when every tenant wants its own segments, and tenants assign media access control (MAC) addresses independently, so addresses overlap. VXLAN answers with a 24-bit segment identifier, the VXLAN Network Identifier (VNI), which the RFC says allows up to 16 M segments in one administrative domain (16,777,216 in the Linux documentation's arithmetic). The VNI scopes the inner frame, so overlapping MAC addresses in different segments never cross over. It is an encapsulation and a framework, not a security boundary, and, as the later Geneve specification observes, the VXLAN packet format has carried a wide variety of control planes since.

The encapsulation. A VXLAN tunnel endpoint (VTEP) takes the original Ethernet frame, without its frame check sequence (FCS), and prepends an 8-byte VXLAN header, a UDP (User Datagram Protocol) header, an outer IP (Internet Protocol) header and an outer Ethernet header, in which a VLAN tag is optional. The VXLAN header holds 8 bits of flags, in which the I flag must be set to 1 for a valid VNI, 24 reserved bits, the 24-bit VNI and 8 more reserved bits; reserved fields are sent as zero and ignored on receipt. The UDP destination port is 4789, assigned by IANA (the Internet Assigned Numbers Authority), and must be configurable because early implementations used others. The source port should be a hash of the inner frame's headers, preferably in the dynamic range 49152 to 65535, which gives the equal-cost multipath (ECMP) hashing of the underlay the entropy it needs to spread different flows across links; the UDP checksum should be sent as zero. The arithmetic follows: the outer IP packet is the inner frame plus 36 bytes (VXLAN 8, UDP 8, and 20 for an IPv4 (IP version 4) header), so a full 1,500-byte inner IP packet with its 14-byte Ethernet header becomes a 1,550-byte outer packet, 1,554 with an inner 802.1Q tag and 1,570 over an IPv6 (IP version 6) underlay. Extreme Networks' Switch Engine guide states the same in its own terms: up to a 54-byte header, and an IP MTU (maximum transmission unit) of at least 1,554 bytes on the network-side interfaces and on every transit node.

How endpoints learn. RFC 7348 describes flood and learn. The receiving VTEP checks that the VNI is valid and that a host on it owns the inner destination MAC, strips the outer headers and delivers the frame, which never shows any trace of the tunnel; it also records the inner source MAC against the outer source IP, so the reply need not be flooded. Broadcast, unknown unicast and multicast (BUM) frames go to an IP multicast group mapped to the VNI, with VTEPs sending (*,G) joins and the underlay running Protocol Independent Multicast Sparse Mode (PIM-SM), or Internet Group Management Protocol (IGMP) snooping on a Layer 2 underlay. Underlays without multicast use head-end replication instead: Extreme's guide calls this unicast VXLAN, in which each BUM frame is copied to every remote endpoint, against multicast VXLAN, which needs multicast in the Layer 3 network. Linux describes its implementation as a 1 to N network, not a point-to-point tunnel, that learns like a bridge or uses static forwarding entries.

Where it came from, and where it is going. VMware and Cisco announced VXLAN at VMworld on 30 August 2011, with Arista Networks, Emulex, Broadcom and Intel, and sent a draft specification to the Internet Engineering Task Force (IETF); The Register reported VMware's chief technology officer, Steve Herrod, presenting the technical preview, and the 24-bit VNI with its 16 million segments was in the draft from the start. IANA registered port 4789 on 19 April 2013. RFC 7348's authors came from Storvisor, Cumulus Networks, Arista, Broadcom, Cisco, VMware, Intel and Red Hat. Because it came through the Independent stream, VXLAN had no IETF process for extending its header. That is changing: the IETF's draft-ietf-nvo3-rfc7348bis-12, dated 22 October 2026, obsoletes RFC 7348 on publication, moves VXLAN into the IETF stream, and allows extensions that add to the header with registration at IANA, while keeping the format fully compatible. On 5 November 2026 the IETF Datatracker showed it in the RFC Editor queue, intended as Informational, and IANA's port registry already cites it for 4789; until an RFC number is assigned, RFC 7348 remains the reference.

The control plane most fabrics use. Flooding and data-plane learning scale poorly, and RFC 8365 (March 2018, Standards Track) specifies the replacement: Ethernet virtual private network (EVPN), carried in the Border Gateway Protocol (BGP), as the control plane of a network virtualization overlay. BGP distributes MAC and IP reachability, so unknown unicast and Address Resolution Protocol (ARP) frames need not be flooded; route reflectors replace a full mesh of sessions; and auto-discovery tells each endpoint which peers share a segment and which encapsulation they use. The VNI travels in the MPLS (Multiprotocol Label Switching) Label1 field of the MAC/IP Advertisement route and in the P-Multicast Service Interface (PMSI) Tunnel attribute of the Inclusive Multicast Ethernet Tag (IMET) route, using all 24 bits, and the BGP Encapsulation Extended Community says whether the data plane is VXLAN, NVGRE (Network Virtualization using Generic Routing Encapsulation), MPLS or MPLS in Generic Routing Encapsulation (GRE). Not every VXLAN fabric uses EVPN. Extreme's Switch Engine can advertise each VNI and endpoint in OSPFv2 (Open Shortest Path First version 2) as a type 11 opaque link state advertisement (LSA) with opaque type 128 and the VNI in the remaining 24 bits, or carry them in multiprotocol BGP with a proprietary address family (the ipv4-vxlan capability, ExtremeXOS 22.3 or later), beside a standard l2vpn-evpn capability.

On the command line. On Linux, ip link add vxlan0 type vxlan id 42 group 239.1.1.1 dev eth1 dstport 4789 creates an interface for VNI 42 that floods unknown traffic to multicast group 239.1.1.1; bridge fdb add and bridge fdb show manage its forwarding table; and ethtool --show-tunnels lists the UDP ports a network interface card (NIC) offloads. The dstport argument matters, because the kernel's own default is 8472: the Linux implementation predates IANA's choice, and the driver keeps 8472 for backwards compatibility, a number IANA has registered since 2008 to Overlay Transport Virtualization (OTV). A Linux VTEP left at its default and a switch at 4789 never exchange a packet. On a FortiGate the equivalent is config system vxlan, with interface, vni, ip-version, remote-ip, multicast-ttl and dstport (default 4789), which creates an interface of type vxlan, and diagnose sys vxlan fdb list shows what it has learned. On Extreme Switch Engine a switch acting as VTEP is a VXLAN gateway, Layer 2 when it bridges VXLAN segments to VLANs and Layer 3 when it also routes between them.

What goes wrong. The maximum transmission unit (MTU) first. RFC 7348 says VTEPs must not fragment VXLAN packets, intermediate routers may, and the destination VTEP may silently discard the fragments, so a frame that grows past the underlay's MTU can vanish with no error at the sender; the RFC recommends raising the MTU of the whole physical network and allows path MTU discovery as an alternative. Inner tags next: a decapsulated frame carrying an inner VLAN tag should be discarded unless explicitly configured otherwise, and an encapsulating VTEP should not add one, which surprises anyone who expects a trunk to pass through. Security last, and most important. The RFC's own security section says a MAC-over-IP mechanism significantly extends the attack surface of Layer 2: rogue hosts can join the multicast groups that carry a segment's broadcast traffic, or source MAC-over-UDP frames into the transport network to inject traffic and hijack MAC addresses, and the protocol itself has no measures against either. Its suggestions are administrative control of who runs VTEPs, IEEE (Institute of Electrical and Electronics Engineers) 802.1X admission control, 5-tuple access control lists (ACLs) on the physical switches, IPsec (IP security) to authenticate and encrypt the tunnels, and a dedicated VLAN for VXLAN traffic. In practice that means UDP 4789 should never be reachable from outside the underlay.

Its neighbours. An IEEE 802.1Q VLAN identifier has 12 bits; a VNI has 24, and a VXLAN segment is usually bound to a VLAN at the edge. Geneve, RFC 8926 (November 2020, Standards Track, UDP port 6081), was designed as the general successor, with variable-length options, and states the lesson VXLAN taught: settle on a data format and leave control planes to differ. VXLAN-GPE (Generic Protocol Extension) has its own port, 4790. Extreme's other fabric, Shortest Path Bridging (SPB) in Fabric Engine, solves the same segment-scale problem without UDP, and Extreme's Switch Engine, which is not an SPB node, can act as client, proxy and even server of Fabric Attach on VXLAN overlays, binding edge VLANs to network service identifiers (NSIs) through extensions to the Link Layer Discovery Protocol (LLDP). Whichever is chosen, the underlay stays an ordinary routed network, which is the whole point: VXLAN lets Layer 2 segments outlive the end of Layer 2.

underlay-overlay.def: The two-layer view of modern networks: the underlay is the physical routed plumbing; the overlay is the virtual topology tunneled on top of it.
underlay-overlay.context: When the overlay misbehaves, the underlay is where you troubleshoot; conflating the two is the classic modern-network confusion.
underlay-overlay.depth:
An underlay is the physical network that actually moves packets; an overlay is a virtual network built on top of it by encapsulating traffic so that endpoints appear adjacent when they are not. VXLAN, GRE, IPsec tunnels and SD-WAN (software-defined wide area network) all build overlays, and the underlay is whatever carries them.

The separation buys independence, which is the whole point. An overlay can present a consistent addressing and policy model across data centres, clouds and offices whose underlying networks are owned by different people and cannot be changed, and workloads can move without renumbering. That is why virtualization and multi-cloud designs depend on it entirely.

The cost is that troubleshooting now requires two mental models at once. Overlay reachability can be perfect while the underlay is dropping packets, and vice versa, and the classic symptom is a tunnel that establishes correctly and then fails on large transfers because encapsulation overhead exceeded the underlay's MTU. Anyone diagnosing an overlay problem needs to establish which layer is broken before anything else, because the tools and the owners differ.

out-of-band-management.def: A separate management path - console servers, dedicated ports, even 4G - that still works when the production network is the thing that broke.
out-of-band-management.context: The difference between fixing a dead core switch from home and driving to the site at 3 a.m.
out-of-band-management.depth:
Out-of-band management is the ability to reach a device through a path that does not depend on the thing you are trying to fix. A serial console on a terminal server, a dedicated management processor with its own network interface, a cellular modem at a remote site: all of them exist so that a broken network does not also remove your ability to repair it.

The failure it prevents is the one everybody eventually experiences. A configuration change to the routing or the firewall is applied, it is wrong, and the change severs the connection you were making it over, leaving a device that is running, healthy, and unreachable. Without another path, the fix is a physical visit, which at a remote site is hours and at a distant one is days.

The security consideration is that this is by definition a path around your controls. A management processor with its own network stack, its own credentials and firmware that is patched on a different schedule from the operating system is an attractive target that many organizations forget they have. Out-of-band access needs to be genuinely isolated, genuinely monitored, and included in the inventory, or it becomes the way in rather than the way back.

loopback-interface.def: A virtual interface that never goes down, giving the router a stable identity for routing protocols and management regardless of physical link state.
loopback-interface.context: BGP sessions and router IDs anchor to loopbacks precisely because cables fail and loopbacks do not.

asymmetric-routing.def: Asymmetric routing: traffic between two hosts that goes out by one path and comes back by another; perfectly legal IP behaviour, and normal on the internet, that quietly breaks stateful firewalls, NAT (network address translation) devices and strict source checks that expect to see both directions.
asymmetric-routing.context: Common wherever multihoming exists; the cure is state sharing between firewalls or accepting the asymmetry by design. IP (Internet Protocol) routes each packet on its destination alone, and every router and every AS (autonomous system) chooses its own exit, so the reply to a packet follows whatever path the reverse lookups produce, not the path the request took.
