Above the optical layer, the Broadband Forum's TR-069, first published in May 2004 and transposed by the European Telecommunications Standards Institute (ETSI) as ES 203 069, defines the CPE WAN Management Protocol (CWMP) between customer premises equipment (CPE) and an auto-configuration server (ACS). It provisions a device when it first connects to the access network and re-provisions it at any later time, including on the ACS's own initiative, either individually or by vendor, model or software version, and it manages firmware images. The CPE is the Hypertext Transfer Protocol (HTTP) client, so a device behind network address translation (NAT) can still be reached through the connection it opens.

Network devices and platforms. The Internet Engineering Task Force (IETF) specification for Secure Zero Touch Provisioning, Request for Comments (RFC) 8572 (April 2019), covers switches and routers that boot in a factory-default state: the device finds bootstrap data on removable storage, through the Domain Name System (DNS) or the Dynamic Host Configuration Protocol (DHCP), or from a bootstrap server, verifies it against an ownership voucher, updates its boot image, commits an initial configuration, runs any scripts, and then opens Network Configuration Protocol (NETCONF) or RESTCONF sessions to its management system. The word also has a narrower, product-specific meaning. On F5 BIG-IP, resource provisioning allocates memory, disk space and processing capacity among licensed modules at one of four levels: None/Disabled, Minimum, Nominal or Dedicated, the last giving one module everything and setting all others to None. F5's documentation warns that the system must be provisioned before it is configured, because provisioning afterwards loses the configuration, and changes are made in the TMOS Shell (tmsh), for example modify sys provision avr level nominal, followed by a reboot.

Identity provisioning. The same word covers account creation and entitlement assignment. The System for Cross-domain Identity Management (SCIM), RFC 7643 and RFC 7644 of September 2015, standardizes it as an HTTP application programming interface (API) between an identity source and services such as cloud applications: a POST to /Users creates an account, a DELETE removes it, and the active attribute records administrative status, where false typically means suspended. Authenticator enrolment is provisioning too: the de facto otpauth://TYPE/LABEL?PARAMETERS format, usually delivered as a QR code, carries a required Base32 secret without padding and a strongly recommended issuer.

Deprovisioning is the half that fails silently. Nobody notices a service that still works or an account that still authenticates after it should have stopped, which is why the National Institute of Standards and Technology (NIST) makes it a control in Special Publication (SP) 800-53 Rev. 5 (September 2020): AC-2(3) requires disabling accounts within a defined period once they have expired, are no longer associated with a person, violate policy or have been inactive too long, and AC-2(4) requires automatic auditing of account creation, modification, enabling, disabling and removal. In SCIM terms the choice between setting active to false and deleting the user matters, because a suspended account can be restored and a deleted one cannot. Whatever the domain, the reliable finding in an audit is the thing that was never turned off.

walled-garden.def: A restricted network state where the subscriber can reach only the provider's portal - used for unpaid bills, activation, or infected hosts.
walled-garden.context: The 'your account needs attention' page that answers every URL you type.
walled-garden.depth:
A walled garden is a platform where the operator controls what may be installed, published or connected, and the term originally described online services that kept subscribers inside their own content rather than the wider internet. It now most often describes application stores and closed ecosystems.

The argument in favour is genuine and should not be dismissed. Curation means malware is rarer, payment and privacy behaviour can be enforced rather than requested, and an ordinary person can install software without evaluating its provenance. Those are real protections that the open alternative does not provide, and most users benefit from them without noticing.

The costs are equally real and are borne differently. The operator decides what exists, which is editorial power exercised commercially and occasionally politically, developers accept terms they cannot negotiate, and the absence of an alternative distribution channel means a removal is a business ending rather than an inconvenience. The regulatory attention now directed at app stores is an argument about whether that concentration is acceptable, and the technical question of security is genuinely entangled with the commercial question of control.

sla.def: Service Level Agreement: the contract's measurable promises - availability, repair time, throughput - and the penalties when they slip.
sla.context: 99.9% allows 8.8 hours down a year; every nine multiplies the price.

mttr.def: Mean Time To Repair: the average clock from failure to restoration - the operational number behind every SLA (service level agreement) repair promise.
mttr.context: Its siblings MTBF and MTTF measure how often things break; MTTR measures how long you suffer.

attenuation.def: Signal loss over distance and through obstacles, measured in dB - the budget every link spends whether copper, fibre, or radio.
attenuation.context: In fibre measured per kilometre; in DSL it decided your plan; in Wi-Fi it is the wall between you and the router.

snr.def: Signal-to-Noise Ratio: how far the signal stands above the noise floor, in dB - the single number that decides whether a link can run its rated speed.
snr.context: Every modulation scheme has an SNR price; margin is what keeps the link alive on a rainy day.

node-split.def: Dividing a congested cable or PON serving area into two smaller ones, halving the subscribers who share the same capacity.
node-split.context: The capacity lever of shared-medium networks: fewer neighbours per node, more speed per neighbour.

aerial-vs-underground.def: The two ways outside plant reaches customers: on poles (cheap, fast, storm-exposed) or buried (costly, slow, backhoe-exposed).
aerial-vs-underground.context: Every ISP's build map is a negotiation between these two economics.
aerial-vs-underground.depth:
Aerial plant is cable strung on poles; underground plant is cable in ducts or buried. The choice is made once and determines the economics and failure modes of that route for decades.

Aerial is dramatically cheaper to install and to repair, because the cable is visible and reachable, and a crew can be at the fault in an hour. It is also exposed to everything: storms, ice loading, vehicle strikes on poles, vegetation, and the shared-pole disputes that arise when power, telephone and cable operators all attach to the same structure. Underground survives weather almost entirely and costs several times as much per metre, more in a city, and when it does fail the repair means locating the fault precisely and then excavating.

The operational consequence is that outage patterns are predictable from the plant type. A region with aerial distribution has weather-correlated outages and short repair times; underground has rare failures and long ones. Anyone reading availability figures for an access network is reading a fact about civil engineering choices made long before the service existed.

pole-attachment.def: The regulated right to hang cables on utility poles owned by power or phone companies - rented space, strict rules, long queues.
pole-attachment.context: Make-ready work and attachment fees shape where competitive fibre actually gets built.

upstream-downstream.def: The two directions of an access link: downstream towards the subscriber, upstream towards the internet - historically sized very unequally.
upstream-downstream.context: Video calls and cloud backups made the skinny upstream everyone's problem.
upstream-downstream.depth:
Upstream and downstream describe direction relative to you, and the words are used in at least three unrelated ways that regularly collide in the same conversation. In access networks, downstream is towards the subscriber and upstream is towards the provider, which is why residential connections are asymmetric.

In routing and business relationships, an upstream is the provider you buy transit from and a downstream is the customer who buys from you, which encodes money rather than direction. In software supply chains, upstream is the project you take code from and downstream is whoever takes yours, so a patch sent upstream travels towards the origin, and an upstream security fix flows down to everyone else.

The collisions are real and worth catching. A conversation about an upstream problem may mean the provider, the origin project, or the direction of traffic, and the three have different owners and different fixes. The habit that avoids it is naming the thing rather than the direction, since the extra three words cost nothing and the ambiguity costs a misdirected escalation.

dhcp-option-82.def: The relay information option: the access device stamps each DHCP request with the physical line it arrived on, giving the ISP per-port identity.
dhcp-option-82.context: How IPoE networks know which customer is which without a login.

wifi-site-survey.def: Measuring actual coverage, interference, and neighbour networks on site before or after placing access points - the map versus the guess.
wifi-site-survey.context: The difference between 'the router is in the living room' and knowing why the bedroom gets nothing.

mesh-wifi.def: Multiple cooperating access nodes forming one seamless network, relaying wirelessly where cable cannot reach.
mesh-wifi.context: Each wireless hop spends airtime twice; wired backhaul between nodes is the quiet upgrade.

ss7.def: Signaling System 7: the signalling network that sets up phone calls and SMS worldwide - designed for a closed club of trusted carriers.
ss7.context: That trust model is why SS7 access enables call interception and SMS hijacking today.

number-porting.def: Moving a phone number between carriers while keeping it - a regulated right, a database update, and a fraud vector when hijacked.
number-porting.context: SIM-swap attacks are porting's evil twin: same mechanism, stolen identity.

service-desk.def: The single point of contact between users and IT: intake, triage, resolution or escalation, and the record of it all.
service-desk.context: ITIL distinguishes it from a help desk by scope - the desk owns the whole service relationship, not just fixes.

ticket.def: The unit of support work: one tracked record per issue or request, with an identifier, status, owner, priority and history; if it is not in the ticket, it did not happen. In authentication the word means something else: a sealed credential, as in Kerberos or Transport Layer Security (TLS) session resumption.
ticket.context: Also the unit of accountability: metrics, service level agreements (SLAs) and 3 a.m. escalations all hang off it. It is where the response and resolution clocks start, where severity is set, and where the next engineer finds out what has already been tried, which is why a vague first line costs more time than any other part of the process.
ticket.depth:
A hospital chart for a network. The clearest statement of what a ticket is for comes from network operations rather than from a help desk. Request for Comments (RFC) 1297, written by D. Johnson of Merit Network in January 1992 as a wishlist for network operations centre (NOC) trouble ticket systems, compares the ticket to a hospital chart: a record that coordinates the work of several people on one problem, so that any operator can come up to speed and take the next step without finding whoever worked on it last, who may be on another task, gone home or on holiday. It lists the purposes a ticket system serves: short-term memory across shifts; scheduling, with open problems sorted by priority; dispatching, by putting a name in an assigned-to field; an alarm clock, because most of the time a ticket is open it is waiting for something, so every wait should carry a timer, including the escalation time by which a telephone company has promised to call back; and oversight and statistics for engineers and managers.

What goes in it. RFC 1297's structure has aged well. A ticket opens with fixed fields: when the problem started, who opened the ticket, the severity, possibly separating the customer's severity from the NOC's priority because the two can differ, and a one-line description for reports; then who reported it, the machines, network and addresses involved, the next action, the time of the next alarm, who it is dispatched to and a single owner responsible overall. The body is a series of free-text updates, each stamped with the time and the operator, with the option to record when something actually happened rather than when it was typed, and room to paste raw evidence such as a user's traceroute output. The RFC's guidance on fields is still the right one: fixed fields cost operators time and push them towards canned answers that may not describe the situation, so use them only where the system fills them automatically or a report actually uses them, and define different ticket types for different classes of problem.

Incidents, requests, problems. Information technology (IT) service management, as ITIL (the Information Technology Infrastructure Library) frames it, records different kinds of work differently. An incident is an unplanned interruption or reduction in quality of an IT service; a request for service is a formal request from a user for something to be provided, such as information or advice, a password reset or a workstation for a new user; a problem is the cause of one or more incidents, usually unknown when its record is created; a change is a planned modification with its own approvals. They run on different clocks and answer different questions, so a queue that mixes them produces meaningless metrics, and closing an incident with a workaround says nothing about whether the problem behind it is solved.

Severity, priority and the clock. Vendor support contracts turn severity into time. F5's support guidelines define four case severities: 1, when the device will not power up or pass traffic and critical business activity is stopped; 2, when business activity is significantly impaired; 3, when service is degraded; 4, for how-to questions, non-critical issues and feature requests. The target initial responses are one hour for the first two, four business hours and the next business day for the others, and initial response is defined precisely as the time from case creation until an engineer first tries to contact the customer and logs it; a Severity 1 case also notifies support managers at once. Two lessons generalize. Response is not resolution: the service level agreement (SLA) usually measures how fast someone engages, not how fast the fault is fixed. And severity is impact, which is why choosing it honestly, with the evidence in the first update, gets a case to the right engineer faster than raising it.

The tools. Ticket systems descend from two lines. Defect trackers such as Bugzilla, written by Terry Weissman for mozilla.org in 1998 and released as version 2.0 on 19 September 1998, track bugs and change requests in software and say outright that they are not support ticket systems. Request trackers such as Request Tracker, an open-source system in use for more than 25 years, receive mail sent to addresses like support@ or security@, turn each message into a ticket in a queue, and run automation on every transaction. Service desk suites and security orchestration platforms add structure on top, but the core record RFC 1297 described, an owner, a state, a timer and a history, is the same.

The other ticket. In security protocols a ticket is a credential, not a work item. Kerberos, specified in RFC 4120 (July 2005, obsoleting RFC 1510), defines a ticket as a record that helps a client authenticate itself to a server, containing the client's identity, a session key, a timestamp and other information, all sealed with the server's secret key, and valid only when presented with a fresh authenticator. A client first obtains a ticket-granting ticket (TGT) and then uses it with the ticket-granting server for each service. The Golden Ticket technique in MITRE ATT&CK (T1558.001) is the attack on that design: with the password hash of the KRBTGT account, which encrypts and signs all Kerberos tickets, an attacker can forge ticket-granting tickets for any account in an Active Directory domain. Transport Layer Security (TLS) uses tickets for resumption: RFC 5077 (January 2008) lets a server store session state in a ticket encrypted and integrity-protected with a key only it knows, so a stolen ticket is useless without that key, and TLS 1.3 (RFC 8446) caps a ticket's lifetime at 604,800 seconds, seven days. When an engineer says the ticket expired, the context decides which of these they mean.

incident-vs-request.def: The great ITIL fork: an incident is something broken; a request is something wanted - different queues, clocks, and expectations.
incident-vs-request.context: Misfiling one as the other is how a password reset gets a major-incident bridge call.
incident-vs-request.depth:
An incident is something broken that should be working; a request is somebody asking for something new or different. The distinction sounds bureaucratic and it determines almost everything about how the work is handled: urgency, who is authorized, whether change control applies, and which clock is running.

The reason it matters is that treating one as the other fails in both directions. A genuine outage entered as a service request sits in a queue behind password resets while a business function is down. A request for new access raised as an incident bypasses the approval that exists specifically to prevent people granting themselves things, which is how audit findings are generated.

The judgement calls are where practice actually lives. A slow system is an incident if it used to be fast and a request if it was always this slow and someone now wants better. A feature that never worked is arguably a defect rather than an outage. Getting the classification right at intake is worth more than any amount of process downstream, because everything after it inherits the initial decision, and misclassification is rarely revisited once the ticket is moving.

severity-levels.def: The impact-and-urgency ladder for incidents: P1 is everyone-down-drop-everything, P4 is a papercut with a queue.
severity-levels.context: The perpetual negotiation: every caller's issue is a P1 to the caller.

escalation.def: Moving an issue to people with more expertise, more authority or more resources when its current owner cannot, or should not, resolve it alone: functionally to deeper skill, hierarchically to management.
escalation.context: Knowing when to escalate is the skill; escalating with a clean handoff is the craft.
escalation.depth:
Two kinds, two triggers. Escalation is moving an issue to someone with more expertise, more authority or more context than its current owner. The glossary of ITIL (originally the Information Technology Infrastructure Library), in its 2011 edition, defines it as an activity that obtains additional resources when they are needed to meet service level targets or customer expectations, most often in incident management, problem management and the handling of complaints, and names two types. Functional escalation transfers the work to a team with a higher level of expertise; hierarchic escalation brings in management, at least for information when an incident is serious (a Priority 1, in Emory University's service management glossary), and to obtain decisions or resources when investigation and resolution are taking too long. Keeping them apart matters because they answer different questions. Functional escalation says this needs a specialist; hierarchic escalation says this needs a decision or resources the current owner cannot authorize; and an incident often needs one without the other.

The National Institute of Standards and Technology (NIST) draws the same line with other words. In Special Publication (SP) 800-61 Revision 3, of April 2025, outcome RS.MA-04 reads incidents are escalated or elevated as needed, with the note that escalation generally means increasing resources or time frames, while elevation usually means involving a higher level of management. The same guide asks that triage, prioritization, escalation, elevation and the decision to start recovery all rest on one set of risk evaluation factors (asset criticality, functional and data impact, the stage of the observed activity, the threat actor, recoverability), that the organization's standard method for calculating cybersecurity risk inform the decision on when to escalate or elevate, and that every ongoing incident be tracked and validated so that one needing more resources or a different strategy is caught quickly. Read side by side, NIST's escalation is ITIL's functional kind and its elevation is ITIL's hierarchic kind.

Escalation is what moves work through the support tiers. In the ITIL V3 incident process as Stefan Kempter's process wiki documents it, first-level support diagnoses and resolves what it can with the knowledge base and predefined incident models; what it cannot resolve must be escalated to a specialist group in second-level support, which is functional escalation, and second level may in turn bring in suppliers and vendors, which ITIL calls third-level support. The escalation rules are written in advance. Triggers combine the severity of the incident, so that severe incidents are escalated immediately, with its duration, so that an incident not resolved within the maximum resolution time agreed in the service level agreements (SLAs) escalates; ideally the ticketing system fires them, not a person. Each trigger maps to a level of an escalation hierarchy, which in the wiki's example runs from first-level support to the incident manager, the manager of the data centre and the chief information officer (CIO). ITIL also recognizes user escalation, raised by a user whose incident is delayed or whose service has not been restored.

On-call tooling turns the duration trigger into configuration. A PagerDuty escalation policy is an ordered set of rules, also called levels: the targets on the first rule are notified the moment an incident triggers, each responder has until the escalation timeout to acknowledge, resolve or reassign it, and if nobody acts the incident moves to the next rule and its targets are notified. The default timeout is 30 minutes, a level with several targets cannot be set below three minutes, and the whole policy can repeat up to nine times if nobody acknowledges. The mechanism is deliberately indifferent to how the first responder feels about the problem: silence is the trigger.

Deciding to escalate by hand is harder, and the best guidance makes that mechanical too. In Google's Site Reliability Engineering (SRE) book, the chapter on managing incidents written by Andrew Stribblehill gives three conditions, any one of which makes an event an incident with a formal response: a second team is needed to fix it, the outage is visible to customers, or the issue is still unsolved after an hour's concentrated analysis. It adds that declaring early and closing out after a simple fix is better than spinning up the incident framework hours into a growing problem, and tells responders who start to feel panicky or overwhelmed to ask for more support. Good escalation policy defines the trigger by elapsed time and impact rather than by the handler's confidence, precisely because confidence is the thing least reliable under pressure, and the person deepest in a problem is the worst placed to judge whether the fix is five minutes away.

The failure modes sit at both extremes. Escalating too readily trains the next tier to expect unfiltered work and erodes the first tier's own capability. Escalating too late is the more expensive one, because an incident handled for two hours by someone out of their depth is two hours of blast radius that nobody was containing. The SRE chapter's portrait of an unmanaged incident shows the late version: an on-call engineer, absorbed in the technical problem, reverts a release that does not help, wakes the original developer at 3:30 a.m. in her time zone, is pressed by executives for an estimate, and loses track of who is changing what, until a well-meaning colleague freelances a production change that kills the remaining servers. Everyone, the book observes, was doing their job as they saw it; what was missing was a declared incident with an incident commander able to escalate, delegate and keep everyone else informed.

Escalating with a clean handoff is the craft. The same chapter asks that incident command be handed over explicitly, with the outgoing commander stating that the other person is now the incident commander and not leaving the call until that is firmly acknowledged, and that the handover be announced to everyone working the incident. Escalation to a vendor follows the same rule, in writing. F5's 2011 technical support guidelines set a one-hour target response for Severity 1 and 2 cases and say that a case logged as Severity 1 immediately notifies the support managers, so that it is assigned to an appropriately skilled engineer: the severity the customer chooses is itself an escalation decision. A case that states the business impact, the exact version and what has already been ruled out can be worked on arrival; one that does not comes back with questions, and the clock restarts.

The word has an unrelated meaning in security. Privilege escalation, tactic TA0004 in MITRE ATT&CK (Adversarial Tactics, Techniques and Common Knowledge), covers the techniques adversaries use to gain higher-level permissions on a system or network after entering with unprivileged access, by exploiting weaknesses, misconfigurations and vulnerabilities. It shares nothing with support escalation except the direction of travel, and an alert or a ticket that just says escalation needs its context read before anyone reacts.

tier-1-2-3.def: The layered support model: L1 handles volume with scripts and known fixes, L2 brings expertise, L3 is the people who built or own the thing.
tier-1-2-3.context: Each tier exists to protect the next one's time.

first-call-resolution.def: The percentage of issues closed in the first contact, no callbacks, no escalation - the metric that best predicts user happiness.
first-call-resolution.context: Easy to inflate by closing tickets prematurely, which is why it pairs with reopen rate.

knowledge-base.def: A searchable, maintained collection of articles recording known issues with their causes and fixes, and answers to recurring questions, kept so that the next person with the same problem finds the answer instead of solving it again: support's compound interest, paid in one resolved ticket at a time.
knowledge-base.context: What makes a knowledge base is retrieval and reuse, not storage: a share full of documents nobody searches is an archive. The best-known discipline for building one is Knowledge-Centered Success (KCS), a methodology of the non-profit Consortium for Service Innovation whose letters stood first for Knowledge-Centered Support and, from version 6, for Knowledge-Centered Service. Its central rule is to write and improve the article while solving the case, in the requester's own words, rather than afterwards. In ITIL (Information Technology Infrastructure Library) terms the knowledge base feeds the service knowledge management system, and its sharpest part is the known error database, where problem management records a root cause and a workaround. Vendors run the largest public ones: Microsoft identifies updates by their Knowledge Base (KB) article numbers, and F5's iHealth checks a device snapshot against its database of known issues.
knowledge-base.depth:
What it is, and what it is not. The 2011 glossary of ITIL (Information Technology Infrastructure Library) defines a knowledge base as a logical database containing data and information used by the service knowledge management system (SKMS), and knowledge management as the process that makes perspectives, experience and information available in the right place at the right time, improving efficiency by reducing the need to rediscover knowledge. The glossary of KCS (Knowledge-Centered Service, as version 6 of the method was called) is blunter: a technology built for the storage and retrieval of a collection of knowledge. Retrieval is the operative word. A wiki of design documents, a ticket history and a folder of runbooks all hold knowledge, but a knowledge base is organized around the question someone will bring to it and is judged by whether they find the answer. It is not a runbook, which tells someone how to carry out a known task, although a good article often links to one. And it has nothing to do with knowledge-based authentication (KBA), the security questions that the National Institute of Standards and Technology (NIST), in Special Publication 800-63B-4, forbids verifiers from prompting subscribers to use when choosing passwords.

The ITIL neighbours. The part of a knowledge base with the most operational weight is the known error. ITIL defines a known error as a problem that has a documented root cause and a workaround, created and managed by problem management and sometimes identified by development teams or suppliers, and the known error database (KEDB) as the store of those records, created by problem management and used by incident and problem management, either inside the configuration management system or elsewhere in the SKMS. The flow is the point: an incident is restored with a workaround, problem management finds the cause, the known error record tells the next person who meets the same symptom what to do while the permanent fix is pending, and the record is retired when the fix ships. The same glossary sets out the Data-to-Information-to-Knowledge-to-Wisdom (DIKW) ladder that the word knowledge stands on.

KCS, and why its name keeps changing. The method most support organizations cite is KCS, developed and maintained by the Consortium for Service Innovation, a non-profit association that is also the only body certifying people in it and designating tools as KCS Verified or KCS Aligned; KCS is the Consortium's registered service mark. The letters have stayed while the words changed. Version 6 of the Practices Guide renamed Knowledge-Centered Support to Knowledge-Centered Service, to reflect use outside support and the idea of service science coined at IBM Research, and the current Knowledge-Centered Success Practices Guide presents the method as an enterprise-wide framework rather than a support model. The Consortium names its intellectual sources: Deming's quality concepts, and Nonaka and Takeuchi's book The Knowledge-Creating Company, a constant reference in KCS's formative years. Version 6 organizes eight practices into two reinforcing loops, an idea taken from research on complex adaptive systems: the Solve Loop, done by each person on each request, and the Evolve Loop, done by the organization over the collection of requests and articles.

The Solve Loop. Its four practices are Capture, Structure, Reuse and Improve. Searching the knowledge base is part of handling a request, under the slogan search early, search often, so that nobody solves again what is already solved; the words the responder typed into the search are kept, because if no article exists they become the start of a new one, and if one exists but was not found, they show what it should also say. Capture records the requester's context in their own words while the context exists, which turns tacit knowledge, things people know without knowing they know, into findable text. Structure means a simple template and a crisp style. Improve is summed up as reuse is review: whoever uses an article and finds it wrong or unclear must flag it or fix it, depending on their confidence and their rights. The Knowledge-Centered Success edition reorders the loop to begin with Reuse, the most common activity, and adds that a new article is created only on demand, when none exists.

What an article looks like. The KCS glossary names the fields. Issue holds the question or symptom as the requester described it; Environment holds the products, versions, hardware, software and network relevant to it, with the standing question of whether anything changed recently; Resolution holds the fix; Cause holds the underlying or root cause. Articles are written in complete thoughts rather than complete sentences. Each carries a state combining confidence, audience (formerly called visibility) and governance: Not Validated signals low confidence in content or structure, Validated means complete, reusable and compliant with the content standard. Rights follow proficiency. A KCS Candidate can create internal articles and edit only their own; a KCS Contributor creates, modifies and reviews articles for a defined audience; a KCS Publisher publishes to an external audience; coaches develop the others, and a Knowledge Domain Expert looks after the health of the knowledge base as a whole. In the new edition the licensing model behind these roles is called the proficiency model, to avoid confusion with software licences.

How it fails. The Consortium's own list of ditches is the best checklist. Putting goals on activities, such as articles written per week, buys volume and duplicates; reuse, the number of times an article has been applied, is the measure of value, and self-service success, the share of users who find what they need on their own, is the outcome. Treating the knowledge base as a project that someone else writes after the fact produces articles nobody trusts, which is why the guide insists that KCS is not something done in addition to solving problems but the way problems are solved. And the idea that a good knowledge base lets an organization answer with lower-skilled, lower-cost staff is, in the guide's word, false: applying an article takes the judgment to decide whether it really matches the case. Stale content is the slow failure. An article that was right for one software version is wrong after the next, and only a practice of review during use keeps a large base honest. Audience is the security failure: an internal article can hold hostnames, configuration fragments or workarounds that should never reach the public side, which is why publishing externally is a separate right.

Vendor knowledge bases in daily work. For most engineers the knowledge base they use most belongs to a vendor. Microsoft states that each security update comes with a security bulletin and a Microsoft Knowledge Base (KB) article, and its updates are known by the article number: Get-HotFix in PowerShell lists installed fixes by HotFixID values such as KB4495590, read from the Win32_QuickFixEngineering management class, with the caveat that updates installed by Windows Installer or from the Windows Update site are not listed there, so a missing KB number in that output does not prove a missing patch. F5 turns its knowledge base into an automated check: a qkview snapshot uploaded to iHealth is evaluated against a database of known issues, common mistakes and published best practices, and the iHealth application programming interface (API) returns each diagnostic as a hit or a miss for that device, with troubleshooting, upgrade and known-issue information. Support engineers at any vendor search their internal base with the exact error string a customer reports, which is why a verbatim message in a case is worth more than a paraphrase.

Beyond support. Security uses the word in the same sense. MITRE describes ATT&CK as a globally accessible knowledge base of adversary tactics and techniques based on real-world observations, used as the foundation for threat models and methodologies in industry and government: curated, structured and built to be reused rather than read once. What the support version and the security version share is the property that separates a knowledge base from a pile of documents. Each entry exists because a real case needed it, each is shaped to be found by the next person with the same question, and each is corrected by the people who use it.

itil.def: The IT service management framework: the shared vocabulary of incidents, problems, changes, and services that lets operations teams and their tickets speak one language.
itil.context: Born in the late-1980s UK government (the CCTA's Infrastructure Library of good-practice books), ITIL grew into the world's default ITSM canon: the incident/problem/change trinity, service levels, and the service desk as a discipline all trace here. Stewardship moved to Axelos in 2013 and to PeopleCert in 2021; ITIL 4 (2019) reframed the process catalogue as a service value system with practices, guiding principles, and an explicit peace treaty with Agile and DevOps. The certification ladder (Foundation upward) is the industry's most common ops credential, and the reason half the world's ticket fields are named what they are named.

problem-management.def: The ITIL practice that hunts the cause behind recurring incidents: incidents restore service, problems remove the reason it broke.
problem-management.context: Ten identical tickets closed is ten incidents; one root cause removed is problem management.

change-management-itsm.def: The gate through which production changes pass: assessed for risk, scheduled in windows, approved, and rollback-ready.
change-management-itsm.context: The CAB (change advisory board) is its parliament; emergency changes are its loophole and its lesson generator.

cmdb.def: Configuration Management Database: the inventory of every asset and the relationships between them - what talks to what, and who screams when it dies.
cmdb.context: Every organization has one; in most, it was accurate once.

asset-management.def: Tracking hardware and software through their whole lifecycle - procurement, assignment, patching, retirement - so licenses, budgets, and audits reconcile.
asset-management.context: The unglamorous discipline that decides whether an audit is a formality or an archaeology dig.

remote-desktop.def: Taking over a user's screen and input from afar - RDP, VNC, and their commercial cousins - support's teleportation.
remote-desktop.context: Also an attack surface: exposed RDP was ransomware's favourite front door for years.

golden-image.def: The blessed master build of an operating system plus standard apps and settings, cloned onto every new machine.
golden-image.context: Its drift over time is why 'reimage it' remains support's nuclear option.

gpo.def: Group Policy Object: Windows domain settings pushed centrally to users and machines - wallpaper to password policy, mapped drives to lockdown.
gpo.context: gpupdate /force is the incantation; 'it is a GPO' is the diagnosis.

active-directory.def: Microsoft's directory service, formally Active Directory Domain Services (AD DS): the domain's phone book and its security authority, holding the users, groups and computers and the permissions that bind them, and authenticating every one of them.
active-directory.context: Active Directory Domain Services (AD DS) is the crown jewel of most corporate networks, which is why attackers head straight for it. Microsoft describes it as a directory service that stores directory data and makes it available to network users and administrators: user accounts with names, passwords and phone numbers, shared resources such as servers, volumes and printers, and the computer accounts of joined machines. Security is integrated through sign-in authentication and access control on the objects in the directory, so one network username and password reaches everything, and every domain controller holds a complete copy of its domain. Applications read it over LDAP (Lightweight Directory Access Protocol), users authenticate with Kerberos and fall back to NTLM (NT LAN Manager) where Kerberos cannot be used, and it is the password store behind most RADIUS (Remote Authentication Dial-In User Service), 802.1X and VPN (virtual private network) logins in a Windows estate, which is why authentication, authorization and accounting (AAA) designs keep returning to it.
active-directory.depth:
Active Directory, strictly Active Directory Domain Services (AD DS), is the directory role of Windows Server; the short form AD and the wider family of roles that share the name are set out in the AD entry. Microsoft defines a directory as a hierarchical structure that stores information about objects on a network, organized logically on top of a structured data store. Its centrality is the point and also the risk: because one sign-in reaches resources anywhere on the network, compromising a domain controller compromises not a server but every identity the organization has. It is not Microsoft Entra ID, the cloud service once called Azure Active Directory, and it is not simply an LDAP (Lightweight Directory Access Protocol) server, although it answers LDAP.

The logical model has three levels. A forest is the top container: one or more domains that share a schema (the class and attribute definitions), a configuration (sites and replication) and a global catalogue for forest-wide search, and Microsoft's planning guide states that domains in one forest are automatically linked by two-way, transitive trusts. A domain is a partition of the forest, so data is replicated only where it is needed; it is the unit of network-wide identity, its domain controllers store the accounts and their credentials, such as passwords or certificates, and it can extend authentication to users of domains outside its forest through explicit trusts. Inside a domain, organizational units (OUs) group objects for administration: Group Policy is linked to them and authority is delegated over them, with control decided by the access control lists (ACLs) on the OU and its objects. The model is called logical because it is independent of how many domain controllers there are and how the network is laid out. Clients find domain controllers through the Domain Name System (DNS): controllers publish service (SRV) records through DNS dynamic update, and a client looking for a directory server asks for the LDAP-over-TCP (Transmission Control Protocol) record of the domain, which is why broken DNS so often presents as broken Active Directory.

Microsoft lists four components beside the store itself: the schema, which defines the classes of objects and attributes, the constraints on them and the format of their names; the global catalogue, which holds information about every object so that a search finds it whichever domain holds the data; the query and index mechanism, through which objects are published and found; and the replication service. Every domain controller in a domain takes part in replication and holds a complete copy of the domain's directory, and any change reaches all of them. Replication is multimaster. Microsoft Press's Introducing Windows 2000 Server explains that an update can be written on any controller, that each change carries a 64-bit update sequence number (USN) from a per-server counter so that partners request only what they have not yet seen, that per-property version numbers detect two simultaneous edits of the same attribute, and that the collision is resolved in favour of the later timestamp, one reason controllers must keep their clocks synchronized. Functional levels decide which features a domain or forest can use and which Windows Server versions may run as its controllers; the current levels are Windows Server 2025, supported only by Windows Server 2025 controllers, Windows Server 2016, still the newest level for Windows Server 2019 and 2022, and Windows Server 2012 R2.

Under the single sign-in sit protocols with entries of their own. Kerberos version 5, as the Internet Engineering Task Force (IETF) defines it, with Microsoft's extensions, is the preferred method: the Key Distribution Center (KDC) runs on every domain controller and uses the AD DS database as its account database. At sign-in the client obtains a ticket-granting ticket (TGT), presents it to ask for a service ticket for each service, and the service checks that ticket without calling a domain controller unless it needs to validate the Privilege Attribute Certificate (PAC). Kerberos also gives mutual authentication and delegation, which lets a front-end service act for the user towards a back end. NTLM (NT LAN Manager) remains for what cannot use Kerberos, such as workgroup machines, local accounts and applications that still ask for it: a challenge-response family covering LAN Manager versions 1 and 2 and NTLM versions 1 and 2, in which the resource server must contact a domain controller to verify each new client and the client has no way to verify the server. LDAP, in versions 2 and 3 from the first release, is how applications search the directory and check passwords by binding, and Group Policy pushes configuration from the directory to the machines. From Windows Server 2025, Kerberos ignores the old SupportedEncryptionTypes registry value, and Microsoft points administrators to Group Policy for the allowed encryption types.

Before Active Directory, Windows NT kept users, groups and computers in NT domains, which suited small and medium networks, forced large ones into many domains joined by trusts, and took changes only at a primary domain controller. Windows 2000 Server introduced Active Directory to replace that model, and Network World dates the official release to 17 February 2000. Microsoft Press's book on the release lists what was new: multimaster replication, so that no single controller is critical; services located through DNS and its dynamic update protocol, Request for Comments (RFC) 2136, instead of NetBIOS (Network Basic Input/Output System) names resolved by WINS (Windows Internet Name Service); every object named by an LDAP distinguished name; users signing in with a user principal name (UPN) that survives moves and renames; delegated administration over subtrees instead of all-powerful Domain Admins rights; and trusts that are bidirectional and transitive. Rival directory vendors were unimpressed, Network World recalled ten years later, and Novell pointed out that the administrator could not be blocked from any file or folder.

The cloud neighbour is Microsoft Entra ID, and the names cause real confusion. Microsoft announced on 11 July 2023 that Azure Active Directory (Azure AD) was becoming Microsoft Entra ID, with the new name appearing in products from August 2023 and service plan display names changing on 1 October 2023. The reasons it gives are the multicloud, multiplatform scope of the product, the unity of the Entra family and, explicitly, avoiding confusion with Windows Server Active Directory; only the name changed, not login addresses, application programming interfaces (APIs), PowerShell cmdlets or licensing. The on-premises products keep their names: Active Directory, AD DS and Active Directory Federation Services (AD FS). Microsoft presents Entra ID as Identity as a Service (IDaaS) and said in 2023 that it protected more than 720,000 organizations; existing Active Directory organizations use Microsoft Entra Connect to synchronize their identities into it, and Microsoft notes that Active Directory itself does not support software as a service (SaaS) applications natively and needs a federation system such as AD FS for them.

Microsoft's guidance on securing domain controllers states the stakes: a controller can read and write anything in the AD DS database, so once one is compromised the forest can never be considered trustworthy again unless it is recovered from a known good backup and the gaps are closed, and a prepared attacker can do irreparable damage in minutes or hours. The best-known techniques follow from the Kerberos design. Kerberoasting needs only an ordinary domain account: anyone holding a TGT may request a service ticket for any account with a service principal name (SPN), part of that ticket is encrypted with a key derived from the service account's password, and the attacker takes it away and guesses passwords offline. Microsoft wrote in October 2024 that graphics processing units (GPUs) were making the attack more effective, that RC4 (Rivest Cipher 4) is the weakest case because it uses no salt and no iterated hash when it turns a password into a key, and that it intends to disable RC4 by default in a future update of Windows 11 24H2 and Windows Server 2025. Its remedies are group managed service accounts (gMSAs), whose passwords are 120 random characters, the delegated managed service accounts (dMSAs) of Windows Server 2025, passwords of at least 14 characters where neither is possible, and AES (Advanced Encryption Standard) for service tickets. A Golden Ticket is the end state: KRBTGT is the KDC's own service account, whose key encrypts and signs every Kerberos ticket, and whoever holds its password hash can forge TGTs for any account. MITRE's catalogue of attacker techniques lists the ways to that hash: credential dumping on a domain controller, or DCSync, in which an account with replication rights, such as a member of Domain Admins or Enterprise Admins, asks a controller to replicate password data as if it were another controller, a feature of the Mimikatz lsadump module.

The defence is to treat domain controllers as a class of their own, which is Microsoft's own advice: dedicated racks or cages, Trusted Platform Module (TPM) chips and BitLocker on every volume, read-only domain controllers (RODCs) where a branch cannot lock a room, the Server Core installation, administration only from privileged access workstations or secure jump hosts, and Remote Desktop Protocol (RDP) to controllers allowed by Group Policy only from authorized systems. Add a patching urgency of their own, tiered administration so that a compromised workstation never holds credentials that reach a controller, and monitoring for the behaviour that precedes escalation, such as one user suddenly requesting many service tickets, or tickets with RC4 encryption, both of which Microsoft names as Kerberoasting signals. The Protected Users group, enforced by controllers from the Windows Server 2012 R2 functional level, denies its members NTLM, DES (Data Encryption Standard) and RC4 in Kerberos pre-authentication and any delegation, and stops their TGTs being renewed beyond four hours. Most published attack chains against enterprises end at Active Directory, and an organization that treats its controllers as ordinary infrastructure has misjudged where its real perimeter is.

For network and security engineers the directory is the back end of almost every AAA (authentication, authorization and accounting) design. A RADIUS (Remote Authentication Dial-In User Service) server checking a PEAP (Protected Extensible Authentication Protocol) login with MS-CHAP-V2 (version 2 of Microsoft's dialect of the Challenge Handshake Authentication Protocol) verifies the response against the password-derived hash the domain holds, which is why FortiAuthenticator must join the domain to do it: its administration guide asks for the Kerberos realm in upper case, the domain's NetBIOS name and a NetBIOS name for the appliance, and recommends a non-administrator account delegated only to manage computer objects, while Fortinet's own troubleshooting note sends a join that reports joined but not connected to the settings and the clock first. BIG-IP Access Policy Manager (APM) authenticates against Active Directory with Kerberos in its AD Auth action; its AD Query action authenticates nothing, but reads the user's memberOf attribute, optionally expanded to nested groups and the primary group, into session variables that the policy then branches on. Since BIG-IP 17.0 the bundled Kerberos library (krb5 1.18) no longer supports single DES, so old accounts that still depend on it fail with a KDC encryption type error. A policy engine choosing a VLAN (virtual local area network) reads group membership over LDAP in the same way, a TACACS+ (Terminal Access Controller Access-Control System Plus) server authenticating an administrator binds to the domain, and a web portal does the same for a sponsored guest. The directory's groups are therefore the roles of a role-based model whether or not anyone called them that, and privilege creep and separation of duties describe what happens to those groups when nobody reviews them.

sso.def: Single sign-on (SSO): authenticating once to an identity service and then reaching many applications without logging in again, usually through a federation protocol such as SAML (Security Assertion Markup Language) or OpenID Connect, or through Kerberos tickets inside a Windows domain.
sso.context: Single sign-on (SSO) moves the login out of each application and into one place. An identity provider, or a Kerberos key distribution centre, authenticates the user once; every application then accepts a signed assertion, token or ticket instead of keeping a password of its own. The gains are real: one strong login to protect, one place to enforce multi-factor authentication, one switch to turn an account off. So is the price. The identity service becomes a single point of failure and the most valuable target on the network, and once the login is hardened, attackers go after what outlives it: session cookies, tokens and the IdP's signing keys.
sso.depth:
NIST (National Institute of Standards and Technology) SP (Special Publication) 800-63-4 defines single sign-on (SSO) as an authentication process by which one account and its authenticators are used to access multiple applications in a seamless manner, generally implemented with a federation protocol. SP 800-63C-4 adds the federation view: the subscriber uses many relying parties (RPs) without separate authenticators at each, and federation is preferred when application and account are not administered in a common security domain. The definition rules out two look-alikes. The same password typed into every application is password reuse, because each application still verifies a secret of its own; a password manager or a gateway that replays stored credentials gives the user an SSO experience while the back ends still see passwords.

Three mechanisms deliver it. Federation protocols send the browser to an identity provider (IdP), which authenticates the user or reuses the session it already holds and returns a signed assertion: a SAML (Security Assertion Markup Language) assertion or an OpenID Connect (OIDC) ID token, which the application checks for signature, issuer, audience, validity window and replay before opening its own session. Kerberos does the job inside a Windows domain: at logon the client proves the user's identity to the key distribution centre (KDC) and receives a ticket-granting ticket (TGT), then presents it to obtain a service ticket for each service without sending the password again; in Windows Server the KDC runs on every domain controller, over the Active Directory Domain Services database. The third is credential caching and proxying at a gateway: F5 BIG-IP Access Policy Manager (APM) caches the identity collected by its access policy in a session database and logs the user in to each back end with one of its methods, HTTP (Hypertext Transfer Protocol) Basic, NTLM (NT LAN Manager) v1 and v2, Kerberos, form-based, forms client-initiated, OAuth Bearer, or its SAML IdP service.

The lineage is long. Kerberos Versions 1 to 4 were designed at the Massachusetts Institute of Technology's (MIT) Project Athena by Steve Miller and Clifford Neuman, with Jerome Saltzer and Jeffrey Schiller; Version 5 is RFC (Request for Comments) 4120, published in July 2005 to obsolete RFC 1510. SAML V1.0 became an OASIS (Organization for the Advancement of Structured Information Standards) standard in November 2002, V1.1 in September 2003 and V2.0 in March 2005; OpenID Connect followed as a final specification in 2014.

The benefits are larger than convenience. SSO removes one password per application, so there are fewer secrets to phish, reuse or reset; it puts multi-factor policy in one place instead of in every application's login page; and it makes removal a single action, provided the IdP also tells the applications. SP 800-63C-4 asks the IdP to signal downstream RPs when an account is terminated, because otherwise the RP may keep an account that nobody can reach through the IdP but an attacker can still target.

Sessions are where the remaining risk lives, because SSO creates at least two of them. SP 800-63B-4 notes that the IdP and the RP manage sessions separately: when an RP session expires, a still-valid IdP session can issue a new assertion without asking the user anything, and the RP is the authority on whether its reauthentication rules were met. It sets reauthentication ceilings by authenticator assurance level (AAL): an overall timeout that should be no more than 30 days at AAL1; 24 hours overall and 1 hour of inactivity at AAL2; 12 hours overall and, as a recommendation, 15 minutes of inactivity at AAL3. Logout is weaker than login: SP 800-63C-4 states that ending the session at the IdP will not necessarily end the sessions the user holds at RPs, unless the protocol, such as OIDC front-channel or back-channel logout, or a shared signal carries the event.

Concentration cuts both ways. On 15 March 2021, from about 19:00 UTC (Coordinated Universal Time), applications that depended on Azure Active Directory (Azure AD) began failing to authenticate users: an automated key-rotation job had removed a signing key that had been marked to be retained, Azure AD published the changed key metadata, and applications refreshed it and stopped trusting tokens signed with that key. Microsoft rolled the metadata back at 21:05 UTC, but cached copies lingered, and the last residual impact was declared mitigated at 09:25 UTC on 16 March. The other edge is compromise. NIST warns that attacks on an IdP propagate to every RP that trusts it, so a stolen IdP administrator account or signing key is not one application but all of them, and identity infrastructure deserves the strongest protection available.

Attackers have adapted by going after the session instead of the password. In July 2022 Microsoft described an adversary-in-the-middle (AiTM) phishing campaign that had targeted more than 10,000 organizations since September 2021: a proxy built with kits such as Evilginx2 relayed the real sign-in page, captured the password and the session cookie, and replayed the cookie, which already carried a multi-factor claim, so the second factor was skipped rather than broken; payment fraud followed in as little as five minutes. In October 2023 Okta revoked session tokens found in HTTP Archive (HAR) files that an attacker had read in its support system. SP 800-63B-4 counts manual-entry codes and out-of-band approvals as not phishing-resistant and accepts only cryptographic methods bound to the channel or to the verifier's name, such as WebAuthn (Web Authentication) with FIDO2 (Fast Identity Online 2); short, device-bound sessions and conditional access limit what a stolen cookie is worth.

Vendor products use the word loosely, so read what each one delivers. Fortinet Single Sign-On (FSSO) does not log anyone in to an application: agents watch Windows logons and pass user, address and group to the FortiGate, so identity-based firewall policies apply without a second prompt. The collector agent talks to the FortiGate on TCP (Transmission Control Protocol) port 8000, listens on UDP (User Datagram Protocol) port 8002 for domain controller agents, and up to five collector agents can be configured for redundancy. In APM, the SSO object is the unit to review: F5 states that a misconfigured object for HTTP Basic, NTLM, Kerberos or OAuth Bearer can disable SSO for every method in the user's session when that resource is reached, with the two form methods the only exceptions.

The neighbours are easily confused. Federation is the trust arrangement between separately run parties and SSO the experience it produces, though NIST notes that the federation process is sometimes known as single sign-on; multi-factor authentication (MFA) is how strongly the one login is done, not how often; OAuth 2.0 delegates access to APIs (application programming interfaces) and becomes sign-in only through OIDC.

mdm.def: Mobile Device Management: enrolling phones, tablets, and laptops under central policy - configure, patch, locate, and wipe from one console.
mdm.context: The truce line of BYOD: your device, the company's rules on the work part of it.
mdm.depth:
Mobile device management enrols devices under a policy that can enforce encryption, require a passcode, push configuration and wipe remotely. On corporate-owned hardware that is straightforward; on personal devices it is a negotiation, because the same capabilities that protect company data also reach the owner's life.

The distinction that resolves most of it is between managing the device and managing the workspace. Application-level containment separates corporate data into a space that can be wiped independently, which gives the organization what it actually needs and leaves the rest alone. Deployments that skip that distinction generate resistance that is entirely rational, and the predictable outcome is people routing work through personal accounts the policy cannot see at all.

byod.def: Bring Your Own Device: employees working from personal hardware - cheaper fleets, happier users, and a security perimeter made of other people's phones.
byod.context: Containerization and MDM exist to make the acronym survivable.

patch-management.def: The cycle of testing and deploying software updates across the fleet - balancing the risk of the bug against the risk of the fix.
patch-management.context: Patch Tuesday made it a calendar; unpatched known vulnerabilities remain the most preventable breach cause.

rma.def: Return Merchandise Authorization: the vendor's blessing to send hardware back - the number without which the box comes home unopened.
rma.context: Advance replacement ships the new unit first; standard RMA teaches patience.
rma.depth:
An RMA is the process for returning failed hardware, and the operational reality is that the paperwork takes longer than the fault. Identifying the failure is minutes; obtaining an authorization number, arranging shipment, waiting for the replacement and installing it is days to weeks depending on contract and geography.

That gap is what spares inventory exists to close, and the calculation is straightforward: the cost of holding a spare against the cost of the outage its absence extends. Contracts express it as response time, and the figure worth reading is what the response actually commits to, since next business day means a part dispatched rather than a system restored. In distant locations the shipping time dominates every other term, which is why a support agreement written for one country reads very differently in another.

warm-cold-boot.def: Restarting without cutting power versus from full power-off - the cold boot clears states the warm one preserves.
warm-cold-boot.context: Why 'turn it off and on again' sometimes fixes what 'restart' did not.
warm-cold-boot.depth:
A cold boot is a full power cycle; a warm boot is a restart that leaves power applied. The difference is not pedantry, because it determines what state survives, and the state that survives is exactly what you may be trying to clear.

Hardware is the usual reason it matters. A network interface, storage controller or peripheral that has entered a confused condition may be reset by its own firmware on a warm restart and only genuinely reinitialized when power is removed, so a device that keeps misbehaving across reboots often needs the power actually cut. Remote administration typically offers only the warm option, which is why managed power distribution units exist.

The security dimension is the cold boot attack, which inverts the assumption. Memory does not clear instantly when power is removed, and cooling the modules extends retention long enough to move them to another machine and read out encryption keys that the running system believed were safely in volatile storage. That is why full disk encryption designs care about what is in memory when a machine is locked or suspended, and why suspend-to-disk with the key evicted is a meaningfully different security posture from a locked screen.

safe-mode.def: Booting with minimal drivers and services: if the problem vanishes here, something loaded at startup is the suspect.
safe-mode.context: Diagnosis by subtraction - the OS's own isolation test.

event-viewer.def: The operating system's diary of errors, warnings, and audits - where 'it just crashed' becomes a source, an ID, and a timestamp.
event-viewer.context: Windows' Event Viewer and Unix's journals: same idea, the machine wrote down what happened.

driver.def: The software that teaches the operating system to speak to a specific piece of hardware - and the first suspect when that hardware misbehaves.
driver.context: Kernel-adjacent by nature, which is why a bad one can take the whole system down with it.

full-disk-encryption.def: Encrypting the entire drive so a lost or stolen machine leaks nothing - BitLocker, FileVault, LUKS - unlocked at boot, transparent after.
full-disk-encryption.context: Turns 'laptop stolen from car' from a breach notification into a hardware expense.

password-manager.def: A vault that generates and stores a unique strong password per site, unlocked by one master secret - the practical end of password reuse.
password-manager.context: The advice that survived every other password rule: length beats complexity, uniqueness beats both.

least-privilege-desktop.def: Daily work in an unprivileged account, elevation only when needed: the desktop version of least privilege, and malware's least favourite policy.
least-privilege-desktop.context: Most commodity malware simply fails without local admin.
least-privilege-desktop.depth:
Running a desktop without administrative rights is the single most effective endpoint control available, and it is unpopular for reasons that are worth engaging with rather than dismissing. A substantial share of malware that requires elevation simply fails on a standard user account, and a substantial share of the remainder is limited to that user's own data.

The objection is real: some software genuinely needs elevation, some legacy applications write to locations that require it, and users doing technical work install things constantly. A policy that makes people raise a ticket for every installation converts a security control into a productivity tax, and the predictable result is blanket exceptions that quietly restore the original state.

What works is targeted rather than absolute. Application allowlisting removes the need to install arbitrary software, just-in-time elevation grants rights for a task and takes them back, and separate accounts let an administrator do administrative work without browsing the web as one. The failure mode to avoid is the middle position: a policy strict enough to be resented, with enough exceptions that it protects nothing, which is where organizations land when the control is implemented without addressing the workflow it broke.

shadow-copy.def: Snapshots are fast local restore points sharing the original's fate; backups live elsewhere and survive it - only the second answers ransomware.
shadow-copy.context: The 3-2-1 rule: three copies, two media, one off-site.
shadow-copy.depth:
A shadow copy is a point-in-time snapshot of a volume taken while it is in use, so that files locked by running applications can still be backed up consistently. Windows calls the mechanism Volume Shadow Copy Service, and the same idea appears everywhere under different names.

Its everyday value is the previous versions feature, which lets a user recover a file they overwrote an hour ago without involving anyone. That quietly resolves an enormous number of support requests, and the fact that most users do not know it exists is a genuine documentation failure rather than a technical one.

Its role in ransomware is why it now gets security attention. Deleting shadow copies is a standard early step for ransomware, precisely because they would otherwise make recovery trivial, and the command to do it is well known enough that its execution is a high-quality detection signal. That has driven both protections on the deletion path and the harder lesson underneath: a backup that lives on the machine being attacked, reachable by an administrator on that machine, is a convenience feature rather than a backup, and the copy that survives is the one somewhere else entirely.

layer-8.def: The unofficial OSI layer above application: the human - where a startling share of network problems actually occur.
layer-8.context: Said with a smile in the NOC (network operations centre); the polite cousin of PEBKAC.

percussive-maintenance.def: The time-honored art of fixing a device by striking it firmly - occasionally effective on oxidized contacts, always effective on morale.
percussive-maintenance.context: Immortalized across generations of field lore; not covered by warranty.

have-you-tried-turning-it-off.def: Support's opening liturgy and its most statistically justified question: a restart clears the accumulated state where most transient faults live.
have-you-tried-turning-it-off.context: Canonized by The IT Crowd; annoying precisely because it works.
have-you-tried-turning-it-off.depth:
Have you tried turning it off and on again is a punchline about support laziness, and it is also genuinely the highest-yield first question in troubleshooting. That tension is worth taking seriously rather than resolving in either direction.

It works because a restart discards accumulated state, and accumulated state is where most faults live. Leaked memory, exhausted handles, a cached value that is now wrong, a thread stuck waiting on something that will never arrive, a driver in a condition its author never tested: none of these are in the code as written, they are in what the code became after running for a month. Restarting returns the system to the only configuration that was ever deliberately designed.

The professional objection is that it destroys the evidence, and that is correct and important. A restart fixes the symptom and guarantees the cause remains unknown, so the discipline is to capture state first, logs, memory, connection tables, whatever the situation allows, and then restart. Do it in that order and you get both the service back and the ability to prevent a recurrence. Do it in the other order and you will be here again, without having learned anything.

ticket-ping-pong.def: A ticket bounced between teams, each reassigning it as not-mine - the organizational failure mode where routing replaces resolving.
ticket-ping-pong.context: The cure is ownership: whoever holds it, drives it, even across team lines.

user-error-codes.def: The joke 'error codes' for user-caused issues - ID-10-T, PICNIC, layer 8 - support's private shorthand, best kept private.
user-error-codes.context: Funny in the break room, career-limiting in the ticket notes.

onboarding-offboarding.def: The account-and-access lifecycle at hiring and departure: created and granted on day one, revoked completely on the last - the second half is the audit finding.
onboarding-offboarding.context: Orphaned accounts of departed employees are a perennial breach vector.
onboarding-offboarding.depth:
Onboarding and offboarding are the joiner and leaver processes, and the asymmetry between them is one of the most reliable findings in any access review. Onboarding is highly visible, because a new person who cannot work complains immediately and loudly, and offboarding is invisible, because an account that still functions after someone leaves generates no complaint from anyone.

That asymmetry produces the predictable outcome. Access accumulates at the individual level too, since a person moving between roles gains the new permissions and rarely loses the old ones, which is privilege creep and ends with long-serving employees holding access no single role would ever justify. Nobody decided that; it is the sum of many reasonable individual decisions.

The fixes are structural rather than procedural. Automated deprovisioning driven by the authoritative HR record removes the dependency on somebody remembering, role-based access makes a change of role a replacement rather than an addition, and periodic recertification forces someone to affirm that access is still needed. The test of whether any of it works is simple and rarely run: pick someone who left three months ago and try to find what they can still reach.

kba-security-questions.def: Knowledge-based authentication - mother's maiden name, first pet - identity proofs from an era before social media published the answers.
kba-security-questions.context: Treat them as passwords: generate nonsense and store it in the manager.

remote-hands.def: Data-center staff acting as your on-site body: swap the drive, read the LEDs, move the cable - your eyes and hands, billed by the quarter hour.
remote-hands.context: The instructions must survive contact with someone who has never seen your rack.
remote-hands.depth:
Remote hands is a data centre service where facility staff perform physical tasks on your behalf: reseating a cable, power-cycling a device, reading what is on a console screen, swapping a drive. You describe what you need, someone who is already on site does it.

Its value is time rather than skill. The staff are not expected to diagnose your problem, and asking them to is where the service goes wrong; they are a pair of hands in a building you would otherwise need to reach. The organizations that use it well send precise, unambiguous, single-step instructions with photographs and exact labels, because the person receiving them has no context and is standing in a loud room full of nearly identical equipment.

The discipline it enforces is worth having anyway. Writing instructions that a competent stranger can execute without knowing your architecture is the same discipline as writing a runbook, and if you cannot describe the task that precisely, the task is probably not understood well enough to be done safely by anyone. Labelling matters enormously here, and a rack where the labels are wrong is one where remote hands will confidently unplug the wrong thing.

maintenance-window.def: A scheduled, announced and bounded period, chosen for low impact, in which changes to a production system are allowed, with the rollback planned in advance; work outside it needs the justification of an emergency. The ITIL (Information Technology Infrastructure Library) glossary calls it a change window.
maintenance-window.context: The reason so much of IT (information technology) happens at 2 a.m. on a Sunday. A maintenance window puts risky work where the fewest users are, tells them beforehand, and gives the engineers a fixed start, a fixed end and a point of no return. It may recur (every Sunday from 02:00 to 04:00, or the second Tuesday of the month) or be booked once for a single change, and it usually carries three agreements: the service may be degraded or unavailable inside it; that time is not held against the service level agreement (SLA); and anything urgent enough to be done outside it goes through the emergency change procedure. On a network it is also when routing is steered away from a device before anyone touches it. Services that have no quiet hour are pushing the practice towards upgrades that roll through redundant members without stopping the service.
maintenance-window.depth:
The term comes from IT (information technology) service management. The 2011 glossary of ITIL (Information Technology Infrastructure Library) defines a change window as a regular, agreed time when changes or releases may be implemented with minimal impact on services, adds that change windows are usually documented in service level agreements (SLAs), and treats release window as a synonym. Maintenance window is the name operations teams and cloud providers use for the same thing. Two neighbours are often confused with it. Planned downtime, in the same glossary, is agreed time when a service will not be available; a window is permission and a time box, and a well-run one may cause no downtime at all. A blackout window, or change freeze, is the opposite: ServiceNow's change module defines blackout windows as times during which normal change activity should not be scheduled and maintenance windows as times during which change requests should be scheduled, and its conflict detection checks a change request against both.

A window has a start, an end, a scope, an owner and an audience that was told in advance. The end is the hard part. The ITIL vocabulary separates back-out (restoring a service to a previous baseline) from remediation in general, and a window has to contain the change, its verification and, if needed, the back-out and the check after it. The latest moment to begin backing out is therefore the end of the window minus the rehearsed back-out time minus the time to verify, and a change still unconfirmed at that moment has failed even if it looks close. One university's change management glossary makes the point in its definitions: a change that exceeded its maintenance window counts as an unsuccessful change, alongside one that was backed out or caused an incident. A window can also be weaker than it sounds. On Amazon's Relational Database Service (RDS) the weekly window fixes when pending operations start and does not limit how long they run, so maintenance can continue past the stated end.

The hour is chosen by traffic. Amazon Web Services (AWS) says the window should fall at the time of lowest usage, gives every RDS database instance a weekly window of 30 minutes, and when the customer picks none assigns one at random inside an 8-hour block per region: 03:00 to 11:00 UTC (Coordinated Universal Time) for US East, 00:00 to 08:00 UTC for São Paulo. Microsoft plans maintenance of its online services for the hours when usage is historically lowest in each regional time zone and notifies customers no later than five days ahead. Hence the early hours of a Sunday. A window stated without its time zone is a classic way to start a change an hour early or a day late.

The link to the SLA is arithmetic. Availability is calculated from agreed service time and downtime, and 99.9 per cent over a year leaves about 8.8 hours, 99.99 per cent about 53 minutes and five nines 5.26 minutes. A weekly 30-minute window used in full is 26 hours a year. So a contract either carves the window out or forbids using it for outages. Google's Cloud SQL agreement does the first for its Enterprise edition: downtime that is part of scheduled maintenance is not counted, and that maintenance is performed only inside the window the customer configured.
