ITIL names the alternative continuous operation, a design that eliminates planned downtime of the service even though individual components go down.

On a network, the window opens by moving traffic away. For Border Gateway Protocol (BGP) sessions, Request for Comments (RFC) 8326 of March 2018 standardizes the well-known community GRACEFUL_SHUTDOWN (65535:0): the operator tags the routes of the session about to be closed, the neighbours lower their local preference, 0 being the recommended value, and the old path stays usable while better ones are selected, which reduces or eliminates the packets lost during convergence. RFC 9003 lets the router that closes the session say why, in up to 255 octets; the example in its predecessor, RFC 8203, is a ticket number followed by the words software upgrade; back in 2 hours. RFC 8327, a Best Current Practice, applies the same thinking to work on the layer below, such as an internet exchange's switching fabric: tear the BGP sessions down before starting. It warns that detection usually takes a hold timer of 90 to 180 seconds and that a router with a slow control plane and full routes may need as much as 15 minutes to converge, so the operator should watch traffic drain instead of trusting a fixed grace period. For Open Shortest Path First (OSPF), RFC 6987 describes advertising all of a router's non-stub links at the maximum metric, 0xffff, so that neighbours stop using it for transit, one stated use being the graceful removal and reintroduction of the router.

Redundant appliances are upgraded inside windows too. F5 recommends upgrading BIG-IP software during a scheduled maintenance window because, while the members of a device group run different versions, connection mirroring does not work; its procedure forces one device offline at a time. Fortinet tells administrators to back up the configuration, schedule a maintenance window and confirm the upgrade path before upgrading a FortiGate high availability (HA) cluster; the default uninterrupted upgrade does the subordinate units first, elects a new primary from them and upgrades the former primary last, while the faster interrupted mode (set upgrade-mode simultaneous) reboots everything at once. The window exists even for an upgrade designed to be invisible, because for its duration the cluster has less redundancy than usual.

Announcements and alarms are part of the mechanism. Carriers and exchanges send notices that customers must turn into calendar entries and tickets, and a draft Best Current Operational Practice from the North American Network Operators' Group (NANOG) proposes a machine-readable form: an iCalendar object carrying the provider, the account, a maintenance identifier, the service object affected, a status and one of four impact levels (NO-IMPACT, REDUCED-REDUNDANCY, DEGRADED, OUTAGE). Its authors name manual handling and time zone conversion as the sources of error. On the monitoring side, a maintenance window in a paging system such as PagerDuty disables the service's integrations so that no new incidents trigger until it ends. That stops the expected alarms, and it also means a real failure inside the window pages nobody unless someone is watching the graphs.

Windows collide with security. The patch management guide of the United States National Institute of Standards and Technology (NIST), Special Publication 800-40 Revision 4 of April 2022, observes that business owners see patching as scheduled downtime plus the risk of more, and that routine patching is therefore postponed, which gives attackers additional windows of opportunity. Its example maintenance groups include data centre equipment that must adhere to scheduled outage windows for all non-emergency situations and assets that can only be rebooted during a monthly maintenance outage. The exception is the emergency change, which ITIL defines as one that must be introduced as soon as possible, for example to resolve a major incident or implement a security patch, and which has its own approval body. NIST's advice for emergency patching is the routine approach on a highly accelerated schedule, not the absence of one.

A window limits who is affected if the change fails at once; it does nothing for the quality of the change. Google's site reliability engineers report that roughly 70 per cent of outages are due to changes in a live system. On 4 October 2021 a command issued during a routine maintenance job at Facebook, meant to assess backbone capacity, took down every backbone link; a bug in the tool that audits such commands let it through, the company's DNS servers withdrew their BGP announcements, and the out-of-band network was down as well, so engineers had to go on site. On 8 July 2022 Rogers, in the sixth phase of a seven-phase core upgrade, removed an access control list (ACL) policy filter from its distribution routers during the maintenance window; the flood of routes crashed the core, and more than 12 million customers lost service from 4:58 on 8 July to 7:00 the next morning, Eastern Daylight Time. The report commissioned by the Canadian regulator notes that the process had rated the whole upgrade High risk and then, because the earlier phases had gone well, downgraded the sixth phase to Low, so it received no extra scrutiny, higher approval or lab test.

The modern criticism follows from those cases. A night window concentrates changes into large, rare, tired sessions, and the practices that Google credits with raising both speed and safety run the other way: progressive rollouts, quick and accurate detection, and safe rollback, automated so that fatigue and inattention are taken out of the loop. Cloud services now sell the option, as when AWS suggests a blue/green deployment to minimize the downtime of a database upgrade. The window keeps its place where there is a single device with no peer, state that cannot be drained, or a contract that requires notice. The figures worth keeping are five days of notice, 90 to 180 seconds of hold timer, 15 minutes of worst-case convergence, and the rule that the back-out must fit inside the window as well.

vpc.def: Virtual Private Cloud: your own logically isolated network inside a public cloud - address space, subnets, routing, and gateways, defined in software.
vpc.context: The cloud's answer to 'where does my network live now?'; every workload sits inside one.

security-group.def: A security group is a cloud platform's stateful virtual firewall attached to instances or their network interfaces: allow rules for inbound and outbound traffic, with return traffic permitted automatically and anything inbound denied unless a rule allows it.
security-group.context: It follows the instance wherever it moves: the rule set is tied to the workload, not the wire. That makes it the cloud's native form of microsegmentation, especially when one group's rules refer to another group rather than to addresses (the web tier may reach the database tier on one port, whatever their IP addresses are today). The name is Amazon's, from EC2 (Elastic Compute Cloud) in 2006, and it does not mean the same thing everywhere: AWS (Amazon Web Services) and OpenStack groups hold allow rules only, combined into one set, while Azure's network security groups add deny rules and priorities, and Google calls the equivalent VPC (virtual private cloud) firewall rules. In Active Directory the same two words name something unrelated, a group of users that receives permissions.
security-group.depth:
What it is. AWS (Amazon Web Services) describes a security group as controlling the traffic that is allowed to reach and leave the resources it is associated with, acting as a virtual firewall: once a group is associated with an EC2 (Elastic Compute Cloud) instance, it controls that instance's inbound and outbound traffic. Inbound rules name a source, a protocol and a port range; outbound rules name a destination, a protocol and a port range; the source or destination can be an IPv4 or IPv6 CIDR (Classless Inter-Domain Routing) block, a managed prefix list or another security group. Three properties define its behaviour. It is stateful: the response to a request an instance sent is allowed back in regardless of the inbound rules, and the response to allowed inbound traffic is allowed out regardless of the outbound rules. It holds allow rules only, never deny rules. And when several groups are associated with one resource, their rules are aggregated into a single set, so, unlike an ACL (access control list), order plays no part: a packet is permitted if any rule in any of the groups permits it. A newly created group has no inbound rules, so nothing gets in, and one outbound rule allowing all traffic, which can be removed; with no outbound rules nothing leaves. Changes apply immediately to every resource associated with the group.

Where it came from. Jeff Barr's 2013 history of EC2 recalls that when the service launched in 2006 each instance received a public IP address and could have a security group, attached at launch time, for ingress filtering; Amazon later named that platform EC2-Classic. The VPC (virtual private cloud) followed in 2009, and in 2011 an upgrade brought enhanced security groups with both ingress and egress filtering and the ability to change membership on running instances, together with routing tables and network ACLs between subnets. The outbound default of allow all, still in place today, is a trace of that history: the first security groups filtered only what came in.

Groups that refer to groups. The feature that turns a security group from a host firewall into a segmentation tool is referencing. When a rule names another security group as its source or destination, it applies to every instance associated with that group, communicating over their private IP addresses on the specified protocol and port, so a database group can admit port 5432 only from members of the application group, however many application instances exist and whatever addresses they hold. References work within a VPC and across VPC peering connections and transit gateways, and a reference to a group in a peer VPC that is deleted becomes a stale rule that has to be cleaned up. Every VPC also comes with a group named default, which allows inbound traffic from its own members and all outbound traffic, and is applied automatically to any resource launched without a group; AWS recommends creating purpose-specific groups instead, and AWS Security Hub's control EC2.2 flags any default group that allows inbound or outbound traffic at all.

Limits and blind spots. The defaults are 2,500 security groups per Region, 60 inbound and 60 outbound rules per group (counted separately for IPv4 and IPv6) and five groups per network interface, adjustable up to 16, as long as rules per group multiplied by groups per interface stays at or below 1,000. Some traffic never meets a security group: AWS lists the Amazon DNS resolver, Amazon DHCP (Dynamic Host Configuration Protocol), the EC2 instance metadata service, ECS (Elastic Container Service) task metadata, Windows licence activation, the Amazon Time Sync Service and the reserved addresses of the VPC router. The neighbouring control, the network ACL, works at the subnet boundary instead of the interface, is stateless, and uses numbered allow and deny rules evaluated from the lowest number, which is why the two are normally used together: the security group for precise per-workload policy, the network ACL for coarse subnet-wide denies.

Azure's network security group. Microsoft's equivalent shares the idea and differs in the details that cause mistakes when people move between clouds. A network security group can be associated with a subnet or a network interface, and its rules carry a priority from 100 to 4096; they are processed in priority order, and processing stops at the first match, so a lower-numbered rule shadows a higher one, as in any ACL. Rules can allow or deny, matched on the five-tuple of source, source port, destination, destination port and protocol. Every group ends with default rules that cannot be deleted: inbound AllowVnetInBound at 65000, AllowAzureLoadBalancerInBound at 65001 and DenyAllInBound at 65500, and outbound AllowVnetOutBound at 65000, AllowInternetOutBound at 65001 and DenyAllOutBound at 65500. Flow records make it stateful, and removing a rule that allowed a connection does not interrupt connections already established; new rules affect only new connections. Rules can use service tags such as VirtualNetwork, AzureLoadBalancer and Internet, and application security groups, which group virtual machines so that policy is written about roles instead of addresses, Azure's counterpart of referencing one security group from another. Security admin rules from Azure Virtual Network Manager are evaluated before any network security group rule, and the host services on 168.63.129.16 and 169.254.169.254 are not subject to network security groups by default.

Google and OpenStack. Google Cloud does not use the name: its VPC firewall rules are stateful, carry allow or deny actions with numeric priorities, cannot be made to deny response traffic, are targeted at instances by network tags or service accounts, and fall back to implied actions when no rule applies; the default network arrives with permissive pre-populated rules such as default-allow-internal at priority 65534. Connection tracking has a ceiling per machine type, 130,000 connections per vCPU up to 1,040,000 for instances with more than eight, beyond which the longest-idle connections stop being tracked. OpenStack's Neutron keeps the AWS model closely: a security group is a container for virtual firewall rules at the port level, with a default deny policy and allow rules only, several groups per port combine additively, and the firewall driver translates the rules into the host's packet filter, such as iptables; each project's default group allows all egress and denies all ingress.

How they go wrong. The commonest failure is a rule opened to 0.0.0.0/0 on a port that should never face the internet. Security Hub rates control EC2.19 critical and lists 24 high-risk ports that should never accept unrestricted ingress, among them 22 (SSH, Secure Shell), 23 (Telnet), 25 (SMTP, Simple Mail Transfer Protocol), 445 (CIFS, Common Internet File System), 1433 and 1434 (Microsoft SQL Server), 3306 (MySQL), 3389 (RDP, Remote Desktop Protocol), 5432 (PostgreSQL) and 9200 and 9300; separate controls watch ports 22 and 3389. The second failure is the outbound default: a group whose all-traffic egress rule is never removed gives a compromised instance an open road out. The third is sprawl, with dozens of groups, overlapping rules and stale references that nobody can explain, inside a rule budget of 60 per group. Finally, a name collision causes real confusion in hybrid estates: in Active Directory a security group is a group of users or computers used to assign permissions, as opposed to a distribution group, which is only a mailing list and cannot appear in a DACL (discretionary access control list). A ticket that says a user must be added to the security group may mean either.

nacl.def: The stateless subnet-level filter in cloud networks: numbered allow and deny rules evaluated in order, both directions filtered independently.
nacl.context: Stateless means return traffic needs its own rule - the classic NACL lesson, learned once per engineer.

route-table.def: The per-subnet routing decisions of a VPC: which destinations go to the internet gateway, the NAT (network address translation), the peering, or the tunnel.
route-table.context: The first place to look when a cloud subnet 'has no internet'.

internet-gateway.def: The VPC component that gives public subnets a door to the internet - horizontally scaled, no bandwidth knob, no single box to fail.
internet-gateway.context: Its presence in the route table is what makes a subnet 'public'.

nat-gateway.def: The managed service that lets private subnets reach out to the internet without being reachable from it - outbound yes, inbound no.
nat-gateway.context: Billed per hour and per gigabyte processed, which is how it becomes a surprise line item.

elastic-ip.def: A static public address you own and can remap between instances - identity that survives the workload behind it.
elastic-ip.context: The cloud's answer to 'the IP must not change'; scarce IPv4 makes idle ones billable.

availability-zone.def: One or more data centres with independent power, cooling, and network inside a region - close enough for sync replication, far enough to fail separately.
availability-zone.context: Multi-AZ is the first rung of cloud resilience; same-AZ redundancy is a shared fate.

transit-gateway.def: The cloud's central router: VPCs, VPNs, and interconnects attach to one hub instead of meshing with each other.
transit-gateway.context: Turns N-squared peerings into N attachments - the hub-and-spoke pattern as a managed service.

vpc-peering.def: A private one-to-one link between two VPCs, routing their address spaces to each other - non-transitive by design.
vpc-peering.context: Peering A-B and B-C does not connect A to C; that gap is why transit gateways exist.

hub-and-spoke.def: The topology where everything connects through a central hub instead of to each other - fewer links, central control, one very important middle.
hub-and-spoke.context: The design behind transit gateways, SD-WAN (software-defined wide area network) backbones, and most airline maps.
hub-and-spoke.depth:
Hub and spoke is a topology where sites connect to a central location rather than to each other, and every conversation between two spokes passes through the hub. It was the default enterprise design for decades because the hub was where the applications, the internet connection and the security controls lived.

Its virtue is control and its cost is the path. Traffic from one branch to another travels to the centre and back, which adds latency proportional to how far the centre is from both, and the hub becomes both a bottleneck and a single point of failure that requires expensive redundancy. When the applications were genuinely in the data centre, the extra distance was buying something real.

That justification weakened when the applications moved. If the destination is a cloud service, backhauling a branch's internet traffic to a distant hub in order to inspect it is paying latency for a security control that could be applied closer, which is the entire argument behind SD-WAN and the SASE (secure access service edge) model. The topology is not obsolete, since regulated traffic and internal systems still justify it, but it is now a choice rather than the assumption.

dedicated-interconnect.def: A private physical circuit from your premises into the cloud provider's edge - predictable latency, real bandwidth, no public internet in the path.
dedicated-interconnect.context: AWS Direct Connect, Azure ExpressRoute, Google Cloud Interconnect: three names, one idea.

privatelink.def: Consuming a service through a private address inside your own VPC, so the traffic never touches the public internet.
privatelink.context: The pattern that keeps 'call the API' from meaning 'cross the internet'.

public-vs-private-subnet.def: The basic VPC split: public subnets route to the internet gateway and can be reached; private subnets reach out through NAT (network address translation) and cannot.
public-vs-private-subnet.context: Load balancers in public, workloads in private: the pattern behind most cloud reference architectures.
public-vs-private-subnet.depth:
In cloud networking a public subnet has a route to an internet gateway and a private one does not, and that single routing difference is the entire distinction. It is not about addresses, and a resource in a private subnet may hold a perfectly ordinary address that simply has no path outward.

The pattern this produces is the standard reference architecture: load balancers in the public subnet, application servers and databases in private subnets, and outbound access for the private tier through a NAT gateway that permits egress without permitting inbound. That arrangement means a compromised application server cannot be reached directly from the internet even if it is listening.

Two mistakes recur often enough to be worth naming. A resource placed in a private subnet with a public address attached is not private, because the route is what matters and someone will assume the address implies isolation. And the outbound path is frequently forgotten in threat modelling: a private subnet with unrestricted egress lets an attacker exfiltrate data and reach command infrastructure freely, so the control that matters is often on the way out rather than the way in.

flow-logs.def: The cloud's NetFlow: records of accepted and rejected connections per interface, subnet, or VPC - who talked to whom, and who was refused.
flow-logs.context: The first evidence pulled in cloud incident response; REJECT lines are free reconnaissance detection.

cdn.def: Content delivery network: a distributed set of servers that caches copies of a site's content at edge locations close to users, so that requests are answered from nearby instead of from the origin.
cdn.context: Latency physics as a product: a content delivery network (CDN) cannot make packets travel faster, so it shortens the trip by answering from a cache in a point of presence (PoP) near the user. It is also the shield that absorbs traffic spikes and much DDoS (distributed denial of service), because the load lands on the provider's many edges and not on a single origin. The parts are a request-routing system that steers each user to an edge, through Domain Name System (DNS) answers or anycast, surrogate caches that follow the caching rules of the Hypertext Transfer Protocol (HTTP), and a control system that pushes configuration to all of them at once. That last part is the catch: a CDN stands in front of every site it serves, terminates their encrypted connections, and can take all of them down together.
cdn.depth:
The Internet Engineering Task Force (IETF) defines a content delivery network (CDN), which it also calls a content distribution network, in Request for Comments (RFC) 6707 of September 2012: network infrastructure in which the network elements cooperate at layers 4 through 7 for more effective delivery of content to user agents. Typically it has four parts: a request routing system, a distribution system made of surrogates, a logging system and a control system. A surrogate is what everybody calls a cache or an edge server: it stores requested content so that the same content can be delivered to many users without crossing the network core again each time. The benefits the same document lists are reduced delivery cost, better quality of experience and more robust delivery. What a CDN is not is a host. Cloudflare's own introduction says a CDN does not host content and cannot replace web hosting, and the older caching taxonomy, RFC 3040, places the surrogate where it belongs: it is a reverse proxy, a gateway delegated the authority to act on behalf of one or more origin servers.

Request routing is the hard part, and there are three ways to do it. The CDN interconnection framework, RFC 7336 (August 2014), describes the first two. DNS (Domain Name System) redirection returns different addresses for the same name according to load or to where the client is; in its usual form the site's name is an alias, a CNAME (canonical name) record, pointing into the CDN's domain, whose authoritative servers choose the edge. It is invisible to the user and cacheable, but the authoritative server sees only the address of the resolver that asked, not the user's, which misplaces anyone using a distant public resolver, and the answer lives as long as its time to live (TTL). The Client Subnet option of Extension Mechanisms for DNS (EDNS), RFC 7871 of May 2016, patches that by letting the resolver pass a truncated client prefix, 24 bits for Internet Protocol version 4 (IPv4) and 56 for version 6 by its privacy recommendation. HTTP (Hypertext Transfer Protocol) redirection with a 302 or 307 answer sees the real client and the request, at the cost of an extra round trip that is never cached. The third way is anycast: the same addresses are announced from every location and routing delivers each user to the nearest data centre that has capacity.

Once the request reaches an edge, ordinary HTTP caching decides the rest. In RFC 9111 (June 2022) a CDN edge is a shared cache, one that stores responses for reuse by more than one user, as opposed to the private cache in a browser. The origin steers it with Cache-Control: s-maxage overrides max-age for shared caches only, private forbids a shared cache to store the response at all, and a response to a request that carried an Authorization field may be reused only if a directive such as public or s-maxage allows it. The cache key is at least the request method and the target address, extended by any request fields the response names in Vary, and the Age field tells the client how many seconds ago the response was generated or validated at the origin. Because a site often wants its CDN to keep an object longer than browsers do, RFC 9213 (June 2022) added a field aimed at CDN caches alone: Cache-Control: max-age=60, s-maxage=120 together with CDN-Cache-Control: max-age=600 gives browsers one minute, other shared caches two and the CDN ten. RFC 9211 standardized the debugging field vendors had each invented, Cache-Status, which reports a hit with its remaining lifetime or the reason a request was forwarded.

The industry began as an answer to a challenge. Akamai's history places it at the Massachusetts Institute of Technology (MIT) in early 1995, when Tim Berners-Lee asked colleagues to invent a fundamentally better way to deliver content. Tom Leighton, a professor of applied mathematics, took it as a problem in algorithms; Danny Lewin came to MIT to work with him in the autumn of 1996; in 1997 their business plan was one of six finalists among 100 entries in the MIT $50K Entrepreneurship Competition, and on 20 August 1998 they incorporated Akamai. The company delivered its first live traffic in February 1999, a single pixel on the Disney site, and launched commercial service that April with Yahoo! as a charter customer. The vocabulary followed the business: RFC 3040 catalogued replication and caching in January 2001, RFC 3466 proposed a model for interconnecting content networks in February 2003, and RFC 6707 and RFC 7336 replaced it once network operators had begun building CDNs of their own.

Scale is counted in locations and in interconnections. Akamai says its edge network spans more than 600 cities. Cloudflare lists data centres in 348 cities, 67 of them in Latin America and the Caribbean, more than 13,000 network interconnections, and claims that 95 per cent of the internet-connected population is within 50 milliseconds of one. Large content owners build their own: Netflix's Open Connect places its appliances inside the networks of over a thousand internet service providers (ISPs) at no charge, steers traffic to them through Border Gateway Protocol (BGP) sessions with the provider, and peers without settlement elsewhere. Brazil has a public variant. OpenCDN, an initiative of the Brazilian Internet Steering Committee (CGI.br) and the Brazilian Network Information Center (NIC.br), hosts the caches of participating CDNs on shared infrastructure at IX.br exchange points, on the estimate that about 70 per cent of a typical provider's traffic comes from the largest CDNs; a provider receives that content locally through a bilateral BGP session with autonomous system 61580, and the service runs in Belo Horizonte, Belém, Brasília, Manaus, Recife and Salvador.

Standing in front of the origin makes a CDN a security device whether or not it is sold as one. Anycast spreads an attack across every data centre, so a flood is absorbed as long as the network's capacity exceeds it. The price is that the edge terminates Transport Layer Security (TLS) and handles the traffic of many customers in the same processes. On 23 February 2017 Cloudflare reported what became known as Cloudbleed: a flaw in an HTML (HyperText Markup Language) parser on its edge servers ran past the end of a buffer and returned memory containing cookies, authentication tokens and request bodies belonging to other sites. Tavis Ormandy of Google's Project Zero found it; the worst period was 13 to 18 February, when about one request in 3,300,000 could leak; some of the data had been stored by search engines; customers' private keys were not exposed, because TLS was terminated in a separate process.

The other shared fate is availability. On 8 June 2021 a valid configuration change by one Fastly customer triggered a bug that had been deployed on 12 May, and 85 per cent of Fastly's network returned errors from 09:47 UTC (Coordinated Universal Time); the company detected it within a minute and had 95 per cent of the network back within 49 minutes. On 18 November 2025, from 11:20 UTC, Cloudflare's network failed to deliver core traffic. There was no attack: a change to database permissions doubled the size of a feature file used by its bot management system, the file exceeded a limit in the proxy software, and because it was regenerated every five minutes and propagated to every machine, the network failed, recovered and failed again until the file was replaced. Core traffic was largely normal by 14:30 and everything by 17:06, and the company called it its worst outage since 2019. The pattern in both is the control system doing exactly what it was built for, distributing one change everywhere in seconds. RFC 8586 notes the usual hedge, more than one CDN in front of an origin, and defines the CDN-Loop field because such chains sometimes loop.

The everyday mistakes are about what is allowed into the shared cache. RFC 9111 warns that poisoning a shared cache spreads malicious content to many clients at once, a common vector being differences in how proxies and user agents parse a message, and that deployment flaws lead to the caching of information thought to be private. Its sharpest note is that a Set-Cookie field does not inhibit caching: a cacheable response that carries one can be, and often is, reused for other users, so a personalized page needs an explicit private or no-store directive. Stale objects are the opposite problem: RFC 9213 observes that publishers are more comfortable giving a generous lifetime to a cache they can invalidate, such as their CDN, than to caches they cannot reach. When a page misbehaves behind a CDN, the first things to read are the alias chain in the DNS answer, the Age field and the Cache-Status field.

pop.def: Point of Presence: a provider's physical edge site - where the CDN (content delivery network) caches, the transit hands off, and the backbone touches the ground.
pop.context: Counted in the hundreds by global networks; 'nearest PoP' decides your first-hop latency.

egress-cost.def: The per-gigabyte charge for data leaving the cloud - in is free, out is billed, and architecture quietly bends around that asymmetry.
egress-cost.context: The economics behind data gravity and many multi-cloud disappointments.

sd-wan.def: Software-Defined WAN: branch connectivity steered by central policy over any mix of links - MPLS (Multiprotocol Label Switching), broadband, LTE - chosen per application in real time.
sd-wan.context: The technology that turned 'the branch router' into 'the branch policy'.

l4-vs-l7-load-balancing.def: Balancing on addresses and ports versus on the application itself: L4 is fast and blind, L7 reads HTTP and routes by path, header, or cookie.
l4-vs-l7-load-balancing.context: The NLB/ALB split in cloud menus; TLS termination is the toll gate into L7.
l4-vs-l7-load-balancing.depth:
Layer 4 load balancing makes its decision from addresses and ports without examining content; layer 7 parses the application protocol and can route on hostname, path, header or cookie. The difference determines what the load balancer can do and how much it costs to do it.

Layer 4 is fast, protocol-agnostic and largely transparent, since it moves packets without terminating the connection. Layer 7 must terminate the connection, decrypt if it is encrypted, parse the request and open a second connection to the server, which is far more work and buys correspondingly more: content-based routing, session persistence by cookie, header manipulation, request-level retry, and the ability to apply a web application firewall at all.

The practical choice follows from what you need to decide. If routing depends only on which pool of identical servers should receive the traffic, layer 4 is the right tool and the cheaper one. The moment routing depends on the content of the request, or you need to inspect it, layer 7 is not optional. Most real deployments run both at different tiers, which is why understanding where a decision is being made is the first step in diagnosing why traffic went somewhere unexpected.

health-check.def: The periodic probe that decides whether a target receives traffic, keeps its routes or gets restarted: an 'are you alive?' question asked on a timer, with consequences attached to the answer.
health-check.context: Shallow checks lie (the port is open while the application behind it is dead); deep checks that test dependencies can fail every member at once and cascade; and the timers, how often to ask, how long to wait and how many answers to count before changing state, decide whether failover is fast or flapping. Tuning them is an art form. The same idea appears as monitors on F5 BIG-IP, link monitors and SD-WAN (software-defined wide area network) performance SLAs (service level agreements) on FortiGate, liveness, readiness and startup probes in Kubernetes, and target health checks in AWS (Amazon Web Services) Elastic Load Balancing.
health-check.depth:
A health check is a diagnostic run on a schedule with an action attached. Kubernetes' description is the cleanest general one: a probe is a diagnostic performed periodically, either by executing code inside the container or by making a network request, and based on the results the system restarts an unhealthy container or stops sending traffic to one that is not ready. Every implementation answers the same three questions: what exactly to test, how often and how patiently to test it, and what to do when the answer changes. F5's documentation separates health monitors, which check availability, from performance monitors, which check performance and load, and separates the methods as well. Active monitoring sends its own probes on a schedule and can look for a specific response, at the price of extra traffic and of being slow to mark a member down. Passive monitoring watches real client requests, adds no traffic and can mark a member down quickly while there is traffic, but cannot check for a specific response and can be slow to mark a member up again.

On BIG-IP the default http monitor probes every 5 seconds with a 16-second timeout, which follows F5's rule that the timeout should be three times the interval plus one second, so a member is declared down only after it has missed three probes and a second more. The content-checking monitor types for HTTP (Hypertext Transfer Protocol), plain or secured, and TCP (Transmission Control Protocol) carry a Send String, most often GET /, and a Receive String to look for in the answer; with both empty only a connection check is made. A Receive Disable String adds a third state, so a page can say up, down or up but disabled, which lets a server drain itself without being marked failed. Reverse mode inverts the test, marking a member down when a string such as Error appears, and Transparent mode sends the probe through a member, typically a firewall, to check what lies behind it. Two settings exist precisely because a quick success can be wrong. Manual Resume keeps a resource down after a failure until an administrator re-enables it, and F5's own example is a web server whose index.html answers as soon as it restarts while the rest of the site is not yet ready. Time Until Up marks a member up only after every response over a set number of seconds has been correct.

FortiGate has two related mechanisms. The link monitor, configured under config system link-monitor, probes a server through a chosen gateway from a source interface with ping, TCP or UDP (User Datagram Protocol) echo, plain or secured HTTP, or TWAMP (two-way active measurement protocol); its interval defaults to 500 milliseconds, it declares the server down after failtime failures and recovered after recoverytime successes, both 5 by default, and it removes static routes when the link fails, in FortiOS 7.2 only the routes listed in the monitor, or all routes through that interface and gateway if none are listed. SD-WAN (software-defined wide area network) performance SLAs (service level agreements), configured as health checks under config system sdwan, measure each member link actively, passively from real sessions, or passively with probes when there is no traffic, against up to two servers, so that a failed server does not condemn a healthy link. They track latency and jitter over the last 30 probes (5 milliseconds by default) and packet loss over the last 100 (0 per cent by default), and Fortinet's guide says plainly that the failures-before-inactive and restore-after counts exist to prevent flapping, the endless transfer of traffic back and forth between links. A member is Dead or Alive by reachability and, separately, In-SLA or Out-of-SLA by quality: Lowest Cost (SLA) rules prefer members that are both alive and in SLA, while Manual and Best Quality rules look only at Dead or Alive. When a member has several health checks, all of them must fail before its routes are removed.

Kubernetes splits the question three ways. A startup probe runs only while the container starts; liveness and readiness probes wait until it succeeds, and if it fails the kubelet kills the container. A liveness probe decides when to restart a container, to catch states such as a deadlock where the process runs but cannot make progress. A readiness probe decides when a container may receive traffic, and a failure removes the Pod's address from the EndpointSlices of every matching Service without restarting anything. The defaults are a probe every 10 seconds with a 1-second timeout, three consecutive failures to fail and one success to recover (and success thresholds must be 1 for liveness and startup), and an HTTP probe succeeds on any status from 200 to 399. A slow-starting application gets a startup probe sized to its worst case, failureThreshold times periodSeconds, 30 times 10 seconds giving 300 seconds in the documentation's example. The documentation's caution is the one most often learned the hard way: liveness probes must truly indicate an unrecoverable failure, because a wrong one restarts containers under high load, which fails client requests and pushes more work onto the remaining Pods, a cascading failure.

The Application Load Balancer of Amazon Web Services (AWS) checks each target every 30 seconds by default, with a 5-second timeout, 2 consecutive failures to mark it unhealthy and 5 successes to mark it healthy again, and a success code of 200 unless configured otherwise. Its most important behaviour is at the edge: if every target in a target group is unhealthy, the load balancer routes to all of them anyway, failing open. Amazon's Builders' Library article on health checks explains why, distinguishing liveness checks (is the process there and reachable), local health checks (can this server do its work, using resources it does not share with its peers) and dependency health checks (can it reach what it depends on). Its advice is to let the load balancer act only on liveness and local checks, which fail for reasons truly local to one server, such as a bad disk, and to leave dependency checks to separate monitoring with thresholds, rate limits and humans in the loop.

The classic failure is the check that tests the wrong thing. A TCP check that an open port answers says nothing about the application behind it, and F5's index.html example shows that even an HTTP check can pass before the service is ready. The Builders' Library opens with the worst version: a web server with a rare bug that rendered blank error pages on every request did not know it was unhealthy, became faster than its healthy peers, and was sent a disproportionate share of traffic by a load balancer that favoured fast servers. Algorithms such as least requests turn a failing server into a black hole, and with ten servers one bad one already caps the fleet at 90 per cent availability or less. The opposite failure is the check that tests too much. A dependency check fails on every server at once when the shared dependency has a problem, so automation removes the whole fleet for a fault no server could fix; that is why load balancers fail open and why Kubernetes warns about liveness probes.

Flapping sits between the two. A check that is too sensitive, or a dependency that is slow or returns a low error rate, makes members go in and out of service, which the Builders' Library describes for servers sharing a struggling data store; every transition costs connections, cache warmth and sometimes a failover. The tools against it are hysteresis and patience: FortiGate's separate failure and recovery counts, BIG-IP's Time Until Up and Manual Resume, Kubernetes' failure and success thresholds. The arithmetic is worth doing before an outage rather than during one. With the defaults above, a FortiGate link monitor reacts in about 2.5 seconds (5 failures at 500 milliseconds), a BIG-IP http monitor in 16 seconds, a Kubernetes liveness probe in about 30 seconds, and an AWS target in about a minute (2 failures at 30 seconds). Fast detection and stable state pull in opposite directions, and the right setting is the one chosen deliberately for the service behind it. A last case is the zombie, a server cut off or powered down for a long time that comes back running old software; Amazon's answer is to have health checks report the running version so that central monitoring can keep stale servers out of service.

autoscaling.def: Capacity that follows demand: instances added on load, removed in quiet - elasticity as the cloud's founding promise.
autoscaling.context: Scale-out is easy; scale-in without dropping connections is where the craft lives.

bastion-host.def: The one hardened, audited entry point for administrative access to a private network - a jump host by design rather than accident.
bastion-host.context: Modern clouds replace it with session-brokered access, but the concept - one guarded door - endures.

cloud-vpn.def: The managed IPsec tunnel between your premises and your VPC - the quick, encrypted, internet-riding alternative to a dedicated circuit.
cloud-vpn.context: Minutes to stand up versus weeks for an interconnect; jitter is the price of the shortcut.

private-dns-zone.def: DNS names that resolve only inside your VPCs - internal service names invisible to the public internet.
private-dns-zone.context: Split-horizon as a managed service: the same name can answer differently inside and out.

ipam.def: IP Address Management: the system of record for who owns which range - allocations, assignments, and conflicts, tracked instead of remembered.
ipam.context: The spreadsheet it replaces is the most dangerous file in networking.

byoip.def: Bring Your Own IP: advertising your own address blocks from the cloud provider's network - your reputation and whitelistings, their infrastructure.
byoip.context: Migration without renumbering; the addresses move, the incumbents' firewall rules keep working.

cold-potato-hot-potato.def: Two philosophies for carrying traffic: hot-potato hands it to the next network as soon as possible; cold-potato keeps it on your backbone as long as possible.
cold-potato-hot-potato.context: Clouds sell cold-potato as 'premium tier': more of the journey on their fibre, less on the open internet.
cold-potato-hot-potato.depth:
Hot potato routing hands traffic to the destination network as soon as possible, at the nearest exchange point, so the sending network carries it the shortest distance. Cold potato routing carries traffic on your own backbone as far as possible before handing it over.

The choice is economic before it is technical. Hot potato minimizes your transit costs and pushes the carrying cost onto the receiving network, which is the default for most peering relationships. Cold potato costs the sender more and is what a content provider chooses when it wants control over quality: keeping traffic on your own well-managed network until it is close to the user means fewer variables and better measured performance.

It explains asymmetric routing, which is one of the more confusing things to diagnose. If both networks apply hot potato, traffic from A to B leaves at one exchange and the return traffic leaves at a completely different one, so the two directions take physically different paths with different latency and different failure modes. Anyone troubleshooting a one-way problem is usually looking at this, and looking only at the outbound path will not find it.

shared-vpc.def: One centrally administered network shared into many projects or accounts - the platform team owns the plumbing, product teams deploy into it.
shared-vpc.context: Governance made topological: subnets as a service, guardrails included.

eni.def: Elastic Network Interface: the cloud's detachable virtual NIC - addresses, security groups, and MAC that can move between instances.
eni.context: Failover by interface migration: the replacement instance inherits the network identity.

five-tuple.def: The connection's fingerprint: source IP, source port, destination IP, destination port, protocol - the key by which firewalls, NATs, and balancers track flows.
five-tuple.context: Hash it and you get ECMP and load-balancer stickiness; change any element and it is a new flow.

east-west-north-south.def: The two axes of data-center traffic: north-south crosses the perimeter to users; east-west flows between servers inside.
east-west-north-south.context: Microservices made east-west dominant - and made perimeter-only security obsolete.
east-west-north-south.depth:
North-south traffic crosses the boundary of your environment; east-west traffic moves between systems inside it. The terms come from how network diagrams are conventionally drawn, and the ratio between the two changed the security industry.

The classical model concentrated everything at the north-south boundary, because that was where the untrusted world was, and traffic inside the perimeter was assumed to be legitimate. Modern architectures inverted the proportions: microservices, virtualization and distributed storage mean the overwhelming majority of packets in a data centre never cross the boundary at all, and a perimeter control sees none of them.

That is the whole argument for microsegmentation and for zero trust as applied inside a network. An attacker who gets in has to move laterally to reach anything valuable, and lateral movement is east-west, which historically meant moving through the part of the network nobody was watching. Instrumenting and controlling east-west traffic is expensive and awkward precisely because it is high volume and internal, which is exactly why it went uncontrolled for so long.

sdn.def: Software-Defined Networking: separating the control plane from the forwarding plane, so the network is programmed centrally instead of configured box by box.
sdn.context: The idea that made clouds possible; OpenFlow was its manifesto, APIs are its legacy.

nfv.def: Network Functions Virtualization: firewalls, routers, and gateways as software on standard servers instead of dedicated appliances.
nfv.context: The carrier movement that turned racks of boxes into racks of compute; 5G cores run on it.

gslb.def: Global Server Load Balancing (GSLB): traffic steering done in the Domain Name System (DNS) across sites and regions, in which an authoritative server answers each resolver with the address of the healthiest, closest or least-loaded destination.
gslb.context: Global server load balancing (GSLB) answers Domain Name System (DNS) queries for one name with the address of the healthiest, closest or least-loaded site, so users are steered between data centres or cloud regions before they open a connection. It is failover at the speed of TTLs (time to live values), and the discipline behind every 'active-active across regions' claim.
gslb.depth:
Global server load balancing (GSLB) answers a question local load balancing cannot: not which server, but which site. When an application runs in more than one data centre or region, something has to decide which one a given user reaches, and because that decision has to happen before any connection is made, it is usually made in the Domain Name System (DNS). In practice a GSLB is an authoritative DNS server, or a cloud service acting as one, that owns the name of the application and answers each query with an Internet Protocol (IP) address chosen at that moment from what it knows about the health and load of every site and about who is asking. It is not in the data path. No user traffic passes through it; once the answer is given, the client connects straight to the address it received, where a local load balancer picks the server. Two tiers, two different questions.

The idea is as old as the DNS hacks it grew out of. Request for Comments (RFC) 1794, written by Thomas Brisco of Rutgers University in April 1995, records that around 1986 several schemes appeared as modifications to the Berkeley Internet Name Domain (BIND) server, the best known being Bryan Beecher's Shuffle Address records and Marshall Rose's Round Robin code, which simply rotated the addresses of a cluster of similar machines. The same document already states the trade that still defines the technique: where the right answer changes quickly, the time to live (TTL) of the records handed out has to be very low, and the BIND of the day treated anything under 300 seconds as irrational and substituted 300.

F5's BIG-IP DNS, formerly Global Traffic Manager (GTM), shows the modern form. Its documentation describes tiered GSLB: a query for a wide IP, the name being balanced, is sent first to the best available pool and then to the best available virtual server in that pool, each choice made by a preferred method with an alternate and a fallback behind it. The static methods follow a fixed pattern: Global Availability (the first available entry of an ordered list, the classic active-standby), Ratio, Round Robin, Static Persist (a hash of the resolver's address, so that the same resolver keeps getting the same site), Topology (location of the requester matched against topology records), and the last-resort Fallback IP, Drop Packet and Return to DNS. The dynamic methods use measurements collected by the big3d agents in each data centre: Round Trip Time, Hops, Completion Rate, Least Connections, CPU, Packet Rate, Kilobytes/Second, Quality of Service, Virtual Server Score and Virtual Server Capacity.

Other products do the same things under other names. NetScaler defines GSLB sites and GSLB virtual servers, answers as an authoritative DNS service and has its sites exchange metrics over its proprietary Metric Exchange Protocol (MEP). The cloud providers sell it as a property of their DNS: Amazon Route 53 offers simple, weighted, latency, geolocation, geoproximity, IP-based, multivalue answer and failover routing, the last being its name for active-passive, and Azure Traffic Manager offers Priority, Weighted, Performance, Geographic, Multivalue and Subnet. Underneath the vocabulary there are only four ingredients: a list of sites, a health verdict for each, a preference rule, and a TTL.

That DNS dependency is the source of most surprises. The answer is cached by resolvers and by the client, so a change does not take effect everywhere the moment you make it, and a TTL that seemed sensible during design becomes a failover delay during an outage. Health monitoring decides whether a site is eligible at all, and topology rules decide who is preferred. The usual shorthand, that the most specific matching rule wins, is close but not exact: on BIG-IP DNS the topology records are sorted with the most specific request source first (Longest Match, the default), and that order governs the weight with which each pool or pool member is scored. Caches are also outside the operator's control: a BIND resolver can be configured to keep every answer for a minimum of up to 90 seconds (min-cache-ttl) whatever TTL was sent. And caching distorts ratios. Microsoft's Traffic Manager documentation warns that when clients sit behind a small number of recursive resolvers, weighted distribution can be significantly skewed, and adds that the effect is common to all DNS-based traffic routing systems.

The second structural limit is that a GSLB sees the resolver, not the user. RFC 7871 (May 2016) states it exactly: authoritative servers that tailor answers to location use the source address of the incoming query, and since most queries come from recursive resolvers, that address is the resolver's. This is harmless while the resolver is near its users and misleading when it is a large public service far away. F5's method descriptions are honest about it, measuring round trip time and hops to the client's local DNS (LDNS), not to the client. The Client Subnet option of the Extension Mechanisms for DNS (EDNS) lets a resolver pass part of the user's network along, at a cost in privacy that the RFC itself acknowledges; Route 53 documents using it to estimate a user's location, and a BIG-IP DNS profile can insert it (edns0-client-subnet-insert) for queries that arrive without one.

The failure modes are worth knowing in advance. A site that is up but degraded may still pass a naive health check. A resolver far from the user makes the geographic decision look wrong when it is working exactly as configured. And an aggressive TTL that gives you fast failover also multiplies query load, which is the trade you are actually choosing. To these the method tables add a few of their own: a Fallback IP is returned without being monitored, so it can point at a dead site; a user whose resolver changes, or whose record expires in the middle of a session, may be sent to another site, which is what Static Persist and replicated session state exist to soften; and an active-active claim is only as good as the data replication behind it, since DNS can move users in seconds while their data may not have followed.

The main alternative moves the decision from DNS into routing. Anycast, as RFC 4786 (December 2006) defines it, makes one service address available in multiple, discrete, autonomous locations, so that packets are routed to one of them; there is no cached answer to wait out, but also far less control over who goes where. The two are often combined, with the GSLB's own DNS listeners reached by anycast, and a content delivery network (CDN) is in effect a GSLB operated by someone else. The design questions do not change with the product: what the health check really proves, which resolver the decision is being made for, how long a wrong answer can live in a cache, and what happens to a session that lands on a different site.

virtual-appliance.def: A vendor's network function shipped as a VM image - the firewall or load balancer you rack by launching instead of lifting.
virtual-appliance.context: The bridge era between hardware boxes and cloud-native services; licensing came along for the ride.

shared-responsibility-model.def: The cloud's division of labor: the provider secures the infrastructure, the customer secures what they build and configure on it.
shared-responsibility-model.context: Security OF the cloud versus security IN the cloud; most cloud breaches happen on the customer's side of the line.

iam.def: Identity and Access Management: who exists, what they may do, and under which conditions - the permission fabric of the cloud.
iam.context: In the cloud, identity is the perimeter; an over-broad IAM policy is an open firewall port by another name.

rbac.def: Role-Based Access Control: permissions granted to roles, people assigned to roles - access managed by job, not by individual favour.
rbac.context: ABAC extends it with attributes (department, time, device); both exist to make revocation possible. NIST's project page gives the lineage: Ferraiolo and Kuhn's 1992 paper "introduced formal model for role based access control", a framework followed in 1996, the unified NIST model in 2000, and the model was "adopted as American National Standard 359-2004 by the American National Standards Institute" in February 2004 and "revised as INCITS 359-2012". The standard's reference model "defines sets of basic RBAC elements (i.e., users, roles, permissions, operations and objects)": a permission is an operation on an object, a role collects permissions, a user is assigned roles, and a session activates some of them. NIST states the case for it as cost: RBAC "has become the predominant model for advanced access control because it reduces" the cost of security administration, and an RTI International analysis of December 2010 estimated it "to have saved industry $1.1 billion over multiple years" through reduced employee downtime and more efficient provisioning and policy administration. The model's characteristic failure is role explosion, when every exception becomes a role; its characteristic strength is that a role can be reviewed once where a thousand individual grants cannot.
rbac.depth:
Role-based access control grants permissions to roles and assigns people to roles, rather than granting permissions to individuals. The benefit is reviewability: a role can be examined once and understood, where a thousand individual grants cannot. The idea is older than its name, but the formal model and the standard are American and dated. NIST's project page records that Ferraiolo and Kuhn's 1992 paper "introduced formal model for role based access control", that Sandhu and colleagues proposed a framework in 1996, and that NIST unified the two in 2000; the unified model "was adopted as American National Standard 359-2004 by the American National Standards Institute" in February 2004 and "revised as INCITS 359-2012" in 2012. The standard's reference model "defines sets of basic RBAC elements (i.e., users, roles, permissions, operations and objects)": an operation on an object is a permission, a role is a named collection of permissions, a user is assigned to roles, and a session is a user's activation of some of them. Hierarchies let a senior role inherit a junior one's permissions, and constraints express separation of duties, so that two roles that must not be held together cannot be.

NIST's argument for the model is economic before it is anything else. Its page says that RBAC "has become the predominant model for advanced access control because it reduces" the cost of security administration, and it cites an RTI International analysis of December 2010 that estimated RBAC "to have saved industry $1.1 billion over multiple years", the savings coming from "reduced employee downtime, more efficient provisioning, and more efficient access control policy administration". The mechanism of the saving is the one every administrator knows: a new hire in a known job gets the job's roles on day one instead of a ticket per system, and a leaver loses everything by losing the roles.

Its characteristic failure is role explosion. Every exception becomes a new role, the set grows past the point anyone can reason about, and the model provides the paperwork of governance without the clarity it was adopted for. The discipline is to keep roles aligned to job functions rather than to requests, to handle genuine exceptions as time-bounded grants rather than permanent roles, and to review the set periodically, because a role nobody can explain is a role nobody should be assigned. The second failure is the one the privilege creep entry describes: people change jobs and keep the roles of the old one, so that the model's clean picture of who may do what drifts from the truth unless the assignments are reviewed on a schedule, which is what NIST's control catalogue asks for in AC-6(7).

The alternatives are refinements rather than replacements. Attribute-based access control, in NIST SP 800-162's definition, decides each request by evaluating attributes of the subject, the object, the operation and the environment against policy, which handles the cases roles cannot, such as access that depends on the time of day, the device in use or a relationship between the requester and the record. Most real systems combine the two, roles for the bulk of access and attributes for the conditions, and the ABAC entry sets them side by side. Separation of duties, which the standard's constrained model expresses as roles that cannot be held or activated together, has its own entry, as does least privilege, the principle both models exist to implement.

In network and security operations the roles are often the groups of a directory: a RADIUS (Remote Authentication Dial-In User Service) or TACACS+ server maps an Active Directory group to a VLAN (virtual local area network), a device privilege level or a command set, a cloud platform maps a group to a set of permissions, and a policy engine's rules are written against group membership. Those groups are an RBAC model whether or not anyone drew it, and reviewing them is the access review the Microsoft documentation describes and the control catalogue requires.

service-account.def: An identity for software rather than a person: the account and credentials under which pipelines, scheduled jobs, applications and other workloads authenticate and are authorized, distinct from any human user's account.
service-account.context: Unrotated keys on forgotten service accounts are among the most common cloud breach entry points: Datadog's 2026 State of Cloud Security calls long-lived credentials one of the most common root causes of publicly documented cloud breaches year after year, and found active keys created within the past year on 41 per cent of Google Cloud service accounts. Every platform has its own form. Google Cloud and Kubernetes call it a service account; Amazon Web Services (AWS) gives workloads IAM (identity and access management) roles; Azure has managed identities and service principals; Active Directory has managed service accounts; a firewall has an administrator for its REST (representational state transfer) application programming interface (API). The direction of travel is the same everywhere: let the platform issue short-lived credentials to the workload, so that there is no key to leak, and keep permanent secrets for the cases that cannot avoid them, with an owner, an expiry and the narrowest permissions.
service-account.depth:
What it is, and what it is not. Kubernetes defines a service account as a type of non-human account that provides a distinct identity; Google Cloud as a special kind of account used by an application or compute workload rather than a person, identified by an email address and used to make authorized calls to application programming interfaces (APIs). The identity matters for three reasons: permissions are granted to it, actions are logged against it, and it can be disabled without affecting anyone's personal access. A service account is not a shared administrator login that several people use, which defeats all three, and it is not the credential itself: a key, a password or a token is how the account proves who it is, and the modern trend is to make that proof short-lived and issued by the platform rather than stored. Google Cloud distinguishes user-managed service accounts, which customers create; default service accounts, user-managed accounts created automatically when certain services are enabled; and service agents, which Google creates and manages so that its services can act on a customer's resources.

Two ways to prove identity. A workload can hold a long-lived secret, or it can ask the platform for a short-lived credential each time. Google Cloud supports both: attached service accounts and impersonation obtain short-lived credentials automatically, while a service account key, a private key the customer downloads, signs a JSON Web Token (JWT) that is exchanged for an access token. Google's own guidance treats the key as the problem. Its best-practice page lists the threats: credential leakage, privilege escalation with a poorly secured key, information disclosure, non-repudiation (an attacker acting through a service account hides their own identity) and malicious credential configurations. It asks that keys never be committed to source repositories or embedded in binaries, that they be rotated and given expiry times, that unused keys be found, and that secret scanning be enabled. Since 3 May 2024 every new Google Cloud organization is created with baseline constraints that disable service account key creation and key upload and stop default service accounts from receiving the broad Editor role automatically.

The same idea on the other clouds. Amazon Web Services (AWS) has no object called a service account; its IAM (identity and access management) best practices say to require workloads to use temporary credentials through IAM roles, to use IAM Roles Anywhere with X.509 certificates from an organization's public key infrastructure for workloads outside AWS, or to exchange a JSON Web Token from an external identity provider through AssumeRoleWithWebIdentity, and to keep long-term access keys for the cases that cannot use roles, using last-used information to update and remove them safely. Azure's managed identities go further: the credentials are not even accessible to the customer. A system-assigned identity is tied to one resource and deleted with it; a user-assigned identity is a standalone resource that several resources can share; both are special service principals in Microsoft Entra ID and cost nothing extra.

Kubernetes. Every namespace gets a ServiceAccount called default, with no permissions beyond the API discovery granted to all authenticated principals when role-based access control (RBAC) is on, and every pod receives the credentials of its service account unless automountServiceAccountToken is set to false. How those credentials work changed with the security thinking. Before v1.22 the pod was given a long-lived, static token stored as a Secret, and until v1.24 such a permanent token was created automatically for every service account; since v1.22 the kubelet obtains a short-lived, automatically rotating token through the TokenRequest API and mounts it as a projected volume. The LegacyServiceAccountTokenNoAutoGeneration feature gate, on by default from v1.24, stopped the automatic permanent tokens and was removed at general availability in v1.27. Indefinite tokens can still be created by hand, and the documentation warns about the security implications.

Active Directory and Kerberoasting. Windows services have long run under ordinary domain accounts whose passwords were set once by an administrator and never changed, which is exactly what Kerberoasting exploits. Kerberos requires a service principal name (SPN) to be associated with a service logon account; any user with a valid ticket-granting ticket can request a service ticket for it, and when the ticket is encrypted with RC4 (Rivest Cipher 4, encryption type 23) the key is the service account's password hash, so the ticket can be attacked offline. MITRE ATT&CK lists it as T1558.003, updated on 4 November 2026. Microsoft's answer is the managed service account. The standalone version, introduced with Windows Server 2008 R2 and Windows 7, gives a single server automatic password management and simplified SPN management; the group Managed Service Account (gMSA) extends it to farms of servers, the domain controller computing the password from a key provided by the Key Distribution Service, and member hosts fetching the current and preceding passwords when they need them. A long random password that changes on a schedule turns an offline cracking attack into a waste of time.

On network and security devices. Automation against firewalls, load balancers and switches needs accounts too, and the same rules apply. FortiOS, for example, has a dedicated REST (representational state transfer) API administrator: only a super_admin can create one; it takes an administrator profile that should grant the minimum permissions needed, and Fortinet recommends against the super_admin profile for it; trusted hosts are mandatory and 0.0.0.0/0 is refused; a client certificate can be required in addition to the token; and the generated token is shown only once. Scripts that log in over SSH (Secure Shell) or the API under a person's account make the audit trail lie about who acted and break when that person leaves; a dedicated account per automation, with its own credential and its own permissions, keeps both the logs and the off-boarding honest.

What goes wrong. Datadog's State of Cloud Security, updated in November 2026, calls long-lived credentials one of the most common root causes of publicly documented cloud breaches year after year, and its data shows why: active keys created within the past year on 43 per cent of AWS IAM users, 41 per cent of Google Cloud service accounts and 66 per cent of Entra ID app registrations, and a rising share of keys older than three years in AWS and Google Cloud since 2024; for build pipelines it recommends OpenID Connect, keyless authentication, instead of stored cloud keys. MITRE's catalogue of valid cloud accounts records APT28 using compromised Office 365 service accounts with Global Administrator privileges to collect email and APT29 using service principal credentials in Exchange. The recurring pattern is a service account created for one project, given broad rights to make it work, issued a key that was copied into a repository or a pipeline, and forgotten when the project ended. The countermeasures follow the platforms' own guidance: an owner and a purpose for every account, one identity per workload, least privilege, platform-issued short-lived credentials wherever possible, expiry and rotation for the keys that remain, monitoring of last use, and disabling before deleting so that a forgotten dependency announces itself.

workload-identity.def: Workloads proving who they are through the platform itself - short-lived, automatically issued credentials instead of long-lived secrets in files.
workload-identity.context: The end state of 'no keys to steal': the platform vouches for the pod, the pod never holds a password.

imds.def: Instance Metadata Service: the link-local endpoint (169.254.169.254) where a cloud instance asks about itself - and collects its temporary credentials.
imds.context: The crown-jewel target of SSRF attacks; IMDSv2's session tokens exist because of that history.
imds.depth:
The instance metadata service is a link-local endpoint a cloud instance queries to learn about itself, including temporary credentials for the role it runs as. Its convenience is exactly its danger.

Because it is reachable from the instance with no authentication, any vulnerability that lets an attacker make the instance issue a request on their behalf, most commonly server-side request forgery, retrieves those credentials. That is the mechanism behind several very large cloud breaches. The mitigation is the second version of the protocol, which requires a token obtained by a PUT with a hop limit that ordinary forgery cannot satisfy, and enforcing it rather than merely enabling it is the part that gets missed.

ssrf.def: Server-side request forgery (SSRF): making a server send requests to destinations the attacker chooses, so that they reach internal addresses and services the attacker could never reach directly.
ssrf.context: Server-side request forgery (SSRF) happens when an application fetches a URL (uniform resource locator) that a user supplied, or helped to build, without making sure the request goes only where it should. The request leaves from the server's own position, behind the firewalls and access lists, so it can reach loopback, private addresses, internal administration interfaces and the cloud instance metadata service at 169.254.169.254, which hands out the credentials of the role attached to the machine. It is the technique behind the 2019 Capital One breach: one forged request to the metadata service, credentials out. OWASP (Open Worldwide Application Security Project) gave it its own Top 10 category, A10, in 2021, and folded it into Broken Access Control in the 2025 edition.
ssrf.depth:
Server-side request forgery (SSRF) turns a server into a confused deputy. MITRE's Common Weakness Enumeration files it as CWE-918: the web server receives a URL (uniform resource locator) or similar request from an upstream component and retrieves its contents without sufficiently ensuring that the request is sent to the expected destination; an older name for the same flaw is XSPA (Cross Site Port Attack). The application has a legitimate reason to fetch, such as rendering a link preview, importing a file, calling a webhook or retrieving an image, and the attacker either supplies a completely different URL or manipulates how the URL is built, for instance with path traversal. Because the request originates from the server, it arrives from a trusted position inside the network. The OWASP (Open Worldwide Application Security Project) prevention cheat sheet adds two points that are easy to miss: SSRF is not limited to HTTP (Hypertext Transfer Protocol), since a fetching library may speak FTP (File Transfer Protocol), SMB (Server Message Block) or SMTP (Simple Mail Transfer Protocol) and accept schemes such as file, phar, gopher, data and dict; and an application vulnerable to XML (Extensible Markup Language) external entity (XXE) injection can be driven into SSRF through its parser.

What the attacker reaches is whatever the server can. OWASP's own attack page lists the cloud metadata interface at 169.254.169.254, where configuration and sometimes authentication keys can be extracted; NoSQL databases such as MongoDB that expose REST (representational state transfer) interfaces on HTTP ports, often without authentication because they were expected to be internal; internal REST services; and local files through file URIs. The 2021 edition of the OWASP Top 10 adds the reconnaissance case: in an unsegmented network the attacker maps internal hosts and open ports from the connection results, or simply from how long a connection takes to succeed or be refused. The blind form, in which the response never comes back to the attacker, still scans, still triggers actions on internal services, and still reaches anything that acts on a single request.

Cloud environments made this substantially worse. Amazon Web Services (AWS) describes its EC2 (Elastic Compute Cloud) Instance Metadata Service (IMDS) as attached locally to every instance on the link-local address 169.254.169.254, reachable only by software on the instance, and serving, among other metadata, the credentials for any IAM (identity and access management) role attached to it. A successful SSRF against a cloud workload can therefore escalate from an odd HTTP fetch to valid API (application programming interface) credentials in a single step. On 19 November 2019 AWS published IMDSv2, written up by Colm MacCarthaigh as defence in depth against four kinds of failure: open web application firewalls (WAFs), open reverse proxies, unpatched SSRF and instances misconfigured as open routers or NAT (network address translation) devices. A session now starts with an HTTP PUT that returns a secret token, valid for up to six hours (21,600 seconds), which every later request must carry in a header; PUT is a method that open WAFs and reverse proxies rarely pass; no token is issued to a caller whose request carries an X-Forwarded-For header; and the response carrying the token leaves with an IP (Internet Protocol) TTL (time to live) of 1, so it dies at the first hop if the instance forwards it. AWS says its analysis of real vulnerabilities found the PUT-plus-token combination protects against the vast majority of SSRF cases, and that it is always strictly stronger than requiring a static header. The EC2 guide still lets an instance answer IMDSv1, IMDSv2 or both by default; configured for IMDSv2 only, IMDSv1 calls fail. Google Cloud's metadata.google.internal and Azure's metadata service at 169.254.169.254 sit in the same place in the design, which is why the OWASP cheat sheet puts all three at the top of its minimum block list.

The case everyone cites is Capital One. The superseding indictment in United States v. Paige A. Thompson (No. CR19-0159, Western District of Washington, filed 17 June 2021) describes the scheme without using the acronym: certain customers of a cloud computing company had misconfigured web application firewalls that let commands sent from outside reach and be executed by their servers; those commands obtained the security credentials of accounts or roles that had permission to view and copy stored data; the credentials were used to list and copy storage buckets; and from Capital One's servers came data on approximately 100,000,000 people who had applied for its credit cards. On 24 October 2019 Senators Ron Wyden and Elizabeth Warren, asking the Federal Trade Commission to investigate Amazon, called the technique a server side request forgery (SSRF). The Office of the Comptroller of the Currency (OCC) assessed an 80 million dollar civil money penalty on 6 August 2020 for the bank's failure to establish effective risk assessment before migrating significant information technology operations to the public cloud, and for not correcting the deficiencies in time. On 17 June 2022 a federal jury in Seattle convicted Thompson of wire fraud and five counts of unauthorized access to and damage of a protected computer, and acquitted her of access device fraud and aggravated identity theft; the prosecutors counted more than 30 victim entities and more than 100 million affected American customers. The chain is the lesson: a component that forwarded requests it should not have, a metadata service that answered them, and a role whose permissions reached the data.

OWASP's ranking traces how the industry learned to weigh it. In the Top 10 of 2021 SSRF entered as A10, added from the community survey where it came first rather than from the contributed test data: a single CWE, an incidence rate of 2.72 per cent, an average weighted exploit score of 8.28 and impact of 6.72, coverage of 67.72 per cent, 9,503 occurrences and 385 CVEs (Common Vulnerabilities and Exposures). The authors wrote that the data showed a relatively low incidence with above-average exploit and impact ratings, and that a single-CWE entry like this might be rolled into a larger category in a future edition. The 2025 edition did exactly that: its introduction says SSRF has been rolled into A01:2025 Broken Access Control, which keeps first place with 40 mapped CWEs, CWE-918 among them, found in 3.73 per cent of tested applications on average.
