The anti-spam community separated message submission from mail transport: clients submit authenticated mail on port 587 under the Message Submission standard, now RFC 6409 (2011), described operationally in RFC 5068 (BCP 134), while port 25 stays for server-to-server transport, so the MAAWG (Messaging Anti-Abuse Working Group) recommendation for residential networks is to require authentication, configure clients for 587/TCP and block outbound 25/TCP from every machine that is not an MTA (mail transfer agent) or explicitly authorized. Brazil adopted it formally: the Brazilian Internet Steering Committee (CGI.br) recommended it in resolution CGI.br/RES/2009/02/P of 2009, the consumer protection department of the Ministry of Justice issued a technical note on its consequences for users, and a cooperation agreement among Anatel, CGI.br, the telecom operators' union SindiTelebrasil and internet provider associations put it into effect. Cloud providers do the same for their tenants: Google Cloud blocks egress to TCP port 25 of external addresses by default, and Microsoft says Azure subscriptions created after 15 November 2017 may be unable to send mail directly on port 25 and recommends authenticated relay on 587.

Open by default in the cloud. In every major cloud the outbound direction starts open. Jeff Barr's 2013 history of EC2 (Elastic Compute Cloud) recalls that the 2006 security group did ingress filtering only, and that egress filtering arrived with the enhanced security groups of 2011; today a newly created AWS (Amazon Web Services) security group has no inbound rules and one outbound rule allowing all traffic, which can be removed, and with no outbound rules nothing may leave. Azure network security groups end with AllowInternetOutBound at priority 65001, above the final DenyAllOutBound at 65500, and Google's VPC (virtual private cloud) firewall has implied allow-egress rules. There are also paths the filters cannot see: AWS security groups do not filter traffic to and from the Amazon DNS resolver, DHCP (Dynamic Host Configuration Protocol), the instance metadata service and the time service, and Azure exempts its host services on 168.63.129.16 and 169.254.169.254 from network security groups by default. A tunnel through the provider's own resolver therefore passes any security-group egress rule, and has to be stopped with DNS-layer controls instead.

Doing it in practice. Servers are the easy half and the most valuable one, because their legitimate outbound needs are short and stable: DNS to the internal resolvers, time to defined NTP (Network Time Protocol) servers, updates through a repository mirror or an authenticated proxy, and the specific partners or APIs (application programming interfaces) the application calls; everything else is denied and logged. DMZ (demilitarized zone) hosts deserve this first, since a compromised public server that can open any outbound connection is a ready-made command channel. User networks are harder, because users browse everywhere; the workable model is to force web traffic through a proxy or a cloud security service where it can be inspected, and to deny direct outbound connections on other ports. Denied outbound attempts are among the best detection signals a network produces: a database server trying to reach an unknown internet address has no innocent explanation that the logs cannot settle quickly.

What it cannot do. Egress filtering decides which connections leave, not what they carry. MITRE's technique T1567, Exfiltration Over Web Service, describes adversaries using popular web services precisely because hosts are probably already talking to them and firewall rules probably already permit them, with SSL (Secure Sockets Layer) and TLS encryption adding cover; a filter that allows the sanctioned file-sharing service allows the attacker's account on it too. Closing that gap needs content and identity controls, such as DLP (data loss prevention), inspection at a proxy and tenant restrictions, on top of the address and port rules. The filter also does nothing about traffic that never crosses it, which is why internal segmentation and egress control are complementary rather than alternatives.

honeypot.def: A decoy system or resource built to be attacked: no legitimate user ever touches it, so every interaction with it is a signal of probing, intrusion or misuse.
honeypot.context: A honeypot has no production purpose, which is its whole value: there is no normal traffic to tune out, so a connection, a login attempt or a file being opened is worth an alert. Designs range from research sensors on the internet, which collect the scanning, password guessing and malware that arrive every day, to enterprise tripwires inside the network, placed where only an intruder moving laterally would look. Low-interaction honeypots emulate a few services cheaply; high-interaction ones are real or proxied systems that show the attacker's whole session but must be contained so they cannot be used against others. Its network sibling is the honeynet, and its smallest form is the honeytoken or canary token: a fake credential, document or key that raises an alarm when used.
honeypot.depth:
A honeypot is a system or resource whose only job is to be attacked. RFC (Request for Comments) 4949, the Internet Security Glossary of August 2007, defines it as a system, such as a web server, or a system resource, such as a file on a server, designed to be attractive to potential crackers and intruders, like honey is attractive to bears; NIST's glossary carries the same wording. RFC 4949 adds a usage note worth keeping in mind for international writing: other cultures may use a different metaphor, so the term should be defined when first used. What makes a honeypot useful is not deception for its own sake but the absence of legitimate use. A production server sees millions of normal events among which an attack must be found; a honeypot sees none, so every connection, login attempt or file access is already suspicious, and alerts from it have almost no false positives.

The idea is older than the word's popularity. From August 1986 Clifford Stoll, tracking an intruder through the computers of Lawrence Berkeley Laboratory, needed the attacker to stay connected long enough for telephone technicians to complete a trace. As he wrote in Communications of the ACM (Association for Computing Machinery) in May 1988, he baited the intruder with files of fictitious text that looked like memos about computer support for the "Strategic Defense Initiative", a mailing list and form letters from a nonexistent secretary, protected so that only their owner and the system manager could read them and alarmed so that any reading was noticed. The intruder found them and spent more than an hour reading, long enough for the trace; months later a letter asking to join the fictitious mailing list arrived from the United States, evidence that the information had travelled onward. Stoll called the technique little more than catching flies with honey, and his account is the Learn article on The Cuckoo's Egg. RFC 4949 even records a formal term for the practice, entrapment, in the narrow technical sense of planting apparent flaws to detect penetration attempts or confuse an intruder.

Deception then became a tool and a research discipline. Fred Cohen's Deception ToolKit, discussed on its mailing list from March 1998, ran fake services and answered on TCP port 365 as a signal that deception was in use, on the theory stated in its FAQ that if enough people use deception, attackers become so unsure that they cannot proceed. The Honeynet Project, founded in 1999, turned honeypots into an instrument for studying attackers, with the mission to learn the tools, tactics and motives involved in computer and network attacks and share the lessons, and published its findings in the Know Your Enemy whitepapers; a honeynet is the project's term for a whole network of honeypots built to be compromised and watched. Brazil has its own long-running sensor network: CERT.br maintains a distributed honeypots project, part of the honeyTARG Honeynet Project, of low-interaction honeypots running Honeyd at partner organizations, among them INPE, BNDES and Petrobras, spread across Brazilian IPv4 address space, which notifies the CSIRTs (computer security incident response teams) of networks that attack the sensors and publishes daily and hourly statistics.

Honeypots are classified by how much of a system they offer. A low-interaction honeypot emulates a handful of services or banners, such as Honeyd in the CERT.br network: cheap to run, safe, and enough to record who scans which ports. A medium-interaction honeypot emulates more: Cowrie, an SSH (Secure Shell) and Telnet honeypot derived from Kippo, logs brute-force login attempts and then presents an emulated UNIX shell written in Python, so that the attacker's commands and downloads are recorded without a real operating system behind them. A high-interaction honeypot is a real system, or in Cowrie's proxy mode a real system behind an SSH and Telnet proxy, which shows the full intrusion but can be taken over and used to attack others, so it needs strict outbound filtering, monitoring and a plan for shutting it down. The smallest unit is the honeytoken, a single resource with no legitimate use: a fake password in a script, a document, an AWS (Amazon Web Services) API (application programming interface) key, a database row. Thinkst's free Canarytokens describe themselves as motion sensors for networks, computers and clouds, placed where nobody should be poking around and designed to look juicy to attackers.

Placement decides what a honeypot detects. On the internet, a honeypot is a research sensor: it receives the constant background of scanning, password guessing and worm traffic, which is data for threat intelligence and blocklists, not an incident. Inside the network it becomes a tripwire. An attacker who has a foothold and starts discovery and lateral movement cannot easily tell a decoy from a real server, and the first touch on a decoy is high-confidence evidence of an intrusion already under way. Commercial deception platforms package this. FortiDeceptor, for example, deploys decoy virtual machines that appear as real endpoints on monitored VLANs (virtual local area networks) or subnets, generates lures from real documents and directory user names, and plants deception tokens on real endpoints as breadcrumbs that lead an intruder towards a decoy, so that the first credential an intruder harvests may itself be the alarm.

The limits are practical ones. A honeypot detects only what touches it, so it complements rather than replaces monitoring of production systems. A convincing decoy needs maintenance: stale banners, impossible configurations or an empty file system give it away, and fingerprinting of common honeypot software is a game attackers also play. A high-interaction honeypot that is compromised and not contained becomes a launch point for attacks on third parties, and collecting attackers' sessions can raise data-protection questions about what is stored. Its neighbours differ in purpose: a tarpit deliberately slows connections to waste an attacker's time; a darknet or network telescope passively records traffic to unused address space without answering it; an IDS (intrusion detection system) watches real traffic for known patterns. The dates worth keeping are 1986 for Stoll's bait files, 1998 for the Deception ToolKit and 1999 for the Honeynet Project.

canary-token.def: A booby-trapped credential, file, or link that phones home when touched - fake AWS keys that alarm the moment someone tries them.
canary-token.context: Detection at the cost of a text file; the modern descendant of the marked bill.

attack-surface.def: The sum of the points where an attacker can try to get into a system, act on it or get data out of it: exposed services and ports, APIs (application programming interfaces), login and management interfaces, integrations, stored credentials and the people who can be persuaded.
attack-surface.context: Every feature adds to it, every decommission subtracts; managing it is subtraction as a discipline.
attack-surface.depth:
NIST (National Institute of Standards and Technology) defines the attack surface as the set of points on the boundary of a system, a system element or an environment where an attacker can try to enter, cause an effect on, or extract data from it. OWASP's (Open Worldwide Application Security Project) analysis guide widens the list for an application: the entry and exit points, the code that protects them (authentication, authorization, logging, validation), the valuable data inside, from keys and secrets to personal data, and the code that protects that data, overlaid with the kinds of user who can reach each point, of which the two extremes, anonymous users and highly privileged administrators, deserve most attention. In an organization the list runs on to exposed ports, third-party integrations, browser-facing code and the humans who can be phoned. The attack surface is not the set of vulnerabilities: it measures what can be attacked, not what is broken, and a large surface of good code is still more exposure than a small one.

The idea was turned into a measure at Microsoft. In an MSDN article written after the Windows Server 2003 security audit, Michael Howard argued that you cannot predict tomorrow's vulnerabilities, but a feature that is not running by default cannot be attacked, and proposed counting a product's relative attackability: list the points through which products have historically been attacked, weight each one (a service running by default under the SYSTEM account with a socket open to the world weighs heavily), and compare versions. By that count a default Windows Server 2003 had roughly half the attack surface of Windows 2000, partly because IIS (Internet Information Services) 6.0 was no longer installed by default; Howard warned that the figure says nothing about code quality. In a 2003 paper, Measuring Relative Attack Surfaces, Howard, Jon Pincus and Jeannette Wing generalized his Relative Attack Surface Quotient (RASQ): count a system's attack opportunities instead of its bugs or vulnerability reports, along three dimensions, targets and enablers, channels and protocols, and access rights, starting from Howard's 17 attack vectors (open sockets, weak access control lists, dynamic web pages, enabled guest accounts among them), which they extended to 20; OWASP notes that Carnegie Mellon researchers later turned this into a formal metric.

Reduction is the cheapest security work available, because a component that is not reachable does not need to be defended, patched or monitored. OWASP lists the usual moves: simplify the model, with fewer user levels and no confidential data kept that is not absolutely needed; turn off features and interfaces that are not used; and add operational controls such as a web application firewall in front of what must stay exposed. NIST's Secure Software Development Framework (SP 800-218, February 2022) names attack surface mapping, alongside threat modelling, as a form of risk modelling developers should use in practice PW.1.1.

It grows silently because expansion accompanies ordinary progress. OWASP notes that an application's attack surface normally increases over time as interfaces, user types and integrations are added, and that deploying several versions, keeping unused features just in case, and leaving old backups and unused code all enlarge it, backups being an often ignored part of it. Not every addition counts the same: one more page built like the others adds little risk, while a new web API (application programming interface), a file upload from the Internet, or any change to session management, authentication, authorization, roles, administrative functions, secrets handling or trust relationships needs review. Nobody ever proposes to increase the attack surface, and yet it increases with each sprint, which is why periodic inventory beats intention as a control.

The parts that hurt most are the ones nobody knew about. A decommissioned service whose DNS (Domain Name System) record still resolves is the classic case: Microsoft documents how a CNAME (canonical name) record left pointing at a deprovisioned cloud resource becomes dangling, and how an attacker who provisions a resource under the same name receives the organization's traffic, a subdomain takeover. Management planes are the other. CVE-2022-1388, published on 5 May 2022, let undisclosed requests bypass authentication on the iControl REST interface of F5 BIG-IP; CVE-2022-40684, published on 18 October 2022, let an unauthenticated attacker operate the administrative interface of FortiOS, FortiProxy and FortiSwitchManager through crafted HTTP (Hypertext Transfer Protocol) or HTTPS requests. Both scored 9.8 under CVSS (Common Vulnerability Scoring System) 3.1 and both were in CISA's (Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency) Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalogue within days, and both mattered most where the management interface was reachable from networks that had no business reaching it. A forgotten staging environment holding production data, or an administrative page opened during a migration and never closed, fail the same way.

Attackers enumerate systematically and find these reliably, so the version of the exercise that works is discovery from the outside in, not from the architecture diagram. For web applications OWASP suggests crawling with a dynamic testing tool such as ZAP, or exporting the entry points a web application firewall already knows; for microservices and cloud-native systems it advises prioritizing whatever is reachable from an attack source such as Internet traffic, even when it sits behind proxies, load balancers and ingress controllers and scales without warning. The output should be compared with the inventory: anything found that nobody claims is either shadow IT (information technology) or a leftover, and both are to be owned or removed.

Neighbouring terms divide the problem. An attack vector is the specific path an attack takes across the surface; a threat model asks what can go wrong and uses the surface as input; blast radius measures how far damage spreads once something is breached; least privilege and segmentation shrink what each exposed point can reach. Worth remembering: Windows Server 2003 at roughly half the surface of Windows 2000, 17 attack vectors in Howard's original count, and two critical management-interface flaws of 2022, both scored 9.8.

iaas-paas-saas.def: The cloud's three service layers: rent the infrastructure, rent the platform, or rent the finished application - each trading control for convenience.
iaas-paas-saas.context: The shared-responsibility line moves with the letter: the higher the layer, the more the provider owns.

tokenization.def: Replacing sensitive values with meaningless stand-ins, keeping the real data in one guarded vault - the token is useless anywhere else.
tokenization.context: How payment systems shrink their compliance scope: most systems only ever see the token.

lgpd.def: Lei Geral de Proteção de Dados Pessoais (LGPD): Brazil's general data protection law, Law 13.709 of 14 August 2018, governing the processing of personal data on principles inspired by the European GDPR (General Data Protection Regulation), with Brazilian teeth: its own legal bases, its own deadlines and its own regulator.
lgpd.context: In force since 18 September 2020, with sanctions applicable since 1 August 2021, and enforced by the ANPD (Agência Nacional de Proteção de Dados, the National Data Protection Agency, an Autoridade until September 2025). Article 7 lists ten legal bases, of which consent and legitimate interest are only two. Article 18 gives the data subject, the titular, rights that include access, correction, portability and deletion. Article 48, with the agency's Resolution 15 of 2024, gives a controller three working days to communicate a security incident that may cause relevant risk or harm. Article 52 sets fines of up to 2% of revenue in Brazil, limited to R$ 50 million per infraction. Since Constitutional Amendment 115 of 2022, the protection of personal data is also a fundamental right in the Brazilian Constitution.
lgpd.depth:
The LGPD (Lei Geral de Proteção de Dados Pessoais) is Brazil's general data protection law, in force since 2020 and closely modelled on the GDPR (General Data Protection Regulation) of the European Union. It applies to any processing of personal data of people in Brazil, regardless of where the processing organization sits, which is the extraterritorial reach that makes it relevant to companies with no Brazilian presence. Article 3 says so in three clauses: the law applies whatever the country of the organization's seat or the country where the data are located, provided that the processing takes place in Brazilian territory, or that it aims at offering goods or services to, or processing the data of, individuals located there, or that the data were collected there. Article 4 lists what is outside: processing by a natural person for exclusively private and non-economic purposes, journalistic, artistic and academic purposes, and public security, national defence, state security and criminal investigation, which are left to specific legislation.

The dates need care, because the law arrived in stages. It began as bill PLC (Projeto de Lei da Câmara) 53/2018, which the Senate approved unanimously in July 2018, and was sanctioned by President Michel Temer on 14 August 2018. Provisional Measure 869 of 27 December 2018, converted into Law 13.853 of 8 July 2019, gave it the name Lei Geral de Proteção de Dados Pessoais and created the regulator, the ANPD (then the Autoridade Nacional de Proteção de Dados). Under article 65 the articles on the ANPD took effect on 28 December 2018 and the rest 24 months after publication; a provisional measure of 2020 tried to postpone that, the Senate struck the postponement out, and the law entered into force on Friday, 18 September 2020. The articles on administrative sanctions, 52 to 54, were deferred by Law 14.010 of 2020 to 1 August 2021. On 10 February 2022, Constitutional Amendment 115 added to article 5 of the Constitution the right to the protection of personal data, including in digital media, and reserved legislation on the subject to the federal Union.

Its vocabulary, in article 5, is the part that reaches a system design. Personal data (dado pessoal) is information related to an identified or identifiable natural person. Sensitive personal data covers racial or ethnic origin, religious conviction, political opinion, membership of a union or of a religious, philosophical or political organization, health, sex life, and genetic or biometric data. Anonymized data are outside the law unless the anonymization can be reversed with reasonable effort (article 12). The titular is the person the data refer to. The controlador (controller) is whoever takes the decisions about the processing; the operador (the GDPR's processor) processes on the controller's behalf and must follow its instructions (article 39); together they are the agentes de tratamento. The encarregado, the officer the GDPR calls a data protection officer, is the channel between the controller, the data subjects and the ANPD. And tratamento, processing, is defined by a list of some twenty operations that runs from collection through storage and transmission to deletion, so that merely holding data is processing.

The structure will look familiar to anyone who has worked with the European regime. Processing requires a legal basis, of which consent is only one and often not the most appropriate. Data subjects hold rights of access, correction, portability, and deletion. Controllers and operators have distinct obligations, and the ANPD is the supervisory authority with enforcement powers including fines calculated against Brazilian revenue. Article 6 states ten principles: purpose, adequacy, necessity, free access, data quality, transparency, security, prevention, non-discrimination, and accountability. Article 7 states the ten bases: consent; a legal or regulatory obligation of the controller; public policy carried out by the public administration; studies by research bodies; performance of a contract to which the data subject is party; the regular exercise of rights in judicial, administrative or arbitral proceedings; protection of life or physical safety; protection of health in procedures by health professionals and services; the legitimate interests of the controller or a third party; and the protection of credit. Consent, where it is the basis, must be demonstrable, with the burden of proof on the controller, must refer to specific purposes, generic authorizations being void, and can be revoked at any time (article 8).

Two categories are treated more strictly. Sensitive data may be processed with consent given in a specific and highlighted way for specific purposes, or without consent only in the cases article 11 lists, which include legal obligation, the exercise of rights, protection of life and health, and the prevention of fraud and the security of the data subject in identification and authentication processes in electronic systems. Legitimate interest and credit protection do not appear in that list. The data of children must be processed in their best interest, and for children article 14 requires specific and highlighted consent from at least one parent or legal guardian.

The rights of article 18 read like a feature list: confirmation that processing exists, access, correction of incomplete, inaccurate or outdated data, anonymization, blocking or deletion of unnecessary or excessive data, portability to another supplier, deletion of data processed on the basis of consent, information about the entities with which data were shared, information about the possibility of refusing consent, and revocation of consent. Article 19 puts a clock on the first two: confirmation or access is provided immediately in simplified form, or within 15 days as a clear and complete declaration, and the data must be stored in a format that favours the exercise of the right of access.

Security is an obligation of both controller and operator. Article 46 requires technical and administrative measures able to protect personal data from unauthorized access and from accidental or unlawful destruction, loss, alteration or communication, observed from the design phase of the product or service through to its execution. Article 37 requires both to keep a record of the processing operations they carry out, article 38 allows the ANPD to demand a data protection impact report, and article 41 requires the controller to appoint an officer and publish that person's contact details. Under article 48 the controller must communicate to the ANPD and to the data subjects any security incident that may cause relevant risk or harm, within a reasonable time defined by the authority; the ANPD defined it in Resolution CD/ANPD 15 of 24 April 2024 (CD is the Conselho Diretor, the board of directors) as three working days, counted for the data subjects from the moment the controller learns that the incident affected personal data, with twenty working days to complement the information and all periods doubled for small processing agents. The same article tells the authority to weigh, when judging gravity, whether technical measures had made the affected data unintelligible to unauthorized third parties, which is the law's own argument for encryption.

Enforcement is administrative and graduated. Article 52 lists the sanctions: a warning with a deadline for corrective measures; a simple fine of up to 2% of the revenue of the company, group or conglomerate in Brazil in its last financial year, excluding taxes, limited in total to R$ 50 million per infraction; a daily fine within the same limit; publication of the infraction; blocking or deletion of the data concerned; and, since 2019, partial suspension of the database or of the processing activity for up to six months, and partial or total prohibition of processing. The ANPD approved its regulation on dosimetry in Resolution 4 of 24 February 2023 and published its first fine on 6 July 2023, against a very small company that had offered a list of voters' WhatsApp contacts: R$ 14,400 in total, for processing without a legal basis and for an infraction of the ANPD's inspection regulation, plus a warning for having no officer. The regulator itself has changed with the law. It began work in November 2020 as an authority attached to the Presidency of the Republic with five directors; Provisional Measure 1.317 of 17 September 2025, converted into Law 15.352 of 25 February 2026, made it the Agência Nacional de Proteção de Dados, a special-nature autarchy linked to the Ministry of Justice and Public Security with the autonomy of a regulatory agency, 200 new specialist posts and the additional task of regulating the Digital Statute of the Child and Adolescent, the ECA (Estatuto da Criança e do Adolescente) Digital, Law 15.211 of 2025.

International transfers are allowed only in the cases of article 33, among them transfer to countries or international organizations with an adequate level of protection, standard contractual clauses, global corporate rules, and the specific and highlighted consent of the data subject. The ANPD approved its transfer regulation and the content of the standard clauses in Resolution 19 of 23 August 2024, and on 26 January 2026, in Resolution 32, recognized the European Union as providing an adequate level of protection; the European Commission adopted its own adequacy decision for Brazil at the same time, so that the two decisions are mutual.

The differences matter more than the similarities in practice. The Brazilian law lists more legal bases than the European one, including protection of credit, and it interacts with a large body of existing Brazilian consumer and civil law rather than replacing it. The count is ten bases against the six of article 6 of the GDPR, none of which concerns credit. Article 64 says that the rights and principles of the LGPD do not exclude others in Brazilian law or in treaties, article 45 leaves violations within consumer relations under consumer legislation, and article 52 states that its sanctions do not replace those of the Consumer Defence Code. Treating an existing GDPR programme as automatically sufficient is the common mistake: the shape transfers, the specifics do not, and the supervisory authority is a different institution with its own priorities. The numbers worth remembering are 13.709 and 14 August 2018, 18 September 2020 and 1 August 2021, ten bases, three working days, 2% and R$ 50 million.

anpd.def: Agência Nacional de Proteção de Dados (ANPD): Brazil's data protection regulator, which regulates, enforces and interprets the LGPD (Lei Geral de Proteção de Dados Pessoais). It began work in 2020 as the Autoridade Nacional de Proteção de Dados and became a regulatory agency under Provisional Measure 1.317 of September 2025, converted into Law 15.352 of February 2026, which kept the acronym.
anpd.context: The ANPD (Agência Nacional de Proteção de Dados) issues the regulations that turn the principles of the LGPD (Lei Geral de Proteção de Dados Pessoais) into checklists, such as the three-working-day deadline for reporting a security incident; it alone applies the law's sanctions and has the last administrative word on how the law is read. It is the Brazilian counterpart of Europe's data protection authorities (DPAs), with one difference of shape: a single national agency, a special-nature autarchy linked to the Ministry of Justice and Public Security, run by a board of five directors approved by the Senate. Since 2026 it also regulates the ECA (Estatuto da Criança e do Adolescente) Digital, the digital statute for children and adolescents, and in January 2026 it recognized the European Union as adequate while the European Commission did the same for Brazil.
anpd.depth:
What it is. The ANPD (Agência Nacional de Proteção de Dados) is the body that article 55-A of the LGPD (Lei Geral de Proteção de Dados Pessoais), Law 13.709 of 2018, creates to supervise the law: a special-nature autarchy linked to the Ministry of Justice and Public Security, with functional, technical, decision-making, administrative and financial autonomy and its own assets, seated in the Federal District under the general law of regulatory agencies, Law 13.848 of 2019. Its existence answers a question the law alone does not: who interprets it, who investigates, and what a sanction actually looks like. Article 55-K answers the first and the last directly. Applying the LGPD's sanctions is exclusively the ANPD's power, its competences prevail over the related competences of other public bodies wherever the protection of personal data is concerned, and it is the central body for interpreting the law and setting the rules and guidelines for implementing it.

How it got here. As sanctioned in August 2018 the law had its article 55 vetoed; Provisional Measure 869 of 27 December 2018, converted into Law 13.853 of 8 July 2019, added articles 55-A to 55-L, which created the authority, and Decree 10.474 of 26 August 2020 gave the authority its structure. In the agency's own account it started in November 2020 as an authority linked to the Presidency of the Republic, five directors in one room. Provisional Measure 1.124 of 13 June 2022, converted into Law 14.460 of 25 October 2022, revoked the original clauses of article 55-A and article 55-B. The decisive change came with Provisional Measure 1.317 of 17 September 2025, published on 18 September and in force on publication: it made the authority the Agência Nacional de Proteção de Dados, a regulatory agency like the others listed in Law 13.848, created a career of data protection regulation specialists and an internal audit unit, and kept the directors' mandates running. Congress converted it, with changes, into Law 15.352, approved by the Senate on 24 February 2026 and published on 25 February; the law turns 797 vacant posts from other careers into 200 specialist posts to be filled by public examination. Decree 12.881 of 2026 and the board's Resolution 33 of 6 April 2026 completed the restructuring, with six superintendencies and the audit unit; by then the agency counted about 500 people. Enforcement built up gradually rather than arriving with the statute, which is normal for a new regulator and has a practical consequence: for its first years, much of the law was waiting for the regulations that would make it concrete.

How it is governed. Article 55-C lists its organs: the board of directors (Conselho Diretor), the highest body; the National Council for the Protection of Personal Data and Privacy; an internal affairs office; an ombudsman; a legal office; the audit unit; and the administrative and specialized units. The board has five directors, one of them the Director-President, chosen by the President of the Republic and appointed after approval by the Senate, from Brazilians of spotless reputation with higher education and recognized expertise. Mandates are four years, and the first board's were staggered at two, three, four, five and six years so that they would never all end together; a director loses office only by resignation, final criminal conviction or dismissal after a disciplinary process. Waldemar Gonçalves Ortunho Junior was the Director-President in 2026. The national council, set by article 58-A, has 23 representatives drawn from the federal executive, both houses of Congress, the national councils of justice and of the public prosecution service, the Brazilian Internet Steering Committee (CGI.br, Comitê Gestor da Internet no Brasil), civil society, research institutions, unions and business, and advises rather than decides.

What it can do. Article 55-J lists 24 competences. The ones that reach an engineering team are these: issuing regulations and procedures on data protection, including on the data protection impact report for high-risk processing; inspecting and applying sanctions through an administrative process that guarantees defence and appeal; hearing a data subject's petition against a controller once the data subject has complained to the controller and the complaint was not resolved in time; carrying out or ordering audits of processing, including by public bodies; signing commitments with processing agents to end an irregularity or legal uncertainty; writing simplified rules and longer deadlines for small businesses and self-declared startups; cooperating with data protection authorities abroad; and deciding, at the administrative level and with final effect, how the law is interpreted. The same article requires public consultation and a regulatory impact analysis before any regulation, and minimum intervention when it imposes conditions on private processing. Law 15.352 added a second statute to its remit: the ECA (Estatuto da Criança e do Adolescente) Digital, the Estatuto Digital da Criança e do Adolescente, Law 15.211 of 2025, in force since 17 March 2026, which the government gave as one of the main reasons for the new structure.

The rules it has written. The agency's guidance is where the law's ambiguities get resolved, so compliance work that reads only the statute and not the regulator's output is reading half the material. The resolutions of its board (CD/ANPD) that matter most to a technical team are: number 1 of 28 October 2021, on inspection and the sanctioning process; number 2 of 27 January 2022, on small processing agents; number 4 of 24 February 2023, on how sanctions are calculated (dosimetry); number 15 of 24 April 2024, on communicating security incidents, which sets three working days for the communication to the ANPD and three working days, counted from the moment the controller learns that personal data were affected, for the communication to data subjects; number 18 of 16 July 2024, on the encarregado, the data protection officer; number 19 of 23 August 2024, on international transfers and the content of Brazil's standard contractual clauses; and number 32 of 26 January 2026, recognizing the European Union as adequate.

How it enforces. The first fine shows the scale at which the regime started. On 6 July 2023 the agency published sanctions against Telekall Infoservice, a microenterprise found to be offering a list of voters' WhatsApp contacts for campaign material in the 2020 municipal election in Ubatuba, São Paulo: fines for processing without a legal basis (article 7 of the LGPD) and for breaching the inspection regulation, each limited to 2% of the company's gross revenue, R$ 14,400 in total, and a warning for having no encarregado (article 41). A year later it used a different tool on one of the largest processors in the country. On 2 July 2024 it published a preventive measure ordering the immediate suspension of Meta's new privacy policy, which allowed public posts on Facebook, Instagram and WhatsApp to be used to train Meta's artificial intelligence, with a daily fine of R$ 50,000 for non-compliance and five working days to comply, citing the imminent risk of serious and irreparable harm to data subjects' fundamental rights; it later rejected Meta's request for reconsideration and eventually suspended the measure. The sanctions themselves are in article 52 of the LGPD: a warning with a deadline for corrective measures, a simple fine of up to 2% of revenue in Brazil limited to R$ 50 million per infraction, a daily fine within the same limit, publication of the infraction, blocking or deletion of the data, and suspension of the database or of the processing activity for up to six months, extendable once; the Meta order, by contrast, came before any case had been decided.

Where it sits among its neighbours. It is the Brazilian counterpart of the European Union's supervisory authorities, but where the General Data Protection Regulation (GDPR) has one authority per Member State coordinated by the European Data Protection Board, Brazil has a single national agency. It does not replace the courts, the consumer protection system or the sectoral regulators: article 55-J tells it to coordinate with the regulators of specific sectors of the economy and of government, and to keep a permanent forum with them, while article 55-K gives it precedence on data protection itself. Internationally it is the counterparty in adequacy. Its Resolution 32 of 26 January 2026 recognized the European Union as providing an adequate level of protection, the European Commission's adequacy decision for Brazil bears the same date, and the Commission announced the mutual decisions on 27 January 2026 as creating the biggest area of free and safe data flows in the world; the next day Commissioner Michael McGrath and the ANPD's Director-President issued a joint statement.

The numbers worth remembering: Law 13.709 of 2018, which it enforces; 2020, when it started; five directors with four-year mandates; three working days to report an incident; Provisional Measure 1.317 of 17 September 2025 and Law 15.352 of 25 February 2026, which made it an agency; 200 specialist posts; and 26 January 2026, mutual adequacy with the European Union.

ccpa.def: California's consumer privacy law: rights to know, delete, and opt out of the sale of personal information - amended and hardened by the CPRA.
ccpa.context: The de facto US baseline in the absence of a federal law; 'Do Not Sell or Share' links exist because of it.

dpo.def: Data Protection Officer: the designated guardian of a data protection program - advisor inside, contact point for regulators and data subjects outside.
dpo.context: Mandatory in many GDPR scenarios and named in the LGPD as 'encarregado'.

dpia.def: Data Protection Impact Assessment: the structured 'what could this do to people?' analysis required before high-risk processing begins.
dpia.context: The LGPD's cousin is the RIPD; both exist so risk is examined before launch, not after headlines.

dsar.def: Data Subject Access Request: a person exercising their right to see the data held about them - and the clock that starts when they ask.
dsar.context: GDPR gives one month, extendable; the operational test of whether a privacy program actually works.

right-to-erasure.def: The right to have personal data deleted when there is no longer a lawful reason to keep it - popularly, the right to be forgotten.
right-to-erasure.context: Not absolute: legal obligations, contracts, and free expression can outweigh it, case by case.

data-portability.def: The right to take your data with you in a machine-readable format - and, where feasible, have it sent straight to the next provider.
data-portability.context: The anti-lock-in right: your history should not be the switching cost.

consent.def: One lawful basis among several: a freely given, specific, informed, unambiguous yes - revocable as easily as it was given.
consent.context: Pre-ticked boxes and bundled agreements fail every adjective in the definition.

legitimate-interest.def: The lawful basis for processing without consent when the controller's genuine need outweighs the person's rights - after a documented balancing test.
legitimate-interest.context: The most flexible basis and the most abused claim; the three-part test is necessity, purpose, balance.

purpose-limitation.def: Data collected for one stated purpose may not be quietly reused for another - the principle that keeps datasets from wandering.
purpose-limitation.context: The reason 'we might find it useful later' is not a collection strategy.

data-controller.def: The party that decides why and how personal data is processed - and therefore the one accountable for it.
data-controller.context: The LGPD's 'controlador'; deciding the purpose is what makes you one, regardless of who holds the servers.

data-processor.def: The party processing personal data on a controller's documented instructions - the cloud provider, the SaaS, the payroll bureau.
data-processor.context: The LGPD's 'operador'; step outside the instructions and you become a controller with a controller's liability.

data-processing-agreement.def: The contract binding a processor to the controller's instructions: security measures, sub-processors, breach duties, and deletion at the end.
data-processing-agreement.context: The document vendor security reviews orbit around; GDPR Article 28 dictates its skeleton.

standard-contractual-clauses.def: The EU's pre-approved contract terms that make personal data transfers to other countries lawful - protection by contract where law alone does not reach.
standard-contractual-clauses.context: The workhorse of international transfers, especially since Schrems II demanded case-by-case safeguards.

privacy-by-design.def: Building data protection into systems from the first sketch - minimization, defaults, and safeguards as architecture, not as patches.
privacy-by-design.context: Codified in GDPR Article 25; its slogan form: the most protective setting is the default setting.

pseudonymization.def: Replacing identifiers with pseudonyms while keeping the mapping elsewhere - reversible by design, protective in the meantime.
pseudonymization.context: Still personal data under GDPR and LGPD, because the key exists; anonymization is the one-way sibling.

anonymization.def: Transforming data so individuals can no longer be identified by any reasonably available means - the exit door from data protection law.
anonymization.context: Harder than it looks: re-identification research keeps proving 'anonymized' datasets talkative.

k-anonymity.def: A dataset property where every person is indistinguishable from at least k-1 others on the quasi-identifiers: each hides in a crowd of size k.
k-anonymity.context: The same idea protects Have I Been Pwned's password checks: a client sends only a five-character prefix of a password's hash and receives the whole crowd of hashes sharing it, so the service cannot tell which one was asked about.

differential-privacy.def: A mathematical guarantee: query answers barely change whether or not any one person is in the dataset - privacy as provable noise.
differential-privacy.context: Used by the US Census and big-tech telemetry; epsilon is the knob between truth and protection.

data-retention.def: Keeping data only as long as its purpose requires, then deleting on schedule - the discipline that shrinks both risk and discovery scope.
data-retention.context: Every breach is smaller when the archive is; 'forever' is not a retention period.

cookie-banner.def: The consent interface for non-essential tracking - born of the ePrivacy rules and GDPR consent standards, degraded by design into a click-through ritual.
cookie-banner.context: Reject must be as easy as accept for the consent to be valid; dark patterns here draw regulatory fire.

tracking-pixel.def: An invisible one-pixel image or beacon whose loading reports that you opened the page or email - presence-tracking disguised as content.
tracking-pixel.context: Email open rates are built on it; blocking remote images is the countermeasure.

browser-fingerprinting.def: Identifying a browser by its combination of traits - fonts, canvas rendering, hardware, settings - unique enough to track without any cookie.
browser-fingerprinting.context: The post-cookie tracking frontier; the EFF's Cover Your Tracks demonstrates how loud a 'private' browser is.

global-privacy-control.def: A browser signal declaring 'do not sell or share my data' automatically on every site - opt-out as a setting instead of a per-site chore.
global-privacy-control.context: Where DNT died of voluntariness, GPC gained legal force: California enforces honouring it.

do-not-track.def: The browser header that politely asked sites not to track - and, lacking any legal force, was almost universally ignored.
do-not-track.context: The cautionary tale GPC learned from: a signal without enforcement is a preference, not a protection.

privacy-enhancing-technologies.def: The toolbox that lets data be used while exposing less of it: differential privacy, homomorphic encryption, secure multiparty computation, federated learning.
privacy-enhancing-technologies.context: The research field where 'compute on data you cannot read' stopped being a contradiction.

data-breach-notification.def: The legal duty to report a personal-data breach to the authority and, when risk is high, to the affected people - on a clock that starts at discovery.
data-breach-notification.context: GDPR's famous 72 hours to the authority; the LGPD requires notice 'in reasonable time' per ANPD rules.

special-category-data.def: The data whose misuse cuts deepest - health, biometrics, beliefs, orientation, genetics - locked behind stricter conditions than ordinary personal data.
special-category-data.context: The LGPD calls it 'dado pessoal sensível'; consent here must usually be explicit and specific.

biometric-data.def: Measurements of the body used to identify the person - fingerprints, face geometry, voice, gait - identifiers you cannot rotate after a breach.
biometric-data.context: A password can be changed; a face cannot. That asymmetry is the whole policy debate.

data-residency.def: Requirements that certain data physically remain within a jurisdiction's borders - law expressed as region selection.
data-residency.context: Why cloud providers open local regions and why architecture diagrams now carry flags.

cross-border-transfer.def: Moving personal data between jurisdictions - lawful only through recognized mechanisms: adequacy decisions, contractual clauses, or specific exceptions.
cross-border-transfer.context: The LGPD's chapter on international transfer mirrors the GDPR's; geography became a compliance property of data.

schrems-ii.def: The judgment of 16 July 2020 in which the Court of Justice of the European Union invalidated the Privacy Shield between the European Union and the United States and made every exporter using standard contractual clauses answer for the law of the destination country: the second time complaints by Max Schrems, begun while he was an Austrian law student, brought down a transatlantic framework.
schrems-ii.context: Max Schrems challenged Facebook's transfers of his data to the United States (US) over the reach of American surveillance, and the Court of Justice of the European Union (CJEU) agreed with him twice: the Safe Harbour decision fell on 6 October 2015 (Schrems I) and the Privacy Shield on 16 July 2020 (Schrems II). The second judgment, in Case C-311/18, kept the standard contractual clauses alive but on a condition that changed what signing them means: the exporter must check whether the destination country's law lets its authorities reach the data beyond what is strictly necessary, and stop the transfer if the clauses cannot be honoured there. A successor, the Data Privacy Framework, has applied since July 2023 and is itself under challenge.
schrems-ii.depth:
Schrems II is the 2020 decision in which the Court of Justice of the European Union (CJEU), sitting as a Grand Chamber in Case C-311/18, Data Protection Commissioner v Facebook Ireland and Maximillian Schrems, invalidated the Privacy Shield framework governing transfers of personal data from the European Union (EU) to the United States (US), on the grounds that US surveillance law did not provide protection essentially equivalent to European standards. It made two findings in opposite directions on the same day. Commission Decision 2016/1250 of 12 July 2016, the Privacy Shield adequacy decision, was declared invalid, with immediate effect. Commission Decision 2010/87 on standard contractual clauses (SCCs) was declared valid. Both findings rest on the General Data Protection Regulation (GDPR) of 27 April 2016 read with the Charter of Fundamental Rights: a transfer outside the Union needs either an adequacy decision or appropriate safeguards with enforceable rights and effective remedies.

How the case got there. Schrems, a Facebook user since 2008, began complaining to Ireland's data protection authority in 2011 while studying law, including a semester at Santa Clara University in California. After Edward Snowden's revelations in 2013 about the National Security Agency (NSA), he complained that Facebook Ireland's transfers to its parent's servers in the United States were not protected against American surveillance. The Irish authority rejected the complaint because of the Commission's Safe Harbour Decision 2000/520 of 26 July 2000, and the High Court referred the matter to Luxembourg. On 6 October 2015, in Case C-362/14 (Schrems I), the Court declared the Safe Harbour Decision invalid and held that an adequacy decision cannot remove a national authority's power to examine a complaint about a transfer. Facebook then relied on SCCs, Schrems reformulated his complaint, and the Irish authority itself went to the High Court to ask whether the clauses were valid; Ms Justice Costello referred the questions to the CJEU on 3 October 2017. In the meantime the Commission had adopted the Privacy Shield, which the Court examined as well.

What the Court said about the clauses. The GDPR applies to a commercial transfer even if the data may later be processed by the destination country's authorities for national security. People whose data leave under SCCs must receive a level of protection essentially equivalent to the one the GDPR guarantees, and the assessment has to weigh both the contract between exporter and importer and, as regards any access by the authorities of the third country, the relevant aspects of its legal system. The clauses are not invalid merely because, being a contract, they cannot bind a foreign government; they survive because Decision 2010/87 obliges the exporter and the importer to verify, before any transfer, that the level of protection is respected, obliges the importer to say when it cannot comply, and obliges the exporter then to suspend the transfer or end the contract. Where there is no valid adequacy decision and the clauses cannot be complied with in the destination country, the supervisory authorities must suspend or prohibit the transfer if the exporter has not done so itself.

What it said about the United States. The Court looked at section 702 of the Foreign Intelligence Surveillance Act (FISA), Executive Order 12333 and Presidential Policy Directive 28, and found that the limitations on protection arising from US law were not circumscribed in a way that satisfies requirements essentially equivalent to those of EU law, because the surveillance programmes based on them are not limited to what is strictly necessary; for certain programmes the provisions show no limits on the power they confer and no guarantees for non-US persons, and they give data subjects no actionable rights before the courts against the US authorities. The Ombudsperson mechanism the Privacy Shield had created was neither independent of the executive nor empowered to adopt decisions binding on the intelligence services. The judgment also recorded the Irish High Court's finding that Executive Order 12333 allows the NSA to access submarine cables and to collect and retain data before it arrives in the United States, which turns the cable landing station into part of the legal analysis.

The practical consequence was immediate and awkward. More than 5,000 US companies had been relying on the Privacy Shield, and the alternative contractual mechanisms remained valid but now required a case-by-case assessment of whether the destination country's law would undermine them; for the United States the honest answer was frequently that it would. It made a routine compliance question into a genuine legal analysis, usually called a transfer impact assessment. The European Data Protection Board (EDPB) set out how to do it in its Recommendations 01/2020, adopted in final form on 18 June 2021: know your transfers, identify the transfer tool, assess whether it is effective in the destination's law and practice, adopt supplementary measures, take the procedural steps, and re-evaluate at intervals. In June 2021 the Commission adopted new SCCs for transfers outside the European Economic Area. The cost of getting it wrong became concrete in May 2023, when Ireland's Data Protection Commission fined Meta 1.2 billion euros, under a binding decision of the EDPB, for continuing transfers to the United States after Schrems II on the 2021 clauses with supplementary measures that did not address the risks the Court had identified, and ordered it to suspend them within five months.

It is worth understanding as a technology issue rather than a legal one, because the responses are architectural. The EDPB's own worked cases say so. Data stored abroad only for backup, encrypted before transmission with state-of-the-art algorithms correctly implemented, with keys reliably managed and retained solely by the exporter or by a trusted entity in the European Economic Area or an equivalent jurisdiction, is an effective supplementary measure. Data that a cloud provider or other processor must see in the clear to do its job, in a country whose law allows disproportionate access, has no effective technical measure in the current state of the art, and transport encryption plus encryption at rest, even together, do not change that. That is why data residency requirements, regional processing, encryption where the provider cannot access the keys, and confidential computing all became commercially significant as answers to a court decision; and it is why choosing a European region on a console settles nothing by itself if the provider holding the keys can be compelled by another country's law.

The question has not been resolved so much as repeatedly renegotiated. Schrems II was the second such invalidation, following Safe Harbour, brought by the same litigant. The United States answered with Executive Order 14086 of October 2022, which added safeguards to signals intelligence, and an Attorney General regulation creating a Data Protection Review Court; on that basis the Commission adopted the EU-US Data Privacy Framework adequacy decision, 2023/1795, on 10 July 2023, and reviewed it for the first time on 9 October 2024. On 3 September 2025 the EU General Court dismissed an action for its annulment, Case T-553/23, Latombe v Commission, finding the review court sufficiently independent; the appeal, C-703/25 P, was pending in September 2026. On 29 June 2026 the US Supreme Court, in Trump v. Slaughter, held that commissioners of the Federal Trade Commission (FTC), the framework's main commercial enforcement authority, can be removed at will, overruling Humphrey's Executor; the EDPB asked the Commission on 31 July 2026 to assess the effect, and the noyb organization Schrems co-founded in 2017 had written on 30 June calling for an orderly withdrawal. The framework remains in force while those questions are answered.

Schrems II also shaped the transfer rules of other countries. Brazil's LGPD (Lei Geral de Proteção de Dados Pessoais) has its own chapter on international transfers, with adequacy and standard clauses; its regulator, the ANPD (Agência Nacional de Proteção de Dados), and the European Commission adopted mutual adequacy decisions dated 26 January 2026, after an assessment in which, under article 45 of the GDPR, the access of public authorities to personal data is one of the elements the Commission must examine. The numbers worth remembering: C-362/14 and 6 October 2015; C-311/18 and 16 July 2020; Decisions 2000/520, 2016/1250, 2010/87 and 2023/1795; more than 5,000 companies; and 1.2 billion euros.

metadata.def: Data about data: who contacted whom, when, from where and how often, everything except the content, and often more revealing than it. In engineering, also the descriptive records systems publish about themselves, such as cloud instance or federation metadata.
metadata.context: A former director of the National Security Agency (NSA) and the Central Intelligence Agency (CIA), Michael Hayden, said in 2014 that 'we kill people based on metadata', and the candour became the field's defining quote because it conceded the critics' point: the pattern of communications can reveal as much as their content. Engineers meet the word in several working senses too: flow records describing traffic, the metadata service a cloud instance queries for its own identity and credentials, and the metadata documents that let identity providers and service providers trust one another.
metadata.depth:
One word, several meanings, one property. The National Institute of Standards and Technology (NIST) glossary collects the definitions side by side. The shortest, from its forensics guide SP 800-86 (SP for Special Publication), is data about data, which for file systems means information about a file's contents rather than the contents. SP 800-53 Revision 5 is more precise: information describing the characteristics of data, divided into structural metadata (format, syntax, semantics) and descriptive metadata (such as security labels). Key management guidance (SP 800-57) uses the word for a key's attributes: its constraints, permitted uses and ownership. What the senses share is that metadata is what a system needs in order to handle the data, and therefore what it cannot easily hide: a network has to see addresses to route a packet, a resolver has to see a name to answer it, and a federation partner has to see a key to verify a signature.

Communications metadata, the privacy sense. In a debate with the Georgetown constitutional law professor David Cole at Johns Hopkins University in April 2014, General Michael Hayden, director of the NSA (National Security Agency) from 1999 to 2005 and of the CIA (Central Intelligence Agency) from 2006 to 2009, agreed with the description that metadata can tell the government everything about a person it targets, and said: we kill people based on metadata. In the same breath he added that this was not what the agency did with the telephone records it had been receiving from telephone companies since October 2001, which it kept, in his words, in a lockbox. Cole used the remark in the New York Review of Books to argue that official reassurances about metadata collection were misleading, and a White House review panel had already recommended ending the bulk collection of Americans' records. Two years later Jonathan Mayer, Patrick Mutchler and John Mitchell of Stanford published a crowdsourced study of real telephone metadata in the Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences (PNAS): the records were highly interconnected, individuals could be re-identified with little effort, and the data supported sensitive inferences about the people behind the numbers.

The law has reached the same conclusion. When the Court of Justice of the European Union struck down the Data Retention Directive on 8 April 2014 in Digital Rights Ireland, it described data that identified the source and destination of a communication, its date, time, duration and type, the equipment and the location, but never the content, and held that taken as a whole they may allow very precise conclusions about people's private lives: daily habits, places of residence, movements, activities and social relationships, with retention likely to create a feeling of constant surveillance. Brazil's Marco Civil da Internet (Law 12.965 of 2014) defines exactly this kind of data as connection records, holding the start and end time, the duration and the Internet Protocol (IP) address used, and application access records, holding the time an application was used from a given IP address, and makes their disclosure conditional on a court order.

Network metadata, the operational sense. The same property that worries privacy lawyers is what makes flow records useful to engineers. The IP Flow Information Export (IPFIX) protocol, RFC 7011 (Request for Comments 7011, Internet Standard 77, September 2013), defines a flow as a set of packets passing an observation point during a time interval and sharing common properties, such as addresses and ports taken from packet header fields; its version number, 10, is one more than the NetFlow version 9 it grew out of. A flow record says who talked to whom, when, for how long and how much, with no payload at all, and that is enough for capacity planning, anomaly detection and incident scoping, and for an investigator reconstructing an intrusion.

Encryption protects content, not metadata. RFC 8744, published by Christian Huitema in July 2020, sets out what the Server Name Indication (SNI) extension of Transport Layer Security (TLS) exposes: the client sends the name of the server it wants in cleartext in the ClientHello, and middleboxes learned to use it for censorship, network operators' content filtering, quality-of-service (QoS) treatment, enterprise blocking and decisions to exempt sensitive sites, such as banks and health services, from interception; the RFC adds that the SNI is probably also collected as metadata by pervasive surveillance actors. Before TLS 1.3 the server certificate travelled in cleartext and exposed the same name, so hiding the SNI alone gained little; TLS 1.3 encrypts the certificate, which is what made encrypting the SNI worth specifying. Packet sizes, timing and destination addresses remain visible regardless.

Cloud instance metadata, the attack-surface sense. Amazon EC2 (Elastic Compute Cloud) gives every instance an Instance Metadata Service (IMDS) at the link-local address 169.254.169.254, and at fd00:ec2::254 over IPv6 on Nitro-based instances, from which software on the instance reads its own configuration and the temporary credentials of its role. Version 1 is a plain request and response; version 2, which an instance can be configured to require, starts with a PUT to the token path carrying a time to live of one second to six hours (21,600 seconds) and then presents that token on every read. The announcement of version 2 by Amazon Web Services (AWS) on 19 November 2019, by Colm MacCárthaigh, explains each layer: open web application firewalls (WAFs) and reverse proxies very rarely forward PUT requests; the service refuses a token to any caller whose request carries an X-Forwarded-For header; the response carrying the token leaves with an IP time to live of 1, so it dies on the first hop if the instance has been misconfigured as a router or NAT (network address translation) device; and a required static header alone only stops server-side request forgery (SSRF) bugs in which the attacker controls the uniform resource locator (URL) and nothing else.

Federation metadata, the trust sense. In Security Assertion Markup Language (SAML) 2.0, metadata is the signed configuration that identity providers and service providers exchange before any user signs in. The metadata specification of OASIS (the Organization for the Advancement of Structured Information Standards), an OASIS Standard of 15 March 2005 edited by Scott Cantor, Jahan Moreh, Rob Philpott and Eve Maler, makes the EntityDescriptor the primary unit, identified by an entityID of up to 1,024 characters and containing one role descriptor per function; each KeyDescriptor carries a certificate marked for signing or encryption; the root element must carry a validUntil or cacheDuration attribute; and most elements can be individually signed. An entity may publish its metadata at the URL that is its entityID, and https is strongly recommended. Because the signing keys travel in the metadata and partners cache it, a certificate rollover reaches a partner only when its copy is refreshed, and the specification itself warns that metadata is not an authoritative statement of what a system can actually do.

Handling metadata well. In every sense, metadata deserves the protection given to the data it describes, and sometimes more, because it is collected by default, kept longer and shared more widely. The defences follow from the sources above: minimize what is logged and retained, aggregate where individual records are not needed, put access to stored communications records behind legal process, encrypt the parts of a protocol that can be encrypted without breaking routing, require tokens and hop limits on local metadata services, and treat federation metadata as a signed, expiring trust anchor rather than a configuration file.

profiling.def: Automated evaluation of a person from their data, to analyse or predict aspects such as behaviour, interests, reliability, economic situation, health or movements: the model of a person that decisions are made against.
profiling.context: The European Union's General Data Protection Regulation (GDPR) defines it in Article 4(4) as automated processing of personal data used to evaluate personal aspects of a natural person, and Brazil's Lei Geral de Proteção de Dados (LGPD) treats the data that builds a behavioural profile as personal data. Both laws grant rights around purely automated decisions with significant effects: GDPR Article 22 a right not to be subject to them without safeguards that include human intervention, LGPD Article 20 a right to request their review and an explanation of the criteria. Profiling is not the same as identification: a profile infers what a person is likely to do or be, and the inference can be wrong, sensitive, or both.
profiling.depth:
The legal definition is broad on purpose. Article 4(4) of the GDPR (General Data Protection Regulation) calls profiling any form of automated processing of personal data that uses the data to evaluate personal aspects of a natural person, in particular to analyse or predict performance at work, economic situation, health, personal preferences, interests, reliability, behaviour, location or movements. The Article 29 Working Party's guidelines, adopted in 2017 and revised on 6 February 2018 (document WP251rev.01), break it into three elements: the processing is automated, it is carried out on personal data, and its objective is to evaluate personal aspects. The word is "any form", not "solely": a human in the loop does not take an activity out of the definition. The guidelines describe it as a series of statistical deductions that infer something about an individual from the qualities of others who appear statistically similar, and they draw the line at purpose: sorting customers by age or sex only to produce aggregate statistics, with no conclusion drawn about any one person, is not profiling.

The same guidelines borrow from the Council of Europe's Recommendation CM/Rec(2010)13 of 23 November 2010 a three-stage picture that maps directly onto real systems: data collection, automated analysis to find correlations, and the application of those correlations to an individual to predict present or future behaviour. They then separate three uses. General profiling builds and keeps the model; decision-making based on profiling uses it to inform a human decision; and solely automated decision-making, including profiling, with legal or similarly significant effects is the case Article 22(1) restricts. Recital 71 of the regulation gives the two classic examples, the automatic refusal of an online credit application and e-recruiting without human intervention, and the guidelines add decisions on access to health services, to employment and to education. Targeted advertising usually falls short of that threshold, but the guidelines say it can cross it through intrusive tracking across websites, devices and services, through exploiting known vulnerabilities (regular adverts for high-interest loans to someone in financial difficulty), or through differential pricing that effectively bars someone from a service. Separately, Article 21 gives an unconditional right to object to profiling for direct marketing.

Article 22 allows such decisions only where they are necessary for a contract, authorized by European Union or national law with safeguards, or based on explicit consent. The European Commission's own illustration is an online bank whose algorithm decides on a loan and its interest rate: the applicant must be told that they may express a point of view, contest the result and have the decision reviewed by a person. The guidelines close the obvious loophole. A controller cannot fabricate human involvement: someone who routinely applies automatically generated profiles without any actual influence on the result leaves the decision solely automated, and real oversight must be carried out by someone with the authority and competence to change the outcome, looking at all the relevant data. Profiling can also trigger the duty to run a DPIA (data protection impact assessment).

Brazil's LGPD (Lei Geral de Proteção de Dados) reaches the same territory by its own route. Article 12, paragraph 2, says that data used to form the behavioural profile of an identified natural person may be treated as personal data, which matters because profiling systems often claim to work on anonymous data. Article 20 gives the data subject the right to request review of decisions taken solely on automated processing that affect their interests, expressly including decisions that define their personal, professional, consumer or credit profile or aspects of their personality; the controller must provide clear and adequate information on the criteria and procedures used, subject to commercial and industrial secrecy, and where it withholds them on that ground the ANPD (Agência Nacional de Proteção de Dados) may audit the processing for discriminatory aspects. The text as enacted in 2018 said the review would be carried out by a natural person. Provisional Measure 869 of 27 December 2018, converted into Law 13.853 of 8 July 2019, removed those words, and a paragraph 3 added by that law was vetoed, so the Brazilian right is to a review and an explanation, without the statutory guarantee of a human reviewer that the European text provides.

Credit scoring is where the law has been tested hardest. In Case C-634/21, SCHUFA Holding, decided on 7 December 2023, the Court of Justice of the European Union (CJEU) held that a credit agency's automated score is itself an automated individual decision under Article 22 when the banks that buy it attribute a determining role to it in granting credit, so the agency cannot shelter behind the bank's formal decision. In Case C-203/22, Dun & Bradstreet Austria, decided on 27 February 2025, a mobile operator had refused a customer a contract of 10 euros a month on the strength of an automated credit assessment; the court ruled that the controller must explain the procedure and principles actually applied, so the person can see which of their data were used and how, that the mere communication of an algorithm is not such an explanation, and that alleged trade secrets go to the supervisory authority or court, which decides how much the person may see. Brazil's Superior Tribunal de Justiça (STJ) settled the local version in Súmula 550, approved on 14 October 2015: a credit score is a statistical method of risk assessment rather than a database, so it needs no consent, but the consumer may ask which personal information was weighed and from which sources.

What makes profiling a privacy problem rather than a statistics exercise is what it can infer. Michal Kosinski, David Stillwell and Thore Graepel showed in the Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences in 2013 that Facebook Likes from more than 58,000 volunteers predicted sexual orientation, ethnicity, religious and political views, personality traits and more: their model told homosexual from heterosexual men in 88 per cent of cases, African Americans from Caucasian Americans in 95 per cent and Democrats from Republicans in 85 per cent. The United States Federal Trade Commission (FTC), reporting on 27 May 2014 on nine data brokers, found billions of data elements on nearly every American consumer (one broker alone held 1.4 billion transactions and 700 billion data elements) combined into inferred ethnicity, income, religion, political leaning, age and health, and sold as segments with names such as Urban Scramble and Mobile Mixers, both concentrated on low-income minority households, or as health segments such as pregnancy, diabetes and high cholesterol. Innocuous inputs can yield special-category outputs, which is why purpose limitation and data minimization are aimed at the model as much as at the raw data.

Security engineering profiles people too, usually without calling it that. UEBA (user and entity behaviour analytics) learns each user's normal pattern and scores deviation. Netskope's Advanced UBA (user behaviour analytics), for example, scores users with a User Confidence Index (UCI), raises an alert when a user's score drops below a threshold within 24 hours, and lets Real-time Protection policies use the score as a traffic criterion, so a low score can change what a user is allowed to do inline. Evaluating an employee's reliability and behaviour from activity logs is profiling in the sense of Article 4(4) and of the LGPD, and the same obligations follow: a stated purpose, a legal basis, an impact assessment where the risk is high, and meaningful human review before a score turns into a consequence for the person. The European Union's Artificial Intelligence Act goes further for the systems it lists in its Annex III (employment, credit and access to essential services among them): Article 6(3) says such a system is always high-risk when it performs profiling of natural persons.

Two neighbouring uses of the word are a different thing. Device profiling in network access control (NAC) classifies endpoints, not people: FortiNAC's device profiling rules, for instance, categorize rogue hosts as they connect by comparing each against the enabled rules until one matches. Performance profiling in software measures where a program spends its time. Browser fingerprinting and tracking pixels sit upstream: they identify and follow a person so that a profile can be built, and the profile is what decisions are then made against.

data-broker.def: A company whose product is other people: profiles assembled from purchases, apps, public records, and location trails, sold to whoever pays.
data-broker.context: The industry most people have never heard of that has heard all about them.

opt-in-vs-opt-out.def: The two default postures of consent: nothing happens until you say yes, versus everything happens until you say no - defaults decide outcomes at population scale.
opt-in-vs-opt-out.context: The single design choice with the largest privacy impact; participation rates swing enormously on it.
opt-in-vs-opt-out.depth:
Opt-in requires an affirmative act before something applies; opt-out applies by default and requires an act to escape. The distinction sounds procedural and it determines outcomes, because defaults are what most people get.

The empirical finding is consistent and large: participation rates differ enormously between the two, in organ donation, retirement savings, marketing consent and every other domain measured. People are not indifferent, they are busy, and the default is what happens when attention is scarce. That makes the choice of default a design decision with a predictable result rather than a neutral starting position.

In data protection this is why the legal texts specify it.
