GDPR requires consent to be freely given, specific, informed and unambiguous, which rules out pre-ticked boxes and consent bundled into terms of service. LGPD follows the same shape. The engineering consequence is that opt-in is a system requirement rather than a policy preference: recording what was consented to, when, and for what purpose is a data model decision, and retrofitting it into a system that assumed opt-out is substantially harder than building it in.

surveillance-capitalism.def: The business model of predicting and steering behaviour from harvested personal data - attention in, predictions out, advertisers billed.
surveillance-capitalism.context: Coined and dissected by Shoshana Zuboff (2019); the term that gave the debate its name.

nat-firewall-myth.def: The belief that address translation is a security control, so that a network behind NAT (Network Address Translation) needs no firewall. NAT blocks unsolicited inbound connections only as a side effect of having no mapping for them; it applies no policy, logs no decisions and does nothing about outbound or internal traffic. A stateful firewall does.
nat-firewall-myth.context: The confusion comes from home routers that bundle translation and stateful filtering in one box and one setting. The Internet Engineering Task Force (IETF) has said for decades that translating addresses does not provide security in itself: RFC (Request for Comments) 4864 in 2007 set out how IPv6 (Internet Protocol version 6) gets the protection people attributed to NAT (Network Address Translation) without translating anything, and RFC 2993 warned in 2000 that NAT creates the illusion of a security barrier without the managed intent of a firewall. IPv6, which needs no NAT, reopened the debate in reverse.
nat-firewall-myth.depth:
The belief, stated exactly: because a NAT (Network Address Translation) device stops outsiders from opening connections to hosts behind it, it is a firewall, and a network behind one is protected; the corollary, often heard when IPv6 (Internet Protocol version 6) is planned, is that removing NAT removes security. Nobody designed NAT as a security device. K. Egevang and P. Francis proposed it in RFC (Request for Comments) 1631 in May 1994 as a short-term answer to the depletion of IPv4 (Internet Protocol version 4) addresses, reusing addresses inside stub domains and translating at the border; the memo noted a privacy side effect and said of security only that 'Security issues are not discussed in this memo'. RFC 3022 replaced it in January 2001 under the name traditional NAT. The Internet Engineering Task Force (IETF) recorded the folk view as early as August 1999, in RFC 2663: many people view a traditional NAT router as a one-way session traffic filter, and dynamic assignment makes it harder to point at a specific inside host; the same paragraph adds that NAT routers may be used in conjunction with firewalls to filter unwanted traffic, which is the point the myth drops.

Why NAT looks like a firewall. Network Address and Port Translation (NAPT), the form every home router runs, keeps a table of sessions that inside hosts have started; a packet arriving from outside that matches no entry has no inside address to go to and is discarded. RFC 4864 (May 2007) describes the effect precisely: the perceived security of NAT comes from the lack of pre-established or permanent mapping state, it is often used as a better-than-nothing level of protection because it needs no management, and the same level of protection would also be available from a basic firewall, which would improve on it by not letting state persist as different clients reuse the same private address. The RFC calls the role, often marketed as a firewall, an arbitrary artefact. RFC 4787 (January 2007) separates the two halves that home boxes blur: how a NAT maps addresses and ports makes no difference to security, and 'the security properties are fully determined by which packets the NAT allows in and which it does not', that is, by its filtering behaviour. It even recommends endpoint-independent filtering where application transparency matters, under which an inside host that sends one packet anywhere can then be reached on that mapping by any external host.

What translation does not do. RFC 4864 states it in one sentence: 'The act of translating address bits within the header does not provide security in itself.' Its example is static NAT with all inbound ports mapped to one machine, whose exposure is then identical to having no NAT at all. A firewall evaluates traffic against a policy someone wrote, logs what it denied, and applies rules outbound and between internal zones; a translation table has no policy, no notion of allowed and denied, no record of decisions it never made, and no opinion about anything an inside host chooses to start. The same RFC notes that attackers know private address space well and use methods such as trojan horses that readily penetrate NAT boundaries, because malware calling out creates exactly the state NAT is built to honour. RFC 2993 (November 2000) went further: NAT, particularly NAPT, has the potential to lower overall security because it creates the illusion of a security barrier without the managed intent of a firewall, and barriers drawn on that assumption treat every threat as external. The result is familiar in incident work: flat internal networks behind a box everyone assumed was protecting them, where one compromised host reaches every other without crossing a single control.

NAT also opens holes on request, by design. The Port Control Protocol (PCP), RFC 6887 of April 2013, exists so that a host can tell a NAT or simple firewall how to translate and forward incoming packets, and it interworks with the UPnP (Universal Plug and Play) Internet Gateway Device protocol that consumer routers have long offered for the same purpose. Application Level Gateways (ALGs), which read inside protocols such as SIP (Session Initiation Protocol) and FTP (File Transfer Protocol) to open the extra ports they negotiate, can be steered from outside. Samy Kamkar's NAT Slipstreaming, released on 31 October 2020 and extended on 26 January 2021 with Ben Seri and Gregory Vishnipolsky of Armis, let an attacker reach any TCP (Transmission Control Protocol) or UDP (User Datagram Protocol) service behind a victim's NAT simply because the victim visited a web page: the browser was made to emit what looked like SIP signalling on port 5060, and the router's SIP ALG, which Kamkar found enabled by default on most routers, opened the pinhole itself. It was a modern version of his own NAT Pinning technique from 2010.

Implementations treat the two functions as separate, and reading them that way removes the confusion. In Linux nftables, NAT rules live in their own chain type: only the first packet of a flow is matched against them to set up a binding, later packets reuse the binding through the nf_conntrack engine without any rule lookup, and putting a NAT rule in a filter chain is simply an error. Accept and drop decisions belong to the filter chains, which are where a policy, its counters and its logs live. Commercial firewalls make the same split in their own vocabulary; translation is an attribute of a rule or a separate rulebase, while the decision to permit a flow at all comes from the security policy.

IPv6 shows what the protection really is. RFC 4864's answer, called Local Network Protection, keeps a clear inside-outside boundary with stateful filtering, privacy addresses and unique local addresses, and concludes that IPv6 can deliver the benefits people attributed to IPv4 NAT without translation; it also says plainly that an IPv6 host directly connected to the internet is about as vulnerable as an IPv4 host, and recommends firewalls and intrusion detection systems (IDSs) for those who want boundary protection. RFC 6092 (January 2011) specifies that boundary for residential gateways: filter state activated by traffic from interior nodes, a protocol for applications to solicit inbound traffic (REC-48), and a transparent mode that forwards all unsolicited flows, which must be easy to select and may be the default (REC-49). RFC 7084 (November 2013) asks IPv6 customer edge routers to support RFC 6092 but takes no position on whether it is enabled by default. The protection is therefore a stateful filter that may or may not be switched on, exactly as it always was behind IPv4 NAT; the network that had no firewall policy simply discovers it on the day it turns on IPv6.

The part of the belief that is right: on a dynamic NAPT gateway with no port forwarding, unsolicited inbound connections to inside hosts really are dropped, and RFC 4864 grants that this stateful behaviour offers a measure of protection against a variety of straightforward network attacks and that the benefit may be partially real; translation also hides internal addressing and topology, the privacy effect RFC 1631 noticed in 1994. What to say instead is that NAT is an addressing tool and the stateful filter is the security control, and they should be configured, reviewed and logged as two things. In practice: write an explicit default-deny inbound policy for IPv4 and IPv6 alike, add egress filtering and segmentation so that internal compromise does not travel freely, disable UPnP and ALGs such as SIP on edge devices that do not need them, check the IPv6 customer edge for transparent mode, and verify behaviour from the state table and the filter counters rather than from the presence of private addresses.

incognito-myth.def: The belief that private browsing (Incognito in Chrome, Private Browsing in Safari and Firefox, InPrivate in Edge) makes the user anonymous. It stops the browser keeping history, cookies and site data on the device after the session; websites, the network, the internet provider and any account the user signs in to see the same as before.
incognito-myth.context: Every browser vendor says so in its own documentation: Google's help page states that Incognito does not make you invisible, Mozilla that a private window does not make you anonymous or hide your address or location. A 2018 study of 460 people found the browsers' own explanations failed to correct most misconceptions, and a US class action over tracking in Incognito mode was settled in April 2024 on terms under which Google agreed to rewrite its disclosures and delete or remediate billions of records of private browsing.
incognito-myth.depth:
The belief, stated exactly: opening an Incognito or private window hides what a person does online, from the sites visited, from the employer or school network, from the internet service provider (ISP) and sometimes even from malware. What the feature does is local. Google's Chrome help page says Chrome does not retain site data or a record of the sites visited once the Incognito session ends, keeps cookies and site data only temporarily during it, and keeps bookmarks and downloaded files afterwards; and then, in the same breath, that Incognito does not make the user invisible, because websites visited, including Google sites, and organizations that manage the network, such as a school, an employer or an internet service provider, may be able to observe the activity. Mozilla's page for Firefox is blunter: a private window does not make you anonymous online, does not hide your IP (Internet Protocol) address or location, and leaves activity visible to sites, search engines, internet providers or an employer. Microsoft describes InPrivate in Edge as not saving history, cookies, site data or form entries on the device and limiting local tracking, while downloads and favourites stay.

Why the stronger belief is so common. The names do the work: 'Incognito', 'Private Browsing' and 'InPrivate' promise more than a cleared history. In a 2018 study presented at the Web Conference in Lyon, Yuxi Wu, Blase Ur and colleagues showed 460 participants one of 13 explanations, the desktop and mobile disclosures of six browsers plus a control, and asked about twenty scenarios. The disclosures failed to correct most misconceptions. 56.3 per cent believed searches made while signed in to a Google account would not be saved in private mode; 40.2 per cent thought websites could not estimate the user's location; 22.0, 37.0 and 22.6 per cent believed ISPs, employers and the government respectively could not track them; 27.1 per cent thought private mode protected better against viruses and malware; 25.2 per cent thought sites could not see their IP address; and some assumed the mode included a VPN (virtual private network). The misreading is not only a user problem: in the Brown v. Google class action, the plaintiffs' filing cites Google employees raising in 2013 the incorrect conclusions users drew from the Incognito splash screen.

What actually happens on the wire is unchanged. The request leaves from the same address over the same network, so the café, the corporate proxy, the ISP and the destination all see what they would see in a normal window; HTTPS (Hypertext Transfer Protocol Secure) hides the page contents from the network but not the domain names, in either mode. The site receives the same IP address and enough browser characteristics to fingerprint it: when the EFF (Electronic Frontier Foundation) sampled 470,161 browsers in 2010, 83.6 per cent had a unique fingerprint. Signing in ends the question altogether: Mozilla notes that once a user signs in, the site knows who they are for the rest of the session in either window type, and the 2018 study's single most common misconception was exactly that signed-in searches would vanish. And nothing in a private window protects against malware already on the machine, which sees the screen and the keyboard whatever the browser is doing.

The case that put a price on the gap. Brown v. Google, filed in June 2020 in the Northern District of California (case 4:20-cv-03664), alleged that Google collected data from users' private browsing sessions through its services embedded in other websites. The plaintiffs' unopposed motion for final approval, filed on 1 April 2024, describes the settlement: Google rewrites its disclosures, so that the Incognito splash screen now says Incognito 'won't change how data is collected by websites you visit and the services they use, including Google', and its privacy policy says that activity on third-party sites using Google services is collected regardless of browsing mode; Google must delete or remediate billions of records reflecting private browsing collected in December 2023 and earlier; for five years Incognito must block third-party cookies by default; the private-browsing detection bits the plaintiffs found must be deleted; and individual damages claims were not released. The filing put the class at about 136 million people. These are the plaintiffs' descriptions in a court filing; the point for practitioners is the disclosure Google now shows, which states the limit in its own words.

The modes have grown more protective since, and they differ. Chrome's help page says third-party cookies are blocked by default in Incognito. Mozilla lists Total Cookie Protection, which stops a tracker on one site seeing what was done on another, fewer device details exposed to fingerprinting scripts in private windows, and a Global Privacy Control signal asking sites not to sell or share data, honoured or not at the site's discretion. Apple's Safari isolates each tab's browsing from the others in Private Browsing, turns on advanced tracking and fingerprinting protection by default there, blocking known fingerprinting data collectors, and strips known tracking parameters from web addresses. All of that reduces cross-site tracking by third parties inside the browser. None of it changes the IP address, the network path or what a site a person signs in to records about them.

The part of the belief that is right: private browsing is a genuine privacy tool against one threat model, someone with access to the same device or browser profile afterwards. It keeps a gift search off the shared family laptop, keeps a session from leaving cookies on a hotel business-centre computer, and lets a person sign in to a second account without signing out of the first; modern versions also blunt some third-party tracking. It is a narrow guarantee, stated accurately by the vendors, and the problem is that the name and the dark window suggest a wider one.

What to say instead is to match the tool to the observer. Against people who share the device, private browsing works, though downloaded files and new bookmarks remain, as all four vendors note. Against the local network, encrypted connections and encrypted DNS (Domain Name System) help; against the ISP or the local network as a whole, a trusted VPN moves the point of observation; against websites and trackers, tracker blocking, fingerprinting protection and not signing in matter more than the window's colour; against all of them at once, Tor Browser is the tool designed for anonymity. In an organization, say plainly in awareness material that an Incognito window does not hide traffic from the corporate proxy, the security service edge or the logs, so nobody relies on it, in either direction.

https-padlock-myth.def: The belief that a padlock (or https) in the address bar means a site is safe or legitimate. It means the connection is encrypted with TLS (Transport Layer Security) to a server that proved control of the name shown; it says nothing about who runs the site or what it wants. Phishing sites obtain certificates in minutes, often for free.
https-padlock-myth.context: By 2019 most phishing pages served valid HTTPS (Hypertext Transfer Protocol Secure), and the US Federal Bureau of Investigation (FBI) warned that June that criminals were banking on the public's trust in the lock icon. Browsers have demoted the padlock ever since: Chrome dropped the word 'Secure' in 2018 and replaced the lock itself with a neutral icon in 2023, because it never indicated trustworthiness and nearly all phishing sites showed it.
https-padlock-myth.depth:
The belief, stated exactly: when the browser shows a padlock, or the address starts with https, the site is genuine and safe to give a password or a card number to. What the padlock actually certifies is narrower. The connection is protected by TLS (Transport Layer Security), so nobody on the path can read or alter it, and the server presented a certificate, issued by a certification authority (CA) the browser trusts, for the domain name in the address bar. The CA/Browser Forum's Baseline Requirements, version 2.3.1 adopted in September 2026, state the scope directly: of the four certificate types (domain validated, individual validated, organization validated and extended validation), all provide the same level of assurance of the device identity, meaning the domain name or IP (Internet Protocol) address, and a domain validated (DV) certificate may carry nothing about its subject beyond a country and a name derived from the domain. Roger Dingledine and Nick Mathewson summarized the gap in 2006: many users read the lock as 'You can safely enter personal information', when its meaning is closer to 'Nobody can read your information on its way to the named website'.

Why people believe it. They were taught to. The FBI's (Federal Bureau of Investigation) Internet Crime Complaint Center (IC3) noted in its June 2019 announcement that cyber security training had focused on encouraging people to look for the lock icon, and the US Federal Trade Commission's 2011 public Wi-Fi advice told consumers to look for https and the lock throughout a site. Browsers reinforced it: until September 2018 Chrome labelled HTTPS (Hypertext Transfer Protocol Secure) pages 'Secure' in the address bar, which the Anti-Phishing Working Group (APWG) pointed out is another word for safe. In an informal PhishLabs poll in November 2017, more than 80 per cent of respondents believed the green lock meant a site was legitimate, safe, or both; research from 2021 cited by Chrome's security team found that only 11 per cent of participants understood the lock's precise meaning.

Why the check stopped working. When certificates were expensive and manual, having one loosely correlated with being an established business. Free, automated domain validation removed that correlation, as it was always going to. Let's Encrypt, which was set up to issue DV certificates, said so before it launched, in a post of October 2015: a DV certificate asserts that a public key belongs to a domain and says nothing else about a site's content or who runs it; certification authorities are not positioned to police content; and since attackers can shop among CAs, the bar is set by the weakest. It checked names against Google Safe Browsing at first and stopped on 10 January 2019. The APWG's quarterly reports show what followed. At the end of 2016 fewer than 5 per cent of phishing sites used HTTPS; by the last quarter of 2017 nearly a third did; in the third quarter of 2019 68 per cent; and by the first quarter of 2021 the share had levelled off at about 83 per cent, with 94.5 per cent of those certificates domain validated. Phishers mostly use domains they registered themselves: for two of the most phished brands, nearly three-quarters of HTTPS phishing sites in 2017 sat on maliciously registered domains rather than hacked ones. The same 2021 report found only 56 per cent of the phishing sites Axur tracked in Brazil on HTTPS, against 83 per cent worldwide, a reminder that the lag is regional, not a protection.

The official warnings and the browsers' response. The IC3's public service announcement I-061019-PSA of 10 June 2019, 'Cyber Actors Exploit Secure Websites In Phishing Campaigns', said criminals were banking on the public's trust of https and the lock icon, and advised people to check for misspellings or wrong domains and not to trust a site just because it shows a lock. Chrome had already begun changing its indicators: the Chromium team announced in May 2018 that Chrome 69 would drop the 'Secure' wording and the https scheme and that Chrome 70 would show a red 'not secure' warning when users type into pages served over plain HTTP (Hypertext Transfer Protocol), on the principle that the web should be safe by default and only exceptions flagged. In May 2023 it announced that Chrome 117 would replace the lock with a neutral tune icon, stating that the lock does not indicate trustworthiness and that nearly all phishing sites use HTTPS, while over 95 per cent of page loads on Windows were by then encrypted. Identity indicators fared no better: a Google field experiment published at USENIX Security 2019 found that removing the extended validation (EV) display left most measures of user behaviour unchanged, and in 14 design iterations no variation significantly improved users' understanding. The APWG's 2021 count of phishing sites with EV certificates was 11, all of them hacked legitimate sites.

The part of the belief that is right. The padlock is a real guarantee about the channel: a café network, a compromised router or an ISP (internet service provider) cannot read or modify the traffic, and the server did prove control of that exact name to a CA within a bounded time, which the Baseline Requirements keep shortening, from a 200-day maximum certificate lifetime from 15 March 2026 to 100 days from 15 March 2027 and 47 days from 15 March 2029. Its absence still matters: a login form on plain HTTP, or a certificate warning, is a genuine reason to stop. What the padlock cannot do is tell a user that the name is the right one.

That makes the domain name the thing to check, and it is harder than it looks. The part that matters is the registrable domain immediately before the first single slash after the scheme, read right to left: bank.example.com.attacker.net belongs to attacker.net. Lookalike characters make it worse; Chromium's documentation gives the example of ebay.com spelled with a Cyrillic 'a', which is why browsers display confusable internationalized names in punycode, the form beginning xn--, under policies that since Chrome 51 ignore the user's language settings. The same document points to the more reliable checks: Safe Browsing warnings, and password managers, which will not fill a password into a domain that is not exactly the right one, so a manager that offers nothing on a familiar-looking login page is itself a warning.

What a practitioner should teach instead: the lock means private, not trustworthy; the address is the identity, and it has to be read; and the strongest defences take the decision away from the eye. Password managers and passkeys bind a credential to the real domain, which is why the UK's National Cyber Security Centre recommended passkeys as the default login in April 2026 partly for their resistance to phishing. Arrive at sensitive sites from a bookmark or by typing the name rather than from a link; treat 'secure' in a message as a claim to verify, not a property; and in awareness training retire the instruction to 'look for the padlock', replacing it with 'look at the domain, and let the password manager look too'.

vpn-anonymity-myth.def: The belief that a commercial VPN (virtual private network) makes its user anonymous. A VPN moves trust from the local network and the internet provider to the VPN company: it hides traffic from the café network and the user's address from websites, while the provider itself sees what the internet provider used to see.
vpn-anonymity-myth.context: A consumer VPN (virtual private network) encrypts traffic between a device and the provider's server, so the local network and the internet service provider (ISP) see only a tunnel and websites see the provider's address instead of the user's. Everything else that identifies a person passes through untouched: account logins, cookies, tracking pixels and browser fingerprints, plus whatever leaks around a misconfigured tunnel, such as DNS (Domain Name System) queries, IPv6 (Internet Protocol version 6) traffic or WebRTC (Web Real-Time Communication) address discovery. The provider inherits the ISP's view, under the laws of its own jurisdiction, and 'no-logs' promises have been contradicted both in court records and in exposed databases. A useful tool for choosing who observes the traffic; the wrong word for what it delivers.
vpn-anonymity-myth.depth:
The belief, stated exactly: connecting through a commercial VPN (virtual private network) makes the user anonymous, so that neither websites nor anyone else can tell who is behind the traffic. What a consumer VPN actually does is narrower. The client builds an encrypted tunnel from the device to a server the provider runs, and from there the traffic leaves for the internet under the provider's IP (Internet Protocol) address. The Electronic Frontier Foundation (EFF) states both halves of the result in its Surveillance Self-Defense guide, last reviewed on 28 July 2026: the tunnel hides outgoing traffic from the ISP (internet service provider) and from the owner of the local network, and the browsing data the ISP used to see becomes visible to the VPN provider instead. Its verdict on the belief takes one sentence: a VPN is not a tool for anonymity.

Why people believe it. VPNs began as a way to send data privately across public networks between sites and remote staff, and the consumer market sold them as something larger. The authors of a measurement study of 62 providers, presented at the 2018 Internet Measurement Conference (IMC), describe VPNs as now marketed broadly as a privacy-preserving technology that hides not only traffic but personal information such as browsing history from ISPs and governments alike, and they found that many of the review sites buyers rely on are supported by affiliate programmes. In December 2021 the Consumer Reports digital lab screened 51 VPNs for Windows 10 and compared 16 in depth; in July 2022 Representative Anna Eshoo and Senator Ron Wyden cited that work in a letter asking the US Federal Trade Commission (FTC) to act, saying 75 per cent of leading providers had misrepresented their products and technology, that some advertised a 'military-grade encryption' that does not exist, and that providers marketing 'total anonymity' had sold user data. The FTC's own consumer advice of February 2018 had already told people to check whether a VPN app encrypts at all and whether it shares information with third parties.

What is actually true is that a VPN moves trust; it does not remove it. HTTPS (Hypertext Transfer Protocol Secure) protects content but not metadata, as the EFF explained in a separate article in January 2020: whoever sits on the path sees the domain names a user visits, when, and the sizes of the pages and files transferred. A VPN does not abolish that position; it decides who occupies it. The provider sits where the ISP sat, with the same view, and it is subject to the laws of the countries it operates in, where, the EFF notes, a government can demand the data or subpoena it. Whether the trade is an improvement depends on whom the user has more reason to fear: on a hostile hotel network, or under an ISP that sells browsing records, a reputable provider is the better observer; a provider of unknown ownership may be a worse one. 'No logs' is a claim, not a property an outsider can check, and the EFF guide says so plainly: a claim is not a guarantee, and an audit cannot show that practices were not changed after it. The weakness is structural, not a matter of picking a better brand. Roger Dingledine and Nick Mathewson, two of Tor's designers, put it in 2006: a single-hop proxy service gives comparatively weak protection, because a compromised proxy can observe all of its users' actions, an eavesdropper need watch only that one proxy to correlate the timing of every user's traffic, and all users must trust the company not to reveal what they do.

The record shows why that caution is earned. In October 2017 the US Department of Justice charged Ryan Lin, then 24, of Newton, Massachusetts, over a cyberstalking campaign run through anonymizing services; according to the criminal complaint as reported by The Register, the provider PureVPN was able to determine that its service had been used by the same customer from two originating IP addresses, which investigators linked to his workplace and his home. He was sentenced to 210 months in prison in October 2018. In July 2020 researchers at Comparitech and vpnMentor found an unsecured Elasticsearch cluster holding about 1.2 TB, some 1,083,997,361 log entries, from seven Hong Kong-based services (UFO VPN, FAST VPN, Free VPN, Super VPN, Flash VPN, Secure VPN and Rabbit VPN) that all advertised themselves as no-log providers and shared one white-label operator; the records included user IP addresses, connection timestamps, websites visited and, by the researchers' account, plain-text passwords.

The tunnel itself leaks more often than users assume. The 2018 IMC study by Mohammad Taha Khan and colleagues tested 62 commercial providers: 25 services, 58 per cent of those the test applied to, leaked user traffic when the tunnel failed, a failure the authors point out an ISP or a government can induce at will by blocking connections or spoofing TCP (Transmission Control Protocol) resets; of 43 providers with their own client software, 12 sent IPv6 (Internet Protocol version 6) traffic outside the tunnel and two leaked DNS (Domain Name System) queries; about 10 per cent showed evidence of intercepting or manipulating traffic; and 5 to 30 per cent of advertised vantage points, at 10 per cent of providers, appeared to sit in a country other than the one advertised. An earlier study of 283 Android apps holding the VPN permission, drawn from more than 1.4 million apps on Google Play and presented at IMC 2016, found that 18 per cent tunnelled without encryption, about 84 per cent did not carry IPv6 and 66 per cent did not carry DNS through the tunnel, 75 per cent embedded third-party tracking libraries, and over 38 per cent showed some malware presence according to VirusTotal. Browsers add a leak of their own: RFC (Request for Comments) 8828, the 2021 Internet Engineering Task Force (IETF) standard on WebRTC (Web Real-Time Communication) address handling, records that with a split-tunnel VPN, WebRTC can discover both the VPN's public address and the ISP address underneath it, and ranks this as the most significant of its concerns precisely because some users rely on a VPN for anonymity.

Even a perfect tunnel changes only one identifier, the source address. The EFF lists what it leaves alone: GPS (Global Positioning System) location, web cookies, tracking pixels and fingerprinting; and signing in to an account identifies the user completely, whatever path the packets took. Fingerprinting is the identifier that survives the most. Between 27 January and 15 February 2010 Peter Eckersley of the EFF collected fingerprints from 470,161 browsers that visited the Panopticlick test site, a sample of privacy-conscious volunteers: 83.6 per cent were unique, 94.2 per cent of those with Flash or Java, and the distribution carried at least 18.1 bits of entropy, so that a browser picked at random would at best share its fingerprint with one in 286,777 others. None of those attributes changes when the exit address does.

The part of the belief that is right explains why it persists. A VPN really does hide the sites a user contacts from the café network and from the home ISP, really does keep the user's own address from the sites visited, and really does move the apparent location, which makes it a sound tool against local snooping, ISP-level data collection and geographic or national filtering. The 2018 IMC authors also found commercial VPNs, on the whole, less likely to intercept or tamper with traffic than other kinds of traffic proxy studied before them. And in enterprise remote access, anonymity was never the point: the corporate tunnel authenticates the user by design.

What to say instead: a VPN changes who can observe the traffic, and choosing one well means naming the observer to be avoided. For someone who needs anonymity rather than a different observer, the EFF guide points to Tor, a network conceived, in the Tor Project's own history, to be operated by many parties with diverse interests and run today on thousands of volunteer relays rather than one company's servers; the Tor Project in turn advises against adding a VPN to Tor unless the user knows how to configure both without weakening Tor's protections. For everyone else the checks are concrete: a provider whose ownership and jurisdiction are known; a kill switch that is on by default, since Khan and colleagues treated default-off kill switches as unsafe; IPv6 and DNS carried through the tunnel or blocked; a browser that keeps WebRTC on the default route (Mode 2 or stricter in RFC 8828) rather than enumerating every interface; and the understanding that logging in, accepting cookies or running an unhardened browser undoes the address change entirely.

five-ghz-myth.def: The belief that 5 GHz Wi-Fi is simply better than 2.4 GHz, so the higher band should always be preferred. Higher bands carry more data and suffer less congestion, but lose more signal with distance and through many building materials: 5 GHz usually wins near the access point, 2.4 GHz often wins several walls away. It is physics, not a quality tier.
five-ghz-myth.context: Free-space loss grows with frequency and absorption in common building materials grows with it too, so each step up in band trades range and penetration for spectrum and capacity; the propagation trade-off is reflected in how the 802.11 bands are planned and used. Band steering exists to choose per client and per position, and 6 GHz repeats the trade one band higher, under rules that now differ by country: the United States opened 1,200 MHz in 2020, while Brazil will limit Wi-Fi to the lower 500 MHz of the band from March 2027.
five-ghz-myth.depth:
The belief, stated exactly: 5 GHz Wi-Fi is the better band, so devices should always use it and 2.4 GHz is a legacy fallback to switch off when possible; by extension, 6 GHz is better still. It is half right, which is why it lasts. The higher band has far more room. Fortinet's channel-planning guide counts only three non-overlapping channels at 2.4 GHz in most of the world (1, 6 and 11) against 25 channels at 5 GHz, and its Wi-Fi 6 access points allow 20, 40 and 80 MHz channels at 5 GHz but only 20 MHz at 2.4 GHz, so the same radio can use a channel four times wider. The 2.4 GHz band is also shared with everything else in the industrial, scientific and medical (ISM) allocation: the ITU (International Telecommunication Union) designates 2450 plus or minus 50 MHz for ISM equipment, and a 1995 report by the US National Telecommunications and Information Administration (NTIA) counted about 80 million domestic microwave ovens in the United States and over 200 million worldwide working in it.

The half that is wrong is range, and it starts with plain geometry. ITU-R Recommendation P.525-5 (November 2024) gives the free-space basic transmission loss between isotropic antennas as 32.4 + 20 log f + 20 log d decibels, with f in megahertz and d in kilometres. The frequency term does not mean that air absorbs 5 GHz more; it comes from the effective aperture of the receiving antenna, which for an isotropic antenna is the wavelength squared over 4 pi, so a shorter wavelength collects less of the same power density. Worked from that formula, a 10-metre path loses 60.0 dB at 2,400 MHz, 67.2 dB at 5,500 MHz and 68.7 dB at 6,500 MHz: about 7 dB more at 5 GHz and nearly 9 dB more at 6 GHz before a single wall. Because loss rises by about 6 dB per doubling of distance, a 7 dB handicap means the 5 GHz signal reaches the same level at a little under half the distance.

Walls widen the gap, unevenly. ITU-R P.2040-4 (September 2025), the recommendation on building materials, notes that the conductivity of most materials increases with frequency and gives a dielectric-limit attenuation rate of 1636 times the conductivity divided by the square root of the relative permittivity, in dB per metre, together with fitted models for common materials. Evaluated with its own Table 3, concrete attenuates about 65 dB per metre at 2.4 GHz, 125 at 5.5 GHz and 143 at 6.5 GHz, so 10 cm of concrete costs roughly 6.5, 12.5 and 14 dB respectively; glass rises from about 8 to 23 dB per metre between 2.4 and 5.5 GHz and plasterboard from about 19 to 42, small numbers for thin panes and boards; brick barely changes, from about 23 to 26. These are bulk figures for the material alone: the recommendation's plane-wave methods ignore spreading loss, and real walls add reflections, layers, reinforcement and metal. The practical reading is that the penalty for a higher band depends on what the building is made of, and is largest in exactly the concrete-and-glass offices where people expect Wi-Fi to work everywhere.

Put together, the trade is simple to state. Near the access point, with a good signal, the higher band delivers more throughput because it has wider, cleaner channels; at the edge of the cell, or through heavy walls, the lower band may give the better signal-to-noise ratio (SNR) and therefore the better connection, because a weak fast link negotiates down and retries while a strong slow one holds. Vendors build that judgement into the equipment rather than preferring one band blindly. Fortinet's frequency handoff, for example, steers a dual-band client to 5 GHz only when its 5 GHz signal is strong, by declining to answer its join request on 2.4 GHz; if the client's 5 GHz signal is weak, its second attempt on 2.4 GHz is accepted.

The 5 GHz band has a reliability caveat of its own. Fortinet's guide notes that sixteen of the 25 channels are shared with military, weather radar and satellite systems, and that an access point which detects radar must move to another channel, as regulation requires. Those channels are worth using, and the same guide says administrators should not be afraid of them, but a 5 GHz cell on a radar-shared channel can change channel abruptly, which a 2.4 GHz cell will not do for that reason.

The 6 GHz band repeats the pattern one step higher, and adds a regulatory one. The US Federal Communications Commission (FCC) opened 1,200 MHz at 5.925 to 7.125 GHz for unlicensed use on 23 April 2020, indoor low-power across the whole band and standard power in 850 MHz under automated frequency coordination (AFC), increasing the spectrum available to Wi-Fi by nearly a factor of five. Other regulators have since divided the band. Ofcom's statement of 20 July 2026 keeps Wi-Fi in 5925 to 6425 MHz, gives it priority in 6425 to 6585 MHz and makes 6585 to 7125 MHz a mobile-priority portion where Wi-Fi may operate only under AFC control. Brazil's Anatel, which in February 2021 had kept all 1,200 MHz for unlicensed use, decided in August 2026 (Acórdão 203 and Ato 10.400, as reported by Teletime and TeleSemana) to restrict Wi-Fi equipment to 5,925 to 6,425 MHz from 1 March 2027, reserving the upper part for mobile networks after co-channel tests showed severe degradation on both sides, while leaving a later review open. The extra capacity of 6 GHz is real; how much of it a given country allows is now a local question.

The part of the belief that is right: in most offices and homes, clients near an access point are better served at 5 or 6 GHz, 2.4 GHz is crowded with its three channels and its neighbours, and a design that pushes capable clients up is sound. What a practitioner should say instead is that the bands are different tools with different failure modes. When a wireless complaint comes in, establish first which band, channel, signal level and SNR the client actually has, since a client holding on to a band that is wrong for where it stands is a common cause; survey each band separately and expect 5 and 6 GHz cells to be smaller; keep 2.4 GHz at 20 MHz on channels 1, 6 and 11 for the devices and distances that need it rather than switching it off; use radar-shared 5 GHz channels but watch for radar-triggered channel changes; and check the local regulator before planning 6 GHz, especially in Brazil from 2027.

mac-permanence-myth.def: The belief that a device's MAC (Media Access Control) address is a fixed, unique hardware identity. The burned-in address still exists, but operating systems now present randomized, locally administered addresses to Wi-Fi networks by default, and any interface's address can be changed in software with one command.
mac-permanence-myth.context: iOS, iPadOS and macOS, Android and Windows all offer MAC (Media Access Control) address randomization against tracking, on by default for new Wi-Fi networks on Android 10 and later and iOS 14 and later; the IEEE (Institute of Electrical and Electronics Engineers) formalized local address usage in 802c-2017, and 802.11bh-2024 now defines how networks operate with changing addresses. Tracking by MAC address and security built on MAC addresses both lost their footing, quietly.
mac-permanence-myth.depth:
The belief, stated exactly: every network interface carries a MAC (Media Access Control) address burned in at the factory, unique in the world and fixed for the life of the device, so the address identifies the device and can be used to track it, to admit it or to bill it. The first half was the design. The IEEE (Institute of Electrical and Electronics Engineers) Registration Authority assigns blocks of universally administered addresses so that, as RFC (Request for Comments) 9797 of June 2025 puts it, a node can be attached to any LAN (local area network) in the world with assurance that its address is unique there. Two bits in the first octet carry the rules: the first marks an individual or a group address, and the second, the Universal/Local (U/L) bit, says whether the address was assigned universally (0, registered with the IEEE) or locally (1, not registered). Locally administered addresses only have to be unique within their broadcast domain.

Why the belief held for so long. For most of Ethernet's history nothing changed the address in practice, and tools, textbooks and asset databases treated it as a serial number: a hardware address in the DHCP (Dynamic Host Configuration Protocol) server, a sticky entry in switch port security, a line in an access-control list on a wireless controller. The permanence was never a property of the protocol, though. The address the network sees is whatever the driver puts in the frame, and on Linux one command changes it: the ip-link manual documents 'address LLADDRESS' as changing the station address of the interface. Redundancy protocols depend on it: VRRP (Virtual Router Redundancy Protocol) version 3, RFC 5798 of March 2010, has whichever router is master answer from a shared virtual address, 00-00-5E-00-01 followed by the virtual router ID for IPv4 (Internet Protocol version 4), so the same MAC moves between boxes by design.

What changed is privacy. RFC 9797 notes that in 802.11 the source and destination MAC addresses are sent unencrypted even on encrypted networks, so a stable universal address is readable by anyone nearby, and Microsoft's own support page says that the address a scanning device broadcasts can be used by shopping malls, stores and other public areas to track movement. That was a business: in April 2015 the US Federal Trade Commission (FTC) settled with Nomi Technologies, which had collected the MAC addresses of about nine million shoppers' devices in the first nine months of 2013, hashed but still trackable over time. Standards work followed. An IEEE 802 privacy tutorial in July 2014 led the 802 Executive Committee to create a privacy study group on 18 July 2014; experiments at IETF (Internet Engineering Task Force) meetings 91 and 92 and the IEEE 802 plenary in Berlin, between November 2014 and March 2015, found that random addresses almost never collided but that other identifiers such as the DHCP client identifier could still be correlated. IEEE 802c, approved on 15 June 2017 and published on 25 August 2017, added the Structured Local Address Plan (SLAP), which divides local space by the second hexadecimal digit and sets aside the Administratively Assigned Identifier quadrant (second digit 2) for addresses assigned arbitrarily, for example randomly; IEEE 802.11aq introduced a randomization mechanism in 2018, and IEEE 802E-2020 recommends temporary identifiers wherever a permanent one is not compelling.

The operating systems now randomize by default. Android sets the locally administered bit and clears the group bit, keeping the other 46 bits random; from Android 10 the randomized address is the default, persistent per network (derived from the SSID, or service set identifier, the security type or, for Passpoint, the FQDN, the fully qualified domain name) and kept until a factory reset, and from Android 12 some networks get non-persistent addresses re-randomized at a new connection once a DHCP lease has expired and the device has been away more than 4 hours, or the address is more than 24 hours old. Apple devices use a different address for each network from iOS 14; from iOS 18, iPadOS 18, macOS Sequoia 15, watchOS 11 and visionOS 2 each network is set to Off, Fixed or Rotating, with Fixed the default on WPA2 (Wi-Fi Protected Access 2) or stronger networks and Rotating, a new address every two weeks, the default on open or weak ones. Windows offers random hardware addresses for all networks or for chosen ones where the hardware supports it. A randomized address therefore has no vendor at all: the bits where an OUI (organizationally unique identifier) would sit are random.

Randomization has its own limits, which is the part of the belief that survives. Jeremy Martin and colleagues at the US Naval Academy showed at PoPETs (Proceedings on Privacy Enhancing Technologies) 2017 that devices often sent frames with their true global address when they should have used a random one, that passive fingerprinting defeated randomization on about 96 per cent of Android phones, and that a flaw in how chipsets handled low-level control frames, present in every device they tested, allowed active tracking. RFC 9797 makes the same point from the network side: devices may keep using other stable identifiers that defeat the purpose. And the uniqueness half of the belief still largely holds where it matters, inside one broadcast domain: universal assignments are unique by registration, and the 2014-2015 experiments found duplicate random addresses negligible.

The consequences land on ordinary network administration. RFC 9797 lists them: an 802.1X authenticator that maps a device to its MAC address closes the port when the address changes until the AAA (authentication, authorization and accounting) server confirms the new one; DHCPv4 servers lose track of which leases are valid and can exhaust a scope, since a released address is held for a while in case the old MAC returns; routers and neighbours see cache churn and extra ARP (Address Resolution Protocol) and Neighbor Discovery traffic; and home parental controls or blocklists keyed to a MAC address simply stop applying. IEEE 802.11bh-2024, published on 3 June 2025, constrains the timing: an address may not change during an association, only through disconnection and reconnection, at the cost of fresh authentication. MAC-based access control was always weak, because the address travels in clear and is set in software, so a permitted one can be observed and copied; it is now also unreliable, because a legitimate device may present a different address on each network or every two weeks.

What to say instead: a MAC address is a link-layer label the device chooses, usually stable per network, sometimes rotating, and never a proof of identity. For identity, use something the device proves rather than announces: 802.1X with certificate-based EAP-TLS (Extensible Authentication Protocol with Transport Layer Security) on managed networks, or a captive portal or account login on guest ones. Where a stable address is genuinely needed for a managed fleet, Apple documents an MDM (mobile device management) profile that turns private addresses off for enrolled devices on the organization's network, and Android exposes a per-network setting; on secured networks the defaults (Fixed on Apple, persistent on Android) already keep one address per network. Shorten DHCP leases on guest networks to avoid scope exhaustion, treat any OUI lookup on a locally administered address as meaningless, and retire MAC filtering as a security control, keeping it at most as an inventory hint.

bandwidth-latency-myth.def: The belief that a plan with more megabits per second makes everything online faster. Bandwidth is how much data a path carries per second; latency is how long each exchange takes. Beyond a modest rate, web pages, calls and games are limited by round trips and queueing delay, which a bigger plan does not reduce.
bandwidth-latency-myth.context: Jim Gettys, with Kathleen Nichols, showed in 2011 that oversized and permanently full buffers in modems, home routers and operating systems added from hundreds of milliseconds to several seconds of delay on lines sold as fast, a problem named bufferbloat. Active queue management (AQM), such as FQ-CoDel (Flow Queue Controlled Delay) and CAKE (Common Applications Kept Enhanced), fixes what a faster plan cannot, and the figure that predicts how a connection feels is its latency under load, not its peak throughput on an idle line.
bandwidth-latency-myth.depth:
The belief is sold with the product. Access plans are priced by their headline rate, speed tests lead with megabits per second, and a large download does finish sooner on a faster line, so faster comes to mean more bandwidth. Stuart Cheshire complained in 1996 that modem boxes proudly printed 14.4, 28.8 and 33.6 kbps and never mentioned latency, although every transfer depends on hundreds of small control messages whose speed is governed by delay, not by rate. The bufferbloat project puts the same point in one sentence: the perceived speed of the internet is much more a function of latency, the time to get a response, than of bandwidth, the ability to ship bulk.

The two quantities are independent. Bandwidth is the rate at which a path can carry bits; latency is the time a given bit, or a given request and its answer, takes to make the trip. The bufferbloat project's road analogy keeps them apart: bandwidth is how much the cars carry from one end to the other per second, latency is how long any one car takes. Cheshire credits David Cheriton at Stanford with the asymmetry that matters: bandwidth can always be bought by putting links in parallel, as ISDN (Integrated Services Digital Network) bonding joined two 64 kbit/s channels into 128 kbit/s, but no amount of money turns a link with bad latency into one with good latency. The classic extreme case is a truck full of disks, enormous bandwidth and terrible latency. Amazon Web Services (AWS) launched Snowmobile on 30 November 2016, a 45-foot container holding up to 100 PB, because moving that much data across the internet could take years; if such a truck spends a week on the road, it delivers 8 times 10 to the 17th power bits in 604,800 seconds, an average of about 1.3 Tbit/s, with a latency of a week, after about 10 days of loading at 1 Tbit/s.

Latency has a floor that no purchase moves. Light in optical fibre travels at roughly two thirds of its speed in vacuum, about 200,000 km per second, and recommendation G.114 of the ITU-T (Telecommunication Standardization Sector of the International Telecommunication Union) uses 5 microseconds per kilometre for digital optical fibre systems, so every 1,000 km of fibre costs 5 ms each way and 10 ms per round trip before any equipment is counted. Cheshire's example in 1996 was Stanford to Boston, 4,320 km: a theoretical minimum round trip of 43.2 ms against a measured ping of about 85 ms, already within a factor of two of physics. G.114 gives 12 ms of propagation for a satellite at 400 km altitude and 260 ms at 36,000 km, the geostationary orbit, and sets its own thresholds for planning: one-way delay should not exceed 400 ms, and below 150 ms most applications, speech or data, see essentially transparent interactivity. A server on another continent stays on another continent whatever the access plan.

Most of what people do online is made of small exchanges, and small exchanges are paid in round trips. Cheshire's arithmetic is the cleanest illustration: ten characters, 80 bits, take 2.4 ms to transmit over a 33 kbit/s modem, but arrive after 102.4 ms because the modems add 100 ms. TCP (Transmission Control Protocol) makes the dependence structural. RFC (Request for Comments) 7323 explains that the receive window field is 16 bits, so without the Window Scale option no more than 64 KiB can be outstanding, and when the bandwidth-delay product of a path exceeds 64 KiB the window, not the link, limits throughput: 65,536 bytes per 100 ms round trip is about 5.24 Mbit/s, and the same window over a 10 ms round trip gives ten times as much. A new connection also starts cautiously. RFC 6928 raised the initial window in 2013 to 10 segments, at most 14,600 bytes in the first round trip, and the experiments behind it showed gains above 20 per cent on high round-trip paths and only about 5 per cent on short ones. A page built from dozens of objects, each costing several round trips, is therefore bound by delay long before a 100 or 500 Mbit/s plan runs out of capacity.

The delay that surprises people is not distance but queueing. Bufferbloat is the undesirable latency that comes from a router or other equipment buffering too much data. Equipment makers, taught to hate packet loss, put large buffers everywhere; under load a bulk transfer fills them, and every other packet, a voice frame or a DNS (Domain Name System) query, waits behind the backlog. Gettys and Nichols reported in 2011, in Queue, the magazine of the Association for Computing Machinery, more than 1.2 seconds of latency on a path whose uncongested round trip was under 10 ms, eight seconds at Gettys's own home router, and a 2007 study in which DSL (digital subscriber line) upstream queues often exceeded 600 ms and cable queues generally exceeded one second. Full buffers also hide the losses TCP uses as its congestion signal, and they note that its reaction time grows with the square of the overbuffering. The project's warning goes to the root of the myth: bufferbloat masquerades as underprovisioning, buying fatter pipes does not fix it, and buying larger buffers makes it worse.

The fixes are queue management, not capacity. The IETF (Internet Engineering Task Force) published RFC 7567 in July 2015 as Best Current Practice 197, a strong recommendation for testing, standardizing and widely deploying AQM (active queue management), replacing the earlier advice of RFC 2309. CoDel (Controlled Delay), by Kathleen Nichols and Van Jacobson, watches how long packets sit in the queue and drops or marks them when that time stays above a target; RFC 8289 describes it as needing no configuration in normal deployments. FQ-CoDel (Flow Queue CoDel), RFC 8290 of January 2018, whose authors include Gettys and Dave Taht, hashes traffic into 1,024 queues by default, runs CoDel on each with a 5 ms target and a 100 ms interval, and so isolates low-rate traffic such as DNS, web and videoconferencing from bulk flows; it is in the mainline Linux kernel as fq_codel and on by default in several distributions. CAKE (Common Applications Kept Enhanced), a queue discipline, adds a shaper, and its manual says most people need only to set the bandwidth parameter. The shaper matters because a queue can only be managed where it forms: shaping a home router or firewall slightly below the access rate moves the queue out of the modem and into a device that manages it well. The L4S (Low Latency, Low Loss, and Scalable Throughput) architecture of RFC 9330, January 2023, goes after the cause from the sending side, arguing that queuing delay originates in capacity-seeking congestion controllers and pairing new ones with ECN (Explicit Congestion Notification) marking. Prioritization alone is not a substitute: the bufferbloat project calls QoS (quality of service) a blind alley until buffers are reduced and managed, after which it can be layered on top.

Measuring the right thing ends the argument. A speed test on an idle line reports the two numbers a plan sells, peak throughput and idle ping, and neither predicts what happens to a call while someone else uploads photos. The IETF's working group on IP (Internet Protocol) performance measurement is standardizing the Responsiveness Test, draft-ietf-ippm-responsiveness-09 of July 2026, which saturates the connection and measures round trips during that load, reporting round-trips per minute (RPM), 60,000 divided by the round-trip time in milliseconds, so that a 50 ms working latency reads as 1,200 RPM; Apple's networkQuality tool implements it. The draft's authors write that the common belief that a video call must suffer while someone streams a 4K film has no technical basis, because queue management solved it; what is missing is awareness and deployment.

None of this makes bandwidth irrelevant. It decides how long a large file, a backup or an operating system image takes; it decides how many simultaneous streams a household or a branch office can run; and on long fat networks, as RFC 7323 calls high bandwidth-delay paths, the window has to grow with the product of the two. The practical order for a slow-feeling connection is: measure latency under load rather than idle throughput, enable AQM at the real bottleneck (the customer premises router, the firewall's egress, the access concentrator), shape just below the line rate if the bottleneck device cannot manage its queue, bring servers closer with a content delivery network or a nearer region, and only then decide whether a faster plan is worth paying for.

password-rotation-myth.def: The belief that forcing password changes on a schedule, every 30, 60 or 90 days, makes accounts safer. People answer expiry with predictable variants of the old password, and NIST (National Institute of Standards and Technology), the UK's National Cyber Security Centre and Microsoft reversed the advice: long unique passwords, screened against breach lists, changed on evidence of compromise.
password-rotation-myth.context: The National Institute of Standards and Technology's (NIST) SP (Special Publication) 800-63B advised against periodic changes in 2017 and has forbidden requiring them since its fourth revision in 2025, while still demanding a forced change on evidence of compromise; it also drops composition rules in favour of length, blocklists and password managers. The UK National Cyber Security Centre (NCSC) dropped expiry in 2015 and Microsoft removed it from its Windows security baseline in 2019. Where the rule survives, it is usually because a compliance regime or an audit checklist still asks for it.
password-rotation-myth.depth:
The belief, stated exactly: making every user replace their password after a fixed interval, commonly 90 days, limits the damage from stolen passwords, so shorter intervals mean better security. The reasoning is not foolish, and Microsoft's own 2019 explanation states it fairly: periodic expiration is a defence only against the chance that a password, or its hash, is stolen during its validity interval and then used by someone else. The rule became the default almost everywhere. Windows ships with a maximum password age of 42 days, and Microsoft's security baseline recommended 60 days, and 90 before that, until it dropped the setting.

The organizations that issued the advice reversed it. The UK National Cyber Security Centre (NCSC) explicitly advised against regular expiry in its Password Guidance of 2015, and a 2016 NCSC blog post by Emma W explained why: forced changes produce new passwords similar to the old ones, reused from other services, written down or forgotten, with the lockouts and service-desk resets that follow; in the post's words, the more often users are forced to change passwords, the greater the overall vulnerability to attack. NIST (National Institute of Standards and Technology) SP (Special Publication) 800-63B of June 2017 said verifiers 'should not' require memorized secrets to be changed arbitrarily, for example periodically, but 'shall' force a change if there is evidence of compromise. Its fourth revision, SP 800-63B-4, published in July 2025 and replacing the 2017 text from 1 August 2025, hardened that to 'shall not': verifiers may not require subscribers to change passwords periodically, keeping the obligation to force a change on evidence of compromise. In its April 2019 draft baseline for Windows 10 version 1903, Microsoft removed the password-expiration policies and called periodic password expiration an ancient and obsolete mitigation of very low value.

The evidence is behavioural, not cryptographic. Yinqian Zhang, Fabian Monrose and Michael Reiter, at the 2010 ACM (Association for Computing Machinery) Conference on Computer and Communications Security (CCS), presented what they called the first large-scale study of whether expiration achieves its purpose, cutting off an attacker who already holds the password; their abstract describes a dataset of over 7,700 accounts and an algorithm that searches for a user's new password starting from the old one. The US Federal Trade Commission's (FTC) Chief Technologist, Lorrie Cranor, summarized the result in March 2016: with the previous password and the hashed password file, an attacker could guess the current password for 41 per cent of accounts within 3 seconds per account on a typical 2009 research computer, and for 17 per cent of accounts in fewer than five tries. She also cited a Carleton University study concluding that frequent changes hamper such an attacker only a little. NIST's own appendix on password strength explains the mechanism with its standard example: a user who would have chosen 'password' picks 'Password1' when a digit and capital are required, and 'Password1!' when a symbol is added. Expiry produces the same pattern over time: Password1, then Password2.

The arithmetic of the defence is weak even before behaviour is counted. Microsoft's baseline post asks how many days a thief should be allowed to keep using a stolen password, and notes that 42 or 90 days is a ridiculously long time for that; if there is evidence of theft the password should be changed at once, and if there is no theft the rotation buys nothing. An attacker who has the old password often derives the new one, as the 2010 study measured. And the commonest modern attack on passwords does not wait for an interval at all: credentials leaked from one site are replayed against others, which SP 800-63B-4 calls password stuffing and answers with distinct passwords per service, not with rotation. Human-assisted resets add their own weakness, since the same NIST document warns that recovery handled by people carries a risk of social engineering, and frequent expiry multiplies those resets.

What the current standard asks for instead is specific. SP 800-63B-4 requires passwords used as a single factor to be at least 15 characters, allows shorter ones only within multi-factor authentication (MFA) and then no fewer than eight, says verifiers should permit at least 64 characters and accept Unicode, counting each code point as one character, and forbids any other composition rule such as mandatory mixtures of character types. New passwords must be checked, whole, against a blocklist of commonly used, expected or compromised values; hints and knowledge-based security questions are forbidden; the entire password must be verified, never truncated; password managers and autofill must be allowed and pasting should be; and online guessing is contained by rate limiting, with no more than 100 consecutive failed attempts before the authenticator is disabled. Microsoft's 2019 list of better controls is the same in operational terms: banned-password lists, MFA, and detection of password-guessing and anomalous logon attempts; the NCSC adds showing users their last login attempt so that they can report one they did not make.

Why the rule persists anyway is mostly paperwork. Microsoft described the audit problem directly: compliance scans count settings out of line with the baseline, so an organization with strong protections that chose 365 days, or no expiry, would be marked down for it. Some regimes still write the interval into their text. The PCI (Payment Card Industry) DSS (Data Security Standard) version 4 requirement 8.3.9, as the PCI Security Standards Council's frequently asked question (FAQ) number 1590 of March 2025 explains, applies only where a password or passphrase is the sole authentication factor; in that case the password must be changed at least every 90 days or the account's security posture must be analysed dynamically, and with MFA in place the requirement does not apply. An expiry period is easy to configure, easy to audit and easy to show a regulator, which is how a control can outlive the evidence that produced it.

The part of the belief that is right is that a compromised password must be replaced, quickly, and that is exactly what both NIST revisions keep as a 'shall'. Where nothing detects compromise, where passwords are the only factor, or where a regime such as PCI DSS demands it, a bounded lifetime is a crude stand-in for detection, and it remains legal and available: Microsoft pointed out that the expiration option is still in Windows, only no longer recommended. What should be said instead is that rotation is a response to evidence, not a calendar ritual. Change a password when it appears in a breach corpus, when the blocklist check fails, after a suspicious login, or when someone leaves who knew a shared secret; otherwise make it long, unique and stored in a password manager, put MFA in front of it, and watch for guessing. Better still, remove the password: in April 2026 the NCSC said passkeys should be consumers' first choice of login, at least as secure as the strongest password combined with two-step verification, and stopped recommending passwords where passkeys are available.

file-deletion-myth.def: The belief that pressing delete, emptying the recycle bin or formatting a disk removes the data. Normally only the file's directory entry and allocation are released; the contents stay on the medium until something overwrites them, which is why undelete tools and forensic recovery work.
file-deletion-myth.context: The National Institute of Standards and Technology (NIST) guide to media sanitization, Special Publication (SP) 800-88, replaces the idea of "deleting" with three graded methods: clear, which defeats simple recovery through the normal interface; purge, which defeats laboratory recovery and leaves the device usable; and destroy. Solid-state drives (SSDs) broke the old shortcut of overwriting the data: wear levelling and spare flash keep stale copies where the host cannot write, so the drive's own sanitize command, and above all cryptographic erase (destroying the key of data that was encrypted from the start), became the practical purge.
file-deletion-myth.depth:
The belief is reasonable from the user's side of the screen. The file disappears from the folder, the recycle bin is emptied, and the format command of early Microsoft systems warned that all data on the drive would be lost, which Simson Garfinkel and Abhi Shelat found users reading as a promise. Underneath, deletion is bookkeeping. Their 2003 paper describes the File Allocation Table (FAT) case exactly: the operating system changes the first character of the file's directory entry to mark it deleted and moves its clusters to the free list, and the file's data is never touched. They note that many other file systems behave the same way, which is why undelete programs exist and why a deleted file is better described as unreferenced storage waiting to be reused.

The evidence of what that means in practice came from the second-hand market. Between November 2000 and August 2002 Garfinkel and Shelat, then at the Massachusetts Institute of Technology, bought 158 used hard drives, mostly through eBay auctions, and imaged the 129 that worked. Only 12 (9 per cent) had been properly sanitized by overwriting every sector with zeros; 83 still held mountable file systems; 51 of those appeared freshly formatted, and 19 of the 51 still held recoverable data from earlier use; 30 of the 46 drives that would not mount had more than a thousand sectors of recoverable data. One drive held 3,722 credit card numbers. The paper opens with institutional cases of the same failure, among them a Veterans Administration medical centre in Indianapolis that retired 139 computers in August 2002 whose drives were found to hold patient information and 44 credit card numbers.

On magnetic disks the classic answer was to overwrite, and that is where the multi-pass folklore comes from. Peter Gutmann's 1996 paper on secure deletion proposed a 35-pass sequence, but it was designed to cover a blend of recording encodings reaching back to MFM (modified frequency modulation) drives. His later epilogue is blunt: people came to treat the 35 passes as a kind of voodoo incantation, no drive ever needs all of them, and for modern PRML (partial-response maximum-likelihood) drives a few passes of random scrubbing is the best that can be done. The National Institute of Standards and Technology (NIST), in the 2014 revision of its Special Publication (SP) 800-88, put the modern position plainly: for magnetic media, a single overwrite pass with a fixed pattern such as binary zeros typically hinders recovery even with state of the art laboratory techniques. The 2025 revision records where the rituals came from, multiple passes based on DoD (Department of Defense) 5220.22-M ranging from one pass to as many as 39, and notes that the DoD removed overwriting specifications from the National Industrial Security Program Operating Manual (NISPOM) in 2006. The remaining weakness of overwriting on a hard disk drive (HDD) is not the number of passes but reach: the normal read and write interface does not touch sectors the drive has retired as defective.

Flash storage changed the problem rather than solving it. An SSD (solid-state drive) keeps a flash translation layer between the logical block addresses the computer writes and the physical pages that hold the data, writes updates out of place, and moves data around for wear levelling and garbage collection. Michael Wei and colleagues at the University of California, San Diego, presented the measurements in February 2011: the drives they tested held 6 to 25 per cent more physical flash than their advertised capacity, and after writing 1,000 small files they found up to 16 stale copies of some of them. Ordinary file deletion left 4.3 to 91.3 per cent of the data recoverable on SSDs and 99.4 per cent on a flash memory key, and even a 35-pass overwrite of a single file left 0.8 to 4.3 per cent behind; none of the single-file techniques worked. Overwriting the whole visible address space twice was usually, but not always, enough. NIST's 2025 text gives the same arithmetic in its own example, a device with 1,024 GB of physical flash and 900 GB available to the user, and concludes that spare cells and wear levelling make it infeasible for a user to sanitize all previous data by overwriting.

Trimming complicates the story in both directions. Drives that speak ATA (Advanced Technology Attachment) accept a command called TRIM, by which the host tells the drive that a range of blocks is no longer in use; Microsoft's documentation also calls the notification unmap. With it, the operating system reports freed blocks so the drive can erase them during its own housekeeping. Windows calls these delete notifications and reports their state with the command "fsutil behavior query DisableDeleteNotify"; Linux sends them with fstrim, whose manual suggests once a week for most desktops and servers, or continuously with the discard mount option. Graeme Bell and Richard Boddington showed in 2010 that SSDs can destroy traditionally recoverable data on their own, without any instruction from the computer, which is bad news for forensic examiners. Yet Wei and colleagues found that TRIM has no reliable effect on data security. The honest summary is that deletion on an SSD may happen to be final, may not, and the owner cannot tell which.

The standards replace the word delete with three graded methods. NIST SP 800-88 Revision 2, by Ramaswamy Chandramouli and Eric Hibbard, published in September 2025 (Revision 1 was withdrawn on 26 September 2025), defines clear as logical techniques applied to every user-addressable location through the normal interface, typically one overwrite pass or a factory reset, protecting against simple non-invasive recovery. Purge must make recovery infeasible with state of the art laboratory techniques while leaving the device reusable, using dedicated sanitize commands for overwrite, block erase or cryptographic erase, with the IEEE (Institute of Electrical and Electronics Engineers) 2883 standard named for media-specific techniques. Destroy means disintegrate, incinerate, melt, pulverize or shred; drilling or bending only partly damages a device, pulverizing and shredding should be avoided for anything but the lowest categories of data, and degaussing is not an approved destroy technique and should not be used on flash at all. NIST's frequently asked questions on the revision, published on 16 July 2026, add that multi-pass overwriting is unnecessary and can shorten the life of flash media.

Built-in commands are not automatically trustworthy. Of the 12 SSDs Wei's team tested, eight reported support for the ATA Security feature set, but of the seven whose results could be verified only four executed the Security Erase Unit command reliably, and one, drive B, reported success while every byte remained and its file system still mounted. NIST makes the same point without names: dedicated commands reach more of the medium, but they require trust that the vendor implemented them as described. That is why Revision 2 separates verification, checking that a technique completed without error, from validation, an organization's decision that the result is good enough for the sensitivity of the data, and why a sanitization programme records each job in a certificate.

Cryptographic erase is the answer that survives every medium, provided it was planned from the start. If everything written to the device was encrypted, sanitizing the key renders the ciphertext unreadable wherever copies sit; the self-encrypting drive Wei's team tested performed it in under a second. NIST's conditions are strict: Federal Information Processing Standards (FIPS) 140 validated cryptographic modules for United States federal agencies, no sensitive data stored in plaintext before the keys were set, a security strength of at least 128 bits, random number entropy at least equal to the key length, and zeroization of every key involved, including wrapping keys. In cloud storage, where the customer never touches the physical media, NIST calls cryptographic erase often the only viable purge, which makes key management the real sanitization control. Wei's team added the caveat that matters: the method depends on the controller really erasing its key store, which the owner usually cannot inspect.

What to do instead follows from the evidence. Turn on full-disk encryption before the first sensitive byte is written, so that disposal can be a key operation rather than a hope. Retire a device with the purge its type supports, followed by verification and a recorded certificate, and destroy media that have failed or whose interface is obsolete, by the methods the standard still accepts. On a hard disk still in service, Windows cipher with the w option overwrites the free space of a whole volume; on an SSD the same tool cannot reach spare or retired blocks. Remember that the file is rarely the only copy: backups, shadow copies, replicas, synchronized folders and cloud versioning all keep data after the original is deleted, and a deletion request under privacy law has to reach them too.

someone-elses-computer.def: A slogan made famous by a sticker, "there is no cloud, it's just someone else's computer": accurate about where the data physically sits and who controls the machine, misleading as a description of what a cloud service sells, which is elastic, metered, self-service capacity and a provider's operations behind an interface.
someone-elses-computer.context: The line was in circulation by December 2013, when the security commentator Graham Cluley proposed replacing every "cloud" with "somebody else's computer", and became a meme through Chris Watterston's sticker, conceived in late 2014 and photographed around the world from 2015. It works as a prompt about trust, location, jurisdiction and dependence; it fails as a definition, because NIST (the National Institute of Standards and Technology) defines cloud computing by properties no single borrowed computer has, and because the providers' shared responsibility models say exactly which parts of the machine remain the customer's problem.
someone-elses-computer.depth:
