The phrase has a traceable history. On 2 December 2013 the trade publication Computing published Danny Palmer's interview with Graham Cluley under the headline that the word cloud should be replaced with somebody else's computer, quoting him: "I'd like to suggest a new phrase so that every time we say cloud we say 'somebody else's computer'." On his own blog the next day Cluley explained the intent: the trendy word had encouraged organizations to ship data off to providers without thinking about how sensitive data could be exposed, especially unencrypted, and he was not saying cloud services should be avoided at all costs. In September 2016 he looked back on the remark as having become a minor meme.

What made it a meme was a sticker. Chris Watterston dates his frustration to late 2014, after years of setting up phones and tablets whose owners nodded blankly through the iCloud or OneDrive step, and with businesses that used the word without explaining it. He designed an 8.13 by 6.45 cm die-cut sticker reading "There is no cloud, it's just someone else's computer" and had it printed by StickerMule; his post of 13 February 2016 collects photographs posted from April 2015 onward, from Toronto, San Francisco, Melbourne, Rome and Berlin. The Free Software Foundation Europe (FSFE) runs its own variant in a campaign of stickers and postcards, "There is no cloud, just other people's computers". By 2017 the Computer History Museum could introduce an essay with the line as a familiar quip.

The word it mocks is older and vaguer. The Massachusetts Institute of Technology's magazine Technology Review traced the earliest known use of "cloud computing" in print to a late-1996 business plan at Compaq, written by a group that included George Favaloro and Sean O'Sullivan, while noting that many date the modern use to 9 August 2006, when Google's chief executive Eric Schmidt said "We call it cloud computing, they should be in a cloud somewhere." The same 2011 article records that the United States government, unsure what counted as cloud computing for procurement, asked NIST (the National Institute of Standards and Technology) for a definition, which opens by admitting that the term means different things to different people.

The half that is true is the physical and legal half. NIST's own definition describes resource pooling: the provider's resources serve many customers in a multi-tenant model, with a sense of location independence in which the customer generally has no control or knowledge of the exact location, though it may choose one at a higher level such as a country, a state or a datacentre. So the data does sit on a particular machine in a particular building under a particular jurisdiction, which is what data residency arguments are about. The provider's people can, in some circumstances, reach it: Microsoft documents that most of its operations and support need no access to customer data, and offers Customer Lockbox so that a customer can approve or reject the rare request when an engineer does need it, for a support ticket or a problem Microsoft found itself. And the provider's failure is a failure the customer can only wait out. On 28 February 2017 an authorized member of the Amazon S3 (Simple Storage Service) team, following an established playbook, entered one input to a command incorrectly at 9:37 a.m. Pacific Standard Time and removed far more servers than intended; the index subsystem, which every read, listing, write and deletion in the Northern Virginia region needs, and the placement subsystem both required a full restart, storage was not fully back until 1:54 p.m., and until 11:37 a.m. Amazon could not even update its Service Health Dashboard, because the dashboard depended on S3. Prices, service retirements and terms are likewise set on someone else's schedule.

The half that is wrong is the definition. NIST Special Publication (SP) 800-145, by Peter Mell and Timothy Grance, September 2011, defines cloud computing as a model for enabling ubiquitous, convenient, on-demand network access to a shared pool of configurable computing resources that can be rapidly provisioned and released with minimal management effort or service provider interaction, and requires five essential characteristics: on-demand self-service, broad network access, resource pooling, rapid elasticity and measured service. A server rented in someone else's rack has none of the last three by default. To the consumer, NIST adds, the capabilities often appear unlimited and can be appropriated in any quantity at any time, which is the property behind the thousand machines for an hour that no single computer offers. The definition also separates a physical layer from an abstraction layer, the software that delivers those characteristics. The sticker describes only the first. Watterston's own post, after the joke, quotes the NIST-derived definition, so the slogan and its correction travelled together from the start.

The precise version of whose computer it is lives in the providers' shared responsibility documents. Amazon Web Services (AWS) calls it security of the cloud against security in the cloud: AWS operates everything from the host operating system and virtualization layer down to the physical security of its facilities, while on EC2 (Elastic Compute Cloud), an infrastructure service, the customer patches the guest operating system, runs the applications and configures the security groups, and on abstracted services such as S3 and DynamoDB the customer still owns its data, its encryption choices, the classification of its assets and its IAM (identity and access management) permissions. Physical and environmental controls are inherited outright; patching, configuration management and staff training are shared, each side doing its own half. Microsoft states the floor in one sentence: for every cloud deployment type, from IaaS (infrastructure as a service) through PaaS (platform as a service) to SaaS (software as a service), the customer owns its data and identities. Google argues the model stops short of producing secure outcomes and calls its alternative shared fate, adding guidance, attested infrastructure code and insurance options. None of the three says the computer is entirely someone else's.

The honest reframing is that a cloud customer rents someone else's operations department, under contract, with a published division of labour. What is bought is elasticity, metering and a team that runs physical security, power, hardware replacement and the patching of hosts and hypervisors at any hour, at a scale few organizations can match; what is given up is location control, a share of visibility, and independence from that provider's mistakes. The Computer History Museum's essay makes the historical point: time-sharing firms such as Tymshare already ran users' data and programs on remote shared machines, handling about 450,000 interactive sessions a month by 1975, so the arrangement is not new, only the scale. The slogan stays useful in the sense Cluley meant it, as a question to ask before data leaves: where will it live, who can reach it, who holds the keys, and what happens when their computer is down.

quantum-breaks-everything-myth.def: The belief that a quantum computer will break all encryption. Shor's algorithm would break today's public-key cryptography (RSA, that is Rivest-Shamir-Adleman, Diffie-Hellman and elliptic curves) on a large fault-tolerant machine that does not yet exist; symmetric ciphers and hashes are only modestly affected, and standardized replacements for the vulnerable part were published in 2024.
quantum-breaks-everything-myth.context: The National Institute of Standards and Technology (NIST) published its first post-quantum standards in August 2024, FIPS (Federal Information Processing Standard) 203, 204 and 205, so that migration happens before a cryptanalytically relevant quantum computer does. The vulnerable part is public-key cryptography, used for key exchange and signatures; AES (Advanced Encryption Standard) and SHA-2 (Secure Hash Algorithm 2) stay in service. The risk already present is 'harvest now, decrypt later': traffic recorded today under quantum-vulnerable key exchange can be read once such a machine exists, which is why hybrid post-quantum key agreement is already the default in major browsers.
quantum-breaks-everything-myth.depth:
The belief, stated exactly: once a large quantum computer exists, every kind of encryption falls at once, so either everything is already lost or nothing can be done until the machine appears. Both conclusions are wrong, and the reason is that quantum computers attack specific mathematical problems, not encryption in general. In November 1994 Peter Shor, then at AT&T, presented at the Symposium on Foundations of Computer Science in Santa Fe efficient algorithms for factoring integers and computing discrete logarithms on a hypothetical quantum computer, running in a number of steps polynomial in the size of the input. Those two problems are the foundation of the public-key systems in use today: RSA (Rivest-Shamir-Adleman), finite-field Diffie-Hellman (DH) and the elliptic-curve schemes ECDH (elliptic-curve Diffie-Hellman), ECDSA (Elliptic Curve Digital Signature Algorithm) and EdDSA (Edwards-curve Digital Signature Algorithm). A machine able to run Shor's algorithm at scale would not weaken them; it would break them outright, recovering private keys from public ones.

Why the stronger belief is so common. In everyday language 'encryption' is one thing, and the public messaging has not always helped. The National Institute of Standards and Technology's (NIST) own announcement of the finished standards in August 2024 spoke of quantum computers that could break the current encryption that protects just about everything done online, and its March 2025 release said a sufficiently powerful quantum computer, if one is ever built, would be able to break that defence. Both sentences are about public-key cryptography, the part that negotiates keys and signs things, but read without that qualifier they become the myth. The other source is the bulk-encryption layer itself: people know that a TLS (Transport Layer Security) session is encrypted with AES (Advanced Encryption Standard) and assume that what breaks one breaks the other.

What is actually true about symmetric cryptography and hashes. The quantum attack on them is Lov Grover's search algorithm, presented in May 1996, which finds a target among N unsorted possibilities in about the square root of N steps. Taken at face value, that halves the effective key length: a 128-bit key would offer about 64 bits of protection against brute force and a 256-bit key about 128, which is where the common advice to double symmetric key sizes comes from. NIST's own reading is more relaxed. Its answers to frequently asked questions (FAQ) on post-quantum cryptography point out that quantum hardware will likely be more expensive than classical hardware and that a 1997 proof by Zalka shows that the full quadratic speedup requires all of Grover's steps to run in series, while real attacks run massively in parallel; it concludes that Grover's algorithm will quite likely provide little or no advantage against AES, that AES-128 will remain secure for decades, and that applications can keep using AES with 128, 192 or 256-bit keys. NIST IR (Interagency Report) 8547, finalized in October 2026, says the same thing in policy form: approved symmetric primitives with at least 128 bits of classical strength are believed to meet the lowest post-quantum security category, which is itself defined as key search on AES-128, while the few 112-bit symmetric standards are to be disallowed in 2030 regardless of quantum computing.

The machine does not exist yet, and nobody knows exactly when it will. NIST IR 8547 states that there are no existing cryptanalytically relevant quantum computers that currently threaten security, and defines one as a quantum computer capable of actually attacking real-world cryptographic systems that would be infeasible to attack classically. The resource estimates have nonetheless moved quickly. In 2019 Craig Gidney and Ekerå estimated that factoring a 2048-bit RSA modulus would take eight hours on a machine of 20 million noisy qubits; in May 2025 Gidney brought that to less than a week with fewer than one million noisy qubits, assuming a 0.1 per cent gate error rate, a surface-code cycle of 1 microsecond and a control-system reaction time of 10 microseconds. Cloudflare, reviewing the field in October 2025, noted the other side of the ledger: the largest number honestly factored on a quantum computer was still 15. Algorithms move too, in both directions: in April 2024 a preprint by Yilei Chen claimed a new quantum algorithm for certain lattice problems, close to those behind the new standards, and experts found a fundamental bug in it within ten days.

Why the urgency does not depend on the date. NIST IR 8547 frames it with Mosca's theorem: if data must stay secret for X years and migration takes Y years, the move must start before X plus Y exceeds Z, the time until a cryptanalytically relevant quantum computer is built. The attack that makes this real today is 'harvest now, decrypt later' (HNDL): an adversary records traffic protected by quantum-vulnerable key exchange now and decrypts it later, so anything whose confidentiality must outlast the uncertainty is already exposed. The same report notes that signatures are not vulnerable to HNDL, since a signature only has to resist forgery until it is verified, but that their migration is still urgent because it is slower and involves more parties, and that earlier cryptographic transitions took 10 to 20 years from standard to full deployment.

What the standards settle. NIST began its selection in 2015 and assessed 82 algorithms from 25 countries; on 13 August 2024 it published FIPS (Federal Information Processing Standard) 203, ML-KEM (Module-Lattice-Based Key-Encapsulation Mechanism) in three parameter sets (ML-KEM-512, 768 and 1024), and FIPS 204 and 205, the ML-DSA (Module-Lattice-Based Digital Signature Algorithm) and SLH-DSA (Stateless Hash-Based Digital Signature Algorithm) signatures. A fourth signature, FN-DSA (FFT, fast Fourier transform, over NTRU-Lattice-Based Digital Signature Algorithm) from the FALCON submission, is to be published as FIPS 206, and on 11 March 2025 NIST chose HQC (Hamming Quasi-Cyclic), built on error-correcting codes rather than lattices, as a backup key-encapsulation mechanism, with a final standard expected in 2027. The backup exists because post-quantum algorithms can fail in ordinary ways: in July 2022 Wouter Castryck and Thomas Decru of KU Leuven published a classical key-recovery attack that broke SIKEp434, an isogeny-based fourth-round candidate, in about ten minutes on a single core. That is why deployments pair the new algorithms with a classical one in hybrid mode, which NIST accommodates in FIPS 140 validation: X25519MLKEM768, combining X25519 with ML-KEM-768, is what Cloudflare reported in October 2025 as enabled by default in recent major browsers, OpenSSL, Go and Apple's operating systems, and it carried the majority of human-initiated traffic to Cloudflare by the end of that month.

The deadlines are now explicit. The final NIST IR 8547 deprecates the quantum-vulnerable public-key algorithms (RSA, ECDSA and EdDSA signatures, DH and MQV (Menezes-Qu-Vanstone) key agreement, RSA-based key establishment) after 2030 and disallows them under NIST standards after 2035, keeping National Security Memorandum 10's 2035 target for completing the federal migration; under Executive Order 14412 and Office of Management and Budget (OMB) memorandum M-26-15, US high value assets and high impact systems must adopt post-quantum key establishment by 31 December 2030 and post-quantum signatures by 31 December 2031, and agencies must support TLS 1.3 by 2 January 2030. The UK National Cyber Security Centre (NCSC), in guidance of 20 March 2025, set three dates for organizations: complete discovery and assessment by 2028, finish the highest-priority migrations by 2031 and complete migration by 2035, adding that small organizations on commodity information technology should migrate largely through vendor updates.

The part of the belief that is right: the public-key cryptography the internet runs on today will not survive a cryptanalytically relevant quantum computer, the break will be total rather than a weakening, and recordings made before the switch will be readable afterwards. What to say instead is narrower and more useful: quantum computing threatens key exchange and signatures, not encryption as a whole; the replacements are standardized and already deployed in hybrid form; and the work is a migration with a long tail. In practice that means an inventory of where RSA and elliptic curves are used, priority for key establishment protecting data with a long confidentiality life, hybrid key agreement enabled wherever TLS 1.3 stacks support it, AES with keys of at least 128 bits and SHA-2 or SHA-3 hashes kept as they are, and an early start on certificates and signatures, which change most slowly.

tor-criminals-myth.def: The belief that Tor is used mainly or only by criminals. Measurement says otherwise: on an average day the large majority of Tor users reach the ordinary web, and the network was designed, and in large part funded, to protect people who need not to be tracked; the criminal share is real but concentrated in onion services, a small fraction of use.
tor-criminals-myth.context: Tor, a name that originally stood for The Onion Routing, carries a few million users a day through thousands of volunteer relays, and its reputation comes almost entirely from onion services, the corner that hosts darknet markets. Peer-reviewed measurement puts the users who visit onion services at about one in fifteen on an average day; the rest use Tor to read the ordinary web without being tracked or filtered. Onion routing began at the US Naval Research Laboratory (NRL) in 1995, and the reason it was released to everyone is the reason the myth misreads it: anonymity needs a varied crowd, so a network used by only one kind of person would protect nobody.
tor-criminals-myth.depth:
The belief, stated exactly: Tor, the anonymity network whose name originally stood for The Onion Routing, exists for, and is used mostly by, criminals, so that Tor traffic on a network is itself evidence of wrongdoing. It survives for understandable reasons. The best-known uses of Tor in the news are the darknet markets, from Silk Road to AlphaBay, and the onion services that host abuse material; Tor Browser is what ransomware notes tell their victims to install in order to pay, as the Tor Project's own answers to frequently asked questions (FAQ) on abuse acknowledge; and 'Tor' and 'dark web' are used as synonyms. The conflation is the error. Tor is first a way to reach the ordinary internet through a circuit of volunteer-operated relays, built one hop at a time, so that no individual relay ever knows the complete path between the user and the destination; onion services, sites that exist only inside the network, are one feature of it, not the whole.

Where it came from. In 1995 David Goldschlag, Michael Reed and Paul Syverson at the US Naval Research Laboratory (NRL) asked whether internet connections could be built that did not reveal who was talking to whom, even to someone watching the network. In the early 2000s Roger Dingledine, joined soon after by Nick Mathewson, worked on an NRL onion routing project with Syverson and named it Tor; the network went live in October 2002 under a free software licence, and by the end of 2003 it had about a dozen volunteer nodes. The design paper, 'Tor: The Second-Generation Onion Router', was presented at the 13th USENIX Security Symposium in August 2004. The Electronic Frontier Foundation (EFF) funded the work from 2004, the Tor Project, Inc. was founded as a 501(c)(3) nonprofit in 2006, bridges for censored users followed in 2007, and the Tor Project's own history credits the network with a role in the Arab Spring from late 2010 and in the 2013 Snowden disclosures.

The reason a navy lab released its tool to the public is the argument that undoes the myth. Dingledine and Mathewson set it out in 'Anonymity Loves Company', presented at the Workshop on the Economics of Information Security (WEIS) in Cambridge in June 2006: an anonymity network hides users among users, the protection grows with the anonymity set, and no organization can build such a network for its own sole use, because any connection entering or leaving a private agency network would be linkable to that agency. To protect anyone, the network has to accept everyone, and the paper lists who that meant: ordinary citizens avoiding advertising profiles, companies hiding research from competitors, and law enforcement and intelligence agencies working online without being noticed. The Tor Project's page on its users adds journalists and their sources through SecureDrop, which news organizations including the Associated Press, The Washington Post, The New York Times, the CBC (Canadian Broadcasting Corporation) and ProPublica use, activists, abuse survivors, and police officers whose own IP (Internet Protocol) ranges would otherwise give an investigation away.

What the measurements say. Tor Metrics, which estimates users from directory requests rather than counting them, gave a mean of about 3.19 million directly connecting users a day in September 2026, plus about 224,000 connecting through bridges, carried by about 9,430 relays and 2,340 bridges; the largest shares that month came from the United States (18.27 per cent), Germany (9.59 per cent), Finland, the United Kingdom and Brazil, which contributed about 145,000 daily users (4.56 per cent). These are model estimates: the same series jumped above 64 million on 29 October 2026 before falling back, an anomaly no one should read as a surge of people. The best peer-reviewed answer to what those users do is a study by Eric Jardine, Andrew Lindner and Gareth Owenson, published in the Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences (PNAS) on 30 November 2020. Running 1 per cent of Tor's guard relays from 31 December 2018 to 18 August 2019, they found that on an average country-day about 6.7 per cent of Tor clients connected to onion services, and upwards of 93 per cent went to sites on the ordinary web; the onion share was about 7.8 per cent in countries Freedom House rates as free and about 4.8 per cent in those it rates not free. Users behind bridges, typically the most censored, were not in the sample.

The part of the belief that is right deserves to be stated as plainly. Onion services, as a category, are heavily illicit. Daniel Moore and Thomas Rid of King's College London crawled 5,205 live onion sites for a study published in 2016 and classified 2,723 of them by content: 1,547, about 57 per cent, hosted illicit material, chiefly drugs, finance (money laundering and the trade in stolen cards), hacking, extremism and illegitimate pornography. A 2015 study by Gareth Owen and Nick Savage, cited in the PNAS paper, found that about 82 per cent of requests to onion services over six months went to child abuse imagery sites, in a period that coincided with the FBI (Federal Bureau of Investigation) investigation of the Playpen site; and the market economy grew from the 3,877 vendor accounts on Silk Road at its closure in October 2013 to about 40,000 on AlphaBay in 2017 while overall Tor use stayed roughly flat. Jardine and his co-authors built their estimate on exactly that pattern, assuming onion-service users are more likely to be engaged in illicit activity than clear-web users, while noting that Facebook and The New York Times run onion services and that plenty of illicit content sits on the ordinary web. The honest summary is that criminal use is real, concentrated in one feature, and a small minority of daily users.

Why the network cannot simply exclude the criminals. A Tor that could keep out bad actors would have to identify its users, and the Tor Project's abuse FAQ says that building that in would be adding a backdoor, opening its vulnerable users to hostile regimes; its design prevents anyone, its own developers included, from tracing a user. The same FAQ argues that criminals have other options, from botnets and stolen phones to hacked hosting accounts, and that traditional police techniques remain effective: interviewing suspects, writing-style analysis, analysis of the content itself, sting operations, keyboard taps and physical investigation. The Silk Road case is the standard illustration: according to the 2013 criminal complaint, as Bruce Schneier summarized it, Ross Ulbricht was traced through a 2011 Bitcoin Talk post that gave his Gmail address and a Stack Overflow question about reaching a Tor hidden service, not through any break of Tor. Anonymity that works for the journalist works for the criminal by the same mechanism, which is not a flaw in the implementation but the definition of the property.

The funding history makes the tension concrete rather than resolving it. For the fiscal year from July 2023 to June 2024 the Tor Project's audited statement shows revenue and support of 8,005,661 dollars; of revenue as reported on its tax filing, about 35.08 per cent came from US government funds, down from 53.5 per cent in 2021-2022, including 2,121,049 dollars from the State Department's Bureau of Democracy, Human Rights, and Labor for censorship circumvention in China, Hong Kong and Tibet, with corporations and nonprofits at 21.59 per cent, foundations at 18.67 per cent, individual donors at 15.61 per cent, and the Swedish agency Sida also among the funders. The government that prosecuted Silk Road's operator also pays to keep the network that carried it running, for the reason the NRL understood in 1995: a network used only by spies hides no spies, and one used only by criminals would hide no criminals either.

What a practitioner should do or say instead. Treat Tor as what the data shows: mostly private reading of the ordinary web, with a small, disproportionately criminal onion-service corner. A site that suffers abuse from Tor exits has, in the Tor Project's own words, easier options than a ban, such as requiring registration for posting while letting anonymous users read, and the project publishes an exit relay list, and a list that can be queried over DNS (Domain Name System), for operators who decide to block anyway; the cost of a ban is the hundreds of thousands of people the FAQ describes as using Tor for ordinary data hygiene. Inside an enterprise, Tor from a managed host is a policy question and worth investigating, because it bypasses inspection, not because it proves a crime. And in public argument, the useful sentence is the one the evidence supports: most Tor users are not criminals, most onion services are not benign, and an anonymity network only protects anyone if it protects everyone.

public-wifi-panic.def: The belief that joining public Wi-Fi means instant hacking. It was true when most web traffic was unencrypted; with HTTPS (Hypertext Transfer Protocol Secure) now on nearly all navigations, the hotspot sees metadata such as domain names, not content, and the real risks are narrower: fake networks and portals, stray unencrypted connections and unpatched devices.
public-wifi-panic.context: The warning dates from the web of plain HTTP (Hypertext Transfer Protocol), when a free browser extension called Firesheep (2010) let anyone on an open network take over other people's logged-in sessions with a double-click. The US Federal Trade Commission (FTC) told consumers in 2011 that most hotspots were not secure; by 2023 its advice was that, because of widespread encryption, connecting through public Wi-Fi is usually safe, and the Electronic Frontier Foundation (EFF) had already called the old advice mostly out of date in 2020. Caution about what stays visible and what can be spoofed, yes; panic, no.
public-wifi-panic.depth:
The belief, stated exactly: connecting to a café, hotel or airport network is dangerous in itself, because anyone else on it can read what you send and take over your accounts. For most of the 2000s that was simply accurate. Sites typically encrypted the login form and nothing after it, so the session cookie that kept a user signed in crossed the air in plain HTTP (Hypertext Transfer Protocol). On 24 October 2010 Eric Butler released Firesheep at the ToorCon 12 conference, a Firefox extension that captured those cookies on any busy open network and showed each victim's name and photo; as he put it, cookies were basically shouted through the air, and a double-click logged the attacker in as someone else. The US Federal Trade Commission (FTC) advised in February 2011 that most Wi-Fi hotspots did not encrypt information and were not secure, and that a hotspot was secure only if it asked for a WPA (Wi-Fi Protected Access) password. The advice was proportionate to the threat.

Then the web encrypted. The Electronic Frontier Foundation (EFF) traces the turn to that same year: Firesheep pushed site owners to deploy HTTPS (HTTP Secure) on every page, Google had made it the default for all Gmail users, and certificates later became free through Let's Encrypt, which the EFF helped launch. HTTP Strict Transport Security (HSTS), standardized as RFC (Request for Comments) 6797 in November 2012, lets a site tell browsers to use only secure connections to it from then on. Google's Chrome team reported in October 2025 that the share of Chrome navigations over HTTPS rose from around 30 to 45 per cent in 2015 to the 95 to 99 per cent range around 2020 before levelling off; counting public sites only, it was nearly 97 per cent on Linux, 98 per cent on Windows and over 99 per cent on Android and macOS. The same team announced that, from Chrome 154 in October 2026, the browser's 'Always Use Secure Connections' setting for public sites would be on by default, so that Chrome asks before the first visit to any public site without HTTPS. The official advice moved with the data: the FTC's consumer page, dated February 2023, now says that because of the widespread use of encryption, connecting through a public Wi-Fi network is usually safe, and the EFF wrote in January 2020 that the advice to avoid public Wi-Fi was mostly out of date, closing with 'You can cross public Wi-Fi off your list'.

What the network still sees is metadata, and it is worth stating precisely. HTTPS protects content but not metadata: anyone on the path, the café's network included, can see the domain names a device contacts, when, and the sizes of the pages and files transferred, but not the pages within a site, the login name or the messages sent. That is the same view the home internet service provider (ISP) has every day. Name lookups add to it: DNS (Domain Name System) queries travel in clear text unless the device uses DNS over TLS (Transport Layer Security), standardized in RFC 7858 in May 2016, or DNS over HTTPS, RFC 8484 of October 2018.

The password on the café wall changes less than people think. RFC 8110, published by the Internet Engineering Task Force (IETF) in March 2017, describes exactly that case, a pre-shared key (PSK) printed on a sandwich board or a menu, and calls the belief that it protects the wireless medium from passive sniffing erroneous: anyone who knows the PSK and observes the four-way handshake can compute a client's traffic keys, and an attacker who missed it can force a new one with a forged deauthenticate frame. The same RFC defines Opportunistic Wireless Encryption (OWE), sold by the Wi-Fi Alliance as Wi-Fi Enhanced Open, which uses a Diffie-Hellman exchange to give every client its own keys on a network without a password; but it states plainly that OWE provides no authentication and secures only the radio link, not end-to-end traffic. So the 2011 rule that only a password-protected hotspot is secure is out of date in both directions: the shared password does not stop a neighbour, and an open network can be encrypted.

What remains worth caring about is narrower, and each item has a mechanism. The first is the stray unencrypted connection: Google's team notes that an attacker needs only a single insecure navigation, that many HTTP requests are invisible because they immediately redirect to HTTPS, and that software to hijack navigations is readily available; HSTS closes that gap only after the first visit, which RFC 6797 discusses as its bootstrap man-in-the-middle vulnerability. The second is the captive portal: RFC 8952 (November 2020) records that current portals typically forge DNS or HTTP responses and that some attempt a man-in-the-middle proxy of HTTPS, which teaches users to click through warnings at the moment they should not. The third is the fake network: neither a shared password nor OWE authenticates the access point, so a rogue device can advertise the same network name, run its own portal and harvest whatever a user types into it; the FTC's warning that scammers create fake websites and encrypt them applies with full force. The fourth is the device itself: the EFF notes that software with bugs exploitable only from the local network carries somewhat more risk on a shared network, and Google observes that HTTP to private addresses can be abused by an attacker on the same local network.

Guidance differs because audiences differ, not because the facts do. The US National Security Agency (NSA), writing in July 2021 for teleworkers on National Security Systems, in the Department of Defense and in the Defense Industrial Base, advised avoiding public Wi-Fi in favour of a personal or corporate hotspot with strong authentication and encryption, using a personal or corporate VPN (virtual private network) when public Wi-Fi cannot be avoided, and disabling Wi-Fi, Bluetooth and NFC (Near-Field Communication) when not in use, since attackers can compromise devices over all three. For someone whose metadata is itself sensitive, or who is a likely target, that is sound. For the ordinary user checking email over HTTPS, the FTC and EFF position holds: the encryption that matters runs end to end, between the device and the site, whatever the radio link is doing.

The part of the belief that is right: a public network is a shared medium run by someone you do not know, it reveals which services you use and when, it can be impersonated, and it is the natural place to meet a fake portal or a device that has not been patched. What a practitioner should say instead is specific. Keep operating systems and browsers updated; leave HTTPS-only or 'Always Use Secure Connections' on; use encrypted DNS; treat a certificate warning on a public network as a stop sign rather than a hurdle; never type credentials into a portal page that asks for more than the venue needs; prefer a phone's own hotspot or a trusted VPN when the metadata or the target matters; and in enterprise settings rely on per-application encryption and device posture rather than on which network the laptop happens to be on. The threat did not disappear; it shrank to something that can be named.

aead.def: A cipher that encrypts and authenticates in one step, so tampering fails as a single operation: decryption returns either the original plaintext or an error, never altered data.
aead.context: Authenticated Encryption with Associated Data (AEAD), given a common interface in Request for Comments (RFC) 5116, combines confidentiality and integrity in one primitive, such as AES-GCM (Advanced Encryption Standard in Galois/Counter Mode), AES-CCM (Counter with CBC-MAC) and ChaCha20-Poly1305. The associated data is information such as a packet header that must stay readable yet must not be altered. Transport Layer Security (TLS) 1.3 permits AEAD ciphers only, because the older construction that applied a message authentication code (MAC) and then encrypted in cipher block chaining (CBC) mode kept producing padding-oracle attacks. The price is strictness about nonces: a nonce must never repeat under the same key.
aead.depth:
AEAD (Authenticated Encryption with Associated Data) packages encryption and authentication into a single operation, which sounds like convenience and is actually a safety mechanism. The historical alternative was composing a cipher with a separate message authentication code (MAC), and the composition was where implementations went wrong: authenticate the wrong thing, or do it in the wrong order, and the result is a padding oracle rather than a protocol. In 2000 Mihir Bellare and Chanathip Namprempre analysed the three ways of composing the two, Encrypt-and-MAC, MAC-then-encrypt and Encrypt-then-MAC, and showed that they are not equally sound. Transport Layer Security (TLS) had chosen MAC-then-encrypt in the 1990s, and Request for Comments (RFC) 7457 records the consequence: padding oracle attacks, among them Lucky Thirteen (CVE-2013-0169) and, against SSL (Secure Sockets Layer) 3.0, POODLE (CVE-2014-3566).

The idea got its name from Phillip Rogaway, whose paper Authenticated-Encryption with Associated-Data, dated 20 September 2002, observed that the problem had long been handled in practice but had never been given a definition or even a name. The Internet Engineering Task Force (IETF) turned it into an interface in RFC 5116, written by David McGrew and published in January 2008. Encryption takes four inputs, each an octet string: a secret key K, a nonce N, the plaintext P and the associated data A. It returns one output, the ciphertext C, which includes an authentication tag. Decryption takes K, N, A and C and returns either P or the symbol FAIL. There is no third outcome, and that is the point: an application cannot be handed plaintext that failed its integrity check.

The associated data is the piece people overlook. Some fields must be visible to work at all, such as headers a router needs to read, yet still must not be tampered with. AEAD covers them with the authentication tag while leaving them unencrypted, so integrity extends beyond the ciphertext to the context around it. Rogaway's own example was a packet header. In IPsec (Internet Protocol Security), RFC 4106 puts the Security Parameters Index (SPI) and the sequence number of the Encapsulating Security Payload (ESP) into the associated data; in TLS 1.3 it is the record header; in QUIC it is the packet header up to and including the packet number.

Three algorithms carry almost all of the traffic. AES-GCM, the Advanced Encryption Standard (AES) in Galois/Counter Mode, was specified by the National Institute of Standards and Technology (NIST) in Special Publication 800-38D in November 2007; it recommends a 96-bit initialization vector (IV), which is the nonce, and allows tags of 128, 120, 112, 104 or 96 bits. AES-CCM, Counter with CBC-MAC (cipher block chaining message authentication code), is the older NIST mode, from May 2004. ChaCha20-Poly1305, in RFC 8439 of June 2018, pairs a stream cipher with a 256-bit key and a 96-bit nonce with a one-time authenticator. In the RFC 5116 definitions the AES-GCM and AES-CCM ciphertexts are exactly 16 octets longer than the plaintext, the size of the tag, and the recommended nonce is 12 octets. The registry kept by the Internet Assigned Numbers Authority (IANA) has since grown past thirty entries, including OCB, AES-GCM-SIV and, from RFC 10032 of September 2026, the AEGIS family; NIST's lightweight standard of August 2025, SP 800-232, adds Ascon for constrained devices.

TLS shows the transition. Version 1.2 (RFC 5246, August 2008) introduced AEAD ciphers as an option beside stream and CBC (cipher block chaining) ciphers, and RFC 5288 defined the first AES-GCM suites in the same month. Version 1.3, now specified in RFC 9846, pruned every legacy algorithm, so that all that remain are AEAD: AES-128-GCM, AES-256-GCM, ChaCha20-Poly1305 and two CCM variants. It also removed a choice that had caused trouble. In TLS 1.2 part of the nonce travelled explicitly in each record; in TLS 1.3 the nonce is never sent, being the 64-bit record sequence number combined by exclusive OR with a secret per-connection IV. Any decryption failure produces the same bad_record_mac alert, so an attacker learns nothing from the manner of failing. OpenSSH offers the same primitives under the names chacha20-poly1305@openssh.com, aes128-gcm@openssh.com and aes256-gcm@openssh.com.

The rule that matters operationally is that AEAD trades one class of failure for another. It removes composition mistakes and it is unforgiving about nonce reuse. RFC 5116 requires every nonce used with a given key to be distinct, and says that an inadvertent repeat in GCM undermines the confidentiality of the two messages and all of the authenticity and integrity protection provided by that key. NIST explains why: from two ciphertexts made with the same IV an adversary is likely to determine the hash subkey, the internal authentication key, and can then forge at will. So repeating a nonce in GCM does not degrade security gracefully. This is not theoretical. In 2016 Hanno Böck and colleagues scanned the internet and found 184 HTTPS (Hypertext Transfer Protocol Secure) servers repeating nonces, which fully broke the authenticity of their connections, and more than 70,000 choosing nonces at random, which is safe only for a limited number of records.

The limits are therefore part of the algorithm. NIST requires that the chance of an IV repeating under one key stay below 2 to the power -32, and caps a key at 2 to the power 32 invocations unless 96-bit IVs are generated deterministically, for example from a counter. TLS 1.3 sets a traffic limit as well: with AES-GCM about 24 million full-size records may be protected under one set of keys, after which the connection must update its keys or close, whereas with ChaCha20-Poly1305 the sequence number would wrap first. Where unique nonces cannot be guaranteed, as in a restored virtual machine, a nonce misuse-resistant design such as AES-GCM-SIV (RFC 8452, April 2019) does not fail catastrophically when one repeats.

AEAD has precise boundaries. It protects a message against reading and alteration, but it does not hide its length, does not stop a valid message from being replayed (protocols add sequence numbers for that) and does not agree on the key, which is the job of the handshake. It also differs from the stopgap that TLS adopted for CBC suites in RFC 7366, encrypt-then-MAC, which repairs the order of the two operations but still has two algorithms and two keys. TLS 1.3 kept only AEAD ciphers precisely because the alternatives had accumulated a decade of attacks, and the remaining sharp edge is nonce management rather than cipher choice.

aes.def: The Advanced Encryption Standard: the symmetric block cipher NIST (National Institute of Standards and Technology) selected from an open competition and published as FIPS (Federal Information Processing Standard) 197 in 2001, which encrypts 128-bit blocks under 128-, 192- or 256-bit keys and protects most bulk encrypted data today.
aes.context: Advanced Encryption Standard (AES), published by NIST (National Institute of Standards and Technology) as FIPS (Federal Information Processing Standard) 197 and originally the Rijndael cipher, encrypts data in 128-bit blocks with 128-, 192-, or 256-bit keys. It is the workhorse behind TLS (Transport Layer Security) record protection, disk encryption, and VPNs (virtual private networks).
aes.depth:
The Advanced Encryption Standard (AES) is FIPS (Federal Information Processing Standard) 197, published by NIST (National Institute of Standards and Technology) on 26 November 2001 and updated on 9 May 2023 with editorial changes only, none to the algorithm. It specifies three members of the Rijndael family designed by Joan Daemen and Vincent Rijmen, AES-128, AES-192 and AES-256; all three transform data in 128-bit blocks, and the number is the key length, not a quality rating. AES is a block cipher and nothing more: it turns one 16-byte block into another under a key. Everything that makes it safe for real messages, chaining blocks, randomizing repeated inputs, detecting tampering, belongs to the mode of operation built around it.

It was chosen in the open. NIST announced the effort on 2 January 1997 and on 12 September 1997 called for an unclassified, publicly disclosed algorithm, available royalty-free worldwide. On 20 August 1998 it presented fifteen candidates from around the world at the first AES candidate conference; five finalists, MARS, RC6, Rijndael, Serpent and Twofish, went through a second round of public analysis that closed on 15 May 2000, after a third conference in New York on 13 and 14 April. On 2 October 2000 NIST announced Rijndael, published a draft standard in February 2001 and the final FIPS 197 that November. Conformance testing followed under the Cryptographic Algorithm Validation Program (CAVP), which had validated more than 5,700 AES implementations by 2020.

Inside, AES works on a state of 16 bytes arranged as a four-by-four array. After an initial AddRoundKey, each round applies SubBytes (a fixed substitution table on every byte), ShiftRows (rotating the last three rows by different offsets), MixColumns (mixing the bytes within each column) and AddRoundKey (combining a round key); the final round omits MixColumns. AES-128 runs 10 rounds, AES-192 12 and AES-256 14, with round keys expanded from the 4-, 6- or 8-word key into a schedule of 4(Nr + 1) words, and the byte arithmetic is in the finite field defined by x^8 + x^4 + x^3 + x + 1. FIPS 197 admits no other Rijndael configuration, but NIST has looked beyond it: in August 2024 it signalled interest in Rijndael-256, with 256-bit blocks and a single 256-bit key, for applications that encrypt very large volumes, and asked for comments on a draft standard by 25 June 2025.

AES has resisted practical cryptanalysis for a quarter of a century. The best key-recovery attacks on the full cipher, the biclique attacks Andrey Bogdanov, Dmitry Khovratovich and Christian Rechberger published in 2011, cost 2^126.1 operations for AES-128, 2^189.7 for AES-192 and 2^254.4 for AES-256, and their authors state that they do not threaten practical use; Alex Biryukov and Khovratovich's 2009 attack on AES-256 at 2^99.5 needs related keys rather than a single unknown key. 128 bits therefore remains entirely adequate against classical attack. The usual reason to choose 256 is policy or a post-quantum margin. Grover's algorithm gives a quantum computer a quadratic speedup in key search, which at face value would halve the effective key length and make AES-256 behave like AES-128; NIST's own assessment is that cost and the difficulty of running Grover in parallel make it quite likely to give little or no advantage, that AES-128 will remain secure for decades, and its transition report of October 2026 says it does not expect to move away from AES at all, using AES-128, AES-192 and AES-256 as the reference points for post-quantum security categories 1, 3 and 5. That is a far gentler outlook than public-key cryptography faces.

Speed depends on hardware. RFC (Request for Comments) 8439 (June 2018) records that AES is four to ten times as fast as Triple DES (Data Encryption Standard) on most modern platforms and very fast on dedicated hardware, but considerably slower without it, where ChaCha20 runs about three times as fast in software. On x86 processors a single instruction, AESENC, performs a whole round on a 128-bit state, with wider forms processing several blocks at once, so on such machines AES is typically faster than the software alternatives people reach for when they think they are optimizing. Hardware matters for a second reason: FIPS 197 itself warns that software implementations on platforms that use a cache can leak key-dependent information through cache timing, and RFC 8439 notes that many AES implementations are vulnerable to cache-collision timing attacks.

The mistake that actually causes breaches is the mode, not the cipher. SP (Special Publication) 800-38A (December 2001) defined five confidentiality modes: ECB (Electronic Codebook), CBC (Cipher Block Chaining), CFB (Cipher Feedback), OFB (Output Feedback) and CTR (Counter). In ECB every identical plaintext block encrypts to the same ciphertext block under a given key, which leaks structure so visibly that an image encrypted that way stays recognizable, and NIST decided in 2023 to revise SP 800-38A and limit ECB to uses other NIST guidance specifically allows. CBC without authentication invites padding oracle attacks: RFC 7457 traces them to the MAC-then-encrypt design of TLS (Transport Layer Security), where the message authentication code (MAC) is computed before encryption, through Lucky Thirteen (CVE-2013-0169) and POODLE (CVE-2014-3566), and names AES-GCM or encrypt-then-MAC as the fix. Modern practice is an AEAD (authenticated encryption with associated data) mode such as GCM (Galois/Counter Mode), where encryption and authentication happen together and the remaining discipline is never repeating a nonce, since SP 800-38D treats IV (initialization vector) uniqueness as almost as important as the key. Storage uses XTS-AES (SP 800-38E, January 2010), which protects confidentiality on disks but authenticates nothing.

AES is everywhere bulk data is encrypted. TLS 1.3, now RFC 9846 of July 2026, requires every compliant application to implement TLS_AES_128_GCM_SHA256 and recommends TLS_AES_256_GCM_SHA384 alongside ChaCha20-Poly1305; disk and storage encryption, Wi-Fi and VPN (virtual private network) tunnels use it as well. Its neighbours are its predecessor DES and Triple DES, its software-friendly alternative ChaCha20, and the modes that turn it into something usable. Numbers worth keeping: 128-bit blocks; 10, 12 and 14 rounds; 15 candidates and 5 finalists; Rijndael chosen on 2 October 2000; and 2^126.1, the best known cost of breaking AES-128 without related keys.

cbc.def: Cipher block chaining (CBC): a block-cipher mode of operation that combines each plaintext block with the previous ciphertext block by exclusive OR (XOR) before encrypting it. It provides confidentiality only, with no integrity of its own.
cbc.context: Cipher Block Chaining, defined in Special Publication (SP) 800-38A of NIST (the United States National Institute of Standards and Technology), XORs each plaintext block with the previous ciphertext block before encrypting, XOR being the bitwise exclusive OR, starting from an initialization vector (IV). It needs a separate MAC (message authentication code) for integrity, and the way TLS combined the two, MAC first and encryption second, produced the Lucky Thirteen and POODLE padding attacks, while the predictable IV of TLS 1.0 produced BEAST. TLS 1.3 drops CBC entirely in favour of AEAD (authenticated encryption with associated data).
cbc.depth:
Cipher block chaining (CBC) XORs each plaintext block with the previous ciphertext block before encrypting, XOR being the bitwise exclusive OR, so identical blocks produce different output and the structure that ECB (electronic codebook) mode leaks is hidden. In the notation of NIST (National Institute of Standards and Technology) Special Publication (SP) 800-38A, written by Morris Dworkin and published in December 2001, the first ciphertext block is the cipher applied to the first plaintext block XORed with an initialization vector (IV), and each later block is the cipher applied to the plaintext block XORed with the ciphertext block before it; decryption applies the inverse cipher to each ciphertext block and XORs the result with the previous one. The publication lists CBC as one of five confidentiality modes, beside ECB, cipher feedback (CFB), output feedback (OFB) and counter (CTR), and the word confidentiality is exact: the mode hides data and does nothing else.

It needs an unpredictable initialization vector for the first block. SP 800-38A is precise about what that means: the IV need not be secret, and may travel with the ciphertext, but for any given plaintext it must not be possible to predict the IV that will be used. It recommends two ways to make one: encrypt a nonce, such as a counter or message number, under the same key, or take a random block from an approved random number generator. The IV is one block long, which in the TLS 1.2 cipher table means 8 bytes for 3DES (triple Data Encryption Standard) and 16 bytes for AES (Advanced Encryption Standard).

Because the cipher works on whole blocks, the plaintext must be padded to a multiple of the block size, and the padding is where much of CBC's history happened. NIST's own example appends a single 1 bit and then as many 0 bits as needed. The method almost everyone uses is the one in the Cryptographic Message Syntax (CMS) of RFC (Request for Comments) 5652, a format derived from PKCS #7, which is the name the padding still goes by: add k minus (length mod k) octets, each holding that same number, and pad every message, even one that already fills its last block, so that the padding can always be removed without ambiguity. TLS block ciphers pad in a similar way, with up to 255 bytes that each hold the padding length. A 2010 addendum to SP 800-38A defines three variants of ciphertext stealing, which borrow bits from the penultimate ciphertext block so that the data does not grow at all.

Two operational properties follow from the chaining. Encryption is serial, since each block needs the previous ciphertext block, while decryption can run in parallel, since all the ciphertext is already there. And errors propagate in a specific pattern: a bit error in one ciphertext block garbles the whole of that block on decryption and flips exactly the same bit positions in the next block, leaving everything else intact. The second half of that sentence is the dangerous one, because what a line error does by accident an attacker can do on purpose.

Its defining weakness is that it provides no integrity. Without a separate authentication step an attacker can modify ciphertext and the recipient decrypts garbage without knowing it was tampered with, which is the basis of padding oracle attacks. A padding oracle is any observable difference in how a receiver treats well-formed and malformed padding, an error message or merely a difference in timing; S. Vaudenay showed at the EUROCRYPT conference of 2002 that such a difference lets an attacker recover plaintext without the key. Microsoft's guidance to developers states the conclusion for application code: it is no longer safe to decrypt CBC data with verifiable padding, such as PKCS #7, without first ensuring the integrity of the ciphertext, and the safe pattern is encrypt-then-sign, with the MAC (message authentication code) checked in constant time before any decryption, noting that TLS on the connection does not protect data handled this way.

The mode is older than the standards most engineers cite for it. IBM filed the patent Message verification and transmission error detection by block chaining on 26 April 1976, naming William F. Ehrsam, Carl H. W. Meyer, John L. Smith and Walter L. Tuchman, and it was published on 14 February 1978. The United States National Bureau of Standards made CBC one of the four modes of DES (the Data Encryption Standard) in FIPS (Federal Information Processing Standard) 81 on 2 December 1980, beside ECB, CFB and OFB; FIPS 81 was withdrawn on 19 May 2005, by which time SP 800-38A had restated the modes for any approved block cipher. NIST has announced that it plans to revise SP 800-38A.

In TLS the history can be read version by version. A CBC record carries the content, then its MAC, then the padding, all encrypted together: MAC-then-encrypt. Through TLS 1.0 the IV of each record was the last ciphertext block of the previous one, which an eavesdropper has already seen; the BEAST attack of 2011, catalogued as CVE (Common Vulnerabilities and Exposures) identifier CVE-2011-3389, used that predictability to decrypt parts of a message, specifically HTTP cookies. TLS 1.1 (RFC 4346, April 2006) had already replaced the implicit IV with an explicit one in every record and made padding errors indistinguishable from MAC errors by using the same bad_record_mac alert. TLS 1.2 (RFC 5246, August 2008) kept CBC, made TLS_RSA_WITH_AES_128_CBC_SHA its mandatory cipher suite, and warned that record processing time must be essentially the same whether or not the padding is correct, while admitting that its recommended fix leaves a small timing channel. Lucky Thirteen (CVE-2013-0169), published by N. AlFardan and K. Paterson in 2013, measured that channel, and POODLE (CVE-2014-3566) needed no timing at all against the looser padding of SSL (Secure Sockets Layer) 3.0.

The remedies came in two forms. RFC 7366, written by P. Gutmann of the University of Auckland and published in September 2014, lets TLS peers negotiate encrypt-then-MAC, so that the MAC covers the ciphertext and is checked before anything is decrypted, and describes MAC-then-encrypt as the subject of a number of security vulnerabilities over a period of many years. The other form was to stop bolting two primitives together: AEAD (authenticated encryption with associated data) modes such as AES-GCM (Galois/Counter Mode) encrypt and authenticate in one operation. That is why modern practice is AEAD rather than CBC plus a bolted-on MAC, and why TLS 1.3 (RFC 8446, August 2018, obsoleted in July 2026 by RFC 9846, which specifies the same version) removed CBC entirely rather than continuing to specify how to use it carefully: its symmetric algorithms were pruned of everything considered legacy, and those that remain are all AEAD. SSH (Secure Shell) took the same road; OpenSSH 6.7, released on 6 October 2014, removed CBC ciphers from its default set as unsafe algorithms.

CBC is still everywhere an engineer looks. It is the CBC in the names of TLS 1.2 cipher suites, where the hash at the end of the name is the separate MAC; on a load balancer or firewall, removing those suites from a cipher string is how the mode is retired in practice. It is the default shape of file encryption with the openssl enc command, as in the option -aes-256-cbc: the manual states that block ciphers there use PKCS #7 padding, that this gives only a rudimentary check which random data passes better than one time in 256, and that the command does not and will not support authenticated modes such as CCM (Counter with CBC-MAC) and GCM. And it survives inside an authenticated mode, since CCM uses the chaining as its MAC. The numbers worth keeping are the block sizes, 8 bytes for 3DES and 16 for AES, the dates 1976, 1980 and 2001, and the three identifiers CVE-2011-3389, CVE-2013-0169 and CVE-2014-3566.

gcm.def: Galois/Counter Mode (GCM): a block-cipher mode of operation, specified by NIST (the US National Institute of Standards and Technology) in 2007, that encrypts with a counter and authenticates with a polynomial hash over a binary Galois field, turning a 128-bit block cipher such as AES (Advanced Encryption Standard) into an AEAD (authenticated encryption with associated data) algorithm.
gcm.context: Galois/Counter Mode (GCM), designed by David McGrew and John Viega and specified in NIST (National Institute of Standards and Technology) Special Publication 800-38D in November 2007, combines counter-mode encryption with GHASH, a keyed hash computed by multiplication in a 128-bit binary field, and outputs a ciphertext as long as the plaintext plus an authentication tag, normally 128 bits. AES-GCM, the Advanced Encryption Standard (AES) in this mode, is the cipher suite every TLS (Transport Layer Security) 1.3 implementation must support and the default of Ethernet's MACsec (Media Access Control Security), and it protects IPsec (Internet Protocol Security), SSH (Secure Shell) and QUIC traffic. Its one sharp edge is the initialization vector (IV), its nonce: if an IV ever repeats under the same key, an attacker can recover the authentication key and forge messages at will, so the standard makes IV uniqueness a requirement and caps randomly chosen IVs at 2^32 messages per key.
gcm.depth:
GCM (Galois/Counter Mode) is a mode of operation, not a cipher. It takes an approved block cipher with a 128-bit block and a key of at least 128 bits, which in practice means AES (the Advanced Encryption Standard), and builds from it an algorithm for AEAD (authenticated encryption with associated data). NIST (the National Institute of Standards and Technology) specified it in Special Publication (SP) 800-38D, written by Morris Dworkin and published in November 2007, together with GMAC, its specialization for authenticating data that is not encrypted. Encryption takes four inputs, the key, an initialization vector (IV), the plaintext and the additional authenticated data (AAD), and returns a ciphertext of exactly the plaintext's length plus a tag. The tag length is a security parameter: 128, 120, 112, 104 or 96 bits in general, and 64 or 32 bits only for applications that meet the conditions of the standard's Appendix C, with one fixed length tied to each key. Decryption returns the plaintext or FAIL and nothing in between, which is the AEAD contract described in the entry on AEAD.

The mechanism has three steps. The hash subkey, H, is the block cipher applied to the all-zero block. The pre-counter block is made from the IV: with the recommended 96-bit IV it is the IV followed by 31 zero bits and a single 1; an IV of any other length is first compressed with GHASH. The plaintext is then encrypted in counter mode starting from the next counter value, where the increment touches only the rightmost 32 bits of the block. Finally GHASH, keyed with H, runs over the AAD and the ciphertext, each padded to whole blocks and followed by their two 64-bit lengths, and the result is encrypted with the cipher output for the pre-counter block and truncated to the tag length. GHASH multiplies by H in the field of 2^128 elements defined by the polynomial x^128 + x^7 + x^2 + x + 1, so the tag is in effect a polynomial in H whose coefficients are the data blocks. Antoine Joux described it as a variation on the Wegman-Carter construction, a universal hash whose output is encrypted, and NIST approves GHASH only inside GCM, since on its own it is not a cryptographic hash function. The standard lists the engineering virtues that made the mode popular: both directions can be parallelized, only the forward cipher is ever used, the data lengths need not be known in advance, and the tag can be checked before anything is decrypted. One invocation may protect up to 2^39 minus 256 bits of plaintext, just under 64 GiB (gibibytes), and up to 2^64 minus 1 bits of AAD.

David McGrew, then at Cisco, and John Viega designed the mode and submitted it to NIST. Their paper on its security and performance, posted to the IACR (International Association for Cryptologic Research) ePrint archive in August 2004 with an extended abstract at the INDOCRYPT 2004 conference, argued that it was the most efficient mode for high-speed packet networks and that it could take IVs of any length, act as a stand-alone MAC (message authentication code) and work as an incremental MAC. The IETF (Internet Engineering Task Force) adopted it before NIST had finished: RFC (Request for Comments) 4106 put AES-GCM into the IPsec (Internet Protocol Security) Encapsulating Security Payload (ESP) in June 2005, and RFC 4543 defined AES-GMAC for ESP and the Authentication Header (AH) in May 2006, giving integrity without confidentiality. The review left two warnings on the record. Niels Ferguson showed on 20 May 2005 that short tags are weaker than their length implies, with forgeries succeeding far more often than 2^-32 for a 32-bit tag, and that each successful forgery leaks information about the authentication key. Joux then showed that a repeated IV lets an adversary recover H, after which the mode is no longer authenticated at all; he called it the forbidden attack. SP 800-38D absorbed both: Appendix C confines 32-bit and 64-bit tags to uses such as voice carried over the Secure Real-time Transport Protocol (SRTP) on UDP (User Datagram Protocol), with tables that limit the packet size and the number of decryption attempts per key, and Section 8 turns IV uniqueness into a formal requirement.

That requirement is the rule that matters. The probability that the encryption function is ever invoked with the same IV and key on two different sets of input shall be no greater than 2^-32, and NIST calls compliance almost as important as keeping the key secret. Appendix A explains why. Plain counter mode with a repeated counter loses confidentiality for the blocks involved and lets an attacker flip plaintext bits at will; GCM adds a tag precisely to stop that, but from two messages encrypted under one IV an adversary is likely to determine H, and can then compute a valid tag for any ciphertext and AAD it chooses. Two constructions meet the rule. The deterministic one splits the IV into a fixed field that identifies the device or context and an invocation field, typically a counter, that never repeats within it. The random one draws the IV from an approved random bit generator, and then, as in every case other than 96-bit deterministic IVs, the total number of encryptions under one key shall not exceed 2^32. The failures are operational rather than mathematical: a counter that resets after a process restart, two cluster members sharing a key and a counter, a virtual machine restored from a snapshot or cloned, a random generator used far beyond its bound. None of them shows up in testing, and each lets an attacker forge rather than merely read.

TLS (Transport Layer Security) shows both the problem and its repair. RFC 5288, from J. Salowey, A. Choudhury and D. McGrew of Cisco Systems in August 2008, defined the first AES-GCM cipher suites, for TLS 1.2 only, such as TLS_RSA_WITH_AES_128_GCM_SHA256 (code 0x00,0x9C), and RFC 5289, published by Eric Rescorla the same month, added the elliptic-curve versions such as TLS_ECDHE_RSA_WITH_AES_128_GCM_SHA256 (0xC0,0x2F). Its 12-byte nonce is a 4-byte salt derived during the handshake and never sent, plus an 8-byte nonce_explicit carried in every record, which must be distinct for each record and may be the 64-bit sequence number. The SHA256 or SHA384 at the end of such a suite names the hash of the pseudorandom function (PRF) used in the handshake, not a record MAC, because GCM needs none. Leaving the nonce to each implementer is what Hanno Böck and four colleagues measured in 2016: an internet-wide scan found 184 HTTPS (Hypertext Transfer Protocol Secure) servers repeating nonces, which fully breaks the authenticity of their connections, and more than 70,000 choosing them at random. TLS 1.3 removed the choice by deriving the nonce from the record sequence number and never transmitting it, as the AEAD entry explains. RFC 9846, which specifies TLS 1.3 since July 2026, makes TLS_AES_128_GCM_SHA256 mandatory to implement and limits AES-GCM to 2^24.5 full-size records, about 24 million, under one set of keys. QUIC, which takes its keys from TLS 1.3, protects its Initial and Retry packets with AES-128-GCM, sets a confidentiality limit of 2^23 packets per key and closes the connection after 2^52 packets that fail authentication.

The mode is just as central below the application layer. In IPsec, RFC 4106 forms the nonce from a 4-byte salt fixed for the life of the security association and the 8-byte IV carried in each ESP packet, which must not repeat for a key and is most naturally a counter; it requires support for a 16-octet integrity check value (ICV), allows 8 or 12 octets and forbids a zero-length one. Linux names these transforms rfc4106(gcm(aes)) and rfc4543(gcm(aes)) when IPsec states are configured with ip xfrm, and FortiOS lists AES128GCM and AES256GCM among its IPsec proposals, available with IKEv2 (Internet Key Exchange version 2). On Ethernet, GCM-AES-128 is the mandatory Default Cipher Suite of IEEE (Institute of Electrical and Electronics Engineers) 802.1AE MAC Security, with GCM-AES-256 added by its first amendment. SSH (Secure Shell) received AES-GCM in RFC 5647, written at the National Security Agency in August 2009, but that RFC's rules for negotiating the algorithm proved awkward, and OpenSSH and other implementations negotiate aes128-gcm@openssh.com and aes256-gcm@openssh.com under different rules.

Its neighbours are easy to place. CCM, Counter with Cipher Block Chaining-Message Authentication Code (SP 800-38C, 2004), uses the same counter encryption with a CBC-MAC (cipher block chaining message authentication code) instead of a field multiplication; ChaCha20-Poly1305 (RFC 8439) is considerably faster than AES in software on processors that lack AES hardware. All three are AEADs with the same strict nonce rule. Against CBC (cipher block chaining) with a separate HMAC (hash-based message authentication code), GCM removes the MAC-then-encrypt order that produced padding oracles, as the CBC entry recounts. Where uniqueness cannot be guaranteed, AES-GCM-SIV (RFC 8452, April 2019, by Shay Gueron, Adam Langley and Yehuda Lindell) is nonce misuse-resistant: a repeated nonce reveals only that two identical plaintexts were encrypted, instead of the catastrophic failure that GCM suffers.

The standard is being revised. NIST began reviewing SP 800-38D in August 2021, proposed a revision on 23 August 2023, and announced on 5 March 2024 that the new edition will remove tags shorter than 96 bits, state explicitly that the IV construction of TLS 1.3 is approved, clarify the guidance on IV construction and update the references. The numbers worth keeping are a 128-bit block, a 96-bit IV, a 128-bit tag by default, a 2^-32 ceiling on the chance of any IV repeating, 2^32 messages per key with random IVs, and the per-key limits of 2^24.5 TLS 1.3 records and 2^23 QUIC packets.

ccm.def: Counter with CBC-MAC (CCM): a block-cipher mode for authenticated encryption with associated data (AEAD) that computes a CBC-MAC tag over the data and then encrypts data and tag in counter mode, with one key; defined for 128-bit block ciphers, in practice AES (Advanced Encryption Standard).
ccm.context: Counter with CBC-MAC (CCM), specified by NIST (the National Institute of Standards and Technology) in Special Publication (SP) 800-38C and by the IETF (Internet Engineering Task Force) in RFC (Request for Comments) 3610, is an AEAD (authenticated encryption with associated data) construction that uses AES (Advanced Encryption Standard) twice per block: once in a CBC-MAC (cipher block chaining message authentication code) over the associated data and plaintext, once in counter mode to encrypt. It needs only the block cipher's forward direction, which keeps hardware small, and it is the cipher of Wi-Fi's CCMP (Counter Mode with CBC-MAC Protocol) in WPA2, of IPsec CCM, of the IoT (Internet of Things) TLS (Transport Layer Security) profiles and of two TLS 1.3 suites, used where GCM (Galois/Counter Mode) is undesirable, as on constrained links. The price is two passes over the data and a message length that must be known in advance. The CCM_8 variant truncates the tag to 8 bytes to save overhead, which measurably weakens integrity: each forgery attempt succeeds with probability up to 1 in 2 to the 64th, and IANA (Internet Assigned Numbers Authority) lists TLS_AES_128_CCM_8_SHA256 as not recommended.
ccm.depth:
What it is. Counter with CBC-MAC (CCM), an AEAD (authenticated encryption with associated data) mode, combines two older mechanisms under a single key: CBC-MAC, the cipher block chaining message authentication code, which runs the block cipher in CBC mode over a formatted block that encodes the nonce, the lengths and the flags, then over the associated data and the plaintext, and keeps the last block as the tag; and counter (CTR) mode, which encrypts the plaintext and the tag with a keystream generated from counter blocks derived from the same nonce. Decryption reverses the order: decrypt, recompute the MAC (message authentication code), and release the plaintext only if the tags match. NIST (the National Institute of Standards and Technology) specifies it in Special Publication (SP) 800-38C (Morris Dworkin, May 2004, updated 20 July 2007) for block ciphers with 128-bit blocks, which in practice means AES (Advanced Encryption Standard), and notes that it therefore cannot be used with Triple DES (Data Encryption Standard), whose block is 64 bits. The key must be used for CCM only, and the total number of block-cipher invocations over its lifetime is capped at 2 to the 61st. NIST announced in April 2025 that it has decided to revise the document.

The parameters. RFC (Request for Comments) 3610 (Doug Whiting, Russ Housley and Niels Ferguson, September 2003) defines two choices. M is the tag length, 4 to 16 octets in steps of 2, a trade-off between message expansion and the chance that an attacker can modify a message undetected. L is the size of the length field, 2 to 8 octets, a trade-off between the maximum message size and the size of the nonce, which is 15 minus L octets: L of 2 allows a 13-byte nonce and messages up to 64 KiB, L of 8 a 7-byte nonce and enormous messages. Within one key a nonce must never repeat, because the counter blocks would repeat with it. SP 800-38C expresses the tag length Tlen in bits, any multiple of 16 from 32 to 128, and says a value under 64 shall not be used without careful analysis of the risk of accepting inauthentic data, and only where the protocol limits how many times verification can fail under one key; it puts the chance that a single forged ciphertext passes at no more than 1 in 2 to the Tlen. The authors of RFC 3610 released all their rights to the public domain and stated that they knew of no patent covering CCM.

Why it exists, and what it costs. CCM was the mandatory encryption algorithm of the IEEE 802.11 draft that became 802.11i, which Phillip Rogaway and David Wagner noted in A Critique of CCM, posted on 15 April 2003, where they listed its limitations. The ones engineers notice are structural. It is two-pass, one pass for the MAC and one for the encryption, so it costs two block-cipher calls per block where GCM (Galois/Counter Mode) costs one plus a multiplication in a binary field. It is not online: the formatted first block encodes the message length, so a sender must know the length before it can start. In exchange it needs only the forward direction of the cipher, one key and no extra primitive, which is exactly what small hardware wants; RFC 6655 (David McGrew and Daniel Bailey, July 2012) calls AES-CCM amenable to compact implementations and suitable for constrained environments.

Where it runs. Wi-Fi is the largest deployment. NIST SP 800-97 (February 2007, withdrawn on 31 December 2025 as technologically outdated, with readers referred to IEEE 802.11) describes CCMP, the Counter Mode with Cipher Block Chaining MAC Protocol of WPA2 (Wi-Fi Protected Access 2), as CCM with AES and a single 128-bit temporal key, protecting the packet data and parts of the 802.11 header, with a 48-bit packet number building the nonce; it was mandatory for robust security network compliance and, of WEP (Wired Equivalent Privacy), TKIP (Temporal Key Integrity Protocol) and CCMP, the only one whose core algorithm is approved under FIPS (Federal Information Processing Standards). IPsec (Internet Protocol Security) uses it in ESP (Encapsulating Security Payload) under RFC 4309 (Russ Housley, December 2005), which requires 8- and 16-octet integrity check values, allows 12, fixes L at 4 and forbids using a nonce and key combination twice. In TLS (Transport Layer Security), RFC 6655 added AES-CCM suites for TLS 1.2 and DTLS (Datagram Transport Layer Security), including CCM_8 suites with 8-octet tags, and RFC 7925 (July 2016), the TLS and DTLS profile for the Internet of Things (IoT), makes TLS_PSK_WITH_AES_128_CCM_8 mandatory to implement for pre-shared keys and TLS_ECDHE_ECDSA_WITH_AES_128_CCM_8 for certificates. TLS 1.3, specified since July 2026 in RFC 9846, keeps two of its five suites for CCM: TLS_AES_128_CCM_SHA256, codepoint 0x13,0x04, and TLS_AES_128_CCM_8_SHA256, 0x13,0x05.

What goes wrong. The short tag is the weakness that is designed in. An 8-byte tag gives a forger at most a 1 in 2 to the 64th chance per attempt, which SP 800-38C accepts only where the number of failed verifications is bounded, and the IANA (Internet Assigned Numbers Authority) TLS registry, last updated 5 November 2026, marks TLS_AES_128_CCM_8_SHA256 as not recommended, following an IESG (Internet Engineering Steering Group) action of 16 August 2018, while TLS_AES_128_CCM_SHA256 stays recommended. In the same registry the TLS 1.2 CCM suites built on RSA (Rivest-Shamir-Adleman) or finite-field Diffie-Hellman key exchange are now marked discouraged, because RFC 10015 (Nimrod Aviram, July 2026) forbids those key exchanges in TLS 1.2; the mode is not the reason. The other failure is nonce reuse, as with every counter-based mode: KRACK, published by Mathy Vanhoef in 2017, made WPA2 devices reinstall a key in use and reset the packet number that forms the CCMP nonce, and it worked even on networks that used only AES. CCM's integrity holds only if the nonce never repeats under a key, and the protocol, not the mode, has to guarantee that.

Its neighbours. GCM is the other NIST AEAD mode for 128-bit block ciphers: counter-mode encryption plus GHASH, a polynomial hash over a binary field. ChaCha20-Poly1305 is the stream-cipher alternative. CBC with HMAC (hash-based message authentication code), the TLS 1.2 construction that preceded AEAD, applied the MAC before encryption and paid for it in padding oracles. What sets CCM apart from all of them is that it needs nothing but the forward direction of one block cipher under one key.

Numbers worth remembering: tags of 4 to 16 bytes, 16 in CCM and 8 in CCM_8; nonces of 7 to 13 bytes, as 15 minus L; 2 to the 61st block-cipher calls per key; a 48-bit packet number in CCMP; codepoints 0x13,0x04 and 0x13,0x05 in TLS 1.3; and 1 in 2 to the 64th as the forgery chance per attempt with an 8-byte tag.

prf.def: A function that stretches a secret into as much key material as a protocol needs.
prf.context: A Pseudorandom Function takes a key and inputs and produces output indistinguishable from random. In TLS it derives the session keys from the negotiated secret; the cipher suite's trailing hash names the PRF hash in TLS 1.2.

rsa.def: RSA (Rivest-Shamir-Adleman) is the public-key cryptosystem published in 1978 whose security rests on the difficulty of factoring the product of two large primes; it is used for digital signatures and, historically, for key transport, and is specified today in PKCS #1 (Public-Key Cryptography Standards #1) version 2.2, RFC (Request for Comments) 8017.
rsa.context: Rivest-Shamir-Adleman (RSA), specified for the internet in RFC (Request for Comments) 8017, is a public-key cryptosystem based on the difficulty of factoring large numbers. In modern TLS (Transport Layer Security) it authenticates the server through its certificate and signatures; its use for key transport is gone from TLS 1.3 because it lacks forward secrecy: whoever later obtains the server's private key can decrypt every recorded session. Its keys are large for the security they give, and like every classical public-key algorithm it has a known expiry condition: a large enough quantum computer.
rsa.depth:
