RSA (Rivest-Shamir-Adleman) was the first practical public-key system to be published and, for decades, the default answer to both key exchange and signatures. Ronald Rivest, Adi Shamir and Leonard Adleman of the Massachusetts Institute of Technology (MIT) Laboratory for Computer Science described it in Communications of the ACM (Association for Computing Machinery) in February 1978, crediting Diffie and Hellman with the concept of a public-key cryptosystem but noting that they had offered no practical implementation. MIT's patent, US 4,405,829, was filed on 14 December 1977, granted on 20 September 1983 and expired in 2000. The idea had been found before in secret: in 1973 Clifford Cocks of GCHQ (Government Communications Headquarters), the British signals intelligence agency, described essentially the same scheme in a classified paper, which GCHQ released on 16 December 1997.

Its security rests on factoring being hard: multiplying two large primes is easy, recovering them from the product is not, and everything else follows from that asymmetry. The public key is the modulus n, the product of two secret primes p and q, and an exponent e; the private exponent d satisfies e times d congruent to 1 modulo (p-1)(q-1). Encryption raises a message, represented as a number, to the power e modulo n; decryption raises the result to d. Signing is the reverse use: only the holder of d can produce a value that anyone can check with e. The authors recommended a modulus of about 200 decimal digits and estimated that factoring one would take 3.8 billion years with the methods of the day; RSA-200 was factored on 9 May 2005, and the record for an RSA challenge number is RSA-250, 250 digits, factored on 28 February 2020 by a team of six: Boudot, Gaudry, Guillevic, Heninger, Thomé and Zimmermann.

The working specification is PKCS #1, from RSA Laboratories' Public-Key Cryptography Standards: versions 1.0 to 1.3 circulated in February and March 1991, 1.4 was part of the public release of 3 June 1991, 1.5 became RFC (Request for Comments) 2313, version 2.0 introduced OAEP (Optimal Asymmetric Encryption Padding), and version 2.2 is RFC 8017, published in November 2016. It defines two encryption schemes and two signature schemes. RSAES-OAEP is required for new applications and RSAES-PKCS1-v1_5 is kept only for compatibility; RSASSA-PSS (the Probabilistic Signature Scheme) is required in new applications, and RSASSA-PKCS1-v1_5 is kept for compatibility although no attacks on it are known. The US National Institute of Standards and Technology (NIST) adopts the same RFC 8017 algorithm in its Digital Signature Standard, FIPS (Federal Information Processing Standard) 186-5, of 3 February 2023.

Textbook RSA, the bare exponentiation without padding, is broken in ways that are easy to demonstrate, which is why OAEP and PSS exist and why nobody should implement the primitive directly. Even the old padding is a trap. In 1998 Daniel Bleichenbacher showed that valid PKCS #1 v1.5 ciphertexts can be produced without knowing the plaintext, so a server that reveals, by any difference in behaviour, whether a ciphertext decrypted to correct padding becomes an oracle that eventually decrypts a recorded key exchange. In December 2017 Hanno Böck, Juraj Somorovsky and Craig Young published ROBOT, the Return Of Bleichenbacher's Oracle Threat, a 19-year-old flaw still present in products from at least seven vendors, among them F5 BIG-IP (CVE-2017-6168, a Common Vulnerabilities and Exposures entry), Citrix, Radware, Cisco and Palo Alto Networks, and on 27 of the top 100 web domains, Facebook and PayPal included. Their fix was to disable every cipher suite whose name starts with TLS_RSA; suites that use RSA only to sign an ephemeral Diffie-Hellman exchange were not affected.

That fix is also the direction the protocols took. Transport Layer Security (TLS) 1.3, first published as RFC 8446 in August 2018 and revised as RFC 9846 in July 2026, removed static RSA and static Diffie-Hellman cipher suites, so every key exchange now provides forward secrecy. RSA survives there as an authentication algorithm: handshake signatures use RSASSA-PSS (rsa_pss_rsae_sha256 and its siblings), while PKCS #1 v1.5 signature identifiers are kept only for signatures inside certificates.

The reason RSA is receding is arithmetic rather than any break. Equivalent security requires much larger keys than elliptic curves. NIST Special Publication (SP) 800-57 Part 1 (Revision 5, May 2020) equates a 2,048-bit modulus with 112 bits of security, 3,072 bits with 128 bits, the level of a 256-bit curve, 7,680 bits with 192 and 15,360 bits with 256, against curves of 384 and 512 bits for the last two; the gap widens as the level rises. Larger keys mean slower private-key operations and bigger handshakes, which is why newer deployments use ECDSA (the Elliptic Curve Digital Signature Algorithm) and Ed25519 for signatures while RSA persists mostly in certificates and in systems too entrenched to change. Key generation is a risk of its own: ROCA, the Return of Coppersmith's Attack (CVE-2017-15361), disclosed on 16 October 2017, found that a library in Infineon chips generated RSA keys with a structure that made about 760,000 confirmed keys factorable, a 1,024-bit key for 40 to 80 US dollars of cloud computing and a 2,048-bit key for 20,000 to 40,000.

Factoring is exactly the problem a sufficiently large quantum computer would solve efficiently: SP 800-57 warns that Shor's algorithms are projected to defeat the approved asymmetric algorithms, so RSA sits squarely in the category of cryptography with a known expiry condition, which is what post-quantum migration planning is about. NIST Interagency Report (IR) 8547, finalized on 27 October 2026, deprecates RSA signatures and RSA key establishment after 2030 and disallows them under NIST standards after 2035, replacing an earlier plan to disallow 112-bit public-key schemes on 1 January 2031; the most sensitive US federal systems must move key establishment to post-quantum cryptography by 31 December 2030 and signatures by 31 December 2031.

Numbers worth remembering: 1978 for the paper, 2048 bits for 112-bit security and 3072 for 128, RSA-250 as the public factoring record, OAEP and PSS as the only paddings for new work, and 2030 and 2035 as the NIST deprecation and disallowance years.

ecdsa.def: The Elliptic Curve Digital Signature Algorithm (ECDSA): a digital signature scheme over elliptic-curve groups, specified in Federal Information Processing Standard (FIPS) 186-5, that matches the security of RSA (Rivest, Shamir, Adleman) with far smaller keys (a 256-bit curve against a 3072-bit modulus) but needs a fresh secret number for every signature.
ecdsa.context: The Elliptic Curve Digital Signature Algorithm (ECDSA), standardized by NIST (the National Institute of Standards and Technology) in FIPS (Federal Information Processing Standard) 186-5, provides digital signatures with far smaller keys than RSA (Rivest, Shamir, Adleman) at equivalent security, which is why modern certificates, TLS (Transport Layer Security) handshakes and DNSSEC (DNS Security Extensions) zones increasingly use ECDSA keys, most often on the P-256 curve. Its weak point is the per-signature secret number: reuse it, or let it leak a few bits, and the private key can be computed from public signatures. Deterministic nonces, defined in Request for Comments (RFC) 6979, and the Edwards-curve Digital Signature Algorithm (EdDSA) remove that dependency, and NIST plans to deprecate ECDSA after 2030 and disallow it after 2035 as signatures move to post-quantum algorithms.
ecdsa.depth:
The Elliptic Curve Digital Signature Algorithm (ECDSA) is one of three signature techniques approved by Federal Information Processing Standard (FIPS) 186-5, the Digital Signature Standard the National Institute of Standards and Technology (NIST) published on 3 February 2023 to replace FIPS 186-4 of July 2013. The other two are RSA (Rivest, Shamir, Adleman), adopted from Request for Comments (RFC) 8017, and EdDSA (the Edwards-curve Digital Signature Algorithm) from RFC 8032. ECDSA itself is specified in the standard, having originally been defined in the now-withdrawn ANS (American National Standard) X9.62, and FIPS 186-5 also approves the deterministic variant of RFC 6979; the recommended curves now live in NIST SP (Special Publication) 800-186. The older DSA (Digital Signature Algorithm) is no longer specified and may only be used to verify signatures made earlier. The purpose is the usual one for signatures: detecting modification, authenticating the signer and giving the recipient evidence that a third party can check, which the standard calls non-repudiation.

The algorithm is short. The industry reference, Standards for Efficient Cryptography (SEC) 1 version 2.0 from Certicom Research, dated 21 May 2009, specifies it on a curve with a base point G of prime order n, a private key d and a public key Q = dG. To sign, the signer picks an ephemeral key pair, a secret integer k and the point R = kG; takes r as the x-coordinate of R reduced modulo n; hashes the message and truncates the hash to the bit length of n to get e; and computes s = k^-1 (e + r d) mod n, starting again if r or s comes out zero. The signature is the pair (r, s), two integers each as long as n, so 32 bytes apiece on a 256-bit curve. Verification needs only Q, the hash and the signature. SEC 1 notes that (r, -s mod n) is an equally valid signature, a malleability that systems using signatures as identifiers have to account for.

The size advantage is the reason for its spread among systems that speak TLS (Transport Layer Security), sign certificates or sign Domain Name System (DNS) zones. SEC 2 version 2.0 (27 January 2010) tabulates the strength of its recommended curves against RSA: secp256r1 and secp256k1 give 128-bit security, comparable to a 3072-bit RSA modulus; secp384r1 gives 192 bits against 7,680; secp521r1 gives 256 bits against 15,360. secp256r1 is the curve NIST calls P-256, and it is the default almost everywhere. TLS 1.3 (RFC 8446, August 2018) defines the signature schemes ecdsa_secp256r1_sha256 (0x0403), ecdsa_secp384r1_sha384 (0x0503) and ecdsa_secp521r1_sha512 (0x0603) beside ed25519 (0x0807) and ed448 (0x0808), and makes ecdsa_secp256r1_sha256 mandatory to implement. The Baseline Requirements of the CA/Browser Forum, the body where certificate authorities and browser makers set the rules, allow publicly trusted ECDSA keys only on P-256, P-384 or P-521, encoded with the id-ecPublicKey identifier (1.2.840.10045.2.1) and a named curve (secp256r1 is 1.2.840.10045.3.1.7) rather than explicit parameters.

Everything depends on k. SEC 1 is explicit that both the static private key and every per-signature k must be chosen securely: an attacker who learns a single k can recover the private key and then forge signatures at will, and even a small bias in k can leak the key gradually across many signatures. Reusing k is the extreme case. Two signatures made with the same k share the same r, and subtracting one s from the other cancels the private key term, so the difference of the two hashes divided by the difference of the two s values gives k, and k gives the private key; no curve has to be broken. RFC 6979 adds the engineering view: k must be chosen randomly and uniformly with a cryptographically secure process, good randomness is hard to guarantee on embedded devices such as smartcards, where deterministic RSA is often preferred despite its cost, and the randomized nature of ECDSA makes implementations hard to test, so failures tend to be discovered after deployment and after an attack.

The record bears that out. At the 27th Chaos Communication Congress (27C3) on 29 December 2010, the group fail0verflow (bushing, marcan and sven) presented Console Hacking 2010 on the PlayStation 3 (PS3), subtitled PS3 Epic Fail. Their slides explain that a random value must be used for every signature because two signatures with the same value give up both it and the private key, and they summarize Sony's ECDSA code with a random-number function that returns a constant; with the PS3 private keys, anyone could sign code the console would accept. Randomness failures recur in the Common Vulnerabilities and Exposures (CVE) records. CVE-2013-7372 records that the SecureRandom implementation in Android before 4.4, from Apache Harmony, produced predictable output when not seeded, and was exploited in the wild against Bitcoin wallet applications in August 2013. CVE-2019-15809, the Minerva case, records smart cards from Athena on an Atmel toolbox that used a fast ECDSA routine leaking the bit length of the nonce through timing, so that a local attacker measuring hundreds to thousands of signatures could compute the private key. Verification can fail as well: CVE-2020-0601 was a spoofing flaw in how Windows CryptoAPI validated elliptic-curve certificates, scored 8.1 and added on 3 November 2021 to the Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalogue of the Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency (CISA).

The standard answers are to stop drawing k from a random number generator. RFC 6979 (August 2013, T. Pornin) derives k deterministically from the private key and the message hash with an HMAC (hash-based message authentication code) construction, the HMAC_DRBG generator, so that the mapping from messages to k values is indistinguishable from random to anyone without the key; the signatures remain ordinary ECDSA signatures that unmodified verifiers accept, and only key generation still needs randomness. EdDSA, its neighbour, builds the same idea in. RFC 8032 (January 2017, S. Josefsson and I. Liusvaara) describes it as a variant of Schnorr signatures on Edwards curves that needs no unique random number per signature, resists side channels better, uses complete formulas with no exceptional points, and has 32-byte public keys and 64-byte signatures for Ed25519 (57 and 114 bytes for Ed448). FIPS 186-5 approves both, which is why new protocols often choose Ed25519 while certificate ecosystems remain on P-256 ECDSA.

The longer horizon is quantum. ECDSA, like RSA and EdDSA, is vulnerable to Shor's algorithm on a cryptanalytically relevant quantum computer, and NIST Interagency Report (IR) 8547, Transition to Post-Quantum Cryptography Standards, published in final form in October 2026 after a draft of 12 November 2024, sets the dates: ECDSA at 112 bits of security and above is deprecated after 2030 and disallowed under NIST standards after 2035, with ML-DSA (FIPS 204), SLH-DSA (FIPS 205) and the stateful hash-based Leighton-Micali Signature (LMS) and eXtended Merkle Signature Scheme (XMSS) as the replacements. NIST notes that its earlier guidance had projected disallowing 112-bit public-key schemes on 1 January 2031, and that federal high-value and high-impact systems face earlier deadlines under Executive Order 14412 and OMB (Office of Management and Budget) Memorandum M-26-15, including post-quantum signatures for the most sensitive systems by 31 December 2031. Until then, the practical rules are the ones the failures teach: use P-256 or larger with a vetted library, prefer deterministic nonces or Ed25519 where the protocol allows, and plan the inventory for the move to post-quantum signatures.

sha.def: The family of cryptographic hash functions standardized by the United States government: SHA-1, the SHA-2 group (SHA-224 to SHA-512) and the SHA-3 group, each turning a message of any length into a fixed-size digest that cannot feasibly be reversed or matched by another message.
sha.context: Secure Hash Algorithm (SHA) is the family published by the National Institute of Standards and Technology (NIST) in Federal Information Processing Standards (FIPS) 180-4 and 202. It includes SHA-256 and SHA-384, used for integrity checks, certificate signatures and as the hash inside HMAC (keyed-hash message authentication code). A digest is a fixed-length fingerprint, 256 bits or 64 hexadecimal characters for SHA-256, and any change to the input changes it. SHA-1 is broken for collision resistance, with a real collision published in 2017, and NIST wants it gone by 31 December 2030. SHA-3, standardized in 2015, is an alternative to SHA-2 built on a different design, not its replacement.
sha.depth:
A Secure Hash Algorithm (SHA) takes a message of almost any length and produces a short, fixed-length value, the message digest. Federal Information Processing Standards (FIPS) Publication 180-4, the Secure Hash Standard of the National Institute of Standards and Technology (NIST), says what makes such a function secure: it is computationally infeasible to find a message that corresponds to a given digest, or to find two different messages with the same digest, and any change to a message will, with very high probability, change the digest. NIST names three properties: preimage resistance, second preimage resistance and collision resistance. A hash is not encryption, since there is no key and nothing to decrypt, and by itself it authenticates nobody: anyone can recompute the digest of an altered message. It becomes a security mechanism when a digital signature or a keyed construction is applied on top of it.

The family has three generations. The first SHA appeared in FIPS 180 on 11 May 1993 and was withdrawn on 17 April 1995, the day FIPS 180-1 published SHA-1, which NIST describes as a slightly modified version. FIPS 180-2, in August 2002, added SHA-256, SHA-384 and SHA-512, the group now called SHA-2; SHA-224 arrived with a change notice in February 2004; FIPS 180-3 followed in October 2008; and FIPS 180-4, in March 2012, brought the count to seven with SHA-512/224 and SHA-512/256. The current text is dated August 2015, and in March 2023 NIST decided to revise it again. SHA-3 came from a public competition that NIST announced on 2 November 2007, after the attacks of 2004 and 2005 on older hash functions, and closed on 2 October 2012 by choosing the algorithm Keccak; it was standardized as FIPS 202 in August 2015.

SHA-1 and SHA-2 share one construction. The message is padded with a single 1 bit, then zeros, then its own length, so that it fills a whole number of blocks; each block is expanded into a message schedule and mixed into a running state, and the final state is the digest. The sizes are the numbers worth remembering. SHA-1 uses 512-bit blocks, 32-bit words, eighty steps per block and a 160-bit digest. SHA-224 and SHA-256 use 512-bit blocks, 32-bit words and sixty-four steps; SHA-384, SHA-512 and the two SHA-512/t variants use 1024-bit blocks, 64-bit words and eighty steps. Messages may be up to 2 to the power 64 bits long for the 512-bit-block functions and 2 to the power 128 for the others. SHA-224 is SHA-256 with different initial values and the output cut to 224 bits, and SHA-384 relates to SHA-512 in the same way. The constants are deliberately unremarkable: the first bits of the fractional parts of the cube roots of the first primes, with initial values taken from square roots.

Strength follows from digest length. Against collisions a function offers at most half its output size: NIST's table gives 128 bits for SHA-256, 192 for SHA-384, 256 for SHA-512, and less than 80 for SHA-1; against preimages the full length applies. NIST's policy since 2012 has encouraged SHA-256 at a minimum wherever interoperability is needed. In hexadecimal a SHA-1 digest is 40 characters, SHA-256 is 64, SHA-384 is 96 and SHA-512 is 128, which is often the quickest way to tell which function produced a value. A handy check of any implementation is the three-letter message abc, whose SHA-256 digest begins ba7816bf, one of the test vectors reproduced in Request for Comments (RFC) 6234.

SHA-1 is the cautionary tale. NIST deprecated it in 2011 and disallowed it for digital signatures at the end of 2013, citing the attack by Wang and colleagues and the growing reach of brute force. On 23 February 2017 researchers from CWI Amsterdam and Google (Marc Stevens, Elie Bursztein, Pierre Karpman, Ange Albertini and Yarik Markov) published the first real collision: two PDF (Portable Document Format) files with different contents and the same SHA-1 digest. The work took the equivalent of 2 to the power 63.1 SHA-1 computations, about nine quintillion, or 6,500 years of processor time and 110 years of graphics processor time, more than 100,000 times faster than brute force. In January 2020 Gaëtan Leurent and Thomas Peyrin went further with SHA-1 is a Shambles, the first chosen-prefix collision, in which the attacker picks both starting texts: 900 graphics cards for two months, about 75,000 US dollars, and a demonstration that forged a certification on a PGP (Pretty Good Privacy) key (CVE-2019-14855). Their summary was that every attack practical on MD5 (the Message-Digest Algorithm of RFC 1321) was now practical on SHA-1. On 15 December 2022 NIST announced that SHA-1 should be phased out by 31 December 2030, that a future FIPS 180-5 will remove it, and that modules still using it after that date will not be eligible for federal purchase.

The break is specific, and the rules reflect that. Collisions defeat signatures, so NIST Special Publication 800-131A disallows SHA-1 for generating digital signatures while still accepting it elsewhere, and NIST's policy keeps it permitted inside HMAC (keyed-hash message authentication code), key derivation and random number generation. Leurent and Peyrin said the same from the attacker's side: HMAC with SHA-1 seems relatively safe and preimage resistance is unbroken, though they recommend removing it everywhere. RFC 9155, of December 2021, deprecates MD5 and SHA-1 as signature hashes in TLS (Transport Layer Security) 1.2 and explicitly leaves HMAC with SHA-1 in record protection alone. For public certificates the CA/Browser Forum adopted its SHA-1 Sunset ballot on 16 October 2014 and, in ballot SC097, set 15 September 2026 as the end of all remaining SHA-1 signatures in certificates and revocation lists.

SHA-3 is not a longer SHA-2 but a different machine. It uses the sponge construction around a single permutation of 1600 bits applied in 24 rounds, with a capacity equal to twice the digest length. FIPS 202 defines four fixed-length functions, SHA3-224, SHA3-256, SHA3-384 and SHA3-512, and two extendable-output functions, SHAKE128 and SHAKE256, whose output can be as long as the caller asks. Keccak came from a team that includes Guido Bertoni, Joan Daemen, Michaël Peeters and Gilles Van Assche. One structural difference matters in practice. SHA-1 and SHA-2 have what the Keccak team calls the length-extension weakness, which is why a keyed digest is computed with the nested HMAC construction and never by simply hashing a key followed by a message; SHA-3 was designed to resist that attack. The standard says SHA-3 supplements the earlier functions, and NIST's position is that there is no need to move applications from SHA-2 to SHA-3.

In daily work the family appears mostly as names and commands. The cipher suites of TLS 1.3 end with the hash they use for key derivation: TLS_AES_128_GCM_SHA256, which every implementation must support, TLS_AES_256_GCM_SHA384 and TLS_CHACHA20_POLY1305_SHA256. In the older TLS 1.2 names a bare SHA, as in TLS_RSA_WITH_AES_128_CBC_SHA, means HMAC with SHA-1 and a 20-byte output, a frequent misreading when cipher lists are audited. On Linux the GNU tools sha224sum, sha256sum, sha384sum and sha512sum print and verify digests; openssl dgst defaults to SHA-256; and in PowerShell Get-FileHash does the same. The whole point of a published digest is that a download can be checked against it, which only helps when the digest came from somewhere the attacker could not also change.

What SHA is not for is storing passwords. The functions are designed to be fast, and a fast hash lets an attacker who steals a database try guesses at enormous rates; the OWASP Foundation's password storage guidance says plainly that fast algorithms such as SHA-256 are not suitable and points to Argon2id, scrypt, bcrypt or PBKDF2 (the password-based key derivation function of RFC 8018), the last of which wraps HMAC with SHA-256 in hundreds of thousands of iterations. The neighbours follow the same division of labour: SHA provides the fingerprint, HMAC adds a key, a signature adds an identity, and a password hash adds deliberate cost.

md5.def: MD5 (Message-Digest Algorithm 5) is a hash function designed by Ronald Rivest and published as RFC (Request for Comments) 1321 in April 1992 that maps any input to a 128-bit digest; practical collisions since 2004 make it unsafe wherever collision resistance matters.
md5.context: Message-Digest Algorithm 5 (MD5, RFC 1321) was once ubiquitous, in signatures, certificates and download checksums, but collisions have been cheap to compute for two decades. It survives as a non-security checksum and inside legacy protocols such as RADIUS (Remote Authentication Dial-In User Service), and must never be used where collision resistance matters: signatures, certificates, or any check an attacker can feed with chosen input.
md5.depth:
What it is. MD5, the Message-Digest Algorithm 5, was published by Ronald L. Rivest of the MIT Laboratory for Computer Science and RSA Data Security as RFC (Request for Comments) 1321 in April 1992. It takes a message of any length, pads it with a single 1 bit and zeros until its length is 448 modulo 512, appends the original length as a 64-bit value, and processes the result in 512-bit blocks through four rounds that update a 128-bit state; the final state is the digest, usually written as 32 hexadecimal characters. Rivest described it as an extension of MD4, slightly slower but more conservative: a fourth round, a unique additive constant per step, and changes meant to speed up the avalanche effect. The RFC stated its purpose plainly: digital signatures, where a large file is compressed before being signed with a private key under a scheme such as RSA.

The promise and how it broke. RFC 1321 conjectured that finding two messages with the same digest would cost on the order of 2^64 operations and finding a message for a given digest 2^128. RFC 6151 (March 2011, S. Turner of IECA and L. Chen of NIST) records the erosion: pseudo-collisions for the compression function in 1993, a compression-function collision in 1996, and in August 2004 the first full MD5 collisions, published by Xiaoyun Wang, Dengguo Feng, Xuejia Lai and Hongbo Yu, with the techniques detailed at EUROCRYPT 2005. Within a few years collisions took about a minute on a 1.6 GHz notebook and, by one 2007 claim, 10 seconds or less on a 2.6 GHz Pentium 4. Preimage resistance has held up far better: the best attack RFC 6151 cites costs 2^123.4, still impractical. The distinction matters: MD5 is broken for collisions, the property signatures depend on, not for reversing a digest.

Chosen prefixes made it practical. A plain collision gives two random-looking blocks with the same digest. A chosen-prefix collision lets the attacker start from two different meaningful prefixes, a harmless document and a harmful one, and append blocks that make the digests equal. Marc Stevens built the method in his 2007 master's thesis and published it with Arjen Lenstra and Benne de Weger at EUROCRYPT 2007, and on 30 December 2008, at the 25th Chaos Communication Congress, Alexander Sotirov, Stevens, Jacob Appelbaum, Lenstra, David Molnar, Dag Arne Osvik and de Weger showed a rogue certificate authority certificate: a commercial CA (certificate authority) still signing with MD5 issued them an ordinary website certificate whose signature was equally valid for a CA certificate of their own. The computation ran on about 200 PlayStation 3 consoles at EPFL (the Swiss Federal Institute of Technology in Lausanne), and the certificates bought for testing cost about USD 700. CERT/CC (the CERT Coordination Center) published VU#836068 the next day and told developers, CAs and users to avoid MD5 in any capacity.

The attacks that followed. In June 2012 Microsoft revoked trust in two Microsoft Enforced Licensing intermediate CAs after active attacks with unauthorized certificates derived from them, and on 7 June Stevens, at CWI (Centrum Wiskunde & Informatica) in Amsterdam, showed that the Flame espionage malware had used a previously unknown variant of a chosen-prefix collision to pass as a legitimate Microsoft security update. In July 2024 BlastRADIUS (CVE-2024-3596), by Sharon Goldberg, Miro Haller, Nadia Heninger, Mike Milano, Dan Shumow, Marc Stevens and Adam Suhl, turned the same technique on RADIUS (Remote Authentication Dial-In User Service): an attacker on the path between a network access server and its RADIUS server could change an Access-Reject into an Access-Accept by forging the MD5-based Response Authenticator, computing each collision in 3 to 6 minutes. The fix was to require the separate Message-Authenticator attribute, first in every response, which every RADIUS vendor the researchers knew of had implemented. What changed was not RADIUS but the cost of a chosen-prefix collision, as the researchers note: MD5 collisions dated from 2004, but none had been thought exploitable inside RADIUS.

Where it still lives, and whether that is wrong. MD5 remains in md5sum, which GNU coreutils now calls a legacy interface to cksum with the instruction not to use MD5 for security related purposes; in old protocols such as the TCP MD5 signature option for BGP (Border Gateway Protocol) sessions, RFC 2385 of August 1998, which RFC 5925's TCP Authentication Option replaced in June 2010; and in HMAC-MD5, which RFC 6151 says it is not urgent to stop using, because HMAC depends on different properties, while advising that new protocols should not use it. The useful test is whether an adversary chooses any of the input. A checksum against accidental corruption, or a hash key in a data structure, has no adversary, and MD5 still works there, although CERT/CC's stronger advice is to avoid it everywhere so that it does not drift into a place where an adversary appears. A signature, a certificate, a file allow-list, a deduplication store fed by users, or any integrity check on downloaded code does have one.

Passwords were wrong for another reason. MD5 was designed to be fast on 32-bit machines, and speed is exactly what password storage must not have. NIST's SP (Special Publication) 800-63B-4 (July 2025) requires passwords to be salted and hashed with a password hashing scheme that takes a salt of at least 32 bits and a cost factor raised over time, because attackers holding a stolen database compute many billions of hashes per second. An unsalted or salted MD5 password hash fails that requirement whatever its collision properties.

Numbers worth remembering: a 128-bit digest, 512-bit blocks, four rounds, the 2^64 collision bound that fell to seconds, 2004 for the first collisions, 2008 for the rogue CA, 2012 for Flame, 2024 for BlastRADIUS.

dtls.def: TLS (Transport Layer Security) adapted to run over UDP (User Datagram Protocol) instead of TCP (Transmission Control Protocol): the same handshake and record protection, rebuilt to survive lost, duplicated and reordered packets.
dtls.context: Datagram Transport Layer Security (DTLS), whose current version 1.3 is Request for Comments (RFC) 9147, brings the confidentiality and integrity of TLS (Transport Layer Security) to datagram transports that can reorder or lose packets. It is used for things like VPN (virtual private network) data channels and real-time media, where a delayed packet is worth less than a lost one. Each record carries its own sequence number so that it can be decrypted alone, the handshake does its own retransmission and fragmentation, and a cookie exchange stops a forged source address from turning the server into an amplifier.
dtls.depth:
DTLS (Datagram Transport Layer Security) is TLS (Transport Layer Security) adapted for datagrams, and it exists because TLS assumes a reliable, ordered stream that UDP (User Datagram Protocol) does not provide. Applications that need encryption without the head-of-line blocking of TCP (Transmission Control Protocol) cannot simply run TLS over UDP, because a single lost record would break the stream the protocol depends on. The design paper by Nagendra Modadugu and Eric Rescorla named the applications that were stuck: video conferencing, internet telephony and online games, all delay-sensitive, which could choose only among IPsec (Internet Protocol Security), a home-made security protocol or a move to TCP. Their answer was to change TLS as little as possible, and the specification still says DTLS is deliberately as similar to TLS as it can be, to minimize new security invention and reuse code.

Request for Comments (RFC) 9147 lists exactly four reasons why TLS cannot run over datagrams, and the adaptation is the answer to each. TLS numbers its records implicitly, so one missing record makes every later one undecipherable; DTLS writes a sequence number into each record, which makes records independently decryptable. The TLS handshake is lock-step and assumes its messages arrive in order; DTLS gives handshake messages their own sequence numbers and a retransmission timer. Handshake messages can be larger than a datagram, in theory up to 2 to the power 24 minus 1 bytes against the usual limit of less than 1500; DTLS adds a fragment offset and a fragment length to each handshake message. And a datagram server can be abused against third parties, which the cookie exchange addresses. What DTLS does not add is reliability for application data: lost and reordered application datagrams stay lost and reordered, by design.

The cookie exchange has a specific reason. Without it an attacker can make the server allocate state and perform expensive cryptography for a client that never existed, or send connection requests with the forged source address of a victim, who then receives the much larger reply, a certificate chain for instance. DTLS borrowed the stateless cookie technique of Photuris and of IKE (Internet Key Exchange), the key exchange of IPsec: the server answers the first ClientHello with a small message carrying a cookie and does nothing more until the client repeats its request with the cookie, proving that it can receive at the address it claims. In DTLS 1.0 and 1.2 that message is HelloVerifyRequest; DTLS 1.3 uses the HelloRetryRequest of TLS 1.3 with a cookie extension. The exchange is optional for the server, and that option has a history. In December 2020 Citrix warned of a distributed denial-of-service pattern that exhausted the outbound bandwidth of its ADC and Gateway appliances through DTLS; its remedy, released in January 2021, was a build in which administrators enable HelloVerifyRequest in each DTLS profile.

Versions follow TLS, with one number missing. DTLS 1.0 (RFC 4347, April 2006) was written as a delta from TLS 1.1, and DTLS 1.2 (RFC 6347, January 2012) as a delta from TLS 1.2; there is no DTLS 1.1, the number having been skipped to line up with TLS. DTLS 1.3 (RFC 9147, April 2022, by Eric Rescorla, Hannes Tschofenig and Nagendra Modadugu) is a Proposed Standard based on TLS 1.3 and gives the same guarantees except for order protection and non-replayability. On the wire the versions are 0xfeff, 0xfefd and 0xfefc, counting downwards. RFC 8996 has forbidden negotiating DTLS 1.0 since March 2021. Version 1.3 keeps only AEAD (authenticated encryption with associated data) ciphers, shortens the record header, encrypts the record sequence numbers, adds an ACK message so that a peer can say which handshake records arrived, and brings in connection identifiers.

The numbers that matter in a capture are few. A DTLS 1.2 record carries a 2-byte epoch, which counts key changes, and a 48-bit sequence number in front of the usual length, 13 bytes of header where TLS has 5. The handshake timer starts at 1 second and doubles on each retransmission, up to at least 60 seconds; for DTLS-SRTP the specification recommends 400 milliseconds, because a call cannot wait. Replay protection is an optional sliding window of received record numbers, the technique of IPsec. RC4 (Rivest Cipher 4) was banned from DTLS from the start, since a stream cipher cannot decrypt a record without all the previous ones. Path MTU (maximum transmission unit) discovery is left mostly to the application. The connection identifier answers a problem of NAT (network address translation): a DTLS association used to be identified by the peer's address and port, so a rebinding in the middle, common with battery-powered devices that sleep, killed it and forced a new handshake. RFC 9146 added the identifier to DTLS 1.2 in March 2022, and RFC 9853 added a return routability check to go with it in March 2026.

Where it shows up in practice is worth knowing. WebRTC, the real-time communication suite built into browsers, requires DTLS: the handshake supplies the keys for the Secure Real-time Transport Protocol (SRTP) that protects the media, under RFC 5764, and carries the data channels. The Constrained Application Protocol (CoAP) of small devices runs over DTLS under the coaps scheme, by default on port 5684. Wireless controllers wrap CAPWAP (Control And Provisioning of Wireless Access Points) in DTLS, with control on UDP port 5246 and data on 5247. Many VPN (virtual private network) products use it for the data channel, and the Zscaler tunnel does too. FortiGate offers it for SSL VPN (set dtls-tunnel enable) with the stated purpose of avoiding the retransmission problems of TCP inside TCP. On F5 BIG-IP Access Policy Manager (APM) a network access resource has a DTLS check box with default port 4433, served by a second virtual server on the same address as the HTTPS (Hypertext Transfer Protocol Secure) one, and compression is not active when DTLS is used.

The operational habits follow from the transport. A DTLS tunnel needs its UDP port open end to end, so products pair it with a TLS connection on TCP that is established first and stays available when UDP is filtered; a tunnel that works but feels slow is often one that fell back. Datagrams that exceed the path MTU are dropped or fragmented below the protocol, so tunnel overhead has to be counted. Support for version 1.3 is still arriving: the OpenSSL project lists DTLS 1.3 among the features of its 4.1 release, a section of its news file still marked as under development when read.

QUIC solves the same problem differently, building its own reliability and encryption together over UDP rather than adapting TLS records. RFC 9001 says it uses keys from a TLS 1.3 handshake but carries no TLS records at all, taking over the record layer's job itself, and that is the route HTTP/3 (RFC 9114, June 2022) took. The division of labour is now fairly clean: QUIC where an application wants reliable streams without TCP, DTLS where it wants plain datagrams that are merely protected, and DTLS-SRTP where DTLS only supplies the keys.

ocsp.def: The Online Certificate Status Protocol (OCSP): a request and response protocol, specified in Request for Comments (RFC) 6960, by which a client asks a certificate authority's responder whether one certificate is good, revoked or unknown, and receives a signed, dated answer.
ocsp.context: The Online Certificate Status Protocol (OCSP), defined in Request for Comments (RFC) 6960, lets a client ask a responder whether a certificate is still valid, an alternative to downloading large certificate revocation lists (CRLs). OCSP stapling lets the server present the signed answer itself, avoiding a separate round trip and the privacy leak of the client asking. Since the forum where certificate authorities (CAs) and browser makers set the rules, the CA/Browser Forum, made OCSP optional in 2023, large CAs such as Let's Encrypt have switched their responders off, and browsers increasingly check revocation against lists pushed to them, such as Firefox's CRLite.
ocsp.depth:
The Online Certificate Status Protocol (OCSP) answers a question certificates cannot answer themselves: has this certificate been revoked since it was issued. A certificate carries its own expiry, but revocation is a decision made afterwards, so the client has to ask somewhere. Request for Comments (RFC) 6960 (June 2013, obsoleting RFC 2560 and RFC 6277) describes OCSP as a way to determine a certificate's current status without requiring certificate revocation lists (CRLs). The request names the certificate by a CertID: a hash algorithm, the hash of the issuer's distinguished name, the hash of the issuer's public key and the serial number. The responder, usually found through the certificate's Authority Information Access extension, returns a signed response with one of three statuses, good, revoked or unknown, plus thisUpdate and nextUpdate times that bound its freshness and a producedAt time; an optional nonce extension binds response to request against replay. Errors (malformedRequest, internalError, tryLater, sigRequired, unauthorized) are not signed. Over HTTP (Hypertext Transfer Protocol), requests under 255 bytes after encoding may use GET so that caches can serve them, and larger ones use POST with the content type application/ocsp-request; openssl ocsp, with -issuer, -cert, -url, -nonce and -resp_text, is the usual way to ask by hand.

The statuses are narrower than they sound. RFC 6960 says good means only that no certificate with that serial number, within its validity interval, is revoked; it does not mean the certificate was ever issued. The 2013 revision therefore allowed responders to answer revoked for serial numbers the certificate authority (CA) never issued, and kept unknown for requests it cannot speak to, such as an issuer it does not serve. The DigiNotar breach of 2011 showed why. Fox-IT's report for the Dutch government found rogue certificates whose serial numbers did not appear in the CA's records, so the responder could not tell them apart from good ones; on 1 September 2011, on Fox-IT's advice, it was switched to a whitelist of known valid certificates, effectively revoking every unknown one. The same OCSP logs were the measure of the damage: requests for the rogue google.com certificate came from 298,140 unique IP (Internet Protocol) addresses, a figure that missed every user of Internet Explorer 6, which sent no OCSP requests at all.

The naive design had two serious problems. Every client contacting the CA for every connection is a privacy leak, since the authority learns which sites a given IP address visits; Let's Encrypt noted that even a CA that keeps no such logs could be legally compelled to collect them, and Mozilla adds that OCSP usually travels over unencrypted HTTP, so every on-path observer learns it too. It is also a performance dependency: Mozilla measured OCSP requests blocking the TLS (Transport Layer Security) handshake for 100 ms at the median, and a slow or unreachable responder delays or breaks the connection. Worse, clients that fail open, which Let's Encrypt says most implementations do, gain no security at all against an attacker who can also block the responder; as RFC 7633 puts it, a client cannot draw any conclusion from missing status information unless it knows the legitimate server would have provided it.

Stapling is the fix that stuck, for a while. RFC 6066 (January 2011) defined the status_request extension: the client asks for status in its hello, and the server, which fetches its own signed OCSP response periodically, sends it in a certificate_status handshake message (type 22), with a bad_certificate_status_response alert (113) for a response the client rejects. The client gets a fresh answer with no extra request, no privacy leak and no third-party dependency in the connection path. RFC 6961 (June 2013) added status_request_v2 (17) so that status for intermediate CA certificates could be stapled too, but TLS 1.3, RFC 8446 (August 2018), obsoleted it: the response now travels in a status_request extension attached to the certificate entry it covers, and servers must ignore status_request_v2. With OpenSSL, s_client -status asks for a stapled response and prints whatever comes back.

Must-staple goes further by marking the certificate as requiring it, which closes the fail-open hole. RFC 7633 (October 2015, P. Hallam-Baker) defines the TLS Feature extension, id-pe-tlsfeature (id-pe 24); a certificate that lists status_request lets the client fail immediately when no response is stapled, with no need to query the responder, which also removes the denial-of-service attack on the client or on the responder. In practice it never became a default. Let's Encrypt, which had offered it for years, wrote in December 2024 that Must-Staple had failed to get wide browser support and that popular web servers still implemented stapling in ways that created serious risks of downtime; it began refusing new Must-Staple requests on 30 January 2025 and refused all of them from 7 May 2025.

The policy turn came from the root programmes. CA/Browser Forum Ballot SC-063, proposed by Ryan Dickson and Chris Clements of Google's Chrome Root Program and endorsed by Microsoft and Sectigo, was voted on from 6 to 13 July 2023, with 28 certificate issuers and 3 certificate consumers in favour and one issuer against. It made OCSP optional for publicly trusted CAs, required CRLs, full or partitioned, republished within 24 hours of a revocation and at least every seven days (four if certificates carry no OCSP pointer), and defined short-lived certificates, initially up to ten days and up to seven from 15 March 2026, that need neither a CRL nor an OCSP pointer because expiry does the revoking. Let's Encrypt, citing privacy and the cost of running the service, announced its intent to leave OCSP on 23 July 2024, dropped OCSP URLs from new certificates on 7 May 2025 and turned its responders off on 6 August 2025, after a peak of about 340 billion requests a month, more than 140,000 a second at its content delivery network (CDN).

What replaces it is revocation pushed to the client. Mozilla's CRLite, enabled for all desktop Firefox users from version 137 and described by John Schanck on 19 August 2025, compresses the set of all revoked certificates that appear in Certificate Transparency logs into a structure Firefox downloads, updates every 12 hours and queries locally on every connection: about 300 kB a day, a 4 MB snapshot every 45 days plus deltas, against roughly 300 MB for the 3,000 or so CRLs the CAs in Mozilla's root store disclose. Mozilla announced that Firefox 142 would stop using OCSP for domain-validated certificates. The broader direction of travel is shorter certificate lifetimes, which reduce the window revocation is needed for in the first place; with seven-day certificates, the attacker holding a stolen key has, at most, a week.

sni.def: Server Name Indication (SNI) is a Transport Layer Security (TLS) extension in which the client names the host it wants in its ClientHello, so that a server holding many sites on one IP (Internet Protocol) address can choose the right certificate and configuration before encryption begins.
sni.context: Defined first in RFC (Request for Comments) 3546 in 2003 and today in RFC 6066, section 3, Server Name Indication (SNI) carries one DNS (Domain Name System) hostname, in ASCII with no trailing dot and never an IP (Internet Protocol) literal, in the server_name extension of the TLS (Transport Layer Security) ClientHello. Servers use it to pick a certificate and policy; load balancers and firewalls read it to route, filter or decide what to decrypt. It travels unencrypted in TLS 1.2 and TLS 1.3 alike, the gap that Encrypted Client Hello (ECH, RFC 9849, March 2026) closes.
sni.depth:
Why it exists. Server Name Indication (SNI) solves a sequencing problem. In HTTPS (Hypertext Transfer Protocol Secure) the requested hostname travels in the HTTP Host header, but that header arrives inside the encrypted session, and the server has to present its certificate before any of it can be decrypted. RFC (Request for Comments) 6066 states the gap plainly: TLS (Transport Layer Security) gave the client no way to tell the server the name of the server it is contacting, which mattered for servers hosting several virtual servers at one network address. Without SNI one address and port could present only one certificate, or one certificate naming every site behind it; RFC 9525 notes that the second option makes every named site only as safe as the weakest server holding that certificate.

On the wire. The client puts a server_name extension, type 0, in its ClientHello. It carries a ServerNameList whose only defined name type is host_name (0); the hostname is a byte string of 1 to 65,535 octets, the fully qualified DNS (Domain Name System) name in ASCII without a trailing dot, with internationalized names sent as A-labels and compared without regard to case. Literal IPv4 and IPv6 addresses are not permitted, and the list may hold only one name of each type; earlier versions allowed several, but clients sent one and could not tell which the server had chosen. A server that used the name answers with an empty server_name extension, in the ServerHello for TLS 1.2 and in EncryptedExtensions for TLS 1.3. A server that does not recognize the name may abort with a fatal unrecognized_name alert (112) or carry on; a warning-level alert is not recommended because clients react to it unpredictably. On resumption the name must match, or the server falls back to a full handshake.

History and status. SNI first appeared in RFC 3546 (June 2003), the TLS extensions document that updated TLS 1.0, passed through RFC 4366, and has been specified in RFC 6066 (January 2011, Donald Eastlake 3rd) since. TLS 1.3, RFC 8446 (August 2018), made it mandatory to implement: every implementation must support it for applications that can use it, clients should send it when applicable, and a server may require it, answering a ClientHello without it with a missing_extension alert. RFC 9525 (November 2023), the current rules for checking a server's identity, observes that SNI is no longer new but commonplace.

The privacy cost. The hostname was meant for the server, but it crosses the network in clear text, and RFC 8744 (July 2020) records that the security considerations of RFC 3546, RFC 4366 and RFC 6066 never flagged that. Middlebox developers found it useful: for censorship, for ISP (internet service provider) filtering and parental controls, for assigning QoS (quality of service) profiles, for enterprise firewalls blocking sites, and for exempting healthcare or banking sites from TLS inspection; the same RFC says pervasive surveillance probably collects it too. TLS 1.3 encrypted the certificate but left the ClientHello, and with it SNI, readable. Several proposals to encrypt SNI were rejected after security reviews found plausible attacks.

Encrypted Client Hello. RFC 9849 (March 2026, Eric Rescorla, Kazuho Oku, Nick Sullivan and Christopher Wood) calls plaintext SNI perhaps the most sensitive information left unencrypted in TLS 1.3. With Encrypted Client Hello (ECH) the client builds a private ClientHelloInner, encrypts it to the server's public key with HPKE (Hybrid Public Key Encryption), and sends it inside a ClientHelloOuter whose visible SNI names the provider's client-facing server. That server either decrypts and passes the inner hello to the backend, in shared mode the same machine and in split mode a separate origin, or rejects ECH and finishes with the outer hello so the client can retry with a fresh configuration. The configuration is published in DNS through SVCB (service binding) and HTTPS records under RFC 9848. ECH also hides the ALPN (Application-Layer Protocol Negotiation) list, but it reveals the provider, and the target can still leak through plaintext DNS queries or the server's IP address. It works with TLS 1.3, DTLS (Datagram TLS) 1.3 and later versions.

In the products. On F5 BIG-IP, several client SSL (Secure Sockets Layer) profiles can share one virtual server from version 11.1.0, each with a Server Name; the profile marked Default SSL Profile for SNI answers when nothing matches, a client that sends no SNI gets that default certificate, and Require Peer SNI Support makes the system drop such clients instead. FortiGate certificate inspection looks only at the headers up to the SSL/TLS layer; its server certificate SNI check compares the ClientHello name with the certificate's CN (common name) or SAN (subject alternative name) and, on a mismatch, either filters on the certificate's CN (enable) or closes the connection (strict). With OpenSSL, s_client -servername sets the name, the host given to -connect is used automatically when it looks like a DNS name, the default since 1.1.1, and -noservername sends none, which is how to reproduce what an old or IP-addressed client sees.

What goes wrong. Most SNI incidents look like certificate errors and are name-selection errors. A client connecting by IP address sends no SNI, so it receives whatever the server presents by default; RFC 9525 adds that a server meant to be reached by address has to present that identity on connections without SNI. A client that negotiates one name in SNI and requests another in the Host header gets a certificate for the first, which RFC 6066 anticipates by saying the client should not request a different name at the application layer. A load balancer that routes on SNI while the application routes on Host, or a wildcard certificate that covers one name and not the other, produces the same symptom. The diagnosis is nearly always the same question: which name was the decision made on? Capturing the ClientHello, or repeating the connection with s_client and an explicit -servername, answers it.

alpn.def: Application-Layer Protocol Negotiation (ALPN) is the Transport Layer Security (TLS) extension, defined in Request for Comments (RFC) 7301, in which a client lists the application protocols it can speak, such as h2 or http/1.1, and the server picks one inside the handshake, so that no extra round trip is needed.
alpn.context: Application-Layer Protocol Negotiation (ALPN), Request for Comments (RFC) 7301, lets client and server agree during the Transport Layer Security (TLS) handshake on the protocol that will run over the connection, for example h2 for HTTP/2 (Hypertext Transfer Protocol version 2), avoiding an extra negotiation round trip. The client sends its list, most preferred first, in the ClientHello; the server returns exactly one name or ends the handshake with a no_application_protocol alert. HTTP/2 over TLS, HTTP/3 and QUIC all depend on it, and because the client's list travels in the ClientHello, firewalls, load balancers and fingerprinting tools read it too.
alpn.depth:
Application-Layer Protocol Negotiation (ALPN) solves a problem created by the success of port 443. Request for Comments (RFC) 7301 (July 2014, by S. Friedl of Cisco, A. Popov of Microsoft, A. Langley of Google and E. Stephan of Orange) starts from the observation that application protocols are increasingly carried inside Transport Layer Security (TLS), to use the secure paths already open on port 443 almost everywhere, and that when several protocols share one server port the two ends must agree, for each connection, on which one to speak. Doing that after the handshake would cost a round trip; ALPN does it inside the handshake. The work was requested by the HTTPbis working group of the Internet Engineering Task Force (IETF) to negotiate HTTP/2 (Hypertext Transfer Protocol version 2) over TLS, but the mechanism is generic, and it also lets a server present a different certificate for each application protocol if it wishes.

The mechanism is one extension, application_layer_protocol_negotiation, type 16. In the ClientHello its data is a ProtocolNameList: the protocols the client supports, in descending order of preference, each an opaque, non-empty byte string of up to 255 octets registered with the Internet Assigned Numbers Authority (IANA); empty strings are forbidden and names must not be truncated. The server ignores names it does not recognize and is expected to hold its own list in preference order: it should choose the most preferred protocol that it supports and the client also offered, and return a list holding exactly one name. If nothing matches, it must end the handshake with the fatal no_application_protocol alert, number 120. The choice is definitive for the connection, and a server must not select one protocol and then speak another. Without the extension the protocol is whatever the port implies, which is how it was always determined before ALPN.

The names live in the IANA registry Application-Layer Protocol Negotiation (ALPN) Protocol IDs, which RFC 7301 created under the Expert Review policy with http/1.1, spdy/1, spdy/2 and spdy/3 as its first entries. It now has 59 rows: h2 (HTTP/2 over TLS, RFC 9113), h3 (HTTP/3, RFC 9114), http/1.0 and http/0.9, acme-tls/1, dot for DNS (Domain Name System) over TLS and doq for DNS over QUIC, imap, pop3, ftp, smb, postgresql, mqtt, radius/1.0 and radius/1.1, among others. Sixteen of the rows are two-octet values from 0x0A 0x0A to 0xFA 0xFA, reserved by RFC 8701 (January 2020) for GREASE (Generate Random Extensions And Sustain Extensibility), which a client may advertise so that servers keep handling unknown values correctly. One entry is a trap: h2c, HTTP/2 over cleartext TCP (Transmission Control Protocol), is registered only to reserve the name and is not allowed to appear in a TLS ALPN negotiation.

The web is where ALPN matters most. RFC 9113 (June 2022, obsoleting RFC 7540), the current HTTP/2 specification, says that a client requesting an https URI (uniform resource identifier) uses TLS with ALPN, that HTTP/2 over TLS uses the identifier h2, and that h2c must never be sent by a client or selected by a server; HTTP/2 over TLS must use TLS protocol negotiation, and prior knowledge (sending the HTTP/2 connection preface straight away) is only for cleartext TCP. The same RFC deprecated the old upgrade to h2c through the Upgrade header as never widely deployed. HTTP/3 runs over QUIC on UDP (User Datagram Protocol) rather than TCP, so RFC 9114 (June 2022) has the client use the token h3 in the QUIC handshake, an origin advertise it beforehand through the Alt-Svc response header or the HTTP/2 ALTSVC frame, and a client fall back to TCP-based HTTP when UDP is blocked. The Domain Name System (DNS) can carry the same information before the first connection: the SVCB (service binding) and HTTPS records of RFC 9460 (November 2023) have an alpn parameter listing the identifiers an endpoint supports, and from it the client also learns the transport, QUIC over UDP or TLS over TCP.

In QUIC the extension is not optional. RFC 9001 (May 2021) requires authenticated protocol negotiation from the handshake, makes ALPN the mechanism unless another is agreed, and has either endpoint close the connection immediately with no_application_protocol, carried as QUIC error 0x0178, when no protocol is negotiated; the server must also choose a protocol compatible with the QUIC version the client selected. TLS 1.3, now RFC 9846 (July 2026, obsoleting RFC 8446), moved the server's half: the extension is allowed in the ClientHello and in EncryptedExtensions, so the server's choice travels encrypted while the client's offer remains visible. Session resumption ties the protocol to the keys: the parameters of 0-RTT (zero round-trip time) early data, the ALPN protocol among them, are those of the pre-shared key in use, and a TLS implementation must not automatically resend rejected early data unless the new connection selected the same ALPN protocol.

ALPN replaced an earlier design. Next Protocol Negotiation (NPN), described in Internet-Drafts by Adam Langley of Google (the fourth revision is dated May 2012), was used to negotiate SPDY on port 443 and worked the other way round: the server listed its protocols in the ServerHello and the client made the choice, sending it in an encrypted message just before its Finished message, so the selected protocol was hidden from the network. ALPN moved the decision to the server and into the clear, and RFC 7301 explains why: a plaintext selection lets network elements give a connection differentiated service when the port does not identify the protocol, lets a server choose a certificate or reroute the connection according to the protocol, and avoids false confidence about hiding it; if the protocol has to be hidden, renegotiation after the connection is established is the way to do it. OpenSSL's s_client still documents both switches, -alpn and -nextprotoneg, states that ALPN is the IETF standard and replaces NPN, and refuses -nextprotoneg together with -tls1_3.

Visibility cuts both ways. The security section of RFC 7301 says that ALPN does not affect the security of the TLS session but provides an externally visible marker of the application protocol, which observers used to infer from the port, and warns that clients on TLS 1.2 and earlier send the identifiers in the clear, so an identifier that could leak personal information should not be used where it would be visible. The protection side was measured by the ALPACA study of Marcus Brinkmann and seven co-authors (USENIX Security Symposium 2021). TLS does not bind a connection to the intended application protocol, so a man-in-the-middle can redirect TLS traffic to another service that accepts the same certificate, for instance from a web server to an SMTP (Simple Mail Transfer Protocol), IMAP (Internet Message Access Protocol), POP3 (Post Office Protocol version 3) or FTP (File Transfer Protocol) server under a shared wildcard certificate; they found 1.4 million web servers generally exposed to such cross-protocol confusion and 114,000 attackable through an exploitable application server, and discussed ALPN and SNI (Server Name Indication) as mitigations. RFC 9113 had already noted that completing a handshake with an ALPN identifier for HTTP/2 is sufficient protection against cross-protocol attacks, because it is a positive indication that the server is willing to speak HTTP/2.

On the command line, openssl s_client -connect host:443 -alpn h2,http/1.1 offers both protocols, most desirable first, and reports which one the server chose; without -alpn nothing is offered at all. curl enables ALPN by default whenever its TLS library supports it, uses it to negotiate HTTP/2 for https URLs and can switch it off with --no-alpn; its manual adds that curl does not itself insist on TLS 1.2 or later for HTTP/2, as the specification requires, unless --tlsv1.2 is given. In Wireshark the field tls.handshake.extensions_alpn_str shows the offered and chosen names. On F5 BIG-IP the HTTP/2 profile's activation-modes setting decides what makes a connection HTTP/2: alpn, the default, relies on the TLS negotiation, so clients that support only HTTP/1.1 carry on as if HTTP/2 were absent, while always treats every connection as HTTP/2; enforce-tls-requirements, enabled by default, applies the TLS conditions of the HTTP/2 specification. The ACME (Automatic Certificate Management Environment) tls-alpn-01 challenge of RFC 8737 (February 2020) shows the mechanism doing something other than choosing HTTP: the validation server connects on TCP port 443, negotiates acme-tls/1 with the domain being validated in SNI, and expects a special certificate that carries the answer to the challenge.

Most ALPN trouble shows up as a protocol mismatch rather than a clear error. A client that offers only h2 to a server without HTTP/2 gets alert 120 in TLS or error 0x0178 in QUIC; a device that terminates TLS answers ALPN from its own configuration, not the backend's, which is exactly what the BIG-IP activation setting controls; and a client that sends no extension simply gets the port's default protocol. The neighbours are easily confused. SNI, another ClientHello extension, names the host the client wants, while ALPN names the protocol. Alt-Svc and the HTTPS DNS record announce in advance which protocols an endpoint offers, and ALPN makes the actual choice on each connection. GREASE values in the list are deliberate noise, not protocols. The numbers worth remembering are extension 16, alert 120, QUIC error 0x0178, names of up to 255 octets, and the tokens http/1.1, h2 and h3.

ecdhe.def: Ephemeral Elliptic Curve Diffie-Hellman: a key agreement in which both sides of a session generate fresh elliptic-curve key pairs, derive a shared secret and then discard the private halves, so recorded traffic stays safe even if a long-term key later leaks.
ecdhe.context: Ephemeral Elliptic Curve Diffie-Hellman (ECDHE) is the key exchange behind almost every modern Transport Layer Security (TLS) connection: RFC (Request for Comments) 8422 defined it for TLS 1.2 until RFC 9846, the July 2026 revision of TLS 1.3, obsoleted that document, and in TLS 1.3 every public-key exchange is ephemeral. In TLS 1.2 it is the one public-key exchange that RFC 10015 (July 2026) leaves untouched: that document deprecates RSA (Rivest-Shamir-Adleman) and finite-field Diffie-Hellman key exchange and discourages static elliptic-curve Diffie-Hellman (ECDH). The ephemeral part means the private keys exist for one handshake only, which is what gives forward secrecy; the elliptic-curve part keeps the keys small and fast (32 bytes for X25519). It agrees on a secret but proves nothing about identity, so a certificate signature still does the authentication.
ecdhe.depth:
ECDHE (Ephemeral Elliptic Curve Diffie-Hellman) is Diffie-Hellman key agreement carried out in an elliptic-curve group, with key pairs that live for a single handshake. Each side picks a random private value, sends the matching public value (a point on the curve, or for X25519 only a 32-byte coordinate) and combines its own private value with the peer's public one; both arrive at the same shared secret, and an eavesdropper who saw both public values cannot compute it. In Transport Layer Security (TLS) that secret is not the session key itself but the input from which the key schedule derives the traffic keys. Two things it is not. It is not authentication: on its own it is open to a man-in-the-middle like any unauthenticated exchange, which is why the server signs its key share in TLS 1.2 and signs the entire handshake (the CertificateVerify message) in TLS 1.3, with the private key behind its certificate. And it is not static ECDH (Elliptic Curve Diffie-Hellman), where the server's elliptic-curve key sits in its certificate and serves every connection; Request for Comments (RFC) 8422 removed the ECDH_RSA and ECDH_ECDSA key exchanges from its specification, and RFC 10015 (July 2026) formally discourages the static ECDH cipher suites in TLS 1.2, which the registry of the Internet Assigned Numbers Authority (IANA) now marks D, for discouraged.

For TLS 1.2 and earlier the rules were written in RFC 8422 (August 2018), which obsoleted RFC 4492 and was itself obsoleted by RFC 9846 in July 2026. It defines three key exchange algorithms, all ephemeral: ECDHE_ECDSA, authenticated by an ECDSA (Elliptic Curve Digital Signature Algorithm) or EdDSA (Edwards-curve Digital Signature Algorithm) signature; ECDHE_RSA, authenticated by an RSA (Rivest-Shamir-Adleman) signature, so a server can keep its existing RSA certificate; and ECDH_anon, with no signature and therefore exposed to man-in-the-middle attacks. The server's ephemeral public key travels in the ServerKeyExchange message with the named curve and a signature over both, made with the private key of the server's certificate; the client answers with its own ephemeral key in ClientKeyExchange, and the shared secret becomes the premaster secret. The key exchange is part of the cipher suite name, so TLS_ECDHE_ECDSA_WITH_AES_128_GCM_SHA256 (code 0xC0,0x2B) reads as ECDHE key agreement, ECDSA authentication, then the record cipher and hash. RFC 8422 is frank about cost: ECDHE_RSA is more expensive for the server than the old RSA key exchange, which provides no forward secrecy. Its housekeeping still shapes the wire: of the 25 curves RFC 4492 had defined, only three had seen much use, so curves 1 to 22 and the explicit-curve options were deprecated, leaving secp256r1 (23), secp384r1 (24) and secp521r1 (25), with X25519 (29) and X448 (30) added; every point format except uncompressed was dropped as well.

TLS 1.3 made the ephemeral exchange the only public-key option. RFC 8446 (August 2018) removed the static RSA and Diffie-Hellman cipher suites so that all public-key based key exchange mechanisms provide forward secrecy, and RFC 9846 (July 2026), the revised TLS 1.3 specification, keeps that rule while obsoleting RFC 8446, the TLS 1.2 specification RFC 5246, and RFC 8422 itself. The key exchange also left the cipher suite: a TLS 1.3 suite such as TLS_AES_128_GCM_SHA256 names only record protection and hash, and the group is negotiated on its own. The client lists the groups it supports in the supported_groups extension (type 10) and, in key_share (type 51), sends public values for the groups it guesses the server will choose; the server answers with its own share in the ServerHello, or, if no guess fits, with a HelloRetryRequest naming a group, and the client starts the handshake again. A compliant implementation must support key exchange with secp256r1 (the P-256 curve of the National Institute of Standards and Technology, NIST) and should support X25519. Encodings are fixed per group: a P-256 share is an uncompressed point of 65 bytes (one format byte and two 32-byte coordinates) whose validity the peer must check, and an X25519 share is 32 bytes. One exception to the forward-secrecy rule remains: a session resumed with a pre-shared key (PSK) in the psk_ke mode, without a fresh Diffie-Hellman exchange, gives up forward secrecy for its application data, while psk_dhe_ke keeps it.

X25519, the group most connections now use, comes from RFC 7748 (January 2016), an informational document of the Crypto Forum Research Group of the Internet Research Task Force (IRTF). It specifies curve25519, a Montgomery curve over the prime 2^255 minus 19 for the 128-bit security level, and curve448, over 2^448 minus 2^224 minus 1, for about 224 bits, both chosen because they lend themselves to constant-time implementation. The exchange is short enough to state whole: each side generates 32 random bytes, sends X25519 of that value and the base point 9, then computes X25519 of its own secret and the peer's value, and both hold the same 32 bytes. A peer that sends a point of small order forces the result to all zeros, so a TLS implementation must check for an all-zero premaster secret and abort. The other common curves, secp256r1, secp384r1 and secp521r1, are the ones RFC 8422 calls the NIST curves because NIST originally standardized them. With them the check is different: each party must verify that the x and y values it received satisfy the curve equation, and RFC 8422 says what skipping that costs, an attacker learning enough to recover the entire private key in a few requests if the key is not really ephemeral.

What the ephemeral part buys is forward secrecy, and its value is retrospective. Under RSA key transport the client encrypts the premaster secret to the server's long-term RSA key, so anyone who records the traffic and later obtains that key can decrypt every recorded session. With ECDHE there is no such master key: the private values are discarded when the handshake ends, and the server's long-term key only signs. RFC 8422 attaches a condition that is easy to miss: the algorithms provide forward secrecy if and only if fresh ephemeral keys are generated and used, and also destroyed after use, so a server that reuses one ECDHE key across many connections for speed quietly brings back a long-lived secret. Static RSA endangers even TLS 1.3: RFC 9846 warns that a server which still accepts static RSA in older versions may let an attacker impersonate it in TLS 1.3 connections through Bleichenbacher-type attacks, and that the cure is to disable static RSA across all versions. The old objection to ephemeral exchange was cost, and it faded as elliptic-curve arithmetic became cheap; F5 BIG-IP 21.1 goes further and offloads X25519 to Intel QuickAssist Technology (QAT) hardware, enabled by default on both client-side and server-side SSL (Secure Sockets Layer) profiles.

ECDHE has one weakness that no curve choice fixes. RFC 10024 notes that any passive observer with a cryptographically relevant quantum computer could recover the ephemeral scalar from the public value, so traffic recorded today could be read later: the threat to the key exchange is already running, even though the machine does not yet exist. The answer is a hybrid, written down in two documents of 2026. RFC 9954 (July 2026, Informational) gives the construction for TLS 1.3: run several key exchanges at once, concatenate their shares and their secrets, and stay secure unless every component is broken. RFC 10024 (August 2026, Standards Track) defines three groups that pair ECDHE with ML-KEM (Module-Lattice-Based Key Encapsulation Mechanism), standardized by NIST as FIPS (Federal Information Processing Standard) 203 in August 2024: X25519MLKEM768 (code point 4588, 0x11EC, the only one of the three marked Recommended in the registry of the Internet Assigned Numbers Authority, IANA), SecP256r1MLKEM768 (4587) and SecP384r1MLKEM1024 (4589). The X25519MLKEM768 client share is 1,216 bytes (a 1,184-byte ML-KEM encapsulation key and the 32-byte X25519 share), the server share 1,120 bytes, and the combined secret 64 bytes. The order inside differs on purpose: X25519MLKEM768 puts the ML-KEM secret first, the two NIST-curve groups put the ECDHE secret first, because NIST approves key derivation over two secrets when the first comes from a FIPS-approved scheme, which decides whether the elliptic-curve or the ML-KEM implementation must be certified. The pre-standard X25519Kyber768Draft00 (25497) and SecP256r1Kyber768Draft00 (25498) entries are now marked obsolete in the IANA registry.

Clients moved before the RFC was published. Google's Chrome team wrote on 13 September 2024 that Chrome 131 would replace the experimental Kyber hybrid (code point 0x6399) with the ML-KEM hybrid at 0x11EC and send a key share for it in the first ClientHello, and would not support both at once. Mozilla's enterprise reference states that Firefox offers hybrid X25519 plus ML-KEM-768 by default, with a PostQuantumKeyAgreementEnabled policy to switch it. OpenSSL 3.5.0, released on 8 April 2025, made X25519MLKEM768 and X25519 its default key shares and its default group list prefer the hybrids. Middleboxes felt it first. Fortinet documented in November 2024 that Chrome 131, Edge 131 and Firefox 132 failed with ERR_SSL_PROTOCOL_ERROR through FortiGate flow-based deep inspection because of the ML-KEM group, while proxy-based inspection was unaffected; the fix was an IPS (intrusion prevention system) engine update (engine 7.1026 is the default in FortiOS 7.6.1), with proxy-based or certificate inspection as workarounds. The FortiOS 8.0 guide now lists X25519MLKEM768, SecP256r1MLKEM768 and SecP384r1MLKEM1024 for SSL deep inspection in both proxy and flow mode.

On F5 BIG-IP the groups live in cipher rules. A cipher rule lists cipher suites, a DH (Diffie-Hellman) Groups field naming the key exchange groups (secp256r1, secp384r1 and X25519 in the classical case) and signature algorithms; a cipher group combines rules and builds the string the system actually negotiates with, and is attached to a Client SSL or Server SSL profile. F5 recommends the pre-built rule /Common/f5-default and ships a pre-built /Common/f5-ecc group. Its post-quantum chapter dates each hybrid: X25519KYBER768 from 17.5.0, X25519MLKEM768 from 17.5.1, P256rMLKEM768 and P384rMLKEM1024 from 21.1, all for TLS 1.3 only and entered in the same dh-groups list as the classical groups, as in X25519MLKEM768:X25519KYBER768:P256rMLKEM768:P384rMLKEM1024:DEFAULT. Because a hybrid is negotiated rather than imposed, a client that knows nothing of ML-KEM simply lands on a classical ECDHE group further down the list. From the command line, openssl s_client takes a -groups list, which is the quickest way to see which groups a server will accept.

The neighbours are easy to confuse. DHE (ephemeral Diffie-Hellman) is the same ephemeral exchange in finite-field groups (ffdhe2048 to ffdhe8192, code points 256 to 260 in the same registry), where a share is as long as the group's prime (256 bytes for ffdhe2048); ECDH without the final E is the static variant that RFC 8422 removed; ECDSA and EdDSA are signature algorithms, not key exchanges, so in ECDHE_RSA the curve does the agreement and RSA only signs. The numbers worth remembering are the TLS Supported Groups code points 23 (secp256r1), 24 (secp384r1), 29 (x25519), 30 (x448) and 4588 (X25519MLKEM768); the share sizes 32 bytes for X25519, 65 for P-256 and 1,216 for the hybrid client share; and the two extension numbers, supported_groups 10 and key_share 51.

ssh.def: Secure Shell (SSH) is the standard protocol for encrypted remote login, command execution, file transfer and port forwarding over an untrusted network, defined by the IETF (Internet Engineering Task Force) in RFCs 4251 to 4254 and served by default on TCP (Transmission Control Protocol) port 22.
ssh.context: Secure Shell (SSH), whose architecture is RFC (Request for Comments) 4251, replaced Telnet and the Berkeley r-commands by encrypting the whole session, passwords included. The same encrypted connection also carries SCP (Secure Copy Protocol), SFTP (SSH File Transfer Protocol), NETCONF (Network Configuration Protocol) and port-forwarding tunnels. The server proves its identity with a host key the client must already trust; the user then proves theirs with a key pair, a password or another method. Its practical weak spot is not the cryptography but the first connection to a host whose key nobody has checked.
ssh.depth:
Secure Shell (SSH) began as an answer to a break-in. In 1995 a password sniffer was found on a server attached to the backbone of the Finnish university network, its database holding thousands of user names and passwords, and Tatu Ylönen of Helsinki University of Technology wrote that spring a replacement for Telnet and rlogin that encrypted everything. In July 1995 he asked the Internet Assigned Numbers Authority (IANA) for port 22, free and conveniently between Telnet on 23 and the File Transfer Protocol (FTP) on 21; Joyce Reynolds assigned it within a day, and ssh-1.0.0 was announced on 12 July 1995. Ylönen founded SSH Communications Security in December 1995 and later took the protocol to the Internet Engineering Task Force (IETF).

The free code did not stay free. Releases after ssh 1.2.12 carried increasingly restrictive licences, so in 1999 OpenBSD developers forked the 1.2.12 code by way of Björn Grönvall's OSSH. The initial import was made on 26 September 1999 and OpenSSH shipped about two months later with OpenBSD 2.6; Markus Friedl then added SSH protocol 2 and SFTP (SSH File Transfer Protocol).

The IETF standard, protocol version 2, was published in January 2006 as RFCs (Requests for Comments) 4251 to 4254, by Ylönen with Chris Lonvick of Cisco as editor. It has three layers. The Transport Layer Protocol (RFC 4253) gives server authentication, confidentiality and integrity with perfect forward secrecy; the User Authentication Protocol (RFC 4252) authenticates the client; the Connection Protocol (RFC 4254) multiplexes the tunnel into channels.
