llm.context: A Large Language Model is a transformer-based model trained on huge corpora to predict text, powering chat assistants, code tools, and retrieval systems. Its scale is what gives it broad capability.
llm.depth:
A large language model predicts likely continuations of text, having been trained on a very large corpus. That framing matters because it explains both the capability and the characteristic failure: fluency is what it optimizes for, and fluency is not accuracy.

For technical work the practical consequences are specific. Output is plausible by construction, so a wrong answer looks exactly like a right one and must be verified against a source rather than assessed by how confident it sounds. It reflects its training data, including the outdated and the incorrect. And anything typed into a hosted model is disclosed to that service, which is a straightforward data handling question that policy has generally been slower to address than usage has been to spread.

rag.def: A technique that feeds an AI model retrieved documents so its answers are grounded.
rag.context: Retrieval-Augmented Generation fetches relevant context from a knowledge source and supplies it to the model at query time, reducing hallucination and letting the model cite information it was not trained on.

rest.def: Representational State Transfer (REST) is the architectural style Roy Fielding defined in his 2000 dissertation for distributed hypermedia systems such as the Web. In everyday use, a REST API (application programming interface) exposes resources at URIs (Uniform Resource Identifiers) and acts on them with standard HTTP (Hypertext Transfer Protocol) methods and status codes.
rest.context: Representational State Transfer (REST) is a set of constraints, not a protocol or a standard: Roy Fielding worked it out while writing the HTTP (Hypertext Transfer Protocol) specifications and published it in chapter 5 of his 2000 dissertation. Its centre is the uniform interface: anything worth naming is a resource with an identifier, clients work on representations of it (a JSON (JavaScript Object Notation) or XML (Extensible Markup Language) document, say), each message describes itself, and each request carries all the state the server needs. HTTP is the uniform interface the Web actually uses, so in practice a REST API (application programming interface) means resources at URLs (Uniform Resource Locators), GET to read, POST, PUT, PATCH and DELETE to change, and status codes to report. That is where network engineers meet it: F5 BIG-IP's iControl REST, the FortiOS REST API and RESTCONF, the standards-track REST-style configuration protocol, all work this way. Fielding reserves the word for interfaces driven by hypertext links, which many so-called REST APIs are not; the older alternative, SOAP (once Simple Object Access Protocol), wraps each call in an XML envelope and uses HTTP only as a carrier.
rest.depth:
Representational State Transfer (REST) comes from one document: Roy T. Fielding's doctoral dissertation, Architectural Styles and the Design of Network-based Software Architectures, submitted to the University of California, Irvine in 2000 under a committee chaired by Richard N. Taylor. Chapter 5 defines the style. Chapter 6 tells where it came from: Fielding co-authored the HTTP/1.0 (Hypertext Transfer Protocol) specification with Henrik Frystyk Nielsen, was the primary architect of HTTP/1.1 and revised the URI (Uniform Resource Identifier) generic syntax, and the first edition of REST was developed between October 1994 and August 1995 as a way to communicate Web concepts while those specifications were written. It was first called the HTTP object model, a name that people misread as the implementation model of an HTTP server. The new name was meant to evoke a well-designed Web application: a network of pages forming a virtual state machine, through which the user progresses by selecting links, each choice transferring the next state to the user.

REST is a set of constraints, and Fielding derives it by adding them one at a time to a style with no constraints at all. Client-server separates the user interface from data storage. Stateless means each request must carry everything needed to understand it, so session state lives entirely on the client; the price, in Fielding's words, is repetitive data sent with every interaction. Cache requires each response to be labelled, implicitly or explicitly, as cacheable or not, at the price of possibly stale data. The uniform interface, the feature he calls central, simplifies the system and makes interactions visible, but degrades efficiency because information travels in a standardized form rather than one shaped to each application. Layered system lets proxies, gateways and firewalls sit in the path, each component seeing only the next layer, which adds latency that shared caches can offset. Code on demand, downloading scripts or applets to the client, is the only optional constraint, because it reduces visibility.

The uniform interface itself has four constraints: identification of resources; manipulation of resources through representations; self-descriptive messages; and hypermedia as the engine of application state (HATEOAS). A resource is any information that can be named, a document, a collection, a service such as today's weather in Los Angeles, even a person, and Fielding defines it as a conceptual mapping to a set of entities, not the entity it maps to at a given moment. A client never handles the resource itself, only representations of it, a JSON (JavaScript Object Notation) document or an image, with metadata that says how to read them. Statelessness has four stated benefits: servers keep no application state between requests, requests can be processed in parallel, an intermediary can understand any request in isolation, and everything that affects whether a cached response can be reused is in the request.

HTTP is where the style became concrete, and RFC (Request for Comments) 9110, HTTP Semantics, published in June 2022 as Internet Standard 97 with Fielding as its first editor, states the same ideas in protocol terms. The target of a request is a resource, most resources are identified by a URI, and a representation reflects a past, current or desired state of the resource. HTTP separates identification from request semantics by putting the semantics in the method. GET, HEAD, OPTIONS and TRACE are safe, essentially read-only; PUT, DELETE and the safe methods are idempotent, so a client whose connection drops before the response arrives can repeat the request automatically. POST is neither, and PATCH, defined in RFC 5789 (March 2010) for partial modification because PUT replaces a whole representation, is neither safe nor idempotent either. That distinction is what lets crawlers and caches prefetch safely, and it is also why a retried POST can create a second object.

What the industry calls a REST API (application programming interface) is usually less than Fielding meant. In October 2008 he wrote that he was frustrated by the number of people calling any HTTP-based interface a REST API, called one such interface RPC (remote procedure call) and said that if the engine of application state is not driven by hypertext, it cannot be RESTful. Leonard Richardson's maturity model, as Martin Fowler described it on 18 March 2010, grades the gap: level 0 uses HTTP as a tunnel for remote procedure calls to a single endpoint, level 1 introduces resources, level 2 uses the HTTP methods and status codes as HTTP defines them, and level 3 adds hypermedia controls, links in each response that tell the client what it can do next. Fowler adds that Fielding has made it clear that level 3 is a precondition of REST. The device APIs below are documented at level 2: resources at published URLs (Uniform Resource Locators), standard methods, JSON bodies, and a client that learns the URL structure from the vendor's reference rather than discovering it from links.

The contrast that made REST popular was SOAP (once Simple Object Access Protocol). The World Wide Web Consortium (W3C) Recommendation for SOAP 1.2, whose second edition is dated 27 April 2007, describes a lightweight protocol for exchanging structured information: an XML (Extensible Markup Language) messaging framework whose envelope can travel over a variety of underlying protocols, HTTP being one binding among several. Version 1.1 had expanded the name as Simple Object Access Protocol; 1.2 says SOAP is no longer an acronym. Fowler places SOAP at level 0: the same remote procedure call mechanism as posting plain XML to one endpoint, only wrapped in an envelope, whereas a REST interface uses HTTP's own methods, status codes and caching rules. F5 said exactly this when it introduced iControl REST as an evolution of its SOAP-based iControl: rather than a SOAP approach, it uses REST, and anything that can be done from the command line can be done through it.

On network equipment REST shows up as the management API. BIG-IP's iControl REST maps the configuration tree onto URLs under /mgmt/tm, so F5's own example creates a pool by posting JSON to /mgmt/tm/ltm/pool. Authentication can be Basic, but F5 documents a token route: POST the credentials with loginProviderName tmos to /mgmt/shared/authn/login, then send the token in the X-F5-Auth-Token header; tokens expire after 1200 seconds by default and can be extended to 36,000 at most. FortiOS accepts only token-based authentication: the token is shown once when the REST API administrator is created, HTTPS (HTTP Secure) is enforced, the token should travel as Authorization: Bearer in the header rather than as a URL parameter, the administrator should have the minimum permissions required, and trusted hosts should limit where calls come from, 0.0.0.0/0 not being allowed. A simple read is GET /api/v2/cmdb/firewall/address. RESTCONF, RFC 8040 of January 2017, is the standards-track version for configuration modelled in the YANG data modelling language: an HTTP interface following REST principles over the datastore model of NETCONF (Network Configuration Protocol), editing data with POST, PUT, PATCH and DELETE.

The security consequence is that a REST management API is the administrative interface, reachable by anything that can open an HTTPS connection to it, and its flaws are administrator compromises. The CVE (Common Vulnerabilities and Exposures) entry CVE-2022-1388, published on 5 May 2022, let undisclosed requests bypass iControl REST authentication on BIG-IP versions 11.6.x to 16.1.x before the fixed releases; it scored 9.8 under CVSS (Common Vulnerability Scoring System) 3.1, and CISA (Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency) listed it as known exploited on 10 May 2022. CVE-2022-40684 let an unauthenticated attacker operate the administrative interface of FortiOS 7.0.0 to 7.0.6 and 7.2.0 to 7.2.1, FortiProxy and FortiSwitchManager with crafted HTTP or HTTPS requests, also 9.8, and was on CISA's list from 11 October 2022. The controls the vendors describe are the ones that limit the damage: source restrictions such as trusted hosts, tokens scoped to the least privilege a script needs, short token lifetimes, and certificate verification left on in every client.

The numbers worth keeping: one dissertation in 2000, a style first written down between October 1994 and August 1995, six constraints of which one, code on demand, is optional, four interface constraints, four safe methods in RFC 9110 and two more idempotent ones, PUT and DELETE, with POST and PATCH being neither. The stateless and uniform-interface constraints are deliberate trades of efficiency for scalability, visibility and independent evolution, which is why a REST call is often chattier than a purpose-built protocol, and why caches, proxies and inspection devices can make sense of it.

soap.def: An older, XML-based protocol for structured web-service messages.
soap.context: Simple Object Access Protocol (W3C) wraps requests in a rigid XML envelope with its own standards for security and transactions. Heavier than REST, it persists in enterprise and legacy integrations.

cli.def: A command-line interface (CLI) is a text interface in which a person or a script types commands that a program parses and executes, and reads the replies as text: the shell on a host, or the management console of a router, switch or firewall.
cli.context: A Command-Line Interface (CLI) accepts typed commands rather than mouse clicks. On network gear and servers it is the primary control surface, scriptable and precise in a way graphical interfaces are not: a saved sequence of commands can be replayed, reviewed and versioned. The same properties cut both ways. A command does exactly what it says, including the wrong thing, and text written for people is a fragile contract for programs, a weakness the 2002 IAB (Internet Architecture Board) network management workshop recorded plainly; structured interfaces such as NETCONF (Network Configuration Protocol) exist alongside it for that reason.
cli.depth:
What it is. A command-line interface (CLI) reads a line of text, splits it into a command and its arguments, runs it and prints the result as text. The program doing the reading is a command interpreter: on a host it is the shell, which the 1978 Bell System Technical Journal foreword to the UNIX papers, by M. D. McIlroy, E. N. Pinson and B. A. Tague, called the most visible system interface, a command language interpreter through which other programs are called into execution singly or in combination; on a network device it is part of the firmware. The CLI is the interface, not the terminal it is displayed on and not the transport that carries it. RFC (Request for Comments) 3535, the report of the 2002 IAB (Internet Architecture Board) network management workshop, noted that network access to device CLIs had traditionally used Telnet, with SSH (Secure Shell) gaining ground because of Telnet's security problems.

Where it came from. CTSS (Compatible Time-Sharing System), one of the first time-sharing systems, was built at the MIT (Massachusetts Institute of Technology) Computation Center by a team led by Fernando Corbató and first demonstrated in November 1961. Louis Pouzin recalls that after writing dozens of CTSS commands in 1963 and 1964, he wanted commands usable as building blocks for more commands, and wrote RUNCOM to run command scripts with argument substitution, so that long jobs could run overnight; at the end of 1964 or the beginning of 1965 he coined the word shell for the command language he proposed for Multics. Unix began in 1969 with Ken Thompson's work on a cast-off PDP-7, and the 1978 foreword set out the maxims its tools follow, among them that the output of every program should be expected to become the input to another, as yet unknown, program, that output should not be cluttered with extraneous information, and that programs should avoid stringently columnar or binary input formats and not insist on interactive input.

Why it composes. A CLI is text in and text out, and the shell joins the two. In the POSIX (Portable Operating System Interface) shell, a pipeline connects the standard output of each command to the standard input of the next, so the output of one command becomes the input of another; the work becomes a script, and the script becomes something that can be reviewed, versioned and run identically a thousand times. Every command also returns an exit status that the next line can test through the special parameter ?: POSIX fixes 127 for a command that was not found, 126 for one found but not executable, and a value greater than 128 for one killed by a signal. PowerShell keeps the pipeline but passes objects instead of text, which removes the parsing step and ties both ends to the same object model.

Conventions that make it predictable. The POSIX utility syntax guidelines, in IEEE (Institute of Electrical and Electronics Engineers) Std 1003.1-2024, ask for utility names of two to nine lowercase characters, single-character options introduced by a hyphen, options without arguments that can be grouped behind one hyphen, options before operands, and the first double hyphen as the end of options, so that a file name beginning with a hyphen can still be passed; -W is reserved for vendor options. The GNU Coding Standards add long-named options such as --verbose, note that GNU getopt accepts options anywhere among the arguments unless the double hyphen is used, which POSIX does not, and require every program to support --version and --help. The trade against a graphical interface is discoverability: a graphical interface shows what is available, a command line requires knowing it, which is why good help output and error messages that name the correction matter more in a CLI than anywhere else.

On network devices. RFC 3535 gives the operator's case for the device CLI: it is task-oriented and easy for people, a saved sequence of commands can be replayed and edited with ordinary text tools, it needs no special client, and most CLIs offer context-sensitive help. Cisco IOS is the familiar example: user EXEC mode at the Router> prompt, privileged EXEC at Router# after enable, global configuration at Router(config)# after configure terminal, a question mark that lists the commands available in each mode, and abbreviation to any unique prefix, so that configure terminal becomes config t. F5 BIG-IP has tmsh, the Traffic Management Shell, hierarchical and modular, with Tab completion of commands and object names; FortiOS uses a small grammar of config, edit, set, unset, next and end.

When a change takes effect. The vendors disagree, and the difference catches people out. In tmsh every change applies to the running configuration at once, and save /sys config is what writes it to the stored configuration files that survive a reboot. In FortiOS, next saves the table entry being edited, end saves the configuration and leaves the config block, and abort leaves without saving. Junos separates the steps: commands change a candidate configuration, commit checks its syntax and activates it, commit confirmed rolls it back automatically unless it is confirmed within 10 minutes by default, and up to 49 earlier configurations are kept for rollback. RFC 3535 had already asked that distributing a configuration and activating it be distinct operations.

Security. A CLI on a network device is privileged access to the whole box, and RFC 3535 observes that CLI access control, where it exists, is usually command-oriented rather than data-oriented and often ad hoc. TACACS+ (Terminal Access Controller Access-Control System Plus, RFC 8907, September 2020) is the common answer: a device can ask the server to authorize each command, with the command name in the cmd argument and its arguments in cmd-arg, or authorize a whole session at once, and it can account for every command typed. Programs that build command lines from input they receive are the other risk. MITRE's CWE-78 (Common Weakness Enumeration) describes OS (operating system) command injection: a product constructs all or part of a command from externally influenced input without neutralizing the special elements that could change it.

Where it falls short. RFC 3535 lists the weaknesses that matter for automation: many CLIs lack a common data model, so the same command can behave differently on different devices from the same vendor; output written for people is troublesome to parse; syntax and semantics are not versioned, so scripts break across software releases; and proprietary syntax does not carry across a mixed estate. Scraping CLI output with regular expressions works until the next release changes a column. Structured interfaces answer that: NETCONF (Network Configuration Protocol, RFC 6241, June 2011) installs, manipulates and deletes device configuration with XML (Extensible Markup Language) encoded data and remote procedure calls. The CLI remains where engineers learn a device, configure it the first time and troubleshoot it when everything else has failed.

saml.def: Security Assertion Markup Language (SAML) is an OASIS (Organization for the Advancement of Structured Information Standards) standard, at version 2.0 since March 2005, in which an identity provider vouches for a user to a service provider with digitally signed XML (Extensible Markup Language) assertions; it underpins most enterprise web single sign-on.
saml.context: Security Assertion Markup Language (SAML) lets an identity provider (IdP) vouch for a user to a service provider (SP) through signed XML (Extensible Markup Language) assertions, and it is the backbone of much enterprise single sign-on (SSO). The user's browser carries the messages between the two, so the application never sees the password and the IdP does not need to reach the application directly. OpenID Connect (OIDC), built on OAuth 2.0 and JSON Web Tokens (JWTs), is the more modern alternative for the same job.
saml.depth:
Security Assertion Markup Language (SAML) is, in the words of the technical overview published by OASIS (Organization for the Advancement of Structured Information Standards), an XML-based framework for describing and exchanging security information between on-line business partners, XML being the Extensible Markup Language. The OASIS Security Services Technical Committee first met in January 2001; SAML 1.0 became an OASIS Standard in November 2002 and 1.1 in September 2003, the month the Liberty Alliance contributed its Identity Federation Framework to OASIS; and SAML 2.0, the version in use today, became an OASIS Standard in March 2005, its core specification dated 15 March 2005 and edited by Scott Cantor, John Kemp, Rob Philpott and Eve Maler. What SAML is not matters as much: it does not authenticate anyone. The identity provider (IdP) logs the user in by whatever means it has, and SAML carries the result, signed, to the service provider (SP).

The unit is the assertion. An assertion names an issuer and a subject (a name identifier plus subject confirmation data), may carry a signature, and holds statements of three kinds: an authentication statement (this user logged in at this time), an attribute statement (this user's e-mail, groups or roles) and an authorization decision statement. Its Conditions element limits where and when it may be used: NotBefore and NotOnOrAfter bound the validity window, AudienceRestriction names the SP it was issued for, and OneTimeUse forbids keeping it. The core specification is candid about the weak point of any time window: some clock skew between systems will always be present, so an issuer cannot make an assertion short-lived without risking that it expires before it arrives.

The shape worth holding in your head is the Web Browser SSO (single sign-on) profile. In the SP-initiated flow the user reaches the application, the SP redirects the browser to the IdP with an AuthnRequest, the user authenticates there, and the IdP sends back a Response containing the assertion, delivered through the browser to the SP's assertion consumer service; in the IdP-initiated flow the user starts at the IdP portal and the SP receives an unsolicited Response. The bindings decide how the messages travel. The Hypertext Transfer Protocol (HTTP) Redirect binding compresses the XML with DEFLATE, base64-encodes it and URL-encodes it (URL being Uniform Resource Locator) into a SAMLRequest or SAMLResponse parameter, with any signature carried in SigAlg and Signature parameters; the HTTP POST binding base64-encodes the XML, without compression, into a hidden form field that the browser submits; the Artifact binding sends only a reference that the SP resolves over a back channel, usually the SOAP (originally Simple Object Access Protocol) binding. RelayState, the value that brings the user back to the page they asked for, must not exceed 80 bytes.

Debugging means reading those messages, so the first step is always to decode them: base64 for POST, base64 plus inflate for Redirect. The profile then fixes what the SP must check: every signature present on the assertion or the response, which with the POST binding must exist; that the Recipient matches the assertion consumer service URL the message arrived at; that NotOnOrAfter has not passed, subject to the allowed clock skew; and that InResponseTo equals the ID of the original AuthnRequest, or is absent for an unsolicited response. Most real failures map onto that list and are mundane: the audience does not match the SP's entity ID, the assertion has expired, the two systems' clocks disagree, the signature does not validate against the certificate the SP has on file, or the attribute the application needs is not sent under the name it expects.

On F5 BIG-IP Access Policy Manager (APM), the SP role is a SAML SP service bound to one or more IdP connectors, created from the IdP's metadata or a template, and a SAML Auth agent in the access policy. Authentication requests go by POST, the default, or Redirect; the assertion consumer service accepts POST, the default, or Artifact; single logout works over HTTP-POST only; and signed assertions are expected by default, checked against the IdP's assertion verification certificate imported into the BIG-IP store.

The security history is about XML signatures, not SAML's logic. In August 2012 Juraj Somorovsky and colleagues at USENIX Security analysed 14 major SAML frameworks and found critical XML Signature wrapping flaws in 11, including Salesforce, Shibboleth and IBM XS40: the signature verified one element while the application read another. The same pattern returned in March 2025, when GitHub Security Lab showed that ruby-saml up to 1.17.0 (Common Vulnerabilities and Exposures entries CVE-2025-25291 and CVE-2025-25292, fixed in 1.18.0) parsed each document with two XML parsers that could pick different Signature elements, so a single valid signature, even one taken from signed IdP metadata, was enough to log in as anyone. The other risk is the signing key itself. In November 2017 CyberArk named Golden SAML, after the Kerberos golden ticket: whoever holds an IdP's token-signing private key can forge a response for any user to any federated service, and on Active Directory Federation Services (AD FS) the AD FS user account was enough to reach it. MITRE ATT&CK lists the technique as T1606.002 and records that APT29 created tokens with compromised SAML signing certificates in the SolarWinds compromise.

SAML's longevity is often mistaken for stagnation. It persists because it does what enterprises need, integrates with nearly every enterprise application, and has no compelling reason to be replaced in deployments that already work; OpenID Connect (OIDC), which carries identity as a signed JSON Web Token (JWT) instead of XML, is the usual choice for new work. Numbers worth remembering: version 2.0 since March 2005, three statement types, the Redirect, POST, Artifact and SOAP bindings, and RelayState capped at 80 bytes.

ike.def: Internet Key Exchange (IKE), the protocol with which two IPsec (Internet Protocol Security) peers authenticate each other, agree on algorithms and derive the keys of the security associations that protect their traffic; version 2 is RFC (Request for Comments) 7296.
ike.context: Internet Key Exchange (IKE) runs over UDP port 500, or 4500 when a NAT (network address translation) device sits in the path, and sets up what an IPsec (Internet Protocol Security) virtual private network (VPN) tunnel needs before any encrypted traffic flows: it authenticates the peers, agrees on the algorithms and derives the keys. It produces two kinds of security association (SA): one that protects IKE's own messages and one or more that protect the traffic itself. IKEv2 (RFC 7296) is the current version; IKEv1 has been deprecated since 2023 but still runs in many networks.
ike.depth:
What it does. RFC (Request for Comments) 7296 describes Internet Key Exchange (IKE) as the component of IPsec (Internet Protocol Security) that performs mutual authentication between two parties and establishes and maintains security associations (SAs), the shared state of keys and algorithms that each side needs. It does not carry user traffic. That is the job of ESP (Encapsulating Security Payload), whose keys IKE derives: the IKE SA protects IKE's own conversation, and each Child SA (an IPsec SA in IKEv1 language) protects one direction of traffic between agreed address ranges. IKE normally sends and listens on UDP (User Datagram Protocol) port 500, and moves to port 4500 when a NAT (network address translation) device is detected, so that ESP can be wrapped in UDP and survive address translation. Every site-to-site or remote-access IPsec virtual private network (VPN) starts with an IKE negotiation, which is why IKE is where most IPsec failures are found.

Version 1 and its two phases. The first version was published in November 1998 as three documents: RFC 2407 (the IPsec Domain of Interpretation), RFC 2408 (ISAKMP, the Internet Security Association and Key Management Protocol) and RFC 2409 (IKE itself), the last by D. Harkins and D. Carrel of Cisco Systems. RFC 2409 gave the field its vocabulary. Phase 1 establishes an authenticated, protected channel, the ISAKMP SA, with either Main Mode or Aggressive Mode; Phase 2 then negotiates the SAs that protect traffic, with Quick Mode. Engineers still speak of phase 1 and phase 2 on IKEv2 devices, and vendors' configuration screens still use the words, even though IKEv2 has no phases in that sense.

Version 2. IKEv2 first appeared in RFC 4306 of December 2005, edited by C. Kaufman of Microsoft, which replaced all three IKEv1 documents and was deliberately not backward compatible. It was clarified in RFC 4718, consolidated in RFC 5996, and republished as RFC 7296 in October 2014, which made it an Internet Standard, STD 79; it has since been updated by RFCs 7427, 7670, 8247, 8983, 9370 and 9827, the last of which, in November 2025, renamed the Extended Sequence Numbers transform type to Sequence Numbers. Appendix A of RFC 7296 lists what the revision set out to fix: one document instead of three, with NAT traversal, extensible authentication and remote address assignment built in; a single four-message initial exchange in place of eight different ones; a reliable, sequenced protocol in which every message is acknowledged, so that creating a Child SA takes two messages instead of three; a responder that does no significant work until the initiator proves it can receive at its claimed address, which blunts denial-of-service floods; and traffic selectors carried in payloads of their own.

The exchanges. An IKEv2 negotiation starts with IKE_SA_INIT, which agrees on the cryptographic algorithms and exchanges nonces and Diffie-Hellman values, and continues with IKE_AUTH, protected by keys from the first exchange, which proves each side's identity and normally creates the first Child SA as well: four messages, two round trips. CREATE_CHILD_SA adds further Child SAs and rekeys existing ones; INFORMATIONAL carries deletions, errors and liveness checks. The requester is responsible for retransmission, because UDP itself guarantees nothing. RFC 9370 (May 2023) added an IKE_INTERMEDIATE stage in which up to seven additional key exchanges, transform types 6 to 12, can follow the first, which is how a post-quantum algorithm is combined with a classical Diffie-Hellman exchange; a working group draft, draft-ietf-ipsecme-ikev2-mlkem, revised in July 2026 and intended as a Proposed Standard, specifies ML-KEM (the module-lattice key encapsulation mechanism) for that role.

Reading a failure. The two-stage structure is still the first diagnostic question, because which stage failed narrows the cause sharply. A failure in IKEv1 phase 1, or in IKE_SA_INIT and the authentication part of IKE_AUTH, points at authentication, identity or a proposal mismatch: NO_PROPOSAL_CHOSEN means no common algorithm set, INVALID_KE_PAYLOAD means the initiator guessed the wrong Diffie-Hellman group and must retry with the one the responder named, and AUTHENTICATION_FAILED means credentials or identities did not match, in which case no IKE SA is created. A failure in phase 2, or in the Child SA part of IKE_AUTH or CREATE_CHILD_SA, points at mismatched traffic selectors or transform sets, meaning the peers authenticated and then disagreed about what to protect. RFC 7296 is explicit about the confusing case: when the Child SA in IKE_AUTH fails with errors such as NO_PROPOSAL_CHOSEN, TS_UNACCEPTABLE or SINGLE_PAIR_REQUIRED, the IKE SA is still created, so the tunnel looks up while no traffic passes. Mixing versions between endpoints is a category of failure of its own: an IKEv2 initiator and an IKEv1-only responder never agree on anything.

On a FortiGate. FortiOS offers IKE version 2 only for route-based VPNs and uses version 1 otherwise, so policy-based tunnels are still IKEv1. With IKEv2 the choice between aggressive and main mode disappears, XAUTH (extended authentication) is not available and EAP (Extensible Authentication Protocol) can be used instead; IKEv2 fragmentation follows RFC 7383. Fortinet's remote-access client dropped IKEv1 with FortiClient 7.4.4, which means old dial-up tunnels have to move to IKEv2 when clients are upgraded. Whatever the vendor, the same two questions apply first: did the IKE SA come up, and did the Child SA come up.

Security history. In 2018 Dennis Felsch, Martin Grothe, Jörg Schwenk, Adam Czubak and Marcin Szymanek showed at USENIX Security that reusing one RSA key pair across IKE versions and modes allows cross-protocol authentication bypass: a Bleichenbacher oracle in the IKEv1 mode that authenticates with RSA-encrypted nonces broke that mode and, through the shared key, RSA signature authentication in both IKEv1 and IKEv2. They also described an offline dictionary attack against the pre-shared key (PSK) modes, so a weak shared secret is crackable by anyone who captures a handshake. Cisco (CVE-2018-0131), Huawei (CVE-2017-17305), Clavister (CVE-2018-8753) and ZyXEL (CVE-2018-9129) issued fixes or removed the mode. The defences are ordinary: one key pair per purpose, long random pre-shared keys or certificates, and no legacy modes left enabled.

The end of IKEv1. RFC 9395 (April 2023), edited by P. Wouters, deprecated IKEv1 and moved RFCs 2407, 2408 and 2409 to Historic status. Its reasons read like an audit checklist: development stopped more than a decade earlier; many IKEv1 systems are past end of life and will never be patched; some vendors have frozen their IKEv1 code while still shipping it; IKEv1 can be abused for packet amplification (CVE-2016-5361); and in practice IKEv1 negotiates dated defaults such as AES-CBC, SHA1 and Diffie-Hellman groups 1 or 2. RFC 7296 itself keeps the 768-bit group 1 only for historic reasons and says its strength may not be sufficient. The RFC's advice is to replace IKEv1-only systems and not to import an IKEv1 configuration into IKEv2 without updating its algorithms, which is the step most migrations skip.

ntp.def: Network Time Protocol (NTP): the protocol that keeps the clocks of networked systems agreeing with one another and with Coordinated Universal Time (UTC), by exchanging timestamps with servers over User Datagram Protocol (UDP) port 123.
ntp.context: The Network Time Protocol (NTP) is one of those dependencies nobody lists until it breaks, and then everything breaks at once: certificates are checked against the clock, Kerberos rejects messages outside a five-minute skew by default, and logs from machines that disagree about the time cannot be put in order. A client measures its offset from several servers, discards the ones that disagree, and slews or steps its clock towards the survivors. Unauthenticated NTP is an attack surface, because whoever controls a system's time controls what it believes is expired; Network Time Security (NTS) closes that gap, and most deployments still do not use it.
ntp.depth:
Why it matters. Clock agreement is a dependency that fails in confusing ways. Certificates are valid only between their notBefore and notAfter times, so a device whose time is wrong rejects good certificates and may accept expired ones; Request for Comments (RFC) 8915, the Network Time Security (NTS) specification, spends a section on the problem that a client cannot strictly check a certificate's validity period before it has the right time. The Kerberos implementation from MIT tolerates a clock skew of 300 seconds, five minutes, by default, so an authentication failure that looks like a password problem is often a clock problem. And log correlation is meaningless without a shared timebase: the standard for syslog over the User Datagram Protocol (UDP), RFC 5426, warns that messages from hosts whose clocks are not synchronized cannot be ordered, so an incident timeline built from unsynchronized logs is fiction.

What it is and where it came from. The Network Time Protocol (NTP) is the work of David L. Mills, first specified in RFC 958 of September 1985 while he was at M/A-COM Linkabit, revised as NTP version 3 in RFC 1305 of March 1992 from the University of Delaware, and defined today by RFC 5905 of June 2010, NTP version 4, by D. Mills, J. Martin, J. Burbank and W. Kasch, which obsoletes RFC 1305 and the Simple Network Time Protocol (SNTP) document, RFC 4330. It runs over UDP port 123. In the usual client-server mode a client sends a request stamped with its transmit time T1; the server records the arrival T2 and its own transmit time T3; the client records the arrival T4. RFC 5905 then computes the offset as one half of ((T2 minus T1) plus (T3 minus T4)) and the round-trip delay as (T4 minus T1) minus (T3 minus T2). Because the offset formula splits the round trip evenly, a path whose two directions differ in delay shows up as clock error.

Choosing whom to believe. A client normally polls several servers, at intervals that RFC 5905 bounds between 2^4 seconds (16 s) and 2^17 seconds (about 36 hours). Its selection algorithm applies Byzantine fault detection to discard falsetickers, clocks whose time is inconsistent, keeps the truechimers, and then clusters and averages the survivors. The best-practice document, RFC 8633 of July 2019, asks for at least four independent, diverse sources, and gives a cautionary case from the June 2015 leap second: some operators smeared the leap second across several hours and others did not, so clients with two sources of each kind could not decide which time was right. Four sources from one provider are not four sources.

Strata and timestamps. Every NTP packet carries a stratum. In RFC 5905's table, 1 is a primary server, for example one equipped with a Global Positioning System (GPS) receiver; 2 to 15 are secondary servers synchronized over NTP, each layer adding one; 16 means unsynchronized, and 0 in a packet means unspecified or invalid, which is also how a server sends a Kiss-o'-Death packet telling a client to back off. The reference clock itself, a GPS receiver or an atomic standard, is commonly called stratum 0. Timestamps are 64 bits: 32 bits of seconds since 0 h on 1 January 1900, which span 136 years, and 32 bits of fraction, a resolution of 232 picoseconds. The seconds field therefore wraps in 2036, and RFC 5905 names 8 February 2036 as the first day of era 1; the Unix epoch, 1 January 1970, is 2,208,988,800 in NTP seconds. A 2-bit leap indicator warns of a leap second (1 for a 61-second last minute, 2 for 59) or marks the clock unsynchronized (3), and the General Conference on Weights and Measures decided in 2022 to let the difference between UT1, the time scale that follows the Earth's rotation, and Coordinated Universal Time (UTC) grow larger in, or before, 2035, which is expected to end leap seconds for at least a century.

How the clock is corrected. NTP disciplines the clock rather than simply setting it, but it does not only slew. RFC 5905 treats an offset below the step threshold of 125 milliseconds as an ordinary adjustment, steps the clock only after the offset has stayed above 125 milliseconds for the stepout interval of 900 seconds, which resists steps during heavy congestion, and gives up with a diagnostic if the offset exceeds the panic threshold of 1000 seconds. A step can move time backwards, which software that assumes monotonic time handles badly. That is why chrony normally slews, speeding up or slowing down the clock, and steps only when told to with makestep, for example makestep 0.1 3 to step if the error exceeds 0.1 seconds during the first three updates, and why its manual recommends stepping only at boot, before programs that rely on time moving forwards have started.

Security. Unauthenticated NTP is a place to attack: an attacker who controls a system's time can expire its certificates, break its Kerberos or make it accept something it would otherwise reject as stale. RFC 5905 defined a symmetric-key message authentication code using MD5; RFC 8633 now calls MD5 too weak, recommends AES-128-CMAC, and reminds operators that NTP has no key exchange, so every key must be distributed out of band, one per association. Network Time Security, RFC 8915 of September 2020, removes that burden: an NTS Key Establishment handshake over Transport Layer Security (TLS) 1.3 on Transmission Control Protocol (TCP) port 4460 authenticates the server with an ordinary certificate and hands the client encrypted cookies, and each later NTP packet is protected with AEAD_AES_SIV_CMAC_256, while the server keeps no per-client state. chrony enables it with the nts option on a server line. The other recurring abuse is volume: RFC 8633 warns that Mode 6 control messages can be used for amplification attacks and should be blocked from outside the organization, and RFC 9109 of August 2021 asks clients to use a random source port instead of 123 to resist blind off-path attacks. NTP has authentication, and most deployments still do not use it.

In practice. Every managed device needs at least an NTP server list and a time zone: on F5 BIG-IP that is sys ntp servers, none by default, and sys ntp timezone; on Linux, chrony or another daemon. The checklist follows RFC 8633: four or more independent, diverse sources, NTS or keyed authentication where the platform allows it, Mode 6 queries blocked from outside, and monitoring of every time source so that a server out of step is noticed quickly. The numbers to remember are UDP 123, TCP 4460 for NTS-KE, strata 1 to 15 and 16 for unsynchronized, 125 ms, 900 s and 1000 s, the 1900 epoch and its 2036 wrap, and Kerberos's five minutes.

icmp.def: Internet Control Message Protocol (ICMP) is the error-reporting and diagnostic protocol built into IP (Internet Protocol): routers and hosts use it to tell a sender that a packet was undeliverable, expired or too big, and ping uses its Echo messages.
icmp.context: Internet Control Message Protocol (ICMP), defined in RFC (Request for Comments) 792, carries reachability errors and diagnostics rather than user data. Ping and traceroute are built on it, Path MTU (maximum transmission unit) Discovery depends on it, and ICMPv6 also carries IPv6 neighbour and router discovery, so a firewall's handling of ICMP decides how well a network reports its own problems.
icmp.depth:
What it is. Internet Control Message Protocol (ICMP), Request for Comments (RFC) 792 (September 1981, Jon Postel), is how a router or destination host reports a problem back to the source. It rides inside IP (Internet Protocol) as if it were a higher-level protocol, with protocol number 1 in the IANA (Internet Assigned Numbers Authority) registry, but the RFC calls it an integral part of IP that every IP module must implement. Its purpose is feedback, not reliability: there is no guarantee that a datagram is delivered or that an error comes back. Two rules stop it feeding on itself: no ICMP message is sent about an ICMP message, and errors are reported only for the first fragment of a fragmented datagram. IPv6 has its own version, ICMPv6, RFC 4443 (March 2006), carried as next header 58, with error types 0 to 127 and informational types 128 to 255.

Format and types. Every message starts with a type, a code and a checksum. The IANA registry (last updated 29 October 2026) lists the familiar ones: 0 Echo Reply, 3 Destination Unreachable, 5 Redirect, 8 Echo, 11 Time Exceeded, 12 Parameter Problem, 13 and 14 Timestamp. Destination Unreachable carries the most detail in its code: 0 network, 1 host, 2 protocol, 3 port, 4 fragmentation needed and Don't Fragment set, and, added later, 9 and 10 (RFC 1122), which RFC 1812 says were meant for military end-to-end encryption devices, and 13, Communication Administratively Prohibited, which RFC 1812 tells routers to send when they drop a packet by administrative filtering, while allowing an option to stay silent. Time Exceeded has two codes: 0, time to live exceeded in transit, and 1, fragment reassembly time exceeded. An error quotes the offending packet so the sender can match it to a connection: RFC 792 asked for the IP header plus 64 bits of data, and RFC 1812 (June 1995) told routers to include as much as possible up to a 576-byte ICMP datagram, because 8 bytes had become too little once tunnels wrapped packets inside packets. RFC 4884 (April 2007) added a multi-part extension structure at the end of selected messages for further information.

Ping and traceroute. Ping is Echo (8) answered by Echo Reply (0), or 128 and 129 in ICMPv6. RFC 1812 requires every router to run an Echo server able to answer a request at least as large as 576 bytes or the MTU (maximum transmission unit) of any attached network, whichever is larger, and allows it to ignore echoes sent to broadcast or multicast addresses. Traceroute reads the Time Exceeded, code 0, that each router returns when a probe's TTL (time to live) runs out. Which address a router uses as the source of that error matters when reading the output: on Linux, icmp_errors_use_inbound_ifaddr is off by default, so errors come from the primary address of the outgoing interface, and the kernel documentation notes that enabling it gives the behaviour many administrators expect from a router, the address of the interface the packet arrived on.

The message nobody may block. Path MTU Discovery (PMTUD), RFC 1191 (November 1990, Jeffrey Mogul and Steve Deering), defined a Next-Hop MTU field in Destination Unreachable, code 4, so a router dropping an oversized packet marked Don't Fragment can tell the sender what size would fit; ICMPv6 calls the same message Packet Too Big. If it never arrives, the sender never shrinks its packets and connections stall as soon as large data flows. RFC 2979 (October 2000) records that firewalls commonly block ICMP on a perception that it is a source of vulnerabilities and so create black holes, rules that a firewall which lets out packets with Don't Fragment set must not block the Fragmentation Needed errors that answer them, and adds that blocking Echo, Echo Reply and Redirect is proper, if unfriendly. RFC 8900 (BCP 230, September 2020) puts it on operators: they must make PMTUD work, including generating Packet Too Big, may rate-limit ICMP, and must not filter ICMPv6 Packet Too Big unless it is known to be forged.

IPv6 depends on it more. Neighbor Discovery, router advertisements and path MTU all travel as ICMPv6, so a blanket deny breaks IPv6 outright. RFC 4890 (May 2007) lists what a firewall must not drop in transit: Destination Unreachable (all codes), Packet Too Big, Time Exceeded code 0, Parameter Problem codes 1 and 2, and Echo Request and Response, adding that address scanning is much less of a risk in IPv6, so there is no need to filter echo requests as IPv4 practice did.

What was retired. Source Quench (type 4) was meant for congestion control. Router generation of it was deprecated by RFC 1812 in 1995, and RFC 6633 (May 2012) deprecated any reaction to it by transport protocols such as TCP (Transmission Control Protocol), calling it an ineffective and unfair antidote for congestion. RFC 6918 (April 2013) formally deprecated a list of types long unused in practice, among them Information Request and Reply (15 and 16), Address Mask Request and Reply (17 and 18) and the experimental Traceroute message (30). Redirect (5) survives, and RFC 2979 regards blocking it entirely as proper.

Rate limits. Generating errors costs a router processing time and reverse-path bandwidth, so RFC 1812 says a router should be able to limit the rate of Destination Unreachable, Redirect, Time Exceeded and Parameter Problem, and RFC 4443 makes rate limiting mandatory for ICMPv6 errors, recommending a token bucket. Linux defaults are documented: icmp_ratelimit spaces responses to each target by 1,000 milliseconds for the types in icmp_ratemask, by default Destination Unreachable, Source Quench, Time Exceeded and Parameter Problem, and icmp_msgs_per_sec caps the whole host at 10,000 a second. Asterisks in a traceroute, or loss in a ping to a router's own address, therefore describe the router's control plane, not necessarily the traffic it forwards.

Abuse. The smurf attack, CERT Advisory CA-98.01 of 5 January 1998, sent forged echo requests to IP directed-broadcast addresses with the victim's address as source, so every host on the intermediary network replied to the victim. The advisory's fixes are still the baseline: disable IP-directed broadcast on all routers, configure hosts to ignore ICMP sent to broadcast addresses, which Linux does by default (icmp_echo_ignore_broadcasts is 1), and filter outgoing packets whose source address belongs to another network. RFC 5927 (July 2010) describes forged ICMP errors used against TCP for blind connection resets and throughput reduction, even from off the path, and the countermeasures stacks adopted. Parsing bugs matter too: CVE (Common Vulnerabilities and Exposures) 2020-16898, published on 16 October 2020, was remote code execution in the Windows TCP/IP stack through crafted ICMPv6 Router Advertisements, rated 8.8.

sql.def: SQL (Structured Query Language) is the standard declarative language for defining, querying and changing data in relational databases, standardized as ISO/IEC (International Organization for Standardization and International Electrotechnical Commission) 9075 and descended from IBM's SEQUEL (Structured English Query Language) of 1974.
sql.context: Structured Query Language (SQL), standardized as ISO/IEC (International Organization for Standardization and International Electrotechnical Commission) 9075, with current parts dated 2023, reads and writes data in relational databases: the query states what result is wanted and the database decides how to get it. It descends from Edgar F. Codd's 1970 relational model and from SEQUEL (Structured English Query Language), designed at IBM by Donald Chamberlin and Raymond Boyce. Every product speaks its own dialect of it. SQL injection, untrusted input that ends up changing the syntax of a query, is one of the oldest and most damaging web vulnerabilities.
sql.depth:
SQL (Structured Query Language) is the language in which applications and people define, query and change data held in relational databases. It is declarative: a statement such as a SELECT names the tables, the columns and the conditions of the result it wants, and the database management system (DBMS) decides how to find it, which is why the same query can be fast or slow depending on indexes and on the optimizer rather than on how it was written. The standard is the ISO/IEC (International Organization for Standardization and International Electrotechnical Commission) 9075 series, maintained by subcommittee 32 of Joint Technical Committee 1 (JTC 1/SC 32). Its Part 1, Framework, is in its sixth edition, published in June 2023 and replacing the 2016 edition; it sets out the conceptual framework that the other parts use to define the grammar and the results of processing SQL statements. The 2023 round also added Part 16, Property Graph Queries (SQL/PGQ), which defines ways for SQL to represent property graphs and query them, and has since received a 2026 corrigendum. What SQL is not is a single product: each database product speaks its own dialect of it, and OWASP's prevention guidance notes that even the escaping rules differ between dialects, which matters a great deal for security.

The idea came first. In June 1970 Edgar F. Codd of the IBM Research Laboratory in San Jose published A Relational Model of Data for Large Shared Data Banks in Communications of the ACM (Association for Computing Machinery), volume 13, number 6. Its opening argument is still the reason relational databases exist: future users of large data banks must be protected from having to know how the data is organized inside the machine, and their programs should keep working when that internal representation changes. The tree-structured and network models of the day tied programs to physical structure; Codd proposed a model based on n-ary relations, a normal form for them and a universal data sublanguage, and called the goal data independence. Don Chamberlin later summed it up for IBM: relationships between data items should be based on the items' values, not on separately specified linking or nesting. Codd became an IBM Fellow in 1976, received the Turing Award in 1981 and died in 2003.

The language came from Chamberlin and Raymond Boyce at the same laboratory. Their paper SEQUEL: A Structured English Query Language, presented at an ACM workshop on data description, access and control in May 1974, described keyword English templates for working with tables that avoided the bound variables and quantifiers of formal logic while matching the power of the first-order predicate calculus, aimed at professional programmers and occasional users alike. IBM's System R project, begun in 1973, turned the theory into an industrial implementation: Patricia Selinger's cost-based optimizer made relational queries efficient, Raymond Lorie built a compiler that saved query plans for reuse, and the work led to IBM's DB2, first shipped in 1983 on IBM mainframes. SEQUEL was later renamed SQL, by most accounts because of a trademark conflict, a reason the history sources give only as a presumption.

Standardization followed the products. The American National Standards Institute (ANSI) approved X3.135-1986, Database Language SQL, on 16 October 1986, the work of technical committee X3H2, and the National Bureau of Standards adopted it for US federal use as FIPS PUB 127 (Federal Information Processing Standards Publication) in 1987; it specified the syntax and semantics of the interfaces for defining and accessing SQL databases. The international series grew from there into today's ISO/IEC 9075, whose parts carry the 2023 dates, and the dialects that products ship are what make portable SQL a discipline rather than a default.

SQL injection is the security term every engineer meets first, and its mechanism is simple. The OWASP (Open Worldwide Application Security Project) cheat sheet defines it as untrusted data becoming part of a query's SQL syntax and so modifying the logic of the request; MITRE's CWE-89 (Common Weakness Enumeration) describes a product that builds an SQL command from externally influenced input without neutralizing the special elements that could change it. The classic case is an application that concatenates a form field into the text of a SELECT statement, so that characters meant as data close the string and continue as code. The input does not have to come straight from a browser: OWASP lists HTTP (Hypertext Transfer Protocol) requests, LDAP (Lightweight Directory Access Protocol) directories, email, third-party APIs (application programming interfaces) and the database itself, the last being the second-order case where stored data is later concatenated into another query. The consequences depend on the database's features and privileges: reading data, inserting, updating or deleting it, administrative operations such as shutting the DBMS down, reading or writing files and, in some cases, running operating system commands, which is why OWASP tells you to consider it high impact. It remains near the top of every list: CWE-89 ranks second in the 2025 CWE Top 25, with four of its CVEs (Common Vulnerabilities and Exposures) in the KEV (Known Exploited Vulnerabilities) catalogue, and OWASP's Top 10 for 2025 counts more than 14,000 CVEs for SQL injection inside the A05 Injection category, low in frequency and high in impact.

The cure is structural, not a filter. OWASP's primary defence is the parameterized query: define the SQL structure separately from its data values, then bind the values through the database API, for instance with a question mark as the placeholder in a prepared statement, so that whatever the user typed is treated as a literal value and can never change the syntax. Concatenating untrusted text into the query before preparing it defeats the protection. Placeholders stand for data values only, not for table names, column names or keywords such as ASC and DESC, so those structural choices must come from a fixed allow-list of application-owned values. Manual escaping is strongly discouraged, because escaping rules differ between dialects and even with configuration (MySQL's NO_BACKSLASH_ESCAPES mode is OWASP's example). The same flaw appears one level up and one level down: ORM (object-relational mapping) query languages such as Hibernate's HQL can be injected in exactly the same way, and binding the arguments of a stored procedure protects the call but not any dynamic SQL the procedure assembles inside itself. OWASP adds a limit worth remembering: parameter binding stops input from changing SQL syntax, but it does not decide whether the caller may see the matching row, which is an authorization question. Least privilege limits the blast radius, and OWASP is blunt that application accounts must never hold DBA (database administrator) rights.

The incidents show why the defaults matter. CVE-2023-34362, a SQL injection in the Progress MOVEit Transfer web application, let an unauthenticated attacker reach the application's database and alter or delete its contents; the NVD (National Vulnerability Database) records exploitation in the wild in May and June 2023, and CISA (Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency) added it to the KEV catalogue on 2 June 2023. Network defences catch some of this. On F5 BIG-IP the application security module classifies SQL-Injection as an attack type, ships a SQL Injection Signatures set, puts new signatures into staging for seven days by default, logging matches without blocking, and rates each signature for accuracy (the likelihood of false positives) and risk; FortiWeb and other web application firewalls (WAFs) work on the same principle. A WAF is a layer, not the fix: OWASP keeps a separate article on bypassing WAFs with SQL injection, and the only complete answer is a query whose structure the input cannot touch. The numbers worth remembering: 1970 for Codd, 1974 for SEQUEL, 1986 for the first ANSI standard, 2023 for the current ISO/IEC 9075 parts, and CWE-89.

l7.def: Layer 7 (L7) is the application layer, the top layer of the Open Systems Interconnection (OSI) reference model, where application protocols such as the Hypertext Transfer Protocol (HTTP) live.
l7.context: Layer 7 is the top of the seven-layer Open Systems Interconnection (OSI) model, the layer of application protocols. Operating at L7 lets a device understand the Hypertext Transfer Protocol (HTTP), make routing decisions on the address of the resource requested, and defend applications, as a web application firewall (WAF) does. The price is that the device has to terminate the connection, and usually the encryption, in order to read the message, which makes it a proxy; a device working at Layer 4 forwards on addresses and ports without looking inside.
l7.depth:
What the standard says. The seven layers come from the Basic Reference Model of Open Systems Interconnection (OSI), published as ISO/IEC 7498-1 and, with identical text, as Recommendation X.200 of the Telecommunication Standardization Sector of the International Telecommunication Union (ITU-T), approved on 1 July 1994. The 1994 edition replaced the first edition of 1984, and ISO's catalogue still lists it as current, last confirmed in 2000. Clause 6.1.2 names the layers from the top: Application (7), Presentation (6), Session (5), Transport (4), Network (3), Data Link (2) and Physical (1). Of the Application Layer the text says that, as the highest layer, it provides the sole means for the application process to access the OSI environment, and therefore has no boundary with a higher layer. The standard also says what it is for: a common basis for coordinating the development of standards, not an implementation specification.

What Layer 7 is not. It is not the application. In the model, the application process, the program or person doing the information processing, sits outside the seven layers; what lives in Layer 7 is the application-entity, the part of the process that communicates, speaking an application protocol with its peer. A browser and a web server are application processes; the Hypertext Transfer Protocol (HTTP) between them is Layer 7. This is why a device that works at Layer 7 understands requests and responses but knows nothing of what the program behind them will do.

The Internet's shorter stack. The Internet protocol suite never adopted the upper three layers separately. Request for Comments (RFC) 1122 (October 1989) describes its application layer as the top layer of the suite, not subdivided further, which essentially combines the functions of the Presentation and Application layers of the OSI model; its examples were Telnet, the File Transfer Protocol (FTP) and the Simple Mail Transfer Protocol (SMTP). HTTP defines itself the same way, as a stateless application-level protocol (RFC 9110, June 2022). So in everyday speech Layer 7 means everything above the transport, and the numbers 5 and 6 are almost never heard. The OSI numbering survived as vocabulary even though the stack that engineers run is the Internet's.

What working at Layer 7 costs. F5's own comparison is the clearest. A Layer 4 load balancer forwards packets with no regard to the content of the messages. A Layer 7 load balancer terminates the network traffic and reads the message within, decides on the content, for example the path in the request or a cookie, and then opens a new connection of the Transmission Control Protocol (TCP) to the chosen server, or reuses one. It is more demanding of the processor, it can change the content on the way through (compression, encryption), and by buffering it shields servers from slow clients; such a device, F5 notes, is often called a reverse proxy. The cloud menus use the same two numbers. Amazon's Application Load Balancer functions at the application layer, the seventh layer of the OSI model, and routes on the content of the application traffic by listener rules; its Network Load Balancer functions at the fourth layer, picks a target by protocol and port, and handles millions of requests per second.

Where the switch is. On every product there is a specific setting that turns Layer 7 awareness on. On F5 BIG-IP, a local traffic policy inspects requests and responses much as an iRule does, and a rule that tests the request path automatically makes the policy require the HTTP profile: without that profile the virtual server sees a byte stream. On a FortiGate, application control uses the protocol decoders of the intrusion prevention system (IPS) to recognize applications even on non-standard ports, and the inspection mode of the policy decides how deep the device goes: flow mode, the default, inspects packet by packet with fewer resources, while proxy mode buffers the whole payload and is required for the web application firewall (WAF) profile, the explicit web proxy and zero trust network access (ZTNA). In Kubernetes, an Ingress exposes HTTP and HTTPS (HTTP Secure) routes to services; that interface is now frozen, and the recommended Gateway interface expresses the same idea with an HTTPRoute.

Encryption is the gate. Nearly all Layer 7 traffic now travels inside Transport Layer Security (TLS), and a device that does not hold the keys sees only the transport. Layer 7 features therefore begin with decryption: FortiGate documents application detection over decrypted traffic, and the load balancers above terminate the encrypted connection before they read a request. The consequence is architectural. Every Layer 7 device is a place where traffic exists in clear text and where private keys are kept, which is a reason to count such devices and to review their configuration as carefully as that of the servers behind them.

Attacks at Layer 7. A flood aimed at the application layer does not need bandwidth. Cloudflare's description is that such attacks target the top layer of the model, where HTTP GET and POST requests occur, and work because of an asymmetry: a request costs the client almost nothing, while the server may have to query a database to answer it, and the requests are hard to tell from legitimate ones. The mitigations are Layer 7 tools too: a challenge that a script cannot pass, a WAF, reputation of source addresses. The record shows the scale. The HTTP/2 Rapid Reset attacks that began on 25 August 2023 peaked just above 201 million requests per second from a botnet of about 20,000 machines, by opening streams and cancelling them at once; the flaw is catalogued as CVE-2023-44487 in the Common Vulnerabilities and Exposures list, published on 10 October 2023 with a severity score of 7.5. Layer 7 attacks are counted in requests per second, not in bits per second.

Reading the label. When a datasheet says Layer 7, the useful questions are which protocols it actually parses, whether it decrypts, and whether it proxies the connection or inspects a copy of the packets. When a ticket says a Layer 7 problem, it means that addressing, routing and the transport handshake have been checked and the fault is in the request or the response. And when a firewall rule is said to be Layer 4, it means the rule sees addresses and ports and nothing of the conversation they carry.

as3.def: An F5 extension for declaratively configuring application services via JSON.
as3.context: Application Services 3 Extension takes a JSON declaration of the desired application configuration and makes BIG-IP match it, a declarative alternative to imperative tmsh commands, delivered over a REST endpoint.
as3.depth:
AS3 takes a JSON declaration of what an application should look like and makes the BIG-IP match it, which is a different proposition from a script that issues commands. You describe the desired end state, the extension works out the difference, and running the same declaration twice produces the same result rather than a second copy of everything.

That idempotence is the whole argument for it. Imperative configuration drifts, because a script that adds a pool member has no opinion about the pool member somebody added by hand last month, and reconciling that gap is the work nobody budgets for. A declaration is comparable to what is deployed, which makes configuration reviewable in a pull request and recoverable from a repository rather than from a backup.

The practical caution is scope. A declaration owns a tenant completely, so anything present in that tenant and absent from the declaration is removed, which is correct behaviour and a genuinely unpleasant surprise the first time it deletes something a colleague added outside the workflow. The migration to declarative is therefore organizational before it is technical: it only works if everybody stops editing by hand.

aws.def: Amazon Web Services (AWS), Amazon's cloud computing business: compute, storage, networking, databases and hundreds of other services, offered on demand through programmable interfaces, metered by use and run from regions around the world.
aws.context: Amazon Web Services (AWS) is the largest public cloud provider, with 26 per cent of cloud infrastructure spending in the third quarter of 2026 by Synergy Research Group's estimate, offering on-demand infrastructure and managed services from 39 geographic regions. For network and security engineers it is as much a destination as a platform: many integrations, including telemetry destinations such as CloudWatch and S3 (Simple Storage Service), virtual appliances and private interconnects, target AWS.
aws.depth:
AWS (Amazon Web Services) is the cloud computing business of Amazon, and the company reports it as a separate segment. For the third quarter of 2026 Amazon reported AWS sales of $46.0 billion, 39 per cent more than a year earlier and an annualized run rate of $184 billion, with operating income of $17.8 billion against $11.4 billion a year before. Synergy Research Group estimated the whole cloud infrastructure services market in that quarter at $167.7 billion, up 55 per cent, with Amazon leading at 26 per cent, followed by Microsoft at 19 per cent and Google at 16 per cent, the latter two growing faster. AWS describes its own customer base as millions of customers, from startups to government agencies, and its home page counts a portfolio of over 240 services.

Its public history begins with a queue. On 3 November 2004 Amazon opened the Simple Queue Service (SQS) for beta testing, describing it as a reliable, highly scalable hosted queue for buffering messages between distributed application components; it reached production in 2006. The launches that defined the model came that year. On 14 March 2006 Jeff Barr announced Amazon S3 (Simple Storage Service): objects of up to 5 GB, each with a user-defined key, metadata and an access control list, reached through SOAP (Simple Object Access Protocol) and REST (Representational State Transfer) interfaces, designed for 99.99 per cent availability with data stored in multiple locations, priced at 15 cents per GB per month and 20 cents per GB transferred. On 25 August 2006 he announced the limited beta of Amazon EC2 (Elastic Compute Cloud): a virtual CPU (central processing unit) equivalent to a 1.7 GHz Xeon processor with 1.75 GB of memory, 160 GB of local disk and 250 Mb/s of network bandwidth, for 10 cents per clock hour, built on the Xen virtual machine monitor and booted from Amazon Machine Images stored as S3 objects. Everything that followed kept the same pattern: an application programming interface (API) first, a meter on every resource, and no commitment beyond what is used.

The infrastructure is organized into regions and zones. The marketing page counts 124 Availability Zones in 39 geographic regions, with Saudi Arabia and Chile announced; the user guide lists 34 regions available to an ordinary account, because the AWS GovCloud (US) regions and the two regions in China are reached only through separate account types, and requires regions introduced after 20 March 2019 to be enabled before use. São Paulo, sa-east-1, is one of the older regions that need no opt-in. Every public region has at least three Availability Zones, separate groups of data centres up to about 100 km apart, and AWS's fault isolation guidance says a region's infrastructure and software services are independent of other regions, with documented exceptions.

The exceptions matter. Some AWS services are global, and their control planes live in one region while their data planes are distributed: AWS Identity and Access Management (IAM), Organizations, Route 53 and CloudFront are managed from us-east-1, Northern Virginia. A running workload elsewhere keeps working when us-east-1 has trouble, but changes to identity, DNS (Domain Name System) records or content distribution may not, which is why AWS's own whitepaper warns against putting a global control plane in a recovery path.

Security on AWS is divided by contract. The shared responsibility model separates security of the cloud, which AWS owns, from security in the cloud, which the customer owns. On EC2, an infrastructure service, the customer patches the guest operating system, runs the applications and configures the security groups; on abstracted services such as S3 and DynamoDB, AWS runs the operating system and platform and the customer still manages its data, encryption options, the classification of its assets and its IAM permissions. Physical and environmental controls are inherited from AWS outright, while patching, configuration management and staff training are shared, each party doing its own part.

One example every engineer meets is the instance metadata service (IMDS), which answers inside each instance at 169.254.169.254, or fd00:ec2::254 over IPv6 (Internet Protocol version 6), and can hand out temporary credentials for the instance's role, which makes it the prize in any SSRF (server-side request forgery) attack. Version 2, IMDSv2, requires a session token obtained in a separate request and valid for between one second and six hours; the response carrying the token has an Internet Protocol (IP) hop limit of 1 by default, so it does not travel beyond the instance, and token requests that carry an X-Forwarded-For header are refused. Both versions are accepted by default, and an instance can be configured to accept IMDSv2 only, after which version 1 calls fail.

AWS documents its own failures. It commits to publishing a post-event summary when an issue has broad and significant customer impact, and keeps each for at least five years; the list holds 18 summaries, from an EC2 and database disruption in Northern Virginia on 21 April 2011 to the DynamoDB disruption of October 2025, and 11 of the 18 concern Northern Virginia. On 28 February 2017 one command input entered incorrectly removed more S3 servers than intended and took the service down in that region for hours, along with the status dashboard that depended on it. On 7 December 2021, at 7:30 a.m. Pacific time, an automated scaling activity triggered a surge of connections from clients in AWS's internal network that congested the devices linking it to the main network; the operators lost their monitoring, EC2 programming interfaces returned errors from 7:33 a.m., new instance launches recovered only at 2:40 p.m., and Route 53 changes were impaired until 2:30 p.m., while running instances were unaffected. From the night of 19 October to the afternoon of 20 October 2025 a latent defect in DynamoDB's automated DNS management left its regional endpoint unresolvable and cascaded through dependent services. Each summary separates the control plane, which creates and changes resources, from the data plane, which serves running workloads, and in each the data plane held up better.

For network and security engineers AWS is often a destination rather than a platform. Telemetry from appliances is streamed to CloudWatch or written to S3; virtual editions of firewalls and application delivery controllers run inside customers' virtual private clouds; AWS Direct Connect ties a data centre to a region through a cross-connect ordered with a letter of authorization; and the identity, logging and metadata services above shape how those appliances are deployed and attacked. Knowing which parts of an architecture are regional, which are global and which side of the shared responsibility line each control falls on is most of what designing on AWS safely means.

fips.def: Federal Information Processing Standards (FIPS) are standards for US federal computer systems, developed by the National Institute of Standards and Technology (NIST) and approved by the Secretary of Commerce; the best known define approved cryptographic algorithms and the requirements a cryptographic module must meet to be validated.
fips.context: Federal Information Processing Standards (FIPS) are the National Institute of Standards and Technology (NIST) publications that define approved cryptographic algorithms, the Advanced Encryption Standard (AES) in FIPS 197 and the post-quantum ML-KEM (Module-Lattice-Based Key-Encapsulation Mechanism) in FIPS 203 among them, and the requirements systems must meet for government use. In the field the word usually means FIPS 140, the cryptographic-module standard, and FIPS mode, the setting that restricts a product to its validated module and approved algorithms.
fips.depth:
What a FIPS is. NIST's own definition is that Federal Information Processing Standards are standards for federal computer systems, developed by NIST and approved by the Secretary of Commerce under the Information Technology Management Reform Act of 1996 and the Computer Security Act of 1987, and written when no acceptable industry standard meets a government requirement. Not every FIPS is mandatory: each has an applicability section saying when it applies, and none applies to national security systems. Where one does apply there is no escape hatch, because the waiver process of the 1987 Act disappeared with the Federal Information Security Management Act (FISMA) of 2002, and FISMA's obligations reach contractors and state agencies running federal programmes as well as federal agencies. NIST also notes that many private-sector organizations adopt them voluntarily. A FIPS is a standard, not a product certificate; the distinction between an algorithm that is FIPS-approved and a module that is FIPS-validated is the one most vendor claims blur.

The current set. On 12 November 2026 NIST's list held 13 final FIPS. The cryptographic ones are FIPS 197, the Advanced Encryption Standard (AES), published on 26 November 2001 and editorially updated on 9 May 2023 with no technical change, which specifies the Rijndael ciphers AES-128, AES-192 and AES-256, all on 128-bit blocks; FIPS 180-4 (August 2015), the Secure Hash Standard with the Secure Hash Algorithms (SHA) SHA-1, SHA-224, SHA-256, SHA-384, SHA-512, SHA-512/224 and SHA-512/256; FIPS 202 (August 2015), SHA-3, built on Keccak, with four hash functions and the SHAKE128 and SHAKE256 extendable-output functions; FIPS 198-1 (July 2008) for the keyed-hash message authentication code (HMAC); FIPS 186-5 (February 2023), the Digital Signature Standard; and the three post-quantum standards of 13 August 2024. Beside them sit FIPS 140-2 and 140-3 for cryptographic modules, FIPS 199 and 200 for categorizing and protecting federal systems, and FIPS 201-3 (January 2022) for the personal identity verification (PIV) cards of federal employees and contractors. NIST has announced revisions of both hash standards.

Categorization and baselines. FIPS 199 (February 2004) asks of each kind of information and each system what a loss of confidentiality, integrity or availability would do, and grades the potential impact LOW for a limited adverse effect, MODERATE for a serious one and HIGH for a severe or catastrophic one. FIPS 200 (March 2006), the second of the two standards FISMA required, turns that category into minimum security requirements and a risk-based process for selecting the security controls that meet them. These two are why federal and federally inspired programmes talk in terms of low, moderate and high baselines.

FIPS 140-3 and the validation programme. The Secretary of Commerce approved FIPS 140-3 on 22 March 2019, effective 22 September 2019, superseding FIPS 140-2 of December 2002. Instead of stating module requirements itself it references ISO/IEC (International Organization for Standardization and International Electrotechnical Commission) 19790:2012, the international module standard, with testing under ISO/IEC 24759:2017.
