It defines four increasing qualitative security levels across eleven areas, from module specification, interfaces and roles to physical security, sensitive security parameter management, self-tests and life-cycle assurance. Validation is the job of the Cryptographic Module Validation Program (CMVP), run jointly by NIST and the Canadian Centre for Cyber Security: independent Cryptographic and Security Testing Laboratories (CSTLs), accredited under the National Voluntary Laboratory Accreditation Program (NVLAP), test the module and CMVP reviews and issues the certificate. The programme counts more than 1,000 active and more than 5,000 validated modules. It accepted FIPS 140-3 submissions from 22 September 2020 and no new FIPS 140-2 certificates after 1 April 2022; certificates stay active for five years, two for interim validations; and FIPS 140-2 modules could be bought for new systems only until 21 September 2026, after which they moved to the Historical List, usable in existing systems only. CMVP's position on the alternative is blunt: non-validated cryptography is viewed as providing no protection, the data in effect plaintext, so where cryptography is required it must be validated.

Retirements and the post-quantum set. Algorithms leave the list as well. SHA-1, standardized in FIPS 180-1 in 1995 as a slight modification of the 1993 SHA, is to be phased out by 31 December 2030; a FIPS 180-5 will remove it, and modules still using it after that date will not be permitted for federal purchase. The replacements for public-key cryptography arrived on 13 August 2024, after a process that began in 2015 and assessed 82 algorithms from 25 countries: FIPS 203 specifies ML-KEM, formerly CRYSTALS-Kyber, a key-encapsulation mechanism based on the Module Learning with Errors problem, with parameter sets ML-KEM-512, ML-KEM-768 and ML-KEM-1024; FIPS 204 specifies ML-DSA (Module-Lattice-Based Digital Signature Algorithm), formerly CRYSTALS-Dilithium, the primary signature standard; FIPS 205 specifies SLH-DSA (Stateless Hash-Based Digital Signature Algorithm), formerly SPHINCS+, a backup built on different mathematics. NIST announced FN-DSA (FFT over NTRU-Lattice-Based Digital Signature Algorithm, FFT being the fast Fourier transform), from FALCON, as draft FIPS 206; on 12 November 2026 the list of final FIPS still ended at 205.

What FIPS mode means. A product does not become validated by supporting AES. Validation attaches to a specific module, version and tested configuration, and each certificate carries caveats. The BIG-IP software module, certificate #5487 (FIPS 140-3, overall Level 1, for BIG-IP Virtual Edition, validated on 14 August 2026, active until its sunset on 20 November 2029, replacing the interim certificate #4895), is valid only when operated in approved mode and when installed, initialized and configured as its Security Policy specifies. FIPS mode is the switch that puts a product into that approved mode: only approved algorithms and key sizes, the validated module in the data path, self-tests at start-up and on demand, and an error state that stops cryptography rather than continue unchecked.

F5 BIG-IP. On hardware, Platform FIPS needs the Full-Box FIPS add-on licence and gives device-level FIPS 140-3 validation at Level 2 on specific platforms, with tamper-evident stickers in the installation kit; it exists since BIG-IP 13.1.0, but only the platforms and versions listed in F5's security policies are validated. With the licence the system enters FIPS-enabled mode during boot, switches its SSL (Secure Sockets Layer) cipher suites to FIPS-compliant ones and runs the required self-tests; a failed test halts the system, the fips_monitor daemon watches for errors, and a system integrity test fails if files of the underlying operating system are changed directly rather than through tmsh, the Configuration utility or the F5 APIs (application programming interfaces). The mode shows in the db variable security.fips140.compliance and in /config/f5_public/fips.conf, which holds 1 when it is on. With a FIPS 140-3 licence the management plane is restricted too: Secure Shell (SSH) accepts only aes128-ctr, aes256-ctr, aes128-cbc and aes256-cbc, hmac-sha1 and hmac-sha2-256, and ecdh-sha2-nistp256 and nistp384 key exchange, and a service indicator logs approved sessions in /var/log/audit. A module that keeps failing its self-tests after several reboots leaves the box unusable until reinstalled, which F5 documents in plain words.

FortiGate. FortiOS calls it FIPS-CC (FIPS and Common Criteria) mode: config system fips-cc, set status enable. The prompt asks for the admin password twice, warns that most configuration will be lost, and reboots, so it belongs in a provisioning plan, not a maintenance window. At boot the unit runs self-tests of AES, HMAC, RSA (Rivest-Shamir-Adleman) and the Elliptic Curve Digital Signature Algorithm (ECDSA), of the key derivation functions (KDFs) of Transport Layer Security (TLS), SSH and Internet Key Exchange (IKE), of firmware integrity and of its random bit generator (RBG). Newer releases replaced the USB (Universal Serial Bus) entropy token once needed in FIPS mode with a built-in entropy source based on central processing unit (CPU) jitter that, Fortinet states, continues to meet FIPS 140-3. In FortiOS 8.0 FIPS-CC mode installs the OpenSSL FIPS provider globally at start-up, defaults to TLS 1.2 and 1.3, allows only Diffie-Hellman groups of 2048 bits or more, limits RADIUS (Remote Authentication Dial-In User Service) to PAP (Password Authentication Protocol) over TLS, and offers execute fips kat ossl-fips-provider-test to rerun the known-answer tests by hand.

Linux. The kernel's switch is the fips=1 boot parameter. It sets fips_enabled, readable at /proc/sys/crypto/fips_enabled together with fips_name and fips_version; with it set, the kernel's crypto test manager refuses algorithms not marked as allowed in FIPS mode and panics if a self-test fails. User space is the library's business: in OpenSSL 3 the FIPS module is a provider, the old FIPS_mode() and FIPS_mode_set() calls are gone, and applications that use low-level APIs, engines or custom methods bypass the module and so fall outside it. A Linux system is in FIPS mode only when the kernel switch, the validated libraries and the applications all line up.

What goes wrong. The common failures are predictable. A product is described as FIPS compliant when it merely implements approved algorithms; a validated module is run outside its approved mode or on a version or platform its certificate does not list; a certificate sunsets or moves to the Historical List unnoticed, as every FIPS 140-2 certificate did in September 2026; and switching the mode on breaks whatever depended on SHA-1 signatures, small Diffie-Hellman groups, old TLS versions or RADIUS without TLS. The numbers to keep are FIPS 140-3 of 2019 with its four levels, five years of certificate life, 21 September 2026 for FIPS 140-2, 31 December 2030 for SHA-1, and 13 August 2024 for FIPS 203, 204 and 205.

ml-kem.def: ML-KEM (Module-Lattice-Based Key-Encapsulation Mechanism) is the post-quantum key-encapsulation algorithm that NIST (the United States National Institute of Standards and Technology) standardized as FIPS 203 in August 2024, derived from CRYSTALS-Kyber, by which two parties establish a 32-byte shared secret that a quantum computer is not known to be able to recover.
ml-kem.context: Module-Lattice-Based Key-Encapsulation Mechanism (ML-KEM), Federal Information Processing Standard (FIPS) 203 from the United States National Institute of Standards and Technology (NIST), derived from Kyber, is a lattice-based scheme designed to resist quantum attacks. Its security rests on the Module Learning With Errors problem; it comes in three sizes, ML-KEM-512, 768 and 1024, with 768 as NIST's recommended default. It is deployed in hybrid TLS (Transport Layer Security) key exchanges alongside classical ECDHE (Elliptic Curve Diffie-Hellman Ephemeral), most often as X25519MLKEM768, and in SSH (Secure Shell), so that recorded traffic stays confidential even if one of the two components is broken.
ml-kem.depth:
ML-KEM (Module-Lattice-Based Key-Encapsulation Mechanism) is the post-quantum key establishment algorithm that the United States National Institute of Standards and Technology (NIST) standardized as FIPS 203 (Federal Information Processing Standard 203) on 13 August 2024, derived from the CRYSTALS-Kyber submission. NIST's announcement called FIPS 203 the primary standard for general encryption, praised its comparatively small keys and its speed, and described the three standards published that day as the result of an eight-year effort that began with a call for submissions in 2016. It takes over the key exchange half of TLS (Transport Layer Security), the part currently done by elliptic curve Diffie-Hellman, whose security rests on a problem a large quantum computer would solve efficiently: NIST's transition report, IR 8547 (an interagency or internal report), states that the elliptic curve and RSA (Rivest-Shamir-Adleman) key establishment schemes are all vulnerable to Shor's algorithm on a cryptanalytically relevant quantum computer.

The name describes the mechanism. It is a key-encapsulation mechanism (KEM) rather than a key exchange, and FIPS 203 explains the difference with Alice and Bob: Alice generates a decapsulation key, which she keeps, and an encapsulation key, which she publishes; Bob uses her encapsulation key to produce one copy of a shared secret together with a ciphertext, and sends the ciphertext; Alice combines it with her decapsulation key to compute the other copy. Only the holder of the private key can decapsulate. Security rests on the hardness of the Module Learning With Errors problem. Internally, FIPS 203 first builds a public-key encryption scheme, K-PKE, and then turns it into a KEM with a variant of the Fujisaki-Okamoto transform, which is why ML-KEM is believed to meet IND-CCA2 (indistinguishability under adaptive chosen-ciphertext attack) security; the decapsulation key includes a random 32-byte value used for implicit rejection: decapsulation re-encrypts the recovered message and, if the result does not match the ciphertext received, returns a key derived from that secret value and the ciphertext instead of an error. The shared secret is always 256 bits, usable directly as a symmetric key or as input to key derivation.

Three parameter sets exist, ML-KEM-512, 768 and 1024, with 768 the common default; NIST's IR 8547 recommends ML-KEM-768 as the default because it gives a large security margin at a reasonable cost, and places the three in security categories 1, 3 and 5. All work on polynomials of 256 coefficients modulo the prime 3329; the module rank k is 2, 3 or 4, and the required strength of the random bit generator is 128, 192 or 256 bits. The sizes are what engineers notice: the encapsulation key is 800, 1,184 or 1,568 bytes, the decapsulation key 1,632, 2,400 or 3,168 bytes, the ciphertext 768, 1,088 or 1,568 bytes, and the shared secret 32 bytes in every case. FIPS 203 also gives the probability that decapsulation simply fails, which is about 2 to the power minus 138.8, minus 164.8 and minus 174.8 for the three sets. For comparison, an X25519 public share is 32 bytes.

ML-KEM is not quite Kyber. Appendix C of FIPS 203 lists the changes from the third-round Kyber specification: the shared secret is fixed at 256 bits instead of a variable length; encapsulation uses a different variant of the Fujisaki-Okamoto transform that no longer hashes the ciphertext into the shared secret; the initial randomness is no longer hashed first, because the standard requires a NIST-approved random bit generator; and explicit input checks were added, so that, for example, an encapsulation key must decode to integers modulo q without any reduction. After the initial public draft of 24 August 2023, domain separation was added to key generation so that a key stored as a seed cannot be misused at a different security level. The practical result, as Chrome's engineers wrote on 13 September 2024, is that final ML-KEM is incompatible with the Kyber already deployed: Chrome 131 moved its hybrid key share from codepoint 0x6399 (X25519 with Kyber768) to 0x11EC (X25519 with ML-KEM-768) and dropped the old one rather than support both, because post-quantum key shares are too big to offer two predictions in one ClientHello.

The urgency is harvest now, decrypt later. An adversary recording encrypted traffic today can decrypt it whenever a capable quantum computer arrives, so anything requiring long-term confidentiality is already exposed regardless of when that happens; NIST's IR 8547 (final version, October 2026) names the threat in those words and gives medical records and government secrets as examples of data whose value outlives the encryption. The same report sets the clock: NIST will deprecate quantum-vulnerable public-key cryptography after 2030 and disallow it under its standards after 2035, while United States federal directives require the government's most sensitive systems to use post-quantum key establishment by 31 December 2030. It also states that ML-KEM is, for now, the only approved post-quantum KEM based on public-key cryptography.

This is why deployments pair ML-KEM with a classical algorithm in hybrid mode: if the lattice assumption were ever broken, the classical half still holds. RFC 10024 (Request for Comments 10024, August 2026, by K. Kwiatkowski, P. Kampanakis, B. E. Westerbaan and D. Stebila) defines three hybrid groups for TLS 1.3 that combine ML-KEM with ECDHE (Elliptic Curve Diffie-Hellman Ephemeral): X25519MLKEM768 (4588, 0x11EC), the only one marked Recommended; SecP256r1MLKEM768 (0x11EB), for cases where both shared secrets must come from FIPS-approved mechanisms; and SecP384r1MLKEM1024 (0x11ED), for higher-security FIPS environments. In X25519MLKEM768 the client's key share is 1,216 bytes (1,184 for ML-KEM and 32 for X25519) and the server's 1,120 bytes (a 1,088-byte ciphertext plus 32), against 32 bytes for X25519 alone; the two shared secrets are concatenated, ML-KEM's first, an order chosen so that a FIPS-approved derivation can be used. The RFC also marks the pre-standard Kyber codepoints as deprecated and warns that its security analysis relies on the TLS 1.3 transcript, so the same hybridization cannot be assumed secure in other protocols. NIST selected the code-based HQC in March 2025 as a structurally different backup for exactly that reason: built on error-correcting codes rather than structured lattices, with a draft standard expected about a year later and a final one in 2027.

Deployment is already broad. Chrome offers X25519MLKEM768 from version 131, and Google implemented ML-KEM in its BoringSSL library. OpenSSH 9.9 (19 September 2024) added the hybrid mlkem768x25519-sha256 key exchange, and OpenSSH 10.0 (9 April 2025) made it the default, describing it as no less strong than curve25519-sha256 and considerably faster than the previous default. F5's BIG-IP 21.1 added SecP256r1MLKEM768 and SecP384r1MLKEM1024 to TLS on both the client and the server side, so a virtual server can negotiate post-quantum key establishment with browsers and with back ends. In a capture, a hybrid handshake is easy to spot: a ClientHello whose key_share carries group 0x11EC with more than a kilobyte of data.

The pitfalls are mostly about size and implementation. A key share of 1,216 bytes no longer fits the assumptions of software that expected a few dozen, and a client that guesses wrong pays a round trip, which is why Chrome's engineers called extra round trips particularly costly with large post-quantum algorithms and proposed letting servers advertise their groups in DNS (Domain Name System). RFC 10024 urges implementations resistant to side-channel attacks, especially remote ones, and points out that the encapsulation randomness drawn from the random bit generator is recovered exactly by the holder of the decapsulation key, so a weak generator leaks its other outputs to the peer. In FIPS deployments the order of the shared secrets decides which component must be certified: the ML-KEM implementation for X25519MLKEM768, the elliptic curve one for the two NIST-curve groups. And ML-KEM protects confidentiality only: certificates and handshake signatures remain RSA or ECDSA (Elliptic Curve Digital Signature Algorithm) until ML-DSA (Module-Lattice-Based Digital Signature Algorithm, FIPS 204) replaces them, which matters less for recorded traffic but fully for forgery once a quantum computer exists.

The numbers worth remembering are FIPS 203 of 13 August 2024; the three sets 512, 768 and 1024 at categories 1, 3 and 5, with 768 the default; 1,184-byte encapsulation keys and 1,088-byte ciphertexts for ML-KEM-768; a 32-byte shared secret; 0x11EC for X25519MLKEM768, which replaced Kyber's 0x6399; HQC as the backup expected in 2027; and NIST's 2030 deprecation and 2035 disallowance of quantum-vulnerable key establishment.

qat.def: Intel hardware that offloads cryptography and compression from the CPU.
qat.context: QuickAssist Technology accelerates encryption, decryption, and compression in dedicated silicon, freeing CPU cycles. On appliances it can materially raise TLS throughput when enabled.

rpm.def: A package format and manager used by Red Hat-family Linux systems.
rpm.context: RPM Package Manager is both the .rpm package format and the tooling that installs, upgrades, and tracks software on distributions like RHEL and Fedora. BIG-IP's software volumes are built from RPMs.

stp.def: In local area networking STP stands for two different things: Spanning Tree Protocol, and Shielded Twisted Pair.
stp.context: Two different things share these letters: Spanning Tree Protocol, and Shielded Twisted Pair. The two diagnoses have nothing in common.
stp.depth:
Two unrelated things share these three letters, and confusing them is common enough to be worth a moment. The sentence around the acronym usually settles it. Root bridges, BPDUs (bridge protocol data units), VLANs (virtual local area networks), blocked ports and convergence times mean the protocol; categories, screens, drain wires, connectors and grounding mean the cable. In a data centre both can turn up in the same ticket, which is exactly when it pays to ask.

Spanning Tree Protocol. This is the Layer 2 protocol that prevents switching loops by electing a root bridge, computing a loop-free tree across a redundant mesh and blocking the links outside it. It is needed because, as RFC (Request for Comments) 6325 puts it, the Ethernet header contains no hop count or time to live (TTL) field, so a loop that forms is never cleaned up by the frames themselves. STP is what the acronym means in almost every switching conversation, and its successors kept the name in theirs: RSTP (Rapid Spanning Tree Protocol), first 802.1w and then part of 802.1D-2004, and MSTP (Multiple Spanning Tree Protocol), first 802.1s. Since 802.1Q-2014, approved on 3 November 2014, superseded 802.1D-2004, all three live in IEEE (Institute of Electrical and Electronics Engineers) 802.1Q. The spanning-tree entry covers the algorithm, the timers, the versions and the guards.

Which STP is running. In strict use STP names only the original 802.1D protocol, with its 30-second-plus convergence, but in daily speech it covers the whole family, and that matters when two switches disagree. A Cisco Catalyst 9300 runs Rapid PVST+ (Rapid Per-VLAN Spanning Tree Plus), one rapid tree per VLAN, out of the box, while PVST+, Cisco's per-VLAN version of classic 802.1D, and MSTP are options. The standard protocols send their BPDUs to the bridge group address 01-80-C2-00-00-00; Cisco's Per-VLAN Spanning Tree uses its own address, 01-00-0C-CC-CC-CD. Saying 'STP is enabled' therefore says little: the useful statement names the mode, RSTP, MSTP or Rapid PVST+, and which switch is meant to be root.

Shielded twisted pair. This is a cable construction: twisted pairs with a conductive screen of foil, braid or both. ISO/IEC 11801, the cabling standard of the International Organization for Standardization (ISO) and the International Electrotechnical Commission (IEC), names its variants by where the screen sits, in designations that its 2010 edition gives in an informative annex, meaning they are not required for compliance: F/UTP for an overall foil over unscreened pairs, often called FTP (foiled twisted pair); U/FTP for individually foiled pairs; S/FTP for a braid over foiled pairs, often called STP or PiMF (pairs in metal foil); SF/UTP for braid and foil over unscreened pairs. Catalogues use STP loosely for several of them, so 'STP cable' on a purchase order is not a specification; the ISO designation is. The term is older than structured cabling: IBM launched its Token Ring product on 15 October 1985 at 4 Mbit/s over shielded twisted pair with its own data connector, and it was Ethernet's move to cheaper unshielded cable with 10BASE-T and 100BASE-TX that made shielding the exception. The shielded-twisted-pair entry covers the constructions and when each is worth its cost.

The practical catch with the cable. A screen helps only when it is continuous through every connector and bonded into the building's telecommunications grounding system. Belden recommends bonding the shield at both ends, requires the foil to make good contact with the connector housing, warns against breaking the screen with an unshielded patch cord, and cites ANSI/TIA-607-C, a standard of the Telecommunications Industry Association approved by the American National Standards Institute (ANSI), for bonding the shield to the busbars; without proper bonding, a difference in common-mode potential between ground connections drives current and creates a ground loop that induces noise onto the cabling.

A third reading, in telephone networks. Telecommunications engineers meet STP as the signal transfer point of Signalling System No. 7 (SS7). RFC 4666, one of the specifications for carrying SS7 signalling over IP (Internet Protocol) networks, defines it as a node in the SS7 network that provides network access and performs message routing, screening and transfer of signalling messages. In an operator's core, 'the STP pair' is a pair of signalling routers and has nothing to do with either switches or cable.

When they meet. 'We had an STP problem in the data centre' could mean a root bridge in the wrong place, a forwarding loop after someone disabled BPDU protection, or a screen bonded to nothing, and no measurement taken for one tells you anything about the other. The cure is vocabulary: write RSTP, MSTP or Rapid PVST+ for the protocol, write S/FTP, F/UTP or U/FTP for the cable, and keep the bare acronym out of tickets and purchase orders.

tps.def: A throughput measure counting transactions handled each second.
tps.context: Transactions Per Second measures processing rate, and on some platforms it is also a licensed capacity limit - for example an SSL TPS ceiling that caps how many handshakes per second a licence permits.

bados.def: A defence that detects denial-of-service by learning normal traffic behaviour.
bados.context: Behavioural Denial of Service protection builds a baseline of normal traffic and mitigates deviations automatically, catching application-layer attacks that signature-based defences miss.
bados.depth:
Behavioural denial of service defence learns what normal traffic looks like for an application and treats significant deviation as an attack, rather than matching known signatures. It exists because application-layer floods consist of individually legitimate requests that no signature can distinguish.

The trade is the one every anomaly-based control makes. A baseline learned during unusual conditions encodes those conditions as normal, and a genuine traffic surge from a legitimate campaign looks exactly like the thing it is built to stop. That is why these systems are usually run in a learning mode long enough to see a full business cycle, and why a mitigation that engages during a product launch is a support incident rather than a success.

c3d.def: An F5 feature that re-signs client certificates for backend mutual TLS.
c3d.context: Client Certificate Constrained Delegation lets BIG-IP terminate a client's TLS and then present a freshly generated certificate representing that client to the backend, preserving identity across a re-encryption boundary.

ehf.def: An out-of-band fix F5 issues for a specific urgent problem.
ehf.context: An Engineering Hotfix is a targeted patch delivered outside the normal release cadence to address a specific defect, later rolled into a maintenance release.

df.def: DF is the model suffix F5 gives to appliances built with a factory-installed, FIPS-validated (Federal Information Processing Standards) hardware security module (HSM) and dual solid-state drives (SSDs): the BIG-IP i5820-DF, i7820-DF and i15820-DF, and the rSeries r5920-DF and r10920-DF.
df.context: In F5's model names the suffix marks the FIPS (Federal Information Processing Standards) variant of a platform. The platform guides describe each DF model as the member of its series that carries a FIPS-validated hardware security module (HSM) as a factory-installed option, with dual solid-state drives (SSDs); F5 does not spell out the two letters, and nothing in the guides makes it a cooling designation. The detail matters whenever a model list is read: in release notes, in the platforms a software version supports, and above all in compliance work, because the HSM inside carries its own Level 3 validation from the National Institute of Standards and Technology (NIST) while the appliance as a whole does not, and a software version keeps the device's FIPS standing only if F5 lists that version as validated.
df.depth:
DF is a suffix on F5 hardware model numbers, not a product of its own. F5's platform guides use it on five appliances: in the BIG-IP iSeries, the i5820-DF, the i7820-DF and the i15820-DF; in the rSeries, which run F5OS, the r5920-DF and the r10920-DF. Each guide says the same two things about its DF model: the series is available with a FIPS-validated (Federal Information Processing Standards) hardware security module (HSM) as a factory-installed option, and these platforms have dual solid-state drives (SSDs). The guides group them under series labels such as i5000F, i7000F and i15000F, which is how the specification tables name them. F5 does not expand the two letters anywhere in its platform guides, FIPS administration guides or certification tables. The older gloss 'dual-fan' does not match the documentation: the guides for the i5000, i15000 and r10000 series describe a single removable fan tray at the back of the chassis, and no guide ties a fan option to the DF models. What the documentation ties to DF is the HSM and the pair of drives.

The neighbouring suffixes follow the same pattern. The i11000 Series comes as the i11400-DS, i11600-DS and i11800-DS, which the platform guide describes as three levels of SSL (Secure Sockets Layer) offload, all with dual SSDs and high-performance SSL hardware, and the rSeries has the r12600-DS, r12800-DS and r12900-DS; dual drives are the feature the DS and DF models share. The i15000 Series also exists in a Network Equipment-Building System (NEBS) compliant version, the i15000-N. Before the DF names, F5's FIPS appliance was the 10350v-F, also written 10350v-FIPS; it appears beside the DF models in F5's FIPS documentation and certification tables, which is why a model list for FIPS work is longer than the DF models alone.

What is inside. F5's certifications page names the integrated module in every DF appliance as the NITROXIII CNN35XX-NFBE HSM Family, which the Cryptographic Module Validation Program (CMVP) of the National Institute of Standards and Technology (NIST) attributes to Marvell, formerly Cavium. Two certificates cover it. Certificate 4263, a FIPS 140-2 validation at overall Level 3 first issued on 13 July 2022, is the one F5 lists for the 10350v-F, i5820-DF, i7820-DF and i15820-DF; NIST now shows it as Historical, moved to the historical list due to sunsetting, which means federal agencies should not include it in new procurements. Certificate 4700, a FIPS 140-3 validation at overall Level 3 first issued on 30 May 2024 and updated on 1 June 2026, is the one F5 lists for the r5920-DF and r10920-DF; it is Active, with a sunset date of 29 May 2029. Both describe a hardware module of the multi-chip embedded kind.

Two validations, two levels. F5 is explicit that the integrated HSM is FIPS-validated but that the BIG-IP systems are not themselves validated at FIPS 140-2 or 140-3 Level 3. The system software has validations of its own: the same certifications page, last updated on 26 August 2026, lists BIG-IP 17.1.0.1 and 17.5 as FIPS 140-3 Level 2 on rSeries and iSeries hardware, a list that includes the DF models among ordinary ones, and BIG-IP Virtual Edition (VE) at Level 1. A DF appliance therefore combines a Level 2 validation of the device's software cryptographic module with a Level 3 validation of the key store inside it. F5's FIPS notes add a scope limit: only the Local Traffic Manager (LTM) and Advanced Firewall Manager (AFM) modules are included in the F5 Device and F5 vCMP (Virtual Clustered Multiprocessing) Cryptographic Modules, so only traffic handled by those modules counts as processed in a FIPS-approved way.

Putting the HSM to work on the iSeries. The module must be initialized before use, which is normally done once, from the BIG-IP command shell, tmsh, with run util fips-util init, and it can be done before the system is licensed or configured. Initialization deletes every key in the HSM and makes any previously exported key unusable, asks for a Security Officer password (the word default is refused), and creates a security domain whose label, up to 50 characters with F5FIPS as the default, must be identical on every peer unit that is to synchronize keys with it. In a device group each unit's HSM is initialized and the peers join the first unit's security domain; the label and password are what an operator needs to keep safe, because without them a replacement unit cannot join.

On the rSeries the model changes. The HSM is managed from the F5OS system command-line interface (CLI), not from inside BIG-IP. After initialization its resources sit in one default FIPS partition, PARTITION_1, which F5 also calls a virtual HSM; to create more, resources are first released from the default and then assigned. A partition can hold from 1 to 1,000,000 keys; the r5000-DF platforms support up to 24 FIPS partitions and 32 acceleration devices, the r10000-DF platforms up to 32 partitions and 63 acceleration devices; key management then happens per tenant, in tmsh. F5's rSeries training material gives the r10920-DF in numbers: one rack unit, 24 physical cores and 48 virtual CPUs (central processing units), of which 12 are reserved for F5OS, 256 GB of memory, two 1 TB SSDs mirrored as RAID-1 (redundant array of independent disks), four 100/40 Gb and sixteen 25/10 Gb ports, and power supplies with a keyed C15 connector shared with the r10000 and r12000.

Where it bites. Software updates are the first trap. F5's FIPS notes tell operators to check a version's FIPS validation status on the certifications page before installing any update or hotfix: the system will apply any update, but if the version has not been validated the device is no longer considered FIPS validated. Firmware is the second. The HSM's firmware is upgraded separately with F5's n3fips-firmware-upgrade utility, supported on the i5820-DF, i7820-DF, i15820-DF and 10350-F, which needs a reboot and therefore a maintenance window; the keys should be backed up first with n3fipsutil, and if the module was re-initialized with a different password the utility fails on upgrade, export and backup. The third is careless re-initialization, which erases every key the module holds. In all three cases the model name is the first thing to check, because the procedure depends on whether the box is an iSeries DF, an rSeries DF or the older 10350v-F.

Other things called DF. Outside F5's price list the two letters mean something else. In the Internet Protocol version 4 (IPv4) header, defined in RFC (Request for Comments) 791 of September 1981, DF is bit 1 of the flags field, Don't Fragment: when it is set the datagram may not be fragmented and is discarded instead. Path MTU (maximum transmission unit) discovery, specified in RFC 1191 in November 1990, is built on that bit: a host sends datagrams with DF set and learns the path's MTU from the 'fragmentation needed and DF set' messages that come back. On Unix and Linux systems df is the POSIX (Portable Operating System Interface) utility that reports free disk space. A search for DF in an F5 context, a packet capture or a shell session will land on three unrelated things.

ja3.def: A fingerprint of a TLS client built from the fields in its ClientHello.
ja3.context: JA3 hashes a set of ClientHello fields - TLS version, cipher list, extensions - into a short signature (an MD5 hash) that often identifies the client software or malware family, regardless of IP. JA4 is its more robust successor.
ja3.depth:
JA3 turns a TLS Client Hello into a short fingerprint by hashing the ordered list of things a client offers: version, cipher suites, extensions, curves and point formats. Different software makes different choices in a different order, so the hash identifies the implementation without decrypting anything at all.

That property is why it spread. A defender can spot a known malware family by its handshake even inside encrypted traffic, and can flag a client claiming to be a browser in its user agent while handshaking like a scripting library. The signal is metadata rather than content, which is precisely what makes it usable where inspection is impossible or unwelcome.

Its limits are equally worth stating. A fingerprint identifies software, not intent, so a match is a lead rather than a verdict, and legitimate tools share hashes with unpleasant ones. Attackers learned to mimic browser handshakes deliberately, which is straightforward once the target is known. And TLS libraries began randomizing extension order, breaking the assumption the technique rests on, which is why JA4 exists and why treating a fingerprint as identity rather than as a hint ages badly.

ja4.def: A newer, more robust family of TLS and network fingerprints.
ja4.context: JA4 (part of the JA4+ suite) improves on JA3 with a more structured, harder-to-evade fingerprint of the ClientHello, and adds companion fingerprints for other protocols. It resists the ordering tricks that let clients dodge JA3.
ja4.depth:
JA4 is the successor to JA3, and it exists because the original stopped working. JA3 hashed the ordered list of what a TLS client offers, which identified software reliably until libraries began randomizing extension order deliberately, at which point the same client produced a different hash on every connection.

The redesign fixes that and more. JA4 sorts the fields it hashes so ordering no longer matters, and it produces a human-readable structure rather than one opaque digest, so an analyst can see which component of a fingerprint changed instead of only that it changed. It also covers more than the client handshake, extending the same approach to server responses, HTTP behaviour and other protocols.

The strategic point survives both versions. Fingerprinting identifies implementations, not intentions, so it belongs in correlation and triage rather than in blocking decisions made alone. And it remains an arms race: any signal derived from what a client voluntarily sends can eventually be imitated by a client that knows it is being measured, which is why the technique is a useful input and never a verdict.

spbm.def: Shortest Path Bridging MAC mode (SPBM; MAC, media access control) is the form of IEEE (Institute of Electrical and Electronics Engineers) 802.1aq that carries Ethernet frames across a backbone in MAC-in-MAC encapsulation, with IS-IS (Intermediate System to Intermediate System) computing the shortest paths and a 24-bit service identifier, the I-SID, naming each service.
spbm.context: Shortest Path Bridging MAC mode (SPBM; MAC, media access control), standardized as IEEE (Institute of Electrical and Electronics Engineers) 802.1aq, creates a loop-free, shortest-path Ethernet fabric controlled by the IS-IS (Intermediate System to Intermediate System) routing protocol, replacing spanning tree with true multipath forwarding across a provider or campus backbone. Backbone Edge Bridges (BEBs) wrap customer frames in IEEE 802.1ah Provider Backbone Bridging headers addressed to each other's backbone MAC addresses; Backbone Core Bridges (BCBs) forward on those addresses alone and never see a customer address. Each service, a stretched VLAN (virtual local area network) or a routed VRF (virtual routing and forwarding instance), is a 24-bit Service Instance Identifier (I-SID) configured only at the edges. Extreme Networks sells its implementation as Fabric Connect, in the operating system now called Fabric Engine.
spbm.depth:
The standard. Shortest Path Bridging (SPB) is IEEE (Institute of Electrical and Electronics Engineers) 802.1aq, whose project page gives its full title as Virtual Bridged Local Area Networks, Amendment 8: Shortest Path Bridging. Its scope is shortest path bridging of unicast and multicast frames, with protocols that calculate multiple active topologies able to share learnt station location information. The project was authorized on 22 September 2005, draft 0.1 was posted on 4 March 2006 and the standard was approved on 29 March 2012; Wikipedia records that IEEE 802.1Q-2014, Bridges and Bridged Networks, incorporates it. SPB has two modes. In SPBV, the VLAN identifier (VID) mode, the services are virtual local area networks (VLANs); in SPBM, the media access control (MAC) mode, they are delineated by service instance identifiers and carried in Provider Backbone Bridging encapsulation, and the two can coexist. RFC (Request for Comments) 6329 gives the practical design goals: networks of about 100 nodes for SPBV and 1,000 for SPBM. When engineers say SPB in a campus or data centre today they almost always mean SPBM.

The control plane is IS-IS. RFC 6329, published by the IETF (Internet Engineering Task Force) in April 2012 with editors from Alcatel-Lucent and Huawei and authors from Ericsson, Ciena and Avaya, documents what 802.1aq adds to Intermediate System to Intermediate System (IS-IS): a small number of TLVs (type, length, value elements) and sub-TLVs, a Network Layer Protocol Identifier (NLPID) of 0xC1, and no change to the state machine. Every bridge's IS-IS System ID doubles as its backbone MAC (media access control) address, the BMAC, and the link-state database carries the BMACs and the service identifiers each node offers. Each node computes shortest path trees from every other node and programs its forwarding tables from that computation alone; no backbone address is ever learned from traffic. The paths are symmetric (the route from A to B is the route from B to A) and congruent for unicast and multicast, which, as the RFC notes, preserves packet ordering and keeps operations, administration and maintenance (OAM) traffic on the path it is testing. Equal-cost paths are spread by Equal Cost Tree (ECT) algorithms: the RFC defines a set of 16, each a tie-breaking rule identified by a 32-bit value such as the default 00-80-C2-01, and binds each to a backbone VLAN, which is why Extreme tells operators always to configure two B-VLANs so that load is distributed over both.

The data plane is MAC-in-MAC. SPBM forwards customer traffic in the encapsulation of IEEE 802.1ah, Provider Backbone Bridges, approved on 12 June 2008 to let providers interconnect bridged networks at a scale of at least 2 to the power 20 service VLANs. The ingress edge, a Backbone Edge Bridge (BEB), wraps the customer frame in a backbone header: a backbone destination and source MAC (BMAC-DA and BMAC-SA), a backbone VLAN tag with EtherType 0x88A8, and an instance tag with EtherType 0x88E7 whose 32-bit field carries the 24-bit Service Instance Identifier (I-SID). Counted from those fields, that is 22 octets added to every frame. Extreme's guide stresses what follows: because the header stays the same across the network, no node swaps a label or does a route lookup; the core never learns customer MAC addresses; and a loop in an access network does not disturb forwarding in the backbone. The core switches, Backbone Core Bridges (BCBs), forward on the BMAC-DA only and are unaware of the services they carry. RFC 6329 adds the safety net: a transit node checks the backbone source address and VLAN against the port the frame arrived on and discards it if the forwarding table points elsewhere, an ingress check the RFC calls a very powerful loop mitigation mechanism.

What a B-VLAN is. A backbone VLAN looks like a VLAN in the configuration and behaves like none. Extreme's documentation lists the changes: flooding, broadcasting and source address learning are disabled, ports cannot be added by hand (every port with IS-IS enabled joins automatically), and the forwarding information base is programmed by IS-IS instead of being learned. Internally SPB takes spanning tree group 63 or Multiple Spanning Tree Instance 62, which must be freed before SPBM can be configured, and Rapid Spanning Tree Protocol (RSTP) mode does not support SPBM at all. That is how SPBM retires spanning tree from the core: spanning tree guarantees a loop-free topology by disabling links, so redundant capacity sits idle waiting for a failure, whereas SPBM computes shortest paths across all links and uses them, and redundancy becomes productive rather than reserved.

Services are I-SIDs. A 24-bit I-SID allows 16,777,216 service instances, and in Extreme's terms each one is a Virtual Services Network (VSN). A Layer 2 VSN maps one customer VLAN to an I-SID and stretches it across the backbone as an any-to-any LAN (local area network), with MAC learning at the edges; a Layer 3 VSN maps one VRF (virtual routing and forwarding instance) to an I-SID, always as a full mesh, with IS-IS carrying the routes between the VRFs; IP (Internet Protocol) Shortcuts route the global table across the fabric with no I-SID at all; and Inter-VSN routing joins Layer 2 VSNs. The point where traditional networking meets the fabric is the User Network Interface (UNI): a VLAN UNI maps a VLAN on the whole switch, a Switched UNI maps a VLAN on one port (so the same VLAN ID can mean different services on different ports), a Transparent Port UNI maps everything arriving on a port, tagged or not, and an E-Tree UNI builds hub-and-leaf private VLANs across the fabric. Multicast gets its own I-SIDs too, a data I-SID per stream inside the scope of a VSN. Adding a service means configuring only the BEBs involved; Extreme's guide says the core switches never need to be touched, which removes the change window that traditionally accompanies extending a VLAN across a campus.

On Extreme hardware. Extreme Networks implements SPBM as Fabric Connect in Fabric Engine, the name that VOSS (VSP Operating System Software) took on Universal hardware. The Fabric Engine 9.4 user guide, dated 23 July 2026, lists the 4220, 5320, 5420, 5520, 5720, 7520, 7720 and 7830 Series, and notes that the 5420 and 5520 ran VOSS before Fabric Engine 8.6. Every node also has an SPBM nickname, a short identifier distinct from its System ID; since release 8.10 a switch joining the fabric assigns itself a random one from F.F0.00 to F.FF.FF after 10 seconds, enough for 4,096 devices, and replaces it if it finds a nickname server. The command show isis spbm ip-unicast-fib lists the IS-IS routes the fabric has computed. Extreme's other operating system, Switch Engine, is not an SPB node: it reaches the fabric through Fabric Attach, which uses extensions to the Link Layer Discovery Protocol (LLDP) of IEEE 802.1AB so that devices without SPB, MAC-in-MAC or I-SID support can ask the edge to bind a VLAN to a service, up to 94 such mappings.

What it does not protect. SPBM guarantees a loop-free backbone, not a loop-free customer network. Extreme's restrictions page says a loop at customer VLAN level across the network-to-network interface (NNI) ports cannot be detected by the fabric, because bridge protocol data units (BPDUs) are not carried across the SPBM tunnel, and recommends its Simple Loop Prevention Protocol (SLPP) on the customer VLANs, never on the B-VLANs, whose topology IS-IS already controls. Interoperability arrived late: the first public multivendor demonstration was the backbone of Interop 2013 in Las Vegas, more than a year after approval, and implementations remain concentrated among few vendors.

Its neighbours. Against the Spanning Tree Protocol (STP), SPBM trades blocked links for computed paths. Against Multiprotocol Label Switching (MPLS), Extreme's own pitch is that SPBM gives carrier-grade virtualization with a single link-state protocol in the core and without the layered protocols of MPLS; RFC 6329 and the standard make no such comparison. Against VXLAN (Virtual Extensible LAN) with EVPN (Ethernet virtual private network), both use a 24-bit service identifier, the VNI in VXLAN and the I-SID in SPBM, but VXLAN rides over any routed IP network in UDP (User Datagram Protocol) while SPBM is native Ethernet with its own link-state control plane. The practical trade is unfamiliarity: the vocabulary (BEB, BCB, B-VLAN, I-SID, UNI, NNI, nickname) and the troubleshooting differ from the spanning tree world most engineers grew up in, and that learning curve, more than any technical shortfall, often decides whether a fabric gets deployed.

is-is.def: Intermediate System to Intermediate System (IS-IS) is a link-state interior gateway protocol (IGP) from the Open Systems Interconnection (OSI) world, extended to route IP (Internet Protocol) by RFC (Request for Comments) 1195: every router floods a description of its links and computes shortest paths over the shared map, as in OSPF (Open Shortest Path First).
is-is.context: IS-IS (Intermediate System to Intermediate System) plays the same game as OSPF (Open Shortest Path First), flooding the map and running Dijkstra's shortest path first (SPF) computation, with a different pedigree and two habits that aged well. Its packets travel directly on the link layer as OSI (Open Systems Interconnection) packets, never inside IP (Internet Protocol), so they cannot be routed to a router from afar and anyone who wants to inject them has to be on the link; and everything it carries is a type-length-value (TLV) element that routers pass on even when they do not understand it, so IPv6 (Internet Protocol version 6), traffic engineering, Segment Routing and Shortest Path Bridging arrived as new TLVs rather than as new protocol versions. Its two levels (Level 1 inside an area, Level 2 between areas) map loosely onto OSPF's areas and area 0. Large service providers run it in their backbones; enterprises mostly meet it inside data centre underlays and Ethernet fabrics such as Extreme Networks' Fabric Connect.
is-is.depth:
Intermediate System to Intermediate System (IS-IS) is a link-state routing protocol: each router describes its own links in a link state PDU (protocol data unit, LSP), floods that description to every router at its level, and runs Dijkstra's shortest path first (SPF) computation over the identical database that results. Intermediate system is the Open Systems Interconnection (OSI) word for a router. The standard comes from the International Organization for Standardization (ISO) and the International Electrotechnical Commission (IEC) as ISO/IEC 10589, whose title still spells routeing the British way: an intra-domain routeing information exchange protocol for use with the connectionless-mode network service of ISO 8473. The first edition appeared in November 1992 and the second, still the current one, in November 2002. RFC (Request for Comments) 1142, edited by D. Oran of Digital Equipment Corporation in February 1990, had republished an earlier ISO draft proposal (DP), DP 10589; RFC 7142 moved it to Historic in February 2014 because that draft differed in a considerable number of significant respects from the final standard, and asked that references point to ISO/IEC 10589:2002.

RFC 1195, written by R. Callon of Digital Equipment Corporation in December 1990, made it integrated IS-IS: a single interior gateway protocol (IGP) for pure IP (Internet Protocol), pure OSI and dual environments, with one two-level hierarchy for both. The alternative it argued against was Ships in the Night, separate protocols such as OSPF (Open Shortest Path First) for IP and IS-IS for OSI competing for the same router's resources. IP arrived as new fields: protocols supported (code 129), IP interface address (132), IP internal reachability (128) and IP external reachability (130). Even an IP-only router still needs an OSI-style address, which IS-IS uses and nothing else does.

The detail that sets it apart in operation is the encapsulation. RFC 1195 says IS-IS packets travel by the normal method for OSI packets on each link type, so every IS-IS router, IP-only ones included, must receive them that way. On an Ethernet local area network (LAN) that means the OSI network layer service access point 0xFE, the IS-IS protocol discriminator 0x83 (binary 10000011), and the multicast destinations 01-80-C2-00-00-14 for all Level 1 intermediate systems and 01-80-C2-00-00-15 for all Level 2, values from the constants table that RFC 1142 reproduced. There is no IP header to route, so no host across the internet can reach a router's IS-IS process: an attacker has to be attached to the link. That is a smaller attack surface, not immunity. It also means an IP capture filter never matches IS-IS; pcap-filter has its own isis qualifier and the PDU keywords l1, l2, iih, lsp, csnp and psnp.

Addresses follow the OSI model. A router's network entity title (NET) is a network service access point (NSAP) address whose last octet, the NSAP selector, is 00; in front of it sit the area address and a system identifier that RFC 3719 fixes at six octets. Juniper's example, 49.0001.1921.6800.1001.00, reads as authority and format identifier (AFI) 49, area 0001, system ID 1921.6800.1001 and selector 00, and Juniper recommends building the system ID from an interface address because it helps when troubleshooting. Extreme Networks' Fabric Engine defaults the system ID to the chassis base MAC (media access control) address, insists that it be unicast, takes a manual area of up to 13 bytes and supports one manual area, although the protocol allows three.

The hierarchy has two levels instead of numbered areas. Level 1 routers know the topology of their own area and send everything else to a Level 2 router in it; Level 2 routers route between areas; and one router can be both. A Level 1-2 router that reaches other areas sets the attached (ATT) bit in its Level 1 LSP, and Level 1 routers install a default route towards the nearest such router. The backbone is not an area 0 but the set of Level 2 routers, and RFC 1195 requires that set to be connected: Level 1 links cannot repair a partitioned Level 2. Prefixes leaked from Level 2 down into Level 1 carry the up/down bit, so they may only travel further down, which closes the loop that redistribution in both directions would open when the original source withdraws a prefix.

Four kinds of PDU do the work: hellos (IIHs) discover and keep neighbours, LSPs describe each router, complete sequence number PDUs (CSNPs) list the whole database, and partial ones (PSNPs) request or acknowledge single LSPs. On a LAN one router per level becomes the designated intermediate system (DIS) and originates a pseudonode LSP for the segment, which turns n-squared adjacencies into n. Cisco gives the rules: priority 64 by default, configurable from 0 to 127, then the highest subnetwork point of attachment (SNPA), which is the MAC address; no backup DIS; and a preemptive election, unlike OSPF's designated router. The DIS multicasts a CSNP every 10 seconds by default. Point-to-point links originally declared a neighbour up on one hello heard, so a link failing in one direction could be noticed by one side only; RFC 5303 (October 2008) added a three-way handshake in option 240. Extreme's Fabric Engine runs every IS-IS link point-to-point and supports no broadcast links at all.

The clocks are generous. ISO fixed the LSP MaxAge at 1200 seconds with a 15-minute refresh, and RFC 3719 reports that both proved too short in some networks, producing a steady flow of updates when nothing changes; FRRouting accepts lifetimes from 350 to 65535 seconds, and RFC 5303 speaks of refresh periods of up to 18 hours. A hello's holding time was ISO's multiplier of 10 times the hello interval, but most implementations default to 3, and RFC 3719 warns that values below 3 make adjacencies flap.

Extensibility is the habit that aged best. A PDU body is a run of type-length-value (TLV) elements, one octet of type and one of length, and RFC 1195 repeats ISO's rule that codes a router does not recognize are ignored and passed on unchanged in flooded LSPs. That rule let IP ride inside an OSI protocol in 1990 and has carried every change since. RFC 5308 (October 2008) routes IPv6 (Internet Protocol version 6) with TLV 236 for reachability, TLV 232 for interface addresses and the network layer protocol identifier 142 (0x8E), whereas OSPF had to move from version 2 to version 3 for the same job, as RFC 5340 says. RFC 5305 added traffic engineering sub-TLVs, RFC 6329 (April 2012) carried IEEE (Institute of Electrical and Electronics Engineers) 802.1aq Shortest Path Bridging (SPB), and RFC 8667 (December 2019) carries Segment Routing on a Multiprotocol Label Switching (MPLS) data plane.

Metrics are where old configurations bite. The original default metric has 6 bits, 0 to 63, and ISO capped a whole path at 1023; Junos gives every link 10 by default and, unlike OSPF, derives nothing from bandwidth, so an untouched network routes by hop count. RFC 5305 (October 2008, obsoleting RFC 3784) brought wide metrics: TLV 22, extended IS reachability, with a 24-bit link metric, and TLV 135, extended IP reachability, with a 32-bit prefix metric. A link advertised at 16,777,215, the 24-bit maximum, is left out of normal SPF, and path metrics stop at 4,261,412,864 (0xFE000000). The two styles travel in different TLVs, so RFC 3787 says narrow metrics must continue while any router lacks wide support and sets out a five-step migration through a phase of sending both. FRRouting offers metric-style narrow, transition and wide and defaults to wide; Junos sends both pairs until wide-metrics-only is configured.

Authentication was weak at birth: RFC 1195 defined a cleartext password and said plainly that it gives no useful protection against intentional misbehaviour. RFC 5304 (October 2008) added HMAC-MD5 (keyed-hash message authentication code with Message Digest 5) as authentication type 54, and RFC 5310 (February 2009) a generic form for HMAC with SHA-1 (Secure Hash Algorithm 1) and SHA-2. Even then a digest confirms only that the sender held the area or domain key, not which router originated the PDU, so a rogue or compromised router on the link remains the threat that matters. Scope varies by vendor: Fabric Engine authenticates hellos only, per interface, with simple, MD5 or HMAC-SHA-256 and a shared key of at most 16 characters. The overload bit is the operator's other lever: an overloaded router is no longer used for transit but stays reachable for its own destinations, and RFC 3787 records the habit of setting it after a reboot until BGP (Border Gateway Protocol) has converged, which FRRouting exposes as set-overload-bit on-startup.

RFC 6232 says IS-IS has been widely used in large-scale IP networks because of its scalability and fast convergence, and FRRouting that it is widely used in ISP (internet service provider) and carrier backbones. Enterprises more often run OSPF, largely because vendor documentation, training and hiring lean that way, and meet IS-IS inside data centre underlays and Ethernet fabrics: Extreme Networks' Fabric Connect uses it as the single control plane of SPBM (Shortest Path Bridging MAC mode), where every node also needs a unique nickname. The vocabulary is the main obstacle for engineers coming from OSPF, since areas become levels, routers become intermediate systems and addresses become NSAPs. Under the words the concepts map closely, and learning the translation once beats treating IS-IS as a different discipline.

exos.def: ExtremeXOS (EXOS) is Extreme Networks' modular, Linux-based switch operating system, introduced with the BlackDiamond 10K in December 2003 and called Switch Engine on Universal hardware since release 31.6.
exos.context: EXOS is short for ExtremeXOS, usually expanded as Extreme Operating System: the network operating system (OS) of Extreme Networks switches. It runs as separate memory-protected processes on a Linux kernel, so a failed process can be restarted, and a feature package upgraded, without replacing the whole image. Its command-line interface (CLI) is flat: every line is a complete command (create, configure, enable, disable, delete, unconfigure) that takes effect at once in the running configuration and survives a reboot only after save configuration. Scripting is built in, from CLI scripts and event-triggered Universal Port profiles to Python on the switch and a REST (representational state transfer) application programming interface (API). On Universal hardware the same system has been named Switch Engine since release 31.6, beside Fabric Engine, the renamed VOSS (VSP Operating System Software), and a switch can be changed from one to the other at the cost of its configuration.
exos.depth:
ExtremeXOS, abbreviated EXOS, is the operating system of Extreme Networks' Ethernet switches, and it now travels under two names. Extreme's documentation states that release 31.6 introduced new names for the network operating systems running on Universal hardware: ExtremeXOS was renamed Switch Engine, and VOSS (VSP Operating System Software) was renamed Fabric Engine, with every reference to ExtremeXOS in the guides applying to Switch Engine 31.6 and later. The Switch Engine 34.1.1 User Guide, published on 1 November 2026, lists the Universal series as 4120, 4220, 5120, 5320, 5420, 5520, 5720, 7520 and 7720. Older ExtremeSwitching and Summit models, such as the X440-G2, X620 and X670-G2, keep the ExtremeXOS name, and the old name has not left the new hardware either: the boot menu of a Universal switch still offers entries labelled EXOS, and core image files still end in .xos.

The system dates from December 2003. Extreme launched the BlackDiamond 10K chassis with what it then called ExtremeWare XOS, reported at the time (Converge Digest, 7 December 2003) as an all-new UNIX-based software platform with a modular architecture and open interfaces in XML (Extensible Markup Language) and POSIX (Portable Operating System Interface). It succeeded ExtremeWare, the company's first-generation system, which Wikipedia describes as based on VxWorks, and the same article dates the first release, version 10.1, to February 2004; the command reference agrees to the extent that its oldest commands, save configuration among them, are recorded as first available in ExtremeXOS 10.1. Underneath is Linux. The release notes name the kernel for each release: 4.14 in ExtremeXOS 30.1 (January 2019), and in Switch Engine 34.1.1 kernel 6.12 on the 4220, 5320, 5420, 5520, 5720, 7520 and 7720 and kernel 5.10 on the 4120 and 5120. The system also ships BusyBox, which is how it entered the history of open-source licensing: on 17 July 2008 the Software Freedom Law Center sued Extreme in the Southern District of New York on behalf of the BusyBox developers Erik Andersen and Rob Landley, alleging that the company distributed BusyBox in violation of the GNU General Public License (GPL), and on 6 October 2008 the parties announced a settlement and the dismissal of the case.

What the Linux base buys is isolation. The user guide describes a distributed architecture of separate binary images organized into discrete software modules that exchange messages, in which each function runs as a memory-protected process under real-time scheduling, so that a process with a memory fault cannot touch the memory of another. Routing protocols, the CLI (command-line interface) itself, the configuration manager and the device manager all appear as separate entries in the output of show process, each with a restart count, and restart process terminates and restarts one of them (bgp, ospf, lldp, snmpMaster or exsshd, for instance) without rebooting the switch. The same structure allows two kinds of software file. A core image (.xos) can be installed only on the inactive one of the two partitions, primary and secondary; a modular package (.xmod) adds or upgrades a feature and needs only its own processes terminated and started again. Image names carry a platform prefix: rzg2 for the 4120 and 5120, summit_arm for the 4220, 5320, 5420 and 5520, onie for the 5720, 7520 and 7720.

The configuration model is what engineers notice first when coming from other vendors. There are no nested modes: each line is a complete command that begins with a verb (create, configure, enable, disable, delete, unconfigure) and names its object, as in create vlan engineering tag 100 followed by configure vlan engineering add ports 1:1 tagged. A command acts on the running configuration the moment it is entered; nothing accumulates in a candidate configuration waiting to be committed. Persistence is a separate, deliberate step: save configuration writes the runtime state to non-volatile memory, by default to the file used at the last reboot, and the saved file takes effect at the next reboot. Configuration files are XML with a .cfg extension; primary and secondary are, in the command reference's words, just conveniences for primary.cfg and secondary.cfg; use configuration selects the file for the next boot; and an ASCII (American Standard Code for Information Interchange) script form with the extension .xsf can be uploaded, edited and replayed with load script. Automatic saving exists but is off by default. The consequence cuts both ways: a change tested and never saved vanishes at the next reboot, and a mistake is live the moment it is typed. The prompt shows the privilege: a hash sign for an administrator account, a greater-than sign for a read-only user.

Several defaults and names differ from what other systems teach. On a new switch every port is an untagged member of a virtual local area network (VLAN) named Default, with tag 1, and because an untagged port can belong to only one VLAN it has to be removed from Default before it can join another untagged. Giving a VLAN an Internet Protocol (IP) address does not route: IP forwarding is disabled by default and is switched on with enable ipforwarding. Link aggregation is called load sharing: enable sharing with a grouping builds a link aggregation group (LAG) that is afterwards addressed by its master port, hashes on layer 2 addresses unless told otherwise, and negotiates with the Link Aggregation Control Protocol (LACP) only when the lacp keyword is added. Ports on a stack are written slot:port. Routing lives in virtual routers (VRs), three of which exist from boot and cannot be deleted or renamed: VR-Mgmt, which owns the management port and the Mgmt VLAN and runs no routing protocol; VR-Control, used for communication between the switch's own subsystems; and VR-Default, where the data ports and the Default VLAN start. That is why commands such as download take a vr argument. Extreme switches also describe themselves to one another with the Extreme Discovery Protocol (EDP), enabled on all ports by default, beside the standard Link Layer Discovery Protocol (LLDP).

For redundancy the system offers three mechanisms of its own beside the Spanning Tree Protocol (STP). SummitStack joins switches, numbered as slots 1 to 8, into one logical switch with a single IP address and a single point of authentication, run by a primary node. Multi-switch link aggregation (MLAG) lets two separate switches, joined by an inter-switch connection (ISC), present one aggregated link to a third device. Ethernet Automatic Protection Switching (EAPS), which Extreme published as the informational Request for Comments (RFC) 3619 in October 2003, protects a ring: a master node blocks its secondary port for the protected VLANs, sends health-check messages around a dedicated control VLAN, and unblocks the port when they stop arriving or a transit node reports a link down. The RFC claims convergence in less than one second, often in less than 50 milliseconds, independent of the number of nodes in the ring.

Scripting is the part worth learning early, because the system has several layers of it. CLI scripting stores commands, with variables and functions, in a script file. Universal Port wraps such scripts in profiles that the switch runs by itself when something happens (a user logs in or out, a device is detected on a port, a time of day arrives, a log event fires), which is how a telephone can receive its VLAN, its Power over Ethernet (PoE) budget and its quality-of-service settings on being plugged in, with no external controller. Python scripting arrived in ExtremeXOS 15.6: scripts are started with run script or load script, call the CLI through the exsh module, can use the bundled pexpect module for interactive commands, and can be registered as permanent processes with create process and its python-module option; it requires FIPS (Federal Information Processing Standards) mode to be off. For external automation there is a REST (representational state transfer) application programming interface (API) served by an OpenAPI server under /rest/openapi, RESTCONF under /rest/restconf, token authentication with a default lifetime of 24 hours, the Chalet web interface on the same ports, and cloud management through ExtremeCloud IQ.

Its relationship to Extreme's fabric is one of attachment. Switch Engine is not a Shortest Path Bridging (SPB) node. Facing a fabric built on Shortest Path Bridging MAC (SPBM), the media access control (MAC) mode that Fabric Engine runs, it acts as a Fabric Attach client or proxy: it uses extensions to LLDP to ask the fabric edge to bind a VLAN to a service identifier, with a limit of 94 such mappings, and it can itself be the Fabric Attach server for overlays built on Virtual Extensible LAN (VXLAN). On Universal hardware the alternative is to change the operating system altogether, from ExtremeCloud IQ, from the boot menu, or by downloading a VOSS image. Extreme's caution is explicit: changing the network operating system deletes all configuration files, debug information, logs, events and statistics of the previous one. It is a rebuild, not a migration. At first start-up the switch asks whether to change the switch operating system to VOSS, and the answer that keeps Switch Engine is N.

Licensing follows the hardware. Universal switches include a Base licence covering layer 2 switching, layer 3 routing and dynamic routing protocols; a Premier licence adds enhanced Border Gateway Protocol (BGP) and Open Shortest Path First (OSPF) support, multicast routing, the Precision Time Protocol and application hosting on some models; MACsec, the link-level encryption of the Institute of Electrical and Electronics Engineers (IEEE) standard 802.1AE, is licensed separately; and licences come as perpetual, as subscriptions, or as a built-in trial of 30 days extendable to 120. For anyone certified on one Extreme system and working on the other, the conceptual gap is small and the recurring daily friction is translation between two command sets: Switch Engine's flat, verb-first lines against Fabric Engine's CLI of nested modes (User EXEC, Privileged EXEC, Global Configuration, interface configuration).

rip.def: The Routing Information Protocol (RIP) is one of the first dynamic routing protocols used on the internet: a distance-vector protocol with hop count as its only metric, 15 hops as its horizon and 'routing by rumour' as its method.
rip.context: RIP, described in Request for Comments (RFC) 1058 and refined as RIPv2 in RFC 2453, is pure distance-vector: every 30 seconds each router tells its neighbours the distances it believes, and everyone trusts the rumours. Hop count is the only metric, so a 10 Gb/s link counts the same as a modem line, and 16 means unreachable, which caps any RIP network at 15 hops and gives the count-to-infinity failure its ceiling. Split horizon, poison reverse and hold-down timers are the folk remedies every networking student memorizes. Obsolete in serious networks, immortal in teaching: RIP is where the problems that Open Shortest Path First (OSPF) and the Enhanced Interior Gateway Routing Protocol (EIGRP) solve are first felt.
rip.depth:
What it is. The Routing Information Protocol (RIP) is the oldest interior routing protocol still encountered. It is a distance-vector protocol: each router keeps, for every destination, a distance and the first router on the way, and learns both from what its neighbours announce. It was designed, in the words of its first specification, for moderate-size networks using reasonably homogeneous technology, and was not intended for more complex environments. Its only metric is hop count, capped at fifteen so that a loop terminates, and it runs over the User Datagram Protocol (UDP) on port 520. It is simple enough to configure without understanding it, which is both its appeal and its problem.

Where it came from. The mathematics is the Bellman-Ford algorithm, which Request for Comments (RFC) 1058 traces to Bellman's equation and to Ford and Fulkerson, and which was used for routing in the ARPANET (Advanced Research Projects Agency Network) as early as 1969. The protocol itself descends from Xerox: the Gateway Information Protocol of the PUP protocols became the Routing Information Protocol of Xerox Network Systems (XNS), and the routed program shipped with Berkeley Unix was largely the same thing with a more general address format and updates limited to one every 30 seconds. By the time Charles Hedrick of Rutgers University wrote RFC 1058 in June 1988 it was already a de facto standard, implemented by most vendors of gateways; the RFC documented existing practice. Gary Malkin's RIP version 2 followed as RFC 1388 (January 1993), RFC 1723 (November 1994) and finally RFC 2453 (November 1998), which is Internet Standard 56. RFC 1923 (March 1996) made the case for retiring version 1, calling it one of the first dynamic routing protocols used in the internet and no longer applicable there; RFC 1058 is now classed as Historic.

The packet. A RIP message has a four-octet header, a command (1 for a request, 2 for a response), a version and two zero octets, followed by 1 to 25 route entries of 20 octets each. In version 1 an entry carries an address family identifier, an IPv4 address and a metric, with the rest zero; because no mask travels with the address, the receiver has to assume the classful one. Version 2 fills the unused space with a route tag, a subnet mask and a next hop, which makes variable-length subnets possible, and sends to the multicast address 224.0.0.9 instead of broadcasting. The metric is 1 to 15, and 16 is infinity, unreachable. A router adds the cost of the receiving network to each metric it hears, never going above 16. Authentication, where used, occupies the first entry, marked by the family 0xFFFF; type 2 is a 16-octet password sent in plain text.

The clock. Every 30 seconds, offset by a random 0 to 5 seconds so that routers do not synchronize, a router sends its complete table to every neighbour. A route that is not refreshed for 180 seconds, six missed updates, times out: its metric is set to 16 and it is advertised as unreachable for a further 120 seconds of garbage collection before it is deleted. Triggered updates, sent as soon as a metric changes, spread bad news faster than the 30-second cycle.

Counting to infinity. The weakness of rumour is that a router can be told about a route by the neighbour that learned it from that very router. When a network fails, two routers can then offer it to each other, each adding one hop, until the metric reaches 16; RFC 2453 says infinity was chosen to be as small as possible precisely so that this counting stops quickly, and that it cannot be raised without breaking compatibility with older versions. The standard remedies narrow the window. Split horizon, which RIP must use, omits a route from updates sent to the neighbour it was learned from; poisoned reverse, which it should use, sends it back with metric 16; triggered updates shorten the time during which wrong beliefs circulate. The hold-down timer of the classroom is not in the RFC at all: it comes from implementations such as Cisco's, whose timers basic command takes update, invalid, holddown and flush values and removes a silent route after 240 seconds.

Its limitations are structural. Hop count ignores bandwidth entirely, so a route over three fast links loses to one over two slow ones. The diameter is 15 hops. The whole table is repeated every 30 seconds whether or not anything changed, and convergence is slow enough that the workarounds carry names like split horizon and poison reverse. Version 1 adds a trap of its own: it is classful, so subnets of one network separated by another network cannot be told apart. Defaults keep the trap alive. Cisco IOS XE still, by default, receives versions 1 and 2 but sends only version 1 and summarizes automatically at classful boundaries, which is why version 2 and no auto-summary are the first two lines of any RIP configuration there; FRRouting, by contrast, sends version 2 by default.

Security is weak by design. Version 1 has no authentication, so any host on the segment can inject routes. Version 2's simple password crosses the wire in clear text, and it is the default mode on Cisco. Authentication keyed with message digest algorithm 5 (MD5) was added by RFC 2082 (January 1997), which RFC 4822 (February 2007) replaced with a scheme that adds the Secure Hash Algorithm (SHA) family with a keyed-hash message authentication code (HMAC) and urges migration away from keyed MD5. Authentication protects updates, not questions: the FRRouting manual warns that unless version 1 is disabled a router will still answer version 1 requests, so anyone who can reach it can read its whole routing table. Marking user-facing interfaces passive, so that no updates are sent there, is the other standard precaution.

Where it still is. FortiGate documents RIP versions 1 and 2 and RIPng under config router rip, with the same 30, 180 and 120-second timers. F5 BIG-IP runs RIP and RIPng as daemons of its advanced routing modules. ExtremeXOS supports it while listing its limits against Open Shortest Path First (OSPF) and Intermediate System to Intermediate System (IS-IS): 15 hops, bandwidth spent on periodic broadcasts of the whole table, slow convergence, no notion of link cost, no areas. In FRRouting its administrative distance is 120, so a route learned from almost any other protocol is preferred, and show ip rip and show ip rip status display what it has learned. RIPng (RFC 2080, January 1997) is the same protocol for IPv6, on UDP port 521 and the multicast group FF02::9, with a prefix length in each entry. The distance-vector idea itself is not obsolete: Babel (RFC 8966, January 2021) is a loop-avoiding distance-vector protocol built for wired networks and wireless meshes. RIP proper survives in small networks and in equipment too old to run anything else, and encountering it in a modern environment is usually a signal that a segment has not been reviewed in a long time.

beb.def: An edge device in an Ethernet fabric that encapsulates traffic into the backbone.
beb.context: A Backbone Edge Bridge (IEEE 802.1ah) sits at the boundary of a provider-backbone or SPBM fabric, wrapping customer frames in backbone MAC headers so the core forwards on backbone addresses - the entry and exit points of the fabric.
beb.depth:
A Backbone Edge Bridge is where customer traffic enters a provider backbone fabric and where the encapsulation happens. It wraps the customer frame inside a provider MAC header, which is what keeps the core from ever learning customer addresses, and it is the only place in the fabric that needs to know a service exists.

That containment is the point of the architecture. A core switch forwards on backbone addresses alone, so its address table stays proportional to the size of the fabric rather than to the number of endpoints connected to it. Adding ten thousand devices at the edges changes nothing in the middle, which is what makes very large layer two fabrics practical at all.

The operational consequence is that provisioning is an edge activity. Extending a service means configuring the bridges at the two ends and nothing between them, so there is no core change window, no reconfiguration of transit devices, and no risk of a mistake in the middle affecting services that had nothing to do with the change. That property, rather than any raw performance claim, is what makes the model attractive to people who have spent a career extending VLANs across a campus.

set-us-up-the-bomb.def: Another garbled line from the same 1991 game's opening as "all your base", now shorthand for a system suddenly and catastrophically compromised.
set-us-up-the-bomb.context: From Zero Wing's notoriously mistranslated intro (the captain is told "Somebody set up us the bomb"), the phrase spread with the "all your base are belong to us" meme in the early 2000s. In ops culture it is affectionate shorthand for the moment an incident begins - the alarm that says something has just gone very wrong.
set-us-up-the-bomb.depth:
All your base are belong to us and somebody set us up the bomb come from the 1989 English localization of the game Zero Wing, whose translation was mangled badly enough to become one of the internet's earliest and most durable memes when it resurfaced in the early 2000s.

The technical interest is in why the translation failed the way it did. Japanese grammar carries information through particles and context that English carries through word order and articles, and a literal substitution produces sentences that are grammatically wrong in a way that still gestures at meaning. That is the same failure mode machine translation produced for decades and the reason localization is a discipline rather than a lookup.

Its persistence in engineering vocabulary is the second half. The phrases became a shorthand for total compromise, deployed when a system is comprehensively owned, which is a small demonstration of how technical communities recruit their idiom from shared cultural artefacts rather than from technical sources. A generation of engineers quotes a badly translated shoot-em-up because they were all in the same places online at the same time.

oidc.def: An identity layer on top of OAuth 2.0 for authenticating users: the authorization server signs an ID token that tells the application who the user is, who vouches for that and for which client the statement was made.
