oidc.context: OpenID Connect (OIDC) adds authentication to the OAuth 2.0 authorization framework. The OpenID Provider (OP) authenticates the user and issues a signed ID token, a JWT (JSON Web Token; JSON is JavaScript Object Notation), which the application, called the Relying Party (RP), validates to learn who signed in; an access token issued alongside it can fetch further claims from the UserInfo endpoint. Ratified by the OpenID Foundation on 26 February 2014, it is the modern successor to much of what the Security Assertion Markup Language (SAML) did for web single sign-on (SSO), and unlike SAML it was designed for mobile and native applications as well.
oidc.depth:
OpenID Connect (OIDC) exists because OAuth deliberately did not answer the identity question, and everyone needed it answered. OAuth 2.0 (RFC, Request for Comments, 6749, October 2012) is a delegation framework: it lets an application call an API (application programming interface) on a user's behalf, and says nothing standard about who that user is. Providers filled the gap with private recipes such as Facebook Connect and Sign In with Twitter, each with its own profile call and its own field names. OIDC is the standard recipe. Its core specification describes it as a simple identity layer on top of OAuth 2.0 that lets a client verify the identity of the end user from the authentication performed by an authorization server, and obtain basic profile information in an interoperable way. The same endpoints and flows are used; what is added is an ID token that asserts who the user is and a UserInfo endpoint for the rest.

The roles get new names. The authorization server that authenticates users is the OpenID Provider (OP), often called the identity provider, and the application that outsources sign-in to it is the Relying Party (RP). A request becomes an OIDC request by carrying the scope value openid. Authentication can follow three paths: the Authorization Code Flow (response_type=code), in which every token comes from the token endpoint and none is revealed to the browser; the Implicit Flow (response_type=id_token token, or id_token alone), in which every token comes back through the browser from the authorization endpoint; and the Hybrid Flow, which mixes the two. Current OAuth security practice, RFC 9700, tells clients not to use response types that put access tokens in the authorization response, which leaves the code flow, with Proof Key for Code Exchange (PKCE), as the normal choice. Four further scopes request sets of claims: profile, email, address and phone.

The distinction worth holding is between the two tokens the client receives. The access token is for calling APIs, and the application should treat it as opaque: its audience is the protected resource, not the client, and plain OAuth defines neither its format nor any audience restriction. The ID token is for the application itself, is always a JWT (JSON Web Token, RFC 7519; JSON is JavaScript Object Notation) and contains claims about the authentication. Sending an ID token to an API, or trusting an access token as proof of identity, is a common and consequential mix-up. The second error is the dangerous one: a naive client that logs a user in because some access token fetched a valid profile will accept a token that was issued to a different application.

Five claims are required in every ID token. The issuer, iss, is a case-sensitive https URL (Uniform Resource Locator). The subject, sub, is an identifier of at most 255 ASCII (American Standard Code for Information Interchange) characters that is locally unique and never reassigned within the issuer. The audience, aud, must contain the client_id of the Relying Party. The expiry, exp, and the time of issue, iat, are numbers of seconds since 1970-01-01T00:00:00Z. Optional claims carry the context: auth_time (when the user actually authenticated), nonce, acr and amr (the class and the methods of authentication), and azp (the authorized party). The token must be signed with JSON Web Signature (JWS), every provider must support RS256, that is RSA (Rivest-Shamir-Adleman) with SHA-256 (Secure Hash Algorithm, 256-bit), and the value none is permitted only when the token comes straight from the token endpoint and the client registered for it explicitly. The specification also warns that the expiry of an ID token is unrelated to the lifetime of the session between the RP and the OP.

Validation is not optional decoration. The issuer must exactly match the provider the client trusts. The audience must contain the client's own client_id, and a token listing additional audiences the client does not trust must be rejected. The signature must verify under the keys the issuer publishes, with the algorithm the client expects. The current time must be before exp, with a leeway for clock skew that the specification puts at no more than a few minutes. If a nonce was sent in the request, the same value must come back in the token, so that a token replayed from another session is refused. And if the client then calls the UserInfo endpoint, the sub it returns must exactly match the sub of the ID token, or the response must not be used. Skip any of these and the result is single sign-on that signs anyone in.

The choice of user key is where real deployments have failed. The specification states that iss and sub, used together, are the only claims a Relying Party can rely on as a stable identifier; an issuer may reuse an email value for different users over time, and a user's email may change. In June 2023 the security company Descope published nOAuth: applications accepting sign-in from any Microsoft Azure Active Directory tenant that matched accounts on the email claim could be taken over, because in that provider the claim was both mutable and unverified. Microsoft responded with new claims that let an application tell whether an email address is domain-verified.

Configuration is meant to be discovered, not typed. A provider publishes a JSON document at the path /.well-known/openid-configuration under its issuer, and the Discovery specification makes issuer and jwks_uri (the location of the signing keys) required members, with token_endpoint required unless only the Implicit Flow is offered. Microsoft's identity platform gives every app registration such a document. On F5 BIG-IP Access Policy Manager (APM) acting as OAuth client and resource server, the OpenID Connect setting of the OAuth Client agent is Disabled by default, offers the Authorization code or Hybrid flow once enabled, and the provider object can discover endpoints and keys from the issuer's document at a chosen frequency.

The name is older than the protocol. OpenID Authentication 2.0, final on 5 December 2007, was a decentralized scheme in which a user proved control of an identifier without any central authority approving providers or relying parties; according to the OpenID Foundation it relied on XML (Extensible Markup Language) and a custom signature scheme that implementations often got wrong. OpenID Connect kept the goal and rebuilt it on OAuth 2.0 and JWT. The foundation's members ratified it on 26 February 2014, by which time Google, Microsoft, Deutsche Telekom, salesforce.com, Ping Identity and Nomura Research Institute had implemented it and more than 20 implementations had been tested against one another. The core text was last corrected in errata set 2 of 15 December 2023, and in October 2024 nine of the specifications were published by the International Organization for Standardization (ISO) and the International Electrotechnical Commission (IEC) as ISO/IEC 26131:2024 to 26139:2024. Logout came later and separately, in RP-Initiated Logout 1.0 (12 September 2022) and the front-channel and back-channel logout specifications.

Its main neighbour is SAML (Security Assertion Markup Language) 2.0, an OASIS standard of 15 March 2005. The foundation's own comparison is that SAML is an XML-based federation technology designed only for web-based applications, that OIDC satisfies the same use cases with a simpler, JSON-based protocol and also serves native and mobile apps, and that the two will coexist for a long time, which matches what enterprise identity providers show: both, side by side. The other neighbour is OAuth itself. A deployment that needs only delegated API access needs no ID token, and one that needs to know who signed in should not try to derive it from an access token.

jwk.def: A JSON Web Key (JWK) is a JSON (JavaScript Object Notation) object that represents one cryptographic key, public, private or symmetric, defined in Request for Comments (RFC) 7517; its kty member names the key type and the other members carry the key's numbers and its intended use.
jwk.context: JSON Web Key (JWK), Request for Comments (RFC) 7517, encodes a public or private key as a JSON (JavaScript Object Notation) object, the format signing keys are published in for JSON Web Token (JWT) verification. A collection of them is a JWK Set (JWKS). Every JWK has kty, the key type (RSA, EC, oct, OKP or AKP); an RSA public key adds its modulus n and exponent e, an elliptic curve key its curve and coordinates, and optional members such as kid, use and alg tell a verifier which key it is and what it is for. A key served at a public endpoint must contain public members only.
jwk.depth:
A JWK (JSON Web Key) is a cryptographic key expressed as JSON (JavaScript Object Notation) rather than as PEM (Privacy-Enhanced Mail) or DER (Distinguished Encoding Rules), which is what makes it convenient for web protocols where everything else is already JSON. Request for Comments (RFC) 7517, written by M. Jones and published in May 2015, defines it as a JSON data structure that represents a cryptographic key, and the same RFC defines the JWK Set, a JSON object whose keys member is an array of JWKs. Names are short on purpose, because a goal is compactness, and the RFC states what a JWK is not meant to be: a new kind of certificate chain, a certified key or a replacement for X.509 certificates. A JWK carries numbers and labels, not a validity period or an issuer's signature.

The key type field determines which other fields are present. The kty member is the only one every JWK must have, and RFC 7518, JSON Web Algorithms (JWA), defined the first three types: RSA (Rivest-Shamir-Adleman), required of implementations; EC (elliptic curve), recommended with a plus sign meaning the requirement is likely to rise; and oct, an octet sequence used for symmetric keys. RSA keys carry modulus and exponent: n and e, each a big-endian unsigned integer in base64url, so the common exponent 65537 is always written AQAB; the private form adds d and the factors and CRT (Chinese remainder theorem) values p, q, dp, dq and qi. The RFC warns that some libraries prefix an extra zero octet to the modulus, giving 257 octets for a 2048-bit key instead of 256, and that it must be dropped. Elliptic curve keys carry a curve name and coordinates: crv (P-256, P-384 or P-521), x and y, each exactly the size of a coordinate on that curve (66 octets for P-521, for instance), plus d for the private key; point compression is not supported. Symmetric keys carry the key value itself in k, and should state an alg. Two types came later: OKP (octet key pair), from RFC 8037 (January 2017), for Ed25519, Ed448, X25519 and X448, with crv, x and, for private keys only, d; and AKP (algorithm key pair), from RFC 9964 (May 2026), for the post-quantum ML-DSA (Module-Lattice-Based Digital Signature Algorithm) signatures, with pub and a private key that may be given only as a 32-byte seed in priv.

The common members say what the key is for. The use member takes sig for signatures or enc for encryption, key agreement and key wrapping; key_ops lists operations (sign, verify, encrypt, decrypt, wrapKey, unwrapKey, deriveKey, deriveBits), deliberately matching the key usages of the Web Cryptography API, and the RFC advises against unrelated combinations because of the danger of using one key with several algorithms. The two should not be used together, and if they are, they must agree. The alg member names the one algorithm intended for the key, such as RS256 or ES256, which is exactly the binding the JSON Web Token best current practice asks for. A key can also bring its certificate: x5c holds a chain of X.509 certificates in standard base64 (not base64url) DER, the first containing the same public key, x5u points to one by URL (Uniform Resource Locator), and x5t and x5t#S256 carry SHA-1 (Secure Hash Algorithm 1) and SHA-256 (its 256-bit successor) thumbprints of the certificate. Members a reader does not understand must be ignored, and duplicate member names must be rejected or resolved to the last one.

The field worth understanding first is the key identifier. kid is an arbitrary label whose only job is to let a token say which key signed it, so that a verifier holding several keys can select the right one without trial and error. RFC 7517 says it is used to match a specific key, for instance to choose among the keys of a set during key rollover; its structure is unspecified, distinct keys in a set should have distinct values, and it is compared with the kid header of a JSON Web Signature (JWS), which RFC 7515 calls a hint. Rotation depends entirely on this, and a signing key with no identifier forces consumers to try every key they hold, which works until it quietly does not.

A common way to make a kid that cannot collide by accident is the JWK thumbprint of RFC 7638 (September 2015, M. Jones and N. Sakimura). It is computed by building a JSON object from only the required members of the key, ordered lexicographically by member name and with no whitespace, then hashing its UTF-8 bytes, usually with SHA-256 and encoding the result in base64url. The members are e, kty and n for RSA; crv, kty, x and y for EC; crv, kty and x for OKP; and k and kty for a symmetric key. The thumbprint of a private key is defined as that of its public key, so both halves of a pair share it. RFC 9278 (August 2022) wraps it in a URI (uniform resource identifier), urn:ietf:params:oauth:jwk-thumbprint followed by the hash name and the value, for contexts that need identifiers in URI form.

The dangerous case is the symmetric key type, and private keys in general. A JWK can legitimately carry a private or secret key, so publishing a key set built carelessly from a keystore can expose exactly what it was meant to protect: an RSA key exported with d, p and q, or an oct key whose k is the shared secret itself. RFC 7517 requires that access to non-public key material by parties without legitimate access be prevented, and recommends an Encrypted JWK, a JSON Web Encryption (JWE) object whose plaintext is the JWK and whose cty header is jwk+json, whenever such a key could be observed. The rule is that anything served at a public endpoint must contain public halves only, and a quick audit of what your set actually serves is worth doing once rather than discovering the answer from someone else. A useful test is mechanical: for RSA and EC no member named d may appear, for OKP no d, for AKP no priv, and no oct key at all.

The other classic failure is trusting a key because a token brought it. RFC 7515 defines a jwk header parameter, the public key that corresponds to the signing key, carried inside the JWS itself. A verifier that uses it has let the sender choose the key. CVE-2018-0114 records that Cisco's node-jose library before version 0.11.0 did exactly that: an attacker could strip the original signature, place a public key of their own in the header and re-sign the token with the matching private key, and the library accepted it. RFC 7517's own security considerations give the principle: place no more trust in data secured by a key than in the method by which the key was obtained. A verifier should take keys only from configuration or from the issuer's published set, never from the token.

In practice JWKs travel between formats constantly. An identity provider's set is fetched over HTTPS (Hypertext Transfer Protocol Secure) and its keys are converted to the PEM or DER forms that libraries and appliances expect; a gateway may need the reverse. The conversions are mechanical but have sharp edges: the base64url encoding (with no padding) used for n, e, x, y and k differs from the standard base64 used inside x5c; integers must not carry the leading zero byte that ASN.1 (Abstract Syntax Notation One) encoders add to positive numbers; and EC coordinates must be padded to the full length of the curve. Checking a key by its thumbprint on both sides of a conversion is the quickest way to prove nothing changed.

Its neighbours are easy to tell apart. A JWK is a single key and a JWKS is the set that holds several; JWS and JWE are the signed and encrypted messages that use them; JWT is the token format built on JWS and JWE; and an X.509 certificate binds a key to a name, a validity period and an issuer's signature, which a bare JWK does not. The numbers worth remembering are RFC 7517 and RFC 7518 of May 2015, the five key types RSA, EC, oct, OKP and AKP, AQAB for the exponent 65537, the 256-octet modulus of a 2048-bit key, RFC 7638 for thumbprints, and CVE-2018-0114 for the embedded-key mistake.

jwks.def: A JSON (JavaScript Object Notation) document whose keys array lists the public keys a service signs its tokens with, published at a known address so that whoever receives those tokens can fetch the keys and verify the signatures.
jwks.context: A JSON Web Key Set (JWKS) is a JSON (JavaScript Object Notation) object with a keys array in which each element is a JSON Web Key (JWK) describing one key; the format comes from Request for Comments (RFC) 7517. An OpenID Connect provider or OAuth authorization server publishes its set at the address its metadata gives as jwks_uri, and every JSON Web Token (JWT) it signs names the key used in its kid header. Relying parties fetch and cache the set to verify JWT signatures and to follow key rotation without manual reconfiguration: the signer adds a new key and starts using it, and a verifier that meets an unfamiliar kid fetches the set again.
jwks.depth:
A JSON Web Key Set (JWKS) is how a service publishes the public keys needed to verify its tokens, usually at a well-known URL (Uniform Resource Locator) that clients fetch and cache. It exists so that key rotation does not require coordinating a configuration change with every consumer, which was the operational nightmare of shipping certificates by hand. The format is defined in Request for Comments (RFC) 7517, JSON Web Key (JWK), written by Michael Jones of Microsoft and published in May 2015, where it is called a JWK Set: a JSON (JavaScript Object Notation) object that must have a member named keys whose value is an array of JWKs. The order of the array implies no preference, members a parser does not understand must be ignored, and keys of an unknown type should be skipped, so a set can grow new kinds of key without breaking old readers. Its media type is application/jwk-set+json.

Each element describes one key. The only member required of every key is kty, the key type, and the registry kept by the Internet Assigned Numbers Authority (IANA) lists five: RSA (Rivest-Shamir-Adleman), EC (elliptic curve), oct (an octet sequence, that is, a symmetric key), OKP (octet string key pairs, added by RFC 8037 in January 2017 for the Ed25519, Ed448, X25519 and X448 algorithms) and AKP (algorithm key pair, added by RFC 9964 in May 2026 for the post-quantum signature scheme ML-DSA, the Module-Lattice-Based Digital Signature Standard). The remaining members depend on the type: an RSA public key carries its modulus n and exponent e, encoded as base64url. Optional members say what the key is for and which one it is: use (sig for signatures, enc for encryption), key_ops, alg, the key identifier kid and x5c, an X.509 certificate chain for the same key. The RFC advises against using use and key_ops together, and RFC 7518 warns of a classic encoding slip, libraries that return 257 octets for a 2048-bit modulus because of a leading zero.

Where the set lives is fixed by the protocols that use it. OpenID Connect Discovery makes jwks_uri a required member of the provider's metadata and requires the https scheme. The set holds the provider's signing keys and may also hold its encryption keys, in which case every key must declare its use. OAuth authorization servers publish their endpoints the same way in the metadata document of RFC 8414. Google's discovery document, for example, points to https://www.googleapis.com/oauth2/v3/certs. On the token side, the header of a signed token, a JSON Web Signature (JWS), carries kid, which RFC 7515 calls a hint indicating which key was used and a way for the signer to signal a change of key.

Rotation works because the set holds several keys at once and each token names the one that signed it. OpenID Connect Core describes the procedure: the signer publishes its keys at jwks_uri, rolls over by adding new keys to the set, begins using a new key at its discretion, and signals the change through kid; the verifier goes back to jwks_uri when it sees an unfamiliar kid; and the set should retain recently decommissioned keys for a reasonable period. In practice that means publishing the new key, waiting for consumers to refresh their cache, then signing with it, and retiring the old key only after every token signed by it has expired. Doing those steps in the wrong order is the classic self-inflicted outage: signing with a key nobody has fetched yet fails every validation at once. Verifiers cannot assume a schedule either. Microsoft states that its signing keys roll periodically, can be rolled immediately in an emergency, with no guaranteed interval, and that there is always more than one valid key in the document.

The caching behaviour is where subtle failures live. Cache too aggressively and a rotation breaks the verifier; refetch on every token and authentication depends on an outbound HTTP (Hypertext Transfer Protocol) call in the hot path. The usual answer is a cache with a bounded lifetime plus a single refetch when an unknown key identifier appears, rate-limited so that a flood of bogus identifiers cannot become a self-inflicted denial of service. Microsoft's published algorithm has exactly that shape: cache each key under its kid with a time to live of 24 hours, refresh every hour in the background, refresh on an unknown kid but never more often than every 5 minutes, and keep the last known good set if a fetch fails. Google says its keys change infrequently and can be cached according to the cache directives of the HTTP response.

Products expose the same decisions as settings. In NGINX Plus, the auth_jwt_key_request directive fetches a JSON Web Key Set through a subrequest and auth_jwt_key_file reads one from disk, while auth_jwt_key_cache defaults to 0, meaning no caching, so the documentation recommends caching the key file explicitly. F5 BIG-IP Access Policy Manager (APM), as OAuth client or resource server, validates incoming JSON Web Tokens (JWTs) with JWKs that it either discovers from the issuer's metadata document at a configured frequency or takes from manual configuration.

A JWKS proves nothing by itself; the trust comes from where it was fetched. RFC 7517 says one should place no more trust in data secured by a key than in the method by which the key was obtained, which is why jwks_uri must be https and why the address must come from the issuer's own configuration. A token can also name its key source, through the jku header (a JWK Set address) or the jwk header (the key itself), and a verifier that honours them lets the attacker choose the key. RFC 8725, the JWT best current practice of February 2020, warns that blindly following jku can also turn the verifier into a server-side request forgery (SSRF) tool, that kid values must be validated before they are used in a lookup, and that each key must be used with exactly one algorithm. The last rule answers a famous substitution: a token marked RS256 is changed to HS256 (a keyed hash using SHA-256, Secure Hash Algorithm with a 256-bit digest), and a careless library verifies it using the RSA public key, which the JWKS has just published to the world, as the shared secret (CVE-2015-9235). The reverse mistake is publishing too much: private and symmetric keys must never appear in a public set.

Its neighbours are easy to tell apart. A JWK is one key, a JWKS the set. A JWK thumbprint (RFC 7638, September 2015) is a hash over a canonical form of a key's required members and is a common way to generate a kid. An X.509 certificate binds a key to a name, a validity period and an issuer's signature; a bare JWK does none of that, and none of its common parameters carries an expiry date, which is why the x5c member exists for deployments that want the certificate's attributes as well. What the JWKS adds to all of them is a place and a refresh habit: one address, fetched over Transport Layer Security (TLS), where the current keys can always be found.

pss.def: A randomized RSA signature scheme, more robust than the older deterministic padding.
pss.context: Probabilistic Signature Scheme (RSASSA-PSS, RFC 8017) adds randomized salt to RSA signatures, giving stronger security proofs than the legacy PKCS#1 v1.5 padding. It is the recommended RSA signature padding in modern protocols.

hqc.def: A code-based post-quantum key-encapsulation algorithm selected by NIST as a backup.
hqc.context: Hamming Quasi-Cyclic is a code-based key-encapsulation mechanism NIST selected in 2025 as a backup to the lattice-based ML-KEM, so that post-quantum security does not rest on a single mathematical assumption.
hqc.depth:
HQC is a code-based key encapsulation mechanism selected by NIST as a backup to ML-KEM. Its purpose is diversity: ML-KEM rests on lattice problems, and standardizing a second algorithm resting on a different mathematical foundation means a breakthrough against one does not leave the world without an option.

That reasoning is worth understanding because it is unusual. Normally standards bodies pick the best candidate and stop; here the risk being managed is that post-quantum assumptions are younger and less attacked than RSA's were, so hedging across families is prudent rather than indecisive. HQC has larger keys and ciphertexts than ML-KEM, which is why it is the reserve rather than the default.

ecdh.def: Elliptic-curve Diffie-Hellman (ECDH): Diffie-Hellman key agreement in the group of points on an elliptic curve, where each side multiplies the other's public point by its own private number and both obtain the same shared point; with static keys it has no forward secrecy, with fresh keys per session (ECDHE) it does.
ecdh.context: Elliptic-curve Diffie-Hellman (ECDH) is the Diffie-Hellman idea moved from numbers modulo a prime to points on a curve. Each party has a private number d and a public point Q, equal to d times a base point; each computes its own d times the other's Q, and both reach the same point, whose x-coordinate becomes the shared secret. Because the best known attacks on curves are far slower, a 256-bit curve matches a 3,072-bit finite field or RSA (Rivest-Shamir-Adleman) key, so the public values are 32 bytes for X25519 and 65 for an uncompressed P-256 point. ECDH names the primitive whatever the key lifetime: with a long-term key on one side it has no forward secrecy, which is why TLS (Transport Layer Security) 1.3 allows only the ephemeral form, ECDHE (elliptic-curve Diffie-Hellman ephemeral). Like every Diffie-Hellman it authenticates nobody, and a peer's point must be validated before use, or a crafted one can leak the private key.
ecdh.depth:
What it is. Standards for Efficient Cryptography 1 (SEC 1), version 2.0, published by Certicom Research on 21 May 2009, specifies two primitives. In the plain elliptic curve Diffie-Hellman primitive, party U multiplies the other party's public key QV by its own private key dU to get a point P, rejects the result if P is the point at infinity, and outputs the x-coordinate of P as the shared secret; in the cofactor variant it multiplies by the curve's cofactor h as well, which SEC 1 says gives efficient resistance to attacks like small subgroup attacks. Both sides reach the same point because dU times dV times the base point is the same whichever order the multiplications run. Elliptic-curve Diffie-Hellman (ECDH) is therefore exactly Diffie-Hellman in another group, and it inherits the same limits: the output is a field element, not yet a key, so it goes through a key derivation function (KDF); and nothing in it proves who the other party is. The National Institute of Standards and Technology (NIST) puts the curve and finite-field versions side by side in Special Publication (SP) 800-56A Revision 3 (April 2018), naming each scheme by how many ephemeral and static keys each side contributes, and announced in January 2026 that it will update that document.

Why curves won. NIST SP 800-57 Part 1 Revision 5 (May 2020) rates an elliptic curve of 256 to 383 bits at 128 bits of security, the same as a 3,072-bit finite field or RSA (Rivest-Shamir-Adleman) modulus, and a curve of 512 bits or more at 256 bits, where the finite field and RSA need 15,360 bits; it adds that all these estimates will be significantly affected when quantum computing becomes practical. The sizes on the wire follow. In Transport Layer Security (TLS) 1.3, specified since July 2026 in RFC (Request for Comments) 9846, a P-256 share is an uncompressed point, a format byte and two 32-byte coordinates, 65 bytes in all; P-384 coordinates take 48 bytes and P-521 coordinates 66; an X25519 share is 32 bytes and an X448 share 56. A 2,048-bit finite-field share, by contrast, is 256 bytes and buys less security. RFC 9846 requires every implementation to support key exchange with secp256r1, which is NIST P-256, codepoint 0x0017, and recommends X25519, codepoint 0x001D.

The curves. The NIST prime curves P-256, P-384 and P-521 are short Weierstrass curves, named secp256r1, secp384r1 and secp521r1 in the SEC registry and in TLS. Curve25519 came from Daniel J. Bernstein, whose paper dated 9 February 2006 announced record speeds, 832,457 Pentium III cycles for a shared-secret computation, together with free key compression, free key validation and protection against timing attacks; in his words, every 32-byte string is accepted as a Curve25519 public key, while typical ECDH functions can be broken if users do not validate public keys. RFC 7748, by Adam Langley, Mike Hamburg and Sean Turner for the Crypto Forum Research Group (CFRG) in January 2016, specified the X25519 and X448 functions: they work on the u-coordinate alone, with base point 9, decode every private key by clearing and setting fixed bits, and use a ladder whose conditional swap should run in constant time. Two parties exchange X25519 of their secret and 9, then each computes X25519 of its own secret and the other's value, and RFC 7748 asks them to run a KDF over the result and both public values. NIST SP 800-186 (February 2023) added two Edwards curves interoperable with the CFRG ones to the curves recommended for United States government use, alongside the Weierstrass curves. Brainpool curves also survive in IPsec (Internet Protocol Security) as groups 27 to 30.

Validation, the part that fails. A point received from a peer must be a valid point on the agreed curve. If it is not, the arithmetic still produces an answer, but on a different and much weaker curve, and a party that reuses its private key across many exchanges leaks it piece by piece; this is the invalid curve attack. CVE-2015-7940 recorded it in the Bouncy Castle Java library before version 1.51, which did not check that a point lay on the curve and so let remote attackers obtain private keys through a series of crafted ECDH key exchanges. RFC 9846 therefore requires TLS 1.3 peers using P-256, P-384 or P-521 to check that the point is not the point at infinity, that both coordinates are in range and that they satisfy the curve equation, and to use the cofactor primitive with the x-coordinate kept at full length, leading zeros included. X25519 and X448 accept any 32 or 56 bytes by design, but a small-order input makes the output all zeros, so RFC 9846 requires an implementation to check for the all-zero value and abort, which RFC 7748 suggests doing by ORing the bytes together to avoid a timing side channel.

Static and ephemeral. ECDH says nothing about how long a key lives. TLS 1.2 once offered static ECDH, in which the server's certificate carried a fixed ECDH public key; RFC 8422 (Yoav Nir, Simon Josefsson and Manuel Pégourié-Gonnard, August 2018) removed the ECDH_RSA and ECDH_ECDSA key exchanges, noting that certificates with a fixed ECDH key saw very little implementation, deprecated explicit curves and compressed points, and is itself obsoleted by RFC 9846, under which every TLS 1.3 key share is ephemeral. RFC 10015 (July 2026) closes the remaining door in TLS 1.2: clients SHOULD NOT offer and servers SHOULD NOT select static ECDH suites, because invalid curve attacks exploit exactly that kind of secret reuse and implementations often miss one of the many required mitigations. Static keys still have a place when they are used for authentication and paired with ephemeral ones. WireGuard runs the Noise_IK handshake over Curve25519 and mixes four results into its chaining key: the initiator's ephemeral key with the responder's static key, the two static keys, the two ephemeral keys, and the responder's ephemeral key with the initiator's static key, so that the static keys identify the peers and the ephemeral ones give forward secrecy; it also accepts an optional pre-shared key for post-quantum resistance. Hybrid Public Key Encryption (HPKE), RFC 9180 (February 2022), turns ECDH into a key-encapsulation mechanism: to encrypt to a recipient's public key, the sender generates an ephemeral key pair and computes ECDH between its new private key and the recipient's public key, and Messaging Layer Security and TLS Encrypted ClientHello are built on it. SEC 1 uses the same pattern in ECIES (Elliptic Curve Integrated Encryption Scheme).

Where engineers configure it. In TLS 1.2 it appears as the ECDHE (elliptic-curve Diffie-Hellman ephemeral) cipher suites, in TLS 1.3 as the supported_groups and key_share extensions. Secure Shell (SSH) names it curve25519-sha256 and curve448-sha512 in RFC 8731 (February 2020), which records that the curve25519-sha256@libssh.org method was already widely deployed in libssh and OpenSSH before the RFC. In IKEv2 (Internet Key Exchange version 2) the elliptic-curve groups are 19 to 21 for the NIST curves and, since RFC 8031 (Yoav Nir and Simon Josefsson, December 2016), 31 and 32 for Curve25519 and Curve448, and they are chosen with the same group setting as the finite-field ones. The post-quantum change comes in alongside rather than in place: RFC 10024 (August 2026) pairs X25519 or a NIST curve with ML-KEM (Module-Lattice-Based Key-Encapsulation Mechanism) in groups such as X25519MLKEM768, whose client share of 1,216 bytes is the 1,184-byte ML-KEM encapsulation key followed by the 32-byte X25519 share, an order the RFC itself calls reversed for historical reasons, so the session holds as long as either component does.

Numbers worth remembering: 32 bytes for an X25519 public value and 56 for X448; 65 bytes for an uncompressed P-256 point; a 256-bit curve equal to 3,072-bit RSA at 128 bits of security; base point 9 for X25519; TLS codepoints 0x0017 for secp256r1 and 0x001D for x25519; IKE groups 19 and 31; and the three checks for a Weierstrass point: not at infinity, coordinates in range, on the curve.

rs256.def: RS256 is the JSON Web Algorithms (JWA) identifier for an RSA (Rivest-Shamir-Adleman) signature in the PKCS #1 v1.5 (Public-Key Cryptography Standards number 1) format over a SHA-256 (Secure Hash Algorithm, 256-bit) hash: the most widely deployed way to sign a JSON Web Token (JWT), verifiable with the signer's public key alone.
rs256.context: RS256 is a JSON Web Algorithm identifier (RFC 7518, Request for Comments) for an RSA (Rivest-Shamir-Adleman) signature using SHA-256 (Secure Hash Algorithm, 256-bit), formally RSASSA-PKCS1-v1_5 with SHA-256. It is one of the most common JSON Web Token (JWT) signing algorithms, paired with a public key published in a JSON Web Key Set (JWKS): the issuer signs with its private key, and any number of services verify with the public key without being able to forge anything. RFC 7518 requires keys of at least 2048 bits, OpenID Connect makes it mandatory for providers, and its main rivals are ES256 (ECDSA on the P-256 curve) for size and PS256 (RSA with PSS padding) for the more modern padding.
rs256.depth:
RS256 is a name, not a new algorithm. Request for Comments (RFC) 7518, JSON Web Algorithms (JWA), written by M. Jones and published in May 2015, defines it as the value of the alg header that marks a JSON Web Signature (JWS) computed with RSASSA-PKCS1-v1_5, the RSA (Rivest-Shamir-Adleman) signature scheme of PKCS #1 (Public-Key Cryptography Standards number 1) version 1.5, using SHA-256 (the 256-bit Secure Hash Algorithm). The same operation exists everywhere under other names: Appendix A of the RFC maps it to SHA256withRSA in Java, to the XML (Extensible Markup Language) Signature URI (uniform resource identifier) ending rsa-sha256 and to the object identifier 1.2.840.113549.1.1.11 used in X.509 certificates. RS256 signs a JSON Web Token (JWT) with a private key so that verification needs only the corresponding public key. It is a signature, not encryption; it is not PS256, which uses the newer PSS (Probabilistic Signature Scheme) padding; and it is not HS256, a keyed hash in which the same secret both signs and verifies.

The mechanics are short. The JWS signing input is the base64url-encoded header, a dot and the base64url-encoded payload. The signer hashes it with SHA-256 and builds the encoded message that RFC 8017 (PKCS #1 version 2.2, November 2016) specifies: the bytes 0x00 and 0x01, a run of 0xff bytes at least eight long, a 0x00 byte, and then T, the DER (Distinguished Encoding Rules) encoding of a DigestInfo structure that names SHA-256 and carries the 32-byte hash. That block, as long as the RSA modulus, is raised to the private exponent, and the result is the signature, an octet string exactly as long as the modulus: 256 bytes for a 2048-bit key, which base64url turns into the 342 characters of the token's third segment. Verification raises the signature to the public exponent, rebuilds the expected encoding from the received header and payload, and compares. The padding has no random component, so the same key and the same input always produce the same signature. RFC 7518 adds one hard rule: a key of 2048 bits or larger must be used.

That asymmetry is why it became the default for anything involving more than one party: an identity provider signs, any number of services verify, and none of them holds anything that could forge a token. This is what makes JSON Web Key Set (JWKS) endpoints work. The provider publishes its public keys, verifiers fetch and cache them, each token's kid header names the key that signed it, rotation happens without coordinating with every consumer, and the private key never leaves the issuer. OpenID Connect builds on exactly that arrangement. Its Core specification requires every OpenID provider to support signing ID tokens with RS256, unless it only returns them from the token endpoint and lets clients register for none, and says the alg should be the default of RS256 unless the client registered another algorithm. Even the token hashes follow from it: when the ID token's alg is RS256, the at_hash claim is the left-most 128 bits of the SHA-256 hash of the access token, base64url-encoded.

The standards treat RS256 as established rather than preferred. RFC 7518 lists HS256 as Required, RS256 as Recommended, ES256 as Recommended+ (a level likely to rise in a future version) and PS256 and none as Optional, and the registry of the Internet Assigned Numbers Authority (IANA), last updated on 29 September 2026, still carries RS256 as Recommended. PKCS #1 itself is more pointed: RFC 8017 says that although no attacks are known against RSASSA-PKCS1-v1_5, RSASSA-PSS is required in new applications for robustness, and the older scheme is included only for compatibility with existing applications, with a gradual transition to PSS recommended as a precaution. In its favour, the version 1.5 encoding embeds an identifier of the hash function, so a forger would have to find collisions in SHA-256 itself; attacking a different hash function gains nothing. The JOSE (JSON Object Signing and Encryption) registry also shows where things are heading: RS1, RSA with SHA-1 (Secure Hash Algorithm 1), is Prohibited, the generic EdDSA identifier is Deprecated in favour of fully specified names, and ML-DSA-44, ML-DSA-65 and ML-DSA-87, the post-quantum signatures, were registered by RFC 9964 in May 2026.

The famous failures were in libraries, not in RSA. JSON Web Token Best Current Practices, RFC 8725 (February 2020, Best Current Practice 225, by Y. Sheffer, D. Hardt and M. Jones), records two attacks made possible because a token names its own algorithm: an attacker changes alg to none and some libraries accept the token without checking any signature, or changes RS256 into HS256 and some libraries verify an HMAC (hash-based message authentication code) using the RSA public key as the shared secret. Since that key is public by design, often in the very JWKS the verifier fetches, anyone could then mint tokens the server accepted. CVE-2015-9235 records the case of the jsonwebtoken module for Node.js before version 4.2.2, in which a token meant for the RS or ES family could be replaced by one signed with an HS algorithm. The cure is in the same RFC: libraries must let the caller fix the set of acceptable algorithms and use no other, must check that alg matches the operation, and must use each key with exactly one algorithm; RFC 7515 had already said that which algorithms are acceptable is the application's decision.

The trade against HS256 is cost and key size, and both matter less than they used to. RSA verification is fast even though signing is not, and verification is the operation that happens constantly, at every service that receives a token. Where RS256 is genuinely under pressure is from elliptic curve alternatives: ES256 offers security at least comparable to RS256 with much smaller keys and signatures, a 64-octet signature against 256 bytes for a 2048-bit RSA key, and a JWT is a thing that travels in an HTTP (Hypertext Transfer Protocol) header, where size is not free. ES256 has its own sharp edge, which RFC 8725 points out: ECDSA (Elliptic Curve Digital Signature Algorithm) needs a unique random value for every signature, and predictable values can leak the private key, so libraries should use the deterministic variant; RS256's deterministic padding has no such requirement.

The longer horizon is quantum. NIST (the United States National Institute of Standards and Technology) states in IR 8547 (an interagency or internal report), Transition to Post-Quantum Cryptography Standards (final version, October 2026), that RSA, ECDSA and EdDSA signatures are all vulnerable to Shor's algorithm on a cryptanalytically relevant quantum computer, and schedules them, at 112 bits of classical security strength and above, to be deprecated after 2030 and disallowed after 2035 under its standards; the replacements are ML-DSA (Module-Lattice-Based Digital Signature Algorithm, Federal Information Processing Standard (FIPS) 204) and SLH-DSA (FIPS 205). For signed tokens, which live minutes or hours, the risk is forgery after a quantum computer exists rather than decryption of old traffic, so the practical consequence is planning: verifiers whose allowed-algorithm list can grow to include the ML-DSA identifiers, and issuers able to publish new key types in their JWKS when the time comes.

In practice an RS256 token is easy to recognize. Its first segment decodes to a header whose alg member reads RS256 and whose kid member names a key; its third segment is 342 base64url characters for a 2048-bit key, 512 for a 3072-bit key and 683 for a 4096-bit one, because the signature is always as long as the modulus. The matching JWK (JSON Web Key) has kty set to RSA, carries the modulus n and exponent e, and may declare alg RS256 to bind the key to this one algorithm, which is what RFC 8725 asks for. Debugging usually comes down to three checks: that the verifier accepts RS256 explicitly rather than whatever the header says, that the kid in the token exists in the set the verifier cached, and that the key is RSA and at least 2048 bits.

The neighbours are easily confused. RS384 and RS512 are the same scheme with SHA-384 and SHA-512 and gain little in practice; PS256 is RSA with PSS padding and SHA-256, randomized by a salt; HS256 is symmetric, so every verifier could also forge; ES256 is ECDSA on the P-256 curve; and none means no signature at all. The numbers worth remembering are RFC 7518 section 3.3, the 2048-bit minimum, signatures of 256 bytes or 342 base64url characters at that size, the object identifier 1.2.840.113549.1.1.11, CVE-2015-9235 for the HS256 substitution, and 2030 and 2035 for NIST's deprecation and disallowance of quantum-vulnerable signatures.

es256.def: ES256 is the JSON Web Algorithms (JWA) identifier for an ECDSA (Elliptic Curve Digital Signature Algorithm) signature on the P-256 curve with SHA-256 (Secure Hash Algorithm, 256-bit), used to sign JSON Web Tokens and other JWS (JSON Web Signature) objects; the signature is exactly 64 bytes, the values R and S side by side.
es256.context: ES256 is defined in section 3.4 of RFC (Request for Comments) 7518 and marked Recommended+ in the IANA (Internet Assigned Numbers Authority) registry for JOSE (JSON Object Signing and Encryption), the plus meaning its requirement is expected to rise. It offers security comparable to RS256 with much smaller keys and signatures, 64 bytes against the 256 of RS256 with a 2048-bit key, a real saving in a token that travels in an HTTP header on every request. The same algorithm is COSE (CBOR Object Signing and Encryption) value -7, the default credential type of WebAuthn (Web Authentication). Its weak point is implementation: every signature needs a fresh secret number, so libraries should derive it deterministically, as RFC 6979 describes.
es256.depth:
What it is. RFC (Request for Comments) 7518, JSON Web Algorithms (JWA), written by Michael Jones and published in May 2015, defines, for the security formats built on JSON (JavaScript Object Notation), ES256 in section 3.4 as ECDSA (Elliptic Curve Digital Signature Algorithm) using the P-256 curve and the SHA-256 (Secure Hash Algorithm, 256-bit) hash. The signer runs ECDSA over the JWS (JSON Web Signature) Signing Input, which RFC 7515 defines as the Base64url-encoded protected header and payload joined by a period, and obtains the pair R and S, two 256-bit unsigned integers. Each is written as a 32-octet big-endian sequence, never shortened to drop leading zeros, and the two are concatenated, R first, into a 64-octet value; a verifier must reject anything that is not exactly 64 octets. The siblings follow the same pattern with ES384 (P-384 and SHA-384) and ES512, which, contrary to what the name suggests, uses the P-521 curve with SHA-512. A public key for ES256 published as a JWK (JSON Web Key) has kty EC, crv P-256, and x and y coordinates encoded at the full size of the curve, 32 octets each. RFC 7518 lists ES256 as Recommended+, and the IANA (Internet Assigned Numbers Authority) JOSE (JSON Object Signing and Encryption) registry, last updated on 29 September 2026, still does: the plus means the requirement is likely to be strengthened in a future version.

How the signature is made, and why randomness matters. FIPS (Federal Information Processing Standard) 186-5, published by NIST (National Institute of Standards and Technology) on 3 February 2023, specifies ECDSA, with the curves themselves in Special Publication 800-186. Each signature uses a per-message secret number. If that number repeats, or is even partly predictable, the private key can be computed from the signatures, and RFC 8725, the JSON Web Token (JWT) Best Current Practices of February 2020, warns that a few predictable bits across messages may be enough. The defence is deterministic ECDSA: RFC 6979, by Thomas Pornin in August 2013, derives the number from the private key and the message hash through HMAC_DRBG, so that the same message and key always give the same signature and no random source is needed at signing time. The signatures remain ordinary ECDSA, verifiable by unmodified code, which is why RFC 8725 says JWT libraries SHOULD implement it, and FIPS 186-5 now approves deterministic ECDSA in its section 6.3.2 for exactly this reason: a per-message number that depends on message and key protects against signatures made with insufficient randomness.

Why choose it. RFC 7518 itself gives the reason: ECDSA provides security equivalent to RSA (Rivest-Shamir-Adleman) with shorter keys and greater speed for many operations, so its signatures are substantially smaller. The arithmetic shows it in a token. An ES256 signature of 64 bytes becomes 86 Base64url characters; an RS256 signature with the 2048-bit minimum key that RFC 7518 requires is 256 bytes, 342 characters, and the key pair is far larger. Against HS256 the difference is trust rather than size: an HS256 tag is checked with the same shared secret that creates it, so every verifier can also forge, while ES256 is verified with a public key that can be published openly in a JWK Set. That combination, small and asymmetric, is why OpenID Connect providers, ACME (Automatic Certificate Management Environment) clients and many APIs use it; RFC 8555's own examples sign ACME requests with ES256, and Neil Madden noted in 2022 that many OIDC (OpenID Connect) providers use ECDSA-signed JWTs.

The same algorithm in WebAuthn. In the binary world of COSE (CBOR Object Signing and Encryption, where CBOR is the Concise Binary Object Representation of RFC 8949), ES256 is the number -7, and it is the backbone of passkeys. The W3C (World Wide Web Consortium) Recommendation for Web Authentication Level 3, published on 25 August 2026, says relying parties that want to support a wide range of authenticators SHOULD offer -8 (EdDSA), -7 (ES256) and -257 (RS256), uses -7 and -257 as the defaults when a site offers none, and requires browsers to expose the public key of a -7 credential on curve P-256. Madden observed that almost all WebAuthn devices in real use, YubiKeys included, sign with ECDSA. One detail catches developers: WebAuthn section 6.5.5 requires an ES256 assertion signature to be an ASN.1 (Abstract Syntax Notation One) DER (Distinguished Encoding Rules) Ecdsa-Sig-Value, the SEQUENCE of two INTEGERs that RFC 3279 defines for X.509, whose length varies; JWS requires the fixed 64-byte concatenation. Moving a signature between the two worlds needs an explicit conversion, and a converter that drops or adds a leading zero produces signatures that fail.

A name with two meanings. RFC 9864, Fully-Specified Algorithms for JOSE and COSE, by Michael B. Jones and Orie Steele in October 2025, separates fully specified identifiers, which fix every parameter, from polymorphic ones, which leave the curve to the key. ES256 in JOSE is fully specified, since P-256 is part of its definition; ES256 in COSE is polymorphic, because -7 means ECDSA with SHA-256 on whatever curve the key names. RFC 9864 therefore created ESP256 (-9), with ESP384 (-51) and ESP512 (-52), and the IANA COSE registry, updated on 25 August 2026, now marks -7 as Deprecated. WebAuthn Level 3 nonetheless keeps -7: it calls -9 NOT RECOMMENDED in pubKeyCredParams and tells sites to use -7 instead or in addition, because its own rules already pin -7 to P-256. In JOSE, ES256 is unaffected and remains Recommended+. Not to be confused with ES256K, registered by RFC 8812 in August 2020, which uses the secp256k1 curve instead and is merely Optional.

What goes wrong. The famous failure is the repeated secret number. At the 27th Chaos Communication Congress, on 29 December 2010, the fail0verflow team showed that from a pair of PlayStation 3 signatures that used the same per-message value they could compute the value and Sony's private key, and with the private key they could sign software themselves. The most dramatic verifier bug came in April 2022: CVE-2022-21449, which Madden named Psychic Signatures, let Java 15 to 18, before the April 2022 Critical Patch Update, accept a signature whose r and s were both zero as valid for any message and any key, because the check that both lie between 1 and n minus 1 was lost when the elliptic curve code was rewritten from C++ into Java in Java 15. Oracle scored it 7.5 under CVSS (Common Vulnerability Scoring System); ForgeRock, Madden's employer, graded it 10.0, since it bypassed ES256 tokens, WebAuthn assertions and anything else verified with ECDSA. The everyday failures are quieter: accepting whatever alg a token header names, which RFC 8725 forbids by requiring an explicit allow-list and one algorithm per key; confusing the DER and raw signature formats; and generating signatures with a weak random source instead of a deterministic implementation.

Neighbours and the horizon. RS256 and PS256 sign with RSA and produce large signatures; HS256 is symmetric; Ed25519 is now the fully specified JOSE name for EdDSA on that curve; ES384 and ES512 are the same construction on larger curves. ES256 is not quantum-safe. NIST Internal Report (IR) 8547, final in October 2026, deprecates ECDSA at every approved strength after 2030 and disallows it after 2035, and the IANA JOSE registry already lists ML-DSA-44, ML-DSA-65 and ML-DSA-87 from RFC 9964 as Optional identifiers. Numbers worth remembering: P-256 and SHA-256; 32 bytes per coordinate and per signature half; 64 bytes or 86 Base64url characters per signature; COSE -7, and -9 for ESP256; Recommended+ in JOSE; RFC 7518 of May 2015, RFC 6979 of August 2013 and RFC 9864 of October 2025; and 2030 and 2035 in the post-quantum transition.

acme.def: The Automatic Certificate Management Environment (ACME), Request for Comments (RFC) 8555: a protocol in which a client proves to a certificate authority that it controls a domain name or Internet Protocol (IP) address through automated challenges, then orders, downloads, renews and revokes certificates without human steps.
acme.context: The Automatic Certificate Management Environment (ACME), Request for Comments (RFC) 8555, is the protocol behind Let's Encrypt and the many certificate authorities (CAs) that now offer the same interface. It lets a client prove domain control and obtain certificates without human interaction, which is why free, auto-renewing TLS (Transport Layer Security) became universal, and why the industry can now shorten certificate lifetimes from a year towards 47 days without asking people to do more work.
acme.depth:
The Automatic Certificate Management Environment (ACME) turned certificate issuance from a purchasing process into an API (application programming interface) call, and that single change is a large part of why HTTPS (Hypertext Transfer Protocol Secure) went from a minority of the web to most of it. Request for Comments (RFC) 8555 (March 2019, by R. Barnes, J. Hoffman-Andrews, D. McCarney of Let's Encrypt and J. Kasten) starts from the problem: certificate authorities (CAs) in the Web PKI (public key infrastructure) must verify that an applicant legitimately represents the names in a certificate, and that verification was done through a collection of ad hoc mechanisms. Before it, getting a certificate meant a vendor, a payment and manual verification, which is a fine annual ritual and a terrible thing to do every sixty days. ACME messages are JSON (JavaScript Object Notation) objects signed as JWS (JSON Web Signature) and sent over HTTPS; the client discovers the server's resources from a directory (newNonce, newAccount, newOrder, revokeCert and keyChange), registers an account key, places an order listing the identifiers it wants, satisfies one challenge per authorization, finalizes the order with a certificate signing request (CSR) and downloads the certificate. The RFC calls it Automatic; its companion RFCs say Automated.

The protocol's core is proving control of a name. Every challenge binds the CA's random token to the client's account through a key authorization, the token, a full stop and the base64url thumbprint of the account key. Validation over the Hypertext Transfer Protocol (HTTP), http-01, serves that string at /.well-known/acme-challenge/ followed by the token, fetched over TCP (Transmission Control Protocol) port 80; DNS (Domain Name System) validation (dns-01) publishes the base64url SHA-256 (Secure Hash Algorithm, 256-bit) digest of it as a TXT record at _acme-challenge under the name being validated. RFC 8737 (February 2020, R.B. Shoemaker) added tls-alpn-01, answered on TCP port 443 by negotiating the ALPN (Application-Layer Protocol Negotiation) protocol acme-tls/1 and presenting a self-signed certificate that carries an acmeIdentifier extension, and RFC 8738 added the ip identifier type, validated by http-01 or tls-alpn-01 but never by dns-01. The DNS method is the one that scales to wildcards and to hosts with no public web server; Let's Encrypt calls it the only choice for wildcards or infrastructure that should not be exposed. That is why it dominates in infrastructure work and why automating DNS updates, with its propagation delays and DNS API credentials scattered through the pipeline, becomes the real integration effort; a new IETF (Internet Engineering Task Force) draft, DNS-PERSIST-01, which Let's Encrypt announced on 18 February 2026, replaces the repeated record with a standing TXT record at _validation-persist that names the CA and the authorized ACME account.

Let's Encrypt, run by the nonprofit Internet Security Research Group (ISRG), issued its first publicly trusted certificate on 14 September 2015. It reached its millionth certificate in March 2016, a million a day by September 2018, a billion in total in 2020 and often ten million a day by late 2025, and over roughly its first five years the share of Firefox connections using HTTPS rose from below 30 per cent to about 80 per cent, where it has stayed. The protocol kept growing with it. RFC 9773 (June 2025, A. Gable) defines ACME Renewal Information (ARI): the server publishes, for each certificate, a suggested renewal window with a start and an end, and the client's next order names the certificate it replaces, which lets a CA spread load and ask for early renewal when a certificate must be replaced.

Short lifetimes are the design intent, not a limitation. If renewal is automated, ninety days is no harder than a year, and it dramatically shortens the window in which a compromised key stays useful. The CA/Browser Forum has now made that the rule for everyone. Ballot SC-081v3, proposed by Clint Wilson of Apple and endorsed by Sectigo, Google Chrome and Mozilla, passed with 25 certificate issuers in favour, none against and five abstaining, and all four browser makers in favour; its review period ran from 13 April to 13 May 2025. The Baseline Requirements (version 2.3.1) now cap publicly trusted TLS (Transport Layer Security) certificates at 200 days from 15 March 2026, 100 days from 15 March 2027 and 47 days from 15 March 2029, with the reuse of domain and IP (Internet Protocol) validation data falling to 200, 100 and finally 10 days on the same dates. The ballot's reasoning is blunt: revocation is unreliable at scale, while certificate validity periods, and their enforcement by relying parties, are incredibly reliable.

Let's Encrypt is moving ahead of the floor. Its 90-day certificates go to 64 days by default on 10 February 2027, with authorization reuse cut from 30 days to 10, and to 45 days with seven hours of reuse on 16 February 2028; an opt-in tlsserver profile has issued 45-day certificates since 13 May 2026, and it expects the last 90-day certificate to expire on 11 May 2027. Since 15 January 2026 a shortlived profile has offered certificates valid for 160 hours, just over six days, and certificates for IPv4 and IPv6 (Internet Protocol versions 4 and 6) addresses, which must be short-lived. Its advice for clients without ARI is to renew at about two thirds of the lifetime, and to search cron jobs, wrapper scripts and runbooks for hard-coded renewal intervals of 83, 80 or 60 days, which will silently stop working. Root programmes push from the other side: Mozilla's Root Store Policy 3.1 requires CAs applying for new roots to demonstrate automated validation, issuance and renewal, renewing test certificates at least every 30 days.

The network vendors have followed. F5's BIG-IP 21.1.0 added native ACMEv2 protocol support that handles certificate provisioning, renewal and deployment automatically, against any ACMEv2-compliant CA, naming ZeroSSL, DigiCert, Buypass, Google Trust Services and SSL.com alongside Let's Encrypt. FortiOS uses ACME to obtain the FortiGate's own administration certificate: the client listens on a publicly reachable interface (not a loopback), uses tls-alpn-01 on TCP 443 by default and falls back to http-01 on TCP 80 if 443 is busy, and is configured with config system acme and a local certificate whose enroll-protocol is acme2; a virtual IP on those ports will capture the challenge instead, which can also be used deliberately to let servers behind the FortiGate answer their own. Fortinet notes that the self-signed tls-alpn-01 certificate often shows up in security scans, and that this is expected.

The corollary is that automation is not optional. A manual ACME workflow gives all the frequency and none of the benefit, and the outage comes at whatever hour the certificate expires. What remains for operators is deployment and monitoring: renewing on the CA's schedule rather than a fixed one, reloading the services that use the certificate, alerting when a renewal fails, and making sure the DNS credentials or open port 80 that validation needs are themselves secured.

fqdn.def: Fully Qualified Domain Name (FQDN): a domain name written out with every label up to the root of the Domain Name System (DNS), such as www.example.com., so that it identifies one node whatever the context in which it is read.
fqdn.context: A Fully Qualified Domain Name (FQDN) gives the full path from the host to the root of the Domain Name System (DNS), like www.example.com with a final dot, leaving no ambiguity about which domain is meant, as opposed to a short or relative name that depends on a search suffix. In everyday use the final dot is dropped and the name is still called fully qualified, which is where most of the confusion about the term comes from.
fqdn.depth:
A Fully Qualified Domain Name (FQDN) is a name in the Domain Name System (DNS) that carries all of its labels, so it means the same thing wherever it is typed. Request for Comments (RFC) 9499, the DNS terminology document of March 2024, is frank that the term is ambiguous. Strictly, a fully qualified name includes every label, the zero-length label of the root among them, and is written with a terminating dot, as in www.example.net followed by a dot; but because every name ends at the same root, names are usually written without it and are still called fully qualified. The RFC traces the term to RFC 819 of August 1982, by Zaw-Sing Su and Jon Postel, which speaks of a complete, fully qualified, name built by concatenating simple names. The Internet Users' Glossary (RFC 1983, August 1996) gives the working definition most engineers use: the full name of a system, not just its hostname, so that venera is a hostname and venera.isi.edu is an FQDN. The opposite is a partially qualified or relative name, one or more of whose last labels are left out and which can only be understood from context.

The limits come from the wire format. A name is a list of labels ordered from the most specific to the root; each label holds 0 to 63 octets and only the root label may be empty; and the whole name may occupy at most 255 octets, counting one length octet in front of each label and one octet for the root (RFC 1035 and RFC 9499). It follows by arithmetic that the longest name that can be written in text, dots included and final dot omitted, has 253 characters. RFC 9499 distinguishes three ways of writing the same name: the wire format, the presentation format of zone files, in which a fully qualified name always shows the final dot, and the common display format of applications and prose, in which the dot is optional and rarely shown. Comparison ignores case (RFC 4343). Host names are a narrower set than domain names: letters, digits and hyphens, with RFC 1123 relaxing the older rule of RFC 952 so that the first character may be a digit, and requiring software to handle 63 characters and preferably 255. Names in other scripts travel as labels that begin with xn-- (RFC 5890).

The final dot is where the term stops being pedantry. RFC 1034 uses it to tell an absolute name, which ends with the root and therefore with a dot, from a relative one, which local software completes from an origin or a search list. In a zone file the rule is literal: RFC 1035 says names that end in a dot are absolute and names that do not are relative to the origin, so a record whose target is written mail.example.com without the dot, inside the zone example.com, points at mail.example.com.example.com. It is one of the commonest zone errors there is, and the reason careful operators always type the dot in record data.

On a client the same question is settled by the search list. In the Linux resolver configuration, resolv.conf, the search list defaults to the local domain, and a name with fewer dots than the ndots option, 1 by default and capped at 15, is tried with each search domain in turn; a name with at least that many dots is tried first as it stands. Up to glibc 2.25 the list was limited to six domains and 256 characters, and it has been unlimited since 2.26. Kubernetes shows what the setting costs: a Pod is given a search list of its namespace, svc.cluster.local and cluster.local, with ndots:5, so an external name with fewer than five dots is first tried under each of those suffixes, and only a final dot makes the lookup go straight out.

Guessing at unqualified names has a security history. RFC 1535 (October 1993) described resolvers that, given any name not ending in a dot, appended pieces of the local domain before trying the name itself: a user at Tech.ACES.COM asking for UnivHost.University.EDU caused queries for that name under Tech.ACES.COM, then ACES.COM, then COM, and only then the real one. Someone had registered EDU.COM, and a single wildcard alias there could have captured every connection from a .com site to a .edu host. The correction was the behaviour ndots now encodes, trying a name that contains dots as absolute first. Mail took the stricter line: RFC 5321 expects the names in the Simple Mail Transfer Protocol (SMTP) to be FQDNs and forbids relays from inferring them from partial names.

The practical places where the distinction bites are certificates, host configuration and directory services. The rules for checking a server's identity in Transport Layer Security (TLS), RFC 9525 (November 2023, replacing RFC 6125), cover FQDNs only and call names that are not fully qualified out of scope, which is why a certificate issued for intranet.corp.example does not match a browser pointed at the bare name intranet. On Linux, hostname -f prints the FQDN, described as the name including the DNS domain, and hostname -s the short name, cut at the first dot. In Active Directory, Microsoft documents 63 bytes for each label and 255 bytes for the FQDN, with the further rule that the FQDN of a domain controller must be smaller than 155 bytes.

Network devices use the word for objects that are resolved, not typed. A FortiGate FQDN address is a firewall address defined by name: the firewall resolves it through DNS, keeps a cache of every address returned and follows the time to live (TTL) of the records, so that the policy tracks the service as its addresses change. What the policy matches is therefore the firewall's own answer, and a client that asks a different resolver may be sent to an address the firewall never learnt. On an F5 BIG-IP a node may be an IP (Internet Protocol) address or an FQDN; with Auto Populate, enabled by default, the system creates an ephemeral node for each address in the answer and deletes those that disappear from it, and the administrator states whether the name is to be resolved to addresses of version 4 or of version 6 of the protocol.

It helps to keep the neighbours apart. A hostname, in the everyday sense, is the first label, or the machine's own short name. A domain name is any name in the tree, qualified or not. A registered domain is the part bought from a registry, one label below a public suffix. An FQDN is a complete name for one node, and it is only a name: it carries no scheme, port or path, which belong to the Uniform Resource Locator (URL) built around it. The numbers worth remembering are 63 octets for a label, 255 for a name on the wire, 253 characters in text, and an ndots of 1 on an ordinary Linux host against 5 in a Kubernetes Pod.

san.def: SAN (subject alternative name): the X.509 certificate extension, object identifier 2.5.29.17 in RFC (Request for Comments) 5280, that lists the identities a certificate is valid for, such as DNS names, IP addresses and email addresses. TLS clients match a server's name against this list, no longer against the subject's common name.
san.context: SAN (subject alternative name) is where a certificate's names actually live. RFC (Request for Comments) 5280 defines it as a list of entries of nine possible types, of which DNS names, IP addresses, email addresses and URIs (Uniform Resource Identifiers) are the usual ones, and requires the certificate authority (CA) to verify every entry. Clients no longer consult the old Common Name: Firefox 48 and Chrome 58 ignore it, Go 1.15 disabled the fallback, and RFC 9525 of November 2023 forbids using it to identify a service. A certificate must therefore list in its SAN every hostname it serves. One certificate can carry many names, a wildcard and specific names side by side, and public CAs accept only DNS names and IP addresses there.
san.depth:
What it is. The SAN (subject alternative name) extension, defined in section 4.2.1.6 of RFC (Request for Comments) 5280, binds identities to the subject of a certificate in addition to, or in place of, the subject's distinguished name. Its object identifier is id-ce 17, which is 2.5.29.17. The value is a sequence of at least one GeneralName, a choice of nine types told apart by context tags 0 to 8: otherName, rfc822Name (an email address), dNSName, x400Address, directoryName, ediPartyName, uniformResourceIdentifier, iPAddress and registeredID. Several types and several entries of each may appear together, which is what lets one certificate serve many hostnames. Because the extension is considered definitively bound to the public key, RFC 5280 requires the certificate authority (CA) to verify every part of it; a name in the SAN is a claim the issuer has checked. otherName carries locally defined forms behind an object identifier: RFC 5280 gives a Kerberos principal name as the example, and Microsoft's Active Directory can map a certificate to a user account through a UPN (user principal name) carried there.

How entries are written. A dNSName is an IA5String in the preferred name syntax of the DNS (Domain Name System) specifications; letter case carries no meaning and a single space is forbidden. An iPAddress is an octet string in network byte order, exactly four octets for IPv4 (Internet Protocol version 4) and exactly sixteen for IPv6. An rfc822Name is a bare mailbox, local part, at sign and domain, with no display name and no angle brackets. A URI (Uniform Resource Identifier) must be absolute, with a scheme, and if it has an authority its host must be a fully qualified domain name or an IP address. Empty entries are not allowed. If a certificate's subject is an empty sequence, so that the SAN holds its only identities, the extension must be present and marked critical; otherwise conforming CAs should mark it non-critical. On the semantics of wildcards RFC 5280 is silent: they are left to the applications that use them.

From the common name to the SAN. Early web certificates carried the server's name in the subject's Common Name (CN). RFC 2818, HTTP Over TLS, written by Eric Rescorla in May 2000 and now obsoleted by RFC 9110, already said that a dNSName in the SAN must be used as the identity when present, that the CN was existing practice but deprecated, and that a wildcard matched any single domain component or fragment: *.a.com matched foo.a.com but not bar.foo.a.com, and even f*.com matched foo.com. RFC 6125, by Peter Saint-Andre and Jeff Hodges, tightened the rules in March 2011, and RFC 9525, Service Identity in TLS, by Peter Saint-Andre and Rich Salz in November 2023, finished the job: the Common Name must not be used to identify a service because it is essentially free-form text, the identity can only be expressed in the subjectAltNames, and a wildcard is legal only as the complete left-most label, once, matching exactly one label. Software followed. Firefox 48 and then Chrome 58, announced in March 2017, stopped matching on the subject, so a certificate with its name only in the CN produces NET::ERR_CERT_COMMON_NAME_INVALID, and the enterprise policy that restored the fallback for locally installed roots was removed in Chrome 66. Go 1.15 disabled the fallback by default, leaving GODEBUG x509ignoreCN=0 as a temporary escape. Python's ssl module is the outlier worth knowing: SSLContext.hostname_checks_common_name, added in 3.7, still defaults to true and falls back to the CN when a certificate has no SAN at all.

The rules for public certificates. Version 2.3.1 of the CA/Browser Forum's Baseline Requirements, dated 4 October 2026, requires the SAN in every subscriber certificate, with at least one dNSName or iPAddress, and permits no other type: no email addresses, URIs or otherName entries in a public TLS server certificate. Each dNSName must be a fully qualified domain name or a wildcard domain name, an asterisk and a dot in front of a fully qualified name, that the CA has validated; it must not be an internal name, meaning one that does not end in a top-level domain in IANA's (Internet Assigned Numbers Authority) root zone; since 15 March 2026 it must not end in an IP address reverse zone suffix; and it must not carry the trailing dot of the root. Each iPAddress must be validated and must not fall in a reserved block of the IANA special-purpose registries. The extension is critical only when the subject is empty, and a commonName, if present at all, must be a character-for-character copy of one SAN value. Issuers set their own ceilings on top: Let's Encrypt allows up to 100 identifiers, DNS names or IP addresses, in one certificate, depending on the profile.

Reading and requesting it. openssl x509 -in cert.pem -noout -ext subjectAltName prints just this extension, and it is the first field to inspect when a certificate is rejected for a name it obviously covers, because the name is often present in the CN and absent from the SAN. openssl req -addext "subjectAltName = DNS:foo.co.uk" puts names into a request, where they travel in the extensionRequest attribute; in ACME (Automatic Certificate Management Environment), RFC 8555, the order's DNS identifiers must appear in the common name or in that requested SAN. FortiGate's certificate request form has a Subject Alternative Name field that takes several types at once, written as DNS:example.fortinet.com, IP:192.168.99.101 or email:user2@fortinet.com.

What goes wrong. A wildcard matches exactly one label, so *.example.com covers www.example.com but neither a.b.example.com nor the bare example.com, which has to be listed separately. Every name in a public certificate is published in Certificate Transparency logs, which exist precisely so that domain owners and anyone else can monitor issuance; internal hostnames placed in a public certificate become publicly enumerable, a genuine reconnaissance gift and an argument for private PKI (public key infrastructure) on internal names. A certificate shared by many services widens the blast radius: RFC 9525 warns that cross-protocol attacks such as ALPACA become possible when two different protocol services use the same certificate, and recommends restricted identifiers or separate certificates. The most damaging failure is letting the wrong party choose the SAN. In June 2021 Will Schroeder and Lee Christensen of SpecterOps showed in Certified Pre-Owned that an Active Directory Certificate Services template that lets the enrollee supply the subject, combined with a client authentication purpose, lets an ordinary user request a certificate carrying another user's UPN in its SAN and then authenticate as that user; they catalogued it as ESC1. Whoever controls what goes into the SAN controls who the certificate says its holder is.

Neighbours and numbers. The issuer alternative name extension is the same structure for the issuer; the name constraints extension of a CA certificate limits which SAN values the CAs and certificates below it may contain; the Common Name survives only as a decorative copy. Numbers worth remembering: 2.5.29.17; nine name types, tagged 0 to 8, with dNSName at 2 and iPAddress at 7; four or sixteen octets for an address; Firefox 48, Chrome 58, Chrome 66, Go 1.15 and Python 3.7 in the retirement of the CN; RFC 2818 of 2000 and RFC 9525 of 2023; and up to 100 names in one Let's Encrypt certificate.

isrg.def: The nonprofit that runs Let's Encrypt.
isrg.context: Internet Security Research Group is the nonprofit behind Let's Encrypt, whose ISRG Root X1 certificate anchors the free, automated certificates that a large share of the web now uses.
isrg.depth:
ISRG is the non-profit that runs Let's Encrypt, and its achievement is not the certificate authority but the automation. ACME made issuance a machine-to-machine protocol, which turned a manual annual purchase into something a server does for itself every sixty days.

That single change is most of the reason HTTPS went from a minority of web traffic to nearly all of it. The side effects are the interesting part: certificates stopped signalling legitimacy, because anyone can get one in seconds, and short lifetimes made revocation less critical while making automation mandatory. A site that cannot renew automatically now has an outage on a timer, which is a different operational risk from the one the old model carried.

ios.def: Cisco's long-standing operating system for routers and switches.
ios.context: Internetwork Operating System is Cisco's classic network OS and command-line style. Its conventions (`enable`, `configure terminal`) are so widespread that many other vendors offer an IOS-like CLI mode for familiarity. Not to be confused with Apple's iOS.

fa.def: A protocol that auto-attaches edge switches to an Ethernet fabric.
