fa.context: Fabric Attach lets an edge switch join a fabric and signal VLAN-to-service mappings automatically over LLDP, so the edge does not have to run the fabric's control protocol (IS-IS/SPBM) itself.

sike.def: A post-quantum candidate that was dramatically broken in 2022.
sike.context: Supersingular Isogeny Key Encapsulation was a promising isogeny-based post-quantum scheme, advanced to the fourth round of the NIST (National Institute of Standards and Technology) post-quantum standardization, until Wouter Castryck and Thomas Decru broke it in 2022. The first version of their paper, posted on 30 July 2022, recovered a SIKEp434 key in about an hour on a single core; the revised version, published at EUROCRYPT 2023, does it in about ten minutes. It is a cautionary tale in why the NIST process hedges across different mathematical families.

totp.def: A Time-based One-Time Password (TOTP), defined in RFC 6238, is a short code, usually six digits, computed with HMAC (hash-based message authentication code) from a shared secret and the current time in 30-second steps, so that an authenticator app and a server produce the same value without communicating.
totp.context: Time-based One-Time Password (RFC 6238, Request for Comments) derives a short code from a shared secret and the current time using HMAC (hash-based message authentication code), so authenticator apps and servers compute the same value independently. It is the basis of most app-based two-factor authentication (2FA), the commonest second factor in multi-factor authentication (MFA). It stops a stolen password from completing a login on its own, but a code that a person can read and type can also be relayed by a phishing proxy within its validity window, so NIST (National Institute of Standards and Technology) classes OTP authentication as not phishing-resistant.
totp.depth:
TOTP is the six digits from an authenticator app, and the mechanism is simpler than most people assume. The server and the device share a secret established once at enrolment, both know the current time, and both compute the same HMAC (hash-based message authentication code) over the current time window. Nothing is transmitted between them, which is why it works on a phone in airplane mode. RFC (Request for Comments) 6238, published in May 2011 by David M'Raihi, Salah Machani, Mingliang Pei and Johan Rydell, defines it as the time-based variant of HOTP (HMAC-based one-time password): a value T derived from the clock replaces HOTP's counter. T is the current Unix time minus T0, divided by the time step X and rounded down, with T0 = 0 and X = 30 seconds by default, so T is 1 at Unix time 59 and 2 at Unix time 60. The RFC also requires T to be held in more than 32 bits once time passes the year 2038.

The engine underneath is HOTP, RFC 4226 of December 2005. HOTP computes HMAC-SHA-1 over the shared key and an 8-byte counter, then applies dynamic truncation: the low-order 4 bits of the last byte of the 20-byte result choose an offset, the 31 bits found there are read as an integer, and that integer modulo 10 to the power of the number of digits is the code. RFC 4226 requires at least six digits, a shared secret of at least 128 bits and recommends 160. TOTP keeps all of that, swaps the counter for T, and allows HMAC-SHA-256 or HMAC-SHA-512 in place of HMAC-SHA-1. The SHA-1 (Secure Hash Algorithm 1) inside the default is not the weakness it would be in a signature: HMAC depends on the secrecy of the key, not on collision resistance, and the security of a six-digit code is set by its length and by the server's limits on guessing.

Enrolment is where the secret travels, usually once, as a QR (quick response) code. The de facto format is the otpauth URI (uniform resource identifier) documented by Google Authenticator: otpauth, the type (totp or hotp), a label naming the account, and parameters, of which the secret, written in Base32 without padding, is the only one required; the defaults are SHA1, 6 digits and a period of 30 seconds, and an issuer parameter is strongly recommended so that the app can tell accounts apart. The same page notes that Google Authenticator's implementations ignored the algorithm and period parameters, and the digits parameter on Android and BlackBerry, which is why a server configured for SHA-256, eight digits or a 60-second period can produce codes that a popular app never matches. Whoever sees that QR code, in a screenshot, a ticket or a shoulder-surfed screen, holds the secret and can generate valid codes for as long as it lives.

The time window explains every quirk. Codes usually last thirty seconds, servers typically accept the adjacent window to tolerate clock drift and slow typing, and a device whose clock has drifted badly will produce codes that are correct for a moment nobody else is in. RFC 6238 recommends allowing at most one time step for network delay, notes that a larger window exposes a larger window for attacks, and chose 30 seconds as the balance between security and usability; a user who has just used a code must wait for the next step before a new one appears. For drift it recommends a limit on how many steps a device may be out of step, gives the example that accepting two steps backward tolerates about 89 seconds of drift, and suggests that the server record the drift it detects for each token and apply it next time; a token unused for a long time may drift beyond any threshold and need resynchronizing through some other form of authentication. Clock skew is the first thing to check when a user swears their app is broken, which puts the Network Time Protocol (NTP) on both sides squarely in the authentication path.

One-time has to be enforced by the server, not assumed. RFC 6238 says a verifier must not accept the second attempt of an OTP after the first has been validated, and NIST Special Publication (SP) 800-63B-4 says verifiers shall accept a given OTP only once while it is valid, and may warn the user when a duplicate suggests that someone else got in first. Guessing is the other limit. Six digits are a million possibilities, so RFC 4226 recommends a throttling parameter that caps failed attempts, or a growing delay such as 5 seconds after the first failure and 10 after the second, applied across login sessions so that parallel guessing does not get around it; SP 800-63B-4 requires rate limiting for any OTP shorter than 64 bits and caps consecutive failed attempts on one authenticator at no more than 100 before it is disabled.

The server's copy of the secret is the part that is easy to forget. Unlike a password, which a verifier stores as a salted hash, a TOTP secret must be held in a form the server can use, because it has to compute the same HMAC. RFC 4226 therefore recommends encrypting stored secrets with tamper-resistant hardware and decrypting each one only while a code is being checked, and SP 800-63B-4 requires the keys to be strongly protected by access controls limited to the software components that need them. A leak of that table compromises every enrolled second factor at once, and the remedy is re-enrolment, not a password reset. The same document asks that a user moving to a new phone bind the app there and invalidate the old one, or export the key into a sync fabric meeting its requirements.

NIST's guideline fixes TOTP's place. SP 800-63B-4 classes a single-factor OTP authenticator, hardware token or phone app, as something you have, requires its key and algorithm to provide at least 112 bits of security strength, allows its output to be truncated to six decimal digits, requires a clock-based nonce to change at least every two minutes, and asks for a TOTP lifetime set by the expected clock drift plus an allowance for network delay and for the user typing the code. It also states plainly that OTP authentication is not phishing-resistant, and phishing resistance is required at its highest level, AAL3 (authenticator assurance level 3), so TOTP can serve as a second factor at AAL2 but not as the authenticator for AAL3.

The important limit is what TOTP does not defend against. It stops password reuse and credential stuffing outright, because a stolen password no longer completes a login. It does not stop real-time phishing: a proxy that relays the code as the user types it is inside the window and the code is still valid. Microsoft's threat intelligence team described such a campaign on 12 July 2022: adversary-in-the-middle (AiTM) phishing sites placed a proxy between the user and the real sign-in page, captured the password and the session cookie, and so skipped authentication even for users with multi-factor authentication enabled, targeting more than 10,000 organizations since September 2021; Microsoft stressed that this was not a vulnerability in MFA but a theft of the session it produced. That is the gap hardware keys and passkeys close by verifying the site's origin, and it is why TOTP is a large improvement rather than a final answer.

The neighbours differ by what moves and what proves possession. HOTP counts events instead of time, so a code stays valid until used and the counters can fall out of step; an SMS (Short Message Service) code is generated by the server and delivered over the phone network, which adds interception and SIM swap risks that TOTP does not have; a push approval moves the decision to a prompt; a passkey or FIDO2 (Fast Identity Online 2) key signs a challenge bound to the site's origin. The numbers worth remembering are RFC 6238 of May 2011 and RFC 4226 of December 2005; T0 = 0 and 30-second steps; six digits and a million possibilities; a secret of 128 bits at least and 160 recommended by RFC 4226, 112 bits of strength by NIST; one step of tolerated delay; about 89 seconds for two backward steps; at most 100 consecutive failures; and 2038 for the 32-bit time limit.

hotp.def: HOTP (HMAC-based One-Time Password), defined in RFC (Request for Comments) 4226, computes a short numeric code from a shared secret key and a counter that advances with every code, rather than from the clock, so a token with no clock and a single button can produce codes that a server can check.
hotp.context: HOTP (HMAC-based One-Time Password), RFC (Request for Comments) 4226 of December 2005, derives each code from a shared secret and an incrementing 8-byte counter: HMAC-SHA-1 (hash-based message authentication code with Secure Hash Algorithm 1) over the counter, cut by dynamic truncation to six or more digits. TOTP (Time-based One-Time Password) is HOTP with the counter replaced by time. HOTP itself is used where a counter is easier to keep in step than a clock: hardware tokens with a button, smart cards, YubiKey slots. Its quirks follow from the counter: a code stays valid until it is used, and the token and the server drift apart whenever a code is generated but not submitted.
hotp.depth:
Origin and purpose. HOTP (HMAC-based One-Time Password) is RFC (Request for Comments) 4226, published in December 2005 by David M'Raihi, Mihir Bellare, Frank Hoornaert, David Naccache and Ohad Ranen, all members of OATH (Initiative for Open Authentication), an industry initiative created in 2004 to make strong authentication interoperable. Its introduction blamed the slow spread of two-factor authentication on proprietary tokens and closed specifications, and set out requirements for cheap hardware: the algorithm must be counter-based so that it can run in SIM (subscriber identity module) cards, Java smart cards and USB (Universal Serial Bus) dongles, must work on tokens with no keypad, must show a value of at least six digits, must allow the counter to be resynchronized, and must use a shared secret of at least 128 bits, with 160 recommended. A token with a button and a display, or a key you touch, can do this without a clock, which is exactly why counter-based codes suit devices that time-based codes do not.

The algorithm. HOTP(K,C) = Truncate(HMAC-SHA-1(K,C)): an HMAC (hash-based message authentication code) using SHA-1 (Secure Hash Algorithm 1) over an 8-byte counter C with the token's unique secret K, read high-order byte first. The 20-byte result is cut by dynamic truncation: the low four bits of the last byte give an offset from 0 to 15, the four bytes starting there are taken, the top bit is masked off to avoid signed arithmetic, and the resulting 31-bit number modulo 10 to the power of the digit count is the code. Implementations must produce at least 6 digits and may produce 7 or 8. The RFC's worked example takes the HMAC bytes ending in 5a, so the offset is 10, the bytes there are 50 ef 7f 19, and the code is 872921. Its test vectors use the ASCII (American Standard Code for Information Interchange) secret 12345678901234567890: counter 0 gives 755224, counter 1 gives 287082 and counter 2 gives 359152, which makes any implementation easy to check. TOTP (Time-based One-Time Password), RFC 6238 of May 2011, is HOTP with C replaced by the number of 30-second steps since the Unix epoch, and it may use HMAC-SHA-256 or HMAC-SHA-512.

The counter and its drift. The token advances its counter each time a code is requested; the server advances its copy only after a successful check. A user who presses the button and never submits the code therefore moves the token ahead of the server. RFC 4226 handles this with a look-ahead parameter s: the server computes the next s values and accepts a match among them, then jumps its counter past it. When the token has drifted beyond that window, the RFC suggests resynchronization by asking for a sequence of two or three consecutive codes, since forging a run of valid codes is much harder than guessing one; the token needs re-synchronizing, not replacing. Appendix E.4 describes a better method for clients that can send their counter along with the code: the server accepts if the client's counter is ahead by no more than s and the code is valid for it, so the window can grow without weakening security. The window cannot grow freely otherwise, because it is part of the attack surface.

Security in numbers. The RFC's analysis concludes that the truncated outputs are, for practical purposes, uniform and independent, so the best attack is brute force, and it approximates the attacker's chance of success as s times v divided by 10 to the power of the digit count, where s is the look-ahead window and v the number of verification attempts. With six digits, a window of 10 and 10 attempts, that is 100 in a million. Hence the throttling parameter T: the server should lock the token after T failures, or impose growing delays, 5 seconds after the first failure and 10 after the second in the RFC's example, and the delays must apply across login sessions so that parallel guessing does not get around them. NIST's (National Institute of Standards and Technology) SP (Special Publication) 800-63B, in its fourth revision of 2025, sets the outer limit at no more than 100 consecutive failed attempts per authenticator, requires the key and algorithm to give at least 112 bits of strength, requires the counter, which it calls the nonce, to be unique over the authenticator's lifetime, and requires the verifier to accept a given code only once.

Secrets and provisioning. A HOTP secret cannot be stored as a hash, because the server must compute the same HMAC. RFC 4226 discusses two ways to manage it: generate each secret randomly and store it protected, or derive each token's secret from a master key held in tamper-resistant hardware, for example as a hash of the master key and the token's serial number, so the individual secrets need never be stored. Software authenticators are usually provisioned with an otpauth URI (Uniform Resource Identifier), often as a QR (Quick Response) code; in the key URI format that Google Authenticator documented, the type is hotp and a counter parameter is required to set the initial counter, while digits may be 6 or 8. On a YubiKey, ykman otp hotp programs an HMAC-SHA1 OATH-HOTP credential into slot 1 or 2, and a touch or an NFC (near-field communication) scan types the code; Yubico's documentation notes that this slot keeps a 4-byte counter, good for 4,294,967,295 codes, with a 20-byte secret, that a validation server is needed to check the codes, and that its newer OATH application is preferred for new deployments. RFC 6287 of June 2011, OCRA (OATH Challenge-Response Algorithm), extends the same family to challenge and response.

What it protects against, and what it does not. A HOTP code defeats the replay of a stolen static password and of a code that has already been used, provided the server accepts each value only once. It stays valid until it is used, which is kinder to a slow typist than TOTP's 30-second step and gives an interceptor a longer window; a TOTP code expires within its time step regardless. Neither resists real-time phishing: SP 800-63B states plainly that OTP (one-time password) authentication is not phishing-resistant, because the user can be led to type the code into a page that relays it at once. The gap is closed by origin-bound credentials such as WebAuthn (Web Authentication) passkeys, which the W3C (World Wide Web Consortium) Recommendation scopes to a relying party so that only its origins can use them. HOTP is also not encryption: RFC 4226 notes that it provides no confidentiality and should run over a secure channel.

Numbers worth remembering: RFC 4226 of December 2005; an 8-byte counter in the algorithm, 4 bytes on a YubiKey slot; a 20-byte HMAC-SHA-1 output and a 31-bit dynamic value; six digits at least, seven or eight possible; 128-bit secrets at minimum and 160 recommended; success probability s times v over 10 to the power of the digits; 755224 as the first test value; and at most 100 consecutive failures under SP 800-63B.

qr.def: Quick Response (QR) code: a two-dimensional matrix barcode, created by Denso Wave in 1994, that a phone camera or scanner reads quickly from any angle and that stores up to a few thousand characters, most often a web address, with built-in error correction.
qr.context: Quick Response (QR) code is a matrix barcode standardized as ISO/IEC (International Organization for Standardization and International Electrotechnical Commission) 18004: square modules in 40 sizes from 21 by 21 to 177 by 177, three corner patterns that let a reader find it at any angle, and Reed-Solomon error correction at four levels. It encodes text, and what the text means is a separate convention: a URL (Uniform Resource Locator), a Wi-Fi configuration, a payment request such as Brazil's Pix, or the otpauth URI (Uniform Resource Identifier) that provisions an authenticator app, so that a phone camera can enrol a time-based one-time password (TOTP) secret in one scan. Two consequences follow. An enrolment code is the secret itself, so a screenshot of it is a copy of the second factor. And because nobody can read a QR code by eye, it hides its destination, which phishing by QR code (quishing) exploits.
qr.depth:
A QR (Quick Response) code is a matrix symbology: an array of nominally square modules, dark for a binary one and light for a zero, arranged in an overall square, as the standard of the International Organization for Standardization and the International Electrotechnical Commission, ISO/IEC 18004, describes it. It is not a link, an application or a protocol. The symbol carries a string of characters, and the meaning of that string, whether a web address, a contact card or a payment request, belongs to conventions layered above the standard and to the software that reads it. The name is also narrower than everyday use suggests: Denso Wave states that the word QR Code is its registered trademark in Japan and other countries, that the trademark covers the word and not the pattern, and that no licence is needed to use codes that follow the Japanese or the international standard.

Denso Wave, then a division of Denso Corporation, announced the code in 1994. Its own account starts in Japanese retail and manufacturing: linear barcodes held only about 20 alphanumeric characters, and users of Denso's barcode readers asked for a code that could also carry Kanji and Kana. Masahiro Hara led the development with one other team member, and where other two-dimensional codes of the time aimed at packing in as much information as possible, his aim was a code that could be read fast. The answer was the position detection pattern, the nested squares in the corners. The team surveyed fliers, magazines and cardboard boxes for the ratio of black to white least likely to appear in print by accident and settled on 1:1:3:1:1, which a reader can search for whatever the angle of scanning, through all 360 degrees. After a year and a half the result held about 7,000 numerals and, by the company's measure, was read more than ten times faster than other codes; hence quick response. The car industry adopted it for electronic kanban, food, pharmaceutical and contact lens makers for traceability, and from 2002 Japanese mobile phones with a reading feature brought it to the general public.

Standardization followed quickly. Denso Wave lists approval as an AIM International (Automatic Identification Manufacturers International) standard in October 1997, by the Japanese Electronic Industry Development Association in March 1998, as Japanese Industrial Standards (JIS) X 0510 in January 1999 and as ISO/IEC 18004 in June 2000; Micro QR Code entered JIS X 0510 in November 2004, and GS1 approved QR Code as a standard for mobile phones in December 2011. The international standard has had four editions. The first, of 2000, was based on QR code model 2; the second, of 2006, added Micro QR Code and symbols printed in mirror image or with reversed reflectance, light on dark; the third, of February 2015, is withdrawn; the fourth, ISO/IEC 18004:2024, was published in August 2024 by Joint Technical Committee 1, Subcommittee 31, runs to 111 pages, adopts continuous grading of fixed pattern damage under ISO/IEC 15415 and clarifies the reference decoding algorithm. The catalogue already marks it as due for revision. On patents, Denso Wave says it has waived its rights under Japanese patent 2938338 for standardized QR Codes only, and asks anyone considering a code that deviates from the standards to contact the patent holders first.

The anatomy explains the reading speed. A finder pattern sits at three corners (at a single corner in Micro QR Code) and gives the reader the symbol's position, size and inclination. A separator one module wide, all light, sets each finder pattern apart from the rest; timing patterns, alternating dark and light modules, let the decoder determine module coordinates; and alignment patterns, the main addition of model 2, assist navigation in larger symbols. Everything else is the encoding region, which holds the data and error correction codewords together with two small fields: format information, without which the remainder cannot be decoded, and, in certain symbols, version information. The data area is masked, meaning it is combined by exclusive-or with a mask pattern, to reduce the occurrence of patterns that would interfere with fast processing of the image. Orientation does not matter: the standard lists the symbology as independent of both rotation and reflection. Around the symbol Denso Wave requires a margin at least four modules wide, two for Micro QR Code.

Sizes are called versions. Version 1 is 21 by 21 modules and each version adds four modules per side, up to version 40 at 177 by 177; Micro QR Code runs from M1 at 11 by 11 to M4 at 17 by 17 in steps of two. Data is written in modes, each announced by a mode indicator and a character count: numeric (the digits), alphanumeric (digits, upper-case letters and nine other characters, among them the space, the full stop, the solidus and the colon), byte (ISO/IEC 8859-1 by default) and Kanji, compacted into 13 bits a character. Extended channel interpretations (ECI) declare other character sets, such as Arabic, Cyrillic or Greek, and structured append spreads one message over up to 16 symbols that can be scanned in any order. The ceiling, at version 40 with the lowest error correction, is 7,089 digits, 4,296 alphanumeric characters, 2,953 bytes or 1,817 Kanji. Because the alphanumeric mode has no lower-case letters, a web address written entirely in capitals can encode more efficiently, a trick that works only if the server answers the capitalized path.

Error correction is Reed-Solomon, chosen at one of four levels that allow recovery of about 7 per cent (L), 15 per cent (M), 25 per cent (Q) or 30 per cent (H) of the symbol's codewords; Micro QR Code has no level H, and its smallest version only detects errors. Denso Wave explains the cost: Reed-Solomon needs two codewords for every codeword to be corrected, so protecting 50 of 100 data codewords takes 100 more, 200 in all, of which 50 can be restored, and that 25 per cent is level Q. The method corrects whole bytes and suits burst errors, which is what dirt and damage produce. Redundancy is paid for in size. More data or a higher level means a higher version, and at a fixed printed width a higher version means smaller modules, which is why a long tracking link turns into a dense code that is harder to print and to read. Denso Wave's worked example: 100 digits at level M fit version 3 (29 by 29); printed at 400 dots per inch with four dots per module, the module is 0.254 mm and the symbol 7.366 mm, or 9.398 mm with its margin.

What a reader does after decoding depends on recognizing the text. The ZXing project's catalogue of barcode contents lists the conventions in common use: a URL (Uniform Resource Locator) with its scheme, which a reader should show and ask about before opening; mailto, tel, sms and geo URIs (Uniform Resource Identifiers); contact cards in the compact MECARD format of the Japanese carrier NTT DoCoMo or as vCard; and a Wi-Fi configuration in a similar syntax, carrying the authentication type, the network name and the password, which joins a phone to a network after a prompt. Payments use the same carrier. Brazil's BR Code, the Central Bank's standard for payment QR codes, adopts the merchant-presented mode of the QR Code Specification for Payment Systems of EMV (the card-payment specifications maintained by EMVCo), lets one code carry several payment arrangements, ends with a four-character check field, and underlies Pix: a static Pix code holds all its payment data, a dynamic one holds a URL that the payer's bank application fetches from the receiver's institution at reading time, and Pix Copia e Cola is exactly the same string, pasted as text.

In identity work the QR code is the usual way to provision an authenticator application. The Key URI format published with Google Authenticator encodes otpauth://TYPE/LABEL?PARAMETERS, where the type is totp, for the time-based one-time password (TOTP) of Request for Comments (RFC) 6238 of May 2011, or hotp, for the counter-based HMAC-based one-time password (HOTP) of RFC 4226 of December 2005, HMAC being keyed hashing for message authentication. The label names the account, preferably prefixed by the issuer; the secret parameter is required and is the shared key in Base32 without padding; issuer is strongly recommended; algorithm (SHA1 by default, or SHA256 or SHA512), digits (6 by default, or 8) and period (30 seconds by default) are optional, and the document warns that Google's own applications ignore some of them; hotp also requires an initial counter. The consequence is easy to miss: the image contains the secret in clear, so whoever photographs or screenshots an enrolment code holds the same second factor as the user. Passkeys use a QR code differently, to start the FIDO Alliance's cross-device authentication, in which a phone holding the passkey signs a session in on another device over the hybrid transport of the Client-to-Authenticator Protocol (CTAP). The Wi-Fi Alliance's Wi-Fi Easy Connect likewise provisions devices that have no rich user interface by scanning a QR code on the product.

The opacity that makes a QR code convenient also makes it a phishing tool, since a person cannot read the destination before scanning. The Federal Bureau of Investigation (FBI) warned on 18 January 2022 that criminals tamper with both digital and physical codes, for example with a sticker placed over the original, to send victims to sites that steal login and financial information or to redirect a payment. The United Kingdom's National Cyber Security Centre (NCSC) wrote on 8 February 2024 that fraud with codes in open spaces such as stations and car parks is small compared with other cyber fraud, but that QR codes in phishing emails, a technique sometimes called quishing, are increasing, for three reasons a defender should note: the code disguises a link that people have learned to distrust, not all email security tools scan images, and the victim usually scans with a personal phone that may lack the protections of an employer's computer. The advice of both agencies is modest: read the address the scanner shows before opening it, use the scanner built into the phone, do not install an application from a code, and reach payment and login pages by an address already known. Nothing in the symbol identifies its author; error correction protects against damage, not against substitution.

The family is wider than the familiar square. Model 1, the original, stops at version 14 (73 by 73 modules, 1,167 digits), and the standard recommends it only for closed systems; today the name QR Code normally means model 2 and its successors. Micro QR Code needs a single finder pattern and holds at most 35 digits. The rectangular rMQR Code, for narrow spaces, has its own standard, ISO/IEC 23941:2022. Denso Wave also lists iQR Code (2008), SQRC, which restricts who can read the content, and Frame QR (2014), with a canvas area for letters and images. The figures worth remembering are 40 versions, 21 to 177 modules per side, four correction levels of 7, 15, 25 and 30 per cent, 2,953 bytes at most, and a margin of four modules.

dnssec.def: Extensions to the Domain Name System (DNS) that let a validating resolver verify, through digital signatures and a chain of trust from a configured key, that DNS data comes from the zone's owner and has not been altered, including signed proof that a name or record type does not exist.
dnssec.context: Domain Name System Security Extensions (DNSSEC) sign the records, not the connection. A validating resolver follows a chain of trust from a configured trust anchor, normally the root zone's key-signing key, through a Delegation Signer (DS) record at each delegation, down to the signature on the answer, and returns an error rather than a forged or altered answer. It adds no encryption: queries and answers stay readable to anyone on the path. Request for Comments (RFC) 9364 (February 2023) made it Best Current Practice 237.
dnssec.depth:
What it protects, and what it does not. The Domain Name System Security Extensions (DNSSEC) sign DNS data, not DNS connections. Request for Comments (RFC) 4033 describes origin authentication and integrity for DNS data, including authenticated denial of existence: object security, not channel security. The key that signs belongs to the zone, not to the servers that publish it, so a signed resource record set (RRset) can still be checked after any cache, forwarder or secondary. The same RFC lists the gaps: no confidentiality, by deliberate design choice; no protection against denial of service; nothing for zone transfers or dynamic updates, left to TSIG (transaction signature) and SIG(0); and parent-side glue and NS records stay unsigned.

The records and the bits. RFC 4034 defines four record types. DNSKEY (type 48) publishes a zone's public keys; its flags read 256 for a zone key and 257 when the Secure Entry Point bit is also set. RRSIG (type 46) signs one RRset and carries, among other fields, 4-octet expiration and inception times and a 2-octet key tag naming the signing key. DS (type 43) sits in the parent at the delegation and holds a digest of a key in the child. NSEC (type 47) links each name to the next in canonical order and lists the types present, so a negative answer can be signed like any other. RFC 4033 adds the CD (checking disabled) and AD (authenticated data) header bits, requires EDNS0 (Extension Mechanisms for DNS) because signed answers are larger, and uses the DO (DNSSEC OK) bit, which a resolver sets to ask for the DNSSEC records. The split between a key-signing key (KSK), the 257 key the parent's DS points to, and a zone-signing key (ZSK) is convention: validation does not distinguish them.

Validation and its four verdicts. A validator starts from at least one trust anchor, a configured DNSKEY or the DS hash of one, and builds the chain: the root's keys, the DS the root signs for the next zone, that zone's DNSKEY matching it, and so on down to the RRSIG over the answer. RFC 4033 names four outcomes. Secure means every signature verified. Insecure means the chain reached a delegation with signed proof that no DS exists, so everything below is provably unsigned. Bogus means data that should have validated did not, from missing or expired signatures to an unsupported algorithm. Indeterminate means no trust anchor covers that part of the tree. RFC 4035 sets the signalling: a recursive server sets AD only when it considers every RRset in the answer and authority sections authentic, and when no signature validates it must return RCODE 2, SERVFAIL, giving the data only to a query with CD set. No reason is given, so a SERVFAIL that turns into an answer with dig +cd is the classic sign of a signing fault, not a dead server.

Proving that nothing is there. An NSEC chain lets anyone walk from name to name and list a whole zone, as RFC 4033 itself warns. NSEC3 (RFC 5155, March 2008) chains hashed names instead and adds opt-out for large zones made mostly of unsigned delegations; RFC 6840 (February 2013), the omnibus update now counted as core, made it as much a part of DNSSEC as NSEC. Hashing proved a modest defence: RFC 9276 (August 2022, BCP 236) prefers NSEC when NSEC3's features are not needed, requires an iteration count of 0, because extra iterations feed CPU-exhaustion attacks, and advises no salt, which reduces the parameters to NSEC3PARAM 1 0 0 -.

Three attempts and a best current practice. RFC 9364 counts today's DNSSEC as the third iteration, after RFC 2065 (January 1997) and RFC 2535 (March 1999), neither deployed at scale; the core is RFC 4033, 4034 and 4035 of March 2005, by Arends, Austein, Larson, Massey and Rose, plus RFC 6840. RFC 9364 makes DNSSEC the best current practice for origin authentication of DNS data, with no Standards Track alternative, and records the gap: fewer than 10% of domain names used for websites signed and around a third of queries to recursive resolvers validated.

Algorithms now live in registries. RFC 9904 (November 2025) obsoletes RFC 8624 and moves the requirements into the IANA (Internet Assigned Numbers Authority) DNSSEC registries: RSAMD5 (algorithm 1) and DSA (3) are forbidden, RSASHA256 (8) and ECDSAP256SHA256 (13) must be implemented for signing and validation, ED25519 (15) is recommended, and a new DS must not use the SHA-1 digest (1) while SHA-256 (2) is recommended. RFC 9905, the same month, deprecates RSASHA1 (5) and RSASHA1-NSEC3-SHA1 (7) for new keys, signatures and DS records, and tells validators to treat them as unsupported, so a zone signed only with them silently becomes insecure.

The root key. KSK-2010 (key tag 19036) signed the root from 15 July 2010 to 11 October 2018, when KSK-2017 (key tag 20326) took over in a rollover carried out with the RFC 5011 automated trust anchor update method. The second rollover came on 11 October 2026: KSK-2024 (key tag 38696), in the root zone since 11 January 2025, now signs, and IANA schedules KSK-2017 for revocation on 11 January 2027 and removal on 22 March 2027. IANA's note is plain: validating resolvers must have updated trust anchors to keep validating the root.

What goes wrong. Signatures expire, so a zone whose re-signing stops goes bogus everywhere at once; a key rolled without updating the DS at the parent breaks the chain; and RFC 4033 warns that validation can make whole legitimate zones unreachable. CDS and CDNSKEY records (RFC 7344) let a child publish the DS it wants, and negative trust anchors (RFC 7646) switch validation off for one broken domain. RFC 4033 also predicted denial of service against validation code; KeyTrap, CVE-2023-50387, found by Haya Schulmann's team at the ATHENE research centre and published on 14 February 2024, showed how far: a zone with many DNSKEY and RRSIG records forces a validator to try every combination, so a single packet could exhaust a resolver's CPU and stall BIND 9 for up to 16 hours. The requirement dated from RFC 2535; vendors patched by 13 February 2024, and the researchers argue that full prevention needs revised standards.

In practice. dig +dnssec sets the DO bit so RRSIG records come back, the ad flag shows that the resolver validated, dig +cd asks it not to, and delv repeats the validation locally and explains failures. F5 BIG-IP DNS signs zones itself with a KSK and a ZSK in overlapping generations; its 21.1 manual suggests, after the NIST (National Institute of Standards and Technology) guide, ZSK rollover at 21 days within a 30-day expiration and KSK at 340 within 365, and requires NTP (Network Time Protocol) synchronization. It offers RSA/SHA1, RSA/SHA256 and RSA/SHA512; after RFC 9905 only the last two belong in a new zone.

Why it is worth the trouble. CVE-2008-1447, the Kaminsky bug of 8 July 2008, poisoned recursive caches by exploiting too little randomness in transaction identifiers and source ports. Randomness only raises the attacker's cost; a validated signature makes a forged answer fail however well it guesses. DANE (DNS-Based Authentication of Named Entities, RFC 6698) builds on it. A stub resolver that does not validate still trusts its recursive server, and RFC 4033 tells it to protect that last hop with channel security.

dnskey.def: The DNSKEY record (DNS Public Key, type 48) publishes at a zone's apex the public keys whose private halves sign that zone under DNSSEC (the Domain Name System Security Extensions), so that a resolver can check the zone's RRSIG (resource record signature) records.
dnskey.context: A DNSKEY record (RFC 4034) holds a public key a resolver uses to verify a zone's DNSSEC (Domain Name System Security Extensions) signatures, together with a flags field that marks it as a zone key and, by convention, as a key-signing key, a protocol field fixed at 3 and an algorithm number. A digest of the key is published as a DS (Delegation Signer) record in the parent zone, which is what links the zone into the chain of trust that starts at the root; at the root itself, the key-signing key is the trust anchor configured in every validating resolver.
dnskey.depth:
What it is. DNSKEY is resource record type 48, defined for the Domain Name System (DNS) Security Extensions, DNSSEC, in Request for Comments (RFC) 4034 of March 2005 by Roy Arends, Rob Austein, Matt Larson, Dan Massey and Scott Rose. It is still a Proposed Standard and has been updated by RFC 4470, 6014, 6840, 6944, 9077, 9824 and 9905. A zone publishes its DNSKEY records at its apex, and each one holds a public key whose private half produced some of the zone's RRSIG (resource record signature) records. A validator that meets an RRSIG looks up the DNSKEY RRset of the signer's name, picks candidates by algorithm and key tag, and verifies. A DNSKEY is not a trust anchor by itself and not a certificate: it is believed only because a DS (Delegation Signer) record in the parent, signed in turn by the parent's keys, vouches for it, or because a resolver has it configured as a trust anchor, as every validator has for the root.

The four fields. The RDATA (record data) is a 2-octet Flags field, a 1-octet Protocol field, a 1-octet Algorithm field and the public key, shown in Base64 in zone files and dig output. Bit 7 of the flags is the Zone Key flag, value 256 in decimal: a key without it MUST NOT be used to verify signatures over record sets. Bit 15 is the Secure Entry Point (SEP) flag, adding 1, so a key-signing key normally reads 257. RFC 4034 is explicit that SEP is only a hint to signing and debugging software, and that validators MUST NOT change their behaviour because of it. RFC 5011 (September 2007) later took bit 8 as the REVOKE flag, adding 128, so a revoked key-signing key reads 385. The Protocol field MUST be 3 and is kept only for compatibility. The remaining flag bits are reserved: zero on creation, ignored on receipt.

Algorithms. The algorithm number points into the IANA (Internet Assigned Numbers Authority) DNSSEC algorithm registry, last updated on 10 August 2026. Algorithm 8 (RSA/SHA-256) and algorithm 13 (ECDSA, the Elliptic Curve Digital Signature Algorithm, on curve P-256 with SHA-256) are RECOMMENDED for signing and MUST be implemented; 15 (Ed25519) is RECOMMENDED; 14 (P-384) and 16 (Ed448) are MAY. RFC 9905 (November 2025) ruled that RSASHA1 (5) and RSASHA1-NSEC3-SHA1 (7) MUST NOT be used to create DNSKEY or RRSIG records: validator software must still be able to check them, because some zones still use them, but operators of validating resolvers are told to treat them as unsupported, which leaves such zones insecure rather than broken. RSA/MD5 (1), DSA (3 and 6) and the old GOST algorithm (12) are MUST NOT on every count. Algorithm 0 never appears in a valid DNSKEY; RFC 8078 gives it a meaning only in CDS and CDNSKEY records, as the request to delete a delegation's DS records.

Key tags and the DS link. Each DNSKEY has a key tag, a 16-bit value computed over its RDATA by the algorithm in Appendix B of RFC 4034, which RRSIG and DS records carry so a validator can pick the right key quickly. The RFC warns that two keys can share a tag and that implementations MUST NOT assume a tag is unique. That warning became a vulnerability in February 2024: KeyTrap, CVE (Common Vulnerabilities and Exposures) 2023-50387, rated 7.5 under CVSS (Common Vulnerability Scoring System) 3.1, showed that a zone serving many DNSKEY and RRSIG records with colliding tags makes a validator try every combination. Its finders at the German ATHENE centre, Elias Heftrig, Haya Schulmann, Niklas Vogel and Michael Waidner, reported that a single DNS packet could stall the widely used implementations and public resolvers, and BIND9 (Berkeley Internet Name Domain, version 9) for up to 16 hours; ISC (Internet Systems Consortium) fixed BIND in 9.16.48, 9.18.24 and 9.19.21 by limiting the work. The DS record that ties a DNSKEY to its parent is a digest of the key's owner name concatenated with its RDATA, so any change to the flags, the algorithm or the key produces a different DS.

Key-signing and zone-signing keys. Zones conventionally use two kinds of key. A key-signing key (KSK) signs only the apex DNSKEY RRset and is the one the parent's DS record points to; a zone-signing key (ZSK) signs everything else. RFC 6781, DNSSEC Operational Practices, Version 2 (December 2012), stresses that the split is purely operational: validation does not distinguish the two, and a zone may use a Single-Type Signing Scheme in which one key does both. The split exists to make rotation tractable. Changing the ZSK is a local operation, done by pre-publishing the new key before it signs anything or by signing everything twice for a while, and the new DNSKEY RRset is simply re-signed with the unchanged KSK. Changing the KSK requires a new DS record at the parent, which involves the registrar and the parent's TTL (time to live), or a trust anchor update if the key is one. The split also lets the KSK live offline or in an HSM (hardware security module) while the ZSK stays where daily changes are made. Under the SEP convention a KSK's flags field is odd and a ZSK's even.

What goes wrong. A mismatch between the DS at the parent and the DNSKEY at the child breaks validation entirely, and because DNSSEC fails closed the zone disappears for validating resolvers, which answer SERVFAIL, while appearing perfectly healthy to everyone else; KSK changes at the registrar are where most DNSSEC outages originate. Cached data stretches the damage: when Slack pulled the DS record for slack.com from the .com zone during its failed DNSSEC rollout on 30 September 2021, errors subsided only as resolver caches flushed and the 24-hour TTL on the DS expired. RFC 7344 (September 2014) began automating the parent side with two child-published records, CDS (type 59) and CDNSKEY (type 60), which state the DS the child wants; RFC 8078 (March 2017) lets a parent act on them and adds the delete signal. Signatures also expire: an RRSIG carries an inception and an expiration time, so a signer that stops re-signing makes its zone fail on a date rather than at the moment of the mistake.

The root's keys. The root KSK is the trust anchor every validating resolver carries, and IANA publishes the set in root-anchors.xml: key tag 19036 from 2010, 20326 (KSK-2017, valid from 2 February 2017) and 38696 (KSK-2024, valid from 18 July 2024), all algorithm 8. The first rollover, from 19036 to 20326, took place in October 2018 after a one-year postponement for outreach. KSK-2024, generated after an upgrade of the HSMs, was published in the root zone on 11 January 2025, became trusted under RFC 5011 on 10 February 2025, after the 30-day add hold-down that RFC sets, and began signing on 11 October 2026; KSK-2017 is to be published with the REVOKE bit on 11 January 2027 and removed on 22 March 2027. ICANN (the Internet Corporation for Assigned Names and Numbers) reported more than 95 per cent of reporting resolvers ready and told operators to look for 38696 in bind.keys (BIND), root.key (Unbound, PowerDNS Recursor) or root.keys (Knot Resolver). Asked on 12 November 2026, Google Public DNS returned the root DNSKEY RRset with one key of flags 256 and two of flags 257, all algorithm 8, and a single RRSIG over it from key tag 38696 with an original TTL of 172,800 seconds, valid from 10 November to 1 December 2026.

Numbers worth remembering. Type 48; Protocol always 3; flags 256 for a ZSK, 257 for a KSK, 385 for a revoked KSK; algorithms 8, 13 and 15 for new signing, 5 and 7 no longer; a 16-bit key tag that is not unique; a 30-day add hold-down for new trust anchors; and 38696, the root KSK since 11 October 2026.

nsec.def: The NSEC (Next Secure) record, type 47 in the Domain Name System (DNS), names the next existing name in a signed zone and lists the record types present at its own name, so that DNSSEC (the DNS Security Extensions) can prove with a signature that a name or a type does not exist.
nsec.context: Next Secure (NSEC) records, defined in Request for Comments (RFC) 4034, chain the existing names of a zone signed with the Domain Name System (DNS) Security Extensions (DNSSEC) in canonical order, each one pointing to the next. Because the gap between two neighbours is signed, a resolver can prove authenticated denial of existence, that a queried name or type really is absent, instead of trusting an unsigned not found that anyone on the path could forge.
nsec.depth:
The problem it solves. A signature covers data, and a negative answer has no data to sign: there is no record for nonexistent.example.com to carry an RRSIG (resource record signature). NSEC proves a name does not exist by signing a statement that no names sort between two neighbouring ones. Next Secure is resource record type 47, defined in Request for Comments (RFC) 4034 of March 2005 for the Domain Name System (DNS) Security Extensions (DNSSEC), with the server and resolver rules in RFC 4035. Each NSEC lists two things: the next owner name in the zone's canonical order that holds authoritative data or a delegation, and the set of types present at its own owner name. The complete set forms a chain through every authoritative name in the zone, and the last record points back to the apex, closing the ring.

The record. The RDATA (record data) is the Next Domain Name followed by the Type Bit Maps field. The type space is cut into 256 window blocks; each block present is written as its number, a bitmap length of 1 to 32 octets, and a bitmap in which bit n stands for type n of that window. RFC 4034's example reads alfa.example.com. 86400 IN NSEC host.example.com. (A MX RRSIG NSEC TYPE1234): host.example.com is the next name, and A (address), MX (mail exchange), RRSIG, NSEC and the unknown type 1234 exist at alfa. Three rules follow from the chain. Every authoritative name must be in it, so in a signed zone an RRSIG and an NSEC sit next to a CNAME (canonical name) record, an explicit change to RFC 1034's rule that nothing coexists with a CNAME. A wildcard owner name is treated as the literal label asterisk and chained like any other. The TTL (time to live) of an NSEC follows negative caching: RFC 4034 tied it to the SOA (start of authority) minimum field, and RFC 9077 (July 2021) tightened that to the lesser of the SOA's MINIMUM field and the SOA's own TTL, because the old wording let a denial outlive its intended lifetime.

The proofs. RFC 4035 section 3.1.3 says which records a signed answer must carry in its authority section. For no data (the name exists, the type does not), one NSEC at the name itself suffices: the type is absent from its bitmap. For a name error, NXDOMAIN, two facts need proving: that no exact match exists, by an NSEC whose range covers the name, and that no wildcard could have produced one, by an NSEC covering the wildcard name that would have matched; sometimes one record proves both. A wildcard answer must come with an NSEC showing that no closer name existed, and a wildcard no-data answer combines the two cases. If the records do not fit, the server sets the TC (truncated) bit, and the client retries over TCP (Transmission Control Protocol). An empty non-terminal, a name with no records of its own but with names below it, is answered in the name-error form.

The root, read today. On 12 November 2026 Google Public DNS answered a query for the nonexistent top-level name nonexistent-label-zq. with NXDOMAIN and the AD (authenticated data) bit set, and its authority section held exactly the two proofs. The record nokia. NSEC norton. NS DS RRSIG NSEC shows that nothing exists between nokia and norton, where the queried label would sort, and that nokia itself is a delegation with NS (name server) and DS (delegation signer) records. The record . NSEC aaa. NS SOA RRSIG NSEC DNSKEY TYPE63 covers the asterisk, which sorts before aaa, so no wildcard exists at the root either; TYPE63 is ZONEMD, the zone message digest of RFC 8976 (February 2021), printed by number. Both were signed by the zone-signing key with key tag 8763 and carried an original TTL of 86,400 seconds, the same as the SOA minimum in that answer. The root zone is public, so the chain gives away nothing that is not published anyway.

Aggressive use. Because an NSEC proves a whole range empty, a validating resolver can reuse it. RFC 8198 (July 2017, Kazunori Fujiwara, Akira Kato and Warren Kumari) lets validating resolvers synthesize negative answers for any name inside a cached NSEC or NSEC3 range, and positive answers from cached wildcards, which saves round trips, keeps queries from reaching authoritative servers, and helps against some denial-of-service floods of random names. The same mechanism makes a wrong NSEC expensive. In Slack's failed DNSSEC rollout of 30 September 2021, Amazon Route 53 generated signed NSEC answers for names under a wildcard without the extra information a wildcard proof needs; an AAAA query for app.slack.com, which correctly had no AAAA record, produced an NSEC that some public resolvers, Google Public DNS among them, cached as proof that nothing at all existed at that name, so the A lookups that should have followed failed, and some users could not reach Slack for 24 hours.

Zone walking. The side effect of the chain is zone enumeration: following NSEC records from one name to the next walks the entire zone and reveals every name in it, and RFC 5155 calls this trivial, done simply by querying names that do not exist. For a public zone that may be acceptable, and for many it is a meaningful information leak: RFC 5155 notes that an enumerated zone can feed lists of probable e-mail addresses for spam or drive WHOIS lookups of registrant data that registries may be legally obliged to protect, and that NSEC makes registry bans on copying zone data unenforceable. That is precisely the problem NSEC3 (RFC 5155, March 2008) was created to address, by chaining hashes of names instead of names, with opt-out for delegation-heavy zones. Its successor guidance cuts the other way, though: RFC 9276 (BCP 236, August 2022) says NSEC SHOULD be used in preference to NSEC3 unless NSEC3's features are actually needed, because hashing costs authoritative servers and validators real computation, and that NSEC3 must use zero extra iterations and should use no salt.

Signing on the fly. Online signers solve walking differently. RFC 4470 (April 2006, Samuel Weiler and Johan Ihren) has the authoritative server generate and sign, at query time, an NSEC whose range is as small as possible around the queried name, using epsilon functions to compute names just before and just after it, so the answer proves the denial and reveals no real neighbour. RFC 9824, Compact Denial of Existence (Standards Track, September 2025, Shumon Huque, Christian Elmerot and Olafur Gudmundsson), goes further: for a nonexistent name the server claims that the name exists but has no data of the queried type, a NODATA answer with response code NOERROR, proved by a single NSEC such as a.example.com. NSEC \000.a.example.com. RRSIG NSEC NXNAME, whose bitmap holds only RRSIG, NSEC and the new meta-type NXNAME (type 128). That replaces up to two NSEC or three NSEC3 records with one, shrinks the response, removes walking and the offline dictionary attack on NSEC3 hashes, and lets a resolver that sets the new Compact Answers OK (CO) flag in EDNS (Extension Mechanisms for DNS) get NXDOMAIN restored. The price of both methods is that the authoritative server must hold a signing key and sign as it answers.

Numbers worth remembering. Type 47; 256 window blocks with bitmaps of up to 32 octets; one NSEC for no data, up to two for NXDOMAIN; a TTL no longer than the lesser of the SOA MINIMUM and the SOA TTL; NXNAME 128 for compact denial; and RFC 4034, 4035, 4470, 5155, 8198, 9077, 9276 and 9824 as the chain of documents.

nsec3.def: A hashed version of NSEC that hides a zone's contents.
nsec3.context: Next Secure version 3 (RFC 5155) provides the same authenticated denial as NSEC but over hashed names, so an attacker cannot walk the chain to enumerate every name in the zone.
nsec3.depth:
NSEC3 does what NSEC does, proving non-existence, but over hashed names, so following the chain yields hashes rather than the names themselves. It was introduced to stop trivial zone enumeration.

The protection is real and weaker than it appears. A hash of a name is subject to offline guessing, and tooling exists to recover a large fraction of a typical zone's names from a collected NSEC3 chain, especially where names are short or predictable. Opt-out mode reduces signing overhead for large delegation-heavy zones at the cost of leaving unsigned delegations unproven. The honest summary is that NSEC3 raises the cost of enumeration rather than preventing it.

tld.def: A top-level domain (TLD) is the last label of a fully qualified domain name, the one directly under the unnamed root of the Domain Name System (DNS), such as com, org, br or a newer generic name; each is delegated from the root zone to the registry that runs it.
tld.context: A top-level domain (TLD) is the rightmost part of a domain name, sitting directly under the DNS (Domain Name System) root. IANA (the Internet Assigned Numbers Authority) records each one in the root zone with the name servers of the registry that operates it, and the DS (Delegation Signer) record at this level is where a DNSSEC (DNS Security Extensions) chain of trust from the root continues downward. TLDs come as country codes, mostly the two-letter ISO 3166 codes, and as generic names, from the original com, org and net to more than a thousand added since 2012.
tld.depth:
What it is, and what it is not. In www.example.com the top-level domain (TLD) is com: the rightmost label, directly under the root of the Domain Name System (DNS), whose own name is empty. Each TLD is a zone of its own, delegated from the root zone by NS (name server) records pointing to the servers of the registry that runs it and, when the TLD is signed, a DS (Delegation Signer) record. IANA (the Internet Assigned Numbers Authority) states that it manages the DNS root zone with these delegations, and publishes them in its Root Zone Database. A TLD is not the same thing as the boundary at which people register names: co.uk is a public suffix but not a TLD, which is why Mozilla's Public Suffix List exists, originally so that browsers would not let one site set supercookies for a whole suffix. And not every last label is a TLD on the public internet: some are reserved never to be one.

Where they came from. Request for Comments (RFC) 920, Domain Requirements, written by J. Postel and J. Reynolds of ISI (the Information Sciences Institute) in October 1984, set out the first top-level domains: ARPA for the existing ARPA-Internet hosts, meant to be transitional, then GOV, EDU, COM, MIL and ORG, and the two-letter codes identifying countries. A decade later RFC 1591 (March 1994, Postel) listed the generic TLDs as EDU, COM, NET, ORG, GOV, MIL and INT, added the two-letter country codes from ISO 3166, and judged it extremely unlikely that any other TLDs would be created. The same memo set the rule that has kept the country list out of politics ever since: IANA is not in the business of deciding what is and what is not a country, so it follows the ISO 3166 list.

How many there are. On 12 November 2026 IANA's Root Zone Database held 1,603 entries, of which 1,436 were active: 1,126 generic, 309 country-code and one special-use domain, .arpa, managed by the IAB (Internet Architecture Board). Of the active ones, 151 are internationalized domain names (IDNs), 90 generic and 61 country-code, which travel in the DNS as A-labels beginning with the ACE (ASCII-compatible encoding) prefix xn--, as RFC 5890 (August 2010) defines; the longest TLD is the 24-character xn--vermgensberatung-pwb, and the longest in plain ASCII (American Standard Code for Information Interchange) is travelersinsurance, at 18. IANA's own list, version 2026111200, also counted 1,436, of which 248 have two letters, and the root zone with serial 2026111201 carried name servers for the same 1,436 and DS records for 1,350 of them, so about one in sixteen TLDs is still unsigned. The database also keeps history: 139 retired generic TLDs, four retired country codes (.an, .tp, .yu and .zr), eleven retired IDN test domains, five country codes eligible but never delegated (.bl, .bq, .eh, .mf and .um), and eight special-use names reserved so that they never resolve publicly: .alt, .example, .internal, .invalid, .local, .localhost, .onion and .test.

Generic TLDs. After RFC 1591 the generic list grew in steps, and then in rounds run by ICANN (the Internet Corporation for Assigned Names and Numbers). The 2012 round produced more than 1,200 new generic TLDs (gTLDs), from brands such as .microsoft and .sky to places such as .africa and .berlin and words such as .bank and .eco; the 139 retired generic entries are largely the other side of that story, names given back. The 2026 Round, the first in more than a decade, opened on 30 April 2026 with IDN applications accepted in 27 scripts, closed at 23:59 UTC (Coordinated Universal Time) on 12 August 2026 with 1,663 applications, of which ICANN confirmed on 22 September that 1,616 had paid and would proceed, and the applied-for strings and contention sets were revealed on 7 October 2026.

Country codes. Country-code TLDs (ccTLDs) are run under local policy by whoever IANA records as manager, often a national non-profit, sometimes a government, sometimes a company. Brazil's .br is managed by the Comitê Gestor da Internet no Brasil (CGI.br), with Registro .br as technical contact, an RDAP (Registration Data Access Protocol) service at rdap.registro.br, WHOIS at whois.registro.br, six servers from a.dns.br to f.dns.br, and a DS record 38298 13 2, meaning a key with tag 38298, algorithm 13 (ECDSA, the Elliptic Curve Digital Signature Algorithm, on P-256 with SHA-256) and digest type 2, SHA-256, the digest IANA marks RECOMMENDED for delegations. Not every ccTLD follows the ISO list mechanically: .uk is run by Nominet UK while .gb, also active, is recorded with IANA as a reserved domain; .eu belongs to EURid; and .su is still active under the Russian Institute for Development of Public Networks.

How resolution reaches them. A resolver that starts cold asks a root server about a name, receives a referral listing the TLD's servers, asks one of those, and is referred again to the domain's own servers; dig +trace prints each step. In the root zone the NS records of a TLD carry a TTL (time to live) of 172,800 seconds, two days, and its DS record 86,400 seconds, so a change of TLD servers or keys takes that long to be seen everywhere. For DNSSEC (the DNS Security Extensions) the TLD is the second link: the root zone signs each TLD's DS record with its own zone-signing key, key tag 8763 on 12 November 2026, and the TLD's DNSKEY (DNS public key) record must match that DS for anything below it to validate. com, for example, publishes DS 19718 13 2 in the root.

What goes wrong. Code that assumes TLDs have two or three letters rejects valid addresses at the very long generic names and every IDN; code that ships a hardcoded TLD list goes stale, because names are added in rounds and retired one by one, which is why IANA's list carries a version number and date. Treating the last label as the registrable boundary makes the mistake the Public Suffix List exists to prevent, for example confusing co.uk with a company. Inventing a private suffix for an internal network risks a clash with a real TLD later; the special-use names exist precisely so that .test, .example, .invalid and .localhost never resolve publicly, and .internal is reserved for use within private networks not intended for the global internet. Finally, a TLD can stop existing: .yu, .tp, .zr and .an were retired, and with them every name below.

Numbers worth remembering. 1,436 delegated TLDs on 12 November 2026: 1,126 generic, 309 country-code, 151 of them IDNs, and 1,350 signed; 248 two-letter codes; 1,663 applications in the 2026 Round; two days for a TLD's NS records and one for its DS in the root zone; and RFC 920 (1984) and RFC 1591 (1994) as the documents that began it all.

pac.def: Proxy Auto-Config: a JavaScript file whose FindProxyForURL function the browser calls for each request to decide whether to connect directly or through a proxy, and which proxies to try in order.
pac.context: A Proxy Auto-Config (PAC) file defines a FindProxyForURL function the browser calls for each request, returning which proxy (if any) to use. It allows fine-grained, per-destination proxy rules without hardcoding a single proxy: internal names go direct, everything else goes to the inspection proxy, with a second proxy or a direct connection as fallback. The browser learns the file's address from its settings, from a management policy or from Web Proxy Auto-Discovery (WPAD). The format comes from Netscape Navigator 2.0 and was never standardized, which is why browsers differ at the edges.
pac.depth:
A PAC (Proxy Auto-Config) file is JavaScript that a browser runs to decide, per request, which proxy to use. One function, FindProxyForURL(url, host), receives the address being fetched and its host name and returns a string naming a proxy, a list of fallbacks, or a direct connection. Netscape introduced it in Navigator 2.0, in the same release that introduced JavaScript, and its description of the file format is dated March 1996. Nobody ever standardized it. The caching taxonomy published as Request for Comments (RFC) 3040 in January 2001 could only cite Netscape's page as the best known reference, and already noted that interoperability of PAC files is not high, because different browsers interpret the same script slightly differently. The helper library Netscape wrote survives in Firefox and was reused in Chromium; Microsoft wrote its own. That tiny interface is how organizations have steered web traffic for three decades, and it long outlived the era it was designed for.

The return value has its own small grammar. DIRECT means no proxy; PROXY host:port names an HTTP (Hypertext Transfer Protocol) proxy; SOCKS host:port names a SOCKS server; current browsers also accept HTTP, HTTPS, SOCKS4 and SOCKS5 as keywords. Several entries separated by semicolons form a fallback list tried from left to right, as in PROXY proxy1:8080; PROXY proxy2:8080; DIRECT. What happens when one fails depends on the client. Chrome marks a proxy that failed as bad for five minutes and moves it to the end of the list, and counts only connection-level failures, such as not resolving the proxy's name or not completing the Transmission Control Protocol (TCP) connection. The behaviour Mozilla documents retries an unresponsive proxy after 30 minutes and, when every proxy is down and the list has no DIRECT, asks the user whether to connect directly.

Inside the function, a set of predefined helpers does the matching. isPlainHostName, dnsDomainIs, localHostOrDomainIs, dnsDomainLevels and shExpMatch are pure string comparisons. isInNet, isResolvable and dnsResolve consult the Domain Name System (DNS), and Mozilla's documentation says their use should be carefully considered: when a proxy is then used, the proxy resolves the name again, which doubles the load on the DNS server. weekdayRange, dateRange and timeRange test the clock, and alert writes to a log. myIpAddress returns the client's own address and is ambiguous on a machine with several interfaces; Chrome picks the address it would use to reach the public internet and returns 127.0.0.1 on failure. For Internet Protocol version 6 (IPv6), Microsoft added variants with an Ex suffix, which Chromium supports and Firefox does not.

What the script is allowed to see has shrunk. In the original Netscape implementation the first argument was the full address of the resource. Since Chrome 52 the path, query and fragment of https addresses are stripped before the call, for security reasons, so the script sees only the scheme, host and port; the option to turn that off was removed in Chrome 75, and Firefox strips them too unless a preference says otherwise. A rule that sends one path of an HTTPS site to a different proxy therefore no longer works anywhere that matters.

Delivery has rules of its own. The file is conventionally named proxy.pac and served with the MIME (Multipurpose Internet Mail Extensions) type application/x-ns-proxy-autoconfig, although Chrome does not enforce the type. Chrome requires the download to finish within 30 seconds, with a response code of exactly 200 and a body under 1 MB; it never fetches the file through a proxy, cannot prompt for credentials to get it, keeps it for at most 12 hours or until the network changes, and reads it as ISO-8859-1 unless told otherwise, not as UTF-8. On Windows, the WinHTTP library accepts only http and https addresses for the file, not a local file path. The address itself is either configured or discovered by Web Proxy Auto-Discovery (WPAD), whose only goal, in the words of RFC 3040, is to locate the PAC file: Chrome tries option 252 of the Dynamic Host Configuration Protocol (DHCP) first, on Windows and ChromeOS only, and then a DNS lookup for the bare name wpad.

Its persistence is explained by what it can express. Send internal domains direct, route everything else through inspection, bypass a payment provider that breaks under interception, fall back to a second proxy if the first is unreachable, all evaluated on the client without touching the network. Cloud security services still lean on it because it works everywhere a browser does. Netskope publishes a PAC template for its Cloud Explicit Proxy that lists the domains not to proxy, sends the identity provider direct and returns the tenant's proxy on port 8081 for the rest; a FortiGate can host the file itself and serve it over HTTPS; F5's SSL Orchestrator guide lists browser settings, PAC and WPAD as the three ways clients find an explicit proxy.

The failure modes are worth knowing before deploying one. The function runs on every request, so expensive logic, particularly DNS resolution inside the file, adds latency to all browsing. Ordering matters because the script is ordinary code and the first return statement reached wins, so a broad rule placed early silently swallows the specific rules beneath it. And an error can fail closed or fail open depending on the client. When Chrome cannot fetch the file it falls back silently to DIRECT, or to the manually configured proxy on Windows, unless the PAC was marked mandatory, in which case every request fails with ERR_MANDATORY_PROXY_CONFIGURATION_FAILED; it retries after 8 seconds, 32 seconds and 2 minutes, then every 4 hours. A silent fall to DIRECT in a network that allows direct egress means browsing without inspection and without anybody noticing, which is why testing the file matters as much as writing it. Mozilla's page uses the pactester utility for that, and Chrome's network log shows the list a script returned and which proxies were marked bad.

The security history belongs mostly to discovery. A PAC file is code that decides where every request goes, so whoever can supply it can route a victim's browsing through a proxy of their choice. DNS-based WPAD asks for the unqualified name wpad, which the resolver completes with each suffix in the search list; a long list produces a slow cascade of failed lookups, and a suffix outside the organization's control lets an outsider answer. The growth in top-level domains made that worse, since names once private to a company became registrable, a problem known as the WPAD name collision. Microsoft's bulletin MS16-077 of 14 June 2016, titled Security Update for WPAD, corrected how Windows performs proxy discovery after flaws that allowed elevation of privilege, tracked as CVE-2016-3213, CVE-2016-3236 and CVE-2016-3299 (CVE stands for Common Vulnerabilities and Exposures). The practical consequence is that the file's address deserves the same care as the proxy itself: a name the organization controls, served over HTTPS, as the FortiGate option for delivering the file through its captive portal assumes.

wpad.def: A method for browsers to find a PAC file automatically.
wpad.context: Web Proxy Auto-Discovery lets a browser locate a proxy config (PAC) file via DHCP or DNS without manual setup. Convenient but a classic attack surface, since a rogue WPAD response can redirect traffic through an attacker's proxy.

mime.def: Multipurpose Internet Mail Extensions (MIME): the IETF (Internet Engineering Task Force) standards that let an email carry text beyond ASCII (American Standard Code for Information Interchange), attachments and multipart bodies, and whose type/subtype labels, the media types such as text/html, became the way the web and many other protocols declare what a stream of bytes is.
mime.context: Multipurpose Internet Mail Extensions (MIME), first published in 1992 and restated in RFC (Request for Comments) 2045 to 2049 in 1996, added to mail the headers that say what a body is and how it was encoded for transport: Content-Type with a type, a subtype and parameters, and Content-Transfer-Encoding such as base64. The type/subtype system it created is the registry in which text/html, image/png and application/json now live, and HTTP (Hypertext Transfer Protocol) adopted it to label every response. The label is also a security control, because a recipient that ignores it and guesses can be tricked into running what was meant to be displayed.
mime.depth:
The problem MIME (Multipurpose Internet Mail Extensions) solved was that Internet mail had been specified for text alone. RFC (Request for Comments) 2045 states it plainly: the message format of Internet Standard 11, RFC 822, described headers in US-ASCII (the United States version of the American Standard Code for Information Interchange) in detail and left the body as flat US-ASCII text, and SMTP (Simple Mail Transfer Protocol) carried relatively short lines of 7-bit US-ASCII, so anything else had to be converted into printable characters before it could be sent. Nathaniel Borenstein of Bellcore and his co-author Freed of Innosoft published the first MIME specification as RFC 1341 in June 1992; it was revised, and in November 1996 it was restated as a set of five documents: RFC 2045 for the format of message bodies, RFC 2046 for the media types, RFC 2047 for non-ASCII text in headers, RFC 2048 for registration procedures and RFC 2049 for conformance. MIME was designed to be orthogonal to RFC 822 rather than a revision of it, which is why a MIME message is still an ordinary message to any relay that does not look inside.

RFC 2045 defines five header fields: MIME-Version, Content-Type, Content-Transfer-Encoding, Content-ID and Content-Description. Content-Type carries a top-level type, a subtype and optional parameters, as in text/plain; charset=us-ascii, which is also the default assumed when the field is absent. Type, subtype and parameter names are case-insensitive. Parameters belong to the type: charset applies to text, and boundary is required for every multipart subtype. A sixth field, Content-Disposition, came later in RFC 2183 (August 1997) to say whether a part should be shown inline or offered as an attachment, with a suggested filename; the same document warns that a receiving agent should not use that filename blindly and should ignore any directory path in it, an early statement of a path traversal defence.

RFC 2046 defined seven initial top-level types. Five are discrete (text, image, audio, video and application) and two are composite (multipart and message). A multipart body is divided by a boundary string of 1 to 70 characters chosen not to occur in the content; each part starts after a line of two hyphens followed by the boundary, and the closing delimiter adds two more hyphens. The subtypes say how the parts relate: mixed for independent parts in order, alternative for versions of the same content in order of increasing faithfulness (so a reader shows the last part it can display, which is why HTML (Hypertext Markup Language) mail carries a plain-text part first), digest for a collection of messages, and parallel for parts meant to be presented together. The message type encapsulates whole messages, as message/rfc822 does for a forwarded mail. Unknown subtypes degrade safely by rule: an unrecognized text subtype is treated as plain text, and an unrecognized image subtype as application/octet-stream, opaque bytes.

Content-Transfer-Encoding answers a different question, how the bytes survive a 7-bit path. The values are 7bit, 8bit, binary, quoted-printable and base64. Quoted-printable keeps mostly-ASCII text readable; base64 uses a 65-character subset of US-ASCII (64 symbols plus the equals sign for padding), turning every 24 bits of input into four 6-bit groups, so the encoded size is four characters for every three bytes, and encoded lines must not exceed 76 characters. Headers needed their own mechanism, because a Subject line cannot carry a body encoding: RFC 2047 defined the encoded-word, a token that starts with an equals sign and a question mark, names a charset and the encoding Q or B, carries the encoded text and ends with a question mark and an equals sign, at most 75 characters long. Mail can now carry UTF-8 (the 8-bit Unicode Transformation Format) directly in headers under RFC 6532 (February 2012), but encoded-words remain everywhere in archives and in the headers of ordinary messages.

The type names outgrew mail through their registry. RFC 6838 (Best Current Practice 13, January 2013) sets the procedure: types in the standards tree are either approved by the IESG (Internet Engineering Steering Group) for IETF (Internet Engineering Task Force) specifications or registered by a recognized standards-related organization, the vendor tree takes names beginning with vnd., the personal or vanity tree names beginning with prs., and the unregistered x. tree is strongly discouraged; names beginning with x- are no longer considered part of it, and a widely deployed x- type may be registered under its existing name in another tree. It also defines structured syntax suffixes, which is why application/ld+json or image/svg+xml can be recognized as JSON (JavaScript Object Notation) or XML (Extensible Markup Language) by software that knows nothing else about them. The IANA (Internet Assigned Numbers Authority) registry, last updated on 10 November 2026, now has ten top-level registries (application, audio, font, haptics, image, message, model, multipart, text and video) holding about 2,400 entries, more than 1,800 of them under application, with designated experts reviewing the vendor and personal trees.

HTTP (Hypertext Transfer Protocol) took the media types and the Content-Type field but not the mail plumbing. RFC 9110 (June 2022) says a sender should generate Content-Type unless the type is unknown, and that without it a recipient may assume application/octet-stream or examine the data. It then names the hazard: some user agents examine content and override the declared type, and this MIME sniffing risks drawing incorrect conclusions that can expose users to privilege escalation; it adds that distinct media types often share one data format and differ only in how the data is meant to be processed, which inspection alone cannot tell.

The WHATWG (Web Hypertext Application Technology Working Group) MIME Sniffing Standard, last updated on 19 October 2026, exists because browsers had diverged in how they guessed, with security consequences. Its example is the classic one: an honest server lets users upload files and serves them with a harmless type, believing the browser will treat a contribution as an image, while the browser decides the bytes are HTML and runs the scripts inside, giving the attacker the user's session and a cross-site scripting foothold. The standard's algorithm, which originated in research by Adam Barth, Juan Caballero and Dawn Song, reads a resource header of up to 1,445 bytes and matches byte patterns; when the no-sniff flag is set, the declared type is used as given. That flag comes from the X-Content-Type-Options response header, whose only value is nosniff; under the WHATWG Fetch Standard a response with that header is blocked if it is requested as a script and its type is not a JavaScript MIME type, or as a stylesheet and its type is not text/css. The defensive pattern follows directly: send an accurate Content-Type with an explicit charset, send nosniff, serve files that users upload from a separate origin, and add Content-Disposition: attachment when a file is meant to be downloaded rather than rendered.
