For the network and security engineer, MIME is the layer where declared type and real content can disagree, and every inspection device has to decide which to trust. A mail gateway splits multipart messages into parts, decodes base64 and quoted-printable and scans each part, and an attachment whose declared type, filename and actual bytes tell three different stories is a standard evasion. A web application firewall chooses its parser for a request body from the Content-Type it is given, so a JSON body labelled as a form, or a multipart upload with an unusual boundary, tests whether the device parses what the server will parse. In a packet capture the same evidence sits in plain sight: the Content-Type and Content-Transfer-Encoding headers, the boundary lines, and the base64 blocks broken at 76 characters.

mdn.def: Mozilla's widely used web-technology documentation site.
mdn.context: Mozilla Developer Network is the reference documentation many developers treat as the canonical description of HTML, CSS, JavaScript, and HTTP behaviour in browsers.

hs256.def: HS256 is the JSON Web Algorithms (JWA) identifier for HMAC (hash-based message authentication code) computed with SHA-256 (Secure Hash Algorithm, 256-bit): a symmetric way to protect a JSON Web Token (JWT) in which one shared secret both creates and verifies the 32-byte tag.
hs256.context: HS256 is the identifier, defined in RFC (Request for Comments) 7518, for HMAC (hash-based message authentication code) with SHA-256 (Secure Hash Algorithm, 256-bit). The base64url header and payload of a JSON Web Token (JWT) are run through HMAC under a shared key of at least 256 bits, and the 32-byte result is the signature. Every conforming JWT library must support it, and it is fast and compact, but the same secret both creates and verifies the tag, so every service that can check a token can also forge one. That suits a single party validating its own tokens; tokens checked by many services belong with asymmetric algorithms such as RS256. Its two classic failures are a human-chosen secret, which falls to offline guessing once one token leaks, and a verifier that lets the token's alg header choose the algorithm, so that an RS256 public key ends up used as an HMAC secret.
hs256.depth:
HS256 is a name for a combination, not a new algorithm. Request for Comments (RFC) 7518, JSON Web Algorithms (JWA), written by M. Jones and published in May 2015, defines it in section 3.2 as the value of the alg header parameter that marks a JSON Web Signature (JWS) computed with HMAC (hash-based message authentication code) over SHA-256 (the 256-bit Secure Hash Algorithm). The recipe is exact: run the HMAC of RFC 2104 with SHA-256 as the hash function, the JWS signing input as the text and the shared key as the key, and the HMAC output is the JWS signature. The signing input is the base64url-encoded header, a period and the base64url-encoded payload, so the tag covers both. Strictly it is a MAC (message authentication code), not a digital signature: the specifications call its output a signature for uniformity, but RFC 7518 states precisely what it proves, that whoever generated it was in possession of the key. It is not RS256, where a private key signs and a public key verifies, and it is not PBES2-HS256+A128KW, an entry in the same registry that uses HMAC with SHA-256 inside password-based key wrapping for encryption rather than to protect a token.

The construction underneath is older than the token format by almost twenty years. RFC 2104, by Hugo Krawczyk, Mihir Bellare and Ran Canetti, February 1997, defines HMAC as H(K XOR opad, H(K XOR ipad, text)): the key is padded to the hash function's block length B and combined with two fixed strings, ipad (the byte 0x36 repeated B times) and opad (the byte 0x5C repeated B times), and the hash runs twice, inner then outer. For SHA-256 the block is 64 bytes, as the test cases of RFC 4231 note, and the output is 32 bytes. Keys longer than the block are hashed first, which quietly reduces them to 32 bytes, and RFC 2104 strongly discourages keys shorter than the output because they lower the strength of the function. A JWS protected with HS256 therefore ends in a 32-byte tag, which base64url turns into 43 characters: the worked example in Appendix A.1 of RFC 7515 ends in the segment dBjftJeZ4CVP-mB92K27uhbUJU1p1r_wW1gFWFOEjXk, made with a 64-byte key written as a JSON Web Key (JWK) whose kty is oct.

RFC 7518 sets one hard rule for the key: it must be at least as long as the hash output, 256 bits for HS256, 384 for HS384 and 512 for HS512. The reason it gives is the analysis in section 5.3.4 of NIST (National Institute of Standards and Technology) Special Publication 800-107, cited in the RFC by a misprint as 800-117, under which the effective security strength of HMAC is the lower of the key's strength and twice the size of the internal hash value; a shorter or guessable key makes the key, not SHA-256, the weak link. As a JWK such a secret has kty set to oct (octet sequence), carries its value base64url-encoded in the k member, and should declare alg so the key is bound to one algorithm. Verification is the same computation repeated: the receiver computes the HMAC of the header and payload it received and compares the result with the decoded signature, and RFC 7518 requires that comparison to run in constant time to thwart timing attacks. An ordinary comparison that returns at the first differing byte tells a patient attacker, through response times, how much of a forged tag was right.

The failure that belongs to HS256 alone is the weak secret. RFC 8725, JSON Web Token Best Current Practices (February 2020), describes applications that protect tokens with HS256 but supply a key with insufficient entropy, such as a human-memorable password, and notes that such keys fall to offline brute-force or dictionary attacks once an attacker holds a single token. The arithmetic is unforgiving: every token carries a message and its valid tag side by side, so guesses can be tested on the attacker's own hardware, with no server to rate-limit them, no lockout and no log entry. The same RFC therefore says that human-memorizable passwords must not be used directly as the key to a keyed MAC such as HS256. A key drawn from a cryptographically secure random generator, 32 bytes or more, puts guessing out of reach; a phrase from a configuration template, or the placeholder in a tutorial, does not.

HS256 is the floor of the whole format. RFC 7518 lists it as Required, the only signing or MAC algorithm at that level, with HS384 and HS512 Optional, RS256 Recommended and ES256 Recommended+; RFC 7519, the JSON Web Token (JWT) specification, says that of the signature and MAC algorithms only HS256 and none must be implemented by conforming implementations, and recommends RS256 and ES256 as well. The registry of the Internet Assigned Numbers Authority (IANA), last updated on 29 September 2026, still lists HS256 as Required. Universal support is not the same as being the right choice: it means every library can produce and accept HS256 tokens, which is exactly why a verifier must decide for itself which algorithms it will accept.

OpenID Connect shows where HS256 fits by design. Its Core specification allows ID tokens and request objects to be protected with HS256, HS384 or HS512, and when they are, the key is the octets of the UTF-8 representation of the client_secret the provider issued to that client; a client using the client_secret_jwt method authenticates at the token endpoint with a JWT protected the same way. Section 16.19 then turns the RFC's key rule into a secret length: for HS256 the client_secret must contain at least 32 octets, and almost certainly should contain more, because such secrets tend to use a restricted alphabet. Symmetric signatures must not be used by public clients, which by definition cannot keep a secret, and the default ID token algorithm remains RS256. The pattern is the general one: HS256 belongs between two parties that already share a secret and can both be trusted to hold it.

The symmetry that makes HS256 fast and compact is also its structural limit. One secret both creates and verifies the tag, so every service that can check a token can also mint one. With one service issuing and validating its own tokens that costs nothing. Once tokens cross a boundary the design changes: five validating services means five copies of a signing key, any one of them, or anyone who compromises any one of them, can forge tokens indistinguishable from real ones, and a token cannot show which copy produced it. Rotation is harder too. An asymmetric issuer adds a new public key to its JSON Web Key Set (JWKS), names it in the kid header of new tokens and lets verifiers fetch it, as OpenID Connect describes; a new HMAC secret has to reach every verifier through a confidential channel before the first token protected with it arrives. With more than one verifier an asymmetric algorithm such as RS256 or ES256 is the correct answer, and the size penalty is real but rarely decisive: 43 characters of signature for HS256 against 342 for RS256 with a 2048-bit key.

HS256 is also the second half of the best-known JWT attack, although the flaw lies in verifiers rather than in HMAC. RFC 8725 records that an RS256 token can be altered to say HS256, and that some libraries would then verify an HMAC using the RSA (Rivest-Shamir-Adleman) public key as the shared secret; since that key is public by design, often in the very key set the verifier downloads, anyone could compute a valid tag. CVE-2015-9235 is the recorded case: in the jsonwebtoken module for Node.js before version 4.2.2, a token meant for the RS or ES family could be replaced by one protected with an HS algorithm, bypassing verification. The defence is the same RFC's first rule: libraries must let the caller specify the set of acceptable algorithms and use no other, must check that alg matches the operation actually performed, and must use each key with exactly one algorithm. The server decides which algorithm is acceptable, never the token; a verifier configured for RS256 rejects an HS256 token outright, and a key object holding an RSA public key is never handed to an HMAC routine.

On the post-quantum horizon HS256 sits on the safe side of the line. NIST Interagency Report (IR) 8547, Transition to Post-Quantum Cryptography Standards (final version, October 2026), plans the retirement of RSA and elliptic curve signatures, but states that NIST's symmetric standards, hash functions included, are significantly less vulnerable to known quantum attacks than public-key cryptography, and that approved symmetric primitives with at least 128 bits of classical security are believed to meet at least the first of its five security categories. What is changing is the paperwork around HMAC. NIST has proposed withdrawing FIPS (Federal Information Processing Standard) 198-1, its HMAC standard, and published Special Publication 800-224, a new specification of HMAC by Meltem Sönmez Turan and Luís Brandão, as an initial public draft on 28 June 2024, with the final version expected when FIPS 198-1 is withdrawn; SP 800-107 Revision 1 (August 2012), the document behind RFC 7518's key-size rule, has carried a note since 20 December 2022 announcing that it too will be withdrawn.

On the wire an HS256 token is easy to recognize. Its header decodes to an alg member of HS256, usually beside typ JWT; its third segment is 43 base64url characters, against 64 for HS384 and 86 for HS512; and any JWK describing the key has kty oct and must never appear in a public key set, since publishing it publishes the power to sign. When verification fails between two systems that share a secret, the first suspect is the key's bytes rather than the algorithm: both sides must feed HMAC exactly the same octets, and OpenID Connect, for one, specifies the UTF-8 octets of the client_secret, not a base64 decoding of it. RFC 4231 (December 2005, M. Nystrom) publishes test vectors for HMAC-SHA-256, and Appendix A.1 of RFC 7515 gives a complete HS256 token with its key, which is enough to prove an implementation right before it meets real traffic.

The neighbours are easy to tell apart once the key model is clear. HS384 and HS512 are the same construction with SHA-384 and SHA-512 and longer minimum keys; RS256 and PS256 are RSA signatures that anyone with the public key can verify; ES256 is ECDSA (Elliptic Curve Digital Signature Algorithm) on the P-256 curve; none means no signature or MAC at all. The numbers worth remembering are RFC 7518 section 3.2; a key of at least 256 bits; a 32-byte tag that encodes to 43 characters; at least 32 octets of client_secret in OpenID Connect; Required in the JOSE (JSON Object Signing and Encryption) registry and the only signing algorithm RFC 7519 makes mandatory; and CVE-2015-9235, fixed in jsonwebtoken 4.2.2, for the substitution of HS256 into an RS256 verifier.

kdf.def: A function that produces cryptographic keys from other secret material: quickly, from a strong secret such as a Diffie-Hellman result or a master key, or deliberately slowly and with a salt, from a weak human password.
kdf.context: A key derivation function (KDF) turns input keying material into the keys a protocol needs, in the right number and length. Two families do two different jobs. Fast KDFs built on HMAC (hash-based message authentication code), such as HKDF (HMAC-based Extract-and-Expand Key Derivation Function, Request for Comments 5869) and the methods of the National Institute of Standards and Technology (NIST) in Special Publications 800-56C and 800-108, start from a secret that already has full entropy, typically a Diffie-Hellman result, and expand it into separate keys for each direction and purpose; Transport Layer Security (TLS) 1.3, IKEv2 (Internet Key Exchange version 2) and SSH (Secure Shell) all reach their session keys this way. Password-based KDFs, PBKDF2 (Password-Based Key Derivation Function 2), scrypt and Argon2, with bcrypt as a close relative, are slow on purpose and take a salt and a tunable cost, because no derivation can add entropy a password lacks: all they can do is make every guess expensive. A fast KDF or a bare hash applied to a password is the mistake that turns a stolen database into a list of cracked credentials.
kdf.depth:
What it is, and what it is not. The National Institute of Standards and Technology (NIST) defines a key derivation function (KDF) as a function that, with the input of a cryptographic key or shared secret and possibly other data, generates a binary string called keying material, which the protocol then cuts into the keys it needs. A KDF encrypts nothing, and nothing is ever decrypted out of it; it is built from hash functions or message authentication codes, but it is more than a bare hash, because it binds its output to a purpose and a length. Two different jobs share the name. One starts from a secret that already has plenty of entropy, such as a Diffie-Hellman result or a master key, and turns it into several independent keys; it should be fast. The other starts from a human password, which has little entropy, and makes each guess at it expensive; it must be slow. The specification of the HMAC-based Extract-and-Expand Key Derivation Function (HKDF) draws the line itself: extraction can concentrate the entropy that is there but cannot amplify it, and a password-based KDF needs a salt and an intentional slowing of the computation, which HKDF does not provide.

Extract, then expand. HKDF (HMAC-based Extract-and-Expand Key Derivation Function), published by Hugo Krawczyk and Pasi Eronen as Request for Comments (RFC) 5869 in May 2010, is the pattern most modern protocols copy. Its extract stage computes HMAC (hash-based message authentication code) keyed with an optional salt over the input keying material and returns a pseudorandom key exactly one hash output long; the stage exists because inputs such as a Diffie-Hellman value are not uniformly distributed, and an attacker may know or even influence part of them. Its expand stage runs HMAC under that pseudorandom key over the previous block, an info string and a one-byte counter, as many times as needed, up to 255 times the hash length, which is 8,160 bytes with SHA-256 (Secure Hash Algorithm, 256-bit). The info string is what keeps keys apart: the same secret expanded under different labels yields keys that reveal nothing about one another, so an encryption key and an integrity key never have to share bytes. When the input is already a uniformly random key, extraction can be skipped and expansion used alone.

NIST's constructions. Special Publication (SP) 800-56C Revision 2 (August 2020; Elaine Barker, Lily Chen and Richard Davis) covers the shared secrets produced by the key-establishment schemes of SP 800-56A and SP 800-56B, in two forms: a one-step derivation that runs a hash function, HMAC or KMAC (Keccak-based message authentication code) over the shared secret and its context, and a two-step procedure of randomness extraction followed by key expansion, which is the HKDF pattern in NIST's vocabulary. SP 800-108 Revision 1 (August 2022, updated 2 February 2024; Lily Chen) covers the next step, deriving more keys from a key that already exists, with HMAC, CMAC (cipher-based message authentication code) or KMAC as the pseudorandom function. In its counter mode each block is the pseudorandom function, keyed with the derivation key, computed over a counter, a label, a zero byte, a context and the output length; the feedback and double-pipeline modes chain blocks instead, and KMAC can produce the whole output in one call. The document advises HMAC or KMAC rather than CMAC, because with CMAC a party who knows the derivation key and can choose enough of the input can force derived blocks to predetermined values. Both texts are moving: NIST announced in January 2026 that it will revise SP 800-56C, and on 4 November 2026 it opened a pre-draft call for comments on SP 800-108, due on 18 December 2026.

Where engineers meet the fast kind. Every secure transport derives its working keys this way, and none of them is slow, because the input is a key-exchange result with full entropy. Transport Layer Security (TLS) 1.3, specified since July 2026 in RFC 9846, runs its whole key schedule on HKDF: HKDF-Extract absorbs the pre-shared key, if there is one, and then the shared secret of the asymmetric key exchange, and HKDF-Expand-Label, whose labels all begin with tls13 and a space, derives separate client and server handshake and application traffic secrets, each bound to a hash of the handshake transcript. Internet Key Exchange version 2 (IKEv2), RFC 7296, computes SKEYSEED as its pseudorandom function keyed with the two nonces over the ephemeral Diffie-Hellman secret, then expands it with prf+ into seven keys taken in order: SK_d, from which the keys of child security associations are derived, SK_ai and SK_ar for integrity, SK_ei and SK_er for encryption, and SK_pi and SK_pr for generating the authentication payload, one of each pair per direction. Secure Shell (SSH), RFC 4253, hashes the shared secret, the exchange hash and the session identifier together with a different single letter, A to F, to produce the initial IV (initialization vector), the encryption key and the integrity key for each direction.

Where engineers meet the slow kind. WPA2-Personal (Wi-Fi Protected Access 2) turns a passphrase into its 256-bit pre-shared key with PBKDF2 (Password-Based Key Derivation Function 2) over SHA-1, using the network name, the SSID (service set identifier), as the salt and 4,096 iterations; the Wireshark Foundation's key generator computes exactly that in the browser. The salt is therefore only as unique as the network name. Cisco's guide to protecting secrets on its network devices (last updated 12 March 2026) lists IOS XE type 8 secrets as PBKDF2 with SHA-256, an 80-bit salt and 20,000 iterations, and type 9 as scrypt with an 80-bit salt and 16,384 iterations; it calls types 8, 9 and 10 secure and type 9 generally the stronger, says type 5 secrets, which use MD5 (Message Digest 5), are converted to type 9 automatically from IOS XE 16.12.x, and says type 7, a reversible Vigenère cipher, should be treated as plain text. On Linux disks, LUKS1 (Linux Unified Key Setup) supports PBKDF2 only, LUKS2 adds memory-hard Argon2, and cryptsetup benchmarks the machine to choose the costs.

Password-based derivation. PBKDF2 is defined in PKCS #5 (Public-Key Cryptography Standards number 5) version 2.1, RFC 8018 (January 2017; Kathleen Moriarty as editor, Burt Kaliski and Andreas Rusch), which obsoletes RFC 2898 and states the arithmetic plainly: an iteration count c adds log2(c) bits of work against trial-based attacks such as brute force and dictionaries. For the count it defers to NIST SP 800-132 (December 2010), which requires the randomly generated part of the salt to be at least 128 bits and the derived key at least 112 bits, asks for an iteration count as large as users will tolerate, recommends a minimum of 1,000 and suggests 10,000,000 for especially critical keys; NIST announced in May 2023 that it plans to revise SP 800-132. The 1,000 of 2010 is no guide today: the OWASP (Open Worldwide Application Security Project) Password Storage Cheat Sheet asks for at least 600,000 iterations of PBKDF2 with HMAC-SHA-256 where compliance with FIPS 140 (Federal Information Processing Standard 140) is required, which is worth about 19.2 bits of work.

Memory-hard functions. Iteration alone makes each guess slower but no larger, and fast hashes let attackers make large numbers of guesses quickly on graphics processing units (GPUs) and custom hardware. scrypt, which Colin Percival presented at BSDCan in May 2009 and published as RFC 7914 (August 2016, with Simon Josefsson), is based on memory-hard functions, which its abstract says offer added protection against attacks using custom hardware: every guess needs a large block of memory, not just arithmetic. Argon2, the winner of the 2015 Password Hashing Competition, is RFC 9106 (September 2021; Alex Biryukov, Daniel Dinu, Dmitry Khovratovich and Simon Josefsson), an Informational document of the Crypto Forum Research Group of the Internet Research Task Force (IRTF). Argon2d uses data-dependent memory access and suits proof-of-work, Argon2i uses data-independent access to resist timing side channels, and Argon2id, the primary variant that every implementation must support, runs as Argon2i for the first half of the first pass and as Argon2d for the rest. Its parameters are memory m, passes t and lanes p; the RFC's first recommended option is t=1, p=4 and 2 GiB with a 128-bit salt, and its second, for machines that cannot spare that, t=3, p=4 and 64 MiB. OWASP's floor is lower: 19 MiB, two passes and one lane. For scrypt it asks for a cost N of 2 to the 17th power, a block size r of 8 and p of 1, and for bcrypt, kept for legacy systems, a work factor of 10 or more, remembering that bcrypt reads at most 72 bytes of password.

What goes wrong. The commonest failure is the wrong family: a fast KDF, or a bare hash such as SHA-256, applied to a password, which OWASP calls unsuitable because it lets an attacker make large numbers of guesses quickly and which RFC 5869 rules out for HKDF in so many words. The second is parameters fixed once and never revisited: a count that was generous when it was chosen becomes cheap as hardware improves, and the Cisco type 8 figures, 20,000 PBKDF2 iterations and an 80-bit salt, sit well below the 600,000 iterations OWASP asks of new systems and the 128-bit random salt of SP 800-132. The third is one derived key reused for two purposes, which the label, info and context inputs of every modern KDF exist to prevent. The fourth is believing a KDF adds strength: a 256-bit key derived from an eight-character password is exactly as guessable as the password, only slower to test, and a key derived from a weak random source inherits the weakness. The fifth is cost without limits: OWASP recalls a denial of service published against Django in 2013, where PBKDF2 implementations that reprocessed a very long password on every iteration made one login expensive enough to be an attack. Migration is possible because a well-designed record stores the algorithm and work factor beside the salt, for example in the PHC (Password Hashing Competition) string format, so each password can be rehashed with stronger settings the next time its owner logs in.

Numbers worth remembering: 255 times the hash length as the limit of one HKDF expansion; the label prefix tls13 in TLS 1.3 and the seven SK keys of IKEv2; 128 bits for the random part of a PBKDF2 salt and 112 bits for the derived key under SP 800-132; 600,000 iterations of PBKDF2-HMAC-SHA-256, and 19 MiB, two passes and one lane for Argon2id, as OWASP's floors; 4,096 iterations with the SSID as salt in WPA2-Personal; and log2(c), the bits of work an iteration count c adds.

der.def: Distinguished Encoding Rules (DER): the canonical subset of the Basic Encoding Rules (BER) for ASN.1 (Abstract Syntax Notation One) data, specified in the International Telecommunication Union's Recommendation X.690, under which every value has exactly one byte encoding. X.509 certificates, revocation lists and keys are signed, hashed and exchanged in it.
der.context: Distinguished Encoding Rules (DER) is a binary tag, length and value format: each element is a tag naming its type, a length and the contents, and constructed types such as SEQUENCE nest further elements inside. What makes it distinguished is that ITU-T (International Telecommunication Union Telecommunication Standardization Sector) Recommendation X.690 removes every choice the Basic Encoding Rules (BER) leave open, so lengths are definite and minimal, sets are sorted and default values are omitted. That determinism is why RFC (Request for Comments) 5280 has certificates and CRLs (certificate revocation lists) signed over their DER bytes, and why certificate fingerprints are hashes of DER. PEM (Privacy-Enhanced Mail) is the same DER in Base64 between BEGIN and END lines, so the two forms convert losslessly with one command.
der.depth:
What it is. Distinguished Encoding Rules (DER) is one of three sets of encoding rules in Recommendation X.690 of the ITU-T (International Telecommunication Union Telecommunication Standardization Sector), published identically as ISO/IEC (International Organization for Standardization and International Electrotechnical Commission) 8825-1; the other two are the Basic Encoding Rules (BER) and the Canonical Encoding Rules (CER). The edition in force is X.690 (02/2021), corrected by an erratum in September 2021, and the earlier standards were X.208 for the notation and X.209 for the encodings. The notation, ASN.1 (Abstract Syntax Notation One), now defined in X.680, describes data structures independently of any programming language; the encoding rules turn values of those structures into bytes. DER is therefore neither a certificate format nor a file type. It serializes any ASN.1 value, and on the internet it carries certificates, CRLs (certificate revocation lists), PKCS #10 (Public-Key Cryptography Standards number 10) certification requests, PKCS #8 private keys, PKCS #7 and CMS (Cryptographic Message Syntax) messages and PKCS #12 files. The Let's Encrypt guide to the subject gives the historical reason it won: ASN.1 dates from 1984 and already existed when certificates (1988) and HTTPS (1994) were invented.

How an element is laid out. Every DER element is what Microsoft's documentation calls a TLV (tag, length, value) triplet: identifier octets that give the type, length octets that count the contents, and the contents themselves. Universal tags cover the building blocks. An INTEGER is tag 02, so the bytes 02 03 01 00 01 are a three-byte INTEGER whose value is 65,537; a SEQUENCE, the constructed type that holds a certificate's fields, starts with 30. Lengths come in two forms. The short form is one byte from 0 to 127; in the long form the top bit of the first byte is set and its remaining seven bits say how many length bytes follow. A certificate whose contents run from 256 to 65,535 bytes therefore opens with 30 82 and two length bytes, which is why its Base64 text so often begins with MII. Integers are two's complement with the top bit as the sign, so a positive value whose first byte would have that bit set needs a leading zero byte: 255 is encoded as 00 FF, because FF alone would mean minus one.

What makes it distinguished. BER leaves the encoder choices and DER removes them. Clause 10 of X.690 requires the definite form of length in the minimum number of octets, forbids the constructed, fragmented form for bit strings, octet strings and character strings, and orders the components of a SET by their tags. Clause 11, shared with CER, adds the rest: a BOOLEAN TRUE is a single octet with all eight bits set, unused bits at the end of a BIT STRING are zero, a component equal to its DEFAULT value is left out, the members of a SET OF are sorted in ascending order of their encodings, and GeneralizedTime and UTCTime values end in Z, always carry the seconds and drop trailing zeros from any fraction. BER also allows the indefinite length, written as the single byte 80 and closed by the two bytes 00 00, which suits a sender that does not know the size in advance. CER is canonical as well but makes the opposite choice: constructed encodings must use the indefinite form and strings longer than 1,000 octets are cut into 1,000-octet fragments, which suits streaming, while DER suits the small signed objects of public key infrastructure.

Why canonical matters. A signature and a hash are computed over bytes, not over meaning. RFC (Request for Comments) 5280, the internet profile of X.509, says that the data to be signed is encoded with DER, that the signatureValue is computed over the DER-encoded tbsCertificate, and that CRLs are handled the same way. If one certificate could be written two ways, issuer and verifier could hash different bytes and the signature would fail, or a lenient parser could be led to accept bytes the issuer never signed. RFC 7468 gives three reasons to encode with DER: a signature is computed over the DER encoding, so supplying anything else is senseless; hashes used for identification are computed over DER; and definite lengths let a parser know its memory needs up front. Identification is everywhere. openssl x509 -fingerprint prints the digest of the DER encoding of the whole certificate, and the x5t#S256 member of a JWK (JSON Web Key, a key written in JavaScript Object Notation) is the SHA-256 (Secure Hash Algorithm, 256-bit) thumbprint of the certificate's DER bytes. PEM (Privacy-Enhanced Mail) text is not canonical, because whitespace and labels can vary, so the security considerations of RFC 7468 say that anyone who needs a canonical form must decode to DER first.

Where it shows up. RFC 7468 recommends .crt for the text form of a certificate, notes that many tools still write the text form to .cer files, and recalls that the application/pkix-cert registration of RFC 2585 says each .cer file holds exactly one certificate in DER. In practice .crt, .cer and .key files may hold either encoding, and file extensions prove nothing: the reliable test is to decode. OpenSSL 3.0 and later read keys, single certificates and CRLs in DER, PEM or PKCS #12 without being told which, and enforce a format only when -inform names it. openssl x509 -in cert.der -outform PEM -out cert.pem converts in one step, losslessly, because PEM adds nothing but armour. openssl asn1parse -inform DER -in file -i walks the TLV tree with indentation, and -strparse with an offset descends into a structure embedded in an octet string, such as an extension value. The OpenSSL manual adds a caution: a command that reads a single DER object may stop once it has decoded it, so trailing data is not necessarily examined, and success does not prove that the file is one valid DER object. Inside JSON, DER travels as Base64: the x5c member of a JWK carries a certificate chain as an array of Base64 (not base64url) DER certificates, the one holding the key first.

What goes wrong. The hazards lie in parsers that are more lenient than DER. On 24 September 2014 Mozilla Foundation Security Advisory (MFSA) 2014-73 disclosed that Network Security Services (NSS), the library behind Firefox and, at the time, Chrome on Windows and OS X, parsed the ASN.1 values inside RSA (Rivest-Shamir-Adleman) signatures too leniently. Antoine Delignat-Lavaud of Inria's Prosecco team, and independently Intel Security's Advanced Threat Research team, showed that this allowed a variant of Daniel Bleichenbacher's signature forgery, so certificates could be forged. Recorded in the Common Vulnerabilities and Exposures (CVE) list as CVE-2014-1568 and rated critical by Mozilla, it was fixed in NSS 3.16.2.1, 3.16.5 and 3.17.1, Firefox 32.0.3 and Chrome 37.0.2062.124. The Let's Encrypt guide gives the matching warning to anyone writing a decoder: never trust a decoded length until it has been checked against the bytes actually available. The everyday failure is milder. An appliance import screen that expects PEM rejects a DER file, or the reverse, and the certificate gets blamed for what is only its wrapping; a rejected file is far more often the wrong encoding than the wrong certificate.

Neighbours. BER is the permissive parent, CER the canonical sibling for streaming, PER (Packed Encoding Rules) the compact relative for links where every byte counts, and XER (XML Encoding Rules) the form in XML (Extensible Markup Language). PEM is not an encoding rule at all, only a text wrapper around DER. One contrast catches developers who move between certificate code and web-token code. In X.509, RFC 3279 carries an ECDSA (Elliptic Curve Digital Signature Algorithm) signature as an ASN.1 SEQUENCE of two INTEGERs, r and s, so its length varies with their values; the JSON Web Algorithms specification, RFC 7518, requires an ES256 (ECDSA using P-256 and SHA-256) signature to be exactly 64 octets, R and S as 32-octet big-endian numbers placed side by side. Code that moves a signature from one world to the other has to convert it explicitly.

Numbers worth remembering: tag 30 for SEQUENCE and 02 for INTEGER; a short-form length of at most 127; 80 as the indefinite-length marker of BER, never valid in DER; FF as the only encoding of TRUE; validity dates as UTCTime through 2049 and GeneralizedTime from 2050, both ending in Z with seconds, as RFC 5280 requires; and MII as the opening of most Base64-encoded certificates.

crl.def: A Certificate Revocation List (CRL) is a signed, time-stamped list, published by a certificate authority (CA) or a CRL issuer it has delegated, of the serial numbers of certificates revoked before their expiry, with the date of each revocation and the date by which the next list will appear.
crl.context: A Certificate Revocation List (CRL), profiled for the internet in Request for Comments (RFC) 5280, is a signed list a certificate authority (CA) publishes of certificates no longer valid before their expiry. A relying party fetches a suitably recent list, usually from the address in the certificate's CRL Distribution Points extension, verifies the issuer's signature and looks for the serial number; the Online Certificate Status Protocol (OCSP) is the lighter per-certificate alternative. Since 2023 the CA/Browser Forum has required CRLs and made OCSP optional for public CAs, and browsers now consume CRLs indirectly, through vendor-compiled lists such as Chrome's CRLSets and Firefox's CRLite.
crl.depth:
A Certificate Revocation List (CRL) is the revocation mechanism that X.509 itself defines, and the original one. Request for Comments (RFC) 5280, the internet profile of X.509 certificates and CRLs (May 2008, by D. Cooper, S. Santesson, S. Farrell, S. Boeyen, R. Housley and W. Polk, a Proposed Standard since updated by six later RFCs), describes it as a time-stamped list identifying revoked certificates, signed by a certificate authority (CA) or by a CRL issuer the CA has authorized, and made freely available in a public repository. A certificate is issued to be used for its whole validity period, but a change of name, the end of the relationship between subject and CA (an employee who leaves, for example) or the compromise or suspected compromise of the private key can invalidate it earlier, and the CA then revokes it. A relying party checks the certificate's signature and validity dates and also obtains a suitably recent CRL and confirms that the serial number is not on it. Because the list is signed, it can travel exactly as certificates do, through untrusted servers and over untrusted channels. The glossary of the United States National Institute of Standards and Technology (NIST) gives the short form: a list of revoked public key certificates created and digitally signed by a certification authority.

What a CRL is not matters as much. It does not list every certificate a CA has issued, only the revoked ones within its scope, and it does not keep expired ones: RFC 5280 lets an entry be removed once it has appeared on one regularly scheduled CRL issued after the certificate's validity period ends, so the list follows the revoked certificates that are still unexpired rather than growing forever. Absence from the list says nothing about whether a certificate was ever issued, and the list is only as current as its last issue. The profile names time granularity as the method's main limitation: CRLs are issued periodically, hourly, daily or weekly, and a revocation reported now will not reliably reach relying parties until every CRL currently in circulation is due to be replaced.

The object is a signed ASN.1 (Abstract Syntax Notation One) structure, CertificateList, made of the part to be signed (tbsCertList), the signature algorithm and the signature value. The signed part carries a version, the signature algorithm, the issuer name, thisUpdate (the issue date), nextUpdate (the date by which the next CRL will be issued, which may come earlier but never later) and the revoked certificates, each identified by serial number with its revocationDate and optional entry extensions; when nothing is revoked the list is absent altogether. Dates are encoded as UTCTime up to 2049 and GeneralizedTime from 2050. A CRL that conforms to the profile must be version 2, must carry nextUpdate even though the ASN.1 marks it optional, and must include two extensions: the authority key identifier, which says which issuer key signed it, and the CRL number, a non-critical, monotonically increasing sequence number of up to 20 octets that tells a relying party which of two lists supersedes the other.

Each entry can say why the certificate was revoked. The reasonCode entry extension takes the values unspecified (0), keyCompromise (1), cACompromise (2), affiliationChanged (3), superseded (4), cessationOfOperation (5), certificateHold (6), removeFromCRL (8), privilegeWithdrawn (9) and aACompromise (10); value 7 is not used. RFC 5280 asks issuers to leave the extension out rather than write unspecified, reserves removeFromCRL for delta CRLs, where it means that a certificate has expired or come off hold, and treats every other code as revoked; certificateHold is the one reversible state. A second entry extension, the invalidity date, records when the key is known or suspected to have been compromised, which can be earlier than the revocation date, the moment the CA processed the revocation.

A relying party finds the list through the certificate's CRL Distribution Points extension. An HTTP (Hypertext Transfer Protocol) address there must point to a single CRL encoded in DER (Distinguished Encoding Rules), which the server should label with the media type application/pkix-crl; an LDAP (Lightweight Directory Access Protocol) address must name the directory entry and the attribute that hold the CRL; and the profile wants at least one address of either kind. Every CRL has a scope, the set of certificates that could appear on it. A full and complete CRL covers everything the CA issued; the critical issuing distribution point extension can narrow a list to end-entity certificates, CA certificates or certain reason codes, which is how a large population is partitioned into smaller lists; an indirect CRL covers certificates issued by another entity. A delta CRL lists only the changes since a referenced base CRL, carries the critical delta CRL indicator with the base list's number, shares one numbering sequence with the complete lists, and is located through the Freshest CRL extension (id-ce 46). Conforming applications must process complete version 1 and version 2 CRLs covering all certificates of one CA, but need not support deltas, indirect CRLs or other scopes, and the validation algorithm of section 6.3, which assumes a local cache refreshed once nextUpdate has passed, ends in one of three answers: revoked, unrevoked or undetermined.

Size is the classic objection, and it is real. Let's Encrypt, which at its founding chose to support only the Online Certificate Status Protocol (OCSP), counted more than 200 million active certificates in September 2022 and calculated that revoking them all at once would produce a CRL of over 8 gigabytes; it split its lists into 128 shards of at most 70 megabytes each, with arithmetic that keeps every certificate in the same shard whenever the lists are reissued. It built them because the Apple and Mozilla root programmes required every CA to publish, before 1 October 2022, CRLs that together cover all its certificates, with their addresses disclosed in the Common CA Database (CCADB). The CA/Browser Forum then reversed the old order: Ballot SC-063, voted in July 2023, made OCSP optional and CRLs mandatory for publicly trusted TLS (Transport Layer Security) certificates, allowed partitioned or sharded CRLs that together equal a full and complete one, and required a new CRL within 24 hours of recording a revocation and at least every seven days, or every four days when the certificates carry no OCSP pointer. Short-lived certificates, up to ten days and up to seven from 15 March 2026, need neither a distribution point nor an OCSP pointer, because expiry does the revoking. Let's Encrypt switched OCSP off on 6 August 2025 and since then publishes revocation exclusively through CRLs.

Browsers rarely fetch CRLs themselves. Let's Encrypt summed up the old position bluntly: CRLs are so inefficient that most browsers do not check them, and OCSP is so unreliable that most browsers do not check it either. The answer it described is the browser-summarized CRL, which the browser vendor downloads centrally, compresses and pushes to every installed copy. Chrome does not generally perform online OCSP or CRL checks; its CRLSets, the primary means by which it blocks certificates in an emergency, are built by crawling the CRLs disclosed to the CCADB and, for intermediates, those discovered through Certificate Transparency (CT), each fetched at most every few hours and verified against its signing certificate, and they carry a subset of the revocations found; chrome://components shows the version in use. Firefox's CRLite, enabled for all desktop users from Firefox 137, encodes every revocation that appears in CT logs for an average of 300 kB a day, against roughly 300 MB for the some 3,000 CRLs that the CAs in Mozilla's root store disclose. In both designs the CRL is still the source of truth; what changed is that the client stopped downloading it during the connection. A live check that fails open protects little against an attacker able to block it, and one that fails closed turns every unreachable distribution point into an outage, which is why the browsers moved the fetching out of the connection path.

Outside browsers, CRLs are checked directly, and that is where engineers meet them: virtual private network (VPN) gateways, mutual TLS and enterprise PKI (public key infrastructure). With OpenSSL, openssl crl -in ca.crl -inform DER -text -noout prints a list, -nextupdate and -crlnumber print single fields and -CAfile verifies its signature; openssl verify with -crl_check checks the end-entity certificate against a CRL and fails when no valid one can be found, -crl_check_all extends that to the whole chain, -use_deltas enables delta CRLs and -extended_crl indirect ones. On Windows, certutil -verify -urlfetch retrieves and verifies the AIA (Authority Information Access) certificates and CDP (CRL distribution point) lists of a certificate, certutil -URL tests the addresses, certutil -URLcache CRL lists or deletes the cached lists, and on a Windows certification authority certutil -CRL publishes new base and delta CRLs. A FortiGate keeps CRLs under config vpn certificate crl and can refresh them from an HTTP URL (uniform resource locator), an LDAP server or an SCEP ("Simple Certificate Enrollment Protocol") server, with update-interval in seconds and 0 meaning update only when the list expires. On F5 BIG-IP a client SSL (Secure Sockets Layer) profile can carry CRL files for client certificate authentication, and Access Policy Manager (APM) offers a CRLDP (CRL distribution point) authentication server that retrieves the list from an LDAP address, a directory path or an HTTP URL.

The failures are mostly operational. Once nextUpdate has passed, the RFC 5280 algorithm needs a current CRL, and OpenSSL's -crl_check, for one, raises an error when it cannot find a valid list, so a CA that misses its publication date makes strictly checking relying parties reject certificates that were never revoked; an internal CA whose distribution point is reachable only inside the network does the same to anyone validating from outside. RFC 9608 (June 2024, by R. Housley, T. Okubo and J. Mandel) handles the opposite case: its noRevAvail extension (id-ce 56) marks a certificate for which the CA publishes no revocation information at all, typically because it lives for less than the time needed to detect, report and distribute a revocation; such a certificate must carry no CRL or OCSP pointers, CA certificates may not use it, and path validation skips the revocation check. Among the neighbours, OCSP answers the same question one certificate at a time, OCSP stapling lets the server deliver that answer, and short certificate lifetimes make revocation matter less, which is the direction the industry has taken. The numbers worth keeping are version 2, CRL numbers of up to 20 octets, reason code 7 unused, 24 hours and seven days under the CA/Browser Forum rules, and 128 shards at Let's Encrypt.

pem.def: A text encoding for certificates, keys and related structures: the binary DER (Distinguished Encoding Rules) bytes are Base64-encoded and placed between a BEGIN line and an END line whose label names the content.
pem.context: PEM (Privacy-Enhanced Mail) is the familiar text format that opens with a line reading -----BEGIN CERTIFICATE-----. Its rules are written down in Request for Comments (RFC) 7468. Despite the name from the mail era, it is now the standard way to store and paste certificates and keys encoded in DER (Distinguished Encoding Rules) as ASCII (American Standard Code for Information Interchange) text: the label on the BEGIN line says whether the block is a certificate, a certificate request, a revocation list or a key, and one file may hold several blocks, as a server certificate followed by its chain does.
pem.depth:
PEM is the format certificates and keys usually arrive in: Base64 wrapped between BEGIN and END lines that name what the block contains. The armour exists because binary DER (Distinguished Encoding Rules) survives copying and pasting badly, and PEM is what made it possible to email a certificate without corrupting it. Request for Comments (RFC) 7468 gives the same reasons: a binary format cannot be interchanged in textual transports such as email or text documents, and text is easy to edit, so a user can build a certificate chain by concatenating blocks with copy and paste. PEM is an encoding and nothing more. It adds no encryption and no integrity, the bytes inside are the same DER that a binary file would hold, and the name says nothing about what the block is, which is the label's job.

The rules were only written down in April 2015, in RFC 7468, Textual Encodings of PKIX, PKCS, and CMS Structures, by Simon Josefsson and Sean Leonard. The document says candidly that it records de facto behaviour: for reasons that boil down to non-coordination or inattention, libraries had implemented encodings similar to, but not identical with, the original. A block begins with a line made of five hyphens, the word BEGIN, one space, a label and five more hyphens, and ends with the matching END line carrying the same label. Between them is base64 as defined in section 4 of RFC 4648. A generator must wrap the base64 at exactly 64 characters per line, except the last, and must not emit other whitespace; a parser may accept other line lengths and must cope with any newline convention. Text before the BEGIN line is allowed, which is why tools can print a readable summary above a certificate, and a file may contain several blocks.

The label on the BEGIN line is the part worth reading carefully. RFC 7468 defines nine: CERTIFICATE, X509 CRL (a certificate revocation list), CERTIFICATE REQUEST (with NEW CERTIFICATE REQUEST noted as widespread), PKCS7 and CMS (Public-Key Cryptography Standards number 7 and its successor, the Cryptographic Message Syntax), PRIVATE KEY (the PKCS #8 container, now called OneAsymmetricKey), ENCRYPTED PRIVATE KEY, ATTRIBUTE CERTIFICATE and PUBLIC KEY (a SubjectPublicKeyInfo structure). All of these are containers that name the algorithm inside. Two older labels remain common and are not in the RFC: RSA PRIVATE KEY, which OpenSSL calls the traditional format, and EC PRIVATE KEY, described in RFC 5915 of June 2010 for elliptic curve keys. CERTIFICATE, PRIVATE KEY, RSA PRIVATE KEY and PUBLIC KEY are different things, and the classic incident is a private key pasted where a certificate belonged, or a chain assembled in the wrong order.

The traditional key formats carry a second relic. An encrypted key written the old way has two header lines after the BEGIN line, Proc-Type: 4,ENCRYPTED and DEK-Info with the cipher name and an initialization vector. They come straight from the mail format, and RFC 7468 does not permit headers at all. OpenSSL's documentation calls the technique non-standard and gives the reason to avoid it: the encryption key is derived from the passphrase with an iteration count of 1, against 2048 for its PKCS #8 routines, so new applications should write ENCRYPTED PRIVATE KEY blocks.

The name is a fossil. Privacy Enhancement for Internet Electronic Mail was a project of the Internet's Privacy Task Force, written up by John Linn in RFC 989 (February 1987), revised in RFC 1040 (January 1988) and RFC 1113 (August 1989), and published in final form as the four documents RFC 1421 to 1424 in February 1993. Its messages were delimited by a line reading BEGIN PRIVACY-ENHANCED MESSAGE between rows of hyphens, and its printable encoding already used lines of exactly 64 characters. The encapsulation idea came from Marshall Rose's proposal in RFC 934. As secure mail the design did not last, but the wrapper outlived it, and RFC 7468 lists OpenPGP's ASCII (American Standard Code for Information Interchange) armor and the OpenSSH key file format as variations of the same idea. OpenSSH now writes new private keys in its own format, and its ssh-keygen tool keeps a -m PEM option for the legacy one.

Underneath is DER, one of the encoding rules for Abstract Syntax Notation One (ASN.1) in ITU-T Recommendation X.690 of the International Telecommunication Union, whose edition in force dates from February 2021. RFC 7468 explains why DER matters: it is the one canonical choice among the Basic Encoding Rules (BER) encodings of a value, and a digital signature is computed over it. The text form is not canonical. The same certificate can be wrapped with different whitespace or labels, so the RFC warns against fingerprinting or comparing the text and says to decode to DER first. A practical consequence of the DER start is visible to the eye: the RFC's certificate examples begin with the letters MII, which is what base64 makes of the bytes 0x30 0x82 that open a DER structure a few hundred to a few thousand bytes long.

File names prove little. RFC 7468 recommends the extension .crt for the text form and admits that many tools write the same text to .cer files, while the registered media type application/pkix-cert says a .cer file holds exactly one certificate in DER. Certbot, the Let's Encrypt client, writes privkey.pem, fullchain.pem (the server certificate first, followed by any intermediates), cert.pem and chain.pem. The reliable test is to decode: openssl x509 -in cert.pem -noout -text prints a certificate, -inform and -outform convert between DER and PEM, and since OpenSSL 3.0 the commands detect the input format by themselves. On Windows, certutil -encode and -decode convert a file to and from Base64. On F5 BIG-IP the import screen offers separate types for a key, a certificate or certificate bundle, a PKCS #12 file and an archive.

Order matters when a file holds a chain: the server certificate comes first, then the intermediates towards the root. The current specification of Transport Layer Security (TLS) 1.3, RFC 9846 of July 2026, puts it as a rule of the protocol: the sender's certificate must come first, each following certificate should directly certify the one before it, and the trust anchor may be left out. The nginx documentation gives the same instruction for the combined file and describes one failure exactly: with the order reversed nginx refuses to start and reports a key values mismatch, because it tried the private key against the first certificate in the bundle. On other servers a chain assembled backwards produces validation failures that can look like expiry problems.

The failure modes are pedestrian and frequent. Windows line endings inside a PEM file break some parsers, a missing trailing newline breaks others, and an invisible character introduced by a word processor breaks everything. RFC 7468 records how uneven the tolerance is: most parsers ignore blanks at the ends of lines, but blanks at the beginning of a line or in the middle of the base64 are far less compatible. When a certificate that is definitely correct is definitely rejected, decoding the file to inspect what it actually contains resolves it faster than re-issuing.

sid.def: An identifier that maps a service to a fabric-wide virtual network.
sid.context: In Shortest Path Bridging, a Service Instance Identifier (I-SID) tags traffic so the fabric knows which virtual network a frame belongs to, decoupling the service from any specific VLAN and letting the edge signal membership without running the core protocol.

rpz.def: A Response Policy Zone (RPZ) is a specially built Domain Name System (DNS) zone whose records are rules, not data, telling a recursive resolver to rewrite, block or pass the answers it would otherwise give, by policy.
rpz.context: A Response Policy Zone (RPZ) lets a recursive resolver override Domain Name System (DNS) answers, returning NXDOMAIN (no such name), an empty answer, a walled-garden address or a custom record, for names, addresses or name servers listed on a policy feed such as a threat-intelligence list. Each rule is an ordinary resource record set whose owner name is the trigger and whose data is the action, so the feed travels between provider and subscribers by ordinary zone transfer, and DNS becomes an enforcement point without any new protocol.
rpz.depth:
What it is. Response Policy Zones (RPZ) are what their authors, Paul Vixie and Vernon Schryver, call DNS Firewalls: a way of expressing Domain Name System (DNS) response policy inside specially constructed zones, which recursive servers load and apply to return modified results. Vixie and Schryver designed RPZ in 2009; Schryver wrote the first patch for BIND (Berkeley Internet Name Domain) in late 2009, patches for BIND 9.4, 9.6 and 9.7 circulated from 2010, and the BIND 9 Administrator Reference Manual described it the same year. It never became a Request for Comments (RFC). The specification lives in Internet-Drafts: draft-vixie-dns-rpz, whose revision 04 dated 16 December 2016 is marked replaced and expired, and draft-vixie-dnsop-dns-rpz-00 of June 2018, intended as Informational and now expired, with no formal standing in the IETF (Internet Engineering Task Force) process. It is free to implement, and besides BIND it runs in Unbound (QNAME and response-address triggers from 1.10.0, the full set from 1.14.0), PowerDNS Recursor and F5 BIG-IP DNS. It is how most DNS filtering is implemented, from malware blocking to content control.

How a rule is written. Each rule is an RRset (resource record set): the owner name is the trigger and the record data is the action. A policy zone has an SOA (start of authority) and NS (name server) records like any zone, so a provider publishes it on a primary and subscribers pull it by AXFR or IXFR (full or incremental zone transfer) after a NOTIFY. The six actions reuse CNAME (canonical name) records in ways ordinary DNS never needs. example.com CNAME . returns NXDOMAIN and is the most used; CNAME *. returns NODATA, an empty answer for every type; CNAME rpz-passthru. exempts a name or a client from the rules below it; CNAME rpz-drop. sends nothing back at all, not even an error; CNAME rpz-tcp-only. answers UDP (User Datagram Protocol) queries with a truncated response that forces a retry over TCP (Transmission Control Protocol), a defence against reflection attacks similar to the slip setting of response rate limiting; and Local Data, any other record, returns that record instead, typically a CNAME or an address record pointing at a walled garden that explains the block. The odd encodings are history: RPZ started with only name triggers and NXDOMAIN, and a CNAME to the root was a legal record nobody otherwise used.

Five triggers. The QNAME trigger matches the name asked, as example.com for the name itself or *.example.com for everything below it. The client IP (Internet Protocol) address trigger, labels ending in rpz-client-ip, matches who is asking. The response IP trigger, rpz-ip, matches addresses that appear in the answer, so a whole hosting range can be blocked whatever names point into it. NSDNAME, rpz-nsdname, matches the names of the authoritative servers for the queried name, and NSIP, rpz-nsip, their addresses, which catches every domain a known-bad name server hosts. Addresses are written as a prefix length followed by the octets in reverse, so 192.0.2.0/24 becomes 24.0.2.0.192 and 2001:db8::3/128 becomes 128.3.zz.db8.2001, with zz standing for the double colon. The triggers arrived in stages: Format 1 had only QNAME, Format 2 added response IP, NSDNAME and NSIP, and Format 3 added rpz-passthru and wildcards in local data.

Precedence and cost. A resolver can subscribe to several zones at once, and when rules in different zones match, the zone listed earlier wins; inside a zone, further rules rank the matches by name, trigger type and prefix length. That is why a local exception zone of PASSTHRU rules goes first in the list. In BIND the response-policy statement names the zones and can override a feed's actions per zone (cname, disabled, drop, given, no-op, nodata, nxdomain, passthru, tcp-only), log hits, cap the TTL (time to live) of rewritten answers with max-policy-ttl, and switch the costly NSIP and NSDNAME triggers on or off. The ISC (Internet Systems Consortium) manual is candid about the cost: each policy zone means one to four extra database lookups per query, and four zones using all four kinds of response trigger need 17 times as many lookups as a server with none.

Signatures and honesty. A rewritten answer cannot carry valid signatures. By default BIND applies RPZ only to queries that do not ask for DNSSEC (DNS Security Extensions) data, DO (DNSSEC OK) set to 0, or to names whose original zone has no DNSSEC records; with break-dnssec yes it rewrites everything, and the specification warns that a client which validates for itself then reacts as if its cache had been poisoned. The draft is plain about what RPZ does: it gives untruthful DNS results to consenting stub resolvers, and a stub that does not consent can opt out by using another recursive server. Extended DNS Errors (RFC 8914, October 2020) make the lie declarable: code 15 Blocked for the operator's own security policy, 16 Censored for a requirement imposed from outside, such as a court order, 17 Filtered for a filter the client asked for, and 18 Prohibited; BIND sets them per zone with the ede option, and PowerDNS Recursor can add an extended error on an RPZ hit.

Protecting the feed. A policy zone is itself sensitive: it lists criminals' infrastructure, it crosses the network in cleartext like any zone transfer, and a forged transfer is a policy injection, so the draft says TSIG (Transaction Signature) SHOULD protect it, and the PowerDNS documentation adds that an RPZ provider must be treated as a trusted entity, because a malicious feed can change any answer. The draft also names a counterintelligence leak: a resolver that rewrites a QNAME match without first finishing recursion sends no query to the listed domain's servers, so an attacker watching their own authoritative servers can infer who uses RPZ and whether they are listed; implementations SHOULD let that optimization be disabled, which in BIND is qname-wait-recurse. On F5 BIG-IP DNS, release 21.1 moved from a single feed with one global response to up to 65,535 RPZ feeds per DNS cache in a configurable precedence order, TSIG with HMAC-SHA-512 (hash-based message authentication code) for their transfers, the full action set including Given and Disabled overrides, per-name address answers instead of one global walled-garden address, and client IP and response IP triggers. F5's Bug ID 2310621 records a gap in 21.1.0 to 21.1.0.3: when the upstream server answers SERVFAIL, the query is never evaluated against RPZ policy.

Strengths and objections. Its strengths and the objections to it are the same mechanism seen from different sides. It is fast, cheap and effective against threats that depend on resolving a name, such as malware reaching its command-and-control domains or a user following a phishing link, and it is also a censorship tool that lies to the client by design; RFC 8914 needed a separate code, Censored, for exactly that use. It fails against anything using hardcoded addresses or its own encrypted resolver: RFC 8484 states that filtering systems relying on unsecured DNS will not function where DNS over HTTPS (Hypertext Transfer Protocol Secure) is used. That is why encrypted DNS on endpoints is in direct tension with network-level filtering, and why that tension remains an ongoing argument rather than a settled question.

Numbers worth remembering. Six actions and five triggers; CNAME . for NXDOMAIN and CNAME *. for NODATA; the rpz-passthru, rpz-drop, rpz-tcp-only, rpz-ip, rpz-nsip, rpz-nsdname and rpz-client-ip labels; the earlier zone wins; EDE (Extended DNS Error) codes 15, 16 and 17; up to 65,535 feeds per DNS cache on BIG-IP 21.1; and no RFC, only expired drafts, behind a mechanism that runs in most large resolvers.

cert.def: CERT, once an acronym for Computer Emergency Response Team and now a registered mark of Carnegie Mellon University, names the CERT Coordination Center (CERT/CC), set up after the Morris worm of November 1988, and loosely the incident response teams modelled on it. The generic term is CSIRT (computer security incident response team).
cert.context: A computer security incident response team (CSIRT), still often called a CERT, handles and coordinates the response to cybersecurity incidents for a defined constituency: one organization, a sector, a product line or a whole country. The first was the CERT Coordination Center at Carnegie Mellon University's Software Engineering Institute, created at DARPA's (Defense Advanced Research Projects Agency) request after the Internet worm of November 1988; national teams such as CERT.br followed. National CERTs publish threat feeds and advisories that downstream defenders consume, receive reports about the networks in their country, and coordinate the disclosure of vulnerabilities between researchers and vendors. Carnegie Mellon owns CERT as a registered mark and asks that it not be used as a generic word.
cert.depth:
The CERT Coordination Center (CERT/CC) was born of the first internet-scale incident. After the Internet worm of November 1988, the Morris worm, the Defense Advanced Research Projects Agency (DARPA) charged the Software Engineering Institute (SEI), a federally funded research and development centre that the Department of Defense had established at Carnegie Mellon University in 1984, with setting up a centre to coordinate communication among experts during security emergencies and to help prevent incidents like the worm. The SEI's magazine Bridge described the new team in March 1990 and quoted William Scherlis of DARPA: the worm was a sad signal of the end of the era of widespread trust in the Internet community. Richard Pethia directed it from 1988 to 2016, while it grew from a small incident-response group into the SEI's CERT Division, a research organization of more than 200 people.

Pethia's testimony to a United States Senate subcommittee on 5 June 1996 set out the mission as it had been defined: run a 24-hour point of contact for security emergencies on the internet, help experts communicate, be a central point for identifying vulnerabilities and working with technology producers to fix them, serve as a model for other incident response teams, raise awareness and conduct research. His numbers show how fast the work grew. In 1989, its first full year, the centre handled 132 reported incidents; by 1995 more than 2,400 a year were reported, and by mid-1996 it had responded to over 7,600 incidents in all and issued 119 advisories, sent directly to more than 100,000 sites. Advisories went out only once a repair or workaround existed, together with instructions for installing it.

The name is now a trademark, and the owner is particular about it. Carnegie Mellon's guidelines say that although CERT was once an acronym, it has been a registered mark owned by the university since 1997; licensees should not define CERT as an acronym and should not use it as a generic term for a category of organizations, for which the right word is computer security incident response team (CSIRT). Over the years the university granted many teams permission to use the mark in their names, which is why so many national teams are called CERT-something; it has since stopped licensing the mark outside the United States, and tells non-US teams to consult their own trademark counsel. In practice the industry uses CERT, CSIRT and, for teams that handle vulnerabilities in a vendor's own products, PSIRT (product security incident response team) loosely and interchangeably; in formal writing, CSIRT is the safe choice.

The defining feature of a CSIRT is its constituency. RFC (Request for Comments) 2350, Best Current Practice 21, written by N. Brownlee and E. Guttman in June 1998, defines a CSIRT as a team that performs, coordinates and supports the response to security incidents that involve sites within a defined constituency, and says each team should publish who belongs to that constituency, what services it offers, its policies and how to report an incident. It provides a template that teams still use: CERT.br's own RFC 2350 description, version 1.6, is dated 12 January 2026. For the incident-handling process itself, NIST's (National Institute of Standards and Technology) SP (Special Publication) 800-61 Revision 3, published in April 2025, replaced the 2012 Revision 2 and now places incident response inside the risk-management activities of the Cybersecurity Framework 2.0.

One team could never serve the whole internet, and DARPA planned for that from the start. According to Pethia, the CERT model presumed many response organizations, each serving its own community, and DARPA worked with NIST to create a forum where they could cooperate: the Forum of Incident Response and Security Teams (FIRST). FIRST dates its idea to 1989 and its founding to 1990, and today it gathers government, commercial, academic and product security teams. It also hosts the special interest groups behind several standards defenders use daily: CVSS (Common Vulnerability Scoring System), TLP (Traffic Light Protocol) for marking how far shared information may travel, and EPSS (Exploit Prediction Scoring System).

National teams are the CSIRTs most engineers meet. In Brazil, CERT.br, formerly NBSO, was created in June 1997 on the initiative of the Brazilian Internet Steering Committee (CGI.br), following a report of August 1996, and is maintained by NIC.br. It describes itself as the national CSIRT of last resort: its constituency is every network using IP (Internet Protocol) addresses or autonomous system numbers allocated to Brazil and every domain under .br, it is the focal point for incident notifications when no other contact is known, it alerts Brazilian networks involved in malicious activity and it helps new teams start. It is a FIRST member and accredited by Trusted Introducer, and it keeps a list of Brazilian CSIRTs, such as CAIS at the national research network RNP, admitting only teams that have operated for six months, are recognized by their constituency, have two listed teams as sponsors and answer periodic tests. In the European Union (EU) the NIS (network and information systems security) Directive of 6 July 2016 created, and NIS2 strengthened, a CSIRTs Network of the teams each member state appoints plus CERT-EU, the team for the EU's own institutions, with ENISA (European Union Agency for Cybersecurity) as its secretariat.

The CERT/CC itself still coordinates vulnerability disclosure, now sponsored by the United States Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency (CISA), through its Vulnerability Notes database and the coordination platform VINCE (Vulnerability Information and Coordination Environment). Its policy is to disclose a reported vulnerability 45 days after the initial report whether or not vendors have patches or workarounds, earlier or later in extenuating circumstances such as active exploitation, and to credit the reporter unless asked not to. For a network or security engineer the practical points follow: know which CSIRT covers your address space and how it will contact you, because notifications about your compromised hosts usually arrive from one; subscribe to the advisories of your national team and of your vendors' product teams; and if your organization runs its own team, publish an RFC 2350 description so that others know how to reach it. The dates worth keeping are November 1988 for the worm and the CERT/CC, 1990 for FIRST, 1997 for both the CERT mark and CERT.br, and 1998 for RFC 2350.

pva.def: F5 hardware that accelerates simple Layer 4 traffic.
pva.context: Packet Velocity ASIC is BIG-IP's hardware fast path. In full or assisted mode it offloads established, simple flows to silicon, freeing the software TMM for connections that need Layer 7 processing.
pva.depth:
Packet Velocity ASIC is F5 hardware that forwards simple flows without involving the general-purpose processor, so a connection that needs no inspection is handled at silicon speed while anything requiring policy goes to software.

That split is the general pattern in network hardware and worth understanding beyond the specific product. Throughput figures on a datasheet usually describe the fast path, and the number that matters for a real deployment is what happens when the features are enabled that force traffic into software. Knowing which of your traffic qualifies for offload, and which does not, is what makes a capacity estimate meaningful rather than optimistic.

icap.def: A protocol for handing HTTP content to an external service for adaptation.
icap.context: Internet Content Adaptation Protocol (RFC 3507) lets a proxy pass request or response bodies to a separate server - for antivirus scanning, DLP (data loss prevention), or content rewriting - and splice the result back into the flow.

eui.def: An IEEE identifier format used to build IPv6 interface IDs.
eui.context: Extended Unique Identifier, in its EUI-64 form, derives a 64-bit interface identifier from a device's MAC address. IPv6 SLAAC historically used it to auto-generate the host part of an address.
eui.depth:
IPv6 uses a modified EUI-64: insert the octets ff and fe between the two halves of a 48-bit MAC, company ID and vendor-supplied part, and invert the universal/local bit, the next-to-lowest bit of the first octet. MAC 00-00-5E-00-53-01 becomes the interface identifier 0200:5eff:fe00:5301, so the link-local address is fe80::200:5eff:fe00:5301. RFC 2464's own example turns 34-56-78-9A-BC-DE into 36-56-78-FF-FE-9A-BC-DE.

The process runs backwards just as easily, which is the problem. A fixed identifier lets observers follow a host from network to network, and the OUI plus the fixed ff fe shrinks the search space of an address scan. RFC 8064 (February 2017) therefore recommends RFC 7217's stable identifiers, which change from one network to the next, and advises against embedding a stable MAC; Linux's addr_gen_mode nevertheless still defaults to EUI-64.

RFC 7136 adds a caution for anyone reading addresses: the identifier is opaque, and ff fe in the middle might come from another method, so a recovered MAC may never have existed. The IPv6 Toolkit shows a MAC whenever bytes 11 and 12 are ff and fe, and the OUI lookup reads its vendor and U/L bit.

dad.def: An IPv6 check that a chosen address is not already in use.
dad.context: Duplicate Address Detection (RFC 4862) has a node send a neighbour solicitation for its own tentative address before using it; if anyone answers, the address is a duplicate and cannot be claimed.
dad.depth:
Duplicate address detection is the check an IPv6 host performs before using an address, sending a neighbour solicitation for its own candidate address and treating any answer as proof someone else has it. It runs on every address including the link-local one.

The failure it produces is distinctive: an interface that comes up and then has no usable address, logged as a duplicate. The usual causes are a genuinely duplicated static assignment, a loop that reflects the host's own solicitation back to it, or a network with a device answering for everything. That second case is worth remembering, because a switching loop presents as an addressing failure rather than as a loop, and the message points at the wrong layer.

ldns.def: The DNS server that queries a GSLB (global server load balancing) system on a client's behalf, and whose address the GSLB takes as the client's location.
ldns.context: A load-balancing term rather than a DNS standard one: RFC 9499 has no entry for it, and the role is usually played by a recursive resolver. A GSLB system such as BIG-IP DNS sees only the LDNS address, so a client behind a distant resolver can get the answer meant for the resolver's location.
ldns.depth:
F5's BIG-IP DNS manuals use the word throughout. In Topology load balancing, the request source statement of each topology record names the origin LDNS of a request, as an IP subnet, a region, an ISP, a state, a country or a continent, and the system places the LDNS address with an IP geolocation database. Longest Match sorting, the default, puts the most specific LDNS subnet first.

The proxy holds only while resolver and client are close. RFC 7871 (May 2016, Informational) observes that most queries reach authoritative servers from intermediate recursive resolvers, carrying the resolver's address, and that centralized resolvers, often far from the clients they serve, draw less than desirable answers from topology-sensitive servers. Its remedy is the EDNS Client Subnet option, code 8: the resolver forwards a truncated client prefix, and the reply's scope prefix length says how much of that prefix the answer covers.

BIG-IP DNS uses it when topology-prefer-edns0-client-subnet is enabled, globally or per wide IP: topology then matches on the ECS address and falls back to the source address when a query carries none. The price is privacy and cache pressure. RFC 7871 recommends the feature be off by default in nameserver software, asks resolvers to truncate IPv4 addresses to 24 bits and IPv6 to 56, and admits that, designed from scratch, it would probably look different.

isp.def: An internet service provider (ISP) is an organization that connects customers to the internet: it sells access to homes and businesses and, at wholesale, transit to other networks, carrying their traffic towards every destination it can reach.
isp.context: An internet service provider (ISP) connects subscribers to the internet and, behind them, buys or exchanges reachability with other networks: transit bought from a larger provider, peering exchanged with equals, often across an internet exchange point (IXP). What a subscriber actually gets ranges from web-only access behind address translation to full connectivity with static public addresses. In geographic DNS (Domain Name System) and topology decisions, the ISP of the resolving network can be one of the attributes used to steer a client towards a nearby data centre.
isp.depth:
What the term covers. Request for Comments (RFC) 4084 (Terminology for Describing Internet Connectivity, Best Current Practice 104, May 2005) was written because providers sold very different products under the single word internet, and it ranks them by capability. Web connectivity reaches only HTTP (Hypertext Transfer Protocol) and HTTPS (HTTP Secure) services, often through a filtering proxy, with private and short-lived addresses. Client connectivity without a public address gives general access through NAT (network address translation), so servers and most peer-to-peer functions do not work. Client-only service with a public address supports most virtual private network (VPN) connections but may prohibit servers by contract or filtering. Firewalled connectivity puts a provider-managed firewall in front of static public addresses at the customer's request. Full Internet connectivity means static public addresses with no filtering proxies, interception proxies, NAT or port restrictions, only bandwidth limits and abuse rules. The RFC asks providers to disclose what they block or divert, especially blocks on outbound mail to external SMTP (Simple Mail Transfer Protocol) servers or on other TCP (Transmission Control Protocol) messaging ports, whether customers must use the provider's DNS (Domain Name System) servers, and whether ICMP (Internet Control Message Protocol), and so ping and traceroute, is filtered.

Transit, peering and the tiers. Behind the subscriber edge an ISP has to reach every other network, and it does so in two ways.
