Transit, in William Norton's definition, is the business relationship in which an ISP, also called a transit provider, sells access to the whole internet; outside the residential market it is usually priced per megabit per second and billed on the 95th percentile, taking a month of 5-minute samples, discarding the top 5 per cent and charging for the highest that remains. Peering is the exchange of traffic between two networks for their own customers only, often without payment. Norton defines a Tier 1 ISP functionally: one that reaches the entire routing table of an internet region only through settlement-free peering, paying no one for any destination; a Tier 2 ISP buys transit to reach at least some destinations. Tier 1 networks are few, between 1 and 15 per region, peer with one another in a full mesh mostly over private interconnects, form the default-free zone, and tend towards restrictive peering policies because every new peer is a lost transit customer. He also warns that the term is overloaded, used loosely for size or quality, and that the test is hard to apply from outside because peering contracts are usually confidential.

How the relationships show up in routing. Border Gateway Protocol (BGP) carries these business relationships as export rules, and RFC 9234 (May 2022) writes them into the protocol as roles. A provider may send any route to its customer; a customer may send its provider only its own and its customers' routes; a peer may send another peer only its own and its customers' routes; route servers at exchanges and their clients follow the same pattern. Breaking those rules, for example announcing routes learned from one transit provider to another, is a route leak, the failure RFC 9234's roles and its Only to Customer attribute were designed to detect. The RFC adds that the roles describe propagation, not necessarily who pays whom.

Exchange points. An internet exchange point (IXP), in the Internet Society's words, is a physical and usually neutral location where networks meet to exchange local traffic through a switch, and associations of ISPs are among the five kinds of organization that build them. Without one, traffic between two providers in the same town can travel thousands of miles through other countries before it arrives. An ISP that connects to an exchange can peer with many networks over one port, either session by session or through the exchange's route servers, and every bit exchanged there is a bit not bought as transit.

Addresses and attribution. Since Internet Protocol (IP) version 4 addresses, IPv4, ran short, many access ISPs number subscribers behind Carrier-Grade NAT (CGN), and RFC 6598 (BCP 153, April 2012) reserved 100.64.0.0/10 as shared address space for the links between CGN devices and customer premises equipment, distinct from the private RFC 1918 ranges. That is RFC 4084's client connectivity without a public address, and it changes how a subscriber is identified: many customers share one public address at the same moment, so an address and a time alone no longer point to one subscriber.

The United States. The Federal Communications Commission (FCC) regulates the access service under the name broadband internet access service, defined in Title 47 of the Code of Federal Regulations (CFR), section 8.1, as a mass-market retail service by wire or radio that can send data to and receive data from all or substantially all internet endpoints, dial-up excluded. Part 8 requires providers to publish their network management practices, performance and commercial terms and, since 2024, to show a standard broadband consumer label at the point of sale, and it defines a reasonable network management practice as one appropriate and tailored to a legitimate network management purpose. The classification underneath has swung back and forth; on 2 January 2025, in Ohio Telecom Association v. FCC, the Sixth Circuit vacated the FCC's 2024 order, holding that broadband internet access is an information service rather than a telecommunications service under Title II, which removed the federal net neutrality rules that order had reimposed.

Brazil. Anatel (Agência Nacional de Telecomunicações) licenses fixed access under the Serviço de Comunicação Multimídia (SCM), a collective-interest fixed telecommunications service that explicitly includes providing internet connection; the authorization costs R$ 400. Brazil's market is unusually fragmented: Anatel's report for the second quarter of 2025 counted 11,951 authorized fixed broadband providers and 10,523 more operating under an exemption, about 22,500 in all, and put 56.4 per cent of fixed broadband in the hands of small providers. Anatel defines a small provider (prestadora de pequeno porte) as a group with less than 5 per cent of the national market in each retail market it serves (Resolução nº 783, 3 September 2025), and according to its 2026 structural network plan small providers are the only fixed broadband option in about a third of the country's municipalities. In July 2025 Anatel suspended the exemption that had let providers with up to 5,000 accesses operate without an authorization, giving them until 25 October 2025 to apply, a move aimed at organized crime's use of local internet businesses in Rio de Janeiro.

The Marco Civil da Internet. Lei nº 12.965 of 23 April 2014, in force 60 days after its publication, sets the rules every Brazilian connection provider works under. Article 9 obliges whoever transmits, switches or routes to treat all data packets equally, without distinction by content, origin and destination, service, terminal or application; discrimination or degradation may arise only from technical requirements indispensable to the service and from the prioritization of emergency services, under presidential regulation after hearing the Comitê Gestor da Internet and Anatel, and connection providers may not block, monitor, filter or analyse packet content. Article 13 makes the administrator of the autonomous system keep connection records, confidential and secured, for one year, a duty that cannot be transferred, with release only on a court order; article 14 forbids connection providers to keep records of which applications a subscriber used, while article 15 makes commercial application providers keep their access records for six months. The connection record, as article 5 defines it, is the start and end date and time, the duration and the IP address used; it does not mention a source port, which is exactly the datum that separates subscribers behind CGN.

Where the term appears in network engineering. Global server load balancing uses the ISP as a location attribute: F5 BIG-IP DNS topology records can match the source of a request by subnet, region, ISP, state, country or continent, using a geolocation database that carries ISP and organization data for IPv4 addresses only. The source it sees is the local DNS resolver that asked, so the ISP attribute describes the subscriber only when the subscriber uses that ISP's resolver, which is one of the questions RFC 4084 says a provider should answer.

bind.def: BIND (Berkeley Internet Name Domain) is the open-source Domain Name System (DNS) server software written at the University of California, Berkeley in the 1980s and maintained since 1994 by Internet Systems Consortium (ISC); its daemon, named, serves zones authoritatively, resolves and caches recursively, or does both.
bind.context: Berkeley Internet Name Domain (BIND) is the Domain Name System (DNS) server of Internet Systems Consortium (ISC), which describes it as the first, oldest and most commonly deployed DNS solution, known to more network engineers than any other. Its named.conf syntax and zone files are where most engineers learn DNS configuration. On F5 BIG-IP DNS a local BIND instance, managed through ZoneRunner, sits at the end of the query-processing line: with the DNS profile's Use BIND Server on BIG-IP setting enabled, a query that no wide IP, DNS Express zone or cache answers falls through to it.
bind.depth:
What it is, and what it is not. BIND is software, not a protocol: the Domain Name System (DNS) is defined by Request for Comments (RFC) 1034 and RFC 1035, both written by Paul Mockapetris and published in November 1987, and BIND is one implementation of them, long treated as the de facto reference. The distribution centres on named, the server daemon, with a set of companions: dig for queries, named-checkconf and named-checkzone to validate configuration and zone files before loading them, and rndc to control a running server. One named can act as an authoritative server, primary or secondary, publishing zones from master files in the format RFC 1035 defines; as a recursive resolver that chases referrals from the root and caches the answers; or as both at once, which is exactly the combination its own vendor advises against. Internet Systems Consortium (ISC) lists its uses from the DNS Security Extensions (DNSSEC) signed root zone and many top-level domains (TLDs) to hosting providers with many small zones, enterprises with internal and external zones, and service providers running large resolver farms. BIND 9 is released under the Mozilla Public License (MPL) 2.0.

Where it came from. The DNS was described in RFC 882 and RFC 883 in 1983 and officially began with RFC 920 in 1984; the first working name server, Jeeves, was written by Mockapetris in 1983 and 1984 for Digital Equipment Corporation (DEC) TOPS-20 machines at the University of Southern California Information Sciences Institute and SRI International's Network Information Center. A server for Unix followed soon after: BIND, written by graduate students at Berkeley under a grant from the Defense Advanced Research Projects Agency (DARPA), with Douglas Terry, Mark Painter, David Riggle and Songnian Zhou as the first team. The Computer Systems Research Group (CSRG) maintained it up to version 4.8.3; Kevin Dunlap, on loan from DEC, worked on it from 1985 to 1987; DEC then released 4.9 and 4.9.1 with Paul Vixie as the primary caretaker, and in 1994 Vixie Enterprises sponsored 4.9.2. ISC was founded the same year by Vixie, Carl Malamud and Rick Adams so that an independent body would maintain BIND, and every version from 4.9.3 on is ISC's. Bob Halley and Vixie released BIND 8 in May 1997; BIND 9, released in September 2000, rewrote nearly all of the architecture, and versions 4 and 8 are deprecated.

Versions and support. ISC supports three branches at a time: a stable branch, an extended-support version (ESV) and a development branch. In November 2026 its page lists 9.20.30, released in October 2026, as both current stable and ESV with end of life in the second quarter of 2028, and 9.21.27 as development. BIND 9.18, released on 26 January 2022, reached end of life with the 17 June 2026 release after four and a half years, and ISC has deferred the next stable branch, 9.22, until at least the end of 2026. Operating-system packages are often built with different defaults and some carry version numbers of their own that do not map exactly to ISC's, so the version string named reports is the one to check against advisories.

Recursion and its defaults. RFC 1034 makes recursive service optional and lets a name server restrict who may use it; a server advertises willingness with the recursion available (RA) bit, and a client asks with recursion desired (RD). In BIND recursion is on by default, and the reference manual documents how the permission is inherited: allow-recursion, when not set, takes the value of allow-query-cache, then of allow-query, and only if neither is set falls back to localnets and localhost. By that rule a server opened to the world with allow-query any, and given neither an explicit allow-recursion nor recursion no, answers recursive queries from anyone. An open resolver is a reflector: the Common Vulnerabilities and Exposures (CVE) entry CVE-2020-8616, posted on 19 May 2020, showed that crafted referrals could make BIND issue a very large number of fetches, degrading the server and turning it into a reflector with a high amplification factor. ISC's best-practice guide is blunt: run separate server sets for authoritative and recursive service, and an Internet-facing authoritative server should not recurse for any client at all. Combining the roles also couples their failures, since a fault that breaks the authoritative side breaks recursion too.

Hardening the rest. ISC recommends a server dedicated to DNS; running named as an unprivileged user with -u, after which on Linux it keeps only the capabilities to bind privileged ports and set resource limits, which is its form of privilege separation; chroot de-emphasized on such a server rather than required; DNSSEC signing for public zones; and Response Rate Limiting (RRL) on authoritative servers, which groups clients into buckets of a /24 for IPv4 and a /56 for IPv6 and, with slip 2, answers every other limited query with a small truncated response that prompts a legitimate client to retry over TCP (Transmission Control Protocol). ISC's own example of why this matters: a 36-byte query for isc.org of type ANY drew a 3,576-byte response, nearly a hundredfold amplification, and RRL has been part of BIND since 9.10. Views give split-horizon DNS, and ISC names their two usual failures: internal data leaking through a wrong access control list (ACL) on zone transfers, and external clients, such as a user whose virtual private network (VPN) did not come up, receiving the external view; a separate internal zone such as int.example.com avoids both by design. RFC 1035 fixes the numbers that sit under all of this: port 53 over UDP (User Datagram Protocol) and TCP, classic UDP messages of 512 octets or less, and a 16-bit message ID.

A long security record. ISC's advisory list holds 201 CVE identifiers from 1999 to October 2026, partly the price of being the most deployed target and partly the weight of decades of features. The 1999 entries already include a run of named bugs such as the nxt bug; CVE-2002-1219 allowed remote execution of code. CVE-2008-1447, posted on 8 July 2008, was the Kaminsky cache-poisoning attack, which ISC described as a weakness inherent to the DNS protocol rather than to any implementation: the 16-bit Query ID was too small a barrier, DNSSEC was the only definitive fix, and the patched releases made spoofing harder by randomizing the UDP source port of every query. CVE-2015-5477, posted on 28 July 2015, let one crafted TKEY query trip a REQUIRE assertion and stop every BIND 9 from 9.1.0 onward, authoritative or recursive, and no ACL helped because the faulty code ran before those checks; a proof of concept was public. KeyTrap, CVE-2023-50387, posted on 13 February 2024 alongside the NSEC3 closest-encloser issue CVE-2023-50868, let crafted DNSSEC-signed zones exhaust the central processing unit (CPU) of a validating resolver.

2026, the year the reports multiplied. In May 2026 ISC wrote that large language models had made vulnerabilities far easier to find and that it was triaging reports at more than ten times historic levels. It dropped its informal practice of one security release per quarter: security fixes now come in every monthly maintenance release, reproduction tests are published with each disclosure because they are mostly discoverable anyway, users are told to take the latest maintenance version rather than work out which release introduced a flaw, and CVEs may now be issued for medium-severity issues with Common Vulnerability Scoring System (CVSS) scores of 5 to 7, while early notifications remain reserved for 7 and above. The record shows the effect: 7 CVEs in each of 2024 and 2025 against 36 dated 2026 by 21 October, with 14 fixed in 9.20.29 on 16 September alone and two releases, 9.20.25 and 9.20.28, withdrawn. The operational answer is the one ISC gives: subscribe to bind-announce and patch monthly.

BIND inside BIG-IP DNS. F5's BIG-IP DNS ships a local BIND instance that the ZoneRunner utility manages: it imports and edits zone files, edits named.conf with a syntax check that guards against a file that would stop BIND, and keeps a default view named external; by default that BIND allows zone transfers only from localhost. In the DNS profile, the Use BIND Server on BIG-IP setting (use-local-bind in tmsh) forwards to it the requests that neither the global traffic manager (GTM) wide IPs nor DNS Express handled, and unhandled-query-action, allow by default, decides what happens to a query that matches neither. F5's own manual recommends sending cache misses to a pool of DNS servers rather than to the local BIND, because BIND is slower than several external resolvers, and it notes that stub zones are a BIND-specific feature to use only when needed. On a BIG-IP the local BIND is best treated as an editing surface and a last resort, not as the main answering engine.

ips.def: Intrusion prevention system (IPS): a control that inspects traffic or host activity for signs of attack and, unlike a detection-only sensor, can stop what it detects, normally because it sits inline in the path of the traffic.
ips.context: An intrusion prevention system inspects traffic in the data path and can drop or reset connections matching known attack signatures or anomalies, sitting inline unlike a passive detection-only sensor. NIST (National Institute of Standards and Technology) Special Publication 800-94 defines it as software with all the capabilities of an intrusion detection system (IDS) that can also attempt to stop possible incidents, and observes that the prevention features can usually be switched off, which turns the same product back into an IDS. That one difference changes the risk: a false positive in detection is an alert to dismiss, while a false positive in prevention is legitimate traffic blocked. Today the function is most often a profile inside a firewall, driven by signatures in a rule language that the open-source engines Snort and Suricata made common.
ips.depth:
The standard description is in NIST (National Institute of Standards and Technology) Special Publication (SP) 800-94, written by Karen Scarfone and Peter Mell and published in February 2007. Intrusion detection is the process of monitoring the events occurring in a computer system or network and analysing them for signs of possible incidents; intrusion prevention is the process of performing intrusion detection and attempting to stop detected possible incidents. An intrusion detection system (IDS) is software that automates the first, and an intrusion prevention system (IPS) is software that has all the capabilities of an IDS and can also attempt to stop possible incidents. Because administrators can usually disable the prevention features, the guide writes IDPS (intrusion detection and prevention systems) for both. A later NIST definition adds the aim: to stop the activity, ideally before it reaches its targets.

SP 800-94 sorts what an IPS can do into three groups. It can stop the attack itself, by terminating the network connection or user session, or by blocking access to the target from the offending account or IP address. It can change the security environment, by reconfiguring a firewall, router or switch, or even a host-based firewall on the target. And it can change the attack's content, removing an infected attachment and delivering the cleaned message, or acting as a proxy that normalizes requests so that some attacks are discarded on the way through. The guide also names four types of product: network-based, wireless, network behaviour analysis (which looks for unusual flows such as a distributed denial-of-service attack) and host-based. In everyday use IPS means the first.

Detection comes in three methods, and products combine them. Signature-based detection compares observed activity with patterns of known threats; it is very effective against those and largely ineffective against unknown threats and variants, and the guide's example is a signature for an attachment called freepics.exe that fails to match freepics2.exe. Anomaly-based detection compares activity with a profile of normal behaviour built over a training period of days or weeks; it can catch threats nobody has described, at the price of many false positives. Stateful protocol analysis compares activity with vendor-written profiles of how each protocol should behave in each state, for example which FTP (File Transfer Protocol) commands make sense before authentication; some vendors call a form of it deep packet inspection (DPI).

Placement decides whether prevention is possible. An inline sensor is deployed so that the traffic it monitors must pass through it, much like a firewall, and the primary reason to deploy it that way is to stop attacks by blocking traffic. A passive sensor monitors a copy, taken from a switch's spanning port or from a network tap. A passive sensor can only try to end a TCP session by sending reset packets to both endpoints, a technique known as session sniping that often arrives too late, does nothing for UDP or ICMP (Internet Control Message Protocol), and is not widely used any more. An inline sensor can drop or reject the traffic, throttle the bandwidth a protocol may use, or sanitize part of a packet. Either kind can ask another device to act, for instance moving a compromised host to a quarantine VLAN (virtual local area network). The guide's rule is simple: deploy sensors inline if prevention methods will be used and passive if they will not.

The products came in that order. Internet Security Systems, founded in April 1994, released RealSecure 1.0 on 19 August 1997; WheelGroup, formed in October 1995 to sell NetRanger, was bought by Cisco in February 1998; and Marty Roesch released the first version of Snort on 22 December 1998. Snort's home page now calls it the foremost open-source intrusion prevention system in the world: rules define malicious network activity, the engine finds packets that match and generates alerts, and it can be deployed inline to stop those packets. Its rules come in a free Community Ruleset and a Subscriber Ruleset developed by Cisco Talos, since Cisco completed its purchase of Sourcefire, the company behind Snort, on 7 October 2013 for about 2.7 billion United States dollars. Suricata, developed by the non-profit Open Information Security Foundation (OISF) under version 2 of the GNU General Public License, is another open-source engine.

The rule language shows the difference between detecting and preventing in one word. A Suricata rule begins with an action: alert generates an alert, pass stops further inspection, drop discards the packet and generates an alert, and reject, rejectsrc, rejectdst and rejectboth send a TCP reset or an ICMP error to one side or both; in IPS mode any reject also drops. To run inline on Linux, Suricata either receives packets from the kernel's Netfilter queue (NFQUEUE), fed by an iptables or nftables rule, at layer 3, or bridges two interfaces at layer 2 with AF_PACKET in copy mode, where the value ips drops and the value tap only watches. The queue has a bypass option so that the link stays up if the engine is not running, which is the fail-open question in miniature.

That question, and the false positive, are what an operator actually manages. NIST says plainly that no IDPS detects with complete accuracy, that false positives and false negatives cannot both be eliminated, and that a new deployment produces many false positives until it is tuned; many sensors therefore offer a learning or simulation mode that suppresses every prevention action and reports what would have been blocked. The usual rollout follows from that: detect only, then block for the signatures that proved quiet, then block by default. Load is the other risk. An inline sensor that drops packets under high load disrupts the network and one that falls behind adds latency, so the guide recommends sensors that recognize overload and either pass traffic without full analysis or drop low-priority traffic. FortiGate exposes the choice as a setting called fail-open, triggered when the IPS engine's socket buffer is full: it is disabled by default, so sessions are dropped, and when enabled traffic continues to flow without IPS scanning.

Two limits are structural. A network IPS cannot detect attacks inside encrypted traffic, which the guide lists as VPN (virtual private network) connections, HTTPS and SSH (Secure Shell) sessions; the payload has to be inspected before it is encrypted or after it is decrypted, which in practice means pairing the IPS with TLS inspection or moving detection to the host. And attackers practise evasion, changing the format or timing of an attack so that it looks different to the sensor and has the same effect on the target; the defence is a sensor that processes the traffic the way the target would.

In current equipment the IPS is seldom a separate box. On a FortiGate it is a security profile, an IPS sensor built from individual signatures and from filters that select signatures by attribute, attached to a firewall policy; each entry takes an action of Allow, Monitor, Block, Reset, Quarantine or the signature's default, and rate-based signatures fire only after a count is reached within a duration, 60 seconds by default. On F5 BIG-IP the Network Firewall offers protocol inspection profiles, whose items are arranged by service, can be extended with custom items written as valid Snort rules, and are assigned to a firewall rule or directly to a virtual server. MITRE ATT&CK records the control as mitigation M1031, Network Intrusion Prevention: use intrusion detection signatures to block traffic at network boundaries.

Its neighbours differ by what they look at. A firewall decides on addresses, ports and state; an IPS inspects traffic the firewall has already allowed. A WAF (web application firewall) applies the same idea to HTTP requests for one application, and DLP (data loss prevention) looks for content leaving rather than attacks arriving. A signature that blocks the exploitation of a flaw before the vendor's fix is installed is what the field calls virtual patching, and it is the most common reason an IPS earns its place in a change window.

wad.def: The FortiGate process that handles proxy-based inspection.
wad.context: The Web Application Daemon is FortiGate's user-space proxy process. In proxy-based SSL inspection and web filtering, WAD terminates and re-originates the session so security profiles can see the full content.

ntlm.def: A legacy Microsoft challenge-response authentication protocol.
ntlm.context: NT LAN Manager authenticates a user via a challenge-response exchange without sending the password. Still seen in Windows environments, it is weaker than Kerberos and a frequent relay-attack target. Microsoft's open specification MS-NLMP, at version 37.0 of 30 March 2026 on the day it was read, describes it as "a challenge-response style authentication protocol" in which "the server sends a challenge to the client. The client then sends back a response that is a function of the challenge, the user's password, and possibly other information." There are connection-oriented and connectionless variants, and "each of these variants has three versions: LM, NTLMv1, and NTLMv2", with the same message flow and different response functions. The three messages are NEGOTIATE, CHALLENGE and AUTHENTICATE, each beginning with the eight-byte signature NTLMSSP followed by a null, a MessageType (0x00000001 for NEGOTIATE), the NegotiateFlags, and offset-and-length fields pointing into a payload that carries the domain, workstation and, in the last message, the responses. Application protocols embed those messages, which is why NTLM appears inside HTTP, SMB and LDAP (Lightweight Directory Access Protocol) alike, and why disabling it is an inventory problem before it is a configuration one.
ntlm.depth:
NTLM is the authentication protocol Windows used before Kerberos, and it survives because compatibility outlives design intent. It is a challenge-response scheme: the server sends a challenge, the client proves knowledge of the password hash without sending it, and no third party is consulted. Microsoft's own open specification, MS-NLMP, which on the day it was read stood at version 37.0 of 30 March 2026, puts the scope in one sentence: it "specifies the NT LAN Manager (NTLM) Authentication Protocol, used in Windows for authentication between clients and servers", and adds that "NTLM is used by application protocols to authenticate remote users and, optionally, to provide session security when requested by the application". That last clause is why NTLM is found inside so many other protocols: it is not a protocol you connect to but a sequence of messages that HTTP, SMB, LDAP and others carry in their own authentication headers.

The specification's overview describes the shape every version shares. NTLM "is a challenge-response style authentication protocol": "the server sends a challenge to the client. The client then sends back a response that is a function of the challenge, the user's password, and possibly other information." There are two variants, connection-oriented, in which a NEGOTIATE message from the client precedes the server's CHALLENGE and the client's AUTHENTICATE, and connectionless, which cannot send a NEGOTIATE_MESSAGE at all; and the document says that "each of these variants has three versions: LM, NTLMv1, and NTLMv2. The message flow for all three is the same; the only differences are the function used to compute various response fields from the challenge, and which response fields are set." LM is the LAN Manager response, NTLMv1 the first NT response and NTLMv2 the one still in use, and the first two are the ones a hardened domain refuses.

The messages themselves are plain structures, which is what makes NTLM easy to decode in a capture. The NEGOTIATE_MESSAGE of section 2.2.1.1 begins with a Signature, "an 8-byte character array that MUST contain the ASCII string ('N','T','L','M','S','S','P','\0')", followed by a MessageType of 0x00000001, the NegotiateFlags that advertise what the client supports, DomainNameFields and WorkstationFields, each a length, a maximum length and an offset into the payload, an optional Version structure present only when the NTLMSSP_NEGOTIATE_VERSION flag is set, and the Payload that the offsets point into. The CHALLENGE and AUTHENTICATE messages follow the same pattern with the server's challenge and the client's responses in place of the names. Anyone who has seen the string TlRMTVNTUAAB at the start of an HTTP Authorization header has seen a NEGOTIATE message: it is the Base64 of that signature and message type.

That last property, no third party consulted, is why it lingers. Kerberos needs a domain controller reachable at the moment of authentication; NTLM does not, so it remains the fallback when a machine connects by IP address rather than name, when the service principal name is missing or wrong, or when anything about the Kerberos path fails. Most surviving NTLM traffic in a modern domain is a Kerberos failure nobody diagnosed. Its weaknesses are structural rather than incidental. The password hash functions as the credential, so stealing it is as good as knowing the password, which is pass-the-hash. Relay attacks forward an authentication attempt to a different service, and the protocol offers no channel binding by default to stop them. The direction of travel is disabling it entirely, and the practical obstacle is always an inventory problem: finding what still depends on it before turning it off, which means auditing the authentication events on domain controllers and the application servers that still accept the NTLMSSP header. The NTLM article walks through the three messages and the versions, and the Active Directory and Kerberos entries describe the protocol that replaced it.

spn.def: The name a Kerberos client uses to request a service ticket.
spn.context: A Service Principal Name uniquely identifies a service instance in Kerberos, tied to the account running it. A misregistered SPN is a classic cause of single sign-on failures.
spn.depth:
A service principal name identifies a service instance in Kerberos, tying a service and host to the account that runs it. A client constructs the name from what it is connecting to and asks the KDC for a ticket for it.

Nearly all Kerberos failures are SPN failures. A missing name means no ticket can be issued and the client silently falls back to NTLM, which is why a password prompt appears where single sign-on should have been seamless. A duplicate name registered on two accounts breaks authentication for both. And because the client builds the name from the address it used, connecting by IP address or by an alias that is not registered produces the same failure, which is why the first question in any Kerberos problem is what name the client actually asked for.

esp.def: The IPsec protocol that encrypts and authenticates packet payloads.
esp.context: Encapsulating Security Payload (RFC 4303) is the IPsec component that provides confidentiality and integrity for tunneled traffic. A capture taken outside the tunnel sees only ESP, not the protected inner packets.
esp.depth:
Encapsulating Security Payload is the IPsec protocol that actually protects traffic, providing confidentiality, integrity and authentication. It is IP protocol 50, not a UDP or TCP port, which is the fact that explains most of its operational difficulty.

Because it has no ports, address translation cannot rewrite it and stateful firewalls often cannot track it, which is why NAT traversal encapsulates it in UDP. Tunnel mode protects the entire original packet and is what site-to-site VPNs use; transport mode protects only the payload and is used between hosts. Its sibling AH provides integrity without encryption and is essentially unused, because integrity without confidentiality is rarely what anyone wants.

vip.def: A virtual IP (VIP) address is an IP (Internet Protocol) address that belongs to a service rather than to one machine's interface: the address clients connect to on a load balancer, or an address that moves between redundant devices and is answered by whichever one currently owns it.
vip.context: A virtual IP (VIP) is the front-door address a load balancer or virtual server listens on, and the address a redundancy protocol hands from one device to another. Vendors name the object differently: on F5 BIG-IP the IP is a virtual address and each address-and-port listener on it is a virtual server; on a FortiGate a VIP is a destination network address translation (NAT) object that maps an external address to an internal one; in the Virtual Router Redundancy Protocol (VRRP) it is the virtual router's address. Whoever owns a VIP answers Address Resolution Protocol (ARP) requests for it, so ownership and failover are visible in ARP. Traffic completing at the VIP but never reaching a pool member points to a problem on the server side of the proxy.
vip.depth:
What it is, and what it is not. A virtual IP (VIP) is an Internet Protocol (IP) address that identifies a service, not a host. Clients send to it; something answers for it; what sits behind it, one server, a pool of servers or a pair of firewalls taking turns, is hidden from the client. The Linux Virtual Server project, whose introduction page dates from May 1998, put the idea in the terms load balancing still uses: a cluster of real servers that users interact with as if it were a single high-performance virtual server, a virtual service on a single IP address. A VIP is not a physical interface address, not a DNS (Domain Name System) name, and not the same thing as a virtual server: on most platforms the virtual server is the listener (address, port and the processing attached to it), and the VIP is only its address.

The load-balancer VIP on F5 BIG-IP. F5's documentation draws the line exactly. A virtual address is the specific node or network IP address with which a virtual server is associated: for a virtual server at 192.168.20.10:80, the virtual address is 192.168.20.10, and the same address can carry 192.168.20.10:80, 192.168.20.10:443 and 192.168.20.10:161 at once. A virtual address cannot be created on its own; BIG-IP creates it with the first virtual server that uses it and, with Auto Delete set, removes it with the last. Its properties decide how the network sees it. BIG-IP associates the address with a media access control (MAC) address, answers ARP (Address Resolution Protocol) requests for it and sends gratuitous ARP for it; ARP can be switched off, which F5 reserves for the rare case of so many virtual addresses that ARP activity affects performance. ICMP (Internet Control Message Protocol) Echo can be Disabled, Always (regardless of availability) or Selective, answering when any or all of its virtual servers are available. Route Advertisement injects a route for the address into dynamic routing when it is available, by the same any, all or always calculation. Each virtual address also belongs to a traffic group, the unit that fails over between BIG-IP devices, and disabling a virtual address stops every virtual server on it.

Not every BIG-IP listener load balances. A Standard virtual server sends traffic to a pool; Forwarding (Layer 2) and Forwarding (IP) virtual servers have no pool and forward packets to their destination; a Performance (Layer 4) virtual server uses a Fast L4 profile; a Reject virtual server refuses traffic; a Stateless virtual server keeps no connection-table entries. Wildcard virtual servers use a network address instead of a host address, catching traffic that matches no specific virtual server: a default wildcard on port 0 handles every service, port-specific wildcards one service each. This is why the existing rule of thumb holds: a connection that completes at the VIP but never reaches a pool member has passed the client side of the proxy, and the fault lies on the server side, in the pool, its monitors, its members or the path back from them.

The return path. A VIP that rewrites only the destination needs the replies to come back through it. The Linux Virtual Server documentation states the rule for its network address translation (NAT) mode bluntly: the default route of the real servers must be the virtual server. When that cannot be arranged, load balancers also rewrite the source address (source NAT, SNAT), so servers reply to the load balancer itself. The other answer is to avoid rewriting at all. In Linux Virtual Server direct routing, which its documentation compares to IBM's NetDispatcher, the load balancer and every real server carry the VIP: the balancer receives the request, picks a server and forwards the frame to it on the same physical segment, and the server answers the client directly. That design creates the classic VIP failure, documented by the project as the ARP problem: if the real servers answer ARP requests for the VIP, there is a race condition with no winner, and packets for the VIP go now to the balancer, now to a server. The fix is to configure the VIP on a non-ARP interface of each real server, so that only the balancer claims it.

The firewall VIP on a FortiGate. FortiOS uses the word for a different object. A static virtual IP maps an external address to an internal one, which Fortinet's guide calls destination NAT (network address translation): config firewall vip, then set extip to the address the FortiGate listens on, extintf to the interface the policy's source interface must match (any allows every policy) and mappedip to the internal address or range; portforward with a mappedport adds port translation. The VIP object, not the internal server's address, is then the destination of the firewall policy. One default bites people: arp-reply is enabled, so the FortiGate answers ARP for the external address as soon as the VIP exists, whether or not a policy uses it, and treats that address as local. Fortinet's advice is to delete unused VIPs, because the FortiGate will not forward traffic for such an address by the routing table.

The redundancy VIP. A default gateway shared by two routers is also a VIP. VRRP (Virtual Router Redundancy Protocol) version 3, RFC (Request for Comments) 9568 of April 2024, which obsoletes RFC 5798, lets a group of routers serve one or more virtual IPv4 (Internet Protocol version 4) or IPv6 (Internet Protocol version 6) addresses; the router forwarding for them is now called the Active Router, a change the RFC makes under the inclusive language guidelines of the Internet Engineering Task Force (IETF), and the router that holds the addresses on a real interface is the IP address owner. The virtual router answers from a virtual MAC address built from the organizationally unique identifier (OUI) of IANA (the Internet Assigned Numbers Authority): 00-00-5E-00-01 followed by the virtual router identifier (VRID) for IPv4 and 00-00-5E-00-02 followed by the VRID for IPv6, so up to 255 virtual routers per local area network (LAN) for each. Because the MAC address moves with the role, hosts' ARP caches stay valid through a failover; the new Active Router still broadcasts a gratuitous ARP for each IPv4 address, and sends unsolicited Neighbor Advertisements for IPv6, so that switches relearn which port the MAC now sits behind. BIG-IP and FortiGate high-availability pairs move their VIPs the same way in principle, announcing the new owner with gratuitous ARP.

The VIP with no owner at all. Kubernetes takes the idea furthest. A Service's clusterIP is a virtual IP that no interface holds: kube-proxy, which runs on every node, watches the Service and EndpointSlice objects and programs each node to capture traffic sent to the clusterIP and port and redirect it to one of the endpoints, usually a Pod. The programming depends on the mode, iptables, ipvs, nftables or kernelspace, and the ipvs mode is deprecated since Kubernetes v1.35 and will be disabled by default from v1.40. The VIP exists only as rules, on every node at once.

Pitfalls and neighbours. An answer to ping proves only that the VIP is owned: on BIG-IP, ICMP Echo set to Always replies regardless of availability, so a reachable VIP can front a pool with every member down. Two owners are worse than none: the Linux Virtual Server ARP race and a forgotten FortiGate VIP both come from a device claiming an address it should not. Failover depends on gratuitous ARP reaching the switches, and a VIP that moved without being announced leaves traffic going to the old owner until caches expire. Anycast, finally, is a different answer to the same wish: RFC 4786 describes it as making a service address available to the routing system at nodes in two or more discrete locations, so many devices own the address at once and routing chooses between them, where a VIP in the senses above has one owner at a time.

first.def: The global body of incident-response teams behind CVSS and EPSS.
first.context: The Forum of Incident Response and Security Teams is the international association that maintains standards like CVSS and EPSS. Its work gives defenders a common language for scoring and prioritizing vulnerabilities.

epss.def: A data-driven score estimating the odds a vulnerability gets exploited.
epss.context: Exploit Prediction Scoring System estimates the probability that a given vulnerability will be exploited in the wild in the near term. It complements CVSS severity by adding a likelihood dimension to prioritization.
epss.depth:
EPSS estimates the probability that a vulnerability will be exploited in the wild in the near term, using observed data rather than the structural characteristics CVSS scores. It exists because severity and likelihood are different questions and the industry had only been measuring one.

The practical consequence is a much smaller worklist. The overwhelming majority of vulnerabilities are never exploited, and a high CVSS score with a low EPSS probability is a different situation from one where both are high. Used well it prioritizes; used carelessly it deprioritizes something that is trivially exploitable in your specific environment, since a model of the general population knows nothing about which of your systems is exposed.

pkce.def: An extension to the OAuth 2.0 authorization code flow in which the client commits to a one-time secret when it starts the request and reveals it when it redeems the code, so that an intercepted authorization code is useless to anyone else.
pkce.context: Proof Key for Code Exchange (PKCE, pronounced "pixy"), defined in Request for Comments (RFC) 7636, binds an authorization code to the client that requested it. The client invents a random code verifier, sends only its hash (the code challenge) with the authorization request and presents the verifier itself when it exchanges the code for tokens; the authorization server recomputes the hash and refuses the exchange if the two do not match. It stops an intercepted code from being redeemed by an attacker. Published in 2015 for mobile apps that cannot keep a client secret, it is now required for every public OAuth client, recommended for confidential ones, and built into the authorization code grant by the OAuth 2.1 draft.
pkce.depth:
PKCE (Proof Key for Code Exchange) closes a hole that mobile and single-page applications opened. The authorization code flow of OAuth 2.0, defined in Request for Comments (RFC) 6749 of October 2012, assumed the client could keep a secret, which a server can and a phone app or a browser bundle cannot, since anyone can decompile it or view its source. RFC 7636 puts it flatly: secrets provisioned in client binary applications cannot be considered confidential. Without a secret, whoever intercepts the authorization code can redeem it. On a phone the interception is easy to arrange: a malicious app registers the same custom URI (Uniform Resource Identifier) scheme as the legitimate one, receives the redirect that carries the code and takes it to the token endpoint. The RFC lists the preconditions and adds that the attack had been observed in the wild.

The fix is small. For every authorization request the client creates a code verifier, a high-entropy random string of 43 to 128 characters drawn from the unreserved URI characters: letters, digits, hyphen, full stop, underscore and tilde. The recommended recipe is 32 random octets encoded as base64url without padding, which yields exactly 43 characters and 256 bits of entropy. From the verifier the client derives the code challenge. With the S256 method the challenge is the base64url encoding of the SHA-256 (Secure Hash Algorithm, 256-bit) digest of the verifier's ASCII (American Standard Code for Information Interchange) bytes, again 43 characters; with the plain method it is the verifier itself. The client adds two parameters to the authorization request, code_challenge and code_challenge_method (which defaults to plain when absent), and one to the token request, code_verifier. The server binds the challenge and the method to the code it issues, repeats the transformation when the code comes back, carries on if the values are equal and answers invalid_grant if they are not. A server that requires PKCE and receives no challenge answers invalid_request.

An intercepted code is now useless without the verifier, which stays inside the client until the token request, and that request travels under Transport Layer Security (TLS) straight to the authorization server. RFC 8252 calls the mechanism a proof-of-possession extension, and the phrase marks its limits. PKCE proves that whoever redeems the code is whoever asked for it; it does not authenticate the application, so a public client remains a public client, and it does nothing for an access token after it has been issued. The verifier also needs no salt. The RFC explains why: unlike a password, it already carries 256 bits of entropy, so adding a public value before hashing would not increase the number of guesses a brute-force search needs.

The plain method protects only against an attacker who sees the authorization response. Anyone able to read the request as well (the RFC's example is an operating system leaking HTTP, Hypertext Transfer Protocol, log information) learns the verifier directly. For that reason RFC 7636 makes S256 mandatory to implement on servers, obliges a client that can use S256 to use it, forbids falling back to plain after trying S256 and says plain should not be used in new implementations. The IANA (Internet Assigned Numbers Authority) registry of PKCE code challenge methods still holds exactly two entries, plain and S256. A second downgrade lives on the server side: an authorization server that enforces PKCE only when code_challenge is present invites an attacker to strip the parameter. RFC 9700 therefore requires servers to reject a token request that carries a code_verifier when the authorization request had no code_challenge, and observes that servers which make PKCE mandatory are immune by construction.

The specification was written in the OAuth working group of the Internet Engineering Task Force (IETF) under the draft name draft-ietf-oauth-spop, and was published in September 2015 as RFC 7636, Proof Key for Code Exchange by OAuth Public Clients, a Proposed Standard by Nat Sakimura, John Bradley and Naveen Agarwal. RFC 8252 (October 2017), the best current practice for native apps, made it mandatory for public native clients and for the servers that serve them. What began as a mobile workaround then became the general recommendation. RFC 9700, the OAuth 2.0 security best current practice of January 2025, says public clients MUST use PKCE, recommends it for confidential clients because it also defeats authorization code injection and, as a side effect, cross-site request forgery (CSRF), and requires every authorization server to support it. RFC 10017 (August 2026) repeats the rule for browser-based applications. The OAuth 2.1 draft, at revision 17 on 31 October 2026 and still not an RFC, folds the two parameters into the authorization code grant itself, removes the plain method on the grounds that any device able to run TLS 1.2 already has SHA-256, and omits the implicit grant.

In deployments, defaults are worth checking rather than assuming. A client can discover support from the code_challenge_methods_supported array in the authorization server metadata of RFC 8414; if the member is missing, the server does not support PKCE. Microsoft's identity platform requires code_challenge for single-page apps that use the authorization code flow and recommends it for every application type, yet accepts both plain and S256. On F5 BIG-IP Access Policy Manager (APM) acting as authorization server, the 17.1 documentation shows the Require PKCE option cleared by default for a client application, and once it is selected the Allow Plain Code Challenge option appears already ticked. To test an implementation, Appendix B of RFC 7636 supplies a known pair: the verifier dBjftJeZ4CVP-mB92K27uhbUJU1p1r_wW1gFWFOEjXk gives the S256 challenge E9Melhoa2OwvFrEMTJguCHaoeK1t8URWbuGJSstw-cM.

The usual mistakes follow from the rules. Ordinary base64 output fails, because the plus sign, the slash and the padding equals sign are outside the permitted alphabet; Appendix A of the RFC shows the conversion to base64url. A constant or reused verifier defeats the purpose, and RFC 9700 requires the challenge to be specific to the transaction and bound to the user agent in which it started. A client that treats an error on S256 as a cue to retry with plain has been downgraded, since the RFC notes that such an error can only mean a faulty server or an attacker in the path.

PKCE has neighbours that are easily confused with it. The state parameter and the OpenID Connect (OIDC) nonce also tie a response to the request that caused it; RFC 9700 lets a client rely on PKCE for CSRF protection once it knows the server supports it, and lets confidential OIDC clients use the nonce instead, though the OAuth 2.1 draft points out that the server-side check is stronger, because the server can refuse to issue tokens at all, whereas a nonce mismatch is noticed only after they have been issued. A client secret answers a different question, which application is calling. For anything interactive today the choice is authorization code with PKCE, and the implicit flow it displaced is discouraged for exactly the reasons PKCE addresses.

eigrp.def: Enhanced Interior Gateway Routing Protocol (EIGRP): Cisco's advanced distance-vector routing protocol, whose DUAL (Diffusing Update Algorithm) keeps loop-free backup routes precomputed, so that a router holding one switches to it at once, without recomputation or flooding.
eigrp.context: EIGRP (Enhanced Interior Gateway Routing Protocol) grew out of Cisco's earlier IGRP (Interior Gateway Routing Protocol), whose composite bandwidth-and-delay metric it kept and scaled up, and stayed proprietary for about two decades until Cisco published it as informational RFC (Request for Comments) 7868 in May 2016. Its heart is DUAL (Diffusing Update Algorithm), from research by J. J. Garcia-Luna-Aceves at SRI International: for each destination a router tracks feasible successors, neighbours whose reported distance proves them loop-free, so when the best path dies the backup is promoted without recomputation or flooding. That is why the classic praise is fast convergence. The trade: excellent inside Cisco networks, historically a lock-in lever, and still the exam counterweight to the open link-state model of OSPF (Open Shortest Path First).
eigrp.depth:
EIGRP (Enhanced Interior Gateway Routing Protocol) is Cisco's interior gateway protocol (IGP): distance-vector at its core, with features borrowed from link-state designs, converging quickly because it keeps precomputed backup routes it can switch to without recalculating. Its specification, RFC (Request for Comments) 7868, calls it a routing protocol based on distance-vector technology whose specific algorithm is DUAL (Diffusing Update Algorithm). A router never holds a map of the topology the way an OSPF (Open Shortest Path First) or IS-IS (Intermediate System to Intermediate System) router does; it knows, for each destination, the distance each neighbour reports and its own cost to that neighbour. EIGRP runs directly over IP as protocol number 88, sends its packets to the multicast groups 224.0.0.10 for IPv4 and FF02::A for IPv6 on multicast-capable links, and carries its own reliable transport: hellos go out once as unacknowledged multicast, while updates, queries and replies are acknowledged, so EIGRP needs no periodic refresh of the whole table.

It descends from IGRP (Interior Gateway Routing Protocol), Cisco's earlier protocol. Cisco's introduction to IGRP argues that the hop count of RIP (Routing Information Protocol), a number from 1 to 15, was too small a range for large networks, and gives IGRP a composite 24-bit metric built from delay, the bandwidth of the narrowest segment, channel occupancy and reliability, with full routing tables sent to neighbours every 90 seconds. RFC 7868 says one of EIGRP's original goals was to enhance IGRP, which is why it used the same composite metric with every term multiplied by 256, turning 24 bits into 32. The FRRouting documentation dates EIGRP's development to the 1990s. The algorithm came from outside Cisco: J. J. Garcia-Luna-Aceves at SRI International published a unified approach to loop-free routing using distance vectors or link states at SIGCOMM in 1989, and Loop-Free Routing Using Diffusing Computations in the first issue of IEEE/ACM Transactions on Networking in 1993. For about two decades EIGRP was Cisco's alone. Cisco submitted an Internet-Draft on 28 February 2013, went through five revisions and saw it published as RFC 7868 on 25 May 2016, written by authors from Cisco, Cumulus Networks, the University of Zilina and LinkedIn. It came through the Independent Submission stream: the IETF (Internet Engineering Task Force) datatracker records that the document is not endorsed by the IETF and has no formal standing in its standards process.

DUAL rests on a handful of definitions that every EIGRP engineer ends up reading in show ip eigrp topology. The reported distance (RD) is a neighbour's own distance to the destination, as it advertises it. The feasible distance (FD) is the lowest total metric the router has known for that destination since the route last went from active to passive; as RFC 7868 stresses, it is a historical record, not necessarily the cost of the current best path. The feasibility condition, which EIGRP implements as the Source Node Condition, is met by a neighbour whose RD is lower than the router's FD, in other words a neighbour closer to the destination than the router itself has been since the route last settled; such a neighbour cannot be routing back through this router, so its path is guaranteed loop-free. The successor is the neighbour on the least-cost path that meets the condition; a feasible successor meets it without being the best. When the successor fails and a feasible successor exists, the router switches to it locally, informs its neighbours, and nobody else has to recompute: RFC 7868 describes DUAL as obtaining loop freedom at every instant throughout a route computation, with routers not affected by a change left out of it.

When no feasible successor exists the price arrives. The route goes active, is considered unusable, and the router sends queries to its neighbours and waits for every reply; neighbours without an answer query theirs in turn, a diffusing computation that can sweep across the whole domain. A route that stays active too long is stuck in active (SIA): Cisco's implementation allows 3 minutes, sends an SIA-QUERY at the halfway point (90 seconds by default) that a neighbour must answer with a reply or an SIA-REPLY, allows at most three SIA-REPLY messages, and then either deletes the routes through the silent neighbour or resets the adjacency with it. A slow or congested link at the edge of a large flat domain is the classic trigger, which is what stub routing is for: a router configured as a stub tells its neighbours so, hub devices stop querying it and answer for it, by default it advertises only its connected and summary routes, and Cisco presents it as the usual design for hub-and-spoke networks and as a way to avoid SIA over limited WAN (wide area network) links.

The metric is the most misread part of the protocol. The classic composite formula multiplies by 256 a weighted sum of bandwidth, a load-dependent bandwidth term and delay, then scales it by a reliability quotient; the weights are the K-values, and with the defaults (K1 and K3 equal to 1, K2, K4 and K5 equal to 0, the reliability quotient then taken as 1) it reduces to 256 times the sum of two numbers: 10 to the power 7 divided by the minimum bandwidth along the path in kbit/s, and the sum of the outgoing interface delays in tens of microseconds. Bandwidth is therefore the narrowest link and delay the accumulated total. A path whose slowest link runs at 10 Mbit/s (10,000 kbit/s) and whose delays add up to 2,000 units (20 milliseconds) scores 256 times 3,000, or 768,000. Load and reliability are expressed from 1 to 255 and are not measured continuously, which is one reason the defaults leave them out of the calculation. The classic formula runs out of resolution at modern speeds, since 10 to the 7 divided by a 10 Gbit/s link's 10,000,000 kbit/s is already 1; RFC 7868's wide metrics change both the packet encoding and the formula so that paths are compared on the computed time, in picoseconds, that information takes to cross the links, with vector metrics for throughput, latency, load, reliability, MTU (maximum transmission unit) and hop count. Two neighbours must agree on the K-values, which travel in every hello, or they never form an adjacency.

The operational defaults are worth knowing by heart. Hellos go out every 5 seconds on high-bandwidth links and every 60 seconds on low-bandwidth multipoint links, and the hold time is three times the hello interval, 15 or 180 seconds. Two routers become neighbours only with the same autonomous system (AS) number, a 16-bit field from 1 to 65,535 that RFC 7868 notes is used indirectly as an authentication value, and the same K-values; real authentication uses the MD5 (Message Digest 5) or SHA2 (Secure Hash Algorithm 2) types the specification defines. In the Cisco routing table, internal EIGRP routes carry administrative distance 90, ahead of OSPF at 110, external routes redistributed into EIGRP carry 170, behind every IGP, and a summary route created by EIGRP carries 5. EIGRP is also the IGP that can spread traffic over paths of unequal cost: the variance command sets a multiplier, and a feasible successor whose metric falls within the best metric times that multiplier is used alongside the successor. In the topology table, A marks a route that is active and P one that is passive; a list of routes stuck in A is the first sign of trouble.

The practical consideration is that publication is not the same as multi-vendor support. Outside Cisco's own operating systems the open-source FRRouting suite ships an eigrpd daemon implementing RFC 7868, but real interoperability across commercial vendors remains limited, so choosing EIGRP is largely choosing a single-vendor network, a legitimate decision when made deliberately and a trap when made by accident. OSPF is the standards-based alternative with genuine multi-vendor implementation, and the comparison is an old one in networking, the same one DECnet lost: an integrated stack against an open one. The usual failure modes follow from the design: SIA storms in large domains with no stubs or summarization, adjacencies that never form because of mismatched AS numbers or K-values, and redistribution loops at the boundary with OSPF, where the 110 against 170 ordering decides which copy of a route a router believes.

as.def: A network under one administrative routing policy, identified by an ASN.
as.context: An autonomous system is a collection of IP prefixes under a single routing policy, identified by an autonomous system number. BGP exchanges reachability between autonomous systems, and AS boundaries are natural places to summarize routes.

ca.def: A certificate authority (CA), also called a certification authority, is an organization trusted to issue, and to revoke, the digital certificates that bind public keys to names. Its signature is what lets a relying party that trusts the CA trust a certificate it has never seen before.
ca.context: A certificate authority (CA) is the entity whose signature makes a TLS (Transport Layer Security) certificate trusted. Browsers and operating systems ship a set of trusted root CAs; a certificate is valid only if it chains to one of them, and the CA is also who revokes certificates, through a CRL (certificate revocation list) or OCSP (Online Certificate Status Protocol), which public CAs have been allowed to drop since 2024. Any trusted root can sign for any name, so a single compromised or careless CA endangers sites that never did business with it, as DigiNotar showed in 2011.
ca.depth:
What it is. The NIST (National Institute of Standards and Technology) glossary calls a certificate authority (CA) a trusted entity that issues and revokes public key certificates, and, in another source, the entity in a PKI (public key infrastructure) responsible for issuing certificates and exacting compliance to a PKI policy, also known as a certification authority. What a CA sells is a signature plus a promise: RFC (Request for Comments) 5280 defines a certificate's validity period as the interval during which the CA warrants that it will maintain information about the certificate's status. It does not vouch for the honesty of the subject; for a domain-validated certificate it vouches only that the applicant controlled the name when it checked.

The hierarchy. The CA/Browser Forum's Baseline Requirements define a root CA as the top-level authority whose root certificate is distributed by application software suppliers (browser and operating system makers) and which issues subordinate CA certificates; a subordinate, or intermediate, CA is one whose certificate is signed by the root or by another subordinate. The root's private key may sign only the root's own self-signed certificate, subordinate and cross-certified CA certificates, infrastructure certificates and certificates for verifying OCSP (Online Certificate Status Protocol) responses, never a server's certificate, which is why every public TLS (Transport Layer Security) chain has at least one intermediate. A cross-certificate is one CA signing another's key to establish trust between them. RFC 5280 leaves the choice of trust anchor to local policy.

Who decides whom to trust. Root programs do. The Baseline Requirements, in force since 1 July 2012, state that they are not mandatory for CAs until application software suppliers adopt and enforce them, and the suppliers do: Mozilla's Root Store Policy, version 3.1 in effect since 1 July 2026, requires CA operators to follow the Baseline Requirements and the Common CA Database (CCADB) Policy and to pass audits under WebTrust or ETSI (European Telecommunications Standards Institute) EN 319 411-1. In the CA/Browser Forum itself the two sides vote separately: a ballot needs two-thirds of the certificate issuers and a simple majority of the certificate consumers, which are Apple, Google, Microsoft and Mozilla.

How a CA checks a domain. Section 3.2.2.4 of the Baseline Requirements numbers 22 domain validation methods, ten of them now retired, including the open-ended Any Other Method. The survivors include email to a constructed address (admin, administrator, webmaster, hostmaster or postmaster at the domain), a random value placed in DNS (Domain Name System), a file on the website, the ACME (Automatic Certificate Management Environment) HTTP (Hypertext Transfer Protocol) challenge of RFC 8555 (March 2019), TLS with ALPN (Application-Layer Protocol Negotiation), and a persistent DNS TXT record. Since 15 March 2025 a CA must also corroborate the result from at least two remote network perspectives, so that a Border Gateway Protocol (BGP) hijack of one path cannot fool it; with two to five perspectives one may disagree, with six or more two.

Limiting which CA may issue. Any publicly trusted CA can technically sign for any name. CAA (Certification Authority Authorization), RFC 8659 of November 2019, which obsoleted RFC 6844, lets a domain holder publish in DNS which CAs may issue for it: the issue property for ordinary certificates, issuewild for wildcards, and iodef for where to report requests that break the policy. The Baseline Requirements make every public CA retrieve and process CAA records for each dNSName before issuing. A record set that names only the CAs actually in use, with an iodef contact, narrows who can issue; Certificate Transparency monitoring shows what was issued anyway; and openssl x509 -issuer shows which CA really signed a given certificate.

Revocation. RFC 5280 gives the classic reasons to revoke early: a change of name, a change of association between subject and CA, and compromise or suspected compromise of the private key. Status was published in CRLs (certificate revocation lists) or answered live by OCSP, specified in RFC 6960 (June 2013). The Baseline Requirements set deadlines of 24 hours for some reasons and five days for others, and Ballot SC063, effective 15 March 2024, made OCSP optional and CRLs mandatory; short-lived certificates, seven days or less since 15 March 2026, are exempt from revocation. Let's Encrypt switched its OCSP service off on 6 August 2025, citing privacy, because every OCSP query tells the CA which site is being visited from which IP (Internet Protocol) address; at its peak the service answered about 340 billion requests a month, more than 140,000 a second at the CDN (content delivery network).

Free and automated. Let's Encrypt, run by the non-profit Internet Security Research Group (ISRG), describes itself as a free, automated and open CA; its model, ACME clients renewing certificates without human involvement, is what the shrinking certificate lifetimes now assume.

When CAs fail. On 29 August 2011 Google reported attempted man-in-the-middle attacks on its users, primarily in Iran, using a fraudulent certificate for Google issued by DigiNotar, a CA that should never have issued one; Chrome detected it, Mozilla and Microsoft acted, and on 3 September Google rejected all DigiNotar CAs following the Dutch government's findings. Distrust can also be slow and deliberate: after announcing it would stop trusting the Symantec CA, including the Thawte, VeriSign, Equifax, GeoTrust and RapidSSL brands, Chrome 66 rejected Symantec certificates issued before 1 June 2016, and Chrome 70, released in October 2018, showed full-screen warnings for the rest of the legacy Symantec PKI; DigiCert had acquired Symantec's CA business. Certificate Transparency logs exist so that misissuance like DigiNotar's is seen quickly.

Private and national CAs. The Baseline Requirements do not cover enterprises that run their own PKI for internal purposes with roots no software supplier distributes; such CAs are trusted only where an administrator installs them, which is exactly how TLS inspection proxies work. Brazil runs a national PKI for legal signatures: Medida Provisória 2.200-2 of 24 August 2001 created ICP-Brasil (Infra-Estrutura de Chaves Públicas Brasileira, the Brazilian public key infrastructure) to guarantee the authenticity, integrity and legal validity of electronic documents, with a policy committee over a chain of a root CA (AC Raiz), CAs (ACs) and registration authorities (ARs), and made the National Institute of Information Technology (ITI) the AC Raiz. Declarations signed through ICP-Brasil are presumed true with respect to their signatories, while other certificates remain valid evidence when the parties accept them.

pin.def: A short numeric secret used to authenticate a person.
pin.context: A personal identification number is a short numeric code used to prove identity, as on a bank card. Being short, a PIN has a tiny keyspace, so it relies on limited attempts or a hardware secure element rather than resistance to offline guessing.

otp.def: A one-time password (OTP) is an authentication value that the verifier accepts only once, derived from a shared secret and a moving factor such as a counter, the clock or a hash chain, or sent by the verifier itself, so that a captured value gives an eavesdropper nothing to replay. The same acronym also names the one-time pad of classical cryptography.
otp.context: A one-time password (OTP) is used once and then becomes invalid, which defeats the replay of a captured code. HOTP (HMAC-based One-Time Password, counter-based) and TOTP (Time-based One-Time Password) are the two common ways to generate them for MFA (multi-factor authentication), while older systems such as S/KEY used a chain of hashes and many services simply send a code by text message. An OTP is strong against password reuse and credential stuffing, because a stolen password alone no longer suffices, but it is not phishing-resistant: a user can be led to type the code into an attacker's page that relays it at once. NIST (National Institute of Standards and Technology) states that limit in its authentication guidelines, and it is the gap that passkeys close.
otp.depth:
Two meanings, one acronym. NIST's (National Institute of Standards and Technology) glossary lists OTP (one-time password) as the abbreviation of two unrelated things: the one-time password of authentication, drawn from its digital identity guidelines, and the one-time pad of cryptography, drawn from US government security glossaries. In networking and security practice the acronym almost always means the first, and the distinction matters because the security properties are nothing alike. SP (Special Publication) 800-63B, revision 4, defines the authentication kind as a secret generated by an authenticator and used only once to prove possession of that authenticator.

Where the idea came from. Leslie Lamport published Password Authentication with Insecure Communication in Communications of the ACM (Association for Computing Machinery) in November 1981, a three-page paper he later called his only publication in cryptography: a way to use one password to log in many times without letting an eavesdropper in. The trick is a hash chain. Bellcore built it into S/KEY, described by N. Haller in RFC (Request for Comments) 1760 in February 1995, and the IETF (Internet Engineering Task Force) standardized the result as the OTP system of RFC 2289, by N. Haller, C. Metz, P. Nesser and M. Straw, in February 1998. The user's pass-phrase, at least 10 characters, is joined to a seed the server sends in clear and hashed repeatedly; the first password is the result of N hash iterations, the next of N minus 1, and so on. The server stores only the last password it accepted and checks a new one by hashing it once and comparing, so an eavesdropper who sees one password would have to invert the hash to produce the next, and no secret is stored on the server at all. MD5 (Message Digest 5) support is mandatory, SHA (Secure Hash Algorithm) should be supported and MD4 may be; the output is folded to 64 bits and can be typed as six short words from a 2048-word dictionary, 11 bits each with a 2-bit checksum, such as OUST COAT FOAL MUG BEAK TOTE, in answer to a challenge such as otp-md5 487 dog2.

What RFC 2289 already knew. The standard is candid about its limits. It protects only against passive eavesdropping and replay; it does not protect the privacy of the session, and it does not stop active attacks such as session hijacking. It also describes the race attack: an attacker who watches most of a password being typed can guess the last word and race the legitimate user to finish, which is why conforming servers must refuse simultaneous authentication sessions for the same user, with a timeout so that the lock cannot itself become a denial of service. These two observations, that a one-time value can be relayed and that it can be raced, are still the core of every OTP threat model.

The OATH generation. The codes in authenticator apps and hardware tokens today come from two algorithms of the OATH (Initiative for Open Authentication) family. HOTP (HMAC-based One-Time Password), RFC 4226 of December 2005, computes an HMAC (hash-based message authentication code) with SHA-1 over a shared secret and an 8-byte counter and truncates it to at least six digits; TOTP (Time-based One-Time Password), RFC 6238 of May 2011, replaces the counter with the number of 30-second steps since the Unix epoch. Both reverse one property of S/KEY: the verifier must hold the same secret as the token, because it recomputes the code, so the server's secret store becomes a target. Many services instead send a code by SMS (Short Message Service) or voice call. SP 800-63B treats that as an out-of-band secret: at least six random digits, valid for no more than 10 minutes and only once, and it classes delivery over the PSTN (Public Switched Telephone Network) as a restricted authenticator, telling verifiers to look for risk signs such as a SIM (subscriber identity module) change, a number port or a device swap before relying on it, and to offer every user an alternative.

What a one-time value does and does not stop. SP 800-63B requires a verifier to accept a given OTP only once while it is valid, which is the replay resistance the name promises, to limit consecutive failed attempts on one authenticator to no more than 100, and to use keys of at least 112 bits of strength. Under those rules an OTP is strong against password reuse and credential stuffing: a password copied from one breach no longer opens an account on its own. It is weak against real-time phishing, and NIST says so directly: OTP authentication is not phishing-resistant. In July 2022 Microsoft's threat intelligence team described an AiTM (adversary-in-the-middle) campaign that had targeted more than 10,000 organizations since September 2021 with the Evilginx2 kit: a proxy sat between the user and the real sign-in page, relayed the password and the code, and kept the session cookie, so the attacker was signed in whatever second factor the user had. Microsoft's recommended answer was phishing-resistant MFA (multi-factor authentication), based on FIDO2 security keys or on certificates, together with conditional access that re-evaluates a stolen cookie when it is used.

The other OTP. The one-time pad combines each character of a message with a character of a random key. The Crypto Museum traces it to a description by the banker Frank Miller in 1882 and to its reinvention in 1917 by Gilbert Vernam and Joseph Mauborgne, and lists the rules that make it absolutely safe: the key must be truly random, at least as long as the plaintext, exist in only two copies, be used only once and be destroyed after use. In his 1949 paper Communication Theory of Secrecy Systems, in the Bell System Technical Journal, Claude Shannon proved that every theoretically unbreakable cipher must meet the same requirements as the one-time pad. That proof is also its practical verdict: securely delivering a truly random key as long as the message is the same problem as securely delivering the message.

Numbers worth remembering: Lamport's paper of November 1981; RFC 1760 of 1995, RFC 2289 of 1998, RFC 4226 of 2005 and RFC 6238 of 2011; 64-bit S/KEY values written as six words of 11 bits from a 2048-word dictionary; six digits and 30 seconds for the common app codes; 10 minutes for an out-of-band code; one use per code, at most 100 consecutive failures and 112 bits of key strength under SP 800-63B; and more than 10,000 organizations in the 2022 AiTM campaign that showed what OTPs cannot stop.

acs.def: The endpoint where a SAML response is delivered to the application.
acs.context: The Assertion Consumer Service is the URL at the service provider that receives and processes a SAML assertion from the identity provider. A response must be sent to the exact registered ACS, which is part of what stops assertion redirection attacks.

dcv.def: Proving you control a domain before a certificate is issued.
dcv.context: Domain Control Validation is how a CA confirms the requester controls the domain, via an HTTP, DNS, or email challenge. Baseline Requirements keep shrinking how long a DCV result can be reused, tightening certificate issuance.
dcv.depth:
Domain control validation is how a certificate authority establishes that the requester controls the name before issuing. The methods are publishing a token in DNS, serving a file over HTTP, or responding to a challenge during a TLS handshake.

The security of the entire public certificate system rests on this step, which is why the attacks worth worrying about target it rather than the cryptography: a BGP (Border Gateway Protocol) hijack that redirects the validation request, a DNS compromise, or a dangling subdomain pointing at infrastructure someone else can claim. Multi-perspective validation, where the authority checks from several network vantage points, is the mitigation for the routing-based version and is now standard practice.
