F5 describes two flavours: Secure Mesh, the layer 3 to 7 networking and security stack with routing, segmentation, IPsec (Internet Protocol Security) to third-party devices, site-to-site fabric, SNAT (source network address translation), network firewall, BGP (Border Gateway Protocol) advertisement of VIPs (virtual IP addresses), load balancing, forward proxy and WAF; and App Stack, a managed Kubernetes platform for running the customer's own applications on the same nodes. Configuration and state live in ETCD, whose quorum for n members is n/2 + 1, so tolerating one failure takes three nodes: F5 recommends a three-node cluster for production, with each node in a separate availability zone in the cloud, and a single node only for tests and proofs of concept.

Network placement comes in two modes. On a stick, a single interface carries both ingress and egress traffic and the CE acts as a proxy, load balancer or gateway. As default gateway, the first interface is the outside network (SITE_LOCAL_OUTSIDE, addressed by DHCP, the Dynamic Host Configuration Protocol) and the second the inside network (SITE_LOCAL_INSIDE), with routing and firewalling between them, local internet breakout and, if a DHCP server is enabled, the CE serving as the inside network's default gateway. Where a CE can be deployed is listed in F5's ecosystem reference: AWS (Amazon Web Services), Azure and GCP (Google Cloud Platform) through automated cloud-site workflows or Secure Mesh Site v2, and OCI (Oracle Cloud Infrastructure), managed Kubernetes services, Hyper-V, VMware ESXi 7.0 or later, OpenStack, Nutanix AHV, bare metal and OpenShift Virtualization through Secure Mesh Site v2. That newer workflow removed the old certified-hardware objects, lets the operator choose REs, and uses a single registration endpoint; F5 marks some providers as early access, for proofs of concept only.

Registration is zero-touch provisioning with a token. The tenant generates a token in the site-creation workflow and places it in the image, in cloud-init or in the Kubernetes spec; the node boots, finds an interface that can reach the Global Controller and calls home with the token and its hardware details; once the registration is approved, the controller picks two REs by GeoIP proximity of the public address the request came from (or uses the ones the operator named), and sends them down with the CE's identity, PKI (public key infrastructure) certificates that the system rotates, and the tunnel configuration. The CE then negotiates IPsec and SSL (Secure Sockets Layer) tunnels to both REs, preferring IPsec and falling back to SSL when IPsec cannot be established, which is why UDP (User Datagram Protocol) port 4500 is optional in F5's firewall reference, and a distributed control plane running in the REs takes over. Those tunnels carry management and control, and data traffic too if the operator wants the F5 global network as a backbone; site-to-site traffic can instead use tunnels built directly between CEs.

The allowlist is where most deployments stall, and F5 publishes it as one reference with a plain-text version for automation. For Secure Mesh Site v2 the mandatory egress rules are small: TCP (Transmission Control Protocol) 443 to the registration address 159.60.141.140, TCP 80 and 443 between the CE and the RE ranges of each geography, UDP 4500 for IPsec (optional, because the SSL fallback exists), UDP 123 for the REs' NTP (Network Time Protocol), DNS (Domain Name System) and NTP to Google's public servers (8.8.8.8 and 8.8.4.4, and the 216.239.35.x time servers) unless custom servers were configured, and either the single F5-owned wildcard *.volterra.io or its list of FQDNs (fully qualified domain names), since F5 removed every third-party wildcard from that set. Legacy sites need a far longer list of cloud and registry ranges. F5 warns that IP addresses can change without its knowledge and calls domain-based rules the preferred method, notes that port 65500 is the CE's local user interface and API, and asks that nodes in a three-node site be allowed to talk freely over their outside interfaces. Its troubleshooting advice is blunt: when an application stays stuck in connecting, review the firewall or proxy allowlist first.

A registered CE is the start, not the finish. An HTTP (Hypertext Transfer Protocol) load balancer serves a private application through a CE by naming an origin pool whose servers are defined by IP address or DNS name on given sites, together with the site or virtual site and the inside network, outside network or a segment, plus an optional SNAT pool. A CE that shows online but has no route to the origin on the network the pool names will register perfectly and serve nothing. The Secure Mesh Site v2 caveats are worth knowing before the first change window: a site with HA (high availability) disabled has exactly one node; HA nodes must be powered on at least 90 seconds apart and must have identical processors, memory and disk; nodes are not resized after deployment; and interfaces are added with every node of the site powered down.

The abbreviation also has an older, unrelated meaning. In MPLS (Multiprotocol Label Switching) VPNs (virtual private networks) as RFC (Request for Comments) 4364 describes them, each customer site contains one or more customer edge (CE) devices, routers or hosts attached to the provider edge (PE) routers of the service provider. That CE belongs to the customer and is usually a plain router; F5's CE is software that F5 manages centrally, and the two meet only in name.

opt.def: OPT (option) is the pseudo-record, resource record type 41, placed in the additional section of a Domain Name System (DNS) message to carry the Extension Mechanisms for DNS (EDNS): the sender's UDP (User Datagram Protocol) payload size, extra response-code bits, a version, flags and a list of options.
opt.context: The OPT record, defined in Request for Comments (RFC) 6891, is not a real resource record but a container in the additional section of a Domain Name System (DNS) message that carries the metadata of the Extension Mechanisms for DNS (EDNS), such as the buffer size and flags. dig shows it as the OPT pseudo-section. It exists only on the wire, one per message, between one sender and the next server, and is never stored in a zone or a cache.
opt.depth:
The OPT record is a pseudo-record that appears in the additional section of a Domain Name System (DNS) message and never exists in a zone; it is the container that the Extension Mechanisms for DNS (EDNS) use. It advertises the message size its sender can receive and carries option codes for extensions. Request for Comments (RFC) 6891 (April 2013), which replaced Paul Vixie's RFC 2671 of August 1999, calls it a pseudo-RR (resource record) or meta-RR: it has type number 41, it carries no DNS data, only control information about one question-and-answer exchange, and it must not be cached, forwarded, or stored in or loaded from a zone file. The headword is short for option; the registry of the Internet Assigned Numbers Authority (IANA) simply lists the type as OPT.

Its trick is to reuse the layout of an ordinary record for other purposes, so that old parsers can step over it. NAME is the root, a single zero byte. TYPE is 41. CLASS, 16 bits, is no class at all but the requestor's UDP (User Datagram Protocol) payload size, the largest message it can accept. The 32 bits of the TTL (time to live) field are split in three: eight bits of extended RCODE (response code), which become the upper bits of a 12-bit code; eight bits of version, always 0 so far; and sixteen flag bits, of which the first is DO (DNSSEC OK, RFC 3225 of December 2001), by which a requestor asks for the records of the DNS Security Extensions (DNSSEC), the second is CO (Compact Answers OK, RFC 9824 of September 2025), and the rest are zero. RDLEN gives the length of the data, and the data is a list of options, each a 16-bit code, a 16-bit length and that many bytes. An OPT record with no options is therefore eleven bytes long: one for the name, two for the type, two for the size, four for the former TTL and two for a zero length.

The rules about its presence are strict. A message may hold only one OPT record, and a query with more than one must be answered with FORMERR (format error). It may sit anywhere in the additional section, except that a TSIG (transaction signature) or SIG(0) record, when present, still has to come last. A responder that implements EDNS must put an OPT record in its reply whenever the request had one, and must not when the request had none. A server that does not implement EDNS answers FORMERR without an OPT record; a server that does, but found the record malformed, answers FORMERR with one, which is how the two cases are told apart. Even a truncated response must contain at least the header, the question and the OPT record. An option code the receiver does not understand is ignored, which is what lets new options be deployed without breaking anything.

The record is hop by hop. It describes one transaction between two parties, so a recursive resolver does not pass the client's OPT record on to the authoritative server: it builds its own, with its own buffer size and flags, and builds another for the answer it gives the client. RFC 6891 draws the line for boxes in the middle. One that merely forwards requests to a resolver must neither modify nor delete the OPT contents in either direction, and must not limit DNS over UDP to 512 bytes; one that answers queries or forwards intelligently should process the record and treat the incoming and outgoing requests as separate transactions. A device that edits options sits in the second group: on an F5 BIG-IP, for example, the DNS profile setting edns0-client-subnet-insert adds the Client Subnet option to queries that arrive without one and removes it again from the responses to those clients.

In dig the record is the block headed OPT PSEUDOSECTION, with a line such as EDNS: version: 0, flags: do; udp: 1232, followed by any options (a cookie, a server identifier, a client subnet, an extended error). It is also the reason the header line so often says ADDITIONAL: 1 when no additional record is printed below: the count includes the OPT record. The option +bufsize sets the advertised size, anywhere from 0 to 65,535. In Wireshark the record appears among the additional records with the root as its name and type OPT, and the display filter dns.resp.type == 41 finds it; the fields worth knowing are dns.rr.udp_payload_size, dns.resp.ext_rcode, dns.resp.edns0_version, dns.resp.z.do and dns.opt.code. tcpdump compresses it into the count of additional records, printed in square brackets as a number followed by au. A decoder that does not know the type shows the fields raw, which is where a baffling class of 1232 or 4096 and an enormous TTL come from.

The reason it is worth knowing separately is diagnostic. Packet captures of DNS problems frequently show an OPT record with a buffer size that does not match what the path can carry, which produces truncation and retry behaviour that looks like intermittent failure: the answer is larger than a link on the way allows, the fragments are dropped, and the client waits before trying again or falling back to the Transmission Control Protocol (TCP). Lowering the advertised size is a standard workaround for a path that fragments badly, and recognizing OPT in a capture is what turns an unexplained DNS slowdown into a specific and fixable problem of path MTU (maximum transmission unit). RFC 9715 (January 2025) recommends advertising no more than 1,400 bytes; Unbound's edns-buffer-size defaults to 1,232, the value that fits the minimum IPv6 (Internet Protocol version 6) link of 1,280 bytes, and its manual notes that 512 gets past even the worst path at the price of excessive fallback to TCP. The same RFC 6891 warns of both extremes: a very large size invites drops and retransmissions with no hope of success, since some devices reject fragmented UDP, and a very small one pushes load on to TCP, especially with DNSSEC.

Three misreadings are common. The size in the record is the sender's receive capacity, not the size of the message that carries it, and each side states its own. The DO flag is a request for signatures and proofs, not a statement that the sender validates them. And the absence of an OPT record in an answer to a query that had one is information, not noise: either the server does not speak EDNS, or something between the two ends removed the record, and the comparison of the same query sent with +noedns, with the default record and over TCP usually says which. The details of sizes, options and the history of their deployment belong to EDNS itself; the OPT record is simply where all of it is written on the wire.

edns.def: Extension Mechanisms for DNS (Domain Name System), also written EDNS0 or EDNS(0): a backward-compatible extension of the DNS message, specified in RFC (Request for Comments) 6891, that adds an OPT pseudo-record to advertise UDP (User Datagram Protocol) payloads larger than 512 bytes and to carry extra flags, a longer response code and options.
edns.context: Extension Mechanisms for DNS (EDNS), standardized in Request for Comments (RFC) 6891, let the Domain Name System (DNS) carry larger responses, signal support for the DNS Security Extensions (DNSSEC), and pass options, all through the OPT pseudo-record, without breaking the legacy message format. A requestor adds one OPT record to the additional section of its query, stating the largest User Datagram Protocol (UDP) payload it can receive and which features it understands; a server that also speaks EDNS answers with its own. Nearly everything added to DNS since 1999 rides on it: DNSSEC, Client Subnet, cookies, padding for encrypted DNS and extended error codes.
edns.depth:
The Domain Name System (DNS) message format of 1987 has fixed fields that ran out. Request for Comments (RFC) 1035 restricts messages carried over the User Datagram Protocol (UDP) to 512 bytes, with longer ones truncated and the TC (truncation) bit set; the response code has four bits, so sixteen values; and a requestor has no way to say what it is capable of. Extension Mechanisms for DNS (EDNS) is the backward-compatible fix. Paul Vixie wrote the first specification, RFC 2671, in August 1999 as EDNS0; RFC 6891 of April 2013, by Joao Damas, Michael Graff and Vixie, revised it from deployment experience, is Internet Standard 75, and also retired the binary labels of RFC 2673. The zero is a version number, and version 0 is still the only one in the registry of the Internet Assigned Numbers Authority (IANA).

Everything is carried in one pseudo-record of type OPT, number 41, placed in the additional section of the message. It holds no DNS data, exists only on the wire and never in a zone file, must not be cached or forwarded, and may appear only once per message. Its fields are those of an ordinary resource record put to other uses. NAME is the root, a single zero byte. CLASS, 16 bits, is the requestor's UDP payload size, the largest message it can reassemble; values below 512 are treated as 512. The 32 bits of the time to live (TTL) field are split into an extended RCODE (response code) of 8 bits, which supplies the upper bits of a 12-bit response code, a version of 8 bits, the DO flag, by which a requestor asks for the records of the DNS Security Extensions (DNSSEC) and whose name stands for DNSSEC OK, and 15 further flag bits that stay zero until a later specification defines them. The record data is a list of options, each a 16-bit code, a 16-bit length and that many bytes of data; a code the receiver does not understand must be ignored.

Negotiation is implicit. An OPT record in a query means the requestor implements that version of EDNS; a responder that does must put an OPT record in its answer, and one that receives a query without OPT must not. A server that has never heard of EDNS answers FORMERR (format error) with no OPT record, which tells the requestor to retry with plain DNS; a server that implements EDNS but not the requested version answers BADVERS, response code 16, a value that only fits because of the extended RCODE. The requestor may remember for a short time that a server lacks EDNS, but RFC 6891 says no fallback should be made when DNSSEC or another EDNS-only feature is required. A response that still does not fit comes back truncated and the query is repeated over the Transmission Control Protocol (TCP), which RFC 7766 (March 2016) made mandatory for every general-purpose implementation.

DNSSEC is the reason EDNS became universal. The DO bit, defined in RFC 3225 in December 2001, is the first bit of the EDNS flags, and a server adds signatures and keys to an answer only when it is set. RFC 4035 requires a validating resolver to send OPT with DO set on every query, to accept messages of at least 1,220 bytes and preferably 4,000. Without EDNS, DNSSEC and several later extensions would simply not fit.

What size to advertise has changed with experience. RFC 6891 suggested 4,096 bytes as a starting point, falling back to something between 1,280 and 1,410 and finally to 512, and warned that a very large value guarantees fragmentation at the Internet Protocol (IP) layer and that some devices reject fragmented UDP. Fragments turned out to be both unreliable and a way to forge part of an answer, so DNS Flag Day 2020, on 1 October 2020, set the default the main open-source servers now ship, 1,232 bytes: the minimum IP version 6 (IPv6) link size of 1,280 minus 48 bytes of IPv6 and UDP headers. In BIND that is edns-udp-size 1232 and max-udp-size 1232, in Unbound edns-buffer-size: 1232. RFC 9715 (January 2025), written by Kazunori Fujiwara and Vixie, recommends a maximum DNS payload of 1,400 bytes over UDP, with smaller values allowed, and advises requestors to drop fragmented responses without reassembling them. A smaller buffer means more truncation, so TCP on port 53 must work end to end; the Flag Day page reminds operators that some firewalls still block it.

The options are where new features land, and IANA keeps the list. NSID, code 3 (RFC 5001, August 2007), asks a server to identify itself, which is how one tells the instances of an anycast service apart. Client Subnet, code 8, passes part of the client's address to authoritative servers. COOKIE, code 10 (RFC 7873, May 2016), is a lightweight defence against off-path forgery and against the use of a server for amplification. Code 11 (RFC 7828) lets a server signal how long an idle TCP session may stay open, Padding, code 12 (RFC 7830), hides message sizes on encrypted transports, and Extended DNS Error, code 15 (RFC 8914, October 2020), finally says why an answer was SERVFAIL (server failure), a code used for many sorts of error, a DNSSEC validation failure among them. As of 9 November 2026 codes up to 26 are assigned, 65001 to 65534 are reserved for local or experimental use, and two high numbers are registered to Cisco, for its Umbrella service. The flags registry holds DO in bit 0 and, since RFC 9824, CO (Compact Answers OK) in bit 1.

The operational trouble is middleboxes. Firewalls and load balancers that reject DNS messages containing an OPT record, or any message over 512 bytes, cause failures that look like intermittent resolution problems, and falling back to TCP is slower and sometimes blocked as well. RFC 6891 is explicit that a conformant middlebox must not limit DNS over UDP to 512 bytes and that one which merely forwards queries must neither modify nor delete the OPT record. For years resolvers hid the breakage by retrying without EDNS after a timeout, at a price RFC 8906 (September 2020) spells out: packet loss was misread as lack of EDNS support, and DNSSEC validation then failed for no visible reason. DNS Flag Day 2019 ended the practice. From about 1 February 2019, BIND 9.14.0, Knot Resolver, PowerDNS Recursor 4.2.0 and Unbound 1.9.0 treat a server that does not answer EDNS queries as dead, and the announcement told operators that firewalls must not drop DNS packets with EDNS extensions, naming older Juniper SRX software that did so by default. A resolver that works for simple names and fails for signed ones is usually meeting one of these devices.

With dig the whole mechanism can be exercised by hand. The output shows an OPT pseudosection whenever the server answered with EDNS. The option +noedns sends a plain 1987 query and +edns=0 an explicit version 0; +bufsize sets the advertised size; +dnssec, or +do, sets the DO bit; +nsid, +subnet, +padding and +ednsopt send individual options, and +cookie is on by default. Comparing a query sent with +noedns, the same query with +dnssec and a large +bufsize, and the same again with +tcp is the quickest way to prove that something on the path dislikes OPT records, large UDP messages or TCP port 53.

sirt.def: F5's team that handles security incidents and advisories.
sirt.context: The Security Incident Response Team at F5 investigates and coordinates responses to security issues in F5 products, publishing advisories and responding to reports, often in the same week a vulnerability is disclosed.

adsp.def: F5's unified platform branding for application delivery and security.
adsp.context: Application Delivery and Security Platform is F5's umbrella name for its converged delivery and security offering. It signals the direction customers are pointed towards when planning around F5's evolving product portfolio.

ad.def: AD stands for Active Directory, Microsoft's directory service; in everyday use it means Active Directory Domain Services (AD DS), the Windows domain, though the name also covers sibling Windows Server roles for certificates, federation and application directories. In routing, AD means administrative distance instead.
ad.context: In a Windows shop, "the AD" is the domain: the domain controllers and the users, groups and computers they hold, authenticated with Kerberos or NTLM (NT LAN Manager) and read over LDAP (Lightweight Directory Access Protocol). Microsoft uses the same two letters for several Windows Server roles, AD DS for the domain, AD CS (Active Directory Certificate Services) for certificates, AD FS (Active Directory Federation Services) for federation and AD LDS (Active Directory Lightweight Directory Services) for application directories, and once used them for Azure AD, the cloud service now called Microsoft Entra ID. Network and security products borrow the abbreviation for their integrations: access policies often query an AD agent or an AD Query step to resolve who a user is and which groups decide what they may reach. Read in a routing table, AD is administrative distance, a different thing entirely.
ad.depth:
The two letters are an abbreviation, and the first job is knowing which Active Directory is meant. Microsoft itself describes three Active Directory-based identity solutions that share a common name and technology but meet different needs. Active Directory Domain Services (AD DS) is the self-managed domain: in Microsoft's words an enterprise-ready LDAP (Lightweight Directory Access Protocol) server that provides identity and authentication, computer object management, Group Policy and trusts, and the central component of most on-premises Windows estates. Microsoft Entra ID, formerly Azure AD, is the cloud identity service, which can be synchronized with an on-premises AD DS so that users keep one identity. Microsoft Entra Domain Services is a managed domain offering a subset of AD DS features (domain join, Group Policy, LDAP, Kerberos and NTLM authentication) without forests, sites or replication links to design and with the domain controllers patched by Microsoft, though forest trusts to an on-premises domain remain possible. When someone says AD without qualification they nearly always mean AD DS; how that domain works, from forests and trusts to Kerberoasting, is the subject of the Active Directory entry.

AD LDS (Active Directory Lightweight Directory Services) is the role most often forgotten. Microsoft describes it as an LDAP directory service for directory-enabled applications, without the dependencies and domain-related restrictions of AD DS: it runs on member or stand-alone servers, one server can host several instances, each with its own independently managed schema, and it avoids the overhead of domains and forests and the single forest-wide schema. It was formerly called Active Directory Application Mode (ADAM), and it can take a copy of data synchronized from AD DS. It is the answer when an application needs its own directory and its own object classes and nobody wants to extend the domain's schema to hold them.

AD CS (Active Directory Certificate Services) is Microsoft's public key infrastructure (PKI) role. It runs root and subordinate certification authorities (CAs), offers web enrolment for certificates and certificate revocation lists (CRLs), an Online Responder that answers revocation status requests with signed responses, the Network Device Enrollment Service that lets routers and other devices without domain accounts obtain certificates, Trusted Platform Module (TPM) key attestation, and enrolment web services for machines outside the domain; Microsoft's current overview adds support for ML-DSA (Module-Lattice-Based Digital Signature Algorithm), the post-quantum signature algorithm standardized by NIST (National Institute of Standards and Technology). Its value and its danger come from the same integration: the directory's identities fill in certificates automatically, and Group Policy decides which users and machines may request which kinds. In June 2021 Will Schroeder and Lee Christensen of SpecterOps published Certified Pre-Owned, arguing that AD CS had been relatively overlooked while the rest of Active Directory was scrutinized. An enterprise CA issues certificates from templates that are themselves directory objects, certificate-based sign-in maps a certificate to an account by the user principal name (UPN) in its subject alternative name (SAN), and a template that lets the requester choose that name while allowing domain authentication lets an ordinary user obtain a certificate for anyone, including a domain administrator. They tagged the attack paths ESC1 onwards and wrote that nearly every environment with AD CS they had examined for these misconfigurations was vulnerable.

AD FS (Active Directory Federation Services) does federation: it shares identity and entitlement rights across security and enterprise boundaries and extends the single sign-on that works inside one organization to Internet-facing applications used by customers, partners and suppliers, with OpenID Connect and OAuth flows as well as the older protocols. Microsoft's comparison notes that Active Directory alone does not support SaaS (software as a service) applications natively and needs a federation system such as AD FS for them, which is why so many estates ran one. Microsoft's own overview now opens with the advice not to upgrade AD FS but to migrate to Microsoft Entra ID instead. AD RMS (Active Directory Rights Management Services) completes the family: information rights management in which the permissions travel inside the protected file, so a document can be barred from printing, forwarding or copying wherever it goes, although Microsoft lists what it cannot stop, from malware capturing the content to a recipient photographing the screen or retyping it.

The cloud name is where the abbreviation now misleads. Microsoft announced on 11 July 2023 that Azure Active Directory was becoming Microsoft Entra ID; its naming guidance says Azure Active Directory, Azure AD and AAD are replaced, discourages any acronym, and offers ME-ID only where space forces one. The rename deliberately left Windows Server Active Directory alone, so AD DS and AD FS keep their names, and Azure AD B2C kept its own while ceasing to be sold to new customers from 1 May 2025. Documents written before 2023 therefore say Azure AD for what is now Entra ID, and a request in 2026 to integrate with AD can mean the on-premises domain, the cloud tenant or a managed domain; asking which saves a design.

Network and security products use AD as shorthand for their directory integrations. FortiGate's Fortinet Single Sign-On (FSSO) learns who is behind an IP (Internet Protocol) address from agents: a domain controller (DC) agent installed on every controller, or a collector agent that polls the controllers itself, reports each logon with its workstation address and the user's domain local and global security groups; the collector agent talks to the FortiGate on TCP (Transmission Control Protocol) port 8000, listens on UDP (User Datagram Protocol) port 8002 for DC agents, and a FortiGate can list up to five collectors for redundancy. Firewall policies then match the group rather than the address. BIG-IP Access Policy Manager (APM) names its access policy items AD Auth and AD Query, the second reading the user's memberOf attribute, optionally with nested groups and the primary group, into session variables without authenticating anything. In both, AD is the source of truth for group membership, and a stale group in the directory becomes a wrong decision at the firewall.

Outside identity, the same two letters mean administrative distance, and network engineers meet that sense daily. Cisco defines it as a value used to rank the trustworthiness of routing information sources: when two protocols offer a route to the same prefix, the lower distance wins. The defaults worth remembering are 0 for a connected interface, 1 for a static route, 20 for external BGP (Border Gateway Protocol), 110 for OSPF (Open Shortest Path First), 200 for internal BGP and 255 for a source the router never installs. In a routing discussion "AD 110" is OSPF, not a directory, and a floating static route is a static route given a deliberately higher AD, Cisco's example uses 250 behind OSPF, so that it is installed only when the primary route is removed. Context decides the reading; in a glossary of networking and security terms both senses are live.

l4.def: The transport layer, handling ports and connections like TCP/UDP.
l4.context: Layer 4 of the OSI model is the transport layer, where TCP and UDP live. L4 load balancing forwards based on IP and port without inspecting application content, which is faster but blind to Layer 7 details like hostnames or URLs.

yaml.def: YAML Ain't Markup Language (YAML), a human-friendly data serialization language whose structure is carried by indentation; specified at yaml.org since 2004, now at version 1.2 (revision 1.2.2, 2021), and best known as the configuration format of Ansible, Kubernetes and CI (continuous integration) pipelines.
yaml.context: YAML (YAML Ain't Markup Language) is an indentation-based serialization format popular for configuration files, infrastructure manifests and continuous integration (CI) pipelines. It adds what hand-written JSON (JavaScript Object Notation) lacks, such as comments, references between nodes and multi-line strings, and since version 1.2 every JSON document is also valid YAML, though not the reverse. Its readability comes with sharp edges: indentation is syntax, unquoted values are given types by guessing (the country code NO turning into false under YAML 1.1 rules is the famous case), and loaders that can build arbitrary language objects have turned configuration files into code execution.
yaml.depth:
YAML is a recursive acronym, YAML Ain't Markup Language, and the specification describes it as a human-friendly, cross-language, Unicode-based data serialization language designed around the native data types of dynamic programming languages, useful for everything from configuration files to messaging, object persistence and data auditing. It was designed by Clark Evans, Oren Ben-Kiki and Ingy döt Net over three years on the yaml-core mailing list, growing out of Clark's and Oren's work on SML-DEV, a list about simplifying XML (Extensible Markup Language), and Ingy's plain-text serialization module for Perl. The first YAML framework was written in Perl in 2001, and Ruby became the first language to ship one in its core distribution, in 2003.

The versions and their dates matter, because parsers still disagree about which one they implement. The 1.0 final draft is dated 29 January 2004. The 1.1 final draft is dated 18 January 2005 on its own page (the specification index lists 30 December 2004). Around then, the 1.2.2 history recalls, the authors noticed that JSON (JavaScript Object Notation) was by sheer coincidence almost a complete subset of YAML, and in 2006 Kyrylo Simonov produced PyYAML and LibYAML, the libraries many other frameworks are built on or modelled after. Revision 1.2.0, dated 21 July 2009, set out to bring YAML into compliance with JSON as an official subset: it changed the implicit typing rules to align with JSON's productions, so booleans became true or false and the empty scalar null, removed the Unicode line breaks, and defined three built-in rule sets. Revision 1.2.1 followed on 1 October 2009. Revision 1.2.2, dated 1 October 2021, makes no normative change to the language: it corrects errors, adds clarity, moves the source to Markdown, and was the first new revision in twelve years, the work of a language design team that had been meeting regularly since 2020.

The relationship with JSON is one way. YAML 1.2 is a superset of JSON, so a valid JSON document is valid YAML 1.2, but a YAML file with comments, anchors or block scalars is not JSON. The spec even admits a small gap: its JSON-schema float expression accepts a number ending in a bare dot, which JSON does not, and that could not be fixed in 1.2.2. On input a processor must support the Unicode transformation formats (UTF) UTF-8 and UTF-16, and for JSON compatibility UTF-32 as well. What YAML adds is what makes it pleasant by hand: comments introduced by a hash sign, anchors marked with an ampersand and aliases marked with an asterisk so that a node can be defined once and referenced elsewhere, literal block scalars that keep their line breaks and folded ones that turn them into spaces, and optional document markers, three dashes to start and three dots to end.

The cost is that whitespace is syntax. Indentation decides structure, and the specification states that tab characters must not be used in indentation, since different systems treat tabs differently, which surprises anyone whose editor inserts them; tabs remain legal elsewhere, inside separating white space for example. A single misplaced space changes structure rather than raising an obvious error, and the failure often appears far from the edit, as a key nested one level deeper than intended. A colon followed by a space always starts a mapping, so Ansible's own guide has to warn that a value containing one must be quoted, and that a value starting with the double brace of a Jinja2 template variable must be quoted too, or YAML reads the brace as the start of a mapping.

The famous trap is implicit typing. A plain, unquoted scalar is matched against a list of patterns, and the list changed between versions. YAML 1.1's boolean type accepts y, yes, n, no, on and off, each in lower case, capitalized or upper case, alongside true and false; its integer type reads a leading zero as octal and accepts sexagesimal values such as 190:20:30. YAML 1.2's core schema keeps only true and false (in three capitalizations) as booleans, writes octal with a 0o prefix, and resolves anything that matches no pattern to a string. Parsers that still apply 1.1 rules produce the Norway problem, told by the author of StrictYAML: a list of country codes worked for GB, IE, FR and DE, then loading NO through PyYAML returned False and took a website down. The same essay shows a version number 9.3 loading as a float while 3.5.3 stayed a string, and a surname Null loading as None. The defence is to quote anything that must stay a string; Ansible's guide tells users to quote a literal yes or False, and version numbers such as 1.0, and to write booleans as lowercase true and false to satisfy yamllint's defaults. Kubernetes has gone further with KYAML, a stricter subset it documents for its own manifests: flow style with braces and brackets, every string double-quoted, aimed squarely at whitespace sensitivity and implicit type coercion while staying readable by existing YAML parsers.

The more dangerous trap is the loader. YAML has tags, and libraries that map tags to native types can construct arbitrary objects. PyYAML's own documentation warns that it is not safe to call yaml.load with data from an untrusted source, because yaml.load is as powerful as pickle.load and may call any Python function, and points to yaml.safe_load, which recognizes only standard YAML tags. The National Vulnerability Database (NVD) records the history in Common Vulnerabilities and Exposures (CVE) entries: CVE-2017-18342, rated 9.8 under CVSS (Common Vulnerability Scoring System) 3.1, for yaml.load executing arbitrary code before PyYAML 5.1, which deprecated the plain call and introduced an explicit UnsafeLoader; CVE-2020-1747, for the full_load path and its FullLoader before 5.3.1, abused through the python/object/new constructor; and CVE-2020-14343, an incomplete fix for that one, closed in 5.4. Java has the same class: CVE-2022-1471 says SnakeYAML's Constructor does not restrict the types it instantiates, so attacker-supplied YAML can lead to remote code execution, and recommends SafeConstructor and version 2.0 or later. Parsing alone can also exhaust a server: CVE-2019-11253 let authorized users send malicious YAML or JSON that drove the Kubernetes API (application programming interface) server to excessive CPU (central processing unit) or memory use, and before Kubernetes 1.14 the default role-based access control (RBAC) policy let anonymous users trigger it.

Where engineers meet YAML is configuration as code. Ansible playbooks are expressed in YAML, and nearly every file starts with a list of dictionaries. Kubernetes manifests are YAML by convention, although JSON is accepted, and kubectl converts them to JSON or another supported format before calling the API. GitHub Actions workflows must be YAML files with a .yml or .yaml extension in the repository's .github/workflows directory. Network automation inherits all of this: a variables file that holds a VLAN (virtual local area network) list, an interface description or a firmware version is exactly where a leading zero, a bare no or a 1.10 that becomes 1.1 does its damage. The practical rules follow from the history: know which version your parser implements, quote strings that could look like anything else, load untrusted input only with a safe loader, and validate the result against a schema rather than trusting that a file which parses cleanly means what it says.

jws.def: A standard for signing data represented as JSON.
jws.context: JSON Web Signature (RFC 7515) defines how to sign a payload and encode the signature compactly. It underlies signed JWTs; notably its 'none' algorithm, meant for unsecured tokens, is a classic source of verification bugs.
jws.depth:
JSON Web Signature is the signing half of the JOSE family and the structure underneath a signed JWT: a header, a payload and a signature, base64url encoded and joined by dots.

Its recurring danger is the algorithm field in the header, which describes what the sender used and must never be what the receiver trusts. Accepting the header's claim allows the none algorithm and the RS256-to-HS256 confusion attack. The correct implementation fixes the acceptable algorithm out of band and rejects anything else, and libraries that made this the default rather than an option removed a whole class of vulnerability from the ecosystem.

pdf.def: PDF (Portable Document Format) is a file format for fixed-layout documents, specified by Adobe from 1993 and standardized by the International Organization for Standardization (ISO) as ISO 32000-1:2008 (PDF 1.7) and ISO 32000-2 (PDF 2.0). Besides text, fonts and images, a PDF can carry forms, scripts, embedded files and actions, which is why it is also a common malware carrier.
pdf.context: Portable Document Format (PDF), standardized by ISO (International Organization for Standardization) as ISO 32000, preserves a document's exact layout across devices: fonts, images and vector graphics are described with an imaging model derived from PostScript, so the page looks the same on any screen or printer. That fidelity is why contracts, invoices, manuals and course material travel as PDF, and why attackers like it: a PDF can also run JavaScript, launch actions and carry embedded files, and readers have a long CVE (Common Vulnerabilities and Exposures) history. In server-side contexts, PDF or screenshot generators are a common SSRF (server-side request forgery) vector because they fetch URLs (Uniform Resource Locators) while rendering. PDF/A is the archival subset that forbids most of the risky features.
pdf.depth:
PDF (Portable Document Format) began at Adobe. According to Adobe, co-founder John Warnock launched the Camelot Project in 1991 with the aim of moving paper documents into digital form, and by 1992 it had become PDF. The foreword of the ISO (International Organization for Standardization) standard says Adobe published the complete PDF specification in 1993 and kept developing it, through versions 1.0 to 1.7, until 2007; the last Adobe edition, PDF Reference, sixth edition, of November 2006, describes PDF 1.7. At the core is an imaging model derived from the PostScript page description language, which is what makes a PDF look the same everywhere: fonts are embedded or referenced, pages are drawn by vector and raster operators, and nothing reflows. The goal the standard states is to let users exchange and view documents independently of the environment in which they were created, viewed or printed.

Standardization came in two steps. On 29 January 2007 Adobe announced that it would release the full PDF 1.7 specification to ANSI (American National Standards Institute) and AIIM, the enterprise content management association, for publication by ISO. ISO's committee TC 171/SC 2 adopted it under a fast-track procedure, approved it in January 2008 and put ISO 32000-1:2008 on sale in July 2008; ISO last confirmed it in 2023, and Adobe offers a free copy whose technical content is identical. PDF 2.0, ISO 32000-2, was first published in July 2017 and replaced by the dated revision ISO 32000-2:2020, which fixed problems found during early adoption and corrected many clauses that PDF 1.7 shares. Since 5 April 2023 it has been available at no cost from the PDF Association, with Adobe, Apryse and Foxit sponsoring the access. Specialized subsets were already ISO standards by 2008, among them PDF/X for print exchange and PDF/A for archiving.

The file structure explains several security properties. A PDF begins with a header of %PDF- followed by a version, 1.0 to 1.7 in ISO 32000-1, and consists of numbered objects, a cross-reference table that locates them and a trailer that points to the document catalogue. Changes can be saved as incremental updates: the standard says they are appended to the end of the file, leaving the original contents intact. That lets small changes to a large file be saved quickly, but it means content that looks deleted in an edited PDF may still be inside the file, and that one file can hold several versions of the same document. Object streams, compression filters and hex-escaped names (for example /J#53 for /JS) let the same structure be written in many ways, which defeats naive string matching.

The features attackers use are part of the standard. An OpenAction entry in the catalogue, or additional-actions (AA) entries on pages and fields, runs something when the document or a page opens. A JavaScript action executes a script written against Adobe's JavaScript for Acrobat API (application programming interface); a launch action launches an application or opens or prints another document; embedded file streams, introduced in PDF 1.3, put whole files inside the PDF; and interactive forms can use XFA (XML Forms Architecture). Didier Stevens, whose pdfid tool triages suspicious files by counting exactly these keywords (/JS, /JavaScript, /AA, /OpenAction, /Launch, /RichMedia, /JBIG2Decode, /XFA, /ObjStm and /Encrypt), reports that almost all the malicious PDFs he has found in the wild contained JavaScript triggered by an automatic action, and that most had only one page; the combination of an automatic action and JavaScript is what makes a document very suspicious. The analysis then moves to his pdf-parser to extract the objects.

The vulnerability record is long and still growing. CVE (Common Vulnerabilities and Exposures) 2009-0927 was a stack-based buffer overflow reachable through the getIcon method of a Collab object in Adobe Reader and Acrobat 9 before 9.1, 8 before 8.1.3 and 7 before 7.1.1; CISA (Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency) added it to its Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalogue in March 2022, thirteen years later. CVE-2010-1240 needed no memory corruption at all: Reader and Acrobat did not restrict the text of the Launch File warning dialog, so a PDF could tell the user that clicking Open would decrypt a message and then run a local program. CVE-2023-26369, an out-of-bounds write in Acrobat Reader that ran code when a victim opened a malicious file, was published on 13 September 2023 and listed as known exploited the next day. Browser viewers are attack surface too: CVE-2024-4367, a missing type check in font handling in PDF.js, the viewer built into Firefox, allowed arbitrary JavaScript in the PDF.js context before Firefox 126, Firefox ESR (Extended Support Release) 115.11 and Thunderbird 115.11.

Delivery is mostly email. MITRE ATT&CK's technique T1566.001, spearphishing attachment, lists PDFs beside Office documents, executables and archives as the usual attachments and records groups that sent tailored PDFs carrying exploits or nothing but a link to an attacker-controlled landing page; a PDF with one convincing button and no script passes many filters that look for code. The server side has its own problem. Services that turn HTML (Hypertext Markup Language) into PDF render it with a browser engine, and the engine fetches whatever the HTML references: the NVD (National Vulnerability Database) records CVE-2022-35583, in which wkhtmltopdf 0.12.6 could be made to fetch an internal address through an injected iframe, scored 9.8. Any PDF or screenshot generator that accepts user-supplied HTML or URLs (Uniform Resource Locators) therefore needs the same egress controls as any other SSRF (server-side request forgery) target.

PDF/A is the deliberate opposite. ISO 19005-1:2005, published in October 2005 and still current, defines a profile of PDF 1.4 for long-term preservation. As the Library of Congress summarizes it, audio and video are forbidden, JavaScript and executable file launches are prohibited, every font must be embedded, encryption is not allowed and XMP (Extensible Metadata Platform) metadata is mandatory, with conformance level A meeting every requirement and level B only those for reliable visual appearance. For security teams that makes PDF/A a useful policy target for archived records: a file that validates as PDF/A carries no scripts and no launch actions, while ordinary PDF, the format the industry actually exchanges, can carry all of them.

bsd.def: Berkeley Software Distribution (BSD): the line of Unix releases produced at the University of California, Berkeley, from 1977 to 1995, and the systems descended from it (FreeBSD, NetBSD, OpenBSD). The name also labels what that work left behind: the permissive BSD licences, the sockets interface and the original syslog message format.
bsd.context: Berkeley Software Distribution (BSD) began in 1977 as a tape of additions to Bell Labs Unix assembled by Bill Joy at the University of California, Berkeley, and grew into a complete operating system whose networking code, paid for by the Defense Advanced Research Projects Agency (DARPA), made TCP/IP (Transmission Control Protocol/Internet Protocol) a normal part of Unix. An engineer meets the name in four places: the operating systems that descend from it (FreeBSD, NetBSD, OpenBSD and the BSD layer of Apple's kernel); the permissive BSD licences; the sockets programming interface; and BSD syslog, the original, loosely specified log message format that Request for Comments (RFC) 3164 described and RFC 5424 later replaced.
bsd.depth:
Berkeley Software Distribution (BSD) now names three different things. It is a series of Unix releases made at the University of California, Berkeley, between 1977 and 1995, most of them by the Computer Systems Research Group (CSRG). It is the family of operating systems that descend from the last of those releases: FreeBSD, NetBSD, OpenBSD and DragonFly BSD, plus the BSD layer inside Apple's kernel. And it is an adjective attached to what Berkeley gave the rest of the industry: the BSD licences, BSD sockets, the BSD Packet Filter and BSD syslog. No current product is called simply BSD, and none of these systems is a Linux distribution: each project maintains its own kernel and its own userland together, in FreeBSD's case in a single repository.

Unix reached Berkeley in January 1974, when a Version 4 tape was installed on a PDP-11/45 shared by three departments. Ken Thompson spent the 1975 to 1976 academic year there on sabbatical, and two graduate students who arrived that autumn, Bill Joy and Chuck Haley, began improving the system. Early in 1977 Joy assembled the first Berkeley Software Distribution, a tape holding a Pascal system and the ex editor, and sent out about thirty copies. The second distribution (2BSD) followed in mid-1978 with the vi editor and termcap. 3BSD, shipped in December 1979, was the first for the 32-bit VAX and added a virtual memory kernel. These dates come from the account written by Marshall Kirk McKusick, who was part of the group.

The step that matters to network engineers was paid for by the Defense Advanced Research Projects Agency (DARPA), which wanted one operating system across its research sites and chose Unix for its portability. Professor Bob Fabry obtained an 18-month contract starting in April 1980 and set up the CSRG, with Joy leading development. 4BSD came out in October 1980 and 4.1BSD in June 1981; the numbering stayed at 4 because AT&T objected that a 5BSD would be confused with its own System V. 4.2BSD, released in August 1983, integrated an implementation of TCP/IP (Transmission Control Protocol/Internet Protocol) supplied by Rob Gurwitz of Bolt, Beranek and Newman (BBN), behind a new interprocess communication interface designed to carry more than one protocol family, together with McKusick's fast file system. More than 1,000 site licences were issued within eighteen months, and most Unix vendors shipped 4.2BSD in preference to System V, which at the time had neither networking nor the fast file system. For 4.3BSD (June 1986) DARPA had an independent laboratory compare Berkeley's TCP/IP code with BBN's, and kept Berkeley's.

That interface is the sockets API (application programming interface), which Request for Comments (RFC) 3493 of the Internet Engineering Task Force (IETF) calls the de facto standard for TCP/IP applications, on Unix and elsewhere. The same RFC still gives separate socket address structures for 4.3BSD-based and 4.4BSD-based systems, because 4.4BSD shrank the family field to 8 bits to make room for a length field. Other Berkeley names survive in daily use. RFC 2001 records that fast retransmit first appeared in the 4.3BSD Tahoe release and fast recovery in 4.3BSD Reno, which is where the TCP variants Tahoe, Reno and NewReno (RFC 6582) get their names. The remote commands rcp, rsh and rlogin date from the development snapshot of April 1982; the r prefix marked them as temporary. BIND (Berkeley Internet Name Domain), the name server, began as a graduate-student project under a DARPA grant and was maintained by the CSRG up to version 4.8.3. RFC 1122 even carries a footnote on a Berkeley mistake: 4.2BSD put zeros where the standard broadcast address has ones, so hosts are asked to accept both forms.

The BSD Packet Filter (BPF) is the piece closest to daily troubleshooting. Steven McCanne and Van Jacobson of Lawrence Berkeley Laboratory presented it at the Winter 1993 USENIX conference: a small register machine in the kernel, with an accumulator, an index register and a scratch memory store, that discards unwanted packets before they are copied to user space. They measured its filter evaluator at up to 20 times faster than the stack-based design it replaced, and the capture path as a whole at up to 100 times faster than Sun's equivalent on the same hardware. The compiler that turns a filter expression into BPF instructions shipped as part of tcpdump, so a tcpdump capture filter is, underneath, a program for that machine.

BSD syslog is the sense that appears in device configuration. The syslog daemon and protocol were invented by Eric Allman and spread with Berkeley's TCP/IP systems; nobody specified them until RFC 3164, The BSD syslog Protocol, an Informational document of August 2001 that describes observed behaviour. Its message travels over the User Datagram Protocol (UDP) to port 514, fits in 1,024 bytes and has three parts: a priority value (PRI) in angle brackets, computed as the facility number times 8 plus the severity, so that facility local4 at severity notice gives 165; a header with a timestamp in the form Mmm dd hh:mm:ss, in local time with neither year nor time zone, followed by the hostname; and the message, which opens with a tag of at most 32 alphanumeric characters naming the program. RFC 5424 obsoleted it in March 2009, adding a version number, a timestamp derived from RFC 3339 that carries the year, fractions of a second and the offset from universal time, structured data, and Transport Layer Security (TLS) as the transport every implementation must support. Its authors found that real implementations agreed on little beyond the leading priority value. Devices still offer both: on a Palo Alto Networks firewall, for example, the format of a syslog server profile is BSD, the default, or IETF.

The licence came out of a commercial request. Vendors building TCP/IP products wanted Berkeley's networking code without paying for an AT&T source licence, and in June 1989 the university published Networking Release 1 under terms that asked only that the copyright notices be kept and that product documentation credit the university. The classic text has four clauses: keep the notice in source, reproduce it with binaries, acknowledge the university in all advertising, and do not use its name to endorse derived products. On 22 July 1999 William Hoskins, director of Berkeley's Office of Technology Licensing, deleted the advertising clause. That leaves the three-clause licence, which the Software Package Data Exchange (SPDX) list identifies as BSD-3-Clause and which is also called New or Modified BSD; dropping the endorsement clause as well gives the two-clause licence (BSD-2-Clause, also Simplified or FreeBSD), which the NetBSD Foundation adopted for its own code in 2008. The phrase BSD licence therefore says little until the identifier is named.

The licence is arguably the more consequential export. Permissive terms allow the code to be folded into closed products with no reciprocal obligation, which is why BSD-derived networking code ended up in commercial operating systems, in appliances and in the network stacks of devices whose vendors never contributed anything back. McKusick notes that even the vendors that returned to System V carried over large parts of 4.3BSD, the networking subsystem above all. The projects treat this as intended: FreeBSD's handbook lists incorporation into closed products among the system's strengths and prefers the BSD licence to the GNU General Public License (GPL) where it has the choice, and OpenBSD's goals state that the GPL is not acceptable for new code, because the aim is source that anyone can use for any purpose. Whether that is the licence working as designed or a failure to sustain the commons is the long-running argument between the permissive and copyleft camps, and it is a disagreement about incentives, not about technology. Some large users give back by choice: Netflix says the improvements it makes to FreeBSD for its Open Connect appliances are contributed upstream.

Freeing the rest of the system took a lawsuit. Networking Release 2 (June 1991) contained everything except six kernel files that still derived from AT&T code; Bill Jolitz wrote replacements and released 386/BSD for 386-based personal computers, and Berkeley Software Design, Incorporated (BSDI) began selling a supported version in January 1992 for 995 dollars. Unix System Laboratories (USL), AT&T's Unix subsidiary, sued BSDI and then the university. A federal judge refused an injunction, Novell bought USL, and the settlement of January 1994 removed three files out of 18,000 and added USL copyright notices to about 70. The unencumbered result, 4.4BSD-Lite, was released in June 1994, and after Release 2 in June 1995 the CSRG was disbanded. NetBSD (version 0.8 on 20 April 1993) and FreeBSD (1.0 in December 1993) had both started from Networking Release 2 and 386/BSD and had to rebase on 4.4BSD-Lite. OpenBSD split from NetBSD in the mid-1990s with security as its focus, and DragonFly BSD forked from FreeBSD 4.8 in June 2003.

Their code is closer than most engineers think. OpenSSH comes from OpenBSD, first shipped with OpenBSD 2.6 on 1 December 1999, and so does the pf packet filter, imported on 24 June 2001; OpenBSD itself reached release 8.0, its 61st, on 20 October 2026. Juniper describes Junos OS as based on a FreeBSD kernel, pfSense is a customized FreeBSD distribution managed through a web interface, Netflix serves video from FreeBSD, and Apple documents the BSD portion of the OS X kernel as derived primarily from FreeBSD. Three misreadings are common. BSD in a logging menu means the RFC 3164 format, whatever operating system the device runs. A BSD-format log line has no year and no time zone, so a collector in another zone, or an archive that crosses New Year, has to supply both; RFC 5424 suggests adding the current year and the collector's time zone when converting. And BSD-based does not mean interchangeable: the systems have been separate code bases for more than three decades.

pri.def: The priority value (PRI) at the start of every syslog message: a number from 0 to 191, written between angle brackets, that encodes the message's facility and severity as facility times 8 plus severity.
pri.context: The PRI (priority value) is the number in angle brackets at the start of a syslog line, defined in RFC (Request for Comments) 5424 and described for the older BSD (Berkeley Software Distribution) format in RFC 3164. It packs two values into one integer, the facility (0 to 23, which subsystem sent it) and the severity (0 to 7, how urgent it is), and both come back with one division: the quotient by 8 is the facility, the remainder the severity.
pri.depth:
The PRI (priority value) is the first field of a syslog message, and RFC (Request for Comments) 5424, The Syslog Protocol (March 2009, Rainer Gerhards), defines it exactly. The PRI part is three, four or five characters long: an opening angle bracket, one to three decimal digits, and a closing angle bracket. The number between the brackets is the Priority value (PRIVAL), its range is 0 to 191, and leading zeros are forbidden, so a zero may follow the bracket only when the value itself is 0. In an RFC 5424 message the PRI is followed immediately by the VERSION field, currently 1; in the older BSD (Berkeley Software Distribution) format that RFC 3164 described in August 2001 it is followed by the timestamp. The PRI is the one thing every implementation shares: RFC 5424's own appendix says research found very little in common between syslog implementations on different platforms, except that messages start with the PRIVAL in angle brackets, and that the new protocol kept the PRI syntax and semantics so that legacy systems could still put messages into the right bins. Despite the name, it is a label for sorting and filtering, not a queueing priority.

The arithmetic is the whole mechanism. RFC 5424 computes the value by multiplying the facility number by 8 and adding the severity. Facilities run from 0 to 23 and severities from 0 to 7, which gives 24 times 8, or 192 possible values, hence 0 to 191. Decoding is the reverse: divide by 8, and the whole-number quotient is the facility and the remainder the severity. Since 8 is 2 to the power 3, the low three bits of the number are the severity and the bits above them the facility. RFC 5424's own example message starts with the PRI value 34 in angle brackets: 34 divided by 8 is 4 remainder 2, facility 4 (security and authorization) and severity 2 (critical), which fits a message reporting that su root failed. Its other examples are 0, a kernel emergency, and 165, which is 20 times 8 plus 5, local4 at Notice. The util-linux logger manual gives a fourth: local0.info, facility 16 and level 6, becomes 134. Two values deserve memorizing for diagnosis. 13 is user.notice, 1 times 8 plus 5: it is the default of logger on Linux, and RFC 3164 also made it the value a relay inserts, together with a timestamp, when a message arrives with no valid PRI, so a flood of 13s at a collector can mean the senders are not writing a PRI at all. And 189, local7 at notice, is what the FortiGate default facility produces at that severity.

The facility table in RFC 5424 is: 0 kernel messages, 1 user-level messages, 2 mail system, 3 system daemons, 4 security/authorization messages, 5 messages generated internally by syslogd, 6 line printer subsystem, 7 network news subsystem, 8 UUCP (Unix-to-Unix Copy) subsystem, 9 clock daemon, 10 security/authorization messages, 11 FTP (File Transfer Protocol) daemon, 12 NTP (Network Time Protocol) subsystem, 13 log audit, 14 log alert, 15 clock daemon, and 16 to 23, local use 0 to 7 (local0 to local7). The duplicates are history, and RFC 3164 records it: operating systems were found using facilities 4, 10, 13 and 14 for similar security, authorization, audit and alert messages, and both 9 and 15 for clock (cron and at) messages. On Linux the names are the syslog(3) constants, where LOG_AUTHPRIV is the private security channel, LOG_CRON is the clock daemon and LOG_USER is the default facility for a program that names none. RFC 5424 is careful to call the facility and severity tables not normative but often used; only the ranges are mandatory. The eight local facilities are where network equipment lives, because their meaning is left to the site: one team's local7 is firewalls, another's is switches, and the convention has to be written down.

The severity table runs the other way from intuition, with the most urgent first: 0 Emergency (system is unusable), 1 Alert (action must be taken immediately), 2 Critical, 3 Error, 4 Warning, 5 Notice (normal but significant condition), 6 Informational and 7 Debug. RFC 5424's implementer guidance asks that debugging and testing messages use 7 and that 0 be kept for very high importance, such as a serious hardware failure or imminent power failure, and it adds a warning every SIEM (security information and event management) engineer learns the hard way: severities are subjective, and a relay or collector should not assume that all originators share the same definition.

The word priority causes most of the confusion, because the field means three different things depending on who uses it. In RFC 5424 the Priority value is the combined number. In the classic selector syntax that rsyslog keeps, facility.priority, the priority is only the severity, and mail.err logs messages of err and every more severe level, not one exact value. rsyslog's syslogpriority property returns the same number as syslogseverity, for historical reasons, while its pri property returns the undecoded PRI and pri-text prints it as facility.severity followed by the number. And FortiGate's config log syslogd setting has a priority option, default or low, which sets the transmission priority of the log traffic and has nothing to do with the PRI. Knowing that facility and severity are packed together is what turns a confusing filter into an obvious one. A rule written against a raw PRI value catches one facility and severity combination rather than a severity across all sources: matching 34 finds critical authorization messages and nothing else. Comparing raw PRI values as if they were severities is worse, because the PRI value 40 (facility 5, Emergency) is larger than the PRI value 7 (kernel, Debug). A collector told to keep everything at or above a threshold, or to keep only certain facilities, may silently drop a facility nobody thought about, which is how a device whose default facility changed disappears from a dashboard without an error. The same rsyslog documentation that accepts decimal numbers in selectors tells you not to use them.

Each platform sets the facility its own way. A Linux program passes the facility to openlog or syslog and the level with each message; from the shell, logger -p local3.info sends a message as informational in the local3 facility, logger defaults to user.notice, its --prio-prefix option reads a PRI already present at the start of each input line, and --rfc3164 or --rfc5424 choose the format for a remote server. On a FortiGate the remote syslog facility is set under config log syslogd setting with set facility, which defaults to local7 and accepts the names kernel through clock and local0 through local7; the same block chooses the format (default, csv, cef or rfc5424), the transport mode (udp, legacy-reliable after RFC 3195 or reliable after RFC 6587) and the port, 514 by default. On F5 BIG-IP, a remote-syslog log destination formats messages into syslog and hands them to a Remote High-Speed Log destination; its default-facility, local0 unless changed and limited to local0 through local7, and its default-severity, info unless changed, apply to messages that do not already carry them, so such a message arrives as the PRI value 134, and its format is rfc3164 by default, with rfc5424 and legacy-bigip as the alternatives. BIG-IP's own system logging uses the same eight severity names, from Emergency to Debug, with a minimum level for each event type.

The PRI does not change with the transport. Syslog over UDP (User Datagram Protocol) uses port 514, as RFC 3164 recorded and RFC 5426 (March 2009) kept; syslog over TLS (Transport Layer Security) uses TCP (Transmission Control Protocol) port 6514 under RFC 5425; and RFC 6587 (April 2012, published with Historic status) documents how syslog messages are framed over plain TCP. RFC 5424 supports UDP but does not recommend it, and recommends TLS. What does change between formats is everything after the PRI: an RFC 3164 timestamp has no year and no time zone, while an RFC 5424 message adds VERSION, a full timestamp, APP-NAME, PROCID, MSGID and structured data. The protocol itself is older than any RFC. RFC 3164 describes it as originally developed on the BSD TCP/IP implementations and credits Eric Allman as the original inventor and author of the syslog daemon and protocol, and RFC 3164 is Informational because it described observed behaviour rather than a standard. The numbers worth keeping in mind: multiply by 8, facilities 0 to 23, severities 0 to 7 with 0 the most severe, a maximum of 191, three to five characters with the brackets, 13 as the inserted default, and ports 514 and 6514.

snat.def: Source network address translation (SNAT): rewriting the source IP (Internet Protocol) address, and usually the source port, of connections as they pass through a device, so that replies come back to that device; F5's BIG-IP documentation also expands it as secure network address translation.
snat.context: Source network address translation (SNAT) makes connections appear to originate from the device's address rather than the client's. On BIG-IP it ensures return traffic comes back through the proxy, at the cost of hiding the original client IP (Internet Protocol) address from the server; on firewalls and Linux routers it is how a private network shares a few public addresses. Every translated connection needs a free source port on the translation address, so one address can carry only about 65,000 connections to any one destination, and port exhaustion under load is SNAT's characteristic failure.
snat.depth:
What it is. Network address translation (NAT) comes in two directions: destination NAT rewrites where a packet is going, as a virtual server or port forward does, and source NAT rewrites where it appears to come from. RFC (Request for Comments) 3022 (January 2001) defines the two traditional forms: Basic NAT maps one set of IP addresses onto another, and NAPT (network address port translation) maps many addresses and their TCP (Transmission Control Protocol) and UDP (User Datagram Protocol) ports onto a single address and its ports. SNAT is the vendor name for applying either in the source direction; F5's own manuals expand it both as secure network address translation and as source network address translation. On a firewall or home router SNAT is how private hosts reach the internet through a few public addresses. On a load balancer it usually exists to solve a routing problem rather than an addressing one.

The return-traffic problem on BIG-IP. F5's routing manual describes the normal case first: servers on the same subnet as the BIG-IP, clients elsewhere, and the BIG-IP as the servers' default gateway, so replies pass back through it and are translated from the pool member's address to the virtual server's. When that does not hold, a server replies directly, the client sees a response from an address it never contacted and rejects it. F5 lists the cases: clients and servers on the same network (the fix it calls virtual server bounceback), servers whose default route cannot point at the BIG-IP, and OneConnect connection reuse, where without SNAT the server-side source address remains that of whichever client opened the connection. An inbound SNAT translates the client's source address to a BIG-IP address, so the server answers the BIG-IP, which holds the connection state and can return the reply correctly; an outbound SNAT hides servers' private addresses when they open connections to the outside.

The kinds of SNAT on BIG-IP. A standard SNAT object maps one or more origin addresses to a specific translation address, to a SNAT pool or to automap; a SNAT pool can also be assigned directly to a virtual server, and an intelligent SNAT chooses the translation in an iRule. Compared with a BIG-IP NAT, which maps exactly one address and leaves all ports of the internal node open, a SNAT can map many origins to one translation address, supports only TCP and UDP by default, is tracked as connections, and is enabled on all VLANs (virtual local area networks) by default. Automap is the common choice: the system builds a SNAT pool from its own self IP addresses, preferring the floating self IPs on the egress VLAN so the address moves with a failover, and alternating among them if there are several. The trap F5 documents is a missing floating self IP on the egress VLAN, or one that was converted from a static self IP, in which case automap may use an address that is not the one intended. SNAT pool members are used in a least-connections fashion, and one pool may hold addresses from several egress networks.

The arithmetic of port exhaustion. Every translated connection needs a source port on the translation address that no other connection from that address to the same remote socket is using. A port is a 16-bit number, so each SNAT address has 65,535 of them; BIG-IP tries to preserve the client's source port and translates it only when that port is already in use. Because a connection is identified by the full socket pair (source address, source port, destination address, destination port), one SNAT address can carry more than 65,535 connections in total, but only about 65,535 at once to any single pool member. F5's guidance is to treat 65,535 concurrent connections as the practical capacity of one SNAT address and to add addresses, through a SNAT pool or more self IPs for automap, when more are needed. Exhaustion shows up as connections failing intermittently under load rather than as an error that names itself; BIG-IP can warn before it happens with the traffic-control settings port-find-threshold-warning (enabled by default), port-find-threshold-trigger (8 failed attempts to find a free port) and port-find-threshold-timeout (30 seconds), which log an error and raise an SNMP (Simple Network Management Protocol) alert.

The client address it hides. After SNAT the server sees the BIG-IP's address on every connection, which breaks source-based access control and makes server logs useless for attribution unless the original address travels some other way. For HTTP (Hypertext Transfer Protocol) the usual answer is a header: BIG-IP's HTTP profile can insert X-Forwarded-For, an option disabled by default, and RFC 7239 (June 2014) standardized the Forwarded header for the same purpose, noting X-Forwarded-For as its non-standard predecessor. For protocols with no such header the client address is simply gone from the server's point of view, which is the strongest argument for routing return traffic through the BIG-IP instead, where the network allows it.

On FortiGate. FortiOS performs SNAT in the firewall policy, by default to the outgoing interface address, or through IP pools. An overload pool behaves like interface NAT spread over several addresses, with 60,416 ports per address, and maps each internal host to a pool address by its source address modulo the number of pool addresses; a one-to-one pool disables port translation and gives each internal host its own address; a fixed port range pool assigns each internal address a predictable slice of ports; and port block allocation hands out blocks, so with a block size of 128 and 8 blocks per user one external address yields 472 blocks, 1,024 ports per user and room for 59 users. Central SNAT moves all of this into its own table, read top-down after the security policy has matched; it is off by default, and when enabled the per-policy NAT option is skipped, while policy-based NGFW (next-generation firewall) mode implies it.

On Linux. In iptables the SNAT target, valid in the nat table's POSTROUTING and INPUT chains, rewrites the source of a connection's packets to an address or range given with --to-source, optionally with a port range; without one, the kernel keeps ports below 512 below 512, ports from 512 to 1023 below 1024 and others at 1024 or above, and changes no port where it can avoid it, while --random and --random-fully randomize the mapping and --persistent keeps a client on the same address. MASQUERADE is SNAT to whatever address the outgoing interface currently has, meant for dynamically assigned addresses; it also forgets its connections when the interface goes down, which is why the manual says a host with a static address should use SNAT instead.

How a NAT ought to behave. RFC 4787 (January 2007, Best Current Practice BCP 127), later updated by RFC 6888 for carrier-grade NAT and by RFC 7857, sets behaviour for NATs that translate UDP: endpoint-independent mapping, so a host keeps the same external address and port whatever it talks to; paired address pooling, so one internal host always gets the same external address; no port overloading; preservation of the well-known and ephemeral port ranges; UDP mapping timers of no less than two minutes, five or more recommended; hairpinning; and UDP ALGs (application level gateways) turned off by default. A firewall that SNATs a whole site to the internet should meet these; a load balancer's SNAT towards a server pool is a different job, but the same port arithmetic governs both.

msrdp.def: Microsoft's protocol for remote graphical desktop sessions.
msrdp.context: Microsoft Remote Desktop Protocol carries remote desktop sessions. MSRDP persistence on a load balancer uses the session's routing token to keep a reconnecting client on the same backend server.

wccp.def: A protocol for transparently redirecting traffic to a cache or proxy.
wccp.context: Web Cache Communication Protocol lets a router redirect selected traffic to a cache or security appliance without the client being configured for it. It is one way transparent proxy interception is set up.

hsts.def: HTTP Strict Transport Security (HSTS) is a response header, Strict-Transport-Security, with which a site tells browsers to use only HTTPS (Hypertext Transfer Protocol Secure) for its host name, and optionally its subdomains, for a stated number of seconds, and to refuse to connect when the certificate is not valid.
hsts.context: HTTP Strict Transport Security (HSTS), Request for Comments (RFC) 6797, tells a browser to only ever connect to a site over HTTPS (Hypertext Transfer Protocol Secure), refusing plaintext and blocking click-through on certificate warnings. It defends against downgrade and stripping attacks. The policy is learned from a header received over a secure connection, so the very first visit stays exposed unless the name is on a browser's preload list. A long max-age with includeSubDomains is a commitment that browsers keep even if the site later wants plain HTTP (Hypertext Transfer Protocol) on some host.
hsts.depth:
HSTS (HTTP Strict Transport Security) closes a gap that HTTPS (Hypertext Transfer Protocol Secure) alone leaves open. A user typing a bare hostname makes an initial plaintext request, and an attacker positioned on the path can intercept that first request and keep the entire session on HTTP, stripping the upgrade before it happens. The redirect to HTTPS is only as trustworthy as the request that received it. Request for Comments (RFC) 6797, published in November 2012 by J. Hodges of PayPal, C. Jackson of Carnegie Mellon University and A. Barth of Google, frames the threats concretely: passive sniffing on wireless networks, tools such as the Firesheep browser extension that collected other users' session cookies, and sites that supported HTTPS without forcing it. It refines ForceHTTPS, the proposal Jackson and Barth presented at the WWW2008 conference, replacing its cookie with a response header and letting a policy cover a whole domain subtree.

The mechanism is one header, sent only over HTTPS: Strict-Transport-Security: max-age=31536000; includeSubDomains. The max-age directive is required and gives, in seconds, how long the browser must remember the host as a Known HSTS Host; the valueless includeSubDomains extends the policy to every subdomain; and max-age=0 tells the browser to forget the policy. While the policy lasts, the browser rewrites any http URL for that host to https before sending anything, changing port 80 to 443, so subsequent visits go straight to HTTPS with no interceptable first request. The RFC forbids a host to send the header over plain HTTP and requires browsers to ignore it if it arrives that way, since an attacker could inject it; only the first such header in a response counts; and a host addressed by an IP (Internet Protocol) literal is never recorded.
