MDN Web Docs adds two practical points: the host is identified by its domain name alone, and the policy applies to all of its ports. For the plaintext side the RFC advises a permanent redirect, such as a 301, to the https form of the requested address.

The second half of the policy is about errors. RFC 6797 says that any warning or error in setting up the secure connection, an expired, mismatched or untrusted certificate among them, must end the connection with no user recourse: no dialog offering to proceed, just failure, as with a server error. It calls click-through a recipe for a man-in-the-middle attack, and says that a site issuing an HSTS policy implicitly opts into this behaviour. The same RFC asks browsers to refuse mixed security context loads from an HSTS host. This is where HSTS turns into an availability decision: a certificate that expires on an HSTS site takes the site down for every returning visitor, with no button that lets them through.

HSTS cannot protect a first contact. RFC 6797 names this the bootstrap MITM (man-in-the-middle) vulnerability: a user who types or follows an http address for a host the browser does not yet know is exposed during that first exchange. Preloading closes the remaining hole by shipping the policy inside the browser itself, which means even the very first visit is protected; the RFC compares such a pre-loaded list to root certificates embedded in browsers at the factory. Chrome maintains the list that matters, built into the browser and used as the base for the lists of Firefox, Safari, Internet Explorer 11 and Edge. Its submission site, hstspreload.org, sets the requirements: a valid certificate; a redirect from HTTP to HTTPS on the same host if port 80 is open; HTTPS on every subdomain, including the www name and internal names that are not publicly reachable; and, on the base domain, a header with max-age of at least 31,536,000 seconds (one year), includeSubDomains and the preload directive, which is not part of RFC 6797 and which MDN describes as outside the specification. New entries are hard-coded into Chrome's source and take several months to reach the stable release, and chrome://net-internals/#hsts shows whether a name is listed.

The guidance on preloading has turned. The same site now says that many browsers, Chrome and Safari among them, automatically upgrade all HTTP navigations to HTTPS regardless of a domain's HSTS policy, that preloading only adds value when those upgrades fail in the presence of an active attacker, and that while HSTS is recommended, HSTS preloading is not. It asks projects that generate configurations never to include the preload directive by default, because operators who tried it that way have found themselves on the list with subdomains that cannot serve HTTPS.

The commitment is the part to think about before deploying. A long max-age is a promise browsers will keep even if you later want to serve something over HTTP, and includeSubDomains extends that promise to hosts you may not have inventoried. Preload removal is slow, measured in browser release cycles: hstspreload.org warns that a removal takes months to reach users through a Chrome update and that it cannot guarantee anything for other browsers. Deploy with a short duration first, confirm every subdomain genuinely serves HTTPS, then raise it, because the failure mode is your own site becoming unreachable with no quick undo. The site's suggested ramp is max-age=300 (five minutes), then 604800 (one week), then 2592000 (one month), each with includeSubDomains, waiting the full max-age at each stage and watching for broken pages before moving on.

On equipment the header is usually one setting away. An F5 BIG-IP HTTP profile carries an hsts block with mode (disabled by default), maximum-age (16,070,400 seconds, about 186 days, by default), include-subdomains (enabled by default once HSTS is on) and preload (disabled by default), so a virtual server can add the header for applications that do not send it. To check a site, curl -sI https://www.example.com prints the response headers, among them Strict-Transport-Security when it is present, and curl's --hsts option keeps its own HSTS cache and upgrades later http transfers to hosts in it.

HSTS now has a DNS (Domain Name System) relative. RFC 9460 (November 2023) says that an HTTPS resource record directs the client to use only secure transport for that host, similar to HSTS: before an http request the client should look the record up, and if one exists, behave as though it had received a 307 (Temporary Redirect) to the https URL. Because DNS is often insecure, clients must trust that signal no more than a cleartext 307, but they may also remove the user recourse on certificate errors, so origins that publish the record must not rely on users clicking through. HSTS has limits of its own that the RFC lists: an attacker who can manipulate the Network Time Protocol (NTP) can make a policy expire early on clients that trust it, and a bogus root certificate installed by phishing combined with DNS cache poisoning defeats it, because HSTS checks that a certificate is valid, not which authority issued it.

Its neighbours do different jobs. The Secure attribute keeps a cookie off plaintext connections, and includeSubDomains is what lets HSTS protect domain cookies shared with subdomains; certificate pinning and Certificate Transparency address a wrongly issued but valid certificate, which HSTS accepts; and the padlock alone says only that this connection is encrypted, not that the next one will be. The numbers worth remembering are RFC 6797 of November 2012, max-age in seconds with 31,536,000 for one year and the preload minimum, the ramp of 300, 604,800 and 2,592,000, port 80 rewritten to 443, a 301 redirect on the plaintext side, 307 as the behaviour of an HTTPS record, and 16,070,400 as BIG-IP's default maximum age.

lb.def: A device or service that spreads traffic across multiple servers.
lb.context: A load balancer distributes client requests across a pool of backends for scale and availability. In F5 Distributed Cloud the load balancer object also anchors routing, security, and origin-pool configuration.

l3.def: The network layer, where IP routing happens.
l3.context: Layer 3 of the OSI model is the network layer, home to IP addressing and routing. An L3 proxy or forwarding decision operates on IP addresses, one layer below the transport (L4) and application (L7) layers.

asn.def: The number that identifies an autonomous system, a network or group of networks under one routing policy, in BGP (Border Gateway Protocol) and in the internet number registries; 16 bits originally, 32 bits since 2007.
asn.context: An autonomous system number (ASN) uniquely identifies an autonomous system in BGP (Border Gateway Protocol): every network a route crosses adds its ASN to the route's AS path. Policies can match on a specific ASN to permit or deny routes from a given network, such as blocking a known-bad provider. Public ASNs come from IANA (the Internet Assigned Numbers Authority) through the five regional internet registries; 64512 to 65534 and 4200000000 to 4294967294 are for private use, and 0, 23456, 65535 and 4294967295 have special meanings.
asn.depth:
What it identifies. RFC (Request for Comments) 1930 of March 1996, by J. Hawkinson and T. Bates, defines the thing being numbered: an autonomous system (AS) is a connected group of one or more IP (Internet Protocol) prefixes run by one or more network operators which has a single and clearly defined routing policy. The same document sets the test for needing one: an AS, and so an autonomous system number (ASN), is only needed when a network's routing policy differs from that of its border gateway peers, which in practice means a multihomed network, one connected to more than one service provider, under a policy of its own. A single-homed site, even with several prefixes, has the same policy as its provider's other customers and belongs in the provider's AS; the RFC stresses that the number represents routing policy, not administrative ownership.

What BGP does with it. In BGP (Border Gateway Protocol), RFC 4271, the ASN appears from the first message: the OPEN carries the sender's number in a field called My Autonomous System. Each AS that passes a route on adds its number to the route's AS_PATH, so the path is a list of ASNs from the neighbour back to the origin, and an AS may prepend its own number more than once to make a path look longer and less attractive. The same list is BGP's loop protection: a router scans the path and excludes any route in which its own ASN already appears. That is why two sites of one company that use the same ASN cannot learn each other's routes across a provider without special configuration, and why policy written against ASNs, such as accepting a customer's routes only with the customer's ASN as origin or refusing anything that crosses a given network, is the everyday language of routing policy.

From 16 to 32 bits. RFC 1930 described the space as a 16-bit integer, 65,535 numbers, of which some 5,100 had been allocated and a little under 600 were routed at the time; it expected a successor protocol to arrive before exhaustion. Instead BGP grew. RFC 4893 (May 2007), by Q. Vohra and E. Chen, and its replacement RFC 6793 (December 2012) define four-octet ASNs: speakers announce support with capability code 65, carry full paths in the new optional transitive attributes AS4_PATH (17) and AS4_AGGREGATOR (18), and show older two-octet speakers the reserved number AS_TRANS, 23456, wherever a four-octet ASN cannot be expressed in 16 bits, which keeps the path length correct. A router that sees 23456 in a path is looking at a four-octet ASN through an old speaker, not at a real network. The 16-bit pool is gone: the registry of IANA (the Internet Assigned Numbers Authority) shows its last block, 64396 to 64495, allocated to the RIPE NCC (Réseaux IP Européens Network Coordination Centre) on 29 July 2016. The 32-bit blocks begin at 131072, and the registry was still recording new allocations in 2026, such as 216476 to 219547 to RIPE NCC on 1 June 2026.

Writing it down. RFC 5396 (December 2008), by G. Huston and G. Michaelson of APNIC, settled the notation: asplain, the plain decimal value, is to be used by all documents, systems and user interfaces. The older alternatives survive in some configurations: asdot+ writes every number as two 16-bit halves joined by a dot, and asdot writes numbers below 65536 plainly and the rest as two halves, so the number 65546 is 1.10 in asdot. When a filter or a ticket mixes the two forms, the same network can look like two.

Who hands them out. IANA allocates ASNs in blocks to the five regional internet registries (RIRs): AFRINIC, APNIC, ARIN, LACNIC and RIPE NCC, which allocate or assign them to network operators under their own policies, and an operator obtains one from the registry of its region. Latin America and the Caribbean are served by LACNIC, whose blocks in the IANA registry include 27648 to 28671, allocated in November 2002, and the four-octet range from 262144, first allocated on 29 November 2006, with the most recent block, 274845 to 275868, on 19 November 2025. The same registry lists, for each RIR, the WHOIS and RDAP (Registration Data Access Protocol) servers where the holder of a given ASN can be looked up.

The special numbers. Several values are reserved, and IANA keeps them in a special-purpose registry created in 2014. AS 0 is reserved: RFC 7607 (August 2015) says a BGP speaker must not originate or propagate a route with AS 0 in its path attributes, codifying what at least two implementations already did, because RPKI (Resource Public Key Infrastructure) uses a ROA (Route Origin Authorization) naming AS 0 to say that a prefix should not be routed at all. 23456 is AS_TRANS. 64496 to 64511 and 65536 to 65551 are reserved for documentation and sample code (RFC 5398), the numbers to use in training material and examples. 64512 to 65534, 1,023 numbers, and 4200000000 to 4294967294, 94,967,295 numbers, are for private use (RFC 6996, July 2013), and the last number of each space, 65535 and 4294967295, is reserved and not to be used by operators (RFC 7300, July 2014).

Private ASNs in practice. RFC 6996 requires private ASNs to be removed from AS path attributes, AS4_PATH included, before routes are advertised to the internet, warns that some implementations fail to remove them when a path mixes private and public numbers, and allows ordinary AS path filtering to stop prefixes originating from private ASNs from leaking out. Inside networks they are everywhere. RFC 7938 (August 2016), by P. Lapukhov, A. Premji and J. Mitchell, describes BGP as the only routing protocol of large data centres built as Clos fabrics: EBGP (external BGP) sessions on every link, private ASNs from 64512 to 65534, one ASN for all Tier 1 switches and one per Tier 2 cluster. Because 1,023 numbers run out, it describes reusing the same ASNs, such as 65001 to 65032, at Tier 3 in every cluster, with the non-standard but widely implemented Allowas-in feature to accept routes that carry the router's own ASN, or moving to four-octet private ASNs where every device supports them.

What an ASN proves, and what it does not. An ASN in a path is a claim, not evidence: BGP itself does not authenticate who originated a route or which networks it really crossed. Route origin validation with RPKI checks only the last number in the path, the origin, against the ROAs published for the prefix, which is why a route leak, a correct origin carried along the wrong path, passes it. Operators therefore combine three habits: filter customers by their registered ASNs and prefixes, publish ROAs for their own address space, and treat 23456, private ranges and AS 0 in a path from the internet as signs of a configuration problem somewhere upstream.

rng.def: A source of random values, ideally unpredictable.
rng.context: A random number generator produces the randomness that security depends on. A weak or predictable RNG, not a flaw in a scheme like UUIDv4, is usually the real cause when supposedly unique or secret values collide or are guessed.

ulid.def: A sortable, unique identifier alternative to UUID.
ulid.context: Universally Unique Lexicographically Sortable Identifier encodes a timestamp plus randomness so IDs sort roughly by creation time while staying unique. It was a popular answer to UUIDv4's lack of ordering before UUIDv7 arrived.
ulid.depth:
A ULID is a unique identifier that sorts lexicographically by creation time, encoding a timestamp followed by randomness. It exists because UUID version 4 is entirely random, which makes it a poor database key.

The reason is index locality. Random keys insert at arbitrary points in a B-tree, fragmenting pages and dirtying many of them per batch of writes; time-ordered keys append, which keeps the working set small and the index compact. The trade is that a ULID leaks its creation time to anyone who sees it, and remains guessable in ordering, so it is right for internal keys and wrong for anything where an identifier should reveal nothing. UUID version 7 standardizes the same idea.

ecma.def: A standards body behind JavaScript and JSON specifications.
ecma.context: European Computer Manufacturers Association, now Ecma International, publishes standards including ECMAScript (JavaScript) and ECMA-404, one of the two specifications that define JSON.

cdata.def: An XML section whose content is not parsed as markup.
cdata.context: A character data section lets an XML document include raw text - like code or markup - without the parser interpreting angle brackets and ampersands. It is written as a CDATA block so special characters need no escaping.
cdata.depth:
A CDATA section tells an XML parser to treat its content as literal characters rather than markup, which is how a document embeds a fragment containing angle brackets without escaping every one.

It is a formatting convenience with a security edge. Filters and validators that scan XML for dangerous content sometimes fail to inspect inside CDATA, so a payload placed there can pass a check that would have caught it elsewhere. The rule that follows is the general one for parsing: validation must happen after the document is fully parsed into its logical structure, not against its serialized text, because the text form has more than one way to say the same thing.

lcs.def: The longest sequence common to two inputs, keeping order.
lcs.context: The longest common subsequence is the basis of most diff tools: the longest ordered (but not necessarily contiguous) run of elements shared by two files. What is left over becomes the additions and deletions a diff shows.
lcs.depth:
The longest common subsequence is the longest sequence of elements appearing in the same order in two inputs, though not necessarily adjacently. It is the algorithm behind every diff you have ever read.

Understanding it explains why diffs sometimes look wrong. The algorithm finds a minimal edit script, not the change a human made, so moving a block of code appears as a deletion and an insertion, and a small edit inside a repetitive region can align against the wrong instance and produce a confusing hunk. Modern tools add heuristics for exactly this reason, and knowing the underlying algorithm is what makes an odd diff explicable rather than mysterious.

nvd.def: The National Vulnerability Database (NVD) is the United States government's public repository of vulnerability data, run by NIST (National Institute of Standards and Technology) since 2005: it takes every CVE (Common Vulnerabilities and Exposures) record and adds severity scores, weakness types and affected-product lists.
nvd.context: The National Vulnerability Database, run by NIST (National Institute of Standards and Technology), enriches CVE (Common Vulnerabilities and Exposures) entries with CVSS (Common Vulnerability Scoring System) scores and other metadata: weakness types, lists of affected products and the exploitation data of CISA (the Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency). Reproducing a published score for a vulnerability, NVD's or the reporting vendor's, is a good check that a CVSS calculation matches the source, and where the two differ the vectors show why. Since April 2026 NIST enriches by priority, exploited and federally used software first, so many records arrive with less than they used to.
nvd.depth:
The National Vulnerability Database (NVD) is a NIST (National Institute of Standards and Technology) programme, and NIST describes it as the United States government repository of standards-based vulnerability management data represented using the Security Content Automation Protocol (SCAP), with databases of security checklist references, security-related software flaws, misconfigurations, product names and impact metrics. It is not the CVE (Common Vulnerabilities and Exposures) List. The CVE Program states plainly that the two are separate: MITRE launched the CVE List as a community effort in 1999, NIST launched the NVD in 2005, and the NVD is built upon and fully synchronized with the CVE List, so that every published CVE record appears there and the NVD adds information on top, fix references, severity scores and impact ratings among it. It is not a CVE Numbering Authority (CNA), which assigns identifiers and writes the original records, and it is not CISA's Known Exploited Vulnerabilities (KEV) catalogue, although it now carries that catalogue's data.

Its ancestry is older than its name. NIST's own history of its security automation work records that NIST developed the Internet Categorization of Attacks Toolkit (ICAT) in 1999, changed the database in 2000 to identify vulnerabilities instead of attacks and put it online as the ICAT Metabase, which identified 644 vulnerabilities at release and described each with more than 20 attributes, a fine-grained search that most databases did not offer at the time. By 2005 it had about 2 million visits a year, and that year NIST launched the NVD based on, and replacing, ICAT, sponsored by the Department of Homeland Security (DHS) and adopting CVE as its identifier. The same history notes that during periods of increased cyber stress the NVD overtakes time.gov as NIST's most visited resource.

Enrichment is the NVD's real product, and one record shows all of it. For CVE-2021-44228, Log4Shell, the NVD's application programming interface (API) returns the CNA's description and affected versions from Apache; NVD's own CVSS 3.1 assessment, marked as the primary source, with a base score of 10.0 and the vector AV:N/AC:L/PR:N/UI:N/S:C/C:H/I:H/A:H, beside an older CVSS 2 score of 9.3; weakness types from the Common Weakness Enumeration (CWE), CWE-20, CWE-400 and CWE-502 from Apache and CWE-917 from NVD; configurations listing affected products as Common Platform Enumeration (CPE) match criteria with version ranges; an SSVC (Stakeholder-Specific Vulnerability Categorization) assessment from CISA in its coordinator role, with exploitation active, automatable yes and technical impact total; and four fields copied from the KEV catalogue, of which cisaExploitAdd (10 December 2021) and cisaActionDue (24 December 2021) are the dates of addition and of the federal deadline. The status of that record is Analyzed, which is what every record used to reach.

Scores come from more than one source, and they do not always agree. The record for CVE-2021-26855, the Microsoft Exchange Server flaw exploited in 2021, carries Microsoft's CVSS 3.1 score of 9.1 and NVD's of 9.8; the vectors differ only in availability impact, none in Microsoft's reading and high in NVD's. Reproducing a published score for a vulnerability is a good check that a CVSS calculation matches the source, and when two published scores differ, the vectors, not the numbers, show where the analysts disagreed. NVD scores are Base scores only: they say how severe a flaw is in general, not how much risk it poses in a particular network.

The NVD has struggled to keep up since early 2024. On 15 April 2026 NIST explained why and what it would change: CVE submissions rose 263 per cent between 2020 and 2025 and in the first three months of 2026 ran nearly a third above the same period a year earlier, and although NIST enriched nearly 42,000 CVEs in 2025, 45 per cent more than in any earlier year, that was not enough. From that day it enriches first the CVEs in the KEV catalogue, aiming at one business day, then CVEs for software used within the federal government and for critical software as defined by Executive Order 14028; everything else is still listed but marked Lowest Priority, not scheduled for immediate enrichment, and can be requested by email. Backlogged CVEs published in the NVD before 1 March 2026 moved to Not Scheduled, a backlog that never contained KEV entries; NIST stopped routinely adding its own severity score when the CNA had already supplied one; and modified records are re-analysed only when a change materially affects the enrichment. A CVE being in the NVD no longer implies that NIST has scored it or listed its affected products.

CISA fills part of the gap from the other side of the record. Its Vulnrichment project publishes CISA's enrichment of public CVE records as an Authorized Data Publisher (ADP), a programme launched in 2024: SSVC decision points for new and recent CVEs, and a CWE and a CVSS score for higher-risk ones where the evidence supports them. CISA stopped adding CPE strings on 10 December 2024, never overwrites the CNA's own container, and removes its assessments when the CNA later supplies its own. The CVE Services record for Log4Shell shows the result as a container titled CISA ADP Vulnrichment, and the NVD record shows the same SSVC data under CISA's identifier.

The NVD is read by machines more than by people. Its web pages are rendered by script in the browser, but the CVE API answers plain HTTPS requests with JSON (JavaScript Object Notation) in a format it labels NVD_CVE version 2.0, at services.nvd.nist.gov/rest/json/cves/2.0, with parameters such as cveId for one record and hasKev for the records that carry KEV data. On 12 November 2026 it held 424,694 CVE records, of which 1,779 matched hasKev. Each record carries a vulnStatus, and the fields that matter for triage are the metrics with their sources, the weaknesses, the configurations and, where present, cisaExploitAdd, cisaActionDue, cisaRequiredAction and cisaVulnerabilityName.

The pitfalls follow from what enrichment is. A vulnerability scanner that finds affected software by matching CPE names against the NVD finds nothing for a record that has not been enriched, so a quiet scan of new software may mean only that NIST has not reached those records; the CNA's own affected-version data, which the API now returns alongside, fills some of that gap. A score copied from the NVD without its vector cannot be checked, and a Base score alone is not a priority: exploitation evidence from KEV, the probability estimates of EPSS (the Exploit Prediction Scoring System) and the local exposure of the asset change the order in which patches go out. And the NVD's own priorities now favour federal software, which is not the same list as any particular organization's software.

The neighbours divide the work. The CVE Program, run by MITRE and the CNAs, names vulnerabilities; the NVD, run by NIST, enriches them; FIRST (the Forum of Incident Response and Security Teams) maintains CVSS; CISA's KEV catalogue records which are exploited; CPE and CWE are the dictionaries of products and weakness types that the NVD's enrichment uses. The numbers worth remembering are 1999 for the CVE List and for ICAT, 2005 for the NVD; 644 vulnerabilities in the first ICAT Metabase; 263 per cent growth in submissions from 2020 to 2025 and nearly 42,000 records enriched in 2025; 15 April 2026 for risk-based enrichment and 1 March 2026 as the backlog cut-off; one business day as the target for KEV records; and 424,694 records on 12 November 2026.

ajax.def: A technique for updating a web page without a full reload.
ajax.context: Asynchronous JavaScript and XML refers to making background HTTP requests from a page and updating it in place. The name predates JSON, which has largely replaced XML as the payload, but the term stuck for in-page dynamic requests.
ajax.depth:
AJAX named the technique of fetching data in the background and updating part of a page without a full reload. The name is a period piece, since it specifies XML and almost everything now uses JSON, but the shift it described was fundamental: pages became applications.

Everything since inherits both the capability and its costs. Browser history, bookmarking and the back button all stop working unless the application explicitly manages them, screen readers need to be told the page changed, and content that never appears in the initial HTML is invisible to anything that does not execute JavaScript. Those are the same trade-offs single-page applications still make, which is why the term is dated and the consequences are not.

sec1.def: A standard format for encoding elliptic-curve private keys.
sec1.context: Standards for Efficient Cryptography 1 defines an elliptic-curve key encoding, distinct from the PKCS#1 (RSA) and PKCS#8 (generic) formats. A private key file may be in any of these, wrapped in either PEM or DER.

captcha.def: A challenge meant to tell humans and bots apart.
captcha.context: Completely Automated Public Turing test to tell Computers and Humans Apart is a challenge, like distorted text or image selection, that is easy for people and hard for bots. It is a last-resort defence because it adds real user friction.
captcha.depth:
CAPTCHA tries to distinguish humans from automated clients, and the arms race has been running long enough that the premise is now shaky: machine vision solves the visual puzzles better than people do, and commercial solving services provide humans at low cost regardless.

What replaced the puzzle is behavioural and cryptographic. Risk scoring from browsing signals, proof-of-work challenges that cost an attacker more than a user, and attestation approaches that vouch for a client without identifying it are all attempts to keep the property while dropping the puzzle. The accessibility cost of the old approach was always severe, and any discussion of these systems that omits blind and motor-impaired users is describing a solution that excludes people to keep out machines.

gui.def: Graphical user interface (GUI): a way of operating software through visual elements on a screen, such as windows, icons, menus and buttons, chosen with a pointing device or by touch instead of typed commands.
gui.context: A graphical user interface (GUI) lets a user operate software through windows, buttons and menus rather than typed commands. On BIG-IP some tasks are only practical through the GUI, while others are faster from the CLI (command-line interface). On network and security devices the GUI is usually a web application served from the management interface over HTTPS (Hypertext Transfer Protocol Secure): the Configuration utility on an F5 BIG-IP, the web interface of a FortiGate. It is the easiest surface to learn and to read state from, the hardest to script, repeat or audit, and, being a web server on the management plane, a part of the device that must be kept off the internet.
gui.depth:
A graphical user interface (GUI, pronounced gooey or spelled out) presents a program as pictures the user acts on directly: the pointer is moved to an object and the object is opened, dragged or pressed. The usual vocabulary is abbreviated WIMP, for windows, icons, menus and pointer. What it replaced was the command-line interface (CLI), in which the user types instructions as text, and GUIs were introduced in reaction to the steep learning curve of command lines. What it is not is equally useful to hold on to. A GUI is one face of a system, not the system; the same configuration is normally reachable through a CLI and through an application programming interface (API), and the three do not always expose the same things.

The ideas are older than the personal computer. In 1963 Ivan Sutherland published Sketchpad, his doctoral thesis at the Massachusetts Institute of Technology (MIT), a real-time drawing system worked with a light pen. On 9 December 1968 Douglas Engelbart and his team from the Stanford Research Institute spent 90 minutes at the Fall Joint Computer Conference in San Francisco showing their oN-Line System (NLS) to an audience of about a thousand: the first public demonstration of the mouse, of hypermedia and of on-screen video conferencing, in a system that already had multiple windows. Xerox's Palo Alto Research Center (PARC) turned those ideas into the Alto, dated 1973 by most accounts and 1974 in the Computer History Museum's timeline: a graphics-based monochrome display of 600 by 800 pixels, a mouse, movable windows and icons, a word processor that printed what the screen showed (what you see is what you get, WYSIWYG) and the overlapping windows of the Smalltalk environment. The first Alto cost Xerox 12,000 dollars, and the machine was never sold as a product.

Commercial history is a string of firsts that depend on the wording. Wikipedia gives the PERQ workstation of 1979 as the first commercially available computer with a GUI; Xerox sold its own in 1981 as the 8010 Information System, the Star; the Computer History Museum calls the Apple Lisa of 1983 the first commercial personal computer with one and the Macintosh of 1984, at 2,500 dollars, the first successful one. Microsoft released Windows 1.0 on 20 November 1985 for 99 dollars, as a shell on top of MS-DOS with tiled windows. IBM's Common User Access guidelines then became the basis of the conventions shared by Windows, OS/2 and the Unix Motif toolkit, which is why most desktops behave alike. On Unix the windowing layer is the X Window System, begun in MIT's Project Athena in 1984 and at protocol version 11 (hence X11) since September 1987. X is network-transparent: the program drawing a window and the server that owns the screen can be on different machines, which is why X11 still appears in lists of remote management protocols. Its intended replacement, Wayland, reached version 1.0 in 2012. Touch screens brought the post-WIMP style, popularized by the iPhone in 2007 and the iPad in 2010.

On network and security equipment the GUI is a web application running on the device. F5's documentation describes the BIG-IP Configuration utility as the browser-based system and network management tool, and the same product is also named the Traffic Management User Interface (TMUI); beside it sit the Traffic Management Shell (tmsh), which is the CLI, and the iControl REST (representational state transfer) API. A FortiGate has the same pair of faces, and Fortinet states the asymmetry outright: the CLI can be used in lieu of the GUI, and some settings are not available in the GUI at all. A FortiGate's GUI can also hide what is there. Its Feature Visibility page controls which features appear, and some are invisible by default, so the absence of a menu does not prove the absence of configuration.

The opposite case exists too, and it is what the remark about BIG-IP in the short definition refers to. The Access Policy Manager's visual policy editor is, in F5's words, a screen on which to configure a per-session or per-request policy using visual elements: actions joined by branches that end in Allow or Deny. A policy drawn as a flow chart is far easier to read there than as the text that stores it. Dashboards, traffic graphs and topology maps are the other things a GUI does better than any command. Bulk edits, searches across hundreds of objects and anything that must be done identically on twenty devices go the other way, and are faster from the CLI or an API.

The engineering weakness of a GUI is that a click leaves no script. A change made by hand in a browser cannot be reviewed before it happens, replayed on the next device or compared with last month's. F5's own automation documentation groups the GUI with tmsh and the imperative REST API as interfaces that carry out one instruction at a time, and contrasts all three with a declaration of the desired end state. The general comparison runs the same way: command lines are lighter and more efficient once learned, at the price of commands that are hard to discover, while a GUI lets a newcomer find a function without knowing its name. Teams that automate tend to keep the GUI for reading and for rare tasks, and to send changes through text that can be versioned.

A GUI is also code that has to be present and patched. Microsoft's Server Core installation of Windows Server has no desktop by design and, in Microsoft's words, a smaller attack surface due to a smaller code base; it is administered from the command line, from PowerShell or from graphical tools running on another machine. Appliances cannot drop their web interface so easily, and it has been one of their most attacked components. CVE-2020-5902 (Common Vulnerabilities and Exposures), published on 1 July 2020, was remote code execution in undisclosed pages of the BIG-IP TMUI, scored 9.8 by the National Vulnerability Database under version 3.1 of the Common Vulnerability Scoring System (CVSS). CVE-2022-40684 let an unauthenticated attacker operate the administrative interface of FortiOS, FortiProxy and FortiSwitchManager with crafted HTTP or HTTPS requests (9.8). CVE-2023-20198 in the web UI of Cisco IOS XE, scored 10.0, was used to create a local account through a privilege 15 command. CVE-2024-0012 was an authentication bypass in the management web interface of Palo Alto Networks PAN-OS. All four are in the Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalogue of the United States Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency (CISA).

The defence is a matter of placement, and it has been written into policy. CISA's Binding Operational Directive 23-02 of 13 June 2023 covers the networked management interfaces of routers, switches, firewalls, virtual private network (VPN) concentrators, proxies, load balancers and out-of-band server controllers, over protocols that include HTTP, HTTPS, Secure Shell (SSH), Telnet, the Simple Network Management Protocol (SNMP), the Remote Desktop Protocol (RDP), Virtual Network Computing (VNC) and X11. Within 14 days of being notified by CISA, or of discovering an exposed interface itself, a federal agency must either remove it from the internet, so that it answers only from an internal network, preferably an isolated management network, or place it behind a zero trust policy enforcement point. The vendor's description of CVE-2024-0012 makes the same point: the risk is greatly reduced when the management web interface accepts only trusted internal addresses. The dates worth keeping are 1968 for the demonstration, 1973 for the Alto, 1984 for the Macintosh and for X, and 1985 for Windows; the rule worth keeping is that the GUI belongs on the management network and nowhere else.

dh.def: Diffie-Hellman (DH) is the key agreement, published in 1976, in which each of two parties combines its own secret exponent with the other's public value so that both reach the same shared secret over an open channel; its security rests on the difficulty of discrete logarithms, and on its own it authenticates neither side.
dh.context: Diffie-Hellman (DH) works in a group fixed by a public prime p and generator g: each side picks a secret x, sends g to the power x modulo p, and raises what it receives to its own secret, so both arrive at g to the power of the product of the two secrets while an eavesdropper sees only the public values. The strength lies in the group: 2,048-bit safe-prime groups, IKE (Internet Key Exchange) group 14 or TLS (Transport Layer Security) ffdhe2048, are today's floor, 512-bit export groups were broken outright and 1,024-bit groups are within reach of a well-funded attacker, and the elliptic-curve form, ECDH (elliptic-curve Diffie-Hellman), does the same job with far smaller numbers. Used with fresh secrets for every session, the ephemeral form written DHE, it gives forward secrecy; with static or reused secrets it does not. It has no authentication of its own, so a certificate signature, a host key or a pre-shared key must bind the exchange to an identity.
dh.depth:
What it is, and what it is not. Whitfield Diffie and Martin Hellman published the scheme in New Directions in Cryptography, IEEE Transactions on Information Theory, November 1976, as a public key distribution system resting on the apparent difficulty of computing logarithms over a finite field. Their version was a directory: each user chose a secret X, placed Y, a fixed primitive element raised to X modulo a prime q, in a public file with name and address, and any two users computed the same key from their own secret and the other's entry. They took the square root of q as a fair measure of the attacker's work and warned that a much faster algorithm for logarithms would break the system. Diffie-Hellman (DH) is key agreement, not encryption: nothing is encrypted, neither side chooses the result, and the output is a shared number, not yet a key. It is not authentication either: an attacker in the middle can run one exchange with each side, which is why every protocol that uses it signs or otherwise authenticates the exchange. The history, Ralph Merkle's independent work and the earlier classified discovery at GCHQ (Government Communications Headquarters) are told under key exchange.

The arithmetic, as standardized. Request for Comments (RFC) 2631, written by Eric Rescorla in June 1999 on the basis of the ANSI X9.42 draft, is the Internet's reference text. Its parameters are a prime p, a prime q that divides p minus 1, and a generator g of the subgroup of order q; each party's private value x gives a public value y equal to g to the x modulo p, and the shared secret ZZ is g to the power of xa times xb modulo p, which each side computes as the other's y raised to its own x. Before using a received y, a party may check that it lies between 2 and p minus 1 and that y to the power q modulo p equals 1; the purpose, in the RFC's words, is to prevent a small subgroup attack on the sender's key pair. RFC 2631 describes ephemeral-static and static-static modes for the Cryptographic Message Syntax (CMS), and it never uses ZZ directly: it hashes ZZ with SHA-1 (Secure Hash Algorithm 1) and context to make a key-encryption key, noting that ZZ is the only source of secret entropy, so the derived key can be no stronger than ZZ. Modern protocols do the same with a key derivation function (KDF).

Groups, the part that decides the strength. A safe prime is a prime p for which (p minus 1)/2 is also prime, so the group has no small subgroups for an attacker to exploit. RFC 3526 (Tero Kivinen and Mika Kojo, May 2003) defined the MODP (modular exponential) groups still used in IPsec (Internet Protocol Security): 1,536 bits as group 5 and 2,048, 3,072, 4,096, 6,144 and 8,192 bits as groups 14 to 18, all with generator 2 and with primes built from the binary expansion of pi, so that nobody could have chosen them to hide a weakness. Its own table estimates the 2,048-bit group at between 110 and 160 bits of strength, far below the 1,024 bits the 1976 square-root measure would have suggested. RFC 7919 (Daniel Kahn Gillmor, August 2016) did the same for TLS with the ffdhe groups of 2,048 to 8,192 bits, safe primes derived from the constant e, because in TLS 1.2 the server sent arbitrary p and g in its ServerKeyExchange message, had to choose them without knowing what the client could accept, and the client had no efficient way to verify that a new group was sound. NIST (National Institute of Standards and Technology) Special Publication (SP) 800-56A Revision 3 (April 2018) approves exactly those two families, with parameters of the form p, q equal to (p minus 1)/2, and g equal to 2, rates the 2,048-bit groups at 112 bits of security, requires a safe-prime group for anything above 112 bits and allows the older FIPS (Federal Information Processing Standard) 186-type parameters only for backward compatibility. It names its schemes by the number of ephemeral and static keys on each side, dhEphem being C(2e, 0s), and also covers MQV (Menezes-Qu-Vanstone); NIST announced in January 2026 that it will update the document.

Where it is configured. In IPsec the group is a numbered transform: the IANA (Internet Assigned Numbers Authority) registry now titled Key Exchange Method Transform IDs (last updated 10 November 2026) lists 1 (768 bits, deprecated by RFC 8247), 2 (1,024 bits), 5 and 14 to 18 as MODP groups, 19 to 21 as elliptic-curve groups, 22 to 24 as the RFC 5114 groups with small prime-order subgroups (22 deprecated), 27 to 30 as Brainpool curves, 31 and 32 as Curve25519 and Curve448, and 35 to 37 as ML-KEM (Module-Lattice-Based Key-Encapsulation Mechanism). On a FortiGate running FortiOS 7.6.5, set dhgrp under config vpn ipsec phase2-interface takes a list from those numbers and set pfs enable makes every child security association run a fresh exchange, which is what perfect forward secrecy means in IPsec. In TLS 1.3, specified since July 2026 in RFC 9846, only the named ffdhe groups remain, codepoints 0x0100 for ffdhe2048 upwards; each public value is padded with zeros to the size of p, so a 2,048-bit share is always 256 bytes, against 32 for X25519. TLS 1.2 is a different story: RFC 10015 (Nimrod Aviram, July 2026) now says that TLS 1.2 clients MUST NOT offer and servers MUST NOT select finite-field DHE (ephemeral Diffie-Hellman) cipher suites, or the static DH ones, because version 1.2 has no way to negotiate the group, a client cannot check a server's custom group for small subgroups, and key reuse opens timing side channels; it leaves finite-field DHE allowed in TLS 1.3, where those problems do not arise. For Secure Shell (SSH), RFC 8270 (December 2017) made 2,048 bits the minimum acceptable modulus for the group-exchange method of RFC 4419.

What goes wrong. Small groups first. Logjam, disclosed in May 2015 and catalogued as CVE-2015-4000, let a man in the middle downgrade TLS connections to export-grade 512-bit Diffie-Hellman. Its authors, David Adrian and thirteen colleagues, implemented the number field sieve: after a week-long precomputation for one 512-bit group they could compute any logarithm in it in about a minute, and 82 per cent of vulnerable servers used a single such group. The same work judged a 1,024-bit group within nation-state resources and, because a few standardized groups serve millions of servers, estimated that one such precomputation would expose 18 per cent of popular HTTPS sites and a second 66 per cent of IPsec VPNs (virtual private networks) and 26 per cent of SSH servers. That is why 2,048 bits is the floor. Second, groups with small subgroups and peers that skip validation. RFC 6989 (Yoav Sheffer and Scott Fluhrer, July 2013) explains that the RFC 5114 groups have a composite (p minus 1)/2 and leak information about a private value that is reused, and adds recipient tests to IKEv2 (Internet Key Exchange version 2); CVE-2016-0701 was the same failure in OpenSSL 1.0.2 before 1.0.2f, where DH_check_pub_key did not ensure a prime was appropriate and a remote attacker could discover a private exponent over multiple handshakes, as demonstrated with a number from an X9.42 file. TLS 1.3 answers with a mandatory check that 1 is less than Y and Y is less than p minus 1, which stops a peer forcing the exchange into a small subgroup. Third, reuse. The Raccoon attack, published in September 2020 by Robert Merget, Marcus Brinkmann, Nimrod Aviram, Juraj Somorovsky, Johannes Mittmann and Jörg Schwenk, used the fact that TLS 1.2 and earlier strip leading zero bytes from the premaster secret: hashing inputs of different lengths takes measurably different time, and a server that reuses its DH value, statically or by recycling ephemeral keys, becomes an oracle. Its authors call it very hard to exploit; OpenSSL fixed it as CVE-2020-1968 in 1.0.2w, the attack does not apply to ECDH (elliptic-curve Diffie-Hellman), and TLS 1.3 keeps the zeros by padding the shared secret to the length of p.

Its neighbours. ECDH is the same protocol in a different group, an elliptic curve, where the best known attacks are so much slower that NIST SP 800-57 Part 1 rates a 256-bit curve and a 3,072-bit finite field alike at 128 bits of security, and it has replaced finite-field DH almost everywhere for speed and size. RSA (Rivest-Shamir-Adleman) key transport is the opposite design: one side chooses the secret and encrypts it to the other, so the long-term key decrypts every recorded session, which is why TLS 1.3 removed it. MQV adds the parties' static keys into the computation so that the agreement itself authenticates them. ML-KEM is not Diffie-Hellman at all but a key-encapsulation mechanism, which is why RFC 9846 replaced the wording that assumed elliptic-curve or finite-field DH with the neutral asymmetric shared secret.

Numbers worth remembering: 1976 for the paper; generator 2 and a safe prime for every modern finite-field group; group 14 and ffdhe2048, 2,048 bits, rated at 112 bits of security by NIST; 256 bytes for a 2,048-bit public value against 32 for X25519; IKE group 31 for Curve25519; the check 1 less than Y less than p minus 1; and 2,048 bits as the minimum for SSH group exchange since RFC 8270.

iis.def: Microsoft's web server software for Windows.
iis.context: Internet Information Services is the web server built into Windows Server. Its URL and path handling quirks, like accepting backslashes as separators, are a common source of WAF (web application firewall) evasion tricks that attackers use to slip past signature matching.

beast.def: BEAST (Browser Exploit Against SSL/TLS) is the attack Juliano Rizzo and Thai Duong demonstrated in September 2011 (CVE-2011-3389) that recovered secrets such as session cookies from SSL 3.0 and TLS 1.0 (Transport Layer Security) connections by exploiting the predictable initialization vector of CBC (cipher block chaining) mode.
beast.context: In SSL 3.0 and TLS 1.0 each record's initialization vector is the last ciphertext block of the previous record, so an attacker who can see the traffic and make the victim's browser send chosen data knows the IV before the next block is encrypted and can test guesses at a secret one byte at a time. The weakness had been described in 2002 and fixed in TLS 1.1 in 2006; Rizzo and Duong showed it working from a browser, with a script or applet in the victim's browser and a network position. The responses were 1/n-1 record splitting in browsers and SChannel, a brief server-side preference for RC4 that was itself prohibited in 2015, and the slow move to TLS 1.1, TLS 1.2 and authenticated encryption, which TLS 1.3 made the only option. BEAST opened the run of named TLS attacks that followed through the next decade.
beast.depth:
What it is. BEAST is a chosen-plaintext attack on the record layer of SSL (Secure Sockets Layer) 3.0 and TLS (Transport Layer Security) 1.0 when they use a block cipher in CBC (cipher block chaining) mode. The National Vulnerability Database (NVD) describes CVE-2011-3389 as SSL encrypting data with CBC mode and chained initialization vectors, which lets a man-in-the-middle obtain plaintext HTTP headers through a blockwise chosen-boundary attack, in conjunction with code in the browser using the HTML5 WebSocket API, Java's URLConnection or Silverlight's WebClient. It does not break AES (Advanced Encryption Standard) or Triple DES, and it does not touch the server: Duong stressed that BEAST never sent a packet to the servers whose sessions it read. It is a client-side attack on how the protocol chains records, and the IETF's own summary, RFC (Request for Comments) 7457, puts it in one line: BEAST uses TLS 1.0's predictable initialization vector to decrypt parts of a packet, specifically HTTP cookies.

How it works. CBC mode combines each plaintext block with the previous ciphertext block before encrypting it, and needs an unpredictable initialization vector (IV) for the first block. SSL 3.0 and TLS 1.0 took a shortcut: the IV of each record after the first is the last ciphertext block of the record before. An observer on the network has therefore already seen the IV of the next record. If that observer can also choose a block the browser will encrypt next, it can make the input to the cipher equal to what it was for an earlier block containing a secret, and tell from the ciphertext whether a guess was right. Rizzo and Duong's contribution was the chosen boundary: by controlling the length of a request, they shifted the secret so that only one unknown byte fell in the block being tested, which reduces the guessing to at most 256 tries per byte and recovers a cookie byte by byte. The attacker needs two things at once: a position to watch and inject traffic, and an agent in the victim's browser that can send requests to the target site on the same TLS connection, which is what the WebSocket, Java and Silverlight routes provided.

Why it was old news, and why it was news. Bodo Möller's note on OpenSSL's site, last updated in 2004, records the weakness from a February 2002 exchange with Wei Dai and the observation, credited there to Phil Rogaway, that CBC is not secure against chosen plaintexts when the IV can be predicted; Möller judged that for most application protocols such attacks were not really feasible. OpenSSL added a countermeasure in version 0.9.6d on 9 May 2002, sending an empty record before real data so that the IV of the live record was not known in advance, and had to make it switchable in 0.9.6e on 30 July 2002 because some implementations, notably Microsoft's browser, rejected empty fragments. TLS 1.1, RFC 4346 of April 2006, replaced the implicit IV with an explicit one specifically to protect against CBC attacks. Duong's account of how BEAST came about starts with Rizzo reading that very note in December 2010; the browser, with JavaScript running next to an encrypted session, was the setting that made the old weakness practical.

The disclosure. Duong writes that by mid-May 2011 they had a paper, which they sent to Google, Mozilla, Apple, Microsoft, Opera and Oracle; Mozilla's bug 665814 became the shared discussion board. Fixing it was hard because every proposed change broke some existing SSL software, and OpenSSL's old countermeasure was off by default because of Internet Explorer 6. The CVE was published on 6 September 2011, Rizzo and Duong gave the talk and a live demonstration at the Ekoparty conference in Buenos Aires in late September, and Microsoft published Security Advisory 2588513 on 26 September. By then WebSockets had changed for unrelated reasons in a way that stopped that route, so the demonstration used Java and Silverlight agents.

The fixes. Browsers settled on 1/n-1 record splitting, which Adam Langley of Google described in January 2012: each CBC record is split in two, the first carrying a single byte of application data, which effectively randomizes the IV of the rest. OpenSSL's older 0/n split, the empty record, had failed because many stacks read an empty record as end of file; 1/n-1 broke code that assumed an HTTP request arrives in a single read, and Chrome rolled it back in version 15 after large sites failed, shipped it in Chrome 16, and was followed by Microsoft's January 2012 update and Firefox 10. Microsoft's bulletin MS12-006 of 10 January 2012, rated Important, changed how the SChannel component sends and receives encrypted records and noted that TLS 1.1, TLS 1.2 and suites without CBC were not affected. On servers the quick advice of 2011, Microsoft's among it, was to put RC4 suites first, because a stream cipher has no CBC IV; that respite was short, since RFC 7457 recorded that RC4 could no longer be considered sufficient and RFC 7465 of February 2015 forbade RC4 in TLS altogether. The durable fix was the protocol version: RFC 8996 of March 2021 states that TLS 1.0 and 1.1 must not be used, and TLS 1.3 has no CBC suites at all.

Where it shows up today. Scanners still report BEAST against any server that accepts TLS 1.0 with CBC suites, and the useful reading of that finding is about the protocol version, not the cipher. On F5 BIG-IP the client SSL profile carries the OpenSSL-derived option list, and its tmsh reference gives dont-insert-empty-fragments, the switch that disables the empty-fragment countermeasure for SSL 3.0 and TLS 1.0 CBC ciphers, as part of the default options; with TLS 1.0 disabled, as current practice requires, the option no longer matters. The same applies to any appliance whose cipher configuration predates 2012: if a BEAST finding appears, the fix is to retire TLS 1.0, not to reorder ciphers back towards RC4.

What it started. BEAST showed that a weakness recorded and fixed in the specification years earlier stays exploitable for as long as the old version is negotiable, and that the attacker's position in the browser changes what counts as practical. It opened a decade of named TLS attacks, CRIME, Lucky Thirteen, POODLE, FREAK, Sweet32 and others, each removing a feature the protocol had kept for compatibility, until TLS 1.3 kept only authenticated encryption. The NVD's score for BEAST, 4.3 under version 2 of the Common Vulnerability Scoring System (CVSS), says little about the effect it had on the protocol's design.

The numbers worth remembering. 2002, the weakness described and OpenSSL's empty-fragment countermeasure; April 2006, explicit IVs in TLS 1.1; 6 September 2011, CVE-2011-3389; late September 2011, Ekoparty; 10 January 2012, MS12-006; 1/n-1 record splitting from Chrome 16 and Firefox 10; at most 256 guesses per byte; February 2015, RC4 prohibited; March 2021, TLS 1.0 and 1.1 deprecated.

poodle.def: A 2014 attack that forces a downgrade to SSL (Secure Sockets Layer) 3.0 in order to exploit the broken padding of its CBC (cipher block chaining) cipher suites. Its identifier in the CVE (Common Vulnerabilities and Exposures) list is CVE-2014-3566.
poodle.context: Padding Oracle On Downgraded Legacy Encryption abused the fact that a client would fall back to SSL (Secure Sockets Layer) 3.0, whose padding could be probed byte by byte to recover data. It effectively ended SSL 3.0 in the field. Bodo Möller, Thai Duong and Krzysztof Kotowicz of Google published it on 14 October 2014; within months browsers had switched SSL 3.0 off, the IETF (Internet Engineering Task Force) had standardized a signal against forced fallback, and in June 2015 RFC (Request for Comments) 7568 ruled that SSL 3.0 must not be used at all.
poodle.depth:
POODLE exploited SSL (Secure Sockets Layer) 3.0's padding, which was not covered by the message authentication code (MAC), allowing an attacker to modify padding bytes and learn plaintext one byte at a time by observing whether the connection failed. The protocol was long obsolete when the attack was published: Google's announcement on 14 October 2014 called it nearly 18 years old, and the later standard that retired it notes that it was released in 1996 and replaced by TLS 1.0 in 1999. The name stands for Padding Oracle On Downgraded Legacy Encryption, and each word carries part of the story.

The padding half is a difference between two specifications. A CBC (cipher block chaining) record in SSL 3.0 holds the content, then its MAC, then padding, then a final byte giving the padding's length, and the specification, preserved as the historic RFC (Request for Comments) 6101, says only how long the padding may be, nothing about what the padding bytes contain. The MAC is computed before the padding is added, so the receiver has no way to tell genuine padding from altered padding. TLS closed the gap by rule; in the words of TLS 1.2, every padding byte must be filled with the padding length value, and the receiver must check this padding. The CVE (Common Vulnerabilities and Exposures) record words the flaw exactly: SSL 3.0 uses nondeterministic CBC padding, which makes it easier for man-in-the-middle attackers to obtain cleartext data via a padding-oracle attack. RFC 7457, the catalogue of attacks on TLS published by the IETF (Internet Engineering Task Force), places it in the padding oracle family as the variant that needs no timing measurement, and adds that on SSL 3.0 it has no known mitigation.

The reason it mattered anyway is downgrade. Clients and servers negotiated the best mutually supported version, and many implementations would retry with older versions if a handshake failed, which meant an attacker who could interfere with connections could force both sides down to SSL 3.0 even though both supported something modern. Google's post describes exactly that: browsers retried failed connections with older protocol versions to work around buggy servers, and a network attacker can cause the failures. The vulnerability was in a protocol nobody wanted to use and everyone still accepted. Mozilla measured how little it was wanted: about 0.3 per cent of Firefox's HTTPS connections used SSL 3.0 on the day of the announcement.

The response had three layers, and they arrived in order of difficulty. Browsers went first: Mozilla announced the same day that SSL 3.0 would be disabled by default in Firefox 34, due on 25 November 2014, and Google said it would begin by disabling the fallback in Chrome and hoped to remove SSL 3.0 from its client products completely in the following months. The protocol fix was the TLS Fallback Signaling Cipher Suite Value (SCSV), which Chrome and Google's servers had already supported since February 2014 and which became RFC 7507 in April 2015. A client that is retrying with a lower version than it really supports adds the value TLS_FALLBACK_SCSV, numbered 0x56,0x00, to its list of cipher suites; a server that supports something higher answers with the fatal alert inappropriate_fallback, number 86, and the forced downgrade fails in the open. Finally, in June 2015, RFC 7568 made the retirement normative: SSLv3 must not be used, negotiation of SSLv3 from any version of TLS must not be permitted, and a party that receives a hello with version 3.0 must refuse it. The RFC explains why patching was not an option: the fix for the flawed MAC-then-encrypt construction relies on extensions, which SSL 3.0 does not have.

The attack then came back in TLS, which is the part an operator of network equipment should remember. On 8 December 2014 Adam Langley of Google reported that some TLS implementations did not check the padding bytes either, having reused an SSL 3.0 decoding routine, and so could be attacked in the same way without any downgrade; he named F5 and A10, both of which issued patches. The F5 case is CVE-2014-8730: the SSL profiles component of BIG-IP, when using TLS 1.x before TLS 1.2, did not properly check CBC padding bytes when terminating connections, a variant of CVE-2014-3566. A second return came in 2019 with CVE-2019-6593, also known as Zombie POODLE and GOLDENDOODLE, a chosen ciphertext attack against CBC ciphers on BIG-IP 11.5.1 to 11.5.4, 11.6.1 and 12.1.0 virtual servers with a Client SSL profile. In both cases the protocol was not at fault; an implementation was not enforcing what the protocol required.

The fixes are the durable part. Downgrade protection mechanisms make a forced fallback detectable, and the broader lesson was that supporting an obsolete protocol for compatibility is supporting it for attackers, since they choose which version is negotiated. TLS 1.3 built the protection into the handshake itself: a server that supports 1.3 but is negotiating an older version must set the last eight bytes of its random value to a fixed marker, and a client that sees the marker when it had offered 1.3 aborts. The same version removed CBC, keeping only AEAD (authenticated encryption with associated data) ciphers, so the padding question no longer exists. That reasoning is why deprecation eventually became removal rather than discouragement, and why modern guidance is to disable old versions outright rather than to prefer new ones.

In practice POODLE survives as a line in scanner reports and as a configuration habit. A finding that names CVE-2014-3566 means a listener still accepts SSL 3.0, and the remedy is to switch the version off in the TLS profile, not to reorder ciphers; on equipment that terminates TLS for others, such as a load balancer, the same check should confirm that no CBC suite is offered below TLS 1.2 without a current fix. Among its neighbours, BEAST (2011) attacked the predictable initialization vector of CBC in TLS 1.0, Lucky Thirteen (2013) attacked the timing of padding checks in TLS itself, and DROWN (CVE-2016-0800, March 2016) used a flaw of the even older SSL 2.0 to decrypt TLS traffic. The numbers worth keeping: 14 October 2014, CVE-2014-3566, 0x56,0x00 and alert 86, RFC 7507 and RFC 7568, and the 265 references that the CVE record had accumulated by 2026, a fair measure of how many products had kept an eighteen-year-old protocol switched on.

crime.def: A 2012 attack recovering secrets by observing the size of compressed TLS requests.
crime.context: Compression Ratio Info-leak Made Easy exploited TLS-level compression: injecting guesses and watching the compressed length reveal when a guess matched secret content like a session cookie. The fix was to disable TLS compression.
crime.depth:
CRIME attacked compression rather than encryption. TLS could compress data before encrypting it, and compression works by finding repetition, so the size of the encrypted output leaks information about how much the plaintext repeated. An attacker who can inject content into a request and observe its encrypted length can determine, guess by guess, whether their injection matched a secret already present, such as a session cookie.

The elegance and the horror are the same thing: the encryption is not broken at all. Every guarantee about confidentiality of content holds, and the length of the ciphertext, which no design treated as sensitive, gives the secret away. It is the clearest practical demonstration that side channels are not exotic and that metadata about encrypted data can be as revealing as the data.

The immediate fix was disabling TLS compression, which was straightforward. The follow-on attacks were not, because compression also happens at the HTTP layer, where it is far too valuable to disable, and defending that required separating secrets from attacker-controlled content and masking tokens per request. That is a much harder engineering problem, which is why this family persisted long after the original was closed.

breach.def: A 2013 variant of CRIME that targets HTTP response compression instead of TLS.
breach.context: Browser Reconnaissance and Exfiltration via Adaptive Compression of Hypertext works even without TLS compression by attacking gzip at the HTTP layer, inferring secrets reflected in compressed responses. Mitigations include masking tokens and disabling reflection of user input.
breach.depth:
BREACH is CRIME's successor and applies the same compression side channel to HTTP response bodies rather than to TLS itself. Because HTTP compression is used essentially everywhere and disabling it costs real bandwidth and performance, the easy remedy that closed CRIME was unavailable.

The conditions are specific and common: the response must be compressed, must reflect some attacker-supplied input, and must contain a secret such as an anti-forgery token in the same body. Given those, an attacker measures response sizes across many crafted requests and extracts the secret character by character.

The defences are all uncomfortable trade-offs, which is why it is still a live consideration. Masking tokens with a per-request random value works and requires application changes. Adding random padding to responses raises the cost of the attack without eliminating it and wastes bandwidth. Separating secrets from reflected content is correct and requires knowing where all your secrets appear. BREACH is a good illustration that some vulnerabilities cannot be patched, only designed around, and that a genuinely useful feature can be the thing that makes an attack possible.

grease.def: GREASE (Generate Random Extensions And Sustain Extensibility) is a TLS (Transport Layer Security) mechanism, defined in RFC (Request for Comments) 8701, in which clients and servers advertise reserved, meaningless values among their real ones, so that peers which wrongly reject unknown values fail at once instead of years later.
grease.context: GREASE (Generate Random Extensions And Sustain Extensibility), RFC (Request for Comments) 8701 of January 2020, reserves sixteen two-byte values, 0x0A0A, 0x1A1A and so on to 0xFAFA, for TLS (Transport Layer Security) implementations to slip at random into cipher suite, extension, group, signature algorithm, version and ALPN (Application-Layer Protocol Negotiation) lists. A correct peer ignores them; one that chokes on unknown values breaks now, while it is cheap to fix, instead of when a real extension ships, so servers and middleboxes learn to ignore what they do not recognize. QUIC has adopted the same idea. Because the values change between connections, fingerprinting methods such as JA3 and JA4 strip them before hashing.
grease.depth:
The problem it solves. TLS (Transport Layer Security) follows a model where one side, usually the client, advertises a list of capabilities and the other selects from it, and the selecting side must ignore values it does not know so that new capabilities can be added later. RFC (Request for Comments) 8701, written by David Benjamin of Google and published in January 2020, describes what goes wrong: a bug that rejects unknown values still interoperates with every existing peer, so it spreads through the ecosystem unnoticed, and when a new value is finally defined, the updated peers discover that the metaphorical joint has rusted shut and the value cannot be deployed without failures. The name, GREASE (Generate Random Extensions And Sustain Extensibility), continues the metaphor; the RFC credits the rusted joint image to Adam Langley. The mechanism is deliberately mundane: reserve values that mean nothing, advertise them at random, and any peer that mishandles an unknown value breaks immediately and visibly, during development and early deployment, rather than years later when a real extension arrives and the failure is somebody else's emergency.

The values. RFC 8701 reserves sixteen values for cipher suites and ALPN (Application-Layer Protocol Negotiation) identifiers, the byte pairs 0x0A 0x0A, 0x1A 0x1A and so on up to 0xFA 0xFA, and the same sixteen as two-byte numbers, 0x0A0A, 0x1A1A, through 0xFAFA, for extensions, named groups, signature algorithms and versions; in decimal the first named group is 2570 and the last 64250. Eight single-byte values, 0x0B, 0x2A, 0x49, 0x68, 0x87, 0xA6, 0xC5 and 0xE4, are reserved for PSK (pre-shared key) key exchange modes. The values were allocated sparsely to discourage servers from special-casing them, follow one pattern across all types, avoid every existing registry entry, and can never become real TLS or DTLS (Datagram TLS) version numbers. A client may put one or more of them in its cipher suites, extensions with arbitrary length and contents, supported groups and even a key share with any bytes, signature algorithms, supported versions, PSK modes and ALPN list; a TLS 1.3 server may add GREASE extensions and signature algorithms to a CertificateRequest, and GREASE extensions to a NewSessionTicket. Both sides must treat a GREASE value that the peer actually selects as a fatal error, and RFC 9846, the July 2026 revision of TLS 1.3, builds the rule into the core protocol: a client must support every non-GREASE parameter it advertises, and a server must ignore every unrecognized cipher suite, extension and parameter.

How to send them. RFC 8701 asks implementations to choose GREASE values at random, so that peers learn to ignore all unknown values rather than a particular one, and to balance diversity against determinism: a client that moves GREASE values to random positions on every connection fails against a broken server only some of the time, and automatic retries can hide the failure, while one that keeps positions fixed for a software release tests fewer cases but finds bugs reliably. It also says implementations should not retry with GREASE disabled after a failure. Fallback retries with a feature switched off were the industry's old answer to interoperability problems, and they let an active attacker silently disable new features; GREASE exists partly to make such fallbacks unnecessary. The values cannot be negotiated, so they have no direct effect on the security of a connection.

Why the history matters. TLS 1.2 and earlier negotiated versions by the highest mutually supported version: the client announced the newest version it knew, and the server picked. RFC 9170, an IAB (Internet Architecture Board) document by Martin Thomson and Tommy Pauly of December 2021, records that clients could not advertise a new version without a non-trivial share of sessions failing because of bugs in servers and middleboxes, and that this intolerance was so severe that TLS 1.3 abandoned the scheme. The protocol now freezes the old version field, legacy_version, at 0x0303, the number for TLS 1.2, and moves the real negotiation into the supported_versions extension, and its middlebox compatibility mode, adopted after field measurements found that many middleboxes misbehaved on TLS 1.3, makes the handshake look like a TLS 1.2 session resumption with a non-empty session identifier and dummy change_cipher_spec records. The same document notes that TLS broke when new signature algorithm values were introduced. GREASE is the inoculation against a repeat: by putting GREASE versions into supported_versions and GREASE entries into every list, clients keep the new extension points in constant use. RFC 9170 is candid about the limits: greasing is superficial, exercising only a small part of an extension mechanism; it cannot protect version negotiation of the old highest-version kind; and although it has revealed problems in TLS, its efficacy has not been proven more generally. Its broader lesson generalizes: only active use keeps an extension point working.

Beyond TLS. QUIC adopted the idea from the start. RFC 9000, QUIC version 1, of May 2021, reserves every version number of the form 0x?a?a?a?a, any value whose low four bits are 1010 in every byte, so that version negotiation is exercised, and reserves transport parameters with identifiers of the form 31 times N plus 27, which carry arbitrary values and exist only to make peers ignore unknown parameters. RFC 9287, Greasing the QUIC Bit, by Martin Thomson in August 2022, adds the grease_quic_bit transport parameter, 0x2ab2, with which an endpoint tells its peer that it may set the second-most significant bit of packets, normally fixed, to any value, so that networks cannot come to depend on it.

What it looks like on the wire, and in fingerprints. In a capture of a modern browser's ClientHello, GREASE appears as unknown cipher suites with numbers such as 0x1A1A or 0xCACA, extensions of the same pattern with varying length and contents, and extra groups or versions that the server never chooses. Because the values vary between connections, passive fingerprinting has to remove them. The JA3 documentation says it ignores Google's GREASE values completely so that programs using GREASE can still be identified with a single JA3 hash, and the JA4 specification tells implementers to ignore GREASE values everywhere: in the version taken from supported_versions, in the counts of cipher suites and extensions and in the sorted lists that are hashed. The privacy angle runs the other way too: RFC 8701 warns that an implementation that does not choose its GREASE values at random may make itself, or even individual users, easier to fingerprint. Numbers worth remembering: RFC 8701 of January 2020; sixteen two-byte values from 0x0A0A to 0xFAFA and eight PSK mode values; 0x0303 as the frozen TLS 1.3 legacy version; 0x?a?a?a?a and 31 times N plus 27 in QUIC; and 0x2ab2 for the greased QUIC bit.

logjam.def: Logjam is the 2015 attack on Transport Layer Security (TLS) in which a man-in-the-middle downgrades a Diffie-Hellman (DH) key exchange to 512-bit export-grade parameters and then computes the session key, made practical because most servers shared the same few primes; it is tracked as CVE-2015-4000.
logjam.context: Logjam tricked servers into using export-grade Diffie-Hellman (DH) groups small enough to break, then computed the shared secret in time to complete the handshake. It revealed how many servers reused the same well-known primes, making precomputation attacks practical: one week of computation per 512-bit prime, then about a minute per connection. The same study warned that a single precomputation against a common 1024-bit prime, within reach of a nation-state, would expose a large share of HTTPS, SSH (Secure Shell) and IPsec VPN (virtual private network) traffic. The remedy was to disable export suites, prefer elliptic curve Diffie-Hellman and use groups of 2048 bits or more; TLS 1.3 later removed the conditions altogether, and in July 2026 RFC (Request for Comments) 10015 deprecated finite-field Diffie-Hellman cipher suites in TLS 1.2.
logjam.depth:
Logjam attacked Diffie-Hellman (DH) key exchange, downgrading connections to export-grade parameters and exploiting a property of the mathematics: a large precomputation against a single commonly used prime makes individual exchanges using that prime cheap to break afterwards. It was disclosed in May 2015 by fourteen researchers from CNRS (the French National Centre for Scientific Research), Inria, Microsoft Research, Johns Hopkins University, the University of Michigan and the University of Pennsylvania, among them David Adrian, Karthikeyan Bhargavan, Zakir Durumeric, Matthew Green, J. Alex Halderman and Nadia Heninger, and published as Imperfect Forward Secrecy: How Diffie-Hellman Fails in Practice at the ACM (Association for Computing Machinery) Conference on Computer and Communications Security in Denver in October 2015. The CVE (Common Vulnerabilities and Exposures) record, CVE-2015-4000, was published on 21 May 2015. The authors framed it as a flaw in the Transport Layer Security (TLS) protocol itself rather than in any implementation, reminiscent of the FREAK attack but aimed at ephemeral Diffie-Hellman instead of RSA (Rivest-Shamir-Adleman) key exchange.

The weak parameters were a relic of policy. To comply with United States export restrictions on cryptography in the 1990s, SSL (Secure Sockets Layer) 3.0 and TLS 1.0 included reduced-strength export cipher suites, among them DHE_EXPORT, which limited the Diffie-Hellman prime to 512 bits. No modern client needed them, but many servers still offered them two decades later: 8.4 per cent of the Alexa top million HTTPS (Hypertext Transfer Protocol Secure) domains, and 3.4 per cent of all HTTPS servers with browser-trusted certificates, accepted DHE_EXPORT when the paper was written. Before disclosure, Internet Explorer, Chrome, Firefox and Opera all accepted 512-bit primes, and Safari accepted groups as small as 16 bits.

The protocol flaw is in what the server signs. When a server chooses DHE_EXPORT it sends a signed ServerKeyExchange message carrying a 512-bit prime, and that message is structurally identical to the one sent for ordinary DHE; critically, the signed portion does not say which cipher suite the server chose. The CVE record describes the consequence: a man-in-the-middle rewrites the client's hello to ask for DHE_EXPORT and rewrites the server's hello to say DHE, and the client, seeing a valid signature, accepts a 512-bit group as if it were a normal one. To complete the handshake unnoticed the attacker then needs the discrete logarithm of one side's public value quickly enough to forge the Finished messages, which is where the mathematics came in. The paper noted that all such attacks would be prevented by also signing the cipher suite in ServerKeyExchange, and expected TLS 1.3 to fix the flaw.

The mathematics made it fast. The best attack on finite-field Diffie-Hellman, the number field sieve, spends almost all its effort on stages that depend only on the prime, not on any individual key exchange. The team ran that precomputation for three 512-bit primes, including the two most used for DHE_EXPORT; it took about a week each, after which individual discrete logarithms took a median of 70 seconds. The important finding was about reuse. A small number of standard primes were hardcoded into widely deployed software and used by an enormous fraction of servers: 92.3 per cent of the domains that allowed DHE_EXPORT used one of just two primes, one shipped with Apache and used by 82 per cent of them, another with mod_ssl at 10 per cent. One very expensive precomputation therefore compromised a very large population.

The researchers then asked what the same economics meant for groups nobody considered export-grade.
