They estimated that 768-bit groups are within range of academic teams and that 1024-bit groups may plausibly be within range of state-level attackers, and they measured what a single such computation would expose: the most common 1024-bit group would allow passive eavesdropping on 18 per cent of popular HTTPS sites, and a second one would allow decryption of traffic to 66 per cent of IPsec VPNs (Internet Protocol Security virtual private networks) and 26 per cent of SSH (Secure Shell) servers, largely because Internet Key Exchange (IKE) implementations relied on the fixed Oakley groups of 768 and 1024 bits. The researchers noted this was within reach of a well-resourced state actor, and observed that it would explain certain capabilities that had been described publicly without a plausible mechanism: a close reading of published NSA (National Security Agency) documents, they wrote, shows that the agency's attacks on VPNs are consistent with having achieved such a break. That part of the work needed no downgrade at all, only passive collection and a prime shared by millions of hosts.

The fixes came quickly on the client side. As a result of the disclosure, Internet Explorer, Firefox and Chrome began raising the minimum Diffie-Hellman group they accept to 1024 bits, with OpenSSL and Safari expected to follow. The OpenSSL advisory of 11 June 2015 made TLS clients reject handshakes with DH parameters shorter than 768 bits, a limit it said would rise to 1024 in a future release, in versions 1.0.2b and 1.0.1n; the fix was written by Emilia Käsper and Kurt Roeckx. For servers the researchers published a deployment guide with three rules: disable export cipher suites, which no modern client relies on; prefer ephemeral elliptic curve Diffie-Hellman (ECDHE), against which the precomputation does not give the same advantage; and use a Diffie-Hellman group of 2048 bits or more with a safe prime, generated for example with openssl dhparam -out dhparams.pem 2048 and loaded with SSLOpenSSLConfCmd DHParameters in Apache 2.4.8 or later or with ssl_dhparam in nginx.

The standards then removed the conditions. RFC 7919 (Request for Comments 7919, August 2016, by D. Gillmor) let TLS 1.2 clients and servers negotiate finite-field groups by name, ffdhe2048, ffdhe3072, ffdhe4096, ffdhe6144 and ffdhe8192, codes 256 to 260 in the Supported Groups registry, so that a client no longer has to accept whatever prime a server sends; a server that cannot meet the client's groups ends the handshake with insufficient_security (71), and a client that still accepts custom groups must reject any below 768 bits and should reject any below 1024. It recommends at least 3072 bits for systems meant to last, and deliberately did not reuse the IKE groups, because using the same groups in many protocols increases the value of cracking any one of them. TLS 1.3, now RFC 9846 (July 2026, obsoleting RFC 8446), removed custom ephemeral Diffie-Hellman groups entirely, keeps finite-field Diffie-Hellman only as named groups beginning with ffdhe2048 (0x0100), signs the entire handshake in CertificateVerify, and adds a downgrade sentinel: a TLS 1.3 server that negotiates TLS 1.2 must end its random value with the bytes 44 4F 57 4E 47 52 44 01, which a TLS 1.3 client checks for.

TLS 1.2 itself was settled in July 2026: RFC 10015 says clients must not offer, and servers must not select, any finite-field Diffie-Hellman cipher suite, ephemeral or static, and the registry of the Internet Assigned Numbers Authority (IANA) marks those suites D, for discouraged; finite-field groups stay allowed in TLS 1.3. Its reasons read like Logjam's legacy: TLS 1.2 has no way to negotiate the group, custom groups became widespread partly through the advice that followed Logjam, a client cannot practically check the structure of a server's custom group, a handful of very large computations against standard groups still exposes much traffic, and a reused secret opens the Raccoon timing attack.

The remediation was to use larger parameters and to stop sharing small ones, and the deeper change was philosophical. Logjam is a good example of a vulnerability that is not a coding error at all: every implementation followed the specification correctly, and the weakness came from a defaults decision made years earlier for compatibility, export suites kept switched on long after the policy behind them had gone. Sharing itself was not the problem once groups became large enough; RFC 7919's named groups are shared by design, but at 2048 bits and above no precomputation is known to be within reach, whereas a 512-bit or 1024-bit prime common to millions of hosts concentrated the value of a single computation. Reviewing what your cryptography is actually configured with, rather than that it is present, is the practice this produced: a scan for export suites and for DH groups under 2048 bits, on web servers, mail servers, VPN gateways and load balancers alike, is the check Logjam made routine.

Among its neighbours, FREAK (also 2015) forced export-grade RSA rather than Diffie-Hellman and was an implementation bug, while Logjam was a protocol flaw; DROWN (2016) attacked TLS through servers that still spoke SSLv2; and POODLE (2014) exploited SSL 3.0's CBC (cipher block chaining) padding. All four turned leftover compatibility options into attacks. The numbers worth remembering are 512 bits for DHE_EXPORT, a week of precomputation and about a minute per connection, 8.4 per cent of the top million HTTPS domains vulnerable at disclosure, 82 per cent of them on Apache's prime, 18, 66 and 26 per cent of HTTPS, VPN and SSH servers exposed by breaking a common 1024-bit group, 768 bits as OpenSSL's first client floor, and 2048 bits as the minimum worth deploying.

freak.def: FREAK (Factoring RSA Export Keys): a 2015 man-in-the-middle attack on TLS (Transport Layer Security) in which a client that asked for normal RSA (Rivest-Shamir-Adleman) key exchange accepted a 512-bit export-grade key, which an attacker could factor to read and alter the session; CVE-2015-0204 in OpenSSL, with parallel flaws in Microsoft and Apple libraries.
freak.context: FREAK (Factoring RSA Export Keys), announced on 3 March 2015 by Karthikeyan Bhargavan's team at INRIA (the French national institute for computer science research) and Microsoft Research, combined two leftovers. Servers still accepted the RSA_EXPORT cipher suites that United States export law had required in the 1990s, which cap the RSA (Rivest-Shamir-Adleman) key used for key exchange at 512 bits; and the TLS (Transport Layer Security) state machines of OpenSSL, Microsoft Schannel and Apple Secure Transport accepted such a temporary key even when the client had not asked for export cryptography. A man-in-the-middle could therefore downgrade the key exchange, factor the 512-bit modulus in hours of rented computing, and decrypt or alter the session. At disclosure 36.7 per cent of HTTPS (Hypertext Transfer Protocol Secure) servers with browser-trusted certificates accepted export RSA. The remedy was to patch the clients and remove export suites from servers; TLS 1.3 later removed RSA key exchange altogether.
freak.depth:
FREAK (Factoring RSA Export Keys) is the name given to a downgrade attack on TLS (Transport Layer Security) published on 3 March 2015. It needed two things to be true at once: a server that still accepted export-grade RSA (Rivest-Shamir-Adleman) cipher suites, and a client whose TLS implementation would accept an export-grade key it had not asked for. Neither half alone was a new idea; the combination turned out to be common. The flaw was not in RSA, nor in the strong cipher suites anyone intended to use, but in a mode of the protocol that had been obsolete for fifteen years and had never been removed.

The export suites were law turned into protocol. TLS 1.0, published as RFC (Request for Comments) 2246 in January 1999, still carried a note that under United States export law RSA moduli larger than 512 bits could not be used for key exchange in software exported from the US. Its RSA_EXPORT method let a server whose certificate held a larger key sign a temporary RSA key of 512 bits or less and use that for the key exchange, paired with 40-bit symmetric ciphers in suites such as TLS_RSA_EXPORT_WITH_RC4_40_MD5, code 0x00,0x03. Their names start with EXP or contain EXPORT, which is how they appear in cipher strings. The legal requirement was lifted for commercial software on 14 January 2000, when the Commerce Department's Bureau of Export Administration allowed any encryption software to be exported to non-government users in every destination except a short list of sanctioned states. RFC 4346, TLS 1.1, recorded the consequence in April 2006: the export suites were now unacceptably weak, implementations must not negotiate them in TLS 1.1, and clients must check that a server has not chosen one. Servers kept offering them anyway, because nothing forced their removal.

The bug was found by formal methods. Benjamin Beurdouche, Karthikeyan Bhargavan, Antoine Delignat-Lavaud, Cédric Fournet, Markulf Kohlweiss, Alfredo Pironti, Pierre-Yves Strub and Jean Karim Zinzindohoue, of INRIA (the French national institute for computer science research), Microsoft Research and IMDEA in Madrid, systematically tested the state machines of open-source TLS libraries, the logic that decides which message may follow which, and found that each mode was implemented correctly on its own while the composition was not. Their paper, A Messy State of the Union, appeared at the 2015 IEEE (Institute of Electrical and Electronics Engineers) Symposium on Security and Privacy. Bhargavan had reported the OpenSSL case on 22 October 2014. OpenSSL fixed it on 8 January 2015 in versions 1.0.1k, 1.0.0p and 0.9.8zd as CVE (Common Vulnerabilities and Exposures) identifier CVE-2015-0204, with a fix by Stephen Henson, and at first rated it low. The public announcement on 3 March was coordinated by Matthew Green of Johns Hopkins University, with internet-wide measurements by J. Alex Halderman, Zakir Durumeric and David Adrian of the University of Michigan.

What happened on the wire can be told in a few steps, and it is the same shape that Logjam used against Diffie-Hellman in May 2015. The client offers an ordinary RSA cipher suite. An attacker in the path rewrites the offer to ask for export RSA. The server, which still supports it, answers with a temporary 512-bit RSA key signed by its real certificate key, so the signature checks out. The vulnerable client accepts that key although the suite it believes it negotiated never uses one, and encrypts the premaster secret to it. Anyone who has factored the 512-bit modulus can now recover the session keys, read the traffic and inject content. Factoring was the expensive part, and two facts made it cheap. Nadia Heninger, then at the University of Pennsylvania, factored 512-bit keys on rented cloud machines in about 7.5 hours for about 104 US dollars each. And servers did not make a new export key per connection: Apache's mod_ssl, by default, generated one when it started and reused it until it stopped, so a single factorization unlocked every session that could be intercepted for the life of the process.

The exposure was wide. On the day of the announcement the University of Michigan team counted export RSA on 36.7 per cent of HTTPS (Hypertext Transfer Protocol Secure) servers with browser-trusted certificates, much of it on content delivery networks, 26.3 per cent of all HTTPS servers and 9.6 per cent of the Alexa top million domains; Ed Felten noted that the National Security Agency's own site was among them. The client side proved wider than first thought. Within days CVE-2015-1637 covered Microsoft's Schannel, which Microsoft called the publicly disclosed FREAK technique, an industry-wide issue, in advisory 3046015 of 5 March and bulletin MS15-031 of 10 March 2015; CVE-2015-1067 covered Apple's Secure Transport in iOS before 8.2 and OS X through 10.10.2; and the Michigan team listed Chrome on macOS and Android, Safari, the stock Android browser, the BlackBerry browser and Opera on macOS as vulnerable, while Chrome on Windows and current Firefox were safe. OpenSSL raised its own rating of CVE-2015-0204 from low to high on 19 March, because server support for export suites had turned out to be far more common than assumed.

The response came from both ends. Clients were patched to refuse a temporary RSA key outside an export suite. Server operators were told to disable export suites outright, together with other known-weak suites, and to enable forward secrecy, and to test the result with a scanner such as the Qualys SSL Labs server test; the Michigan team warned that software must not offer export suites even as a last resort, because a patched library is no protection if the suites remain enabled. The Michigan tracker's final figures show export RSA down to 6.5 per cent of browser-trusted HTTPS servers. OpenSSL removed export ciphers from its DEFAULT list in 1.0.2a on 19 March 2015 and dropped all 40-bit and 56-bit ciphers and ephemeral RSA key exchange in 1.1.0 on 25 August 2016. TLS 1.3, specified today in RFC 9846, removed static RSA key exchange entirely, so that every key exchange provides forward secrecy and the whole class of RSA downgrade has nothing left to target. On a load balancer or firewall the practical check is the same as for Logjam and DROWN: no cipher whose name contains EXP or EXPORT should appear in any client-side or server-side profile.

Why it is remembered. Felten drew the lesson on the day of disclosure: the deliberate weakening of exportable cryptography in the 1990s boomeranged on the agency that had wanted it, undermining the security of its own site twenty years later, and anyone asking to modify a security system to preserve their own access should be asked what the side effects will be. Green put it more bluntly. That is why FREAK, with Logjam and DROWN, is cited whenever exceptional access to encryption is proposed: a weakness introduced to satisfy a government requirement outlived the requirement by fifteen years and was then turned against the users of the very networks it was meant to protect. The technical lesson is just as durable. A protocol that negotiates downward needs every peer to enforce the same rules, and dead options are a liability until they are deleted from the code, not merely left unused. The identifiers worth remembering are CVE-2015-0204, CVE-2015-1637 and CVE-2015-1067, the 512-bit export limit and the dates 3 March 2015 and 14 January 2000.

drown.def: A 2016 attack that breaks TLS by exploiting a server's support for obsolete SSLv2.
drown.context: Decrypting RSA with Obsolete and Weakened eNcryption used a still-enabled SSLv2 endpoint sharing the same RSA key as a cross-protocol oracle to decrypt modern TLS sessions. The lesson was to fully disable SSLv2 everywhere a key is used.
drown.depth:
DROWN broke modern TLS connections by attacking an obsolete protocol running somewhere else. If a server still supported SSLv2 anywhere, even on a different port or a different service sharing the same certificate and key, an attacker could use that weak endpoint as an oracle to decrypt sessions from the modern, correctly configured one.

That cross-protocol shape is the lesson. The vulnerable server did not have to be the one under attack; it only had to share key material. Mail servers were a common culprit, because a certificate reused across web and mail meant a forgotten SSLv2-capable mail daemon undermined the website nobody thought was related to it.

The remediation is the general principle it demonstrates: an obsolete protocol is not disabled until it is disabled everywhere the key appears, and key reuse across services silently couples their security. Inventory is the actual defence, which is unglamorous and is why this class keeps recurring. Anyone confident their TLS configuration is modern should confirm what else holds the same private key.

lucky13.def: A 2013 timing attack against CBC padding in TLS.
lucky13.context: Lucky Thirteen measured tiny timing differences in how TLS processed CBC padding to recover plaintext byte by byte. It reinforced the case for moving away from CBC mode towards AEAD ciphers.
lucky13.depth:
Lucky Thirteen is a timing attack on TLS's older CBC construction. The protocol computed the MAC over the plaintext and then padded, so the amount of work a server did when rejecting a record depended on the padding, and that dependence was measurable as a tiny timing difference.

The difficulty of exploiting it is part of what makes it instructive. The signal is microseconds, requires many thousands of attempts, and is easiest with network proximity, so it sits at the edge of practicality. It was still worth fixing, because attacks only improve, and a measurable side channel is a vulnerability whose exploitation cost is a moving number.

The structural fix was ordering. MAC-then-encrypt puts the integrity check on data that has already been processed, which is what creates the timing dependence; encrypt-then-MAC and the AEAD modes that replaced both verify integrity before touching the plaintext at all. TLS 1.3 removed CBC entirely for this reason. The general lesson is that constant-time behaviour is a design property rather than an implementation detail you can add later.

sweet32.def: Sweet32 is the 2016 attack by Karthikeyan Bhargavan and Gaëtan Leurent of Inria (CVE-2016-2183 for TLS, CVE-2016-6329 for OpenVPN) that recovers secrets such as HTTP cookies from long-lived connections encrypted with 64-bit block ciphers like Triple DES and Blowfish, using block collisions that become likely after about 32 GB under one key.
sweet32.context: A block cipher with n-bit blocks is only safe in modes such as CBC (cipher block chaining) for well under 2 to the power n/2 blocks per key; for 64-bit blocks that birthday bound is about 32 GB, which a fast link carries in under an hour. Sweet32 turned that textbook limit into an attack: malicious JavaScript in the victim's browser made it send the same cookie in a vast number of requests over one Triple DES HTTPS connection, and a passive observer of about 785 GB of traffic recovered the cookie in under two days in the lab; the same applied to OpenVPN, whose default cipher was Blowfish. The response combined retiring 64-bit ciphers (OpenSSL disabled 3DES by default, NIST moved to disallow it in TLS and IPsec, OpenVPN switched to AES-GCM) with data limits per key for what remained.
sweet32.depth:
What it is. Sweet32 is not a break of Triple DES or Blowfish as ciphers; neither has a practical key-recovery attack. It exploits their 64-bit block size. Bhargavan and Leurent's site sets out the arithmetic: modes of operation such as CBC, CTR (counter mode), GCM and OCB are unsafe beyond about 2 to the power n/2 blocks of data under one key, which is about 256 exabytes for AES's 128-bit blocks but only 32 GB for 64-bit blocks. The National Vulnerability Database (NVD) describes CVE-2016-2183 as DES and Triple DES, as used in TLS (Transport Layer Security), SSH (Secure Shell) and IPsec, having a birthday bound of about four billion blocks, which lets an attacker obtain cleartext from a long-duration session, demonstrated against HTTPS with Triple DES in CBC mode; CVE-2016-6329 records the same for OpenVPN with a 64-bit cipher, demonstrated with Blowfish. Cryptographers had always required keys to be changed well before that point, but standards bodies recommended rekeying only just before it and many implementations enforced no limit at all.

How a collision leaks data. In CBC each ciphertext block is the encryption of the plaintext block combined by XOR with the previous ciphertext block. The block cipher is a permutation, so if two ciphertext blocks are ever equal, their inputs were equal, and the XOR of the two plaintext blocks equals the XOR of the two preceding ciphertext blocks, which the attacker can see. On its own that reveals only the XOR of two unknown blocks. It becomes an attack when a fixed secret is sent over and over and much of the surrounding plaintext is known: then a collision between a block holding the secret and a known block reveals the secret outright. HTTP over TLS fits exactly, because an authentication cookie travels with every request and most of the other headers are predictable or chosen by the attacker. The attack is expected to succeed once 2 to the power s copies of the secret and 2 to the power t known blocks have been encrypted, with s plus t at least 64.

What the researchers showed. The attacker is a man in the browser plus a passive observer: JavaScript planted in the victim's browser makes it send huge numbers of requests to the target site over one persistent HTTP/1.1 connection, and the observer records the encrypted traffic. Their attack needs about 2 to the 29.1 short requests of 512 bytes, 280 GB in total, or 2 to the 27.6 longer ones of 4 kB, 785 GB, and in their demonstration it recovered a secure cookie in less than two days. It worked because Triple DES was still everywhere: it was the mandatory cipher of TLS 1.0 and 1.1, nearly all HTTPS servers supported it, roughly 1 to 2 per cent of HTTPS connections from mainstream browsers used it, and about 1.1 per cent of the top 100,000 sites supported AES but preferred 3DES. Servers also had to allow very long connections, and 72 of the top 10,000, 0.6 per cent, accepted at least 800,000 requests on one connection. For VPNs (virtual private networks) the case was easier: Blowfish in CBC mode was OpenVPN's default, OpenVPN tunnels are long-lived by design, and in its pre-shared-key mode the keys never change at all.

The disclosure and the responses. The researchers reported to the OpenVPN team, website operators, browser vendors and TLS libraries, and published in August 2016, with the CVE record for TLS dated 1 September and the paper presented at ACM CCS (Conference on Computer and Communications Security) that autumn. The responses show both available strategies. Retirement: OpenSSL moved the 3DES suites from its HIGH list to MEDIUM in the 1.0.1 and 1.0.2 branches and disabled them by default in 1.1.0; Akamai offered customers the option to drop 3DES; Apple disabled it on icloud.com and urged customers to do the same; Microsoft removed 3DES from its TLS False Start list; OpenVPN 2.3.12 warned users of 64-bit ciphers and 2.4 added cipher negotiation, defaulting to AES-GCM between peers that support it. Limits: Mozilla added per-connection data limits for all cipher suites in NSS 3.27, for Firefox 51, because about 1 per cent of browser connections still used 3DES and switching it off would have broken too many sites; OpenVPN advised renegotiating every 64 MB with reneg-bytes where the cipher could not be changed. In July 2017 NIST announced that it would cut the amount of data allowed under one Triple DES 3-key bundle from 2 to the 32 to 2 to the 20 blocks in the next revision of SP 800-67, would disallow Triple DES in TLS and IPsec, and urged all users to migrate to AES. SP 800-67 Revision 2 followed in November 2017 and was itself withdrawn on 1 January 2024.

Where it shows up now. Vulnerability scanners still report Sweet32, or CVE-2016-2183, against any TLS, SSH or IPsec endpoint that offers a 64-bit block cipher, including the TLS_RSA_WITH_3DES_EDE_CBC_SHA suite that was once mandatory, and VPN concentrators and older appliances are the usual hits. The NVD scores the TLS record 7.5 under CVSS (Common Vulnerability Scoring System) 3.1, high confidentiality impact, which makes the finding prominent in reports even though exploitation needs a browser agent and a very long connection. The practical fix is to remove 3DES and Blowfish from the offered suites; RFC (Request for Comments) 9325, the current best practice for TLS, already forbids TLS 1.0 and 1.1, advises against suites under 128 bits of security, and notes that 168-bit 3DES gives only 112 bits of effective strength. In OpenVPN that means an AES-GCM cipher, which 2.4 and later negotiate by default.

Retire or rekey. Rekeying is a legitimate defence against a birthday bound, and it is what NSS, OpenVPN's 64 MB limit and NIST's 2 to the 20 blocks all do; the researchers themselves list frequent rekeying as the alternative to stopping use of 64-bit ciphers. Its weakness is that it depends on every implementation enforcing a limit that many had never enforced, and the researchers noted that limits close to the bound can still be attacked across many sessions at higher cost. Replacing the cipher removes the condition instead of managing it, which is why the lasting outcome was retirement. The general lesson is that block size, like key size and nonce size, sets a volume of use beyond which the guarantee stops holding, and that faster networks reach those volumes sooner.

The numbers worth remembering. 64-bit blocks and a birthday bound of 2 to the 32 blocks, 32 GB; 256 EB for 128-bit blocks; 785 GB, or 280 GB with short requests, and under two days for the demonstration; 1 to 2 per cent of HTTPS connections on 3DES in 2016; CVE-2016-2183 and CVE-2016-6329; 64 MB as OpenVPN's renegotiation figure; 2 to the 20 blocks as NIST's planned limit; Triple DES's 112 bits of effective strength.

robot.def: A 2017 return of a classic RSA padding oracle affecting many TLS stacks.
robot.context: Return Of Bleichenbacher's Oracle Threat showed that a 1998 RSA PKCS#1 v1.5 padding attack still worked against numerous modern implementations. It underscored how hard it is to fully retire a flawed cryptographic construction.
robot.depth:
ROBOT is the return of an attack first published in 1998. Bleichenbacher showed that a server which reveals whether an RSA-encrypted message had valid padding can be used as an oracle to decrypt traffic, one query at a time. Nearly twenty years later, researchers found that many major implementations were still vulnerable.

The recurrence is the finding. The original fix required servers to behave identically for valid and invalid padding, which is difficult to implement correctly and impossible to verify by testing the happy path. Implementations diverged in small ways over the years, and the differences were enough. Some products were vulnerable through a distinguishable error message, others through timing.

That is a strong argument for removing dangerous constructions rather than defending them. TLS 1.3 dropped RSA key exchange entirely, which eliminates the class rather than requiring every implementation to keep getting a subtle behaviour right forever. When a mitigation depends on every implementer avoiding a specific mistake in perpetuity, some of them will not, and the failure will be quiet.

raccoon-attack.def: A 2020 timing attack on TLS-DH that can recover the session key in rare cases.
raccoon-attack.context: The Raccoon attack exploited how TLS derived the premaster secret from Diffie-Hellman, where leading zero bytes and timing could leak enough to reconstruct the key. It is another reason ephemeral DH parameters and constant-time code matter.
raccoon-attack.depth:
The Raccoon attack targets a timing side channel in TLS's Diffie-Hellman key derivation. Leading zero bytes in the shared secret were stripped before hashing, so the length of the input varied, and that variation was observable in how long the hash took.

It is genuinely hard to exploit: it requires precise measurement, a large number of handshakes, and a server reusing the same ephemeral key across connections, which good practice already forbids. The researchers were clear about the limited practicality, and that honesty is worth noting because inflated severity claims are a real problem in vulnerability disclosure.

Its value is as an illustration of where side channels hide. The flaw is not in the mathematics of Diffie-Hellman or in the hash function; it is in a small encoding decision about how to represent a number before hashing it. That is the level at which cryptographic implementations actually fail, and it is why constant-time discipline has to extend to serialization and encoding rather than stopping at the primitives.

spectre.def: A 2018 class of attacks abusing CPU speculative execution to leak memory.
spectre.context: Spectre tricks a processor into speculatively accessing data it should not, then reads it through cache side channels. It affected nearly all modern CPUs and forced deep changes in browsers, operating systems, and hardware design.
spectre.depth:
Spectre exploits speculative execution, the technique processors use to guess which branch a program will take and start work early. When the guess is wrong the results are discarded, but the effects on the cache are not, and measuring which memory is now cached reveals what the processor speculatively touched.

What made it a landmark is that it was not a bug in any implementation. Speculative execution is a deliberate design that every high-performance processor of the era used, and the vulnerability is in the concept, which means it could not be patched away without giving up decades of performance work. Variants continued to appear for years because the underlying technique keeps offering new observable side effects.

The mitigations are correspondingly unsatisfying: compiler barriers that inhibit speculation at sensitive points, microcode updates, and process isolation strong enough that speculation cannot cross a boundary that matters. Each costs performance, some of it significant, and browsers additionally reduced timer precision because the attack needs accurate measurement. Spectre is the clearest demonstration available that an optimization can be a security boundary violation, and that performance and isolation are in genuine tension rather than merely competing for budget.

meltdown.def: A 2018 attack letting user programs read protected kernel memory via speculative execution.
meltdown.context: Meltdown broke the isolation between user space and the kernel on affected CPUs, allowing arbitrary kernel memory to be read. The main mitigation, kernel page-table isolation, carried a measurable performance cost.
meltdown.depth:
Meltdown broke the boundary between user programs and kernel memory on affected processors, allowing an ordinary program to read memory it had no permission to see. It was disclosed alongside Spectre and is frequently confused with it, though it is narrower and, importantly, fixable.

The mechanism is that a processor could speculatively read privileged memory and act on the value before the permission check completed, leaving cache traces that revealed the contents. Unlike Spectre, this was closer to an implementation flaw than an inherent property of speculation, which is why the mitigation could be architectural.

That mitigation was kernel page table isolation, which separates kernel and user address spaces so the privileged memory is simply not mapped when user code runs. It works and it costs, because every system call now requires switching address spaces, and workloads that make many syscalls saw substantial slowdowns. Meltdown is therefore a clean case study in security costing performance in a way that is measurable, unavoidable and paid by everyone, which is a more honest description of most security engineering than the usual framing.

roca.def: A 2017 flaw in RSA key generation in certain chips that made keys factorable.
roca.context: Return of Coppersmith's Attack exploited a weak RSA keygen routine in a widely used cryptographic library, so affected public keys could be factored. It forced reissuance of many smartcards, TPMs, and identity certificates.
roca.depth:
ROCA was a flaw in a widely used cryptographic library's RSA key generation, which produced primes with a structure that made the resulting public keys factorable far more cheaply than their size implied. The library was embedded in smartcards, trusted platform modules and national identity cards.

The scale is what makes it instructive. Keys generated over years by hardware from a major manufacturer were affected, including government identity documents that had to be suspended, and the flaw was detectable from the public key alone, which meant anyone could scan for vulnerable keys without any access to the systems holding them.

It illustrates a risk that is easy to underrate: the concentration of trust in a small number of cryptographic implementations. Hardware security modules and secure elements are chosen precisely because they are supposed to be more trustworthy than general-purpose software, and that concentration means a single defect propagates into millions of devices that cannot be patched, only replaced. ROCA is the strongest available argument for diversity in cryptographic implementations, and for treating hardware as something to verify rather than to assume.

sloth.def: A 2016 set of attacks abusing obsolete hashes like MD5 in TLS negotiation.
sloth.context: Security Losses from Obsolete and Truncated Transcript Hashes showed that allowing weak hashes such as MD5 in TLS signatures enabled transcript-collision and downgrade attacks. It pushed removal of MD5-based signatures from TLS.
sloth.depth:
SLOTH attacked protocols still using weak hash functions in their handshake signatures. The name stands for security losses from obsolete and truncated transcript hashes, and the finding was that transcript collisions could be used to impersonate a party during TLS, IKE or SSH negotiation.

The important detail is where the weak hash was. Everyone had stopped using MD5 and SHA-1 for certificates, and the deprecation campaigns focused there. But the same functions survived inside handshake signature negotiation, where they attracted no attention because nobody thought of the handshake as a place hashes lived.

That is the generalizable lesson: deprecating a primitive means finding every place it is used, and the ones that get missed are the internal, unglamorous uses that no compliance checklist enumerates. A scanner that reports a certificate's signature algorithm says nothing about what the handshake negotiated. Removing a weak algorithm requires an inventory of uses rather than an inventory of certificates.

terrapin.def: A 2023 attack that can weaken or truncate the SSH handshake.
terrapin.context: Terrapin manipulated sequence numbers during the SSH handshake to strip messages and downgrade security in specific configurations. It prompted updates to OpenSSH and other SSH implementations.
terrapin.depth:
Terrapin attacked SSH by manipulating sequence numbers during the handshake, allowing an attacker positioned in the network to delete messages from the beginning of the encrypted connection without detection. The effect is that security features negotiated at the start can be silently stripped.

Its interest is in what it says about integrity at boundaries. The SSH transport protects data after the handshake, and the handshake itself had a window where message deletion was not covered by the integrity checks that protect everything afterwards. That is a seam, and seams between protocol phases are where this whole family of attacks lives, alongside downgrade attacks and renegotiation flaws in TLS.

The practical remediation was a strict key exchange mode that both ends must support, which means the fix arrives only when both client and server are updated. That is the recurring difficulty with protocol vulnerabilities as opposed to implementation ones: patching your own side is insufficient, deployment is gated by the slowest participant, and the vulnerable configuration remains negotiable until support is removed rather than merely deprecated.

alpaca.def: A 2021 cross-protocol attack that confuses TLS services sharing a certificate.
alpaca.context: Application Layer Protocol Confusion Analysing Cross-protocol Attacks redirected a TLS connection meant for one service to another that shared the certificate, exploiting mismatched application-layer expectations. Strict SNI and ALPN checking mitigate it.
alpaca.depth:
ALPACA is a cross-protocol attack on TLS. A certificate valid for a hostname can be presented by any service on that host, so an attacker who can redirect a connection may deliver a browser's HTTPS request to a different TLS service entirely, such as an FTP or mail server sharing the same certificate.

The confusion that results is the exploit. The second service does not speak HTTP, but it may echo parts of the request in an error message, and a browser interpreting that response as HTML can be made to execute content in the origin's context. The TLS layer is not broken at any point: both endpoints authenticate correctly, and the mismatch is entirely about which application protocol was expected.

The defence is application layer protocol negotiation, enforced strictly, so that a server refuses a connection whose negotiated protocol it does not implement. The broader lesson is about certificate scope: a wildcard certificate shared across many services means those services can be substituted for one another, and the convenience of one certificate everywhere is exactly the property being exploited.

krack.def: KRACK (key reinstallation attack) is the class of attacks on WPA2 that Mathy Vanhoef published on 16 October 2017: by replaying handshake messages, an attacker in radio range makes a Wi-Fi client or access point reinstall a key already in use, which resets its packet numbers and replay counters, so traffic can be replayed, decrypted and, with some ciphers, forged.
krack.context: The weakness was in the IEEE 802.11 standard's handshakes, not in one product, so every correct implementation was likely affected: the four-way handshake that every protected network runs, the group key, PeerKey, TDLS (Tunneled Direct-Link Setup), WNM (Wireless Network Management) sleep and 802.11r fast transition handshakes, ten CVE identifiers in all. The cipher was never broken; the handshake let a key be installed twice, and the counters that serve as nonces went back to their starting values. Linux and Android 6.0 clients were worse off still, installing an all-zero key. CERT/CC coordinated the disclosure and patches were out on the day; they were backwards-compatible, so patched and unpatched devices keep working together, and changing the Wi-Fi password does nothing. The episode showed that a handshake with formal security proofs can still fail when the proofs do not model when a key is installed.
krack.depth:
What it is. KRACK, short for key reinstallation attack, is a family of attacks on the handshakes defined by IEEE 802.11 for Wi-Fi Protected Access (WPA and WPA2). Vanhoef and Piessens's paper describes the four-way handshake it targets as 14 years old, first introduced in 2003 under the name WPA, when the Wi-Fi Alliance began certifying devices against draft D3.0 of the 802.11i amendment before the final version was ratified as WPA2; every protected Wi-Fi network, personal or enterprise, uses it to derive a fresh session key. CERT/CC's note VU#228519 is blunt about scope: the vulnerabilities are in the standard itself rather than individual implementations, so any correct implementation is likely affected. KRACK does not reveal the network password or the pairwise master key, and it is not an attack on AES (Advanced Encryption Standard). It is an attack on the moment a key is put into use.

How it works. In the four-way handshake the access point and the client exchange random values and derive a session key; in message 3 the access point tells the client to install it, and the client confirms in message 4. Radio loses frames, so the standard has the access point retransmit message 3 if message 4 does not arrive, and the client accepts the retransmission and installs the key again. An attacker who has placed itself between the two on the radio channel can hold back message 4, collect the retransmitted message 3 and deliver it, so that the client reinstalls a key it is already using. Installing a key resets the transmit packet number, which the encryption protocol uses as its nonce, and the receive replay counter to their initial values. Nonce reuse under the same key is exactly what these protocols forbid: with AES-CCMP (Counter Mode with CBC-MAC Protocol) an attacker can replay and decrypt frames but not forge them, which is still enough to hijack TCP connections and inject content into unencrypted HTTP; with WPA-TKIP (Temporal Key Integrity Protocol) and with GCMP (Galois/Counter Mode Protocol), whose authentication key can be recovered when nonces repeat, frames can also be forged. The same idea applies to the group key handshake and to the fast transition handshake of 802.11r, where it is the access point that reinstalls the key.

The identifiers and the worst case. CERT/CC lists ten CVE identifiers: CVE-2017-13077 to 13079 for the pairwise, group and integrity group keys in the four-way handshake; 13080 and 13081 for the group key handshake; 13082 for an access point accepting a retransmitted 802.11r reassociation request; 13084 for the PeerKey handshake; 13086 for TDLS; and 13087 and 13088 for WNM sleep mode responses. The National Vulnerability Database scores CVE-2017-13077 at 6.8 under the Common Vulnerability Scoring System (CVSS) version 3.0, adjacent network and high complexity, and the 802.11r case, CVE-2017-13082, at 8.1. The implementation finding was worse than the protocol one: wpa_supplicant 2.4 and 2.5, the common Linux client, and Android 6.0 and later, which uses a modified copy, cleared parts of the session key from memory after installing it, as a remark in the standard suggests, so a replayed message 3 made them install an all-zero key; the paper put the share of Android devices exposed to that variant at 31.2 per cent and the krackattacks.com site at half, and the hostapd and wpa_supplicant advisory confirmed an all-zero key case in version 2.6 as well.

Why a proven handshake broke. The four-way handshake had formal proofs of security, and Vanhoef's own answer to the obvious question is precise: the attacks do not violate any property the proofs established. The negotiated key stays secret, both sides still authenticate each other, and handshake messages still cannot be forged. What the proofs did not model was key installation; the formal models never said when, or how many times, a negotiated key should be installed, and 802.11i defined the state machine only in textual descriptions scattered through the amendment. The flaw lived in that gap between a proven protocol and the behaviour the standard left unspecified. Vanhoef found it while checking a claim about OpenBSD's handshake code for another paper, when a call that installs the key during message 3 processing caught his attention.

The disclosure. Vanhoef notified the vendors whose products he had tested around 14 July 2017, realized from their replies that this was a protocol flaw rather than a set of bugs, and asked CERT/CC to coordinate; CERT/CC sent its broad notification on 28 August, with ICASI helping vendors collaborate. OpenBSD, notified on 15 July, objected to sitting on a fix for a month and was allowed to patch silently, releasing errata on 30 August; Vanhoef later called that a bad decision, since others could rediscover the flaw from the patch, and said OpenBSD would in future be told closer to the end of an embargo. The paper had been submitted for review on 19 May 2017. Publication came on 16 October 2017, with CERT/CC's note, vendor advisories and patches on the same day, and the paper was presented at the ACM Conference on Computer and Communications Security (CCS) on 1 November. The Wi-Fi Alliance said that day it had no evidence of malicious exploitation, that patched and unpatched devices would keep working together, and that it now required testing for the vulnerability in its certification labs, using a detection tool built on Vanhoef's own.

What had to be patched, and where. The fixes were backwards-compatible: a patched device sends the same handshake messages at the same moments but refuses to install a key twice. That is why Vanhoef answered that WPA3 was not needed and that changing the Wi-Fi password neither prevented nor mitigated anything. Clients carried most of the risk; access points were exposed mainly if they supported 802.11r fast transition or acted as clients themselves, as repeaters and mesh nodes do, which made enterprise networks the main infrastructure to update, although some vendors found implementation bugs beyond that. Fortinet's advisory of the same day shows the pattern: FortiGate Wi-Fi models were affected only in Wi-Fi client mode and FortiAP only as a mesh leaf, by the five four-way and group key identifiers, while Meru access points and FortiWLC controllers were affected in mesh mode, with the service assurance module or with 802.11r enabled; a later fix for CVE-2017-13077 was needed to pass the Wi-Fi Alliance's Security Detection 2017 test plan. Access points could also be modified to protect unpatched clients by not retransmitting message 3 of the four-way handshake or message 1 of the group key handshake, and hostapd offered such an option, but only for clients connected to that access point. The devices that never got patched, from handheld scanners to embedded equipment, are the lasting exposure.

What followed. The Wi-Fi Alliance introduced WPA3 on 25 June 2018, with Simultaneous Authentication of Equals (SAE) for personal networks and a 192-bit suite for enterprise ones, while keeping WPA2 mandatory for certified devices. WPA3 answers a different weakness, offline guessing of a captured password exchange; as the Dragonblood paper of 2019 by Vanhoef and Eyal Ronen notes, WPA3 defines no new protocols, and the key SAE negotiates is then used in WPA2's four-way handshake, so the KRACK fixes, not WPA3, are what protect that step. The broader lesson is about the scope of assurance: a specification that does not say when a state change may happen will be implemented in several incompatible ways, and a proof covers only the question it was asked.

The numbers worth remembering. Ten CVE identifiers, CVE-2017-13077 to 13088 (13083 and 13085 not used); message 3 of the four-way handshake as the replayed message; vendors told on 14 July and 28 August 2017; public on 16 October 2017; CCS on 1 November 2017; an all-zero key in wpa_supplicant 2.4 and 2.5 and Android 6.0; CVSS 6.8 for the four-way handshake case and 8.1 for 802.11r; WPA3 announced on 25 June 2018.

rowhammer.def: A hardware attack that flips memory bits by rapidly accessing neighbouring rows.
rowhammer.context: Rowhammer exploits electrical interference in dense DRAM: hammering one row can flip bits in an adjacent row, corrupting memory and enabling privilege escalation. It blurs the line between software and hardware security.
rowhammer.depth:
Rowhammer is a physical attack expressed in software. Repeatedly accessing one row of memory cells at high speed can, through electrical interference, flip a bit in an adjacent row that the attacker has no permission to touch. It requires no software vulnerability at all.

The consequences are severe because a single flipped bit in the right place is enough. Researchers demonstrated privilege escalation by flipping bits in page table entries, escaping virtual machines, and defeating memory protections that were working exactly as designed. The security model assumed memory is reliable storage, and Rowhammer shows that at sufficient density it is a physical system with analogue failure modes.

Mitigations have been partial and repeatedly circumvented. Error correcting memory helps and does not eliminate it, refresh rate changes raise the cost, and targeted row refresh implementations have been shown vulnerable to newer patterns. It is a good illustration that abstractions leak downward as well as upward: software security reasoning rests on assumptions about hardware, and when the hardware stops satisfying them, no amount of correct software fixes it.

bluekeep.def: A 2019 wormable flaw in Microsoft Remote Desktop Services.
bluekeep.context: BlueKeep was a pre-authentication remote code execution bug in RDP that could self-propagate like WannaCry. Its severity prompted rare patches even for out-of-support Windows versions.
bluekeep.depth:
BlueKeep was a pre-authentication remote code execution flaw in Windows Remote Desktop, meaning an attacker needed no credentials at all to run code on an exposed machine. It was wormable, and Microsoft took the unusual step of issuing patches for operating systems long out of support.

That decision is the interesting part. Releasing fixes for end-of-life systems contradicts the entire incentive structure of support lifecycles, and Microsoft did it because the alternative was a self-propagating worm across a very large installed base of machines nobody was going to replace. It is a rare case of a vendor absorbing cost to prevent an externality.

The mass exploitation that was widely predicted did not really materialize, and the reasons are worth noting because they inform how to read the next warning. The vulnerability was difficult to exploit reliably without crashing the target, patches went out ahead of working public exploits, and the coordinated warnings were unusually loud. That is a case of the ecosystem working, and the fact that a predicted catastrophe did not happen is weak evidence about whether the warning was warranted, which is the prevention paradox again.

zerologon.def: A 2020 flaw letting attackers take over a Windows domain controller.
zerologon.context: Zerologon exploited a cryptographic weakness in the Netlogon protocol so that an attacker on the network could reset a domain controller's machine password and seize control. It was rated maximum severity.
zerologon.depth:
Zerologon was a flaw in the Netlogon protocol that allowed an unauthenticated attacker with network access to a domain controller to set the machine account password to empty and take over the entire Active Directory domain. The severity rating was maximum and the exploitation was, in the end, remarkably simple.

The cause was a cryptographic misuse rather than a memory bug. A custom authentication scheme used AES in a mode with a fixed initialization vector of zeros, which meant an attacker sending all-zero input had a usefully high chance of producing a valid result by simply retrying a few hundred times. The primitive was strong and the way it was applied was not.

The remediation was staged over months because enforcing the corrected protocol immediately would have broken older devices that spoke the flawed version, which is the recurring shape of enterprise security work: the fix is known quickly and the deployment is gated by compatibility with things nobody controls. Zerologon is also the clearest available argument that domain controllers are a category of asset requiring different treatment, since compromising one is not compromising a server but compromising every identity in the organization.

printnightmare.def: A 2021 set of flaws in the Windows Print Spooler enabling remote code execution.
printnightmare.context: PrintNightmare abused the Print Spooler service, which runs with high privileges and is enabled by default, to run attacker code and escalate to system. It led to emergency patches and guidance to disable the spooler where not needed.
printnightmare.depth:
PrintNightmare was a series of vulnerabilities in the Windows Print Spooler allowing privilege escalation and remote code execution. It became notorious partly because the disclosure was accidental, with proof-of-concept code published before the fix was ready, and partly because the initial patches were incomplete.

The underlying problem is architectural and older than the bugs. The spooler runs with high privilege, is enabled by default on virtually every Windows system including domain controllers, and accepts driver installation from remote sources by design, because that is how network printing was supposed to work. Printing was designed in an era with different assumptions about who is on your network.

The advice that emerged was blunt and correct: disable the spooler on machines that do not print, particularly domain controllers. That is a good illustration of attack surface reduction beating patching as a strategy, because the vulnerability class kept producing new instances while a disabled service produced none. It also illustrates that default-enabled legacy services are a category of risk that patching never resolves, since the next one in the same component is already being written.

proxylogon.def: A 2021 chain of Microsoft Exchange flaws exploited widely in the wild.
proxylogon.context: ProxyLogon combined a server-side request forgery with further bugs to achieve unauthenticated remote code execution on on-premises Exchange servers. It was mass-exploited before patches were widely applied.
proxylogon.depth:
ProxyLogon was a chain of vulnerabilities in on-premises Microsoft Exchange, combining a server-side request forgery with a file write to achieve unauthenticated remote code execution. Mass exploitation began before most organizations had patched, and a very large number of Exchange servers worldwide were compromised.

What made it consequential is who runs Exchange on premises. By that point most large enterprises had moved to hosted mail, so the affected population skewed towards smaller organizations, local government, schools and businesses without dedicated security staff, precisely the population least able to detect a compromise or respond to one. The victims were selected by the technology rather than by the attacker.

The aftermath included a genuinely unusual event: a court-authorized operation in which the FBI removed web shells from compromised servers without the owners' involvement. That was legally novel, ethically contested and a reasonable response to the fact that thousands of organizations did not know they were compromised. It is worth knowing about, because it set a precedent for what governments may do about vulnerable infrastructure that its owners cannot manage.

proxyshell.def: A 2021 Exchange exploit chain related to ProxyLogon.
proxyshell.context: ProxyShell chained three Exchange vulnerabilities to reach remote code execution, and like ProxyLogon it was heavily exploited by multiple threat actors. Together they made Exchange patching an urgent priority that year.
proxyshell.depth:
ProxyShell was a second chain of Exchange vulnerabilities disclosed after ProxyLogon, following the same pattern of combining several flaws into unauthenticated remote code execution, and exploited heavily by ransomware operators against organizations that had patched the first chain and not the second.

The pattern it demonstrates is worth naming: a product that produces one serious vulnerability chain frequently produces another, because the underlying architecture and the assumptions that allowed the first are still present. Attackers who invested in understanding a codebase for the first campaign are also the best-placed people to find the next issue, so research concentrates rather than disperses.

The strategic consequence for defenders is that a single patch is not a resolution when the same component keeps producing exploitable chains. That reasoning is what moved many organizations off on-premises Exchange entirely, which is a legitimate response and a form of risk transfer rather than risk elimination, since the hosted alternative concentrates the same risk somewhere with better staffing and a much larger blast radius when it does fail.

mirai.def: Mirai is the malware and botnet that, from August 2016, took over internet-of-things (IoT) devices such as cameras, video recorders and home routers, mostly by logging in with factory-default passwords, and used hundreds of thousands of them for record distributed denial-of-service (DDoS) attacks, among them one on the Domain Name System (DNS) provider Dyn.
mirai.context: Mirai scanned for internet-of-things devices with default credentials and enlisted them into a botnet that took down major services through massive traffic floods: about 620 Gbit/s against a journalist's site in September 2016, and an attack on Dyn's name servers in October that disrupted Twitter, Amazon, Netflix and other sites for many users. Its source code was released publicly at the end of September 2016, spawning many variants. Its three authors, then college-age, pleaded guilty in December 2017 and, for extensive cooperation with the Federal Bureau of Investigation (FBI), were sentenced to probation, community service and restitution; the lasting response was regulatory, laws that forbid shipping devices with a shared default password.
mirai.depth:
What it was. The measurement study that a team from Georgia Tech, Akamai, Google, Cloudflare and several universities published at USENIX Security in 2017 describes Mirai as a worm-like family of malware that infected internet-of-things (IoT) devices and corralled them into a distributed denial-of-service (DDoS) botnet; the name, it notes, is Japanese for the future. The botnet surfaced on 1 August 2016, infected nearly 65,000 devices in its first 20 hours and settled at a steady population of 200,000 to 300,000, with a brief peak of 600,000 at the end of November 2016. The devices were digital video recorders (DVRs), Internet Protocol (IP) cameras, routers and printers, and their mix followed the market shares and design decisions of a handful of consumer electronics makers. Infections clustered in a few countries: Brazil, Colombia and Vietnam together accounted for 41.5 per cent, and on the day of the Krebs attack Telefônica Brasil's network alone held 3.4 per cent of all bots. The US Department of Justice, describing the case, puts it in one sentence: the botnet infected wireless cameras, routers and digital video recorders without their owners' knowledge or permission and, at its peak, consisted of hundreds of thousands of compromised devices.

How it spread. The paper reconstructs the mechanism from the released code, and the mechanism is the lesson. Each bot sent fast, stateless probes to pseudorandom IPv4 (Internet Protocol version 4) addresses on telnet, Transmission Control Protocol (TCP) ports 23 and 2323; when one answered, it tried ten username and password pairs chosen at random from a built-in list of 62, a list that largely absorbed that of an older IoT botnet family, BASHLITE, and added credentials specific to consumer routers and cameras. A successful login was reported to a separate server, and a separate loader then logged in, identified the device's architecture and installed the matching binary. The bot hid by deleting its file and disguising its process name, killed competing malware and anything listening on telnet or the Secure Shell (SSH) port, and, because it lived only in memory, did not survive a reboot. Why it found so many victims is explained by the devices. Researchers at Flashpoint told Brian Krebs that cameras and DVRs from one Chinese maker, XiongMai, had a password hard-coded in the firmware and reachable over telnet and SSH that the owner could not change, and that the web administration panel did not even know existed; a scan they ran on 6 October 2016 found more than 515,000 such systems exposed.

Not only passwords. The common summary, that Mirai exploited nothing and simply logged in, is true of the original strain and incomplete as a description of the case. The Justice Department says the three authors also tried to find known and previously undisclosed vulnerabilities to take control of devices. And after the source release, variants added exploits: from 26 November 2016 the measurement team saw Mirai-fingerprinted scans on TCP port 7547, used by the CPE WAN Management Protocol (CWMP), an HTTP-based protocol for the remote management of home routers, modems and other customer premises equipment, exploiting a remote code execution flaw in a configuration endpoint, which caused a new spike in infections and an outage at Deutsche Telekom; the operator patched its routers quickly through its own automatic update mechanism, and the attacker was arrested on 23 February 2017.

The attacks. Mirai's first famous target was a journalist. On 20 September 2016, from about 20:00 Eastern time, KrebsOnSecurity was hit by an attack first measured at 665 Gbit/s and then put at about 620 Gbit/s, nearly double the largest Akamai had seen, 363 Gbit/s earlier that year. What struck Akamai was its composition: no reflection or amplification, but SYN (synchronize), GET and POST floods that require real connections, and a large volume of traffic shaped as generic routing encapsulation (GRE) packets, whose source cannot be spoofed, which pointed to a very large collection of hacked machines. Attacks on the hosting provider OVH had begun on 18 September. On 21 October attacks on Dyn, a Domain Name System (DNS) provider, made Twitter, Amazon, Tumblr, Reddit, Spotify and Netflix hard to reach for many users. The paper counted 107,500 addresses attacking Dyn, 71 per cent of which also appeared as Mirai scanners, sending SYN floods on DNS port 53 with ACK (acknowledgement) and GRE floods; later commands targeted Dyn and PlayStation infrastructure together, and the Dyn addresses attacked were linked to PlayStation's name servers, a clue to motive. Attacks on Lonestar Cell, a Liberian telecom operator, began on 31 October. Across September 2016 to February 2017 the team observed 15,194 attack commands from 146 operator clusters, against game servers, telecom operators, anti-DDoS providers and many unrelated sites: Hypertext Transfer Protocol (HTTP) floods and User Datagram Protocol (UDP), ACK, SYN and GRE floods.

The source release and the variants. At the end of September 2016 the code was posted on Hack Forums, the date the paper gives as 30 September; the Justice Department confirms that Paras Jha posted it on a criminal forum in the fall of 2016 and that other criminals have since used Mirai variants in other attacks. Releasing code is a known way to blur attribution, since many operators then run near-identical botnets. The measurement team collected 1,028 distinct samples, found competing operators, and used DNS data to separate strains.

The case. The author's identity was made public in January 2017. On 8 December 2017, in the District of Alaska, Paras Jha, Josiah White and Dalton Norman pleaded guilty to conspiracy to violate the Computer Fraud and Abuse Act by creating and operating Mirai in the summer and fall of 2016; Jha and Norman also admitted running a second botnet of over 100,000 mainly US home routers for advertising click fraud from December 2016 to February 2017, and Jha separately pleaded guilty in New Jersey to DDoS attacks on Rutgers University between November 2014 and September 2016, which repeatedly took down the university's central authentication server. On 18 September 2018 each was sentenced in Alaska to five years' probation, 2,500 hours of community service and 127,000 dollars in restitution, and gave up cryptocurrency seized in the investigation; the prosecutors explained the sentences by extensive cooperation with the FBI, which had substantially contributed to other complex cybercrime investigations and to the wider defensive effort, and which they had to continue. On 26 October 2018 a New Jersey court added, for the Rutgers attacks, six months of home incarceration, five years of supervised release and 8.6 million dollars in restitution for Jha.

What defenders took from it. The paper's authors draw the defensive lessons from the desktop worm era. Hardening first: an unsophisticated dictionary attack compromised hundreds of thousands of devices, randomized default passwords would be only a first step, and devices should be closed by default, limit remote access to the local network or specific providers, and use address space layout randomization, isolation and least privilege. Then automatic updates, signed and with rollback, which is exactly what let Deutsche Telekom recover. Then notification, the hardest part, because consumer devices carry no public sign of ownership and no channel to their owners. For an enterprise the same reading applies: inventory what is reachable rather than what is managed, keep telnet and remote management off the internet, and watch outbound traffic, since a compromised camera is a weapon pointed at someone else. Mitigating the floods themselves is a matter of capacity and filtering upstream, which the Learn article on what actually absorbs a DDoS attack explains.

Why the fix was a law. Device security of this kind is an externality: the manufacturer competes on price, the owner, who noticed nothing, suffers no harm, and the cost falls on third parties such as a journalist, a hosting provider or the users of a DNS provider, so no participant in the sale had a reason to fix it. The paper itself concludes that this is a space where IoT requires non-technical intervention. The regulatory answer came years later. In the United Kingdom, the product security regulations in force since 29 April 2024 require that any password on a consumer connectable product be unique per product or set by the user, and neither an incremental pattern nor derived from a serial number unless through accepted cryptography; that the manufacturer publish a contact for reporting security issues; and that it publish the period for which security updates will be provided, which cannot then be shortened. Those three requirements map directly onto what Mirai exploited: a shared default, nobody to tell, and devices that were never going to be patched.

notpetya.def: The destructive malware outbreak of 27 June 2017, disguised as ransomware and delivered through the update channel of a Ukrainian accounting package.
notpetya.context: NotPetya spread using the same EternalBlue exploit as WannaCry, together with stolen administrator credentials, but was designed to destroy data rather than collect ransom. It caused billions of dollars in damage to global companies, and the United States and the United Kingdom attribute it to the Russian military.
notpetya.depth:
NotPetya presented as ransomware and was not. It encrypted systems and displayed a demand for 300 dollars in bitcoin, but the encryption was constructed so that recovery was impossible even with payment, which means the ransom was camouflage for destruction. Kaspersky showed why on 28 June 2017: the installation identifier on the ransom screen, which in real ransomware of the Petya family carries the information the attacker needs to recover the key, was plain random data, so nobody could derive a decryption key from it. The single mailbox given for payment confirmation had already been closed by its provider. Cisco Talos assessed with high confidence that the intent was destructive and not economic, and the United Kingdom's statement of 2018 put it in one line: the attack masqueraded as a criminal enterprise but its purpose was principally to disrupt. The name records the confusion of the first hours. The code resembled the Petya ransomware of 2016, so it was first reported as Petya, PetrWrap or GoldenEye; Kaspersky called it ExPetr, Talos Nyetya and ESET Diskcoder.C.

Its spread was through a compromised update mechanism for Ukrainian accounting software, which is a supply chain attack in its purest form: the malicious code arrived under the vendor's own name, through the trusted channel, from the vendor's server. The software was M.E.Doc, made by the Ukrainian company Intellect Service and used to deal with the Ukrainian tax system. ESET found a backdoor injected into one of its legitimate modules, a .NET library, in at least three updates, those of 14 April, 15 May and 22 June 2017. The backdoor collected each installation's EDRPOU number, the legal entity identifier of every organization doing business in Ukraine, along with proxy and mail settings, and it took its orders through the product's ordinary update checks to the official server, so there was no separate command and control (C2) address to block. Talos, invited in by the vendor, established that an administrator's credentials had been stolen and that the update server had been reconfigured to pass requests to a machine outside; its logs bracket the active infection phase between 09:11:59 and 12:31:12 Coordinated Universal Time (UTC) on 27 June. Microsoft's telemetry saw the M.E.Doc updater process launch the malware at about 10:30.

It then propagated laterally using stolen credentials and a leaked exploit, which meant organizations with a single Ukrainian subsidiary lost their entire global network within hours. Unlike WannaCry it had no component for scanning the internet; it was built to exhaust the network it landed in. It dropped a credential dumping tool with code similarities to Mimikatz, reused the sessions and passwords it found, and copied itself to other machines with two legitimate Windows administration mechanisms, PsExec and Windows Management Instrumentation (WMI). Where that failed it used two exploits for version 1 of the Server Message Block protocol (SMBv1) leaked by the group calling itself the Shadow Brokers: EternalBlue, CVE-2017-0144 in the Common Vulnerabilities and Exposures (CVE) list, and EternalRomance, CVE-2017-0145, both fixed by Microsoft in bulletin MS17-010 on 14 March 2017. It looked for Transmission Control Protocol (TCP) ports 139 and 445, and on a domain controller it asked the Dynamic Host Configuration Protocol (DHCP) service for every subnet and client to build its target list. The consequence is the point most often missed: a fully patched machine fell all the same if an administrator's credentials were valid on it.

On each machine the sequence was short. With the highest privileges the malware overwrote the master boot record (MBR) and scheduled a reboot between 10 and 60 minutes later; after the reboot it encrypted the Master File Table of the disk's New Technology File System (NTFS) partitions behind a fake disk-check screen and then showed the ransom note. Files with extensions from a hard-coded list were also encrypted with a 128-bit Advanced Encryption Standard (AES) key, itself encrypted with the attackers' 2048-bit RSA public key. When Kaspersky wrote on the day of the outbreak the bitcoin wallet had received 24 payments worth 2.54 bitcoin, under 6,000 dollars.

The damage is estimated in the billions and is the most expensive cyberattack on record. Microsoft counted more than 12,500 machines hit in Ukraine and infections in another 64 countries, Brazil among them. Wired's reconstruction gives the cost by company: Merck 870 million dollars, FedEx through its subsidiary TNT Express 400 million, Saint-Gobain 384 million, Maersk 300 million, Mondelez 188 million and Reckitt Benckiser 129 million, and a total above 10 billion dollars according to a White House assessment confirmed by the former homeland security adviser Tom Bossert. The White House statement of 15 February 2018 called it the most destructive and costly cyber-attack in history.

Maersk is the case engineers remember. The entry point was one computer in Odessa on which a finance executive had asked for M.E.Doc to be installed. Within hours the company that handles close to a fifth of the world's shipping capacity had 17 of its 76 port terminals stopped, and it later rebuilt 4,000 servers and 45,000 personal computers in ten days. Server backups existed, three to seven days old. What did not exist was a backup of Active Directory: the roughly 150 domain controllers replicated to one another, and all of them were wiped at once. The single surviving copy was on a domain controller in Ghana that a power cut had knocked offline before the attack; because the link was too slow to transfer several hundred gigabytes, the disk was carried by hand through Nigeria to the recovery centre in England. Maersk's chairman put the cost at 250 to 300 million dollars.

Attribution came in stages. ESET tied the outbreak within days to the group it calls TeleBots, already known for destructive KillDisk attacks in Ukraine in which ransom had never been the priority; Talos declined to name a state. On 15 February 2018 the United States and the United Kingdom attributed it to the Russian military, the British National Cyber Security Centre assessing that the Russian military was almost certainly responsible. On 19 October 2020 the United States Department of Justice announced charges against six officers of Unit 74455 of the Russian Main Intelligence Directorate (GRU), the unit researchers track as the Sandworm Team, citing nearly 1 billion dollars in losses to just three victims: the Heritage Valley Health System in Pennsylvania, TNT Express and a large United States pharmaceutical manufacturer.

The aftermath produced a legal question that mattered more than the malware. Insurers denied claims under war exclusions on the basis of the state attribution, and the resulting litigation reshaped how cyber insurance is written. Mondelez, which reported 1,700 servers and 24,000 laptops affected, sued Zurich American in 2018 after the insurer invoked an exclusion for hostile or warlike action in time of peace or war by a government or sovereign power; the parties settled in 2022 on undisclosed terms. Merck, with more than 40,000 machines infected, took the same question to judgment: on 1 May 2023 the Appellate Division of the Superior Court of New Jersey held, with 699,475,000 dollars of coverage in dispute, that such an exclusion requires the involvement of military action and did not reach a cyberattack on an accounting software provider. The traditional wording, in other words, did not make the loss uninsurable. The market's answer was to write wording that would. Lloyd's Market Bulletin Y5381 of 16 August 2022 requires every standalone cyber-attack policy starting or renewing from 31 March 2023 to exclude losses from state-backed cyber-attacks that significantly impair a state's ability to function or its security capabilities, and to set out how such an attack will be attributed. NotPetya is therefore the case that moved a destructive state attack from an unlitigated possibility into a named exclusion, a category of risk most organizations had never considered.

What it teaches is mostly about architecture. Microsoft's advice at the time was to apply MS17-010, disable SMBv1, block ports 139 and 445 between machines that have no reason to share files, restrict remote WMI, and protect privileged credentials, because the worm travelled further on stolen administrator sessions than on its exploits. Maersk's recovery adds the lesson about identity infrastructure: replication is not backup, and a directory whose every copy is online can be destroyed in one pass. The reason it mattered that a firm had one office in Ukraine is the flat internal network that let a workstation in Odessa reach domain controllers everywhere. And the update channel that started it all is trusted by design, which is why the outbreak sits beside the SolarWinds compromise as a reference case for software supply chain risk.

The numbers worth remembering: 27 June 2017; three backdoored updates, in April, May and June; an infection window of about three hours and twenty minutes; a reboot within 10 to 60 minutes; a 300-dollar demand that could never be honoured; 12,500 machines in Ukraine and 64 other countries; 45,000 personal computers and 4,000 servers at Maersk alone; more than 10 billion dollars in total; and MS17-010, published 105 days before the outbreak.

spring4shell.def: A 2022 remote code execution flaw in the Spring Framework for Java.
spring4shell.context: Spring4Shell let attackers achieve remote code execution through data binding in certain Spring configurations. Coming shortly after Log4Shell, it renewed attention on the risk carried by ubiquitous Java dependencies.
spring4shell.depth:
Spring4Shell was a remote code execution vulnerability in the Spring Framework, disclosed shortly after Log4Shell and inevitably compared to it. The comparison is instructive mostly for how different the two turned out to be.

Log4Shell was trivially exploitable in almost any deployment that logged user input, which is nearly all of them. Spring4Shell required a specific combination of Java version, deployment packaging and configuration, so the vulnerable population was a fraction of the framework's users. The initial reporting did not make that distinction, and a great many teams spent a weekend on an emergency that did not apply to them.

That gap between disclosure and applicability is the durable point. Severity scores describe the worst case, not your case, and the useful question during a disclosure is whether the preconditions hold in your environment rather than how high the number is. Teams that could answer that quickly, because they knew what they ran and how it was configured, spent an hour where others spent days. Inventory is what converts a headline into a decision.

flapping.def: An interface, adjacency or route that keeps going down and up, again and again: never quite dead, never quite stable.
flapping.context: A flapping link resets protocol adjacencies on every transition, so one bad SFP (small form-factor pluggable) transceiver or loose patch cable can ripple through OSPF (Open Shortest Path First) and BGP (Border Gateway Protocol) far beyond the port itself. BGP even grew a defence, route flap damping, because a single flapping route can churn tables across the wider internet. The fix is almost never at the layer where the flapping is noticed: it is at the lowest layer that is changing state.
flapping.depth:
What the word covers. Flapping is a state that oscillates: up, down, up, down, often faster than anyone can react. It happens at every layer, and the layers feed each other. A physical link loses and regains carrier; the routing adjacency over it, an OSPF (Open Shortest Path First) neighbour or a BGP (Border Gateway Protocol) session, is torn down and rebuilt; the routes learned over it are withdrawn and announced again; and a monitoring system watching the service behind it sends an alert and a recovery, then another alert. Juniper's documentation describes the mechanism in one line: each time an interface changes state, an advertisement goes to the upper-level routing protocols. It also sorts physical flaps into two kinds that need different treatment: nearly instantaneous bursts lasting milliseconds, typical of transport equipment between two routers, and periodic flaps lasting seconds.

Why a flap costs more than an outage. A link that fails and stays down costs one convergence. A link that flaps costs one on every transition. In OSPF the rule is explicit: RFC (Request for Comments) 2328 says that on the InterfaceDown event all interface variables are reset, timers are disabled and every neighbour connection associated with the interface is destroyed, so each return of the link means a new adjacency, a new database exchange and a new shortest-path calculation on every router in the area. Ivan Pepelnjak's analysis of the problem makes the trade-off plain: a network tuned for fast convergence detects failures and reroutes quickly, and for the same reason becomes highly susceptible to repetitive failures, with traffic constantly rerouted as adjacencies come and go and significant data loss along the way.
