Detection mechanisms can create flaps as well as react to them: RFC 5880 warns that a system running many BFD (Bidirectional Forwarding Detection) sessions or very short intervals can become CPU-bound (limited by its central processing unit), and that such failures have been seen repeatedly in hello-based protocols, so timers set too aggressively make a stable link look as if it were flapping.

Damping the interface. The first defence holds the news back. Junos hold timers ignore every transition during the hold time after a link goes down or comes up, and advertise the new state only if it is still true when the timer expires; Juniper recommends similar damping on both ends of a link and notes that damping only makes sense where routing protocols are listening. Cisco's answer for longer flaps, IP Event Dampening, applies the same mathematics as BGP route flap damping to the interface: each flap adds a penalty, fixed at 1,000 in Cisco IOS, the penalty decays with a half-life, and the interface is reported down to the routing protocols while the penalty is above the suppress threshold. The defaults, as ipSpace.net documents them, are a half-life of 5 seconds, a reuse threshold of 1,000, a suppress threshold of 2,000 and a maximum suppress time of 20 seconds, configured with the dampening command on physical interfaces only and read with show dampening interface and show interface dampening. Arista added a similar feature in EOS 4.32.0F.

Route flap damping in BGP. On the internet the problem appeared one level up. RIPE-378 (2006), a document of the Routing Working Group of RIPE (Réseaux IP Européens), recalls that in the early 1990s the fast growth in announced prefixes, denser meshing between providers and rising instability began to hurt backbone routers, since every prefix that became unreachable produced updates that rippled across the internet. RFC 2439, BGP Route Flap Damping, published in November 1998 by Curtis Villamizar of ANS, Ravi Chandra of Cisco and Ramesh Govindan of ISI, answered with a figure of merit kept for each route: it grows with every change, decays over time with a half-life, and suppresses the route while it is high, until there is some confidence the route has stabilized. RFC 7196 lists the defaults that Cisco and Juniper still ship: a penalty of 1,000 for a withdrawal, 500 for an attribute change, 0 (Cisco) or 1,000 (Juniper) for a re-advertisement, a suppress threshold of 2,000 (Cisco) or 3,000 (Juniper), a half-life of 15 minutes, a reuse threshold of 750 and a maximum suppression of 60 minutes.

How damping came to hurt the innocent. The defaults turned out to be too aggressive. RIPE-378 warned in 2006 that common simple configurations can do more harm than good, and RIPE-580 (7 January 2013) explained why: BGP path hunting, the extra updates a richly connected topology produces whenever a route changes (in RFC 7196's words, topological richness amplifies the number of update messages), generates enough of them for default settings to suppress a prefix after only a few real flaps, so damping was deprecated for over-damping. RFC 7196 (May 2014) put it bluntly: damping severely penalized sites for being well connected, and many operators turned it off. The measurements in RIPE-580 show the trade: with a suppress threshold of 2,000, 14 per cent of prefixes were suppressed for a 47 per cent cut in churn; at 6,000, 2.1 per cent for 19 per cent; at 12,000, 0.63 per cent for 11.26 per cent. Because a small number of prefixes flap rapidly and cause a disproportionate share of updates, both documents bring damping back with higher numbers: vendors should raise the maximum penalty to at least 50,000, and operators should set a suppress threshold of at least 6,000, or 12,000 if conservative, while RFC 7196 asks vendors not to change the old defaults under existing configurations. A router running damping with factory values is therefore still applying the 1998 settings that the 2013 and 2014 documents call overly aggressive.

Flapping in monitoring. The word means the same thing in a monitoring system, with a different remedy. Nagios defines flapping as a host or service changing state too frequently, producing a storm of problem and recovery notifications, and notes that the cause can be thresholds set too low as well as a real network problem. It keeps the last 21 check results, in which at most 20 state changes can occur, computes a percent state change that weights recent changes more heavily, and declares flapping when that value rises above a high threshold and over only when it falls below a separate low one, the same hysteresis that keeps damping from switching on and off. While a host is flapping, alerting on each change would only feed alert fatigue.

Reading a flap. The useful question is which layer is changing state first, since everything above it is consequence. An interface whose carrier drops points at the physical layer: the optic, the cable, the patch panel, or the transport equipment between two routers that Juniper's documentation singles out. A BGP session that resets while the interface underneath stays up points at the session itself: hold timers, a BFD configuration too aggressive for the box, or a path problem. A route that flaps with a stable session points further away, at the origin or a network along the path. Damping changes none of these causes; it only limits how far the noise spreads, and a suppressed interface or route is still broken until someone fixes the bottom layer. Flapping should not be confused with MAC flapping, in which one MAC (media access control) address is learned alternately on two switch ports, a sign of a loop or of duplicated addresses rather than of a link going up and down.

fat-finger.def: To cause an outage with a typo - the wrong command, the wrong device, or one digit off in a config line.
fat-finger.context: Half the war stories in networking start with a fat-fingered prefix, VLAN (virtual local area network), or a reload typed into the wrong window. Change windows, peer review, and commit-confirm exist not because engineers are careless, but because everyone's fingers slip eventually.

cruft.def: The accumulated leftover junk in a system - old configs, dead code, objects nobody dares delete.
cruft.context: Every long-lived firewall policy and codebase grows cruft: rules for servers decommissioned years ago, objects named test2-DO-NOT-DELETE. Cleaning it is unglamorous and essential, because cruft is where surprises hide.

bit-bucket.def: The imaginary place discarded data goes - the destination of everything sent to /dev/null.
bit-bucket.context: Dropped packets, silenced logs, and ignored alerts all land in the bit bucket. On Unix it has a real address, /dev/null: the device that accepts everything and stores nothing.

thundering-herd.def: What happens when a crowd of clients all wake up, retry, or reconnect at exactly the same moment.
thundering-herd.context: A cache entry expires and a thousand requests hit the origin at once; a switch reboots and every device re-authenticates together. The fixes are jitter, backoff, and request coalescing - anything that turns a stampede back into a queue.

hairpin-nat.def: Reaching your own public address from inside your own network - the traffic goes out to the NAT and hairpins straight back in.
hairpin-nat.context: Without hairpin (loopback) NAT support, an internal client asking for the company's public IP gets nowhere, which is why split-horizon DNS often answers with the internal address instead. The name is the shape the traffic draws: out, U-turn, back.
hairpin-nat.depth:
RFC 4787 defines the case precisely: two hosts sit behind one NAT, X1 sends to the external address and port the NAT allocated to X2, and the NAT must relay the traffic back inside. Its REQ-9 makes hairpinning a MUST for UDP and RFC 5382 does the same for TCP. The behaviour required is that X2 sees the packet arrive from X1's external address and port, not from its private one.

In a worked example with the NAT at 203.0.113.1, a packet from 10.0.0.2:40000 to 203.0.113.1:51234 is delivered to 10.0.0.10:51234 with source 203.0.113.1:40000. RFC 5128 notes that not all deployed NATs support hairpinning, and that even where they do, two peers on the same network do better to reach each other's private endpoints directly, because the detour through the NAT adds latency and load.

eyeball-network.def: An ISP whose customers are people watching screens - the networks where the eyeballs are.
eyeball-network.context: Peering economics splits the internet into eyeball networks (residential ISPs, mobile carriers) and content networks (CDNs, clouds). Content wants to reach eyeballs, eyeballs want content close, and interconnection disputes between the two are where most peering drama lives.

five-nines.def: 99.999% availability - about five minutes of downtime allowed per year.
five-nines.context: The classic telecom gold standard. Each added nine costs roughly ten times more than the last: four nines is under an hour of downtime a year, five is minutes, six is seconds. The honest question is never whether you can hit five nines, but which failures the users actually feel.

war-room.def: The room, physical or virtual, where an incident's responders gather until the thing is fixed.
war-room.context: A war room concentrates the people, the timeline, and the decision-making in one place during a major outage. The modern version is a bridge call plus a dedicated chat channel; the ritual matters more than the walls.

snowflake-server.def: A server so hand-crafted and unique that nobody could rebuild it from scratch.
snowflake-server.context: Years of manual tweaks make a snowflake: beautiful, fragile, and unreproducible. The remedy is the cattle model - configuration as code, rebuildable from a definition - so that no machine is precious.

configuration-drift.def: The slow divergence between what a system is supposed to look like and what it actually runs.
configuration-drift.context: One emergency hotfix here, one manual tweak there, and six months later no two of the 'identical' devices match. Drift is why audits surprise people, and why declarative tooling keeps re-asserting the desired state instead of trusting the last change.

crash-cart.def: The wheeled cart with a monitor, keyboard, and cables that gets pushed to a server that stopped answering the network.
crash-cart.context: When SSH is dead and the out-of-band card was never configured, the crash cart is the last resort: console access at walking speed. Datacenters keep one per aisle for exactly that day.

tarpit.def: A defensive trick that answers attackers extremely slowly, wasting their time instead of refusing them.
tarpit.context: A tarpit accepts the connection and then drips out bytes, holding scanners and spam bots for minutes on what should take milliseconds. The German original, Teergrube, gave the technique its name during the spam wars.

script-kiddie.def: An attacker who runs other people's exploit tools without understanding how they work.
script-kiddie.context: Dismissive but useful: script kiddies are the background noise of the internet, scanning everything with downloaded kits. The insult hides a serious point - automation means even unskilled attackers find unpatched systems, so 'nobody would bother attacking us' has never been true.

shoulder-surfing.def: Stealing information the analog way: reading someone's screen or keyboard over their shoulder.
shoulder-surfing.context: Airport lounges, trains, and open-plan offices are the classic venues. Privacy screens, screen-lock habits, and not typing passwords during a projected demo are the countermeasures - the oldest attack in the book still works.

dumpster-diving.def: Recovering sensitive information from the trash - printouts, sticky notes, unwiped drives.
dumpster-diving.context: Old-school reconnaissance that still delivers: org charts, invoices, and password notes leave the building through the bin. Shredders and disk-wipe policies exist because the perimeter includes the dumpster.

juice-jacking.def: The attack theory that a public USB charging port could push malware or pull data while it charges your phone.
juice-jacking.context: USB carries data and power on the same connector, which makes the attack plausible; confirmed in-the-wild cases are rare, but the fix is cheap - a power-only cable, a data blocker, or simply your own charger.

bricked.def: Rendered as functional as a brick - a device so broken it will not even boot.
bricked.context: A failed firmware update is the classic cause: half-written flash, no bootloader, no recovery. Soft-bricked means a rescue path exists (safe mode, TFTP boot, console); hard-bricked means it is now a paperweight with ports.

borked.def: Broken, in the resigned voice of someone who has to fix it - as in 'the upgrade borked the standby unit'.
borked.context: Less formal than 'failed', more printable than the alternatives. A word for the state between working and diagnosed.

nuke-and-pave.def: To stop debugging a sick machine and simply wipe it and reinstall from scratch.
nuke-and-pave.context: At some point the honest cost-benefit says rebuilding beats untangling. Cheap and safe when configs are code and data is backed up; terrifying exactly when they are not - which is the real lesson.

dependency-hell.def: The state where software cannot be installed or upgraded because its dependencies' versions conflict.
dependency-hell.context: Package A needs libfoo 1.x, package B needs 2.x, and you need both. Windows called it DLL hell; every language ecosystem reinvents it. Lockfiles, vendoring, and containers are all, at heart, escapes from dependency hell.

braindump.def: A verbatim collection of leaked real exam questions, sold or shared so candidates can memorize their way to a certification.
braindump.context: The dark economy of the certification world. Using dumps violates every vendor's exam agreement, gets certifications revoked, and produces paper cert-holders who collapse at the first real device. The word also has an innocent sense - writing down everything you know before leaving a project - so context matters.

alert-fatigue.def: The numbness that sets in when monitoring pages so often that real alerts drown among the false ones.
alert-fatigue.context: Every ignored alarm trains the on-call brain that alarms do not matter, right up until one does. The cure is ruthless: every alert must be actionable, or it gets tuned, aggregated, or deleted.
alert-fatigue.depth:
Alert fatigue is the failure mode where a monitoring system works exactly as designed and stops protecting anything. Every alert is technically correct, and there are far too many, so the humans receiving them learn to dismiss without reading. The system is healthy on paper; the response capability is gone.

Where the term comes from. Hospitals named it first, as alarm fatigue. The Joint Commission devoted its Sentinel Event Alert of 8 April 2013 to medical device alarms: it estimated that between 85 and 99 per cent of alarm signals do not require clinical intervention, described clinicians who become desensitized to the sound and overwhelmed by information, and counted 98 alarm-related events in its voluntary database between January 2009 and June 2012, 80 of which ended in death. The Agency for Healthcare Research and Quality's summary of the alert adds the point that matters for any field: because reporting is voluntary, those numbers are a small part of the real total. The mechanism carries over to a network operations centre or a security operations centre (SOC) unchanged, which is why the jargon of operations and security borrowed the name.

It is a design problem rather than a discipline problem, which is the part organizations get wrong when they respond by telling analysts to be more careful. Attention is finite and habituation is automatic. A queue that produces hundreds of low-value notifications trains exactly the behaviour that will miss the one that mattered, and blaming the person for that outcome guarantees it recurs.

The operations view. Google's site reliability engineering book puts the cost in plain terms. In the chapter on monitoring, Rob Ewaschuk writes that paging a human is an expensive use of an employee's time, and that when pages occur too frequently people second-guess, skim or even ignore them, sometimes ignoring a real page masked by the noise, so that outages last longer. His rules follow from that: every page should be actionable; every page should require intelligence, because a page that merits only a robotic response should not be a page; and an engineer can react with urgency only a few times a day before becoming fatigued. The chapter on being on call turns that into arithmetic: handling an incident, from root-cause analysis to the postmortem and the bug fixes, takes about six hours on average, so a 12-hour shift can absorb at most two, the distribution of pages should be very flat with a median of zero, and no more than 25 per cent of an engineer's time should be spent on call.

The security view. Security monitoring has the same problem with a worse signal. Bushra Alahmadi, Louise Axon and Ivan Martinovic of the University of Oxford surveyed 20 SOC practitioners, who confirmed high false-positive rates requiring manual validation, then interviewed 21; their USENIX Security 2022 paper found that most of what analysts call false positives are benign triggers, true alarms explained by legitimate behaviour in the organization, and that the tedium of validating them causes alarm burnout and, eventually, desensitization. Their prescription is aimed at the tools rather than the people: alarms should be Reliable, Explainable, Analytical, Contextual and Transferable, so that an analyst can validate one quickly and act. Palantir's incident response team describes the same decay from the engineering side: alerts that went to production without documentation or peer review gained a reputation for low quality, which led to fatigue and alerting apathy.

The case everyone cites. At Target in 2013 the detection worked and the response did not. The US Senate Commerce Committee's majority staff report of 26 March 2014 records that the company's FireEye system raised urgent alerts with each installation of the data exfiltration malware between 30 November and 3 December, that the security team neither reacted nor let the software delete the malware automatically, and that the alert, with the generic name malware.binary, may have been viewed as a false positive if the system was frequently alarming. Target did not find the breach itself: the report notes that it learned of it from the Department of Justice on 12 December, and on 19 December it confirmed that some 40 million credit and debit cards had been compromised. The tool did its job; the alert had to compete with everything else on the console, and lost.

The fixes are unglamorous. Alert on conditions that require a decision rather than on facts that are merely true. Give every alert an owner and a documented action, and delete the ones that have neither. Track how often each rule fires and what fraction was actionable, then tune or remove the worst offenders. The UK National Cyber Security Centre (NCSC) adds the practices a SOC can adopt: keep the number of alerts to the absolute minimum so that each one that fires can be properly investigated; feed triage outcomes back into the detection logic; combine detections, since a real attack usually trips several and a single detection firing in isolation is more likely to be wrong; and review the most frequently triggered alerts regularly, being cautiously open to removing those with high false-positive rates. A short queue of alerts people actually read protects more than a comprehensive one they have learned to ignore.

The opposite failure. Suppression is the easiest cure and the most dangerous one. The NCSC warns that allow lists must be strictly bounded by object and time, or they become perpetual and a way to evade monitoring. A preprint posted to arXiv on 31 August 2026 by Sudaroli Dhananjeyan and Kumaran U measured what happens when they are not: across nine years of the public SigmaHQ rule corpus, exclusions added to quieten noisy rules outnumbered those withdrawn by 1,642 to 304, and an estimated 86.7 per cent were still in force three years later. Every one of those decisions relieved fatigue on the day it was made; collectively they narrowed what the rules could see. A team fighting alert fatigue should therefore count its suppressions as carefully as its alerts, and give each one an owner and an expiry date.

Neighbours, and the numbers worth keeping. Alert fatigue is the human cost of poor detection engineering and the commonest way a SOC loses an intrusion it had already detected; toil is its operational cousin, the repetitive manual work that grows when alerts are answered by hand; triage and escalation are the processes it degrades first; and service level objectives (SLOs) are the operations answer to it, since paging on a threat to the objective rather than on every symptom cuts the noise at the source. Worth remembering: 85 to 99 per cent of hospital alarms needing no intervention in 2013; two incidents per 12-hour shift as Google's ceiling; and the Target alerts of late November 2013, which fired on time and changed nothing.

alarm-storm.def: One real failure detonating into thousands of secondary alarms across the monitoring system.
alarm-storm.context: A core link dies and every device behind it screams at once, burying the root cause under its own symptoms. Event correlation and topology-aware suppression exist to turn the storm back into a single actionable page.

gray-failure.def: A failure that is real but not clean - the system is degraded in a way the health checks do not see.
gray-failure.context: The disk that is slow but not dead, the link dropping one packet in a thousand. Gray failures are nastier than outages because everything reports green while users suffer; catching them means measuring what users experience, not just whether the process is up.

goodput.def: The throughput that actually matters: useful application data delivered, after all the overhead and retransmissions.
goodput.context: A link can show high throughput while goodput is terrible - retransmissions, headers, and duplicate data all count as traffic but not as progress. It is the difference between the speedometer and actually arriving.

bufferbloat.def: Latency caused by oversized buffers: routers queue so much that packets arrive very late instead of being usefully dropped.
bufferbloat.context: Big buffers were meant to prevent loss, but a full deep buffer means every packet waits in a long line - which is why one big upload can make video calls stutter. Smart queue management (CoDel, FQ-CoDel, CAKE) drains the bloat.

microburst.def: A traffic spike so brief that it overflows a switch buffer and drops packets, yet vanishes inside the utilization averages.
microburst.context: The five-minute graph shows 30% while a two-millisecond burst overruns the port and TCP quietly retransmits. Classic in storage and trading networks; catching one takes high-resolution counters or buffer-drop statistics, not prettier averages.

elephant-flow.def: A single long-lived flow so large it dominates a link - one elephant among thousands of mice.
elephant-flow.context: Backups, replication, and bulk transfers are the elephants; interactive traffic is the mice. One elephant can fill a queue and trample the mice's latency, which is why QoS, ECMP hashing, and flow-aware scheduling all care about telling them apart.

living-off-the-land.def: Attacking with the tools already installed on the victim's systems, so nothing malicious ever has to be downloaded.
living-off-the-land.context: PowerShell, WMI, certutil, PsExec: all legitimate, all signed, all abusable. It defeats naive antivirus because there is no malware file to find; defenders answer with behavioural detection and with logging what the built-in tools are doing.

magic-smoke.def: The smoke inside electronics that, once released, can never be put back - the joke explanation for why fried hardware stays dead.
magic-smoke.context: 'You let the magic smoke out' is how engineers pronounce a component dead after a miswire or a power surge. The humor encodes a truth: electronics fail visibly exactly once.

tribal-knowledge.def: The critical operational knowledge that lives only in certain people's heads, never in the documentation.
tribal-knowledge.context: Why the failover script must run twice, which port is really connected where - the things you learn by asking the right veteran. It is the raw material of the bus factor, and writing it down is how teams stop being hostage to it.

flag-day.def: A cutover where everything must change at once, with no coexistence between old and new.
flag-day.context: The name honours the original: 1 January 1983, when the ARPANET switched from NCP to TCP/IP in a single day. Protocol designers have avoided flag days ever since - it is why IPv6 was built to run alongside IPv4 rather than replace it overnight.

forklift-upgrade.def: An upgrade so total that the old equipment leaves on a forklift - nothing is reused, everything is replaced.
forklift-upgrade.context: The opposite of an incremental migration: new chassis, new architecture, new cabling. Sometimes it genuinely beats nursing the installed base; vendors, naturally, tend to agree.

sev1.def: The highest incident severity: the service is down, customers feel it, and everything else can wait.
sev1.context: Declaring a SEV1 is a deliberate act - it summons the war room, wakes the escalation chain, and starts the clock on communications. Most organizations run SEV1 through SEV4; arguing about the number mid-incident is a smell of its own.

its-always-dns.def: The troubleshooting proverb that whatever the symptom, the root cause will turn out to be DNS.
its-always-dns.context: Half joke, half statistics: name resolution touches everything, fails in creative ways, and hides behind symptoms that look like anything else. The haiku version is canon: it's not DNS - there's no way it's DNS - it was DNS.
its-always-dns.depth:
It's always DNS is the standard joke of incident response, deployed the moment a problem is inexplicable, and its persistence is diagnostic rather than merely funny. DNS genuinely is implicated in a disproportionate share of outages.

The reason is structural. Almost every action begins with a name resolution, so a DNS failure presents as everything being broken simultaneously rather than as a DNS error, which is exactly the shape that makes a problem hard to localize. Caching means the symptom appears at unpredictable times and in unpredictable places, and a change to a record propagates on a schedule set by TTLs somebody chose months ago. Failures are also frequently partial, affecting one resolver's view and not another's, which produces the impossible reports where a service is down for half the staff.

The corollary experienced engineers actually use is that DNS should therefore be the first thing eliminated rather than the first thing blamed. Resolving the name from several vantage points, checking whether the answer matches expectation, and confirming which resolver answered takes under a minute and either finds the problem or removes a large branch of the search tree. The joke is a heuristic, and it earns its place.

works-on-my-machine.def: The developer's classic defence when code fails everywhere except their own laptop.
works-on-my-machine.context: The phrase that launched a thousand containers. The gap between 'my machine' and production - versions, paths, environment variables, data - is precisely what reproducible builds, CI, and Docker exist to close.
works-on-my-machine.depth:
It works on my machine is the defence that ends a conversation and the phrase that named an entire category of problem: software behaves differently in different environments, and the developer's environment is the least representative one available.

The causes are mundane and numerous. Different library versions, a dependency installed globally years ago and forgotten, environment variables set in a shell profile, file paths that exist only locally, a database with test data shaped unlike production, a timezone, a locale, more memory, no latency. None of these are in the repository, which is exactly why the code appears correct and behaves differently.

The industry's response was to make the environment part of the artefact. Containers, declarative dependency manifests, lockfiles and infrastructure as code all exist to close the gap between what is committed and what actually runs, and the joke about shipping your machine to the customer is the honest description of what a container image is. The phrase survives as shorthand for a failure of reproducibility, and the useful response to hearing it is curiosity about what differs rather than an argument about whose machine is correct.

s-in-iot.def: The joke that the S in IoT stands for security - there is no S, and too often no security either.
s-in-iot.context: A one-line audit of an industry: default passwords, unpatchable firmware, devices that outlive their vendors. Botnets like Mirai turned the punchline into an operational fact.
s-in-iot.depth:
The S in IoT stands for security is a joke that works because there is no S in IoT. It names a real and structural condition rather than a series of individual failures.

The economics explain it completely. Connected devices compete on price in a market where security is invisible at purchase, so the manufacturer's incentive is to omit it. The firmware is frequently assembled from vendor code with unknown provenance, updates require infrastructure the manufacturer must fund for the life of the device, and that life is often longer than the company's interest in the product. A camera bought today may be running unpatched software in a decade because there is no mechanism and no obligation.

That the joke has survived unchanged for years is itself the point. Mirai demonstrated the consequences, regulation has begun to address the incentive with default password bans and mandatory update periods, and the installed base of devices that predate any of it will remain connected for a very long time. The practical position for anyone running a network is to assume these devices are compromised, segment them accordingly, and not depend on the manufacturer for anything.

trust-but-verify.def: The old proverb of cooperative suspicion - accept the claim, then check it anyway.
trust-but-verify.context: A Russian proverb that Reagan made famous in arms control and IT made a habit. Zero trust sharpened it into 'never trust, always verify': identity and posture are checked continuously, not once at the door.
trust-but-verify.depth:
Trust but verify entered technical vocabulary from arms-control diplomacy, where it described treaties whose provisions were backed by inspection. Applied to systems, it names the position between paranoia and credulity: proceed on the assumption things are working, and independently confirm that they are.

The verification half is what usually gets dropped. A backup job that reports success is trusted; a restore that has never been attempted is the verification nobody ran. A firewall rule believed to be in place, a monitoring alert believed to fire, a failover believed to work: each is a trust that has never been tested, and the pattern is the same one that hope is not a strategy describes from the other direction.

It sits awkwardly beside zero trust, and the tension is worth stating rather than resolving glibly. Zero trust says do not grant access on the basis of network position; trust but verify says do not act on an assumption without confirming it. They are compatible and they are not the same, and using the phrases interchangeably, which happens in vendor material constantly, muddies both.

assume-breach.def: The security posture that plans as if attackers are already inside, because someday they will be.
assume-breach.context: It reframes the job from building a perfect wall to limiting what a successful intruder can reach: segmentation, least privilege, detection, rehearsed response. The grim industry version: there are two kinds of companies - those that have been breached, and those that do not know it yet.
assume-breach.depth:
Assume breach is the posture that treats compromise as a current condition rather than a future possibility, and its value is in what it changes about where effort goes. If prevention is assumed to work, investment concentrates at the perimeter; if compromise is assumed, detection, containment and recovery become equally important.

The evidence supports the posture. Dwell time, the interval between intrusion and discovery, has historically been measured in months, and organizations frequently learn of a breach from an outside party rather than from their own monitoring. Any model that assumes you would know is contradicted by the data.

What it changes in practice is concrete. Segmentation so a foothold does not become the whole network, least privilege so a compromised account is not a compromised environment, monitoring for lateral movement rather than only at the boundary, and incident response that is rehearsed rather than documented. It also changes design questions: not whether this can be breached, but what an attacker can reach from here, how quickly it would be visible, and how the blast radius is bounded. That is a more useful question because it has an answer.

never-touch-a-running-system.def: The conservative operator's creed: if it works, leave it alone.
never-touch-a-running-system.context: Born from hard experience with fragile systems, and half-obsolete in the patch-or-be-breached era: not touching a running system also means not patching it. The modern compromise is making change safe enough to do routinely rather than avoiding it.
never-touch-a-running-system.depth:
Never touch a running system is the instinct that anything currently working should be left alone, and it is genuinely correct about a narrow class of situation and catastrophic as a general policy.

The narrow correctness is real: an unnecessary change to a production system that has no fault is pure risk with no benefit, and a great many outages are caused by maintenance nobody needed to perform. Change is the leading cause of incidents in most environments, which is exactly why change management exists.

The catastrophic version is the system nobody has touched for six years, running an operating system with no remaining support, with an undocumented configuration, on hardware whose replacement is no longer manufactured. It is not stable, it is fragile in a way that has not been tested, and the accumulated distance between it and everything around it grows continuously while nobody looks. That is bit rot, and the day it finally fails, the people who understood it have left and the recovery is an archaeology project rather than a restore. The defensible reading is do not change without reason, and never being able to change safely is itself the reason.

read-only-friday.def: The ops tradition of making no production changes on Friday, because weekends exist.
read-only-friday.context: A deploy at five on Friday has a way of becoming a Saturday incident with half the team unreachable. Mature CI/CD (continuous integration and continuous delivery) teams argue the rule away - if deploys are that risky, fix the deploys - but the instinct it encodes is respect for blast radius and for people's time off.
read-only-friday.depth:
Read-only Friday is the convention of not deploying changes late in the week, and the reasoning is entirely about recovery rather than about the change itself. A deployment that breaks on Tuesday afternoon meets a full team, an alert audience and a working day in which to fix it. The same deployment on Friday evening meets whoever is on call, at a weekend rate of attention, with the people who understand the change unreachable.

The practice is sensible and it is also a symptom worth reading. A team that cannot deploy safely on Friday cannot deploy safely at all; they have simply arranged for failures to land at a convenient hour. The underlying weaknesses are the same ones that make any deployment risky: no confident rollback, insufficient automated verification, changes large enough that failure is hard to localize, and a release process that depends on specific people being awake.

Which is why the mature position is to treat it as a temporary control while fixing the cause. Organizations with genuinely reversible deployments, progressive rollout and automatic rollback deploy on Friday without ceremony, not because they are braver but because the failure costs an alert rather than a weekend. Keeping the rule forever is choosing to live with the fragility rather than to remove it.

hope-is-not-a-strategy.def: The SRE reminder that wishing a system stays up is not the same as engineering it to.
hope-is-not-a-strategy.context: Popularized by Google's SRE culture: reliability comes from measured objectives, error budgets, and rehearsed failure, not optimism. If the plan for a risk is 'it probably won't happen', there is no plan.
hope-is-not-a-strategy.depth:
Hope is not a strategy is the observation that an unverified assumption is not a plan, and it names a specific failure: believing something will work because nobody has evidence that it will not. It is a staple of site reliability engineering for a good reason.

The instances are everywhere once you look for them. Backups that have never been restored are hope. Failover that has never been exercised is hope. A runbook written once and never followed is hope. Capacity that has never been load tested is hope. In each case the belief may well be correct, and the point is that nobody knows, and the moment of discovery is scheduled by circumstance rather than by you.

The discipline that follows is testing the assumption deliberately and on your own timetable: restore a backup on a schedule and verify the contents, fail over during business hours with everyone watching, run the runbook as an exercise, load test to the point of failure so you know where it is. Every one of those converts a hope into either a fact or a repair, and the cost of finding out on purpose is invariably lower than the cost of finding out otherwise.

you-build-it-you-run-it.def: The DevOps principle that the team that writes a service also operates it in production.
you-build-it-you-run-it.context: Werner Vogels' phrase from Amazon, and the cultural end of throwing code over the wall: nothing teaches operability like being the one who gets paged. Ownership closes the loop between design decisions and 3 a.m. reality.
you-build-it-you-run-it.depth:
You build it, you run it is Werner Vogels's description of Amazon's model, and its point is about incentives rather than staffing. When the team that wrote the software carries the pager for it, the cost of a poor logging decision, a missing metric or an unclear failure mode is paid by the people who chose them, and behaviour changes accordingly.

The traditional alternative, developers writing and a separate operations team running, produces a predictable pathology. Operational quality is somebody else's requirement, so it loses to features consistently, and the operations team inherits systems they cannot change and are accountable for anyway. Everything that fell between the two groups became a wall of confusion, which is the problem the whole DevOps movement was formed around.

The honest caveats matter. It requires real investment in tooling, or it is simply a transfer of burden; it needs on-call to be humane, compensated and staffed enough to sustain, or it becomes attrition; and it does not eliminate specialist operations expertise, since platform, network and database work remain genuine disciplines. Applied without those, the slogan describes a cost shift rather than an improvement.

single-pane-of-glass.def: The perennial vendor promise of one dashboard that shows everything - and the engineer's shorthand for doubting it.
single-pane-of-glass.context: Every management product pitches one; most environments end up with a dozen single panes of glass. Useful as an aspiration, ironic as a description - usually said with one eyebrow raised.
single-pane-of-glass.depth:
A single pane of glass is the promise of one console showing everything, and it appears in nearly every management product's marketing because the underlying pain is genuine: an operator switching between nine tools during an incident is losing time and context at exactly the wrong moment.

The reason it rarely arrives is that consolidation is a data problem rather than a display problem. Each source has its own model of what an entity is, its own identifiers, its own timing and its own semantics for the same word, and reconciling those is the actual work. A dashboard that displays nine tools in nine panels has not consolidated anything, it has relocated the switching.

The failure mode is the pane that becomes another thing to maintain: incomplete because the tenth tool was never integrated, stale because a source changed its format, and distrusted because operators learned it disagrees with the underlying systems. At that point people go back to the original tools and the pane becomes the tenth. What works better is usually narrower: consolidating alerting so there is one queue, or correlating identity across sources so a search finds everything about one host, rather than attempting a universal view.

two-is-one-one-is-none.def: The redundancy proverb: with two you can lose one; with one, a single failure leaves you with nothing.
two-is-one-one-is-none.context: Military in origin and native to network design: dual power feeds, dual supervisors, HA pairs, two of everything on the critical path. The corollary every operator learns: untested redundancy counts as one.
two-is-one-one-is-none.depth:
Two is one and one is none is a military maxim about equipment redundancy, adopted into infrastructure because the arithmetic is identical. A single component has no margin: when it fails, the capability is gone. Two components means one can fail and the capability survives, which is the only configuration that tolerates the thing you know will eventually happen.

The way it fails in practice is through hidden commonality. Two power supplies fed from the same circuit are one power supply. Two servers in the same rack, two links through the same conduit, two availability zones with a shared control plane, two administrators who both learned the system from the same person: each pair looks redundant and shares a failure mode. Finding those requires asking what both copies depend on, which is a different question from counting them.

The other half is that untested redundancy is decorative. A secondary that has never carried load, a failover that has never been exercised, a spare that has never been powered on: each is assumed rather than known to work, and the assumption is tested for the first time during the incident. Redundancy that has not been exercised is closer to one than to two.

fail-open-vs-fail-closed.def: The design choice of what a control does when it breaks: allow everything through, or block everything.
fail-open-vs-fail-closed.context: A fire door fails open because life beats security; a vault fails closed for the opposite reason. Every inline control faces the same choice - an IPS (intrusion prevention system) that fails open keeps the business running but unprotected, while failing closed is safe and is also an outage. The right answer is a decision, never a default.
fail-open-vs-fail-closed.depth:
When a control cannot make a decision, it either allows the traffic or blocks it, and choosing between those is one of the most consequential design decisions in any security system. Fail open preserves availability, fail closed preserves the security property.

Neither is correct in general, which is what makes it a decision rather than a rule. A door lock that fails closed during a fire kills people; a door lock that fails open during a power cut is not a lock. In technology the same tension appears constantly: an authentication service that fails open lets everyone in, and one that fails closed stops the business entirely, and both outcomes have been serious incidents at large companies.

What matters is choosing deliberately, per control, and documenting the reasoning, because the default is usually whatever the implementer happened to code. The questions that decide it are what the failure allows an attacker to do, what it costs the organization per minute, and whether the failure is likely to be induced by an attacker specifically to trigger it. That last one is the subtle case: a control that fails open is a control an attacker will try to break rather than bypass.

crunchy-outside-chewy-center.def: The classic critique of perimeter-only security: a hard shell around a soft, defenseless inside.
crunchy-outside-chewy-center.context: Bill Cheswick's 1990 description of firewalled networks - a sort of crunchy shell around a soft, chewy centre - is still the sharpest one-liner about why one perimeter is not a strategy. Everything from segmentation to zero trust is an answer to it.
crunchy-outside-chewy-center.depth:
A hard crunchy outside with a soft chewy centre is the vivid description of perimeter-only security, and it is the same critique as castle and moat delivered with more contempt. The point of the phrasing is that the interior is not merely less defended, it is undefended, and everyone involved knows it.

What makes the interior soft is usually accumulation rather than decision. Flat networks because segmentation was deferred, service accounts with broad rights because scoping them was harder, credentials reused across systems because rotation was painful, management interfaces reachable from anywhere inside because that was convenient, and no monitoring of internal traffic because the volume was high and the value was assumed low.

The consequence is that the entire security posture rests on nobody getting through the shell, which is a bet against an attacker who only needs one phishing email to work. Fixing it is unglamorous and slow: segment, scope, monitor east-west, and remove the shared credentials, none of which produces a visible improvement until the day it contains something. That is why it is consistently underfunded relative to perimeter products, and why the phrase persists as a diagnosis.

castle-and-moat.def: The perimeter security model: strong walls at the edge, broad trust for anyone already inside.
castle-and-moat.context: It matched the world where everything lived in one building behind one firewall. Cloud, SaaS, and remote work dissolved the moat - the resources left the castle - which is the whole argument for zero trust's per-request verification.
castle-and-moat.depth:
Castle and moat describes perimeter security: a hard boundary with controlled crossings, and an interior where traffic is trusted because it got past the wall. It was the dominant model for decades and it was reasonable while the assumptions held, which were that valuable things were inside, users were inside, and the boundary was crossable only in known places.

Every one of those assumptions failed. Applications moved to providers outside the wall, users worked from anywhere, mobile devices left and returned carrying whatever they picked up, and partner integrations opened crossings nobody drew on the diagram. A perimeter around an empty castle protects nothing.

The failure mode when it collapses is that the interior was never designed to resist anything, so a single compromised endpoint has flat access to everything. That is the observation that produced zero trust, and the honest reading is not that perimeters were wrong but that they became insufficient: a boundary is still worth having, and it can no longer be the only place a decision is made. The replacement is authorization per request rather than trust by location.

pcap-or-it-didnt-happen.def: The network engineer's evidence standard: claims about traffic are settled by a packet capture, not by opinion.
pcap-or-it-didnt-happen.context: Applications blame the network, the network blames the application, and the pcap ends the argument, because packets do not lie. It is the profession's version of 'citation needed'.
pcap-or-it-didnt-happen.depth:
A packet capture is ground truth, and the phrase is deployed when someone describes network behaviour that logs and counters do not corroborate. Everything else in the diagnostic chain is an interpretation: application logs record what the application believed, device counters record what the device counted, and both can be wrong or absent for the case at hand.

The value is settling disagreements that would otherwise persist. When a client team says the requests are being sent and a server team says they are not arriving, a capture at both ends ends the discussion in minutes, and it does so without either side needing to be trusted. That is why the phrase carries a slight edge: it is usually said to someone whose account is not being accepted.

The honest limits deserve stating alongside. Encryption means you observe metadata rather than content unless you can decrypt, which requires keys and raises its own questions. Capturing at scale is expensive and rolling buffers are usually short, so the capture that matters is often the one nobody was running. And capture points are themselves a design choice, since a capture on the wrong side of a translating device shows a true picture of the wrong thing.

check-layer-1.def: The first commandment of troubleshooting: before anything clever, confirm the cable, the port, the power.
check-layer-1.context: The OSI model doubles as a debugging ladder, and an embarrassing share of 'routing problems' end at an unplugged patch lead or a dead SFP. Start at the bottom; the physical layer has no sense of humor.
check-layer-1.depth:
Check layer one is the reminder that a great many problems presented as complex are a cable, a port, a transceiver, or power. It is said with a certain weariness because it is said after someone has spent an hour on the routing table.

The reason the physical layer gets skipped is that it is boring and invisible from a terminal. An engineer diagnosing remotely sees interface counters and configuration, both of which are abstractions over something physical that may be half-seated, kinked behind a rack, plugged into the neighbouring port, or an optic operating at a wavelength the far end does not use. Error counters incrementing steadily are the tell, and they are frequently on a screen nobody looked at.

The discipline is to check it first rather than last, because it is cheap to check and expensive to skip. Is the link up, is it at the expected speed and duplex, are errors incrementing, does the optic report sensible light levels, is it in the port the documentation claims. Five minutes of that eliminates a large fraction of possibilities, and the alternative is discovering at midnight that the answer was a cable somebody moved during the day.

schroedingers-backup.def: The state of any backup that has never been restored: simultaneously good and bad until someone opens the box.
schroedingers-backup.context: Backup jobs succeed for years while quietly producing nothing restorable - wrong scope, silent corruption, expired credentials. The operational form of the proverb: a backup does not exist until a restore has been tested.
schroedingers-backup.depth:
The state of any backup is unknown until a restore is attempted. The joke is precise, and the underlying claim is that an untested backup exists in superposition: it is simultaneously a working recovery plan and a directory of useless files, and only the restore collapses it.

The failure modes are numerous and quiet. The job succeeded but excluded a directory added last year. The database was backed up while running without a consistent snapshot, so the file is present and unusable. The encryption key is stored in the system being restored. The tapes are fine and the drive that reads them has been decommissioned. The retention policy silently rotated away the only copy from before the corruption. In every case the monitoring is green, because backup software reports on whether it ran.

The only remedy is restoring on a schedule, to separate hardware, verifying the contents rather than the exit code, and timing how long it takes so the recovery objective is measured rather than assumed. Organizations that do this discover problems on an ordinary Tuesday. The ones that do not discover the same problems during the incident that made them matter.

three-two-one-backup.def: The backup rule of thumb: three copies of the data, on two different media, with one copy off-site.
three-two-one-backup.context: Simple enough to remember mid-disaster, and it survives most single failures: device death, site loss, even ransomware if the off-site copy is offline or immutable. The modern extension is 3-2-1-1-0: one copy offline, zero restore errors.
three-two-one-backup.depth:
Three copies of the data, on two different media types, with one held offsite. The rule is old, it predates cloud storage entirely, and it survives because each number defends against a different failure that the others do not.

Three copies means a single corruption does not exhaust your options, since the production copy and one backup can both be bad. Two media types defends against a systemic fault in one technology, a firmware defect affecting an entire drive model, or a format nothing can read any more. One offsite copy defends against everything that is geographic: fire, flood, theft, and the building being inaccessible.

Ransomware forced an addition, usually written as one immutable or offline copy, because an attacker with administrative access will delete backups they can reach, and a backup system reachable from the network is a backup system inside the blast radius. The other half of the rule that nobody writes down is that a backup nobody has restored is not a backup, it is a belief about a backup, and the only way to convert one into the other is to actually try it.

raid-is-not-a-backup.def: The storage truth that redundancy protects against disk failure, not against deletion, corruption, or ransomware.
raid-is-not-a-backup.context: RAID keeps a volume alive when a drive dies - and faithfully mirrors every mistake to all disks at once. Deleted the file? It is gone, redundantly. Availability and recoverability are different problems; a backup solves the second one.
raid-is-not-a-backup.depth:
RAID protects against a disk failing. It does not protect against anything else, and the list of anything else is where all the data loss actually happens: deletion, corruption, ransomware, a botched migration, a controller writing garbage, fire, theft, and someone typing a command against the wrong host.

The confusion is understandable, because RAID does produce a redundant copy and redundancy sounds like backup. The difference is that a mirror is synchronous: whatever happens to the primary happens to the copy immediately, including deletion. A backup is a point-in-time copy that is deliberately not synchronized, which is precisely the property that lets you go back to before the mistake.

The same reasoning applies more broadly than people apply it. Cloud storage replication is not a backup for the same reason, since a deleted object is deleted in every replica, and a synchronized folder propagates encryption by ransomware to every device within minutes. The question that separates the two categories is simple: if I destroy the data right now, deliberately, does this mechanism still have it? If the answer is no, it is availability, not backup.

security-is-a-process.def: Bruce Schneier's reminder that security is a process, not a product - nothing you buy makes you done.
security-is-a-process.context: Products help, but threats move, configurations drift, and people change; what endures is the loop of assessing, patching, monitoring, and responding. Anyone selling total security in a box is selling the noun without the verb.
security-is-a-process.depth:
Bruce Schneier's formulation is that security is a process, not a product, and it is aimed at the assumption that a purchase can resolve a security problem. Products are components in a process; they are not the thing itself, and treating a deployment as a conclusion is how organizations end up well equipped and badly protected.

The reasoning is that the environment moves continuously. New vulnerabilities are disclosed, attackers change technique, the systems being defended change every sprint, staff join and leave, and business requirements alter what is acceptable. A configuration that was correct in March is a set of assumptions that have been decaying since. Nothing about that is fixable by buying a better version of the same appliance.

What the process actually consists of is unglamorous and continuous: knowing what you have, patching it, monitoring it, reviewing access, rehearsing incidents, and revisiting decisions when the conditions that justified them change. None of it produces a certificate to hang on a wall, which is precisely why it competes badly for budget against a product that does. The organizations that do it well tend to be the ones that stopped asking what to buy and started asking what to operate.

dont-roll-your-own-crypto.def: The first commandment of applied cryptography: use the vetted algorithms and libraries, never your homemade ones.
dont-roll-your-own-crypto.context: Designing crypto that others cannot break is one of the hardest problems in the field, and every homemade cipher looks unbreakable to its author - Schneier's law in action. Rolling your own means your mistakes ship without ever meeting the years of public attack that hardened AES and TLS.
dont-roll-your-own-crypto.depth:
Don't roll your own crypto is the field's most repeated advice, and it means do not implement primitives yourself, not do not learn how they work. The distinction gets lost, and the confusion produces engineers who use cryptography without understanding it, which is its own hazard.

The reason it holds is that cryptographic code fails silently. Ordinary code that is wrong usually misbehaves visibly; a cipher implemented wrongly still produces output that looks random, still decrypts correctly with your own implementation, and passes every test you would think to write. The defects are timing variation, weak randomness, and nonce reuse, none of which are detectable from the output.

The honest scope is narrower than the slogan. Do not implement AES. Do use a well-reviewed library, and understand it well enough to choose the mode, manage the keys and avoid reusing a nonce, because those are your decisions and the library will let you get them wrong. Somebody has to write the libraries, and the people who do are the ones who ignored the advice deliberately and then submitted their work for years of attack. That is the legitimate path, and it starts with study rather than with shipping.

key-management-is-hard.def: The crypto veteran's summary: encrypting data is the easy part; protecting, rotating, and not losing the keys is the hard part.
key-management-is-hard.context: The algorithms are free and vetted; what fails in practice is the key left in a repository, the certificate nobody renewed, the HSM (hardware security module) nobody can operate. It is the two-hard-things joke of the crypto world, and the reason key-management systems exist.
key-management-is-hard.depth:
Key management is the part of cryptography that actually fails. The algorithms are the well-understood component, extensively reviewed and rarely broken in deployment; what breaks is generating keys with poor entropy, storing them in a repository, distributing them over a channel that is not itself protected, failing to rotate them, and having no procedure for revocation.

The recursion is what makes it hard rather than merely tedious. Protecting a key requires another key, and protecting that one requires another, and the chain has to terminate somewhere in a hardware root, a passphrase in a person's memory, or an institutional procedure. Every real system resolves that regress by putting trust in something non-cryptographic, and where it terminates is the actual security boundary.

The operational consequence is that the interesting questions are procedural. Who can access the key, how would you know if they did, what happens when the person who set it up leaves, and can you actually revoke it in an emergency or is that a documented intention nobody has tested. Those questions are answerable, and a system with strong algorithms and unanswered key management questions is not protected by the algorithms.

rough-consensus-and-running-code.def: The IETF's working philosophy: standards emerge from broad agreement plus implementations that actually work.
rough-consensus-and-running-code.context: David Clark's 1992 formulation - we reject kings, presidents and voting; we believe in rough consensus and running code - is why internet protocols are proven in interop before they are finished on paper. It is the cultural DNA behind every RFC this site teaches.
rough-consensus-and-running-code.depth:
We reject kings, presidents and voting. We believe in rough consensus and running code. David Clark's line describes how the IETF makes decisions, and it is a genuine alternative to both authority and formal ballot.

Rough consensus means no formal vote and no requirement of unanimity: the chair judges whether objections have been addressed, not whether everyone agrees, and a persistent minority does not hold a veto. Running code means a proposal with two interoperating implementations outweighs an elegant specification nobody has built. Together they select for what works over what wins an argument.

The honest limits are worth stating because the phrase gets used as an unqualified virtue. Rough consensus rewards those who can attend meetings and sustain long participation, which favours the well-funded, and running code favours whoever already has engineers. The IETF has debated its own capture by large implementers repeatedly. It nonetheless produced TCP/IP, HTTP and TLS, which is a stronger record than most standards bodies with more formal legitimacy, and the tension between openness and effectiveness is a live one rather than a solved one.

turtles-all-the-way-down.def: The recursion joke applied to trust: every layer rests on another layer, and eventually you must simply stand somewhere.
turtles-all-the-way-down.context: PKI (public key infrastructure) ends at self-signed root CAs, DNS at the root servers, secure boot at a burned-in key - every chain of trust bottoms out in an anchor taken on faith. Naming the turtles is how you find out what you are actually trusting.
turtles-all-the-way-down.depth:
Turtles all the way down comes from an anecdote about cosmology: the world rests on a turtle, and that turtle rests on another, and it is turtles all the way down. In computing it describes an abstraction stack with no obvious bottom.

A running program sits on a runtime, on an operating system, on a hypervisor, on firmware, on microcode, on silicon that is itself an abstraction over physics. Every layer presents a simplified model of the one below and every layer is leaky, which is why a problem can originate at a depth nobody in the room is equipped to consider.

The honest version acknowledges that the regress does terminate, and where it terminates matters. Trust bottoms out in hardware you did not fabricate, running microcode you cannot read, made by a supply chain you cannot audit, which is exactly the anxiety that Thompson's trusting trust argument formalizes. The practical response is not paralysis but knowing which turtle you are standing on: a debugging session goes badly when the participants have different assumptions about how far down the problem could be.

second-system-effect.def: Fred Brooks's warning that the successor to a successful system tends to be overengineered with every idea saved up from the first.
second-system-effect.context: The first system was kept humble by ignorance; the second gets all the features its designers wished for, and sinks under them. Protocols, products, and rewrites all fall for it - restraint is a second-system skill.
second-system-effect.depth:
Fred Brooks observed that the second system a designer builds is the most dangerous one they will ever build. The first is constrained by inexperience and caution, so it stays lean. The second carries every idea that was deferred from the first, and the designer now has enough confidence to believe all of them are achievable at once.

The result is over-generalization: features nobody asked for, abstractions for requirements that have not appeared, configurability where a decision would do, and a scope that grows faster than the understanding supporting it. It is the specific mechanism behind a great many ambitious rewrites that never shipped, and it is driven by competence rather than incompetence.

The defence is structural rather than a matter of self-restraint. Requiring each addition to be justified by a current need rather than an anticipated one, shipping incrementally so reality intervenes early, and having someone empowered to say no to the designer are all versions of the same thing: forcing the second system to earn its features the way the first one did. Brooks's own suggestion was simply awareness, on the grounds that a designer who knows about the effect is meaningfully less likely to produce it.

patch-tuesday-exploit-wednesday.def: The rhythm of Windows security: fixes ship on the second Tuesday, and reverse-engineered attacks follow within days.
patch-tuesday-exploit-wednesday.context: Microsoft's predictable cadence gave defenders a schedule - and gave attackers a diff to reverse into working exploits before slow organizations patch. The window between patch release and patch deployment is the whole game.
patch-tuesday-exploit-wednesday.depth:
Patch Tuesday, exploit Wednesday describes the consequence of predictable release schedules. Microsoft ships fixes on the second Tuesday of the month, and attackers reverse-engineer those patches to find the vulnerability they fix, then attack the population that has not applied them yet.

The mechanism is worth understanding because it is counterintuitive. A patch is a description of a vulnerability: diffing the fixed binary against the previous one reveals what changed and therefore what was wrong, and that analysis is routine and fast. Publishing the fix starts a race in which the defender must deploy across an estate and the attacker only needs one unpatched target.

The scheduling trade is genuine on both sides. Predictable dates let organizations plan testing and change windows, which measurably increases how many patches actually get applied; they also give attackers a known starting gun. Out-of-band releases for severe issues are the escape valve. The practical response is to shorten the window rather than to wish the schedule away: prioritize by exploitability rather than by severity score alone, and treat the days after a release as the period of elevated risk that they demonstrably are.

demo-gods.def: The capricious deities who decide whether a live demo works - having behaved perfectly in every rehearsal.
demo-gods.context: Every instructor and presenter knows the liturgy: the lab that ran flawlessly all week fails the moment an audience appears. Offerings include pre-recorded fallbacks, snapshots, and never typing live what a script can type for you.
demo-gods.depth:
The demo gods are the imaginary deities who decide whether a demonstration works, invoked because the failure rate of demos is so much higher than the failure rate of the same system in normal use that it feels supernatural.

The causes are mundane once enumerated. The demo machine is on a different network, the projector changes the resolution, the presenter is typing under observation and makes errors they never make alone, the dataset is fresh rather than the one that was tested, an update installed overnight, and a cache that is always warm is cold. Every one of those is a real environmental difference, and their conjunction is why demos fail more.

Treating it as luck is the actual mistake, because the mitigations are all boring and effective: rehearse on the exact machine and network you will present on, record a video fallback, disable updates and notifications, prepare the state in advance rather than building it live, and know which step you can skip if time is short. The engineers whose demos succeed are not favoured by anything, they have simply removed the variables.

greenfield-vs-brownfield.def: Building on an empty field versus building inside what already exists - the two starting conditions of every project.
greenfield-vs-brownfield.context: Greenfield means freedom and no users; brownfield means constraints, migrations, and the installed base paying the bills. Most real work is brownfield, which is why 'how do we get there from here' matters more than the target architecture.
greenfield-vs-brownfield.depth:
Greenfield is building with no existing constraints; brownfield is building into a system that already exists, with its data, its integrations, its users and its accumulated decisions. Almost all real work is brownfield, and almost all writing about software assumes greenfield.

That mismatch explains a lot of frustrated engineering. Advice that assumes you can choose the architecture, the language and the data model is useless when the answer to all three is already deployed and carrying traffic. Estimates derived from greenfield experience are systematically low in brownfield, because the work is not building the feature, it is discovering what the existing system actually does, which is never quite what it is documented to do.

The honest framing is that brownfield is the harder discipline and the more valuable one. It demands archaeology, migration paths, backwards compatibility and the ability to change something while it stays running. Greenfield is enjoyable and it is also where the future brownfield problems are created, which is why the most useful question during a greenfield project is what this will be like to change in five years.

hot-warm-cold-standby.def: The three temperatures of a backup system: running and synchronized, running but behind, or powered off until needed.
hot-warm-cold-standby.context: The temperature buys recovery time: a hot standby takes over in seconds, a cold one after hours of restore. Cost scales the same way, which makes the choice a business decision wearing a technical costume.
hot-warm-cold-standby.depth:
Standby configurations describe how ready a secondary is, and the terms map to a spectrum of cost against recovery time. Hot means running and synchronized, able to take over in seconds. Warm means running but behind, needing some catch-up. Cold means the equipment exists and must be started, configured and loaded before it is useful.

The choice is an economic decision disguised as a technical one, and it should be driven by two numbers agreed with the business rather than by engineering preference: how much time may pass before service resumes, and how much data may be lost. Those two determine which configuration is required, and everything else is implementation.

The failure that recurs is a mismatch nobody noticed. A cold standby documented as meeting a four-hour objective, where nobody has measured how long the restore actually takes, is a plan that will be discovered to be wrong during its first use. And a hot standby whose synchronization has silently broken is worse than a cold one, because the readiness is assumed. Both cases are resolved by the same practice: exercise the failover on a schedule and time it.

active-active-vs-active-passive.def: The two shapes of high availability: both nodes serving traffic, or one serving while the other waits.
active-active-vs-active-passive.context: Active-passive is simpler to reason about and idles half the hardware; active-active uses everything and doubles the failure modes - notably the risk that each node runs fine alone but the pair cannot agree who owns what. BIG-IP HA pairs, firewall clusters, and databases all wrestle with the same trade.
active-active-vs-active-passive.depth:
Active-passive keeps a standby idle until failure; active-active runs both simultaneously and shares load. The second sounds strictly better, since the hardware is doing work rather than waiting, and the trade underneath is real and frequently underestimated.

Active-active requires the application to tolerate concurrency across sites. State has to be shared or partitioned, writes have to be reconciled, and the sequencing problems that a single active node made impossible are now live. Split brain is the characteristic failure: the two sides lose contact, both continue believing they are authoritative, and the data diverges in ways that must eventually be merged by a human.

Active-passive avoids all of that by having one authority, at the cost of idle capacity and a failover that must be tested. It is also easier to reason about during an incident, which is worth more than it sounds. The honest guidance is that active-active is right when you genuinely need the capacity or the latency of being close to users, and that choosing it for elegance means adopting a distributed systems problem you did not previously have.

baby-giant.def: A frame slightly over the classic 1518-byte Ethernet maximum: a tag or label added a few bytes to a standard packet.
baby-giant.context: One 802.1Q tag turns a full 1518-byte frame into 1522 bytes: the tag sits in the frame header and the 1500-byte payload is unchanged. MPLS (Multiprotocol Label Switching) labels differ: RFC 3032 counts each 4-byte label inside the payload, so a 1500-byte IP packet under two labels needs a link MTU of 1508.
baby-giant.depth:
A baby giant is a frame slightly larger than the classic 1518-byte Ethernet maximum, because a VLAN tag or an MPLS label stack added a few bytes to a packet of standard size. IEEE 802.3 itself names the 1522-octet Q-tagged frame and an envelope frame of up to 2000 octets. It is not a jumbo frame: a jumbo frame grows the payload by thousands of bytes, a baby giant grows the frame by a handful.

Where the bytes go matters. A VLAN tag rides in the frame header and leaves the IP MTU at 1500. MPLS labels sit inside the frame payload, 4 octets each (RFC 3032, sections 2.1 and 3.1), so a full 1500-byte IP packet under one label needs 1504 bytes of payload and under two needs 1508; on a link left at 1500 the labelled path carries 1496 or 1492 bytes of IP instead.

The failure is quiet and specific. A switch or interface not configured for the extra bytes drops these frames while passing everything else, so a trunk carrying tagged or labelled traffic loses full-size packets and passes small ones. The symptom is the familiar small-works-large-fails pattern, and the fix is a system or MPLS MTU adjustment rather than jumbo frame configuration.

brownout.def: A service that is up but deliberately or visibly degraded - dimmed, like the power-grid original, rather than dark.
brownout.context: Feature brownouts are also a communication tool: briefly degrading a deprecated API warns integrators that the real shutdown is coming, in a way release notes never manage. The involuntary kind is just a grey failure with better branding.

dark-launch.def: Shipping a feature to production silently, running it on real traffic before any user can see it.
dark-launch.context: The code path executes, metrics and error rates accumulate, and the audience is zero - the feature flag stays off. It converts the scariest moment of a launch into a rehearsal with production-grade data.

tiger-team.def: A small, hand-picked group pulled out of normal structure to attack one hard problem until it yields.
tiger-team.context: The name comes from 1960s aerospace and earned immortality with Apollo 13's rescue effort. In security the term overlaps with red teams, but a tiger team is defined by its mission and temporariness, not by playing the adversary.

cowboy-coding.def: Development with no process between the idea and production: no review, no tests, no branch, just push.
cowboy-coding.context: Thrilling in a prototype, lethal in anything shared. The cowboy is not always wrong - speed has value - but the debt lands on whoever maintains the code, which is why teams fence the pasture with CI and review.

firefighting.def: Operating in permanent emergency mode: all effort goes to the incident of the day, none to preventing the next one.
firefighting.context: The trap is self-sustaining - time spent extinguishing leaves no time for fireproofing, which guarantees more fires. Escaping requires deliberately protecting non-urgent work, which is exactly what burning teams feel they cannot afford.

top-talkers.def: The hosts, flows, or applications consuming the most bandwidth on a link - the first list every traffic tool shows.
top-talkers.context: NetFlow, sFlow, and every monitoring dashboard lead with top talkers because the distribution is brutally unequal: a handful of conversations usually own the link. It answers the eternal question 'what is eating the WAN' in one sorted column.

clean-pipe.def: Internet transit that arrives already scrubbed of DDoS (distributed denial of service) traffic - the provider filters the flood upstream and delivers only the clean flow.
clean-pipe.context: Sold by carriers and mitigation providers as a service: attack traffic is absorbed in their scrubbing centres, close to its sources, instead of saturating the customer's last mile. The metaphor is exact - the pipe is the same, the water is filtered before it reaches you.

swivel-chair.def: Integrating two systems with a human who swivels between screens, reading from one and retyping into the other.
swivel-chair.context: The oldest middleware in the world, and still everywhere: ticket data copied into the change system, alarms retyped into spreadsheets. Every swivel is latency, toil, and a transcription error waiting to happen - which is why 'swivel-chair integration' is usually said while writing the automation ticket.

shelfware.def: Software an organization bought, licensed, and never actually deployed - value sitting on a shelf.
shelfware.context: Born from bundle deals, over-optimistic projects, and compliance purchases. Security suffers a special variant: the tool is installed but never tuned, generating a comforting line item and no protection. License audits exist largely to find it.

vaporware.def: A product announced with fanfare that never ships - or ships so late and so diminished that the announcement was the product.
vaporware.context: A vintage industry word from the era of pre-announcements designed to freeze competitors' sales. The defensive reflex it taught still applies to roadmap slides: ship dates are facts, announcements are marketing.
