authentication-policy-tree.def: PingFederate's runtime decision tree for authentication: nodes are authentication sources and selectors, Fail and Success branches express fallbacks, reusable fragments capture common sequences, and every successful path ends by fulfilling a policy contract.
authentication-policy-tree.context: One tree routes different populations differently - corporate network tries Kerberos and falls back to the form, sensitive applications add a second factor.

opentoken.def: Ping Identity's encrypted token format for integration kits: the authenticated identity travels between PingFederate and an application as an OpenToken carried by cookie, query parameter, or POST.
opentoken.context: The OpenToken adapter runs both directions - handing a user to an agent-equipped application after SSO (single sign-on), or accepting one the application already authenticated.
opentoken.depth:
OpenToken is Ping Identity's encrypted token format used by its integration kits, carrying attributes from the identity provider to an application in a compact encrypted blob rather than in a signed XML assertion.

Its role is worth understanding as a pattern rather than a product. Integration kits exist because applications that cannot speak SAML or OIDC natively still need federated identity, so an agent handles the protocol and hands the result to the application in a simpler form. The security boundary therefore moves to the shared key between the agent and the application, which is where deployments go wrong: a default or widely-copied key means anyone who knows it can mint an assertion of identity.

data-store.def: A reusable connection definition to an external identity source - an LDAP (Lightweight Directory Access Protocol) directory with failover hosts and a service bind, or a JDBC database with its driver and validation query - configured once and referenced by validators, attribute lookups, and provisioning.
data-store.context: The indirection is the point: rotate the service credential or move the directory, and every consumer follows one changed definition.

identity-provider.def: The party in a federation that authenticates the user and vouches for the result to other services: in SAML (Security Assertion Markup Language) it issues signed assertions to service providers; in OpenID Connect the same role is the OpenID Provider, issuing ID tokens to relying parties.
identity-provider.context: Every federation names one side the identity provider (IdP) and the other the service provider or relying party: one authenticates, the other trusts. The IdP holds the login page, the multi-factor policy, the session and the signing key; each application keeps only the IdP's issuer name and verification key, checks the signed statement that arrives, and runs its own session from there. That concentration is the whole benefit, one place to enforce strong authentication and to switch an account off, and the whole risk, because whoever can make the IdP sign, or can steal what it signs with, is trusted by everything downstream.
identity-provider.depth:
An identity provider (IdP) is, in the words of NIST (National Institute of Standards and Technology) SP (Special Publication) 800-63-4, the party in a federation transaction that creates an assertion for the subscriber and transmits it to the relying party (RP). The OASIS (Organization for the Advancement of Structured Information Standards) glossary for SAML (Security Assertion Markup Language) 2.0, dated 15 March 2005, calls it a kind of service provider that creates, maintains and manages identity information for principals and authenticates them to other service providers within a federation; in OpenID Connect (OIDC) the same role is the OpenID Provider (OP), an OAuth 2.0 authorization server that can authenticate the end-user and give a relying party claims about that event. An IdP is not the account of record: NIST separates it from the credential service provider (CSP), which establishes the subscriber account, and calls the IdP the bridge between that account and the RP. Nor does it decide what the user may do in an application; in the SAML technical overview's example the IdP states who the user is, how they authenticated and which attributes they hold, and the service provider applies its own access policy.

The vocabulary shifts with protocol and decade. SAML 1.x spoke of an asserting party and a relying party; SAML 2.0 and WS-Federation say IdP and service provider (SP); OIDC says OP and RP; NIST says IdP and RP. PingFederate's documentation adopts IdP and SP for every specification, calls the IdP the SAML authority, and adds the SAML 2.0 IdP discovery role, which works out which IdP a user belongs to. Roles stack: PingFederate can also act as an OP, and a federation proxy is an RP towards an upstream IdP while acting as the IdP for the applications behind it.

The exchange has the same shape in both main protocols. The RP sends the browser to the IdP with a request; the IdP authenticates the user, or reuses a session it already holds, and returns a signed assertion. In OIDC that assertion is the ID token, a JSON Web Token (JWT) whose required claims are iss (the issuer, an https web address), sub (a subject identifier of at most 255 characters, never reassigned), aud (which must contain the RP's client_id), exp and iat, plus auth_time when the RP sets a maximum authentication age and nonce to tie the token to the request. Delivery is front channel, through the browser, as in the SAML Web Browser SSO (single sign-on) profile, or back channel, where the browser carries only a reference that the RP redeems at the IdP, as in the SAML Artifact binding and the OIDC authorization code flow; NIST requires that reference to be single-use and bound to one authenticated RP, and recommends a validity of no more than five minutes. The ID token's expiry, the OIDC specification warns, is unrelated to the session lifetime between RP and OP.

The names settled in the SAML era. SAML V1.0 became an OASIS standard in November 2002 and V1.1 followed in September 2003; SAML V2.0, approved in March 2005, unified SAML 1.1 with Internet2's Shibboleth and the Liberty Alliance's Identity Federation Framework. The OpenID Connect final specification launched on 26 February 2014; Core with errata set 2 is dated 15 December 2023, and on 7 October 2024 the OpenID Foundation announced nine OIDC specifications published as ISO/IEC (International Organization for Standardization and International Electrotechnical Commission) standards, Core as ISO/IEC 26131:2024. NIST SP 800-63C-4, Federation and Assertions, superseded SP 800-63C in July 2025.

SP 800-63C-4 grades federation by Federation Assurance Level (FAL). FAL1 requires an assertion signed with approved cryptography, restricted to a named audience, and accepted only once by each RP. FAL2 adds strong protection against assertion injection, RP-started transactions, a single audience, identifiers free of plaintext personal information, and a trust agreement set up in advance; federal IdPs at FAL2 or above must keep signing keys in modules validated at FIPS 140 (Federal Information Processing Standard 140) Level 1 or higher. FAL3 is written for a compromised IdP: the RP must also verify that the subscriber holds an authenticator, named in a holder-of-key assertion or bound at the RP. Through a proxy, the FAL is the lowest anywhere on the path, and the revision covers subscriber-controlled wallets, which present attribute bundles signed by the CSP, alongside the general-purpose IdP.

In practice the role is played by identity services such as Microsoft Entra ID, Active Directory Federation Services (AD FS), Okta and PingFederate, and by devices already in the traffic path. F5 BIG-IP Access Policy Manager (APM) can act as a SAML IdP: a SAML IdP service, which APM treats as one more type of SSO service, is bound to SP connectors, one per external SP, created from the SP's metadata, from a vendor template or by hand, and an artifact resolution service lets it hand out artifacts in place of assertions.

Concentration is the price. NIST states that successful attacks on the IdP can propagate to every RP that relies on it and move laterally between them. The most valuable thing an IdP holds is its signing key. MITRE ATT&CK (Adversarial Tactics, Techniques, and Common Knowledge) technique T1606.002 describes forging SAML tokens with any permissions and lifetimes once an adversary holds a valid token-signing certificate, records that APT29 did so during the SolarWinds compromise, and starts containment with rotating that certificate. In July 2023 Microsoft reported that Storm-0558 had, from 15 May, used forged tokens to read email at about 25 organizations, with an inactive Microsoft account (MSA) consumer signing key that a validation flaw let be trusted for Azure AD tokens too. Sessions are the second target: in October 2023 Okta found that an attacker with a stolen credential had read HTTP Archive (HAR) files uploaded to its support system, files that can carry cookies and session tokens, and revoked the tokens embedded in them. Protocols add their own traps: RFC (Request for Comments) 9700, the OAuth 2.0 security best current practice of January 2025, describes mix-up attacks, where a client using several authorization servers, one hostile, is tricked into sending a code meant for an honest one to the attacker, and NIST counts refusing unsolicited IdP-initiated logins among the protections against assertion injection.

The neighbours differ in what they own. The SP or RP consumes the assertion and runs its own session; the CSP owns the account and its authenticators; a SAML attribute authority answers attribute queries without authenticating anyone; an OAuth authorization server issues access tokens for APIs (application programming interfaces) and is an OP only when it also authenticates the user and issues ID tokens. Worth remembering: SAML 2.0 in 2005, OIDC in 2014, FAL1 to FAL3, five minutes for a back-channel reference.

service-provider.def: In federated identity, the application side: the party that relies on assertions or tokens from an identity provider to grant access, the Security Assertion Markup Language (SAML) service provider or OpenID Connect relying party. In networking, also the operator that sells connectivity to customers.
service-provider.context: Service-provider-initiated (SP-initiated) sign-on starts here: the user arrives at the application first, and it sends them to the identity provider with a request to authenticate, then checks the assertion that comes back before creating its own session. The service provider never sees the password; what it has to get right is the signature, the audience, the recipient and the expiry of every assertion, because everything it grants rests on them.
service-provider.depth:
One role, three vocabularies. The Organization for the Advancement of Structured Information Standards (OASIS) glossary for SAML 2.0, an OASIS Standard of 15 March 2005, defines a service provider broadly, as a role a system entity takes on when it provides services to principals or to other entities, and defines an identity provider as a kind of service provider, the one that creates and manages identity information and authenticates principals for the others; the word relying party names the function, an entity that decides to act on information from another, as a SAML relying party acts on assertions from an asserting party. OpenID Connect Core 1.0 (errata set 2, December 2023) calls the same participant the Relying Party, an OAuth 2.0 client application that requires end-user authentication and claims from an OpenID Provider. The National Institute of Standards and Technology (NIST), in Special Publication (SP) 800-63C-4 of July 2025, also says relying party (RP): an entity that relies on a verifier's assertion of a subscriber's identity, and federation is authenticating a subscriber to an RP without the RP ever verifying the subscriber's authenticators itself. In everyday federation work, SAML SP, OpenID Connect RP and NIST RP are the same thing: the application that trusts someone else to say who the user is.

Who starts the sign-on. The SAML 2.0 Technical Overview describes two flows. In identity-provider-initiated (IdP-initiated) single sign-on the user authenticates at the identity provider first and is then sent to a resource at the SP, with an assertion the SP never asked for. In the more common SP-initiated flow the user goes to the application, which sends them to the identity provider with an authentication request; the identity provider then produces an assertion for the SP. SAML 2.0 supports both, and its profiles say that an unsolicited response must not carry the InResponseTo attribute that would tie it to a request. NIST's guidance takes sides. At federation assurance level 2 (FAL2) the federation transaction shall be initiated by the RP, at FAL1 it should be, and among its protections against assertion injection, an attacker forcing an RP to accept an assertion meant for someone else, it lists prohibiting IdP-initiated processes, except where an outside party only signals the RP to start a transaction of its own. Convenience portals that launch applications from an identity provider are therefore a deliberate trade against injection risk.

What a SAML SP must check. The Web Browser SSO (single sign-on) profile lists the obligations regardless of binding. The SP must verify any signatures on the response or the assertions; check that the Recipient in each bearer subject confirmation matches the assertion consumer service URL (uniform resource locator) it was delivered to; check that NotOnOrAfter has not passed, allowing for clock skew between the providers; check that InResponseTo equals the identifier of its own authentication request, unless the response was unsolicited; and discard any assertion that is invalid or whose confirmation requirements cannot be met. With the HTTP (Hypertext Transfer Protocol) POST binding the assertions must be signed, and the SP must prevent replay by remembering the identifiers of assertions it has used until their NotOnOrAfter time passes. NIST adds that every RP shall check that the audience of an assertion contains its own identifier. Each of these checks closes a specific attack: a missing audience check lets an assertion minted for one application open another, and a missing replay cache lets a captured POST be resubmitted.

The same job in OpenID Connect. An OpenID Connect relying party validates the ID token (identity token) in the same spirit: the issuer identifier obtained from discovery must exactly match the iss claim; the aud claim must contain the relying party's own client_id, and a token listing additional audiences the client does not trust must be rejected; the signature must be verified with the issuer's keys, although an ID token received directly from the token endpoint over TLS (Transport Layer Security) may rely on server validation instead; the current time must be before exp; and if a nonce was sent in the request, the token's nonce must match it, which is also the replay defence. iat can be used to limit how long nonces need to be stored. The structures differ, signed XML (Extensible Markup Language) in SAML and a JSON (JavaScript Object Notation) Web Token in OpenID Connect, but the relying party's questions are the same: who issued this, was it meant for me, is it still valid, and is it an answer to my own request.

The trust root is the identity provider's key, and that is the attack. MITRE ATT&CK (Adversarial Tactics, Techniques and Common Knowledge) records the technique as T1606.002, Forge Web Credentials: SAML Tokens: an adversary who obtains a valid token-signing certificate can forge SAML tokens with any permissions and any lifetime, and every service provider that trusts that certificate will accept them, because the signature is genuine. The default token lifetime is one hour, but the NotOnOrAfter value can set any period. During the SolarWinds compromise the advanced persistent threat (APT) group tracked as APT29 created tokens with compromised SAML signing certificates. Since nothing at the SP looks wrong, detection has to correlate across systems, for example a validly signed token with no preceding Kerberos authentication at the identity provider. For the SP the lesson is to trust a specific issuer and a specific key, refresh partner metadata deliberately, keep accepted lifetimes short and log every assertion's issuer, audience and validity window.

In practice: F5 BIG-IP Access Policy Manager (APM) as an SP. In version 16.1, APM acts as a service provider through three objects: a SAML SP service, which is one of its AAA (authentication, authorization and accounting) services; one or more SAML IdP connectors describing the external identity providers; and an access policy containing a SAML Auth agent that calls the SP service. When one SP service is bound to several IdP connectors, for example to serve several businesses or universities, APM chooses the identity provider by matching criteria on session variables, such as a landing path in the session.server.landinguri variable, and it performs that discovery only for SP-initiated connections. For step-up authentication the SAML Auth agent goes into a subroutine of a per-request policy, so that a user can be asked for a stronger authentication when moving to a more sensitive resource.

The other service provider: the network operator. In routing, a service provider is the operator that carries customers' traffic, and the term is formal in the standards. Request for Comments (RFC) 4364 of February 2006, which obsoleted RFC 2547 and defines virtual private networks built with the Border Gateway Protocol (BGP) and Multiprotocol Label Switching (MPLS), describes how a service provider uses an Internet Protocol (IP) backbone to provide IP virtual private networks (VPNs) for its customers: customer edge (CE) routers send their routes to the provider edge (PE) routers, BGP carries each VPN's routes among the PE routers while keeping overlapping address spaces separate, and the provider's core routers, the P routers, never attach to customer devices. Brazilian law draws a legal version of the same line: the Marco Civil da Internet distinguishes the provision of connection, whose autonomous system administrator keeps connection records for one year, from application providers, which keep application access records for six months.

Reading the abbreviation. SP means service provider in both SAML and MPLS documents, and NIST's identity guidance adds credential service provider (CSP) for the party that issues and manages credentials. Because the SAML glossary makes an identity provider a kind of service provider, even the federation sense depends on context: in SAML configuration screens SP almost always means the relying application, while in a carrier contract it means the operator. Read the surrounding protocol before deciding which one a ticket, a log or a vendor document is talking about.

zero-trust-exchange.def: Zscaler's globally distributed proxy platform: every connection terminates at a Service Edge, is identified and inspected, then completed onward - sources connect to the Exchange, the Exchange connects to destinations.
zero-trust-exchange.context: The architectural sentence behind ZIA, ZPA, and ZDX: nothing traverses, everything is brokered.

zia.def: Zscaler Internet Access (ZIA): the outbound half of Zscaler's Zero Trust Exchange, a cloud proxy that applies secure web gateway, cloud firewall, sandbox and data protection policy between users or workloads and the internet and SaaS (software as a service) applications.
zia.context: ZIA (Zscaler Internet Access) only protects what reaches it, so every deployment starts with forwarding: the Client Connector agent and its Z-Tunnel from devices, GRE (Generic Routing Encapsulation) or IPsec (Internet Protocol Security) tunnels from sites, PAC (proxy auto-config) files steering browsers, or proxy chaining from an existing proxy. Once traffic arrives at the nearest Zscaler service edge it is decrypted, inspected against the organization's policy and logged, then sent on or blocked; what is deliberately not decrypted, the bypass list, decides how much of that protection is real.
zia.depth:
Zscaler describes ZIA (Zscaler Internet Access) as a secure internet and web gateway delivered in the cloud as part of its Zero Trust Exchange, and, in its traffic forwarding reference architecture, as an advanced web proxy built for the cloud. Users anywhere are directed to the nearest ZIA Service Edge, and each edge performs full TLS (Transport Layer Security) interception, web proxying, firewalling and anti-malware scanning under the same authentication and policy. Its 2026 data sheet calls ZIA a security service edge (SSE) platform and lists the modules sold under the name: a cloud secure web gateway (SWG) with URL (uniform resource locator) filtering; a CASB (cloud access security broker); cloud DLP (data loss prevention) with exact data match and optical character recognition; the Zscaler Firewall with a cloud IPS (intrusion prevention system) for all ports and protocols; a sandbox; an isolating browser; digital experience monitoring; branch connectivity; and DNS (Domain Name System) security. Its sibling, ZPA (Zscaler Private Access), covers private applications; ZIA is the side that faces the internet.

The Zero Trust Exchange, in Zscaler's own definition, is a cloud native platform built on zero trust architecture that establishes trust from user identity and context (location, device, application, content) and then creates direct user-to-application connections, using a proxy rather than a passthrough design. The proxy is the point. A firewall in the path sees packets; a proxy terminates the connection, so it can reassemble a whole object and hand it to a sandbox or a DLP engine, which is the argument Zscaler makes against inspecting on next-generation firewalls. Gartner's definition of a secure web gateway, which Zscaler quotes, requires URL filtering, malicious code detection and filtering, and application controls for popular web applications; ZIA's policy layers (URL filtering, cloud application control, file type control, firewall rules) are built on that model.

The edges are Zscaler's own infrastructure. The 2024 reference architecture puts ZIA Service Edges in more than 150 data centres, including peering at internet exchanges; Zscaler's public feed of enforcement node address ranges for the zscaler.net cloud lists 106 city-named data centre entries, among them São Paulo, São Paulo II, São Paulo IV and Rio de Janeiro I, the ranges that firewalls and partner allowlists have to permit. The same service can be extended into a customer's own premises with a ZIA Private Service Edge (an appliance) or a Virtual Service Edge (a virtual machine), but Zscaler's guide says that in most cases it does not recommend them: they make sense where geopolitical conditions mean traffic would otherwise be intercepted locally or carried abroad before inspection, or where a single site sustains 1 GB or more of traffic, and even then the logs still go to Zscaler's logging infrastructure.

ZIA only protects what reaches it, and Zscaler's forwarding guide divides the ways in two. Transparent forwarding serves fixed sites: Branch Connector appliances or virtual machines that build tunnels for both ZIA and ZPA; GRE (Generic Routing Encapsulation) tunnels, which Zscaler recommends whenever possible because they carry everything with little overhead, built in primary and secondary pairs from each internet egress and each ISP (internet service provider) and requiring a static address; IPsec (Internet Protocol Security) tunnels, with NULL encryption because the traffic is already encrypted, perfect forward secrecy disabled and NAT (network address translation) traversal supported; and dedicated proxy ports, a subscription that requires authentication for every user. The numbers matter in design: if users are translated by NAT before entering a tunnel, they all look like one user, load balancing inside the data centre stops and the location is limited to 250 Mbps; beyond 1 Gbps a site adds tunnels from separate public addresses and keeps each internal address on the same tunnel, or users are asked to authenticate again and again. Mapping private Internet Protocol (IP) addresses to authenticated users, the feature Zscaler calls Surrogate IP, is recommended for every transparent method. Explicit forwarding serves mobile users: Zscaler Client Connector, the agent that also serves ZPA and ZDX (Zscaler Digital Experience), captures traffic with a virtual adapter and carries it in a Z-Tunnel to the nearest edge chosen by geolocation, pausing for captive portals for a configurable 1 to 60 minutes; or PAC (proxy auto-config) files, a JavaScript mechanism Netscape introduced with Navigator 2.0 in 1996, which Zscaler serves with the two nearest edges filled in and recommends only when nothing else works. Proxy chaining from an existing on-premises proxy is described as a transitional design, because such proxies usually fail over only by hand.

Inspection depends on decrypting. When TLS inspection is on, the Zscaler edge intercepts the client's HTTPS (Hypertext Transfer Protocol over TLS) request, opens its own TLS session to the destination and validates the server's certificate, then completes a second handshake with the browser using a server certificate signed by the Zscaler intermediate CA (certificate authority) or by the organization's own intermediate, which the device must trust. Zscaler says that around 70 per cent of the traffic its cloud processes is encrypted. Its TLS inspection guide treats the rollout as a project with phases: settle the legal and privacy objections first, with a data processing agreement and an acceptable use policy explained to users; enrol a root CA, preferably the organization's own; then enable inspection for a pilot group. It also recommends blocking Google's QUIC (which the guide expands as Quick UDP Internet Connections, UDP being the User Datagram Protocol), because inspection relies on TCP (Transmission Control Protocol) session information and browsers fall back to TCP when QUIC is blocked.

Most of the operational difficulty sits in what is deliberately not inspected. Zscaler's guide lists the usual bypasses: banking and finance destinations, healthcare destinations, functions that require traffic that cannot be decrypted, applications that use certificate pinning and break under interception, and parts of Microsoft 365 that misbehave when inspected. It tells administrators to choose bypasses only after consulting legal counsel for the region concerned, and says Zscaler strongly recommends inspecting all traffic and bypassing only in extreme circumstances. Developer environments are a recurring exception that the guide calls a risk to accept knowingly. Every entry on the bypass list is a hole in the coverage being paid for, so getting it right is as much a policy and legal conversation as a technical one.

The architectural trade is plain. Policy follows the user rather than the office, so a laptop is filtered the same way at headquarters, at home or in an airport, and the organization stops backhauling traffic to a central firewall. In exchange, every connection takes an extra hop to an edge the organization did not build, decryption happens on Zscaler's infrastructure under its data processing terms, and availability depends on reaching a healthy edge, which is why Zscaler's forwarding designs pair every primary tunnel or edge with a secondary one, and why a plan is needed for the device that cannot reach either. Zscaler's own data sheet answers the residency question with egress NAT, geolocalized content and in-country data logging, which are features to verify in the contract rather than assume.

zpa.def: Zscaler Private Access (ZPA): Zscaler's zero trust network access (ZTNA) service, announced in April 2016, which joins an authorized user to one private application at a time through a cloud broker, the ZPA Service Edge, to which both the user's Client Connector and an App Connector beside the application connect outbound.
zpa.context: ZPA (Zscaler Private Access) is the inbound half of Zscaler's Zero Trust Exchange, the sibling of Zscaler Internet Access (ZIA), and it replaces the remote-access VPN (virtual private network) rather than extending it. Nothing beside the application listens for the internet: an App Connector next to it dials out over TLS (Transport Layer Security) to the Zscaler cloud, the Client Connector on the user's device dials out too, and a Service Edge checks policy and stitches the two outbound tunnels together, carrying each user session to each application in its own Microtunnel. What a user may reach is defined as application segments, named by fully qualified domain name (FQDN) or IP address and port, grouped into segment groups and allowed by access policy rules that read identity attributes and device posture. Access therefore attaches to applications, never to networks, and an application nobody has defined is simply unreachable.
zpa.depth:
What it is, and what it is not. Zscaler Private Access (ZPA) is Zscaler's product in the zero trust network access (ZTNA) category; the general architecture, the vocabulary of policy engines and enforcement points and the comparison with other vendors belong to the ZTNA entry, and what follows is how Zscaler builds it. Zscaler's 2025 data sheet describes ZPA as a cloud-native service that gives users direct connectivity to private applications while minimizing the attack surface and eliminating lateral movement, delivered as part of its Zero Trust Exchange and built on a security service edge (SSE) framework; its counterpart for traffic bound to the internet is Zscaler Internet Access (ZIA). It is not a virtual private network (VPN): the device is not given a place on an internal subnet, and a session reaches one defined application and nothing else. Nor is it a gateway waiting on the internet for connections: in the normal deployment nothing on the customer's side accepts an inbound connection at all, which is why the same data sheet says the inside-out connections between user and application mean that applications and their IP addresses are never exposed.

Where it came from. Zscaler announced Zscaler Private Access in San Jose on 26 April 2016 as a new service extending its cloud security platform to internal applications. The announcement framed the problem as the VPN's: typical implementations give users access to the entire network they connect to, a fact exploited in a number of breaches. The new service decoupled applications from the physical network to give granular, per-user access to applications in the corporate network, in a data centre or in a public cloud such as Amazon's, with no additional hardware. Zscaler's chief information officer, Patrick Foxhoven, put the design goal as making a company's most precious internal assets dark to the outside world. Two early users were quoted: an infrastructure architect at MAN Diesel & Turbo, who wanted to give users access to a single application and not to his entire network, and a security manager at SAS, who valued microsegmentation that had previously needed a VPN combined with network access control (NAC). SiliconANGLE, reporting the launch on 3 May 2016, noted that a select group of customers had already been using it for some time.

How a session is built. Two parties dial out and one broker joins them. After enrolment, Zscaler Client Connector on the user's device opens one TLS (Transport Layer Security) connection for ZPA, the client tunnel, to the nearest ZPA Public Service Edge. Its first destination, any.broker.prod.zpath.net, resolves only to Public Service Edges; the two sides authenticate each other with mutual TLS, and the client's certificate tells the Service Edge which customer tenant it belongs to. Control and data travel to that one Service Edge, and the Client Connector is never connected to more than one at a time. On the application side, an App Connector, a lightweight virtual machine or package deployed beside the applications, opens a control channel to an optimal Public Service Edge, downloads the set of applications it is responsible for and keeps advertising its availability and the health check status of those applications; application data then travels over separate TLS data connections. When the user asks for an application, the Service Edge checks policy, the client starts a connection carried in a Microtunnel inside its client tunnel, the App Connector is signalled to build a Microtunnel of its own for that session, and the Service Edge stitches the two outbound tunnels together. Even when many users reach the same application, each user session has its own set of Microtunnels.

What is configured. In Zscaler's reference architecture an application is a fully qualified domain name (FQDN), a local domain name or an IP address defined on a standard set of ports, and every application must sit in an application segment, a set of applications on shared ports across one or more back-end servers. Segments are combined into segment groups for policy, and Zscaler recommends naming applications by FQDN wherever possible. Access policy rules name the segments or segment groups they control and the context they require: Security Assertion Markup Language (SAML) attributes from the identity provider (IdP), such as group membership or role, attributes kept current through the System for Cross-domain Identity Management (SCIM), device posture, access type and network location. The guide's worked example turns observed traffic into policy: engineering users seen reaching a source code server on TCP port 443 and a jump host on port 22 become an engineering segment group allowed to members of the Engineering group, while finance users get a separate group for their reporting server. Segments are also tied to the App Connector groups that can reach them, and ZPA chooses a path dynamically, taking into account how close each App Connector is to the requesting user.

Inventory is the work. Because nothing undefined is reachable, a deployment begins by finding out what exists. Zscaler names three sources of that knowledge: asking application owners, mining existing logs and data sources, and ZPA's own application discovery, which it recommends wherever possible. In discovery mode ZPA is first set up to let a set of users reach a wide range of destinations, typically wildcard domains or large IP subnets, and the traffic that results produces a list of discovered applications from which granular segments and rules are then written. The same guidance warns about the transition: broad segments tied to many App Connector groups in different places generate unnecessary health checks, or none at all when they exceed what a group can handle, which degrades path selection, so App Connectors should be grouped by physical or logical location. The cost of the model is that anything nobody remembered to onboard simply does not work, which is exactly why migrations surface applications nobody knew were still running.

Brokers on the premises. Sending a user in the head office to the cloud and back to reach a server in the next room adds latency, so Zscaler also delivers the broker as software the customer runs. A ZPA Private Service Edge is a single-tenant instance, available as a lightweight virtual machine or as an RPM package and usually placed in the demilitarized zone (DMZ), that provides the complete broker function of a Public Service Edge; the customer manages its operating system and Zscaler manages the service. For an on-premises user connecting through a local Private Service Edge and a local App Connector, control-plane and data-plane traffic stay inside the network, and only management traffic, configuration and logging, goes to the cloud. Private Service Edges do not talk to each other, only down to local App Connectors and Client Connectors and up to a Public Service Edge, while each App Connector keeps a private control channel to every Private Service Edge of its tenant that it can reach. The feature is disabled by default and is switched on by Zscaler, and a Private Service Edge can also serve remote users in countries where there is no ZPA cloud service. The 2025 data sheet adds a Business Continuity Mode: with Private Service Edges and private cloud controllers deployed, ZPA switches over automatically so that policy and authentication are still enforced when the ZPA cloud cannot be reached.

Access without the agent. Not every user can install Client Connector, and contractors and partners rarely should. ZPA Browser Access lets a user authenticate and reach a web application from an ordinary browser; integrated browser isolation streams only pixels to an unmanaged device, so the application's data stays off it; and Privileged Remote Access gives isolated, clientless remote desktop access to internal systems over Remote Desktop Protocol (RDP), Secure Shell (SSH) and Virtual Network Computing (VNC), which the data sheet aims at operational technology (OT) sites and third-party vendors who would otherwise come in through jump hosts and VPNs. Records of user activity leave through the Log Streaming Service (LSS) to a security information and event management (SIEM) system.

Inspection, when it is wanted. Brokering decides who reaches what; it does not look inside the traffic. ZPA AppProtection, formerly called Inspection, adds that step at the App Connector: when a user's transactions reach it, the App Connector terminates the TLS session, inspects the request and, if it is allowed, forwards it into the Microtunnel built for that session. The controls are predefined web application firewall rules against the Open Worldwide Application Security Project (OWASP) Top 10, such as Structured Query Language (SQL) injection and cross-site scripting (XSS); detection of port scanners and other network discovery tools; controls written by Zscaler's ThreatLabZ team against attacks reported as Common Vulnerabilities and Exposures (CVE); WebSocket controls; and custom regular expressions. Each control has a paranoia level from 1 to 4, and raising it makes the control consider more inputs, which catches more and blocks more legitimate traffic, so Zscaler advises changing it one step at a time and watching the result. A match either allows the request or blocks it and redirects the user, for instance to an acceptable use policy page.

Where it goes wrong. Firewalls in front of App Connectors and Private Service Edges must allow outbound connections to the Public Service Edge address ranges Zscaler publishes as its Cloud Enforcement Node Ranges, and need nothing inbound. When a customer runs ZIA as well, Client Connector may reach ZPA by way of a ZIA Public Service Edge, and the geolocation step that chooses the nearest broker then sees the ZIA egress address rather than the user's; the reference architecture fixes this by bypassing any.broker.prod.zpath.net out of ZIA or by defining trusted networks. And the broker is a dependency of its own. NIST (National Institute of Standards and Technology) Special Publication 800-207 warns that disrupting the policy components, by a denial-of-service attack or a route hijack, can halt an enterprise's access to its resources, and that hosting enforcement in a well-secured cloud or replicating it across locations mitigates the risk without eliminating it; Private Service Edges and Business Continuity Mode are Zscaler's answer to that warning.

Why it is worth the trouble. A compromised VPN session gives an attacker a network position to explore laterally; a compromised ZPA session gives them one application. That is a genuine reduction in blast radius, not an elimination of risk: SP 800-207 notes that an attacker holding a valid account still reaches whatever that account was granted, and that a well-built zero trust architecture should only keep it from reaching resources outside its normal purview. Applications that only dial out are absent from internet scanning rather than defended against it, which is the property Foxhoven described in 2016 as making assets dark. Vendor figures deserve to be read as vendor figures: the 2025 data sheet quotes Zscaler's own ThreatLabz 2025 VPN Risk Report, in which 92 per cent of respondents shared concerns that unpatched VPN flaws directly lead to ransomware incidents. The other cost is portability. Segments, groups and rules are written in Zscaler's own model, and SP 800-207 lists reliance on proprietary formats as a threat in its own right, since leaving one provider can mean a long programme of translating policy rules into another's.

Neighbours. ZIA is the outbound half of the same platform and shares the Client Connector with ZPA; the Zero Trust Exchange is Zscaler's name for the whole; ZTNA is the category, in which Netskope's Publishers and FortiGate's access proxy solve the same problem with different mechanisms; and SSE and SASE (secure access service edge) are the bundles in which it is usually bought. The names worth keeping straight are the four components of every session (Client Connector, Service Edge, App Connector, Microtunnel), the three layers of configuration (application segment, segment group, access policy) and the date the model began, 26 April 2016.

zdx.def: Zscaler Digital Experience: endpoint-to-application experience monitoring riding the same vantage points as the brokered data path.
zdx.context: Device, network, and app health measured from where the traffic actually flows.
zdx.depth:
ZDX measures what a user actually experiences rather than what the infrastructure reports, which addresses the oldest complaint in operations: every dashboard is green and the application is slow. It does that by measuring from the endpoint, along the real path, to the real application.

The value is in decomposition. When a session is bad, the useful question is which segment is responsible, and the candidates are the device itself, the local network, the path to the security edge, the internet in between, and the application. Measurement from the endpoint can separate those, which turns an argument between teams into a location, and that is usually the entire content of the escalation.

The honest caveat is that this is telemetry, not omniscience. Scores are composites, and a composite can hide a single dreadful component inside an acceptable average, so the score is a starting point for investigation rather than a verdict. Endpoint measurement also means device conditions, a saturated laptop or an overloaded wireless adapter, register as network problems until someone looks closely. Reading the components rather than the number is the skill worth having.

zcc.def: Zscaler Client Connector: the endpoint agent that authenticates the user, classifies the network state, and forwards traffic per its forwarding profile.
zcc.context: Two documents rule it: forwarding profile (plumbing) and app profile (platform policy).
zcc.depth:
Zscaler Client Connector is the agent that decides, on the endpoint, what happens to each packet before anything else can. That decision is driven by forwarding profiles, which key on where the device is: on a trusted network, on a VPN (virtual private network), or off-network entirely, with separate behaviour configured for the internet service and the private access service.

The tunnel choice underneath matters more than it looks. Z-Tunnel 1.0 forwards proxy-aware traffic using CONNECT requests, much like a traditional proxy, which is fine for ordinary web traffic and blind to everything else. Z-Tunnel 2.0 carries all endpoint traffic over DTLS or TLS regardless of port or protocol, which is what makes non-web traffic inspectable. On Windows there is a further choice between a route-based virtual adapter and a filter driver that captures traffic without creating one, and the filter driver interoperates far better with other VPN clients.

This is why most user-reported problems are really forwarding-profile problems. A device that thinks it is on a trusted network behaves completely differently from one that does not, and captive portals, unexpected trusted-network detection, and the wrong tunnel version account for a large share of tickets that first look like cloud outages.

public-service-edge.def: Zscaler's enforcement node in its worldwide data centres: terminates sessions, applies identity and policy, originates the onward connection; packet data stays in memory, never on disk.
public-service-edge.context: Formerly ZEN in older docs; the Private Service Edge is its single-tenant sibling.

app-connector.def: ZPA's lightweight VM/container beside a private application, making only outbound TLS connections to Service Edges - enrolled with a provisioning key, discovering apps via its own DNS vantage.
app-connector.context: No inbound listener means the app is absent from the reachable internet, not hidden behind something.

microtunnel.def: ZPA's per-application, per-user-session thread riding inside the TLS connections from client and App Connector, stitched at a Service Edge.
microtunnel.context: The granularity is the security model: three apps, three Microtunnels.
microtunnel.depth:
A Microtunnel establishes an encrypted path to a single application rather than to a network, which is the mechanical expression of per-application access. Three applications means three tunnels, and each one is independently authorized, so reaching one grants nothing towards the others.

That granularity is the security model rather than an implementation detail. A conventional tunnel is a pipe onto a segment, and everything reachable through it is reachable by whoever holds the session. Splitting per application means a compromised session yields exactly one destination, and the segment those applications sit on remains invisible because it was never the thing being connected to.

The operational trade is the same one every per-application model carries: the inventory becomes the system. Each application must be defined, published and maintained, and anything nobody onboarded simply does not work, which surfaces forgotten dependencies during migration. That is genuinely painful and genuinely valuable, since the applications nobody remembered are also the ones nobody was patching.

z-tunnel.def: Client Connector's transport to a Service Edge: 1.0 is an HTTP CONNECT tunnel shaped for web; 2.0 speaks TLS/DTLS and carries all ports and protocols.
z-tunnel.context: New deployments steer to 2.0 - the all-traffic device tunnel.
z-tunnel.depth:
Z-Tunnel is the transport a Zscaler client uses to reach a service edge, and the version in use determines what can be inspected at all. Version 1.0 forwards proxy-aware traffic using CONNECT requests, in the manner of a traditional proxy, which handles ordinary web browsing and is simply blind to everything else on the device.

Version 2.0 changes the scope rather than the encryption. It carries all endpoint traffic over DTLS, falling back to TLS where UDP is blocked, regardless of port or protocol, which is what makes non-web traffic subject to policy. That is the actual reason to migrate: not speed, but coverage of the traffic that was previously invisible.

The practical consequences show up as support tickets. An application that worked before a migration and fails afterwards is usually one that was never being inspected and now is. A network that blocks the UDP the tunnel prefers forces a fallback that behaves differently under load. And on Windows the choice between a route-based virtual adapter and a filter driver interacts with any other VPN (virtual private network) client on the machine, which is why that setting appears in so many escalations that first look like cloud problems.

surrogate-ip.def: ZIA mechanism mapping a known internal IP to an authenticated user for a period, so traffic that cannot carry credentials still gets user-level policy.
surrogate-ip.context: The proxy-auth fallback for the unauthenticatable - printers, tools, embedded clients.

forwarding-profile.def: ZCC's traffic-plumbing document: for each network state (on/off/VPN trusted) it assigns the forwarding action - Z-Tunnel 1.0/2.0, Tunnel with Local Proxy, Enforce Proxy, or None for ZIA; Tunnel or None for ZPA.
forwarding-profile.context: The state machine that lets the agent stand down where a location tunnel already carries the site.

trusted-network.def: A ZCC-detected network condition defined by admin criteria - preferably the static DNS servers and search domains over dynamic hostname resolution.
trusted-network.context: A flaky criterion misclassifies the network and applies the wrong forwarding action.

gre.def: Generic Routing Encapsulation (GRE): a minimal envelope that carries one network-layer packet inside another, adding 24 bytes over IPv4 (a 4-byte GRE header and a 20-byte outer header carrying Internet Protocol number 47), with no encryption, no authentication and no session.
gre.context: Generic Routing Encapsulation (GRE) wraps a packet of any protocol, named by its EtherType, in a 4-byte header and an outer IP (Internet Protocol) header addressed to the far tunnel endpoint, so two routers that are many hops apart behave like neighbours on one link. That is why it still carries routing protocols and multicast inside IPsec (IP Security) tunnels and why cloud security services accept a whole site's traffic over it. What it adds is overhead and nothing else: no encryption, no authentication, no state. The overhead is small, 24 bytes against the up to roughly 58 that IPsec's ESP (Encapsulating Security Payload) adds, so GRE leaves the highest ceiling of the common tunnels, yet the tunnel MTU (maximum transmission unit) still drops to 1,476 on a 1,500-byte path and somebody has to clamp the TCP (Transmission Control Protocol) maximum segment size.
gre.depth:
What it is. Generic Routing Encapsulation (GRE) is specified in RFC (Request for Comments) 2784, published in March 2000 by Dino Farinacci, Tony Li, Stan Hanks, David Meyer and Paul Traina as a Proposed Standard. Its model has three layers: a payload packet, a GRE header, and a delivery header of whatever protocol carries the result, and the RFC describes itself as the intersection of GRE as already deployed by multiple vendors. That deployment began with RFC 1701 and RFC 1702 of October 1994, informational documents from Hanks of NetSmiths and Li, Farinacci and Traina of cisco Systems, whose header carried routing, key, sequence number and strict source route flags and a recursion control field. RFC 2784 deprecated all of those; RFC 2890 (September 2000) brought back two as options, a Key to identify a traffic flow within a tunnel and a Sequence Number, and RFC 9601 (August 2024) updated RFC 2784 on propagating Explicit Congestion Notification. GRE is not IP-in-IP: the Internet Assigned Numbers Authority (IANA) lists IPv4 encapsulation (RFC 2003) as protocol 4 and GRE as protocol 47, and where IP-in-IP carries only IP, GRE names its payload by EtherType and so can carry almost anything; RFC 7676 (October 2015) added IPv6 as payload or delivery protocol.

The header and the 24 bytes. The base header is 4 octets: a C bit saying whether a checksum is present, twelve reserved bits (a receiver discards the packet if bits 1 to 5 are set, unless it implements RFC 1701), a 3-bit version that must be 0, and a 2-octet Protocol Type holding the payload's EtherType, 0x800 for IPv4. With C set, a 2-octet checksum and 2 reserved octets follow; with RFC 2890's K and S bits set, a 4-octet key and a 4-octet sequence number. The header is therefore 4, 8, 12 or 16 octets. Over IPv4 the delivery header is a 20-octet IP header with protocol 47, and the familiar figure follows: 20 plus 4 is 24 bytes, so a 1,500-byte path leaves a tunnel MTU (maximum transmission unit) of 1,476, and a TCP (Transmission Control Protocol) segment inside it can carry 1,476 minus 40, or 1,436 bytes, the maximum segment size (MSS) both Cisco's and Netskope's documentation arrive at. A key adds 4 more bytes, a checksum another 4.

What the endpoints do, and what they do not. When the payload is IPv4, RFC 2784 says the decapsulating endpoint forwards by the inner destination address, decrements the inner TTL (time to live), and must discard a packet whose inner destination is the encapsulator itself, because that is a loop. Nothing more is defined: no handshake, no session, no encryption and no authentication, so the tunnel interface is up because it is configured, not because the far end answers. RFC 2784's security section notes the operational consequence: filtering by content requires a firewall that looks inside the GRE packet, or filtering at the tunnel endpoints, and terminating the tunnel on the firewall may be preferable.

Why it survives: GRE over IPsec. Its value is what it will carry. Cisco's documentation puts the classic case directly: IPsec (IP Security) does not support IPv4 multicast, GRE does, so a GRE tunnel first encapsulates the dynamic routing protocol and IPsec then encrypts the GRE packet; OSPF (Open Shortest Path First), EIGRP (Enhanced Interior Gateway Routing Protocol) or BGP (Border Gateway Protocol) adjacencies then form across the tunnel as if the routers shared a link. FortiOS documents the same design: an IPsec interface whose phase 2 selectors carry only protocol 47, a config system gre-tunnel entry using the IPsec interface's addresses as its endpoints, and static or dynamic routes pointing into the GRE tunnel. The order of operations matters for size: Cisco notes that GRE fragments before it encapsulates, while IPsec encrypts before it fragments, and recommends an MTU of 1,400 on GRE-over-IPsec tunnels because it covers the common combinations (its tables give 1,440 for transport mode and 1,420 for tunnel mode), with ESP (Encapsulating Security Payload) overhead not exceeding about 58 bytes.

Steering a site to a cloud service. Cloud security services use GRE to receive a whole site's traffic from an edge router without software on every device. Netskope's GRE guide works the numbers from a 1,500-byte WAN (wide area network) interface, GRE MTU 1,476 and GRE MSS 1,436, and its Cisco IOS example sets ip tcp adjust-mss 1436 on the tunnel; it warns against NAT (network address translation) of endpoint addresses before the tunnel, because the service would see one address for everybody, requires a user's traffic to stay in one tunnel, and strongly recommends ICMP (Internet Control Message Protocol) keepalive probes, every 20 seconds with 5 retries every 6 seconds, staggered across tunnels to the same point of presence.

Keepalives. Because GRE has no session, a dead far end leaves the tunnel interface up and traffic disappearing into it. Cisco's keepalive works by reflection: the router builds a packet addressed to itself, wraps it in GRE with a Protocol Type of 0 and sends it inside a packet to the far end, which simply decapsulates it and routes it back; each sent keepalive increments a counter that a returned one resets, and when the counter reaches the configured retries the line protocol goes down, while only keepalives continue to be processed. The command is keepalive with a period and a retry count, 10 seconds and 3 by default, and it is off by default; Cisco notes that keepalives are ordinary packets and can be dropped under load, and that they are supported only in GRE/IP mode.

MTU, MSS and path MTU discovery. The failure is always the overhead: the tunnel comes up, small packets pass and large transfers hang, because hosts still send 1,500-byte packets into a 1,476-byte tunnel. Cisco's routers by default do not run path MTU discovery on the GRE packets they generate and clear DF (Don't Fragment) in the outer header, so tunnel packets can be fragmented; tunnel path-mtu-discovery copies DF from the inner header and lets the tunnel MTU shrink when the path requires it, and Cisco recommends using it together with ip mtu. For TCP the cleaner fix is MSS clamping, ip tcp adjust-mss on the tunnel interface, which rewrites the MSS in SYN (synchronize) packets so the hosts never build oversized segments. On Linux, ip tunnel add with mode gre creates the tunnel, with key, seq and csum options for the RFC 2890 and checksum fields; path MTU discovery on the tunnel is on by default, a fixed ttl implies it, and ignore-df suppresses the DF bit.

Recursive routing. The outer packet is routed like any other, so the route to the far endpoint must stay in the underlay. If a routing protocol running over the tunnel ever offers a better route to the tunnel destination through the tunnel itself, each encapsulated packet is sent back into the tunnel; Cisco IOS detects this, logs %TUN-5-RECURDOWN, disables the tunnel for a few minutes and, if the configuration is wrong, keeps flapping it along with the OSPF, EIGRP or BGP neighbours over it. The fix is a more specific static route, typically a /32, to the tunnel destination over the physical path.

Neighbours in the family. NVGRE (RFC 7637, September 2015) reuses the GRE Key for network virtualization, a 24-bit Virtual Subnet ID and an 8-bit FlowID; GRE-in-UDP (RFC 8086, March 2017) adds a UDP (User Datagram Protocol) header so that the source port gives equal-cost multipath (ECMP) hashing some entropy; RFC 4023 (March 2005) carries MPLS (Multiprotocol Label Switching) in GRE. Encryption and authentication always come from somewhere else, most often IPsec around it.

nat-t.def: NAT Traversal: IPsec's repair for address translation - detecting NAT in IKE and re-wrapping ESP in UDP/4500 so per-flow ports exist again.
nat-t.context: The port-varies property that also lets multiple tunnels share one source IP.
nat-t.depth:
NAT traversal lets IPsec work through address translation, which it otherwise cannot, because ESP has no ports for a translator to rewrite and its integrity check covers fields that translation modifies.

The solution is to encapsulate ESP in UDP on port 4500, giving the translator something it understands and leaving the protected payload intact. Detection happens during the key exchange, where both ends compare hashes of what they think the addresses are and notice when they disagree. Keepalives are needed because a translation entry expires on idle, and a tunnel that works and then silently stops after a quiet period is almost always this.

mss-clamping.def: Rewriting TCP's advertised Maximum Segment Size downward in the SYN so segments fit a tunnel's reduced MTU without fragmentation or black holes.
mss-clamping.context: The device-side escape from PMTUD failures: fix the promise, not the path.
mss-clamping.depth:
MSS clamping is a router rewriting the Maximum Segment Size that endpoints advertise in their TCP handshake, lowering it so segments fit through a tunnel whose overhead the endpoints know nothing about.

It exists because the correct mechanism fails in practice. Path MTU discovery is supposed to handle this by having a router report that a packet was too large, but the ICMP messages carrying that report are widely filtered, so the sender never learns and simply retries forever. The symptom is the familiar one: the connection establishes, small requests work, and anything large hangs, which points at everything except the real cause.

Clamping is honestly a workaround rather than a fix, and worth understanding as such. It is a middlebox altering a negotiation between two endpoints who never agreed to it, which is the layering violation the internet architecture was designed to avoid, and it is standard practice on essentially every VPN (virtual private network) and GRE deployment because the alternative does not work. It is also a good illustration of why protocol evolution is difficult: the network is full of devices making decisions the endpoints cannot see.

app-profile.def: The Zscaler Client Connector policy object that decides per-application handling on the device: which destinations bypass the tunnel via its PAC logic, and platform-specific behaviour per operating system.
app-profile.context: Pairs with the forwarding profile: forwarding decides HOW traffic leaves the device; the app profile decides WHAT gets special handling.

posture-profile.def: A named device-state check evaluated by Zscaler Client Connector - disk encryption, OS state, certificate presence, and similar signals - consumed by ZPA access rules as conditions and surfaced to ZIA as device trust.
posture-profile.context: The mechanism that makes access decisions follow the device's current state, per session, not just the user's identity.

app-segment.def: ZPA's unit of application definition: a set of FQDNs, wildcards, or IP addresses plus their ports, naming what can be reached. Access policy matches top-down against the most specific segment.
app-segment.context: Zero trust names applications instead of networks; the application segment is where the naming happens.

segment-group.def: A ZPA collection of application segments used as the policy axis: access rules commonly target segment groups, so grouping strategy is policy strategy.
segment-group.context: Pairs with server groups (the reachability axis, binding segments to App Connector groups).

private-service-edge.def: A ZPA Service Edge instance the customer hosts in their own environment, brokering the same stitched Microtunnels as the cloud's Public Service Edges but keeping the meeting point local.
private-service-edge.context: Chosen for latency or data-path locality when user, connector, and application all live close together.

ssma.def: Single Scan, Multi-Action: the ZIA Service Edge design where content is scanned once and every enabled engine acts on that single pass, instead of daisy-chaining separate inspection devices.
ssma.context: The architectural answer to appliance sprawl - one proxy transit, all verdicts.

zidentity.def: Zscaler's unified identity layer for the Zero Trust Exchange: one place to integrate identity providers and manage admin and user identity across the platform's services.
zidentity.context: Identity is the new perimeter's control plane; ZIdentity is where the platform centralizes it.

telesp.def: Telecomunicações de São Paulo: the Telebrás system's São Paulo fixed-line operator (1973-1998), successor to the CTB's São Paulo operations; acquired by Spain's Telefónica in the 1998 privatization, becoming Telefônica Brasil (the Vivo brand from 2012). Under Telefónica it launched São Paulo's ADSL broadband, Speedy, in 1999.
telesp.context: The company whose copper pair carried this site's author onto always-on internet in 1999.
telesp.depth:
Telesp was the São Paulo operator within the Telebras system and, by virtue of the state's size, the largest piece of the whole. When the system was privatized in 1998 it went to a Spanish buyer, and the copper pairs it had spent decades installing became the physical layer of the country's first consumer broadband.

That transition is the part worth stating clearly. The same pair of copper wires that had carried a voice line, often after a long wait to obtain it, was reused to carry always-on internet through ADSL. No new cable was laid to most homes; the value came from new equipment at each end of an existing wire, which is why broadband arrived first and fastest wherever the incumbent's copper already was.

For a generation of Brazilian technologists, that copper pair is where the internet stopped being something you dialled and started being something that was simply on. This site's author came online that way in 1999. The infrastructure inherited from a state monopoly, sold to a foreign operator, and repurposed by a technology nobody had in mind when the wire was installed is a reasonable summary of how most countries actually got connected.

telebras.def: Telecomunicações Brasileiras S.A.: the state holding that organized Brazil's telecom operators from 1972; the whole system - three fixed holdings, Embratel, and eight cellular holdings - was privatized in twelve auctions on 29 July 1998, the largest privatization in Brazilian history.
telebras.context: The monopoly era's name; its breakup is the hinge of Brazil's telecom timeline.
telebras.depth:
Telebras was the state holding company that owned Brazilian telecommunications, a system of operating companies under one federal roof, and for a quarter of a century it was simply how telephony existed in the country. Its breakup in July 1998 was among the largest privatizations attempted anywhere at the time.

The monopoly era is remembered for two things that sound contradictory and both happened. Telebras built genuine national infrastructure and funded serious research through its own centre, reaching places no commercial calculation would have reached. It also produced waiting lists measured in years and a line so scarce it was treated as an asset: people bought and sold telephone lines, and a residential line appeared on balance sheets as property.

The breakup replaced one problem with a different one. Competition and privatization ended the queue, put mobile telephony within reach of ordinary incomes, and transferred the network to operators answerable to shareholders rather than to a ministry. It also required inventing a referee where none had existed, which is why Anatel arrives at the same moment. Everything about Brazilian telecom regulation since is downstream of that year.

embratel.def: Empresa Brasileira de Telecomunicações: Brazil's long-distance and data carrier, created in 1965 and folded into the Telebrás system; ran the country's first commercial internet trial in December 1994; privatized in 1998 to MCI WorldCom, sold to Telmex in 2004, incorporated into Claro in 2015.
embratel.context: The backbone company - long distance, international, and the first commercial internet on-ramp.
embratel.depth:
Embratel was created in the 1960s to build what Brazil did not have: long distance and international connectivity across a country of continental size, where linking two cities was a national infrastructure project rather than a commercial decision. Satellite earth stations, microwave chains and eventually fibre were all its work.

Its second life is the one that matters to this site. When commercial internet arrived in Brazil in the mid-1990s, Embratel operated the backbone it ran on and was the on-ramp through which the country connected to the rest of the network. The academic connection through FAPESP had carried Brazil's traffic until then; the commercial era began on Embratel's circuits.

That sequence, a state company building the physical plant over decades and a commercial internet arriving to use it, is the pattern almost everywhere. The infrastructure is expensive, slow to build, and unattractive to private capital until it already exists, at which point it looks obvious. Reading the history in that order makes the privatization debates of the 1990s more legible: what was being sold had been built by an entity that could afford to be patient.

anatel.def: Agência Nacional de Telecomunicações: Brazil's telecom regulator, created by the Lei Geral de Telecomunicações (Law 9.472, July 1997) to set rules and supervise the privatized sector in the public interest.
anatel.context: The referee the 1998 privatization required - regulation moved from ministry to agency.
anatel.depth:
Anatel was created by the General Telecommunications Law of 1997 and exists because privatization required it. A state monopoly needs no referee, since the operator and the policymaker are the same institution; the moment competing private operators exist, somebody has to allocate spectrum, arbitrate interconnection, set quality obligations and decide disputes.

The design decision worth noticing is independence. Anatel was constituted as an agency with its own budget and fixed-term appointments rather than as a department of a ministry, which was a deliberate attempt to insulate technical regulation from electoral cycles. That model was applied across several Brazilian sectors in the same period and remains contested, since independence from politics is also distance from democratic accountability.

Its scope is telecommunications rather than the internet, and the distinction matters and is frequently lost. Anatel regulates the carriers, the spectrum and the infrastructure; internet governance sits with CGI.br, a multistakeholder committee that is not a regulator at all. Brazil deliberately kept those separate, which is unusual internationally and is the reason the country's internet policy and its telecom policy can diverge.

cgi-br.def: Comitê Gestor da Internet no Brasil: the multistakeholder Internet Steering Committee created in 1995 by the Science & Technology and Communications ministries to set internet directives and policies in Brazil, including governance of the .br domain.
cgi-br.context: Brazil's answer to internet governance - policy by committee rather than by carrier.
cgi-br.depth:
CGI.br is the Brazilian Internet Steering Committee, created in 1995 with representation from government, the private sector, civil society and the academic community. The composition is the substance: no single sector holds a majority, and the civil society and academic seats are filled by election within their own constituencies rather than by appointment.

It was established years before multistakeholder governance became the standard international vocabulary, which gave Brazil an unusually strong diplomatic position when those debates arrived. The 2009 Decálogo set out ten principles including network neutrality, privacy, freedom of expression and the inimputability of the network, five years before the Marco Civil made several of them statute.

The design decision worth appreciating is what it is not. CGI.br is not a regulator and has no enforcement power; Anatel regulates carriers and CGI.br governs the internet, and Brazil deliberately kept those apart. That separation is uncommon and it is the reason the country's internet policy has been able to develop on its own logic rather than as an appendix to telecommunications law.

nic-br.def: Núcleo de Informação e Coordenação do Ponto BR: the entity that implements CGI.br's decisions - formalized in 2003, operating the .br registry (Registro.br) since 2005, plus measurement, IX, and security functions.
nic-br.context: The operational arm: where .br domains, Brazilian IP allocation, and traffic exchange actually run.
nic-br.depth:
NIC.br is the non-profit created in 2005 to execute what CGI.br decides, and it is where Brazilian internet governance becomes operational infrastructure rather than policy. Its arms do the work: Registro.br runs the .br domain, CERT.br handles national incident response, and CEPTRO.br operates IX.br and drives IPv6 adoption.

The funding model deserves attention because it explains the independence. NIC.br is financed largely by domain registration fees rather than by government appropriation, which means it can maintain long-term technical programmes without an annual political negotiation. That is why IX.br could be built out across dozens of cities on a timeline that no budget cycle would have tolerated.

The result is a set of national capabilities that many larger countries lack: a distributed exchange system that keeps domestic traffic domestic, measurement and IPv6 programmes with genuine reach, and an incident response function with standing. It is a good argument that governance structure and technical outcome are connected, since the same work under a ministry with annual funding would look very different.

fapesp.def: Fundação de Amparo à Pesquisa do Estado de São Paulo: São Paulo's research-funding foundation whose data-processing team built Brazil's academic network (ANSP), received Jon Postel's delegation of the .br domain in 1989, made the country's first TCP/IP connection in 1991 (to ESnet via Fermilab), and ran .br registration until NIC.br took over.
fapesp.context: A research funder that accidentally became a country's internet registry - for sixteen years.
fapesp.depth:
FAPESP is the São Paulo state research foundation, funded by a constitutionally guaranteed share of state tax revenue, and that funding model is why it could do what it did. A guaranteed percentage means long-horizon commitments survive changes of government, which is precisely what infrastructure research requires and almost never gets.

Its place in this history is not as a funder but as an operator. FAPESP built and ran ANSP, connected it to Fermilab, and for roughly five years that single link carried essentially all Brazilian internet traffic to the outside world. It also administered the .br domain and IP address allocation, functions it took on because somebody had to and no other institution existed to do it.

That is an unusual role for a research foundation and it explains the shape of Brazilian internet governance afterwards. The registry function eventually moved to NIC.br, the academic network work continued through RNP and later KyaTera, and the institutional habit of treating the internet as research infrastructure rather than as a telecommunications product survived the transition. Countries where the internet arrived through a carrier ended up with different assumptions.

usp.def: Universidade de São Paulo: Brazil's largest research university and a founding participant of the ANSP academic network - Brazilian internet history runs through its physics and engineering departments' need to reach colleagues abroad.
usp.context: One of the campuses whose email envy bootstrapped a national network.
usp.depth:
The University of São Paulo is the largest and most research-intensive university in Brazil, and in this history it is one of the institutions on the far end of the first academic network links. ANSP connected it, and the physicists whose collaborations motivated the Fermilab connection worked there.

Its role is worth stating precisely because it is easy to overstate. USP did not build the Brazilian internet; FAPESP funded and operated the network, and RNP built the national backbone. What USP supplied was demand and expertise: the researchers who needed international connectivity badly enough to justify it, and the people who knew how to make it work once it existed.

That pattern is the ordinary one and worth recognizing. Research networks are built because researchers have a concrete problem that requires them, not because someone anticipated the internet. The physics collaboration that wanted to exchange data with Illinois produced, as a side effect, the country's first international link, and everything commercial that followed used infrastructure and expertise that existed because of an academic requirement nobody would have funded as a communications project.

unicamp.def: Universidade Estadual de Campinas: the Campinas state research university, a founding ANSP participant alongside USP and UNESP in the pre-internet academic networking that became Brazil's on-ramp.
unicamp.context: The other São Paulo campus in the founding story.
unicamp.depth:
Unicamp, the State University of Campinas, is a research university deliberately created in the 1960s in a region that became Brazil's densest concentration of technology industry and research institutes. It was one of the institutions ANSP connected, and it sits at the centre of what is sometimes called the Brazilian technology corridor.

Its significance here is regional rather than singular. Campinas holds a cluster of universities, research centres and manufacturing that developed together, and the academic network links between them mattered because the collaboration was already happening. Connectivity followed proximity and shared work rather than creating it.

The broader point is that technology geography is built rather than found. That concentration exists because of decisions about where to put a university and what to fund around it, made decades before anyone could have described the payoff, and the returns arrived on a timescale no quarterly process would have sanctioned. Anyone arguing about how a country develops technical capability is arguing about that kind of patience, and Campinas is one of the clearer natural experiments available.

pots.def: Plain Old Telephone Service: the analog telephone network - a voice in the 300-3400 Hz band over a dedicated twisted pair for the duration of a call. Dial-up internet was data squeezed through its voice channel, one occupied line at a time.
pots.context: The retronym the internet made necessary - and then made historical.
pots.depth:
Plain old telephone service is the analogue line that carried voice for a century, powered from the exchange so it worked when the building lost electricity. That property is the one worth remembering, because everything that replaced it does not have it.

Its retirement is an ongoing infrastructure change with real consequences. Alarm panels, lift emergency phones, fax machines, medical alert devices and payment terminals were all designed against a line that supplied its own power and was assumed always present. Migrating them to IP is not a like-for-like swap, and the classes of failure introduced, most obviously that a power cut now takes the phone with it, are why the transition has been slower and more contested than the technology alone would suggest.

adsl.def: Asymmetric Digital Subscriber Line: broadband over the existing telephone pair by frequency division - voice below ~4 kHz, data above, a DSLAM terminating the data side at the exchange. Asymmetric because downstream gets most of the spectrum. Its arrival made home connections always-on.
adsl.context: The technology that let the same copper carry the internet full-time - the beginning of POTS's end.
adsl.depth:
ADSL carried broadband over ordinary telephone copper by using frequencies above the voice band, which is why a filter at each socket kept the two from interfering. Asymmetric described the split: much more capacity downstream than up, matching what browsing looked like at the time.

Its defining constraint was distance. Attenuation rises with line length, so the achievable rate fell off sharply with distance from the exchange, and two subscribers on the same package could receive very different service for reasons of geography alone. That single fact shaped a generation of complaints and is the reason cabinet-based deployments shortening the copper run mattered more than any protocol improvement.

hfc.def: Hybrid Fiber-Coaxial: the cable-TV plant architecture - fibre from the headend to neighborhood nodes, coaxial for the final drop - that DOCSIS turned into a shared broadband network.
hfc.context: Why the television cable in the wall can carry gigabit internet.
hfc.depth:
Hybrid fibre-coaxial runs fibre to a neighbourhood node and coaxial cable for the last stretch, which is how cable operators upgraded without replacing the drop to every home. It is the physical plant DOCSIS runs on.

The characteristic it produces is shared capacity per node. Everyone served by one node contends for the same spectrum, so performance depends on how many subscribers are on that segment and what they are doing, which is why node splits are the standard remedy for congestion.
