It also means an operator's advertised speed is achievable and not guaranteed, and the difference between the two is a function of local subscriber density rather than of the customer's equipment.

leo-constellation.def: A fleet of satellites in Low Earth Orbit - hundreds of kilometres up rather than geostationary's 35,786 km - trading one motionless satellite for thousands of moving ones: latency drops to tens of milliseconds, at the cost of constant handoffs, phased-array terminals, and fleet logistics. Starlink is the operating example at scale.
leo-constellation.context: Satellite internet without the half-second physics tax.

lora.def: A long-range, low-power radio technique (Semtech's chirp spread spectrum) and, via LoRaWAN (the LoRa Alliance's network specification), an LPWAN architecture: kilometres of range, years of battery, bytes of payload, gateways forwarding whatever they hear.
lora.context: The network for whispers - sensors that must live for years on a coin cell.
lora.depth:
LoRa takes the opposite bet from Wi-Fi, and understanding the trade explains everything else about it. It uses a spread spectrum modulation in sub-gigahertz unlicensed bands to achieve kilometres of range and years of battery life, and it pays for that with data rates measured in hundreds of bits per second.

That budget shapes what you can build. A sensor sending a temperature reading every fifteen minutes fits comfortably; anything resembling a stream does not. The lower the data rate, the further the signal reaches, so range and throughput are directly exchangeable per message, and the adaptive schemes that pick this automatically are optimizing that exact trade.

The constraint people meet late is regulatory duty cycle. Unlicensed sub-gigahertz bands limit how much of each hour a device may transmit, which caps message frequency independently of anything in your design, and the limits differ by region. A device that works in testing and fails in production is often one whose retry logic is exceeding what the band permits, which is a compliance ceiling rather than a bug in the radio.

pager.def: A pocket radio receiver, known in Brazil as the bip, that listens to a one-way paging network: transmitters broadcast every message to every pager in range, and each pager displays only those carrying its own address. Classic services relayed callers' messages through human operators; POCSAG (Post Office Code Standardization Advisory Group) and Motorola's FLEX carried the digital formats.
pager.context: Reachability before real time. The classic pager has no transmitter, so it cannot be located, cannot confirm delivery and cannot congest anything; a network of powerful transmitters broadcasting the same signal reaches it deep inside buildings, and its receiver sleeps through most of the broadcast, which spares the battery. That is why hospitals and emergency services kept pagers long after consumers moved to mobile phones, and why on-call engineers still say they were paged when the alert arrived on a phone. It is also a privacy lesson: in the classic service a human operator heard every message and typed it, and on the air most pages still travel unencrypted and unauthenticated, readable by anyone with a cheap software-defined radio within tens of kilometres.
pager.depth:
What it is, and what it is not. A pager is a radio receiver tuned to a paging network. Transmitters broadcast every message on a shared channel, every pager in range listens, and each one acts only on the messages that carry its own address. The classic device has no transmitter at all, so the network never learns where it is or whether a message arrived; that is the design, not a missing feature. Three neighbours share the word. Two-way paging, such as Motorola's ReFLEX, adds a return channel to the same kind of network. In operations, to page someone now means to send an urgent alert to whatever the on-call engineer carries, usually a phone. And the pager of a command-line interface, more or less, is the program that shows output one screen at a time, which scripts driving network devices switch off; it shares only the name.

Where it came from. The Lemelson-MIT Program credits Al Gross, who had patented a handheld two-way radio, the walkie-talkie, in 1938, with inventing and patenting the telephone pager in 1949: a pocket-sized receiver with circuitry that responded selectively to specific signals. The doctors at a Philadelphia medical convention that year mostly worried that it would upset their patients or interrupt their golf; New York's Jewish Hospital adopted his system in 1950, and the Federal Communications Commission (FCC), to which he demonstrated it that year, approved his transceivers in 1958. Trend Micro's account has physicians carrying pagers from the 1950s, receiving pages up to 25 miles from a single tower, transistorized pagers in the 1960s, and the general public taking them up only in the 1990s, shortly before SMS (Short Message Service) on mobile phones took the use away. Japan shows the whole curve: pagers there peaked at about 10 million units in 1996, the operator that had introduced them ended its service in 2007, and the last provider, Tokyo Telemessage, announced in December 2018 that it would close in September 2019, with about 1,500 users left.

The first common code. The format most pagers spoke came out of the British Post Office. An international group of engineers began meeting in 1976 to design a code for wide-area paging, chaired by R. H. Tridgell; it took its name from the Post Office Code Standardization Advisory Group (POCSAG), and in February 1981 the CCIR (Comité consultatif international pour la radio), forerunner of the Radiocommunication Sector of the International Telecommunication Union (ITU-R), accepted it as Radiopaging Code No. 1. Today it is Annex 1 of Recommendation ITU-R M.584-2, approved in November 1997 and in force. A transmission opens with a preamble of alternating ones and zeros at least 576 bits long, one batch plus one codeword, so that receivers can lock on. Then come batches: a synchronization codeword followed by eight frames of two codewords each. Every codeword is 32 bits, 21 information bits followed by 10 check bits of a cyclic code and an even-parity bit, enough to correct up to two bit errors per codeword. The pager population is split into eight groups by the three least significant bits of each 21-bit identity, and a pager examines address codewords only in its own frame, which is what lets it sleep the rest of the time. An address codeword starts with a 0 and carries the other 18 identity bits plus two function bits that select one of four addresses per pager, 2 to the power 23 addresses in all, over 8 million; message codewords start with a 1 and carry 20 message bits. Numeric pages use 4-bit characters (digits, space, hyphen, brackets and a U for urgent), five to a codeword; alphanumeric pages use the 7-bit International Alphabet No. 5. The original rate was 512 bit/s, later 1,200 and 2,400 bit/s, sent by frequency-shift keying (FSK) with a 4.5 kHz shift in 25 kHz channels, narrowed to 12.5 kHz channels where regulators required it, as the FCC did before 2013.

FLEX and its two-way successor. Motorola's FLEX is synchronous where POCSAG is batch by batch. As the Japanese variant FLEX-TD, set in 1995 by the Association of Radio Industries and Businesses (ARIB), is described in Annex 2 of the same Recommendation, an hour divides into 15 cycles of 128 frames, so a cycle lasts 4 minutes and a frame 1.875 s: a sync of 115 ms and 11 interleaved blocks of 160 ms. Frames run at 1,600, 3,200 or 6,400 bit/s with two- or four-level FSK, the codeword is the same 32-bit word as POCSAG's with two-bit correction, and interleaving eight words per block lets a pager survive bursts of 32 consecutive bit errors at 3,200 bit/s and 64 at 6,400. A pager knows which frames can carry its address and keeps its receiver off for most of the cycle, which is where the long battery life comes from. Roaming uses a simulcast system identifier (SSID), naming the coverage area, or a network identifier. ReFLEX added the uplink: forward channels at 1,600 to 6,400 bit/s and return channels from 800 to 9,600 bit/s, first for a messaging service the carrier MTEL launched in the mid-1990s.

Why the networks outlived the consumers. The argument is architectural, and much of the published case comes from the industry itself. An engineering paper on ReFLEX for first responders, posted by the FCC's Public Safety and Homeland Security Bureau in December 2005, describes simulcast networks of transmitters with up to 3,500 W of effective radiated power on antennas of 300 feet or more, all sending the same signal, against cellular sites of about 100 W on 90-foot masts; the overlapping coverage gives redundancy and better penetration inside buildings, and because messages are sent one after another on dedicated narrowband channels, coverage does not change with traffic load: a device that works at a spot once works there whatever the load. After Hurricane Katrina, the chief executive of USA Mobility told the FCC's review panel that paging, fed to its transmitters by satellite rather than landlines, was restored within 48 hours in the worst-hit areas. Hospitals add their own reasons: Trend Micro notes that cellular coverage can be weak inside large hospital complexes and that phones are still prohibited in parts of hospitals in several countries. The counter-case was put by the United Kingdom on 23 February 2019, when the health secretary ordered the National Health Service (NHS) to phase pagers out of non-emergency use by the end of 2021: it ran about 130,000 pagers at 6.6 million pounds a year, more than one in ten of all pagers in the world, only one UK provider was left, and a 2017 pilot of phones and apps had saved junior doctors 48 minutes a shift. Pagers could stay for emergencies, such as a Wi-Fi failure.

What goes wrong: the air is a broadcast. Paging was designed before anyone expected receivers to be cheap, and most pages are neither encrypted nor authenticated. In 2016 Stephen Hilt and Philippe Lin of Trend Micro showed what that means in practice. With software-defined radio and a dongle costing about 20 US dollars, they passively observed 54,976,553 pages in the United States between 25 January and 25 April 2016; 18,368,210 were alphanumeric, and 2,075,765 of those came from hospitals or healthcare centres, carrying names, dates of birth, diagnoses and other protected health information that the Health Insurance Portability and Accountability Act (HIPAA) of 1996 is meant to keep private, readable tens of kilometres from the transmitter. In a test environment they also sent spoofed POCSAG pages, because a pager has no way to tell who transmitted. The researchers point out that intercepting such traffic is a crime in most countries. The practical conclusions for anyone who still runs paging: treat every page as published, send a callback number or a ticket reference instead of the content, and never let a page act as an authenticated command.

What goes wrong: the device itself. In September 2024 thousands of pagers and radios exploded at once across Lebanon and Syria; United Nations human rights experts, in a statement on 19 September 2024, described the devices as maliciously manipulated, reported at least 32 people killed and about 3,250 injured, and called the attacks violations of international law. For engineers the episode moved the threat model of a fleet device from its radio link to its supply chain: a device bought in bulk from one source can be altered before it is ever switched on, which is a hardware question that no encryption of the channel answers.

Brazil and the bip. In Brazil the service was regulated as the Serviço Especial de Radiochamada, one-way paging. In February 1999 the board of the National Telecommunications Agency (Anatel) approved its authorization plan, later formalized as Resolution 171 of 8 October 1999, adding the 929 MHz band to the 931 MHz band already in use and licensing operators at national, regional and local levels. Classic Brazilian service ran through operators: the caller telephoned a call centre, an attendant took the message and typed it, and it reached the subscriber's bip. By December 2002 the trade press was describing a market emptied by mobile phones and their messaging, with Mobitel, Teletrim, Conectel and TWW (formerly Pagenet) as the largest survivors and Mobitel earning about 20 reais a month per user. Anatel's Resolution 617 of 19 June 2013 revoked the 1999 plan and folded the remaining paging authorizations into the Serviço Limitado Privado.

The word in operations. On-call vocabulary kept the pager after the hardware. Google's Site Reliability Engineering book notes that the page-receiving device is typically a phone, with pages delivered by email, SMS, automated voice call or app, and sets response times of about 5 minutes for user-facing services and 30 minutes for less time-critical ones. Its rules for sustainable on-call are paging rules: paging alerts should match symptoms that threaten a service level objective (SLO) and be actionable, a shift should see at most two incidents in 12 hours, and a team overwhelmed by a service can give the pager back to its developers. Numbers worth keeping: 1949 for the invention, 1981 for POCSAG at the CCIR, 512, 1,200 and 2,400 bit/s for POCSAG, 1,600 to 6,400 bit/s for FLEX, 32-bit codewords with 21 information bits, 1.875 s frames, and tens of kilometres for the reach of an unencrypted page.

cci.def: Cloud Confidence Index - Netskope's 0-100 risk rating for tens of thousands of cloud applications, scored against objective criteria adapted from the Cloud Security Alliance's guidance and grouped into enterprise-readiness categories such as certifications and compliance, data protection, access control, auditability, disaster recovery, and legal/privacy terms.
cci.context: CCI levels (excellent, high, medium, low, poor) are usable directly in policy - steering, coaching, or blocking by risk tier rather than by naming apps one at a time. Named verbatim in the Netskope blueprints' monitoring domain, and the subject of this site's Cloud Confidence Index article.
cci.depth:
The Cloud Confidence Index is Netskope's risk rating for cloud applications, scoring each on attributes such as encryption, certifications, data ownership terms and administrative controls. Its purpose is to turn discovery into a decision.

The reason a rating like this exists at all is scale. An organization's shadow IT discovery typically returns hundreds or thousands of distinct services, which is far too many to evaluate individually, and a score gives a defensible basis for tiering them into sanctioned, tolerated and blocked. The honest caveat is that any single vendor's index reflects that vendor's criteria and weightings, so it is a starting point for policy rather than an objective measurement of risk.

newedge.def: Netskope's privately operated global network of data centres - the infrastructure the Netskope One security cloud runs on. Every data centre provides full compute for single-pass inspection, with extensive peering close to users and to the major SaaS providers.
newedge.context: The architectural answer to 'where does the proxy live': not in a few hub regions with backhaul, but at points of presence engineered for low round-trip time. The platform-architecture article on this site draws the full picture.
newedge.depth:
NewEdge is the answer to a question every cloud security platform must answer: where does the inspection actually happen. Concentrating it in a few large regions means users far from one pay latency on every request, and backhaul is precisely the cost the architecture was supposed to remove.

The alternative is many points of presence, peered directly with the networks users and applications already use, so traffic enters the security fabric close to where it starts and leaves close to where it is going. Direct peering matters more than the count of locations: a nearby point of presence reached over a congested transit path is not nearby in any sense that affects a user.

The reason this is worth understanding rather than accepting is that it determines the failure modes. Performance complaints in cloud security platforms are usually path problems rather than inspection problems, and knowing whether traffic reaches a well-peered nearby edge or is being carried across a continent first is what distinguishes a tuning exercise from an architecture one. It is also the property that no datasheet number captures, since a location list says nothing about how traffic gets there.

block-cipher.def: A symmetric cipher that transforms fixed-size blocks of data under a key, 128 bits for AES (Advanced Encryption Standard), and relies on a mode of operation to encrypt messages of real length.
block-cipher.context: A block cipher is a keyed permutation: for each key it maps every possible block of n bits to a different block, and the same key and block always give the same output. That determinism is why it never encrypts a message directly: a mode of operation chains it, counts with it or authenticates with it, and the mode is where the security lives or dies. CBC's (cipher block chaining) padding history produced a decade of oracles, while the AEAD (authenticated encryption with associated data) modes, GCM (Galois/Counter Mode) and CCM (Counter with CBC-MAC), weld integrity in; TLS (Transport Layer Security) 1.3 permits only AEAD algorithms, and its block-cipher ones are exactly AES (Advanced Encryption Standard) in GCM and CCM. Block size matters as much as key size: 64-bit blocks, as in Triple DES (Data Encryption Standard), wear out after tens of gigabytes under one key. AES is the block cipher of the internet largely because AES-NI (AES New Instructions) silicon makes it fast, and free of the table lookups that leak timing, nearly everywhere.
block-cipher.depth:
What it is. A block cipher takes a key and a block of fixed size and returns a block of the same size, and for each key the mapping is a permutation that can be inverted only with the key. FIPS (Federal Information Processing Standard) 197, which specifies the Advanced Encryption Standard (AES), calls its two functions Cipher and InvCipher and notes that neutral terms are appropriate because block ciphers have applications besides encryption: they also build message authentication codes, key derivation functions, random bit generators and key wrapping. AES is three members of the Rijndael family designed by Joan Daemen and Vincent Rijmen, which NIST (National Institute of Standards and Technology) announced in 2000 as the winner of its open competition: AES-128, AES-192 and AES-256 all transform 128-bit blocks and run 10, 12 and 14 rounds respectively, and the suffix is the key length. FIPS 197 was published on 26 November 2001 and updated on 9 May 2023 with extensive editorial changes and no technical change. Rijndael itself supports block and key sizes from 128 to 256 bits in 32-bit steps; AES fixed the block at 128.

Modes, where it becomes useful. Because a block cipher is deterministic, encrypting a long message block by block under one key leaks its structure: NIST Special Publication (SP) 800-38A (Morris Dworkin, December 2001) states that in ECB (electronic codebook) mode, under a given key, a given plaintext block always encrypts to the same ciphertext block. SP 800-38A defines five confidentiality modes, ECB, CBC (cipher block chaining), CFB (cipher feedback), OFB (output feedback) and CTR (counter), leaves padding outside its scope with one example method in an appendix, and has an addendum defining three ciphertext-stealing variants of CBC. The rest of the 800-38 series adds CMAC (cipher-based message authentication code) for authentication (38B), CCM (Counter with CBC-MAC, 38C) and GCM (Galois/Counter Mode) with GMAC (38D) for authenticated encryption, XTS-AES for storage (38E), key wrapping (38F) and format-preserving encryption with FF1 and FF3 (38G). CFB, OFB and CTR turn the block cipher into a keystream generator, so they behave as stream ciphers; CBC and ECB need padding or ciphertext stealing; GCM and CCM add the integrity that the confidentiality modes lack. NIST has said since April 2023 that it plans to revise SP 800-38A, and the initial public draft of SP 800-131A Revision 3 (21 October 2024, comments closed 4 December 2024, still a draft) proposes to disallow ECB for encrypting secret data, allowing it only to decrypt legacy data and, per NIST IR (Interagency Report) 8459, for non-confidentiality uses such as challenge-response and IV (initialization vector) generation, while keeping CBC, CFB, CTR and OFB acceptable and CCM, GCM and XTS-AES acceptable for 128-bit block ciphers; FF3 would be disallowed.

Block size, the limit nobody configures. A block cipher with n-bit blocks starts to repeat blocks, by the birthday paradox, after about 2 to the n/2 blocks under one key, and in CBC a collision leaks the XOR (exclusive OR) of two plaintext blocks. For 64-bit ciphers that is 2 to the 32nd blocks, 32 GB, which a fast connection can carry in less than an hour, and which Karthikeyan Bhargavan and Gaëtan Leurent turned into the Sweet32 attack (ACM CCS 2016, CVE-2016-2183 and CVE-2016-6329): by watching a long-lived Triple DES (Data Encryption Standard) HTTPS connection they recovered a secure cookie from about 785 GB of traffic in under two days, and showed the same against OpenVPN, whose default cipher was then Blowfish, another 64-bit design. Triple DES was still used for about 1 to 2 per cent of HTTPS connections at the time. NIST withdrew SP 800-67 Revision 2, its Triple DES recommendation, on 1 January 2024, and the Revision 3 draft of SP 800-131A lists TDEA (Triple Data Encryption Algorithm) encryption as disallowed and decryption as legacy use only; DES itself, FIPS 46-3 of 25 October 1999, was withdrawn on 19 May 2005. AES's 128-bit block pushes the bound to 2 to the 64th blocks, ample for most uses, but NIST's own review of AES and its modes, begun in 2021, found data limits increasingly relevant, and in August 2024 NIST indicated interest in Rijndael-256, the 256-bit-block member of the family with a single 256-bit key; its pre-draft call for comments, published as SP 800-197 in December 2024, closed on 25 June 2025, and in January 2026 NIST told a workshop that it plans to revise FIPS 197 to include Rijndael-256, as a complement to AES rather than a replacement, together with a family of wide-block modes it calls accordions.

Inside AES. Each round of AES applies four transformations to a 4-by-4 array of bytes, SubBytes, ShiftRows, MixColumns and AddRoundKey, with round keys expanded from the cipher key; the S-box that SubBytes applies to every byte is, in the standard's words, a non-linear substitution table. FIPS 197 warns that a physical implementation may leak key-dependent information through side channels such as computation time, and that cache-timing attacks may affect AES implementations on software platforms that use a cache to speed up memory access, which is what classic table-based software does. Intel's AES New Instructions (AES-NI), described by Shay Gueron in a white paper whose revision 3.01 dates from September 2012, perform the rounds in hardware without lookup tables and with data-independent latency, which the paper says eliminates the major timing and cache attacks on table-based software AES; it reports speedups of more than an order of magnitude for parallelizable modes and about two to three times for serial modes such as CBC encryption. NIST's January 2026 presentation credits AES-NI with the high performance that made AES the default almost everywhere.

Where engineers meet it. In Transport Layer Security (TLS) 1.3, specified since July 2026 in RFC (Request for Comments) 9846, the symmetric algorithms were pruned of everything considered legacy and only AEAD (authenticated encryption with associated data) algorithms remain: of the five cipher suites, four are AES in GCM or CCM mode and the fifth is ChaCha20-Poly1305, a stream cipher. TLS 1.2 still carries CBC suites, whose problems RFC 7905 cited in 2016 as a reason for adding ChaCha20-Poly1305 and which Google's 2014 note tied to padding oracles such as Lucky Thirteen; the cbc, beast and lucky13 entries tell that history. IPsec (Internet Protocol Security) offers AES in CBC and GCM, disk encryption uses XTS-AES, and Sweet32 is the reason 3DES and Blowfish proposals should be gone from VPN (virtual private network) and TLS configurations. The SP 800-131A draft adds that AES-128, AES-192 and AES-256 are expected to remain secure for the foreseeable future even with the impact of quantum computers, so the post-quantum migration replaces public-key algorithms, not block ciphers.

Its neighbours. A stream cipher generates a keystream and needs no block alignment; a block cipher in CTR mode is one. A hash function has no key and no inverse; a block cipher has both. AEAD is an interface that a block-cipher mode such as GCM or CCM, or a stream cipher with an authenticator, can provide. An IV or nonce is the per-message input a mode needs, and its rules differ by mode: unpredictable for CBC and CFB, unique for OFB and CTR.

Numbers worth remembering: 128-bit blocks and 10, 12 or 14 rounds for AES; 64-bit blocks for DES, Triple DES and Blowfish, and 785 GB for Sweet32's cookie; 2 to the n/2 blocks as the birthday bound; five modes in SP 800-38A; 26 November 2001 for FIPS 197; 1 January 2024 for the withdrawal of SP 800-67; and 256 bits, block and key, for the planned Rijndael-256.

stream-cipher.def: A symmetric cipher that encrypts data of any length by combining it, usually by exclusive OR (XOR), with a pseudorandom keystream generated from a key and a nonce, so no block alignment or padding is needed; ChaCha20 is the current standard example and RC4 the broken former one.
stream-cipher.context: A stream cipher turns a short key and a nonce into a long keystream and XORs (exclusive ORs) it over the data, byte for byte, so ciphertext is exactly as long as plaintext and there is no padding to attack. ChaCha20 (RFC 8439, Request for Comments, paired with the Poly1305 authenticator) is the modern member: constant-time in software and, in Google's 2014 measurements, three times faster than AES-GCM (Advanced Encryption Standard in Galois/Counter Mode) on devices without AES hardware acceleration, which is why mobile fleets favour it. Its infamous predecessor RC4 accumulated keystream biases until RFC 7465 banned it from TLS (Transport Layer Security) entirely in 2015. Two rules decide everything: a key and nonce pair must never be reused, or the XOR of two ciphertexts gives the XOR of two plaintexts, and the ciphertext must be authenticated, because flipping a ciphertext bit flips the same plaintext bit.
stream-cipher.depth:
What it is. A stream cipher generates a keystream from a key and a nonce and combines it with the plaintext, almost always by exclusive OR (XOR); decryption regenerates the same keystream and XORs it away. The idea descends from Gilbert Vernam's printing-telegraph cipher, described in a 1926 paper, and from Claude Shannon's Communication Theory of Secrecy Systems, which grew out of a confidential report dated 1 September 1946: Shannon defined perfect secrecy, showed that it needs at least as much key as message, and named the Vernam system, a never-repeating random key added to the message, as the system that achieves it. That is the one-time pad. A stream cipher gives up perfect secrecy for practicality: it stretches a short key into a keystream that is only computationally indistinguishable from random, so its security rests on the generator, and on never producing the same keystream twice. A stream cipher is not defined by its internals, and block ciphers become stream ciphers through their modes. NIST (National Institute of Standards and Technology) Special Publication (SP) 800-38A (Morris Dworkin, December 2001) specifies the output feedback (OFB) and counter (CTR) modes as running the block cipher to produce output blocks that are XORed with the plaintext, and CTR is the encryption half of AES-GCM (Advanced Encryption Standard in Galois/Counter Mode), so most encrypted traffic today is, in function, stream encryption.

The first rule: never reuse a keystream. If two messages are encrypted under the same key and nonce, XORing the two ciphertexts cancels the keystream and leaves the XOR of the two plaintexts, as RFC (Request for Comments) 8439 states for ChaCha20; from there, any known or guessable plaintext reveals the other. SP 800-38A puts the same point for OFB: a reused IV (initialization vector) plus one known plaintext block exposes the corresponding block of every other message encrypted with that IV, and in CTR all counters under a key must be distinct. The defence is bookkeeping, not mathematics: a counter that never wraps, a nonce space partitioned between senders that share a key, and keys rotated well before the counter runs out.

The second rule: authenticate the ciphertext. XOR is malleable: flipping a bit of the ciphertext flips exactly the same bit of the plaintext, and the receiver cannot tell unless something checks integrity. That is why modern stream ciphers ship as AEAD (authenticated encryption with associated data) constructions, ChaCha20 paired with Poly1305, and why a checksum is not enough. WEP (Wired Equivalent Privacy) showed both rules failing at once. Nikita Borisov, Ian Goldberg and David Wagner, at MobiCom in July 2001, described its encryption as the RC4 keystream of a per-packet IV v concatenated with the shared key k, with a CRC-32 (cyclic redundancy check) inside the encrypted payload for integrity. The IV field was only 24 bits wide: a busy access point sending 1,500-byte packets at an average of 5 Mbit/s would exhaust it in less than half a day, and an implementation choosing IVs at random could expect a collision after about 5,000 packets, a few minutes of traffic. Because CRC-32 is not a cryptographic authentication code, an attacker could also alter messages and fix the checksum without knowing the key. The same year Scott Fluhrer, Itsik Mantin and Adi Shamir published weaknesses in the key scheduling algorithm of RC4 itself, at Selected Areas in Cryptography 2001.

RC4 in TLS. RC4 lived on for years as the only stream cipher in Transport Layer Security (TLS), often preferred by servers. In March 2013 Nadhem AlFardan, Daniel Bernstein, Kenneth Paterson, Bertram Poettering and Jacob Schuldt showed that single-byte biases in the first 256 bytes of RC4 keystreams let an attacker recover plaintext that is sent repeatedly in the same position across many connections, reliably with about 2 to the 30th sessions and for some bytes with 2 to the 24th; their page also covers biases in TKIP (Temporal Key Integrity Protocol), the interim cipher of WPA (Wi-Fi Protected Access). RFC 7465 (Andrei Popov, February 2015) concluded that RC4 could no longer be seen as providing sufficient security, cited attacks then needing 2 to the 26th sessions or 13 times 2 to the 30th encryptions, and required that TLS clients and servers never negotiate RC4 cipher suites in any version.

ChaCha20. Daniel J. Bernstein published ChaCha, a variant of Salsa20, on 28 January 2008: ChaCha8, ChaCha12 and ChaCha20 modify the 8-, 12- and 20-round Salsa20 ciphers to improve diffusion per round while keeping their speed. RFC 8439 (Yoav Nir and Adam Langley, June 2018, obsoleting RFC 7539) fixes the version the Internet uses: a 256-bit key, a 96-bit nonce and a 32-bit block counter; each block of keystream is 64 bytes, produced by 20 rounds made only of 32-bit additions, XORs and fixed rotations, which can and should be implemented in constant time. The original ChaCha had a 64-bit nonce and a 64-bit counter; the layout of the IETF (Internet Engineering Task Force) limits one key and nonce pair to 2 to the 32nd blocks, 256 GB, and says that when several senders share a key, the nonce space must be partitioned so they never collide. Poly1305 takes a one-time key derived from ChaCha20 and produces a 16-byte tag over the ciphertext and the associated data.

Where it runs. RFC 7905 (June 2016, by Adam Langley and colleagues) defined ChaCha20-Poly1305 cipher suites for TLS and DTLS (Datagram Transport Layer Security), explicitly to replace RC4 and to answer concerns about the performance and ease of software implementation of AES-GCM. Google had already deployed it in Chrome, writing on 24 April 2014 that the suite ran three times faster than AES-GCM on devices without AES hardware acceleration, including most Android phones, and that ChaCha20 is immune to padding oracles such as Lucky13 and, by design, to timing attacks. TLS 1.3, specified since July 2026 in RFC 9846, makes TLS_AES_128_GCM_SHA256 mandatory and TLS_CHACHA20_POLY1305_SHA256 a SHOULD. WireGuard uses ChaCha20 with Poly1305 for all its data, and Secure Shell (SSH) offers it too. A sound cipher does not make a sound protocol, though: the Terrapin attack published by Fabian Bäumer, Marcus Brinkmann and Jörg Schwenk showed that a man in the middle could adjust SSH sequence numbers during the handshake and silently delete the first messages of the secure channel, including the extension negotiation, when the connection used ChaCha20-Poly1305 or CBC (cipher block chaining) with Encrypt-then-MAC; the fix, a strict key exchange mode, changed the protocol, not the cipher.

Its neighbours. A block cipher encrypts fixed-size blocks and needs a mode to handle real messages; in CTR or OFB mode it behaves as a stream cipher and inherits both rules above. AEAD is the interface that packages a stream-style cipher with its authenticator. The nonce or IV is the per-message input that keeps keystreams apart, and a salt is something else, an input to hashing and key derivation. Google's speed comparison was made on devices without AES hardware, and TLS 1.3 keeps both families on its list, AES-GCM as the mandatory suite and ChaCha20-Poly1305 as the recommended one.

Numbers worth remembering: 256-bit key, 96-bit nonce, 32-bit counter and 64-byte blocks in RFC 8439; 2 to the 32nd blocks, 256 GB, per key and nonce; a 16-byte Poly1305 tag; 24 bits of WEP IV and about 5,000 packets to a random collision; RFC 7465 of February 2015 for the end of RC4 in TLS; and three times AES-GCM's speed on phones without AES hardware, in Google's 2014 figures.

key-exchange.def: Key exchange is how two parties arrive at a shared secret key over a channel others can read, by key agreement, key transport or key encapsulation; it is the part of a cipher suite or protocol handshake that decides whether recorded traffic stays sealed.
key-exchange.context: Ephemeral Diffie-Hellman, today usually ECDHE (elliptic-curve Diffie-Hellman ephemeral) on X25519 or P-256, generates fresh keys for every connection and so gives forward secrecy; static RSA (Rivest-Shamir-Adleman) key transport does not, which is why TLS (Transport Layer Security) 1.3 removed it and made ephemeral exchange structural, and in July 2026 RFC (Request for Comments) 10015 deprecated RSA key exchange in TLS 1.2 as well. The post-quantum transition happens here too: the hybrid X25519MLKEM768 group runs a classical curve and ML-KEM (Module-Lattice-Based Key-Encapsulation Mechanism) side by side, so the session stays secret if either one holds.
key-exchange.depth:
Key exchange, or key establishment in NIST (National Institute of Standards and Technology) language, comes in three shapes. In key agreement both sides contribute and neither chooses the result: Diffie-Hellman over a finite field or an elliptic curve, the subject of NIST Special Publication (SP) 800-56A Revision 3 (April 2018), which also covers MQV (Menezes-Qu-Vanstone). In key transport one side picks the secret and encrypts it to the other's public key, as RSA (Rivest-Shamir-Adleman) did in older Transport Layer Security (TLS). In key encapsulation, the post-quantum pattern of FIPS (Federal Information Processing Standard) 203, one side encapsulates a fresh secret to the other's encapsulation key and both end with the same shared key. What key exchange does not do on its own is authenticate: an attacker in the middle of an unauthenticated exchange simply runs one exchange with each side, which is the man-in-the-middle case RFC (Request for Comments) 4251 describes for Secure Shell (SSH). Protocols therefore bind the exchange to an identity: TLS with a certificate signature, SSH with the host key, Internet Key Exchange version 2 (IKEv2) in its IKE_AUTH exchange.

The idea was published by Whitfield Diffie and Martin Hellman in New Directions in Cryptography, IEEE (Institute of Electrical and Electronics Engineers) Transactions on Information Theory, November 1976. They posed the public key distribution problem, two users who communicate back and forth until they arrive at a key in common, with an eavesdropper unable to compute it from what was overheard, and solved it with the difficulty of computing logarithms in a finite field: each side publishes alpha to the power of its secret, modulo a prime q, and both arrive at alpha to the product of the two secrets. They credited Ralph Merkle with an independent public key distribution system whose cost to an attacker grew only with the square of the cost to the users. In Britain, M. J. Williamson of GCHQ (Government Communications Headquarters) had found a remarkably similar classified algorithm in 1974, made public only on 16 December 1997.

Elliptic curves made the exchange small. X25519, specified in RFC 7748 (January 2016) over the prime 2 to the power 255 minus 19, gives about 128 bits of security with 32-byte public values; X448 gives about 224 bits with 56 bytes. TLS 1.3, first RFC 8446 (August 2018) and now RFC 9846 (July 2026), carries the exchange in two extensions: supported_groups lists what the client can do and key_share carries one or more ready-made public values in descending order of preference, so that a matching guess completes the exchange in the first round trip. If the server picks a group the client offered no share for, it must answer with a HelloRetryRequest and the handshake costs an extra round trip. The registry spans secp256r1, secp384r1, secp521r1, x25519, x448 and the finite-field groups ffdhe2048 to ffdhe8192; every implementation must support secp256r1 (NIST P-256) and should support X25519.

Forward secrecy is the reason ephemeral exchange won. With RSA key transport, the server's long-term private key decrypts the premaster secret of every session ever recorded, so stealing it later opens the archive. With ephemeral Diffie-Hellman, each connection's secret is computed from values that are discarded afterwards, and a later key theft gains nothing. RFC 9846 states the result plainly: static RSA and Diffie-Hellman cipher suites were removed, and all public-key key exchange in TLS 1.3 provides forward secrecy. The one exception is resumption with a pre-shared key in psk_ke mode, which sends no key_share at all; psk_dhe_ke adds a fresh exchange.

The same choice runs through the other protocols. For Secure Shell, RFC 9142 (January 2022) rates the old 1,024-bit diffie-hellman-group1-sha1 at about 80 bits and demotes it to SHOULD NOT, makes diffie-hellman-group14-sha256 the one MUST and recommends curve25519-sha256; OpenSSH went further, making the hybrid sntrup761x25519-sha512 its default in version 9.0 (8 April 2022) and mlkem768x25519-sha256 in 10.0 (9 April 2025). For IPsec (Internet Protocol Security), RFC 8247 (September 2017) requires Diffie-Hellman group 14 (2,048-bit) in IKEv2, recommends group 19 (256-bit elliptic curve), says groups 2 and 5 should not be used and forbids group 1 (768-bit); a group mismatch is a classic reason for a tunnel's first phase to fail.

What goes wrong is usually size and downgrade. Logjam, disclosed on 20 May 2015 by a team including David Adrian, Zakir Durumeric, J. Alex Halderman and Matthew Green, let a man in the middle downgrade TLS connections to 512-bit export-grade Diffie-Hellman; 8.4 per cent of the top million HTTPS (Hypertext Transfer Protocol Secure) domains were initially vulnerable. The same work showed that, because most of the cost of breaking a group is a precomputation that depends only on the prime, a nation-state could break a 1,024-bit group, and that the most widely shared 1,024-bit primes would expose 18 per cent of the top million HTTPS domains, 66 per cent of VPN (virtual private network) servers and 26 per cent of SSH servers. The fixes were to drop export suites, use groups of 2,048 bits or more and prefer elliptic-curve Diffie-Hellman. For TLS 1.2 and Datagram TLS 1.2 the standards went further in July 2026: RFC 10015 says clients must not offer, and servers must not select, cipher suites that use RSA key transport or finite-field Diffie-Hellman, ephemeral or static, and should not use static elliptic-curve Diffie-Hellman, and the registry of the Internet Assigned Numbers Authority (IANA) now marks all of them D, for discouraged.

The post-quantum transition happens here first, because of what NIST Interagency Report (IR) 8547 calls harvest now, decrypt later: traffic recorded today can be decrypted once a quantum computer can run Shor's algorithm, and IR 8547 (October 2026) deprecates finite-field and elliptic-curve Diffie-Hellman and RSA key establishment after 2030 and disallows them after 2035. FIPS 203 (13 August 2024) standardized ML-KEM (Module-Lattice-Based Key-Encapsulation Mechanism), built on the Module Learning with Errors problem, in three sizes, ML-KEM-512, ML-KEM-768 and ML-KEM-1024. The web did not swap one for the other but combined them: RFC 10024 (August 2026) defines X25519MLKEM768, codepoint 0x11EC and the only one of its three hybrids marked Recommended, along with SecP256r1MLKEM768 and SecP384r1MLKEM1024, each secure as long as either component holds. The price is size: the client share is 1,216 bytes (1,184 for ML-KEM and 32 for X25519) and the server's 1,120 bytes, against 32 for X25519 alone, which is why Chrome's engineers wrote in September 2024 that post-quantum shares are too big to send two guesses at once. Chrome 131 moved from the draft Kyber codepoint 0x6399 to 0x11EC, since the final ML-KEM is incompatible with the earlier Kyber.

Numbers worth remembering: 1976 for the paper, 32 bytes for an X25519 share, P-256 as the mandatory TLS 1.3 group, 2,048 bits as the floor for finite-field groups, 0x11EC and 1,216 bytes for X25519MLKEM768, and 2030 and 2035 for NIST's deprecation and disallowance of classical key establishment.

nist.def: The National Institute of Standards and Technology (NIST) is the US Department of Commerce agency, founded in 1901, whose cryptographic standards and security guidance, from AES to the post-quantum algorithms and the Cybersecurity Framework, serve as engineering baselines far beyond the US government.
nist.context: The National Institute of Standards and Technology (NIST) publishes FIPS (Federal Information Processing Standards) and the SP (Special Publication) 800 series that security engineering cites constantly: SP 800-52 Rev. 2 for TLS (Transport Layer Security) configuration, SP 800-38A for block cipher modes, SP 800-53 for security controls. It ran the open competitions that selected AES (Advanced Encryption Standard) and SHA-3, its post-quantum process produced ML-KEM and ML-DSA, and its Cybersecurity Framework (CSF) anchors countless compliance programmes. It is not a regulator: outside US federal systems adoption is voluntary, which makes its influence the more remarkable.
nist.depth:
What it is. The National Institute of Standards and Technology (NIST) was founded in 1901 as the National Bureau of Standards, created by Congress because the United States had a second-rate measurement infrastructure compared with the United Kingdom and Germany; it was renamed in 1988 and is part of the Department of Commerce. Security is one strand of a much wider mission in measurement science, but it is the strand most engineers meet, through the Computer Security Resource Center and its two publication families. FIPS (Federal Information Processing Standards) are standards, binding on US federal systems; SPs (Special Publications), above all the 800 series, are recommendations and guidelines. NIST's own Cybersecurity Framework FAQ states the point that matters to everyone else: NIST is not a regulatory agency, and most organizations use its work voluntarily. Publications written by NIST employees are not subject to US copyright, which helps explain why they spread.

Open competitions. NIST's most influential cryptographic work came from public contests. The AES (Advanced Encryption Standard) effort was announced on 2 January 1997 with a call for an unclassified, royalty-free block cipher with 128-bit blocks and 128, 192 and 256-bit keys; fifteen candidates were presented in August 1998, five finalists (MARS, RC6, Rijndael, Serpent and Twofish) survived the first round, and Rijndael was selected on 2 October 2000, becoming FIPS 197 on 26 November 2001. The SHA-3 competition ran from 2 November 2007 to 2 October 2012, when Keccak won; FIPS 202 followed in August 2015. The post-quantum process produced FIPS 203 (ML-KEM, a module-lattice key-encapsulation mechanism), FIPS 204 (ML-DSA, a lattice signature) and FIPS 205 (SLH-DSA, a stateless hash-based signature), all published on 13 August 2024, and NIST later selected HQC as an alternative to ML-KEM, with its own FIPS still in development.

The documents engineers actually use. SP 800-38A (December 2001) defines the block cipher modes of operation; SP 800-52 Rev. 2 (August 2019) is the federal guide to selecting and configuring TLS (Transport Layer Security); SP 800-53 Rev. 5 (September 2020) is the security and privacy control catalogue behind most federal and many private compliance regimes; FIPS 140-3 (22 March 2019) sets the requirements cryptographic modules are validated against, which is what a vendor means by a FIPS-validated mode. The Cybersecurity Framework (CSF) 2.0, published on 26 February 2024, is a taxonomy of outcomes rather than a process, organized in six functions, Govern, Identify, Protect, Detect, Respond and Recover, with Govern new in 2.0; it says what to achieve and leaves the how to other references. Executive Order 13800 made it mandatory for US federal agencies; elsewhere it is chosen, and widely.

The post-quantum deadline. NIST IR (Interagency Report) 8547, finalized in October 2026, sets the calendar every product roadmap now cites: quantum-vulnerable public-key algorithms, RSA, ECDSA (Elliptic Curve Digital Signature Algorithm), EdDSA, Diffie-Hellman and their relatives, are deprecated after 2030 and disallowed under NIST standards after 2035. Federal high-impact systems must move faster, adopting post-quantum key establishment by 31 December 2030 and post-quantum signatures by 31 December 2031 under Executive Order 14412 and OMB (Office of Management and Budget) Memorandum M-26-15, and agencies must support TLS 1.3 by 2 January 2030.

Standards versus recommendations. The distinction worth holding is between what NIST standardizes and what it recommends. A FIPS-approved algorithm is a requirement for US federal systems and a strong signal everywhere else; a special publication is guidance, and the good ones show the evidence behind it. Passwords are the clearest case of guidance changing on evidence. SP 800-63B (June 2017) said verifiers should not require memorized secrets to be changed periodically; its successor in SP 800-63-4 (July 2025) says they shall not, forbids composition rules, and sets a 15-character minimum for passwords used alone, citing breached-password research showing that users respond to such rules predictably, Password1! after password. That reversal of the rotation habit is a better argument for reading NIST's reasoning than for treating any publication as settled.

When trust broke. In September 2013 news reports raised doubts about Dual_EC_DRBG, a random bit generator in SP 800-90A. NIST recommended against it at once, removed it from Rev. 1 in April 2014, told vendors to reconfigure modules that used it by default, and opened a review of its own cryptographic standards process (NIST IR 7977). The episode is why practitioners still read the rationale behind a NIST recommendation, not just the result. NIST also runs the National Vulnerability Database, which enriches CVE (Common Vulnerabilities and Exposures) records and moved to risk-based prioritization in April 2026.

mitre.def: The MITRE Corporation: a US not-for-profit, founded in 1958, that operates federally funded research and development centres and, for security practitioners, is the home of the ATT&CK knowledge base, the CVE (Common Vulnerabilities and Exposures) Program and the CWE (Common Weakness Enumeration) list.
mitre.context: MITRE (the name is not an acronym) stewards the common vocabularies of security operations: the CVE (Common Vulnerabilities and Exposures) Program, which gives each publicly known vulnerability an identifier and which MITRE operates under contract to CISA (the US Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency); CWE (Common Weakness Enumeration), which classifies the weakness types behind them; CAPEC (Common Attack Pattern Enumeration and Classification), a catalogue of attack patterns; and the ATT&CK knowledge base of adversary tactics and techniques that detection engineering, threat intelligence and purple teams are organized around, with D3FEND as its defensive counterpart. Its technique numbers are cited everywhere, from SIEM (security information and event management) rules to vendor reports, and they change: ATT&CK is released twice a year, and in 2026 "Defense Evasion" was split into two tactics and several techniques were renumbered, so an identifier should be quoted with the version or date it was read.
mitre.depth:
The MITRE Corporation is a not-for-profit organization that runs research and development for the United States government. It began in 1958, sponsored by the US Air Force, to help architect SAGE (the Semi-Automatic Ground Environment), the Cold War air-defence network that MIT's Lincoln Laboratory had designed and that MIT no longer wished to manage. As Simson Garfinkel recounted in MIT Technology Review in 2023, James McCormack, MIT's vice president for industrial and government relations, and two Boston attorneys signed the certificate incorporating The MITRE Corporation on 17 July 1958; the working name had been Cape Cod Corporation. Where the name came from is unclear. The company's former website stated that MITRE is not an acronym but the name of the company, and that McCormack wanted a name that was meaningless and without connotations; the popular reading, MIT Research and Engineering, runs against the wish of MIT's leadership to distance the Institute from SAGE. Today MITRE says it operates six of the 42 federally funded research and development centres (FFRDCs) in existence, with laboratories in Bedford, Massachusetts and McLean, Virginia. Whitfield Diffie worked there from June 1965 to December 1969.

For network and security engineers MITRE matters for a narrower reason: it maintains the shared names the field uses for vulnerabilities, weaknesses and adversary behaviour. The oldest is CVE (Common Vulnerabilities and Exposures). David E. Mann and Steven M. Christey of MITRE described the idea in a white paper, Towards a Common Enumeration of Vulnerabilities, dated 8 January 1999 and presented at a workshop on vulnerability databases at Purdue University on 21 and 22 January. A working group, later the first 19-member CVE editorial board, created the original 321 entries, and the list was launched publicly in September 1999; by December 2000, 29 organizations had declared 43 products compatible. The problem it solved is still the one that matters: when two scanners, an intrusion detection system and a vendor advisory all describe the same flaw, a CVE identifier says that they are talking about the same thing. A CVE record names a vulnerability and nothing more; severity comes from CVSS (the Common Vulnerability Scoring System), maintained by FIRST, enrichment from NIST's NVD (National Vulnerability Database), and exploitation status from CISA's Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalogue, which is why the entries on those terms are separate.

The CVE Program's dependence on a single government contract became visible in April 2025. The contract between CISA (the Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency) and MITRE, worth 57.8 million US dollars, was due to expire on 16 April, and MITRE warned that it had no renewal in place; on the evening of 15 April CISA exercised an option extending it for 11 months, to 16 March 2026, as The Record reported. The scare came as volume was rising, from 28,818 CVE identifiers assigned in 2023 to 40,009 in 2024. In March 2026 CSO Online reported that CISA and MITRE had renegotiated the contract to remove the fixed expiry, with the program reportedly moved to a protected line of CISA's budget. Identifiers themselves are assigned by CVE Numbering Authorities (CNAs) authorized by the program, not only by MITRE: the records show F5 assigning CVE-2022-1388 for its own BIG-IP, Microsoft CVE-2015-1637 for Windows and Red Hat CVE-2015-0204 for OpenSSL.

Two companion catalogues sit underneath. CWE (Common Weakness Enumeration), which marks twenty years in 2026, is a community-developed list of software and hardware weaknesses: conditions that can lead to vulnerabilities, such as CWE-89 for SQL injection or CWE-787 for out-of-bounds write. It is sponsored by CISA and managed by the Homeland Security Systems Engineering and Development Institute, one of the centres MITRE operates, and its annual Top 25 ranks the weaknesses behind recent CVEs. CAPEC (Common Attack Pattern Enumeration and Classification), established under the Department of Homeland Security's software assurance initiative and first released in 2007, catalogues how attackers exploit those weaknesses. Read together, the chain runs from an attack pattern in CAPEC to a weakness in CWE, a specific vulnerability in CVE and a score in CVSS.

ATT&CK is the catalogue most engineers now meet first. MITRE started it in 2013 to document the tactics, techniques and procedures that advanced persistent threats used against Windows enterprise networks, for an internal research project called FMX on using endpoint telemetry to detect intruders after compromise. The first model dates from September 2013; the public release in May 2015 had 96 techniques under 9 tactics. It grew to macOS and Linux as ATT&CK for Enterprise in 2017, gained PRE-ATT&CK and Mobile the same year, Cloud in 2019 and ICS (industrial control systems) in 2020. Its grammar is simple: a tactic is the adversary's goal, the why, such as Credential Access; a technique is how the goal is reached, such as T1110 Brute Force; sub-techniques refine it; and groups, software and campaigns record who has been seen doing it. The FAQ calls it complementary to the Cyber Kill Chain, at a lower level of detail, with tactics that are unordered because real intrusions do not move in a straight line. MITRE's design paper lists the uses that made it popular: adversary emulation, red teaming, building behavioural analytics and assessing defensive gaps, which is what a purple team does when it walks a list of techniques and checks which ones the SOC (security operations centre) can see.

ATT&CK is versioned and it moves. It is released twice a year; version 20 came out on 13 October 2026, and as read on 12 November 2026 Enterprise ATT&CK holds 15 tactics, 227 techniques, 479 sub-techniques, 178 groups, 842 pieces of software, 57 campaigns and 44 mitigations. Version 19, on 28 April 2026, split the old "Defense Evasion" tactic into Stealth, which keeps the identifier TA0005, and "Defense Impairment", TA0112, and moved techniques accordingly: T1656 Impersonation now redirects to T1684.001, Social Engineering: Impersonation, and T1562.008 to T1685.002. Detection content, threat reports and SIEM (security information and event management) rules written before then still carry the old numbers. The defensive mirror is D3FEND, a knowledge graph of countermeasures built in part from more than 500 countermeasure patents filed between 2001 and 2018 and mapped onto offensive techniques, funded by the National Security Agency's Cybersecurity Directorate.

The common pitfalls are about attribution and precision. MITRE is an organization, ATT&CK one of its products and CVE a program it operates for CISA, and the three are often blurred. A CVE identifier is not a severity, a CWE identifier is not a vulnerability, and an ATT&CK technique number is not stable across versions, so reports should cite the version or the date read. The numbers worth keeping are 1958 for the company, September 1999 and 321 entries for CVE, 2007 for CAPEC, 2013 and May 2015 for ATT&CK, and version 20 with 15 Enterprise tactics as of November 2026.

ietf.def: The Internet Engineering Task Force (IETF) is the open, membership-free standards body that develops the internet's core protocols, such as the Transmission Control Protocol (TCP) and Transport Layer Security (TLS), and publishes them as Requests for Comments (RFCs) after work in public groups that decide by rough consensus, not by vote.
ietf.context: The Internet Engineering Task Force (IETF) works by rough consensus and running code: open working groups, organized into areas and steered by the Internet Engineering Steering Group (IESG), turn Internet-Drafts into Requests for Comments (RFCs), which is where the Transmission Control Protocol (TCP), the Hypertext Transfer Protocol (HTTP), Transport Layer Security (TLS), the Domain Name System (DNS) and most of what an engineer decodes in a capture are specified. There is no membership and no membership fee; anyone can join a working group's mailing list, and the only charge is meeting registration. It works beside the Internet Assigned Numbers Authority (IANA), which keeps the registries its documents create, and the RFC Editor, which publishes them.
ietf.depth:
What it is, and what it is not. The introduction published by the Internet Engineering Task Force (IETF) dates it to 1986; Request for Comments (RFC) 8700 puts the first meeting in January of that year. It calls itself the premier standards development organization for the internet, makes voluntary standards, and adds that in no way does the IETF control, or even patrol, the internet. Its mission statement, RFC 3935 (October 2004, Harald Alvestrand), a Best Current Practice (BCP 95), sets the goal as making the internet work better, through high-quality, relevant documents: protocol standards, best current practices and informational documents. The same RFC lists five cardinal principles: an open process, technical competence, a volunteer core, rough consensus and running code, and protocol ownership, which means that the IETF takes responsibility for every aspect of a protocol it owns and does not try to control protocols it does not.

Who takes part. There is no membership. Anyone participates by joining a working group mailing list or registering for a meeting, every participant is a volunteer acting as an individual, including those paid to be there, and the IETF counts over 7,000 active participants in any one year. The only fee is meeting registration, with waivers so that it does not become a barrier. Participation is not free of obligations: the Note Well, which participants are regularly shown, reminds them that by taking part they agree to the IETF's processes, that anyone aware of a patent on a contribution owned or controlled by them, their employer or sponsor must disclose it or stay out of the discussion (RFC 8179, BCP 79), and that contributions are licensed under RFC 5378 (BCP 78).

How it is organized. Working groups, each with a charter and a mailing list that carries all official work, sit in areas managed by one or two Area Directors (ADs); RFC 2418 (BCP 25, September 1998) counted eight areas, and the Datatracker now lists seven: Applications and Real-Time (ART), General (GEN), Internet (INT), Operations and Management (OPS), Routing (RTG), Security (SEC) and Web and Internet Transport (WIT). The ADs and the IETF Chair form the Internet Engineering Steering Group (IESG), which manages the standards process and gives final approval to Internet Standards. ADs serve two-year terms and are chosen by the Nominating Committee (NomCom) under RFC 8713 (BCP 10, February 2020): a chair, two liaisons, an advisor and 10 voting volunteers picked at random from a pool, with no more than two sharing a primary affiliation. Under RFC 8711 (BCP 101, February 2020), the IETF Administration LLC, a disregarded limited liability company (LLC) of the Internet Society, is the corporate legal home of the IETF, the Internet Architecture Board (IAB) and the Internet Research Task Force (IRTF) and funds the RFC Editor.

How a document moves. Anyone may write an Internet-Draft on any topic, and a working group may adopt it. A draft expires 185 days after it is posted unless a new version replaces it or it is in a protected state such as IESG processing. A finished document needs IESG approval and the consensus of the IETF as a whole before the RFC Editor edits it and gives it a number. Promotion beyond Proposed Standard follows RFC 6410: at least two independent interoperating implementations with widespread deployment, no errata that would break interoperation, and an IETF-wide Last Call of at least four weeks.

Rough consensus. RFC 7282 (June 2014, Pete Resnick) opens with the aphorism almost every participant knows, from Dave Clark's plenary presentation at the twenty-fourth IETF in July 1992: we reject kings, presidents and voting; we believe in rough consensus and running code. Full consensus is not required because it would let one intransigent person who keeps saying no stop the process cold. Instead a chair may declare rough consensus once an objection has been truly considered and the group has made an informed decision that it has been answered or is not a technical problem serious enough to stop work. Humming replaces a show of hands so that nobody counts. The section titles carry the method: lack of disagreement is more important than agreement; rough consensus is achieved when all issues are addressed, but not necessarily accommodated; and humming should be the start of a conversation, not the end.

Running code and the meetings. The other half of the motto is the requirement for implementations before promotion, inherited from RFC 2026's demand for two independent and interoperable implementations from different code bases. Most work happens on mailing lists, but there are three week-long working meetings a year, with hackathons and no exposition hall, averaging 1,000 to 1,500 people onsite and more than 600 remotely. IETF 126 in Vienna in July 2026 drew 1,224 participants onsite and 555 online, and IETF 127 runs in San Francisco from 14 to 20 November 2026.

What it has produced, and at what status. The Transmission Control Protocol (TCP) is RFC 9293 (August 2022), an Internet Standard as STD 7, and Hypertext Transfer Protocol (HTTP) semantics are RFC 9110 (June 2022), STD 97. Much of what carries traffic today is still a Proposed Standard: QUIC is RFC 9000 (May 2021), HTTP/3 is RFC 9114 (June 2022), and Transport Layer Security (TLS) 1.3, first RFC 8446 in August 2018, was respecified as RFC 9846 in July 2026, which obsoletes it. That is not a warning about maturity; RFC 6410 itself records that the vast majority of standards-track documents never advance, so Proposed Standard is where most of the deployed internet lives.

Neighbours. The IETF shares its legal home and its publication channel with two siblings: the IRTF, which works on longer-term research, and the IAB, which gives long-range technical direction; both publish RFCs through their own streams, which the IETF does not generally review. The Internet Assigned Numbers Authority (IANA) keeps the protocol registries that IETF documents create through their IANA Considerations sections, and the RFC Production Center edits and publishes. Outside that family, the link layers beneath the Internet Protocol (IP) are largely the work of the 802 committee of the Institute of Electrical and Electronics Engineers (IEEE).

Common misreadings. An Internet-Draft, however widely deployed, is not an IETF standard, and the IETF asks that drafts be cited only as work in progress. An Informational RFC describing a vendor protocol does not represent IETF consensus: RFC 2026 says an Informational specification does not represent an internet community consensus or recommendation. A hum is not a vote, and under RFC 2026 a working group decision can be disputed, first with the chairs, then with the Area Director. Numbers worth keeping: 1986 for the first meeting, 185 days for a draft, four weeks for the Last Call that makes an Internet Standard, two independent implementations, seven areas, and BCP 9 for the process itself.

cloud-security-alliance.def: The industry body that defines how cloud security is assessed and attested.
cloud-security-alliance.context: CSA's Cloud Controls Matrix (CCM) is the de facto control framework for cloud providers, and the STAR registry publishes provider self-assessments and certifications against it - the acronym you meet on every vendor trust-center page. It also runs the CCSK certificate and the shared-responsibility research that SASE (secure access service edge) and zero-trust vendor conversations lean on.

sans.def: The best-known commercial training institute in security operations, and home of the GIAC certifications and the Internet Storm Center.
sans.context: SANS courses and their GIAC exams are the operational counterpart to vendor certifications: incident response, forensics, detection, offensive skills. Its Internet Storm Center is a long-running community sensor and daily-diary institution, and its free resources (posters, cheat sheets, reading room) circulate far beyond paying students.

isc2.def: The certification body behind the CISSP - the credential most often gatekeeping senior security roles.
isc2.context: ISC2 (formerly styled (ISC)², rebranded in 2023) maintains the CISSP, CCSP for cloud, and a members' code of ethics with real teeth: certified members can be stripped for violations. Where SANS/GIAC test hands-on depth, ISC2 credentials test breadth of the common body of knowledge - which is exactly why hiring pipelines lean on them.

eff.def: The nonprofit defending civil liberties in the digital world, and the maker of Certbot.
eff.context: Founded in 1990, the Electronic Frontier Foundation litigates, lobbies, and builds: it was a founding partner of the effort that became Let's Encrypt, and it ships Certbot, the client that made free certificates operationally trivial. Its research and scorecards (device privacy, data practices) are standing references in privacy engineering.
eff.depth:
The EFF (Electronic Frontier Foundation) was founded in July 1990 because, in its own account, none of the existing civil-liberties groups understood the technology well enough to see what the Secret Service raids of that spring meant. The raids were chasing the E911 (Enhanced 911) document, and one of them, on 1 March 1990, took all the electronic equipment and an upcoming game book from Steve Jackson Games, an Austin publisher that was never charged. Jackson laid off nearly half his staff, and when the computers came back every message on the company's bulletin board had been opened and deleted. Mitch Kapor, John Perry Barlow and John Gilmore, with help from Steve Wozniak, unveiled the organization and its first case on the same day: a lawsuit for the publisher and its bulletin-board users against the Secret Service. Barlow's own history, written that November, dates the announcement to 10 July 1990 at the National Press Club in Washington and records that one of the foundation's first acts was a grant of 275,000 dollars to Computer Professionals for Social Responsibility for work on computing and civil liberties.

That case produced the first court holding that electronic mail deserves at least as much protection as a telephone call; more than three years after the raid a federal court awarded the publisher damages and legal fees. The next landmark is one every open-source cryptographer relies on: in Bernstein v. Department of Justice, filed in 1995, the courts held that source code is speech protected by the First Amendment and that rules requiring a licence to publish it were unconstitutional. Daniel Bernstein, then a graduate student at Berkeley, wanted to publish an encryption algorithm he called Snuffle, a paper about it and its source code. Under the Arms Export Control Act and the International Traffic in Arms Regulations (ITAR) he would have had to submit the work for review, register as an arms dealer and obtain a licence. After four years and one change of regulation the Court of Appeals for the Ninth Circuit ruled for him, and the government rewrote its export rules.

The foundation also answered a technical question with hardware: the DES (Data Encryption Standard) Cracker, whose design John Gilmore led, showed publicly that the cipher the government still called secure could be broken in about a week. The measured result was better than that. The machine, the first unclassified hardware built to search the 56-bit key space, cost less than 250,000 dollars and on 17 July 1998 won RSA Laboratories' DES Challenge II in under three days, where the previous record, set by tens of thousands of networked computers, was 39 days. On 19 January 1999, working with the Distributed.Net network of nearly 100,000 personal computers, it won DES Challenge III in 22 hours and 15 minutes, testing 245 billion keys per second when the key turned up. The design, including chip and software source code, was published as a book, Cracking DES.

Surveillance became the long case. In Hepting v. AT&T, filed on 31 January 2006, the foundation sued the carrier on behalf of its customers, with evidence from a former AT&T technician, Mark Klein, that copies of internet traffic were being routed to a secret room in San Francisco controlled by the National Security Agency (NSA). Congress answered in 2008 with the FISA Amendments Act, amending the Foreign Intelligence Surveillance Act (FISA) to give the carriers retroactive immunity; the case was dismissed in June 2009 and the Supreme Court declined to hear it in October 2012. The follow-on case, Jewel v. NSA, filed in 2008 against the agencies themselves, challenged the bulk collection of telephone records, the collection of internet metadata and the interception at backbone facilities later known as Upstream. It lasted until June 2022, when the Supreme Court refused to take it, leaving the programmes untested on the merits because of state secrets.

The rhetoric of the early years has its own monument. On 8 February 1996, from Davos, Barlow published A Declaration of the Independence of Cyberspace, addressed to the governments of the industrial world, those weary giants of flesh and steel, which the foundation still hosts. It is a period piece and is worth reading as one; the organization's practice was always more concrete than its founding prose.

The through-line is that the people writing rules about a technology should understand it, and that where they do not, the remedy is evidence: a court record, a published paper, a working machine. In later decades the same instinct turned into software, Certbot among it, which made encrypting a web server routine and no longer a project. The path is documented. Peter Eckersley of the EFF and the researcher Alex Halderman met at the RSA Conference in 2012 and began designing automated certificate issuance, including the first drafts of what became the Automatic Certificate Management Environment (ACME) protocol. They joined a parallel effort at Mozilla, and on 18 November 2014 Let's Encrypt was announced by Mozilla, Cisco, Akamai, the EFF, IdenTrust and researchers at the University of Michigan, working through the Internet Security Research Group (ISRG). It began service in 2015. Eckersley's team wrote the original client, which on 12 May 2016 moved from ISRG to the EFF under the name Certbot.

Certbot itself is, in its makers' words, a free, open source tool for automatically using Let's Encrypt certificates on manually administered websites to enable HTTPS (Hypertext Transfer Protocol Secure). It runs from the command line of the web server, proves control of the domain through ACME, installs the certificate and keeps renewing it. Its companion, the HTTPS Everywhere browser extension, has been retired because it won: major browsers now have an HTTPS-only mode, and by 2021 about 90 per cent of web page visits were already encrypted.

The research side produces instruments as well as reports. Panopticlick, launched in 2010, measured how unique a browser's configuration is and published the result at the Privacy Enhancing Technologies Symposium, which made browser fingerprinting a standard topic; it gained tracker-blocker tests in 2015 and was relaunched in 2020 as Cover Your Tracks. Privacy Badger is a browser extension that blocks trackers by observing their behaviour, with no curated list, and sends the Global Privacy Control and Do Not Track signals. Surveillance Self-Defense is the foundation's guide to protecting communications, and the Atlas of Surveillance and Street Level Surveillance sites stand beside it in the foundation's list of tools. The Who Has Your Back reports grade companies against published criteria; the 2019 edition assessed sixteen companies on six points of content moderation policy, and only Reddit earned all six.

What it is now. The EFF is a donor-funded nonprofit under section 501(c)(3) of the United States tax code, based in San Francisco, which describes its methods as impact litigation, policy analysis, grassroots activism and technology development. Its issue list in 2026 runs from free speech, privacy and security to transparency, international work, creativity and innovation, and artificial intelligence. Nicole Ozer has been its executive director since June 2026; she previously founded and led the Technology and Civil Liberties Program at the American Civil Liberties Union (ACLU) of Northern California.

For a network or security engineer the dates and numbers worth keeping are these: 10 July 1990 for the founding; 1995 to 1999 for Bernstein and the principle that code is speech; 17 July 1998 and under three days for 56-bit DES, at a cost under 250,000 dollars; 31 January 2006 for Hepting and the secret room in San Francisco; 18 November 2014 for Let's Encrypt; and 12 May 2016 for Certbot.

ieee.def: The Institute of Electrical and Electronics Engineers (IEEE) is the professional association, formed in 1963, whose standards arm publishes the 802 family: Ethernet (802.3), Wi-Fi (802.11) and bridging, virtual local area networks (VLANs) and port access control (802.1), the link layers almost every Internet Protocol (IP) network runs on.
ieee.context: The Institute of Electrical and Electronics Engineers (IEEE) writes its networking standards through the IEEE 802 LAN/MAN Standards Committee (LMSC), named for local and metropolitan area networks, whose working groups own the lower two layers: 802.3 for Ethernet, 802.11 for wireless LANs, 802.1 for bridging, virtual LANs (VLANs) and port authentication, 802.15 for wireless personal area networks. The numbering is a precise vocabulary: an uppercase letter after the group number marks a standalone standard, lowercase letters an amendment, and a year the edition, so 802.1Q-2022 and 802.11be-2024 each name one exact document. Unlike Requests for Comments (RFCs), IEEE standards are sold, though the 802 family becomes free to download six months after publication.
ieee.depth:
What it is. The Institute of Electrical and Electronics Engineers (IEEE) is a professional association, not a government agency or a regulator, and it calls itself the world's largest technical professional organization; its standards arm, the IEEE Standards Association (IEEE SA), cites more than 417,000 members and standards participants in more than 160 countries. Its standards are voluntary: they matter because vendors implement them and buyers ask for them. Networking engineers meet IEEE almost entirely through one committee, 802, but the same organization publishes standards on power, safety, instrumentation and much else.

Where it came from. According to the IEEE History Center, the American Institute of Electrical Engineers (AIEE) was formed in New York in the spring of 1884, held its first technical meeting in Philadelphia that October, and drew its early leaders from telegraphy, power and the telephone: its founding president was Norvin Green of Western Union, and Thomas Edison and Alexander Graham Bell were among the early figures. Radio brought a second society in 1912, the Institute of Radio Engineers (IRE), which grew faster from the 1940s and was the larger of the two by 1957. On 1 January 1963 they merged into the IEEE, which started with 150,000 members, 140,000 of them in the United States.

How 802 began. The IEEE milestone that commemorates the committee tells the story. Maris Graube, at Tektronix, found the IEEE-488 instrument bus, limited to 20 metres of cable, too short to automate more than one room of a laboratory and, on 29 August 1979, submitted a Project Authorization Request (PAR) for a local network for computer interconnection. An evening meeting at the COMPCON conference in San Francisco on 28 February 1980 drew at least 79 people, and on 13 March 1980 the IEEE Standards Board approved the PAR as IEEE Standard Project No. 802, sponsored by the Computer Society. The goal in Graube's view was about 100 devices at roughly one megabit per second over a kilometre of cable. Consensus on one technology proved impossible: Digital Equipment Corporation, Intel and Xerox (DIX) had their Ethernet Blue Book, IBM would not back a standard that was not its own, and the committee split the work into CSMA/CD (carrier sense multiple access with collision detection, 802.3), token bus (802.4) and token ring (802.5), with logical link control (802.2) above them and bridging (802.1) beside. The three access standards were published in 1985 and later adopted by ISO/IEC JTC 1 as the ISO/IEC 8802 series. The milestone names the four groups that proved transformative by 1999: 802.1, 802.3, 802.11 and 802.15.

The committee today. The home page of the IEEE 802 LAN/MAN Standards Committee (LMSC) lists five working groups, 802.1 (Higher Layer LAN Protocols), 802.3 (Ethernet), 802.11 (Wireless LAN), 802.15 (Wireless Specialty Networks) and 802.19 (Wireless Coexistence), and two technical advisory groups, 802.18 (Radio Regulatory) and 802.24 (Vertical Applications), and keeps a separate list of hibernating and disbanded groups. A standard starts as a PAR, is drafted by a working group, and is approved through a Standards Association ballot (formerly called a Sponsor ballot) by a ballot pool of those who sign up to vote. The groups meet in plenary and interim sessions; the 802.1 agendas for the November 2026 plenary are for Bangkok.
