Reading the numbers. The 802.1 working group publishes the grammar. Uppercase letters after 802.1 identify standalone standards and lowercase letters identify amendments, formerly called supplements, and no two projects may differ only in case. In the longer forms the uppercase letters name the standard being amended and the lowercase pair the project, so 802.1Qat amends 802.1Q, while 802.1Q-REV marks a revision, a change too extensive for an amendment. A year suffix names the edition, and a P prefix (P802.3dj) marks a project whose drafts are not yet a standard. The current editions include IEEE Std 802.3-2022, 802.1Q-2022, 802.1X-2020 for port-based network access control and 802.1AE-2018 for Media Access Control (MAC) Security, each with a revision in progress, and 802.11-2024, published on 28 April 2025. The 802.1 group is also where bridging and the spanning tree protocol of 802.1D come from. Amendments follow on: 802.11be-2024, which the 802.11 group itself notes is known in the industry as Wi-Fi 7, was published on 22 July 2025, and 802.11bi-2026 on 23 October 2026. The label is the precise way to ask a question: a switch that supports 802.1Q and a switch that supports virtual local area networks (VLANs) are different claims, and a product that ships against a P802.11 draft has implemented a document that can still change.

Ethernet keeps moving. The 802.3 working group's active list in November 2026 includes P802.3dj for 200 Gb/s, 400 Gb/s, 800 Gb/s and 1.6 Tb/s Ethernet, P802.3dv for 400 Gb/s per lane signalling, automotive and single-pair Power over Ethernet projects, the eighteenth maintenance revision of 802.3-2022 and an ad hoc assessing Ethernet for artificial intelligence (AI) workloads. The milestone's summary of the committee's achievement is that its groups wrote the specifications accepted worldwide as defining MAC and the physical layers in wired and wireless equipment.

The registries. IEEE also hands out identifiers. Its Registration Authority, under the IEEE SA Board of Governors, assigns an Organizationally Unique Identifier (OUI) with every MA-L (MAC Address Block Large) assignment, together with large blocks of EUI-48 and EUI-64 values usable as MAC addresses, Bluetooth device addresses or Ethernet addresses; MA-M and MA-S assignments give smaller blocks, the latter under a 36-bit OUI-36; and a Company ID (CID) is a 24-bit identifier that cannot generate EUI-48 values. The same authority runs the EtherType registry, the value that tells a receiver how to interpret the data field of an Ethernet frame, and publishes the full public listings that every OUI lookup uses.

Access and cost. Requests for Comments (RFCs) are free from the day they appear; IEEE standards are sold. The exception that matters to network engineers is the Get IEEE 802 programme, whose guidelines were signed on 3 February 2016: individual current 802 standards become free to the public six months after publication, while drafts, editions and inactive standards are excluded, IEEE remains the sole copyright holder and the terms of use forbid redistribution. Drafts are available to voting members of the working group or for purchase.

Neighbours and misreadings. The IEEE 802 committee defines the MAC and physical layers; the Internet Engineering Task Force (IETF) defines the Internet Protocol (IP) and what runs above it, so a VLAN tag is an IEEE matter and the IP packet it carries is an IETF one. The Wi-Fi Alliance is a separate international trade association that drives the adoption of 802.11-based technology and owns the Wi-Fi trademark; Wi-Fi 7 is the industry's name, 802.11be is the standard. Amendments are listed in the front matter of the base standard's current revision, so an amendment label tells you when a feature arrived and the base standard tells you where it lives now. The dates worth keeping: 1884, 1912 and 1963 for the institution; 13 March 1980 for Project 802; 1985 for the first 802.3 standard; six months before an 802 standard becomes free.

eia-tia.def: The standards lineage behind structured cabling - the TIA-568 family that defines the categories, connectors, and distances of every wiring closet.
eia-tia.context: The Telecommunications Industry Association (successor to the EIA side of the old EIA/TIA partnership) publishes ANSI/TIA-568 and its siblings: the cable category definitions (Cat 5e, 6, 6A, 8), the T568A/T568B pinouts, channel lengths, and the data-center and pathways standards. When a datasheet says 'meets Cat 6A', this is whose test limits it means.
eia-tia.depth:
EIA/TIA standards govern structured cabling: what a cable must be capable of, how far it may run, how outlets and patch panels are labelled, and how a telecommunications room is laid out. They are the reason a building's cabling is predictable to someone who did not install it.

The one people meet first is the pin assignment, and the useful fact is that T568A and T568B are electrically equivalent as long as both ends match. The standards also carry the distance limits that get ignored, most often the hundred-metre channel for copper, and a link that works at eighty metres and fails at a hundred and twenty is not a mystery, it is the specification being enforced by physics.

defcon.def: DEF CON is the hacker convention Jeff Moss started in Las Vegas in June 1993 as a farewell party for a bulletin board network, now held every summer for tens of thousands of people and often called the world's largest hacker conference: cash at the door, volunteer Goons, themed villages, contests, and the original capture-the-flag (CTF) competition.
defcon.context: Founded by Jeff Moss (The Dark Tangent), DEF CON grew from a send-off for a Canadian hacking network into the annual gathering of the field: villages for every specialty, from lockpicking and car hacking to voting machines and aerospace; the flagship capture-the-flag (CTF) contest, run since 1996; badges that are puzzles and hardware projects in themselves; and the red-shirted volunteer Goons who keep a crowd of some 25,000 to 30,000 functioning. Talks regularly make world news, and the culture around them, the spot the fed contest, the Wall of Sheep, the Black Badge, is half the institution. Black Hat, also created by Moss, runs in the days just before it, which is why the two together are called hacker summer camp.
defcon.depth:
Where it came from. In Moss's own account on the DEF CON site, the event began in 1993 as a closing party for Platinum Net, a hacking network built on the FidoNet protocol and run out of Canada, for which his bulletin board system was the main United States hub; the network's organizer was moving away with his family and left early, so Moss invited the members of the other networks his board belonged to, and everyone on the #hack chat channel, instead. DEF CON 1 ran from 9 to 11 June 1993 at the Sands Hotel and Casino, with speakers including Dan Farmer and the Arizona prosecutor Gail Thackeray, and about a hundred people came; the second year nearly doubled that. The name was chosen to avoid any season (there were already SummerCon, HoHoCon and PumpCon): DEF are the letters on the 3 key of a telephone, which phone phreaks would notice, DEF CON is military shorthand for a defence readiness condition, and in the film WarGames the Seattle teenager David Lightman chooses Las Vegas as a target, while Moss lived in Seattle and was planning a convention in Vegas.

How it grew. The archive shows the conference moving through ever larger venues: the Alexis Park from 1999 to 2005, the Riviera to 2010, the Rio to 2014, then the Paris and Bally's, Caesars Palace and Caesars Forum. Attendance was estimated at about 30,000 at DEF CON 27 in 2019. In 2020 the in-person event was cancelled and replaced by an online DEF CON Safe Mode on the same dates, and DEF CON 29 in 2021 returned with a vaccination requirement. In February 2024 Caesars Entertainment cancelled its contract and the conference moved to the Las Vegas Convention Center, where DEF CON 34 took place from 6 to 9 August 2026 in the West Hall; DEF CON 35 is set for 5 to 8 August 2027, under the theme The Age of Experimentation. Registration still works the old way alongside online pre-registration: for DEF CON 34 the cash line at the door, known as LineCon, charged 520 dollars, and pre-registrants were guaranteed a human badge even if the run sold out.

How it runs. The DEF CON frequently asked questions (FAQ) page describes the Goons as the staff, with roles from safety and speaker coordination to the vendor area and network operations, and explains that new Goons are typically inducted by friends of existing ones because every position involves trust; the Goons page says plainly that without them DEF CON would not happen. Around the main talk tracks sit villages, dedicated spaces for one subject with their own talks, labs and contests (aerospace, car hacking, the Internet of Things, social engineering, voting machines and many more), and dozens of contests from Hacker Jeopardy to scavenger hunts. The highest prize is the Black Badge, which gives its holder free entry for life; in 2016 one went to Mayhem, the autonomous system from ForAllSecure that won the Cyber Grand Challenge of the Defense Advanced Research Projects Agency (DARPA) at DEF CON 24, the first non-human holder. Badges themselves are electronic or not, change every year and usually hide a puzzle; the DEF CON 34 badge was built around the Baochip-1x, a chip of open-source silicon. The Wall of Sheep, which first appeared in 2002 and projects credentials it captures in the clear on the conference network, now runs the Packet Hacking Village, and the FAQ still lists spot the fed among the activities.

The capture-the-flag contest. The DEF CON capture-the-flag (CTF) contest has run every year since DEF CON 4 in 1996 and is one of the few major contests in the attack and defence format, in which each team must keep its own services running while exploiting everyone else's. A qualifying round was introduced in 2003 as the game grew, and the organization has passed through successive volunteer groups, from the Goons themselves to Kenshoto, DDTEK, the Legitimate Business Syndicate, the Order of the Overflow and, since 2022, the Nautilus Institute. Its inventions travel: in 2017 the Legitimate Business Syndicate built an entire processor architecture, cLEMENCy, with nine-bit bytes, to break every team's tools at once, and the format has been copied by other conferences, universities and military exercises. The team Maple Mallard Magistrates won each final from 2022 to 2025.

Disclosure and the law. DEF CON is where research that vendors would prefer to keep private gets presented, and its history includes arrests, injunctions and talks pulled under legal pressure. On 10 July 1999 the Cult of the Dead Cow released Back Orifice 2000 from its stage. On 16 July 2001, the day after DEF CON 9, the Russian programmer Dmitry Sklyarov was arrested in Las Vegas under the anti-circumvention provisions of the United States Digital Millennium Copyright Act (DMCA) for work on software that removed the protection from Adobe's e-book format; he was allowed home in December 2001, and a jury acquitted his employer, ElcomSoft, on 16 December 2002. In 2008 the Massachusetts Bay Transportation Authority (MBTA) obtained an order stopping three Massachusetts Institute of Technology (MIT) students from presenting their research on Boston's fare cards, arguing under the Computer Fraud and Abuse Act (CFAA); after the case was dismissed, the authority and the students agreed in December 2008 to work together on the system's security. The best-known suppressed talk of that era, Michael Lynn's on Cisco routers in 2005, was in fact at Black Hat. The lesson the community drew is that a venue willing to platform uncomfortable findings changes what researchers will work on, because the alternative to public disclosure is not silence but a private market.

The federal relationship. Agents from the Federal Bureau of Investigation (FBI), the Department of Defense, the Postal Inspection Service and the Department of Homeland Security attend as a matter of routine, and agencies recruit in the same rooms where people demonstrate breaking federal systems. In 2012 the director of the National Security Agency, General Keith Alexander, gave the keynote; in July 2013, after the surveillance disclosures, Moss asked federal agencies for the first time to stay away that year. In 2017 the Voting Machine Village breached dozens of voting machines in public and published a report on United States election equipment. That uneasy coexistence took decades to negotiate, and it is the mechanism by which offensive knowledge reaches defensive practice at all.

Beyond Las Vegas. DEF CON's first event outside the United States was DEF CON China Beta in Beijing in May 2018. In 2025 it offered programming in Bahrain, and on 28 to 30 April 2026 it held the first DEF CON Singapore at Marina Bay Sands; DEF CON Singapore 2 is announced for 4 to 6 March 2027 at the same venue, directly after Black Hat's Singapore event, while a DEF CON Middle East planned for Bahrain was postponed in July 2026 because of the security situation in the region. Year round, DEF CON Groups meet locally, numbered after telephone area codes in the United States. For visitors from Latin America the August week is also a meeting point: the Brazilian community's own BRHueCon was held in Las Vegas on 3 August 2026, the Monday before DEF CON 34.

How to read it. DEF CON is the community institution and Black Hat its commercial sibling, the same research presented once to people whose employers need an invoice and once to people who pay in cash. Its scale now dwarfs the origin story, and much of its value is in the hallways and villages rather than on the main stages: it is where careers start, where research areas such as car and medical device hacking were born in public, and where regional events from Buenos Aires to São Paulo took their models, from the volunteer staff to the CTF. The numbers worth remembering are 1993 for the first, about 100 people then and about 30,000 at the peak before the pandemic, 1996 for the first CTF, and the second week of August in Las Vegas.

black-hat.def: Black Hat is the commercial security conference Jeff Moss founded in Las Vegas in 1997 and Informa owns today: peer-reviewed research Briefings, paid Trainings, the Arsenal of open-source tool demonstrations and a Business Hall, held in the days before DEF CON, with further editions in Europe, Asia, India, the Middle East and Africa, and Canada.
black-hat.context: Moss started Black Hat in 1997 as the counterpart of DEF CON that a company could send its engineers to, and Black Hat USA still anchors the Las Vegas week the community calls hacker summer camp. Its Briefings are one of the field's main venues for disclosing vulnerability research, and its Business Hall is where the vendor industry meets that research; the 2026 edition counted more than 23,000 verified attendees. Owned since 2005 by CMP Media and its successors, and now part of Informa, it runs a calendar of regional events from Toronto to Riyadh and, since September 2026, the Brazilian Mind The Sec has joined its family. It remains the conference companies budget for when DEF CON reads as too informal.
black-hat.depth:
Origin. The first Black Hat was held from 7 to 10 July 1997 in Las Vegas, immediately before DEF CON 5, presented by DEF CON Communications and Cambridge Technology Partners. It was pitched at the computer industry, which was promised a look into the minds of its adversaries: in the organizers' words, only the Black Hat Briefings would put a company's engineers and software programmers face to face with the leading computer security experts and hackers. When CMP Media announced its purchase in 2005, it described the same mission, Moss's aim to mix the best minds of the computer underground with security professionals in global corporations and federal agencies. The pairing has defined both events since: the corporate Briefings and paid Trainings first, then the community conference in the same city the same week.

Owners. CMP Media, a subsidiary of the British group United Business Media (UBM), announced on 15 November 2005 that it had acquired Black Hat Inc., with Moss continuing to run the conference as Director of Black Hat; at the time it already offered briefings and training on three continents. Informa took over UBM in June 2018, and after a reorganization in 2025 Black Hat sits in the Informa Festivals division. The organizer's own pages are now headed Black Hat, by Informa, and its press contacts use Informa addresses. Moss remains associated with it as chair of the Black Hat Review Board, the group that selects the Briefings.

How it is put together. The Briefings are the peer-reviewed talks, grouped in tracks from reverse engineering to identity and privacy, plus keynotes; the 2026 edition announced more than 100 of them. The Trainings, more than 100 courses in 2026, are multi-day paid classes taught by vendors and independent professionals, which over the years have included the National Security Agency's information assurance course and classes by Cisco and Offensive Security. The Arsenal, added in 2010, gives authors of open-source security tools their own stage: live demonstrations at stations where attendees can ask questions and sometimes use the tools. The Business Hall is the vendor expo. In 2026 the Trainings ran from Saturday 1 to Tuesday 4 August, the Briefings on Wednesday 5 and Thursday 6 August, and the Business Hall, with the Arsenal inside it, from 4 to 6 August, opening on the Tuesday afternoon for the first time, all at the Mandalay Bay Convention Center; the organizers reported more than 23,000 verified attendees, over 15 per cent more than the year before, and billed the edition as the 29th anniversary event. DEF CON 34 began on 6 August, the day the Briefings ended.

The calendar. Black Hat started as a single Las Vegas conference and is now a series. As read on 12 November 2026, its upcoming events were SecTor in Toronto (6 to 8 October 2026), Black Hat India in Bengaluru (27 to 30 October), Black Hat Middle East and Africa in Malham, near Riyadh (1 to 3 December), Black Hat Europe at ExCeL London (7 to 10 December) and Black Hat Asia 2027 at Marina Bay Sands in Singapore, with dates still to be announced; the 2026 Asia edition was held there from 21 to 24 April. DEF CON's own Singapore event, from 4 to 6 March 2027, is announced to follow directly after Black Hat's. Brazil has had two brushes with the brand: a Black Hat Regional Summit São Paulo at the Transamérica Expo Center in late November 2013, repeated only in 2014, and, in September 2026, the announcement at the opening of Mind The Sec, São Paulo's largest corporate security conference, that the event had joined the Black Hat family under Informa.

The disclosure fights. Black Hat's most cited moment is about disclosure. In July 2005 the researcher Michael Lynn, then at Internet Security Systems (ISS), was due to present a way to turn a buffer overflow in Cisco's router operating system, IOS, into full control of the router, when it had been believed such bugs could only crash it. At the last minute Cisco persuaded ISS to cancel the talk, and Cisco staff ripped his paper out of every copy of the printed proceedings; Lynn quit his job and gave the presentation anyway, and Cisco went to court for an injunction, settling on terms under which Lynn would destroy his material and not disclose it further. Ed Felten's account, written that week, is still the clearest short version, and the episode became a standard case in the argument over who controls vulnerability information.

Talks that changed practice. Several of the best-known demonstrations in security history were Black Hat Briefings. In 2008 Dan Kaminsky coordinated a multi-vendor patch for a fundamental weakness in the Domain Name System (DNS), released on 8 July, and kept the details back for his Black Hat talk; they leaked on 21 July, before he could give it, and the talk went ahead regardless. In 2010 Barnaby Jack made two automated teller machines (ATMs) dispense cash on stage, the demonstration that gave jackpotting its name; he died in July 2013, a week before a scheduled Black Hat talk on attacking implanted heart devices. In 2015 Charlie Miller and Chris Valasek timed the publication of part of their remote attack on the Jeep Cherokee to a Black Hat talk, after sharing the research with Chrysler for nearly nine months; Chrysler released a patch on 16 July, before the conference. Each case shows the role the event plays: a fixed date in August that gives coordinated disclosure a deadline.

Hazards of the venue. A conference full of security researchers is a hostile environment by design. Wikipedia's history records that in 2008 three men were expelled for sniffing the press room network, that in 2009 the websites of several researchers, among them Kaminsky's, were defaced with leaked passwords and private email days before the conference, and that the same year a USB (Universal Serial Bus) drive passed among attendees turned out to be infected with Conficker. Attendees learn to treat the conference network, the hotel and anything plugged into their laptop as untrusted, which is part of the education.

Black Hat and DEF CON. The two events share a founder, a city and a week, and differ in almost everything else: Black Hat sells badges and corporate passes, peer-reviews its Briefings, sells training, and is organized by a commercial events company; DEF CON takes cash at the door and is run by volunteers. Researchers frequently present the same work at both, once for the people whose employers need an invoice and once for the community. For Latin American readers the relationship has a local echo: the corporate Mind The Sec and the community events such as the Hackers to Hackers Conference (H2HC) and BSides São Paulo are separate venues for separate audiences, and with Mind The Sec now inside Black Hat the parallel has become literal.

chaos-computer-club.def: Germany's Chaos Computer Club (CCC), founded in 1981 and registered as an association in 1986: Europe's largest hacker association, with over 8,000 members, and one of its oldest, political and deeply serious about technology and civil rights.
chaos-computer-club.context: Founded in 1981, the Chaos Computer Club (CCC) made its name with the Btx hack of November 1984, which exposed the flaws of the Bundespost's videotex system by billing a Hamburg savings bank about 135,000 marks overnight through the club's own paid page and then handing the money back. Its annual Chaos Communication Congress, held since 1984 between Christmas and New Year, and the open-air Chaos Communication Camp are institutions; its magazine Die Datenschleuder and its expert submissions to courts and parliaments define the club's blend of hands-on hacking and public-interest advocacy.
chaos-computer-club.depth:
What it is. The Chaos Computer Club (CCC) describes itself as one of the longest established and most influential civil society organizations dealing with the security and privacy aspects of technology in the German-speaking world, and its German page calls the registered association the largest organized hacker association, with over 8,000 members. It is something no other country quite produced: a hacker organization with institutional standing, whose experts, by the club's own account, contribute opinions and statements to bodies ranging from the Federal Constitutional Court to data protection authorities. It is decentralized by design. Local groups called Erfa-Kreise (from Erfahrungsaustausch, exchange of experience), about thirty of them, plus smaller Chaostreffs, run their own meetings, talks and workshops across Germany and in neighbouring countries, and the association's statutes and a Declaration of Incompatibility set out what membership commits people to.

Origins. The club traces its roots to 1981, when hackers who called themselves Komputerfrieks met at the Kommune 1 table of the Berlin newspaper taz during the tu-wat congress, saw what the new electronic data networks could do and wanted to put them to creative use. The meeting led to an informal founding, the meetings continued regularly in Hamburg, and in 1984 the club held its first Chaos Communication Congress and published the first issue of Die Datenschleuder, its magazine for data travellers. In 1986, to rule out legal misunderstandings, the CCC was registered as an association (eingetragener Verein) for the promotion of freedom of information and of a human right to at least worldwide unhindered communication.

The Btx hack, November 1984. Btx (Bildschirmtext) was the Bundespost's videotex service, launched in 1983, on which subscribers could call up pages from providers for shopping, travel and banking, and providers could charge a fee per page view. Die Zeit, reporting on 30 November 1984, explained the flaw: a page held at most 1,626 characters, and when providers overfilled a page the program sometimes pushed fragments of its own memory onto the screen, in which Steffen Wernéry and his club mates found the Btx identifier and password of the Hamburger Sparkasse. The club, a registered Btx provider, set up a donation page charging 9.97 marks, just under the 9.99 limit, and had a home computer call it with the bank's credentials continuously; heise's 2024 reconstruction counts 13,504 calls on the night of 16 to 17 November, 134,634.88 marks, while Die Zeit gave about 135,000 marks between 6:00 pm on Saturday and 1:00 pm on Sunday. Die Zeit also reported that the money was transferred back to the savings bank. The Bundespost's technical manager for Btx still maintained thirty years later that someone must have given the club the password; the club had written to data protection authorities and to the Bundespost about gaps in the system in October 1984, and Wau Holland had spoken about them at the DAFTA (Datenschutzfachtagung) data protection conference earlier in November. The press release that followed asked who carried the risk if the Bundespost was not liable for such errors, and called for a ban on financial transactions on Btx.

The ethic. The club's statement of hacker ethics takes the principles Steven Levy wrote down in Hackers: Heroes of the Computer Revolution (1984), from unlimited access to computers to judging hackers by what they do, and adds two lines of its own from the 1980s: do not litter other people's data, and make public data available, protect private data. The CCC says the additions came out of intense discussion after some individuals from the scene offered their know-how to the Soviet KGB (Committee for State Security), and as intrusions into other people's systems came to be seen as counterproductive. That is the episode known as the KGB hack, and the ethic is the club's answer to it: the CCC treats its rules as guidelines for discussion rather than dogma, but the line between public-interest demonstration and selling access was drawn there.

Demonstrations as argument. The Btx template, proving a claim by doing it in public, recurs through the club's history. In 2008 Die Datenschleuder printed, on plastic foil in about 4,000 copies, the fingerprint of the interior minister Wolfgang Schäuble, a leading advocate of fingerprints in passports, lifted by a supporter from a glass he had used at a public event; German passports had carried fingerprints in a biometric chip since November 2007, and the CCC had published instructions for copying fingerprints since 2004. On 8 October 2011 the club published its analysis of a police trojan sent to it anonymously, sold as source telecommunications interception (Quellen-TKÜ), which was supposed to be limited to internet telephony: it could take browser screenshots, download and run arbitrary further programs, and so be extended to switch on microphone or camera for room surveillance; its commands were neither encrypted nor authenticated, so anyone on the internet could take control of an infected machine, and its traffic ran through a rented server in the United States.

In front of the courts. The club's campaign against voting computers, run with the Dutch foundation Wij vertrouwen stemcomputers niet after hackers had manipulated Nedap machines in the Netherlands in 2006, fed into the Federal Constitutional Court's judgment announced on 3 March 2009 (2 BvC 3/07, 2 BvC 4/07). The court held that the use of voting machines requires that the essential steps of voting and of determining the result can be checked by citizens reliably and without specialist knowledge, a requirement of the principle of the public nature of elections, and declared the Federal Voting Machines Ordinance under which the 2005 Bundestag election had used them unconstitutional. The 2011 trojan analysis was framed the same way, against the limits the court had set on 27 February 2008 for secret access to computers.

The congress and the camp. The Chaos Communication Congress has run since 1984; its editions are numbered, and the 40th, 40C3, is scheduled for 27 to 30 December 2026 in the Hamburg Messehallen, after a move announced in July 2026. Its summer counterpart, the Chaos Communication Camp, is an international five-day open-air event for hackers; the 2023 edition ran from 15 to 19 August at Ziegeleipark Mildenberg in Zehdenick. The club also points to art projects such as Blinkenlights among the actions that made its name, and its local Erfa spaces are among the hackerspaces the wider movement grew from.

Why it matters to engineers. The CCC's lasting contribution is a method: a security claim made by a vendor or a ministry is tested in public, the result is published with enough detail to be checked, and the demonstration is designed so that it cannot be dismissed as theft or vandalism. Btx showed that a provider's terms making users liable for everything done under their code were unrealistic; the fingerprint showed that a biometric is a credential you leave on every glass; the trojan showed that a lawful-interception tool without authentication is a backdoor for everyone. Each is a design lesson as much as a political one.

2600-magazine.def: The Hacker Quarterly: the printed voice of hacker culture since 1984, and the origin of the HOPE conference and the Friday 2600 meetings.
2600-magazine.context: Edited by Emmanuel Goldstein (Eric Corley) and named for the 2600 Hz phreaking tone, 2600 has published reader-submitted explorations of systems for four decades, fought landmark legal battles (notably the DeCSS case), and seeded a worldwide network of first-Friday meetups. Its HOPE conference (Hackers On Planet Earth) carries the same lineage - and the magazine's editor opened the very first YSTS in São Paulo, tying this entry to the Brazilian scene.
2600-magazine.depth:
2600, named for the phreaking tone and edited by Emmanuel Goldstein, has published reader-submitted technical material continuously since 1984, in print, on paper, quarterly. It also organizes the physical meetings that happen in cities worldwide on the first Friday of the month.

Its significance is distribution before the internet made distribution trivial. A teenager in a small town with no local community could buy a magazine at a bookshop and find out that other people existed, what they were doing, and how. For a great many people who later became security professionals, that was the entry point, and the physical object mattered precisely because nothing else reached them.

It has been controversial throughout and has usually been on the receiving end of the legal action rather than the sending end, most prominently in the DeCSS case. What the magazine consistently argued is that publishing technical information is speech, and that a society which criminalizes explanation ends up with a population that cannot evaluate the systems governing it. That argument has aged well, and the magazine still arrives quarterly.

ysts.def: You Sh0t the Sheriff (YSTS) is a single-day, invitation-only information security conference held in São Paulo each May since 2007, grown out of the ISTS podcast: tickets are not sold, guests come through sponsors, and the venue is revealed only to those confirmed. Its eighteenth edition was on 18 May 2026, the Monday after BSides São Paulo.
ysts.context: Founded by Luiz Eduardo dos Santos, Nelson Murilo Rufino, the author of chkrootkit, and Willian Caprino, it started as a podcast: ISTS, 'i sh0t the sheriff', recording since 2006 and still going. The conference followed in 2007 and kept the podcast's register. Three refusals define it: attendance by invitation through a sponsor, a venue disclosed only to confirmed attendees, and a headcount the founders keep fixed on principle, having said at the tenth edition that they work to keep it the same size. Jeff Moss, who created DEF CON and Black Hat, joined its fourteenth edition in 2022 for a remote fireside chat, and Cris Thomas of the L0pht has spoken there, alongside the people who carry the Brazilian scene.
ysts.depth:
The podcast came first. ISTS, i sh0t the sheriff, describes itself as the Brazilian information security podcast since 2006, made by Luiz Eduardo dos Santos, Nelson Murilo and Willian Caprino; its 143rd episode came out on 30 December 2024, scripted by the three and produced by Halfmouth Podcasts. The conference grew out of that conversation rather than being conceived as an event, and it kept the podcast's tone: unhurried, opinionated and closer to a talk among peers than to a lecture. The founders are known for their own work as well: Nelson Murilo is the main author of chkrootkit, the tool that locally checks a system for signs of a rootkit, written with Klaus Steding-Jessen of CERT.br, whose version 0.60 shipped on 11 October 2026.

What the event is. YSTS packs hand-picked national and international speakers into a single day in São Paulo and calls itself the most exclusive information security conference in Brazil, bringing together the most influential people in the Brazilian sector in an informal, relaxed setting; its site addresses three audiences at once, hackers, chief information security officers and the visitor. Its distinguishing choice is deliberate smallness. Attendance is by invitation from a sponsor, and Anchises Moraes, the calendar's chronicler, summarizes it in 2026 as one of the most traditional events of the market, exclusive to sponsors' guests and therefore much sought after. In 2011 the organizers still put a small number of tickets on sale beside the sponsors' invitations; by 2022 the event sold none. The venue is chosen carefully and kept secret, revealed only to those confirmed to attend, and has historically been a place that feels nothing like a conference hall: the tenth edition, in 2016, was held at Villa Bisutti, and the founders have described choosing bars and pubs for the early ones. The organization trades as STS Produções e Eventos.

The editions. The numbering gives the history: the fifth edition was on 16 May 2011, the tenth in 2016, the fourteenth on 23 May 2022 and the eighteenth on 18 May 2026. At the tenth, Kaspersky's Securelist reported, the three founders opened by contrasting the first edition with the tenth, more mature and professional but still a challenge to put on, and described their work to keep the event the same size, believing growth would cost them the quality. For 2027 the preliminary calendar puts it on Monday 17 May. YSTS is scheduled immediately after Security BSides São Paulo, the free community conference held the weekend before, and the same people move between the two: the open event on the Saturday and Sunday, the closed one on the Monday.

Who has been in the room. The programme has mixed people who built the international scene with those who built the Brazilian one. In May 2011 Deviant Ollam, of the lockpicking group TOOOL, opened the fifth edition with the basics of lockpicking and sold kits to the room, in what Moraes recorded as a record audience; at the same edition Fabio Assolini, a Kaspersky analyst, explained how Brazilian criminals put stolen personal data to work, two days after a talk on the history of Brazilian banking trojans at the network security working group meeting of NIC.br, the Grupo de Trabalho em Segurança de Redes (GTS). The InfoSec Arena, a debate built on questions sent in by the audience, was one of the formats that only work at that size. In 2022 Jeff Moss, founder of DEF CON and Black Hat, joined YSTS 14 for a remote fireside chat with the audience, and Cris Thomas, Space Rogue of the L0pht, was back on the programme. Moraes ranked YSTS among his best Brazilian events of 2024, with Mind The Sec, the Hackers to Hackers Conference (H2HC) and BSides São Paulo.

Why keep it small. The reasoning behind the cap is the same one behind ShmooCon's attendance limit in the United States, arrived at independently: a room where everyone can plausibly meet everyone produces different conversations from a hall of two thousand, and the value of a security event is often less the talks than who you end up standing next to. YSTS makes that explicit by bringing technical and managerial audiences into the same room for one day, which in most conferences is a slogan and here is a seating plan. Curating the audience is unfashionable, and it does produce the thing it aims at.

The cost, and the balance. The trade is the obvious one and worth naming. A curated event is by definition exclusionary, and who gets invited reflects who the organizers and sponsors already know, which is how professional networks reproduce themselves and how newcomers stay outside. In São Paulo the answer has been to put the opposite model next to it rather than to argue about the door: BSides São Paulo, free and open, on the weekend before. A healthy scene needs both, the open event anyone can walk into and the small, dense one where the people who run things talk to each other for a day, and a country with only one of them is missing something. The numbers worth remembering are 2006 for the podcast, 2007 for the first conference, a single day in May, and eighteen editions by 2026.

bsides-sao-paulo.def: The community-run, free security conference of São Paulo, born as the Conferência O Outro Lado inside Garoa Hacker Clube on 15 May 2011, a Security BSides event since 2012, and by 2026, with 3,431 people at its twenty-first edition, one of the largest BSides events anywhere.
bsides-sao-paulo.context: Co0L BSidesSP, today Security BSides São Paulo, is part of the global Security BSides movement: volunteer-organized, free to attend and deliberately community-first, with more than twenty villages run by their own communities, a capture-the-flag (CTF) competition, the lightning talks and the Brazilian Arsenal of open-source tools it introduced in 2013, and a children's village, BSides4Kids. It traditionally runs the weekend before YSTS; the 2026 edition, on 16 and 17 May, marked fifteen years since the first one was held inside Garoa. The food has always been free too: barbecue from the first edition, then hot dogs and feijoada cooked by volunteers, and in the hotel years pastries by the hundreds.
bsides-sao-paulo.depth:
What it is. Security BSides São Paulo (BSidesSP) describes itself as a conference about information security and hacker culture, organized by people who work in the field to promote innovation, discussion and the exchange of knowledge among security researchers, professionals and students, and to spread the positive values of hacker culture. It is run by volunteers, independently and without profit, with the stated commitment of being free and accessible, under the motto from the community to the community. Since 2017 it has been held once a year, on the weekend before the You Sh0t the Sheriff (YSTS) conference: a Saturday of short trainings and competitions, then a Sunday of talks, villages and stalls. Its organizers call it the second largest event of the Brazilian security community, after the Hackers to Hackers Conference (H2HC). Much of its history is written down by one of those organizers, Anchises Moraes, whose blog is the main record used here.

Where the BSides idea came from. The global movement began in the summer of 2009, after the Black Hat conference announced its speaker line-up and a group of security people, among them Mike Murray, Chris Nickerson, Mike Dahn, Davi Ottenheimer and Anton Chuvakin, started an open conversation about talks that had not been accepted; another conversation about the politics of security conferences, and the wish for a friendlier event, joined it. Dahn first wanted to call it Security Fringe. Security BSides 1.0 was held in a house in Las Vegas on 29 and 30 July 2009, alongside Black Hat, and focused on conversation and interaction with peers. In 2010 the Las Vegas event drew about 650 people, and BSides events ran in cities from Berlin and Ottawa to Austin and San Francisco; in 2011 the movement passed 40 events, and Security BSides was incorporated in California, today as a non-profit organization. The model is volunteer-run, free or near-free and open to first-time speakers, and the BSidesSP organizers count the circuit in more than 60 countries.

The São Paulo beginning. At 13:00 on Saturday 15 May 2011 the first Conferência O Outro Lado (CoOL), the event that gave rise to BSidesSP, opened at the former headquarters of the Garoa Hacker Clube, São Paulo's hackerspace: 84 people, nine talks and two workshops in the small rooms of the space, with a barbecue in the internal yard, everything free. The idea from the start was an informal, relaxed and inclusive event with content from the newest beginner to the most experienced professional, and with room for the wider culture of hacking. In 2012 the organizers of Security BSides in the United States approved it as the official BSides of São Paulo, which is why it was long known as Co0L BSidesSP.

Twice a year, then once. For its first years the conference ran two or three editions a year, fourteen editions and one BSidesLatam (in 2016) by 2017. The seventh, on 24 November 2013 at Fatec in São Caetano do Sul, was nicknamed the Black Hat Edition because it fell on the Sunday before the first Black Hat event in Brazil, and introduced several things that stayed: the Brazilian Arsenal, a space for developers of Brazilian open-source security tools; a CTF; ten-minute lightning talks; and a reshaped hacker job fair. In May 2017 the fourteenth edition at PUC-SP set a record of 770 people, and in October the organizers decided to hold only one edition a year, because the event had outgrown a team of five people taking the strategic and financial decisions and twelve friends helping on the day, all working in their free time, and the university venue had become too small at lunch and at the closing ceremony. They chose the first half of the year, which has fewer large events, and the weekend before YSTS, which takes place on Mondays.

Pause and return. The 2018 edition drew 1,245 participants from 2,051 registrations, and the May 2019 edition, the sixteenth, about 1,200. The organizers chose not to hold editions in 2020 and 2021, judging that in-person participation is one of the main benefits of a BSides, and skipped May 2022 at the peak of the Omicron variant; the seventeenth edition took place on Sunday 20 November 2022 at PUC-SP's Consolação campus, in a single day, with a CTF run with HackaFlag, barbecue, an open bar and hot dogs offered by a group of volunteer security professionals, under the theme Peace, Love and Hacking. In 2023 the eighteenth edition, on 24 and 25 June, moved to the convention centre of the Novotel Jaraguá in central São Paulo, which brought bigger rooms closer together and also restrictions: no bar, no skewers and no volunteer hot dogs. It received 1,123 people.

The years of growth. The nineteenth edition, on 18 and 19 May 2024, broke every record: 3,542 registrations, 1,795 people on the Sunday, villages doubled from seven in 2019 to fourteen on a floor of their own, and a CTF organized by the Hack in Cariri community, under the theme Pwnd IA. The twentieth, on 17 and 18 May 2025, received 109 talk proposals, cut talks from 50 to 40 minutes to fit 32 into the main tracks instead of 24, and had 17 villages, 17 teams in the CTF, 202 volunteers, 29 sponsors and, for the first time, a sponsor exhibition area; 2,307 people came on the Sunday and 2,725 over the two days, from 5,529 registrations, and 880 pastries were served. Free registrations ran out in days, which led the organizers to a crowdfunding campaign in 2026 to raise capacity and keep the event free. The twenty-first edition, on 16 and 17 May 2026, celebrated fifteen years: 3,431 people over the two days, 54 per cent of the 6,312 confirmed registrations, 3,120 of them on the Sunday, 22 villages and a CTF again run by Hack in Cariri.

How the villages work. Each village is organized by its own community, which takes a dedicated room and is responsible for its own programme; the conference only provides the space, free of charge, and since 2026 runs a single call for papers for all of them. The 2026 list shows the range: aerospace, Apple red teaming, application security, biohacking, car hacking, careers, chief information security officers, awareness, Cyber Women, digital investigation, exploits, forensics, human intelligence, artificial intelligence, industrial control systems, mobile security, open-source intelligence, quantum computing and red teaming, plus the hackerspace Dumont and the children's space, BSides4Kids. One measure of what that space does came at the 2025 closing ceremony, when a prize went to someone who had attended the kids' village in 2013 as a child.

Why the model matters. The open call for papers is the whole mechanism. A researcher with no reputation cannot get accepted at an established conference, and cannot build a reputation without presenting somewhere, which is a loop that keeps new voices out unless something breaks it. BSides breaks it on purpose, accepting people who have never presented and treating the first talk as the point rather than a risk; the 2026 crowdfunding appeal states the aim as giving a stage to speakers who do not reach the big events and making room for people starting in the field. What it produces is a pipeline rather than a single event: speakers who start at BSides go on to larger conferences, and the community hears from people without employers who fund conference travel. Running it on volunteer effort and a small budget is genuinely hard, and the movement's persistence across dozens of cities is a quiet argument that the barrier was never talent.

garoa-hacker-clube.def: São Paulo's hackerspace, which describes itself as Brazil's first: an idea from June 2009, a 12 square metre basement opened on 28 August 2010, a non-profit association founded on 20 February 2011, and the room where BSidesSP (Security BSides São Paulo) was born.
garoa-hacker-clube.context: Garoa (the name is the city's famous drizzle) is a member-run space in the classic hackerspace tradition: open weekly activities, electronics benches with soldering stations and oscilloscopes, retrocomputing, lockpicking, cryptography nights, and a wiki-documented culture of projects, all free and open to anyone. Beyond its own walls it has been an incubator for the local scene: the first edition of what became BSidesSP (Security BSides São Paulo) was held inside it on 15 May 2011, its events archive records Garoa at H2HC (Hackers to Hackers Conference) and Roadsec and a hackerspace area at Campus Party, and it keeps the list of the Brazilian hackerspaces that followed it.
garoa-hacker-clube.depth:
What it is. Garoa Hacker Clube describes itself as an open, collaborative place that gives technology enthusiasts space and infrastructure for projects in security, hardware, electronics, robotics, model railways and rocketry, software, biology, music, visual arts or whatever else they think of: a community laboratory where people meet, share and collaborate. Its inventory is a working bench: a 3D printer, Arduino boards and assorted components, basic woodworking tools, soldering and rework stations, electronic instruments (oscilloscopes, function generators, multimeters and regulated power supplies), old hardware, a kitchen equipped for brewing beer, a games room and a small library. Everything is run by volunteers, every activity is free and open, and the club states plainly that it is not a company and sells no services.

How it is run. Garoa is a registered non-profit civil association, created, in its own words, so that individual members would not have to answer personally for the lease and the bills. It has statutes, internal rules and a code of conduct, elects an executive board and a fiscal council every two years, and is steered between elections by a council of associates, the Conselho Manda-Chuva, which meets monthly. It has no agreements with any company, government or university; the money comes from members' monthly dues and donations, and the occasional company donation, usually equipment, is accepted without anything in return. Its tax registration came through on 16 August 2011.

Origins. The idea took shape from June 2009 in an online community on Ning under the provisional name hackerSPace, which survives as the name of a mailing list. Anchises Moraes, one of the twelve founders, has written that it was a collective effort by people who barely knew each other, and that he first met the idea at the Ekoparty conference in 2009 in a talk by Philippe Langlois of the Paris hackerspace /tmp/lab. The group presented the project publicly at Campus Party in January 2010, held its first in-person meeting on 15 July 2010 at the Escritório Piloto of the University of São Paulo's Escola Politécnica (Poli), with the support of its free-software study group PoliGNU, chose the name on 14 October 2010, and on 28 August 2010 had already opened its first permanent space: a 12 square metre basement, once used for parties, in the Casa da Cultura Digital, which waived the rent for the first six months. The founding assembly took place on Saturday 20 February 2011, and the minutes were signed at Unix time 1298244863, which the club treats as its epoch zero.

Three headquarters. The first regular activity was the Noite do Arduino, on Thursdays from November 2010, and over time the club spread into a second basement used mostly as storage. In February 2013 it moved to a single-storey house in Pinheiros, decorated by members and visitors; by the end of 2014 it counted more than 40 paying associates, about 2,100 people on its mailing list and an estimated 3,000 people who had attended its activities, and in January 2018 more than 3,400 on the list. In-person activities stopped during the COVID-19 pandemic while the house was kept, and the club has since moved to a nearby townhouse, its third headquarters, five minutes' walk from Pinheiros metro station.

What happens there. Its calendar in November 2026 shows the pattern: an Open Hack Night every Thursday evening, a fortnightly Micro Sábado and IoTrem night, a monthly Python Lab, the council's meeting and a Noite de Relâmpagos of lightning talks, plus one-off sessions such as building a minimal function generator or a data science group. Anyone, member or not, may propose an event through the mailing list, events are free and need no registration. The archive of past events reads like a map of the scene's interests: Arduino nights, CarnaHacking during Carnival from 2011 to 2016, lockpicking, Noites Criptonicas on cryptography, capture-the-flag (CTF) competitions, a debate on government cyber-espionage, a talk on the Azeredo bill, Hackids and Jovem Hacker sessions, Garoa appearances at H2HC (Hackers to Hackers Conference) and Roadsec, and a Dumont Hackerspace area at Campus Party in most years from 2015 to 2024.

Where BSidesSP (Security BSides São Paulo) began. At 13:00 on Saturday 15 May 2011, three months after the founding, the first Conferência O Outro Lado (CoOL) opened at Garoa's then headquarters: 84 people, nine talks and two workshops spread through the space's small rooms, with a barbecue in the internal yard, everything free. In 2012 the organizers obtained approval from Security BSides for it to become the official São Paulo edition, and the club's own history records that the first editions of BSidesSP were held in that basement space.

Seeding a network. In September 2011 Anchises Moraes joked that Brazil already had 11 hackerspaces, in binary: Garoa, Fundação Hacker Space in the east of São Paulo, and the Laboratório Hacker de Campinas, which opened on 12 October 2011 as the third in operation. Garoa counts fostering new spaces as part of its mission, keeps a page on how to start one, and its list of Brazilian hackerspaces, last updated on 6 October 2026, names 32 in fourteen states and the Federal District, from Raul Hacker Club in Salvador and Calango Hacker Club in Brasília to GaragemHacker in Curitiba.

Why it matters. The model matters more than any single project. A hackerspace is infrastructure for the kind of learning institutions cannot schedule, where the bench, the soldering iron and the person who already knows how are in the same room and free to use; for people without university access or an employer paying for equipment, that combination is the difference between curiosity and capability. In Brazil equipment is expensive relative to income, imported components carry real cost and delay, and formal technical education is unevenly distributed, which is why a shared physical space with tools and expertise has outsized importance, and why the volunteers who keep the lights on do more consequential work than the label suggests.

mente-binaria.def: The Brazilian nonprofit teaching computing and security from first principles - free courses, an active forum, and open-source tooling.
mente-binaria.context: Founded by researcher Fernando Merces, Mente Binaria is formally a nonprofit teaching and research institution: its free CERO (reverse engineering) and AMO (malware analysis) courses run on the Papo Binario YouTube channel, its forum community spans beginners to veterans, it maintains open-source tools like readpe (born as pev), and programs like CodeHERS bring women into reverse engineering. Portuguese-language, foundations-first - a rare and load-bearing institution in the Brazilian scene.

h2hc.def: Hackers to Hackers Conference: the Brazilian security research conference founded in 2004 and held in São Paulo since 2008, often described as the oldest of its kind in Latin America.
h2hc.context: H2HC (Hackers to Hackers Conference) is the deep-technical anchor of the Brazilian calendar: vulnerability research, exploitation, reverse engineering, hardware. It sits at the research end of the spectrum, with international headliners alongside Brazilian researchers, a second track of talks labelled H2HC University, trainings, a magazine and a capture the flag (CTF) contest. Its reputation for a playfully 'hostile' hallway culture is worn as a badge: it is the room where the technical bar is highest.
h2hc.depth:
H2HC, the Hackers to Hackers Conference, is the deep-technical anchor of the Brazilian security calendar: vulnerability research, exploitation, reverse engineering and low-level work, presented to an audience expected to follow it. It has run since 2004, which makes it one of the longest-standing technical conferences in Latin America. Its own description is plain: a conference organized by people who work in information security research and development, with talks and trainings by members of the corporate world, research groups and the underground community, built to show techniques not seen in public before. The reason it gives for showing attacks is the one the whole field rests on: those who attack usually know many techniques, so the analysts, auditors and administrators who defend have to know them too, and the better protection against flaws nobody has reported is to understand a class of problem deeply, not to apply the vendor's fixes and hope that no one arrives with a 0day.

Where it came from. The account assembled by Anchises Moraes, the Brazilian security blogger who has followed the event since its second edition, is that the idea came from three members of the underground community who had met at an event in São Paulo and drew the rest of that community in over Internet Relay Chat (IRC). They wanted a technical, hands-on meeting where people who knew one another online could meet in person, and where, unlike the slide-only conferences of the time, every talk had to carry a practical demonstration; the name, from hackers to hackers, says as much. It was organized at first under the names of the groups Front The Scene and Clube dos Mercenários, later joined by Security OpenSource. The first edition was planned for São Paulo on 24 and 25 July 2004; the venue withdrew, and it took place in Brasília in November 2004. The 2004 programme kept in the conference archive had talks on attacks on Wi-Fi networks, honeypot detection, attack signatures and cryptography on clusters. The next two editions were held in São Paulo colleges, the fourth, in 2007, returned to Brasília, and from 2008 the conference stayed in São Paulo, moving into a hotel, the Novotel Morumbi, with the sixth edition in 2009. There was one extra edition abroad, H2HC Cancún, in 2010. Accounts of exactly who founded it differ, and that dispute is not needed to describe the event.

Who ran it. Rodrigo Rubira Branco joined the organization during the first edition and became the lead organizer at the fifth, in 2008, when the committee of about eight people was divided and behind schedule; he invited Filipe Balestra to run it with him. The two led it for sixteen more years. Branco's farewell letter of 25 November 2024 gives the internal numbers: about 1,000 hours of his own time a year; an event run entirely by volunteers, with no employees, the organizers taking no money and all revenue reinvested; tickets donated to people who could not pay; and no marketing budget. He announced that from 2025 every responsibility would rest with Balestra.

Its defining choice is to refuse to broaden. Many conferences drift towards management tracks and vendor keynotes as they grow, because that is where the sponsorship is, and H2HC's refusal to do that keeps a specific kind of work possible: research that takes months, cannot be summarized in a slide, and has an audience of a few hundred people worldwide who genuinely understand it. Branco's letter describes the same thing from the inside: he says he constantly held back the event's growth, and that the agreement when he took over was to keep the original spirit, that people should meet, that hacking is a counter-culture and that knowledge should not be controlled. The choice has not gone unquestioned. Anchises records that when companies began sponsoring the event in 2008, part of the underground accused it of having gone commercial.

What an edition looks like. The edition branded 21 Years was held on 14 and 15 December 2024 at the Novotel Center Norte. According to its call for papers the main auditorium holds up to 600 people and a parallel track up to 200, every talk in the main auditorium is given in English or translated simultaneously into English, and the selection committee prefers talks with a practical demonstration; the same page puts attendance at about 1,500 a day, while Branco's letter of that November speaks of about 3,000 a day, more than 20 villages and more than 18 international speakers. The 2024 programme shows the level: keynotes by Cristofaro Mune and by Gerardo Richarte, and talks on Linux kernel security by Alexander Popov, on alternate Spectre vulnerabilities by Johannes Wikner of ETH Zurich, on security assessment of internet protocols by Fernando Gont, and a case study of client-side attacks on automated teller machines by Filipe Balestra and Wendel Guglielmetti. Around the talks there are trainings, a capture the flag (CTF) contest, the electronic badges that have become a tradition, and the track of talks the archive labels H2HC University. H2HC Magazine had reached issue 17, each issue with a digital object identifier (DOI). Slides and videos from 2004 to 2019 are published on GitHub and YouTube.

The gaps in the record. The conference is not an unbroken annual series. In August 2020 the organizers cancelled that year's edition because of the COVID-19 pandemic, for the first time in 17 years, and declined to hold it online, arguing that no online format offered the interaction the event was created for; it stayed suspended in 2021 and returned in 2022. The 2023 edition was celebrated as the twentieth anniversary, with the villages so prominent that some talks were delivered as silent talks over radio headsets. Then, in the first year after the handover, there was no edition at all: the cancellation of H2HC 2025, expected for 13 and 14 December, was communicated on 19 November 2025, with the statement that the event would be held the following year, and the official website had by then been offline for months. Several communities organized the 307 Temporary Security Conference on the same weekend at the Pontifical Catholic University of São Paulo (PUC-SP), with about 500 people on the first day. Anchises's calendar for 2026, as last updated on 8 September 2026, lists the second 307 conference for 5 and 6 December and no date for H2HC.

That matters more in a country whose researchers are largely invisible to the international scene. Deep technical work needs a venue where it will be judged by peers and not by novelty, and without one the researchers either present abroad or stop. Sustaining that venue for two decades, almost always in the same city and with the same standard, is the kind of unglamorous institutional work that fields depend on and rarely credit. The year without an edition showed how much it depended on a very small number of people, and also that the community it had formed was able to put a replacement together in under two months.

How it differs from its neighbours. In the Brazilian calendar its neighbours are You Sh0t the Sheriff, Mind the Sec and the Security BSides events, the São Paulo one a free community meeting of about a thousand people; H2HC is the one whose main programme is original offensive and low-level research, with international speakers at a time when, as Anchises noted of 2023, most Brazilian events had stopped bringing them. Its phrase for itself, in the organizers' 2020 statement, is a way for hackers to meet, exchange ideas and learn from one another. The local description is shorter: quality content, a great deal of quarrelling and a great deal of banter.

The dates worth remembering: November 2004 in Brasília for the first edition; 2008 for the move to São Paulo for good and for the Branco and Balestra organization; 2009 for the first hotel edition; 2020 and 2021 without the event; 14 and 15 December 2024 for the edition called 21 Years; 25 November 2024 for Branco's farewell; and 19 November 2025 for the cancellation of that year's edition.

mind-the-sec.def: São Paulo's corporate-scale information security conference and trade fair, launched by Flipside in 2015 and held each September, where the Brazilian market's decision-makers meet the vendor ecosystem; in September 2026 it passed to Informa, the organizer of Black Hat.
mind-the-sec.context: Mind The Sec occupies the enterprise end of the Brazilian conference spectrum: three days, expo-heavy and aimed at executives, the counterpart to the community events (BSidesSP, H2HC) on the same calendar. The 2026 edition, its twelfth, ran from 15 to 17 September at the Transamérica Expo Center in São Paulo, with more than 500 speakers and an expected 17,500 visitors. It was created by Flipside, the company that also ran the Roadsec hacker festival, and at its 2026 opening its founder announced that it had joined the Black Hat family. For practitioners it is the market-watching stop: who is selling what to whom in Brazilian security.
mind-the-sec.depth:
What it is. Mind The Sec is a commercial conference and business fair for information security, held once a year in São Paulo and aimed, in its organizer's words, at the people who actually think about and decide security in Brazil. It combines a paid congress, with tracks for delegates, keynotes and executive programmes, with a large exhibition where vendors take stands and give free talks. Its organizers bill it as the largest cybersecurity event in Latin America, and on its site, read in November 2026, as the largest in the Southern Hemisphere; the twelfth edition, from 15 to 17 September 2026 at the Transamérica Expo Center, occupied more than 17,000 square metres, announced more than 500 Brazilian and international speakers and expected more than 17,500 participants, sold in Starter, Expo, Professional and Business ticket categories, with an on-demand ticket that in 2025 gave 180 days of access to the recorded talks. It is not a hacker conference: the research-led and community events of the same calendar, such as H2HC and BSidesSP, have their own entries.

How it began. Mind The Sec was born large. Flipside created it in 2015 to replace SecureBrasil, an event it had run with (ISC)², and held the first edition on 26 and 27 August 2015: two days, three tracks of talks divided into management, technology and solutions, and Bruce Schneier as keynote speaker. Anchises Moraes, who has reviewed the year's Brazilian security events on his blog since 2011, voted it, with Roadsec, the best Brazilian event of that year, a new event that attracted the profession's senior people from the start.

The family of events. Around 2018 Flipside described the São Paulo edition as receiving more than 900 people over two days, added that Rio de Janeiro had hosted a one-day version for 300 people since 2017, and announced a Mind The Sec Summit to take content and networking to six of the country's capitals that year, for influencers and purchasing decision-makers only. A Mind The Sec Club offered relationship events for chief-level executives. Moraes later listed the chapters of the story as SecureBrasil, Mind The Sec, Roadsec, the regional Mind The Sec editions, the Hackaflag capture-the-flag (CTF) championship and the Club.

Through the pandemic. In 2020, when in-person events stopped, Mind The Sec was one of the few security events that carried on, testing new formats. Flipside had already experimented with online platforms through the weekly Roadsec@Home sessions, and the online Mind The Sec of that year ran one day longer than earlier editions, with three simultaneous tracks plus question-and-answer sessions, about 40 sponsors and, for the first time, a free registration tier with limited access; executives of the Club received kits to cook their own lunch at home under a chef's guidance.

The years of scale. After the pandemic the event moved to the Transamérica Expo Center, in 2022 by Moraes's account, and grew past every other Brazilian security event. Moraes counted more than 10,000 participants and 100 sponsors in 2023, when it filled two halls, and 10,000 participants and 140 sponsors at the tenth edition, from 17 to 19 September 2024, which he called practically flawless, with Mikko Hyppönen among its speakers. The organizer's own release for 2025 said more than 14,000 visitors had come to the previous edition; the figures differ by source and are best read as orders of magnitude. The 2025 edition, from 16 to 18 September, expected more than 16,000 people from more than 200 companies, with Paula Januszkiewicz, Trey Ford and Gary McGraw as headline speakers; the 2026 programme had Jon DiMaggio, Wendy Nather and Chris Wysopal as keynotes and, for the first time, put the congress and the exhibition on the same floor. Growth brought complaints too: Moraes wrote of a crowded exhibition and badly used space in 2023, and in 2024 of a confusing agenda in which attendees could not tell open talks from those reserved for delegates who had paid for expensive passes.

Flipside and Roadsec. Mind The Sec and Roadsec were run by the same company, Flipside, and Moraes describes Anderson Ramos as the founder of Mind The Sec. The two were deliberate opposites: one corporate, expo-heavy and in São Paulo; the other a travelling festival taking hacker culture to the state capitals. By 2023 both had lost their regional editions while setting records in São Paulo. Then, in 2024, Roadsec did not happen; its last edition remains that of 15 July 2023. Moraes's personal reading, which matches the assessment heard more widely in the scene, was that Mind The Sec had grown so large that the company had no breath left to run the other event. That is a specific and instructive thing to watch: the profitable event did not out-compete the community event in any market, it out-competed it for the attention of the people who ran both. The space did not stay empty. Moraes singled out 2024 for the appearance of several regional, community-run events, so the calendar now has more small events outside São Paulo than it had when one large organizer served those cities directly; whether that is better depends on what one values, and the honest answer is that it is different.

Black Hat arrives. On 18 September 2026 Moraes reported that, after more than a year of market rumours, it was official: Mind The Sec had joined the Black Hat family. Ramos had shared the news without much fanfare at the opening of the 2026 edition, and on the Thursday, the last day, the staff wore shirts reading Mind The Sec by Black Hat. Black Hat is organized by Informa, which, Moraes wrote, is the company that bought Mind The Sec. It was not Black Hat's first approach to Brazil: a Black Hat Regional Summit São Paulo was held in late November 2013 at the same Transamérica Expo Center and was repeated only in 2014. The event's release of 15 September 2026 quoted two co-chief executives of Mind The Sec, Liz Kazi and Carlos Bellini. When its site was read on 12 November 2026 it still carried only the Mind The Sec name, offering pre-reservations for 2027; what the event will be called is, as Moraes put it, an open question.

Why practitioners go. For an engineer the value is mostly in the hall, not in the keynotes: it is where the Brazilian market shows which vendors are selling which products to which buyers, which integrators and distributors are present, and which buzzwords are in season (in 2024 Moraes listed artificial intelligence, ransomware, open-source intelligence, supply chain attacks and zero trust). Its calls for papers, tools, workshops and trainings give practitioners a route onto its stages, but its centre of gravity is the decision-maker, and the research-led and community events remain the places for deep technical content. The numbers worth keeping: first edition on 26 and 27 August 2015, the tenth in September 2024, the twelfth from 15 to 17 September 2026, and the Black Hat announcement at that edition's opening.

f5-devcentral.def: F5's official technical community, online since 2003 and now at community.f5.com: forums, technical articles and shared code, with more than two decades of iRules knowledge and an MVP programme that recognizes its leading contributors each year.
f5-devcentral.context: DevCentral (today at community.f5.com) is where F5 practitioners publish deep-dive articles, answer configuration questions, and share iRules and automation; much of the working knowledge of BIG-IP outside the official documentation lives there. Its MVP programme recognizes standing contributors annually. It began in 2003 as a home for developers using iControl, the BIG-IP API (application programming interface), and grew up with iRules, the Tcl-based traffic scripting of BIG-IP. It is a community and not a support channel: validated answers and support cases belong to the MyF5 portal, and code shared on DevCentral carries the warning that F5 has not validated it.
f5-devcentral.depth:
F5 describes DevCentral as an online technical community where engineers and practitioners collaborate, share knowledge and solve problems related to F5 technologies and industry trends, and its support page counts more than 300,000 F5 users in it. It is run and moderated by F5, whose staff write the section called F5 Technical Articles, but most forum answers come from other customers and partners. That makes it different from the two things it is most often confused with. It is not the knowledge base: the validated articles, the software downloads and the support cases are in the MyF5 portal. And it is not support: the community guidelines say plainly that the community is largely made up of unpaid volunteers and that there should never be an expectation of free on-demand support.

Its origin is an API (application programming interface). According to Joe Pruitt, who built it, the first iControl software development kit (SDK), for the Common Object Request Broker Architecture (CORBA), was released on 25 May 2001, with the SOAP (Simple Object Access Protocol) version a few months behind. F5 was then a hardware company whose product support was not ready to help application developers, so in 2003 DevCentral was created to support them, and in his words it was born on a PC under his desk. Pruitt moved to the community full time in 2007. The community marked its 20th anniversary in June 2023.

What made it indispensable was iRules. BIG-IP version 9 rewrote the data plane as the Traffic Management Operating System (TMOS), and iRules, the scripting feature that F5's reference still introduces as a powerful and flexible way to manage network traffic and that is built on the Tcl language, needed worked examples more than manuals. The winners of the first contest, called iRule, Do You?, were announced on 31 October 2005. The iRules Wiki opened on DevCentral on 30 January 2006 and stayed there until May 2019, when it moved to F5's CloudDocs site, where the master lists of commands, events and operators, the changes by BIG-IP version and the list of disabled Tcl commands are kept today. The contest itself came back in 2026, at F5's AppWorld conference, with 10,000 dollars in prizes.

The site today has four main sections. Technical Forums is the question-and-answer board, by far the largest part, with 68,080 topics when its category list was read on 12 November 2026. F5 Technical Articles (6,460 topics) are written by F5 staff. Community CodeShare (1,420) holds members' iRules, scripts and automation, posted from a template that asks for the problem solved, the steps and the version tested on. F5 Security Insights (235) carries commentary from F5 Labs and F5's security practitioners. Around these sit curated Article Series (DevCentral Basics, an iRules series, iControl, SYN cookies, HTTP), the DevCentral Connects livestream group, events and regional user groups, among them one for Latin America, described in Spanish and carrying posts in Portuguese. In all, the site's own statistics showed 77,401 topics and 308,355 posts that day, with 691 users active in the previous 30 days.

The address has outlived several platforms, and each move broke something. A relaunch on 24 January 2022, announced under the title Ch-ch-ch-ch-changes, followed an earlier platform change that the team said had not worked out as hoped: usernames lost their spaces and were cut to 15 characters, the Questions section became Forums, CodeShare was folded into a section called CrowdSRC, and followed articles, bookmarks and private messages were not carried over. CodeShare returned as a section of its own in September 2022 after members asked for it. In 2026 the community moved again, to the Discourse forum software: the present instance was created on 23 March 2026 and its welcome post is dated 14 September 2026. The practical lesson is that a DevCentral link in an old runbook or ticket may no longer resolve, and the article is usually easier to find by its title.

The MVP award is the community's recognition scheme; F5 uses the initials without expanding them. It was created in January 2010, when the first class of seven was announced, to honour members who contribute without incentive. It is given annually to a select group of the most active, knowledgeable and impactful members, for a one-year term that can be renewed without limit, and F5 publishes no rubric for earning it: nominations come from the community, and help given outside the site, on Reddit, GitHub or Stack Overflow or at user groups, counts as well. Holders get a badge on their profile, access to a private group, and technical deep-dive and preview sessions with F5's subject matter experts, and they give feedback to F5's product team. The 2026 cohort, announced on 4 March 2026, has 37 members. It is recognition of contribution, not a certification obtained by examination.

Used well, DevCentral is the fastest way to learn how a BIG-IP feature behaves in practice; used carelessly, it is a source of stale or untested configuration. Four habits follow from its own rules. Check the version: answers span more than twenty years of releases, and the CloudDocs pages list which iRules commands and events exist in which version. Treat shared code as a starting point: the CodeShare category states that community-contributed content is not validated by F5 and is used at the reader's own risk. Sanitize what is posted: the guidelines forbid passwords and unsanitized code, in private messages too. And say when an answer was machine-written: the guidelines, at version 1.2 of 6 January 2025, require a reply generated wholly or partly by a large language model (LLM) to be labelled as such.

For anything that affects production with a deadline, the community is the wrong queue. F5's support page lists help with iRules scripts among the services of its Standard and Premium support contracts, and security fixes are published through its advisories; forum threads discuss those advisories, they do not replace them. The useful division of labour is this: the manuals say what a feature is, the knowledge base says what is broken and how F5 fixes it, and DevCentral shows what other engineers did with it.

fortinet-community.def: Fortinet's official user community - forums, knowledge-base articles, and ideas exchange for the FortiGate ecosystem.
fortinet-community.context: The Fortinet Community (community.fortinet.com, successor to the FUSE community brand) is the vendor-run home for FortiOS questions and answers, moderated knowledge-base articles, and product idea submissions. For day-to-day FortiGate troubleshooting it is the first stop after the docs - and alongside it, the independent r/fortinet subreddit carries a notably active practitioner culture.

apisec-university.def: Free, certificate-granting API-security training - the fastest on-ramp into the OWASP API Top 10 world.
apisec-university.context: APIsec University offers free online courses - API Security Fundamentals, the OWASP API Security Top 10, API authentication, gateway best practices, API penetration testing - with completion badges via Credly and certifications like CASA and ACP, serving well over a hundred thousand students. It also runs the free APISEC|CON online conference. Vendor-adjacent but genuinely educational: the courses stand on their own.
