reddit.def: The threaded, voted discussion platform whose networking and vendor subreddits carry an outsized share of real-world troubleshooting.
reddit.context: Beyond the front page, Reddit's technical subreddits are working infrastructure: r/networking for vendor-neutral engineering discussion, and per-vendor communities (r/fortinet notably active; equivalents exist across the platforms this site covers) where practitioners compare notes faster than official channels. Unofficial by nature - verify against vendor documentation - but for 'has anyone else seen this', frequently the fastest answer on the internet.

iso-27001.def: The international standard for an information security management system (ISMS) - the certification most vendor trust centres lead with.
iso-27001.context: ISO/IEC 27001 (current revision 27001:2022) certifies that an organization runs a documented, audited system for managing information-security risk across sites, development, support, and data centres. Certificates run three years with annual surveillance audits. All three vendors this site's instructor teaches - F5, Netskope, Extreme - hold it, alongside its cloud siblings 27017 and 27018.

iso-27017.def: The cloud-security extension of ISO 27001 - controls specific to being, or using, a cloud service provider.
iso-27017.context: ISO/IEC 27017:2015 supplements ISO 27002/27001 with cloud-specific guidance: shared responsibility, virtual-machine hardening, administrator operations, tenant isolation. It is not a standalone certification so much as a cloud overlay, which is why it almost always appears bundled with 27001 and 27018 on a provider's compliance page.

iso-27018.def: The privacy extension of ISO 27001 - protecting personally identifiable information processed in the public cloud.
iso-27018.context: ISO/IEC 27018:2019 sets controls for cloud providers acting as processors of PII: consent, transparency about sub-processors, data return and deletion, and restrictions on using customer data for advertising. It maps closely to GDPR obligations, and rounds out the 27001/27017/27018 trio that cloud vendors present together.

fedramp.def: The US government's standardized security-authorization program for cloud services - High, Moderate, and Low baselines.
fedramp.context: FedRAMP lets a cloud service be assessed once, against NIST SP 800-53 controls, and reused across federal agencies. The baselines scale with data sensitivity; FedRAMP High covers the government's most sensitive unclassified data. Netskope's GovCloud holds FedRAMP High; F5's Distributed Cloud carries FedRAMP authorizations - the credential public-sector buyers look for first.

pci-dss.def: The Payment Card Industry Data Security Standard (PCI DSS): the baseline of technical and operational security requirements, set by the PCI Security Standards Council, for every entity that stores, processes or transmits payment card account data or can affect the security of the environment that does; version 4.0.1, published in June 2024, is the only active version.
pci-dss.context: PCI DSS is set by the PCI (Payment Card Industry) Security Standards Council, founded in 2006 by the card brands American Express, Discover, JCB, Mastercard and Visa, and defines a baseline of network, encryption, access-control and monitoring requirements in twelve requirements. It is contractual rather than governmental: the brands and acquiring banks decide who must comply and how compliance is validated, and non-compliance carries fines and lost processing rights. It is a common scope item on vendor trust centres even when the vendor never directly handles card data, because customers deploy their products in cardholder environments, and because a provider of managed firewalls or hosting that can affect that environment is itself a service provider in the standard's own definition.
pci-dss.depth:
What it is, and what it is not. The PCI Data Security Standard (PCI DSS), in the words of the PCI Security Standards Council (PCI SSC) that maintains it, provides a baseline of technical and operational requirements designed to protect payment account data. Its audience is any entity that stores, processes or transmits cardholder data or sensitive authentication data, or could affect the security of the environment where they live: merchants, processors, acquirers, issuers and service providers alike. It is not a law. The Council itself says that whether an entity must comply, or must prove it, is decided by those who run compliance programmes, the payment brands, acquirers and payment facilitators, and that it does not set compliance validation responsibilities itself. Where the standard conflicts with law, the law applies. Some United States states have borrowed from it anyway: Minnesota in 2007 prohibited keeping some card data more than 48 hours after authorization, Nevada wrote compliance into state law two years later, and Washington followed in 2010.

Where it came from. Before 2004 each brand ran its own programme: Visa's Cardholder Information Security Program, Mastercard's Site Data Protection, American Express's Data Security Operating Policy, Discover's Information Security and Compliance and JCB's Data Security Program, each with its own requirements and its own validation. Version 1.0 of a combined standard was released on 15 December 2004, and in 2006 American Express, Discover, JCB International, MasterCard and Visa founded the Council, which they own and govern in equal shares; each incorporates PCI DSS into its own compliance programme and recognizes the assessors the Council qualifies. Versions followed in 2006, 2008, 2010 and onwards; 3.2.1 was retired on 31 March 2024. Version 4.0, published in March 2022, was the largest revision since 1.0. Version 4.0.1, published on 11 June 2024 after a request for comments that ran from December 2023 to January 2024, is a limited revision with no new or deleted requirements; 4.0 was retired on 31 December 2024, and the requirements that 4.0 had future-dated became effective on 31 March 2025. In November 2026 the Council's library still presents 4.0.1 as the current standard.

The data it protects. Account data is cardholder data, sensitive authentication data, or both. Cardholder data is at minimum the full PAN (primary account number), the number that identifies the issuer and the account, and may also include the cardholder's name, the expiration date and the service code. Sensitive authentication data (SAD) is what authenticates the cardholder or authorizes the transaction: card verification codes, full track data from the magnetic stripe or its equivalent on a chip, PINs and PIN blocks. The Council's glossary describes SAD as data that may be transmitted or processed but not stored, which is the single most important rule in the standard: a system that keeps the full track or the security code after authorization has a problem no compensating control fixes. The glossary also separates masking, which hides part of a PAN on screens and receipts, from truncation, which removes digits from a stored or transmitted PAN; tokenization replaces the PAN with an index token; and version 4.0.1 clarified how keyed cryptographic hashes can be used to render a PAN unreadable.

The twelve requirements. Version 4.0.1 groups them under six goals. Build and maintain a secure network and systems: 1, install and maintain network security controls (the term that replaced firewall in 4.0), and 2, apply secure configurations to all system components. Protect account data: 3, protect stored account data, and 4, protect cardholder data with strong cryptography during transmission over open, public networks. Maintain a vulnerability management programme: 5, protect all systems and networks from malicious software, and 6, develop and maintain secure systems and software. Implement strong access control measures: 7, restrict access by business need to know; 8, identify users and authenticate access; and 9, restrict physical access. Regularly monitor and test networks: 10, log and monitor all access, and 11, test security of systems and networks regularly. Maintain an information security policy: 12, support information security with organizational policies and programmes. Each requirement comes with testing procedures for the assessor and guidance on its intent. Version 4 added a customized approach, in which an entity meets a requirement's stated objective with its own control, beside the defined approach of following the requirement as written.

Scope is where network engineers come in. The cardholder data environment (CDE) is the people, processes and system components that store, process or transmit cardholder data or SAD, plus every system component that has unrestricted connectivity to them, whether or not it touches card data itself. Scoping is identifying all of that, and segmentation, which the glossary also calls isolation, is what keeps everything else out: the firewalls, access control lists, VLANs (virtual local area networks) and jump hosts that separate the CDE are what decide whether an assessment covers twenty servers or the whole company. A flat network puts every host in scope. The same logic explains the trust centres: the standard's definition of a service provider includes companies that provide services that control or could affect the security of card data, naming managed firewall and intrusion detection providers and hosting providers, so a vendor's cloud or managed service can be in its customers' scope even if it never sees a card number.

How compliance is proved. The brands sort merchants into levels by annual transaction volume, typically Level 1 above six million transactions a year down to Level 4 below 20,000, though the thresholds and the number of levels vary by brand. Large entities are assessed by a Qualified Security Assessor (QSA), an independent firm qualified by the Council, which produces a Report on Compliance (ROC) and an Attestation of Compliance (AOC); an Internal Security Assessor (ISA) can run assessments inside its own organization; smaller merchants complete a Self-Assessment Questionnaire (SAQ) matched to how they take payments. External vulnerability scans for Requirement 11.3.2 must come from an Approved Scanning Vendor (ASV) whose scan solution the Council has tested. What an entity must use, SAQ or ROC, is set by its acquirer or the brands, not by the Council.

What version 4 changed for engineers. Multi-factor authentication (MFA) is required for all access into the CDE, not only administrative access, with an applicability note in 4.0.1 exempting accounts that authenticate only with phishing-resistant factors. Version 4.0.1 also restored the earlier wording that patches must be installed within 30 days only for critical vulnerabilities. The new e-commerce requirements took longest to settle: Requirements 6.4.3 and 11.6.1 address the security of payment pages, 6.4.3 by managing the scripts that run on them, with a targeted risk analysis under 12.3.1 supporting 11.6.1, all effective from 31 March 2025. The payment page itself is defined broadly, including a form displayed in an inline frame inside a non-payment page. In January 2025 the Council removed 6.4.3, 11.6.1 and 12.3.1 from SAQ A, for merchants who have outsourced all account data functions, and added instead an eligibility criterion that the merchant confirm its site is not susceptible to attacks from scripts; it stressed that the requirements themselves remain in the standard.

What goes wrong. Validation is a point-in-time statement, and the record shows the gap. A former Visa chief enterprise risk officer, Ellen Richey, said in 2018 that no compromised entity had yet been found to be in compliance at the time of its breach; yet Heartland Payment Systems had been validated as compliant before its 2008 breach of more than one hundred million card numbers, Hannaford and TJX had also been validated before being breached in attacks attributed to Albert Gonzalez, and more than forty million Target customer accounts were compromised in December 2013. Tools age too. The PCI Compliance report in the Application Security Manager of F5 BIG-IP, still documented for version 17.5 in July 2026, maps a security policy against PCI-DSS 3.2, and its table still mentions 1.2, so an auditor reading that report is reading against a retired version; the same product's default masking of credit card numbers in request logs is more directly useful, because a web application firewall log full of PANs brings the logging system into scope. The web application firewall's place in the standard is older than many assume: the Council announced in April 2008 that Requirement 6.6, which offered either application code review or an application firewall for public-facing web applications, would become effective on 30 June 2008.

Its neighbours. The General Data Protection Regulation (GDPR) and Brazil's LGPD (Lei Geral de Proteção de Dados Pessoais) are laws about personal data in general, enforced by public authorities; PCI DSS is a contractual standard about one kind of data, enforced through the payment chain. ISO/IEC 27001 certifies a management system and a SOC 2 report attests to controls over time; neither substitutes for a PCI DSS assessment, although the evidence overlaps. The Council also owns sister standards for other parts of the chain, among them Point-to-Point Encryption (P2PE), PIN Transaction Security (PTS) for terminals and hardware security modules, 3-D Secure and the Secure Software Standard; the older PA-DSS (Payment Application Data Security Standard) is listed as retired. The numbers worth remembering: 12 requirements under 6 goals; version 4.0.1 of June 2024; 31 December 2024, when 4.0 was retired; 31 March 2025, when the future-dated requirements took effect; and 2004 and 2006, the first standard and the Council.

hipaa.def: The US healthcare-privacy law governing protected health information (PHI).
hipaa.context: HIPAA (1996) sets the confidentiality, integrity, and availability requirements for PHI, and its Security and Privacy Rules flow down to vendors as business associates. A vendor stating HIPAA alignment means its controls and its Business Associate Agreement support customers in regulated healthcare - a standard line on the trust centres of infrastructure vendors serving that sector.

csa-star.def: The Cloud Security Alliance's public registry of cloud-provider security postures - self-assessment through third-party certification.
csa-star.context: STAR (Security, Trust, Assurance and Risk) builds on the CSA Cloud Controls Matrix: Level 1 is a published self-assessment, Level 2 adds third-party certification (often paired with ISO 27001), all mapped to leading standards. It is the transparency layer of cloud compliance, letting buyers compare providers against one cloud-specific control framework - and it ties every vendor trust centre back to the CSA.

cyber-essentials.def: The UK government's baseline cyber-hygiene certification, run by the NCSC.
cyber-essentials.context: Cyber Essentials sets five basic technical controls (firewalls, secure configuration, access control, malware protection, patch management); Cyber Essentials Plus adds hands-on verification. It is deliberately entry-level - required for many UK public-sector contracts - and appears on vendor trust centres as evidence of the fundamentals, distinct from the depth of ISO 27001.

c5.def: Germany's government-backed cloud-security attestation, defined by the BSI.
c5.context: The Cloud Computing Compliance Criteria Catalogue (C5) was introduced by Germany's Federal Office for Information Security (BSI) to give a consistent, auditable baseline for cloud providers serving the German market. An auditor attests against the catalogue; the result is widely recognized across German and EU public and private sectors - the German counterpart to schemes like ENS (Spain) and IRAP (Australia) that cluster on multinational trust centres.

irap.def: Australia's assessment framework letting cloud services be validated against the government's security manual.
irap.context: IRAP (Information Security Registered Assessors Program) trains and endorses assessors who evaluate systems against the Australian Signals Directorate's Information Security Manual (ISM). An IRAP assessment tells Australian government customers which controls are in place and how responsibility is shared - the Australian analogue to FedRAMP, and a standard entry on the trust centres of vendors selling into that market.

data-privacy-framework.def: The mechanism for lawfully transferring personal data from the EU/UK/Switzerland to certified US companies.
data-privacy-framework.context: The EU-U.S. Data Privacy Framework (DPF), with its UK and Swiss extensions, replaced the invalidated Privacy Shield. US companies self-certify to the Department of Commerce that they meet EU-equivalent protections, enabling transatlantic data flows without additional transfer mechanisms. It sits alongside GDPR on privacy-focused trust centres as the transfer-compliance answer.

nis2.def: The EU directive massively expanding cybersecurity obligations across essential and important sectors.
nis2.context: NIS2 (Directive (EU) 2022/2555) widens the original NIS scope to far more sectors, tightens incident-reporting timelines, and adds management accountability with real penalties. It is transposed into each member state's national law, and its arrival is why vendor trust centres and blogs (Extreme's among them) now foreground NIS2 readiness for European customers.

802-1q.def: The Institute of Electrical and Electronics Engineers (IEEE) standard for bridges and virtual local area networks (VLANs), best known for the four-byte tag it inserts into an Ethernet frame to say which VLAN the frame belongs to: the reason one physical link can carry many separate layer 2 networks.
802-1q.context: The Institute of Electrical and Electronics Engineers (IEEE) standard 802.1Q inserts a 4-byte tag after the source address of an Ethernet frame: the EtherType 0x8100, then a 3-bit priority, a 1-bit drop eligible indicator and a 12-bit VLAN identifier, of which 1 to 4094 name real virtual local area networks (VLANs). A link that carries tagged frames between switches is a trunk; an access port sends and receives untagged frames and places them in one VLAN. The standard itself is much larger than the tag: its current edition, 802.1Q-2022, Bridges and Bridged Networks, is the home of bridging, spanning tree and provider bridging, maintained by the 802.1 working group, the architecture arm of the 802 family.
802-1q.depth:
What the standard is. The Institute of Electrical and Electronics Engineers (IEEE) standard 802.1Q began as the virtual local area network (VLAN) standard: the IEEE 802.1ad project page describes its own work as an amendment to IEEE Std 802.1Q-1998, and Request for Comments (RFC) 4363 of January 2006 still cites the 2003 edition by its old title, Virtual Bridged Local Area Networks. It has since become the bridging standard as a whole. The active edition, IEEE 802.1Q-2022, is titled Bridges and Bridged Networks; it supersedes 802.1Q-2018, has been amended by 802.1Qcj-2023 through 802.1Qdy-2025, and specifies how the media access control (MAC) service is supported by bridged networks and the operation of MAC Bridges and VLAN Bridges, with their management, protocols and algorithms. The old bridging standard, 802.1D, has been folded into it. It belongs to the 802.1 Working Group, which is chartered for the architecture of 802 local and metropolitan area networks, internetworking among 802 networks, security, management and the protocol layers above the MAC.

The tag. Cisco's description of the frame format is exact: 802.1Q inserts a 4-byte field between the Source Address and the Type/Length field of the original frame. The first two bytes are the Tag Protocol Identifier (TPID), 0x8100, sitting exactly where an untagged frame keeps its EtherType, so a receiver that reads that position knows a tag follows; the Internet Assigned Numbers Authority (IANA) lists 0x8100 as the Customer VLAN Tag Type, formerly called the Q-Tag, and notes it was initially assigned to Wellfleet. The next two bytes, the Tag Control Information, hold three fields: a 3-bit Priority Code Point (PCP), 0 to 7, the class-of-service value often still called 802.1p; a 1-bit Drop Eligible Indicator (DEI); and the 12-bit VLAN identifier (VID). The original EtherType follows the tag. Because the frame has changed, the switch that adds or removes a tag recomputes the frame check sequence, and a tagged frame can reach 1522 bytes instead of 1518.

The values that matter. Twelve bits give 4,096 values, and two are not ordinary VLANs. VID 0 is the null VLAN ID: a priority-tagged frame carries a PCP and no VLAN, and a bridge assigns it a VLAN on entry. VID 0xFFF, 4095, is reserved for implementation use, which is why management information bases treat it as a wildcard and the IEEE's own YANG model gives a VLAN identifier the range 1 to 4094. VID 1 is the default, used to classify untagged frames on the way into a bridge port. The single bit beside the VID changed meaning over time: it was the Canonical Format Indicator (CFI), which signalled an embedded source-routing information field, and according to a 2013 contribution by Stephen Haddock to the 802.1 group, 802.1Q-2011 replaced it on customer tags with the DEI that 802.1ad-2005 had introduced for provider tags, so that a frame can be marked as eligible for dropping under congestion.

How a bridge port uses it. The standard's vocabulary is not the vendors'. Each bridge port has a port VLAN identifier (PVID), the VID it gives to untagged frames, 1 by default in the IEEE YANG model; for each VLAN there is a member set, the ports that may send it, and an untagged set, the ports that send it without a tag. Ingress filtering, which discards frames arriving on a port outside the VLAN's member set, is disabled by default in the same model. Vendors map that onto their own words: Cisco's access port is a port whose PVID is its only VLAN, sent untagged, and its trunk's native VLAN is the PVID of a port in many member sets; ExtremeXOS adds ports to a VLAN as tagged or untagged; Linux exposes PVID and per-port VLAN membership directly once VLAN filtering is switched on in its bridge, and creates a tagged subinterface with ip link add link eth0 name eth0.100 type vlan id 100, where the protocol may be 802.1Q or 802.1ad.

Stacking tags. Service providers needed to carry many customers' VLANs without those customers having to coordinate, and the answer was a second, outer tag. IEEE 802.1ad, Provider Bridges, approved on 8 December 2005 and published on 26 May 2006 with Tony Jeffree as editor, let a service provider offer the equivalent of separate local area networks to many users over its own bridged network. Its service tag (S-Tag) uses its own EtherType, 0x88A8, which IANA lists as the IEEE Std 802.1Q Service VLAN tag identifier; the IEEE YANG model explains the name, recording that the S-VLAN, originally introduced in 802.1ad, was incorporated into 802.1Q in 2011. The outer tag comes first on the wire and the customer tag after it, a layout usually called Q-in-Q. Packet filters have to be told: in tcpdump, the first vlan keyword shifts the offsets for the rest of the expression by four bytes, and vlan 100 && vlan 200 matches VLAN 200 carried inside VLAN 100.

What goes wrong. The tag is only as safe as the configuration around it. The native VLAN, sent untagged on a trunk, is the source of double tagging: an attacker on it sends a frame with two tags, the first switch strips the outer one as native, and the next delivers the frame into the VLAN named by the inner one, a unidirectional attack that is stopped by moving the native VLAN to an unused identifier or by tagging it. Captures mislead in quieter ways. A filter written for untagged traffic decodes the wrong offsets on a tagged link unless it says vlan, and, as the Wireshark wiki warns, a capture on the host where the VLANs are configured will probably not show the tags, because the driver or the adapter strips them before the capture library sees them; a mirror port on the switch shows them reliably. And the four extra bytes still catch equipment out: a device that enforces a 1518-byte maximum discards full-size tagged frames, which shows up as large transfers stalling while small ones succeed.

Limits and successors. A 12-bit identifier means 4,094 VLANs per bridged domain. RFC 7348, which documents Virtual eXtensible Local Area Network (VXLAN), calls that limit inadequate for multi-tenant data centres and replaces the VID with a 24-bit segment identifier allowing up to 16 million segments, carried over the Internet Protocol (IP) instead of inside the Ethernet header. Stacking two tags multiplies the space instead, to at most 4,094 times 4,094 combinations. The numbers to remember are 0x8100 and 0x88A8, 4 bytes, 3 plus 1 plus 12 bits, VLANs 1 to 4094, PVID 1 by default, 1522 bytes, and the years 2005, 2011 and 2022.

802-1x.def: Port-based network access control - the IEEE standard that makes a switch port or access point authenticate before it forwards traffic.
802-1x.context: 802.1X frames the handshake: a supplicant (the device), an authenticator (the switch or AP), and an authentication server (usually RADIUS) exchange EAP over LAN until the port opens or stays closed. The standard defines that carriage, EAPOL, for wired 802 networks and for 802.11; the authenticator periodically invites a supplicant with an EAP-Request Identity sent to the multicast address 01:80:C2:00:00:03, the supplicant answers with its identity, and from there the switch relays EAP packets to the server inside RADIUS (Remote Authentication Dial-In User Service) EAP-Message attributes and acts only on the final accept or reject. It is the enforcement layer under enterprise Wi-Fi (WPA2/WPA3-Enterprise) and wired NAC, and pairs naturally with 802.1Q to place authenticated devices into the right VLAN: RFC 3580 specifies the three tunnel attributes a server returns for that, Tunnel-Type VLAN (13), Tunnel-Medium-Type 802 (6) and Tunnel-Private-Group-ID carrying the VLAN number as a string. The method inside the EAP envelope is a separate decision, and the fallbacks for devices without a supplicant, MAB and web authentication, are separate mechanisms that the same port can be configured to try in order.
802-1x.depth:
802.1X authenticates a device before its switch port or wireless association carries any traffic, using EAP to carry the exchange between the supplicant, the switch and a RADIUS server. It moves access control from a physical assumption to an identity check. The standard, part of the IEEE 802.1 family, is described in the encyclopaedia article as "an IEEE Standard for port-based network access control", and its history is short enough to tell: 802.1X-2001 defined the mechanism for Ethernet, Token Ring and FDDI; 802.1X-2004 extended it to 802.11 wireless and added supplicant-side port entities; 802.1X-2010 revised EAPOL to work with 802.1AE MACsec link encryption and 802.1AR device identity certificates. The problem it addressed is sometimes called hardware addition, the plugging of an unauthorized device into a live port, and the article recalls a 2005 incident at a large retailer as the kind of event the standard exists to prevent.

The model has three parties and two ports. The supplicant is the software on the device asking for access; the authenticator is the switch or access point whose port the device is on; the authentication server, typically a RADIUS server speaking EAP, decides. The article puts it in one line: "The authenticator acts like a security guard". On the authenticator, 802.1X-2001 defines a controlled port, which forwards traffic only after authentication, and an uncontrolled port, which always passes the EAPOL frames the authentication itself needs, with a Port Access Entity managing the state. Initiation is simple: the authenticator periodically sends an EAP-Request Identity frame to the group address 01:80:C2:00:00:03, the supplicant answers with an EAP-Response Identity, the authenticator wraps that in a RADIUS Access-Request, and the server replies in an Access-Challenge that proposes the EAP method. From then on the switch relays EAP packets it does not interpret, encapsulated per RFC 3579 in EAP-Message attributes (79) protected by a Message-Authenticator (80), and acts on the final Access-Accept or Access-Reject.

The consequence people underestimate is the shift in what a port means. Without 802.1X, a live wall jack is a trust decision made by whoever ran the cable, and a conference room, a lobby and a printer alcove are all inside the perimeter. With it, the port is nothing until an identity is presented, and the server's answer can carry policy: RFC 3580, the IEEE 802.1X RADIUS Usage Guidelines of September 2003 by Congdon, Aboba, Smith, Zorn and Roese, specifies the attributes that make the port behave. VLAN assignment uses three of them together, Tunnel-Type set to VLAN (13), Tunnel-Medium-Type set to 802 (6) and Tunnel-Private-Group-ID carrying the VLAN identifier as a string, so that the same physical port lands a finance laptop and a visitor's phone in different networks. NAS-Port-Type tells the server whether the request came from Ethernet (15) or Wireless-IEEE 802.11 (19); Calling-Station-Id carries the device's MAC address in upper-case hexadecimal with hyphens, and Called-Station-Id carries the port or access point's MAC with the SSID appended after a colon on wireless; Session-Timeout with Termination-Action set to RADIUS-Request tells the port how many seconds to allow before re-authenticating. Every one of these is a knob a policy engine turns.

The standard's limits were documented early and are still true. The article records Steve Riley's 2005 analysis, drawing on research by Svyatoslav Pidgorny, of a man-in-the-middle attack in which an attacker shares an authenticated port through a hub after the legitimate device has authenticated, since the port, once open, does not re-check per frame; the suggested mitigation was IPsec, and the standard's later answer was 802.1X-2010's integration with MACsec, which encrypts and authenticates every frame on the link. EAPOL-Logoff frames travel in the clear and can be trivially spoofed to knock an authenticated device off a port. And the devices that cannot run a supplicant at all, printers, cameras, badge readers and the long tail of embedded things, need a fallback: MAC Authentication Bypass, in which the switch submits the MAC address as the credential, and web authentication, in which a browser login is forced, both of which the same port can be configured to try after 802.1X times out. Those fallbacks are where most real deployments spend their policy effort, and each has its own entry.

What 802.1X does not decide is the method inside the EAP envelope, and that decision carries most of the security. EAP-TLS with certificates on every device is the strongest and the most administration; TEAP chains machine and user proofs; PEAP and EAP-TTLS protect a password inside a TLS tunnel and are only as safe as the client's validation of the server's certificate; EAP-pwd needs no certificates at all. The article on 802.1X and the EAP methods lays the options side by side, and the RADIUS entry carries the other half of every conversation described here.

802-3.def: 802.3 is both the Ethernet working group of the Institute of Electrical and Electronics Engineers (IEEE) and the standard it maintains, IEEE Std 802.3: every wired Ethernet speed and medium, the frame format, and Power over Ethernet (PoE).
802-3.context: The 802.3 working group of the Institute of Electrical and Electronics Engineers (IEEE) has carried Ethernet from 10BASE5 coaxial cable in 1985 to hundreds of gigabits per second. Each addition arrives as a lettered amendment and is later folded into a revision of the one standard; the edition in force is IEEE Std 802.3-2022, titled simply IEEE Standard for Ethernet. It defines Power over Ethernet (PoE) across 802.3af, 802.3at and the four-pair 802.3bt. It inherited the 1500-byte data field from the Ethernet of Digital Equipment Corporation, Intel and Xerox (DIX) and has repeatedly declined to standardize jumbo frames, which is why 9000-byte support is a vendor convention and not a clause. Its neighbours in the IEEE 802 committee are 802.1, which owns bridging and virtual local area network (VLAN) tagging, and 802.11, the wireless group.
802-3.depth:
One number, two things. The 802 committee of the Institute of Electrical and Electronics Engineers (IEEE), formally the Standards Committee for local area networks (LAN) and metropolitan area networks (MAN), gives each technology to a working group, and 802.3 is its Ethernet Working Group; its neighbours are 802.1 (Higher Layer LAN Protocols, which includes bridging) and 802.11 (Wireless LAN). The same number names the document the group maintains. IEEE Std 802.3-2022, approved on 13 May 2022 and published on 29 July 2022, superseded the 2018 edition, which had superseded that of 2015. Its abstract is a fair map of the contents: operation from 1 Mb/s to 400 Gb/s with one common media access control (MAC) specification and management information base; a MAC that specifies both shared-medium (half duplex) and full duplex operation; physical layer devices (PHYs) for coaxial cable, twisted pair, optical fibre and electrical backplanes; repeaters for speeds up to 1000 Mb/s; and the provision of power over twisted pair. Older editions and amendments carry the title Carrier Sense Multiple Access with Collision Detection (CSMA/CD) Access Method and Physical Layer Specifications; the current title is just IEEE Standard for Ethernet.

How the paper works. New work is a project with a letter suffix, run by a task force: after 802.3z the letters doubled (802.3ab, 802.3ad), and the series has now reached 802.3dj and beyond. An approved project is an amendment to the base standard, and every few years a revision merges the amendments into a new edition. The 2018 edition collected 14 amendments, from 802.3bt-2018 to 802.3cv-2021; the 2022 edition has 12 approved so far, from 802.3ck-2022 to 802.3dk-2026, two corrigenda and eight proposed amendments. As read on 12 November 2026, the group's page lists as active, among others, P802.3dj (200 Gb/s, 400 Gb/s, 800 Gb/s and 1.6 Tb/s), P802.3dv (signalling at 400 Gb/s per lane) and the next revision of the base standard, and names David Law as chair. The practical consequence is that a name on a datasheet, such as 802.3bt, points at a document that stops existing on its own once a revision absorbs it; the content lives on as clauses. Three clause numbers are quoted often enough to be worth knowing: Clause 28 is auto-negotiation, Clause 33 is Power over Ethernet (PoE) and Clause 78 is Energy Efficient Ethernet.

The speeds, in order. IEEE Std 802.3-1985 specified the MAC and 10BASE5, 10 Mb/s over 500 metres of coaxial cable. Then came 10BASE2, also on coaxial cable (802.3a-1988, 185 metres), 10BASE-T on twisted pair (802.3i-1990, 100 metres), Fast Ethernet (802.3u, approved on 14 June 1995), full duplex and flow control (802.3x, 20 March 1997), Gigabit Ethernet (802.3z, July 1998) and its twisted-pair form, 1000BASE-T (802.3ab, June 1999), link aggregation (802.3ad, March 2000), 10 Gb/s (802.3ae-2002), Ethernet in the First Mile for access networks (802.3ah-2004), 10GBASE-T (802.3an-2006), 40 and 100 Gb/s (802.3ba, June 2010), Energy Efficient Ethernet (802.3az, September 2010), 2.5GBASE-T and 5GBASE-T (802.3bz, 22 September 2016), 200 and 400 Gb/s (802.3bs, 6 December 2017), 10 Mb/s on a single pair for cars and factories (802.3cg, 7 November 2019) and 800 Gb/s (802.3df, 16 February 2024). The names follow a loose grammar. The group's chair wrote in 2009 that the nomenclature had never been particularly consistent from project to project: broadly, the first letter after the dash gives the medium or wavelength, the second the coding or reach, and at 10 Gb/s and above a trailing number counts lanes.

The frame. What every one of those physical layers carries has barely changed: a 7-octet preamble and a 1-octet start frame delimiter, then 6 octets of destination address, 6 of source address, 2 of Length/Type, 46 to 1500 octets of client data and padding, and a 4-octet frame check sequence (FCS). That gives the 64-octet minimum and the 1518-octet maximum of a basic frame. The two-octet field has a history. The original IEEE standard defined it as a length, to be followed by a Logical Link Control (LLC) header, while the earlier Ethernet of Digital Equipment Corporation, Intel and Xerox (DIX) used it as a type, and the Internet followed DIX: Request for Comments (RFC) 894 of April 1984 put the Internet Protocol (IP) directly behind type 0800 hexadecimal, and RFC 1122 required every host to send and accept that format and to default to it, treating the LLC form of RFC 1042 as an option. The IEEE closed the gap in the 802.3x supplement, which declared values of 0x0600 (1536) and above to be types and values up to 0x05DC (1500) to be lengths; until then, as Rich Seifert wrote to the 802.1 mailing list in April 1996 while that draft was in progress, 802.3 said nothing about type values. That is why a capture shows nearly all IP traffic as Ethernet II frames although the cabling, switches and transceivers are all 802.3.

Why there is no jumbo clause. The frame has grown twice, and both times only around the data. A tagged frame may be 1522 octets to make room for the 802.1Q tag, and the Frame Expansion project, 802.3as-2006, created the envelope frame of up to 2000 octets for stacked tags and security headers. Its objectives, approved on 18 November 2004, are explicit: maintain the maximum data field length of 1500 octets, and increase the frame size exclusively for optional prefix and suffix fields; the task force chose 2000 octets in March 2005. The chair's 2011 overview summarizes the position in four words, jumbo frames not supported, while the Ethernet Alliance had conceded in 2009 that jumbo frames are not going away. So the sizes are whatever each maker decided. ExtremeXOS defines a jumbo frame as anything larger than 1522 bytes including the cyclic redundancy check and accepts a configured size from 1,523 to 9,216; F5 BIG-IP gives each virtual local area network (VLAN) a maximum transmission unit (MTU) of 1500 by default and counts it without the layer 2 header. Two devices that both claim jumbo support can therefore disagree by a few octets about the same frame, and that disagreement is a drop, not a negotiation.

Power over Ethernet. Power over the data cable is an 802.3 specification in three steps. IEEE Std 802.3af-2003, approved in June 2003, defined what is now called Type 1: 15.4 W at the power sourcing equipment (PSE) and 13 W guaranteed at the powered device (PD). IEEE Std 802.3at-2009 added Type 2 with 30 W at the source and 25.5 W at the device. IEEE Std 802.3bt-2018, approved on 27 September 2018, added Types 3 and 4, which can use all four pairs: 60 W and 90 W at the source, 51 W and 71.3 W at the device. The Types interoperate, with the obvious limit that a high-power device behind an older source receives only what that source can give.

Where the number shows up, and what it is not. In the Link Layer Discovery Protocol (LLDP), the 802.3 group has its own organizationally specific elements under the identifier 00-12-0F: MAC/PHY Configuration/Status, Power via MDI (the medium dependent interface), Link Aggregation and Maximum Frame Size, which is how a device tells its neighbour its speed and duplex state and its power needs. What 802.3 does not cover is equally useful to know. The VLAN tag, bridging and spanning tree belong to 802.1, although 802.3 enlarged the frame for the tag; LLC is 802.2; Wi-Fi is 802.11 and shares only the address format. And 802.3 is not only the modern switched, full-duplex Ethernet: the half-duplex CSMA/CD procedure and repeaters are still in the standard, for speeds up to 1000 Mb/s.

wifi.def: Wi-Fi is the Wi-Fi Alliance's registered name for wireless local area networking built on the IEEE (Institute of Electrical and Electronics Engineers) 802.11 standards, and the mark of its Wi-Fi CERTIFIED interoperability programme: the IEEE writes the standard, the Alliance owns the name and certifies products.
wifi.context: Every Wi-Fi generation is an IEEE (Institute of Electrical and Electronics Engineers) 802.11 amendment: Wi-Fi 4 is 802.11n, Wi-Fi 5 is 802.11ac, Wi-Fi 6 and 6E are 802.11ax, Wi-Fi 7 is 802.11be-2024. The IEEE 802.11 working group writes the standard; the Wi-Fi Alliance owns the Wi-Fi trademark and runs the interoperability certification, which is why marketing says Wi-Fi 7 while datasheets say 802.11be. Underneath every generation sits the same constraint: a radio channel is a shared, half-duplex medium, so devices take turns and the airtime a slow or distant client uses is airtime no one else has. Security rides on top through Wi-Fi Protected Access (WPA2 and WPA3), certified separately from the speed generations.
wifi.depth:
Two bodies share the word. The IEEE (Institute of Electrical and Electronics Engineers) 802.11 working group writes the standard for wireless local area networks: its first project was authorized on 21 March 1991 and the original IEEE 802.11 was approved on 26 June 1997. The Wi-Fi Alliance certifies products against it. Six companies founded it in 1999 as the Wireless Ethernet Compatibility Alliance; in 2000 it adopted the name Wi-Fi for its work and became the Wi-Fi Alliance, and the first Wi-Fi CERTIFIED products, at up to 11 Mbps, appeared that year. Wi-Fi is a registered trademark of the Alliance. The plain Wi-Fi name, the Wi-Fi Protected Access marks WPA2 and WPA3, and the generation names Wi-Fi 4 to Wi-Fi 7 are offered for public use without a licence, but the Wi-Fi CERTIFIED marks are reserved for members whose products pass certification. That is the practical difference between a device that implements 802.11 and one that is certified: the second has been tested for interoperability against a test bed of other vendors' equipment.

The standard grows by amendments, each named with letters and the year it was approved, that are later folded into a consolidated revision. On the IEEE's own timeline, 802.11a, a higher-speed physical layer for 5 GHz, and 802.11b, the same for 2.4 GHz, were both approved on 16 September 1999; 802.11g, a higher rate for 2.4 GHz, on 12 June 2003; 802.11n, High Throughput, on 11 September 2009; 802.11ac, Very High Throughput below 6 GHz, on 11 December 2013; 802.11ax, High Efficiency WLAN (wireless local area network), on 9 February 2021, published on 19 May 2021; and 802.11be, Extremely High Throughput, on 26 September 2024, published on 22 July 2025. 802.11be's stated aim is at least 30 Gbit/s at the MAC (medium access control) service access point, on carrier frequencies between 1 and 7.250 GHz, while staying compatible with earlier devices in 2.4, 5 and 6 GHz. The working group's timeline of 27 October 2026 lists the projects now under way, among them 802.11bn, Ultra High Reliability, whose draft 2.0 drew 77 per cent approval in a letter ballot of 2 September 2026, and 802.11bt, post-quantum cryptography, authorized in September 2025.

The generation numbers are newer than most of the standards they name. On 3 October 2018 the Wi-Fi Alliance announced Wi-Fi 6 for devices supporting 802.11ax and applied the scheme backwards: Wi-Fi 5 for 802.11ac and Wi-Fi 4 for 802.11n. From then on, certification programmes based on major 802.11 releases took generational names, starting with Wi-Fi CERTIFIED 6 in 2019. Wi-Fi 6E is Wi-Fi 6 extended into the 6 GHz band, which the Alliance describes as the first new spectrum made available to Wi-Fi since 1999, opened in 2020. Wi-Fi CERTIFIED 7 (Wi-Fi 7 being, in the words of Extreme Networks' guide, officially known as IEEE 802.11be) launched on 8 January 2024, eight months before the IEEE approved the amendment. Its headline features are 320 MHz channels where a country makes 6 GHz available, Multi-Link Operation across bands, 4K QAM (quadrature amplitude modulation) with transmission rates 20 per cent higher than Wi-Fi 6's 1024 QAM, 512-frame compressed block acknowledgements and several resource units for one station. The Alliance now describes a Wi-Fi 8 built around reliability and access points that coordinate instead of competing for spectrum. Its own pages are not consistent about dates (the timeline places Wi-Fi 4 in 2007 and Wi-Fi 5 in 2013, the technology page in 2009 and 2014), so the IEEE approval dates are the ones to quote.

The constraint behind every generation is that the medium is shared and half duplex. Cisco Meraki's documentation puts it plainly: 802.11 is a shared medium, and the half-duplex nature of wireless together with protocol overhead means that aggregate throughput is typically 50 per cent or less of the advertised data rate. Every device on a channel takes turns, so a slow client transmitting for a long time consumes the airtime of several fast ones, and management frames go out at the lowest rate the network allows. Meraki's high-density guidance follows from that: more than five SSIDs (service set identifiers) can consume 20 per cent or more of the airtime in management frames alone, raising the minimum data rate reduces overhead, and 20 MHz channels are a common recommendation in dense deployments because bonding channels for speed leaves fewer unique channels to reuse and raises co-channel interference. Adding access points on overlapping channels makes the contention worse, not better.

Headline speeds come from wider channels, more spatial streams and denser modulation, all of which need conditions a busy office rarely provides; Meraki notes, for instance, that most phones and tablets have only one or two antennas, which limits the spatial streams they can use. That is why designing for coverage alone, the old method of placing the fewest access points that give acceptable signal strength everywhere, produces a network that shows full bars and performs badly: it ignores how many clients there are, what they can do and what their applications need. The 6 GHz band changed the arithmetic more than any modulation scheme, because it added clean, wide channels that older devices cannot use and therefore cannot slow down, but its availability is set by each country's regulator, so the same Wi-Fi 7 access point offers different channels in different markets.

Security is certified separately, under the Wi-Fi Protected Access (WPA) name. The IEEE's security work sits in amendments such as 802.11i, MAC Security Enhancements, approved on 24 June 2004, and 802.11w, Protected Management Frames, approved on 11 September 2009. In 2017 Mathy Vanhoef of KU Leuven published KRACK (key reinstallation attacks): by manipulating and replaying messages of the WPA2 four-way handshake, an attacker in range could make a victim reinstall a key already in use, reset its nonce and decrypt traffic, against personal and enterprise networks and every cipher, because the flaw was in the standard rather than in one product. It was fixed by backwards-compatible patches to clients and access points, and changing the password did nothing. On 25 June 2018 the Alliance introduced WPA3, citing more than a decade of WPA2: WPA3-Personal replaces the pre-shared-key exchange with Simultaneous Authentication of Equals (SAE) to resist password guessing, WPA3-Enterprise offers the equivalent of 192-bit cryptographic strength, and every WPA3 network must use Protected Management Frames. WPA3 is now mandatory for Wi-Fi CERTIFIED devices, and Wi-Fi Enhanced Open adds unauthenticated encryption to open networks.

WPA3 did not end the story. In April 2019 Vanhoef and Eyal Ronen published Dragonblood: in transition mode, where WPA3 and WPA2 share one password so older clients can still join, an attacker could stand up a rogue WPA2-only network, lure WPA3-capable clients onto it and run a dictionary attack on the captured handshake; implementations of the Dragonfly handshake also leaked timing and cache side channels. Enterprise mode with per-user credentials is a different security model from a shared passphrase, and the friction in moving to it is usually legacy devices that support neither WPA3 nor modern enterprise authentication, which makes it a procurement problem wearing the costume of a technical one. The numbers worth remembering are 1997 for the first standard, 2000 for the Wi-Fi name, Wi-Fi 4, 5, 6 and 7 for 802.11n, ac, ax and be, 2.4, 5 and 6 GHz, 320 MHz as the widest Wi-Fi 7 channel, and 50 per cent as the usual ceiling on real aggregate throughput.

wpa.def: The Wi-Fi Alliance's security scheme for wireless LANs - WPA2 and WPA3 today, replacing the broken WEP.
wpa.context: WPA (Wi-Fi Protected Access) came as an urgent fix for WEP; WPA2 made AES-CCMP the standard; WPA3 (2018) added stronger handshakes (SAE) and forward secrecy. Each has a Personal mode (pre-shared key) and an Enterprise mode that delegates authentication to 802.1X/RADIUS. When a network prompts for 'WPA2-Enterprise', that is WPA riding on the port-based access control from the 802.1 group.

decnet.def: Digital Equipment Corporation's networking suite - the protocol that ran the VAX era, evolving from proprietary roots towards OSI.
decnet.context: DECnet (formally Digital Network Architecture, DNA) connected DEC's PDP and VAX machines from the mid-1970s. Phase IV was the widely deployed peer-to-peer version of the 1980s; Phase V realigned it onto OSI protocols as the industry standardized. It shared 1990s Ethernet segments with AppleTalk and IPX before TCP/IP displaced them all - a name every network engineer of the minicomputer era knew, and part of the lineage behind vendors like Cabletron that grew up wiring those machines.
decnet.depth:
DECnet was Digital Equipment Corporation's networking suite, and for a substantial period it did things TCP/IP could not. Its later phases offered a hierarchical address space, integrated naming, and a routing architecture that OSI standardized, in a coherent stack from a single vendor who supported all of it.

It lost anyway, and the reasons are more interesting than technical inferiority. TCP/IP was not owned by anyone, so it could be implemented by anyone without permission or licence, and it was already installed across the research networks that grew into the internet. A superior protocol tied to one manufacturer competes against a good-enough protocol that every manufacturer can implement, and that contest has a predictable outcome.

The pattern is worth carrying forward because it keeps recurring. Technical merit is one input among several, and openness, installed base and freedom to implement routinely beat it. Anyone evaluating a vendor's integrated stack against an open standard is having the same argument DEC's customers had, and the historical record is not encouraging for the integrated stack, however good it currently is.

xns.def: Xerox's late-1970s protocol architecture - the ancestral design that Novell IPX, and much else, copied.
xns.context: Xerox Network Systems came out of PARC alongside Ethernet itself, and its layered design (the IDP datagram at its core) became the archetype early LAN vendors cloned. Novell's IPX is XNS with the serial numbers filed off; Banyan VINES and others borrowed too. XNS itself saw little direct deployment, but as a template it shaped a generation - notably except AppleTalk, which deliberately went its own way.

appletalk.def: Apple's plug-and-play networking suite of the 1980s and 90s - zero-configuration before the term existed, now discontinued.
appletalk.context: Introduced in 1985, AppleTalk let Macs and LaserWriters self-assign addresses and find each other with no router or server - built into every Mac. It ran over LocalTalk, then EtherTalk (Ethernet) and TokenTalk (Token Ring). Unusually for its era it was not based on Xerox XNS. TCP/IP eroded it through the 1990s, and Apple ended support in Mac OS X 10.6 (Snow Leopard, 2009), pointing users to Bonjour - which carries its zero-config spirit forward on IP.
appletalk.depth:
AppleTalk was Apple's networking suite from the mid-1980s, and its defining property was that it configured itself. Plug in a machine, and it acquired an address, announced itself, and appeared in a browsable list of available printers and file servers, with no administrator involved at any point.

That was extraordinary at the time and it is easy to forget how extraordinary. The contemporary alternative involved manually assigned addresses, configuration files and someone who knew what they were doing. AppleTalk let a school or a design studio have a working network because someone plugged in cables, which is a category difference rather than an improvement.

Its zero-configuration ideas outlived the protocol itself. Apple moved to TCP/IP like everyone else, but the service-discovery concepts reappeared as Bonjour and were standardized as mDNS and DNS-SD, which is how devices still find printers and each other on a local network today. The lesson that survived is that automatic discovery is worth genuine protocol complexity, because the alternative cost is paid by every user forever rather than once by the designers.

ipx.def: Novell NetWare's networking protocols - the LAN standard of the file-server era, derived from Xerox XNS.
ipx.context: IPX (the layer-3 datagram) and SPX (the layer-4 connection protocol) were introduced by Novell in 1983, adapted from Xerox XNS's IDP and SPP. Through the late 1980s and 90s IPX/SPX was the default on NetWare LANs - and, as NetWare dominated file and print, on a huge share of business networks. Windows spoke it too. TCP/IP took over around the Windows XP era, and IPX faded to legacy - the protocol behind the NetWare that vendors like Novell built an empire on.

novell-sap.def: NetWare's Service Advertising Protocol - how servers announced 'here I am, and here's what I offer' across an IPX network.
novell-sap.context: SAP let file servers, print servers, and other NetWare services broadcast their existence and type so clients could find them without central configuration. Convenient at small scale, its periodic broadcasts became a notorious scaling problem on large IPX internetworks - routers had to carry ever-growing SAP tables, and 'SAP storms' were a real operational headache. It is a clean cautionary tale in service discovery that predates today's DNS-based approaches.

sna.def: IBM's mainframe networking architecture - the hierarchical world that predated and long coexisted with TCP/IP in the enterprise.
sna.context: Systems Network Architecture (1974) defined how terminals and controllers reached IBM mainframes, in a rigid hierarchy centred on the host (VTAM). Its link layer was SDLC. For decades SNA and TCP/IP ran side by side in banks and large enterprises, bridged and tunneled (DLSw) as IP won; later APPN added peer routing. Knowing SNA explains a great deal about why enterprise networking evolved the way it did, and about the IBM gear that shaped the industry.

ppp.def: The Point-to-Point Protocol - the standard way to run IP (and more) over a serial link, from dial-up to modern broadband.
ppp.context: PPP frames a point-to-point connection with a Link Control Protocol to bring the line up and Network Control Protocols to carry IP and other layer-3 traffic, plus built-in authentication via PAP or CHAP. It replaced the cruder SLIP, powered the dial-up internet, and lives on inside PPPoE and PPTP. When a broadband link authenticates with a username and password, PPP is usually underneath.

slip.def: The Serial Line Internet Protocol - the minimal, pre-PPP way to put IP packets on a serial line.
slip.context: SLIP does almost nothing: it marks IP packet boundaries on a serial link and no more - no addressing negotiation, no authentication, no support for protocols other than IP, no error detection. It carried the early dial-up internet until PPP, with all the features SLIP lacked, replaced it. A compressed variant (CSLIP) squeezed TCP/IP headers. It survives mainly as history and in tiny embedded contexts.

ml-ppp.def: Multilink PPP - bundling several physical links into one logical PPP connection for more bandwidth.
ml-ppp.context: Multilink PPP (MP) fragments traffic across multiple links - two ISDN B-channels, several serial lines - and reassembles it at the far end, presenting one pipe of their combined capacity. It was the classic way to get more than a single circuit's throughput before cheap high-speed links, common on ISDN and bonded T1s, and it relies on the same LCP/authentication machinery as plain PPP.

chap.def: The Challenge-Handshake Authentication Protocol - PPP's secure alternative to sending a password in the clear.
chap.context: CHAP authenticates by challenge and response: the authenticator sends a random challenge, the peer replies with a hash of the challenge plus a shared secret, and the secret itself never crosses the wire. It can also re-challenge mid-session. Microsoft's MS-CHAP variants extended it. It is the safer of PPP's two authentication options - the other, PAP, sends the password in plaintext - and the pattern recurs throughout network authentication.

pap.def: The Password Authentication Protocol - PPP's simplest, and least safe, way to log in: the password in plaintext.
pap.context: PAP sends the username and password across the link unprotected, in a single exchange. It is trivial to implement and trivial to sniff, which is why CHAP exists and why PAP is only acceptable when the link itself is already encrypted or trusted. It endures as a fallback and as the textbook example of why authentication protocols evolved towards challenge-response and away from sending the secret.

hdlc.def: High-Level Data Link Control - the ISO framing standard that underlies a whole family of serial protocols.
hdlc.context: HDLC defines how to delimit and error-check frames on a synchronous serial link, and it is foundational: X.25's LAPB, Frame Relay, ISDN's LAPD, and Cisco's default serial encapsulation are all HDLC-derived. It descends from IBM's SDLC, generalized by ISO into a vendor-neutral standard. You rarely configure 'HDLC' by name, but its frame structure is quietly under much of classic WAN networking.

sdlc.def: IBM's Synchronous Data Link Control - the link-layer protocol of SNA, and the ancestor of HDLC.
sdlc.context: SDLC (mid-1970s) was IBM's bit-oriented, synchronous link protocol for connecting terminals and controllers into SNA. ISO generalized it into HDLC, which in turn seeded LAPB, LAPD, and the rest of the serial family - so SDLC sits at the root of that tree. In its own right it carried IBM mainframe traffic for decades, and migrating SDLC to IP (SDLC-to-LLC conversion, DLSw) was a standard enterprise project as TCP/IP took over.

frame-relay.def: The packet-switched WAN service that replaced X.25 and defined enterprise connectivity in the 1990s and 2000s.
frame-relay.context: Frame Relay descends directly from X.25 (both trace to the 1976 packet-switching work) but strips out the per-hop error correction X.25 needed on noisy analog lines, betting on cleaner digital links for speed. Sites bought virtual circuits (identified by DLCI) with a committed information rate (CIR) instead of a mesh of leased lines. It was the WAN workhorse until MPLS (Multiprotocol Label Switching) and IP VPNs displaced it - the service a generation of enterprise routers was built to speak.

x25.def: The first widely deployed packet-switching standard - ITU-T's 1976 protocol that ran WANs, ATMs, and card networks for decades.
x25.context: X.25 was finalized by the CCITT (now ITU-T) in 1976 - older than IPv4 and the OSI model - as a virtual-circuit packet service over the noisy analog links of the day, with heavy per-hop error checking (its link layer, LAPB, is HDLC-based). It carried financial transactions, airline reservations, and early corporate WANs; credit-card networks used it into the 2010s, and aviation still does. Frame Relay is its leaner successor. A genuine ancestor of modern packet networking.

x21.def: ITU-T's interface for circuit-switched data networks - the serial physical-layer standard that often sat beneath X.25.
x21.context: X.21 defines the physical and signalling interface between data terminal equipment and a circuit-switched public data network - the connector, voltages, and call-setup handshake. It was used directly on circuit-switched data networks and as the physical layer under X.25 in parts of Europe. Largely historical now, it is the companion 'X-dot' standard to X.25: X.25 the packet protocol, X.21 the serial interface it could ride on.

utp.def: Unshielded twisted pair - the copper cabling that carries almost every wired office connection.
utp.context: UTP bundles four pairs of wires, each pair twisted to cancel interference - no shield, just geometry. It is the default medium of structured cabling: cheap, flexible, terminated on RJ45, and specified by category (Cat 5e, 6, 6A) for what speeds and distances it supports. When shielding is added for noisy environments, the cable stops being 'U' and enters shielded-twisted-pair territory.
utp.depth:
Unshielded twisted pair carries essentially all copper Ethernet, and the twisting is the entire engineering idea. Two conductors carrying equal and opposite signals pick up interference identically, and the receiver subtracts, so noise common to both cancels out.

That is why the untwisting matters at termination. Stripping too much jacket and untwisting the pairs to reach the punchdown degrades exactly the property the cable relies on, and it is the most common cause of a link that certifies badly or negotiates a lower speed than it should. Shielded variants exist for genuinely noisy environments and require proper bonding to ground, which if done wrong performs worse than unshielded cable would have.

shielded-twisted-pair.def: Twisted-pair cable with a conductive screen, of foil, braid or both, around the whole cable, around each pair, or both: named in ISO/IEC 11801 by where the screen sits (F/UTP, U/FTP, S/FTP, SF/UTP and so on), and effective only when that screen is continuous and bonded to ground.
shielded-twisted-pair.context: The international naming reads in two halves around a slash: the letters before it describe the cable's overall screen (U for unscreened, F for foil, S for braid, SF for braid and foil) and the letters after it the screening of each pair, ending in TP for twisted pair. So F/UTP is an overall foil over unscreened pairs, the cable trade catalogues long called FTP; U/FTP foils each pair with no overall screen; and S/FTP puts a braid over individually foiled pairs, the construction often still sold as STP, shielded twisted pair. Shielding earns its place where electromagnetic interference (EMI) is heavy and where alien crosstalk between neighbouring cables limits 10-gigabit copper; Category 7 and 7A require an S/FTP construction, and Category 8 requires a screened cable of some kind. Its condition is a continuous screen, terminated all the way round at every jack and bonded into the telecommunications grounding system.
shielded-twisted-pair.depth:
What the screen does. Twisted pair already fights noise through its twist; a screen adds a physical barrier. In Panduit's description it is a continuous shield, typically aluminium foil, braided copper or both, around the pairs, which keeps the cable's own signals in and external interference out. Two problems make it worth the trouble. One is alien crosstalk, signals from one cable coupling into the cable beside it, which became significant at the frequencies 10GBASE-T needs and which unscreened Category 6A cable can only fight with spacing and tighter twists. The other is electromagnetic interference (EMI) from the equipment around the cable, the concern that keeps shielded systems common in healthcare, defence, aerospace, broadcasting and media production.

Reading the names. The designations come from an informative annex of ISO/IEC 11801, the international cabling standard (Annex E in the 2010 edition, Annex D, 'Acronyms for balanced cables', in Part 1 of the 2017 series); informative means they are not required for compliance, which is why catalogues still mix them with older names. The pattern is XX/YZZ. XX is the overall screen: U for none, F for foil, S for braid, SF for braid and foil. Y is the screen on each pair, with the same letters. ZZ is the element, TP for twisted pair. That gives U/UTP, the ordinary unscreened cable; F/UTP, overall foil over unscreened pairs; U/FTP, foiled pairs with no overall screen; F/FTP, foil over foiled pairs; SF/UTP, braid and foil over unscreened pairs; and S/FTP and SF/FTP, a braid, or braid and foil, over foiled pairs. Fluke Networks notes the trade names that survive alongside: F/UTP is often called FTP and S/FTP often STP, so an order for 'STP cable' can mean any of several constructions.

Bonding and grounding. A screen is a conductor, and it helps only when it is part of an equipotential bonding system. Panduit lists the two jobs that system does, equalizing voltage and giving surge currents a return path, and the standards behind it, among them ANSI/TIA-607-E, ANSI/TIA-942-C and the Institute of Electrical and Electronics Engineers (IEEE) standards 142 and 1100. Equipment and patch panels are bonded to the racks to create one grounding reference, the busbars and bonding backbone of the telecommunications grounding system are inspected for corrosion and loose connections, and each cable screen is terminated with 360-degree contact around the jack so that the shield is continuous through every connection. Belden recommends grounding a shield at both ends with a path to ground of less than 1 ohm, since otherwise a common-mode potential difference can drive current and create a ground loop, and observes that cutting the shield back at one end simply leaves it exposed to the next point of danger; Panduit, more cautiously, calls grounding at both ends sometimes recommended but something that must be done properly to avoid ground loops. Both describe the same discipline: a screen that is bonded everywhere or treated with care everywhere, never one that is left floating where somebody happened to stop.

When to use it. For Category 6 and 6A the choice is open, since both can be built unscreened or screened. For Category 7 and 7A, which are ISO/IEC grades the Telecommunications Industry Association does not recognize, an S/FTP construction is required, and for Category 8 a screened cable is required, with S/FTP the likely construction in 22 American Wire Gauge (AWG) according to Siemon's standards director. The cost is not only the cable, which is stiffer and thicker, but the whole system: screened jacks and panels, bonded racks and installers who terminate the screen properly. Panduit's own example of what goes wrong is instructive: a Category 7A cable fitted with Category 6A shielded connectors is, as a system, a shielded Category 6A link. The practical test is therefore the environment and the plant, not the catalogue: heavy interference, dense bundles running 10-gigabit or faster copper, or a category that demands a screen, in a building whose bonding network exists and is maintained.

The acronym. STP also stands for Spanning Tree Protocol, the switching protocol, which is a common source of confusion in sentences about data centres.

cable-categories.def: The performance grades of twisted-pair cabling: categories for components in both Telecommunications Industry Association (TIA) and ISO/IEC usage, and classes for whole channels in ISO/IEC 11801, from Category 5e (Class D, 100 MHz) to Category 8 (Classes I and II, 2000 MHz).
cable-categories.context: Each grade is specified to a frequency, which determines the Ethernet speeds and distances it supports. Category 5e, Class D, is specified to 100 MHz and carries gigabit Ethernet over a 100 m channel. Category 6, Class E, to 250 MHz, carries 10GBASE-T only over shortened runs, within the limits of the Telecommunications Industry Association's bulletin TSB-155-A. Category 6A, Class EA, to 500 MHz, carries 10GBASE-T over the full 100 m. Categories 7 and 7A, Classes F and FA, to 600 and 1000 MHz, are ISO/IEC grades that TIA does not recognize, require S/FTP cable and use non-RJ45 connectors. Category 8, ISO/IEC Classes I and II, to 2000 MHz, supports 25GBASE-T and 40GBASE-T over channels of only 30 m with two connectors, and requires screened cable. A channel is graded by its weakest part: a Category 6A link patched with Category 5e cords is a Category 5e channel.
cable-categories.depth:
Where the categories came from. The first TIA cabling standard of 1991 was followed by technical bulletins giving cable and connector specifications for Categories 3, 4 and 5, which 568-A absorbed in 1995; Category 5e was defined in an addendum of 1999. The later grades raised the specified frequency: Category 6 to 250 MHz, Category 6A to 500 MHz, enough for 10GBASE-T over the full 100 m, and the higher grades to 600, 1000 and 2000 MHz for shielded, short-reach or data centre use.

Categories and classes. ISO/IEC 11801 separates the component, graded by category, from the channel built out of components, graded by class: Class D from Category 5e, E from 6, EA from 6A, F from 7, FA from 7A, and I and II from Categories 8.1 and 8.2. TIA uses the category for both and does not recognize Category 7 or 7A, which require S/FTP construction and non-RJ45 interfaces of the IEC 61076-3 family; Panduit's own technical brief describes them as recognized mainly in Europe, with little adoption elsewhere and no path to 25GBASE-T or 40GBASE-T. The connector matters as much as the cable: Categories 5e to 6A and Category 8.1 use the IEC 60603-7 modular jack, the RJ45 style, while 7, 7A and 8.2 do not.

Category 8. Category 8 broke the pattern of earlier grades in three ways, as Siemon's standards director set out: it is characterized to 2000 MHz, it is limited to a 30 m channel with two connectors, and it requires shielded cable, most likely 22 AWG (American Wire Gauge) S/FTP. ISO/IEC recognizes two classes, Class I on the RJ45-style connector and Class II on non-RJ45 interfaces, and TIA's Category 8 corresponds to Class I, which lets a jack-to-jack link be installed now and patched with Category 6A cords until the equipment changes. These channels are aimed at server-to-switch connections at the edge of the data centre, and they are not supersets of Class FA below 1000 MHz.

What the grade does not say. A category on the cable jacket describes a component, and a channel is only as good as its worst component, so cords, jacks and panels have to be of the same grade or better. The standards also move: ANSI/TIA-568.2-E of October 2024 added direct current (DC) resistance unbalance limits for Categories 5e, 6 and 6A, so links certified to the previous edition may not meet the current one, and it now carries an annex on delivering power over twisted pair, which ties the choice of category to Power over Ethernet and to how tightly cables are bundled.

rj45.def: The eight-position modular jack and plug on the end of nearly every Ethernet cord, properly the 8P8C (eight position, eight contact) connector of IEC 60603-7; 'RJ45' is a name borrowed from the telephone network.
rj45.context: RJ stands for registered jack, a family of telephone network interface jacks. The original RJ45 used keying, so an ordinary 8P8C plug fits an RJ45 receptacle but not the other way round, and what the industry calls RJ45 connectors are, in Arrow's words, in fact 8P8C modular connectors. The name stuck to every eight-pin modular connector anyway. In the cabling standards the interface is IEC 60603-7, used by Categories 5e to 6A and by Category 8.1 (ISO/IEC Class I, the equivalent of the Telecommunications Industry Association's Category 8); Category 7, 7A and 8.2 systems use other connectors. It terminates four twisted pairs in the T568A or T568B order, as plugs on cords and as keystone jacks in panels and outlets.
rj45.depth:
The name. Registered jacks were defined as standard interfaces for connecting equipment to the telephone network, and that is still where they belong: in the United States, the rules for customer premises wiring require plugs and jacks used with inside wiring to conform to the technical criteria published by the Administrative Council for Terminal Attachments (ACTA), whose connector requirements document is TIA-1096-A. RJ45 was one of those telephone interfaces, and it used keying. Ethernet borrowed the shape of the eight-position modular connector, not the registered jack, but the shorter name was already in every catalogue and stayed there.

The connector. 8P8C describes the geometry: eight positions, spaced about 1 mm apart, each fitted with a contact. The cabling standards specify it as IEC 60603-7, in versions graded to the category of the system, and ISO/IEC 11801-1 groups Categories 5, 6, 6A and 8.1 around the same jack face. That shared interface is what lets a Category 8 Class I link accept Category 6A cords, while the systems that abandoned it for other interfaces, Categories 7, 7A and 8.2, have stayed niche, Panduit noting very limited adoption of Categories 7 and 7A outside Europe.

In practice. Each of the four pairs lands on a fixed pair of positions under the T568A or T568B assignment, and the same plug or jack serves gigabit, multi-gigabit and powered links. Category matters at the connector as much as in the cable, since a channel is graded by its weakest component and a jack of a lower grade turns the whole channel into that grade.

t568a-t568b.def: The two TIA-568 pinouts for terminating twisted pair on RJ45 - identical performance, different wire-to-pin order.
t568a-t568b.context: T568A and T568B differ only in swapping the green and orange pairs' positions. Either works; what matters is consistency - both ends the same scheme yields a straight-through cable, one end of each yields a crossover. B is the de facto habit in much of the market, A is preferred in some government and residential specs. The rule every installer learns: pick one scheme per site and never mix.
t568a-t568b.depth:
T568A and T568B are the two standard pin assignments for eight-position modular plugs, differing only in whether the orange and green pairs are swapped. Electrically they are equivalent, and a link works as long as both ends use the same one.

The rule that follows is simple and constantly broken: pick one and use it throughout a site. Mixing them produces a crossover cable, which modern equipment with automatic MDI-X detection will silently accommodate, which is worse than failing because the inconsistency survives undetected until someone connects equipment that does not. Labelling the standard in the wiring closet is the whole of the discipline.

crossover-cable.def: A patch cord wired T568A on one end and T568B on the other - once required to connect like devices, now made obsolete by auto-MDIX.
crossover-cable.context: Ethernet's transmit and receive pairs had to line up: connecting a PC to a switch used a straight-through cable, but PC-to-PC or switch-to-switch needed the pairs crossed. Gigabit-era auto-MDIX let ports detect and swap electronically, so any modern port pair works with any cable. The crossover survives as a toolbox relic, a lab trick for ancient gear, and a recurring exam question.

plenum.def: The fire rating that decides where a cable may legally run - plenum (CMP) for air-handling spaces, riser (CMR) for vertical shafts.
plenum.context: Air-handling plenums spread smoke fast, so cable jacketed for those spaces (CMP) must burn slowly and emit little smoke; riser-rated CMR handles floor-to-floor shafts; general-purpose ratings cover the rest. Ratings nest downward - plenum can substitute for riser, never the reverse. Outside North America the parallel vocabulary is LSZH (low smoke, zero halogen). It is the code-compliance dimension of cabling, enforced by inspectors rather than by link testers.
plenum.depth:
Plenum-rated cable is required in spaces used for air return, typically above suspended ceilings, because those spaces move air throughout a building. The rating is about what the jacket does in a fire: ordinary PVC produces dense toxic smoke that the ventilation system would then distribute everywhere.

This is a building code requirement rather than a networking preference, and it is enforced by inspection. The cable costs several times more, which is why the temptation to run a few metres of ordinary cable through a ceiling is real and why it is a genuinely dangerous economy. If air moves through the space, the cable in it needs the rating, and the question of whether a given ceiling is a plenum is one for the building's mechanical drawings rather than for the network team.

single-mode-fiber.def: The long-haul fibre: a core so narrow light travels one path - distance measured in tens of kilometres, not hundreds of meters.
single-mode-fiber.context: Single-mode fibre's ~9-micron core admits a single propagation mode, eliminating the modal dispersion that limits multimode, so runs stretch from campus links to intercontinental cables. Standardized as OS1/OS2, usually yellow-jacketed, and driven by laser optics that historically cost more than multimode's - a gap that has narrowed enough that many new builds simply choose single-mode everywhere.
single-mode-fiber.depth:
Single-mode fibre's core is so small, 8 to 10 microns, that light can travel only one way down it, and with one mode there is no modal dispersion; its limits are attenuation and chromatic dispersion instead, which is why it carries kilometres. The ordinary single-mode fibre is ITU-T G.652, with its 'zero-dispersion wavelength around 1310 nm'; the G.657 family is bend-insensitive, and its Category A fibres comply with G.652.

Optics run at 1310 and 1550 nm. Cabling standards grade it OS1, cabled for premises with attenuation of up to 1 dB per km, and OS2, cabled for outdoor use; a current fibre such as Corning's SMF-28 Ultra is specified at no more than 0.32 dB per km at 1310 nm and 0.18 at 1550.

The connectors carry the polish in their colour: blue for the flat UPC face, green for the angled APC face, and the two must never be mated.

multimode-fiber.def: The short-reach fibre of buildings and data centres - a wide core, cheaper optics, distances of hundreds of meters.
multimode-fiber.context: Multimode's 50-micron core (62.5 in legacy OM1) carries many light paths at once; their spread (modal dispersion) is what caps distance as speeds rise. Grades OM1 through OM5 mark the progression - OM3 and OM4 (aqua) are the laser-optimized workhorses for 10-100 Gb/s inside facilities, OM5 (lime) adds wideband support for multi-wavelength short reach. The trade against single-mode is classic: cheaper transceivers, shorter reach.
multimode-fiber.depth:
The Fiber Optic Association gives the core sizes, 'almost always 50 or 62.5 microns', inside a 125-micron cladding. A core that wide admits many modes, paths of slightly different lengths, so a pulse spreads as it travels, and the faster the signal the shorter the distance before pulses blur. The grades track the fight against that spreading: one Cisco 10GBASE-SR module reaches 33 m on OM1, 82 m on OM2, 300 m on OM3 and 400 m on OM4, all at 850 nm.
