Above 10 Gb/s, speed came from parallel fibres as much as from faster light: 100GBASE-SR4 uses four lanes each way on an MPO connector, and 400G SR8 uses eight pairs, both to about 100 m on OM4. OM5 is, in Fluke Networks' words, 'a version of the OM4 fibre with additional bandwidth characterization at 953 nm', for short-reach wavelength multiplexing.

The jacket says the grade: orange for OM1 and OM2, aqua for OM3 and OM4 (violet for OM4 in much of Europe), lime green for OM5.

transceiver.def: The pluggable module that gives a switch port its personality - copper or fibre, short reach or long, one lineage from GBIC to OSFP.
transceiver.context: Instead of fixing the optics at manufacture, ports take standardized pluggables: the chunky GBIC gave way to the SFP, then SFP+ (10G), SFP28 (25G), the quad-lane QSFP+ / QSFP28 (40/100G), and QSFP-DD and OSFP at 400G and beyond. The module choice - SR, LR, DAC twinax, RJ45 copper - decides medium and distance; the form factor decides what fits the port. Vendor lock-in games on 'unsupported' third-party optics are a running industry argument.
transceiver.depth:
The transceiver is where a port's physical layer actually lives. A switch built with empty cages leaves the medium and the reach to the module: short-reach multimode at 850 nm, long-reach single-mode at 1310, copper over twisted pair, or a direct-attach cable. The IEEE's names say which: in 10GBASE-SR, BASE is baseband, S short wavelength and R the scrambled 64B/66B coding; in 100GBASE-SR4, the final 4 counts lanes on parallel fibre.

Reach belongs to the pair, module and fibre, never to the module alone. The same 10GBASE-SR module that covers 400 m of OM4 covers 33 m of OM1, and an LR module is specified for single-mode fibre, not multimode. That is why a transceiver swap is the first suspect after a cabling change, and the module's own diagnostics, its transmitted and received power, are the first numbers to read.

media-converter.def: The small box that translates one physical medium to another - classically copper Ethernet to fibre and back.
media-converter.context: A media converter bridges a link's two halves at layer 1/2: extend a copper run beyond 100 m by jumping onto fibre, connect a copper-only device to a fibre plant, or join multimode to single-mode segments. Standalone units and chassis versions exist; many modern deployments prefer a switch with SFP ports doing the same job. Simple, cheap, and a classic silent point of failure worth labelling.

poe-injector.def: The midspan device that adds Power over Ethernet to a link whose switch cannot supply it.
poe-injector.context: An injector sits between a non-PoE switch port and a powered device, inserting DC onto the pairs per 802.3af/at/bt so a distant access point or camera runs without local mains. The reverse device - a splitter - extracts power back out for gear that lacks PoE input. Injectors solve the one-off case; at scale, PoE switching in the closet replaces the wall-wart forest.

wiring-closet.def: The telecom room where a floor's cabling terminates - patch panels, switches, and the boundary between horizontal and backbone cabling.
wiring-closet.context: Structured cabling pulls every outlet's horizontal run back to a telecom room (TR): panels in front, switch ports patched behind, backbone links riser-ing to the main distribution frame. The MDF/IDF vocabulary maps onto it - the main room and the per-floor intermediate ones. Its unglamorous disciplines - labelling, cable management, cooling, locked doors - decide whether the site is maintainable in five years.
wiring-closet.depth:
A wiring closet is where horizontal cabling from a floor terminates and where the switches serving it live. Its constraint is the hundred-metre copper limit, which sets how much floor area one closet can serve and therefore how many a building needs.

What determines whether it stays workable is discipline rather than design. Labelling that matches the outlets, patch cords of the right length, cable management that lets a single cord be traced, and a record of what is patched where are all cheap at installation and nearly impossible to retrofit. The alternative is the closet everyone recognizes, where the fastest way to find a run is to unplug something and see who complains.

rack.def: The 19-inch frame that standardizes how equipment mounts - and the rack unit (U), the 1.75-inch height quantum everything is measured in.
rack.context: The 19-inch rack predates computing (telephone exchanges used it), and its grammar is universal: equipment height in U (1U = 1.75 in / 44.45 mm), typical enclosures 42U, two-post relay racks for patching versus four-post cabinets for servers, square-hole rails and cage nuts. 'It's 2U' communicates instantly across every vendor - one of networking's quiet, total standardizations.

hot-cold-aisle.def: The data-center layout that keeps equipment intake air separate from exhaust - rows face front-to-front and back-to-back.
hot-cold-aisle.context: Racks arranged so all fronts (intakes) share a cold aisle fed by cooling, and all rears (exhausts) share a hot aisle returning to the CRAC/CRAH units, stop hot exhaust from recirculating into intakes. Containment - doors and panels sealing one aisle or the other - sharpens the separation and the efficiency numbers (PUE). Blanking panels in empty rack slots are the humble detail that makes the whole scheme work.

data-center-tiers.def: The Uptime Institute's I-to-IV classification of data-center resilience - from basic capacity to fault tolerance.
data-center-tiers.context: Tier I is basic capacity; Tier II adds redundant components; Tier III is concurrently maintainable (any component can be serviced without shutting production down, the common enterprise/colo target); Tier IV is fault-tolerant, riding through equipment failures. The tiers describe facility topology - power and cooling paths - not operations quality. Distinct from the identically-worded ISP transit tiers and support tiers; three unrelated ladders sharing one word.

atm.def: Asynchronous Transfer Mode - the 1990s bet that all traffic, voice to data, should ride fixed 53-byte cells with hard QoS. Ethernet and IP won instead.
atm.context: ATM cut everything into 48-byte payloads behind 5-byte headers, switched by VPI/VCI circuit labels, with service classes (CBR, VBR, ABR, UBR) giving telcos the guarantees they trusted. It ran the B-ISDN vision over SONET/SDH at OC-3 and OC-12, carried DSL's back end for years, and dominated carrier cores around the turn of the century. What killed it: the ~10% cell-tax overhead, the complexity of adaptation layers like AAL5 and of pretending to be a LAN, and Ethernet ports that got fast and cheap faster than ATM could. MPLS (Multiprotocol Label Switching) took the traffic-engineering ideas and left the cells behind.
atm.depth:
ATM carried everything in fixed 53-byte cells, a size chosen by committee compromise between voice and data requirements, and it promised deterministic quality of service that IP could not offer. For a period in the 1990s it was widely expected to become the universal network layer.

It lost, and the reasons are instructive. The cell tax, five bytes of header per forty-eight of payload, wasted around ten percent of capacity, the equipment was expensive, and running IP over it required an adaptation layer that added complexity to the thing everyone actually wanted to use. Ethernet got faster and cheaper on a curve ATM could not match, which is the same story as DECnet and Token Ring: good enough and open beat better and closed.

lane.def: LAN Emulation - the ATM Forum's scheme for making a cell network impersonate Ethernet. Famously the moment many engineers decided ATM to the desktop was a bad idea.
lane.context: Because every LAN protocol assumed broadcast and MAC addresses, LANE bolted them onto point-to-point ATM with a cast of servers: the LEC client in every host, a LES to resolve MACs to ATM addresses, a LECS for configuration, and the aptly-named BUS - the Broadcast and Unknown Server - through which all broadcast traffic funneled. Every piece was a bottleneck and a single point of failure, troubleshooting meant tracing calls through all of them, and the whole edifice existed to emulate what a cheap Ethernet switch simply did. It survives as the cautionary tale about emulating the thing you were supposed to replace.

sonet.def: Synchronous Optical Network - the telco standard that made optical transport a synchronized hierarchy with 50-millisecond healing rings. SDH is its international twin.
sonet.context: SONET (ANSI/Telcordia, North America) and SDH (ITU-T G.707, everywhere else) organized fibre transport into a rigid TDM hierarchy built from the 51.84 Mb/s STS-1, with add/drop multiplexers on protected rings that restored service within 50 ms of a fibre cut - the number that defined carrier-grade for a generation. Voice, ATM, and packet links all rode inside its containers. Packet-optical transport and OTN have largely displaced it, but its framing, its OAM discipline, and the 50 ms reflex still shape how operators think.

pos.def: Packet over SONET - IP straight onto the optical hierarchy in PPP framing, skipping ATM's cell tax. The backbone link of the early-2000s internet core.
pos.context: PoS (RFC 2615) wraps packets in HDLC-like PPP framing directly inside SONET/SDH payloads, so an OC-48 or OC-192 between two core routers carries IP with almost no overhead and none of ATM's segmentation machinery. Through the 1990s-2000s it was how the big router vendors sold the internet core, and the OC-192 PoS interface was the prestige port of its day. Ethernet at 10G and beyond, cheaper per port and end-to-end, eventually took the role; PoS remains the clean example of removing a layer instead of managing it.

dwdm.def: Dense Wavelength Division Multiplexing - many independent light colours down one fibre. The reason a single strand can carry terabits and the backbone of every long-haul network.
dwdm.context: DWDM packs dozens of tightly-spaced wavelengths (the ITU-T G.694.1 grid in the C-band, 100/50 GHz spacing and now flexible grids) onto one fibre pair, each lambda its own independent link. Erbium-doped fibre amplifiers made it practical by boosting all channels at once without electronics, and coherent optics pushed each wavelength from 10G to 100G, 400G and beyond. It is how submarine cables, national backbones, and metro rings scale - and why leasing 'a lambda' is a product. Its coarser sibling CWDM spaces channels wider for cheaper short-haul gear.

oc-levels.def: The SONET Optical Carrier ladder - OC-3, OC-12, OC-48, OC-192 - every rung 51.84 Mb/s times n, with SDH's STM names for the same speeds.
oc-levels.context: OC-n means n times the 51.84 Mb/s STS-1: OC-3 at 155 Mb/s (SDH STM-1), OC-12 at 622 (STM-4), OC-48 at 2.5 Gb/s (STM-16), OC-192 at 10 Gb/s (STM-64), OC-768 at 40 Gb/s (STM-256). A 'c' suffix (OC-3c) meant concatenated - one big pipe rather than channelized subdivisions. For two decades these names WERE the speed vocabulary of carrier links and router interfaces; reading old network diagrams, RFPs, or war stories requires the ladder, even now that Ethernet names took over.

igp.def: An interior gateway protocol (IGP) is any routing protocol that routers use to exchange routing information within a single autonomous system (AS); the ones in use are OSPF (Open Shortest Path First), IS-IS (Intermediate System to Intermediate System), EIGRP (Enhanced Interior Gateway Routing Protocol) and RIP (Routing Information Protocol).
igp.context: An interior gateway protocol (IGP) gives the routers of one organization fast, complete knowledge of that organization's own topology. Link-state protocols, OSPF (Open Shortest Path First) and IS-IS (Intermediate System to Intermediate System), flood a map of routers and links and let every router compute its own shortest paths; older distance-vector protocols such as RIP (Routing Information Protocol) passed on rumours of distance instead. IGPs are built for quick convergence and internal metrics, and they deliberately do not carry the whole internet: that problem of scale and policy belongs to the exterior side, BGP (Border Gateway Protocol). In MPLS (Multiprotocol Label Switching) networks the IGP also provides the reachability that the labels follow, which is why IGP design remains a carrier's craft.
igp.depth:
An interior gateway protocol (IGP) is a class of protocol, not a protocol. The specification of the Border Gateway Protocol (BGP), RFC (Request for Comments) 4271 of January 2006, defines an IGP as a routing protocol used to exchange routing information among routers within a single autonomous system (AS), and its classic definition of an AS rests on it: a set of routers under one technical administration, using an IGP and common metrics to route packets inside the AS and an inter-AS protocol to reach other ASes. The same text records that one AS now commonly runs several IGPs and several sets of metrics, while still presenting a single coherent interior routing plan to the outside. What an IGP is not: internal BGP (iBGP) also runs between routers of one AS, but it is a session type of the exterior protocol, and large BGP deployments typically rely on an IGP to resolve the next hops iBGP advertises, as RFC 7938 notes. The members of the class in use today are OSPF (Open Shortest Path First), IS-IS (Intermediate System to Intermediate System), EIGRP (Enhanced Interior Gateway Routing Protocol) and the older RIP (Routing Information Protocol).

The name comes from the early 1980s, when routers were called gateways. In RFC 827 (October 1982), which proposed the Exterior Gateway Protocol (EGP), Eric C. Rosen of Bolt Beranek and Newman (BBN) wrote that the internet was expected to evolve into separate autonomous systems, each a set of relatively homogeneous gateways whose routing algorithm would be a private matter, never implemented outside the domain. The core gateways would keep running the old Gateway-Gateway Protocol (GGP), and gateways in other autonomous systems could use their own Interior Gateway Protocols, exchanging only reachability at the border through EGP. RFC 1812 (June 1995) tells the same story from the router's side: traditional routing protocols came to be called interior gateway protocols, and each site acquired a strange new beast called an exterior gateway, which spoke EGP to the BBN core gateways, then the internet backbone, while speaking its IGP to the routers at home, with both protocols wanting to fill the same routing table.

RFC 1812, the requirements for routers running Internet Protocol version 4 (IPv4), lists what any IGP should do whatever its algorithm: respond quickly to changes in the internal topology; keep a flapping circuit from causing continuous routing updates; converge quickly to loop-free routing; use minimal bandwidth; offer equal-cost routes so that load can be split; and authenticate routing updates. It sorts the IGPs of its day into distance-vector and link-state, and requires that a router implementing any routing protocol other than static routes implement OSPF. The family has stayed small. RIP, in its version 2 specification, RFC 2453, counts hops and treats 16 as infinity. OSPF version 2, RFC 2328 of April 1998, is a link-state protocol carried directly over the Internet Protocol (IP) as protocol number 89, each router running the Dijkstra algorithm over a shared database. IS-IS came from the OSI (Open Systems Interconnection) world and was extended by RFC 1195 in December 1990 to serve pure IP, pure OSI and dual environments. EIGRP, Cisco's protocol, was published as an informational RFC, RFC 7868, only in May 2016; it is distance-vector technology made loop-free by DUAL (Diffusing Update Algorithm). When BGP-4 (version 4 of BGP) made inter-domain routing classless, RFC 1930 (March 1996) drew the consequence for the inside: the IGP must carry classless routes too, OSPF and IS-IS being its examples.

The design differences from BGP follow from the trust boundary. Inside its own network an operator controls every router, wants traffic moved within moments of a link failure, and can believe the information being flooded, so an IGP is built for speed and correctness rather than for policy and distrust. Link-state protocols have every router build the same map and compute paths independently, which converges quickly and scales through areas; distance-vector protocols tell neighbours about destinations rather than about topology. In practice most enterprises run OSPF, while IS-IS is, in the words of the FRRouting documentation, widely used in large networks such as ISP (internet service provider) and carrier backbones; the deciding factors are usually operational familiarity and tooling rather than protocol capability. RFC 1930 adds two practical points: the process tag many routers require for an IGP instance need not be globally unique (an AS number or a private-use number will do), and running an IGP is no reason to register an AS number.

The discipline that keeps large networks predictable is a division of labour. The IGP carries the infrastructure, meaning links, router loopbacks and the addresses that BGP uses as next hops, and it should stay small and stable; BGP carries everything else, customer prefixes and the internet's routes. RFC 4271 builds this dependency into BGP itself: inside a transit AS the consistent view of interior routes comes from the IGP, and step (e) of the decision process prefers, among otherwise equal routes, the one whose NEXT_HOP has the lowest interior cost as computed from the routing table, which is how IGP metrics end up choosing the exit point. In 1995, RFC 1772 described the timing hazard between the two layers: a border router can learn of a new exit before the IGP is able to route traffic to it, and in that window incorrect routing or black holes occur, so interior routing should converge on the proper exit before the route is advertised to external peers. One label needs care: a BGP route whose ORIGIN attribute reads IGP (value 0) was not necessarily learned from an IGP; the value says only that the reachability information is interior to the originating AS.

The boundary is where the interesting failures live. The moment external routes are redistributed into an IGP wholesale, convergence time and CPU (central processing unit) load both suffer, and a flap somewhere else becomes the receiving network's problem. RFC 1812 sets the rules for any router running two interior protocols at once: it must be able to exchange routes between them, must provide some mechanism for avoiding routing loops when the exchange runs in both directions, and must provide a priority mechanism for choosing between routes from independent processes, because different IGPs use metrics with nothing in common. That priority is what Cisco calls administrative distance (AD): a local value, never advertised, used only when several sources offer the same prefix, the lowest winning. Cisco's defaults are connected 0, static 1, EIGRP summary 5, external BGP 20, internal EIGRP 90, IGRP (Interior Gateway Routing Protocol) 100, OSPF 110, IS-IS 115, RIP 120, EGP 140, ODR (On Demand Routing) 160, external EIGRP 170, internal BGP 200, and 255 for an unknown source. With those numbers a prefix the IGP knows beats the same prefix learned over internal BGP, while a route from an external BGP neighbour beats every IGP.

In service provider networks the IGP is also the foundation of MPLS (Multiprotocol Label Switching). The Label Distribution Protocol (LDP), RFC 5036 (October 2007), builds label switched paths (LSPs) by mapping network-layer routing information onto them, each router splicing its incoming label to the one assigned by the next hop that routing has chosen, so labelled traffic follows the IGP's paths. RFC 5443 (March 2009) deals with what happens when the two disagree: if the IGP is up on a link but LDP is not, labelled traffic is black-holed, which matters for MPLS virtual private networks (VPNs) and for BGP-free cores whose routers carry no external routes at all. The fix is for the IGP to advertise that link at maximum cost until LDP is ready: LSInfinity (0xFFFF) in OSPF, and 2^24 minus 2 in IS-IS, because a link at the absolute maximum of 2^24 minus 1 would drop out of the topology altogether. Segment routing, RFC 8402 (July 2018), goes a step further and lets the link-state IGP distribute the labels itself, as prefix, node, anycast and adjacency segment identifiers (SIDs) encoded as MPLS labels, with no separate label protocol.

Convergence is the figure IGPs are judged by. RFC 5714, the IP Fast Reroute framework (January 2010), records that disruptions after a failure traditionally lasted at least several seconds, and that advances in routers had reduced this to under a second for carefully configured networks using link-state IGPs, still too slow for some services. Its answer, and that of the loop-free alternates of RFC 5286 (September 2008), is to precompute backup next hops so that the router adjacent to a failure repairs it locally while the rest of the network reconverges. Detection is the other half of the budget. OSPF's sample values for a local area network are a hello every 10 seconds and a dead interval of some multiple of it, say four, and the Bidirectional Forwarding Detection (BFD) specification, RFC 5880 (June 2010), notes that routing-protocol hellos detect failures no better than a second, far too long for some applications, which is why BFD runs beside the IGP to do the detecting.

Data centres are where the IGP's monopoly inside the AS has been challenged. RFC 7938 (August 2016), written by engineers from Facebook and Arista Networks, observes that fully routed data centre designs commonly use an IGP such as OSPF, and proposes running external BGP (EBGP) as the only protocol in large Clos fabrics instead. It lists the reasons BGP had not been used that way, among them the belief that it converges much more slowly than IGPs and that it needs an IGP to resolve next hops, and answers that BGP propagates only the best path, so a failure is masked as soon as an alternative is found, while the event propagation scope of a link-state IGP is an entire area. The argument is about flooding scope and simplicity at that scale; in campus, enterprise and carrier backbones the IGP keeps its job.

egp.def: Exterior Gateway Protocol - the class of protocols that route BETWEEN autonomous systems, and also the name of the specific 1980s protocol BGP replaced.
egp.context: The term does double duty. As a class, EGP means inter-domain routing - today effectively synonymous with BGP, where policy, business relationships, and reachability matter more than shortest paths. As a proper noun, EGP (RFC 904, 1984) was the actual protocol of the early internet's tree-shaped topology; its inability to handle arbitrary meshes is precisely what BGP was invented to fix in 1989. Exam answers and old documents use both senses, so the disambiguation is worth carrying.
egp.depth:
EGP names both a specific obsolete protocol and the class of protocols that route between autonomous systems, in contrast to interior protocols that route within one. Only the class sense is current, and BGP is its sole surviving member.

The distinction the class captures is about trust and policy rather than about algorithms. An interior protocol optimizes a path within one administration where everyone shares an objective; an exterior protocol carries routes between organizations with different commercial interests, so it must express policy and cannot simply prefer the shortest path. That is why BGP's decision process is a list of policy tie-breakers rather than a metric, and why understanding it means understanding business relationships.

t1.def: The North American 1.544 Mb/s digital carrier - 24 channels of 64 kb/s, the DS1, the leased line a generation of WANs was built from.
t1.context: T1 comes from Bell's T-carrier hierarchy: 24 DS0 timeslots of 64 kb/s each plus framing yields 1.544 Mb/s, delivered channelized (each slot its own voice or data circuit) or clear-channel as one pipe. The ladder continues to T3/DS3 at 44.736 Mb/s (28 T1s), above which SONET's OC levels take over. For decades 'a T1' meant business-grade connectivity itself - Frame Relay, PPP leased lines, and PBX trunks all rode it - and its 24-channel arithmetic still surfaces in PRI voice (23B+D). North America and Japan territory; the rest of the world runs E1.

e1.def: The international 2.048 Mb/s digital carrier - 32 timeslots of 64 kb/s, the E-carrier answer to T1, and the line Brazilian networking grew up on.
e1.context: E1 divides 2.048 Mb/s into 32 timeslots: 30 usable channels, slot 0 for framing and slot 16 classically for signalling (30B+D in ISDN PRI terms), on G.703 physical interfaces. The hierarchy steps to E3 at 34.368 Mb/s before SONET/SDH absorbs the ladder. Everywhere outside North America and Japan, 'dois megas' - two megs - was the business circuit, the Frame Relay access line, and the voice trunk of the dial-up-to-broadband decades. The T1/E1 split is the classic reminder that even the plumbing of telecom forked by region - same 64 kb/s DNA, different arithmetic.

sampasec.def: São Paulo's CitySec - the informal monthly bar meetup of the city's security professionals and enthusiasts, third Wednesday of the month.
sampasec.context: SampaSec follows the CitySec model - the informal, no-agenda security meetup format that spread worldwide from the idea of Richard Bejtlich, Chris Walsh, and Adam Shostack - and has anchored São Paulo's scene since around 2010, alongside Brazilian siblings like CamSec (Campinas), PoASec (Porto Alegre), and SSASec (Salvador). No talks required, no badge, no dress code: the point is the room - students, veterans, researchers, and the occasional recruiter, around a table. It is the connective tissue between the city's bigger fixtures: many a BSidesSP village, YSTS hallway conversation, and Garoa project traces back to a SampaSec table.
sampasec.depth:
Sampasec is a São Paulo security conference whose name folds Sampa, the city's own nickname for itself, into the word security. That naming is a small thing and it signals something real: an event that belongs to a city rather than one that could be held anywhere.

Its place in the Brazilian calendar is alongside H2HC, Roadsec, BSidesSP and YSTS, and the useful observation is the density rather than any single event. One city sustaining several distinct security conferences, each with a different format and audience, is a sign of a community large enough to support specialization: deep technical research in one venue, career entry in another, curated networking in a third.

That density took two decades to build and is easy to underestimate from outside. A country with one conference has a scene that depends on whoever organizes it; a country with five has an ecosystem that survives any one of them ending. The unglamorous work of running these events, mostly by volunteers and mostly unpaid, is what the difference is made of.

dpd.def: Dead Peer Detection - how an IPsec endpoint learns its IKE partner is gone: an on-demand are-you-there exchange, so dead tunnels get torn down and failover can happen.
dpd.context: IPsec tunnels fail silently: packets simply stop arriving, and without liveness checks a gateway will happily encrypt into a void for hours. DPD (RFC 3706, from the IKEv1 era) replaced wasteful periodic keepalives with an on-demand design - only when traffic is outbound and nothing has been heard back does the peer send an R-U-THERE notification and await the acknowledgement; a few misses and the security associations are torn down, freeing the tunnel to re-establish or fail over. IKEv2 built the equivalent liveness check into its informational exchanges, but the DPD name survives in vendor UIs and tunnel configurations everywhere - usually as an interval, a retry count, and the eternal judgment call between detecting failure fast and flapping on a lossy WAN.

igmp.def: Internet Group Management Protocol: how IPv4 hosts tell the routers on their link which multicast groups they want to receive.
igmp.context: Hosts send membership reports, and one querier per link polls them with general queries to 224.0.0.1, so a router keeps a group only while someone on the link still wants it. IGMPv3, now RFC 9776 (2025), adds source filtering. Switches snoop the same messages to send multicast only to ports that asked; PIM builds the trees between routers.
igmp.depth:
Version 1 came with RFC 1112; version 2, RFC 2236 (1997), added the Leave Group message for low leave latency and querier election by lowest IP address; version 3 adds source filtering, interest in a group only from some sources or from all but some. RFC 9776, an Internet Standard of March 2025, obsoletes RFC 3376 as the IGMPv3 specification and still updates RFC 2236, since IGMPv3 must handle version 2 reports and leaves. IGMPv3 reports go to 224.0.0.22, where all IGMPv3 routers listen.

The defaults are a robustness variable of 2, a query interval of 125 seconds and a query response interval of 10 seconds. A router forgets a group when no report arrives within the Group Membership Interval: 2 times 125 plus 10, or 260 seconds, under RFC 2236, and 2 times 125 plus 2 times 10, or 270 seconds, under RFC 9776, which changed the formula to resolve an erratum. The five minutes often quoted matches neither. A silent querier is replaced after the Other Querier Present Interval, 255 seconds.

A snooping switch, in RFC 4541's Informational advice, forwards reports only towards router ports, found from queries whose source is not 0.0.0.0, and sends group traffic only to ports that reported, but forwards 224.0.0.0/24 on all ports. With no querier, entries time out and the switch either floods the group as unregistered traffic or stops delivering it, as its policy dictates. IPv6 does the same with MLD: MLDv2, RFC 9777, is a translation of IGMPv3, with reports sent to ff02::16.

pim.def: Protocol Independent Multicast - the routing of multicast: building the delivery trees that carry one stream to many networks, using whatever unicast routing table already exists.
pim.context: The 'protocol independent' is the design: PIM does not compute its own topology - it borrows the unicast table (OSPF's, IS-IS's, BGP's) for its reverse-path checks. PIM Sparse Mode (RFC 7761), the mode that won, starts every group on a shared tree rooted at a rendezvous point - the meeting place where sources and receivers find each other - written (*,G); once traffic flows, receivers' routers can switch to the shortest-path tree straight to the source, written (S,G). Dense mode's flood-and-prune survives mostly in labs, and SSM drops the rendezvous point entirely when receivers know their source. In practice, multicast troubleshooting is PIM troubleshooting: where is the RP, does the RPF check pass, and which tree is this packet on.

dvmrp.def: Distance Vector Multicast Routing Protocol - the first multicast routing protocol, and the engine of the MBone: RIP's logic, pointed at delivery trees.
dvmrp.context: DVMRP (RFC 1075, 1988) built multicast's proof of concept: a RIP-like distance-vector exchange defining reverse paths, and flood-and-prune delivery - send the stream everywhere, let uninterested branches prune themselves, repeat as prunes expire. Its monument is the MBone, the 1990s virtual multicast backbone of DVMRP tunnels over the unicast internet, over which IETF meetings, NASA missions, and a famous Rolling Stones concert were streamed years before 'streaming' was a word anyone used. The flood-and-prune economics could not scale, PIM Sparse Mode replaced it, and DVMRP retired into history - the protocol that showed multicast could work at all.

cobit.def: ISACA's governance framework for enterprise IT - the auditor's answer to the question ITIL doesn't ask: who decides, who is accountable, and how do we prove it.
cobit.context: COBIT (now versioned as COBIT 2019) descends from ISACA's audit heritage, and it shows: the framework separates GOVERNANCE (evaluate, direct, monitor - the board's job) from MANAGEMENT (plan, build, run, monitor - the executives' job) and maps objectives, processes, and maturity so that control can be designed and audited. Where ITIL tells operations how to run services, COBIT tells the organization how to govern the whole IT estate - which is why the two are exam-question neighbours and real-world colleagues: COBIT sets the requirements, ITIL is one way to meet them.

agile.def: The 2001 Manifesto and everything it unleashed - individuals over processes, working software over documentation, responding to change over following the plan.
agile.context: Seventeen practitioners met at a Utah ski lodge in February 2001 and distilled a decade of lightweight-methods rebellion into four values and twelve principles. The word became an umbrella: Scrum's sprints and standups, Kanban's flow, XP's engineering practices all shelter under it, and half the vocabulary of modern work - backlog, retro, velocity, MVP - leaked out of it into everything. The honest reading for infrastructure people: Agile is a bet that feedback beats prediction, and it wins exactly where requirements genuinely cannot be known up front - which is why 'agile transformation' succeeds in product teams and turns to ritual theater where the work is actually operations.

okr.def: Objectives and Key Results - Andy Grove's goal-setting discipline from Intel: a qualitative ambition, measured by a few brutally quantitative results.
okr.context: An Objective says where you are going ('make the platform the obvious choice'); its Key Results say how you will know you arrived (numbers, dates, thresholds - graded, not vibes). Grove built the practice at Intel; John Doerr carried it to a forty-person Google in 1999, and its spread from there made it the tech industry's default planning grammar, popularized in Doerr's Measure What Matters. The discipline that separates working OKRs from wall decoration: key results are outcomes, not tasks; ambitious enough that 70 percent is a good score; and few enough to remember without looking.

kanban.def: Toyota's pull system, adapted to knowledge work: visualize the flow, limit work in progress, and let capacity pull tasks instead of schedules pushing them.
kanban.context: The kanban (signboard) cards of the Toyota Production System signaled upstream stations to produce only what downstream consumed - inventory replaced by information. David Anderson's mid-2000s adaptation brought the idea to software and operations: a board whose columns are the workflow's real states, cards that are the work, and the one rule that does all the heavy lifting - WIP limits, which convert 'everything is in progress' into finished things leaving the board. For operations teams, kanban usually fits better than sprints: interrupt-driven work has no respect for two-week boxes, but it flows beautifully through a limited pipe.

furukawa.def: Furukawa Electric LatAm - the name on Brazil's structured cabling for decades: the Curitiba-based operation of Japan's 1884-founded Furukawa Electric, whose cabling brand now carries the Lightera name.
furukawa.context: Ask a Brazilian installer whose cable is in the wall and the answer is usually Furukawa: the LatAm operation (headquartered in Curitiba, with plants there, in Santa Rita do Sapucaí, and beyond) made the brand synonymous with cabeamento estruturado, aligned to TIA/ISO and Brazil's own ABNT NBR 14565. Its FCP program - Furukawa Certified Professional, delivered through authorized centres with mandatory official training before the exam, and recognized by BICSI towards the RCDD - is one of the market's pioneering cabling certifications and a rite of passage for the country's infrastructure trade. The recent rebrand puts Lightera on the certifications and solutions; the installers still say Furukawa.

cisco-certifications.def: The certification ladder that defined the industry: CCNA to prove you can run a network, CCNP to prove you can build one, CCIE to prove it under lab pressure.
cisco-certifications.context: Since the CCIE arrived in 1993 - years before the associate tiers existed - Cisco's ladder has been networking's common currency: the CCNA as the profession's entry ticket, the CCNP as the working engineer's credential, and the CCIE's eight-hour hands-on lab as the industry's most feared and most respected exam, whose holders cite their number the way pilots log hours. The 2020 restructure consolidated the sprawl (one CCNA, specialization tracks, DevNet added for automation) without changing the social fact: on a résumé in this industry, these three acronyms need no explanation.

cissp.def: The management-level security certification - (ISC)2's flagship since 1994: eight domains, a mile wide, and the credential security leadership job posts ask for by name.
cissp.context: The CISSP covers the Common Body of Knowledge's eight domains - from security and risk management through architecture, network security, IAM, testing, and operations - at deliberately managerial altitude: the running joke 'a mile wide and an inch deep' is also the design. Five years of paid experience is required (candidates who pass early hold Associate status until they earn it), plus endorsement and continuing education. It signals breadth and governance fluency rather than hands-on depth - which is exactly why CISOs' job descriptions ask for it and why hands-on practitioners pair it with technical certs rather than replacing them.

cwnp.def: The vendor-neutral Wi-Fi certification body - and CWNA, its flagship: the credential that proves you understand radio, not just controllers.
cwnp.context: CWNP (Certified Wireless Network Professionals, established 1999) built the wireless track no vendor could: RF behaviour, spectrum, antennas, and 802.11 mechanics taught without a product attached. The CWNA (Wireless Network Administrator) is the foundation everything stacks on - CWSP for security, CWDP for design, CWAP for analysis - culminating in the CWNE, the expert tier earned by portfolio and endorsement rather than one exam. In a field where most training is a vendor's UI in disguise, the CWNP ladder is where engineers go to learn why the survey looks the way it does.

roadsec.def: Roadsec was the travelling Brazilian hacking and security festival that Flipside launched at the end of 2013 and billed as Latin America's largest hacker festival: one-day regional editions in state capitals each year, closing with a São Paulo mega-edition of talks, workshops, villages, music and the Hackaflag capture-the-flag (CTF) final. Its last edition was in 2023.
roadsec.context: Roadsec inverted the conference formula: instead of making Brazil's hackers travel to one city, the festival travelled to them, a caravan through the state capitals that culminated each year in a mega-edition in São Paulo. The format was deliberately a festival, not a conference: career talks beside hardware villages, robot building beside serious research, and at the centre Hackaflag, the capture-the-flag (CTF) championship whose regional rounds along the tour crowned a national champion. For a generation of Brazilian students far from the São Paulo and Rio axis, a Roadsec stop was the first time the security community came to their town, which was precisely the point. The same company, Flipside, ran Mind The Sec at the corporate end of the calendar; the regional editions of both had ended by 2023, Roadsec skipped 2024 and has not returned, and in September 2026 Mind The Sec passed to Informa, the organizer of Black Hat.
roadsec.depth:
What it was. Anchises Moraes, the chronicler of Brazilian security events, described Roadsec in 2014 as an event that had emerged at the end of 2013 with an unusual purpose: to be an itinerant information security event, with editions in several Brazilian cities, ending the year with a closing edition in São Paulo. Its organizer, Flipside, described it around 2018 as a roadshow taking a full day of hacking, security and technology content around the country, with four years on the road, more than 50 editions and more than 25,000 participants, and called the São Paulo closing edition, with almost 24 hours of programme, the largest hacker festival on the continent. Its own site kept the slogan to the end: O Maior Festival Hacker da América Latina.

The first year. In 2014 the caravan held regional editions in nine capitals with more than 2,000 participants, then closed in São Paulo on 2 December at Audio Club, in Água Branca. The programme already had the shape the festival kept: talks (among them Diego Aranha on the Você Fiscal project), workshops on Lego Mindstorms robots, lockpicking, Anki Drive and drone piloting, DJs, and a concert by the band Ira!. In the morning São Paulo held its own qualifier of the Hackaflag capture-the-flag (CTF) championship, and in the afternoon a final joined the winners from every state; Symantec sponsored it, with a trip to Silicon Valley as the prize. Roadsec also set out to support local communities, backing the hackerspace in every city it visited that had an active one.

Why travel. The argument behind the format is about geography. As Moraes put it in 2014, few cities outside São Paulo host frequent security events, and in a country of continental scale, where a domestic flight can cost more than a monthly wage, asking people to come to São Paulo filters out most of them. Expertise concentrates where events are, events are where the money is, and the money is in a few cities, so talent outside them stays invisible to an industry that complains about a shortage of it. Taking the event to the people is one of the few interventions that addresses that mechanism rather than the symptom.

A festival, not a conference. The São Paulo edition of 11 November 2017 had 5,000 registrations, almost ten hours of content in six tracks and 41 talks (career, application security, hacking, technology and communities among them), a robot competition, a live biochip implant on the main stage and a Hackaflag final broadcast with commentators; it also showed the format's costs, with crowded halls, noisy stages and food prices attendees complained about. Talks sat beside hardware hacking, lockpicking, drones and music, which lowered the barrier for people who would never have described themselves as belonging at a security event; Moraes credited Roadsec with popularizing capture-the-flag competitions across Brazil through Hackaflag, and later with positioning itself as a tech recruitment event. Its record with international headliners was mixed: a talk by John Draper, Captain Crunch, was cancelled days before the 2017 edition.

Pandemic and peak. When the 2020 lockdown stopped events, Flipside ran Roadsec@Home, a free weekly online edition on the Hopin platform whose donations went to Brazilian hackerspaces. The festival came back in person on 9 July 2022 in a larger hall, with more than 4,000 people and ten simultaneous stages, drawing many people early in their careers. The 2023 edition, the ninth, held on 15 July 2023 at Arca in Vila Leopoldina, São Paulo, was the largest on paper: eight thematic tracks across 11 stages and 110 sessions, villages for open-source intelligence (OSINT), mobile, application security, hardware and children, the Hackaflag final, an exhibition and a recruitment fair (the 2022 edition had offered more than 2,000 vacancies), over 14 hours. By then the regional caravan was gone: Moraes's review of 2023 noted that both Roadsec and Mind The Sec had lost their regional editions while setting records in São Paulo.

Hackaflag. The championship outgrew the festival. Flipside presented Hackaflag as a platform combining a capture-the-flag competition, a bounty programme and hands-on training, with video lessons and virtual laboratories in a Hackaflag Academy, and listed it with its awareness software Eskive as one of the company's five business lines. Its finals were the competitive centre of each São Paulo edition, from the 2014 national final to the #HFBR23 final of 2023.

The company behind it. Flipside, which marked twelve years in July 2020, describes itself as a security awareness company and ran both ends of the Brazilian calendar: Roadsec for the community and Mind The Sec for the corporate market, plus regional and executive versions of the latter, the research conference Sacicon and the media outlet The Hack. Its chief executive, Anderson Ramos, who speaks of having founded the company and is described by Moraes as the founder of Mind The Sec, appeared among the 2023 masters of ceremonies; in 2020 Flipside said its events and training had reached more than 200,000 people. The two events were deliberate opposites, one corporate, expo-heavy and in São Paulo, the other a festival taking hacker culture to the state capitals, and that pairing explains much of the shape of the Brazilian calendar in the decade they ran together.

The disappearance. In 2024 Roadsec did not happen. Flipside announced nothing, and until 31 December said the festival might still take place that year; Mind The Sec meanwhile held its tenth edition with 10,000 participants and 140 sponsors. Moraes's personal reading was that Mind The Sec had grown so large that the company had no breath left for Roadsec, which is also the assessment heard more widely in the scene. A return was promised for July 2025; by September 2025 Moraes wrote that the end of Roadsec seemed sealed. What makes it instructive is the mechanism: the profitable event did not out-compete the community one in any market, it out-competed it for the attention of the people who ran both. The space did not stay empty. Moraes singled out 2024 for the appearance of several regional events, community conferences in cities the caravan used to visit, so the calendar now has more small events outside São Paulo than when one large organizer served those cities directly; whether that is better depends on what one values, and the honest answer is that it is different.

Epilogue. In September 2026, at the opening of that year's Mind The Sec, Anderson Ramos announced that the event had joined the Black Hat family; Informa, the company that organizes Black Hat, had bought it. In his account of the news Moraes listed Roadsec and Hackaflag among the chapters of the history that led there. The festival's site still showed its 2023 edition in November 2026.

cryptorave.def: São Paulo's crowdfunded cryptoactivism marathon, held since 2014: about 24 uninterrupted hours of talks and workshops on privacy, security, cryptography and freedom online, free and open to anyone, run by volunteers, and refusing sponsorship from companies and non-governmental organizations.
cryptorave.context: Inspired by the international CryptoParty movement, whose gatherings teach people with no prior knowledge to protect themselves online, CryptoRave scaled the house party into what its organizers call Brazil's largest open and free cryptography and security event: talks, hands-on workshops, an install fest and art running through the night in a public building. The tenth edition, on 8 and 9 May 2026, took over the Biblioteca Mário de Andrade under the theme '85 seconds to the end of the world'. The funding model is the politics: an all-or-nothing crowdfunding campaign instead of sponsors, so the programme answers to no vendor. Where most security events talk to professionals, CryptoRave deliberately talks to everyone, journalists, activists, neighbours, on the theory that privacy fails unless it is popular.
cryptorave.depth:
What it is. The organizers describe CryptoRave as an annual event in São Paulo that gathers, in 24 hours followed by a party, a wide range of activities on security, cryptography, hacking, anonymity, privacy and freedom online; it is open and free, and it is a collective effort to spread the fundamental ideas of privacy and freedom on the internet and to widen the use of digital security practices and tools, encrypted communication among them. It began in 2014, in its own words as a reaction to disclosures that confirmed governments and corporations were keeping the world's population under constant surveillance. Its crowdfunding page names the audience it wants: activists, hackers, journalists, teachers, cypherpunks, students, nerds, artists and anyone curious about collective security practices and the protection of personal data. Anchises Moraes, the chronicler of the Brazilian security calendar, put the difference plainly: its target audience is end users.

The CryptoParty root. CryptoParty describes itself as a decentralized movement with events all over the world whose goal is to pass on knowledge about protecting yourself in the digital space, from encrypted communication to preventing web tracking and securing computers and smartphones. Its gatherings are open to everyone but meant especially for people without prior knowledge, they are free, and attendees bring their own devices to try the tools there and then. CryptoRave kept those principles and changed the scale: instead of an evening in someone's living room, a night and a day in a public building, with dozens of rooms running at once. The install fest is the direct descendant of the CryptoParty table: practically every edition has had one, a space where volunteers help people install free operating systems and tools on their own machines, so that people leave with encryption configured on their own devices rather than with the knowledge that encryption exists.

The editions. The 2018 edition, on 4 and 5 May, had more than 100 activities, running without a break from 19:00 on Friday to 19:00 on Saturday, followed by a party. The sixth, in 2019, raised 135 per cent of its crowdfunding goal, about R$ 94,000 from more than 440 backers, and the organizers added a one-afternoon Criptofesta of basic workshops in December that year. The event was suspended during the COVID-19 pandemic and returned on 5 and 6 May 2023, then ran on 10 and 11 May 2024 and, as the ninth edition, on 16 and 17 May 2025, from 18:00 on Friday to 05:00 and again from 08:00 to 17:00 on Saturday, 150 metres from Security BSides São Paulo, which held its own edition that weekend. The tenth took place on 8 and 9 May 2026 at the Biblioteca Mário de Andrade, on Rua da Consolação beside Anhangabaú metro station; the campaign counted thirteen years of the event.

The money, and the rule. CryptoRave is financed by an all-or-nothing crowdfunding campaign on the Catarse platform: if the goal is missed, nothing is collected. The 2026 campaign succeeded on 11 April 2026, with 363 backers giving R$ 80,611.17, 107 per cent of a R$ 75,000 goal, and the site also takes Bitcoin and sells merchandise at the event. The campaign states the rule behind it: CryptoRave is independent and volunteer-run, led by the collectives Actantes, MariaLab and Saravá, it pays none of its participants, and it accepts no sponsorship from companies or from non-governmental organizations, so that the money raised covers only the costs of the event, with no fee for organizers or speakers. The site's sponsor section is the list of individual backers, names in alphabetical order. Support of other kinds is credited separately: in 2026 the Heinrich Böll Foundation, the Chaos Computer Club, the library itself, the city's culture secretariat and the Escola de Ativismo. The distinction between support and sponsorship is the point; the programme is chosen by the community, and nobody buys a slot.

The 2026 programme. The published schedule lists 104 sessions in twelve spaces, the rooms named after Aaron Swartz, Ada Lovelace, Alan Turing, Chelsea Manning, Edward Snowden, Ian Murdock and Tula Pilar, plus the garden, the terrace, permanent installations and the Install Fest room. There were 61 talks, 29 hands-on workshops, five round tables, seven permanent activities, a film and an art performance, all proposed by the community through an open call. The largest tracks were technopolitics (27 sessions); technology and intersectionalities of gender, sexuality, race and class (19); the latest advances and vulnerabilities in information security and privacy (12); art and free technologies (12); hacking and exploring the limits of the internet (11); and workshops on installing and using secure communication and data protection tools (10), with smaller tracks on the climate crisis and autonomous infrastructure, internet governance and regulation, and activities for children. The opening round table, at 19:00 on Friday, was titled Crypto roots against the end of the world; a session on Meshtastic, billed as autonomous wireless communication, ran at 02:00; the closing round table started at 17:00 on Saturday. The campaign lists people who have spoken at past editions, among them Jérémie Zimmermann, Peter Sunde, James Bamford, Eva Galperin, Dave Maass, Anne Roth, Chelsea Manning, and the Brazilian cryptographers Paulo Barreto and Diego Aranha.

The theme, and the format. The 2026 theme borrowed the Doomsday Clock: on 27 January 2026 the Bulletin of the Atomic Scientists set it at 85 seconds to midnight, the closest it has ever been, and the campaign said CryptoRave was approaching those 85 seconds while celebrating its trajectory from its roots. The overnight-in-public choice is not incidental. Holding the event in a library or cultural centre rather than a hotel makes it accessible to people who could never expense a conference ticket, and running it through the night gives it the feel of an occupation rather than a seminar. The slogan on the campaign page states the argument in one line: if surveillance is centralized, resistance will be distributed. An anti-harassment policy applies in every space for the whole 24 hours.

The politics, stated rather than sanitized. CryptoRave emerged from a movement that treats privacy as a civil right and surveillance as something to be resisted, in a country with its own history of both, and its tracks on technopolitics and intersectionality make that explicit. Whether or not one shares the framing, it explains the format: a teaching event built on the belief that the knowledge should be distributed as widely as possible, which is why nobody is charged for it. For a security engineer the lesson is practical. The weakest point of most protection schemes is the person using them, and CryptoRave is one of the few events in the Brazilian calendar that works on that point directly, with the people outside the profession, while the professional conferences, such as BSides São Paulo a few streets away, talk to each other.

gts-gter.def: NIC.br's twin working groups - GTS for network security, GTER for network engineering and operations: the free meetings where Brazil's internet operators compare notes, twice a year, for decades.
gts-gter.context: GTER (Grupo de Trabalho em Engenharia e Operacao de Redes) is the older sibling; GTS (Grupo de Trabalho em Seguranca de Redes) grew from a GTER security subgroup launched at Comdex-SP in 1996 - the same lineage that produced CERT.br in 1997. The joint meetings, free to attend and streamed, anchor the Semana de Infraestrutura da Internet no Brasil each December (GTER 55 | GTS 41 in 2026) and carry the country's operational memory: BGP incidents, DDoS (distributed denial of service) seasons, IPv6 migration, all presented by the operators who lived them. The Premio Alberto Courrege Gomide honours the community's technical elders. If Brazilian network operations has a hallway track, it is here.

campus-party.def: Campus Party is the technology festival that began in Spain in 1997 as a LAN (local area network) party and is known for its camping: thousands of campuseiros pitching tents inside the venue for days of talks, workshops, hackathons and round-the-clock connectivity; in Brazil, where it arrived in São Paulo in 2008, it has held more than 50 editions.
campus-party.context: Born in Spain as a gathering of networked gamers and scaled into a travelling festival, Campus Party found its largest audiences in Brazil, where editions since 2008 turned the acampamento into a rite of passage: sleep in the tent, live on the arena floor, code through the night on famously generous bandwidth. The programme spans robotics, astronomy, games, startups, free software and security, breadth being the point, and the national edition has been held in Brasília since 2025. It is not a security conference and never claimed to be; it is where a great many Brazilian technologists first found their tribe, and where security often reached them first as one subject among many.
campus-party.depth:
Where it came from. Campus Party's Brazilian organizers date its birth to Spain in 1997, as a digital culture gathering that joined technology, creativity and living together, later known as one of the largest networked gatherings in the world. Wikipedia's history fills in the detail: a Spanish youth organization, EnRED, wanted to hold a small private local area network (LAN) party at the youth centre in Benalmádena, in Andalusia, and Paco Ragageles suggested expanding it into what was first called the Ben-Al Party. The second edition, in April 1998, attracted five times as many participants; in April 1999 Ragageles and a group of partners, among them Belinda Galiano, founded the non-profit E3 Futura, which set up Futura Networks to organize the festivals, and in 2000 the event moved to the science museum of Valencia's City of Arts and Sciences and grew to 1,600 participants over six days.

How it spread. From 2008 Campus Party expanded into Latin America, first to Brazil and Colombia and later to Argentina, Paraguay, Uruguay and El Salvador; in the 2010s it held a continental European edition in Berlin (2012), its first United Kingdom edition in London (2013) and one in Utrecht (2016), and reached Canada and Singapore. The Brazilian organizers counted more than 70 editions in 31 countries by 2025, and the global site's counters claim 700,000 campuseros, 7,200 speakers, 1,600 communities and 900 universities. Its list of famous participants, the extraordinary campuseros, includes Tim Berners-Lee, Vinton Cerf, Steve Wozniak and Al Gore, the last at Campus Party Brasil.

Brazil. The first Latin American edition was held in São Paulo in February 2008, at the São Paulo Art Biennial pavilion; from 2009 to 2011 it occupied the Centro de Exposições Imigrantes, and in 2012 it moved to Anhembi to fit its growing public. By the organizers' count Brazil has since hosted more than 50 editions, in person and digital, in 14 states, with an average of more than 100,000 visitors to the free Open Area at each full edition, and regional editions in Recife, Goiânia, Salvador, Manaus, Belo Horizonte and Natal among others. São Paulo remains the historical reference, but from 2025 Brasília became the national edition: CPBR17, the seventh in Brasília and the seventeenth national edition, filled the Arena BRB Mané Garrincha for five days from 18 to 22 June 2025, and the rules for Campus Party Brasil 2026, the eighteenth, set it for 3 to 6 June 2026, organized by the Instituto Campus Party, with travel support for selected speakers living outside Brasília. Shorter formats carry the brand further: Campus Party Weekend editions in Teresina, Aracaju, Pato Branco and Petrolina, the third in Teresina on 21 and 22 November 2026 with a free programme, and one-day Campus Day editions in Boa Vista, Campina Grande, Caruaru, Petrolina and Canindé de São Francisco.

How it works. A full edition has three layers. The Open Area is free, with talks, workshops and exhibitions for all ages; the Arena is the ticketed, immersive core of talks, workshops, hackathons, communities and large meetings; and the Camping is where, in the organizers' words, the experience runs 24 hours a day and connections happen at any hour, open to ticket holders with camping and to those who come through volunteering, caravans or communities. Campuseiros propose content through a call for talks, communities run their own spaces, and the event publishes a free scientific journal from submitted work. Its stated objective, in the 2026 rules, is the digital inclusion of Brazilian citizens, sharing, learning and teaching digital knowledge in a healthy setting of entertainment and talks. Hackathons are a fixture: in 2019 the organizers ran the Desafio Zé Gotinha with the Ministry of Health to build tools for vaccination surveillance and coverage.

The camping is the mechanism. The camping is not a gimmick. A conference you attend during the day and leave produces sessions; days living inside the venue produce the thing that actually changes careers, which is sustained contact with peers who are equally obsessed. Most of what participants describe afterwards happened between the talks rather than during them, and the organizers' own description of the camping, an experience that has no hour to end, says the same thing.

Free software and digital inclusion. Free software is rooted in the event's origins, and Brazil's editions were a stage for it: Jon 'maddog' Hall of Linux International spoke at Campus Party Brazil in 2011 to mark the twentieth anniversary of Linux, and on 17 January 2011 Ragageles and Telefónica's Latin American president announced at the Brazilian edition an initiative called Something Better, meant to promote responsible use of the internet and address privacy, piracy, spam and cyberbullying. Security fits the same pattern: it appears at Campus Party as one track and one community among many, beside robotics, astronomy, games and startups, which is precisely how many young Brazilians first met it.

Its significance in Brazil. For a great many attendees Campus Party was the first time being interested in technology stopped feeling like an isolated trait and started to look like membership of something with size and momentum. That transition is hard to engineer deliberately and impossible to measure afterwards, which is why events like it are consistently undervalued by everyone except the people they changed. For the security community specifically, it sits upstream of the specialist events: the people who later run or attend the Hackers to Hackers Conference (H2HC), BSides São Paulo, CryptoRave or Roadsec often met the field there first, and the free-software congress Latinoware, held in Foz do Iguaçu, is its closest relative in the Brazilian calendar.

latinoware.def: The Latin American congress of free software and open technologies, held every year since 2004 in Foz do Iguaçu (except 2005, in Curitiba), organized by Itaipu Binacional and its technology park, now Itaipu Parquetec, which hosted it for many editions.
latinoware.context: Latinoware grew alongside Brazil's strong free-software movement into one of the region's largest gatherings of free/libre and open-source software (FLOSS): community, government and academia meeting at the edge of the Itaipu binational dam for talks, tutorials and install fests across every corner of the open ecosystem, kernels to content licences. Its location is its symbol: open technology discussed at the border of three countries, Brazil, Argentina and Paraguay, under the patronage of a monument to shared infrastructure. For the networking trade it matters as the place where the Linux, BSD and open tooling communities that underpin every NOC (network operations centre) meet their Latin American contributors.
latinoware.depth:
What it is. Latinoware, in its current name the Congresso Latino-americano de Software Livre e Tecnologias Abertas (Latin American Congress of Free Software and Open Technologies), is a three-day annual event of talks, workshops, short courses and technical sessions for students, professionals, researchers, developers, teachers and leaders from the public and private sectors. It is organized by Itaipu Binacional, the binational company that runs the Itaipu hydroelectric dam, and by its associated technology park, Itaipu Parquetec, formerly the Parque Tecnológico Itaipu (PTI). Its twenty-third edition took place from 14 to 16 October 2026 at the Grand Carimã Resort and Convention Center in Foz do Iguaçu. It is not a security conference, though it now has a capture-the-flag (CTF) competition, and not a vendor fair, though it has exhibitors: its identity is the community of free and open technologies, now broadened well beyond the operating system.

Where it came from. The event grew out of Itaipu's own adoption of free software. According to the organizers' history, published in September 2026, Itaipu joined the federal government's Technical Committee for the Implementation of Free Software in 2003, with the involvement of its board and its information technology department, and figures of the Brazilian free software movement such as Sérgio Amadeu and Djalma Valois helped persuade the company; at the same time, conversations at an international free software conference in Curitiba produced the idea of a meeting with a Latin American calling. The first edition took place in November 2004 in Foz do Iguaçu, presenting Itaipu's free software programme under the slogan Ele não é diferente... É Livre (It is not different... it is free), with Jon maddog Hall among the guests, beginning a relationship with the event that has lasted ever since.

Foz, Curitiba and the park. In 2005 the event went to Curitiba; from 2006 it returned to Foz do Iguaçu and began its long relationship with the PTI. The third edition, opened at the park on 16 November 2006, was promoted by Itaipu Binacional and the Paraná state information technology company Celepar, expected about 1,300 people and 60 speakers, and was described at the time as the second largest free software event in South America; Itaipu's Brazilian director-general, Jorge Samek, presented it as a way to build a pool of open-source companies and skilled labour in the tri-border region, and the programme showcased the state government's open-source systems and the open protocols Itaipu itself had adopted. The venue has not always been the park: the 2018 edition gathered some 4,000 people at Foz do Iguaçu's convention centre, and the 2026 edition moved to a resort convention centre in the city.

Growth and the names on stage. Over the following years university caravans brought students from across Brazil, and the programme widened from free software itself to networks, infrastructure, security, development, databases and programming languages, then to open hardware (Arduino, Raspberry Pi, embedded systems, robotics and maker culture) and the internet of things. The eighth edition, in 2011, registered more than 4,200 participants and had on its stage Rasmus Lerdorf, the creator of PHP, Alexei Vladishev, the developer of the Zabbix monitoring system, and maddog Hall, who closed the event by marking twenty years of Linux. The organizers count more than 78,000 participants in total over the event's history.

A year of doubt. In September 2019 the organizers called off the sixteenth edition, planned for 9 to 11 October, citing internal contractual procedures that left no time to hold it, at a moment when Itaipu's new management was cutting agreements and sponsorships; the trade site Baguete noted that the event depended on its organizers' money and that the federal government, which appoints the directors of both Itaipu and its park, no longer had free software among its priorities. In October Itaipu's park announced new dates, 27 to 29 November 2019, with more than 100 activities and 4,000 people expected. The same year saw the decline of Brazil's other great free software event, the FISL (Fórum Internacional Software Livre) of Porto Alegre, cancelled for lack of sponsors in 2017, held in a much reduced form in 2018 and called off in Porto Alegre in 2019 after eighteen editions there. Latinoware survived; in 2020 and 2021 it went online, reaching people who could never have travelled to Foz do Iguaçu, and it returned in person in 2022.

What it covers now. The twentieth edition was held in 2023. The organizers describe the programme as following the field: security, privacy, data protection and technological sovereignty; education, with computational thinking, educational robotics, accessibility and neurodiversity; art, music and illustration made with open tools; and, since 2024 and 2025, artificial intelligence and innovation. A scientific track, Latin.Science, received a record 265 submissions in 2025. The 2026 edition combined the main programme with a CTF, the eighth Latinoware hackathon, on the theme of Brazil's statute protecting children and adolescents online and solutions built with free software, a programming marathon, robot sumo and a pop culture festival.

Why it matters to engineers. Most of the tools a network or security engineer runs are free software: the Linux and BSD systems under appliances and servers, monitoring such as Zabbix, the languages that glue automation together. Latinoware is one of the few places in Latin America where the people who build, package and teach those tools meet the people who use them, in Portuguese and Spanish, and where students from outside the São Paulo and Rio de Janeiro axis get a first contact with that community. Its history also shows how much open-technology events in Brazil depend on public patrons: a binational dam made this one possible, and a change of management in 2019 nearly ended it. The dates worth keeping are November 2004 for the first edition, 2005 for the year in Curitiba, 2019 for the postponement, 2020 and 2021 for the online years, and 14 to 16 October 2026 for the twenty-third edition.

ekoparty.def: Latin America's biggest hacking conference: Buenos Aires, every year since 2001, where the region's security community - and more than a few world-class vulnerabilities - come out on stage.
ekoparty.context: Founded in 2001 by five Argentine hackers, Ekoparty grew from a small local gathering into the continent's meeting point: 10,000-plus attendees, villages, wargames, lockpicking, wardriving heritage, and a week of trainings around the core days (the 22nd edition runs at the Centro de Convenciones de Buenos Aires in 2026). Its stage has world stature - the BEAST TLS attack was unveiled at Ekoparty 2011, CRIME followed there in 2012 - proof that first-rank offensive research speaks Spanish and Portuguese too. For Latin American researchers, an Ekoparty talk is the hometown equivalent of a Vegas main stage.
ekoparty.depth:
Ekoparty began in 2001 as a small gathering of five Argentine hackers and became the meeting point for security research across Latin America, drawing tens of thousands to Buenos Aires for a week of trainings, villages, wargames and talks.

Its significance is regional rather than merely large. Serious offensive security research in Latin America had no obvious venue: the major conferences were in the northern hemisphere, expensive to reach and conducted in English, so work done in the region was either presented abroad or not at all. Ekoparty created somewhere for that work to be presented in Spanish, to the people it was most relevant to, without a visa application.

The pattern is worth noticing because it repeats. A technical community that cannot gather does not develop a shared standard of what good work looks like, and the researchers stay isolated from each other while remaining perfectly aware of the international scene. Conferences function as the thing that turns scattered practitioners into a field, which is why the regional ones matter disproportionately to the people who could not have attended the others.

dragonjar.def: DragonJAR is a Colombian security community, grown from a Spanish-language forum into a company and into the DragonJAR Security Conference (DragonJARCON), which calls itself the largest hacker conference in Colombia and gives every main-stage talk in Spanish: 13 editions from 2014 to 2026, the last two in Medellín.
dragonjar.context: DragonJAR began as one of the Spanish-speaking world's most active security communities and forums, and its conference inherited that character: technical talks, tools and research by and for the regional community, with the all-Spanish rule as an explicit accessibility position, that world-class content should not require English. The founder, Jaime Andrés Restrepo, built a company on the same name, and the conference, run from offices in Manizales and held in Bogotá and then Medellín in recent years, draws speakers from Argentina, Mexico, Spain and Peru as much as from Colombia. Alongside Ekoparty in Buenos Aires and 8.8 in Santiago it forms the spine of the Latin American circuit, and its speakers travel the other events as a who's who of Spanish-language security research.
dragonjar.depth:
Community first. DragonJAR grew from a Colombian security community and its Spanish-language forum into a conference, and the sequence matters: the community existed first and the event became its annual gathering rather than the reverse. Its pages count the community's age at more than twenty years on the home page and twenty-five on the company page, and fourteen years as a business, DragonJAR Soluciones y Seguridad Informática, which sells penetration testing and training and says its team includes people who have ranked in the global top 100 on the bug bounty platforms HackerOne, YesWeHack and Intigriti. The community side still runs a blog, forums, newsletters and a video channel, and the conference's offices are in Manizales.

The conference. The DragonJAR Security Conference, DragonJARCON for short, describes itself as the largest hacker conference in Colombia and as an international congress of hackers and cybersecurity organized by the DragonJAR Community, for professionals, pentesters, researchers, students, security leaders and academics, with content on ethical hacking, penetration testing, web and mobile security, malware analysis, threat intelligence and bug bounty, and lately on artificial intelligence applied to offensive work. Its official history lists editions every year from 2014 to 2026, 238 talks in all, each linked to a free recording; the founder's own record dates the first edition to 8 to 10 May 2014. The 2023 and 2024 editions were held in Bogotá, on 7 and 8 September 2023 and on 26 and 27 September 2024; the twelfth, on 10 and 11 September 2025, and the thirteenth, on 10 and 11 September 2026 at the Centro de Eventos El Tesoro, in Medellín. In November 2026 the site already invited visitors to register for news of the 2027 edition.

The Spanish rule. The conference's frequently asked questions (FAQ) page answers the question of language directly: all the research presented on the main stage is in Spanish, given by Spanish-speaking researchers with a proven track record, with no simultaneous translation and no subtitles. Its archive calls itself a decade of offensive security research in Spanish. The speaker list shows what that produces: of the 238 talks in the official history, the largest groups of speakers are from Colombia (53), Argentina (47), Mexico and Spain (31 each) and Peru (20), followed by Uruguay, Ecuador, Bolivia and Chile, a pan-Hispanic programme rather than a national one. A regional observer, Corporación Colombia Digital, singled out its practical workshops in Spanish and its preference for technical content over formats driven by marketing.

Why language matters. Its significance is linguistic before it is technical. A great deal of security knowledge exists only in English, which puts a comprehension tax on every practitioner who does not read it fluently, and the tax compounds because the material is dense and precision matters. A forum and a conference operating in Spanish removed that tax for a region, and the archive of accumulated questions, answers and recorded talks is arguably worth more than any individual event. Translation is not the same as native-language production: a community that discusses problems in its own language develops its own vocabulary, its own worked examples and its own experts, rather than remaining a downstream consumer of somebody else's. That is a structural difference in how expertise develops, not merely a convenience, and the pattern recurs across non-English technical communities.

The founder's own research. Jaime Andrés Restrepo, who founded the community and the conference, keeps a public record of 71 documented participations in events in ten countries between 2008 and 2026, from Ekoparty in Buenos Aires and 8.8 in Santiago to Hacker Halted in Atlanta. His best-known line of research was on cars sold in Latin America: in October 2014 he spoke on keyless car hacking at the fourth 8.8 in Santiago, and on 18 April 2015 he gave 'Hackeando Carros en Latinoamérica' at the Latin American tour of the Open Worldwide Application Security Project (OWASP), the OWASP Latam Tour, in Lima. It is a clean statement of the circuit's argument: the vehicles, banking systems and devices sold in the region need researchers in the region, because nobody elsewhere has a reason to test them.

Its place in the circuit. DragonJAR belongs to the generation of independent Latin American conferences built locally rather than imported, with Ekoparty in Argentina, 8.8 in Chile and the Hackers to Hackers Conference (H2HC) in Brazil. Its distinguishing choices are the community behind it and the rule that the main stage speaks Spanish; its position is that of Colombia's largest hacker event, with a regional rather than national audience, and its archive is a free public collection of security talks in Spanish. The numbers worth remembering are 2014 for the first conference, 13 editions by 2026, 238 recorded talks, and a community more than two decades old.

8dot8.def: The 8.8 Computer Security Conference, Chile's technical hacking conference: founded in Santiago in 2011, '100% técnico y académico' by its own description, and wrapped every year in a different pop-culture theme, from The Matrix to Unreal.
8dot8.context: Founded in Santiago in 2011 by Gabriel Bergel, who still opens it as co-founder and chief executive, the 8.8 Computer Security Conference set out to share information, democratize knowledge and build community, and by its own count has grown into a regional institution: in 16 years more than 90 events, more than 500 speakers and more than 27,000 attendees across eight countries, plus offshoots such as 8.8 Gobierno, run with the Chilean government's CSIRT (computer security incident response team). The signature is tone: rigorous technical content inside a colourful frame soaked in pop culture, so that the fifteenth-anniversary edition of 2025 was 8.8 Matrix and the 2026 edition is 8.8 Unreal. With Ekoparty in Argentina and DragonJAR in Colombia it completes the southern circuit in which Latin America's security scene talks to itself.
8dot8.depth:
The 8.8 Computer Security Conference, written 8dot8 in its web address and social accounts, is Chile's hacker conference. Its own description, repeated in every press release, is a 100 per cent technical and academic event whose main aim is to share information, democratize knowledge and build community, which goes beyond theory and does it in a colourful frame with constant references to pop culture; it now calls itself the only itinerant conference, and one of the most influential hacker conferences, in Latin America.
