The name echoes the magnitude of the Maule earthquake of 27 February 2010, 8.8 in the United States Geological Survey's catalogue, a year before the first edition: a national catastrophe rather than a technology, which asserts local identity instead of borrowing the look of the northern conferences it is compared with.

It began on 18 November 2011 at the Cine Arte Normandie in Santiago, with speakers from Germany, Argentina, Brazil, Chile, the United States and Italy, among them researchers from Cisco, McAfee, DreamLab Technologies, Trustwave SpiderLabs, Onapsis and Core. Gabriel Bergel, its founder and organizer, told The Clinic that day that the aim was a different kind of conference, not oriented to governance and management or to commerce, but showing the techniques being used to exploit platforms and systems, the latest attacks and how they were carried out, repelled or fixed. The local backdrop was the 2011 wave of Anonymous attacks in support of the student movement and against HidroAysén, which kept the Ministry of Education's website down for weeks and also hit the sites of HidroAysén and the National Energy Council, while Bergel singled out code injection against banks as the most dangerous threat. Interviewed in 2016, he called 8.8 the first hacking conference in Chile, listed what was uncertain beforehand (a venue, sponsors, whether the police would agree, whether anyone would come, whether serving free beer was wise) and recalled that 400 people arrived, the press came, and the event reached prime-time television.

The second edition, on 18 and 19 October 2012 in the same cinema at Tarapacá 1181, brought Raoul Chiesa, known for breaking into the Bank of Italy's servers in the 1990s, and César Cerrudo, with cloud and mobile threats as the year's themes; ESET Latin America presented its research on the Dorkbot botnet and ran a malware analysis challenge across both days. The format settled quickly. Bergel wrote in 2022 that since 2012 the conference had been held in the third week of October, the month Chile has declared for cybersecurity since 2018; the Cine Arte Normandie was its home; entry that year was free; and each edition opens with his introduction and the start of a capture the flag (CTF) competition with a cash prize for the team that captures the most flags.

The edition names carry the pop-culture frame. The twelfth, in 2022, was 8.8 Real, with Eva Galperin, director of cybersecurity at the Electronic Frontier Foundation (EFF), giving the keynote on who deserves cybersecurity on her first visit to Chile, and Brazil's Eduardo Izycki dismantling the belief that Latin American states stay out of state-sponsored offensive operations, with three cases and the purchase of offensive capabilities by thirteen countries. The fourteenth, in 2024, saw Chile's Carabineros take part for the first time, presenting an artificial intelligence (AI) system called Proyecto Sitia that helps recover stolen vehicles, and Jaime Andrés Restrepo of DragonJAR warning about AI-driven cybercrime. For its fifteenth anniversary, on 2 and 3 October 2025, the conference became 8.8 Matrix, after the 1999 film, and moved to a new venue, the Centro Cultural CA660 in Las Condes, with Galperin back as keynote and the usual two days of talks, workshops, live hacking and CTF.

The sixteenth edition, 8.8 Unreal, asks whether you trust what you see. Its premise is that generative AI shapes perception, so that the conscious mind knows a fabricated video is fantasy while the subconscious takes it as real, and that criminals use generative AI and reverse engineering to alter the behaviour of networks, infrastructure and users and so hide their attacks. The Santiago agenda for 1 and 2 October 2026 at CA660 ran from Beau Woods, a collaborator of I Am The Cavalry, on building a better cyberpunk future and César Cerrudo's Countdown to Skynet to a dissection of a smishing campaign against Chilean users, an AI agent acting as the operator in real intrusions, virtual machine and container escapes, Linux kernel flaws from Dirty COW onwards, a radio-frequency assessment methodology from Mexico's Electronic Cats, digital evidence in oral trials, and Group-IB's chief executive Dmitry Volkov. The call for papers lists application security, reverse engineering, vulnerability exploitation, malware, social engineering, forensics, connected devices, cryptography, privacy and AI.

It no longer happens only in Santiago. Bergel said in 2016 that 8.8 also ran in La Paz, Bolivia, with Lima to follow, and the 2026 calendar has Peru on 6 May, 8.8 Gobierno on 13 May, Mexico on 29 and 31 July, a Las Vegas event on 4 August during the Black Hat and DEF CON week, Ecuador on 24 and 25 September, Chile on 1 and 2 October, an armed forces edition (FF.AA.) on 7 October and Brazil on 26 November. 8.8 Gobierno began on 13 May 2021 as an online conference developed with the CSIRT (computer security incident response team) of Chile's Ministry of the Interior, opened by the minister, with Tõnu Tammer of Estonia's national incident response team and Carlos Landeros, then director of the government CSIRT, among the speakers. Around the conference now sit an academy teaching hacking with AI, defence and governance courses, a foundation and a merchandise store.

The organizers' own figures vary with the date and the outlet, and should be read as theirs: the home page counts 15 years, more than 90 events, more than 500 experts and more than 27,000 attendees; a February 2026 announcement says 16 years and eight countries; a report from the October 2026 edition gives more than 25,000 attendees and 450 speakers. Its place in the region is clearer than any number. Ekoparty in Argentina, DragonJAR in Colombia, H2HC and Roadsec in Brazil and 8.8 in Chile each emerged because researchers in a country had no venue that was reachable, affordable and run in a language they worked in, and Bergel in 2016 named DragonJAR, founded by his friend Jaime Restrepo, as the largest security community in Latin America. Read together they describe a region building its own technical institutions rather than waiting to be included in someone else's.

fenasoft.def: Brazil's giant computing fair of the 1990s: the Anhembi pavilions, endless entry queues, and a nation meeting the personal computer - all at once.
fenasoft.context: Created by Max Gonçalves, the Feira Nacional de Software opened at Rio's RioCentro in March 1987 and moved to São Paulo in 1990, just as Brazil's market reserve on computing was crumbling - and the timing made it a phenomenon. At the Parque Anhembi it became, by every account, Latin America's largest computing fair: some 670,000 visitors in 1992, 800,000 and more than a thousand exhibitors in 1993, deals measured in billions, and lines outside the park that became part of the memory itself. For the generation that entered computing in 1990s Brazil, walking those pavilions - diskettes, first portables, the arrival of the consumer internet - was the pilgrimage. The 2000s pivot to a corporate-only event quietly ended the loucura; the word most used to remember the 1990s editions is exactly that one.
fenasoft.depth:
Fenasoft mattered because of when it happened. It opened in 1987 and moved to São Paulo in 1990, exactly as the market reserve was collapsing, so it became the place where a country that had spent a decade legally insulated from foreign computing got to see what everyone else had been using.

The scale it reached is hard to convey now. Hundreds of thousands of visitors queued at Anhembi to touch hardware they had only read about, in an era before the web made the international market visible from a desk. For a generation of Brazilian technologists it was the annual event where the industry became real, where you saw the machines, met the vendors, and discovered the size of the thing you had joined.

Its decline says as much as its rise. A trade fair whose value was giving physical access to products and information stopped being necessary once the internet provided both continuously and for free. Fenasoft did not fail so much as complete: it existed to solve the problem of distance from the global industry, and that problem was solved by the network the fair itself had helped people imagine.

shmoocon.def: The Washington, D.C. hacker convention that stayed small, cheap, and beloved on purpose - held every winter from 2005 until its farewell edition in 2025.
shmoocon.context: Organized by The Shmoo Group, ShmooCon inverted the industry's growth logic: roughly two thousand seats at the Washington Hilton, tickets priced to be affordable, and demand so fierce that sales sold out in seconds - a ritual of its own. The format was fixed and loved: a first day of rapid-fire talks called One Track Mind, then two days across Build It, Belay It, and Bring It On, plus fixtures like Hack Fortress and the TOOOL lockpick village. After twenty years the organizers closed it on their own terms with the 2025 edition - a conference that ended not by fading but by finishing, which in this industry is its own kind of distinction.
shmoocon.depth:
ShmooCon inverted the growth logic every other conference followed. Roughly two thousand seats, tickets priced to be affordable rather than expensable, and sales that famously sold out in seconds, because the organizers chose a size and refused to exceed it.

That refusal is the whole design. A conference that grows to fill demand becomes a trade show: sponsors set the tone, hallway conversations stop being possible, and the people who made it worth attending stop coming. Capping attendance keeps the density of expertise high and keeps a first-time attendee within conversational distance of researchers whose work they have read.

The trade is real and worth naming honestly. Deliberate scarcity means many people who would benefit cannot get in, and a lottery-style scramble favours those watching the clock at the right moment. The community's answer has been to publish talks openly afterwards, which shares the content while accepting that the room itself, the part that actually mattered, does not scale.

troopers.def: ERNW's Heidelberg conference - the one experienced European practitioners name when they can only pick one: trainings, three tracks, and roundtables where speakers and attendees argue as equals.
troopers.context: Running since 2008 at Heidelberg's Print Media Academy under the motto of making the world a safer place, TROOPERS built its reputation on density rather than scale: two days of high-end trainings, two of talks (the Active Directory and Entra ID track has become a signature that gathers Europe's identity-security researchers like nowhere else), and a closing day of roundtables. The culture shows in the details - electronic badges with a soldering corner to modify them, the IPv6 Security Summit heritage, a town small enough that the conference takes over its evenings. Modest in size, outsized in the respect it commands.
troopers.depth:
TROOPERS built its reputation on density rather than scale, running since 2008 in Heidelberg with two days of high-end training before two days of talks, under a motto about making the world a safer place that the programme takes literally.

Its distinguishing characteristic is the subject matter. Where many conferences chase whatever is newly fashionable, TROOPERS has consistently platformed research into the unglamorous infrastructure everything else depends on: telecommunications signalling, IPv6, industrial control, enterprise directory internals. That research rarely trends and matters enormously, because the systems involved are difficult to test, expensive to replace, and quietly load-bearing for everything above them.

The format follows from that focus. Small enough that speakers stay for the whole event rather than flying in for a slot, technical enough that the audience can challenge the work, and repeated annually with the same community, which is how a venue develops the shared standards that make deep work possible. It is a good illustration that a conference's value comes from who returns rather than from how many attend once.

hitb.def: Hack In The Box - the 'deep-knowledge' security conference born in Kuala Lumpur in the early 2000s, whose stages have moved across Asia, Europe, and the Middle East.
hitb.context: HITBSecConf made its name on technical depth - multi-track research talks, serious trainings, and its capture-the-flag heritage - and on geography: it was for years the gravitational centre of the Asian security research scene, with the Amsterdam editions of the 2010s serving as its celebrated European counterpart until that chapter closed for good in 2023. The conference continues where it began and beyond, in Asia and the Middle East, keeping its founding proposition intact: research-grade content, no filler, and a stage that made clear world-class security research was never a Western monopoly.
hitb.depth:
HITBSecConf made its name on two things: technical depth, through multi-track research talks and serious trainings with a capture-the-flag heritage, and geography, by becoming for years the gravitational centre of the Asian security research scene.

The geographic point is the substantive one. Research communities need somewhere to gather, and when the recognized venues are all in one hemisphere the effect is not merely inconvenience. Work gets presented to the wrong audience or not at all, regional expertise stays invisible to the international field, and practitioners who cannot travel remain isolated from each other while being perfectly aware of what they are missing.

Its later expansion to European editions changed the shape without changing the argument. A conference that establishes itself as the place where serious work in a region is presented creates a feedback loop: good research goes there because the audience is there, and the audience comes because the research is. Breaking into that loop from nothing is difficult, which is why the venues that manage it matter far beyond their attendance figures.

nullcon.def: India's flagship hacker conference, grown out of null - the country's largest open security community - and held on the beaches of Goa since 2010.
nullcon.context: null (styled n|u) is a registered not-for-profit and India's largest active security community, with chapters across Bangalore, Mumbai, Pune, Delhi, and beyond, built on free monthly meets and open exchange of research. Nullcon is its conference arm - run and marketed by Payatu - and it scaled the community's ethos into an international event: hardcore technical talks, trainings, a hardware village, and the Goa setting that became part of the brand (a Berlin edition extends the season). Its rise tracks India's rise in the global security industry, and for the subcontinent's researchers it is the home main stage.
nullcon.depth:
Nullcon grew out of null, the registered not-for-profit that is India's largest active security community, built on free monthly meets and open chapters across Bangalore, Mumbai, Pune, Delhi and beyond. The conference is the annual visible peak of something that runs all year.

That order matters, and it is the reverse of the usual. Most conferences are events that later grow a community; null was a community that eventually grew a conference, which means the meets are the substance and the conference is the summary. A free monthly meeting in a dozen cities reaches vastly more people over a year than any annual event, and it reaches the ones who could never afford a ticket.

The chapter model is worth studying by anyone trying to build a technical community elsewhere. It is cheap, it does not depend on sponsorship to survive, it scales by finding one committed organizer per city rather than by growing a central operation, and it produces local expertise that stays local. Conferences are visible and communities are durable, and the ones that last usually got the order right.

rsa-conference.def: The industry's biggest stage: born in 1991 as a small gathering of cryptographers, now the annual San Francisco mega-show where the security business shows what it is selling this year.
rsa-conference.context: RSA Conference began as a seminar convened by RSA Data Security for the tiny community arguing about cryptography - the Cryptographers' Panel survives as the ritual link to that origin - and grew with the industry into its trade fair: tens of thousands of attendees, an expo floor of acronyms competing for the same budgets, and the year's marketing theses on every banner. The honest reading practitioners share: the talks are uneven but the signal is real - walk the floor and you know what the industry believes, or wants you to believe, this year. Black Hat is where research premieres; RSA is where it gets productized.

cisco-live.def: The vendor mega-event that began as Networkers: certification labs, the World of Solutions floor, and the annual pilgrimage of the Cisco-certified.
cisco-live.context: Cisco's user conference traces to the late-1980s Networkers gatherings and scaled with the company into a multi-city institution (US and international editions) that defined what a vendor flagship event is: deep technical breakouts taught by the people who wrote the features, on-site certification testing where careers are minted, the NetVet culture of decades-long returnees, and a show floor - the World of Solutions - that doubles as the ecosystem's family reunion. Its DNA is the interesting part: unlike a trade show, the centre of gravity is education, which is why generations of network engineers date their skills by which Cisco Live they attended.

mwc.def: Mobile World Congress - the GSMA's Barcelona mega-show where the telecom industry announces its year: handsets, networks, and roughly a hundred thousand badge-wearers.
mwc.context: Descended from the GSM World Congress of the 1990s and its 3GSM years in Cannes, the event moved to Barcelona in 2006, took the MWC name, and became the industry's calendar anchor at the Fira Gran Via: phone launches for the headlines, but the real business in the halls where operators, equipment vendors, and now cloud and chip companies negotiate the next generation - each G's hype cycle has premiered here. Satellite editions extend the brand, and for anyone in ISP or carrier work, MWC week is when the roadmaps that will land in your network get announced to everyone at once.

nanog.def: The North American Network Operators' Group: the town hall where the people who actually run the internet compare notes - three meetings a year and one legendary mailing list, since 1994.
nanog.context: NANOG grew out of the NSFNET era's regional-techs meetings and kept that founding character: operators presenting to operators about routing incidents, peering, DDoS (distributed denial of service) weather, and the operational truth behind the marketing. The mailing list is an institution in its own right - decades of outage post-mortems and blunt engineering argument - and the term hallway track might as well have been coined for its corridors, where peering deals are struck over coffee. Regional siblings worldwide (Brazil's GTS/GTER plays the same role at home, LACNOG for the region) share the model: no vendor keynotes at the centre, just the network, as operated.

lacnic.def: The Latin American and Caribbean internet registry - the steward of the region's IP addresses and AS numbers, whose twice-yearly meetings double as the region's operator congress.
lacnic.context: One of the five regional internet registries, LACNIC (established 2002, headquartered in Montevideo) allocates IPv4, IPv6, and autonomous system numbers across Latin America and the Caribbean, and runs the open policy forum where the community writes its own allocation rules. The meetings are the events: held around the region jointly with LACNOG, the operators' group, they concentrate the continent's BGP, peering, IPv6, and security conversations in one week - with fellowship programs that deliberately pull new engineers into the room. For a region that entered the IPv4-exhaustion era early, LACNIC's meetings are where the transition has been argued, measured, and engineered.

network-topology.def: The shape of a network: how nodes are connected, drawn either as the cables actually run or as the traffic actually flows.
network-topology.context: The distinction that trips people up is physical versus logical topology, and they are frequently different. Classic Ethernet wired as a star through a hub behaved logically as a bus, because every frame still reached every port and every station still contended for the same medium. Ask which one someone means before you argue about the diagram.

bus-topology.def: A single shared cable that every station taps into, with terminators at each end.
bus-topology.context: The original Ethernet: 10BASE5 thicknet with vampire taps, then 10BASE2 thinnet with BNC tees. One shared medium means one collision domain, so stations had to take turns, and a single break or a missing terminator took the whole segment down. That fragility is exactly why the star replaced it, though the bus survives conceptually in wireless, where the air is the shared medium.

star-topology.def: Every node connects to a central device, and nothing connects directly to anything else.
star-topology.context: The topology that won. A switch at the centre gives each station its own collision domain and turns a cable fault into a one-port problem instead of a network outage, which is why structured cabling standardized on home runs to a wiring closet. The obvious objection is the centre as a single point of failure, answered in practice by stacking, chassis redundancy, or dual-homing to two switches.

ring-topology.def: Each node connects to exactly two neighbours, forming a closed loop that traffic travels around.
ring-topology.context: Token Ring and FDDI made it famous: a token circulating the loop granted the right to transmit, which produced deterministic, collision-free behaviour that Ethernet could not match at the time. Dual counter-rotating rings gave FDDI its self-healing wrap on a break. Ethernet's economics eventually won anyway, but rings never left, they moved into the metro and optical layer, where SONET/SDH and resilient ring protocols still exploit the same property.

mesh-topology.def: Nodes connect to many other nodes directly, so traffic has multiple independent paths.
mesh-topology.context: A full mesh connects every node to every other, which costs n(n-1)/2 links and stops scaling almost immediately, so real designs use partial mesh: rich connectivity where it pays, sparse elsewhere. The internet's inter-AS core is the largest working example, and wireless mesh applies the same idea where cabling is impractical. Redundancy is the point, and the price is complexity in routing and troubleshooting.

tree-topology.def: A hierarchy of stars: a root branching into layers, with no loops in the intended design.
tree-topology.context: The classic campus three-tier build, core to distribution to access, is a tree, and its virtue is that aggregation and policy land at predictable layers. Because the design assumes no loops, an accidental one is a broadcast storm, which is why spanning tree exists as the automatic loop-breaker. Modern data centres largely abandoned the strict tree for spine-leaf, wanting equal-cost paths rather than a single upward branch.

hybrid-topology.def: Any real network: a mix of topologies stitched together, chosen per layer for what that layer needs.
hybrid-topology.context: Nobody designs a pure anything. A typical enterprise is star at the access layer, meshed between core switches, ring in the metro carrier that connects the sites, and logically point-to-point across every VPN (virtual private network) tunnel. The textbook topologies are worth knowing precisely so you can name the pieces of the hybrid you are actually looking at.

client-server.def: An architecture where requesting clients talk to a designated server that holds the resource and answers.
client-server.context: The asymmetry is the whole design: the server is always listening, is addressable and administered, and the client initiates. That centralization is what makes access control, backup, and auditing tractable, and it is why nearly every enterprise protocol, HTTP, LDAP (Lightweight Directory Access Protocol), SMTP, SQL, works this way. The cost is that the server is both the bottleneck and the target.
client-server.depth:
Client-server splits an application between a requester and a provider, with the server holding the shared state and enforcing the rules. It is the dominant model because centralizing authority makes consistency, access control and auditing tractable.

Its properties follow from that centralization. The server is a single point of failure and a single point of trust, scaling means making it bigger or making many of them agree, and every client depends on its availability. The alternative pushes work and trust to the edges and gets resilience at the cost of consistency, which is why almost every real system is a hybrid: peer-to-peer distribution of bulk data, client-server for the decisions about it.

peer-to-peer.def: An architecture where every node is both client and server, providing resources to the others directly.
peer-to-peer.context: Peers discover each other and exchange without a central authority holding the data, which gives P2P its resilience and its bandwidth economics: the more participants, the more capacity, exactly inverting the client-server curve. BitTorrent, blockchain gossip, and Windows file sharing between two desktops are all the same model. The trade is governance, since there is no single place to enforce policy or revoke access.
peer-to-peer.depth:
Peer-to-peer has no privileged node, with each participant acting as both client and server. Capacity grows as participants join rather than being consumed by them, which is the property that makes it superb for distribution and awkward for anything requiring agreement.

That awkwardness is where most of the interesting engineering sits. Without a central authority, discovering peers, establishing trust, resisting participants who lie, and deciding what is true when nodes disagree all become explicit problems that a server would have solved implicitly. Consensus protocols and reputation systems are the answers, and they cost latency and complexity, which is why peer-to-peer wins for content distribution and mostly loses for transactions.

host-to-host.def: A direct association between two endpoints, with no intermediary acting as the resource.
host-to-host.context: The term shows up in two places worth separating. In TCP/IP's layered model, the host-to-host layer is the transport layer, TCP and UDP, whose job is end-to-end delivery between two hosts regardless of the routers in between. In topology talk, host-to-host means a plain point-to-point link, a crossover cable or a serial WAN circuit. Both senses share the idea: two ends, symmetric, no server in the middle.

quality-assurance.def: The discipline of building confidence that software does what it should, before users find out otherwise.
quality-assurance.context: Worth separating from testing: testing is an activity, QA is the whole practice of process, standards, and evidence that makes quality predictable rather than lucky. The distinction shows up in job titles too, where a QA engineer today writes at least as much code as the developers under test.

regression-testing.def: Re-running existing tests to confirm that a change did not break something that already worked.
regression-testing.context: The name is the point: a regression is progress running backwards, and the whole reason a suite accumulates is that every bug fixed once should stay fixed. Mature teams add a test reproducing each bug at the moment they fix it, so the suite becomes a memory of everything that ever went wrong. Skipping it under deadline pressure is the classic false economy behind the emergency hotfix a week later.

test-automation.def: Letting machines execute tests, so they run on every change instead of when someone has time.
test-automation.context: Automation buys repeatability and speed, which is what makes continuous integration possible at all, since nobody manually regression-tests on every commit. The trap is treating coverage percentage as the goal: a suite full of brittle tests asserting implementation details costs more to maintain than the bugs it catches. Unit tests are cheap and fast, end-to-end tests are slow and truthful, and the ratio between them is a real design decision.

semantic-versioning.def: The MAJOR.MINOR.PATCH convention, where each number carries a promise about compatibility.
semantic-versioning.context: Under SemVer, PATCH means backward-compatible fixes, MINOR means backward-compatible additions, and MAJOR means you broke something and callers must read the notes. Its value is entirely social: it lets a dependency manager reason about upgrades automatically, which only works while publishers keep the promise. Version 0.y.z is the explicit escape hatch meaning nothing is stable yet.

patch.def: A change applied to existing software or firmware to fix a defect or close a vulnerability; in source code, the set of differences (a diff) that the patch program applies to a file. Patching is the act; patch management is doing it across every asset, quickly enough and verifiably.
patch.context: The noun is older than most of the software it now ships in: the Association for Computing Machinery's first glossary of programming terms, in June 1954, defined a patch as a section of coding inserted into a routine to correct a mistake, and suppliers later mailed fixes as segments of paper tape or punched cards to be cut in by hand. In security work patching is the least glamorous control and one of the most effective, because so many exploited flaws already have a fix: WannaCry and the Equifax breach in 2017 both used vulnerabilities patched two months earlier. The practical difficulty is never the patch itself but the change window: proving the fix will not break production is what patch management actually consists of.
patch.depth:
What counts as a patch. The National Institute of Standards and Technology (NIST) glossary carries two definitions. One, taken from ISO/IEC 19770-2, the software identification standard of the International Organization for Standardization (ISO) and the International Electrotechnical Commission (IEC), is narrow: a component that, once installed, modifies the files or settings of another component without changing its version number. The other, from NIST's older guides to web and mail servers, is the working sense: a repair job, the immediate solution handed to users, not necessarily the best one (developers often find a better fix for the next release), usually shipped as a replacement for or an insertion into compiled code. NIST Special Publication (SP) 800-40 Revision 4 (April 2022) defines patching as applying a change to installed software, whether firmware, operating system or application, that corrects security or functionality problems or adds capabilities, and treats patches, updates and upgrades under the same management process.

Where the word comes from, and the programmer's sense. The Association for Computing Machinery (ACM) committee on nomenclature, chaired by Grace Murray Hopper, defined a patch in June 1954 as a section of coding inserted into a routine, usually by transferring control to the patch and back again, to correct a mistake or alter the routine; linguists on the American Dialect Society list point to that glossary as the earliest dictionary citation and doubt the popular story that the word began with patches stuck on punched cards, although such patches were really made. Fixes later travelled as segments of paper tape or card decks for the recipient to cut in, and the Jargon File remembers instructions keyed in from front-panel switches and IBM's absolute hexadecimal patches, applied on top of each other until the code grew scar tissue. In Unix a patch became a diff: the output of diff, which the patch program written by Larry Wall applies to source files. The GNU manual's image is exact: diff subtracts one file from another, patch adds the difference back. That is the sense in which open-source contributors still send a patch.

The patch is a disclosure. A fix shows where the flaw was. In May 2008 David Brumley, Pongsin Poosankam, Dawn Song and Jiang Zheng showed at the Institute of Electrical and Electronics Engineers (IEEE) Symposium on Security and Privacy that an exploit could be generated automatically from the patched binary, sometimes in a few minutes, by finding the input checks the patch added and constructing inputs that fail them. The clock therefore starts at release, not at disclosure. The argument came back in 2026. On 6 July F5 announced monthly hardened releases on the third Wednesday of each month from 15 July, limited detail about each fix and security notifications a month later, a delay meant to give customers time to update first. On 13 August, one release later, it moved to a six-week cadence from 2 September and paused regular notifications, saying that current artificial intelligence (AI) models reason from a diff, a partial description or a version range to a working attack chain, so that the window it had created for defenders was a window for attackers too; on 14 October it renamed hardened releases critical releases.

Cadence. Predictability was Microsoft's answer to sporadic releases: Patch Tuesday, the release of security updates on the second Tuesday of each month, was conceived and implemented in 2003. Fortinet's product security incident response team (PSIRT) publishes its advisories on the second Tuesday of the month as well. A fixed day lets operations plan maintenance windows; out-of-band releases remain for flaws already under attack.

The process. SP 800-40 Rev. 4, by Murugiah Souppaya and Karen Scarfone, frames patching as preventive maintenance, a cost of doing business like servicing a vehicle fleet. Patching is one way to mitigate risk; the others are accepting it, transferring it (insurance) and avoiding it (decommissioning the asset). Its steps are concrete: prioritize, schedule, acquire, validate the patch's authenticity and integrity because it may come from a rogue source or be tampered with, test, distribute, install, restart or reconfigure where needed, resolve side effects, verify that the patch took effect, and keep monitoring, because a patch can be uninstalled by a user or an attacker, an unpatched version restored from a backup, or a device reset to a vulnerable factory state. It plans for four situations, routine patching, emergency patching, emergency mitigation and unpatchable assets, and states the trade-off plainly: deploying faster shortens the attacker's window and raises the risk of disruption; testing longer does the reverse. Control SI-2 of SP 800-53 turns this into requirements: test updates for effectiveness and side effects, install them within a period the organization defines, and run flaw remediation through configuration management.

A rate, not a percentage. SP 800-40 calls overly simple metrics, such as the share of vulnerabilities patched, not actionable, and proposes instead the percentage of assets patched by each plan's deadline with the mean and median time, by asset importance and vulnerability importance. Equifax shows why. Its policy required critical vulnerabilities to be patched within 48 hours; its security staff learned of the Apache Struts flaw from the United States Computer Emergency Readiness Team on 8 March 2017 and circulated an alert to more than 400 people, but the developer who knew where Struts ran was not on the list, scans missed it, and the company had no complete asset inventory. Attackers entered on 13 May 2017 and stayed 78 days; the breach involved the personal data of more than 145 million Americans. A 2015 internal audit had already found a backlog of more than 8,500 unpatched vulnerabilities and an honour system for patching. The Senate investigators' summary is the rule: if a vulnerability cannot be found, it cannot be patched.

What to patch first. Severity alone is a weak guide; evidence of exploitation is a better one. The Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency's (CISA) Binding Operational Directive 22-01 of November 2021 told federal agencies to remediate listed vulnerabilities within two weeks, or six months for those with Common Vulnerabilities and Exposures (CVE) identifiers assigned before 2021, until BOD 26-04 revoked and replaced it on 10 June 2026; its Known Exploited Vulnerabilities (KEV) catalogue held 1,779 entries in the 10 November 2026 version, 361 of them marked as used in ransomware campaigns. Verizon's 2025 Data Breach Investigations Report put exploitation of vulnerabilities as the initial vector in 20 per cent of breaches, up 34 per cent, with zero-days against perimeter devices and virtual private networks (VPNs) prominent. WannaCry is the standard lesson: Microsoft published bulletin MS17-010, rated Critical, on 14 March 2017; the worm spread on 12 May; the National Audit Office found that at least 81 of 236 English hospital trusts were affected, that every infected organization ran unpatched or unsupported Windows, and that managing internet-facing firewalls would also have protected them.

When the patch cannot go in yet. Live patching narrows the reboot problem: the Linux kernel's livepatch redirects calls to fixed functions through ftrace, under a consistency model that decides when the new code may run. Virtual patching, a web application firewall or intrusion prevention rule that blocks the exploit, covers the gap between a fix that exists and a fix that is deployed, which F5's August 2026 note also recommended; it is mitigation, not remediation. Neighbours worth separating: a hotfix is an urgent patch outside the normal cycle, a backport carries a fix to an older branch, an upgrade changes the version, and an unpatchable asset needs compensating controls for as long as it stays in service.

hotfix.def: An urgent, narrowly scoped fix shipped outside the normal release cycle.
hotfix.context: A hotfix trades process for speed: it skips the queue because something is on fire, which means it also skips much of the testing that normally catches side effects. The discipline that keeps hotfixes safe is merging them back into the mainline immediately, since the classic disaster is an emergency fix that quietly disappears in the next scheduled release and the outage returns.

vi.def: The modal terminal editor that is on essentially every Unix-like system, and its dominant modern successor Vim.
vi.context: Modal means keystrokes mean different things depending on mode, which is why newcomers get stuck unable to exit and veterans edit at speed without leaving the home row. Learning it is not nostalgia but insurance: vi is what exists on the rescue shell, the appliance console, and the container with nothing else installed. The minimum survival kit is i to insert, Escape to leave insert, and :wq to write and quit.

nano.def: A small, unmodal terminal editor that shows its own shortcuts along the bottom of the screen.
nano.context: Nano's virtue is that it requires nothing to be known in advance, since the control keys are printed right there, which is why distributions install it as the default for editing a config file quickly. It succeeded Pico from the Pine mail client. For a two-line change on a box you are not going to live on, it is the right tool and not a lesser one.

emacs.def: The extensible editor from the GNU project, closer to a programmable environment that happens to edit text.
emacs.context: Nearly all of Emacs is written in its own Lisp dialect and can be redefined while running, which is what people mean when they joke that it is a fine operating system lacking only a decent editor. Its rivalry with vi is the oldest running joke in the field, the editor war, and both sides are correct: one optimizes for editing keystrokes, the other for reshaping the tool itself.

gdb.def: The GNU debugger: it runs a program under control so you can stop it, inspect it, and step through it.
gdb.context: The core moves are a breakpoint to pause at a chosen line, backtrace to see the call stack that got you there, print to read variables, and step or next to advance. It is the tool that turns a crash into an explanation, since a segfault plus a backtrace usually names the offending line immediately. Security researchers and reverse engineers use the same tool from the other direction, watching memory as a program mishandles it.

memory-leak.def: Memory that a program allocates and never releases, so its footprint grows until something gives.
memory-leak.context: Not a crash but a slow bleed, which is what makes it hard: the process is fine for hours or weeks, then the machine starts swapping and the incident begins far from the cause. The classic fingerprint is a service that behaves perfectly after a restart, which is why nightly restarts became a folk remedy instead of a fix. Detectors like Valgrind and the address sanitizers exist precisely because the symptom appears so far from the allocation.

buffer-overflow.def: Writing more data into a buffer than it can hold, so the excess lands in adjacent memory that was never meant to receive it.
buffer-overflow.context: The mechanism is simple enough to state in one line: a fixed-size buffer, an unchecked copy, and whatever sat next to it in memory gets overwritten. Historically what sat next to a stack buffer was the saved return address, so a long enough input could redirect execution when the function returned, which is what made this the defining vulnerability class of the 1990s and the engine of the Morris worm and Code Red. Everything about modern process hardening is a response to it: stack canaries to detect the overwrite, NX/DEP so overwritten data cannot execute, ASLR so the attacker cannot predict addresses, and bounds-checked or memory-safe languages so the write never happens. It is CWE-787, still near the top of the CWE Top 25 thirty years on.
buffer-overflow.depth:
A buffer overflow writes past the end of allocated memory, corrupting whatever sits beyond it. On the stack that is often the saved return address, which is why the classic exploit redirects execution to attacker-supplied code.

Decades of mitigation made the classic version hard rather than impossible: stack canaries detect the overwrite, non-executable memory stops the payload running where it was written, and address randomization removes the fixed targets. Each was answered, respectively, by canary leaks, return-oriented programming and information disclosure, which is why the durable answer is memory-safe languages rather than another layer of defence on an unsafe one.

stack-overflow.def: Exhausting the call stack, usually through recursion that never reaches its base case.
stack-overflow.context: Worth keeping distinct from a buffer overflow on the stack, which is a different bug with a similar-sounding name. Here nothing is overwritten maliciously, the stack simply hits its limit and the process dies, typically with a stack overflow exception or a segmentation fault. The fix is almost always algorithmic, a missing termination condition or converting deep recursion to iteration, and it is the bug that gave the famous programming site its name.

integer-overflow.def: An arithmetic result too large for its type, so the value silently wraps around instead of growing.
integer-overflow.context: Add one to the maximum signed 32-bit integer and you land on the most negative one, which is only a curiosity until the wrapped value is used as a size. The dangerous pattern is a length calculation that overflows to something tiny, passes a sanity check because it now looks small, and is then used to allocate a buffer that the real data overruns, which is how integer overflows become memory-corruption bugs. Ariane 5 famously destroyed itself on a related conversion error. Mitigations are checked arithmetic, wider types, and treating any size arithmetic on untrusted input as suspect. It is CWE-190.

null-pointer-dereference.def: Following a pointer that holds null, so the program reads or writes address zero and is stopped by the operating system.
null-pointer-dereference.context: Rodolfo Nützmann calls this the zero pointer, and the usual cause is prosaic: a function returned null on failure and nobody checked. On modern systems it is a reliable crash rather than a takeover, because the zero page is deliberately left unmapped, which is precisely the mitigation, and it explains why the same bug was far more dangerous on older systems where low memory could be mapped. Its real cost is availability, since an attacker who can force the null path repeatedly has a denial of service. It is CWE-476, and in a debugger it is the fastest bug to diagnose: the backtrace names the line.

use-after-free.def: Using a pointer to memory that has already been released, back when it still meant something.
use-after-free.context: The pointer is now dangling: the allocator may have handed that block to something else entirely, so the program is reading or writing another object's data through the wrong lens. It is more dangerous than a plain crash because the contents are attacker-influenceable if they can control what gets allocated into the freed space, which makes it a mainstay of modern browser and kernel exploitation, and the reason double-free is treated as its sibling. Defenses are ownership discipline, setting pointers to null after freeing, hardened allocators, and ultimately languages that make the pattern unrepresentable. It is CWE-416.
use-after-free.depth:
Use after free accesses memory that has already been released, at which point the allocator may have handed it to something else. The danger is not the read itself but that an attacker who controls what gets allocated into that space controls what the stale pointer now points at.

It is harder to reason about than an overflow because the bug and its consequence are separated in time and often in code. Sanitizers find it during testing by delaying reuse and poisoning freed regions, hardened allocators make exploitation less reliable, and neither eliminates it. It is the most common serious memory bug in modern C and C++ codebases, which is much of the reason for the ownership models in newer languages.

memory-safety.def: The property of never accessing memory outside what a program legitimately owns, in space or in time.
memory-safety.context: Two halves: spatial safety means staying inside an object's bounds, and temporal safety means only touching it while it is alive, which is why buffer overflows and use-after-free are the same problem viewed on different axes. The industry conclusion, stated by CISA, the NSA, and Microsoft alike, is that roughly seventy percent of serious vulnerabilities in large C and C++ codebases are memory-safety bugs, which is what put Rust, Go, Java, and modern C++ practice at the centre of the conversation. Rewriting everything is not realistic, so the practical answer is memory-safe languages for new components plus hardening and sanitizers for the code that stays.
memory-safety.depth:
Memory safety means a program cannot read or write outside what it legitimately owns. Languages that guarantee it eliminate overflows, use-after-free, double frees and data races on memory by construction rather than by discipline.

The numbers behind the industry's shift are stark: multiple large vendors have reported that around two thirds of their serious vulnerabilities are memory safety issues, and that proportion has been stable for years despite enormous investment in finding them. That is the argument for changing the material rather than inspecting it harder. The honest counterweight is that rewriting working systems is expensive and risky, which is why the practical advice is to write new components in safe languages and to harden rather than replace the old ones.

stack-canary.def: A known value placed between local buffers and the saved return address, checked before a function returns.
stack-canary.context: The name is the coal-mine metaphor: if the canary is dead, something wrote past the buffer, and the program aborts instead of returning into whatever now sits in that slot. Compilers add it automatically under flags like -fstack-protector, and it is cheap, which is why it is on by default nearly everywhere. It detects rather than prevents, and it only guards the contiguous-overwrite case, so it is one layer among several, not the answer on its own.

aslr.def: Randomizing where a process's memory regions land, so their addresses differ on every run.
aslr.context: Exploitation generally requires knowing where something is, so shuffling the stack, heap, libraries, and with PIE the executable itself turns a reliable attack into a guess. Its weakness is anything that leaks an address, since one leaked pointer can derandomize an entire region, which is why information disclosure bugs are rated more seriously than their direct impact suggests. Paired with NX and canaries, it is the third leg of standard process hardening.
aslr.depth:
Address space layout randomization places code and data at unpredictable addresses so an exploit cannot rely on knowing where anything is. It converts a reliable attack into one that must first discover the layout.

Its effectiveness depends entirely on entropy and on nothing leaking. On 32-bit systems the available randomness was small enough to brute force; a single information disclosure that reveals one address often defeats the whole scheme, because everything in that module shifts together. It is a genuine and cheap mitigation that raises exploitation cost, and describing it as protection rather than as an obstacle overstates what it does.

nx-bit.def: Marking memory pages as either writable or executable, but never both, so injected data cannot run as code.
nx-bit.context: The hardware bit is NX or XD; Windows calls the policy DEP, and the general principle is W xor X. It ended the simplest form of exploitation, where an attacker wrote instructions into a buffer and jumped to them, and it is the reason attackers moved to reusing code already present and legitimately executable in the process. That escalation is the honest lesson of this whole family: each mitigation raised the cost substantially without ending the game, which is why they are deployed together rather than chosen between.

fuzzing.def: Feeding a program vast quantities of malformed or random input to see what makes it crash.
fuzzing.context: A crash is a lead, since a program that mishandles input badly enough to die may mishandle it exploitably, and fuzzers find in hours what code review misses for years. Modern coverage-guided fuzzers like AFL and libFuzzer mutate inputs and keep the ones that reach new code paths, which is why they are paired with sanitizers that turn silent corruption into a loud, reproducible failure. It sits on both sides of the fence: the same tool serves a vendor hardening a parser and a researcher hunting for bugs in it.

cwe.def: A community catalogue of software weakness types, each with a stable identifier like CWE-787.
cwe.context: The distinction from CVE is the one to hold: a CVE is one specific vulnerability in one specific product, while a CWE is the category of mistake behind it, so a CVE report says what broke and its CWE says why. MITRE publishes the CWE Top 25 most dangerous weaknesses annually, which is the register the memory-safety classes keep appearing on. It is the vocabulary secure-code reviews and static analysis tools report in.
cwe.depth:
CWE catalogues weakness types rather than individual vulnerabilities: the class of mistake, such as improper input validation or use after free, as opposed to CVE's naming of a specific instance in a specific product. The pairing is that a CVE is an occurrence and its CWE is the reason.

That distinction is what makes CWE useful for prevention rather than response. A list of CVEs tells you what to patch; a distribution of CWEs tells you what your development process keeps producing, which is actionable in a different way. The Top 25 is the widely cited artefact, and it is more useful read as a curriculum for where to invest in training and tooling than as another checklist.

ether.def: The imaginary medium light was once thought to travel through, and the wink in the name Ethernet.
ether.context: Nineteenth-century physics assumed waves needed a medium, so it posited the luminiferous aether filling all space; the Michelson-Morley experiment of 1887 famously failed to detect it, and relativity later dispensed with it entirely. When Metcalfe and Boggs named their 1973 network Ethernet, the joke was deliberate: the shared coaxial cable was the omnipresent medium every station transmitted into, a working ether for packets even though physics had abandoned the real one. Engineers still say a lost packet vanished into the ether, and the pun is the whole point.
ether.depth:
The name Ethernet comes from the luminiferous aether, the medium nineteenth-century physics assumed light needed in order to propagate. The Michelson-Morley experiment failed to detect it in 1887 and relativity eventually dispensed with the idea entirely, leaving a word for something that does not exist.

Metcalfe chose it deliberately and the metaphor is precise. Original Ethernet was a shared coaxial cable that every station could hear, so the cable behaved as a passive medium carrying signals to everyone, exactly the role the aether was invented to play. Collisions happened because two stations could transmit into the same medium at once, which is why the protocol needed detection and backoff at all.

The irony is that modern Ethernet has no shared medium. Switched, full-duplex links mean each station has a private path, collisions do not occur, and the collision detection the name implies is vestigial. The word survived because it names a family of standards and a connector rather than a mechanism, which is a common fate: the technology was replaced underneath the name, and everyone kept saying it because the alternative was renaming everything.

daemon.def: A long-running background process, with no controlling terminal, that waits to do its job for the system or for other programs; the name comes from a benevolent spirit, Maxwell's daemon, not from a demon.
daemon.context: The term comes from Maxwell's demon in physics, chosen by Fernando Corbató's group at Project MAC of the MIT (Massachusetts Institute of Technology) around 1963 for a helpful process that works unseen; the conventional d suffix (sshd, httpd, crond) marks them. A daemon has no controlling terminal and is usually started at boot by the service manager, which is exactly why a hung one is invisible until something depending on it fails. On Windows the same idea is called a service. BSD (Berkeley Software Distribution) Unix even adopted the little horned mascot, insisting it was a daemon and never a demon.
daemon.depth:
What it is. The Linux daemon(7) manual page defines a daemon as a service process that runs in the background and supervises the system or provides functionality to other processes. It has no controlling terminal and no user in front of it; it is started by the system, usually at boot, and it answers to signals, sockets, timers and files rather than to a keyboard. The name describes a role, not a kind of program: sshd, the OpenSSH server, is a daemon, and so are a syslog collector, a cron scheduler and the control-plane processes of a load balancer or firewall. Names conventionally end in d, as in sshd, httpd and crond, or, on F5 BIG-IP, mcpd, bigd and gtmd.

Where the word came from. Asked about the origin in an exchange published by the etymology column Take Our Word For It, Fernando Corbató confirmed that his group at MIT's (Massachusetts Institute of Technology) Project MAC began using the term around 1963, when they worked on the IBM 7094, and said the use was inspired by Maxwell's daemon of physics and thermodynamics, an imaginary agent that sorted molecules of different speeds and worked tirelessly in the background. They fancifully applied it to background processes that tirelessly performed system chores. The backronym Disk And Executive MONitor, sometimes offered as the origin, was new to him. The spelling is the older form of demon: the FreeBSD project quotes Evi Nemeth's Unix System Administration Handbook calling the equation of daemon with demon an egregious misunderstanding, since the Greek daemon was closer to a guardian spirit. The mascot of BSD (Berkeley Software Distribution) Unix, the BSD Daemon, copyright 1988 by Marshall Kirk McKusick, owes its earliest and most popular renditions to John Lasseter.

How a traditional daemon detaches. daemon(7) lists fifteen steps a SysV-style daemon performs when it starts. It closes inherited file descriptors, resets signal handlers and the signal mask, and sanitizes the environment; calls fork() to create a background process; calls setsid() in the child to detach from any terminal and start a new session; forks again so that it can never reacquire a terminal; exits the first child so the daemon is re-parented to init, process 1; connects standard input, output and error to /dev/null; resets the umask to 0; changes the working directory to / so it does not hold a mount point busy; writes a PID (process identifier) file so that it cannot be started twice; drops privileges where it can; and tells the original process that initialization is complete before that process exits. Each step closes a specific trap, from a daemon that dies when its terminal closes to one that blocks an unmount.

New-style daemons. Under systemd none of that is needed. The service manager starts the daemon already detached, with clean signals and environment and its output connected to the journal, and the daemon is expected to report readiness through sd_notify(3) with READY=1, shut down cleanly on SIGTERM, reload its configuration on SIGHUP where that applies, and return a meaningful exit code. Socket-based activation moves the creation of the listening socket into the service manager, which can then start daemons in parallel and hold connections while one restarts. In a unit file, Type= tells systemd how start-up completion is signalled (simple, exec, forking, oneshot, dbus, notify, notify-reload or idle), and Restart= decides whether a dead daemon comes back; its default is no.

The same idea on Windows. Windows calls these services. A service application conforms to the interface rules of the Service Control Manager (SCM), can start automatically at boot or on demand, and runs even when no user is logged on. Microsoft describes Windows services, formerly NT services, as long-running executables that run in their own Windows sessions, can be paused and restarted, show no user interface, and can run under an account different from the logged-on user's. The vocabulary differs; the operating questions, who starts it, under which identity, and who notices when it stops, are the same.

Why a hung daemon is invisible. Nobody watches a daemon's terminal, because it has none, so a daemon that is alive but stuck looks healthy to anything that only checks whether the process exists. The fix is a heartbeat. systemd's WatchdogSec= requires the service to send WATCHDOG=1 at regular intervals; if the gap grows longer than the configured time, the service is put in a failed state, terminated with SIGABRT, and restarted if Restart= is set to on-failure, on-watchdog, on-abnormal or always. F5 BIG-IP builds the same idea into high availability: sys daemon-ha enables heartbeat monitoring by default for all its daemons except named, with restart as the most common heartbeat action, and for critical daemons such as tmm, mcpd, bigd and gtmd a daemon that stops running triggers an action whose most common default is go-offline-downlinks, so that the peer takes over. tmsh restart sys service mcpd restarts one by name, and drops the tmsh session that depended on it.

Why daemons are a security boundary. A daemon usually listens on the network and often starts with more privilege than it needs, which is why daemon(7) includes dropping privileges among its steps. The cost of getting that wrong was shown by regreSSHion, CVE-2024-6387 (Common Vulnerabilities and Exposures), published by Qualys on 1 July 2024: a signal handler race in sshd, triggered when a client fails to authenticate within LoginGraceTime (120 seconds by default), allowed unauthenticated remote code execution as root on glibc-based Linux systems because it hit sshd's privileged code, which was not sandboxed. It was a regression of CVE-2006-5051, reintroduced in OpenSSH 8.5p1 and fixed in 9.8p1; setting LoginGraceTime to 0 removed the remote code execution at the price of exposing sshd to connection exhaustion. Least privilege, sandboxing and keeping long-lived listeners patched are the general lessons.

host-to-multihost.def: One sender reaching many receivers at once: the one-to-many communication pattern.
host-to-multihost.context: Broadcast and multicast are its everyday forms, and the design question is always who is obliged to process the copy. Broadcast forces every station on the segment to look; multicast delivers only to those who subscribed, which is why streaming and routing protocols prefer it. The pattern's dark twin is the amplification attack, where a small one-to-many request is abused to flood a victim. Contrast with its mirror, multihost-to-host.

multihost-to-host.def: Many senders converging on one receiver: the many-to-one pattern, also called incast.
multihost-to-host.context: It is the shape of a load balancer's back end, a log collector, and a database under fan-in, and it is where congestion is born, because a single link or buffer becomes the meeting point for traffic that left many places at once. Pushed past capacity by design, the same pattern is a distributed denial of service: thousands of hosts aimed at one. Incast collapse in data centres, where synchronized responses overrun a switch buffer, is the benign version of the same physics.

promiscuous-mode.def: A network interface setting that accepts every frame on the wire, not just those addressed to it.
promiscuous-mode.context: Normally a NIC ignores frames whose destination MAC is not its own; promiscuous mode disables that filter so a capture tool can see the whole segment, which is what Wireshark and tcpdump rely on. On a shared medium like old hubbed Ethernet or open wireless (where the equivalent is monitor mode) that meant seeing everyone's traffic, so switched networks and a SPAN/mirror port became the sanctioned way to feed a sensor. The setting is neutral, and the same capability serves both the troubleshooter and the eavesdropper.

deep-web.def: Everything on the web that search engines do not index, which is most of it.
deep-web.context: The deep web is mundane and enormous: your webmail inbox, banking portal, paywalled journals, and any page behind a login or a query form. The persistent confusion is treating it as sinister, when it simply means not crawlable. The dark web is a tiny, deliberately hidden subset of it, reachable only with specific software, and conflating the two makes ordinary private pages sound like a crime scene.
deep-web.depth:
The deep web is everything a search engine has not indexed: content behind logins, database results generated on request, private documents, internal systems. It is the overwhelming majority of what exists online and almost none of it is mysterious.

The term is constantly conflated with the dark web in popular coverage, and the conflation is a category error rather than an exaggeration. Your bank statement is deep web. So is every page of every internal wiki. The distinction that matters is between not indexed, which describes most of the internet, and requiring specific software to reach, which describes something much smaller and much more specific.

dark-web.def: The subset of the deep web reachable only through anonymity networks, where sites hide their location as well as their content.
dark-web.context: Its defining technology is onion routing via Tor, whose hidden services (the .onion addresses) conceal server and visitor alike. The result is genuinely mixed: whistleblower drop boxes, censored-press mirrors, and privacy forums share the space with the marketplaces the headlines fixate on, from Silk Road onward, which trade in illicit goods and settle in cryptocurrency. Its honest framing is a tool, not a place, and anonymity is what it provides to everyone who arrives, for any reason.
dark-web.depth:
The dark web is content reachable only through anonymity networks, most often Tor hidden services. It is a small fraction of the deep web, which is itself most of the internet, and the numbers routinely quoted in media coverage inflate it by orders of magnitude.

Its composition is more mundane than its reputation. Alongside the criminal markets that generate coverage sit mirrors of news organizations, secure document submission for journalists, forums for people in countries where the open web is monitored, and a large amount of nothing much. The technology is the same in every case, because anonymity that could distinguish between users would not be anonymity, and that is a property rather than an oversight.

darknet.def: An overlay network that runs on the public internet but is reachable only with specific software, configuration, or authorization.
darknet.context: The word predates its reputation: a 2002 Microsoft Research paper used darknet for any private distribution network, and friend-to-friend systems like Freenet and I2P fit the definition as much as Tor does. A darknet is the underlying private network; the dark web is the websites people run on top of one. Keeping the two distinct is the difference between naming a road and naming the shops along it.
darknet.depth:
Darknet is the older and broader term, originally describing any network that is not publicly routed: private overlays, closed file-sharing networks, and in some usages the unallocated address space that receives only unsolicited traffic.

That last usage is worth separating because it is genuinely different and useful. A darknet in the network-telescope sense is a block of routed but unused addresses, and everything arriving there is by definition unsolicited: scanning, worm propagation, backscatter from spoofed attacks. Watching one is a cheap and effective way to measure internet-wide malicious activity, and it has nothing to do with the dark web the term is usually confused with.

ttp.def: Tactics, techniques, and procedures: the layered description of how a threat actor operates.
ttp.context: The layers ascend in specificity: a tactic is the goal (gain initial access), a technique is the general method (phishing), and a procedure is the concrete way this actor does it (a lure impersonating a specific vendor with a particular payload). TTPs (tactics, techniques and procedures) are the most durable thing you can track about an adversary, because they can rent new infrastructure overnight but cannot easily change how they think, which is exactly the insight behind MITRE ATT&CK. Compare the shorter-lived indicator of compromise (IoC).
ttp.depth:
What the phrase means. The National Institute of Standards and Technology (NIST) defines tactics, techniques and procedures (TTPs) as the behaviour of an actor, described at three levels: a tactic is the highest-level description of that behaviour, techniques describe it in more detail in the context of a tactic, and procedures give a lower-level, highly detailed description in the context of a technique. The definition comes from its guide to sharing cyber threat information, SP 800-150, and is repeated in its incident response recommendations, SP 800-61 Revision 3 of April 2025. The term is almost always plural, because an actor is characterized by a set of them. TTPs are not indicators: an IP address, a domain or a file hash is something an actor uses, while a TTP is what the actor does. Nor are they tools, which David Bianco's Pyramid of Pain ranks one level lower, or vulnerabilities, which are weaknesses in the defender's systems that a technique may exploit. For network engineers there is one more trap: TTP is also the name of the Template Text Parser, a Python library for turning show command output and configuration text into structured data, which has nothing to do with threat actors.

Where it came from. The triad is military doctrine. Writing for the Modern War Institute at West Point in 2016, John Spencer recalled that the US Army's former field manual FM 3-0 defined doctrine as fundamental principles; tactics, techniques and procedures; and terms and symbols. In that usage tactics are the employment and ordered arrangement of forces in relation to each other; techniques are non-prescriptive ways or methods used to perform missions, functions or tasks, and the main way units pass on lessons learned; and procedures are standard, detailed steps that prescribe how to perform specific tasks, executed in the same manner regardless of circumstances. Security borrowed the words and shifted their meaning. A tactic became the adversary's goal rather than an arrangement of forces, and a procedure became something observed rather than prescribed: in threat intelligence, a procedure is an actor's habit, the specific way it was seen to carry out a technique, not a manual it is required to follow.

The three layers in practice. MITRE ATT&CK, which began in 2013 precisely to document the TTPs of advanced persistent threats against Windows networks, gives the clearest working definitions. Tactics are the why, the adversary's tactical goal, such as credential access; techniques are the how, such as dumping credentials; sub-techniques sit one level lower, such as reading the Local Security Authority secrets; and procedures are the specific implementation seen in the wild, such as using PowerShell to inject into lsass.exe and scrape credentials from its memory. That example also shows why procedures resist tidy classification: one procedure combines several techniques, here PowerShell, process injection and credential dumping. In the phishing case, the tactic is initial access, the technique is phishing, and the procedure is the particular lure, sender and payload a given group reuses from campaign to campaign.

Why defenders track them. Bianco's Pyramid of Pain, first posted on 1 March 2013, explains the value by cost to the attacker. At the bottom, hash values change with any edit to a file and IP addresses and domains can be replaced overnight; above them sit network and host artefacts and tools; at the apex are TTPs. Detecting and responding at that level means operating directly on adversary behaviour, for example detecting pass-the-hash itself rather than the program used to perform it, and if the response is fast enough it forces the adversary into the most time-consuming change of all: learning new behaviours. That is the reasoning behind the remark that an adversary can rent new infrastructure overnight but cannot easily change how it thinks, and it is why durable detections, threat-informed testing and threat intelligence reports are all written in terms of TTPs.

Where the term turns up. Threat intelligence reports describe actors by their TTPs and, increasingly, map them to ATT&CK identifiers. Incident reviews use them as an improvement target: NIST's outcome ID.IM-03 cites identifying TTPs that are not currently being blocked by safeguards or flagged by detection technologies as an example of the improvements found in lessons-learned meetings. Regulated testing is specified in them: the European Central Bank's TIBER-EU framework requires red-team tests that mimic the tactics, techniques and procedures of real-life attackers, based on threat intelligence prepared for the tested entity. The vocabulary has also travelled beyond intrusion: the DISARM framework, formed in 2022 by teams from MITRE, Florida International University and CogSecCollab, catalogues the TTPs of disinformation creators in a Red framework and those of responders in a Blue framework, in the style of ATT&CK.

What goes wrong. The first error is treating TTPs as fixed. They are durable compared with indicators, not permanent: ATT&CK version 20, released on 13 October 2026, added techniques focused on and enabled by artificial intelligence (AI) because adversaries had started using them. The second is attribution by TTP alone. Common techniques, such as phishing or abusing valid accounts, are used by many actors, so a match at technique level says little about who is responsible; procedures, with their specific habits, carry more weight, and even they can be copied. The third is vagueness: a report that lists tactics only, such as persistence or exfiltration, has described the shape of an intrusion but given a defender nothing to detect. A usable TTP description says what was done, on which platform, with which data source likely to see it.

Neighbours. Indicators of compromise (IoCs) are the short-lived, machine-matchable counterpart; MITRE ATT&CK is the catalogue that gives TTPs shared names and numbers; the cyber kill chain is the older, ordered model of an intrusion's phases; an advanced persistent threat (APT) is the kind of actor the vocabulary was built to describe; an attack vector is the path in, which a technique exploits; detection engineering and red teaming are the two disciplines that turn TTPs into rules and into tests.

attack-vector.def: The specific path or means by which an attacker reaches and compromises a target: the route in, such as an email attachment, an exposed service or a removable drive, as distinct from the flaw exploited at the end of it.
attack-vector.context: Phishing email, exposed RDP (Remote Desktop Protocol), a vulnerable dependency, a USB (Universal Serial Bus) drop, a compromised supplier: each is a vector, and the collection of all of them is the attack surface. The distinction that matters operationally is vector versus vulnerability, since the vector is the route in and the vulnerability is the flaw it exploits on arrival. Reducing vectors, closing unused paths, is often cheaper than patching every flaw behind them, which is why attack-surface reduction is a control in its own right. The term has a second, narrower sense in vulnerability scoring: CVSS (the Common Vulnerability Scoring System) has an Attack Vector metric, Network, Adjacent, Local or Physical, which records how close an attacker must be to exploit a flaw, not which route a real intrusion took.
attack-vector.depth:
An attack vector is the route by which an attacker gets from where they are to the thing they want to compromise. An email with a malicious attachment, a web page that exploits a browser, an internet-facing Virtual Private Network (VPN) gateway with an unpatched flaw, a valid password bought from a broker, a USB (Universal Serial Bus) drive left in a car park and a software update from a compromised supplier are all vectors. What sits at the end of the route, the bug in the parser or the weak password, is the vulnerability; what the attacker then does is the technique. Keeping the three apart is what makes an incident report or a risk register precise.

The vocabulary has been standardized more than once, with slightly different aims. NIST (the United States National Institute of Standards and Technology), in its Computer Security Incident Handling Guide, SP (Special Publication) 800-61 Revision 2 of August 2012, listed common attack vectors so that teams could prepare handling procedures for each: external or removable media, attrition (brute force, including distributed denial of service), web, email, impersonation (spoofing, man-in-the-middle, rogue access points and even SQL injection), improper usage by authorized users, loss or theft of equipment, and other. It said plainly that the list was not a definitive classification. That edition was withdrawn on 3 April 2025 and replaced by Revision 3, which reorganizes incident response around the Cybersecurity Framework (CSF) 2.0 and keeps the idea only in passing: monitor email, web, file sharing, collaboration services and other common attack vectors, and use threat modelling to understand attack vectors, attack surfaces and lateral paths. The old categories remain a useful checklist. The MITRE Corporation's ATT&CK knowledge base gives the most detailed modern catalogue. Its Initial Access tactic, TA0001, consists, in its own words, of techniques that use various entry vectors to gain an initial foothold, and as read on 12 November 2026 it holds eleven: T1566 Phishing, T1190 Exploit Public-Facing Application, T1133 External Remote Services, T1078 Valid Accounts, T1195 Supply Chain Compromise, T1199 Trusted Relationship, T1189 Drive-by Compromise, T1091 Replication Through Removable Media, T1200 Hardware Additions, T1659 Content Injection and T1669 Wi-Fi Networks.

The word also has a narrow, formal meaning that is easy to confuse with the everyday one. In the Common Vulnerability Scoring System (CVSS), maintained by FIRST (the Forum of Incident Response and Security Teams), Attack Vector (AV) is a base metric of a vulnerability, not a description of an intrusion. It records the context in which exploitation is possible, and the score rises the more remote the attacker can be, on the assumption that more people can reach a flaw across a network than one that needs a hand on the device. Version 4.0 defines four values. Network (N): the vulnerable component is bound to the network stack and the attacker can be anywhere up to the whole internet, one or more routers away. Adjacent (A): the attack is limited to a logically adjacent topology, the same Bluetooth or 802.11 radio range, the same IP (Internet Protocol) subnet, or a limited administrative domain such as an MPLS (Multiprotocol Label Switching) network, with an ARP (Address Resolution Protocol) or IPv6 neighbour discovery flood as the example. Local (L): the attacker needs local access, at the console or over a terminal session such as SSH (Secure Shell), or relies on a user opening a malicious document. Physical (P): the attacker must touch the device, as in a cold boot attack or a direct memory access attack through a peripheral port. The specification's own guidance for borderline cases is that anything launchable across a wide area network or from outside the adjacent administrative domain is Network. A third sense is unrelated altogether: the CVSS vector string, such as one beginning CVSS:4.0/AV:N, is just the text encoding of all the metric values, and the AV in it is only one of them.

Which vectors matter most changes with defences and with attacker economics, and the best evidence comes from incident responders. Mandiant's M-Trends 2026 report, published on 23 March 2026 from its 2025 investigations, found exploits to be the most common initial infection vector for the sixth consecutive year, in 32 per cent of intrusions.
