Highly interactive voice phishing rose to second place at 11 per cent, as with groups that call IT help desks to get around multi-factor authentication, while email phishing fell to 6 per cent as automated controls improved. Prior compromise, access left behind by an earlier intruder and handed on, was third at 10 per cent overall and first in ransomware cases at 30 per cent. Espionage groups favoured edge devices such as VPN gateways and routers, which rarely carry endpoint detection, and the report estimated the mean time to exploit at about minus seven days, meaning that exploitation now routinely begins before a patch is available. Figures like these are a sample of one firm's caseload, not a census, but they explain why edge appliances and identity help desks receive so much attention.

For defenders the useful habit is to list vectors, not only vulnerabilities. A vulnerability scanner answers which flaws exist; a vector inventory answers which of them anyone can reach, and from where. That is the attack surface, which NIST's glossary defines, after SP 800-53 Revision 5, as the set of points on the boundary of a system, a system element or an environment where an attacker can try to enter, cause an effect on, or extract data from it. Closing a vector often removes a whole class of exposure at once: a management interface reachable only from a jump host, an RDP (Remote Desktop Protocol) service moved behind a VPN or a zero trust access broker, USB storage disabled by policy, macros blocked in documents from the internet. Endpoint products build the idea in; Microsoft Defender for Endpoint, for example, ships attack surface reduction rules that block executable content arriving by email or webmail, stop Office applications from creating child processes and stop untrusted, unsigned processes from running from USB drives.

The pitfalls are mostly about language. Vector and vulnerability are often used interchangeably, which hides whether a fix closed the route or only one flaw along it. A CVSS score with AV:N does not mean the flaw was exploited over the network in a given incident, only that it could be. Threat vector, entry vector and initial access vector are used as synonyms for the same idea; ATT&CK's own term for the stage is Initial Access, and its technique numbers, unlike the everyday words, are precise, though MITRE does revise them, so they should be quoted as read on a given date. The numbers worth keeping are the four CVSS values N, A, L and P, the eleven Initial Access techniques of TA0001 as of November 2026, and Mandiant's 32 per cent for exploits as the leading vector of 2025.

ioc.def: A forensic artifact that indicates a system may have been breached: a hash, an IP, a domain, a filename, a registry key.
ioc.context: IoCs are how detection scales, since a SIEM (security information and event management) can match millions of events against a feed of known-bad indicators automatically. Their weakness is their strength inverted: they are cheap for an attacker to change, a new domain or a recompiled binary defeats a signature instantly, which is why indicators sit at the bottom of the Pyramid of Pain and TTPs sit at the top. Good detection uses both, IoCs for speed and behaviour for durability.

open-graph.def: A small set of HTML meta tags that tell other sites how to display a link to your page - the title, image, and description in the preview card.
open-graph.context: Introduced by Facebook in 2010 and specified at ogp.me, Open Graph turns a page into a shareable object through tags in the head like og:title, og:image, og:description, og:url, and og:type. Its reach far outgrew Facebook: paste a link into Slack, Discord, LinkedIn, WhatsApp, iMessage, or X and the rich preview you see is almost always read from these tags (X layers its own twitter:card tags on top, falling back to OG). The most common real-world lesson is that the crawler reads the STATIC HTML, so a link preview reflects whatever OG tags are in the served markup, not anything rendered later by JavaScript - which is why single-page apps so often paste as a blank card until they pre-render their tags. This very site generates an OG image per page at build time for exactly this reason.

tor.def: An anonymity network that routes traffic through three volunteer relays, each peeling one layer of encryption, so no single relay knows both ends.
tor.context: Onion routing came out of the US Naval Research Laboratory in the 1990s, and the paradox is the design: a network used only by spies would identify its users as spies, so it had to be public and popular to work at all. The three-hop circuit splits knowledge (the guard sees you, the exit sees your destination, neither sees both), and .onion addresses are public keys rather than registered names, so they authenticate the server by construction. Worth correcting the usual assumption: only a small single-digit share of Tor traffic reaches onion services, and the rest simply exits to the ordinary web.
tor.depth:
Tor routes traffic through several relays with layered encryption, so that no single relay knows both who sent a message and where it is going. That is its entire guarantee, and it is a strong one within its threat model. The word covers four things, as the project's own support pages point out: the program that runs on a client or a relay, the network of volunteer relays, Tor Browser (a modified Firefox) and the non-profit Tor Project that maintains them. It is written Tor, not TOR, although it began as an acronym: the project's history says Roger Dingledine chose the name, which stood for The Onion Routing, to tell the Naval Research Laboratory's work apart from other onion routing efforts, and the 2004 design paper is titled Tor: The Second-Generation Onion Router.

The idea dates from 1995, when David Goldschlag, Michael G. Reed and Paul Syverson at the laboratory asked whether connections could be made that do not reveal who is talking to whom, even to someone monitoring the network. Dingledine began working with Syverson in the early 2000s and Nick Mathewson joined soon after. On 20 September 2002 Dingledine announced a pre-alpha, tor-0.0.0, with the words that the onion routing network was functional and deployed; the project dates the initial deployment, with the code under a free and open licence, to October 2002. By the end of 2003 there were about a dozen volunteer nodes, and the design paper, presented at the USENIX Security Symposium of 2004, reported 32. The Electronic Frontier Foundation (EFF) began funding the work in 2004, The Tor Project, Inc. was founded as a non-profit in 2006, bridges against censorship followed from 2007 and Tor Browser from 2008.

A client learns the network from a consensus, a list of relays voted on and signed by a small set of directory authorities whose identities ship with the software; the consensus of 12 November 2026, 08:00 UTC (Coordinated Universal Time), was signed by eight of them and listed 9,460 running relays. From it the client picks a path, the exit first, then the entry guard, then the middle, never using the same relay twice, two relays of one declared family, or two in the same /16 of IPv4 address space. It then builds the circuit one hop at a time, negotiating a separate session key with each relay, the telescoping construction that gave Tor forward secrecy: once the keys are deleted, a relay compromised later cannot decrypt old traffic. Data travels in fixed-length cells, 512 bytes in the original design and 514 on current link protocols (a 4-byte circuit identifier, a 1-byte command and a 509-byte body), inside TLS (Transport Layer Security) connections between relays, whose record framing must not reveal the type or contents of the cells. The guard is deliberately long-lived. If entry and exit were both chosen at random for every circuit, an adversary running a fraction k/N of the network would see both ends of (k/N) squared of all circuits, and over enough circuits every user would eventually be caught; the guard specification therefore has clients keep a small set of primary guards (three) for a lifetime of 120 days.

An onion service removes the exit. Client and service each build a circuit to a rendezvous point, having found each other through introduction points and descriptors published in a directory, and neither learns the other's address. The .onion name is not registered anywhere: it is the base32 encoding of the service's 32-byte ed25519 public key, a 2-byte checksum and a version byte, 56 characters in all, so reaching the name and authenticating the server are one act. This is version 3, first supported in Tor 0.3.2.9 of 9 January 2018, which replaced the SHA1, DH and RSA1024 of the earlier design with SHA3, ed25519 and curve25519; support for version 2 was removed from the code in release 0.4.6 on 15 July 2021, and stable clients disabled it on 15 October 2021. RFC (Request for Comments) 7686, of October 2015, reserves .onion as a special-use domain name: software that does not speak Tor should not look such names up, and resolvers must answer NXDOMAIN. An .onion query arriving at a corporate DNS (Domain Name System) resolver is therefore a leak from a misconfigured client, not the way these services are reached.

The network's size is published daily by Tor Metrics. As read on 12 November 2026 there were about 9,500 relays, some 4,300 of them with the Guard flag and 2,750 with the Exit flag, and about 2,500 bridges; relays advertised roughly 1,240 Gbit/s and carried about 475 to 505. Onion-service traffic relayed at rendezvous points was estimated at 11 to 14 Gbit/s in the first days of November, two to three per cent of the bandwidth consumed, which is the measured basis for saying that nearly all Tor traffic exits to the ordinary web. Directly connecting users were estimated at about 3 million a day, with the United States first at about 18 per cent, Germany second at about 9 per cent and Brazil fifth at just under 5 per cent in the days from 6 to 9 November. The figures are estimates derived from directory requests, and they can be distorted: between 28 October and 4 November 2026 the estimate jumped as high as 64.5 million a day before falling back, which lifts the 90-day averages on the default table (United States 20.6 per cent, Germany 10.6, Brazil third at 5.8) without changing the order of the first two.

What Tor does not defend against is the endpoints and the correlation. The design paper says it plainly: a global passive adversary is the threat most often assumed in theory, and Tor, like all practical low-latency systems, does not protect against one. The support pages repeat it for the practical case: an observer who can see both the user and either the destination or the exit relay can correlate the timing and volume of traffic entering and leaving, and Tor does not defend against that threat model. The exit relay also sees whatever the destination would see, so content is only as private as the encryption used end to end, and because a circuit is reused for several connections, anonymous and identifying traffic sent together can be linked at the exit. A user who logs into an identifying account, or runs a browser configured differently from everyone else's, deanonymizes themselves regardless of the network; Tor Browser exists to make all its users look the same, and changing its settings undoes that. Using Tor well is a discipline rather than an installation.

Because the relay list is public, a censor can block every relay, which is what bridges and pluggable transports answer. Bridges are relays that are not listed publicly. The transports disguise the traffic itself: obfs4 makes it look random and resists scanning for bridges, meek makes it look like a visit to a major website behind a cloud provider, Snowflake passes it through volunteers' proxies so that it resembles a video call, and WebTunnel makes it look like HTTPS to a website. In early November 2026 bridges served some 215,000 to 230,000 users a day, about 100,000 of them through obfs4, 55,000 to 60,000 through Snowflake and 40,000 to 44,000 through WebTunnel, and over the previous ninety days Russia accounted for 42 per cent of bridge users, followed by the United States and Iran at about 11 per cent each.

For those who operate a network or a service, the same openness cuts the other way. The Tor Project publishes its exit relay list and a DNS-based lookup, and says that an up-to-date list of Tor addresses is easy to build; it asks operators to consider application-level limits, such as restricting posting, before banning, and to remember that each relay has its own exit policy. Security products package the list: BIG-IP's IP intelligence has a tor_proxy category for addresses acting as Tor exit nodes, and FortiGate's Internet Service Database has an object for known exit nodes, with Application Control signatures as an alternative. These catch traffic arriving from Tor. Traffic leaving for Tor is harder, since bridges and transports exist precisely to defeat lists and protocol recognition, so a block by address stops the default configuration and little else. On a host, the tor program listens for applications on SOCKS port 9050 by default. And a single-hop service, whether a proxy or a commercial VPN (virtual private network), is not a smaller Tor: Tor's support pages contrast its distributed trust, relays run by different people so that no single one can learn what a user is doing, with the one-hop provider, which knows both who its users are and what they browse.

reserva-de-mercado.def: The Brazilian policy that legally reserved the domestic computer market for nationally-owned companies from 1984 to 1992.
reserva-de-mercado.context: Lei 7.232/1984 established the Politica Nacional de Informatica with an eight-year term written into it, and it passed unanimously on a coalition of nationalist military officers, domestic industry, and the left opposition. In practice it produced clones of the ZX81, Apple II, MSX, and IBM PC sold late and expensive, a smuggling route through Paraguay, and a Section 301 trade fight with Washington that ended in Reagan announcing sanctions in 1987. The reserve expired on schedule in October 1992. The hardware bet failed, but the engineering generation it trained is a direct ancestor of Brazilian banking automation and of firms like Cyclades and Datacom.
reserva-de-mercado.depth:
The market reserve was Brazil's attempt to build a domestic computing industry by law. The 1984 legislation reserved segments of the market for Brazilian-owned firms, and it passed unanimously on a coalition that is hard to imagine now: nationalist military officers, domestic manufacturers, and the left opposition, each supporting it for different reasons.

The results were genuinely mixed and both halves are usually omitted depending on who is telling it. It created real engineering capability, a domestic industry, and a generation of professionals who learned by building rather than importing. It also produced expensive machines a generation behind, a smuggling economy, and a software culture shaped by scarcity, where cracking and cloning were normal because the legitimate path was closed.

Its end coincided with the opening of the 1990s, which is why Fenasoft in that period functioned as a national revelation. The lasting question it poses has not aged: whether protection builds capability or preserves inefficiency is an argument every country with an industrial policy is still having, and Brazil ran the experiment at scale with a clear start and end date, which makes it unusually good evidence for both sides.

amateur-radio.def: A licensed radio service for self-training, experimentation, and non-commercial communication, with allocations across the whole spectrum.
amateur-radio.context: The licence is the distinction: examinations, a callsign issued under an ITU treaty allocation, and permission to build and modify your own transmitting equipment, which is almost unique in modern radio. Amateurs run everything from Morse on a wire antenna to microwave links and satellites. The service earns its spectrum partly through emergency communications, because a station with a battery and an antenna keeps working when towers, exchanges, and the internet do not.

callsign.def: A unique identifier issued to a licensed radio station, structured as prefix, digit, and suffix.
callsign.context: The prefix range is allocated to a country by the International Telecommunication Union, so a callsign is legible worldwide without explanation. Brazil holds the entire PPA to PYZ block plus ZV to ZZ for special stations, and Anatel issues within it using a two-letter-plus-digit scheme where the digit is regional: PY2 is São Paulo, PY1 Rio de Janeiro, PY4 Minas Gerais. The letter series also signals licence class in Brazil, so a PU station is distinguishable from a PY one on the air.

morse-code.def: Encoding of characters as short and long tones, sent as an on-off keyed carrier and known on the air as CW.
morse-code.context: It survives because of an engineering fact rather than nostalgia: a trained ear extracts Morse from noise that renders voice unintelligible, in a fraction of the bandwidth. When propagation collapses, CW is often the only thing still getting through. It is sent with a straight key, a paddle driving an electronic keyer, or a computer, and the Q-code abbreviations that grew around it, like QTH for location and QRM for interference, became the shared vocabulary of the whole hobby.

repeater.def: A station or device that receives a signal and retransmits it to extend its reach. In radio, especially amateur radio, a station on high ground that receives on one frequency and simultaneously retransmits on another, extending the range of low-power stations; in Ethernet, a physical-layer device that regenerates signals between segments, of which the hub is the multiport form.
repeater.context: Two settings catch newcomers out. The offset is the difference between the repeater's input and output frequencies, and reversing it means you hear everyone while nobody hears you. CTCSS (Continuous Tone-Coded Squelch System) is a sub-audible tone proving you are a legitimate user rather than distant interference, so the right frequency with the wrong tone produces the same silence as the wrong frequency. Amateur repeaters are almost always built, sited, and maintained by volunteers at their own expense. In networking the word names a layer 1 device instead, which the hub entry covers.
repeater.depth:
What a radio repeater does. A handheld or mobile radio on the VHF (very high frequency) and UHF (ultra high frequency) bands reaches roughly as far as it can see, so a repeater sits somewhere high, a hilltop, a tower or a tall building, and retransmits what it hears. United States regulations define it as an amateur station that simultaneously retransmits the transmission of another amateur station on a different channel or channels. The simplest one is an FM (frequency modulation) receiver on one frequency wired to an FM transmitter on another: when the receiver hears a signal, the transmitter is keyed and repeats it. Every low-power station inside the repeater's coverage can then talk to every other one, and groups built around emergency communication depend on them.

The offset. Because the repeater listens and transmits at the same moment, the two frequencies must differ, and a user's radio must transmit on the repeater's input while listening on its output. The difference is the offset, and the two frequencies together are a repeater pair. On the United States 2-metre band the standard offset is 600 kHz: the ARRL (American Radio Relay League) band plan puts repeater inputs from 146.01 to 146.37 MHz with outputs from 146.61 to 146.97, and outputs from 147.00 to 147.39 with inputs from 147.60 to 147.99, while 146.40 to 146.58 MHz stays simplex with 146.52 as the national calling frequency. Modern radios apply the standard split automatically, so a repeater is announced by its output and the direction of the shift, and the radio works out the rest. Set the shift backwards and the symptom is distinctive: every user is heard perfectly, and nobody hears you.

The tone. Most repeaters will not key up for just any carrier. Tone access with CTCSS (Continuous Tone-Coded Squelch System), also called PL (Private Line), after the Motorola trademark, adds a low-frequency audio tone, between 67 and 254.1 Hz, to every transmission; the repeater's receiver opens only when it hears the right tone, which keeps distant stations, interference and other repeaters on the same pair from triggering it. The tones are called sub-audible because radios filter them out of the speaker, not because they are below human hearing. Regulation allows exactly this kind of gatekeeping: the United States rules for repeater stations state that limiting a repeater's use to certain user stations is permissible. A wrong tone produces the same silence as a wrong frequency, which is why both settings belong in any repeater listing.

Inside the box. A repeater transmitting at full power a few hundred kilohertz from its own receiver would deafen itself, so it either uses two well-separated antennas or a duplexer, a set of filters that lets the transmitter and receiver share one antenna without the output drowning the input. A timeout timer cuts off a transmission that runs too long, typically 30 seconds on systems built for emergency traffic and up to three minutes or more elsewhere, and a short tone after each over tells users the timer has reset. Many repeaters are controlled remotely by audio tones on a control channel and may be automatically controlled, and some offer an autopatch to the telephone network. Variants include cross-band repeaters, which retransmit from one band to another so that simple filters suffice; digipeaters, which store and forward packet radio and other digital modes; and amateur satellites, which are repeaters in orbit.

Rules and coordination. In the United States the rules set out who may run a repeater (a Technician licence holder or above) and where: only on the 10-metre band and higher frequencies, excluding segments such as 144.0 to 144.5 and 145.5 to 146.0 MHz. Every amateur station, repeaters included, must transmit its call sign at the end of each communication and at least every 10 minutes during one. Pairs are assigned by volunteer frequency coordinators, which the rules define as bodies that recommend channels and technical parameters to avoid or minimize interference; coordination is not legally required, but when a coordinated and an uncoordinated repeater interfere, the uncoordinated one bears primary responsibility for fixing it. And the rules protect the people who run the machines: a control operator is not accountable for violating traffic that the repeater retransmitted inadvertently. Repeaters are almost always built, sited, powered and maintained by clubs and individuals at their own expense, and the hobby's local infrastructure is largely volunteer-built.

The network sense. In Ethernet a repeater is a physical-layer device that receives a signal on one segment and regenerates it onto others, extending a cable run without looking at addresses. IEEE (Institute of Electrical and Electronics Engineers) 802.3 defines one per generation of shared Ethernet: Clause 9, the repeater unit for 10 Mb/s baseband networks, Clause 27 for 100 Mb/s and Clause 41 for 1000 Mb/s, and the repeater MIB of the IETF (Internet Engineering Task Force) (management information base), RFC (Request for Comments) 2108 of February 1997, manages them, including the auto-partition state that isolates a misbehaving port. Every segment joined by repeaters forms one collision domain, which is why the multiport repeater, the hub, was replaced by the switch; the hub entry covers that history, the repeater classes and the rules that limited how many could be chained. Wireless networks reuse the idea: a Wi-Fi repeater or extender relays frames between radios, and 802.11 provides a four-address frame for it, with both To DS and From DS set (DS being the distribution system), in which the receiver, transmitter, destination and source addresses all differ.

What the two senses share is the trade they make. A radio repeater doubles the airtime every conversation uses and adds a single point of failure on a hilltop; an Ethernet repeater extends the medium and the collision domain with it; a single-radio Wi-Fi repeater sends every frame twice on the same shared channel. Each buys reach and pays in capacity, which is why all three are planned rather than added.

citizens-band.def: A small licence-free or lightly-licensed radio allocation near 27 MHz with fixed channels and low power limits.
citizens-band.context: Worth keeping firmly distinct from amateur radio, which the equipment can superficially resemble. CB has no examination, no individually-issued callsign, fixed channels, and tight power limits; amateur radio is a licensed service with allocations across the spectrum and permission to build your own transmitters. Sitting at the top of HF, CB occasionally propagates by sky wave during high solar activity, which is why distant stations sometimes appear on a channel that should be local.

radio-spectrum.def: The range of electromagnetic frequencies used for radio, conventionally divided into bands from VLF to EHF.
radio-spectrum.context: One trade governs the whole thing: low frequencies travel far and carry little, high frequencies carry enormous amounts and stop at the first obstacle. Long wavelengths diffract around terrain and buildings, short ones behave increasingly like light, and available bandwidth scales with frequency. Every allocation decision, from submarine communications at a few kilohertz to millimetre-wave 5G, is a position taken on that single trade.

propagation.def: How a radio signal actually travels from transmitter to receiver, which depends far more on frequency than on power.
propagation.context: Three modes explain nearly everything. Ground wave follows the earth's surface and dominates below about 2 MHz. Sky wave, between roughly 2 and 30 MHz, is refracted by the ionosphere back to earth and can cross oceans in multiple hops. Line of sight takes over above about 30 MHz. The ionosphere varies by day and night, season, and the eleven-year solar cycle, which is why an HF path that worked this morning can be dead this afternoon.

hf.def: High frequency, 3 to 30 MHz: the shortwave range where signals refract off the ionosphere and travel worldwide.
hf.context: This is the band that makes intercontinental contact possible with modest equipment, because sky wave propagation does the work that power cannot. A hundred watts into a wire antenna can reach another continent, which no amount of power at 2.4 GHz will achieve. The cost is variability: conditions shift with the time of day, the season, and solar activity, so choosing the right frequency for the path is the core operating skill. International broadcasting, long-distance maritime and aeronautical services, and most amateur DX live here.

vhf-uhf.def: Very high frequency (30 to 300 MHz) and ultra high frequency (300 MHz to 3 GHz): the line-of-sight bands.
vhf-uhf.context: Above roughly 30 MHz the ionosphere generally stops bending signals back, so coverage is limited by the horizon and by obstructions, which is why antenna height matters so much. VHF carries FM broadcasting, air traffic control, and marine radio; UHF carries mobile telephony, Wi-Fi, Bluetooth, GPS, and most television. Both are reliable and predictable compared with HF, and tropospheric ducting occasionally carries them far beyond the horizon anyway.

ism-band.def: Industrial, scientific and medical bands: spectrum usable without an individual licence, subject to power and interference rules.
ism-band.context: These allocations made consumer wireless possible. Wi-Fi and Bluetooth share 2.4 GHz with microwave ovens and much else, which is exactly why that band is congested, and the 5 and 6 GHz Wi-Fi bands trade range for room. LoRa takes the opposite bet in the sub-GHz ISM allocations, accepting very low data rates to get kilometres of range and years of battery life. Licence-exempt does not mean rule-free: duty cycle and power limits are what keep the bands usable.

apache-httpd.def: The web server that ran most of the internet for the best part of two decades, begun in 1995 as coordinated patches to a server nobody was maintaining.
apache-httpd.context: Its original model gives every connection its own process, which is robust and flexible and expensive in memory. That cost is the constraint NGINX was written against, and later Apache multi-processing modules - especially event - answered it from the other direction.

a-patchy-server.def: The oldest explanation of how Apache got its name: it was a server made of patches.
a-patchy-server.context: The project's own FAQ said so from 1996 to 2001. Brian Behlendorf said in 2000 that the name honoured the Apache people, then said in 2007 that it was the patches after all, and the foundation today credits the tribe. Both stories are in the record and neither has been retracted cleanly, which is why the origin is treated as disputed.

apache-software-foundation.def: The non-profit incorporated in June 1999 so the Apache projects would outlive any individual volunteer.
apache-software-foundation.context: Formed from the eight-person Apache Group with Brian Behlendorf as first president. The structure is the reason the ASF now stewards hundreds of projects rather than one web server.

c10k.def: The problem, named in 1999, of handling ten thousand simultaneous connections on one machine.
c10k.context: Not a hardware question but an architectural one: a server giving each connection its own process or thread runs out of memory and scheduler long before it runs out of CPU. The answer was the event loop, which is what NGINX and Apache's event module both use.

altavista.def: The search engine that led the web before Google, built at DEC as a way to stress-test a processor.
altavista.context: Launched 15 December 1995 with an index of sixteen million documents and full Boolean search, at a time when the alternative was a hand-maintained directory. Its owners then rebuilt it as a portal to compete with Yahoo, which meant competing on everything except the thing it was best at. Sold to Overture in 2003 for about six percent of its valuation three years earlier, and shut down by Yahoo on 8 July 2013.

babel-fish.def: The web's first machine-translation service, shipped by AltaVista.
babel-fish.context: Named for the creature in The Hitchhiker's Guide to the Galaxy that translates any language when placed in your ear. It outlived its parent under Yahoo's brand and now redirects to Microsoft's translator.

scooter-crawler.def: AltaVista's web crawler, written by Louis Monier at DEC.
scooter-crawler.context: The half of AltaVista that actually stressed the hardware, which was the original point of the project. Switched off around 2004 when Yahoo replaced the engine with its own, leaving the AltaVista brand as a front end for someone else's results.

pagerank.def: Google's ranking idea: score a page by who links to it, weighting links from well-linked pages more heavily.
pagerank.context: It measures something a page's own author does not control, which is why it resisted the keyword-stuffing that was defeating the search engines of the mid-1990s. Begun as a Stanford project called BackRub in January 1996. Page and Brin offered it to AltaVista for a million dollars in 1998 and were turned down.

googol.def: The digit one followed by a hundred zeros, and the word Google is a misspelling of it.
googol.context: Chosen to suggest the scale of the index the founders intended to build. The mathematical term itself was coined by a nine-year-old asked to name a very large number.

six-degrees-of-separation.def: The idea that any two people are connected by a chain of about six acquaintances - and the name of the first social network.
six-degrees-of-separation.context: SixDegrees.com launched in 1997 with profiles, friends lists and the ability to see how you connected to any other member: every feature social networks still have. It reached 3.5 million users and failed anyway, because in the late 1990s most of the people those users knew were not online at all. The idea was right and the infrastructure had not arrived.

large-language-model.def: A model trained on very large amounts of text to predict what comes next, which turns out to be enough to do a great many other things.
large-language-model.context: The capability people find surprising is emergent rather than designed: nobody wrote rules for summarizing or translating or writing code. Worth holding onto when reading claims about what these systems 'understand' - next-token prediction at scale is what is actually happening, and how much that explains is genuinely contested.

transformer-architecture.def: The 2017 neural-network design that made modern language models practical, built on self-attention.
transformer-architecture.context: Introduced in a Google paper titled 'Attention Is All You Need'. Its advantage over what came before is that it processes a whole sequence in parallel rather than one token at a time, which is what made training on internet-scale text affordable. Every large language model in current use is a descendant.

generative-ai.def: Systems that produce new text, images, audio or code rather than classifying or ranking existing material.
generative-ai.context: The technology was not new in November 2022; the access was. ChatGPT's launch on 30 November 2022 reached a hundred million monthly users in two months, and what changed was that using a language model stopped requiring an API key or any idea of what a transformer is. Capability had been improving for years in public view.

ognl.def: An expression language for reading and writing Java object properties, used as a configuration feature by some products and as an attack vehicle against others.
ognl.context: The two halves of that sentence are the same fact. OGNL is powerful because an expression can reach into a running application's objects and call methods on them, which is exactly what makes it useful for mapping an attribute in an identity product and catastrophic when an application evaluates something a stranger sent. Apache Struts spent years patching a family of flaws with one shape: reach the object that enforces OGNL's own restrictions, switch it off, then call anything. PingFederate takes the opposite approach to the same power, gating expression authoring behind an administrative role separate from the one that configures everything else, on the reasoning that someone who can write expressions can run code on the server and that is a different permission from configuring a connection.

nice-framework-work-role-categories.def: The five high-level groupings the NICE Framework uses to organize cybersecurity work: Oversight and Governance, Design and Development, Implementation and Operation, Protection and Defense, and Investigation.
nice-framework-work-role-categories.context: Five high-level groupings the NICE Framework uses to organize cybersecurity work - not seven, since two moved to the DoD framework in 2025. A Work Role is a bundle of responsibility, not a job title.
nice-framework-work-role-categories.depth: Five, not seven, and that is the first thing to know because most articles and course outlines still say seven. The NICE Framework - the NICE Workforce Framework for Cybersecurity, published by NIST as SP 800-181 - exists to give cybersecurity work a common vocabulary, so that a job advert, a curriculum and a certification can all be describing the same thing. Its components are built from Task, Knowledge and Skill statements, the atoms of the system: a Task is work to be done, Knowledge and Skill are what somebody needs in order to do it. Work Roles group those statements into areas of responsibility, and the Work Role Categories group the roles. There are currently 42 Work Roles across the five categories, alongside 11 Competency Areas which sit on a separate axis and describe a learner's capability in a domain rather than a position in an organization - among them AI Security, Cyber Resiliency, Operational Technology Security and Supply Chain Security. The most common misuse is to read a Work Role as a job title. It is not one. A Work Role is a bundle of responsibility that may appear in many differently titled jobs, and a single real job usually combines several: the person who administers your firewalls may hold parts of Implementation and Operation, Protection and Defense, and on a bad week Investigation. Mapping a vacancy to exactly one role is a sign the mapping is wrong. The version trap is worth spelling out. The components are versioned separately from the publication, so SP 800-181 Revision 1 dates from November 2020 while the components have moved several times since: v1.0.0 in March 2024 introduced the current category names and Competency Areas, v2.0.0 in March 2025 removed Cyberspace Effects and Cyberspace Intelligence entirely - those Work Roles now live in the DoD Cyber Workforce Framework, for harmonization between the two - and v2.1.0 in December 2025 revised Cybercrime Investigation and the AI Security competency. Anything citing seven categories is describing the framework as it stood before March 2025, and anything citing Securely Provision, Operate and Maintain, or Collect and Operate is describing it as it stood before November 2020. If you are building a curriculum or mapping a team against it, check the current components release rather than the publication number, because the publication number has not changed while the content has.

dod.def: The United States Department of Defense.
dod.context: Appears throughout security standards work for a reason that is structural rather than patriotic: the department buys enormous quantities of technology, and its procurement requirements become de facto standards for everyone who wants to sell to it. Several frameworks and certifications on this site exist in their current shape because a defence buyer needed them to.

nist-csrc.def: The Computer Security Resource Center, NIST's publication hub for its security standards, guidance and reference data.
nist-csrc.context: The practical value is that it is the canonical location. Security standards circulate as PDFs attached to emails and quoted in slide decks, and those copies go stale silently while keeping the same document number. If a control, a definition or a framework matters enough to cite, cite it from here, where the version and its status are stated. This is also where you discover that a publication you have been quoting was withdrawn or superseded years ago.

nist-csf.def: The NIST Cybersecurity Framework: a voluntary structure for organizing security work around a small set of high-level functions.
nist-csf.context: Deliberately not a checklist, which is what people most often want it to be. It describes outcomes rather than controls, so it can sit above whatever control set an organization already uses, and version 2.0 in 2024 added a Govern function alongside the original Identify, Protect, Detect, Respond and Recover. The useful discipline it imposes is proportion: an organization that can describe its Detect and Respond work in one sentence each, while Protect runs to four pages, has just learned something about itself.

inmetro.def: Brazil's national metrology, quality and technology institute, responsible for measurement standards and conformity assessment.
inmetro.context: Matters to networking more than it looks, because conformity assessment is what decides whether equipment may legally be sold and installed in Brazil. A product that is standard elsewhere can require local certification here, which is one of several reasons why what is practical to buy differs by country - a point the distributor entries on this site make from the commercial side.

abnt.def: The Brazilian Association of Technical Standards: Brazil's national standards body and its ISO member.
abnt.context: Its NBR standards are where international standards become locally binding text, sometimes adopted verbatim as ABNT NBR ISO/IEC and sometimes with national annexes. For anyone working in Brazil this is the difference between an international standard being a reference and being a requirement, and the numbering matters: ABNT NBR ISO/IEC 27001 and ISO/IEC 27001 are the same standard, cited two ways, and a contract will usually name one of them specifically.

hyperlink.def: A reference from one document to another that a reader can follow directly, and the mechanism the web is built on.
hyperlink.context: A reference from one document to another that a reader can follow, and the mechanism the web is built on. Its defining property is that it is allowed to break.
hyperlink.depth: The idea predates the web by decades and the web's contribution was to make it one-directional and allowed to break. Earlier hypertext systems tried to guarantee that every link resolved, which requires central coordination and does not scale past one organization. Berners-Lee's design permits a link to point at something that has moved or vanished, and accepts the resulting rot as the price of letting anyone publish without asking permission. Almost every subsequent argument about the web - link rot, deep linking, whether a site may forbid inbound links, what a URL is allowed to reveal - descends from that one decision to let links fail.

dod-cyber-workforce-framework.def: The United States Department of Defense's own catalogue of cyber work roles, aligned with but distinct from the NICE Framework.
dod-cyber-workforce-framework.context: The US Department of Defense's own catalogue of cyber work roles, aligned with but distinct from the NICE Framework, which transferred two categories to it in 2025.
dod-cyber-workforce-framework.depth: Two frameworks describing the same trade for different audiences, and since March 2025 they are formally connected: NICE removed its Cyberspace Effects and Cyberspace Intelligence categories and the roles in them moved here, explicitly to harmonize the two. The division that leaves is coherent. NICE now covers cybersecurity work as any organization might practise it - governance, design, implementation, defence, investigation - while the DCWF additionally covers work that only a military carries out, which is where offensive cyberspace operations and intelligence roles live. If you are mapping a civilian team, NICE is the right instrument. If you are reading a role description that mentions cyberspace effects, you are reading the defence framework, and possibly a document written before the split that has not been updated. The practical consequence for anyone outside the United States is that both frameworks leak into commercial job adverts and training syllabi worldwide, because contractors adopt the vocabulary of the buyer.

niprnet.def: The unclassified but sensitive network of the US Department of Defense, and the one with controlled connections to the public internet.
niprnet.context: The US Department of Defense's unclassified-but-sensitive network, and the first of three tiers separated by classification onto physically distinct infrastructure.
niprnet.depth: The first of three tiers, and the reason to understand the set rather than any single member. Defence networks are separated by classification level onto physically distinct infrastructure: unclassified-but-sensitive here, secret on SIPRNet, top secret and compartmented on JWICS. The separation is not a firewall rule or a VLAN. It is different cable, different equipment, different rooms, and a user who needs two levels sits at two terminals. This is the strongest form of the principle every enterprise network implements weakly: that the cheapest way to stop traffic crossing a boundary is not to build the boundary at all. Where information genuinely must cross, it goes through a cross-domain solution - a deliberately narrow, heavily inspected, usually one-directional gateway that exists precisely because the alternative is connecting the networks. Enterprise architects meet the same problem at smaller scale whenever a production network must accept something from a development one, and generally solve it with a rule where the defence answer would be a wire that is not there.

siprnet.def: The US Department of Defense network for information classified up to secret, physically separate from both the unclassified network and the public internet.
siprnet.context: The US network for information classified up to secret, physically separate from the internet - and the tier whose best-documented failure was an insider, not an intrusion.
siprnet.depth: The middle tier of the three, and the one whose failure mode is best documented. The 2010 disclosure of a very large volume of diplomatic cables did not involve breaching the network's separation from the internet: it involved someone with legitimate access to the network copying material they were entitled to reach. That distinction is the whole lesson. Physical separation defends comprehensively against outsiders and not at all against insiders, and a network whose perimeter is a wire that does not exist can still be emptied by anybody already inside it. The response was not more separation but more granular access control, monitoring of bulk access patterns, and restrictions on removable media - all of which are the ordinary tools of an enterprise, applied late. Any organization that describes its most sensitive system as safe because it is not connected to anything should read that sequence carefully.

jwics.def: The US intelligence community's network for top secret and compartmented information, the most restricted of the three tiers.
jwics.context: The US intelligence community's network for top secret and compartmented information, and the tier where the usability cost of separation becomes the mechanism rather than a flaw.
jwics.depth: The top of the model, and where the trade-off becomes visible. Each step up in classification buys stronger separation and pays for it in usability: fewer terminals, fewer places you can work, more friction moving anything between levels, and a growing population of people who need information they cannot reach from where they are sitting. That friction is not an implementation flaw, it is the mechanism - the security comes precisely from the cost of moving between levels. Organizations that copy the model without accepting the cost end up with the friction and not the security, because a boundary people routinely work around is a boundary in name. The general form of the lesson appears throughout this site: a control that is expensive to comply with will be complied with less, and the design question is always whether the expense is buying something proportional.

siscomis.def: Brazil's military satellite communications system, providing the armed forces with sovereign links independent of commercial or foreign infrastructure.
siscomis.context: Brazil's military satellite communications system, giving the armed forces links independent of commercial or foreign infrastructure.
siscomis.depth: Begun in the 1980s and now a component of the wider military command and control system, SISCOMIS exists to answer a question every country eventually asks: what happens to your command links if the satellites, cables or ground stations you depend on belong to somebody else. Its ground stations are distributed across Brazilian territory, and the Geostationary Defence and Communications Satellite launched for it carries an X band reserved for the armed forces alongside a Ka band used for the national broadband programme - a dual-use arrangement that funds sovereign military capacity with civilian demand. The concept worth taking from it is not military. Sovereignty over infrastructure is a design property, not a policy statement: a network is independent to exactly the degree that its physical layer, its orbital slots and its spare parts are, and no amount of encryption changes who owns the transponder.

rnp.def: Brazil's national education and research network: the academic backbone created in 1989, and the infrastructure the Brazilian internet was actually built on.
rnp.context: Brazil's national education and research network, created in 1989, and the infrastructure the Brazilian internet was actually built on.
rnp.depth: The Brazilian internet started in universities, not in commerce, and the sequence is worth knowing precisely because the popular version compresses it. Before RNP existed there were separate international links: one from the national scientific computing laboratory in Rio to the University of Maryland at 9,600 bits per second, and one from São Paulo's state research foundation to Fermilab in Chicago at 4,800, running DECnet and reaching the physics and academic networks of the time. The Rio link came first, by about three months. It also mattered least. It never evolved, and was switched off in 1996 at exactly the speed it had started at, while the São Paulo link grew into the thing everything else attached to. Being first and being the one that matters are different achievements, and this is a clean example of the gap. By May 1989 the country had three disconnected islands of academic connectivity, two in Rio and one in São Paulo, which could reach each other only by going abroad and coming back. RNP was created that September to fix exactly that: build a national backbone, and spread the use of networks in a country where almost nobody had seen one. The first national TCP/IP connection followed in February 1991, the backbone carried the Rio-92 summit, and by the mid-nineties it reached most states through points of presence in their capitals with regional networks hanging off them. Then the decision that made it the country's spine rather than a university facility: in 1995 RNP began carrying commercial traffic as well as academic, and became the backbone of the Brazilian internet. It still runs the academic network, now called Rede Ipê, with a point of presence in every state and the federal district. The general lesson has nothing to do with Brazil. National internets are usually built by whoever was already connecting universities, because that community had the requirement, the international relationships and the tolerance for unreliable infrastructure a decade before anyone could sell the service.

sntp.def: Simple Network Time Protocol: a reduced subset of NTP that speaks the same wire protocol with far less of the algorithm behind it.
sntp.context: A reduced subset of NTP that speaks the same wire protocol with far less algorithm behind it. Never configure an SNTP client as a time source for anything else.
sntp.depth: The confusion worth clearing up is that SNTP is not a different protocol. It is defined as a subset of NTP, uses the same packet format and the same port, and a server cannot tell whether a client is running a full implementation or a simple one. The difference is entirely in what the client does with the answer. Full NTP polls several sources, discards outliers, weighs the survivors, estimates the frequency error of the local oscillator and corrects for it continuously. SNTP typically asks one server and applies the result. That is fine for a device that needs to be roughly right - an access point, a camera, a small appliance - and unsuitable for anything that will be used as a time source for something else, because errors do not average out when there is nothing to average. The practical rule is the one that gets violated in every network eventually: an SNTP client must never be configured as a server for other devices, because it will faithfully propagate a bad answer it had no means of detecting.

ptp.def: Precision Time Protocol, IEEE 1588: time synchronization to sub-microsecond accuracy, achieved by putting timestamps in hardware rather than software.
ptp.context: IEEE 1588: time synchronization to sub-microsecond accuracy, achieved by timestamping in hardware rather than software, with switches along the path participating.
ptp.depth: NTP is accurate to a few milliseconds over a normal network, which is ample for logs and certificates and useless for a power substation, a broadcast facility, a mobile base station or a trading floor. PTP closes the gap by attacking the largest source of error, which is not the network but the operating system: a timestamp taken in software has already been delayed by scheduling, interrupts and buffering by an unknown and variable amount. PTP timestamps in the network interface hardware, as close to the wire as the design allows, and switches along the path participate rather than just forwarding - a transparent clock measures how long a packet spent inside it and writes that into a correction field, while a boundary clock terminates the timing and regenerates it. That participation is the point and the deployment difficulty: PTP accuracy is a property of the whole path, so a single switch that neither corrects nor regenerates will quietly cap what the whole domain can achieve. Industry profiles constrain the many options for particular uses, including telecom profiles for mobile networks and financial ones written against regulatory timestamping requirements. The general lesson transfers beyond timing: when the error you care about is introduced by the layers between your measurement and the wire, the fix is to move the measurement, not to average harder.

darpa.def: The United States defence research agency created in 1958, and the funder of the network that became the internet.
darpa.context: The US defence research agency created in 1958 that funded the network which became the internet - though it did not invent packet switching, which was arrived at independently elsewhere.
darpa.depth: Founded within months of Sputnik, on the reasoning that the United States had been strategically surprised and should not be again, with a mandate to fund research too speculative for anyone else. The structure is the interesting part and it is widely imitated and rarely reproduced: small permanent staff, programme managers hired on fixed terms of a few years, and a deliberate expectation that most programmes will fail. A manager arrives with a problem, funds work at universities and companies, and leaves - which means the agency cannot easily develop the institutional attachment to a failing programme that keeps ordinary funding bodies pouring money into things that are not working. The networking work matters here for a specific reason worth being precise about. DARPA did not invent packet switching; that was arrived at independently by Paul Baran at RAND and Donald Davies at the National Physical Laboratory in Britain, working on different problems. What DARPA did was fund the building of a working network at a scale that proved the idea, and then fund the protocols that let separate networks join. J.C.R. Licklider's role is worth knowing too: his 1960 paper on human-computer symbiosis and his memos to what he jokingly addressed as the Intergalactic Computer Network described interactive, networked computing years before there was hardware to do it, and he then held the budget that made people build it. The general point is that the agency's contribution was rarely the idea. It was the patience and the money to find out whether the idea worked, sustained across the decade that answering usually takes.

arpanet.def: The Advanced Research Projects Agency Network (ARPANET): the packet-switched network built under contract to the United States Department of Defense's research agency from 1968, which joined its first four sites in 1969, switched to TCP/IP (Transmission Control Protocol/Internet Protocol) on 1 January 1983 and was decommissioned in 1990.
arpanet.context: The first node went in at the University of California, Los Angeles (UCLA) in September 1969, the first host-to-host message reached the Stanford Research Institute (SRI) on 29 October, and the University of California, Santa Barbara and the University of Utah completed four sites by the end of the year. Its design separated the network from the computers on it: each host connected to an Interface Message Processor (IMP), a minicomputer from Bolt Beranek and Newman (BBN) that did the packet switching, so incompatible machines only had to agree on how to talk to the IMP and to each other. Two common stories about it are wrong. It was not built to survive a nuclear war: its builders trace that rumour to a separate RAND study on secure military voice, while the ARPANET itself was meant for sharing scarce and expensive computers. And the internet is not simply the ARPANET grown large: it is the interconnection of separate networks through gateways, an idea Bob Kahn and Vint Cerf worked out in 1973 and 1974, with the ARPANET as its first member.
arpanet.depth:
What it was, and what it was not. The Advanced Research Projects Agency Network (ARPANET) was one network, not a network of networks. Its parts were Interface Message Processors (IMPs), the packet switches, joined by leased lines, and the host computers attached to them; and the host protocol it ran for its first decade, the Network Control Protocol (NCP), assumed that the ARPANET would be the only network in existence. As the Internet Society's history puts it, NCP could not address anything beyond a destination IMP and left end-to-end reliability to the network, so that lost packets would bring it to a grinding halt. The internet is a different design: independent networks of any type joined by gateways, with the hosts responsible for reliability. The ARPANET was that internet's first member and its proving ground, not its earlier name. What it proved was packet switching at scale. In the telephone network a path is set up first and the whole call then runs over that circuit; in the ARPANET each small chunk of data carried its destination address and was routed at every IMP on the way, so addressing, routing, flow and congestion control and error detection all had to be designed from scratch. The Institute of Electrical and Electronics Engineers (IEEE) milestone that marks it calls it the first network based on packet switching and demand access, and sets it against earlier specialized networks that linked specific machines of a similar type: the ARPANET was meant to let machines communicate irrespective of type.

Where the idea came from. J. C. R. Licklider wrote memos in August 1962 about a Galactic Network of interconnected computers and became the first head of the computer research programme at the Advanced Research Projects Agency (ARPA) that October; the Defense Advanced Research Projects Agency (DARPA) still cites his memo to the ARPA research community of 25 April 1963. Leonard Kleinrock, then at the Massachusetts Institute of Technology (MIT), published the first paper on packet switching theory in July 1961 and a book on it in 1964, and in 1965 Lawrence Roberts and Thomas Merrill connected the TX-2 computer in Massachusetts to the Q-32 in California over a dial-up line, which showed that time-shared computers could work together and that the circuit-switched telephone system was inadequate for the job. Roberts went to ARPA in late 1966 and published his plan for the ARPANET in 1967. At the same conference Donald Davies and Roger Scantlebury of the United Kingdom's National Physical Laboratory (NPL) presented a packet network design, and Scantlebury told Roberts about Paul Baran and others at the RAND Corporation, who had written about packet switching for secure military voice in 1964. The work at MIT (1961 to 1967), at RAND (1962 to 1965) and at NPL (1964 to 1967) had gone on in parallel without any of the researchers knowing of the others. The ARPANET took the word packet from NPL, and the planned line speed went up from 2.4 kbit/s to 50 kbit/s.

The nuclear war story. That the ARPANET was built to survive a nuclear attack is the most repeated claim about it, and the history written by its builders, with Kleinrock, Kahn, Roberts and Cerf among the authors, calls it a false rumour that started from the RAND study: only that unrelated study, on secure voice, considered nuclear war. The ARPANET's motivation was resource sharing, letting research groups use expensive time-sharing computers at other sites instead of duplicating them; Cerf and Kahn's 1974 paper opens by naming the sharing of computer resources as a principal reason for building packet networks at all. Two qualifications keep the correction honest. The same history notes that the later internetting work did emphasize robustness and survivability, including withstanding the loss of large portions of the underlying networks. And DARPA's own page today lists secure communication among the ARPANET's original goals and presents packet switching as a way not to depend on any single node. Robustness was a property the design had and its sponsors valued; nuclear survivability was never its brief.

How it was built. ARPA issued its request for quotation for the IMPs in August 1968, and in December a group headed by Frank Heart at Bolt Beranek and Newman (BBN) won it, with Bob Kahn playing a major role in the architecture; Howard Frank's team at Network Analysis Corporation designed the topology and its economics, and Kleinrock's group at the University of California, Los Angeles (UCLA) built the measurement system. Each IMP was a Honeywell DDP-516 minicomputer running BBN's software, AT&T supplied dedicated lines carrying 50,000 bits per second between them, and the contract called for one IMP a month from 1 September 1969. The split between subnetwork and hosts was deliberate: a failing host would not disturb the communications subnetwork, and a failing subnetwork would not stop any host. Request for Comments (RFC) 1, 'Host Software', written by Steve Crocker at UCLA on 7 April 1969, records the division of labour: BBN specified the IMP software, and the host groups had to agree on the host software among themselves. It also records the first message format: up to 8,080 bits behind a 16-bit header holding a 5-bit destination, an 8-bit link number, a trace bit that asked the IMPs to report on the message to the Network Measurement Center at UCLA, and two spare bits. The early network had problems any network engineer will recognize. The original routing had each IMP send its neighbours its view of the network so often that packets looped without arriving, and the cure was to update less often; and the addressing first chosen allowed at most 64 IMPs with four hosts each, which proved far too few.

The first years. BBN installed the first IMP at UCLA in September 1969 and the first host was connected; the Stanford Research Institute (SRI), home of Doug Engelbart's project, followed a month later, and the first host-to-host message went from Kleinrock's laboratory to SRI. The UCLA log entry that DARPA reproduces dates it 29 October 1969 at 22:30 Pacific time, from Boelter Hall 3420. The University of California, Santa Barbara and the University of Utah made four nodes by the end of 1969, and by June 1970 two cross-country lines joined MIT, BBN and Harvard to six West Coast IMPs. The Network Working Group under Crocker finished NCP in December 1970 and the sites implemented it during 1971 and 1972; in October 1971 representatives of the first sites met at MIT to try logging in to each other's machines. In October 1972 Kahn organized the first public demonstration, at the International Computer Communication Conference (ICCC) in Washington, with 40 terminals serving about 1,000 attendees. Email arrived in the same period: the Internet Society's history dates Ray Tomlinson's send and read software at BBN to March 1972, other accounts put the first messages between researchers in 1971, and Roberts wrote the first program to list, read selectively, file, forward and answer messages in July 1972. Email was the largest network application for more than a decade. SRI also ran the Network Information Center, led by Elizabeth (Jake) Feinler, which kept the tables mapping host names to addresses and the directory of RFCs.

Growth, and a new owner. In 1973 an IMP in Hawaii linked the University of Hawaii by radio and satellite rather than wire, and an IMP in London followed over satellite. Between 1973 and 1975 the network grew from 30 to 57 nodes and moved from experiment towards operational service. A proposal to hand it to a common carrier such as AT&T was rejected, and in the second half of 1975 its administration passed to the Defense Communications Agency (DCA). Meanwhile, in DARPA's account, the military wanted a mobile network that could link vehicles, aircraft and ships, which leased telephone lines could not do, so its researchers built packet networks over radio and satellite as well; by 1973 there were four different packet switching technologies, and the next problem was to make separate networks talk to one another.

From one network to an internet. Kahn introduced the idea of open-architecture networking shortly after arriving at DARPA in 1972, in the packet radio programme. NCP could not serve it, so in the spring of 1973 he asked Vint Cerf, then at Stanford and closely involved in NCP, to design a new protocol with him. The first written version circulated as INWG 39 at a meeting of the International Network Working Group (INWG) at the University of Sussex in September 1973, and the refined paper, 'A Protocol for Packet Network Intercommunication', appeared in the IEEE Transactions on Communications in May 1974. It introduced the GATEWAY as the interface between networks and placed sequencing, flow control and end-to-end error checking in the hosts. DARPA then let three contracts to implement it, at Stanford, BBN and University College London (UCL), and within about a year there were three implementations that interoperated. The Transmission Control Protocol/Internet Protocol (TCP/IP) suite became a defence standard in 1980.

The flag day, 1 January 1983. The ARPANET's own switch from NCP to TCP/IP is often described as an overnight cutover with no transition. It was a flag day, but one planned over years. Jon Postel's RFC 801, the NCP/TCP Transition Plan of November 1981, required every host organization to begin implementing IP and TCP no later than 1 January 1982 and new hosts to implement only IP/TCP. Because hosts could not convert simultaneously, dual-protocol hosts would relay Telnet, file transfer and mail between NCP-only and TCP-only hosts from November 1981. Its milestones were normal internet service by July 1982, the last NCP-only host converted by November 1982, and full internet service in January 1983, with NCP removed from service and the relays ended. The Internet Society's history says the transition went surprisingly smoothly, which produced buttons reading 'I survived the TCP/IP transition'; another history notes that it was not quite completed on time. The move also allowed the network to be divided: later in 1983 the roughly 140 nodes serving 320 computers were split into an ARPANET for research and MILNET for unclassified defence traffic, connected by a gateway.

The end, and what is left of it. As the National Science Foundation Network (NSFNET), set up in 1985, and other networks took over the backbone role, the ARPANET was phased out and decommissioned in 1990; by then, in the Internet Society's words, TCP/IP had supplanted or marginalized most other wide-area protocols worldwide. The traces an engineer still meets are concrete. Every reverse lookup runs under the arpa top-level domain: RFC 3172 (September 2001) records that it was created in the first deployment of the Domain Name System (DNS) as a transition mechanism from the ARPANET host tables and as the home of IPv4 (Internet Protocol version 4) reverse mapping, and that in 2000 the name was redesignated Address and Routing Parameter Area to reduce confusion with the old network, so a PTR (pointer) query for an address is still a query under in-addr.arpa. The RFC series that Crocker began in 1969 is still how internet protocols are written down. And the IMP's separation of the switching machine from the computers it served survives as the division between routers and hosts.

infovia-brasilia.def: The Brazilian federal government's own metropolitan network in Brasília, running on state-owned fibre and operated by Serpro exclusively for public bodies.
infovia-brasilia.context: The Brazilian federal government's own metropolitan network in Brasília, on state-owned fibre, operated for public bodies only - a private network in the strict physical sense.
infovia-brasilia.depth: Twenty years old and almost unknown outside the people who use it, which is the ordinary condition of working infrastructure. The design decision that matters is ownership: the fibre belongs to a ministry rather than to a carrier, and the network is operated by the state data-processing company for government entities only. That makes it a private network in the strict sense - not a virtual private network riding somebody else's infrastructure, but physically separate cable that no commercial operator touches. The reasoning is the same as the reasoning behind military satellite systems and behind the Telebrás monopoly before privatization: an organization that cannot survive its supplier changing terms, being acquired, or being compelled by a foreign jurisdiction will eventually build its own. What it now carries goes well beyond connectivity - hosting, colocation, cloud services and custom networks for digital government - which is the predictable trajectory. A network built for one purpose acquires services because the network is already there and already trusted, and the marginal cost of adding something to infrastructure you already operate is far below the cost of procuring it. That is also the risk: everything ends up depending on one network, and its protection becomes a national concern rather than an operational one. Which is exactly what happened after a wave of attacks on federal sites, when responsibility for defending it was assigned explicitly rather than assumed.

cdciber.def: Brazil's military cyber defence centre, created in 2010 under the Ministry of Defence and later expanded into a full command.
cdciber.context: Brazil's military cyber defence centre, created 2010. Its first assignment was monitoring a United Nations conference, which is how such organizations usually begin.
cdciber.depth: Created by ministerial order in August 2010 and inaugurated the following year, with a first assignment that says a great deal about how such organizations actually begin: monitoring the network of the Rio+20 United Nations conference in June 2012. Not a war, not an incident - an event with a fixed date, a defined perimeter and a guaranteed audience. That is the standard way a new capability gets built, because a scheduled event supplies a deadline, a budget and a visible result, and the resulting organization outlives the event that justified it. The team assembled for it is the more interesting detail: army, air force and navy personnel alongside technicians from the federal police cybercrime unit and the telecommunications regulator. Cyber defence forces organizations to mix in ways conventional defence does not, because the infrastructure being defended is civilian, the expertise is scattered across agencies that do not normally share a room, and the attacker does not respect the boundary between crime and conflict. The subsequent cooperation with the federal data-processing company - including forensic computing training - reflects the same reality: the state's operational knowledge of its own networks sat in a civilian company, and the military needed it. Every country works through some version of this problem, and the arrangements it produces are usually more revealing than the doctrine written about them.

sisbin.def: The Brazilian Intelligence System, established in 1999, coordinating intelligence activity across federal bodies with ABIN as its central organ.
sisbin.context: The Brazilian Intelligence System, established 1999. Its communications security centre, founded 1982, develops sovereign cryptographic algorithms rather than importing them.
sisbin.depth: Worth an entry here for one component rather than for the system itself. CEPESC, the communications security research centre inside ABIN, was created in 1982 for a specific and clearly stated reason: Brazil could not guarantee the confidentiality of its own government communications. It develops state cryptographic algorithms - meaning sovereign, nationally designed cryptography rather than imported implementations. That is a decision several countries make and it carries a real trade-off worth understanding. Cryptography reviewed by the global research community benefits from decades of adversarial analysis by people with no stake in whether it holds; national cryptography is reviewed by a much smaller group, often one that cannot publish. The argument for it is that an imported implementation is trusted on somebody else's word, may contain weaknesses its authors know about, and can be withdrawn or restricted by an export regime - which is not hypothetical, since export controls on cryptography shaped what was legally shippable for decades. The argument against is that fewer eyes find fewer flaws. Neither argument wins outright, and a country's position on it usually reflects how much it expects to be able to trust its suppliers. The intelligence system also connects to the incident-response layer through the government response team serving federal administration, alongside the national team that serves the public - a separation that most countries maintain and that is worth understanding, because they answer to different people and publish very different amounts.

vlc.def: The VideoLAN Client: a free, open-source media player that began in 1996 as a student project to stream video across a French university's campus network, and became one of the most widely installed pieces of software ever written.
vlc.context: The media player that plays what nothing else will, because it carries its own decoders rather than asking the operating system. A 1996 student project that became one of the most installed programs ever written.
vlc.depth: The reason it plays what nothing else will is an architectural decision, not a feature list. Most media players ask the operating system to decode a file, which means they play whatever codecs the machine happens to have installed and fail on everything else - and the failure is opaque, because the player genuinely does not know what it is looking at. VLC carries its own decoders. That makes the download larger, puts the maintenance burden of a very long list of formats on the project rather than on Microsoft or Apple, and drags the whole thing into the patent and licensing thicket around video codecs. What it buys is that the question of why a file will not play stops depending on the machine. The general lesson is worth taking out of the media context entirely: depending on the platform's shared components makes you quick to build and hostage to what the platform has installed, and choosing to carry your own is choosing predictability over convenience. Anyone who has shipped software that works on the developer's laptop and not on the customer's has met the same trade from the losing side. The rest of the story is unusual in ways worth recording. It was a student project at École Centrale Paris in 1996, intended to move video around the campus network rather than to become anything; the code belonged to the school, and its release under the GPL in 2001 required the institution's permission, which is a detail anybody whose employer owns their side projects will recognize. The orange traffic cone is not a metaphor for anything - it references the cones collected by the school's networking students' association, which makes it a piece of student mischief that ended up as one of the most recognizable icons in computing. The project separated from the school and became a non-profit in 2009, passed six billion downloads by 2025, and has been funded partly by public money, including a European Parliament bug bounty in 2017 aimed at improving European infrastructure. Its president Jean-Baptiste Kempf, who took it over around 2006 when the project had stalled, is widely reported to have turned down offers worth tens of millions to bundle advertising or tracking into the installer - a story that circulated heavily in late 2025 from a single interview, so it is worth treating as attributed rather than established. What is established is the outcome: no adverts, no telemetry, no paid tier, after nearly thirty years. One of the project's authors, Olivier Pomel, later co-founded Datadog, and the connection is less coincidental than it looks - writing software that copes with malformed input from the entire world is unusually good preparation for building a platform that ingests telemetry from every system a company runs.

archive-formats.def: Container formats that bundle files together, compress them, or both - and the distinction between those two jobs is the thing most people never learn.
archive-formats.context: Archiving and compressing are different jobs. tar bundles files and compresses nothing; gzip compresses a stream and knows nothing about files. ZIP does both, which is why it can extract one file instantly and a .tar.gz cannot.
archive-formats.depth: The first thing to understand is that archiving and compressing are two different jobs, and the Unix world keeps them separate while the Windows world does not. tar is a tape archiver: it concatenates many files into one, preserving names, permissions, ownership and directory structure, and it compresses nothing at all. gzip compresses a single stream and knows nothing about files, names or directories. Put them together and you get .tar.gz, the two-step that trips up everyone coming from the other tradition: tar makes the many into one, gzip makes the one smaller. This is why you cannot extract a single file from a .tar.gz without decompressing everything before it, and why a .zip can pull one file out of a thousand instantly. ZIP does both jobs in one format, compressing each file separately and keeping an index at the end, which costs a little compression efficiency and buys random access. Neither design is wrong; they were solving different problems, and the difference still shows up every time somebody waits four minutes to extract one configuration file from a large tarball. The rest of the family divides along the same lines. 7z is a container with strong compression, usually LZMA, open-source tooling and a genuine efficiency advantage on large similar files, because it can compress across file boundaries in what is called a solid archive - the same trick that makes it slow at extracting one item. RAR is proprietary: the decompressor is documented and free to implement, the compressor is not, so only the vendor's software can create one, which is unusual in a world of open formats and is the reason RAR persists in some communities and is absent from others. ISO is not compression at all.
