It is a sector-by-sector image of an optical disc, a filesystem in a file, which is why mounting one shows a directory tree rather than needing extraction, and why an ISO of a 700 MB disc is 700 MB whether the disc was full or nearly empty. CAB is Microsoft's cabinet format, used inside installers and driver packages, and most people only ever meet it indirectly. On the utilities: 7-Zip is free, open source and written substantially by one person, Igor Pavlov, and it reads nearly everything while writing 7z and ZIP well; WinRAR is commercial, is the only thing that creates RAR archives, and has its own entry here for reasons that have nothing to do with technology; WinZip was the commercial standard of the 1990s and is the reason a generation says zip as a verb; PowerArchiver, PeaZip, Bandizip and others occupy the same space with different trade-offs between price, format coverage and how much they try to sell you. The formats above are the survivors, and the era before them is worth recovering, because one of its requirements has vanished so completely that the software built around it went too. In the DOS and bulletin-board years the competition was fierce and the names are half-forgotten: ARJ, written by Robert Jung, whose name it carries; LHA and its LZH format, from Haruyasu Yoshizaki in Japan, which was free to use and consequently ended up embedded in a great many other products; ZOO; and PKZIP defending the ground it had taken from ARC. Compression ratios were argued over the way frame rates are now, and the differences were real, because a file that took nine minutes to download at 2400 baud instead of eleven was a meaningful improvement. But the feature that decided which archiver you actually used was multi-volume archiving: splitting one archive across several floppy disks, each of which had to be individually reliable, in a period when disks failed constantly. ARJ was very good at this, which is why so many people who used it remember it fondly and cannot quite say what it did better - it did the thing that made a 20 MB file movable at all when nothing you owned could hold 20 MB. That requirement disappeared entirely, first to writable optical discs and then to networks, and the formats optimized for it disappeared with it. They were not defeated on compression or on licensing. The problem they existed to solve stopped being a problem, which is a more complete kind of ending than losing. Two security notes belong in any honest description. Archives are an attack surface: a zip bomb is a small file that expands to something enormous, designed to exhaust whatever is scanning it, and path traversal in archives - extracting a file whose stored name contains ../ and lands outside the target directory - has produced a long line of vulnerabilities across many extraction libraries. Encrypted archives are also the oldest way to move a payload past a scanner that cannot see inside them. If you are writing code that extracts archives supplied by anyone else, treat the filenames inside as hostile input, because they are.

winrar-licence.def: WinRAR's forty-day trial has never stopped working, on any version, for about thirty years - which turns out to be a business model rather than an oversight.
winrar-licence.context: WinRAR's forty-day trial has never stopped working, on any version, for about thirty years - which turns out to be a business model rather than an oversight.
winrar-licence.depth: WinRAR ships with a forty-day evaluation period. When it ends, the software displays a reminder asking you to buy a licence, and then continues working. It has behaved this way for roughly three decades, across every version, on hundreds of millions of installations, and RARLAB has never changed it. The result is one of the most-used pieces of commercial software on Earth being one of the least-paid-for, and a running joke that has outlived most of the people who started telling it. The interesting part is not the joke. It is that the arrangement is deliberate and appears to work. A nag screen that never escalates is a business model built on the observation that individuals will not pay and organizations will, because an organization cannot run unlicensed software that displays a purchase reminder on a projector during an audit. So the trial that never expires is not a failure of enforcement; it is enforcement aimed precisely at the population that can be enforced against, and a gift to everyone else. Compare that with the two alternatives actually available - crippleware that stops working, driving people to a crack, or free-with-advertising, driving people to something quieter - and the strange middle option looks less like an oversight than like somebody who understood their market. There is a second, smaller thing, and it is the part that is not a joke. Buying a WinRAR licence is a genuinely unusual act. It costs little, nobody checks, the software works either way, and the only person who knows is you. A tool you have used for twenty years without paying is a debt in the only sense that matters, which is that somebody did work you benefited from. The author of this site bought one, which almost nobody does.

zip-and-the-lawsuit.def: The 1988 lawsuit that was meant to protect the ARC format, and instead produced ZIP.
zip-and-the-lawsuit.context: The 1988 lawsuit meant to protect the ARC format instead ended it, because its target designed ZIP and published the specification for anyone to implement.
zip-and-the-lawsuit.depth: Before ZIP there was ARC, and a young programmer named Phil Katz wrote a faster implementation of it called PKARC. The company behind ARC sued him in 1988 for copying its format and code, and won enough that Katz stopped distributing it. His response was to design a new format from scratch and publish the specification so that anybody could implement it without asking permission. He called it ZIP, reportedly because it was meant to be quicker than ARC. The lawsuit intended to protect a format ended it, and created the one that replaced it so completely that most people have never heard of the thing it replaced. That is the whole lesson and it recurs constantly: a format's value comes from ubiquity, ubiquity comes from anybody being able to implement it, and litigating against implementers is a way of guaranteeing that a competing format becomes ubiquitous instead. The industry keeps relearning it, usually while a lawyer is explaining why this case is different. ZIP is now in operating systems, browsers, office documents, application packages and firmware, and the ARC company is a footnote in a story about the format that beat it. The rest is less cheerful and should not be omitted from a piece of lore that celebrates an outcome. Katz did not benefit from what he built in any way that lasted. He struggled with alcoholism through the 1990s, withdrew from the company that carried his initials, and was found dead in a hotel room in 2000 at the age of thirty-seven. The format he wrote is on essentially every computing device manufactured since. Both of those sentences are true and the second one does not follow from the first.

deflate.def: The compression algorithm inside ZIP, PNG, Git and most of the web; the file format that wraps it; and the library that implements both.
deflate.context: The compression algorithm inside ZIP, PNG, Git and most compressed web traffic; gzip is the file format wrapping it, zlib the library nearly everything calls.
deflate.depth: Three names for closely related things, and separating them is the first step to not being confused by them. DEFLATE is the algorithm. gzip is a file format wrapping DEFLATE with a header, a checksum and a length. zlib is both a slightly different wrapper and, more importantly, the library almost everything actually uses to do any of it. DEFLATE itself is two old ideas stacked. First LZ77: as you read the input, replace anything you have seen before with a short reference back to where you saw it, so the second occurrence of a repeated phrase costs a few bytes instead of its full length. Then Huffman coding: having produced that stream of literals and back-references, count how often each symbol occurs and give the common ones short codes and the rare ones long codes. Neither half was new when DEFLATE was specified in 1951 - the RFC number is a coincidence worth enjoying - and the combination is not clever so much as extremely well balanced: fast enough to run on everything, good enough that improving on it rarely justifies the change. The result is probably the most-executed compression algorithm in history, and almost nobody can name it. It is inside every ZIP file, every PNG image, every Git object, and every HTTP response served with content-encoding gzip, which is to say most of the web. The reason gzip exists at all is a patent, and this is the part worth knowing. Unix had a compression tool called compress, which used LZW - an algorithm covered by Unisys patents, the same patents that made GIF legally uncomfortable for years and eventually pushed the web towards PNG. Jean-loup Gailly and Mark Adler wrote gzip specifically to be a free replacement that infringed nothing, and zlib followed as the reusable library. Both outlived the patents, the tool they replaced, and the format the patents damaged. A patent intended to capture a market instead motivated the free thing that replaced it - which is the same shape as the lawsuit that produced ZIP, in the same decade, in the same corner of computing. One security consequence deserves stating because it surprises people who understand both halves separately. Compression leaks information about what it compressed. If an attacker can inject text into something that is compressed and then encrypted, they can learn whether their guess appears elsewhere in the plaintext by watching the compressed length change - guessing a secret one character at a time without breaking any cryptography. That is the mechanism behind the CRIME and BREACH attacks, both of which have their own entries here. Encryption hides content; it does not hide size, and compressing before encrypting turns size into a channel. The practical rule is unglamorous and absolute: do not compress attacker-influenced data together with secrets in the same encrypted stream.

bhack.def: BHack is the annual information security conference of Belo Horizonte, Minas Gerais, held since 2012 and in its sixteenth edition on 28 and 29 November 2026: a technical, community-rooted event and one of those that made the Brazilian scene something other than a São Paulo scene.
bhack.context: Technical rather than corporate, and outside São Paulo: one of the regional conferences that exist in inverse proportion to how well the commercial circuit serves the regions. Its own pitch is to serve the information security public of Minas Gerais, and the chronicler of the Brazilian calendar, Anchises Moraes, ranks it with Nullbyte in Salvador for technical quality, just behind the two big São Paulo technical events, H2HC and BSides São Paulo.
bhack.depth:
What it is. BHack describes itself as a conference that, since 2012, has set out to meet the needs of the Minas Gerais public in information security, and that in its sixteenth edition has become one of the most important annual events on the national circuit. The 2026 edition is scheduled for two days, 28 and 29 November, at the MinasCentro convention centre in central Belo Horizonte, with talks pitched, in its own words, at everyone who deals with information security, integrating managers and technicians, plus a capture-the-flag (CTF) competition run with the FireShell team, training sessions and the merchandise that every Brazilian community event now sells, made by Imaginário Nerd, the T-shirt maker that also supplies H2HC and BSides São Paulo. Tickets are sold through Sympla; it is a paid event, unlike the free BSides São Paulo. Moraes's 2026 calendar note sums up its standing: a traditional event of the Belo Horizonte security community, one of the main Brazilian events with a technical and research focus, always with good technical talks and with the community present.

The early years. Moraes's review of 2013 records the second edition, on 22 and 23 June 2013, as an event that was giving the security market in Belo Horizonte a push: a good mix of technical and managerial talks in two simultaneous tracks, with excellent speakers, marred only by rooms in separate buildings that made switching tracks hard. In June 2015 he reported a talk at BHack by the lawyer Walter Capanema on the Marco Civil da Internet, Brazil's internet civil rights law, a year after it came into force. The fourth edition, in 2016, is the low point in his record: the date moved from June to November, the final date appeared on the website only about two weeks beforehand, and it clashed with the São Paulo weekend of Roadsec and BSides. The first two editions had been very good and the 2015 one had had problems, so on top of the confusion there was doubt whether the event would recover.

The recovery. It did. Moraes's review of 2022 congratulated BHack for being an important regional event of the security community that had kept going online through the COVID-19 pandemic and came back strongly in person that year. In his review of 2023 he named it, with NullByte, BSides Vitória and BSides João Pessoa, as the best of the year outside the Rio de Janeiro and São Paulo axis, and noted that the Masters of Pwnage trading cards, a community project launched at BSides São Paulo, had an extra print run at BHack. In his review of 2024 he placed it, with Nullbyte, at the top for technical quality, beside H2HC and BSides São Paulo, the largest Brazilian technical events. That is the community assessment worth recording: after some quieter years it recovered the standing of its early editions and went back to being where the region's better practitioners actually turn up.

The regional generation. BHack belongs to a generation of conferences run by local communities on local budgets. Moraes's review of 2016 already saw the north-east gaining strength, with the third Nullbyte in Salvador, the second Jampasec in João Pessoa and the new Broken Wall Security Conference in Recife. Jampasec was later replaced by BSides João Pessoa, which he describes as one of the traditional events of the north-east; Bxsec in Santos disappeared during the pandemic and was back on his 2026 calendar as a conference drawing people from the coast, the interior and the capital of São Paulo state. Brazilian security has a heavy São Paulo gravity: the large commercial conferences are there, the vendor ecosystem is there, and for years an engineer in Minas Gerais, Bahia or Rio Grande do Sul either travelled or missed out. These events push against that, and they exist because somebody local decided to run one.

Why the regional circuit grew. The structural point is not about Brazil. Regional technical conferences exist in inverse proportion to how well the commercial circuit serves the regions, and the clearest illustration came after the pandemic. In his review of 2023 Moraes noted that the two largest events by attendance, Roadsec and Mind The Sec, had lost their regional editions even as their São Paulo editions set records for audience and sponsors, and he listed the disappearance of those regional events, which left several cities, communities and professionals orphaned of local events, among the year's disappointments. A year later he singled out the rise of several regional events in 2024 as a very important movement for the growth of the community across the country. Local community events multiplied into the space the largest organizer had left. Anyone who has wondered why a scene is thriving in a city with no industry presence should keep the sequence in mind: the absence is often the cause.

Where it sits in the calendar. On the 2026 calendar BHack sits between Nullbyte in Salvador on 7 November and the 307 Temporary Security Conference on 5 and 6 December, at the end of the busy second half of the year. Its mix is that of the better regional events: a technical core, a CTF, training, a slot for management and law, and an audience that comes from the region rather than flying in. For a practitioner in Minas Gerais it is the event where the state's security community meets; for the national scene it is one of the reasons the best Brazilian talks are no longer given only in São Paulo.

security-leaders.def: The executive end of the Brazilian security calendar - where the people who sign things meet, rather than the people who configure them.
security-leaders.context: Risk, governance and budget rather than technique. Technical conferences transmit skill; executive ones transmit priorities, and neither substitutes for the other.
security-leaders.depth: The executive end of the Brazilian security calendar: risk, governance, budget and the conversations that happen between people who sign things rather than configure them. It runs a São Paulo flagship alongside regional editions - seven of them in 2024 - which makes it one of the few commercial circuits that actually reaches beyond the capital consistently. Its usefulness depends entirely on what you go for. As a place to learn a technique it is the wrong room; the technical events on the same calendar exist for that. As a place to understand what the market believes, what buyers are being told, and which concerns have reached the level where somebody with a budget is worried about them, it is unusually informative - and those are genuinely different kinds of knowledge that engineers routinely conflate. A practitioner who has never sat in an executive security conference tends to be surprised by how much of the decision-making they complain about is visible in advance, discussed openly, months before it lands on them as a policy. The general observation the Brazilian calendar supports better than most is that a security scene needs both kinds of event and they do not substitute for one another. The technical conferences transmit skill; the executive ones transmit priorities. An engineer who attends only the first is repeatedly surprised by decisions, and an executive who attends only the second is repeatedly surprised by reality.

tac.def: The vendor's technical assistance centre: the engineers you reach when a product itself, rather than your configuration of it, may be at fault.
tac.context: Opening a TAC case is a handover, and it succeeds or fails on the same things any handover does: what was reported, what has been established as true, what was ruled out and how, and what has already been changed. A case that arrives as “it is broken” gets a reply asking for the things the first message should have carried.

bisection.def: Halving a search space repeatedly until one candidate remains, so that a thousand possibilities take ten tests rather than a thousand.
bisection.context: It is arithmetic rather than opinion: each test that eliminates half the remaining candidates costs one step and buys a doubling. The prerequisite is a reliable test - something that answers yes or no the same way every time - and where the fault is intermittent, bisection stalls until that test exists.

workaround.def: A change that restores function without addressing why it broke, and which therefore continues until somebody actively ends it.
workaround.context: The distinction from a fix is not which is better but that only one of them concludes. ITIL (the Information Technology Infrastructure Library) defines a workaround as a solution that reduces or eliminates the impact of an incident or problem for which a full resolution is not yet available, and pairs it with the known error that problem management records until the real fix ships. Vendors publish workarounds for the same reason, to cover the time before an upgrade. A workaround kept under pressure and never documented becomes configuration nobody can explain, which is how a temporary routing exception survives four years and outlives the person who applied it.
workaround.depth:
The formal definition comes from IT (information technology) service management. ITIL (the Information Technology Infrastructure Library) 4 defines a workaround as a solution that reduces or eliminates the impact of an incident or problem for which a full resolution is not yet available, and adds that some workarounds reduce the likelihood of incidents. The neighbouring terms place it precisely. An incident is an unplanned interruption to a service or a reduction in its quality; a problem is a cause, or potential cause, of one or more incidents; and in the ITIL 2011 vocabulary a known error is a problem with a documented root cause and a workaround, recorded in a known error database (KEDB). The earlier wording called the workaround a temporary solution, and that adjective carries the whole management burden: a workaround is defined by what it is waiting for.

Problem management is the practice that owns the wait. Once a problem is diagnosed it becomes a known error, problem management hands the workaround to incident management so the service desk can apply it to repeat incidents, and it invokes change management when the permanent solution needs a change; when that solution is deployed, the problem record is formally closed. ITIL 4 describes problem management as one of 34 practices rather than a fixed process, but the shape is the same. A workaround that is applied without a problem record is therefore invisible to the only process designed to retire it.

Security uses the word in the same sense, and the scoring systems make the gradation explicit. The CVSS (Common Vulnerability Scoring System) version 3.1 Remediation Level metric says workarounds or hotfixes may offer interim remediation until an official patch or upgrade is issued, and its values grade them: Workaround (W) means an unofficial, non-vendor solution, sometimes a user-made patch or steps to mitigate; Temporary Fix (T) covers an official but temporary fix, including a vendor's hotfix, tool or workaround; Official Fix (O) means a complete vendor solution. The less official and permanent the fix, the higher the score. The CVE (Common Vulnerabilities and Exposures) record format keeps the same distinction in data, with separate fields for workarounds and mitigations and for solutions and remediations, and the CERT/CC (CERT Coordination Center) discloses reported vulnerabilities after 45 days whether or not vendors have produced patches or workarounds.

Vendor advisories are where network engineers meet workarounds most often, and they show both the value and the limits. Fortinet's FG-IR-22-377, published on 10 October 2022 for an authentication bypass in the FortiOS administrative interface, gave as its workaround disabling the HTTP (Hypertext Transfer Protocol) and HTTPS (HTTP Secure) administrative interface or limiting the addresses that could reach it with local-in policies, beside the list of fixed versions. FG-IR-24-015, published on 8 February 2024 for an out-of-bounds write in the SSL (Secure Sockets Layer) VPN (virtual private network) daemon, gave the workaround of disabling SSL VPN and warned in capitals that disabling web mode is NOT a valid workaround: a partial measure that looks like a fix is worse than none. For F5's CVE-2022-1388, CERT-EU summarized F5's temporary workarounds until a fixed version could be installed, blocking iControl REST (F5's management application programming interface) through the self IP (Internet Protocol) addresses and the management interface or changing the httpd configuration, and noted that versions 11 and 12 would get no patch at all. For those versions the workaround was the permanent state.

Workarounds have side effects, and vendors track them as bugs. F5's bug tracker lists Bug ID 2461221, opened on 18 August 2026: the workaround for an earlier bug, Bug ID 694707 (hardware crypto offload is not compatible with HTTP/3 and QUIC), which is to disable hardware acceleration with tmsh modify sys db crypto.hwacceleration value disable, may degrade performance for every other virtual server that uses encryption; the record lists neither a workaround nor a fix. A workaround applied to one service changed the behaviour of others on the same device, and the person who applied it months earlier may not be the one who sees the degradation.

The risk of a permanent workaround is the risk Ward Cunningham described for code in 1992, when he compared shipping first-time code to going into debt: a little debt speeds things up as long as it is paid back promptly, and the danger occurs when the debt is not repaid, because every minute spent on not-quite-right code counts as interest. A routing exception, a disabled inspection profile, a firewall rule opened for a vendor's test or a hardware feature turned off for one application all accrue that interest. They also interact with what comes later: an upgrade can make the workaround unnecessary, harmful or silently ineffective, which is why reading release notes against the list of active workarounds is part of change review.

The practical discipline follows from the definitions. Record every workaround against a problem or a vulnerability, with the condition that ends it (the fixed version, the vendor bug ID, the date of the planned change) and the owner who will remove it; treat its removal as a change in its own right; and, when the vendor offers both a workaround and a fix, schedule the fix rather than letting the workaround become the configuration. The United States CISA (Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency) states the hierarchy in its Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalogue: in the 10 November 2026 edition about half of its 1,779 entries require applying updates per vendor instructions, and most of the rest require applying mitigations per vendor instructions or discontinuing use of the product if mitigations are unavailable. A workaround is a legitimate step on that path, as long as everyone knows it is a step.

severity.def: How bad a fault, a vulnerability or an event is, judged by its effect rather than by how loudly it is reported: for incidents, the impact on the business; for vulnerabilities and log messages, a rating on a published scale.
severity.context: Severity is not priority: severity describes the incident, priority describes what gets worked first, and conflating them is how the person who shouts loudest sets the queue. In practice severity is negotiated rather than measured, which is why the criteria are worth writing down before the outage rather than during it.
severity.depth:
Three scales share the word. Operations teams rate incidents, vulnerability management rates flaws, and logging systems rate messages, and in all three the number describes impact, not the order of work. Atlassian's incident guidance puts the distinction in one line each: severity is a measurement of impact, priority a measurement of urgency. Usually they agree, but not always; its example is a typo in the headline of a company's home page, low in severity because nothing stops working, yet high in priority because of what it does to the brand. The reverse also happens, a serious fault in a system nobody uses until month end.

Incident severity. Most incident schemes number downwards, so SEV-1 is the worst. PagerDuty's public incident response guide defines five levels: SEV-1 is a critical issue that warrants public notification and executive liaison, such as a system actively impacting a large number of customers, functionality impaired long enough to break the service level agreement (SLA), or a security vulnerability exposing customer data; SEV-2 is a critical system issue impacting many customers; anything at SEV-2 or above is a major incident that triggers the full response process with an incident commander; SEV-3 covers partial loss of function or a service left with no redundancy; SEV-4 a minor issue such as one failed node in a cluster; and SEV-5 a cosmetic bug that becomes a ticket. Two rules in the same guide carry most of the value: when unsure between two levels, treat the incident as the higher one and argue about it in the postmortem, not during the outage; and write the definitions specifically, usually as a percentage of users or accounts affected. Atlassian uses three levels and adds that team size, on-call schedules, traffic patterns and incident frequency should shape where the lines fall.

Vendor support severity. Opening a case with a vendor's technical assistance centre (TAC) means picking a severity, and each vendor publishes what it means and what it buys. F5's support guidelines, for example, define Severity 1 as conditions preventing critical business activities, including a device that will not power up or pass traffic; Severity 2 as conditions preventing or significantly impairing high-level business activities; Severity 3 as degradation of service or functionality; and Severity 4 as how-to questions, non-critical troubleshooting and feature requests. Severity 1 and 2 carry a one-hour target for initial response, defined as the first attempt to contact the customer, Severity 3 four business hours and Severity 4 the next business day, and a Severity 1 case alerts support managers immediately. A severity on a case is therefore a claim about business impact that the engineer opening it should be able to defend with facts about who and what is affected.

Vulnerability severity. The Common Vulnerability Scoring System (CVSS), owned by FIRST (Forum of Incident Response and Security Teams), describes itself as a framework for communicating the characteristics and severity of software vulnerabilities. Version 4.0, first published on 1 November 2023 and at document version 1.2 since 18 June 2024, maps every score to an optional qualitative scale: None 0.0, Low 0.1 to 3.9, Medium 4.0 to 6.9, High 7.0 to 8.9 and Critical 9.0 to 10.0. It also asks that scores be labelled by the metric groups used, CVSS-B for Base alone, CVSS-BT with Threat, CVSS-BE with Environmental and CVSS-BTE with both, and notes that publishers such as the National Vulnerability Database (NVD) typically provide only CVSS-B. The user guide is blunt about the limit: the Base score measures severity, not risk, and should not be used alone to assess risk; a CVSS-BTE score, built with the threat picture and the local environment, is much closer to it.

Message severity. Syslog has the oldest and simplest scale. Request for Comments (RFC) 5424 (March 2009) defines eight severities, 0 Emergency (system is unusable), 1 Alert, 2 Critical, 3 Error, 4 Warning, 5 Notice, 6 Informational and 7 Debug, and packs severity and facility into one number, the Priority, computed as facility times 8 plus severity: a Notice from facility local4 (20) is 165 and is written in the header as 165 between angle brackets, with no leading zeros. As with SEV levels, lower numbers are worse, which is worth remembering when a filter says "severity 3 and above" and somebody has to decide which direction above means.

What goes wrong. Severity inflation is the commonest failure: if every case is a SEV-1, the scale stops carrying information and the person who shouts loudest sets the queue. The opposite failure is a severity argued over while the outage continues. Both have the same cure, written criteria agreed before the incident, expressed in observable terms such as users affected, revenue blocked or redundancy lost, and reviewed afterwards. For vulnerabilities the parallel mistake is treating a published CVSS-B Critical as an instruction rather than an input, without asking whether the vulnerable component is exposed or whether an exploit exists.

Numbers worth remembering: SEV-1 as the worst level in most schemes; F5's one-hour target for Severity 1 and 2; CVSS bands breaking at 0.1, 4.0, 7.0 and 9.0; and syslog's 0 to 7, with Priority equal to facility times 8 plus severity.

triage.def: Sorting incoming problems by severity and urgency and routing each to the right owner, so that the queue reflects impact rather than arrival order.
triage.context: The name comes from battlefield medicine and carries the same uncomfortable implication: triage is the decision about what will not be worked on yet. Done well it is invisible; done badly it shows up as a critical fault sitting behind a printer request.
triage.depth:
What it is, and what it is not. Triage is the first decision taken about a problem report, before anyone tries to fix it: is this real, how bad is it, how fast does it need an answer, and who should own it. It is not diagnosis and it is not repair. The National Institute of Standards and Technology (NIST) puts the steps in that order in Special Publication (SP) 800-61 Revision 3, its incident response guide of April 2025. Outcome RS.MA-02, incident reports are triaged and validated, begins with a preliminary review to verify that an incident has actually occurred and then estimates its severity and the urgency of the response; RS.MA-03 follows with a more detailed review that categorizes the incident by type, such as data breach, ransomware, account takeover or denial of service, and prioritizes it by scope, likely impact, time-critical nature and the resources available. The same section states the principle behind the definition in one line: because of resource limitations, incidents should not be handled on a first-come, first-served basis.

How the decision is made. NIST calls evaluating an incident's overall risk and applying the appropriate prioritization perhaps the most critical decision points in the whole response, and asks that triage, prioritization, escalation and the decision to start recovery all rest on one agreed set of risk evaluation factors, which may be simple or very complex depending on the organization's maturity. Its examples are asset criticality, the functional impact of the incident, its data impact, the stage the observed activity has reached, the characterization of the threat actor, and recoverability. Revision 3, written by Alexander Nelson, Sanjay Rekhi, Murugiah Souppaya and Karen Scarfone, superseded the Revision 2 of August 2012 with a full rewrite organized as a Cybersecurity Framework (CSF) 2.0 Community Profile, so triage now sits in the Respond function, after Detect has declared an incident and before Recover. Triage is also not a single moment: RS.MA-04 asks that the status of every ongoing incident be tracked and validated, so that those needing more resources or a different strategy are found quickly. A priority set at intake is expected to change.

Triage in operations. Google's Site Reliability Engineering (SRE) book, in the chapter on effective troubleshooting written by Chris Jones, places triage straight after the problem report, and a good report states the expected behaviour, the actual behaviour and, if possible, how to reproduce it. The range of severity is wide, from one user under very specific circumstances with a workaround to a complete global outage, and the response should match it: an all-hands emergency is right for the second and overkill for the first. The chapter's central instruction is counterintuitive. In a major outage, ignore the instinct to find the root cause and first make the system work as well as it can, by diverting traffic from a broken cluster to healthy ones, dropping traffic wholesale to prevent a cascading failure, or disabling subsystems to lighten the load. Stopping the bleeding comes first, while still preserving evidence such as logs for the root-cause analysis later. The book borrows the rule taught to novice pilots, fly the airplane, and adds that if a bug may cause unrecoverable data corruption, freezing the system can be better than letting it run.

Severity and priority are different numbers. Severity says how bad the problem is; priority says where it goes in the queue, which also depends on urgency and on who is free to take it. PagerDuty's public incident response documentation uses five levels, SEV-1 to SEV-5, the lower number the more urgent: SEV-1 is a critical issue that warrants public notification and liaison with executive teams, SEV-5 a cosmetic issue that does not affect customers' ability to use the product, and anything above SEV-3 is automatically a major incident with a more intensive response. Its rule for doubt is the most useful part: if it is unclear whether an incident is a SEV-2 or a SEV-1, treat it as the higher one, because the middle of an incident is not the time to litigate severities; the choice is reviewed in the postmortem. Service desks in the ITIL tradition (originally the Information Technology Infrastructure Library) derive priority from impact and urgency instead. BMC Helix Service Desk 23.3, for example, gives each impact category and urgency level a numeric weight and adds them: a significant or large impact (5) with critical urgency (20) totals 25 and becomes a Critical priority, while a minor or localized impact (1) with the same urgency totals 21, and what that becomes depends on how the administrator mapped the ranges.

When the triage happens at a vendor, the customer's own severity choice sets the clock. F5's technical support guidelines, in a 2011 datasheet, define four case severities: Severity 1 when conditions on the device prevent critical business activities, or the device will not power up or is not passing traffic; Severity 2 when they prevent or significantly impair high-level commerce or business activities; Severity 3 for degradation of service or functionality; and Severity 4 for how-to questions, non-critical troubleshooting and feature requests. The target initial responses were one hour for Severities 1 and 2, four business hours for Severity 3 and the next business day for Severity 4, and a case logged as Severity 1 notified the support managers at once so that it could be assigned to a suitably skilled engineer. A case that states its business impact plainly is triaged at the right level on the first read; one that does not is graded on what it says.

Bug and vulnerability triage. Software projects triage defects the same way. Mozilla's process for Firefox requires every component to have a named triage owner, asks that new bugs be assessed daily so that security bugs can be actioned quickly and that every new bug be fully triaged, or under active investigation, within one week, and expects new S1 and sec-critical bugs to be assigned within two business days. A report without steps to reproduce goes back to its author with a needinfo request, which is a legitimate triage outcome rather than a delay. Vulnerability queues need the same care with their numbers. The Forum of Incident Response and Security Teams (FIRST) describes the Base metrics of the Common Vulnerability Scoring System (CVSS) version 4.0 as a reasonable worst-case impact across deployed environments, and asks consumers to add Threat and Environmental metrics and to feed the result into a process that also weighs regulatory requirements, the number of customers affected, monetary loss, threat to life or property and reputation. Sorting a backlog by Base score alone is a severity sort, not triage.

Where the word comes from. Merriam-Webster traces triage to French, from trier, to sort, and dates the first known English use in the medical sense to 1918; its second sense, assigning priority to projects according to where resources are best used, most needed or most likely to succeed, is the one engineering borrowed. A 2017 review in Acute Medicine and Surgery by Hiroyuki Nakao, Isao Ukai and Joji Kotani finds the word in the British wool trade in 1727 and for sorting coffee beans around 1830, and credits Napoleon's military surgeon Dominique-Jean Larrey (1766–1842) with its battlefield form: at the Battle of Jena in 1806 the French army sorted casualties into three grades by the severity of their wounds, irrespective of rank. The civilian Simple Triage and Rapid Treatment (START) method was developed in California in the 1980s by Hoag Hospital and the Newport Beach Fire Department. The logic that crossed over to engineering is Larrey's: severity decides the order, not rank.

What goes wrong. The commonest failure is triage by volume, where the loudest or most senior reporter is served first. The SRE chapter's remedy is structural: open a ticket for every issue, even those received by email or instant message, and discourage reporting problems directly to a person, because such reports are of lower quality, invisible to the rest of the team, and concentrate the work on whoever the reporters happen to know rather than on the engineer on duty. The opposite failures are severity inflation, where everything arrives as the top severity and the scale stops meaning anything, and the frozen priority, where an incident triaged as minor in the morning is still minor in the queue in the afternoon although its scope has grown. Written criteria, a rule for doubt that errs upwards, and re-triage of every open item, as RS.MA-04 asks, address all three.

postmortem.def: A written account, after an incident is resolved, of what happened and what should change.
postmortem.context: The useful ones are blameless by construction: they describe what the system allowed rather than who did it, because a review that stops at human error stops people telling you about mistakes. A postmortem that produces no change to a system, a process or a piece of documentation was a meeting.

post-incident-review.def: The meeting or document that examines an incident after service is restored, to decide what changes as a result.
post-incident-review.context: Distinct from the technical root cause work: the review asks what the organization should do differently, which frequently has no engineering answer at all. Where the cause was a decision nobody made (a certificate nobody owned, a forecast nobody read), the finding belongs in the review rather than in a ticket.
post-incident-review.depth:
What it is, and the names it goes by. A post-incident review (PIR) is the organization's structured look back at an incident once the service is stable again: what happened, why the system allowed it, how the response went, and what will change. The thing itself is old and the names vary by community. Site reliability engineers and most of the software industry say postmortem, and Google's book defines one as a written record of an incident, its impact, the actions taken to mitigate or resolve it, its root causes and the follow-up actions to prevent recurrence. Microsoft publishes Post Incident Reviews for Azure; Amazon Web Services publishes Post-Event Summaries; the National Institute of Standards and Technology (NIST) speaks of lessons-learned meetings and follow-up reports. The two terms overlap almost completely in use; where a distinction is drawn, the postmortem is the written account and the review is the meeting, and the decisions, that turn the account into changes. A review is not root cause analysis, which is one input to it; not a forensic investigation, which establishes facts to an evidentiary standard and keeps a chain of custody; and not a legal analysis of liability. Mixing those purposes in one meeting usually spoils all three.

When to hold one. Google's chapter lists the triggers it uses: user-visible downtime or degradation beyond a threshold, data loss of any kind, on-call intervention such as a release rollback or rerouting of traffic, a resolution time above a threshold, and a monitoring failure, which usually means the incident was discovered by hand. It insists on two rules around them: the criteria must be defined before an incident, so that nobody argues about whether this one qualifies, and any stakeholder may request a review for an event that meets none of them. The monitoring trigger deserves attention from security teams in particular: an intrusion found by a customer, a bank or a journalist is a detection failure as well as a breach, and it merits its own line of inquiry. In the same book, an incident is defined for on-call purposes as the sequence of events and alerts related to the same root cause that would be discussed in the same postmortem, and handling one, the postmortem included, takes about six hours on average, which is why reviews have to be budgeted rather than squeezed in.

How security incident response treats it. NIST's incident response recommendations, Special Publication (SP) 800-61 Revision 3 of April 2025, changed the picture. Its predecessor of August 2012 drew a circular life cycle in which formal post-incident activity identified improvements and fed them back into preparation, an approach that fitted a time when incidents were rare, narrow and over in a day or two. The 2025 text places improvement in the Identify function of the Cybersecurity Framework 2.0 as the Improvement category (ID.IM), and says lessons learned should often be shared as soon as they are identified rather than held until recovery concludes, because recovery now takes weeks or months. The review meeting survives: its note to outcome ID.IM-03 says improvements are often identified when writing follow-up reports or holding lessons-learned meetings as recovery concludes, especially after a major incident, to review what happened, what actions were taken and how effective they were, and to hear from all parties involved. The improvements may land in the incident response programme itself or elsewhere, for example by identifying the adversary's tactics, techniques and procedures (TTPs) that no safeguard blocked and no detection flagged.

Blameless, and why. The review works only if people say what they actually saw and did. John Allspaw, writing for Etsy's engineering blog on 22 May 2012, described the practice that made the term common: engineers whose actions contributed to an incident give a detailed account, what actions they took at what time, what effects they observed, the expectations and assumptions they had, and their understanding of the timeline, without fear of punishment or retribution. He tied it to the idea of a Just Culture, which balances safety and accountability, and to the search for the second story, the circumstances that made an action reasonable at the time. Google's chapter says the blameless culture originated in healthcare and avionics, where mistakes can be fatal, and that a blamelessly written review assumes everyone acted with good intentions on the information they had. Richard Cook's treatise How Complex Systems Fail, written at the University of Chicago between 1998 and 2000, gives the theory: post-accident attribution to a single root cause is fundamentally wrong, because accidents need several contributors at once, and hindsight bias distorts every judgement of human performance made after the outcome is known.

What it produces. The output is decisions, with owners and dates. Some are engineering changes; many are not: a certificate that expired because nobody owned it, or a capacity forecast that nobody read, is a gap in the organization's decisions, and a ticket in an engineering queue will not close it. Google adds a discipline about the document itself. Drafts are assessed by a group of senior engineers for completeness, then shared as widely as the knowledge is useful, with personal data kept out, and added to a repository of past incidents; 'an unreviewed postmortem might as well never have existed', and the chapter recommends regular review sessions so that no draft is left unfinished.

Public reviews. The large cloud providers now publish theirs. Microsoft's Azure status history keeps Post Incident Reviews for five years; from 20 November 2019 it published one for every issue it communicated about publicly, and from 1 June 2022 for broad issues as defined in its documentation. Each answers the same questions: what happened, what went wrong and why, how did the provider respond, how is it making incidents like this less likely or less impactful, and how can its communications be more useful, and some come with an incident retrospective video. Amazon Web Services commits to a public Post-Event Summary when an issue has broad and significant customer impact, such as the failure of a significant percentage of control plane calls, a significant part of a service's infrastructure, or a total power or significant network failure; summaries stay available for at least five years and give the scope of impact, the contributing factors and the actions taken, and its list ran, when read, from a compute and database service disruption in US East on 21 April 2011, through an event in the South America region (SA-EAST-1) on 17 December 2013, to the DynamoDB disruption in Northern Virginia on 19 October 2025. For customers these documents are evidence for their own reviews: a provider's account of an outage is a timeline the customer did not have to reconstruct.

What goes wrong. Blame is the first failure: a review that ends at human error teaches people to report less and later, and leaves the conditions that made the error easy in place. The second is no follow-through: actions without owners or dates, or reviewed once and never again. The third is selection: only the spectacular incidents get reviewed, while the near misses and the slow detections, which carry the same lessons more cheaply, are closed without comment. The fourth is a single root cause, which Cook's argument rules out, written into the summary because the template has one box for it. The fifth is timing: holding every lesson until recovery is complete, which NIST's 2025 revision explicitly advises against.

Neighbours. The postmortem is the written account, and blameless is the stance it is written in; root cause analysis is one of the inputs and should yield causes in the plural; the Swiss cheese model is the picture of several defences failing at once; a tabletop exercise rehearses the response before an incident and is often the first place a review's actions are tested. Mean time to recovery (MTTR) and service level objectives (SLOs) are the measures a review is usually trying to improve, and change management is where many of its actions end up.

observer-effect.def: When the act of measuring changes the behaviour being measured, so the fault disappears while you are watching for it.
observer-effect.context: Enabling debug logging slows a process just enough that a race no longer loses; attaching a capture changes buffering. The effect is not a nuisance to be worked around - it is a finding. A fault that vanishes under observation is telling you it depends on timing, which narrows the search considerably.

regression.def: A defect introduced by a change, in which something that previously worked stops working or works measurably worse.
regression.context: The word carries a specific accusation: not that the software is faulty in general, but that it got worse in a known direction at a known moment. That makes regressions the most tractable class of bug, because the change that caused one is usually still visible in the log.
regression.depth:
The Linux kernel's documentation gives the working definition most engineers use: it is a regression if an application or practical use case that runs fine with one kernel works worse or not at all with a newer version built with a similar configuration. Its examples are deliberately ordinary, a wireless driver that works in 5.13 and in 5.14 does not work at all, works significantly slower or misbehaves, or an application that suddenly behaves erratically because something changed in procfs or sysfs. The definition has two edges worth keeping. A bug that was always present is not a regression, however serious, because nothing that worked has stopped; and a regression does not have to be a crash, since slower, hungrier or merely different behaviour of something that used to work is enough. Statistics uses the same word for fitting a model to data, an unrelated sense.

The kernel treats the matter as a rule rather than a preference. "We don't cause regressions" is described as the first rule of Linux kernel development, established by Linus Torvalds and enforced by him, and the documentation spells out its consequences. Most regressions should be fixed within two weeks. A regression that the user could avoid by updating some other software is almost always still a regression. Performance counts only when the difference is significant: a 5 per cent slow-down in a micro-benchmark is unlikely to qualify unless it also moves a broad benchmark by more than 1 per cent. Security fixes may cause one only in extremely rare cases, where they are accepted as the lesser evil. And time matters: a change that broke something can usually be reverted if the problem is reported before the release, but a few weeks later software may depend on follow-up changes, and reverting everything would then be a regression for those users. Reports carry the range in which the problem appeared, for the tracking bot regzbot, in the form of an introduced line naming the last good and first bad versions.

That range is what makes regressions tractable. Because one version is known good and a later one known bad, the search space is bounded, and git bisect turns the search into binary search for the commit that introduced the bug. The engineer marks revisions good and bad (or old and new, for changes that are not bugs), Git checks out the midpoint, and each answer halves what remains, so a range of about a thousand commits is settled in about ten tests. The search can be automated with git bisect run and a script that exits 0 when the revision is good, with any code from 1 to 127 except 125 when it is bad, and with 125 when the revision cannot be tested and must be skipped; 126 and 127 are avoided because POSIX (Portable Operating System Interface) shells use them for a command that cannot be executed or found. When a regression arrived through a merged branch, the --first-parent option names the merge itself as the culprit and ignores broken intermediate commits on the branch.

The discipline that prevents regressions is named after them. The IEEE (Institute of Electrical and Electronics Engineers) software engineering glossary, IEEE 610.12-1990, and its successor, ISO/IEC/IEEE 24765, the vocabulary shared by the International Organization for Standardization (ISO), the International Electrotechnical Commission (IEC) and the IEEE, define regression testing as the selective retesting of a system or component to verify that modifications have not caused unintended effects and that it still complies with its specified requirements. In practice that means a suite of tests that once passed and must keep passing on every change, and the habit of adding a test for each fixed bug, so that if the bug returns it fails a build instead of reaching a user.

Security has its own regressions, and they are the most expensive kind because the original fix gave everyone confidence. CVE-2024-6387 in the CVE (Common Vulnerabilities and Exposures) list, published on 1 July 2024, is described in the National Vulnerability Database as a security regression of CVE-2006-5051: a race condition in the signal handling of OpenSSH's server that an unauthenticated remote attacker can trigger by failing to authenticate within the allowed time. The OpenSSH 9.8 release notes of the same day say the flaw was present in Portable OpenSSH from 8.5p1 to 9.7p1 inclusive, may allow arbitrary code execution with root privileges, and had been demonstrated on 32-bit Linux systems using glibc and ASLR (address space layout randomization) after six to eight hours of continuous connections on average in the lab, while OpenBSD was not vulnerable. A vulnerability fixed in 2006 had returned years later, which is the case for keeping a test for every security fix as well as for every functional one.

Network and security teams meet regressions mostly through upgrades. A new firmware or software train fixes the bug that justified the upgrade and breaks something that worked, often in a feature the upgrade never mentioned; the defences are the ones the definition suggests. Record how the system behaved before the change so that worse can be measured rather than argued; keep the previous image and a tested way back to it; read the vendor's lists of resolved and known issues for the target release; and test the paths that matter in a lab or a canary before the whole estate moves. When a regression does reach production, the choice is between rolling back, which restores the known-good version and gives up whatever the upgrade fixed, and a workaround, which keeps both, at the price of carrying a deviation until the vendor's fix arrives.

The vocabulary around the word is worth knowing because it shortens conversations. The regression range is the interval between the last known-good and the first known-bad version; the first bad commit is what bisection finds; a performance regression is a slowdown with no functional change; and a known regression is one the vendor has acknowledged in release notes. Saying that a problem is a regression, and naming the range, gives a vendor's support engineers the most useful single fact they can receive: not that the product is broken, but where to look.

failover.def: Failover is the switch of a service from a failed or failing component to a redundant standby, ideally automatic, which restores availability without repairing the fault.
failover.context: It is containment rather than cure, and it carries costs worth naming out loud: failing over to a standby that shares the fault takes down the survivor, and a contained problem often stops alerting, which means nobody is watching the thing that is still broken.
failover.depth:
What it is. NIST (National Institute of Standards and Technology), in the glossary drawn from SP (Special Publication) 800-53 Rev. 5, defines failover as the capability to switch over automatically, typically without human intervention or warning, to a redundant or standby system when the active one fails or terminates abnormally. Every design has the same three parts: detection, deciding that the active unit is gone; decision, choosing which unit takes over; and takeover, moving the service's identity, its IP (Internet Protocol) addresses, its MAC (media access control) address and sometimes its sessions, to the new unit. Failback, returning to the original unit once it recovers, is a separate decision, and often the riskier one.

Detection is a trade-off between speed and false alarms. VRRP (Virtual Router Redundancy Protocol) version 3, RFC (Request for Comments) 9568 of April 2024, which obsoleted RFC 5798 and renamed the master the Active Router, sends advertisements every 100 centiseconds by default. A Backup declares the Active down after three missed intervals plus a skew time of ((256 minus priority) times the interval) divided by 256, so the highest-priority backup moves first; the RFC puts election at under 4 seconds by default and below 1/25 of a second when tuned. A FortiGate cluster sends heartbeats every 200 ms by default and assumes its peer has failed after 6 are lost, 1.2 seconds; Fortinet's own example of 2-second heartbeats with a threshold of 30 waits a full minute. BFD (Bidirectional Forwarding Detection, RFC 5880, June 2010) generalizes the arithmetic: detection time is the peer's detect multiplier times the agreed transmit interval. Every vendor says the same thing in its own words: a lower threshold reacts faster and produces more false failovers when a busy peer or a congested link merely delays the heartbeat.

Takeover means moving an identity. A VRRP virtual router answers with a well-known MAC address, 00-00-5E-00-01 followed by the virtual router ID for IPv4, and the new Active Router broadcasts gratuitous ARP (Address Resolution Protocol) so switches and hosts learn where that address now lives. F5 BIG-IP generalizes the idea as traffic groups: floating self IP addresses, virtual addresses and SNAT (source network address translation) addresses that float together to another device in a Sync-Failover device group, up to 127 floating groups per device group. Its triggers show what is worth watching: system fail-safe on service heartbeats, gateway fail-safe on upstream routers, VLAN (virtual local area network) fail-safe on lost traffic, and HA (high availability) groups that score trunks, pool members and cluster members. A MAC masquerade address keeps the MAC constant across units and, in F5's words, reduces the risk of dropped connections; auto-failback is optional and off unless enabled; F5 recommends port 1026 for failover communication between units.

Split brain. When the two units lose sight of each other but not of the network, both conclude the other is dead and both go active, with duplicate addresses and divergent state. Fortinet's guidance for clusters stretched across buildings or regions describes exactly how it happens: heartbeats need a layer 2 path, distance adds transit time, and once delay, latency and loss exceed the lost-heartbeat threshold the cluster splits. Its remedies are the general ones: longer intervals and higher thresholds on long links, several heartbeat interfaces over different paths, and QoS (quality of service) priority for heartbeat traffic. Larger systems replace the pair with a quorum, so that a minority partition cannot promote itself.

When failover is the outage. On 21 October 2018, at 22:52 UTC (Coordinated Universal Time), routine replacement of failing 100G optical equipment cut GitHub's primary US East Coast data centre off from its network hub for 43 seconds. Orchestrator, the tool managing its MySQL topologies, built on Raft consensus, did what it was configured to do: nodes on the West Coast and in a public cloud formed a quorum and failed the database primaries over to the West Coast. When connectivity returned, the East Coast held a few seconds of writes the West had never received and the West had begun taking new ones, so failing back was no longer safe, and applications in the East could not tolerate cross-country latency to their databases. Service was degraded for 24 hours and 11 minutes while engineers chose consistency over speed. Every component behaved correctly; the failover policy allowed a topology the applications could not support.

Containment, not cure. The fault is still there after a failover, and two consequences follow. A standby that shares the fault, the same software defect, the same synchronized bad configuration, the same upstream dependency, fails the moment it takes the load, taking down the survivor. And a contained problem often stops alerting, so nobody is watching the component that is still broken while the cluster runs without a spare. Failover that is never exercised is a hypothesis; the honest test is to trigger it deliberately and measure what the users saw.

Neighbours. Load balancing spreads traffic across healthy members in active-active fashion, and its health checks are a form of failure detection; failover in the strict sense moves a service between an active and a standby. GSLB (global server load balancing) applies the same idea between sites through DNS (Domain Name System). RTO (recovery time objective) and RPO (recovery point objective) state how fast the switch must be and how much data loss is acceptable, which is exactly the trade GitHub had to make by hand.

incident.def: An incident is an unplanned interruption or reduction in quality of a service or, in security, an occurrence that jeopardizes the confidentiality, integrity or availability of information or systems or violates security policy: something that needs a response now, as distinct from a request for something new.
incident.context: An incident and a service request need different queues and different clocks: the incident is restored as fast as possible, the request is fulfilled on an agreed schedule. Treating a request as an incident inflates the numbers; treating an incident as a request buries it, and where both are logged in the same system the classification is usually the first thing to get wrong. Security adds a second test: not every alert or adverse event is an incident, and the moment one is declared starts the clocks for escalation and, where personal data is involved, for regulators.
incident.depth:
Two definitions, one word. In information technology (IT) service management, ITIL 2011 defined an incident as an unplanned interruption to an IT service or reduction in its quality, and included a failure of a configuration item that has not yet affected the service, such as the loss of one disk in a mirror set; the ISO 20000 objective for the process is to restore agreed service as soon as possible. In security, the National Institute of Standards and Technology (NIST) Special Publication (SP) 800-61 Rev. 3 (April 2025) quotes the United States Federal Information Security Modernization Act (FISMA) of 2014: an occurrence that actually or imminently jeopardizes, without lawful authority, the integrity, confidentiality or availability of information or an information system, or constitutes a violation or imminent threat of violation of law, security policies, security procedures or acceptable use policies. The first is about service; the second is about harm and authority, and a security incident can leave every service running.

Event, adverse event, incident. The same NIST guide keeps the vocabulary in layers. An event is any observable occurrence involving computing assets, such as a login attempt, a software update or an application answering a request. An adverse event is any event with a negative consequence, whatever the cause, from a natural disaster or a power failure to an attack. Whether adverse cybersecurity events add up to an incident usually needs further analysis, which is why triage exists. The guide's examples of incidents read like a recent threat report: a botnet flooding an internet-facing service, stolen administrative credentials at a software-as-a-service provider, an intrusion that reaches industrial control systems, ransomware with data theft, phishing that leads to financial fraud, a new vulnerability exploited in network management appliances, and a vendor's software compromised before it reaches customers.

Declaring one. Google's Site Reliability Engineering (SRE) book gives a test that avoids arguing about definitions while an outage runs: declare an incident if a second team is needed to fix the problem, if the outage is visible to customers, or if the issue is unsolved after an hour's concentrated analysis. Its incident management is based on the Incident Command System, with roles kept separate: the incident commander holds the overall state and every role not delegated, operations is the only group allowed to change the system, communication issues periodic updates and keeps the incident document current, and planning handles the longer-term work, from filing bugs and arranging handoffs to tracking how the system has drifted from normal. There is a recognized command post, a live incident document, and an explicit handoff of command, said aloud and acknowledged. The priorities are stated in one line: stop the bleeding, restore service, and preserve the evidence for finding the root cause.

The security life cycle, old and new. SP 800-61 Rev. 2 (August 2012) described four phases: preparation; detection and analysis; containment, eradication and recovery; and post-incident activity, ending in a report on the cause and cost of the incident and the steps to prevent the next one. Rev. 3 retires that circle. It explains that in 2012 incidents were relatively rare, narrow and usually handled within a day or two, whereas today they are frequent, damaging and can take weeks or months to recover from. It maps response onto the six Functions of the NIST Cybersecurity Framework (CSF) 2.0: Govern, Identify and Protect as the broader preparation, Detect, Respond and Recover as incident response proper, with an Improvement Category (ID.IM) through which lessons are fed back as soon as they are learned rather than after recovery ends.

Clocks set by law. Declaring an incident can start legal deadlines. Under Article 33 of the European Union's General Data Protection Regulation (GDPR), a controller must notify the supervisory authority of a personal data breach without undue delay and, where feasible, within 72 hours of becoming aware of it, with reasons for any delay. The NIS2 Directive, (EU) 2022/2555, sets three steps for significant incidents in Article 23: an early warning within 24 hours, an incident notification within 72 hours and a final report within one month of that notification. In Brazil, Resolução CD/ANPD nº 15 of 24 April 2024 requires the controller to inform the ANPD (Agência Nacional de Proteção de Dados, the Autoridade Nacional until Provisional Measure 1.317 took effect on 18 September 2025, converted into Law 15.352 of 25 February 2026) within three working days of learning that personal data were affected, and to inform the data subjects within the same period. These clocks run from awareness, so the log of when a responder first knew something is itself evidence.

What goes wrong. The common failures are misclassification and slow declaration: a security incident handled as an ordinary service ticket loses the evidence that the SRE priorities and NIST's analysis depend on, and a service incident left in a request queue misses its restoration target. Responders who start repairing before anyone holds command change the system in uncoordinated ways, which is exactly what separating the operations role prevents. And restoring service without preserving evidence, the third of the SRE priorities, leaves nothing for the root-cause analysis that follows.

Numbers worth remembering: one hour of unsolved analysis as a declaration trigger, four life-cycle phases in 2012 and six CSF Functions in 2025, 24 hours, 72 hours and one month under NIS2, 72 hours under the GDPR, and three working days for the ANPD in Brazil.

intermittent-fault.def: A failure that occurs unpredictably and cannot be triggered on demand, so it cannot be tested against directly.
intermittent-fault.context: The instinct is to keep trying to reproduce it. The better move is to stop trying to trigger it and start trying to catch it: instrument the path, leave the capture running, and define in advance what evidence would settle the question. “Cannot reproduce” describes your laboratory, not the fault.

handover.def: Transferring a problem to another person or team, along with the state of understanding that goes with it.
handover.context: Escalation is not letting go of a ticket; it is this. A good handover carries what was reported, what is established as true rather than suspected, what was ruled out and how, what was about to be tried, and - not optional - what has already been changed. The expensive ones are those where the receiving engineer spends an hour discovering the system is not in the state the documentation describes.

rate-limiting.def: Capping how often something may happen, such as requests, connections, packets or responses per client in a given time, to protect a system from load it cannot absorb.
rate-limiting.context: Used as containment it buys time without fixing anything, and it moves the problem rather than removing it: whatever was rate limited is still trying, and the queue it forms is now somebody's capacity problem. The retry that masks a slow dependency becomes a thundering herd when the dependency stops entirely.
rate-limiting.depth:
What is being limited. A rate limit counts events, requests, new connections, packets, bytes or responses, against a key, such as a client address, a user, an API (application programming interface) key or a destination, over time, and acts when the count runs ahead of the allowed rate. It is not the same as a concurrency limit, and products keep the two apart: F5 BIG-IP offers a Connection Limit for concurrent connections and a separate Connection Rate Limit for new connections per second, on virtual servers, pool members and nodes; NGINX has limit_req for request rate, limit_conn for concurrent connections and limit_rate for bandwidth. Acting on excess also comes in two kinds. Policing decides conformance and drops, marks or rejects what does not conform; shaping delays the excess in a queue and sends it later. Request for Comments (RFC) 3290, the informal management model for Differentiated Services (Diffserv) routers (May 2002), assigns the leaky bucket mainly to shaping traffic as it leaves an interface and the token bucket to measuring whether arriving traffic conforms.

The token bucket. Both models are relationships between a rate R, a burst size B and an interval t, with R = B/t. RFC 3290's example is an information rate of 1.2 Mbps with a 1,500-byte burst: 1,200,000 bits per second, a 12,000-bit burst and a 10-millisecond interval, so conforming traffic arrives at worst as 100 bursts of 1,500 bytes a second. Tokens accumulate at rate R up to B, each packet spends tokens equal to its size, and a stream conforms to a simple bucket if in any interval t it delivers at most R times t plus B. Variable-length packets create a dilemma when fewer tokens remain than the packet needs: accepting it and letting the bucket go negative is loose conformance, rejecting it until enough tokens accrue is strict, and either way up to one maximum transmission unit (MTU) of capacity can shift between intervals. Real meters often stack buckets: the single rate three colour marker of RFC 2697 (September 1999) meters a Committed Information Rate (CIR) with a Committed Burst Size (CBS) and an Excess Burst Size (EBS), marking packets green, yellow or red. The Linux token bucket filter, tc qdisc tbf, is a pure shaper built the same way: tokens roughly correspond to bytes with a minimum cost per packet, the bucket starts full for one burst, packets wait in a limited queue when it is empty, and an optional peakrate is a second, very small bucket. Its manual notes a hardware-independent limit: the kernel throttles in units of one jiffy, so perfect shaping at HZ=100 means about 100 packets of 1,000 bytes a second, roughly 1 Mbit/s.

The leaky bucket. A leaky bucket drains at a constant rate and releases a packet only when all of its bits would have been allowed, never borrowing from future capacity, which with a coarse clock adds jitter to the shaped stream. NGINX's limit_req module uses this method for requests. limit_req_zone binds a key, typically $binary_remote_addr, to a shared-memory zone with a rate in requests per second or per minute (30r/m is half a request per second); limit_req applies it with an optional burst. Excess requests are delayed to the configured rate until more than burst are waiting, and only then rejected; nodelay serves the burst at once while still counting it, and delay=, since version 1.15.7, sets how many may pass before delaying starts. The sizing is documented: the binary address is 4 bytes for IPv4 (Internet Protocol version 4) or 16 for IPv6, each state takes 64 bytes on 32-bit platforms and 128 on 64-bit ones, so one megabyte holds about 16,000 or 8,000 states, the least recently used state is evicted when the zone fills, and requests with an empty key are not counted at all. limit_req_dry_run, since 1.17.1, counts without enforcing, which is how a new limit should start. One default surprises people: rejected requests get limit_req_status, which is 503, not 429.

Signalling it over HTTP (Hypertext Transfer Protocol). RFC 6585 (April 2012) defined 429 Too Many Requests: the user has sent too many requests in a given amount of time. The response should explain the condition and may carry Retry-After, and a 429 must not be stored by a cache. The RFC deliberately leaves the policy open: a server may count per resource, across the whole server or across a set of servers, and may identify the user by credentials or by a cookie. Retry-After itself is defined in RFC 9110 (June 2022), section 10.2.3, as either an HTTP-date or a number of seconds; sent with 503 it says how long the service is expected to be unavailable. What HTTP still lacks is a standard way to announce the limit before it is hit. The IETF (Internet Engineering Task Force) httpapi working group's draft-ietf-httpapi-ratelimit-headers, at revision 11 of 23 May 2026 and expiring on 24 November 2026, is an active working group document, not an RFC. It defines RateLimit-Policy, with a quota q, a quota unit qu (requests, content-bytes or concurrent-requests), a window w in seconds and a partition key pk, and RateLimit, with the remaining quota r and the seconds t until the window resets: RateLimit-Policy: "default";q=100;w=10 and RateLimit: "default";r=50;t=30.

In the network layer. Routers rate-limit their own control-plane output. RFC 1812 (June 1995) says a router should be able to limit the ICMP (Internet Control Message Protocol) errors it sends, by count, by timer or by bandwidth; RFC 4443 makes it a must for ICMPv6, recommends a token bucket, gives B=10 and N=10 per second as possible defaults for a small device, and warns against limiters that cannot cope with bursts such as traceroute's. That is why traceroute shows asterisks at healthy routers. Authoritative DNS (Domain Name System) servers face the opposite problem, being used as amplifiers: Internet Systems Consortium (ISC) measured a 36-byte query for isc.org of type ANY drawing a 3,576-byte response, nearly a hundredfold, and the Response Rate Limiting (RRL) of BIND (Berkeley Internet Name Domain), part of BIND since 9.10, limits identical responses per client bucket of a /24 in IPv4 or a /56 in IPv6, answering a fraction with truncated responses so that real clients can retry over TCP (Transmission Control Protocol).

On F5 and Fortinet equipment. On BIG-IP the connection rate limit can be keyed per virtual object, the default, or per source address, per destination address or a combination, and the difference matters: with the default, one abusive client exhausts the limit for everyone. The per-source mode had its own history; F5 bug 420341, opened on 1 May 2013 and fixed in 12.0.0, throttled every other client once one source exceeded its limit. FortiGate applies DoS (denial of service) policies before security policies, so floods are cut before they reach more expensive inspection, using predefined anomaly sensors with recommended thresholds: tcp_syn_flood at 2,000 packets per second to one destination, tcp_port_scan at 1,000 per second from one source, udp_flood at 2,000, icmp_flood at 250, icmp_sweep at 100 sessions per second, and 5,000 concurrent sessions for the TCP, UDP (User Datagram Protocol) and IP per-source and per-destination session anomalies. The recommended values are starting points to tune against a baseline, not limits that fit every network.

Choosing the key. Every limiter is only as good as the identity it counts. Per-address limits punish everyone who shares an address: ISC warns that RRL may limit innocent hosts behind a large NAT (network address translation) and offers exempt-clients, and the same applies to carrier-grade NAT, corporate proxies and mobile gateways in front of a web limiter. Per-user or per-key limits need authentication first, which is why RFC 6585 mentions credentials and cookies, and limits enforced across several servers must either share state or accept some overshoot.
