An attacker who controls many addresses, as in credential stuffing from a botnet, stays under any per-address limit, so per-account and global limits are needed beside it.

The client side. A rejected client usually retries, and if every client retries on the same schedule the retries arrive together. Marc Brooker's 2015 analysis for Amazon Web Services (AWS) showed that exponential backoff alone still produces clusters of calls with idle gaps between them, that adding random jitter spreads them to an almost constant rate and, with 100 contending clients, cut the number of calls by more than half, and that the variant he called Full Jitter did the least work; by May 2023 most AWS software development kits (SDKs) supported exponential backoff with jitter in their standard and adaptive retry modes. A well-behaved client honours Retry-After when present, backs off exponentially with jitter when it is not, and caps its retries; a server that returns 429 or 503 without Retry-After leaves every client to guess.

The numbers to keep. HTTP 429 for too many requests, Retry-After in seconds or as a date, NGINX's default rejection status of 503, R = B/t and conformance as R times t plus B, RFC 4443's B=10 and N=10 per second for ICMPv6 errors, RRL buckets of /24 and /56, and FortiGate's 2,000 SYN (synchronize) packets per second as the starting threshold for a flood.

ops-escalation.def: Handing a problem to someone with more authority, more knowledge, or the ownership needed to act on it.
ops-escalation.context: The useful question is not whether you could solve it but whether you are the fastest path to it being solved. Escalating late is the failure of the competent, and it persists because escalation is treated as a confession - which is a cultural problem no advice to individuals will fix.

containment.def: Limiting how far a fault or an incident spreads and how much it affects, without yet addressing why it happened.
containment.context: Failing over, disabling a feature, blocking a source, isolating a segment or a host: none of these repairs anything, they put a boundary around the damage. The incident guidance of the National Institute of Standards and Technology (NIST) defines containment as preventing the expansion of an incident and notes that most incidents need some of it. Most incidents end at containment, which is the normal shape of the work, but a report that calls the result 'resolved' rather than 'bounded' describes a problem that is still live.
containment.depth:
What it is, and what it is not. In NIST's current guidance, Special Publication (SP) 800-61 Revision 3 (April 2025), containment is the outcome RS.MI-01, Incidents are contained, and the note under it is short: containment refers to preventing the expansion of an incident, it can prevent additional damage and avoid overwhelming the organization's resources, and most incidents require some form of it. The next outcome draws the line that matters. Eradication, RS.MI-02, means eliminating persistence mechanisms and entry points, deleting malware, disabling breached accounts and mitigating every exploited vulnerability, and recovery, under the Recover function, restores systems, confirms they work and remediates what let the incident happen. Containment does none of that. It changes how far the problem reaches, not whether the problem exists, which is why it can be done quickly, under uncertainty, and before anyone knows the cause.

From a phase to an outcome. Revision 2, the Computer Security Incident Handling Guide of August 2012 by Paul Cichonski, Tom Millar, Tim Grance and Karen Scarfone, drew incident response as a cycle of four phases: preparation; detection and analysis; containment, eradication and recovery; and post-incident activity, with activity often looping from the third phase back to detection as new infected hosts turned up. NIST withdrew it on 3 April 2025, superseded in its entirety by Revision 3, written by Alex Nelson, Sanjay Rekhi, Murugiah Souppaya and Karen Scarfone as a full rewrite organized as a Community Profile of the Cybersecurity Framework (CSF) 2.0. Revision 3 explains the change: the old cycle fitted a time when incidents were rare, narrow and handled within a day or two by a separate team, whereas today they are frequent, more damaging and take weeks or months to recover from, so response belongs inside risk management across all six CSF Functions, Govern, Identify, Protect, Detect, Respond and Recover, and lessons should be shared as soon as they are found. Containment survives as part of Incident Mitigation, RS.MI, defined as activities performed to prevent expansion of an event and mitigate its effects.

Choosing a strategy. Revision 2's advice on choosing a containment strategy is still the clearest list of trade-offs, and Revision 3 carries its essentials forward. Strategies differ by incident type, since containing email-borne malware is nothing like containing a distributed denial-of-service (DDoS) attack, so each major type should have its own documented strategy and criteria. The criteria are the potential damage to and theft of resources, the need to preserve evidence, service availability, the time and resources the strategy needs, its effectiveness (partial or full containment) and its duration. On duration Revision 2 gave concrete classes: an emergency workaround to be removed in four hours, a temporary workaround to be removed in two weeks, or a permanent solution; Revision 3 keeps the same classes in terms of hours, two weeks or permanence. Revision 3 adds automation: security tools and the security features of operating systems and network devices can quarantine malware, move a compromised endpoint to an isolated remediation network or halt an infected container on their own, and internet service providers and cloud providers can be authorized in advance to contain large DDoS attacks, while handlers must still be able to choose and apply containment by hand.

Where containment goes wrong. Both revisions warn about delaying containment to watch an attacker in a sandbox: it should be discussed with the legal department first, and the delay is dangerous because the attacker can escalate access or compromise other systems; Revision 2 added that an organization which knowingly lets a compromise continue may be liable if the compromised system is used to attack others. Revision 2 also describes containment that causes damage: a malicious process that periodically pings another host may overwrite or encrypt the disk when disconnection makes the pings fail, so handlers should not assume that a disconnected host is safe. Evidence is the other tension, since wiping or rebuilding contains quickly and destroys what the investigation needed. The general rule is that a containment action is itself a change, made under pressure, and needs the same question every change needs: what else does this reach?

The cost of not having it. The Knight Capital incident is the operational textbook case, as the US Securities and Exchange Commission (SEC) recorded it in its order of 16 October 2013. On 1 August 2012 Knight's order router, SMARS, sent millions of orders into the market over 45 minutes from 212 incoming parent orders, obtaining more than 4 million executions in 154 stocks for more than 397 million shares, and Knight lost over 460 million dollars. Knight had no procedures to halt SMARS in response to its own aberrant activity, and the response it improvised made things worse: removing the new code from the seven servers that had been deployed correctly caused more incoming parent orders to activate the old defective code. The lesson for containment is twofold. A stop switch has to exist before the incident, and a rollback is a containment action only if someone has checked which way it moves the failure.

Containment designed in. Engineering borrowed the idea from ships, where watertight bulkheads keep a breach in one compartment. Michael Nygard's Release It! (second edition, January 2018) lists bulkheads among its stability patterns alongside timeouts, circuit breakers, load shedding, back pressure and governors, under the broader heading of stopping crack propagation before a local fault becomes a cascading failure. Amazon Web Services' Well-Architected Framework makes the arithmetic explicit in REL10-BP03: a cell-based architecture runs the workload as several isolated cells that share no state, routed by a partition key such as a customer ID through a deliberately simple routing layer, so that with 10 cells serving 100 requests a failure in one leaves 90 per cent unaffected. Its listed anti-patterns are the ways containment erodes: cells allowed to grow without bound, changes deployed to all cells at once, state or components shared between cells, and logic piled into the router. Rolling changes out cell by cell is itself containment applied in advance, and it also contains poison pill requests, inputs that crash whatever processes them. In networks the same idea is segmentation, from VLANs (virtual local area networks) to microsegmentation, which decides in advance how far a compromised host can reach.

Calling it by its name. The common levers are the ones already in place: fail over to a healthy peer, disable a feature or a route, block a source address, isolate a host or a segment, revoke a credential, limit a rate. Each buys time and none removes the cause. Containment measures are also temporary by design, as NIST's duration classes imply, so each one is a debt to be tracked: an emergency block that nobody removes becomes a permanent, undocumented policy, and a rate limit left in place quietly becomes someone else's capacity problem. The honest status for an incident after containment is bounded, with the eradication and recovery work still listed as open, and the post-incident review should record not only what contained the problem but how long the containment took, because that interval set most of the cost.

carterfone.def: The 1968 FCC decision that let equipment the telephone company had not made be attached to the telephone network.
carterfone.context: Before it, the carrier decided what could touch its lines, and the answer was almost always its own equipment. The Carterfone was an acoustic coupler for linking a two-way radio to a phone call, and the ruling that allowed it established a principle far larger than the device: the network had to accept attachments that did it no harm. Every modem, multiplexer and data device sold by somebody other than the carrier descends from that opening, which is why an FCC decision about a radio accessory turns up at the start of so many company histories.

computer-inquiry.def: The FCC proceedings that drew a line between regulated communications and unregulated data processing.
computer-inquiry.context: The question sounds administrative and decided the shape of an industry: if a service both moves data and computes on it, is it a telephone service subject to tariffs, or a computer service that anybody may sell? Computer Inquiry I asked it; Computer Inquiry II answered it by separating basic transmission from enhanced services built on top. That separation is why value-added networks could exist as businesses, and why the carriers had to offer the underlying capacity to competitors who then sold against them.

imp.def: Interface Message Processor: the ARPANET's packet switch, a separate minicomputer sitting between a host and the network.
imp.context: Putting the network's logic in its own machine was a design decision with consequences. Hosts differed wildly, and asking each to implement the network directly would have made the network hostage to the slowest vendor; the IMP presented one interface and absorbed the difference. It is the ancestor of the router as a distinct box rather than a function of a computer, and the reason the first network engineers worked on equipment nobody else in the building understood.

ncp.def: Network Control Program: the ARPANET host protocol that TCP/IP replaced.
ncp.context: NCP assumed the network beneath it was reliable, which the single ARPANET was, and that assumption is exactly what stopped it scaling to a network of networks. TCP's separation of a reliable conversation from an unreliable delivery service was the answer, and the cutover on 1 January 1983 is one of the few flag days in this history that actually happened. Anybody who has argued about where reliability belongs in a stack is repeating an argument NCP lost.

statistical-multiplexer.def: A multiplexer that allocates line capacity on demand rather than by fixed time slot.
statistical-multiplexer.context: Terminals are idle most of the time, so a fixed slot per terminal wastes most of a line. The statistical multiplexer buffers and interleaves instead, giving capacity to whoever is transmitting, and sold on the arithmetic: fewer leased lines for the same terminal count. It also introduced queueing and therefore variable delay, which is the trade every shared-capacity technology since has made. The companies built on it were substantial and mostly did not survive the arrival of networks that did the same thing end to end.

data-pbx.def: A switch that connected terminals to computers the way a PBX connected telephones to lines.
data-pbx.context: In a building with more terminals than computer ports, something had to decide who got connected to what, and the data PBX (or CBX, when the vendor wanted to sound computerized) did it as a circuit switch. It was a good answer to a question that stopped being asked: local area networks let a terminal reach any host without a switch in the middle deciding, and the market closed faster than its vendors expected. It is one of the clearest cases of a product that was correct and was overtaken.

gosip.def: GOSIP (Government Open Systems Interconnection Profile) was a government procurement specification of the late 1980s and early 1990s that fixed which Open Systems Interconnection (OSI) protocols and options agencies had to buy, in the United States as Federal Information Processing Standard (FIPS) 146, mandatory from August 1990 until 1995, and in the United Kingdom as a profile from 1988.
gosip.context: Both the United States and the United Kingdom used buying power to try to make OSI the standard, on the reasoning that a large enough customer can create a market. It did not work, and the reason is instructive: TCP/IP (Transmission Control Protocol/Internet Protocol) was already running, already interoperating and already cheaper to deploy, while OSI arrived as a specification that vendors were still implementing, with routing, network management and directory standards unfinished. GOSIP itself only required agencies to buy OSI, not to use it or to stop using anything else, and in 1995 the United States replaced it with a profile that pointed to Internet Engineering Task Force (IETF) standards. A mandate can compel purchase; it cannot compel a technology to be ready.
gosip.depth:
What it was exactly. A profile, not a protocol. The Open Systems Interconnection (OSI) standards left implementers many options, some of them incompatible, so two products that both conformed to OSI could still fail to talk to each other. GOSIP picked one configuration: a subset of OSI protocols, with the options and parameters agreed by vendors and users at the OSI Implementors Workshops that the National Bureau of Standards, later the National Institute of Standards and Technology (NIST), had hosted four times a year since 1983. In the United States it was a Federal Information Processing Standard (FIPS), and, as Request for Comments (RFC) 1169 stressed, a procurement specification: it said what agencies must buy when they needed the functions it covered, not what they must run. Phill Gross, who had helped draft RFC 1169, put it in one line on a public mailing list in 1991: government network purchasers had to buy OSI, but nothing said they had to use it.

Where it came from. In September 1986 the National Bureau of Standards held the first meeting of government agencies wanting a Government OSI Profile, with representatives of 19 organizations, to coordinate the acquisition and operation of OSI products by the federal government. Its author, John Heafner, described the aim as a procurement specification that referenced the work of the American National Standards Institute (ANSI), the International Organization for Standardization (ISO), the International Telegraph and Telephone Consultative Committee (CCITT) and the Institute of Electrical and Electronics Engineers (IEEE) rather than rewriting it, and NIST's Gerard (Jerry) Mulvenna noted that the Department of Defense was a major contributor. The military had already moved: a memorandum of 2 July 1987, published as RFC 1039, adopted the OSI message handling and file transfer protocols defined in the GOSIP draft of 22 April 1987 as experimental co-standards to the Department of Defense's own protocols (MIL-STD 1777, 1778, 1780 and 1781), planned to make OSI the sole mandatory suite two years after GOSIP became a FIPS, and told the Defense Communications Agency to join the Corporation for Open Systems. IEEE Spectrum's history of OSI traces that policy to a 1985 National Research Council recommendation that the Department of Defense migrate from TCP/IP to OSI.

Versions and dates. GOSIP Version 1 was published in August 1988 after a comment period that began as early as January 1987, adopted as FIPS 146 in February 1989 and made mandatory in federal solicitations from 15 August 1990. NIST's Special Publication 500-163, the GOSIP Users' Guide of August 1989, explained it for planners. Version 2, FIPS 146-1, dated 3 April 1991, superseded the first: its additional protocols took effect on 3 October 1991 and had to be cited in solicitations initiated after 3 October 1992, and the rule for later versions was a mandate about a year after each took effect, roughly 18 months after promulgation. Every version allowed agencies to buy other protocols, proprietary ones included, alongside the profile.

What it specified. Version 1 covered two applications, the X.400 Message Handling Systems (MHS) and File Transfer, Access and Management (FTAM), over four network technologies: X.25, carrier-sense multiple access with collision detection (ISO 8802-3, the Ethernet family), token bus (ISO 8802-4) and token ring (ISO 8802-5). In the middle it was deliberately narrow. To guarantee interoperable data transfer it made one transport protocol, class 4 of ISO 8073, and one network protocol, the Connectionless Network Protocol (CLNP) of ISO 8473, mandatory, with the ISO 8327 session protocol above. Version 2 added the Virtual Terminal service, the Integrated Services Digital Network (ISDN), documents in the Office Document Architecture (ODA) format carried by MHS and FTAM, the End System to Intermediate System (ES-IS) protocol, and optionally the connection-oriented network service and a connectionless transport. For addressing, GOSIP used network service access point (NSAP) addresses under authority and format identifier 47 and international code designator 0005, assigned to NIST, which specified the rest of the structure and delegated the assignment of values to the General Services Administration (GSA).

How the mandate actually worked. By 1990 the misunderstanding was common enough that the Internet Activities Board (IAB), coordinating with the Federal Networking Council, published RFC 1169, written by Vint Cerf and NIST's Kevin Mills, as its official view. GOSIP did not mandate an immediate or total transition to OSI; it applied to new networks and major upgrades, not to adding devices to an existing non-GOSIP network; it was not exclusive, so other protocol families could be bought and used on the same network; heads of agencies could grant waivers when compliance would prevent an agency from accomplishing its mission or cause adverse financial effects not offset by government-wide savings; and NIST had no enforcement role. The same document gave the reasons TCP/IP would stay: a large installed base, limited deployment of commercial OSI products and incomplete OSI standards for routing, network management and directory services. The Internet Engineering Task Force (IETF) devoted one of its eight areas to OSI integration and sat on the GOSIP Advanced Requirements Group, and the plan included routing ISO 8473 packets on the National Science Foundation's NSFnet backbone and gateways between OSI and TCP/IP applications.

Beyond the United States. The United Kingdom's Central Computer and Telecommunications Agency (CCTA) published its own GOSIP in 1988 and began work that year with France and West Germany on the European Procurement Handbook for Open Systems (EPHOS), published in 1990 as a European GOSIP; the fourth and final UK GOSIP appeared in 1991, and Australia and New Zealand issued a joint GOSIP Version 3 in 1993. The idea of a government profile spread as widely as the protocols it profiled did not.

The end. On 14 September 1994 NIST proposed revising FIPS 146-1, and on 15 May 1995 the Federal Register announced the Secretary of Commerce's approval of FIPS 146-2, renamed Profiles for Open Systems Internetworking Technologies (POSIT). Its explanation is one sentence long in effect: it removed the requirement that federal agencies specify GOSIP protocols when acquiring networking products and services. In its place agencies were told to use open, voluntary standards such as those of the IETF, the International Telecommunication Union's standardization sector (ITU-T) and ISO, with the Internet Official Protocol Standards (RFC 1610) among the related documents and an updated OSI profile, the Industry/Government Open Systems Specification (IGOSS), available for those who still wanted OSI. From 1995 interest in OSI implementations declined, although the Defense Message System kept the OSI X.400 and X.500 protocols for their security features.

Why it failed, and what survived. IEEE Spectrum's history notes that the Internet was still a research network through the 1980s, closed to commercial traffic on the subsidized backbone until 1992, which made OSI look like the only option for businesses at the moment the mandates were written; by 1989 the OSI advocate Brian Carpenter was giving a talk called 'Is OSI Too Late?' to a standing ovation. A mandate can compel purchase; it cannot compel a technology to be ready, and in the years GOSIP was in force agencies bought OSI to comply and ran TCP/IP to work. What survived is the method, which FIPS 146-2 itself kept: the profile as a procurement tool, a fixed set of options from larger open standards so that products from different vendors interoperate, with NIST planning further profiles and agencies urged to buy components tested for interoperability.

osinet.def: OSINET: the Open Systems Interconnection (OSI) test network and membership organization that the United States National Bureau of Standards (NBS, later NIST) hosted from 1984, on which vendors and government users joined their implementations over X.25 to check that OSI products from different suppliers actually interoperated.
osinet.context: Conformance to a specification and interoperation with another vendor's product are different properties, and Open Systems Interconnection (OSI) made the gap between them visible. OSINET existed to close it by testing implementations against each other rather than against a document: its members, from IBM, Digital and Sun to the Defense Communications Agency, put real systems on a shared X.25 network and ran agreed tests between pairs. The effort was serious and the lesson outlived the protocols: interoperability is demonstrated, not declared, which is the same argument that later made Interop a trade show worth attending.
osinet.depth:
What it was. OSINET was two things with one name: a network, made of subnetworks, intermediate systems and end systems, and the organization that ran it. The general agreements document that the National Institute of Standards and Technology (NIST) published in August 1989 describes it as an international organization established in 1984 to foster the development, promotion and deployment of Open Systems Interconnection (OSI) through interoperation tests and testing; its members were potential users and potential suppliers of OSI products, industry user companies, government agencies and vendors, and although NIST, the former National Bureau of Standards (NBS), hosted it, the members governed it, through a Steering Committee that approved every project and a Technical Committee that did the technical work. It was not a standards body and it did not certify products in general; it was the place where products were made to talk to each other before customers tried.

Why it was needed. The same document states the problem without decoration. Open systems are those able to communicate with other open systems that adhere to the same base standards, yet because communications standards are necessarily complex there is no absolute assurance that implementations will interwork over the whole range of functions the standards specify. Interoperation testing between pairs of implementations gives some evidence that they can interwork, at least over the tests carried out, but no guarantee, and OSINET made no claim that its results were complete. The OSI standards also left implementers options, some of them incompatible, which is why NBS had hosted OSI Implementors Workshops four times a year since 1983 to agree on which options to use, as Request for Comments (RFC) 1169 records. Gerard Mulvenna, who was responsible for OSINET at NBS, told the historian James Pelkey that it arose in 1984 and 1985 when vendors meeting in one place were saying there had to be a better way of running interoperability testing of their products: they wanted to simulate the real environment their products would be sold into, and competitors cooperated because it was in their own interest.

The network. The backbone was X.25. In the implementation agreements revised in July 1987 it was provided by AT&T's ACCUNET and Wang's WANGPAC; by 1991 the providers were AT&T and US Sprint, and the messaging project also reached European public networks such as PSS and Transpac. An end system could attach to X.25 directly or sit on a local area network, carrier-sense multiple access with collision detection (CSMA/CD) or token bus, behind an intermediate system. So that every member could reach every other and the shared services, all end systems had to run a common stack from at least March 1986 to March 1989: the International Organization for Standardization (ISO) connectionless internetwork protocol (CLNP), ISO transport class 4 and the ISO session protocol's basic combined subset with full duplex, as specified in the NBS workshop agreements. The services planned on top were a bulletin board, a host name server, an application directory, a list of site contacts and the results of network management experiments. The costs of membership were the X.25 installation, monthly and traffic charges, with no fee beyond them.

Who was on it. The July 1987 agreements list 24 participating sites: the US Army, the Department of Agriculture, the Navy, the Defense Communications Agency and the Defense Logistics Agency; AT&T; Boeing Computer Services, General Motors and the MITRE Corporation; the computer makers Digital Equipment Corporation, Hewlett-Packard, Honeywell Bull, IBM, International Computers Limited (ICL), NCR, Sun Microsystems, Unisys and Wang; the protocol software houses Retix, Touch Communications and the Wollongong Group; Charles River Data Systems, TASC and NBS itself. The rules kept it a working network rather than a list of logos. A member had to put an operational end system or intermediate system on OSINET within six months of joining, had to attend three of the four most recent meetings of the Implementors' Workshop to stay eligible, and had one vote however large it was.

How the testing worked. Pelkey's history distinguishes two services. For conformance, NBS used a test gateway first built for the Autofact '85 manufacturing show: a vendor arranged its tests in advance, connected to the NBS gateway over ACCUNET at the agreed time and tested its implementation of the first four OSI layers, for X.25, token bus and CSMA/CD, so that NBS acted as the certifying body for those layers; File Transfer, Access and Management (FTAM) was tested separately. For interoperability, vendors arranged tests with each other, interconnected their products over OSINET and ran each other's tests, and a customer could require all its vendors to pass them. NBS also offered an application-layer gateway between the Department of Defense (DoD) protocols and OSI, for mail between the Simple Mail Transfer Protocol (SMTP) and X.400 and for file transfer between the File Transfer Protocol (FTP) and FTAM; Mulvenna described its purpose as helping the TCP/IP (Transmission Control Protocol/Internet Protocol) world work with OSI and pushing it, gently, in OSI's direction. By 1989 the approved projects were X.400 messaging, directory services, FTAM Phase II and testing of that gateway. The messaging project's stated goals included verifying that the X.400 profile agreed at the workshop was a complete and unambiguous specification for interoperation, and feeding back to the workshop where it was not: the testbed was also a way of debugging the agreements.

Registration and procurement. By 1989 OSINET had added testing and registration of announced products, meant to give some confidence beyond conformance testing that implementations could interwork. Testing parties agreed privately, voluntarily and bilaterally to run specific interoperation tests; successful results were filed as a supplier's declaration of interoperation (SDI) in the Network Registration Service, an online database at NIST, with supporting documents such as the protocol implementation conformance statement (PICS) and the test report; only suppliers could register, and the data were meant to be public and referenced in the procurement of open systems. By the August 1991 specification the Test and Registration service was owned by OSINET Corporation, listed products tested for interoperability with Message Handling System (MHS) and FTAM protocol suites against profiles such as US GOSIP (Government OSI Profile) Version 1 MHS, and ran on a Digital MicroVAX II under VAX/VMS 5.1 with an ORACLE version 6 database reachable by dial-up at 2,400 or 1,200 bit/s. The Corporation for Open Systems (COS) had become OSINET Corporation's secretariat, and the service's computer was to move from NIST to COS headquarters in August and September 1991.

The limits. OSINET started late: Pelkey records that its development fell behind because the people needed were reassigned to the Autofact '85 demonstration, and that NBS afterwards had to solicit resources from voluntary participants. Its testing covered a lot of protocol and very little market. The obvious barrier was the growing installed base of TCP/IP, since a customer already running working TCP/IP products had little reason to replace them, and customers wanted seven-layer interoperability tests, while NBS had said it would not do for layers five to seven what it did for the lower four. That gap is why NBS created COS and handed it rights to its test tools. None of this made OSI arrive sooner, and the protocols OSINET tested lost the protocol wars. The method did not lose: a shared network, agreed test suites, pairwise tests between competitors, published declarations of what actually interworked, and the explicit admission that passing a test proves only what the test covered.

cos-corporation.def: The Corporation for Open Systems (COS), later COS International: a non-profit consortium of mainly US computer and communications vendors, set up in 1985 and 1986 with test tools handed over by the National Bureau of Standards, to test Open Systems Interconnection (OSI) products and certify their conformance with a product mark known as the gold dot.
cos-corporation.context: When a standard is large enough that no two implementations agree, somebody has to say which ones count. The Corporation for Open Systems (COS) was the industry's attempt to be that somebody, funded by the vendors whose products it would judge. It produced real testing work and could not solve the underlying problem: the specification kept moving, and the market it was certifying for was being taken by protocols that had shipped. Its own staff found that a product could pass the conformance suite and still fail to talk to another vendor's, which is the distinction between conformance and interoperability in its plainest form.
cos-corporation.depth:
What it was. The Department of Defense, announcing its OSI policy in a memorandum of July 1987 published as Request for Comments (RFC) 1039, described the Corporation for Open Systems (COS) as a non-profit consortium formed to deal with testing and other operational issues relating to Open Systems Interconnection (OSI) protocols, and told the Defense Communications Agency to join it as the department's representative; at the request of the Office of Management and Budget, the armed services were not to join directly. A Datapro technology report of 1991 gives the fuller picture: a non-profit research and development consortium in McLean, Virginia, with an annual budget of 10 million dollars, whose mission was to open worldwide markets for OSI and, later, Integrated Services Digital Network (ISDN) products through certification, conformance test products and cooperation with other organizations. It was explicit that it was not in the business of reinventing standards; its job was to accelerate the use of existing ones by testing and certifying products against them.

Who created it. The accounts differ in emphasis, and both are probably right. Datapro says that in 1985 major US vendors, having concluded that cooperation among vendors and users would be critical to open standards, officially announced their support and formed COS. The historian James Pelkey tells it from the government side: the National Bureau of Standards (NBS) had built conformance tests for the lower four OSI layers and made clear it would not do the same for layers five to seven, so it created a non-profit body, COS, and transferred to it non-exclusive rights to its testing and gateway intellectual property and some related assets. Rosenthal, one of the NBS officials Pelkey interviewed, put the logic bluntly in 1988: the bureau had the test technology and the Reagan administration had a privatization mindset, so what better than to get COS out of it. The trade press greeted the announcement warmly in the first quarter of 1986, and on 14 May 1986 the consortium filed its notification under the National Cooperative Research Act, the law that limits antitrust damages for registered joint research ventures.

Members and money. By 1991 COS listed about 60 member companies, mostly information technology vendors such as Apple, AT&T, Digital Equipment, Hewlett-Packard, IBM, Intel, Sun Microsystems and Texas Instruments, plus software and local area network vendors, several federal agencies and a few large end users, and an affiliate programme of more than 40 universities and non-profit bodies. Regular and corporate research members paid 25,000 dollars a year; senior research members, with revenues above 150 million dollars, paid the same fee plus a research fee of 175,000 dollars, which is the 200,000 dollars in annual dues that members were already grumbling about in 1988. The contrast with the other camp was obvious to contemporaries: at the first Transmission Control Protocol/Internet Protocol (TCP/IP) Vendors Workshop in August 1986 vendors were disappointed that no certification and conformance testing process existed for TCP/IP at all, and in 1987 an Ungermann-Bass marketing manager, Barton Burstein, summed up the market as an OSI side with no product but a COS with a tremendous budget, against a TCP/IP side five or six times as populous with Dan Lynch and his answering machine. Lynch, who ran the TCP/IP workshops that became Interop, called his own vendor alliance the Coalition for Working Systems, a jab at COS that needed no explanation.

The gold dot, and how testing worked. The centre of COS's work was the COS Mark Licensing Program. The mark, informally the gold dot and developed with the help of Underwriters Laboratories, was meant as a seal of approval: impartial verification that an OSI or ISDN product conformed to the standards and would interoperate with other vendors' products. Because OSI contains many optional classes, subsets and parameters, products were tested against a COS Stack Specification, a fixed profile of OSI options, the same profiling idea that the Government OSI Profile (GOSIP) applied to federal buying. Tests were available at COS's own laboratory, through licences to third-party testing organizations and through licences to vendors to test themselves. Besides the OSI upper layers, the laboratory offered conformance testing of Institute of Electrical and Electronics Engineers (IEEE) 802.3 (CSMA/CD, carrier-sense multiple access with collision detection), 802.4 token bus at layers 1 and 2, X.25, the OSI internetwork protocol, File Transfer, Access and Management (FTAM) and the Message Handling System (MHS); testing cost 1,000 dollars a day, and test licences, including ten for the Manufacturing Automation Protocol (MAP) and its office counterpart, ran from 5,500 to 135,000 dollars per protocol.

The criticism. It came quickly. Pelkey lists COS turning down test tools Europeans had already developed and changing its membership rules repeatedly, and in June 1987 Data Communications reported that COS had chosen TCP/IP, not OSI, for its own internal network, because its computer vendor, Sun, did not yet support OSI; a COS researcher answered that it might look bad but they did plan to migrate. At the Enterprise Networking Event (ENE) in Baltimore on 5 to 9 June 1988, the OSI showcase COS sponsored with the MAP/TOP Users Group and the Society of Manufacturing Engineers, members complained that their dues were being wasted, that the group was poorly managed and that comprehensive conformance testing at the show would be delayed; the trade press wrote of the gulf between COS promises and COS deliveries. Pelkey's judgement is that COS became a convenient scapegoat for problems endemic to ten years of OSI: no products, eroding confidence and a habit of promising more than it delivered. Datapro in 1991 added that COS had failed to attract end-user members and was criticized as slow and not impartial, since its members could not always reconcile their business interests with open standards.

The view from the laboratory. Michael Grant, who built and ran the COS testing laboratory, described it on the Internet Society's internet-history list in May 2026. Vendors came in and set up their equipment; most failures to communicate turned out to be addressing problems, found by reading protocol traces. There was no OSI internet to connect to: no authority assigned globally unique X.400 mail addresses, so they were made up; transport class 0 ran over X.25 and class 4 over the connectionless network protocol, and nobody could say what happened when one end used each. COS staff communicated with vendors over Unix dial-up mail links and by fax, because management would not allow a dial-up internet connection for years. COS sold expensive OSI testers running on Sun hardware, yet even a product that passed the test suite could not talk to another implementation without a great deal of configuration; then the vendors started leaving the consortium and the layoffs began. It is one witness, and it says in practice what OSINET's own rules conceded in principle: a test between implementations gives some evidence that they interwork over the range tested, and no guarantee beyond it.

What became of it. COS adapted. By 1991 it was shifting from running a laboratory to providing a model for third-party testers, had brokered an industry consensus on National ISDN 1, and had become the secretariat of OSINET Corporation, with the OSINET Test and Registration service moved from the National Institute of Standards and Technology (NIST) to COS headquarters in August and September 1991. A Federal Register notice of June 1995 shows the Corporation for Open Systems International still filing as a joint research venture, with members including the General Services Administration and Hewlett-Packard leaving at the end of 1994, a COS SONET (synchronous optical network) Interoperability Forum, and a new group on digital video home terminals. The OSI mission had gone; the testing institution had found other standards to test.

interop.def: The trade show that began as a TCP/IP interoperability demonstration and became the industry's proving ground.
interop.context: Its founding idea was that vendors would connect their equipment to one live network on the show floor, in public, where failure was visible. That is a genuinely uncomfortable proposition for a vendor and it is why the event mattered: buyers could see interoperation rather than read about it. The show hall network became a standing demonstration that TCP/IP worked between competitors, which no specification and no consortium had managed to establish.

ene.def: Enterprise Network Event: the 1988 trade show positioned as the OSI counterpart to the TCP/IP demonstrations.
ene.context: Held as OSI's procurement mandates were at their most confident, it was intended to show enterprise buyers a coherent OSI ecosystem. What it showed instead, read with hindsight, is how much of that ecosystem was still described rather than shipped. The two 1988 shows are worth reading together: one demonstrated a working network between rivals, the other demonstrated an intention.

iccc-demonstration.def: The 1972 public demonstration of the ARPANET at the International Conference on Computer Communication.
iccc-demonstration.context: Before it, packet switching was a funded research result that most computing professionals had not seen work. The demonstration put terminals in a Washington hotel connected to hosts across the country, running real applications for anybody who walked up. It converted a paper technology into an observed one, and much of the commercial interest that followed traces to people who were in that room.

project-mac.def: The MIT time-sharing research project whose people and ideas seeded much of computer communications.
project-mac.context: Its subject was making one computer serve many users at once, which is not networking, and it produced a generation who then built networks. That is the pattern worth noticing: the interactive computing tradition trained people to think about resource sharing, contention and fairness, and those are the problems a network has. Reading the ARPANET's early personnel is largely reading a list of people who passed through time-sharing research first.

idcma.def: Independent Data Communications Manufacturers Association: the trade body for vendors competing with the carriers.
idcma.context: After the interconnect decisions there was an industry of companies selling equipment the telephone company had not built, and it needed a voice in proceedings that would decide whether it could keep doing so. IDCMA was that voice. It is a reminder that a market opened by a regulator stays open only while somebody argues for it, and that a great deal of the technical history in this period was settled in hearings rather than in laboratories.

channel-vendor.def: In the vocabulary of the technology supply chain, the company that makes the product (hardware, software or a cloud service) and owns its design, code, roadmap and support lifecycle, as distinct from the distributors, resellers, integrators and service providers that sell, install or operate it.
channel-vendor.context: Most of the industry's stories are vendor stories, because a vendor is where a thing gets built before anybody knows what it is for. The word does real work in a channel conversation: it identifies who owns the roadmap, who fixes the defect, and who cannot be routed around when something is broken at the product level rather than the configuration level. An engineer who says "escalate to the vendor" is naming a specific escalation destination, not a generic supplier.
channel-vendor.depth:
In channel vocabulary a vendor is the maker: the company whose name is on the product and whose engineers wrote its code, designed its hardware or run its service. F5, Cisco and Fortinet are vendors in this sense. Around the vendor sit the other roles of the supply chain: the distributor, which buys from vendors and sells to resellers rather than to end users; the reseller or integrator, which sells to and implements for the customer; the services company, which consults, operates or manages; the carrier, which moves traffic; the data centre operator, which houses equipment; and the training and standards bodies. A company can hold several roles at once, and many large ones do, but the vendor role is defined by ownership of the product, not by who sends the invoice.

General usage is looser, which is a frequent source of confusion. The glossary of the National Institute of Standards and Technology (NIST) defines a vendor simply as a commercial supplier of software or hardware, and its definition of supplier, taken from NIST Special Publication (SP) 800-53 Revision 5, deliberately includes developers and manufacturers, systems integrators, vendors, product resellers and third-party partners alike. Procurement departments follow that broad sense and call whoever bills them the vendor, which is how a reseller ends up in the vendor list of a purchasing system. The channel sense narrows the word to the manufacturer, sometimes called the OEM (original equipment manufacturer), and the distinction matters as soon as something goes wrong: the reseller can replace a box, but only the maker can change what the box does.

The clearest thing only a vendor can do is fix the product, and the vulnerability system is built around that. The CVE (Common Vulnerabilities and Exposures) Program's operational rules for CNAs (CVE Numbering Authorities), version 4.1.0, effective 14 May 2025, say that many CNAs are suppliers that assign CVE identifiers and publish records for vulnerabilities in products they own, develop or maintain, typically through a PSIRT (product security incident response team), with scopes written as narrowly as one supplier's products, or its supported and end-of-life products. Vendors also set the rhythm of disclosure. Fortinet's PSIRT policy, for example, describes a global team that receives, investigates and publicly reports vulnerabilities, scores them with CVSS (Common Vulnerability Scoring System) version 3.1, publishes advisories on the second Tuesday of each month, goes out of cycle for critical issues and earlier still under active exploitation, covers products that have not reached end-of-life, and runs no bug bounty. Whatever the reseller's contract says, the patch comes from the vendor's release.

The vendor also owns time. It decides how long each version is supported, and its calendar becomes its customers' upgrade plan. F5 announced on its DevCentral community in June 2025 that BIG-IP 16.1.x would reach End of Technical Support on 31 July 2025, pointing customers to its BIG-IP software support policy, article K5903, and noting that staying on supported software is what keeps both technical support and software development support. Fortinet's PSIRT scope stops at end-of-life in the same way. A version past its vendor's end of support is not merely old: no one is obliged to analyse a new defect in it or ship a fix, which is why lifecycle dates appear in audit findings and why an engineer reading a release note checks the support phase before the feature list.

Escalation runs to the vendor for the same reason. Partners and internal teams handle configuration; when the behaviour is wrong in the product itself, the case goes to the vendor's technical support organization, often called the TAC (technical assistance centre), where engineers can reproduce the issue, consult the developers and file the defect. That is why "escalate to the vendor" names a specific destination rather than a generic supplier, and why vendors gate that path behind support contracts and serial numbers: the right to have the maker look at a problem is part of what is sold.

Vendors rarely reach every customer directly; they build channels. F5's Unity+ Partner Program, for instance, has one track for value-added resellers, offering margins, priority access to product announcements and promotions, and technical training, and another for cloud services, through which hosted and managed service providers resell F5 capabilities under utility billing, bring-your-own-licence, subscription or volume licensing. The licensing model is itself a vendor decision, and so is the partner tier that determines which resellers can quote which products. Training follows the same line: the vendor writes the official curriculum and authorizes who may deliver it.

Regulation adds obligations that fall on the maker or its local representative. In Brazil, the national telecommunications agency Anatel (Agência Nacional de Telecomunicações) requires telecommunications products to carry a certificate of conformity issued by a designated certification body and to be homologated by Anatel before they are sold; its 2018 description of the model placed data communication equipment in category III, and recorded 6,843 homologation certificates issued in 2017. The regulation Anatel published on 25 October 2019 lists who may request conformity assessment and homologation: the manufacturer, the commercial representative of a foreign company, and any person or company for its own use. For a foreign vendor, a Brazilian representative is therefore part of the route to market, not an optional extra.

The word is also used against vendors. Vendor lock-in describes the cost of leaving a maker's proprietary features, formats or licences; vendor-neutral describes certifications, standards and advice that favour none of them; and supply-chain risk management treats each vendor as a party whose code, update channel and support lifetime have to be trusted. Each of these uses rests on the same definition: the vendor is the one party in the chain that controls what the product is, and so the one whose decisions everyone downstream inherits.

channel-distributor.def: A company that buys from technology vendors and sells to resellers, integrators and service providers rather than to the organizations that use the equipment: the middle tier of two-tier distribution.
channel-distributor.context: Invisible to most engineers and decisive for what they can actually buy. A distributor decides which products it will stock, finance and support in a given country, and a vendor's line card is theoretical until somebody local carries it. In markets with currency controls, import duty and long lead times, that decision is the difference between a product existing and a product being available. Distributors also run the credit: the reseller who installed your firewall was very likely financed by one.
channel-distributor.depth:
In the two-tier model the vendor sells to a small number of distributors, the distributors sell to resellers, integrators and service providers, and those sell to the organizations that run the equipment. Fortinet's annual report for 2025 describes its own business in exactly those terms: it primarily sells through a two-tier distribution model, to distributors that sell to resellers, to service providers and to MSSPs (managed security service providers), and sells directly only in certain cases, to large service providers, major systems integrators and large end users. A distributor is therefore not the vendor, which owns the roadmap and fixes the code, and not the reseller, which holds the relationship with the customer and does the installation. It is the wholesaler between them, and in many countries the vendor's commercial relationship runs through the distributor rather than through the reseller whose logo is on the proposal.

The model did not end with hardware in boxes. Microsoft's CSP (Cloud Solution Provider) programme has the same two tiers for cloud subscriptions. A direct-bill partner buys from Microsoft and must sell to, bill, manage and support its customers on its own, which requires its own sales, billing and support infrastructure; an indirect reseller instead buys from a distributor, which collaborates with it on marketing, customer support and billing. Microsoft's documentation, last updated in May 2026, now calls these firms distributors, having formerly called them indirect providers. Whether the product is a chassis or a licence key, the distributor's job is the same: carry the vendor's catalogue, the paperwork and the risk for resellers too small to carry them alone.

What that job contains shows in the annual report of a broadline distributor. TD SYNNEX, for its fiscal year ended 30 November 2025, describes itself as a global distributor and solutions aggregator with an active base of more than 150,000 reseller customers, products from about 2,500 OEMs (original equipment manufacturers) and 168 distribution and administrative facilities. Its services include outsourced fulfilment, configure-to-order assembly, marketing on behalf of vendors, pre-sales and post-sales technical support, and financing. The financing is the part engineers rarely see: customers generally pay 30 days after the invoice and some get longer terms, and some resellers buy under third-party floor plan financing whose cost is subsidized by the vendor or paid by the distributor. A reseller that wins a project larger than its balance sheet can still deliver it, because somebody else carries the receivable.

The distributor also carries inventory, and the contracts with vendors are built around that risk. TD SYNNEX reports that many suppliers give it limited protection against a fall in the value of stock caused by a supplier's price cut (price protection), the right to return slow-moving stock (stock rotation), and rebates and discounts for volume and early payment. The vendor side shows the same arrangement from the other end: Fortinet's report says it may permit distributors and resellers to return products in limited circumstances, offers extended payment terms to certain distributors, and lists as a risk that channel partners may buy more inventory than they can sell. For an engineer the practical consequence is lead time. A part the local distributor holds can ship this week; a part it does not stock has to be ordered from the vendor, imported and cleared, and the project plan has to absorb the difference.

The tier is small and concentrated. Fortinet names Arrow Electronics, Exclusive, Ingram Micro and TD Synnex among its distributors, and its segment note shows three distributors accounting for 28, 15 and 12 per cent of its revenue in 2025, 55 per cent between them, with one distributor holding 32 per cent of its net accounts receivable at the end of the year. F5's report for its fiscal year ended 30 September 2025 states that two worldwide distributors accounted for 33.3 per cent of its total net revenue. Read from the vendor's side, a handful of wholesalers stand between it and most of its customers; read from the market's side, a vendor that loses its distributor in a country effectively leaves that country until another one signs.

Distributors differ in how much engineering they add, and the industry distinguishes broadline houses, which move thousands of vendors' products at volume, from value-added distributors (VADs), which carry fewer lines and add design, integration and training. Arrow's Global ECS (Enterprise Computing Solutions) segment, about 30 per cent of Arrow's 2025 sales, calls itself a value-added provider and offers its customers engineering and integration support, warehousing and logistics, marketing resources and authorized hardware and software training. Exclusive Networks, founded in Paris in 2003, describes itself as a cybersecurity go-to-market specialist with more than 320 vendors, more than 20,000 reseller partners and offices in over 50 countries, and lists pre-sales consulting and solution design, financing, logistics, training and certification and technical support among its services, with one technical engineer for every three salespeople. Those engineers are the reason a small reseller can quote a large security project: the bill of materials, the proof of concept and the first enablement course often come from the distributor rather than from the reseller or the vendor.

Brazil shows why the context matters. The census of Abradisti, the Brazilian association of information technology distributors, put the country's ICT (information and communications technology) distribution business at R$ 30.7 billion in 2025, 7 per cent up on the year before, and noted that interest rates near 14.5 per cent make credit and working capital more expensive, which is precisely the cost a distributor carries on behalf of its resellers. The same census series attributed part of the resellers' 10.7 per cent revenue growth in 2024 to an 11.3 per cent rise in the dollar, which directly moves the price of hardware, software and telecommunications equipment, and recorded a 10 per cent fall in 2023 when public-sector spending, about a fifth of the market, dropped. A distributor that imports in dollars and sells on credit in reais is exposed to both rates at once, which is why its credit limits and its stocking decisions shape what local customers can buy.

For the engineer the tier shows up at predictable moments. Part numbers, licence SKUs (stock keeping units) and support contracts on a quote are usually priced from a distributor's catalogue; a product announced by the vendor may not yet be orderable locally because no distributor has listed it; a return of faulty hardware under an RMA (return merchandise authorization) may travel back through the same chain; and the technical help a reseller cannot give may come from the distributor's engineers before anyone opens a case with the vendor's TAC (Technical Assistance Center). None of this appears in a datasheet, but it decides how fast a design becomes an installed system.

channel-reseller.def: The company that sells and installs somebody else's products for the organization that will run them; also called a value-added reseller or integrator.
channel-reseller.context: Their skill is not the products: it is making a portfolio assembled for commercial reasons behave like a system. A reseller arrives at an estate somebody else designed, with vendors who each assume they are the only one present, and has to produce something coherent from parts that were never tested together. That is a real discipline and it is largely undocumented, because every vendor's material describes a world containing only that vendor.
channel-reseller.depth:
Where it sits. In the channel vocabulary the reseller, or integrator, is the company that sells to and implements for the end user, between the distributor, which buys from the vendor and sells to resellers, and the organization that will run the equipment. Fortinet's annual report for 2025 describes the arrangement from the vendor's side: it primarily sells through a two-tier distribution model, in which distributors sell to resellers, service providers and managed security service providers (MSSPs), which in turn sell to end customers, and it sells directly only in certain cases, to large service providers, major systems integrators and large end users. The same report says that substantially all of its revenue comes from sales by channel partners, distributors and resellers included. For most buyers, then, the reseller is the only company in the chain they ever deal with: it writes the proposal, signs the contract and sends the engineers.

What the names mean. Value-added reseller (VAR), integrator and systems integrator overlap in use. The glossary of the United States National Institute of Standards and Technology (NIST) lists systems integrators, vendors and product resellers together as suppliers, organizations that agree with an acquirer to supply a product or service, and defines a system integrator by its customized services: development, testing, operations and maintenance done for the buyer. The value in value-added is that work. A box shifter that only resells is a different business, and Brazil's census of resellers shows how different. The survey of 1,360 resellers by Abradisti, the association of information technology distributors, separates value-added resellers, volume resellers, online stores, commercial representatives and retail automation specialists; in 2024, when the resellers' revenue grew 10.7 per cent overall, value-added resellers grew 14.7 per cent and volume resellers 5.1 per cent. The census also attributed part of that growth to an 11.3 per cent rise in the dollar, which moves the price of hardware, software and telecommunications equipment directly, recorded a 10 per cent fall in 2023 when public spending dropped, and put the public sector at about a fifth of the market.

What a vendor gives a reseller, and expects back. Partner programmes formalize the relationship. F5's Unity+ Partner Program for value-added resellers offers increased margins on F5 products, priority access to product announcements, promotions and technical training, qualified leads, dedicated partner resources and joint marketing funds, beside a separate programme for cloud service providers. The tiers in such programmes are tied to trained and certified staff, which is how a vendor makes sure the company installing its product can configure it. In cloud subscriptions Microsoft draws the line by who supports the customer. Under its Cloud Solution Provider programme an indirect reseller buys from a distributor that collaborates with it on marketing, customer support and billing, while a direct-bill partner buys from Microsoft and must sell to, bill, manage and support its customers on its own, a status open only after at least 12 months as an indirect reseller and USD one million in trailing twelve-month revenue. The commercial tier decides who answers the telephone.

What integration actually is. The context of this role is that no vendor documents the estate the customer actually has. Each vendor's material describes its product alone, and the reseller's engineers are the ones who make a firewall from one vendor, a load balancer from another, a switching fabric from a third and an identity provider from a fourth agree on addressing, routing, authentication, logging and failure behaviour. The reseller sizes the solution, often runs the proof of concept, stages and installs, migrates the old configuration, writes the as-built documentation and takes the first support call. Small resellers lean on their distributor's systems engineers for sizing and design, and on the vendor's technical assistance centre (TAC) once a defect is in the product rather than the configuration. The value a good integrator adds is mostly knowledge of how products from different vendors behave together, which is the knowledge no single vendor has an incentive to write down.

What the vendor worries about. A vendor that reaches customers through resellers carries their conduct. Fortinet lists as a risk that it could face liability if channel partners misrepresent the functionality of its products to end customers, says it depends on its partners worldwide to comply with legal and regulatory requirements, and screens partners and suppliers as part of its anti-corruption programme. For the buyer the same dependence runs the other way: the warranty, the support contract and the software licence normally reach the customer through the authorized chain, which is why serial numbers and contract entitlements are checked before a support case is accepted and why a product bought outside that chain may arrive without any of them.

Why the authorized channel matters. The counterfeit Cisco case prosecuted in New Jersey shows what sits outside it. A company owner was sentenced on 1 May 2024 to 78 months in prison and ordered to pay USD 100 million in restitution to Cisco for a scheme in which older, lower-model devices were modified to look like new, higher-end Cisco products, with counterfeit labels, packaging and documentation, and sold through about 15 Amazon and at least 10 eBay storefronts run by at least 19 companies. The network took in more than USD 100 million, and its devices turned up in hospitals, schools, government agencies and military platforms supporting fighter aircraft. For a network engineer the lesson is concrete: a switch bought from an unauthorized seller is a supply-chain risk before it is a cost saving, and the reseller's authorization is part of the bill of materials.

What it means for the engineer. The reseller is usually the counterparty on the purchase order and the first line on the support contract, so renewals, returns under an RMA (return merchandise authorization) and the escalation path often run through it before they reach the vendor. Its project team may be the only people who know why a configuration looks the way it does. When the reseller changes, the documentation it leaves behind is the estate's memory. The numbers worth remembering: two tiers between vendor and user; substantially all of Fortinet's revenue through channel partners; 12 months and USD one million for a Microsoft direct-bill partner; 1,360 resellers in Brazil's census and 14.7 per cent growth for its value-added segment in 2024; and 78 months for trafficking counterfeit Cisco equipment.

channel-services.def: A company that sells people and process rather than product: consulting, outsourcing, managed operations.
channel-services.context: Harder to explain to a market and harder to scale than a product business, because the thing being sold is judgement and judgement does not have a bill of materials. The commercial shape matters operationally: a managed-services contract moves the pager, and whoever holds the pager ends up owning decisions the contract never mentioned. Reading a services agreement as a technical document (what is monitored, what may be changed without asking, who declares an incident) explains more about how an estate behaves than most architecture diagrams.

channel-carrier.def: An operator that carries somebody else's traffic over its own or leased transmission facilities: the regulated layer of cables, radio, rights of way and interconnection that everything above it assumes.
channel-carrier.context: Enterprise networking treats the carrier as a line on a diagram, which is why carrier problems are so disorienting when they arrive: the abstraction was doing a great deal of work. Underneath it are rights of way, conduit, undersea cable, regulated interconnection and a completely different commercial clock, in which circuits are provisioned in weeks, not minutes. Several of the oldest entries in this field's history are really about who was permitted to lay cable where, or to attach what to whose line, which are legal questions that determined technical topologies.
channel-carrier.depth:
In channel vocabulary a carrier is the telecommunications operator: the company that moves traffic it did not originate, between points its customers choose, over facilities it builds, licenses or leases. It sits beside the other roles of the supply chain (the vendor that makes the equipment, the distributor and reseller that sell it, the services company that runs it, the data centre operator that houses it) and many large firms combine it with them; a carrier that also runs colocation and managed services is common. What defines the role is the transport itself, and the law in most countries defines it with some care, because carriers have been regulated longer than any other part of the industry.

United States law gives the classic formulation. Title 47 of the United States Code, section 153, defines a common carrier, or simply a carrier, as any person engaged as a common carrier for hire in interstate or foreign communication by wire or radio, and excludes broadcasters from the term while they broadcast. Its definition of telecommunications captures the essence of the job: transmission, between or among points specified by the user, of information of the user's choosing, without change in the form or content of the information as sent and received. A telecommunications carrier is a provider of telecommunications services, offered for a fee directly to the public regardless of the facilities used, and is treated as a common carrier only to the extent that it provides them. The International Telecommunication Union (ITU) uses the older word operator: its Constitution defines an operating agency as any individual, company, corporation or governmental agency operating a telecommunication installation intended for an international service, and a recognized operating agency as one that runs a public correspondence or broadcasting service and carries the obligations its member state imposes under the treaty.

Brazil's General Telecommunications Law, Lei 9.472 of 16 July 1997, draws the same line in its own terms. Article 60 defines a telecommunications service as the set of activities that makes the offer of telecommunication possible, and telecommunication as the transmission, emission or reception, by wire, radio, optical means or any other electromagnetic process, of symbols, characters, signals, writing, images, sounds or information of any nature. Article 61 then defines the value-added service, which adds new utilities to a telecommunications service that supports it, and states that it is not a telecommunications service: its provider is a user of the supporting service, with that user's rights and duties. The distinction between the carrier and the service that rides on it is therefore written into the law. Article 63 splits telecommunications services into a public regime, provided under concession or permission with obligations of universal service and continuity, and a private regime. The law also created the regulator, Anatel (Agência Nacional de Telecomunicações), and opened the way for the privatization of the state Telebrás System, sold on 29 July 1998 in 12 consecutive auctions at the Rio de Janeiro stock exchange, three fixed-line holdings, one long-distance holding (Embratel) and eight cellular holdings, for R$ 22 billion according to BNDES (the Brazilian Development Bank), which ran the sale.

The physical side of carrying is mostly a matter of permission. Article 73 of the Brazilian law gives providers of collective-interest telecommunications services the right to use the poles, ducts, conduits and easements owned or controlled by other telecommunications or public utility providers, on non-discriminatory terms and at fair and reasonable prices, because a network that cannot reach a building does not exist. Article 146 treats networks as integrated routes of free circulation: interconnection between them is mandatory, their integrated operation must be assured nationally and internationally, and the right of property over a network is conditioned on its social function. Interconnection is defined as the link between functionally compatible networks that lets the users of one communicate with the users of another, which is the legal form of what engineers call peering, transit and termination.

The boundary between carrier and customer has a history of its own. In the United States the telephone companies' tariffs long forbade subscribers to attach their own interconnecting devices to the lines. On 26 June 1968 the Federal Communications Commission (FCC) decided the Carterfone case: Thomas Carter's device, which coupled a two-way radio base station to a telephone handset and had been made since 1959, with about 4,500 produced and 3,500 sold by 1966, had been banned under tariff FCC No. 132 of AT&T (American Telephone and Telegraph). The Commission held the tariff unreasonable, discriminatory and unlawful because it prohibited interconnecting devices that do not adversely affect the telephone system, applying the earlier Hush-A-Phone principle that a subscriber may use the telephone in ways that are privately beneficial without being publicly detrimental. Data networking inherited the boundary in the ITU-T (ITU Telecommunication Standardization Sector) Recommendation X.25, the interface between data terminal equipment (DTE) and data circuit-terminating equipment (DCE) for terminals connected to public data networks by dedicated circuit; the DCE side faces the carrier's network, the DTE is the customer's, and that demarcation survives in every network termination point and customer premises equipment contract.

Much of the substrate is not on land. TeleGeography tracks more than 600 active and planned submarine cables as of 2026, with over 1.5 million km in service. They were traditionally owned by consortia of carriers, private cables arrived in the late 1990s, and the largest new investors are now content providers such as Google, Meta, Microsoft and Amazon, whose deployed capacity has outpaced that of internet backbone operators. Satellites account for 0.37 per cent of United States international capacity, by FCC figures TeleGeography cites. Cables fail about 200 times a year, two thirds of the time because of fishing gear and anchors, and are designed for a minimum life of 25 years, which is why carriers and their large customers spread capacity across several cables rather than trusting one.

The commercial clock is different from the one engineers working in software expect. A circuit involves a site survey, physical work, a cross-connect in somebody's building and paperwork between companies, and the cloud providers' own documentation reflects that clock. For a dedicated port of its Direct Connect service, Amazon Web Services (AWS) issues a Letter of Authorization and Connecting Facility Assignment (LOA-CFA), which the customer's network provider needs in order to order the cross connect; a request for more information must be answered within 7 days or the connection is deleted; and billing starts when the port comes up or 90 days after the letter is issued, whichever comes first. The virtual interface on top can be configured in minutes; the fibre under it cannot.

For the engineer the practical lessons follow from those facts. Two circuits from two carriers may share a duct, a pole route or a landing station, so diversity has to be checked on the route maps, not assumed from the invoices. The demarcation point decides who troubleshoots what, and a service level agreement describes a refund, not an outcome. And because carriers are licensed and few, they are the layer through which states act on the network, from interconnection rules to orders to restrict service, which is why a carrier problem so often turns out to be a legal or commercial problem wearing a technical symptom.

channel-datacentre.def: Colocation, hosting and interconnection: the businesses that own the places where networks physically meet.
channel-datacentre.context: A property business with network effects, which is a stranger combination than it sounds. The value of a facility is not its floor space but who else is already inside it, because a cross-connect to a network in the same building is cheaper, faster and more reliable than reaching it any other way. That is why a small number of buildings carry a wildly disproportionate share of a region's traffic, and why an outage in one of them is a news event rather than a customer incident.

channel-training.def: The companies and bodies that decide what competence looks like in a technology and who may claim it.
channel-training.context: An authorized centre is the layer most vendor documentation never mentions, and it is what closes the distance between a certification existing and an engineer being able to get it. A course that runs only in English, only across a currency barrier and only in another time zone is a course most local engineers will not take. The certification also does commercial work nobody discusses openly: partner tiers are gated on how many certified staff a company employs, so training is a purchasing requirement dressed as an educational one.

channel-standards.def: In the vocabulary of the technology supply chain, an organization whose output is an agreement rather than a product: the standards bodies, consortia, industry associations, laboratories and foundations that write specifications, test conformance or certify interoperability, and on which the vendors' products are built.
channel-standards.context: A standard is an agreement about what two implementations owe each other, and the interesting question is always who is in the room. Bodies funded by the vendors they regulate produce different specifications from bodies funded by governments or by nobody, and the Open Systems Interconnection (OSI) period is the clearest demonstration: enormous institutional weight, conformance testing, procurement mandates, and a competing stack that shipped. Conformance to a specification and interoperation with another vendor's product are different properties, and the gap between them is where standards bodies earn or lose their authority.
channel-standards.depth:
What the word covers. In the channel vocabulary that sorts the industry into vendors, distributors, resellers, services companies, carriers, data centre operators, training organizations and media, the standards body is the one that sells no box. Its output is a document, a test or a mark, and the category is wider than the formal standards organizations. It runs from treaty bodies through national standards institutes, professional societies and open engineering communities to industry consortia that exist to certify one technology, and it includes the government laboratories and research centres that wrote or tested specifications. Many organizations hold this role beside another one, which is why a research institute or a vendor can appear in the category too: the role is defined by producing agreements other people build on, not by being incapable of selling anything.

Who is in the room. Membership decides what a body is. The International Telecommunication Union (ITU), established in 1865 to manage the first international telegraph networks, is a United Nations specialized agency whose members are 194 states, with more than 1,000 companies, universities and international and regional organizations alongside them. The International Organization for Standardization (ISO) and the International Electrotechnical Commission (IEC) federate national standards bodies, and Brazil's is a good example of what those are: the Associação Brasileira de Normas Técnicas (ABNT), founded on 28 September 1940, is a private non-profit entity recognized by the federal government as the national standardization forum, a founding member of ISO and a member of the IEC since its foundation, and it publishes the Brazilian standards known as ABNT NBR (Norma Brasileira).
