The IEEE Standards Association (IEEE SA), under which the IEEE 802 standards committee for local and metropolitan area networks (LAN/MAN) maintains the Ethernet (802.3) and wireless local area network (802.11) standards through an open and accredited process, describes itself as a consensus-building organization of individuals and organizations with collaborators in more than 160 countries. The Internet Engineering Task Force (IETF) has no voting members at all. Industry consortia have member companies: the Wi-Fi Alliance began in 1999, when six companies formed the Wireless Ethernet Compatibility Alliance to make wireless LAN (local area network) products interoperate, and took its present name in 2000, the year the term Wi-Fi was introduced and the first Wi-Fi CERTIFIED products were announced.

How a decision is made. The IETF is the clearest case of process as product. RFC (Request for Comments) 7282 says the IETF is not supposed to be run by majority rule; working groups hum rather than vote, and rough consensus is reached when every objection has been addressed, though not necessarily accommodated, so that the absence of sustained disagreement matters more than the number in favour. What it calls an Internet Standard has a demanding definition in RFC 2026 of October 1996: a specification that is stable and well understood, technically competent, with multiple, independent and interoperable implementations and substantial operational experience, significant public support, and recognizable usefulness. RFC 6410 of October 2011 cut the ladder from three maturity levels to two, Proposed Standard and Internet Standard, because the middle step, Draft Standard, had stopped meaning anything, and dropped the annual review of documents stuck below the top. A working draft that is not advanced simply expires after six months. The definition puts running code into the meaning of the word standard, and that is a choice other bodies did not make.

Conformance is not interoperability. The National Bureau of Standards, later the National Institute of Standards and Technology (NIST), hosted OSINET to test Open Systems Interconnection (OSI) products, and its 1989 general agreement said plainly that interoperation testing between pairs of implementations gives some evidence that they can interwork over the tests carried out, but no guarantee of general interworking. The vendor consortium that ran OSI conformance testing in the United States, the Corporation for Open Systems (COS), found the same thing from the inside. Michael Grant, who built and ran its testing lab, recalled on the Internet Society's history list in May 2026 that even when an implementation passed the test suite it could not talk to another without a great deal of configuration, that there was no OSI internet to connect to, and that vendors eventually left the consortium. A certification mark that is earned by testing products against each other, as the Wi-Fi Alliance's is, answers a different question from a conformance certificate earned against a test suite.

Authority without implementations. The OSI period also shows the limits of a mandate. The United States Government OSI Profile (GOSIP) was published in August 1988, adopted as Federal Information Processing Standard (FIPS) 146 in February 1989 and made a federal procurement requirement from August 1990; RFC 1169, the Internet Activities Board's official view written by Vint Cerf and NIST's Kevin Mills, stressed that it was a procurement specification with waiver procedures, not an order to abandon TCP/IP. On 15 May 1995 NIST published the approval of FIPS 146-2, which removed the requirement that agencies specify GOSIP protocols at all and pointed them to open, voluntary standards from the IETF, the ITU's telecommunication sector and ISO. Seven years of procurement weight had not produced a network people used; the stack with interoperable implementations had.

Why it matters to an engineer. A datasheet's list of RFC numbers and IEEE clauses is the vendor's own claim of conformance; a certification mark is a third party's statement that a product passed a defined test; and neither says that two products from different vendors will work together in a particular network. The standards body behind each reference also explains what the reference is worth. An IETF Proposed Standard may still change; an Internet Standard has interoperable implementations by definition; an ITU-T (ITU Telecommunication Standardization Sector) Recommendation was agreed among member states and sector members; an ABNT NBR may be referenced by Brazilian regulation and procurement. Knowing who wrote a specification, and how they decided, tells you how much testing it has already had.

Where it sits among the other roles. The vendor owns a product's code and roadmap; the distributor carries stock, credit and logistics; the reseller or integrator installs; the training organization teaches; the standards body defines the agreements all of them depend on. The roles overlap in practice, because vendors staff the working groups, distributors and resellers run interoperability labs for their customers and certification bodies sell training, but the distinction holds where it matters: a standards body's authority comes from being trusted by competitors, and it lasts only as long as its specifications describe products that actually interoperate. The numbers worth remembering: 1865 for the ITU, 1940 for ABNT, 1999 and 2000 for the Wi-Fi Alliance, RFC 2026 and RFC 6410 for the IETF's two maturity levels, and August 1990 and May 1995, the start and the end of the GOSIP mandate.

firmware.def: Code stored in a chip of a device and run from its processor's reset vector, or as an extension of other firmware.
firmware.context: Firmware is the set of instructions a device's own processor runs, like any program; what sets it apart is where it runs and how it fails. Boot firmware runs first at power-on and loads the operating system, a new image often takes effect only after a reset, and a corrupted one can leave a server or switch unable to boot at all.
firmware.depth:
What the word means. NIST (National Institute of Standards and Technology) Special Publication (SP) 800-193, the Platform Firmware Resiliency Guidelines of May 2018, defines firmware as code in a chip that sits at its processor's reset vector or extends other firmware, such as expansion ROMs (read-only memories). The older definition, which the NIST glossary carries from RFC (Request for Comments) 4949, stresses where it lives: programs and data stored in hardware, typically ROM or PROM (programmable read-only memory), such that they cannot be dynamically written or modified during execution, whereas software can. The word itself is usually traced to Ascher Opler's article Fourth-Generation Software in Datamation in January 1967, which the Oxford English Dictionary treats as the first citation: he proposed it for microprograms resident in a computer's control memory that specialize its logic, for example to emulate another machine. Flash memory has since made firmware rewritable in the field, which is exactly why its integrity became a security subject.

Where it runs. A platform holds many firmware-bearing devices: besides the boot firmware, storage and network controllers, graphics processors and service processors carry their own. SP 800-193 singles out the BMC (Baseboard Management Controller) on servers and the ME (Management Engine) on clients, out-of-band management devices that let administrators manage a machine without its operating system running, which is why their firmware must not weaken the host's integrity. NIST SP 800-147 (April 2011) calls the system BIOS (Basic Input/Output System) the first software the main CPU (central processing unit) runs at power-on: it initializes and tests the hardware, may load CPU microcode patches and loads the operating system. UEFI (Unified Extensible Firmware Interface) 2.10, released in August 2022, specifies the interface between that firmware and the OS (operating system) loader; the UEFI Forum's current version is 2.11, released in December 2024.

How it is updated. Firmware used to be rarely changed in the field; SP 800-193 notes that updates grew more common with its complexity, and asks that only authentic, authorized images be applied. A Root of Trust for Update checks each image's digital signature against its key store, and a version check can refuse a rollback to older firmware with known vulnerabilities, with a deliberate rollback perhaps requiring a physically present user. The guideline names three logical roots, for update, detection and recovery, which may share components. UEFI's Firmware Management Protocol reports each image's LowestSupportedImageVersion, the floor below which it will not go, and flags images that need a device reset before they take effect.

Secure Boot and its keys. UEFI Secure Boot extends the signature check from the firmware to everything it loads. The UEFI 2.11 specification builds it on keys: a Platform Key establishes trust between the platform owner and the firmware, Key Exchange Keys establish trust between each operating system and the firmware, and an authorized and a forbidden signature database (db and dbx) decide which images may run. While no Platform Key is enrolled the platform is in setup mode and the keys and databases can be changed without authentication. The chain is only as strong as its keys. In PKfail, reported by Binarly in July 2024 and documented by CERT/CC as VU#455367, test Platform Keys, often labelled DO NOT TRUST and meant only for development, were found in production firmware from many vendors; anyone holding such a private key can sign modules that run during boot with Secure Boot enabled, and CERT/CC notes that UEFI firmware is largely invisible to EDR (endpoint detection and response) tools.

What attacks look like. In September 2018 ESET reported LoJax, the first UEFI rootkit found in the wild, used by the Sednit group: it wrote a malicious UEFI module into the SPI (Serial Peripheral Interface) flash chip that holds the firmware, so it survived both an operating system reinstall and a hard disk replacement, and removing it meant re-flashing the firmware; ESET later corrected its advice to say that Secure Boot would not have stopped it. In March 2023 ESET's Martin Smolár analysed BlackLotus, sold on hacking forums for 5,000 dollars, the first publicly known UEFI bootkit able to bypass Secure Boot on fully patched Windows 11. It exploited CVE-2022-21894, fixed in January 2022, which still worked because the vulnerable but validly signed boot binaries had not been added to the dbx revocation list.

Why failure is so expensive. SP 800-193 warns that an attack on platform firmware can render a system inoperable, perhaps permanently or until the manufacturer reprograms it, and that losing one device that is crucial to booting can stop the whole platform. It therefore asks for protection, detection and recovery together. Recovery comes in two forms: manual, where someone physically present during boot writes a known good image, and automatic, from a backup image kept apart from the corrupted one, for example in a second flash chip or a protected region of storage. A device with neither is one bad flash away from a return to the factory.

On network devices. Network vendors use the word firmware for the whole operating system image, and the same principles apply. Fortinet signs FortiOS firmware images, and its antivirus and IPS (intrusion prevention system) engine files, with both its own CA (certificate authority) and a third-party CA; at the High BIOS security level a FortiGate accepts only certified images, at Low it warns but installs, and at boot the BIOS checks secure hashes before the kernel loads and halts with a system integrity failure if a protected file has been altered. Cisco's account of SYNful Knock, published on 8 October 2015, shows why that matters: attackers implanted modified Cisco IOS images on routers, not through a vulnerability but with compromised administrative credentials or physical access. Cisco's answer was SHA-512 (Secure Hash Algorithm) hashes for its images, reinstallation of a known-good image verified against its hash, and trust anchors with secure boot that reject unsigned modifications. Verifying an image's published hash before installing it is the cheapest firmware control there is.

fw-vs-sw.def: The distinction a vendor draws between code that is part of the device and code that runs on top of it - and the reason it decides who fixes your problem.
fw-vs-sw.context: The line moves by vendor and it is rarely technical. On a network appliance the whole operating system is often called firmware; on a server the same layer would be an OS, and the firmware would be the BIOS and the controllers beneath it. What makes the distinction worth knowing is commercial and procedural: firmware and software frequently have different support lifecycles, different release cadences, different licences and different escalation paths inside the vendor. An engineer who says “that is a firmware issue” is often making a routing decision about which team owns it, not a claim about where the bug lives.

microcode.def: A layer inside a processor that implements its published instruction set in terms of simpler internal operations.
microcode.context: It is the reason a processor's behaviour can change without the silicon changing. An instruction a program issues is not necessarily executed directly by hardware; on many processors it is decoded into a sequence of internal steps the chip's designers can revise after manufacture. That became widely visible when speculative-execution vulnerabilities were mitigated partly by microcode updates - patches that alter what a processor does, shipped through firmware, for a defect in something most people think of as fixed at the foundry.

asic.def: Application-Specific Integrated Circuit: a chip built to do one job, fast, and incapable of being repurposed.
asic.context: In networking it is the reason a switch forwards at line rate while a general-purpose processor cannot. The trade is stark and worth stating: an ASIC is dramatically faster and cheaper per port than software forwarding, and it is fixed at manufacture - a feature the silicon does not implement is a feature the box will never have, whatever the release notes say. That is why “supported in software but not in hardware” has real operational consequences: the same feature can mean line rate on one platform and a punt to the control-plane processor on another.

fpga.def: Field-Programmable Gate Array: a chip whose logic can be rewired after it is manufactured.
fpga.context: It occupies the space between a general-purpose processor and an ASIC: slower and more expensive per unit than fixed silicon, far faster than software for the right problem, and - crucially - changeable. Vendors use them to ship hardware before a protocol is finished, to serve markets too small to justify a custom chip, and to fix in the field what would otherwise need a silicon respin. When a release note says a feature now runs in hardware on a platform that previously punted it to the processor, an FPGA is often what changed.

embedded-system.def: A computer built into something that is not thought of as a computer, with a fixed job and usually nobody watching it.
embedded-system.context: Almost every device on a network is one: the switch, the access point, the power distribution unit, the camera, the building's air handling. What makes them an operational category rather than a hardware one is the assumptions they carry - long service lives, patching that requires an outage, credentials that were set once, and vendors who may not exist by the time a vulnerability is published. An estate's real attack surface is usually not the servers somebody maintains; it is the several hundred small computers nobody has logged into since installation.

dot.def: Domain Name System (DNS) queries and responses carried inside Transport Layer Security (TLS) over TCP (Transmission Control Protocol) on a dedicated port, 853: DNS over TLS (DoT), specified in Request for Comments (RFC) 7858 in May 2016.
dot.context: Domain Name System (DNS) over Transport Layer Security (TLS), or DoT, encrypts the same leg as DNS over HTTPS (DoH, HTTPS being Hypertext Transfer Protocol Secure): the hop between a device's stub resolver and its recursive resolver, protected by the same TLS. What differs is visibility. DoT keeps the classic DNS wire format and runs it on a port of its own, 853, so a network that looks can see that the traffic is DNS without decrypting it, and can block it, redirect it or permit it deliberately, as a matter of policy rather than of parsing; DoH travels on port 443 among ordinary web traffic. Neither hides the query from the resolver that answers it, and neither proves an answer genuine, which remains the job of DNSSEC (the DNS Security Extensions).
dot.depth:
What it is. Running the Domain Name System (DNS) over Transport Layer Security (TLS), DNS over TLS (DoT) is defined by Request for Comments (RFC) 7858, published in May 2016 on the Internet Engineering Task Force (IETF) Standards Track and still a Proposed Standard, by Zi Hu, Liang Zhu and John Heidemann of the University of Southern California Information Sciences Institute (USC/ISI), Allison Mankin, Duane Wessels of Verisign Labs and Paul Hoffman of ICANN (the Internet Corporation for Assigned Names and Numbers). Its purpose is to remove the eavesdropping and on-path tampering described in RFC 7626, a privacy analysis since replaced by RFC 9076 (July 2021). Under the charter of the working group that wrote it, DPRIVE, its scope is the leg from the stub resolver on a device to its recursive resolver, though the RFC leaves room for the recursive-to-authoritative leg. What it is not matters as much: DoT protects the channel, not the data. The resolver at the far end still sees every name asked, and only DNSSEC (the DNS Security Extensions) proves that an answer is the one the zone owner published.

How a session works. A server that offers DoT MUST listen for TCP (Transmission Control Protocol) connections on port 853, and a client that wants privacy MUST connect there, unless both sides have agreed on another port; that port MUST NOT be 53, so that nobody has to guess whether a connection on the classic port is encrypted, and a downgrade is harder to slip in. The first exchange on the connection is the TLS handshake. Port 853 MUST NOT carry cleartext DNS, and no cleartext may follow a failed handshake. Inside the session every message is preceded by the two-octet length field that DNS over TCP has used since RFC 1035, written together with the message so that both leave in one TCP segment. Clients SHOULD pipeline queries instead of waiting for each answer, and because answers can return in any order they MUST match them by message ID (identifier) and, when a question section is present, by name, class and type. Connections are meant to stay open and be reused; either side may close an idle one, and TCP Fast Open and TLS session resumption (RFC 5077) cut the cost of reconnecting. IANA (the Internet Assigned Numbers Authority) registered the service name domain-s on TCP port 853 on 8 October 2015; the same number over UDP (User Datagram Protocol) is reserved for DNS over DTLS (Datagram Transport Layer Security, RFC 8094, Experimental, February 2017) and for DNS over QUIC (DoQ, RFC 9250, May 2022).

Why a port of its own. The dedicated port was a choice the RFC explains. Early drafts upgraded an ordinary connection instead, a STARTTLS for DNS: the client set a TLS OK bit in the EDNS(0) (Extension Mechanisms for DNS) flags and sent a dummy query for the name STARTTLS, type TXT (text), class CH (Chaos), and a willing server answered with the bit set. That would have kept DNS on port 53 with no new firewall rules, and let a busy server decline. It was dropped for three recorded reasons: nobody knew whether middleboxes would pass an EDNS(0) flag that had not changed in years, a stripped bit would make a downgrade attack indistinguishable from a broken middlebox, and the dummy query cost an extra round trip. A rival DNS over DTLS proposal claimed it could share port 53 only because a server that did not speak DTLS read the encrypted query as a response, with the QR (query or response) bit set, which the authors called unfortunate. One well-known port for both was the cleaner answer.

Authentication profiles. Encryption without authentication defeats only a passive listener, and the profiles say how much a client insists on. RFC 7858 defined an opportunistic privacy profile and an out-of-band key-pinned profile, in which the client holds a set of SPKI (Subject Public Key Info) fingerprints for the server, with a backup pin, and treats a mismatch as a failure. RFC 8310 (March 2018, by Sara Dickinson, Daniel Kahn Gillmor and Tirumaleswar Reddy), which updates RFC 7858, defines the two usage profiles in use today. Strict Privacy requires an encrypted and authenticated connection and fails hard without one, defending against active attackers too. Opportunistic Privacy follows the opportunistic security of RFC 7435: the client may end up with an encrypted and authenticated connection, an encrypted but unauthenticated one, or cleartext, and keeps resolving in every case. A strict client authenticates the server against an authentication domain name (ADN), checked through a PKIX (Public Key Infrastructure using X.509) certificate or DANE (DNS-Based Authentication of Named Entities), or against a pin set. The same RFC sets the TLS profile: TLS 1.2 or later only, never TLS compression, session resumption without server-side state, and EDNS(0) padding (RFC 7830) so that message sizes stop giving names away. RFC 8467 (Experimental, October 2018) supplies the padding policy, queries to a multiple of 128 octets and responses to a multiple of 468, a block chosen so that three of them still fit a typical MTU (maximum transmission unit). Cloudflare's own kdig example shows the effect: 408 bytes of padding bring a response to exactly 468.

Clients and resolvers. Support arrived in operating systems before browsers. Android 9 (Pie) added Private DNS, announced on 13 April 2018 by Erik Kline of Android and Ben Schwartz of Jigsaw: by default the device upgrades to DoT whenever the network's resolver supports it, and when the user enters a resolver hostname, Android sends every query to that server over TLS or marks the network as having no internet access, which is the Strict profile in practice. On Linux, systemd-resolved has had DNSOverTLS= since version 239: yes requires DoT and lets every lookup fail if the server does not offer it; opportunistic tries it and falls back, which the manual warns is open to downgrade by a forged response and, because the server is not authenticated, to a man-in-the-middle; the default is no. Writing the server as address#server_name gives it the name for the certificate check and for SNI (Server Name Indication). For testing, dig in BIND (Berkeley Internet Name Domain) 9.20 has +tls, which moves the port to 853, +tls-ca to validate the certificate and +tls-hostname to name what it must match; Cloudflare documents kdig -d @1.1.1.1 +tls-ca +tls-host=one.one.one.one example.com. Cloudflare answers DoT on 1.1.1.1, 1.0.0.1, 2606:4700:4700::1111 and 2606:4700:4700::1001, port 853, and by name at one.one.one.one, with TLS 1.3 and 1.2. Google Public DNS answers at dns.google on port 853 with TLS 1.3, TCP Fast Open and the DNS-over-TCP requirements of RFC 7766, and may close connections that sit idle too long or have carried many queries. Google re-enabled EDNS Client Subnet (ECS) on its DoT service on 27 June 2019, having launched without it, a reminder that encryption on the path says nothing about what the resolver passes on.

On a FortiGate. FortiOS meets DoT in two roles. As a client, version 6.4 enforces it for the unit's own lookups with set dns-over-tls enforce under config system dns, and its manual warned that the default FortiGuard DNS servers of that release did not support DoT and dropped the packets. From 7.0.4 the FortiGuard servers 96.45.45.45 and 96.45.46.46 are reached over DoT by default, shown as set protocol dot with set server-hostname globalsdns.fortinet.net, the name the certificate is checked against, while low-encryption models stay on cleartext UDP port 53. As an inspection point, FortiOS before 7.0 let DoT pass through its DNS proxy silently; from 7.0 the proxy hands DoT queries to the DNS proxy so that the DNS filter profile applies, which works only with full SSL (Secure Sockets Layer) deep inspection and with DNS over TLS enabled in the profile's protocol port mapping.

Beyond the stub. The same transport now reaches past the stub-to-recursive leg. Zone transfer (XFR) over TLS, XoT (RFC 9103, August 2021), carries zone transfers between primary and secondary servers on port 853, with the ALPN (Application-Layer Protocol Negotiation) token dot and TLS 1.3 or later only, because TSIG (Transaction Signature) authorizes a transfer and protects its integrity but never encrypted it. RFC 9539 (Experimental, February 2024) lets recursive resolvers try DoT or DoQ towards authoritative servers on port 853 unilaterally: no authentication is required, a self-issued certificate will do, the answers must be identical to those over cleartext, and the protection holds against a passive monitor only. Discovery uses service binding: an SVCB (service binding) record with alpn=dot advertises DoT, on port 853 unless another port is given (RFC 9461), the same machinery that DNS over HTTPS (DoH, HTTPS being Hypertext Transfer Protocol Secure) uses.

What goes wrong. An opportunistic client can be pushed back to cleartext by anyone who blocks port 853 or forges a refusal, and it does not say so; a strict client fails closed, which is safer, and is also how a captive portal or a firewall that drops 853 turns into a network that seems to have no internet. RFC 8932, the Best Current Practice for DNS privacy service operators (BCP 232, October 2020), lists the threats specific to DoT: known attacks on TLS, traffic analysis, client tracking through transport identifiers, and blocking of the well-known port. Its mitigations include padding to RFC 8467, serving clients that decline session resumption or DNS cookies no worse than others, and offering DoT on port 443 as well as 853, with the dot ALPN value telling it apart from DNS over HTTPS on the same address.

DoT against DoH. The practical difference is not cryptographic, since both protect the query in transit; it is whether the traffic announces what it is. DoT on port 853 can be allowed to the enterprise's designated resolvers, denied everywhere else or redirected by an operator who has an opinion; DNS over HTTPS (DoH) on 443 can only be managed by blocking known resolver endpoints or by controlling the client. That is why enterprises that permit encrypted DNS at all tend to prefer DoT, while browsers chose DoH: Firefox began enabling DoH by default for users in the United States on 25 February 2020, with Cloudflare as the default resolver, whereas Android's system-wide Private DNS is DoT. The numbers worth remembering are TCP port 853 (domain-s) and never 53 for TLS, UDP 853 for DoQ and DTLS, the ALPN token dot, the two-octet length prefix, TLS 1.2 as the floor for DoT and 1.3 for XoT, padding blocks of 128 and 468 octets, and RFC 7858, 8310, 9103 and 9539.

ecs.def: An EDNS option that forwards part of the client's address to the authoritative server.
ecs.context: EDNS Client Subnet lets a recursive resolver tell an authoritative server roughly where the client is, so a content network can answer with a nearby server rather than one near the resolver. It improves routing for users of large public resolvers and leaks the client's approximate location to every authoritative server queried.
ecs.depth: ECS exists because anycast solved the wrong half of the problem: it puts the resolver near the user, but the authoritative server answers based on where the resolver is, not where the user is. Forwarding a truncated client subnet fixes the answer and creates a privacy question, which is why public resolvers differ on it - some send it for performance, some refuse on principle, and the choice is invisible to the person whose location is or is not being shared.

dns-filtering.def: Blocking or rewriting DNS answers to stop clients reaching chosen domains.
dns-filtering.context: Because every connection to a named host starts with a lookup, refusing to answer stops the connection before it is attempted - no session to inspect, no port to match, and it works for protocols nobody has written a parser for. The same mechanism is sold as response policy zones, protective DNS, a secure web gateway's DNS layer, and a vendor DNS filter with category ratings.
dns-filtering.depth: The control is high-leverage and low-visibility: it applies to every device on a network without an agent, including printers, cameras and visitors' laptops, and it produces almost no evidence of working correctly. Its two failure modes are silent and opposite - a block returned as NXDOMAIN is indistinguishable from a domain that does not exist, so it reads as an outage; and a client using its own resolver is never filtered at all, so the queries that were never seen appear on no report.

gambiarra.def: Brazilian Portuguese, feminine noun. An improvised fix built from whatever is to hand - precarious, unorthodox, and working. The word carries admiration and disapproval at the same time, and Brazilians hear both.
gambiarra.context: The word started literal. In nineteenth-century theatre a gambiarra was a row of lamps hung above the footlights to light the stage frontally and kill shadows; the dictionary sense is an improvised electrical extension, a long wire with a lamp at the end, carried to wherever light was needed. How that became the modern sense is where the accounts stop agreeing: one has actors tripping over the cabling until the word soured, another has genuinely bad wiring taking the name by association. The etymology is disputed too - the philologist Antenor Nascentes proposed gâmbia, borrowed from the Italian gamba, leg, with the augmentative and sometimes pejorative suffix -arra, and framed even his own reasoning as a question: because the light falls on the actors' legs? It also means an illegal power tap, and, in some registers, an affair.
gambiarra.depth: In technology the word arrived intact. A gambiarra is the SSH tunnel that has been up for three years, the crossover made by hand - a cabo bacalhau, a codfish cable - the loop that exists because the vendor's feature does not, the paperclip in the reset hole. Brazilian developers coined POG, programação orientada a gambiarra, gambiarra-oriented programming, which is a joke that everybody has shipped. Related words divide the ground: quebra-galho is a stopgap, remendo a patch, jeitinho the social manoeuvre rather than the physical one, and gato specifically the illegal tap. What no English word carries is the double charge. Kludge and bodge are insults; hack is a compliment; jury-rig is neutral and nautical. Gambiarra is all three at once, and the pride in it is real: the thing works, it cost nothing, and somebody clever did it under constraint. The nearest relatives are elsewhere - jugaad in India, which the University of Oxford's informality researchers place in the same family as the Brazilian jeitinho, système D in France and West Africa, desenrascanço in Portugal, костыль (a crutch) in Russian code review, houtje-touwtje in Dutch, atar con alambre in Argentina. Every one of them keeps part of the meaning and drops another part. That is why the word stays in Portuguese on this site, in every language: translating it would be the first gambiarra.

jeitinho.def: Brazilian Portuguese. The knack of getting something done by going around a rule rather than through it - usually with charm, usually without money changing hands, and usually at a small cost to somebody who is following the rule.
jeitinho.context: Where a gambiarra bends a material, a jeitinho bends a procedure. It lives in the gap between the impersonal law and the personal relationship: the queue skipped because you know the doorman, the form accepted after hours because somebody made a call, the deadline that moves because you asked well. Brazilians describe it with pride and with unease in the same breath, and the phrase that carries it - dar um jeitinho, to give it a little way - is a diminutive doing a lot of work: the -inho makes the manoeuvre sound small and forgivable.
jeitinho.depth: For anyone working across Brazilian organizations the concept is operationally real. A change that goes in without a window, an access granted on a WhatsApp message, an exception that becomes the practice - each is a jeitinho, and each is the reason a control that exists on paper fails in an audit. That is the honest half. The other half is that it also names a genuine social competence in a system where formal channels are slow and unevenly applied, which is why the same person may condemn it in the abstract and rely on it on a Tuesday. Oxford's informality researchers catalogue it beside jugaad in India, blat in Russia and guanxi in China: different cultures, the same human answer to a rule that does not fit the case. Its technical cousin is gambiarra - the improvised fix in the physical or digital world - and the distinction worth keeping is that one bends a rule and the other bends a wire.

open-source.def: Software under a licence meeting the Open Source Initiative's ten criteria: free redistribution, available source code, permission for derived works, and no discrimination against people or fields of use. The term was coined in 1998 (Christine Peterson) as a business-friendlier name for what the four freedoms already described.
open-source.context: Open source and free software describe almost exactly the same set of licences with different emphases: a practical argument about the development model versus a moral argument about user freedom. The umbrella acronyms FOSS (free and open-source software) and FLOSS (free/libre and open-source software) name the shared territory. Source-available is not the same thing: readable code whose licence withholds modification or redistribution fails both definitions.
open-source.depth:
What it is exactly. The Open Source Definition (OSD), kept by the Open Source Initiative (OSI), opens with the sentence that settles most arguments: open source doesn't just mean access to the source code. It then sets ten criteria for a licence. The licence must allow free redistribution, including selling the software as part of an aggregate, with no royalty (1). The source code must be included or easily obtainable, in the form a programmer would prefer for modifying it, and deliberately obfuscated source does not count (2). Modifications and derived works must be allowed and distributable under the same terms (3). The author may require modified versions to carry a different name or to be distributed as patches (4). The licence may not discriminate against persons or groups (5) or against fields of endeavour, such as business or genetic research (6). The rights pass to everyone who receives the program with no further licence to sign (7), do not depend on the program being part of a particular distribution (8), place no restriction on other software shipped alongside (9), and may not depend on any individual technology or style of interface (10). The current text is version 1.9, last modified on 22 March 2007. Open source is therefore a property of a licence, certified by a review process, and says nothing about who governs a project, how it is funded or whether anyone has audited the code.

Where the words came from. Christine Peterson, then executive director of the Foresight Institute, has told the story herself. Meetings at Foresight in late 1997 had identified free software as a route to better security and reliability and kept stumbling on the name, because newcomers assume that free refers to price. When Netscape announced that it would release its browser's source code, Eric Raymond came to California to help, and on 2 February 1998 a group met at Foresight's office in Los Altos. Peterson came up with open source software that week; at a brainstorm at VA Research on 5 February the Linux programmer Todd Anderson argued for it, Raymond endorsed it, and the room settled on it. The OSI's own history dates the strategy session to 3 February 1998 in Palo Alto. By late February O'Reilly and Netscape were using the term, and in the same weeks Raymond and Bruce Perens founded the OSI, with Raymond as president, to explain and protect the label.

The definition is older than the name. Perens had drafted the Debian Free Software Guidelines, which the Debian developers refined in a month-long electronic mail conference in June 1997 and ratified on 5 July 1997 as part of the Debian Social Contract. In February 1998 he removed the Debian-specific references and the result became the OSD. The OSI published its first formal list of approved licences by October 1999, added the tenth criterion in 2004 to deal with click-wrap licensing, and in 2006 issued a report on licence proliferation that sorted the list into categories.

Free software and open source. Richard Stallman's essay on the difference starts from the common ground: the two terms stand for almost the same range of programs. Free software is defined by four freedoms, numbered from zero: to run the program for any purpose, to study and change it, to redistribute copies, and to distribute modified versions, with access to the source as a precondition for the second and fourth. Free refers to liberty, and the GNU Project is explicit that free software can be commercial and that copies can be sold. In Stallman's account all released free software would qualify as open source, and nearly all open source software is free software; the difference is one of values, a movement for users' freedom on one side and an argument from practical advantage on the other. His exceptions are instructive. A few OSI-approved licences are too restrictive to be free. And a device that checks signatures so that only the manufacturer's build will run, a practice he calls tivoization, can ship executables built from open source that the owner cannot usefully replace, which is how many Android products carry the Linux kernel.

The licence families. The OSI's list marks a dozen licences as popular with a strong community: the Apache License 2.0, the two-clause and three-clause Berkeley Software Distribution (BSD) licences, the Massachusetts Institute of Technology (MIT) licence, the Mozilla Public License 2.0, the Eclipse Public License 2.0, the Common Development and Distribution License 1.0, and versions 2 and 3 of the GNU General Public License (GPL) with the Lesser and Library variants. They divide into permissive licences, which ask for little more than attribution, and copyleft licences, which require derived works to be distributed under the same terms. The software a network engineer touches every day covers the range: the Linux kernel is under GPL version 2 only, nginx is under the two-clause BSD licence, and OpenSSL moved to the Apache License 2.0 with release 3.0, earlier releases remaining under the dual OpenSSL and SSLeay licence. Licences are named unambiguously by the identifiers of the Software Package Data Exchange (SPDX) list, at version 3.29.0 in September 2026, such as GPL-2.0-only, BSD-2-Clause and Apache-2.0; the kernel requires an SPDX identifier line in every source file.

What it is not. It is not source-available software. The OSI's statement of 19 January 2021 on the Server Side Public License (SSPL) is the clearest example: the licence had been submitted for approval and withdrawn when it became clear it would not pass, and when Elastic adopted it in order to stop cloud providers offering its software as a service, the OSI called the result fauxpen source, because a restriction on a field of endeavour breaks the sixth criterion. The code can be read; the rights that make it open source are gone. Nor does open source mean free of charge, since the first criterion protects the right to sell, or unowned, since every one of these licences rests on the author's copyright.

The newest extension concerns artificial intelligence (AI). The OSI's Open Source AI Definition, version 1.0, applies the same four freedoms, to use, study, modify and share, to an AI system, and says what the preferred form for modification is when the artefact is a trained model: sufficiently detailed information about the training data, the complete code used to train and run the system, and the parameters, such as the weights. A model whose weights can be downloaded but whose training cannot be reproduced does not meet it.

What it means in operation. A permissive or copyleft licence gives the right to inspect and fix the code that runs in a product; it does not supply the people to do so. The XZ Utils backdoor of 2024 began with pressure on a maintainer who had to remind his critics that the compression library on which so many systems depended was an unpaid hobby project. For an organization that ships or operates software the practical duties are to know which components are present and under which licence, which is what SPDX identifiers and a software bill of materials record, to honour the conditions attached to redistribution, and to treat a relicensing announcement as a supply event: when a vendor moves a product from an OSI-approved licence to a source-available one, the earlier releases remain open source and the community's usual answer is a fork.

The dates and numbers worth remembering: 5 July 1997 for the Debian guidelines; February 1998 for the term and for the OSI; ten criteria in the definition, at version 1.9 since 2007; four freedoms, counted from zero; October 1999 for the first list of approved licences; 19 January 2021 for the statement on the SSPL; and version 1.0 of the Open Source AI Definition for the extension to models.

free-software.def: Software whose users have the four freedoms of the Free Software Definition: run for any purpose (0), study and change (1, which requires source), redistribute copies (2), and distribute modified versions (3). Free refers to liberty, not price - free as in freedom, not free as in beer.
free-software.context: Portuguese resolves the famous English ambiguity outright: livre (liberty) and gratuito (price) are different words, which is why software livre needs no footnote. A program can be gratis without being free (freeware) and free without being gratis - selling free software is explicitly permitted.

copyleft.def: A licensing mechanism (the GPL family) that permits modification and redistribution on one condition: the redistributed version must carry the same freedoms forward. Copyright law used against its usual grain - the share-alike rule is the mechanism, the pun is the philosophy.
copyleft.context: The counterpart family is permissive licensing (MIT, BSD, Apache): keep the notice and otherwise do as you like, including closing the code into proprietary products. Copyleft protects the freedom of the code downstream; permissive maximizes the freedom of the next developer. Both families sit fully inside the free-software and open-source definitions.

norad.def: The binational United States-Canada command (1958) that watches North American airspace - and, since 1985, aerospace - for attack, headquartered at Peterson with its hardened alternate inside Cheyenne Mountain. One command, two countries, one warning picture: a Canadian officer can order the defence of American skies and vice versa.
norad.context: Networking and security keep meeting NORAD's shadow: its 1950s automation produced SAGE (for which the modem was invented, and whose alumni built the ARPANET); the film WarGames rattled Reagan into NSDD-145, the first US computer-security policy; its 1979 training-tape and 1980 failed-chip false alerts are the canonical integrity case studies; Cheyenne Mountain is the archetype of the air-gapped facility; and every December it famously tracks Santa.
norad.depth: Networking and security people keep meeting NORAD's shadow. Its 1950s automation problem produced SAGE, the continent-spanning air-defense computer system for which the telephone modem was invented and real-time computing was industrialized - the school that trained the generation who later built the ARPANET. Feeding it required the DEW Line radars across the Arctic and the White Alice troposcatter network: network communications engineering at heroic scale, decades before fibre. In 1983 the film WarGames put a teenager inside a fictional NORAD computer; a rattled President Reagan asked whether it could really happen, and the answer became NSDD-145, the first US national policy on computer security, with the Computer Fraud and Abuse Act following - modern cyber law begins with a movie about this command. The legend that Kevin Mitnick hacked NORAD (he did not) fed the same era's mythology. Its false alerts - a training tape loaded into the live system in 1979, a failed chip in 1980 that painted incoming missiles - are still the canonical case studies for integrity and fail-safe design. Cheyenne Mountain remains the archetype of the air-gapped facility, policy debates still reach for 'a NORAD for cyber' whenever collective defence is proposed, and every December the command that watches for missiles also, famously, tracks Santa - a goodwill operation running since a misprinted 1955 phone number, and today one of the internet's great seasonal traffic events.

phreaking.def: The exploration and manipulation of the telephone network, the craft that preceded computer hacking and took the ph of phone for its name. Its golden age ran on in-band signalling: the network carried its control tones on the same line as the voice, so whoever could produce the tones could command the switch.
phreaking.context: A 2,600 Hz tone told long-distance trunks that a line was idle; a toy whistle from a cereal box happened to produce it, and a blue box automated the rest by adding the network's own multifrequency (MF) dialling tones. The Bell System had published those frequencies in its technical journal, Esquire made the people public in October 1971, and the scene's longest-running magazine, 2600: The Hacker Quarterly, took the frequency as its name. The cure was to move signalling off the voice path, which AT&T began in 1976 and the industry completed with Signalling System No. 7 (SS7). Phreaking's people, ethics and folklore flowed straight into the computer underground: the first generation of famous hackers were phone phreaks first.
phreaking.depth:
The word and its limits. The Jargon File gives two senses: the art and science of cracking the phone network, for example to make free long-distance calls, and by extension security cracking in any other context, especially on communications networks. It also records the culture's own rule, a gentleman's agreement that phreaking as an intellectual game and a form of exploration was acceptable while serious theft of service was taboo, and the newsletter that carried it, TAP, which the Federal Bureau of Investigation (FBI) tracked in New York, as the Technological American Party, in a single file with the Youth International Party Line (YIPL). The same entry dates the end of that ethos to the mid-1980s, when wider spread of the techniques reached less scrupulous hands and changes in the network made technical ingenuity less effective, so that phreaking came to depend on stolen calling-card numbers, and the prosecutions of gangs such as the 414 group turned the game ugly. Phreaking is therefore not a synonym for toll fraud, though it shades into it; at its classic core it is the study of a network's signalling from the outside, by people who were not supposed to speak its language.

The design that made it possible. The Bell System Technical Journal of November 1960 set out the signalling of the long-distance network in an article by C. Breen and C. A. Dahlbom. Single-frequency (SF) signalling put a tone on an idle trunk and removed it when the trunk was seized; it had used 1,600 cycles during the war, because emergency facilities cut off around 1,750, and was raised to 2,600 cycles afterwards, with current circuits on 2,400 or 2,600. Because the tone sat inside the voice band, the receiver had to guard against speech by treating any other energy as a sign that someone was talking. The article states the Bell System's philosophy plainly: in-band signalling over non-metallic facilities, out-of-band direct current over metallic pairs. In-band was economical, since the same channel served both, and it was the flaw: a caller who put 2,600 cycles on the line was indistinguishable from the switch at the far end.

The address language. The same article published the multifrequency (MF) pulsing code operators used to send numbers between offices: six frequencies spaced 200 cycles apart from 700 to 1,700, each digit a pair of two out of five of them (the digit 5, for instance, 900 plus 1,300 cycles), with an opening signal of 1,100 plus 1,700 that prepared the far receiver and a closing one of 1,500 plus 1,700 that ended the digits. A blue box was simply a generator of these tones plus the 2,600 cycle supervisory tone: the tone made the far end treat the trunk as free for a new call, and the box then addressed it in the network's own code, as an operator's keyset would have. The phreaks Rosenbaum interviewed said the equipment accepted any tone within about thirty cycles of the real one, which is why blind phreaks could do it with electric organs and tape recorders. A further international plan in the 1960 article, line signals on 2,400 and 2,600 cycles, became the International Telegraph and Telephone Consultative Committee (CCITT) System No. 5, which the Bell System described in 1978 as the in-band system still used on undersea cables and satellite circuits.

How the secret got out. The frequencies were never secret in the cryptographic sense; they were engineering literature. In Ron Rosenbaum's Esquire article of October 1971, the blue box maker he called Gilbertson says the phone company made one big mistake in letting a technical journal publish the actual multifrequency tones, and claims that Bell had the issue withdrawn from engineering libraries too late. The historian Phil Lapsley lists the Breen and Dahlbom article as the one often cited as giving away the keys to the kingdom, alongside earlier public descriptions of the same systems from 1949, 1951 and 1954. The Esquire piece, and a syndicated newspaper article the same month, did for the people what the journal had done for the tones: they made a scattered underground visible to anyone who could read.

The people. Joe Engressia, born on 25 May 1949 and blind from birth, learned to dial with the hookswitch at four or five and, by his New York Times obituary's account, discovered about four years later that he could disconnect a call by whistling, because his whistle matched the 2,600-cycle tone; the University of South Florida dropped him after he was caught making calls for friends at a dollar a call, he was convicted of phone fraud in Memphis in 1971, later worked for Mountain Bell finding faults in its network, took Joybubbles as his legal name in 1991 and died on 8 August 2007. John Draper took the name Captain Crunch from the cereal-box whistle that produced 2,600 cycles; Rosenbaum reported that he used it to make calls free for friends while serving with the Air Force in England. A 1986 profile counted three convictions: in 1972, with probation, in 1976, with four months in jail, and a third later, and quoted his view that prison spread the techniques to people far more interested in free calls than he had been.

Wozniak and Jobs. Steve Wozniak read the Esquire article in the autumn of 1971, the day before starting classes at Berkeley, called Steve Jobs, and the two went that hour to the library of the Stanford Linear Accelerator Center (SLAC), where they found an international telephone standard listing the frequencies. Wozniak then designed a digital blue box timed by a quartz crystal, so that it did not drift with temperature as analogue boxes did; he used the handle Berkeley Blue and Jobs Oaf Tobar, and they sought out Draper. Jobs set the price at about 170 dollars, and they sold boxes in the Berkeley dormitories; Wozniak guessed 30 or 40 in all, Jobs remembered nearer a hundred. Wozniak also used one to reach the Vatican posing as Henry Kissinger. In 2022 he still described the box as having tricks he never equalled in his Apple designs, and insisted they had done it for fun.

The fix. The Bell System's own journal named the problem in 1978: voice-frequency signalling on circuits customers used was vulnerable to interference and susceptible to fraud, and expensive to equip on every channel. The answer was Common Channel Interoffice Signaling (CCIS), which in May 1976 first linked a No. 4A toll crossbar office in Madison, Wisconsin, with the first No. 4 ESS (Electronic Switching System) toll office in Chicago. CCIS carried all supervisory and address signals on data links between the processors of the switching offices, completely separate from the talking paths, and its designers wrote that fraudulent manipulation of the telephone network is eliminated in an all-CCIS environment. The international counterpart, CCITT System No. 6, was approved in October 1976, and its successor, Signalling System No. 7 (SS7), introduced in ITU-T (International Telecommunication Union Telecommunication Standardization Sector) Recommendation Q.700, is what the world's networks still use. The tone a caller makes no longer means anything to the switch, which is the engineering lesson phreaking left to every protocol since: keep the control plane out of the data channel.

After the boxes. With the tones disarmed, the crossover with the computer underground that the Jargon File describes became the culture's main line, and its press moved with it: 2600: The Hacker Quarterly, named for the frequency, was still on sale in its autumn 2026 issue. Brazil had its own version of the economic motive, with long-distance calls expensive: in 1995 Jornal Nacional reported a payphone fraud in São Paulo, recalled by the Diário Online in 2025, in which a fault in the phones' memory let long-distance calls run without charging the card, costing the state operator Telesp more than 10 million reais before two men were arrested in Praça da Sé. Draper himself was announced for the Roadsec festival in São Paulo on 11 November 2017, though the talk was cancelled days before the event.

The descendants. The idea that a network trusts whoever speaks its signalling language outlived in-band tones. SS7 took the signalling out of the voice channel but not out of reach: at the Chaos Communication Congress in December 2014 Tobias Engel showed that companies were selling the ability to locate a phone number to within 50 metres from the other side of the world. In March 2018 the European Union Agency for Cybersecurity (ENISA) assessed the risk in interconnection signalling, SS7, Diameter and 5G, as medium to high. The principle behind any defence is the 1976 fix in a new setting: do not let the party at the other end of a channel issue commands simply because it can produce the right signal.

cult-of-the-dead-cow.def: The oldest continuously active hacker group in the United States, formed in Lubbock, Texas in 1984 - equal parts security research, absurdist zine and political theatre. It coined the word hacktivism and shipped the remote-administration tool Back Orifice at DEF CON in 1998 to humiliate Microsoft into taking Windows security seriously.
cult-of-the-dead-cow.context: The Back Orifice launch is the template every provocative disclosure has followed since: a working tool, a stage, a press corps, and a vendor with no good answer. cDc later spun off Hacktivismo, focused on circumvention tools for censored networks. Its alumni turn up everywhere in the field - and in 2019 a journalist revealed that a young member writing as Psychedelic Warlord had grown up to be a US presidential candidate, Beto O'Rourke.

legion-of-doom.def: The most influential American hacker group of the 1980s, founded around 1984 by a phreak calling himself Lex Luthor and named after the Super Friends villains. Its members were deep telephone-switch specialists whose technical files, published in Phrack, taught a generation how the phone network actually worked.
legion-of-doom.context: LOD's rivalry with the New York crew Masters of Deception became the Great Hacker War, the first documented gang conflict inside the underground. The group's spread of an internal BellSouth document about the 911 system - valued absurdly at $79,449 - triggered the Neidorf prosecution and the crackdown known as Operation Sundevil. Several members went on to found respectable security consultancies, a career arc the field would repeat for decades.

masters-of-deception.def: The New York hacker crew of the late 1980s and early 1990s, formed around Mark Abene (Phiber Optik) after his split from the Legion of Doom - younger, more urban and more publicly defiant than their Texan rivals, and deeply at home inside the switches of the regional telephone companies.
masters-of-deception.context: The LOD-MOD feud - the Great Hacker War - ran on hijacked conference bridges and pride rather than damage, but the 1992 federal indictments treated it as organized crime, and Abene served a year. New York threw him a welcome-home party and New York magazine put him on its list of the city's smartest people; the case is the cleanest early example of a culture and a courtroom holding irreconcilable views of the same behaviour.

operation-sundevil.def: The United States Secret Service operation of May 1990, run from Phoenix with Arizona's racketeering prosecutors: coordinated raids on 7, 8 and 9 May in a dozen or more cities (the official release said twelve, John Perry Barlow wrote fourteen) that seized bulletin board systems, computers and floppy disks, aimed at credit-card and telephone-code fraud.
operation-sundevil.context: The operation is remembered less for its convictions, which were few, than for the crackdown around it, which the public folded into its name. On 1 March 1990 a separate Chicago-led task force raided Steve Jackson Games, a tabletop publisher, and seized the manuscript of a cyberpunk role-playing book as a supposed handbook for computer crime; separately, the government's case against Phrack's Craig Neidorf collapsed when the defence showed that a BellSouth document on the same Enhanced 911 (E911) system, valued by the prosecution at 79,449 dollars, could be ordered from a catalogue for 13 dollars. The fiascos convinced Mitch Kapor and John Perry Barlow to found the Electronic Frontier Foundation (EFF), and gave Bruce Sterling his book The Hacker Crackdown.
operation-sundevil.depth:
What it was, and what it was not. Bruce Sterling, whose 1992 book is the standard account, draws the line carefully. Operation Sundevil was based in Arizona, the work of the Phoenix office of the Secret Service and the Arizona Attorney General's office, and it was a crackdown on the traditional scourges of the underground, credit-card theft and the abuse of stolen telephone calling codes, not on computer intrusion or attacks on telephone switches. Its targets were chosen over an investigation lasting two full years. The Chicago Computer Fraud and Abuse Task Force, which pursued the Legion of Doom and the BellSouth Enhanced 911 (E911) document, and the New York State Police's own actions were never part of Sundevil, yet after the May raids police secrecy, panic in the underground and a puzzled press folded the whole 1990 crackdown into its name; Sterling notes that the Secret Service's Washington office helped the confusion by answering freedom-of-information requests about Sundevil with the cases of Knight Lightning and the Atlanta Three. The name came from Arizona State University's Sun Devil football stadium, near the local Secret Service headquarters. The conflation was there from the start: Barlow's own essay Crime and Puzzlement, written that year, called the January 1990 raids on New York hackers and the pursuit of the Legion of Doom the visible phase of Operation Sun Devil.

The raids. The press release of the United States Attorney's office in Phoenix announced twenty-seven search warrants executed on 8 May 1990, three arrests and 150 agents in twelve cities; local press counts gave thirteen, fourteen and sixteen, and Barlow's history of the Electronic Frontier Foundation (EFF), written that November, says fourteen. Sterling lists raids from 7 to 9 May in Cincinnati, Detroit, Los Angeles, Miami, Newark, Phoenix, Tucson, Richmond, San Diego, San Jose, Pittsburgh and San Francisco, five in the New York City area, four in Plano, Texas, and one in Chicago, most of them in homes rather than offices. About forty-two computer systems were seized, roughly twenty-five of them running bulletin board systems (BBSs), along with an estimated 23,000 floppy disks. The organizers had a list of at least three hundred boards they considered worth a warrant; with perhaps 30,000 boards in the country, the seizures took about one tenth of one per cent of them. The agents were seeking computers, not people: there were four arrests, one of them on weapons charges.

The message. Sterling reads Sundevil's motives as largely political, a public-relations effort aimed at several audiences. At the press conference in Phoenix on 9 May 1990, Garry M. Jenkins, the Secret Service's assistant director and the highest federal official to take a public role in the crackdown, said the service was sending a clear message to hackers who believed they could avoid detection by hiding behind the relative anonymity of their computer terminals, and that many suspects were no longer misguided teenagers but high-tech operators. Officials put the telephone companies' losses at a figure that may run into millions of dollars, and credit went to the Secret Service, Assistant United States Attorney Tim Holtzen and Arizona's Assistant Attorney General Gail Thackeray. The other audiences were the telephone and credit-card companies, which wanted to see action, and law enforcement itself, to which the operation was offered as proof that computer crime could be policed.

How a seizure worked. Sterling describes the method: agents entered through every door at once, moved suspects away from the machines so nothing could be erased, and a two-agent team, a finder who knew what the warrant sought and a recorder who photographed the equipment and its cabling, inventoried what was taken. Computer-crime warrants of the time were written to cover computers, almost anything attached to them and almost any document around them, and agents were urged to seize the lot, so the 23,000 disks held pirated software and stolen codes but also legitimate programs, business records and private mail. That is the point an engineer should keep: taking a board took every user's stored messages with it, and the law had not yet decided what that meant.

The raid that was not Sundevil. On 1 March 1990 the Chicago task force raided Steve Jackson Games in Austin, Texas. By the company's account armed agents, with Austin police and a civilian expert from the phone company, took four computers, two laser printers and loose hard disks, including the machine that ran the company's Illuminati BBS, and the files of GURPS (Generic Universal Role Playing System) Cyberpunk, a book about to go to print, which an agent called a handbook for computer crime; Jackson's answer, in Sterling's telling, was that it was science fiction. Some files came back on 26 March and most of the hardware on 21 June; the book was rebuilt from backups and notes, and the company survived by laying off half its staff. When the sealed affidavit was finally released on 21 October 1990 it showed that the target was the book's writer, Loyd Blankenship, who ran a legal board from home that discussed the computer underground and had reposted Phrack; the manuscript was a target of opportunity. At Craig Neidorf's trial, on 25 July 1990, his lawyer showed a BellSouth witness the catalogue document BellSouth E911 Service Interfaces, priced at 13 dollars, and asked whether it did not contain about twice the detail Phrack had printed; two days later, on 27 July 1990, the case against Neidorf collapsed.

In court. Steve Jackson Games and four users of its board sued in May 1991 with the EFF's backing. In 1993 the federal district court in Texas found that the Secret Service had violated the Privacy Protection Act and awarded the company 51,040 dollars in damages, found a violation of Title II of the Electronic Communications Privacy Act (ECPA) for seizing stored electronic communications and awarded 1,000 dollars in statutory damages to each individual plaintiff, plus 195,000 dollars in attorneys' fees and about 57,000 dollars in costs; it also found that the 162 unread private e-mails on the board had been read and deleted. On 31 October 1994 the Fifth Circuit rejected the appeal on the last count: taking a computer that holds e-mail not yet read by its addressees is not an interception under the Wiretap Act, because the statute does not apply interception to communications in electronic storage. That line between intercepting traffic in transit and accessing stored messages is one engineers and lawyers have argued over since.

What came out of it. Barlow wrote that the list of outrages that spring, the game publisher, the boards confiscated with undelivered mail, Sundevil's more than 40 computers and 23,000 disks, and the Neidorf prosecution, is what moved him to write Crime and Puzzlement and, with Mitch Kapor, to found the EFF after a meeting in Pinedale, Wyoming, in June 1990. Steve Wozniak offered to match Kapor's contributions and John Gilmore offered six-figure support, and the foundation was announced at the National Press Club on 10 July 1990 with Steve Jackson beside the founders. Sterling, a science fiction writer, turned to reporting and published The Hacker Crackdown in 1992, later giving it away as free electronic text. The operation's own record is thin by comparison: few prosecutions, seized boards that included many with no connection to fraud, and a reputation, deserved or not, as the moment American law enforcement met the online world without understanding it.

the-kgb-hack.def: The late-1980s West German intrusion ring that sold access to US military and research systems to the Soviet KGB for cash and drugs - the far end of the trail Cliff Stoll followed from a 75-cent accounting error.
the-kgb-hack.context: Its most haunted figure was Karl Koch, alias Hagbard Celine after a character in the Illuminatus! trilogy, a young man convinced the number 23 governed reality. He confessed, was granted amnesty, and in 1989 was found burned to death in a forest outside Hanover - officially a suicide, endlessly disputed. The story gave German cinema the film 23 and the hacker scene its most cautionary legend: the first documented case of computer intrusion sold to a foreign intelligence service, and a reminder of what the underground's drift towards espionage cost the people inside it.

wank-worm.def: Worms Against Nuclear Killers: the anti-nuclear worm that hit NASA and US Department of Energy DECnet systems in October 1989, days before the Galileo probe launched with a plutonium power source. Infected terminals greeted operators with a banner announcing WANK and the line 'You talk of times of peace for all, and then prepare for war.'
wank-worm.context: It is generally regarded as the first hacktivist worm - protest rather than profit or curiosity - and it forced NASA into a scramble at the worst possible moment. Never definitively attributed, it is widely believed to have come from the Melbourne scene later chronicled in the book Underground, whose researcher was Julian Assange.

mafiaboy.def: The alias of Michael Calce, the Montreal fifteen-year-old whose distributed denial-of-service (DDoS) attacks of February 2000, which he called Project Rivolta, knocked Yahoo!, Amazon, eBay, CNN, Dell, E*Trade and others offline from university machines he had compromised; sentenced in youth court in 2001, he later became a security consultant and author.
mafiaboy.context: The attacks landed at the peak of dot-com optimism and punctured it: the idea that a teenager with borrowed computers could switch off the internet's biggest brands reached the White House, where President Clinton met industry and security experts within a week, and helped make distributed denial of service (DDoS) a permanent line in every risk register. Calce was sentenced in Montreal's youth court in September 2001 to eight months of open custody, served in a group home, and a year of probation and, in the pattern the field keeps repeating, grew up into a security consultant and author.
mafiaboy.depth:
What happened. On the morning of 7 February 2000 Yahoo, then one of the web's most visited sites, was knocked offline for about three hours. Over the following days the attacks reached eBay, Buy.com, Amazon.com, CNN.com and E*Trade; Dell was among the later targets named in court. CNN.com and the more than 1,200 sites it hosted were unreachable for more than four hours on 8 February. None of the sites was broken into: each was flooded with traffic from many machines at once, a distributed denial-of-service (DDoS) attack, so that legitimate visitors could not get through. The Yankee Group estimated the cost to the industry at about 1.2 billion dollars, a figure that was widely repeated and never tested in court.

The tools were already known. Dave Dittrich of the University of Washington, who analysed the first DDoS kits, later published the timeline. The trinoo agent was found on mass-compromised Solaris systems in the second half of 1999, and analyses of it and of Tribe Flood Network (TFN) were finished that October; the CERT Coordination Center (CERT/CC, CERT standing for Computer Emergency Response Team) held a workshop on distributed intruder tools in November 1999, issued an incident note on 18 November and an advisory on 28 December, and jointly with a federal response team published Advisory 2000-01 on denial-of-service developments on 3 January 2000; Dittrich's analysis of stacheldraht went to the BUGTRAQ list on 30 December 1999. His conclusion was that any site reading CERT notes or BUGTRAQ knew about these tools months before February 2000; the first attacks on e-commerce sites began on 7 February, the day Steve Bellovin gave a talk on denial of service at the NANOG (North American Network Operators' Group) meeting in San Jose.

How he did it. In a 2008 interview Calce said that by the day of the Yahoo attack he had broken into perhaps 40 per cent of the major universities in the United States, using exploits for Solaris, HP-UX and Linux and for BIND (Berkeley Internet Name Domain), the dominant DNS (Domain Name System) server, all picked up online. He took denial-of-service code written by a hacker called Sinkhole and built a way to aim his roughly 200 university networks at one target at the same moment; he said he was surprised it worked and kept going to see whether Yahoo had been a fluke. The University of California, Santa Barbara was one of the victims: its network programmer found two machines compromised, one used in an attack, and pieces left behind. Officials at the time called the attacker a script kiddie using an existing script and sloppy methods; Calce has since rejected that label. He told NPR in 2015 that the purpose was to intimidate rival hacker groups, and Wikipedia records his name for the operation, Rivolta, Italian for rebellion.

The response. On 15 February 2000 President Clinton told technology executives and security experts at the White House that the disruptions at several websites the week before showed how vulnerabilities at one place on the net could create risks for all; he had asked Congress for 2 billion dollars for cybersecurity and released 9 million at once, and welcomed an industry mechanism to share security information. The Royal Canadian Mounted Police (RCMP) and the FBI (Federal Bureau of Investigation) worked the case together for two months. Calce, who had moved from AOL chat rooms to the EFnet network of Internet Relay Chat (IRC), had boasted about the attacks in IRC channels, and Michael Lyle of Recourse Technologies was among those who reported the boasting. The RCMP arrested him in a late-night raid in April 2000; Attorney General Janet Reno announced the arrest on 19 April. He was charged with two counts of mischief to data over the CNN attack, released on bail and barred from computers except for supervised schoolwork.

The case. In August 2000 the RCMP added 64 charges: 54 counts of illegal access to computers and two each for Yahoo, Amazon, Dell, eBay and Outlaw.net. In January 2001 he changed his plea and admitted 55 of 66 counts, according to Computerworld; The Register and CBC put the number at 56. On 12 September 2001 Judge Gilles Ouellet of the Quebec youth court sentenced him to eight months of detention followed by a year of probation, calling it a grave matter that weakened the entire electronic communication system. The prosecutor, Louis Miville-Deschenes, had asked for a year; the maximum was two; the defence had asked for no detention and called eight months too much. He served the time in a group home, open custody in the court's terms, where he could attend school and a part-time job. The conditions barred him from profiting from the case during probation, from owning software that was not commercially available and from talking to other hackers online, and required him to tell police which internet service provider he used; he also had to give 250 dollars to charity for breaching bail by being suspended from school. Canadian law kept his name out of the record because he was a minor.

Afterwards. He stayed silent for eight years. In October 2008 he gave his first public interviews and published, with the Montreal journalist Craig Silverman, Mafiaboy: How I Cracked the Internet and Why It's Still Broken, which presented his story as a cautionary tale. He said the group home changed him, that he wanted to help ordinary users who had replaced universities and corporations as the main targets, and that he now worked helping companies protect themselves. In 2015 he described himself to NPR as a white hat hacker and argued that, whatever its cost, the attack had forced a real focus on security.

What it taught. The lesson for network engineers is in the architecture rather than the person. The attacking machines were ordinary university servers with known holes, the agents were public tools with published analyses, and the traffic came from thousands of legitimate-looking sources, so filtering by source address could not stop it and the victims depended on upstream capacity and on their providers. Mudge, who attended Clinton's meeting, had told the Senate two years earlier that the backbone operators would not pay the small cost of inspecting packets. The February 2000 attacks are why DDoS became a line item for every operator and why ingress filtering against spoofed sources, scrubbing capacity and incident coordination between providers stopped being optional.

back-orifice.def: The remote-administration tool for Windows released by the Cult of the Dead Cow at DEF CON in August 1998, its name a joke at the expense of Microsoft's BackOffice. It gave an operator near-total control of a remote Windows machine over a small, quiet network channel.
back-orifice.context: cDc's argument was that Windows security was so weak the only way to force the issue was to hand everyone the proof; Microsoft's argument was that a tool is not a lecture. Both were right, and the episode set the enduring template for the full-disclosure debate. Back Orifice also popularized the remote access trojan as a category, and its 1999 successor BO2k was released as open source - which is how a stunt became, briefly, a legitimate administration tool.

kaminsky-dns-flaw.def: The Kaminsky DNS flaw (CVE-2008-1447) is the cache-poisoning technique Dan Kaminsky found in early 2008, which let an off-path attacker take over a whole domain in a recursive resolver's cache within seconds instead of days, and the industry-wide fix of 8 July 2008 that answered it by randomizing resolvers' source ports.
kaminsky-dns-flaw.context: Cache poisoning was known; what Kaminsky showed was that it no longer had to wait for cached answers to expire. By asking a resolver about names that could not be in its cache and racing forged replies that carried a referral for the entire domain, an attacker could retry at will, and one win redirected every name in the zone, with everything that trusts names behind it: web sessions, mail, even the certificates that secure banking sites. The response became the reference case for coordinated disclosure: sixteen experts met in secret at Microsoft's Redmond campus on 31 March 2008, more than 80 vendors were brought into one coordinated release on the same day, and Kaminsky explained the details at Black Hat on 6 August, after they had partly leaked. The fix bought entropy rather than certainty, so it also gave DNSSEC (Domain Name System Security Extensions) its strongest argument. Kaminsky, who died in April 2021, is remembered as much for how he handled the finding as for the finding itself.
kaminsky-dns-flaw.depth:
What it is. A recursive resolver sends a question to an authoritative server over UDP (User Datagram Protocol) and accepts the first reply that matches it. CERT/CC's vulnerability note VU#800113 sets out why matching was weak in 2008: the DNS (Domain Name System) transaction ID is 16 bits, so even a perfectly random one falls to 32,768 attempts on average; several implementations had weak ID generators; some sent several identical queries at once, inviting a birthday attack; and many sent every query from one fixed source port, sometimes 53 itself, so the port added nothing an attacker had to guess. All of that was published before Kaminsky. What kept poisoning slow was the time to live (TTL): an attacker who lost the race let the real answer into the cache and had to wait until it expired before trying again for that name. The National Vulnerability Database (NVD) record for CVE-2008-1447, which calls it the Kaminsky bug, describes what changed: a birthday attack that uses in-bailiwick referrals to poison recursive resolvers, related to insufficient randomness of transaction IDs and source ports.

The technique, at the level a defender needs it. Kaminsky came to it sideways, according to MIT Technology Review: he was working on a way to get around the TTL so that a provider could steer users to the best server for each request, and realized that bypassing the TTL broke the security of DNS.
