An attacker asks the target resolver for names under the victim's domain that cannot already be cached, so the resolver must go out and ask each time, and races each outgoing query with forged replies. The forged replies do not just answer the meaningless name; they carry a referral, naming servers for the whole domain and their addresses, which a resolver accepts because they fall within the domain being asked about. A lost race costs nothing, because the next query uses a new name; a single win puts the attacker's server in the cache as the authority for every name in the zone until the referral expires. Technology Review listed what that meant: users sent to phishing copies of real sites, sensitive mail intercepted, and forged versions of the certificates that secure banking sessions, because all of them ride on names resolving correctly; the impact went far beyond pointing a browser at the wrong page.

The secret summer. Kaminsky called Paul Vixie of the Internet Systems Consortium (ISC), maintainer of BIND, and then went wider. On 31 March 2008, The Register reported, sixteen internet and security experts met on Microsoft's campus in Redmond to confirm the problem, agree a fix and set a timetable, and decided that the only workable approach was a simultaneous release, because a patched resolver is still exposed while others are not and because a single vendor's patch would reveal the bug to anyone who compared the code. The group chose a stopgap that would be easy to deploy and would mask the nature of the flaw. CERT/CC's records show vendors being notified from 14 April 2008, and its note lists more than ninety vendors. On Tuesday 8 July 2008, Microsoft's regular patch day, Kaminsky and the vendors released fixes together (VU#800113 lists 91 vendor records, 84 of them notified, 37 found affected): Microsoft's bulletin MS08-037, rated Important, covered the Windows DNS client and server and credited Kaminsky for CVE-2008-1447; ISC shipped BIND 9.5.0-P1, 9.4.2-P1 and 9.3.5-P1, its advisory listing all BIND 8 and nearly every BIND 9 version as affected; CERT/CC published VU#800113. Kaminsky asked other researchers not to speculate until he presented at Black Hat a month later.

The leak and the talk. The month did not hold. On 21 July Halvar Flake posted his guess at the mechanism and a researcher at Matasano Security corrected the details in a blog post of his own, which put the essentials in public a fortnight before the talk. Kaminsky presented 'Black Ops 2008: It's The End Of The Cache As We Know It' at Black Hat on 6 August 2008, a day earlier than ISC's advisory had said, to a room where people filled every seat and most of the floor, and he was also listed on the DEF CON 16 programme that week. The episode set the pattern every later embargo has had to face: a patch is itself a description of the vulnerability, so once fixes ship the defenders are racing whoever reads the changes fastest. Technology Review recorded the other argument too, that publicizing the flaw so loudly was either grandstanding or a necessary way to make people patch.

What the fix bought. The patch was per-query source port randomization, an idea whose original conception and implementation in a DNS resolver CERT/CC credits to Daniel J. Bernstein. CERT/CC estimates it adds about 16 bits to what an attacker must guess, roughly 32 in all, and RFC (Request for Comments) 5452, published in January 2009, made it a requirement: resolvers must use an unpredictable source port from as large a range as practicable and an unpredictable query ID over the full 16 bits. The RFC's own arithmetic shows the gain: against a single port, a stream of forged answers reaches a 50 per cent chance of success within 7 seconds, while with 64,000 ports the same rate needs about 116 hours, and matching the single-port odds would take more than 285 Gb/s. That is resilience, not immunity, and ISC said so on the day: DNSSEC is the only full solution, and patched BIND provides increased resilience. The NVD's current scoring reflects the residual difficulty, with a version 3.1 base score of 6.8 and high attack complexity.

What operators had to do, and still check. Patching the resolver was not enough on its own. CERT/CC warned that routers, firewalls and other devices doing port address translation (PAT) rewrite source ports and can strip the randomness the resolver added, so a patched resolver behind a translating firewall may still send predictable ports; ISC added that firewalls restricting the UDP ports a resolver may use reduce security, and that the patch cost noticeable performance on resolvers at 10,000 queries per second or more until optimized releases arrived. CERT/CC also advised restricting who may ask a resolver for recursion, since an open resolver lets anyone trigger the queries the attack needs, and noted that stub resolvers on clients needed the same randomization. The quickest practical test is still to look at a capture of a resolver's outgoing queries and see whether the source ports vary; the lasting fix is DNSSEC validation on the resolver and signed zones on the authoritative side.

The person. Kaminsky was at IOActive when he found the flaw, as Microsoft's and CERT/CC's credits record, and he chose to coordinate rather than publish. The New York Times obituary of April 2021 described him as the security researcher known for discovering a fundamental flaw in the fabric of the internet; he died that month in San Francisco, aged 42. The flaw is often cited with his name because the handling, as much as the bug, became the template: private notice to the maintainer, a closed working group of competitors, one release day, then full disclosure.

The numbers worth remembering. A 16-bit transaction ID and 32,768 attempts on average; about 16 more bits from source port randomization; 31 March 2008 in Redmond; 8 July 2008, 84 vendors notified and 91 listed, CVE-2008-1447, VU#800113 and MS08-037; 21 July, the leak; 6 August, the Black Hat talk; RFC 5452 in January 2009, with 7 seconds against 116 hours and 285 Gb/s.

the-jeep-hack.def: The 2015 demonstration by Charlie Miller and Chris Valasek that a Jeep Cherokee could be taken over remotely over the cellular network - through the entertainment head unit and onto the vehicle's internal bus - reaching the transmission, brakes and steering while a journalist drove it on a public highway.
the-jeep-hack.context: Wired published the drive; Fiat Chrysler recalled 1.4 million vehicles, the first cybersecurity recall in automotive history; the Black Hat and DEF CON talks that followed turned car security from a curiosity into a regulated discipline. The technical moral is old and familiar: an infotainment radio and a brake controller had no business sharing a bus without a boundary between them.

barnaby-jack.def: The New Zealand-born security researcher whose live demonstration at Black Hat USA 2010 made two automated teller machines (ATMs) dispense cash on stage, a result he called jackpotting, and who went on to show wireless attacks on insulin pumps and implantable heart devices; he died in San Francisco in July 2013, aged 35.
barnaby-jack.context: He spent his career on embedded systems that their makers assumed nobody would take apart: Windows kernel drivers at eEye, then ATMs, then medical implants. In 2011 he showed that Medtronic insulin pumps within 300 feet could be found and ordered to empty their reservoirs, and in 2012 that bedside transmitters for pacemakers and implantable defibrillators could be made to deliver 830-volt shocks from tens of feet away. Medtronic changed its designs, and an official of the US Food and Drug Administration (FDA) credited his work with contributing importantly to progress in the field. He died a week before he was due to present new heart-device research at Black Hat in 2013. His method was the public demonstration, made after the vendor had been told: he said his aim was to make people look again at systems presumed locked down.
barnaby-jack.depth:
Who he was. Barnaby Jack was a New Zealand-born researcher whose subject, across a short career, was software that runs inside machines: kernel drivers, cash dispensers, insulin pumps and cardiac implants. He mattered to security less for any single bug than for showing, on stage and in front of the vendors, that embedded devices trusted with money and lives had been built without the defensive engineering that ordinary operating systems had been forced to adopt. He said as much in 2010: the companies that make ATMs are not Microsoft, and have not had ten years of continuous attack to teach them.

Kernel exploitation. His first reputation was in Windows exploitation; Stuart McClure, who later worked with him at McAfee, had given him one of his first jobs, and by 2005 he was at eEye. In February 2005 eEye's Marc Maiffret introduced his paper 'Remote Windows Kernel Exploitation: Step Into the Ring 0', recalling that more than five years earlier Jack had written a seminal paper on Windows buffer overflow exploitation; the new one argued that as host-based security products moved code into the kernel, kernel drivers were not getting the scrutiny applied to user-mode code. He presented it at Black Hat USA 2005.

ATMs. In 2009 he was due to show ATM vulnerabilities at Black Hat, but his employer, Juniper Networks, cancelled the talk weeks before the conference after an unnamed ATM vendor raised concerns; Jack later said it was pulled because patches were not yet available. On 28 July 2010, by then at IOActive, he brought two retail ATMs, made by Tranax and Triton and both running Windows CE, onto the Black Hat stage. Against the Tranax he used an authentication bypass in the remote monitoring feature, reachable over the internet or dial-up and enabled by default, with a tool he called Dillinger, to upload a rootkit he called Scrooge; a key sequence or a special card then opened a hidden menu, and the machine paid out 50 bills under the word 'Jackpot!'. Scrooge also captured the magnetic-stripe data of other customers' cards. The Triton fell to physical access: a single key, sold online, opened the front panel of every machine of that model, and a Universal Serial Bus (USB) stick installed the same malware. He estimated that about 95 per cent of retail ATMs were on dial-up and could be found by war-dialing or by querying Internet Protocol (IP) addresses, said he had found a game-over flaw in every ATM he had examined, four for four, and asked manufacturers for better locks, executable signing at kernel level and rigorous code review. Both vendors had patched before the talk. The result was what he called jackpotting, and a clip of the demonstration had been viewed more than 2.6 million times by 2013.

Insulin pumps. At McAfee he turned to medical devices. At the Hacker Halted conference in Miami in October 2011 he showed that Medtronic insulin pumps, which communicate on 900 MHz without encryption, could be located within 300 feet by a custom antenna and software, which answered with their serial numbers; earlier research by Jerome Radcliffe at DEF CON that year had needed the serial number in advance. His software overrode the restriction on wireless dose commands and suppressed the vibration and tone that warn the patient, so that a pump could be made to deliver its whole reservoir of about 300 units. Medtronic said it was evaluating encryption and would set up an industry working group, while maintaining that the risk of a deliberate attack was low.

Heart devices. Back at IOActive, as director of embedded device security, he presented at the Breakpoint conference in Melbourne in October 2012 an attack on the bedside transmitters that had replaced the programming wand for pacemakers and implantable cardioverter-defibrillators (ICDs). A special wireless command made devices within about 30 to 50 feet return their model and serial numbers, which was enough to authenticate to them; from a laptop he could rewrite firmware and trigger 830-volt shocks. In the transmitter software he found no obfuscation and even credentials for what appeared to be the manufacturer's development server, which led him to describe a worst case of a compromised programmer spreading rogue firmware from implant to implant. He notified the manufacturers, did not name them, and said his aim was to make them review the security of their code and not only the traditional safety mechanisms.

Death and the disputes around it. He was found dead at his home in San Francisco on 25 July 2013, a week before he was due to present 'Implantable Medical Devices: Hacking Humans' at Black Hat on 1 August; police ruled out foul play, and an autopsy released in January 2014 found an accidental overdose of several drugs with no sign of trauma. Black Hat left his session empty in his memory. The timing produced speculation that the record does not support, and a related story deserves correcting: in October 2013 the former US Vice President Dick Cheney said his doctor had disabled the wireless function of his defibrillator in 2007, years before Jack's heart-device work, so that decision cannot have been a response to it. The other argument he left behind is about method. Vendors such as Medtronic stressed how low the real-world risk was; Jack's position was that a public demonstration, after notification, was what made manufacturers act. Reuters reported in 2013 that his insulin pump research had prompted Medtronic to revamp the way it designs its products, and William Maisel of the Food and Drug Administration (FDA) said the work of Jack and others had contributed importantly to progress in the field.

wall-of-sheep.def: The DEF CON installation that sniffs the conference network for credentials sent in the clear and projects the partially masked usernames on a giant screen, for everyone to see and laugh at.
wall-of-sheep.context: It is education by public embarrassment, and it worked: a generation of professionals learned what a plaintext protocol really means by watching colleagues appear on the wall. The Wall is also a quiet historical record of encryption's spread - it used to fill up in minutes with mail and web logins, and the rise of ubiquitous TLS slowly starved it. DEF CON's broader folklore lives in the same spirit: the hostile network you are warned never to trust, the badge that is a hardware puzzle, and the Spot the Fed game.

pwnie-awards.def: The security industry's annual awards, handed out at Black Hat since 2007 as a gold-painted toy pony - honouring the year's best server-side and client-side bugs alongside categories no one wants to win, chiefly Lamest Vendor Response and Most Epic Fail.
pwnie-awards.context: The Pwnies are the field's self-policing mechanism dressed as a joke: a vendor that bullies a researcher or dismisses a real bug gets its name read aloud to a ballroom of the people it depends on. Winning the technical categories is a genuine career marker; the shame categories have changed disclosure behaviour more than several regulations.

pwn2own.def: The hacking contest founded at CanSecWest in 2007 where researchers compromise fully patched software - browsers, operating systems, phones, and later cars - live, for cash and for the device itself. Working exploits are handed to the vendors under coordinated disclosure.
pwn2own.context: It began as an argument: a Mac was put on a table with a sign saying take it if you can, after years of claims that the platform was immune. Pwn2Own turned the zero-day into a legitimate market with rules, gave vendors a hard annual deadline they cannot spin, and is where much of the public evidence about browser and phone security actually comes from.

wargames.def: The film in which a Seattle teenager dials into what he thinks is a games company and reaches a NORAD war-planning computer, nearly starting a nuclear exchange before teaching the machine that some games cannot be won.
wargames.context: No other work of fiction has moved computer security further. President Reagan watched it, asked his Joint Chiefs whether it could really happen, and the answer led to NSDD-145, the first US national policy on computer security, with the Computer Fraud and Abuse Act arriving in its wake. It gave the world the phrase war dialing, the sentence 'Shall we play a game?', and a generation's decision to get a modem. Its release also coincided with the 414s arrests, so the newspapers had a real story and a movie poster on the same week.

sneakers-film.def: The caper film about a team of physical and technical penetration testers hired to steal a black box that breaks all cryptography - written with real cryptographers consulting, and beloved by the field for getting the work right.
sneakers-film.context: It is the most technically respectable hacker movie ever made: the tradecraft is social engineering, dumpster diving, lock bypass and tailgating rather than neon typing, and the crew is a plausible red team decades before the term went mainstream. The anagram Setec Astronomy - too many secrets - and the closing 'It's all about the information' still get quoted in talks, and the film is routinely the answer when practitioners are asked which movie their job actually resembles.

hackers-film.def: The rollerblading, neon-soaked teen movie whose depiction of hacking is almost entirely fantasy and whose cultural influence on hackers is almost entirely real - source of the war cry 'Hack the planet!'
hackers-film.context: Practitioners mock it and quote it in the same breath. Underneath the flying 3D filesystems it gets two things exactly right: that social engineering and dumpster diving beat technical wizardry most days, and that the underground was a social scene before it was a profession. Its promotional website was famously defaced by real hackers within days, which is the most fitting review any film has ever received.

hackers-heroes-book.def: Steven Levy's history of the first three hacker generations - the MIT model-railroad and PDP crowd, the Homebrew hardware builders, and the early game programmers - and the book that first wrote down the hacker ethic.
hackers-heroes-book.context: Levy's principles are the field's oldest creed: access to computers should be unlimited and hands-on, all information should be free, mistrust authority and promote decentralization, judge hackers by their hacking rather than their credentials, and computers can change your life for the better. Every argument about open source, disclosure and platform control since has been an argument with this list.

the-art-of-deception.def: Kevin Mitnick's first book after prison: a collection of social-engineering stories, each dissected into the technique that made it work and the control that would have stopped it. The thesis is one line - the human is the vulnerability no patch reaches.
the-art-of-deception.context: It turned social engineering from folklore into a teachable discipline with named moves: pretexting, authority, urgency, reciprocity, the helpful stranger. Security-awareness training as an industry essentially descends from this book, and its case studies are still the ones instructors reach for. Mitnick's later Ghost in the Wires tells the same life from the inside, as a chase story.

underground-book.def: Suelette Dreyfus's narrative history of the Australian computer underground of the late 1980s and early 1990s, researched by a young hacker known as Mendax - later the world's most recognizable name in leaking, Julian Assange.
underground-book.context: The book is the best surviving portrait of a national scene that never got Hollywood's attention: the International Subversives, the NASA and Nortel intrusions, the WANK worm's likely birthplace, and the police work that ended it. It was released free online years before that was normal, and it remains the standard answer when someone asks what the underground actually felt like from inside.

countdown-to-zero-day.def: Kim Zetter's reconstruction of Stuxnet: how a worm carrying four zero-days crossed an air gap into Natanz, spun Iranian centrifuges to destruction while replaying recorded normal readings to the operators, and was found only because it escaped into the wild.
countdown-to-zero-day.context: The book is the field's standard account of the first cyberweapon to cause physical damage, and of the analysis - largely by antivirus researchers in Belarus, Russia and Germany - that reverse-engineered a nation-state operation from a sample. It is also the clearest telling of the argument the incident opened and never closed: once a state builds and loses control of such a tool, everyone lives in the blast radius.

anonymous.def: The leaderless online collective that emerged from imageboard culture around 2003 and became, from 2008, the public face of hacktivism, identified by the Guy Fawkes mask and the line 'We are Legion.' Anyone can act as Anonymous, which is the point and the problem.
anonymous.context: Project Chanology against Scientology in 2008 moved it from pranks to protest; Operation Payback defended WikiLeaks by knocking payment processors offline; later operations touched Tunisia, Egypt, police departments and accounts of the Islamic State (ISIS). Having no membership makes it impossible to disband and impossible to hold accountable: actions range from genuine whistleblowing to mistaken doxxing of innocent people. Its subgroups and splinters, LulzSec above all, ended in arrests built on informants. In networking the same word also names unauthenticated access: anonymous cipher suites, anonymous File Transfer Protocol (FTP) and the anonymous outer identity of 802.1X.
anonymous.depth:
The collective: where it came from. Anonymous began in 2003 on 4chan, an imageboard where posting without a name was the default, and the name came from that anonymity: the joke was that the crowd posting as Anonymous was one entity, a hive mind. Users of its /b/ board organized mass pranks, such as the raid of 12 July 2006 in which identical avatars blocked regular members of the Finnish social network Habbo Hotel from its virtual pool. The few rules that later circulated were not to disclose one's identity, not to talk about the group and not to attack the media, and the tagline that became its signature runs: We are Anonymous. We are Legion. We do not forgive. We do not forget. Expect us. When United States prosecutors described it in March 2012 they called it a loose confederation of computer hackers and others, active since at least 2008, which is as close to a definition as an organization without members can get.

Project Chanology, 2008: from pranks to protest. On 15 January 2008 the blog Gawker posted a video of Tom Cruise praising Scientology, and the Church answered with a copyright cease-and-desist letter. 4chan users retaliated with prank calls, black faxes meant to waste ink, and distributed denial-of-service (DDoS) attacks on Church websites, first with general-purpose load tools and within days with the Low Orbit Ion Cannon (LOIC), a stress-testing program that flooded a server with TCP (Transmission Control Protocol) or UDP (User Datagram Protocol) packets. LOIC became the signature weapon and the cause of many arrests, because it did nothing to hide the user's Internet Protocol (IP) address, a fact some channel operators misrepresented to new volunteers. On 10 February 2008 thousands joined protests outside Scientology buildings in 142 cities in 43 countries. Because the protesters were meant to stay anonymous, they wore masks, and the one available everywhere was the Guy Fawkes mask from the 2006 film V for Vendetta. The British Broadcasting Corporation (BBC) traced it to the image David Lloyd drew for Alan Moore's graphic novel and noted the irony that Warner Bros, which made the masks to promote the film, profits from every one sold.

Operation Payback, 2010: the WikiLeaks campaign. The operation began in September 2010 against anti-piracy firms and turned in December, after WikiLeaks began releasing United States diplomatic cables and Amazon, PayPal, MasterCard and Visa cut it off. On 8 December attacks took PayPal.com down for an hour and disrupted the Visa and MasterCard sites. According to one participant the LOIC volunteers did little and two hackers' botnets did most of the work, a claim others dispute. PayPal put its cost at 5.5 million US dollars and gave the Federal Bureau of Investigation (FBI) the IP addresses of 1,000 attackers, which led to at least 14 arrests; on 5 December 2013, 13 of the PayPal 14 pleaded guilty. The prosecutors' 2012 account confirms the frame: members took responsibility for denial-of-service attacks on Visa, MasterCard and PayPal as retaliation for their refusal to process donations to WikiLeaks.

After 2010: a widening range, and the failures. Operation Tunisia began in January 2011 in support of the uprising, with a script to protect Tunisians' browsers from government surveillance and attacks that took government websites offline; Operation Egypt followed with the activist group Telecomix. On 5 November 2013 the Million Mask March gathered protesters in 400 cities. The failures belong in the same account, because the same structure produced them. During the Ferguson protests of August 2014, an Anonymous account published what it said was the name of the police officer who had shot Michael Brown; the police said the name was wrong, and Twitter suspended the account. After the Paris attacks of November 2015 the collective declared war on ISIS and claimed to have taken down 3,824 accounts, then more than 5,000, then 20,000; the published list included the accounts of Barack Obama, Hillary Clinton, The New York Times and BBC News.

LulzSec, and how it ended. In May 2011 a handful of people behind the earlier attacks on the security firm HBGary formed Lulz Security, LulzSec. The Department of Justice's charges of 6 March 2012 list what they and the predecessor group Internet Feds did: hacks of Fine Gael, an Irish political party; of HBGary and HBGary Federal, with data on 80,000 user accounts; of Fox, with data on more than 70,000 X-Factor contestants; of PBS (the Public Broadcasting Service), in retaliation for a Frontline programme; of Sony Pictures, with data on about 100,000 users; and of Bethesda Softworks, with about 200,000. The same release disclosed that Hector Xavier Monsegur, known as Sabu, had pleaded guilty on 15 August 2011 to a 12-count information; he had been arrested in secret on 7 June 2011, during the group's 50 days of lulz, which it declared over on 26 June, and worked as an informant from then on. The Stratfor intrusion of December 2011, by the AntiSec offshoot, took account data on about 860,000 subscribers and 60,000 credit cards, with more than 700,000 dollars in fraudulent charges. A movement with no vetting was rolled up through one person, and the people identified were caught by ordinary operational mistakes.

What the structure means. The absence of membership is the design and the weakness at once. Nobody can expel anyone, so nothing done under the mask can be disowned; nobody can be held to account, so every legitimate action shares a name with harassment and with mistaken accusations; and anyone can borrow the brand, which is why claims made under it need the same scepticism as claims made by any anonymous source. For defenders the lesson of the decade is operational: most Anonymous-branded attacks were denial of service and SQL (Structured Query Language) injection against neglected web applications, and most of the people prosecuted were identified through addresses, reused handles and an informant, not through any technical brilliance on either side.

The technical sense: anonymous means unauthenticated. In Transport Layer Security (TLS), anonymous key exchange is Diffie-Hellman in which neither side is authenticated. RFC 5246 (Request for Comments 5246), the TLS 1.2 specification of August 2008, lists the DH_anon cipher suites, such as TLS_DH_anon_WITH_AES_128_CBC_SHA (0x00,0x34), warns that the mode is vulnerable to man-in-the-middle attacks and protects only against passive eavesdropping, says the suites MUST NOT be used unless the application explicitly asks for anonymous key exchange, and adds that a non-anonymous key exchange whose certificate is never verified is equivalent to an anonymous one. Anonymous FTP, described in RFC 1635 of May 1994, is an account literally called anonymous that archive sites created for public retrieval: limited rights, usually no uploads, and any string accepted as the password, by convention guest or the user's e-mail address. In 802.1X networks, RFC 7542 (May 2015) on the Network Access Identifier notes that the current practice in tunnelled EAP (Extensible Authentication Protocol) methods such as TTLS (Tunneled Transport Layer Security) is an outer identity of the form anonymous@realm, which lets the visited network route the request to the home domain without learning the username, while the real identity travels inside the protected inner exchange.

The legal sense: anonymity is a threshold, not a label. The General Data Protection Regulation (GDPR), in recital 26, does not apply to anonymous information, meaning data that does not relate to an identifiable person, but treats pseudonymized data that can be attributed to a person with additional information as personal data, and judges identifiability by all the means reasonably likely to be used, singling out included, taking into account cost, time and the technology available. The collective's own history is the best illustration of why that bar is high: thousands of volunteers believed they were anonymous while their tool sent their IP addresses to the target.

lulzsec.def: Lulz Security (LulzSec), the six-person splinter from Anonymous that ran a fifty-day spree in 2011 (Sony Pictures, PBS, the CIA's public site, an FBI affiliate, games companies), announcing each breach on Twitter under a cartoon logo and mocking the victims' security, until its best-known member turned out to be an FBI informant.
lulzsec.context: Technically most of it was ordinary SQL (Structured Query Language) injection against neglected websites and denial of service from botnets, which was the uncomfortable lesson: the systems were that easy. The ending is the darker lesson. The leader, Sabu, had been arrested early, pleaded guilty in August 2011 and kept running the crew online as a cooperating witness for the Federal Bureau of Investigation (FBI), which is how the charges arrived all at once in March 2012. LulzSec is the standard case study in how a movement with no accountability structure gets rolled up through one person.
lulzsec.depth:
Where it came from. LulzSec grew out of Anonymous, the leaderless collective that has its own entry. According to the charges the United States Department of Justice unsealed on 6 March 2012, a smaller crew calling itself Internet Feds had already broken into the website of the Irish political party Fine Gael, into the security firms HBGary and HBGary Federal, from which it took data on 80,000 user accounts, and into systems of Fox Broadcasting, from which it took data on more than 70,000 people who had applied to the talent show X-Factor. In May 2011, after the publicity those attacks brought, four of its members formed a new group, Lulz Security; the prosecutors name Hector Xavier Monsegur, known as Sabu, Ryan Ackroyd (Kayla), Jake Davis (Topiary) and Darren Martyn (pwnsauce) as its principal members. The group's own farewell statement and later reporting put its core at six people. The name came from lulz, internet slang for laughs at someone else's expense, and the motto was Laughing at your security since 2011.

The fifty days. Between May and late June 2011 the group published a steady stream of breaches and outages, announced on its Twitter account, which Davis ran as its publicist, and on a website decorated with ASCII-art boats. The Department of Justice lists the hack of the Public Broadcasting Service (PBS), in retaliation for what the group saw as an unfavourable episode of the news programme Frontline, after which it posted a false story that two dead rappers were alive; the theft of data on about 100,000 users of Sony Pictures Entertainment's website; and the theft of data on about 200,000 users of the games company Bethesda Softworks. Monsegur's guilty plea also covered the hack of InfraGard Members Alliance, an organization affiliated with the FBI, whose Atlanta chapter site the group defaced. On 13 June it published data from a server behind the United States Senate's public website, which Senate officials said did not compromise the Senate's network. On 15 June it claimed a denial-of-service outage of cia.gov with the message Tango down; the site was back within two hours. Games companies and services, among them Nintendo and EVE Online, and the United Kingdom's Serious Organised Crime Agency (SOCA) were hit by denial of service, and on 23 June the group dumped documents from the Arizona Department of Public Safety. On 26 June it announced that the fifty days were over and the group was disbanding; on 18 July some of the same people redirected visitors of The Sun's website to a fake story that Rupert Murdoch had died. With Anonymous it also launched Operation AntiSec, whose name was later carried by the crew that breached Stratfor.

How it was done. Little of it was sophisticated, which is the part defenders remember. The group worked by finding badly secured websites and taking what they exposed, using well-known techniques such as SQL (Structured Query Language) injection; the breach of Sony Pictures' film website, for which two associates were later sentenced, was an SQL injection. Its outages came from distributed denial of service (DDoS): a British associate supplied a botnet of around 100,000 compromised computers that, the court in London heard, he also sold access to for up to 2,500 pounds a month. Much of the damage came from publishing what was taken: e-mail addresses and passwords released as torrents and on file-sharing sites, whose reuse on other services security professionals singled out as the real danger. The lesson for an engineer is the boring one: parameterized queries, input validation, a web application firewall in front of legacy applications, hashed and salted passwords, and capacity or a scrubbing service against floods would have stopped most of the fifty days.

The informant. Monsegur had been arrested in June 2011, in the middle of the spree. He pleaded guilty on 15 August 2011 to a twelve-count information (computer hacking conspiracies, computer hacking, hacking in furtherance of fraud, conspiracy to commit access device fraud and bank fraud, and aggravated identity theft) under a cooperation agreement, and at the government's direction went back online. The plea stayed sealed until 6 March 2012, when the Department of Justice charged Ackroyd, Davis, Martyn and Donncha O'Cearbhaill with computer hacking conspiracy, O'Cearbhaill also with disclosing an intercepted communication: in January 2012 he had broken into the personal e-mail account of an officer of the Irish police, the Garda, who had forwarded work messages to a personal account, and so recorded and leaked an international conference call between the FBI, the Garda and others about the investigation of Anonymous. The day before, Jeremy Hammond of the AntiSec offshoot had been arrested in Chicago for the December 2011 breach of the intelligence firm Stratfor, which exposed account data of about 860,000 subscribers and 60,000 credit cards used for more than 700,000 dollars of fraudulent charges. When Monsegur was sentenced on 27 May 2014, prosecutors said his cooperation had let them identify, locate and arrest eight co-conspirators, including Hammond, and prevent or mitigate more than 300 planned attacks; Judge Loretta Preska called it truly extraordinary and sentenced him to time served (he had served seven months) and one year of supervised release.

The sentences. In London, at Southwark Crown Court on 16 May 2013, Judge Deborah Taylor sentenced four people who had pleaded guilty, saying they had wreaked havoc and destruction while hiding behind aliases and seeking maximum publicity: Ryan Cleary, the botnet supplier, who also admitted breaking into United States Air Force systems, received 32 months; Ackroyd, who had searched for vulnerable sites under the persona Kayla and admitted stealing data from Sony, 30 months; Davis, the group's publicist, 24 months in a young offenders' institution; and Mustafa Al-Bassam (tflow), still at school at the time of the attacks, a 20-month suspended sentence with 300 hours of unpaid work. The prosecution described the group as seeing themselves as latter-day pirates driven by anarchic self-amusement. In the United States, Cody Kretsinger (recursion) received a year and a day in April 2013 and Raynaldo Rivera (neuron) 366 days in August 2013, with 13 months of home detention, 1,000 hours of community service and 605,663 dollars of restitution to Sony Pictures, for the Sony Pictures breach; neither was in the core group. Hammond, for Stratfor and other intrusions, received ten years on 15 November 2013.

Why it is still taught. LulzSec is the standard case study in how a movement with no accountability structure gets rolled up through one person: a group whose members knew each other only by handles could not vet anyone, so the moment its most trusted member was compromised the whole network was visible to the people watching him. It is also a lesson about attention. The group's power came from publicity, every breach timed and announced for maximum effect, and the same publicity brought the FBI, Scotland Yard's e-crime unit and the Irish Garda together against it. For defenders the uncomfortable conclusion of 2011 holds: the targets were large organizations with security budgets, and what failed was basic hygiene on public web applications, password storage and reuse, and capacity against floods, not exotic defences against exotic attacks.

shadow-brokers.def: The unidentified group that in 2016 and 2017 published stolen offensive tooling attributed to the elite hacking unit of the United States National Security Agency (NSA), first exploits for firewalls from Cisco, Fortinet and others, then Windows exploits including EternalBlue, which attacks the Server Message Block (SMB) file-sharing protocol.
shadow-brokers.context: The Shadow Brokers appeared on 13 August 2016 offering to auction what they said were the cyber weapons of the Equation Group, the threat actor Kaspersky had exposed in 2015 and that is widely tied to the NSA (National Security Agency); Kaspersky's analysis of the sample confirmed the link within days. The consequences arrived after the Windows dump of 14 April 2017: EternalBlue powered WannaCry in May 2017 and NotPetya a month later, which the White House called the most destructive and costly cyberattack in history, striking hospitals, ports and factories that had nothing to do with intelligence work. The leak is the defining case in the vulnerabilities equities debate: a government stockpiling secret flaws is one custody failure away from arming everyone, and this is the case where that actually happened.
shadow-brokers.depth:
What the name covers. The Shadow Brokers is the name an anonymous person or group used, from August 2016 to 2017, to publish and try to sell hacking tools it said it had taken from the Equation Group, the threat actor that Kaspersky researchers had described in 2015 as one of the most advanced hacking operations ever found, with links to the Stuxnet and Flame platforms. Several outlets noted that the name probably comes from a character in the Mass Effect video games, an information broker who always sells to the highest bidder. The tools themselves came to be attributed to the Tailored Access Operations unit of the United States National Security Agency (NSA); Microsoft's president wrote in May 2017 that the exploits used by WannaCry had been drawn from those stolen from the NSA. Who the Shadow Brokers were, and how they obtained the material, has never been established on the public record: in 2019 David Aitel, a computer scientist formerly employed by the NSA, summed up the state of knowledge as not knowing whether even the most common theory, Russian involvement, was right.

The first dump, and the auction. On 13 August 2016 a Twitter account announced a Pastebin page, a GitHub repository and a Tumblr post in broken English: the group said it had followed Equation Group traffic, hacked it and found many cyber weapons, and it offered to auction them for one million bitcoins, then worth more than 500 million dollars. A free sample of about 256 megabytes came with the offer. Researchers who looked at it on the first day found mostly batch and Python scripts, dated most recently to 2013, with implants and exploits for routers and firewalls from Cisco, Juniper, Fortinet's FortiGate and the Chinese vendor Topsec; many doubted the sale was ever the point and read the release as an attempt to embarrass the United States government, possibly obtained from a staging or command-and-control server rather than from the unit's own networks. On 16 August Kaspersky settled the authenticity question with a cryptographic fingerprint: more than 300 files in the archive implemented the RC5 and RC6 ciphers in 24 forms using the unusual negative constant minus 0x61C88647, functionally identical to the code in known Equation Group malware, which led the firm to state with a high degree of confidence that the tools were related.

What it meant for network engineers. The first dump was about the network edge, not desktops. Cisco was alerted to the postings on 15 August 2016 and on 17 August published advisory cisco-sa-20160817-asa-snmp, CVE-2016-6366: a buffer overflow in the Simple Network Management Protocol (SNMP) code of the Adaptive Security Appliance (ASA) software that could reload the device or execute code, affecting SNMP versions 1, 2c and 3, triggered only by IPv4 traffic sent to the device and requiring the attacker to know the SNMP community string or, for version 3, valid credentials. The advisory stated that the exploit had been publicly disclosed by the alleged Shadow Brokers group, listed the ASA 5500 and 5500-X, the ASAv, Firepower appliances running ASA or Firepower Threat Defense and the Industrial Security Appliance 3000 among the affected platforms, and noted that the Firewall Services Module and PIX firewalls were past end of software support and would get no fix. Fortinet published FG-IR-16-023 the same day, CVE-2016-6909: a cookie parser buffer overflow in FortiOS firmware released before August 2012 (4.3.8 and earlier, 4.2.12 and earlier, 4.1.10 and earlier, and FortiSwitch 3.4.2 and earlier) that a crafted HTTP request could use to take over execution, with FortiOS 5.x not affected. The flaw had been reported to Fortinet in August 2012 and fixed in 4.3.9, so the dump weaponized a four-year-old bug against devices nobody had upgraded. The workarounds both vendors gave are the lasting lesson: SNMP restricted to known managers with strong credentials, and administrative HTTP and HTTPS access disabled or limited to a short list of trusted hosts.

Going dark, and coming back. On 31 October 2016 the group published a list of servers it said the Equation Group had compromised, with the names of seven further tools. On 12 January 2017 it posted a farewell: it was deleting its accounts after its offer to release the whole cache for 10,000 bitcoins, then more than 8.2 million dollars, had found no buyer, and as a parting shot it published 61 Windows binaries, of which only one had previously been uploaded to the VirusTotal scanning service and many of which the most widely used malware defences did not detect. The silence lasted three months. On 8 April 2017 a post on its Medium account released the password to the encrypted archive of the year before, saying it was partly a response to the United States strike on a Syrian airfield.

The Windows dump of 14 April 2017. The next release, on the Friday before the Easter weekend, was close to 300 megabytes and was immediately called the most damaging yet: compiled exploits for a long line of Windows versions with names such as ETERNALBLUE, ETERNALROMANCE, ETERNALSYNERGY and ETERNALCHAMPION against Server Message Block (SMB), EXPLODINGCAN against IIS 6.0, ESTEEMAUDIT against Remote Desktop on Windows XP and Server 2003 and ESKIMOROLL against Kerberos on domain controllers, a framework called FUZZBUNCH that loads them much as Metasploit loads modules, and evidence of intrusions into the SWIFT banking systems of several banks. Microsoft's Security Response Center answered the next day that most of the exploits were already patched: EternalBlue, EternalChampion, EternalRomance and EternalSynergy by bulletin MS17-010 of 14 March 2017, others by updates going back to MS08-067 and MS09-050, while three (EnglishmanDentist, EsteemAudit and ExplodingCan) did not reproduce on supported platforms, meaning Windows 7 and later or Exchange 2010 and later. Ars Technica corrected its first report accordingly: none of the exploits was a zero-day against supported Microsoft products. That a fix had shipped a month before the leak led to speculation that Microsoft had been tipped off in advance.

What the tools did next. Unpatched machines are what turned a leak into a catastrophe. EternalBlue carries kernel shellcode that loads the DoublePulsar backdoor, and more than 200,000 systems were reported infected with tools from the April dump within two weeks. On 12 May 2017 WannaCry used EternalBlue to spread as a worm; Microsoft's president Brad Smith wrote two days later that, although the patch had been out since 14 March, many computers remained unpatched, so hospitals, businesses, governments and home computers were affected. On 27 June 2017 NotPetya arrived through a Ukrainian accounting software update and spread inside networks with stolen credentials and with EternalBlue (CVE-2017-0144) and EternalRomance (CVE-2017-0145); in February 2018 the White House attributed it to the Russian military and called it the most destructive and costly cyberattack in history, with billions of dollars of damage across Europe, Asia and the Americas. Microsoft's advice that June is the defender's summary of the whole episode: install MS17-010, disable SMBv1, block SMB on port 445 at the router or firewall, and consider blocking ports 139 and 445 between machines with no reason to share files. Both outbreaks have their own entries.

The equities argument. Brad Smith used WannaCry to argue against the stockpiling of vulnerabilities by governments: exploits in the hands of governments had repeatedly leaked into the public domain and caused widespread damage, and the equivalent with conventional weapons would be the United States military having some of its Tomahawk missiles stolen. Microsoft's call was for governments to report vulnerabilities to vendors rather than stockpile, sell or exploit them. The United States government's answer came on 15 November 2017, when the White House published the unclassified charter of its Vulnerabilities Equities Policy and Process (VEP), the interagency procedure for deciding whether to disclose a newly found flaw or restrict it temporarily for national security and law enforcement purposes such as intelligence collection and military operations. The charter states that in the vast majority of cases responsibly disclosing a newly discovered vulnerability is clearly in the national interest, creates an Equities Review Board that meets monthly, makes the NSA the process's executive secretariat and requires an annual report. Whatever one thinks of the balance it strikes, the Shadow Brokers case is the one both sides cite: a government that keeps secret flaws is one custody failure away from arming everyone, and here that failure happened.

Lessons that outlast the drama. Three are worth carrying into any network. Patch latency is the real exposure window: the Windows exploits were fixed a month before they leaked and still caused the two outbreaks, and the firewall exploit Fortinet had fixed in 2012 was still usable in 2016 against devices left on old firmware. End of support is a security property: Cisco's advisory had no fix to offer for the PIX and the Firewall Services Module. And management planes are attack surface: the August dump went after SNMP and administrative web interfaces, which is why management access belongs on a separate, filtered network with SNMP restricted to known pollers and strong credentials. The names worth remembering are 13 August 2016 for the first post, 17 August 2016 for the Cisco and Fortinet advisories, 14 March 2017 for MS17-010, 14 April 2017 for the Windows dump, 12 May and 27 June 2017 for WannaCry and NotPetya, and 15 November 2017 for the published VEP charter.

hacktivism.def: Hacking done to make a political or social point rather than money, from website defacements and denial-of-service floods to leaks and tools that get around censorship; the word is usually credited to Omega, a member of the Cult of the Dead Cow, who used it in an e-mail to the group in 1996.
hacktivism.context: Its own practitioners have argued about its methods from the start. The Electronic Disturbance Theater's FloodNet virtual sit-ins of 1998 and the Electrohippies' action against the World Trade Organization in 1999 presented mass page-reloading as the online counterpart of a street sit-in; Oxblood Ruffin of the Cult of the Dead Cow answered that blocking a website silences its owner, and defined hacktivism as using technology to improve human rights across electronic media. American and British courts treated the floods of Anonymous and the intrusions of LulzSec as computer crime, and states have since hidden behind hacktivist personas: a 2018 US indictment says Russian military intelligence invented Guccifer 2.0, which claimed to be a lone Romanian hacker.
hacktivism.depth:
The word. The coinage is usually credited to Omega, a member of the Cult of the Dead Cow (cDc), who used it in an e-mail to the group in 1996, partly in jest, for hacking with a political purpose; Wikipedia records an earlier printed use, in a 1995 Minneapolis magazine article about Shu Lea Cheang's film Fresh Kill. Oxblood Ruffin, the cDc's 'chief evangelist for hacktivism', set out to narrow it. Taking Article 19 of the Universal Declaration of Human Rights as the hook, he defined hacktivism as 'using technology to improve human rights across electronic media', and in a paper given at Yale Law School in 2004 he excluded web defacement and denial of service (DoS) by name, since both abridge the expression of whoever runs the target.

Precursors and sit-ins. The motive is older than the name: in October 1989, as the Computer Emergency Response Team (CERT) at Carnegie Mellon University reported, a worm crossing a National Aeronautics and Space Administration (NASA) network over DECnet set system announcements to a banner reading Worms Against Nuclear Killers. The Electronic Disturbance Theater, co-founded by Ricardo Dominguez, wrote FloodNet, a Java applet that reloaded a target page over and over, and from April 1998 staged virtual sit-ins with it in solidarity with the Zapatistas, against the website of Mexico's President Zedillo and, on 9 September 1998, against the Pentagon and the Frankfurt Stock Exchange as well. In December 1999 five British activists, the Electrohippies, ran a virtual sit-in against the World Trade Organization during the Seattle protests and estimated that more than 452,000 people joined it.

Hacktivismo. Ruffin drafted the framework of Hacktivismo, a cDc offshoot, at DEF CON in 1999, and it grew into an international group of technologists, lawyers, human-rights workers and artists building tools for people behind national firewalls, among them Peekabooty, for reaching the open web, and Camera/Shy, which hid censored material in innocuous web pages by steganography. Its declaration, which Ruffin drafted in June 2000 and Fred von Lohmann of the Electronic Frontier Foundation (EFF) helped to tighten, was published on 4 July 2001; it holds that 'state sponsored censorship of the Internet erodes peaceful and civilized coexistence, affects the exercise of democracy, and endangers the socioeconomic development of nations.'

The constructive strand. Tor was funded by the EFF from 2004, became a non-profit in 2006, began building bridges around government firewalls in 2007 and, by its own account, was instrumental during the Arab Spring. The Citizen Lab of the University of Toronto released Psiphon as open-source software in December 2006 so that people could give friends and family behind censorship a way out. SecureDrop, the open-source system through which whistleblowers send documents to newsrooms, began as DeadDrop, written by Aaron Swartz in 2012; the Freedom of the Press Foundation took it over in October 2013.

Anonymous and LulzSec. Anonymous's Project Chanology took on the Church of Scientology in 2008 with flooding software, prank calls and black faxes, then with masked street pickets in several countries. Its Operation Payback, aimed at organizations fighting file-sharing, hit PayPal from 6 to 10 December 2010 as Operation Avenge Assange, after the company stopped handling donations to WikiLeaks. On 19 July 2011 the Federal Bureau of Investigation (FBI) arrested 14 people over the PayPal attacks, and 13 pleaded guilty in December 2013. In March 2012 prosecutors revealed that Hector Xavier Monsegur, known as Sabu, who had founded LulzSec with three others in May 2011, had pleaded guilty the previous August and was cooperating; in May 2014 he was sentenced to time served, the judge citing help that disrupted hundreds of attacks. Jeremy Hammond, of AntiSec, another Anonymous offshoot, received 10 years in November 2013 for the hack of the intelligence firm Stratfor, and in London in May 2013 three British LulzSec members and an associate received sentences from 20 months suspended to 32 months.

Borrowed masks. In July 2018 a US grand jury indicted 12 officers of Russia's military intelligence service, the GRU (Main Intelligence Directorate), and the Department of Justice said they had invented Guccifer 2.0, a persona that falsely claimed to be a lone Romanian hacker. In April 2024 Mandiant reported that the same service's sabotage unit Sandworm, which it now designates Advanced Persistent Threat 44 (APT44), cultivates hacktivist identities for its information operations, from Anonymous Poland and Guccifer 2.0 to the Telegram channels XakNet Team, CyberArmyofRussia_Reborn and Solntsepek. In January 2024 CyberArmyofRussia_Reborn, which Google's Threat Analysis Group assesses APT44 created and controls, posted videos claiming to manipulate controls at Polish and American water utilities, claims Mandiant could not independently verify.

Protest or crime. The PayPal defendants were charged with conspiracy and with intentional damage to a protected computer, which the Computer Fraud and Abuse Act (CFAA), 18 U.S.C. 1030, defines as knowingly transmitting a program, information, code or command and thereby intentionally causing damage without authorization; that count carries up to 10 years. Defenders argue from civil disobedience: Dominguez set the virtual sit-in beside Gandhi, Martin Luther King Jr and Thoreau as blockage that disrupts the everyday flow of power; the Electrohippies called such actions directly analogous to street demonstrations, with a democratic guarantee in the mass participation they require; and a 2013 petition on the White House website likened distributed denial of service (DDoS) to an Occupy protest, gathering 6,048 of the 25,000 signatures it needed. Critics answer that blocking a site silences its owner: Ruffin compared DoS to shouting someone down at a town-hall meeting; in 1998 the cDc, the L0pht, the Chaos Computer Club, 2600 and Phrack rebuked a group that had declared cyberwar on Iraq and China, since 'one cannot legitimately hope to improve a nation's free access to information by working to disable its data networks'; and Ron Deibert of the Citizen Lab added that a physical sit-in demands physical risk and a flood does not. Prosecutors point to cost, 8.9 million dollars in one Operation Payback case by the Department of Justice's estimate; critics of the law ask for leniency where nobody sought personal gain, and in 2014 a federal judge in Virginia asked why felonies were pursued there when the California PayPal case had ended in misdemeanours with almost no prison time.

war-dialing.def: Dialing whole ranges of telephone numbers automatically to find the ones answered by a modem - the reconnaissance technique of the dial-up era, and the direct ancestor of the port scan.
war-dialing.context: The name comes from WarGames, whose protagonist does exactly this to find a games company and reaches NORAD instead; the film named the technique retroactively, and tools like ToneLoc made it routine. The war- prefix then spread across security vocabulary to wardriving, warwalking and warchalking for wireless.

irc.def: The text chat protocol written by Jarkko Oikarinen in Finland in 1988: servers federate into a network, users join channels prefixed with #, and the whole thing is simple enough to speak by hand over a raw socket. Standardized late, in RFC 1459 and its successors.
irc.context: IRC was where open source, the security underground and most of internet culture actually lived for two decades - Linux kernel work, warez trading, the Anonymous operations, and the first incident-response calls all happened in channels. Its bot ecosystem taught a generation to automate, then taught attackers the same trick: early botnets were literally IRC clients that joined a channel and waited for the operator to type commands, which is why so much command and control still looks like chat.

usenet.def: The distributed discussion system built in 1979-1980 by Duke and UNC graduate students on top of UUCP, later carried by NNTP: articles posted to hierarchical newsgroups flood from server to server, with no central host and no owner.
usenet.context: It was the internet's public square before the web, and it invented most of what online life still runs on - FAQ, flame war, spam, sockpuppet, netiquette, and the September that never ended. Linus Torvalds announced Linux on comp.os.minix; Tim Berners-Lee announced the web on alt.hypertext; the alt hierarchy existed precisely because someone objected to central approval. Its flood-fill design is also the ancestor of every eventually-consistent replication scheme since.

uucp.def: The 1970s Bell Labs suite that let one Unix machine dial another over a modem to exchange files, mail and commands - store-and-forward networking for people with no network, only telephones.
uucp.context: Addresses were bang paths that spelled out the physical route a message would take, hop by hop: mymachine!theirmachine!you. Mail took days and everyone knew which links were reliable. UUCP carried Usenet, connected the pre-internet Unix world into the UUCPNET, and taught the operational reflexes - queue, retry, forward, tolerate the link being down - that resurface every time a system has to work over an unreliable path.

r-commands.def: The Berkeley remote-access family - rlogin for a shell, rsh to run one command, rcp to copy files, rexec to execute with a password - that ran the Unix world before SSH, authenticating on trust files (.rhosts, hosts.equiv) that said, in effect, this machine vouches for that machine.
r-commands.context: Everything travelled in the clear, and the trust was based on source IP address and hostname, both forgeable. A single compromised host with a permissive .rhosts could cascade through an entire cluster - which is precisely how the Morris worm and a generation of intrusions moved laterally. SSH exists because of these tools, replaced them command for command, and their retirement is the canonical example of an entire protocol family removed rather than patched.

xauth.def: The authorization layer of the X Window System: xauth manages the MIT-MAGIC-COOKIE tokens that let a client open a window on your display, and X11 forwarding tunnels that protocol over SSH so a remote program can draw on your local screen.
xauth.context: X's model is inverted from what people expect - the display is the server and the application is the client - and its old alternative to cookies, xhost +, disabled access control entirely, which meant any host on the network could open windows, read your keystrokes and screenshot your session. That is why xhost + is a classic audit finding, and why SSH forwarding with proper cookie handling replaced it. Trusted forwarding still hands the remote side real power over your desktop, which is the modern caution.

blockchain.def: An append-only ledger of batched transactions in which each block carries the cryptographic hash of the one before it, so altering any past record changes every hash after it. Combined with a consensus rule that decides which chain counts, it lets mutually distrustful parties agree on an order of events with no central authority.
blockchain.context: The data structure is old - hash chains and Merkle trees, plus Haber and Stornetta's 1991 timestamping work - and the 2008 Bitcoin paper's real contribution was the incentive layer that makes rewriting history expensive. What blockchains actually guarantee is narrow and worth stating precisely: ordering and tamper-evidence, not truth. Garbage written correctly to a chain is permanent garbage, and most problems reached for by the word are solved better by a database with an audit log.

war-driving.def: Driving around with a wireless card, an antenna and a GPS, logging every access point you pass - mapping the radio landscape of a city. Named after war dialing by Peter Shipley, who did the first systematic survey around 1999 to 2000.
war-driving.context: The findings were the argument: early surveys found most networks open or on WEP, which turned a theoretical weakness into a photograph of an entire city's exposure. Warchalking, briefly, marked open networks in chalk on pavements. The practice is legal in most places when it only listens, and it produced lasting public goods - the crowd-sourced access-point databases that phones now use to fix their position indoors are, in origin, war driving at planetary scale. DEF CON's wireless village still runs the sport version.

l0pht.def: The Boston hacker group of 1992 to 2000: a rented loft full of salvaged hardware where Mudge, Weld Pond, Space Rogue, Kingpin, Brian Oblivion, John Tan and Stefan Von Neumann did vulnerability research and published it free, testified to the United States Senate in May 1998, and in January 2000 became part of the consultancy @stake.
l0pht.context: The L0pht built L0phtCrack, the Windows password auditor that made the weakness of the LAN Manager (local area network manager, LM) password hash undeniable, and ran the Hacker News Network. On 19 May 1998 its seven members told a Senate committee, under their handles, that they could make the internet unusable for the entire nation in under thirty minutes. They then did what the underground rarely does: they went legitimate as @stake, a venture-funded consultancy that took in a large share of the industry's first professional generation and was bought by Symantec in 2004. Mudge later spent three years directing cybersecurity research at DARPA (Defense Advanced Research Projects Agency), moved to Google, and in 2022 testified to the Senate again as a Twitter whistleblower; Weld Pond and Dildog founded Veracode.
l0pht.depth:
What it was. L0pht Heavy Industries (the name is pronounced loft) was a group of Boston-area hackers active from 1992 to 2000, and it was a place before it was a brand. In the written statement its members gave the Senate in 1998 they dated it to early 1992, when one member's accumulated test and computer equipment had to leave home and a loft was rented nearby; to share the rent of the old warehouse, others were recruited from a Boston bulletin board system (BBS), the Black Crawling Systems. It began as a storage locker for surplus gear, grew a small lab and an internal network, and, in their words, the actual L0pht was born in late 1993, when its Linux machine went onto the internet over a 28.8 modem link to a local provider. The Washington Post's 2015 account places that first clubhouse in a loft above a carpentry shop in Boston's South End, filled largely with hardware pulled from dumpsters. The members called themselves grey hats, between the avowedly virtuous white hats and the outlaw black hats, and their statement described the ambition as a consumer-reports body for security, tied to no large vendor, that would publish who was helping users and who was selling snake oil.

Who was in it, in their own words. Seven members testified: Mudge, Weld Pond, Kingpin, John Tan, Space Rogue, Brian Oblivion and Stefan Von Neumann, and their introductions to the committee are a cross-section of 1990s hacking. Weld Pond described himself as a programmer with more than ten years in commercial software, working on vulnerabilities in Microsoft's business version of Windows and on L0phtCrack. Kingpin, the youngest, was an electrical engineer and hardware hacker. Space Rogue, with no formal computer training, was assessing proximity devices such as toll tags and access cards. Brian Oblivion worked on wireless and satellite communications, and the statement records him as an advocate of the free, unrestricted use of encryption who wanted the export laws revisited. Stefan Von Neumann, with the group since 1993, worked on high-power electronics and the convergence of power and data distribution. The statement says the L0pht had issued at least 19 security advisories, which had prompted official incident-response advisories and patches from Microsoft, Sun, FreeBSD, Cygnus (for Kerberos) and Bellcore. Later members include Dildog and Silicosis.

L0phtCrack, and what it proved. L0phtCrack, first released in 1997, recovers Windows passwords from their stored hashes by dictionary and brute-force attack, which made it a password auditor in an administrator's hands. Its target was the LAN Manager (local area network manager, LM) hash, which Windows kept computing beside its stronger hash for compatibility with older clients. At a hacker conference in August 1997, as the Washington Post later told it, Mudge singled out the design: a 14-character password field was split into two seven-character halves stored separately, so an attacker faced two short passwords instead of one long one, and a password of seven characters or fewer left a recognizable value in the unused half, telling the attacker half the work was already done. He also reported a network where 700 users shared the single password CHANGEME. Microsoft's documentation now says the same in quieter words: when a password of fewer than 15 characters is set, Windows generates an LM hash as well as the stronger one and stores both in the Security Accounts Manager (SAM) database or in Active Directory, and the LM hash is relatively weak and prone to fast brute-force attack. The countermeasures are the NoLMHash policy, which appears in Group Policy as Network security: Do not store LAN Manager hash value on next password change and was disabled by default before Windows Vista and Windows Server 2008 and enabled from them on, or a password of at least 15 characters, for which Windows stores an LM value that cannot be used to authenticate.

Paying the rent. A physical space has bills, and the products existed partly to pay them: a pager-decoder kit, compact-disc copies of the Black Crawling Systems archives, then L0phtCrack, whose command-line version was free and whose graphical version was sold. The Hacker News Network followed, a popular online newsletter run by Space Rogue that spread word of security discoveries and drew enough readers to attract advertisers, whom the group kept off its main site, l0pht.com. The Post also records regular gatherings at a Boston bar where anyone who revealed a new vulnerability got a free beer. By the end of the decade the Justice Department and the Securities and Exchange Commission had hired the L0pht as consultants, according to USA Today.

The Senate, 19 May 1998. The Committee on Governmental Affairs, chaired by Fred Thompson, heard the seven as its second panel at the hearing Weak Computer Security in Government: Is the Public at Risk? (S. Hrg. 105-609); the chairman explained that, because of the sensitivity of the work done at the L0pht, they would use their hacker names. The line that made headlines is in their written statement: in under 30 minutes the seven could very trivially make the internet unusable for the entire nation, cutting communication between the United States and other countries and leaving the major backbone providers, MCI and AT&T among them, unable to route traffic to each other, findings they said they had given to the appropriate agencies. The printed record does not name the protocol; the Post later identified the flaws as those of the Border Gateway Protocol (BGP). Mudge told the senators that one of them could do it with a few packets, that backbone operators stayed exposed because inspecting traffic at even 1 millisecond per packet would cost them speed a competitor could sell, and that vendors often fixed software only after the L0pht went public, because companies want to ignore problems as long as possible: it is cheaper for them. For the group the hearing meant fame, down to a Trivial Pursuit question about what the L0pht said it could cripple in 30 minutes.

Going legitimate. In January 2000 the group was acquired by @stake, a Cambridge, Massachusetts start-up backed by 10 million dollars of venture capital, as USA Today reported on 10 January; Mudge became vice president of research, a former Compaq senior vice president became chairman, and the firm billed itself as a pure-play web security consultancy beholden to no software maker. Mudge's explanation was that the L0pht lacked the management expertise and business savvy to handle everyone coming to it. The oral history Decipher published in 2025 names the backer as Battery Ventures and records the community's charge that the group had sold out; Weld Pond, Chris Wysopal, told the Post that the community they came from thought they were selling out to the Man, which of course they were. Commercial life tested the old habits. Microsoft, the L0pht's longtime target, hired @stake and demanded nondisclosure agreements about what it found; the Hacker News Network became a corporate Security News Network; and in September 2003 @stake fired its chief technology officer, Dan Geer, after he co-authored a study on how Microsoft's dominance undermined security. Symantec announced its acquisition of @stake on 16 September 2004 and completed it on 8 October.

Afterlives. L0phtCrack outlived @stake: Symantec owned it from 2004 and stopped selling it, and in January 2009 original authors, among them Peiter Zatko (Mudge), Chris Wysopal and Christien Rioux (Dildog), bought it back. Terahash bought it in 2020, it was repossessed in July 2021 after Terahash defaulted on the instalment loan, and on 17 October 2021 version 7.2.0 was released as open source. Wysopal and Dildog founded the application security company Veracode in 2006. Zatko spent three years directing cybersecurity research at the Defense Advanced Research Projects Agency (DARPA) before moving to Google, and on 13 September 2022 was back before the Senate, this time its Judiciary Committee, as a whistleblower about Twitter. On 22 May 2018, almost exactly 20 years after the hearing, Weld Pond, Space Rogue (Cris Thomas), Mudge and Kingpin (Joe Grand, hardware designer and founder of Grand Idea Studio) returned to Capitol Hill for a Congressional Internet Caucus Academy briefing titled after the Post's verdict: a disaster foretold, and ignored.

What still applies. The technical lesson is the LM hash itself: a compatibility format kept alive long after it was known to be weak and switched off only by a policy whose default changed with Windows Vista and Windows Server 2008, which is why old domains, old images and old local accounts are worth checking for stored LM values, and why the related NT LAN Manager (NTLM) authentication family is its own migration project. The structural lesson is the one the members put to the senators: operators knowingly left a backbone weakness open because defending against it cost speed, and vendors waited for publication before patching because silence was cheaper. The professional lesson is @stake's: independent research could say anything partly because nobody was paying for it, and the trade from a loft to a client list changed what could be published, a tension every disclosure policy since has had to settle.

the-scene.def: The underground release culture: crews competing to be first to crack and distribute software, games, music and film, on invitation-only servers, for reputation and nothing else. Related to but distinct from the demoscene, which competes on making art in tiny amounts of code.
the-scene.context: The Scene invented an entire economy without money: strict rules on release quality, the NFO (information) file with its logo in American Standard Code for Information Interchange (ASCII) art and its greetings, courier races between topsites, and permanent bans for anyone who leaked to the public internet. Its aesthetic (the art, the handles, the crew loyalties) shaped hacker culture broadly, and its distribution technique arguably taught the industry more about content delivery than any vendor did. Ask about it and you will hear a decades-long argument about whether it was theft, sport, or preservation.
the-scene.depth:
What it is, and what it is not. Martin Paul Eve, who wrote the first scholarly book on it, defines the Warez Scene as a worldwide, underground, organized network of pirate groups specializing in obtaining and illegally releasing digital media, free of charge, before their official sale dates; warez is a derivative of software. It has no central leadership or location. The United States Department of Justice described its place in the chain in 2004: release groups are the first-providers, the original source for most pirated works traded online, which reach secure top-level servers within minutes and public channels within hours. That last step is not the Scene's doing. Eve reproduces the usual piracy pyramid, with topsites and release groups at the top, then File eXchange Protocol (FXP) boards, private torrent trackers, public trackers and other peer-to-peer mechanisms, and bootleggers at the bottom, and stresses that the Scene's own ethos strictly forbids putting its releases on public peer-to-peer networks. Nor is it the demoscene, which shares its ancestry and is entirely legal.

Where it came from. The Scene began on dial-up bulletin board systems (BBSes), where the first groups removed copy protection from games for the home computers of the early 1980s and signed their work, and it moved to File Transfer Protocol (FTP) servers on the internet in the mid-to-late 1990s. For part of that history the law lagged behind: Eve quotes the archivist Ben Garrett's remark that not-for-profit software piracy was not a criminal act when information files first became popular, and that the change began with the World Intellectual Property Organization (WIPO) Copyright Treaty of December 1996, which gave software the protection of literary works and criminalized bypassing copy protection. A subculture that had advertised itself openly became a closed one.

The machinery. A release group obtains a title, often through a supplier who, according to the Department of Justice, is a company insider, strips the protection and packages the result. It uploads to the topsites it is affiliated with: FTP servers with very high bandwidth and storage, run by a site operator (siteop). When the upload is complete on all of them the group runs the pre command, which makes the release visible on every affiliated site at the same moment and has a bot announce it in the site's invitation-only Internet Relay Chat (IRC) channel. From there couriers race it to other sites using FXP, which is FTP used to transfer files directly between two remote servers. A site pays in credit, commonly three bytes of download for every byte uploaded, and ranks its couriers in a weekly scoreboard, the weektop, on which their accounts depend. Access is guarded with the tools of the period: a login accepted only from a known host and ident reply (the identification protocol of Request for Comments (RFC) 1413), encrypted sessions, and bouncers, which are proxies that hide the server's real address.

The release as a document. Every release is a folder: the content, often split into RAR archive volumes, a Simple File Verification (SFV) file holding checksums of each volume so that a transfer can be verified, and an NFO file. The NFO, short for information, states what the release is and who made it, usually under a logo drawn in American Standard Code for Information Interchange (ASCII) characters and followed by greetings to other groups. It was introduced in 1990 by a member of The Humble Guys, known as Fabulous Furlough, with the group's release of the game Knights of Legend, and has been called the press release of the warez scene. A script on the topsite, the zipscript, checks integrity while the upload is still in progress.

The rules. Each category, such as MP3 music, television, lossless audio or 0day, has a written rule set agreed by the groups themselves. A release that breaks the rules or has a technical fault is nuked, that is, flagged as bad, at the level of one site or of the whole Scene, and the uploader loses credit. A release that duplicates an earlier one is a dupe, which is why groups consult a dupecheck database before releasing. A corrected version by another group carries the tag PROPER, and by the same group REPACK. The gravest sanction is the SceneBan, a lifetime ban for a serious infraction. The word 0day belongs to this vocabulary: Eve's glossary derives it from access that comes zero days since release and notes that it also names a category of small applications. Wired's account of the security term zero-day traces it to the same bulletin board usage, where zero-day software was software not yet released.

An economy of reputation. Eve's thesis is that the Scene is an aesthetic subculture and an alternative reality game, fixated on originality, whose members play for enjoyment and reputational capital and not for material wealth. The groups say the same in their own NFO files. SKIDROW wrote that it releases because it can and for the thrill of winning over competing groups, and told readers who liked a game to support the developer; MYTH wrote that it was against any profit or commercialization of piracy and bought its own originals. A former member of DrinkOrDie put it more bluntly: it is all about stature. Eve adds the necessary qualification that, whatever the ethos, the Scene very likely feeds the commercial bootleg markets below it, and that its culture of ranking and one-upmanship sits badly with the communal ideals often attached to piracy.
