Raids are the other documentary record. Eve notes an early Operation Cyber Strike in 1997 against the bulletin boards. On 11 December 2001 the United States announced three operations, Buccaneer, Bandwidth and Digital Piratez, with about 100 search warrants; Buccaneer alone, led by the Customs Service, executed 58 at once and was aimed at DrinkOrDie, a group of about 40 members. Operation Fastlink, announced on 22 April 2004, ran more than 120 searches in 27 American states and 10 other countries, identified nearly 100 people and seized more than 200 computers, 30 of them servers, one holding 65,000 titles; its targets included Fairlight, Kalisto, Echelon, Class and Project X. Operation Site Down, on 30 June 2005, added more than 90 searches in eleven countries and took down at least eight major distribution sites. None of it ended the practice: the figures collected on Wikipedia put the Scene at more than 100 active groups and 1,000 releases a day in 2012, and at more than 400 groups, 2,000 releases a day and 11 million releases in total by 2023.

The demoscene is the branch that kept the art and dropped the piracy. Crackers of the early 1980s put a screen crediting themselves in front of the games they had opened, first as plain text on the Apple II and soon as animated introductions with music, the crack intros or cracktros. In 1986 the Dutch Commodore 64 groups 1001 Crew and The Judges were producing pure demos with no game attached, and the intro became a form of its own, judged at gatherings called demoparties in categories defined by size: a 64k intro must fit in 65,536 bytes and a 4K intro in 4,096. Assembly, in Helsinki, is the largest of these parties. The Humble Guys themselves later became a demo group and took the NFO with them. In April 2020 Finland entered the demoscene in its national inventory of intangible cultural heritage under the convention of the United Nations Educational, Scientific and Cultural Organization (UNESCO), the first digital subculture so listed, and by April 2026 Germany, Poland, Switzerland, the Netherlands, Sweden, France and Norway had done the same.

What a network engineer recognizes in it is a distribution system built from ordinary parts. Replication to many sites at one instant, server-to-server transfer so that the bulk of the data never touches a client, checksums verified during the transfer, a database consulted to prevent duplicates, automatic announcements over IRC and an access list keyed to source address are all techniques that later became routine in legitimate content delivery and release engineering. The Scene assembled them in the 1990s for a purpose that Eve himself calls highly illegal in almost every aspect of its operations, and policed them with nothing but reputation.

The numbers and names worth remembering: bulletin boards first, FTP topsites from the mid-to-late 1990s; 1990 for the first NFO; three to one for the usual credit ratio; RFC 1413 for ident; 58 warrants in Buccaneer in 2001, more than 120 searches in Fastlink in 2004 and more than 90 in Site Down in 2005; 65,536 and 4,096 bytes for the two classic intro sizes; and April 2020 for the first heritage listing of the demoscene.

leet.def: Elite, spelled the way the bulletin-board underground spelled it: letters replaced by digits and symbols, 3 for E, 1 for L, 7 for T. 31337 is eleet, and remains a running joke that shows up as port numbers, version strings and CTF flags.
leet.context: The orthography began as evasion - keyword filters on BBSs looking for forbidden words - and hardened into an in-group marker: writing it fluently proved you belonged, overusing it proved the opposite. It gave the field a vocabulary that survives in earnest, from pwn to the 1337 port. Understanding the register matters when reading old files, because a text that looks like noise is often precise technical writing wearing a costume.

lamer.def: The underground's ladder of contempt, and the distinctions matter. A newbie or newb is simply new and willing to learn. A noob (or n00b) is new and unwilling - demanding answers, ignoring the manual. A lamer is neither new nor learning, claiming credit for others' work. A script kiddie runs tools they cannot read or modify.
lamer.context: The gradations encode the culture's actual value system: ignorance is fine and temporary, laziness and posturing are not, and status comes from what you can build or break yourself. RTFM and read the fine manual belong to the same tradition of harsh induction. The words also matter operationally - script kiddie describes a real and large threat class, since mass-scanning commodity exploits compromise more systems every year than any elite crew ever did.

defcon-goons.def: The volunteer staff who run DEF CON - identifiable by their red shirts, and the reason a conference of tens of thousands of hackers works at all. Goons handle lines, rooms, speakers, contests, safety and the moment something goes wrong, and every one of them pays their own way to be there.
defcon-goons.context: The role is unpaid, invitation-earned and jealously guarded: goons are chosen from people who have already given years to the community, and departments run from A/V and Info Booth to Speaker Ops and NOC (network operations centre). The shouted line management is theatre with a purpose - a crowd this size moves safely because someone with authority and a voice is willing to be the villain for ten minutes. Goons also carry the culture's unwritten rules to newcomers, which is why the badge on the shirt is treated as a genuine honour rather than a job title.

jeff-moss.def: The founder of DEF CON, which began in 1993 as a farewell party for a friend's bulletin-board network and became the largest hacker gathering in the world, and of Black Hat, its commercial sibling for the people who had to expense the trip.
jeff-moss.context: Moss's real achievement was building an institution that the underground would still accept: DEF CON is deliberately cash-only at the door, structurally suspicious of surveillance, and run by unpaid Goons rather than an events company. He later served on the US Homeland Security Advisory Council and as ICANN's chief security officer, becoming the field's most credible translator between hackers and governments - the same bridge the L0pht walked into the Senate in 1998.

mudge.def: Peiter C. Zatko, the L0pht's best-known member: author of the 1995 note How to write Buffer Overflows and of L0phtCrack, first witness of the L0pht's 1998 Senate testimony, later DARPA (Defense Advanced Research Projects Agency) programme manager, Twitter's security lead and whistleblower, and DARPA's chief information officer from 2024.
mudge.context: Mudge is the clearest single example of the underground-to-institution arc: the man who told senators under his handle in 1998 that the seven L0pht members could make the internet unusable within 30 minutes later ran DARPA's (Defense Advanced Research Projects Agency) Cyber Fast Track, funding hacker-scale research on hacker-scale timelines. In 2022, months after Twitter fired him, he became a whistleblower against it, telling Congress and regulators that its security had been misrepresented to its board and regulators, which Twitter disputed: the hacker habit of disclosure, applied at personal cost at the top of the industry.
mudge.depth:
Why he matters. Peiter C. Zatko, known by the handle Mudge, links almost every stage of how hacking became a profession. He was the most visible member of the L0pht, the Boston-area group that published advisories and tools in the 1990s; he opened its testimony to a United States Senate committee in 1998; he co-founded the consultancy that grew out of it; and he then spent three decades moving between government research, large technology companies and public argument about security. The constant thread is the one his Senate committee biography named in 1998, when it called him a strong proponent of full disclosure, and the one he restated to another Senate committee in 2022: tell the institution quietly first, and go public if it will not fix the problem.

The L0pht years. The 1998 hearing record says he started tinkering with computers in 1975, received degrees in music and held jobs ranging from software development to code breaking for large organizations. His note How to write Buffer Overflows, dated 20 October 1995, began as a reminder to himself: it walks through crashing a test program that overflows a buffer in syslog, reading the registers in gdb and overwriting the instruction pointer so that the processor jumps to code the attacker supplied, one of the first public papers on the technique. At the hearing he described L0phtCrack, written with Weld Pond, as a tool for showing administrators and users the insecurity of Microsoft's passwords; it was first released in 1997 as a tool for testing password strength and recovering Windows passwords by dictionary and brute-force attack. He listed advisories that had prompted vendor patches, often only after publication, and his committee biography credited him with exposing problems in Microsoft's encryption, Bellcore's one-time password scheme and Kerberos. With Bruce Schneier he published a 1998 cryptanalysis of Microsoft's PPTP (Point-to-Point Tunneling Protocol) at an ACM (Association for Computing Machinery) conference; Microsoft responded with MS-CHAPv2 (Microsoft Challenge Handshake Authentication Protocol version 2), and their 1999 follow-up found that it dropped the LAN Manager (local area network manager) hash and the reused encryption key but still derived a key only as strong as the user's password. CNET later credited him with AntiSniff, which it described as the first remote detector of machines in promiscuous mode used by the Defense Department.

The Senate, 19 May 1998. The Committee on Governmental Affairs, chaired by Fred Thompson, held the hearing Weak Computer Security in Government: Is the Public at Risk? (S. Hrg. 105-609). The seven L0pht members testified as Mudge, Weld Pond, Brian Oblivion, Kingpin, Space Rogue, John Tan and Stefan Von Neumann, because of the sensitivity of their work, and Mudge spoke first. He told the senators that companies want to ignore problems as long as possible because it is cheaper for them, and that if you are looking for computer security, then the internet is not the place to be. Asked whether the seven could make the internet unusable for the entire nation within 30 minutes, he answered that it was correct, and that one of them could do it with just a few packets. He explained the mechanism in operator terms: with the old protocols it was trivial to separate the major long-haul providers so that AT&T could not talk to MCI, PSINet or AlterNet, and the backbone operators would not pay to stop it, because inspecting traffic even at 1 millisecond per packet would cost them speed their competitors could sell. He had opened by calling the invitation a very great step forward and saying the group was thrilled that the government was starting to approach the hacker community, since hackers brought a tremendous asset to the table.

@stake, BBN and the White House. CNET's 2010 profile records that he started the corporate information security group at BBN Technologies in the 1990s, was chief executive of L0pht Heavy Industries when the group incorporated, and founded @stake, the consultancy it became, where CNN records him as chief scientist; Symantec acquired @stake in 2004. On 15 February 2000, the week after denial-of-service attacks had disrupted several major websites, President Clinton met technology executives and security experts at the White House; FCW's participant list names Peiter Zatko of @stake among them, alongside Vint Cerf, Whitfield Diffie, Gene Spafford and Howard Schmidt. From 2004 he was back at BBN as a division scientist and technical director in its National Intelligence Research and Applications department. L0phtCrack had its own afterlife: Symantec owned it from 2004 to 2009, when Zatko and other original authors bought it back; it was sold to Terahash in 2020, repossessed in July 2021 after a loan default, and released as open source, version 7.2.0, on 17 October 2021.

DARPA, 2010 to 2013. CNET reported on 10 February 2010 that he would join DARPA (Defense Advanced Research Projects Agency) in mid-March as a programme manager in the Strategic Technologies Office, with a goal of funding researchers at hacker spaces, start-ups and boutique firms: "I want revolutionary changes. I don't want evolutionary ones." He helped stand up the Information Innovation Office (I2O), and his best-known programme there was Cyber Fast Track. Its research announcement, DARPA-RA-11-52 of 3 August 2011, names him as technical point of contact and sets out the design: many small cyber security projects with results in less than 12 months, a preference for shorter efforts, payment only on delivered milestones, firm fixed price subcontracts placed through a Federal Supply Schedule contractor within about 10 working days of selection, and an explicit exclusion of research that only improves the existing state of practice. It was built for individuals and small firms with little experience of government contracting. His 2022 Senate statement says this service earned him the Office of the Secretary of Defense's medal for exceptional public service.

Google, Stripe and Twitter. In April 2013 The Register reported that he was leaving DARPA after three years for an unspecified role at Motorola Mobility's Advanced Technology and Projects (ATAP) division at Google, following his former DARPA director Regina Dugan; CNN adds that he later helped build the security team at the payments company Stripe. Twitter hired him in November 2020, after the July 2020 compromise of high-profile accounts in a cryptocurrency scam, and his Senate statement describes the role as Security Lead, reporting to chief executive Jack Dorsey, with responsibility for information security, privacy engineering, physical security, information technology and Twitter Services. Dorsey's successor, Parag Agrawal, fired him in January 2022; Twitter said it was for poor performance.

The disclosure and the hearing. In July 2022 he sent a disclosure of roughly 200 pages to lawmakers and regulators, which CNN and the Washington Post reported on 23 August 2022. It alleged that Twitter gave far too many employees access to sensitive user data, that one or more employees might be working for a foreign intelligence service, and that Agrawal had misled the board by discouraging a full account of the company's security weaknesses. He was represented by Whistleblower Aid. Twitter's answer, as CNN reported it, was that security and privacy had long been company-wide priorities and that what it had seen was a narrative riddled with inconsistencies and inaccuracies that lacked important context; the dispute also reached Elon Musk's legal fight over his 44 billion dollar purchase of the company, in which Musk's lawyers subpoenaed him. On 13 September 2022 he testified before the Senate Judiciary Committee, chaired by Senator Durbin, that he had found 10 years of overdue critical security issues, had reported them repeatedly inside the company and had turned to regulators only when those reports went unheeded.

Back to government. Defense One reports that he joined CISA (Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency) in September 2023 as a part-time senior technical adviser, where MeriTalk places him on its Secure by Design work, and MeriTalk adds a period as executive in residence at Rapid7. DARPA confirmed that he became its chief information officer in June 2024; he announced the return on X on 6 August 2024. Across the whole record the pattern holds: the same argument he made to the Senate as a hacker in 1998, that vendors fix what is made public and the public pays for what is hidden, is the one he made as an executive in 2022.

phiber-optik.def: The New York phone-switch specialist who left the Legion of Doom to found Masters of Deception, became the most visible hacker of the early 1990s, and served a year in federal prison in 1994 for conspiracy.
phiber-optik.context: Abene mattered because he argued in public. He taught, gave interviews, and insisted that exploring systems was not the same as damaging them, at a moment when prosecutors were making the opposite case. New York magazine named him one of the city's hundred smartest people the year he went in; the city threw him a party when he came out. His case, more than any other, is why the field still distinguishes curiosity from harm when it writes its own history.

the-mentor.def: The Legion of Doom member who, hours after his 1986 arrest, wrote the short essay published in Phrack as The Conscience of a Hacker - universally known as the Hacker Manifesto - and who later, by coincidence of employment, wrote the cyberpunk game manual the Secret Service seized in the Steve Jackson Games raid.
the-mentor.context: The Manifesto is the most reprinted text the culture produced: a defence of curiosity as a crime of the mind, written by a teenager and quoted ever since in films, talks and courtrooms. Blankenship's second brush with the law is the more instructive one - his GURPS Cyberpunk manuscript was confiscated as a supposed hacking manual, and the fiasco helped bring the Electronic Frontier Foundation into existence.

joybubbles.def: The blind phone phreak with perfect pitch who discovered as a boy, about four years after learning to dial at four or five, that whistling a particular tone into a receiver made the network obey - and who could produce 2600 Hz with his mouth, no equipment at all.
joybubbles.context: Engressia mapped the telephone system by ear over decades, was expelled and prosecuted for it, and was named in the 1971 Esquire article that made phreaking public. He legally renamed himself Joybubbles in 1991 and declared himself perpetually five years old. The scene remembers him as its gentlest figure and its purest case: he wanted to understand the network, never to profit from it, and he is the reason the culture's founding story is about curiosity rather than theft.

cliff-stoll.def: The Berkeley astronomer turned accidental investigator who, told in 1986 to reconcile a 75-cent accounting discrepancy, followed it to a West German intruder selling material from US military systems to the Soviet KGB, and wrote it up in Communications of the ACM (Association for Computing Machinery) and as The Cuckoo's Egg.
cliff-stoll.context: Stoll improvised working incident response before it had a name: he kept a paper logbook, printed every session, baited the intruder with an invented defence project, a documented early case of what the field now calls a honeypot, and spent months persuading agencies that the case was real. Much of what modern practice does, the timeline, evidence handling, caution about attribution, patient monitoring instead of instant disconnection, appears in his 1988 write-up. He then wrote books arguing against the internet's promoters, taught physics, and now sells glass Klein bottles, which the field finds delightful.
cliff-stoll.depth:
Clifford Stoll, born in Buffalo, New York, in 1950, took a degree in astronomy at the State University of New York at Buffalo and a PhD at the University of Arizona in 1980. In 1986 he was designing telescope optics at Lawrence Berkeley Laboratory (LBL) when his grant ran out; as he put it to California Magazine, the lab recycled used astronomers, and he moved downstairs to the computer centre as a systems manager. On his second day his boss gave him a 75-cent discrepancy in the computer usage accounts, which he traced to an unauthorized user who had used about nine seconds of time without paying. His own technical account, in Communications of the ACM in May 1988, describes the same start more drily: the lab's accounting program could not balance because a new account had been created without a billing address, and soon afterwards the National Computer Security Center reported that someone from LBL had tried to break into one of its computers over MILNET.

What made the case a model was the decision to watch rather than lock the door. Stoll and his colleagues put line printers and recorders on every incoming port, capturing every keystroke, and saw the intruder use a bug in the movemail feature of the Gnu-Emacs editor, which ran with system privileges, to become system manager. They chose printers over online monitors because monitoring software runs privileged, could add holes, and might have warned him. They kept a detailed logbook, like a laboratory notebook, which months later yielded clues they had missed. Over the next ten months the intruder attacked about 450 computers and got into more than 30, mostly military and defence-contractor systems reached through LBL's links to ARPANET and MILNET. He used no new methods: known holes, default accounts and passwords (which worked on about five per cent of the machines he tried), passwords left in files and mail, dictionary attacks on stolen password files run on his own machine, and Trojan horses to collect more. He searched for words such as nuclear, sdi, kh-11 and norad.

Tracing him took the cooperation of telephone companies, Tymnet and the West German Bundespost. Tymnet's X.25 calling addresses pointed to universities in Bremen and Karlsruhe and a dial-up modem in another German city, and Stoll found other clues in hindsight: round-trip times that implied an overseas link, AT&T rather than Berkeley Unix commands, German passwords. To hold the intruder on the line long enough for a trace, the team created files of invented memos about computers supporting the Strategic Defense Initiative (SDI), with a mailing list and form letters from a secretary who did not exist, protected them, and set alarms on them. He read them for more than an hour and the trace was completed; months later a letter arrived in the United States asking to be put on the SDI mailing list, which convinced Stoll he was watching espionage and handed that side to the FBI. The paper calls the method little more than catching flies with honey and suggests alarmed bait files as a way to detect and classify intruders. In later interviews Stoll named the operation Showerhead.

The intruder was Markus Hess, of Hanover, who with Dirk Brzezinski and Peter Carl had been selling material to the Soviet KGB, for US$54,000 according to Wikipedia's account. West German police raided the group in March 1989, and Hess and his associates were tried in 1990, with Stoll flying out to testify. Hess was convicted of espionage and given a 20-month suspended sentence according to the Associated Press as cited by Wikipedia; Stoll's own recollection in 2016 was that of five people involved, one turned state's evidence, one died, his body found burned in a forest, and the rest received two years, suspended, by then the Berlin Wall had fallen. The case also showed how unready the institutions were: Stoll recalls that agencies hesitated over jurisdiction and had never handled a computer break-in, and the 1988 paper records that the FBI and its West German counterpart, the BKA, ran parallel investigations.

The paper's lessons still read like an incident-response syllabus. The first days were confused because nobody knew what the response should be; the accounting files misled because system clocks had drifted by minutes, and the LAN's connection logs had drifted by hours and were in a format nobody knew. Closing out an intruder upon discovery, Stoll wrote, may be a premature reflex, because determining the damage and helping investigators argue for leaving the system open; the cost under California law of the computing, network time and tracing exceeded US$100,000; and the only guaranteed clean-up, rebuilding every system from source and changing every password overnight, was impractical for a lab of over a thousand users, so they settled on password expiry, removing shared and expired accounts, continued monitoring and user education. Security, he concluded, is a human problem that technical solutions alone cannot solve.

The story reached a wide audience as The Cuckoo's Egg (Doubleday, 1989), named, as Stoll explains it, after the bird that lays its egg in another's nest, and as the 1990 NOVA docudrama The KGB, the Computer, and Me, in which he played himself. Fame did not suit him. In Silicon Snake Oil (1995) and a Newsweek essay of 27 February 1995 he called the claims of internet visionaries baloney and wrote that no online database would replace your daily newspaper; when the essay resurfaced in 2010 he called it one of his most public howlers. High-Tech Heretic followed in 1999. He taught physics to schoolchildren, and since 1994 has sold blown-glass Klein bottles, made with friends who ran a scientific glassware shop in Berkeley, under the name Acme Klein Bottles.

tsutomu-shimomura.def: The San Diego Supercomputer Center researcher whose own machines were broken into on Christmas Day 1994 with IP (Internet Protocol) address spoofing and TCP (Transmission Control Protocol) sequence-number prediction, and who then led the technical hunt that ended with Kevin Mitnick's arrest in February 1995.
tsutomu-shimomura.context: The intrusion itself was a landmark: a working demonstration, documented with his own packet logs, that a TCP (Transmission Control Protocol) connection could be forged from a trusted host's address by predicting the target's sequence numbers, the attack Robert Morris had described in 1985 and Steven Bellovin in 1989. The CERT advisory written about it is the one cited at the top of RFC (Request for Comments) 1948, the defence that gave each connection its own sequence space. The chase, written up with the New York Times journalist John Markoff as Takedown, made both men famous and remains fiercely disputed: reviewers called the book self-regarding, the journalist Jonathan Littman accused Markoff of taking part in the manhunt he reported, and reviewers of the book called Mitnick only the apparent attacker.
tsutomu-shimomura.depth:
Tsutomu Shimomura was born in Nagoya on 23 October 1964, the son of Osamu Shimomura, who shared the 2008 Nobel Prize in Chemistry and records in his Nobel biography returning to Princeton in December 1965 with his wife and their one-year-old son. He grew up in Princeton, studied physics at Caltech under Richard Feynman, worked at Los Alamos National Laboratory on lattice gas automata, and in 1989 became a research scientist in computational physics at the University of California, San Diego, and a senior fellow at the San Diego Supercomputer Center (SDSC). He was known in security circles before 1995; in 1992 he testified to a congressional subcommittee on the privacy and security of cellular telephones.

His own account of the break-in, posted to comp.security.misc and comp.protocols.tcp-ip on 25 January 1995 from a talk he had given on 11 January, is one of the clearest attack write-ups of its era, complete with tcpdump excerpts. At 14:09:32 PST on 25 December 1994 finger, showmount and rpcinfo probes from toad.com, where the attacker had root, looked for trust relationships among his machines. About six minutes later a burst of SYN packets from a forged, unused address filled the connection queue of the login port (513) on the server, so that it would no longer answer unexpected SYN-ACKs with resets. Twenty probe connections to the X terminal's shell port then showed that each new initial sequence number was exactly 128,000 higher than the last. The attacker sent a SYN that appeared to come from the server's login port, predicted the X terminal's reply without seeing it, acknowledged it, and sent the rsh command echo + + >>/.rhosts, writing into the trust file of the Unix r-services (rsh, rlogin) that the whole exercise was aimed at. Elapsed time from the first spoofed packet: under 16 seconds. The half-open connections were then reset so the server recovered.

That was only the first of two mechanisms. With root on the X terminal, the attacker compiled and loaded a kernel STREAMS module, tap-2.01, and at about 14:51 used it to take over an already authenticated login session to another system. The CERT Coordination Center's advisory CA-95:01 of 23 January 1995 described the same pair: spoofed packets against applications that authenticate by IP address, which could pass filtering routers not configured to drop incoming packets whose source address belonged to the local network, and a separate tool for seizing terminal sessions on SunOS 4.1.x. Its detection advice is still the basis of anti-spoofing filters: a packet on the external interface with both source and destination addresses in the local domain means an attack is under way. The weaknesses were not new. Robert Morris had described sequence-number guessing in 1985 and Bellovin had analysed it in 1989; Bellovin wrote in 2004 that the attack received little attention until it was used against Shimomura. In May 1996 Bellovin's RFC 1948 opened by citing CA-95:01 and proposed a separate, keyed initial sequence number space for every connection.

The hunt took less than two months. SDSC's 1996 release says the attacker had already broken into service providers such as the WELL and Netcom, and that after a concentrated effort using Internet monitoring techniques Shimomura traced Mitnick to Raleigh, North Carolina, and helped the FBI arrest him on 15 February 1995. Simson Garfinkel's review records that in court the next day Mitnick told him, Tsutomu, I respect your skills. Among the files found was a list of Netcom customers' credit card numbers, though Salon's reviewer noted there was no evidence Mitnick had used it and that copies had circulated in the underground for months. Markoff, whose front-page story in The New York Times on 23 January 1995 had first described the attack, broke the story of the arrest there on 16 February.

The book is where the dispute lives. Takedown, written with Markoff and published by Hyperion (dated 1995 by SDSC, 1996 by most later citations), sold for an advance trade reports put at around $700,000, with film rights to Miramax and a film, Track Down, in 2000. Salon's Scott Rosenberg found in it near-inhuman condescension and argued that the press had turned Mitnick's trespasses into a legend; Jonathan Littman's The Fugitive Game, written from phone conversations with Mitnick during the chase, called him a harmless creep rather than a threat, accused Markoff of being a participant rather than an observer, and questioned the legality of Shimomura's role, concerns Mitnick repeated in his own autobiography, Ghost in the Wires. Garfinkel, reviewing for The Christian Science Monitor, called Mitnick the apparent attacker and observed that the transcripts in the book make him look like the dupe of an accomplice known only as jsz, still at large. The attribution of the Christmas Day intrusion itself has therefore never been as settled as the book's subtitle suggests.

Two of Shimomura's arguments outlasted the quarrel. Rosenberg singled out the book's explanation that the internet had been built for open research rather than secure commerce, that the greatest weaknesses are human, and that corporate firewalls behave like digital Maginot lines that intruders walk around with social engineering. And in January 1996 he joined Matt Blaze, Whitfield Diffie, Ronald Rivest, Bruce Schneier, Eric Thompson and Michael Wiener on Minimal Key Lengths for Symmetric Ciphers to Provide Adequate Commercial Security, which found that 40-bit keys offered virtually no protection, that 56-bit DES (Data Encryption Standard) was increasingly inadequate, and that keys should be at least 75 bits, and 90 bits for anything meant to last twenty years. He later founded the fabless semiconductor company Neofocal Systems and served as its chief executive and chief technology officer until 2016.

adrian-lamo.def: The itinerant intruder of the early 2000s - working from libraries and cafes, breaking into Microsoft, Yahoo!, WorldCom and the New York Times, then telling the victims how he did it and offering to help fix it.
adrian-lamo.context: Lamo is the awkward case the field cannot file cleanly. His method was intrusion followed by unsolicited disclosure, which some read as public service and courts read as crime; the Times added him to its expert source database, then pressed charges. In 2010 he reported Chelsea Manning to the US Army after she confided the WikiLeaks disclosures to him in chat, and much of the hacker community never forgave him. He died in 2018 at thirty-seven, remembered as the era's most contested conscience.

albert-gonzalez.def: The Miami hacker and carder whose crews took more than 170 million payment-card numbers from 2005 to 2008 (TJX and other retailers, Dave and Buster's, then Heartland Payment Systems, 7-Eleven and Hannaford) while he was a paid informant for the US Secret Service; sentenced in 2010 to 20 years, released in 2023.
albert-gonzalez.context: The technique was mundane and therefore damning: war driving to find shops running weak wireless encryption, sniffers inside their networks, then SQL (Structured Query Language) injection against a payment processor's systems. The scale changed the argument: the cases became the reference point for enforcing PCI DSS (Payment Card Industry Data Security Standard), for end-to-end encryption in payment terminals, and for the modern assumption that card data must never sit readable on a retailer's network. His concurrent sentences of 20 years, and 20 years and a day, imposed in March 2010, were described as among the longest ever imposed in the United States for hacking crimes; the Federal Bureau of Prisons records his release on 19 September 2023.
albert-gonzalez.depth:
Why he matters. The US Department of Justice called the ring Albert Gonzalez led the largest hacking and identity theft ring ever prosecuted by the United States government. Between 2005 and 2008 his crews took card data from TJX, BJ's Wholesale Club, OfficeMax, Boston Market, Barnes & Noble, Sports Authority, Dave & Buster's and others, more than 40 million card numbers in the Massachusetts and New York cases, and then from Heartland Payment Systems, 7-Eleven and Hannaford Brothers, more than 130 million in the New Jersey case. Through most of it he was working as a confidential informant for the United States Secret Service. For engineers the lesson is that none of the methods was exotic: an obsolete wireless encryption protocol, cardholder data kept longer and in more places than needed, sniffers on internal networks, a SQL (Structured Query Language) injection on an internet-facing application, and malware checked against antivirus products before use. Each step defeated a control the industry already knew was weak.

The informant. The New Jersey indictment release records that he was arrested in 2003 for his role in ATM (automated teller machine) and debit card fraud; it places the arrest in New Jersey, while Wired places it in New York. He became a confidential informant. Wired reported that under the nickname Cumbajohnny he had been a top administrator of the carding site Shadowcrew, and that the Secret Service put him to work undercover there, where he set up a VPN (virtual private network) the carders used that was in fact wiretapped by the agency's New Jersey office; the operation, Operation Firewall, led to the arrest of 28 members of the site in October 2004. He then took the nickname Segvec and moved to Miami. According to his friend and accomplice Stephen Watt, who pleaded guilty to writing the sniffer used against TJX, the Secret Service paid Gonzalez 75,000 dollars a year in cash; the agency said it would not comment on payments to informants.

TJX and the wireless door. Canada's federal privacy commissioner and Alberta's information and privacy commissioner investigated TJX and its Canadian Winners stores, and their report of 25 September 2007 is the clearest technical record of the first breach. TJX notified them on 17 January 2007 of an intrusion affecting an estimated 45 million payment cards in Canada, the United States, Puerto Rico, the United Kingdom and Ireland. TJX reported that its systems were accessed in July and September 2005 and from mid-May 2006 to mid-January 2007, that no customer information was stolen after 18 December 2006, and that the intruder may have entered from outside two stores in Miami, Florida. The stores' wireless networks were protected with WEP (Wired Equivalent Privacy). TJX decided at the end of September 2005 to move to WPA (Wi-Fi Protected Access), began the conversion in October 2005 and completed the pilot in mid-January 2007. The commissioners found that WEP can be defeated relatively easily, that the IEEE (Institute of Electrical and Electronics Engineers), which wrote it, had recommended moving to WPA in June 2003, that PCI DSS (Payment Card Industry Data Security Standard) version 1.0 of December 2004 had not required WPA but version 1.1 of September 2006 did, and that TJX had kept more personal information, for longer, than it needed; it now purges the relevant log files after 24 to 48 hours. They also faulted it for not segregating cardholder data while the conversion ran and for not detecting the intrusion before December 2006.

The Boston and New York cases. The Eastern District of New York indicted him on 12 May 2008 over the breach of Dave & Buster's payment systems, and he was arrested in Miami that month. On 5 August 2008 federal prosecutors charged eleven people from at least five countries, Gonzalez and two other Miami residents in a Boston indictment and eight others in San Diego, over the hacking of nine companies, including TJX, BJ's Wholesale Club, OfficeMax, Boston Market, Barnes & Noble, Dave & Buster's, Sports Authority, Forever 21 and DSW; Attorney General Michael Mukasey called it the single largest and most complex identity theft case ever charged in the country. According to the court documents, the group found unsecured store wireless networks by wardriving, installed sniffer programs to capture card numbers, sold the numbers and encoded stolen data onto the magnetic stripes of blank cards to withdraw cash from ATMs, and laundered the proceeds through anonymous internet currencies and bank accounts in Eastern Europe.

Heartland and SQL injection. The New Jersey indictment of 17 August 2009 charged him and two unnamed hackers in or near Russia over five corporate breaches, among them Heartland Payment Systems of Princeton, 7-Eleven and Hannaford, with more than 130 million card numbers stolen between October 2006 and May 2008. The method, as the indictment described it, was patient: the group scanned the Fortune 500 list for targets, visited stores to see which point-of-sale terminals they used, staged its tools on servers in New Jersey and abroad, broke in with SQL injection, installed sniffers that intercepted card data in real time, worked through proxies, tested its malware against about twenty leading antivirus products and made it delete traces of itself. Heartland's chairman, Robert Carr, told a Senate committee on 14 September 2009 that the company had announced the breach on 20 January 2009, that the malware captured card data in transit during authorization, data that industry rules did not then require to be encrypted in transit, and that the company had already taken about 32 million dollars in charges in six months. Heartland had been certified as PCI DSS compliant in April 2008; in March 2009 Visa removed it from its list of compliant service providers.

Pleas and sentences. He pleaded guilty in both districts; his plea agreements contemplated 17 to 25 years and the government asked for 25. On 25 March 2010 Judge Patti B. Saris in Boston sentenced him to 20 years for conspiracy, computer fraud, wire fraud, access device fraud and aggravated identity theft, a sentence that also covered the New York charges, with three years of supervised release and a 25,000 dollar fine. The next day Judge Douglas P. Woodlock sentenced him to 20 years and one day on two conspiracy counts in the Heartland case, to run concurrently, with a further 25,000 dollar fine and restitution to be set later. The Justice Department said the sentences were some of the longest ever imposed for hacking crimes. Gonzalez admitted it was foreseeable that his help would let his co-conspirators steal tens of millions of card numbers affecting more than 250 financial institutions; by then six co-conspirators had pleaded guilty in the United States, an Estonian arrested in Germany had been extradited and pleaded guilty, and another co-conspirator had been sentenced in Turkey to 30 years.

The disputed authority. In a habeas petition filed on 24 March 2011, acting as his own lawyer, he asked to withdraw his pleas, arguing that he had believed he was acting for the Secret Service and that his lawyers had never discussed a public authority defence; he also alleged that the Ukrainian carder Maksym Yastremskiy, whose laptop had led investigators to Segvec, had been beaten by Turkish officials to give up its passphrase. His former lawyer, Rene Palomino, answered that Gonzalez had been given the opportunity of a lifetime to work for the Secret Service and had chosen to become a double agent. The Federal Bureau of Prisons inmate locator records his release on 19 September 2023.

What changed. Carr used his testimony to argue for end-to-end encryption, which Heartland called E3: card data made unreadable from the moment of the swipe by tamper-resistant security modules in the terminals and HSMs (hardware security modules) in the processor's network, so that card numbers and magnetic stripe data are never usable inside merchant and processor systems. He also described sharing the Heartland malware with competitors through a new payments council inside the FS-ISAC (Financial Services Information Sharing and Analysis Center), and New Jersey's acting US attorney credited companies that disclosed breaches early with making the arrests possible. Together with the Canadian findings on WEP and data retention, these are the arguments behind today's defaults: strong wireless encryption, cardholder data segregated or tokenized, nothing readable in transit, and monitoring good enough to see an intruder before a card brand does.

gary-mckinnon.def: The Glasgow-born systems administrator who between February 2001 and March 2002 entered 97 US military and NASA (National Aeronautics and Space Administration) computers looking, by his own account, for suppressed evidence of UFOs (unidentified flying objects) and free-energy technology, largely through blank and default administrator passwords; the UK refused to extradite him in 2012.
gary-mckinnon.context: US prosecutors called it the biggest military computer hack of all time and sought his extradition. A decade-long legal fight followed, through the High Court, the House of Lords and the European Court of Human Rights, until on 16 October 2012 the Home Secretary, Theresa May, withdrew the extradition order on human-rights grounds, citing medical evidence about his Asperger's syndrome and depressive illness; in December 2012 the Director of Public Prosecutions decided not to charge him in Britain either. The case is studied twice over: as the defining argument about extradition, forum and proportionality in computer crime, which helped put a forum bar into UK law, and as an uncomfortable audit finding, since some of the world's most sensitive networks were entered by someone who mostly tried passwords nobody had changed.
gary-mckinnon.depth:
Who he is. Gary McKinnon is a British systems administrator, born in Glasgow and living in London, who was 36 and out of work when the UK's National Hi-Tech Crime Unit arrested him in March 2002. He matters to security for two reasons that have little to do with technical brilliance. His intrusions were, in effect, an unsolicited audit of how United States government Windows machines were configured at the turn of the century. And the legal case that followed, over ten years, became the test of how far one state's computer-crime law should reach into another country, and changed UK extradition law.

What the United States alleged. The facts set out in the House of Lords judgment of 30 July 2008 are the US case, which McKinnon contested in part. Between 1 February 2001 and 19 March 2002, working from his home computer in London, he gained unauthorized access to 97 US government computers: 53 belonging to the Army, 26 to the Navy, 16 to NASA (National Aeronautics and Space Administration), one to the Department of Defense and one to the Air Force. He was alleged to have deleted critical operating system files from nine of them, which shut down the Army's Military District of Washington network of more than 2,000 computers for 24 hours, and the repair costs were put at more than 700,000 dollars. After the attacks of 11 September 2001, 300 computers at Naval Weapons Station Earle were made unusable, and the systems reached included ones used to replenish munitions and supplies for the Atlantic fleet. A note left on an Army machine read: 'I am SOLO. I will continue to disrupt at the highest levels.' McKinnon admitted the access in interviews but denied causing real damage.

How he got in. McKinnon's own descriptions are unglamorous. He told IEEE Spectrum that he wrote a small Perl script that let him scan up to 65,000 machines for passwords in under eight minutes, dialled in, and found that many federal workers had never changed default passwords; he said he was amazed at the lack of security. He used a commercial remote-control program, RemotelyAnywhere, to drive the machines and copy files, and described administrator passwords that were easy to guess; once he misjudged the time difference and connected while a user was at the keyboard, who cut him off. Asked about his motive in 2006, he said he knew governments were suppressing antigravity, unidentified flying object (UFO) and free-energy (zero-point energy) technology, which should not be hidden while pensioners could not pay their fuel bills; his inspiration, he said, was Hugo Cornwall's The Hacker's Handbook rather than the film WarGames, and he had been looking both before and after 11 September. He claimed to have glimpsed, over a 56k dial-up link with a NASA desktop reduced to 4-bit colour, an image of a silvery, cigar-shaped object; the claim rests on his word alone.

The American case and the plea offer. A federal court in New Jersey issued an arrest warrant on 31 October 2002, and on 12 November 2002 the US Attorney for the Eastern District of Virginia, Paul McNulty, called it the biggest military computer hack of all time; a Virginia warrant followed on 12 August 2004 and a formal extradition request on 7 October 2004. He faced eight counts of computer fraud, and reports put the theoretical maximum at up to 70 years. The Lords recorded the plea offer made by the prosecutor Scott Stein: agree to extradition and plead guilty to two counts, and the predicted sentence was three to four years, with six to twelve months served in the US before repatriation to finish it in Britain; contest extradition and be convicted, and he could face eight to ten years or more, with no support for repatriation and at best about 15 per cent remission. He declined.

Ten years in the British courts. Bow Street Magistrates' Court issued a UK warrant on 31 March 2005 and Scotland Yard's extradition unit arrested him on 7 June 2005. On 4 July 2006 the Home Secretary, John Reid, signed the extradition order under the Extradition Act 2003; McKinnon had argued, among other things, that he might be treated as an enemy combatant. The High Court rejected his appeal on 3 April 2007, and on 30 July 2008 all five Law Lords dismissed his further appeal, answering the question whether the plea bargaining had been an abuse of process with 'not in this case'. In August 2008 he was diagnosed with Asperger's syndrome, after an assessment by the autism researcher Simon Baron-Cohen among others, and on 28 August 2008 the European Court of Human Rights refused to stay his removal. Successive Home Secretaries, Jacqui Smith and Alan Johnson, refused to halt it on medical grounds, the High Court refused again in July 2009, and in May 2010 Theresa May agreed to adjourn the case while the medical evidence was considered.

The decision and the law it changed. On 16 October 2012 May told the House of Commons that the only question left for her was whether extradition would breach his human rights; having taken her own medical advice, she concluded that it would create so high a risk to his life as to be incompatible with them, withdrew the order, and left any British prosecution to the Director of Public Prosecutions. On 14 December 2012 the Director, Keir Starmer, declined to charge him, because most witnesses and nearly all the physical evidence were in the United States and the prospects of a conviction reflecting the full extent of the alleged criminality were not high. In the same statement May announced a forum bar, and the Crime and Courts Act 2013 inserted it as section 19B of the Extradition Act 2003: a judge must bar extradition by reason of forum if it would not be in the interests of justice, a provision in force from 14 October 2013. She also proposed moving human-rights representations from the Home Secretary to the High Court.

The other side, and what remains. In the United States the lawyer David Rivkin, a former adviser to the Reagan and Bush administrations, saw a loophole: under the decision's logic, he said, anyone claiming a physical or mental problem could commit crimes with impunity. McKinnon's own solicitor, Karen Todner, said the case set no precedent because the medical evidence was unique, and the contrast was drawn at once with Talha Ahsan, also diagnosed with Asperger's, who had been extradited earlier that month. Accounts of the damage also differ: the Lords' summary of the US case has the Washington network down for 24 hours, IEEE Spectrum for about three days. For engineers the enduring finding is the one McKinnon kept repeating, that the systems were ridiculously easy to enter: administrator accounts with passwords nobody had changed, reachable over dial-up and remote-control software, on networks whose loss of a few machines took thousands of others with them.

dvd-jon.def: The Norwegian teenager who in 1999 co-released DeCSS, the program that decrypted DVD content scrambling so films could be played on Linux, and who was prosecuted twice in Norway and acquitted both times.
dvd-jon.context: The case became the defining fight over whether code is speech: DeCSS circulated as a haiku, a T-shirt, a dramatic reading and a prime number, precisely because courts were being asked to suppress what could be written down as text or as a number. Johansen's defence, that he had made a legally purchased disc play on his own computer, was accepted by two Norwegian courts and became a reference point for later interoperability and right-to-repair arguments, while in the United States the same program produced the first court tests of the anti-circumvention rules of the Digital Millennium Copyright Act (DMCA).
dvd-jon.depth:
Who he is. Jon Lech Johansen, born in 1983 and known in Norway as DVD Jon, was 15 when he helped write and publish DeCSS in the autumn of 1999. He was a co-founder of a small group called Masters of Reverse Engineering (MoRE), and two of its members, whom he knew only by their screen names, worked on the program with him. Afterwards he made a career of the same skill: reverse engineering the protection on Apple's iTunes and Microsoft's media formats, then building commercial software that let people move their own media between devices.

What DeCSS did. Commercial DVDs are scrambled with the Content Scrambling System (CSS), licensed by the DVD Copy Control Association (DVD CCA); a licensed player holds keys that let it descramble the film as it plays. In autumn 1999 there was no DVD player for Linux, and the licence terms could not be reconciled with open-source software. The Norwegian appeal court's judgment reconstructs what happened from chat logs on Internet Relay Chat (IRC): on 11 September 1999 Johansen discussed with a contact called 'mdx' how to recover the play keys from a poorly protected software player; on 22 September 'mdx' reported that 'the nomad', said to be German, had recovered the decryption algorithm by reverse engineering the Xing DVD player, whose keys were barely hidden; and the authentication code came from Derek Fawcus via the LiVid (Linux Video) mailing list. Johansen built DeCSS, a Windows program, and posted it in late October 1999; prosecutors said it was downloaded more than 5,000 times in three months. The court noted that DeCSS stores the film decrypted on the hard disk, which is what CSS had been meant to prevent.

The Norwegian prosecution. In January 2000 the Motion Picture Association (MPA) and the DVD CCA complained to Økokrim, Norway's economic crime authority, and on 9 January 2002 Økokrim indicted him under section 145(2) of the criminal code, the provision against breaking a protective device to gain unlawful access to data, which carries up to two years when committed for unlawful gain. His lawyer, Halvor Manshaus, said it was the first time the provision had been used against someone for breaking an encryption system, and stressed that he owned the disc. The indictment's theory was that access was unauthorized because DVDs are sold on condition that buyers use licensed players and respect the copy protection. Prosecutors asked for a 90-day suspended sentence, confiscation of his computer and costs.

Two acquittals. On 7 January 2003 the three judges of the Oslo City Court acquitted him unanimously in a 25-page ruling. The presiding judge, Irene Sogn, found that no one could be convicted of breaking into his own property, that someone who buys a legally produced DVD has legal access to the film even if it is played in a way its makers did not foresee, and that there was no proof that he or anyone else had used the program on pirate copies. Økokrim appealed. The Borgarting Court of Appeal heard the case from 2 to 11 December 2003, with two information technology experts among the lay judges, and on 22 December 2003 unanimously rejected the appeal: unilateral licence conditions cannot validly restrict uses the Copyright Act permits, no evidence showed anyone using DeCSS on illegally acquired films, and his purpose in publishing had been to help build a Linux player. On 5 January 2004 Økokrim confirmed it would not go to the Supreme Court. The Motion Picture Association of America (MPAA) called him a serial hacker and urged Norway to implement the World Intellectual Property Organization (WIPO) Copyright Treaty; in July 2005 Norway adopted a European Union directive that, like the DMCA, outlaws circumvention regardless of purpose.

The American cases and the protest. In the United States, where Johansen was not accused of breaking any law, DeCSS produced the first lawsuits under the DMCA's anti-circumvention provisions. On 20 January 2000 Judge Lewis A. Kaplan of the Southern District of New York enjoined distribution of DeCSS under section 1201(a)(2), and in 2001 the Second Circuit, in Universal City Studios v. Corley, a case against the publisher of 2600: The Hacker Quarterly, held that computer code conveying information is speech but that the DMCA targets its functional side, and upheld an injunction against posting DeCSS and knowingly linking to it. The response was a demonstration that the line could not be drawn. David Touretzky of Carnegie Mellon University collected the results in his Gallery of CSS Descramblers: a descrambler in 434 bytes of C, Seth Schoen's haiku of 12 February 2001 that is a complete and correct description of the algorithm, T-shirts carrying the source code (their seller was sued), a dramatic reading, a square-dance version and an encoding of the code as a prime number. In April 2002 the Electronic Frontier Foundation (EFF) gave its Pioneer Award to the DeCSS writers, accepted by Johansen, for the program that enabled a DVD player on Linux.

After DeCSS. Johansen kept working on the same boundary. In March 2005 he released PyMusique, written with Travis Watkins and Cody Brocious, a Python interface to Apple's iTunes Music Store that let buyers re-download their purchases and saved tracks without digital rights management (DRM), because Apple's FairPlay protection was applied on the client after download. Later that year he moved to San Diego to work on reverse engineering for Michael Robertson at MP3tunes, and he went on to co-found doubleTwist, software for managing media across devices, which in June 2009 rented a transit-authority window beside the entrance of Apple's flagship San Francisco store to advertise itself as the cure for iPhone envy. The legal record he left is unusually clean: two unanimous Norwegian judgments holding that decrypting a disc one has bought is not a break-in, set against American appellate law holding that code is speech whose functional use can still be enjoined.

george-hotz.def: The New Jersey teenager who in 2007, at seventeen, performed the first unlock of the original iPhone from AT&T, and who in 2010 published the root keys of the PlayStation 3 after Sony removed its Linux feature.
george-hotz.context: Sony's lawsuit against him produced one of the largest backlashes in the history of the industry: Anonymous launched Operation Sony, and the PlayStation Network breach that followed weeks later cost the company a hundred million accounts and a reported hundreds of millions of dollars. Whatever the direct causal chain, the episode is the standard case study in how suing a researcher can cost far more than the bug ever would. Hotz went on to work in artificial intelligence and self-driving cars.

hd-moore.def: The creator of Metasploit, the open-source exploitation framework released in 2003 that turned exploit development from artisanal one-off code into a shared platform with modules, payloads and a common interface.
hd-moore.context: Metasploit did for offence what a package manager did for software distribution, and the argument about it has never fully settled - it lowered the barrier for defenders and attackers on the same day. Moore also ran the Month of Browser Bugs, publishing a flaw a day to force vendors to move, and later scanned the entire public IPv4 internet repeatedly to measure what was actually exposed. Both projects share his method: make the uncomfortable truth impossible to ignore.

marcus-hutchins.def: The British malware researcher known online as MalwareTech who, on 12 May 2017, registered a domain he found in the WannaCry ransomware for 10.69 dollars and so triggered the check that stopped the worm spreading; three months later he was arrested in Las Vegas over banking malware he had written years before, and in 2019 he was sentenced to time served.
marcus-hutchins.context: Three months after WannaCry he was arrested in Las Vegas on his way home from DEF CON, charged over the Kronos banking trojan, which prosecutors said he had written and helped sell in 2014 and 2015. He pleaded guilty to two counts in April 2019, and in July 2019 Judge Joseph Peter Stadtmueller sentenced him to time served and a year of supervised release, explicitly weighing what he had done since against what he had done as a teenager. The arc of accidental hero, defendant and respected researcher is the most modern version of the field's oldest story, and it is why the community argues so hard about second chances.
marcus-hutchins.depth:
Who he is. Marcus Hutchins is a British reverse engineer who, in May 2017, was 22, worked from home in England for the Los Angeles security company Kryptos Logic and was known only by his handle, MalwareTech. His work at the time was botnet tracking: he routinely registered unregistered domains found in malware samples, assuming they were command servers, to watch how far and how fast an infection spread and to send its traffic into a sinkhole. That routine is what made him, by accident, the person who stopped the first worm in a decade to attack computers on a massive scale.

What WannaCry was. On Friday 12 May 2017 a ransomware worm began spreading across the world. Cisco Talos's analysis that day showed how: it scanned heavily over TCP port 445, the Server Message Block (SMB) protocol, both inside networks and across the internet, exploiting the vulnerability Microsoft had fixed in bulletin MS17-010 with the ETERNALBLUE exploit and installing the DOUBLEPULSAR backdoor, both from the National Security Agency (NSA) tools leaked by the Shadow Brokers. Before encrypting anything, the code made a Hypertext Transfer Protocol (HTTP) request to a long, almost keyboard-mashed domain, iuqerfsodp9ifjaposdfjhgosurijfaewrwergwea.com; if the request failed, infection continued, and if it succeeded, the malware exited. Cisco's resolvers saw the first lookups at 07:24 UTC. The attack reached about 150 countries and, by later estimates, more than 200,000 computers, and the United Kingdom's National Health Service (NHS) had to turn patients away.

What he did. Hutchins came home at about 2:30 in the afternoon, saw the outbreak, obtained a sample, noticed the unregistered domain and registered it, as he always did, for 10.69 dollars. By his own account he did not know at first what it was for. Testing showed that with the domain resolving the sample stopped, and with the connection blocked it ran; registering it had flipped the condition worldwide. In his write-up he rejected the popular label: he believed it was not a deliberate kill switch but a badly thought out anti-analysis check, a test of whether the code was running in an analysis environment. Kryptos Logic's chief executive, Salim Neino, said he had taken it over on the Friday afternoon, European time, before the outbreak fully reached the United States. Hutchins told the Associated Press that he was definitely not a hero, and ended his post with the only advice that mattered: if you have anything to patch, patch it, because the sinkhole stopped only that sample.

Keeping it alive. The kill switch only worked while the domain answered. Hutchins and his colleague Jamie Hankins spent the following days defending the sinkhole against a botnet operator trying to knock it offline with junk traffic, and at one point law enforcement seized two of their servers in France, believing the domain was spreading WannaCry rather than stopping it. TechCrunch reported in 2019 that keeping that domain up was still the only thing preventing a renewed outbreak.

Arrest and charges. On 2 August 2017, as he waited to fly home after Black Hat and DEF CON, the Federal Bureau of Investigation (FBI) arrested him in Las Vegas. A federal grand jury in the Eastern District of Wisconsin had returned a six-count indictment on 11 July 2017, alleging that between about July 2014 and July 2015 he had helped create and distribute Kronos, malware designed to harvest the usernames and passwords people typed into banking websites, offered on forums from early 2014 and sold on the AlphaBay market on the Tor network. He was 23; he was released shortly afterwards but required to stay in the United States; many researchers defended him, citing his public work against cybercriminals, and hundreds donated to his defence. A superseding indictment raised the count to ten, including a false statements charge.

Plea and sentence. In April 2019 he pleaded guilty to two counts: conspiracy to advertise, distribute and profit from the UPAS Kit and Kronos malware, and an effort to disseminate a device used primarily to intercept electronic communications, each carrying up to five years. 'I regret these actions and accept full responsibility for my mistakes,' he wrote, adding that he had since been using the same skills for constructive purposes. On 26 July 2019 Judge Joseph Peter Stadtmueller sentenced him to time served and one year of supervised release. The judge noted that he had turned away from malware development before the FBI came for him, that a young person may not yet be able to exercise good judgment, and that people with his skills were needed to fix woefully inadequate security; he warned that the conviction might bar him from returning to the United States and suggested he seek a pardon.

The arguments that remain. Prosecutors put their view in an analogy: like a man who spent years robbing banks and then helped design better security systems, he deserved credit for his epiphany but still bore responsibility for what he did. His supporters pointed out that the government had struggled to show specific losses and that almost all the victims were outside the United States. The case sits beside a larger story: the US Justice Department later charged a North Korean man over WannaCry and other attacks, and the outbreak cost the NHS alone more than 100 million dollars. For defenders the technical lessons are durable: an exposed SMB port and an unapplied patch let a leaked exploit become a worm, and a sinkholed domain, once it is load-bearing, has to be defended like production infrastructure.

wau-holland.def: The co-founder of the Chaos Computer Club in 1981 and the author of its ethic - Levy's hacker principles extended with two German additions: do not litter in other people's data, and use public data, protect private data.
wau-holland.context: Holland's club proved its point by doing rather than saying: in 1984 the CCC exploited the Btx videotext system to bill a Hamburg savings bank about 135,000 Deutschmarks overnight (134,634.88 by heise online's 2024 count), then returned it in public with the press watching, forcing the Bundespost to admit a flaw it had denied. That is the CCC method still, technical proof deployed as civic argument, and it is why Germany's hacker scene has spent forty years closer to constitutional politics than to the underground.

aleph-one.def: The 1996 Phrack article by Elias Levy, writing as Aleph One, that explained the stack buffer overflow completely and clearly (stack frames, return addresses, shellcode, NOP (no-operation) sleds) and taught a whole generation how memory corruption actually works; Levy also moderated the Bugtraq disclosure list from 1996 to 2001.
aleph-one.context: It is probably the single most influential technical text the underground produced. It was not the first account of a stack overflow (its introduction lists a recent wave of them), but it was the complete, step-by-step one, and fourteen months later the authors of StackGuard cited it among the cook-book descriptions that had made such exploits easy to build. That is why the article is also the standing exhibit in the disclosure argument, and why its author, as moderator of Bugtraq, was one of that argument's principal voices. The defences that followed, stack canaries, non-executable memory, address randomization and memory-safe languages, are answers to the attack it made common knowledge.
aleph-one.depth:
Aleph One was the handle of Elias Levy. In November 1996 he signed his mail from underground.org and had, since 14 May 1996, been the moderator of Bugtraq, the full-disclosure mailing list Scott Chasin had created on 5 November 1993; the article itself is presented as brought to the reader by BugTraq, r00t and Underground.Org. Phrack's own archive dates issue 49 to 8 November 1996, edited by daemon9, and lists Smashing The Stack For Fun And Profit as file 14 of 16, alongside a Phrack Prophile on Mudge, Project Loki on tunnelling through the Internet Control Message Protocol (ICMP) and Project Hades on weaknesses in TCP.

The article opens with the Jargon File's definition of smashing the stack: on many C implementations, writing past the end of an array declared auto in a routine corrupts the execution stack and can make the routine return to a random address, producing some of the most insidious data-dependent bugs known. Its introduction places it in time: over the previous few months there had been a large increase in buffer overflow vulnerabilities both discovered and exploited, in syslog, splitvt, sendmail 8.7.5, the Linux and FreeBSD mount commands, the Xt library and at. It sets its own scope: stack-based overflows of dynamic buffers on Intel x86 processors running Linux, for a reader with basic assembly language, with virtual memory concepts and the GNU debugger (gdb) helpful but not required.

What it explains, in order, is the machinery an engineer needs to understand the bug class. A process has three regions, text, data and stack. The stack grows towards lower addresses; a function call pushes its arguments, the CALL instruction saves the instruction pointer as the return address, and the procedure prologue saves the old frame pointer and makes room for local variables, so a local buffer sits just below the saved frame pointer and the saved return address. Copy a longer string into that buffer with strcpy(), which has no bounds check, and the copy runs over both: the demonstration ends with the program trying to return to 0x41414141, the letter A repeated. A buffer overflow, the article concludes, lets the attacker change the return address of a function, and therefore the flow of execution.

The second half turns that into code execution. Since the target program rarely contains the code the attacker wants, usually a shell, the article places machine code in the overflowing buffer itself and points the return address back into it, building that code step by step from the system call that starts a program and removing every null byte, because a string copy stops at the first one. The practical problem is that the attacker must guess exactly where the code will land; the article's answer is to fill the front of the buffer with NOP (no-operation) instructions, one byte, 0x90, on Intel, so that a return anywhere into the padding slides down to the code, and to repeat the guessed return address. For buffers too small for the code it uses the program's environment variables instead. It ends with how to find such bugs: standard C library functions that copy or append without bounds checks, strcat(), strcpy(), sprintf(), vsprintf() and gets(), scanf() with an unbounded %s, and hand-written loops of getc() or getchar() without a length check. Free operating systems published their source, and many commercial utilities were derived from the same code; grep, the article says, is your friend. The method was not new; the completeness of the explanation was.

The defenders read it as closely as the attackers. StackGuard, presented at the 7th USENIX Security Symposium in San Antonio on 26 to 29 January 1998, cited the article, as its reference 17, among the cook-book descriptions of stack smashing that had made building buffer-overflow exploits quite easy, and answered with a compiler change: a canary word placed next to the return address and checked before the function returns, randomized so that an attacker cannot simply include it in the overflow. MITRE's Common Weakness Enumeration (CWE) entry for the bug, CWE-121, now lists the descendants: Microsoft Visual Studio's /GS flag, FORTIFY_SOURCE in the GNU Compiler Collection (GCC) on Fedora and Red Hat, StackGuard and ProPolice, plus address space layout randomization (ASLR) and position-independent executables (PIE). It is careful to call all of them defence in depth: canaries catch only some overflows and still end in a denial of service, and an information leak that discloses addresses defeats randomization. The answer that removes the bug class rather than raising its cost is a memory safe language, which the US Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency (CISA) now asks software manufacturers to adopt through published roadmaps.

Bugtraq gave the article its context. Jeremy Rauch, one of SecurityFocus's founders, described it in 1999 as designed from the start as an open forum for the no-holds-barred discussion of security vulnerabilities, on the theory that the only way to improve security is to understand the problems that exist, and recorded the backlash from those who said that arming the hacker enemy would bring chaos. On 28 June 1999 Levy told subscribers that within a week the list would move from netspace.org to securityfocus.com, that he would remain moderator under the same rules, and that SecurityFocus would add a free searchable vulnerability database culled from five years of Bugtraq, a lightly moderated Incidents list for break-ins and malware, and Japanese and Spanish versions of Bugtraq for people more comfortable outside English.

The disclosure argument came to a head in October 2001, when Scott Culp, manager of Microsoft's security response centre, coined the term information anarchy for the publication of vulnerability details and exploits, comparing it to yelling fire in a crowded movie house; his position, as Levy summarized it, was that clamping down on the dissemination of that information would reduce everyone's risk. Levy's reply in The Register on 23 October 2001 said Culp had missed that the movie house was already on fire. A successful attacker needs opportunity, capability and motivation; restricting information targets only capability, and in an open society, he argued, it cannot work, because a small number of malicious users will always obtain it, because nobody can tell a potential attacker from a legitimate user, and because the same information is what researchers, penetration testers and administrators need to understand a problem and verify that a vendor's fix works.

Levy had already stepped down. On 15 October 2001 he wrote that he had moderated Bugtraq nearly continuously, every day, for almost six years, and handed the list to David Ahmad so that he could work on the Attack Registry and Intelligence Service (ARIS) project. On 17 July 2002 Symantec announced it would buy SecurityFocus for about 75 million US dollars in cash, keeping Bugtraq under the SecurityFocus brand alongside the DeepSight threat service and the vulnerability database; the deal closed in August 2002. By 2020 the list had carried almost 80,000 posts, with a peak of 776 in July 2001, but approvals stopped in late February 2020 after Broadcom acquired Symantec's enterprise assets in late 2019 and some of them changed hands again in 2020. A final message on 15 January 2021 announced that the archive would close on 31 January 2021; within days the new owner reversed the decision.

The defensive record can be read against the article step by step: the canary answers the overwritten return address, layout randomization answers the guessed landing address that the NOP padding only approximates, bounds-checked library functions answer the unchecked copies the article told readers to grep for, and memory safe languages remove the out-of-bounds write itself. Phrack, which carried it, was still publishing in 2025, with issue 72 dated 19 August 2025, and the article remains in its archive as file 14 of issue 49.

richard-stallman.def: The MIT AI Lab hacker who, watching the lab's culture dissolve into proprietary software in the early 1980s, launched the GNU Project in 1983, founded the Free Software Foundation in 1985, and wrote the four freedoms and the GPL.
richard-stallman.context: The origin story is a printer: denied the source code to fix a jam notification, he concluded that a program you cannot change is a program that controls you. He then wrote foundational software - GCC, GNU Emacs, GDB, much of the toolchain the world compiles with - which is why the argument had teeth. Uncompromising to the point of alienating allies, and controversial in later years over public remarks, he remains the reason the movement is framed as ethics rather than engineering convenience.

linus-torvalds.def: The Finnish student who announced a free operating-system kernel on the comp.os.minix newsgroup in August 1991, 'just a hobby, won't be big and professional like gnu', and who, in 2005, wrote Git in about ten days after the kernel lost access to its proprietary version-control system.
linus-torvalds.context: Two artifacts, both now infrastructure for the whole industry: the kernel that the Linux Foundation calls the world's most pervasive operating system, which also sits under every Android phone, and the distributed version-control model most developers now use daily. His method is as influential as his code: merciless public review on a mailing list, final authority over what enters the mainline kernel, and a famous temper he publicly stepped back to address in September 2018. Where Richard Stallman argued ethics, Torvalds argued engineering, and between them the movement got both halves.
linus-torvalds.depth:
Linus Torvalds was born in Helsinki on 28 December 1969 and entered the University of Helsinki in 1988. In late August 1991 he posted to comp.os.minix, the newsgroup of Andrew Tanenbaum's teaching system MINIX: I'm doing a (free) operating system (just a hobby, won't be big and professional like gnu) for 386(486) AT clones. It had been brewing since April, he had ported bash 1.08 and gcc 1.40, it was free of any MINIX code, and it was not portable, since it used 386 task switching and would probably never support anything but AT hard disks, as that's all I have. Google's archive timestamps the post 26 August 1991, 06:12 UTC. The irony was not lost later: his master's thesis at Helsinki, in the Linux Foundation's account, was titled Linux: A Portable Operating System.

Two early decisions shaped everything after. The release notes for version 0.12 announced that the copyright would change to the GNU copyleft as of the first of February, removing the condition that the code could not be distributed for money, once contributors agreed, which put the kernel under the GNU General Public License (GPL). And the work was done in public from the first day: the announcement itself asked Usenet readers which features they wanted. Version 1.0 followed in March 1994; the tarball on kernel.org is dated 13 March, and the usual date given is 14 March. Tanenbaum, writing in 2004, supplied the context: MINIX source had been published in 1987 as the appendix to his textbook, comp.os.minix had 40,000 subscribers asking him to turn a teaching system into a production one, the GNU system, in his words, sort of went nowhere, and AT&T's lawsuit against BSDI held up free BSD long enough to give Linux breathing space.

The two men also disagreed in public. Tanenbaum called it a fairly public debate, and in his 2004 notes, written to rebut a claim that Linux had been copied, he stated that to the best of his knowledge Linus wrote the whole kernel himself, that MINIX had influenced the file system layout and the names in the source tree, and that no MINIX code was used. His objection was architectural: MINIX was a microkernel with the memory manager and file system in user space, and Torvalds had written a big monolithic kernel instead, which in Tanenbaum's words messed the design up; his only regret, he wrote, was that Linux was not built on MINIX's microkernel technology.

As the project grew, the bottleneck became Torvalds himself. LWN recalls that in early 1999 Larry McVoy warned that Linus did not scale, and that the 2.4 kernel took almost a year to stabilize.
