From 2002 the kernel used McVoy's proprietary BitKeeper, whose model had no central repository: each developer kept independent trees, and changes were pulled from one to another with full history. Patch flow improved dramatically, but the free licence was binary-only, required changelogs to be published, and forbade users to work on any source code management system at all. In April 2005, after a developer reverse-engineered the BitKeeper protocol, which Torvalds names as Andrew Tridgell, BitMover withdrew the free version and the kernel lost its tool.

Torvalds wrote his own. In a 2015 interview he said Git was self-hosting after about a day, that it came together in about ten days, at which point he made his first kernel commit with it, and that the hard part was not the code but how it organizes the data. Pro Git lists the goals: speed, a simple design, strong support for thousands of parallel branches, full distribution and the ability to handle a project the size of the kernel. Git stores snapshots rather than per-file differences, checksums everything with a SHA-1 hash before storing it and refers to it by that checksum, and keeps the entire history on every local disk, so that corruption is detectable and most operations need no server; Torvalds noted that he commonly does tens of merges a day in the merge window. It took over far beyond the kernel, which he attributed to frustration with every earlier system and to the freedom of private repositories without the politics of write access to a central one.

His management style was as public as the code. He had always been known, as LWN put it, as a harsh critic, and people had been telling him for years that some things should change; on 16 September 2018 he announced a break from kernel work, writing that people in the community had confronted him about his lifetime of not understanding emotions and that his flippant attacks in emails had been both unprofessional and uncalled for, for which he was truly sorry. Greg Kroah-Hartman took over pull requests for the rest of the 4.19 cycle, and the same day the kernel replaced its 2015 code of conflict with a code of conduct based on the Contributor Covenant. LWN's Jonathan Corbet noted that some welcomed the change and others did not, while Torvalds said he strongly wished to keep leading the project once things settled.

He has deliberately avoided working for any of the companies that depend on Linux, saying in 2012 that what he valued most was his neutral status; after the chip start-up Transmeta, which he left in 2003, he worked independently of the kernel's corporate users, and today he is a Linux Foundation fellow and, in its words, the ultimate authority on new code in the standard kernel. In 2012 he shared the Millennium Technology Prize of Technology Academy Finland with the stem-cell researcher Shinya Yamanaka, a pot of one million euros (the Linux Foundation's biography dates the prize to 2008, which the 2012 announcements contradict); he also received the IEEE (Institute of Electrical and Electronics Engineers) Computer Society Computer Pioneer Award in 2014 and was made a fellow of the Computer History Museum. The kernel he started now underlies Android, whose kernels are built from upstream Linux long-term support releases, and, by the Linux Foundation's description, nearly every industry and form factor.

space-rogue.def: The L0pht member who founded the Hacker News Network, testified alongside the rest of the crew before the US Senate in 1998, and has spent the decades since as one of the field's most consistent public voices on research ethics and vendor behaviour.
space-rogue.context: HNN mattered because it was journalism by practitioners at a moment when mainstream coverage of hacking was mostly panic; it set the tone for the security press that followed. He later wrote the L0pht's own history, arguing against the tidy legend the industry prefers, and remains a fixture at DEF CON and Black Hat - proof that the underground's institutional memory is carried by people, not archives.

solar-designer.def: The Russian researcher behind John the Ripper, the password cracker that has been the standard auditing tool since 1996, and behind Openwall - along with early defensive work on non-executable stacks and the return-to-libc attack that showed why that defence alone is not enough.
solar-designer.context: He is the clearest example of a researcher who moves attack and defence in the same career: publishing the technique that defeats a mitigation, then shipping hardening that addresses it. He also runs the oss-security mailing list, which is where a large share of the open-source world's vulnerabilities are coordinated in public. Quiet, rigorous, and enormously influential without the conference-stage persona.

michal-zalewski.def: The Polish researcher who wrote American Fuzzy Lop, the coverage-guided fuzzer that made automated bug-hunting genuinely effective, and the books Silence on the Wire and The Tangled Web on passive reconnaissance and browser security.
michal-zalewski.context: AFL changed the economics of finding memory-corruption bugs: instrument the target, mutate inputs, keep whatever reaches new code, and let a laptop discover crashes that skilled humans missed for years. Nearly every modern fuzzer descends from it, and large parts of open source were audited by it before anyone was paid to. His writing has the same quality as his tools - patient explanations of how information leaks from systems that look silent.

fyodor.def: The author of Nmap, published in Phrack in 1997 and still the standard port scanner and host-discovery tool - the program that taught the industry what its own networks actually expose.
fyodor.context: Nmap's contribution goes beyond scanning: OS fingerprinting by TCP/IP stack quirks, service and version detection, and a scripting engine that turned it into a small vulnerability scanner. It is also a rare piece of security software with cultural reach - it appears on screen in The Matrix Reloaded, which Fyodor documents proudly on the project's Movies page. He also maintains the seclists archives, where much of the field's public discussion has been preserved for decades.

cypherpunks.def: The movement and mailing list founded in 1992 around a single conviction: that widely deployed strong cryptography, not legislation, is what protects privacy from states and corporations. Eric Hughes's manifesto supplied the creed: 'Cypherpunks write code.'
cypherpunks.context: The list worked on much of the modern internet's privacy machinery before it reached the public: its members ran anonymous remailers, which Tim May called quick, if incomplete, implementations of David Chaum's mixes, discussed digital cash years before any system was deployed, and argued through the legal fight over encryption export that became the Crypto Wars. Onion routing itself began at the US Naval Research Laboratory in 1995. The list's alumni built the ecosystem of PGP (Pretty Good Privacy), Tor, BitTorrent and eventually Bitcoin; Satoshi's paper was announced on a descendant list. The name was coined by Jude Milhon, and the movement is where cryptography stopped being a military discipline and became a civil-rights one.
cypherpunks.depth:
A cypherpunk is someone who advocates the widespread use of strong cryptography and privacy-enhancing technology as a means of social and political change. The Cypherpunks, with a capital, were never an organization. Steven Levy, who sat in on their meetings for the cover story of the second issue of Wired in 1993, wrote that it would be wrong to think of them as a formal group: there was a monthly physical meeting, and there was the List. The name fuses cipher with cyberpunk. By Timothy May's account, Jude Milhon, then an editor at the magazine Mondo 2000, quipped at one of the earliest meetings that those present were just a bunch of cypherpunks, and the name was adopted immediately; the Oxford English Dictionary admitted the word in November 2006. It should not be confused with cyberpunk, the fiction genre it borrows from, or with crypto in the later sense of cryptocurrency, although one led to the other.

The group dates from September 1992. May, a former Intel physicist who had retired young, and Eric Hughes, both software engineers with an interest in cryptography, had been talking, and Hughes decided to host a gathering. It met in Oakland, California, in the week that version 2.0 of PGP (Pretty Good Privacy) was released, and diskettes of it were handed out. May read aloud a text he had written in mid-1988 and circulated at the Crypto '88 conference, The Crypto Anarchist Manifesto. John Gilmore, a co-founder of the Electronic Frontier Foundation (EFF), offered his machine toad.com to host a mailing list and the offices of his company, Cygnus Support, for monthly meetings, and the list began almost immediately. It was never large and always loud: May put it at about 500 subscribers in 1994, other counts give 700 that year and an estimated 2,000 in 1997, and Levy found more than 50 messages a day in its first months.

Its creed is Hughes's A Cypherpunk's Manifesto of 9 March 1993, a page of text that still reads as a design brief. Privacy is necessary for an open society in the electronic age, and privacy is not secrecy: it is the power to selectively reveal oneself to the world. Because any party to a transaction can speak about it, privacy requires that each party learn only what the transaction needs, which means anonymous transaction systems, and it requires cryptography. Governments and corporations cannot be expected to grant it. Then the operative lines: Cypherpunks write code; the code is published, free for all to use, worldwide; software cannot be destroyed, and a widely dispersed system cannot be shut down. May's manifesto goes further, towards what he called crypto anarchy, a politics in which encryption, digital money and anonymous networks dissolve the power of governments. The two texts are worth keeping apart: Hughes describes a method, May a programme, and many who adopted the method did not share the programme.

The first code was the anonymous remailer. Hughes wrote the first Cypherpunks remailer in a weekend, by May's account spending the first day learning enough Perl to do it. A message is encrypted in envelopes within envelopes, each addressed to the next remailer, and each remailer strips one layer and forwards the rest, so that no single operator can link sender to recipient. May called these quick, if incomplete, implementations of the digital mixes that David Chaum had described in 1981. The same nesting is what onion routing, begun at the US Naval Research Laboratory in 1995, later applied to live connections instead of stored messages. Digital cash, by contrast, was discussed for years without being deployed, a difference May noted at the time.

The public fight was with the United States government, in what came to be called the Crypto Wars. Cryptographic software was treated as a munition for export, and on 16 April 1993 the administration announced the Escrowed Encryption Standard, known as the Clipper chip: strong encryption for telephones in which every device transmitted a Law Enforcement Access Field (LEAF) holding a copy of the session key, recoverable with keys kept in escrow. May called the announcement a galvanizing event for the group. In August 1994 Matt Blaze of AT&T Bell Laboratories published techniques by which Clipper devices could communicate without sending a valid LEAF, whose integrity rested on a 16-bit checksum. In court, Daniel Bernstein, represented by the EFF, challenged rules that would have required him to register as an arms dealer and obtain a licence before publishing an encryption algorithm and its source code; on 6 May 1999 the Ninth Circuit Court of Appeals held that source code is speech protected by the First Amendment. Philip Zimmermann, who had published PGP in 1991, wrote that in the closing months of 1999 the administration essentially threw out the whole export control regime.

The second line of work, digital money, took longer and ended elsewhere. In 1997 Adam Back proposed hashcash to the list, a proof-of-work stamp meant to make abuse of email and of remailers costly. In 1998 Wei Dai published b-money, a design for money and contracts among untraceable pseudonyms, which opens with the sentence that he is fascinated by Tim May's crypto-anarchy. On 31 October 2008 a message signed Satoshi Nakamoto, titled Bitcoin P2P e-cash paper, reached the Cryptography mailing list, a moderated list that has been described as a successor to cypherpunks and that carries many of the same people. It announced an electronic cash system with no trusted third party and said that new coins are made from Hashcash style proof-of-work; the paper's first reference is b-money and its sixth is Hashcash.

The list itself outgrew its host. After a falling-out over moderation it was migrated in early 1997 from toad.com, which carried on with its existing subscribers, to a set of cross-linked servers, the Cypherpunks Distributed Remailer, built to remove the single point of failure of a central list; the network had at least seven nodes at its peak and a single one by 2005. The people matter more than the servers. Among those counted as cypherpunks are Hal Finney, the main author of PGP 2.0, Adam Back, Wei Dai, Nick Szabo, Bram Cohen, who created BitTorrent, and Julian Assange, who joined the list in late 1993 or early 1994, and the projects usually traced to the list include PGP, FreeS/WAN for opportunistic encryption of network traffic, Off-the-record messaging and Tor.

Two cautions keep the story honest. The movement was small and, by May's own description, largely libertarian; he told Levy that if cryptography were put to a vote among his fellow Americans his side would lose. And its critics' fear, also recorded by Levy in 1993, that anonymous systems would make illegal activity easier, was not answered so much as overtaken by events. What the cypherpunks established is narrower and has lasted: that privacy on a network is built from deployed software, and that an argument about whether cryptography should be allowed is settled in practice by whether it already ships.

jude-milhon.def: The self-taught programmer and civil-rights activist who helped build Community Memory, the first public computerized bulletin board, in 1970s Berkeley, coined the word cypherpunk, and wrote as St. Jude in Mondo 2000.
jude-milhon.context: Milhon insisted that hacking was 'the clever circumvention of imposed limits', a definition that covers code, bodies and laws with equal force, and she spent her life pushing back on the scene's boy-club default; her advice to women entering it was blunt, funny and widely reprinted. She is the corrective to a history told as a list of young men: the culture's vocabulary, its earliest public network and a good part of its politics came from her.
jude-milhon.depth:
Judith Milhon (1939 to 2003), known from the 1980s as St. Jude, was born in Washington, D.C. and brought up in Indiana, according to her Guardian obituary. In the early 1960s she was part of the beat scene in Cleveland, Ohio, and in 1965 she was active in the civil rights movement: she helped to organize the voting rights march from Selma to Montgomery, Alabama, and was jailed for civil disobedience in Jackson, Mississippi.

She taught herself to program. The Guardian dates the start to 1967, after she read a book called Teach Yourself Fortran; her first programming job was for the restaurant and vending company Horn & Hardart in New York. After moving to the San Francisco Bay Area she worked, according to the official biography posted on the WELL after her death, at the Berkeley Computer Company, microcoding the communications controller of its large timesharing machine.

Community Memory is the work most often attached to her name. The Computer History Museum (CHM) lists its original founders as Lee Felsenstein, Efrem Lipkin, Ken Colstad, Jude Milhon and Mark Szpakowski, who in 1972 joined Resource One, a nonprofit set up by three computer science dropouts from the University of California at Berkeley to put computing at the service of the anti-war and anti-establishment movements; Resource One had been given an SDS-940 timesharing computer. In 1973 the group put a terminal in Leopold's Records in Berkeley, next to the shop's paper bulletin board, where musicians and others pinned cards and flyers. The CHM calls it the first public computer-based bulletin board. The Guardian describes a Teletype, with no screen, housed in a cardboard box to muffle its noise and linked to the computer over the telephone network, and adds that it stayed in the record shop only a few months; the CHM records that the last incarnation of the project closed in 1992. Musicians used it to sell instruments and promote concerts, others for typewriter art and electronic poetry, and the speed of adoption surprised founders who had expected the counterculture to be hostile to computers.

In the mid-1980s she joined a Berkeley magazine called High Frontiers, which in 1989 turned to computer counterculture as Mondo 2000. As St. Jude she was its senior editor from 1989 to 1994, writing a column called Irresponsible Journalism, and she also wrote for Wired and The Net. Her books mixed manual and satire: The Cyberpunk Handbook: The Real Cyberpunk Fakebook, with R.U. Sirius and Bart Nagel and a foreword by Bruce Sterling (Random House, 1995 in the Open Library catalogue), and How to Mutate and Take Over the World, with R.U. Sirius (Ballantine, 1996); her online book proposal Hacking the Wetware: The NerdGirl's Pillow Book appeared on the web in 1994.

The word cypherpunk is hers. Timothy May's Cyphernomicon, the group's own FAQ (frequently asked questions), version 0.666 of 10 September 1994, answers the question of where the name came from in two lines: Jude Milhon, then an editor at Mondo 2000, was at the earliest meetings and quipped that they were just a bunch of cypherpunks, and the name was adopted immediately. The same document dates the group to September 1992, with a first meeting hosted by Eric Hughes in the week PGP 2.0 (Pretty Good Privacy) was released, and a mailing list on a machine offered by John Gilmore. The pun on cyberpunk fiction stuck to a movement that argued for strong cryptography in public hands, wrote anonymous remailers and campaigned against key escrow.

Her definition of hacking is quoted in every obituary. In a 1999 interview with Wired, quoted in her obituaries, she called hacking a martial art, a way of defending against politically correct politicians, overly intrusive laws, bigots and narrow-minded people, and defined it as the clever circumvention of imposed limits, whether imposed by your government, your own skills or the laws of physics. The version quoted at her memorial on the WELL adds your IP server and your own personality to the list. Her slogan for women was shorter: girls need modems. In 2003 she told ABC News that women still met prejudice in online communities, where simply being present, honest, reasonably competent and female left everyone aghast.

Judith Milhon died of cancer on 19 July 2003, aged 64; Boing Boing's notice the next day reported her death in Berkeley, and the WELL held a memorial and virtual wake in its Inkwell conference from 1 August 2003. The official biography posted there describes her as considered by many to be the first woman hacker of the personal computing era and as a central figure, under the name St. Jude, in Steven Levy's Hackers: Heroes of the Computer Revolution; the Guardian, more cautiously, calls her one of the first female hackers. Both agree on the record: a civil rights activist who learned Fortran from a book, a co-founder of the first public computer bulletin board, and the editor who named a cryptography movement.

susan-headley.def: Susan Headley, known as Susan or Susy Thunder, the Los Angeles phone phreak of the late 1970s and early 1980s who was among the first masters of social engineering, talking her way into telephone company systems and, by her own account, military ones by voice; she testified in the early cases against Kevin Mitnick's circle and to the US Senate in 1983, and spoke at DEF CON in 1995.
susan-headley.context: She ran in the same circle as the young Kevin Mitnick, testified against her associates under a grant of immunity, explained the phone phreaks' methods on national television and to a Senate subcommittee, and then left the scene, later playing professional poker in Las Vegas, serving as the elected city clerk of California City and, by some accounts, working as a librarian. Her erasure is itself instructive: she appears in the 1991 book Cyberpunk and in scattered interviews, but the histories that made her contemporaries famous mostly wrote her out until a 2022 profile found her. The method she perfected, authority in the voice and homework before the call, is now the foundation of an entire industry's training.
susan-headley.depth:
Why she matters. Susan Headley is the clearest early case of an intruder whose main tool was other people. In the Los Angeles phone underground of the late 1970s and early 1980s, where the network itself was the object of study, she specialized in what she later called psychological subversion: getting a password, a phone number or a door opened by playing a role over the telephone. Her contemporaries' fame rested on the systems they reached; hers rested on how they were reached, and the techniques she described in 1982, 1983 and 1995, impersonation, research before contact, dumpster diving and playing insiders against each other, are the ones security awareness programmes still teach against.

The Los Angeles scene. The 2022 profile by Claire L. Evans in The Verge describes the city's phone culture of the late 1970s: 24-hour conference lines, phreakers who studied the Bell network and met at a Hollywood pizza parlour to compare notes, and a gradual move from the phone network to computer bulletin board systems (BBSes). Headley ran her own four-way conference line and posted on the phreaker board 8BBS. Through Lewis DePayne, known as Roscoe, a student at the University of Southern California, she met Kevin Mitnick. Esquire's 1995 account by Katie Hafner describes the group's routine in the same terms: nights spent diving into dumpsters behind phone company offices for manuals, and social engineering, conning passwords and proprietary information out of employees by calling up as a technician, secretary or supervisor.

The method. Evans records the voice she used: a telephone operator, a clerk or an overworked secretary saying that her boss needed his password changed. Because telephone operators were then almost all women, she was trusted more easily than her male collaborators, and she considered herself at least their equal as a social engineer. The group's dumpster finds, internal jargon, access codes and employee names, turned single calls into longer, more convincing pretexts. On ABC's 20/20 broadcast of 22 April 1982, The Electronic Delinquents, she explained to Geraldo Rivera that when the phone company received an updated manual it simply threw the old one in the bin, and that the phreaks cleaned out the bins and retrieved a lot of knowledge that way. By her own account to Evans, her last major job was physical: after months of searching the trash of a Pacific Bell office in East Los Angeles for the microfiche of unlisted numbers, she walked in at night, told the cleaning crew that she worked there and needed some records, and swapped part of a drawer of the microfiche for discarded library fiche. She was never charged with it, and she told Evans that the best hackers are the ones nobody knows because they were never caught. Some of her claims cannot be checked: she told Hafner she had expertise in cracking military systems, and told Evans she had talked her way past military checkpoints into Area 51; Evans observed that the more far-fetched one of her stories sounded, the more detail she could supply.

The cases. After a falling-out with DePayne in 1981, played out in public on 8BBS, she sent the FBI (Federal Bureau of Investigation) a copy of his handwritten notes with the phone number and passwords of US Leasing, a San Francisco equipment leasing company whose RSTS computer had been wiped after a session she said she had watched, and asked for immunity. DePayne, Mitnick and another phreaker, Mark Ross, were already under investigation by the Los Angeles District Attorney for a physical break-in at a Pacific Bell building downtown, where they took a manual for the company's internal COSMOS database. The District Attorney gave her immunity in exchange for her testimony, and news reports called her only a female conspirator. Evans describes it as one of the first prosecutions for an electronic intrusion under California's computer crime statute, then two years old; Mitnick, a juvenile, received a year's probation and DePayne served 150 days in jail, and Hafner adds that DePayne later had his conviction set aside. Mitnick's own account is the opposite of hers: in his autobiography he called her a wannabe hacker who destroyed the US Leasing system through a backdoor he had created and left his and DePayne's names behind as a red herring.

Going public. Her 20/20 interview was followed by testimony to the United States Senate: the Committee on Governmental Affairs' Subcommittee on Oversight of Government Management held hearings on computer security in the federal government and the private sector on 25 and 26 October 1983, and the printed record lists Susan Headley among its witnesses. The communications scholar Robert W. Gehl describes that testimony as a warning about hacker garbology, rooting through physical and digital trash, and as part of her move from the underground to security consulting, with clients that included the US military. Evans adds that for a time she appeared at security conventions.

DEF CON, 1995. Her talk at DEF CON III in Las Vegas, Social Engineering and Psychological Subversion of Trusted Systems, promised to show how to plan an attack on a hypothetical XYZ Insurance Company knowing nothing but its name and location, without physical access, without dial-up access and without ever needing a password. As Evans summarizes it, she argued that if more than one person has access to a system they can be played against one another, and that even a single administrator is vulnerable simply by being human, and she told a mostly male audience that a woman willing to use seduction had an advantage. She disliked the term social engineering and preferred her own coinage, psychological subversion, or psych-sub.

After the scene. Hafner found her in 1995 in Las Vegas, where she had tried professional poker, and reported that in 1994 she had been elected city clerk of a small California desert town; Evans names it as California City and lists her later work as a proposition poker player at the Stardust and a dealer of ancient Roman coins. She kept her likeness off the internet and spoke to Evans only by telephone. Hafner and John Markoff had included her in Cyberpunk: Outlaws and Hackers on the Computer Frontier (Simon & Schuster, 1991), but for three decades she was mostly a name in other people's stories. The lesson she embodies has not aged: Evans notes that in July 2020 teenagers took over 130 high-profile Twitter accounts by manipulating Twitter employees into giving them access to internal tools, the same move she made with a telephone in 1980.

emmanuel-goldstein.def: The editor of 2600: The Hacker Quarterly since 1984, host of the radio programme Off The Hook, and founder of the HOPE conferences - the closest thing the American underground has to a permanent institution, named for Orwell's fictional dissident.
emmanuel-goldstein.context: 2600 published what the mainstream press would not, organized the monthly Friday meetings that gave isolated teenagers a physical community in dozens of cities, and paid for its principles in court: the magazine was sued by the film industry for linking to DeCSS, losing a landmark case on whether a hyperlink is speech. Corley's constant argument across four decades is that the right to understand technology is not conditional on permission from its owners.

julian-assange.def: The Australian hacker who, as Mendax of the International Subversives, broke into networks including Nortel's, was sentenced for it in Melbourne in 1996, researched the book Underground and co-wrote the deniable-encryption tool Rubberhose; he founded WikiLeaks in 2006 and, after 14 years of Swedish, British and US proceedings, pleaded guilty to one Espionage Act conspiracy count in 2024.
julian-assange.context: Before WikiLeaks he co-wrote the cryptographic deniable-storage tool Rubberhose and researched the book Underground, which remains the definitive account of the Australian scene of his youth. His later career, the 2010 military and diplomatic releases, seven years in Ecuador's London embassy, five years in a British prison fighting extradition and a 2024 plea deal that freed him, divides the hacker community as sharply as any subject in it, along the fault line the culture has argued over since the 1980s: whether releasing information is in itself a public good, and who carries the cost when names are published.
julian-assange.depth:
Why he matters. Julian Assange connects three things that security engineers normally meet separately: the Australian intrusion scene of the early 1990s, the cypherpunk tradition of building cryptography for people under pressure, and the largest publication of classified material of its time. His case is also a record of how a disclosure is argued in court: the hash the prosecution said he tried to crack, the file transfer drop his source used, and a published password that put unredacted diplomatic cables on the internet. WikiLeaks describes itself as a media organization and library founded by its publisher Julian Assange in 2006; the United States charged him for what it calls the obtaining and publication of national defence information. Both descriptions are part of the record.

Mendax inside NorTel. Underground, the 1997 book by Suelette Dreyfus for which Assange was the researcher, tells the story of three Melbourne hackers, Mendax, Prime Suspect and Trax, who called themselves the International Subversives. Its chapter on them is a case study in network design. NorTel's worldwide network held more than 11,000 computers in a flat name space, every system knowing the address of every other; it was firewalled from the internet, so its internal security was relaxed, but the group came in through dial-up lines. A Yellow Pages (YP) directory database served the password files of 400 sites, and root on that one server gave Mendax control over all 400. He collected 1,003 password files, ran the THC password cracker across 40 Sun workstations he found on the network, with a 60,000-word dictionary and a fast crypt implementation by the Queensland academic Eric Young, made about 40,000 guesses per second and cracked some 5,000 passwords, around 100 of them for root accounts, in a few hours. From NorTel's corporate wide area network he also reached Telecom Australia's systems, while reading a NorTel security administrator's mail that refused to connect Telecom because it had too many hackers.

The sentence. The Australian Federal Police raided Prime Suspect, Mendax and Trax in October 1991. According to Underground, Mendax pleaded guilty to eight counts on 29 August 1995 and to eleven more on 9 May 1996, and contested six charges involving the Australian National University, the Royal Melbourne Institute of Technology (RMIT), NorTel and Telecom, on which the prosecution and defence asked the Supreme Court of Victoria to rule on a point of law. The court sent the case back to the County Court, and on 5 December 1996 he pleaded guilty to the remaining six. Judge Ross said he had initially thought the offences justified a jail sentence, but bound by parity with his co-offenders he recorded convictions on all counts and ordered 2,100 Australian dollars in reparation to the university and a three-year good behaviour bond of 5,000 dollars, adding that highly intelligent individuals ought not to behave like this.

Cypherpunk tools. The same period produced Rubberhose, codenamed Marutukku, a disk encryption system that Assange, Dreyfus and Ralf Weinmann wrote for Linux 2.2, NetBSD and FreeBSD between 1997 and 2000. It filled a disk with layers that each decrypt under a different key, plus chaff layers of random data, so that someone forced to hand over a key could reveal a decoy and deny that further layers existed; the name is a joke on rubber-hose cryptanalysis, getting keys by violence. StegFS is now described as the successor to its ideas.

WikiLeaks and 2010. WikiLeaks released a classified US military video, which it titled Collateral Murder, on 5 April 2010; the Afghanistan significant activity reports followed on 25 July, the Iraq reports on 22 October (391,832 of them, by WikiLeaks's count) and, with media partners, redacted versions of the State Department cables from 28 November 2010. Their source was the Army intelligence analyst Chelsea Manning, who was sentenced to 35 years in prison; President Obama commuted the sentence in 2017. The US case, as the 2021 extradition judgment summarizes it, was that Manning uploaded material, including 250,000 cables, over SFTP (the SSH, or Secure Shell, File Transfer Protocol) to a drop box WikiLeaks ran, and that on 8 March 2010 Assange agreed to help crack a password hash stored in the registry of a computer on SIPRNet (Secret Internet Protocol Router Network), the classified military network, saying he had rainbow tables, so that she could log in under an account not assigned to her; he later reported no luck. The unredacted cables became public in late August and early September 2011. The United States says WikiLeaks published them and endangered named sources; the defence says the password to the encrypted file had appeared in a February 2011 book by the Guardian journalist David Leigh, and that other sites such as Cryptome and the Pirate Bay published first. Leigh called that account a complete invention.

Sweden and the embassy. A Swedish judicial authority issued a European arrest warrant on 2 December 2010 over allegations of unlawful coercion, rape and molestation, which he denied. He was arrested in London on 7 December, extradition to Sweden was ordered on 24 February 2011, the UK Supreme Court dismissed his appeal on 30 May 2012, and on 19 June 2012 he entered Ecuador's embassy in London, where he stayed for nearly seven years. Three of the allegations became time-barred on 12 August 2015; the Swedish prosecutor discontinued the case on 19 May 2017, reopened it on 13 May 2019 and discontinued it again on 19 November 2019 because the evidence had weakened with time, while saying that the complainant's account was credible and reliable.

The extradition fight. The United States indicted him on 6 March 2018 for conspiracy to commit computer intrusion. Ecuador ended his asylum and British police arrested him at the embassy on 11 April 2019; he was convicted that day of failing to surrender to bail and sentenced at Southwark Crown Court on 1 May 2019 to 50 weeks. A superseding indictment of 23 May 2019, replaced by a second on 24 June 2020, brought 18 counts, 17 of them under the Espionage Act. On 4 January 2021 District Judge Vanessa Baraitser rejected his other objections, including that the treaty barred extradition for a political offence, but discharged him because his mental condition made extradition oppressive. After the United States gave assurances that he would not be held under special administrative measures and that, if convicted, it would consent to his serving the sentence in Australia, the High Court allowed its appeal on 10 December 2021; the Supreme Court refused permission to appeal on 14 March 2022, saying the application raised no arguable point of law; Home Secretary Priti Patel ordered extradition on 17 June 2022; and Mr Justice Swift refused leave to appeal on the papers on 6 June 2023. On 26 March 2024 the High Court found a real prospect of success on three of nine grounds and gave the United States three weeks to assure it that he could rely on the First Amendment, would not be prejudiced by his nationality and would not face the death penalty; on 20 May 2024, after hearing the assurances, it granted him leave to appeal.

The plea. He was granted bail on 24 June 2024 and flew from Stansted. In the US District Court for the Northern Mariana Islands, in Saipan, before Judge Ramona Manglona, he pleaded guilty to one count of conspiring to obtain and disclose national defence information, the Justice Department announcing it on 25 June in Washington, already 26 June in Saipan. He was sentenced to 62 months, the time he had spent in British custody on the US charges, was barred from returning to the United States without permission, and landed in Canberra that evening. On 1 October 2024 he told the Parliamentary Assembly of the Council of Europe in Strasbourg that he was not free because the system worked but because he had pleaded guilty to journalism: to seeking information from a source, obtaining it and informing the public what it was. The other side of the argument is in the indictment and in his critics' view, reported alongside, that publishing the names of people who had helped US forces put innocent lives at risk and went beyond journalism; press freedom groups such as the Knight First Amendment Institute answered that a successful prosecution would have criminalized much of investigative journalism. WikiLeaks's later publication in 2016 of emails stolen from the Democratic National Committee and Hillary Clinton's campaign by Russian government hackers, which the Mueller report examined but did not charge, sharpened the division further.

bruce-schneier.def: The cryptographer and writer whose 1994 book Applied Cryptography taught a generation of programmers how ciphers work, who designed Blowfish and Twofish, and who then spent decades arguing that the hard problems in security are human and economic rather than mathematical.
bruce-schneier.context: He gave the field several of its most-used ideas: security theatre for measures that perform safety without providing it, the observation that security is a process and not a product, and Schneier's law - anyone can design a cipher they themselves cannot break. His newsletter has run since 1998 and remains one of the few places where the policy, economic and technical sides of the field are argued together.

satan-scanner.def: The free network vulnerability scanner released in April 1995 by Dan Farmer and Wietse Venema - and the first time the industry had a full public argument about whether giving defenders an attacker's tool is responsible.
satan-scanner.context: The press predicted catastrophe on release day; the catastrophe did not arrive, and administrators finally saw their own networks the way an intruder did. Farmer was reportedly let go by his employer for publishing it, and the authors shipped a renaming script so squeamish sites could call it SANTA. Every argument about Metasploit, Nmap and offensive tooling since is a rerun of the SATAN debate, and the accompanying paper - Improving the Security of Your Site by Breaking Into It - is the founding text of penetration testing as a discipline.

john-markoff.def: The New York Times technology reporter whose front-page coverage in the 1990s turned Kevin Mitnick into the world's most famous hacker, and who co-wrote Cyberpunk (1991) and Takedown (1996), the account of Mitnick's capture written with Tsutomu Shimomura.
john-markoff.context: His reporting is the standing case study in how press framing becomes legal reality: descriptions of Mitnick as a threat to national infrastructure fed a prosecution and years of pretrial detention that the underlying facts did not support, and the Free Kevin campaign was aimed as much at the coverage as at the courts. Markoff also chronicled the personal-computer revolution with genuine authority, which is what makes the episode a caution rather than a dismissal - accurate technology journalism and a distorted narrative can come from the same desk.

moonlight-maze.def: The intrusion campaign discovered in 1998 that had been quietly reading US military, NASA, Department of Energy and university systems since at least 1996 - the first sustained state-scale espionage operation ever detected on the internet, and the effective birth of the category later called the advanced persistent threat.
moonlight-maze.context: Investigators traced connections towards Moscow; attribution was never made public with proof, and Russia denied involvement. What makes it foundational is the shape rather than the source: patient, low-noise, years-long access focused on collection rather than damage, using ordinary Unix vulnerabilities and stolen credentials. Researchers in 2016 linked surviving Moonlight Maze code to the Turla toolkit still in use two decades later, which is the clearest evidence anyone has that state operations have continuity measured in generations.

titan-rain.def: The US government's code name for a series of coordinated intrusions from 2003 onward into defence contractors, army installations and NASA - Lockheed Martin, Sandia, Redstone Arsenal - widely attributed in reporting to Chinese state-linked operators.
titan-rain.context: The human story is as instructive as the technical one. Sandia analyst Shawn Carpenter traced the intruders on his own initiative, shared findings with the Army and FBI, and was fired for it; he later won a jury award. The case set the pattern for two decades of industrial and defence espionage reporting, and it forced a shift in doctrine: perimeter defence assumes an attacker who leaves, while an operator who intends to stay for years requires detection, segmentation and hunting - the reasoning that eventually produced the modern security operations centre.

sony-pictures-hack.def: The November 2014 breach in which attackers calling themselves Guardians of Peace destroyed much of Sony Pictures Entertainment's infrastructure with wiper malware and published executives' email, unreleased films, salaries and employee medical records - alongside threats tied to the studio's comedy about assassinating North Korea's leader.
sony-pictures-hack.context: The FBI attributed it to North Korea, an attribution disputed by some researchers at the time and largely accepted since. It rewrote several rulebooks at once: destructive attacks became a board-level scenario rather than a theoretical one, leaked internal email became a weapon aimed at reputations rather than systems, and the film's altered release turned a corporate breach into a question about coercion and speech. Employees suing over their exposed data established that a breach injures the workforce, not only the company.

the-dnc-hack.def: The 2016 compromise of the Democratic National Committee and campaign staff by two separate Russian intelligence groups - designated Cozy Bear and Fancy Bear - whose stolen email was then published through fronts including Guccifer 2.0 and WikiLeaks during a US presidential election.
the-dnc-hack.context: The initial access was a credential-phishing message that looked like a routine password reset, which is the detail everyone should keep: the most consequential political intrusion of the century began the way most breaches do. Its real novelty was doctrinal - the theft was not the operation, the publication was. Once stolen material can be released selectively and amplified, an intrusion becomes an influence campaign, and every election authority since has had to plan for both.

rsa-breach.def: The March 2011 intrusion at RSA Security in which attackers stole material relating to the SecurID two-factor tokens used by tens of thousands of organizations - reaching the company through a phishing email carrying a spreadsheet with a Flash exploit, opened from a junk folder.
rsa-breach.context: Within months an intrusion attempt at Lockheed Martin was tied to the stolen material, and RSA replaced tokens for a large share of its customer base. It is the canonical supply-chain lesson: compromising one security vendor undermines every customer's authentication at once, and trust in a vendor is a dependency exactly like a library or a certificate authority. It also demonstrated that a company whose product is trust can survive the breach but not the silence - RSA's early reticence cost it more than the incident.

target-breach.def: The 2013 holiday-season compromise of about 40 million payment cards and 70 million customer records at the US retailer Target, entered through credentials stolen from a heating and air-conditioning contractor with remote access to the corporate network.
target-breach.context: It is the case that made third-party risk and network segmentation board-level topics: an HVAC vendor's account had no business being able to reach point-of-sale systems. Detection failed at the last step - the monitoring tools fired alerts that nobody actioned - which is the more uncomfortable half of the story, since the controls worked and the process did not. The chief executive resigned, one of the first times a breach visibly ended a career at that level.

max-butler.def: The security researcher turned card thief who, as Iceman, hacked and forcibly merged the rival carding forums of the mid-2000s into his own CardersMarket - a hostile takeover of an entire criminal marketplace - before receiving a thirteen-year sentence in 2010.
max-butler.context: His arc is the field's sharpest cautionary tale because both halves were real: he wrote intrusion-detection signatures and ran a respected security list while also stealing roughly two million card numbers. Kevin Poulsen's book Kingpin reconstructs it in detail. The case is also where the underground economy's structure became legible to outsiders - forums, reputation systems, escrow, vendor ratings - which is the moment researchers stopped treating cybercrime as hacking and started treating it as an industry.

carding.def: The trade in stolen payment-card data and the economy around it: dumps are magnetic-stripe tracks for cloning physical cards, CVVs are card-not-present details for online use, and fullz bundles a card with enough identity data to open accounts in the victim's name.
carding.context: Carding is where cybercrime professionalized. Its forums built reputation scores, escrow services, dispute resolution and vendor reviews - an institutional structure that made specialization possible, so that the person who breaches a retailer, the person who sells the data and the person who cashes it out are three different people. Chip cards and tokenization collapsed the value of dumps; the trade moved to card-not-present fraud and account takeover, which is where it mostly lives now.

aaron-swartz.def: The programmer and activist who co-authored the RSS 1.0 web feed format (RDF Site Summary) at fourteen, helped build Creative Commons, web.py, Open Library and Reddit, founded Demand Progress and wrote the code behind SecureDrop; he died by suicide in 2013, aged 26, while facing federal charges over a bulk download from JSTOR.
aaron-swartz.context: The specification of RSS 1.0 (RDF Site Summary, after the Resource Description Framework), dated December 2000, lists him among the members of the RSS-DEV working group; soon afterwards he joined a World Wide Web Consortium (W3C) working group, and in 2004 he wrote Request for Comments (RFC) 3870, registering the application/rdf+xml media type. In 2012 he developed DeadDrop, the anonymous submission system that became SecureDrop, with Kevin Poulsen managing the project. In 2008 he downloaded about 20 million pages of court records from PACER (Public Access to Court Electronic Records); the Federal Bureau of Investigation (FBI) investigated and nobody was charged. The JSTOR case followed in 2011: JSTOR said the decision to prosecute was the government's and that it had no interest in the matter becoming an ongoing legal case, and a superseding indictment in 2012 carried 13 felony counts. He died on 11 January 2013 and the charges were dismissed three days later. His case made the Computer Fraud and Abuse Act (CFAA) a public argument; Aaron's Law, the reform named for him, was introduced in 2013 and again in 2015.
aaron-swartz.depth:
The specifications. RDF Site Summary (RSS) 1.0, named after the Resource Description Framework (RDF), was published in December 2000 by the RSS-DEV working group, whose twelve listed members include Aaron Swartz of The Info Network; the Internet Hall of Fame notes that he co-authored it at the age of 14 and shortly afterwards joined a working group at the World Wide Web Consortium (W3C) developing common data formats for the web. In September 2004 he was the sole author of RFC 3870, the Request for Comments that registered application/rdf+xml as the media type for the Resource Description Framework. It was the pattern of his career: infrastructure first, written to be reused by people he would never meet.

Creative Commons, web.py, Reddit, Open Library. Creative Commons, announcing his death, called him one of its early architects, who as a teenager helped design the code layer of its licences. He founded the software company Infogami, and when it merged with Reddit he became a co-owner; there he released web.py, the web framework he had written, as free software. He was a developer of the Internet Archive's Open Library, a free book database and digital library open to the public. In 2008 he founded Watchdog.net, for political transparency; in 2010 he founded Demand Progress, which campaigned successfully against two internet censorship bills, the Stop Online Piracy Act and its Senate counterpart, the PROTECT IP Act; and in 2010 and 2011 he studied the influence of money on institutions, politics and public opinion at Harvard's Edmond J. Safra Center for Ethics. In 2012 he wrote DeadDrop, an anonymous document submission system for journalists, with Kevin Poulsen managing the project; The New Yorker launched it as StrongBox in May 2013, and in October 2013 the Freedom of the Press Foundation took it over and renamed it SecureDrop.

PACER and the manifesto. In 2008 he downloaded about 20 million pages of documents from PACER (Public Access to Court Electronic Records), the government-run court records system, during a period when, and at a location where, it was not charging for downloads; the records were in the public domain, and the 19,856,160 pages were given to public.resource.org, Carl Malamud's open government project. The Federal Bureau of Investigation (FBI) investigated and the inquiry ended with no prosecution. The same year a single page dated July 2008, Eremo, Italy, the Guerilla Open Access Manifesto, opened with 'Information is power' and argued that those with access to paywalled scholarship had a duty to share it. Prosecutors later cited it as evidence of intent; the review that MIT commissioned noted that he was not its sole author and that it was unknown whether he wrote the sentences quoted.

The JSTOR case. The indictment unsealed on 19 July 2011 alleged that between September 2010 and January 2011 he had used the network of the Massachusetts Institute of Technology (MIT), including a switch in a restricted wiring closet, to download more than four million articles from JSTOR, the digital archive of academic journals, and charged him with wire fraud and computer fraud offences carrying a maximum of 35 years in prison. JSTOR stated that it had recovered the content, with confirmation that it would not be used or distributed, that the decision to prosecute was the government's and that it had no interest in the matter becoming an ongoing legal case. State charges were dropped in March 2012. A superseding federal indictment on 12 September 2012 carried 13 felony counts, two of wire fraud and eleven under the Computer Fraud and Abuse Act (CFAA). On 11 January 2013, before trial, he died by suicide, aged 26. On 14 January the United States Attorney's office filed a three-line notice dismissing the case because of his death.

Afterwards. MIT's review, led by Hal Abelson and published on 26 July 2013, examined the institute's posture of neutrality during the prosecution. On 20 June 2013 Representative Zoe Lofgren, with bipartisan co-sponsors, introduced H.R. 2454, the Aaron's Law Act, to refocus the CFAA away from violations of terms of service and towards damaging attacks, with a companion bill from Senator Ron Wyden; Lofgren, Wyden and Senator Rand Paul introduced it again on 21 April 2015. The Internet Hall of Fame inducted him posthumously in 2013, and the American Library Association gave him its James Madison Award, also posthumously.

neuromancer.def: William Gibson's 1984 novel, written on a manual typewriter by an author with almost no computer experience, which gave the culture the word cyberspace, the image of the console cowboy, and ICE for intrusion countermeasures.
neuromancer.context: Its influence runs the wrong way round: the fiction shaped the engineering. A generation of hackers, and later the people who built virtual worlds, cryptocurrency and the modern web's metaphors, were reading Gibson first. The famous opening line about a sky the colour of a dead television now reads differently than it did, since televisions changed - which Gibson has noted with amusement. He also supplied the field's most quoted maxim about unevenly distributed futures.

snow-crash.def: Neal Stephenson's 1992 novel, which coined metaverse and popularized avatar in their current senses, and whose plot turns on a virus that infects both computers and human brains through a deep linguistic substrate.
snow-crash.context: It is the more technically literate of the two founding cyberpunk novels and the funnier one - the protagonist is a pizza-delivering hacker literally named Hiro Protagonist. Its ideas seeded a startling amount of real infrastructure: virtual-world design from Second Life onward, corporate metaverse projects three decades later, and the book was famously required reading among early engineers at several large technology companies. The central conceit - that language itself can be an exploit - reads better every year that prompt injection exists.

the-shockwave-rider.def: John Brunner's 1975 novel, which describes a self-replicating program moving through a continent-wide computer network and calls it a tapeworm - the origin of the word worm as a category of malicious software.
the-shockwave-rider.context: The researchers who built the first real worms at Xerox PARC in 1979 took the name directly from Brunner, and the term reached the wider world with the Morris worm in 1988. The novel is also strikingly prescient about the politics: a networked society where data brokering, identity and government records are the real terrain of conflict, written before personal computers existed. Fiction supplied this field its vocabulary well before the artifacts arrived.

ghost-in-the-wires.def: Kevin Mitnick's memoir of his years as a fugitive, written as a chase narrative: the social-engineering calls reconstructed line by line, the identity changes, the surveillance, and the arrest.
ghost-in-the-wires.context: It is the most readable technical account of social engineering ever published, precisely because it shows the preparation rather than the trick - the hours of research that make a two-minute phone call work. Read against Takedown, written from the pursuers' side, it forms the field's clearest example of the same events producing irreconcilable stories, and the honest way to teach it is to assign both and let the discrepancies stand.

takedown-book.def: The account of Kevin Mitnick's 1995 capture written by Tsutomu Shimomura, whose systems Mitnick had broken into, with New York Times reporter John Markoff - later filmed as Track Down.
takedown-book.context: As technical writing on the intrusion itself it is genuinely valuable: the TCP sequence-prediction attack is explained by the person whose machines it was used against. As history it is contested at almost every turn, and the FREE KEVIN campaign treated the book and its authors as part of the injustice rather than observers of it. The lesson worth extracting is about sourcing: when the investigator, the journalist and the publisher are the same three-way relationship, the resulting record needs reading with that structure in mind.

cyberpunk-book.def: Katie Hafner and John Markoff's 1991 book telling three long-form stories from the 1980s underground: the young Kevin Mitnick and his Los Angeles circle, the German KGB hackers around Hanover, and Robert Morris and his worm.
cyberpunk-book.context: It is the first serious attempt at journalism about this subculture rather than panic reporting about it, and its Los Angeles section preserves some of the only substantial published material on Susan Headley, whom later histories mostly dropped. Mitnick disputed his portrayal for decades. Read alongside The Cuckoo's Egg and Underground, it completes the trio of contemporaneous accounts that fixed the 1980s underground in the record before anyone could tidy it up.

the-matrix.def: The Wachowskis' 1999 film about a programmer who discovers reality is a simulation - the most culturally saturating hacker film ever made, and the source of the red pill, bullet time, and an entire visual grammar for cyberspace.
the-matrix.context: The security field's fondness for it is narrower and more specific than the general audience's: in The Matrix Reloaded, Trinity breaks into a power station using a genuine Nmap scan and a real SSH vulnerability of the period, correctly portrayed. Fyodor documents the appearance on Nmap's own site. After decades of films where hacking meant typing loudly at a rotating three-dimensional interface, a sequel that showed an actual port scan bought the franchise permanent goodwill among practitioners.

mr-robot.def: The television series about a security engineer and vigilante hacker whose technical scenes are, by broad agreement among practitioners, the most accurate ever committed to screen - real tools, real command output, plausible operations.
mr-robot.context: The production hired working security professionals as advisors and shot actual sessions rather than invented interfaces: Kali, Metasploit, John the Ripper, a Raspberry Pi in a climate-control closet, social engineering that begins with a pretext and a phone call. Its other achievement is tonal - it portrays the loneliness, the mental-health cost and the moral confusion of the work rather than the glamour, which is why so many people in the field describe it as uncomfortable to watch in the right way.

citizenfour.def: Laura Poitras's documentary, filmed inside the Hong Kong hotel room where Edward Snowden handed the NSA archive to journalists - the disclosure itself, recorded as it happened, and winner of the 2015 Academy Award for documentary feature.
citizenfour.context: For this field the film is less about the politics than about the tradecraft, shown plainly: encrypted mail as the first contact, air-gapped machines, a blanket over the keyboard against ceiling cameras, phones in the minibar fridge, passphrase discipline. It is the clearest existing record of operational security practised under real threat rather than described in a slide deck, and the archive's contents made everything the cypherpunks had argued about mass surveillance a matter of documents rather than suspicion.

ccc-congress.def: The annual conference the Chaos Computer Club has run between Christmas and New Year since 1984 - tens of thousands of attendees, numbered by edition, with a summer outdoor sibling, the Chaos Communication Camp.
ccc-congress.context: It differs from the American conferences in character: talks are political and technical in equal measure, recordings are published free by a volunteer video team within hours, and the whole event is built and run by attendees rather than staff. Congress is where the CCC has demonstrated biometric passport weaknesses, dissected a state surveillance trojan, and repeatedly dismantled electronic voting proposals - a hacker conference that functions as a standing technical opposition rather than an industry gathering.

hope-conference.def: The conference 2600 has organized in New York since 1994, held for most of its history in the Hotel Pennsylvania across from Penn Station, and named after the magazine's founding conviction that hacking belongs to everyone.
hope-conference.context: HOPE is the most explicitly political of the major hacker conferences - heavy on civil liberties, surveillance, whistleblowing and community organizing, with a long tradition of hosting speakers other venues would not, including remote appearances by figures facing prosecution. Its atmosphere is closer to a public assembly than a trade event, which is the point: DEF CON grew into an institution the state now attends, while HOPE deliberately stayed a place where the state is the subject rather than the guest.

capture-the-flag.def: The competitive format in which teams solve security challenges to recover flag strings. Jeopardy style offers categorized puzzles - binary exploitation, reverse engineering, cryptography, web, forensics - while attack-defence gives every team an identical vulnerable network to break into and simultaneously patch.
capture-the-flag.context: DEF CON's CTF has run since 1996 and is the field's world championship, with qualifiers feeding a final that teams train for all year. The format turned out to be the best training method anyone has found: it rewards reading unfamiliar code under time pressure, which is the actual job. Attack-defence in particular teaches the lesson no lecture conveys - that you must fix your own copy of the bug while someone is actively using it against you.

defcon-badge.def: DEF CON's conference badge, which since 2006 has usually been a working piece of electronics carrying a multi-stage puzzle - designed for years by Joe Grand, known as Kingpin - and the seed of the wider badgelife culture of independent hardware badges.
defcon-badge.context: Solving the badge is a competition in itself, drawing teams that work through the conference on ciphers, hidden hardware interfaces and cross-badge protocols. The side effect is educational: thousands of people who had never touched a soldering iron or a serial console learned hardware hacking because the conference pass was itself the lesson. Badgelife grew into an economy of independent creators shipping small runs of custom electronics, which is a hardware-hacking on-ramp disguised as merchandise.

pgp.def: The encryption program Phil Zimmermann released free in 1991, combining public-key and symmetric cryptography for mail and files, and the OpenPGP standard and implementations - notably GnuPG - that grew from it.
pgp.context: PGP introduced most people to public-key cryptography and to the web of trust, a decentralized alternative to certificate authorities in which users sign each other's keys. It also demonstrated the model's limits: key management proved too hard for general use, and its long-lived keys and lack of forward secrecy are why modern messaging moved to different designs. It remains widely used for signing software releases and for journalist contact, and it is the tool whose distribution triggered a three-year criminal investigation of its author.

phil-zimmermann.def: The author of PGP, who released strong encryption free to the public in 1991 and spent three years under US criminal investigation for munitions export because the software left the country.
phil-zimmermann.context: His defence became a landmark of legal creativity: since exporting a book is protected speech, PGP's source code was published as a printed volume by MIT Press, exported lawfully, and scanned back in abroad. The investigation was dropped in 1996 without charges. Zimmermann's stated motive was never commercial - he built it for activists and for people who should not have to justify wanting a private letter, an argument he has repeated for three decades.

clipper-chip.def: The United States government's 1993 proposal for encrypted telephony, formalized as the Escrowed Encryption Standard: the encryption was strong, but every chip's key was split between two government escrow agents, so authorities with legal authorization could decrypt.
clipper-chip.context: It failed politically because a key held by someone else is not your key, and technically because Matt Blaze showed in August 1994 that the Law Enforcement Access Field (LEAF), the block every chip sent so that its traffic could be decrypted, rested on a 16-bit checksum that a determined user could satisfy with a forged value, keeping the encryption while defeating the escrow: the system broken on its own terms. Clipper is the reference point for every later proposal of the same shape, whatever it is called: lawful access, exceptional access, client-side scanning. The engineering objection has never changed: a mechanism built to be opened does not verify who is opening it.
clipper-chip.depth:
What it was. The Clinton White House introduced the Clipper chip on 16 April 1993 as the encryption device for American secure voice equipment, and the National Institute of Standards and Technology (NIST) made it a federal standard on 9 February 1994: FIPS (Federal Information Processing Standard) 185, the Escrowed Encryption Standard (EES). The standard specified the use of a symmetric cipher called SKIPJACK and a method for creating a Law Enforcement Access Field (LEAF), the part of a key escrow system that allows lawfully intercepted traffic to be decrypted, but did not describe either: both were classified, referenced in the standard and implemented only inside tamper-resistant chips. Its use was voluntary for unclassified government applications and for commercial security. There were two chips, Clipper (MYK-78), a drop-in replacement for a Data Encryption Standard (DES) chip that left key negotiation to the host, and Capstone (MYK-80), which added public-key negotiation and digital signatures; Blaze names the AT&T Model 3600 Telephone Security Device as the first application, with a Capstone-based card for laptops to follow.

How the escrow worked. Each chip had a device unique key made of two components of at least 80 bits each, every component generated and stored by a separate escrow agent. Traffic was encrypted with an 80-bit session key in the standard DES modes of operation. With every session the chip produced a 128-bit LEAF: a 32-bit unit identifier, the serial number of the chip; the 80-bit session key encrypted under the unit key; and a 16-bit checksum, the whole encrypted under a family key shared by every interoperable device. A wiretapping agency captured the traffic and the LEAF, decrypted the LEAF with the family key to read the serial number, took the serial number with its legal authorization to the two escrow agents, combined the two half-keys they returned by exclusive-or into the unit key, and used that to recover the session key. The receiving chip enforced the scheme: it would not load an initialization vector whose accompanying LEAF failed its integrity check.

The cipher. SKIPJACK, designed by the National Security Agency (NSA), stayed secret until the agency declassified it, with the Key Exchange Algorithm (KEA), in 1998. Bruce Schneier described it then as a 64-bit block cipher with an 80-bit key and no escrow of its own, the escrow having lived in the key handling around it, and as the first NSA-designed algorithm the public had ever seen; he argued the declassification happened because the Defense Messaging System could not get Fortezza cards installed fast enough and needed the algorithms in software. The standard itself had claimed SKIPJACK gave more protection against key search than DES, which was true of the key length, but nobody outside the government could check the design, and that was the first objection the cryptographic community raised.

Blaze's protocol failure. On 20 August 1994 Matt Blaze of AT&T Bell Laboratories published experiments on a prototype PCMCIA (Personal Computer Memory Card International Association) card that implemented the standard. They worked only through the device's normal interface, with no cryptanalysis and no hardware reverse engineering, and showed that the receiving chip could check the LEAF only through its 16-bit checksum, since it did not know the sender's unit key. A random 128-bit value therefore passed with probability one in 2 to the 16th power, so a rogue application could use its own chip to search for a LEAF that looked valid but carried no usable key: at 38 milliseconds a test, about 42 minutes, or under 45 seconds spread over 60 cards. That was too slow for telephone call set-up but acceptable for electronic mail and stored files, and the result was traffic with the full strength of SKIPJACK and no access for the wiretapper. The fixes Blaze discussed, slower LEAF checks, limits on failed attempts, longer checksums, each cost either legitimate users or the wiretap.

What Blaze did and did not show. He did not break SKIPJACK, and the point has been argued over since. In 2015 the former NSA general counsel Stewart Baker wrote that nothing in the paper questioned the security the chip offered and that the press ignored that caveat; Matthew Green answered that a multimillion-dollar, NSA-designed access system emerging with fundamental flaws in its design matters whether the flaw recovers plaintext or merely lets criminals use the technology in ways they were not supposed to. Both readings agree on the mechanism: the escrow was the fragile part, and it failed in the direction the scheme could least afford, towards the users determined enough to strip it.

Why it died. The objections came from both sides at once. Civil libertarians objected to the arrangement itself; Phil Zimmermann wrote in 1995 that each chip would carry a unique key whose copy sat in a vast government database for wiretap purposes. Cryptographers objected to a classified cipher nobody could evaluate. The technology was also behind its moment: Matthew Green calls Clipper a bit of a dinosaur, a hardware answer proposed on the eve of a revolution in software encryption and network voice, and the standard's devices remained subject to the International Traffic in Arms Regulations (ITAR) for export. The Electronic Frontier Foundation (EFF) records massive public opposition and dates the proposal's death to 1996; NIST formally withdrew FIPS 185 on 19 October 2015.

What it left behind. Clipper fixed the template for every exceptional-access proposal since. The arguments recur unchanged: the escrow database is a single target holding the keys to everything; the access path must itself be secured, so the system's strength rests on a process as well as on mathematics; and a well-resourced adversary can avoid the escrow while ordinary users carry its risk. When many of the same cryptographers revisited the question in Keys Under Doormats in July 2015, they judged that exceptional access would do more damage than it would have twenty years earlier. The phrase golden key used in that later round was itself an echo: the EFF notes it had been the name of a coalition campaign against key escrow nearly twenty years before.

edward-snowden.def: The NSA contractor who in 2013 handed journalists a large archive of documents on US and allied signals-intelligence programmes, then left for Hong Kong and eventually Russia, where he remains beyond the reach of American prosecution.
edward-snowden.context: For this field the significance is technical rather than political: the documents turned longstanding suspicions about bulk collection, tapped inter-datacentre links and weakened cryptographic standards into sourced fact. The industry response was immediate and durable - encryption between datacentres, HTTPS as a default rather than a feature, certificate transparency, and free certificates at scale. The disclosure itself was filmed in the Hong Kong hotel room and released as Citizenfour, which doubles as a record of operational security practised under real threat.

key-escrow.def: Any arrangement in which a copy of a decryption key is held by a third party so encrypted material can be recovered without the owner's cooperation - proposed for law enforcement, and used legitimately inside organizations for recovering data when an employee leaves.
key-escrow.context: The two uses are not the same problem. Corporate escrow has a bounded scope, a known custodian and an auditable process; national escrow proposes a repository of keys to everyone's communications, which is a target of unmatched value and a single point of catastrophic failure. The consensus position among cryptographers, argued since Clipper and restated in the Keys Under Doormats papers, is that exceptional-access systems add complexity and attack surface faster than they add safety.

apt.def: An adversary with the resources and patience to gain access and keep it - typically state-sponsored or state-tolerated, focused on collection over months or years rather than on immediate gain. The term describes the operator's posture, not a specific technique.
apt.context: The phrase came out of US Air Force reporting in the 2000s and hardened into an industry label after Moonlight Maze and Titan Rain. Each word does work: advanced means capable of building tools rather than only buying them, persistent means it comes back after you evict it, threat means a human with intent rather than an automated scan. It is also the field's most abused term - vendors call ordinary criminal crews APTs because it sells, and the correct question about any intrusion is whether the operator will still be trying next quarter.

atp.def: A vendor product category - detonation sandboxes, mail and web filtering with behavioural analysis, endpoint detection bundled under one name - sold as the answer to advanced threats. Three letters away from APT, and constantly confused with it.
atp.context: Keep them straight: APT is the adversary, ATP is the thing you buy because of the adversary. The confusion is not accidental - the product name was built to echo the threat name. The useful discipline when reading a datasheet is to ask which specific behaviours the product detects, because advanced threat protection is a marketing category rather than a defined capability, and two products under the same label may share nothing at all.

mitre-attack.def: The public knowledge base that catalogues what attackers actually do, organized as tactics (the goal: initial access, persistence, exfiltration) and techniques (the method), each with observed procedures and the groups seen using them.
mitre-attack.context: MITRE ATT&CK replaced a decade of vague vendor vocabulary with shared identifiers, so a detection engineer, a red team and a report can all point at the same T-number and mean the same thing. Its two failure modes are worth naming: coverage theatre, where an organization counts techniques it has a rule for and calls that a security programme, and the assumption that the matrix is exhaustive. It catalogues what has been observed and written down, which is not the same as everything possible. It is also versioned and it moves: released each April and October, it split its largest tactic in two in April 2026, so a technique number should be quoted with the version it was read in.
mitre-attack.depth:
What it is, and what it is not. MITRE describes ATT&CK as a globally accessible knowledge base of adversary tactics and techniques based on real-world observations, used as a foundation for threat models and methodologies in the private sector, in government and in the security product and service community. Its source is public: threat intelligence and incident reporting, distilled into common tactics, techniques and procedures (TTPs), plus published research on new techniques close to what adversaries do. MITRE's design paper is explicit about the limits. ATT&CK is not an exhaustive enumeration of attack vectors against software, a job it leaves to MITRE's Common Attack Pattern Enumeration and Classification (CAPEC) and Common Weakness Enumeration (CWE); it is not a checklist; and its frequently asked questions (FAQ) page admits that it tries to include most threat reporting but can only get to so much. It is open for anyone to use at no charge, under terms of use and a trademark rule that the first reference in any text must read MITRE ATT&CK, and that no one may present it as MITRE's endorsement of a product.

The model, field by field. Tactics are the why of an action, the adversary's tactical goal, such as credential access. Techniques are the how, such as dumping credentials. Sub-techniques describe the behaviour at a lower level, such as dumping credentials by reading the Local Security Authority (LSA) secrets. Procedures are the specific implementation seen in the wild, such as an adversary using PowerShell to inject into lsass.exe and scrape credentials from its memory, and they appear in the Procedure Examples section of each technique page; a single procedure often spans several techniques. Each object has an identifier: TA for tactics, a T followed by four digits for techniques, a further three digits for sub-techniques, and separate series for groups, software, campaigns, mitigations and, since version 18, detection strategies and analytics. Credential stuffing, for example, is T1110.004, a sub-technique of Brute Force (T1110) under Credential Access (TA0006), with mitigations M1036 (account use policies), M1032 (multi-factor authentication), M1027 (password policies) and M1018 (user account management) and the detection strategy DET0460. Unlike the Lockheed Martin Cyber Kill Chain, whose phases are ordered, ATT&CK's tactics are unordered and may not all occur in one intrusion, because an adversary's goals change during an operation.

The Enterprise matrix in 2026. As read on 12 November 2026, Enterprise ATT&CK has 15 tactics, in matrix order: Reconnaissance (TA0043), Resource Development (TA0042), Initial Access (TA0001), Execution (TA0002), Persistence (TA0003), Privilege Escalation (TA0004), Stealth (TA0005), "Defense Impairment" (TA0112), Credential Access (TA0006), Discovery (TA0007), Lateral Movement (TA0008), Collection (TA0009), Command and Control (TA0011), Exfiltration (TA0010) and Impact (TA0040). The two in the middle are new as a pair. Version 19, released on 28 April 2026, split the old "Defense Evasion" tactic into Stealth, which kept the identifier TA0005 and covers hiding actions so that they appear as normal behaviour (31 techniques), and "Defense Impairment", TA0112, created on 14 April 2026 for breaking security mechanisms, pipelines and tooling so that defenders cannot see or trust what is happening (18 techniques). Several techniques were revoked in favour of others in the process, so a detection or a report that cites a pre-2026 identifier under the old tactic needs checking against the current release. Mobile and ICS (industrial control systems) have 12 tactics each.

How it grew.
