ATT&CK came out of FMX, a research environment MITRE established in 2010 as a living lab inside its own corporate network, where researchers worked under an assume-breach mentality on detecting advanced persistent threats with endpoint telemetry and behavioural analytics. Periodic cyber game exercises emulated real adversaries in that heavily monitored environment while threat hunters tested their analytic hypotheses, and ATT&CK was the shared catalogue both sides used: scenarios for the emulation team, progress measurement for the defenders. The first model dates from September 2013 and covered Windows enterprise networks; it went public in May 2015 with 96 techniques under 9 tactics. In 2017 it was extended to macOS and Linux as ATT&CK for Enterprise, with PRE-ATT&CK for activity before exploitation and ATT&CK for Mobile alongside; Cloud followed in 2019 as part of Enterprise, as did the Impact tactic; ICS came in 2020, the same year sub-techniques reshaped the technique list. Versioning began with v1.0 on 16 January 2018; major releases now arrive each April and October. Version 18, of 28 October 2025, rebuilt the defensive side, replacing the detection notes inside techniques with Detection Strategies and Analytics and deprecating Data Sources. Version 20, released on 13 October 2026 and current as v20.1, counts 971 pieces of software, 182 groups and 61 campaigns across the three domains, and for Enterprise alone 227 techniques, 479 sub-techniques, 178 groups, 842 pieces of software, 57 campaigns, 44 mitigations, 703 detection strategies, 1,770 analytics and 106 data components.

How it is used. Detection engineers tag each rule with the technique it targets and use the mapping to find gaps; threat intelligence analysts map reports to techniques so that one actor's behaviour can be compared with another's; red teams and adversary emulators build scenarios from the techniques a named group has been seen using, which is how it began in FMX; purple teams run those scenarios with the defenders watching. European threat-led tests under the TIBER-EU framework, for instance, are specified as mimicking the TTPs of real attackers. MITRE publishes the content in several forms: an Excel workbook, the dataset in Structured Threat Information Expression (STIX) 2.0 and 2.1, the ATT&CK Navigator, a web tool for annotating and exploring the matrices that is used to visualize defensive coverage, red and blue team planning and the frequency of detected techniques, and the Workbench, an application for exploring, creating, annotating and sharing extensions of the knowledge base. The FAQ places it beside the other models rather than above them: the Cyber Kill Chain describes the shape of an intrusion at a higher level, and the Diamond Model helps cluster intrusions, with ATT&CK-mapped techniques as one of its inputs.

What goes wrong. Coverage theatre comes first. The design paper calls coverage of every technique unrealistic, notes that some behaviours, such as an administrator running ipconfig.exe, should never be alerted on in isolation, says that anyone mapping to ATT&CK should be able to explain the procedures they cover, and asks the questions a coverage claim must answer: is it data collection or alerting, one analytic or several, visibility or prevention, and has it been tested by a red team or by adversary emulation? A heat map coloured from rule tags answers none of them. The second error is reading the matrix as the universe: it records what has been reported and distilled, so a technique absent from it is unrecorded, not impossible. The third is version drift: identifiers are stable within a release but techniques are revoked, merged and moved, as the 2026 split showed, so a technique number in a report or a detection should carry the version or the date it was read. The last is misuse of the name, which the terms of use address directly: ATT&CK mappings in a product imply no endorsement by MITRE.

Neighbours. TTPs are the concept ATT&CK organizes; indicators of compromise (IoCs) are the short-lived observables it deliberately sits above. The kill chain is the older, ordered model it complements; MITRE is the organization that maintains it, alongside CAPEC and CWE. Detection engineering, security operations centres (SOCs), red, purple and blue teams all use it as their common vocabulary, and two of its tactics, lateral movement and command and control, are everyday terms in their own right.

kill-chain.def: The staged model of an intrusion published by Lockheed Martin analysts in 2011 - reconnaissance, weaponization, delivery, exploitation, installation, command and control, actions on objectives - borrowed from military targeting doctrine.
kill-chain.context: Its value is defensive framing: an intrusion is a sequence, so breaking any link stops the operation, and defenders can invest where interruption is cheapest rather than trying to stop everything. Its limits are equally real - the model assumes a tidy linear campaign, fits malware delivery better than credential abuse or insider misuse, and stops at the objective rather than covering the months an intruder spends moving laterally. ATT&CK largely superseded it for detailed work; the kill chain survives because it explains the shape of an attack to people who do not need a matrix.

dwell-time.def: How long an intruder is inside before anyone notices: measured from first compromise to detection, and the single most honest number a security programme reports about itself.
dwell-time.context: Industry surveys have tracked it falling from many months to weeks over the past decade, driven by better endpoint telemetry and by the rise of ransomware, which announces itself and so shortens the average by being loud. That last point matters: a falling average can mean detection improved or that attackers stopped hiding. The related figure is breakout time, how long from first foothold to lateral movement, which is the window a defender actually has to act.
dwell-time.depth:
What is measured. Mandiant, whose annual M-Trends report is the series most often quoted, defines dwell time as the period an attacker is on a system from compromise to detection, and reports it as a global median across the intrusions its consultants investigated, more than 500,000 hours of them in 2025. Three properties follow from that definition and are easy to forget. It is a median, so a handful of intrusions that lasted years do not move it, which is also why a team's own MTTD (mean time to detect) for the same interval can look very different. It is measured backwards from detection, so the start point is whatever forensic work later establishes as the first compromise, and it can only be as early as the oldest surviving log. And it describes the intrusions someone found and investigated: an intrusion still undetected is not in the sample. Dwell time is also not the time to contain or recover, which the mean time to respond or repair covers, nor the time an attacker needs to spread, which is breakout time.

The long fall. The early numbers explain why the metric became famous. Reporting the M-Trends release of April 2014, SecurityWeek gave Mandiant's figures as 416 days in 2011, 243 in 2012 and 229 in 2013, with the longest presence found in 2013 lasting six years and three months, and only 33 per cent of organizations detecting their breach themselves in 2013, down from 37 per cent the year before. A decade later the number had collapsed: M-Trends 2024, published on 23 April 2024, gave a global median of 10 days for 2023, down from 16 in 2022; M-Trends 2025, a year later, gave 11 days for 2024; and M-Trends 2026, published on 23 March 2026, gave 14 days for 2025, which Mandiant attributes to growing sophistication in evading defences.

Who noticed changes the number. The 2025 report splits the median by the source of detection: 26 days when an external entity notified the victim, 10 days when the organization discovered the activity itself, and 5 days when the adversary notified it, which is what a ransom note is. That last category is why a falling figure can mean that attackers stopped hiding rather than that defenders got faster: Mandiant's own 2024 summary names ransomware among the factors driving dwell time down, a loud intrusion that ends the clock by announcing itself. The same summary puts the shorter figures in proportion: Mandiant's red teams need only five to seven days on average to achieve their objectives, so a median of 10 days still describes many intrusions that finished their work before anyone looked.

The long tail. The median hides the intrusions that matter most to some sectors. For cyber espionage and for North Korean information technology (IT) workers placed inside companies, M-Trends 2026 reports a median of 122 days, and it describes the BRICKSTORM backdoor reaching dwell times of nearly 400 days. Espionage groups, it says, deliberately target edge and core network devices such as virtual private network (VPN) gateways and routers, which typically lack endpoint detection and where file system or memory forensics is hard. Its conclusion joins dwell time to log retention directly: against a 400-day intrusion, a standard 90-day log retention policy leaves an organization blind to the initial access vector and to the full scope of the intrusion. A retention period shorter than a plausible dwell time is a decision, usually unmade, to be unable to answer the first question of the investigation.

Breakout time, the other clock. CrowdStrike introduced breakout time in its 2018 Global Threat Report, defining it as the period between initial access and lateral movement onto another system, and reported an average of 1 hour and 58 minutes. Its 2019 report ranked adversaries by it, with Russian state groups almost eight times faster than the next and eCrime groups averaging over nine hours, and proposed the 1-10-60 rule as a target for defenders: one minute to detect, ten to investigate and one hour to remediate. By the 2026 report, published on 24 February 2026, the average eCrime breakout time for 2025 had fallen to 29 minutes, 65 per cent faster than in 2024, the fastest observed was 27 seconds, and in one intrusion data exfiltration began within four minutes of initial access. Mandiant measures a related interval from another angle: the median time between an initial access event and its hand-off to a second threat group fell from more than eight hours in 2022 to 22 seconds in 2025. Dwell time says how long an intruder stayed unseen; breakout time says how soon after arrival being unseen stopped mattering.

Using the number honestly. A vendor's dwell time describes its own caseload, organizations that called an incident responder, so it is a trend line for the field rather than a benchmark for any one network. Inside an organization the useful version is per incident: the post-incident review records when the intrusion began, how that was established and who detected it, and over several incidents those records show whether detection is improving or whether intrusions simply became louder. The levers are the ones the reports point to: telemetry on the systems attackers actually use, including the edge devices that carry no endpoint agent, retention at least as long as the intrusions worth finding, and detection engineering aimed at the persistence and lateral movement that long dwell times depend on.

tetrade.def: The collective name Kaspersky researchers gave in July 2020 to four Brazilian banking trojan families, Guildma, Javali, Melcoz and Grandoreiro, that matured attacking Brazilian bank customers and then went international, to the rest of Latin America, Spain, Portugal and beyond.
tetrade.context: Brazil has been a world centre of banking malware for two decades, and the Tetrade report is the clearest technical account of why: heavy obfuscation, modular installers, abuse of legitimate Windows tools for execution, command and control (C2) details hidden on ordinary sites such as YouTube, Facebook and Google Docs, and in Grandoreiro's case, by Kaspersky's reading, a malware-as-a-service (MaaS) model in which other criminals rent the toolkit. Grandoreiro became the most widespread of the four, and in January 2024 Brazil's Federal Police, with Interpol, Spanish police and ESET's researchers, moved against the people behind it. The strategic point is that these crews did not need novel exploits: they industrialized social engineering and evasion against a banking population that had gone online early.
tetrade.depth:
What the name covers. The Tetrade is a vendor designation, not a criminal brand: Kaspersky's Global Research and Analysis Team (GReAT) used it in a report published on 14 July 2020 for four large banking trojan families created, developed and spread by Brazilian criminals and by then operating abroad. The report noted that an earlier attempt to go international, in 2011, had been timid, with very basic trojans and little success, and that the 2020 generation was different: modular, heavily obfuscated, with execution chains complicated enough to make analysis a painful process. The four are separate families with separate operators, and other catalogues name them differently: MITRE ATT&CK (Adversarial Tactics, Techniques and Common Knowledge) files Guildma as an associated name of Astaroth (S0373) and lists Javali (S0528), Melcoz (S0530) and Grandoreiro (S0531) as their own software entries. The background the report gives is the Brazilian banking environment itself: at least since 2000 the country's banks had operated amid constant online fraud, and their early adoption of browser plugins, hardware tokens, two-factor authentication and chip cards with a PIN (personal identification number) had not stopped it.

The common method. All four aim to make the fraudulent transaction come from the customer's own computer, because bank anti-fraud systems look for sessions from suspicious machines. Guildma's final module watches which sites and programs the victim opens and, when a bank appears, gives the operator full control of page navigation through a VNC-like (Virtual Network Computing) remote view, the ability to toggle a screen overlay, and prompts for the Short Message Service (SMS) token or the QR (Quick Response) code validation the bank asks for. Melcoz draws an overlay window over the browser while the operator works the session behind it and asks for the secondary password and token, which defeats the second factor the bank relied on. Grandoreiro's operator tool notifies the operator when a victim is online, offers full remote access and can block the victim's access to the bank's site so the transfer is not noticed in time.

Guildma, also known as Astaroth. First seen in 2015 against Brazilian customers only, it spread by email with compressed attachments, Visual Basic Script (VBS) or Windows shortcut (LNK) files dressed as invoices, courier notices or, in 2020, a purchase of alcohol gel; from November 2019 an HTML (Hypertext Markup Language) attachment ran JavaScript to fetch the next stage. It downloads with BITSAdmin, a tool built into Windows and commonly allowlisted, and from late September 2019 hid its payloads in NTFS (New Technology File System) alternate data streams attached to desktop.ini, invisible in Explorer but listed by dir /R. It loads through DLL (dynamic-link library) search-order hijacking of ExtExport.exe, checks for debuggers, virtual machines and analysts' disk serials, then decrypts its next stage, encrypted twice with an XOR-based (exclusive-or) scheme, into svchost.exe by process hollowing. Its command and control (C2) addresses sat encrypted in YouTube and Facebook posts, and in 2020 Kaspersky saw more than 200 new download addresses a day. Microsoft documented the same family in July 2019 as a fileless campaign: a link led to an LNK file that ran WMIC (Windows Management Instrumentation Command-line) with its /Format option to execute script, then Bitsadmin, Certutil and Regsvr32, until the final payload was injected into the Userinit process; Microsoft's point was that fileless does not mean invisible.

Javali and Melcoz. Javali, active since November 2017 against Portuguese- and Spanish-speaking countries and above all Brazil and Mexico, arrives as a Microsoft Installer (MSI) file whose CustomAction runs a VBS downloader; the package it fetches holds legitimate executables vulnerable to DLL sideloading and a malicious library inflated to 602 MB, where the genuine one is about 600 KB, so that multiscanners with upload limits never see it; stripped of empty sections it is 27.5 MB. Its configuration came from a shared Google Docs document, later YouTube, and its targets included cryptocurrency exchanges and Mercado Pago. Melcoz, active in Brazil for years and abroad since at least 2018 in Chile, Mexico, Spain and Portugal, is a customization of Remote Access PC, an open-source remote access trojan (RAT) published on GitHub. MSI packages built with Advanced Installer carry a VBS that loads it either through the AutoIt interpreter or by DLL hijacking of a legitimate executable such as VMware's vmnat.exe; the Brazilian builds were unpacked while those aimed at Chile and Mexico were packed with VMProtect or Themida. A clipboard timer swaps Bitcoin wallet addresses for the criminals' own, and Kaspersky read the Spanish-language campaigns as Brazilian operators working with local coders and money mules.

Grandoreiro. Kaspersky dated it to at least 2016 and MITRE describes it as written in Delphi. In Brazil it was pushed through hacked websites and Google Ads leading to a fake download page; abroad, through spear-phishing. An MSI ran a function in an embedded DLL to fetch the encrypted final payload, first XOR-encrypted with the key 0x0AE2 and later delivered as a base64-encoded ZIP. Each build carried an operator identifier, and a domain generation algorithm (DGA) combined that operator's key with the date to compute a new Google Sites path every day, where the C2 address was posted; payloads were served from short-lived instances of a small Windows web server whose page counter had been relabelled from Hits to Infects. Kaspersky judged it the most widespread of the four and concluded from the many operator identifiers that it ran as malware-as-a-service; MITRE ATT&CK and the X-Force team of IBM (International Business Machines) say the same. ESET, which has tracked it since late 2017, disagrees: its command servers do not allow more than one operator at a time and almost all of its DGA configurations cluster together, so ESET believes a single group, or a few closely cooperating groups, runs it.

The operation of January 2024. ESET's account, published on 30 January 2024, describes a DGA in use since October 2020 that produces one main domain a day plus failsafe domains, 105 distinct configurations, domains registered through No-IP's dynamic DNS (Domain Name System) service and pointed at servers rented mostly from Amazon Web Services (AWS) and Azure, and a design flaw in the network protocol, built on the discontinued RTC Portal (RealThinClient) Delphi components, that let researchers count victims: on average 551 unique victims connected a day, 114 of them new. Spain was the most targeted country from 2020 to 2022, and in 2023 the focus moved to Mexico and Argentina. The same day Brazil's Federal Police executed Operação Grandoreiro: five temporary arrest warrants and 13 search warrants in São Paulo, Santa Catarina, Pará, Goiás and Mato Grosso, against a group suspected of moving about 3.6 million euros since 2019, an investigation opened on a complaint from the Spanish bank CaixaBank and supported by Interpol and Spain's National Police; total losses were put at 110 million euros. It did not end the family. From March 2024 X-Force tracked large new phishing campaigns impersonating tax and electricity authorities in Mexico, Argentina and South Africa, with a variant aimed at more than 1,500 banks in over 60 countries, generating at least 12 C2 domains a day and mailing itself onward through the victim's Outlook client.

Reading it as a defender. Almost every stage is a legitimate component misused: Windows binaries such as BITSAdmin, WMIC, Certutil and Regsvr32 doing download and execution, MSI custom actions, signed executables loading a planted library, AutoIt as an interpreter, and C2 details kept on YouTube, Facebook, Google Docs and Google Sites, services no proxy can block outright. That is why the useful detections are behavioural: a living-off-the-land chain launched from a mail attachment, data written to an alternate data stream, a library hundreds of megabytes larger than the file it impersonates, daily domains on a dynamic DNS provider, and a banking session driven remotely from the customer's own machine. The families are the desktop chapter of a longer Brazilian story whose other chapters are the boleto fraud, the Prilex attacks on point-of-sale terminals and the social engineering of instant Pix payments.

banking-trojan.def: A banking trojan is malware built specifically to steal money from online banking: it captures credentials, injects fake fields into the bank's page, draws a convincing overlay on top of the real application, takes remote control of the victim's own session, or alters payment details as a transfer is submitted.
banking-trojan.context: The global lineage runs from Zeus, around since at least 2007, through its man-in-the-browser descendants. The Brazilian variant is a distinct lineage with its own techniques, driven by local payment instruments: overlay attacks against desktop banking, and manipulation of the boleto, the printed payment slip whose barcode can be rewritten so the money goes elsewhere; families such as Guildma and Grandoreiro later went abroad. Instant payments changed the target rather than removing it: fraud moved to social engineering the victim into authorizing the transfer themselves, and the malware that remains automates the transfer from inside the victim's phone. The defence that actually works is out-of-band confirmation of the destination, with limits and delays the regulator now imposes, not detection of the malware.
banking-trojan.depth:
What it is, and what it is not. A banking trojan is defined by its goal, not its code: it sits on the customer's own device, waits for a banking session and turns it into a transfer the criminal wants. The techniques are a toolkit. It may log keystrokes or grab form fields to steal credentials; inject extra fields into the bank's page to ask for a token or card code the bank never requests; draw a window over the real application so the victim types into the criminal's copy; drive the session remotely, so that the fraudulent transfer comes from the victim's own machine and address; or rewrite the recipient and amount between what the victim sees and what is sent. It overlaps with remote access trojans (RATs) and information stealers, and many families are both; it is distinct from malware that attacks the bank's own infrastructure, such as the cash-machine and point-of-sale malware Prilex.

Man-in-the-browser. The technique at the heart of the desktop generation modifies pages and transaction contents, or inserts extra transactions, invisibly to both the user and the bank, which is why it succeeds whatever encryption or two- and three-factor authentication protects the session: the customer is shown the payment they keyed in while different values are transmitted. It was demonstrated by the Brazilian researcher Augusto Paes de Barros in a presentation on backdoor trends at CNASI (Congresso Nacional de Auditoria de Sistemas, Segurança da Informação e Governança) in São Paulo on 15 September 2005, and the name man-in-the-browser was coined by Philipp Gühring on 27 January 2007. The families that used it include Zeus, its successor SpyEye, Carberp and Gozi, and in a 2014 survey most financial service professionals rated it the greatest threat to online banking.

The Zeus lineage. When the United States Department of Justice moved against Gameover Zeus on 2 June 2014, it described it as the latest version of the Zeus malware, which dates to at least 2007, distinguished by a peer-to-peer structure that made it harder to take down. Security researchers estimated 500,000 to 1 million infected computers, about a quarter of them in the United States, and the FBI (Federal Bureau of Investigation) attributed more than 100 million dollars in losses to it: the botnet captured banking credentials, which were then used to start or redirect wire transfers to accounts the criminals controlled abroad. A grand jury in Pittsburgh indicted Evgeniy Bogachev of Anapa, Russia, as an alleged administrator, on 14 counts including bank fraud and money laundering.

The boleto. Brazil grew its own lineage because it had its own instruments. The boleto bancário, the barcoded payment slip used by consumers and for most business-to-business payments, cannot be charged back like a card payment; it can only be reversed by another transfer. Krebs on Security reported in July 2014 how malware waited until the victim filled in the recipient's details for a boleto payment and then changed the destination, and how RSA had found a ring it called Bolware affecting more than 30 Brazilian banks, with a control panel tracking nearly half a million fraudulent transactions and possible losses of up to 3.75 billion dollars. The same malware disabled the security plug-ins most Brazilian banks required their online customers to install in the browser, leaving them with a false sense of safety.

The Tetrade. In July 2020 Kaspersky's researchers grouped four Brazilian families that had gone abroad. Guildma, also known as Astaroth, active since 2015, used living-off-the-land binaries, NTFS (New Technology File System) alternate data streams and process hollowing, hid its payloads in YouTube and Facebook posts, and gave its operators full control of page navigation, screen overlays and requests for SMS (Short Message Service) tokens and QR (Quick Response) code validation, so that transactions came from the victim's own computer and slipped past anti-fraud systems that flag suspicious machines. Javali, active since November 2017 against customers in Brazil and Mexico, arrived as Microsoft Installer (MSI) attachments and used DLL (dynamic-link library) sideloading. Melcoz reached Chile, Spain and Portugal. Grandoreiro, first seen in 2016 and written in Delphi, used a domain generation algorithm (DGA) and stored command information on Google Sites, ran, in Kaspersky's reading, as malware-as-a-service with many operators (ESET, in January 2024, saw one operator at a time and judged it more likely one group or a few cooperating ones), and had confirmed victims in Brazil, Mexico, Portugal and Spain.

The move to mobile. On Android the overlay survived as MITRE ATT&CK's graphical user interface (GUI) input capture technique: the malware uses accessibility features to learn which application is in the foreground, then either starts its own activity on top of it, which Android 10 restricted, or draws an overlay window, which requires the SYSTEM_ALERT_WINDOW permission. BRATA, documented by Kaspersky in August 2019, targeted only Brazilian victims, had been spreading since January 2019 mostly through the Google Play store in more than 20 variants, many posing as a WhatsApp update after the WhatsApp vulnerability catalogued as Common Vulnerabilities and Exposures (CVE) entry CVE-2019-3568 made news, and used the Accessibility Service for keylogging with real-time screen streaming. The official store, in other words, was part of the distribution channel.

Pix changed the target. Pix, launched in November 2020, made transfers instant, final and free; by March 2023 it carried more than 3 billion transactions a month worth 1.25 trillion reais, and it had 140 million users by May 2023. Irreversible transfers made the malware less necessary, since the efficient attack became persuading the victim to authorize the payment, but where malware remains it automates the same thing: IBM Trusteer's analysis of PixPirate describes a two-application scheme whose hidden component, with no launcher icon, uses the accessibility service to navigate the bank's app, fill in the payee, amount and password and complete a Pix transfer, or to change the payee of a transfer the victim started, while reading, editing and deleting the bank's SMS messages to get past two-factor checks.

Defences that work. The Central Bank answered with friction rather than detection. Resolution BCB No. 142 of 23 September 2021 requires institutions to cap transfers between different natural persons at 1,000 reais between 20:00 and 06:00, to make any limit increase requested through electronic channels wait at least 24 hours, to let customers pre-register the accounts allowed to receive more, and to keep daily records of fraud and attempted fraud; an amendment of 11 September 2025 added a duty, in force from 13 October 2025, to reject payments to accounts under well-founded suspicion of fraud. For the transaction itself, out-of-band verification of the destination and amount defeats man-in-the-browser, but only if the second channel is not on the infected device: SMS codes fall to man-in-the-mobile malware and to the SMS-reading behaviour of families like PixPirate. The defence that actually works is confirming the destination through a channel the malware does not control, backed by limits and delays for unfamiliar recipients, not hoping the malware is detected first.

lei-carolina-dieckmann.def: The Brazilian statute of November 2012 that made unauthorized access to a computing device a crime in its own right, inserting article 154-A into the Penal Code. It took effect in April 2013.
lei-carolina-dieckmann.context: It is named after the actress whose device was compromised and whose private photographs were published in an extortion attempt - a case that made the legislative gap impossible to ignore, since prosecutors until then had to stretch general statutes to reach conduct that was obviously criminal. The pattern is the same one that produced the Computer Fraud and Abuse Act in the United States: a public incident, a fast legislative response, and a text the field then lives with for decades. It was later reinforced by Law 14.155/2021, which raised penalties for electronic fraud and device intrusion.

marco-civil-da-internet.def: Brazil's framework law for internet rights and duties, enacted in 2014: it establishes network neutrality, privacy and freedom of expression as principles, sets data-retention obligations for connection and application providers, and conditions the removal of content on a court order in most cases.
marco-civil-da-internet.context: It was drafted through an unusually open public consultation and was internationally notable for putting user rights before intermediary obligations - a deliberate contrast with laws written primarily to enable takedowns. For practitioners the operative parts are the retention periods, the rules on producing logs, and the liability regime that determines when a platform must act. Its intermediary-liability provisions have been repeatedly litigated, and the balance it struck is under continuous political pressure.

cert-br.def: CERT.br is Brazil's national computer security incident response team (CSIRT) of last resort, created in June 1997 as NBSO and maintained by the Brazilian Network Information Center (NIC.br), the non-profit that runs the .br registry, address allocation and the IX.br exchanges for the multistakeholder Brazilian Internet Steering Committee (CGI.br).
cert-br.context: The arrangement is unusual and worth knowing. Rather than sitting inside a ministry or an intelligence agency, national incident response, the domain registry, the distribution of Internet Protocol (IP) addresses and autonomous system numbers and the exchange-point fabric all sit with the Brazilian Network Information Center (NIC.br), a private non-profit that executes the decisions of a governance committee with government, business, third-sector and academic seats, and that pays for all of it from .br domain registrations. That structure is part of why Brazil built one of the world's largest exchange-point systems, and why CERT.br's incident statistics, honeypot data and awareness material have been public and free for decades: the operator of the infrastructure is also the publisher of its measurements.
cert-br.depth:
What it is. CERT.br, the Centro de Estudos, Resposta e Tratamento de Incidentes de Segurança no Brasil, describes itself as a computer security incident response team (CSIRT) with national responsibility of last resort, maintained by the Brazilian Network Information Center (NIC.br). Its mission is to raise the level of security and the incident handling capacity of networks connected to the internet in Brazil, and its constituency is defined by numbers rather than by sector: any network using resources administered by NIC.br, that is, Internet Protocol (IP) addresses or autonomous system numbers (ASNs) allocated to Brazil, and domains under the .br country code top-level domain. Its description in the format of Request for Comments (RFC) 2350, also known as Best Current Practice (BCP) 21, with its contacts, mission, policies and services, is published on its site. NIC.br, which maintains it, is a private, non-profit civil entity, so CERT.br sits outside government.

Where it came from. CERT.br was created in June 1997, under the name NBSO, on the initiative of the Brazilian Internet Steering Committee (CGI.br), following the recommendations of a report published in August 1996, 'Rumo à Criação de uma Coordenadoria de Segurança de Redes na Internet Brasil', written by the security subgroup of the Grupo de Trabalho de Engenharia e Operação de Redes (GTER), the network engineering and operations working group, at CGI.br's request. Its work serves several of CGI.br's legal attributions, among them promoting studies and recommending procedures and technical standards for the security of internet networks and services, and NIC.br's statutory objective of meeting the security and emergency requirements of the Brazilian internet in cooperation with the responsible bodies. Its services are free to every network in its constituency, except the incident handling courses it teaches under licence from Carnegie Mellon University, and the money comes from .br domain registrations.

What a last-resort CSIRT does. As a national CSIRT of last resort, CERT.br acts as the national point of contact for reporting security incidents, especially when no more specific contact is known, and facilitates communication between professionals and teams in Brazil and abroad. It always tries to find and work through the CSIRTs and security groups of the organizations involved, and failing that the party responsible for the autonomous system concerned. On request it coordinates, supports technical analysis, and supports mitigation and recovery, but it has no access to third parties' premises or systems: its role is to enable other teams to respond. It treats reports as confidential, anonymizes them where possible, never comments on specific incidents, and handles information according to the Traffic Light Protocol (TLP) of the Forum of Incident Response and Security Teams (FIRST), with all five markings from TLP:CLEAR to TLP:RED.

Situational awareness and measurement. The second strand is data. CERT.br runs a distributed honeypot network with sensors in networks across Brazil, to observe attacks against Brazilian address space, and a second honeypot network, SpamPots, with sensors in several countries, to observe abuse of internet infrastructure for sending spam. It receives threat feeds about Brazilian autonomous systems from partners including Team Cymru, the Shadowserver Foundation, Spamhaus and Shodan, groups the findings by ASN and sends weekly notifications to the responsible networks about misconfigured or vulnerable systems, and shares indicators with Brazilian CSIRTs and sector communities through the open-source MISP threat-sharing platform. Its public statistics give annual totals of voluntary incident notifications since 1999 and, since 2016, breakdowns by category, most-scanned ports, and the top source countries and autonomous systems. The same data feeds research: in 2013 João Ceron, Klaus Steding-Jessen and Cristine Hoepers presented an anatomy of abuse against Session Initiation Protocol (SIP) servers at the Brazilian security symposium, SBSeg, drawn from voice over IP (VoIP) attacks captured by honeypots in Brazil, and later papers with university groups traced the Bashlite and Mirai botnets of Internet of Things devices.

Knowledge transfer. The third strand is teaching. CERT.br writes the Cartilha de Segurança para Internet, a series of free booklets of advice for end users, including one on using artificial intelligence safely, which organizations can reprint with their own logo; it fosters cooperation between Brazilian CSIRTs by organizing the yearly Fórum Brasileiro de CSIRTs, keeping discussion lists and a public list of Brazilian CSIRTs; it trains incident handlers, especially for institutions setting up their own team; and it takes part in national and international internet governance discussions to explain technical questions and the possible effects of policy decisions on network security.

International standing. CERT.br has been a full member of FIRST since 15 May 2002, and its staff have served on FIRST's membership committee, its special interest groups on metrics and the CSIRT services framework, the conference programme committee and, in 2012 and 2013, the board of directors, and a CERT.br member chaired FIRST's 2020 annual conference. It also takes part in TF-CSIRT's Trusted Introducer, a partner of the Software Engineering Institute (SEI) at Carnegie Mellon, and a member of the Shadowserver Alliance, the Anti-Phishing Working Group (APWG) and the Messaging, Malware and Mobile Anti-Abuse Working Group (M3AAWG). Cristine Hoepers, at CERT.br since 1999 and its general manager, was inducted into FIRST's Incident Response Hall of Fame, announced on 10 June 2024 at the FIRST conference in Fukuoka, for pioneering work establishing and supporting CSIRTs around the world, the first woman to receive the honour; she has also received M3AAWG's Mary Litynski award. Klaus Steding-Jessen, who shares several of CERT.br's recognitions with her, is the co-author of chkrootkit, the rootkit checker written with Nelson Murilo.

How it fits the CGI.br system. NIC.br, created to implement CGI.br's decisions, is the executive arm behind several services Brazilian engineers use daily: Registro.br for .br domains and for ASNs and IPv4 and IPv6 addresses, CERT.br for incidents, Ceptro.br for the IX.br internet exchanges and the NTP.br legal time service, Cetic.br for indicators and Ceweb.br for the web, plus technical support to LACNIC, the regional internet registry. CGI.br itself is a multistakeholder committee with representatives of government, business, the third sector and academia, whose ten principles for internet governance, of 2009, inspired the legislative proposal for the Marco Civil da Internet. For a network engineer the practical points are three: report incidents involving Brazilian networks to CERT.br when you do not know whom else to call, read its weekly notifications about your ASN rather than filtering them out, and expect any data you send to be handled under TLP.

o-rei-da-internet.def: The 2026 Brazilian biographical crime film directed by Fabrício Bittar, starring João Guilherme as Daniel Nascimento - a teenager who joined one of the country's large online criminal operations in the dial-up era, moved millions through card and banking fraud before turning seventeen, and became the target of a Federal Police investigation.
o-rei-da-internet.context: It is the Brazilian entry in a genre this field knows well, and the same cautions apply as with Hackers or Takedown: a film about a criminal career, narrated by its subject, is a source about the telling rather than about the events. What makes it worth watching anyway is the setting - Brazil's early-2000s fraud underground is the historical root of the banking-malware industry that later went global as the Tetrade, and the film is one of very few popular accounts of it. Reviewers have noted its celebratory tone; the more useful reading is as evidence of how that scene saw itself.

demi-getschko.def: The engineer on the team that made Brazil's first internet connection, at FAPESP in São Paulo, and the person most associated with the country's naming and governance ever since - administrative contact for the .br domain since 1989, member of the Brazilian Internet Steering Committee since its creation in 1995, later an ICANN board member and chief executive of NIC.br.
demi-getschko.context: He was inducted into the Internet Hall of Fame in 2014, the first of seven Brazilians so far. His durable contribution is structural rather than technical: he helped define the shape of the .br name tree and the rules of the registry, and then stayed for three decades to operate them. When people ask why Brazil's internet governance looks unusual - multi-stakeholder, with the registry, the incident response team and the exchange points under one civil body - the answer runs through the choices this generation made and defended.

tadao-takahashi.def: The founder of Brazil's National Education and Research Network (RNP) and the coordinator who turned scattered academic links into a national backbone - inducted into the Internet Hall of Fame in 2017. He died in April 2022.
tadao-takahashi.context: His decisive move was political as much as technical. When the state telecommunications monopoly proposed becoming the single access point for all Brazilian users, with everyone holding one company's email address, Takahashi and colleagues argued the government into a hierarchical, many-provider model instead. That argument is why Brazil got a competitive internet rather than a state portal, and it was won in 1995 in a meeting rather than in a protocol.

carlos-afonso.def: The co-founder, with sociologist Herbert de Souza (Betinho) and Marcos Arruda, of the Brazilian Institute of Social and Economic Analyses (IBASE), and the man behind Alternex, the first internet service in Brazil open to the public, years before commercial providers existed. Inducted into the Internet Hall of Fame in 2021.
carlos-afonso.context: Alternex came out of civil society rather than industry or academia, which is the point: Brazil's first public network access was built by an organization whose purpose was social justice, and it served non-governmental organizations before it served anyone else. Its defining moment was the 1992 Earth Summit in Rio, where Alternex, riding infrastructure assembled with the nascent National Education and Research Network (RNP), provided internet mail to conference participants, the country's first large public demonstration that the network was for everyone.
carlos-afonso.depth:
Carlos Alberto Afonso trained, in the Internet Hall of Fame's words, in engineering and in social and political thought, and had been in exile with Betinho before the political amnesty. After it, he and Marcos Arruda, Betinho's companions in exile, founded with the sociologist Herbert de Souza, known as Betinho, the Brazilian Institute of Social and Economic Analyses (IBASE), a non-profit citizenship organization active from 1981. IBASE's interest in computer networks was there almost from the start: in 1984 it began an initiative in Rio de Janeiro to promote their use with organizations in other countries, part of an international effort called Interdoc that had Canadian government support.

That initiative became Alternex. In Afonso's own account, written for the Association for Progressive Communications (APC) in 2022, it was established on 18 July 1989 as an information exchange service based on email and electronic conferences, after experimental use since 1987; the 2005 history of the Brazilian internet in O Globo describes the same day as the activation of IBASE's first Unix server linked to the internet in the United States over UUCP (Unix-to-Unix Copy), open to civil society groups by dial-up and over the Renpac data network, and quotes Afonso calling it the symbolic birth date of the internet in Brazil. The same timeline counts 159 users on 19 February 1990. The Internet Hall of Fame describes Alternex as a free service for civil society organizations and individuals and as an incubator: it acted as the internet gateway for hundreds of bulletin board systems (BBSs), many of which became some of the country's largest internet service providers (ISPs).

Alternex was part of a network of networks before the internet was one. By late 1989, APC's history records, networks in Sweden, Canada, Brazil (IBASE), Nicaragua and Australia were exchanging traffic with the Institute for Global Communications (IGC) in the United States and GreenNet in the United Kingdom, and in May 1990 the seven organizations founded APC in San Francisco; it received category one consultative status with the United Nations (UN) Economic and Social Council (ECOSOC) in 1995 and now has 73 organizational members. On 1 May 1991 Alternex opened an experimental service to Cuba, daily UUCP sessions over international dial-up between Rio and Havana with Telebit Trailblazer modems, which for the first time let a Cuban institution, the Centre for the Automatic Exchange of Information (CENIAI) of the Institute for Documentation and Information on Science and Technology (IDICT), exchange mail with the world through APC and the internet. Afonso records rates of about 600 characters per second between Rio and San Francisco and 400 between Rio and Havana, at a time when, until 1995, many Brazilian states reached the internet at 960 characters per second; the cost of the calls ended the link, and from 1992 Toronto took over the Cuban gateway at a fifth of the cost.

The 1992 Earth Summit made the case in public. The conference secretary-general, who knew the work of IBASE and APC, invited IBASE to build the Brazilian part of the Global Electronic Network, and at the end of 1990 IBASE proposed a data communication system for the conference, known as ISP/Rio, with technical support from members of APC and of the National Education and Research Network (RNP). Embratel and the other telecommunications companies resisted strangers installing networks and, above all, internet protocols in the country. The work was divided: Tadao Takahashi, who led the building of RNP, took on the government; the IBASE team, with the UN diplomat Janos Pasztor, got the requirement for direct links between the conference areas and the internet written into the host country agreement between the UN and the Brazilian government, which O Globo describes as done against the government's wishes. RNP linked Alternex through the Federal University of Rio de Janeiro (UFRJ) and the São Paulo Research Foundation (Fapesp), Telerj supplied lines between the sites, and the networked rooms ran at Riocentro, at the NGO (non-governmental organization) Forum around the Hotel Glória and at the press centre. There was no web yet; participants exchanged messages and files. The Internet Hall of Fame calls it the first use of the internet at a UN event.

The consequences outlasted the conference. According to O Globo's timeline, the Earth Summit project broke the government's resistance to permanent internet links for RNP, and two permanent 64 kbit/s channels to the United States were finally activated, from São Paulo (Fapesp) and Rio (UFRJ). APC repeated the model, with the IBASE team, for the NGO forums of the UN conferences in Vienna (1993), Cairo (1994) and Beijing (1995). The resistance is part of the record too: Afonso recalls a Telesp executive telling Takahashi that with this new network he wanted to destroy their jobs. And 'first' depends on the side being counted: the academic networks date their own start to links of 1988 and 1991 and to RNP's formal launch in September 1989, while Afonso's date for the civil-society internet is July 1989.

Afonso then helped govern what he had helped connect. The Brazilian Internet Steering Committee (CGI.br) was created on 31 May 1995 to set strategic guidelines for the internet in Brazil, domain registration under .br and IP address allocation, with seats for government, business, the third sector and academia. CGI.br's own register lists him as a member from 3 July 1995 to 22 August 1997 in the seat for service providers, then in the third-sector seat provisionally in 2003 and from 9 January 2004 through successive mandates to 31 May 2017. He pressed, with Takahashi and Marlon Borba, for a Brazilian chapter of the Internet Society from COMDEX 1997; it was established in 2011 and formalized in 2012. He has served on the Multistakeholder Advisory Group (MAG) of the UN Internet Governance Forum (IGF), and after his induction into the Internet Hall of Fame in 2021 sat on its advisory board from 2022 to 2025.

His current work returns to access. He is executive director of Instituto Nupef, which began as a research and training unit within the Third Sector Information Network (Rits) and became a non-profit association in 2009. Nupef runs Tiwa, a non-profit internet service for civil society organizations, social movements and research bodies, and Graúna, a mirror of essential content from pages at risk, with a portable server for community networks where connectivity is poor; and it designs and installs community networks with indigenous, quilombola and other communities in remote parts of the Amazon, training residents to maintain them, while arguing in spectrum policy for rules that let such networks exist.

liane-tarouco.def: The researcher who built the Rede Sul de Teleprocessamento, the first initiative to connect Brazilian universities, wrote the first book on computer networks published in Brazil, and contributed to the country's first internet backbone. Inducted into the Internet Hall of Fame in 2021.
liane-tarouco.context: Her inclusion corrects a familiar distortion. Founding histories are usually told through the people who negotiated with ministries; Tarouco's work was the teaching and the regional plumbing - the textbook a generation learned from and the southern network that proved inter-university connection was practical before there was a national one. She spent her career at UFRGS, and the education side of her contribution is why the field in Brazil had trained people ready when the backbone arrived.

cristine-hoepers.def: The general manager of CERT.br, Brazil's national computer security incident response team (CSIRT), which she joined in 1999; a builder of response teams across Latin America, a honeypot researcher and a leader of Brazil's anti-spam work, and in 2024 the first woman inducted into the Incident Response Hall of Fame of FIRST (Forum of Incident Response and Security Teams).
cristine-hoepers.context: She received the Mary Litynski Award of M3AAWG (Messaging, Malware and Mobile Anti-Abuse Working Group) in 2020 for work reducing online abuse, and in 2024 became the first woman, and the first Brazilian, inducted into FIRST's Incident Response Hall of Fame, a list that also carries Dan Kaminsky. The through-line of her career is capacity building rather than headline findings: teams that did not exist, best practices that had no local text, and long-running measurement published openly, the unglamorous work that determines whether a country can respond at all.
cristine-hoepers.depth:
Who she is. Cristine Hoepers is the general manager of CERT.br (Centro de Estudos, Resposta e Tratamento de Incidentes de Segurança no Brasil), the computer security incident response team (CSIRT) that NIC.br (Núcleo de Informação e Coordenação do Ponto BR) maintains as Brazil's national CSIRT of last resort. She joined it in 1999, attended her first FIRST (Forum of Incident Response and Security Teams) conference in 2000 and holds a Ph.D. in applied computing from INPE (Instituto Nacional de Pesquisas Espaciais), Brazil's National Institute for Space Research, in São José dos Campos. Her work spans three strands that every network operator in Brazil has met: incident coordination, measurement with honeypots, and the operational fight against spam.

The institution. CERT.br began in June 1997 as the NBSO (NIC.br Security Office), created on the initiative of CGI.br (Comitê Gestor da Internet no Brasil) after an August 1996 report by the security subgroup of GTER, the Brazilian network engineering and operations working group (Grupo de Trabalho de Engenharia e Operação de Redes), and it has received incident notifications about networks operating in Brazil since 1999. It serves any network that uses resources administered by NIC.br, meaning IP (Internet Protocol) addresses or ASNs (autonomous system numbers) allocated to Brazil and domains under .br, free of charge, funded by .br registrations. As a team of last resort it has no access to anyone else's systems: it works by finding the CSIRT or, failing that, the operator of the autonomous system involved, and helping them respond. Its public profile follows RFC (Request for Comments) 2350, and its services are described in the terms of the FIRST CSIRT Services Framework, which Hoepers helped develop.

Building teams. According to FIRST, she started CERT.br's CSIRT development programme, which set off the creation of teams across Brazil and helped establish CSIRTs in Latin America and beyond, with training delivered in partnership with the CERT Division of Carnegie Mellon University's Software Engineering Institute (SEI). She has been an SEI-authorized CERT instructor since 2004 and has trained more than 2,000 incident responders; on CERT.br's twentieth anniversary as a licensed SEI partner, the SEI counted more than 2,400 attendees trained by the team's three authorized instructors in courses such as Creating and Managing CSIRTs and Advanced Incident Handling for Technical Staff. At FIRST she served on the Membership Committee, helped bring SIM3 (the Security Incident Management Maturity Model) into its processes and is a SIM3 auditor, sat on the Board of Directors in 2012 and 2013, and was among the first to argue that incident response should have a voice in internet governance, which brought FIRST into forums such as the IGF (Internet Governance Forum). She has been a member of the ITU (International Telecommunication Union) High Level Experts Group, has held roles at LACNIC (the Latin American and Caribbean regional internet registry) and serves on the Board of Commissioners of the OpenCSIRT Foundation.

Honeypots and measurement. With Klaus Steding-Jessen and Antonio Montes of INPE she built Honeynet.BR, planned in December 2001 and operating from March 2002 as joint research between the NBSO and INPE; their 2003 FIRST paper describes a honeynet built entirely from open-source software, with an administrative network that contains outgoing malicious traffic, captures data and raises alerts, and argues for its value to a CSIRT trying to understand threats to its constituency. In September 2003 the NBSO and the Centro de Pesquisas Renato Archer (CenPRA), a research unit of the federal science ministry, deployed the Distributed Honeypots Project, part of the honeyTARG Honeynet Project: low-interaction honeypots running Honeyd, hosted by partner organizations and covering a large share of the Brazilian IPv4 address space, with automatic notification to the CSIRTs of networks that attack them and public daily and hourly statistics of the traffic they receive. FIRST describes her as having started this line of research during her doctorate and as a participant in the conception and deployment of the countrywide network. The sensors later supported academic work she co-authored on Internet of Things (IoT) botnets: the evolution of Bashlite and Mirai, presented at the 2018 symposium on computers and communications of the IEEE (Institute of Electrical and Electronics Engineers), and an adaptive network layer for IoT botnet investigation, published in Sensors in 2019.

Spam and port 25. M3AAWG (Messaging, Malware and Mobile Anti-Abuse Working Group) credits her with leading the technical coordination of Brazil's anti-spam efforts from 2005 to 2013, focused on the abuse of open proxies and open relays and on direct delivery by botnets; FIRST dates the work from 2006 to 2013 and names its instrument, getting network providers to adopt port 25 management. The policy, published on CGI.br's Antispam.br site, separates mail submission from mail transport on residential broadband, following the recommendation of the Messaging Anti-Abuse Working Group: mail providers require authentication for submission (RFC 4954) and their users' clients send on port 587 of TCP (Transmission Control Protocol), while broadband operators block outbound traffic to port 25/TCP from every machine that is not a mail transfer agent or explicitly authorized, so infected machines and open proxies can no longer deliver spam directly. CGI.br recommended it in resolution CGI.br/RES/2009/02/P, and its implementation was the subject of a cooperation agreement between Anatel, CGI.br, the operators' union SindiTelebrasil and associations of internet access providers, supported by public prosecutors and consumer protection bodies.

In the wider community. She attended the Internet Architecture Board's CARIS (Coordinating Attack Response at Internet Scale) workshop in Berlin on 18 June 2015, whose report, RFC 8073, describes CERT.br as Brazil's national focal point for incident reporting that distributes network security honeypots and focuses on network monitoring; FIRST also lists her contributions to OECD (Organisation for Economic Co-operation and Development) work on digital security risk, to the SEI's state of practice of CSIRTs and to the GFCE (Global Forum on Cyber Expertise) guide Getting Started with a National CSIRT. M3AAWG presented her with its Mary Litynski Award at its 48th General Meeting in San Francisco in February 2020; she used the occasion to argue that industries have to recognize and own the abuse of their services, because only criminals gain when a problem is denied. On 10 June 2024, at FIRSTCON24 in Fukuoka, FIRST inducted her into its Incident Response Hall of Fame for pioneering work in establishing and supporting CSIRTs worldwide, the first woman in a group that included Andrew Cormack, Jeffrey Carpenter, Dan Kaminsky, Ian Cook, Don Stikvoort and Klaus-Peter Kossakowski; NIC.br's chief executive, Demi Getschko, called it the result of more than 25 years of dedication to managing security incidents.

chkrootkit.def: chkrootkit is the Unix rootkit detector that Nelson Murilo first released in Brazil on 20 February 1997, later with Klaus Steding-Jessen as co-author: a shell script, helped by a few small C programs, that uses ordinary system tools to look for the signatures and behavioural traces of known rootkits, and that is still maintained, with version 0.60 out in October 2026.
chkrootkit.context: It is probably the most widely deployed piece of security software ever written in Brazil: packaged by the major Linux distributions and security collections, in the FreeBSD ports tree since 2001, tested across the BSD (Berkeley Software Distribution) systems, Solaris, HP-UX and macOS, and reached for by administrators who suspect a compromised machine. The design decision that made it last was choosing to be a portable script over standard utilities rather than a binary tool or a Perl program: it runs where nothing else will install, which is exactly the situation in which it is needed. Its limits come from the same design: it finds what it has signatures for, and it trusts tools that an attacker with root may already have replaced.
chkrootkit.depth:
What it is. The package is a shell script, chkrootkit, that checks system binaries for modification by known rootkits, plus a handful of small C programs for checks a script cannot do well: ifpromisc reports whether a network interface is in promiscuous mode, the mark of an installed sniffer; chklastlog, chkwtmp, chkutmp and, on Solaris, check_wtmpx look for entries deleted from the login records; chkproc and chkdirs look for signs of loadable kernel module (LKM) trojans; and strings is a minimal replacement for the system's own. It must run as root. Run with no arguments it performs every test, or it can be given a list (for example ps, ls and sniffer). Each test prints one of a few verdicts: INFECTED when a command was probably modified by a known rootkit, not infected when no known signature was found, not tested, not found, and vulnerable but disabled when an infected command exists but is not in use.

How it detects. Most tests look for known signatures, strings that particular rootkits leave inside the binaries they replace; the example in the project's frequently asked questions (FAQ) is trojaned versions of ps that contain /dev/ptyp. The authors are blunt about the consequence: an attacker can change a rootkit's source to remove its signature, and when chkrootkit finds no known signature it cannot decide on its own whether a file has been trojaned. For that case there is an expert mode, -x, which dumps suspicious strings from the binaries and leaves the analysis to the administrator. Other tests look at behaviour rather than content. chkproc compares the output of ps with the entries under /proc, because a process hidden from ps by a kernel-level rootkit still has a directory there; on a busy server short-lived processes can make it report false positives. The aliens test looks in default locations for sniffer logs and rootkit configuration files, and the bindshell test looks for listeners on ports associated with backdoors, such as 1524, 31337 and 12321, which is why a defensive tool like PortSentry that binds to unused ports trips it. The README itself warns that the login-record checks only try to detect deletions and guarantee nothing.

The trust problem. The script relies on a short list of ordinary commands, awk, cut, echo, egrep, find, head, id, ls, netstat, ps, strings, sed and uname, and on a compromised machine those are exactly the commands a rootkit replaces. The FAQ's answer to whether they can be trusted is 'probably not', and the tool offers two ways round it. The -p option supplies an alternative path, for example a read-only medium carrying known-good binaries; the -r option scans a different root directory, so that the suspect disk can be mounted on a machine the administrator trusts and examined from there. The README's advice once a trojaned command is found is equally direct: the real problem is that someone has root on the machine, and the best course is to reinstall it from safe media and follow the vendor's security recommendations rather than replace the one command.

Origin. The ChangeLog in the README begins with an initial release on 20 February 1997, followed by version 0.4 five days later, Debian compatibility in June 1997 and FreeBSD fixes in June and August. Checks for loadable kernel module trojans arrived in version 0.17 in September 2000, the -r, -p and -l options in 0.19 that December, Ramen worm detection in January 2001 and the quiet mode in 0.34 in September 2001. In October 2001 the two authors described the method at the third Brazilian information security symposium, SSI 2001, in São José dos Campos: Murilo was then at Pangéia Informática in Brasília and Steding-Jessen at the NIC BR Security Office in Campinas, which CERT.br, created as NBSO in June 1997, describes as its own former name; the README now gives his address at cert.br. Their paper traces the target: from 1989 the underground magazine Phrack published tools to edit the utmp, wtmp and lastlog records; the first rootkits, written for SunOS and then Linux, appeared with sniffers in CERT advisories by 1994; and from 1997 rootkits moved into the kernel as modules that altered system calls such as kill, getdents and read, which is what chkproc and chkdirs were built to catch. In version 0.34 the script alone was 1,985 lines.

Keeping up. The home page lists 75 rootkits, worms and kernel modules the current version detects, from the lrk3 to lrk6 Linux rootkits, t0rn, the Ramen, Lion and Adore worms, the knark and Adore kernel modules, SucKIT and the Slapper worm to families of the last decade: Operation Windigo's Secure Shell (SSH) backdoor (version 0.50, April 2014), the Mumblehard botnet (0.51, October 2016), the Rocke Monero miner (0.53, January 2019), the Umbreon rootkit (0.55), the Kovid rootkit (0.56, December 2022) and BPFDoor (0.58, June 2023). Version 0.59, of 11 October 2025, added detection of the XZ backdoor and of the Bootkitty Unified Extensible Firmware Interface (UEFI) bootkit and a check for processes executed from memory; 0.60, released on 11 October 2026, brought performance work and fixes to chkproc's false positives. It has been tested on Linux from 2.0 to 6.x, FreeBSD up to 15, OpenBSD, NetBSD, Solaris, HP-UX, Tru64, BSDI and macOS.

Where it lives. Debian maintains it through its Security Tools team, with version 0.59 in testing and unstable and 0.58b in stable as read on 12 November 2026; Kali lists it among its forensics tools; it has been in the FreeBSD ports tree since 6 April 2001, under a two-clause BSD licence. The FAQ shows the classic deployment, a nightly cron job that mails the output to root, and O'Reilly's Linux Security Cookbook and Network Security Hacks and Skoudis and Zeltser's Malware: Fighting Malicious Code all teach it. A routine scan is useful for catching the known and the careless; it is not a substitute for examining a suspect system from trusted media.

Its own vulnerability. A tool that runs as root over attacker-controlled files is itself attack surface. Common Vulnerabilities and Exposures (CVE) entry CVE-2014-0476 recorded that the slapper test in chkrootkit before 0.50 did not properly quote file paths, so that on systems where /tmp was not mounted noexec a local user could plant an executable that the scan would then run with root privileges. Version 0.50 fixed it. The lesson is general to security scanners: run current versions, from read-only trusted media where possible, and treat the scanner's privileges as part of the threat model.

Neighbours and limits. MITRE ATT&CK describes rootkits, technique T1014, as programs that hide files, processes, network connections and other components by intercepting and modifying operating system calls, at user or kernel level, which is the behaviour chkrootkit's two families of tests target. Its closest relative is Rootkit Hunter (rkhunter), another script-based scanner whose latest release, 1.4.6, dates from February 2018. A clean chkrootkit result means only that none of the known signatures and anomalies was found: a new or modified rootkit, or one that hides well enough in the kernel, can pass, which is why it is used alongside file integrity monitoring, endpoint detection and offline forensic analysis rather than instead of them.

rodrigo-rubira-branco.def: Rodrigo Rubira Branco (BSDaemon) is a Brazilian vulnerability researcher and exploit writer whose career runs from IBM's Advanced Linux Response Team through Check Point, Qualys and Intel to Amazon Web Services, Google and L3Harris Trenchant, and who organized the Hackers to Hackers Conference (H2HC) in São Paulo from its fifth edition until 2024.
rodrigo-rubira-branco.context: His significance for Brazil is the demonstration effect: low-level security research (kernels, processors, firmware, exploit mitigation) was assumed to happen elsewhere, and a generation of Brazilian researchers followed a path he helped make visible, both through a career inside some of the world's largest technology companies and through H2HC, which he ran on volunteer labour for two decades and described as the place where hacking stays a counterculture and knowledge is not controlled. The local conference culture that grew alongside it is where much of that community still meets.
rodrigo-rubira-branco.depth:
Who he is. Rodrigo Rubira Branco, known by the handle BSDaemon, describes himself as a vulnerability researcher and exploit writer. Most of the public record about him comes from his conference biographies, his published research and the pages of the Hackers to Hackers Conference (H2HC); they show a career spent on the lowest layers of systems, from operating system kernels and debuggers to processor microarchitecture, and a parallel role as the long-time organizer of Latin America's oldest security research conference. He is a member of the RISE Security group and has served on the programme committees of conferences including OffensiveCon, LangSec, Black Hat and Enigma.

Kernels and toolchains. His early posts were in systems engineering and vulnerability research: staff software engineer in IBM's Advanced Linux Response Team (ALRT), also working in IBM's toolchain and debugging team for the PowerPC architecture, then principal security researcher at Scanit and senior vulnerability researcher at COSEINC. He contributed to open-source projects including the Linux kernel and the ebizzy benchmark. His article in Phrack issue 66, 'Power cell buffer overflow', is characteristic of the work: a guide to Linux on the Cell Broadband Engine, to debugging its synergistic processor elements (SPEs) and to exploiting memory overflows on them, written with acknowledged help from his research partner Filipe Balestra.

Finding bugs at scale. As chief security researcher at Check Point in Israel he founded the company's Vulnerability Discovery Team (VDT), which released dozens of vulnerabilities in widely used software, and in 2011 he was recognized as one of the top contributors to Adobe's vulnerability fixes over the previous 12 months. At Qualys, as director of vulnerability and malware research, he founded the Dissect || PE malware analysis project, built on a database of 30 million samples with static and dynamic analysis engines and an open plug-in architecture for researchers. Its first results, presented at Black Hat USA in July 2012 and at Hack In The Box in Kuala Lumpur, ran 51 static tests for anti-debugging, anti-disassembly and anti-virtualization tricks against 4 million samples and found that 88.96 per cent used at least one evasion technique, with anti-virtualization the most common by a wide margin: a measurement, rather than an anecdote, of how much malware is built to detect the sandbox analysing it. At DEF CON 20 the same year he presented 'Overwriting the Exception Handling Cache Pointer: Dwarf Oriented Programming' with James Oakley and Sergey Bratus of Dartmouth College.

Processors and the cloud. At Intel he was chief security researcher, founding and leading the STORM (STrategic Offensive Research and Mitigations) team, and also led the Core Client and BIOS (Basic Input/Output System) teams; at Black Hat USA 2016 he presented DPTrace, a dual-purpose trace for analysing the exploitability of program crashes, and he took part in the closing locknote of Black Hat USA 2020. He then worked as a senior principal engineer at Amazon Web Services, led central processing unit (CPU) and microarchitecture security research at Google, and, by his 2024 biography, was lead security researcher at L3Harris Trenchant. The thread running through these posts is the boundary where hardware assumptions meet software exploitation.

H2HC. Branco joined the organization of the Hackers to Hackers Conference during its first edition, while it was already under way. By the fifth edition the committee of about eight people was divided and late; he offered to leave, the group asked him to stay, and he became lead organizer on the condition of keeping the original spirit, then invited Filipe Balestra to join him. The conference kept a steady cadence: its eighth edition took place on 29 and 30 October 2011 at the Amcham Business Center in São Paulo, and its 21-year edition on 14 and 15 December 2024, with the organization listed as Branco and Balestra. Black Hat's regional advisory board described it as the oldest and biggest security research conference in Latin America.

The farewell. On 25 November 2024 Branco announced that he would leave the organization after that year's edition, handing every responsibility to Balestra. His letter is a rare first-hand account of what running a volunteer research conference costs: about 1,000 hours of his time a year, around 3,000 people a day, more than 20 villages, more than 18 international speakers, a technical magazine, electronic badges, free drinks to make people talk, donated tickets and no marketing budget, with no employees and every cent reinvested. He wrote that for him leading had always been about serving, that growing the event further would require professionalizing it in ways he was not the right person to lead, and that he would go on as a researcher who cares about the world and its people. Anchises Moraes, who transcribed the letter, called H2HC the backbone of the Brazilian security community.

efnet.def: One of the oldest surviving IRC networks, formed in 1990 when a set of servers removed a machine called Eris that accepted connections from anyone - the name is short for Eris Free Net, and it is a policy stated as a network topology.
efnet.context: EFnet's defining choice is what it refuses to run: no central registration services, no ChanServ, no NickServ. Nicknames and channels belong to whoever is holding them right now, which produced decades of takeovers, bot wars and the culture of never leaving a channel empty. That austerity kept it the home of much of the old technical and underground community long after friendlier networks appeared, and it is why EFnet stories are mostly about conflict - the network's design assumes you can defend yourself.

netsplit.def: A partition of an IRC network when the link between servers drops: each side keeps running, users on the far side appear to quit en masse, and when the link returns the two halves merge their state back together.
netsplit.context: The merge is where the exploit lived. On a network without registration services, a channel that becomes empty on one side of a split gives the first person to join it operator status - so a patient attacker would wait for a split, join the isolated empty channel, and inherit control of the whole channel when the halves rejoined. Riding the netsplit is the classic IRC takeover, and the countermeasures it forced - always-on bots, channel guards, eventually services - are the reason later networks look nothing like EFnet. It is also a general lesson: partition plus automatic merge is a security problem, not just an availability one.

the-great-irc-split.def: The 1996 schism that divided the original IRC network into EFnet and IRCnet, largely along an American and European line, after long-running disagreement over server linking policy, nickname handling and who decides.
the-great-irc-split.context: The split is the field's cleanest study of governance failing before technology does. The protocol worked; what broke was the human process for admitting servers and settling disputes, in a design where every server operator holds real power and no mechanism existed to bind them. Every federated system since - mail, social protocols, package registries - meets the same problem, and IRC met it first and loudest. The consequence lasts: instead of one network there are many, and the split is why a user must ask not just whether someone is on IRC but which one.

libera-chat.def: The IRC network founded in May 2021 by the volunteer staff who resigned from freenode after a disputed change of control, taking most of the free-software projects that had used freenode with them within days.
libera-chat.context: freenode had been the default home of open-source project channels for two decades. When its staff concluded the network's ownership had changed hands in a way they could not accept, they left as a body and stood up a replacement, and thousands of projects moved almost immediately - a demonstration that in volunteer infrastructure the community, not the domain name, is the asset. It is the clearest modern case of a fork applied to an organization rather than to code, and it worked because the people who ran the thing were the thing.

midori.def: Microsoft's incubation project, running from around 2008 until it was wound down in 2015, to build an operating system from scratch in managed code - kernel, drivers and applications all memory-safe - as a commercial descendant of the Singularity research OS, designed for concurrency and capability-based isolation.
midori.context: It never shipped, and it is studied anyway because its team published unusually candid retrospectives, chiefly Joe Duffy's series, describing what a language-enforced safe operating system actually costs and what it buys. Ideas from it surfaced later in mainstream work on safe systems programming, async and error handling. Read alongside the memory-safety argument now driving Rust adoption in kernels, Midori reads as an experiment that answered the question a decade before the industry asked it. Note: the name is reused - there is also a lightweight web browser called Midori, unrelated to this project.

leonardo-pigner.def: Co-founder and chief executive of Ekoparty, the Buenos Aires security conference that grew into one of Latin America's largest hacking events, one of the five people credited with starting it in 2001, alongside Juan Pablo Daniel Borgna, Federico Kirschbaum, Jerónimo Basaldúa and Francisco Amato.
leonardo-pigner.context: Pigñer is the founder who stayed operational: he runs the conference as an organization rather than an annual event, with year-round community programmes, publications and training. With Basaldúa he is also credited with building the security firm Base4. The Ekoparty model, a commercially sustainable conference that never stopped being a hacker gathering, is the one many Latin American organizers study, and it is part of why the region has an independent circuit rather than franchised editions of northern events.
leonardo-pigner.depth:
Who he is. Leonardo Pigñer, often Leo, is one of the founders of Ekoparty and, in the press of the 2020s, its chief executive: iProfesional called him its director general ejecutivo in October 2023, Ámbito its CEO (chief executive officer) a few days later, and ITSitio its CEO and co-founder in May 2026. Little of his own biography has been published; the public record is mostly the conference's record, and he appears in it as the person who opens the event, describes its programme and speaks for it to the press. That is itself telling: Ekoparty is less a single annual meeting than an organization that he runs all year, and he is also credited, with Basaldúa, with building the security firm Base4.

Where it came from. Ekoparty's own history traces it to a 2001 meetup of hackers who barely knew each other from chat rooms.
