Around 2000, during Argentina's economic collapse, two of them met in person and formed the Ezkracho Team, or EKO Team, which grew around IRC (Internet Relay Chat), published a technical e-zine called Eko Magazine and organized the first two Ekoparty events at a LAN house called Baires LAN in Villa Urquiza: weekend-long gatherings where people brought their own computers and slept on mattresses the owner provided. The third edition, in 2007 at the Hotel Bauen in Buenos Aires, took the conference format it keeps today, with several talks at once and speakers from abroad; the name was later explained as Electronic K.O. Party. English-language accounts list five founders, Juan Pablo Daniel Borgna, Leonardo Pigñer, Federico Kirschbaum, Jerónimo Basaldúa and Francisco Amato, and date the founding to 2001; the Spanish-language Wikipedia gives 2005.

A venue for research. The conference became a place where international work was released. In September 2011 Juliano Rizzo and Thai Duong chose Ekoparty to unveil BEAST, their attack on version 1.0 of TLS (Transport Layer Security), which could decrypt the encrypted cookies of HTTPS (Hypertext Transfer Protocol Secure) sessions; BEAST stands for Browser Exploit Against SSL/TLS, SSL being the older Secure Sockets Layer. The 2023 programme the organizers announced to the press covered the security of AI (artificial intelligence), weaknesses in VoLTE (Voice over Long-Term Evolution) mobile networks and in the European trunked radio standard TETRA, used worldwide by government agencies, security forces, emergency services and the military, attacks on the integrity of video surveillance streams and honeypots used for counterintelligence, with speakers who included Gottfrid Svartholm, a co-founder of The Pirate Bay, and an opening talk by the veteran researcher Iván Arce on how security and hacking had changed since the 1990s.

Scale and format. The 2023 edition ran from 1 to 3 November at the Centro de Convenciones de Buenos Aires, with free entry, more than 10,000 attendees expected and, in Pigñer's description, nine auditoriums running in parallel for three days, job interviews for people looking for work in the field and the wardriving tour that maps the city's Wi-Fi networks; Ámbito counted more than 170 talks. iProfesional called it the largest hacker gathering in the Spanish-speaking world, and in 2026 ITSitio put annual attendance in Buenos Aires at more than 10,000.

Building talent. Pigñer's public message has been about the shortage of people. Opening the 2023 conference, he said that the Futuro Hacker programme had taken members of the community into schools and that more than 1,500 young people had attended its talks; the programme travels the country in a van called the Ekoneta, encouraging secondary students to study security, and brought more than 300 students to the conference for web hacking workshops and interview practice. Ekoparty's Ekojobs survey, which it calls the first comprehensive study of the cybersecurity labour market in Latin America, found that 70 per cent of the region's security professionals were trained outside traditional education. The year's calendar now includes the main CTF (capture the flag) competition, wardriving, a live bug bounty event with Bug Bounty Argentina, webinars and a zone for start-ups.

Going north. In May 2026 Ekoparty held its first edition in the United States, in Miami on 21 and 22 May, with villages for hardware hacking, bug bounty and car hacking run with communities such as OWASP (Open Worldwide Application Security Project), WiCyS (Women in CyberSecurity) and The Diana Initiative, and an agenda on AI-driven offence, Latin American financial fraud operating across borders and the region's technical talent. Pigñer told ITSitio that Ekoparty had always been a meeting point for Latin America's hacker community, that the organizers had watched researchers, communities and technical talent of a very high level grow in Mexico and across the region, and that Miami was where that talent could meet new opportunities and global players. The same month Ekoparty led a session at New York's Tech Week presenting Argentina's security ecosystem, drawing on its own research, to American companies and investors.

federico-kirschbaum.def: Argentine security researcher and executive, co-founder of Ekoparty (2001) and, with Francisco Amato, of Infobyte and its successor Faraday, the company behind the open-source collaborative penetration-testing and vulnerability management platform of that name; Faraday's CEO (chief executive officer) by 2024 and, by 2026, head of the Security Lab at XBOW.
federico-kirschbaum.context: Kirschbaum represents the pattern that makes the Argentine scene distinctive: the conference and the research companies grew from the same group of people, so talks, tooling and commercial work reinforce each other instead of competing. He has continued presenting original research internationally, including at Black Hat, which is the practical rebuttal to the assumption that serious offensive research happens only in the northern hemisphere.
federico-kirschbaum.depth:
Who he is. Federico Kirschbaum, known as Fede, is an Argentine security researcher whose career runs from the hacker meetups that became Ekoparty to the business of offensive security tooling. His 2010 DEF CON biography describes him as CTO (chief technology officer) of Infobyte Security Research in Buenos Aires, with almost ten years of experience researching and penetration-testing networks and a deep knowledge of computer security and telecommunications, and as one of the founders of Ekoparty; his Black Hat biographies of 2015 and 2016 repeat the role with almost fifteen years of experience. By 2024 Black Hat described him as chief executive and co-founder of Faraday Security, with more than twenty years in the industry, and in May 2026 he was introduced as head of the Security Lab at XBOW, a company building an autonomous offensive security platform.

Ekoparty. The conference's own history traces it to a 2001 meetup of hackers who knew each other from chat rooms and to the Ezkracho, or EKO, Team that grew out of IRC (Internet Relay Chat) around 2000 and published the Eko Magazine e-zine. The first two Ekoparty events were weekend-long gatherings at Baires LAN in Villa Urquiza, where attendees brought their own computers; the third, in 2007 at the Hotel Bauen, took the conference format with multiple talks and foreign speakers. English-language accounts name Kirschbaum among five founders, with Juan Pablo Daniel Borgna, Leonardo Pigñer, Jerónimo Basaldúa and Francisco Amato. In his 2023 interview with the journalist Ryan Naraine he described what made the Argentine scene distinctive, from its exploit writers to the U.S.-centric view of the security industry, and in 2026 he spoke from Ekoparty's first edition in Miami.

Evilgrade. With Amato he presented Evilgrade, You Still Have Pending Upgrades? at DEF CON 18 on 30 July 2010. Evilgrade, which Amato had released in 2008, is a modular framework that impersonates the update servers of applications once an attacker can redirect a victim's DNS (Domain Name System) traffic, through ARP (Address Resolution Protocol) spoofing, DNS cache poisoning, DHCP (Dynamic Host Configuration Protocol) spoofing or a rogue access point, and then delivers the attacker's agent as an update. Its 2.0 release of October 2010 added SSL (Secure Sockets Layer) support to its web server and wildcard DNS matching, and modules for dozens of updaters.

Faraday, the idea. Infobyte released Faraday in 2013, describing it as the first multi-user penetration testing IDE (integrated development environment). In March 2015 Russ McRee's toolsmith column described it as an Integrated Penetration-Test Environment (IPE) designed for the distribution, indexation and analysis of the data generated during a security audit carried out by several people, with plugins for more than 40 tools, among them OpenVAS, BeEF, Arachni, Skipfish and ZAP. Kirschbaum, then Infobyte's CTO and the project lead, explained the reasoning: on real assessments the team always needed to know what other members had found, because sharing partial knowledge of the targets avoided overlap and let discoveries be reused, and on large scopes a vulnerability found in one part of the network can often be exploited somewhere else. The goal was to turn everything a test produces into indexed information distributed to the team in real time, without forcing anyone to change tools or workflow, so that Faraday acted as a bridge between the tools testers already preferred.

Faraday, the product. Today's repository presents Faraday as an open-source vulnerability manager that aggregates and normalizes the results loaded into it and offers views for analysts and managers alike, deployed with Docker and a PostgreSQL database. Kali Linux packages it as python-faraday among its reporting tools, with a terminal that recognizes supported commands such as an nmap scan and imports their results automatically. The company that grew from Infobyte took the product's name, Faraday Security, with Kirschbaum as chief executive; in 2023 he spoke at a security awareness meeting organized by the Buenos Aires City Legislature after a 2022 cyber attack on its infrastructure.

XBOW and AI-driven offence. On the Three Buddy Problem podcast recorded at Ekoparty Miami and published on 25 May 2026, Kirschbaum, as head of XBOW's Security Lab, discussed what happens to offensive security when an autonomous AI (artificial intelligence) hacker can find and exploit real vulnerabilities, including the experience of watching a non-human adversary reason its way to an ASLR (address space layout randomization) bypass. His argument was that penetration testing is not dying but becoming accessible to far more than the world's biggest companies, with humans still needed in the loop, and that Argentina remains an untapped talent pipeline. SC Media's contributor page likewise lists him as leading the XBOW Security Lab and as co-founder of Faraday Security and Ekoparty.

Why he matters. Kirschbaum's line of work, from Evilgrade's attack on trust in the update channel to Faraday's insistence that a team's findings be shared and normalized, and now to automated exploitation, follows the practical questions of a penetration testing practice rather than a single discovery. For engineers on the defending side the useful lesson is Faraday's: findings from many scanners only become actionable when they are deduplicated, correlated across the network and tracked to closure in one place.

francisco-amato.def: Argentine security researcher, co-founder of the Ekoparty conference and of the Infobyte and Faraday security companies, and author of Evilgrade (2008), the framework that showed how software update mechanisms can be abused to deliver an attacker's code to a victim who was doing exactly what security advice told them to do.
francisco-amato.context: Evilgrade landed at the point where the industry was telling everyone to keep software updated, and showed that an update channel without signature verification is a distribution system for whoever controls the network path. The work is a good example of research from the region setting an international agenda: update integrity is now assumed, and part of the reason is that someone built the tool that made the failure undeniable.
francisco-amato.depth:
Who he is. Francisco Amato is an Argentine security researcher and consultant whose 2008 speaker biographies describe his specialities as vulnerability development, blackbox testing and reverse engineering. He ran his own company, ISR (Infobyte Security Research), through which he published audit tools and vulnerabilities in products from Novell, IBM, Sun Microsystems, Apple and Microsoft; he is one of the founders of Ekoparty, the Buenos Aires security conference; and Faraday, the company that grew out of Infobyte, describes him as its co-founder. His best-known work, Evilgrade, belongs in every network engineer's threat model, because it turns a network position into code execution through the one channel users are told to trust.

Ekoparty. The conference's own history says it started in 2001 as a meetup of hackers who barely knew each other from chat rooms. Around 2000, in the middle of Argentina's economic collapse, two of them met in person and formed the Ezkracho Team, or EKO Team, which published a technical e-zine, Eko Magazine, and organized the first two Ekoparty events at a LAN house called Baires LAN in Villa Urquiza: weekend-long gatherings where attendees brought their own computers. The third edition, in 2007 at the Hotel Bauen in Buenos Aires, adopted the conference format it still has, with multiple talks and foreign speakers; the name was later explained as Electronic K.O. Party. English-language accounts list five founders, Juan Pablo Daniel Borgna, Leonardo Pigñer, Federico Kirschbaum, Jerónimo Basaldúa and Francisco Amato, and date the founding to 2001; the Spanish-language Wikipedia gives 2005 and credits the Ezkracho team with them. Amato's 2010 DEF CON biography calls him a founding organizer. The conference grew into a venue where international research premiered: in September 2011 Juliano Rizzo and Thai Duong unveiled at Ekoparty their attack on TLS (Transport Layer Security) 1.0, BEAST, short for Browser Exploit Against SSL/TLS, SSL being the older Secure Sockets Layer.

Infobyte. A company listing published by Python Argentina describes Infobyte LLC as founded in 2001 and offering offensive security services, including what it calls the first red team services in Latin America, with research that ranged from Evilgrade to attacks on a fingerprint reader and a report on tunnels used in bank robberies; in 2013 it released Faraday, which it called the first multi-user penetration testing IDE (integrated development environment). Faraday later became the company's name and product; its open-source vulnerability manager is packaged in Kali Linux, and in August 2023 the company reported that Amato, as co-founder, had shown it at Black Hat in Las Vegas as an open-source vulnerability management tool.

Evilgrade, how it works. Evilgrade is a modular framework that takes advantage of poor upgrade implementations by injecting fake updates. Its targets are updaters that look up a fixed hostname and trust whatever the server there returns: each module lists the virtual hosts it impersonates (for Java, java.sun.com and javadl-esd.sun.com) and the message it will show, and Evilgrade answers those requests itself: it ships its own DNS (Domain Name System) server and web server, each module emulates the update protocol of one application (the hostnames it calls and what it expects back), and the agent it delivers is whatever payload the tester chooses. It needs one precondition, that the attacker can redirect the victim's name resolution. Inside a network that means control of internal DNS, ARP (Address Resolution Protocol) spoofing, DNS cache poisoning, DHCP (Dynamic Host Configuration Protocol) spoofing, TCP (Transmission Control Protocol) hijacking or a rogue Wi-Fi access point; from outside, control of DNS or cache poisoning.

Release and timing. Amato presented and released the tool at the TROOPERS conference on 23 April 2008 under the title You have pending upgrades. Version 1.0.0 is dated 25 July 2008, and on 28 July Infobyte announced it on the Full-Disclosure list with modules for the Java plugin, Winzip, Winamp, Mac OS, OpenOffice, iTunes, the LinkedIn Toolbar, Download Accelerator, Notepad++ and Speedbit, and a demonstration titled Java plugin plus Dan Kaminsky's DNS vulnerability equals remote compromise. The timing was the point: Kaminsky's DNS cache poisoning flaw had been disclosed three weeks earlier and an exploit had just been folded into Metasploit, so, as The Register put it, the man-in-the-middle precondition was no longer much of a problem. The demonstration compromised a fully patched machine through Java's own updater.

Growth. Version 2.0.0, on 29 October 2010, added SSL to the web server, wildcard DNS matching, hashes of the delivered agent and dozens of modules, among them Windows Update for Internet Explorer 6 to 8, Apple Software Update, apt on Ubuntu releases before 10.04 and CPAN (Comprehensive Perl Archive Network); that summer, on 30 July 2010, Amato and Federico Kirschbaum presented it at DEF CON 18 as Evilgrade, You Still Have Pending Upgrades? Later releases added native Windows support (2013), a link to the Faraday platform (2014), modules for vendor update tools from Samsung, Intel, Lenovo, ASUS and Acer, for KeePass (the Common Vulnerabilities and Exposures entry CVE-2016-5119) and a generic one for the Sparkle update framework (2016), SoapUI (2018) and, on 14 December 2020, the SolarWinds Orion updater.

What it teaches. Every Evilgrade module is a record of an updater that trusted the network. The defence is equally specific: the client must verify a digital signature on the update, against a key it already holds, before running anything, and should fetch over TLS with full certificate validation, so that neither a poisoned DNS answer nor an ARP spoof can substitute code. DNSSEC (Domain Name System Security Extensions) and resolver hardening reduce the redirection, but only signed updates remove the payoff. For a penetration tester, the framework is a reminder that a man-in-the-middle position on a LAN (local area network) is worth more than the traffic it can read.

filipe-balestra.def: Filipe Alcarde Balestra is a Brazilian offensive security researcher, founder and director of PRIDE Security, and co-organizer, with Rodrigo Rubira Branco, of the Hackers to Hackers Conference (H2HC) in São Paulo from its fifth edition; he took sole charge of the conference from 2025. His published work includes kernel vulnerabilities and research on attacking automated teller machines (ATMs).
filipe-balestra.context: The handover is worth recording because succession is where volunteer conferences usually die. On 25 November 2024 Branco announced that, after 21 years in the organization, he would step down after that year's edition and that from 2025 every responsibility would rest with Balestra, whom he called one of his best friends and fully able to secure the conference's future. By then H2HC, held in São Paulo since 2004 and described by its organizers as the oldest security research conference in Latin America, drew around 3,000 people a day, with more than 20 villages and more than 18 international speakers, and was run entirely by volunteers. A deliberate, announced transition rather than a quiet ending is a governance achievement as much as a technical community's.
filipe-balestra.depth:
Who he is. Filipe Alcarde Balestra has worked in information security since the 1990s, concentrating on the offensive side: penetration testing, vulnerability research and attacks on physical and financial systems. He founded and directs PRIDE Security, where he works in offensive security, after working for other consultancies in Brazil and abroad. The public record about him is short and comes mainly from his conference biographies and from the pages of the Hackers to Hackers Conference (H2HC); he is better known in the Brazilian community as the person who, with Rodrigo Rubira Branco, kept the country's deepest technical conference running for sixteen years than for any single disclosure.

Research. His biographies credit him with vulnerabilities in widely used software, among them the kernels of FreeBSD and NetBSD, the QNX real-time operating system (RTOS) and Sun Solaris, one of which was cited as a reference in the Syngress book A Guide to Kernel Exploitation: Attacking the Core. They also credit him as co-author of an article in Hakin9 chosen as the best of the magazine's first 100 issues and of an article for Phrack. His collaboration with Branco is on the record in Phrack itself: Branco's article in issue 66 on attacking the Cell Broadband Engine architecture closes by thanking Filipe Balestra, 'my research partner', for ideas, feedback and experience that improved the article and its samples.

ATMs and banks. His more recent public work is on the security of financial infrastructure. At the 2024 edition of H2HC he and Wendel Guglielmetti Henrique presented 'Case study: client-side attacks on ATM', which walked through the anatomy of an automated teller machine (ATM): its most relevant parts, its physical security and its communication standards. The point of the talk was that even with a globally used standard, a real machine may run custom implementations that defeat some published attacks, and it described alternative ways of attacking those implementations, from the locks up to the communication standards, to obtain what the abstract called the so wanted jackpot; jackpotting is the name for forcing an ATM to dispense its cash. At SBSeg 2024, the 24th Brazilian Symposium on Information and Computational Systems Security, organized by the Aeronautics Institute of Technology (ITA) from 16 to 19 September 2024 for the Brazilian Computing Society, he gave a lightning talk titled 'From Physical Access to Domain Admin in a Bank', a title that names the whole path, from physical access to administrative control of a bank's domain.

The conference he runs. H2HC, the Hackers to Hackers Conference, describes itself as organized by people who work in research and development in information security, with the aim of showing techniques that have never been seen or discussed in public. Its stated rationale is the defender's one: finding flaws is not hard, for every flaw reported to a manufacturer others are probably known and unreported, and the best protection against them is to understand how problems occur and build mechanisms that prevent whole classes of flaw, instead of applying vendor fixes and hoping nobody has a zero-day. Its topics run from exploit development, fuzzing and reverse engineering to telecommunications and phone phreaking, hardware hacking, industrial systems and lockpicking. The 2024 edition, billed as H2HC 21 Years, took place on 14 and 15 December 2024 at the Novotel Center Norte in São Paulo; its pages listed the organization as Rodrigo Rubira Branco and Filipe Alcarde Balestra, with Gabriel Negreira Barbosa as editor of the H2HC Magazine. Recordings of the talks have been published on a YouTube channel in Balestra's name.

How he came to organize it. Branco's own account, published when he left, explains Balestra's place. Branco joined the organization during the first edition, while it was already under way. By the fifth edition the committee of about eight people was divided and everything was late; Branco said he would leave, the group decided he should continue, and the agreement was to keep the original spirit: that people should meet, that hacking is a counterculture and that knowledge should not be controlled. Branco then invited his close friend Filipe Balestra to join him, and, in his words, sixteen more years passed.

The succession. In the letter of 25 November 2024 Branco described what the two had built: around 3,000 people a day, more than 20 villages, more than 18 international speakers, a magazine whose technical quality had risen, electronic badges that had become an international reference, free drinks to encourage people to talk, tickets donated to those who could not pay, and no marketing budget. The event had no employees; nobody took a cent, and all income was reinvested. Branco put his own effort at around 1,000 hours a year and said that growing the conference would require professionalizing it, potentially with exclusive dedication, which was not what he wanted to do; he left the choice of path to Balestra, in whom he said he had full confidence. Anchises Moraes, writing the same day, called H2HC the backbone of the Brazilian security community. From 2025 the conference has been Balestra's to run, which makes him, at the time of writing, the person responsible for the oldest security research conference in Latin America surviving its founder's exit.

jaime-andres-restrepo.def: Founder of DragonJAR, the Colombian security company and one of the largest Spanish-speaking security communities, and creator of the DragonJAR Security Conference; recognized in 2022 with Ekoparty's lifetime achievement award.
jaime-andres-restrepo.context: His strategic choice was language. DragonJAR was built in Spanish, for a region whose practitioners were expected to consume security knowledge in English, and the community and forum that grew around it trained a generation that had no other local reference. His own research, notably work on attacking the connected systems of cars sold in Latin America, made the point that regional targets deserve regional researchers, since nobody in the northern hemisphere was testing those particular vehicles.
jaime-andres-restrepo.depth:
Who he is, in his public role. Jaime Andrés Restrepo is a Colombian security consultant, the founder and chief executive of DragonJAR, a company from Manizales that sells penetration testing, ethical hacking and digital forensics, and the creator of the community of the same name. The biography published by Ekoparty when it honoured him describes a Systems and Telecommunications Engineer from the Universidad de Manizales with more than twenty years of work in ethical hacking, penetration testing and digital forensics, a speaker in almost every Spanish-speaking country, and a bug bounty hunter ranked among the top 100 of all time on several platforms.

DragonJAR is two things with one name. The company's own page, as read in November 2026, counts 25 years as a community and 14 as a company. The community came first: a blog, forums, video and, today, a chat server for hacking in Spanish, which Ekoparty calls one of the largest Spanish-speaking information security communities and a reference in the field. The company grew out of it and says that members of its team have figured in the world top 100 on the bug bounty platforms HackerOne, YesWeHack and Intigriti.

The choice of language is stated as policy, not as an accident of geography. The conference's site answers the question of language directly: every talk on the main stage is given in Spanish, by Spanish-speaking researchers with a proven record, with no simultaneous translation and no subtitles, so that technical knowledge arrives directly and with the context of the region. The announcement of the 2026 edition puts it in one line: original research, presented by whoever did it, in the language in which it was thought.

The conference. Before it there was the ACK Security Conference, which he co-founded and organized in Manizales in March 2012. The first DragonJAR Security Conference followed in 2013, with him as founder and organizer, and the 2014 edition ran from 8 to 10 May. By 2023, when it was held in Bogotá on 7 and 8 September, the Colombian press counted more than ten editions, speakers from more than 20 countries and more than 45,000 participants over the decade. It was in Bogotá again on 26 and 27 September 2024, and in Medellín for the twelfth edition on 10 and 11 September 2025 and for the thirteenth on 10 and 11 September 2026, at the Centro de Eventos El Tesoro, with more than 17 specialists from 8 countries, 14 original investigations, technical villages and a capture the flag (CTF) contest. The organization has announced a 2027 edition. The event, known as DragonJARCON, is long associated with Manizales, where the company keeps its offices.

The car research. In January 2014 he received an e-mail from the maker of his car that showed how much the manufacturer knew about his driving. The car carried a telematics unit, sold under the name ChevyStar, with its own 3G connection and its own telephone number, which offered remote locking and unlocking, lights and horn, location and speed alerts. The monthly message listed the distance driven, the top speed, the number of times the speed limit had been passed and the number of hard stops, and was built so that anyone curious could read them. He published the case on 20 January 2014 under the title Sé lo que hicieron el diciembre pasado, asking who may see a car's data, with what consent and with what security. As he wrote two years later, that article was only the tip of the iceberg: the e-mail led him to a much larger set of security problems in the vehicle's connected system, which he disclosed in a talk called Hackeando Carros en Latinoamérica, given at the Open Worldwide Application Security Project (OWASP) Latam Tour in Lima on 18 April 2015 and at the eleventh Ekoparty in Buenos Aires that October. A year later ESET's coverage of car hacking at Ekoparty cited his case, which exploited the car's integrated device, beside the work of Charlie Miller and Chris Valasek.

What that research argued is the point of the whole enterprise. The product was sold with cars in Latin America, and it was examined by someone who owned one. The best-known car hacking of those years, by Charlie Miller and Chris Valasek, was being presented at Black Hat and DEF CON. A region that only reads other people's findings learns about other people's products.

The rest of the record is long and public. His own list documents 71 appearances in 10 countries between 2008 and 2026, each linked to a source: security laboratories and ethical hacking techniques at the SECURINF events in Popayán in 2008 and 2009; forensic analysis of iOS devices at Ekoparty in 2011; penetration testing in the era after the personal computer at 8.8 in Santiago in 2012; a real banking malware robbery, told at several conferences in 2018; what nobody tells you before taking up bug bounty, in 2020, and a keynote on writing a bug bounty report at Ekoparty in 2021; red team exercises in 2022; and, from 2024, how generative artificial intelligence automates deception, the subject of his sessions at Ekoparty Miami and of a keynote at Hacker Halted in Atlanta in 2026. Ekoparty's biography adds the halls of fame he entered by reporting flaws responsibly, among them those of Harvard University, Netflix, Sony, Visa, Mastercard, AT&T, IBM, Yahoo!, General Motors and Alibaba.

The recognition. Ekoparty, the Buenos Aires conference, has given its Premio a la Trayectoria since its tenth year, 2014, to people whose work shaped the community; the first went to Gera Richarte. The 2022 award went to Restrepo, between Verónica Valeros in 2021 and the Latin American hacking pioneer known as Thonhy in 2023. Asked in 2023 why Colombia produces security talent, he pointed to creativity, and noted that many of the country's professionals end up hired abroad, leading technology companies.

The dates worth keeping: 2008 for the first documented talk; March 2012 for the ACK Security Conference in Manizales; 2013 for the first DragonJAR Security Conference; 20 January 2014 for the article on vehicle telemetry; 18 April 2015 and October 2015 for the car talk in Lima and Buenos Aires; 2022 for Ekoparty's award; and 10 and 11 September 2026 for the thirteenth DragonJARCON.

willian-caprino.def: One of the three organizers who created You Sh0t the Sheriff, and the person who has most often explained the event's history and its unusual format in public - a career of more than twenty years in Brazilian information technology and security.
willian-caprino.context: The YSTS founders describe the origin as a reaction: Brazilian security events were becoming either vendor showcases or purely technical gatherings, and they wanted the room where the two audiences argue with each other. Deliberately capping attendance was the mechanism. Caprino is the clearest example of the organiser-as-infrastructure that this scene runs on - people who keep an event alive for two decades while holding a full-time job elsewhere.

anchises-moraes.def: A Brazilian threat intelligence specialist who is one of the founders of Garoa Hacker Clube, Brazil's first hackerspace, where he holds the title of Supreme Chancellor; a founder and organizer of Security BSides São Paulo (BSidesSP); a former director and president of the Brazilian chapter of the Cloud Security Alliance (CSA); and author of the blog AnchisesLandia since 2005.
anchises-moraes.context: He is the connective tissue of the Brazilian scene rather than a researcher known for one finding: the hackerspace, the free community conference, the professional association chapters, the threat intelligence work and two decades of writing that documents the local calendar year by year. Communities need someone who keeps the record and introduces people to each other, and in Brazil that role has largely been his, which is why his blog is a primary source for the history of these events: his post of 25 November 2024 is where the H2HC succession was recorded, and his twice-yearly calendars are how much of the community plans its year.
anchises-moraes.depth:
Who he is. Anchises Moraes is a São Paulo security professional with, in his own account, more than 25 years in information security across small, medium and large companies. He studied computer science at the Institute of Mathematics and Statistics of the University of São Paulo (IME-USP) and took a postgraduate course in marketing at the Escola Superior de Propaganda e Marketing (ESPM), and he teaches on postgraduate courses. His importance to the Brazilian community is less a single technical contribution than the infrastructure he helped build and the record he keeps: a hackerspace, a community conference that now draws thousands, the professional association chapters he led, and a blog that has documented the scene since June 2005.

Threat intelligence. His career has run through threat intelligence. He worked at RSA and at VeriSign's iDefense cyber intelligence group as a threat intelligence specialist for Latin America, then at C6 Bank, where he led the threat intelligence team, was responsible for the bank's bug bounty programme and its cybersecurity research partnership with the Massachusetts Institute of Technology (MIT), and gave himself the title of Cyber Evangelist while running security culture and awareness for staff and customers. Since 2023 he has been Threat Intel Lead at Apura Cyber Intelligence. His recent talks follow the same line: at Mind The Sec on 16 September 2026 he spoke on what really turns threat intelligence into decisions, and at BSides Porto on 29 November 2025 on how Brazil's instant payment system reshaped the country's threat landscape.

Associations and standards. He was a director of the Brazilian chapter of the Information Systems Security Association (ISSA) and its president from 2008 to 2009, and has been director and president of the Brazilian chapter of the Cloud Security Alliance (CSA). He also volunteered on the information security, cybersecurity and privacy protection committee of the Brazilian standards body, the Associação Brasileira de Normas Técnicas (ABNT), committee CE 021.004.027, contributing to the creation and translation of ISO/IEC and ABNT NBR standards. He supports the Latin American women in cybersecurity community WOMCY as a He for She volunteer and sits as a counsellor of the non-profit Mente Binária.

Garoa Hacker Clube. Garoa's own history explains why no single person claims it. Discussion began in June 2009 in a Ning community; the idea was presented publicly at Campus Party in January 2010; the first in-person meeting took place on 15 July 2010 at the Polytechnic School of the University of São Paulo with support from its free software group PoliGNU; and at the end of August 2010 the club opened its first permanent space, a 12 square metre basement lent by the Casa da Cultura Digital, which the club describes as the first Brazilian hackerspace. A non-profit association was set up on 20 February 2011, and in February 2013 the club moved to much larger premises. Its FAQ says it was founded by about a dozen people, some of whom contributed more actively and became founders; Moraes is one, and he was its secretary for 2015 to 2016. Since 2016 he has held the title of Supreme Chancellor (Chanceler Supremo). The title is tongue in cheek but has one real function: the club has no official spokespeople and avoids institutional positions, and press contacts are handled by the Chanceler Supremo for practicality, while any collective position must be discussed openly and ratified by a council the members call the Conselho Manda Chuva.

BSidesSP. Security BSides São Paulo began in 2011 with a first edition held inside Garoa Hacker Clube, as part of the global Security BSides circuit, which runs in more than 60 countries under the motto of a conference from the community to the community. Moraes is one of its founders and organizers. Its growth is the clearest measure of what that work built. The 20th edition, on 17 and 18 May 2025, had 5,529 registrations and 2,725 people across two days, 2,307 of them on the Sunday, up from about 1,800 in 2024; it received 109 talk proposals for 32 slots, ran 17 themed villages and a capture-the-flag championship, and was staffed by 202 volunteers with 29 sponsors. The 21st edition, on 16 and 17 May 2026, marked 15 years. He is also among the founders and organizers of BRHueCon and of the 307 Temporary Security Conference, held in 2025.

The record-keeper. AnchisesLandia has been active since June 2005 and is the reference for much of what is known about the Brazilian scene's recent history. Twice a year he publishes a calendar of the events he considers most relevant; for 2026 he had mapped more than 40 before the year began. On 30 January 2010 he published a list of Brazilian security professionals on Twitter that grew past 700 profiles and was maintained until June 2023. He created and ran the InfoSec Arena at You Sh0t the Sheriff, an audience debate whose topics were submitted on Twitter and paper forms and drawn at random; at its second outing, in May 2011, certification and professional ethics were the most contested subjects. And when Rodrigo Rubira Branco left the organization of the Hackers to Hackers Conference (H2HC), it was on AnchisesLandia, on 25 November 2024, that the farewell letter was transcribed and the conference described as the backbone of the Brazilian security community.

bsides-sp.def: The São Paulo edition of the global Security BSides circuit - a free, community-organised conference on information security and hacker culture, run by working professionals, with talk tracks, villages, a capture-the-flag contest and a pre-event day of mini-trainings.
bsides-sp.context: It began as Conferencia O Outro Lado, hosted at Garoa Hacker Clube for the community around the invite-only YSTS, and grew into the largest free security event in the country. The pairing is the point: BSidesSP happens on the weekend before YSTS, so the people excluded from the closed room have a bigger open one - a deliberate answer to the access problem that invite-only events create, and the reason Brazil's scene has stayed open despite having an exclusive event at its centre.

hacker-scene.def: The community of a place: the people, meetings, boards, conferences, hackerspaces and shared history that make hacking a local culture rather than an individual hobby. Distinct from the Scene, which in release culture means the warez distribution world specifically.
hacker-scene.context: Scenes differ by what they organized around, and the differences persist for decades. The American scene formed around crews and rivalry and was shaped by prosecution; the German one organized as a formal association and ended up testifying before its constitutional court; the Australian one produced a definitive book instead of a legend; the Brazilian one grew out of civil-society networking and a fraud underground, and now runs one of the densest conference calendars anywhere. This site treats each as a subject in its own right rather than as footnotes to the American story.

lista-do-anchises.def: The roster of Brazilian and Portuguese information-security people and organizations that Anchises Moraes has maintained on his blog since January 2010 - started at 72 entries and grown past 770, with every addition dated in a public changelog at the foot of the post.
lista-do-anchises.context: It is the closest thing the Brazilian scene has to a census. Researchers, lawyers, forensic examiners, journalists, police, hackerspaces, conferences, CTF teams and vendors all sit in one alphabetical list, and the update log doubles as a timeline of when each part of the community appeared. Anchises states his criteria openly, marks the most active people in italics, and has removed profiles that turned into self-promotion - editorial judgement applied in public, which is what separates a curated record from a directory. For anyone researching the scene it is the correct starting point, precisely because it is one person's honest list rather than an institution's.

sandro-suffert.def: One of the earliest Brazilian security bloggers - his SSegurança blog compiled the first substantial index of Portuguese-language security blogs in 2008 - and a long-running figure in digital forensics and threat intelligence in Brazil.
sandro-suffert.context: His 2008 blog index and Anchises's 2010 profile list were the two documents that let the Brazilian community see itself for the first time: before them, practitioners knew their own city's people and nobody else's. That is a recurring pattern in this scene - the infrastructure that mattered most early on was not technical but bibliographic, built by people who decided to keep lists.

fabio-assolini.def: The Brazilian malware analyst who heads the Americas and Europe research of Kaspersky's Global Research and Analysis Team (GReAT), and whose published work is the main public record of how Brazilian banking fraud actually operates: boleto manipulation, modem and DNS hijacking, overlay attacks and the families that became known as the Tetrade.
fabio-assolini.context: His significance is documentary. Brazilian banking malware was for years a phenomenon everyone in the region experienced and almost nobody outside it could read about, because the analysis existed only in Portuguese or not at all. Publishing that research in English, with samples and technique names, is what turned a local nuisance into an internationally understood threat class, and it is why the rest of the world eventually recognized Brazilian crews as innovators rather than imitators.
fabio-assolini.depth:
Fabio Assolini joined Kaspersky's Global Research and Analysis Team (GReAT) in July 2009 to focus on Brazil, analysing viruses, attacks and above all the banking trojans that originate there and in the rest of Latin America; he was promoted to senior security researcher in November 2012 and holds a bachelor's degree in computer science. His Securelist author page now gives his title as head of the research centre for the Americas and Europe, Kaspersky's press office in March 2026 as head of the Americas and Europe units of GReAT, and the Brazilian site Canaltech in 2022 as director of GReAT for Latin America. The record he built is unusually network-shaped for a malware analyst: much of Brazilian banking fraud ran through DNS, home routers and payment slips before it ran through endpoints.

The 2011 posts set the pattern. On 30 August 2011 he reported Brazilian banking trojans aimed for the first time at banks in Spain and Portugal and at customers in Cape Verde, the timid first attempt at a global reach that Kaspersky's 2020 Tetrade report would later cite. On 7 November 2011 he described DNS cache poisoning at Brazilian internet service providers (ISPs): users opening Google, YouTube or local portals were told to install a 'Google Defence' plug-in that was a banking trojan, served alongside an exploit for an old Java runtime flaw, CVE-2010-4452 in the Common Vulnerabilities and Exposures (CVE) list. He noted that Brazil then had 73 million connected computers and that the large ISPs averaged three or four million customers each, so one poisoned cache could reach millions of people, and that the Federal Police had just arrested an ISP employee in the south accused of changing the provider's DNS cache for ten months to send every customer to phishing pages.

His best-known network paper, The Tale of One Thousand and One DSL Modems (1 October 2012), documented an attack running since 2011 with one firmware vulnerability, two malicious scripts and 40 malicious DNS servers across modems from six manufacturers, 4.5 million devices in all. The flaw, published in March 2011, was a cross-site request forgery (CSRF) in the modems' administration panel that disclosed the password and let the attacker change the DNS servers, and the affected devices shared a Broadcom chipset. He put the blame on the whole chain: users who never update modem firmware, manufacturers slow to fix, ISPs choosing old cheap models, and Anatel, Brazil's telecommunications agency, whose approval tests check that a modem works but not that it is secure. One seized server's log alone showed more than 14,000 victims.

The boleto work explained a fraud that reached people who never bank online. A boleto is a printed payment slip with a typeable ID line and a barcode; according to the Brazilian Central Bank it carried 21 per cent of all payments in 2011, and 18 per cent of Brazilian e-commerce used it in 2012. In Attacks against Boletos (26 September 2014), and in his Virus Bulletin 2014 talk P0wned by a barcode, he showed trojans, seen from April 2013, that rewrote the slip in the victim's browser as it was generated, first replacing both the ID line and the barcode so the payment went to the criminals' account, later changing only the line and inserting a space that made the barcode unreadable, so that the cashier had to type in the forged number. Newer samples encrypted their payloads the way GameOver Zeus did, which he read as a sign of cooperation with European gangs.

The same paper is also where he disputed a famous figure. In July 2014 RSA's researchers had estimated that boleto fraud might have stolen as much as 3.75 billion US dollars (8.6 billion reais), from 495,793 boletos and 192,227 victims found in criminal control panels. Assolini argued that the total counted every entry in the panels, including slips never paid, payments the banks blocked, test transactions by researchers and criminals and duplicates, averaging an implausible 16,000 reais per boleto, and that counting victims by unique IP address is unreliable in a country where most connections use dynamic addresses. Only the banks, he wrote, can give a real total, and the Brazilian Federation of Banks (FEBRABAN) had put all electronic fraud losses in its worst year, 2011, at 1.5 billion reais, about 680 million dollars.

Later reports widened the frame. Beaches, carnivals and cybercrime (11 November 2015) placed Brazil first in the world in 2014 for both financial malware attacks and phishing, with the local ChePro family second only to ZeuS, and traced techniques imported from Eastern Europe. Large-scale SIM swap fraud (11 April 2019), written with André Tenreiro of Mozambique's Computer Emergency Response Team (CERT-MZ), described one Brazilian gang that had swapped the subscriber identity module (SIM) cards of 5,000 victims, insiders at mobile operators paid 10 to 15 dollars per activated SIM, and the resulting advice to avoid SMS (Short Message Service) text messages as a second authentication factor. The Tetrade report of 14 July 2020, published by GReAT, named four Brazilian families going global, Guildma (also called Astaroth), Javali, Melcoz and Grandoreiro, the last, in Kaspersky's reading, sold as malware-as-a-service (ESET later disputed this) and the most widespread, with remote-control modules that include toggling a screen overlay over the bank's page. In March 2026 Kaspersky described GoPix, which he said the team had followed since 2023 and which had made 90,000 infection attempts, using memory-only implants, proxy auto-configuration (PAC) files to sit in the middle of browser traffic, and malicious Google advertisements to reach customers of Brazilian banks, Pix users and cryptocurrency holders.

In Brazil he is also a regular public voice. He spoke at the fifth You Sh0t the Sheriff in May 2011 on how data leaks were feeding local crime, and at the Fifth Congress on Cybercrime organized by the São Paulo State Federation of Commerce (FECOMERCIO) in August 2013, where the participants judged the new Carolina Dieckmann law too lenient to deter criminals. In 2022 he told Canaltech that Brazilian banking trojans are born internationalized to attack the neighbours, that Brazilian criminals want the password to steal the money now, that they were filling a gap left by European gangs moving to ransomware, and that Kaspersky had worked for years with the Federal Police and Interpol.

rodrigo-montoro.def: Brazilian researcher known as Sp0oKeR, long associated with intrusion detection and detection engineering, and the author of one of the two 2010 lists - his own roster of Brazilian security people on Twitter - that first mapped the community.
rodrigo-montoro.context: He belongs to the detection side of the field rather than the offensive one, which is under-represented in hacker history everywhere: the people who write the rules that catch the attack rarely get the conference legend treatment. His long presence in the Brazilian scene, and the fact that two independent practitioners felt the need to index the community in the same month of 2010, says something about how invisible the scene was to itself before that.

calendario-anchises.def: The calendar of Brazilian and international security events that Anchises Moraes publishes on his blog, AnchisesLandia: a commented list for each half of the year, published since at least 2011, a December preview of the year ahead and a yearly review of how the events went. The 2026 preview mapped more than forty events he considers the most relevant.
calendario-anchises.context: It is the working document of the Brazilian conference circuit: organizers check it for date collisions, speakers plan submissions from it, and it is one of the few places where the regional events (Juazeiro do Norte, Maceió, Natal, Aracaju, Belém, Salvador, Pindamonhangaba) appear next to São Paulo's. He states the filter openly, listing only what he judges relevant and good, with a preference for community and traditional events over commercial ones, which makes it a curated opinion rather than a directory. Its companion is a single-question page he keeps updated about the Hackers to Hackers Conference (H2HC), 'A H2HC foi cancelada?', linked from the calendar as 'Teremos H2HC neste ano?', which is its own comment on how conference scheduling works.
calendario-anchises.depth:
What it is. Every year Anchises Moraes, a Brazilian security professional and one of the organizers of Security BSides São Paulo, publishes on his blog the list of security events he considers the most relevant, in two posts a year, one for each half, with a short description of each event. Since December 2025 he has added a preview of the whole year: the post of 24 December 2025 announced that he had already mapped more than 40 events for 2026, counting only those he considers the most relevant, and asked readers to start planning their year. A third kind of post closes the cycle: the yearly review of how the events went, a frank and light-hearted assessment with awards, which he says he has written since 2011. A separate list covers the BSides conferences, which in Brazil went from five in 2025 to at least nine in 2026.

How far back it goes. The semester format is already visible in a post of 25 February 2011, a list of the main and largest Brazilian events of the first half of that year: the CNASI auditing and security congress in Rio de Janeiro and Brasília, a new Web Security Forum, the first SecureBrasil conference of the International Information System Security Certification Consortium, the seventeenth meeting of NIC.br's network security working group (GTS), the first Conferência O Outro Lado at the Garoa Hacker Clube, which became BSides São Paulo, and You Sh0t the Sheriff (YSTS). The blog's archive also has earlier posts on upcoming events, such as one on the events of December published in November 2009, but 2011 is when the twice-yearly lists and the yearly reviews settle into a series.

The filter. The lists are explicitly opinionated. In the first-semester post of 2026 he writes that he lists only events he finds interesting or relevant to the market or the security community and that, in his view, bring quality content, plus some large information technology (IT) events that also carry security content, such as The Developers Conference; unless stated otherwise, an event is in São Paulo. In the second-semester post he adds that he prefers community events and the most traditional ones and gives little importance to commercial events, preferring to support those he believes bring quality content. He is equally frank about what he leaves out: he confesses a prejudice against events with CISO (chief information security officer) in the name, which he suspects of selling sponsors access to executives, and lists a few for those who like them. That honesty is what makes the calendar useful: it is a recommendation, signed, rather than a database.

What the 2026 lists contained. The preview ran from Oxum Sec in Salvador on 31 January 2026, the first edition of an event organized by people from the Raul Hacker Clube, through Hack in Cariri in Juazeiro do Norte, BSides Rio de Janeiro and Tosconf in Campinas on the same day in March, 0x3 Hacker Conference in Maceió, Fortalsec in Fortaleza and BSides Floripa, CryptoRave, Security BSides São Paulo on 16 and 17 May and YSTS on 18 May, DunaSec in Natal, BSides Recife and BSides Vitória, Cajusec in Aracaju, the fourteenth Fórum Brasileiro de CSIRTs at the end of July, bxsec in Santos, Hack'a Valley in Pindamonhangaba, the 26th SBSeg in Armação dos Búzios from 1 to 4 September, Mind The Sec, XibéSec in Belém and BSides João Pessoa, Latinoware in Foz do Iguaçu, Nullbyte in Salvador on 7 November, BSides Brasília, BHack in Belo Horizonte on 28 and 29 November and the 307 Temporary Security Conference on 5 and 6 December, beside the commercial Security Leaders tour and the banking events FebrabanSEC and Febraban Tech. The international section lists what Brazilians travel to: RSA Conference, the annual conference of the Forum of Incident Response and Security Teams (FIRST), BSidesLV, Black Hat, DEF CON, Ekoparty, 8.8 and BSides Lisbon. By August 2026 the second-semester post already carried a preliminary list for 2027.

Collisions, and one recurring question. The calendar's most practical use is spotting clashes, and the posts say so. In 2026, with many holidays, a World Cup and an election in the same year, he noted SecOps Summit in Porto Alegre and FebrabanSEC on the same days in March, Fortalsec and BSides Floripa both on 25 April, and BSides Fortaleza set in the week of Black Hat and DEF CON, warning that such clashes cost events speakers, attendees and sponsors. His review of 2024 had already named the year's worst choice as having to pick between BSides Vitória and BSides São Paulo, and between BHack and Nullbyte. The running joke is the Hackers to Hackers Conference (H2HC): after the 2025 edition was cancelled, he kept asking whether there would be an H2HC in 2026, wrote in May that nobody knew because no date had been announced despite a promise of the first half of the year, pointed to the 307 Conference on 5 and 6 December, and maintains a one-question page, 'A H2HC foi cancelada?', which he updates when there is news.

What it is not. It is not the only calendar: the posts themselves point readers to InfoSecMap for events worldwide, the Security Leaders roadmap, speakfy and the event calendars of Hekate and Mente Binária. It is not neutral either, and does not try to be; the yearly awards include categories such as best events, biggest surprise, worst clash and best venue. What it adds is continuity and judgement: the same person, an organizer himself, recording the Brazilian calendar every year for over a decade and a half, with the regional events from Juazeiro do Norte to Pindamonhangaba listed beside the São Paulo ones, which is why so much of the community plans its year by it.

nullbyte-con.def: The Nullbyte Security Conference is an annual hacker conference in Salvador, Bahia, run by volunteers on a non-profit basis and devoted to technical, mostly offensive security research; it holds one day each November, marked its tenth anniversary in 2024, met on 7 November 2026 and is announced for 6 November 2027.
nullbyte-con.context: Bahia is one of the clearest counter-examples to the assumption that Brazilian security lives in the southeast. Salvador's community sustains Nullbyte, a second annual event, HackBahia, and since January 2026 a third, Oxum Sec, organized by people from the city's hackerspace, the Raul Hacker Clube; in a country where most technical work is concentrated in a couple of states, that is an achievement of organizing rather than of funding. Nullbyte is the technical one: a single day of talks on attack techniques and research, small enough that speakers and audience mix, and ranked by the calendar's best-known chronicler, Anchises Moraes, with Belo Horizonte's BHack and São Paulo's Hackers to Hackers Conference (H2HC) as an event for the most technical public in the country.
nullbyte-con.depth:
What it is. Nullbyte is a one-day conference held in Salvador each November, organized by volunteers without profit, whose stated purpose, in Anchises Moraes's description after attending, is simply to create a space for exchanging security knowledge and so foster a community of researchers. Its tone is set by its own site, which announces the next edition as the Pwn Party Syndicate inviting the visitor to a true hacker conference and takes as its epigraph the closing lines of The Mentor's hacker manifesto, the passage that ends with the line that we are all alike. The content follows: talks on attack, intrusion and defence techniques, given by researchers rather than vendors. Tickets for the 2027 edition were on sale at 250 reais in the Hacker category and 1,000 reais for a personal sponsor, with a joke tier for cybersecurity digital influencers.

Its size and history. In 2019 Moraes described the sixth edition, held on Saturday 9 November 2019, as a small event of about 100 participants with excellent technical content: seven talks on the programme, a surprise talk by Maycon Vitalli at the end, and a short debate. He placed it in a small family of Brazilian events built around offensive research and the sharing of technical work, which he listed as Jampasec in João Pessoa, DarkWaves in Natal, Alligator and BWCon in Recife and, above all, the Hackers to Hackers Conference (H2HC). In 2024 Nullbyte held a commemorative tenth-anniversary edition, which its archive marks as ten years. Recent editions were held on 8 November 2025 and 7 November 2026, and the organizers have already announced 6 November 2027; the venue description on the site speaks of a twelfth edition in the art cinema of a museum in Salvador's Vitória district.

Hacker culture beyond security. The weekend Moraes described in 2019 had a second day: on Sunday 10 November the Raul Hacker Club, Salvador's hackerspace, hosted Dumont Fest, the first national meeting of Brazilian hackerspaces, with people from Mandacaru in Feira de Santana, Jerimum in Natal, Oxe in Maceió, Garoa in São Paulo and the Raul itself, plus someone planning a hackerspace in Sergipe. He presented the two days as complementary sides of the culture: the technical side, where hacking means information security, and the community side, concerned with technological education and inclusion. The same Raul community later launched Oxum Sec, whose first edition opened the 2026 calendar on 31 January, with a strong focus on supporting the local security community; Moraes's preliminary 2027 list already includes Oxum HC for 30 January 2027.

Its place in the calendar. Moraes, who has reviewed the Brazilian events of each year since 2011, describes Nullbyte as one of the most important events of the community, held every year in Salvador, with excellent technical talks and participation by the leading researchers of the Brazilian community. In his review of 2024 he rated BHack and Nullbyte with H2HC and BSides São Paulo for technical quality, listed Nullbyte with H2HC and BHack under the most technical audience and with BHack, BSides Vitória and BSides João Pessoa among the best events outside the Rio and São Paulo axis, and named it, with DEF CON and H2HC, among the top hacker events that should have the printed edition of Phrack on hand. The same review recorded the year's worst scheduling clash: BHack in Belo Horizonte and Nullbyte in Salvador on the same weekend, forcing people who wanted to attend or speak at both to choose.

The Bahian circuit. Salvador now carries more than one community event. HackBahia, a security community event in the city, was held on 4 October 2025 and is listed for 25 September 2027; Oxum Sec opened 2026; the commercial Security Leaders tour stopped in Salvador on 10 September 2026; and the first BSides in Bahia, in Porto Seguro, was scheduled for 5 December 2026. That density, in a state far from the São Paulo and Rio de Janeiro axis where most Brazilian security events have historically been concentrated, is the point the conference makes simply by existing.

Why events like it matter. Moraes's own explanation in 2019 is the best one: regional events help build and keep a local community of security researchers, encouraging the study of offensive security, and they let people present and meet without travelling to São Paulo. Nullbyte does this in the format that suits a technical community of a few hundred people: a single day, one main room, an opening in the morning and a close in the evening, research talks, and a culture that takes the hacker manifesto at its word. It sits alongside BHack in Belo Horizonte as the pair of regional conferences most often cited for technical depth, and is one of the events that make the Brazilian scene a national one rather than a São Paulo one.

tosconf.def: Tosconf is the annual unconference of the Laboratório Hacker de Campinas (LHC), a hackerspace in Campinas, São Paulo state: a one-day, volunteer-run community event held in the hackerspace itself since 2012, open to any topic, with editions numbered from zero and a name that pokes fun at conference production values.
tosconf.context: Tosconf is the Brazilian scene's joke at the expense of its own professionalization, and it works as a release valve. As events acquire sponsors, badges, expo halls and executive tracks, something has to hold the space for the talk nobody would accept elsewhere and the demo that might not work. The Laboratório Hacker de Campinas holds it in its own building, calls it an unconference, puts information security next to woodworking, brewing and astronomy, and numbers its editions the way a programmer indexes an array. Calling that space shoddy on purpose is a very precise piece of community self-awareness.
tosconf.depth:
What it is. The organizers describe Tosconf as the annual unconference (desconferência in Portuguese) of the Laboratório Hacker de Campinas (LHC): an eclectic event that invites people from the community, from any field, culture and level of skill, to share what they do and to celebrate the spirit of hacker culture. There is practically no restriction on subjects or formats so long as they respect the hackerspace's code of conduct, and the topics its site lists from past years run from electronics, computing and data security to brewing, woodworking, gardening, open data and mechanics. The audience it names is just as mixed: professionals, amateurs, students, researchers and hobbyists. It lasts one day, and every edition so far has fallen on a Saturday; the 2026 edition opened its doors at 08:00 and ran from 08:30 to 18:00, with talks in an upstairs room and workshops in the garage.

The host. The LHC describes itself as a hackerspace in Campinas, in the state of São Paulo, that offers an open, community space where people develop their own projects and bring their communities together, in electronics, robotics, mechanics, computing, games, cooking, the arts or whatever the space allows. It has an electronics laboratory, a woodshop, a technical library, metalworking and brewing equipment, 3D printing and computer numerical control (CNC) machining. All of it is kept up voluntarily by its members, who pay for it and do the administration and maintenance themselves; members have access around the clock, and anyone else can visit when a member is there. Its focus is in-person meetings, and with few exceptions its events are free. Tosconf is the largest of those events, and it happens inside the building: the early programmes allocated sessions to rooms called the Garage, the Studio, the Cave and the Kitchen.

The name and the numbering. The name joins tosca, Portuguese for crude or shoddy, to conf. The numbering is a programmer's joke kept up for over a decade: editions are written as array elements, Tosconf[0] on 26 May 2012, Tosconf[1] on 8 June 2013 and Tosconf[2] on 31 May 2014. After a long gap, the fourth edition was planned for 2020 and postponed because of the COVID-19 pandemic; the 2023 site announced the return in person with Tosconf[3] on 18 March 2023, followed by Tosconf[4] on 23 March 2024, Tosconf[5] on 22 March 2025 and Tosconf[6] on 28 March 2026. The zero-based index produces exactly the off-by-one confusion it invites: the 2024 site calls Tosconf[4] the fifth edition, the 2026 ticket page calls Tosconf[6] the seventh, and the 2026 home page, with text carried over from 2025, still says sixth. The 2014 programme even had a slot titled void *atividade = NULL, a null pointer in C as the name of a session.

What gets presented. The programmes show the range better than any description. The 2013 edition had a lockpicking introduction given by a member of São Paulo's Garoa Hacker Clube, a talk on why your internet is slow, wiretapping from the bottom up, retroprogramming, beer, a coding dojo, building apps for Firefox OS, and building amplifiers and guitars, closing with lightning talks. In 2014 the talks went from Linux kernel modules, drivers and udev, and Go for websockets, to using a cheap software-defined radio (RTL-SDR) to follow air traffic control, mechanical retrocomputing with the slide rule, white-hat hacking, hacktivism, and forging an axe by hand. In 2023 there were astronomy kits, querying public datasets with Structured Query Language (SQL), open-source first-person-view (FPV) drones, the Linux graphics stack, sound on an ESP32 running NuttX, self-hosting, DDoS (distributed denial of service) handling, application security, the reverse engineering of the game Another World, bonsai and kombucha. In 2025 the morning opened with sizing photovoltaic systems, the PHP language ecosystem, slide rules again and the programmable input/output (PIO) blocks of the Raspberry Pi Pico. According to the 2013 site, the first edition in 2012 drew developers, information security researchers and what it called mythical figures of computing.

How it is run. Tosconf is organized by volunteers, members of the LHC or not, who handle the call for papers (publicity, review and building the agenda) along with everything else on the day; the 2023 site asked for more of them so that nobody would be overloaded. Tickets are issued through the LHC's own pretix instance in batches with limited places, and the 2024 edition sold out. The 2026 ticket covered every talk and workshop, coffee and a lunch snack, with drinks sold separately. The event is not sponsor-free in principle: the 2024 site had a sponsors section, and in 2025 it published a sponsorship letter and named a supporter. What keeps it small is the format and the building, not a rule.

In the Brazilian circuit. Anchises Moraes, whose annual calendar is the working map of Brazilian security events, went to tosconf[0] on Saturday 26 May 2012, the LHC's first edition, found it well organized with several interesting talks, and wrote up a steganography talk by Vinícius Berardi; a year later he listed the 8 June 2013 edition among the security events worth visiting. The Learn article on Latin American security conferences places it in the regional circuit beside BHack in Belo Horizonte, Nullbyte in Salvador and CryptoRave in São Paulo, and the article on the Brazilian hacker scene describes the hackerspaces it grows out of. Garoa Hacker Clube in São Paulo is its nearest sibling.

Why it matters. The large Brazilian events are now professional conferences with sponsors, villages, career tracks and executive audiences, and they do that job well. Tosconf keeps the older meaning of hacking in view: curiosity across fields, where a talk on denial-of-service handling sits between a kombucha workshop and a radio receiver tracking aircraft, and where an unfinished project is a reason to present rather than a reason to wait. The joke in the name is aimed at production values, not at the content.

sbseg.def: SBSeg, the Brazilian Symposium on Cybersecurity (Simpósio Brasileiro de Cibersegurança), formerly the Brazilian Symposium on Information and Computational Systems Security, is the annual peer-reviewed academic security conference of the Brazilian Computer Society (SBC), held since 2001 in a different city each year; its 26th edition ran from 1 to 4 September 2026 in Armação dos Búzios.
sbseg.context: It is where Brazilian security research goes through peer review: university groups in cryptography, network and systems security, forensics and privacy present there, and so does applied work such as the honeypot measurements of the national incident response team, CERT.br, whose papers have appeared in its proceedings. The gap between it and the practitioner conferences is narrower in Brazil than in many countries: since 2025 the symposium has an industry track, its programme includes a capture-the-flag (CTF) contest whose 2026 coordinators included CERT.br's general manager, and the same people circulate between it, the Fórum Brasileiro de CSIRTs (the yearly meeting of Brazil's computer security incident response teams) and the community events. That overlap is one of the healthier features of the Brazilian scene.
sbseg.depth:
What it is. SBSeg describes itself as the largest academic event in Brazil in cybersecurity and the country's main scientific forum for information and systems security. It is held annually by the Sociedade Brasileira de Computação (SBC), the non-profit scientific society of Brazilian computing founded in July 1978, under the responsibility of one of the SBC's Special Committees, the Comissão Especial de Cibersegurança (CESeg); the committee was created in 2004 as the Special Committee on Information and Computational Systems Security and keeps a discussion list, seg-l. Until recently the symposium's name followed the committee's: Simpósio Brasileiro em Segurança da Informação e de Sistemas Computacionais. The current name, Simpósio Brasileiro de Cibersegurança, is used on the 2025 and 2026 sites, while the society's digital library still lists it in English as the Brazilian Symposium on Information and Computational Systems Security, and many in the community still call it by the old name.

History and standing. The symposium has run every year since 2001, with 25 editions between 2001 and 2025, and moves to a different city each time, usually hosted by a university's computing department: the recent list runs from Curitiba (2012), Manaus (2013), Belo Horizonte (2014), Florianópolis (2015), Niterói (2016), Brasília (2017), Natal (2018) and São Paulo (2019) to Petrópolis (2020), Belém (2021), Santa Maria (2022), Juiz de Fora (2023), São José dos Campos (2024) and Foz do Iguaçu (2025). In Brazil's evaluation system for academic venues, run by the federal agency CAPES, it is rated Qualis A4, which matters to the graduate students and researchers who publish there. The 2025 edition, from 1 to 4 September at a resort in Foz do Iguaçu, celebrated the silver jubilee with 424 registrations and 419 recorded participants and added, for the first time, a workshop on quantum cybersecurity (WQuSec), a workshop on ethics in cybersecurity and an industry forum and track, alongside the third Women in Cybersecurity session and a fourth hackathon run with the Hackers do Bem programme.

How it is organized. The scientific core is the main track, which in 2026 called for original, unpublished research in two main tracks, cryptography, and security of computer systems and communication networks, over a long list of topics: applied cryptography and cryptanalysis, cryptocurrencies and distributed consensus, malware analysis, auditing and risk, forensics, surveillance and censorship, disinformation, cybersecurity education and ethics, social engineering, human-centred security, security and privacy in machine learning, generative artificial intelligence and large language models in security, hardware security, intrusion detection and response, cloud, Internet of Things and vehicular network security. Around it sit short courses, invited talks, a tools exhibition (the Salão de Ferramentas), a thesis and dissertation contest (CTDSeg), an undergraduate research workshop (WTICG) and satellite workshops, which in 2026 included the sixteenth workshop on digital identity management (WGID), workshops on artificial intelligence (WCIA) and quantum security (WQuSec), and hands-on workshops run by companies. The proceedings are published every year in the SBC's open digital library, SBC OpenLib (SOL).

The 2026 edition. The 26th SBSeg took place in person from 1 to 4 September 2026 at the Ferradura Resort in Armação dos Búzios, about 170 km from Rio de Janeiro, a venue for up to 500 participants, organized by the Universidade Federal Fluminense (UFF), with Dianne Medeiros and Diogo Mattos as general coordinators and Edelberto Franco Silva (UFJF) and Cíntia Borges Margi (USP) coordinating the programme committee. It added a capture-the-flag (CTF) contest, an industry track coordinated by Marcos Simplicio (USP) and Charles Miers (UDESC), and the thesis contest; the CTF was coordinated by Aldri dos Santos (UFMG), Diego Kreutz (UNIPAMPA) and Cristine Hoepers of CERT.br, the national computer emergency response team (CERT). Its supporters included the Brazilian Internet Steering Committee (CGI.br), the Brazilian Network Information Center (NIC.br) and the National Education and Research Network (RNP), and the sponsors ran workshops of their own, a sign that the academic event now openly courts the security industry.

Where practice meets research. The link with the operational community is concrete. In 2013, at the 13th SBSeg in Manaus, João Ceron, Klaus Steding-Jessen and Cristine Hoepers presented an anatomy of abuse against Session Initiation Protocol (SIP) servers, built from the voice over Internet Protocol (VoIP) attack attempts captured by a network of honeypots deployed in Brazil, the kind of measurement CERT.br runs as part of its national incident response work. The traffic runs both ways: in 2021 the CESeg coordinator, Michele Nogueira of the Universidade Federal do Paraná, presented a panorama of the Brazilian academic cybersecurity community at the Grupo de Trabalho em Segurança de Redes (GTS), the network security working group meeting run by NIC.br, describing SBSeg as the main forum among researchers, industry, students and practitioners and the national science and technology institute for cybersecurity, a network of universities and the Army's cyber defence centre led by the State University of Campinas (UNICAMP). Anchises Moraes, whose calendar the community plans its year by, lists SBSeg every year as the main academic security event in the country.

How it differs from its neighbours. Unlike the Hackers to Hackers Conference (H2HC), BSides São Paulo or Nullbyte, SBSeg is a refereed venue: papers are submitted ahead of the event, reviewed by a programme committee and published with page numbers in proceedings that count for academic careers. Unlike the Fórum Brasileiro de CSIRTs, which CERT.br organizes for incident responders under Traffic Light Protocol rules, it is public by design. And because it moves through Brazilian university cities, it comes within reach of students far from São Paulo. For a practitioner the reasons to read it are its tools exhibition, its industry track and the measurement papers on the Brazilian internet; for a student, it is often the first place to present research. The numbers worth remembering are 2001 for the first edition, the first week of September in 2025 and 2026, and 26 editions by 2026.

forum-brasileiro-de-csirts.def: The annual meeting of Brazil's computer security incident response teams (CSIRTs), organized since 2012 by CERT.br, the national CSIRT of last resort run by the Brazilian Network Information Center (NIC.br); its fourteenth edition, in July 2026 in São Paulo, drew 860 participants and was followed by the seventh workshop on the MISP Threat Sharing Platform (MISP).
forum-brasileiro-de-csirts.context: This is the part of the calendar nobody outside the field notices and everybody depends on: the people who answer when a bank, a hospital or a university is compromised, comparing notes once a year. Incident response only works if teams trust each other enough to share indicators before an incident is public, and that trust is built at events like this one rather than through tooling. The Forum makes the trust explicit: every talk carries a Traffic Light Protocol (TLP) label telling the room how far its content may travel, from TLP:CLEAR, publishable, to TLP:RED, for those present only.
forum-brasileiro-de-csirts.depth:
What it is. The organizers describe the Fórum Brasileiro de CSIRTs as an event dedicated to building community and to discussing how organizations stand up to security incidents. It is run by the Centro de Estudos, Resposta e Tratamento de Incidentes de Segurança no Brasil (CERT.br), which was created in June 1997, under the name NBSO, on the initiative of the Brazilian Internet Steering Committee (CGI.br), and describes itself as a computer security incident response team (CSIRT) with national responsibility of last resort: its mission is to raise the security and incident handling capacity of networks connected to the internet in Brazil, which includes helping new CSIRTs get established. CERT.br is maintained by the Brazilian Network Information Center (NIC.br), the non-profit that runs the .br domain, distributes Internet Protocol (IP) addresses and registers autonomous systems in the country. The Forum is free; each event has its own registration through NIC.br's course and event portal, and sponsorship comes in platinum, gold and silver tiers. The audience is the incident handlers themselves: bank, government, telecom, hospital and university teams, and the vendors and researchers who work with them.

How it started, and the editions.
