The first Forum was held on 26 March 2012, the day before the 2012 Symposium of the Forum of Incident Response and Security Teams (FIRST), a joint event that ran from 27 to 30 March. Its programme set the pattern: a special talk by Robin Ruefle of the CERT Coordination Center (CERT/CC) on the evolution of incident management worldwide, the maturity of organizations and current trends; reports on the state of incident handling in different sectors; and case studies submitted by the Brazilian incident response community, with simultaneous translation between Portuguese and English. It then ran every year to 2020: the eighth edition took place on 9 and 10 September 2019, and the ninth moved online, on Zoom Webinar on 9 and 10 September 2020 with shortened sessions, followed by a MISP workshop on 11 September. Its invited speaker that year was Don Stikvoort, then chair of the FIRST special interest group that maintains TLP, co-author of the CERT/CC CSIRT handbook of 2003 and lead author of the Security Incident Management Maturity Model (SIM3), who with Klaus-Peter Kossakowski had started European CSIRT cooperation in 1993. The event's list of past editions has no 2021; it resumed in 2022, and the fourteenth edition took place on 28 and 29 July 2026 at the Amcham Business Center in São Paulo, with the seventh MISP workshop on 30 July. NIC.br reported 860 participants and said the event grows every year.

The TLP rule. All talks at the Forum and its workshops carry a sharing expectation in FIRST's Traffic Light Protocol, and the agenda prints the label next to each title, with the instruction always to respect the label on the speaker's slide and on the screens in the room. CERT.br adheres to the FIRST standard, whose current version, TLP 2.0, has been authoritative since August 2022. Its four labels are TLP:RED, for the eyes and ears of individual recipients only, which in a meeting means those present; TLP:AMBER, limited disclosure on a need-to-know basis within the recipient's organization and its clients, with TLP:AMBER+STRICT restricting it to the organization alone; TLP:GREEN, shareable within the community but not through publicly accessible channels; and TLP:CLEAR, with no limit on disclosure. The labels stay in English in any language, and the standard notes that TLP is distinct from the Chatham House Rule, which lets participants use what they hear without revealing who said it. The 2026 agenda used all five markings, and only some talks published slides. That is what makes the Forum different from a public conference: a team can describe an intrusion it is still handling, under TLP:RED, to the people most likely to see the same attacker next.

What is discussed. The 2026 programme, as NIC.br summarized it, shows the range. Cristine Hoepers, CERT.br's general manager, argued that artificial intelligence widens the old asymmetry between an attacker who needs one flaw and defenders who must cover them all, and that teams should prioritize Common Vulnerabilities and Exposures (CVE) entries by real exposure and exploitability, with the Stakeholder-Specific Vulnerability Categorization (SSVC) framework, rather than by severity scores alone; citing the 2026 Verizon Data Breach Investigations Report, she said vulnerability exploitation had overtaken credential abuse as the leading initial access vector in breaches. A Federal Police expert showed a malware triage pipeline built from free reverse-engineering tools such as Ghidra and JADX linked to large language models through the Model Context Protocol (MCP), with a human validating the output. Other talks covered illicit lookup panels that reuse leaked personal data; network flow telemetry (NetFlow and IPFIX) as evidence for the incident rules of Brazil's National Monetary Council and Central Bank; fraud through governance gaps and Pix interfaces; a hospital's method joining incident response, digital forensics and the General Data Protection Law (LGPD); privileged account protection at the Federal Court of Accounts (TCU); Anatel, the telecom regulator, on uncertified TV boxes carrying the BadBox 2.0 malware and forming botnets for distributed denial of service (DDoS) and fraud; and ransomware as an ecosystem. The published slides include talks from the National Education and Research Network (RNP), the federal government's incident response centre CTIR Gov (Centro de Prevenção, Tratamento e Resposta a Incidentes Cibernéticos de Governo) and the cyber laboratory of the Brazilian Federation of Banks (Febraban).

The MISP workshop. MISP, which NIC.br calls the MISP Threat Sharing Platform, describes itself as an open-source threat intelligence platform and a set of open standards for sharing it: similar organizations are often targeted by the same threat actor, so sharing with and receiving from trusted partners is the key to fast detection, and the platform adds tagging, feeds, visualization and integration with other tools, with free software and open data formats and application programming interface (API). It is developed at the Computer Incident Response Center Luxembourg (CIRCL). The seventh workshop, on 30 July 2026, was a hands-on session on sharing indicators of compromise (IoCs) and threat data, led by Luciano Righetti of the MISP development team, with reports of practical use from the federal data processing service Serpro and from Vision Cybersecurity. For a Brazilian team the workshop is the practical half of the Forum: the talks build the trust, and MISP is the plumbing through which the indicators then move.

Why it matters. Incident response is a team sport played between organizations that are otherwise competitors or strangers, and a CSIRT's most valuable asset is the list of people at other teams it can call at three in the morning. The Forum is where that list is built in Brazil. Its host has spent nearly three decades helping such teams exist: Hoepers, at CERT.br since 1999, was named to FIRST's Incident Response Hall of Fame on 10 June 2024, at the FIRST conference in Fukuoka, for pioneering work establishing and supporting CSIRTs around the world, the first woman so honoured. The Forum is the national counterpart of FIRST's own meetings, and its TLP discipline, its case studies from Brazilian banks, regulators and hospitals, and its pairing with a workshop on sharing tools make it the operational end of a security calendar otherwise dominated by commercial conferences.

bsides-brasil.def: The constellation of Security BSides conferences held across Brazil - São Paulo, Rio de Janeiro, Recife, Florianópolis, Vitória, João Pessoa, Brasília, Fortaleza, Porto Alegre and Curitiba among them - each free, locally organized, and part of the global BSides circuit.
bsides-brasil.context: BSides was designed to be forkable: any community can run one, which is why a country the size of Brazil ended up with a dozen rather than one. The effect is decentralization of the thing that usually centralizes - a student in Recife or Vitória can reach a real security conference without a flight to São Paulo. Read next to the older single-city events, the circuit is the clearest evidence that the Brazilian scene's answer to concentration has been replication rather than expansion.

307conf.def: A São Paulo security conference whose name declares its own impermanence - 307 is the HTTP status code for a temporary redirect - held in December with villages and a community programme.
307conf.context: The joke carries a real idea. Most conferences are built to become institutions, and the cost of that ambition is the succession problem that eventually threatens all of them. An event that announces itself as temporary is free to exist for exactly as long as its organizers want to run it, and to stop without the stopping being a failure. Whether that is wisdom or self-fulfilling prophecy is the kind of argument this scene enjoys having out loud.

linux-kernel.def: The operating-system kernel Linus Torvalds began in 1991, now developed by thousands of contributors from competing companies: monolithic in architecture, released on a fixed cadence of nine to ten weeks, with selected versions carrying years of long-term support.
linux-kernel.context: Two properties explain its reach. Its licence, the GNU General Public License (GPL) version 2, obliges distributors of modified kernels to publish their changes, which makes upstreaming cheaper than maintaining a private fork, so competitors cooperate out of self-interest. And its hardest rule is that userspace must not break: internal interfaces churn freely, but a program that ran yesterday must run tomorrow. Almost everything except the desktop runs on it: servers, phones, routers, cars, industrial controllers and every machine on the supercomputer top list.
linux-kernel.depth:
What it is. Linux is a kernel, the privileged core of an operating system. Architecturally it is monolithic, and that was controversial from the start. On 29 January 1992 Andrew Tanenbaum, the author of MINIX, posted LINUX is obsolete to comp.os.minix, explaining that in a monolithic system the whole operating system, process management, memory management, the file system and the rest, runs as one program in kernel mode, that microkernels which move most of that into separate processes had won the argument among operating system designers, and that Linux was a monolithic style system and a giant step back into the 1970s. Linux stayed monolithic. Its drivers belong in the kernel tree itself, and the ones developed outside it hook in through an internal module application programming interface (API) that the project explicitly does not keep stable.

Where it came from. Torvalds, posting from the University of Helsinki, asked comp.os.minix for the POSIX (Portable Operating System Interface) standard on 3 July 1991. On 25 August 1991, at 20:57 GMT (Greenwich Mean Time), he posted What would you like to see most in minix?: he was doing a free operating system, just a hobby, won't be big and professional like gnu, for 386 and 486 AT clones, brewing since April, with bash 1.08 and gcc 1.40 already ported, free of any MINIX code, not portable because it used 386 task switching, and probably never going to support anything but AT hard disks. In his own 1992 recollection, the 0.01 sources went up on nic.funet.fi around the middle of September 1991, not yet runnable and mostly a token gesture to arl, who had set up the Linux directory there, and 0.02 was announced on 5 October 1991 as free minix-like kernel sources for 386-AT. The kernel now runs on every one of the 500 systems on the June 2026 TOP500 list of supercomputers.

The licence and why it matters. The kernel is provided under the GNU General Public License version 2 only, GPL-2.0, with an explicit exception for system calls, the Linux-syscall-note, as the COPYING file and the kernel's licensing rules state. Section 3 of GPLv2 allows anyone to ship the kernel in object code, inside a router, a phone or a car, only with the complete corresponding source code or a written offer of it valid for at least three years. A vendor that modifies the kernel must therefore publish the modification anyway, and once the code is public the cheapest way to maintain it is to get it merged upstream, where everyone else keeps it working. That economic pull, rather than altruism, is why companies that compete everywhere else contribute to the same tree. The version 2 only choice also means the kernel did not move to GPLv3.

The release cycle. Torvalds maintains the mainline tree. After each release comes a two-week merge window in which new features land, then about seven weeks of bug fixing with a weekly release candidate, rc7 usually being the last, so a new mainline kernel appears every nine to ten weeks. Version numbers carry no meaning beyond order: the major number is increased when the minor one starts looking too big, and the old odd-even scheme, in which 2.1, 2.3 and 2.5 were development series, ended after 2.6. Once released, a mainline kernel becomes a stable series that receives backported fixes, usually weekly, until the next one supersedes it, unless it is chosen as a longterm kernel. On 12 November 2026 kernel.org listed mainline 7.4-rc2, stable 7.3.4, 7.2 at end of life, and six longterm series maintained by Greg Kroah-Hartman and Sasha Levin: 6.18 and 6.12 with projected end of life in December 2028, 6.6 and 6.1 in December 2027, and 5.15 and 5.10 in December 2026. A longterm kernel normally starts with a two-year projection that is extended only if the industry helps support it, and the choice depends on features, distribution and device-maker demand and maintainer workload; LWN expected 7.3, released on 18 October 2026, to be the next.

Who writes it. The 7.3 cycle, according to LWN's statistics, was the first in the project's history to exceed 20,000 commits, 18,765 of them non-merge, adding nearly 920,000 lines and removing about 270,000. They came from 3,021 developers, well past the record of 2,652 set one release earlier, and from 232 identifiable employers, the most active by changesets being AMD, Intel, Google, Qualcomm and Red Hat, with about a fifth of changesets from contributors whose employer was unknown. LWN noted that the cycle was abundantly fuelled by contributions assisted by large language models.

The rule that keeps users. The kernel documentation defines a regression as an application or practical use case that worked with one kernel and works worse or not at all with a newer one built with a similar configuration, and its no regressions rule forbids that; a developer who causes one by accident is expected to fix it quickly. The rule is precise about scope. Developers may change any aspect of the kernel, including interfaces and binary interfaces to userland, as long as no existing application breaks, and the rule covers only interfaces offered to userland, not kernel-internal ones such as the module API that out-of-tree drivers hook into. The stated purpose is that users feel safe updating rather than staying on series that are abandoned or more than a year and a half old. The companion document on driver interfaces makes the other half explicit: there is no stable internal API, the system call interface is the one that is kept, and programs built for kernels older than 0.9 still ran on 2.6, so the way to a driver that keeps working is to get it into the main tree.

The flood of vulnerability identifiers. In February 2024 the kernel project became a Common Vulnerabilities and Exposures (CVE) Numbering Authority (CNA), able to assign CVE identifiers for Linux itself. Its documented policy explains the volume that followed: because almost any kernel bug might be exploitable and exploitability is rarely evident when a fix is written, the assignment team is deliberately cautious and gives a CVE to any bugfix it identifies as potentially security-relevant in the stable releases. CVEs are assigned only after a fix is in a stable tree, tracked by the commit of the original fix, never for unfixed issues or for versions the stable team no longer supports; only the maintainers of the affected subsystem may dispute one; CVEs that other parties assign against supported kernels are to be treated as invalid; and whether a given CVE applies to a given system is explicitly left to the user. Greg Kroah-Hartman's own figures, published around April 2025, counted 4,451 kernel CVEs in 2024 and an average of 92.4 a week, about 13 a day, between 21 January 2024 and 16 April 2025. At that rate triaging CVEs one by one does not scale; tracking a supported stable or longterm series does, which is the behaviour the policy is designed to encourage.

Numbers to remember. 25 August 1991 for the announcement and 5 October 1991 for version 0.02; GPL-2.0 only with the syscall note; a two-week merge window, about seven weeks of release candidates and nine to ten weeks per release; longterm series now projected to December 2026, 2027 and 2028; more than 3,000 developers per release; and 500 of the 500 fastest supercomputers.

gpl.def: The copyleft licence family from the Free Software Foundation: you may use, study, modify and redistribute the software, provided that anything you distribute built from it carries the same freedoms and ships its source.
gpl.context: Version 2 (1991) is what Linux uses. Version 3 (2007) added terms on software patents and on devices built to refuse modified software, and the kernel deliberately stayed on 2 - a split that persists across the ecosystem. The practical difference from permissive licences is who bears the risk of enclosure: permissive terms let anyone take the code private, copyleft terms do not, and which is preferable depends entirely on whether you are trying to maximize adoption or to guarantee that improvements come back.

systemd.def: The init system and service manager adopted by most major Linux distributions, replacing collections of shell scripts with declarative unit files, parallel startup, dependency resolution, and integrated logging, device and network management.
systemd.context: Its technical case is strong and its adoption near-universal, and it remains the most divisive change in the platform's history. The objection is not that it fails but that it absorbed jobs previously done by separate replaceable programs, against the Unix habit of composing small tools. Read it as a governance dispute rather than a technical one: the real question was who decides the shape of the base system when a few large distributions move together, and that question recurs in every commons.

bitkeeper.def: The proprietary distributed version-control system the Linux kernel used from 2002, offered free to the project - and whose withdrawal in 2005, after a dispute over reverse-engineering its protocol, left the kernel abruptly without version control.
bitkeeper.context: Torvalds wrote Git in a matter of weeks to fill the gap, targeting exactly what the kernel needed: speed on a huge tree, distributed operation, and cryptographic integrity of history. The episode is the field's neatest demonstration that infrastructure gets built when someone capable is blocked - and a caution about depending on a tool you cannot fork, however generous the terms look while the relationship is good.

distro.def: A complete operating system assembled around the Linux kernel: the kernel plus userland tools, a package manager, an installer, default configuration, and a promise about how updates will arrive and for how long.
distro.context: Distributions differ far less in software than newcomers expect - the kernel and core tools are largely the same everywhere. What actually separates them is packaging format, release model (fixed, rolling or immutable), what the project defines as its job, and governance. That last one is a technical property, not a political footnote: who decides determines whether your deployment plan survives the next announcement.

package-manager.def: The system that installs, upgrades and removes software while tracking dependencies, file ownership and integrity - apt and dpkg on Debian lineages, dnf and rpm on Red Hat and SUSE, pacman on Arch, apk on Alpine, portage on Gentoo.
package-manager.context: It is the component you interact with most and the one that most defines a distribution's character. The design questions are the same everywhere and answered differently: does it resolve dependencies automatically, does it verify signatures, can it roll back, what happens when two packages want incompatible versions of the same library. Container images and language-level managers layered on top have not removed the problem - they have multiplied the number of places it has to be solved.

centos-stream.def: The 2020 decision to redirect CentOS - until then a free, bug-for-bug rebuild of Red Hat Enterprise Linux - into CentOS Stream, positioned ahead of the enterprise release rather than behind it, and the founding of Rocky Linux and AlmaLinux in response.
centos-stream.context: It is the canonical demonstration that governance is a technical property. No code changed; what changed was who decided and on what terms, and organizations that had built long-lived infrastructure on a free enterprise-compatible base discovered their plan had no owner. The durable lesson for anyone choosing a platform: ask who can change the terms, what their incentives are, and what your exit looks like if they do - before the announcement, not after.

alpine-linux.def: The small, security-oriented distribution built on musl libc and BusyBox rather than glibc and the full GNU utilities - the default base image for a very large share of container workloads because of its size.
alpine-linux.context: Choosing it is a trade, not a free win. Images shrink dramatically and attack surface with them, but musl is not bug-for-bug identical to glibc: software that assumes glibc behaviour - some locale handling, some DNS resolution paths, prebuilt binaries linked against glibc - can misbehave in ways that cost more debugging time than the megabytes saved. The correct question is whether your workload's dependencies are actually tested against musl.

cgroups.def: The Linux kernel facility that limits, accounts for and isolates the resource use of a group of processes - processor time, memory, block input and output, network - and one of the two features that make containers possible.
cgroups.context: Originally built at Google to stop workloads on shared machines from starving each other, it answers the accounting question that virtual machines answered with hardware emulation, at a fraction of the cost. Every memory limit in a container platform, every noisy-neighbour mitigation and every out-of-memory kill you have ever debugged in Kubernetes is cgroups doing its job - which is why the platform's behaviour is only fully explicable at the kernel level.

namespaces.def: The kernel mechanism that gives a process its own view of a system resource - process table, network stack, mount points, hostname, users, inter-process communication - so that what it sees is not what the host sees.
namespaces.context: Namespaces provide the isolation half of containers, as cgroups provide the accounting half. The security consequence is the one most often missed: isolation here is a kernel-enforced illusion, not a hardware boundary, so every container on a host shares one kernel and one kernel vulnerability. Treating containers as if they were virtual machines is the single most common architectural mistake in the field - user namespaces narrow the gap but do not close it.

openwrt.def: The replacement Linux firmware for consumer and small-business network devices, which began after a router vendor's use of Linux obliged them to publish their source under the kernel's licence.
openwrt.context: It is the cleanest real-world demonstration of copyleft working as designed: a company shipped Linux in a product, the licence required the changes back, and a community turned that release into a full independent firmware that now supports hundreds of devices. The practical value today is longevity - OpenWrt keeps devices patched years after their manufacturer has stopped caring, which is the embedded industry's central failure and, so far, its only broadly available answer.

android-linux.def: The most widely deployed Linux system in the world, and a deliberate piece of licence architecture: the copyleft kernel underneath, a permissively licensed framework and a purpose-built C library above it, so manufacturers can ship proprietary layers without publishing them.
android-linux.context: The arrangement is legal, effective and expensive in a way that took a decade to show. Device makers kept large kernel modifications out of the mainline tree, so shipping a security update meant rebasing a private fork - which is a direct cause of the update problem that left phones unpatched. Later work to upstream that support and stabilize the module interface is an attempt to pay down a debt the original boundary created. The general lesson: where you draw the licence line becomes your maintenance burden.

bgp-hijack.def: A BGP (Border Gateway Protocol) hijack is the announcement of address space a network does not hold, so that other networks send it traffic meant for the real holder; it works because routers prefer the most specific announcement and the protocol has no native way to check who is entitled to originate a prefix.
bgp-hijack.context: Impact is global within minutes and depends almost entirely on whether the upstream provider filtered. The dangerous variant is not blackholing but interception: divert, inspect and forward on, so the destination keeps working and the only evidence is latency and a path nobody looks at. Route origin validation with RPKI (Resource Public Key Infrastructure) closes the crude version, an announcement from the wrong AS (autonomous system); it does not close a plausible forged path that names the right origin, which is why monitoring a network's own prefixes remains an operational duty rather than an optional nicety.
bgp-hijack.depth:
A BGP (Border Gateway Protocol) hijack is an announcement in which an autonomous system (AS) originates a prefix it is not authorized to originate, or a more specific part of one, so that some or all of the internet routes the traffic for that space towards it. It comes in a few shapes. An exact-prefix hijack announces the same prefix as the legitimate holder and competes on path length and policy, splitting the internet between the two origins. A sub-prefix hijack announces something longer, a /24 inside a /22, and wins wherever it is accepted, because forwarding follows the longest matching prefix whatever the path. A forged-origin hijack puts the legitimate AS at the end of the path it announces so that origin checks pass. What distinguishes it from a route leak, in the vocabulary of RFC (Request for Comments) 7908, is the object: a leak propagates real routes beyond their intended scope, a hijack originates routes from an origin that has no right to them. Both are mostly accidents, and both are stopped mostly by the same thing, a provider that filters what its customers and peers announce.

It works because BGP was not built to check. RFC 4272 (January 2006) named three fundamental vulnerabilities: nothing strongly protects the integrity and peer authenticity of BGP messages, nothing in BGP validates the authority of an AS to announce reachability for a prefix, and nothing ensures the authenticity of the path attributes an AS announces. The same analysis lists what the consequences can be: blackholes, where traffic is drawn to a router that cannot carry it; delay, along an inferior path; looping; and eavesdropping, where traffic passes through a network that would otherwise never see it. The last is the variant defenders fear most, because an interceptor that forwards traffic on to its real destination leaves the service working and leaves as evidence only extra latency and an unfamiliar AS path.

The case that taught a generation of operators was YouTube in 2008, reconstructed by the RIPE NCC from its Routing Information Service (RIS). At 18:47 UTC (Coordinated Universal Time) on 24 February 2008, Pakistan Telecom (AS17557) began announcing 208.65.153.0/24, a more specific piece of YouTube's 208.65.152.0/22, and its upstream PCCW Global (AS3491) passed the announcement on to the rest of the internet; the RIPE NCC notes that Pakistan aimed to block the YouTube website, and a block meant for one country became a global outage. YouTube (AS36561) answered at 20:07 by announcing the same /24, which only split the traffic because path selection then decided, and at 20:18 by announcing two /25s, which longest-prefix match made win everywhere they were accepted; PCCW withdrew the Pakistan Telecom routes at 21:01. One detail of the RIPE NCC's analysis is a lesson in itself: the /25s were seen by only 21 RIS peers against 105 for the /24, because many networks refuse prefixes longer than /24, which limits how far defensive more-specifics can reach.

Later hijacks show the range of motives and of damage. On 24 April 2018 eNet (AS10297) announced more-specific /24s of the address space Amazon (AS16509) uses for its Route 53 DNS (Domain Name System) servers, propagated through Hurricane Electric (AS6939), for about two hours from 11:05 UTC. Cloudflare's analysis found that the servers on the hijacked space answered only for myetherwallet.com, returning addresses at a Russian provider; resolvers whose routers accepted the route were poisoned, Cloudflare's own 1.1.1.1 in several cities among them, and users who reached the fake site over HTTPS saw a warning for a self-signed certificate, so the attack worked only on those who clicked through it. On 1 April 2020, from 19:28 UTC, Rostelecom (AS12389) originated thousands of prefixes belonging to others; the MANRS (Mutually Agreed Norms for Routing Security) analysis counted 4,569 unique announcements propagated through Rascom (AS20764), 4,255 of them Amazon's and 85 Akamai's, most at prefix lengths never seen before, a pattern resembling a BGP optimizer or internal traffic engineering escaping its network. Level3 and Telia did not pass them on; Cogent (AS174) did. On 27 June 2024 Eletronet (AS267613) originated 1.1.1.1/32, and networks including at least one Tier 1 provider accepted it as a blackhole route, making Cloudflare's resolver unreachable from more than 300 networks in 70 countries.

The defence starts with filtering, because every one of those incidents needed someone upstream to accept and propagate the announcement. RFC 7454 (February 2015, Best Current Practice 194) describes the toolkit: prefix filters on every session, generated automatically from registry data for customers, maximum-prefix limits that shut down a peering whose neighbour suddenly announces far more than it should, and AS path filters. The MANRS initiative turns such practices into commitments that participating network operators, internet exchange points, CDN (content delivery network) and cloud providers and equipment vendors make publicly, and its Observatory measures how well they are kept. NIST (National Institute of Standards and Technology) Special Publication (SP) 800-189 (December 2019), by Kotikalapudi Sriram and Douglas Montgomery, gives the same guidance as a federal recommendation, citing hijacks and route leaks as causes of denial of service, traffic detours and degradation.

Origin validation is the cryptographic layer. With RPKI (Resource Public Key Infrastructure), the holder of a prefix publishes a Route Origin Authorization (ROA) naming the AS allowed to originate it, and routers classify each route as Valid, Invalid or NotFound under RFC 6811 (January 2013); dropping Invalid routes stops exact-prefix and sub-prefix hijacks from a wrong origin, and the incidents above show it: in the Rostelecom case 4,040 of the 4,569 prefixes had valid ROAs for their real origins, so networks enforcing origin validation rejected the hijack, and Cloudflare's 1.1.1.0/24 was signed, so the /32 was Invalid for the networks that checked. RFC 6811 is honest about the limit: an attacker need only prepend the valid origin AS to a forged route to defeat it, and it gives no protection against an AS in the middle or any path validation; the RFC calls it protection against misconfiguration more than security in the strong sense. RFC 9319 (October 2022, Best Current Practice 185) closes part of the gap from the publishing side: loose ROAs using maxLength authorize sub-prefixes nobody announces, which a forged-origin sub-prefix hijack can then claim with a perfectly Valid route, and a June 2017 measurement it cites found 84 per cent of prefixes in maxLength ROAs exposed. Its advice is minimal ROAs that authorize only what is actually announced.

Path validation is the unfinished layer. BGPsec, specified in RFC 8205 (September 2017), signs the AS path hop by hop, but RFC 9319 describes the situation of a substantial and growing number of large networks as RPKI deployed and invalid routes dropped, with BGPsec or anything like it not deployed. The lighter alternative, Autonomous System Provider Authorization (ASPA), in which each AS publishes its upstream providers so that impossible paths can be detected, remains an Internet-Draft: on 12 November 2026 the verification document, draft-ietf-sidrops-aspa-verification-29, stood with the IESG (Internet Engineering Steering Group) in evaluation by the responsible Area Director (AD Evaluation), awaiting a revised draft. Until path validation is common, a forged path that names the right origin passes origin validation.

Response is operational. A network should watch its own prefixes from outside, through public collectors such as RIS and route views, BGPlay-style replays and looking glasses, and alert on any new origin or more-specific announcement. When a hijack starts, the levers are the ones YouTube used: announce the same prefix or more-specifics to compete, accepting that /25s and longer will not travel far and that, as RFC 9319 notes, minimal ROAs can stop defensive more-specifics near the attacker (it recommends publishing them anyway), and call the upstreams of the offending AS, since a withdrawal by the provider that accepted the route ends the event fastest. Higher layers limit the damage: in the Route 53 case, DNSSEC (Domain Name System Security Extensions) signatures would have exposed forged answers, and TLS (Transport Layer Security) certificate validation stood between the hijacker and every user who did not click through the warning.

route-leak.def: The propagation of BGP (Border Gateway Protocol) routes beyond their intended scope, typically passing routes learned from one transit provider or peer to another, so that a network briefly claims to be a path to far more of the internet than it can carry.
route-leak.context: Leaks are usually accidents and are responsible for a large share of the biggest routing outages on record: traffic for major services converges on a network with a fraction of the required capacity and simply drops. What separates a leak from a hijack is what is announced, not intent: RFC (Request for Comments) 7908 defines a leak as a learned route propagated beyond its intended scope, by accident or by malice, whereas a hijack announces routes the announcer has no right to. The defence is largely the same: prefix filtering by the upstream. The recurring lesson is that the failure is rarely only the leaking network; it is the larger provider that accepted and propagated an announcement it should have discarded.
route-leak.depth:
The definition. RFC (Request for Comments) 7908, of June 2016, gives the working definition: a route leak is the propagation of routing announcements beyond their intended scope, that is, an announcement from one autonomous system (AS) to another of a learned BGP (Border Gateway Protocol) route in violation of the intended policies of the receiver, the sender or one of the ASes along the preceding path. Those policies are usually written in terms of business relationships: a customer pays a transit provider to carry its traffic, two peers exchange only their own customers' routes free of charge, and a provider passes everything to its customers. The result, in the RFC's words, can be traffic redirected through an unintended path, open to eavesdropping or traffic analysis, and sometimes overload or a black hole. Leaks can be accidental or malicious but most often arise from accidental misconfiguration. RFC 9234 restates the idea in terms of relationships: prefixes propagated in violation of the assumptions of BGP topology relationships, usually through misconfigured or absent route filtering.

The six types. RFC 7908 sorts observed leaks into six types. Types 1 to 4 violate policy and differ in the roles of the ASes involved. Type 1, the hairpin turn, is a multihomed AS passing a full route from one upstream to another; the RFC's examples include the Dodo-Telstra incident of March 2012 and the Telekom Malaysia leak of about 179,000 prefixes, which Level3 accepted and propagated. Type 2 is a lateral leak, an ISP (internet service provider) passing one peer's route to another peer, which monitoring catches by spotting three very large networks in a row in an AS path, since such networks rarely buy transit from one another. Type 3 sends a transit provider's routes to a peer; type 4 sends a peer's routes to a provider, as in the Hathway-Airtel leak of 336 Google prefixes that disrupted Google services in Europe and Asia. Type 5 is re-origination: a network strips the path and announces a learned prefix as its own, sometimes with a working path onward to the real origin, as in the China Telecom incident of April 2010, and sometimes without, as with Indosat in April 2014, where the traffic was dropped. Type 6 is the accidental leak of internal or more-specific prefixes, which the RFC says happens several times a week, the most conspicuous being about 22,000 more-specific prefixes leaked by AS701 and AS705 in August 2014.

Why a leak becomes an outage. Two mechanisms do the damage. A leaked route can win on path length or local preference at networks that would never have chosen it on purpose, and a leaked more-specific prefix wins outright, because routers prefer the longest match regardless of path. Cloudflare's account of 24 June 2019 shows both and the chain of responsibility. DQE Communications (AS33154) ran a BGP optimizer that split prefixes into more-specifics for internal traffic steering, so Cloudflare's 104.20.0.0/20 became 104.20.0.0/21 and 104.20.8.0/21; DQE passed them to its customer Allegheny Technologies (AS396531), which passed them to its other transit provider, Verizon (AS701), which announced them to the rest of the internet. Traffic for Cloudflare, Amazon, Linode and others converged on networks that could not carry it, and Cloudflare lost about 15 per cent of its global traffic at the worst point. Its conclusion is the recurring lesson of the subject: the leak should have stopped at Verizon, whose lack of filtering on a customer session turned a customer's mistake into a global incident.

Why origin validation does not catch it. A leak usually keeps the true origin at the end of the path, and RPKI (Resource Public Key Infrastructure) route origin validation checks only the origin. Cloudflare's record of 27 June 2024 is the clean example: while 1.1.1.1/32 was being hijacked by ELETRONET (AS267613), 1.1.1.0/24 was leaked upstream by its customer Nova Rede de Telecomunicações (AS262504) and widely propagated by Peer-1 Global Internet Exchange (AS1031). Cloudflare showed that the leaked announcement was RPKI Valid, because the origin was correctly AS13335, while the path itself was invalid. So the line between leak and hijack is drawn by what is announced, not by intent or by what a validator sees: RFC 7908 defines a leak by what is propagated, a learned route carried beyond its intended scope, and allows that it may be accidental or malicious, while a hijack announces routes without the right to them. Even so, a type 5 re-origination looks exactly like a hijack on the wire, and a leak with a valid origin passes the one check that stops most hijacks. The exception is the leaked more-specific: Cloudflare noted in 2019 that a provider validating with RPKI would have seen the leaked /21s as not valid, since its published authorizations did not cover them.

Prevention, in order of maturity. The oldest defence is filtering: a provider accepts from each customer only the prefixes, and the customer ASNs (autonomous system numbers), that the customer is entitled to announce, usually built from Internet Routing Registry (IRR) data; MANRS (Mutually Agreed Norms for Routing Security), the global initiative of network operators, internet exchanges and cloud providers, tracks filtering, anti-spoofing, coordination and IRR and RPKI publication among its members. Cloudflare's 2019 list of what would have stopped the Verizon leak adds the cheapest control of all: a maximum-prefix limit that shuts a session down when a customer suddenly announces far more routes than usual. RFC 8212 (July 2017), by J. Mauch, J. Snijders and G. Hankins, changed the default so that a BGP speaker neither imports nor exports routes on an external session unless an explicit policy says so, which turns a forgotten policy from a leak into a session that carries nothing. Many routers still ship the old behaviour or let it be switched back, so the default should be checked rather than assumed.

Roles and the Only to Customer attribute. RFC 9234 (May 2022) puts the business relationship into the protocol. Each side of a session declares its role, Provider, Customer, Peer, Route Server (RS) or RS-Client, in a BGP Role capability in the OPEN message; mismatched pairs, or a missing capability in strict mode, are refused with the Role Mismatch notification (code 2, subcode 11). The roles then drive a new optional transitive attribute, Only to Customer (OTC), type code 35. A route received from a provider, a peer or a route server is marked with OTC; a route that carries OTC must not be sent to providers, peers or route servers; and a route that arrives with OTC from a customer or an RS-Client, or from a peer with an OTC value other than the peer's own ASN, is a leak and is ineligible. Because the mark travels with the route, the attribute both prevents leaks locally and detects them several hops away. Cloudflare's 2024 analysis notes the catch: it only helps where routers along the path have been configured with roles.

Provider authorization and what remains open. The RPKI-based complement is Autonomous System Provider Authorization (ASPA): each network publishes, as a signed object, the list of its providers, and receivers verify that an AS path is consistent with those declarations, which detects leaks and path manipulation even where the leaking network does nothing. Cloudflare argued that ASPA would have flagged the 2024 leak had the networks involved published and validated it. On 12 November 2026 the verification procedure, draft-ietf-sidrops-aspa-verification, was still an Internet-Draft, submitted to the IESG (Internet Engineering Steering Group) and awaiting a revised version after area director evaluation; its latest revision is dated 16 October 2026. Until roles, OTC and ASPA are widespread, the practical defences are the old ones: strict prefix and AS path filters on every customer session, maximum-prefix limits, an import and export policy on every external session, and monitoring that alerts when one's own prefixes appear behind an unexpected path.

manrs.def: MANRS (Mutually Agreed Norms for Routing Security): a community agreement on baseline routing hygiene: filter the announcements of customers, keep traffic with spoofed source addresses from leaving the network, publish accurate routing data, and coordinate with other operators.
manrs.context: MANRS (Mutually Agreed Norms for Routing Security) is not a standard or a protocol but a published set of commitments with a participant list, which makes it a reputational instrument as much as a technical one. That is the point: most routing incidents are caused by an operator not doing one of four unglamorous things, and no protocol change can force them. When a network is asked why it accepted an impossible announcement, the answer is almost always that nobody had made filtering someone's explicit job. Its actions draw on long-standing practice, ingress filtering, prefix lists built from the IRR (Internet Routing Registry) and origin validation with the RPKI (Resource Public Key Infrastructure), and its Observatory publishes how well participants keep them.
manrs.depth:
MANRS (Mutually Agreed Norms for Routing Security) describes itself as a global initiative that provides crucial fixes to reduce the most common routing threats. It is supported by the Global Cyber Alliance, which provides its secretariat, and partially funded by a five-year grant from the Internet Society. It runs four programmes, each with its own normative actions document: network operators, IXPs (internet exchange points), CDN (content delivery network) and cloud providers, and equipment vendors; on 12 November 2026 its home page counted 1,412 participants across them. It has its own governance: a Steering Committee oversees the application and auditing processes, develops conformance criteria and guides community programmes, a Community Charter sets the principles, and a MANRS Development Process governs changes to the specifications. The committee is elected by the community; the 2026 election closed on 30 October 2026, and the committee's chair at the time was Tony Tauber.

It began with operators. In early 2014 a small group of network operators started what they called the Routing Resilience Manifesto, published a draft set of recommendations in July 2014 for community review, closed the review on 31 August 2014, and launched the final MANRS document and site that year with an initial list of supporters; a survey of routing incidents run with BGPmon was published in December 2014. The Internet Society, which in 2015 held MANRS up as a prime example of its collaborative security approach, supported the initiative until January 2024, when the Global Cyber Alliance took on its secretariat and operational functions; the Internet Society continues to provide funding, advocacy and training through the five-year grant.

For network operators the normative text is MANRS-003.01, approved on 17 May 2021, whose scope is three classes of problem: incorrect routing information, traffic with spoofed source IP addresses, and coordination and collaboration between networks. It grades its actions. Compulsory: Action 1, announce to adjacent networks only the AS (autonomous system) numbers and prefixes the operator or its customers are legitimately authorized to originate, and check that each customer legitimately holds what it announces; Action 3, keep contact data current in the RIR (regional internet registry) or NIR (national internet registry) database or PeeringDB, with an address for operational queries expected to be answered within 72 hours, a telephone number and an abuse address; and Action 4, publicly document intended announcements in the RIR's routing registry, RADB or an RADB-mirrored IRR (Internet Routing Registry), or, in lieu of that, create ROAs. Recommended: Action 2, source address validation for the operator's own infrastructure, its end users and single-homed stub customers, with a test of whether the network can send forged packets using CAIDA's Spoofer software that is required even so; and the RPKI (Resource Public Key Infrastructure) form of Action 4, a valid Route Origin Authorization (ROA) for each prefix the operator originates, with customers encouraged to do the same. Anti-spoofing, which the About page lists among the actions without grading them, is a recommendation in the normative text.

The document is specific about what does not count. It warns that filtering customer announcements by AS-path filters alone is insufficient to prevent catastrophic routing problems at a systemic level; what matters is explicit prefix-level filtering of inbound announcements, especially from customers. To join, a network must describe how its prefix filters are generated and how often they are updated, at least 50 per cent of its autonomous system numbers (ASNs) must be conformant, each ASN must have been visible and announcing prefixes for at least three months without announcing anything it was not authorized to originate in that time, and the operator must have run the CAIDA Spoofer software on at least two network segments using public addresses, with the results in CAIDA's database. Participants can be suspended for failing the actions afterwards. The anti-spoofing action rests on an older standard, BCP 38 (Best Current Practice 38), published as RFC (Request for Comments) 2827 by Paul Ferguson and Daniel Senie in May 2000; the MANRS text names source address validation on cable modem networks, strict unicast reverse path forwarding (uRPF) on routers, and packet filters derived from inbound prefix filters as the usual ways to do it.

The other programmes adapt the same ideas to other roles. For IXPs, MANRS-004.01 (23 April 2018) sets five actions: filtering of route announcements at the route server based on IRR or RPKI data, or both, promotion of MANRS among members, protection of the peering platform with a published policy of traffic not allowed on the fabric (unwanted Ethertypes, link-local and discovery protocols and the like), communication facilities such as member mailing lists and directories, and monitoring and debugging tools; Actions 1 and 2 are mandatory and an exchange must implement at least one more. For CDN and cloud providers, MANRS-005.01 (1 March 2021) requires explicit allow-list filtering with prefix granularity of announcements from non-transit peers and their customers, which matters because such networks peer with very many others, plus anti-spoofing, coordination, publication of routing information in at least one of the IRR or the RPKI, and active promotion of MANRS among peers; using RPKI as the primary source of validation and a standard AS-SET expansion process are optional additional commitments, and monitoring tools for peers are recommended. For equipment vendors, MANRS-006.01 (16 September 2021) asks for product features that let customers implement the other programmes' actions, and for training and technical content that promotes them.

Incidents show why the four things matter. When DQE Communications leaked more-specific routes through Allegheny Technologies to Verizon on 24 June 2019, Cloudflare wrote that the defences it recommended, prefix limits, IRR-based filtering and RPKI, were nicely condensed into MANRS, and its account of struggling to reach the networks involved is the case for the coordination action. The MANRS analysis of the Rostelecom hijack of 1 April 2020 makes the filtering case: had Rascom (AS20764) filtered strictly, the bad announcements would not have spread, Level3 and Telia did not propagate them while Cogent did, and 4,040 of the 4,569 hijacked prefixes had valid ROAs, so origin validation alone would have stopped most of them.

The Observatory turns the commitments into public measurement: it aggregates data from several sources to show, network by network, the state of filtering, anti-spoofing, coordination and routing information in the IRR and the RPKI, and the participant tables list each network's status action by action. Brazil stands out in them. The network operator table read on 12 November 2026 held about 1,200 organizations, of which 349 list Brazil among the areas they serve and 332 serve Brazil alone, against 121 that serve only the United States; in the IXP programme, DE-CIX São Paulo and DE-CIX Rio de Janeiro were approved on 17 December 2025. The limits are those of any voluntary norm: the actions are a baseline, as the document itself says, not a comprehensive solution, they are checked mostly at joining and through public data, and they bind only those who sign. Their strength is that a network that filters its customers' announcements protects everyone else from its customers' mistakes, which is exactly the protection the largest incidents lacked.

submarine-cable.def: The fibre-optic cable laid on the seabed that carries essentially all intercontinental internet traffic - fibre pairs at the core, wrapped in steel and copper, roughly garden-hose thick in deep water and heavily armoured near shore.
submarine-cable.context: Most faults are accidental, caused by fishing gear and anchors in shallow water, and most are invisible to users because traffic reroutes. The dangerous property is correlation: geography forces cables into shared corridors and shared landing areas, so systems bought as independent frequently are not. When assessing resilience the question is never how many cables a country has, but how many physically separate paths, landing points and terrestrial backhauls stand behind them.

landing-station.def: The facility where a submarine cable comes ashore and connects to terrestrial networks - housing the power feed equipment for the cable's optical amplifiers and the transmission gear that hands traffic to carriers.
landing-station.context: It is the concentration point that makes cable diversity misleading. Several cables often land within a short stretch of coast and feed the same backhaul, so a country counting four systems may have one effective failure domain. Landing stations are also the physically accessible end of an otherwise inaccessible asset, which makes them the relevant target for both regulation and interference - the seabed is hard to reach, the building on the beach is not.

cable-repair-ship.def: A specialized vessel held on standby under regional maintenance agreements to repair submarine cable faults - locating the break, grappling the cable off the seabed, splicing new fibre aboard, testing, and returning it to the bottom.
cable-repair-ship.context: The fleet is small, partly ageing and geographically concentrated, and it is the real constraint on recovery time. A typical repair runs one to several weeks: sailing time, weather, depth and queueing behind other faults all add up. Permits to work in another state's waters routinely add more, which is why some outages last far longer than the engineering requires - the delay is diplomatic. Any resilience plan that assumes fast physical repair has not looked at the fleet.

certificate-authority.def: An organization trusted by browsers and operating systems to vouch that a public key belongs to a given name. The set of them a client trusts is its root store - on the order of a hundred-plus organizations across many jurisdictions.
certificate-authority.context: The uncomfortable property is that the model is a flat list: by default any authority in the store can issue for any name anywhere, so the security of every site depends on the weakest member. The counterweights arrived late and from outside the authorities themselves - browser root programmes that set and enforce rules, CAA records that let a domain restrict who may issue for it, and public logging that makes issuance observable. Judge a CA less by its cryptography than by its validation process and its incident history.

diginotar.def: The Dutch certificate authority compromised in 2011, whose fraudulently issued certificates for major services were used to intercept traffic in Iran - and which went bankrupt within weeks of the disclosure.
diginotar.context: It is the reference case for three lessons. A fraudulent certificate produces a normal padlock, so victims see nothing wrong. Trust in this system is revocable but removal has collateral damage - taking DigiNotar out of root stores also broke Dutch government services that depended on it. And the victims were ordinary users of a country under surveillance, which is why this incident, more than any technical argument, drove the industry towards public logging of every certificate issued.

certificate-transparency.def: Certificate Transparency (CT) is the system, specified in Request for Comments (RFC) 6962 and revised in RFC 9162, in which publicly trusted Transport Layer Security (TLS) certificates are recorded in append-only, publicly auditable logs, and browsers refuse certificates that lack proof of logging, so that any issuance for any domain can be seen by anyone.
certificate-transparency.context: Certificate Transparency (CT) changed the security model of the web's public key infrastructure (PKI) rather than strengthening the old one: certificate authorities (CAs) can still misissue, but they cannot do it secretly, and detection moves from practically impossible to within a log's merge delay, usually 24 hours. A log answers each submission with a Signed Certificate Timestamp (SCT), a signed promise to publish, which the CA embeds in the certificate and the browser checks. Domain owners get a free, direct benefit: one that watches the logs for its own names learns quickly when someone certifies them. The broader idea generalizes well beyond certificates: when trust cannot be verified in advance, make the exercise of that trust public and auditable after the fact.
certificate-transparency.depth:
Certificate Transparency (CT) answers a weakness built into the web's public key infrastructure (PKI): any trusted certificate authority (CA) can issue a certificate for any domain, and a CA that has been hacked or is careless can do it for a site it has no business with. Before CT, the project's own account says, trust in CAs rested on audits by accredited third parties that looked at operational practices and history rather than at the technical correctness of what was issued, and a wrongly issued certificate could go unnoticed for a long time. The trigger was 2011. In July of that year an unknown attacker compromised DigiNotar, a Dutch CA, and issued rogue certificates for many domains, more than 500 of which were eventually detected and which were used for man-in-the-middle attacks on traffic from Iran; in February 2012 it emerged that Trustwave had given a customer subordinate root certificates that could have certified almost any domain. The Internet Engineering Task Force (IETF) chartered its Trans working group in September 2012, Google launched its first logs in March 2013, prepopulated with certificates found by its crawler, and Request for Comments (RFC) 6962, by B. Laurie, A. Langley and E. Kasper of Google, was published as an Experimental RFC in June 2013. DigiCert ran the first log outside Google from September 2013.

A log is an append-only list of certificates kept as a Merkle tree over SHA-256 (the 256-bit Secure Hash Algorithm), so that the log can prove two things cheaply: that a given certificate is in it (an inclusion proof) and that its current state extends an earlier one without rewriting it (a consistency proof). The log periodically signs the root as a Signed Tree Head (STH). Anyone may submit a chain, but in practice CAs do, and they solve a chicken-and-egg problem with a precertificate: a copy of the future certificate made unusable by a critical poison extension (OID 1.3.6.1.4.1.11129.2.4.3). The log answers at once with a Signed Certificate Timestamp (SCT), a signed promise to incorporate the entry within the log's Maximum Merge Delay (MMD), usually 24 hours. The CA then embeds the SCTs in the final certificate as an X.509v3 extension (OID 1.3.6.1.4.1.11129.2.4.2); a server can instead deliver them in the TLS (Transport Layer Security) extension signed_certificate_timestamp, number 18, or inside a stapled OCSP (Online Certificate Status Protocol) response. RFC 6962 defines the log's HTTP (Hypertext Transfer Protocol) interface: add-chain and add-pre-chain for submissions, get-sth, get-sth-consistency, get-proof-by-hash and get-entries for readers.

The design spreads the work across roles. Logs record but, as RFC 6962 says plainly, do not themselves detect misissued certificates; they rely on interested parties, domain owners first among them, to watch and act. Monitors fetch the logs and look for certificates of interest, including ones with unusual extensions or CA capabilities. User agents enforce the policy by refusing certificates without valid SCTs. The RFC also lists the two ways a log can misbehave, failing to incorporate a certificate within the MMD or presenting different views of its tree to different parties, and says both are publicly detectable. That happened in 2016, when the Spanish CA and log operator Izenpe reused its production log key for testing, produced a split view and was disqualified as a log operator. An SCT is therefore evidence that a certificate is public, not that it was rightly issued: the RFC notes that the domain owner may not have looked, or the CA may have refused to revoke.

Enforcement came in stages, because requiring CT everywhere at once would have broken large numbers of sites. Chrome required CT for Extended Validation (EV) certificates issued from 1 January 2015, and it paid off within the year. On 14 September 2015 a Thawte-branded CA of Symantec issued an EV precertificate for google.com and www.google.com that Google had neither requested nor authorized; Google found it in the CT logs, where it had been recorded by logs run by Google and by DigiCert, and Symantec attributed it to an internal testing process. In 2017 CT showed that Symantec had misissued thousands of certificates, and all major platforms ultimately distrusted it; the same year CT exposed WoSign and StartCom backdating certificates. Chrome 68 then enforced CT for every TLS server certificate issued after 30 April 2018, Apple for certificates issued after 15 October 2018, and Firefox, after Nightly in version 133 and Beta in 134, from Firefox 135 on desktop.

The browser policies decide how many SCTs are enough. Chrome classifies logs as Pending, Qualified, Usable, ReadOnly, Retired or Rejected. A certificate with embedded SCTs is compliant when at least one comes from a log that is Qualified, Usable or ReadOnly at the time of the check, when SCTs come from at least two distinct logs for a certificate valid for 180 days or less, or three for a longer one, and when at least two different log operators are represented; SCTs delivered through TLS need two, from distinct operators, and SCTs inside stapled OCSP responses are accepted only by versions before Chrome 148. Issuing a non-compliant certificate is not misissuance under Chrome's rules; the certificate simply fails to validate. Apple's policy, published in April 2025, also asks for at least two SCTs, two embedded ones for lifetimes up to 180 days and three for 181 to 398 days, with a cap on how many may come from one operator, and requires at least one SCT from a log compliant with RFC 6962. Firefox compiles in a log list derived from Chromium's, controls enforcement with the preference security.pki.certificate_transparency.mode (0 off, 1 on without enforcement, 2 enforced for roots in Mozilla's programme), and offers disable_for_hosts and disable_for_spki_hashes exceptions modelled on Chrome's enterprise policies.

The protocol itself has moved on more slowly than its deployment. RFC 9162 (December 2021, by B. Laurie, E. Messeri and R. Stradling) defines CT version 2.0 and obsoletes RFC 6962: hash and signature algorithms become registries, precertificates become CMS (Cryptographic Message Syntax) objects so that the poison extension and the duplicated serial number disappear, logs are identified by an OID (object identifier), a TransItem structure wraps the data, a transparency_info TLS extension replaces signed_certificate_timestamp, and submit-entry replaces the two submission calls. The logs browsers actually rely on still speak RFC 6962, which is why Apple insists on at least one RFC 6962 SCT. The change in practice has been in how logs are built: the Static CT API, formerly the Sunlight API (version 1.1.0, March 2026), keeps RFC 6962's submission endpoints and signatures but serves the read side as static files, so that a log is cheaper to run and needs no change from CAs or TLS clients. The scale explains the effort: the project's counter showed more than 2.5 billion certificates logged since 2013 when it was read in November 2026.

For an operator, CT is mainly a free alarm. A domain owner who subscribes to a monitor is told when a precertificate or certificate for its names appears in any log the monitor follows. The ecosystem grew around that service: crt.sh, a search interface over the logs, from September 2015; Facebook's monitoring tool in December 2016; Cloudflare's Nimbus log and Merkle Town in March 2018 and its monitoring service in August 2019; DigiCert's in December 2019; Let's Encrypt's Oak log in May 2019. Microsoft added CT support to Active Directory Certificate Services in April 2018. The natural pairing is with a CAA (Certification Authority Authorization) record, which tells CAs in advance who may issue for a domain, while CT shows afterwards who did. Facebook reported in April 2016 that CT had revealed an internal policy violation in its own certificates, which is the less dramatic but more common way monitoring pays off.

Two consequences catch people out. Transparency is total for public certificates: every name placed in a publicly trusted certificate becomes visible to anyone who reads the logs, so a hostname that should stay private does not belong in one. And enforcement covers only the public web: Chrome applies its policy to publicly trusted certificates, Firefox to roots in Mozilla's programme, so certificates from an enterprise CA, including those minted by a TLS inspection proxy, are not expected to carry SCTs, while a misconfigured exception list can quietly switch CT off for hosts that should have it. CT also does not stop misissuance, revoke anything or judge whether issuance was legitimate; it makes issuance visible, and the remedy, revocation or distrust, comes through the CA and the root programmes.

Among its neighbours, revocation through the Certificate Revocation List (CRL) or OCSP withdraws a certificate after the fact, CAA restricts which CAs may issue, and CT records what was issued; each covers a gap the others leave. The numbers worth remembering are a merge delay usually of 24 hours, two or three SCTs depending on whether a certificate lives more than 180 days, TLS extension 18, the 2013 publication of RFC 6962 and its 2021 successor RFC 9162, and the enforcement dates of 30 April 2018 for Chrome and 15 October 2018 for Apple. The idea travels well beyond certificates: when trust cannot be verified in advance, make every exercise of that trust public and auditable after the fact.

concentration-risk.def: Concentration risk is the exposure created when a large share of unrelated organizations depend on the same provider, region, network, software or authority, so that a single failure, decision or legal order reaches all of them at once.
concentration-risk.context: It is emergent rather than designed: each organization picked the most reliable option available and the aggregate became a shared failure domain. Two things follow that are easy to miss. Individual reliability and systemic fragility can rise together, because the better a provider is, the more of the world routes through it. And concentration is jurisdictional as well as technical: a small number of companies means a small number of legal levers. Regulators now target it explicitly, which is unusual for a property nobody deliberately created: the European Union's Digital Operational Resilience Act (DORA) defines information and communication technology (ICT) concentration risk and, in November 2025, put 19 technology providers under direct supervisory oversight.
concentration-risk.depth:
What it is, and what it is not. A single point of failure is a flaw inside one organization's design; concentration risk is a property of many organizations' designs taken together, each of which may be redundant on paper. It is also distinct from a supply-chain attack, which is deliberate: concentration turns an ordinary failure, a commercial decision or a court order at one provider into a simultaneous event for every customer. Financial regulation has given it a precise form. DORA, Regulation (EU) 2022/2554, defines ICT (information and communication technology) concentration risk as an exposure to one or more related critical ICT third-party service providers that creates enough dependency that their unavailability, failure or other shortfall may endanger a financial entity's ability to deliver critical or important functions, cause it large losses, or endanger the financial stability of the Union as a whole. The last clause is the point: the regulator's concern is not one firm's outage but the same outage in many firms at once.

The shapes it takes. The dependency can be on a provider (a cloud, a content delivery network (CDN), a managed Domain Name System (DNS) service), on one region of a provider, on a piece of software installed everywhere, on an authority such as a certificate issuer or registry, or on a supplier's supplier. DORA's Article 29 names the two tests a financial entity must apply before contracting services that support critical or important functions: whether the provider is not easily substitutable, and whether the entity would end up with several arrangements with the same provider or with closely connected providers. It adds the chain behind the contract: subcontracting, subcontractors in third countries, and the insolvency law that would govern the data if the provider went bankrupt.

A region as a dependency. On 19 and 20 October 2025, Amazon Web Services' (AWS) Northern Virginia region, us-east-1, failed in three overlapping waves. AWS's own summary traces the start to a latent race condition in the automation that manages DynamoDB's DNS records, which left an empty DNS record for the service's regional endpoint, dynamodb.us-east-1.amazonaws.com, that the automation then failed to repair. From 23:48 PDT (Pacific Daylight Time) on 19 October to 02:40 on 20 October, DynamoDB returned increased API (application programming interface) errors, and customers and other AWS services that depended on it could not open new connections; launches of new EC2 (Elastic Compute Cloud) instances then failed from 02:25 to 10:36, and Network Load Balancer connection errors ran from 05:30 to 14:09. The lesson for customers is the depth of the graph: an application with no direct use of DynamoDB could still depend on services that did.

Configuration propagated everywhere. On 18 November 2025, from 11:20 UTC (Coordinated Universal Time), Cloudflare's network failed to deliver core traffic, and users of its customers' sites saw Cloudflare error pages. Matthew Prince's post-mortem states that it was not an attack: a change to a database's permissions made it write duplicate entries into a feature file for the Bot Management system, the file doubled in size, it was propagated to every machine in the network, and the proxy software, which had a size limit below the new file's size, failed. Core traffic was largely flowing by 14:30 and all systems were normal by 17:06; Cloudflare called it its worst outage since 2019, the first in more than six years to stop the majority of core traffic. A platform built to push a change everywhere in seconds pushes a bad change everywhere in seconds.

Few machines, critical ones. Concentration is measured by function, not count. The faulty CrowdStrike software update of July 2024 affected about 8.5 million Windows devices by Microsoft's estimate, less than one per cent of all Windows machines; Microsoft's own explanation of why the impact was so broad is that enterprises running many critical services used CrowdStrike. A single endpoint agent, installed on the machines that matter most, is as concentrated as any cloud.

Regulators move. DORA has applied since 17 January 2025. On 18 November 2025 the three European Supervisory Authorities (ESAs) published the first list of critical ICT third-party providers designated for direct oversight, after collecting the registers of information in which financial entities record their ICT contracts and assessing each provider's systemic importance, its role in critical or important functions and the substitutability of its services. The 19 names include Amazon Web Services EMEA, Google Cloud EMEA, Microsoft Ireland Operations, Oracle, IBM and SAP, the data centre operators Equinix and InterXion, the carriers Deutsche Telekom, Orange and Colt, and services firms such as Accenture, Capgemini, Kyndryl, NTT DATA and Tata Consultancy Services. The United Kingdom built a parallel regime under the Financial Services and Markets Act 2023: HM Treasury may designate a critical third party only if a failure in or disruption to its services could threaten the stability of, or confidence in, the UK financial system, and the Bank of England, Prudential Regulation Authority and Financial Conduct Authority rules took effect on 1 January 2025, with no provider yet designated when the policy was published in November 2024. Their policy statement records a revealing objection: that designation might entrench concentration by acting as a mark of approval, which the regulators answered by saying designation does not make a provider more resilient or better suited than an undesignated one.

Brazil's version. Brazil's National Monetary Council (Conselho Monetário Nacional, CMN) took the reporting route in Resolution CMN No. 4,893 of 26 February 2021: institutions authorized by the Central Bank must tell it, within ten days, when they contract relevant data processing, storage or cloud services, naming the provider, the services and the countries and regions where data may be stored and processed; services abroad require an information-exchange agreement between the Central Bank and the foreign supervisors, and contracts must give the Central Bank access to the data, the backups and the access codes. Knowing which institutions depend on which provider, and under which jurisdiction, is the precondition for measuring concentration at all.

What reduces it. No one can deconcentrate the market alone, but each organization can shrink its own share of the common failure domain. The work starts with a dependency map that includes the unglamorous services, DNS, certificate issuance, identity, package registries and the status page, because those are where hidden common dependencies live; DORA's substitutability question is the right one to ask of each. A second provider counts only if it does not share the first one's failure domain: a second region of the same cloud survives a regional failure but not a control-plane or global configuration failure, and two resellers of one platform are one provider. Designs that degrade, serving cached or read-only content, and failovers rehearsed on a schedule, matter more than a second copy that has never carried traffic. And the contract matters as much as the architecture, since the questions DORA forces, exit plans, subcontracting and the law that applies in insolvency, are concentration risk in its commercial form.

correlated-failure.def: Failures that happen together because the things that failed share something (a control plane, a configuration pipeline, a provider, a physical route, a firmware version) rather than failing independently, as a redundancy calculation assumes.
correlated-failure.context: Redundancy arithmetic assumes independence, and almost nothing is independent. Two providers reselling one platform, a backup in another region of the same cloud, a secondary DNS service peering at the same exchange: all present as diversity and behave as one component. The practical test is not how many vendors appear on the invoice but what happens if any single shared element is removed, and the answer usually has to be traced through the dependency graph rather than recalled from the architecture diagram.
correlated-failure.depth:
What it is, and its relatives. A correlated failure is any set of failures whose probability of occurring together is higher than the product of their separate probabilities, because something links them. Nuclear safety engineering formalized the idea decades before cloud operators rediscovered it. The US Nuclear Regulatory Commission's guidelines on modelling common-cause failures, NUREG/CR-5485 by A. Mosleh, D. M. Rasmuson and F. M. Marshall (November 1998), define a common cause event as the failure or unavailable state of more than one component during the mission time due to the same shared cause, and require two ingredients: a root cause, and a coupling mechanism that lets it reach several components at once. A coupling factor, in their words, is a characteristic of a group of components that identifies them as susceptible to the same causal mechanisms of failure, such as similarity in design, location or environment. Common-mode failure is the older name for the case where the redundant parts fail in the same way. A cascading failure is the dynamic relative: Google's site reliability book defines it as a failure that grows over time as a result of positive feedback, one part failing and raising the probability that others fail. All three break the same assumption.

Why the arithmetic lies. If two components are each available 99.9 per cent of the time and fail independently, both are down together about one millionth of the time, and redundancy looks almost free. The independence is the expensive word. Daniel Ford and colleagues at Google studied a year of live operation of the company's storage fleet and presented the results at OSDI (the USENIX Symposium on Operating Systems Design and Implementation) in 2010: 37 per cent of node failures were part of a burst of at least two nodes, large bursts were associated with shared failure domains such as racks, and models that treated failures as independent overestimated data availability by at least two orders of magnitude, and by eight orders for one erasure-coding scheme. They concluded that the critical element of an availability model is its handling of the frequency and magnitude of correlated failures, that adding replicas helps much less once failures are correlated, and that replicating across cells (separate data centres) was what actually bought availability. Disks tell the same story at smaller scale. Bianca Schroeder and Garth Gibson of Carnegie Mellon University analysed replacement logs for about 100,000 drives for FAST (the USENIX Conference on File and Storage Technologies) in 2007: datasheets promised mean times to failure of 1,000,000 to 1,500,000 hours, a nominal annual failure rate of at most 0.88 per cent, while field replacement rates of 2 to 4 per cent were common and up to 13 per cent was observed, and the time between replacements showed significant correlation, including autocorrelation and long-range dependence. They pointed out that this matters for RAID (redundant array of independent disks), whose safety depends on the chance of a second failure during reconstruction, a chance badly estimated by scaling an annual rate down to a few hours.

Identical parts, identical clocks. The cleanest coupling factor is sameness. In December 2019 Ireland's national CSIRT (computer security incident response team) relayed an HPE (Hewlett Packard Enterprise) advisory: SAS (Serial Attached SCSI, the Small Computer System Interface) solid-state drives with firmware older than HPD8 would fail, with loss of data, at 32,768 hours of operation, which is 2 to the 15th power hours, or about three years and nine months, and drives installed at the same time could therefore fail at approximately the same time. A mirror built from two such drives, bought together and powered on together, had redundancy on paper and none in fact. Same model, same batch, same firmware and same installation date are four coupling factors at once, and spreading purchases, firmware versions and commissioning dates is the cheap defence.

One change, everywhere at once. Software and configuration pipelines couple systems that share no hardware at all.
