On 18 July 2024, according to Microsoft, an update released by the security company CrowdStrike affected an estimated 8.5 million Windows devices, less than one per cent of all Windows machines, yet with broad economic and social impact because the enterprises that used the product ran many critical services; every machine running the same agent and receiving the same update was one failure domain. Cloudflare's outage of 18 November 2025, described by Matthew Prince in the company's post-mortem, began at 11:20 UTC (Coordinated Universal Time) when a change to a database system's permissions made it emit duplicate entries into a feature file used by the Bot Management system; the file doubled in size, was propagated to every machine in the network, and exceeded a size limit in the traffic-routing software, which failed. The engineers first suspected a hyper-scale DDoS (distributed denial-of-service) attack. In both cases the mechanism that made the change fast, a global push, was also the coupling.

Shared dependencies and shared safety logic. The less visible couplings are internal dependencies. AWS (Amazon Web Services) reported that on 19 and 20 October 2025 a latent race condition in the automated DNS management of DynamoDB, in its Northern Virginia (us-east-1) Region, left an incorrect empty DNS record for the service's regional endpoint that the automation failed to repair; customers and other AWS services that depended on DynamoDB could not establish new connections, and the disruption went on to affect EC2 (Elastic Compute Cloud) instance launches and Network Load Balancer health checks, so independent-looking services failed together because they shared one dependency. Facebook's outage of 4 October 2021, explained by Santosh Janardhan the next day, shows a safety mechanism becoming the coupling. A maintenance command meant to assess backbone capacity took down every backbone connection, and a bug in the audit tool failed to stop it. The company's DNS servers were designed to withdraw their BGP (Border Gateway Protocol) advertisements whenever they could not reach the data centres, a sensible local rule; with the whole backbone gone, every site applied it at once, Facebook's DNS vanished from the internet, the loss of DNS broke the internal tools engineers needed, and with out-of-band access also down, staff had to be sent to the data centres in person.

Correlation that clients create. Retries turn a small, partial failure into a synchronized one. Google's chapter on cascading failures, by Mike Ulrich, works through a frontend that retries naively against an overloaded backend: the retries add to the load, the rejected requests grow from 100 to 200 to 300 per second, the backend melts down, and its share of traffic moves to the remaining tasks, overloading them in turn. Its advice is randomized exponential backoff, a cap on retries per request and a server-wide retry budget, for example 60 retries a minute per process, beyond which requests simply fail. Amazon's Builders' Library makes the correlation explicit: retries are selfish, and backing off helps less than it seems because failed calls that back off to the same moment overload the service again when they return, which is why jitter, a random delay, is added. A retry storm is a correlated failure manufactured by well-intentioned clients.

Designing against it. The NUREG guidelines analyse defences against root causes and against coupling factors separately, and the second list is the more useful in networks and clouds. Diversity breaks coupling: different firmware versions, vendors, installation dates, regions and providers, provided they do not share a platform underneath. Staged rollouts break the single global push, so that a bad change reaches one cell, one availability zone or a canary population first. Independent control planes and out-of-band management that does not depend on the production network or its DNS keep the means of repair outside the failure. Retry budgets with jitter keep clients from synchronizing. And the test of any redundancy claim is the one the context states: name every element the redundant parts share, remove each in turn on paper, and see what is left. When the shared element is a provider used by many organizations at once, the same problem appears one level up as concentration risk.

internet-shutdown.def: A government-ordered disconnection of internet access for a population - nationwide or regional, total or limited to mobile data - executed by licensed operators under legal instruction rather than by any technical attack.
internet-shutdown.context: The mechanism is administrative, which is why no protocol change addresses it: connectivity in most countries runs through a handful of licensed operators with licences to lose. The damage is much wider than speech - payments, delivery work, health services, exams, customs and remote contracts all assume connectivity - and it falls hardest on people with no financial buffer. Shutdowns also remove the evidentiary record of whatever prompted them, which is a consequence with a longer tail than the outage itself.

throttling.def: Deliberately reducing available bandwidth until services degrade - video first, then images, then messaging - while the connection technically continues to work.
throttling.context: It is the deniable form of a shutdown and increasingly the preferred one: no outage appears, operators can attribute it to congestion, and users blame their own devices. Achieving most of a blackout's effect without producing an event anyone can point at is precisely the appeal. This is why independent network measurement matters more than it sounds - without a documented, dated technical record, throttling is an argument about whether the internet feels slow, and that is an argument nobody wins.

dpi.def: Examining traffic beyond its headers to classify what protocol or application it carries - used legitimately for network management and troubleshooting, and equally for blocking, throttling and surveillance.
dpi.context: Encryption removed the content but not the shape: modern inspection classifies by handshake characteristics, packet timing and size patterns rather than by reading payloads. That is why circumvention moved from encrypting traffic to making traffic look ordinary, and why pluggable transports and protocol obfuscation exist at all. The arms race is asymmetric in an instructive way - the censor only needs a classification good enough to be politically acceptable, while the tool must be indistinguishable.

prilex.def: Prilex is the Brazilian criminal group, active since 2014, and its malware family that began by jackpotting ATMs (automated teller machines), more than a thousand machines at one bank in 2016 with some 28,000 cards cloned, and then rebuilt itself around point-of-sale (PoS) payment software, manipulating chip card transactions at the PIN pad.
prilex.context: Kaspersky, whose researchers have published most of what is known about it, calls it the most advanced PoS threat they have seen. Its point-of-sale generation works at the PIN pad protocol level rather than through higher-level interfaces, patches the target payment software in memory, hooks Windows libraries and, instead of replaying old card data, asks the victim's chip card for fresh EMV (Europay, Mastercard and Visa) cryptograms to use in fraudulent GHOST transactions; later versions block contactless payments so that customers insert the card. It reaches merchants through fake technicians and remote-access sessions, and it was marketed to other criminals as a kit, although Kaspersky is not sure the sellers were the group itself. Its capability profile, detailed knowledge of Brazilian electronic funds transfer software and payment protocols, suggests insider understanding of the industry it attacked, and it is the clearest case of a Brazilian crew building payment-fraud tooling ahead of what was seen elsewhere.
prilex.depth:
What it is. Prilex names both a Brazilian financially motivated threat actor and its malware. Kaspersky's Global Research and Analysis Team (GReAT), whose 2022 report and Virus Bulletin paper are the main public record, describes an actor active since 2014 that evolved from ATM-focused malware into modular point-of-sale malware, built by criminals with extensive knowledge of the payment market and of the electronic funds transfer (EFT) software, called TEF (transferência eletrônica de fundos) in Brazil, that connects shop tills to card readers and acquirers. It is not a banking trojan that steals online banking credentials, and it is not mass malware: Kaspersky stresses that it is highly targeted and not spread by spam. Its targets are the payment systems themselves.

The ATM attack. During carnival in 2016 a Brazilian bank found that its ATMs had been emptied. According to the law enforcement reports Kaspersky cites, the criminals infected more than 1,000 machines of that one bank in the same incident and had earlier captured enough data to clone 28,000 unique cards used at those machines. They had no physical access to the ATMs: a home-made device combining a 4G router and a Raspberry Pi gave them a foothold on the bank's wireless network, from which they located the ATMs and installed malware written from scratch with privileged knowledge of the ATM network. It patched legitimate ATM software so that the machines would dispense cash on command, the attack known as jackpotting, and also read the magnetic stripes of cards inserted into the infected machines.

The move to the point of sale. In 2016 the group abandoned ATM malware and turned to PoS systems, with its first PoS sample seen in October 2016. The early versions patched libraries of the EFT software to read the track data, the account number, expiry date and other details, as transactions went through. By March 2018 Kaspersky reported a complete toolset: the malware on the merchant's machine, a server for the stolen data and a client application with which a buyer could view, clone and keep statistics on cards, and which turned stolen data into working plastic cards. The victims Kaspersky saw were ordinary Brazilian businesses such as petrol stations, supermarkets and shops. Delivery relied on social engineering rather than exploits: a caller posing as a technician tells the business its PoS software needs updating and either visits or asks staff to install a remote-access tool such as AnyDesk, and at least one PoS vendor warned its customers about exactly this.

Replay, then GHOST. Brazil began migrating to EMV chip cards in 1999, and nearly all cards issued there are chip cards. Prilex's first chip attacks did not break EMV; they exploited acquirers and processors that skipped validations the standard requires, pushing transactions through as chip purchases with data captured earlier, which is why a cloned card could work at almost any terminal in Brazil. Kaspersky links the technique to replay attacks by Brazilian criminals since at least 2014, the kind Brian Krebs described in October 2014, when US banks that had not yet issued chip cards received tens of thousands of dollars of fraudulent charges from Brazil submitted as chip transactions on cards stolen in the Home Depot breach, one small New England bank facing about 120,000 dollars in under two days; it also links it to a 2019 attack on a German bank that lost 1.5 million euros, which the gang claimed. As issuers and processors fixed those gaps, replays stopped working, partly because a replayed cryptogram repeats its Application Transaction Counter and carries the wrong date. The newer versions therefore intercept the conversation between the payment software and the PIN pad during a genuine purchase and ask the customer's card for new cryptograms, which the criminals then use for what the malware's authors call GHOST transactions through a terminal registered to a front company. To do it, the stealer module hooks Windows functions inside the payment process that talks to the PIN pad over its COM port, placing its hook code in unused space inside existing modules rather than in newly allocated memory.

Contactless, and the rules file. In January 2023 Kaspersky described three further versions found during an incident response, the latest numbered 06.03.8080 and dated November 2022. They read a rules file that can block NFC (near-field communication) transactions: the payment software then makes the PIN pad show a contactless error and ask for the card to be inserted, because a tap generates data valid for one transaction only, while an inserted chip card can be made to produce the cryptograms the attack needs. The rules can also select cards by segment, capturing only premium or corporate cards with high limits.

Activity and the service question. Kaspersky's sample timeline shows Prilex highly active in 2020, silent in 2021 and back in 2022 with three new variants. The 2018 release presented the business model, a user-friendly kit with support for its buyers, as the most notable thing about it, and Kaspersky's 2022 report says the group adopted malware-as-a-service and expanded abroad, yet in the same report it gives little weight to a website that appeared in 2019 claiming to sell the group's package, which might be copycats trading on the name. What can be said with confidence is that the tooling circulated beyond its authors.

What defenders take from it. The weak points Prilex used are specific. Point-of-sale computers run general-purpose Windows with remote-access tools, and an unannounced technician or a support call asking to install one is the delivery route, so merchants and their EFT vendors need a verified way to authenticate support. The PIN pad encrypts the PIN, usually with Triple DES, but the computer it is cabled to sees the rest of the transaction, so the integrity of that computer and of the payment software's files decides the outcome; Kaspersky's products detect the family as HEUR:Trojan.Win32.Prilex and HEUR:Trojan.Win64.Prilex. On the issuer and acquirer side, the replay era ended because the EMV checks were finally enforced, and the GHOST era is detectable by the same discipline: cryptograms, counters and dates that do not match the purchase, and terminals registered to companies that do not trade. A sudden contactless failure on a terminal that worked yesterday is itself a signal worth investigating.

The numbers worth remembering. Active since 2014; carnival 2016, more than 1,000 ATMs at one bank and 28,000 cards cloned; first PoS sample in October 2016; EMV migration in Brazil from 1999; 1.5 million euros lost by a German bank in 2019; silent in 2021, three versions in 2022; version 06.03.8080 of November 2022 blocking contactless payments.

ataque-stj-2020.def: The November 2020 ransomware incident at Brazil's Superior Court of Justice, attributed to RansomExx, which encrypted the court's case files, suspended proceedings and deadlines, and took roughly two weeks to restore.
ataque-stj-2020.context: Recovery was possible because backups survived, which is the whole lesson in one clause. Support came from the Federal Police, army intelligence and Microsoft, and the judiciary responded by standing up a body to address protection across the courts. Careful accounts note that the court never publicly confirmed a ransom demand, so descriptions of the extortion side rest on reporting rather than official statement - a distinction worth preserving when this case is cited.

peruhack.def: Peru's annual offensive-security conference in Lima - free to attend, deliberately technical, and explicitly carrying forward the spirit of its predecessor LimaHack, with a lineage the organizers date to 2013.
peruhack.context: Its declared purpose is to show security from the attacker's perspective, through talks, live demonstrations and workshops, and its declared constraint is independence: free admission and no commercial pitch, which the organizers describe as what keeps the technical content objective. The LimaHack-to-PERUHACK handover is the same succession question that faces every volunteer conference in the region, answered here by an explicit continuity of purpose rather than of brand.

bsides-peru.def: The Peruvian edition of the global Security BSides circuit, running since 2018 - community-organised, free of commercial pitches, and built around technical talks on real problems.
bsides-peru.context: Peru now carries both formats that this region tends to produce in pairs: a free community conference and an independent offensive-security event. That pairing is the same structure Brazil arrived at with BSides São Paulo alongside the invite-only YSTS, and it appears to be what a maturing scene converges on - one venue optimized for access, another for depth, rather than one event trying to be both.

security-bsides.def: Security BSides is the worldwide family of community-run information security conferences that began in Las Vegas on 29 and 30 July 2009 with talks Black Hat had no room for, named after the B-side of a vinyl record; by November 2026 its organizers counted 1,389 events in 305 cities in 74 countries.
security-bsides.context: The origin is the whole design. Rather than argue with a selection committee, the first organizers, usually credited as Mike Dahn, Jack Daniel and Chris Nickerson, ran the rejected talks as their own event, then released the format so that anyone could start a local edition under a short set of rules: an open call for papers, low fees, no selling of attendee data or speaking slots, and a name tied to a city. That is why BSides is a circuit rather than an institution: well over a thousand independent conferences sharing a name, a spirit and little else. In regions with one dominant or closed event, the local BSides is usually the open counterpart that appears beside it, a pattern visible in São Paulo, across Brazil and in Peru.
security-bsides.depth:
What it is, and what it is not. BSides is not one conference but a framework for building events for and by the security community, in the words of its global site, and a movement whose stated principles are to expand the conversation, enable people to join the discussion and get people involved. There is no central programme or headquarters: each organizing team is solely responsible for the event it produces and answers to its own community. As of November 2026 the global site counted 1,389 BSides events held in 305 cities in 74 countries, which makes it by far the largest family of security conferences by number of events, although almost every individual event is small, often a single day for a few hundred people.

How it started. In the summer of 2009, shortly after Black Hat announced its speaker line-up, a conversation began on Twitter, Facebook and email, first as an expression of disappointment at not being accepted to speak; the global community's history names Mike Murray, Chris Nickerson, Mike Dahn, Davi Ottenheimer and Anton Chuvakin among those involved. A second conversation, about the politics of conferences and the wish for a friendlier event, ran alongside it. Dahn originally wanted to call the result Security Fringe; friends advised Security BSides instead, after the B-side of a vinyl record. Murray, Dahn and Jennifer Leggio mapped out the business side; Nickerson provided a house in Las Vegas as the venue and gathered sponsors, Dahn built the website, Travis Goodspeed made the badges, and when a family tragedy took Dahn away the week before, Nickerson and Jack Daniel ran the event. Security BSides 1.0 took place on 29 and 30 July 2009, alongside Black Hat, organized almost as an unconference, with talks chosen just before the event through an online community process. Wikipedia credits Dahn, Daniel and Nickerson as the co-founders.

How it grew. In July 2010 Nickerson secured a mansion on the outskirts of Las Vegas with four pools, two tracks, 25 volunteers and about 650 attendees, and BSides events were held that year in Berlin, Ottawa, Dallas, Delaware, Atlanta, Kansas City, Denver, Boston, Austin and San Francisco, each with between 100 and 300 participants. In 2011 the movement passed 40 events, reached Australia and Africa and held its first United Kingdom edition in London, and in March 2011 Dahn registered Security BSides as a corporation in California. That non-profit, Security B-Sides, now runs BSides San Francisco and acts as global steward, holding the intellectual property and handling domains, after its founders concluded that a large central organization would compete with individual events for resources; the organizers of all the events form an informal community council, and a volunteer team maintains the site and mentors new organizers. BSides Las Vegas is still held each August, in the same week as Black Hat and DEF CON, and is counted as part of hacker summer camp; in 2026 it ran from 3 to 5 August.

The rules. The global rules are short. Non-negotiable: a fair and open call for presenters, keeping participants and the steering committee informed, and at least one organizer in the organizers' mailing group. Beyond that, the guidance is that registration should be nominal, with discounts for students, the unemployed and people on low incomes, because entirely free events often see no-show rates above 50 per cent; that participant information must never be sold or shared with sponsors, and badges should carry no barcodes for lead generation; that speaking slots are never sold, sponsors submit through the call for papers like everyone else, and joint events with other organizations are avoided; that organizers should not go into debt; and that event names should refer to a city or town, because state and country names are not permitted. The ideal core team is put at two or three people with six to eight months of planning, and the vocabulary is deliberate: participants, not attendees, and sponsors, not vendors.

Brazil. The São Paulo edition began as the Conferência O Outro Lado (CoOL), held on Saturday 15 May 2011 at the former headquarters of the Garoa Hacker Clube: 84 people, nine talks and two workshops in the hackerspace's small rooms, with a barbecue in the yard, all free. In 2012 the Security BSides organizers in the United States approved it as the official BSides of São Paulo. Fifteen years later, on 16 and 17 May 2026, Security BSides São Paulo received 3,431 people over two days, from 6,312 confirmed registrations, 3,120 of them on the Sunday, which places it among the largest BSides anywhere; it is held on the weekend before the invitation-only You Sh0t the Sheriff (YSTS), which in 2026 took place on Monday 18 May. Because the rules tie each event to a city, Brazil has no national BSides but a constellation: the global chapter list in November 2026 included Brasília, Curitiba, Florianópolis, Fortaleza, João Pessoa, Rio de Janeiro, São Paulo and Vitória, and Anchises Moraes, one of the São Paulo organizers, counted five BSides in Brazil in 2025 and at least nine in 2026, from Rio de Janeiro on 28 March to Brasília on 14 November and Porto Seguro, in Bahia, on 5 December.

The rest of Latin America. The same pattern runs through the region, with BSides in Panama (January 2026), Colombia (April), Mexico City (July) and Chile (November), and in Lima, where the chapter is listed as BSides Peru; in Portugal, Porto and Lisbon hold their own. In most of these places the BSides sits beside an established event rather than replacing it: in São Paulo, for example, next to the invitation-only YSTS and the research-heavy Hackers to Hackers Conference (H2HC), which is the counterpart role the movement was designed for.

Why the model matters, and where it strains. The open call for papers is the whole mechanism. A researcher with no reputation cannot get accepted at an established conference and cannot build a reputation without presenting somewhere, a loop that keeps new voices out unless something breaks it; BSides breaks it on purpose by accepting first-time speakers, and many of them go on to larger stages. The looseness that makes it spread also limits it. The central body has little power beyond the use of the name, so quality and conduct depend on each local team: in 2022, BSides Cleveland was criticized for booking, as an unannounced surprise speaker, a person previously banned by DEF CON, several experts withdrew, and the organizer stepped down in favour of a four-person team supported by the central organizers. The numbers worth remembering are 2009 for the first event, Las Vegas for the first city, more than 1,300 events since, and a rule set that fits on one page.

dmarc.def: DMARC (Domain-based Message Authentication, Reporting, and Conformance) is an email policy published in DNS (the Domain Name System) under which a message passes only if an SPF (Sender Policy Framework) or DKIM (DomainKeys Identified Mail) pass is aligned with the domain in the visible From header.
dmarc.context: SPF (Sender Policy Framework) and DKIM (DomainKeys Identified Mail) authenticate domains the reader never sees; DMARC (Domain-based Message Authentication, Reporting, and Conformance) ties them to the From domain the reader does see and lets that domain ask for reports. Since May 2026 it is Standards Track: RFC (Request for Comments) 9989, with aggregate and failure reporting in RFC 9990 and RFC 9991, which together obsolete the Informational RFC 7489.
dmarc.depth:
What it is. DMARC (Domain-based Message Authentication, Reporting, and Conformance) lets the owner of the domain in a message's From header, the Author Domain, publish in DNS (the Domain Name System) how receivers should treat mail that fails validation, and ask them for reports. It adds no cryptography of its own. SPF (Sender Policy Framework) authenticates the envelope sender, the MAIL FROM of the SMTP (Simple Mail Transfer Protocol) session, and DKIM (DomainKeys Identified Mail) authenticates the d= domain of a signature; neither has to match the From address a person reads. DMARC's contribution is alignment: one of those authenticated domains must belong to the From domain. Its own specification is plain about the limits: a pass says only that the use of the domain was authorized, not that the mail is safe, and carries no value judgement about the message or its sender.

From industry draft to standard. DMARC.org records that, building on efforts begun in 2010, a group of receivers (AOL, Comcast, Gmail, Hotmail, Netease and Yahoo! Mail), senders such as Bank of America, Facebook, Fidelity, JPMorgan Chase, LinkedIn and PayPal, and vendors came together in spring 2011, published the specification on 30 January 2012, circulated it as an Internet-Draft on 31 March 2013 and moved it to the Independent Submissions track on 2 April 2014. It became RFC (Request for Comments) 7489 in March 2015, edited by M. Kucherawy and E. Zwicky, an Informational document from the Independent Submissions Editor rather than an IETF (Internet Engineering Task Force) standard. The IETF's dmarc working group then produced DMARCbis, published in May 2026 as three Proposed Standards: RFC 9989, the protocol, edited by Todd M. Herr and John Levine; RFC 9990, aggregate reporting, edited by Alex Brotman; and RFC 9991, failure reporting, edited by Steven M. Jones and Alessandro Vesely. Together they obsolete RFC 7489, and RFC 9989 also obsoletes RFC 9091 (July 2021), the experimental extension for public suffix domains.

The record. The policy is a TXT (text) record at _dmarc under the domain, such as _dmarc.example.com. It must begin with v=DMARC1, or the whole record is ignored, and unknown tags must be ignored. p sets the policy: none, quarantine or reject, and none if absent. sp covers existing subdomains and np non-existent ones, those for which DNS answers NXDOMAIN; psd says whether the domain is a public suffix domain (y), an organizational domain for itself (n) or unknown (u, the default); t=y marks a policy under test. rua lists the URIs (uniform resource identifiers) for aggregate reports and ruf those for failure reports, every reporter must support mailto:, and without rua no aggregate reports are sent at all; fo chooses which failures trigger a failure report (0, 1, d for DKIM, s for SPF); adkim and aspf choose strict or relaxed alignment for each mechanism. On 12 November 2026 Google Public DNS returned v=DMARC1; p=reject; rua=mailto:mailauth-reports@google.com for _dmarc.google.com, and for _dmarc.gmail.com v=DMARC1; p=none; sp=quarantine with the same reporting address.

Alignment. A message passes when its From domain aligns with a DKIM d= domain or an SPF-validated MAIL FROM, never HELO: relaxed alignment needs the same Organizational Domain, strict needs identical names, and relaxed is the default. SPF can validate both the HELO and the MAIL FROM identities, but DMARC uses only MAIL FROM, and RFC 9989 explains why alignment is required at all: any domain owner, a bad actor included, can publish SPF for its own domain and get an SPF pass, so only an aligned pass proves anything about the From domain. A DKIM signature by a mailing service with its own d= domain, or an SPF pass for a bounce domain at a marketing platform, leaves DMARC failing unless one of them aligns.

The DNS Tree Walk. Against RFC 7489, RFC 9989 replaces the Public Suffix List with a DNS Tree Walk of at most eight queries, which also absorbs public suffix policy from RFC 9091, now obsolete. RFC 7489 had suggested, without requiring, the list at publicsuffix.org, set no refresh interval, and admitted that receivers using different lists could disagree. The walk instead queries _dmarc at the starting name and then removes labels from the left, stopping at a record that carries psd=y or psd=n; a name with eight or more labels is first cut to seven, so a hostile sender cannot force dozens of lookups, and the RFC notes that observed data showed Author Domains of up to seven labels in use. The same walk finds both the policy that applies and the Organizational Domain used for relaxed alignment, which lets large organizations publish DMARC records at several points in their namespace.

What changed in the tags, and the reports. RFC 9989 adds np, psd and t and removes pct, rf and ri: t=y asks receivers to apply one level below the stated policy, the role pct=0 had taken on. pct was meant to phase a policy in by percentage, but operational experience showed it was applied accurately only at 0 or 100, and pct=0 had become the signal by which intermediaries and mailbox providers rewrote the From header to avoid DMARC failures downstream; t=y keeps that signal without the arithmetic. Aggregate reports, XML (Extensible Markup Language) documents, moved to RFC 9990, and failure reports to RFC 9991. Aggregate reports, daily or more often, list for a domain owner each connecting IP (Internet Protocol) address that sent mail in its name and how its messages fared; failure reports describe single messages, carry privacy risk, and may be redacted.

What receivers do. Final handling is always local policy. A receiver may reject a message that passes, and may accept one that fails even under p=reject; RFC 9989 says in section 5.4 that receivers SHOULD NOT reject solely because of p=reject, and in section 7.4 that they MUST NOT reject on p=reject alone and, without other analysis, treat it as quarantine. They should add an Authentication-Results header field (RFC 8601), report any override through the PolicyOverride field of the aggregate report, and change nothing at all for p=none. When rejecting, a full rejection with a 5xy reply to DATA leaves the bounce to the sending server, while a silent discard avoids backscatter at the cost of a false success.

Forwarding and mailing lists. Forwarding breaks SPF, so a p=reject domain MUST sign with DKIM, and domains whose users post to mailing lists SHOULD NOT publish p=reject; the advised path is p=none for at least a month, then quarantine as long. RFC 7960 (September 2016) catalogued the trouble: alumni forwarders, role addresses and mailing lists relay mail from addresses the original SPF record never listed, lists that tag the subject line or add a footer to the body break DKIM signatures too, and a receiver that rejects such mail can get its own users unsubscribed by the list software. ARC, the Authenticated Received Chain (RFC 8617, Experimental, July 2019), lets intermediaries record and sign the authentication results they saw so that a later receiver can judge them. Large mailbox providers now push adoption: since 1 February 2024 Gmail requires every sender to use SPF or DKIM, and senders of more than 5,000 messages a day to use SPF, DKIM and DMARC, with p=none allowed and a From domain aligned with the SPF or DKIM domain. Numbers worth remembering: _dmarc, v=DMARC1, eight queries at most, one month at p=none, and RFC 9989, 9990 and 9991.

arc.def: An experimental email protocol in which each handler of a message records and seals the authentication results it saw.
arc.context: Forwarders break SPF and lists that edit messages break DKIM, so relayed mail from a p=reject domain can fail DMARC. ARC (RFC 8617, Experimental, 2019) lets each intermediary seal what it saw on arrival, and a receiver may accept that record as local policy. RFC 9989 names ARC as the main attempt to fix this and says none has become widely used.
arc.depth:
Each handler adds an ARC Set of three header fields: ARC-Authentication-Results, its assessment on arrival in Authentication-Results syntax; ARC-Message-Signature, a DKIM-like signature that identifies the custodian; and ARC-Seal, which binds the sets into a chain. Instance tags from 1 to 50 order the sets, each holding exactly one of each field, and the chain validation status cv is none, fail or pass.

ARC does not restore a broken SPF or DKIM result; it carries evidence about an earlier one. RFC 8617 lets a DMARC processor accept a chain's assessments as a matter of local policy, and warns that every sealer deserves suspicion, because a malicious actor could seal spam to help it through, and that an intact passing chain can be replayed to many recipients, as with DKIM. Which intermediaries to believe is a policy decision, not a cryptographic one.

RFC 8617 is still Experimental, neither updated nor obsoleted on its RFC Editor page, and it cites RFC 7489, now obsolete. RFC 9989 (May 2026) supports only DKIM and SPF as authentication mechanisms; it records that mailing list software has instead adopted From rewriting, such as the list's own address.

mta-sts.def: A mechanism by which a domain declares that mail sent to it must travel over authenticated TLS, published over HTTPS with a DNS pointer - closing the downgrade gap left by SMTP's opportunistic encryption. DANE solves the same problem using DNSSEC instead.
mta-sts.context: It is routinely confused with SPF, DKIM and DMARC, and it addresses a different problem entirely: those authenticate the sender, this protects the transport. SMTP's encryption is opportunistic by default, so an attacker in path can strip it and the mail flows in clear. Which of the two mechanisms you can deploy is mostly determined by whether your zone is signed - DANE requires DNSSEC, MTA-STS was designed for domains that do not have it.

passkey.def: A public-private key pair created for one specific site, where the private key never leaves the authenticator and the browser will only offer it to the exact origin it was registered for.
passkey.context: The absence of a shared secret is useful - a breached server database yields public keys - but origin binding is the actual innovation. On a lookalike domain the passkey does not appear, and a signature produced for the wrong origin is rejected by the real site, so the user cannot be talked into a mistake the browser will not make. Synced passkeys inherit the security of the platform account holding them, which is a fair trade for consumer services and a deliberate decision to review for administrative access.

webauthn.def: The browser interface websites call to create and use public-key credentials. CTAP is the protocol between browser and external authenticator; FIDO2 is the umbrella term covering both.
webauthn.context: The properties that matter to an implementer: the origin is included in the signed data, so credentials cannot be replayed to a different site; user verification by biometric or device PIN is performed locally and never transmitted, which is the point users most often assume works the other way round; and discoverable credentials allow account selection without a username. Recovery is deliberately out of scope, which is why it is the part every deployment has to design itself - and usually the part that reintroduces the phishable path.

aitm.def: Phishing that proxies the real site in real time: the fake page relays the victim's password and one-time code to the genuine service within their validity window, then steals the resulting session cookie.
aitm.context: It is why most deployed multi-factor authentication does not stop phishing. Codes, push approvals and authenticator apps all fail against it, because anything a person can read out and type can be relayed by someone else. Tooling for this is commodity rather than exotic. Only origin-bound credentials break the pattern, since the signature is tied to the site the browser is actually talking to - which is the argument for treating phishing-resistant authentication as a different category rather than a stronger grade of the same thing.

cross-device-authentication.def: The flow that lets a passkey held on one device authorize a sign-in on another - the site displays a code, the phone scans it, and the two link over Bluetooth Low Energy using the CTAP hybrid transport.
cross-device-authentication.context: The common misreading is that this makes the security of your login depend on Bluetooth. It does not: the exchange carries its own cryptography on top, and Bluetooth is used only to establish that the two devices are physically near each other. That proximity requirement is the anti-phishing property - a remote attacker's page cannot be in the room. It is also what makes passkeys usable without syncing, which matters for anyone deliberately keeping credentials device-bound.

shared-address-space.def: The IPv4 range reserved for the middle layer of carrier-grade NAT, between the subscriber's own private network and the provider's public addresses.
shared-address-space.context: It exists because providers were previously borrowing ordinary private ranges for this purpose, which collided with the ranges customers were already using at home and produced faults nobody could diagnose from either end. Treat an address from this range as a signal rather than a destination: it means the customer sits behind provider translation, so inbound connections will not work and the address does not identify a household.
shared-address-space.depth:
RFC 6598 (April 2012) reserved 100.64.0.0/10, 4,194,304 addresses from 100.64.0.0 to 100.127.255.255, because providers said a /10 was the smallest block that let them deploy CGNs regionally without nesting them. RFC 1918 space remains safe on the CGN-to-CPE link only if the provider knows the CPE copes with the same block on both sides, or that subscribers do not use it, which an unmanaged service cannot know. Numbering the link from someone else's public space, squat space, is forbidden.

The rules are MUSTs: packets with these addresses must not cross provider boundaries, the range must stay out of external DNS zones, and reverse queries for it must not reach the global DNS. The IANA registry marks it forwardable but not globally reachable. One behaviour differs from RFC 1918 space: a CPE given a shared or public WAN address may try 6to4, which then fails.

On a router or Linux host, ip address show to 100.64.0.0/10 finds a WAN address in the range, and a traceroute shows it as an early hop after the home router. The SSRF URL classifier flags such addresses as CGNAT.

port-block-allocation.def: Assigning each subscriber a fixed, predictable block of source ports for the duration of a session, and logging that assignment - rather than logging every individual translation as it happens.
port-block-allocation.context: It is the difference between a retention obligation that is affordable and one that is not: logging moves from per-flow to per-session, and attribution becomes arithmetic rather than a search through a flow database. That matters most where the output is a name given to a court, because a defensible answer requires address, port and timestamp together. The trade is that block size caps a subscriber's simultaneous connections, and an undersized block produces failures users report as random network faults.
port-block-allocation.depth:
Two schemes share the name. In RFC 7768's dynamic form the NAT gives a subscriber a block of ports, for example 2001 to 2300, on the first packet, adds another block when needed and writes one log line per block allocated or released, reducing log volume by the block size; it cites 42.5 TB of per-session logs against 40.6 GB with blocks, for 20,000 subscribers over 60 days, about 1,047 to 1. In RFC 7422's deterministic form the block is a function of the inside address, so only configuration changes and overflow blocks need logging.

RFC 7422's example puts 198.51.100.0/28 behind 192.0.2.1 with a dynamic pool factor of 2, a ratio of 1:16, and (65536 minus 1024)/16 = 4032 ports per inside address: subscriber 1 holds 1024 to 5055 and the dynamic pool runs from 57472 to 65535. A report for port 2001 maps straight back to subscriber 1; one for port 58204 lands in the dynamic pool and needs the log. The CGN must keep a record whenever those parameters change.

The trade sits among RFC 6888's three soft goals, port utilization, log volume and resistance to port guessing, so RFC 7422 asks for random port choice within each block.

source-port-logging.def: Recording the remote source port and an accurate timestamp alongside the remote address, so that a report about an event remains attributable when the address is shared by many subscribers.
source-port-logging.context: Without the port, an abuse report against a carrier-grade NAT address is unanswerable: the provider can only say that some hundreds of customers were behind that address at that moment. Most internet-facing services still log the address alone, which is why so many reports go nowhere and why blocking by address punishes a whole shared pool. It costs one extra field, and it is the single cheapest thing a service operator can do to make the abuse ecosystem work.
source-port-logging.depth:
RFC 6302 (June 2011) asks internet-facing servers to record, with each connection, the source port, a timestamp in UTC accurate to the second from a traceable source such as NTP, and the transport and destination port where a service uses several. The same applies to load balancers logging on behalf of servers, and to IPv6 for consistency.

Precision matters because ports are reused. RFC 6888 only asks a CGN to wait 120 seconds before reallocating a port, some reuse ports almost at once, and RFC 6269 warns that even small clock skew between a server and a densely used CGN makes the subscriber ambiguous. The alternative, logging destinations at the CGN, is weaker: it cannot separate subscribers who reach a popular server at nearly the same time, and RFC 6888 says a CGN should not log destinations at all.

Common servers can do it: Apache with %a and %'{remote}'p in the log format, Postfix with smtpd_client_port_logging, off by default, and OpenSSH with LogLevel VERBOSE. RFC 7768 recorded that IIS, Cyrus IMAP and UW IMAP could not. In Brazil, the Marco Civil's definition of a connection record names date, time, duration and IP address, not the port.

ransomware.def: An intrusion that ends in encrypting the victim's data for payment and, in its modern form, in copying that data out first, so that the threat to publish survives any recovery.
ransomware.context: The operational detail that matters for defence is the order: capable operators locate and destroy backups before encrypting production, because the recovery path is what determines whether anyone pays. So backup design became an adversarial problem rather than an availability one. The double form splits the incident into two decisions: restore, which good backups answer completely, and disclosure, which they do not answer at all and which runs on regulatory clocks of its own.
ransomware.depth:
The National Institute of Standards and Technology (NIST) defines ransomware in Interagency Report (IR) 8374 as a type of malicious attack in which attackers encrypt an organization's data and demand payment to restore access, adding that they may also steal the organization's information and demand a further payment for not disclosing it to authorities, competitors or the public. The #StopRansomware Guide published by the Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency (CISA) with the Multi-State Information Sharing and Analysis Center (MS-ISAC), the National Security Agency (NSA) and the Federal Bureau of Investigation (FBI) puts the mechanism plainly, malware that encrypts files on a device and renders them and the systems that rely on them unusable, and names the second move double extortion: data theft plus the threat to release what was stolen. It also notes the variant that skips encryption altogether and only steals and threatens. In both documents the encryption is the last act of an intrusion, not the intrusion itself; the CISA guide says a ransomware infection may be evidence of a previous, unresolved compromise, and that operators of the precursor malware often sell access to the networks they hold.

The idea is older than the internet economy that now runs it. Virus Bulletin's January 1990 issue analysed the AIDS Information disk: between 8 and 12 December 1989 several thousand diskettes were posted from London to computer users in the United Kingdom, Europe, Africa, Scandinavia and Australia, many to the subscriber list of the magazine PC Business World, obtained by deception; delegates to an AIDS congress held in Stockholm in October 1988 had also been targeted. The disk carried an interactive questionnaire about the disease and a Trojan from a firm calling itself PC Cyborg Corporation. Once installed through a modified AUTOEXEC.BAT it counted reboots, usually 90 in tests, then hid the directories, encrypted the file names with substitution tables built into the program, and demanded payment for leasing the software to a post office box in Panama. Because the tables were in the code, the analyst Jim Bates could write AIDSOUT to remove it and CLEARAID to recover the scrambled names; the attacker's leverage lasted only until somebody read the program.

WannaCry showed what happens when the payload can spread by itself. On Friday 12 May 2017, according to the United Kingdom's National Audit Office (NAO), it reached more than 200,000 computers in at least 100 countries. In England it affected at least 80 of the 236 National Health Service (NHS) trusts, 34 of them infected and locked out of their devices, plus 603 primary care and other NHS organizations including 595 general practices; NHS England counted 6,912 cancelled appointments and estimated more than 19,000. A researcher stopped the locking that evening by activating a kill switch tied to a domain the malware contacted. Every infected NHS organization had unpatched or unsupported Windows, most of them supported Windows 7 machines that a patch Microsoft had issued in March 2017 would have protected; Microsoft's bulletin of that month for the SMBv1 (Server Message Block version 1) server, MS17-010, is dated 14 March, and on 13 May Microsoft took the unusual step of making the update available for Windows XP, Windows 8 and Windows Server 2003. On 19 December 2017 the British government attributed the campaign to the North Korean actors known as the Lazarus Group, putting the total at 300,000 computers in 150 countries.

Colonial Pipeline showed that the cost of ransomware is measured in availability. Its chief executive, Joseph Blount, told a United States Senate committee on 8 June 2021 that an employee found the ransom note of the DarkSide group on a system in the information technology (IT) network just before 5:00 in the morning, Eastern Daylight Time, on Friday 7 May 2021. To keep the malware from reaching the operational technology (OT) network that controls the pipeline, the company halted operations: by 6:10 all 5,500 miles were shut, a system with about 260 delivery points across 13 states and Washington, D.C. that carries nearly half of the fuel consumed on the East Coast. Product began moving again on the evening of Wednesday 12 May. Blount said the attacker had used a legacy virtual private network (VPN) profile that was not meant to be in use, and that he had decided to pay. The Department of Justice put the payment at about 75 bitcoin on 8 May and announced on 7 June 2021 that it had seized 63.7 bitcoin, then about 2.3 million dollars. The encryption hit IT; the shutdown of the physical system was a precaution, and the shortage it caused was the real damage.

Brazil's highest-profile case hit the judiciary. On the afternoon of Tuesday 3 November 2020, as Consultor Jurídico reported the next day, the network of the Superior Tribunal de Justiça (STJ), the country's second-highest court, was attacked while its six panels were in session; the court's president, Humberto Martins, called in the Federal Police and procedural deadlines were suspended until 9 November. On 7 November Migalhas reported the court's confirmation that the attacker had encrypted and blocked access to its data, that the backup of its 255,000 cases had been preserved, that the Army's Cyber Defence Command was helping, and that work was expected to resume on 10 November. The regulatory clock in Brazil is now explicit: the ANPD, Brazil's data protection authority, then the Autoridade Nacional de Proteção de Dados and, since Provisional Measure 1.317 took effect on 18 September 2025 (converted into Law 15.352 of 25 February 2026), the Agência Nacional, issued Resolution CD/ANPD number 15 on 24 April 2024, which requires a controller to notify it within three working days of learning that an incident affected personal data, with twenty working days to complete a preliminary notice.

The CISA guide reads like a map of where these intrusions begin and how they end. The common ways in are internet-facing vulnerabilities and exposed services such as the Remote Desktop Protocol (RDP), compromised credentials, phishing, and precursor malware of the kind it names (QakBot, Emotet, Bumblebee), and the answers it gives are patching with priority for known exploited vulnerabilities, phishing-resistant multi-factor authentication (MFA) for email, VPN and critical systems, unique passwords of at least 15 characters, and centrally managed endpoint detection and response (EDR). On recovery it is blunt about the adversary: many ransomware variants try to find and delete or encrypt accessible backups, which is why backups must be offline, encrypted and regularly tested, why golden images of critical systems speed rebuilding, and why immutable cloud storage needs care, because a misconfiguration there can be costly too. Its response checklist starts with identifying the affected systems and isolating them, taking the network offline at the switch level if many subnets are hit, coordinating out of band so the intruders do not learn they have been seen, and powering devices down only when they cannot be disconnected, since that destroys the artefacts of the infection.

The double form changes what a good recovery buys. Restoring from clean backups ends the outage and answers the extortion over availability completely; it answers the extortion over publication not at all, because the copy is already outside, and the notification duties to regulators and to the people whose data was taken run on their own timetable whatever the restore achieves. NIST's revised profile, IR 8374 Revision 1 of June 2026, which superseded the 2022 version, maps the defences onto the six functions of its Cybersecurity Framework (CSF) 2.0, adding governance to identification, protection, detection, response and recovery, and offers itself as the basis for a ransomware countermeasure playbook. The CISA guide adds the practical step that matters on the worst day: report to CISA or the local FBI field office early, because researchers sometimes release decryptors and law enforcement may know of one.

immutable-backup.def: A backup copy that cannot be altered or deleted for a defined period, even by an administrator - achieved through storage-level object lock, genuinely offline media, or a separate trust domain with its own identity.
immutable-backup.context: The classic 3-2-1 rule - three copies, two media, one off-site - predates an adversary who hunts backups, and every copy it describes can sit behind the same administrative credential. The missing clause is that one copy must fall outside the blast radius of the credentials that manage production, because if a domain administrator can delete the backups then a domain administrator compromise deletes all of them regardless of how many there are. Retention should also outlast plausible dwell time, or every surviving copy already contains the intrusion.

rpo-rto.def: Recovery point objective is how much data you accept losing, measured backwards from the incident; recovery time objective is how long you accept being down. Together they define what a recovery plan must achieve.
rpo-rto.context: Both are frequently written into policy and never validated, which makes them aspirations rather than objectives. The only thing that converts them is a timed restore: run it on a schedule, measure the actual throughput against the real data volume, and compare. The failures that surface are rarely the backup itself - a missing dependency, an identity provider that is part of the outage, a runbook stored inside the environment it describes. An untested restore is a hypothesis, and stating an objective it has never met is worse than stating none.

bcp38.def: The practice of a network verifying that packets leaving it carry source addresses that actually belong to it, and dropping those that do not - blocking address forgery at the point where it originates.
bcp38.context: It is the reason reflection attacks are possible at scale, and its adoption problem is economic rather than technical. A network that filters its own customers' forged packets protects strangers from attacks it will never see, and gains nothing measurable on its own dashboards. The guidance is from the 1990s, uncontroversial, and still not universal - which makes it the clearest case in networking of a control whose beneficiaries and implementers are different people.

amplification-attack.def: Sending small forged requests to public servers so their much larger replies are delivered to a victim - reflection provides the disguise, amplification provides the volume.
amplification-attack.context: Two conditions are required: a protocol whose answer is far larger than its question, usually over UDP, and a network that permits source address forgery. Only the second is fixable at scale, which is why the defence lives at other people's edges rather than at the victim's. The property that makes it hard to answer at the destination is that the arriving traffic comes from legitimate servers behaving correctly - there is nothing malicious to identify, only volume, so the response is capacity rather than filtering.

load-balancer.def: A device or service that accepts client traffic on one address and distributes it across a set of backend servers, tracking which of them are usable.
load-balancer.context: Its algorithm is the least consequential part of its configuration. What determines behaviour in production is the health check that defines which servers exist, the persistence rule that pins clients, and the drain and warm-up behaviour when the set changes. It is also in the path of everything, so it hides individual server failures from users and from operators, which is why per-member metrics matter more than the pool average, and why a pool that looks healthy can contain one member serving errors quickly enough to attract extra traffic.
load-balancer.depth:
What it is. A load balancer publishes one address, the virtual server or VIP (virtual Internet Protocol address), and spreads what arrives there across a pool of servers it currently considers usable. The Hypertext Transfer Protocol (HTTP) specification, RFC (Request for Comments) 9110, lists load balancing among the jobs of a gateway, or reverse proxy, that partitions HTTP services across multiple machines. Two families do it differently. A layer 4 balancer chooses per connection or flow: Amazon Web Services' (AWS) Network Load Balancer picks a target with a flow hash. A layer 7 balancer terminates the protocol and chooses per request: the AWS Application Load Balancer first evaluates listener rules in priority order and only then picks a target from the matching group. Global balancing across sites happens a layer earlier, in the Domain Name System (DNS) answer.

Where it came from. RFC 1794 (April 1995), by T. Brisco of Rutgers University, records that load balancing in DNS first meant clusters of functionally identical machines, and that around 1986 hacks to the Berkeley Internet Name Domain (BIND) server appeared: Bryan Beecher's Shuffle Address records and Marshall Rose's Round Robin code rotated address records, and Matt Madison of TGV ordered them by load using VMS facilities. Its complaint, that load was not actually a factor, still describes plain DNS round robin. DNS has not gone away: clients of an AWS load balancer resolve its name and receive the addresses of its nodes with a time to live (TTL) of 60 seconds, so they can be remapped quickly. At the other end of the scale, Google described Maglev at NSDI (the USENIX Symposium on Networked Systems Design and Implementation) in March 2016: a software layer 4 balancer serving its traffic since 2008, in which one machine saturates a 10 Gbit/s link with small packets, and which uses consistent hashing and connection tracking to limit what a failure disturbs.

Algorithms. The HAProxy 3.2 manual is a compact catalogue. roundrobin uses servers in turn according to their weights, adjusts weights on the fly, and is limited to 4,095 active servers per backend; leastconn sends a connection to the server with fewest connections and is recommended for very long sessions such as LDAP (Lightweight Directory Access Protocol) and SQL (Structured Query Language) database sessions, but not well suited to short-session protocols such as HTTP; source hashes the client address, so a client keeps its server only as long as no server goes up or down; uri hashes the path to raise cache hit rates; random draws two servers by default and takes the less loaded, the power of two random choices, which avoids ever picking the most loaded server. AWS target groups offer round_robin by default, least_outstanding_requests and weighted_random. The choice matters less than it looks; what the balancer believes about its servers matters more.

Health checks define the pool. HAProxy checks every 2,000 milliseconds by default, declares a server dead after 3 consecutive failures and alive again after 2 successes. F5 BIG-IP monitors default to a 5-second interval and a 16-second timeout, following its rule that the timeout should be three times the interval plus one second; a target that does not answer within the timeout is considered down. The arithmetic is worth doing: with those defaults a dead member keeps receiving new connections for up to about 6 seconds on HAProxy and 16 on BIG-IP. What the check tests matters even more. A Transmission Control Protocol (TCP) check succeeds as soon as the connection is established; a content check sends a request such as GET / and looks for an expected string in the reply, and with both strings empty BIG-IP performs only a connection check. A server that accepts connections and answers every request with an error passes the first kind and fails the second.

Persistence and change. Persistence overrides the algorithm to keep a client on one server. Source address affinity, in F5's words, directs requests to the same server based solely on the source address, which collapses when thousands of users arrive from one carrier-grade network address translation (NAT) or proxy address; cookie persistence uses an HTTP cookie, inserted by the balancer by default on BIG-IP. Changing the pool is where outages hide. AWS keeps a deregistered target draining until in-flight requests complete, for a deregistration delay of 300 seconds by default and up to 3,600, and can give a new target a linearly increasing share of traffic over a slow-start period of 30 to 900 seconds, disabled by default.

Who the server thinks is calling. A balancer that translates the source address makes every request look as if it came from the balancer, which is also what guarantees the reply comes back through it: F5 documents source address translation (SNAT) precisely for servers whose default gateway is not the BIG-IP. The client's address then has to travel some other way. At layer 7 it rides in X-Forwarded-For or the standard Forwarded header of RFC 7239 (June 2014), which a server should accept only from proxies it trusts. At layer 4, the PROXY protocol written by Willy Tarreau, first published on 29 October 2010, with a binary format added in 2012, prepends the original connection details to the stream.

Where imbalance comes from. A balancer hides individual failures by design, so the evidence is in per-member statistics, not pool averages. Some imbalance is configuration: AWS keeps cross-zone load balancing always enabled at the load balancer level for Application Load Balancers but disabled by default for Network and Gateway Load Balancers, so a zone with fewer targets carries proportionally more per target. Some is persistence, some is a stale DNS answer, and some is a health check that tests the port instead of the application. The Gateway Load Balancer is the odd one out: it exists to insert appliances such as firewalls into a path, choosing one by a 5-tuple flow hash and exchanging traffic with it over GENEVE (Generic Network Virtualization Encapsulation) on port 6081.

session-persistence.def: Sending a returning client back to the same backend server, because that server holds state the others do not have.
session-persistence.context: It is best understood as an admission that the application is not stateless, and every method carries a cost. Source-address persistence concentrates whole carrier-NAT populations onto one server. Cookie persistence requires terminating the connection. The operational consequence people miss is that persistence and capacity work against each other: adding servers during a peak leaves them idle, because the load you wanted to move is pinned where it already is. Moving state to a shared store is the fix; persistence is what you run until then.

slow-start.def: Two behaviours for changing a pool safely: ramping a newly added member's share of traffic upward over time, and letting an outgoing member finish existing connections before removal.
slow-start.context: A fresh instance has cold caches, an empty connection pool and an unwarmed runtime, so giving it a full share immediately makes it slow, fail its own health check, get ejected and oscillate. Draining has the mirror problem: too short cuts live requests, never-completing blocks maintenance. Both are usually discovered during a release rather than designed, and both matter more than the balancing algorithm - which is why a capacity plan for N servers should be tested at N-1, since that is the state a failure actually puts you in.

detection-engineering.def: Treating each detection as an engineered artefact rather than a switch: a stated hypothesis, the data it requires, logic under version control, a test that proves it fires, a false-positive budget, a named owner and a documented response.
detection-engineering.context: It is the difference between a platform that costs money and a capability that finds intrusions, and it is almost never in the purchase order: the product is a cost, the content is the capability. The load-bearing element is the documented response: an alert nobody knows what to do with is worse than no alert, because it consumes the attention a real one needs and teaches the team that the console lies. Detections without owners are eventually suppressed or ignored, and both look identical on a dashboard.
detection-engineering.depth:
What it is, and what it is not. A security information and event management (SIEM) platform, an endpoint agent or an intrusion detection sensor ships with an engine and some vendor content; detection engineering is the work of writing, testing, deploying, tuning and retiring the logic that turns their telemetry into alerts worth a person's time. The UK National Cyber Security Centre (NCSC) calls the same work content development and use-case development in its guidance for security operations centres (SOCs), and sets out the trade-off at its root. Vendor rules are maintained by large teams who follow new attacker techniques, but they have to serve many customers, so their detection is biased towards the techniques that benefit the widest range of them; bespoke rules fit the organization's own technologies and threats and can be written without waiting for a supplier, but they rely on skilled analysts and on log tools that can be configured with detection logic. It is related to, but not the same as, threat hunting: a hunt is a human search for activity that no rule has flagged, and a good hunt ends either in a finding or in a new detection, so that the next occurrence is caught automatically.

Where the template comes from. The most cited formalization is the Alerting and Detection Strategies (ADS) framework that Palantir's incident response team published in 2017. Its README describes the problem it was built to fix: alerts going to production without documentation or peer review, some of which gained a reputation for low quality and caused fatigue, alerting apathy and wasted engineering time. Every new strategy has to complete nine sections before production: the goal; its categorization against MITRE ATT&CK; a strategy abstract; the technical context an analyst needs; the blind spots and assumptions; the known false positives; validation, meaning a way to produce a true positive on demand; the priority; and the response. Each one, draft or live, is stored in a version-controlled, central location. Most detection programmes since then use a variant of those headings, compressed into the same few questions: what is the hypothesis, what data does it need, how is it tested, what will it get wrong, who owns it and what happens when it fires.

Detection as code. The next step was a shared format. Sigma, the generic signature format for SIEM systems that Thomas Patzke presented at the Hack.lu conference in 2017 and that a group including him and Florian Roth maintains today, describes log events in a simple rule format, so that a detection can be written once and converted into the query language of whichever SIEM the reader runs; its README puts it as being for log files what Snort is for network traffic and YARA is for files. The main SigmaHQ repository held more than 3,000 rules when read in November 2026, split into generic detection rules that target a behaviour or technique, broader threat hunting rules meant as starting points for an analyst, emerging threat rules tied to a specific campaign or vulnerability, compliance rules and placeholder rules; conversion is done with the pySigma library or the Sigma command-line tool, and the content is published under the Detection Rule License 1.1. Treating rules as code brings the rest of software practice with them: pull requests and review, tests in a pipeline, version history that shows who changed a rule and why, and the ability to roll a bad change back.

What to detect. David Bianco's Pyramid of Pain, first posted on 1 March 2013, is still the clearest guide to choosing. It ranks the indicators a defender can deny an adversary, from hash values and IP addresses at the bottom, through domain names, network and host artefacts and tools, to tactics, techniques and procedures (TTPs) at the top. A hash is the most exact indicator and the cheapest for the attacker to change; detecting at the level of TTPs means operating on the behaviour itself, for example detecting pass-the-hash rather than the tool used for it, and if the response is fast enough it forces the adversary to do the most time-consuming thing possible: learn new behaviours. ATT&CK gives those behaviours stable names, and since version 18 of 28 October 2025 it has organized its own defensive content the same way, replacing the detection notes inside each technique with Detection Strategies and Analytics and deprecating its old Data Sources. Version 20, released on 13 October 2026, holds 703 detection strategies and 1,770 analytics for Enterprise alone; the one for credential stuffing, DET0460, carries separate analytics for remote desktop and file-sharing logons, Secure Shell (SSH) and other Unix logins, macOS logins, cloud identity providers, cloud applications and the authentication failures that routers and firewalls send to syslog.

Testing and the lifecycle. The NCSC's guidance treats a detection the way a developer treats a feature. Parsing tests prove that the right fields arrive in the right format, but genuine attacks rarely appear in logs the way one expects, so the use case has to be exercised: red team exercises show what the SOC missed, purple team exercises close the gaps with the SOC as they are found, and open-source test tooling exists for those who build their own platform, with the caveat that running tests on production systems carries risk. Every rule needs a lifecycle with regular reviews of the alerts that fire most, triage feedback that refines the logic, and a willingness to remove alerts with high false-positive rates; a rule that has never fired is not thereby invalid. Allow lists, which exclude specific users or addresses from a use case, are to be strictly bounded by object and time to avoid perpetual exclusions that become a way to evade monitoring. Alerts built on real attack profiles, which fire only when several detections agree, reduce false positives, since a single detection firing in isolation is more likely to be wrong. And the catalogue of detections must itself be protected, because to an attacker it is a list of gaps.

What goes wrong. Coverage theatre is the first trap. MITRE's own design paper for ATT&CK says that coverage of every technique is unrealistic, that the knowledge base is not a checklist, that some behaviours, such as an administrator running ipconfig.exe, should never raise an alert on their own, and that anyone mapping detections to ATT&CK should be able to explain which procedures they actually cover. A heat map of techniques with a rule attached says nothing about whether those rules have ever been seen to fire. The second trap is silent decay. A preprint posted to arXiv on 31 August 2026 by Sudaroli Dhananjeyan and Kumaran U measured exclusions across nine years and 8,234 revisions of the SigmaHQ corpus: exclusions were added 1,642 times and withdrawn 304, a ratio of 5.4 to 1 that rises to 13 to 1 for individual rules; an estimated 86.7 per cent were still in force three years later, regardless of whether the rule was the only coverage for its technique; and 64.1 per cent of the exclusions based on file paths could be satisfied by an unprivileged process that simply chose its file name. Each suppression is reasonable on the day it is made, and together they become an evasion route. The third trap is the oldest: a detection with no owner and no documented response, which degrades into a notification people learn to mute.

Neighbours. Detection engineering feeds the SOC, whose analysts triage what it produces; alert fatigue is its failure measured in human attention; the SIEM, the endpoint detection and response (EDR) agent and the network sensors are the engines it writes for; security orchestration, automation and response (SOAR) automates the response section of a strategy once it is trusted. Indicators of compromise (IoCs) give fast, short-lived detections, TTP-based analytics give durable ones, and a mature programme runs both. Red and purple teams are its test harness, and dwell time, the interval from compromise to detection, is the outcome it exists to shorten.

telemetry-selection.def: Deciding what to collect by asking which questions must be answerable, rather than collecting whatever is available until the licence bill forces cuts.
telemetry-selection.context: Volume-based pricing makes this an economic decision disguised as a technical one, and the sources cut first are frequently the useful ones - proxy and DNS logs are enormous and are also where lateral movement and exfiltration become visible. The consistently high-value set is identity events, endpoint process telemetry, DNS and egress, administrative audit trails, and the cloud control plane. Every omission is a blind spot no amount of correlation can fill, which is why gaps should be recorded deliberately rather than discovered during an investigation.

policy-sprawl.def: The accumulation of rules and exceptions that outgrows anyone's ability to review them, ending in permits nobody can justify and nobody dares remove.
policy-sprawl.context: It is the practical ceiling on granularity: per-workload policy on an estate that cannot maintain per-workload rules produces stale permits that quietly become permanent. A microsegmentation deployment full of allow-any exceptions reports coverage it does not have, and is less honest than a well-run tiered design. The countermeasure is unglamorous - treat exceptions as a register with named owners and review dates, since that list, rather than the policy document, is the real record of where risk sits.

co-channel-interference.def: The throughput loss that occurs when neighbouring access points share a channel: they do not corrupt each other's transmissions, they defer to them, so the available airtime is divided rather than added.
co-channel-interference.context: It is the most misdiagnosed wireless problem, because every signal indicator looks excellent while measured throughput collapses - and the usual response, adding more access points, is what caused it. The related trap is that the slowest client sets the pace: a device at a low data rate occupies the channel far longer to send the same bytes, so one distant laptop can consume the airtime a dozen nearby ones would have shared. Design for capacity means more radios at lower power on planned channels, not stronger signal.

wifi-generations.def: The successive amendments to IEEE 802.11, given retroactive marketing numbers in 2018 - from 2 Mbps in 1997 through MIMO, multi-user transmission, OFDMA, the 6 GHz band, and multi-link operation.
wifi-generations.context: The useful way to read the sequence is that the goal changed. Early generations sold raw modulation rate; from Wi-Fi 6 onward the features sell airtime efficiency and determinism - dividing a channel into resource units so small transmissions share a slot, letting a radio ignore a neighbouring network's traffic instead of deferring to it, and scheduling when battery devices listen. That shift happened because contention, not modulation, is what limits a busy network, which is also why a newer standard helps a crowded room more than it helps a fast laptop.

capwap.def: The standardized protocol between a wireless controller and its access points, carrying configuration, radio management and, optionally, the client data traffic itself.
capwap.context: The architectural decision it exposes is where user traffic goes. Tunnelling everything back to the controller makes policy and mobility simple and turns the controller into a bandwidth bottleneck and a single point of failure; local switching keeps traffic at the edge and pushes policy enforcement out with it. Neither is wrong, and the choice should be made deliberately rather than inherited from a default - particularly in branch sites, where a tunnelled design means a broken uplink stops local traffic that never needed to leave the building.

vint-cerf.def: The co-designer, with Bob Kahn, of TCP/IP - the protocols that turned separate networks into one internet - and joint recipient of the 2004 Turing Award for the work.
vint-cerf.context: Cerf and Kahn did not invent a network; they invented the agreement that lets networks that were never designed for each other exchange packets, which is why the citation reads for internetworking rather than for a protocol. Born in New Haven in June 1943, Cerf has had a hearing impairment since early life and has attributed part of his interest in networking to its promise as another channel for people who cannot use a telephone easily - a detail worth keeping, because the most consequential communications protocol of the century was partly motivated by someone who found the existing one hard to use. He has spent the decades since as the most public advocate the internet has, which is a job nobody appointed him to. He was inducted into the Internet Hall of Fame in its inaugural class of 2012, as a Pioneer.

bob-kahn.def: The co-designer of TCP/IP with Vint Cerf, and the 2004 Turing Award co-recipient, cited for the design and implementation of the internet's basic communications protocols.
bob-kahn.context: The Turing citation is specific about what the pair actually did: they formulated the design principles of internetworking, specified TCP/IP against those requirements, prototyped it, and coordinated the early implementations. That last verb matters more than it looks. A protocol that one team implements is a program; a protocol several teams implement compatibly is a standard, and getting there is coordination work rather than design work. Kahn's later decades went into the institutions around the technology rather than the technology itself, which is the less celebrated half of why any of it still functions.

bob-metcalfe.def: The inventor of Ethernet, at Xerox PARC in 1973, and recipient of the 2022 Turing Award for its invention, standardization and commercialization.
bob-metcalfe.context: The 1973 memo described a broadcast communication network for connecting PARC's Alto computers, and the first Ethernet ran at 2.94 Mbps - roughly ten thousand times faster than the terminal networks it replaced. The word that mattered was in the name: Metcalfe wrote of communication over an ether, which left the medium unspecified and is why the same design later survived twisted pair, fibre and radio. David Boggs, who died in 2022, co-invented it and co-authored the 1976 paper. The third word in the citation is the one engineers skip: after leaving Xerox, Metcalfe drove DEC, Intel and Xerox to a shared 10 Mbps specification rather than keeping it.
