radia-perlman.def: The engineer who invented the spanning tree algorithm at Digital Equipment Corporation in the 1980s, making bridged Ethernet with redundant links survivable, who designed the routing protocol standardized as IS-IS (Intermediate System to Intermediate System), and who wrote the algorithm's poem.
radia-perlman.context: Her 1985 paper let bridges of arbitrary topology agree on a loop-free tree without a central authority, and the Institute of Electrical and Electronics Engineers (IEEE) standardized it in 802.1D in 1990. Every switched network since has run a descendant. She published the algorithm with a poem attached, Algorhyme, whose first lines answer Joyce Kilmer's poem "Trees". She also designed the link-state routing behind IS-IS (Intermediate System to Intermediate System). The nickname she is given, mother of the internet, obscures the actual contribution: not that she connected things, but that she made a redundant network safe to build, which is a different and harder problem. She was inducted into the Internet Hall of Fame in 2014 and the National Inventors Hall of Fame in 2016.
radia-perlman.depth:
Radia Joy Perlman was born in 1951, according to the National Inventors Hall of Fame (Lemelson-MIT gives 1952 and Portsmouth, Virginia), and grew up in New Jersey, the child of two engineers. At the Massachusetts Institute of Technology (MIT) she took bachelor's and master's degrees in mathematics in 1973 and 1976, and while an undergraduate worked as a programmer in the Logo Lab, where she built TORTIS (Toddlers Own Recursive Turtle Interpreter System), hardware and software that let children as young as three assemble programs from physical objects; the Hall of Fame credits it with starting the field of tangible computing. She then joined BBN (Bolt Beranek and Newman) and began designing network protocols.

In 1980 she moved to Digital Equipment Corporation (DEC) to design the routing for DECnet, and that design was adopted as the international standard IS-IS (Intermediate System to Intermediate System). The National Inventors Hall of Fame describes the problem she started from: the routing protocol that worked at ARPANET scale, several hundred routers, would not work for larger networks and needed experts to manage it, and one of her first papers warned that a few bad messages injected into it could crash the network, which then happened. Eric Rosen's RFC 789 documents the event: on 27 October 1980 the ARPANET was unusable for several hours because three routing updates from one node, carrying the 6-bit sequence numbers 8, 40 and 44 after bits were dropped in memory, kept superseding one another in a cycle. Her answer was routing that is self-stabilizing, recovering by itself once misbehaving nodes are disconnected. Her Fault-Tolerant Broadcast of Routing Information (IEEE INFOCOM, April 1983; Computer Networks, December 1983) is cited in the IS-IS specification that David Oran republished as RFC 1142 in February 1990, and Ross Callon's RFC 1195 of December 1990 adapted IS-IS to route IP (Internet Protocol). The Internet Hall of Fame notes that it still flourishes for routing IP today, and Lemelson-MIT credits her with algorithms that made link-state protocols such as IS-IS and OSPF (Open Shortest Path First) efficient and scalable.

The spanning tree came out of a different need. Transparent bridges listened promiscuously on every port, learned where stations were and forwarded between LANs (local area networks) without the stations knowing, but they assumed a loop-free topology. As her 1985 paper puts it, that meant no backup paths, and a single loop could cause severe degradation of the whole extended network through infinitely circulating packets, so that a network could be brought down merely by plugging a cable into the wrong place. Her algorithm, presented at ACM (Association for Computing Machinery) SIGCOMM in 1985, has the bridges compute an acyclic spanning subset of an arbitrary topology between themselves. One bridge, the Root, is elected by lowest ID; on each LAN the bridge closest to the Root, with a tie-breaker, becomes the Designated Bridge and periodically sends HELLO messages to the all-bridges group address, carrying the Root's ID, the path cost, the age of the information and a MAX-AGE timer that the network agrees on. The only information a bridge needs in advance is its own unique ID, the paper says, and convergence time is proportional to the diameter of the network, with memory per bridge and bandwidth per LAN independent of the number of bridges or links. Redundant links stay in place, blocked, until a failure brings them back.

The paper's first page carries a poem next to the abstract, Algorhyme, which opens with Joyce Kilmer's 1914 line rewritten: I think that I shall never see a graph more lovely than a tree, a tree whose crucial property is loop-free connectivity. It walks through the protocol (first the Root must be selected, by ID it is elected; least-cost paths from the Root are traced) and ends: a mesh is made by folks like me, then bridges find a spanning tree. The IEEE (Institute of Electrical and Electronics Engineers) built the algorithm into 802.1D-1990, Media Access Control (MAC) Bridges, approved on 31 May 1990 and published on 8 March 1991. That standard was superseded by 802.1D-1998 and then 802.1D-2004, which in turn was folded into 802.1Q-2014. As she told the National Inventors Hall of Fame, she had assumed spanning tree would be a short-term fix lasting a few months, until deployed hosts could be upgraded to work with routers; it was so simple to manage that it is still everywhere.

She has also been its most precise critic. In a 2013 interview with LACNIC News she said spanning tree was good because it was largely self-configuring, you plug it in and it works, but that it does not make the best use of bandwidth, because a tree offers one path between two points and leaves links idle; and that it was built because people mistook Ethernet, meant for one building, for a protocol that could run a whole network. Her line to the National Inventors Hall of Fame is sharper: she wishes Ethernet had been called Etherlink, because Ethernet is not an entire network but a link in one. Her fix, begun at Sun Microsystems, was TRILL (Transparent Interconnection of Lots of Links). RFC 6325, published in July 2011 with Perlman as first author, specifies Routing Bridges (RBridges) that run IS-IS between themselves, encapsulate frames with a header that includes a hop count so that forwarding stays safe during temporary loops, use multiple paths for unicast and multicast, and terminate the classic spanning tree at their edge.

Her career followed the protocols. She left Digital in 1993 for Novell and joined Sun Microsystems in 1997, where Lemelson-MIT records her as a Distinguished Engineer in 2007; Intel named her director of Network and Security Technology in March 2011, and she was later a fellow at Intel Labs and then a Dell Technologies fellow. Her 1988 MIT doctoral thesis in electrical engineering and computer science, Network Layer Protocols with Byzantine Robustness, supervised by Dave Clark, is about networks that keep working while some participants misbehave. She wrote Interconnections: Bridges, Routers, Switches, and Internetworking Protocols (second edition, Addison-Wesley, 1999) and, with Charlie Kaufman and Mike Speciner, Network Security: Private Communication in a Public World, whose third edition in 2022 added Ray Perlner. The Internet Hall of Fame lists her security work on trust models for public key infrastructure (PKI), data expiration (the ephemerizer, in which destroying a dated key makes the data it protected unreadable) and distributed algorithms resilient to malicious participants, and states her design rule: systems should work with zero configuration, and where configuration is allowed, misconfiguration should not be possible.

She does not like the nickname. In 2011 she told Intel Free Press that mother of the internet was invented by a writer who interviewed her, that it is a title one has no clear way of earning, unlike a doctorate, that no single individual deserves credit for inventing the internet, and that the label oddly emphasizes gender. Her opinions on the protocols she did not design are just as direct: in the 2013 LACNIC interview she called it sad that IPv6 is technically worse than the ISO (International Organization for Standardization) proposal with 20-byte addresses that the internet community set aside in 1992, attributing the choice to rivalry between standards bodies, and described today's user authentication as neither secure nor usable.

The honours are the expected ones, and the patent counts depend on the date of the page: more than 200 US patents according to the National Inventors Hall of Fame, which inducted her in 2016 for robust network routing and bridging; more than 100 on her Internet Hall of Fame page, from her 2014 induction; some 80 in the older Lemelson-MIT profile. She is a member of the National Academy of Engineering, a fellow of the ACM and the IEEE, and has received lifetime achievement awards from ACM SIGCOMM (Special Interest Group on Data Communication) and USENIX. She has taught at the University of Washington, Harvard and MIT, and later co-taught a course based on Network Security at Texas A&M University.

jon-postel.def: The editor of the Request for Comments (RFC) series from its first years until his death in 1998, author or editor of the specifications of the Internet Protocol (IP), ICMP (Internet Control Message Protocol) and TCP (Transmission Control Protocol), and the first director of the Internet Assigned Numbers Authority (IANA), a job he volunteered for and at first did by hand.
jon-postel.context: For almost three decades one person shepherded the documents that define the internet, and the numbering authority that keeps addresses and protocol parameters unique began as him keeping a list. That is the part worth sitting with: the global registry that governments now argue over started as a volunteer's clerical habit at the University of Southern California. His most quoted line, from the 1980 specifications of IP (Internet Protocol) and TCP (Transmission Control Protocol), is the robustness principle: be conservative in what you send, liberal in what you accept. It shaped protocol design for forty years, and in 2023 the Internet Architecture Board (IAB) qualified it in RFC (Request for Comments) 9413, on the grounds that tolerated errors become entrenched and eventually become the specification.
jon-postel.depth:
Jonathan B. Postel came to networking at the University of California, Los Angeles (UCLA). Vint Cerf, from the same high school in the San Fernando Valley, Van Nuys High, recalled in RFC 2468 that they really met as graduate students working for Professor Leonard Kleinrock on the ARPANET project; the Internet Hall of Fame records that Postel was on the UCLA team that set up the network's first node in 1969 and took his PhD in computer science there in 1974. When Steve Crocker invented the Request for Comments (RFC) series, in Cerf's words, Jon became the instant editor, and when the network needed someone to keep track of hosts and protocol identifiers he volunteered to be the Numbers Czar.

RFC 1, Host Software, is dated 7 April 1969. The RFC Editor's own history says the series was managed and edited by Postel for 28 years, funded by the Defense Advanced Research Projects Agency (DARPA) until 1998 and run as a project of the USC (University of Southern California) Information Sciences Institute (ISI) in Marina del Rey. He also edited the 204 Internet Experiment Notes (IENs) of 1977 to 1982, and the same history credits that parallel series for his later, vigorous opposition to any other. Editing meant more than layout. Cerf called him the network's Boswell and wrote in RFC 2555 that he would not let a document out that failed his personal quality filter, so that many bad design decisions were reworked; Danny Cohen, who worked alongside him at ISI from 1977 to 1993, said in RFC 2441 that Postel routinely told authors that earlier work had already treated their subject. He also let the series carry poetry and the April 1 humour RFCs.

In January 1980 ISI published, for DARPA, the DoD (Department of Defense) Standard Internet Protocol as RFC 760 and the DoD Standard Transmission Control Protocol as RFC 761. The User Datagram Protocol (UDP), RFC 768, is his alone and dated 28 August 1980. September 1981 brought the set that defined the internet for decades: RFC 790, Assigned Numbers; RFC 791, Internet Protocol; RFC 792, Internet Control Message Protocol (ICMP); and RFC 793, Transmission Control Protocol (TCP), whose preface mentions nine earlier editions of the ARPA TCP specification and is signed Jon Postel, Editor. RFC 821, the Simple Mail Transfer Protocol (SMTP), followed in August 1982, replacing RFCs 788, 780 and 772. The Internet Hall of Fame counts more than 200 RFCs he wrote or co-wrote, and John Klensin's judgement there is that Cerf and Bob Kahn designed TCP/IP but Postel wrote many of the specifications that let the world use it. He also set the naming work in motion: Paul Mockapetris, who joined ISI in 1978 on a team of about twenty supervised by Postel, recalls him walking into his office and asking whether he would like to work on the domain naming problem.

The sentence the field quotes is his. RFC 760 asked that an implementation be conservative in its sending behaviour and liberal in its receiving behaviour: careful to send well-formed datagrams, but accepting any datagram it could interpret, without objecting to technical errors where the meaning was still clear. RFC 761 compressed it into a general principle of robustness, be conservative in what you do, be liberal in what you accept from others, and RFC 793 repeated it in a section of its own. The Internet Architecture Board (IAB) restated it in June 1996 in RFC 1958, Architectural Principles of the Internet, as be strict when sending and tolerant when receiving. RFC 9413 itself calls it hugely influential in shaping the design of the internet.

The qualification came from inside the institutions he helped build. RFC 9413, Maintaining Robust Protocols, published by the IAB in June 2023 (Martin Thomson and David Schinazi, from a 2018 draft), separates three aspects of the principle. Robustness to software defects and robustness to attacks remain necessary; tolerating unexpected input is, in its words, no longer considered best practice in all scenarios. Its argument is protocol decay: each tolerated error becomes something every other implementation must also tolerate, until a flaw is entrenched as a de facto standard and new implementations have to be bug-for-bug compatible. The remedy it proposes is active protocol maintenance by designers, implementers and operators together, and, where it helps, what it calls virtuous intolerance, an implementation that refuses the error so that the error gets fixed.

The numbers job became the Internet Assigned Numbers Authority (IANA). The Internet Hall of Fame describes it as a task he volunteered for and at first performed manually, which gave numbering and protocol management the stability they needed to scale. By March 1994, when he wrote RFC 1591, Domain Name System Structure and Delegation, IANA was the overall authority for IP (Internet Protocol) addresses, domain names and many other parameters, with day-to-day assignment handled by the Internet Registry and the regional registries. That memo listed the generic top-level domains (EDU, COM, NET, ORG, GOV, MIL and INT) and the two-letter country codes from ISO 3166, judged it extremely unlikely that any other top-level domains would be created, and set the rule that a designated manager is a trustee for the delegated domain with a duty to serve the community, so that concerns about rights and ownership were inappropriate. He was also, Cerf adds, custodian of .US, a founder of the Los Nettos regional network, a founding member of the IAB and the first individual member of the Internet Society, having beaten Steve Wolff in a race to send in the form; he was its trustee from 1993 to 1998. Cohen's summary was that the papers called Jon the director of IANA, but Jon was IANA.

That personal authority was tested in January 1998. Wired News reported on 5 February that Postel, as head of IANA, had asked the operators of six of the internet's dozen root servers to take their daily update from a system he controlled instead of from Network Solutions, which held the US government contract to handle the domain name system and was about to lose its exclusive position; he described it as a test of what problems such a switch might raise. He gave no prior notice. Network Solutions complained of uncertainty and perceived instability and asked who could authorize changes to the infrastructure, and the White House adviser Ira Magaziner, whose administration had just published its own plan, called the timing a bit dicey and said he would give Postel some slack. Later retellings, including the Internet Hall of Fame's in 2012, put the number at eight of twelve operators and note that some saw a routine test and others a statement to the government about who actually ran the root. Either way, it showed how much of the system then rested on one person's word.

He died on 16 October 1998, aged 55, from complications during a heart operation, as the Internet Corporation for Assigned Names and Numbers (ICANN) was being formed; he had been slated to serve as its chief technology officer. Cerf's remembrance, dated the next day and published as RFC 2468, a number Postel's successor as RFC Editor, Joyce Reynolds, chose on purpose, notes that he had completed the incorporation of a successor to his IANA service and had recently received the Silver Medal of the International Telecommunication Union at the Internet Society meeting in Geneva. Cerf also pledged the Jonathan B. Postel Service Award, given to Postel posthumously as its first recipient and still presented every year by the Internet Society, now with a US$20,000 honorarium, for sustained service to the internet community. Today the IANA functions are performed by Public Technical Identifiers, an ICANN affiliate. USC ISI still operates the B root server. The Internet Hall of Fame inducted him in 2012.

paul-vixie.def: The engineer who maintained and then rewrote BIND (Berkeley Internet Name Domain), the most widely used DNS (Domain Name System) server software, co-founded the Internet Software Consortium (now Internet Systems Consortium, ISC), wrote Vixie cron, and created the first successful commercial anti-spam service.
paul-vixie.context: Born in 1963, he has spent a career on the parts of the internet that only get attention when they break. BIND (Berkeley Internet Name Domain) is the name server most of the internet ran on; Vixie cron is still the scheduler Debian and FreeBSD ship; and the anti-spam reputation list he built with Dave Rand established the pattern, a list distributed as DNS (Domain Name System) data so that it needed no new software anywhere, that later produced Response Policy Zones (RPZ), which he designed with Vernon Schryver in 2009 and which shipped from 2010. The through-line is the same each time: put the new capability inside machinery operators already run, because the adoption problem is harder than the design problem.
paul-vixie.depth:
Paul Vixie was born on 23 May 1963 and grew up in San Francisco; by Wikipedia's account he left high school in 1980 and went to work as a programmer. From 1988 to 1993 he was a software engineer at Digital Equipment Corporation (DEC), where, the Internet Hall of Fame records, he started maintaining BIND 4 (Berkeley Internet Name Domain), the name server Berkeley had written. The cron daemon he wrote in the same years carries the notice Copyright 1988, 1990, 1993, 1994 by Paul Vixie in FreeBSD's source to this day, and Debian still describes its cron as Vixie Cron. That double inheritance, the internet's name server and Unix's scheduler, is the shape of the career: infrastructure software that nobody thinks about until it fails.

In 1994, by ISC's own history (other accounts give 1996), he founded the Internet Software Consortium with Carl Malamud and Rick Adams, so that BIND's maintenance, which had passed from the Computer Systems Research Group at Berkeley to DEC and then to his own Vixie Enterprises, would be funded and run by an independent body. IANA (the Internet Assigned Numbers Authority) designated ISC a root name server operator, first as NS.ISC.ORG and then as F.ROOT-SERVERS.NET; ISC has run F-Root since 1994, pioneered anycast for DNS (Domain Name System) service, and today answers on 192.5.5.241 and 2001:500:2f::f from more than 230 F-Root nodes. In 2004 the work moved to Internet Systems Consortium, Inc., a non-profit. Vixie was the primary author and technical architect of BIND 8 and hired many of the people who wrote BIND 9 and BIND 10. The code's security history was not gentle: in 2002, Wikipedia records, he said he held the record for most CERT advisories due to a single author.

His protocol work is the operational plumbing of today's DNS. RFC 1996 (August 1996) defined NOTIFY, so that a primary tells its secondaries a zone has changed instead of waiting for their refresh timers. RFC 2136 (April 1997), which he edited with Susan Thomson, Yakov Rekhter and Jim Bound, defined UPDATE, the dynamic update that lets a DHCP (Dynamic Host Configuration Protocol) server or a host change records in a live zone. RFC 2317 (March 1998, BCP 20), with Havard Eidnes and Geert Jan de Groot, set out classless IN-ADDR.ARPA delegation for reverse zones smaller than a /24. RFC 2671 (August 1999) introduced EDNS0, the Extension Mechanisms for DNS, because messages over UDP (User Datagram Protocol) were limited to 512 octets and requesters needed a way to advertise larger buffers; RFC 6891 (April 2013), with Joao Damas and Michael Graff, replaced it and is Internet Standard 75. The Internet Hall of Fame's summary is that these extensions let the DNS scale beyond its original design and added its first elements of security.

He also wrote down, early, the weakness that would make headlines in 2008. His paper DNS and BIND Security Issues, given at the Fifth USENIX UNIX Security Symposium in Salt Lake City in June 1995, set the goal of getting BIND to the point where its only vulnerabilities were the protocol's, and then listed what could not be fixed in code: with only 16 bits of query ID and 16 bits of UDP port number, it's hard not to be predictable, and an attacker who can spoof source addresses can try them all; the real answer would be DNSSEC (Domain Name System Security Extensions), with signed responses. The same paper made BIND 4.9 stricter about glue records, conceding that this may fly in the face of the robustness principle but that the old behaviour was simply wrong. In 2008, when Dan Kaminsky found a way to make that race practical, he called Vixie, then ISC's president. Vixie told MIT Technology Review it took twenty seconds to explain and twenty more to answer his objections, after which he asked Kaminsky never to repeat it over an unsecured mobile phone; the two then gathered vendors and government experts at Microsoft in Redmond in March, and the coordinated patch shipped on 8 July.

The reputation idea began with spam. RFC 5782, the Internet Research Task Force's 2010 description of DNS blocklists, records that in 1997 Dave Rand and Paul Vixie started keeping a list of IP addresses that had sent them spam, distributed it first as a BGP (Border Gateway Protocol) feed for routers, and called it the Real-time Blackhole List (RBL); because most mail administrators would not take a BGP feed, Rand and Vixie created a DNS-based distribution, which quickly became more popular than the original. The mechanism is the reverse-lookup trick: to ask whether 192.0.2.99 is listed in bad.example.com, a mail server looks up 99.2.0.192.bad.example.com, and an A record (conventionally 127.0.0.2) means yes, with a TXT record giving the reason. The list moved to MAPS (Mail Abuse Prevention System), the California non-profit the Hall of Fame calls the first anti-spam company, and RBL is now a Trend Micro service mark.

Response Policy Zones (RPZ) carried the same idea into the recursive resolver. The specification Vixie and Vernon Schryver published as an Internet-Draft in 2018 says they designed RPZ in 2009, that Schryver wrote the first BIND patch late that year, that patches circulated from 2010, and that the first format had only one trigger, the query name, with the only action being to deny the name existed; later formats added triggers on the IP addresses in a response, on the names and addresses of authoritative name servers, and a passthru action. The policy is itself a DNS zone, so it is distributed by the zone transfers every resolver already supports, and ISC describes it as an open, vendor-neutral standard for DNS firewall data, with feeds from Farsight (now part of DomainTools), Spamhaus, SURBL and ThreatSTOP, and cloud services such as Route 53 DNS Firewall and Quad9. ISC lists DNS Response Rate Limiting (RRL) among the same family of its innovations, and the Hall of Fame credits him with using the DNS for rate limiting as well as response policy.

Outside the code he built institutions. The Hall of Fame credits him with the first neutral commercial internet exchange, the Palo Alto Internet Exchange (PAIX), which Wikipedia dates to 1995; he sat on the board of trustees of the American Registry for Internet Numbers (ARIN) from 2005 to 2013, chairing it in 2008 and 2009 by the Hall of Fame's account; and he was a founding member of the Internet Corporation for Assigned Names and Numbers (ICANN) Root Server System Advisory Committee and its Security and Stability Advisory Committee. He earned a PhD from Keio University in Japan for work on the DNS and DNSSEC. In 2013 he left ISC to found Farsight Security, a passive DNS data company, which DomainTools announced it had acquired on 9 November 2021, quoting him as Farsight's chairman, cofounder and CEO; he then worked at Amazon Web Services (AWS). The Internet Hall of Fame inducted him in 2014.

He argues in public, and the best-known argument is about encryption of DNS. When DNS over HTTPS (DoH) was published as RFC 8484 in October 2018, he wrote that it was a disaster for internet security and that the inmates had taken over the asylum. His case, as The Register reported it, is architectural: DNS is part of the control plane, network operators must be able to monitor and filter it, and DoH is an over-the-top bypass of enterprise and other private networks, so his advice was to use DNS over TLS (Transport Layer Security), RFC 7858, and never DoH. The other side, in the same report, is that DoH's sharing of port 443 with ordinary web traffic is exactly what protects users from networks that would block or watch them, and that the DNS community had failed for decades to deliver private lookups, so browsers went around it. The position is consistent with the rest of his work: a DNS firewall built on RPZ can only enforce policy on queries that reach the resolver it runs on.

grace-hopper.def: The mathematician and US Navy rear admiral who built one of the first compilers, coined the word, and drove the English-language programming that became COBOL.
grace-hopper.context: Born in 1906, she joined the Naval Reserve in 1943 and was assigned to Harvard's Mark I, then wrote the first computer manual in 1946 - the first extensive treatment anywhere of how to program a machine. At Eckert-Mauchly from 1949 she designed a compiler and named the category; her 1957 division produced Flow-Matic, the first English-language data-processing compiler, which is the direct ancestor of COBOL. The argument she had to win was not technical but cultural: that a machine could usefully translate words into instructions, and that programmers need not be mathematicians. She retired from the Navy in 1966, was recalled in 1967, and retired again in 1986 as the oldest officer on active US naval duty, aged 79.

dan-kaminsky.def: The security researcher who in 2008 found a way to make DNS (Domain Name System) cache poisoning fast and reliable against nearly every resolver, and who coordinated a simultaneous multi-vendor patch, released on 8 July 2008, before revealing the details at Black Hat.
dan-kaminsky.context: The weakness was in the protocol, not in one product: DNS (Domain Name System) matched answers to questions with a 16-bit query identifier, and he showed how to win that race reliably. What makes the episode a landmark is the handling. He was 29, working as a penetration tester, and he took the finding to Paul Vixie and then to competing vendors, who shipped a coordinated patch on 8 July 2008, a month before he presented the detail at Black Hat. Source-port randomization was the mitigation; DNSSEC (Domain Name System Security Extensions) was always the real answer. The uncomfortable footnote is that the mitigation was not new, since Daniel J. Bernstein had shipped randomized query ports and warned about BIND's fixed port in 2001, and that a patched BIND was poisoned in about ten hours over gigabit Ethernet a month later. He died in April 2021, at 42.
dan-kaminsky.depth:
Daniel Kaminsky was born in San Francisco on 7 February 1979. His mother told The New York Times that he had taught himself to code by five, and that at eleven his exploration of military systems led an administrator to threaten to cut off the family's connection; they settled on three days offline. He studied at Santa Clara University and worked for Cisco and Avaya before IOActive, the Seattle firm where he was director of penetration testing in 2008. He was already known from Black Hat and DEF CON for using infrastructure in ways its designers had not intended: in 2005, when Sony BMG's copy-protection rootkit was exposed and the company played it down, he used DNS (Domain Name System) cache snooping, asking resolvers whether they had recently looked up the rootkit's domains, to show how widely it had spread. The counts reported differ: more than 568,000 computers in the Times, more than a third of a million networks in The Register, half a million computers on his Internet Hall of Fame page.

The weakness he made practical was old. A resolver accepts an answer if it arrives on the right port with the right 16-bit transaction ID; with a properly random ID, CERT/CC (the CERT Coordination Center) calculates that a blind attacker needs 32,768 attempts on average. Paul Vixie had written in 1995 that 16 bits of ID and 16 bits of port were hard to keep unpredictable; Daniel J. Bernstein wrote in 2001 that his dnscache chose both with a cryptographic generator while BIND reused a single port, so that a hundred thousand guesses were enough against it; Amit Klein showed weak ID generators in several implementations in 2007. What had kept poisoning rare was the TTL (time to live): once a resolver cached the record an attacker wanted, the attacker got very few chances to race the real answer.

Kaminsky found the way around the TTL by accident. MIT Technology Review reported that he was designing a content-delivery trick to make resolvers fetch fresh answers instead of cached ones, and realized after talking it over with a friend that the same trick broke DNS security. Instead of racing for www.example.com, which is cached, the attacker makes the victim resolver look up names that do not exist, 1.example.com, 2.example.com and so on, each one a fresh query and a fresh race, and floods forged replies that claim authority for the whole parent domain. Every miss costs nothing and the next race starts at once, so the TTL no longer limits anything; he told the magazine his test attacks succeeded in as little as ten seconds. The impact reached far beyond web browsing, because mail delivery, software updates and password-reset messages all trust DNS.

He then did the part that made the episode a reference case for coordinated disclosure. He called Vixie, then president of the Internet Systems Consortium (ISC), who told the Times he realized they were looking down the gun barrel of history; the two persuaded Microsoft to host a secret meeting in Redmond in March 2008 with DNS vendors and US government experts, where they settled on a stopgap that most implementations could ship quickly and that did not reveal the flaw. On 8 July 2008 ISC, Microsoft, Cisco and others released patches together, CERT/CC published VU#800113 and the issue became CVE-2008-1447. The patch randomized the source port of every outgoing query, which CERT/CC estimates adds about 16 bits to what an attacker must guess; Kaminsky put the effect as tens of thousands of attempts before and billions after. CERT/CC's note credits Kaminsky with showing the effectiveness and practicality of the attack, Vixie with raising its urgency, and Bernstein with the original idea and implementation of randomized source ports. It also warns that NAT (Network Address Translation) and PAT (Port Address Translation) devices can rewrite source ports and undo the randomization, which is why a resolver behind a firewall or load balancer doing source NAT needs checking. ISC called DNSSEC (Domain Name System Security Extensions) the only full solution. RFC 5452, published in January 2009, made unpredictable source ports a requirement for resolvers.

The secrecy did not hold, and the handling was argued over. Kaminsky asked researchers not to speculate for 30 days; Thomas Ptacek and Dino Dai Zovi publicly doubted the flaw until a conference call converted them, and Dai Zovi worried that it looked like hype for a Black Hat talk. On 21 July Thomas Dullien (Halvar Flake) posted his guess at the mechanism, a detailed explanation briefly appeared on Matasano Security's site, working attack code was public within days, Metasploit shipped modules, and an attack on AT&T servers was seen in the wild. When he finally presented the details at Black Hat on 6 August, he reported that more than 120 million broadband customers had been protected and that 70 per cent of Fortune 500 companies had patched, while 30 to 40 per cent of name servers remained vulnerable. Later that day he received the Pwnie Award for the most overhyped bug, and answered that some people find bugs and some people get bugs fixed. Technology Review summed up the dispute as dangerous grandstanding or a necessary media hack, depending on one's view.

The mitigation was also shown to be partial. In August 2008 Evgeniy Polyakov reported poisoning BIND 9.5.0-P2, the follow-up release with randomized ports, in a little under ten hours using two machines on a Gigabit Ethernet link to the server. Vixie replied that this was a rate-limiting problem comparable to SYN flood protection, nothing like 11 seconds at 10 megabits, and used the moment to argue that it was long past time for end-to-end cryptographic authentication of the DNS. In 2010 ICANN chose Kaminsky as one of 21 Trusted Community Representatives for the signing of the DNS root, one of the seven Recovery Key Share Holders, of whom, as reported at the time, at least five would have to come together to restart the root signing system after a catastrophe.

His later work kept mixing research and repair. He helped build a scanner for Conficker infections, which the Internet Hall of Fame says affected more than nine million computers; co-founded the security company White Ops, later renamed HUMAN, where he was chief scientist; and built DanKam, a phone app for people with colour blindness, along with telemedicine tools for clinicians treating AIDS-related skin disease. In 2016 he told a Black Hat audience that everybody looks busy, but the house still burns, and when the FBI director, James Comey, asked that Apple take the vicious guard dog away and let the bureau pick the lock, he answered that he was that guard dog. Katie Moussouris wrote after his death that the multi-party coordination he championed in 2008 was the catalyst for the formal creation of Microsoft Vulnerability Research. He died at his home in San Francisco on 23 April 2021, aged 42, of diabetic ketoacidosis, and was inducted into the Internet Hall of Fame posthumously that year.

alessandro-volta.def: The physicist whose 1800 pile - stacked zinc and copper discs separated by brine-soaked cloth - produced the first steady electric current.
alessandro-volta.context: Static electricity had been known for centuries and was useless for communication: a discharge is an event, not a signal. The pile gave a current that keeps flowing, and only then is there something to modulate, switch or send. Everything on this timeline after him depends on that one change of kind, from a spark to a supply. His name became the unit, which is a rarer honour than a prize.

hans-christian-orsted.def: The Danish physicist who observed in 1820 that a current-carrying wire deflects a compass needle, showing electricity and magnetism to be one phenomenon.
hans-christian-orsted.context: Every motor, every transformer and every read head over a disk platter is this observation applied on purpose. So is every signal induced onto the wrong pair in a cable bundle: crosstalk is Ørsted's experiment happening when nobody asked for it. Cable design has spent two centuries arranging conductors so that his effect helps rather than interferes.

michael-faraday.def: The experimenter who showed in 1831 that a changing magnetic field induces a current - the reciprocal of Ørsted, and the basis of generation and of every inductive coupling problem since.
michael-faraday.context: It is also, directly, why twisted pair works. Twist the two conductors and the interference induced into each is roughly equal; the receiver reads the difference between them, and the difference is largely clean. A cabling standard is Faraday's law turned into a manufacturing tolerance. He had almost no formal mathematics, which did not stop him from being right, and Maxwell spent the next three decades writing his results down as equations.

james-clerk-maxwell.def: The theorist whose 1865 equations described electricity, magnetism and light as one field, and predicted that electromagnetic waves travel at the speed of light.
james-clerk-maxwell.context: The order matters: the prediction came two decades before anyone demonstrated it. Radio existed on paper long before it existed in a laboratory, which is worth remembering whenever a standard is dismissed for having no implementations yet. Every wireless specification is an engineering treatment of this result, and propagation, attenuation and antenna design are applied Maxwell whether the engineer knows it or not.

heinrich-hertz.def: The physicist who in 1887 built a spark-gap transmitter and a loop receiver and demonstrated the waves Maxwell had predicted, turning radio from mathematics into an engineering problem.
heinrich-hertz.context: He reportedly saw no use for the result, which is the most useful thing about the story: the distance between a demonstration and an application is not a measure of the demonstration. Within fifteen years the same effect was carrying messages across the Atlantic commercially. His name is the unit every spectrum plan, channel width and clock rate is quoted in.

claude-shannon.def: The author of the 1948 paper that founded information theory, and, a decade earlier, of the thesis showing that Boolean algebra describes switching circuits.
claude-shannon.context: Two contributions, either of which would have been a career. The 1937 thesis made digital logic a design discipline rather than a craft. The 1948 paper defined information as a measurable quantity and gave the ceiling on what any channel can carry given its bandwidth and noise - which is why capacity planning is arithmetic rather than opinion, and why every claim about a faster link eventually meets a number Shannon wrote down. Compression, error correction and modulation are all consequences.

alan-turing.def: The mathematician whose 1936 paper defined what computation is, and what no machine can compute - the boundary every computer since has been built inside.
alan-turing.context: The paper was about the limits, not the possibilities: he described a machine in order to prove that some questions have no algorithmic answer. That the description turned out to be a blueprint is one of the field's larger accidents. His wartime cryptanalysis is better known publicly and less foundational technically, and the treatment he received afterwards is part of the record too.

george-boole.def: The mathematician who in 1854 built an algebra of logic, ninety years before anyone had a machine to run it on.
george-boole.context: He was describing reasoning, not circuits. The connection was made by Shannon in 1937, and the gap between the two is the point: a piece of pure mathematics sat unused for three generations and then turned out to be the exact description of how switches behave. Every conditional, every access-control rule and every packet filter is his algebra with an implementation.

john-von-neumann.def: The mathematician whose 1945 EDVAC draft set out the stored-program architecture - instructions held in the same memory as data - that almost every computer still follows.
john-von-neumann.context: The draft circulated with his name alone on it, which is why the architecture carries it; the EDVAC group's work is in there too, and the attribution has been argued over ever since. The design decision that matters is the one people forget is a decision: code and data share a memory, which is what makes software possible and what makes buffer overflows possible, and the same property does both.

guglielmo-marconi.def: The engineer and entrepreneur who turned Hertz's laboratory effect into a transatlantic service, claiming reception of a signal across the Atlantic in 1901.
guglielmo-marconi.context: His technical contribution is contested and his commercial one is not: he built the company, the shore stations and the ship contracts that made wireless a business rather than a demonstration. The pattern is familiar to anyone who has watched a standard win - the person who makes something deployable is frequently not the person who made it work. The claim about the 1901 signal has been questioned on physical grounds ever since, which the record should carry rather than smooth over.

tim-berners-lee.def: The author of the 1989 CERN proposal that became the World Wide Web, and of the first browser, server and page - and the 2016 Turing Award recipient for it.
tim-berners-lee.context: He wrote three things that had to exist together for any of them to be useful: an addressing scheme, a transfer protocol and a markup language. The decision with the longest consequences was not technical: CERN put the specification into the public domain in 1993, and the web spread because nobody had to ask permission or pay a licence. Compare any contemporary networked hypertext system that did neither, and the difference in outcome is almost entirely that.

gordon-moore.def: The Fairchild and later Intel co-founder whose 1965 article observed that the number of components per integrated circuit was doubling on a regular cadence.
gordon-moore.context: It was an observation about economics with a horizon of about a decade, and it became a planning assumption for fifty years - and then, quietly, an industry roadmap that vendors organized themselves to meet, which is a different thing from a law of nature. The useful reading for anyone sizing infrastructure is that the curve was always about cost per transistor rather than speed, and that the two stopped moving together long before anyone announced it.

whitfield-diffie.def: Co-author, with Martin Hellman, of the 1976 paper New Directions in Cryptography, which proposed public-key cryptography and digital signatures and gave the key exchange that bears both their names; joint recipient of the 2015 Turing Award.
whitfield-diffie.context: Before that paper, encryption assumed the two parties had already met, or that a courier had. The paper's move was to separate the key that locks from the key that unlocks, which makes it possible to communicate privately with a stranger, the requirement every later commerce protocol rests on. It described the idea without a practical construction; three people at the Massachusetts Institute of Technology (MIT) supplied one the following year. He later spent decades arguing the policy side in public, testifying to both houses of the US Congress on cryptography.
whitfield-diffie.depth:
Whitfield Diffie (Bailey W. Diffie on the patent) was born on 5 June 1944. His biography on the Association for Computing Machinery (ACM) Turing Award site, written by the historian Jeffrey R. Yost, places his birth in Washington, D.C. and his childhood in Queens, New York; the National Inventors Hall of Fame gives New York City. He took a Bachelor of Science in mathematics at the Massachusetts Institute of Technology (MIT) in 1965 and, to avoid the Vietnam draft, joined the MITRE Corporation, where from 1965 to 1969 he worked on symbolic mathematics software that fed into Macsyma and spent much of his time as a resident guest at MIT's Project MAC artificial intelligence laboratory. In 1969 John McCarthy invited him to the Stanford Artificial Intelligence Laboratory (SAIL), one of the original hubs of the Advanced Research Projects Agency Network (ARPANET), where he was a research programmer until 1973. He had read about cryptography and mathematics as a boy, and David Kahn's The Codebreakers deepened that interest into one in cryptography and privacy, and in one-way functions in particular.

In 1973 and 1974 he travelled to meet the few people doing cryptography in the open, among them the team at IBM's Thomas J. Watson laboratory, which included Horst Feistel and Alan Konheim. Konheim told him to look up Martin Hellman at Stanford. Their first meeting, in the autumn of 1974, was planned as a short one and ran for hours, through dinner and into the evening. Diffie went to work with Hellman as a programmer and in the second half of 1975 enrolled as a doctoral student at Stanford, a degree he never finished; the Swiss Federal Institute of Technology gave him an honorary doctorate in 1992.

New Directions in Cryptography appeared as an invited paper in IEEE Transactions on Information Theory, the journal of the Institute of Electrical and Electronics Engineers (IEEE), volume IT-22, number 6, November 1976, pages 644 to 654. The manuscript was received on 3 June 1976, and parts had already been presented at the IEEE Information Theory Workshop in Lenox, Massachusetts, on 23 to 25 June 1975 and at the International Symposium on Information Theory in Ronneby, Sweden, on 21 to 24 June 1976. Its first sentence is: we stand today on the brink of a revolution in cryptography. The problem it set out was commercial before it was military. Using cryptography required the parties to share a key known to no one else, sent in advance by private courier or registered mail, and it was unrealistic, the authors wrote, to postpone business contacts until keys could be delivered by physical means. In the public key cryptosystem they proposed, enciphering and deciphering are governed by distinct keys E and D such that computing D from E is computationally infeasible, so E can be placed in a public directory and anyone can send its owner a message only the owner can read. They offered techniques but said plainly that the problem was still largely open.

The construction that did work was the public key distribution system, now called Diffie-Hellman key exchange. It rests on the apparent difficulty of computing logarithms in a finite field with a prime number q of elements. Each user chooses a secret X at random and publishes Y, a fixed primitive element alpha raised to the power X mod q; users i and j then each compute the same key, alpha raised to Xi times Xj mod q, from their own secret and the other's public value, while an eavesdropper who sees only the two public values must, as far as anyone knew, take a logarithm. The paper put numbers on the gap: with b = 200 bit quantities, at most 400 multiplications for the legitimate users against roughly 2 to the power 100 operations to take the logarithm. The authors admitted they had no proof that the scheme is secure if logarithms are hard. The same paper defined the digital signature, which it called one-way authentication, a message-dependent signature anyone can recognize as authentic and only its author can produce, and it used one-way functions to show how a login system can store a function of each password instead of the password. It also warned that the public file of keys must be protected from unauthorized modification: the exchange by itself says nothing about who is at the other end, and authenticating public keys is the job that public key infrastructure (PKI) was later built to do.

The paper credits Ralph Merkle, then a student at Berkeley, with independent work on distributing keys over an insecure channel, and states the weakness of his scheme: it required n potential keys to be transmitted before one could be agreed, so with a one-megabit limit on set-up overhead it achieved a cost ratio of only about 10,000 to 1 between attacker and users. Diffie later wrote that he and Hellman had a far more compact solution than Merkle's puzzles, and called Merkle possibly the most inventive character in the public-key saga. On 6 September 1977 Hellman, Diffie and Merkle filed the application that became United States Patent 4,200,770, Cryptographic apparatus and method, granted on 29 April 1980 and assigned to Stanford; Google Patents gives its anticipated expiration as 6 September 1997. The practical public-key cryptosystem that New Directions had left open came from Ron Rivest, Adi Shamir and Leonard Adleman at MIT, first released in 1977; Stanford sublicensed its patent to MIT, and Cylink, founded by Jim Omura, licensed it as well.

Publishing was a fight. In June 1977 Diffie and Hellman published Exhaustive Cryptanalysis of the NBS Data Encryption Standard in the magazine Computer, part of a campaign that, in Stanford's account, included the claim that the National Security Agency (NSA) had pressured IBM into limiting the key of the Data Encryption Standard (DES) of the National Bureau of Standards (NBS) to 56 bits. An NSA employee wrote to the publishers that the authors could face prison under export laws covering military weapons, and Stanford calls these disputes the first crypto wars. The agencies' account is the classified prior art. The ACM biography says that James Ellis at the United Kingdom's Government Communications Headquarters (GCHQ) conceived public-key cryptography in 1969 and 1970 and that Clifford Cocks devised an algorithm to implement it in 1973. The NSA's Center for Cryptologic History records that GCHQ's public disclosure of 1997 credited Ellis, Cocks and Malcolm Williamson, that an NSA memorandum of October 1976 noted that Williamson had described the concept in a top secret paper in 1974, and that Ellis, meeting Diffie in 1982 while his own work was still secret, found him charming, plausible and quite expert. A former NSA director has also claimed that two-key cryptography was found inside the agency a decade before 1976; the ACM biography reports the claim without details, and concludes that the open research community, not classified work, drove the field's practical advances. In 2020 the NSA inducted Diffie into its own Cryptologic Hall of Honor, calling his 1976 contribution a history-making advancement in the protection of privacy and information security.

Diffie's working life after Stanford was in industry. From December 1978 he was manager of secure systems research at Northern Telecom's laboratory, Bell-Northern Research, in Mountain View, California, for about twelve years; in 1991 he joined Sun Microsystems, where he was chief security officer, a vice-president, Distinguished Engineer and Sun Fellow until 2009. The National Inventors Hall of Fame records that in 2010 he joined the Internet Corporation for Assigned Names and Numbers (ICANN) as vice-president for information security and cryptography. Stanford had him as a visiting scholar and affiliate from 2009 to 2012 and then as a consulting scholar at its Center for International Security and Cooperation, and the Royal Society lists him as an honorary visiting professor at Royal Holloway, University of London.

From 1993 the Royal Society describes his main focus as public policy on cryptography, security and privacy. On 11 May 1993, less than a month after the Clipper proposal was made public on 16 April, he gave congressional testimony, opening with thanks to Congressman Boucher and the committee, under the title The Impact of a Secret Cryptographic Standard on Encryption, Privacy, Law Enforcement and Technology. He described the Law Enforcement Exploitation Field each Clipper chip would generate, which a government-held key unique to the chip could decrypt to reveal the session key, compared the design to the keyhole in the back of a school locker's combination lock through which the teachers can always look, and concluded that the proposal was at best premature and at worst damaging to business security and civil rights without improving law enforcement. His ACM biography records testimony before House and Senate subcommittees in the early 1990s and later. With Susan Landau he wrote Privacy on the Line: The Politics of Wiretapping and Encryption (MIT Press, 1998; updated and expanded edition, 2007), which received the 1998 Donald McGannon Award for Social and Ethical Relevance in Communication Policy Research. In 2016 he and Hellman sided with Apple in its dispute with the Federal Bureau of Investigation (FBI) over unlocking an iPhone, Diffie warning that compliance could help totalitarian regimes persecute people.

The honours follow the paper. With Hellman he received the National Computer Systems Security Award of the National Institute of Standards and Technology (NIST) and the NSA in 1996, the Franklin Institute's Levy Medal in 1997 and the IEEE Information Theory Society Golden Jubilee Award in 1998; the ACM Paris Kanellakis Theory and Practice Award for 1996 went to Diffie, Hellman and Merkle for the conception of public-key cryptography and to Rivest, Shamir and Adleman for its first effective realization. The IEEE Kobayashi Award in 1999 and the IEEE Richard W. Hamming Medal in 2010 were shared with Hellman and Merkle. He became a fellow of the International Association for Cryptologic Research (IACR) in 2004 for the invention of public-key cryptography, entered the National Inventors Hall of Fame in 2011, and was elected to the US National Academy of Engineering and to the Royal Society in 2017. The 2015 ACM A.M. Turing Award, shared with Hellman, was announced at the RSA Conference in San Francisco, carried a prize of 1 million US dollars funded by Google and was presented on 11 June 2016.

Every key exchange a network engineer configures descends from section III of the paper. The Secure Shell (SSH) transport protocol, Request for Comments (RFC) 4253 of January 2006, made diffie-hellman-group1-sha1 and diffie-hellman-group14-sha1 its required key exchange methods; Internet Key Exchange version 2 (IKEv2), RFC 7296 of October 2014, runs a Diffie-Hellman exchange in its first message pair to key an IPsec (Internet Protocol Security) tunnel; and TLS 1.3, RFC 8446 of August 2018, removed static RSA and static Diffie-Hellman cipher suites, so that every public-key exchange it allows is ephemeral and provides forward secrecy, over named groups that run from the elliptic curves secp256r1 and x25519 to the finite-field groups ffdhe2048 to ffdhe8192. The paper's warning about the public file still decides the design: an unauthenticated exchange can be run twice by someone in the middle, once with each side, which is why TLS has the server sign the whole handshake in its CertificateVerify message and why IKE authenticates the exchange with certificates or pre-shared keys. The (EC)DHE that RFC 8446 names as a key exchange mode is exactly this: ephemeral Diffie-Hellman, over finite fields or elliptic curves.

martin-hellman.def: Co-author of New Directions in Cryptography and of the key-exchange method that carries his name with Diffie's; joint recipient of the 2015 Turing Award.
martin-hellman.context: His citation is worth reading closely: it credits inventing AND promulgating, which is the pair of verbs this history keeps requiring. The exchange lets two parties agree a shared secret over a channel someone else is listening to, and it is still the thing happening at the start of a TLS session decades later - which is why forward secrecy is available at all. He spent much of his later career on nuclear risk rather than cryptography, which the record should mention rather than tidy away.

ralph-merkle.def: The third name on the public-key patent with Diffie and Hellman, who arrived at the idea independently as a student, and the inventor of the hash tree that carries his name.
ralph-merkle.context: His undergraduate course proposal of 1974 described a way for two parties to agree a secret in public; the instructor turned it down, and the paper that grew from it was rejected in 1975 by an anonymous referee who judged it outside the main stream of cryptography. The Association for Computing Machinery's Kanellakis award for 1996 lists him with Diffie, Hellman, Rivest, Shamir and Adleman for the conception and first effective realization of public-key cryptography. The tree structure he described later became the standard way to prove that one item belongs to a large set without shipping the set, which is why it turns up in certificate transparency, in backups and in ledgers.
ralph-merkle.depth:
Ralph Charles Merkle was born on 2 February 1952, in Berkeley, California, according to the Computer History Museum (CHM); the National Inventors Hall of Fame says he was born and raised in California. The University of California at Berkeley conferred his Bachelor of Arts in computer science on 14 December 1974, a diploma he has scanned onto his own site. He then moved to Stanford, where he took a master's degree in 1977 and a doctorate in electrical engineering in 1979 under Martin Hellman.

The idea came first, in the autumn of 1974, in CS244, the computer security course Lance Hoffman taught at Berkeley. Students had to submit two project proposals, and one of Merkle's described what would later be called public key cryptography. His seven-page proposal set out Method 1, now known as the puzzles method, and a Method 2 that would turn a two-way encryption technique into an apparently one-way technique another site could use to encrypt messages that only the original could decrypt. Hoffman rejected it; Merkle rewrote it as two pages, met the same lack of interest, dropped the course and kept working. Bob Fabry, on the Berkeley faculty, read a draft and told him to publish it and win fame and fortune. In August 1975 he submitted it to Susan Graham, an editor of the Communications of the ACM (Association for Computing Machinery). Her letter of 22 October 1975 enclosed the report of an experienced cryptography expert, never identified, who wrote that the paper was not in the main stream of present cryptography thinking and that experience shows it is extremely dangerous to transmit key information in the clear; Graham herself was bothered that it cited no literature. Merkle's later answer is that there was no literature to cite: the term public key cryptography did not yet exist, and there were no previous workers in the field. He lost the original proposal and found it again in a box on 8 September 2005.

The paper finally appeared as Secure Communications Over Insecure Channels in the Communications of the ACM, volume 21, number 4, April 1978, pages 294 to 299, marked received August 1975 and revised September 1977, almost three years after submission and after others had published. Its central object is the puzzle, a cryptogram meant to be broken: encrypt a message with a strong cipher (the paper suggests Lucifer) but restrict the key space so that a solution costs a chosen amount of work. X sends N puzzles over the open channel, each holding a random identifier and a puzzle key and each costing work proportional to N to solve. Y picks one at random, solves it and sends back only its identifier, and both then use its puzzle key. An eavesdropper does not know which puzzle was chosen and must, on average, solve half of them, so the attacker's work grows as N squared while each legitimate party spends work proportional to N. A quadratic gap is a weak one, which Diffie and Hellman pointed out in New Directions (with a one-megabit limit on set-up traffic, a cost ratio of about 10,000 to 1); Hellman's overview of 1978 limited the scheme to N of about 10,000, roughly 500 kilobits of transmission. What the puzzles proved was the principle: two parties with no shared secret can agree one over a channel the attacker reads.

In 1975 Diffie and Hellman learned of his work; he joined the Stanford group for the summer of 1976 and became Hellman's doctoral student that autumn. On 6 September 1977 Hellman, Diffie and Merkle filed the application that became United States Patent 4,200,770, Cryptographic apparatus and method, granted on 29 April 1980 and assigned to Stanford, which is why his is the third name on the public-key patent. With Hellman he proposed a public-key cryptosystem built on trapdoor knapsacks, Hiding Information and Signatures in Trap Door Knapsacks, in the September 1978 IEEE Transactions on Information Theory, a journal of the Institute of Electrical and Electronics Engineers (IEEE). It did not last: Adi Shamir's A Polynomial Time Algorithm for Breaking the Basic Merkle-Hellman Cryptosystem, published in Advances in Cryptology in 1983, showed that when the public elements are modular multiples of a superincreasing sequence, as Merkle and Hellman had proposed, almost every instance can be solved in polynomial time. Diffie's own judgement, in his ACM biography, is that the knapsack did not lend itself readily to signatures, and that Merkle was possibly the most inventive character in the public-key saga.

The structure that carries his name came out of signatures. His 1979 Stanford thesis was Secrecy, Authentication, and Public Key Systems, and the paper A Certified Digital Signature, submitted to Ron Rivest at the Communications of the ACM in 1979, accepted subject to revisions and resubmitted in November 1979, was never published there: Rivest handed over the editorship, Merkle went to a start-up and the referees never answered. It appeared only at Crypto '89. The paper builds signatures from a conventional one-way function, starting from the Lamport-Diffie one-time signature and the Winternitz improvement, and solves the problem of authenticating many one-time public keys with what it calls tree authentication. Each leaf is hashed; each parent is the hash of its two children; the single value at the top, the root R, authenticates every leaf. To prove one leaf belongs, the sender supplies only the sibling values along the path to the root, log2 n of them, which the paper calls the authentication path: for n = 8, authenticating the fifth item needs that item and three other values. Merkle estimated signatures of 1 to 3 kilobytes, a few thousand applications of the underlying function each and about 20 milliseconds per signature. The method was patented as United States Patent 4,309,569, Method of providing digital signatures, filed on 5 September 1979, granted on 5 January 1982 and assigned to Stanford; Michael Szydlo later showed how to traverse such trees in logarithmic space and time (Eurocrypt 2004).

The tree is now one of the most widely deployed ideas in security engineering. Certificate Transparency, RFC 6962 (Request for Comments 6962, June 2013), has every log keep a binary Merkle Hash Tree over SHA-256 (the 256-bit Secure Hash Algorithm) so that anyone can demand an audit path proving a certificate is in the log and a consistency proof that the log has only been appended to; RFC 9162 (December 2021), version 2.0, keeps the same trees with inclusion and consistency proofs. The Bitcoin paper hashes each block's transactions in a Merkle tree with only the root in the block's hash, so that spent transactions can be pruned and a light client can check a payment with a Merkle branch; its citation for the tree is Merkle's Protocols for public key cryptosystems, from the IEEE Symposium on Security and Privacy of April 1980. Amazon S3 Glacier, an archive storage service, requires a SHA-256 tree hash over 1 MB chunks of every upload, with the root as the checksum of the whole archive. And hash-based signatures have come back for the reason Merkle gave in 2012, when he argued that deployable tree signatures should be developed before quantum computers arrive: RFC 8554 (April 2019), Leighton-Micali Hash-Based Signatures, traces itself to Lamport, Diffie, Winternitz and Merkle and notes that such signatures stay secure against a quantum attacker, and the National Institute of Standards and Technology (NIST) approved the Leighton-Micali Signature (LMS) system and the eXtended Merkle Signature Scheme (XMSS), with their multi-tree variants, in Special Publication (SP) 800-208 in October 2020.

Credit for the key exchange has been argued since. New Directions in Cryptography cites Merkle's work as a partial solution of a different form, and the name that stuck is Diffie-Hellman. In 2002, when IEEE Communications Magazine reprinted his 1978 overview of public key cryptography as a landmark article, Hellman wrote a foreword saying that Diffie and Merkle had independently broken with conventional wisdom, that the system he and Diffie first described was a concept developed by Merkle and should be called Diffie-Hellman-Merkle key exchange if names are to be attached to it, and that a quirk of fate had deprived Merkle of the credit he deserved. Merkle's own home page writes the acronym DHM.

After his doctorate Merkle worked for Elxsi, a small Silicon Valley computer company, and from 1988 turned to nanotechnology, which has occupied him since. He served as an executive editor of the journal Nanotechnology, chaired the Fourth and Fifth Foresight Conferences on Molecular Nanotechnology, won the 1998 Feynman Prize in Nanotechnology for theory, and co-founded the Nanofactory Collaboration with Robert Freitas, with whom he wrote Kinematic Self-Replicating Machines (2004). He was a distinguished professor at the Georgia Institute of Technology from 2003 and returned to California in 2006. His home page lists him as a senior research fellow of the Institute for Molecular Manufacturing and a director of Alcor, the cryonics organization, and the National Inventors Hall of Fame adds a place on the faculty of Singularity University.

The recognition for cryptography came late and in company. The ACM Paris Kanellakis Theory and Practice Award for 1996 went to Adleman, Diffie, Hellman, Merkle, Rivest and Shamir for the conception and first effective realization of public-key cryptography; the IEEE Koji Kobayashi Computers and Communications Award of 1999 went to Diffie, Hellman and Merkle for the revolutionary invention of public key cryptosystems; he received the RSA Award in Mathematics in 2000 and the IEEE Richard W. Hamming Medal in 2010, was named a fellow of the International Association for Cryptologic Research (IACR) in 2008, and in 2011 entered the National Inventors Hall of Fame for Patent 4,200,770 and became a fellow of the CHM for his work, with Diffie and Hellman, on public key cryptography. The 2015 Turing Award went to Diffie and Hellman alone.

ron-rivest.def: The R in RSA: co-author of the 1977 paper that turned public-key cryptography from a proposal into something implementable, and joint recipient of the 2002 Turing Award.
ron-rivest.context: Diffie and Hellman had described what was needed and said plainly that they had no realistic way to build it. Rivest, with Shamir and Adleman at MIT, produced one within a year, and the trio founded RSA Data Security in 1982 - which is how the algorithm reached the products rather than the journals. The Turing citation is precise about the contribution: making public-key cryptography useful in practice. He also wrote the MD and RC families of algorithms, several of which the field later had to retire.

adi-shamir.def: The S in RSA, joint recipient of the 2002 Turing Award, and the author of the secret-sharing scheme that splits a key so that any k of n holders can reconstruct it.
adi-shamir.context: The RSA work is what he is cited for, and the secret sharing may be the more widely deployed idea: it is how a root key can exist without any one person holding it, which is the arrangement used at the ceremonies that sign the DNS root. He also did foundational work on differential cryptanalysis, which is the other half of a cryptographer's job - the field advances as much by breaking constructions as by proposing them.

leonard-adleman.def: The A in RSA and joint recipient of the 2002 Turing Award, later the founder of DNA computing.
leonard-adleman.context: His role in the trio was largely to attack the constructions the other two proposed, which is how the surviving one earned confidence: the published algorithm is the one that outlasted its own co-author trying to break it. That division of labour - propose, attack, keep what survives - is the method the whole field runs on, and it is easier to describe than to practise inside a group of three people who have to agree on a paper afterwards.

james-ellis.def: The GCHQ researcher who conceived non-secret encryption around 1969-70, several years before the public discovery of public-key cryptography, and could tell nobody.
james-ellis.context: The idea existed inside a British intelligence agency and did nothing, because a classified insight changes no protocol, ships in no product and teaches no one. The comparison is the argument for open research stated as an experiment that actually ran: two groups had the same idea, one could publish and one could not, and the entire public-key infrastructure descends from the one that could. Recognition came only after declassification in the late 1990s, by which time he had died.

clifford-cocks.def: The GCHQ mathematician who in 1973 worked out an implementation of Ellis's idea - equivalent in substance to what became RSA - four years before RSA was published.
clifford-cocks.context: He is reported to have done it in an afternoon and then filed it, because there was nothing else to do with it. The work stayed secret until the late 1990s, so it influenced nothing: no standard cites it, no library implements it, and the industry that grew up around the same mathematics grew up entirely on the published version. The episode is the cleanest available answer to whether secrecy or publication produces more capability, and it is not close.

paul-baran.def: The RAND engineer who designed the distributed network - no central switch, messages cut into blocks routed independently - in studies published from 1960 and collected in 1964 as On Distributed Communications.
paul-baran.context: He was asked to find a way for communications to survive a nuclear attack, and the answer he reached was to remove the thing that could be destroyed: the centre. He described taking inspiration from a brain routing around damaged tissue. Two details are worth carrying. The idea was resisted by the telephone company's circuit-switching engineers, who regarded it as unworkable, so the network that replaced theirs was rejected by them first. And the survivability argument is why the internet has no master switch, which is the same property that makes it hard to shut down and hard to govern.

donald-davies.def: The National Physical Laboratory scientist who arrived at the same idea independently in the mid-1960s, named it packet switching, and built a working network at NPL to prove it.
donald-davies.context: Baran had the concept and Davies gave it the word, which is not a small contribution: the term packet is what let engineers, funders and standards bodies talk about the thing without arguing about what to call it. He also did what the theory needed - an actual node, running, at Teddington - and the ARPANET design took from both men, with the terminology coming from him and the resilience argument from Baran. Independent arrival at the same answer, on two continents, is the strongest evidence that the idea was ready rather than lucky.

leonard-kleinrock.def: The queueing theorist whose early-1960s work on delay in networks of nodes underpinned ARPANET performance analysis, and whose UCLA laboratory hosted the first node.
leonard-kleinrock.context: His mathematics is what lets anyone reason about waiting: how long a queue grows, what delay a given load produces, and why a link at ninety per cent utilization behaves nothing like one at fifty. Every capacity conversation is downstream of it. His claim to have originated packet switching is disputed - by Baran, by Davies and by historians who note that the early reports address queueing and delay rather than message blocks - and the honest record keeps the dispute rather than resolving it in either direction.

larry-roberts.def: The ARPA programme manager who decided in 1967 that the network would be packet switched, then funded, designed and managed it into existence.
larry-roberts.context: The decision is the contribution. Two people had proposed the technique and neither could deploy it; Roberts chose it over circuit switching, coordinated the contractors who built the hardware and the university that hosted the first node, and revised the design to take from both proposals rather than picking a camp. This is the role that rarely gets a monument: not the person who has the idea, and not the person who writes the code, but the one who selects among ideas and then carries the consequences of the choice.

van-jacobson.def: The author of Congestion Avoidance and Control, the 1988 work that gave TCP the algorithms - slow start, congestion avoidance, fast retransmit - that stopped the internet collapsing under its own load.
van-jacobson.context: In the mid-1980s the network suffered congestion collapse: throughput between two sites fell by three orders of magnitude, because every sender responded to loss by retransmitting harder. His fix was to make each sender infer the state of a network it cannot see, from the only evidence it has - the timing and loss of its own packets - and to back off. That inference is still what every TCP connection does. It is also why a link can be busy while nothing feels fast, and why bufferbloat took decades to be recognized as the same problem wearing a different hat. He was in the inaugural 2012 class of the Internet Hall of Fame, inducted as an Innovator - the category for people whose contribution was a new use rather than the underlying architecture, which is a fair description of making an existing protocol survive its own success.

nelson-murilo.def: The author of chkrootkit, the rootkit detector that has been part of the Unix security toolkit since the late 1990s, and one of the three founders of the ISTS podcast and the YSTS conference.
nelson-murilo.context: Very few conference founders anywhere have their own code still installed on other people's servers decades later. chkrootkit is still being released (version 0.60 shipped on 11 October 2026), which is an unusual thing to be able to say about any security tool, let alone one written before the industry had a name for the category. He is also one of the three voices on the podcast that has been recording since 2006, and the event grew out of that rather than the other way round.

luiz-eduardo-dos-santos.def: The founder whose idea the ISTS podcast was, and who spent months insisting the three of them record a pilot; co-founder of the YSTS conference that grew out of it.
luiz-eduardo-dos-santos.context: The detail worth keeping is the insistence. The three worked in information security, lived in different cities - he in a different country - and had an affinity for the subject that sometimes converged and sometimes did not. Nothing about that arrangement produces a podcast without somebody pushing, and he pushed for months. Nearly twenty years of continuous recording, and one of the most selective conferences in Latin America, exist because of that.

nelson-brito.def: The creator of T50, the packet injection and stress-testing tool, and the only Brazilian to have presented at PH-Neutral in Berlin, in 2011.
nelson-brito.context: T50 is the kind of tool that gets used far beyond the people who know who wrote it, which is the usual fate of a good one. His research has been published under names like Permutation Oriented Programming and SQL Fingerprint, and his speaking record runs through the Brazilian circuit - IME, CNASI, CONIP, SERPRO, ITA, H2HC, BSides São Paulo and YSTS - as well as that one Berlin appearance, which is worth noting because PH-Neutral was small and did not hand out invitations widely.

deviant-ollam.def: The physical security researcher and TOOOL member whose lockpicking talks put the discipline in front of network audiences that had never considered the door.
deviant-ollam.context: At the fifth edition of YSTS, in May 2011, he opened the event with the basics of lockpicking and sold kits to the room afterwards - which is the whole argument in one gesture, since a lock is a control whose failure mode you can hold in your hand. Physical access defeats most of what the rest of a security programme buys: a server room door, a rack lock and a badge reader sit underneath every network control, and they are usually the least examined part of the estate.

dennis-ritchie.def: The creator of the C programming language and co-creator of Unix, and joint recipient with Ken Thompson of the 1983 Turing Award for the development of generic operating systems theory and the implementation of Unix.
dennis-ritchie.context: The decision that made both last was rewriting Unix in C. Before that, an operating system was written for a machine; afterwards it could be moved to another one, and portability stopped being a research topic and became an expectation. Nearly everything since inherits from that pair: the descendants of C run the kernels and the network stacks, and the shape of Unix - a hierarchy of files, small tools composed together, processes forked from other processes - is still the mental model behind systems that have never run a line of his code.

ken-thompson.def: Co-creator of Unix and joint recipient of the 1983 Turing Award, and author of the Turing lecture that showed a compiler can hide a backdoor no source review would ever find.
ken-thompson.context: The lecture is the part that belongs on a security site. He described a compiler modified to insert a backdoor into a program, and to insert the same modification into any compiler it compiles - so the malicious code disappears from every source file while surviving in every binary.
