The conclusion he drew is the uncomfortable one: you cannot trust code you did not totally create yourself, and reading the source is not enough, because the thing that reads the source is also code. Reproducible builds and supply-chain attestation exist because of an argument he made in 1984.

leslie-lamport.def: The 2013 Turing Award recipient for imposing order on distributed systems: logical clocks, distributed snapshots, Paxos, Byzantine fault tolerance, the safety and liveness distinction - and LaTeX.
leslie-lamport.context: His 1978 paper on time, clocks and the ordering of events is among the most cited in computing, and its point is that in a distributed system there is no global now - only causality, which you can order without a shared clock. Everything downstream depends on that: consensus, replication, and every database that must decide which write happened first. His own line describes the field better than any textbook: a distributed system is one in which the failure of a computer you did not know existed can render your own computer unusable.

barbara-liskov.def: The 2008 Turing Award recipient, cited for practical and theoretical foundations of programming language and system design, especially data abstraction, fault tolerance and distributed computing.
barbara-liskov.context: The substitution principle that carries her name is the one most programmers meet: a subtype must be usable anywhere its supertype is, without the caller needing to know. That is a statement about interfaces rather than about inheritance, and it is why abstraction survives contact with a large codebase. Her distributed systems work matters as much and is credited less - she and her student Brian Oki arrived at view-stamped replication at about the same time as Paxos, independently, which is the second time in this history that two groups reached the same answer without knowing.

tcp.def: The transport that turns a stream of packets into an ordered, reliable byte stream, by numbering what it sends and retransmitting what is not acknowledged.
tcp.context: Everything the Transmission Control Protocol (TCP) does follows from one fact: the network underneath makes no promises. Packets may be lost, duplicated, reordered or delayed, so ordering, retransmission, flow control and congestion control all live in the endpoints rather than in the network. That decision is why the internet could be built from links nobody controlled centrally, and it is also why a single lossy hop degrades a session end to end. The three-way handshake, the sequence numbers and the window are the visible parts; the interesting part is that the sender infers the state of a network it cannot see from the timing of its own packets.
tcp.depth:
The Transmission Control Protocol (TCP) gives two applications a reliable, ordered, full-duplex stream of octets over the Internet Protocol (IP), which only delivers datagrams on a best-effort basis. The connection exists in the endpoints alone: each keeps its state in a Transmission Control Block (TCB), and no router on the path knows it is there. It is a byte stream, not a message service, so the boundaries of an application's writes are not preserved and every protocol above must frame its own messages.

The design begins with Vinton Cerf and Robert Kahn's 'A Protocol for Packet Network Intercommunication', published in May 1974 in IEEE (Institute of Electrical and Electronics Engineers) Transactions on Communications: one transmission control program handling sequencing, flow control, end-to-end error checking and process-to-process connections across dissimilar networks joined by gateways. Addressing and routing were later split out as IP. Request for Comments (RFC) 793, published in September 1981, was the base specification for four decades, patched by errata and by enhancements scattered over many documents, until the Internet Engineering Task Force (IETF) consolidated them in August 2022 as RFC 9293, Internet Standard 7, which obsoletes RFC 793 and six RFCs that had amended it.

The header is 20 bytes without options and at most 60, since the 4-bit Data Offset counts 32-bit words. It carries 16-bit source and destination ports, a 32-bit sequence number (that of the segment's first data octet), a 32-bit Acknowledgment Number (the next octet expected), eight control bits, a 16-bit receive window, a checksum and an urgent pointer. The flags are two for Explicit Congestion Notification (ECN), CWR (Congestion Window Reduced) and ECE (ECN-Echo), then URG (urgent), ACK (acknowledgement), PSH (push), RST (reset), SYN (synchronize) and FIN (no more data). The checksum also covers a pseudo-header from the IP layer, 96 bits for IPv4 and 320 for IPv6 (IP versions 4 and 6), so a segment delivered to the wrong address fails it. The options in the opening segments matter most: Maximum Segment Size (MSS), assumed to be 536 bytes for IPv4 (576 minus 40) or 1220 for IPv6 (1280 minus 60) when the peer sends none; Window Scale; Selective Acknowledgment (SACK); and Timestamps.

A connection opens with the three-way handshake, SYN, SYN-ACK, ACK, in which each side picks an Initial Sequence Number (ISN) and acknowledges the other's; RFC 9293 gives the principal reason for three messages as stopping old duplicate connection initiations from causing confusion. It defines eleven states, from LISTEN, SYN-SENT and SYN-RECEIVED through ESTABLISHED to FIN-WAIT-1, FIN-WAIT-2, CLOSE-WAIT, CLOSING, LAST-ACK, TIME-WAIT and a fictional CLOSED that means no TCB exists. Closing takes a FIN in each direction, so a half-closed connection can still send the other way; a RST aborts at once. The side that closes first stays in TIME-WAIT for twice the Maximum Segment Lifetime (MSL), taken as 2 minutes, so stray segments expire before the same addresses and ports are reused; that is why busy clients and proxies hold thousands of TIME-WAIT sockets.

Reliability is cumulative acknowledgement plus retransmission on a timer. RFC 6298 (June 2011) derives the RTO (Retransmission Timeout) from smoothed round-trip time (RTT) samples, starts it at 1 second instead of the earlier 3, rounds lower values up to 1 second, and doubles it on each expiry. Flow control is the receive window. The 16-bit field caps it at 65,535 bytes, far too little for fast, long paths, so RFC 7323 (September 2014) adds Window Scale, negotiated only in SYN segments, with a shift of at most 14 for a 1 GiB window, and Timestamps for RTT measurement and Protection Against Wrapped Sequences (PAWS). A window smaller than bandwidth times RTT caps throughput whatever the link speed.

Congestion control came out of a crisis. In October 1986 the internet had the first of a series of congestion collapses: throughput between Lawrence Berkeley Laboratory and the University of California at Berkeley, 400 yards and two hops apart, fell from 32 kbit/s to 40 bit/s. Van Jacobson and Michael Karels blamed transport implementations rather than the protocol, and their 1988 paper added seven algorithms to the Berkeley TCP, including RTT variance estimation, exponential retransmit backoff, slow start and fast retransmit, all built on the conservation of packets: a new packet enters the network only when an old one leaves. RFC 5681 (September 2009) now standardizes slow start, congestion avoidance, fast retransmit after three duplicate ACKs, and fast recovery. Most hosts run CUBIC, standardized in RFC 9438 (August 2023), which records it as the default in the Linux, Windows and Apple stacks.

Because an endpoint accepts any segment whose numbers look plausible, TCP has a long security record. Robert Morris described sequence-number guessing in a 1985 Bell Laboratories report, and its exploitation became widely known about ten years later through Tsutomu Shimomura's 1995 account; RFC 1948 (1996), then RFC 6528 (February 2012), answered with ISNs built from a 4-microsecond clock plus a keyed pseudorandom function of addresses and ports, the method RFC 9293 now recommends. The SYN flood, published in Phrack in 1996 and seen in the wild by that September against a provider's mail servers, fills the backlog of half-open connections. RFC 4987 (August 2007) surveys the defences, chiefly SYN cookies, which encode the state in the SYN-ACK's sequence number; Linux enables them by default, yet its documentation calls them a last resort that conflicts with TCP extensions.

In practice, ss -tan on Linux lists every TCP socket and its state. Linux defaults explain many tickets: keepalive probes start after 7200 seconds, matching RFC 9293's rule that keep-alives are off by default with an interval of no less than two hours; tcp_fin_timeout is 60 seconds; and tcp_retries2 of 15 lets a vanished peer go unnoticed for roughly 13 to 30 minutes. A firewall or load balancer whose idle timeout is shorter than the application's keepalive drops connections that both ends think are open. A full proxy such as an F5 BIG-IP virtual server runs separate client-side and server-side TCP profiles, so each side's window and buffers are tuned independently, sized from bandwidth times path delay.

The neighbours define it by contrast. The User Datagram Protocol (UDP), IP protocol 17 where TCP is 6 in the Internet Assigned Numbers Authority (IANA) registry, adds ports and a checksum and nothing more. QUIC (RFC 9000, May 2021) runs several ordered streams in one encrypted connection over UDP, and because a lost packet blocks only the streams whose data it carried, it avoids the head-of-line blocking that a single TCP byte stream cannot.

packet.def: A unit of data with its own header, forwarded independently of whatever came before or after it.
packet.context: The word is Donald Davies's, coined in the mid-1960s for an idea Paul Baran had reached separately, and the naming mattered: it gave engineers, funders and standards bodies a way to discuss the thing without arguing about what to call it. The independence is the whole design. Because each packet carries its own addressing, no device has to remember a conversation, which is what lets a failed link be routed around and what makes the network cheap to scale; it is also why order, reliability and pacing had to be rebuilt at the endpoints.
packet.depth:
Packet is the general word for a block of data that crosses a network as one unit, carrying a header that tells every hop where it is going, so that each node can forward it without knowing anything about the blocks before or after it. Engineers use the word loosely, but the internet's host requirements, Request for Comments (RFC) 1122 (October 1989), give each layer its own term. A segment is the unit of the Transmission Control Protocol (TCP), a TCP header followed by application data; a message is the unit of any transport protocol; an IP datagram is the unit of the Internet Protocol (IP), an IP header followed by a message; a packet is what passes between the internet layer and the link layer, a whole IP datagram or a fragment of one; and a frame is the link-layer unit, a link header followed by a packet. The distinctions have consequences: a capture records frames, a router forwards packets, and an IP version 4 (IPv4) fragment is a packet that is not a complete datagram.

The idea arrived twice. At the RAND Corporation, Paul Baran's studies of 1960 to 1962, collected in 1964 as On Distributed Communications, asked whether a command and control network could survive an attack that destroyed its central switching centres, and answered with a network without central switches whose nodes divided information into message blocks and passed them on by what he called hot-potato routing. At the National Physical Laboratory (NPL) in Britain, Donald Davies and his team developed the same method from 1965, independently, and Davies called the blocks packets; RAND's own history records that his word displaced Baran's. The Internet Society's history adds that the ARPANET, the network of the Advanced Research Projects Agency, adopted the word from NPL's work, that its first node was installed at the University of California, Los Angeles (UCLA), in September 1969, and it credits Leonard Kleinrock with the first paper on packet switching theory, in July 1961. NPL's own network went into service in 1970 for some 200 users.

What packets buy is sharing. A circuit-switched telephone network reserves a path for the whole of a call, whether anyone is speaking or not; a packet network lets every conversation use every link, sending blocks as they are ready, so idle time costs nothing and a link's capacity is divided among whoever has data at that moment. Because each packet carries its own addressing, no node has to remember the conversation, and traffic can be routed around a failed link while the conversation goes on, which was Baran's survivability argument. The price is variability. Packets queue behind one another, so delay changes from packet to packet, and when a queue overflows packets are dropped, which makes loss, reordering and duplication normal events that the endpoints must handle, as TCP does.

Each layer wraps the one above. RFC 894 (April 1984), which defines IP over Ethernet, limits an IP datagram on Ethernet to 1500 octets and pads the data field to at least 46. A full-size TCP packet therefore holds 20 octets of IP header, 20 of TCP header and 1460 of data, and the Ethernet framing adds 18 octets to make a 1518-octet frame, the largest size in RFC 2544's reference table; the smallest Ethernet frame is 64 octets. On the wire every frame is also preceded by a 64-bit preamble and followed by a 96-bit gap, so small packets cost far more than their size suggests: RFC 2544 (March 1999) gives 14,880 frames per second as the maximum for 64-byte frames on 10 Mbit/s Ethernet, against 812 for 1518-byte frames, and the same arithmetic at 10 Gbit/s gives about 14.88 million 64-byte frames per second. That is why routers, firewalls and load balancers are rated in packets per second as well as bits per second, and why a flood of minimum-size packets can exhaust a device whose bandwidth figure looks ample.

A router handles each packet on its own: it reads the destination address, picks the longest matching prefix in its forwarding table, decrements the Time to Live (TTL) or Hop Limit, recomputes the IPv4 header checksum because the TTL has changed, and queues the packet on the outgoing interface. Nothing ties one packet to the next, so packets of one conversation may take different paths when routing changes or load is spread across equal-cost links. A packet larger than a link's Maximum Transmission Unit (MTU) is fragmented in IPv4, while IPv6 (IP version 6) routers never fragment and every IPv6 link must carry 1280 octets. IPv4 packets stop at 65,535 octets; IPv6 jumbograms, defined in RFC 2675 (August 1999), carry payloads from 65,536 up to 4,294,967,295 octets on links that can take them.

Because packets describe themselves, they can be recorded and read later, which is the basis of most network troubleshooting. The classic pcap file that tcpdump and libpcap write starts with a 24-octet header holding the magic number 0xa1b2c3d4 and a snapshot length; packets longer than that are truncated, and each 16-octet record header keeps both the captured length and the original length, so a reader can tell what is missing. tcpdump keeps up to 262,144 bytes of each packet by default; a smaller -s value saves disk at the cost of payload. On a proxy or an address-translating device the same flow appears as different packets on each side, so where a capture is taken decides what it can prove.

Independence is also what attackers exploit. A stateless packet filter judges every packet by its own header, so it cannot tell a reply from an unsolicited packet with the same addresses and flags, and RFC 1858 (October 1995) shows how fragments that hide or overwrite the transport header slip past it; stateful inspection exists to put the conversation back. Nothing in a packet proves its source address either, which is the root of spoofing and reflection attacks and the reason for ingress filtering under Best Current Practice (BCP) 38, RFC 2827.

Numbers worth remembering: 1500 octets of IP datagram on Ethernet, 1518 octets of frame, 64 octets of minimum frame and 46 of minimum payload, 576 octets that every IPv4 host must accept, 1280 octets of IPv6 minimum MTU, 65,535 octets of IPv4 maximum, and 14,880 minimum-size frames per second for every 10 Mbit/s of Ethernet.

packet-switching.def: Forwarding data as independent packets that share links with everyone else's, instead of holding a dedicated path open for the duration of a conversation.
packet-switching.context: The alternative it replaced was circuit switching, where a call reserved a path end to end whether or not anything was being said. Packet switching wins whenever traffic is bursty, which is nearly always in data: the link is shared, the idle moments of one conversation carry another's, and capacity is sold many times over. The costs are the mirror image and they are permanent - no reservation means no guarantee, so delay varies, congestion is possible, and every quality-of-service mechanism since exists to claw back some of what the reservation used to provide for free.

latency.def: The time between sending something and its arrival, distinct from bandwidth, which is how much arrives per second.
latency.context: The two get confused constantly, and the confusion is expensive: adding capacity does nothing for a slow application whose problem is round trips. Latency has four parts: propagation, which is physics and cannot be bought down; serialization, which shrinks as links get faster; queueing, which grows with load and is where most surprises live; and processing. Distance sets a floor no product can beat, which is why a chatty protocol crossing an ocean is slow no matter how much bandwidth is bought, and why moving the work closer is the only real fix.
latency.depth:
What is measured. Latency is a delay, and the Internet Engineering Task Force (IETF) work on Internet Protocol (IP) Performance Metrics defines two of them. One-way delay, RFC (Request for Comments) 7679 (January 2016, Internet Standard 81), is the time from the first bit leaving the source to the last bit reaching the destination, and needs clocks synchronized well enough to trust the subtraction. Round-trip delay, RFC 2681 (September 1999), needs only one clock, which is why ping and every Transmission Control Protocol (TCP) stack measure it, but the RFC lists its weaknesses: the forward and reverse paths may be different routers, queueing may differ by direction even on a symmetric path, and an application may care mostly about one direction. Two readings from it are worth remembering. The minimum round-trip time indicates the delay due only to propagation and transmission, and values above the minimum indicate congestion. The variation in delay is often called jitter, a word RFC 3393 deliberately avoids because it has two meanings; it defines IP packet delay variation instead.

Propagation: the floor. Distance sets a minimum no equipment can lower. ITU-T (the International Telecommunication Union's Telecommunication Standardization Sector) Recommendation G.114 (May 2003) gives planning values of 5 microseconds per kilometre for optical fibre systems, including repeaters and regenerators, and 4 for terrestrial coaxial or radio-relay systems. A 1,000 km fibre path therefore costs about 5 ms each way and 10 ms per round trip before a single router has done anything. Satellites make the same point at scale: G.114 puts propagation between earth stations at 12 ms for a 400 km orbit, 110 ms at 14,000 km and 260 ms at 36,000 km, the geostationary case, one way.

Serialization and processing. Every hop must clock the whole packet onto the wire before the next can start forwarding it, so serialization delay is size divided by rate: a 1,500-byte packet is 12,000 bits, which takes 12 microseconds at 1 Gbit/s and 1.2 ms at 10 Mbit/s. This is the part that faster links genuinely shrink. Processing, the lookup and any inspection, encryption or logging in the path, is usually small per device and adds up across many devices, and a device that terminates and inspects a connection adds its own handshakes as well.

Queueing: where the surprises live. A packet that arrives at a busy link waits behind those already queued, and the wait grows with load. Jim Gettys and Kathleen Nichols named the failure bufferbloat in ACM Queue in 2011: excessively large and frequently full buffers inside the network. Gettys measured more than 1.2 seconds of latency on a path whose unloaded round trip was under 10 ms; a 500 KB buffer draining at 2 Mbit/s accounts for a full second, and a 128 KB buffer on a 3 Mbit/s uplink takes 340 ms to empty. Active queue management attacks it directly. Controlled Delay (CoDel), RFC 8289 (January 2018, Experimental), tracks how long packets sit in the queue, tolerates a standing queue of 5 ms against an interval of 100 ms for the terrestrial internet and drops beyond that. Low Latency, Low Loss, and Scalable Throughput (L4S), RFC 9330 (January 2023), observes that spikes of hundreds of milliseconds are not uncommon even with state-of-the-art queue management, that more link capacity offers diminishing returns if latency is not addressed, and aims at queueing below 1 ms on average and about 2 ms at the 99th percentile.

Why latency caps throughput. TCP can have only one window of unacknowledged data in flight per round trip. RFC 7323 (September 2014) explains the consequence: the 16-bit window field limits the window to 64 KiB, and on a path whose bandwidth-delay product exceeds that, the window, not the link, limits throughput; window scaling, with an exponent limited to 14, allows up to 1 GiB. The arithmetic is unforgiving: 64 KiB per 100 ms round trip is about 5.2 Mbit/s however fast the link. Loss recovery is also paced by time: RFC 6298 (June 2011) sets the initial retransmission timeout to 1 second, down from 3, and rounds any computed value below 1 second up to 1 second.

Round trips in protocols. Each exchange that must finish before the next starts costs a full round trip. A new TCP connection spends one on the three-way handshake (RFC 9293, August 2022), and TLS 1.3 (Transport Layer Security, RFC 8446, August 2018) one more for its full handshake, so the first request on a new connection using the Hypertext Transfer Protocol over TLS (HTTPS) leaves after two round trips, 300 ms at a 150 ms round trip time. TLS 1.3's zero round-trip mode saves one for some application data at the cost of certain security properties, and QUIC (RFC 9000, May 2021), designed for low-latency connection establishment, uses a combined cryptographic and transport handshake. A protocol that makes many sequential round trips is slow over distance for the same reason, and no extra bandwidth changes it.

How much is too much. Jakob Nielsen's limits, published in 1993, still frame user perception: 0.1 second feels instantaneous, 1 second keeps the flow of thought, and 10 seconds is about as long as attention holds. For conversation, ITU-T G.114 finds that below 150 ms one way most applications see essentially transparent interactivity, and recommends not exceeding 400 ms for general network planning. RFC 9330 cites studies in which end-to-end delay above 50 ms, or even 20 ms, starts to feel unnatural for demanding interactive applications. Measure accordingly: compare the current round trip with the path's minimum to separate distance from queueing, and report percentiles, because users notice the tail and averages hide it.

c.def: The general-purpose systems programming language Dennis Ritchie developed at Bell Labs in the early 1970s out of Ken Thompson's B, in which the Unix kernel was rewritten in 1973 and in which most operating systems and network stacks are still written.
c.context: Its bargain is explicit: enough abstraction to be portable, and nothing between the programmer and the memory. That is why it runs everywhere and why it produced whole vulnerability classes: buffer overflows, use-after-free, and the rest of the memory-safety catalogue that newer languages exist to prevent. Both halves of that sentence are true at once, which is the honest way to read fifty years of C. It is not going away either: too much of the world's running software is written in it for a rewrite to be a plan.
c.depth:
What it is. C is a compiled, statically typed, procedural language for systems work: a program is a set of functions and global declarations, translated ahead of time into machine code, with a small standard library. Ritchie named the two ideas most characteristic of it: the relationship between arrays and pointers, and a declaration syntax that mimics expression syntax. A pointer is an address that supports arithmetic, an array is reached through a pointer to its first element, and a string is not a type but a convention, which the current standard defines as a contiguous sequence of characters terminated by and including the first null character. Nothing in the language records how long a buffer is, so nothing stops a copy from running past its end. That single choice explains both the speed and the bug history.

Where it came from. By 1969 Bell Labs had concluded that Multics, its joint venture with MIT (Massachusetts Institute of Technology) and General Electric, would deliver too late and at too high a cost, and the group that went on to build Unix lost its high-level language. Ken Thompson created B in 1969 and 1970, in Ritchie's words BCPL squeezed into 8K bytes of memory and filtered through Thompson's brain; like Martin Richards's BCPL (Basic Combined Programming Language), it was typeless, with one data type, the machine word. On the PDP-11 that no longer fitted: characters and byte addressing needed types, and B's threaded-code compiler produced programs too slow to rewrite the operating system in. In 1971 Ritchie added a character type and a compiler that emitted PDP-11 instructions, called the result NB, for new B, and then C, leaving open whether the name continued the alphabet or the letters of BCPL. The preprocessor arrived around 1972 and 1973, partly at Alan Snyder's urging. By early 1973 the essentials were complete, and in the summer of that year the Unix kernel for the PDP-11 was rewritten in C.

From one machine to many. Between 1977 and 1979 Ritchie, Thompson and Steve Johnson moved Unix to the Interdata 8/32, and Johnson wrote pcc, a compiler meant to be easy to retarget; the language changes of those years were about portability and type safety, and between 1973 and 1980 the type system gained unsigned, long, union and enumeration types. In 1978 Brian Kernighan and Ritchie published The C Programming Language, known as K&R from its authors' initials, and it served as the language reference until a formal standard arrived more than ten years later; a second edition followed in 1988. Its descendants include Objective-C and C++.

The standards. At Doug McIlroy's urging, the American National Standards Institute (ANSI) set up committee X3J11 in the summer of 1983; its standard, X3.159-1989, was finished at the end of 1989 and accepted by the International Organization for Standardization (ISO) as ISO/IEC 9899:1990. Ritchie counted one genuinely important change to the language: function prototypes, putting argument types in a function's signature, with syntax borrowed from C++. The standard is now kept by WG14, the C working group of the joint technical committee of ISO and the International Electrotechnical Commission (IEC), ISO/IEC JTC1/SC22/WG14, whose editions are C90, the 1995 amendment, C99, C11, C17 and C23, ISO/IEC 9899:2024, which reports __STDC_VERSION__ as 202311L. C11 removed the gets function, added threads and atomics, and made the bounds-checking interfaces of Technical Report (TR) 24731-1 optional. C23 made bool, true, false, static_assert and thread_local keywords, added nullptr, #embed, binary literals, typeof and attributes such as nodiscard and fallthrough, added memset_explicit, a memory store the compiler may never elide, for erasing secrets, required two's complement by removing the other sign representations, and dropped old-style function definitions with identifier lists. The next revision, C2y, is in progress; WG14's latest working draft is N3998 of 25 October 2026.

Undefined behaviour. The standard defines undefined behaviour as behaviour, upon use of a nonportable or erroneous construct or of erroneous data, for which it imposes no requirements: anything from ignoring the situation with unpredictable results to stopping the program. An out-of-range array subscript, use of a pointer to an object whose lifetime has ended, the unary * operator applied to an invalid pointer and a signed arithmetic result outside its type's range all qualify. Compilers may assume none of it happens and optimize on that basis. Chris Lattner explained for the LLVM project in May 2011 that because signed overflow is undefined, a compiler may fold X+1 > X to true; GCC (the GNU Compiler Collection) and Clang accept -fwrapv to make signed overflow wrap, at a cost in speed. The practical consequence is that an overflow check written in terms of the overflow it is meant to catch can be deleted by the optimizer.

The security record. Buffer overflow, use-after-free and out-of-bounds read are what that freedom costs at scale. Microsoft's Security Response Centre wrote in July 2019 that about 70 per cent of the vulnerabilities to which Microsoft assigns a Common Vulnerabilities and Exposures (CVE) identifier each year are memory safety issues placed in C and C++ code; the Chromium project reports the same share, around 70 per cent of its high and critical severity security bugs since 2015, half of them use-after-free. Network engineers meet it at the edge. Heartbleed, CVE-2014-0160, was an implementation mistake in OpenSSL's TLS (Transport Layer Security) heartbeat extension, not a protocol flaw, that let anyone on the internet read the memory of systems running OpenSSL 1.0.1 to 1.0.1f, private keys included; it entered the code in December 2011 and was fixed in 1.0.1g on 7 April 2014. CVE-2022-42475, published by Fortinet on 12 December 2022, was a heap-based buffer overflow in sslvpnd, the FortiOS SSL-VPN (Secure Sockets Layer virtual private network) daemon, that gave a remote unauthenticated attacker code execution and was exploited in the wild; one indicator of compromise was a crash log reading Signal 11 received, and signal 11 is SIGSEGV, invalid memory reference, on x86 and ARM Linux.

What is changing. WG14 keeps adding defences at the margin, most recently a provenance-aware memory object model, Technical Specification (TS) 6010, published in May 2025. The larger shift is in where new code is written. Microsoft's 2019 post made the case for memory-safe languages and named Rust; the Linux kernel, written in C and compiled under -std=gnu11, the GNU dialect of ISO C11, or with Clang, also supports Rust under CONFIG_RUST; and Google reported in September 2024 that memory safety issues fell from 76 per cent of Android vulnerabilities in 2019 to 24 per cent in 2024, because the problem is overwhelmingly new code and new code moved to memory-safe languages, while the existing C was left largely alone except for fixes. For anyone operating networks, the kernels, TLS libraries and daemons inside every appliance will stay C for years, so patch cadence and the exposure of management and VPN interfaces are where the language's bargain becomes an operational matter.

unix.def: The operating system Ken Thompson and Dennis Ritchie built at Bell Labs from 1969, whose design (a hierarchical file system, devices as files, small composable tools, processes forked from processes) became the shape almost everything since has copied.
unix.context: What spread was not the code but the model, and the reason is that the model was small enough to reimplement. Linux was written from scratch, the BSDs shed their AT&T code, and macOS is certified against a written specification, so they share a design rather than one source tree; POSIX (the Portable Operating System Interface) exists to write down what they have to agree on. For anyone operating systems today, the inheritance is practical: a shell that pipes one program into another, a filesystem that represents devices as files, and a permission model that predates the internet and still decides who can read what.
unix.depth:
What it is. Ritchie and Thompson's own description, in the paper first published in Communications of the ACM (Association for Computing Machinery) in July 1974, is a general-purpose, multi-user, interactive operating system offering a hierarchical file system with demountable volumes, compatible file, device and inter-process I/O (input/output), asynchronous processes, a command language selectable per user and a high degree of portability. They counted its achievement as showing that a powerful interactive system need not be expensive: it ran on hardware costing as little as 40,000 US dollars, and the main system software took less than two man-years. Today the word has two meanings. UNIX in capitals is a trademark of The Open Group, usable only by systems certified to the Single UNIX Specification; Unix in ordinary speech means the whole family, including Linux and the BSDs, which follow the design without the certificate.

How it began. Bell Labs withdrew from Multics in 1968 and 1969, leaving Thompson, Ritchie, Doug McIlroy and J. F. Ossanna without the interactive system they had come to rely on. Thompson found a little-used PDP-7, first to run a game, Space Travel, then to build a file system, processes, an editor, an assembler and a simple command interpreter, the shell; that is the system Ritchie says was born in 1969, although Brian Kernighan only suggested the name Unix, a pun on Multics, well into 1970. PDP-11 Unix became operational in February 1971, justified by a text-processing service for the Bell Labs patent department. Pipes arrived in 1972 at McIlroy's urging. In the summer of 1973 the kernel was rewritten in C; the new system was about a third larger but far easier to understand and change, and it gained multiprogramming. Thompson and Ritchie presented the first Unix paper at the Symposium on Operating Systems Principles at Purdue in November 1973, and by the 1978 revision of their paper more than 600 installations were in service. In 1983 the two received the ACM Turing Award; the citation says the genius of the Unix system is its framework, which enables programmers to stand on the work of others.

The ideas that lasted. The 1974 paper names three kinds of file: ordinary files, which are just sequences of bytes with no structure imposed, directories, and special files. Every supported device has a special file in /dev, read and written like any other file and covered by the same protection, so a program expecting a file name can be handed a device name. A directory entry holds only a name and an i-number; the i-node it points to holds the owner, the protection bits, the disk addresses, the size, the times and the link count. Protection was ten bits: nine for read, write and execute by the owner, the group and everyone else, and a tenth, set-user-ID, which runs a program with its owner's identity so that privileged programs can be written without administrative help; one user, the super-user, is exempt from the checks altogether. Processes are created by fork, replaced by exec, and collected by wait; the pipe call makes a channel that a parent hands to its children, and a filter is any program that copies its standard input to its standard output with processing. The shell is just a user program that ties these together.

Berkeley and the network. Berkeley received a Version 4 tape in January 1974, and Thompson spent a sabbatical there from the autumn of 1975, bringing up Version 6 with Bill Joy and Chuck Haley among the students who took to it. With funding from DARPA (the Defense Advanced Research Projects Agency), Joy integrated and tuned an early TCP/IP (Transmission Control Protocol and Internet Protocol) implementation, and 4.2BSD (Berkeley Software Distribution) shipped in August 1983; within eighteen months more than 1,000 site licences had been issued, and most Unix vendors shipped it rather than AT&T's System V, which lacked networking. Berkeley released its own networking code as the freely redistributable Networking Release 1 in June 1989 and a much larger Networking Release 2 in June 1991. Unix System Laboratories (USL) sued Berkeley Software Design, Incorporated (BSDI) over a commercial product built on it; the case was settled in January 1994, three of 18,000 files were removed, and 4.4BSD-Lite followed in June 1994, the code on which BSDI, NetBSD and FreeBSD all had to restart their systems.

Standards and the trademark. POSIX, now The Open Group Base Specifications Issue 8, also published as IEEE (Institute of Electrical and Electronics Engineers) Std 1003.1-2024, specifies the interfaces and the shell that portable programs may rely on, including the Epoch, defined as 00:00:00 UTC (Coordinated Universal Time) on 1 January 1970, from which Unix time counts seconds. The Open Group's register of UNIX certified products lists IBM AIX 7 and z/OS 3.1, HPE HP-UX 11i v3, SCO UnixWare and OpenServer, and Apple's macOS 15 Sequoia and macOS 26 Tahoe, certified to UNIX 03. Linux is not on it: its own documentation calls it a clone of Unix written from scratch by Linus Torvalds that aims towards POSIX and Single UNIX Specification compliance.

Where engineers meet it. Most network gear runs a Unix-like system under its command line. Juniper documents that most Junos OS hardware platforms run on an upgraded FreeBSD 10 or later kernel and that Junos OS Evolved is built on a Linux kernel, and Linux sits under a large share of firewalls, load balancers and cloud hosts. The inheritance shows in daily work: rwx permission strings and octal modes in ls -l and chmod, devices under /dev, timestamps in seconds since 1970 in logs and APIs (application programming interfaces), and a shell that composes small tools with pipes. The same design carries its oldest risk. Set-user-ID was meant to let a program act with its owner's rights, and a set-user-ID program owned by the super-user that can be tricked into running something else hands over the whole machine, which is why auditing such files remains a standard hardening step.

kernel.def: The part of an operating system that runs with full hardware privilege, mediating memory, processes, devices and the network for everything else.
kernel.context: The privilege boundary is the point. Ordinary programs cannot touch hardware directly; they ask, through system calls, and the kernel decides. That is what makes isolation between processes possible, and it is why a defect inside the kernel is categorically worse than one in an application: there is nothing above it to contain the damage. It is also why so much security engineering is about reducing what runs there: drivers moved to user space, filtering done in constrained virtual machines, and hypervisors adding a layer beneath it.
kernel.depth:
Two modes of one processor. Microsoft's description of Windows is the clearest general statement. The processor runs in two modes, user mode and kernel mode, and switches between them depending on the code it is executing. Each application runs in user mode inside a process with its own private virtual address space, so it cannot modify another application's data and its crash does not take the others down. All kernel-mode code shares one virtual address space, so a kernel-mode driver is not isolated from other drivers or from the operating system, and if it crashes, the whole operating system crashes. x86 processors offer four protection rings, but most operating systems use only two, ring 0 for the kernel and ring 3 for applications. The doorway between them is the system call, which the Linux manual calls the fundamental interface between an application and the kernel; programs rarely issue one directly and instead call a C library wrapper such as glibc's chdir().

What it contains, and how much. The Linux README lists what a modern Unix-like kernel is expected to provide: true multitasking, virtual memory, shared libraries, demand loading, shared copy-on-write executables, proper memory management and multistack networking including IPv4 and IPv6 (Internet Protocol versions 4 and 6). Where the line is drawn is a design choice. In a monolithic kernel, such as Linux, all operating system services run in kernel mode in the same memory area, which gives fast and direct hardware access at the price of tight coupling, so a bug in one device driver can crash the system. A microkernel moves as much as possible into servers running in user mode around a minimal kernel. Most real kernels sit between the two and are called hybrids, and the argument between Andrew Tanenbaum and Linus Torvalds over Linux's monolithic design is a famous debate about where the line belongs.

The Linux kernel today. Its documentation calls Linux a clone of Unix written from scratch by Linus Torvalds with a loosely knit team across the net; it is written in C, compiled under -std=gnu11, the GNU dialect of ISO (International Organization for Standardization) C11, and now also accepts Rust. On 11 November 2026 kernel.org listed mainline 7.4-rc2, stable 7.3.4, and longterm branches 6.18, 6.12, 6.6, 6.1, 5.15 and 5.10, the last two projected to end in December 2026 and 6.18 and 6.12 in December 2028. A mainline release arrives every nine to ten weeks: two weeks of merge window for new features, then about seven weeks of weekly release candidates, usually ending at rc7; stable updates follow roughly weekly. Running uname -r tells which kernel a box has, and anything after the dash marks a distribution kernel, maintained by the distribution and not by kernel.org.

Why a kernel bug is worse. The isolation that protects processes from each other is enforced by the kernel, so a flaw there defeats it for everyone. Dirty COW, CVE-2016-5195 in the CVE (Common Vulnerabilities and Exposures) list, was a race condition in the memory-management file mm/gup.c, present in Linux 2.x through 4.x before 4.8.3, that let any local user write to a read-only memory mapping through the copy-on-write logic and so gain privileges; it was exploited in the wild in October 2016. Volume is part of the picture too. The kernel team now assigns CVE numbers itself and, because almost any bug at that layer might be exploitable, assigns one to any bug fix it identifies as possibly security-relevant, which is why scanners report so many kernel CVEs and why reachability, not count, should drive the order of patching.

What a crash in kernel mode costs. On 19 July 2024 at 04:09 UTC (Coordinated Universal Time), CrowdStrike released a content configuration update for its Falcon sensor on Windows. A problem in Channel File 291 caused an out-of-bounds memory read in the sensor's Content Interpreter, an exception that could not be handled gracefully, and a Windows operating system crash, the blue screen, on hosts running sensor 7.11 or later that were online until 05:27 UTC. Microsoft estimated that 8.5 million Windows devices were affected, less than one per cent of all Windows machines. Nothing in the incident was a Windows flaw: it was third-party code running where, by design, a crash takes the operating system with it. In November 2024 Microsoft announced the Windows Resiliency Initiative, with new capabilities that let security products such as antivirus run outside kernel mode, in user mode like ordinary applications, and noted that kernel attack surfaces such as Tool Tips had already been moved to user mode.

Shrinking what runs there. The same logic drives eBPF on Linux. It runs sandboxed programs in a privileged context such as the kernel, extending it without changing kernel source code or loading kernel modules, and every program must pass a verifier that guarantees it runs to completion, uses no uninitialized variables and never accesses memory out of bounds before it is compiled just in time. BPF originally stood for Berkeley Packet Filter, and today it carries high-performance networking, load balancing, observability and security tooling. Hypervisors push the other way, putting a further layer of privilege beneath the guest kernel. For an engineer the practical rules follow from the boundary: patch kernels on a schedule that tracks the branch's end of life, prefer user-mode agents and verified extensions to third-party kernel drivers, and treat any local privilege escalation in the kernel as a remote one waiting for its first foothold.

shell.def: The command-language interpreter that reads commands, typed at a terminal or read from a script, and runs them as programs; on Unix-like systems an ordinary program such as sh, bash or zsh, and the interface through which most infrastructure work is still done.
shell.context: Its durability is a design consequence rather than nostalgia. Because Unix tools read text and write text, the shell can compose programs that were never written with each other in mind, and a pipeline assembled in one line does work that would otherwise need a project. That same property is a security surface: a shell interprets what it is given, so anything that builds a command from untrusted input is one quoting mistake away from executing it. Command injection is the shell doing exactly its job on the wrong text.
shell.depth:
What it is, and what it is not. POSIX (the Portable Operating System Interface) defines the shell simply as a command language interpreter. It reads input from a file, from the -c option or from the system and popen library functions, breaks it into words and operators, expands the words, sets up redirections, runs a function, a built-in, an executable file or a script, and collects the exit status. It is not the terminal, which only displays characters and passes keystrokes, and it is not the kernel: on Unix it is an ordinary user program. Dennis Ritchie described the loop that every shell still runs: read a command line, create a child process with fork, have the child exec the command from a file, wait for it to exit, and go back to the start. The same history explains why cd is built into the shell. When fork first arrived, the chdir command stopped working, because it changed the directory of the child created to run it, which promptly exited and left the shell where it was.

Where the word and the idea came from. Louis Pouzin wrote RUNCOM for MIT's (Massachusetts Institute of Technology's) CTSS (Compatible Time-Sharing System) in 1963 and 1964, a program that ran scripts of commands with argument substitution, so people could leave long jobs running overnight. At the end of 1964 or early in 1965 he described how the Multics command language could be built the same way, coined the word shell for it, and left a flowchart from which Glenda Schroeder of MIT and an engineer from General Electric wrote the first Multics shell; the rc in names such as .bashrc is a remnant of RUNCOM. Unix shipped Ken Thompson's shell in Versions 1 to 6, from 1971 to 1975. Redirection with less-than and greater-than came early, inspired by Multics, and pipes appeared in 1972 at the suggestion, or insistence, of Doug McIlroy. The PWB (Programmer's Workbench) or Mashey shell of 1975 to 1977 added variables, including the ancestor of PATH, and the Bourne shell of Version 7 Unix in 1979 added here documents and command substitution and fixed the language most later shells extend.

The shells in use. Bash, the GNU Project's Bourne Again SHell, is sh-compatible, borrows features from the Korn shell and the C shell, and is intended to conform to the IEEE (Institute of Electrical and Electronics Engineers) POSIX shell standard; its maintainer lists bash-5.3 as the current version, under the GNU General Public License version 3, and it is the default interactive shell on most Linux systems. Debian and Ubuntu use dash, a descendant of the Almquist shell, for /bin/sh; BusyBox carries an ash derivative for small embedded systems; and Apple made zsh the default login and interactive shell from macOS 10.15, with bash the default in 10.14 and earlier. A script that must run everywhere targets the POSIX language, now published as The Open Group Base Specifications Issue 8, IEEE Std 1003.1-2024. Vendors also call their command-line interfaces shells, as F5 does with tmsh, the TMOS Shell on BIG-IP, but those are product command languages rather than Unix command interpreters.

How a line becomes a command. POSIX fixes the order: tilde expansion, parameter expansion, command substitution and arithmetic expansion first, from beginning to end; then field splitting of the results; then pathname expansion, unless set -f is in effect; and quote removal last. Single quotes preserve every character literally; double quotes preserve everything except the dollar sign, the backquote and the backslash, so variables still expand inside them but are not split or globbed. That is the root of most shell-script bugs: an unquoted variable holding a file name with a space becomes two arguments, and one holding an asterisk becomes a list of files. A pipeline connects each command's standard output to the next command's standard input, and its exit status is the last command's unless the pipefail option, which POSIX.1-2024 specifies, makes any failure count. The standard also leaves a first line beginning with #! unspecified; running such a script is the operating system's business, not the shell language's.

The security surface. MITRE's CWE-78 (Common Weakness Enumeration) names the failure: a program builds an operating system command from externally influenced input without neutralizing the special elements that could change it. Python's subprocess documentation puts the defence plainly: the module does not call a shell unless asked, and with shell=True quoting whitespace and metacharacters becomes the application's job. Passing an argument list to the program directly, so that no shell parses it, removes the whole class. The shell can also be the vulnerable component itself. Shellshock, the Common Vulnerabilities and Exposures (CVE) entry CVE-2014-6271, published on 24 September 2014, was GNU Bash through 4.3 executing trailing strings after function definitions in environment variable values, reachable through OpenSSH's ForceCommand, Apache's mod_cgi and mod_cgid modules and DHCP (Dynamic Host Configuration Protocol) clients wherever an environment crossed a privilege boundary; the first fix was incomplete, and CVE-2014-7169 covers what remained.

Why it lasts. Every appliance built on a Unix-like system still has a shell underneath its management interface, and an engineer who can read a pipeline, quote a variable and tell a built-in from an external program can work on all of them. The habits that keep that power safe are few and constant: quote every expansion, avoid building commands from strings, run with the least privilege the job needs, and treat any text that reaches an interpreter, a shell included, as code.

compiler.def: A program that translates source code written in one language into another, usually lower-level, form that a machine can execute; Grace Hopper built the A-0 compiler in 1951 and 1952 and is credited with coining the term.
compiler.context: It is worth remembering that the compiler had to be argued for. The idea that a machine could usefully translate human-written text into instructions was not obvious in 1952, and the objection was that a programmer should write the instructions. The compiler is also where trust becomes circular: Ken Thompson's Turing lecture showed that a compiler can insert a backdoor into programs and into future compilers, so inspecting source proves nothing about the binary. Reproducible builds exist to close that loop.
compiler.depth:
A compiler translates a program written in one language, the source, into another, usually lower-level one, typically machine code or object code that is then linked into an executable. That separates it from an interpreter, which executes the source or an intermediate form directly, while just-in-time (JIT) compilation sits between the two by compiling at run time; the LLVM project (whose name, it says, is not an acronym) describes its design as capable of both static and dynamic compilation. Modern compilers are pipelines. A front end parses the language, an optimizer transforms an intermediate representation independent of both source and target (LLVM's is the LLVM IR, intermediate representation), and a code generator emits instructions for a particular processor. GCC, the GNU (GNU's Not Unix) Compiler Collection, shows how far the front ends have spread: C, C++, Objective-C, Fortran, Ada, Go, D, Modula-2, COBOL (Common Business-Oriented Language), Rust and, since an experimental front end was added in November 2025, Algol 68. Around the compiler sit the assembler, the linker and the loader, and the security story of the compiler is really the story of that whole toolchain.

The word and the first working example both trace to Grace Hopper. As head programmer for Remington Rand on the UNIVAC I (Universal Automatic Computer), she and her team produced the A-0 system in 1951 and 1952. Her own description is that she put the subroutines she had been collecting onto tape, gave each a call number, and then only had to write down the call numbers and let the computer find the routines and do the additions: this was the first compiler. The IEEE (Institute of Electrical and Electronics Engineers) Milestone dedicated to it in May 2024 is careful about what it was, a series of specifications that functioned as a linker/loader and a pioneering piece of automatic programming, and it credits her with inventing and coining the term compiler. A-1 and A-2 followed, the A-2 being the first compiler used extensively, then B-0, which became FLOW-MATIC, the line that led to COBOL. The idea had to be sold: Hopper recalled that she had a running compiler and nobody would touch it, because computers could only do arithmetic and could not do programs, and acceptance took about two years.

The argument was settled by FORTRAN (Formula Translation). John Backus received a budget at IBM in 1953, the language was created from 1954, and IBM made the first FORTRAN compiler available to users of the IBM 704 in 1957, after a project planned for six months had taken three years. Skeptics insisted that a program compiled from a high-level language could never be as efficient as one written directly in numerical codes; Backus's team answered with the first optimizing compiler, whose output ran nearly as fast as hand-crafted code. IBM's own history gives the scale of the change: as many as a thousand hand-keyed instructions for a problem could become 47 statements of FORTRAN, and a FORTRAN program could run on any system that had a FORTRAN compiler, which began the separation of software from the hardware it runs on.

Trust in the compiler is circular, and Ken Thompson proved it. In his Turing Award lecture, published in Communications of the ACM (Association for Computing Machinery) in August 1984, he described what he called the cutest program he ever wrote, in three stages: a program that prints its own source, a compiler that learns, and a C compiler carrying two Trojan horses. The first recognized the UNIX login command and miscompiled it to accept a known password as well as the real one; the second recognized the compiler's own source and reinserted both Trojans whenever the compiler was rebuilt. Once that binary was installed, the Trojans could be deleted from the source and would survive indefinitely, with no trace anywhere in source code. His moral was blunt: you can't trust code that you did not totally create yourself, and no amount of source-level verification or scrutiny will protect you from using untrusted code. He added that he could have picked any program-handling program, an assembler, a loader or even hardware microcode, and that the lower the level, the harder such bugs are to find. David A. Wheeler notes that an Air Force evaluation of Multics had already shown compilers could be subverted this way.

Two answers now exist, and both rest on comparing bits. Wheeler's Diverse Double-Compiling (DDC), published at ACSAC (Annual Computer Security Applications Conference) in 2005 and proved formally in his 2009 PhD dissertation at George Mason University, compiles a compiler's source with a second, independently trusted compiler and then compiles the source again with the result; if the final binary is bit-for-bit identical to the one under suspicion, the source accurately represents it. He demonstrated it with GCC, and the GNU Mes bootstrap later used it, rebuilding the Mes C compiler under GNU Guix, Nix and Debian with three major versions of GCC and getting identical results each time. Reproducible builds generalize the idea to all software: a build is reproducible if, given the same source code, build environment and instructions, any party can recreate bit-by-bit identical artifacts, checked with cryptographic hashes. The project traces the idea to GNU tools in the early 1990s; interest returned with Bitcoin's Gitian in 2011 and with Mike Perry's work on the Tor Browser after the surveillance disclosures of 2013; Debian took it up at DebConf13 in July 2013, when a first mass rebuild found 24 per cent of 5,240 source packages reproducible, rising to 67 per cent of 6,887 by the FOSDEM developer conference in 2014. The logic answers Thompson directly: if independent builders get the same bits, a backdoor would have to be in all of their toolchains at once.

The attack has happened in the wild. In September 2015 Palo Alto Networks' Unit 42 described XcodeGhost, which it called the first compiler malware on OS X. Because Apple's Xcode installer was nearly 3 GB and slow to download in China, developers took copies from Baidu's cloud file-sharing service, and the copies of versions 6.1 to 6.4 had been altered: a malicious Mach-O object file named CoreServices sat in one of Xcode's default framework search paths, so the linker added it to every iOS app built with that installation, without the developer's knowledge. Infected apps collected device and app details and sent them to command-and-control servers, and at least two passed Apple's App Store review. The tampering was visible to anyone who checked: code-signing verification of the installers showed the extra files. The lesson is the same as Thompson's, made practical: obtain toolchains from the vendor, verify their signatures, and treat the build machine as part of the product.

The compiler is also a security control in its own right. The OpenSSF (Open Source Security Foundation) Compiler Options Hardening Guide for C and C++, revised in August 2026, recommends for GCC and Clang a baseline that includes -D_FORTIFY_SOURCE=3, -fstack-protector-strong and -fstack-clash-protection, full RELRO (read-only relocation) with -Wl,-z,relro and -Wl,-z,now, position-independent executables with -fPIE -pie, -fcf-protection=full on x86_64, and -Wbidi-chars=any for code meant to be written only left to right. It also recommends, for production code, -fno-delete-null-pointer-checks and -fno-strict-overflow, a reminder that optimizers are allowed to delete a null-pointer check when the code has already dereferenced the pointer; the guide recalls that the Linux kernel builds with that option after such a deletion turned a benign bug into a trivially exploitable one. It also advises a blanket -Werror during development but not in distributed source, where it ties users to particular toolchain versions. The numbers worth remembering: A-0 in 1951 and 1952, FORTRAN in 1957, Thompson's lecture in 1984, Debian's reproducibility push from 2013, XcodeGhost in 2015, and the bit-for-bit comparison that underlies every defence against a dishonest compiler.

consensus.def: The problem of getting several machines to agree on one value when any of them may be slow, may fail, and cannot tell those apart.
consensus.context: It sounds administrative and it is the hardest thing in distributed systems, because a node that has not answered is indistinguishable from a node that is dead. Every replicated database, cluster leader election and configuration store rests on a consensus algorithm, and the practical consequence is a majority rule: an odd number of members, a quorum required to decide, and a minority that must stop rather than proceed alone. That is why a three-node cluster survives one failure and a two-node cluster survives none.
consensus.depth:
Stated exactly, a consensus algorithm lets a collection of processes that can propose values choose a single one of them, and Leslie Lamport's Paxos Made Simple gives the safety requirements in three lines: only a value that has been proposed may be chosen, only a single value is chosen, and a process never learns that a value has been chosen unless it actually has been. Liveness, that some value is eventually chosen, is the part that cannot be guaranteed outright. The practical use is the replicated state machine: each server keeps a state machine and a log of commands, the consensus algorithm keeps the logs identical, and once the cluster has decided on an entry the decision is final. The Raft project's own summary gives the operational shape: such algorithms make progress while any majority of servers is available, so a cluster of five keeps working with two failed, and if more fail it stops making progress but never returns an incorrect result.

The theory begins with faults worse than crashes. Lamport's notes on his own papers credit Reaching Agreement in the Presence of Faults, by Marshall Pease, Robert Shostak and Lamport in the Journal of the Association for Computing Machinery (ACM) in April 1980, with the first precise statement of the consensus problem, and with showing that a faulty processor which sends inconsistent information to the others, a Byzantine fault, defeats any traditional three-processor algorithm: in general 3n+1 processors are needed to tolerate n such faults, or 2n+1 if messages carry digital signatures. The same three authors' The Byzantine Generals Problem, in ACM Transactions on Programming Languages and Systems in July 1982, gave the problem its name and its story of generals, some of them traitors, who must agree whether to attack. Lamport writes that the draft title was The Albanian Generals Problem, until Jack Goldberg pointed out that there were Albanians outside Albania, and that the main reason for writing the paper was to give the problem a name that would attract attention.

Then came the limit. In April 1985 Michael Fischer, Nancy Lynch and Michael Paterson published Impossibility of Distributed Consensus with One Faulty Process in the Journal of the ACM, showing that in a completely asynchronous system, with no assumptions about the relative speed of processes or the delay of messages, no synchronized clocks and therefore no time-outs, every protocol for agreeing even on a single bit has the possibility of never terminating if just one process may fail. The reason is the heart of the whole problem: as the paper puts it, it is impossible for one process to tell whether another has died or is just running very slowly. The FLP result, after its authors' initials, does not make consensus useless; it says that a real algorithm must either assume some timing, through time-outs, or accept that it may stall. Practical systems choose safety always and liveness when the network behaves.

Paxos is Lamport's answer. His notes say he found it while trying to prove impossible what the builders of Echo, a fault-tolerant file system built in the late 1980s at the Digital Equipment Corporation laboratory where he then worked, claimed to do: stay consistent through any number of non-Byzantine faults and make progress whenever a majority of processors worked. He described it as the legislature of a lost Greek island named Paxos, submitted The Part-Time Parliament in 1990, and saw it published only in May 1998 in ACM Transactions on Computer Systems; the parable confused readers so thoroughly that he wrote Paxos Made Simple, 13 pages with no formula more complicated than n1 > n2, published in December 2001. Its agents are proposers, acceptors and learners. A value is chosen when a majority of acceptors have accepted it, which works because any two majorities share at least one acceptor, and numbered proposals let a new proposer discover and respect any value that may already have been chosen. Its first implementation, Lamport recounts through Chandu Thekkath, was in the same laboratory's Petal storage system, and then in the lock server of the Frangipani file system.

Raft was written to be understood. Diego Ongaro and John Ousterhout of Stanford presented In Search of an Understandable Consensus Algorithm at the USENIX Annual Technical Conference in June 2014, where it won the best paper award. Raft manages a replicated log, produces a result equivalent to multi-Paxos and is as efficient, but separates the problem into leader election, log replication and safety, and enforces a stronger degree of coherency to reduce the number of states to reason about. etcd relies on Raft to keep its members consistent, and etcd in turn is the consistent and highly available key-value store that holds all of a Kubernetes cluster's API (application programming interface) data.

The arithmetic of quorums is where operations meets the theory. etcd's documentation states it directly: a quorum is a majority, (n/2)+1 members with the division rounded down, so a cluster of one or two tolerates no failure, three or four tolerate one, five or six tolerate two, and seven tolerates three. An even member adds cost without adding tolerance, and an odd count guarantees that a network partition always leaves one side with a majority that can carry on and be the source of truth when the partition heals; the same page advises no more than seven members, five being what Google's Chubby lock service suggests. If quorum is lost, etcd operates no longer and resumes safely once the network recovers and quorum returns, with Raft enforcing consistency. Apache ZooKeeper gives the same rules for its ensembles: available while a majority is up, three servers as the minimum, an odd number preferred because four machines survive only one failure, and all writes forwarded to a single leader whose followers agree on each proposal through ZooKeeper's atomic messaging protocol, so replicas never diverge. That is the reason a two-node cluster survives no failures: one survivor out of two is not a majority.

Much of what network engineers call clustering is not consensus, and the difference matters when links fail. VRRP (Virtual Router Redundancy Protocol), now version 3 in Request for Comments (RFC) 9568 of April 2024, is an election protocol: the highest-priority router becomes the Active Router for a virtual address, and a Backup that hears no advertisement for its Active_Down_Interval, three advertisement intervals (one second each by default) plus a small priority-based skew, declares the Active down and takes over. There is no vote and no quorum, so if the path between two routers breaks while both stay up, each concludes the other is dead and both forward as Active. F5 BIG-IP device service clustering works the same way at its core. Device trust is a certificate relationship: devices in a local trust domain exchange x509 certificates, some acting as certificate signing peer authorities and others as subordinate non-authorities. A Sync-Failover device group of up to eight devices synchronizes configuration, by pushing the most recent changes from one device to the rest rather than agreeing on a log, and fails traffic groups over when a device stops answering the continual health messages sent to its HA (high availability) self IP (Internet Protocol) address and, if that fails, its management address. With no majority to consult, a pair that loses every failover path goes active on both units; F5's own bug notes describe such Active/Active conditions and recommend multiple redundant failover paths, including the management network. The defence for a two-member design is therefore redundant heartbeat paths and fail-safes, while anything that must never disagree, such as a cluster's configuration store, needs three members and a real consensus algorithm.

quorum.def: The minimum number of members that must agree for a distributed system to act - normally a majority, so that two disjoint groups can never both decide.
quorum.context: The arithmetic is the whole safety argument. If a decision needs more than half the members, then any two decisions must share at least one member, and that member prevents them contradicting each other. It is also why cluster sizing is about odd numbers rather than round ones: five members tolerate two failures, six tolerate the same two and cost more. When a network splits, the side without quorum has to stop serving even though it is healthy, which feels wrong to operators the first time and is the only thing standing between them and split brain.

paxos.def: Leslie Lamport's consensus algorithm, the first proved correct for an asynchronous network where machines may fail, and the basis of most replicated systems built since.
paxos.context: It is famous for two things: being correct, and being hard to understand from the paper, which was written as an allegory about a fictional Greek parliament and took years to be taken seriously. Barbara Liskov and Brian Oki reached an equivalent design independently at about the same time. Most production systems run a variant rather than the original, and Raft was designed explicitly to be the same guarantee explained more simply - which is a rare case of a field admitting that comprehensibility is a property worth optimizing.

raft.def: A consensus algorithm designed to be understandable, giving the same guarantees as Paxos through an explicit leader, an append-only log and a defined election.
raft.context: Its contribution is pedagogical and that is not a small thing: an algorithm that operators can reason about is one they configure correctly, and most consensus outages are configuration rather than mathematics. It separates the problem into leader election, log replication and safety, which also maps onto what a monitoring system can show you. If you run etcd, Consul or a modern distributed store, you are running this, and the practical rule that falls out is the familiar one - odd member counts, and a minority that stops.

byzantine-fault-tolerance.def: Agreement that survives members which do not merely fail, but lie - sending different answers to different peers, whether through corruption or malice.
byzantine-fault-tolerance.context: Ordinary consensus assumes a failed node goes quiet. Byzantine tolerance drops that assumption, which is much harder and much more expensive: the classic result is that agreement needs more than two thirds of members to be honest. Most enterprise systems do not pay for it, and are right not to, because they control every node. It becomes necessary exactly when they do not - blockchains, and any system whose participants are mutually distrustful - which is the real technical distinction between a distributed database and a ledger.

fault-tolerance.def: Continuing to provide service while something is broken - which requires deciding in advance which failures are survivable and paying for that in redundancy.
fault-tolerance.context: The word is used loosely and the useful version is specific: you tolerate the failures you designed for, and no others. That means naming them - one power feed, one disk, one site, one region - and accepting that anything unnamed will take the service down. The recurring mistake is redundancy that shares a dependency: two devices on the same power strip, two links in the same duct, two regions with one identity provider. The second copy only helps if it fails independently, and independence is the property people forget to buy.

abstraction.def: Hiding how something works behind what it does, so callers depend on an interface rather than on an implementation.
abstraction.context: It is the only technique that makes large systems buildable, and it always leaks. Barbara Liskov's work is the rigorous version: a subtype must be usable wherever its supertype is, without the caller needing to know the difference - a statement about interfaces rather than inheritance. The operational corollary is worth stating too. Every abstraction has a failure mode that shows through: the network that pretends to be a local call still has latency, and the storage that pretends to be infinite still has a bill.

douglas-engelbart.def: The engineer who demonstrated the mouse, hypertext, windows, word processing and video conferencing in a single session on 9 December 1968 - the presentation now called the Mother of All Demos.
douglas-engelbart.context: The audience of professionals had never seen a cursor moved by a hand, and the machine driving it sat twenty-five miles away. Almost everything in that ninety minutes is now furniture, which is the strange part: the demonstration is more famous than any product he shipped. His stated aim was not convenience but augmentation - computers as tools for people to handle problems too complex to hold in one head - and he had written that argument down years before he had the hardware to show it. The Turing Award reached him in 1997, twenty-nine years after the demonstration.

margaret-hamilton.def: The director of the Software Engineering Division at the MIT Instrumentation Laboratory, who led the on-board flight software for the Apollo Guidance Computer, and who argued for calling the work engineering at all.
margaret-hamilton.context: She was the first programmer hired for Apollo at MIT, and the naming fight is part of the contribution: software was not treated as a discipline, and insisting on the term software engineering was a claim that it needed the same rigour as the hardware it flew on. The technical legacy is priority scheduling that sheds load rather than failing: during the lunar descent the computer discarded lower-priority work under overload instead of stopping. That is the ancestor of every system designed to degrade rather than die.

elizabeth-feinler.def: The information scientist who ran the Network Information Center from 1972 to 1989 - the Host Naming Registry for the whole internet - and whose group devised the .com, .edu, .gov, .mil, .org and .net scheme and built the first WHOIS server.
elizabeth-feinler.context: Before DNS, every machine on the network was listed in one file that her group maintained and published, updated almost daily by hand. That is the fact worth sitting with: the internet's entire naming authority was a directory service run by a team at SRI, reachable by telephone and post as well as by network. She joined Douglas Engelbart's Augmentation Research Center in 1972 and stayed until the year the registry became too big for a file. She called the NIC the prehistoric Google of its day, and in retirement she organized over 350 boxes of the Engelbart and NIC archives so the record would survive.

hosts-file.def: A local text file that maps host names to IP addresses, descended from HOSTS.TXT, the single host table the early network used before DNS.
hosts-file.context: Before DNS, every host fetched the NIC's HOSTS.TXT by FTP, and RFC 1034 names the cost, growing with the square of the number of hosts, among the reasons DNS was built. The local file survives as /etc/hosts and the Windows hosts file, and an entry in it overrides DNS wherever the system consults it first.
hosts-file.depth:
It began in January 1974, when RFC 608 had the NIC publish an ASCII file of host names and addresses, HOSTS.TXT, regenerated weekly or as the situation warranted. RFC 952 (October 1985), by Harrenstien, Stahl and Feinler, is the final specification: NET, GATEWAY, HOST and DOMAIN entries in colon-separated fields, fetched by FTP from SRI-NIC or through the hostname server. RFC 1034 records why it ended: distribution grew with the square of the number of hosts, and organizations had to wait for the NIC to make their changes visible.

Today's file holds one line per address: the address, the canonical name, then aliases, IPv4 or IPv6, with # starting a comment. On Windows it sits in %WinDir%\System32\Drivers\Etc, typically C:\Windows\System32\drivers\etc. Whether it is read before DNS is configuration, not protocol: on glibc systems the hosts line of /etc/nsswitch.conf lists the sources in order, files meaning /etc/hosts, and the manual's own example puts dns first.

A forgotten entry keeps one machine on an old address while every other follows DNS, and Microsoft lists a modified hosts file as a cause of connectivity problems. getent hosts resolves a name in the nsswitch order, as the C library does, while dig asks name servers directly, so when the two disagree the file or the switch order is the first suspect.

whois.def: The query service that answers who registered a domain or an address block - the first query-based host name and address server, defined in Feinler's group in 1982.
whois.context: It began as a directory of people and machines on a network where everyone was reachable, and that origin explains its problems: a protocol with no structured schema, no authentication and no privacy model, answering in whatever text each registry chooses. Registration data was public because the early network assumed accountability rather than anonymity, and privacy law has since forced most of it behind redaction. RDAP is the structured, authenticated successor, and the transition is slow because the old one still answers.

steve-crocker.def: The author of RFC 1, published 7 April 1969, and the person who chose to call the series Requests for Comments rather than standards.
steve-crocker.context: He later called it a modest and entirely forgettable memo, and the modesty was the design. A graduate student had no authority to declare a standard, so the documents invited disagreement instead of announcing decisions - and that framing is why the series survived the arrival of everyone with more authority than him. The internet's technical documents are still called requests for comments sixty years on, by organizations that could rename them any time they liked.

jcr-licklider.def: The psychologist who ran ARPA's Information Processing Techniques Office from 1962 and addressed his memos to the Members and Affiliates of the Intergalactic Computer Network.
jcr-licklider.context: He did not build the network; he funded the people who did, and described what it should be before the hardware existed. The joke in the name hides a serious specification: an electronic commons open to all, and the main medium of informational interaction for governments, institutions, companies and individuals. That is close to what happened. His other contribution was structural - the money he directed created computer science departments at several universities, which is why the field had people in it a decade later.
