wietse-venema.def: The Dutch security researcher who wrote TCP Wrapper and the Postfix mail server and, with Dan Farmer, the SATAN scanner and The Coroner's Toolkit, tools that made the case for examining your own systems the way an attacker would.
wietse-venema.context: The 1993 paper that announced SATAN was called Improving the security of your site by breaking into it, and the reaction became the story: the San Jose Mercury compared releasing the scanner to handing out rocket launchers at the local library. It shipped anyway, and the position it defended, that defenders need the attacker's view and that withholding the tool protects nobody who is already being scanned, is now the assumption behind every vulnerability scanner sold. Postfix, written later at IBM Research, is the other half of the same instinct: instead of patching the mail server everyone ran, rebuild one from separate, unprivileged processes so that a single bug cannot hand over the whole system.
wietse-venema.depth:
Wietse Zweitze Venema was born on 24 June 1951 and trained as a physicist, with a doctorate from the University of Groningen, before he moved into computing. He spent twelve years as systems architect in the Mathematics and Computing Science department of Eindhoven University of Technology, part of that time writing tools to translate Electronic Data Interchange (EDI) messages, and it was there, defending the university's own machines, that he wrote the tools that made his name. In 1996 he emigrated to the United States and joined IBM's Thomas J. Watson Research Center in New York State, where Postfix was born; he later spent eight years at Google, and he still maintains Postfix.

TCP Wrapper began as a response to one intruder. Around 1990 Eindhoven was under heavy attack by a Dutch cracker who repeatedly obtained root and then ran rm -rf / to erase his tracks. One night Venema noticed the attacker watching the university through the finger service, which asked for no password and kept no record. Rather than switch finger off, he set out to learn where the requests came from. Vendor sources for the network daemons were not available, so he used a swap: inetd, the daemon that waits for connections and starts the right server, was left alone; the vendor's server programs were moved elsewhere, and a few lines of code took their place that logged the remote host name and then ran the real server. Because the wrapper never exchanges data with the client or the server, one binary served telnet, ftp, finger and the rest, and the risk of bugs was tiny. He extended it in stages: access control through two files, /etc/hosts.allow and /etc/hosts.deny, consulted in that order, with unmatched service and host pairs allowed, used first to shut out the open terminal servers the cracker liked; automatic reverse finger probes of suspicious sites; booby traps on unused services such as tftp as an early-warning system; and a check that drops a connection when a host's name and address do not match, which mattered for rsh and rlogin. With the Computer Emergency Response Team (CERT) he traced the attacker to accounts at Stanford, where Stephen Hansen had been watching him, and found that the same man had attacked AT&T Bell Labs' gateway, where Bill Cheswick and colleagues let him into a monitored environment. He was never arrested. Venema described all this at the 3rd UNIX Security Symposium in Baltimore in September 1992, after a Dutch-language talk at the NLUUG and SURF security meeting of 23 April 1992; the last release, 7.6, is still in his archive.

On 2 December 1993 Venema and Dan Farmer posted to Usenet Improving the security of your site by breaking into it, which explained to administrators what crackers had known for a long time and announced a program called SATAN, the Security Administrator Tool for Analyzing Networks. Delivering it took more than a year, during which SATAN became, in Venema's own description, the most famous piece of internet vaporware. A documentation release with a sample database came on 15 March 1995 and the program was scheduled for 5 April 1995. SATAN was written in Perl 5, ran from a web browser (Netscape, Mosaic or Lynx in the README), had to run as superuser to collect data and was built to survey hundreds of hosts, one database per block of 256 addresses; its point, in the authors' words, was to close much of the knowledge gap between intruders and system administrators by proposing how to fix the problems it found. The README ends: SATAN was written to improve Internet security; don't put our work to shame. The press before release was the opposite: the Oakland Tribune likened it to randomly mailing automatic rifles to 5,000 addresses, the Los Angeles Times to handing a gun to a 12-year-old, the San Jose Mercury to distributing high-powered rocket launchers free of charge at your local library or school, and the New York Times carried the complaint that it discovers vulnerabilities for which we have no solutions. On 27 March 1995 TidBITS reported that Farmer and Silicon Graphics had parted company the week before, largely over SATAN, and that the New York Times and National Public Radio were following the story. After release, Nick Christenson observed that the scanner announced itself like a rock concert in the scanned machine's log file. The archive still offers satan-1.1.1 and, separately, Venema's UDP and TCP port scanners from it.

The other side's case deserves stating as its critics made it: a capable scanner, free to anyone, lowers the cost of attack for people who could not have written one, and defenders cannot patch everything at once. The authors' answer was that the holes existed whether or not anyone published a scanner, that attackers already had their own tools, and that a tool which explains every finding helps the administrator more than the intruder. That argument has returned with every jump in capability since, and SATAN's release, with its warnings and its anticlimax, remains the reference case.

Postfix came out of IBM Research, an alternative to the widely used Sendmail whose outside was deliberately Sendmail-compatible and whose inside was completely different. Formerly called VMailer, it was released at the end of 1998 as the IBM Secure Mailer, and John Markoff's New York Times article of December 1998, Sharing Software, IBM to Release Mail Program Blueprint, is credited on the Postfix site with putting open source on the agenda of IBM's chief executive, Lou Gerstner. The design document is a short lesson in least privilege. The initial release had about 30,000 lines of code, so no single mechanism was trusted: most daemons, above all the Simple Mail Transfer Protocol (SMTP) server and client that face the network, run at fixed low privilege inside a chroot jail; activities are insulated in separate processes, so there is no direct path from the network to the local delivery programs, and every program that talks to the outside world is single-threaded; delivery programs run under a resident master daemon with no parent-child relationship to user processes, which removes attacks through inherited signals, open files and environment variables; and no Postfix program is set-uid, a concept the document calls the biggest mistake made in UNIX history. His 1996 USENIX Security paper, Murphy's law and computer security, had already set out the lessons he drew from errors in his own software and in other people's.

Postfix remains under active maintenance: release 3.11.0 shipped on 5 March 2026, and on 7 September 2026 stable 3.11.7 shipped together with legacy releases down to 3.5.28. Features track the mail standards, from opportunistic DNS-Based Authentication of Named Entities (DANE) TLS (Request for Comments (RFC) 7672) in version 2.11 to REQUIRETLS (RFC 8689) in 3.11. Its security record is unusually well documented by its author. When an exploit attributed to a collection of National Security Agency (NSA) tools surfaced in 2017, the Postfix site explained that it targeted Postfix 2.0 to 2.2, through a memory-corruption bug in a workaround for a Sendmail problem, fixed eleven years earlier in 2.2.11. From July 2015 all supported releases stopped enabling export-grade ciphers and SSLv2 and SSLv3 by default, and the site gave one-line fixes for FREAK and Logjam, such as postconf smtpd_tls_exclude_ciphers=EXPORT followed by postfix reload. In December 2023, days before the Christmas break, a security firm published SMTP smuggling, which exploits differing treatment of the end-of-data sequence: a sending service passes on a bare line feed, dot, line feed (or line feed, dot, carriage return, line feed) and the receiving service takes it as the standard carriage return, line feed, dot, carriage return, line feed, so that smuggled SMTP commands inject a spoofed message. Venema traced the weakness to Sendmail's decades-old acceptance of bare line feeds, copied by Postfix and Exim for compatibility, noted that Common Vulnerabilities and Exposures (CVE) identifiers were assigned to all three, and complained that critical information had not reached the Postfix maintainers before publication, which turned it into an unintended zero-day.

The collaboration with Farmer continued in forensics. The Coroner's Toolkit (TCT), a set of programs for the post-mortem analysis of a UNIX system after a break-in, was first presented at a free computer forensic analysis class they gave in August 1999; a column series in Doctor Dobb's Journal followed, and in 2005 their book Forensic Discovery. Venema served a two-year term as chair of the Forum of Incident Response and Security Teams (FIRST), sits on the board of the Digital Forensic Research Workshop (DFRWS), and kept publishing research from IBM, including work on privilege escalation by pathname manipulation at the Network and Distributed System Security (NDSS) symposium in 2010 and, with Vern Paxson and others, bounds on covert communication over DNS at USENIX Security 2013.

The honours came from the communities that used the tools. He received the Security Summit Hall of Fame award in July 1998; the 1999 SAGE (System Administrators Guild) Outstanding Achievement Award, presented at LISA '99 by SAGE president Barb Dijker for his continual work to improve the security of systems; the award of the NLUUG, the Netherlands UNIX users group, in November 2000; the Sendmail Milter Innovation Award in November 2006; the Free Software Foundation's (FSF) Award for the Advancement of Free Software for 2008, presented by Richard Stallman at LibrePlanet in March 2009 for his contributions to network security and his creation of Postfix; and the Information Systems Security Association (ISSA) Hall of Fame in October 2012.

For an engineer today the traces are everywhere and mostly invisible. On a host running Postfix, a mail transfer agent (MTA), the design document is visible in the process list: a resident master daemon starting small single-purpose processes at low privilege, smtpd facing the network and local delivery out of its reach. TCP Wrapper's syntax of daemon, colon, client list in hosts.allow and hosts.deny still turns up on older systems and in audit checklists, though the mechanism is fading: OpenSSH 6.7, released on 6 October 2014, removed sshd's tcpwrappers and libwrap support, and Red Hat describes tcp_wrappers as deprecated and removed in Red Hat Enterprise Linux (RHEL) 8, where the hosts files still ship but filtering belongs to firewalld and systemd. The idea it introduced, a small, auditable filter that logs and decides before the real service ever sees the client, is the idea behind per-service access lists.

katie-moussouris.def: The researcher who created Microsoft's bug bounty programme and helped create the first one at the US Department of Defense, and who has spent the years since arguing about how they should be run.
katie-moussouris.context: The contribution is institutional rather than technical, and it is the harder kind: persuading a company that paying outsiders to find its defects is cheaper than not knowing about them. Her later argument is the one worth carrying - that a bounty is not a security programme, and an organization that cannot fix what it already knows about will not be helped by learning more. Bounties reward finding; nothing in them rewards repairing, which is why the mature version pairs them with a disclosure policy and a fix pipeline.

daniel-j-bernstein.def: The cryptographer and programmer behind qmail and djbdns, and of the curve and cipher designs now widely deployed - and the person who put money behind a security guarantee for his own software.
daniel-j-bernstein.context: The guarantee is the part that changed practice: he offered a cash reward for a verifiable security hole in qmail, which was an unusual claim to make in the 1990s and a workable one because the software was small enough to reason about. His designs are opinionated in the same direction - fewer moving parts, less privilege, no configurability that can be misconfigured. He is also a lasting argument in the field about tone: the technical positions and the public disputes with other implementers arrive together in the record, and both belong in it.
daniel-j-bernstein.depth:
The case that tied his name to the Crypto Wars began with a paper. As a mathematics graduate student at Berkeley he developed an encryption algorithm he called Snuffle and wanted to publish it three ways, as an algorithm, as an explanatory paper and as source code, and to discuss it in classrooms and at conferences. The ITAR (International Traffic in Arms Regulations) scheme required him to submit his ideas for government review, register as an arms dealer and obtain a licence to publish, on pain of civil and criminal penalties.

With the EFF (Electronic Frontier Foundation), and Cindy Cohn as chief counsel, he sued in February 1995. On 15 April 1996 the district court refused the government's motion to dismiss, in a decision the EFF describes as establishing precedent for First Amendment protection of software; in December 1996 Judge Patel held parts of the export regime unconstitutional, and in August 1997, after the controls had moved to the Commerce Department, she struck down the new regulations too. On 6 May 1999 the Ninth Circuit affirmed his right to publish encryption source code.

The government sought a rehearing and the case wound on, but the practical result arrived anyway, and the EFF credits the case with changing US export regulations on encryption software. Its account of John Gilmore, who found the government documents that showed the constitutional problem and helped start the case, puts the outcome plainly: the decision made it legal in 1999 for browsers, websites and software such as PGP to use the encryption of their choice.

rfc.def: A Request for Comments (RFC) is a document in the numbered, permanent series in which internet protocols, operating practices and much else are published, from Proposed Standards to informational notes and April jokes. The modest name dates from 1969, when the first author claimed no authority to set a standard.
rfc.context: Not every Request for Comments (RFC) is a standard: the series carries Proposed Standards and Internet Standards, Best Current Practice, Informational and Experimental documents and the odd April Fools' joke, and the status, not the number, says which. Every RFC is free to read, and once published its text never changes: a mistake becomes an erratum and a revision becomes a new RFC that updates or obsoletes the old one. That is why RFC numbers are cited in configuration guides and code comments across the industry, and why a careful reader checks the status and the Obsoleted by line before trusting one.
rfc.depth:
What the series is, and what it is not. Request for Comments (RFC) 8729, from the Internet Architecture Board (IAB), calls it the archival series dedicated to documenting internet technical specifications, from research contributions to standards, available free of charge to anyone. The number is assigned at publication, and each RFC also has a Digital Object Identifier (DOI) of the form 10.17487/RFC9293. An Internet-Draft is not an RFC: under RFC 2026 drafts have no formal status, are removed after six months without action and are not a means of publishing a specification, so a protocol cited by a draft name is a proposal, however widely deployed.

Where it came from. Steve Crocker of UCLA wrote RFC 1, Host Software, dated 7 April 1969, as notes from the group designing the ARPANET's host protocols. In RFC 8700 (December 2019) he recalls his one rule: a note had to be complete before it got a number, to keep holes out of the sequence. Jon Postel took the series over in 1971, when Crocker left for ARPA, and defined the role of RFC Editor by doing it (RFC 902 formalized it in July 1984); after his death in October 1998 Joyce Reynolds and Bob Braden carried on, and production moved to a contractor, Association Management Solutions (AMS), from October 2009. Governance is now RFC 9280 (June 2022), version 3 of the RFC Editor Model: the open RFC Series Working Group (RSWG) proposes policy, the RFC Series Approval Board (RSAB) approves it, and the RFC Production Center (RPC), contracted by the Internet Engineering Task Force (IETF) Administration LLC, edits and publishes. The index generated on 11 November 2026 runs to RFC 10082; RFC 10000 is marked Not Issued, and the RFC Editor explains such gaps as numbers assigned to documents never published.

Streams. Five streams feed the series, and modern RFCs print the stream at the top left, where older ones said Network Working Group. The IETF stream is the only one that creates Internet Standards; the Internet Research Task Force (IRTF), the IAB and the Independent Submission stream publish the rest; the Editorial stream, created by RFC 9280, publishes the policies of the series itself; documents older than the streams are labelled Legacy. RFC 7841 (May 2016) spells out the consequence: documents from other streams have not had IETF review for security, congestion control or harmful interaction with deployed protocols, and the IETF disclaims any knowledge of their fitness for any purpose.

Status. RFC 2026 (Best Current Practice 9, October 1996, Scott Bradner) set three standards-track levels, Proposed Standard, Draft Standard and Standard, with minimum stays of six months and four months on the first two, and a Draft Standard needed at least two independent and interoperable implementations from different code bases. Off the track sit Experimental, Informational and Historic. RFC 6410 (October 2011) cut the ladder to Proposed Standard and Internet Standard because the vast majority of standards-track documents were published as Proposed Standards and never advanced. Promotion now needs at least two independent interoperating implementations with widespread deployment, no errata that would break interoperation with deployed code, no unused features that greatly increase complexity, and an IETF-wide Last Call of at least four weeks; the RFC is then reclassified without a new document. The 11 November 2026 index shows how rarely that happens: more than 4,400 Proposed Standards against about 100 Internet Standards, with 136 RFCs still at the abandoned Draft Standard level. The status shown is the current one; RFCs older than RFC 1128 mostly carry Unknown.

Subseries and relations. Because an RFC never changes, the series needs names that outlive individual documents. The STD subseries, started with RFC 1311 in March 1992, labels Internet Standards and the BCP subseries, started with RFC 1818 in August 1995, labels Best Current Practice; one STD or BCP number can cover several RFCs and survives their replacement. The Transmission Control Protocol (TCP) shows the mechanics: RFC 793 (September 1981, Jon Postel) was updated by RFCs 1122, 3168, 6093 and 6528 and is now marked obsolete, replaced by RFC 9293 (August 2022), which carries STD 7. Hypertext Transfer Protocol (HTTP) semantics are RFC 9110 (June 2022), STD 97, which obsoletes RFCs 7230 to 7233 and 7235, themselves successors of RFC 2616. BCP 9 groups RFC 2026 with RFC 6410, which updates it. The header records Updates and Obsoletes; only the RFC Editor's info page can show the reverse links, Updated by and Obsoleted by.

Errata. Mistakes are recorded beside the text, never in it. An erratum is Technical or Editorial and is Reported, Verified, Rejected or Held for Document Update; errata appear on the RFC's page and in an HTML version that includes them, but are not incorporated into the TXT, PDF or XML files. RFC 793's page lists 47. A downloaded text file is the specification as published, not as corrected, so check the verified errata before relying on it.

Reading one. The RFC Style Guide, RFC 7322 (September 2014), makes an Abstract and a Security Considerations section mandatory in every RFC, requires an Internet Assigned Numbers Authority (IANA) Considerations section in the Internet-Draft and removes it at publication if it only says there is nothing to do, and gives editors a prime directive: do not change the intended meaning of the text. Requirement words have defined weight under BCP 14: in RFC 2119 (March 1997), MUST, REQUIRED and SHALL are absolute, SHOULD and RECOMMENDED allow valid exceptions whose full implications must be understood, and MAY and OPTIONAL are truly optional, and RFC 8174 (May 2017) clarifies that only the uppercase forms carry that meaning. RFC 7990 (December 2016) moved the canonical format from plain ASCII (American Standard Code for Information Interchange) text to XML in the xml2rfc version 3 vocabulary, from which HTML, plain text and PDF (PDF/A-3 for archiving) are rendered.

The April RFCs are part of the record and carry real statuses. RFC 8700 names RFC 748, the Telnet randomly-lose option, as the first April 1st RFC (the index dates it 1 April 1978). RFC 1149 (1 April 1990, David Waitzman), on Internet Protocol (IP) datagrams over avian carriers, is Experimental and was updated by RFC 2549 and RFC 6214; RFC 3514 (1 April 2003, Steven Bellovin), the security flag in the IPv4 header, is Informational. A joke with a status proves that being an RFC confers no authority by itself.

Before quoting an RFC, check in this order: stream, status, Obsoleted by and Updated by, then verified errata. A datasheet claiming RFC compliance says little until it names the RFC and the MUST-level requirements it meets. The numbers worth remembering: 1969 for RFC 1, BCP 9 for the process, BCP 14 for the key words, six months for a draft, four weeks for the Last Call that promotes a Proposed Standard, and two for the independent implementations it needs.

circuit-switching.def: Reserving a dedicated path end to end for the duration of a conversation, whether or not anything is being sent on it.
circuit-switching.context: It is what the telephone network did, and its properties are the exact inverse of packet switching: guaranteed capacity, constant delay, no congestion - and a link that sits idle while nobody speaks. That waste is affordable for voice and ruinous for data, where traffic arrives in bursts. The distinction still shapes arguments about quality of service: every attempt to give a packet network hard guarantees is an attempt to buy back something circuit switching had, and to pay for it in complexity instead of in reserved capacity.

congestion-control.def: The sender's job of inferring how much the network can carry and slowing down before it collapses - distinct from flow control, which protects the receiver.
congestion-control.context: It exists because the network gives no explicit signal: a sender learns about congestion from its own losses and delays, and reacts. That inference is why a single busy link changes behaviour end to end, and why measuring a network from one endpoint tells you as much about the path as about the host. The classic failure was congestion collapse in the 1980s, when every sender answered loss by retransmitting harder; the modern one is bufferbloat, where oversized buffers hide the loss and the sender never learns to slow down.

cache-poisoning.def: Getting a resolver, proxy or other shared cache to store a forged or attacker-shaped answer, so every later client asking the same question is given the attacker's version until the entry expires.
cache-poisoning.context: The leverage is what makes it serious: one successful injection serves everybody behind that cache until the entry expires, which turns a single race won into a population-scale redirect. In the Domain Name System (DNS) the race was against a 16-bit query identifier, which is why source-port randomization was the emergency mitigation in 2008 and DNSSEC (Domain Name System Security Extensions) the actual answer. The same shape appears wherever something caches on behalf of many: web caches and content delivery networks, Address Resolution Protocol (ARP) tables, and any middlebox that remembers an answer to save asking again.
cache-poisoning.depth:
A cache answers on behalf of an authority so that the authority does not have to be asked again: a recursive resolver for the Domain Name System (DNS), a reverse proxy or content delivery network (CDN) for a web origin, a host's Address Resolution Protocol (ARP) table for the owner of an address. Poisoning means placing a false answer in that store. RFC (Request for Comments) 9111, the HTTP caching standard of June 2022, puts the danger in one sentence: storing malicious content in a cache can extend an attacker's reach to multiple users, and it is especially effective with shared caches. That is the difference from ordinary spoofing, which deceives one victim with one forged reply; a poisoned cache repeats the lie to everyone who asks until the entry expires. It is also different from web cache deception, in which a private response is made to look cacheable and is then served to others, and from cache snooping, which only asks a cache what it already holds.

In DNS the attack is a race over the User Datagram Protocol (UDP). A resolver that has sent a query accepts the first reply that matches it, and RFC 5452 (A. Hubert and R. van Mook, January 2009) lists what must match: the source and destination addresses, the destination port against the query's source port, the query ID, the query name, and the class and type; anything else must be treated as invalid. RFC 3833, the threat analysis of DNS by D. Atkins and R. Austein (August 2004), had already observed that the ID field is only 16 bits and the server port is well known, which leaves 2 to the power 32 combinations of ID and client port at most, and often fewer than 2 to the power 16 in practice because resolvers used fixed or predictable ports and IDs. With a properly random ID and a known port, CERT/CC (the CERT Coordination Center) calculates that a blind attacker needs 32,768 attempts on average, and those attempts must arrive before the genuine answer does.

Time to live (TTL) governs how often the race can be run, and RFC 5452 works the numbers. Against a record with a TTL of 3,600 seconds and a known destination port, an attacker sending 7,000 forged packets per second, about 4.5 Mbit/s, has a 10 per cent chance of success in the first 24 hours and 50 per cent after a week; with a 60-second TTL, 10 per cent comes after 24 minutes, 50 per cent in under 3 hours and 90 per cent after about 9 hours. Once the source port must be guessed as well, the problem space grows by a factor of 64,000 and the same odds need more than 285 Gb/s. Two refinements make things worse for the defender. A birthday attack forces several identical queries to be outstanding at once, so each forged packet only has to match any one of them; and techniques that keep asking for new names reduce the effective TTL to zero, so that with a single source port the 7,000-packet stream reaches 50 per cent within 7 seconds, against about 116 hours with 64,000 ports.

That zero-TTL technique is what Dan Kaminsky made practical in 2008. CVE-2008-1447 describes a birthday attack that uses in-bailiwick referrals to poison recursive resolvers, related to insufficient randomness of DNS transaction IDs and source ports, in BIND 8 and 9, Microsoft DNS and other implementations, and records it as the Kaminsky bug. The fixes shipped together on 8 July 2008, when CERT/CC published Vulnerability Note VU#800113: resolvers began to randomize the source port of every query, which CERT/CC estimates adds approximately 16 bits to what an attacker must guess. The same note warns that a port address translation (PAT) device in front of a resolver can reduce or eliminate that gain by rewriting ports, and that without protocol changes such as DNSSEC these mitigations cannot completely prevent cache poisoning. RFC 5452 then turned the practice into requirements: resolvers must use an unpredictable source port from as large a range as practicable, different ports for simultaneous queries and an unpredictable query ID over the full range 0 to 65,535, should use several addresses unpredictably when they have them, and must accept only records within the domain for which the answering server is authoritative, the bailiwick rule.

Other defences add identity without changing the protocol. An Internet-Draft by Paul Vixie and David Dagon of March 2008 proposed using the 0x20 bit of DNS labels, randomizing the upper and lower case of the query name and requiring the reply to copy it exactly, because even perfectly random IDs leave random and birthday attacks theoretically feasible; the draft expired without becoming an RFC. DNS Cookies, RFC 7873 (D. Eastlake 3rd and M. Andrews, May 2016), protect against forgery and cache poisoning by off-path attackers with a client cookie computed from the two addresses and a client secret of at least 64 bits of entropy. Port randomization itself can be undermined from the side: CVE-2020-25705, published on 17 November 2020, records a flaw in the Linux kernel's ICMP (Internet Control Message Protocol) handling that let an off-path attacker scan open UDP ports quickly and effectively bypass source port randomization, which is why kernel and resolver patches, not configuration alone, are part of the defence.

DNSSEC (Domain Name System Security Extensions) is the actual answer because it changes what is being checked. Every defence above makes a forged packet harder to match; DNSSEC makes a matching forged packet useless, because a validating resolver checks the zone's signatures and classes data that fail validation as bogus, and RFC 4035 (March 2005) requires a validating name server to answer a recursive query with RCODE 2, server failure (SERVFAIL), when it cannot validate the answer, instead of passing the forged data on. It protects only signed zones and only where resolvers validate, which is why the entropy measures remain in place beside it.

Web caches are poisoned differently: nobody has to win a race, because the attacker simply asks. RFC 9111 names one common vector, differences in message parsing between proxies and user agents. The OWASP (Open Worldwide Application Security Project) Web Cache Security Cheat Sheet describes the other as an attacker-controlled request input that changes the response but is not part of the cache key, so the harmful response is stored under a key that ordinary visitors also hit. Its defences are design rules: untrusted inputs outside the cache key must not influence a cacheable response; a body on a GET request or an unkeyed header must not alter one; Forwarded and X-Forwarded headers are trusted only when a trusted proxy set or replaced them; host and scheme are canonicalized before they generate links, redirects or security-sensitive headers; static and dynamic content are separated by hostname or path; and if poisoning happens, every affected cache layer is purged and the key or origin behaviour fixed before caching is re-enabled. Vary is the standard tool for adding request headers to the key, and the most common place to forget it is a response whose Access-Control-Allow-Origin depends on the Origin header.

At layer 2 the cache is the ARP table. Cisco's troubleshooting guide for Dynamic ARP Inspection (DAI) on Catalyst switches (5 August 2024) describes ARP poisoning as sending fake ARP replies so that hosts on the subnet send traffic meant for another host to the attacker, a classic man-in-the-middle position. DAI checks every ARP packet received on an untrusted interface against the IP-to-MAC bindings in the DHCP (Dynamic Host Configuration Protocol) snooping binding database and drops the ones that do not match; trusted interfaces, normally the uplinks, are forwarded without checks, and untrusted ones are limited to 15 ARP packets per second by default. show ip arp inspection and show ip dhcp snooping binding are the first commands to run when DAI drops traffic that ought to pass.

Operations decide whether the defences actually hold. RFC 5452 notes that a stream of 4.5 Mbit/s of unexpected responses may well be noticed by a watchful operator, and that firewalls set to allow outgoing queries from only one DNS source port need reconfiguring; CERT/CC's warning about PAT applies to every resolver behind a firewall or load balancer that translates source ports, and the spread of source ports seen in a capture of the resolver's outgoing queries is the quickest test. Poisoned DNS entries age out with their TTL or are flushed from the resolver; poisoned web entries must be purged from every layer that stored them, browser caches included where the response allowed it.

The neighbours are easy to separate. Spoofing forges one reply; poisoning gets the forgery stored and repeated. Cache deception stores a private response where others can fetch it. A BGP (Border Gateway Protocol) hijack misdirects traffic without touching any cache. The numbers worth remembering are a 16-bit DNS ID and 32,768 attempts on average to guess it; about 16 more bits from source port randomization; 8 July 2008, CVE-2008-1447 and VU#800113; RFC 5452 of January 2009 and its 285 Gb/s figure once ports are random; RFC 7873's 64-bit client secret; and 15 ARP packets per second as DAI's default limit on untrusted ports.

rdap.def: The structured, authenticated successor to WHOIS: the same registration data, returned as JSON over HTTPS, with differentiated access instead of one public answer for everyone.
rdap.context: It exists because WHOIS could not survive privacy law. A single unauthenticated text response cannot show a registrar's staff one thing and an anonymous querier another, so the whole record had to be redacted for everybody. RDAP can distinguish the caller, which is what makes tiered access possible at all. Adoption has been slow for the ordinary reason: the old protocol still answers, and nothing breaks by ignoring the new one.

coordinated-disclosure.def: Reporting a defect privately to whoever can fix it, agreeing a deadline, and publishing after the fix: the compromise the field settled on between full disclosure and silence. Standards and coordinators call it coordinated vulnerability disclosure (CVD).
coordinated-disclosure.context: The deadline is the load-bearing part, and it exists because without one the vendor's incentive is to wait forever. It also rests on an assumption worth stating: the reporter is probably not the only person who can find this, so time spent unpatched is time somebody else may be using. The Kaminsky DNS flaw is the reference case for what the good version looks like, with competing vendors patching on the same day and the detail published a month later, and it is rare because it needed one researcher to organize people who do not usually cooperate.
coordinated-disclosure.depth:
The CERT Coordination Center (CERT/CC), whose guide to coordinated vulnerability disclosure (CVD) is the field's working manual, insists that it is a process, not an event. Publishing an advisory is an action and releasing a fix is an action; neither defines it. The process starts when at least one person becomes aware of a vulnerability in a product, which divides the world into those who know and those who do not, and from then on those who know keep asking two questions: what should I do with this knowledge, and who else needs to know what, and when? It ends when the answers are nothing and nobody. The guide names the roles: the finder who discovers, the reporter who tells, the vendor who fixes, the deployer who must still install the fix, and sometimes a coordinator, a relay or information broker between the others.

The standards give the same activity a vendor's-eye description. ISO/IEC 29147, Vulnerability disclosure, in its second edition of October 2018, confirmed in 2024, sets requirements and recommendations for receiving vulnerability reports and for publishing remediation information, and observes that coordination matters most when several vendors are affected; its companion ISO/IEC 30111 covers what the vendor does between receiving a report and disclosing. FIRST (the Forum of Incident Response and Security Teams) defines disclosure itself as the act of initially providing vulnerability information to a party that was not believed to be previously aware, and notes that the whole process typically contains several such events: reporter to vendor, vendor to other vendors, vendor to customers, everyone to the public.

The name is a correction of an older one. The practice used to be called responsible disclosure, which carried a judgement: a finder who published without the vendor's agreement was, by implication, irresponsible, whatever the vendor had done with the report. In July 2010 Katie Moussouris, writing for the Microsoft Security Response Center, argued that "Responsible Disclosure should be deprecated in favor of something focused on getting the job done", and described CVD as the same premise of private reporting with one addition, a coordinated public disclosure strategy if attacks begin in the wild. The two poles it sits between are full disclosure, in which the finder publishes everything to everyone at once, and silence, in which the finder tells the vendor and nobody ever tells the users.

Deadlines are where policies differ, and the numbers are worth knowing. The CERT/CC discloses vulnerabilities reported to it 45 days after the initial report, regardless of the existence or availability of patches or workarounds, earlier or later only in extenuating circumstances such as active exploitation. Google's Project Zero gives a vendor 90 days after notification to make a patch available; if the patch arrives in time, the technical details follow 30 days after it, the arrangement usually written 90+30; for a vulnerability already exploited in the wild the 90 days become 7; and a grace period of 14 days may be granted when a fix is nearly ready. The CERT guide declines to name a correct figure. Asked whether 45 days is long enough or 90 too short, it answers that it depends, and lists reasons to publish early (evidence of active exploitation; a vendor that fails to respond, is not acting in good faith or denies the vulnerability; knowledge that adversaries have found it) and reasons to hold back (a vendor making progress in good faith; severe impact on safety-critical systems or critical infrastructure).

The same guide explains why no agreement can be absolute: all disclosure agreements are contingent. The parties may feel they have reached a settlement with each other, but the adversary is not a party to it and does not care whether the vendor needs another month to test or the reporter wants to announce at a conference; and because a vulnerability's existence is an observable fact, anyone else who notices it may disclose it on their own terms. It also records how much the calendar matters. Black Hat and DEF CON fall in early August every year, the CERT/CC sees more reports a few months before the big conferences, and vendors are advised to be ready for deadlines that will not move.

The reference case can be read in the CERT/CC's own record. Vulnerability Note VU#800113, Multiple DNS implementations vulnerable to cache poisoning, was released on 8 July 2008 with the CVE (Common Vulnerabilities and Exposures) identifier CVE-2008-1447, crediting Dan Kaminsky of IOActive for identifying how effective and practical cache poisoning had become and Paul Vixie of the Internet Systems Consortium (ISC) for raising the urgency. Its vendor records show the first notifications on 21 April 2008 and a second wave on 5 May, so the embargo held for eleven weeks across dozens of organizations that compete with each other. The shared fix was per-query source port randomization, an idea the note credits to Daniel J. Bernstein, which adds about 16 bits to the 16-bit transaction identifier an attacker has to guess. Nothing on that scale was easy: it needed one finder willing to wait, one coordinator trusted by all sides, and a fix every vendor could ship at once.

Cases with many vendors have their own guidance. FIRST's Guidelines and Practices for Multi-Party Vulnerability Coordination and Disclosure, version 1.1, released in spring 2020 and written with the United States National Telecommunications and Information Administration (NTIA), distinguishes upstream vendors, downstream vendors and peer vendors, such as independent implementers of the same protocol, and works through use cases and the ways they go wrong, beginning with the finder who publishes before a fix exists. Its first recommendation is that every party, vendors above all, publish an actionable policy with timelines and thresholds for disclosure, and that, absent clear evidence that the flaw is already public or being exploited, finders give vendors a reasonable embargo period.

For an organization on the receiving end, the practical minimum is small. RFC (Request for Comments) 9116, published in April 2022, defines security.txt, a text file served under the well-known path of a website in which the Contact and Expires fields must always be present, so that a finder knows where to send a report. A published policy says what is in scope, how quickly a report is acknowledged and what the finder may expect. The CERT guide's warning to vendors who do not bother is that CVD is a social process played over and over by people who share knowledge between rounds: vendors seen as slow or hostile may learn of flaws in their products at the same time as the public.

The law has moved towards the practice. On 19 May 2022 the United States Department of Justice announced a charging policy for the Computer Fraud and Abuse Act that for the first time directs that good-faith security research should not be charged, defining it as accessing a computer solely for good-faith testing, in a manner designed to avoid harm, with the results used primarily to promote security or safety. In the European Union the Cyber Resilience Act, in force since 10 December 2024, requires manufacturers to handle vulnerabilities throughout the lifecycle of their products, with its reporting obligations applying from 11 September 2026 and its main obligations from 11 December 2027.

What goes wrong is usually one of three things. The embargo leaks, because every additional party told is another place it can leak from. The fix gives the flaw away, since anyone can compare the patched code with the old, so the embargo protects the interval before the fix and nothing after it. Or someone hints: the CERT guide's advice on partial information is two words, "Don't tease", because the mere knowledge that a flaw exists in a feature is often enough for a skilled person to find it again.

base64.def: An encoding that represents arbitrary bytes using 64 printable characters, so binary data can travel through channels that only accept text.
base64.context: It is not encryption and not compression: it makes data larger, by roughly a third, in exchange for surviving transports that would mangle raw bytes. The reason it is everywhere is historical: email was text-only, and everything built on that assumption inherited the need. Two practical notes: a variant safe for a Uniform Resource Locator (URL) exists because plus and slash mean something in a URL, and seeing Base64 in a payload tells you nothing about whether the content is safe, which is why decoders belong in every analyst's toolkit rather than in their conclusions.
base64.depth:
What it is, and what it is not. The reference is Request for Comments (RFC) 4648, The Base16, Base32, and Base64 Data Encodings, written by Simon Josefsson and published in October 2006, replacing RFC 3548. Base64 uses a 65-character subset of US-ASCII (the American Standard Code for Information Interchange): 64 characters each carry 6 bits, and the 65th, "=", is padding. It is not encryption: the RFC's security section says base encoding visually hides things such as passwords but provides no computational confidentiality, and notes real incidents in which people pasted a protocol exchange to illustrate a problem and gave away a password. It is not compression either: the MIME (Multipurpose Internet Mail Extensions) standard says the output is consistently about 33 per cent larger, and GNU coreutils puts it at roughly 133 per cent of the original.

How the bits move. The encoder takes three octets, 24 bits, and splits them into four 6-bit groups, each an index into the alphabet: A to Z for 0 to 25, a to z for 26 to 51, the digits for 52 to 61, then + for 62 and / for 63. When the input does not divide by three, one leftover octet becomes two characters followed by "==", and two leftover octets become three characters followed by "=". The RFC's test vectors show it: f is Zg==, fo is Zm8=, foo is Zm9v. The unused low bits of the last character must be set to zero by a conforming encoder; if they are not, several different strings decode to the same bytes, which is why the RFC calls zero pad bits the condition for a canonical encoding.

Where it came from. Privacy Enhanced Mail (PEM), RFC 1421 of February 1993, defined a printable encoding step at 6 bits per character, and MIME, RFC 2045 of November 1996, adopted a Base64 Content-Transfer-Encoding it called virtually identical. The subset was chosen because it is represented identically in every version of ISO 646 (from the International Organization for Standardization), US-ASCII included, and in every version of EBCDIC (Extended Binary Coded Decimal Interchange Code), so mail gateways of the time could not corrupt it. Line lengths are part of the history too: MIME limits encoded lines to 76 characters and PEM to 64, both, as RFC 4648 explains, because of limits in the Simple Mail Transfer Protocol (SMTP). RFC 7468 (April 2015) still requires generators of PEM-style certificate and key files to wrap at exactly 64 characters, while RFC 4648 forbids adding line feeds at all unless the specification using it asks for them.

The URL-safe variant. Plus and slash cause trouble in file names and Uniform Resource Locators (URLs), and RFC 4648 adds that legacy search and index tools treat them as word breaks. Its section 5 therefore defines base64url, identical except that 62 is the minus sign and 63 the underscore; the pad "=" would need percent-encoding in a URL, so it may be dropped when the length is known. The RFC insists that base64url must not be called just base64. JSON (JavaScript Object Notation) Web Signature (JWS), RFC 7515 of May 2015, uses it with every trailing "=" removed and no line breaks or whitespace, which is why a JSON Web Token (JWT) never ends in an equals sign and why feeding one segment to a strict standard decoder fails.

Where engineers meet it. HTTP (Hypertext Transfer Protocol) Basic authentication, RFC 7617 of September 2015, joins the user-id, a colon and the password and encodes the result, so the specification's own example, Aladdin with the password open sesame, travels as Authorization: Basic QWxhZGRpbjpvcGVuIHNlc2FtZQ==, and the RFC states that the scheme is not secure because credentials cross the network as cleartext. RFC 2397 (August 1998) lets a URL carry its content inline: data:, an optional media type, the marker ;base64, a comma and then the encoded bytes, as in the RFC's own data:image/gif;base64, example. Certificates and private keys in PEM files are Base64 between BEGIN and END lines, and SAML (Security Assertion Markup Language) 2.0 messages are compressed and Base64-encoded into the URL in the HTTP Redirect binding, or Base64-encoded into a hidden form field in the POST binding. On the attacking side, PowerShell's -EncodedCommand accepts a Base64 string of a command, which Microsoft documents must be UTF-16LE text, so an analyst who decodes one and sees letters separated by zero bytes is reading exactly what was intended.

Strict and liberal decoders. RFC 4648 says a decoder must reject characters outside the alphabet unless the specification using it says otherwise; MIME says otherwise and tells decoders to ignore them. Ignoring has costs the RFC spells out: the skipped characters become a covert channel to leak data, a way to defeat a string equality comparison, or a trigger for implementation bugs, and a decoder should not break on embedded NUL characters either. GNU base64 shows both habits: it wraps encoded output at 76 characters by default (-w 0 turns that off), decodes with --decode, and has a --ignore-garbage flag to skip unrecognized bytes. Most decoding failures in practice are one of three things: a base64url string fed to a standard decoder, padding stripped by one side and expected by the other, or line breaks added by a tool that wraps.

Numbers worth remembering: 3 bytes in, 4 characters out; 6 bits per character; 64 symbols plus "=" for padding; about 33 per cent overhead; lines of 76 characters in MIME and 64 in PEM; and minus and underscore in place of plus and slash for base64url.

bill-cheswick.def: Co-author of Firewalls and Internet Security in 1994, one of the first books on the subject, written from running AT&T's internet gateway - and the author of the account of watching an intruder inside a deliberately prepared environment.
bill-cheswick.context: An Evening with Berferd is the piece people remember, and it is where the honeypot argument enters the literature: rather than eject the intruder, he watched, recorded and learned what the attacker was actually trying. The book's most durable line is a warning against its own subject, and the authors made it themselves - in many of the access arrangements they studied, the only secure component was the firewall, which attackers simply went around to reach the machines it was said to protect.

steven-bellovin.def: Computer scientist at AT&T Bell Laboratories and later Columbia University who catalogued the design-level security flaws of the TCP/IP (Transmission Control Protocol/Internet Protocol) suite in 1989, co-wrote the 1994 book that defined the network firewall, co-directed the IETF (Internet Engineering Task Force) Security Area, and, years earlier, helped create Usenet.
steven-bellovin.context: His standing description of his own field is the most useful sentence in it: he does research on networks, security, and especially why the two don't get along. That is not a joke about culture. Networking optimizes for reachability and security for restriction, and almost every operational argument between the two teams is a rediscovery of that. His 1989 paper on the TCP/IP (Transmission Control Protocol/Internet Protocol) suite took Robert Morris's 1985 sequence-number attack and set it beside routing, ICMP (Internet Control Message Protocol), DNS (Domain Name System) and authentication attacks, arguing that the flaws were in the protocols and not in any one implementation; by his own later account, the sequence-number attack drew little attention until it was used against Tsutomu Shimomura.
steven-bellovin.depth:
Steven M. Bellovin took a BA at Columbia University in 1972 and an MS (1977) and PhD (1982) in computer science at the University of North Carolina at Chapel Hill, where his dissertation on verifiably correct code generation was supervised by David L. Parnas. As a graduate student he was one of the original designers, and the first implementor, of Netnews. His own history dates the design to the fall of 1979: two Duke graduate students, Tom Truscott and the late Jim Ellis, wanted announcements posted at one university to be read at others, and rather than write a network protocol the group used UUCP, the dial-up copy and remote-execution package that came with Seventh Edition Unix, with Duke polling other sites and being reimbursed for the phone calls. Ellis named it Usenet as a riff on Usenix. Bellovin calls it arguably the first social network, the place where Linux, the World Wide Web and Mosaic were announced, and says its one wrong early decision was failing to plan for success. The three received the 1995 Usenix Lifetime Achievement Award, the Flame, for creating it.

He joined Bell Labs in Murray Hill in 1982 and stayed with AT&T until 2004, as a Distinguished Member of Technical Staff from 1987 and an AT&T Fellow from 1998. His 2004 retrospective explains how security found him. He took charge of one of the first three Ethernet cables in all of AT&T, which grew into a Bell Labs internet routed by VAXes and Suns with second Ethernet boards running Berkeley's routed, and the outages he chased were routing problems caused by misconfiguration, once a new workstation that assigned itself the .1 gateway address. The lesson he drew is the one the field still teaches: anything that could happen by accident could be done deliberately. Robert Morris's discovery of sequence number guessing and an intrusion into AT&T machines by a teenager, caught by detectors Bellovin and colleagues had set for exactly that behaviour, did the rest.

The result was Security Problems in the TCP/IP Protocol Suite, published in Computer Communication Review in April 1989 and already substantially written before the Internet worm of 1988. Its premise was new: the paper set implementation bugs aside and argued that serious flaws were inherent in the protocols themselves. It explained Morris's 1985 attack (a forged connection that completes the three-way handshake without ever seeing the server's reply, because the server's initial sequence number can be predicted) and quantified why: the TCP specification called for the counter to tick about 250,000 times a second, 4.2BSD advanced it by 128 a second and 4.3BSD by 125,000, and the granularity, not the rate, was what mattered. It then walked through source routing, forged RIP (Routing Information Protocol) and EGP (Exterior Gateway Protocol) updates, ICMP (Internet Control Message Protocol) redirects, the finger service and DNS (Domain Name System) resolvers whose query sequence numbers started at 0, and warned that a combined attack on the DNS and routing could be catastrophic. Its conclusions read like a modern hardening guide: relying on the IP source address for authentication is extremely dangerous, sequence numbers must be unpredictable, and hosts should not give away knowledge gratuitously.

It was not received without argument. Stephen Kent published Comments on it in the same journal in July 1989, and Bellovin's 2004 reprint with commentary concedes part of the criticism: he had lumped Berkeley's r-utilities together with standardized protocols, and address-based authentication, the flaw he attacked throughout, was Berkeley's habit rather than anything an RFC (Request for Comments) required; he had also mischaracterized Morris, who used a Berkeley kernel bug to need far fewer packets than flooding. He kept his conclusions, and added that sequence-number attacks received little attention outside his paper until Kevin Mitnick reimplemented Morris's idea against Tsutomu Shimomura. The architectural lesson he drew in 2004 is the one worth keeping: the r-utilities had assumed that TCP sequence numbers carried security properties they were never designed to have. He also noted that by then most real attacks exploited buggy code rather than protocol design, because there was so much easier fruit to pick.

The defence that became the standard is his. RFC 1948, Defending Against Sequence Number Attacks (May 1996), written after CERT Advisory CA-95:01 on IP spoofing, proposed computing each connection's initial sequence number as ISN = M + F(localhost, localport, remotehost, remoteport), where M is the 4-microsecond timer TCP already used and F is a cryptographic hash, MD5 at the time, over the connection's addresses and ports plus a secret. Each connection, each four-tuple, gets a separate sequence number space in which the ISN still advances as the TCP specification requires, with no visible relationship between spaces. In February 2012 RFC 6528, by Fernando Gont and Bellovin, moved the scheme to the Standards Track and obsoleted RFC 1948. His best-known RFC may be another one: RFC 3514 of 1 April 2003, The Security Flag in the IPv4 Header, defines the evil bit, set to 1 on packets with evil intent so that firewalls can drop them, a joke about every security mechanism that relies on the attacker's cooperation.

Firewalls and Internet Security: Repelling the Wily Hacker, written with Bill Cheswick and published by Addison-Wesley in 1994, was built on running AT&T's internet gateway. Its first preface states the strategy plainly: networked hosts offer many services and must trust their peers, so the network should be arranged so that only one computer needs to talk to the outside world, a dedicated firewall gateway. The second edition (2003) added Aviel Rubin, and its full text is now published free under a Creative Commons licence. He kept writing about the perimeter, in There Be Dragons (1992) and in Distributed Firewalls (1999). With Michael Merritt he designed Encrypted Key Exchange (EKE), presented at the IEEE (Institute of Electrical and Electronics Engineers) Symposium on Research in Security and Privacy in May 1992, a password-based protocol designed so that an eavesdropper cannot mount a dictionary attack on the password; it received a test-of-time award in 2019.

In the standards bodies he sat on the Internet Architecture Board (IAB) from 1996 to 2002 and was co-director of the IETF Security Area, and so a member of the Internet Engineering Steering Group, from 2002 to 2004. He was elected to the National Academy of Engineering in 2001, joined the Columbia faculty in 2005, and moved into policy: Chief Technologist of the Federal Trade Commission in 2012 and 2013, Technology Scholar at the Privacy and Civil Liberties Oversight Board in 2016, and member of the Department of Homeland Security's Science and Technology Advisory Committee from 2005 to 2014. He is a co-author of Keys Under Doormats (2015), with Harold Abelson, Ross Anderson, Whitfield Diffie, Susan Landau, Ronald Rivest, Bruce Schneier and others, which argued that mandated government access to encrypted communications would create insecurity; its authors shared an EFF Pioneer Award in 2016. He received the 2007 NIST/NSA National Computer Systems Security Award, entered the Cybersecurity Hall of Fame in 2014, and in 2023 won a second Flame, with Matt Blaze and Landau, for policy work. He also does history: his 2011 Cryptologia paper showed that the one-time pad, generally credited to Gilbert Vernam and Joseph Mauborgne, had been invented about 35 years earlier, in 1882, by a Sacramento banker named Frank Miller. He is now professor emeritus at Columbia and a senior affiliate scholar at Georgetown Law's Institute for Technology Law and Policy; his books include Thinking Security (2016).

firewall.def: A device or function that decides which traffic may pass between networks, enforcing a policy at a boundary.
firewall.context: The name is borrowed from a wall built to stop fire spreading between parts of a building, and the metaphor carries the assumption that has aged worst: that there is an inside and an outside. It was true when an organization had one gateway, and it stopped being true with cloud, remote work and machine-to-machine traffic that never touches the perimeter. The function did not become useless; it multiplied and moved, into hosts, hypervisors, service meshes and cloud policy, which is what segmentation and zero trust are actually describing. The warning Cheswick and Bellovin wrote into their firewall book still applies: an estate where the firewall is the only secure component is one attackers go around rather than through.
firewall.depth:
What it is. NIST (the National Institute of Standards and Technology), in Special Publication 800-41 Revision 1 of September 2009, by Karen Scarfone and Paul Hoffman, defines firewalls as devices or programs that control the flow of network traffic between networks or hosts employing differing security postures. Cheswick, Bellovin and Rubin, in the second edition of Firewalls and Internet Security, are broader still: any device, software or arrangement that limits network access, which already includes the packet filters in most routers and the software in every popular operating system. What a firewall is not is the whole of security: it enforces a policy at the point where traffic crosses it, and has no opinion about traffic that never does.

Where it came from. In March 1989 Jeffrey Mogul of Digital Equipment Corporation's Western Research Laboratory described packet screening for Unix-based gateways: a gateway screen in the Ultrix 3.0 kernel intercepted packets before they were forwarded and asked a user-level daemon, screend, to apply a table-driven policy, so that organizations could restrict inter-organization access to specific hosts and applications. Gil Shwed of Check Point filed on 15 December 1993 for a patent, granted on 25 February 1997, on a filter module that accepts or drops packets according to rules an administrator defines. The first printing of Cheswick and Bellovin's book appeared at the Las Vegas Interop in May 1994, at the same show as the first of many commercial firewall products.

The kinds, in NIST's terms. Packet filtering, on addresses, ports and protocol, is at the core of most modern firewalls, although few sold today do only stateless filtering, and a router with access control lists (ACLs) is a packet filter. Stateful inspection keeps track of each connection in a state table, typically source and destination address, ports and connection state, so a packet that claims to belong to an established Transmission Control Protocol (TCP) connection is checked against the table rather than believed. Application firewalls add stateful protocol analysis, which some vendors call deep packet inspection: they can tell instant messaging hiding on port 80 or refuse the File Transfer Protocol (FTP) put command. An application-proxy gateway never allows a direct connection; each successful attempt becomes two separate connections. Unified threat management (UTM) puts a firewall, malware detection and probe blocking in one system, which simplifies policy and concentrates load. Host-based firewalls protect a single machine, including from hosts on its own subnet that a network firewall never sees.

Policy. NIST recommends deny by default: block all inbound and outbound traffic not expressly permitted. Many firewalls check rules in sequence until one matches, which makes order a matter of correctness, not only of performance: a broad permit placed above a narrow deny silently wins. FortiGate lists policies in the order they are checked, and traffic that matches none of them meets the implicit deny policy and is dropped. Internet Control Message Protocol (ICMP) is where over-tight policies hurt: NIST warns that blocking all of it causes diagnostic and performance problems, and that ICMP type 3 for Internet Protocol version 4 (IPv4) should not be filtered because it carries the messages that path maximum transmission unit (MTU) discovery depends on; ICMPv6 needs its own list, in RFC (Request for Comments) 4890.

Seeing state on Linux. Netfilter's connection tracking names the states a ruleset can match: NEW for a packet that starts a connection or belongs to one not yet seen in both directions, ESTABLISHED once packets have flowed both ways, RELATED for a new connection tied to an existing one, such as FTP data or an ICMP error, and INVALID for a packet associated with no known connection. The usual stateful ruleset accepts ESTABLISHED and RELATED first and then lists the NEW connections that policy allows. How a refusal looks is a choice. DROP discards silently, so the client waits for its own timeout; REJECT answers with an ICMP error, port unreachable by default, or a TCP reset. RFC 1812 asks routers that filter administratively to send ICMP code 13, Communication Administratively Prohibited, and allows an option to suppress it. A connection attempt that hangs until timeout with nothing in any log is the signature of a silent drop.

What goes wrong. A stateful firewall has to see both directions of a conversation: if the reply returns by another path, the device that saw only half of it has no matching state and drops what follows. The firewall is also software exposed at the edge, and therefore a target. On 12 April 2024 Palo Alto Networks disclosed CVE-2024-3400 (Common Vulnerabilities and Exposures), an operating system command injection in the GlobalProtect feature of PAN-OS that let an unauthenticated attacker execute arbitrary code with root privileges on the firewall, rated 10.0 and already under an increasing number of attacks; the box that enforces the boundary can be the way through it.

After the perimeter. Cheswick and Bellovin admitted in their second edition that they had assumed a company would have only a few external connections, easy to keep track of and to firewall, and that the spaghetti topology that followed was a surprise; before AT&T's split, over 300,000 hosts sat behind at least six firewalls plus special arrangements with some 200 business partners. Their fundamental theorem of firewalls still holds: most hosts run too many programs that are too large to be secured one by one, so they are isolated behind something. What changed is where that something sits. NIST SP 800-207 (August 2020) defines zero trust as granting no implicit trust based solely on physical or network location, a response to remote users, personally owned devices and cloud assets outside any enterprise boundary, and directs protection at resources rather than network segments. The firewall function survives that shift: it moves into hosts, hypervisors and cloud policy, and the rules multiply.

packet-filter.def: A packet filter is the simplest firewall function: it decides on each packet independently, by addresses, protocol, ports and the interface it crosses, against an ordered list of rules, with no memory of what came before.
packet-filter.context: Statelessness is both the appeal and the limit. A packet filter is fast, cheap and predictable, and it can be implemented in hardware at line rate, which is why access control lists (ACLs) live on routers and switches rather than only on security appliances. What it cannot do is tell a reply from an unsolicited packet, because that requires remembering the request. Permitting the return traffic therefore means permitting a whole class of packets that merely look like replies, which is the gap stateful inspection was invented to close. The same name also covers the kernel filters that select packets for capture, such as the BSD Packet Filter (BPF) behind tcpdump.
packet-filter.depth:
What it is. The National Institute of Standards and Technology (NIST) calls the packet filter the most basic feature of a firewall. Its guide to firewalls, Special Publication (SP) 800-41 Revision 1 of September 2009, still the current final version, describes the early packet-filter-only firewalls as essentially routing devices that provided access control for host addresses and communication sessions, the wording NIST's glossary keeps as its definition, and calls them stateless inspection firewalls: they do not track the state of each flow, so they cannot associate the requests of one session with each other, and they are not concerned with the content of packets. The decision uses what each packet carries and where it is: the source and destination IP (Internet Protocol) addresses, the protocol, such as the Transmission Control Protocol (TCP), the User Datagram Protocol (UDP) or the Internet Control Message Protocol (ICMP), possibly the source and destination ports, and the interface the packet crosses and in which direction. NIST notes that packet filtering is built into most operating systems and routing devices, that the purest example is a router applying access control lists (ACLs), and that few firewalls sold today do only stateless filtering: it is the core of most of them, not the whole.

Where it came from. Packet filtering began on the gateways that first joined separate organizations' networks. Wikipedia dates the first published work on packet filter firewalls, by engineers at Digital Equipment Corporation (DEC), to 1987, and credits Bill Cheswick and Steve Bellovin at AT&T Bell Labs with carrying the research on. A primary account from the period is Jeffrey Mogul's DEC Western Research Laboratory report 89/4 of March 1989, Simple and Flexible Datagram Access Controls for Unix-based Gateways, a preprint for the Summer 1989 USENIX conference. Its problem statement still describes the job: organizations want to restrict access from other organizations to specific hosts and applications, and one way is to prevent certain packets from entering or leaving through their gateways. Its design kept the policy out of the kernel: the kernel asked a user-level process, screend, to judge every packet it was about to forward, and screend decided from a table-driven configuration file.

The other packet filter. The same words name a second, related thing: the kernel facility that decides which packets a capture program receives. Steven McCanne and Van Jacobson's paper on the BSD Packet Filter (BPF), dated 19 December 1992 and presented at the Winter USENIX conference in January 1993, traces the idea to the CMU/Stanford Packet Filter (CSPF), completed in 1980 from the packet filter of the Xerox Alto, and reports that BPF's register-based evaluator ran up to 20 times faster than the original stack-based design and its buffering made the whole up to 100 times faster than the capture interface Sun shipped at the time. Its expression language, documented today in pcap-filter(7), is what tcpdump and Wireshark capture filters use, and the two meanings meet on F5 BIG-IP, whose packet filter rules are written in tcpdump syntax.

How the rules are read. A packet filter is an ordered list, and the platform's evaluation order and default decide more outcomes than any single rule. In the access control list model that RFC (Request for Comments) 8519 standardizes for configuration, the actions of the first matching entry are applied and later entries are not processed; Cisco's documentation adds the implicit deny all at the end of every ACL, so anything not explicitly permitted is denied. OpenBSD's PF reads the other way round: rules are evaluated from first to last but the last matching rule decides, unless a rule carries the quick keyword, and a packet that matches nothing passes. Extreme Networks' Switch Engine writes each ACL entry as match conditions and an action, permits a match when no action is given, applies ACLs in hardware with no impact on switch performance, and warns that they apply to all traffic, so a deny-all on a port also drops the switch's own OSPF (Open Shortest Path First) or RIP (Routing Information Protocol) adjacencies. F5 BIG-IP packet filters apply only to incoming traffic, are disabled by default, have an Unhandled Packet Action of Accept unless changed to Discard or Reject, and are ordered First, Last or After a named rule. Knowing which of these defaults a platform uses is half of reading its filter correctly.

The reply problem. Statelessness is both the appeal and the limit. What a packet filter cannot do is tell a reply from an unsolicited packet, because that requires remembering the request. Permitting return traffic therefore means permitting a whole class of packets that merely look like replies. Cisco's established keyword is the classic approximation: a rule such as access-list 102 permit tcp any any gt 1023 established passes TCP datagrams that have the acknowledgement (ACK) or reset (RST) bit set, which every reply has and which any sender can also set. UDP has no such bits, so a stateless rule for UDP replies has to open whole port ranges. NIST adds that stateless filters are generally vulnerable to attacks that exploit the TCP/IP specification itself: many cannot detect spoofed addresses or packets using options such as IP source routing, which is why most firewalls that use packet filters also maintain some state. Stateful inspection closes the gap by remembering connections: in Linux's nftables, a connection is new, established, related, invalid or untracked, and a policy of drop followed by ct state established,related accept is the simplest stateful firewall; PF filters statefully by default, keeping state for TCP from the SYN unless a rule says no state. Even BIG-IP's packet filter is not purely stateless in practice: its Filter established connections option is off by default, so packets of existing connections are not filtered at all.

Fragments. A filter that matches on transport headers has to see them, and IP fragmentation can hide them. RFC 1858 (October 1995) describes the tiny fragment attack, in which a sender makes the first fragment so small that TCP header fields such as the flags fall into the second fragment, where port and flag rules do not apply; the minimum fragment of 8 octets that RFC 791 guarantees is not enough. Its remedies are to drop first fragments whose transport header is shorter than the filter needs, or simply to drop TCP fragments with an offset of 1, since such a fragment must exist for the attack to work. The same RFC describes the overlapping fragment attack, in which a later fragment overwrites header fields of an innocent first one at reassembly, and RFC 3128 (June 2001) shows a variant that defeats filters built to RFC 1858. NIST's guide gives the operational side: fragments are common because virtual private networks (VPNs) encapsulate packets, blocking them is a frequent cause of VPN interoperability problems, and reassembling them costs memory and invites denial of service, so the choice is a trade between interoperability and security.

Where stateless filtering is still the right tool. Some jobs need no memory. NIST recommends egress filtering that permits outbound traffic only from the organization's own source addresses, and RFC 2827 (BCP 38, May 2000) asks every network to apply ingress filtering at its edge, dropping packets whose source addresses could not legitimately come from the connected customer, which defeats denial-of-service attacks that rely on spoofed addresses. Infrastructure ACLs on routers and switches protect the control plane at line rate, where a state table would be a target in itself. The classic mistakes are the same everywhere: an order that lets a broad permit shadow a specific deny; a default that silently allows (PF, an Extreme entry with no action, BIG-IP's Accept) or denies (Cisco's implicit deny); a filter that blocks the device's own routing protocols; and a blanket ICMP block, which breaks path MTU (maximum transmission unit) discovery because, as RFC 1191 specifies, hosts learn the path MTU from ICMP Destination Unreachable messages meaning that fragmentation was needed.

stateful-inspection.def: Filtering that remembers connections, so a packet is judged by whether it belongs to a flow the policy already allowed.
stateful-inspection.context: Keeping state is what lets a firewall permit replies without permitting everything that resembles one, and it is why a modern rule set is written in terms of who may initiate rather than which packets may pass. The cost is a table with finite size and entries with timeouts, which turns into two operational facts: a connection idle longer than the timeout is silently dropped and the application sees a hang rather than a refusal, and the table itself is a resource an attacker can exhaust. Most mysterious long-lived session failures are one of those two.
stateful-inspection.depth:
What it does. The United States National Institute of Standards and Technology (NIST), in Special Publication (SP) 800-41 Revision 1 of September 2009, describes stateful inspection as an improvement on packet filtering that tracks the state of connections and blocks packets that deviate from the expected state. It still intercepts packets at the network layer and checks them against the rule base, but each permitted connection is recorded in a state table whose entries typically hold the source and destination addresses, the ports and the connection state. For TCP the guide distinguishes three phases, establishment, use and termination, and counts a long period of inactivity as a form of termination. Every new packet is compared with the table, so a packet forged to look like part of an established connection is dropped if no such connection exists. The simplest implementations accept anything that seems to belong to an open connection; stricter ones follow the TCP state machine and reject, for example, segments whose sequence numbers are out of window. Where the firewall also translates addresses, the network address translation (NAT) mapping lives in the same table. UDP has no handshake or teardown, so the firewall can track only addresses and ports: a DNS response from outside is admitted only if a matching query went out, and the entry disappears when a timer expires. Stateful inspection is not a proxy, since the connection passes through rather than being terminated and reopened, and it is not application inspection: it knows that a flow is legitimate, not what the flow contains.

Where it came from. Remembering conversations appears first in what the history of firewalls calls the second generation: between 1989 and 1990 Dave Presotto, Janardan Sharma and Kshitij Nigam at AT&T Bell Laboratories built circuit-level gateways that remembered which ports two addresses were using. The productized form came from Check Point. Gil Shwed filed United States patent 5,606,668 on 15 December 1993, granted on 25 February 1997 and since expired, for a packet filter module that runs compiled filter code in a small virtual machine, with record and lookup operations that store values in tables for use by later rules and packets. Check Point unveiled FireWall-1 at NetWorld+Interop in 1994, and Shwed later named its stateful inspection engine and its graphical interface as the strengths that turned a niche into a mainstream market. The proxy school never fully conceded: Marcus Ranum, interviewed in 2014, called stateful inspection a 15-year-long digression, on the grounds that the real contest had always been at layer 7, which is roughly where next-generation firewalls went.

The table, in numbers. On Linux the table is netfilter's connection tracking, conntrack.
