Its kernel documentation explains that each entry is inserted twice, once for the original direction and once for the reply, that the maximum number of entries, nf_conntrack_max, defaults to the size of the hash table, and that the hash table defaults to total memory divided by 16,384, never fewer than 1,024 buckets nor more than 262,144. Its default timeouts show how differently protocols are treated: 432,000 seconds (five days) for an established TCP connection, 120 seconds after a FIN, 60 in CLOSE_WAIT, and only 30 seconds for UDP, extended to 120 once a UDP flow looks like a stream. Commercial firewalls are far less patient with idle TCP. A FortiGate keeps an idle session for its default session-ttl of 3,600 seconds, adjustable from 300 to 2,764,800 globally and overridable per protocol, per policy and per service. PAN-OS also defaults to 3,600 seconds for an established TCP session, gives a SYN 5 seconds and a handshake 10, and holds a half-closed session for 120; Palo Alto Networks' own guidance warns that values set too low make sessions sensitive to minor delays and values set too high delay failure detection.

Why idle sessions die. The numbers above meet two older ones. RFC (Request for Comments) 1122 (October 1989) requires that a host's TCP keep-alive interval, where keep-alives are used at all, default to no less than two hours. RFC 5382 (Best Current Practice, BCP, 142, October 2008) requires a NAT that cannot tell whether a TCP connection is alive to wait at least 2 hours 4 minutes before abandoning an established one, and at least 4 minutes for a transitory one; RFC 4787 (BCP 127) asks for UDP mappings of at least two minutes and recommends five or more. A firewall that forgets an idle TCP session after one hour therefore forgets it before the host's first default keep-alive is sent. The next packet on that connection matches no entry, is dropped as invalid or as a new connection that does not begin with a SYN, and neither end receives a reset: database connection pools, SSH (Secure Shell) sessions left open and long polls simply stop answering: the application sees a hang, never a refusal. The fixes are a longer timeout on the specific policy or service, or keep-alives at the application or operating system level set shorter than the firewall's timer, not a global increase that lets the table fill with dead entries.

When the table is the target. Because every permitted flow costs an entry, the table is finite memory that outsiders can make the firewall spend. RFC 4987 (August 2007), on TCP SYN flooding, describes the classic case at the host: the attack exploits the state TCP keeps after receiving a SYN, filling it with half-open connections until legitimate ones cannot be established. Firewalls that screen connection attempts until the handshake completes protect the hosts behind them, but, as the RFC notes, they move the problem onto themselves. Short timers for embryonic sessions, such as PAN-OS's 5 and 10 seconds, limit how long a spoofed SYN can occupy an entry, and on Linux the size of the conntrack table is the first number to check when new connections start failing under load.

What stateful inspection cannot see by itself. Some protocols negotiate a second channel inside the first: the File Transfer Protocol (FTP) announces a data port, the Session Initiation Protocol (SIP) announces media ports, the Trivial File Transfer Protocol (TFTP) answers from a new port. A table keyed on the original five values never matches the second channel, so firewalls add protocol helpers. FortiOS calls them session helpers, bound to a port and protocol, that read the negotiation and open temporary pinholes, for example for FTP data connections or SIP media; Linux's conntrack does the same with its helper modules. Failover is another edge: unless the state table is synchronized to the standby unit, established flows arrive at a firewall that has never seen their handshake, which is why Linux's nf_conntrack_tcp_loose, enabled by default, lets conntrack pick up connections already in progress. And a firewall sees only the packets routed through it, so a design where requests leave through one firewall and replies return through another leaves each with half a conversation and nothing that matches its table.

encoding.def: Encoding is the representation of data in a form that a particular channel or reader can carry or parse: a reversible, keyless transformation that provides no secrecy and no integrity.
encoding.context: The word gets used for three different things, and separating them prevents a family of security mistakes: encoding makes data transportable, encryption makes it unreadable without a key, and hashing makes it unrecoverable. Only the first is reversible by anyone. Layered encodings are also where filters go wrong: a value decoded once may still be encoded, and a check applied at the wrong layer sees something the destination will not. Percent-encoding, Hypertext Markup Language (HTML) entity encoding and Base64 in one Uniform Resource Locator (URL) is not unusual, and every mismatch between what the filter parsed and what the target parses is a bypass.
encoding.depth:
Two layers share the name. Character encoding maps text to bytes: characters become numbers (code points) and the numbers become octets in a scheme such as ASCII (American Standard Code for Information Interchange) or UTF-8, a transformation format for Unicode. Transfer and content encodings work the other way round, turning arbitrary bytes into characters a channel will carry unharmed: Base64 in mail and certificates, percent-encoding in Uniform Resource Locators (URLs), entity encoding in Hypertext Markup Language (HTML). Neither hides anything. Request for Comments (RFC) 4648 says it plainly: base encoding visually hides easily recognized information such as passwords but provides no computational confidentiality, and that misunderstanding has caused security incidents when users posted protocol traces to illustrate some other problem.

From ASCII to Unicode. On 16 October 1969 Vint Cerf's RFC 20 proposed standard 7-bit ASCII, from USAS X3.4-1968, carried in an 8-bit byte whose high-order bit is always 0, for host-to-host connections on the ARPANET; it is now Internet Standard STD 80. Seven bits give 128 codes, enough for English and nothing else. Unicode gives every character a code point from U+0000 to U+10FFFF; version 18.0.0, released on 16 September 2026, added 13,007 characters for a total of 172,808. UTF-8, specified for the internet in RFC 3629 (November 2003, STD 63), encodes each code point in one to four octets, and its design is why it won: code points U+0000 to U+007F are the ASCII octets 00 to 7F, and those octet values never appear inside a multi-byte sequence, so any protocol that parses on ASCII delimiters keeps working. The Encoding Standard of the Web Hypertext Application Technology Working Group (WHATWG), which browsers implement, now states that UTF-8 is the most appropriate encoding for interchange of Unicode and that new protocols and formats must use it exclusively.

What UTF-8 forbids, and why. RFC 3629 prohibits encoding the code points U+D800 to U+DFFF, reserved as UTF-16 surrogates, and limits the range to U+10FFFF; the older ISO/IEC 10646 description allowed values up to U+7FFFFFFF in sequences of up to six bytes, a buffer-sizing trap for any decoder that does not enforce the limit. It also warns that the same visible text can have more than one character sequence: e with an acute accent is either the single code point U+00E9 or U+0065 followed by U+0301, a combining accent, so string matching, indexing and access control that compare raw sequences can disagree with what a user sees. A decoder that guesses the wrong character encoding produces mojibake, text decoded with the wrong table, which is harmless on screen and serious when the garbled value is a username or a path.

Binary to text. RFC 4648 (October 2006) defines Base16 (hexadecimal), Base32 and Base64. Base64 takes 24-bit groups, three octets, and writes each as four characters from a 65-character subset of US-ASCII, 64 symbols plus = for padding, so the output is a third larger than the input, and one or two = signs mark a final group of one or two octets. The URL and filename safe variant, base64url, replaces + and / with the hyphen and the underscore. Base64 reached everyday use through Multipurpose Internet Mail Extensions (MIME): RFC 2045 (November 1996) noted that the Simple Mail Transfer Protocol (SMTP) restricted messages to 7bit US-ASCII and defined the transfer encodings 7bit, 8bit, binary, quoted-printable and base64, with encoded lines of no more than 76 characters. RFC 4648's security considerations are worth reading as a checklist: a decoder that silently ignores non-alphabet characters creates a covert channel and lets two different strings decode to the same bytes, non-significant padding bits can be abused the same way, and case-insensitive Base16 or Base32 handling can make string comparisons fail.

Percent-encoding. RFC 3986 (January 2005, STD 66) defines a percent-encoded octet as % followed by two hexadecimal digits, leaves the unreserved characters (letters, digits, hyphen, full stop, underscore and tilde) unencoded, requires % itself to be written %25, and then states the rule that most bypasses break: implementations must not percent-encode or decode the same string more than once, because decoding an already decoded string can turn data into syntax.

Where filters lose. MITRE's Common Weakness Enumeration entry CWE-174 names the weakness, double decoding: the product decodes the same input twice. The illustration from the Open Worldwide Application Security Project (OWASP) is the dot-dot-slash of path traversal: ../ is %2E%2E%2F, and encoding the % again gives %252E%252E%252F, which passes a filter that decodes once and looks for ../, then becomes ../ when a later component decodes again. Microsoft's Internet Information Services (IIS) suffered both forms. CVE-2000-0884 (a Common Vulnerabilities and Exposures identifier), the Web Server Folder Traversal vulnerability fixed by MS00-078, let attackers read outside the web root on IIS 4.0 and 5.0 with Unicode-encoded characters in the URL, and CVE-2001-0333, fixed by MS01-026, did the same on IIS 5.0 and earlier by encoding the dots and the backslash twice. RFC 3629 cites the related trick of the overlong UTF-8 sequence: a parser that rejects 2F 2E 2E 2F (/../) but accepts the illegal 2F C0 AE 2E 2F lets the same path through, an exploit it records as used by a widespread virus attacking web servers in 2001. The lesson is structural: decode to a canonical form once, validate that form, and do it at the layer that will finally interpret the value.

Encoding as a defence. Encoding is also the main protection against cross-site scripting (XSS), as output encoding. The OWASP prevention cheat sheet asks for context-specific encoding of every variable placed in a page, because browsers parse HTML, JavaScript, URLs and Cascading Style Sheets (CSS) differently: in HTML element content, & becomes &, < becomes <, > becomes >, the double quote " and the single quote '. It also warns that output encoding is not perfect, and that in dangerous contexts, such as directly inside a script element, a comment or a style block, no encoding makes a variable safe. Using the wrong encoding for the context is the same mistake as decoding twice, seen from the other side.

The working rule is to name every layer: which character encoding the bytes are in, which transfer encoding wraps them and which parser will finally read them. Numbers worth keeping: 128 codes in ASCII, U+10FFFF as the last code point, one to four bytes in UTF-8, four output characters for every three input bytes in Base64, 76 characters per MIME line, and %25 for a literal percent sign.

router.def: A device that forwards packets between networks by choosing a next hop from a routing table.
router.context: The decision is per packet and purely local: a router does not know the path, only the next step, and the packet's journey is the sum of independent choices made by machines that never coordinate. That is why traceroute shows a path that may not be the path the next packet takes, and why routing problems are often asymmetric: the way out and the way back are decided by different devices with different tables.
router.depth:
What it is. RFC (Request for Comments) 1812, the requirements for Internet Protocol (IP) version 4 (IPv4) routers, defines a router as a device that performs the network layer forwarding function of the Internet protocol suite; the Open Systems Interconnection (OSI) world called the same thing an intermediate system. What sets it apart from other packet switches is that it examines the IP header as part of switching: it generally removes the link layer header a packet arrived with, modifies the IP header, and adds a new link layer header to send it on. A switch forwards frames within one network by media access control (MAC) address; a router joins networks, and firewalls, load balancers and servers route too. On Linux it is a single setting, net.ipv4.ip_forward, which defaults to 0; setting it to 1 resets the kernel's parameters from host defaults (RFC 1122) to router defaults (RFC 1812).

Where the word came from. The ARPANET's packet switches were Interface Message Processors (IMPs), built by a group headed by Frank Heart at Bolt Beranek and Newman (BBN); the first was installed at the University of California, Los Angeles (UCLA) in September 1969. In the Internet Society's history, the black boxes that connected separate networks would later be called gateways and routers. The Internet Engineering Task Force (IETF) kept the old word for years: RFC 1009 (June 1987), by Braden and Postel, is titled Requirements for Internet Gateways. RFC 1812, edited by Baker of Cisco Systems in June 1995, replaced it and RFC 1716, noting that the older name had largely passed out of favour to avoid confusion with application gateways. It survives in default gateway and in the names Interior and Border Gateway Protocol.

The forwarding decision. For each packet the router looks the destination up in its forwarding table and keeps the most specific match. RFC 1812's own example sends 10.144.2.5 by 10.144.2.0/24 rather than by 10.144.0.0/16 or 10.0.0.0/8, because the /24 has the longest prefix. The result is a next hop and an outgoing interface, never a path. The router then decrements the Time to Live (TTL), an 8-bit field nominally in seconds that RFC 1812 says must drop by at least one at every router, which makes it in effect a hop count; at zero the packet is discarded and an Internet Control Message Protocol (ICMP) Time Exceeded message goes back to the source. IP version 6 (IPv6) renamed the field Hop Limit and, unlike IPv4, leaves fragmentation to the source: RFC 8200 (July 2017) says routers on the path do not fragment. A router never changes the source and destination IP addresses on its own, so they survive end to end unless something translates them, while the MAC addresses are rewritten at every hop.

Two tables, and how they are filled. Routes come from connected networks, static configuration and dynamic routing protocols such as Open Shortest Path First (OSPF), Intermediate System to Intermediate System (IS-IS) and Border Gateway Protocol (BGP). The protocols and the selection logic are the control plane; the per-packet lookup works from the Forwarding Information Base (FIB). In FortiOS terms, the routing table holds the best routes from all protocols and the kernel table is the FIB used for each packet. When two sources offer the same prefix, the lowest administrative distance, a rank of trustworthiness, wins. Cisco's defaults are 0 for connected, 1 for static, 20 for external BGP, 90 for internal Enhanced Interior Gateway Routing Protocol (EIGRP), 110 for OSPF, 115 for IS-IS, 120 for Routing Information Protocol (RIP), 170 for external EIGRP and 200 for internal BGP, and a route with 255 is never installed. FortiGate gives a static route 10 and a default route learned by Dynamic Host Configuration Protocol (DHCP) 5, then breaks ties by priority. Distance only arbitrates between identical prefixes: the most specific route wins first, which is what to check when a static route seems to be ignored.

Load sharing and asymmetry. When several next hops are equally good, routers use equal-cost multipath (ECMP). RFC 2992 (November 2000) analyses the common method, hash-threshold: a hash, a 16-bit cyclic redundancy check (CRC16) for example, over packet header fields selects the next hop, so the packets of one flow stay on one path and are not reordered. The reply is hashed by other routers with other tables, so the path back is often different, and a stateful device in the middle, a firewall or a network address translator, may see only half of a conversation. RFC 3704 (Best Current Practice, BCP, 84, March 2004) meets this in anti-spoofing. Strict reverse path forwarding looks the source address up in the FIB and accepts a packet only if it arrived on the interface the router would use to reach that source; the RFC calls it very reasonable in front of an edge network but applicable only where routing is symmetrical, which between providers using hot-potato routing it normally is not; loose and feasible-path modes exist for that case.

Scale. A router that takes a full internet table carries every announced prefix. In the report of 12 November 2026 the APNIC (Asia Pacific Network Information Centre) research view, AS131072, on bgp.potaroo.net held 1,091,968 IPv4 entries and 265,429 IPv6 entries, all of which have to fit in the FIB of such a router.

What goes wrong. In a routing loop two routers point at each other and a packet bounces until its TTL expires, so, unlike a switching loop, it burns itself out. A more specific route than intended, or a default route pointing at a dead next hop, makes a black hole that drops traffic silently. Directed broadcasts show a default that aged badly: RFC 1812 required routers to forward them unless configured otherwise, attackers used the networks that did as amplifiers in smurf attacks, and RFC 2644 (BCP 34, August 1999) reversed the default, so routers must block receiving and forwarding them. Spoofing follows from the design, since a router forwards on the destination and does not check the source; RFC 2827 (BCP 38, May 2000) asks providers to apply ingress filtering so that traffic with forged source addresses cannot leave from behind their aggregation points.

Seeing it work. traceroute exploits the TTL: it sends probes with increasing TTL values, 3 per hop and up to 30 hops by default on Linux, and each router that discards one answers with Time Exceeded, revealing its address. Each line is a separate measurement, possibly over another ECMP branch, so the output lists routers that replied, not a guaranteed path. On Linux, ip route get followed by an address prints the route the kernel would actually use. On Cisco IOS, show ip route prints each route with its administrative distance and metric in brackets; on a FortiGate, get router info routing-table all does the same, a static default route appearing as [10/0]. Linux sends its own packets with a TTL of 64 by default, so the TTL seen in a capture hints at how many routers a packet crossed.

switch.def: A device that forwards frames within a network by learning which addresses live on which port.
switch.context: It learns by watching: every frame that arrives teaches it where the sender is, and anything it has not learned yet is flooded to every port. That single behaviour explains most of what operators see: a network that works before the table populates, traffic appearing where it should not during a topology change, and the reason a loop is catastrophic rather than merely wasteful, since flooded frames multiply with nothing to stop them.
switch.depth:
In Ethernet networks a switch is a multiport bridge: a device that connects network segments at layer 2 and forwards each frame by its destination media access control (MAC) address. The Linux kernel's bridging documentation describes the role as IEEE (Institute of Electrical and Electronics Engineers) 802.1Q-2022, Bridges and Bridged Networks, defines it: a bridge filters and forwards frames between segments based on the destination MAC address. Each switch port is a segment of its own, frames are filtered and forwarded rather than repeated to everyone as a hub does, and on full-duplex links there is nothing left to collide. A layer 3 switch adds Internet Protocol (IP) routing between virtual local area networks (VLANs) in the same hardware; that part of it is a router, whatever the product is called.

The mechanism is older than the product. In her 1985 paper written at Digital Equipment Corporation, Radia Perlman summarized the transparent bridge it rests on: a bridge listens promiscuously on all its links, keeps a forwarding database whose entries pair a station address with the link in whose direction that station was last seen, builds that database from the source field of each frame, and forwards by the destination field. A frame for a known address leaves by one port only; a frame for an unknown unicast address, and every broadcast, is flooded out of every other port in the VLAN, as the Linux bridge does by default; and an entry that is not refreshed ages out, after 300 seconds by default on a Linux bridge. With VLANs the table takes two keys, address and VLAN, so one switch holds several separate layer 2 networks.

Those habits make loops lethal. Flooding has no memory and an Ethernet frame no hop count, so in a loop a broadcast circulates and multiplies; Perlman's paper warned of severe performance degradation of the entire network from infinitely circulating packets, a network that could be brought down merely by plugging a cable into the wrong place. Her algorithm lets bridges compute, from nothing more than each bridge's own unique identifier, a loop-free spanning tree over an arbitrary topology and keep the remaining links as backups. It became the Spanning Tree Protocol (STP) of IEEE 802.1D, which evolved into the Rapid (RSTP) and Multiple (MSTP) Spanning Tree Protocols; 802.1D-2004 replaced the original protocol with RSTP, its functions moved into 802.1Q by 2014, and 802.1D was withdrawn in 2022. On a Linux bridge STP is off unless stp_state turns it on, and the classic timers show its age: a port spends the forward delay, configurable from 2 to 30 seconds, in each of the listening and learning states before it forwards.

Some frames a bridge must not pass on at all. Destination addresses of the form 01:80:C2:00:00:0X are reserved for link-local control traffic between neighbouring devices, and the multicast group a bridge uses for spanning tree must be one of them; a Linux bridge's group forward mask defaults to 0, so it forwards none of these frames. If learning is switched off on a port, the bridge floods every frame for which it has no entry, which shows what learning is for: without the table, a switch behaves like a hub.

The table is also the attack surface. A frame with a forged source address rewrites the switch's idea of where that address lives, and a flood of random source addresses fills the table: macof, a tool in Dug Song's dsniff suite, floods a switched LAN (local area network) with random MAC addresses, causing some switches to fail open into repeating mode, which makes sniffing easy. The defences limit learning: port security on switches, a cap on dynamically learned entries, which the Linux bridge exposes as IFLA_BR_FDB_MAX_LEARNED, and 802.1X authentication on access ports.

How a switch forwards matters for latency and for errors. Application-specific integrated circuits (ASICs) cut the handling time inside 1990s bridges to tens of microseconds, and Cisco's white paper on the subject explains that a store-and-forward switch receives the whole frame and checks its frame check sequence (FCS) before forwarding, and drops invalid frames, while a cut-through switch begins forwarding soon after reading the destination MAC address and therefore passes corrupted frames on to be discarded downstream. Cut-through, a term coined in the early 1990s, faded as store-and-forward became the norm, and returned in low-latency data centres where it gives a few microseconds per hop regardless of packet size.

In practice, bridge fdb show on Linux lists the learned table and bridge link shows the ports and their state, with per-port switches for learning, unicast flooding and broadcast flooding; managed switches expose the same table as a MAC address table. Because a switch delivers each frame only to the port where its destination lives, a capture host on another port sees broadcasts, floods and its own traffic, not other conversations, which is why captures on switched networks need port mirroring. Vendors build on the same core: a FortiSwitch, for instance, adds storm control, which measures broadcast, unknown unicast and unknown multicast in packets per second and drops the excess.

Numbers worth remembering: 300 seconds of default ageing on a Linux bridge; on the same bridge, a forward delay settable from 2 to 30 seconds per STP state, a hello time from 1 to 10 seconds and a max age from 6 to 40 seconds; and the 4094 VLANs that one 802.1Q switch can keep apart.

bridge.def: A device or function that joins two or more network segments at layer 2, learning where each media access control (MAC) address lives and forwarding only the frames that need to cross, so that the segments behave as one network.
bridge.context: The bridge is the switch's ancestor, and the word survives where the switch's does not: spanning tree still elects a root bridge, the Institute of Electrical and Electronics Engineers (IEEE) standard still specifies bridges rather than switches, and Linux, hypervisors and firewalls in transparent mode still call their software switch a bridge. The original purpose was to cut a shared Ethernet's collision domain in two while keeping one broadcast domain, which is what a modern switch does on every port: the idea did not go away, it multiplied.
bridge.depth:
What it does. The Linux kernel documentation, paraphrasing the Institute of Electrical and Electronics Engineers (IEEE) standard 802.1Q-2022, describes a bridge as a device that connects two or more network segments, operates at the data link layer (layer 2) and filters and forwards frames between segments on the destination media access control (MAC) address. Its plain-English answer to what a bridge does is better still: it transparently forwards traffic between interfaces, joining two or more physical Ethernet networks into one larger logical Ethernet network, and because it looks only at layer 2 headers it is protocol independent, carrying the Internet Protocol (IP) in both versions and older protocols alike. Transparent is the important word. Hosts do not address the bridge or know it is there; they address each other, and the bridge decides which side each frame belongs on.

How it decides. A transparent bridge learns by listening: every frame it receives teaches it that the source address lives behind the arrival port, and it keeps that fact in a forwarding database (FDB) until it ages out, after 300 seconds by default in Linux. A frame for a learned address goes out of that one port, or is dropped if the destination is on the same side it came from, which is the filtering half of the job. A frame for an address not yet learned is flooded out of every port except the one it arrived on, and so are broadcasts and, unless something smarter is configured, multicasts. Classic Ethernet was a shared medium, and the bridge's first value, as one switching study guide puts it, was to segment a LAN (local area network) into two collision domains; the switches that followed provided the same benefit with more interfaces and forwarding in hardware, while a set of connected switches remains one broadcast domain. In the standard's own vocabulary a switch is still a bridge.

Loops, and the protocol that tamed them. Flooding has a price: a bridge sends a broadcast out of every port, so two bridges joined twice hand the same frame back and forth around the loop, copying it each time, which is the broadcast storm the Linux documentation says spanning tree exists to prevent. Radia Perlman, inducted into the Internet Hall of Fame in 2014, designed the spanning tree algorithm that let bridged Ethernet grow into large networks; she later designed TRILL (Transparent Interconnection of Lots of Links), specified in Request for Comments (RFC) 6325 of July 2011 with her as first author, which routes between bridges with the Intermediate System to Intermediate System (IS-IS) protocol and adds a header with a hop count so that forwarding stays safe even during temporary loops. The Spanning Tree Protocol (STP) elects a root bridge: every bridge advertises a bridge identifier made of a configurable priority, 32768 by default in Linux, and its MAC address, and the lowest identifier wins. Each other bridge then picks a root port, the best path towards the root, and each segment a designated port, and every remaining port is set to blocking. Ports move through blocking, listening, learning and forwarding; Linux's defaults are a hello time of 2 seconds, a maximum age of 20 seconds and a forward delay of 15 seconds spent in each of listening and learning.

The standards. Bridging was IEEE 802.1D. According to the Linux documentation, 802.1D-2004 removed the original spanning tree protocol in favour of the Rapid Spanning Tree Protocol (RSTP), by 2014 everything 802.1D defined had moved into IEEE 802.1Q or IEEE 802.1AC, and 802.1D was withdrawn in 2022. The active standard is IEEE 802.1Q-2022, Bridges and Bridged Networks, which supersedes 802.1Q-2018, has been amended through 802.1Qdy-2025, and specifies how the MAC service is supported by bridged networks and the operation of MAC Bridges and VLAN (virtual LAN) Bridges, with their management, protocols and algorithms. The Multiple Spanning Tree Protocol (MSTP) lives there too.

In software. The Linux kernel bridge is created with ip link add br0 type bridge and given ports with ip link set dev eth0 master br0, and it is the usual way to connect virtual machines and containers to a physical network. It has grown into a capable switch: VLAN filtering with a default port VLAN identifier (PVID) for untagged frames, a VLAN protocol of 0x8100 (802.1Q) or 0x88A8 (802.1ad), per-port controls over learning and flooding, a BPDU (bridge protocol data unit) guard that shuts a port when a spanning tree frame arrives and a filter state that keeps STP off untrusted ports. With switchdev, forwarding can be offloaded to a hardware switch that supports it. Filtering bridged traffic is a known trap: the legacy br_netfilter module, which makes bridged packets visible to iptables by pretending they are routed, is scheduled for removal, and the documentation points to nftables instead.

In security appliances. Bridging lets a firewall or load balancer be inserted into a path without readdressing anything. Fortinet's documentation says that in transparent mode the FortiGate acts like a bridge, with all interfaces in the same virtual domain in one layer 2 forwarding domain by default. F5 BIG-IP does it with a VLAN group, which allows layer 2 forwarding between VLANs of the same IP network and offers four modes: translucent, the default, which uses the real MAC address of the remote host with the locally administered bit toggled; transparent, which preserves it; opaque, which answers with the group's own MAC by proxy ARP (Address Resolution Protocol) and forwards at layer 3; and virtual-wire, a two-member bridge that keeps the Ethernet header intact.

What goes wrong. Every bridge in a redundant pair is a loop waiting to happen, which is why BIG-IP leaves bridging on the standby unit (bridge-in-standby) disabled by default and warns that enabling it in the wrong design may cause adverse effects. Spanning tree problems surface as flooding rather than outages: Cisco's note on unicast flooding explains that each topology change notification shortens the forwarding table's ageing time, so a flapping port keeps the network flooding unicast, and recommends PortFast on ports that face end devices. The numbers to keep: 300 seconds of ageing, a priority of 32768, timers of 2, 20 and 15 seconds, 802.1D withdrawn in 2022, and 802.1Q-2022 as the standard that still calls every switch a bridge.

gateway.def: The address a host sends to when the destination is not on its own network, and, more generally, any device that translates between two systems.
gateway.context: The word carries two meanings. A default gateway is a host's exit: a configured address, usually a router, used for anything outside the local subnet. An application gateway translates between protocols or formats. A wrong default gateway cuts one machine off from everything beyond its subnet while its local neighbours still answer.
gateway.depth:
Three meanings. In the early internet the word meant what is now called a router. RFC (Request for Comments) 1812, of June 1995, notes that many older Internet documents call routers gateways, a name that had passed out of favour to avoid confusion with application gateways, and RFC 1122, the host requirements of October 1989, uses gateway throughout; that is why the host-side term is still default gateway, while Internet Protocol version 6 (IPv6) Neighbor Discovery, RFC 4861, says default router. The second meaning is a translator: RFC 2663 defines application level gateways (ALGs) as application-specific agents that let a host in one address realm reach its counterpart in another, rewriting payloads that carry addresses and ports, and observes that they resemble proxies. The third is the cloud's. Amazon Web Services (AWS) describes its internet gateway as a horizontally scaled, redundant and highly available virtual private cloud (VPC) component that is a target in route tables and, for IPv4, performs one-to-one network address translation (NAT) to an instance's public address: a gateway that is a route target, not a box anyone logs into.

The host's decision. RFC 1122 makes it mechanical and mandatory. The host applies its address mask to the destination and to its own address; if the bits match, the destination is on the connected network and the datagram goes to it directly; if not, the destination is accessible only through a gateway. The host then consults its route cache and, with no entry, uses a default gateway, and it must support more than one. The packet sent to the gateway still carries the final destination in its Internet Protocol (IP) header; only the link-layer frame is addressed to the gateway, whose hardware address the host learns with the Address Resolution Protocol (ARP) or, in IPv6, Neighbor Discovery. That is why a default gateway has to be on the host's own subnet, and why its address never appears in a capture taken at the far end.

When the mask is wrong. Before subnetting was universal, RFC 1027 (October 1987) documented proxy ARP, written at the University of Texas at Austin, whose Ethernet joined more than ten buildings and more than a hundred hosts: a subnet gateway answers ARP requests on behalf of hosts on other subnets, so that hosts unaware of subnets can still talk. Where a router still answers this way, a host with too wide a mask reaches off-subnet hosts without using its default gateway at all, and breaks on the day proxy ARP is switched off, which makes a wrong mask look like a router fault.

Where the default comes from. Apart from manual configuration, IPv4 hosts usually learn it from the Dynamic Host Configuration Protocol (DHCP). Option 3, the Router option of RFC 2132 (March 1997), lists router addresses in order of preference. Option 121, the Classless Static Route option of RFC 3442 (December 2002), delivers whole routes, and a client that receives both MUST ignore the Router option, which is why RFC 3442 tells administrators to put the default router in both. Internet Control Message Protocol (ICMP) Router Discovery (RFC 1256, September 1991) offered a protocol alternative. IPv6 hosts learn default routers from Router Advertisements, sent from a link-local address: RFC 4861 (September 2007) gives each a 16-bit Router Lifetime in seconds, where 0 means the sender is not a default router, and limited what routers send to 9000 seconds until RFC 8319 (February 2018) raised the ceiling to 65535.

Dead gateways. RFC 1122 requires the IP layer to detect the failure of a next-hop gateway and choose another, and it is specific about how not to do it: a gateway should not be used indefinitely without positive indication that it works, and hosts must not check a first-hop gateway by pinging it continuously; pinging is allowed only while traffic is going to the gateway and nothing else shows it alive. Networks therefore also make the gateway itself redundant, so that hosts never have to notice a failure.

First-hop redundancy. The Virtual Router Redundancy Protocol (VRRP), version 3 in RFC 9568 (April 2024, obsoleting RFC 5798), lets several routers share a virtual address that hosts use as their default gateway. A virtual router has an identifier from 1 to 255 and a virtual media access control (MAC) address of 00-00-5E-00-01 followed by that identifier for IPv4, or 00-00-5E-00-02 for IPv6. The router that owns the address uses priority 255, backups use 1 to 254 with a default of 100, and priority 0 tells the backups that the Active Router, as the revised terminology calls it, has stopped. Advertisements go out every 100 centiseconds by default with a Time to Live (TTL) or Hop Limit of 255, and anything arriving with less is discarded, so they cannot come from off the link. Cisco's Hot Standby Router Protocol (HSRP), documented in the informational RFC 2281 (March 1998), does the same with virtual MAC addresses 00-00-0C-07-AC followed by the group number. The hosts keep one gateway address; the address moves.

Rogue gateways. Every mechanism that delivers a gateway can deliver a false one. A rogue DHCP server can name itself as the router, which is what DHCP snooping exists to stop: Cisco's Catalyst documentation describes it as a firewall between untrusted hosts and trusted DHCP servers, filtering messages from untrusted sources, and inactive on all virtual LANs (VLANs) by default. A rogue Router Advertisement makes any host on the link a default router for IPv6, which RA-Guard (RFC 6105, February 2011) filters in the layer-2 switches. Option 121 proved sharper still. CVE-2024-3661, published on 6 May 2024 and named TunnelVision by Lizzie Moratti and Dani Cronce of Leviathan Security Group, showed that an attacker on the same local network can push classless static routes that pull traffic away from a virtual private network (VPN) interface onto the physical one, where it can be read or altered: a VPN that relies on routes to steer traffic can be overridden by a more specific one.

Reading it on a machine. On Linux, ip route get followed by an address prints the route the kernel would actually use, which shows at once whether a destination goes via the gateway or directly. On Windows, route print displays the routing table, the default route is the one to 0.0.0.0, and route add 0.0.0.0 mask 0.0.0.0 followed by an address sets a default gateway, kept across restarts only with /p, which stores it in the registry under PersistentRoutes. In AWS the router is implicit: in every subnet the address after the network address, 10.0.0.1 in 10.0.0.0/24, is reserved for the VPC router, and the next one serves the Domain Name System (DNS). A wrong or dead default gateway looks the same everywhere: hosts on the local prefix answer, and everything beyond it disappears.

proxy.def: An intermediary that terminates one connection and makes another on the requester's behalf, rather than forwarding packets.
proxy.context: Terminating is the difference from routing, and everything follows from it: the proxy is a party to the conversation, so it can read, rewrite, cache, authenticate and log; it also becomes a place where plaintext exists, a bottleneck under load, and a single component whose failure is total. Forward proxies act for clients going out, reverse proxies act for servers being reached; the mechanics are the same and only the direction of trust differs.
proxy.depth:
What it is, and what it is not. A proxy terminates the client's connection and opens its own towards the destination, so there are two transport connections where a router or a network address translator leaves one. The Hypertext Transfer Protocol (HTTP) specification, RFC (Request for Comments) 9110 of June 2022, names three kinds of intermediary. A proxy is a message-forwarding agent chosen by the client, usually through local configuration, to receive requests for some types of absolute URI (uniform resource identifier); organizations use one to group their requests through a common intermediary for security services, annotation or shared caching. A gateway, also known as a reverse proxy, acts as the origin server towards the client but forwards requests inbound to one or more other servers, to front legacy or untrusted services, for accelerator caching and for load balancing. A tunnel is a blind relay that, once active, is not a party to the HTTP conversation at all.

Where it came from. In a paper last revised on 24 May 1994, Ari Luotonen and Kevin Altis described World-Wide Web proxies built into cern_httpd, the server developed at CERN: the proxy gave people on closed subnets, who could reach the internet only through a firewall machine, access to the web, and its cache gave shorter response times after the first fetch. Those two motives, controlled egress and caching, still define the forward proxy. Squid, based on the Harvest Cache Daemon of the early 1990s, became the common open-source implementation and normally listens on port 3128. SOCKS took the idea below HTTP: version 5, RFC 1928 (March 1996), is a shim between the application and transport layers that carries both Transmission Control Protocol (TCP) and User Datagram Protocol (UDP) traffic through a firewall, conventionally on TCP port 1080, with GSSAPI (Generic Security Service Application Program Interface) authentication required of implementations and username and password recommended.

On the wire. A client using an explicit proxy puts the full URI in the request line, as in GET http://www.example.org/pub/WWW/TheProject.html HTTP/1.1, the absolute form of RFC 9112, and the proxy answers from its cache or makes the request itself. For HTTPS, HTTP over Transport Layer Security (TLS), the client sends CONNECT with only host and port, such as CONNECT server.example.com:443, and after any 2xx answer the proxy switches to blind forwarding in both directions. RFC 9110 warns that a tunnel to an arbitrary port such as 25 could make the proxy a spam relay, and says proxies supporting CONNECT should restrict it to known ports or a configured list. A proxy that wants credentials answers 407 Proxy Authentication Required with a Proxy-Authenticate challenge and the client retries with Proxy-Authorization; every proxy must add a Via header field to what it forwards. An interception proxy, also called a transparent proxy, differs because the client never chose it: it redirects outgoing TCP port 80 traffic, as on public access points and inside corporate firewalls, and RFC 9110 notes that such intermediaries are indistinguishable at the protocol level from an on-path attacker.

How clients find it. Browsers can be pointed at a proxy auto-configuration (PAC) file, a JavaScript function FindProxyForURL(url, host) introduced with Netscape Navigator 2.0, which returns DIRECT, PROXY host:port or SOCKS host:port, several of them separated by semicolons for failover, served as application/x-ns-proxy-autoconfig. Command-line tools read environment variables: curl honours http_proxy, HTTPS_PROXY, ALL_PROXY and NO_PROXY, and accepts http_proxy only in lower case. The upper-case form is the dangerous one. In mid-2016 the httpoxy disclosures showed that the Common Gateway Interface (CGI) turns a client's Proxy request header into an HTTP_PROXY environment variable, so an attacker could route a web application's outgoing requests through a proxy of his choosing; CVE-2016-5385 (PHP) and CVE-2016-5387 (Apache HTTP Server) were among the Common Vulnerabilities and Exposures (CVE) identifiers, and the advice was to block the Proxy header at the edge.

Encrypted traffic. Through CONNECT a proxy sees the destination host and port and nothing more. To inspect content it must terminate the TLS session itself, presenting certificates from an authority the clients have been made to trust, and open a second TLS session to the server. That decision has a measured cost. Durumeric and colleagues, at the Network and Distributed System Security (NDSS) Symposium in 2017, looked for interception from the Mozilla Firefox update servers, popular e-commerce sites and the Cloudflare network, found more than an order of magnitude more of it than previously estimated, and reported that nearly all interception products reduced connection security and many introduced severe vulnerabilities. A decrypting proxy has to validate the server's certificate at least as strictly as the browser it stands in for.

Reverse and full proxies. In front of servers the split is the point. F5 describes BIG-IP as a full proxy: a client-side connection and a separate server-side connection with a little gap in the middle, never blended, so each side can have its own TCP behaviour, TLS settings and protocol version, and a policy can act on a whole request before any server sees it. The price is that servers see the proxy's address instead of the client's. The de facto fix was X-Forwarded-For; RFC 7239 (June 2014) standardized a Forwarded header field that carries for, by and proto in one field so that the values can be correlated, and warns that it cannot be relied upon, because every node on the way, the client included, can modify it. A server should trust only the entries its own proxies added.

When it goes wrong. Two parsers in a row are a vulnerability waiting for a disagreement. Request smuggling, described by Linhart, Klein, Heled and Orrin in June 2005, exploits differences in how recipients parse a message to hide an extra request inside an apparently harmless one, and RFC 9112 tightened message framing rules to reduce its effectiveness. The rest are configuration failures: an open proxy that relays for anyone, CONNECT allowed to every port, a backend that trusts a client-supplied X-Forwarded-For for access control or logging, and a proxy whose own timeouts and connection limits, invisible to both ends, produce errors that neither client nor server can explain from its own logs.

port.def: A sixteen-bit number that identifies which service or conversation on a host a packet belongs to.
port.context: Ports exist because an address identifies a machine and not a program. The number is a label, not a permission: a service is not safer on a non-standard port, and a port that answers is not evidence of what is listening. Two operational consequences follow. Sixteen bits allow at most 65,536 values, so one client address can hold only as many simultaneous connections to a given server address and port as it has free source ports, which is what runs out under heavy proxying and address translation; and any filter written by port number describes an expectation rather than a fact.
port.depth:
A port is the 16-bit number a transport protocol uses to deliver data to the right process on a host. The Internet Protocol (IP) address gets a datagram to a machine; the destination port in the header of the Transmission Control Protocol (TCP), the User Datagram Protocol (UDP), the Stream Control Transmission Protocol (SCTP) or the Datagram Congestion Control Protocol (DCCP) gets it to a program. IP itself has no ports, as the Linux ip(7) page puts it: they are implemented by the protocols above. Each transport has its own number space, so TCP 53 and UDP 53 are different endpoints that happen to be registered to the same service. An address and a port together make what Request for Comments (RFC) 9293 calls a socket, a connection is a pair of sockets, and with the protocol added this becomes the five-tuple that firewalls, load balancers and Network Address Translation (NAT) devices use to track every flow. The word is overloaded: the port of a switch is a physical interface, a different thing entirely.

Port numbers are as old as the protocols that carry them, in UDP's specification of 1980 and TCP's of 1981, and their assignment was central from the start. From November 1977 to October 1994 the Internet Assigned Numbers Authority (IANA) published its tables in a series of Assigned Numbers RFCs, the last being RFC 1700, Internet Standard 2; RFC 3232 (January 2002) recorded that the series had been replaced by an online database. Today that is the Service Name and Transport Protocol Port Number Registry, run under RFC 6335 (August 2011, Best Current Practice (BCP) 165), which brought TCP and UDP into one procedure with SCTP and DCCP. RFC 6335 also ended the habit of assigning every number for both TCP and UDP whether or not a service used both; from then on the unused protocol's entry is marked Reserved.

RFC 6335 divides the space into three ranges. System Ports, also called well-known ports, run from 0 to 1023; User Ports, or registered ports, from 1024 to 49151; and Dynamic Ports, also called private or ephemeral, from 49152 to 65535, which are never assigned. When it was written, about 76 per cent of System Ports and 9 per cent of User Ports were taken. Values at the edges of each range, such as 0, 1023 and 1024, are reserved, and 1021 and 1022 are set aside for experiments. The assignments every engineer meets daily are few: 22 for Secure Shell (SSH), 25 for the Simple Mail Transfer Protocol (SMTP), 53 for the Domain Name System (DNS), 80 and 443 for the Hypertext Transfer Protocol (HTTP) and its secure form, 123 for the Network Time Protocol (NTP), 179 for the Border Gateway Protocol (BGP) and 3389 for Remote Desktop, registered as ms-wbt-server.

The client side of a connection usually takes an ephemeral port chosen by its operating system: on Linux, connect() or listen() on an unbound socket binds it automatically to a free port. RFC 6056 (January 2011, BCP 156) recommends choosing these unpredictably, so that off-path attackers cannot guess the port of a connection they want to attack blindly, and from the whole range 1024 to 65535 rather than only IANA's dynamic range, because the larger the range, the harder the guess. Implementations differ anyway. Linux defaults to 32768 to 60999 (net.ipv4.ip_local_port_range); Windows moved to 49152 to 65535 with Windows Vista and Windows Server 2008, from 1025 to 5000 before, following the IANA recommendation, and netsh int ipv4 show dynamicport tcp shows the current range.

Sixteen bits set a hard ceiling that operators reach more often than they expect. A connection is unique only by its five-tuple, so one client address talking to one server address and port can hold no more simultaneous connections than it has usable source ports: 28,232 with the Linux default range, 16,384 with the Windows default, and fewer while closed connections sit in TIME-WAIT. Proxies, NAT gateways and load balancers that translate source addresses reach this limit first, because many clients share a few addresses towards the same backend. F5 documents the condition for BIG-IP secure network address translation (SNAT), which rewrites a connection's source address, as ephemeral port exhaustion, in which the SNAT cannot process more connections until source ports become free again, and provides a threshold that logs an error and raises a Simple Network Management Protocol (SNMP) alert. The remedies are more translation addresses, more destination addresses or ports, or shorter holding times.

Unix systems treat ports below 1024 as privileged. On Linux only a process with the CAP_NET_BIND_SERVICE capability may bind them, and the boundary is a per-namespace sysctl, net.ipv4.ip_unprivileged_port_start (default 1024), which an administrator can lower, or set to 0 to remove privileged ports altogether. The check says something about the process on the local host and nothing about the remote side.

A port number is a convention, not an identity. RFC 6335 says so directly: port numbers have meaning only for the two endpoints of a connection, and drawing conclusions about the service behind a flow from the port numbers observed is not always reliable; it calls the use of ports for firewall filtering much less sound than their use as process or protocol identifiers. A rule that allows TCP 443 therefore admits whatever a client chooses to send to that port. Scanning measures exposure from the outside: Nmap's basic scan probes 1,000 TCP ports and reports each in one of six states, open, closed, filtered, unfiltered, open|filtered and closed|filtered, the last two when no answer distinguishes the cases, which is common with UDP. Moving a service to a non-standard port cuts the noise of opportunistic scans; it does not hide the service from a full scan.

In practice, ss -tlnp on Linux lists listening TCP sockets with numeric ports and the owning process, and the services file, usually /etc/services, maps names to numbers locally, which is why tools print ssh instead of 22. The numbers worth keeping: 16 bits, 0 to 65535; well-known 0 to 1023, registered 1024 to 49151, dynamic 49152 to 65535; a Linux ephemeral default of 32768 to 60999; and a Windows default of 49152 to 65535 since Vista.

socket.def: The operating system's handle for one end of a network conversation: an object, created by the socket() call and usually reached through a file descriptor, that is bound to an address, a port and a transport protocol.
socket.context: It is the boundary where networking becomes a programming problem: an application does not build packets, it writes bytes to a descriptor and the kernel does the rest, from the Transmission Control Protocol (TCP) handshake to retransmission. That abstraction is why so much network troubleshooting starts with tools that list sockets rather than capture traffic: the state of a connection is visible on the host, in a table, before anything appears on the wire. A socket is also a finite resource, counted against per-process descriptor limits and the ephemeral port range, and sockets left behind after a close, in TIME-WAIT on the side that closed first or in CLOSE-WAIT when an application forgets to close, are a routine cause of failures on systems that look idle.
socket.depth:
Two meanings, fifty years apart. The word is older than the Transmission Control Protocol (TCP). Request for Comments (RFC) 147, written by J. M. Winett at Lincoln Laboratory and dated 7 May 1971, defined a socket on the network of the day as the unique identification to or from which information is transmitted: a 32-bit number, even for receiving and odd for sending. The TCP specification of September 1981, RFC 793, gave the word its protocol meaning: a port concatenated with the network and host addresses forms a socket, and a pair of sockets uniquely identifies each connection, so one local socket may take part in many connections at once. RFC 9293 of August 2022, which obsoletes RFC 793, keeps the sentence: a connection is defined by a pair of sockets. Add the protocol and the pair becomes the five-tuple that firewalls and load balancers key their tables on. The second meaning, the one programmers use, is the operating system object that holds one end of that conversation.

Where the interface came from. The programming interface is the Berkeley one. Marshall Kirk McKusick's history of Berkeley Unix records that Bill Joy designed the interprocess communication facilities, that he integrated an early TCP/IP (Internet Protocol) implementation from Rob Gurwitz and restructured the internals so that several network protocols could be used at the same time, and that the result shipped as 4.2BSD in August 1983. The Linux manual still gives socket() a history of 4.2BSD and POSIX.1-2001, and the current Portable Operating System Interface (POSIX) standard, published as Institute of Electrical and Electronics Engineers (IEEE) Std 1003.1-2024, says that socket() shall create an unbound socket in a communications domain and return a file descriptor. That last clause is the design decision that matters: on Unix-like systems a socket is a file descriptor, the lowest-numbered free one, so read(), write(), close() and the descriptor limits all apply to it.

What a socket is made of. The call takes three arguments: a domain, a type and a protocol. The domain picks the address family: AF_INET for IPv4, AF_INET6 for IPv6, AF_UNIX for local communication between processes, AF_PACKET for raw link-layer frames and AF_NETLINK for talking to the kernel itself, among more than twenty on Linux. The type picks the semantics: SOCK_STREAM provides sequenced, reliable, two-way, connection-based byte streams, which is TCP in the Internet domains; SOCK_DGRAM provides connectionless, unreliable messages of a fixed maximum length, which is the User Datagram Protocol (UDP); SOCK_SEQPACKET keeps message boundaries on a reliable connection; and SOCK_RAW gives raw protocol access, which is what ping and packet generators need and why they need privileges. A stream socket carries bytes, not messages, so an application that wants records has to mark their edges itself.

The life cycle. A server calls socket(), bind() to a local address and port, listen() to declare that it will accept connections, and accept() for each one, the sequence the Linux listen() manual lists step by step. Each accept() takes the first connection from the queue and returns a new file descriptor for a new connected socket, while the listening socket is unaffected. That is why a busy web server shows one socket in LISTEN on port 443 and thousands of established sockets with the same local port: they differ only in the remote half of the pair. The listen() backlog has meant, since Linux 2.2, the queue of fully established connections waiting for accept(); half-open ones have their own limit; and any backlog larger than /proc/sys/net/core/somaxconn is silently capped to it, a ceiling that defaults to 4096 since Linux 5.4 and was 128 before. A client normally skips bind(): connect() picks an ephemeral source port from /proc/sys/net/ipv4/ip_local_port_range. The Internet Assigned Numbers Authority (IANA) reserves 49152 to 65535 as dynamic ports that are never assigned, in RFC 6335 of August 2011, and operating systems choose their own ranges within or beyond it.

Reading them. Because the kernel keeps every socket in a table, its state can be read before anything is captured. On Linux, ss, which its manual calls another utility to investigate sockets, written by Alexey Kuznetsov, shows TCP sockets with -t, UDP with -u, listeners with -l, numbers instead of names with -n and the owning process with -p, and it filters by any TCP state: established, syn-sent, syn-recv, fin-wait-1, fin-wait-2, time-wait, close-wait, last-ack, closing and listening. A socket stuck in SYN-SENT says the handshake left this host and nothing came back; a pile of SYN-RECV on a server says the opposite.

What goes wrong. Sockets are finite. socket() fails with EMFILE when the per-process limit on open descriptors is reached and with ENFILE when the system-wide limit is; bind() fails with EADDRINUSE when every port in the ephemeral range is in use, the classic failure of a proxy or a client that opens many short connections to one destination. TIME-WAIT is the state RFC 9293 defines as waiting long enough for the peer to receive the final acknowledgement and for delayed segments of the old connection to expire; it is held by the side that closed first, and the specification's Maximum Segment Lifetime (MSL), on which it is based, is taken to be 2 minutes as an engineering choice. Linux leaves tcp_tw_reuse disabled by default, and its manual warns that the older tcp_tw_recycle, present from Linux 2.4 to 4.11, broke clients behind network address translation (NAT). CLOSE-WAIT means the peer has closed and the socket is waiting for the local user to close too; a server that leaks them is a program that never calls close(), and it runs out of descriptors and stops accepting while its processors sit idle. Restarting a server is the other classic: SO_REUSEADDR lets it bind its port again while old connections linger, and on Linux both the old and the new program must have set it, unlike FreeBSD, where only the new one needs to; SO_REUSEPORT, since Linux 3.9, lets several sockets bind the identical address so that many processes can share one listening port.

Scaling and portability. Watching many sockets from one thread is the job of multiplexing: select() and poll(), and on Linux epoll, available since Linux 2.5.44, which reports the descriptors ready for input or output and, in its manual's words, scales well to large numbers of them. Windows took the Berkeley interface and changed it where it had to: in Winsock a socket descriptor is not a file descriptor, the SOCKET type is unsigned, so a failed call must be compared with INVALID_SOCKET rather than tested for -1, and errors come from WSAGetLastError() rather than errno.

Neighbours. A UNIX domain socket uses the same calls with no network at all: it is bound to a filesystem pathname or, on Linux, to an abstract name, and it can pass open file descriptors to another process. A port is a number in a header; a socket is the kernel object that owns it; a connection is a pair of sockets; and getaddrinfo() is the call that turns a name into the addresses a socket can connect to. The numbers worth keeping: 4.2BSD in 1983, the pair of sockets of RFC 793, ports 49152 to 65535 for dynamic use, an MSL of 2 minutes in the specification, and a somaxconn of 4096 on current Linux.

handshake.def: The exchange of messages that sets up a conversation before data flows: it establishes that both sides are present and agrees on the terms, such as sequence numbers, protocol version, algorithms and keys, and in security protocols it also proves who each side is.
handshake.context: Every handshake costs at least one round trip, and that is why latency dominates the experience of a distant service more than bandwidth does: a page needing several connections pays the distance repeatedly before a byte of content moves. It is also the point where capability is negotiated, which makes it the place where downgrade attacks live and the reason modern protocols authenticate the negotiation itself rather than trusting it.
handshake.depth:
Two jobs in one exchange. The NIST (National Institute of Standards and Technology) glossary, following RFC (Request for Comments) 4949, defines a handshake as a protocol dialogue between two systems for identifying and authenticating themselves to each other, or for synchronizing their operations. Transport handshakes do the second job, security handshakes do both, and the result is state that outlives the exchange: a TCP (Transmission Control Protocol) connection, a TLS (Transport Layer Security) session, an IKE (Internet Key Exchange) security association. The handshake creates the session; it is not the session.

The TCP three-way handshake. RFC 9293 (August 2022, Internet Standard 7, obsoleting RFC 793) describes it as SYN, SYN-ACK, ACK, named after the control bits for synchronize sequence numbers (SYN) and acknowledgement field significant (ACK). The initiator sends a SYN carrying its initial sequence number (ISN), a fresh 32-bit value, and moves to SYN-SENT; the responder answers with its own SYN and acknowledges ISN plus one, moving from LISTEN to SYN-RECEIVED; the final ACK puts both in ESTABLISHED, and because an ACK occupies no sequence space, the first data segment carries the same sequence number as that ACK. Simultaneous open, two SYNs crossing, also works. The RFC gives the principal reason for three messages: to stop old duplicate connection requests from causing confusion. It also warns that an off-path attacker who can predict ISNs has a security problem, and a SYN to a port with no listener is answered with a reset.

State before proof. A server in SYN-RECEIVED holds memory for a client that has proved nothing, and that is the SYN flood. RFC 4987 (August 2007) records that it was first publicized in Phrack in 1996, that by September 1996 it had taken down an internet service provider's mail servers, prompting CERT advisory CA-96.21, and that it targets end-host resources rather than bandwidth, so few packets suffice. The defences it documents are a larger backlog, the SYN cache Dave Borman built at BSDi in October 1996, and SYN cookies, which keep no state at all and encode it in the sequence number of the SYN-ACK, rebuilding it from the ACK that comes back. TCP Fast Open (RFC 7413, December 2014, experimental) goes the other way, carrying data in the SYN to save up to one round trip, at the stated cost that SYN data may in rare cases be replayed to the application.

What security handshakes cost. In the TLS 1.2 full handshake (RFC 5246, Figure 1) the client waits for ServerHelloDone, sends its key exchange and Finished, and must then receive the server's Finished: two round trips before application data, on top of TCP's one. TLS 1.3 sends key shares in the first flight, and RFC 9001 notes that, absent packet loss, most new connections are established and secured within a single round trip; a client that guesses the wrong key share group pays an extra round trip through HelloRetryRequest. Resumption allows 0-RTT (zero round-trip time) data, which RFC 9846 says has no forward secrecy guarantee and no protection against replay between connections. QUIC removes the separate transport step: RFC 9000 (May 2021) describes a combined cryptographic and transport handshake carried in CRYPTO frames to minimize connection establishment latency.

The negotiation is the target. Whatever the handshake agrees, the session inherits, so attackers aim at the agreement. Browsers once retried failed connections with lower protocol versions, and RFC 7507 (April 2015) added the TLS_FALLBACK_SCSV signal (signalling cipher suite value), code 0x56 0x00, so a server could refuse an artificial fallback; RFC 8996 later obsoleted it along with TLS 1.0 and 1.1. TLS 1.3 builds the defence in: its handshake is designed so that an active attacker cannot force different parameters, Finished is a MAC (message authentication code) over the entire handshake, and a server that negotiates an older version marks its random value so that a TLS 1.3 client can detect the downgrade.

Other handshakes, same lessons. IKEv2 (RFC 7296, October 2014) normally needs four messages: IKE_SA_INIT negotiates parameters and exchanges nonces and Diffie-Hellman values, and IKE_AUTH carries identities, proves possession of the secrets and sets up the first child security association, with the requester responsible for retransmission. The WPA2 (Wi-Fi Protected Access 2) 4-way handshake confirms that client and access point share the credentials and negotiates a fresh key. In 2017 Mathy Vanhoef of KU Leuven showed with KRACK (key reinstallation attacks) that replaying message 3 makes a client reinstall a key already in use, resetting its nonce and replay counter (CVE-2017-13077 and related Common Vulnerabilities and Exposures identifiers); the handshake's formal proofs held, because they guaranteed a secret key and unforgeable messages, not that a key is installed only once.

Reading one. The failure point usually names the cause: a SYN with no answer suggests a filter or a dead path, a SYN answered by a reset means nothing is listening, and a completed TCP handshake followed by a TLS alert moves the question up a layer. tcpdump with the filter tcp[tcpflags] & tcp-syn != 0 shows only connection openings, openssl s_client shows the TLS exchange, and a full proxy such as F5 BIG-IP performs the TLS handshake the destination servers would normally perform, so the client's handshake ends at the proxy.

authentication.def: Establishing who or what is making a request, by checking evidence such as a password, a cryptographic key or a certificate. It is distinct from authorization, which decides what that identity may then do.
authentication.context: The distinction from authorization is the one most incidents turn on: a system that proves identity correctly and then grants everything to anyone who proved it has authenticated perfectly and authorized nothing. Authentication also happens once and is then represented by a token, a cookie or a session, which is why stealing the representation is usually easier than defeating the check, and why lifetime and revocation matter as much as strength.
authentication.depth:
What it is. The NIST (National Institute of Standards and Technology) glossary, quoting FIPS (Federal Information Processing Standards) 200, defines authentication as verifying the identity of a user, process or device, often as a prerequisite to allowing access. NIST's current guideline, Special Publication (SP) 800-63B-4, published in July 2025 by David Temoshok and colleagues and replacing the 2020 edition, describes the same act in its own vocabulary: a claimant proves control of one or more authenticators bound to a subscriber account, a verifier checks that proof, and the result may be used locally or asserted to a relying party in a federated system. Claiming a name is identification; proving it is authentication; checking someone's real-world identity before the account exists is identity proofing, a separate document in the same series.

Factors and levels. A password is something you know; a physical authenticator is something you have; a biometric match is something you are, but SP 800-63B-4 does not accept a biometric as an authenticator by itself, only together with a physical device. Multi-factor authentication (MFA) means two distinct factors. The guideline sets three authenticator assurance levels (AALs): AAL1, basic confidence, allows a single factor; AAL2, high confidence, requires two factors and must offer a phishing-resistant option; AAL3, very high confidence, requires proof of possession of a key through a public-key cryptographic protocol, with a phishing-resistant authenticator and a non-exportable key.

What changed for passwords. The 2025 guideline is blunt. Passwords used as the only factor must be at least 15 characters long, and 8 when they are one factor of several; verifiers should allow at least 64 characters, must check new passwords against a blocklist of common, expected or compromised values, and must not impose composition rules or require periodic changes, forcing a change only on evidence of compromise. Hints and knowledge-based questions are out. Consecutive failed attempts on one account must be limited to no more than 100 before the authenticator is disabled. And it states plainly that passwords are not phishing-resistant.

Phishing resistance. One-time codes typed by the user, whether from an app, a token or a text message, are not phishing-resistant either, because manual entry does not bind the code to the session being authenticated: an impostor site can relay it to the real one. The guideline recognizes two methods that are: channel binding, which ties the authentication to the protected channel and is the stronger, and verifier name binding, which ties it to the verifier's name. Web Authentication (WebAuthn), a W3C (World Wide Web Consortium) Recommendation at Level 2 since 8 April 2021, implements the second idea for the web: public key credentials scoped to one relying party, so a credential created for one site is useless to a look-alike. Passkeys are built on it.

On the wire. HTTP (Hypertext Transfer Protocol), in RFC (Request for Comments) 9110, provides a challenge-response framework: a 401 (Unauthorized) response must carry a WWW-Authenticate challenge, and 403 (Forbidden) is the different answer for a request that was understood and refused. The Basic scheme, RFC 7617 (September 2015), sends user-id and password in Base64, which is encoding, not encryption; the RFC itself calls it not a secure method of user authentication and says it should not protect sensitive information without enhancements such as HTTPS (HTTP over TLS, Transport Layer Security). Kerberos version 5, RFC 4120 (July 2005), replaces the password on the wire with tickets from a trusted third party, and TLS can authenticate the client with a certificate when the server sends a CertificateRequest, though its specification makes only the server side mandatory.

How it fails. The OWASP (Open Worldwide Application Security Project) Top 10:2025 keeps Authentication Failures at seventh place, as in 2021, covering 36 weakness types: credential stuffing with breached username and password lists, password spraying with predictable variants such as Password1!, Password2!, Password3!, default credentials, missing or weak MFA, session identifiers exposed in URLs (uniform resource locators) or reused after login, and sessions not invalidated at logout or after inactivity. Microsoft's own January 2024 incident shows the ordinary version: Midnight Blizzard, detected on 12 January, used a password spray to compromise a legacy, non-production test tenant account that did not have MFA enabled, and from there a legacy test OAuth application with elevated access to the corporate environment.

What it does not settle. A successful authentication answers one question once. Everything that follows depends on how the result is represented, a session cookie, a Kerberos ticket, a bearer token, and on the separate authorization decision made on every request; SP 800-63B-4 therefore pairs each assurance level with reauthentication timeouts, and the OWASP list puts session handling inside the same category.

authorization.def: Deciding what a party, usually an authenticated one, may do with which resource. It is the check that has to run on every request and every object, not only once at the door.
authorization.context: It is the harder half, because it has to be right per object rather than per person: a system knows who you are once, and must then decide about every record, endpoint and action separately. That is why broken access control is consistently the most common serious web defect, not because the concept is difficult, but because the check has to be repeated everywhere and any single place that forgets it is the whole failure.
authorization.depth:
Two meanings. The NIST (National Institute of Standards and Technology) glossary gives the everyday one: the decision to permit or deny a subject access to system objects, or the privileges so granted. It also records an older, governmental one: the official decision to let an information system operate, formerly called accreditation. Engineers mean the first; auditors sometimes mean the second, and a conversation about authorization can go wrong on that alone.

Separate from authentication, on purpose. HTTP (Hypertext Transfer Protocol) keeps the two apart in its status codes: RFC (Request for Comments) 9110 defines 401 (Unauthorized) for a request lacking valid authentication credentials, which must carry a WWW-Authenticate challenge, and 403 (Forbidden) for a request the server understood and refuses; despite its name, 401 is about authentication. TACACS+ (Terminal Access Controller Access-Control System Plus), documented in RFC 8907 in September 2020, makes the separation of authentication, authorization and accounting its key design element. Authorization there is determining what a user is allowed to do, need not use the same server as authentication, can customize the service (a login shell with a time restriction, say) and is one request and one reply per decision, which is what makes per-command authorization on routers and switches possible. The RFC adds a detail worth knowing: nothing at protocol level ties an authorization request to the authentication that preceded it.

Models. The oldest is the access control list, permissions written per user per object. Role-based access control (RBAC), formalized by David Ferraiolo and Rick Kuhn of NIST in 1992 and adopted by the American National Standards Institute and the International Committee for Information Technology Standards (ANSI/INCITS) as standard 359-2004 on 11 February 2004 (revised in 2012), grants permissions to roles and roles to people, which NIST credits with cutting the cost of administration. Attribute-based access control (ABAC), defined for United States federal agencies in SP (Special Publication) 800-162 (January 2014, updated 2019), evaluates attributes of the subject, the object, the requested operation and the environment against policy, so a rule can say that a clinician may read records of patients in her own ward during her shift.

Zero trust moves the decision. NIST SP 800-207 (August 2020) treats authentication and authorization as discrete functions performed before a session to a resource is established, places the decision in a policy decision point and its execution in a policy enforcement point, grants access per session with the least privilege needed, and states that authentication and authorization to one resource do not automatically grant access to another. Policy may weigh device state, location, time and behaviour, not only who the user is.

Delegation. OAuth 2.0, RFC 6749 (October 2012), is explicitly an authorization framework: it lets a third-party application obtain limited access to an HTTP service on behalf of a resource owner, or on its own behalf, through tokens with scopes; its security guidance was consolidated in RFC 9700, Best Current Practice (BCP) 240, in January 2025. A scope says what kind of thing a client may do; it does not say which records, so the resource server still has to check ownership object by object.

How it fails. The OWASP (Open Worldwide Application Security Project) Top 10:2025 keeps Broken Access Control in first place and reports that every application tested had some form of it, across 40 weakness types: insecure direct object references (IDOR), where changing an identifier exposes someone else's data; missing checks on POST, PUT and DELETE in an API (application programming interface); tampering with a JSON Web Token (JWT, JSON being JavaScript Object Notation), cookie or hidden field to raise privileges; permissive CORS (cross-origin resource sharing); and force browsing to pages the user was never shown. Its advice is that access control works only in trusted server-side code and should deny by default. The textbook case is First American Financial: in May 2019 KrebsOnSecurity reported about 885 million title-insurance files, back to 2003, reachable by changing a sequential nine-digit number in a document link, with no authentication at all. Over-broad grants fail too: in Microsoft's January 2024 incident a legacy test OAuth application with elevated access to the corporate environment turned one compromised test account into access to corporate mailboxes.

In the network.
