Access control lists on interfaces, firewall policies, TACACS+ command authorization and the attributes a RADIUS (Remote Authentication Dial In User Service) server returns with an accept are all authorization decisions; the same rules apply to them as to web code: the decision belongs where the requester cannot alter it, the default should be refusal, and every grant tends to outlive the reason it was made.

certificate.def: A digital certificate, in practice an X.509 certificate, is a signed data structure that binds a public key to an identity, such as a domain name, for a stated validity period. A relying party accepts the binding only if a chain of signatures leads to a certification authority (CA) it already trusts.
certificate.context: Three things fail here, and they fail differently. The name may not match what the client asked for. The period may have ended, which is the outage that arrives on a date somebody could have read months in advance. Or the chain may not lead to a trusted root on that particular machine, which is why a certificate that works in a browser can fail from a server with an older trust store. Nothing about a valid certificate says the operator is honest: only that an authority attested to a name.
certificate.depth:
What it is. The NIST (National Institute of Standards and Technology) glossary, quoting FIPS (Federal Information Processing Standards) 186-5, defines a certificate as a set of data that uniquely identifies a public key and an owner authorized to use the key pair, digitally signed by a certification authority (CA), which binds the key to the owner. A certificate is public by design: it carries the public key, never the private one, and encrypts nothing by itself; its only job is to let a relying party believe that a given key belongs to a given name. On the internet the format is the X.509 version 3 certificate as profiled by RFC (Request for Comments) 5280, published in May 2008 by D. Cooper and colleagues.

Where the format came from. The standardization sector of the International Telecommunication Union (ITU-T) published Recommendation X.509, then titled The Directory: Authentication framework, in November 1988 as part of the X.500 directory series; that is the version 1 format. The 1993 revision of X.500 added two fields, giving version 2. The Privacy Enhanced Mail (PEM) RFCs of 1993 built an internet public key infrastructure on version 1 and found it lacking, so the standards bodies behind X.509 added an extensions field, completing the basic version 3 format in June 1996. The edition in force dates from October 2019.

The structure. A certificate is three things in sequence: tbsCertificate, the body to be signed; the signature algorithm; and the signature value. The body is encoded in ASN.1 (Abstract Syntax Notation One) DER (Distinguished Encoding Rules), so that signer and verifier hash exactly the same bytes. It holds the version (the integer 2 means version 3), a serial number, the issuer's name, the validity, the subject's name, the subject's public key and algorithm, and the extensions. RFC 5280 requires the serial to be positive, unique per issuing CA and no longer than 20 octets; the CA/Browser Forum's Baseline Requirements add, for public TLS (Transport Layer Security) certificates, a non-sequential serial below 2^159 carrying at least 64 bits from a cryptographically secure random generator. Validity is two instants, notBefore and notAfter, inclusive, encoded as UTCTime through 2049 and GeneralizedTime from 2050; a device certificate with no meaningful expiry should carry 99991231235959Z.

The extensions that decide behaviour. basicConstraints says whether the key may sign other certificates (the cA flag) and how long a path below it may be; without cA, the keyCertSign bit of keyUsage must not be set. subjectAltName lists the names the certificate is for. keyUsage limits what the key may do: TLS 1.3 needs digitalSignature, while keyEncipherment serves only older TLS 1.2 suites that the Baseline Requirements call insecure. certificatePolicies records how the CA checked the applicant, through reserved identifiers: 2.23.140.1.2.1 for domain validation, 2.23.140.1.2.2 for organization validation, 2.23.140.1.2.3 for individual validation and 2.23.140.1.1 for extended validation.

Names. RFC 9525 (November 2023), which obsoleted RFC 6125, settles how a TLS client matches a certificate to the server it meant to reach: check DNS (Domain Name System) names only in the dNSName entries of subjectAltName, and never in the subject's Common Name, which it calls essentially free-form text. A wildcard is valid only once, only as the whole left-most label, and matches exactly one label, so *.example.com covers www.example.com but neither example.com nor a.b.example.com. The Baseline Requirements make Common Name not recommended in subscriber certificates and require it, when present, to repeat a subjectAltName value.

The chain. RFC 5280 separates end-entity certificates, issued to subjects that may not issue certificates, from CA certificates, and calls a certificate self-signed when its own key verifies its signature, which is how paths start. Validation starts from a trust anchor, and which anchors to accept is a matter of policy, so the same chain can validate on one machine and fail on another. In TLS 1.3 the server's certificate must come first in the Certificate message, each following one should certify the one before it, and the root may be omitted because the client is expected to hold it; versions before 1.3 required the strict order.

Lifetimes. The CA/Browser Forum's Baseline Requirements, version 2.3.1 of 4 October 2026, cap the validity of publicly trusted TLS server certificates by issue date: 398 days before 15 March 2026, 200 days from that date, 100 days from 15 March 2027 and 47 days from 15 March 2029, counting a day as 86,400 seconds. The schedule came from Ballot SC-081v3, proposed by Clint Wilson of Apple and adopted on 11 April 2025 without a vote against: 25 certificate issuers in favour, five abstaining, and all four certificate consumers (Apple, Google, Microsoft and Mozilla) in favour. The same ballot cuts the reuse of domain validation data to 10 days. Renewal at that pace assumes automation, for which the standard protocol is ACME (Automatic Certificate Management Environment), RFC 8555 of March 2019.

Transparency. Certificate Transparency (CT), specified as an experiment in RFC 6962 by B. Laurie, A. Langley and E. Kasper of Google in June 2013 and revised as version 2.0 in RFC 9162 in December 2021, records issued certificates in publicly auditable, append-only logs, so that anyone can notice the issuance of suspect certificates. A log answers a submission with a Signed Certificate Timestamp (SCT); a CA logs a precertificate before issuance and embeds the SCTs in the final certificate. Chrome requires every publicly trusted TLS certificate to be CT compliant: with embedded SCTs, two from distinct logs for a lifetime of up to 180 days and three beyond, from at least two different log operators.

When certificates break things. On 6 December 2018 Ericsson attributed an outage to an expired certificate in software versions installed with its customers; according to The Register about 32 million people in the United Kingdom lost mobile service on O2 and the networks that use it, with operators in other countries hit too. Trust stores age too: when the DST Root CA X3 cross-signature used by Let's Encrypt expired on 30 September 2021, older devices that did not trust ISRG Root X1, the root of the Internet Security Research Group (ISRG), began showing warnings, and clients on OpenSSL 1.0.x could fail even when they did trust it, because of a verification quirk.

Formats and tools. The same DER bytes are usually wrapped in PEM, the textual encoding described in RFC 7468 (April 2015): base64 between -----BEGIN CERTIFICATE----- and -----END CERTIFICATE----- lines. openssl x509 -in cert.pem -noout -text prints every field and extension; -dates or -enddate shows the validity; -ext subjectAltName prints just the names; -checkend followed by a number of seconds exits non-zero if the certificate expires within that time; and -inform DER reads a binary file.

vulnerability.def: A weakness in a system, its procedures, its controls or its implementation that a threat source could exploit to do something the system was meant to prevent.
vulnerability.context: A vulnerability is not a risk on its own: risk needs a reachable path, a motivated party and something worth reaching. That is why the count of open findings is a poor management number and the count of exploitable, exposed, high-value ones is a useful one. The awkward corollary is that most estates cannot fix everything, so a programme that does not prioritize is choosing by accident, and the choice is being made whether or not anyone writes it down.
vulnerability.depth:
What counts. The NIST (National Institute of Standards and Technology) glossary, following FIPS (Federal Information Processing Standards) 200, defines a vulnerability as a weakness in an information system, system security procedures, internal controls or implementation that could be exploited or triggered by a threat source. The definition is wider than code: a default password, a firewall rule nobody reviews and a skipped approval step all qualify. Three neighbouring words are often blurred. A weakness, in the vocabulary of MITRE's Common Weakness Enumeration (CWE), is a condition in software, firmware, hardware or a service that could contribute to the introduction of vulnerabilities, such as an out-of-bounds read; a vulnerability is a concrete instance in a specific product and version; an exploit is the technique or code that uses it; and risk adds the threat and the consequence.

Naming. The CVE (Common Vulnerabilities and Exposures) list began as a white paper by David E. Mann and Steven M. Christey of MITRE, Towards a Common Enumeration of Vulnerabilities, presented at Purdue University on 21 and 22 January 1999; a working group that became a 19-member editorial board produced the original 321 entries, and the list went public in September 1999. By October 2024 MITRE counted more than 240,000 CVE records and more than 400 CVE Numbering Authorities (CNAs) in 40 countries, the vendors, researchers and coordinators allowed to assign identifiers, with the programme sponsored by the US (United States) Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency (CISA). A CVE identifier names one vulnerability so that a scanner, an advisory and a patch note can be matched; it says nothing by itself about severity. CWE, updated three or four times a year, names the class of mistake behind it.

Severity. The Common Vulnerability Scoring System (CVSS), maintained by FIRST (Forum of Incident Response and Security Teams), reached version 4.0 on 1 November 2023. It has four metric groups: Base, the intrinsic and stable properties; Threat, which replaced the old Temporal group and now centres on exploit maturity; Environmental, the consumer's own context; and Supplemental, attributes such as Safety, Automatable and Recovery that never change the number. Version 4.0 added an Attack Requirements metric, retired Scope, and introduced labels so that a score says what it contains: CVSS-B for Base alone, CVSS-BT, CVSS-BE and CVSS-BTE. Scores map to None (0.0), Low (0.1 to 3.9), Medium (4.0 to 6.9), High (7.0 to 8.9) and Critical (9.0 to 10.0), and the specification tells consumers to add Threat and Environmental metrics before using a score in their own risk assessment. Most published scores are Base only, which is why a Critical label is a statement about the flaw, not about anyone's exposure.

Likelihood. Two public sources answer the question CVSS leaves open. FIRST's Exploit Prediction Scoring System (EPSS) is a data-driven machine-learning model that estimates, every day and for every published CVE, the probability from 0 to 1 that it will be exploited in the wild in the next 30 days. CISA's Known Exploited Vulnerabilities (KEV) catalogue lists vulnerabilities with evidence of exploitation; its catalogue version of 10 November 2026 held 1,779 entries, the first dated 3 November 2021. On 10 June 2026 CISA issued Binding Operational Directive (BOD) 26-04, which harmonizes the earlier BOD 19-02 and BOD 22-01 and tells federal agencies to prioritize by asset exposure, KEV status, exploit automation and post-exploitation technical impact.

One vulnerability, all the signals. Log4Shell, CVE-2021-44228, was published by NVD (National Vulnerability Database) on 10 December 2021: Apache Log4j2 from 2.0-beta9 through 2.15.0 let anyone who could influence a log message trigger JNDI (Java Naming and Directory Interface) lookups that loaded and executed remote code. NVD scored it 10.0 under CVSS 3.1, network vector, low complexity, no privileges, no user interaction, scope changed; CISA added it to KEV the same day with a due date of 24 December 2021 and marks it as used in ransomware campaigns. Heartbleed, CVE-2014-0160, shows the other direction: published in April 2014, it entered KEV only on 4 May 2022, because CISA adds a vulnerability when it has evidence of exploitation, whatever the age of the flaw.

What goes wrong in practice. Treating the CVSS Base score as risk, so that a Critical finding on an isolated test host outranks a Medium one on an internet-facing gateway already in KEV. Counting findings instead of exposure, so dashboards improve while the reachable attack surface does not. Waiting for a CVE before acting, when a vendor advisory or a KEV entry is the stronger signal. And forgetting that procedures and configurations are vulnerabilities too, which scanners mostly do not see.

malware.def: Software or firmware deliberately placed or run on a system for a harmful purpose, serving someone other than its owner: to steal, spy, extort, destroy or keep a way in. Viruses, worms, trojans, rootkits, spyware and ransomware are kinds of it, named more for how they spread or hide than for what they do.
malware.context: The categories (virus, worm, trojan, rootkit, stealer) describe how it spreads and hides rather than what it does, and modern samples mix them freely, which is why classification is less useful operationally than behaviour. The defining property is that it is code executing with legitimate permissions: almost nothing malware does requires a novel capability, only the ability to run as somebody who was already allowed. That is why execution control and privilege reduction outperform detection over time.
malware.depth:
What the definitions agree on. The glossary of the National Institute of Standards and Technology (NIST) collects several, and the common element is intent. The Internet Security Glossary, Request for Comments (RFC) 4949, as adopted by the Committee on National Security Systems, speaks of hardware, firmware or software intentionally included or inserted in a system for a harmful purpose. NIST's control catalogue speaks of software or firmware intended to perform an unauthorized process that harms the confidentiality, integrity or availability of a system, and counts spyware and some forms of adware in. A buggy program that destroys data is not malware; the same destruction written on purpose is. Intent also explains the grey zone: remote administration tools, credential dumpers and scanners are the same code in an administrator's hands and an intruder's.

The virus and the worm. Fred Cohen's 1984 paper, Computer Viruses: Theory and Experiments, gave the first a definition that still holds: a program that can infect other programs by modifying them to include a possibly evolved copy of itself, spreading with the authorizations of every user who runs it. The experiment was conceived on 3 November 1983 for a weekly security seminar, the name was suggested by Len Adleman, and the first virus took eight hours to write on a VAX 11/750 running Unix; demonstrated on 10 November, it obtained all system rights in under an hour in each of five attacks, in under five minutes at best. Cohen also showed that detecting a virus is undecidable in general, by inspection or at run time, the formal reason no scanner can be complete. The worm needed no host program. RFC 1135 describes the one released on the evening of 2 November 1988: it attacked Sun and VAX machines running Berkeley Unix through a debugging feature of sendmail and a buffer overflow in fingerd, then through rexec and rsh trust and password guessing.

The classic categories, and why they fade. NIST Special Publication (SP) 800-83 Revision 1 (July 2013), by Murugiah Souppaya and Karen Scarfone, sets them out. Viruses insert copies of themselves into host programs or files and usually need a user action; compiled viruses include file infectors, boot sector viruses and multipartite ones, interpreted viruses include macro and scripting viruses. Worms are self-replicating and self-contained, spreading through vulnerable network services or by mass mailing. Trojan horses do not replicate and look benign while carrying a hidden purpose. Malicious mobile code arrives from a remote host and runs without explicit instruction. Blended attacks combine methods. Backdoors, bots, remote administration tools, keystroke loggers and rootkits are, strictly speaking, attacker tools that malware delivers, because they cannot infect anything on their own. The guide's own conclusion is the one the entry's context draws: many if not most instances are blended, so the categories are considerably less useful for incident handling than they were, one set of procedures now handles them all, and organizations should not spend time classifying each incident. It also notes the shift to toolkits such as Zeus, SpyEye and Poison Ivy, which let unskilled attackers build customized samples faster than signature-based controls can follow.

Malware and tools. MITRE ATT&CK, the knowledge base of adversary behaviour MITRE started in 2013 and at version 20.1 since 13 October 2026, catalogues about 970 pieces of software used in the behaviour it models and labels each one Malware or Tool. Emotet is malware, a modular downloader for other malware; PsExec is a tool, a free Microsoft utility that the entry describes as used by information technology (IT) administrators and attackers alike. Brazilian banking malware shows how blurred the line runs in practice. Kaspersky's 2020 report on four families it calls the Tetrade (Guildma, Javali, Melcoz and Grandoreiro) describes Guildma, active since at least 2015, downloading its modules with BITSAdmin because it is an allowlisted Windows tool, hiding payloads in alternate data streams of the New Technology File System (NTFS), loading through dynamic-link library (DLL) search-order hijacking and process hollowing, and keeping its command and control addresses in YouTube and Facebook posts, while spreading from Brazil to the rest of Latin America and Europe. Almost every step uses something the operating system already permits.

Detection and its limits. Signature scanning remains the base layer and is honest about its scope: it recognizes what has been seen. Testing it needs no live sample: the EICAR test file, produced by the European Institute for Computer Antivirus Research (EICAR) and the Computer Antivirus Research Organization (CARO), is 68 printable American Standard Code for Information Interchange (ASCII) characters (a file no longer than 128 characters in all) that products detect as if it were a virus. Gateways add their own limits. FortiOS runs flow-based and proxy-based antivirus side by side, flow mode for throughput; in flow mode a file larger than the protocol options' oversize limit is passed by default and bypasses scanning altogether, and suspicious files can be handed to FortiSandbox for behavioural analysis. Endpoint detection and response (EDR) moves the question from what the file is to what the process does, which is where Cohen's result leaves the defender anyway.

Prevention that does not depend on recognition. SP 800-83 recommends application whitelisting, also called application control, for high-security and high-risk environments: in enforcement mode only listed applications may run, in audit mode non-listed ones are logged but allowed, and the guide advises starting in audit mode to find missing entries before enforcing, noting that audit mode detects but never prevents. It adds sandboxing, browser separation and segregation through virtualization as architectural limits on what a successful sample can reach. Least privilege works on the same principle: malware inherits the rights of whoever runs it, so fewer standing rights means less inherited.

Handling an infection. SP 800-83 follows the general incident life cycle (preparation, detection and analysis, containment, eradication and recovery, and post-incident activity) and lists containment by user participation, by automated detection, by disabling services and by disabling connectivity. For stealthy, long-lived intrusions it warns that removal often means reinstalling the operating system and applications and restoring data from known good backups, which is why persistence is a separate question from the sample. Ransomware is the economic engine of the field now: the Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency's (CISA) Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalogue marks 361 of its 1,779 entries as known to be used in ransomware campaigns. The neighbours are distinct: an exploit is the way in, a payload is what the exploit delivers, malware is the code that stays and works, command and control (C2) is how it takes orders, and a botnet is many infected hosts under one operator.

api.def: An application programming interface (API) is a defined way for one program to ask another for something: a contract stating what may be called, with which inputs, and what comes back, independent of how the other side implements it.
api.context: An application programming interface (API) is a promise, and the promise is the security surface: everything the caller can reach is everything an attacker holding a valid credential can reach. Two failures dominate. Authorization is checked at the gateway but not per object, so changing an identifier in a request returns somebody else's record. And an interface grows by addition, so the undocumented endpoint from three years ago is still answering because nothing ever removed it.
api.depth:
What it is, exactly. The glossary of the National Institute of Standards and Technology (NIST), quoting an older NIST report, defines an application programming interface (API) as a system access point or library function with a well-defined syntax, accessible from application programs or user code, that provides well-defined functionality. The word covers two things engineers meet daily: the interface of a library or an operating system, called inside one process, and the network API, reached over the Hypertext Transfer Protocol (HTTP) or another protocol by a program somewhere else. In both, the API is the contract and not the code behind it. The United States Supreme Court drew exactly that line in Google v. Oracle, separating the declaring code that names a task and its inputs from the implementing code that performs it. An endpoint is one entry point of a network API, and a software development kit (SDK) is a library that wraps an API for one language; neither is the API itself.

Where the word came from. The idea is older than the term. In the 1940s Maurice Wilkes and David Wheeler kept the subroutine library for the EDSAC computer on punched tape in a filing cabinet, with a catalogue explaining how to call each routine, and their book on preparing programs for the machine contains what is described as the first published API specification. The phrase application program interface is first recorded in a 1968 paper by Ira Cotton and Frank Greatorex at the AFIPS Fall Joint Computer Conference, describing Fortran subroutine calls that let a graphics program ignore the quirks of its display hardware, the same promise of independence from the implementation that the term still carries. C. J. Date brought it to databases in a 1974 paper comparing the relational and network approaches.

Web APIs and Fielding's constraints. Roy Fielding's 2000 doctoral dissertation at the University of California, Irvine defined Representational State Transfer (REST) as a set of constraints on a distributed hypermedia system: client and server separated; communication stateless, so that each request carries all the information needed to understand it; responses labelled as cacheable or not; a uniform interface; a layered system in which each component sees only the next layer, which is what lets intermediaries balance load, cache and enforce security policy, as firewalls do; and, optionally, code on demand. The uniform interface is itself four constraints: identification of resources, manipulation of resources through representations, self-descriptive messages, and hypermedia as the engine of application state. Most interfaces sold as REST APIs are HTTP with JavaScript Object Notation (JSON) that honour some of these, which is why the label promises less than it seems. The surrounding standards come from the Internet Engineering Task Force (IETF): HTTP semantics in Request for Comments (RFC) 9110, status 429 Too Many Requests in RFC 6585 (April 2012), machine-readable errors in Problem Details for HTTP APIs, RFC 9457 (July 2023), and delegated authorization in OAuth 2.0, RFC 6749 (October 2012).

Describing the contract. The OpenAPI Specification defines a language-agnostic description of an HTTP API that lets humans and programs discover what a service does without reading its source or watching its traffic. It began as Swagger, first released on 10 August 2011; Swagger 2.0 was donated to the OpenAPI Initiative on 31 December 2015, and the specification has since moved through 3.0.0 (26 July 2017), 3.1.0 (15 February 2021) and 3.2.0 (19 September 2025) to 3.2.1, a patch release of 10 September 2026. A description is used to generate documentation, client and server code and tests, and on the security side it is the inventory and the schema against which a gateway or a web application firewall (WAF) can validate requests.

In network operations. Device management has moved from screen-scraping the command line to APIs. The IETF's Network Configuration Protocol, NETCONF (RFC 6241, June 2011), and its HTTP-based counterpart RESTCONF (RFC 8040, January 2017), both Proposed Standards, carry configuration and state modelled in YANG. F5 describes iControl REST as the evolution of its earlier SOAP-based iControl framework, through which anything possible at the BIG-IP command line can be done programmatically, and points automation towards AS3, its declarative API, where the caller states the desired configuration rather than the sequence of calls that produces it.

How APIs fail. The API Security Top 10 of 2023 from the Open Worldwide Application Security Project (OWASP) is the working list. First is Broken Object Level Authorization: APIs expose endpoints that take object identifiers, so every function that reads data using an identifier from the user needs its own authorization check. Then come Broken Authentication; Broken Object Property Level Authorization, which merged the 2019 categories of excessive data exposure and mass assignment; Unrestricted Resource Consumption, where the cost may be bandwidth, processor time or a paid text message per request; Broken Function Level Authorization between regular and administrative functions; Unrestricted Access to Sensitive Business Flows, such as buying tickets or posting comments by automation; Server-Side Request Forgery (SSRF); Security Misconfiguration; Improper Inventory Management, meaning forgotten versions and exposed debug endpoints; and Unsafe Consumption of APIs, the habit of trusting data from a third-party API more than user input. NIST Special Publication (SP) 800-228 (June 2025) frames the defence across the life cycle: identify risk factors in development and at runtime, apply basic and then advanced controls before and during runtime, and choose implementation options incrementally by risk.

A named case. In a Form 8-K dated 19 January 2023, T-Mobile reported that on 5 January it had found a bad actor obtaining data through a single API without authorization, data for about 37 million current postpaid and prepaid accounts: names, billing addresses, email addresses, phone numbers, dates of birth, account numbers and plan features. The company believed the retrieval had begun on or around 25 November 2022. The interface did not expose payment card data or government identifiers, but six weeks of unnoticed bulk retrieval through one endpoint is the pattern the OWASP list describes, and it is why per-client volume, not only authentication, belongs in API logging.

The interface as property. Google v. Oracle, decided on 5 April 2021 by six votes to two, with Justice Breyer writing for the Court, Justice Thomas dissenting with Justice Alito and Justice Barrett not participating, concerned about 11,500 lines of declaring code that Google copied from the Java SE API for Android, 0.4 per cent of the 2.86 million lines in that API. The Court assumed, for argument's sake, that the lines could be copyrighted and held that Google's reimplementation was fair use as a matter of law, noting that much of an interface's value comes from the programmers who have learned it. The question of whether an API is copyrightable at all was left open.

Numbers worth remembering: 1968 for the term, 2000 for REST, 2011 for Swagger, 429 for rate limiting, and API1, the object-level authorization check that OWASP ranks first.

backup.def: A copy of data, configuration or system state kept apart from the original so that it can be restored after loss, corruption or attack. It counts as a control only once a restore from it has been tested.
backup.context: The operational rule is that nobody has backups, only restores, and an untested copy is a belief rather than a control. Three properties decide whether it survives an incident rather than merely a mistake: it must be isolated enough that whoever compromised the system cannot delete or encrypt it, recent enough to stay within the acceptable data loss, and restorable fast enough to stay within the acceptable downtime. Ransomware turned the first of those from a nicety into the whole point.
backup.depth:
What it is, and what it is not. The National Institute of Standards and Technology (NIST) glossary, quoting its contingency planning guide, calls a backup a copy of files and programs made to facilitate recovery if necessary; in key management the same word means a copy of key material kept for recovery during the key's cryptoperiod. The definition says nothing about where the copy lives, and that is where most failures are. A mirror, a replica or a RAID (redundant array of independent disks) set protects against a failed component, but it writes a deletion or an encryption as faithfully as it writes data. NIST Special Publication (SP) 800-53 accepts a redundant secondary system as a way to achieve the effect of backup only when it is geographically separate and can be activated without loss of information. A snapshot on the same storage, credentials and administrative domain shares the original's fate.

How copies are made. NIST SP 800-34 Revision 1 (May 2010) describes three methods. A full backup captures everything selected, is simple to restore from and slow and storage-hungry to take. An incremental backup captures what changed since the last backup of any kind, which is fast and economical but means a restore needs the last full set plus every incremental since. A differential backup captures what changed since the last full backup, so a restore needs only the full set and the latest differential, at the cost of differentials that grow each day; a full backup at the weekend with differentials each evening is the guide's example. For offsite storage it asks three questions: is the site far enough not to be hit by the same disaster, how long does retrieval take, and how secure are the transport, the facility and the people.

The numbers that size it. SP 800-34 defines three objectives. The maximum tolerable downtime (MTD) is the total outage the system owner will accept for a business process. The recovery time objective (RTO) is how long a system resource can stay unavailable before the impact becomes unacceptable, and so normally has to be shorter than the MTD. The recovery point objective (RPO) is the point in time to which data can be recovered from the most recent backup, a measure of how much data loss the process can tolerate, and is not part of the MTD. Backup frequency follows from the RPO; the restore method, and the bandwidth it needs, follow from the RTO. Control CP-9 of SP 800-53 Revision 5 writes this down: back up user-level information, system-level information and system documentation at a frequency consistent with both objectives, and protect the confidentiality, integrity and availability of the copies, with digital signatures and cryptographic hashes as integrity mechanisms.

Testing is the control. CP-9's first two enhancements require testing backup information for media reliability and integrity, for example by decrypting and transporting a random sample from the backup site and comparing it with the primary, and restoring selected system functions from a sample during contingency plan tests. GitLab's outage of 31 January 2017 is the standard demonstration of why. An engineer removed about 300 GB from the primary production database by mistake. The nightly logical backups, made with pg_dump and sent to cloud storage, had been failing silently: the job used pg_dump 9.2 against a PostgreSQL 9.6 database, and the failure emails were rejected because DMARC (Domain-based Message Authentication, Reporting and Conformance) was not enabled for them, so the bucket was empty. Recovery came from a Logical Volume Manager (LVM) snapshot an engineer had taken about six hours earlier to refresh staging; copying it back took around 18 hours over network disks throttled to roughly 60 Mbps. The changes in between were lost: about 5,000 projects, 5,000 comments and 700 new user accounts. Every element is a lesson: monitor the backup job itself, restore regularly, and measure restore throughput, because the RTO is set by it.

Ransomware goes for the backups first. In a survey of 2,974 organizations hit by ransomware, published by Sophos in March 2024, 94 per cent said the attackers had tried to compromise their backups and 57 per cent of those attempts succeeded; victims whose backups were compromised were almost twice as likely to pay, and their median recovery cost, 3 million US dollars, was eight times that of the others. The United Kingdom's National Cyber Security Centre (NCSC) wrote in August 2019 that it had seen ransomware encrypt connected Universal Serial Bus (USB) and network drives holding backups and connected cloud storage too. Its advice: keep at least one backup offline (cold) at any time, connect it only when necessary, never have every copy connected at once, give backup clients no valid credentials while the storage is idle, keep at least three copies on two devices with one offsite (the 3-2-1 rule), and test regularly.

Making the copy hard to destroy. The NCSC's principles for ransomware-resistant cloud backups (November 2024) turn isolation into service features. Block deletion or alteration of a backup once created, or use soft delete with a recovery period, or delay destructive requests with an alert that reaches someone even when the corporate infrastructure is compromised; forbid destructive requests from customer accounts, human or machine, and authorize exceptions out of band. Make it impossible to lock the customer out by deleting accounts, with an out-of-band way back in. Keep backups for a fixed period rather than a fixed number of copies, so an attacker cannot flood the store with corrupted versions. Protect the encryption keys, because deleting a key destroys the data without touching it, and offer an out-of-band key backup on paper. Alert on significant changes and privileged actions. SP 800-53 adds dual authorization for deletion (CP-9(7)), cryptographic protection (CP-9(8)) and storage of critical software in a separate facility or fire-rated container (CP-9(3)).

On network and security devices. A BIG-IP keeps its configuration archive as a user configuration set (UCS): configuration files, licences, user accounts and password information, Domain Name System (DNS) zone files and installed SSL (Secure Sockets Layer) keys and certificates. F5's documentation (version 21.1, updated 2 September 2026) recommends making one before every upgrade, stores archives by default in /var/local/ucs on the device itself, warns that the host name in the file must match the system being restored, and asks for secure storage because of the keys; tmsh save sys ucs can encrypt it with a passphrase or leave the private keys out. FortiGate backs up its configuration in FortiOS format or in YAML (YAML Ain't Markup Language) to the administrator's computer, a USB drive, or a File Transfer Protocol (FTP) or Trivial File Transfer Protocol (TFTP) server, with optional encryption under a password using the Advanced Encryption Standard in Galois/Counter Mode (AES-GCM); its password-masking option replaces secrets with FortinetPasswordMask for files sent to third parties, which makes a masked file something to share rather than something to restore from. A copy that never leaves the appliance fails with it.

The argument after the fact. When Brazil's Superior Tribunal de Justiça (STJ) was hit on 3 November 2020, it suspended deadlines and sessions until 9 November. Press reports attributed the attack to RansomEXX and said more than 1,200 virtual machines had been encrypted and the backups destroyed; the court said the system backup had not been affected and that case data, e-mail and contracts were preserved. The two accounts were never reconciled in public, which is the final point: a backup is worth what can be shown, by a restore, to come back.

session.def: A bounded period of interaction that keeps state across messages that would otherwise be independent. In web security it is the server's memory that a client has already authenticated, carried by a secret (usually a cookie or token) presented with each request; in networking, a tracked flow such as a firewall session table entry.
session.context: Sessions exist because the protocol underneath does not remember anything, so each request must carry proof of a decision made earlier. That proof is bearer material: whoever holds it is treated as the user, which is why session theft skips authentication entirely and why lifetime, binding and revocation are the controls that actually matter. A logout that only clears the client leaves a valid token in the hands of whoever copied it.
session.depth:
One word, several layers. The NIST (National Institute of Standards and Technology) glossary, quoting its SP (Special Publication) 1800-17, defines a session as a persistent interaction between a subscriber and an endpoint that begins with an authentication event, ends with a session termination event, and is bound by a session secret the subscriber's software presents instead of the credentials. Engineers use the same word for a TLS (Transport Layer Security) session that can be resumed, an entry in a firewall's session table and a load balancer's persistence record. What they share is state kept across messages that would otherwise stand alone. HTTP (Hypertext Transfer Protocol) is stateless, and RFC (Request for Comments) 6265, by A. Barth in April 2011, defines the Cookie and Set-Cookie header fields precisely so that servers can maintain a stateful session over it.

The session secret. SP 800-63B-4 (July 2025) sets the rules for authenticated sessions. The secret is issued by the session host in direct response to an authentication event, comes from an approved random bit generator and is at least 64 bits long; used as a bearer token it should not survive a restart of the application or a reboot; and a session may be treated at a lower assurance level than the authentication that created it, never a higher one. Cookies, it says, are not authenticators but short-term secrets, and session cookies must be sent only over HTTPS (HTTP over TLS) and scoped to the fewest hosts and paths, and should be HttpOnly (hidden from scripts, as RFC 6265 defines the attribute), expire with the session, use the __Host- prefix with Path=/, set SameSite=Lax or Strict and hold only an opaque identifier. The OWASP (Open Worldwide Application Security Project) Session Management Cheat Sheet adds that a session identifier is, while it lives, equivalent to the strongest authentication the application uses, that it needs at least 64 bits of entropy from a cryptographically secure generator, and that default names such as PHPSESSID or JSESSIONID announce the framework behind the site.

How long. SP 800-63B-4 ties reauthentication to the authenticator assurance level (AAL): an overall limit of no more than 30 days at AAL1; 24 hours overall and one hour of inactivity at AAL2; 12 hours overall and 15 minutes of inactivity at AAL3. The OWASP cheat sheet quotes common idle timeouts of 2 to 5 minutes for high-value applications and 15 to 30 minutes for low-risk ones, an absolute limit of 4 to 8 hours for a full working day, and insists that an expired session be invalidated on the server, not only in the browser. SP 800-63B-4 also warns that an OAuth access token and its refresh tokens can remain valid long after the session that produced them has ended, so their presence says nothing about whether the user is still there.

How sessions are stolen. Guessing fails against 64 random bits; the practical attacks take or plant the secret. Session fixation works when the application keeps the same identifier after login, which is why the identifier must be renewed after any privilege change; the OWASP Top 10:2025 lists reuse after login, identifiers exposed in URLs (uniform resource locators) and sessions not invalidated at logout among authentication failures. Theft needs no exploit at all when tokens travel in files: between 28 September and 17 October 2023 an intruder in Okta's support system, entering with service account credentials that had been saved to an employee's personal Google profile, read files belonging to 134 customers and used session tokens found in HAR (HTTP Archive) files to hijack the sessions of five of them. Okta's remedy was to bind administrator sessions to network location and require reauthentication when it changes.

From bearer to bound. SP 800-63B-4 points to proof-of-possession designs, such as the emerging Device Bound Session Credentials specification, in which the client proves it holds a key kept in a protected store instead of replaying a copyable string; such secrets may persist, but the lifetime limits still apply. Binding, short lifetimes and server-side revocation are the three answers to the same problem: a session secret is only as safe as the place it is kept.

In network devices. A FortiGate defines a session as a communication channel between two devices or applications and keeps, for each, the addresses, ports, protocol number (1 for ICMP, the Internet Control Message Protocol, 6 for TCP, the Transmission Control Protocol, 17 for UDP, the User Datagram Protocol), state, timers and matching policy ID; diagnose sys session filter narrows the view, diagnose sys session list shows it and diagnose sys session clear removes matching entries. For TCP the proto_state field holds two digits, one per direction, such as 1 for ESTABLISHED or 2 for SYN_SENT; for UDP, which has no states, it only records whether a reply was seen; and the expire field counts down the timeout since the last packet, which is why an idle application connection dies at the firewall long before either end closes it. In TLS 1.3, RFC 9846 replaced the older session identifiers and session tickets with a single pre-shared key (PSK) mechanism for resumption.

throughput.def: How much data actually gets through per unit of time, as opposed to the link's rated capacity, which is a ceiling and not a promise.
throughput.context: The gap between the two is where the interesting questions live. A gigabit link carrying a single TCP (Transmission Control Protocol) session across a continent will not reach a gigabit, because the sender may only have one window's worth of unacknowledged data in flight per round trip. That is why the fix for a slow transfer is often a larger window or more parallel streams rather than a bigger link, and why buying capacity to solve a distance problem is the most common expensive mistake in the field.
throughput.depth:
Two meanings. In benchmarking the word is precise. RFC (Request for Comments) 1242 of July 1991 defines the throughput of a device as the maximum rate at which none of the offered frames are dropped, on the reasoning that even one lost frame can cause significant delays while higher-level protocols time out, and asks for measurements across an assortment of frame sizes. RFC 2544 (March 1999) turns that into a procedure: offer frames at a rate, count what comes out, and if anything is lost reduce the rate and rerun, a binary search whose final trials should each last at least 60 seconds, using the Ethernet frame sizes 64, 128, 256, 512, 1024, 1280 and 1518 bytes. RFC 6815 (November 2012) adds that these methods deliberately overload devices and belong in isolated test environments, not on production networks. In operations the word is looser: the data a path actually delivers per unit of time. RFC 2647 (August 1999) names the useful part goodput, the bits forwarded to the right destination minus any bits lost or retransmitted.

The ceiling the wire sets. Framing alone keeps throughput below the line rate. RFC 6349 counts 1538 bytes on the wire for every full-size Ethernet frame: 1500 of MTU (maximum transmission unit), 14 of Ethernet header, 4 of CRC (cyclic redundancy check), 12 of inter-frame gap, 7 of preamble and 1 of start-of-frame delimiter. That allows at most 8,127 frames per second at 100 Mbit/s, 81,274 at 1 Gbit/s and 812,743 at 10 Gbit/s, and with 40 bytes of IP (Internet Protocol) and TCP (Transmission Control Protocol) headers per packet the maximum TCP throughput on 100 Mbit/s Ethernet is 1460 bytes times 8 bits times 8,127 frames, 94.9 Mbit/s. Small packets do worse, which is why benchmark results are always quoted with a frame size, and jumbo frames do better where every hop supports them.

The ceiling the window sets. A TCP sender may only have a window of unacknowledged data in flight, the smaller of its congestion window and the receiver's advertised window, so RFC 6349 gives TCP throughput as the window in bytes times 8, divided by the round-trip time (RTT). To fill a path, the window must cover the bandwidth-delay product (BDP), the bottleneck bandwidth times the RTT: the RFC's table needs 125 KB for 1 Gbit/s at 1 ms, 375 KB for 10 Gbit/s at 0.3 ms, and about 138 KB for a 44.21 Mbit/s T3 at 25 ms, and it shows a 16 KB window on a 100 Mbit/s path with 5 ms of RTT reaching only 25.6 Mbit/s. The same formula explains the continental case: with 100 ms of RTT a 1 Gbit/s path holds 12.5 MB in flight, while a 64 KiB window delivers about 5.2 Mbit/s. RFC 7323 (September 2014) describes such long, fat networks: the TCP header's 16-bit window field caps the window at 64 KiB, and the Window Scale option, with a shift of at most 14, raises the ceiling to 1 GiB. Both ends must negotiate scaling and have socket buffers large enough to use it.

Loss, congestion and parallel streams. The congestion window is not a setting; RFC 6349 describes it as computed by slow start and congestion avoidance from the path's loss rate, so a path with even modest loss holds the window, and with it the throughput, below what the buffers would allow. That is why parallel streams help: each has its own window, and iperf3's documentation notes that running several with its -P option may give higher throughput than a single stream, while -w sets the socket buffer and, indirectly, the maximum window, which Linux effectively doubles. RFC 6349 turns the comparison into metrics, the TCP Transfer Time Ratio against the ideal, TCP Efficiency in terms of retransmitted bytes, and Buffer Delay, the extra RTT that queueing adds while the test runs. A transfer that is slow on a lightly loaded link is usually a window, a buffer or a loss problem, not a capacity problem.

Datasheet throughput. RFC 1242 observed that a single throughput figure lets vendors report one value that has proven useful in the marketplace, and datasheets still lead with one. The conditions behind it decide what it means. Fortinet, for example, publishes separate IPS (intrusion prevention system), NGFW (next-generation firewall) and Threat Protection throughput figures for each FortiGate, measured with its Enterprise Traffic Mix, a mix of applications and packet sizes close to NSS testing, with logging enabled, each adding inspection to the last: firewall plus IPS, then application control, then malware protection. One appliance therefore has several throughputs, and the one that matters for a design is the figure measured with the features that will be switched on and traffic that resembles the real mix, since a firewall that inspects or proxies traffic does not forward what it drops, which is why RFC 2647 measures goodput rather than gross forwarding.

Reading and testing it. Check units first, since link rates are quoted in bits per second and file transfers in bytes. Test with the protocol the application uses, because a UDP (User Datagram Protocol) stream measures the path and a single TCP stream measures the path plus its window and loss. Measure the RTT and work out the BDP before blaming the link. Keep RFC 2544-style load tests off production networks. When a long-distance transfer is slow, larger windows, tuned buffers or more parallel streams usually help more than a bigger link, because the limit was the distance and the window, not the capacity.

jitter.def: Variation in delay between packets: the reason a call sounds broken on a link whose average latency looks fine.
jitter.context: Real-time media cares about consistency more than speed, because a receiver has to play audio at a steady rate and can only absorb variation by buffering. A jitter buffer trades latency for smoothness, so the cure and the disease are measured in the same unit. This is why an average is the wrong statistic for anything interactive: the ninety-fifth percentile and the spread say what the user experiences, and the mean hides exactly the packets that ruined the call.
jitter.depth:
One word, several meanings. Request for Comments (RFC) 3393 opens by warning that jitter causes confusion because different groups use it differently. The older meaning belongs to transmission engineering: the variation of a signal against the clock it should follow. Recommendation G.810 of the Telecommunication Standardization Sector of the International Telecommunication Union (ITU-T) defines timing jitter as the short-term variations of the significant instants of a timing signal from their ideal positions, at frequencies of 10 Hz and above, and calls the slower variations wander. The meaning used in packet networks is the variation of delay against some reference, and the measurement documents prefer to call it delay variation; RFC 3393 avoids the word jitter wherever it can, and RFC 5481 notes that only the buffer that fights it keeps the name, the de-jitter buffer. A third use is unrelated to both: RFC 5148 uses jittering for deliberately randomizing the timing of protocol messages so that senders do not collide.

How it is measured. Every definition starts from one-way delay and takes a difference. RFC 5481 (March 2009) identifies the two formulations that industry actually implements. Inter-Packet Delay Variation (IPDV) compares each packet with the one before it, so the reference changes with every packet and the values swing positive and negative. Packet Delay Variation (PDV) compares every packet with a single reference, normally the packet with the minimum delay in the sample, so the values are all zero or positive and form a distribution whose upper end is what a receiver must absorb. The number most engineers actually see is neither of these exactly. The Real-time Transport Protocol (RTP), RFC 3550 of July 2003, has each receiver compute an interarrival jitter: for consecutive packets it takes D, the difference between their spacing on arrival and their spacing at the sender, and smooths its absolute value by moving a running estimate one sixteenth of the way towards each new sample: J(i) = J(i-1) + (|D(i-1,i)|-J(i-1))/16. The result is expressed in RTP timestamp units, which depend on the codec clock (8,000 per second for most audio codecs), and is sampled into every reception report. RFC 3550 is careful about what it is worth: a snapshot, not intended to be taken quantitatively, useful for comparing reports over time or between receivers.

Where it comes from. Cisco's voice troubleshooting note gives the plain definition, a variation in the delay of received packets, and the plain cause: a packet was queued or delayed somewhere along the path, usually by congestion, and on slow links by the time it takes to serialize a large packet ahead of it. RFC 3550 adds the diagnostic value: loss tracks persistent congestion, jitter tracks transient congestion, and a rising jitter figure may announce congestion before any packet is lost. Whether it matters depends on the application. The service class table of RFC 4594 (August 2006) marks telephony as very intolerant of loss, delay and jitter alike, and marks most data classes as jitter-tolerant, with the explanation that applications over the Transmission Control Protocol (TCP) buffer data in the endpoint, so a moderate variation in delay does not affect them.

The buffer that hides it. A receiver of real-time media cannot play packets as they arrive; it holds them briefly and releases them at the steady rate of the codec. RFC 5481 states the design problem exactly: the buffer must be big enough to accommodate the expected variation of delay, or packet loss will result, but if it is too large the spontaneity of conversation is lost. Ideally the packet with the minimum transit delay waits the longest and the slowest accommodated packet does not wait at all, so that minimum delay plus maximum buffer time equals maximum delay plus minimum buffer time; anything later than that is discarded. That is why the range of PDV, or its 99.9th percentile, is the statistic that sizes the buffer. Cisco gateways run this playout buffer in an adaptive mode by default, discard out-of-range packets, which are heard as dropouts, and expose it through the playout-delay command. Browsers expose the same machinery in the WebRTC statistics: jitter in seconds computed as in RFC 3550, the accumulated jitterBufferDelay divided by jitterBufferEmittedCount for the average time spent in the buffer, and packetsDiscarded for packets that arrived too late or too early to be played.

The numbers. ITU-T Recommendation Y.1541 sets the usual objectives for Internet Protocol (IP) networks. Its classes 0 and 1, the ones meant for interactive voice, bound delay variation at 50 milliseconds, defined as the 99.9th percentile of transfer delay minus the minimum, with a mean delay of at most 100 ms (class 0) or 400 ms (class 1) and a loss ratio of at most one in a thousand, each evaluated over one minute. ITU-T Recommendation G.114 supplies the delay budget that the buffer eats into: most applications are not significantly affected while one-way delay stays below 150 ms, and 400 ms is the planning limit. Vendors set their own thresholds on top. In FortiGate's software-defined wide area network (SD-WAN) health checks the default jitter threshold is 5 ms, calculated over the last 30 probes. The standards therefore go further than the ninety-fifth percentile: what they bound is the tail, because the tail is what the buffer has to cover.

Keeping it low. Jitter is created in queues, so it is controlled by queueing policy, not by bandwidth alone. The Expedited Forwarding per-hop behaviour of Differentiated Services (RFC 3246, March 2002) exists as a building block for low delay, low jitter and low loss services, and RFC 4594 assigns it to telephony. The broadcast video class shows the other strategy, a deep buffer in place of a strict queue: RFC 4594 assumes a de-jitter buffer of two to eight video frames, from 66 to several hundred milliseconds, which is acceptable only because nobody is talking back.

Measuring and reproducing it. In Wireshark, the RTP Stream Analysis under the Telephony menu applies the RFC 3550 formula to a captured stream and graphs it, provided the clock rate of the payload type is known. On a FortiGate, the Performance SLAs tab under SD-WAN (SLA, service level agreement) lists latency, jitter and packet loss for each health check, measured by active probes or passively from session information. On a Cisco voice gateway, show voice call prints the delay and error statistics of the signal processor for a port. To reproduce a complaint in the laboratory, the Linux netem queue discipline accepts a jitter value after the delay: tc qdisc add dev eth0 root netem delay 100ms 10ms delays each packet by 100 ms plus or minus 10 ms, and distribution normal changes the shape.

Common misreadings. Jitter is not latency: a path with a constant 200 ms delay has no jitter at all, and a path averaging 20 ms can have a great deal. The RTP interarrival figure is a smoothed average, so it cannot be compared with a percentile of PDV or with a contractual 50 ms objective. A figure taken from one direction says nothing about the other, since the definitions are one-way. And the timing jitter of a clock or a line signal, measured in fractions of a bit period, is a different quantity that merely shares the name.

packet-loss.def: Packets that never arrive - discarded by a full queue, corrupted in transit, or dropped by policy.
packet-loss.context: Small percentages do disproportionate damage, because loss is the signal congestion control listens to: one per cent loss can halve a transfer's throughput, since the sender treats it as instruction to slow down. That also means loss is not always a fault to eliminate - a network that never drops is usually one that buffers instead, and the resulting delay is worse for interactive traffic than the drops would have been.

duplex.def: Whether a link can carry traffic in both directions at once (full duplex) or must take turns (half duplex).
duplex.context: Modern switched links are full duplex and the setting is rarely thought about, until there is a mismatch: one end fixed at full duplex and the other, left to negotiate alone, falling back to half. The result is the most misleading fault in networking. The link is up, small pings succeed, and throughput collapses under load with rising errors, because one side transmits whenever it likes while the other treats every overlap as a collision, backs off and retransmits. Cisco's troubleshooting notes place the late collisions and the frame check sequence (FCS) errors on the half-duplex side and the runts on the full-duplex side. It survives as a diagnostic reflex precisely because it looks like anything except what it is. The rule that prevents it is about both ends: auto-negotiation on both, or the same fixed speed and duplex on both, never one of each.
duplex.depth:
The word itself. The telecommunications glossary of the Alliance for Telecommunications Industry Solutions (ATIS) defines duplex operation as transmission that is possible simultaneously in both directions of a channel, with full-duplex and two-way simultaneous operation as synonyms; half-duplex operation as communication in either direction but in only one direction at a time, also called two-way alternate; and simplex operation as transmission in one preassigned direction only. A half-duplex link is therefore still a two-way link; what it lacks is simultaneity. The glossary adds that in radio, duplex generally needs two frequencies, which is why a Wi-Fi cell is half duplex: the stations of the 802.11 standard of the Institute of Electrical and Electronics Engineers (IEEE) share one channel and contend for it with carrier sense multiple access with collision avoidance (CSMA/CA). In Ethernet the word has a narrower, mechanical meaning. A half-duplex port runs carrier sense multiple access with collision detection (CSMA/CD): it listens before sending and treats simultaneous reception as a collision. A full-duplex port does neither.

How Ethernet got there. Ethernet began half duplex by necessity: on a shared medium only one station could transmit, and collision detection settled who went next. In that world, as a Cisco note puts it, collisions are not bad, they are essential to correct operation; the abnormal event is the late collision, one detected after the station has sent the 512th bit of its frame. Hubs kept every port in one collision domain. Switches gave each link exactly two ends, and with two ends and separate transmit and receive paths there is nothing to collide with. IEEE Std 802.3x-1997, approved on 20 March 1997 and published on 18 November 1997, made that official: it added 'an additional, full duplex mode of operation on a speed-independent basis', changed the media access control (MAC) and the 10BASE-T, 10BASE-FL and 100BASE-T physical layers to support it, and added pause-based flow control. On a full-duplex link collision detection is simply switched off.

How the two ends agree. On twisted pair the choice is made by auto-negotiation, defined in Clause 28 of the Fast Ethernet supplement IEEE Std 802.3u (approved on 14 June 1995) and described by Cisco as an optional function of that standard. Each end sends bursts of Fast Link Pulses every 16 milliseconds, give or take 8, that spell out a 16-bit link code word with one bit for each ability: 10BASE-T, 10BASE-T full duplex, 100BASE-TX, 100BASE-TX full duplex and 100BASE-T4. Both ends then apply the same priority list and pick the highest entry they share: 100BASE-TX full duplex, 100BASE-T4, 100BASE-TX, 10BASE-T full duplex, 10BASE-T. At any given speed, full duplex outranks half.

Where the mismatch comes from. Negotiation needs two talkers. A port that hears no Fast Link Pulses falls back on parallel detection, which recognizes the speed from the signal itself, and the rule, in the words of the University of New Hampshire InterOperability Laboratory, is that a device can never parallel detect to a full duplex link. So a negotiating port facing a port fixed at 100 Mb/s full duplex settles on 100 Mb/s half duplex; Cisco's table of combinations labels that row Duplex Mismatch. Nothing brings the link down. The full-duplex end transmits whenever it has a frame; the half-duplex end, already sending, sees a collision, often after the 512-bit window, aborts and backs off. Cisco's signature for it is late collisions and a rapid increase of frame check sequence (FCS) and alignment errors on the half-duplex side and runts on the full-duplex port, with the user-visible symptoms being slow performance, intermittent connectivity and data link errors. Light traffic rarely overlaps, which is why a ping passes and a file transfer crawls. A speed mismatch is different and kinder: the link does not come up at all.

Gigabit and beyond. For 1000BASE-T negotiation is not optional. The standard says that all 1000BASE-T physical layer devices (PHYs) shall support auto-negotiation, and an IEEE interpretation confirms that selecting 1000BASE-T still requires it, because the same exchange decides which end is the timing master; the way to pin a port is to keep negotiating and advertise only 1000BASE-T. Half-duplex Gigabit Ethernet exists on paper: IEEE 802.3z, approved in July 1998, supports it, and Cisco notes that its devices support only full duplex. From 10 Gb/s the question was closed in the objectives. The 10 Gigabit Ethernet task force wrote 'Support full-duplex operation only' in 2001, and the same line appears in the objectives for 10GBASE-T (September 2003) and for 2.5GBASE-T and 5GBASE-T (March 2015). Duplex is thus a property of 10, 100 and 1000 Mb/s copper links and of the auto-negotiation that sets them, which is where it still goes wrong. Half duplex did return once, deliberately: IEEE Std 802.3cg-2019, the 10 Mb/s single-pair Ethernet for automotive and industrial use, defines a short-reach PHY that runs half duplex point to point over 15 metres and, optionally, half-duplex multidrop with at least eight nodes on a 25-metre mixing segment.

On real equipment. On Linux, ethtool with the device name prints the current settings of the interface, and ethtool -s sets speed, duplex half or full and autoneg on or off; the manual says autonegotiation is on by default and should be disabled only if really necessary. Cisco switches negotiate by default, and Cisco's advice is to leave it on for devices that comply with 802.3u, with one rule above all: both sides on, or both sides off. On F5 BIG-IP the media option of net interface in the Traffic Management Shell (tmsh) takes values such as auto, 100baseTX-full and 100baseTX-half. On a FortiGate, set speed under config system interface takes auto (the default), 10half, 10full, 100half, 100full and 1000full, and Fortinet's own tip is that if the FortiGate is set to 100full the device at the other end should be too. On ExtremeXOS the command is configure ports with auto off, a speed and duplex half or full; the guide notes that 1000 Mb/s cannot be set with negotiation off, that 10 and 40 Gb/s ports always run full duplex, and that some switch models have no half-duplex support at all, so that with a partner that does not negotiate they fail to link up instead of limping.

What else depends on it. Duplex leaks into other features. Pause-based flow control arrived in the same supplement as full duplex, 802.3x; FortiSwitch documents that priority-based flow control does not support half-duplex speeds, and ExtremeXOS ties flow control on Gigabit ports to auto-negotiation. Spanning tree reads duplex as a hint about topology: BIG-IP's default link type assumes that full-duplex links are point-to-point and half-duplex links are shared, so a port that has fallen to half duplex also loses the fast point-to-point optimizations. And any collision counter that moves on a port believed to be full duplex is itself the diagnosis: Cisco states that collisions must not be seen on interfaces configured as full duplex.

checksum.def: A small value computed from data so a receiver can notice accidental corruption: detection, not correction, and not protection.
checksum.context: It defends against noise, not against people: an attacker who changes the data simply recomputes the checksum. That is the distinction from a signature or a message authentication code, and confusing them is a real design error rather than a pedantic one. Operationally the surprise is offload: network cards compute checksums in hardware, so a capture taken on the sending host routinely shows them as invalid, which is correct behaviour that has cost many hours of investigation.
checksum.depth:
What it is, exactly. The Internet Security Glossary, Request for Comments (RFC) 4949 of August 2007, defines a checksum as a value computed by a function of a data object's contents and stored or sent with it, so that whoever uses the data later can recompute it and compare; the NIST (National Institute of Standards and Technology) glossary repeats the definition. An error detection code, in the same glossary, detects accidental changes but does not correct them. The limit is stated just as plainly: active wiretapping that changes the data can change the checksum to match, so against an attacker the function must be a cryptographic hash and its result must itself be protected, by a digital signature or a keyed hash such as an HMAC (hash-based message authentication code). Even against noise the protection is statistical; the Wireshark manual reminds its readers that common checksum algorithms cannot guarantee 100 per cent detection.

The Internet checksum. IP (Internet Protocol), TCP (Transmission Control Protocol) and UDP (User Datagram Protocol) share one algorithm, written up by R. Braden, D. Borman and C. Partridge in RFC 1071 (September 1988). Adjacent octets are paired into 16-bit integers and added in one's complement arithmetic, any carry out of the top bit wrapping around into the bottom; the sender clears the field, sums, and stores the complement of the sum; the receiver sums everything including the field and expects all ones, negative zero in one's complement. The design is chosen for speed: the sum can be taken in any order, in either byte order and in parallel on wider words, which mattered because, as the RFC says, the checksum could become a limiting factor on TCP performance.

Where it sits. The IPv4 header checksum of RFC 791 (September 1981) covers the header only and is recomputed and verified at every hop, because fields such as the time to live (TTL) change in transit; the RFC called it provisional and said it might be replaced by a cyclic redundancy check (CRC), which never happened. TCP, now RFC 9293 (August 2022), covers header and data plus a pseudo-header of the addresses, protocol and length, 96 bits for IPv4 and 320 for IPv6, so that a segment delivered to the wrong host fails; its checksum is never optional. UDP, RFC 768 of 28 August 1980, uses the same procedure but lets a sender put zero in the field to mean no checksum, sending a computed zero as all ones instead. IPv6, RFC 8200 of July 2017, dropped the header checksum altogether and in exchange made the UDP checksum mandatory: a zero result is sent as 0xFFFF and receivers discard zero checksums, except in the zero-checksum mode allowed for tunnels; ICMPv6 also began covering the pseudo-header, with Next Header 58, which the Internet Control Message Protocol (ICMP) for IPv4 never did.

Updating it on the fly. Routers decrementing TTL, and network address translation (NAT) rewriting addresses that the TCP and UDP pseudo-headers include, must fix checksums without resumming the whole packet. RFC 1071 gave the incremental formula, RFC 1141 refined it, and RFC 1624 (May 1994) corrected that refinement, which produced 0xFFFF where 0x0000 was required at the boundary between positive and negative zero; its corrected form is HC' = ~(~HC + ~m + m'), with HC the old checksum, m the old field value and m' the new one.

Below IP, a CRC. Ethernet ends every frame with a Frame Check Sequence (FCS), a 32-bit CRC computed by the sending hardware and checked by the receiving hardware, which discards a bad frame before any capture tool sees it; the 64-byte minimum frame size includes those 4 bytes. A CRC protects one link at a time: the frame is checked and rebuilt at each hop, so corruption inside a router or a host's memory sails through with a fresh, valid CRC.

How well it works in practice. Jonathan Stone and Craig Partridge measured it for SIGCOMM 2000 in "When the CRC and TCP Checksum Disagree": in their traces 1 in 30,000 packets failed the TCP checksum even on links whose CRC should have missed only 1 in 4 billion errors; they found nearly 100 distinct error patterns, at every level of the network; and they estimated that the TCP checksum fails to detect an error in roughly 1 in 200 million packets. That is the case for end-to-end integrity above TCP, such as the authenticated encryption of Transport Layer Security (TLS) or a hash checked after a file transfer.

The offload trap. Modern drivers often hand the packet to the network card with the checksum field empty, zero or garbage, and let the hardware fill it in. A capture taken on the sending host sees the packet before that, so Wireshark reports the checksum as invalid even though the packet leaves correct; the effect applies only to packets the capture host itself sends, and received packets should be right. Linux and Windows go further with partial checksums, placing only the pseudo-header's contribution in the field and letting the hardware add the payload. Because an invalid checksum also stops Wireshark from reassembling a stream, recent releases disable checksum validation by default; the alternatives are to turn validation off per protocol or turn offload off in the driver.

Numbers worth remembering: 16-bit one's complement sums for IPv4, TCP and UDP; a 96-bit IPv4 and a 320-bit IPv6 pseudo-header; 0xFFFF in place of a computed zero; a 4-byte CRC-32 FCS on Ethernet; and, from the 2000 study, roughly 1 in 200 million packets with an error the TCP checksum misses.

fragmentation.def: Splitting an IP (Internet Protocol) datagram into smaller pieces, each carrying its own IP header, because it is larger than the maximum transmission unit (MTU) of a link on its path; the pieces are reassembled only at the destination.
fragmentation.context: It is the classic source of faults that pass every simple test: small packets work, the connection establishes, and transfers hang once real data starts. That happens when the message asking the sender to reduce its size is filtered, which is common because the message is ICMP (Internet Control Message Protocol) and somebody blocked ICMP as a precaution. Tunnels make it routine by adding headers to packets already sized for the original path, which is why the first question about any VPN (virtual private network) complaint is the effective maximum size.
fragmentation.depth:
What it is, and what it is not. Fragmentation is the Internet Protocol's (IP's) way of getting a datagram across a link whose maximum transmission unit (MTU) is smaller than the datagram: the datagram is cut into fragments, each a complete IP packet with its own header, and they are put back together only by the destination. It is not TCP (Transmission Control Protocol) segmentation, where the sender sizes its segments by the maximum segment size (MSS) so that IP never has to cut anything, and it is not link-layer fragmentation inside one network, which RFC (Request for Comments) 791 calls network-dependent and leaves out of scope. The rule that routers split and only the destination reassembles goes back to Vint Cerf and Bob Kahn's 1974 paper, which rejected reassembly in gateways because of buffering problems, potential deadlocks and the need for every fragment to pass through the same gateway.

The IPv4 fields. RFC 791 (September 1981) gives every IPv4 header the machinery. Total Length allows datagrams of up to 65,535 octets. Identification, 16 bits, is set by the sender so that the fragments of one datagram can be told apart from those of another, and reassembly matches fragments on source, destination, protocol and identification together. Flags holds a reserved bit, DF (Don't Fragment) and MF (More Fragments). Fragment Offset, 13 bits, says where the fragment's data belongs, in units of 8 octets, which is why every fragment except the last carries a multiple of 8 data octets; 8,192 offsets of 8 octets cover 65,536 octets. Two floors still matter: every IP module must be able to forward a datagram of 68 octets without further fragmentation (a header of up to 60 octets plus the minimum fragment of 8), and every destination must accept a datagram of 576 octets, whole or in fragments. Some options are copied into every fragment, others stay with the first. A worked example: a 4,000-octet datagram (20 octets of header and 3,980 of data) crossing a 1,500-octet link becomes three fragments carrying 1,480 data octets at offset 0, 1,480 at offset 185 and 1,020 at offset 370, the first two with MF set, so 1,500, 1,500 and 1,040 octets on the wire. RFC 791 suggested a reassembly timer starting at 15 seconds that could grow to the maximum TTL (time to live) of about 4.25 minutes; Linux exposes the equivalent as ipfrag_time, with ipfrag_high_thresh capping the memory reassembly may use.

IPv6 changed the rules. Under RFC 8200 (July 2017, Internet Standard STD 86) only the source node may fragment; routers never do. A source that must send a packet larger than the path MTU adds a Fragment header, identified by Next Header value 44, holding a 13-bit offset in 8-octet units, an M (more fragments) flag and a 32-bit Identification that must differ from that of any other fragmented packet sent recently between the same two addresses. Reassembly is abandoned if it is not complete within 60 seconds of the first fragment, and a datagram with overlapping fragments is discarded whole, the rule RFC 5722 introduced in December 2009. Every IPv6 link must carry at least 1,280 octets, and a router that cannot forward a packet sends ICMPv6 (Internet Control Message Protocol for IPv6) Packet Too Big to the source instead. RFC 8200 also stopped the creation of atomic fragments, Fragment headers on packets that are not actually fragmented, after RFC 8021 (January 2017) showed them harmful.

Path MTU discovery, and why it fails. RFC 1191 (November 1990) replaced the old practice of sending no more than 576 octets, or the first-hop MTU, to any off-net destination. The host sets DF on every datagram; a router that cannot forward one without fragmenting drops it and returns ICMP Destination Unreachable, type 3 code 4, 'fragmentation needed and DF set', with the next-hop MTU in a field RFC 1191 defined for it; the host lowers its estimate, and may probe upwards no sooner than 5 minutes after such a message (10 is recommended). RFC 8201 (July 2017, STD 87) does the same for IPv6 with Packet Too Big. The weakness is the dependence on ICMP. RFC 8900 lists transient causes of lost Packet Too Big messages (congestion, corruption, routing loops and rate limiting, which RFC 4443 recommends strictly for ICMPv6) and persistent ones, chief among them security policies that drop the inbound ICMP because no session matches it. The sender keeps retransmitting full-size packets with DF set and never learns why they vanish: the handshake completes, small requests work, the first large response hangs. On Linux the related knobs are ip_no_pmtu_disc and min_pmtu, whose default of 552 is the floor of any cached path MTU.

Probing instead of trusting ICMP. Packetization Layer Path MTU Discovery (PLPMTUD), RFC 4821 (March 2007) for TCP, finds the path MTU with real probe packets and treats their loss as the signal, so it works where ICMP is filtered; RFC 8899 (September 2020) extends it to datagram transports as Datagram PLPMTUD (DPLPMTUD) and names the two failures it handles, the packet black hole (packets of a size the path once carried silently dropped) and the ICMP black hole (Packet Too Big messages that never arrive). Linux turns it on with tcp_mtu_probing: 0 disables it, 1 enables it only when an ICMP black hole is detected, and 2 enables it always, starting from tcp_base_mss and reprobing every 10 minutes as RFC 4821 suggests. Testing by hand is the same idea: ping -M do -s 1472 on Linux, or ping -f -l 1472 on Windows, sends an unfragmentable 1,500-octet IPv4 packet (1,472 octets of data, 8 of ICMP header and 20 of IP header), and stepping the size down until replies return measures the path.
