Fragmentation considered fragile. RFC 8900, published in September 2020 as Best Current Practice (BCP) 230, collects the reasons. NAT (network address translation) devices, including carrier-grade NAT, must virtually reassemble fragments to translate them. Stateless firewalls see the ports only in the first fragment, so they must either accept all later fragments, admitting some attacks, or block them, breaking legitimate traffic. ECMP (equal-cost multipath) and link aggregation hash on five fields when a transport header is present and on three when it is not, so fragments of one flow can take different links. And at high rates the 16-bit IPv4 Identification wraps: RFC 4963 (July 2007) works out that strict conformance would cap a host sending 1,500-octet packets with a 30-second packet lifetime at about 26 Mbps, while filling 1 Gbps takes 65,536 packets in under a second, so fragments of different datagrams are mis-associated and the TCP and UDP (User Datagram Protocol) checksums are too weak to catch every corrupted result; IPv6's 32-bit Identification makes this rarer. Its recommendations are blunt: developers SHOULD NOT build new protocols that rely on IP fragmentation; operators MUST make path MTU discovery work, MUST NOT filter ICMPv6 Packet Too Big messages unless they are known to be forged, and SHOULD NOT filter fragments from or to DNS (Domain Name System) servers.

The attacks. RFC 1858 (October 1995) describes the tiny fragment attack: a first fragment carrying only 8 data octets holds the TCP ports but pushes the TCP flags into the second fragment, so a filter that drops connection requests by testing the SYN (synchronize) and ACK (acknowledgement) flags never sees them. Overlaps are the other classic: CERT Advisory CA-97.28 of 16 December 1997 warned that some TCP/IP reassembly code did not handle overlapping fragments properly, that the widely available Teardrop tool exploited it, that any remote user could crash a vulnerable machine, and that there was no workaround short of vendor patches; the CVE (Common Vulnerabilities and Exposures) list records it as CVE-1999-0015. The Ping o' Death, CVE-1999-0128, was an oversized ICMP echo, and the field arithmetic shows how one can exist: a final fragment at the largest offset, 8,191 units of 8 octets or 65,528 octets, plus its data reassembles to more than the 65,535 octets a datagram may hold. RFC 8900 adds resource exhaustion, attacks on predictable identification values (RFC 7739) and evasion of intrusion detection systems.

DNS and tunnels. DNS over UDP is the largest remaining user of fragmentation, because EDNS(0) (Extension Mechanisms for DNS) lets clients accept large responses and DNSSEC (DNS Security Extensions) signatures make them large. RFC 9715 (January 2025) recommends that responders fit their answers within the smallest of the requestor's offered size, the interface MTU, the network MTU and 1,400 octets, setting the truncation bit so the client retries over TCP when an answer does not fit, and that requestors drop fragmented responses without reassembling them, to avoid cache poisoning; DNS Flag Day 2020 had proposed 1,232 octets, the IPv6 minimum MTU of 1,280 less 48 octets of IPv6 and UDP headers. Tunnels are the everyday case: every encapsulation adds headers to packets already sized for the original path, RFC 8900 itself notes that IPsec tunnel mode and IP-in-IP encapsulation may have no alternative to fragmentation, and the practical remedies are to clamp the TCP MSS at the tunnel, keep ICMP Packet Too Big flowing, and set tunnel MTUs deliberately rather than by default.

container.def: A process, or a small group of processes, isolated by kernel features rather than by a separate operating system, sharing the host's kernel with everything else running on it; in practice, an application packaged with its dependencies as an image and run that way.
container.context: The shared kernel is the whole trade. It makes containers fast to start and cheap to run, and it means the isolation boundary is a set of kernel features rather than a hardware one, so a kernel vulnerability is a boundary vulnerability. That is why the interesting security questions are about what the container may ask the kernel to do (capabilities, system call filtering, whether it runs as root) rather than about the image alone, and why a compromised container on a shared host is a different conversation from a compromised virtual machine.
container.depth:
What the word covers. The National Institute of Standards and Technology (NIST) defines a container as a method for packaging and securely running an application within an application virtualization environment. Its Special Publication (SP) 800-190, the Application Container Security Guide of September 2017 by Murugiah Souppaya, John Morello and Karen Scarfone, places it in a lineage. Hardware virtualization gives each virtual machine (VM) its own virtual hardware and a complete guest operating system (OS); OS virtualization runs several virtualized OSs above one real kernel, as Solaris Zones and FreeBSD jails did from the early 2000s and Linux Containers (LXC) brought to Linux in 2008; application containers, the ones meant today, also share one kernel but normally run a single application each, an analogy to shipping containers that group disparate contents in a standard box. Because the kernel is shared, containers are OS-family specific: a Linux host runs Linux containers, and Windows has had its own since Windows Server 2016.

What the kernel actually does. A container is not a kernel object; it is an ordinary process placed inside several isolation mechanisms at once. Linux namespaces give it a private view of one kind of resource each, and the namespaces(7) manual lists eight: cgroup (the cgroup root directory), IPC (System V interprocess communication and Portable Operating System Interface (POSIX) message queues), network (devices, stacks and ports), mount (mount points), PID (process IDs), time (boot and monotonic clocks), user (user and group IDs) and UTS (host name and domain name). Creating most of them requires the CAP_SYS_ADMIN capability; user namespaces are the exception, creatable without privilege since Linux 3.8. Control groups (cgroups) organize processes into hierarchies whose use of memory, central processing unit (CPU) time and other resources can be limited and monitored; they first shipped in Linux 2.6.24, and the redesigned version 2 became official in Linux 4.5. On top of these, runtimes trim what root inside the container can do. Docker starts containers with a restricted set of capabilities, the kernel's split of root into fine-grained privileges (a web server that only needs to bind a port below 1024 gets net_bind_service and nothing else), and applies a default seccomp profile that works as an allowlist and blocks around 44 of more than 300 system calls.

Images and standards. Docker made the model popular: Solomon Hykes of dotCloud first showed it in a lightning talk at PyCon US on 15 March 2013. The Open Container Initiative (OCI), launched on 22 June 2015 by Docker, CoreOS and others under the Linux Foundation, standardized it in three specifications: the runtime specification (how to run an unpacked filesystem bundle), the image specification (a manifest, filesystem layers and a configuration holding the command, arguments and environment) and the distribution specification (how registries serve images). The runtime that does the low-level work in most stacks is runc, which its maintainers describe as the runtime underneath Docker, CRI-O, containerd and Kubernetes. SP 800-190 describes the operating model that came with it: containers are treated as immutable, destroyed and replaced rather than patched in place, and data lives outside them in databases or persistent volumes, which is what lets organizations move from quarterly releases to daily ones.

Orchestration. Kubernetes does not run containers directly; its smallest deployable unit is the Pod, one or more containers with shared storage and network, always co-located and co-scheduled, an application-specific logical host. Since version 1.24 (3 May 2022) the kubelet no longer contains dockershim, deprecated in 1.20, so clusters use containerd, CRI-O, or the separate cri-dockerd adapter to keep Docker Engine. Traffic reaches Pods through ingress controllers; NGINX Ingress Controller, for example, configures NGINX through the Kubernetes application programming interface (API) and adds VirtualServer and TransportServer resources for content-based routing, traffic splitting and passthrough of Transmission Control Protocol (TCP), User Datagram Protocol (UDP) and Transport Layer Security (TLS) traffic.

The boundary, honestly assessed. SP 800-190 is plain about the cost of the shared kernel: although containers provide strong software-level isolation, sharing a kernel invariably gives a larger inter-object attack surface than hypervisors do, even on minimal container-specific host OSs, so the isolation of container runtimes is not as high as that of hypervisors. Its recommendations follow: put only containers with the same purpose, sensitivity and threat posture on one host kernel; prefer container-specific host OSs, often with read-only file systems; use vulnerability management built for images rather than for long-lived servers; and anchor host integrity in hardware such as a Trusted Platform Module (TPM). Docker's own documentation adds the operational corollary: the daemon runs as root unless rootless mode is used, and anyone allowed to control it can start a container with the host's root directory mounted and change the host file system without restriction, so control of the daemon is control of the host.

Escapes. Two runc vulnerabilities, each with a Common Vulnerabilities and Exposures (CVE) identifier, show what crossing the boundary looks like. CVE-2019-5736, disclosed by runc maintainer Aleksa Sarai on 12 February 2019 and found by Adam Iwaniuk and Borys Popławski, let a malicious container overwrite the host's runc binary and gain root on the host, needing only that some command run as root inside a container built from an attacker's image, or a docker exec into a container the attacker could write to; default AppArmor did not stop it, while user namespaces that do not map host root did. CVE-2024-21626, announced publicly on 1 February 2024, used a leaked file descriptor to allow full container breakouts, scored 8.6, and was fixed in runc 1.1.12. Both reward the same habits: run containers as non-root, use user namespaces, and patch the runtime as seriously as the kernel.

Neighbours. A virtual machine isolates with a hypervisor and its own kernel; a container shares the kernel; a Pod is Kubernetes' grouping of containers; a sidecar is a helper container in the same Pod; an image is the packaged filesystem and configuration a container is started from; and running containers inside VMs, which SP 800-190 depicts as a common deployment, combines the two boundaries.

hypervisor.def: The software layer, also called a virtual machine monitor (VMM), that presents virtual hardware to several guest operating systems on one physical machine, shares out its processors, memory and devices among them, and keeps them apart.
hypervisor.context: It is the strongest common isolation boundary in ordinary infrastructure, because each guest has its own kernel and the hypervisor mediates the hardware, which is why multi-tenant cloud is built on it rather than on containers alone. The cost is that it is also the most privileged software present: whatever compromises it owns every guest at once, and the guests may have no reliable way to notice. Side channels through shared processor resources are the awkward part, because they cross a boundary the design assumed was solid.
hypervisor.depth:
The United States National Institute of Standards and Technology (NIST) describes the hypervisor by analogy in Special Publication (SP) 800-125A Revision 1, Security Recommendations for Server-based Hypervisor Platforms (June 2018): just as an operating system isolates the processes running on a server, the hypervisor isolates the virtual machines (VMs) running on it, and just as an operating system mediates access to devices, the hypervisor mediates access to physical resources across VMs. Processor and memory it virtualizes itself, with or without hardware assistance; devices it handles through software modules that run either in its own kernel or in dedicated device-driver VMs. The word is a variant of supervisor, the old term for an operating system kernel, so a hypervisor is the supervisor of supervisors; IBM coined it around 1970 for software that ran OS/360 and the 7090 emulator at the same time on a System/360 Model 65. The terms are not quite interchangeable: NIST calls virtual machine monitors (VMMs) combined with operating-system services such as scheduling the hypervisor, and in Linux usage the Kernel-based Virtual Machine (KVM) is the hypervisor while QEMU or Cloud Hypervisor is the VMM that uses it. The longer history, from IBM's CP-40 to the Popek and Goldberg requirements and the x86 extensions, is the history of the virtual machine as a whole.

The usual classification comes from Robert P. Goldberg's 1973 thesis, Architectural Principles for Virtual Computer Systems. A Type 1, native or bare-metal hypervisor runs directly on the hardware: Microsoft Hyper-V, Xen and VMware ESXi are the common examples. A Type 2, or hosted, hypervisor runs as a program on a conventional operating system: VirtualBox and VMware Workstation. The line has blurred. KVM is a loadable kernel module, kvm.ko, plus a processor-specific kvm-intel.ko or kvm-amd.ko, that turns Linux itself into the hypervisor, and bhyve does the same for FreeBSD. Hyper-V, though bare-metal, needs at least one root partition running Windows: the virtualization management stack lives there with direct access to the hardware, creates the child partitions that hold the guests through the hypercall application programming interface, and serves their virtual devices through Virtualization Service Providers reached over the VMBus. The distinction that matters for security is NIST's trust model: everything inside a VM is untrusted, the hypervisor kernel and the hardware are trusted, and for a Type 2 hypervisor the whole host operating system is trusted too, which makes its trusted computing base far larger.

SP 800-125A breaks the job into five baseline functions, a useful checklist for any platform. HY-BF1, VM process isolation, schedules the VMs and manages their processor and memory state. HY-BF2, device mediation and access control, makes devices available by emulation, paravirtualization, passthrough or self-virtualizing hardware and controls which VM may use which device. HY-BF3, direct execution of commands from guests, is the hypercall interface of paravirtualized designs. HY-BF4, VM lifecycle management, covers images, start, pause and stop, migration, snapshots and monitoring, and is usually a management daemon running unprivileged on top of the kernel. HY-BF5, management of the platform, covers configuration and patching, including the configuration of the virtual network inside the hypervisor. That last item is the network engineer's point of contact: the first switch a VM's traffic crosses is a software switch inside the hypervisor, and the publication's recommendations include per-VM limits on network and input/output bandwidth (HY-SR-8) so that one guest's denial of service stays its own.

Modern hypervisors lean on the processor. NIST lists the security gains of hardware-assisted virtualization: the extensions provide a host or root mode and a guest or non-root mode, the hypervisor runs in the more privileged host mode, and so exploit code in a guest operating system cannot subvert the hypervisor's controls by privilege alone; second-level page tables such as Intel's Extended Page Tables (EPT) can stop code executing from pages reserved for data; and an IOMMU (input-output memory management unit) remaps DMA (direct memory access) so that a device assigned to one VM cannot write into another's memory. Microsoft makes second-level address translation (SLAT) a requirement for Hyper-V from Windows Server 2016 and uses the IOMMU for the same remapping. Recommendation HY-SR-1 asks that the hypervisor be launched on hardware with measured launch and an attestation process, giving a chain of trust from the hardware through the kernel, its modules and drivers to the management applications; HY-SR-13 asks that live migration be authenticated and carried over a secure connection on a dedicated network segment; and HY-SR-20 asks for the management interface on a dedicated physical NIC (network interface card) or, failing that, a dedicated segment behind a firewall that admits only designated subnets.

The trust placed in the hypervisor is exactly what attackers aim at. A VM escape crosses from guest to host, and exposure is not theoretical: on 4 March 2025 VMware published CVE-2025-22224 in the CVE (Common Vulnerabilities and Exposures) list, a time-of-check to time-of-use race in ESXi and Workstation that let a local administrator inside a VM execute code as the VMX process, the host process that runs that virtual machine, rated 9.3 under CVSS (Common Vulnerability Scoring System) 3.1, together with CVE-2025-22225, an arbitrary kernel write from the VMX process leading to an escape of the sandbox; the United States Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency (CISA) added both to its catalogue of known exploited vulnerabilities the same day. The opposite direction is a hypervisor slipped underneath a running system. Joanna Rutkowska demonstrated Blue Pill at Black Hat on 3 August 2006: a thin hypervisor started under a running Windows Vista, first using AMD-V and later Intel VT-x, that could intercept interrupts, data requests and even the system time, following the virtual-machine-based rootkit concept published at the IEEE (Institute of Electrical and Electronics Engineers) Symposium on Security and Privacy in May 2006. Her claim that it was 100 per cent undetectable was disputed, AMD among the critics, but the point stands that software beneath the kernel controls what the kernel can see.

Shared hardware leaks across the boundary even when the hypervisor is correct. The L1 Terminal Fault (L1TF) family of 2018 is the instructive case for virtualization, tracked for its virtualization aspects as CVE-2018-3646: hyperthreads on affected Intel processors share the L1 data cache, so a malicious guest on one hyperthread can read data that the sibling hyperthread brought into that cache, whether it belongs to the host operating system, host user space or another guest. The Linux kernel documentation lists the defences and their price: flushing the L1 data cache conditionally or unconditionally on entry to a guest, confining guests to dedicated cores, or disabling simultaneous multithreading (SMT) altogether with the nosmt or nosmt=force boot options, and it notes that the full mitigations are not enabled by default because of their performance cost. The Spectre and Meltdown disclosures of the same year belong to the same lesson, and the practical rule for multi-tenant hosts is to decide deliberately whether mutually untrusted guests may share a physical core.

Confidential computing changes the trust model by taking the hypervisor out of it. AMD's Secure Encrypted Virtualization (SEV) encrypts a guest's private memory with a guest-specific key so that a decrypted copy exists only inside the VM, and its Secure Nested Paging extension (SEV-SNP) adds integrity protections; Intel's Trust Domain Extensions (TDX) protect confidential guests from the host and from physical attacks by isolating the guest's register state and encrypting its memory, with a processor-attested TDX module running in a new Secure Arbitration Mode between host and guest. In NIST's 2018 model the hypervisor kernel is trusted; in these designs the cloud operator's hypervisor still schedules the guest but is no longer trusted to read it.

For operations the conclusion is that the hypervisor is infrastructure of the highest privilege and deserves to be run like it. Its management plane belongs on its own network, its patches belong in the same urgent class as the most exposed perimeter device, and its configuration drift is everyone's problem, since every virtual appliance on the host (a BIG-IP Virtual Edition, a FortiGate-VM, a virtual router) inherits its availability, its isolation and its flaws.

logging.def: Logging is recording what happened, as timestamped entries about events in systems and networks, so that it can be answered for later: by an operator during an incident, or by an investigator afterwards.
logging.context: The two audiences want different things and the conflict is rarely resolved deliberately. Operations wants recent, verbose, searchable and cheap; investigation wants complete, tamper-evident and kept for a long time. Estates that optimize only for the first discover during an incident that the window closed before the question was asked. The second recurring failure is that logs live on the machine that generated them, which is the machine an attacker controls.
logging.depth:
What it is. The National Institute of Standards and Technology (NIST) defines a log, in Special Publication (SP) 800-92 (September 2006), as a record of the events occurring within an organization's systems and networks, made of entries that each describe one event, and log management as generating, transmitting, storing, analysing and disposing of that data. The 2023 draft revision, SP 800-92 Rev. 1, adds accessing to the list and recasts the guidance as a planning playbook. Logging is not monitoring: a log is evidence, and only becomes detection when something reads it, which is the job of a security information and event management (SIEM) system or of a person. Nor is it the same as telemetry such as flow records or metrics, which summarize behaviour instead of recording events.

The network's format: syslog. Request for Comments (RFC) 5424 (March 2009) is the syslog protocol, obsoleting the informational description of BSD syslog in RFC 3164 (August 2001). Every message begins with a PRI value between angle brackets that packs two numbers: a facility from 0 to 23 and a severity from 0, Emergency, to 7, Debug, combined as facility times 8 plus severity, so a local4 message at Notice is 165 and appears as <165>. The header continues with a version, a timestamp in RFC 3339 format, a hostname, an application name, a process identifier and a message identifier, then optional structured data. Receivers must accept messages of 480 octets and should accept 2,048. Transport is separate: RFC 5426 puts syslog on User Datagram Protocol (UDP) port 514, which has no acknowledgement, so a lost datagram is simply lost and a forged one is hard to tell from a real one, while RFC 5425 carries it over Transport Layer Security (TLS) on Transmission Control Protocol (TCP) port 6514.

Time is part of the record. A log entry is only useful in relation to others, and correlation across devices fails when clocks disagree. NIST SP 800-92 lists synchronizing each logging host's clock to a common time source among the basic operational duties. The United States Office of Management and Budget memorandum M-21-31 (27 August 2021) goes further and prescribes the format: ISO 8601 and RFC 3339 timestamps with milliseconds and an explicit offset, such as 2021-08-27T14:03:07.123Z for Coordinated Universal Time (UTC).

How long, and where. M-21-31 is the most concrete public baseline. Written after the SolarWinds incident, it sets four maturity tiers from EL0 to EL3, gave federal agencies one year, 18 months and two years to reach EL1, EL2 and EL3, and fixes minimum retention for the required log categories at 12 months in active storage followed by 18 months in cold storage, with full packet capture kept for only 72 hours. It also asks for the controls that make logs credible as evidence: current files backed up promptly to a centralized log server or write-once media, integrity hashes checked periodically and on access, and alerts in near real time when logging stops unexpectedly. NIST adds the mundane failures: log rotation that closes and compresses files on a schedule, and logs that, when full, either overwrite the oldest data or stop logging altogether.

The attacker reads logs too. MITRE ATT&CK catalogues clearing Windows event logs as a defence evasion sub-technique, renumbered T1685.005 in 2026 from T1070.001, with commands as plain as wevtutil cl security and a list of users that includes APT28, APT38 and APT41. Its first mitigation is M1029, Remote Data Storage: forward events to a log server promptly so that nothing worth deleting stays on the compromised host. The Open Worldwide Application Security Project (OWASP) Top 10 of 2021 lists Security Logging and Monitoring Failures as A09, mapped to insufficient logging (CWE-778), improper output neutralization for logs (CWE-117), omission of security-relevant information (CWE-223) and sensitive information in log files (CWE-532), and illustrates it with a children's health plan provider that learned from an outside party that records of more than 3.5 million children had been accessed, in a breach that might have been running since 2013.

What to write, and what never to write. The OWASP Logging Cheat Sheet asks for events that matter to security, such as input validation failures, authentication successes and failures, authorization failures and configuration changes, and warns against excluding events from supposedly known sources such as monitoring systems, auditors or penetration testers. It lists what should be removed, masked, hashed or encrypted before it reaches a log: session identifiers, access tokens, passwords, database connection strings, encryption keys, payment data and sensitive personal data. Logs that capture secrets turn the log store into a target and extend the reach of any breach of it.

The logger as attack surface. Log4Shell, CVE-2021-44228, published on 10 December 2021, showed that the logging code itself sits on the attack path. In Apache Log4j2 from 2.0-beta9 through 2.15.0, an attacker who could control a log message or its parameters could make the library perform a JNDI lookup to a Lightweight Directory Access Protocol (LDAP) server and execute the code it returned; version 2.15.0 disabled the behaviour by default and 2.16.0 removed it. Any string that an application logs is attacker input, and log injection, in which untrusted data containing carriage return and line feed characters creates an entry that looks as if it came from someone else, is the low-tech version of the same mistake.

In practice the decisions are few and easy to postpone: which events each system records, where they are sent and over which transport, which clock they share, how long they are kept and at what cost, who can delete them, and who is alerted when they stop. Numbers worth remembering: severities 0 to 7, PRI equal to facility times 8 plus severity, UDP 514 and TCP 6514, 480 and 2,048 octets, 12 plus 18 months, and 72 hours for full packets.

canary.def: Exposing a change to a small, real slice of traffic first, so the failure is discovered by few rather than by everyone.
canary.context: It works only if two things are true, and both are commonly missing. There must be a signal that distinguishes the canary from the rest, which means metrics segmented by version rather than aggregated. And there must be a rollback that can be executed under pressure by whoever is awake. Without those, a canary is a deployment with extra steps that still fails everywhere, five minutes later than it would have.

rollback.def: Returning a system, a configuration or a database to an earlier known-good state by undoing a change rather than fixing forward, which is only a plan if it has been tried.
rollback.context: The assumption that breaks it is that a change is reversible. Schema migrations, data written in a new format, consumed messages and issued credentials are not undone by redeploying the old version, and discovering that mid-incident is how a short outage becomes a long one. Mature change records therefore state the rollback explicitly and name what it cannot recover, which turns an unexamined hope into a decision somebody made on purpose.
rollback.depth:
Three senses, one idea. In databases, ROLLBACK is a statement of the SQL (Structured Query Language) standard: in PostgreSQL it rolls back the current transaction and causes all the updates the transaction made to be discarded, while COMMIT makes them permanent. In operations, a rollback returns a deployed service or a device configuration to its previous release or revision. In security engineering rollback is also a threat, because an attacker who can reinstall an older, vulnerable version has undone every patch since, and platforms therefore build rollback protection. The first is a guarantee the database enforces, the second a procedure people carry out, the third a capability someone has to deny.

Inside a transaction rollback is exact, but only for what the transaction covers. PostgreSQL can run schema changes, written in data definition language (DDL), inside a transaction and roll them back like any other update, which its project wiki presents as an advantage over competitors. MySQL cannot: its 8.4 reference manual lists ALTER TABLE, CREATE TABLE, DROP TABLE, RENAME TABLE, TRUNCATE TABLE and many other statements as causing an implicit commit, ending any active transaction as if COMMIT had been issued first, and warns that even CREATE TEMPORARY TABLE, which does not commit, cannot be rolled back. The National Institute of Standards and Technology (NIST) treats the mechanism as a control: Special Publication (SP) 800-53 Revision 5 names transaction rollback and transaction journaling as the means of transaction recovery (CP-10(2)), and its secure failure principle (SA-8(24)) describes rolling back to a secure state, possibly the initial one, before the failed component is shut down or replaced.

Network operating systems built rollback into the configuration model. Junos keeps the active configuration as juniper.conf.gz and, on every commit, saves the previous one as juniper.conf.1.gz and moves the older ones down a number, holding up to 49 rollback configurations, the first three in /config and the rest in /var/db/config; the rollback command with a number from 0 to 49 loads one of them as the candidate, which is then committed like any other change. The feature that matters most for remote work is commit confirmed. The new configuration is activated, and unless it is confirmed by a further commit within 10 minutes by default (another number of minutes can be given), the system automatically rolls back to the previous configuration and broadcasts a message to every logged-in user. A change that cuts off the engineer's own management session therefore undoes itself. This is the safest form of rollback because the outcome if nobody acts is the old state.

In software deployment the cheapest rollback is the one designed in. Kubernetes keeps a Deployment's history as old ReplicaSets, ten by default (the revisionHistoryLimit field), and kubectl rollout undo, optionally with --to-revision, returns to one of them; but a revision is created only when the Pod template changes, so a rollback restores the template and nothing else, neither the replica count nor any data the new version wrote, and a ReplicaSet that has been pruned can no longer be rolled back to. Google's site reliability engineering (SRE) books describe the operational patterns. The launch chapter of the first notes that tools installing new software typically watch a new server for a while and automatically roll back a change that fails the validation period. The workbook's chapter on canarying releases, by Alec Warner and Štěpán Davidovič, observes that smaller, self-contained release artefacts are cheaper and easier to roll back; that sending a release which fails 20 per cent of requests to a 5 per cent canary costs a 1 per cent overall error rate while detection and rollback take the same time; and that in blue/green deployment rollback is a trivial reversal of the router change, paid for with twice the resources.

What cannot be reversed by redeployment has to be made reversible by design. The established technique is parallel change, also called expand and contract, which Danilo Sato described on Martin Fowler's site in May 2014. A backward-incompatible change is split into three phases: expand, in which the interface or schema supports both the old and the new forms; migrate, in which every client moves to the new form; and contract, in which the old form is removed. Most database refactorings follow it, and canary and blue/green deployments are applications of it. Until the contract step, rolling the application back is safe because the old schema still works; after it, the only way back is a new change forward. The pattern carries its own warning: a contract phase that is never executed can leave things worse than before the change began.

The best-known rollback on record made things worse. According to the US Securities and Exchange Commission's order of 16 October 2013 (Release No. 70694), Knight Capital, whose trading was about ten per cent of all trading in listed US equities, deployed new code for its automated order router to seven of its eight servers before 1 August 2012. The eighth still held the old Power Peg code, unused since 2003, and the new code had repurposed the flag that used to activate it. From 8:01 a.m., before the 9:30 a.m. open, the system sent 97 emails reporting Power Peg disabled, and nobody acted on them. Once trading began, 212 incoming parent orders produced millions of child orders and about 4 million executions in 154 stocks, more than 397 million shares in about 45 minutes. Trying to fix it, Knight uninstalled the new code from the seven servers where it had been deployed correctly, and the order records that this worsened the problem, causing additional incoming parent orders to activate Power Peg. Knight lost more than 460 million US dollars. The rollback assumed the new code was at fault; the fault was the old code still present, and the rollback spread it to every server.

The standards' version of a rollback that has been tried. NIST SP 800-53 asks organizations to retain an organization-defined number of previous baseline configurations to support rollback (CM-2(3)), and spells out that this includes hardware, software, firmware, configuration files, configuration records and the associated documentation, not just the last running configuration; and to test, validate and document changes before finalizing them (CM-3(2)). Read together, the two controls say what makes a rollback real: the previous state must exist in full, the version it depends on must still be installable, and the way back must have been exercised somewhere other than production. A Junos rollback file restored onto a different software release, or a configuration archive restored onto a device running other firmware, is a new change, not a return.

Rollback as an attack. The Android Open Source Project's documentation of Verified Boot describes the case plainly: even with a completely secure update process, a non-persistent kernel exploit could install an older, more vulnerable version of Android, reboot into it, and use it to install a persistent exploit, after which the attacker owns the device and can disable updates. Rollback protection is the defence: the most recent version is recorded in tamper-evident storage, usually per partition, and the device refuses to boot anything lower. The ability to go back is a privilege, reserved for the owner and denied to the attacker.

single-point-of-failure.def: A component, link, dependency or person whose failure alone stops the service, however much redundancy surrounds it.
single-point-of-failure.context: They are usually found by accident because the obvious ones get removed early and the remaining ones are shared dependencies nobody drew: the identity provider in front of both regions, the certificate authority, the one person who knows the procedure, the DNS (Domain Name System) zone. Redundancy at one layer often hides a single point at another (two data centres on one fibre route, two clusters in one cloud account, two nodes with one power feed), which is why the useful exercise is tracing a dependency rather than counting devices.
single-point-of-failure.depth:
The term comes from reliability engineering, and its oldest formal wording is still the best. MIL-STD-1629A, the United States Department of Defense standard of 24 November 1980 for failure mode, effects and criticality analysis (FMECA), defines a single failure point as the failure of an item which would result in failure of the system and is not compensated for by redundancy or alternative operational procedure. Two details of that sentence matter. An item is anything at any level of the design, from a part to a whole subsystem, so the question can be asked of a power supply, a DNS (Domain Name System) zone or a team. And compensation can be a procedure, not only a spare, which is why a manual workaround that people have actually rehearsed removes an item from the list and an untested one does not. The standard requires a separate list of all single failure points with their criticality, and a final report naming those that could not be eliminated from the design. That is the right frame for networks too: a single point of failure (SPOF) is something to find, write down, and then either remove or accept on purpose.

The arithmetic explains why one is enough to undo everything else. In the series model of the NIST (National Institute of Standards and Technology) handbook of statistical methods, a system fails when its first component fails, so the reliabilities of independent components multiply. In the parallel, or redundant, model the system works while at least one component works, so it is the failure probabilities that multiply. Two units that are each available 99 per cent of the time, in parallel, are both down 0.01 per cent of the time: 99.99 per cent. Put that pair behind one unduplicated element that is available 99.9 per cent of the time and the chain multiplies out to about 99.89 per cent, worse than the single element alone. Both formulas rest on one assumption, that the components fail independently, and most real single points are violations of exactly that assumption.

Network design has been removing the obvious ones for decades, layer by layer. RFC (Request for Comments) 9568, which in April 2024 replaced RFC 5798 as the specification of the Virtual Router Redundancy Protocol (VRRP), states the case for the default gateway: a manually configured default route creates a single point of failure, the loss of the default router isolates every end-host that cannot find another path, and VRRP exists to eliminate that by electing one of several routers to answer for a shared address. RFC 2182, a Best Current Practice of July 1997, does the same for the DNS: every delegated zone must have multiple servers, and the secondaries must be both topologically and geographically dispersed, to minimize the likelihood of a single failure disabling all of them. It adds, dryly, that putting all of a zone's servers on the same segment in the same room almost defeats the requirement. Link aggregation, dual power supplies, clustered firewalls and load balancers and a second upstream provider apply the same idea to a link, a feed, a device and a carrier.

The interesting failures are one level down, in what the duplicated things share. Optical networks have a formal name for it. RFC 4202 (October 2005) defines a shared risk link group (SRLG) as a set of links that share a resource whose failure may affect all of them, gives two fibres in the same conduit as its example, identifies each group by a 32-bit number and says that paths meant to be diverse should have disjoint groups. Two circuits bought from two carriers that cross the same bridge are one circuit for this purpose. Cloud guidance says the same of compute: the reliability pillar of the AWS (Amazon Web Services) Well-Architected Framework advises spreading requests across multiple smaller resources so that they do not share a common point of failure.

Cloudflare's control plane outage of 2 November 2023 is the cleanest worked example. The control plane ran in three independent data centres around Hillsboro, Oregon, each with multiple power feeds and network connections, as a high availability cluster designed to survive the loss of any one. When the largest facility lost power, the cluster did what it was built to do, and the control plane failed anyway: services that were in the cluster depended on two systems, Kafka and ClickHouse, that ran only in the failed building. The company's post mortem says those were non-obvious dependencies, and that it had tested by taking each of the other two facilities offline but never the whole of that one. Inside the facility the same pattern repeated: a ground fault shut down the second utility feed and, as a protective measure, all ten generators; batteries expected to bridge about ten minutes began failing after four; and the building's access control system was not on battery backup, which slowed the people sent to restart the generators.

Other incidents show the shared element in software and in the tools of recovery. On 4 October 2021 a maintenance command disconnected Facebook's entire backbone after a bug in the audit tool that should have stopped it; the company's DNS servers, designed to withdraw their BGP (Border Gateway Protocol) announcements when they cannot reach a data centre, all did so at once, and the loss of DNS then broke the internal tools and the out-of-band access needed to repair the network, so engineers had to be sent on site. On 8 June 2021 a bug that Fastly had deployed on 12 May was triggered by one valid customer configuration change and 85 per cent of its network returned errors; the fault was detected within a minute and 95 per cent of the network was normal within 49 minutes. On 19 July 2024 a CrowdStrike content update released at 04:09 UTC (Coordinated Universal Time) and reverted at 05:27 UTC crashed Windows hosts that received it, an estimated 8.5 million devices by Microsoft's count. In each case the redundant units were geographically separate and logically identical: the same software, the same configuration channel or the same control system was the single point.

Finding them is a matter of method, not of inspiration. The bottom-up method is the one the 1980 standard prescribes: take each item in turn and ask what happens to the system when it fails. The top-down method is to trace what a service needs in order to start, to be reached and to be repaired, including names, identity, certificates, power, the management network and the people on shift, and to mark everything that appears only once. The empirical method is to remove things and watch. The Principles of Chaos Engineering list cascading failures when a single point of failure crashes among the weaknesses to be found by experiment, with real events such as crashed servers and severed connections and a deliberately small blast radius; Meta describes its own drills, in which a service, a data centre or a region is taken offline, and admits it had never simulated the loss of the backbone.

Not every single point should be removed. Cloudflare had left its logging pipeline out of the high availability cluster on purpose, judging that delayed analytics were acceptable, and that part of the design behaved as intended. Redundancy costs money and adds machinery, and the machinery (failover logic, state synchronization, the election between two nodes) can fail in its own ways. The honest outcome of the exercise is the list the old standard asks for: the points that were removed, and the ones that remain because someone decided they could.

exfiltration.def: Getting stolen data out of a network: the unauthorized transfer of information from a system, and the stage at which an intrusion becomes a breach with consequences.
exfiltration.context: It is the last chance to notice, and it is deliberately made to look ordinary: uploads to services the organization already uses, small volumes over long periods, or tunnelling through protocols nobody inspects. The Domain Name System (DNS) is the classic channel precisely because it is allowed everywhere and rarely examined for content. The detectable property is usually shape rather than payload: a volume, a destination or a timing that does not match how that account normally behaves.
exfiltration.depth:
What it is, and what it is not. The National Institute of Standards and Technology (NIST) defines exfiltration, in Special Publication (SP) 800-53 Revision 5, as the unauthorized transfer of information from a system. MITRE ATT&CK, the public knowledge base of adversary behaviour, files it as tactic TA0010 under the plain summary that the adversary is trying to steal data, and places it after the Collection tactic (TA0009): the intruder gathers what it wants, stages it in a central location or directory, often packages it with compression and encryption, and only then moves it out. In the intrusion kill chain that Lockheed Martin researchers introduced in 2011 it sits in the last stage, actions on objectives. Three neighbours are worth keeping apart. Command and control (C2) is the channel an intruder uses to steer its tools, which may or may not also carry the stolen data. Data loss or data leakage includes the unintentional case, and the NIST control text says prevention applies to intentional and unintentional exfiltration alike. A data breach is the event with legal consequences, declared once it is established that the data really left.

The channels. ATT&CK listed ten techniques under the tactic when read on 12 November 2026. Exfiltration Over C2 Channel (T1041) encodes the data into the same protocol that already carries the commands. Exfiltration Over Alternative Protocol (T1048) uses a different one, and the page names File Transfer Protocol (FTP), Simple Mail Transfer Protocol (SMTP), Hypertext Transfer Protocol (HTTP) with or without encryption, the Domain Name System (DNS) and Server Message Block (SMB), noting that ordinary operating system utilities such as curl are enough. Exfiltration Over Web Service (T1567) sends the data to a legitimate external service, with sub-techniques for code repositories, cloud storage, text storage sites and webhooks. Transfer Data to Cloud Account (T1537) moves it to another account on the same cloud provider, so that nothing crosses an external interface a defender is watching. Two techniques leave the monitored network altogether: Exfiltration Over Other Network Medium (T1011), through Wi-Fi, a cellular connection or Bluetooth, and Exfiltration Over Physical Medium (T1052), typically a removable drive, which is how data leaves an air-gapped network. Automated Exfiltration (T1020) includes duplicating traffic with a device's own mirroring feature. Data Transfer Size Limits (T1030) and Scheduled Transfer (T1029) shape the flow to stay under alert thresholds and to blend with normal hours. The newest, AI-Enabled Exfiltration (T1700), created on 22 September 2026, covers prompt injection that instructs an enterprise artificial intelligence (AI) agent to send data out through the tools it is already allowed to use.

Why DNS is the classic covert channel. A compromised host asks for a name under a domain whose name server the attacker controls, and the query reaches that server through the ordinary DNS infrastructure, so the host never has to open a connection to the attacker itself. The stolen bytes travel encoded in the query name, and replies can carry data back in records such as TXT. Request for Comments (RFC) 1035 sets the budget: at most 63 octets per label, 255 per name and 512 per message over the User Datagram Protocol (UDP), all on port 53; and because names admit only a limited character set, the data is first encoded, commonly in base32 or base64. That makes the channel slow and chatty. Unit 42's 2019 survey of the technique points out that UDP has no retransmission, so a tool has to number and reassemble its own pieces, and that moving every document on a system this way would take an age and look hugely suspicious. The tools are old and public: the survey lists OzymanDNS, written by Dan Kaminsky in 2004, and iodine, first released in 2006. ATT&CK records the Helminth malware sending data in chunks of up to 23 bytes per DNS query, and FrameworkPOS tunnelling payment card data over DNS.

Hiding in sanctioned traffic. Most exfiltration needs no covert channel, because the permitted ones are good enough. ATT&CK's note on web services gives the reason: hosts inside the network are probably already talking to the service, firewall rules probably already permit it, and the provider's Transport Layer Security (TLS) encryption hides the content. The tool that recurs in ransomware cases is Rclone, a legitimate command-line program for synchronizing files with cloud storage such as Dropbox, Google Drive, Amazon S3 and MEGA, which ATT&CK ties to the Conti and DarkSide operations. The #StopRansomware Guide published by the Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency (CISA) and its partners lists the common tools as Rclone, Rsync, web-based file storage services, FTP and SFTP, its counterpart over Secure Shell (SSH). Operators also pace themselves: ATT&CK documents one campaign limiting Rclone's bandwidth, the group APT28 splitting archives into chunks smaller than 1 MB, and another campaign cutting encrypted archives into 3 MB parts.

Two cases show the range. In the Target breach of 2013, as reconstructed in a United States Senate committee staff report of 26 March 2014, malware on the point-of-sale terminals collected card data, intermediate servers inside the network held it, and from 2 December 2013 it was sent to an external FTP server through another compromised Target server. Over the next two weeks the attackers collected 11 GB, transmitting between 10:00 and 18:00 Central Standard Time, presumably to hide among the busy shopping hours, with drop servers reported in Russia, Miami and Brazil. The intrusion detection product raised urgent alerts each time the exfiltration malware was installed, and the security team did not react. In the MOVEit Transfer campaign of 2023, described by the Federal Bureau of Investigation (FBI) and CISA in advisory AA23-158A, the CL0P group exploited a previously unknown Structured Query Language (SQL) injection flaw, catalogued as CVE-2023-34362 in the Common Vulnerabilities and Exposures (CVE) list, beginning on 27 May 2023, planted a web shell named LEMURLOOT and used it to steal data from the file transfer product's databases. The advisory notes that since 2021 the group has relied mostly on exfiltration rather than encryption. That is double extortion taken to its end: CISA's guide uses the term for encrypting systems and also threatening to release stolen data, and adds that some actors now use the theft as their sole form of extortion.

What the control catalogues ask for. SP 800-53 treats exfiltration twice. Control SC-7(10), Prevent Exfiltration, requires the organization to prevent it and to conduct exfiltration tests at a frequency it defines; the discussion lists the techniques, among them strict adherence to protocol formats, monitoring for beaconing, disconnecting external network interfaces except when needed, traffic profile analysis to detect deviations from the expected volume and types of traffic, penetration testing, monitoring for steganography and data loss prevention (DLP) tools. Control SI-4(18) requires analysing outbound traffic at the external interfaces and at chosen interior points to detect covert exfiltration. ATT&CK's mitigations say the same in operational terms: DLP to detect and block sensitive uploads (M1057); forcing traffic through proxies and letting only dedicated servers speak protocols such as DNS to the outside (M1037); firewall rules that allow only necessary ports out (M1030); web proxies that enforce which external services may be used (M1021); and identity controls on cloud storage, including temporary tokens in place of permanent credentials (M1018).

On real equipment this becomes a short list of egress decisions. Only the internal DNS servers should be able to send queries to the internet, which removes direct tunnels from every other host and concentrates the evidence in one query log. Security service edge and firewall products add DNS-aware controls: Netskope's DNS Security documentation describes attackers encoding extra content within a DNS query for C2 and data exfiltration, lets an administrator allow or block DNS tunnels, and inspects DNS requests on non-standard ports when all traffic is steered to the service; FortiOS offers a DNS filter profile with FortiGuard category-based domain filtering and botnet C2 domain blocking. For web channels the instrument is DLP, which Netskope's documentation defines as preventing data leakage, also known as data exfiltration, and which can only judge content it can read, so it depends on TLS inspection. The T1537 case, a transfer to another account on a provider the organization already uses, is the one a rule written on domains cannot distinguish from ordinary work.

What detection keys on is shape. CISA's guide lists an abnormal amount of data outgoing over any port among the signs of exfiltration and tells defenders to establish a baseline of normal traffic first. ATT&CK's detection notes for DNS look for long or frequent subdomains, high query volume, encoded patterns and queries issued by processes that are neither browsers nor system components; for alternative protocols they look for transfers by unusual processes, outside working hours or at uncommonly high volume. The useful raw material is therefore plain: byte counts per source and destination, DNS logs that keep the full query name, and proxy logs that record upload sizes.

Once exfiltration of personal data is confirmed, the clock is a regulator's. Article 33 of the European Union's General Data Protection Regulation (GDPR) gives the controller, where feasible, no more than 72 hours after becoming aware of a personal data breach to notify the supervisory authority. In Brazil the national data protection agency (ANPD, Agência Nacional de Proteção de Dados, an Autoridade until Provisional Measure 1.317 took effect on 18 September 2025, converted into Law 15.352 of 25 February 2026), under Resolution CD/ANPD 15 of 24 April 2024, gives the controller three working days to notify the authority and the data subjects, with twenty working days to complete the information.

The numbers worth remembering: 63 octets per DNS label, 255 per name and 512 per classic UDP message; 23 bytes per query in Helminth's channel; 11 GB in two weeks from Target, sent during shop hours; 72 hours under the GDPR and three working days under the ANPD's rule. The Target case also carries the operational lesson: the tooling flagged the exfiltration malware as it arrived and nobody acted, so the last chance to notice is only a chance if somebody owns the alert.

risk.def: The combination of how likely an adverse event is and how much harm it would do, stated so that a decision can be made against it. In information security it is assessed from threat, vulnerability, likelihood and impact.
risk.context: Its usefulness collapses when it becomes a colour on a chart. A risk statement that cannot name the asset, the scenario and the consequence is a mood, and it competes badly against a business case with numbers in it. The other failure is treating the register as the work: recording a risk changes nothing, and an organization with a mature register and no remediation has documented its exposure precisely rather than reduced it.
risk.depth:
Two definitions. The NIST (National Institute of Standards and Technology) glossary carries the security one, from US (United States) federal policy: a measure of the extent to which an entity is threatened by a potential circumstance or event, typically a function of the adverse impact if it happens and the likelihood that it will. It also carries the broader management one, from ISO Guide 73: the effect of uncertainty on objectives, which allows for upside as well as harm. Security work nearly always uses the first. Neither is the same as a vulnerability, which is one input, or a threat, which is another, or a severity score, which describes a flaw rather than an organization's exposure to it.

The factors. NIST Special Publication (SP) 800-30 Revision 1 (September 2012) names the typical risk factors: threat, vulnerability, impact, likelihood and predisposing condition, a condition of the organization or its environment, such as a facility in a hurricane zone, that raises or lowers the chance that a threat event causes harm. It recommends analysing how vulnerabilities chain, because some are reachable only after others have been exploited, and notes that a threat scenario tells a story, which makes it useful for communicating risk as well as analysing it. Assessments happen at three tiers: the organization, the mission or business process, and the information system.

How it is measured, and the limits of each way. SP 800-30 is frank about the trade-offs. Quantitative assessment supports cost-benefit comparison of responses, but its rigour drops when subjective judgements are buried inside the numbers. Qualitative assessment, very low to very high, communicates well, but the small range of values makes prioritizing within it hard, and unless each level is clearly defined different experts will produce significantly different results. Semi-quantitative bins and scales sit between the two; in the guide's own example, scores of 70 and 71 differ insignificantly while 36 and 70 differ greatly, even when a chart colours them alike. FAIR (Factor Analysis of Information Risk), published by The Open Group as the Open FAIR standards O-RT (risk taxonomy) and O-RA (risk analysis), takes the quantitative road and expresses loss exposure in financial terms; its promoters at the FAIR Institute describe it as the only international standard quantitative model, a claim worth reading as theirs.

What can be done with it. NIST lists five responses: accept, avoid, mitigate, share or transfer. The Risk Management Framework in SP 800-37 Revision 2 (December 2018) runs in seven steps, Prepare, Categorize, Select, Implement, Assess, Authorize and Monitor, and its Authorize step is the formal moment when an authorizing official determines that the risk of operating a system is acceptable and issues an authorization to operate. The Cybersecurity Framework (CSF) 2.0 of 26 February 2024 organizes outcomes under six functions, GOVERN, IDENTIFY, PROTECT, DETECT, RESPOND and RECOVER, with GOVERN setting the risk management strategy that tells the other five what to prioritize and linking cybersecurity to enterprise risk management.

Risk that was known. The US Government Accountability Office (GAO) report GAO-18-559 (August 2018) on the 2017 Equifax breach reads like a list of risk factors left open. An Apache Struts vulnerability had been publicly identified two days before attackers scanned for it on 10 March 2017; Equifax's own scan about a week after the identification did not find it on the online dispute portal. Data extraction began on 13 May 2017 and went unnoticed for about 76 days, until routine checks found it on 29 July, partly because a certificate on the device that inspected network traffic had expired about ten months before the breach, so encrypted traffic was not being inspected. At least 145.5 million people were affected. Equifax itself named four factors: identification, detection, segmenting of access to databases, and data governance.

Reading scores as risk. A vulnerability score is an input, not a result: the CVSS (Common Vulnerability Scoring System) version 4.0 specification tells consumers to add threat and environmental context before using a score in their own risk assessment. The same discipline applies to the register: each of the five NIST responses is a decision with an owner and a date, and an entry nobody has decided on is still an open risk, only better documented.

asset.def: Anything of value to an organization that it owns, operates or depends on, whether tangible (hardware, network devices, firmware) or intangible (data, software, services, reputation); in practice, something the organization has to know exists before it can protect it.
asset.context: Inventory is where security programmes quietly fail, because every other control is scoped by it: patching covers what is listed, monitoring watches what is listed, and the machine nobody recorded is the one still running the old version. That is why the NIST (National Institute of Standards and Technology) Cybersecurity Framework starts its Identify function with asset management and the CIS (Center for Internet Security) Controls put enterprise and software inventories first. Cloud and remote work made this permanently harder, since anything can be created in minutes by someone with a card. The honest metric is not the size of the inventory but its drift: how long something can exist before the register knows.
asset.depth:
Definitions of asset vary with who is counting, and the variation matters. The NIST (National Institute of Standards and Technology) glossary collects several. The systems-engineering one in SP (Special Publication) 800-160 Volume 1 Revision 1, published in November 2022 and borrowed from ISO/IEC/IEEE 24765, is the broadest: anything that has value to a person or organization. Volume 2 adds the useful split: an asset is an item of value to stakeholders, tangible (hardware, firmware, computing platforms, network devices) or intangible (people, data, information, software, capability, function, service, trademark, patent, image, reputation), and its value is set by the stakeholders in view of what its loss would cost across the life cycle. The CNSSI (Committee on National Security Systems Instruction) 4009 glossary notes that assets have value, criticality and a degree of reliance, from which protections follow, and an older NIST interagency report lists the things auditors forget: virtual computing platforms, IT (information technology) circuits, and the locks, cabinets and keyboards around the hardware. The common thread is that an asset is defined by value and dependence, not by ownership; a supplier's service the business relies on is an asset in this sense even though someone else runs it.

The NIST Cybersecurity Framework (CSF) 2.0, published on 26 February 2024, organizes outcomes into six Functions, Govern, Identify, Protect, Detect, Respond and Recover, and its Identify function begins with assets: understanding the organization's data, hardware, software, systems, facilities, services and people, its suppliers and the related risks is what lets it prioritize. The Asset Management category, ID.AM, asks that assets be identified and managed in line with their importance to organizational objectives and the risk strategy, and its subcategories spell out the inventories: hardware (ID.AM-01); software, services and systems (ID.AM-02); authorized network communications and internal and external data flows (ID.AM-03); services provided by suppliers (ID.AM-04); prioritization by classification, criticality, resources and impact on the mission (ID.AM-05); data and its metadata (ID.AM-07); and life-cycle management of all of them (ID.AM-08). The next category opens with ID.RA-01, vulnerabilities in assets are identified, validated and recorded, which cannot be done for an asset nobody listed.

The CIS (Center for Internet Security) Critical Security Controls make the same point by ordering: Control 1 is the inventory and control of enterprise assets and Control 2 the inventory and control of software assets, ahead of everything else. Control 1 asks the enterprise to actively manage, meaning inventory, track and correct, all end-user, network, IoT (Internet of Things) and server assets connected physically, virtually, remotely or in the cloud, so that it knows the totality of what must be monitored and protected and can find what is unauthorized or unmanaged. Version 8.1, an iterative update to version 8, revised the asset classes and added the Govern function from CSF 2.0. The CIS assessment specification turns the safeguards into numbers. Safeguard 1.1 asks for each asset's network address if static, hardware address, machine name, owner, department and whether it is approved to connect, including devices regularly connected but not under the enterprise's control, with a review at least twice a year; an inventory more than six months old fails outright. Unauthorized assets are dealt with weekly by removal, denial of remote access or quarantine (1.2); an active discovery tool runs daily (1.3); DHCP (Dynamic Host Configuration Protocol) logs feed the inventory weekly (1.4); and a passive discovery tool does the same (1.5).

Software has its own list. Safeguard 2.1 asks for every licensed program's title, publisher, install date and business purpose, and where appropriate its version, deployment mechanism, decommission date and number of licences, reviewed at least twice a year. Only currently supported software may be authorized, checked monthly, with a documented exception and risk acceptance for anything unsupported that the business still needs (2.2); unauthorized software is removed or given an exception monthly (2.3); and the higher implementation groups add allowlisting of software, libraries and scripts (2.5 to 2.7). For a network engineer the lesson is that a firewall, a load balancer or a switch is both an enterprise asset and a software asset: its operating system version, its support status and its end-of-life date belong in the same record as its serial number.

The failure mode is easy to name and expensive to suffer. The United States Government Accountability Office's report on the 2017 Equifax breach, published on 30 August 2018, counts at least 145.5 million people affected and lists identification among the factors Equifax itself found: the Apache Struts vulnerability was not properly identified as being present on the online dispute portal when patches were installed, the internal alert went to an out-of-date recipient list so the people responsible never received it, and a scan a week later did not detect the vulnerable system. Separately, an expired certificate had stopped a network inspection tool from seeing the attackers' traffic. Each of those is an inventory failure of a different kind: which software runs where, who owns it, and which certificates the security tooling depends on.

Keeping the list true is a process, not a project. NIST's practice guide SP 1800-5 on IT asset management, from September 2018, puts the gap plainly: a physical asset system can say where a computer is, but not what operating system the laptops are running or which devices are vulnerable to the latest threat, and only an IT asset management system that joins physical and virtual records can. The usual sources are the ones the CIS safeguards name (active scanning, passive discovery from traffic, DHCP and IP (Internet Protocol) address management logs, a configuration management database) plus endpoint agents, network access control and the inventory APIs (application programming interfaces) of each cloud account. Reconciling them is where the work is, because each sees a different subset, and the disagreements between sources are the findings.

Cloud and remote work made the problem permanent, because a virtual machine, a bucket or a public API can be created in minutes by anyone with a payment card and an account. The useful measure is therefore not how many assets the register holds but its drift: the time between something appearing on the network or in an account and the register knowing about it. The CIS cadences give a practical target, with discovery daily and unauthorized assets handled within a week. An inventory that is complete but six months old fails the CIS test, and one that is fresh but blind to a cloud account fails the attackers' test.

ids.def: A system that watches traffic or hosts and reports what looks like an attack - and, as an IPS (intrusion prevention system), blocks it.
ids.context: The whole design question is the one letter. Detection produces alerts somebody must read; prevention produces outages when it is wrong. Moving from one to the other converts every false positive from noise into an incident, which is why mature deployments stage it: monitor, then block for a pilot, then block generally, with a date on each step. The second constraint is encryption - a sensor that cannot read the traffic is reduced to metadata, which is why so much of this capability migrated to the endpoint.

hub.def: A hub, properly a repeater hub, is a multiport Ethernet repeater that regenerates the signal it receives on any port out of every other port, so all attached stations share one collision domain and one channel's bandwidth; it is the device switches replaced.
hub.context: Everything plugged into a hub was in one collision domain and could see everyone else's traffic, which is why packet capture used to be trivial and why switching was a security improvement nobody sold as one. The word survives in two useful places: a port mirror (SPAN, Cisco's Switched Port Analyzer) deliberately recreates hub behaviour for monitoring, and wireless is a shared medium by physics, so the old contention arithmetic still applies to a channel even though the cabling stopped working that way decades ago.
hub.depth:
What it is, and what it is not. In IEEE (Institute of Electrical and Electronics Engineers) 802.3 terms a hub is a repeater: Clause 9 of the standard specifies the repeater unit for 10 Mb/s baseband networks, Clause 27 the repeater for 100 Mb/s networks (from the 802.3u Fast Ethernet supplement of 1995) and Clause 41 a repeater for 1000 Mb/s. A repeater works on signals, not on addresses: whatever arrives on one port is regenerated and sent out of every other port, collisions included, so it learns nothing, filters nothing and forwards everything. That is the difference from a bridge or switch, which reads the destination MAC (media access control) address and, as Cisco's documentation puts it, once it has learned where host B is, forwards unicast traffic from A to B only to B's port. The product name confused the two for years: vendors sold switching hubs, and Charles Spurgeon's configuration guide notes that a switching hub is, for collision-domain purposes, just another station, so it ends the shared segment rather than extending it. The word hub also names the centre of a hub-and-spoke topology, which has nothing to do with repeaters.

One collision domain. Half-duplex Ethernet shares one channel by CSMA/CD (carrier sense multiple access with collision detection), and a collision domain is formally a single CSMA/CD network in which two stations transmitting at the same time collide; a single segment, or several segments joined by repeater hubs, is one collision domain. Every station on it shares the medium's bandwidth, sees every frame, and must hear any collision while it is still transmitting, which is what bounds the network's size: the round-trip delay must fit within 512 bit times, the minimum frame, or collisions arrive late, after the sender believes its frame was sent. The repeater has jobs of its own in this scheme. The repeater MIB (management information base) of RFC (Request for Comments) 2108, February 1997, models them from Clauses 9 and 27: a Jam state that propagates a collision to every port, fragment extension of short events by Clause 9 repeaters, and auto-partition protection, which cuts off a port that misbehaves, for example one stuck in endless collisions, until it behaves again.

The 10 Mb/s rules and the 5-4-3 myth. The 802.3 standard gives two ways to verify a multi-segment network: Transmission System Model 1, a set of ready-made rules, and Model 2, a delay calculation for anything else. For 10 Mb/s, Model 1 allows a path between any two stations of up to five segments and four repeater sets; when a path has five segments and four repeaters, up to three may be mixing segments (coaxial segments with more than two attachments) and the rest must be link segments (point-to-point, with exactly two). That is the origin of the 5-4-3 rule, which Spurgeon calls an over-simplification and partly wrong, because its usual wording counts populated segments, those attached to PCs, when the standard counts mixing segments, and an unpopulated coaxial segment is still a mixing segment. With three repeaters and four segments, every segment may be a mixing segment.

Fast Ethernet repeaters. Clause 27 defines two classes, and a repeater must be labelled with a Roman I or II in a circle. A Class I repeater translates incoming line signals to digital form and back, which lets it join segments with different signalling, such as 100BASE-TX or FX with 100BASE-T4, but costs enough bit times that only one Class I repeater fits in a collision domain at maximum cable lengths. A Class II repeater repeats immediately, connects only segment types with the same signalling, and allows two per collision domain. The ten-fold faster bit time shrinks the network accordingly: under Model 1 a station-to-station copper link is limited to 100 m, one repeater allows a copper collision domain of 200 m, and two Class II repeaters 205 m, assuming a 5 m link between them in the wiring closet.

Why hubs disappeared. Two changes removed the reason for them. Bridging, and then multiport switching, gave every port its own collision domain and forwarded unicast frames only where they needed to go, so stations no longer shared one channel's capacity. And full duplex, added to 802.3 by the 802.3x supplement approved in March 1997, let both ends of a point-to-point link transmit at once with no collision detection at all; a repeater, which by design joins more than two stations on one channel, cannot offer that. Once switch ports cost about as much as hub ports, the shared segment had nothing left to recommend it. The repeater clauses remained in the standard as legacy; already in 2003 the 802.3 working group's clause table marked Clause 19, layer management for 10 Mb/s repeaters, as deprecated, and the repeater MIB of the Internet Engineering Task Force (IETF) has not been revised since RFC 2108, which replaced RFC 1516 (September 1993) and RFC 1368 (October 1992).

What it meant for security and capture. On a hub every station receives every frame, so any machine in promiscuous mode could read its neighbours' traffic; Cisco's SPAN documentation makes the point directly, a sniffer attached to a hub sees host A's traffic to host B, while on a switch it does not once B's address has been learned. Switching therefore cut passive eavesdropping on the local segment as a side effect, which is also why capture became harder: the analyser needs a copy of the traffic. SPAN, or port mirroring in general, solves that deliberately, copying the traffic of chosen source ports or VLANs (virtual local area networks) to a destination port where the analyser sits, and an engineer who borrows an old hub for a quick capture is rebuilding the same idea with half-duplex costs: one collision domain, shared bandwidth and, if the hub and the hosts disagree, a duplex mismatch.

Where the idea lives on. Wireless local area networks are shared media by physics: every station on a channel contends for the same airtime, as stations on a coaxial segment did, so the old contention arithmetic still applies even though wired Ethernet stopped working that way decades ago, and IEEE 802.11 avoids collisions with CSMA/CA (collision avoidance) because a radio cannot detect them while transmitting. Clause 41 also defined a Gigabit repeater for half-duplex 1000 Mb/s operation; the hub as a product, though, is a museum piece, and the word now survives mostly as shorthand for anything at the centre of a star.

trunk.def: A link that carries more than one network at once: on most switches, a port that carries several virtual local area networks (VLANs), tagging frames as Institute of Electrical and Electronics Engineers (IEEE) 802.1Q specifies; on F5 BIG-IP and FortiSwitch, a bundle of physical links aggregated into one logical link.
trunk.context: The trunk is where segmentation is enforced and where it is most often quietly undone. A Cisco trunk carries every virtual local area network (VLAN) from 1 to 4094 by default, so one cable can hand a whole estate to whatever is plugged into it, and a native VLAN mismatch between two switches silently merges two networks the diagram says are separate. Both are configuration defects rather than protocol defects, which is why segmentation reviews look at trunk allowed lists before they look at firewall rules. The word is also ambiguous: on several platforms a trunk is link aggregation, not VLAN tagging, so the platform has to be read before the word.
trunk.depth:
Two meanings. On a Cisco Catalyst switch a trunk is, in Cisco's own words, a point-to-point link between one or more Ethernet interfaces and another networking device, carrying many virtual local area networks (VLANs) at once, and IEEE 802.1Q, the tagging standard of the Institute of Electrical and Electronics Engineers (IEEE), is the encapsulation available on every Ethernet interface. On an F5 BIG-IP the same word means something else: F5's reference opens with the sentence that link aggregation allows multiple physical links to be treated as one logical link and is also referred to as trunking. FortiSwitch agrees with F5, configuring its link aggregation groups (LAGs) under config switch trunk. Extreme's ExtremeXOS uses neither sense: it adds ports to a VLAN as tagged or untagged, and calls aggregation sharing, enabled with enable sharing followed by a port and grouping. The safe rule is to read the platform before reading the word.

How a VLAN trunk works. Frames on the trunk carry an 802.1Q tag naming their VLAN, with one exception, the native VLAN: Cisco's rule is that a packet whose VLAN ID matches the outgoing port's native VLAN is sent untagged, and every other one is tagged. The native VLAN is VLAN 1 by default on Cisco, and on HPE Aruba's AOS-CX, whose reference states that VLAN 1 is assigned as the native VLAN of all trunk interfaces by default. By default a Cisco trunk sends and receives traffic for all VLANs, 1 to 4094; the allowed list narrows it, and even VLAN 1 can be removed, though management traffic continues to flow. In ExtremeXOS terms the same design is a port that is a tagged member of many VLANs and an untagged member of at most one, the VLAN named Default unless it is moved.

Negotiation. Cisco switches can form trunks automatically with the Dynamic Trunking Protocol (DTP).
