On the Catalyst 9300 the default mode of every Ethernet interface is dynamic auto, which lets the link become a trunk if the other side asks; dynamic desirable actively tries to make one; and nonegotiate stops the interface sending DTP frames at all. Convenience on uplinks is exposure on access ports: an attacker who answers DTP is treated as a switch and offered every VLAN, the attack known as switch spoofing, which only works where an interface is willing to negotiate.

What goes wrong with VLAN trunks. Cisco warns that the native VLAN must be the same at both ends, and that spanning-tree loops might result if it is not; even without a loop, a mismatch forwards untagged frames from one VLAN into another, joining two networks with no device in between. Double tagging exploits the native VLAN on purpose: an attacker on the native VLAN sends a frame with two tags, the first switch strips the outer one because it matches the native VLAN, and the next switch reads the inner tag and delivers the frame into a VLAN the attacker was never in. It is one-way, but it is enough to deliver a packet. The hardening list is short and well known: carry only the VLANs the far end needs, move the native VLAN to an unused identifier or tag it, and switch trunk negotiation off on every port that faces a host.

How an aggregated trunk works. In IEEE terms link aggregation lets one or more links form a Link Aggregation Group that the layer above treats as a single link; IEEE 802.1AX holds the standard, and its 2012 amendment describes N parallel full-duplex point-to-point links at the same data rate. F5 frames the purpose plainly: more bandwidth at lower cost without new hardware, the aggregate being the sum of the members. The Link Aggregation Control Protocol (LACP) watches the members by exchanging control packets and removes a failed one; on BIG-IP it is disabled by default, for backward compatibility, and without it member links carry traffic as long as the physical layer is up. LACP can run active, sending regardless of the peer, or passive, sending only if the peer is active, and BIG-IP sends its packets every 30 seconds with the default long timeout or every second with the short one. FortiSwitch offers static, LACP active and LACP passive modes.

How traffic is spread. An aggregated trunk does not split a single conversation across links. F5 explains that the distribution function keeps the frames of one conversation from being mis-ordered or duplicated by hashing addresses carried in the frame and sending every frame with the same hash over the same member; its options hash on the destination media access control (MAC) address, on source and destination MAC, or on source and destination IP addresses and ports. ExtremeXOS offers address-based hashing at layer 2, its default, or on layer 3 and layer 4, and a custom algorithm. The consequence is the one that surprises people on day one: four 10 Gbit/s members give 40 Gbit/s to many flows, but one flow still gets at most one member, and a hash that sees too few distinct addresses can load one link while the others idle.

What goes wrong with aggregated trunks. F5 is blunt that both ends must have identical LACP configuration, and that one end with LACP enabled and the other disabled is not a valid configuration. Without LACP a member that fails in a way the physical layer does not notice keeps receiving its share of traffic, which is the case for running LACP. And the two meanings are often stacked: a BIG-IP trunk or a switch LAG commonly carries tagged VLANs, so one logical link is aggregated and tagged at the same time. The numbers to remember: VLANs 1 to 4094, native VLAN 1 by default, LACP every 30 seconds or every second, and one flow per member link.

pat.def: Translating many private addresses onto one public address by also rewriting ports - what most people mean when they say NAT.
pat.context: The port is what makes the sharing possible: the translating device keeps a table mapping each internal conversation to a unique source port on the shared address, and reverses it on the way back. Two consequences follow directly. The table is finite, so a host opening thousands of connections can exhaust it for everyone behind the same address. And attribution collapses - an address in a log identifies the gateway, not the user, which is the problem carrier-scale deployments create everywhere they are used.

vm.def: A complete simulated computer with its own kernel, isolated from its neighbours by the hypervisor rather than by the operating system.
vm.context: Its own kernel is the whole difference from a container, and it decides where each belongs: virtual machines cost more to start and run, and give a boundary that survives a guest kernel bug. That is why untrusted or mutually hostile workloads still land on separate machines rather than separate namespaces. The operational inheritance is snapshots: freezing and restoring a whole system is the most useful thing virtualization gave operations, and the most dangerous thing it gave anyone testing a restore they never rehearsed.
vm.depth:
The glossary of the United States National Institute of Standards and Technology (NIST) carries several definitions of a virtual machine (VM), from the terse, a simulated environment created by virtualization, to the precise, a software-defined complete execution stack consisting of virtualized hardware, an operating system (the guest) and applications. The piece that makes it possible is the hypervisor, also called the virtual machine monitor (VMM): the component that manages the guest operating systems on a host and controls the flow of instructions between them and the physical hardware. The name covers a second, unrelated thing. A process virtual machine, of which the Java Virtual Machine is the best-known example, is an abstract computing machine with its own instruction set that runs as an ordinary application and supports a single process. What follows is about the first kind, the system virtual machine, which stands in for a real computer and runs an entire operating system.

What counts as a proper one was settled in 1974, when Gerald Popek and Robert Goldberg published Formal Requirements for Virtualizable Third Generation Architectures in the journal Communications of the ACM. A monitor must provide equivalence, so a program behaves as it would on the real machine; resource control, so the monitor stays in complete command of the hardware; and efficiency, so that a statistically dominant share of instructions runs directly on the processor. Their first theorem says such a monitor can be built whenever every sensitive instruction, one that could interfere with the monitor, is also privileged and therefore traps when a guest executes it. The technique that follows is trap-and-emulate. The same literature distinguishes a Type I monitor, which runs on the bare machine, from a Type II monitor, which runs as an application on a host operating system.

IBM had it working before the theory. CP-40, built at the company's Cambridge Scientific Center, was in production use from January 1967 and led to CP-67 and then to VM/370, which in 1972 became the first virtual machine operating system IBM sold as a product. The personal computer's processor was another matter. In 2000 John Scott Robin and Cynthia Irvine examined the roughly 250 instructions of the Intel Pentium and found seventeen that were sensitive but not privileged, which made the processor non-virtualizable by the formal test. VMware, founded on 10 February 1998 by Mendel Rosenblum, Diane Greene, Edouard Bugnion, Scott Devine and Edward Wang, had already shipped a way round it in Workstation in May 1999, combining direct execution of user code with binary translation of the kernel code that would not trap; its bare-metal ESX Server followed in 2001 and live migration of running machines, vMotion, in 2003. The Xen project at the University of Cambridge took the other route in 2003, paravirtualization, porting the guest operating system to an idealized machine at a cost it measured as a few per cent at most. Intel and AMD then added virtualization extensions to their processors in 2005 and 2006, which let x86 meet the Popek and Goldberg requirements, and the Linux kernel gained its own hypervisor, the Kernel-based Virtual Machine (KVM), in version 2.6.20. Broadcom completed its acquisition of VMware on 22 November 2023.

In a modern VM the guest's code runs directly on the processor until it does something sensitive, at which point control passes to the hypervisor. Devices are handled in two ways. A hypervisor can emulate real hardware, so that an unmodified guest finds a disk controller or a network card it already has a driver for, or it can offer paravirtualized devices that the guest knows are virtual; virtio is that common framework, and the main platform for input and output in KVM. The disk is usually a file, and that is what makes the characteristic operations possible: a snapshot records the state of the machine at a point in time and sends later writes to an overlay, and a machine that can be captured like that can also be moved to another host while it runs.

The comparison with a container is a comparison of boundaries. Containers on one host share that host's kernel and are separated by features of it; each VM brings its own kernel and is separated by the hypervisor, so a flaw in one guest's kernel stays inside that guest. The price has traditionally been start-up time and memory, and it has been falling: Firecracker, the KVM-based monitor written for multi-tenant container and function services, advertises machines that boot in under 125 milliseconds with under 5 MiB of overhead each, up to 150 new ones per second on a host, and does it partly by emulating only five devices.

That last number is a security decision, because the weak point of a VM boundary has been device emulation. The reference case is VENOM, CVE-2015-3456 in the Common Vulnerabilities and Exposures list, published on 13 May 2015: a flaw in the floppy disk controller that QEMU emulates, used by Xen and KVM alike, let a user inside a guest crash it with an out-of-bounds write or possibly execute arbitrary code. The fewer devices a monitor emulates, the less of this kind of code a guest can reach. NIST's guide to the security of full virtualization, Special Publication 800-125 of January 2011, remains the standing reference for these concerns and for the recommendations that answer them.

Snapshots deserve their warning. Broadcom's guidance for vSphere is blunt: do not use snapshots as backups, because a snapshot file is only a change log of the original virtual disk, not a copy of it; no more than 32 in a chain, and two or three for the sake of performance; and no single snapshot kept for more than 72 hours, since the file grows for as long as it exists and can fill the storage it sits on. A snapshot taken before a change is a way back from that change. It is not a copy of the system, and a restore that has never been rehearsed is a hope.

In networks and security the VM is also a delivery format. F5 documents BIG-IP Virtual Edition for VMware ESXi, Linux KVM, Microsoft Hyper-V, Nutanix AHV, Xen and the public clouds, and Fortinet describes FortiGate-VM as carrying all the security and networking services of its hardware appliances, managed alongside them. The appliance becomes a guest like any other, which means that its capacity, its placement and its recovery now depend on a hypervisor somebody else may operate.

telemetry.def: The measurements a system emits about itself, sent somewhere else to be stored and read.
telemetry.context: The word hides a decision: something chose what to emit, and everything not chosen is invisible no matter how good the analysis is later. That makes telemetry selection an architectural act rather than an operational one, and it is usually made by defaults: the agent's out-of-the-box configuration decides what the organization will be able to investigate for years. The second constraint is cost, which is why the useful question is not what can be collected but what will still be affordable to keep when the estate doubles.
telemetry.depth:
What the word means. Merriam-Webster defines telemetry as the science or process of telemetering data, and as the data so transmitted, with a first known use in 1865: measurement at a distance, sent back to someone who is not there. In software the OpenTelemetry project uses it for data emitted from a system about its behaviour, in the form of traces, metrics and logs, and separates it from observability, the ability to understand a system from the outside by asking it questions without knowing its inner workings. Telemetry is the raw material; observability is what a team can do with it; monitoring and alerting are particular uses. An application is properly instrumented, in OpenTelemetry's words, when developers do not need to add more instrumentation to troubleshoot an issue, which is a test most systems only take during an incident.

Signals and the standard way to carry them. OpenTelemetry, a CNCF (Cloud Native Computing Foundation) project formed by merging OpenTracing and OpenCensus, organizes its clients into signals: tracing, metrics, logs and baggage, which share a context propagation layer but otherwise work independently, so that a web framework or a database client can describe itself through each. It is a framework for generating, exporting and collecting telemetry, deliberately not a backend; storage and visualization are left to tools such as Jaeger or Prometheus or to commercial services. Its wire protocol, OTLP (OpenTelemetry Protocol), carries Protobuf messages over gRPC on port 4317 by default or over HTTP (Hypertext Transfer Protocol) POST on port 4318, in binary or JSON (JavaScript Object Notation) encoding. A vendor-neutral protocol is what lets an organization change backends without re-instrumenting its code.

Network telemetry. RFC (Request for Comments) 9232, the IETF (Internet Engineering Task Force) Network Telemetry Framework of May 2022, describes the shift in networking. Operators long relied on SNMP (Simple Network Management Protocol), the CLI (command-line interface) and syslog, and the RFC calls poll-based, low-frequency collection ill-suited to continuous monitoring: SNMP only exposes what is in a MIB (Management Information Base), and the push mechanisms that existed, traps, syslog and sampled packets, carried only predefined warnings or samples. Telemetry in the newer sense has five accepted characteristics: data is pushed and streamed from the source, even from the forwarding chip, instead of polled; it comes in volumes meant for machines rather than people; it is normalized across devices; it is modelled in advance; and it is fused from many sources. The framework sorts it by where it comes from: the management plane, the control plane, the forwarding plane and external data.

The protocols in practice. Model-driven streaming is typically YANG-Push, defined in RFC 8641 (September 2019), through which a subscriber asks a device for a continuous, customized stream of updates from its YANG datastore instead of polling it. Flow telemetry is IPFIX (IP Flow Information Export, RFC 7011, September 2013), whose message version number, 10, continues from version 9 of Cisco's NetFlow; it sends flow records from an exporting process to a collecting process, by default on port 4739. On F5 BIG-IP, Telemetry Streaming aggregates, normalizes and forwards statistics and events to a consumer application, configured declaratively by posting one JSON declaration to its REST (Representational State Transfer) endpoint rather than by a sequence of commands. In every case the device decides what it can emit, and the configuration decides what it does.

Cost and selection. Telemetry is cheap to emit and expensive to keep, and the expensive part grows with traffic, not with insight. OpenTelemetry calls sampling one of the most effective ways to cut the cost of observability without losing visibility, and is candid about the trade. Head sampling decides at the start of a trace, which is cheap but cannot guarantee that every trace containing an error is kept; tail sampling decides after seeing all or most of a trace's spans, which large systems almost always need, but which is hard to implement and has to change as the system changes. Filtering and aggregation also cut volume, but unlike sampling they do not keep a representative picture. Whatever is dropped at the source, by sampling, filtering or simply never being emitted, cannot be recovered for an investigation later, which is why the selection deserves a design review rather than a default.

Telemetry as data that leaves. Because telemetry is by definition sent somewhere else, it crosses boundaries: from a device to a collector, from a host to a vendor's service, from a production network to an analytics platform. The same streams that make a network observable describe its topology, its users and its traffic, so the collectors, the transport and the retention of telemetry need the same access control and encryption decisions as any other sensitive data, and the destination of every exporter is worth knowing before an incident rather than during one.

metrics.def: Numbers recorded over time as named, labelled time series: cheap to store, fast to query, and unable to explain a single request.
metrics.context: Metrics answer how much and how often, which makes them right for alerting and wrong for investigation: an aggregate says the error rate rose and cannot say which customer, which version or which query. The recurring mistake is averaging, because an average hides the tail users actually experience: if the mean response is fast and the ninety-ninth percentile is terrible, a meaningful fraction of people are having a bad time invisibly.
metrics.depth:
What a metric is. The Prometheus monitoring system stores everything as time series: streams of timestamped values that belong to one metric and one set of labelled dimensions, each series identified by a metric name, such as http_requests_total, and optional key-value labels. OpenTelemetry's data model describes the same thing as streams of data points of a few kinds, Sum, Gauge, Histogram, ExponentialHistogram and a legacy Summary, each with a unit, a description and timestamps in Unix Epoch nanoseconds. What makes metrics cheap is that they are already aggregated: a counter of a million requests costs the same few bytes per sample as a counter of ten. That is also why a metric cannot explain one request. OpenTelemetry's exemplars narrow the gap by attaching to a metric event the trace_id and span_id of a real request that contributed to it, so that a spike on a graph can lead to an actual trace.

The kinds. A counter only goes up, or resets to zero when the process restarts, and Prometheus warns never to use one for a value that can fall, such as the number of running processes; what is graphed is its rate, the difference between two samples divided by the time between them. A gauge goes up and down: a temperature, memory in use, concurrent requests. A histogram counts observations into buckets, and a summary computes configurable quantiles over a sliding time window. OpenTelemetry adds the question of temporality: a cumulative stream reports the full sum since a start time, close to when the process started, while a delta stream reports only what happened in each interval with no overlap, and the choice trades off how restarts are detected, how rates are computed and whether the backend pulls or the source pushes.

Counters on network devices. SNMP (Simple Network Management Protocol) interface counters are the oldest metrics most engineers meet, and RFC (Request for Comments) 2863, the Interfaces Group MIB (Management Information Base) of June 2000, explains their classic trap. A 32-bit ifInOctets counter fed by back-to-back full-size packets wraps in just over 57 minutes at 10 Mbit/s, 5.7 minutes at 100 Mbit/s and 34 seconds at 1 Gbit/s, so a poller slower than the wrap time sees traffic disappear. The RFC therefore requires 64-bit high-capacity octet counters, such as ifHCInOctets, on interfaces faster than 20 Mbit/s, and 64-bit packet counters as well at 650 Mbit/s and above. It also tells a manager to discard any difference computed across a change in ifCounterDiscontinuityTime, and to check sysUpTime for an agent restart, because a counter that resets in mid-interval produces a rate that is simply wrong.

The averaging trap. Google's Site Reliability Engineering (SRE) book, in Rob Ewaschuk's chapter on monitoring distributed systems, names four golden signals, latency, traffic, errors and saturation, and then warns against building on means. A web service with an average latency of 100 ms at 1,000 requests per second might easily have 1 per cent of requests taking 5 seconds, and when a page depends on several such backends, the 99th percentile of one can become the median response of the frontend. The remedy it gives is to count requests in latency buckets, 0 to 10 ms, 10 to 30, 30 to 100, 100 to 300 and so on, with boundaries growing by factors of about three, which is exactly a histogram. Percentiles have a second trap: they do not average. Prometheus puts it bluntly: averaging the precomputed quantiles of several summaries yields statistically nonsensical values, while histogram buckets from many instances can be added and a percentile computed from the total. The true average, when it is wanted, is the rate of the sum divided by the rate of the count.

Cardinality. Every label multiplies. Prometheus reminds instrumenters that every unique combination of key-value label pairs is a new time series, which can dramatically increase the data stored, and tells them not to use labels for dimensions with many values, such as user IDs, email addresses or other unbounded sets. That rule is the practical reason metrics answer how much and how often but not who: the moment a metric is labelled by customer it stops being cheap. Per-request detail belongs in logs and traces, linked back to the metric by an exemplar or a shared identifier.

Alerting, not investigation. Metrics are the right trigger for a page because they are cheap to evaluate continuously and their meaning is stable; the SRE chapter's advice is that a service whose four golden signals are measured, with a human paged when one is problematic or, for saturation, nearly so, is at least decently covered. They are the wrong tool for the next question, which is always which requests, from whom, on which version, and that question is answered by the telemetry that was kept alongside them.

tracing.def: Following one request through every service it touches, with each step recorded and linked by a shared identifier.
tracing.context: It exists because breaking an application into services broke the stack trace: no single machine sees the whole request any more, and the slow step could be anywhere. A trace reassembles that, which is why it is the tool that answers where the time went. Each step is a span, with a start, an end and a parent, and the identifier travels between services in a header, standardized for the Hypertext Transfer Protocol (HTTP) by the World Wide Web Consortium (W3C) as traceparent. The cost is instrumentation and propagation: every service must pass the identifier along, and one that does not becomes a gap where the trail stops, which is usually the oldest component and often the one being blamed.
tracing.depth:
What it is, and what it is not. Distributed tracing records the path of a single request through a system of services as a trace: a tree of spans, each span one unit of work with a name, a start and an end time, a reference to its parent, and whatever attributes the instrumentation attaches. The root span covers the request from start to finish; its descendants show which service called which, in what order, and how long each took, which is why tracing answers questions about latency that averaged metrics cannot. The word has other meanings that engineers meet daily, and they are different tools. Traceroute traces the path of packets hop by hop, not of a request through software. A packet capture on a firewall is often called a trace. The Linux kernel's ftrace is, in its documentation's words, an internal tracer for finding what is going on inside the kernel, used for debugging and for latency analysis outside user space. And a stack trace, or traceback, shows the calls inside one process at the moment of an error. Distributed tracing is what replaced the stack trace once a request stopped living in one process.

Where it came from. The design most systems follow was described by Google in Dapper, a Large-Scale Distributed Systems Tracing Infrastructure, published as Google Technical Report dapper-2010-1 in April 2010 by Benjamin H. Sigelman and seven colleagues. Dapper acknowledged earlier research systems, Magpie and X-Trace, and set three goals: low overhead, transparency to application developers, and deployment everywhere. It met the second by instrumenting a small number of common libraries, the remote procedure call and control-flow libraries every service used, instead of every application. Its data model is the one still in use: a trace tree whose nodes are spans, each with a span id and a parent id, all of them probabilistically unique 64-bit integers, plus a trace id shared by the whole tree, with optional annotations added by the application. The open-source lineage followed. Zipkin, a distributed tracing system that gathers timing data to troubleshoot latency problems, lets an engineer jump from a trace ID found in a log to the whole request. Jaeger was accepted by the Cloud Native Computing Foundation (CNCF) on 13 September 2017 and graduated on 31 October 2019. OpenTelemetry, born from the merger of OpenTracing and OpenCensus, which had separately tried to standardize how code is instrumented, was accepted by the CNCF on 7 May 2019 and graduated on 11 May 2026; it produces and exports traces but is not a backend, leaving storage and display to tools such as Jaeger.

The data model in detail. OpenTelemetry's span carries a name, the parent span ID (empty for a root span), start and end timestamps, a span context, attributes, events, links and a status. The span context is the part that travels: the trace ID, the span's own ID, trace flags and trace state. Status has three values, and the default is Unset, which means the operation completed without an error; Error marks a failure, for example a server returning Hypertext Transfer Protocol (HTTP) status 500; Ok means a developer explicitly marked the span as error-free. Span kind tells a backend how to join spans across processes: a client span is a synchronous outgoing call such as an HTTP request or a database query, a server span the matching incoming call, an internal span work that does not cross a process boundary, and producer and consumer spans the two ends of asynchronous work through a queue, where the consumer may start long after the producer finished. Links tie a span to spans in other traces when the causal relationship is not a parent and child, as when queued work is processed later.

Propagation, the part that breaks. A trace exists only if every hop passes its identity on. For HTTP that is standardized by the World Wide Web Consortium (W3C) Trace Context Recommendation of 23 November 2021. The traceparent header has four fields separated by hyphens: a version (00), a 16-byte trace-id written as 32 hexadecimal characters, an 8-byte parent-id, the ID of the calling span, written as 16, and an 8-bit trace-flags field whose lowest bit is the sampled flag, as in 00-0af7651916cd43dd8448eb211c80319c-b7ad6b7169203331-01. All-zero IDs are invalid, and a receiver must ignore a traceparent with an invalid trace-id or parent-id. The tracestate header carries vendor-specific data alongside, and vendors should propagate at least 512 characters of it. A service that receives no traceparent starts a new trace; one that receives a valid header continues it, adding its own span as the new parent. Every component in the path that does not do this, an old service, a message queue without instrumentation, a proxy that rewrites headers, splits the request into two unrelated traces, and the gap is exactly where nobody can see.

Network devices in the path. Load balancers, reverse proxies and gateways sit on every request, so they either carry the trace or break it. NGINX's ngx_otel_module, packaged for open-source NGINX since 1.25.3 and for NGINX Plus since 1.23.4, adds OpenTelemetry tracing with W3C context propagation and exports spans over OpenTelemetry's own protocol. Its otel_trace_context directive makes the choice explicit: extract continues the trace from the incoming request, inject starts a new context and overwrites any existing headers, propagate does both, so that the proxy appears in the trace as a span between client and backend, and ignore, the default, leaves the headers alone. A proxy configured with inject in the middle of an existing trace cuts it in two; one that is not instrumented at all passes the headers through but appears in the trace as unexplained time between the caller's client span and the backend's server span. The same questions apply to any appliance that terminates and re-originates HTTP: whether it forwards traceparent and tracestate unchanged, rewrites them or drops them.

Sampling and cost. Recording every span of every request is rarely affordable. Dapper's first production version sampled uniformly, one trace in every 1024 candidates, later moving to adaptive rates per service; a span averaged 426 bytes, and trace collection used less than 0.01 per cent of Google's production network traffic. OpenTelemetry distinguishes head sampling, decided at the start, most commonly by consistent probability on the trace ID at a rate such as 5 per cent so that whole traces are kept or dropped together, from tail sampling, decided after all or most spans are in, which can keep every trace that contains an error or exceeds a latency threshold but needs stateful components able to hold large amounts of data. The W3C sampled flag lets a caller share its decision so that downstream services record the same traces, but the specification calls the flags recommendations rather than rules, because callers may be buggy or abusive.

What goes wrong. The security considerations of the Trace Context specification are worth reading by anyone running a public application programming interface (API). Information exposure: traceparent lets one request be correlated with another, and tracestate can reveal which monitoring software the caller runs, so confidential data should never be placed in tracestate, or the header should be removed from requests to external systems. Denial of service: a service that naively continues any incoming trace with the sampled flag set can be overwhelmed with tracing overhead, have its monitoring polluted by forged trace-id collisions, or run up its bill with a hosted tracing vendor; the specification suggests treating authenticated and unauthenticated requests differently and rate-limiting what is recorded. At the edge, that means deciding whether to trust, regenerate or strip traceparent arriving from the internet. Attributes are the other leak: instrumentation that records full Uniform Resource Locators (URLs), headers or query parameters copies whatever sensitive data they carry into the tracing backend. Numbers worth keeping: a 16-byte trace ID, an 8-byte span ID, version 00, flags 01 for sampled, at least 512 characters of tracestate, and Dapper's one in 1024.

retention.def: How long records are kept before they are deleted or destroyed: a decision with legal, financial and investigative consequences that is too often made on storage cost alone.
retention.context: Two opposite pressures meet here and both are legitimate. Investigations need history, and intrusions are frequently discovered months after they began, so a ninety-day window can mean the beginning is already gone before anyone looks. Privacy regulation and litigation exposure push the other way, because data kept is data that can be demanded or leaked. Deciding deliberately is the whole exercise; letting the default win means the answer was set by whoever priced the storage tier.
retention.depth:
A retention period has two edges. The lower edge is how long records must exist, set by law, contract, regulation and the investigations they support; the upper edge is how long they may exist, set by privacy law and by the risk of holding them. The National Institute of Standards and Technology (NIST) writes the lower edge as control AU-11 of Special Publication (SP) 800-53 Revision 5: retain audit records for an organization-defined period consistent with the records retention policy, to support after-the-fact investigation of incidents and to meet regulatory and organizational requirements, until they are no longer needed for administrative, legal, audit or operational purposes, including requests under the Freedom of Information Act (FOIA), subpoenas and law enforcement. The enhancement AU-11(1) adds a requirement that is easy to forget: records kept for years must still be retrievable, which can mean converting them to newer formats, keeping equipment able to read them and keeping the documentation needed to interpret them. Retention that cannot be read back is only storage.

Why investigators want long windows. Mandiant's M-Trends 2026, published on 23 March 2026 from more than 500,000 hours of incident investigations in 2025, puts the global median dwell time, the time an intruder is present before detection, at 14 days, up from 11 the year before; for cyber espionage cases, and for North Korean information technology (IT) workers placed inside companies, the median was 122 days, and backdoors such as Brickstorm, planted on network appliances with little onboard storage, reached dwell times of nearly 400 days. The report's conclusion is blunt: standard 90-day log retention policies leave organizations completely blind to the initial access vector and the full scope of the intrusion. The previous year's edition showed the other variable: the median was 26 days when an outside party raised the alarm and 10 when the organization found the activity itself. Medians hide the long tail, and the long tail is exactly the case where history matters most.

The United States government set a concrete baseline after the SolarWinds compromise. Office of Management and Budget (OMB) memorandum M-21-31, of 27 August 2021, defines event logging maturity tiers for federal agencies and requires the most critical categories of logs to be kept for 12 months in active storage, meaning stored for frequent use and easy access, and a further 18 months in cold data storage, cheaper but still accessible; full packet capture only has to be kept for 72 hours. The memorandum states that these periods are minimums, and asks for integrity checks against log hashes throughout the retention period, because a log that can be quietly edited is worth little as evidence. The hot and cold split is the useful pattern: fast search for the recent months, cheap reach-back for the long tail.

Products encode the same split, and their defaults decide more than policies do. FortiAnalyzer stores every arriving log in a file that is compressed when it rolls and kept as an Archive log, offline, while the same log is inserted into an SQL (Structured Query Language) database as an Analytics log, indexed and searchable. A data policy sets how long each is kept: in version 7.6.1, Keep Logs for Analytics set to 0 means unlimited, Keep Logs for Archive set to 0 means files are deleted once rolled, and the retention check runs every twelve hours. A separate disk utilization threshold starts deleting the oldest Archive files or Analytics tables first when the disk fills. On an undersized appliance the effective retention is therefore whatever the disk holds, regardless of what the policy says, which is the storage tier setting the answer in the most literal way.

The upper edge comes from privacy law. The General Data Protection Regulation (GDPR) makes storage limitation one of its principles in Article 5(1)(e): personal data may be kept in a form that permits identification for no longer than is necessary for the purposes of processing, with an exception for archiving in the public interest, research and statistics under safeguards. Brazil's Lei Geral de Proteção de Dados (LGPD), Law 13.709 of 14 August 2018, says in article 16 that personal data shall be eliminated once processing ends, and authorizes keeping them only to meet a legal or regulatory obligation of the controller, for study by a research body (anonymized where possible), for transfer to a third party within the law, or for the controller's exclusive use once anonymized. A retention schedule is therefore a list of purposes with a period each, not a single number, and the legal basis is what lets an organization answer a deletion request with not yet.

Telecommunications retention is where the two edges have collided in court. The European Union's Data Retention Directive, 2006/24/EC of 15 March 2006, required providers to retain traffic and location data, not content, for between six months and two years. On 8 April 2014, in Digital Rights Ireland (Joined Cases C-293/12 and C-594/12), the Grand Chamber of the Court of Justice of the European Union (CJEU) declared the directive invalid: the data, taken as a whole, may allow very precise conclusions about people's private lives, the interference with privacy was wide-ranging and particularly serious, and the 6 to 24 month period was not tied to objective criteria limiting it to what is strictly necessary. In Tele2 Sverige and Watson (Joined Cases C-203/15 and C-698/15), on 21 December 2016, the Court held that national laws imposing general and indiscriminate retention of all traffic and location data are precluded, while targeted retention to fight serious crime is allowed if limited to what is strictly necessary in the categories of data, the means of communication, the persons concerned and the period.

Brazil chose fixed statutory periods. The Marco Civil da Internet, Law 12.965 of 23 April 2014, defines a connection record as the date and time a connection to the internet starts and ends, its duration and the Internet Protocol (IP) address used, and an application access record as the date and time an application was used from a given IP address. Article 13 obliges the administrator of the autonomous system providing the connection to keep connection records confidentially, in a controlled and secure environment, for one year; the duty cannot be transferred to a third party; police, administrative authorities or the public prosecutor may ask for longer preservation, but must seek a court order within 60 days; and records are disclosed only by court order. Article 14 forbids connection providers to keep application access records at all, and article 15 obliges application providers run as businesses to keep theirs for six months. The two periods are minimums for the provider and the most an investigator can count on.

The end of a retention period is a disposal decision, and it needs the same care. NIST SP 800-88 Revision 2, published in September 2025 by Ramaswamy Chandramouli and Eric Hibbard and superseding the 2014 Revision 1, tells system owners to consult privacy officers, FOIA officers and records retention offices before sanitizing anything, so that nothing under a legal obligation or a hold is destroyed. It defines three methods: clear, which protects against simple non-invasive recovery through the normal user interface; purge, which makes recovery infeasible even with state-of-the-art laboratory techniques while leaving the medium reusable, and which should be preferred to clear when possible; and destroy, which leaves the medium unusable. Cryptographic erase, destroying the key under which the data was encrypted, is one of the purge techniques. Expiring an index entry while copies survive in backups, snapshots and replicas is not the end of retention; it is a record nobody knows they still hold.

forensics.def: Establishing what happened on a system, in a way that survives being questioned afterwards.
forensics.context: The discipline is defined by that second clause. Anyone can look at a machine; forensics is looking without changing what you are looking at, recording how you know, and being able to show later that the evidence is the same evidence. That is why the first action is usually to capture volatile state and isolate rather than to reboot or clean, and why an organization that wipes and reimages a compromised host has chosen recovery speed over ever knowing what happened, which is sometimes the right trade and should be a decision rather than a reflex.
forensics.depth:
What it is, and what it is not. Digital forensics, which the National Institute of Standards and Technology (NIST) also calls computer and network forensics, takes its name from forensic science, the application of science to the law. NIST Special Publication (SP) 800-86, Guide to Integrating Forensic Techniques into Incident Response, written by Karen Kent, Suzanne Chevalier, Tim Grance and Hung Dang and published in August 2006, defines it as the application of science to the identification, collection, examination and analysis of data while preserving the integrity of the information and maintaining a strict chain of custody for the data. The glossary NIST keeps for its publications adds two stricter readings: a United States national security glossary speaks of proper search authority, validation with mathematics, validated tools, repeatability, reporting and possibly expert testimony, and NIST Interagency Report 8006 asks for methods that are demonstrably reliable, accurate and repeatable, so that the result may be used in judicial proceedings. Forensics is therefore not the same thing as incident response, even though the two travel together as DFIR (digital forensics and incident response): response aims to contain the damage and restore service, forensics aims to know what happened and to be able to prove it. Nor is it only for crimes. SP 800-86 lists operational troubleshooting, such as finding where a misconfigured host really is, log correlation across systems, recovery of deleted data, acquiring a departing employee's workstation before its media are sanitized, and regulatory due diligence as ordinary uses of the same tools.

The process. SP 800-86 describes four phases. Collection identifies, labels, records and acquires data from the possible sources while following procedures that preserve its integrity. Examination processes large amounts of collected data, by automated and manual means, to extract what is of interest. Analysis uses legally justifiable methods to answer the questions that prompted the collection, and reporting describes the actions taken, explains how tools and procedures were chosen and says what else needs doing. Integrity is shown rather than asserted. When media are imaged, the guide recommends a write-blocker, a hardware or software tool that prevents the computer from writing to the storage connected to it, and message digests of the original and the copy, computed and compared to show that the image is exact. RFC (Request for Comments) 3227 adds a working rule that is easy to forget: make a bit-level copy of the evidence copy and analyse that, because analysis will almost certainly alter file access times. The media that receive evidence should be forensically clean, which SP 800-86 defines as completely wiped, scanned for malware and verified before use.

The order of volatility. The most quoted page in the field is an Internet Engineering Task Force (IETF) document. RFC 3227, Guidelines for Evidence Collection and Archiving, published in February 2002 as Best Current Practice 55 by Dominique Brezinski and Tom Killalea, tells the collector to proceed from the volatile to the less volatile and gives an example order for a typical system: registers and cache; the routing table, ARP (Address Resolution Protocol) cache, process table, kernel statistics and memory; temporary file systems; disk; remote logging and monitoring data relevant to the system; physical configuration and network topology; and archival media. SP 800-86 gives a finer order for volatile operating system data: network connections first, then login sessions, the contents of memory, running processes, open files, network configuration and, last, the system's time. For network engineers the list is a warning about habits. On a router or a firewall the routing table and the ARP cache sit near the top, together with everything else that lives only in memory, such as a firewall's session table, and a reload to clear a fault is exactly the step that empties them. RFC 3227 also asks the collector to record the extent of the system's clock drift, because every timeline built afterwards depends on it.

Live systems, and why the obvious step is often the wrong one. RFC 3227's list of things to avoid reads like a list of first reactions. Do not shut down until collection is complete, since much evidence is lost and an attacker may have altered the startup and shutdown scripts to destroy it. Do not trust the programs on the system: run collection tools from protected media. Do not run programs that change the access time of every file, and the RFC names tar and xcopy. And note that simply disconnecting or filtering the machine from the network may trigger deadman switches that notice they are off the network and wipe evidence. SP 800-86 explains the trust problem: a fully compromised system may carry rootkits that alter its behaviour at kernel level and return false data to user-level tools, so the collection kit should use statically linked binaries, and even then the tools are no guarantee of accurate results. The shutdown itself is a choice with consequences. A graceful shutdown makes the operating system close open files, delete temporary files and possibly clear the swap file, and it can remove malicious material: memory-resident rootkits may disappear and Trojan horses may erase their traces. Removing power avoids that, but on some operating systems it corrupts files that were open. NIST's guidance is a graceful shutdown in general, unless swap or temporary files matter or the system may hold malware that a shutdown would trigger.

Evidence that holds up. RFC 3227 sets five properties for computer evidence: admissible, conforming to the legal rules for being put before a court; authentic, positively tied to the incident; complete, telling the whole story rather than one perspective; reliable, with nothing in its collection and handling that casts doubt on its authenticity and veracity; and believable, readily understood by a court. Its chain of custody documents where, when and by whom the evidence was discovered and collected, where, when and by whom it was handled or examined, who held it during which period and how it was stored, and when and how each transfer of custody happened. NIST SP 800-61 Revision 3 (April 2025, by Alexander Nelson, Sanjay Rekhi, Murugiah Souppaya and Karen Scarfone, superseding Revision 2 of August 2012), now written as a community profile of the Cybersecurity Framework (CSF) 2.0, turns this into the outcome RS.AN-07: incident data and metadata are collected, and their integrity and provenance are preserved. Its note is realistic: formal chain-of-custody handling might not be performed for every incident, since most malware incidents will not end in prosecution, but the data collected is still evidence. The international reference is ISO/IEC 27037:2012 of the International Organization for Standardization and the International Electrotechnical Commission, which gives guidelines for identifying, collecting, acquiring and preserving potential digital evidence on storage media, mobile devices, cameras including closed-circuit television (CCTV), networked computers and Transmission Control Protocol/Internet Protocol (TCP/IP) networks, and which ISO last confirmed in 2018.

In Brazil the chain of custody is statute. Law 13.964 of 24 December 2019, known as the anticrime law, added articles 158-A to 158-F to the Code of Criminal Procedure. Article 158-A defines the chain of custody as the set of all procedures used to maintain and document the chronological history of a trace collected at crime scenes or from victims, tracking its possession and handling from its recognition to its disposal. Article 158-B divides it into ten stages: recognition, isolation, fixing (recording the trace as found), collection, packaging, transport, receipt, processing, storage and disposal. Article 158-C requires every trace collected during an inquiry or a case to be handled this way, article 158-E requires every Criminalistics Institute to run a custody centre for storing and controlling traces, and article 158-F sends the material back to that centre after examination. A seized disk or a copy of a server's logs is a trace in this sense, and an engineer who hands one over is the first link of the chain.

Tools, testing and limits. NIST's Computer Forensics Tool Testing (CFTT) programme exists because, in its words, law enforcement needs to ensure the reliability of forensic tools: it writes tool specifications, test procedures, criteria and test sets, and publishes test reports with the Science and Technology directorate of the Department of Homeland Security. RFC 3227's own toolkit, ps, ifconfig, netstat, arp, dd and sha1sum among them, is a 2002 snapshot, but its logic has not aged: tools that examine processes and system state, make bit-for-bit copies and compute checksums, carried on trusted media. The limits are worth knowing precisely. A hash proves that a copy matches what was acquired, not that the source was untouched before acquisition. A log is evidence only if it was kept long enough and protected from the intruder, which is the subject of the audit trail entry. A capture of volatile state taken from a system whose kernel lies is a record of the lie. And the start of an intrusion, the figure from which dwell time is measured, is usually established by forensic work after detection, so the quality of that number depends on the quality of this discipline.

chain-of-custody.def: The unbroken record of who held evidence, when, and what they did with it.
chain-of-custody.context: Its purpose is to make an answer defensible rather than merely correct: an investigator who cannot show the evidence was protected from alteration has findings that can be dismissed without being disproved. In practice it is unglamorous - hashes taken at acquisition, copies worked on rather than originals, timestamps, signatures and a log of every transfer. It matters outside courtrooms because the same discipline is what makes an internal incident report survive contact with a vendor, an insurer or a regulator.

change-management.def: The process by which planned changes to production systems are proposed, assessed for risk, approved, scheduled, recorded and verified, so that every change is known before it happens and traceable afterwards.
change-management.context: It exists because most outages are self-inflicted and arrive on purpose, so a record of what changed is the fastest route to what broke. It fails in two opposite directions. Too heavy, and it delays small safe changes until they arrive in large risky batches: the process manufacturing the risk it was meant to control. Too light, and nobody can answer what changed at the hour the graph turned. The useful test is whether the record answers that question in one minute during an incident.
change-management.depth:
The security world's version of the discipline is set out in NIST (National Institute of Standards and Technology) Special Publication 800-128, Guide for Security-Focused Configuration Management of Information Systems, published in August 2011 and updated in October 2019. It describes four phases: planning, identifying and implementing secure baseline configurations, controlling configuration changes, and monitoring. In the control phase, changes are formally identified, proposed, reviewed, analysed for security impact, tested and approved before implementation, and organizations limit unauthorized or undocumented changes with access controls, process automation, change windows and verification and audit. The deciding body is a Configuration Control Board (CCB), a group of two or more people with the collective responsibility and authority to review and approve changes; service management frameworks call the equivalent body a CAB (change advisory board), and the ticket-and-approval workflow of IT (information technology) service management is defined separately. The broader questions are why the workflow exists and how much of it actually helps.

The reason is that the greatest single source of outages is the people responsible for the system. Google's site reliability engineers report that roughly 70 per cent of outages are due to changes in a live system, and the practices they credit are automated: progressive rollouts, quick and accurate detection of problems, and safe rollback, which together limit how many users and operations a bad change can reach, and which take humans out of the loop where fatigue, familiarity and inattention to repetitive tasks cause mistakes. Seen this way, change management is not paperwork around engineering; it is the control that sits in front of the most frequent cause of failure.

Mature processes sort changes by risk so that effort goes where risk is. The model in ServiceNow's change management documentation is typical of the industry. A standard change is pre-authorized, low risk and relatively common, follows a streamlined path and skips peer review and CAB authorization; a normal change needs assessment, peer or technical approval and CAB authorization before implementation; an emergency change, made immediately to resolve a major incident or to apply a security patch, bypasses group and peer review and goes straight to authorization. The design consequence is that the catalogue of standard changes is where a process earns its speed: every routine, rehearsed change moved into it is a change that no longer waits for a meeting, and every emergency change is a reason to ask afterwards why it was not foreseen.

The evidence against heavyweight approval is unusually direct. The DORA (DevOps Research and Assessment) programme, in its 2019 State of DevOps Report, found that change approvals are best implemented through peer review during development, supplemented by automation that detects, prevents and corrects bad changes early. Approval by people outside the team, a change approval board or a senior manager, had a negative impact on software delivery performance, and the research found no evidence that a more formal, external review was associated with lower change failure rates. Such processes slow delivery, which leads to larger batches released less often, each with a bigger impact on production. The same analysis keeps the legitimate goal of approval: segregation of duties, the rule that the author of a change is not its only approver, is a common regulatory requirement, and peer review satisfies it without a weekly board.

Too light fails more loudly. On 1 August 2012 Knight Capital's automated equity router sent more than 4 million orders into the market in 45 minutes while trying to fill 212 customer orders, traded more than 397 million shares and lost more than 460 million dollars. The Securities and Exchange Commission found that new code deployed incorrectly in late July had triggered a defective function left in the router since 2005, that 97 automated emails had flagged the error before the market opened without anyone acting on them, and that the firm lacked adequate controls for deploying and testing code and written procedures for responding to incidents; it paid a 12 million dollar penalty under an order of 16 October 2013. On 19 July 2024 CrowdStrike released a content configuration update for its Windows sensor at 04:09 UTC (Coordinated Universal Time) that crashed the systems receiving it until it was reverted at 05:27 UTC; its preliminary review found that a bug in its content validator had let problematic content pass, and committed to staggered deployment of such updates starting with a canary, and to giving customers more control over their delivery. In both cases the change that hurt was one treated as routine: a deployment, a content update, not a project with a review.

Network operations has its own mechanisms, and the best of them make the safe path the default. Junos, which edits a candidate configuration and commits it as a whole, supports a confirmed commit: the change takes effect, and unless it is confirmed within the deadline (600 seconds, 10 minutes, by default on Junos, adjustable through NETCONF (the Network Configuration Protocol) from 1 second up to 4,294,967,295 seconds) the device rolls back to the previous configuration by itself, so a change that cuts off the operator's own access undoes itself. Pre-change and post-change checks, a saved copy of the running configuration, a tested back-out plan and a maintenance window chosen for low impact complete the picture, and each of them is worth only as much as its last rehearsal.

The record is the half most often neglected. NIST's monitoring phase exists because controlling change is not enough to keep a system in its approved state: automated comparison against the baseline finds components nobody documented, misconfigurations and unauthorized changes, which are as much a security signal as an operational one, since an unrecorded change on a firewall is either a process failure or an intruder. In practice the record is assembled from three sources that should agree: the change ticket, the configuration diff or version history, and the device's own audit log of who changed what and when. When they agree, the question that opens most incident reviews, what changed just before the graph turned, has an answer in a minute; when they do not, the investigation starts by reconstructing history instead of fixing the system.

idempotence.def: The property that doing something twice has the same effect as doing it once.
idempotence.context: It is what makes retrying safe, and retrying is unavoidable: networks lose responses, so a client that got no answer cannot know whether the work happened. Without idempotence the only options are to risk duplicating the action or to risk skipping it. This is why payment interfaces take an idempotency key, why configuration tools describe desired state rather than steps, and why the interesting question about any interface is what happens when the same request arrives twice.

rto-rpo.def: How long recovery may take, and how much recent data may be lost - the two numbers that turn continuity from an aspiration into a design.
rto-rpo.context: They are useful because they cost money in opposite ways. A short recovery time buys standby capacity that sits idle; a short recovery point buys replication and the bandwidth to sustain it. Stating both forces the business to say what an hour of downtime and an hour of lost work are actually worth, which is the conversation continuity planning exists to have. The failure mode is declaring numbers nobody has tested, which produces a plan that is precise and untrue.

secure-boot.def: Checking each stage of startup against a signature before running it, so code that loads before the operating system cannot be replaced silently.
secure-boot.context: It closes a specific gap: anything running before the operating system is above every defence the operating system provides, so a bootkit sees the security software start and can lie to it. The chain has to be rooted in hardware. The trade is control - the same mechanism that stops unsigned malicious code stops unsigned legitimate code, which is why the argument about who holds the signing keys for general-purpose hardware is a genuine one rather than an obstruction.

persistence.def: An attacker's arrangements for surviving a reboot, a password change or a partial cleanup: whatever keeps access to a system after the original way in is closed. MITRE ATT&CK tracks it as tactic TA0003. (In load balancing the same word means session stickiness, a different concept with its own entry.)
persistence.context: It is the difference between an incident that ends and one that returns, and it is why containment is judged by whether the intruder can come back rather than by whether the current session is closed. The mechanisms are almost always legitimate features (scheduled tasks, startup entries, service accounts, mail rules, added credentials on an identity provider), which is why hunting for persistence is a review of configuration rather than a search for files, and why an organization that reimages a host without auditing identity often finds the visitor already waiting.
persistence.depth:
How the field defines it. MITRE ATT&CK, the knowledge base of adversary behaviour that MITRE started in 2013, describes the persistence tactic, TA0003, in one line: the adversary is trying to maintain their foothold. Its techniques are those used to keep access to systems across restarts, changed credentials and other interruptions that could cut access off, and they include any access, action or configuration change that does so, such as replacing or hijacking legitimate code or adding startup code. The tactic was created on 17 October 2018; as read in version 20.1 (13 October 2026) it groups 22 techniques. Read as a list, they are a tour of features administrators use every day: account manipulation, account creation and valid accounts; boot or logon autostart execution and initialization scripts; scheduled tasks and jobs; creating or modifying system processes; event-triggered execution; Office application startup; browser and software extensions; server software components such as web shells; modifying the authentication process; implanting an internal image; pre-OS boot (persistence that loads before the operating system); external remote services; Background Intelligent Transfer Service (BITS) jobs; cloud application integration; power settings; and traffic signalling, where a port opens only after a secret knock.

Identity is the durable layer. Account manipulation (T1098) has seven sub-techniques: additional cloud credentials, additional email delegate permissions, additional cloud roles, Secure Shell (SSH) authorized keys, device registration, additional container cluster roles and additional local or domain groups. Each survives a password reset of the account that was first compromised, because it is not that account. Microsoft's own incident is the clearest public example. Detected on 12 January 2024 and described in guidance for responders on 25 January, Midnight Blizzard sprayed passwords against a legacy, non-production test tenant account that had no multi-factor authentication (MFA), used it to reach a legacy test OAuth application (OAuth being the authorization framework of Request for Comments (RFC) 6749) with elevated access to the corporate environment, created additional malicious OAuth applications and a new user account to consent to them, and granted itself the Exchange Online full_access_as_app role, which reads mailboxes. Microsoft's note on why attackers like this route is the definition of persistence in practice: abusing OAuth lets them keep access to applications even if they lose the account they started with.

In the application and the mailbox. ATT&CK's Outlook Rules sub-technique (T1137.005) describes rules that load whenever Outlook starts and run code when the attacker sends a specially crafted message, so the trigger arrives from outside long after the intrusion. A web shell (T1505.003) is a script placed on an openly accessible web server that gives the attacker a command interface and a gateway into the network; ATT&CK records Sandworm deploying the Neo-REGEORG web shell on an internet-facing server during the 2022 attack on Ukraine's electricity grid. Scheduled execution (T1053) covers at, cron, Windows scheduled tasks, systemd timers and container orchestration jobs.

On network and security devices. Appliances are a favourite place to persist because few organizations inspect them like servers. On 10 April 2025 Fortinet's product security team described a threat actor who, after using known vulnerabilities to get into FortiGate devices, created a symbolic link between the user filesystem and the root filesystem inside the folder that serves the language files of its Secure Sockets Layer virtual private network (SSL-VPN). The change lived in the user filesystem and escaped detection, so devices later upgraded to versions that fixed the original flaws could still give the attacker read-only access to their files. Devices that had never enabled the SSL-VPN were not affected. Fortinet's response shows what eviction takes: an antivirus and intrusion prevention signature that removes the link, FortiOS 7.6.2, 7.4.7, 7.2.11, 7.0.17 and 6.4.16 removing it on upgrade and refusing to serve such links, and advice to treat all configuration as potentially compromised. The same post cites FortiGuard research putting exploitation of known vulnerabilities at an average of 4.76 days after disclosure. ATT&CK also records attackers in the 2025 wiper attacks in Poland setting FortiGate scheduled tasks to run their own command-line scripts weekly, and lists ROMMONkit and TFTP (Trivial File Transfer Protocol) Boot among its pre-OS boot sub-techniques (T1542), where persistence lives in firmware or boot images below anything host software can see, and where the mitigation is boot integrity anchored in a Trusted Platform Module (TPM) and secure boot.

Hunting and eviction. Because the mechanisms are configuration, the hunt is a comparison: scheduled tasks, cron tables and timers, services, autostart entries, SSH authorized_keys files, mailbox rules and delegates, application registrations, consent grants and added credentials in the identity provider, appliance configuration and file systems, each checked against a known good baseline. Two lessons follow from the cases above. Patching closes the way in but does not remove what was left behind, as the FortiGate link showed. Rebuilding a host does not remove persistence held in the identity layer, as the OAuth applications showed. The malware guide of the National Institute of Standards and Technology (NIST) adds that for stealthy, long-lived intrusions removal often means reinstalling the operating system and applications and restoring data from known good backups; the containment question to ask is not whether the session is closed but whether every route back has been found.

Neighbours, and a homonym. Initial access is how an attacker gets in; privilege escalation is how they get more; lateral movement is how they reach other systems; command and control (C2) is how they take instructions; persistence is how they stay, and the P in APT (advanced persistent threat) refers to it. Dwell time, the interval between intrusion and detection, is largely a measure of how well persistence worked. In load balancing, persistence means something unrelated: F5 describes BIG-IP session persistence as tracking session data, such as which pool member served a client, so that the client's requests keep reaching the same pool member, which is covered by the session persistence entry.

command-and-control.def: The channel a compromised host uses to receive instructions and report back, and by extension the infrastructure at the other end of it; usually abbreviated C2.
command-and-control.context: It is the most reliably detectable stage of an intrusion, because it has to be repetitive: something must check in, and checking in leaves a rhythm. That is why detection focuses on beaconing (regular intervals, consistent sizes, a destination no other host in the estate talks to) rather than on content, which is encrypted. Modern channels hide in ordinary services precisely to defeat that, using cloud storage, chat platforms and DNS, so the useful signal is often a host talking to something normal in an abnormal pattern.
command-and-control.depth:
What it is, and where the phrase comes from. In military usage, as the US Department of Defense dictionary quoted in the glossary of the National Institute of Standards and Technology (NIST) puts it, command and control is the exercise of authority and direction by a properly designated commander over assigned and attached forces, through personnel, equipment, communications, facilities and procedures. Security borrowed the phrase for the attacker's side of the same problem: once code is running on a victim, the operator needs a way to tell it what to do and to receive what it finds. In the intrusion kill chain described by Eric Hutchins, Michael Cloppert and Rohan Amin of Lockheed Martin, command and control (C2) is the sixth of seven phases, after installation and before actions on objectives: compromised hosts typically beacon outbound to an internet controller server to establish the channel, and once it is up the intruders have hands on the keyboard inside the network. MITRE ATT&CK has carried it as a tactic, TA0011, since 17 October 2018, defined as the adversary trying to communicate with compromised systems to control them; it is not the same as exfiltration, which ATT&CK keeps as a separate tactic even when the same channel carries the stolen data, nor as lateral movement, which is the spread from host to host inside the network that the channel then directs.

How a channel is built. Inbound connections to an infected host are usually blocked by firewalls and address translation, so the implant calls out, which is why the kill chain describes C2 as outbound beaconing. ATT&CK lists 18 techniques under the tactic, and their names are a catalogue of the ways to blend in: application layer protocols, encrypted channels, protocol tunnelling, proxies, web services, non-standard ports, data encoding and obfuscation, multi-stage and fallback channels, remote access tools, traffic signalling, removable media for isolated networks, and the transfer of further tools down the same channel. Application Layer Protocol, T1071, has five sub-techniques (web protocols, file transfer protocols, mail, DNS, and publish/subscribe protocols), because commands embedded in ordinary protocol traffic pass where unusual protocols would not; inside a network, ATT&CK notes, the hops between a proxy or pivot node and other hosts tend to use SMB (Server Message Block), SSH (Secure Shell) or RDP (Remote Desktop Protocol). The tactic's own description sums up the strategy: adversaries commonly attempt to mimic normal, expected traffic.

Staying reachable. A channel that depends on one address dies with that address, so operators build in ways to find the controller again. Dynamic Resolution, T1568, covers malware that shares an algorithm with the infrastructure so that both sides can compute the day's domain name, IP address or port: fast-flux DNS, domain generation algorithms (DGAs) and DNS calculation are its three sub-techniques, and ATT&CK notes that they also serve as fallback when contact with the primary server is lost. Peer-to-peer designs remove the single controller altogether, and the defenders' answers, from registering generated domains before the operator can to sinkholing them, are a large part of the history of botnets. The lesson for C2 is that blocking an address or a domain buys hours, and denying the mechanism buys months.

How it is detected. Repetition is the weakness, and ATT&CK's detection strategies for the tactic are written around it. For application layer C2, DET0444 looks for common protocols used by processes that do not normally use them, high outbound byte counts, irregular ports, unbalanced traffic or beacon-like intervals, and C2 embedded in TLS or HTTP headers or tunnelled through DNS over HTTPS; for dynamic resolution, DET0039 looks for bursts of DNS queries from processes that do not normally generate network requests, high-entropy or newly registered domain names and repeated failed lookups. Encryption hides the content but not the handshake: JA3, invented at Salesforce in 2017, concatenates the version, cipher suites, extensions, elliptic curves and elliptic curve formats a client offers in its TLS Client Hello and hashes them with MD5 into a 32-character fingerprint, and JA3S does the same for the server's reply, so that the pair identifies a particular malware family talking to its particular controller; the project is no longer maintained by Salesforce, and its creator, John Althouse, carries the idea forward at FoxIO as JA4. Signature sets encode what is already known: the open Emerging Threats malware rules for Suricata 7.0.3 carried 7,322 active signatures with CnC in their names when read in November 2026, 422 of them naming a beacon. David Bianco's Pyramid of Pain explains why the better detections target behaviour: the C2 server's IP address and domain sit near the bottom, cheap to change, while the C2 information embedded in protocols is a network artefact further up and costs the adversary more to alter.

How it is blocked. Most firewalls can refuse traffic to known controllers. On a FortiGate the setting lives in the intrusion prevention system (IPS) sensor's Botnet C&C section, where scanning outgoing connections to botnet sites is set to block or monitor (scan-botnet-connections in the command line); the lists come from FortiGuard, and a hit is logged with the event type botnet and the message Botnet C&C Communication, which is exactly the sort of alert a security operations centre (SOC) should never leave unread. DNS filtering and response policy zones do the same at name resolution, and community blocklists such as abuse.ch's Feodo Tracker publish the controllers of banking and loader families (Dridex, Emotet, TrickBot, QakBot and BazarLoader); when read in November 2026 its datasets were empty. Reputation blocking is a floor, not a strategy: it catches the infrastructure that has already been reported, and a channel that runs through a popular cloud service cannot be blocked by address without blocking the service.

How it is taken down. Because the channel is the operator's lifeline, cutting it is the standard law enforcement play. In August 2023 the US Federal Bureau of Investigation (FBI) redirected Qakbot's botnet traffic to and through servers it controlled, which instructed more than 700,000 infected computers worldwide to download an uninstaller, in an operation spanning seven countries. Private action follows the same logic. In 2023 Microsoft, the software company Fortra and the Health Information Sharing and Analysis Center obtained a US court order against cracked, legacy copies of Fortra's Cobalt Strike, an adversary simulation platform introduced in 2012 and widely abused by criminals, including in attacks on the government of Costa Rica and on Ireland's Health Service Executive; Microsoft described it as a departure, aimed at the tool itself instead of disrupting the command and control of a malware family.

Three spellings, one meaning. C2 is the form in most threat intelligence writing, in the kill chain paper and in David Bianco's Pyramid of Pain, which ranks C2 information embedded in network protocols among the network artefacts a defender can detect and puts backdoors used to establish C2 among the attacker's tools. C&C is the older botnet-era spelling and survives in product interfaces and community feeds: a FortiGate's intrusion prevention system (IPS) sensor has a Botnet C&C section and logs hits with the message Botnet C&C Communication, and abuse.ch's Feodo Tracker describes its subject as botnet command&control (C&C) infrastructure. CnC is the house style of the Emerging Threats signature sets, whose open malware rules for Suricata 7.0.3 carried 7,322 active signatures with CnC in their messages when read in November 2026. MITRE ATT&CK avoids all three and writes the tactic out in full, Command and Control, TA0011. Search tools and log queries should therefore look for all four forms when hunting through a vendor's documentation or a rule set.

The compounds in daily use. A C2 server is the controller the implants call; a C2 channel is the communication path between them, whatever protocol it rides; C2 infrastructure is everything the operator runs to keep that path alive, from domains and virtual servers to redirectors and cloud accounts; C2 traffic is what crosses the wire, and a beacon is one periodic check-in within it. The Structured Threat Information Expression (STIX) 2.1 standard, the OASIS format for exchanging threat intelligence, gives the concept a machine-readable label: its infrastructure type vocabulary includes command-and-control, defined as infrastructure used for command and control (C2), typically a domain name or IP address, alongside a separate botnet type for the hosts that make up a botnet. The JA3 project's README uses the full phrase for one half of its fingerprint pair, labelling JA3S as the fingerprint of the command and control server's response. A C2 framework, finally, is the operator's software suite: the server, the agents it builds and the console that drives them.

C2 frameworks and red teams. The same frameworks serve attackers and testers. Red teams need to emulate an adversary's command channel to test whether a security operations centre (SOC) will notice it, and commercial and open-source frameworks exist for exactly that purpose. Cobalt Strike, introduced in 2012 as an adversary simulation platform and used by red teams in government and industry, is the standard example of the overlap: criminals took to stealing older versions and altering them, until in 2023 Microsoft, its owner Fortra and the Health Information Sharing and Analysis Center obtained a US court order against the cracked copies. For a defender, the practical consequence is that a C2 framework seen on the network is not proof of a criminal intrusion, and not proof of an authorized test either, until someone checks the rules of engagement.

Reading a C2 indicator. Most C2 indicators that reach a defender are addresses and domains: a threat feed listing controller IP addresses, a STIX object of type command-and-control, a blocklist entry. They are useful for hours or days and then go stale, which is why the Pyramid of Pain puts IP addresses and domains near its base. Feodo Tracker is a reminder of how quickly that ground shifts: when read in November 2026 its datasets for the families it tracks, among them Emotet and QakBot, were empty. Fingerprints of how the channel behaves, such as a JA3 and JA3S pair or a beaconing pattern, last longer, and detections written against the C2 technique itself last longest.

The other C2s. Two older meanings still turn up in network and security work and have nothing to do with attackers.
