The US Department of Defense's Trusted Computer System Evaluation Criteria of 26 December 1985, the Orange Book, defined Class C2, Controlled Access Protection, for systems that enforce finer discretionary access control than Class C1 and make users individually accountable through login procedures, auditing of security-relevant events and resource isolation. The class survives as a setting name: SQL Server's c2 audit mode records both failed and successful attempts to access statements and objects in files of up to 200 megabytes, and Microsoft's documentation marks it for removal, noting that the C2 security standard has been superseded by Common Criteria certification. In military writing, C2 keeps its original sense of command over forces.

Neighbours. C2 is the everyday abbreviation, also written C&C and CnC. Beaconing is the observable rhythm of a channel, botnets are fleets of hosts under one command channel, exfiltration often rides it out, and lateral movement is what it directs inside the network. Red teams run the same kind of infrastructure legitimately, which is why their tools keep turning up in criminal hands. The numbers worth keeping: the sixth of seven kill chain phases, ATT&CK tactic TA0011 with 18 techniques in version 20, and a JA3 fingerprint of 32 hexadecimal characters.

key-management.def: Generating, storing, rotating, revoking and retiring cryptographic keys: the part of cryptography that actually fails.
key-management.context: Algorithms are rarely broken in practice; keys are copied, checked into repositories, shared between environments, left on decommissioned hardware and never rotated because nobody knows what would break. The useful questions are therefore administrative: where does this key exist, who can use it, what happens the day it must be replaced, and has that ever been done. An organization that cannot answer the last one has encryption whose strength is untested in the only way that matters.
key-management.depth:
The United States National Institute of Standards and Technology (NIST) defines key management as the activities involving the handling of cryptographic keys and related parameters during their entire life cycle: generation, storage, establishment, entry and output, use and destruction. The reason it deserves a discipline of its own is as old as modern cryptography. In 1883 Auguste Kerckhoffs wrote that a cipher system must not require secrecy and must be able to fall into enemy hands without causing trouble, and that the key must be easy to change. Everything that is secret about a well-designed system is therefore in its keys. NIST's guide says it with a safe: if the combination is known to an adversary, the strongest safe provides no security, and poor key management may easily compromise strong algorithms.

The reference text is NIST Special Publication (SP) 800-57, Recommendation for Key Management, in three parts: general guidance (Part 1, revision 5 of May 2020, by Elaine Barker), best practices for the organizations that manage keys (Part 2, revision 1 of May 2019) and application-specific guidance (Part 3). Part 1 distinguishes nineteen types of key, from private signature keys to symmetric key-wrapping keys, and sets a rule that prevents a surprising number of incidents: in general, a single key shall be used for only one purpose, be it encryption, authentication, key wrapping, random bit generation or digital signatures.

A key has a life with named stages. SP 800-57 gives six states: pre-activation (generated, not yet authorized for use), active, suspended, deactivated, compromised and destroyed. It groups them into four phases, pre-operational, operational, post-operational and destroyed. The post-operational phase is the one administrators forget. A deactivated key no longer protects new data, but it may still be needed to process old data, to decrypt an archive or to verify an old signature, so retiring a key is not the same as deleting it, and deleting it too early destroys the data it protected. Records about a destroyed key may outlive the key itself.

How long a key stays active is its cryptoperiod, the time span during which it is authorized for use. NIST lists what a limit buys: less material for cryptanalysis, less exposure if one key is compromised, and less time for an attacker to work on the key or on the controls around it. Its suggested values are a usable baseline: one to three years for a private signature key, at most two years of originator use for a symmetric data-encryption key, with up to three more years of recipient use, about one year for a symmetric master key, and a single transaction for an ephemeral key-agreement key. Strength has a calendar too. A security strength of 112 bits, which corresponds to RSA (Rivest-Shamir-Adleman) with 2048-bit keys, is acceptable through 2030, and at least 128 bits, the level of AES-128 (Advanced Encryption Standard) or RSA with 3072-bit keys, from 2031. For the quantum-vulnerable signature algorithms NIST's draft transition report of November 2024 goes further, and would disallow them after 2035.

Where a key lives decides who can use it. Keys are arranged in hierarchies, because a key that encrypts data must itself be protected, and the usual way is to encrypt it with another key. Amazon Web Services (AWS) calls this envelope encryption and notes the unavoidable end of the chain: eventually one key must remain in plaintext, so that top-level key, the root key, is kept inside a hardware security module (HSM) validated to FIPS (Federal Information Processing Standards) 140-3 level 3 and never leaves it unencrypted. Modules are graded by that standard, FIPS 140-3, published on 22 March 2019 as the successor of FIPS 140-2, in four increasing levels; the rules for public certification authorities demand level 3 for a CA (certification authority) private key. Network devices use the same pattern on a smaller scale. On F5 BIG-IP, Secure Vault encrypts the passphrases in the configuration, shown with a $M$ prefix, under a master key that is shared by the members of a high-availability group, and encrypts that master key under a unit key unique to each device and held in non-volatile memory on hardware platforms. On FortiGate, private data encryption generates a random master password that encrypts sensitive configuration data, and the Trusted Platform Module (TPM) protects it with a 2048-bit key that never leaves the chip. Fortinet spells out the operational consequence, which applies to every such scheme: a backup taken with one key cannot be restored on a unit that holds a different one.

Rotation is the test of whether a key is managed or merely stored. A managed service makes it a property of the key: AWS Key Management Service (KMS) generates new key material every year by default once automatic rotation is enabled, accepts a custom period or a rotation on demand, and keeps the earlier material so that old ciphertext still decrypts. Outside such a service the organization needs an inventory. SP 800-57 defines it as information about each key that does not include the key itself, such as owner, type, algorithm, application and expiry date, and requires long-term keys to be inventoried when they are generated. Between products, the Key Management Interoperability Protocol (KMIP), an OASIS standard whose version 2.1 dates from 14 December 2020, lets clients and key servers from different vendors speak one protocol.

The incidents are seldom about mathematics. On 24 March 2023 GitHub replaced the RSA key that identifies its SSH (Secure Shell) service after discovering that the private key had been briefly exposed in a public repository, through what it believed to be an inadvertent publication; nothing was known to have been abused, and every user connecting over SSH with RSA still had to update a known_hosts file. In 2023 Microsoft reported that the actor it calls Storm-0558 had acquired a signing key for consumer accounts and used it to forge tokens that opened mailboxes in the OWA and Outlook.com services. Its investigation of September 2023 named as the most probable route a crash dump from April 2021 that left the isolated signing environment for a debugging environment, later reached through an engineer's compromised account; an update of March 2024 added that no dump containing the key had been found. A second failure made the first one matter: the mail system accepted a token for enterprise mail signed with the consumer key, because key scope was not validated, which is the single-purpose rule broken at the verifier.

A compromise needs a rehearsed answer. SP 800-57 states that once a key is compromised its cryptoperiod is no longer valid, and public certification authorities must revoke a certificate within 24 hours of obtaining evidence that its private key was compromised. The neighbouring disciplines differ mainly in what is being managed. A public key infrastructure manages the binding of public keys to names; secrets management handles passwords and tokens with the same habits; key escrow deliberately gives a third party a copy. Key management is the layer beneath all of them: knowing which keys exist, where, for what purpose and until when.

blameless.def: Reviewing an incident to find the conditions that allowed it, rather than the person who acted within them.
blameless.context: The argument for it is practical rather than kind: people who expect blame report less, later and less accurately, and an organization that cannot see its near misses is flying on the subset of events too large to hide. The discipline is asking why the action made sense at the time - what the operator saw, what the tooling suggested, what the pressure was - because a system where one wrong command causes an outage has a design problem that will outlive the person who ran it.

wireguard.def: A VPN (virtual private network) protocol built around a deliberately small codebase and a fixed set of modern cryptographic choices, with no negotiation.
wireguard.context: The absence of negotiation is the design argument. IPsec and TLS let two ends agree on algorithms, which is flexible and is also where downgrade attacks and configuration mismatches live; WireGuard removes the conversation by shipping one suite and versioning the whole protocol if it must change. The trade is real: no algorithm agility means a break in one primitive requires a new protocol version everywhere, and the small feature set pushes identity, policy and address assignment out to whatever wraps it.
wireguard.depth:
What it is. WireGuard is a layer 3 secure tunnel designed by Jason A. Donenfeld and described in his whitepaper, WireGuard: Next Generation Kernel Network Tunnel, a version of which appeared at the Network and Distributed System Security Symposium (NDSS) in 2017. It is implemented as a virtual network interface in the Linux kernel and aims, in the paper's words, to replace IPsec for most use cases as well as user-space and TLS-based solutions such as OpenVPN, while being more secure, faster and easier to use. The Linux implementation is less than 4,000 lines of code, excluding the cryptographic primitives, so that auditing it is easy. It carries IPv4 and IPv6, including either inside the other, and nothing else: it is deliberately layer 3 only, with no Ethernet bridging. Linus Torvalds wrote on the netdev list on 2 August 2018 that maybe the code was not perfect, but that compared to the horrors that are OpenVPN and IPsec it was a work of art, and Linux 5.6, released on 29 March 2020, shipped it in the mainline kernel. What it is not matters as much: it is a tunnel, not a remote-access product, and the paper says plainly that key distribution is the wrong layer for it to address.

Cryptokey routing. The central idea is one table. Each peer is identified only by its public key, a 32-byte Curve25519 point that is 44 characters in Base64, and each key is associated with a list of allowed IP addresses. On the way out, a packet's destination address selects the peer whose allowed IPs contain it, and the packet is encrypted for that peer. On the way in, a packet is decrypted with the session that authenticates it, and the inner source address is then checked against that peer's allowed IPs; if the key does not own the address, the packet is dropped. The same table therefore does authentication, access control and routing. Endpoints are learned rather than fixed: a peer's endpoint is updated to the most recent source address and port of correctly authenticated packets, which is how a laptop roams between networks without renegotiating. The configuration file is equally small: an interface section with a private key and an optional ListenPort, which the wg manual page says is chosen randomly if not specified (its examples use 51820), and one section per peer with its public key, an optional endpoint and its allowed IPs.

The cryptography, and why it does not negotiate. The handshake is an instance of Trevor Perrin's Noise protocol framework, named in the protocol itself as Noise_IKpsk2_25519_ChaChaPoly_BLAKE2s: Curve25519 for elliptic-curve Diffie-Hellman, ChaCha20 with Poly1305 in the authenticated encryption with associated data (AEAD) construction of RFC (Request for Comments) 7539 (since obsoleted by RFC 8439 of June 2018), BLAKE2s for hashing, and the HMAC-based Extract-and-Expand Key Derivation Function (HKDF) of RFC 5869 for key derivation. The paper calls WireGuard cryptographically opinionated: it intentionally lacks cipher and protocol agility, so if holes are found in the primitives all endpoints will have to update, a cost it accepts because, as the continuing torrent of SSL (Secure Sockets Layer) and TLS vulnerabilities shows, cipher agility increases complexity monumentally. The handshake takes one round trip, gives perfect forward secrecy and a high degree of identity hiding, and has known edges the project lists itself: a compromise of a responder's private key together with logs of past handshakes would reveal who sent them, though not the data, and the protocol is not post-quantum secure by default. For the record-now-decrypt-later threat it offers an optional pre-shared 256-bit symmetric key per pair of peers, mixed into the handshake as an extra layer, which the paper describes as a sound trade-off for the extremely paranoid.

Messages and timers. There are four message types: handshake initiation (1), handshake response (2), cookie reply (3) and transport data (4). A transport data message carries exactly 16 bytes of header fields, the type, three reserved bytes, the receiver's index and a 64-bit counter, then the encrypted inner packet and a 16-byte Poly1305 tag, all inside UDP; the inner packet is zero-padded before encryption to complicate traffic analysis, never beyond the path MTU (maximum transmission unit). Replays are rejected with a sliding window of roughly 2,000 counter values. The session machinery is driven by timers rather than by commands: a new handshake is started when a session is 120 seconds old (Rekey-After-Time), a session is refused after 180 seconds (Reject-After-Time), retries come every 5 seconds for up to 90, and a peer that has received data but has nothing to send replies within 10 seconds with a keepalive, an empty transport message. The consequence for troubleshooting is that there is no tunnel to bring up or down: wg show reports each peer's latest handshake and transfer counters, and a peer whose latest handshake is several minutes old has no valid session. Behind NAT (network address translation), a peer that rarely sends but must be reachable needs PersistentKeepalive, from 1 to 65535 seconds and off by default; the manual suggests 25 seconds and says most users will not need it.

Silence as a security property. WireGuard keeps no state before authentication and sends no response to unauthenticated packets, so to a scanner its port looks closed. Authenticating the very first message exposes it to replay, which the design answers with a 12-byte TAI64N timestamp, encrypted and authenticated, of which the responder keeps the greatest per peer. Because each handshake costs a Curve25519 multiplication, a responder under load may answer with a cookie reply instead of processing the message: the cookie is a MAC (message authentication code) of the initiator's IP address under a secret that changes every two minutes, and it is sent encrypted, which the paper presents as an improvement on the clear-text cookies of DTLS (Datagram Transport Layer Security) and IKEv2 (Internet Key Exchange version 2). The project's own list of limitations names the costs of these choices: before the mac2 check engages, handshake computations can use considerable processor (CPU) time; the system clock serves as the monotonic counter, so a clock that jumps forward can lock a user out of their own keys and one controlled by an attacker could let a stored initiation be used later; and roaming without an extra round trip means an active man in the middle can replace a peer's source address.

What it leaves out on purpose. WireGuard runs only over UDP, and the project explicitly refuses to tunnel over TCP because of the poor performance of TCP inside TCP; it does no obfuscation, leaving both to layers above it. A network that blocks outbound UDP therefore blocks WireGuard, which is the exact situation in which TLS-based remote access, discussed in the entry on SSL VPNs (virtual private networks), kept its advantage. Its ChaCha20 and Poly1305 primitives are fast in software on general-purpose processors, and the project notes that dedicated hardware support for them is still limited. The wg-quick helper sets the interface MTU automatically from the endpoint addresses or the default route unless told otherwise, which matters when the tunnel crosses a path with a smaller MTU than expected. And everything an enterprise means by remote access, user identity, multi-factor authentication, group policy, address assignment and key revocation, is outside the protocol: it is supplied by whatever system distributes the keys and writes the allowed IPs, which is why WireGuard so often appears as the data plane underneath a product rather than as the product itself.

accounting.def: The third A in AAA: recording what an authenticated party actually did, for billing, capacity or evidence.
accounting.context: It is the one most often configured last and needed most under pressure, because authentication and authorization answer questions about the present while accounting is the only one that answers questions about the past. In carrier networks it exists to produce an invoice; in enterprise networks it exists so that someone can say which account issued which command on which device, which is exactly the question asked after an outage or an intrusion and exactly the record nobody enabled. RFC 2866 gives RADIUS (Remote Authentication Dial-In User Service) accounting its shape: Accounting-Request packets on UDP 1813 with an Acct-Status-Type of Start (1), Stop (2) or Interim-Update (3), plus Accounting-On (7) and Accounting-Off (8) when a NAS boots or shuts down, carrying Acct-Session-Id, the input and output octet and packet counters, Acct-Session-Time and Acct-Terminate-Cause, each acknowledged by an Accounting-Response and retried with backoff until it is. RFC 8907 gives TACACS+ its accounting exchange with START, STOP and WATCHDOG flags, which on a router means every command an administrator ran. Syslog (RFC 5424) and a device's own configuration change log carry the rest, and NIST's control catalogue says what a record must establish: what happened, when, where, from what source, with what outcome, and the identity of who was involved.
accounting.depth:
Accounting is the part of AAA that produces a record, and the record is the point: authentication decides who may enter and authorization decides what they may do, but only accounting can say afterwards what was done, by which account, on which device, and when. Carriers built it to bill, which is why the RADIUS attributes count octets; enterprises need it for the question that follows every outage and every intrusion, and discover on the day whether it was ever switched on. The protocols that carry it are the same ones that carry authentication, each with an accounting side of its own.

RADIUS accounting is RFC 2866, published in June 2000 by Rigney as an Informational companion to RFC 2865. The network access server sends Accounting-Request packets (code 4) to UDP port 1813 and expects an Accounting-Response (code 5) for each; the RFC recommends that "the client continue attempting to send the Accounting-Request packet until it receives an acknowledgement, using some form of backoff", which is why accounting survives a brief server outage and why a long one produces a flood of delayed records when the server returns. The Acct-Status-Type attribute says what kind of record it is: 1 Start when a session begins, 2 Stop when it ends, 3 Interim-Update at intervals during it, 7 Accounting-On and 8 Accounting-Off when the NAS itself starts or stops serving, with further values for tunnels and 15 for a failed attempt. The attributes carry the measurements: Acct-Session-Id to tie Start, updates and Stop together, Acct-Input-Octets and Acct-Output-Octets, Acct-Input-Packets and Acct-Output-Packets, Acct-Session-Time in seconds, Acct-Terminate-Cause for why it ended, Acct-Delay-Time for how long the record waited, Acct-Multi-Session-Id to link related sessions and Acct-Authentic to say who authenticated it. The Class attribute the server placed in the Access-Accept comes back unmodified, so a tag the policy engine attached at login is on every record. The Request Authenticator of an accounting packet is an MD5 over the packet with sixteen zero octets in the authenticator's place and the shared secret appended, which lets the server detect a record from a client that does not know the secret, and nothing more; the whole record is otherwise in clear text, as everything in RADIUS is without RadSec.

TACACS+ accounting, in RFC 8907 of September 2020, is the third of the protocol's three packet types, 0x03, and its records are about administrators rather than subscribers. The accounting request carries flags, START (0x02) for the beginning of a task, STOP (0x04) for its end and WATCHDOG (0x08) to report that a long task is still in progress, and because TACACS+ authorizes commands one by one, a router configured for command accounting sends a record for each command an administrator executes, with the username, the device, the command line and the time. That stream, kept on a server, is the answer to who changed what; it exists only for devices where it was enabled and only for the period the server retained.

The device's own logs are the complement. Syslog, in RFC 5424 of March 2009, defines a message of a header, structured data and free text, with a priority computed as facility times eight plus severity, severities from 0 Emergency to 7 Debug, facilities 4 and 10 reserved for security and authorization messages and 16 to 23 for local use, and a timestamp derived from RFC 3339; the document specifies the message and leaves transport to others, UDP in RFC 5426 and TLS in RFC 5425, which every implementation must support. Cisco's Configuration Change Notification and Logging feature shows what a device can record on its own: it "allows the tracking of configuration changes entered on a per-session and per-user basis by implementing an archive function" and "saves configuration logs that track each configuration command that is applied, who applied the command, the parser return code (PRC) for the command, and the time the command was applied", with options to hide passwords in the log and to send each entry to syslog. Configuration backup tools close the loop by storing every device's configuration in a version-controlled repository and showing the difference between one day and the next; Oxidized, which describes itself as a network device configuration backup tool and a RANCID replacement, supports over 130 operating system types and writes to git, so that the diff between two commits is the change, even when the command accounting that would have named the author was never enabled.

What a record must contain is written down. NIST's control catalogue, SP 800-53, requires in AU-3 that audit records establish "what type of event occurred", "when the event occurred", "where the event occurred", the "source of the event", the "outcome of the event" and the "identity of any individuals, subjects, or objects/entities associated with the event"; AU-2 asks an organization to "provide a rationale for why the event types selected for logging are deemed to be adequate to support after-the-fact investigations of incidents"; AC-6(9) says simply "log the execution of privileged functions", because, in its discussion, the misuse of privileged functions by insiders or by attackers holding compromised accounts is "a serious and ongoing concern". Read together, those controls are the specification for an enterprise's accounting: RADIUS Start and Stop for every network session, TACACS+ command records for every administrative session, syslog with synchronized clocks from every device, and configuration history that shows what the commands did. The article on who did what and when assembles them into one design, and the regulations that demand it, from SOX to PCI DSS, have entries of their own.

tacacs.def: A protocol for centralizing administrative access to network devices, separating authentication, authorization and accounting into distinct exchanges.
tacacs.context: The separation is the practical difference from RADIUS (Remote Authentication Dial-In User Service): because authorization is its own exchange, a device can ask the server about each command as it is typed, which is how per-command control and full command logging work. That makes it the usual choice for device administration while RADIUS remains usual for network access. RFC 8907 (September 2020) documents the protocol as deployed: TCP port 49, a 12-byte header with major and minor version, type (0x01 authentication, 0x02 authorization, 0x03 accounting), sequence number, flags, session id and length, and a body obfuscated by XOR with MD5-derived padding of the shared secret; the RFC itself says that is "best referred to as 'obfuscation' and not 'encryption'" and that the protocol "does not include a security mechanism that would meet modern-day requirements". Cisco's comparison puts the contrast plainly: "TACACS+ encrypts the entire body of the packet but leaves a standard TACACS+ header." The dependency deserves stating - if the server is unreachable and local fallback was never configured or never tested, the estate becomes unmanageable at exactly the moment somebody needs to log in.
tacacs.depth:
TACACS+ is the protocol a router or switch uses to ask a server whether an administrator may log in, whether that administrator may run the command just typed, and to tell the server that the command was run. It is the descendant of the original TACACS of the ARPANET terminal servers and of Cisco's extended XTACACS, and it carried Cisco's name on it for two decades before it was written down for the record: RFC 8907, The Terminal Access Controller Access-Control System Plus (TACACS+) Protocol, published in September 2020 by Dahm and Ota of Google, Medway Gash of Cisco, Carrel and Grant as an Informational document, describes the protocol as deployed since "The Draft" of 1998, the vendor specification that was never standardized until this document. The TACACS and XTACACS entry covers the ancestors.

The protocol runs over TCP on port 49. Every packet begins with a 12-byte header: a major and minor version, a type octet, 0x01 for authentication, 0x02 for authorization and 0x03 for accounting, a sequence number, flags, a session identifier and the length of the body. The three types are separate conversations, and that separation is the point. A RADIUS Access-Accept combines authentication with whatever authorization the server chooses to attach; a TACACS+ authorization exchange is its own request and reply, which a device can make as often as it likes, including once per command. Cisco's comparison document, which also records that Cisco "seriously evaluated RADIUS as a security protocol before it developed TACACS+", states the consequence: "RADIUS does not allow users to control which commands can be executed on a router", whereas "TACACS+ provides two methods to control the authorization of router commands on a per-user or per-group basis". Accounting is a third exchange with its own flags, START (0x02), STOP (0x04) and WATCHDOG (0x08), so that a session's start, its end and its continued existence can each be recorded; the accounting entry and the article on who did what and when describe what the records contain.

Security is where RFC 8907 is unusually frank for a protocol document. The body of each packet is XORed with a pseudo-pad made of successive MD5 digests, the first computed over the session id, the shared key, the version and the sequence number and each later one over the same values plus the previous digest. The RFC says that this is "best referred to as 'obfuscation' and not 'encryption'", that the protocol "does not include a security mechanism that would meet modern-day requirements", and that it therefore "MUST be deployed over networks that ensure privacy and integrity", separated from other traffic. The header is never obfuscated, which is Cisco's "leaves a standard TACACS+ header". The practical reading is that TACACS+ belongs on a management network, or inside a tunnel, and that the shared key is a secret worth rotating. What is deployed in most estates is the RFC 8907 protocol on a protected network.

The operational risk is availability, and it is the one engineers remember. A device configured to authenticate administrators against TACACS+ servers it cannot reach will fall back to whatever its method list says, and if the list ends at the servers, or the local account at the end of it was never created or its password never tested, nobody can log in to fix the thing that broke the path to the servers. The discipline is a method list that ends in a tested local credential, servers reachable by more than one route, and a periodic exercise in which the fallback is actually used. The second habit is to treat the accounting side as a product in itself: command accounting from every device to a server that keeps it is the record that answers the question asked after every outage and every intrusion, and it exists only on devices where somebody turned it on.

Against RADIUS, the division is stable and worth stating as a rule: TACACS+ for device administration, where per-command authorization and command accounting are the requirement, and RADIUS for network access, where the user or device is being admitted to a port, an SSID or a VPN (virtual private network) and where 802.1X and the EAP methods only exist in RADIUS. Most estates run both, usually from the same policy servers, and the article on TACACS+ device administration walks a login and a command through the three exchanges.

rce.def: Remote code execution (RCE): a defect that lets an attacker run code of their choosing on a system across the network, typically without needing an account on it.
rce.context: A remote code execution (RCE) flaw is the top of the severity scale because it collapses every other step: no phishing, no credential theft, no lateral movement needed to get the first foothold. That is why an unauthenticated one in an internet-facing product produces emergency patching cycles regardless of what the scanner score says; in CVSS (Common Vulnerability Scoring System) terms it usually carries the vector AV:N/PR:N/UI:N (attack vector network, no privileges required, no user interaction) and scores 9.8 or 10. RCE describes an outcome, not a cause: memory corruption, command or code injection and unsafe deserialization all end there. The useful follow-up question is what the code runs as: the same defect is a different incident depending on whether the service was running with least privilege or as root.
rce.depth:
Remote code execution (RCE) is the outcome a defect produces, not a kind of defect. A bug qualifies when someone with network access to a program can make it execute instructions they supply, whether machine code, an operating system command, a script or a class loaded from elsewhere. Arbitrary code execution is the wider term; remote narrows it to an attacker who is not already on the machine. Most advisories add one more qualifier that matters as much as the other two: whether the attacker must first authenticate. An unauthenticated RCE in an internet-facing service is the worst ordinary finding in vulnerability management, because it collapses every other step of an intrusion: no phishing, no stolen password and no lateral movement is needed to get the first foothold.

Many different weaknesses arrive at the same place, and the 2025 edition of MITRE's CWE (Common Weakness Enumeration) Top 25, published in December 2025, shows which ones attackers actually use, through its count of each weakness's CVEs (Common Vulnerabilities and Exposures) in the Known Exploited Vulnerabilities (KEV) catalogue of CISA (the US Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency). Memory-safety errors are one family: out-of-bounds write, CWE-787, ranked fifth with 12 entries in KEV, use after free, CWE-416, seventh with 14, and heap-based buffer overflow, CWE-122, sixteenth with 6. Injection into an interpreter is the other: OS (operating system) command injection, CWE-78, ninth but with 20 KEV entries, more than any other weakness on the list, and code injection, CWE-94, tenth with 7, which CWE defines as building code from externally influenced input without neutralizing the elements that could change its syntax or behaviour. Deserialization of untrusted data, CWE-502, fifteenth with 11, turns an object graph sent by the attacker into live objects whose side effects run code. SQL injection and server-side template injection can end in code execution too when the database or template engine can reach the operating system.

The famous cases show each family. Shellshock, CVE-2014-6271, was GNU Bash through version 4.3 executing trailing strings after function definitions in environment variables, reachable remotely wherever a network service passed attacker input into the environment of a shell: Apache's CGI (Common Gateway Interface) modules, OpenSSH's ForceCommand and DHCP (Dynamic Host Configuration Protocol) clients. EternalBlue, CVE-2017-0144, was a flaw in the SMBv1 (Server Message Block version 1) server of Windows that let remote attackers execute arbitrary code with crafted packets; Microsoft fixed it in MS17-010 on 14 March 2017, and within months it was the spreading mechanism of WannaCrypt and then of the June 2017 Petya variant, as the Learn article on them tells. BlueKeep, CVE-2019-0708, gave an unauthenticated attacker code execution through RDP (Remote Desktop Protocol). Log4Shell, CVE-2021-44228, disclosed in December 2021 and found by Chen Zhaojun of Alibaba Cloud Security Team, let anyone who could get a string into a log message make Apache Log4j 2 load and run code from an attacker's LDAP (Lightweight Directory Access Protocol) server through its JNDI (Java Naming and Directory Interface) lookups; it scored the maximum 10.0, and CISA added it to KEV on the day it was published. Network equipment is no exception. F5 BIG-IP's Traffic Management User Interface, CVE-2020-5902, had RCE in undisclosed pages; FortiOS SSL-VPN (Secure Sockets Layer virtual private network) had a heap-based buffer overflow, CVE-2022-42475, allowing a remote unauthenticated attacker to execute arbitrary code or commands, already exploited when Fortinet published it in December 2022; and an out-of-bounds write in FortiOS, CVE-2024-21762, entered KEV on 9 February 2024, the day it was published.

Reading the score correctly is part of the job. In CVSS (the Common Vulnerability Scoring System), maintained by FIRST, a typical pre-authentication RCE has the vector AV:N/AC:L/PR:N/UI:N, network attack vector, low complexity, no privileges required and no user interaction, with high impact on confidentiality, integrity and availability, which gives 9.8 in version 3.1, or 10.0 when the scope changes as it did for Log4Shell. The same flaw behind a login reads PR:L and drops to 8.8, as NVD (the National Vulnerability Database) scored EternalBlue. Microsoft's severity system makes the threshold explicit in words: Critical means a vulnerability whose exploitation could allow code execution without user interaction, including self-propagating worms, and Microsoft asks customers to apply Critical updates immediately. Scores still mislead in both directions. A 9.8 on a service nobody can reach may wait; a 7.2 that requires administrator privileges on a firewall management interface exposed to the internet may not, because the attacker may already have those privileges from a stolen password. KEV status, exposure and the asset's role decide the urgency more than the base score does.

The defensive response has a fixed order. First reduce exposure: management interfaces, VPN (virtual private network) portals and remote desktop services should not be reachable from the whole internet, and Fortinet's own workaround for CVE-2022-42475 until a patch could be applied was to disable SSL-VPN altogether. Then patch, prioritizing what is in KEV and what faces the internet, and after patching an exploited RCE, hunt: Fortinet's advisory for CVE-2022-42475 told customers to check their systems against published indicators of compromise, because a patch removes the door but not an intruder already inside. Virtual patching on a web application firewall or an intrusion prevention system buys time for web-borne cases such as Log4Shell, at the price of chasing evasions. Underneath all of it sits least privilege. The code an attacker runs inherits the identity of the process it runs in, so the same defect is a different incident when the service runs as an unprivileged account in a container with no outbound internet access than when it runs as root on a host that can reach the domain controllers; egress filtering in particular breaks many RCE chains, since Log4Shell needed the vulnerable server to fetch code from outside. Segmentation then limits what the foothold can reach next, which is where lateral movement begins.

The numbers worth remembering: 9.8 for the canonical AV:N/PR:N/UI:N vector, 10.0 when scope changes; Log4Shell's CVE-2021-44228, EternalBlue's CVE-2017-0144, Shellshock's CVE-2014-6271 and BlueKeep's CVE-2019-0708 as the reference cases; and command injection's 20 KEV entries in the 2025 Top 25 as the reminder that the simplest bug class is still the one exploited most.

lfi.def: Getting an application to read or execute a file the caller chose, by controlling a path it builds from input.
lfi.context: It belongs to the same family as injection: user input reaching an interpreter, in this case the filesystem. Reading is bad enough - configuration files, credentials, keys - and it escalates to execution whenever the application will run what it includes. Filtering the path is the losing strategy for the familiar reason: every encoding, every traversal variant and every layer of normalization between the check and the open is another chance for the two to disagree, which is why the durable fix is to never build a path from input at all.

microservice.def: An architecture that splits an application into independently deployable services communicating over the network.
microservice.context: The promised benefit is organizational before it is technical: teams can ship without coordinating a single release. The cost is that every function call that crossed a process boundary now crosses a network, so failures that were impossible become routine - partial success, timeout, retry storms, and version skew between services that used to be compiled together. That is why tracing, idempotence and backpressure stop being optional, and why splitting a system that one team ships once a week usually buys the costs without the benefit.

graphql.def: A query language for interfaces where the caller specifies exactly which fields it wants, in one request.
graphql.context: It solves a real problem - clients fetching too much or making several round trips - by moving the shape of the response into the caller's hands. That inversion is also the security change: authorization can no longer be checked per endpoint, because there is effectively one endpoint and the caller composes the query. Checks have to live at the field and object level, and a deeply nested query is a resource question as well, which is why depth limits and cost analysis are part of running it rather than refinements.

webhook.def: An arrangement where one system calls a URL you provide when something happens, instead of you polling to ask.
webhook.context: It inverts who initiates, and that inversion carries three obligations people discover late. The endpoint is public, so it must authenticate the caller - usually by verifying a signature over the body, because a URL is not a secret. Delivery is at-least-once, so the handler must be idempotent or duplicates become double charges. And the sender expects a fast answer, so real work belongs on a queue rather than in the request, or a slow handler turns into retries that make the load worse.

pam.def: Controlling and recording the use of administrative accounts - checking credentials out, brokering the session, and rotating the secret afterwards.
pam.context: Its purpose is to make privilege temporary and observable, because standing administrative access is the thing an intruder is looking for and the thing an audit cannot reconcile. Done well it removes shared passwords from human hands entirely. Done badly it becomes a single system holding every credential in the estate, reachable from ordinary workstations - which is why the interesting question about any deployment is what happens to it, and to the business, when that system is unavailable or compromised.

tpm.def: A chip that stores keys and measurements in hardware, so secrets are usable by the machine without being extractable from it.
tpm.context: The property that matters is that a key can be used without being read: software asks the chip to sign or decrypt, and never holds the private material. That is what lets disk encryption unlock without a password on the drive, and what lets a machine prove which software it booted. The limits are worth knowing too - it protects against copying the disk, not against an attacker who already runs code on the running machine as the user the key belongs to.

tabletop.def: Walking a team through a hypothetical incident in a room, to find the gaps before a real one does.
tabletop.context: Its value is that it tests the parts a technical test cannot: who decides, who is called at three in the morning, who talks to customers, and whether the plan assumes a system that will be unavailable during the very event it describes. The recurring discovery is mundane and expensive - the runbook lives on the wiki that is behind the identity provider that is down, or the only person who knows the procedure is the one on holiday. Nothing else finds those cheaply.

capacity.def: How much load a system can carry before its behaviour degrades past what its users accept, which is not the same as the number on the specification.
capacity.context: The useful figure is the point where response time starts climbing, not the point where something stops answering, and those are far apart: queues grow non-linearly, so a system at ninety per cent utilization behaves nothing like one at fifty, and the last ten per cent of nominal capacity is usually unusable in practice. Planning against the rated number rather than the measured knee is the standard way to discover this, always at the least convenient moment.
capacity.depth:
Two definitions, and the gap between them. The ITIL glossary (ITIL, originally the Information Technology Infrastructure Library, in its 2011 edition) defines capacity as the maximum throughput that a configuration item or service can deliver, or for some items, such as a disk drive, its size or volume; capacity management is the process that ensures capacity meets the agreed capacity and performance requirements cost-effectively and in time, split into business, service and component capacity management. Google's site reliability engineering (SRE) book, in Benjamin Treynor Sloss's introduction, adds the qualification that makes the number usable: software becomes slower as load is added, a slowdown is a loss of capacity, and at some point a slowing system stops serving altogether, which amounts to infinite slowness. SRE teams therefore provision to meet a capacity target at a specific response speed. A capacity figure without a latency attached is a maximum throughput measured at a moment nobody would want to live in.

Why the knee exists. The simplest queueing model, the M/M/1 queue (one server, random arrivals at rate lambda, exponentially distributed service at rate mu), makes the shape explicit. Utilization is rho, the ratio lambda over mu; the mean number of requests in the system is rho divided by (1 minus rho); and, by Little's law, the mean time a request spends in the system is 1 divided by (mu minus lambda), which is the bare service time divided by (1 minus rho). At 50 per cent utilization a request therefore takes twice its service time, at 80 per cent five times, at 90 per cent ten times and at 95 per cent twenty times. The model is idealized, but the denominator is the lesson: response time does not grow in proportion to load, it grows with the inverse of the headroom left, which is why the last tenth of nominal capacity costs as much latency as everything before it.

Little's law connects the rates engineers measure. John D. C. Little proved in Operations Research in 1961 that the average number of items in a system equals the arrival rate times the average time each spends there, L = lambda W, and fifty years later described how widely it had spread into operations management and computer architecture. It needs no assumption about the distribution of arrivals or service, so it applies to a firewall as well as to a checkout queue. A device receiving 20,000 new connections per second whose connections last 30 seconds on average holds about 600,000 at any instant; if the average lifetime doubles because a backend slows down, the concurrent count doubles at the same arrival rate. Connections per second and concurrent sessions are two capacities linked by duration, and a slow server consumes the second without touching the first.

What goes wrong when capacity runs out is rarely tidy. The chapter on addressing cascading failures, by Mike Ulrich, describes the sequence: with too little CPU (central processing unit), all requests become slower, so more of them are in flight at once, which raises memory use, active threads and open file descriptors; queues saturate and latency rises further; in garbage-collected runtimes less CPU means slower requests, more memory, more collection and less CPU still, the GC (garbage collection) death spiral. Health checks then fail, load moves to the survivors, and they fail in turn. The scarce resource is often not the one on the specification sheet: threads, descriptors, memory or source ports can run out while the CPU graph still looks comfortable.

Measure capacity in the resource that runs out. The chapter on handling overload, by Alejandro Forero Cuervo, records a lesson learned the hard way: modelling capacity as queries per second is a poor metric, because different queries can cost vastly different amounts and the ratios change, sometimes drastically when a new software version ships. Google found it works better to measure capacity directly in available resources, such as a number of CPU cores and an amount of memory reserved for a service in a datacentre, and in most cases to use CPU consumption as the provisioning signal. The same logic applies to appliances: a throughput number means something only for a stated traffic mix.

That is exactly what the Internet Engineering Task Force asks of security device benchmarks. Request for Comments (RFC) 9411, Benchmarking Methodology for Network Security Device Performance, published in March 2023 by B. Balarajah, C. Rossenhoevel and B. Monkman, obsoleted the firewall methodology of RFC 3511 after 18 years. It requires the device under test to be configured inline with the same parameters and security features as a real or typical deployment, requires any recommended security feature left disabled to be reported with the reason and a note that this may affect performance, and defines the key performance indicators separately: inspected throughput with a documented application traffic mix (applications, share of encrypted traffic, cipher suites, object sizes), TCP (Transmission Control Protocol) connections per second, concurrent connection capacity, and transaction latency, for HTTP (Hypertext Transfer Protocol) and HTTPS (Hypertext Transfer Protocol Secure). A datasheet figure that states none of these was measured on a different network from the one being planned.

Planning is forecasting plus testing. The SRE introduction lists the mandatory steps: an organic demand forecast that extends beyond the lead time needed to acquire capacity, the inclusion of inorganic demand such as launches and marketing campaigns, and regular load testing to correlate raw capacity (servers, disks) with service capacity. It warns that provisioning is riskier than shifting load, because adding capacity means new instances or locations and changes to configuration, load balancers and networking, all of which must be validated. The cascading-failure chapter gives the arithmetic: if every cluster breaks at 5,000 queries per second and peak load is 19,000, four clusters carry the peak at their limit and about six are needed to run at N + 2, able to lose two clusters, one to maintenance and one to failure, without overload. Even then, it notes, losing a major part of the infrastructure, a network partition or an unexpected surge can create pockets of load beyond any plan.

The other capacity: the channel. In information theory the word has an exact ceiling. Claude Shannon's 1948 paper A Mathematical Theory of Communication proves, as its Theorem 17, that a channel of bandwidth W hertz, with white thermal noise of power N and average signal power P, has capacity C = W log2((P + N)/N) bits per second: suitable coding can approach that rate with an arbitrarily small error frequency, and no coding can exceed it without a definite rate of errors. A 3,000 Hz channel with a signal-to-noise ratio of 1,000 (30 dB) therefore tops out near 29,900 bits per second whatever the modem does. Engineering capacity always sits below the physical limit, and planning capacity sits below the engineering one, at the knee.

dhcp-snooping.def: DHCP snooping is a switch feature that lets DHCP (Dynamic Host Configuration Protocol) server replies in only through ports declared trustworthy, and records each lease it sees in a binding table that other port protections use.
dhcp-snooping.context: It exists because DHCP (Dynamic Host Configuration Protocol) has no authentication: any device on the segment can answer, and a client may simply take the first offer it hears. A rogue server can hand out its own address as the gateway or a hostile DNS (Domain Name System) server and quietly become the path for everything. Trusting only the ports that lead to real servers removes that whole class of attack, and the binding table the switch builds while it watches becomes the reference for dynamic ARP (Address Resolution Protocol) inspection and IP source guard.
dhcp-snooping.depth:
What it does. RFC (Request for Comments) 2131, the DHCP (Dynamic Host Configuration Protocol) specification of March 1997, is blunt about security: DHCP in its current form is quite insecure, and unauthorized servers may easily be set up to hand clients false addresses, routers and other information. DHCP snooping is the switch's answer. It divides a switch's ports into trusted and untrusted. Server messages, DHCPOFFER, DHCPACK and DHCPNAK, are forwarded only from trusted ports and dropped on untrusted ones, so a rogue server on an access port reaches nobody. Cisco's Catalyst 9000 troubleshooting guide lists what else an untrusted port drops: DHCPLEASEQUERY, requests whose source MAC (media access control) address does not match the client hardware address inside the message, DHCPRELEASE or DHCPDECLINE arriving on a port other than the one that holds the binding, and relayed packets carrying a gateway address or option 82. It is a layer 2 feature on access switches, not a DHCP server function, and it protects only clients whose traffic crosses a switch that enforces it.

Defaults differ, and they matter. On Juniper switches DHCP snooping is not enabled in the default configuration and is enabled per VLAN (virtual local area network); once it is, trunk ports are trusted and access ports untrusted unless overridden. On Cisco Catalyst every interface is untrusted by default, so the uplink towards the server must be trusted by hand. FortiSwitchOS also treats every port as untrusted and leaves snooping off until it is enabled on a VLAN. RFC 7513 (May 2015), the Internet Engineering Task Force's (IETF) source address validation solution for DHCP by Jun Bi, Jianping Wu, Guang Yao and Fred Baker, states the same rule in standards language: the DHCP-Trust attribute, false by default, decides whether a point of attachment may send server-to-client messages, and messages from attachments without it must be discarded.

The binding table. While it watches, the switch builds a binding table from the lease information in the server's replies, typically MAC address, IP (Internet Protocol) address, remaining lease, VLAN and interface, and deletes each entry when its lease expires or the client releases it. That table is what makes snooping more than a filter: Cisco documents that Dynamic ARP (Address Resolution Protocol) Inspection and IP Source Guard use it, Juniper does the same for IP source guard and dynamic ARP inspection, and FortiSwitch for dynamic ARP inspection, so a host that sets a static address, or answers ARP for someone else's, is caught because no lease backs it. Bindings are lost when the switch reboots unless they are made persistent, which Juniper notes and Cisco handles with a binding database written to a file; after a reload without one, legitimate clients are blocked by the dependent features until they renew. The server messages a switch logs from untrusted ports are a way to find a rogue server; FortiSwitchOS logs "A rogue DHCP server has been detected on the interface" for the first such packet, and can restrict accepted servers to an allowed list of up to 2,048.

Option 82 is where snooping surprises people. RFC 3046 (January 2001) defined the relay agent information option, option 82, whose sub-option 1 is the agent circuit ID and sub-option 2 the agent remote ID, so a server can see which switch port a request came from. Many switches insert it as part of snooping, and on Cisco access switches ip dhcp snooping information option is enabled by default. The access switch is not a relay, so it leaves the relay address (giaddr) at 0.0.0.0, and a distribution switch or router that relays the request but does not itself run snooping drops it, logging that the relay information option exists but giaddr is zero. Cisco's fix in that case is no ip dhcp snooping information option on the access switch, or trusting option 82 where it arrives; FortiSwitchOS makes insertion an explicit per-VLAN choice with dhcp-snooping-option82, and has dhcp-snoop-option82-trust per interface.

The threat is documented. In December 2008 the SANS Internet Storm Center described a DNSChanger variant that installed a raw packet driver and ran a DHCP server on infected PCs, answering every discover with its own offer carrying malicious DNS (Domain Name System) servers, in a race with the legitimate server; a March 2009 variant, similar to Trojan.Flush.M, existed to spread a bad DNS server address with a one-hour lease. In May 2024 Leviathan Security Group published TunnelVision (CVE-2024-3661 in the Common Vulnerabilities and Exposures list, scored 7.6): a rogue DHCP server on the same LAN (local area network) pushes classless static routes in option 121 that are more specific than the VPN's (virtual private network's), so traffic leaves by the physical interface instead of the tunnel, on Windows, Linux, iOS and macOS, but not Android, which ignores option 121. Leviathan's advice to organizations was to enable DHCP snooping and ARP protections on their switches. And because snooping parses frames, it shares the bypass problem of other layer 2 filters: the CERT Coordination Center's (CERT/CC) vulnerability note VU#855201 (September 2022) showed controls of this kind evaded by stacking VLAN 0 and LLC/SNAP (logical link control and subnetwork access protocol) headers, and recommends allowing only needed protocols on access ports.

What it does not cover. Starvation, a flood of requests from spoofed MAC addresses that empties the server's pool, needs another control: a limit on MAC addresses or bindings per port, which Juniper documents as MAC limiting, FortiSwitch as a learning limit (5 entries per untrusted port by default once enabled) and Cisco approaches with ip dhcp snooping limit rate, which caps DHCP packets per second on an untrusted port. Rogue router advertisements in IPv6 (Internet Protocol version 6) need RA-Guard (Router Advertisement Guard), and rogue DHCPv6 servers need DHCPv6-Shield or DHCPv6 snooping, which FortiSwitchOS enables per VLAN with dhcp6-snooping. Virtual switches need their own version: Hyper-V's Set-VMNetworkAdapter -DhcpGuard On drops DHCP server messages from a virtual machine. The commands to know are show ip dhcp snooping and show ip dhcp snooping binding on Cisco, and the binding table, trust state and logged rogue servers on any platform.

region.def: A geographic area in which a cloud provider runs a cluster of data centres, usually split into isolated zones, and the boundary that most of its services, and most of their data, do not cross unless told to.
region.context: It is the unit that matters for both law and failure: data residency is argued in terms of regions, and a regional outage is the largest failure that most workloads in a single provider routinely have to plan for. The trap is assuming multi-region is a checkbox: it means duplicated data with a consistency decision, duplicated deployment pipelines, an egress bill for the traffic between regions, and a careful look at which "global" services still live in one of them.
region.depth:
All three large providers use the word the same way, with different emphasis. Amazon Web Services (AWS) describes Regions as geographical locations where it clusters data centres, each made of multiple independent and physically separate Availability Zones (AZs), with at least three in every public Region, and states that a Region's physical infrastructure and software services are isolated from other Regions, with a few documented exceptions, so that a service failure stays in one Region. Microsoft describes an Azure region as one or more datacentres connected by a high-capacity, low-latency network, typically within a large metropolitan area, and says it offers more than 70 of them. Google Cloud calls regions independent geographic areas made of zones, with three or more zones housed in three or more physical data centres, and notes that its Stockholm, Osaka and Montreal regions still have three zones in one or two buildings while they expand. In every case the region is a logical construct over physical sites, and the documentation, not the name, says how independent those sites are.

The zone is the unit underneath, and its distances explain the design. AWS defines an Availability Zone as one or more discrete data centres with independent, redundant power, networking and connectivity, meaningfully distant from the other zones of the Region, up to 60 miles (about 100 km), to avoid correlated failures, yet close enough for synchronous replication with single-digit millisecond latency; zones share no generators or cooling, are fed from different substations, and receive software deployments at different times. Microsoft gives a similar range, zones typically several kilometres apart and usually within 100 km. Google tells customers to treat a zone as a single failure domain. The practical consequence is that a database can replicate synchronously across zones, with no data lost on a zone failure, but not across regions hundreds or thousands of kilometres apart, where replication becomes asynchronous and a regional failover can lose the last writes.

Names do not always mean the same place. In AWS the code of a zone is the Region code plus a letter, us-east-2a for example, but for accounts created before November 2025 in its oldest Regions the letters were mapped independently per account, so us-east-1a in one account may be a different building from us-east-1a in another; the stable name is the zone's identifier, its AZ ID, such as euw1-az1. Azure does the same with physical and logical zones, mapped differently for each subscription. Two teams who agree to put their systems in zone a may be in different zones, and two who think they are spread out may share one. Regions themselves also vary: AWS documentation lists 34 Regions available to an ordinary account, with GovCloud and China reached only through separate account types, and requires Regions introduced after 20 March 2019, such as Cape Town or Mexico (Central), to be enabled before use, while São Paulo, sa-east-1, is on by default. Its marketing page counts 124 zones in 39 geographic Regions, with Saudi Arabia and Chile announced, and the difference is a reminder that counts depend on what is included.

Isolation has exceptions, and they are where regional failures spread. AWS lists services whose control plane lives in a single Region while their data plane is distributed: Identity and Access Management (IAM), Organizations, account management, Route 53, CloudFront and the certificate manager for CloudFront in us-east-1, and others in us-west-2. The whitepaper warns that depending on a global control plane in a recovery workflow introduces a single point of failure. Azure describes nonregional services, deployed across two or more regions, some of which, such as Microsoft Entra ID, let the customer pick a geography for their data; it also pairs some regions for geo-replication and disaster recovery, pairs that customers cannot choose, while many newer regions are unpaired and rely on availability zones instead. Knowing which services are regional, zonal or global is part of knowing where a workload really runs.

A regional outage is the failure that tests all of this. From 11:48 p.m. on 19 October to 2:20 p.m. on 20 October 2025, Pacific time, the Northern Virginia Region of AWS suffered a chain of failures that began with a latent defect in the automated system managing DynamoDB's DNS (Domain Name System) records, which left the service's regional endpoint unresolvable; services that depended on DynamoDB failed with it, Network Load Balancer connection errors and failed EC2 (Elastic Compute Cloud) instance launches followed, and AWS's post-event summary describes three distinct periods of customer impact. Other Regions kept running, which is the isolation working; workloads that lived only in us-east-1, or whose recovery depended on something that did, had nowhere to go.

The legal meaning of a region is residency. Azure states it most plainly: every region sits within a single geography that serves as a fixed data residency boundary, and customers with residency requirements must choose regions inside the required geography. AWS's own Region guide gives the example of creating resources in Europe to meet legal requirements, and its whitepaper says data created in one Region does not exist in another unless the customer replicates it. Residency is not the whole question, though, because a service can store in one place and process in another. F5's Distributed Cloud data residency reference, updated on 22 September 2026, separates persistent storage locations from non-persistent processing locations: a web application firewall running at a Regional Edge or a Customer Edge may process a request in memory at that edge, while stored data sits where the customer selected, and for Bot Defense the storage location (São Paulo among them) is chosen independently of the scrubbing centre. In that platform a Regional Edge is a point of presence of the provider's own network, and each Customer Edge site connects to two of them, chosen from the public address it registered from unless a label overrides the choice.

Multi-region therefore costs more than a second deployment. Data must be copied, with a decision about consistency that Google, for one, describes as a trade-off between latency and the consistency model in its own multi-regional services; pipelines, secrets and monitoring must exist twice; and traffic between regions is billed. Google Cloud's price list shows the shape: virtual machine traffic between regions costs from $0.02 per GiB within North America or Europe to $0.14 per GiB to or from South America, traffic between zones of one region $0.01 per GiB, and traffic inside a zone on internal addresses nothing. A region is chosen for latency to users, for the services and zones it offers, for the law that applies to it and for price; it is kept honest by testing failover, including the dependencies that quietly live somewhere else.

object-storage.def: Storage addressed by key rather than by path or block, with metadata attached and no filesystem semantics.
object-storage.context: Dropping the filesystem is what makes it scale: no directories to lock, no partial writes to coordinate, objects replaced whole. That also removes what applications expect - no append, no rename that is not a copy, and eventual rather than immediate agreement in some designs. The recurring security failure is not the technology but the permission: a bucket made public to fix an access problem, and never made private again.

block-storage.def: Storage presented to a machine as a raw disk, which the operating system formats and manages itself.
block-storage.context: It is what a database and an operating system expect, because they want to control layout, caching and ordering. The cloud consequence is attachment: a volume belongs to one machine at a time and lives in one zone, which makes it the thing that pins a workload to a location. Anyone designing for failure discovers that moving the compute is easy and moving the disk is the actual project.

shared-responsibility.def: The division of security duties between a cloud provider and its customer - the provider secures the platform, the customer secures what they put on it.
shared-responsibility.context: It is stated in every provider's documentation and misread constantly, because the line moves with the service: with a virtual machine the customer patches the operating system, with a managed database they do not, and with a storage service the provider guarantees durability while the customer alone decides who can read it. Almost every publicized cloud breach sits on the customer side of a line that was published in advance.

multi-tenancy.def: One system serving several customers from shared infrastructure, with isolation enforced by software rather than by separate hardware.
multi-tenancy.context: It is what makes cloud economics work and what makes cloud security interesting: the boundary between two customers is code, and a defect in that code is a cross-tenant issue rather than a bug. The question worth asking of any platform is where the isolation actually lives: separate machines, separate virtual machines, separate processes or databases, or only a customer identifier in a query, because the last one fails to a single missing filter. Each layer of sharing buys efficiency and adds a way for one tenant's activity, failure or attacker to reach another, whether through a software flaw, a side channel in shared hardware or plain contention for the same resources.
multi-tenancy.depth:
What it means. NIST (the US National Institute of Standards and Technology) wrote multi-tenancy into the definition of cloud computing itself. SP (Special Publication) 800-145 by Peter Mell and Timothy Grance (September 2011) lists resource pooling among the essential characteristics: the provider's computing resources are pooled to serve multiple consumers using a multi-tenant model, with physical and virtual resources dynamically assigned and reassigned according to demand, and with a sense of location independence. The companion guide on public cloud security, SP 800-144 by Wayne Jansen and Timothy Grance (December 2011), names the consequence: consumers share components with others unknown to them, so instead of physical separation the cloud depends on logical separation at multiple layers of the stack. In IaaS (infrastructure as a service) that usually means virtual machines from different customers multiplexed on one physical server; in SaaS (software as a service) it often means a single logical instance of an application serving very large numbers of tenants. A tenant is the unit of isolation, normally a customer organization with its own users, data and configuration, which is why multi-tenancy is a different property from merely having many users.

Where the isolation can live. The same spectrum appears in every architecture. At one end each tenant gets dedicated resources; at the other everything is shared and the tenant boundary is a field in a record. The SaaS Lens of AWS (Amazon Web Services) calls the ends silo and pool: a silo gives a tenant dedicated resources, such as a fully independent stack or a separate database, while still sharing identity, onboarding and operations, and a pool shares the resources themselves, which it calls the classic notion of multi-tenancy, with bridge for the mixtures in between. It also states the stakes: crossing the tenant boundary in any form would be a significant and potentially unrecoverable event for a SaaS business. Microsoft's guide to tenancy patterns for Azure SQL Database lays out the database version. Database-per-tenant allows per-tenant schema changes and single-tenant restores and stays manageable at well over 100,000 databases; a multitenant database needs one or more tenant identifier columns and, in Microsoft's words, necessarily sacrifices tenant isolation, so queries must never return data from more than one tenant, a guarantee that row-level security can help enforce.

The filter that goes missing. Row-level security moves the tenant filter from every query into the database, but its exceptions are the classic trap. In PostgreSQL, once row security is enabled on a table every normal read and write must be allowed by a policy, and a table with no policy defaults to deny; but superusers and roles with the BYPASSRLS attribute always bypass row security, and so, normally, does the table's owner, unless the owner is made subject to it with FORCE ROW LEVEL SECURITY. An application that connects as the owner of its own tables therefore gets no protection from policies that look correct in review. PostgreSQL also warns that referential integrity checks, such as unique and foreign key constraints, bypass row security and can leak information through covert channels. These are the mechanics behind the warning that a shared database fails to a single missing filter.

Shared hardware. Below the software, tenants share processors, caches and memory. In 2009 Thomas Ristenpart, Eran Tromer, Hovav Shacham and Stefan Savage showed at the ACM (Association for Computing Machinery) CCS (Conference on Computer and Communications Security) that on Amazon EC2 (Elastic Compute Cloud) an attacker could map the internal infrastructure, work out where a target's virtual machine probably ran, and launch instances until one landed beside it, with a few dollars of instances giving about a 40 per cent chance of co-residence; from there cross-VM (virtual machine) side channels could, among other things, time a user's keystrokes over SSH (Secure Shell). The 2018 disclosures of Meltdown and Spectre made the point at industrial scale: their authors wrote that both attacks work in the cloud and that, depending on the provider's infrastructure, it might be possible to steal data from other customers, with Meltdown potentially affecting essentially every Intel processor with out-of-order execution made since 1995. Contention is the benign version of the same sharing: the noisy neighbour whose load degrades everyone else's performance is a multi-tenancy failure with no attacker at all.

When the platform's own code breaks the boundary. Two 2021 cases in Microsoft Azure show what a cross-tenant flaw looks like. Wiz researchers Nir Ohfeld and Sagi Tzadik reported on 26 August 2021 that the Jupyter Notebook feature of Cosmos DB, added in 2019 and switched on for all Cosmos DB accounts in February 2021, allowed a privilege escalation into other customers' notebooks, from which they harvested primary keys giving full read, write and delete access to the databases of several thousand customers; Microsoft disabled the feature within 48 hours of the report. On 9 September 2021 Yuval Avrahami of Palo Alto Networks' Unit 42 described Azurescape, which they called the first cross-account container takeover in the public cloud: Azure Container Instances ran customer containers on multitenant Kubernetes clusters with runC v1.0.0-rc2, a release of 1 October 2016 vulnerable to known breakouts including CVE-2019-5736 (Common Vulnerabilities and Exposures), so one customer could escape to the node and reach other customers' containers. Microsoft patched it and Unit 42 advised revoking privileged credentials deployed to the service before 31 August 2021. In both cases the customers had done nothing wrong; the shared layer was the vulnerability.

Multi-tenancy in network equipment. Networks partitioned infrastructure for customers long before cloud. A VLAN (virtual local area network) per customer separates layer 2 domains and a VRF (virtual routing and forwarding) instance per customer separates routing tables, and RFC (Request for Comments) 5517, Cisco's description of private VLANs, was written because hosting providers could not give every customer one of the 4094 usable VLANs. Security appliances partition themselves too. FortiOS in multi VDOM (virtual domain) mode lets a FortiGate hold multiple VDOMs that function as independent units, each with its own policies and administrators, around a root VDOM that cannot be deleted. F5's rSeries appliances, under the F5OS platform layer, run tenants: guest systems such as BIG-IP that receive dedicated vCPU (virtual central processing unit) and memory, are restricted to specific VLANs and have their own administrator role, managed much as vCMP guests were on VIPRION chassis, with the number of tenants fixed per model (one on an r2600, four on an r4800). Dedicated cores and memory make these closer to a silo than a pool, which is precisely why operators choose them for customers who must not share fate.

What to ask of any multi-tenant system. Where exactly is the boundary enforced, and by which component: hardware partitioning, a hypervisor, a container runtime, an application filter or a database policy? What is still shared above it, such as the control plane, the identity system, the key management, the management interface and the people who operate it, since a shared layer is a shared failure domain even when data is separated perfectly? How are noisy neighbours limited? Can a single tenant be restored, moved or deleted without touching the others? And what happens to every tenant if the shared layer has a flaw like ChaosDB or Azurescape? The answers decide whether multi-tenancy is an efficiency or a concentration of risk.

egress-fee.def: What a cloud provider charges for data leaving its network - typically free to receive and priced to send.
egress-fee.context: The asymmetry is the strategy: importing data costs nothing and exporting it costs money, so the bill grows with any architecture that moves data out, and shrinks with any that keeps it in. That shapes real decisions - where backups live, whether analytics run next to the data, and how expensive leaving would be. It is worth pricing that last one before it matters rather than during a migration.

pon.def: A fibre access network where one feed is split optically to many homes, with no powered equipment between the exchange and the subscriber.
pon.context: Passive is the economic argument: splitters need no power, no cooling and no maintenance visit, which is what made fibre to the home affordable. The consequences follow directly - the capacity of one feed is shared among everyone on the split, so contention is a design parameter rather than a fault, and every subscriber's downstream traffic physically reaches every other, which is why encryption on the access link is part of the standard rather than an option.

spectrum.def: The range of radio frequencies available for transmission, allocated internationally by the ITU (International Telecommunication Union) and assigned nationally by regulators, who divide it into licensed bands with exclusive rights and unlicensed bands shared under common rules.
spectrum.context: It is the only genuinely finite input in networking: fibre can be laid and processors improved, but a frequency in a place can only be used once at a time. That scarcity explains the two worlds. Licensed spectrum is bought, at auction in most countries, and comes with exclusivity and legal protection; unlicensed spectrum is free and comes with neighbours, because every device must accept the interference of every other device that follows the same rules. Everything difficult about wireless in an office is a consequence of choosing the second, where the interference is other people doing the same thing legally. The 6 GHz band shows the politics live: opened in full for Wi-Fi in the United States in 2020 and in Brazil in 2021, it is now being split with mobile operators in the United Kingdom and, from 2027, in Brazil.
spectrum.depth:
Radio spectrum is governed by treaty before it is governed by any vendor. The ITU (International Telecommunication Union) Radio Regulations, which the ITU calls the binding international treaty that determines how the radio-frequency spectrum is shared between services, run to more than 2,300 pages. Their current text is the 2024 edition: the regulations adopted at the World Radiocommunication Conference (WRC) of 1995 as revised at every conference since, the latest WRC-23 in Dubai. Conferences meet every four years for four weeks, and WRC-23 already set the agenda for WRC-27, including studies on mobile use of 4,400 to 4,800 MHz and 7,125 to 8,400 MHz.
