The international table of allocations runs up to 3,000 GHz and is printed in three columns, because the ITU divides the world into three Regions; the United States lies mainly in Region 2, which is why its national table is built on the Region 2 column.

The vocabulary is precise, and it matters when reading a regulator's decision. An allocation is an entry in the table that gives a band to one or more services (fixed, mobile, broadcasting, radionavigation and so on) under stated conditions; an assignment is an administration's authorization for a particular station to use a particular frequency. The ITU's Master International Frequency Register records assignments that gain international recognition and protection, more than 3.1 million for terrestrial services alone. Harmful interference has a legal definition: interference that endangers a radionavigation or other safety service, or seriously degrades, obstructs or repeatedly interrupts a service operating under the Radio Regulations. Who administers what is national. In the United States the federal table belongs to the NTIA (National Telecommunications and Information Administration) and the non-federal one to the FCC (Federal Communications Commission); in Brazil it is Anatel (Agência Nacional de Telecomunicações), in the United Kingdom Ofcom, and the European Commission harmonizes bands across the European Union.

Licensed spectrum gives its holder exclusive use of a band in an area, and in most markets it is sold. The FCC has auctioned licences since 1994, under the Omnibus Budget Reconciliation Act of 1993; before that it chose licensees by comparative hearings and lotteries. Brazil's 5G auction, whose public session ran on 4, 5 and 9 November 2021, offered 700 MHz, 2.3 GHz, 3.5 GHz and 26 GHz and is described by Anatel as the largest radio-frequency auction in the country's history, with commitments such as building optical backhaul attached. A licence buys legal protection: interference into a licensed band is the regulator's problem to stop.

Unlicensed spectrum gives nobody that protection. The United States rule for unlicensed devices, 47 CFR (Code of Federal Regulations) 15.5, says their users have no vested right to any frequency, may cause no harmful interference, must accept interference from licensed stations, from other devices and from industrial, scientific and medical (ISM) equipment, and must stop operating when the FCC says they are interfering. The ISM bands are where much of this began. ITU footnote 5.150 designates 13,553 to 13,567 kHz, 26,957 to 27,283 kHz, 40.66 to 40.70 MHz, 902 to 928 MHz in Region 2, 2,400 to 2,500 MHz, 5,725 to 5,875 MHz and 24 to 24.25 GHz for equipment that generates and uses radio energy locally for industrial, scientific, medical, domestic or similar purposes other than telecommunications, and requires radio services in those bands to accept the interference it causes. Wi-Fi, Bluetooth and countless sensors live at 2.4 GHz on those terms, which is why that band is crowded and why no one can complain about a neighbour's access point.

The 6 GHz band is the clearest recent example of how a band is opened, and of how quickly the decision can be revisited. On 23 April 2020 the FCC adopted rules, effective on 27 July 2020, opening 1,200 MHz from 5.925 to 7.125 GHz to unlicensed use: the whole band for indoor low-power access points, and standard-power access points indoors and outdoors in two sub-bands under an automated frequency coordination (AFC) system that protects incumbent fixed microwave links, with channels up to 320 MHz wide. On 24 July 2020 Ofcom made 5,925 to 6,425 MHz licence-exempt in the United Kingdom, at 250 mW indoors and 25 mW outdoors. The European Commission's Implementing Decision (EU) 2021/1067 of 17 June 2021 required member states to make 5,945 to 6,425 MHz available for wireless access systems by 1 December 2021, on a non-exclusive, non-interference and non-protected basis. The Wi-Fi Alliance calls 6 GHz the first new spectrum for Wi-Fi since 1999.

Brazil went furthest and then reversed course. Anatel's board proposed the whole 1,200 MHz from 5,925 to 7,125 MHz for unlicensed indoor use on 10 December 2020, against operators who wanted 500 MHz kept for 5G, and confirmed it on 25 February 2021 when it approved the technical requirements. In August 2026, after updating its band plan to reserve 6,425 to 7,125 MHz for collective-interest services, chiefly mobile telephony, Anatel's board unanimously restricted Wi-Fi equipment to 5,925 to 6,425 MHz from 1 March 2027, in Acórdão 203 and Ato 10.400, citing laboratory, field and simulation results that showed relevant degradation when Wi-Fi and IMT (International Mobile Telecommunications) systems share a channel; the trade press reported Wi-Fi throughput falling by about 95 per cent in those tests. Ofcom chose a split instead of a reversal: its January 2026 statement confirmed higher-power Wi-Fi under AFC in the lower band and proposed dividing the upper band at 6,585 MHz, with Wi-Fi priority below and mobile priority above.

The practical consequences for an engineer are three. The constraint on a wireless design is usually regulatory before it is physical: the band sets the power, the power sets the range, and the regulator sets the band, so the same access point offers different channels in São Paulo, London and Dallas. Unlicensed capacity is shared by rule, so the defence against interference is design (channel plans, power, cell size), not a complaint. And allocations move: a band opened to Wi-Fi in one decade can be reassigned to mobile in the next, so equipment certified today may have to be brought into line with new rules, as Anatel's 2027 deadline requires for Wi-Fi devices whose conformity certificates remain valid after it.

ix.def: An internet exchange (IX), or internet exchange point (IXP), is a shared switching fabric where many independent networks connect once and then exchange traffic directly with one another, instead of paying a third party to carry it between them.
ix.context: The Internet Exchange Federation (IX-F) defines it as a facility that interconnects more than two independent autonomous systems (ASes), primarily to exchange internet traffic, without that traffic having to cross any third AS. The participants are access providers, content and cloud networks, carriers and some enterprises; the fabric is usually a shared Ethernet switching platform spread across a metropolitan area; and the routing is Border Gateway Protocol (BGP), either in sessions agreed pair by pair or through the exchange's route servers. The case for one is distance and cost at once: traffic between two networks in the same city stays in the city, and every bit that crosses the exchange is a bit neither side has to buy from a transit provider.
ix.depth:
What it is, and what it is not. The Internet Exchange Federation's definition is narrow on purpose. An internet exchange point is a technical facility, distinct from the organization that runs it; it interconnects only autonomous systems, each operated by a separate legal entity; it needs at least three of them, which is what separates it from a private interconnection between two networks; and it neither provides internet access nor acts as a transit carrier, nor alters the traffic that crosses it. In practice the facility is a layer 2 switching fabric, typically Ethernet, as the Internet Engineering Task Force's route server specification, Request for Comments (RFC) 7947, puts it: each participant connects a router to a port, often in one of several data centres the exchange links together, and from then on reaches every other participant across the same switched network.

How peering across it works. The fabric only carries frames; who sends what to whom is decided in Border Gateway Protocol (BGP). In bilateral peering two participants configure an external BGP session directly between their routers and exchange only the routes they have agreed on, which was the usual model until, in the words of RFC 7947, the overhead of dense interconnection caused substantial scaling problems at larger exchanges. Multilateral peering adds a route server, normally run by the exchange operator: each participant announces its routes once, the route server passes them on to every other client according to policy, and because it never forwards traffic itself it is not a router. It behaves like a route reflector for external BGP, and by default does not add its own autonomous system number to the path, which is why RFC 7948 advises clients to switch off the check that expects it. The same operational guide recommends at least two route servers on each fabric, configured identically, and describes the controls participants use: BGP communities that tell the route server to send a prefix to everyone, to some or to none, and filters built from Internet Routing Registry data. At Brazil's IX.br the multilateral agreement works through route servers in exactly this way, and bilateral peering runs over a private virtual local area network (VLAN) inside the exchange.

Why it matters. The Internet Society puts the problem plainly: without a local exchange, traffic between neighbours can travel thousands of miles through other countries, and sometimes other continents, before it arrives a town away. An exchange keeps that traffic local, which shortens paths and lowers latency, replaces transit that would otherwise be bought, and adds a path that does not depend on any single upstream, which is the resilience argument. Exchanges also attract content: once enough access networks meet in one place, content delivery networks (CDNs) put caches there, and the traffic that matters most to users stops leaving the region at all. That is the logic behind the Internet Society's 2010 goal, set with the African peering community, that 80 per cent of African internet traffic should be accessed within Africa by 2020.

Where they came from. In the United States the model was set during the retirement of the National Science Foundation Network (NSFNET). The carrier MFS had run MAE-East, the Metropolitan Area Ethernet in Washington, since 1992, and the National Science Foundation used it as the model for the network access points it specified in 1993 and awarded in 1994 to Sprint, MFS Datanet and Bellcore, the last on behalf of Ameritech and Pacific Bell. The Routing Arbiter project shipped route servers to those access points in November 1994, two decades before RFC 7947 wrote the practice down, and the NSFNET backbone was switched off on 30 April 1995. In Europe the London Internet Exchange (LINX) was founded in 1994 by five UK providers who wanted to keep local traffic local, and DE-CIX opened in Frankfurt in 1995. Brazil's first exchange, run by the São Paulo Research Foundation (FAPESP) from 1998, became part of the national programme in 2004.

Who runs them, and who is largest. The Internet Society counts five kinds of founder: non-profit organizations, associations of providers, operator-neutral commercial companies, universities or government agencies, and informal groups of networks. LINX is member-owned and not for profit, with one vote per member however large; DE-CIX belongs to a company whose sole shareholder is eco, the Association of the Internet Industry; IX.br is run by the non-profit Brazilian Network Information Center (NIC.br) and financed from .br domain registrations. The Internet Exchange Federation's own reading of what works is that exchanges grow out of trust among local operators, that light or no regulation has suited them best, and that governments have helped to start exchanges but have rarely run them. Claims to be the largest depend on what is counted and are made by the operators themselves: DE-CIX calls Frankfurt the world's leading interconnection platform, with more than 18 Tbit/s at peak; NIC.br calls IX.br São Paulo the world leader in traffic and participants, reporting 32 Tbit/s and more than 2,500 connected networks in March 2026; LINX reports a 13 Tbit/s peak and says one London port reaches more unique networks than any other. None of this changes BGP. An exchange is where BGP sessions become cheap to set up; local preference, communities and filters remain each network's own policy.

federation.def: Accepting an identity proven somewhere else, so a user authenticated by their own organization can reach a service run by another.
federation.context: It moves the trust decision from a password to a relationship: the service no longer stores credentials, it decides which issuers it believes. The consequences are worth naming. Account lifecycle belongs to the issuer, so removing someone at home removes their access everywhere, which is the whole benefit and also means a compromised issuer is a compromise of every service that trusts it.
federation.depth:
NIST (National Institute of Standards and Technology) defines federation as a process that allows for the conveyance of identity and authentication information across a set of networked systems, done interoperably with protocols such as OpenID Connect (OIDC) or SAML (Security Assertion Markup Language). Older definitions describe the structure rather than the process: WS-Federation 1.0, dated 8 July 2003, calls it a collection of realms that have established trust among themselves, a trust that typically includes authentication and may include authorization, and the SAML 2.0 glossary of March 2005 uses the word in two senses, the act of establishing the relationship and the association of identity providers (IdPs) and service providers (SPs) that results. The SAML executive overview of the same year lists what is actually agreed: business agreements, cryptographic trust, and user identifiers or attributes across security and policy domains. Federation is the arrangement; single sign-on is the experience it produces, and NIST notes that federation is also used inside one security domain simply to centralize account management.

Each of those three layers can be set up pair by pair or through a third party. In the bilateral case an IdP and a relying party (RP) exchange metadata and keys directly; at NIST's highest federation assurance level, FAL3, the identifiers of the parties must be established manually and each tied to its verification keys. In the multilateral case a federation authority, in NIST's term, onboards members and gives them a basis to trust each other without pairwise decisions, usually under a trust framework that formalizes the rules. NIST keeps the federation authority and the federation proxy apart: the first manages the trust agreement, the second only relays the protocol, even when one organization runs both. OpenID Federation 1.0, final since 17 February 2026, puts the multilateral model into OIDC: each entity publishes an Entity Statement, a signed JSON Web Token (JWT) about itself and the entities beneath it, and a relying party validates a Trust Chain from the leaf entity up to a Trust Anchor it already trusts, with Trust Marks to certify conformance.

Research and education run the largest multilateral federations. National federations sign and publish their members' metadata, and eduGAIN connects them: its status page lists 84 participant federations. Brazil's is CAFe, the Comunidade Acadêmica Federada run by RNP, an identity management service that joins Brazilian teaching and research institutions so that one account, in a single sign-on model, reaches the services of the user's own institution and those of the other participants; it exports 343 identity providers to eduGAIN, in signed metadata created on 11 November 2026 and valid until 6 December 2026. InCommon in the United States exports 587 identity providers and 1,933 service providers. The OpenID Federation specification uses the same world for its worked example, a service registered with InCommon that wants to accept every provider under the eduGAIN Trust Anchor.

The service still needs a local account, and how it gets one matters. NIST describes three provisioning models: just-in-time, where the RP creates the account the first time an assertion with an unknown identifier arrives, the most common because it needs the least coordination; pre-provisioning, where the IdP pushes or the RP pulls accounts in bulk through a provisioning API (application programming interface), the role filled by SCIM (System for Cross-domain Identity Management), RFC (Request for Comments) 7644 of September 2015; and ephemeral provisioning, where the link lasts only for the session. Lifecycle is where federation pays off or fails. Removing someone at the home organization removes their access to every federated service only if new logins are the sole path in; with just-in-time accounts and no termination signal, NIST warns that the RP accumulates accounts nobody can reach through the IdP but an attacker can still target.

Privacy shapes the identifiers. A pairwise pseudonymous identifier (PPI) gives each RP a different, unguessable identifier for the same person, so that RPs cannot collude to track the subscriber, and at FAL2 and above federated identifiers must not carry plaintext personal information such as an email address. Account linking, one RP account tied to several federated identifiers, is allowed, but it needs an authenticated session with the existing account first. Proxies cut both ways: they can blind IdP and RP from each other, but they see every transaction and can profile the user across both sides.

Because the service now believes whatever its trusted issuers say, the trust configuration itself is the target. MITRE ATT&CK (Adversarial Tactics, Techniques, and Common Knowledge) technique T1484.002 describes adversaries who add or modify trust relationships between domains and tenants: converting an Active Directory domain to a federated one with Active Directory Federation Services (AD FS), adding their own signing certificate so they can mint tokens without stealing the real key, or adding a new federated IdP to an identity tenant such as Okta or AWS IAM Identity Center and authenticating as any user, which in an AWS (Amazon Web Services) Organization reaches every member account. It records APT29 configuring a domain during the SolarWinds compromise to accept tokens signed by its own SAML certificate, Scattered Spider adding a federated IdP with automatic account linking turned on, and Storm-0501 creating a federated domain in a Microsoft Entra tenant as a persistent backdoor. The defences are administrative rather than cryptographic: least privilege on who can change federation settings, alerts on every new trust, certificate or IdP, and NIST's advice that RPs keep their own monitoring, since an attack on one IdP can move laterally to every RP that trusts it.

Neighbouring terms differ in scope. Single sign-on is the user's view; the IdP and RP are the roles inside one transaction; a trust framework is the rulebook; interfederation, as in eduGAIN, is a federation of federations; and directory synchronization copies accounts, where federation passes assertions about them. Dates worth knowing: WS-Federation 1.0 in 2003, SAML 2.0 in 2005, SCIM in 2015 and OpenID Federation 1.0 in 2026.

assertion.def: The signed statement a federation protocol carries: who authenticated, when, how, for which audience, and for how long it is valid.
assertion.context: Every field in it is load-bearing. The audience stops a token issued for one service being replayed at another; the validity window limits how long a stolen one is useful; the authentication method tells the service whether a second factor was actually used. Services that check the signature and ignore the rest accept assertions that were technically valid and not meant for them.
assertion.depth:
The SAML (Security Assertion Markup Language) 2.0 glossary of March 2005 defines an assertion as a piece of data produced by a SAML authority about an act of authentication performed on a subject, attribute information about the subject, or authorization data for the subject with respect to a resource. RFC (Request for Comments) 7521 (May 2015), which brought assertions into OAuth 2.0, generalizes it: a package of information that lets identity and security information be shared across security domains, typically naming a subject, the issuer and the time of issue, and the conditions under which it is valid, and always integrity-protected by the issuer with a digital signature or a message authentication code (MAC). NIST (National Institute of Standards and Technology) SP (Special Publication) 800-63C-4 names the two assertions most deployments use: the SAML Assertion and the ID token of OpenID Connect (OIDC). An assertion is not a session: NIST forbids using its validity window to limit the session at the relying party (RP), and OIDC says the ID token's expiry is unrelated to the session lifetime. Nor is it an API (application programming interface) credential: an OAuth access token authorizes calls to a resource, while an assertion tells a relying party who authenticated.

A SAML 2.0 assertion, as the core specification of 15 March 2005 defines it, carries a Version of 2.0, a unique ID and an IssueInstant in UTC (Coordinated Universal Time) as attributes; an Issuer; an optional XML (Extensible Markup Language) Signature; a Subject; optional Conditions and Advice; and statements. The AuthnStatement records when the subject authenticated (AuthnInstant), an optional SessionIndex and SessionNotOnOrAfter, and the AuthnContext that says how; the AttributeStatement carries attributes; the AuthzDecisionStatement records an authorization decision. Conditions hold NotBefore and NotOnOrAfter, any number of AudienceRestriction elements (the audiences inside one element are alternatives, separate elements must all be satisfied), OneTimeUse and ProxyRestriction, and evaluation yields Valid, Invalid or Indeterminate; an element the RP does not understand makes the whole assertion Indeterminate. One sentence in the specification deserves attention: it defines no relationship between the Issuer named in the assertion and whoever signed it, so binding the two is the RP's job.

How the presenter proves it is the subject is set by the subject confirmation method. SAML defines three: holder-of-key, where the assertion names a key and the presenter must prove possession of it; sender-vouches, where the relying party must use other means; and bearer, where whoever holds the assertion is treated as the subject. Browser single sign-on (SSO) uses bearer, and the profile compensates with strict rules. The bearer SubjectConfirmationData must carry a Recipient equal to the service provider's assertion consumer service URL (Uniform Resource Locator) and a NotOnOrAfter that limits the delivery window, must not carry NotBefore, and must carry InResponseTo equal to the ID of the request when there was one; the assertion must include an AudienceRestriction with the service provider's identifier; under the HTTP (Hypertext Transfer Protocol) POST binding the assertion must be signed; and the service provider must remember used assertion IDs for as long as they would be valid, so that none is accepted twice. Unsolicited responses, sent by the identity provider (IdP) without a request, carry no InResponseTo, which is one reason NIST counts refusing them among the defences against assertion injection.

The OIDC ID token is the same idea in JSON (JavaScript Object Notation): a signed JSON Web Token (JWT) whose iss, sub, aud, exp and iat claims match issuer, subject, audience and validity, with auth_time for the moment of authentication, nonce to bind it to the request, and acr and amr for the authentication context class and the methods used. SP 800-63C-4 lists the checks any RP must make whatever the format: signature, issuer, time window, audience, and the assertion identifier against replay. It asks for a window long enough to process the assertion plus reasonable clock drift and no longer, recommends that the assertion state the authentication method, for example whether the authenticator was phishing-resistant, through Vectors of Trust or authentication context references, and allows encryption with XML Encryption or JSON Web Encryption (JWE). At its highest level, FAL3, a bearer assertion is no longer enough: the RP must also verify an authenticator, named in a holder-of-key assertion or bound at the RP.

Most real failures have been in signature checking, not cryptography. In 2012 Juraj Somorovsky and colleagues, most of them at Ruhr-University Bochum, showed at the USENIX Security Symposium that 11 of 14 major SAML frameworks, Salesforce, Shibboleth and IBM XS40 among them, were vulnerable to XML Signature wrapping: the signature validated one element while the application read another that the attacker had inserted. On 27 February 2018 the CERT Coordination Center (CERT/CC) published VU#475445: several libraries lost the text after an XML comment during canonicalization, so an attacker could alter a name inside a signed assertion without breaking the signature; OneLogin's ruby-saml and python-saml, Shibboleth and Duo Network Gateway (CVE-2018-7340) were on the list. The pattern returned in CVE-2024-45409, published on 10 September 2024: Ruby-SAML before 1.12.3, and from 1.13.0 before 1.17.0, did not properly verify the SAML Response signature, so anyone holding any document signed by the IdP could forge an assertion and log in as any user, scored 10.0 under CVSS (Common Vulnerability Scoring System) 3.1. The lesson is the one the profile already implies: verify the signature over exactly the element you then read, and check every condition, not only the signature.

Neighbouring terms overlap. A claim is one statement inside a JWT; a token is any credential object, assertions included; a SAML artifact or an OIDC authorization code is an assertion reference that the RP exchanges for the assertion over the back channel; a Kerberos ticket plays a similar role inside one realm. Numbers worth remembering: SAML 2.0 core and profiles of 15 March 2005, three confirmation methods, the five-minute ceiling NIST recommends for assertion references, and a CVSS score of 10.0 for a library that verified the wrong thing.

passwordless.def: Authenticating with a key held by a device rather than with a shared secret the user types.
passwordless.context: The property that matters is not convenience: because the credential is bound to the site's origin and never leaves the device, there is nothing for a user to type into a convincing copy of the login page. That defeats phishing structurally rather than by training. The open problems are recovery and enrolment - what happens when the device is lost, and how the first credential is established, which is where the remaining attacks now concentrate.

raid.def: Combining several disks so the array survives losing one - or more, depending on the layout chosen.
raid.context: The sentence that has to accompany it is that RAID is not a backup: it protects against a disk dying, and copies a deletion, a corruption or an encryption faithfully to every member. The second operational fact is rebuild - replacing a failed disk puts the array under sustained load precisely when its redundancy is gone, which is when the second failure tends to arrive.

replication.def: Keeping copies of data, or of state, on more than one machine and updating them as the original changes, so the loss of one does not lose the data.
replication.context: The whole subject is the word 'when'. Synchronous replication confirms a write only after the copy has it, which costs latency proportional to distance and guarantees no loss; asynchronous confirms immediately and accepts that a failure loses whatever had not shipped. That choice is the recovery point objective expressed in engineering, and it cannot be avoided: a system that has not chosen has chosen asynchronous by default.
replication.depth:
NIST (the United States National Institute of Standards and Technology), in Special Publication 800-209 on storage security (October 2020), defines data replication as writing the same data to at least two separate locations and divides it into two kinds: synchronous, the real-time copying of data from a production site to a recovery site, and asynchronous, which involves a delay and may run continuously or at a set frequency, with the delay dictated by the organization's recovery objectives. The recovery point objective (RPO), in NIST's glossary, is the point in time to which data must be recovered after an outage, so an asynchronous lag of five seconds is an RPO of at least five seconds whether or not anybody wrote that number down. Replication is not the same thing as a backup: the same publication distinguishes continuous data protection, which journals changes so that data can be played back to earlier points in time, from replication, which keeps a copy of the present.

PostgreSQL's documentation shows the trade in one database. Streaming replication is asynchronous by default, with a delay typically under one second, and if the primary crashes some committed transactions may never have reached the standby, a loss proportional to the replication delay at the moment of failover. Synchronous replication makes each commit wait for confirmation from one or more standbys, at a level the administrator chooses with synchronous_commit: remote_write waits until the standby has received the commit record and handed it to its own operating system, on until it is on disk in the standby's write-ahead log, and remote_apply until it has replayed it, making it visible to queries there. The documentation states the cost plainly: the minimum wait is the round-trip time between primary and standby. Light in fibre travels at roughly two-thirds of its speed in a vacuum, about 200,000 kilometres per second, so every 100 kilometres of fibre path between the sites adds about a millisecond to each commit, before any equipment delay; that is why synchronous replication is normally confined to metropolitan distances and long-distance copies are asynchronous.

Synchronous replication also changes how a system fails. If the standby that every commit waits for stops answering, PostgreSQL warns that commits may never complete, so high availability needs more potential synchronous standbys than the number required. Its synchronous_standby_names setting offers two policies: FIRST n, where the first n named standbys are synchronous and the next in the list takes over when one fails, and ANY n, a quorum in which a commit waits for any n of the listed standbys. Storage arrays face the same choice. NIST's recommendation DP-SS-R8 asks for automated suspension of input and output when a synchronous replica must never fall behind, and immediately notes the price: the primary then refuses writes whenever it loses contact with its replica, so an attacker who can disrupt the replication path can stop production.

Copies that accept writes in more than one place need agreement on order, which is where replication meets consensus. Raft, like Paxos, keeps a replicated log that drives identical state machines on several servers and makes progress while any majority is available: a cluster of five continues with two servers down, and with three down it stops rather than return an incorrect result. Majorities are what prevent split-brain, two halves of a partitioned cluster each accepting writes the other never sees, and they explain why clusters are built with odd numbers of members. Synchronous, quorum-based and asynchronous replication are therefore three answers to one question: how many copies must hold a write before it counts.

Network engineers run replication long before they meet a database. The secondary name servers of a DNS (Domain Name System) zone are asynchronous replicas: RFC (Request for Comments) 1996 of August 1996 introduced the NOTIFY message because long refresh times left long intervals of incoherence among authoritative servers, letting the primary tell its secondaries that the zone changed instead of waiting to be polled, and RFC 1995 of the same month added the incremental zone transfer (IXFR) so that a small change no longer requires a full transfer (AXFR). Firewall and load balancer clusters replicate state rather than data. With session-pickup enabled, the FortiGate Clustering Protocol (FGCP) synchronizes the primary unit's TCP (Transmission Control Protocol) session table to every cluster member as quickly as possible so that the new primary can resume those sessions after a failover; Fortinet's documentation notes that resumption is not guaranteed, and that UDP (User Datagram Protocol) and ICMP (Internet Control Message Protocol) sessions are synchronized only when connectionless pickup is also enabled. A replica that has not yet received a session is, for that session, a lost write.

The defining weakness of replication is that it copies mistakes as faithfully as data. A deletion, a corrupting bug or ransomware encryption on the primary reaches every synchronous replica at once and every asynchronous one a little later. Some services are designed against this. Amazon S3 (Simple Storage Service) does not, by default, replicate delete markers under its current replication configuration, and when a request deletes a specific object version it removes it from the source but does not replicate that deletion, which Amazon describes as protecting data from malicious deletions. NIST adds the security obligations that follow from having two copies: the replica must carry the same protection as the primary, such as encryption at rest and access restrictions (DP-SS-R5); replication traffic should be encrypted in transit unless the copy stays within one room or enclosure (DP-SS-R7); and arrays that no longer share replicated volumes should not keep a trust relationship (AC-SS-R6), since every replication link is also a path into the other site.

The practical questions for any replicated system follow from all of this. Is it synchronous, quorum-based or asynchronous, and what is the measured lag at peak load rather than at rest? What does the primary do when the replica disappears: stop accepting writes, or carry on alone and widen the window of loss? Who decides which copy is authoritative after a partition, and can both sides ever believe they are? And where is the copy that a deletion or an encryption on the primary cannot reach, because if the answer is nowhere, the system has availability and no backup.

sharding.def: Splitting a dataset across machines by some key, so each holds part of it rather than all of it.
sharding.context: It is what you do when one machine can no longer hold or serve the data, and the shard key is the decision that cannot be undone cheaply. Choose badly and traffic concentrates on one shard while the others idle, or the common query has to visit every shard and the whole point is lost. Everything hard about it - rebalancing, cross-shard transactions, hot keys - descends from that single early choice.

data-at-rest.def: Data sitting in storage rather than moving across a network or being processed in memory, and, in most security conversations, shorthand for encrypting it there.
data-at-rest.context: Encryption at rest defends against a specific threat: someone obtaining the medium. A stolen disk, a decommissioned array, a copied snapshot. It does nothing against an attacker who has access to the running system, because the system must be able to read its own data. That is why it satisfies a compliance requirement more often than it changes an incident, and why the useful question is where the key lives relative to the data.
data-at-rest.depth:
What the term covers. Security engineering splits data into three states: at rest in storage, in transit across a network, and in use in a processor's memory. NIST (the US National Institute of Standards and Technology) draws the first line explicitly in SP (Special Publication) 800-111, its guide to storage encryption for end-user devices by Karen Scarfone, Murugiah Souppaya and Matt Sexton (November 2007), which deals only with the encryption of data at rest (storage) and not with data in motion (transmission), and lists the media it means: the drives of desktops and laptops, phones and other handheld devices, and removable storage such as USB (Universal Serial Bus) flash drives, memory cards, external hard drives and writable CDs and DVDs. The same split runs through servers, storage arrays, backups and cloud object stores. In practice "data at rest" is rarely said for its own sake; it is said because a policy, an audit or a contract requires that data in that state be encrypted.

The layers that can do the encrypting. NIST SP 800-111 describes three classes of technique. Full disk encryption (FDE) encrypts everything on the drive used to boot the computer, operating system included, and permits access only after authentication to the FDE product: the master boot record is redirected to a pre-boot environment that checks the user before the system starts. Volume and virtual disk encryption protect a container or partition, and file and folder encryption protect individual objects, which keeps protection attached to the file wherever it is copied. The guide also covers hardware-based encryption performed by the drive itself, with little performance cost because the operating system takes no part. Above those, databases and applications can encrypt fields or tables, and cloud storage services encrypt on the provider's side: on 5 January 2023 Amazon S3 (Simple Storage Service) began applying server-side encryption with S3-managed keys, using 256-bit AES (Advanced Encryption Standard), to all new objects at no cost and with no change to applications, with customer-provided keys (SSE-C) or keys from the AWS (Amazon Web Services) Key Management Service (SSE-KMS) as alternatives. The higher the layer, the narrower the set of people and processes that see plaintext, and the more work it takes to deploy.

The cipher mode for disks. Storage has a constraint that network encryption does not: a sector has a fixed size, and its ciphertext must fit in the same space. NIST SP 800-38E, by Morris Dworkin (January 2010), approves XTS-AES (the XEX Tweakable Block Cipher with Ciphertext Stealing, applied to AES), the mode specified by the Security in Storage Working Group of the IEEE (Institute of Electrical and Electronics Engineers) in IEEE Std 1619-2007, for confidentiality on storage devices that use fixed-length data units. It is explicit about the price: the mode provides no authentication of the data or its source, because it was designed to encrypt without data expansion, which leaves no room for an authentication tag. Disk encryption of this kind therefore keeps a stolen drive unreadable but does not by itself detect a sector modified while the drive was out of the owner's hands.

At rest means powered off. The protection holds only while the keys are absent from the running machine, and that is a narrower window than most people assume. In 2008, J. Alex Halderman and colleagues from Princeton University, the Electronic Frontier Foundation and Wind River Systems showed at the USENIX Security Symposium that DRAM (dynamic random-access memory) keeps its contents for several seconds after power is lost, even at room temperature and even when removed from the motherboard, long enough to image memory and recover disk encryption keys. An adversary who steals a laptop while an encrypted disk is mounted, even if it is screen-locked or suspended, can reach the data; they demonstrated it against BitLocker, TrueCrypt and FileVault. The practical lesson is that a sleeping laptop is not at rest in the cryptographic sense, while one that has been shut down for long enough to lose its memory is.

Where the encryption really happens. Trusting the storage hardware moves the problem rather than solving it. Carlo Meijer and Bernard van Gastel of Radboud University reverse-engineered the firmware of self-encrypting SSDs (solid-state drives) from three manufacturers that together sold roughly 60 per cent of SSDs between 2014 and 2018, and reported in a paper for the 2019 IEEE Symposium on Security and Privacy that many models allowed complete recovery of the data without knowledge of any secret. The damage spread further because BitLocker, the encryption built into Windows, relied exclusively on the drive's hardware encryption whenever the drive advertised support for it, so data that administrators believed was protected by BitLocker was exposed as well. Their conclusion was that one should not rely solely on hardware encryption; the broader one is that an encryption-at-rest checkbox says nothing about who implemented the cryptography or how well.

The key decides everything. Encryption at rest converts the problem of protecting data into the problem of protecting keys, and the useful question is where the key lives relative to the data. Cloud key services formalize the answer as envelope encryption: AWS describes encrypting plaintext data with a data key and then encrypting the data key under another key, possibly several levels deep, until one root key must remain in plaintext; in AWS KMS (Key Management Service) those root keys never leave hardware security modules validated at FIPS (Federal Information Processing Standard) 140-3 Security Level 3 unencrypted. Separating the key's custody from the data's custody is what turns encryption at rest from a formality into a control: a key held in a separate service, under a separate policy, with its use logged, adds a second authorization and an audit trail to every read. It also gives the cleanest way to destroy data. NIST SP 800-88 Revision 2 (September 2025) recognizes cryptographic erase, sanitizing the keys that protect encrypted data so that recovery becomes infeasible, as a purge technique far faster than overwriting, provided the cryptography's pedigree and the preconditions it lists are met.

What it does not do. Server-side encryption with provider-managed keys is transparent by design, which is its selling point and its limit: Amazon could switch it on for every new S3 object without any change to applications precisely because any request with valid credentials is decrypted automatically. Encryption at rest of that kind protects against lost or recycled drives and copied media inside the provider's custody; it does nothing against a stolen access key, an over-permissive bucket policy or an attacker running inside the application. Customer-managed keys narrow the gap only if their own access policy is stricter than the data's. Encryption in transit and access control remain separate requirements, and the honest description of encryption at rest in most architectures is a strong control against physical loss and a weak one against everything else.

data-in-transit.def: Data moving across a network - and the encryption applied so that whoever carries it cannot read it.
data-in-transit.context: It is the better understood half, and the one where the assumption most often outruns the configuration: traffic is encrypted to the load balancer and plaintext behind it, or encrypted with a certificate nobody validates. The honest audit question is not whether it is encrypted but on which segments, and what each end actually checked before trusting the other.

ssid.def: The Service Set Identifier (SSID) is the name a wireless network advertises: a string of up to 32 octets that identifies a network to people and devices, a label rather than an identity, and trivially copied.
ssid.context: Because the name is only a string, any device can claim it, which is the whole basis of the evil twin: a stronger radio announcing the same network and collecting whatever connects. Hiding it protects nothing, since clients that know it broadcast their search for it and reveal it anyway. What actually distinguishes a legitimate network is the credential exchange behind the name, which is why enterprise authentication and certificate validation on the client are the controls that matter.
ssid.depth:
The Service Set Identifier (SSID) is the name of a Wi-Fi network as the IEEE (Institute of Electrical and Electronics Engineers) 802.11 standard carries it: an element of type 0 placed in beacons, probe responses and association requests, holding between 0 and 32 octets. Microsoft's programming interface for it states the consequences plainly: the maximum length is 32, the value is not a null-terminated ASCII (American Standard Code for Information Interchange) string, its length travels separately, and an SSID of length zero is the wildcard that matches any network, which is what a device sends when it probes for whatever is nearby. Because it is a byte string rather than a terminated text string, how it is displayed is up to each device, and Apple notes that it is case-sensitive. The 32-octet limit is the same constant in the Linux kernel's 802.11 definitions, IEEE80211_MAX_SSID_LEN.

The name is not the network. Each access point radio forms a basic service set (BSS), identified by a BSSID (basic service set identifier), which in an infrastructure network is the radio's MAC (media access control) address; many radios in a building advertise the same SSID, so a client roaming from one to another keeps the name while the BSSID changes. Windows reports the two separately for every network it hears, together with the beacon period in time units of 1,024 microseconds, all taken from the beacon or probe response it received. One access point can also advertise several SSIDs at once, each a different logical network. On a FortiGate wireless controller every SSID is created as a virtual network interface, tunnelled to the controller by default or bridged locally at the FortiAP, with an optional VLAN (virtual local area network) ID, a client limit and, with multiple pre-shared keys, dynamic VLAN assignment; in the command line it is config wireless-controller vap with set ssid, and the factory default name is fortinet.

Because the SSID is only a string, any device can claim it, which is the whole basis of the evil twin. In 2024 the Australian Federal Police charged a man accused of running fake free Wi-Fi networks that mimicked legitimate ones at Perth, Melbourne and Adelaide airports and on domestic flights, with a page that harvested email and social media logins. Nothing in the name lets a client tell such an access point from the real one; on an open network, nothing else does either. Common names make it worse: Apple's guidance asks for a single, unique SSID across all bands and warns against defaults such as linksys or netgear, because devices that know a name will try to join any network that announces it.

Hiding the SSID, which access points call disabling broadcast or a closed network, removes the name from beacons but not from the air: clients that want a hidden network must ask for it by name in their probe requests, wherever they are. Apple states that hiding the network name does not conceal the network from detection or secure it, and that because of how devices search for networks it can expose information identifying the user and the hidden networks they use, such as their home network; its devices show a privacy warning when connected to one. FortiAP keeps Broadcast SSID enabled by default.

What protects a network is what happens after the name. With WPA2 or WPA3 Personal the key depends on the passphrase and, in WPA2, on the SSID as well: the wpa_passphrase tool of wpa_supplicant documents that an ASCII passphrase and the SSID together generate the 256-bit PSK (pre-shared key), so the same passphrase on a differently named network gives a different key. With enterprise authentication, IEEE 802.1X and an EAP (Extensible Authentication Protocol) method such as EAP-TLS (Transport Layer Security), which RFC (Request for Comments) 5216 describes as certificate-based mutual authentication, the network proves itself with a certificate, and a client that validates the server's certificate and name will not hand its credentials to an evil twin. That is why enterprise authentication and certificate validation on the client are the controls that matter, and why profiles that tell clients to accept any server certificate undo most of the protection.

Even with authentication, the name itself is not always protected. In May 2024 Mathy Vanhoef and Héloïse Gollier published the SSID Confusion attack, CVE-2023-52424 in the Common Vulnerabilities and Exposures (CVE) list, which comes from the 802.11 standard: the SSID is not always used to derive the session keys and is not exchanged in protected form during the 4-way handshake, and beacons are not authenticated. Where two networks share credentials, an attacker in the middle can make a client believe it joined one while it actually joined the other: a client can be pushed from a 5 GHz network to a weaker 2.4 GHz one with the same password, an eduroam user to another institution's eduroam, and VPN (virtual private network) clients that switch themselves off on trusted network names can be tricked into turning off. The record lists WEP (Wired Equivalent Privacy), WPA3 SAE (Simultaneous Authentication of Equals) in its hunting-and-pecking loop form, 802.1X/EAP, mesh AMPE (Authenticated Mesh Peering Exchange) and FILS (Fast Initial Link Setup) as affected. The proposed fixes are to include the SSID in key derivation, or to authenticate it as additional data in the 4-way handshake, and to use beacon protection, which Wi-Fi 7 mandates; until then, unique credentials per SSID remove the confusion.

In troubleshooting, the SSID is the first field to check and the least informative. A capture shows it in the SSID element of beacons and probe responses, but the questions that matter are which BSSIDs answer for it, on which bands and channels, with which security settings, and whether a second network somewhere advertises the same name with weaker ones. The numbers worth remembering are element ID 0, a maximum of 32 octets, a wildcard of length 0, and a beacon period counted in time units of 1,024 microseconds.

wpa3.def: The current generation of wireless security, replacing the shared-key handshake that allowed offline password guessing.
wpa3.context: The substantive change is the handshake: the older scheme let anyone who captured a connection attempt guess the passphrase offline at their own pace, and the new one does not, which is why a weak passphrase stops being catastrophic on day one. It also encrypts open networks so that a public hotspot is no longer readable by everyone present. Adoption is the usual story - mixed mode keeps the old handshake available for old clients, and a network in mixed mode has the old properties for anyone who asks for them.

captive-portal.def: A captive portal is the web page a network forces a newly connected client to see, to accept terms, pay or sign in, before granting it wider access; traditionally implemented by intercepting the client's first requests.
captive-portal.context: It has traditionally worked by lying: the network answers DNS (Domain Name System) and HTTP (Hypertext Transfer Protocol) for names it does not own so that the browser lands on the portal instead. That is indistinguishable from an attack, which is precisely why it breaks more every year: certificate validation, HSTS (HTTP Strict Transport Security), encrypted DNS and pinned applications all refuse the interception on purpose. Operating systems now probe a known plain-HTTP address to detect the situation and open a restricted window, which is the industry admitting the technique is a hack it has agreed to accommodate; standards published in 2020 let the network announce the portal instead of faking answers.
captive-portal.depth:
A captive portal holds a newly connected device in a restricted state until its user does something in a web browser: reads an advertisement, accepts an acceptable-use policy, pays, or provides credentials. Request for Comments (RFC) 8952, the Captive Portal Architecture published in November 2020 by Kyle Larose, David Dolson and Heng Liu, describes the three pieces every implementation has: a web server for the portal, an enforcement device that allows or blocks traffic, and some way to tell the user. It is found on hotel, airport, aircraft and café Wi-Fi, on guest networks in companies and hospitals, and on some wired ports. It is not a form of wireless security: the network in front of it is usually open, and the portal decides who may pass, not whether the radio link is protected.

The classic way of telling the user is interception. A device on the restricted network asks for some site; the enforcement device answers the DNS (Domain Name System) query with its own address, or lets the query through and catches the HTTP (Hypertext Transfer Protocol) request, then replies with a redirect to the portal. RFC 8952 states the problem bluntly: current solutions forge DNS or HTTP responses, and some attempt a man-in-the-middle (MITM) proxy of HTTPS (HTTP Secure) to forge those too. RFC 6585 (April 2012) gave the honest version of the reply a status code, 511 Network Authentication Required, meant for intercepting proxies that control network access, never for origin servers and never to be cached, and its Appendix B lists what goes wrong without it: a browser that caches the portal's favicon as the real site's icon, policy files and cross-origin rules read from the wrong server, and non-browser HTTP clients such as calendaring or software updates that receive a login page instead of their data. Products put the same mechanism behind a setting. FortiOS, for instance, turns an interface into a portal with set security-mode captive-portal, after which any HTTP request from an unauthenticated user returns the authentication page; the portal can be local or external, a Wi-Fi network in front of it appears open, and exemption lists let devices such as printers through without logging in.

Interception has been failing for years, by design of the protocols it abuses. Most sites now use TLS (Transport Layer Security), so a redirect injected into an HTTPS connection produces a certificate error, and for sites under HTTP Strict Transport Security (HSTS, RFC 6797, November 2012) browsers must fail with no user recourse, without a dialog offering to proceed. A validating resolver rejects a forged DNS answer, which is why RFC 8952 requires that captive portal solutions must not need forged responses and must permit DNSSEC (DNS Security Extensions) validation. Encrypted DNS and applications that pin their certificates simply see a broken network. Johannes Ullrich of the SANS Internet Storm Center summed it up in July 2026: portals used to catch the plain-HTTP home page many users had, but most sites now use TLS and browsers default to it.

Operating systems therefore detect portals themselves, with a canary request. RFC 8952's appendix describes the method: on joining a network the system fetches a fixed vendor URL (Uniform Resource Locator) over plain HTTP, deliberately without TLS so that the portal can redirect it, and treats any other answer as a sign of captivity. Microsoft's Network Connectivity Status Indicator (NCSI) has fetched www.msftconnecttest.com/connecttest.txt since Windows 10 build 14393 (version 1607), expecting the text Microsoft Connect Test, after www.msftncsi.com/ncsi.txt in earlier versions, and also resolves dns.msftncsi.com, expecting 131.107.255.255; a redirect, an empty answer or different content makes it report local connectivity only and prompt the user. Apple systems fetch captive.apple.com/hotspot-detect.html and expect the word Success; Android uses connectivitycheck.android.com/generate_204 and Chrome www.gstatic.com/generate_204, both expecting status 204 with no content; Firefox loads detectportal.firefox.com/canonical.html. RFC 8952 notes the weaknesses: different tests can disagree, and a malicious or misconfigured network can pass the canary through or impersonate it and leave the device with a false negative. In corporate networks the same probes explain odd symptoms: if a proxy auto-configuration file sends www.msftconnecttest.com to the wrong proxy, NCSI decides there is no internet.

The IETF (Internet Engineering Task Force) replaced guessing with announcement in 2020. RFC 8910 (September 2020, Warren Kumari and Erik Kline) lets the network hand the device a URI (Uniform Resource Identifier) in DHCPv4 (Dynamic Host Configuration Protocol for Internet Protocol version 4) option 114, DHCPv6 option 103 or IPv6 (Internet Protocol version 6) Router Advertisement (RA) option type 37. It replaced RFC 7710 of December 2015, whose DHCPv4 code 160 turned out to conflict with another use, and it defines the special value urn:ietf:params:capport:unrestricted for networks that want to say there is no portal at all. The URI points at the Captive Portal API (application programming interface) of RFC 8908, which answers over TLS with JSON (JavaScript Object Notation) of media type application/captive+json: captive true or false, the user-portal-url to open, which must itself use TLS, an optional venue-info-url, and, where the operator supplies them, seconds-remaining, bytes-remaining and can-extend-session. Apple announced support in iOS 14 and macOS Big Sur in June 2020, noting that when both DHCP and RA advertise the portal the URLs must match. The design means the device learns it is captive without anything being forged, can show the time or data left, and can return to the portal before a session expires instead of having its traffic silently hijacked.

Portals are a favourite disguise for credential theft, because users have been taught to type passwords into whatever page appears when they join a network. In June 2024 the Australian Federal Police (AFP) charged a man who, it alleged, had set up evil twin free Wi-Fi networks at airports in Perth, Melbourne and Adelaide and on domestic flights; an airline's staff had reported a suspicious network in April, and the fake page asked victims to sign in with their email or social media accounts. He was sentenced in November 2025 to seven years and four months' imprisonment for those and other offences, and the AFP's advice was that connecting to free Wi-Fi should never require such logins. The defences are on both sides: users should treat a portal as an untrusted page and never reuse real passwords there, and operators should serve the portal over HTTPS from a name with a valid certificate, as RFC 8908 requires for the portal URL, so that a genuine portal can be told from an impostor.

A portal admits a device, not a person, so it is weak access control. RFC 8952 notes that existing implementations often identify the device by its MAC (media access control) address, or by its IP (Internet Protocol) address, and asks for an identifier that is hard to spoof, because a device that can pass for another inherits its access; the radio link itself stays unencrypted unless the network adds Opportunistic Wireless Encryption (OWE, RFC 8110, March 2017), which encrypts an open network without authenticating it, and the portal can sit on top of that. Where real identity matters, IEEE (Institute of Electrical and Electronics Engineers) 802.1X with RADIUS (Remote Authentication Dial-In User Service) authenticates the user before the port opens at all, and portals remain for guests. When a portal misbehaves the useful checks are short: does the client receive option 114 or RA option 37 and can it reach the API over TLS; does the portal's own name resolve and validate before login (the walled garden must include it, and RFC 8952 adds the OCSP (Online Certificate Status Protocol) responders, revocation lists and NTP (Network Time Protocol) servers needed to validate the API's certificate); are the operating systems' probe hosts allowed through after login; and does the portal answer plain HTTP with a redirect or a 511 rather than interfering with HTTPS.

cache-control.def: The header that tells caches whether a response may be stored, by whom, and for how long.
cache-control.context: Two mistakes recur and both are expensive. Caching something private in a shared cache serves one user's page to another, which is a data breach caused by a header. And caching nothing means every request reaches the origin, which turns a traffic spike into an outage that a correct directive would have absorbed entirely. The directive is small, sits in one place, and decides both.

etag.def: An opaque identifier for a specific version of a resource, used to ask whether a cached copy is still current.
etag.context: It turns a full transfer into a short question: the client sends the tag it holds, and the server answers not-modified if nothing changed. That is the cheapest bandwidth saving on the web. It has a second life in write operations, where sending the tag with an update means the change applies only if nobody else changed it first, which is optimistic concurrency implemented in a header.

websocket.def: A connection that starts as HTTP and then upgrades into a two-way channel that stays open.
websocket.context: It exists because the request-response shape cannot express a server that needs to speak first. The operational consequences are what surprise people: the connection is long-lived, so it holds resources on every proxy and firewall in the path and dies to their idle timeouts; it bypasses the per-request checks a gateway performs, because there is only one request; and it needs its own authorization model, since the credential was checked once at the upgrade and the channel then carries anything.

same-origin.def: The browser rule that script from one site cannot read responses from another, where a site means scheme, host and port together.
same-origin.context: It is the foundation the entire web security model rests on: without it, any page could read your mail by requesting it with your cookies attached. Everything that looks like an exception is a deliberate opening of it - CORS is a server saying who may read its responses, and a cross-site scripting flaw matters precisely because injected code runs as the origin and the policy therefore protects the attacker.

mta.def: The server that accepts mail and passes it on towards its destination.
mta.context: It is one of the last places where a machine accepts unsolicited connections from strangers and then acts on their content, which is why mail infrastructure carries so much of the internet's security history: relay controls, reputation lists, authentication records and content filtering were all invented here first. The operational rule that has not changed is that an agent which accepts and forwards without checking who asked will be found and used within hours.

open-relay.def: A mail server that will forward messages from anyone to anyone - the default in the early internet and a liability ever since.
open-relay.context: It was not a defect originally: forwarding for strangers was cooperative behaviour on a network of colleagues. Spam turned it into free infrastructure for whoever found it, and the response invented the reputation list, which is the mechanism that later spread far beyond mail. It is worth remembering as the clearest case of a design that was correct for the network it was built on and became a vulnerability when the population changed.

attestation.def: A statement by one party that something about another is true, made in a form somebody else is willing to rely on.
attestation.context: It is what a report, a certification and a signed software bill of materials all are, and the useful question is always the same three: who is asserting, what exactly did they check, and what happens if they were wrong. An attestation with a narrow scope and a named responsible party is worth more than a broad one nobody stands behind, which is why reading the scope section is the whole skill.

compliance.def: The state of meeting, and being able to show that one meets, a requirement set from outside: a law, a regulation, a contract or an industry standard. Demonstrating it is a different objective from being secure. In device management and zero trust access the word also names a narrower verdict: whether an endpoint passes a posture policy.
compliance.context: The two overlap and are not the same, and pretending otherwise wastes money in both directions. A control can satisfy a requirement and stop nothing, and a genuine improvement can be invisible to the framework. The useful stance is to treat the requirement as a floor and a forcing function, since it obtains budget and attention that a risk argument could not, while measuring the programme against whether an attacker would actually be stopped.
compliance.depth:
Meeting a requirement, and showing it. The vocabulary of standards bodies puts the weight on demonstration. The National Institute of Standards and Technology (NIST) glossary, quoting ISO/IEC 17000 from the International Organization for Standardization (ISO) and the International Electrotechnical Commission (IEC), defines conformity assessment as an activity that provides demonstration that specified requirements relating to a product, process, system, person or body are fulfilled. Data protection law says the same thing in its own words. Article 5(2) of the European Union's General Data Protection Regulation (GDPR) makes the controller responsible for, and able to demonstrate compliance with, its principles, and calls that accountability; the regulation's recitals tie records of processing to the same purpose. Brazil's Lei Geral de Proteção de Dados (LGPD), Law 13,709 of 14 August 2018, goes a step further in article 6, item X: the principle of accountability is the agent's demonstration that it has adopted effective measures able to prove observance of the law, including the effectiveness of those measures. On paper, at least, the Brazilian text closes the gap between a documented control and a working one.

Where requirements come from. Some are law: the GDPR, the LGPD, the European NIS 2 Directive, successor to the 2016 directive on the security of network and information systems (NIS). Some are contract: the Payment Card Industry Data Security Standard (PCI DSS), which, in the words of a United States Senate staff report, card companies require before allowing merchants to process credit and debit card payments. Some are frameworks an organization adopts or that its customers demand, such as an ISO/IEC 27001 certificate or a System and Organization Controls 2 (SOC 2) report. The NIST Cybersecurity Framework 2.0, published on 26 February 2024, files the whole subject under its Govern function, in Organizational Context: GV.OC-03 asks that legal, regulatory and contractual requirements regarding cybersecurity, including privacy and civil liberties obligations, be understood and managed. In that model compliance is an input to risk management, part of the context decisions are made in, rather than its output.

Why it gets budget. The penalties are written into the texts. NIS 2, Directive (EU) 2022/2555 of 14 December 2022, requires member states to ensure that the management bodies of essential and important entities approve the cybersecurity risk-management measures, oversee their implementation and can be held liable for infringements, and that their members follow training; administrative fines for essential entities reach a maximum of at least 10 million euros or 2 per cent of total worldwide annual turnover, whichever is higher, and for important entities at least 7 million euros or 1.4 per cent. The LGPD's article 52 allows a simple fine of up to 2 per cent of the revenue of the company, group or conglomerate in Brazil in its last financial year, excluding taxes, limited to 50 million reais per infraction. Fines of that size, and personal liability for boards, are what make a requirement move faster than a risk register.

Versions and dates. A compliance programme lives on a calendar. The PCI Security Standards Council published PCI DSS v4.0 in March 2022, retired v3.2.1 on 31 March 2024 and on 11 June 2024 published v4.0.1, a limited revision with corrections and clarifications but no added or deleted requirements; v4.0 was retired on 31 December 2024, and the requirements that v4.0 had dated for the future became effective on 31 March 2025. An assessment against a retired version proves only that the organization once met a standard nobody now applies.

Compliant, and breached. The case everyone cites is Target. The Senate Commerce Committee's majority staff report of 26 March 2014 records that Target's chief financial officer testified the company had been certified in September 2013 as compliant with PCI DSS; in November and December 2013 attackers took the financial and personal information of as many as 110 million customers, having entered with a credential belonging to Fazio Mechanical Services, an HVAC (heating, ventilation and air conditioning) and refrigeration contractor. The report quotes Target's own filing that an independent third-party assessor had found the cardholder data network compliant that autumn, and lists requirements that, applied in depth, bore directly on the intrusion: removing or changing unneeded default accounts (requirement 2.1) and monitoring the integrity of critical system files (requirement 11.5). The certificate described a scope, a sample and a date; the attack used a contractor's access and arrived two to three months later.

Configuration compliance. Engineers meet the word most often in a scanner's report. NIST Special Publication (SP) 800-70 Revision 4, the National Checklist Program guide of February 2018, describes a security configuration checklist, also called a lockdown guide, hardening guide, Security Technical Implementation Guide (STIG) or benchmark, as instructions for configuring a product for an environment, verifying that it was configured properly and identifying unauthorized changes; checklists written in the Security Content Automation Protocol (SCAP) can be checked by machine. The Center for Internet Security (CIS) publishes the CIS Benchmarks, consensus-based configuration recommendations for more than 25 vendor product families. A compliance score against one of these is a reading of configuration, a useful one, and says nothing about exposures the checklist never mentions.

Device compliance. In endpoint management and zero trust network access (ZTNA), compliance is a per-device verdict. Microsoft Intune evaluates compliance policies on managed devices (a minimum operating system version, not jailbroken or rooted, a threat level reported by integrated security software) and Microsoft Entra Conditional Access can block devices that fail. The trap is a default: the tenant-wide setting for devices with no compliance policy assigned is Compliant, which Microsoft describes as the security feature being off, and it advises switching it to Not compliant when Conditional Access depends on the result; a device that does not report within the validity period, 30 days by default and configurable from 1 to 120, is treated as noncompliant. Fortinet's FortiClient Endpoint Management Server (EMS) does the equivalent with Zero Trust tagging rules (antivirus installed, running and current, a certificate, a list of Common Vulnerabilities and Exposures (CVE) identifiers, a file, the FortiClient version), and FortiGate pulls the resulting tags over the EMS Fabric connector as read-only dynamic address objects that ZTNA, firewall and network access control (NAC) policies can match.

Neighbours. An audit is the independent examination that tests compliance and reports on it; attestation is a practitioner's report on management's assertion that it complies; risk is what the organization is actually exposed to, which a requirement approximates and never fully describes. The difference between a met requirement and a stopped attacker is the subject of the separate entry on why compliance is not security, and it explains why the useful questions about any framework are what it leaves out and how recently anyone checked.

5g.def: The fifth generation of mobile networking, defined as much by network architecture as by radio speed.
5g.context: The headline figure is throughput and the durable changes are elsewhere: a core network built as software functions rather than fixed boxes, and network slicing, which lets one physical network present several logical ones with different guarantees. The security consequence follows the architecture - when the core is software running in data centres, mobile network security becomes a cloud and supply-chain problem rather than a telecom one.

lte.def: The fourth-generation mobile standard, and the point at which mobile networks became entirely packet-based.
lte.context: Dropping the circuit-switched path is the historically important part: voice stopped being a separate system and became an application on the data network, which is why call quality became a quality-of-service problem rather than a switching one. Most of the world still runs on it, and it remains the fallback that carries service when the newer radio is unavailable - which makes its security properties current rather than historical.

sim.def: The module holding a subscriber's identity and the key that authenticates them to a mobile network.
sim.context: It is a hardware credential, and treating it as one explains both its strength and its most exploited weakness. The key never leaves the card, which is genuinely strong. The account behind it, however, is transferable by a support agent - which is what SIM swapping attacks, and why anything that treats possession of a phone number as proof of identity inherits the security of a call centre rather than of cryptography.

cloud-iam.def: The permission system of a cloud platform - who and what may call which interface on which resource.
cloud-iam.context: It differs from traditional access control in that machines are first-class subjects: most of the identities in a mature account are workloads, not people, and their credentials are issued automatically. That is the improvement and the risk, because a permissive role attached to a compute instance is reachable by anything that can run code on it. The recurring finding is scope - wildcards granted during setup and never narrowed, because nobody knows which of them is now load-bearing.

spot-instance.def: Spare cloud capacity sold cheaply on the condition that it can be taken back with little warning.
spot-instance.context: It is the clearest example of price expressing a guarantee: the same machine costs a fraction of the on-demand rate because the provider keeps the right to reclaim it. That makes it excellent for work that can be interrupted and restarted, and a trap for anything holding state. Designing for it is the same discipline as designing for failure, which is why teams that use it well tend to have better recovery behaviour everywhere else.

edge-computing.def: Running computation near where data is produced or consumed, instead of sending it to a central location first.
edge-computing.context: The motive is usually latency and sometimes law: physics puts a floor under a round trip to a distant region, and data residency rules can forbid the trip entirely. The cost is operational multiplication - the same workload now runs in many places you do not physically control, with the update, monitoring and key management problems that follow. It is a distribution decision before it is a technology.

deprovisioning.def: Removing an identity's access when a person leaves or a role changes - the half of the lifecycle nobody is waiting on.
deprovisioning.context: Provisioning has an impatient audience and deprovisioning has none, which is why access accumulates and departures leave accounts behind. The dangerous residue is rarely the main directory account, which someone does disable, but everything federated, local or machine-to-machine that was granted separately: a key in a repository, an account on a supplier's portal, a token in a scheduled job. The measurable question is how long after a departure the last credential dies.

transaction.def: A group of operations that either all take effect or none do, leaving no visible half-finished state; in network protocols, by extension, one request matched with the responses that complete it.
transaction.context: The guarantee is what lets a system be reasoned about at all: money moves between two accounts without a moment where it exists in neither. It is also expensive, and distributed systems spend most of their design effort deciding how much of it to give up, which is why the interesting question about any storage system is what it promises across machines rather than within one.
transaction.depth:
Where the concept comes from. Jim Gray, then at Tandem Computers, set it out in The Transaction Concept: Virtues and Limitations, a technical report of June 1981 presented at the Very Large Databases conference that September. He defined a transaction as a transformation of state with three properties: atomicity, all or nothing; durability, effects that survive failures; and consistency, a correct transformation that obeys the system's constraints. His model was the contract, and his example the wedding: the parties negotiate for as long as they like, then a minister asks each whether they agree, and only if both say yes is the marriage pronounced. Every transaction has exactly one of two outcomes, committed or aborted; the effects of an aborted transaction are never visible to others; and a committed one can only be corrected by running another, which Gray called a compensating transaction, as when an underpaid employee is paid the difference rather than the payroll being un-run. In December 1983 Theo Haerder and Andreas Reuter, in ACM Computing Surveys, the journal of the Association for Computing Machinery (ACM), added isolation to the list and named the set ACID (atomicity, consistency, isolation, durability), proposing it as the acid test of a database system's quality.

Isolation is the property that is negotiable. The SQL (Structured Query Language) standard of 1992 defines four isolation levels by the anomalies each forbids: dirty reads of uncommitted data, non-repeatable reads, and phantoms, rows that appear in a repeated query. In 1995 Hal Berenson, Phil Bernstein, Jim Gray, Jim Melton, Elizabeth O'Neil and Patrick O'Neil showed that those definitions do not characterize several real implementations, and defined snapshot isolation: each transaction reads from a snapshot of the committed data as of its start, and a transaction commits only if no concurrent transaction has already committed a write to the same data, the first-committer-wins rule that prevents lost updates. Snapshot isolation is still not serializable. In their example two transactions each read x and y, each is written to keep x + y positive, and each updates a different one of the two; each is correct alone, both commit, and the constraint is broken, the anomaly now called write skew.

What a real database promises. PostgreSQL accepts all four standard levels but implements three, treating Read Uncommitted as Read Committed, which is its default. At Read Committed each statement sees a snapshot taken when it starts, so two SELECT statements inside one transaction can return different data if another transaction commits in between.
