Its Serializable level is implemented as Serializable Snapshot Isolation, snapshot isolation plus monitoring for the dangerous patterns, and when it detects one it aborts a transaction with a serialization failure; applications must be written to retry. Choosing a stronger level does not make conflicts disappear, it turns silent anomalies into errors the application has to handle.

How atomicity and durability are made cheap. PostgreSQL's documentation describes write-ahead logging (WAL) as a standard method: changes to the data files are written only after the log records describing them have been flushed to permanent storage, so at commit only the log, written sequentially, has to reach the disk, and after a crash the database replays it to restore the data files. ROLLBACK discards everything a transaction did, and COMMIT makes it permanent. The boundary of what can be rolled back is a property of the engine, not of the SQL: MySQL's reference manual lists data definition language (DDL) statements such as ALTER TABLE, CREATE TABLE and DROP TABLE as causing an implicit commit, ending any open transaction as if COMMIT had been issued, so a schema migration in MySQL cannot be wrapped in one transaction and undone.

Across machines, transactions become a protocol. Two-phase commit has every participant first prepare, making its part durable and promising to commit, before a coordinator tells all of them to commit. PostgreSQL exposes the participant side as PREPARE TRANSACTION, which stores the transaction's full state on disk so that it can still be committed after a crash, and warns that it exists for external transaction managers rather than applications: a prepared transaction keeps its locks, interferes with the reclaiming of storage by VACUUM, and if forgotten can force the server to shut down to prevent transaction identifier wraparound, which is why the feature is best left disabled, with max_prepared_transactions at zero, where nothing manages it. The cost of that blocking is why many distributed designs give up the global transaction and fall back on Gray's other idea, a sequence of local transactions with compensating transactions to undo the earlier steps if a later one fails.

In network protocols the word means a request and its replies. The Session Initiation Protocol (SIP), Request for Comments (RFC) 3261 of June 2002, defines a SIP transaction as all the messages from the client's first request up to the final, non-1xx, response; for an INVITE that ends in a failure response the transaction also includes the ACK, while the ACK for a successful 2xx response is a transaction of its own. Each transaction has a client side and a server side, implemented in user agents and stateful proxies, and its own timers: Timer B, the INVITE transaction timeout, is 64 times T1, and T1 defaults to 500 ms, so a call attempt with no final answer gives up after 32 seconds. When SIP traces show a retransmitted request, the question is which transaction it belongs to, not which call.

Transaction identifiers are how stateless messages are matched, and they are also attack surface. In the Domain Name System (DNS), RFC 1035 of November 1987 gives every query a 16-bit identifier (ID) that the server copies into the reply so the client can match it to the outstanding question. In the Dynamic Host Configuration Protocol (DHCP), RFC 2131 of March 1997 gives each exchange a 4-byte xid, a random number the client chooses to associate the server's replies with its requests. RFC 5452, published in January 2009 by A. Hubert and R. van Mook, spells out the consequence for DNS: an off-path attacker forging answers must guess the ID, which with all 16 bits truly random takes 32,768 attempts on average, and anecdotal evidence suggested some implementations used only 14 bits. Randomizing the source port adds up to another 16 bits of guessing over about 64,512 usable ports, which is why resolvers were patched to randomize both and to validate them in every response.

What goes wrong. Long-running transactions hold locks and old row versions, so a session left idle inside an open transaction can block writers and stop storage from being reclaimed. Retries without idempotence turn one intended transfer into two when a commit succeeded but its acknowledgement was lost. Application code that reads, decides and then writes in separate transactions recreates the races the database would have prevented. And the guarantees stop at the boundary of one system: a transaction that commits in the database while the message announcing it is sent separately can leave the two disagreeing, which is the half-finished state the concept was invented to rule out.

data-classification.def: Deciding which data is sensitive and how each class must be handled - the step every other data control depends on.
data-classification.context: It fails in a specific way: a scheme with five levels that nobody applies is worse than two levels that everyone does, because controls keyed to labels do nothing when the labels are absent or wrong. The workable version is coarse, automatic where possible, and tied to a consequence people can see. If nothing behaves differently once something is labelled confidential, the exercise produced paperwork rather than protection.

bssid.def: The identifier of one specific radio in a wireless network - in practice the access point's own address, as distinct from the network name.
bssid.context: One name can be served by hundreds of radios, and the client chooses between them; the identifier is how you tell which one it actually joined. That makes it the field that matters in wireless troubleshooting, because a complaint about the network is usually a complaint about one access point, and the aggregate hides it. It is also how a rogue announcing your network name is distinguished from your own equipment.

channel-width.def: How much spectrum one wireless channel occupies - wider carries more per transmission and leaves fewer non-overlapping channels.
channel-width.context: It is the clearest trade in wireless design and the most commonly got wrong: the widest setting gives the best single-client speed test and the worst dense-deployment behaviour, because every neighbouring access point now overlaps and they take turns instead of working in parallel. In an office the right answer is usually narrower than the default, which is an argument that has to be made against a number everyone can see on a laptop.

eap-tls.def: Wireless and wired authentication using certificates on both sides, rather than a shared password.
eap-tls.context: RFC 5216 (Simon, Aboba and Hurst of Microsoft, March 2008, Standards Track, obsoleting RFC 2716) specifies EAP-TLS at EAP Type 13: a TLS handshake carried in EAP packets, in which the server presents a certificate, the client presents one too, and both derive keying material; the RFC defines fragmentation with an L bit (a four-octet TLS Message Length is included) and an M bit (more fragments follow), because a handshake with certificates does not fit in one lock-step EAP packet. The exported keys follow a fixed recipe, the TLS pseudo-random function over the master secret with the label "client EAP encryption" and the two random values, with the first 64 octets as the MSK and the next 64 as the EMSK, which is what the access point turns into link encryption keys. It is the strongest common option because there is no passphrase to share, post or take to a former employer, and each device authenticates as itself. The cost is a certificate lifecycle for every endpoint, which is the reason deployments stall. The frequent misconfiguration is worth naming: a client that does not validate the server's certificate will happily authenticate to an impostor, which turns the strongest option into a credential-harvesting opportunity.
eap-tls.depth:
EAP-TLS is the method the other EAP methods are measured against, because it is the one that removes the password. RFC 5216, published in March 2008 by Simon, Aboba and Hurst of Microsoft as a Standards Track document and obsoleting RFC 2716, specifies it at EAP Type 13. The method is a TLS handshake carried inside EAP Request and Response packets: the server presents its certificate, the client presents its own, each verifies the other against its trust anchors, and the handshake's result is keying material for the link. The RFC describes it as providing certificate-based mutual authentication and key derivation, and that combination, both sides proving identity with a certificate and a key coming out of the exchange, is what makes it the strongest option in the family and the only one in which there is no secret a human could write on a sticky note.

The mechanics have one feature that every other TLS-based method inherited. EAP is a lock-step protocol with small packets, and a TLS handshake carrying certificates and chains is not small, so RFC 5216 defines fragmentation: a flags octet with an L bit, meaning a four-octet TLS Message Length field is present, and an M bit, meaning more fragments follow, with the receiver of a fragment answering, in the RFC's words, "with EAP-Type=EAP-TLS and no data". Dozens of round trips between supplicant, switch and RADIUS (Remote Authentication Dial-In User Service) server are normal, and a slow or lossy link between the switch and the server shows up as authentication timeouts long before it shows up as anything else. Once the handshake completes, the key material is exported by a fixed recipe: the TLS pseudo-random function over the master secret with the label "client EAP encryption" and the client and server random values, producing 128 octets of which the first 64 are the Master Session Key and the next 64 the Extended Master Session Key. The use of those keys, the RFC says, "is specific to the lower layer"; in enterprise Wi-Fi that lower layer is the one that encrypts the link, which is how an 802.1X-authenticated session gets keys of its own without anyone configuring them.

The strength comes with a lifecycle. Every endpoint needs a certificate issued to it, a private key kept on it, renewal before expiry and revocation when the device is lost or retired, and the server needs a certificate the clients will trust. Organizations with a device-management platform and a certificate authority that can enrol devices automatically find this routine; organizations without one find it the reason the project stalls, and often settle for a tunnelled password method on the way. RFC 5216 also notes a privacy limitation: a peer configured to keep its identity private, by withholding its certificate until the server is authenticated, typically cannot authenticate with a server that does not support that option, so privacy is a feature to be designed in on both sides.

The misconfiguration that undoes the method deserves its own paragraph. Mutual authentication is only mutual if the client checks the server's certificate against a trusted authority and an expected name. A supplicant set to skip that check will complete the handshake with any access point that presents a certificate, and while EAP-TLS gives an impostor no password to steal, it gives them an authenticated client to attach to a hostile network, and it trains users to accept whatever appears. The setting is on the client, is enforced by management policy, and should be verified on every device class that joins the network, which is the same discipline PEAP and EAP-TTLS need for a more dangerous reason.

Where it fits: EAP-TLS for every device that can hold a certificate, which today includes laptops, phones and tablets under management and a growing share of printers and controllers; TEAP where machine and user must be proven together or where credentials are to be provisioned inside the tunnel; PEAP and EAP-TTLS where a password back end is the constraint; MAB for the devices that can do nothing at all. The 802.1X entry covers the carriage, the RADIUS entry the server side, and the article on 802.1X and the EAP methods sets the choices side by side.

http2.def: The second major version of the Hypertext Transfer Protocol (HTTP): a binary framing layer that carries many concurrent requests and responses as independent streams over one TCP (Transmission Control Protocol) connection and compresses their header fields, without changing what a request means.
http2.context: HTTP/2 fixed the main waste of HTTP/1.1 (Hypertext Transfer Protocol version 1.1): browsers opened several TCP (Transmission Control Protocol) connections to each server and queued requests behind one another, because a connection could usefully carry only one response at a time. It gives every request and response its own stream inside one connection, interleaves their frames and compresses repetitive header fields. The limitation is inherited from underneath: the streams are independent to HTTP but not to TCP, so one lost or reordered packet stalls every stream on the connection. That transport-level head-of-line blocking is what HTTP/3 removes by running over QUIC. The other legacy is operational: one long-lived connection carrying hundreds of streams behaves differently through proxies, load balancers and denial-of-service defences than many short ones.
http2.depth:
What it is, and what it is not. RFC (Request for Comments) 9113, published by the IETF (Internet Engineering Task Force) in June 2022, calls HTTP/2 an optimized expression of the semantics of the Hypertext Transfer Protocol (HTTP). The semantics themselves are defined once for every version in RFC 9110; HTTP/2 changes only how messages travel. It runs over one TCP (Transmission Control Protocol) connection opened by the client and is not a new transport, and the specification states plainly that TCP head-of-line blocking is not addressed. RFC 9113 obsoletes RFC 7540, the original specification of May 2015, and RFC 8740, which had defined its use over TLS (Transport Layer Security) 1.3.

Where it came from. HTTP/2 grew out of SPDY, an experimental protocol from Google's Let's make the web faster initiative, whose Chromium white paper reported page-load speed-ups of 27 to 60 per cent over plain TCP on the top 25 websites with 1 per cent packet loss. Mike Belshe and Roberto Peon put SPDY before the IETF as an Internet-Draft in February 2012. RFC 7540, which they wrote with Martin Thomson as editor, credits a long list of SPDY contributors, and its header compression, HPACK, appeared alongside it as RFC 7541 by Peon and Herve Ruellan.

Starting a connection. Over TLS the protocol is named h2 in ALPN (Application-Layer Protocol Negotiation), the octets 0x68 and 0x32, so the version is agreed inside the TLS handshake without adding a round trip, as RFC 7301 intended. RFC 9113 requires TLS 1.2 or later and SNI (Server Name Indication); under TLS 1.2 it forbids TLS compression and renegotiation, requires TLS_ECDHE_RSA_WITH_AES_128_GCM_SHA256, and lists prohibited cipher suites that a peer may refuse with INADEQUATE_SECURITY. In cleartext, the h2c token for the HTTP/1.1 Upgrade header was never widely deployed and is now deprecated; what remains is prior knowledge, which curl requests with --http2-prior-knowledge. The client then sends a 24-octet preface, the text PRI * HTTP/2.0 and SM separated by blank lines, followed by a SETTINGS frame; the server answers with its own SETTINGS frame.

Frames and streams. Every frame has a fixed 9-octet header: a 24-bit Length, an 8-bit Type, 8 bits of Flags, one reserved bit and a 31-bit Stream Identifier. Payloads may not exceed 16,384 octets unless the receiver raises SETTINGS_MAX_FRAME_SIZE, whose ceiling is 16,777,215. The ten frame types run from DATA (0x00) to CONTINUATION (0x09). Clients open odd-numbered streams, servers even-numbered ones, and stream 0 carries connection control. A request is a HEADERS frame, plus CONTINUATION frames when the field block does not fit, then DATA frames. The request line becomes the pseudo-header fields :method, :scheme, :authority and :path (and :status in responses), field names must be lowercase, connection-specific fields such as Connection, Keep-Alive, Transfer-Encoding and Upgrade are forbidden, and chunked transfer encoding cannot be used, because DATA frames carry the content.

Flow control, settings and errors. Every stream and the connection as a whole start with a flow-control window of 65,535 octets, which the receiver raises with WINDOW_UPDATE frames up to 2 to the power 31 minus 1. SETTINGS frames carry each side's parameters and are acknowledged; SETTINGS_MAX_CONCURRENT_STREAMS, for instance, starts unlimited, with a recommended minimum of 100. A stream error is answered with RST_STREAM and spares the other streams; a connection error ends with GOAWAY, which names the last stream processed; and the code ENHANCE_YOUR_CALM (0x0b) exists for a peer whose behaviour might be generating excessive load.

Header compression. SPDY compressed HTTP/1.1's repetitive header fields with DEFLATE until the CRIME (Compression Ratio Info-leak Made Easy) attack exposed the risk, so HPACK took an approach its authors call intentionally simple and inflexible: a static table of 61 common fields, a dynamic table both sides maintain (4,096 octets by default) and a static Huffman code for literals. RFC 7541 admits that the dynamic table can still be probed by an attacker who can choose fields and observe their encoded length, even through TLS; values that must not be guessed can be sent as never-indexed literals. The state lives per connection, and a receiver must decompress every field block, even for a stream it is about to discard, or close the whole connection with COMPRESSION_ERROR.

Two features that did not survive deployment. RFC 7540's dependency-tree priorities were, in RFC 9113's own words, not successful; they are deprecated in favour of RFC 9218 by Kazuho Oku and Lucas Pardue, a Priority header field carrying an urgency from 0 to 7, 3 by default, and an incremental flag, plus a PRIORITY_UPDATE frame for HTTP/2 and HTTP/3. Server push, a PUSH_PROMISE followed by an unrequested response on an even-numbered stream, fared worse. Google announced on 18 August 2022 that Chrome 106 would disable it by default, since only 1.25 per cent of HTTP/2 sites used it (later 0.7 per cent) and results were mixed, with many regressions, and pointed to 103 Early Hints.

What it did not fix. Fewer connections mean less competition between flows, and they replace the browser habit of pooling up to six TCP connections per host. RFC 9114 states the catch: HTTP/2's parallelism is invisible to TCP's loss recovery, so one lost or reordered packet stalls every active transaction. HTTP/3 keeps the semantics and moves the streams into QUIC, which recovers loss per stream. F5 BIG-IP carries HTTP/2 on both the client and the server side only through its message-routing proxy, the HTTP MRF Router option, instead of the connection-oriented TCP proxy, and that mode rules out OneConnect, hash and SSL (Secure Sockets Layer) persistence and connection mirroring; F5 also lists NTLM (NT LAN Manager) authentication as incompatible with HTTP/2.

A history of resource exhaustion. Most HTTP/2 security problems share one shape: a cheap frame forces the server to allocate state or do work. The CERT Coordination Center's VU#605641 of 13 August 2019 covered eight implementation flaws, CVE (Common Vulnerabilities and Exposures) entries CVE-2019-9511 to CVE-2019-9518, seven reported by Jonathan Looney of Netflix and one by Piotr Sikora of Google. Rapid Reset, CVE-2023-44487, was exploited in the wild from August to October 2023 and disclosed on 10 October by Cloudflare with Google and AWS (Amazon Web Services): the client opens a stream and cancels it at once with RST_STREAM, and because cancelled streams stop counting against SETTINGS_MAX_CONCURRENT_STREAMS, the limit never bites. Cloudflare saw a peak just above 201 million requests per second from a botnet of only 20,000 machines. On 3 April 2024 VU#421644, reported by Bartek Nowotarski, described CONTINUATION floods: header blocks that never set END_HEADERS exhausted memory, or the CPU (central processing unit) when Huffman-encoded, in implementations including Node.js (CVE-2024-27983), and because such a request never completes, CERT warns that it may only be visible in raw traffic.

http3.def: HTTP/3 is the version of the Hypertext Transfer Protocol (HTTP) that runs over QUIC on UDP (User Datagram Protocol), standardized as RFC (Request for Comments) 9114 in June 2022, so that a lost packet stalls only the stream it belongs to rather than every request on the connection.
http3.context: Moving the transport onto UDP (User Datagram Protocol) is what removes head-of-line blocking, and it has consequences beyond speed. The transport is encrypted, so middleboxes see far less and classifying traffic by inspection largely stops working. A connection can survive a change of client address, which is why a phone moving between networks keeps its session. And networks that block UDP force the client back to HTTP/2 over TCP (Transmission Control Protocol), which usually works and quietly costs the benefit.
http3.depth:
What it is. HTTP/3 is RFC (Request for Comments) 9114, edited by Mike Bishop and published in June 2022 as a Proposed Standard: a mapping of HTTP semantics, the methods, status codes and fields defined once for every version in RFC 9110, onto the QUIC transport. It is not a new HTTP. What changed is the layer underneath. HTTP/1.1 sends text and, having no multiplexing, opens several TCP (Transmission Control Protocol) connections to work in parallel, which RFC 9114 notes is bad for congestion control because TCP does not share it across connections. HTTP/2 added binary framing and multiplexing without touching the transport, but its parallel streams are invisible to TCP's loss recovery, so one lost or reordered packet stalls every transaction on the connection. QUIC provides streams, per-stream flow control and per-stream reliability with congestion control across the whole connection, and it builds in TLS (Transport Layer Security) 1.3, so a loss now stalls only the stream that lost data.

The transport underneath. QUIC was published in May 2021 as three documents. RFC 9000 defines the protocol: a connection-oriented, stateful exchange whose packets are carried in UDP (User Datagram Protocol) datagrams to ease deployment in existing networks, with every packet authenticated in full and as much of it encrypted as is practical; bidirectional and unidirectional streams; and connection identifiers that let a connection move to a new path, which in version 1 only the client may do, as a phone does when it leaves Wi-Fi for a mobile network or a NAT (network address translation) device rebinds its port. RFC 9001 integrates the TLS handshake, either a full 1-RTT (round-trip time) handshake or 0-RTT, in which a returning client sends application data immediately; RFC 9001 warns that 0-RTT data can be replayed by an attacker and must not carry anything that would cause unwanted effects if repeated. RFC 9002 covers loss detection and congestion control, with a default controller similar to TCP NewReno. Two defensive numbers are worth remembering: a client's first datagrams must carry at least 1,200 bytes of UDP payload, and until a peer's address is validated a server may send no more than three times what it received, the anti-amplification limit that stops QUIC being used as a reflector.

How HTTP maps onto it. Each request and response uses one client-initiated bidirectional QUIC stream. Each side also opens a unidirectional control stream, and QPACK needs two more, so both endpoints must allow the peer at least three unidirectional streams. The frames are familiar from HTTP/2 but fewer: DATA (0x00), HEADERS (0x01), SETTINGS (0x04, sent only at the start of the connection), PUSH_PROMISE (0x05) and GOAWAY (0x07) remain, while RST_STREAM, PING, WINDOW_UPDATE and CONTINUATION are gone because QUIC already provides stream reset, liveness and flow control, and HTTP/3 itself defines no priority signalling (the Extensible Prioritization Scheme, RFC 9218, also from June 2022, fills that role). The frame type space grew from 8 bits to 62. Field compression is QPACK, RFC 9204: HPACK, the HTTP/2 scheme, would reintroduce head-of-line blocking because it assumes a total ordering of frames across all streams, so QPACK keeps HPACK's ideas but moves table updates onto separate encoder and decoder streams and lets each implementation trade compression ratio against the risk of a blocked stream.

Finding an HTTP/3 server. A client cannot simply connect, because nothing in a web address says the server listens on UDP. RFC 9114 gives three routes. A client may try QUIC directly on the URL's port and select HTTP/3 with the Application-Layer Protocol Negotiation (ALPN) token h3. An origin already reached over TCP may advertise HTTP/3 with the Alt-Svc response field of RFC 7838 (April 2016), for example Alt-Svc: h3=":50781" for UDP port 50781 on the same host; the advertisement stays fresh for 24 hours unless its ma parameter says otherwise. And since November 2023 the DNS (Domain Name System) record type called HTTPS (after HTTP Secure), defined in RFC 9460 as resource record type 65, can carry alpn=h3 so the client knows before it opens any connection. Because HTTP/3 does not use TCP, it cannot be the direct route for a plain http address. When QUIC cannot be established, for example because UDP is blocked, RFC 9114 says clients SHOULD fall back to a TCP-based version of HTTP; RFC 9308 cites measurements finding that between 3 and 5 per cent of networks block all UDP, which is why every HTTP/3 deployment is also an HTTP/2 deployment.

Where the name came from. QUIC began at Google, in Daniel Stenberg's description as more or less HTTP/2 encrypted over UDP; when the work moved to the Internet Engineering Task Force (IETF) it was split into a general transport and a separate HTTP mapping, informally iQUIC as against Google's gQUIC, with the HTTP part known as hq. On 28 October 2018 Mark Nottingham proposed to the QUIC working group that the HTTP document be renamed HTTP/3 with the final ALPN token h3, to stop people confusing the transport with the HTTP binding; the HTTP working group reached consensus on the name at IETF 103 in November 2018, the same month that LiteSpeed announced, on 7 November, that it and Facebook had completed the first interoperation between two HTTP/3 implementations.

How much of the web uses it. The two common measures count different things. W3Techs reported in November 2026 that 40.8 per cent of all websites use HTTP/3, which counts sites that offer it. Cloudflare's Radar Year in Review, published on 15 December 2025, counts requests: across 2025, 21 per cent of requests to Cloudflare used HTTP/3, 50 per cent HTTP/2 and 29 per cent HTTP/1.x, shares largely unchanged from 2024; 15 countries or regions sent more than a third of their requests over HTTP/3, led by Georgia at 38 per cent, and seven, among them Singapore and Ireland, were below 10 per cent because of the volume of HTTP/1.x traffic from bots. A site that offers HTTP/3 still serves many of its requests over HTTP/2.

What it means for the network. RFC 9312, the IETF's manual for operators, is direct about what is left to see. The TLS ClientHello, including any Server Name Indication (SNI), is still readable unless it is encrypted; QUIC version 1 offers an optional spin bit so that passive observers can estimate round-trip time; and HTTP/3 uses UDP port 443 by convention, but so does Microsoft's SMB (Server Message Block) over QUIC by default, and DNS over QUIC (RFC 9250) also exists, so a UDP port number alone does not identify the application. UDP is also the most common vector for distributed denial of service, and some networks block or throttle it; RFC 9312 recommends policing per flow rather than dropping random packets, because random loss lets handshakes complete, prevents the fallback to TCP and leaves the connections suffering heavy loss. Blocking UDP port 443 outright is the blunt version of the same policy: browsers fall back to HTTP/2 over TCP, where existing inspection works, at the cost of everything HTTP/3 was for.

On F5 BIG-IP and FortiGate. F5's documentation for BIG-IP Local Traffic Manager (LTM) 15.1.0 through 21.1.0 builds an HTTP/3 virtual server with protocol UDP, the udp profile on the client side and a TCP profile (F5 recommends f5-tcp-lan) on the server side, the clientssl-quic profile because TLS 1.3 is required, the HTTP MRF Router (the HTTP router of F5's Message Routing Framework) enabled, and a QUIC profile and an HTTP3 profile; the system decrypts the QUIC traffic and sends it to the pool over TCP, so the servers behind it need not speak HTTP/3 at all. The tmsh reference lists the QUIC profile's limits on concurrent bidirectional and unidirectional streams and a spin-bit switch, and gives the HTTP3 profile's header table a default of 4,096 bytes. The 21.1 documentation adds Web Application Firewall (WAF) inspection of client-side HTTP/3 through the standard pipeline, provided HTTP/3 discovery is configured with Alt-Svc or DNS HTTPS records. On FortiGate, FortiOS inspects HTTP/3 in flow mode, and its guide notes that Chrome may switch the connection to HTTP/2 when deep inspection is applied because of its sensitivity to the added delay; FortiOS 7.2.4 stopped blocking QUIC by default in application control (the allow-quic option was removed), leaving manual blocking through the QUIC application signature 40169 for proxy mode, and in 7.6 the HTTPS and DNS over TLS options of an SSL/SSH (Secure Sockets Layer/Secure Shell) inspection profile enable QUIC inspection with set quic inspect.

user-agent.def: The client program that makes requests for a user (a browser, a crawler, a script) and the User-Agent header in which it identifies itself: a claim, not a fact, and one of the oldest lies on the web.
user-agent.context: The string is famously accreted: browsers claim to be other browsers because sites once tested for names instead of capabilities, so almost every modern agent asserts a lineage it does not have. Two practical points survive that history. Anything security-relevant that depends on it is trivially bypassed, since the client chooses what to send. And it is a fingerprinting input, which is why browsers are now reducing what it reveals rather than adding to it.
user-agent.depth:
The term has two senses, and specifications keep them apart. In RFC (Request for Comments) 9110, the current definition of HTTP (Hypertext Transfer Protocol) semantics, published in June 2022, a user agent is any client program that initiates a request. Browsers are the familiar case but, the document says, only a small percentage of implementations: the others include spiders, command-line tools, household appliances, firmware update scripts and mobile apps, often with no person present at the time of the request. Other protocols use the word the same way: in SIP (Session Initiation Protocol) a user agent is the logical entity that acts as client and server for a call, and mail architecture speaks of the message user agent (MUA). In everyday use, though, the user agent is the second sense: the string that the program sends about itself in the User-Agent request header.

The header's grammar is simple. Its value is one or more product identifiers, each a name with an optional slash and version, and each followed by zero or more comments in parentheses, listed by convention in decreasing order of significance. A client should send it in every request; it must not carry advertising; it should not contain needlessly fine-grained detail, which RFC 9110 says increases request latency and the risk of a user being identified against their wishes; and implementations are encouraged not to use the product tokens of other implementations to declare compatibility with them, since that defeats the purpose of the field. The example the RFC prints, CERN-LineMode/2.15 libwww/2.17b3, is the same one that RFC 1945 printed for HTTP/1.0 in May 1996. That older text already listed the three uses the header still has: statistics, tracing protocol violations, and tailoring responses to avoid the limitations of particular agents. The third is where the trouble started.

The accretion is documented in Aaron Andersen's history, written for WebAIM in 2008. NCSA Mosaic called itself NCSA_Mosaic/2.0 (Windows 3.1). Netscape, whose code name was Mozilla, sent Mozilla/1.0 (Win3.1), and when sites began sending frames only to clients that said Mozilla, Internet Explorer shipped as Mozilla/1.22 (compatible; MSIE 2.0; Windows 95). The pattern repeated with each engine that mattered: Konqueror added (KHTML, like Gecko) to be served the pages written for Gecko, Safari kept that phrase and added AppleWebKit, and the first Chrome announced itself as Mozilla/5.0, AppleWebKit, KHTML like Gecko, Chrome and Safari all at once. MDN Web Docs states the outcome plainly: Mozilla/5.0 is the token that says a browser is Mozilla-compatible, and for historical reasons almost every browser sends it.

The fiction is now written into the standard. The HTML (Hypertext Markup Language) specification maintained by the WHATWG (Web Hypertext Application Technology Working Group) requires the script-visible properties to return fixed values in every browser: appCodeName is Mozilla, appName is Netscape and product is Gecko. It defines three navigator compatibility modes, Chrome, Gecko and WebKit, which decide only whether productSub reads 20030107 or 20100101 and whether vendor reads Google Inc., Apple Computer, Inc. or nothing. Its advice to authors is that client detection should be limited to known current versions, with unknown and future versions assumed to be compliant.

A current desktop Chrome string reads Mozilla/5.0 (Windows NT 10.0; Win64; x64) AppleWebKit/537.36 (KHTML, like Gecko) Chrome/143.0.0.0 Safari/537.36, the example on MDN as read on 12 November 2026. Only two parts carry information: the platform comment and the Chrome major version. Edge appends an Edg token and Opera an OPR token to the same string. Firefox sends Mozilla/5.0, a platform comment with an rv value, Gecko/20100101 (a fixed string on desktop) and Firefox with its version. Safari puts a Version token before Safari/605.1.15, and the other browsers on an iPhone, being built on WebKit, look like Safari.

Since 2022 the string has been getting shorter. Chromium's User-Agent Reduction replaced the minor version numbers with 0.0.0 from Chrome 101 (fully rolled out on 13 June 2022), reduced the desktop string from Chrome 107 (7 February 2023) and the Android string from Chrome 110 (11 May 2023), and finished in Chrome 113. The platform part became one of a few literal values that do not change when the system is updated: Windows NT 10.0; Win64; x64, Macintosh; Intel Mac OS X 10_15_7, X11; Linux x86_64 and, for every Android phone, Linux; Android 10; K. Operating-system versions and device models can therefore no longer be read from an access log. The detail moved to User-Agent Client Hints: Sec-CH-UA, Sec-CH-UA-Mobile and Sec-CH-UA-Platform are sent by default, and anything more precise, such as the model or the full version list, only after the server asks for it in an Accept-CH response header, the mechanism of the experimental RFC 8942 of February 2021. Chromium states no plans to reduce the string on iOS or in Android WebView.

Programs that are not browsers are usually more candid, because they have no pages to be denied. curl sends curl and its version, and its -A option sets any other string or, given an empty argument, removes the header. Well-behaved crawlers follow RFC 9309, the Robots Exclusion Protocol of September 2022: the name they obey in robots.txt should be a substring of their User-Agent, as in Mozilla/5.0 (compatible; Googlebot/2.1; +http://www.google.com/bot.html), and the string should describe their purpose. Because anyone can send that string, Google documents how to check it: a reverse DNS (Domain Name System) lookup on the source address, a name under googlebot.com, google.com or googleusercontent.com, and a forward lookup that returns the same address, or a match against its published address ranges.

For whoever operates the server, the header is a log field and an input, never an identity. Apache's Combined Log Format records it as the last field of every line, and on a BIG-IP an iRule reads it with the HTTP::header command. It is chosen by the client, so a rule that allows or blocks on it stops only clients that tell the truth; RFC 9309 says the same of robots.txt, whose rules are not a form of access authorization. Detection that has to resist lying compares the claim with things the client cannot change as easily, such as the TLS (Transport Layer Security) handshake fingerprints of the JA3 method that Salesforce published in 2017, and treats a browser string arriving with a script's handshake as the finding. On the page itself, MDN's advice is to test for the feature needed instead of parsing the string, which it calls very hard to do reliably and a frequent cause of bugs.

spam-filter.def: The system deciding which incoming mail reaches a person - the most consequential automated judgement most organizations run.
spam-filter.context: It is a false-positive problem more than a detection problem: missing spam is an annoyance and blocking an invoice, a job offer or a customer reply is a business incident, which is why quarantine and release exist at all. It is also the first control an attacker tests, because delivery is the precondition for phishing, and the reason authentication records for a domain matter to everyone who receives its mail rather than only to its owner.

audit.def: An independent, systematic and documented examination of evidence against stated criteria (a control framework, a standard, a policy or a law) that ends in a conclusion someone outside the activity can rely on. In logging, the same word names the records an examination reads: audit records, audit logs and the audit trail.
audit.context: Independence is the product: an internal review can find more and convince fewer. What auditors test is usually a sample against a stated control, which means the result says the control worked on those occasions rather than always, a distinction worth holding on to when a clean report meets a real incident. The useful preparation is not tidying evidence before the visit but keeping records that are produced by the process anyway.
audit.depth:
Two definitions, one word. The glossary of the National Institute of Standards and Technology (NIST) carries two lineages. The first, which the Committee on National Security Systems took from ISO 30401:2018, a standard of the International Organization for Standardization (ISO), calls an audit a systematic, independent and documented process for obtaining audit evidence and evaluating it objectively to determine the extent to which the audit criteria are fulfilled; an audit can be internal (first party, run by the organization itself or by an outside party on its behalf) or external (second or third party), and one audit can combine several disciplines. The second, the one NIST Special Publication (SP) 800-12 and SP 800-53 Revision 5 use, is the security sense: an independent review and examination of records and activities to assess the adequacy of system controls and ensure compliance with established policies and operational procedures, with older versions adding the recommendation of changes. NIST's entry for security audit adds a warning worth keeping: some publications use audit together with, or as a synonym for, inspection or assessment, and the terms are not interchangeable.

What it is not. In SP 800-53 the work an organization does to check its own controls is a separate control, CA-2 (Control Assessments): at a defined frequency, determine whether the controls are implemented correctly, operating as intended and producing the desired outcome, and write a report. The control's own discussion says that external audits, including those by regulatory agencies, are outside its scope, and penetration testing (CA-8) and continuous monitoring (CA-7) are separate controls again. A vulnerability scan, a penetration test or a configuration score from a compliance tool can all be evidence in an audit. None of them is one, because none compares evidence with stated criteria and ends in an opinion somebody else is entitled to rely on.

The other sense: audit records. NIST defines an audit record as an individual entry in an audit log related to an audited event, and SP 800-53 gives the subject a whole family, Audit and Accountability (AU), numbered AU-1 to AU-16. Two of its controls explain why the records matter to the examination. AU-9 requires that audit information and the logging tools themselves be protected from unauthorized access, modification and deletion, with an alert when that happens; its first enhancement asks for hardware-enforced write-once media and points out that tape cartridges, Universal Serial Bus (USB) drives and rewritable discs are write-protected, not write-once. AU-11 keeps records for a defined period to support after-the-fact investigations and retention rules, and its enhancement deals with records kept for years, which can mean converting formats or keeping equipment that can still read them. A log that the people it describes can edit is not evidence.

On a real device. F5 documents both kinds of record for BIG-IP (version 21.1, page updated 22 July 2026). Login attempts go to /var/log/secure: successful ones for command-line sessions, failed ones for the command line, the Configuration utility and iControl. Configuration changes go to /var/log/audit whenever an object such as a virtual server or a pool is created, modified or deleted, whether by a user, by the system or by loading configuration. The detail that catches people is the default. Audit logging of configuration changes, set with tmsh modify sys daemon-log-settings mcpd audit, ships disabled, and its levels select the initiator rather than the severity: enabled records user-initiated changes, verbose adds configuration loads, and the highest level adds changes the system makes itself. Audit logging of tmsh commands, by contrast, defaults to on and records every command typed, including those that change nothing. An auditor asking who changed a pool last March gets an answer only if somebody switched the first one on in advance and shipped the file somewhere the administrators could not edit.

Independence, written into rules. The SP 800-53 enhancement CA-2(1) describes independent assessors as free of any actual or perceived conflict of interest: they do not assess their own work, act as management or employees of the organization, or put themselves in a position of advocacy for it; where an organization is too small for that, independence can come from having the results reviewed by an independent team. The Institute of Internal Auditors' 2024 Global Internal Audit Standards, to which internal audit functions are expected to conform, are organized in five domains and fifteen principles, among them Maintain Objectivity and Positioned Independently. For listed companies in the United States the Sarbanes-Oxley Act (Public Law 107-204, 30 July 2002) made independence law: section 201 forbids the accounting firm that audits a company from also providing it, at the same time, with services such as financial information systems design and implementation or outsourced internal audit; section 203 bars a lead or reviewing audit partner who has served the company in each of the five previous fiscal years; and section 404 requires management to assess internal control over financial reporting every year and the auditor to attest to that assessment.

A point in time, or a period. The distinction that matters most when reading a report is its time frame. The American Institute of Certified Public Accountants (AICPA) defines two kinds of System and Organization Controls 2 (SOC 2) examination on controls relevant to security, availability, processing integrity, confidentiality or privacy. A type 1 report covers the service organization's description of its system and whether the controls were suitably designed as of a point in time. A type 2 report adds whether they operated effectively throughout a period, with a detailed description of the auditor's tests and their results; the auditor may not mix the two by giving a design opinion on some controls and an effectiveness opinion on others. The guide also states that controls can only provide reasonable assurance. The criteria are the 2017 trust services criteria and the 2018 description criteria, both revised in 2022, and the AICPA has published exposure drafts for 2027 versions. A type 1 says the controls existed and were well designed on one day; the test results in a type 2 are where exceptions are recorded.

Management system audits. For the ISO family of management systems the guidance is ISO 19011, Guidelines for auditing management systems, which covers audit principles, managing an audit programme, conducting audits and auditor competence. ISO lists its 2018 third edition as withdrawn; the 2026 edition, published in the United Kingdom as BS EN ISO 19011:2026, expands the guidance on remote and hybrid audits in line with ISO/IEC TS 17012:2024 (IEC being the International Electrotechnical Commission) and expects auditors to evaluate cloud platforms, data analytics and decisions made by artificial intelligence (AI). Certification audits against ISO/IEC 27001 are governed separately: the certification body must meet ISO/IEC 17021-1 and its information security extension, ISO/IEC 27006-1:2024, which replaced the 2015 edition and sets requirements for impartiality, auditor competence and minimum audit duration, with more room for remote auditing.

When the audit is the weak link. In May 2026 the AICPA told its peer reviewers how to deal with firms issuing SOC 2 reports at high volume through third-party compliance platforms. The risk it named is engagements that are not designed around the client's own risks and so produce identical reports, risk assessments, sample sizes and testing procedures; peer review calls such engagements nonconforming, and reviewers who suspect it are to pull about five engagements from different partners and compare them with each other and with the prior year, under a structured monitoring process starting 1 June 2026. The AICPA also said it was looking into anonymously published allegations about a compliance vendor that offers SOC (System and Organization Controls) reporting services, and that it would act against members found not to have followed professional standards, not to be enrolled in peer review, or to be unlicensed. For anyone receiving a report, that is the reason to read who signed it, the period it covers and the tests behind the opinion, not only the cover page.

Neighbours. Compliance is the state of meeting a requirement; an audit is one way of demonstrating it to somebody else. Attestation is the accountant's word for a report on another party's assertion, which is why the AICPA describes SOC 2 as an assertion-based examination of management's description and controls. Accounting, the third A of authentication, authorization and accounting (AAA), and the audit trail produce the records; the audit reads them. An assessment, a scan or a test can be run by the team that operates the system; an audit, in every definition above, needs independence from the activity it examines.

control-framework.def: A published set of controls used as a common reference - so an organization can describe what it does in terms others recognize.
control-framework.context: Its value is shared vocabulary rather than novelty: nothing in a framework is unknown to a competent practitioner, and the point is that a customer, an insurer and a regulator can all read the same map. The failure is adopting one as a to-do list, which produces uniform coverage rather than defence where it is needed. Frameworks describe what to consider, and the organization still has to decide what its own risk demands.

luigi-galvani.def: The physician who saw dead frog legs twitch at the touch of dissimilar metals in 1780 and called it animal electricity.
luigi-galvani.context: His explanation was wrong and his observation was not, which is the useful shape of the story. Volta disputed the theory - arguing the twitch came from the contact of two metals rather than from anything in the animal - and that disagreement is what drove him to build the pile. A mistaken interpretation of a correct experiment produced the first steady current, and the word galvanic survived attached to the idea he got wrong.

charles-augustin-de-coulomb.def: The French engineer who turned the torsion balance into an instrument for measuring charge, and proved the electric force follows an inverse square law.
charles-augustin-de-coulomb.context: Before him there were devices to generate, store and detect static electricity and no easy way to say how much. He did not invent the balance - John Michell had used a similar one for gravity - but he was the first to point it at charge, and measurement is what turned electricity from a phenomenon people demonstrated into a quantity people could reason about. The field became a science when it acquired a number.

andre-marie-ampere.def: The physicist who turned Ørsted's observation into electrodynamics, and who first drew the distinction between current and voltage.
andre-marie-ampere.context: Ørsted's experiment was reproduced at the Paris Academy in September 1820; Ampère presented his first reflections on it a week later and spent the following six years turning it into mathematics. The speed matters less than the difference in kind: Ørsted observed that a current deflects a needle, and Ampère produced a theory that predicted by how much. Separating current from voltage is the distinction every practical electrical measurement rests on, and the unit of the first carries his name.

georg-ohm.def: The German physicist whose 1827 law relates voltage, current and resistance - the first thing anyone learns about circuits, and the last thing they stop using.
georg-ohm.context: The law was poorly received when published and he waited years for recognition, which is a recurring pattern in this timeline rather than an anecdote. What it gave the field was a design tool: with three quantities related by one equation, a circuit can be reasoned about before it is built. Every cable length calculation, every power budget and every fault involving a bad connection is downstream of it.

james-prescott-joule.def: The physicist who showed that electrical energy, heat and mechanical work are the same quantity in different forms.
james-prescott-joule.context: Establishing that energy is conserved across electrical, thermal and chemical processes is what makes a power budget possible: the watts that enter a device leave it as work and heat, and none of them disappear. Every cooling calculation in a data centre is his result applied at scale, and the reason a dense rack is a thermal problem before it is anything else. Joule heating is also why a bad connection warms up, which is one of the oldest diagnostic signs in the trade.

samuel-morse.def: The portrait painter whose code turned electricity into a message, sent from Washington to Baltimore on 24 May 1844.
samuel-morse.context: Cooke and Wheatstone built a working telegraph in England at the same time, using moving needles; Morse used sound, and encoding is what made his version travel. The choice is the first appearance of a decision this whole field keeps repeating - that the encoding matters more than the medium. His code is also the older half of a partnership rarely stated: Alfred Vail and Leonard Gale worked on it and are usually left out, which makes this the first attribution problem on the timeline rather than the last.

nikola-tesla.def: The engineer whose alternating-current systems and 1891 resonant transformer made high frequency and high voltage into tools rather than curiosities.
nikola-tesla.context: Direct current loses too much over distance to serve a city, and alternating current can be transformed up for transmission and down for use - which is why the grid every data centre draws from is his design rather than his rival's. The resonant coil matters here for a second reason: producing and tuning high-frequency oscillation is the same problem radio had to solve, and the work fed straight into it. He is also the clearest case on this timeline of reputation and reward diverging completely from contribution.

william-crookes.def: The chemist whose partially evacuated tube let cathode rays be seen and studied, and which every later display and vacuum device descends from.
william-crookes.context: Pumping most of the air out of a glass tube and passing a current through it produced something nobody could account for, and the instruments built to study it produced the electron, the X-ray and the cathode ray tube. The apparatus outlived every theory offered to explain it. That is the ordinary sequence in this field and it is worth stating: a tool built to investigate a puzzle usually turns out to be more durable than the answer it was built to find.

lee-de-forest.def: The engineer who added a third electrode to a vacuum tube in 1906, producing the first device that could amplify a signal.
lee-de-forest.context: He built it as a detector and did not grasp what he had; its amplifying capability was only realized after 1912. Amplification is the property that made long-distance telephony, radio and eventually computing possible, because a signal that can be rebuilt at intervals can travel indefinitely - which is the same argument as a repeater, a regenerator and, later, a router. The pattern is worth marking: the inventor of the most consequential component of the era spent six years not understanding its most important property.

sarbanes-oxley.def: The 2002 United States law on corporate financial reporting that made internal controls, including access control, a matter of legal liability for company officers.
sarbanes-oxley.context: It is a finance law and it reshaped security purchasing, which is why it belongs in a technical glossary. By making executives answerable for the integrity of financial systems, it turned identity governance, change control and audit logging from good practice into obligations someone signs for. Static analysis and identity governance both became enterprise categories in its wake. The pattern recurs throughout the industry's history: compliance creates markets faster than threats do, and it moves the buying decision from the people who operate a control to the people who have to certify it.

x509.def: X.509 is the certificate format published by the ITU (International Telecommunication Union) in 1988 and profiled for the internet in RFC (Request for Comments) 5280, binding a name to a public key with an issuer's signature.
x509.context: It carries the subject, the public key, the validity dates, the issuer and the extensions that decide what the certificate may be used for, all signed by the issuing authority. It comes from the same standards programme as the X.500 directory, which is why its structures feel like a directory's and why so many operational problems are really encoding problems. Most certificate faults in practice are not cryptographic: a missing intermediate, a name that does not match, or dates nobody was watching.
x509.depth:
X.509 began as part of the X.500 directory. ITU-T, the standardization sector of the International Telecommunication Union and formerly the CCITT (International Telegraph and Telephone Consultative Committee), published Recommendation X.509, The Directory: Authentication framework, in November 1988, in step with ISO/IEC 9594-8 from the International Organization for Standardization and the International Electrotechnical Commission; that is the version 1 certificate. The 1993 revision added two fields, the issuer and subject unique identifiers, giving version 2. When the internet's Privacy Enhanced Mail (PEM) specifications of 1993 tried to build a public key infrastructure (PKI) on version 1, the format proved too rigid, and ISO/IEC, ITU-T and the X9 committee of ANSI (American National Standards Institute) added extensions, completing version 3 in June 1996. ITU-T has revised the text many times since (1997, 2000, when it was renamed Public-key and attribute certificate frameworks, 2005, 2008, 2012, 2016), and the edition in force is October 2019. The internet profile, which says how to use it on the web, in mail, for user authentication and for IPsec (Internet Protocol Security), is RFC (Request for Comments) 2459 of January 1999, replaced by RFC 3280 in April 2002 and by RFC 5280 in May 2008, which nine later RFCs have amended.

A certificate is a to-be-signed body followed by the issuer's signature algorithm and signature over it. The body holds the version (version 3 is encoded as the integer 2), a serial number, the signature algorithm, the issuer's distinguished name, the validity period, the subject's distinguished name, the subject public key with its algorithm, the optional unique identifiers, and the extensions. Everything is described in ASN.1 (Abstract Syntax Notation One) and signed in its DER (Distinguished Encoding Rules) form, so a single changed byte breaks the signature. RFC 5280 tightens the details that trip implementations: a serial number must be a positive integer unique for each certificate from a given CA (certification authority) and no longer than 20 octets; validity dates through 2049 are encoded as UTCTime with a two-digit year, and dates from 2050 must use GeneralizedTime; a certificate meant never to expire uses the notAfter value 99991231235959Z.

Extensions are where version 3 does its work, and each carries a critical flag: a relying party must reject a certificate with a critical extension it does not recognize, and may ignore an unrecognized non-critical one. The ones met every day are basic constraints (is this a CA, and how many CAs may follow it in a path), key usage and extended key usage (what the key may sign or be used for, such as server or client authentication), subject alternative name (the Domain Name System (DNS) names, Internet Protocol (IP) addresses or e-mail addresses the certificate is for), authority and subject key identifiers (which tie each certificate to the key that signed it and so link a chain), CRL (certificate revocation list) distribution points, and authority information access, which points to the issuer's certificate and to an OCSP (Online Certificate Status Protocol) responder.

Names are the most common source of confusion. The subject is a directory-style distinguished name, and for years web clients matched the host name against its common name. RFC 9525 (November 2023, replacing RFC 6125) now says the common name must not be used to identify a service, because it is essentially free-form text; the identity belongs in the subject alternative name. The CA/Browser Forum's Baseline Requirements, version 2.3.1 of 4 October 2026, make the common name in a server certificate not recommended and, if present, a copy of a subject alternative name. A certificate whose only correct name is in the common name, or whose subject alternative name lacks the host name actually typed, is the classic name mismatch.

Dates are the other half of the faults, and they are getting shorter. Under the same Baseline Requirements a publicly trusted server certificate issued before 15 March 2026 could be valid for up to 398 days; from that date the maximum is 200 days, from 15 March 2027 100 days, and from 15 March 2029 47 days. The schedule comes from ballot SC-081v3, proposed by Apple's Clint Wilson with Sectigo, Google Chrome and Mozilla endorsing, and passed in April 2025 with 25 issuers in favour, none against and 5 abstaining, and all 4 voting consumers in favour. At 47 days, renewal by hand stops being viable and automation becomes the only workable practice.

Chains fail in ways the signature maths never sees. A server that sends its own certificate without the intermediate works in a browser that has cached or fetched the intermediate and fails in a script or appliance that has not. Trust anchors expire too: Let's Encrypt's old cross-signing root, DST Root CA X3, expired on 30 September 2021; devices that had never received ISRG Root X1 started showing warnings, and clients using OpenSSL 1.0.x could fail even when they did trust ISRG Root X1, because of a quirk in certificate verification, which is why Let's Encrypt recommended OpenSSL 1.1.0 or later.

Reading a certificate is the first diagnostic step. openssl x509 -in cert.pem -noout -text prints the whole structure; -dates, -subject, -issuer and -ext pull out single parts; -fingerprint hashes the DER encoding; and -checkend 86400 exits nonzero if the certificate expires within a day, which makes it a monitoring check. Many apparent certificate faults are encoding faults: a binary DER file handed to a tool that expects PEM (Privacy Enhanced Mail) text, which RFC 7468 (April 2015) defines as base64 between -----BEGIN CERTIFICATE----- and -----END CERTIFICATE----- lines, or a bundle with the certificates in the wrong order.

Numbers worth remembering: 1988 for the first edition and 1996 for version 3, the integer 2 meaning version 3, 20 octets for a serial number, 2049 as the last UTCTime year, RFC 5280 as the profile, and 398, 200, 100 and 47 days as the shrinking maximum lifetime of a public server certificate.

jean-charles-peltier.def: The clockmaker who found in 1834 that passing current through a junction of two dissimilar metals heats one side and cools the other, depending on direction.
jean-charles-peltier.context: He was a watchmaker who retired at thirty to do science, and what he found is the only way to move heat with no moving parts and no working fluid. It stayed a curiosity for about 120 years, because it needs semiconductors to be efficient enough to matter - which makes it a clean case of a correct discovery waiting for a material that did not exist yet. The devices built on it now hold laser temperatures steady inside optical transceivers, so a discovery from 1834 is what keeps a wavelength where the specification says it should be.

leon-foucault.def: The physicist who demonstrated the Earth's rotation with a pendulum in 1851, discovered eddy currents, and gave the gyroscope its name.
leon-foucault.context: The pendulum is what he is remembered for and the eddy currents are what the industry actually pays for. Currents induced in a conductor by a changing magnetic field are the loss that every transformer and motor is designed to minimize, and the effect that induction heating, metal detectors and magnetic braking are designed to exploit - the same phenomenon counted as waste in one application and as the product in another. He also belongs to a recurring pattern: he built his own instruments, including the knife-edge test still used on telescope mirrors, and people who make their own tools tend to see what the users of those tools cannot.

james-watt.def: The engineer who in 1788 put a spinning-weight governor on a steam engine, creating the mechanical ancestor of every control loop in computing.
james-watt.context: The attribution deserves care: Huygens had built centrifugal governors in the seventeenth century for windmills, and Watt adapted one rather than inventing it - though the adaptation mattered enough that he is often credited anyway. What the device is, precisely, is a closed loop with no human in it: the engine's speed raises the weights, the weights close the throttle, the throttle slows the engine. James Clerk Maxwell turned it into mathematics in 1868, and everything from congestion control to autoscaling to a datacentre's cooling is a descendant of that paper rather than of the hardware.

john-logie-baird.def: The engineer who demonstrated working television to the Royal Institution on 26 January 1926, to an audience that did not appear to realize what it had seen.
john-logie-baird.context: Not one attending member published a comment afterwards. The only first-hand account was a short item in The Times two days later, and a prospective investor visiting that April concluded it would be an error of judgment to bring the equipment to market. The date is now treated as the birth of television and was, on the day, unremarkable to the experts in the room - which places it beside Kao being ridiculed and Ohm being ignored. Baird's mechanical system then lost within a decade to all-electronic television built on the cathode ray tube, whose lineage runs back to Crookes: first to a working demonstration, and not the design that won.

edward-weston.def: The engineer who made electricity measurable in the field, with the first accurate portable direct-reading meters and a cell stable enough to calibrate them.
edward-weston.context: He did not set out to sell instruments. He was working on dynamos and found the available meters too clumsy and slow for his own experiments, so he built better ones - and they worked well enough that in 1888 he abandoned everything else. The list of what he had to invent to get there is the real story: permanent magnets that stayed permanent, conductors that ignored temperature, springs with low resistance and no magnetism, and pointer damping from Foucault's eddy currents. His 1893 cell then served as the international standard for electromotive force from 1911 until 1990, which means the volt was defined by a wet chemical cell for most of the twentieth century. An industry cannot be billed, tuned or trusted until it can be measured, and this is the man who closed that gap.

alexander-graham-bell.def: The teacher of the deaf whose 1876 patent on transmitting speech electrically created the network that every later one was built on top of.
alexander-graham-bell.context: The telephone matters here for an unglamorous reason: it produced the wires. Decades of digital communication ran over a plant built for voice, which is why modems, leased lines and the first broadband all had to work within constraints set by a nineteenth-century speech circuit. His work with deaf students is what led him to the mechanics of speech and hearing in the first place - the machine came out of teaching rather than out of telegraphy. His name is now attached to the medal given for contributions to communications engineering, which several people in this catalogue have received.

lan.def: A local area network (LAN) is a network confined to a limited area, typically a home, a building or a campus under one administration, in which every attached device can reach every other directly, today almost always over Ethernet or Wi-Fi.
lan.context: The defining property was never only distance. It was that the owner runs the cable, so moving a byte costs nothing extra and a round trip is short enough to ignore, and protocols designed for a local area quietly assume both, then misbehave when the network they run on is stretched or moved. In engineering terms a local area network (LAN) is one layer 2 domain: the reach of a broadcast, where hosts find each other with the Address Resolution Protocol (ARP) and frames travel without a router. Virtual LANs, overlays and cloud subnets have since detached the word from geography, and security practice has turned local from a statement about trust into one it no longer accepts.
lan.depth:
What the term names. The National Institute of Standards and Technology (NIST) glossary defines a local area network (LAN), in the wording of its industrial control system and other guides, as a group of computers and other devices dispersed over a relatively limited area and connected by a communications link that enables any device to interact with any other on the network. Both halves matter. The limited area is the old part of the definition; the any-to-any reachability is the part an engineer tests. In practice a LAN is the span of one layer 2 network, the reach of a limited broadcast, which Request for Comments (RFC) 1122 describes as received by every host on the connected physical network and never forwarded outside it. A router marks its edge, which is why one building can hold dozens of LANs and one LAN, stretched with the right tools, can span cities.

Where it came from. Robert Metcalfe, then a researcher at the Xerox Palo Alto Research Center (PARC), wrote the memo proposing an Ethernet on 22 May 1973, according to the Computer History Museum. Ethernet was first specified jointly by Digital Equipment Corporation, Intel and Xerox, which is why its original form is called DIX Ethernet, from the companies' initials. The Institute of Electrical and Electronics Engineers (IEEE) began its 802 work in 1980, and Ethernet became IEEE Std 802.3-1985; the project number itself, 802, has no significance beyond being the next number available. The committee standardized rivals too, Token Bus as 802.4 and Token Ring as 802.5, and both working groups have since been disbanded: Ethernet won the wired LAN, and 802.11 Wi-Fi the wireless one.

Who defines it now. The IEEE 802 LAN/MAN Standards Committee develops standards for local, metropolitan and other area networks, and names its most widely used ones as Ethernet, bridging and virtual bridged LANs, and wireless LAN, the work of the 802.3, 802.1 and 802.11 working groups. The family is deliberately limited to networks that carry variable-size packets, which leaves out cell-switched and isochronous networks. Its umbrella document, IEEE Std 802-2024, Overview and Architecture, approved on 11 December 2024 and published on 21 March 2025 to supersede the 2014 edition, sets the reference models, the structure of IEEE 802 media access control (MAC) addresses and the way higher layer protocols are identified. The metropolitan area network (MAN) and the personal area network (PAN) sit beside the LAN in the same family.

What made local local. The economic difference came first. On a LAN the operator owns the cable, so capacity has no per-byte price and round trips are short, and protocols written for that setting take both for granted. The Transmission Control Protocol (TCP) shows the cost of the assumption: its header carries a 16-bit window, so without extensions no more than 64 KiB can be in flight, and RFC 7323 of September 2014 explains that on long, fat networks, whose bandwidth-delay product exceeds 64 KiB, that window caps throughput. On a 1 Gbit/s LAN with a 0.5 ms round trip the product is about 62 KB and the limit never bites; across a 100 ms wide area path at the same rate it is 12.5 MB, and an unscaled connection crawls. Other protocols are local by design: the Address Resolution Protocol (ARP) and the first message of the Dynamic Host Configuration Protocol (DHCP) are broadcasts that stop at the router, and Multicast DNS, RFC 6762 of February 2013, exists to resolve names on the local link in the absence of any conventional Domain Name System (DNS) server.

How the word left geography. IEEE 802.1Q made the LAN logical: a virtual LAN (VLAN) is a separate layer 2 network that shares switches and cables with others, so one switch can carry many LANs and one LAN can run through several buildings. Overlays went further. Virtual eXtensible Local Area Network (VXLAN), documented in RFC 7348 of August 2014, carries layer 2 frames over a layer 3 network to stretch a LAN between data centres, explicitly because the 4094-VLAN limit was too small for multi-tenant clouds; each segment has a 24-bit identifier, which allows up to 16 million of them. Cloud providers then gave customers the vocabulary without the wire: Amazon describes a virtual private cloud as a logically isolated virtual network whose subnets and route tables will be familiar to anyone with an existing network.

Trust was the last property to go. For decades the inside of the LAN was treated as trusted and the firewall at its edge as the boundary, the castle-and-moat model. NIST's zero trust architecture, Special Publication (SP) 800-207 of August 2020, rejects exactly that: zero trust assumes no implicit trust granted to assets or user accounts based solely on their physical or network location, and the parenthesis names local area networks versus the internet. In other words, being on the LAN still decides whether a device can broadcast to its neighbours, but it no longer decides whether it should be believed. That is the practical lesson for anything that authenticates by source address or trusts a protocol because it never leaves the link.

Neighbours and numbers. A wireless LAN (WLAN) is a LAN whose medium is radio; a campus network joins many LANs with routers; a wide area network (WAN) connects sites over links someone else usually owns. The things worth remembering are the dates, 1973 for the Ethernet memo, 1980 for IEEE 802 and 1985 for IEEE Std 802.3-1985, and the boundaries: one LAN equals one broadcast domain, 4094 usable VLAN identifiers, 16 million VXLAN segments, and a 64 KiB TCP window that only a LAN can fill without scaling.

wan.def: Wide area network (WAN): a network that connects sites spread over a larger area than a local network can reach, almost always over circuits or services that a carrier owns and bills for; in enterprise use, the network between branches, data centres, the cloud and the internet.
wan.context: Every design decision about a wide area network (WAN) descends from the link being rented. Bandwidth is metered, latency is set by geography and the speed of light in fibre (about 5 microseconds per kilometre in the planning figure of ITU-T, the International Telecommunication Union's standardization sector), and the circuit can fail in ways you cannot inspect. Compression, caching, deduplication, traffic shaping and the whole WAN optimization category exist because a megabyte across a wide area costs money and a megabyte across a local one does not, and SD-WAN (software-defined WAN) exists because enterprises wanted to buy cheaper internet links and still steer each application onto the path that suits it.
wan.depth:
What the term means. NIST's (National Institute of Standards and Technology) glossary, quoting its industrial control systems guide SP 800-82r3, defines a wide area network (WAN) as a physical or logical network that provides data communications to a larger number of independent users than a local area network (LAN) typically serves, usually spread over a larger geographic area, where a LAN covers a relatively limited area. There is no distance in the definition, and in practice the line is drawn by ownership: inside a building or campus the organization owns the cabling, between sites it buys circuits or services from carriers. MEF's SD-WAN standard describes what those services can be: Ethernet services, IP (Internet Protocol) services, internet access and layer 1 connectivity, reached over DSL (digital subscriber line), hybrid fibre-coaxial cable, LTE (Long Term Evolution) mobile, fibre, Wi-Fi or Ethernet, and billed either at a flat rate for a given bandwidth or by usage.

The physics that cannot be bought. Bandwidth can be upgraded; distance cannot. ITU-T (International Telecommunication Union, Telecommunication Standardization Sector) Recommendation G.114 gives a planning value of 5 microseconds per kilometre for digital optical fibre systems, repeaters included, so every 1,000 km of fibre path adds about 5 ms one way and a 10,000 km route about 50 ms one way, 100 ms for the round trip, before any queueing. A geostationary satellite hop at 36,000 km altitude costs 260 ms one way between earth stations. G.114 recommends that one-way delay not exceed 400 ms for general network planning and notes that below 150 ms most applications are not significantly affected. Protocols written for a LAN feel this first: Fortinet's WAN optimization guide names Windows file sharing and Exchange email as applications that work fine locally and suffer from bandwidth limits and latency across a WAN, because every request waits a round trip.

From leased lines to label switching. The classic WAN was the leased line, a dedicated digital circuit such as the North American DS1 (Digital Signal 1), whose management objects RFC (Request for Comments) 4805 still models at 1.544 Mbps per link. MPLS (Multiprotocol Label Switching), specified in RFC 3031 (January 2001, Eric Rosen, Arun Viswanathan and Ross Callon), became the carrier technology that replaced most of them. In ordinary IP forwarding every router re-examines each packet's header and assigns it to a forwarding equivalence class; in MPLS that assignment is made once, at the ingress, and encoded as a short fixed-length label, and each following router uses the label as an index to find the next hop and a new label, without analysing the IP header again. RFC 3032 gives each label stack entry 4 octets: a 20-bit label, 3 experimental bits, a bottom-of-stack bit and an 8-bit TTL (time to live).

The MPLS service enterprises bought. What carriers sold as an MPLS WAN is usually the BGP/MPLS IP VPN (Border Gateway Protocol, virtual private network) of RFC 4364 (February 2006, obsoleting RFC 2547 of March 1999). It uses a peer model: the customer's edge (CE) routers send their routes to the provider's edge (PE) routers, the customer sees no overlay, CE routers at different sites do not peer with each other, and packets are tunnelled across the backbone so the core routers never learn the customer routes. Each PE keeps a separate VRF (virtual routing and forwarding) table per customer, and an 8-byte Route Distinguisher lets two customers use the same private addresses. Classes of service were part of the product and the price: TeleGeography models MPLS port pricing as 10 per cent voice and video, 30 per cent real-time data and 60 per cent best effort, because enterprises rarely buy all-best-effort MPLS when internet access would do.

The WAN as a cost centre. The numbers explain the last decade. TeleGeography's November 2025 pricing analysis found median 100 Mbps MPLS port prices 7.3 times higher than business broadband on average across the cities it surveyed, from 2.8 times in Rome to 20.2 times in Sofia, with dedicated internet access (DIA) at 3.5 times broadband (1.6 to 8.9 times); an earlier TeleGeography analysis (April 2020) noted that local access alone can be as much as half the cost of a site, and that on-net internet access in multi-tenant buildings often carries no local access charge. Its WAN Manager Survey, reported in August 2026, found DIA on 53.88 per cent of enterprise sites on average and MPLS on 22 per cent, with 96 per cent of respondents using DIA somewhere and 74 per cent still using MPLS somewhere. Before SD-WAN, the answer to expensive bandwidth was WAN optimization: Fortinet's byte caching, for example, splits data into chunks, labels each with a hash, sends the hashes instead of the data when the far end already holds them, and works across applications, so a file seen in an email is not sent again when it is downloaded from a web page.

SD-WAN as a standard. MEF 70, published in July 2019 and since superseded by MEF 70.2 (October 2023), defines the externally visible behaviour of an SD-WAN (software-defined WAN) service between a subscriber and a provider.
