The service is an overlay over one or more Underlay Connectivity Services (UCS), each public (internet access) or private, flat-rate or usage-based, and any of them can be designated as a backup. The SD-WAN Edge, usually at the subscriber's premises, does everything the underlays do not: it identifies application flows, applies policies and routes; Tunnel Virtual Connections join pairs of edges across one underlay, each with its own delay, bandwidth and encryption characteristics, and a path between two sites is one tunnel or a chain of them. The point of the standard is that policy, not topology, decides where each application's traffic goes.

Fortinet Secure SD-WAN in practice. On FortiGate, interfaces of any type, physical, aggregate, VLAN (virtual LAN) or IPsec (IP Security) tunnel, become SD-WAN members inside zones, by default the zone virtual-wan-link; the zone is used in firewall policies and the whole SD-WAN in static routes. Performance SLAs (service level agreements) probe a server through each member and compare latency, jitter and packet loss against thresholds, such as 10 ms of latency and 5 ms of jitter in Fortinet's Gmail example. SD-WAN rules then pick a member per application with a strategy: manual, best quality, lowest cost (SLA), which takes the cheapest member that meets the SLA (cost 0 being the lowest), or maximize bandwidth (SLA), which spreads traffic over the members that meet it. Overlays add ADVPN (Auto-Discovery VPN) shortcuts between spokes, adaptive forward error correction and packet duplication for loss-sensitive traffic.

What goes wrong. A rented circuit fails in ways the customer cannot see inside: an outage is easy, a brownout of loss and jitter is not, which is why SLA probing replaced simple link-up checks. Internet underlays carry no class of service end to end, so voice quality depends on picking the right path rather than on marking, and every overlay tunnel costs MTU (maximum transmission unit) that has to be accounted for with MSS (maximum segment size) clamping. Physics still wins: no SD-WAN policy makes a 10,000 km path shorter than 50 ms one way. And the economics have moved the WAN's job: with applications in the cloud and DIA the default underlay, the question is less how to connect branches to headquarters than how to reach the internet and cloud securely from each site, which is where SASE (secure access service edge) designs take over.

man.def: Metropolitan area network (MAN): a network across a city, larger than one site and smaller than a carrier's long-haul.
man.context: It is the least used of the three terms and describes a real situation: a university, a hospital group or a municipality with several buildings across a city, joined by fibre they either own or lease dark. What makes it its own category is that the economics sit between the other two: the link is not free, and it is not metered per byte either, so the design choices belong to neither.
man.depth:
What the term means. A metropolitan area network (MAN) is a scale and a situation rather than a technology. The usual definition is a network that interconnects users and computing resources across a region the size of a city, most often by joining the local area networks (LANs) of several sites into one larger network, which may in turn give efficient access to a wide area network (WAN); point-to-point links between the sites of one organization count as well. The boundaries are soft on both sides. Below it sits the campus network, buildings joined over private ground; above it the long-haul WAN, where distance and leased capacity dominate the design. In daily speech engineers rarely say MAN at all: they say metro, as in metro Ethernet, metro ring or metro fibre, which is part of why the acronym survives mostly in textbooks and in the name of a standards committee.

The committee that carries the name. The Institute of Electrical and Electronics Engineers (IEEE) standards body behind Ethernet and Wi-Fi is the IEEE 802 LAN/MAN Standards Committee (LMSC). Its own 2004 overview records that the first meeting of Project 802, then the IEEE Computer Society's Local Network Standards Committee, was held in February 1980, that the number 802 was simply the next in the sequence the IEEE was issuing to standards projects, and that the scope later grew to include metropolitan area networks. The committee still describes its work as standards for local, metropolitan and other area networks, and Wireless MAN is among the families it lists. The name outlived the MAN standards themselves.

The standards that tried to own the city. Three IEEE working groups wrote technologies specifically for metropolitan networks, and none became the way cities are wired. IEEE 802.6-1990 defined the Distributed Queue Dual Bus (DQDB), a shared medium access protocol over two counterflowing, unidirectional buses that offered the usual connectionless service to the logical link control sublayer, with isochronous and connection-oriented services as optional extras. It was approved on 6 December 1990, published on 3 July 1991, reaffirmed in 1997 and withdrawn on 7 February 2003, and the 802.6 working group appears among the disbanded groups in the committee's 2004 overview. IEEE 802.17 tackled the fibre rings that, in its own description, were widely deployed in metropolitan and wide area networks but ran protocols not optimized for packets; its Resilient Packet Ring (RPR) base standard is 802.17-2004, and the group lists its planned work as finished, with no active projects. IEEE 802.16 wrote the WirelessMAN standards for broadband wireless metropolitan networks, the basis of WiMAX; its last revision, IEEE Std 802.16-2017, was published on 2 March 2018, the group entered hibernation a week later, and its page now marks it disbanded, with maintenance passed to the 802.15 working group.

How cities are actually wired. What won was fibre, and on it Ethernet. Telephone companies began offering dark fibre, fibre with no equipment attached, to customers who wanted to join their buildings, and universities and research institutions adopted dark fibre as their metropolitan backbone; in West Berlin the BERCOM project linked the mainframes of publicly funded universities and research institutes over fibre the Deutsche Bundespost had already laid. Dense wavelength division multiplexing (DWDM) later let carriers sell wavelengths on existing metropolitan fibre instead of a dedicated pair per customer. Metro Ethernet rings became the common backbone, and their failure handling shows the layer 2 inheritance: rings that did not route IP ran spanning tree variants, each ring with its own root bridge, because a switched network cannot tolerate a loop. The Metro Ethernet Forum, set up to define best practice for these networks, ended up defining carrier Ethernet services in general. Metropolitan exchange points then joined the pieces to the rest of the internet, as the entry on internet exchanges describes.

The Brazilian case. The clearest current example of a MAN built on owned fibre is the Redecomep programme (Redes Comunitárias de Educação e Pesquisa) of the Brazilian National Education and Research Network (RNP). It builds high-speed networks in metropolitan regions and in inland cities that have two or more federal teaching and research institutions; in state capitals each network connects directly to RNP's point of presence (PoP), and inland an aggregation point carries it to the PoP in the capital. Its funding model shows the in-between economics at work: consortia of the member organizations make it possible to own the fibre, which RNP describes as self-sustaining. RNP reports 54 metropolitan networks in operation, with more than 4,000 km of fibre and more than 500 participating institutions.

What changes in the design. Because a MAN is usually owned fibre or leased dark fibre rather than a metered service, capacity is set by the optics at each end rather than by a contract, and the hard questions move elsewhere. Protection matters more than bandwidth: a backhoe in one street should not isolate a hospital, which is why metropolitan designs favour rings and physically diverse paths, and why ring protocols, from RPR to spanning tree, keep recurring in its history. Layer 2 stretched across a city carries layer 2 risks across a city, so a loop or a broadcast storm is no longer confined to one building. And fibre that crosses public streets is outside the organization's walls, which is worth remembering when deciding what may travel over it unencrypted.

wlan.def: Wireless local area network: a local area network whose medium is shared air rather than dedicated cable.
wlan.context: It is a local area network in addressing and a completely different animal in behaviour, because the switch removed collisions from the wired world and nothing can remove them from the air. Capacity falls with the number of talkers rather than with distance, the client decides when to roam and the network cannot make it, and interference comes from neighbours and appliances you do not control. Treating it as cable that happens to be invisible is the most common design error in this area.

pan.def: Personal area network: the few metres around one person, where devices pair with each other rather than joining an infrastructure.
pan.context: The interesting property is that it has no administrator. Pairing is a decision made by whoever is holding the device, which is why the security model is consent at a moment rather than policy over time, and why enterprise control over this layer is weak wherever it exists at all. Headsets, keyboards, wearables and vehicle links all sit here, and all of them are network attach points that no inventory contains.

can-campus.def: Campus area network: several local area networks across adjacent buildings under one owner, joined by cable that owner controls.
can-campus.context: It is the scale at which the vendor certification tracks are actually taught, and the scale where the hard problems first appear: several buildings means a distribution layer, redundant paths, spanning tree or its successors, and a routing decision between floors. Not to be confused with the controller area network of the same acronym, which is an in-vehicle bus and an entirely different subject.

overlay-network.def: A network built on top of another one, whose links are tunnels across the network beneath it.
overlay-network.context: The one underneath is the underlay, and the split is the dominant pattern in modern infrastructure: route the underlay simply and reliably, and express everything the application wants in the overlay. The uncomfortable part is that a fault in the underlay appears in the overlay as something else entirely, so the layer that made the design tractable is also the layer that makes the diagnosis hard.

geneve.def: Generic Network Virtualization Encapsulation: a tunnelling format designed to carry arbitrary metadata rather than a fixed set of fields.
geneve.context: Its whole argument is with its predecessors. Earlier encapsulations fixed their header fields at design time, so anything the designers had not anticipated required a new protocol; this one carries extensible options so the format outlives the requirements. Whether that generality was worth the parsing cost is a live disagreement, and hardware support has been the deciding factor rather than elegance.

nvgre.def: Network Virtualization using Generic Routing Encapsulation: a network virtualization scheme carrying tenant traffic inside an existing tunnelling protocol.
nvgre.context: It reused an encapsulation that already existed rather than defining a new one, which is a reasonable instinct and cost it the market: the field it used for load distribution was not one that existing hardware hashed on, so traffic did not spread across links the way operators expected. It is worth keeping in the record as a case where reusing a standard was the more conservative choice and the less successful one.

ray-tomlinson.def: The BBN engineer who in 1971 made a message reach a person on a different machine, and picked the at sign to say which one.
ray-tomlinson.context: Nobody asked him to. A colleague's description is that it was not an assignment at all - he was fooling around, looking for something to do with the ARPANET - and he built it by grafting code from his own file transfer program onto a local messaging tool. The addressing convention he improvised in an afternoon has outlived every system designed to replace it, and the mailbox went on to become the recovery path for nearly every other account a person owns, which is a role no specification ever assigned it.

robert-taylor.def: The research director who started the ARPANET in 1966 and then used his agency's budget leverage to conscript the man who built it.
robert-taylor.context: He wanted Larry Roberts to run the project and Roberts declined. Taylor then established that the Defense Department supplied fifty-one per cent of Lincoln Lab's funding, and asked the agency's director to inform the lab's director that sending Roberts would be in everyone's interest. Roberts, by his own account not particularly eager, was at the Pentagon within months. The most consequential networking project of the century began with a program manager who did not want the job, which is worth remembering against every account of invention driven purely by enthusiasm. Taylor's stated objective was plainer than the later mythology: to let people separated geographically discover and exploit common interests.

howard-frank.def: The engineer who decided where the ARPANET's links should actually go, treating network shape as an optimization problem.
howard-frank.context: Somebody had to choose which sites connected to which, and how many links were enough to survive failures without paying for redundancy nobody needed. He came to that question from work on the survivability of national assets in wartime and from optimizing pipeline networks, which is why the answer arrived as operations research rather than as engineering intuition. The topology of the first network was a calculation, and the discipline he founded - designing a network by analysing it before building it - is the one every capacity plan since has been an instance of.

david-clark.def: The architect who put the internet's governing philosophy into one sentence in 1992: no kings, no presidents, no voting - rough consensus and running code.
david-clark.context: It is the most quoted line in internet governance and it is usually read as a slogan about openness. It is more useful read as a description of a decision procedure, and one with consequences that recur: a system that advances by rough consensus and working implementations will adopt any improvement one party can deploy alone, and will stall on every improvement that requires everybody to agree at once. Secure routing, DNSSEC and email authentication all waited decades for exactly that reason. The sentence explains both why the internet could be built without permission and why parts of it cannot be repaired.

tcl.def: Tool Command Language (Tcl): a scripting language John Ousterhout conceived in 1987 and built at Berkeley from 1988 to be embedded inside other people's programs, so that each tool would not invent a command language of its own.
tcl.context: Ousterhout built it out of frustration that every tool he encountered had grown its own half-designed scripting language, and he shipped it as a C library precisely so an application could gain a scripting layer without recompiling. That design decision determined where it ended up: Tcl is rarely the language you choose for a project and frequently the language you find inside a product you bought. It is the scripting layer of network test equipment, the language F5 iRules are written in, and, through Don Libes's Expect extension of 1990, the way a generation automated devices that only offered a terminal. Anyone who learned it to drive one vendor's tool has usually found it waiting inside another one years later.
tcl.depth:
What it is. Tcl (Tool Command Language) is an interpreted language built as a library: an application links the interpreter, registers its own commands and lets people script it. Ousterhout set it three goals. It had to be extensible, so that an application's own commands would look as if they had been designed in from the start; simple and generic, so that it would not limit what applications could add; and good at integration, because the interesting work would come from the application and the language's job was to glue the pieces together. Tk, the graphical toolkit he built on it from late 1988, was the first big proof of the model, and the pairing Tcl/Tk is still how many people first meet the language.

Twelve rules. The whole syntax is the twelve rules of the Tcl manual page, which users call the dodekalogue. A script is a string of commands separated by newlines or semicolons. Each command is evaluated in two steps: the interpreter splits it into words and performs substitutions, the same way for every command, and then the first word selects the routine, which may interpret its other words however it likes, as an integer, a variable name, a list or another script. That is why if, while and proc are ordinary commands rather than keywords. A word in double quotes is grouped but still substituted; a word that begins with an open brace runs to the matching close brace and is taken literally, with no substitution except backslash-newline; square brackets run a nested script and insert its result; a dollar sign inserts a variable's value. Each character is processed exactly once, from left to right, so a value inserted by substitution is never parsed again.

Why braces matter. That one-pass rule is what makes ordinary Tcl safe, and the commands that parse their argument a second time are where it stops. An unbraced argument to expr is substituted twice: the Tcler's Wiki page on bracing expressions shows that set y [expr $x + 3], with x holding a bracketed exec call, would run that command, likens the problem to SQL (Structured Query Language) injection, and adds that unbraced expressions also run slower and can lose precision through numeric to string to numeric conversions. In BIG-IP iRules, which act on request headers and content chosen by whoever sent the request, bracing is the difference between handling a value and executing it. Numbers hide a second trap: Tcl 8 reads a leading zero as octal, so 08 is not a valid number, and Tcl 9 dropped that reading in favour of an explicit 0o prefix.

Where it came from. Ousterhout's students at the University of California, Berkeley, had written interactive integrated circuit design tools such as Magic and Crystal, each with a command language that ended up weak and quirky and could not be carried to the next tool. In the fall of 1987, on sabbatical at DEC's (Digital Equipment Corporation's) Western Research Laboratory, he had the idea of an embeddable command language; he started work early in 1988, used the first version in a text editor that spring, and gave copies away in 1989. After his paper at the USENIX conference of January 1990 he put the source code on Berkeley's FTP (File Transfer Protocol) site, and one listener, Don Libes of NIST (the National Institute of Standards and Technology), went home, built Expect on it in three weeks and presented it that summer; Expect became the first widely distributed Tcl application. Users grew from a few in 1989 to several tens of thousands in 1993.

From Sun to the Core Team. Ousterhout joined Sun Microsystems in May 1994, where the team ported Tcl to Windows and the Macintosh, overhauled input and output and added sockets for network applications, built a bytecode compiler that sped scripts up by as much as ten times, and added Safe-Tcl for running untrusted scripts. He founded Scriptics in January 1998, which released Tcl/Tk 8.1 in April 1999 with Unicode support, thread safety and Henry Spencer's new regular expression package. In 1998 Tcl received the ACM (Association for Computing Machinery) Software System Award and the USENIX Software Tools User Group Award. After Scriptics, renamed Ajuba Solutions, was acquired in 2000, the Tcl Core Team took over and still steers the language through Tcl Improvement Proposals (TIPs). Tcl 8.5 arrived in December 2007 with new datatypes, bignums and lambdas, and Tcl 8.6 in December 2012 with the TclOO object system.

Where engineers meet it. F5 documents that iRules, the BIG-IP traffic scripting feature, use the industry-standard Tcl with a subset of commands disabled, and keeps per-version lists of those commands. Cisco IOS has offered a Tcl shell since 12.3(2)T: tclsh, entered from privileged EXEC mode, runs Tcl 8.3.4 commands and adds exec and ios_config to drive the command line, SNMP (Simple Network Management Protocol) get and set on MIB (management information base) objects, and TCP (Transmission Control Protocol) and UDP (User Datagram Protocol) sockets. VIAVI's TestCenter traffic generator lists Tcl among the languages of its native API (application programming interface), beside Python, Perl, Java, C, C#, C++ and Ruby. And Expect, still Tcl underneath, drives the devices that have nothing better than a prompt.

Versions now. Tcl 9.0, released in September 2024, raised data values past 2 GB, covered the full Unicode code point range, added encoding profiles, zip filesystems and epoll and kqueue event notifiers, and broke a few things on purpose: unqualified variable names now resolve in the current namespace rather than the global one, reading input in the wrong encoding raises an error by default, a tilde in a path no longer means the home directory, and leading-zero octal is gone. The 9.0 line reached 9.0.4 on 26 June 2026, Tcl/Tk 9.1.0 followed on 29 September 2026 with a unicode command for normalization, a monotonic microsecond timer and lfilter, and 8.6.18 is the legacy line. Embedded interpreters lag far behind: an IOS router runs 8.3.4, which predates the 8.5 and 8.6 features, and Expect's own maintained repository still awaits a production Tcl 9 port, so the first question for any Tcl script is which interpreter will run it.

expect.def: The Tcl extension, written by Don Libes at the US National Institute of Standards and Technology (NIST) and first presented in 1990, that automates programs which only offer an interactive terminal.
expect.context: It exists because a great deal of infrastructure has no interface except the one built for a human typing at a prompt. Expect drives that interface: wait for this text, send that text, handle the case where neither arrives. Every network automation effort before vendors shipped usable programmatic interfaces was some version of it, and a surprising amount of production tooling still is. The honest assessment is that screen-scraping a command line is fragile and was always the wrong shape, and that it was also the only thing available for two decades, which is why the skill outlived every prediction of its retirement.
expect.depth:
What it is. Its manual calls Expect a program that talks to other interactive programs according to a script: it knows what output to expect from a program and what the correct response is, uses an interpreted language, Tcl (Tool Command Language), for branching and control, and lets a person take over the session and hand it back. The name comes from the send and expect sequences of uucp, kermit and other modem control programs, generalized so that it can drive any program. NIST (the National Institute of Standards and Technology) lists telnet, ftp, passwd, fsck, rlogin and tip as typical targets, and testing those programs as a second use. Expectk combines Expect with the Tk toolkit, and libexpect offers the same machinery to C and C++ without Tcl. It is not a protocol or an API (application programming interface); it reads and writes the character stream a human would see.

How it works. The spawn command starts a program with its standard input, output and error connected to Expect through a pseudo-terminal (pty), and sets spawn_id to the current process. The send command writes to it, and expect waits until the output matches one of a list of patterns: glob-style by default, regular expressions with -re, exact strings with -ex. Patterns are unanchored, and because Expect is not line oriented, ^ and $ match the start and end of the data in its buffer rather than of a line. On a match, the matched and previously unmatched output goes into expect_out(buffer), with up to nine regular-expression substrings in expect_out(1,string) to expect_out(9,string). The default timeout is 10 seconds, set timeout 30 changes it and -1 means wait forever; the special patterns timeout, eof, default and full_buffer catch the other outcomes. More than 2000 bytes of output can push earlier bytes out of the buffer unless match_max raises the limit. The exp_continue command keeps the same expect waiting, which is how a loop answers several prompts in any order, and interact gives the keyboard back to the user.

Where it came from. Libes conceived Expect in September 1987; the bulk of version 2 was designed and written between January and April 1990 and presented at the Summer 1990 USENIX conference in Anaheim, 11 to 15 June 1990, as expect: Curing Those Uncontrollable Fits of Interaction, followed that October by a paper for system administrators at the USENIX Large Systems Administration Conference, LISA IV. About half of it was rewritten for Tcl 6.0 in October 1991; Expect 4, with Tk support, reached production in August 1993, Expect 5, matching Tcl 7.0, in March 1994, and it was substantially rewritten for Tcl 8.2 in the summer of 1999. Libes's book Exploring Expect, 602 pages, was published by O'Reilly in 1995. Because its design and implementation were paid for in part by the US government, Expect is in the public domain, and NIST still lists it as public domain software.

Where it stands. The home page on core.tcl-lang.org gives 5.45.4, created on 4 February 2018, as the current version, and Debian packages 5.45.4 in bookworm and in testing. The same page now says the repository is no longer maintained and points to a port under the tcltk-depot organization that builds on Tcl 8.6 and 9; that port carries the version 6.0a0 and calls itself a work in progress, not production-ready, with no published release. For anyone depending on Expect, a Tcl 9 migration is therefore an open question, not a solved one.

The tools around it. autoexpect watches a person work through a session and writes an Expect script that reproduces it, which saves time on straight-line scripts but produces code that must be tidied before it handles anything unexpected. DejaGnu, a test framework built on Expect, has been used to test GCC (the GNU Compiler Collection). The distribution ships examples still found on many systems, among them kibitz, passmass, mkpasswd and unbuffer. Pexpect brings the same model to Python as a pure Python module that needs neither Tcl nor Expect, running wherever Python's pty module does.

What goes wrong. Most failures come from the manual's own caveats. Prompts differ by user, shell and device, so the manual suggests describing the end of a prompt as a regular expression, such as (%|#|\$) followed by a space and the end of the buffer, and warns that a pattern not tied to the end of the output lets a response land in the middle of text still arriving. The terminal driver turns a newline into carriage return plus line feed, so matching two lines needs \r\n, and a program in raw mode wants a real carriage return, which is why scripts send \r rather than \n. A missing timeout pattern is silent: the implicit action is to do nothing, and the script carries on as if the prompt had appeared. Long command output can overflow the default 2000-byte window. Passwords are the security problem: the manual shows stty -echo to read one at run time instead of embedding it in the script, and Libes wrote a 1994 LISA paper on handling passwords safely in background processes. When a script misbehaves, exp_internal 1 prints every character received and every match attempted.

Its place now. Expect remains the tool of last resort for any device or product whose only interface is a command line built for people, and the reasons it is fragile are structural: it matches text meant for eyes, so a changed banner, prompt or pager breaks it. Where a structured interface exists, such as NETCONF (Network Configuration Protocol) or a REST (representational state transfer) API returning JSON (JavaScript Object Notation), that is the better contract; Expect is what is left when none does.

rfc-2544.def: The 1999 benchmarking methodology that defined how a network device's throughput, latency, frame loss and burst tolerance are to be measured.
rfc-2544.context: Its introduction is unusually blunt for a standards document: vendors engage in specsmanship, it says, involving smoke and mirrors to confuse the people buying their products. The whole methodology exists to make performance claims comparable, by fixing the frame sizes, the trial durations and the reporting so that two vendors' numbers mean the same thing. It also has a sequel worth knowing about: the IETF later published an applicability statement titled Use on Production Networks Considered Harmful, because a test that deliberately drives a device to its loss threshold does exactly that to whatever else is running.

traffic-generation.def: Producing synthetic traffic with known properties in order to measure what a device or network does with it.
traffic-generation.context: The point is not volume, it is control: you know exactly what was sent, so anything missing, late or reordered is attributable. That is why the discipline sits closer to instrumentation than to networking, and why the equipment is bought by test labs, carriers accepting a circuit, and vendors who must publish a number. The harder use is scenario recreation - reproducing a fault that happened once in production, under conditions you control, until it happens on demand. Most difficult problems are not solved by inspecting the broken system but by rebuilding the circumstances that broke it.

line-rate.def: The theoretical maximum a link can carry for a given frame size - and the claim that benchmarking exists to check.
line-rate.context: It is a property of the medium and the frame size together, not of the interface speed alone, because per-frame overhead means small frames reach a lower bit rate than large ones on the same wire. This is why a device advertised at line rate may be honest at 1518-byte frames and nowhere near it at 64 bytes, and why any benchmark that does not state the frame size has not stated anything. The number a vendor prints and the number an operator measures usually differ for this reason rather than through dishonesty.

werner-zorn.def: The Karlsruhe professor who connected Germany to the internet in 1984, and China three years later.
werner-zorn.context: He had been proposing the connection since 1982, and the first message - received by his colleague Michael Rotert on 3 August 1984 - was a welcome from MIT, making Germany the second country outside the United States to be reached. What he did next is the part usually left out: in 1987 he connected China to the same network through Germany. A national connection is normally told as a national achievement, and this one was performed twice by the same man for two countries, one of which was not his.

jun-murai.def: The Keio professor who built Japan's first inter-university network in 1984 and the research consortium that followed it.
jun-murai.context: JUNET came first, then WIDE, which carried the country's first real internet traffic over leased lines. The detail worth keeping is the route: Japan's international link to the United States was established through Hawaii, with help from the University of Hawaii - the same institution that had put a packet radio network across four islands thirteen years earlier because it could not lay cable. The place that solved its own isolation ended up being how somebody else's was solved.

nii-quaynor.def: The Ghanaian scientist recognized for pioneering internet development across Africa.
nii-quaynor.context: The technical work of connecting a country is largely the same everywhere; what differs is how much of the surrounding apparatus you have to build yourself. Where a European or Japanese pioneer could assume universities with budgets, existing leased circuits and a regulator that had heard of data, the equivalent work across much of Africa meant assembling the institutions alongside the infrastructure. That the person who connected Germany and the person who connected Japan are far easier to name than the person who did comparable work for a continent is itself worth noticing.

kanchana-kanchanasut.def: The computer scientist credited with bringing the internet to Thailand, and with obtaining the country's domain.
kanchana-kanchanasut.context: Securing a country-code domain sounds administrative and is closer to foundational: it is the point at which a country stops being a set of hosts inside somebody else's namespace and becomes an addressable place with its own registry, its own policy and its own dispute over who runs it. Nearly every national internet story in this catalogue has that moment in it, and it is almost always accomplished by one or two academics doing paperwork nobody else understood the importance of.

stephen-wolff.def: The programme director who built the American research backbone and, from the start, planned for it to stop needing him.
stephen-wolff.context: Taking over NSFNET in 1986, he identified two needs at once: infrastructure for the academic community, and a strategy to put that infrastructure on a footing ultimately independent of federal funding. The mechanism was to push the regional networks towards commercial customers so that scale would lower everyone's costs. Federal support for the backbone ended in April 1995, on purpose. A public official whose stated objective was to make his own programme unnecessary is rare enough in any field to be worth recording, and the commercial internet is what that decision produced.

david-farber.def: The organizer of CSNET, and one half of the 1981 agreement that let one network's traffic cross another's without anyone counting it.
david-farber.context: CSNET existed because most computer science departments were not eligible for the ARPANET, and the arrangement he negotiated with Robert Kahn let CSNET traffic ride ARPANET infrastructure on a statistical, no-metered-settlements basis. That phrase is worth pausing on. Two organizations agreed to carry each other's traffic without measuring or billing it, because measuring would have cost more than it was worth - and that principle, invented as an accounting convenience between two American agencies, is how networks interconnect worldwide to this day. His CSNET software is also what Karlsruhe used to bring Germany online three years later.

glenn-ricart.def: The man who built the first place where separate networks met as equals, and who led the first TCP/IP implementation for the IBM PC.
glenn-ricart.context: An exchange point is an unglamorous room where networks that do not own each other agree to hand over traffic, and it is the physical form of the interconnection principle. Before one exists, every pair of networks needs its own private arrangement; afterwards, joining once reaches everybody present. Every internet exchange since - and the entire peering economy that decides how traffic actually flows between continents - is that room repeated. The second achievement is easy to underrate: TCP/IP on the IBM PC is what moved the protocol off institutional machines and onto desks.

danny-cohen.def: The engineer who put real-time voice and video onto a packet network in 1973, by adapting a flight simulator.
danny-cohen.context: The ARPANET was built to move files and messages, where arriving late is an inconvenience. He adapted a visual flight simulator to run across it, which requires the opposite property: a packet that arrives late is worse than one that never arrives at all. That is the first application of packet switching to real time, and every argument since about jitter buffers, quality of service and whether the internet can carry a phone call descends from someone attaching a simulator to a research network to see what would happen.

peter-eckersley.def: The Australian computer scientist, for years the EFF's (Electronic Frontier Foundation) chief computer scientist, who co-founded Let's Encrypt and led the client that became Certbot, removing the price and most of the labour of encrypting a website, and whose 2010 Panopticlick study measured how identifiable web browsers are.
peter-eckersley.context: Two threads meet in one person. Encryption stayed off most of the web for years because a certificate was a budget line and a chore, and removing both arguably changed the security posture of the internet more than any single protocol did; the EFF credits the work he began for making web encryption so common it is nearly invisible, starting with a conversation at a conference in 2012 about automating what everyone did by hand. And at the EFF (Electronic Frontier Foundation) he showed, with Panopticlick, that letting people see exactly what a tracker could read about their browser argued the privacy case better than any explanation. He died in 2022, at 43. A remembrance quoted a colleague summing up the first achievement: deprecating a billion-dollar industry overnight, and providing better security for internet users everywhere.
peter-eckersley.depth:
Peter Eckersley was born in Melbourne and studied mathematics, physics and computer science at the University of Melbourne before joining the Electronic Frontier Foundation (EFF) in San Francisco in 2006 as a staff technologist, a role that then meant advising the foundation's lawyers and activists so that their work was technically correct. His early passion, in the EFF's words, was the mismatch between copyright law and how the internet works, and he finished his PhD in computer science and law at Melbourne in 2012, on digital copyright and its alternatives. With Seth Schoen, the EFF's first staff technologist, he began to build software rather than only advise, and the two created the foundation's Technology Projects Team. He stayed twelve years and became chief computer scientist.

His first widely noticed work was on network neutrality. In 2007 he and collaborators ran what the Internet Hall of Fame calls the first controlled tests of ISP (internet service provider) interference with peer-to-peer protocols, showing that Comcast disrupted BitTorrent with forged TCP (Transmission Control Protocol) reset packets, and the EFF released Switzerland, a tool to tell users whether their provider was tampering with their traffic. He documented further violations, argued for keeping computing platforms open and for open wireless networks, and, after a call from his friend Aaron Swartz, was a driving force in the campaign against the SOPA and PIPA blacklist bills.

Panopticlick turned a privacy argument into a measurement. Between 27 January and 15 February 2010 the EFF invited visitors to panopticlick.eff.org to test their browsers, and his paper How Unique Is Your Web Browser? analysed 470,161 fingerprints built from values any site can collect: the user-agent string, HTTP (Hypertext Transfer Protocol) accept headers, whether cookies were enabled, screen resolution, time zone, the list of plugins and their versions, system fonts and a partial supercookie test. The distribution carried at least 18.1 bits of entropy, so that a randomly chosen browser would at best share its fingerprint with one in 286,777 others; 83.6 per cent of the browsers were unique, and 94.2 per cent of those with Flash or Java. Fingerprints changed often, but a simple heuristic linked an upgraded browser to its earlier fingerprint correctly 99.1 per cent of the time. The paper also named a paradox: an anti-fingerprinting measure used by too few people can make them more identifiable, not less. The EFF also lists its Privacy Badger extension among his projects.

He then turned to the web's encryption. The SSL Observatory, presented at DEF CON 18, downloaded every publicly visible SSL (Secure Sockets Layer) certificate on the IPv4 internet to search for vulnerabilities and document the practices of certificate authorities, and mapped some 650 organizations that acted as certificate authorities trusted, directly or indirectly, by Mozilla or Microsoft. The Internet Hall of Fame credits it with uncovering widespread vulnerabilities and misconfigurations; the EFF now describes certificate transparency as its successor. HTTPS Everywhere, the browser extension that rewrote requests to use HTTPS wherever a site supported it, ran for more than ten years; its goal, the EFF wrote in 2021, was always to become redundant, and it went into maintenance mode in 2022 once mainstream browsers offered their own HTTPS-only modes.

Let's Encrypt began, by its own account, when he met the University of Michigan researcher Alex Halderman at the RSA Conference in 2012 and the two started planning technology to automate getting HTTPS certificates, including early designs for what became the ACME (Automatic Certificate Management Environment) protocol. They joined a parallel effort by Josh Aas and Eric Rescorla at Mozilla, and the four built a free, automated certificate authority run for the public benefit, which began service in 2015. The EFF says he used the Snowden-era slide showing where SSL was added and removed inside a large network to build the coalition that made it happen. He led the first ACME client, which became Certbot, maintained by the EFF and designed to automate the whole HTTPS deployment rather than just fetch a certificate, and he served on the Let's Encrypt board. ACME became a Standards Track RFC (Request for Comments), RFC 8555, in March 2019, with him named in its acknowledgements. The EFF counted 100 million certificates by 2017 and over a billion issued to more than 280 million websites by 2022, by which time, it said, about 90 per cent of web page visits used HTTPS; the Internet Hall of Fame calls Let's Encrypt the largest public certificate authority in the world.

In 2018 he left the EFF to become director of research at the Partnership on AI, working on the misuse of machine learning, and in 2021 he co-founded the AI Objectives Institute. He died in San Francisco on 2 September 2022, aged 43 according to Sophos (Wikipedia gives his birth year as 1978), from complications of treatment for a colon cancer diagnosed shortly before. The EFF's tribute noted that his single-minded passion could sometimes lead him to step on toes and gloss over problems, alongside the tenacity that kept Let's Encrypt going through what it called an endless series of blockages and setbacks. The Internet Hall of Fame inducted him posthumously in 2023.

douglas-comer.def: The Purdue professor who wrote the books that taught a generation how the internet actually works.
douglas-comer.context: His citation is worth reading carefully, because of what it honours. A hall of fame otherwise full of people who invented protocols admitted someone for EXPLAINING them: the first series of textbooks setting out the scientific principles under the design, and the earliest formal guidance for building things that use it. The three volumes appeared in 1987 and went into sixteen languages. He did plenty besides - an original Internet Architecture Board member, an early network offering connections before ISPs existed, Cisco's first head of research - but the record puts the teaching first. One detail measures what those editions spanned: the first was written when the internet connected about five thousand computers, and by the fourth it was over fifty-six million. The same book, revised across four orders of magnitude of the thing it described.

randy-bush.def: The operator who spent forty years helping other countries build their own networks, and who later went after the routing system's security.
randy-bush.context: He was in the inaugural Hall of Fame class, and not for inventing anything: the citation is for the Network Startup Resource Center, which began in 1988 as volunteering when engineers in Africa and Latin America asked for help getting connected. His account of the motive is unsentimental - there were capable scientists going out of date because they were isolated - and so is his description of the era: the internet then was scientists and non-governmental organizations, not social media.
randy-bush.depth:
The model was the important part. The centre works with local engineers who run their own infrastructure, supplying training, technical information and donated equipment rather than operating anything itself. That is the difference between building a network for somewhere and leaving one behind, and it is the same distinction the entry on Africa's connection turns on: what is scarce is rarely the technical work, it is the surrounding apparatus, and an outsider can either supply that permanently or help build it locally.

He did a great deal besides. He was Verio's founding engineer, chaired the IETF's DNS working group for a decade, sat on ARIN's founding board, and helped start NANOG and AFRINIC. From 2000 he turned to the question of whether the routing system can be trusted at all, catalysing the work that became RPKI - which is a fitting second act for someone who spent the previous decade helping people join a network on the assumption that its routing told the truth.

ira-fuchs.def: The CUNY administrator who built the academic network for everyone the ARPANET had left out, starting with one link to Yale in 1981.
ira-fuchs.context: He gave the motive himself, without dressing it up: he was envious of ARPANET users. The ARPANET served defence-funded mathematics and physics, and the rest of the university - the humanities, the liberal arts, everyone without the right grant - had nothing. So he built a network whose entry condition was that you agree to connect the next institution along. It reached 1,400 universities in 49 countries and was the first academic network to reach Japan, Israel, the USSR and most of western Europe. The name began as Because It’s There and became Because It’s Time, he said, because it sounded better. And the origin is the detail worth keeping: he traced the whole idea to being a teenager with a ham radio in Queens, talking to strangers across the world from his bedroom - the same article of faith, applied to institutions instead of individuals.

adiel-akplogan.def: The Togolese engineer who helped bring the first TCP/IP connection to his country, then built the registry that allocates addresses for a continent.
adiel-akplogan.context: The Quaynor entry notes that connecting Africa meant assembling the institutions alongside the infrastructure. This is what that looked like in one career. He helped establish Togo's first TCP/IP connection in 1996, worked on several of the earliest West African providers, advised the internet development strategy of half a dozen countries, and then in 2003 helped found AFRINIC - the body that decides who gets which addresses across Africa - and ran it for a decade. He intended to stay two years. The origin is worth keeping because it is so unlike the usual founding story: an intern, promised a permanent job if he could fix what others could not, who worked three days and nights and produced a working prototype on French Minitel technology. He called that the start of the journey to the internet in Togo.

kees-neggers.def: The Dutch network director behind the first European backbone, and behind the exchange that made Amsterdam a place traffic goes.
kees-neggers.context: Ebone, which he led in 1991, was Europe's first cross-border backbone, and its founding idea is the one worth carrying: Open Exchanges - neutral places where any network could meet any other, rather than a hierarchy of who buys transit from whom. The exchange point entry for Glenn Ricart describes that room in the abstract; he is a large part of why Europe ended up with several, and why Amsterdam in particular became somewhere the world's traffic passes through rather than around. The list under his name is almost entirely institutions - RARE, TERENA, the RIPE registry, the Amsterdam exchange, a fibre consortium - which is the same shape as the other entries here whose work was making arrangements between organizations hold.

mike-jensen.def: The engineer who spent decades connecting the organizations nobody was going to connect commercially.
mike-jensen.context: His networks served the nonprofit sector first, which is an unusual starting point: most connectivity arrives because somebody expects to bill for it, and his did not. The Association for Progressive Communications, which he helped found in 1992, exists on that premise still. And the method in the citation is worth noting because it is so unglamorous - he travelled the continent, organization by organization, helping each one get online or get a better link. There is no protocol here and no product. It is the observation that a network reaches wherever somebody was willing to go and do the work, which is why coverage maps have always tracked effort as much as economics.

karen-banks.def: The GreenNet engineer whose gateway carried mail for sixty partner organizations across three continents, using the wrong technology on purpose.
karen-banks.context: GnFido ran on store-and-forward - fidonet and uucp - rather than a permanent internet link, because for most of its correspondents no permanent link existed or could be afforded. It was the inferior technology by every measure except the one that mattered, which was that it worked where the better one did not, and for thousands of people it was the only affordable electronic communication available. In 1995 the programme she helped found took forty women to the UN conference in Beijing and gave ten thousand delegates email and web access, some of them for the first time in their lives; the same group then got communications written into the Beijing Platform for Action, the first intergovernmental policy to treat women's access to these technologies as a matter of rights. Her own summary of thirty years is the line to keep: it is one thing to have access to the technologies and the pipes, but it is the people who make the network.

hardware-implant.def: Something added to a device during manufacture or transit that the buyer cannot see and the vendor may not know about.
hardware-implant.context: Most supply chain cases carry an information payload: a beacon in a router, a backdoor in a library, a rootkit in a controller. The mechanism does not require that. On 17 and 18 September 2024 thousands of pagers and hundreds of radios carried by members of Hezbollah detonated across Lebanon and Syria; 42 people were reported dead by 22 September, at least 12 of them civilians, with thousands injured across 150 hospitals. UN human rights experts condemned the attacks as potential war crimes, holding that the indiscriminate nature of simultaneous detonations breached international law; Israel's president denied involvement. The commercial detail is the transferable one. The brand on the pagers was licensed: a Taiwanese firm said the model was designed, made and sold by a Budapest company under a trademark agreement, and that the devices used a chip it does not use. The name on a product and the maker of a product are routinely different entities, entirely lawfully, and a buyer inspecting the label learns nothing about either. An implant can also lie dormant for years and wake on a message, which is a property it shares with software - the difference is only in what the payload does.

al-gore.def: United States senator, later vice president, whose 1991 legislation funded the research network and the supercomputing centre from which the commercial internet emerged; better known for a sentence he did not say.
al-gore.context: Two facts sit on either side of the name. The first is what the legislation did. As a senator in the 1980s Gore pushed to join several dozen unconnected federal networks into one, and in January 1991 he introduced the bill that became the High Performance Computing Act, signed that December. It authorized about six hundred million dollars, funded the National Research and Education Network that carried the internet out of computer science into universities at large, and strengthened the supercomputing centres - among them NCSA in Illinois, where a group of students then wrote Mosaic, the browser that made the web a public thing. Andreessen, who led that group, said that left to private industry it would not have happened for years. The second fact is the quotation. On CNN in March 1999 Gore said he had taken the initiative in creating the internet - a claim about legislation, and an accurate one - which was cut down to the word invented and became a joke that outlived the facts. The people who wrote the internet's protocols answered it: Cerf and Kahn wrote in 2000 that no elected official had made a greater contribution over a longer period. The second fact is the one everybody knows. The first is the one that happened.

jaap-akkerhuis.def: Dutch network engineer who helped build Europe's first international internet gateways at CWI in Amsterdam, later steered the .nl registry, and now sits on the body that assigns the world's two-letter country codes.
jaap-akkerhuis.context: He began in 1977 at the Mathematical Centre in Amsterdam, in the small team under Teus Hagen that did most of the actual networking as the institute became the hub of European computer networks, and he spent the nights and weekends setting up and debugging the first international gateways, reaching as far as Australia by way of Japan and Korea. One detail says how he worked: before the first official public connection between Europe and America existed, he persuaded Jon Postel to allocate him a range of addresses in advance, so that when the connection came there would be no collisions. Seven years in the United States followed, at Carnegie Mellon, mtXinu and Bell Labs, and then the first independent Dutch ISP in 1995, and from 1999 the .nl registry, where the domain count passed a million and his applied work made signing names cryptographically at scale a practical thing. He is now Vice-Chair of the agency that maintains ISO 3166, the list of two-letter country codes - the codes beneath every national domain, and the ones this site's own statistics page uses to name where readers are. Inducted into the Internet Hall of Fame in 2017, the fourth Dutch member; knighted in April 2026.

tarek-kamel.def: Egyptian engineer who established his country's first internet connection in the 1990s, built the regional gateway through which neighbouring countries first reached the network, and served as minister when the state switched it off.
tarek-kamel.context: An engineer with a Munich doctorate who grew up between German and Egyptian cultures, he ran the networking department of the Egyptian cabinet's information centre from 1992, established the country's first connection to the internet, brought in commercial service, and founded the local chapter of the Internet Society - and because Egypt became the gateway, several neighbouring Arab countries reached the network through the link he built. He helped found AFRINIC, the region's address registry, and joined the ministry at its formation in 1999, becoming minister of communications from 2004 to 2011. The hard part of the record is January 2011: in the final weeks of the Mubarak government the state shut down internet access across the country, and he was the sitting minister. The head of ICANN later stated that he had not been responsible for the shutdown and had worked, at real risk to himself and his family, to restore service as fast as it could be restored. Both facts stand. A state's decision and a minister's conduct inside it are not the same question, and the record does not resolve them into one. He went on to ICANN in 2012 as the first senior advisor from the developing world, and was inducted into the Internet Hall of Fame in 2025, six years after his death. He is, among other things, the case of the person who built the switch being in the room when it was thrown.

yvonne-marie-andres.def: California schoolteacher who, given a computer with no software in 1984, wrote her own and built a store-and-forward network that connected twelve thousand schools before the web existed.
yvonne-marie-andres.context: She was teaching low-achieving children in Oceanside when Apple gave every California school a computer with nothing on it. So she and Al Rogers, another San Diego teacher, wrote what was missing: a free word processor first, then FrEdMail - Free Educational Electronic Mail - built from a bulletin-board program a teenager had written and lent them. It ran on an Apple IIe and worked the way FidoNet and the African store-and-forward links in this catalogue worked: children wrote in class, the work went to a floppy, and in the middle of the night, when the school's one phone line was free and the rates were lowest, the machine dialled the next school and passed it on. A story could take days to cross the country, but it was affordable, which was the point. In 1991 the network was gatewayed onto the NSFNET; at its peak it joined twelve thousand schools through three hundred and fifty nodes. In 1993 it became Global SchoolNet, the 1992 Global Schoolhouse having already put students in four places on two continents onto a shared watershed study over desktop video. She wrote the first teacher's guide to the internet. The pattern recurs among the pioneers - the tool did not exist, so the person who needed it built it - with the difference that the person was a primary-school teacher and the network was made of a donated computer, a borrowed program and the night rate.

craig-newmark.def: Programmer whose 1995 email list of San Francisco events became Craigslist, the site that moved classified advertising onto the internet and, by the same act, out of the newspapers.
craig-newmark.context: The training is the part usually left out. A computer-science master's thesis on information security, seventeen years at IBM, then a move to San Francisco in 1993 as a systems security architect at a brokerage - and in 1995, from that job, an email to friends listing what was on in the city. People asked to be added; then they asked for jobs, apartments and things for sale, and he added those. By 1999 it was a company, and it became one of the most used sites on the internet by running on almost nothing: mostly free listings, a tiny staff, and a stated reliance on the users themselves to police what was posted. Two facts stand against each other and both are recorded. The site is widely held to have taken from newspapers the classified revenue that local journalism ran on, and the resulting news deserts are laid at its door; and its founder has since given, by his own account, some six hundred million dollars, first to journalism and then, increasingly, to cybersecurity and to military families. A security engineer built a trust system, watched what it did to an older one, and has spent the proceeds on the two things his thesis and his conscience pointed at.

teus-hagen.def: Dutch computer scientist who ran the networking team at Amsterdam's Mathematical Centre and in 1982 started EUnet, the first public wide-area network in Europe, as a dial-up service of the Unix user group he chaired.
teus-hagen.context: He ran the Computer Laboratory's small networking team at the Mathematical Centre - Akkerhuis, Beertema, McKie and Karrenberg - and that team is why Amsterdam became the junction of European networking before the internet reached it. Hagen founded the Dutch Unix user group and then the European one, chaired the European group through the whole decade from 1980, and in 1982 started EUnet as its dial-up service: store-and-forward mail and news over UUCP between four countries at first, the United Kingdom, the Netherlands, Denmark and Sweden, with the Dutch node at the institute. It was the first public wide-area network in Europe, and it grew to a thousand sites in twenty-one countries by 1989 - a working continental network built by a user group, on telephone lines, before any of the official research networks that were supposed to provide one. It was one of his own people who wrote the report arguing that Europe should adopt TCP/IP, and the institute that opened the first connection to the American network in 1988. From 1992 to 2008 he chaired NLnet, which grew out of EUnet into the first Dutch ISP and now funds free internet research; the Hall of Fame inducted him in 2013. The pattern is the volunteer one: the network that connected Europe first was nobody's job.

piet-beertema.def: System administrator at Amsterdam's Mathematical Centre who ran the machine at the junction of European network traffic, registered .nl, and on 17 November 1988 at 2:28 in the afternoon received the message that put Europe on the internet.
piet-beertema.context: He met his first computer at the aerospace laboratory in 1965, joined the Mathematical Centre in 1966 and never left. The machine he ran there, mcvax, was the junction through which most of Europe's mail and news passed to and from America, which made him the person who registered .nl in 1986 and, after years of preparation, the one who received the confirmation on 17 November 1988 that the institute was on the American research network - the first institution outside North America, a short while after INRIA in France. The other thing he is remembered for happened four years earlier and says something about the network he ran. On 1 April 1984, seven months after a Korean airliner had been shot down, he posted from a fictitious Moscow machine, as the Soviet general secretary, that the USSR was joining Usenet. It was the first online April Fool with international reach; he revealed himself two weeks later, by which time, he said, it had worried the Pentagon. When a real Moscow site joined in 1990, readers needed convincing it was not another prank, and its administrator named the gateway kremvax - a joke made true after the fact. A machine in Amsterdam was, in 1984, well enough connected that a message from it could alarm a superpower; four years later the same machine connected the continent.

daniel-karrenberg.def: German network engineer who helped build EUnet, wrote the report that argued Europe should run TCP/IP, co-founded RIPE, and in 1992 set up the world's first regional internet registry - intending to be finished with the internet a year later.
daniel-karrenberg.context: A network administrator at Dortmund from 1981, he helped set up EUnet the following year and joined the Amsterdam team in 1987, where he built the links to the American network and wrote the report arguing that European networking should run on TCP/IP rather than the standards the continent's institutions preferred - one of the decisions on which everything since depended. In 1989 he co-founded RIPE, the forum where European operators coordinate, and in April 1992 he set up the RIPE NCC, the first regional internet registry in the world, the body that has handed out Europe's addresses ever since; the four other registries copied the model. His own account of the plan is the best part: he meant to establish the registry and, by April 1993, be done with the internet and move on to something interesting, and instead ran it until 2000 and served as its chief scientist until 2013, building the measurement systems - the routing information service, the Atlas probes, the DNS monitors - through which the internet's operators observe the internet. Inducted in the Hall of Fame's first class in 2012, he used the speech to say the point of a hall of fame was to name the people who actually built the thing before the history books were written, and pledged to push for it. The entries around this one are, in part, that pledge kept.

jim-mckie.def: Member of the Amsterdam team that put Europe on Usenet, who in 1982 told the continent's Unix users that the Mathematical Centre would call anyone, and who later worked at Bell Labs on Plan 9, the successor to Unix.
jim-mckie.context: The first link across the Atlantic, from Digital's decvax to Amsterdam's mcvax, was held up into 1982 by something small: an autodialling modem that satisfied European telephone standards was hard to get. Once it worked, somebody had to tell Europe, and that was McKie. At the European Unix Users Group meeting in Paris in the spring of 1982 the Mathematical Centre announced it was connected to Usenet and would call, or be called by, any group site on the continent - the moment, the record says, that began the transformation of the European Unix community into a networked one. He wrote it up as Where Is Europe for the 1983 Usenix conference in Toronto, and a posting of his from that August survives in the archives, signed mcvax!jim, on the cost of sending news to aliens - the aliens being Europeans, and the cost being the phone bill. He was one of the small team under Hagen, with Akkerhuis, Beertema and Karrenberg, that did the institute's networking. Then he went to the source: Bell Labs lists him among the department that built Plan 9, the system Ritchie, Pike and Thompson's group designed from the late 1980s for a world of networked machines rather than one shared one. He had spent the early eighties making Unix machines talk across an ocean, and spent the next decade at the lab that made Unix, building the system that assumed the network from the start.

marisa-bellisario.def: Italian executive who, from 1981, turned the state telecommunications manufacturer Italtel from what the press called a national scandal into a profitable company, and whose planned merger into a group of European scale was cancelled, her foundation records, because a partner would not have a woman as chief executive.
marisa-bellisario.context: She came up through Olivetti in its electronic years, went to America in 1965, ran Olivetti's American company from 1979 and repaired its balance sheet, and in October 1980 accepted the state holding's offer of the hardest job in Italian industry. Italtel had six plants, twenty-nine thousand employees, very low productivity, high absenteeism and heavy losses; the press called it a nightmare and a national scandal, and she wrote later that it was worse than described. Co-general manager from the start of 1981, sole managing director from that August, she replaced the management, started new projects, and carried the plan through against the unions and part of the press. In three years turnover went from 503 billion lire to 1,300 billion, with a substantial profit, and the share of women among the company's graduates went from five per cent to twenty-seven. The merger with Fiat's Telettra that would have made an Italian equipment group of European scale did not happen; the foundation that bears her name states plainly that Fiat would not give her the chief executive's chair because she was a woman, and that the sector's growth stalled with it. She died in office in August 1988, at fifty-three. The Italtel entry records what became of the company; this is the person who gave it the decade it had.

ssl-vpn.def: Remote access carried inside a TLS session on port 443, either through a browser portal or an agent, so that it crosses networks that permit little else.
ssl-vpn.context: The appeal was always practical rather than cryptographic: a hotel or airport network that blocks almost everything still allows outbound 443, so a tunnel disguised as web traffic gets through where IPsec does not. The cost is the shape of what has to listen. A concentrator terminates TLS, parses attacker-controlled input through an HTTP stack and often a web application, must be reachable from the whole internet, and usually sits inside the firewall itself, which is why the same class of pre-authentication flaw has recurred across unrelated vendors' products for a decade. Fortinet removed tunnel mode entirely in FortiOS 7.6.3, keeping browser access under the name Agentless VPN (virtual private network), and other vendors have retired product lines or hardware generations. The industry is not abandoning TLS or remote access; it is abandoning the full-tunnel, appliance-terminated form as the default, in favour of brokered per-application access.
ssl-vpn.depth:
What the term covers. The National Institute of Standards and Technology (NIST) wrote the reference description in Special Publication (SP) 800-113, Guide to SSL VPNs, published in July 2008 by Sheila Frankel, Paul Hoffman, Angela Orebaugh and Richard Park. An SSL VPN (virtual private network) is one or more devices to which users connect with a web browser, the traffic protected by Secure Sockets Layer (SSL) or its successor, Transport Layer Security (TLS), which is why the guide accepts TLS VPN as an equal name. It distinguishes two kinds. A portal VPN gives the user a single TLS connection to a web site, a page that leads to many internal resources after the user authenticates. A tunnel VPN carries multiple services, including applications and protocols that are not web-based, through a tunnel running under SSL, and so acts as a network-layer VPN for both TCP and UDP; it needs active content in the browser, or a client installed on the machine, which in turn needs administrative rights. Tunnels can be full, sending all traffic to the organization, or split, sending only the organization's traffic through the tunnel. NIST was explicit in 2008 that SSL VPNs were not intended to replace IPsec VPNs and that the two were complementary. The name has outlived its protocol: SSL 3.0 was deprecated by RFC (Request for Comments) 7568 in June 2015, which says it must not be used, so every product sold as an SSL VPN today runs TLS, and many move their data channel to DTLS (Datagram Transport Layer Security), the datagram form of TLS described in its own entry.

Where it sits. SP 800-113 describes the practical requirement plainly: port 443 on the firewall's external address must be open so that users can start sessions. It also lists the placements, and the one that became the norm, the SSL VPN as a function of the firewall itself, has advantages the guide spells out: no holes between an external VPN device and the internal network, and traffic to internal hosts still passing the firewall's rules. The guide's list of expected features shows what a concentrator grew into: endpoint security that checks the host before admitting it, cache cleaners that remove sensitive data from the client after the session, and intrusion prevention on the decrypted traffic. Each of those is more code running on the device that faces the internet.

The pre-authentication record. The vulnerability catalogue reads like a description of that device; the identifiers below are Common Vulnerabilities and Exposures (CVE) entries. CVE-2019-11510, published on 8 May 2019, let an unauthenticated attacker read arbitrary files on Pulse Connect Secure with a crafted uniform resource identifier (URI); CVE-2018-13379, published on 4 June 2019, was a path traversal in the FortiOS SSL VPN web portal that let an unauthenticated attacker download system files; CVE-2019-19781, published on 27 December 2019, was a directory traversal in Citrix Application Delivery Controller (ADC) and Gateway. All three entered the Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency's Known Exploited Vulnerabilities (KEV) catalogue on 3 November 2021. Fortinet's SSL-VPN then accumulated CVE-2022-42475, a heap-based buffer overflow allowing remote unauthenticated code execution, added to KEV on 13 December 2022; CVE-2023-27997, another heap overflow, added on 13 June 2023; and CVE-2024-21762, an out-of-bounds write, added on 9 February 2024. Ivanti Connect Secure, the former Pulse product, had CVE-2023-46805, an authentication bypass in its web component, and CVE-2024-21887, a command injection in its web components reachable once authenticated, both added to KEV on 10 January 2024; used together, the first supplies the authentication the second requires. The pattern is consistent: the flaws are in the HTTP and web layer that must run before anyone has logged in, so multi-factor authentication, which protects the session, does nothing for a flaw in the doorway.

Patched is not the same as clean. On 10 April 2025 Fortinet's product security team described what a threat actor had done with three of those flaws, FG-IR-22-398, FG-IR-23-097 and FG-IR-24-015, which the National Vulnerability Database (NVD) links to CVE-2022-42475, CVE-2023-27997 and CVE-2024-21762. After gaining access, the actor created a symbolic link joining the user filesystem to the root filesystem inside the folder used to serve the SSL-VPN's language files. Because the change sat in the user filesystem it escaped detection, and it survived upgrades that fixed the original vulnerabilities, leaving read-only access to files that may include the device's configuration. Fortinet added an antivirus and IPS (intrusion prevention system) signature to remove the link, changed FortiOS 7.6.2, 7.4.7, 7.2.11, 7.0.17 and 6.4.16 to remove it on upgrade and to stop the SSL-VPN serving such links, and noted that devices that had never enabled SSL-VPN were not affected. The operational lesson is general: a concentrator that was ever exploitable should be checked for the vendor's published indicators and have every credential it could read rotated, not merely be upgraded.

The Fortinet change. FortiOS 7.6.3 replaced SSL VPN tunnel mode with IPsec VPN on every FortiGate model. The release notes say the IPsec replacement can be configured to use TCP port 443, that tunnel mode is no longer available in the graphical interface or the command line, that its settings will not be upgraded from previous versions, and that customers must migrate before upgrading to keep remote access working. The browser mode survives under a new name, Agentless VPN, except on the small FortiGate 40F, 60F, 61F and 90G-family models with 2 GB of RAM (random access memory), where it is gone too; the notes tell administrators to confirm the memory with diagnose hardware sysinfo conserve and to consider IPsec dial-up instead. Moving remote access to IPsec over TCP 443 keeps the property that made SSL VPNs popular, crossing networks that allow little but HTTPS, while taking the web application out of the path that runs before authentication.

What replaces it, and what does not change. The successors are IPsec with an internet key exchange (IKE) front end, smaller tunnels such as WireGuard for site and device links, and zero trust network access (ZTNA), in which a broker grants one application at a time instead of a network segment, as the entries on those terms describe. None of them removes the need for something listening on the internet: a ZTNA broker or a security service edge also terminates TLS from clients, and WireGuard, which runs only over UDP, cannot cross a network that permits nothing but TCP 443. What changes is the size and shape of the code exposed before authentication and whether a successful login yields a network or a single application. For an SSL VPN still in service the near-term measures follow from its record: track the vendor's advisories against the KEV catalogue, reduce who can reach the portal, prefer certificate-backed and multi-factor authentication for the session while remembering that neither helps against a pre-authentication flaw, and plan the migration on the vendor's timetable rather than discovering it in an upgrade window.

l2tp.def: Layer Two Tunneling Protocol: carries PPP frames across an IP network, providing no encryption of its own, which is why it is almost always paired with IPsec.
l2tp.context: It came from merging two earlier proposals, Cisco's L2F and Microsoft's PPTP, and its job is narrow: take the point-to-point session a dial-up user would have had with an access server and carry it over an IP network instead, so the user appears to terminate where the network wants rather than where the modem was. On its own it authenticates the tunnel and encrypts nothing, which is the detail practitioners most often get wrong. The pairing written as L2TP/IPsec puts the whole L2TP session inside an IPsec transport-mode association, so IPsec supplies confidentiality and integrity and L2TP supplies the PPP semantics - user authentication, address assignment, multiprotocol carriage. It persists mainly because it is built into consumer operating systems and home routers, which makes it the fallback that works without installing anything, and it is a poor choice where a modern option exists.

ikev2.def: Internet Key Exchange version 2: the negotiation that authenticates both ends of an IPsec tunnel and establishes the keys, replacing a first version whose complexity was its main flaw.
ikev2.context: Version 1 grew several negotiation modes with subtly different security properties, and aggressive mode in particular could expose a hash of the pre-shared key to a passive observer. Version 2 collapsed that into one exchange of four messages, made the request-response pairing explicit so that retransmission and dead-peer detection actually work, and built in the NAT traversal and mobility handling that version 1 had bolted on. For an operator the practical differences are that a version 2 tunnel survives a change of address - a laptop moving from wired to mobile - and that the failure modes are legible, because each exchange has a matching response rather than a state machine to infer. It is the default for any new deployment, and the reason a remote-access migration away from a browser-based tunnel usually lands here.

split-tunnel.def: Sending only the traffic destined for corporate resources through the tunnel, and letting everything else go straight out to the internet.
split-tunnel.context: The alternative, full tunnelling, sends everything through the concentrator, which gives the security team one place to inspect and log but makes them the carrier for every video call and software update the workforce generates. Full tunnelling collapsed as a default in 2020, when concentrators sized for a fraction of the workforce met all of it at once and the arithmetic stopped working. The argument against splitting is that traffic which never crosses the tunnel is never inspected, and that a compromised laptop has a foot in both networks at the same time. The argument for it is capacity and user experience, and the honest position is that neither wins on principle: it is a decision about where inspection happens, and moving inspection to the endpoint or to a cloud-delivered service is what makes splitting defensible rather than merely cheaper.

pptp.def: Point-to-Point Tunneling Protocol: the first widely deployed remote-access VPN (virtual private network), broken repeatedly since 1998 and retained only as a lesson.
pptp.context: It shipped in Windows in the mid-1990s and made remote access ordinary, which is its real contribution.
