It was also cryptanalysed almost immediately: Schneier and Mudge published against the original in 1998, and against the revised MS-CHAPv2 authentication in 1999, and by 2012 the remaining protection could be reduced to a single brute-force problem solvable by a rented service in hours. The flaw that matters is structural rather than incidental - the encryption keys were derived from the user's password, so the strength of the tunnel could never exceed the strength of a password. It is disabled or removed in current operating systems. It appears here because it is the clearest example in this catalogue of a protocol that was not repaired but replaced, and because equipment still offers it.

openvpn.def: An open-source tunnel that runs its own protocol over UDP or TCP using TLS for key exchange, independent of any vendor's appliance.
openvpn.context: It occupies the space between the two families: like an SSL VPN (virtual private network) it can hide inside port 443 and traverse restrictive networks, and like IPsec it is a full network tunnel with no web application in front of it. That combination, plus an implementation that runs on everything and is auditable by anyone, made it the default for people who did not want to buy a concentrator - community and commercial VPN services, small offices, and laboratories. The cost is throughput, because the data path runs in user space and each packet crosses the kernel boundary, and configuration surface, because the flexibility that makes it portable also makes it easy to deploy badly. It is the reference point against which WireGuard's argument about size is usually made.

man-in-the-middle.def: An attacker positioned between two parties who each believe they are talking directly to the other, able to read and alter what passes.
man-in-the-middle.context: The formal definition calls it active wiretapping: the attacker does not merely observe but terminates each side and can modify what it forwards. The position can be reached by lying on the local network, by controlling a router or wireless access point, by poisoning name resolution, or simply by being the proxy the user configured. That last case is why the term needs care in professional use: a developer's debugging proxy and a corporate inspection appliance perform the identical operation and are not attacks, because consent was given. Encryption does not prevent the position; it prevents the reading, and only for as long as the certificate presented is not one the client will accept. That is why the defences are all about identity rather than confidentiality: certificate pinning, mutual authentication, and the transparency logs that make a wrongly issued certificate visible. Some organizations now write it as machine-in-the-middle or adversary-in-the-middle to avoid the gendered term.
man-in-the-middle.depth:
Request for Comments (RFC) 4949, the Internet Security Glossary that R. Shirey published in August 2007, defines a man-in-the-middle (MITM) attack as a form of active wiretapping in which the attacker intercepts and selectively modifies communicated data in order to masquerade as one or more of the entities in a communication. Its worked example is the textbook case: two parties agree a session key with the Diffie-Hellman-Merkle algorithm but without data origin authentication, so a third party can block their direct exchange, pose as each party to the other, establish a separate session key with each, and run as a clandestine proxy that captures or changes whatever they believe they are sending only to each other. The word that separates it from eavesdropping is active: a passive tap only reads, while a man in the middle terminates each side and decides what to forward, what to alter and what to drop.

The National Institute of Standards and Technology (NIST) glossary words it operationally: an attacker positioned between two communicating parties in order to intercept or alter the data travelling between them. The definition it takes from Special Publication (SP) 1800-21B adds the identity case, with the attacker between claimant and verifier, between registrant and credential service provider during enrolment, or between subscriber and provider while an authenticator is being bound. The names vary more than the idea. NIST lists MitM and MITM and writes person (man)-in-the-middle; MITRE's catalogue of adversary behaviour files the technique as adversary-in-the-middle (AiTM), T1557, created on 11 February 2020, and names interception of credentials, access tokens and session cookies among its uses; RFC 3833 says monkey-in-the-middle; machine-in-the-middle is another variant.

Reaching the position is the first half of every MITM, and on a local network it is cheap, because the protocols that steer traffic believe whoever answers. MITRE's four sub-techniques read like a list of those protocols. In cache poisoning of the Address Resolution Protocol (ARP), which maps IPv4 (Internet Protocol version 4) addresses to link-layer MAC (media access control) addresses, the attacker answers a victim's broadcast request faster than the real owner, or sends an unsolicited gratuitous reply claiming the address, and because ARP is stateless and unauthenticated the victim caches the false binding, usually for its default gateway. In spoofing of the Dynamic Host Configuration Protocol (DHCP), a rogue server answers first and hands clients its own DNS (Domain Name System) servers; on IPv6 (Internet Protocol version 6) it can answer a DHCPv6 INFORMATION-REQUEST, message code 11, without assigning an address at all. In name-resolution poisoning it answers the fallback protocols LLMNR (Link-Local Multicast Name Resolution, on UDP (User Datagram Protocol) port 5355), NBT-NS (NetBIOS Name Service, UDP 137) and multicast DNS (UDP 5353), so a Windows host looking for a server it cannot find sends its authentication, with the user's password hash, to the attacker, which can crack it offline or relay it to a real server. The evil twin does the same on Wi-Fi: an access point broadcasting a legitimate network's SSID (service set identifier), with a stronger signal.

The local defences live in the network rather than on the hosts. For ARP poisoning MITRE lists DHCP snooping with dynamic ARP inspection on the switches, which bind each address mapping learned from DHCP to a switch port and drop replies that contradict it, static ARP entries where the network is small enough, and hosts that refuse to update their cache from gratuitous replies. For the family as a whole it adds encrypting sensitive traffic, disabling legacy protocols that nothing needs, segmentation that limits how much one foothold can reach, and training users to distrust certificate errors.

Further out the target is name resolution. RFC 3833, the threat analysis of the DNS that D. Atkins and R. Austein wrote in August 2004 because the threats the DNS Security Extensions (DNSSEC) were meant to stop had never been written down, puts packet interception first: monkey-in-the-middle attacks, and eavesdropping combined with spoofed responses that beat the real answer back to the resolver. The DNS makes this easy because a query or response normally travels in one unsigned, unencrypted UDP packet. An attacker who cannot see the query must guess the 16-bit query identifier (ID) and the client port, at most 2 to the power 32 combinations and, when the port is fixed or predictable, often fewer than 2 to the power 16; combined with knowledge of the query names, that guess is enough to inject bogus data.

Encryption does not stop anyone taking the position; it decides what the position is worth. Against Transport Layer Security (TLS) the attacker must present a certificate the client accepts, meaning a chain to an anchor the client trusts and a name that matches the service. RFC 9525 (November 2023), which replaced RFC 6125, governs that name check and says the Common Name attribute must not be used to identify a service. Most practical interception therefore attacks the client's decision rather than the cryptography. For the Hypertext Transfer Protocol (HTTP), RFC 6797 defined HTTP Strict Transport Security (HSTS) in November 2012, written by J. Hodges, C. Jackson and A. Barth against a named habit: browsers let users click through certificate errors, and that click-through insecurity leaks session cookies to whoever sits in the middle. A site that sends the Strict-Transport-Security header field, with its required max-age directive and optionally includeSubDomains, tells the browser to use only secure connections to it and to treat any TLS error as fatal, with no user recourse. The RFC names the gap it leaves, the bootstrap MITM vulnerability of a first visit typed or linked as an http address, which pre-loaded lists shipped inside browsers close; MITRE also lists downgrade to weaker protocol versions as a way in. Certificate pinning goes further: the client knows in advance which certificate, usually which issuer, to expect, and severs the connection on a mismatch. Certificate Transparency, now RFC 9162 (December 2021, experimental, obsoleting RFC 6962), covers the case pinning cannot scale to, a genuine but wrongly issued certificate, by logging certificates publicly so that anyone can audit certificate authority (CA) activity and notice suspect issuance.

That case has a name: DigiNotar. The final report that Fox-IT wrote for the Dutch Ministry of the Interior and Kingdom Relations, Black Tulip, dated 13 August 2012, reconstructs it. The outer network was breached on 17 June 2011, the segment holding the CA servers was reached on 1 July, the first rogue certificate was issued on 10 July, all eight CA servers were compromised, and a non-exhaustive list of 531 rogue certificates was identified. A rogue wildcard certificate for google.com was then used for weeks in a large-scale MITM against about 300,000 users, almost all in Iran. It came to light on 28 August 2011, when a Gmail user posted on a Google support forum that Chrome had blocked Google with a certificate warning; Chrome, the report notes, checked Google's certificates with pinning on top of standard validation. Requests to DigiNotar's Online Certificate Status Protocol (OCSP) responder for that one certificate came from 298,140 unique Internet Protocol (IP) addresses, 95 per cent of them in Iran, spread over 143 autonomous systems, a count the report calls a very rough approximation. The Dutch government publicly revoked its trust on 3 September, DigiNotar filed a bankruptcy petition on 19 September, and the Court of Haarlem declared it bankrupt on 20 September 2011. Every browser that trusted DigiNotar had validated correctly; the attack worked because the anchor itself had been subverted.

With consent, the same mechanics are an ordinary enterprise control. Fortinet's FortiOS 7.6.5 guide says that with deep inspection the FortiGate impersonates the recipient of the originating SSL (Secure Sockets Layer) session, decrypts and inspects the content, then re-encrypts it and sends it to the real recipient, for mail and file-transfer protocols over TLS as well as for web traffic. It re-signs server certificates with a stored CA, Fortinet_CA_SSL by default, Fortinet_CA_Untrusted, or the organization's own uploaded CA; browsers warn until Fortinet_CA_SSL is in the clients' trusted root store, usually pushed by Active Directory group policy, and Fortinet says never to import Fortinet_CA_Untrusted. F5's SSL Orchestrator deployment guide describes the forward-proxy version step by step: the BIG-IP pauses the client's handshake at the Client Hello, completes its own handshake with the real server and validates that server's certificate, then forges a new certificate carrying the original's names and most of its attributes, signed by a local CA the internal clients must trust, so that two separate TLS sessions replace one. The guide is explicit that certificate pinning, being solely a function of the client, defeats any decrypting intermediary, which is why it ships a Pinners bypass category, and that browsers keep working because they accept locally installed roots. Technically nothing separates this from an attack except the root in the trust store and the policy that put it there; operationally, the inspecting device inherits the server-validation duty the client gave up, and the exemptions for categories such as finance and banking are where privacy rules meet it.

arp-poisoning.def: Answering the local network's address resolution requests with a lie, so that traffic for another machine is delivered to you instead.
arp-poisoning.context: Address resolution was specified in 1982 to solve one problem - find the hardware address for a protocol address - and it solved it by asking the whole segment and believing whatever came back. There is no authentication, no state, and no way for the asker to tell a legitimate reply from a crafted one; a machine can also send unsolicited replies that hosts will cache. Everything else follows. Placing yourself between two hosts on the same segment, or between a host and its default gateway, requires only that you answer first and keep answering. Switching never addressed this, because a switch forwards on the basis of the same learned mappings. The mitigations are all switch features and all optional: dynamic ARP inspection validating replies against DHCP bindings, DHCP snooping to build those bindings, port security limiting addresses per port, and 802.1X to authenticate the device before it may speak at all. Forty-four years after the specification the protocol is unchanged, and the defence remains a configuration decision somebody has to make.

certificate-pinning.def: Requiring that a server present one specific certificate or public key, rather than any certificate a trusted authority will sign.
certificate-pinning.context: Ordinary validation asks whether some authority the device trusts vouches for this name, which means any of hundreds of authorities, or any authority installed on the device, will do. Pinning narrows that to a named key, normally a SHA-256 (Secure Hash Algorithm, 256-bit) hash of the certificate's public key information, and so defeats interception even when the intercepting certificate is technically valid. It is standard in mobile applications and in anything talking to a fixed backend. The browser version, HTTP Public Key Pinning (HPKP), was specified in 2015 and abandoned: a site that pinned a key and then lost it made itself unreachable to returning visitors for the lifetime of the pin, and the failure was unrecoverable, so Chrome and Firefox removed it, leaving Certificate Transparency as the main safeguard against misissued certificates. The operational consequence in an enterprise is unavoidable: an application that pins correctly will simply fail behind an inspecting proxy, and the resolution is always an exception list rather than a technical reconciliation.
certificate-pinning.depth:
What a pin is. RFC (Request for Comments) 7469 defines a pin as a relationship between a hostname and a cryptographic identity, one or more of the public keys in a chain of X.509 certificates, and pin validation as the check that a host still authenticates with that identity. Ordinary TLS (Transport Layer Security) validation asks whether a chain leads to any trusted root and names the host; pinning adds a second, narrower question: does the chain contain one of these particular keys? The usual pin is an SPKI (SubjectPublicKeyInfo) fingerprint, the hash of the DER-encoded (Distinguished Encoding Rules) structure that holds the key and its algorithm, written in Base64. RFC 7469, Android and Apple all use SHA-256 (Secure Hash Algorithm, 256-bit), so a pin is 32 bytes, 44 Base64 characters. Pinning the key rather than the whole certificate is what the OWASP (Open Worldwide Application Security Project) cheat sheet encourages, because the key with its algorithm survives a renewal that reuses it, while a certificate pin breaks at every reissue. Apple's guidance states the property that matters most: pinning can only tighten trust, never loosen it, and the chain must still pass the platform's normal validation.

What to pin. OWASP sets out the trade-off. Pinning a root CA (certificate authority) is generally not recommended, because it implies trusting every intermediate under it; pinning an issuing or intermediate CA reduces the risk but still accepts anything that CA issues, not only the application's own certificates; pinning the leaf is recommended, provided a backup is included, such as the intermediate or a set of alternative keys, so that a failed or rotated leaf does not brick the application. Every serious scheme insists on a backup. RFC 7469 refused to record a host's pins unless at least one of them did not appear in the current chain, the backup pin for a key pair kept offline. Android's documentation says to include a backup key or be ready to push an application update to restore connectivity, and Apple's says that an app expecting specific keys refuses to connect once the server deploys new ones, until the app is updated. Certificate lifetimes make this sharper every year. Under Ballot SC081v3 of the CA/Browser Forum, adopted on 11 April 2025, and version 2.3.1 of the Baseline Requirements, public TLS certificates issued from 15 March 2026 may last at most 200 days, from 15 March 2027 at most 100 days, and from 15 March 2029 at most 47 days; a pin on a leaf key that changes at each renewal has to change with it.

How applications pin today. On Android the Network Security Configuration file declares a pin-set for a domain, each pin a Base64 SHA-256 digest of a SubjectPublicKeyInfo, and accepts an expiration date after which pinning stops; Google's documentation warns that the expiration avoids stranded users but may let attackers bypass the pins. A trust-anchors element can carry overridePins, so that chains signed by the CAs it names skip pinning altogether. Apple platforms read NSPinnedDomains inside NSAppTransportSecurity in the app's Info.plist, with NSPinnedCAIdentities or NSPinnedLeafIdentities holding SPKI-SHA256-BASE64 values. Apple's article of 14 January 2021 gives the pipeline to compute one: openssl x509 -noout -pubkey extracts the key, openssl pkey -pubin -outform der turns it into DER, openssl dgst -sha256 -binary hashes it, and openssl enc -base64 encodes the result. The same article opens with a warning worth quoting in substance: pinning is not required, and in most cases it should be avoided.

The browser experiment. RFC 7469, by Chris Evans, Chris Palmer and Ryan Sleevi of Google, published in April 2015 on the Standards Track, let a site send a Public-Key-Pins header with pin-sha256 directives, a mandatory max-age, an optional includeSubDomains and a report-uri, plus a Public-Key-Pins-Report-Only variant for testing. It was trust on first use: a browser learned the pins on its first error-free visit and enforced them until max-age ran out. The RFC let browsers cap max-age, giving 5,184,000 seconds (60 days) as an example, and let them skip pin validation when a chain ended at a user-installed trust anchor, so enterprise inspection was not blocked. Its own security section described hostile pinning: an attacker holding a valid certificate for a domain, through misissuance or as the domain's previous owner, could send pins of its choosing and lock the real owner out for as long as the maximum max-age. The cure proved worse than the disease. Chrome removed HPKP (HTTP Public Key Pinning) in version 72, citing very low adoption and the risks of denial of service and hostile pinning, and Firefox removed it in version 72 in January 2020. Scott Helme, who ran a reporting service for it, counted about 3,500 sites in the top million at its peak and about 650 at the end, and pointed to Certificate Transparency and CAA (Certification Authority Authorization) records as the partial replacements. RFC 7469 has never been formally obsoleted; it simply has no implementations left in browsers.

Where pinning earned its reputation. Browsers had also shipped built-in pins for a few high-value sites. The Black Tulip report on the DigiNotar breach, written by Fox-IT for the Dutch government and dated 13 August 2012, records that Chrome performed certificate pinning on Google certificates, and that on 28 August 2011 a Gmail user, a customer of the Iranian provider ParsOnline, posted on a Google support forum the warning Chrome had shown him for a rogue *.google.com certificate issued by DigiNotar. That certificate had been used for weeks in a man-in-the-middle attack on about 300,000 users, almost all in Iran. Google's security blog of 29 August said that Chrome users were protected because Chrome detected the fraudulent certificate, and announced that DigiNotar would be disabled in Chrome. A pin did what ordinary validation could not: the rogue certificate chained to a trusted root and named the right host.

Pinning and inspection. A TLS inspection device presents certificates signed by its own CA, which the managed devices are told to trust; an application that pins the real key rejects the substitute, correctly from its own point of view, and nothing on the proxy can change that. The vendors' answer is a bypass list. Netskope's documentation says that its predefined certificate-pinned applications bypass the Netskope cloud by default and that custom ones can be defined under Settings, Security Cloud Platform, App Definition, Certificate Pinned Apps and added as steering exceptions. Mobile platforms add a second cause that looks the same: Android apps targeting Android 7.0 (API level 24) and later trust only the system CAs unless their configuration says otherwise, so a corporate CA installed by the user is ignored even by apps that do not pin; only Android 6.0 and earlier trust user-added CAs by default. When an application refuses the proxy, the resolution is an exception for that application, not a cleverer certificate.

What goes wrong, and the numbers. The classic failure is self-inflicted: a key lost, a CA changed or a leaf renewed with a new key, and every installed copy of the application stops connecting until users update. Pinning a root trusts too much and pinning a single leaf without a backup trusts too little; expiry dates on pins trade safety for availability; and shorter certificate lifetimes multiply the moments when a pin and a key can drift apart. Numbers worth remembering: SHA-256 over the DER SubjectPublicKeyInfo, 32 bytes or 44 Base64 characters per pin; RFC 7469 of April 2015 and its 60-day example cap; Chrome 72 and Firefox 72 for the end of HPKP; 28 August 2011 for the DigiNotar warning; and 200, 100 and 47 days as the public certificate lifetimes from 2026, 2027 and 2029.

ssl-inspection.def: An organization terminating and re-encrypting its own users' encrypted sessions in order to inspect the contents, using a certificate authority it installs on every managed device.
ssl-inspection.context: Technically it is a man-in-the-middle performed with the organization's consent rather than the individual user's, and every property of that position applies: the device holds the plaintext of every session it inspects and a private key that every managed device trusts, which makes it the most valuable single object on the network. National security guidance has been explicit that the inspection point becomes a high-value target and that breaking end-to-end protection introduces risks to be weighed against the visibility gained. Three practical frictions recur. Pinned applications fail rather than degrade, so an exception list is unavoidable. Certificate errors that would have warned a user about a genuine attack are now generated and resolved by the appliance, so the user sees nothing either way. And the shift towards encrypting the handshake itself, including the name of the site being visited, is progressively removing the metadata that name-based policy depends on.

ssl-stripping.def: Keeping a victim on plain HTTP by rewriting the links that would have taken them to HTTPS, while the attacker speaks HTTPS to the real server.
ssl-stripping.context: Presented by Moxie Marlinspike in 2009, the technique exploited the fact that users almost never type the scheme: they arrive at a site over plain HTTP and are redirected, or they follow a link. An attacker in the path rewrites those redirects and links so the victim's side of the conversation is never encrypted at all, while the attacker's side to the server is - so the server sees a normal secure session and the victim sees a page that simply lacks a padlock nobody was looking for. It required no invalid certificate and produced no warning, which is what made it effective. HTTP Strict Transport Security is the direct answer: a site instructs the browser to use HTTPS for that name for a stated period, so there is no plain-text first request to intercept, and preload lists carry the instruction before the first visit. The technique is largely historical for major sites and remains relevant wherever a redirect from plain HTTP is still the entry point.

rfc-2549.def: An April Fools' RFC from 1999 that adds quality of service to the pigeon-based IP transport of RFC 1149.
rfc-2549.context: RFC 2549 keeps the deadpan of its predecessor while layering on class-of-service handling, queue management and the observation that the carriers are self-regulating: high-priority traffic is simply carried by faster birds. It also notes that the protocol has a built-in loss mechanism in the form of predators. The joke works because everything it describes is a real QoS concern stated without a single false note.

rfc-6214.def: A 2011 April Fools' RFC that formally adapts RFC 1149's avian carrier transport to IPv6.
rfc-6214.context: Published on 1 April 2011, RFC 6214 exists because IPv6 migration documents were being written for every other transport and the authors followed the pattern to its conclusion. The serious content underneath is a checklist of what actually changes when a protocol moves to IPv6 - address size, header format, neighbour discovery - applied to a carrier that flaps. Twenty-one years separate it from RFC 1149, which is a long time for a joke to stay maintained.

http-420.def: A non-standard HTTP status code once returned by Twitter's API for rate limiting, named Enhance Your Calm.
http-420.context: 420 has never been registered with IANA and does not appear in RFC 9110. Twitter used it for rate-limited clients before moving to the standard 429 Too Many Requests, and a few frameworks have since borrowed it for their own purposes. Encountering it in the wild tells you something about the service's age rather than about the request: it is a fossil of an era when large APIs invented status codes rather than waiting for the registry.

ieee-802-11.def: The standard of the Institute of Electrical and Electronics Engineers (IEEE) for wireless local area networks (WLANs), IEEE 802.11: one medium access control (MAC) layer over a family of physical layers, extended by lettered amendments. It is what almost everyone means by Wi-Fi.
ieee-802-11.context: IEEE (Institute of Electrical and Electronics Engineers) 802.11 specifies the physical layer (PHY) and the medium access control (MAC) layer of a wireless LAN (local area network); the throughput amendments among the letters that follow it (a, b, g, n, ac, ax, be) mark generations of modulation, channel width and multi-user behaviour. Wi-Fi is the certification brand of the Wi-Fi Alliance rather than the standard itself, which is why marketing names such as Wi-Fi 6 map onto amendments like 802.11ax rather than replacing them. Naming the amendment rather than the brand is usually the faster way to end an argument about what a device actually supports.
ieee-802-11.depth:
What it is. IEEE (Institute of Electrical and Electronics Engineers) Std 802.11 is Part 11 of the IEEE 802 family of local and metropolitan area network standards, titled Wireless LAN Medium Access Control (MAC) and Physical Layer (PHY) Specifications. The IEEE states its scope in one sentence: it defines one medium access control and several physical layer specifications for wireless connectivity for fixed, portable and moving stations within a local area. One MAC over many PHYs is the key to reading it. Each amendment changes or adds to that single MAC and adds physical layers with new modulation, coding, channel widths or bands; none starts a new standard, and each is eventually folded into a consolidated edition. The Wi-Fi name is not part of it: that belongs to the Wi-Fi Alliance, which certifies products against 802.11 and numbers its generations, and the wifi entry covers that side. The current edition is IEEE 802.11-2024, approved by the IEEE Standards Association (IEEE SA) Standards Board on 26 September 2024 and published on 28 April 2025, and it is available through the IEEE GET Program, the sponsored-access scheme that includes the 802 standards.

How it grew. The project authorization request (PAR) for the original standard was approved on 21 March 1991, and IEEE 802.11-1997 was approved on 26 June 1997. It offered two raw data rates, 1 and 2 Mbit/s, over infrared or over frequency-hopping or direct-sequence spread spectrum (DSSS) in the 2.4 GHz industrial, scientific and medical (ISM) band, and it already defined carrier sense multiple access with collision avoidance (CSMA/CA) as the access method, a choice that gives up a large share of raw capacity in exchange for reliability over radio. A clarified edition, 802.11-1999, was approved on 18 March 1999, and on 16 September of that year came 802.11a, a physical layer for 5 GHz, and 802.11b, which raised the 2.4 GHz rate to 11 Mbit/s. Since then the working group has periodically rolled its amendments into a new edition: 802.11-2007 absorbed a, b, d, e, g, h, i and j; 802.11-2012 absorbed k, n, p, r, s, u, v, w, y and z; 802.11-2016 took in aa, ac, ad, ae and af; 802.11-2020 took in ah, ai, aj, ak and aq; and 802.11-2024 incorporated the seven amendments published from 2021 to 2024 (ax, ay, ba, az, bd, bb and bc) and two corrigenda. A maintenance task group, TGmf, is preparing the next edition; its draft 3.0 drew 774 comments in a working group recirculation ballot around the September 2026 interim session.

Reading the letters. Each amendment is written by a task group named after it (TGax produced 802.11ax), and the letters are handed out in sequence: after 802.11z came 802.11aa, and after 802.11az came 802.11ba. Only a few are throughput generations, namely a, b, g, n, ac, ax and be, with bn, Ultra High Reliability, which the working group itself calls Wi-Fi 8, now in ballot. Most of the alphabet does something else: 802.11i-2004, MAC Security Enhancements; 802.11e-2005, quality of service (QoS) enhancements to the MAC; 802.11k-2008, Radio Resource Measurement, and 802.11r-2008, Fast Roaming; 802.11w-2009, Protected Management Frames; 802.11p-2010, wireless access in the vehicular environment; 802.11s-2011, mesh networking; 802.11u-2011 and 802.11v-2011, interworking with external networks and wireless network management; 802.11ad-2012 and 802.11ay-2021 for 60 GHz; 802.11ah-2016 below 1 GHz; 802.11az-2022, positioning; 802.11bb-2023, light communications. The latest show where the work has moved: 802.11bh, randomized and changing MAC addresses, published on 3 June 2025; 802.11bk, 320 MHz positioning, and 802.11bf, WLAN sensing, both published in September 2025; and 802.11bi, enhanced privacy protection, published on 23 October 2026. Projects under way include bp (ambient power, for stations that run on harvested energy), bq (operation between 42 and 71 GHz that always depends on a link below 7.25 GHz), br (enhanced light communications) and bt (post-quantum cryptography), whose first draft passed its initial working group ballot with 651 comments.

The frame. Every 802.11 frame starts with a two-octet Frame Control field: a 2-bit protocol version, a 2-bit type (management, control, data or extension), a 4-bit subtype and eight flags: To DS and From DS (DS being the distribution system that joins access points to the wired network), More Fragments, Retry, Power Management, More Data, Protected and Order. A 2-octet Duration/ID field, three 6-octet addresses and a 2-octet Sequence Control field follow, with an optional fourth address: a header of 24 octets, or 30 with Address 4, plus 2 octets of QoS Control on QoS data frames. The frame body, the MAC service data unit (MSDU), carries up to 2,304 octets, extended to 7,920 for the 60 GHz directional multi-gigabit (DMG) physical layers of 802.11ad, and a 4-octet frame check sequence (FCS) closes the frame; the Linux kernel sizes the largest classic frame at 2,352 bytes, from a 30-byte header, 2 bytes of QoS Control, the 2,304-byte body, 12 bytes of encryption overhead and the FCS. A network name, the service set identifier (SSID), is at most 32 octets. Bridging between 802.11 and the other 802 LANs was the subject of 802.11c, a supplement to the MAC bridge standard later rolled into 802.11d, and on a host the adapter or its driver usually rewrites data frames with Ethernet headers before the operating system sees them.

Four addresses, not two. Ethernet needs a source and a destination; a wireless frame often crosses the air between two radios that are neither, so 802.11 also distinguishes the receiver address (RA) from the transmitter address (TA). The To DS and From DS bits say how to read the address fields, and the table in the Linux kernel's 802.11 header sets it out. With neither bit set (stations talking directly, in an independent basic service set or over direct link setup), Address 1 is the destination, Address 2 the source and Address 3 the basic service set identifier (BSSID). From an access point to a station (From DS), Address 1 is the destination, Address 2 the BSSID and Address 3 the original source. From a station towards the access point (To DS), Address 1 is the BSSID, Address 2 the source and Address 3 the final destination. With both bits set, as on a wireless distribution system link between access points, the four fields carry receiver, transmitter, destination and source. Wireshark accordingly has separate filter fields for wlan.ra and wlan.ta, for wlan.da and wlan.sa, and wlan.bssid for the cell.

How the MAC behaves. There are three frame types on the air. Management frames, in Cisco's description, let stations establish and maintain communications: the beacons an access point sends periodically to announce its presence, probe requests and responses, authentication and deauthentication, association and disassociation. Control frames assist delivery: request to send (RTS), clear to send (CTS) and acknowledgement (ACK). Data frames carry the payload from higher layers. A receiver that finds no errors returns an ACK, and a sender that gets none can retransmit, which is why every unicast exchange on the air costs at least two frames. Time in the MAC is counted in time units (TUs) of 1,024 microseconds, introduced with 802.11-1999, so beacon intervals and similar timers are set in TUs rather than milliseconds. In Wireshark the subtypes filter by number: wlan.fc.type_subtype == 0x08 for beacons, 0x04 for probe requests, 0x0b for authentication, 0x00 for association requests and 0x1d for acknowledgements.

Capturing it. An ordinary capture on a laptop shows little of this. The Wireshark project's capture guide explains that without monitor mode an adapter may deliver only data frames, with fake Ethernet headers in place of the 802.11 header and no radio information such as data rate or signal strength, and that promiscuous mode, possible in theory on many 802.11 adapters, often does not work in practice. Association, roaming and authentication problems are therefore diagnosed from a monitor-mode capture, where beacons, probes, retries and acknowledgements are visible, not from the client's own interface.

Reading device claims. Because one letter can mean throughput, security, roaming or positioning, a datasheet line such as 802.11a/b/g/n/ac/ax names the physical layers a radio supports and says nothing about k, r, v or w, which have to be checked on their own. And since 802.11bh standardized randomized and changing MAC addresses, a client's MAC address is no longer a dependable long-term identity for access lists or inventory. The numbers worth keeping are 1991 for the project, the editions of 1997, 1999, 2007, 2012, 2016, 2020 and 2024, one MAC over many PHYs, three frame types, up to four addresses, a 24- or 30-octet header, 2,304 octets of body, a 32-octet SSID and a 1,024-microsecond time unit.

ieee-802-1d.def: The IEEE standard for MAC bridges, which introduced the Spanning Tree Protocol.
ieee-802-1d.context: 802.1D is the document that makes an Ethernet network with redundant links survivable: without it a loop floods the segment until nothing passes. The original convergence behaviour was slow enough that it became its own class of outage, which is why 802.1w rapid reconvergence and later shortest-path bridging exist. Most engineers meet 802.1D through its failure mode rather than through its text.

six-ghz-wifi.def: The 5.925-7.125 GHz band opened to unlicensed Wi-Fi, roughly tripling the spectrum available to wireless LANs.
six-ghz-wifi.context: Regulators began releasing 6 GHz in 2020, and it carries far more non-overlapping wide channels than 2.4 or 5 GHz - the reason it is attractive in dense deployments. The trade-off is physics rather than protocol: higher frequencies attenuate faster and pass through walls less well, so coverage per access point falls even as capacity rises. Devices must also support it, which is what Wi-Fi 6E and later certifications indicate.

silent-failure.def: A fault that produces no error anywhere: the system completes its work, reports success, and does the wrong thing.
silent-failure.context: The defining property is not that the failure is small but that nothing in the system disagrees with it. An access point given a DHCP (Dynamic Host Configuration Protocol) option 43 value in another vendor's encoding completes its lease, reads a value it cannot parse, and never joins a controller. A firewall rule shadowed by a broader rule above it is correct, enabled, and never evaluated, and Palo Alto's own documentation notes that Commit and Push does not report shadowing. A security signature left in staging appears in the log, contributes to a request's rating, and blocks nothing. In each case the artefact everyone inspects looks right, because it is right; what changed is the thing reading it. The diagnostic cost is what makes the category worth naming: an error message points at itself, so the work is repair. A silent failure points at nothing, so the work is first proving which of the things that appear to be working actually is. Guardrails that only report problems are therefore weaker than they look, and a check that passes on an empty input, a missing file or an unparsed regex is itself a silent failure wearing a green tick.
silent-failure.depth:
What the term covers, and its neighbours. A silent failure is defined by the absence of disagreement, not by its size: every component that could complain is satisfied. That separates it from three things it is often confused with. A crash, a fail-stop failure in the vocabulary of the gray failure paper, announces itself by stopping. A gray failure, which has its own entry, is the case that Peng Huang and colleagues at Microsoft Research and Azure described in 2017 as differential observability: the system's failure detectors see health while the applications that use it suffer, so at least one observer knows. In a silent failure no observer knows until a person goes looking. And fail open against fail closed, also an entry of its own, is a design choice about what a control does when it breaks; a control that fails open without logging that it did so has turned that choice into a silent failure. The cases below share one mechanism: something reads a correct artefact under an assumption that no longer holds, and the protocol, product or check is built to tolerate rather than reject what it does not understand.

The standard that tells the receiver to stay quiet. RFC (Request for Comments) 2132 (March 1997, by Steve Alexander and Ralph Droms) defines DHCP (Dynamic Host Configuration Protocol) option 43 as an opaque object interpreted by vendor-specific code, with the vendor named elsewhere, in the vendor class identifier. Its rules for the unexpected are explicit: servers not equipped to interpret the vendor-specific information sent by a client must ignore it, and clients that do not receive the information they want should try to operate without it, possibly in a degraded mode. Both rules are sensible for interoperability, and together they guarantee that a wrongly encoded value is never rejected: the access point simply carries on without a controller address, as the entries on option 43 and its generator explain in detail.

Rules that are right and never reached. Palo Alto Networks' rulebase guidance, updated on 16 January 2026, defines shadowing as placing a broad rule with the same match criteria above a more specific one, so that traffic intended for the specific rule matches the general one first. Its example is a general rule blocking a social network placed above a rule allowing the marketing group to use it: the allow rule is valid, enabled and never matched. It adds a quieter cause, an address object that is named individually in one rule and also belongs to a group used in another. The detection is there but easy to miss: a commit on the firewall validates for shadow rules and raises a warning, the Rule Shadow tab of the Last Push State Details lists them, Commit and Push does not provide shadowing information, and the list is not persistent across commit operations, so the guide tells administrators to capture it by script, screenshot or even photograph. Any first-match rule base behaves the same way, which is why reading a rule in isolation proves nothing about whether it ever fires.

Controls that log but do not act. F5's documentation for BIG-IP Advanced WAF (web application firewall) version 17.5 states the staging rule plainly: entities and attack signatures in staging do not cause violations and consequently are not blocked, and a violation set to alarm or block on an entity in staging is not enforced. A policy can therefore be in blocking mode, the signature can match and be visible in the request log, and the attack still reaches the application. Staging exists for good reasons, to let a new signature prove it does not block legitimate traffic, but a signature that never leaves staging is a control that only appears to exist, and nothing on the dashboard will turn red to say so.

The network that eats the evidence. RFC 2923 (September 2000, by Kevin Lahey) catalogued the classic network case, the PMTUD (path maximum transmission unit discovery) black hole, described in the entry on that mechanism. A sender sets the Don't Fragment bit and relies on an ICMP (Internet Control Message Protocol) Fragmentation Needed message to learn that a packet is too large; firewalls, the RFC notes, are often misconfigured to suppress all ICMP, so the message never arrives and the sender keeps trying the same size. The RFC's own description of the symptom is the description of a silent failure: it is especially difficult to debug because pings and some interactive TCP connections work, while bulk transfers fail with the first large packet and the connection eventually times out. Its recommendation is telling: hosts that implement black hole detection should probably log the black holes they detect, so that someone can fix them.

Below the network: corruption nobody reports. In End-to-End Arguments in System Design, published in November 1984 as a revision of a 1981 conference paper, J. H. Saltzer, D. P. Reed and D. D. Clark of the Massachusetts Institute of Technology (MIT) told the too-real story behind their argument. A network of gateways checked a checksum on every hop, and application programmers assumed the network was therefore reliable; but data was unprotected while it sat in each gateway, one gateway developed a transient fault that swapped a byte pair about once in every million bytes, and operating system source files passed through it repeatedly were corrupted, until their owners had to compare them by hand with old listings. Four decades later the same pattern appears in silicon. Engineers at Meta reported in February 2021 that silent data corruptions are not captured by a processor's error reporting at all, propagate up the stack as application problems, can take months of debugging, and that running silent-error tests across hundreds of thousands of machines for more than 18 months had found hundreds of faulty CPUs (central processing units).

How to make the silence speak. Every remedy above has the same shape: a positive check, made by whoever cares about the result, that the intended effect actually happened. Saltzer, Reed and Clark's answer to the corrupting gateway was an end-to-end checksum compared by the two ends before the transfer is declared committed; Huang and colleagues argue for bridging the gap between what the system's detectors see and what applications measure end to end. Operationally that means sending test traffic a rule should block and confirming that it is blocked, confirming that an access point actually joined its controller rather than that it got a lease, moving staged signatures to enforcement on a schedule, capturing shadow lists before the next commit erases them, and giving every automated guard a known-bad sample it must reject, so that a guard that silently stopped testing fails loudly instead. When a silent failure is suspected, the first task is to establish which of the apparently healthy components is not, and bisection is usually the fastest way to do it: halve the space of things that appear to work until the one that does not is the only one left.

dongle.def: A small piece of hardware you plug into a port to make something work: originally to prove you had paid for software, now usually to give a machine back a capability it shipped without.
dongle.context: The object is ordinary; the word has a history. Its earliest print appearance is in Byte, October 1981, in a passage about software piracy in the United Kingdom, and the account that survives scrutiny traces it to Wordcraft 80, a word processor for Commodore hardware. In a 1982 letter to Personal Computer World, Mike Lake recalled Graham Heggie of Analog Electronics of Coventry asking what they were going to call this dongle thingy, and the name stuck to the thing before anyone agreed what the name meant. The likeliest derivation is simply dangle, because it hung off the back of the machine, and that is still not settled. What is settled is the invented origin: in 1992 Rainbow Technologies ran an advertisement attributing the word to a person named Don Gall. There was no such inventor. The claim was a marketing joke, and it has been repeated as fact ever since.
dongle.depth:
The early ones were pass-through devices on a parallel or serial port, sitting between the computer and the printer so the port still worked; the software refused to run unless it could interrogate the thing. Modern protection dongles are secure cryptoprocessors that hold keys and execute instructions rather than merely answering a challenge, which is a different security argument: the secret never has to be present in the software at all.

Then the meaning inverted. A dongle used to be what a vendor made you carry so their software would run. It is now what you carry so your own hardware will run: the Bluetooth adapter on a laptop whose radio was left out, the USB-C to everything-else adapter, the streaming stick. Same shape, same port, opposite purpose. The complaint changed from paying for permission to paying for the ports you used to have.

The Don Gall story is worth keeping for its own sake. A vendor printed a fabricated etymology in a trade magazine as a joke, and the joke outran the correction by decades, which is roughly what happens to every confident origin story nobody checks.

ascii.def: American Standard Code for Information Interchange (ASCII): the 7-bit character code that numbers 0 to 127 the English letters, the digits, punctuation and 33 control codes; the first 128 code points of Unicode.
ascii.context: Its 128 codes sit under almost everything a network engineer reads: Hypertext Transfer Protocol (HTTP) header fields, Simple Mail Transfer Protocol (SMTP) commands, host names in their ASCII form, configuration files. Seven bits leave no room for accented letters, which is why so many 8-bit charsets were built on top of it, and it survives inside UTF-8 byte for byte. RFC 20 (1969) reproduces the 1968 version of the standard, then called the USA Standard Code for Information Interchange. A browser told a page is in "ascii" reads windows-1252 instead.
ascii.depth:
What it is. ASCII (American Standard Code for Information Interchange) assigns a 7-bit number, 0 to 127, to each of 128 positions. Its table is eight columns of sixteen rows: columns 0 and 1 hold 32 control characters, column 2 begins with the space, and position 7/15, decimal 127, holds DEL, which brings the non-printing codes to 33 and leaves 95 graphic characters, the space included. The order was chosen with machines in mind. The Linux ascii(7) page points out that upper and lower case letters differ by a single bit, as do the digit 2 and the double quote, which made mechanical and simple electronic keyboards easier to build, and RFC (Request for Comments) 20 says that when characters are sorted, their sequence is simply their binary value. The standard was published in 1968 by the United States of America Standards Institute (USASI) as USAS X3.4-1968; the edition cited by later Internet standards is ANSI (American National Standards Institute) X3.4-1986.

ASCII on the network. On 16 October 1969 Vint Cerf, at UCLA (University of California, Los Angeles), proposed in RFC 20 that ARPANET hosts exchange standard 7-bit ASCII embedded in an 8-bit byte whose high-order bit is always 0, and attached the code table from USAS X3.4-1968. The same page already shows the line-ending problem: SRI (Stanford Research Institute) used a period as its end-of-line character and UCLA used carriage return, 0x0D. RFC 20 is now Internet Standard STD 80, and its rule of a 7-bit code in an octet with the top bit cleared is still how SMTP (Simple Mail Transfer Protocol) defines its commands and replies in RFC 5321, where every line ends with carriage return and line feed, 0D 0A.

The control characters. Most of the 32 controls were written for teleprinters and data links, not screens. RFC 20 groups them: communication controls such as SOH (Start of Heading), STX (Start of Text), ETX (End of Text), EOT (End of Transmission), ENQ (Enquiry), ACK (Acknowledge), NAK (Negative Acknowledge), SYN (Synchronous Idle) and DLE (Data Link Escape), the vocabulary of character-oriented link protocols; format effectors such as carriage return, line feed and horizontal tab; and four information separators, FS, GS, RS and US (file, group, record and unit separator), nested in that order. DEL was meant to obliterate unwanted characters punched in paper tape, and RFC 20 notes that in the strict sense it is not a control character at all. The ones that matter today are NUL, which C uses to end strings, tab, line feed and carriage return, and ESC (0x1B), which begins the escape sequences terminals use for colour and cursor movement.

National variants and the 8th bit. ASCII was American, and RFC 20 marks the positions that should not be used in international interchange without agreement between sender and recipient, among them the backslash, the square brackets, the vertical line, the circumflex, the grave accent and the tilde, and allows the pound sterling sign in place of the number sign at 2/3. Ecma International's ECMA-6, first published in April 1965 and in its sixth edition since December 1991, is the counterpart of ISO/IEC 646 (the International Organization for Standardization and the International Electrotechnical Commission): a 7-bit set with national options and an International Reference Version (IRV) in which those options are fixed, and ascii(7) calls ISO/IEC 646-IRV ASCII's international counterpart. Eight-bit sets such as ISO/IEC 8859-1 then kept ASCII as their lower half and used the upper 128 values for accented letters, one regional set at a time.

What "ascii" means to a browser. Because ISO/IEC 646 never mapped bytes 0x80 to 0xFF, software disagrees about them. The WHATWG (Web Hypertext Application Technology Working Group) Encoding Standard, which browsers implement, settles the question for the web: the labels ascii, us-ascii, ansi_x3.4-1968, latin1 and iso-8859-1 all mean windows-1252, a superset of both, so a browser decodes byte 0x80 as the euro sign, U+20AC. Other libraries reject such bytes or map them differently, which is how one log line renders differently in two tools.

Inside Unicode and UTF-8. Unicode's first 128 code points, U+0000 to U+007F, are ASCII, and UTF-8 (the 8-bit Unicode Transformation Format) keeps them as the same single bytes, 00 to 7F. RFC 3629 adds the property that makes this safe: any octet with an ASCII value stands only for that ASCII character and never appears inside a longer sequence, so a parser that splits on spaces, colons or line ends works unchanged on UTF-8 text. RFC 5198 of March 2008 formalized the move, replacing the old Network Virtual Terminal assumption of ASCII text with Net-Unicode: UTF-8, normalized, with CRLF line endings.

Where it still rules. HTTP (Hypertext Transfer Protocol) field values, says RFC 9110, are usually constrained to US-ASCII, and newly defined fields should use only visible US-ASCII characters, space and horizontal tab. Domain name labels in the traditional form are LDH (letters, digits, hyphen) labels of ASCII letters, digits and hyphens, at most 63 octets, and an internationalized name travels in DNS (Domain Name System) as an A-label that begins xn-- and carries Punycode, which is what a host name in its ASCII form means. Command-line interfaces, configuration files, syslog and most wire protocols' keywords are ASCII for the same reason: it is the one character set every system agrees on.

unicode.def: The standard that gives every character of every writing system a number, a name and a set of properties; version 18.0 counts 172,808 characters.
unicode.context: Unicode is the catalogue, not the bytes: a code point such as U+00E9 becomes bytes only through an encoding form, almost always UTF-8 (the 8-bit Unicode Transformation Format). Most text bugs a network engineer meets live in the gap between the two: lengths counted in different units, characters that draw as nothing, letters from another script that look identical, and bytes read in the wrong charset. Each version adds characters, so software with older data may not know a character that newer text contains.
unicode.depth:
What it defines. Unicode assigns code points, integers in a codespace that runs from 0 to 10FFFF in hexadecimal, written U+0000 to U+10FFFF. The codespace is divided into 17 planes of 65,536 code points each, numbered 0 to 16, which makes 1,114,112 code points in all; Plane 0, the Basic Multilingual Plane (BMP), covers U+0000 to U+FFFF, and Planes 1 to 16 are the supplementary planes. The block U+D800 to U+DFFF is set aside as surrogate code points for UTF-16, the 16-bit Unicode Transformation Format, and never holds a character, so the values a text can actually contain, the Unicode scalar values, are everything else. Beyond the numbers, the standard gives each character a name and properties such as its script, its general category, its case mappings and how it combines with its neighbours, published as the Unicode Character Database, plus algorithms for sorting, line breaking, bidirectional display and normalization. How the numbers become bytes is a separate layer: the glossary lists seven character encoding schemes, UTF-8 (the 8-bit form), UTF-16 in big-endian, little-endian and marked forms, and the same three for UTF-32.

Where it came from. The Consortium's own history says Unicode began in late 1987 in discussions among Joe Becker, Lee Collins and Mark Davis, engineers at Xerox and Apple, and that the name stood for three goals: universal, uniform and unique. The first design was a fixed-width 16-bit code, and when Unicode, Inc. was incorporated in California on 3 January 1991 its stated purpose was a 16-bit encoding for over 60,000 graphic characters. Unicode 1.0 followed in October 1991. The same year the working group of ISO (the International Organization for Standardization) and IEC (the International Electrotechnical Commission) responsible for ISO/IEC 10646 and the Consortium agreed to maintain one universal standard, and the two have kept their character codes and encoding forms synchronized since; Unicode adds the properties, algorithms and implementation rules that ISO/IEC 10646 does not carry. Sixteen bits did not last: the codespace now reaches U+10FFFF, which is why UTF-16 needs surrogate pairs and why the old fixed-width idea survives only in UTF-32.

Versions and stability. Unicode 2.0 appeared in July 1996, 3.1 in March 2001, 6.0 in October 2010, and Unicode 18.0, dated 16 September 2026, added 13,007 characters for a total of 172,808, including three new scripts, Proto-Cuneiform, Jurchen and Seal. Five technical standards move in step with each version, among them UTS (Unicode Technical Standard) #39 on security mechanisms and UTS #46 on compatibility processing for internationalized domain names. What makes the growth safe to depend on is the stability policy: since Unicode 2.0 an encoded character is never moved or removed, and its name is never changed, and since 4.1 a string normalized under one version stays identical when normalized under any later one. A newer version can only add, which is also why a device or library with old data shows a character it does not know as a box or a question mark.

One text, several spellings. Different code point sequences can mean the same thing. Unicode Standard Annex #15 defines canonical equivalence, where sequences represent the same abstract character and should look and behave the same, such as a precomposed C with cedilla and a plain C followed by a combining cedilla, or the ohm sign and the Greek capital omega; and compatibility equivalence, a weaker relation between forms that mean the same but may look different. Four normalization forms follow: NFD and NFC (Normalization Forms D and C), which decompose or compose by canonical equivalence, and NFKD and NFKC, which also fold compatibility variants. Comparing two strings that have not been normalized the same way is how one user name becomes two accounts, and how a filter that checks one form misses an attack sent in another.

Lookalikes and invisible controls. A character set this large contains many letters that look alike across scripts, and UTS #39 exists, in its own words, because incorrect usage can expose programs or systems to security attacks. It defines single-script, mixed-script and whole-script confusables and a skeleton function: two strings are confusable when their skeletons are equal, which is the basis for flagging a domain name spelled with a Cyrillic letter that looks Latin. Display order is a second channel. CVE-2021-42574 (Common Vulnerabilities and Exposures), published on 1 November 2021 and known as Trojan Source after the University of Cambridge work by Nicholas Boucher and Ross Anderson, showed that bidirectional control characters placed in comments and strings can make source code display in an order different from the one a compiler reads, so a reviewer approves logic that is not the logic that runs; a homoglyph variant is tracked as CVE-2021-42694. The Consortium's response points to its security considerations report, to UTS #39 and to the identifier rules of UAX (Unicode Standard Annex) #31.

Where engineers meet it. Every layer that handles names or text inherits these rules. Internationalized domain names reach the DNS (Domain Name System) as A-labels that begin with xn-- and carry Punycode, so the same host has a Unicode form for people and an ASCII (American Standard Code for Information Interchange) form for the wire. Lengths depend on the unit: the Unicode Consortium notes that Java and Windows use UTF-16 internally, where a supplementary-plane character such as most emoji counts as two code units, UTF-8 counts bytes, and what a user sees as one character can be several code points forming one grapheme cluster. Firewalls, web application firewalls and log pipelines that inspect text have to decide which form they compare, and the safe default is to decode strictly, normalize once, check for mixed scripts and invisible controls in identifiers, and only then match.

utf-8.def: UTF-8 (Unicode Transformation Format, 8-bit): the encoding that writes each Unicode code point as one to four bytes and keeps ASCII (American Standard Code for Information Interchange) as single bytes; the encoding the web requires.
utf-8.context: Its design is why it won: ASCII (American Standard Code for Information Interchange) text is already valid UTF-8, no byte of a longer character falls in the ASCII range, and the first byte of each character says how long it is, so a reader can find its place anywhere in a stream. Its byte patterns are strict too: C0, C1 and F5 to FF never appear, and a decoder that meets ill-formed bytes replaces them with U+FFFD instead of guessing. Text that shows Ã© where é belongs is UTF-8 read in the wrong charset.
utf-8.depth:
What it is, exactly. UTF-8 is an encoding form: it turns Unicode character numbers, the code points from U+0000 to U+10FFFF, into octets, and nothing more. RFC (Request for Comments) 3629, published in November 2003 as Internet Standard STD 63, gives the whole scheme in four rows. U+0000 to U+007F take one octet, 0xxxxxxx; U+0080 to U+07FF take two, 110xxxxx 10xxxxxx; U+0800 to U+FFFF take three, 1110xxxx followed by two 10xxxxxx; and U+10000 to U+10FFFF take four, 11110xxx followed by three continuation octets. The rows are mutually exclusive, so each character has exactly one valid encoding. The RFC's own examples show the result: the four characters A, not-identical-to, capital alpha and full stop become 41 E2 89 A2 CE 91 2E; and the three Korean syllables of hangugeo take nine octets. By the same table, é, U+00E9, becomes C3 A9. UTF-8 is not Unicode, which is the catalogue of characters, and it is not a byte-for-byte charset like Latin-1: above 0x7F every character costs at least two bytes.

Why the design works. RFC 3629 lists the properties. Code points U+0000 to U+007F are the ASCII (American Standard Code for Information Interchange) octets 00 to 7F, so plain ASCII is already valid UTF-8, and those octet values never appear inside a longer sequence, so file systems, C's printf and any protocol that splits on spaces, colons, slashes or line ends keep working. The first octet of a sequence states its length, continuation octets always begin with the bits 10, and character boundaries can therefore be found from anywhere in a stream. The octets C0, C1 and F5 to FF never occur. Sorting UTF-8 strings byte by byte gives the same order as sorting by code point, which the RFC itself calls of limited interest because code point order is almost never culturally valid. The surrogate range U+D800 to U+DFFF, reserved for UTF-16, the 16-bit Unicode Transformation Format, may not be encoded at all.

Who designed it. Rob Pike's account is that Ken Thompson worked out the bit-packing on a placemat in a New Jersey diner one night around September 1992, after IBM and X/Open contacts asked the two of them to review a proposal called FSS/UTF. Plan 9 had been using ISO 10646's original UTF and its developers disliked it; Pike's list of requirements included resynchronizing a byte stream picked up mid-run while losing less than one character, which FSS/UTF lacked. Thompson wrote the packing code that night, Pike converted the C and graphics libraries, and within days Plan 9 ran on nothing else; Thompson mailed the modified FSS-UTF proposal on 8 September 1992. The two described the conversion at the Winter 1993 USENIX conference in San Diego. Pike also wrote that the story that IBM designed it and Plan 9 merely implemented it probably began with RFC 2279.

From RFC 2279 to the web's only encoding. RFC 3629 obsoleted RFC 2279 and changed it in ways that matter to implementers: it restricted the range to U+10FFFF, the space UTF-16 can reach, where ISO/IEC 10646's description had allowed values up to U+7FFFFFFF in sequences of five and six bytes; it made Unicode the normative source; and it turned the old advice against decoding invalid sequences into a firm must not. The IETF (Internet Engineering Task Force) had already set its policy in RFC 2277 of January 1998: every protocol must identify the charset of its text and must be able to use UTF-8. The WHATWG (Web Hypertext Application Technology Working Group) Encoding Standard, which browsers implement, now calls UTF-8 the most appropriate encoding for interchange of Unicode and requires authors and all new protocols and formats to use it, and W3Techs measured it on 99.1 per cent of websites with a known encoding in November 2026. Operating systems split along older lines: the Unicode Consortium notes that Java and Windows use UTF-16 internally, while Linux and Unix systems use UTF-8, which is why Python 3.15 made UTF-8 its default encoding for files and pipes and why that change mostly affects Windows.

What goes wrong. Strictness is a security property. RFC 3629 warns of a parser that blocks NUL as the byte 00 but accepts the illegal two-byte form C0 80, or blocks /../ as 2F 2E 2E 2F but accepts 2F C0 AE 2E 2F, and notes that this last trick was used by a widespread virus attacking web servers in 2001; CVE-2000-0884, the IIS (Internet Information Services) 4.0 and 5.0 Web Server Folder Traversal flaw, let attackers read files outside the web root through malformed URLs (Uniform Resource Locators) containing Unicode-encoded characters. The same RFC warns that a decoder that does not cap the range at U+10FFFF must size its buffers for the old five- and six-byte forms. The Unicode Consortium's rule is that a conformant process must not interpret ill-formed sequences as characters, though it may substitute U+FFFD, and the WHATWG decoder enforces exact byte ranges: after E0 the next byte must be A0 to BF, after ED 80 to 9F, which excludes the surrogates, after F0 90 to BF and after F4 80 to 8F. It also forbids an error from swallowing a following ASCII byte, after a real case in which a bad lead byte ate the quotation mark that closed a JSON (JavaScript Object Notation) string.

The byte order mark and mojibake. U+FEFF, zero width no-break space, serves as a byte order mark (BOM) in UTF-16 and UTF-32; in UTF-8 it always appears as EF BB BF and says nothing about byte order, because UTF-8 has none. RFC 3629 allows it as a signature at the start of a stream but advises against stripping it without good reason, and browsers let a BOM override a declared label. Tools that do not expect it show three stray bytes, or ï»¿ when the file is read as windows-1252. The everyday failure is the same misreading in reverse: é stored as C3 A9 and decoded as windows-1252 prints as Ã©, while Latin-1 bytes decoded as UTF-8 turn into U+FFFD replacement characters. Lengths differ too: an HTTP (Hypertext Transfer Protocol) Content-Length or a 63-octet DNS (Domain Name System) label counts bytes, not characters, and one accented letter counts two.

byte-order-mark.def: U+FEFF at the very start of a text: in UTF-16 and UTF-32 (the 16-bit and 32-bit Unicode Transformation Formats) it says which byte order the text uses, and in UTF-8 it serves only as a signature that the text is UTF-8.
byte-order-mark.context: In UTF-16 (16-bit Unicode Transformation Format) it reads FE FF in big-endian order and FF FE in little-endian; in UTF-8 it is EF BB BF and says nothing about byte order, only that the text is very probably UTF-8. A browser trusts it over any charset label. Elsewhere it is often unwelcome: it is invisible in most editors, RFC (Request for Comments) 8259 forbids adding one to JSON (JavaScript Object Notation) sent over a network, and a parser that does not expect one sees an extra character (JavaScript's JSON.parse rejects a text that starts with one).
byte-order-mark.depth:
The byte order mark (BOM) is not a special code but an ordinary character put to a second use. Code point U+FEFF is named ZERO WIDTH NO-BREAK SPACE, and RFC (Request for Comments) 3629, the UTF-8 (8-bit Unicode Transformation Format) specification of November 2003, explains the nickname: prepended to a stream of characters it acts as a signature, telling a receiver that the stream is Unicode, which encoding form it uses and, for encodings with units longer than one byte, in which order the bytes of each unit are serialized. The Unicode Consortium's FAQ (frequently asked questions) on the subject gives the five byte patterns to recognize: 00 00 FE FF for UTF-32 big-endian, FF FE 00 00 for UTF-32 little-endian, FE FF for UTF-16 big-endian, FF FE for UTF-16 little-endian and EF BB BF for UTF-8. The trick that makes it work for byte order is that the swapped value, U+FFFE, is a noncharacter that should never occur in text, so a receiver that reads FF FE where it expected FE FF knows it must reverse each pair of bytes.

One character doing two jobs created an ambiguity that the standards have been closing ever since. In the middle of a text U+FEFF is a zero-width no-break space, and RFC 3629 says that anywhere other than the beginning of a stream it must be interpreted with those semantics and must not be taken as a signature. At the very start it may be either. Unicode 3.2 added U+2060 WORD JOINER, with the same joining behaviour and no signature role, and recommended it for all word joining, so that an initial U+FEFF can eventually be read as a BOM with confidence; the FAQ repeats that a U+FEFF found mid-text should be treated as a zero-width no-break space and is part of the content. RFC 3629 also warns against stripping an initial signature without good reason, because a process at another layer, such as a digital signature or a character count, may depend on every character being present, and against leaving it when strings are concatenated, because the join then contains an invisible character.

Labels and the mark are meant to be alternatives. When text is labelled UTF-16BE, UTF-16LE, UTF-32BE or UTF-32LE, the FAQ says a BOM is neither necessary nor permitted, and any U+FEFF is content. Text labelled simply UTF-16 may carry one: RFC 2781 (February 2000) says that if it begins FE FF it can be read as big-endian, if FF FE as little-endian, and otherwise it should be read as big-endian, the same default the FAQ gives for plain Unicode text of unknown byte order. Databases and fields with a declared type need no mark at all, and the FAQ points out a quieter cost of adding one anyway: two fields with exactly the same visible content are no longer binary-equal when only one starts with a BOM.

UTF-8 has no byte order to declare, since its unit is a single byte, so there the mark is purely a signature, and that is where most trouble comes from. The FAQ notes that some recipients of UTF-8 do not expect it and that it interferes with any protocol or file format that expects specific ASCII (American Standard Code for Information Interchange) characters at the beginning, its example being the #! line of a Unix shell script, which no longer starts with #! once three bytes precede it. RFC 3629 tells protocol designers to forbid the signature for elements they already mandate to be UTF-8. Python's documentation records the origin of the habit: Microsoft adopted the UTF-8 signature for Notepad, which Python supports as the utf-8-sig codec, writing the three bytes on encoding and skipping them on decoding, while adding that in UTF-8 the BOM is discouraged and should generally be avoided. It also explains the classic symptom: read as ISO-8859-1, the bytes EF BB BF appear as the three characters small i with diaeresis, right-pointing double angle quotation mark and inverted question mark, the stray marks at the top of a badly decoded file.

Browsers give the mark the last word. The WHATWG (Web Hypertext Application Technology Working Group) Encoding Standard, last updated on 19 October 2026, decodes every resource by first sniffing up to three bytes: EF BB BF selects UTF-8, FE FF UTF-16BE and FF FE UTF-16LE, and the bytes are then consumed. For compatibility with deployed content the standard makes the BOM more authoritative than anything else, and admits that where HTTP (Hypertext Transfer Protocol) is used this violates the semantics of the Content-Type header, so a page served as one charset but starting with a BOM is decoded by the BOM. The table has no UTF-32 entry, so a file beginning FF FE 00 00 is taken for UTF-16LE. For other standards the same document distinguishes UTF-8 decode, which removes a leading BOM and is meant for new formats, from UTF-8 decode without BOM, meant for identifiers and protocol byte sequences.

JSON (JavaScript Object Notation) is where the mark most often breaks an integration. RFC 8259 (December 2017), section 8.1, requires JSON exchanged outside a closed ecosystem to be UTF-8, forbids implementations to add a byte order mark to a JSON text transmitted over a network, and allows parsers to ignore one rather than treat it as an error. Ignoring is optional, and JavaScript does not do it in JSON.parse: the ECMAScript specification requires the function to accept exactly the format of ECMA-404, without extensions, and to throw a SyntaxError for any text that is not valid JSON, while JSON's grammar allows only space, horizontal tab, line feed and carriage return as whitespace. A file saved with a BOM and read into a string intact therefore fails to parse in JavaScript and may parse elsewhere, which is exactly the kind of difference that survives testing.

On the engineer's workstation the mark usually arrives from a Windows tool. Microsoft's PowerShell documentation states that Windows PowerShell writes a BOM with any Unicode encoding except UTF-7, while PowerShell 6 and later default to UTF-8 without one; that Windows PowerShell reads a BOM-less script containing non-ASCII characters in the legacy code page that Windows calls ANSI (after the American National Standards Institute), so such scripts need the BOM there; and that files with the UTF-8 BOM are problematic on Unix-like platforms, where cat, sed, awk and some editors do not know how to treat it. Its advice for compatibility is to avoid BOMs in UTF-8 files. The practical consequences for network and security work are configuration snippets, CSV (comma-separated values) imports, certificates, YAML (YAML Ain't Markup Language) files and scripts that move between a Windows desktop and a Linux host or an appliance: a first line that does not match, a header field whose name has an invisible prefix, or two values that look identical and compare unequal. A hex dump of the first bytes settles the question at once, and a BOM-aware decoder such as Python's utf-8-sig removes the mark cleanly when it is not wanted.

mojibake.def: Garbled text produced when bytes written in one charset are read in another: café shown as cafÃ©, don’t as donâ€™t.
mojibake.context: It is almost never random. Each pair of charsets garbles in its own recognizable way: UTF-8 read as windows-1252 fills a text with Ã and â€, a DOS code page shows box-drawing characters, EBCDIC read as Latin-1 turns every space into @. Because the wrong reading usually keeps every byte, the damage can often be undone by encoding the text back with the charset that misread it and decoding it with the right one; a byte that was replaced with ? or dropped is gone for good.

easter-egg-header.def: A response header that carries a tribute, a joke or an invitation, placed where only people who read headers will find it.
easter-egg-header.context: HTTP lets a server send any header it likes, and a name beginning with X- was for decades the convention for a private one. Operators have used that freedom for things that are not protocol: Slashdot answered every request with a Futurama quote, Automattic hid a job offer, Airbnb's infrastructure team said hello, and after Terry Pratchett died in 2015 thousands of sites began sending his name in the overhead. None of it changes what the page does; all of it is found with one curl -I. The genre has three rules its best examples keep: it costs the reader nothing, it is true (a real invitation, a real tribute), and it is addressed to the people who would look.

x-clacks-overhead.def: The HTTP header thousands of sites send in Terry Pratchett's memory: X-Clacks-Overhead: GNU Terry Pratchett.
x-clacks-overhead.context: In Pratchett's Going Postal the clacks are semaphore towers that relay messages across the Discworld, and a message's overhead can carry control codes: G, send it on to the next tower; N, do not log it; U, at the end of the line, turn it around and send it back. A name sent with GNU circulates forever, because, as the book has it, a man is not dead while his name is still spoken. When Pratchett died on 12 March 2015, readers on r/discworld proposed putting his name in the one overhead the internet has, and within days Apache and Nginx snippets, a WordPress plugin and a Chrome extension that lights up when the header is present were in circulation. The header is still sent by a great many servers, and this one is among them.
x-clacks-overhead.depth: The clacks of the Discworld novels are an optical telegraph: towers with shuttered lamps, each repeating what the previous one showed, so that a message crosses a continent in hours. In Going Postal (2004) the system has grown its own culture, including the overhead, the housekeeping codes sent along with the traffic. Three of them matter to the memorial. G tells a tower to pass the message on. N tells it not to log the message. U tells the tower at the end of the line to turn the message around and send it back the way it came. A name sent with all three never stops moving through the towers and is never written down, which is how the clacks operators keep a dead colleague's name alive: the book's line is that a man is not dead while his name is still spoken. Terry Pratchett died on 12 March 2015. Within days, readers on the Discworld subreddit asked what the internet's overhead would be, and settled on an HTTP response header, which is exactly a piece of housekeeping sent along with the traffic and seen only by the machines and the people who look. The name X-Clacks-Overhead follows the X- convention for private headers of the time; the value is GNU Terry Pratchett. Configuration snippets for Apache (a Header set line) and Nginx (add_header) appeared on 15 March 2015, then a WordPress plugin, then browser extensions that show a small marker when a site sends it. Reddit itself added it.
