The L-Space wiki, the Discworld fan encyclopaedia, lists later adopters, among them Minecraft, which carries GNU Terry Pratchett as splash text number 338 from Java Edition 1.8.5. The header does nothing. Browsers ignore it; caches pass it through; it adds a few dozen bytes to every response. That is the point: a tribute that costs the reader nothing and is found only by someone who went looking, which is the shape of the best things in this corner of the web, and the reason it is the model for the other hidden headers in this glossary.

x-fry-x-bender.def: Slashdot's response headers carrying a random Futurama quote, named for the characters who said it.
x-fry-x-bender.context: For years every response from slashdot.org included one extra header, X-Fry, X-Bender or X-Lrrr, whose value was a line from Futurama chosen at random per request. Nothing read it but the people who ran curl -I against the site, which on Slashdot was a fair share of the readership. It is the purest form of the easter egg header: no purpose, no recruitment, a joke addressed to exactly the audience that would get it. The How-To Geek write-up that catalogued hidden headers used it as the opening example, and a commandlinefu one-liner existed solely to fetch a fresh quote.

x-hacker.def: Automattic's recruiting header on WordPress.com and its VIP-hosted sites: an invitation to apply, for whoever is reading the headers.
x-hacker.context: Responses from Automattic's platforms have carried an X-hacker header in several wordings over the years, the best known being an invitation to visit the company's jobs page and apply to join the fun, mentioning this header, and the shorter Want root? Visit join.a8c.com and mention this header. The logic is sound: a person inspecting response headers of a blog platform is a person the platform might want to hire, and mention this header makes the candidate's path traceable. Wikimedia's engineers noticed it on blog.wikimedia.org, which was hosted on WordPress VIP, and filed a ticket about it. The same company's page cache announces itself with a sillier header, x-nananana.

x-hi-human.def: Airbnb's response header greeting whoever reads it, with a hiring address from the Production Infrastructure team.
x-hi-human.context: Troy Hunt's March 2015 survey of recruitment messages hidden in sites found Airbnb answering with X-Hi-Human: The Production Infrastructure team added this header. Come work with us!, followed by an engineer's hiring address. It sits with X-hacker in the recruiting branch of the genre, and it is the friendlier of the two: a greeting first, the offer second. Hunt's point in collecting them was that the people who deconstruct a site to see how it is built are precisely the people worth reaching, and a header reaches them at the moment they are paying attention.

x-nananana-batcache.def: The header Batcache, Automattic's WordPress page cache, uses to say a page came from the cache, named with the Batman theme.
x-nananana-batcache.context: Batcache is a memcached-backed full-page cache for WordPress, written at Automattic and used on WordPress.com and the hosts built on its stack. Its source opens with the comment nananananananananananananananana BATCACHE!!!, and the production deployments answer with a header named x-nananana whose value reports the cache state, Batcache-Hit when the page was served from the cache. Pressable's documentation tells customers to look for exactly that header to confirm the cache is working. It is a diagnostic header that happens to be a joke, which is the rarest and best kind: it earns its place in the response and smiles while it does.

http-451-unavailable-for-legal-reasons.def: The HTTP status code for a resource withheld because of a legal demand, numbered after Fahrenheit 451.
http-451-unavailable-for-legal-reasons.context: RFC 7725, published in February 2016 and written by Tim Bray, defines status code 451 for use when resource access is denied as a consequence of legal demands, so that a block ordered by a court or a government is distinguishable from an ordinary 403. The number is a literary choice: Ray Bradbury's Fahrenheit 451 is the novel about burning books, and the RFC's acknowledgements end with Thanks also to Ray Bradbury. Unlike 418 it is a real, standards-track code with a real job, which is why it is listed as a term and not as lore; it belongs with the hidden messages because the nod is deliberate and written into the document itself.

qradar.def: The security intelligence platform Q1 Labs built in Fredericton, sold to IBM in 2011, and split in 2024 between IBM, which kept the on-premises product, and Palo Alto Networks, which bought the SaaS version.
qradar.context: QRadar began as the product of Q1 Labs, a 2001 spinout from the University of New Brunswick that had moved to Waltham, Massachusetts by 2011. The trade press of the day described it as log, threat and compliance management with flow and event processors that read network and security events and application flow data: in later vocabulary, a SIEM with a strong flow side, sold to 1,800 clients. IBM announced the purchase on 4 October 2011, closed it on 26 October and made Q1 Labs' chief executive the general manager of a new Security Systems division. On 4 September 2024 Palo Alto Networks completed its acquisition of the QRadar SaaS assets, offering free migration to Cortex XSIAM, while QRadar on premises stayed with IBM and keeps receiving its features and fixes. One product name, two owners, two roads.
qradar.depth:
What the product did, in the words of 2011. TechCrunch described Q1 Labs' QRadar as log, threat and compliance management solutions, with flow and event processors for processing network and security events and network and application flow data. That sentence is a fair summary of what a security information and event management system was expected to do then and still is: collect logs from everything, normalize them, correlate events across sources, and raise the ones that matter as offences for an analyst. The flow side was QRadar's distinguishing habit, because Q1 Labs had come at the problem from network behaviour rather than from the log archive, and the product kept a native view of who talked to whom alongside the event stream.

The company. Q1 Labs was founded in Fredericton, New Brunswick, in 2001 as a spinout from the University of New Brunswick; by the time of the sale it was based in Waltham, Massachusetts, with a strong presence still in Fredericton. IBM announced the acquisition on 4 October 2011 with financial terms undisclosed and closed it on 26 October 2011; Brendan Hannigan, Q1 Labs' chief executive, became general manager of IBM's newly formed Security Systems Division. Buying a company to found a division is a different act from buying a product to fill a gap, and the division's name told the market which it was.

The split. On 4 September 2024 Palo Alto Networks announced from Santa Clara that it had completed the acquisition of IBM's QRadar Software as a Service assets. The release draws the line precisely: QRadar clients who wish to remain on QRadar on premises continue to receive IBM features and support, including security, usability and critical bug fixes, updates to existing connectors and the ability to expand consumption; eligible SaaS customers are offered free migration services, with IBM Consulting, to the Cortex XSIAM platform; and IBM acts as a preferred managed security services provider for the shift. Read practically, the cloud product became an on-ramp into a competitor's platform and the on-premises product became an installed base in maintenance.

Why it is on this glossary. The author's generation of network engineers met QRadar as the console into which their firewall and switch logs disappeared, and the one that produced the offence ticket at three in the morning. Knowing which owner now holds which half matters when a customer asks what to do with a QRadar estate, and the answer differs for the two halves. The companion record on the industry timeline carries the sources and dates.

tamograph.def: TamoSoft's Wi-Fi planning and site survey software, which performs passive, active and predictive surveys on Windows and macOS, from a privately held Christchurch company founded in 1998.
tamograph.context: TamoGraph Site Survey is one of the three survey tools a wireless engineer is likely to carry, beside Ekahau's and the MetaGeek line now at Oscium. TamoSoft describes it as Wi-Fi planning and site survey software that helps you create and maintain reliable networks, with passive, active and predictive surveys, the last also called RF modelling, and full support of 802.11be (Wi-Fi 7), 802.11ax (Wi-Fi 6 and 6E) and 802.11ac as well as the legacy standards. It runs on Windows 10, 11 and Server 2016 to 2022 and on macOS from Monterey to Tahoe. The company behind it, TamoSoft Ltd, was founded in 1998, is privately held, is headquartered in Christchurch, New Zealand, and serves customers in over 100 countries with a wired and a wireless packet analyser, a private LTE and 5G planning tool and a throughput tester beside the survey product.
tamograph.depth:
The three survey types, in TamoSoft's own vocabulary. A passive survey listens: the engineer walks the floor plan and the software records what every access point's beacons look like from each point, signal, noise, channel, interference. An active survey connects: it associates to the network under test and measures what a client actually gets, throughput and round trips, at each point. A predictive survey, which the product also calls RF modelling, needs no walking at all: it draws the building's walls and materials, places virtual access points and computes the expected coverage, so a design can be argued about before anybody buys hardware. Most real projects use all three in order, predict, install, verify.

Standards and platforms. The product page lists full support of 802.11be, which is Wi-Fi 7, 802.11ax, which is Wi-Fi 6 and 6E, and 802.11ac, Wi-Fi 5, plus the legacy standards. It is available for Windows and for macOS; the Windows requirement is Windows 10, 11, Server 2016, 2019 or 2022, the macOS requirement Monterey, Ventura, Sonoma, Sequoia or Tahoe. The video tour on the page refers to TamoGraph 4.0.

The company. TamoSoft Ltd is, in its own words, a privately held company with headquarters in Christchurch, New Zealand, founded in 1998, with customers from over 100 countries. Its about page describes the catalogue without naming the products: a wireless site survey and RF modelling tool, a network monitor and packet analyser for wired networks, another for wireless 802.11 a/b/g/n/ac/ax/be networks, a design and planning tool for 4G LTE and 5G NR private cellular networks, and a utility for testing wireless or wired network performance.

Where it sits. Of the three survey tools on this site, Ekahau began as a University of Helsinki research group and now belongs to Ookla and, through it, Accenture; the MetaGeek tools began as a Boise side project and have had two owners since 2022; TamoGraph is the one whose company has stayed where it started. The industry record carries the dates for all three.

hp-openview.def: The former name of Hewlett-Packard's network and systems management family, built on Network Node Manager, an SNMP network monitor; rebranded HP BTO Software in 2007 and sold with HP Software to Micro Focus in 2017.
hp-openview.context: For twenty years HP OpenView was what a large enterprise meant by network management. Its foundational product was Network Node Manager, network monitoring software based on SNMP that discovered a network and drew its map, used on its own or with other management software such as CiscoWorks; around it HP assembled a family of modules and third-party products in a common framework. The family grew by acquisition, Novadigm and its Radia suite in April 2004, Peregrine Systems' IT asset and service management in December 2005, Mercury Interactive in November 2006, Opsware, and in early 2007 HP rebranded the whole line HP BTO (Business Technology Optimisation) Software under its HP Software Division; the OpenView and Mercury names were phased out. HP Software passed to Hewlett Packard Enterprise at the 2015 split and was sold to Micro Focus in a merger completed on 1 September 2017. The name survives in the vocabulary of everyone who ran a network operations centre before 2007.
hp-openview.depth:
What the name covered. HP OpenView was the former name for a Hewlett-Packard product family that consisted of network and systems management products. It provided large-scale system and network management of an organization's IT infrastructure, with optional modules from HP and third-party management software connecting within a common framework. The product at the base was Network Node Manager, NNM, which polled devices over SNMP, the Simple Network Management Protocol, discovered how they were connected and presented the result as a map with status colours. Everything the operations centre did, alarms, trend graphs, escalation, hung off that map.

The acquisitions that made it a suite. In April 2004 HP bought Novadigm and its Radia suite; in December 2005 it acquired Peregrine Systems, whose IT asset and service management software was integrated into OpenView; in November 2006 it completed the purchase of Mercury Interactive and integrated its applications; Opsware followed. Each purchase widened the family from the network towards the service desk, the application and the data centre, which is the same path every management vendor walked in those years.

The end of the name. In early 2007, alongside the integration of the Mercury, Peregrine and Opsware products, the OpenView products were rebranded under the HP Software Division as HP BTO Software, and the OpenView and Mercury names were phased out; HP OpenCall kept its name. HP Software became part of Hewlett Packard Enterprise after the 2015 split of Hewlett-Packard, and HPE Software was sold to Micro Focus, the merger completing on 1 September 2017. The article this entry rests on does not give a launch year for OpenView, so none is stated here.

Why it still matters. The division of labour OpenView taught, discovery, polling, event correlation, trend collection, a map as the operator's primary instrument, is the division of labour the open source monitors on this glossary (Nagios, Zabbix, OpenNMS) and the commercial ones (PRTG, SolarWinds Orion) inherited, usually at a fraction of the price and without the framework. When an engineer who learned on NNM says the new tool has no map, this is what they mean.

solarwinds-orion.def: SolarWinds' self-hosted monitoring platform, the base for Network Performance Monitor and its sibling modules, and the software whose signed updates carried the SUNBURST backdoor in 2020; its modules now run on the renamed SolarWinds Platform.
solarwinds-orion.context: SolarWinds describes the Orion Platform, in the past tense, as a comprehensive, scalable infrastructure monitoring and management platform designed for the era of network and infrastructure monitoring modules and restricted to self-hosted deployment; its modules, Network Performance Monitor, NetFlow Traffic Analyzer, Network Configuration Manager, IP Address Manager, Server & Application Monitor, Virtualization Manager, Storage Resource Monitor and Web Performance Monitor, are now self-hosted on the SolarWinds Platform, which the company calls a new, more expansive platform built with Secure by Design principles. The reason the old name is known far outside network operations is SUNBURST: on 13 December 2020 FireEye disclosed that trojanized Orion updates, digitally signed by SolarWinds, carried a backdoor in SolarWinds.Orion.Core.BusinessLayer.dll, and the same day CISA's Emergency Directive 21-01 ordered federal agencies to disconnect or power down Orion versions 2019.4 through 2020.2.1 HF1. The full story is in the Learn article on the SolarWinds compromise.
solarwinds-orion.depth:
The platform. Orion was the common base on which SolarWinds' modules installed: Network Performance Monitor for device and interface health, NetFlow Traffic Analyzer for flow records, Network Configuration Manager for configuration backup and change, IP Address Manager, Server & Application Monitor, Virtualization Manager, Storage Resource Monitor and Web Performance Monitor. It ran on the customer's own servers, which is what the company means today when it says the Orion Platform was restricted to self-hosted deployment. The company's current page is titled 'Orion modules are now self-hosted on the SolarWinds Platform' and presents the successor as a new, more expansive platform rather than a rebranding, built with Secure by Design principles.

Why a monitoring platform is a target. A network monitoring server holds credentials for everything it watches: SNMP community strings and users, Windows service accounts, SSH keys for configuration backup, API tokens for the hypervisors. It sits where it can reach every segment, because reaching every segment is its job. That is why compromising the vendor's update was worth the effort to the actor who did it, and why the directive's first instruction was not to patch but to disconnect.

SUNBURST, in the disclosers' words. FireEye, on 13 December 2020: a supply chain attack trojanizing SolarWinds Orion business software updates in order to distribute malware it called SUNBURST, inside SolarWinds.Orion.Core.BusinessLayer.dll, a SolarWinds digitally signed component of the Orion software framework that contains a backdoor communicating over HTTP to third-party servers; after an initial dormant period of up to two weeks it retrieved and executed jobs, transferring and executing files, profiling the system, rebooting it, disabling services, and found its command server through a domain generation algorithm under avsvmcloud[.]com. CISA's Emergency Directive 21-01, the same day, named Orion Platform 2019.4 HF5, 2020.2 RC1 and RC2, 2020.2 and 2020.2 HF1 and required agencies to disconnect or power down the products, image the hosts, analyse stored traffic and report by noon on 14 December. SolarWinds' own 8-K of 14 December said the vulnerability existed in updates released between March and June 2020 and that fewer than 18,000 of its roughly 33,000 Orion maintenance customers were believed to have installed them.

What changed afterwards. The company's platform page, its Secure by Design language and the regulatory history recorded on the SolarWinds entry of the industry timeline are the consequences; the Learn article on the compromise tells the sequence from the September 2019 intrusion to the 2024 court ruling. For an operator the lesson is older than the incident: the monitoring system is a crown jewel, and its update channel is part of the attack surface.

prtg.def: Paessler's monitoring software, named Paessler Router Traffic Grapher, which counts and licenses everything in sensors, one sensor per measured value, with a free edition up to 100 of them.
prtg.context: PRTG is the monitoring tool the mid-market learned by downloading. Paessler's own definition of its unit is the thing to understand: in PRTG, sensors are the basic monitoring elements, one sensor usually monitors one measured value in your network, the traffic of a switch port, the CPU load of a server, the free space on a disk, and on average you need about five to ten sensors per device or one per switch port. Licensing follows the same unit: the freeware edition is free of charge for up to 100 sensors, and the subscription tiers run from PRTG 500 to PRTG 10000, each named for the number of aspects it can monitor. It runs on Windows servers and supports distributed monitoring across an unlimited number of remote locations through probes. The editions are PRTG Network Monitor, PRTG Enterprise Monitor, PRTG Hosted Monitor and an MSP (managed service provider) edition. Paessler, founded in Nuremberg in 1997, has its own entry on the industry record; MRTG, whose name PRTG echoes, has the entry beside this one.
prtg.depth:
The sensor model. Most monitoring products count devices; PRTG counts measurements. Paessler puts it plainly on the product page: sensors are the basic monitoring elements, and one sensor usually monitors one measured value in your network, for example the traffic of a switch port, the CPU load of a server, or the free space on a disk drive. The rule of thumb the page gives is five to ten sensors per device, or one sensor per switch port, which is also the honest way to size a licence: a 48-port access switch with a few system sensors is about fifty sensors on its own, and a tier is exhausted faster than a device count would suggest.

Editions and licensing. The product family on Paessler's site is PRTG Network Monitor, PRTG Enterprise Monitor, PRTG Hosted Monitor and a PRTG MSP Edition. The freeware edition of PRTG Network Monitor is free of charge for up to 100 sensors, which is how most engineers first met it. The subscription tiers on the product page at the time of reading were PRTG 500, 1000, 2500, 5000 and 10000, each described as monitoring up to that many aspects of your devices. PRTG Network Monitor runs on Windows servers, and distributed monitoring across an unlimited number of remote locations is part of the design: remote probes collect locally and report to the core.

What it monitors. Paessler describes integrated support of all important technologies and protocols and groups the capabilities by what is watched, network devices, virtual environments, applications, websites, databases, cloud services and environmental parameters, with SNMP and an HTTP API named explicitly and custom sensors as the extension point. The page claims twenty years of monitoring expertise, which matches the company's own founding in Nuremberg in 1997.

The name. PRTG stands for Paessler Router Traffic Grapher, a deliberate echo of MRTG, the Multi Router Traffic Grapher that Tobias Oetiker published in 1995 and that drew the first traffic graphs most network engineers ever saw. The lineage is the point: the five-minute traffic graph of a router interface became a commercial product with ten thousand sensors behind it, and the glossary entry for MRTG tells the first half of that story.

mrtg.def: The Multi Router Traffic Grapher, Tobias Oetiker's free SNMP tool that polls two counters every five minutes and draws the daily, weekly, monthly and yearly traffic graphs that became the universal picture of a busy link.
mrtg.context: MRTG was born of one slow link. In Oetiker's own account to the LISA conference of December 1998, in the summer of 1994 De Montfort University in Leicester had one 64 kbit Internet link for more than a thousand networked computers and could not get a faster one for another year, so he wrote a tool that queried the gateway router's octet counters every five minutes, derived the average transfer rate for each interval and generated a web page with four graphs showing the rates for the last day, week, month and year. The graphs did not make the link faster, but they were, he wrote, a key argument to convince management that a faster link was needed. Published on the Internet in spring 1995, it spread quickly; Dave Rand contributed a small C program called rateup that moved the heavy work out of the Perl script, and after a year of beta testing MRTG-2.0 was released in January 1997 under the GNU GPL. The RRD Tool that grew out of it became the time-series store behind a generation of monitoring.
mrtg.depth:
How it works. MRTG uses SNMP, the Simple Network Management Protocol, to send a request carrying two object identifiers to a device; the device looks them up in its management information base and returns the raw counter values, typically the octets in and out of an interface. MRTG records the values in a log beside the previous readings, computes the rates, and writes an HTML page per target with four graphs, GIF or PNG, plotting the two values against time over a day, a week, a month and a year, the inbound as a filled green area and the outbound as a blue line. It can also run a script instead of an SNMP query and graph whatever integer the script prints, which is how MRTG ended up graphing CPU fan speeds and firewall rule hits. The Y axis scales itself; the page carries the maximum, average and current values; thresholds can send warning mail. It is written in Perl and runs on Windows, Linux, Unix, Mac OS and NetWare.

The design decision that mattered. MRTG logged its data to an ASCII file that it rewrote every five minutes, consolidating older readings so the file never grew. That consolidation is why the yearly graph is coarse and the daily graph is fine, and it is the idea that Oetiker's Round Robin Database Tool later generalized: a store of fixed size in which old data loses resolution instead of taking space. RRDtool, Cacti and Munin all stand on it.

The history, from the author's paper. The original MRTG was a Perl script that called external utilities to do the SNMP queries and to create the GIF images. Once it spread in 1995, users reported two problems, scalability and portability. Dave Rand's rateup, in C, took over the two most processor-intensive tasks; the SNMP portability problem was solved by switching from CMU's snmpget to Simon Leinen's pure-Perl SNMP module, which to Oetiker's surprise worked under Windows NT without change. The result of almost a year of beta testing was MRTG-2.0 in January 1997, available under the terms of the GNU GPL. The paper was presented at LISA XII in Boston, 6 to 11 December 1998, by which time MRTG-3 and the RRD Tool were already in development.

Why the entry exists. Before dashboards, there was the MRTG page: a wall of green-and-blue graphs that every network operations centre of the late 1990s and 2000s kept open, and that told you at a glance when a link filled. PRTG took its name from it, Cacti took its database, and every traffic graph on every modern tool is a descendant. The author's own career in networking began in the year the tool was published, which is reason enough for it to be here.

hp-ux.def: Hewlett Packard Unix, HP's System V Unix for the HP 9000 and later the Itanium-based Integrity servers, first released in the early 1980s and out of support since 31 December 2025.
hp-ux.context: HP-UX was one of the three great commercial Unixes of the enterprise data centre, beside Sun's Solaris and IBM's AIX. It is based on Unix System V, initially System III, and its first release is dated 1982 in the encyclopaedia's infobox and 1984 in its prose, a discrepancy recorded here rather than resolved. Early versions ran the HP Integral PC and the HP 9000 Series 200, 300 and 400 on Motorola 68000 processors and the Series 500 on HP's own FOCUS architecture; later ones ran PA-RISC and, at the end, Intel's Itanium in the HPE Integrity servers. It was the first Unix to offer access control lists for file permissions and among the first with a built-in logical volume manager; HP-UX 11i was certified to The Open Group's UNIX 03. The last release, 2025.11i v3, came on 22 May 2025, and following the discontinuation of Itanium, support ended on 31 December 2025, with mature support without sustaining engineering on Integrity through at least 2028.
hp-ux.depth:
Lineage. HP-UX, from Hewlett Packard Unix, is a proprietary implementation of Unix developed by Hewlett-Packard and later Hewlett Packard Enterprise, based on Unix System V and initially on System III. The encyclopaedia article this entry rests on dates the initial release to 1982 in its infobox and says 'first released in 1984' in its text; both figures stand here because the article states both.

Hardware. The early versions supported the HP Integral PC and the HP 9000 Series 200, 300 and 400 on the Motorola 68000 family, and the HP 9000 Series 500 on HP's proprietary FOCUS architecture; later HP 9000 models used HP's PA-RISC instruction set, and the final versions support the HPE Integrity Servers on Intel's Itanium architecture. The platform list in the infobox is therefore 68k, FOCUS, PA-RISC and IA-64, which is a complete history of HP's own processor choices in four words.

What it did first. HP-UX was the first Unix to offer access control lists for file access permissions as an alternative to the standard Unix permission bits, and among the first to include a built-in logical volume manager; the article marks both claims as needing a citation, and the caveat travels with them. HP-UX 11i offers a clustered file system with shared disks, HP Serviceguard as its cluster solution and Global Workload Management for balancing workloads. HP-UX 11i was certified to The Open Group's UNIX 03 standard; previous releases to UNIX 95.

The end. The latest release is 2025.11i v3 of 22 May 2025. Following the discontinuation of Itanium processors, support for HP-UX ended on 31 December 2025; the article describes the current state as mature support on HPE Integrity without sustaining engineering through at least 2028, and the infobox's working state as discontinued. An operating system that began on 68000 desktops and ended on Itanium servers forty-odd years later is a reasonable definition of a platform.

For the network engineer. HP-UX machines are still met in telecommunications billing, manufacturing and finance, usually running something nobody dares migrate; the practical knowledge is that their TCP/IP stack and tooling differ from Linux in the ways System V differs from BSD, and that the Hewlett-Packard record on the industry timeline carries the corporate story around them.

solaris.def: Sun Microsystems' Unix from 1992 onwards, built on System V Release 4 and marketed under a new name when Sun left its BSD-based SunOS behind; now Oracle Solaris, with OpenSolaris's open source fork living on as Illumos.
solaris.context: Solaris is SunOS 5 under a marketing name. On 4 September 1991 Sun announced that its next major operating system release would switch from the BSD-derived source base of SunOS to one based on AT&T's System V Release 4, and from that point used Solaris as an overbrand covering the operating system, the OpenWindows desktop and Open Network Computing; SunOS 4.1.1 was rebranded Solaris 1.0, and SunOS 5.0 became part of Solaris 2.0. Solaris superseded SunOS in 1993, reached x86 with Solaris 2.1 in June 1993 and a single SPARC and x86 source base with 2.4 in 1994, and became known for scalability on SPARC and for originating DTrace, ZFS and Time Slider. In June 2005 Sun released most of the code under the CDDL as OpenSolaris; after Oracle's 2010 acquisition the OpenSolaris distribution was discontinued and public updates to the kernel source stopped, so Solaris 11 is effectively closed again, and the community forked the code as Illumos. Oracle released Solaris 11.4 in 2018; the current code base supports 64-bit SPARC and x86-64.
solaris.depth:
The switch from BSD. In 1987 AT&T and Sun announced a collaboration to merge the most popular Unix flavours of the time, BSD with the features then unique to SunOS, System V and Xenix, into System V Release 4. On 4 September 1991 Sun announced that its next major release would move from its BSD-derived source to SVR4; the internal designation stayed SunOS 5, but the marketing name became Solaris, justified as an overbrand covering the operating system, OpenWindows and Open Network Computing. Sun immediately applied the new name backwards, so SunOS 4.1.1 shipped as Solaris 1.0, and the SVR4 system arrived as Solaris 2.0. Customers went on calling the BSD line SunOS, which is why the two names coexist in every old runbook.

The releases that mattered. Solaris superseded SunOS in 1993. The first two Solaris 2 releases were SPARC only; an x86 version of 2.1 came in June 1993, and 2.4 in 1994 supported SPARC and x86 from one source. The release numbering dropped the '2.' with Solaris 7, so Solaris 7 carries SunOS 5.7 and the current Solaris 11.4 carries SunOS 5.11 at its core. Solaris 10 brought 64-bit x86 applications, zones (the branded zones that later ran Linux applications) and the features the system is remembered for: DTrace, the dynamic tracing framework, and ZFS, the file system with built-in volume management and snapshots, with Time Slider as the desktop face of the snapshots.

Open, then closed again. In June 2005 Sun released most of the Solaris code base under the Common Development and Distribution License and founded the OpenSolaris project to build a developer and user community. After Oracle acquired Sun in 2010 the OpenSolaris distribution was discontinued, and Oracle later stopped providing public updates to the source code of the Solaris kernel, effectively turning Solaris 11 back into a closed-source proprietary operating system. OpenSolaris was forked as Illumos and lives on through several Illumos distributions. Oracle kept developing Solaris after a large layoff of its engineering staff and released 11.4 in 2018.

Where it is met today. Solaris runs on SPARC and x86-64 servers in the kinds of estates that bought Sun in the 1990s and 2000s: telecommunications, banking, big databases. For a network engineer the practical inheritance is the vocabulary, zones, ZFS pools, and the knowledge that the host's tooling is System V and not Linux. The SunOS entry tells the BSD half; the Sun Microsystems record on the industry timeline tells the company's story to its end inside Oracle on 27 January 2010.

sunos.def: Sun Microsystems' original Unix, BSD-based, shipped from 1982 to version 4.1.4 of September 1994; the name is used for releases 1.0 to 4.1.4, after which the System V Release 4 line was sold as Solaris.
sunos.context: SunOS is the Berkeley half of Sun's history. Sun developed it for its workstations and servers from 1982, and the name is usually used only for versions 1.0 to 4.1.4, which were based on BSD, while versions 5.0 and later are based on Unix System V Release 4 and marketed as Solaris. SunOS 1 ran the Sun-2; SunOS 2 the Sun-2 and Sun-3; SunOS 4 the Sun-2, Sun-3, the Sun386i and the Sun-4 SPARC machines, and 4.1.2 brought Sun's first multiprocessor support with a single kernel lock. Its heritage is Bill Joy's: a primary developer of the Berkeley Software Distribution joined Sun soon after its founding and is counted as a founder. In 1987 AT&T and Sun announced the merger of BSD, System V and Xenix into SVR4, and on 4 September 1991 Sun announced the switch; the last SunOS 4 release was 4.1.4, Solaris 1.1.2, in 1994, shipped until 27 December 1998 and supported until 30 September 2003. Many of the conventions a Unix engineer thinks of as Sun's came from this line.
sunos.depth:
What it was. SunOS is a Unix-branded operating system developed by Sun Microsystems for its workstation and server computers from 1982 until the mid-1990s. It was a BSD system, which placed Sun on the Berkeley side of the great Unix divide of the 1980s against the System V camp of AT&T and most other vendors, and that choice shaped the network: Sun was an early advocate of Unix-based networked computing, promoting TCP/IP and especially its own Network File System, and its motto, coined by John Gage, was The Network is the Computer.

Hardware and releases. SunOS 1 supported only the Sun-2 series, including Sun-1 systems upgraded with Sun-2 processor boards; SunOS 2 the Sun-2 and the 68020-based Sun-3; SunOS 4 the Sun-2 until 4.0.3, the Sun-3 until 4.1.1, the Sun386i in 4.0 to 4.0.2 and the Sun-4 SPARC architecture, with a SunOS 3.2 release having given preliminary Sun-4 support earlier. SunOS 4.1.2 introduced support for Sun's first sun4m multiprocessor machines, the SPARCserver 600MP series, with a single kernel lock, so only one processor at a time could execute in the kernel. The last release of SunOS 4 was 4.1.4, also named Solaris 1.1.2, in 1994; it supported sun4, sun4c and sun4m, not sun4d. Sun continued to ship 4.1.3 and 4.1.4 until 27 December 1998 and supported them until 30 September 2003.

The renaming. In 1987 AT&T and Sun announced they were collaborating to merge BSD, including many features then unique to SunOS, System V and Xenix into what became System V Release 4. On 4 September 1991 Sun announced that its next major release would switch from the BSD-derived source base to one based on SVR4; the internal designation would be SunOS 5, but Sun began using the marketing name Solaris as an overbrand for the operating system, OpenWindows and ONC. Although the SVR4 system was not expected to ship in volume until the following year, Sun immediately applied the new name to the current release: SunOS 4.1.1 became Solaris 1.0, SunOS 5.0 became part of Solaris 2.0, and each later SunOS 4.1.x micro release received a Solaris 1.x name, which customers mostly ignored.

Why a network glossary keeps it. NFS and much of the way a Unix host thinks about a network were born or matured on this line, and the habit of calling the whole family SunOS survived the renaming by decades: Solaris 11.4 still carries SunOS 5.11 at its core. The Solaris entry carries the second half; the Sun Microsystems record on the industry timeline carries the company.

irix.def: Silicon Graphics' Unix for its MIPS workstations and servers, System V with BSD extensions, named from release 3.0 in 1988 and ended with 6.5.30 in August 2006; the birthplace of XFS and OpenGL.
irix.context: IRIX, a portmanteau of IRIS and UNIX, is the discontinued operating system Silicon Graphics developed to run on its proprietary MIPS workstations and servers; it is based on Unix System V with BSD extensions, and both the XFS file system and the OpenGL graphics API were originally developed by SGI for it. SGI began using the IRIX name with the 1988 release 3.0 for the IRIS 4D series, earlier releases being identified only as 4D1-2.2 and the like, and before the IRIS 4D the company had shipped GL2, based on UniSoft's UniPlus System V. The final release was 6.5.30 on 16 August 2006; updates up to 6.5.22 were free downloads and later ones required a support contract. On 6 September 2006 SGI announced the end of the MIPS and IRIX product lines, production ended on 29 December 2006 with final deliveries in March 2007, and support ended in December 2013. Much of its core technology, XFS above all, was open-sourced and ported by SGI to Linux, which is the operating system SGI's Itanium machines ran instead.
irix.depth:
Origins. SGI began using the name IRIX in the 1988 release 3.0 of its operating system for the IRIS 4D series of workstations and servers; previous releases carried only a release number prefixed 4D1-, such as 4D1-2.2, and the prefix stayed in official documentation afterwards. Before the IRIS 4D, SGI bundled the GL2 operating system, based on UniSoft UniPlus System V Unix, with its proprietary MEX windowing system. IRIX 3.x was System V Release 3 with 4.3BSD enhancements and the 4Sight windowing system; later releases moved to the SVR4-derived base the infobox records as SVR4.1ES, with a POSIX userland and the IRIX Interactive Desktop.

What it gave the industry. XFS, the file system that now ships in every Linux distribution, was written for IRIX, as was OpenGL, the graphics API that SGI reformed out of its proprietary IRIS GL in 1992 and licensed to its own competitors under an industry review board. Both outlived the system they were built for; the Silicon Graphics record on the industry timeline tells how OpenGL came to be licensed and how an SGI Crimson running the fsn file navigator ended up in Jurassic Park.

Decline and end. Updates from 6.5.x to the 6.5.22 maintenance release were available as free downloads; 6.5.23 and higher required an active Silicon Graphics support contract. A 2001 Computerworld review found IRIX in a critical state as SGI moved its effort to Linux and to the Windows-based Visual Workstations, and MIPS and IRIX customers persuaded SGI to continue supporting the platform through 2006. On 6 September 2006 an SGI press release announced the end of the MIPS and IRIX product lines; production ended on 29 December 2006, with final deliveries in March 2007 except by special arrangement, and support ended in December 2013 with no further updates. The final release, 6.5.30, is dated 16 August 2006. SGI's Itanium systems ran SUSE Linux Enterprise Server with SGI enhancements, and QuickTransit let old MIPS/IRIX applications run on them in emulation.

For the reader of this glossary. IRIX is the Unix of the film studio and the wind tunnel rather than of the data centre, which is why a network engineer meets it rarely and remembers it well; it is one of the four vendor Unixes, with HP-UX, Solaris and AIX, that defined what a workstation network looked like before Linux, and as the system that gave Linux its best file system.

aix.def: Advanced Interactive eXecutive, IBM's proprietary Unix, first released in February 1986 for the RT PC and still current on Power servers; System V with 4.3BSD extensions, and the first operating system with a journaling file system.
aix.context: AIX is the vendor Unix that did not end. IBM has developed and sold it since 1986, the name stands for Advanced Interactive eXecutive, and the current versions run IBM's Power ISA servers and workstations alongside IBM i and Linux; the latest release at the time of reading is 7.3 TL4 of December 2025. It was originally released for the IBM RT PC RISC workstation in 1986 and has since run the RS/6000, Power and PowerPC systems, System i, System/370 mainframes, PS/2 personal computers and the Apple Network Server. It is based on Unix System V with 4.3BSD-compatible extensions and is certified to the UNIX 03 and UNIX V7 specifications of the Single UNIX Specification, from AIX 5.3 and 7.2 TL5 respectively; older versions were certified to UNIX 95 and 98. AIX was the first operating system to implement a journaling file system, and IBM has continuously added processor, disk and network virtualization, dynamic hardware allocation including fractional processor units, and reliability engineering derived from its mainframes. The kernel is monolithic with dynamically loadable modules; the default shell is ksh88.
aix.depth:
Background. IBM's involvement with Unix began in 1979, when it helped Bell Labs port Unix to the System/370 as a build host for the 5ESS switch's software; Unix itself had begun at Bell Labs in the early 1970s on DEC minicomputers and had been ported to the S/370 at Princeton by 1976, a port that became Amdahl's UTS. AIX arrived in February 1986 for the IBM RT PC, IBM's RISC workstation, and has since supported the RS/6000 series and the Power and PowerPC systems that followed, IBM System i, System/370 and ESA/390 mainframes, PS/2 personal computers, the Apple Network Server and, for a time, Itanium. Today it is supported on IBM Power Systems alongside IBM i and Linux.

What kind of Unix. AIX is based on Unix System V with 4.3BSD-compatible extensions, with a POSIX and Single UNIX Specification userland. It is certified to UNIX 03 from AIX 5.3 and to UNIX V7 from AIX 7.2 TL5; older versions were certified to UNIX 95 and UNIX 98. The kernel is monolithic with dynamically loadable modules; the default interface is the Korn shell, ksh88, with the Common Desktop Environment and optionally Plasma or GNOME on the desktop. It is written in C, closed source, formerly source-available.

Firsts and engineering. AIX was the first operating system to implement a journaling file system. IBM has continuously enhanced it with processor, disk and network virtualization, dynamic hardware resource allocation including fractional processor units, and reliability engineering concepts derived from its mainframe designs, which is the context in which most administrators meet those features. The current release line is 7.3, with technology level 4 released in December 2025, and the working state is current.

Why it belongs beside the others. HP-UX reached its end of support on 31 December 2025, Solaris became closed again after 2010, IRIX ended in 2006; AIX is the one of the four vendor Unixes still being released on a vendor's own processor architecture. For a network engineer the relevant facts are that the host runs System V tooling with IBM's own additions, that its network stack is configured through IBM's utilities rather than Linux's, and that the machines it runs on sit at the centre of the estates, banks, airlines, insurers, where the oldest and most critical applications live. The IBM record on the industry timeline carries the company.

openvms.def: Virtual Memory System: the operating system DEC announced with the VAX-11/780 in 1977 as VAX/VMS, renamed OpenVMS in 1992, ported to Alpha, Itanium and now x86-64, and developed since 2014 by VMS Software Inc.
openvms.context: VMS is the other great operating system lineage of the minicomputer era, and the one that did not die with its maker. Digital Equipment Corporation announced VAX/VMS, Virtual Address eXtension and Virtual Memory System, alongside the VAX-11/780 in 1977, with Dave Cutler, Dick Hustvedt and Peter Lipman as technical project leaders of the Star and Starlet projects that produced the machine and the system. It is a multi-user, multiprocessing, virtual memory operating system with high availability through clustering, the ability to distribute one system over many physical machines, and its customers are banks and financial service providers, hospitals, telecommunications operators, network information services and manufacturers. In July 1992 DEC renamed it OpenVMS to signal support for open-systems standards such as POSIX and Unix compatibility and to drop the VAX from the name as the Alpha port arrived; the name was first used with OpenVMS AXP V1.0 in November 1992. It has since been ported to the Itanium-based HPE Integrity servers and to x86-64, and since 2014 it is developed and supported by VMS Software Inc., whose x86-64 early adopter kit shipped in May 2020.
openvms.depth:
Origins. OpenVMS, often referred to simply as VMS, was first announced by Digital Equipment Corporation as VAX/VMS alongside the VAX-11/780 minicomputer in 1977. The Star project produced the VAX architecture and the Starlet project its operating system, with software engineers Dave Cutler, Dick Hustvedt and Peter Lipman as technical project leaders. The system is multi-user, multiprocessing and virtual-memory based, and from early on offered clustering: the ability to distribute the system over multiple physical machines, so that a cluster survives the loss of a member. That is the property its remaining customers pay for.

The renaming and the ports. During the 1980s DEC planned to replace the VAX and VMS with the PRISM architecture and the MICA operating system; that plan ended, and led to the Alpha architecture instead. In July 1992 DEC renamed VAX/VMS to OpenVMS as an indication of its support of open systems industry standards such as POSIX and Unix compatibility, and to drop the VAX connection since a migration to a different architecture was under way. The OpenVMS name was first used with the OpenVMS AXP V1.0 release in November 1992, and DEC began using OpenVMS VAX with V6.0 in June 1993. The system was subsequently ported to the Itanium-based HPE Integrity servers and, most recently, to x86-64. The VAX architecture mechanisms the system depends on, its four privilege levels among them, are implemented on Alpha, Itanium and x86-64 either by mapping to the hardware or by emulation, via PALcode on Alpha and in software on the other two.

VMS Software Inc. and x86-64. Since 2014 OpenVMS has been developed and supported by VMS Software Inc., VSI, which on securing the rights from HP announced its intention to port the system to x86-64. The port targets specific HPE and Dell servers and virtual machine hypervisors; VMware support was announced in 2020 and Hyper-V explored. The port replaced the proprietary GEM compiler back end with LLVM, changed the boot process to start from a memory disk, and simulates the four privilege levels in software. In May 2020 the V9.0 Early Adopter's Kit went to a small number of customers as a VirtualBox image with cross compilers running on Itanium; in 2021 the port was demonstrated on an Intel Atom single-board computer. HPE ended its OpenVMS Hobbyist Program in March 2020, and VSI launched a Community License Program in July 2020 covering Alpha, Integrity and x86-64.

Why a network glossary keeps it. Two reasons. The people: Cutler went on to Microsoft, where Windows NT was, in the encyclopaedia's phrase on the DEC record, made possible by former Digital engineers, which is why NT's internals read like VMS to anyone who knew both. And the installations: OpenVMS clusters still run billing, trading, hospital and manufacturing systems that cannot be stopped, and the network engineer who inherits one needs to know that DECnet may still be on the wire beside TCP/IP. The Digital Equipment Corporation record on the industry timeline carries the company from the Maynard mill to Compaq.

nagios.def: The open source monitoring system Ethan Galstad released as NetSaint on 14 March 1999 and renamed Nagios in 2002; a scheduler that runs plugins and reads their exit codes, with a St. Paul company behind it since 2007 and a family of forks around it.
nagios.context: Nagios is an open source network and infrastructure monitoring system that watches hosts, services and network devices, sends alerts when components fail and again when they recover. Ethan Galstad released NetSaint 0.0.1 on 14 March 1999 with host and service monitoring via plugins and notifications by e-mail and pager; in 2002, after the owners of a similarly named trademark raised a legal challenge, he renamed it Nagios, a recursive acronym for Nagios Ain't Gonna Insist On Sainthood, with 'agios' the Greek for saint. The design is a plugin model: Nagios Core performs no checks itself but executes external programs that test one service or resource and return 0 for OK, 1 for warning, 2 for critical or 3 for unknown, so anyone who can write a script can monitor anything. It is written in C, licensed under the GPLv2, and runs on Linux and other Unix systems. Galstad founded Nagios Enterprises in 2007 in St. Paul, Minnesota, for commercial support and the proprietary Nagios XI; Icinga forked the project in May 2009, and the 2014 redirection of the nagios-plugins.org domain produced the separate Monitoring Plugins project.
nagios.depth:
The model. Nagios Core does not perform monitoring checks directly. Its scheduler runs check plugins at configured intervals, processes the results and triggers notifications; each plugin tests a specific service or resource and returns a status code, 0 OK, 1 WARNING, 2 CRITICAL, 3 UNKNOWN, with a line of text. Hundreds of community-developed plugins exist for specific services and hardware, and the architecture is why the system spread through the 2000s: the monitoring server knew nothing about Oracle, printers or UPS batteries, and did not need to, because someone had written a forty-line script that did. Written in C, it runs on Linux and other Unix systems under the GPLv2.

The history. Galstad released NetSaint 0.0.1 on 14 March 1999; it was registered on SourceForge about two months before the project that became OpenNMS. In 2002 the owners of a similarly named trademark raised a legal challenge and, although an agreement was reached, Galstad changed the name to avoid future disputes, choosing Nagios, which links to the old name through the Greek 'agios'. Nagios 2.0 in February 2006 brought a redesigned web interface and the Event Broker module API, which let third-party software reach the internal data structures; 3.0 in March 2008 added adaptive monitoring and better performance for large installations; 4.0 in September 2013 added worker processes for parallel check execution and a redesigned CGI interface.

The company and the products. Galstad founded Nagios Enterprises in 2007 in St. Paul, Minnesota, to provide commercial support and the proprietary Nagios XI; the company's own history says Nagios began in 1999 when he developed the open source Nagios Core engine. The product line today is Nagios XI, the enterprise product, Nagios Core, the open source engine, Nagios Log Server, Nagios Network Analyzer for flow analysis and Nagios Fusion for a view across many servers.

The forks, which are part of the story. In May 2009 a group of community developers forked Nagios as Icinga, citing slow development, lack of community involvement in decisions and insufficient response to submitted patches; Icinga initially kept compatibility with Nagios plugins and configuration files, and Icinga 2 in 2014 was a ground-up rewrite with a new configuration language and distributed monitoring. On 16 January 2014 Nagios Enterprises redirected the nagios-plugins.org domain to a server it controlled without notifying the community plugin team; the displaced maintainers continued their work as Monitoring Plugins at monitoring-plugins.org. Shinken (2009), Naemon (2013) and Checkmk are the other derivatives of the plugin model. A project that made monitoring a community craft then lived through what a community does when it disagrees, and the result is that a Nagios plugin written in 2004 still runs on half a dozen systems today.

Beside the others. Zabbix kept one company and one code base; OpenNMS kept a foundation-like governance beside its company; Nagios kept the simplest possible contract between the scheduler and the check, and that simplicity is why it is still the first monitoring system many engineers install. The Nagios record on the industry timeline carries the company's dates.

zabbix.def: An open source monitoring platform created by Alexei Vladishev in 2001, released as 1.0 in 2004 and backed since 2005 by a company in Riga; it collects over SNMP, IPMI, JMX and its own agents into a relational database and has been under the AGPLv3 since 7.0.
zabbix.context: Zabbix monitors networks, servers, virtual machines and cloud services: it collects metrics via SNMP, IPMI, JMX and custom agents, stores them in a relational database, PostgreSQL, MySQL or MariaDB, Oracle or TimescaleDB, and provides alerting, visualization and reporting through a web front end. Alexei Vladishev started it in 2001 as an internal monitoring tool and released the first stable version, 1.0, in 2004; the company's own history begins in 2005 with a small group of passionate individuals led by Vladishev, who is still chief executive and founder, headquartered in Latvia with offices in the USA, Brazil, Mexico, Japan and France. The server and the original agent are written in C, the newer agent2 in Go, the web front end in PHP, and a Java gateway handles JMX; proxies collect at remote sites and forward to the server. Version 3.0 in February 2016 was the first long-term support release; 7.0 LTS in June 2024 changed the licence from GPLv2 to AGPLv3 and added browser-based synthetic monitoring. The company's one-line description of its model: free and open source software backed by a mature, reliable vendor.
zabbix.depth:
Architecture. The Zabbix server collects data from agents and other sources, evaluates trigger conditions, sends alerts and stores data in a relational database; supported databases include PostgreSQL, MySQL and MariaDB, Oracle and TimescaleDB as a PostgreSQL extension for time series. For distributed monitoring, Zabbix proxies collect data at remote sites and forward it to the central server, reducing bandwidth and buffering locally if the connection drops, which is how a Brazilian branch network reports to a head office through thin links. The original agent, in C, runs on Linux and Unix systems; agent2, written in Go from version 4.0, executes checks concurrently and takes plugins; a Java gateway handles JMX; and agentless collection over SNMP and IPMI covers the devices that cannot run anything.

Versions as a map of the trade. 1.0 appeared in 2004 and 1.1 later that year, after which development branches took odd numbers and stable releases even ones. 1.8 in December 2009 added auto-discovery and auto-registration of hosts; 2.0 in May 2012 the screen-based dashboards and template inheritance; 3.0 in February 2016, the first long-term support release, encryption between agent and server and predictive trigger functions; 4.0 in October 2018 the Go agent with a plugin architecture; 5.0 LTS in May 2020 a monitoring proxy for distributed environments and SAML authentication; 6.0 LTS in February 2022 high-availability clustering for the server, Kubernetes monitoring and machine-learning anomaly detection; 7.0 LTS in June 2024 browser-based synthetic monitoring, an improved API, proxy load balancing and the licence change from GPLv2 to AGPLv3.

The company. Zabbix SIA, also written Zabbix LLC, is based in Riga, Latvia; its about page says it began in 2005 with a small group of passionate individuals led by Alexei Vladishev, names him chief executive and founder, and lists offices in the USA, Brazil, Mexico, Japan and France with headquarters in Latvia. The model is stated in one sentence, free and open source software backed by a mature reliable vendor, and it has not changed in twenty years: the software costs nothing, the company sells support, training, certification and consulting.

Where it sits. Beside Nagios, which spread through plugins and forks, and OpenNMS, which nearly died twice before its company existed, Zabbix is the monitoring project that kept one founder, one company and one code base from the start, and its Brazilian office is why the name is as familiar in São Paulo as in Riga. The Zabbix record on the industry timeline carries the dates; the Grafana entry describes the dashboard many Zabbix installations now wear.

grafana.def: The open source analytics and visualization application Torkel Ödegaard released in January 2014, which draws dashboards over other systems' metrics, logs and traces without storing them itself; the product of Grafana Labs and the face of the LGTM observability stack.
grafana.context: Grafana connects to time-series databases and other data sources and lets a user build dashboards that display metrics, logs and traces; it stores none of that telemetry itself, querying the backends when a dashboard renders and combining several sources in one panel, and keeps only dashboards, users, annotations and alert state in a small database of its own. Core data sources include Prometheus, Graphite, InfluxDB and OpenTSDB for metrics, Loki and Elasticsearch for logs, Tempo, Jaeger and Zipkin for traces, Pyroscope for profiles and MySQL, PostgreSQL and SQL Server. Torkel Ödegaard created it in December 2013, by Grafana Labs' account, and released it in January 2014 as an outgrowth of work on Graphite at Orbitz, with a user interface originally based on version 3 of Kibana; the name combines Graphite and Kibana. The back end is Go and the front end TypeScript and React, shipped as a single binary with a plugin system for data sources, panels and apps; dashboards are JSON and can be version-controlled. Licensed under the AGPLv3 since 2021 (Apache 2.0 before), with Grafana Cloud and Grafana Enterprise as the commercial forms.
grafana.depth:
What it does and does not do. Grafana is a web application for analytics and visualization. It does not store the metrics, logs or traces it shows: when a dashboard is rendered it queries the external data sources it has been pointed at and can combine results from several of them in a single panel. It maintains its own relational database, SQLite by default or MySQL or PostgreSQL, for dashboards, users, annotations and alert state only. That separation is the design decision that made it the front end to everyone else's telemetry, and the reason a Grafana dashboard can sit on top of Zabbix, Prometheus and a SQL warehouse at once.

Data sources and plugins. Core data sources shipped with Grafana include Prometheus, Graphite, InfluxDB and OpenTSDB for metrics; Loki and Elasticsearch for logs; Tempo, Jaeger and Zipkin for traces; Pyroscope and Parca for profiles; and MySQL, PostgreSQL and Microsoft SQL Server. Other back ends, OpenSearch and Splunk among them, arrive as separately installed plugins. Plugins fall into three categories, data source plugins for querying back ends, panel plugins for visualization types and app plugins for bundled functionality. Dashboards are defined as JSON documents, can be provisioned from files, version-controlled and shared through Grafana's public dashboard library; alerting rules can be defined against any data source with notifications to e-mail, Slack, PagerDuty and other channels. The back end is written in Go and the front end in TypeScript with React, and the whole runs as a single binary.

Origins. Grafana Labs' own page says that in December 2013, looking for a better way to make data more accessible and interactive, Torkel Ödegaard created an open source dashboarding tool he called Grafana; the encyclopaedia dates the first release to January 2014, as an outgrowth of his work on Graphite at Orbitz, initially targeting Graphite and InfluxDB, with a user interface originally based on version 3 of Kibana. The name combines Graphite and Kibana. The company around it was founded in 2014 as Raintank and later took the product's name; Ödegaard, Raj Dutt and Anthony Woods are its co-founders.

The stack and the licence. Grafana Labs built or acquired the rest of what it calls the LGTM stack, Loki for logs, Grafana for dashboards, Tempo for traces and Mimir for metrics, and maintains k6, Pyroscope, Faro, Beyla and Alloy as well. Since 2021 Grafana has been licensed under the AGPLv3, having been Apache 2.0 before, the same move Zabbix made with 7.0 in 2024 and a cousin of the dispute recorded on the Elastic entry of the industry timeline. Grafana Cloud is the managed service, with Adaptive Telemetry and Grafana Assistant among its additions; Grafana Enterprise is the self-managed commercial edition with LDAP (Lightweight Directory Access Protocol) team synchronization, data source permissions and reporting.

For the network engineer. Grafana is where the SNMP counters a Zabbix or Prometheus collector gathers end up on the wall of the operations centre, in the place where the MRTG page hung in 1998; the entries for MRTG, PRTG, Nagios and Zabbix tell the collectors' side, and the Grafana Labs record on the industry timeline tells the company's.

netware.def: Novell's network operating system, the file and print server of the LAN era: file sharing instead of disk sharing in 1983, hardware-independent NetWare 286 in 1986, NLMs with NetWare 386 in 1989, a directory service in 1993, TCP/IP as the core protocol in 1998, and a last service pack in May 2009.
netware.context: NetWare is the discontinued network operating system Novell developed from 1983 to the final update, 6.5 SP8 of 6 May 2009, after which Open Enterprise Server carried its services on a SUSE Linux kernel. It evolved from one idea, file sharing instead of disk sharing: by controlling access at the level of files rather than whole disks it could lock files and enforce access control, when every competitor of 1983 shared raw disks, and IBM's 1984 endorsement of the approach helped it spread. It ran cooperative multitasking on a dedicated PC, spoke its own IPX protocol with NCP, the NetWare Core Protocol, on top, mapped DOS drive letters to server volumes through a resident client, and became hardware-independent with NetWare 286 in 1986, when any 80286 machine with a supported disk and network card could be a server. NetWare 386 (3.x, 1989) brought 32-bit protected mode and the NetWare Loadable Module; NetWare 4 (1993) brought NetWare Directory Services, an X.500-style global directory six years before Active Directory; NetWare 5 (October 1998) switched the core protocol to TCP/IP, a decision bitterly contested inside Novell, and 6.5 (2003) shipped with PHP, MySQL, OpenSSH and bash. Novell said its 90 million users would be supported until at least 2015.
netware.depth:
The idea. NetWare originated from consulting work by SuperSet Software, a group founded by Drew Major, Dale Neibaur, Kyle Powell and later Mark Hurst out of their classwork at Brigham Young University from October 1981. Ray Noorda engaged them in 1981 to build a CP/M disk-sharing system for the Motorola 68000 hardware Novell then sold; in 1983, privately convinced that CP/M was doomed, the team built a file-sharing system for the newly introduced IBM PC instead, and wrote Snipes, a text-mode game, to test and demonstrate it, the first network application written for a commercial personal computer. The product, first called ShareNet or S-Net, was NetWare: file sharing instead of disk sharing, so that access could be controlled and files locked at the level of the individual file, when all competing products of 1983 shared raw disks. IBM's validation of the approach in 1984 helped it along.

How it worked. A NetWare server shares disk space as volumes; DOS clients run a terminate-and-stay-resident program that maps a drive letter to a volume after logging in, and print to the server's printers as if they were local. The protocol is NCP, the NetWare Core Protocol, a request-reply design that trusted the network: a request carries a sequence number and the reply is its acknowledgement, which cut transactions by two thirds against the protocols of the day; NCP ran natively over IPX/SPX. The server was a special-purpose, non-preemptive operating system that cached the whole file allocation table and directory in RAM and used every spare byte as file cache, which is where its benchmark advantage of five to ten times over Microsoft's and Banyan's products came from, and why an uninterruptible power supply was effectively compulsory.

The generations. NetWare 68 ran on Novell's own 68000 server; NetWare 86 and Advanced NetWare 86 (1985) moved it to Intel PCs; Advanced NetWare 286 of 1986 used the 80286's 16-bit protected mode to address 16 MiB, supported 256 MB volumes, mirrored disks (SFT), tracked transactions (TTS) and, decisively, was hardware-independent, with eighteen makers' network cards supported at launch and licences keyed to a card or, later, to serialized diskettes. NetWare 386 arrived in 1989, was renamed 3.0 in 1990 and reached 3.11 in 1991: 32-bit protected mode, 1 TB volumes, and the NetWare Loadable Module, which let disk drivers, network drivers, antivirus, backup, databases and web servers load into the server at ring 0 with no memory protection and the ABEND that followed a badly behaved one. NetWare 4 in 1993 replaced the per-server bindery with NetWare Directory Services, a global directory based on ISO X.500 concepts, renamed Novell Directory Services and in February 2004 eDirectory; Microsoft released Active Directory six years later. GroupWise, ZENworks and BorderManager were built on it. 4.11 of 1996 brought the first full 32-bit Windows client and the NetWare Administrator, and was bundled with a web server, TCP/IP and Netscape as IntranetWare.

TCP/IP and the end. Novell had used IPX/SPX from the start and was poorly placed for the Internet of 1995; limited TCP/IP support existed in 3.x and 4.x, and the IPX/IP gateway and NWIP eased the transition. With NetWare 5 in October 1998 the primary NCP interface switched from IPX/SPX to TCP/IP, a decision bitterly contested inside the company; chief executive Eric Schmidt's line was that the market had spoken and TCP/IP had won. NetWare 5 added a graphical console, Novell Storage Services, a Java virtual machine, directory-enabled DNS, DHCP and PKI (public key infrastructure), SAN support and Novell Cluster Services; 5.1 of January 2000 WebSphere and web management; 6.0 of October 2001 per-user licensing and 32-node clusters; 6.5 of August 2003 PHP, MySQL, OpenSSH, bash, iSCSI and a user portal. The last service pack, 6.5 SP8, came in May 2009. Open Enterprise Server, announced 2003 and first released in March 2005, offers the NetWare services on SUSE Linux Enterprise Server, with the NetWare kernel an option until OES 11 in late 2011; general support for 6.5 SP8 ended in 2010, extended support at the end of 2015 and self support at the end of 2017.

The market, and why it ended. IDC reported a 53 per cent share of network operating systems for NetWare in 1988 against 17.1 for MS-Net and 8.5 for AppleTalk, and before Windows NT Server arrived Novell claimed 90 per cent of PC-based servers. Three things ended it, in the encyclopaedia's account: a text console at a time when Windows had won the administrator; the choice of IPX over TCP/IP as the Internet arrived; and Microsoft's bundling of file and print into the operating system every desktop already ran. The profession the product created, the CNEs and CNAs, has its own entry; the Novell record on the industry timeline carries the company from the Superset team to OpenText.

novell-certifications.def: Novell's certification ladder, the first in the IT industry: the Certified Novell Instructor from 1986, the Certified Novell Engineer from 1989 or 1990, the Certified Novell Administrator from 1992 and the Master CNE from 1995, with over 150,000 CNEs by 1999.
novell-certifications.context: Before the CCNA there was the CNE. By Novell's own account, in a release from BrainShare '96 in Salt Lake City on 20 March 1996 celebrating a decade of certification, Novell pioneered IT certification in 1986 with the Certified Novell Instructor programme, introduced the CNE in 1990, the Certified Novell Administrator in 1992 and the Master CNE in 1995, and by then counted more than 4,000 CNIs, 82,000 CNEs, 93,000 CNAs and 6,500 Master CNEs, taught through 1,450 Novell Authorized Education Centers and 150 academic partners and tested at more than a thousand Sylvan Prometric centres, with the one millionth test delivered in 1995. A second Novell release, filed in March 1999 and celebrating ten years of the CNE, calls it the industry's first information technology certification, says it was introduced in 1989, and counts more than 150,000 CNEs and nearly a million certifications granted or in progress; the two releases disagree on the CNE's launch year and both figures are recorded here. The CNE was expanded as Certified NetWare Engineer in the early years and as Certified Novell Engineer later, the second being the form Novell trademarked in 1999.
novell-certifications.depth:
The ladder. The Certified Novell Administrator, the CNA, certified the person who ran a NetWare server day to day: users, printers, rights, backups. The Certified Novell Engineer, the CNE, certified the person who designed and built the network, and in the 1990s it was the credential a career in corporate networking was built on; the Master CNE, from 1995, sat above it for specialists. The Certified Novell Instructor, the CNI, certified the people who taught the courses at the Novell Authorized Education Centers, and it came first: Novell's own 1996 release says the company pioneered IT certification in 1986 with the CNI programme. The 1999 release lists the then-current family as CNE, Master CNE, CNA, CNI and Certified Internet Professional.

The numbers, from Novell's releases. March 1996: more than 4,000 CNIs worldwide, more than 82,000 CNEs, more than 93,000 CNA certificants, 6,500 Master CNEs, 1,450 Novell Authorized Education Centers globally, 150 Novell Education Academic Partners, more than 1,000 Sylvan Prometric testing centres, and the one millionth test delivered in 1995. March 1999: more than 150,000 CNEs worldwide, and nearly one million Novell certifications granted or in progress during the decade; the same release marks fifteen years of BrainShare, Novell's conference.

The discrepancy. Novell's 1996 release states that the CNE was introduced in 1990; its 1999 release, celebrating a decade of the programme that month, states that it was introduced in 1989. Both documents are Novell's own and both are cited on this entry; the disagreement is recorded rather than resolved, which is how this site treats a conflict between primary sources. The dateline of the 1999 release reads March 1998 in its text while the release is filed under March 1999 and speaks of a decade since 1989; that too is noted.

Why it matters to anyone who was not there. Every vendor certification ladder that followed, Cisco's CCNA, CCNP and CCIE (which arrived in 1993, after the CNE) and the F5, Fortinet, Extreme and Netskope programmes the author of this site teaches today, is built on the pattern Novell established: an administrator tier, an engineer tier, a master tier, and an instructor certification above them for the people allowed to teach the official curriculum through authorized centres. The authorized training centre, the proctored test at a third-party centre, the course number and the exam number as a profession's shared vocabulary all date from here. The NetWare entry describes the product the ladder was built on; the Novell record on the industry timeline carries the company.

notes-and-domino.def: Lotus Notes, the client, and Domino, the server: the collaborative platform Ray Ozzie's Iris Associates built for Lotus from 1984 and shipped in December 1989, bought with Lotus by IBM in 1995 and owned by HCL since July 2019; a replicated document database with mail, calendars, directory, applications and public-key security built in.
notes-and-domino.context: HCL Notes, formerly Lotus Notes and then IBM Notes, is a proprietary collaborative software platform whose client is called Notes and whose server is branded Domino. It provides e-mail, calendars, to-do lists, contacts, discussion forums, file sharing, websites, instant messaging, blogs, document libraries, user directories and custom applications, all built on one storage model: the Notes Storage Facility, the .nsf file that holds an application's design and its data together, replicated between servers and between server and client so that a user works offline on a local replica and synchronizes on the next connection. Its chief inspiration was PLATO Notes, the discussion system David Woolley created at the University of Illinois in 1973 and that Ray Ozzie used there; Ozzie's deal with Mitch Kapor formed Iris Associates in 1984, Lotus beta-tested the product so long it was called vaporware, and Price Waterhouse bought 10,000 copies before the December 1989 release, the largest single sale of PC software to that date. Lotus bought Iris in 1994, IBM bought Lotus in 1995 primarily for Notes, the server took the Domino name in 1996 when its HTTP add-on was folded in, IBM dropped the Lotus brand in 2012 and sold the products to HCL in a $1.8 billion deal announced on 6 December 2018 and completed in July 2019. Domino 14.0 shipped on 7 December 2023.
notes-and-domino.depth:
The origin. Lotus Notes's chief inspiration was PLATO Notes, created by David R. Woolley at the University of Illinois in 1973: user-created discussion groups, in today's terms, and part of the foundation of an online community that thrived on PLATO for more than twenty years. Ray Ozzie worked with PLATO as a student there in the 1970s, and when PC network technology emerged he made a deal with Lotus founder Mitch Kapor that formed Iris Associates in 1984 to combine the capabilities of PCs with the collaborative tools PLATO had pioneered; product development stayed under Ozzie and Iris, sales and marketing under Lotus. Lotus beta-tested Notes for so long that it was considered vaporware before the December 1989 release, and was unsure how to sell it, since Lotus sold through retail and Notes's corporate customers would buy direct and need support; Price Waterhouse bought 10,000 copies before the official release, the largest single sale of PC software. After the success of Notes R3, Lotus purchased Iris in 1994, and in 1995 IBM purchased Lotus primarily to acquire Notes; the HCL Notes article gives the price as $3.2 billion, the Lotus Software article cited on the Lotus record gives $3.5 billion, and both figures are recorded here.

The design. The standard storage mechanism in Domino is a document-database format, the Notes Storage Facility, whose .nsf file normally contains both an application's design and its data. A database can be replicated between servers and between server and client, so a local replica on the Notes client lets a user fully use the databases while offline, with changes synchronized when client and server next connect; many servers can hold the same information and many users can work on it. Security is granular, from ten parameters at the database level down to individual fields in specific records. Lotus Notes was the first widely adopted software product to use public-key cryptography for client-server and server-server authentication and for encryption of data. Until United States export law changed in 2000, IBM and Lotus could not export versions supporting symmetric keys longer than 40 bits; in 1997 Lotus negotiated an agreement with the NSA allowing export of 64-bit keys of which 24 bits were encrypted to a special key and included in the message, a 'workload reduction factor' that protected users outside the United States against private-sector espionage but not against the US government, and that many considered a backdoor. Domino can also reach relational databases through the Enterprise Integrator, ODBC or XPages, the Jakarta Faces-based technology IBM released in 2008 to surface Domino applications to browsers.

The names. Before release 4.5 the Lotus Notes brand covered both client and server. In 1996 Lotus released an HTTP server add-on for the Notes 4 server called Domino, which rendered Notes documents as web pages in real time; later that year the Domino web server was integrated into release 4.5 of the core server and the whole server program was rebranded Domino, while only the client kept the Lotus Notes name. In November 2012 IBM announced it would drop the Lotus brand and identify the products as IBM Notes and IBM Domino. On 6 December 2018 IBM announced the sale of a number of software products to HCL for $1.8 billion, Notes and Domino among them, and the acquisition completed in July 2019; since then they are HCL Notes and HCL Domino under HCLSoftware. The platform runs on AIX, IBM i, Linux, macOS and Windows; the 9.x Standard client is Java on Eclipse, earlier clients C++; the stable release at the time of reading is 14.0.0 of 7 December 2023, and HCL's product page presents HCL Domino 2026 as a 'Secure Enterprise AI and Collaboration Platform' and a rapid application development platform with Notes, Nomad, Verse, Domino Leap, Domino IQ and Domino Workspace around it, a platform that already powers thousands of business-critical applications.

Why a networking glossary keeps it. Because of what the Lotus record on the industry timeline says of the product: organizations built their actual business processes inside it, and a business process is far harder to migrate than a file format, which is why the same software has outlived three owners. Because Domino competes, in the encyclopaedia's words, with products from Microsoft, Google and Zimbra and is compared with SharePoint, so the network engineer still meets Domino servers replicating across WAN links and Notes traffic in firewall rules. And because the public-key story, a commercial product with certificate-based authentication in 1989 and an export-control compromise in 1997, is a chapter of the crypto wars told elsewhere on this site.
