pascal.def: Niklaus Wirth's imperative, procedural programming language of 1970, designed as a small, efficient language to encourage structured programming and data structuring; the teaching language of the 1980s, displaced by C, and the root of Object Pascal and Delphi.
pascal.context: Pascal is an imperative and procedural programming language designed by Niklaus Wirth and named after Blaise Pascal, the French mathematician, philosopher and physicist. Wirth developed it on the pattern of ALGOL 60: having worked on ALGOL W, he abandoned the ALGOL X standardization process in 1968, improved ALGOL W further and released the result as Pascal in 1970, a small, efficient language intended to encourage good programming practice through structured programming and data structuring. It became very successful in the 1970s on the minicomputer market, compilers appeared for the microcomputers as that field emerged in the late 1970s, UCSD Pascal among them, and in the 1980s it was widely used as a teaching language in university programming courses and in production for commercial software. It was displaced by C during the late 1980s and early 1990s as Unix systems became popular and especially with the release of C++, and Brian Kernighan's 1981 article 'Why Pascal is Not My Favorite Programming Language' set out the case against it. A derivative, Object Pascal, designed for object-oriented programming in 1985, was used by Apple for the Lisa and Macintosh and by Borland, and grew into Delphi on Windows; Free Pascal and GNU Pascal keep the language alive.
pascal.depth:
Design. Wirth designed Pascal as a small, efficient language, with static, strong and safe typing and lexical scope, intended to encourage good programming practices through structured programming and data structuring: records, enumerations, subranges, sets and pointers as the vocabulary of data, and the procedure and function as the unit of program. It is named after Blaise Pascal, and its family is the Wirth line that runs from ALGOL W through Pascal to Modula-2 and Oberon. The list of languages it influenced in the encyclopaedia's infobox includes Ada, C#, Go, Java, Modula, Oberon, Object Pascal, Standard ML, VHDL and the structured text of industrial controllers.

Rise. Pascal became very successful in the 1970s, notably on the burgeoning minicomputer market; compilers were also available for many microcomputers as the field emerged in the late 1970s, UCSD Pascal with its portable p-code among them. It was widely used as a teaching language in university-level programming courses in the 1980s and in production settings for writing commercial software in the same period. The major implementations the encyclopaedia lists range from the CDC 6000 and ICL 1900 to the PDP-11, the IBM System/370, VSI Pascal on OpenVMS, Delphi, Free Pascal and GNU Pascal. A generation of engineers, the author included, met structured programming through it.

Decline and critique. Pascal was displaced by the C programming language during the late 1980s and early 1990s as Unix-based systems became popular, and especially with the release of C++. Brian Kernighan, who had popularized C, outlined his criticisms in 1981 in 'Why Pascal is Not My Favorite Programming Language', an article every Pascal programmer eventually read and argued with; the glossary's 'Real Programmers Don't Use Pascal' entry records the folklore side of the same quarrel.

Descendants. A derivative named Object Pascal, designed for object-oriented programming, was developed in 1985; it was used by Apple Computer for the Lisa and Macintosh machines and by Borland in the late 1980s, and later developed into Delphi on the Microsoft Windows platform. Turbo Pascal, Borland's compiler and editor of 1983, has its own entry because it is the form in which most people met the language; Free Pascal and GNU Pascal, the latter having adopted some of the Pascal-SC extensions, continue it as free software. The Borland record on the industry timeline tells how a $49.95 compiler made the language a mass-market product.

turbo-pascal.def: Borland's software development system of 20 November 1983, a Pascal compiler with an integrated editor for CP/M, CP/M-86 and MS-DOS, written by Anders Hejlsberg, famous for compiling very fast and for selling by mail order at $49.95 when professional tools cost hundreds.
turbo-pascal.context: Turbo Pascal is a compiler and integrated development environment for Pascal, originally developed by Anders Hejlsberg at Borland and notable for its very fast compiling; with the later Turbo C it made Borland a leader in PC development tools. Philippe Kahn's idea was to package everything a programmer needed, a custom text editor, the compiler and the means to produce an executable, in one integrated toolkit with much better performance and resource use than the professional tools of the day, and to sell it by direct mail order for US$49.95 without retailers or resellers, when vendors aimed their tools at professionals and the price of a basic set plus a profiler ran into the hundreds of dollars. The compiler descends from the Blue Label Pascal Hejlsberg wrote in 1981 for the Nascom microcomputer's NasSys cassette system; Borland licensed the PolyPascal core from his Danish company Poly Data, added the user interface and editor, and after a release as Compas Pascal for CP/M shipped Turbo Pascal on 20 November 1983 for CP/M, CP/M-86 and DOS. Hejlsberg joined Borland and was the architect of every version of the compiler and of the first three versions of Delphi, before going on to C# and .NET at Microsoft. Object-oriented features arrived with 5.5; by 1995 Delphi replaced it.
turbo-pascal.depth:
What was new. In 1983 writing a program meant an editor, then a compiler, then a linker, each a separate program loaded in turn from floppy disks, and vendors of development tools aimed their products at professional developers at professional prices. Kahn's idea, in the encyclopaedia's words, was to package all these functions in an integrated programming toolkit designed to have much better performance and resource utilization than the usual professional development tools, and to charge a low price for a package integrating a custom text editor, compiler and all functionality needed to produce executable programs. The program was sold by direct mail order for US$49.95, without going through established sales channels. Fast compilation was the experience: the compiler was in memory with the editor, an error dropped the cursor on the line, and the cycle that had taken minutes took seconds.

Lineage. The Turbo Pascal compiler was based on the Blue Label Pascal compiler Anders Hejlsberg produced in 1981 for the NasSys cassette-based operating system of the Nascom microcomputer. Borland licensed Hejlsberg's PolyPascal compiler core, Poly Data being the name of his company in Denmark, and added the user interface and editor; the compiler was first released as Compas Pascal for CP/M and then, on 20 November 1983, as Turbo Pascal for CP/M, including the Apple II with a Z-80 SoftCard and the Commodore 64 with a CP/M cartridge, for CP/M-86 and for DOS. Hejlsberg joined the company as an employee and was the architect for all versions of the Turbo Pascal compiler and the first three versions of Borland Delphi.

Versions. From version 5.5 object-oriented programming features were introduced, classes, inheritance, constructors and destructors; Borland called its language Object Pascal, greatly extended later as the language underlying Delphi. For versions 6 and 7, the last two, a lower-priced Turbo Pascal and a more expensive Borland Pascal were sold, the latter oriented to professional development with more libraries and standard library source code, and Borland Pascal 7 had Windows support. By 1995 Borland had dropped Turbo and Borland Pascal and replaced them with the rapid application development environment Delphi, based on Object Pascal. Borland later released several versions as freeware once they became 'antique software': 1.0 for DOS on 1 February 2000, 3.02 on 10 February 2000, 5.5 on 21 February 2002 and the French 7.01 in 2000; most are still downloadable from the successor site at Embarcadero.

Why it is remembered. The 1985 West Coast Computer Faire review quoted on the Borland record said the legend of Turbo Pascal had reached mythic proportions, with firms planning in marketing meetings to become the next Borland. The reason is in the price and the loop: a professional's instrument made cheap enough for a student, and a compile fast enough to learn by. A great many network engineers of the author's generation wrote their first real programs in it, and the structured habits Pascal taught travelled into every configuration they wrote afterwards. The Pascal entry carries the language; the Borland record on the industry timeline carries the company from this compiler to Micro Focus.

dbase.def: The microcomputer database management system and programming language Ashton-Tate sold from 1980 as dBASE II, the most successful of its day: a database engine, a query system, a forms engine and a language in one package, whose dialect became the xBase family of dBASE III, FoxPro and Clipper.
dbase.context: dBase was one of the first database management systems for microcomputers and the most successful in its day: a core database engine, a query system, a forms engine and a programming language tying them together. It began as Vulcan, which Wayne Ratliff wrote for PTDOS in 1978 in 8080 assembly language to pick football pools, modelled on JPLDIS, a Univac program from the Jet Propulsion Laboratory; the CP/M port caught Ashton-Tate's attention in 1980, and the company licensed it, released it as dBASE II at $700 with an unusual guarantee, a crippled trial copy and a sealed full disk returnable within thirty days, and shipped it for the IBM PC in September 1982. By early 1984 it reportedly held 70 per cent of the microcomputer database market with 150,000 copies sold, a catalogue of 700 applications written in its language and more than thirty books teaching it; dBASE III shipped in July 1984 and was ported to Unix and VMS, and by the mid-1980s Ashton-Tate was one of the Big Three with Lotus and Microsoft. The xBase clones, FoxBASE+ and FoxPro, Clipper and others, could not displace it until dBASE IV 1.0 of October 1988 shipped so buggy that users left; within one year Borland bought Ashton-Tate, Microsoft bought Fox Software and Computer Associates bought Nantucket.
dbase.depth:
What it was. The dBase system included the core database engine, a query system, a forms engine and a programming language that tied all of these components together, and the language is why it mattered beyond its own tables: a dBASE program was a text file of commands over tables stored in .dbf files, a format other software still imports. The interactive dot prompt let a user type commands directly, and the RunTime product of February 1983 let developers distribute applications to customers who did not own the full product. The infobox credits Cecil Wayne Ratliff as developer, dates the first appearance to 1979 and the final release, dBASE 2019, to that year.

Origins. In the late 1960s Fred Thompson at JPL used a Tymshare product named RETRIEVE; Jeb Long wrote JPLDIS for the Univac 1108 in its image; and in 1978 Wayne Ratliff, a Martin Marietta programmer, wrote Vulcan for PTDOS in Intel 8080 assembly, modelled on JPLDIS, to help him pick football pools. The CP/M port caught the attention of George Tate and Hal Lashlee in 1980; they licensed it in 1981 on a one-page agreement with generous royalties and sold it as dBASE II. It cost $700. Customers received a crippled version and a separate sealed disk with the full one, returnable unopened within thirty days, which likely persuaded many to risk the price. The IBM PC port shipped in September 1982, and as hard disks grew the product became one of the first database titles to sell in volume.

The peak. By early 1984 InfoWorld estimated Ashton-Tate to be the world's sixth-largest microcomputer software company on $35 million of 1983 sales; dBASE II reportedly had 70 per cent of the microcomputer database market with more than 150,000 copies sold, the company published a catalogue of more than 700 applications written in the language, and more than thirty books and courses taught it, while other companies produced hundreds of utilities around it. Ratliff's own explanation was that the software was incomplete, with omissions other developers filled, and that the gaps built the ecosystem. PC Magazine wrote that the share would be the envy of Procter & Gamble or General Motors. dBASE III was announced in May and shipped in July 1984, then ported to Unix and VMS; dBASE III Plus was 63 per cent of fiscal 1987 revenue.

The fall. dBASE went 22 months without an update while competitors shipped. dBASE IV 1.0 arrived in October 1988 to good reviews until, by spring 1989, users found the bugs; Ed Esber admitted in August 1989 that it had shipped too early, and 1.1 did not ship until July 1990, by which time many customers had moved to the xBase products, FoxBASE+ and FoxPro, Clipper and others, that implemented the same language better. In the early 1990s xBase was the leading platform for business applications, and within a year the three top firms were bought: Borland purchased Ashton-Tate, Microsoft bought Fox Software and Computer Associates acquired Nantucket. Borland brought out a revised dBASE IV in 1992 described as designed for programmers rather than ordinary users, and the Justice Department required it to end its lawsuit against Fox and allow other companies to use the dBASE/xBase language without the threat of legal action. By the opening decade of this century most of the original xBase products had faded; in 2022 products known as dBase still existed, owned by dBase LLC, and The Register reported the dBase website ceased to operate in 2026.

Why it is on this glossary. Every small business system the author's generation inherited in Brazil in the 1990s, stock, billing, the clinic's patient list, was a dBASE or Clipper application on a NetWare share, and the .dbf file is still the lowest common denominator of data exchange. The Clipper entry tells the compiler's half; the Ashton-Tate, Borland and Nantucket records on the industry timeline carry the companies.

clipper.def: Nantucket's compiler for the dBASE III language, first released in 1985, which turned interpreted database programs into standalone DOS executables; millions of small-business applications were built in it before Computer Associates bought it in 1992, and its last release was CA-Clipper 5.3b in 1997.
clipper.context: Clipper is an xBase compiler that implements a variant of the xBase language: it was created as a replacement for Ashton-Tate's dBASE III, and its advantage was that a program could be compiled and executed on DOS as a standalone application rather than run inside the dBASE interpreter, the one major dBASE feature it never implemented being the interactive dot prompt. Nantucket Corporation, started in 1984 by Barry ReBell on the management side and Brian Russell on the technical side with Larry Heimendinger as president, shipped the first release, Winter '84, on 25 May 1985 and named the next ones for seasons, Summer '85, Winter '85, Autumn '86 and the Summer '87 of 21 December 1987 that became the long-lived standard, before Clipper 5.0 in 1990 and 5.01 in April 1991. Between 1985 and 1992 millions of Clipper applications were built, typically for small businesses, and for banks and insurers as front ends to the mainframe. In 1992 Computer Associates bought the company for 190 million dollars and renamed the product CA-Clipper; 5.2 came in 1993, 5.3 in 1995 and the final 5.3b on 20 May 1997. Under its new owner Clipper failed to move from DOS to Windows and almost no new commercial applications were written in it after 1995; Harbour, xHarbour, Xbase++ and FlagShip keep the language alive today.
clipper.depth:
What it was and why it won. Clipper, from Nantucket Corporation and later Computer Associates, started as a native-code compiler for dBASE III databases and later evolved. dBASE ran programs through its interpreter and needed the dBASE product on every machine; Clipper compiled the same language into a DOS executable that ran on its own, faster, without licence fees per seat, and without exposing the source. The one major dBASE feature it did not implement was the interactive dot prompt, which mattered less to the developer shipping an application than to the user exploring a table. In the years between 1985 and 1992 millions of Clipper applications were built, typically for small businesses dealing with client management and inventory; for many smaller businesses a Clipper application designed to their needs was their first experience of software development, and many applications for banking and insurance companies were developed where the system was too small for the mainframe or as a front end to one.

The language grew. As the product matured it added elements of C and Pascal, object-oriented programming and the code-block data type, which hybridized dBASE macros, string evaluation, with function pointers, becoming far more powerful than the original language; Nantucket's Aspen project later matured into the Windows native-code CA-Visual Objects compiler. The releases: Nantucket Clipper Winter '84 on 25 May 1985, Summer '85, Winter '85 on 29 January 1986, Autumn '86 on 31 October 1986, Summer '87 on 21 December 1987, 5.00 in 1990, 5.01 on 15 April 1991 and 5.01 Rev. 129 on 31 March 1992; then CA Clipper 5.20 on 15 February 1993 with 5.2a to 5.2e through February 1995, 5.30 on 26 June 1995, 5.3a on 20 May 1996 and 5.3b on 20 May 1997, the last. The November 1991 New York Times reported Nantucket's success in convincing Soviet developers that buying was preferable to pirating: 2,000 copies sold in the Soviet Union against 250,000 worldwide.

The company and the sale. Nantucket Corporation was started in 1984 by Barry ReBell, management, and Brian Russell, technical, with Larry Heimendinger as president. In 1992 the company was sold to Computer Associates for 190 million dollars and the product was renamed CA-Clipper. It was one of three sales within a year: Borland bought Ashton-Tate and its dBASE, Microsoft bought Fox Software and its FoxPro, and Computer Associates bought Nantucket, as the xBase market peaked.

Decline and afterlife. In the early 1990s, under new ownership, Clipper failed to transition from DOS to Windows, and as a result almost no new commercial applications were written in it after 1995. By then the classically trained programmer expected strong typing, which the original dBASE language lacked; Visual Objects added it optionally, and the four languages that took over, Visual Basic, Microsoft Access, Delphi and PowerBuilder, all provided it. The language itself is actively implemented and extended by others: Xbase++ from Alaska Software and FlagShip commercially, and Harbour and xHarbour as free GPL projects, portable to DOS, Windows, Linux, Unix and macOS with extended libraries. For the network engineer the relevance is practical: a Clipper application on a shared .dbf directory is the reason many NetWare and later Windows file shares existed, its record locking is why the share had to be a real file server, and some of those applications are still running in 2026 on Harbour. The dBASE entry carries the language's parent; the Nantucket, Ashton-Tate and Borland records on the industry timeline carry the companies.

eap.def: The Extensible Authentication Protocol of RFC 3748: a framework of four packet codes that carries any of dozens of authentication methods between a peer and an authenticator, usually over PPP or Ethernet, without needing IP.
eap.context: EAP is not an authentication method; it is the envelope the methods travel in. RFC 3748 (June 2004) defines four codes, Request, Response, Success and Failure, and a Type octet on Requests and Responses that names the method: 1 Identity, 2 Notification, 3 Nak, 4 MD5-Challenge, 5 One-Time Password, 6 Generic Token Card, 254 Expanded Types and 255 Experimental. Everything an enterprise actually deploys, EAP-TLS, PEAP, EAP-TTLS, EAP-FAST, TEAP, EAP-pwd, EAP-SIM and EAP-AKA, is a Type carried inside that envelope. The RFC calls it a lock-step protocol (one Request, one Response, no pipelining) that typically runs directly over data link layers such as PPP or IEEE 802, which is why a device can be authenticated before it has an address. The authenticator, a switch, access point or dial-in server, may act as a pass-through agent, relaying each EAP packet to a backend server inside RADIUS (Remote Authentication Dial-In User Service) EAP-Message attributes (RFC 3579) and acting only on the final Success or Failure. 802.1X is EAP over LAN; the method inside is a separate decision, and the hardest one in a Wi-Fi design.
eap.depth:
The Extensible Authentication Protocol was written so that the link layer would not have to be rewritten every time somebody invented a new way to prove identity. RFC 3748, published in June 2004 by Aboba, Blunk, Vollbrecht, Carlson and Levkowetz, obsoleting RFC 2284, defines a packet of four fields, Code, Identifier, Length and Data, and four codes: 1 Request, 2 Response, 3 Success and 4 Failure. Requests and Responses carry a Type octet in the first position of the Data field, and the Type is where the methods live. The base document itself assigns only the plumbing types: 1 Identity, 2 Notification, 3 Nak (the peer's way of saying it does not support the proposed method and listing the ones it does), 4 MD5-Challenge, 5 One-Time Password, 6 Generic Token Card, 254 Expanded Types for vendor-specific methods and 255 Experimental. Every method that matters in a network today, EAP-TLS at Type 13, EAP-TTLS at 21, PEAP at 25, EAP-FAST at 43, EAP-pwd at 52, TEAP at 55, EAP-SIM at 18 and EAP-AKA at 23, is specified in a document of its own and rides in that Type field.

Two properties of the envelope explain where EAP shows up. The RFC states that EAP "typically runs directly over data link layers such as PPP or IEEE 802, without requiring IP", which is the whole reason it can gate a switch port or a wireless association: the device has no address yet, may never get one, and still has to be identified. And the RFC describes it as a "lock step" protocol, one Request outstanding at a time, each answered by exactly one Response, with retransmission handled by the authenticator and no pipelining. That simplicity costs round trips (a TLS-based method needs many) and it is why EAP conversations over slow or lossy links feel sluggish, but it keeps the state machine small enough to live in a switch ASIC's companion CPU.

The third design decision is the one that created the AAA industry as it exists. The authenticator, the device the peer is physically attached to, does not have to understand the method at all. RFC 3748 allows it to act as a pass-through agent for a backend authentication server, and RFC 3579 (Aboba and Calhoun, September 2003) specifies how: the switch or access point forwards each EAP packet to a RADIUS server encapsulated in EAP-Message attributes (type 79), and every RADIUS packet that carries an EAP-Message must also carry a Message-Authenticator attribute (type 80) to protect it. Where an EAP packet is larger than one attribute, several EAP-Message attributes are placed in order, consecutively, and concatenated at the far end. The switch therefore sees a conversation it cannot read between the supplicant and the server, and acts only on the final Access-Accept or Access-Reject, which carries the EAP Success or Failure. Changing the authentication method in an estate is a change on the server and the clients; the hundreds of switches in between do not care.

That separation is also where the arguments start. Because the methods are independent documents, they differ in what they protect: MD5-Challenge (Type 4, in the base RFC) is a bare challenge-response whose security claims the RFC lists as "Mutual authentication: No" and "Key derivation: No", which rules it out wherever the link needs keys from the authentication, as a wireless link does; the TLS-based methods authenticate the server with a certificate and derive keying material; the tunnelled methods (PEAP, EAP-TTLS, EAP-FAST, TEAP) run a weaker legacy exchange inside a TLS tunnel so that a password can be used without exposing it to the air. The practical consequence for a designer is that "we use 802.1X" says nothing about security until the method is named, and that the common failure in deployments, a client that does not validate the server's certificate inside the chosen method, is a method-level setting that the framework cannot enforce.

The entries on each method in this glossary carry their own RFC facts: EAP-TLS and its certificate on both sides, PEAP and its expired draft, EAP-TTLS and the legacy methods inside it, EAP-FAST and the Protected Access Credential, TEAP and its chaining, EAP-pwd and its password-only exchange, EAP-SIM and EAP-AKA and the operator's SIM. The 802.1X entry covers the LAN carriage (EAPOL), and the RADIUS entry covers the other side of the pass-through.

peap.def: Protected EAP, EAP Type 25: a TLS tunnel authenticated by the server's certificate, inside which a second, weaker EAP method (in practice almost always EAP-MSCHAPv2) authenticates the user with a password.
peap.context: PEAP solves the problem that passwords cannot travel safely in a bare EAP exchange: part one is a TLS handshake in which the server presents a certificate and the client checks it, and part two runs zero or more EAP methods inside the resulting tunnel, protected from eavesdropping and from a rogue authenticator. The specification, draft-josefsson-pppext-eap-tls-eap-10, Protected EAP Protocol (PEAP) Version 2, of 15 October 2004, is an expired Internet-Draft by Palekar, Simon, Salowey, Zhou, Zorn and Josefsson; it assigns Type 25 and describes the goals as protection against rogue authenticators, protection of the confidentiality and integrity of the inner exchange, and identity privacy for the peer. It mandates a Crypto-Binding TLV that ties the inner method to the outer tunnel. The entire security of a PEAP deployment rests on one client setting: whether the supplicant validates the server certificate and the name on it. A client that does not will complete the tunnel with any access point that offers a certificate, and hand its MSCHAPv2 exchange to whoever is on the other end. PEAP with EAP-MSCHAPv2 is the method that made enterprise Wi-Fi possible with Active Directory passwords, and the one that most needs that setting checked.
peap.depth:
Protected EAP was designed for a world in which the thing an enterprise had was a password database and the thing it wanted was wireless authentication. Bare EAP methods that use passwords expose them, or at least expose a challenge-response that can be attacked offline, to anyone in radio range; a certificate for every client, the EAP-TLS answer, was more administration than most organizations would take on. PEAP's answer was to borrow TLS for the first half of the conversation. The draft, draft-josefsson-pppext-eap-tls-eap-10 of 15 October 2004, titled Protected EAP Protocol (PEAP) Version 2 and written by Palekar, Simon, Salowey, Zhou, Zorn and Josefsson, describes it in two parts. In part one the server responds to the peer with a PEAP/Start, a TLS handshake follows using certificate-based ciphersuites, and the server is authenticated by its certificate; the peer may or may not present one. In part two, inside the tunnel the handshake produced, "zero or more EAP methods" run. In practice the inner method is almost always EAP-MSCHAPv2, which is why the combination is written PEAP-MSCHAPv2 and why it maps so naturally onto a Windows domain.

The draft states the goals plainly. PEAPv2 "uses TLS to protect against rogue authenticators, protect against various attacks on the confidentiality and integrity of the inner EAP method exchange and provide EAP peer identity privacy". Identity privacy matters because the EAP Identity exchange that starts every 802.1X conversation happens before any tunnel exists: the outer identity is sent in the clear, and PEAP lets it be a placeholder, with the real username disclosed only inside the tunnel. The draft also makes the Crypto-Binding TLV mandatory, a construction that proves to both sides that the peer who completed the inner method is the same peer who built the outer tunnel; without such binding, tunnelled methods are open to a man-in-the-middle who runs the inner method with the victim and the outer tunnel with the server.

The status of the document is worth recording accurately. The specification is an expired Internet-Draft; PEAP reached ubiquity through implementations, above all the Windows supplicant and the server products that matched it, rather than through a published standard, and the version most widely deployed is not the one the draft describes as version 2. For a practitioner the consequence is that interoperability details live in vendor documentation and in testing, not in an RFC that can be cited against a vendor.

The security of PEAP is almost entirely a client configuration question. The tunnel protects the inner exchange only against parties outside the tunnel; if the supplicant accepts any server certificate, the tunnel can be terminated by an impostor access point, and the inner MSCHAPv2 exchange, challenge and response, is delivered to the attacker, who can attack it offline. Every supplicant therefore has a setting to validate the server certificate, usually with a list of trusted certification authorities and an expected server name, and the difference between a secure PEAP deployment and a credential-harvesting opportunity is whether that setting is enforced, by policy, on every device. Devices outside management, personal phones joining a corporate SSID, are where it is most often left off, and they are also the devices whose users will click through any warning.

Against its siblings, PEAP sits between EAP-TLS, which authenticates the client with a certificate and has no password to steal, and EAP-TTLS, which also builds a TLS tunnel but allows non-EAP legacy methods such as PAP and CHAP inside it. TEAP, the standards-track tunnel method of RFC 7170, was written to replace this generation with one that can chain user and machine authentication and provision credentials inside the tunnel. Where PEAP remains, and it remains almost everywhere passwords are used for Wi-Fi, the design questions are the inner method, the certificate on the server, and the validation on the clients.

eap-ttls.def: EAP Tunneled TLS of RFC 5281, EAP Type 21: a TLS tunnel authenticated by the server, inside which the client can authenticate with almost anything, including PAP, CHAP, MS-CHAP and MS-CHAP-V2 as well as another EAP method.
eap-ttls.context: RFC 5281 (Funk and Blake-Wilson, August 2008, Informational) specifies EAP-TTLSv0 in two phases: a handshake phase in which the server is authenticated by TLS, and a data phase in which the client is authenticated inside the tunnel by "an arbitrary authentication mechanism", which "may itself be EAP, or it may be a legacy protocol such as PAP, CHAP, MS-CHAP, or MS-CHAP-V2". That is its difference from PEAP, which only carries EAP inside the tunnel: EAP-TTLS can front a RADIUS (Remote Authentication Dial-In User Service) or directory backend that only knows how to check a plain password, because PAP inside the tunnel delivers the password to the server in a form it can verify against any store. The RFC allows one-way authentication, the server by certificate and the client by password, and it tells the client that the outer identity "SHOULD NOT include the actual name of the user", using a blank or an anonymous value so that the real identity is only disclosed inside the tunnel. The TTLS server may itself proxy the inner authentication to the user's home AAA server, which is how roaming federations work across administrative domains. As with every tunnelled method, the client must validate the server's certificate or the tunnel protects nothing.
eap-ttls.depth:
EAP-TTLS was written for the authentication back ends that enterprises actually had: directories and RADIUS servers that could verify a plain password, or a legacy challenge-response, but could not run an EAP method themselves. RFC 5281, published in August 2008 by Funk and Blake-Wilson as an Informational document, specifies EAP-TTLSv0 at EAP Type 21 and describes a two-phase exchange. The handshake phase is a TLS negotiation in which the server authenticates to the client with a certificate and the two derive keys; the client may present a certificate too, but the RFC explicitly allows one-way server authentication. The data phase then runs inside the tunnel, where the client authenticates with "an arbitrary authentication mechanism": the RFC says it "may itself be EAP, or it may be a legacy protocol such as PAP, CHAP, MS-CHAP, or MS-CHAP-V2".

That sentence is the practical distinction between EAP-TTLS and PEAP. PEAP tunnels EAP and only EAP, so the inner exchange has to be an EAP method such as EAP-MSCHAPv2, and the back end has to support what that method needs. EAP-TTLS with PAP inside the tunnel hands the server the password itself, protected by TLS on the way, and the server can verify it against anything, including a directory that stores passwords in a form only a plain bind can check. That is why EAP-TTLS/PAP is the usual recommendation when the user store is an LDAP (Lightweight Directory Access Protocol) directory without the hashes MSCHAPv2 needs, and why it appears so often in university and federation deployments.

The RFC takes identity privacy seriously. The EAP Identity exchange precedes the tunnel and is visible to anyone listening, so the outer identity "SHOULD NOT include the actual name of the user"; the client should send a blank username or the string anonymous, keeping any realm part needed for routing, and disclose the real identity only in the data phase. Routing is the other feature that made EAP-TTLS a federation protocol: the TTLS server that terminates the tunnel need not hold the user's credential at all. It may act as a proxy, forwarding the inner authentication to the home AAA server of the user's realm, so that a visitor's password is checked by the visitor's own institution while the visited network only learns that the answer was yes.

The security caveats are those of every tunnelled method. The tunnel is only as trustworthy as the client's check of the server certificate; a supplicant that accepts any certificate will build its tunnel with an impostor and deliver its inner credential, which in the PAP case is the password in clear text inside the attacker's tunnel. The inner legacy method adds nothing to security, it only inherits the tunnel's, so the server certificate, the trust anchor on the client and the expected server name are the controls that matter. And because the inner method can be as weak as PAP, the server side must not expose the inner credential to anything outside the TLS termination point: the back-end path from the TTLS server to the directory is a second place a password can be seen.

In the family tree, EAP-TTLS sits beside PEAP as the second of the tunnelled password methods, with EAP-FAST and then TEAP (RFC 7170) as the later generation that added credential provisioning and cryptographic binding of the inner exchange to the outer tunnel. Where a client can hold a certificate, EAP-TLS removes the password from the picture altogether; where it cannot, EAP-TTLS is the method that lets almost any back end participate.

eap-fast.def: Flexible Authentication via Secure Tunneling, Cisco's EAP Type 43 of RFC 4851: a TLS tunnel that can be established with a Protected Access Credential rather than a server certificate, with the real authentication carried as TLVs inside it.
eap-fast.context: RFC 4851 (Cam-Winget, McGrew, Salowey and Zhou of Cisco, May 2007, Informational) specifies EAP-FAST in two phases: a TLS tunnel, then an exchange of type-length-value objects inside it that carries the inner authentication. What distinguishes it is the Protected Access Credential, the PAC: a PAC-Key, a 32-octet secret shared between peer and server; a PAC-Opaque, a ticket the server can decode but the peer cannot; and PAC-Info, the authority's identity and the credential's lifetime. With a PAC the tunnel can be re-established without server-side state and without a certificate exchange, which was the point for constrained devices and for sites that did not run a PKI (public key infrastructure). The RFC lists the design goals as mutual authentication, immunity to passive dictionary attacks, protection against man-in-the-middle attacks, and efficiency for devices with limited resources. RFC 7170 records that EAP-FAST "has been widely adopted" and that the IETF's EMU working group took it as the basis for TEAP, the standards-track tunnel method. Its weak point in operation was always PAC provisioning: how the first PAC reaches a device safely is a deployment decision, not something the method can guarantee on its own.
eap-fast.depth:
EAP-FAST was Cisco's answer to a problem it had partly created. Password-based wireless authentication needed a tunnel, and the tunnelled methods of the day, PEAP and EAP-TTLS, anchored that tunnel in a server certificate, which meant a certificate authority, a trust anchor on every client and a validation setting that users could turn off. RFC 4851, published in May 2007 by Cam-Winget, McGrew, Salowey and Zhou, all of Cisco, as an Informational document, specifies Flexible Authentication via Secure Tunneling at EAP Type 43. Phase one establishes a TLS tunnel; phase two runs an exchange of TLVs, type-length-value objects, inside it, and the inner authentication, the result, and any additional data travel as TLVs. The structure is close to PEAP's, but the way the tunnel can be built is not.

The Protected Access Credential is the method's signature idea. The RFC defines a PAC in three parts: the PAC-Key, a 32-octet secret shared between the peer and the server; the PAC-Opaque, a ticket that the server created and only the server can interpret, which the peer stores and presents; and PAC-Info, which carries the identity of the authority that issued it and the credential's lifetime. A peer holding a PAC can re-establish the tunnel with it, without a certificate exchange and, in the RFC's words, without the server having to keep state for that peer, since everything the server needs is inside the opaque ticket it wrote. The design goals the RFC lists are mutual authentication, immunity to passive dictionary attacks, protection against man-in-the-middle attacks, and efficiency for devices with limited resources, and the PAC serves the last of those directly.

The PAC also created the method's characteristic operational problem. The first PAC has to get onto the device somehow, and however it is done, that first delivery is the moment the whole scheme's trust is established. Deployments provisioned PACs out of band, or allowed an in-band provisioning exchange whose security properties depended on the mode chosen, and the configuration of that step, on servers and on supplicants, became the thing engineers spent their time on. The method also remained a vendor specification: Informational status, Cisco authorship, and strongest support in Cisco's own clients and servers.

Its legacy is TEAP. RFC 7170, the Tunnel Extensible Authentication Protocol of May 2014 and a Standards Track document, says in its own text that EAP-FAST "has been widely adopted" and was "adopted by the EMU working group as the basis for the standard tunnel-based EAP method". TEAP keeps the TLS tunnel and the TLV structure, keeps PAC provisioning as one option beside certificate provisioning, adds a mandatory Crypto-Binding TLV, and allows several inner methods in sequence, which is how user and machine authentication can be chained in one conversation. A designer meeting EAP-FAST today is usually meeting an older Cisco estate, and the question is whether to move it to TEAP or, where clients can hold certificates, to EAP-TLS.

teap.def: The Tunnel Extensible Authentication Protocol of RFC 7170, EAP Type 55: the standards-track tunnel method that runs zero or more inner EAP methods inside a mutually authenticated TLS tunnel, binds them cryptographically to it, and can provision credentials along the way.
teap.context: RFC 7170 (Zhou, Cam-Winget and Salowey of Cisco and Hanna of Infineon, May 2014, Standards Track) defines TEAP version 1 as "a tunnel-based EAP method that enables secure communication between a peer and a server by using the Transport Layer Security (TLS) protocol to establish a mutually authenticated tunnel". Inside the tunnel, type-length-value objects carry "zero or more EAP methods", which is the feature the market calls EAP chaining: a machine certificate and a user credential can be authenticated in one conversation, so a policy can distinguish a corporate laptop with a logged-in employee from either alone. The tunnel can also provision a Protected Access Credential or a certificate to the peer, and it can carry a password. Two protections are built in rather than optional: a Crypto-Binding TLV that ties each inner method's result to the outer tunnel, defeating the tunnel man-in-the-middle, and EAP channel binding, which lets the peer and server confirm they agree about the network they are on. TEAP is the IETF's successor to PEAP, EAP-TTLS and EAP-FAST, and the RFC records that EAP-FAST was the basis the working group started from.
teap.depth:
By 2014 the IETF had three tunnelled EAP methods in wide use, two of them never published as standards, and a list of things all three lacked. RFC 7170, published in May 2014 by Zhou, Cam-Winget and Salowey of Cisco and Hanna of Infineon as a Standards Track document, is the result of the EMU working group's effort to replace them with one. It defines TEAP version 1 at EAP Type 55 as "a tunnel-based EAP method that enables secure communication between a peer and a server by using the Transport Layer Security (TLS) protocol to establish a mutually authenticated tunnel". The RFC itself names its ancestry: EAP-FAST "has been widely adopted" and was "adopted by the EMU working group as the basis for the standard tunnel-based EAP method". Readers of the EAP-FAST entry will recognize the shape, a TLS tunnel followed by TLVs.

What happens inside the tunnel is where TEAP goes further than its predecessors. The RFC allows "zero or more EAP methods within the protected tunnel", run in sequence, each with its own result. That sequence is what vendors sell as EAP chaining: a device can prove it is a managed machine, with a certificate, and then the user can prove who they are, with a password or a second certificate, in a single 802.1X conversation, and the server can authorize on the combination. Before TEAP the two facts had to be established in separate authentications and correlated by inference, which is why policies that said "corporate device and known user" were so hard to write honestly.

The tunnel is also a provisioning channel. TEAP can provision a Protected Access Credential, the PAC inherited from EAP-FAST, or a certificate, inside the tunnel, so that a device which arrives with only a password can leave with a stronger credential for next time. Passwords themselves can be carried, which keeps the directory-only back end in play. And two protections that were optional or absent in the earlier methods are built in. The Crypto-Binding TLV binds the result of each inner method to the tunnel that carried it, so an attacker cannot relay an inner exchange between a victim and a server while holding the outer tunnel with each; the earlier generation's exposure to that man-in-the-middle was one of the motivations for the work. EAP channel binding lets the peer and the server check that they agree about the network the peer is attached to, which closes a class of attacks in which a rogue network relays a legitimate authentication.

Adoption has followed the usual curve for a method that needs both supplicants and servers: operating-system supplicants and the major AAA servers added it, with the chaining feature as the draw, and estates with existing PEAP or EAP-FAST deployments have moved as their clients allowed. For a designer the decision is now between EAP-TLS for devices that can hold certificates and TEAP where chaining, provisioning or a password back end is required; PEAP and EAP-TTLS remain for compatibility, and the method matrix in the 802.1X and EAP methods article sets the four side by side.

eap-mschapv2.def: Microsoft's CHAP version 2 of RFC 2759, a challenge-response that proves a password without sending it and adds mutual authentication, carried inside EAP and, in practice, inside the PEAP or EAP-TTLS tunnel.
eap-mschapv2.context: RFC 2759 (Zorn of Microsoft, January 2000, Informational) specifies MS-CHAP-V2. Its advance over the first version is mutual authentication, achieved "by piggybacking a peer challenge on the Response packet and an authenticator response on the Success packet": the client answers the server's challenge and sends its own 16-octet Peer-Challenge; the 24-octet NT-Response is computed from the challenges and an MD4 hash of the password using DES; the server then proves it knew the password too. The method needs the server to hold the NT hash of the password, which is why it fits Active Directory and does not fit directories that store passwords in other forms. On its own, over the air, the exchange can be captured and attacked offline, and the RFC already advises that the authenticator "SHOULD limit the number of password retries"; wrapped as an EAP method inside PEAP (PEAP-MSCHAPv2) or EAP-TTLS, the tunnel hides the exchange from eavesdroppers, which is the only configuration in which it should appear on a network today. The tunnel protects nothing if the client does not validate the server's certificate.
eap-mschapv2.depth:
MS-CHAP-V2 is the challenge-response at the bottom of most password-based enterprise Wi-Fi, and it predates Wi-Fi: RFC 2759, published in January 2000 by Glen Zorn of Microsoft as an Informational document, specifies it as a PPP authentication protocol, Microsoft's second extension of CHAP, for dial-up and VPN (virtual private network) clients. The RFC describes the improvement over version 1 as mutual authentication, obtained "by piggybacking a peer challenge on the Response packet and an authenticator response on the Success packet". The server sends a challenge; the client's Response packet carries a 16-octet Peer-Challenge of its own and a 24-octet NT-Response derived from both challenges and an MD4 hash of the user's password, with DES as the cipher; on success the server returns an authenticator response that proves it also knew the password. Neither side ever sends the password, and the client learns whether the server was genuine, which CHAP alone could not tell it.

The protocol's dependence on the NT hash shaped where it could be used. Because the server must compute the same function of the password that the client did, it has to hold the password in the MD4 form Windows stores, or the clear password; a directory that stores salted hashes of another kind cannot verify MS-CHAP-V2 at all. That is why the method pairs naturally with Active Directory, why RADIUS (Remote Authentication Dial-In User Service) servers that front a domain speak it fluently, and why sites with an LDAP (Lightweight Directory Access Protocol) directory of a different lineage are steered towards EAP-TTLS with PAP inside the tunnel instead.

As an EAP method, MS-CHAP-V2 is carried in Request and Response packets and known as EAP-MSCHAPv2; its proper home is inside a tunnel. The challenge-response exchange, captured from the air, can be attacked offline against the password, and the cryptography of the response is DES on a 1990s design; RFC 2759 itself advises that the authenticator "SHOULD limit the number of password retries" against online guessing, and the offline exposure is addressed only by hiding the exchange. PEAP's expired draft describes the inner EAP methods it protects, and RFC 5281 lists MS-CHAP-V2 among the legacy methods EAP-TTLS can carry; PEAP with EAP-MSCHAPv2 inside became the default enterprise Wi-Fi configuration for Windows networks because it combined a method the domain could verify with a tunnel the air could not read.

The security of that arrangement is therefore the tunnel's, and the tunnel's security is the client's certificate validation. An attacker who can persuade a supplicant to complete a TLS tunnel with an impostor access point receives the MSCHAPv2 challenge-response inside it and can attack it offline, which turns a wireless network into a password-collection device; the only defence is a supplicant configured to trust a named server certificate and nothing else. Engineers asked why their security team wants certificates on clients, the EAP-TLS answer, can point at this paragraph: with EAP-TLS there is no password exchange to collect. Where passwords remain, as they do on most networks, EAP-MSCHAPv2 inside PEAP with validation enforced on every client is the configuration, and the retries limit on the server is the second control the RFC already asked for.

eap-pwd.def: EAP Authentication Using Only a Password, RFC 5931 at EAP Type 52: a password-authenticated key exchange that is secure against offline dictionary attacks even with a weak password, and needs no certificates or PKI (public key infrastructure) on either side.
eap-pwd.context: RFC 5931 (Harkins and Zorn, August 2010, Informational) presents EAP-pwd as "a robust authentication method that is secure even when used with a weak password in the presence of a strong adversary". The password "may be a low-entropy one and may be drawn from some set of possible passwords, like a dictionary", and the method still gives an eavesdropper nothing to attack offline: each run of the protocol tests exactly one guess, which is the property that distinguishes a password-authenticated key exchange from a challenge-response such as MS-CHAP-V2. The exchange has three parts, Identity, Commit and Confirm, authenticates both sides, derives the MSK and EMSK that 802.1X needs for link keys, and does so without certificates, so there is no server certificate for a client to fail to validate. Its limits are deployment ones: the server must hold the password or a form of it the method can use, support in supplicants and servers has been narrower than for the tunnelled methods, and the property it offers, no offline guessing, is the one WPA3's handshake later brought to personal networks.
eap-pwd.depth:
Most password methods in the EAP family protect the password by hiding the exchange inside a TLS tunnel; EAP-pwd protects it by changing the mathematics so that there is nothing useful to hide. RFC 5931, published in August 2010 by Harkins and Zorn as an Informational document, specifies EAP Authentication Using Only a Password at EAP Type 52 and states its claim directly: it is "a robust authentication method that is secure even when used with a weak password in the presence of a strong adversary". The RFC is explicit that the password "may be a low-entropy one and may be drawn from some set of possible passwords, like a dictionary", and that the method still resists offline attack.

The mechanism is a password-authenticated key exchange. Rather than sending a function of the password that a listener can test against candidate passwords at leisure, which is what every challenge-response does, the two sides first use their identities and the agreed ciphersuite "to fix an element in the negotiated group called the Password Element", derived from the password, and then prove in the Commit and Confirm exchanges that each holds the same element. The RFC states the requirement it meets: "any advantage an adversary can gain must be directly related to the number of interactions she makes with an honest protocol participant and not through computation", and in its security considerations, "the best advantage an attacker can gain in a single active attack is to determine whether a single guess at the password was correct". An eavesdropper learns nothing to test offline; an active attacker buys one guess per run, and the server can count runs and lock the account. The WPA3 entry describes the same property arriving in personal Wi-Fi, where the older handshake had allowed exactly the offline guessing this design forbids.

Two consequences follow for a network designer. The first is that EAP-pwd needs no certificates and no PKI: there is no server certificate, so there is no client-side validation setting to be left off, which removes the failure that undermines PEAP and EAP-TTLS deployments. The method authenticates both sides, in the RFC's security claims "by proving possession of a shared password", and an MSK and EMSK are derived from the shared secret, so it is complete on its own. The second is that the server must have the password in a form the method can use, which is a question to ask of the directory before choosing it.

The method's adoption has been narrower than its properties might suggest. The tunnelled methods arrived first, were built into the dominant operating-system supplicants and the servers that matched them, and solved the password problem well enough for the organizations that could manage certificate validation; EAP-pwd's support in clients and servers has been partial, and sites choosing it have to confirm both ends. Where it is available it is the method that lets a password be used over the air without a PKI and without the offline exposure of MS-CHAP-V2, and that is a short list.

eap-sim-aka.def: The EAP methods that let a mobile operator's SIM authenticate a device to a network: EAP-SIM (RFC 4186, Type 18) using GSM credentials and EAP-AKA (RFC 4187, Type 23) using the UMTS Authentication and Key Agreement of the USIM.
eap-sim-aka.context: RFC 4187 (Arkko of Ericsson and Haverinen of Nokia, January 2006, Informational) specifies EAP-AKA, EAP Type 23. The authentication runs the same AKA exchange the mobile network uses: the operator's authentication centre produces a random challenge (RAND) and an authentication token (AUTN), the USIM in the device checks the token and returns a result (RES), and the two sides derive keys; the network is authenticated to the SIM as well as the SIM to the network. The RFC positions it against EAP-SIM of RFC 4186, EAP Type 18, which uses the GSM algorithms, with "substantially longer key lengths and mutual authentication" as the differences. Both offer optional identity privacy through pseudonyms, so the permanent identity is not sent on every connection, and fast re-authentication, so a device that recently authenticated can reconnect without a round trip to the home operator. These are the methods under operator Wi-Fi offload and roaming: the credential is the SIM the subscriber already has, the authentication server is the operator's, and the visited network is a pass-through authenticator like any other 802.1X deployment.
eap-sim-aka.depth:
A mobile phone carries a credential that was designed from the start for remote authentication, the SIM, and these two EAP methods let a Wi-Fi network use it. RFC 4187, published in January 2006 by Arkko of Ericsson and Haverinen of Nokia as an Informational document, specifies EAP-AKA at EAP Type 23, the EAP method for the UMTS Authentication and Key Agreement; its companion RFC 4186 specifies EAP-SIM at Type 18 for the older GSM credentials. Both wrap an exchange the mobile network already performs: the operator's authentication centre generates a random challenge, RAND, and in the AKA case an authentication token, AUTN; the (U)SIM in the device computes a response, RES, and session keys; and the server compares. In AKA the token lets the SIM verify that the challenge came from its own operator, so authentication is mutual.

RFC 4187 states the differences from EAP-SIM as "substantially longer key lengths and mutual authentication", which is a polite way of saying that the GSM algorithms had the weaknesses GSM had, and that EAP-AKA is the method operators moved to as USIMs became universal. Both methods add two features on top of the cellular exchange. Identity privacy lets the server issue pseudonyms so that the permanent subscriber identity is not transmitted on every connection, which matters on a radio medium where the first EAP Identity packet is sent in the clear. Fast re-authentication lets a device that authenticated recently reconnect using keys derived from the earlier run, without another round trip to the home operator's authentication centre, which is what makes handover between access points tolerable.

The architecture is pure 802.1X. The access point or controller is a pass-through authenticator; the RADIUS (Remote Authentication Dial-In User Service) conversation travels, often through proxies and across operator boundaries, to a server that can reach the subscriber's home authentication centre; the visited network learns only that the answer was yes and whatever authorization attributes the home network chose to send. Everything that makes roaming work at the cellular layer, the home and visited operators and the agreements between them, reappears here at the Wi-Fi layer, and the AAA proxies in between are where the engineering lives.

For an enterprise network designer the methods are mostly something to recognize rather than to deploy: they appear when an operator's offload or roaming service is hosted on an enterprise or venue network, when a device's supplicant offers them in the method list, and in the server logs of any RADIUS proxy that participates in such a service. Where they are deployed, the operational questions are the ones RFC 4187 already raises: whether pseudonyms are issued so identities are not leaked, how fast re-authentication is bounded, and how the path to the home operator is protected, which is where RadSec and the roaming federations enter.

radius-coa.def: The Dynamic Authorization Extensions to RADIUS of RFC 5176: Disconnect-Request and CoA-Request messages a server sends to a network access server on UDP 3799 to end a session or change its authorization while it is running.
radius-coa.context: Base RADIUS is request-response from the network access server; once it has issued an Access-Accept the server has no way to speak until the NAS asks again. RFC 5176 (Chiba, Dommety and Eklund of Cisco, Mitton of RSA and Aboba of Microsoft, January 2008, Informational, obsoleting RFC 3576) reverses the direction. It defines six codes: 40 Disconnect-Request, 41 Disconnect-ACK, 42 Disconnect-NAK, 43 CoA-Request, 44 CoA-ACK and 45 CoA-NAK. The RFC states that "for either Disconnect-Request or CoA-Request packets UDP port 3799 is used as the destination port", and it names the roles the other way round from normal RADIUS: the Dynamic Authorization Client, which initiates, sits on the server side, and the Dynamic Authorization Server, which receives and acts, is the NAS. A Disconnect ends the session the request identifies; a CoA changes its attributes, typically the VLAN, a filter or a session timeout. A NAS that cannot apply a requested attribute answers CoA-NAK with an Error-Cause of 401 (Unsupported Attribute). CoA is the mechanism under every policy engine's quarantine, posture change and guest expiry: the device stays attached, and the port's authorization changes under it.
radius-coa.depth:
RADIUS as RFC 2865 defines it has one direction of initiative. The network access server asks, the server answers, and after the Access-Accept the server is silent until the NAS has a reason to ask again, which may be hours or, on a wired port, never. Any policy decision that arrives after the session started, a device found to be infected, a guest account expiring, an administrator wanting a port moved to another VLAN, had no channel to travel on. RFC 5176, Dynamic Authorization Extensions to Remote Authentication Dial In User Service, published in January 2008 by Chiba, Dommety and Eklund of Cisco, Mitton of RSA and Aboba of Microsoft as an Informational document obsoleting RFC 3576, supplies that channel.

The extension defines six packet codes that reuse the RADIUS packet format. 40 is Disconnect-Request, answered by 41 Disconnect-ACK or 42 Disconnect-NAK; 43 is CoA-Request, Change of Authorization, answered by 44 CoA-ACK or 45 CoA-NAK. The RFC specifies the destination: "for either Disconnect-Request or CoA-Request packets UDP port 3799 is used as the destination port". Because the initiative is reversed, the RFC also reverses the names: the Dynamic Authorization Client is the party that sends the request, which is the policy server or something acting for it, and the Dynamic Authorization Server is the party that receives it and acts, which is the NAS. A packet capture on a switch therefore shows the switch answering on 3799, which surprises engineers used to seeing it only as a client on 1812 and 1813.

A request identifies the session it is about with the same attributes the session was built from, User-Name, Calling-Station-Id, Acct-Session-Id and the NAS's own identifiers, and a CoA-Request carries the attributes that are to change. The common cases are a new VLAN through the tunnel attributes, a new filter, a shortened Session-Timeout, or a request that the NAS re-authenticate the device. Where the NAS cannot honour an attribute it answers with CoA-NAK and an Error-Cause, and the RFC assigns 401, Unsupported Attribute, to the case where the NAS does not implement what was asked; other Error-Cause values distinguish a session it cannot find from a request it will not accept.

In practice CoA is the mechanism under almost every feature a network access control product advertises as dynamic. Posture assessment that quarantines a device after it has connected, guest access that expires at a set time, a security tool that asks for an endpoint to be isolated, an administrator clicking "re-authenticate" in a console: each ends in a Disconnect-Request or a CoA-Request to the switch or controller the device is on. The device stays attached and the port's authorization changes under it, which is both the feature and the thing to test, since a NAS that silently ignores a CoA leaves the policy engine believing a quarantine happened.

Two operational facts follow. The NAS must be configured to accept dynamic authorization from the specific servers, with the shared secret, on port 3799, and a firewall between the server and the access layer must allow the reverse direction, which the original RADIUS flows never needed. And the shared secret and MD5 protection are the same as base RADIUS, so a server that can send CoA to a switch can disconnect anyone on it; RadSec's TLS protection extends to these messages where both ends support it, and the RadSec entry describes the transport.

radsec.def: RADIUS (Remote Authentication Dial-In User Service) over TLS, RFC 6614: the whole RADIUS packet carried inside a TLS session on TCP port 2083, with both ends authenticated by X.509 certificates and the RADIUS shared secret fixed to the literal string "radsec".
radsec.context: RFC 6614 (Winter of RESTENA, McCauley, Venaas and Wierenga of Cisco, May 2012, Experimental) starts from a plain statement: "RADIUS security is based on the MD5 algorithm, which has been proven to be insecure", and only the password attribute was ever hidden anyway. RadSec "wraps the entire RADIUS packet payload into a TLS stream" over TCP, on port 2083, with mutual X.509 authentication, so the usernames, MAC addresses, EAP exchanges and policy attributes that plain RADIUS sends in the clear are encrypted and the peers are authenticated by certificates rather than by a shared secret per pair. Because the RADIUS packet format still requires a secret for its internal MD5 computations, the RFC fixes it to the string radsec. The main use the RFC names is roaming across administrative domains, where RADIUS proxies belonging to different organizations forward each other's authentications over the public Internet and a per-pair shared secret does not scale; large federations of universities and operators are the motivating case. Inside an enterprise it is the answer to the audit finding that authentication traffic between switches and the policy servers crosses the network unencrypted.
radsec.depth:
RADIUS leaves almost everything it carries in clear text and authenticates its packets with MD5 and a shared secret, a design the protocol's own successor documents stopped defending. RFC 6614, Transport Layer Security (TLS) Encryption for RADIUS, published in May 2012 by Winter of RESTENA, McCauley, Venaas and Wierenga of Cisco as an Experimental document, opens with the diagnosis: "RADIUS security is based on the MD5 algorithm, which has been proven to be insecure". Its remedy is not a new protocol but a new transport. RadSec "wraps the entire RADIUS packet payload into a TLS stream", carried over TCP on port 2083, and authenticates both ends with X.509 certificates.

The design keeps the packets and changes what surrounds them. A RADIUS packet inside the TLS stream is byte for byte the packet RFC 2865 defines, codes, identifier, authenticator and attributes, so servers, proxies and the attribute dictionaries are unchanged and a TLS-terminating front end can hand ordinary RADIUS to an existing back end. Because the format's internal MD5 computations, the User-Password hiding and the response authenticator, still need a shared secret, RFC 6614 fixes it: the secret is the literal string radsec, which carries no security and is there only so the arithmetic can be performed. Security comes from TLS: confidentiality for the usernames, MAC addresses, EAP exchanges and policy attributes that plain RADIUS exposes, integrity for every attribute rather than only the password, and peer authentication by certificate, which replaces the per-pair secret that had to be configured on both ends of every relationship.

The RFC names roaming across administrative domains as the main use, and the motivating deployments were the federations in which universities and operators forward each other's authentications so that a visitor's credentials are checked at home. In such a federation a RADIUS proxy may talk to hundreds of peers it does not operate, over networks nobody controls; a shared secret per pair is unmanageable and the clear-text payload is unacceptable. Certificates issued by a federation authority solve both, and a TCP connection with TLS also gives the proxies something UDP RADIUS never had, a reliable, long-lived channel whose health is observable.

For an enterprise the case is simpler and increasingly common. Auditors who find that every 802.1X conversation and every administrator login crosses the campus or the WAN in a protocol whose only protection is MD5 over a shared secret want it encrypted, and RadSec is how the switches, controllers and policy servers that support it do that. The caveats are support and operations: a device has to implement RadSec on the NAS side as well as the server side; certificates have to be issued to switches and controllers and renewed; and the reverse-direction messages of RFC 5176, Disconnect and Change of Authorization, are protected only where both ends carry them over the same TLS session.

The status is worth stating precisely. RFC 6614 is Experimental, and the IETF's subsequent work on RADIUS transport continued after it; what is deployed under the name RadSec today is this document's protocol, TLS on TCP 2083 with the fixed secret, implemented by the major AAA servers and a growing list of network equipment. The RADIUS entry describes what is being protected, and the article on RADIUS end to end shows where the transport sits in a full conversation.

tacacs-xtacacs.def: The original Terminal Access Controller Access-Control System of the ARPANET, documented in RFC 1492, and Cisco's extended XTACACS: the clear-text, port-49 ancestors of TACACS+, which shares their name and almost nothing else.
tacacs-xtacacs.context: RFC 1492, An Access Control Protocol, Sometimes Called TACACS, published in July 1993 by Finseth of the University of Minnesota as an Informational document, records a protocol created to control access to dial-up lines on the ARPANET. A terminal server sends a username and password to a server on port 49, by UDP or TCP, and receives accept or reject; the credentials travel in clear text. The RFC notes that "Cisco Systems terminal servers implement an extended version of this TACACS protocol", which is XTACACS, with "more types of authentication requests and more types of response codes" than the original. TACACS+ kept the name and the port and replaced everything else: it is a Cisco design of the 1990s, written down in "The Draft" of 1998 and finally documented by RFC 8907 in September 2020, with three separate conversations for authentication, authorization and accounting and a body obfuscated with the shared key. The three are not interoperable, and the plus sign is the whole difference: a device offering "TACACS" in a 1990s menu meant one of the first two, and anything deployed today means the third.
tacacs-xtacacs.depth:
The name TACACS covers three protocols that share a port and a purpose and nothing else, and the history is short enough to keep straight. The first is the ARPANET's. RFC 1492, An Access Control Protocol, Sometimes Called TACACS, published in July 1993 by Finseth of the University of Minnesota as an Informational document, describes a protocol that was created to control access to dial-up lines on the ARPANET: a terminal server that a user has dialled into sends the username and password to an access control server on port 49, over UDP or TCP, and the server answers accept or reject. The document records the protocol as it was found running rather than as a design, which is why its title hedges, and it is explicit that the credentials travel in clear text.

The second is Cisco's extension. RFC 1492 notes that "Cisco Systems terminal servers implement an extended version of this TACACS protocol", known as XTACACS, with "more types of authentication requests and more types of response codes" than the original: the server could be asked not only whether a user might log in, but about connections and other events, and could answer with more than yes or no. It remained a simple query protocol with the same exposure of credentials, and it is the one that early Cisco documentation and configuration keywords mean by the bare word.

The third is TACACS+, which kept the name and TCP port 49 and replaced the design. RFC 8907 of September 2020, the first document to describe it formally, records that it is based on "The Draft" of 1998, a vendor specification circulated for years without being standardized, and that the plus-sign protocol has three distinct packet types for authentication, authorization and accounting, a 12-byte header and a body obfuscated by XOR with MD5-derived padding of a shared key. None of the three interoperates with the others; a TACACS+ server cannot answer an XTACACS client, and a device configured for one is not configured for the other.

For a reader today the distinction matters in two places. In old documentation and in the memory of engineers who ran terminal servers, TACACS means one of the first two, and the warnings about clear-text passwords attached to it are true of them. In anything deployed now the word means TACACS+, whose own weaknesses are of a different kind, obfuscation rather than encryption and a dependence on a protected management network, and whose strengths, per-command authorization and command accounting, the first two never had. The TACACS+ entry covers the living protocol.

mab.def: MAC Authentication Bypass: the 802.1X fallback in which a switch, finding no supplicant on a port, submits the device's MAC address to the RADIUS (Remote Authentication Dial-In User Service) server as its identity, so that printers, phones and other things that cannot authenticate are admitted by a list.
mab.context: Cisco's configuration guide describes MAB as "a MAC-address-based authentication mechanism" for "platforms with no supplicant or not under administrative control", and names the devices: cash registers, fax machines, printers. The mechanism is a RADIUS request built by the switch: "MAB generates a RADIUS request with a MAC address in the Calling-Station-Id (attribute 31) and Service-Type (attribute 6) with a value of 10", Call Check in RFC 2865's list, the value that tells the server to decide on the station identifier rather than on a user. The encyclopaedia's description of the sequence is the one engineers recognize: the port first tries 802.1X, and if nothing answers it authenticates with the MAC address as both username and password. The guide also records that "before standalone MAB support was available, MAB could be configured only as a failover method for 802.1x authentication", and that standalone MAB works on switched ports only. The weakness is the credential: a MAC address is printed on the device and visible on the wire, so MAB admits anything that spoofs an allowed address, which is why the authorization it returns should be a restricted VLAN or filter and why profiling, checking that the device behaves like the printer it claims to be, grew up around it.
mab.depth:
Every 802.1X deployment meets the same wall within a week: the devices that cannot run a supplicant. Printers, IP phones from before the standard, cameras, badge readers, building controllers, lab instruments and the long tail of embedded equipment have no way to answer an EAP-Request Identity, and a port that insists on one simply never opens. MAC Authentication Bypass is the fallback the industry settled on. Cisco's IOS configuration guide, Configuring MAC Authentication Bypass, describes it as "a MAC-address-based authentication mechanism that allows clients in a network to integrate with the Cisco Identity Based Networking Services (IBNS) and Network Admission Control (NAC) strategy using the client MAC address", intended for "platforms with no supplicant or not under administrative control", and it names the examples that every network has: cash registers, fax machines, printers.

The mechanism is simple and entirely on the switch. When 802.1X on a port times out without a supplicant answering, the switch takes the source MAC address of the first frame it sees and builds a RADIUS Access-Request around it. The guide specifies the shape: "MAB generates a RADIUS request with a MAC address in the Calling-Station-Id (attribute 31) and Service-Type (attribute 6) with a value of 10". RFC 3580 fixes the Calling-Station-Id format for 802.1X as the MAC in upper-case hexadecimal with hyphens between octets, and Service-Type 10 is Call Check, which RFC 2865 defines as the NAS asking the server to accept or reject a call "typically based on the Called-Station-Id or Calling-Station-Id attributes", so the server knows to consult a list of addresses rather than a directory of users. The encyclopaedia article on 802.1X describes the sequence the same way: the port first checks for 802.1X and, finding none, authenticates with the device's MAC address as username and password. The guide adds a piece of history, that "before standalone MAB support was available, MAB could be configured only as a failover method for 802.1x authentication", and that standalone MAB is supported on switched ports only; the usual configuration today is an order, 802.1X first, MAB second and web authentication third.

The weakness is the credential. A MAC address is not a secret: it is printed on a label, visible to anyone on the same segment, and trivially changed on most operating systems. MAB therefore admits anything that presents an allowed address, and an attacker who unplugs a printer and clones its MAC inherits whatever the printer was authorized for. The mitigations are about authorization rather than authentication: the RADIUS server returns a restricted VLAN or a downloadable filter for MAB sessions, so that a cloned printer address reaches the print server and nothing else; and profiling, in which the policy engine watches the device's traffic, its DHCP options, its browser strings and its protocols, and withdraws the session, with a RADIUS Change of Authorization, when the thing claiming to be a printer starts behaving like a laptop. The RADIUS CoA entry describes that mechanism.

Operationally MAB is a database problem. Somebody has to maintain the list of permitted addresses, with an owner and a purpose for each, and the list decays as devices are replaced; most deployments feed it from a discovery or asset system rather than by hand, and the audit question is not whether MAB is on but who may add to the list and how an entry is retired. The accounting records MAB sessions generate, Start and Stop with the Calling-Station-Id, are the trail that shows which port a given device was on and when, which is useful far beyond security.

The design rule that follows is to treat MAB as an admission policy for things, with the least authorization that lets each kind of thing work, rather than as authentication. Where a device can hold a certificate, EAP-TLS replaces it; where it cannot, MAB plus a restricted authorization plus profiling is the state of the art, and the web authentication entry covers the third fallback, for the devices that have a browser but no supplicant.

webauth.def: Web authentication: the switch or controller feature that intercepts a new client's first browser request, serves a login page, checks the credentials against a RADIUS (Remote Authentication Dial-In User Service) server and only then opens the port or session, for people on devices that cannot do 802.1X.
webauth.context: Cisco's Catalyst 9300 security guide describes the feature, "known as web authentication proxy", as the way "to authenticate end users on host systems that do not run the IEEE 802.1x supplicant". The sequence is the one every hotel guest has met: "The user initiates an HTTP session", "the HTTP traffic is intercepted, and authorization is initiated. The switch sends the login page to the user", the credentials go to the authentication server, and "if the authentication succeeds, the switch downloads and activates the user's access policy from the authentication server"; on failure the switch serves a fail page, and after the maximum number of attempts "the switch sends the login expired page, and the host is placed in a watch list". The guide describes the switch as "an intermediary (proxy) between the client and the authentication server", detects hosts by ARP and DHCP snooping, and states a limit that explains much modern grief: "HTTPS traffic interception for central web authentication redirect is not supported." The IETF's answer to interception, RFC 8952's captive portal architecture with the DHCP and router advertisement options of RFC 8910, is the standards side; the captive portal entry has the user's view. In the fallback order of a port, web authentication comes after 802.1X and MAB.
webauth.depth:
