Web authentication is the third way onto an authenticated port, after 802.1X for devices with a supplicant and MAC Authentication Bypass for things on a list, and it is the one built for people: a visitor with a laptop that has no supplicant configured, a contractor on a personal device, a student on a campus network. Cisco's Catalyst 9300 security configuration guide, in its chapter on configuring web-based authentication, says to use the feature, "known as web authentication proxy, to authenticate end users on host systems that do not run the IEEE 802.1x supplicant". The design is a man-in-the-middle performed by the network on purpose: the switch sits between the browser and the authentication server and, in the guide's words under Device Roles, "acts as an intermediary (proxy) between the client and the authentication server, requesting identity information from the client, verifying that information with the authentication server, and relaying a response to the client".

The sequence in the guide's Authentication Process section is the one a user experiences as a login page appearing from nowhere. "The user initiates an HTTP session"; "the HTTP traffic is intercepted, and authorization is initiated. The switch sends the login page to the user"; the user enters credentials, which the switch sends to the authentication server over RADIUS; "if the authentication succeeds, the switch downloads and activates the user's access policy from the authentication server" and shows a success page. On failure "the switch sends the login fail page. The user retries the login. If the maximum number of attempts fails, the switch sends the login expired page, and the host is placed in a watch list." The four pages, Login, Success, Fail and Expire, are customizable, and a Local Web Authentication Banner can carry an organization's text or logo on the login page and the result pop-ups. Before any of that can happen the switch has to notice the host, and the guide lists the triggers for a Layer 2 port: an ARP-based trigger that catches hosts with static or dynamic addresses, dynamic ARP inspection, and DHCP snooping, which notifies web authentication when a binding is created. The session is re-authenticated when a host on a Layer 2 interface stops answering ARP probes, or when a host on a Layer 3 interface sends nothing within the idle timeout.

The mechanism's dependence on interception is also its decline, and the guide states the limit without softening: "HTTPS traffic interception for central web authentication redirect is not supported." A browser whose first request is an HTTPS one, which is now most browsers' first request, cannot be redirected without a certificate warning, and the same is true of applications with pinned certificates and of encrypted DNS. The IETF's response was to stop pretending. RFC 8952, Captive Portal Architecture, of November 2020, describes an architecture of user equipment, a provisioning service, a captive portal API server, an enforcement device and a captive portal signal, in which the network tells the device, rather than tricks it, that a portal exists; it states that "solutions MUST NOT require the forging of responses from DNS or HTTP servers". RFC 8910, of September 2020, gives the network the means: DHCPv4 option 114, DHCPv6 option 103 and router advertisement option 37 carry the URI of the captive portal API, replacing a deprecated option 160 that had misbehaved in the field. Operating systems that implement this learn of the portal at address assignment and open it themselves. The captive portal entry describes the user-side view of the same history.

In enterprise deployments the names matter. Local web authentication is the feature described above, with the switch or controller serving the pages; central web authentication moves the portal to the policy engine, with the switch redirecting to it and the engine returning the authorization, usually with a RADIUS Change of Authorization once the user has logged in, which is the configuration the HTTPS limit above is about. Either way the identity established is a person's, checked against the same RADIUS servers and directories as everything else, and the authorization that follows should be the visitor's, a VLAN or a filter that reaches the Internet and nothing internal.

The fallback order on a port is the design summary: 802.1X first, because it authenticates the device with a credential; MAB second, for the things on a list; web authentication third, for the people on devices that can do neither. The 802.1X and MAB entries cover the first two, and the article on web authentication and captive portals sets the enterprise feature beside the standards that are replacing interception.

privilege-creep.def: The slow accumulation of access rights by a person or an account as jobs change and old permissions are never withdrawn, until what they can do bears no relation to what they need to do.
privilege-creep.context: Nobody grants privilege creep; it is what happens when permissions are added for each new task, project or transfer and removed for none, so that a ten-year employee can still reach the systems of every team they have passed through. NIST's control catalogue names the dynamic without the slang: in AC-6(7) it says that "the need for certain assigned user privileges may change over time to reflect changes in organizational mission and business functions, environments of operation, technologies, or threats", and requires a periodic review of assigned privileges to "validate the need for such privileges" and to "reassign or remove privileges, if necessary". Microsoft's documentation on access reviews asks the same two questions of every organization: "As people move teams or leave the company, how do you make sure that their old access is removed?" and warns that "excessive access rights can lead to compromises" and "can also lead to audit findings as they indicate a lack of control over access". The cure is procedural, not technical: joiner, mover and leaver processes tied to the HR record, roles instead of individual grants, time-bounded exceptions, and reviews in which an owner has to say yes to each entitlement again or it is removed.
privilege-creep.depth:
Privilege creep is the name practitioners give to a drift rather than a decision. A person is hired into one job and given the access it needs; they help on a project and are added to its systems; they move to another team and gain that team's groups; they cover for a colleague on leave and inherit an administrator role for the duration; and at no point does anyone remove what the previous step granted, because removal has no deadline and no requester. After a few years the account can reach systems of every team it has passed through, and the picture an access control model paints of who may do what has quietly stopped being true. Service accounts creep the same way, with the difference that nobody is ever transferred away from them.

The standards describe the condition without using the slang. NIST's control catalogue, in the enhancement AC-6(7) Review of User Privileges, says that "the need for certain assigned user privileges may change over time to reflect changes in organizational mission and business functions, environments of operation, technologies, or threats", that "a periodic review of assigned user privileges is necessary to determine if the rationale for assigning such privileges remains valid", and that "if the need cannot be revalidated, organizations take appropriate corrective actions"; the control itself requires organizations to review assigned privileges at a defined frequency "to validate the need for such privileges" and to "reassign or remove privileges, if necessary, to correctly reflect organizational mission and business needs". The account management control AC-2 attacks the sources of the drift: it requires notification when accounts are no longer required, "when users are terminated or transferred" and "when system usage or need-to-know changes for an individual", and asks organizations to "align account management processes with personnel termination and transfer processes", which is the joiner-mover-leaver discipline in regulatory prose.

The vendors who sell the remedy describe the symptom in the same words. Microsoft's overview of access reviews in its identity governance product opens with the questions "As new employees join, how do you ensure they have the access they need to be productive?" and "As people move teams or leave the company, how do you make sure that their old access is removed?", and gives the two consequences: "Excessive access rights can lead to compromises" and "excessive access rights can also lead to audit findings as they indicate a lack of control over access". The product's answer is the one the control describes, recurring reviews, weekly to annual, in which the owners of a group, an application or a role are told to approve or deny each person's continued access, with denial removing it.

Why it matters is the blast radius. An attacker who compromises a crept account inherits years of accumulated reach, and the lateral movement that makes up most of a breach narrative is often not escalation at all but the ordinary use of permissions a person should have lost long ago. The insider case is the same account used by its owner, and the separation of duties entry explains why a single person who has accumulated both halves of a controlled process is a control failure even when no harm has happened. Auditors therefore treat accumulated access as evidence of absent control, which is the second consequence Microsoft names.

The cure is procedural, and the technical measures only make the procedure cheap. Roles rather than individual grants, so that a transfer is a change of role and the old role's permissions leave with it; exceptions granted with an expiry date rather than permanently; account management tied to the personnel record so that transfers and departures trigger removal automatically; reviews in which an owner must positively re-approve each entitlement or it lapses; and logging of privileged actions, which the catalogue's AC-6(9) requires, so that the privileges an account actually uses can be compared with the ones it holds. Least privilege is the principle, RBAC and ABAC are the models, and privilege creep is what happens to any of them without a schedule.

abac.def: Attribute-Based Access Control: authorization decided per request by evaluating attributes of the subject, the object, the operation and the environment against policy, rather than by looking up a role.
abac.context: NIST SP 800-162, Guide to Attribute Based Access Control (ABAC) Definition and Considerations, by Hu, Ferraiolo and Kuhn of NIST with Schnitzer, Sandlin, Miller and Scarfone, published in January 2014 and last updated on 2 August 2019, defines it in one sentence: "ABAC is a logical access control methodology where authorization to perform a set of operations is determined by evaluating attributes associated with the subject, object, requested operations, and, in some cases, environment conditions against policy, rules, or relationships that describe the allowable operations for a given set of attributes." Where a role-based model asks what role the requester holds, an attribute-based policy asks about the requester's department and clearance, the record's classification and owner, the operation, and conditions such as the time, the location and the device, and can express rules such as a clinician may read the records of patients on their own ward during their shift. The price is that the policy, the attribute sources and their freshness become the system: a stale attribute is a wrong decision. In practice it layers on roles rather than replacing them, and the conditions attached to a network session, device posture, time of day, location of the port, are attribute-based decisions whether or not the policy engine uses the acronym.
abac.depth:
Attribute-based access control answers the question role-based control cannot: what if the right answer depends on something about this request, right now, and not only on who is asking. NIST's guide to the subject, Special Publication 800-162, Guide to Attribute Based Access Control (ABAC) Definition and Considerations, written by Hu, Ferraiolo and Kuhn of NIST with Schnitzer of Booz Allen Hamilton, Sandlin and Miller of MITRE and Scarfone, published in January 2014 and last updated on 2 August 2019, gives the definition that the field uses: "ABAC is a logical access control methodology where authorization to perform a set of operations is determined by evaluating attributes associated with the subject, object, requested operations, and, in some cases, environment conditions against policy, rules, or relationships that describe the allowable operations for a given set of attributes."

Each word in that sentence is a component. Subject attributes describe the requester: department, job title, clearance, training completed, employment status. Object attributes describe the thing requested: classification, owner, project, the ward a patient is on. The requested operation is read, write, approve, delete. Environment conditions are what is true at the moment of the request: time of day, the network the request arrives from, the posture of the device, whether a second factor was used. The policy is a set of rules over those attributes, and an access decision is the evaluation of the rules for one request. Nothing has to be pre-computed per user, which is the attraction: a rule such as a clinician may read the records of patients on the ward they are assigned to, during their shift, needs no role per ward per shift, only attributes that are kept current.

The cost is that the attributes are now the system. A role-based model fails when roles multiply; an attribute-based model fails when an attribute is stale, missing or sourced from a system nobody owns, because a wrong attribute produces a confident wrong decision at every request. The guide's title, with its word considerations, signals how much of the document is about governance: who is authoritative for each attribute, how it is kept fresh, how policies are written, tested and audited, and how a decision can be explained afterwards. Auditing is harder than with roles, since there is no static list of who may do what to review, only policies and the attribute values that held at the time; logging the attributes used for each decision becomes part of the design.

In practice the two models coexist. Roles carry the bulk of an organization's entitlements, because most access really does follow the job, and attributes add the conditions: this role, but only from a managed device; this role, but only during business hours; this permission, but only on records the requester owns. Network access control engines have worked this way for years without using the acronym: an 802.1X or MAB session's authorization is decided from the identity, the device's posture and profile, the location of the port or the SSID and the time, and changed with a RADIUS (Remote Authentication Dial-In User Service) Change of Authorization when an attribute changes. The RBAC entry describes the model this one refines, and the least privilege entry the principle both exist to serve.

separation-of-duties.def: The control that no single person should hold enough privilege to misuse a system alone, so that completing a sensitive action requires two people, or two roles that the same person cannot hold.
separation-of-duties.context: NIST's glossary, citing SP 800-192, defines separation of duty as "the principle that no user should be given enough privileges to misuse the system on their own", with the classic example: "the person authorizing a paycheck should not also be the one who can prepare them". It "can be enforced either statically (by defining conflicting roles, i.e., roles which cannot be executed by the same user) or dynamically (by enforcing the control at access time)", which is the static and dynamic separation that the RBAC model expresses as constraints on roles. The control catalogue's AC-5 requires organizations to identify and document the duties to be separated and to "define system access authorizations to support separation of duties", and explains that the control "addresses the potential for abuse of authorized privileges and helps to reduce the risk of malevolent activity without collusion", with the example that "security personnel who administer access control functions do not also administer audit functions". The principle is Saltzer and Schroeder's separation of privilege of 1974 in organizational form: "a protection mechanism that requires two keys to unlock it is more robust and flexible than one that allows access to the presenter of only a single key".
separation-of-duties.depth:
Separation of duties is the control that refuses to trust any one person completely, and it is older than computing: the bookkeeper who records the payments does not sign the cheques. NIST's glossary, citing Special Publication 800-192, defines it as "the principle that no user should be given enough privileges to misuse the system on their own", gives the canonical example, "the person authorizing a paycheck should not also be the one who can prepare them", and names the two ways of enforcing it: "either statically (by defining conflicting roles, i.e., roles which cannot be executed by the same user) or dynamically (by enforcing the control at access time)". Static separation says the two roles may never both be assigned to one person; dynamic separation allows the assignment but forbids both being active in the same session, so that the person who can both prepare and approve cannot do both to the same transaction.

The principle's computing ancestor is the one Saltzer and Schroeder listed just before least privilege. Their separation of privilege reads: "Where feasible, a protection mechanism that requires two keys to unlock it is more robust and flexible than one that allows access to the presenter of only a single key." They credit Needham in 1973 with pointing out its relevance to computer systems, and the reasoning is the organizational one: once the two keys are held by different programs, organizations or people, no single accident, deception or breach of trust is sufficient to compromise what they protect.

The control catalogue turns it into a requirement. AC-5, Separation of Duties, asks organizations to identify and document the duties that must be separated and to "define system access authorizations to support separation of duties". Its discussion explains the aim, that the control "addresses the potential for abuse of authorized privileges and helps to reduce the risk of malevolent activity without collusion": a control that one person can defeat alone is defeated by one dishonest or one compromised person, while a control that needs two makes them conspire, which is harder, rarer and more often detected. The examples the catalogue gives are the ones infrastructure teams recognize: "dividing mission or business functions and support functions among different individuals or roles, conducting system support functions with different individuals, and ensuring that security personnel who administer access control functions do not also administer audit functions". The last is the one most often missed in small teams, where the administrator of the systems is also the administrator of the log server that would record their actions.

In the access models, separation of duties is a constraint. The RBAC model expresses it as mutually exclusive roles, static or dynamic, and an attribute-based policy can express it as a rule that the approver of a record may not be its author. In operations it is a change process in which the engineer who writes a configuration change is not the one who approves it, a deployment pipeline in which the person who can merge code cannot alone promote it to production, a key ceremony that needs two custodians, and an accounting design in which the people who administer the network devices cannot alter the TACACS+ and syslog records of what they did. Privilege creep is its slow enemy: a person who accumulates roles across transfers eventually holds both halves of a separated duty without anyone having decided it, which is why the catalogue says separation "is enforced through the account management activities" of AC-2 and why access reviews check conflicting combinations as well as excess.

The entries beside this one complete the picture: least privilege for the principle that each person should hold the minimum, RBAC and ABAC for the models that express the constraints, privilege creep for the drift that erodes them, and accounting for the records that let a reviewer see whether the separation held.

as-400.def: IBM's Application System/400, the midrange computer announced in June 1988 and released that August, whose operating system and architecture survive today as IBM i on Power Systems: a single-level store, an object-based machine interface and an integrated relational database that have kept forty-year-old applications running on current hardware.
as-400.context: The AS/400 was the Silverlake system, built by a skunkworks at IBM Rochester, Minnesota, named after a lake in the town and officially under way from December 1985 after the company-wide Fort Knox project to unify its midrange lines had failed; IBM announced it on 21 June 1988 with more than 1,000 software packages and released it in August as the successor to the System/36 and System/38. Its operating system, OS/400, descends from the System/38's and was released on 26 August 1988; it became i5/OS in 2004 and IBM i in 2008, the i standing for integrated. The architecture is the reason the line still exists: the Technology Independent Machine Interface presents applications with a platform-independent instruction set that is translated to native code below it, so that when IBM replaced the 48-bit IMPI processors with 64-bit PowerPC-derived chips in 1995 the applications did not notice, and again when POWER4 arrived in 2001. By the end of 1990 an estimated 111,000 systems were installed and the line earned $14 billion that year; about 500,000 had shipped by 1997. The hardware was renamed AS/400e in 1997, eServer iSeries in 2000, eServer i5 in 2004 and System i in 2006, and in 2008 it merged with the System p into IBM Power Systems. IBM i 7.6 shipped on 18 April 2025, with RPM and YUM packaging for open-source software and TN5250 still carrying the green screens.
as-400.depth:
The AS/400 is the computer that proved an architecture could outlive every piece of hardware it ran on. IBM's Application System/400, in the encyclopaedia's account, was a family of midrange computers announced in June 1988, on 21 June as the Silverlake system with more than 1,000 software packages available at launch, and released in August of that year as the successor to the System/36 and the System/38. It came out of IBM Rochester, in Minnesota, where a skunkworks named for Silver Lake in the town had been officially at work since December 1985 after Fort Knox, the company's attempt from 1982 to consolidate the System/36, System/38, 8100, Series/1 and 4300 lines on a single 801-based processor, had failed. The numbers that followed explain why the name still carries weight: an estimated 111,000 installations by the end of 1990 and annual revenue of $14 billion that year, 250,000 systems by 1994 and about 500,000 shipped by 1997.

The idea underneath is the Technology Independent Machine Interface, TIMI, inherited from the System/38. Applications are compiled to a platform-independent instruction set and translated to the processor's native code below that interface, so that the processor can change without the applications being recompiled or even knowing. The article records the proof. The first machines used the 48-bit CISC IMPI processors of the System/38 lineage; in 1995 IBM moved the line to 64-bit PowerPC-derived processors, the RS64 family, following Frank Soltis's 1991 proposal, made at Jack Kuehler's request, to adopt a PowerPC variant for the AS/400 after an in-house design had been cancelled; POWER4 followed in 2001, then POWER5 and POWER6; and through all of it the applications written for the 1988 machine kept running. Few platforms can make that claim across a change of word size and instruction set, and it is the reason so much of the world's inventory, banking and manufacturing still runs on this line.

The operating system carries the other half of the design. OS/400, released on 26 August 1988, is described in the IBM i article as an evolution of the System/38's Control Program Facility with compatibility layers for the System/36's SSP and for AIX; it exposes the Machine Interface for hardware independence, uses object-based addressing on a single-level store, in which memory and disk form one address space and every thing on the system is a typed object, and integrates a relational database so tightly that the database is not a product installed on the system but a property of it. It was renamed i5/OS in 2004, when the hardware became the eServer i5, and IBM i in 2008, "the i standing for integrated". Fixes arrive as PTFs, program temporary fixes; open-source software arrives through RPM packages and YUM; and the terminal protocol of the green screen is TN5250, which is why that number appears in firewall rules at companies that have never bought a terminal.

The hardware's names changed with IBM's marketing. The AS/400 Advanced Series came in 1994 and the AS/400e in 1997; in 2000 the line became the eServer iSeries, sharing the POWER4 processor with the pSeries; in 2004 the eServer i5; in 2006 the System i; and in 2008 IBM consolidated the System i and the System p into IBM Power Systems, so that IBM i and AIX share one hardware line. The infobox of the AS/400 article records the original line as discontinued on 30 September 2013, which is a statement about the name rather than the platform: IBM i 7.6 was released on 18 April 2025, and the RS/6000, announced in February 1990 as an internal competitor, became the sibling it now shares hardware with.

For a reader of this glossary the AS/400 sits beside AIX, OpenVMS and the Unixes as one of the long-lived enterprise platforms a network engineer meets rather than administers: the host behind a TN5250 session, the system whose batch jobs define the maintenance window, the box in the corner of the data centre that cannot be patched on the project's timetable because it is the business. IBM's industry record carries the company's side of the story.

osi-model.def: The seven-layer reference model of network communication, from the physical signal at layer 1 to the application at layer 7.
osi-model.context: A standard, not folklore: ISO/IEC 7498-1:1994 and ITU-T X.200, both still in force. Its protocols lost to TCP/IP, but its numbering became the industry's vocabulary for saying where a problem lives.
osi-model.depth:
The internet's own architecture never had seven layers. RFC 1122, the host requirements of 1989, lists four, application, transport, internet and link, and says its application layer 'essentially combines the functions of the top two layers' of the OSI model, presentation and application. Session has no protocol of its own in the internet suite to point at.

What survived is the map. 'Layer 2' means the link and its frames, 'Layer 3' the IP packet and routing, 'Layer 4' TCP and UDP and their ports, 'Layer 7' the application; the numbers let a network team and an application team agree in one sentence on which half of a problem is whose. The map bends wherever one device does several jobs, a load balancer terminating TLS or a tunnel carrying Layer 2 inside UDP, which is why engineers use the layers as a vocabulary rather than a law.

oui.def: The organizationally unique identifier (OUI) is the 24-bit prefix that the Registration Authority of the Institute of Electrical and Electronics Engineers (IEEE) assigns to an organization. It forms the first three octets of the media access control (MAC) addresses that organization issues, and identifies it inside other protocols.
oui.context: The Registration Authority of the Institute of Electrical and Electronics Engineers (IEEE) sells media access control (MAC) address space in three sizes. A MAC Address Block Large (MA-L) brings an organizationally unique identifier (OUI) of its own and 2^24 (about 16.8 million) 48-bit addresses, which the IEEE calls EUI-48 (48-bit Extended Unique Identifier). A MAC Address Block Medium (MA-M) brings 2^20 addresses under a 28-bit prefix and a MAC Address Block Small (MA-S) 2^12 under a 36-bit one; both share their first 24 bits with other buyers, so a lookup that reads only three octets cannot name their owner. Two bits of the first octet decide whether a lookup means anything at all: the group bit marks multicast and broadcast, and the local bit marks an address set by software, such as the randomized Wi-Fi addresses that phones now use by default, which have no vendor. The same 24-bit number also labels vendor-specific fields in other protocols, from the Subnetwork Access Protocol (SNAP) header to the organizationally specific elements of the Link Layer Discovery Protocol (LLDP).
oui.depth:
What it is, exactly. The guidelines of the Registration Authority of the Institute of Electrical and Electronics Engineers (IEEE) define the organizationally unique identifier (OUI) as 'a 24-bit (three octet) sequence' that identifies a company, organization, entity, manufacturer or vendor. Octet 0 is the most significant; its lowest bit is called the M bit and the next one the X bit, and in every OUI the IEEE assigns both are zero. The IEEE writes an OUI as octets separated by hyphens (AC-DE-48 is its own example) or as six hexadecimal digits. Extended with 24 more bits chosen by the assignee, an OUI becomes a 48-bit Extended Unique Identifier (EUI-48), which is what a media access control (MAC) address is when it is globally unique; extended with 40 bits, it becomes an EUI-64. An OUI is not an address, and it does not certify who built a device: it names the organization that registered the block. Its sibling, the Company ID (CID), comes from the same 24-bit space with the X bit set to one and, by rule, cannot be used to build EUI-48 or EUI-64 values.

What is sold. The Registration Authority assigns address blocks in three sizes. A MAC Address Block Large (MA-L) includes an OUI and yields 2^24 EUI-48 and 2^40 EUI-64 identifiers. A MAC Address Block Medium (MA-M) yields 2^20 and 2^36 under a 28-bit prefix and 'does not include an OUI assignment': its first 24 bits are an OUI that stays assigned to the IEEE, so sixteen buyers share it. A MAC Address Block Small (MA-S) yields 2^12 and 2^28 under a 36-bit prefix called an OUI-36, again cut from an OUI the IEEE holds. The medium and small blocks have existed since 1 January 2014; the MA-S replaced the Individual Address Block (IAB), a block of 4,096 addresses that the IEEE cut from just two of its own OUIs, 00-50-C2 and then 40-D8-55. The rules are written to save space: a first-time customer cannot buy an MA-L, and a further block is granted only on certification that at least 95 per cent of the current one is in use. The public listings downloaded on 12 November 2026 held 40,481 MA-L, 6,685 MA-M and 7,275 MA-S assignments, 224 CIDs and 4,575 historical IABs. Of the MA-L rows, 1,593 were in the name of Apple, 1,416 of Huawei Technologies, 1,257 of Cisco Systems and 442 of the IEEE Registration Authority itself, the bases from which the smaller blocks are cut; 107 were listed as Private, an option that publishes the assignment and withholds the name of the assignee.

Where it came from. Ethernet was first specified by Digital Equipment Corporation, Intel and Xerox, and its address blocks were at first handed out by Xerox; Request for Comments (RFC) 9542 records that the IEEE Registration Authority has been the registration authority for Ethernet parameters since 1986. The registry still shows the origin. The prefix 00-00-00 is registered to Xerox Corporation, and the guidelines note that about 18 of the 24-bit BlockIDs assigned to early Ethernet implementers, before IEEE Std 802.3-1985 was approved, have the X bit set to one, which no modern OUI may have; the listing holds exactly 18 such rows today, among them 02-60-8C (3Com) and AA-00-03 and AA-00-04 (Digital Equipment Corporation). When the IEEE 802 committee began its work in 1980 the 48-bit space was meant to last 100 years, and the Registration Authority still manages it towards 2080: new high-volume applications are pushed to EUI-64, and the older name MAC-48 is declared obsolete in favour of EUI-48.

Two bits to read first. When an identifier is used as a MAC address, the M bit is the individual/group (I/G) bit and the X bit is the universal/local (U/L) bit. Ethernet transmits each octet lowest bit first, the reverse of the order in which the Internet Engineering Task Force (IETF) writes bits, so the I/G bit is the first bit of a destination address to reach the wire. In hexadecimal the second digit gives both bits away: an odd digit is a group address (multicast or broadcast), and 2, 6, A or E is a locally administered unicast address. In either case the first three octets are not an OUI, and a lookup has nothing to say. Since the amendment IEEE Std 802c-2017 the local space has an optional structure, the Structured Local Address Plan (SLAP), which uses the next two bits, Y and Z, to split it into four quadrants: administratively assigned, extended local (where addresses built from a CID live, a CID having M, X, Y and Z equal to 0, 1, 0 and 1), standard assigned, and reserved.

Why a lookup so often finds nobody. A universal address follows its device, and RFC 9724 (March 2025) describes the result: on a shared medium, especially over the air, it is relatively easy to track a device by observing its address, both in the probe requests it sends while scanning and in the frames it exchanges once associated. The remedy uses the local bit to generate random addresses. IEEE Std 802.11aq specified a randomization mechanism in 2018, and the operating systems made it the default. Android sets the locally administered bit to 1 and the unicast bit to 0 and randomizes the other 46 bits; it has done so by default since Android 10, keeping one address per network until a factory reset, and from Android 12 re-randomizes it in some cases. Apple devices use a different private Wi-Fi address for each network from iOS 14, and from iOS 18 and macOS Sequoia 15 can rotate it every two weeks. Windows offers random hardware addresses for all networks or for a chosen one. For the engineer this ends several habits at once. A randomized address has no vendor, so the honest result of looking one up is none; and anything keyed on a stable address, from reservations and allow-lists to remembering a device at a captive portal, either needs the persistent form or another identifier, which is why Apple tells organizations to update their Wi-Fi security or to switch the feature off through a device management profile.

Beyond addresses. The same three octets identify organizations inside other protocols. In the Subnetwork Access Protocol (SNAP) header of IEEE 802.2 Logical Link Control (LLC), the octets AA-AA-03 are followed by an OUI and a two-octet protocol number that the owner of the OUI assigns; RFC 1042 (February 1988) carries the Internet Protocol (IP) this way, with an organization code of zero followed by the EtherType. EtherType 88-B7, the OUI Extended EtherType, does the same job without LLC. In the Link Layer Discovery Protocol (LLDP), every organizationally specific type-length-value (TLV) element has type 127 and begins with an OUI and a one-octet subtype: 00-80-C2 for IEEE 802.1, 00-12-0F for IEEE 802.3 and 00-12-BB for the Telecommunications Industry Association's LLDP-MED (Media Endpoint Discovery). The IEEE's guidelines add World Wide Names in storage and clock identities in IEEE Std 1588, and its registry pages add Bluetooth device addresses. The Internet Assigned Numbers Authority (IANA) holds an OUI of its own, 00-00-5E: the virtual MAC addresses of the Virtual Router Redundancy Protocol (VRRP), 00-00-5E-00-01-00 to 00-00-5E-00-01-FF, come from it, and so does a range reserved for documentation, 00-00-5E-00-53-00 to 00-00-5E-00-53-FF, the MAC counterpart of an example domain name.

The OUI also leaked into layer 3. RFC 4291 (February 2006) built IPv6 interface identifiers from a MAC address by inserting FF-FE between the OUI and the device part and inverting the universal/local bit, the Modified EUI-64 format, so an address formed by stateless address autoconfiguration (SLAAC) carried the maker's prefix and the device's own number wherever the device went. RFC 8064 (February 2017) changed the recommendation: stable link-layer addresses should not be embedded in interface identifiers, and the opaque scheme of RFC 7217 is the default for stable addresses. The IEEE itself now deprecates the mapping of an EUI-48 to an EUI-64, because with MA-M and MA-S blocks it can create duplicates.

In practice. Wireshark resolves the prefix of every address it shows from data taken from the IEEE Registration Authority, compiled into the program in current versions and printable with tshark -G manuf; its manuf format writes prefixes with colons and accepts a length after the address (00:50:C2:00:30:00/36), which is what the smaller blocks need. The IEEE's own advice for a search is the same: if the first 24 bits match an OUI assigned to the IEEE Registration Authority, search the first 28 or 36 bits, because the owner is one level down. The listing is also where to check a vendor. On 12 November 2026 it had 00-01-D7 registered to F5, 00-09-0F to Fortinet, 00-E0-2B to Extreme Networks, 00-00-0C to Cisco Systems, and 00-0C-29 and 00-50-56 to VMware; large makers hold many blocks, so one prefix is never the whole answer.

What goes wrong. A prefix names a registrant, which may be the maker of the network chip or module (Intel, Texas Instruments and Espressif hold hundreds of MA-L blocks each) and not the brand on the case. Uniqueness is a policy, not a guarantee: the IEEE says it makes a concerted effort to avoid duplicate assignments, does not guarantee that none has occurred, and depends on assignees using their blocks properly. And an OUI authenticates nothing. Any Linux host can change the station address of an interface with ip link set and the address keyword, so a rule that trusts a prefix trusts whoever types it. Switches that place a port in the voice network when the source address matches a table of telephone makers' OUIs, as Cisco's small business switches do, are the usual example.

ethertype.def: The two-octet field after the source address of an Ethernet frame, or after a VLAN (virtual local area network) tag, that names the protocol carried inside: 0x0800 for IPv4 (Internet Protocol version 4), 0x86DD for IPv6 (Internet Protocol version 6), 0x0806 for ARP (Address Resolution Protocol).
ethertype.context: Values of 0x0600 (1536) and above are types; values up to 1500 (0x05DC) are a length, the original IEEE (Institute of Electrical and Electronics Engineers) 802.3 reading of the same field, and are followed by an 802.2 Logical Link Control (LLC) header that labels the payload in its own way. The IEEE Registration Authority assigns EtherTypes; IANA (the Internet Assigned Numbers Authority) keeps an informational list of those the internet uses. Tags are announced the same way: 0x8100 opens an IEEE 802.1Q tag, and the EtherType of the payload follows four octets later.
ethertype.depth:
EtherType is a 16-bit protocol identifier carried in an Ethernet frame. In the simplest case it follows the destination and source media access control (MAC) addresses, six octets each, so it closes the 14-octet header that Linux describes in its if_ether.h constants (ETH_ALEN 6, ETH_HLEN 14, ETH_DATA_LEN 1500), and it tells the receiver which protocol handler gets the data that follows. RFC (Request for Comments) 9542, the Best Current Practice of the Internet Engineering Task Force (IETF) on IEEE (Institute of Electrical and Electronics Engineers) 802 parameters, published in April 2024 and obsoleting RFC 7042, defines EtherTypes as 16-bit identifiers that, read as unsigned integers, are equal to or larger than 0x0600. It sets them beside the other way an 802 frame can label its contents: a length field followed by a pair of 8-bit link service access points (LSAPs), one for the destination handler and one for the source, which is the Logical Link Control (LLC) format. An EtherType names the protocol directly inside the frame and nothing deeper; the transport and the application are the business of the headers that follow.

One field, two meanings, settled by a threshold. Ethernet was first specified by Digital Equipment Corporation, Intel and Xerox, hence the name DIX (Digital, Intel, Xerox) Ethernet, and that version used the field as a type. IEEE 802.3 first used it as a length and later accepted both readings. Rich Seifert described the rule to the IEEE 802.1 list on 18 April 1996 while the 802.3x supplement was in draft: values of 0x0600 (1536) or more are Type fields, values of 0x05DC (1500) or less are Length fields, and 0x05DD to 0x05FF are left undefined, in intent kept back for a larger frame once VLAN (virtual local area network) tags arrived; the existing 802.3, he noted, said nothing about Type values. IEEE 802.3x-1997 made the rule part of the standard. RFC 9542 states it from the internet's side: EtherTypes are 'equal to or larger than 0x0600', and a length must stay below 0x5DD 'or it could be mistaken as an EtherType'. A type carries no length, and the minimum Ethernet payload is 46 octets, so a protocol carried by EtherType needs its own length field when short messages are padded. RFC 894 (Charles Hornig, April 1984), which set 0x0800 for IP (Internet Protocol) over Ethernet, says exactly that: the data field is padded with zeros to the minimum, and the padding is not counted in the IP header's total length.

Who assigns them. Xerox kept the list at first; RFC 9542 records that the IEEE Registration Authority has been responsible since 1986, and the IEEE public listing still shows the earliest history, with 0x0600, the lowest type, assigned to Xerox, 0x0800 registered to Xerox for IPv4 (Internet Protocol version 4), and a few hundred values below 0x0600 marked invalid as an EtherType since 1983. The listing holds about 3,560 distinct values, some 745 of them registered as private, without the protocol named. A new public assignment costs US$4,170, and the Registration Authority does not accept requests for a chosen value. IANA (the Internet Assigned Numbers Authority) does not assign EtherTypes at all: its IEEE 802 Numbers page is an informational copy of those of interest to internet protocols, last updated on 3 November 2024 and maintained with an expert, Donald Eastlake. Because the space is scarce, an Internet Engineering Steering Group (IESG) statement of 1 May 2023 says the IEEE will not assign an EtherType to a new IETF protocol until the IESG has approved it for publication, and that requests for IETF protocols now go through the IESG. For development there are two Local Experimental EtherTypes, 0x88B5 and 0x88B6, which no product should ship with.

The values worth remembering. 0x0800 is IPv4, 0x0806 ARP (Address Resolution Protocol), 0x8035 RARP (Reverse Address Resolution Protocol) and 0x86DD IPv6 (Internet Protocol version 6). 0x8100 is the Customer VLAN tag of IEEE 802.1Q, listed by IANA as the 'Customer VLAN Tag Type (C-Tag, formerly called the Q-Tag)' and initially registered to Wellfleet; 0x88A8 is the Service VLAN tag (S-Tag) of provider bridging, which the IEEE listing also names as the Backbone VLAN tag (B-Tag); 0x88E7 is the instance tag of Provider Backbone Bridging. 0x8847 and 0x8848 are MPLS (Multiprotocol Label Switching), the second for upstream-assigned labels; 0x8863 and 0x8864 are the discovery and session stages of PPPoE (Point-to-Point Protocol over Ethernet); 0x8809 is the Slow Protocols type that carries the Link Aggregation Control Protocol (LACP) and Ethernet OAM (operations, administration and maintenance); 0x888E is IEEE 802.1X port-based access control, which Linux calls ETH_P_PAE; 0x88CC is the Link Layer Discovery Protocol (LLDP); 0x88E5 is MACsec (media access control security, IEEE 802.1AE); 0x88F7 is the Precision Time Protocol of IEEE 1588; and 0x894F is the Network Service Header of RFC 8300.

Tags are EtherTypes too. RFC 9542 describes a tag as a fixed-length prefix identified by an EtherType and followed by another tag, the real EtherType, or an LSAP; tags carry no length of their own, and in the RFC's words a device cannot, in general, safely process anything past an EtherType it does not understand. An 802.1Q tag is four octets starting with 0x8100, so a receiver that finds it reads the EtherType of the payload four octets later. Provider networks stack a second, outer tag, standardized as 0x88A8. Before that value existed some equipment used 0x9100, which Wikipedia lists as a pre-standard Q-in-Q value and the Linux header keeps as ETH_P_QINQ1, marked deprecated and not an officially registered value; it has no entry in the IEEE listing. The mismatch still matters. Extreme Networks' Switch Engine, which calls a stacked VLAN a VMAN (virtual metropolitan area network), its own name for IEEE 802.1ad provider bridging, sends 0x88a8 by default, lets an operator set a primary and, since ExtremeXOS 12.1, a secondary value with configure vman ethertype, and warns that a VMAN crossing a third-party device must use the ethertype that device expects.

The other ways an EtherType travels. On 802 media that do not carry a type field, the Subnetwork Access Protocol (SNAP) carries one inside LLC: RFC 1042 (J. Postel and J. Reynolds, February 1988) puts IP and ARP on 802.3, 802.4 and 802.5 networks with both service access points set to 170 (0xAA), control 3, a 3-octet organization code of zero and then the EtherType, 2048 for IP and 2054 for ARP, in an 8-octet LLC and SNAP header. RFC 9542 adds the reverse case: the OUI (organizationally unique identifier) Extended EtherType 0x88B7, followed by an OUI and a 2-octet protocol number, labels a protocol defined by an organization rather than by the IEEE. EtherTypes also appear outside Ethernet framing altogether, in the protocol type field of Generic Routing Encapsulation (GRE), in the Geneve encapsulation header and in Next Hop Resolution Protocol messages.

Where the two readings still collide. Jumbo frames of around 9,000 octets cannot express their length in a Length field without falling into the EtherType range, which broke the LLC frames that Intermediate System to Intermediate System (IS-IS) uses. Wikipedia records that the IETF IS-IS working group proposed 0x8870 to mark LLC frames longer than 1,500 octets, that the IEEE 802.3 working group first rejected it, and that 802.1 adopted it about 15 years later in 802.1AC-2016, briefly as 0xC9D1 until a 2018 corrigendum restored 0x8870; RFC 9542 now names 0x8870 as the LLC encapsulation EtherType, a length indication of nonspecific length. Security devices care about the threshold as well. Cisco's ASA (Adaptive Security Appliance) documentation for transparent (bridging) mode says the firewall drops packets that lack a valid EtherType of 0x600 or more, with exceptions for bridge protocol data units (BPDUs) and IS-IS, that BPDUs pass by default and need an EtherType access control list (ACL) to be denied, and that non-IP traffic such as AppleTalk, IPX (Internetwork Packet Exchange), BPDUs and MPLS passes only when an EtherType ACL permits it.

In captures and filters. Wireshark exposes the field as eth.type, an unsigned 16-bit value, or as eth.len when it holds a length, and since version 1.8.0 flags values in the undefined gap as eth.invalid_lentype; the zeros added to reach the minimum size show up as eth.padding. In tcpdump and libpcap, ether proto takes a number or a name (ether proto 0x88cc selects LLDP; arp, ip and ip6 are among the names), and the vlan and mpls keywords move the decoding offsets by four octets each time they appear, so a filter written for untagged traffic silently misses the same packets on a trunk unless vlan is added. On Linux, a packet socket binds to one EtherType or to ETH_P_ALL (0x0003), a pseudo-value that is not an EtherType and that the header annotates 'be careful'. When a capture shows an EtherType it cannot decode, the protocol inside is one the tool does not know, not a broken frame; when it shows a value between 1501 and 1535, the frame itself is malformed.

fcs.def: The four-octet checksum at the end of an Ethernet frame, a 32-bit cyclic redundancy check (CRC-32) that the receiver recomputes to detect corruption.
fcs.context: A frame whose frame check sequence (FCS) does not match is dropped without a word; the only trace is an FCS or CRC (cyclic redundancy check) error counter on the receiving port. The check protects one link at a time, not the path: a switch that changes the frame, adding or removing a VLAN (virtual local area network) tag, computes a new FCS, and a cut-through switch may already have forwarded a damaged frame before it could check, marking it as bad on the way out.
fcs.depth:
What it covers. The frame check sequence (FCS) is the last field of every Ethernet frame: four octets holding a 32-bit cyclic redundancy check (CRC-32). The sender's media access control (MAC) logic computes it, in one vendor's words, over the frame bytes that include the source address, destination address, length, data and pad, so it runs from the destination address to the end of the padding and leaves out the preamble, the start frame delimiter (SFD) and itself. The generator polynomial is x to the 32nd plus x to the 26th, 23rd, 22nd, 16th, 12th, 11th, 10th, 8th, 7th, 5th, 4th and 2nd powers, plus x, plus 1; Philip Koopman writes it as the hexadecimal number 0x82608EDB and notes that it is irreducible but not primitive. It has been in the Ethernet standard of the Institute of Electrical and Electronics Engineers (IEEE) since its 1985 edition, ANSI/IEEE Std 802.3-1985. The four octets are counted in the frame sizes engineers quote: the 64-octet minimum and the 1518-octet maximum of an untagged frame both include the FCS.

One link at a time. Because the FCS covers the addresses and the Length/Type field, any device that rewrites them must compute a new one. Cisco's description of 802.1Q trunking says it directly: because the frame is altered, the trunking device recomputes the FCS on the modified frame, which is also why a tagged frame can reach 1522 bytes and must be at least 68. The consequence is easy to miss: the FCS proves that a frame crossed the last link intact, not that it is the frame the original sender built. Corruption inside a switch, between the check on the way in and the new FCS on the way out, is invisible to it, and end-to-end integrity is left to the checksums of the protocols above.

How strong it is. A CRC's strength is measured by its Hamming distance (HD): a code with HD of m detects every error of m minus 1 flipped bits or fewer. Koopman's 2002 survey found the IEEE 802.3 polynomial grossly suboptimal for its main job: at an Ethernet MTU (maximum transmission unit) of 1500 bytes, a 12,112-bit data word, it guarantees detection of three independent bit errors (HD 4), where the best 32-bit polynomial could guarantee five (HD 6). Its guarantees by length are HD 8 or better up to 91 bits, 7 to 171 bits, 6 to 268, 5 to 2,974, 4 to 91,607 and 3 beyond that, and, like any 32-bit CRC, it detects every burst of 32 bits or fewer. By that table a 9000-byte jumbo payload, about 72,000 bits with the header, still sits inside the HD 4 range, while frames longer than about 11,450 bytes fall to HD 3. Most errors outside the guarantees are still caught; the guarantee is what the code promises against the worst case.

What the receiver does. The receiving port computes the CRC again over the same bytes and compares. If they differ, the frame is discarded and a counter goes up; Ethernet never asks for it again. Whatever runs above, usually TCP (Transmission Control Protocol), notices the loss and recovers, slowly, so a link that loses one frame in a thousand feels far worse than the number suggests. Cisco's counter documentation names the family: FCS-Err counts frames of valid size with a bad FCS and no other error; Align-Err counts frames that do not end on a byte boundary and also fail the CRC; runts are frames shorter than 64 bytes with a bad CRC; giants are frames longer than 1518 bytes with a bad FCS; and input errors roll several of these up. The same counters appear as show interfaces counters errors on Cisco switches, as RX errors in ip -s link show on Linux and as Received Errors in netstat -e on Windows.

What a rising counter means. An FCS counter is a physical-layer symptom read at Layer 2. Cisco's list of causes is hardware almost from top to bottom: a damaged copper or fibre cable or direct attach cable, a failing transceiver, a bad patch panel port, a faulty switch port or line card, a malfunctioning network interface card (NIC) in a host, with an MTU mismatch as the one configuration cause on the list. Dirty fibre connectors and electrical noise belong to the same physical family. The classic non-physical cause is a duplex mismatch: Cisco's guidance is that if the FCS, CRC, alignment or runt counters increment, check for a duplex mismatch, and its auto-negotiation document places the rapid increase of FCS and alignment errors on the half-duplex side, with runts on the full-duplex port; there they climb with load, since more traffic means more simultaneous transmissions for the half-duplex side to break off.

Cut-through switching changes the picture. A store-and-forward switch receives the whole frame, checks the FCS and drops a bad frame at the ingress port, so the error is counted where it entered. A cut-through switch starts sending as soon as it has read the header, before the FCS has arrived, so by the time the check fails the corrupt frame is already on its way: the switch counts an input error on the ingress port and an output error on every egress port that sent it. Some cut-through platforms then stomp the frame, computing its CRC, inverting it and writing that into the FCS so that every device downstream recognizes it as bad, which is why one damaged frame can raise counters on several switches. Cisco's method for finding the real fault follows the trail: look for a link where one end counts incrementing input errors and the other end counts no output errors; that link is where the corruption happens. Engineers who chase the first counter they see in a cut-through fabric often replace the wrong optic.

Why captures rarely show it. The Wireshark wiki notes that most Ethernet interfaces do not hand the FCS to Wireshark or other applications, or are not configured by their drivers to do so, and that a frame with a wrong CRC is thrown away by the receiving host. A capture therefore usually shows neither the four FCS octets nor the corrupted frames themselves, and the 64-byte minimum, which includes the FCS, appears in a capture as 60 bytes of header, data and padding. Bad frames are found in interface counters, not in packet captures, unless the capture hardware is set to keep them.

auto-negotiation.def: The exchange in which two twisted-pair Ethernet ports advertise their speeds and duplex modes and settle on the best they share.
auto-negotiation.context: Defined in Clause 28 of IEEE 802.3 and carried in bursts of link pulses. Optional at 10 and 100 Mb/s, mandatory from 1000BASE-T on.
auto-negotiation.depth:
Cisco describes it as 'an optional function of the IEEE 802.3u Fast Ethernet standard that enables devices to automatically exchange information over a link about speed and duplex abilities'. The information travels in Fast Link Pulse bursts, which the University of New Hampshire's lab describes as 'simply a sequence of 10BASE-T Normal Link Pulses', sent every 16 ms, give or take 8.

From Gigabit on copper it stopped being optional: an IEEE interpretation confirms that 'selecting 1000BASE-T mode of operation still requires that Auto-Negotiation be used', because negotiation is also where the two ends settle which one is the clock master. Fibre at a fixed speed usually does not negotiate speed at all.

Its weak point is a neighbour that does not negotiate. The negotiating side then falls back on parallel detection, which can sense speed from the signal but never full duplex, so it settles on half: the origin of most duplex mismatches. Leave both ends on auto, or fix both.

native-vlan.def: The VLAN whose frames cross an 802.1Q trunk without a tag, and into which a trunk port places any untagged frame it receives.
native-vlan.context: VLAN 1 by default on Cisco and on Aruba's AOS-CX. Two ends that disagree merge two VLANs; the standard's own name for the idea is the port's PVID.
native-vlan.depth:
Cisco's rule for a trunk's egress is the definition at work: 'If a packet has a VLAN ID that is the same as the outgoing port native VLAN ID, the packet is sent untagged; otherwise, the device sends the packet with a tag.' On the way in, an untagged frame is assigned to the native VLAN. If the two ends of a trunk disagree about which VLAN that is, traffic from one VLAN arrives in another, and Cisco warns that 'spanning-tree loops might result'.

The native VLAN is also the hinge of a classic attack. A frame with two tags, the outer one matching the trunk's native VLAN, which is also the attacker's own access VLAN, loses that outer tag at the first switch and crosses the trunk into the VLAN of the inner one. Cisco's campus design guide gives the standard answer: 'Assign the native VLAN to an unused ID or use the Tagged Native VLAN option to avoid VLAN hopping.' Many switches can tag the native VLAN too, which removes the untagged exception altogether.

bpdu.def: The frame spanning tree switches exchange to elect a root bridge and decide which ports forward and which block.
bpdu.context: Sent to the bridge group address 01-80-C2-00-00-00, every two seconds by default from the root. A BPDU arriving on a port that faces a host is a warning sign, which BPDU Guard turns into a shut port.
bpdu.depth:
BPDUs carry everything the election needs: the sender's bridge ID, a priority and a MAC address, the ID of the bridge it believes is root, and its cost to reach it. The lowest bridge ID wins; Cisco's default priority is 32768, settable from 0 to 61440 in steps of 4096. The root sends configuration BPDUs every hello interval, 2 seconds by default, and the other switches relay them, so a switch that stops hearing them knows the topology has changed.

Because a BPDU can claim to be anything, a port that faces users should never accept one. Cisco's BPDU Guard 'shuts the port down by placing it in the errdisable state' when a BPDU arrives on a port configured for end devices, which stops a stray switch, or a crafted frame, from winning the election. In the rapid version of the protocol, BPDUs also work as keepalives: three missed hellos and a neighbour's information ages out at once.

rstp.def: The rapid version of spanning tree, IEEE 802.1w, which converges in moments by handshake instead of waiting out timers.
rstp.context: Incorporated into 802.1D-2004, which obsoleted the original protocol. Cisco's Rapid PVST+ runs one RSTP instance per VLAN.
rstp.depth:
Classic spanning tree waits: a port moves through listening and learning on 15-second forward delays, and an indirect failure can take 50 seconds with default timers. RSTP replaces most of the waiting with an exchange between neighbours: a switch 'sets the proposal bit on the BPDUs it sends out', and once the other end answers with an agreement the port can move to forwarding at once, which Cisco puts 'sometimes in the order of a few hundred milliseconds'.

The handshake only works where two switches face each other, so RSTP moves quickly on point-to-point links and on edge ports, the ports facing hosts, which go straight to forwarding and lose that status the moment a BPDU arrives. It also renames the roles: the old blocking port becomes an alternate (a backup path to the root through another switch) or a backup (a second link to the same segment), and the disabled, blocking and listening states merge into one, discarding.

link-aggregation.def: Several parallel Ethernet links grouped so that both ends treat them as one logical link, for more capacity and for resilience.
link-aggregation.context: Standardized by the Institute of Electrical and Electronics Engineers (IEEE) as 802.1AX today, and as 802.3ad before it. Every vendor has its own word: EtherChannel or port channel at Cisco, aggregated Ethernet at Juniper, a bond on Linux, a trunk on F5 BIG-IP, where Cisco's trunk means something else: a link carrying several tagged VLANs (virtual local area networks). The Link Aggregation Control Protocol (LACP) is what lets the two ends negotiate the group and notice a member that stops working; a group built without it relies on both sides being configured identically.
link-aggregation.depth:
What the standard says it is. IEEE (Institute of Electrical and Electronics Engineers) 802.1AX defines the goal in one sentence: one or more parallel full-duplex point-to-point links are aggregated together to form a Link Aggregation Group (LAG), such that a MAC (media access control) client can treat the LAG as if it were a single link. Everything above the group sees one interface with one address and the combined capacity. Spanning tree therefore sees one link and blocks nothing, and if a member fails the group keeps carrying traffic on the remaining members, losing capacity but not connectivity. F5's documentation gives the arithmetic in its simplest form: four Fast Ethernet links of 100 Mbit/s, aggregated, make a single 400 Mbit/s link. What a LAG is not is a way to make any one conversation faster, which is the first thing people expect of it and the subject of the fourth paragraph below.

From 802.3ad to 802.1AX. The work began in the IEEE 802.3 Trunking Study Group, became the P802.3ad task force, and was approved as IEEE 802.3ad-2000 at the March 2000 meeting of the IEEE Standards Board, as Clause 43 of the Ethernet standard. In 2007 the 802.1 and 802.3 working groups concluded that future development of link aggregation belonged in 802.1, and a new project request moved the protocol of Clause 43 into a standard of its own: IEEE 802.1AX-2008, approved in September 2008 together with IEEE 802.3-2008. The current edition, 802.1AX-2020, edited by Stephen Haddock and Jessy Rouyer, was approved on 30 January 2020; it also specifies the Distributed Resilient Network Interconnect (DRNI), a resilient interconnect between one to three nodes in one network and one to three nodes in another, separately administered one, which is the standard's answer to bundles that end on two switches. The amendment 802.1AXdz-2025 adds YANG modules for configuration and status, approved on 10 September 2025 and published on 17 October 2025. Vendor documentation still says 802.3ad almost everywhere, Juniper, F5 and the Linux bonding driver included; it means the same protocol.

LACP, and why a static group is risky. The Link Aggregation Control Protocol (LACP) runs on every member: each end sends LACP data units (LACPDUs), carried under EtherType 0x8809, the value IANA (Internet Assigned Numbers Authority) lists for the Slow Protocols, which carry link aggregation and Ethernet operations, administration and maintenance (OAM) among others, and a link joins the group only when both ends agree. A port in active mode starts the exchange and a passive one only answers, so two passive ends never form a group; F5 makes active its default and warns that with both peers passive no control packets are sent. Identity decides membership: Cisco builds the LACP system ID from a system priority, 32768 by default with lower values preferred, and the switch MAC address, and uses port priority, also 32768 by default, to choose which links are active and which wait in hot standby. The timers matter for failure detection. Cisco's default rate is one LACPDU every 30 seconds with a fast option of one second; the Linux bonding driver asks its partner for the slow rate by default; F5 documents both, with long (30 seconds) as its default, and removes a member after three consecutive packets without a response, which is three seconds with the short timer and ninety with the long. A static group, Cisco's mode on, has none of this. Cisco warns that a misconfigured group can cause packet loss or spanning-tree loops, and Aruba spells out why: a static LAG exchanges no keepalives, so it cannot detect a member that has failed without its light going out, and a misconfiguration on one side is difficult to troubleshoot because no signalling passes between the two peers.

One flow, one link. A LAG does not split frames across its members. Each sender computes a hash from fields of the frame and maps every frame with the same hash to the same member, so that, in F5's words, frames belonging to one conversation are neither mis-ordered nor duplicated at the receiving end. The consequence is the rule that surprises people: a single flow never runs faster than one member. A group of four one-gigabit links serves many flows at up to four gigabits in total and one large transfer at one; the Linux documentation says plainly that even with ports in the hash a single connection will not span multiple links. The inputs differ by platform and default: the Catalyst 9300 hashes on source MAC address unless told otherwise; F5 BIG-IP defaults to source and destination IP (Internet Protocol) addresses; Linux in its XOR (exclusive or) and 802.3ad modes defaults to the source and destination MAC addresses combined with the packet type, reduced modulo the number of members. Few flows therefore spread unevenly, and a design that hashes only on MAC addresses sends almost everything that crosses a router over one member, since every such frame carries the router's address. Each end chooses independently for the traffic it transmits, so the path out and the path back need not be the same member. F5 recommends aggregating links in powers of two for the most even result.

The rules members follow. Every member must match. Cisco asks for the same speed and duplex on all ports, the same VLAN (virtual local area network) for access ports or trunk configuration with the same allowed VLAN range, and notes that different native VLANs keep ports from forming a channel; misconfigured ports are suspended to avoid loops, and an LACP port that receives no LACP response is suspended too unless standalone mode is enabled (on that default the 17.12 guide contradicts itself). Juniper requires the same speed and full duplex on every member. The size of a group is a platform limit, not a protocol one: the Catalyst 9300 takes up to 16 LACP ports, of which eight are active and eight in hot standby, and up to 128 EtherChannels per switch; BIG-IP trunks take 16 or 32 members depending on platform and version; Juniper's limits vary by switch model.

On servers and appliances. The Linux bonding driver has seven modes, of which only mode 4, named 802.3ad, speaks LACP. Its default is balance-rr, round robin, which sends packets over the members in turn and is the one mode that spreads a single flow, at the cost of reordering; active-backup uses one member at a time and needs nothing from the switch; balance-tlb and balance-alb balance without special switch support. The HOWTO insists that link monitoring, miimon or ARP (Address Resolution Protocol) monitoring, be configured, or serious network degradation will occur during link failures. F5 BIG-IP calls the group a trunk, runs LACP as an option through a service called lacpd, uses the lowest-numbered interface's MAC address and treats that interface as the reference link, and adds a link selection policy that the standard does not have: Auto aggregates the links whose speed and duplex match the reference link, while Maximum Bandwidth picks whichever subset of members gives the trunk the most capacity at the moment.

What goes wrong. The vocabulary trips people first: an F5 trunk is a LAG, while a Cisco trunk port is a single link carrying several VLAN tags, and an engineer reading both vendors' configurations side by side must keep the two apart. Then come the mismatches: one end in LACP and the other static, members with different speeds or allowed VLANs, or a cable that lands on a different switch, which LACP detects because the partner's system ID does not match. Slow timers hide a member that fails silently for up to ninety seconds. And capacity planning goes wrong when a group is sized by its total and then asked to carry one big backup stream, which will use one member no matter how many are bundled.

link-state-routing.def: A routing method in which every router floods a description of its own links and computes paths from the shared map.
link-state-routing.context: It is the family of OSPF and IS-IS. Each router keeps a link-state database that is identical on every router of an area, and runs Dijkstra's algorithm on it with itself as root. Changes travel as flooded advertisements of each router's local state.
link-state-routing.depth:
RFC 2328 describes the database as a collection of each router's local state, its usable interfaces and reachable neighbours, distributed by flooding. All routers run the same algorithm in parallel and each builds a tree of shortest paths with itself as root; only the next hop from that tree is used for forwarding. The standard calls this a departure from the Bellman-Ford base of the older TCP/IP routing protocols.

Two safeguards keep the map consistent. A link is used only if the router at the far end lists a link back, and every advertisement carries a sequence number, a checksum and an age, which decide which copy is newer. RFC 4593 recalls why this matters: errors in a router of the original ARPANET link-state algorithm created three instances of one advertisement, which flooded continuously until the whole network was power cycled.

Scale comes from hierarchy, areas in OSPF and levels in IS-IS. A router keeps a separate database for each area it joins, and between OSPF areas only summaries pass, which FRRouting describes as distance-vector routing between areas. FRRouting also notes that the calculation is mostly negligible on modern CPUs; the real burden is flooding and the database as an area grows.

lsa.def: The unit of an OSPF link-state database: one router's or one network's local state, flooded to every router in its scope.
lsa.context: Every OSPF router describes its own links in a router-LSA, the designated router of a LAN adds a network-LSA, border routers add summaries and AS boundary routers add external routes. The type sets the flooding scope: one area, one NSSA or the whole AS.
lsa.depth:
RFC 2328 defines five types. Type 1 router-LSAs and type 2 network-LSAs describe topology and stay inside one area. Type 3 and type 4 summary-LSAs come from area border routers and describe networks and AS boundary routers outside the area. Type 5 AS-external-LSAs are flooded throughout the AS. RFC 3101 adds type 7 for a not-so-stubby area, translated into type 5 at its border, and types 9 to 11 are the opaque LSAs.

Three header fields identify an LSA, LS type, Link State ID and Advertising Router, and three decide which copy is newer: sequence number, checksum and age. Sequence numbers start at 0x80000001. An originator refreshes each of its LSAs every 30 minutes even when nothing has changed, an LSA whose age reaches MaxAge, one hour, is flushed and no longer used, and only the originator may age its own LSAs early.

FRRouting's show ip ospf database lists them by type with age, sequence number and checksum, and its documentation notes that stale LSAs left by a router that vanished without flushing them are not abnormal and do little harm. Forged ones are another matter: RFC 4593 warns that an LSA with the wrong Advertising Router makes every receiver compute an incorrect tree.

ospf-area.def: A group of OSPF networks and routers that shares one link-state database, its topology hidden from the rest of the domain.
ospf-area.context: Areas bound flooding and computation: routers inside an area know its full map, routers outside see only summaries. Area 0 is the backbone that carries traffic between areas, and stub and not-so-stubby areas (NSSAs) change which external routes enter an area.
ospf-area.depth:
RFC 2328 gives the backbone, area 0.0.0.0, three duties: it contains every area border router, carries routing between non-backbone areas, and must be contiguous, if need be through virtual links configured across a non-backbone area. Inter-area routing therefore takes the shape of a star with the backbone as hub. If the backbone partitions, parts of the AS become unreachable; a non-backbone area that partitions simply becomes two areas.

A stub area receives no AS-external-LSAs; its routers reach external destinations through a default summary from the border router, which shrinks their database. It suits an area with a single exit, cannot carry a virtual link and cannot contain an AS boundary router. Totally stubby is industry usage for a stub whose border routers also withhold most summaries, FRRouting's stub no-summary. An NSSA, defined in RFC 3101, does the opposite of shrinking: it may import external routes as type 7 LSAs, which its border routers translate into type 5.

Neighbours must agree on the area ID and on the stub or NSSA flag carried in their Hellos, or the adjacency never forms.

designated-router.def: The router an OSPF broadcast network elects to speak for the segment, with a backup designated router ready to replace it.
designated-router.context: On a LAN with several OSPF routers, each becomes adjacent only to the designated router and its backup, not to every other router, and the designated router originates the network-LSA for the segment. The election goes by priority, then router ID, and is not pre-emptive.
designated-router.depth:
RFC 2328 gives the reason: a designated router reduces the number of adjacencies on a broadcast network, and with them routing traffic and database size. Five routers in a full mesh would need 10 adjacencies; with a designated router and a backup they need 7. Two routers that are neither stop at the 2-Way state with each other, which is normal. The designated router multicasts its updates to AllSPFRouters, 224.0.0.5, and both it and the backup also listen on AllDRouters, 224.0.0.6.

The highest Router Priority wins, ties go to the highest router ID, and priority 0 makes a router ineligible. A router that finds a designated router already in place accepts it regardless of priority, so a returning router with a higher priority comes back as backup, not as designated router. RFC 2328 accepts that unpredictability because each change costs a moment of lost connectivity while the databases converge again. The backup is already adjacent to everyone and takes over when the designated router fails.

A link that joins only two routers needs no election: configured as point-to-point, it forms its adjacency directly, and FRRouting lists such a neighbour as Full/- rather than Full/DR.

dijkstras-algorithm.def: The shortest-path method link-state routers run: the closest tentative node's distance is final, so it is fixed next.
dijkstras-algorithm.context: Edsger Dijkstra designed it in 1956 to demonstrate the ARMAC computer and published it in 1959. OSPF and IS-IS name it as the basis of their route calculation, which is why routers call it SPF, shortest path first.
dijkstras-algorithm.depth:
The 1959 note in Numerische Mathematik is three pages long and solves two problems, the minimum spanning tree first and the shortest path second. It builds the shortest paths from the starting node in order of increasing length, so each node's distance is settled before any longer one. In 1993 Dijkstra wrote that he designed it without pencil and paper, over coffee on a café terrace in Amsterdam, only for a demonstration.

RFC 2328 states the router's version: at each iteration the candidate closest to the root is guaranteed to be shortest, joins the tree, and its neighbours are examined. When two paths tie, both next hops are kept, so strictly the result is not a tree. The specification does not require this exact method, only that any other algorithm produce an identical tree.

The guarantee needs non-negative costs, and OSPF goes further: every interface cost must be greater than zero. RFC 1195 gives the cost of the computation as the square of the number of nodes, lower on sparse networks, and FRRouting's documentation calls it mostly negligible on modern CPUs. What routers do limit is how often it runs: RFC 8405 standardizes a back-off that delays SPF when events arrive close together.

nsap-net.def: The OSI-style address every IS-IS router needs: an area address, a system ID and a selector of 00.
nsap-net.context: Even an IP-only router running IS-IS must carry one, and uses it only for IS-IS. It reads as the area, then a six-octet system ID that names the router in the domain, then the selector: 49.0001.1920.0000.2001.00 is a router in area 49.0001.
nsap-net.depth:
An NSAP address divides into an area address, a system identifier and a one-octet selector; a NET is an NSAP whose selector is 00. Juniper's documentation gives NETs a length of 8 to 20 octets, the simplest 10, with an area part of 1 to 13 octets. RFC 3719 says an implementation MUST use a system ID length of 6, which has proved ample because the ID matters only inside the routing domain.

The system ID is usually minted from something already unique. Juniper recommends an interface IP address in binary-coded decimal: 192.0.2.1, padded to 192.000.002.001, becomes 1920.0000.2001. RFC 1195 instead prepends hex 02 00 to the address, giving 0200.c000.0201, which cannot collide with an ID taken from a MAC address because 02 sets the bit that globally assigned MACs leave clear.

Every ID must be unique in the domain, and Juniper notes that an all-zero system ID is illegal and forms no adjacency. Level 1 routers refuse neighbours whose area addresses do not overlap their own, so a mistyped area shows up as a missing adjacency; FRRouting's show isis summary prints the NET and system ID in use.

overload-bit.def: A flag in an IS-IS router's LSP that tells other routers not to use it for transit, while still reaching it as a destination.
overload-bit.context: ISO 10589 defined it for a router whose link-state database had overflowed. Operators now also set it on purpose for a set time after a reboot, so traffic avoids a router whose BGP routes have not yet converged.
overload-bit.depth:
As RFC 3787 restates ISO 10589, a router in the LSP Database Overload condition sets the bit in its non-pseudonode LSP number zero, and other systems must not use it as a transit router. It may still be used to reach systems directly attached to it, since it may be their only path. In FRRouting's show isis database the bit is the OL in the ATT/P/OL column.

Its meaning has since been, in RFC 3787's word, overloaded.
