When a router running BGP and IS-IS reboots, IS-IS converges first and the router attracts traffic it cannot yet deliver, discarding packets for destinations learned only through BGP. RFC 3277 describes that transient black hole and the cure, setting the bit until BGP has converged, a mechanism it says had been deployed in several large IS-IS networks for years. FRRouting offers set-overload-bit, and set-overload-bit on-startup with a duration in seconds.

OSPF reaches the same end differently: under RFC 6987, a router advertises its transit links at the maximum metric, so others avoid paths through it while still reaching its own networks.

discard-route.def: A discard route is a route whose next hop is nowhere: installed for a summary prefix, it drops traffic for the parts of the summary that are not reachable instead of letting that traffic follow a less-specific route; the same mechanism, called a blackhole or null route, is used to drop attack traffic on purpose.
discard-route.context: A router that advertises a summary installs one, usually pointing to Null0 or a blackhole. Without it, a packet for a dead component matches the router's default route and is sent back the way it came, looping until its TTL (time to live) runs out. Longest-prefix match keeps it harmless: every component the router can still reach is a longer prefix and wins, so only traffic for the missing pieces lands on the discard entry. OSPF (Open Shortest Path First) installs one automatically for each area range it summarizes, operators add them by hand next to every aggregate they announce in BGP (Border Gateway Protocol), and the same route type, triggered remotely, is how providers drop traffic aimed at the target of a denial-of-service attack.
discard-route.depth:
RFC (Request for Comments) 4632, the current Classless Inter-Domain Routing (CIDR) specification (August 2006, Best Current Practice 122), states the rule in its second aggregation rule: a router that generates an aggregate route for several more-specific routes must discard packets that match the aggregate but none of the more-specific routes; in other words, the next hop for the aggregate should be the null destination, which is necessary to prevent forwarding loops when some addresses the aggregate covers are not reachable. Its predecessor, RFC 1519 (September 1993), had already given the implementation: the border router keeps a sink route for each of its aggregations. RFC 4632 says the same thing in practice, that the rule is typically implemented by installing a discard or null route for every aggregated prefix one network advertises to another. A discard route is therefore not a failure state but a deliberate entry in the routing table, with a prefix, a distance and a next hop that drops whatever matches.

The loop it prevents is easiest to see with RFC 4632's own example. A provider holds 192.168.0.0/16 and assigns 192.168.64.0/19 to a customer, which advertises its /19 back to the provider and receives the provider's /16, or simply a default route. If the customer loses internal reachability to 192.168.65.0/24, traffic for 192.168.65.1 still arrives from the provider following the customer's /19; inside the customer's network the most specific match is now the provider's /16 or the default, so the packet goes back up to the provider, which sends it down again, and the two bounce it until its TTL (time to live) expires, taking link capacity with them. With a discard route for the /19 the customer drops the packet at the border instead. RFC 4632 names the default route (0.0.0.0/0) as the special case: a network must never follow the default to destinations that are part of its own aggregated advertisements.

Longest-prefix match is what makes this safe. Every component the router can still reach is a longer prefix than the summary, so it wins over the discard entry; only the components that have vanished fall through to it, and the discard entry, being longer than the default, wins over the default in turn. That is why a discard route never hides a reachable subnet and why it needs no maintenance as components come and go. The same logic tells an operator where not to put one: a discard route for a prefix shorter than a route the router should follow elsewhere, or for space it does not actually own, silently drops traffic that had a valid path.

Routing protocols build the entry in. OSPF (Open Shortest Path First) does it in the specification itself: RFC 2328 says that before the routing table lookup begins, discard entries should be inserted for each of the router's active area address ranges, an area range being active if it contains at least one network reachable by intra-area paths, and a footnote explains that the entries are necessary to ensure that summarization at area boundaries cannot cause packet looping. When the best match is one of those entries, the packet is dropped and an ICMP (Internet Control Message Protocol) destination unreachable is returned to its source. Cisco's EIGRP (Enhanced Interior Gateway Routing Protocol) installs a summary route of its own whenever it summarizes, at administrative distance 5 in Cisco's table, lower than any learned route for the same prefix. For BGP (Border Gateway Protocol) aggregates the habit is manual: operators create a static route to Null0 for each prefix they announce, which both satisfies RFC 4632's rule and keeps the announcement stable, since the aggregate no longer depends on any one component being up.

What happens to the dropped packet depends on the route type, and the difference matters. Linux distinguishes four kinds in ip-route(8): blackhole discards silently and gives local senders EINVAL; unreachable discards and generates an ICMP host unreachable, EHOSTUNREACH locally; prohibit generates communication administratively prohibited, EACCES locally; and throw, used with policy routing, ends the lookup in that table as if no route had been found. FRRouting accepts Null0 or blackhole as the gateway of a static route for a route that drops everything, and reject for one that answers with ICMP destination unreachable. Junos has a discard interface, dsc, that drops silently with no ICMP message, and Juniper's documentation gives the reason to prefer silence on an exposed router: answering every unroutable packet with an ICMP error lets an attacker who spoofs the victim's source address turn the router into a reflector. The polite reject is better inside an enterprise, where a fast unreachable saves an application from waiting for its connection to time out.

A discard route with a high distance is a safety net. FRRouting's documentation shows ip route 10.0.0.0/8 null0 255 installed next to the real static routes for the same prefix: while the gateways are reachable they win, and when they are not, the blackhole at distance 255 keeps traffic for 10.0.0.0/8 from matching a less-specific route such as the default. Fortinet gives the same advice for site-to-site VPNs (virtual private networks): a static route for the branch networks, 10.0.0.0/14 in its example, with distance 254 and blackhole enabled, so that while a tunnel is down, traffic destined for private branch addresses is dropped instead of following the default route out of the internet interface. The floating discard route is the difference between an outage and an outage that also sends internal traffic unencrypted towards the provider.

The same mechanism is a denial-of-service tool. RFC 3882 (September 2004) described using BGP communities to trigger black-holing of a destination remotely, and RFC 5635 (August 2009) the standard design: a discard route on every edge router pointing to the null interface for a reserved next-hop address, such as one from the 192.0.2.0/24 documentation range or from private space, after which announcing the attacked address in BGP with that next hop makes every edge router drop its traffic. The RFC is frank that this completes the attack, since the target becomes unreachable, but minimizes collateral damage to everything that shares the links; coupled with unicast reverse path forwarding (uRPF) the same trick filters by source instead. Between networks, RFC 7999 (October 2016) registered the well-known BLACKHOLE community, 0xFFFF029A or 65535:666 (666 being the value operators had long used), and noted that while prefixes longer than /24 for IPv4 or /48 for IPv6 are usually refused, blackhole announcements should be as specific as possible, typically /32 or /128. For IPv6, RFC 6666 (August 2012) had IANA (Internet Assigned Numbers Authority) set aside 0100::/64 as a discard-only prefix for exactly these designs.

The price is visibility. RFC 4632 notes that when a site has moved to another provider and its old provider's aggregate still covers it, the old provider's discard route drops the traffic correctly, but traceroute and similar tools then point at the network advertising the aggregate, not at the one that stopped advertising the more-specific prefix; the RFC's remedy is better education of operators, not a change in routing. A trace that dies at the first router of a network that legitimately owns the address space, with no ICMP reply or with a destination unreachable from that router, is the signature of a discard route doing its job.

gtsm.def: GTSM (Generalized TTL Security Mechanism): a check that accepts a protocol's packets only when they arrive with TTL (time to live) 255, or IPv6 Hop Limit 255, so they cannot have crossed a router on the way.
gtsm.context: RFC (Request for Comments) 5082 defines GTSM (Generalized TTL Security Mechanism): senders set the TTL (time to live) or Hop Limit to 255, and since every router decrements it, a receiver that demands 255 drops packets forged from further away. BFD (Bidirectional Forwarding Detection), VRRP (Virtual Router Redundancy Protocol) and directly connected BGP (Border Gateway Protocol) sessions use it; it is no substitute for authentication.
gtsm.depth:
RFC (Request for Comments) 5082, published in October 2007 by Vijay Gill, John Heasley, David Meyer, Pekka Savola and Carlos Pignataro, defines the Generalized TTL Security Mechanism (GTSM) and obsoletes RFC 3682, the Experimental version of February 2004. Its purpose is narrow and practical: to protect a router's IP control plane from attacks that work by exhausting its CPU (central processing unit), such as a flood of forged BGP (Border Gateway Protocol) packets aimed at a peering address. It rests on an observation about topology, that the vast majority of protocol peerings are between adjacent routers, and on one about the IP header, that TTL (time to live) spoofing is considered nearly impossible: every router decrements the TTL by one as it forwards a packet, so no packet can arrive with more than the sender set minus the number of routers it crossed. If the sender sets 255, the maximum, a packet that has crossed even one router arrives with 254 at most. An expected value therefore gives, in the RFC's words, a simple and reasonably robust defence against forged protocol packets from outside the network. The mechanism applies identically to the IPv4 TTL and the IPv6 Hop Limit, and the RFC credits the original idea of using the TTL to protect BGP to Paul Traina, Jon Stewart and others before it was generalized.

The procedure has two halves. Every packet of a GTSM-enabled session must leave with TTL 255, including the ICMP (Internet Control Message Protocol) error messages related to it, which RFC 3682 had not covered, and the TTL must not be decremented on the way out by architectures that would otherwise do so. On receipt, packets addressed to the control plane fall into three classes: Unknown, which cannot be tied to any GTSM-enabled session; Trusted, which belong to one and carry the expected TTL; and Dangerous, which belong to one but carry an unexpected TTL and so may be spoofed. By default an implementation should keep Dangerous packets from competing for resources with the other two, must not drop Trusted or Unknown packets as part of GTSM, and may drop Dangerous ones. There is no negotiation: GTSM is configured by hand, on both peers, per session or per group.

Where the check sits decides how much it protects. The RFC assumes the router can classify packets and give them separate queues or processing quotas before they reach a scarce resource, and states plainly that the closer GTSM processing is done to the line-rate hardware, the more resistant the system is to denial of service. A check made in software after the packet has already reached the routing process stops forged sessions from being accepted but does little for the CPU it was meant to protect. That is also why GTSM pairs naturally with strict ingress filtering of spoofed source addresses on untrusted interfaces, which the RFC names as necessary for maximal protection.

Protocols adopted it in two ways, as an option bolted on and as a rule built in. For BGP, RFC 7454 (February 2015, Best Current Practice 194) explains the switch: instead of sending TCP packets with TTL 1, as external BGP between neighbours traditionally does, speakers send them with TTL 255 and the receiver checks for 255, which effectively prevents all spoofing attacks from third parties not directly connected to the same subnet; network administrators SHOULD implement it on directly connected peerings, and, like MD5 (Message Digest 5) protection, it must be configured on both ends. FRRouting implements it as the command "neighbor PEER ttl-security hops NUMBER", which admits only neighbours that many hops away and cannot be combined with ebgp-multihop on the same neighbour. Single-hop BFD (Bidirectional Forwarding Detection), RFC 5881 (June 2010), builds it in: without authentication, control packets must be sent with TTL or Hop Limit 255 and discarded on receipt if the value is anything else; with authentication the packets are still sent at 255, and the check may be made before the cryptographic one to save work. VRRP (Virtual Router Redundancy Protocol) version 3, RFC 9568 (April 2024), requires TTL and Hop Limit 255 and discards anything else, which, its security section says, limits most of its vulnerabilities to attacks on the local network. RFC 6720 (August 2012) added GTSM to the Label Distribution Protocol (LDP), using a bit RFC 5036 had reserved.

OSPF (Open Shortest Path First) shows the opposite approach to the same problem of keeping protocol packets local. RFC 2328 sets the IP TTL of packets sent to OSPF's multicast addresses to 1, so that they never travel more than a single hop. TTL 1 controls where a packet can go; it does nothing about where a received packet came from, since a packet crafted far away can still arrive with TTL 1 after its sender set a higher value. GTSM's 255 inverts the logic: it cannot stop a packet from travelling, but it proves on arrival that the packet did not.

The limits are in RFC 5082 itself. GTSM is not a substitute for authentication and does not protect against an insider on the wire spoofing or replaying packets; it cannot protect against an attacker as close as the legitimate peer, so on a shared segment every host on that segment is as trusted as the neighbour; an attacker directly connected to another interface can disturb a protected session by spoofing the peer's address unless ingress filtering is applied there; a tunnel that is not integrity-protected can deliver a packet with TTL 255 from anywhere, so over tunnels GTSM is only as good as the tunnel; and non-initial IP fragments carry no transport ports, so they are classified as Unknown. Multi-hop use, checking for 254 or 253 instead of 255, appears only in a non-normative appendix: RFC 5082 restricts its scope to the single-hop case because its security properties are clearer, and RFC 7454 notes that multi-hop GTSM is less effective because anyone inside the TTL diameter could spoof the TTL. That is why multihop BFD relies on authentication instead, and why RFC 5880 notes that GTSM applied to BFD echo packets loses one from the TTL as the packet is looped back, leaving echo spoofing possible from one hop away.

The numbers worth remembering are few. Send at 255 and require 255 for directly connected peers; anything lower means at least one router in between. External BGP's traditional TTL of 1, OSPF's TTL of 1 for multicast and GTSM's 255 are three different uses of the same eight bits: the first two limit how far a packet may travel, the third checks how far it has travelled.

path-vector-routing.def: A routing method in which each route carries the list of autonomous systems it has crossed, not just a distance.
path-vector-routing.context: BGP works this way. RFC 4274 calls its algorithm a modified distance vector, referred to as path vector, that uses path information to avoid the traditional distance-vector problems. The reader meets the idea when comparing routing families and when reading the AS path column of a BGP table.
path-vector-routing.depth:
With each destination a BGP speaker sends the list of autonomous systems (ASes) the announcement has traversed. RFC 4271 says that list is enough to build a graph of AS connectivity, from which routing loops may be pruned and some policy enforced at the AS level. A speaker prepends its own AS number when it advertises a route to an external peer, and leaves the path unchanged towards internal peers.

Loop prevention is therefore a scan rather than a count: a router checks whether its own AS number appears anywhere in the AS_PATH, and a route that contains it is excluded from the decision. Path length also takes part in choosing a route, as the first tie-break after the degree of preference: the route with the fewest AS numbers wins, an AS_SET counting as one.

Two misreadings are common. RFC 4274 describes BGP as neither a pure distance-vector nor a pure link-state algorithm. And the path records the announcement, not the packets: after aggregation the actual path may not be the one the AS_PATH shows (RFC 4271, section 5.1.6), and nothing internal to BGP protects that list against being modified or forged (RFC 4272).

ebgp-and-ibgp.def: The two kinds of BGP session: external, between routers in different autonomous systems, and internal, within one.
ebgp-and-ibgp.context: RFC 4271 calls a peer in a different AS external and one in the same AS internal, abbreviated EBGP and IBGP. The session type changes the rules: what a speaker adds to a route, which attributes travel, which route wins a tie and, inside the AS, a requirement that every speaker peer with every other.
ebgp-and-ibgp.depth:
On an eBGP session a speaker prepends its own AS number to the AS_PATH and by default puts the address it uses for that session in NEXT_HOP; towards an internal peer it must not modify the AS_PATH. LOCAL_PREF goes to internal peers only and must not be sent to external ones, except within a confederation. In the decision process, if any candidate was received over eBGP, the iBGP-learned routes are removed. RFC 4271 also suggests a slower advertisement pace for eBGP, 30 seconds, than for iBGP, 5 seconds.

The full-mesh rule comes from one sentence of section 9.2: a speaker that receives an UPDATE from an internal peer shall not re-distribute it to other internal peers, unless it acts as a route reflector. Every iBGP speaker must therefore peer with every other, n(n-1)/2 sessions for n speakers: 45 for ten, 4,950 for a hundred. RFC 4456 says the requirement clearly does not scale.

Two remedies replace the mesh. Route reflection (RFC 4456) lets chosen speakers pass iBGP routes on to their clients; a confederation (RFC 5065) splits the AS into member ASes that appear as one AS from outside, so the sessions inside follow the inter-domain model. Since RFC 8212 (July 2017), an eBGP session with no explicit import or export policy accepts and sends nothing.

route-reflector.def: An iBGP speaker allowed to pass routes learned from one internal peer on to others, so the AS needs no full mesh.
route-reflector.context: Route reflection, RFC 4456 (April 2006), is the alternative to the full mesh of internal BGP sessions, which needs n(n-1)/2 sessions for n speakers. The reader meets it in iBGP designs and in route details, where the ORIGINATOR_ID and CLUSTER_LIST attributes mark a route that was reflected.
route-reflector.depth:
A route reflector and its client peers form a cluster. The rules are short: a route from a non-client iBGP peer is reflected to all clients; a route from a client is reflected to all non-client peers and to the other clients. Only the non-clients must remain fully meshed; the clients need not be (RFC 4456, sections 5 and 6). It is the exception RFC 4271 itself names in the rule that otherwise forbids passing an internal peer's routes to other internal peers.

Relaxing that rule needs loop guards, so RFC 4456 adds two optional non-transitive attributes, type codes 9 and 10 in the IANA registry. ORIGINATOR_ID carries the BGP Identifier of the route's originator in the local AS, and a router should ignore a route that carries its own identifier there. CLUSTER_LIST records the clusters the route has been reflected through, and a reflector should ignore an advertisement whose list already holds its own CLUSTER_ID.

The gain is the arithmetic of the mesh: ten speakers need 45 iBGP sessions in a full mesh and a hundred need 4,950, while the clients of a reflector need no mesh among themselves. Confederations (RFC 5065) are the other remedy, splitting the AS rather than relaxing the rule.

local-preference.def: The BGP attribute that carries an autonomous system's own preference for a route to its internal peers; higher wins.
local-preference.context: LOCAL_PREF, type code 5 in RFC 4271, is how an operator states which exit it prefers for a destination. It is set by local policy, sent only to iBGP peers, and compared before the AS path length is even considered, so it overrides every tie-break that follows.
local-preference.depth:
RFC 4271's decision process starts by giving each route a degree of preference. For a route from an internal peer that is either the LOCAL_PREF value or a value computed from local policy; for an external route the speaker computes it from preconfigured policy, and the higher degree of preference must be preferred. How that policy works is a local matter. Only routes that tie on it go on to the tie-breaks: shortest AS_PATH, lowest ORIGIN, lowest MED and the rest.

The attribute never leaves the AS. It shall be included in every UPDATE sent to internal peers and must not be sent to external peers, except within a BGP confederation. A neighbouring AS therefore cannot set it for you; its own means of influencing how traffic enters it are MED and communities that the receiving AS has agreed to act on.

Two consequences are worth seeing. A route given LOCAL_PREF 200 by import policy beats a route with a shorter AS path, because the comparison never reaches path length. In FRRouting's BGP table the LocPrf column holds the value, and the header states the default, Default local pref 100. Implementations may add steps of their own before it: FRRouting, for one, checks a router-local weight first.

multi-exit-discriminator.def: An optional BGP attribute by which a neighbouring AS suggests which of several links into it to use; lower wins.
multi-exit-discriminator.context: MULTI_EXIT_DISC, type code 4 in RFC 4271, is meant for external links: it discriminates among multiple exit or entry points to the same neighbouring AS. The reader meets it in the Metric column of a BGP table and at step c of the best-path decision, where only routes from the same neighbouring AS are compared.
multi-exit-discriminator.depth:
The attribute is optional and non-transitive. All other factors being equal, the exit point with the lower value should be preferred, and a MED received from a neighbouring AS must not be propagated to other neighbouring ASes. RFC 4271 also requires a locally configurable mechanism to remove it from a route, so the receiver decides whether to honour it at all.

In the decision process it comes third among the tie-breaks, after AS_PATH length and ORIGIN, and it is comparable only between routes learned from the same neighbouring AS, which is read from the AS_PATH. A route without a MED counts as having the lowest possible value. Two links into one AS carrying MED 50 and MED 10 resolve to the link with 10; the same two values from two different ASes do not compete on MED at all, and the choice falls to the later steps.

It is easy to overrate. It is a hint from the neighbour, weaker than the receiving AS's own degree of preference, so a LOCAL_PREF set by import policy overrides it. FRRouting prints it in the Metric column of its BGP table, which invites confusion with an interior metric; the interior cost to the NEXT_HOP is a separate, later step.

bgp-communities.def: Numeric tags attached to BGP routes so that networks can group destinations and request how they are treated.
bgp-communities.context: The COMMUNITIES attribute (RFC 1997, August 1996, type code 8) carries four-octet tags; large communities (RFC 8092, February 2017, type code 32) carry twelve-octet ones. The reader meets them in route details and in providers' policies, where a tag can mean learned from a customer or do not export to a given AS.
bgp-communities.depth:
RFC 1997 defines a community as a group of destinations that share some common property, and the attribute as optional and transitive. By convention a four-octet value holds an AS number in the first two octets and a value defined by that AS in the last two. A speaker may use the tags to control which routing information it accepts, prefers or passes on to other neighbours.

Some values are well known. NO_EXPORT (0xFFFFFF01) keeps a route inside the AS or confederation, NO_ADVERTISE (0xFFFFFF02) keeps it from every BGP peer, and NO_EXPORT_SUBCONFED (0xFFFFFF03) completes the original set. The IANA registry has since added others, among them BLACKHOLE (RFC 7999) and GRACEFUL_SHUTDOWN (RFC 8326).

Four-octet AS numbers broke the convention, because a two-octet field cannot hold a four-octet AS number. Large communities answer with a four-octet global administrator and two four-octet operator-defined fields, written like 64496:4294967295:2. RFC 8195's examples separate tags that inform, such as 64497:3:2 for a route learned from a customer, from tags that request an action, such as 64497:4:64498 for do not export to AS 64498. An action tag is a request: it works only where the receiving AS defines and honours it.

bgpsec.def: A BGP extension in which every AS on the path signs the route announcement, so the AS path itself can be verified.
bgpsec.context: BGPsec (RFC 8205, September 2017) is the path-validation layer meant to supplement RPKI origin validation, which checks only who originated a prefix. The reader meets it in routing-security discussions as a finished standard that, in 2024, the US government found not yet implemented by commercial router vendors.
bgpsec.depth:
It works through an optional non-transitive path attribute that carries digital signatures produced by each AS that propagates the UPDATE. The assurance is that every AS listed has explicitly authorized the advertisement of the route to the next AS in the path. RFC 8205 presents it as a supplement to origin validation; used together, the two are meant to prevent a wide variety of route hijacking attacks.

Partial deployment is the hard part. If an AS on the path does not support BGPsec, the signed UPDATE is converted to an unsigned one before it is forwarded to that AS, and the assurance for that path is lost; RFC 8207 describes the result as islands of assured paths. It also protects the control plane only: it does not guarantee that data packets follow the indicated path.

Deployment is where it stops. In 2015 BCP 194 still called it ongoing work that could not be implemented. The Office of the National Cyber Director's roadmap of September 2024 says the standards were completed in 2017 and prototype reference implementations exist, but the standard has yet to be implemented by commercial router vendors, and it names two barriers: it changes the format of BGP messages, and it typically requires routers to process signatures.

aspa.def: A signed RPKI object in which an AS names its transit providers, so that routers can check an AS path for leaks.
aspa.context: Autonomous System Provider Authorization is still work in progress: on 19 October 2026 its profile and verification documents were IETF Internet-Drafts, revision 29, and no ASPA RFC existed. It targets what origin validation cannot see, a route with the right origin on the wrong path.
aspa.depth:
The profile draft defines an ASPA as a digitally signed object through which the holder of an AS number authorizes one or more other ASes as its transit providers. The verification draft uses those objects to check a route's AS_PATH, adding means to detect and mitigate route leaks and AS_PATH manipulations. The objects are published in the global Resource Public Key Infrastructure (RPKI), the system that also holds ROAs.

The status, as the IETF datatracker showed it on 19 October 2026: draft-ietf-sidrops-aspa-verification-29 of 16 October 2026 and draft-ietf-sidrops-aspa-profile-29 of 29 July 2026, both at WG Consensus: Waiting for Write-Up, with the IESG state I-D Exists. The RFC index of 16 October 2026 lists no ASPA RFC. The profile draft itself reports roughly 2,400 ASPA objects published as of July 2026, a figure from the draft rather than from a measurement.

Expectations are cautious. The US roadmap of September 2024 said the ASPA standards were nearing completion. Cloudflare, writing after the 1.1.1.1 incident of 27 June 2024, in which the leaked route was RPKI Valid, called ASPA a long-term effort that depends on networks, especially large providers, rejecting invalid AS paths based on ASPA objects.

bgp-hold-time.def: How long a BGP speaker waits without hearing from its peer before it declares the session dead and closes it.
bgp-hold-time.context: Each side offers a Hold Time in its OPEN message, and RFC 4271 section 4.2 makes both use the smaller of the two; KEEPALIVE messages stop it from expiring. It sets how long a silent peer can go unnoticed, up to 90 seconds with the suggested default, which is why faster detection is left to a dedicated protocol such as BFD.
bgp-hold-time.depth:
On receiving an OPEN, a speaker must set its Hold Timer to the smaller of its own configured Hold Time and the one received. The value must be zero or at least three seconds, and the other side has no veto: an implementation may only reject the connection on the basis of the Hold Time. A router configured for 180 seconds whose peer offers 9 therefore runs at 9.

RFC 4271 section 10 suggests 90 seconds for the Hold Time and a third of it for the keepalive interval; a KEEPALIVE is a bare 19-octet header and must not be sent more often than once per second. Implementations set their own defaults and controls. FRRouting configures both values per neighbour, keepalive first, and offers a minimum hold time below which it refuses to establish a session.

When nothing arrives within the Hold Time, the speaker sends a NOTIFICATION with the Hold Timer Expired error code and closes the connection, and a verified erratum (ID 2838) adds that it deletes all routes associated with that connection. With the suggested 90 seconds, a peer that has gone silent can keep its routes in use for up to 90 seconds before that happens.

neighbor-discovery-protocol.def: The IPv6 protocol, carried in ICMPv6, by which nodes on a link find each other, their routers and link-layer addresses.
neighbor-discovery-protocol.context: Neighbor Discovery (RFC 4861) does what ARP, ICMP Router Discovery and ICMP Redirect did in IPv4, and adds unreachability detection. Every address resolution, router choice and duplicate check on an IPv6 link runs through it, so dropping its messages breaks IPv6 outright.
neighbor-discovery-protocol.depth:
It is five ICMPv6 messages, types 133 to 137: Router Solicitation and Router Advertisement, Neighbor Solicitation and Neighbor Advertisement, and Redirect. All are sent with a hop limit of 255 and receivers check it, so a message that crossed a router is rejected; fragmented ND messages must be ignored. Resolution takes one multicast solicitation to the target's solicited-node group, carrying the asker's MAC, and one unicast advertisement back, after which both ends hold an entry.

Each Neighbor Cache entry moves through INCOMPLETE, REACHABLE, STALE, DELAY and PROBE. With default timers reachability lasts a random 15 to 45 seconds; a stale entry waits 5 seconds after the next packet, then sends three unicast probes one second apart and is deleted if none is answered.

The protocol trusts the link. Nothing tells a host which neighbours may send Router Advertisements or whether an advertiser owns the address it claims, so rogue RAs, mostly accidental, and spoofed advertisements send packets to unexpected places, and a scan of a /64 can fill a router's cache from off-link. SEND adds signatures but RFC 9099 says it should not be relied upon; RA-Guard, rate limits and right-sized subnets are what is used. On Linux, ip -6 neigh show lists the cache with its states.

icmpv6.def: Internet Control Message Protocol version 6 (ICMPv6) is the control and error protocol of Internet Protocol version 6 (IPv6). It reports delivery errors, carries ping, and transports Neighbor Discovery and the multicast listener messages, so IPv6 cannot work without it.
icmpv6.context: ICMPv6, specified in Request for Comments (RFC) 4443, is identified by the value 58 in the Next Header field of the Internet Protocol version 6 (IPv6) header and, unlike the Internet Control Message Protocol (ICMP) in many IPv4 policies, cannot be treated as optional: every IPv6 node must implement it, and address resolution, router discovery, duplicate address detection and Path MTU (maximum transmission unit) Discovery all ride on it. Routers never fragment IPv6 packets, so the Packet Too Big message is the only way a sender learns that a path is narrower than its packets. Blanket ICMPv6 filtering is a self-inflicted outage; RFC 4890 lists the message types that a firewall must let through.
icmpv6.depth:
What it is. ICMPv6 is the form the Internet Control Message Protocol (ICMP) takes in Internet Protocol version 6 (IPv6). Its specification, Request for Comments (RFC) 4443, by Alex Conta, Stephen Deering and Mukesh Gupta, was published in March 2006 and is now Internet Standard 89; it replaced RFC 2463 of December 1998, which had replaced the first specification, RFC 1885 of December 1995, and it is updated by RFC 4884 (April 2007), which lets some messages carry extension objects. The text is blunt about status: ICMPv6 is an integral part of IPv6, and every node must implement the base protocol fully. It is not a transport protocol and has no ports. An ICMPv6 message follows the IPv6 header, and any extension headers, and is announced by the value 58 in the preceding Next Header field, where the ICMP of IPv4 is protocol 1.

The message. Every message begins with an 8-bit Type, an 8-bit Code and a 16-bit Checksum, followed by a body whose layout the type decides. The checksum is computed over the message plus a pseudo-header of IPv6 fields (addresses, length and the value 58), which RFC 4443 marks as a change from IPv4, where the ICMP checksum covers the ICMP message alone. The high bit of the type splits the space in two: types 0 to 127 are errors and types 128 to 255 are informational. A node that receives an error of a type it does not know must hand it to the upper layer that sent the offending packet; an unknown informational message is silently discarded. The base specification defines four errors and two informational messages. Destination Unreachable (type 1) has codes for no route (0), administratively prohibited (1), beyond the scope of the source address (2), address unreachable (3), port unreachable (4), source address failed ingress or egress policy (5) and reject route (6). Packet Too Big (type 2) carries the maximum transmission unit (MTU) of the next-hop link. Time Exceeded (type 3) reports a hop limit exceeded in transit (code 0) or a fragment reassembly timeout (code 1). Parameter Problem (type 4) points at the offending octet. Echo Request (128) and Echo Reply (129) carry an Identifier and a Sequence Number, and every node must answer echo. Each error has exactly 32 bits of type-specific data and then as much of the packet that caused it as fits without the whole message exceeding the minimum IPv6 MTU of 1,280 octets; RFC 792 gave IPv4 only the header and the first 64 bits of data.

When errors are sent, and how often. An ICMPv6 error is never originated in response to another ICMPv6 error or to a Redirect, to a packet whose source address does not identify a single node, or to a packet sent to a multicast or broadcast destination, with two exceptions for the last rule: Packet Too Big, so that Path MTU Discovery works for multicast, and Parameter Problem code 2. Rate limiting is mandatory. RFC 4443 recommends a token bucket and suggests a burst of 10 and an average of 10 messages a second for a small device, and it calls a plain timer unreasonable because bursty tools such as traceroute need several errors at once. Implementations follow it: Linux has net.ipv6.icmp.ratelimit, 100 milliseconds by default, applied to the types in ratemask, by default every error except Packet Too Big; Cisco IOS XE has ipv6 icmp error-interval, 100 milliseconds with a bucket of 10 tokens by default. A router that answers some traceroute probes and not others is usually showing this limiter, not loss.

What rides on it. The registry of the Internet Assigned Numbers Authority (IANA), last updated on 30 October 2026, shows how much of IPv6 is ICMPv6. Types 133 to 137 are Neighbor Discovery (RFC 4861, September 2007): Router Solicitation, Router Advertisement, Neighbor Solicitation, Neighbor Advertisement and Redirect, which together do what the Address Resolution Protocol (ARP), ICMP Router Discovery and ICMP Redirect do in IPv4. Types 130 to 132 are Multicast Listener Discovery (MLD), by which a router learns which multicast addresses have listeners on its links, and type 143 is the version 2 report, now specified by RFC 9777 (March 2025, Internet Standard 101), which obsoleted RFC 3810. Types 144 to 147 serve Mobile IPv6, 148 and 149 the certification paths of SEcure Neighbor Discovery (SEND), and 160 and 161 are the Extended Echo of RFC 8335 (February 2018), which asks a node for the status of an interface, its own or a directly connected neighbour's. The code registries have grown as well: Destination Unreachable now runs to code 9 and Parameter Problem to code 10, most of the additions reporting problems with extension headers.

Path MTU Discovery. In IPv6 only the source fragments, and every link must carry 1,280 octets (RFC 8200, July 2017). A router that cannot forward a packet because it is larger than the outgoing link's MTU must send Packet Too Big, and the source lowers its estimate of the path, never below 1,280 (RFC 8201, July 2017). When a filter drops that message, RFC 8201 describes exactly what the user sees: connections that complete the three-way handshake of the Transmission Control Protocol (TCP) and then hang when data is transferred, the black-hole connection. RFC 7915 notes that it is not unusual for networks to drop Packet Too Big, which is why translators need special care and why RFC 4821 defines a discovery method that probes at the packetization layer and does not depend on ICMPv6 at all.

Filtering it properly. RFC 4890 (May 2007) is the reference. Through a firewall, the messages that must not be dropped are Destination Unreachable with all codes, Packet Too Big, Time Exceeded code 0, Parameter Problem codes 1 and 2, and Echo Request and Reply; the document argues that address scanning is far less of a threat in IPv6 and that filtering echo is unnecessary. Neighbor Discovery and MLD need no transit rule, because they are link-local by construction: a Neighbor Discovery message is valid only if it arrives with a Hop Limit of 255, which proves that no router forwarded it. For traffic addressed to the device itself the same errors, Neighbor Discovery and MLD must be accepted if the node is to take part in IPv6, and Redirect (137) is the one type for which an explicit policy decision should be taken. RFC 9099 (August 2021) repeats the advice for operators: accept the ICMPv6 messages that Neighbor Discovery and Path MTU Discovery need.

What goes wrong on the link. Any node on a link can send a Router Advertisement, and a rogue one, malicious or just misconfigured, can give hosts a wrong router or a wrong prefix. Router Advertisement Guard (RA-Guard, RFC 6105, February 2011) filters advertisements in the switches; attackers evaded early implementations by fragmenting the packet, so RFC 6980 (August 2013) forbade the Fragment header in Neighbor Discovery messages. From off the link, scanning a /64 forces the last router to attempt address resolution for addresses that do not exist, so that new devices cannot join and new flows cannot be set up (RFC 6583, March 2012); the mitigation is to rate-limit Neighbor Solicitations and to bound the state kept for unresolved addresses. Implementations fail too: the Common Vulnerabilities and Exposures entry CVE-2020-16898, published in October 2020, was remote code execution in the Windows TCP/IP stack through crafted Router Advertisements, scored 8.8 with an adjacent attack vector. And because errors are passed to upper layers, RFC 4443 asks those layers to validate an error against the embedded packet before acting on it.

In captures and on devices. In tcpdump, icmp6 is an abbreviation for ip6 proto 58, and the named values select single types, as in icmp6[icmp6type] == icmp6-packettoobig or icmp6-neighborsolicit; the manual warns that the abbreviation assumes a packet with no extension headers, and offers ip6 protochain 58 to follow the chain. In Wireshark the fields are icmpv6.type and icmpv6.code, with an icmpv6.nd family for Neighbor Discovery. On Linux, accept_ra and accept_redirects decide per interface whether advertisements and redirects are honoured, and both default to off when the host forwards. On F5 BIG-IP, show net ndp in the Traffic Management Shell (tmsh) prints the neighbour table that these messages build. On an ip6tables firewall the match is -p icmpv6 with --icmpv6-type, as in the example script that closes RFC 4890.

router-advertisement.def: A router advertisement (RA) is the ICMPv6 (Internet Control Message Protocol for IPv6) message, type 134, in which an IPv6 router announces itself, its prefixes and how hosts on the link should configure themselves.
router-advertisement.context: Router advertisements are how an IPv6 (Internet Protocol version 6) host learns its default router, its on-link prefixes and whether SLAAC (stateless address autoconfiguration) or DHCPv6 (Dynamic Host Configuration Protocol for IPv6) is on offer; DHCPv6 has no way to supply the default route. Without one a host keeps only its link-local address; a rogue one takes over its default router.
router-advertisement.depth:
A router advertisement (RA) is message type 134 of ICMPv6 (Internet Control Message Protocol for IPv6), defined with the rest of Neighbor Discovery in Request for Comments (RFC) 4861 of September 2007, the IPv6 (Internet Protocol version 6) counterpart of the ICMP (Internet Control Message Protocol) router discovery of IPv4 (version 4). Routers send them unsolicited to the all-nodes multicast address, by default at intervals of up to 600 seconds (the allowed range is 4 to 1,800), and in answer to a Router Solicitation (type 133), which a host sends up to three times, four seconds apart, after a random delay of up to one second when an interface comes up. A new router interface sends its first three advertisements at intervals of no more than 16 seconds, solicited answers are delayed by up to half a second, and RFC 4861 asks for no more than one multicast RA every three seconds, although FRRouting documents that it allows faster retransmission by default to speed convergence. The source must be the router's link-local address and the hop limit 255, and a host must silently discard any RA that fails either check, which proves the packet was not forwarded from another link.

The fixed part is short. Cur Hop Limit suggests the hop limit hosts should use; the M (managed address configuration) flag says addresses are available from DHCPv6 (Dynamic Host Configuration Protocol for IPv6), and the O (other configuration) flag says other information, such as DNS (Domain Name System) settings, is; neither flag forces anything, they only signal. Router Lifetime, in seconds, says how long the sender may be used as a default router; senders limit it to 9,000 seconds, it defaults to three times the maximum advertisement interval (1,800 seconds with defaults), and zero means do not use this router as a default at all, while still accepting its other information. Reachable Time and Retrans Timer, in milliseconds, tune neighbour unreachability detection. RFC 4191 (November 2005) put a two-bit default router preference in the flags byte, 01 high, 00 medium (the default), 11 low, and added a Route Information option, type 24, for more-specific routes; Wireshark exposes these as icmpv6.nd.ra.flag.m, .o, .prf and related fields.

The options do the configuring. The Source Link-Layer Address option (type 1) saves hosts a Neighbor Solicitation; the MTU (maximum transmission unit) option (type 5) sets the link MTU; each Prefix Information option (type 3) carries a prefix with an L flag for on-link determination, an A flag that permits SLAAC (stateless address autoconfiguration, RFC 4862), and valid and preferred lifetimes that default to 30 days and 7 days. Later RFCs moved more configuration into the RA: the Recursive DNS Server option (RDNSS, type 25) and DNS Search List (type 31) in RFC 8106 (March 2017), the NAT64 prefix (PREF64, type 38) in RFC 8781 (April 2020), the captive portal API address (type 37) in RFC 8910 (September 2020) and encrypted DNS resolver discovery (type 144) in RFC 9463 (November 2023). The default route itself comes only from the RA's Router Lifetime, which is why a network can run without any DHCPv6 server but not without RAs.

Hosts decide what to accept, and implementations differ. Linux learns from RAs only while forwarding is disabled, unless accept_ra is set to 2, and sends solicitations only when it would accept the answers; accept_ra_defrtr and accept_ra_pinfo switch off the default router and prefix parts separately, and the learned default route gets metric 1024 by default. On the router side, FRRouting sends RAs on an interface unless ipv6 nd suppress-ra is configured, with an interval of 600 seconds, a router lifetime of 1,800 and prefix lifetimes of 30 and 7 days by default; rdisc6, from the ndisc6 package, solicits and prints the RAs on a link from user space, and in Wireshark they are icmpv6.type == 134.

Lifetimes are where RAs cause the slowest failures. To stop a forged RA from expiring every address on a link, RFC 4862 forbids an unauthenticated RA from cutting an address's remaining valid lifetime below two hours, so after a prefix changes, as when a home router reboots and its provider delegates a new prefix, hosts can keep a stale address for days. RFC 9096 (August 2021) therefore asks customer edge routers to advertise preferred and valid lifetimes no longer than 45 and 90 minutes (2,700 and 5,400 seconds) and to deprecate stale prefixes actively; Linux now offers ra_honor_pio_life to obey the advertised lifetime instead of the two-hour rule.

Trust is the other problem: any node on the link can send an RA. RFC 6104 (February 2011) found that the common case is accidental, not malicious: a misconfigured router, or a laptop whose connection sharing turns it into a router, advertising itself as a default gateway and a prefix that leads nowhere. RA-Guard (RFC 6105, February 2011) filters advertisements in the switch, admitting them only on ports facing real routers; FortiSwitch implements it as policies that check the M and O flags, the hop limit, the router preference and the allowed source addresses and prefixes, and drop every RA arriving from a host port. Attackers evaded early RA-Guard implementations by hiding the RA behind IPv6 extension headers or fragments, as RFC 7113 (February 2014) describes, so RFC 6980 (August 2013) forbade the Fragment header in Neighbor Discovery messages. SEcure Neighbor Discovery (SEND, RFC 3971, March 2005) can sign RAs but has seen little deployment, and RAs are also parsed by every host on the link: CVE-2020-16898 in the Common Vulnerabilities and Exposures list, published on 16 October 2020 and scored 8.8, was remote code execution in the Windows TCP/IP (Transmission Control Protocol/Internet Protocol) stack through crafted Router Advertisements.

When IPv6 misbehaves on a link, the RA answers most of the first questions. A host with only a link-local address has received no valid RA, or one without an A-flagged prefix and no DHCPv6; a host with two default routers or an unexpected prefix is seeing a second, often rogue, advertiser; a host that has addresses but no DNS servers needs RDNSS or the O flag and DHCPv6; and a host that keeps an old prefix after renumbering is obeying the two-hour rule. The numbers worth remembering are type 134 (and 133 for the solicitation), hop limit 255, a 600-second default interval, a 1,800-second default router lifetime with 9,000 as the ceiling, prefix lifetimes of 30 and 7 days, the two-hour floor, and option types 3, 5, 24, 25, 31, 37 and 38.

ra-guard.def: RA-Guard (Router Advertisement Guard) is a switch feature, described in RFC (Request for Comments) 6105, that drops IPv6 (Internet Protocol version 6) Router Advertisements arriving on ports where no router is supposed to be, so that a host cannot make itself the default router of its neighbours.
ra-guard.context: RA-Guard (RFC, Request for Comments, 6105) is the practical answer to rogue router advertisements, which are far more often a misconfigured host than an attacker. It filters in the layer 2 fabric as a lighter alternative to SEND (SEcure Neighbor Discovery), and works only where hosts' traffic passes through switches that apply it. Its weak point has always been parsing: RAs (router advertisements) hidden behind IPv6 (Internet Protocol version 6) extension headers, fragments or unusual layer 2 encapsulations have slipped past implementations, which is why RFC 7113 tells switches to parse the whole header chain.
ra-guard.depth:
The problem it solves. In IPv6 (Internet Protocol version 6) a host learns its default router, its prefixes and often its DNS (Domain Name System) servers from Router Advertisements (RAs), and nothing in Neighbor Discovery says which nodes on a link may send them. RFC (Request for Comments) 6104, Tim Chown and Stig Venaas's problem statement of February 2011, found the common case to be accidental rather than malicious, more frequent on shared wireless networks but seen on wired ones too: a laptop running Windows Internet Connection Sharing that turns itself into a 6to4 gateway, or a router plugged in the wrong way round, advertising a default route and a prefix that lead nowhere. An attacker can do the same deliberately to put itself in the path of every host on the link. SEND (SEcure Neighbor Discovery, RFC 3971) can sign RAs but has seen little deployment, so the defence moved into the switch.

How it works. RFC 6105 (February 2011), by Eric Levy-Abegnoli, Gunter Van de Velde, Ciprian Popoviciu and Janos Mohacsi, describes a framework rather than a protocol: an access switch examines RAs and forwards only valid ones. In its simplest form the switch is told which port leads to the router: that port may forward RAs and every other port blocks them. Stateless RA-Guard decides from what is in the message and in the switch's configuration: the sender's link-layer address, the receiving port, the source IP (Internet Protocol) address, the advertised prefixes and the router priority, each checked against allowed values. Stateful RA-Guard learns legitimate senders, either during a learning period an administrator starts when a new router is installed, or by validating SEND, in which case only the switch and the routers need certificates. Because a valid RA must come from a link-local address with a hop limit of 255 (RFC 4861 section 6.1.2), RA-Guard is a strictly first-hop control, and RFC 9099 (August 2021) still recommends it, with SAVI (Source Address Validation Improvement), as a first line of defence against common attacks and misconfigured hosts, including on networks that use DHCPv6 (Dynamic Host Configuration Protocol for IPv6), since hosts there still take their default router from RAs.

How it was evaded. Early implementations looked for the ICMPv6 (Internet Control Message Protocol for IPv6) header at a fixed place, so attackers hid the RA behind IPv6 extension headers, or split it across fragments so that the switch never saw the ICMPv6 type in the first fragment. CVE-2011-2395 in the Common Vulnerabilities and Exposures list, published on 9 June 2011, recorded exactly that against Cisco IOS switches: a fragmented packet whose RA sat in the second fragment. In 2014 RFC 7113, by Fernando Gont, reported the fragment variant effective against every existing implementation, and its rules are now the test of a good one: pass packets whose source is not link-local or whose hop limit is not 255, since neither can be a valid RA; parse the entire header chain with no fixed byte limit; drop first fragments that do not contain the whole chain, which RFC 7112 (January 2014) requires them to; drop RAs and packets with unrecognized Next Header values, with that last behaviour configurable but defaulting to drop; and log what is dropped as a security fault. RFC 6980 (August 2013) made fragmented Neighbor Discovery messages invalid in the first place, with only SEND certificate advertisements excepted. The layer 2 variant came later: on 27 September 2022 CERT/CC (the CERT Coordination Center) published VU#855201, with CVE-2021-27853, CVE-2021-27854, CVE-2021-27861 and CVE-2021-27862, after Etienne Champetier showed that stacking VLAN (virtual local area network) 0 priority tags and 802.2 LLC/SNAP (logical link control and subnetwork access protocol) headers, or exploiting Ethernet to Wi-Fi conversion, let RAs past RA Guard, dynamic ARP (Address Resolution Protocol) inspection and ND (Neighbor Discovery) protection on many vendors' switches.

On real equipment. Cisco IOS XE builds it from an ipv6 nd raguard policy whose device-role is host or router, with optional checks on hop-limit, managed-config-flag, other-config-flag, router-preference maximum, match ipv6 access-list for allowed sources and match ra prefix-list for allowed prefixes, plus trusted-port to switch policing off, attached to an interface with ipv6 nd raguard attach-policy; in host mode all RAs and redirects are dropped, it works only on ingress, not on EtherChannels, and offers no protection where IPv6 is tunnelled. FortiSwitchOS has the same model as config switch raguard-policy, with device-role, managed-flag, other-flag, max-hop-limit, min-hop-limit, max-router-preference, match-src-addr and match-prefix, applied per interface and VLAN list. Extreme Networks Fabric Engine enables it with ipv6 fhs enable and ipv6 fhs ra-guard enable, and documents it as disabled by default. Hypervisors have their own version: Hyper-V's Set-VMNetworkAdapter -RouterGuard On drops Router Advertisement and Redirection messages from unauthorized virtual machines, alongside -DhcpGuard for rogue DHCP (Dynamic Host Configuration Protocol) servers.

Its limits are topological. RA-Guard protects only hosts whose traffic to each other crosses a switch that enforces it, so it does nothing on shared media, between virtual machines on an unprotected virtual switch, or between Wi-Fi clients that an access point bridges directly. RFC 9099 warns that RA-Guard and SAVI may not work as expected, or may even be harmful, where several routers share a link, and that home-network devices which legitimately send RAs need an exception, while recommending that it be strongly considered as a default on managed Wi-Fi and campus networks. It also covers only RAs: rogue DHCPv6 servers need the companion filter, DHCPv6-Shield (RFC 7610), which discards server messages except on designated ports, and the IPv4 equivalents are DHCP snooping and dynamic ARP inspection. CERT/CC's advice after VU#855201 applies to all of them: allow only the protocols an access port needs.

The numbers worth keeping: RFC 6105 for the framework, RFC 7113 for the parsing rules, RFC 6980 and RFC 7112 for fragments, RFC 9099 for operations; ICMPv6 type 134, hop limit 255, a link-local source; and the bypass families, extension headers and fragments (2011 to 2014) and VLAN 0 or LLC/SNAP stacking (2022). A deployment check is simple: from a host port, send an RA (rdisc6 lists them, and tools that forge them exist for testing) and confirm that the neighbouring hosts never install it, then repeat with an extension header and with fragmentation.

solicited-node-multicast.def: The IPv6 multicast group, ff02::1:ff00:0/104 plus an address's last 24 bits, that Neighbor Discovery asks instead of broadcasting.
solicited-node-multicast.context: Where ARP broadcasts to every host, IPv6 has no broadcast and sends address resolution and duplicate address detection to the solicited-node group of the target, which every node joins for each of its unicast and anycast addresses. Only the nodes sharing those 24 bits are interrupted.
solicited-node-multicast.depth:
The group is built by appending the low-order 24 bits of the address to ff02::1:ff00:0/104, which gives 2^24, or 16,777,216, possible groups. For 2001:db8::200:5eff:fe00:5301 the bits are 00 53 01 and the group is ff02::1:ff00:5301. Its link-local twin, fe80::200:5eff:fe00:5301, falls in the same group, by intent: addresses that differ only in their high-order bits share one, so a node joins fewer groups.

On Ethernet an IPv6 multicast is sent to a MAC address made of 33:33 and the last four octets of the group, here 33:33:ff:00:53:01, whose group bit marks it as multicast. Nodes join with MLD; a switch without MLD snooping still delivers the frame to every port, so the gain is fewer interrupts on other nodes rather than less traffic on the wire.

Duplicate address detection uses the same group: before using a tentative address a node joins its solicited-node group and sends a Neighbor Solicitation to it from the unspecified address. In Python's ipaddress the group is the prefix ORed with the address masked to 0xFFFFFF; the IPv6 Toolkit classifies the result as link-local multicast but does not derive it.

unique-local-address.def: An IPv6 address in fc00::/7, meant for use inside a site or between cooperating sites and not routed on the internet.
unique-local-address.context: Unique local addresses (RFC 4193) are the nearest IPv6 counterpart to RFC 1918 space, with one difference that matters: each site picks a random 40-bit Global ID, so the prefix is meant to be globally unique and a leak should not collide with anyone. They give no security by themselves.
unique-local-address.depth:
The address splits into the 7-bit fc00::/7 prefix, an L bit, a 40-bit Global ID, a 16-bit Subnet ID and the 64-bit interface identifier. Only L set to 1, locally assigned, is defined, so every ULA in use begins with fd. The Global ID must not be sequential or a well-known number: RFC 4193 derives it from a SHA-1 hash of the time of day and an EUI-64, keeping the low 40 bits, which makes fd00::/48 an invalid choice.

Their default scope is global, so only policy keeps them in. RFC 4193 asks exterior routing sessions and site borders to drop fc00::/7 by default, keeps their AAAA and PTR records out of the global DNS and expects them to reuse the global plan's subnet IDs when both run together; IANA marks the block not globally reachable.

Address selection treats them as a last choice: RFC 6724's default table gives fc00::/7 precedence 3 against 35 for IPv4, so by default a dual-stack host prefers an IPv4 destination to a ULA one. The IPv6 Toolkit labels these addresses unique local.

dhcpv6.def: DHCPv6 (Dynamic Host Configuration Protocol for IPv6, Internet Protocol version 6) is the IPv6 counterpart of DHCP: a server leases addresses, delegates whole prefixes to routers or simply hands out options such as DNS (Domain Name System) servers, but never the default router, which only Router Advertisements supply.
dhcpv6.context: DHCPv6 (Dynamic Host Configuration Protocol for IPv6) is now RFC (Request for Comments) 9915, Internet Standard 102 since January 2026, obsoleting RFC 8415. It runs beside or instead of SLAAC (stateless address autoconfiguration): it is how ISPs (internet service providers) delegate a prefix to a subscriber's router, how a network keeps a lease and a log for each address, and how hosts learn DNS (Domain Name System) and other options. It never supplies the default router or the on-link prefix; only Router Advertisements do, so no IPv6 network runs on DHCPv6 alone.
dhcpv6.depth:
What it is. DHCPv6 (Dynamic Host Configuration Protocol for IPv6, Internet Protocol version 6) was first specified in Request for Comments (RFC) 3315 in July 2003, edited by Ralph Droms; prefix delegation (RFC 3633) and stateless service (RFC 3736) followed as separate documents. RFC 8415 (November 2018) folded those and four other RFCs into one specification, and RFC 9915, published in January 2026 by Tomek Mrugalski, Bernie Volz, Michael Richardson, Sheng Jiang and Timothy Winters, obsoletes RFC 8415 and makes DHCPv6 an Internet Standard, STD 102. The 2026 revision removed three optional features that were rarely deployed: the IA_TA option for temporary addresses (a client can request and release an ordinary address instead), the Server Unicast option and the UseMulticast status code, so clients now always multicast. It is not DHCP (version 4) with longer addresses: the message format, the ports, the client identifier and the relationship with routers are all different.

The packets. Clients listen on UDP (User Datagram Protocol) port 546 and send to port 547, where servers and relay agents listen, normally to the link-scoped multicast group ff02::1:2 (All_DHCP_Relay_Agents_and_Servers); relay agents can reach every server in a site at ff05::1:3 (All_DHCP_Servers). The client normally sends from its link-local address, which, as RFC 9915 puts it, every interface where DHCPv6 is useful has, so DHCPv6 works before the host has any global address. Message types run from 1 to 13: Solicit, Advertise, Request, Confirm, Renew, Rebind, Reply, Release, Decline, Reconfigure, Information-request, Relay-forward and Relay-reply. A stateful assignment is Solicit, Advertise, Request and Reply, or just Solicit and Reply when both sides agree to Rapid Commit (option 14); stateless DHCPv6 is a single Information-request and Reply that carries options and no lease. In Wireshark the exchange is dhcpv6.msgtype.

Leases live in identity associations. An IA_NA (identity association for non-temporary addresses, option 3) holds addresses, an IA_PD (identity association for prefix delegation, option 25) holds delegated prefixes, and each carries a T1, after which the client renews with the server that granted it, and a T2, after which it rebinds with any server; RFC 9915 recommends 0.5 and 0.8 times the shortest preferred lifetime. Clients and servers identify themselves with a DUID (DHCP Unique Identifier) of type 1 (link-layer address plus time), 2 (vendor-assigned, based on an enterprise number), 3 (link-layer address) or 4 (UUID, universally unique identifier), and the standard says DUIDs are opaque and may only be compared for equality. That is the first trap for anyone used to IPv4: a DHCPv6 reservation is keyed on the DUID, not the MAC (media access control) address, and a reimaged host or a dual-boot machine may present a different DUID. RFC 6939 (May 2013) lets the first-hop relay add the client's link-layer address as option 79 for servers that need it.

Two gaps catch people out. An address from an IA Address option implies no prefix: RFC 9915 forbids forming an implicit prefix of any length other than 128, and RFC 5942 (July 2010) says that assigning an address, by SLAAC (stateless address autoconfiguration), DHCPv6 or by hand, must never by itself make a prefix on-link. And there is no default-router option at all: RFC 4862 states that the only mechanism to configure the default router's address automatically is the Router Advertisement (RA). A host on a DHCPv6-managed network therefore still needs RAs for its gateway and on-link prefixes, and a network that turns RAs off to force DHCPv6 gets hosts that hold an address and cannot leave the link. The RA's M flag says addresses are available through DHCPv6 and the O flag says other configuration is, but both only signal: RFC 4861 erratum 8055, held for document update in May 2025, notes that M=0 does not stop a node from attempting DHCPv6, since the router cannot know that no server exists.

Prefix delegation is the part that providers rely on. A subscriber's router asks with an IA_PD, receives a prefix, often a /48 or /56, cuts it into /64s, one per link, and advertises them in its own RAs, never for longer than the delegation's own lifetimes; when it releases a prefix it must first have advertised it with zero lifetimes. The same mechanism has now reached hosts. RFC 9663 (October 2024) describes delegating a unique prefix to each client on a large shared network, RFC 9762 (June 2025) added the P flag to the RA's Prefix Information Option to say the network prefers this to SLAAC or address leases (a host that honours P ignores the A flag), and Android's networking team announced in September 2025 that DHCPv6 prefix delegation was rolling out to most devices on Android 11 and later, arguing that both SLAAC and IA_NA make the network keep state for every address. RFC 9686 (December 2024) goes the other way, letting a host register an address it generated itself so that the DHCPv6 server's logs stay complete.

Where it runs, and how it fails. Relays work as in IPv4 but encapsulate: a relay wraps the client's message in a Relay-forward, adds options such as the interface identifier, and unwraps the server's Relay-reply. RFC 6221 (May 2011) defined a Lightweight DHCPv6 Relay Agent (LDRA) for access switches and digital subscriber line (DSL) access multiplexers that do not route IPv6 but must still tag which port a request came from, the IPv6 counterpart of option 82. On a FortiGate the server is config system dhcp6 server, with subnet, interface and Domain Name System (DNS) server settings, and FortiOS documents stateful, stateless, prefix delegation and relay modes; on the server side the Internet Systems Consortium (ISC) ended maintenance of ISC DHCP at the end of 2022 and points users to Kea. The classic fault is a rogue server on the link, whether a misconfigured home router or an attacker answering Solicits first. RFC 7610 (August 2015), DHCPv6-Shield, has the switch drop DHCPv6 server messages on every port not explicitly configured for a server, the analogue of RA-Guard, and requires it to parse the full IPv6 header chain so that extension headers cannot hide a reply; it protects hosts only, and does nothing about rogue RAs or attacks on the servers. The numbers to keep are UDP 546 and 547, ff02::1:2 and ff05::1:3, message types 1 to 13, options 3, 14, 25 and 79, DUID types 1 to 4, T1 and T2 at 0.5 and 0.8, and RFC 9915.

nat64.def: NAT64 (Network Address and Protocol Translation from IPv6 Clients to IPv4 Servers) is the stateful translator of Request for Comments (RFC) 6146: it lets clients that have only IPv6 (Internet Protocol version 6) open sessions to servers that have only IPv4 (version 4), sharing a few public IPv4 addresses among them by translating ports as well as addresses.
nat64.context: Stateful NAT64 is how networks that give hosts only IPv6 (Internet Protocol version 6), mobile networks among them, still reach the IPv4 (version 4) internet. It works with DNS64 (DNS extensions for NAT64), a resolver function that answers for an IPv4-only name with a synthesized AAAA record, the record type that holds an IPv6 address: the server's IPv4 address placed inside a translation prefix, normally the well-known 64:ff9b::/96. The client connects to that IPv6 address, and the NAT64 reads the IPv4 destination from its last 32 bits and maps the client to a public IPv4 address and port. Anything that never asks the Domain Name System (DNS), such as an application holding an IPv4 literal, fails unless the host adds the customer-side translator of 464XLAT.
nat64.depth:
What it is, and what it is not. Request for Comments (RFC) 6146, written by Marcelo Bagnulo, Philip Matthews and Iljitsch van Beijnum and published in April 2011, specifies stateful NAT64: a translator that lets IPv6-only (Internet Protocol version 6) clients reach IPv4 (version 4) servers using unicast UDP (User Datagram Protocol), TCP (Transmission Control Protocol) or ICMP (Internet Control Message Protocol). It rewrites each packet's headers with the stateless translation algorithm, SIIT (Stateless IP/ICMP Translation, now RFC 7915 of June 2016, which obsoleted RFC 6145), and adds per-flow state so that many IPv6 clients can share one or a few IPv4 addresses. That makes it different from SIIT on its own, which maps addresses 1:1 and keeps no state, and from DS-Lite (Dual-Stack Lite), which carries IPv4 packets inside IPv6 instead of translating them. Without existing state only the IPv6 side can open a session; IPv4-initiated traffic reaches an IPv6 host only through a statically configured binding.

The address arithmetic comes from RFC 6052 (October 2010). An IPv4-embedded IPv6 address is a prefix of 32, 40, 48, 56, 64 or 96 bits followed by the 32-bit IPv4 address, with bits 64 to 71 always zero for compatibility with the interface identifier format, so the shorter prefixes split the IPv4 address around that octet. The Well-Known Prefix, 64:ff9b::/96, takes only the /96 form: 192.0.2.33 becomes 64:ff9b::c000:221, also written 64:ff9b::192.0.2.33. It must never carry a non-global IPv4 address such as an RFC 1918 one, and translators must drop packets that combine the two. An operator who needs to translate towards private IPv4 space uses a Network-Specific Prefix from its own allocation, or since RFC 8215 (August 2017) the local-use 64:ff9b:1::/48. The Internet Assigned Numbers Authority (IANA) lists both: 64:ff9b::/96 (allocated 2010-10) as globally reachable, 64:ff9b:1::/48 (2017-06) as not.

A session step by step. DNS64, the Domain Name System (DNS) extension of RFC 6147 (April 2011), sits in the recursive resolver: when a name has no AAAA record, the record type that holds an IPv6 address, it fetches the A record and synthesizes a AAAA from the prefix and the IPv4 address; when a real AAAA exists, it should return that instead, ignoring answers in excluded ranges such as ::ffff:0:0/96. The client sends to the synthesized address, routing delivers the packet to the translator, and the NAT64 takes the IPv4 destination from the address, picks an IPv4 address and port from its pool and records the mapping in a Binding Information Base (BIB), of which it keeps three (TCP, UDP and ICMP query), each with its own session table. Mappings must be endpoint-independent, the same external address and port for a given IPv6 source whatever it talks to, and filtering may be endpoint-independent or address-dependent, which keeps NAT64 compatible with the usual NAT (network address translation) traversal techniques such as ICE (Interactive Connectivity Establishment). Hairpinning lets two IPv6 hosts behind the same translator reach each other through its IPv4 addresses. DNS64 and NAT64 never talk to each other: RFC 6147 says the only state they share is the prefix and an optional set of static parameters, configured identically on both, which is why a mismatched prefix fails silently.

The state has lifetimes, and they are the numbers that show up in tickets. RFC 6146 inherits them from the NAT behaviour RFCs: UDP mappings live at least 2 minutes (UDP_MIN) and by default at least 5 (UDP_DEFAULT); an established TCP session survives 2 hours idle (TCP_EST), plus 4 minutes in the transitory state (TCP_TRANS); an unsolicited inbound SYN waits 6 seconds (TCP_INCOMING_SYN); fragments wait at least 2 seconds; ICMP query sessions last 60 seconds by default. Because many subscribers share each public IPv4 address, a NAT64 run by a provider raises the same logging and attribution questions as carrier-grade NAT, and the same answers apply, including port-block allocation, which FortiOS documents for NAT64 on a page of its own.

How hosts learn the prefix. RFC 7050 (November 2013) lets a host ask for the AAAA records of ipv4only.arpa, a name whose only real A records are 192.0.0.170 and 192.0.0.171, and read the prefix out of the synthesized answer; RFC 8880 (August 2020) made ipv4only.arpa a special-use name, and IANA's IPv4 registry lists the pair as NAT64/DNS64 Discovery, reserved by protocol. A network can also announce the prefix directly in Router Advertisements with the PREF64 option, type 38, of RFC 8781 (April 2020). Knowing the prefix matters because of 464XLAT (RFC 6877, April 2013, written by Masataka Mawatari, Masanobu Kawashima and Cameron Byrne of T-Mobile USA): a stateless customer-side translator (CLAT) on the host or the home router gives applications a private IPv4 address and an IPv4 default route, translates 1:1 into IPv6, and hands the traffic to the provider-side translator (PLAT), which is an ordinary RFC 6146 NAT64. IPv4 literals and IPv4-only sockets then work, because they never needed DNS64.

Where it shows up. Apple has required since 1 June 2016 that every app submitted to the App Store work on an IPv6-only network, and tells developers to test on a DNS64/NAT64 network. RFC 8925 (October 2020) defined DHCPv4 option 108, IPv6-Only Preferred, so that a host able to live without IPv4 (usually because it has a CLAT) declines an IPv4 lease for V6ONLY_WAIT seconds, 1,800 by default and never less than 300, while legacy hosts on the same network still get IPv4: the IPv6-mostly design. Microsoft opened a public preview of Windows CLAT on 9 June 2026, discovering the prefix from PREF64 by default with ipv4only.arpa as the alternative, honouring option 108 and managed with netsh interface clat; OSnews reported general availability in Windows 11 25H2 from build 26200.9550 on 28 October 2026. On a FortiGate (FortiOS 7.4.3), config system dns64 enables the DNS proxy's synthesis with a dns64-prefix that defaults to 64:ff9b::/96, and the translation itself is a firewall policy with nat64 enabled, an IPv6 virtual IP with an embedded IPv4 address and an IPv4 pool with nat64 enabled. Fortinet's worked example embeds a 172.16.200.0/24 server under 64:ff9b::, fine in a lab but exactly what RFC 6052 forbids for the Well-Known Prefix on a real network. Public DNS64 resolvers exist, Google's at 2001:4860:4860::6464 and 2001:4860:4860::64, but they help only where a NAT64 on 64:ff9b::/96 is reachable.

What breaks. Protocols that protect IP (Internet Protocol) header information are, in RFC 6146's words, essentially incompatible with NAT64: IPsec AH (Authentication Header) fails in both modes and ESP (Encapsulating Security Payload) in transport mode, and UDP encapsulation restores end-to-end IPsec. Application protocols that carry addresses in their payload, SIP (Session Initiation Protocol) and FTP (File Transfer Protocol) among them, need an application-level gateway. A DNSSEC (DNS Security Extensions) validator that does not know about DNS64 may reject synthesized answers as tampered with, so validation behind a DNS64 has to understand synthesis or trust the resolver. Devices and applications that use a resolver other than the network's, including encrypted DNS over TLS (DoT) or HTTPS (DoH), which RFC 8683 notes declared DNS64 out of scope, get no synthesized answers and fall back to failing IPv4, unless a CLAT is present. The numbers worth keeping are 64:ff9b::/96 and 64:ff9b:1::/48, 192.0.0.170 and 192.0.0.171 behind ipv4only.arpa, PREF64 (type 38) in Router Advertisements, option 108 in DHCPv4, and RFCs 6146, 6147, 6052, 7915 and 6877.

ds-lite.def: A broadband design that carries subscribers' IPv4 inside IPv6 to a carrier NAT, so the access network can be IPv6-only.
ds-lite.context: Dual-Stack Lite (RFC 6333) gives each home native IPv6 plus IPv4 tunnelled to the provider's AFTR and translated there. RFC 9313 reports it as the most common of the IPv4-as-a-service methods in broadband, and it brings all the logging and attribution issues of carrier-grade NAT.
ds-lite.depth:
The customer's B4 element wraps each IPv4 packet in IPv6, IP protocol 4, without changing its address family; the AFTR, an IPv4-in-IPv6 tunnel endpoint and an IPv4-to-IPv4 NAT on one node, unwraps it and translates it to a shared public address. Because no family translation happens, applications that carry IPv4 literals in their payloads are much simpler to support. RFC 6333 numbers the tunnel ends from 192.0.0.0/29: 192.0.0.1 for the AFTR, 192.0.0.2 for the B4.

Since many subscribers share the same inside address, the AFTR tells them apart by the B4's IPv6 address. RFC 6888 applies paired pooling per subscriber rather than per inside address, and names that IPv6 address as the subscriber identifier in the CGN's logs; RFC 7422's deterministic mapping recovers it but loses the inner IPv4 address.

Encapsulation costs 40 bytes: on a 1500-byte path the inner IPv4 MTU is 1460 and the IPv4 MSS 1420, and RFC 6333 asks operators to raise link MTUs, since path MTU discovery is not reliable here. On Linux a B4 tunnel uses mode ipip6. Lightweight 4over6 moves the NAT into the customer's equipment to remove per-flow state from the provider.

464xlat.def: IPv4 access across an IPv6-only network by translating twice: statelessly on the device, statefully at the provider.
464xlat.context: 464XLAT (RFC 6877) keeps IPv4-only applications and IPv4 literals working on IPv6-only networks, notably cellular ones, by pairing a translator on the device (CLAT) with a NAT64 in the network (PLAT). It translates and does not encapsulate: nothing is tunnelled.
464xlat.depth:
The CLAT gives local applications a private IPv4 address and a default route, from the 192.0.0.0/29 range reserved for systems that need IPv4 addresses but emit no IPv4 packets, and translates their packets one to one into IPv6. The PLAT, an ordinary stateful NAT64, translates them back and shares global IPv4 addresses among many clients. IPv4 exists only inside the device.

Most traffic never touches the CLAT. The CLAT translates only when an IPv4 literal or an IPv4-only socket requires it; applications that use names get synthesized AAAA records from DNS64 and go straight to the NAT64, and native IPv6 needs no translation. RFC 9313 cites a cellular deployment where, to the end of 2018, 75% of traffic was IPv6 end to end, 24% went through DNS64 and NAT64, and under 1% used the CLAT as well.
