It is not full IPv4. It supports only clients reaching servers with global IPv4 addresses, so IPv4 peer-to-peer and inbound connections do not work. The provider side keeps per-flow state, and where data-retention laws apply each PLAT entry must be logged, as at any carrier-grade NAT.

6to4.def: 6to4 is an automatic tunnelling method, defined in Request for Comments (RFC) 3056 in 2001, that gives any site with a public IPv4 (Internet Protocol version 4) address an IPv6 (version 6) prefix built from that address, 2002 followed by the 32-bit IPv4 address, and carries the IPv6 packets inside IPv4 to the endpoint written in each destination address.
6to4.context: 6to4, defined in RFC (Request for Comments) 3056, gave every public IPv4 (Internet Protocol version 4) address a /48 of IPv6 (version 6) under 2002::/16, with no tunnel to configure, and reached native IPv6 through relay routers, often found through the anycast address 192.88.99.1. Asymmetric and black-holed relays and filtered protocol 41 made it fail often enough that RFC 7526 deprecated the anycast relays in 2015 and required 6to4 to ship disabled, and RFC 6343 notes that rogue Router Advertisements often carry a 2002::/16 prefix.
6to4.depth:
What it is. Request for Comments (RFC) 3056, written by Brian Carpenter and Keith Moore and published in February 2001, connected IPv6 (Internet Protocol version 6) sites across an IPv4 (version 4) internet without any tunnel being configured by hand. The Internet Assigned Numbers Authority (IANA) set aside 2002::/16 for it, and a site whose border router holds the public IPv4 address V4ADDR owns the prefix 2002:V4ADDR::/48 with no further assignment: illustratively, 192.0.2.33 gives 2002:c000:221::/48. That address must be one duly allocated by a registry, never RFC 1918 private space. To reach another 6to4 site the router reads the IPv4 tunnel endpoint straight from the destination's 2002 prefix and sends the IPv6 packet inside IPv4 with protocol number 41, the same as a configured 6in4 tunnel, so the whole IPv4 internet behaves as one unicast point-to-point link layer. It is not GRE (Generic Routing Encapsulation), which adds its own header, and not Teredo, which wraps IPv6 in UDP (User Datagram Protocol) to cross NAT (network address translation) devices that drop protocol 41.

Relays connect it to the rest of IPv6. Native IPv6 networks cannot reach 2002::/16 by themselves, so relay routers advertise a route to 2002::/16 into native routing, accept the native traffic and tunnel it over IPv4 to the V4ADDR embedded in the destination; in the other direction a 6to4 router sends everything that is not 6to4 to a relay as its IPv6 default route. The two directions are independent, so the outbound packet usually crosses one relay and the reply the relay topologically nearest to the remote network, often a different one run by someone else. RFC 3068 (June 2001), from Christian Huitema of Microsoft, removed the last piece of configuration by giving relays an anycast address, 192.88.99.1 in 192.88.99.0/24, or 2002:c058:6301:: in its 6to4 form, so that a 6to4 router could simply point its default route at the nearest relay. Windows exposed all of this: Set-Net6to4Configuration takes a State of Default, Automatic, Enabled or Disabled and a RelayName, mirroring the netsh interface 6to4 context.

Why it failed. Nobody operated those relays on anyone's behalf, and RFC 6343 (August 2011), Brian Carpenter's advisory guidelines, collected the evidence: one experiment by Emile Aben of the RIPE NCC (RIPE Network Coordination Centre, a regional internet registry) recorded failures in 9 to 20 per cent of all 6to4 connection attempts (about 15 per cent on average, with weekdays worse than weekends, and that counting only failures on the return path), and one by Geoff Huston in 9 to 19 per cent of 6to4 clients. The failure modes have names: an outbound black hole, where packets sent to 192.88.99.1 are silently dropped; no return relay, where the reply never finds its way back; asymmetric, overloaded relays with highly variable round-trip times; protocol 41 blocked by firewalls and NAT boxes near users; and path MTU (maximum transmission unit) discovery failures, because encapsulation lowers the path MTU below the usual 1,500 bytes. Dual-stack hosts hid the damage by falling back to IPv4 after 7 to 20 seconds, so users experienced slow sites rather than broken ones, and content providers measured a fraction of 1 per cent of connections to dual-stack servers lost to 6to4. RFC 6724 (September 2012) codified the lesson in default address selection: in its policy table native IPv6 has precedence 40, IPv4-mapped addresses (that is, IPv4) 35, 2002::/16 only 30 and Teredo's 2001::/32 5, so a correctly behaving host prefers plain IPv4 over a 6to4 path.

It also had a security cost. RFC 3964 (December 2004, Pekka Savola and Chirayu Patel) pointed out that a 6to4 router must accept protocol 41 from any node on the IPv4 internet, which invites denial of service and makes it easy to spoof IPv6 source addresses, and that relays can be used to reflect traffic. A quieter problem showed up on campus networks: RFC 6343 reports that observers at the University of Southampton, Tim Chown and James Morse, and at other sites found rogue Router Advertisements often conveying a 2002::/16 prefix, sent by devices acting as connection-sharing routers. Windows' own Set-Net6to4Configuration has an AutoSharing setting that, by default, forwards 6to4 prefixes when Internet Connection Sharing is on, which is exactly that kind of behaviour, and RA-Guard (Router Advertisement Guard) on access switches is the usual defence.

Deprecation, not removal. RFC 7526 (May 2015, Best Current Practice BCP 196, Ole Troan and Brian Carpenter) formally deprecated anycast 6to4 and the address 192.88.99.1, declaring it no longer a useful service of last resort, obsoleted RFC 3068 and the 6to4 provider managed tunnels of RFC 6732, and ruled that 192.88.99.0/24 must not be reassigned except by a future IETF (Internet Engineering Task Force) Standards Action. Unicast 6to4 and 2002::/16 were not deprecated, and the address selection rules were left as they were. The implementation rules changed: anycast 6to4 is not recommended in new code and must be off by default; hosts must ship unicast 6to4 disabled too; routers must ship 6to4 disabled, and enabling IPv6 forwarding must not switch it on. IANA's registries show the result: 2002::/16 still listed as 6to4 (allocated 2001-02), and 192.88.99.0/24 as Deprecated (6to4 Relay Anycast), allocated 2001-06 and terminated 2015-03, with only 192.88.99.2/32 still in use, as the 6a44 relay anycast address.

The idea that survived is 6rd. In 2007 the French provider Free, of the Iliad group, took Rémi Després's proposal and in five weeks, from 7 November to 11 December, made native-looking IPv6 available to more than 1,500,000 residential customers, as RFC 5569 (January 2010) records. The trick was to use the 6to4 arithmetic under the provider's own prefix instead of 2002::/16, so that every relay is inside the provider's network and the return path is no longer a stranger's. RFC 5969 (August 2010, Mark Townsley and Ole Troan) standardized it and says plainly that, unlike 6to4, 6rd is for use only where a service provider closely manages the delivery of IPv6 service.

On a live network. A 6to4 address is easy to recognize: anything in 2002::/16, whose next 32 bits are an IPv4 address. Python's ipaddress module reports that embedded address through the sixtofour property (None for anything else), and the IPv6 Toolkit labels 2002::/16 addresses as 6to4 without extracting it. On Linux, 6to4, 6in4 and 6rd tunnels are all sit devices in ip tunnel, which also takes 6rd-prefix and 6rd-relay_prefix options. On Windows, the DisabledComponents registry value under the Tcpip6 parameters has separate bits for tunnel, 6to4, ISATAP (Intra-Site Automatic Tunnel Addressing Protocol) and Teredo interfaces, and Microsoft recommends the 0x20 bit, which prefers IPv4, over disabling IPv6 outright. On a perimeter firewall, IP protocol 41 arriving from or leaving for arbitrary IPv4 addresses is either a deliberate tunnel or an unmanaged IPv6 path around the IPv6 policy, and should be treated as one or the other. The numbers to keep are 2002::/16 and the /48 per IPv4 address, protocol 41, 192.88.99.1 (deprecated since May 2015), precedence 30 against IPv4's 35, and RFCs 3056, 3068, 6343, 7526 and 5969.

teredo.def: Teredo is an IPv6 (Internet Protocol version 6) transition method of last resort, defined in Request for Comments (RFC) 4380 in 2006, that carries IPv6 packets inside UDP (User Datagram Protocol) over IPv4 so that a host behind an IPv4 NAT (network address translation) device can still obtain a global IPv6 address and reach IPv6 peers.
teredo.context: Teredo (RFC, Request for Comments, 4380) was designed as IPv6 (Internet Protocol version 6) access of last resort, for hosts behind a NAT (network address translation) that can use no other transition scheme. A Teredo server on UDP (User Datagram Protocol) port 3544 tells the client how its NAT maps it, the client's address in 2001::/32 encodes that mapping, and relays connect Teredo clients to native IPv6. RFC 6724 gives it precedence 5, far below native IPv6 at 40 and IPv4 at 35, and Microsoft shipped it in Windows, where Xbox multiplayer gaming used it for NAT traversal.
teredo.depth:
What it is. Teredo was designed by Christian Huitema of Microsoft and published as Request for Comments (RFC) 4380 in February 2006, as an IPv6 (Internet Protocol version 6) provider of last resort: a way for a host that sits behind an IPv4 (version 4) NAT (network address translation) device, and so cannot use 6to4 or a configured tunnel because the NAT drops IP protocol 41, to get a global IPv6 address anyway. It wraps each IPv6 packet in a UDP (User Datagram Protocol) datagram that the NAT can translate like any other. Three roles take part. A Teredo client is the host itself; a Teredo server, a node with a global IPv4 address listening on UDP port 3544, helps the client learn its NAT mapping and relays the first contact; a Teredo relay is an IPv6 router that receives traffic for Teredo clients from the native IPv6 internet and forwards it over the Teredo service. The service prefix is 2001::/32, listed by the Internet Assigned Numbers Authority (IANA) as TEREDO, allocated in 2006-01 inside the IETF (Internet Engineering Task Force) protocol assignments block 2001::/23. RFC 5991 (September 2010) and RFC 6081 (January 2011), from Microsoft's Dave Thaler with colleagues on the first, and RFC 9601 (August 2024), on propagating explicit congestion notification through tunnels, update it.

The address carries the NAT traversal in its 128 bits: the 32-bit prefix, the Teredo server's IPv4 address, 16 bits of flags, then the client's mapped UDP port and mapped public IPv4 address, both obfuscated by inverting every bit (an exclusive OR with 0xFFFF and 0xFFFFFFFF) so that NATs which rewrite addresses found in payloads leave them alone. Illustratively, with server 192.0.2.45 and a mapping of 203.0.113.20:40000, the address is 2001:0:c000:22d:3c5a:63bf:34ff:8eeb, where 63bf is 40000 (9c40) exclusive-ORed with ffff and 34ff:8eeb is cb00:7114 exclusive-ORed with ffffffff. The flags were meant to sit where the top of a modified EUI-64 (64-bit Extended Unique Identifier) interface identifier sits, with the universal and group bits at zero; RFC 4380 let only one of them, the cone bit, vary. RFC 5991 found that this made Teredo addresses easy to guess, since the server field has low entropy and ports are often predictable, and replaced most flag bits with 12 random bits, observing that without them an attacker who knows the server faces a search space of only 16 bits, worse than the 24 bits of a SLAAC (stateless address autoconfiguration) address whose interface card vendor is known.

How it gets through the NAT. The client qualifies first: it sends a Router Solicitation to its server inside UDP, and the reply comes back with an origin indication telling the client the address and port its NAT presented. Before two parties exchange real traffic they send bubbles, minimal IPv6 packets made of a header with next header value 59 (no next header) and nothing else, whose only purpose is to create mappings in the NATs along the way. RFC 4380 supported clients behind cone, restricted cone and port-restricted cone NATs and said that bubble exchanges would often fail behind symmetric NATs, whose port choice the peer cannot predict. RFC 5991 dropped the first phase of qualification and with it the cone bit, at the cost of more indirect bubbles, and RFC 6081 added six extensions: symmetric NAT support, a UPnP (Universal Plug and Play) extension, port-preserving and sequential-port symmetric NAT support, hairpinning, and server load reduction. Hosts should assume a link MTU (maximum transmission unit) of 1,280 bytes on the Teredo interface, the IPv6 minimum, so that the extra IPv4 and UDP headers never push a packet past a real link's limit.

How it performed. RFC 6724 (September 2012) ranks 2001::/32 at precedence 5 in the default address selection table, against 40 for native IPv6, 35 for IPv4 and 30 for 6to4, so a well-behaved dual-stack host uses Teredo only when nothing else is available. In December 2010 Geoff Huston found Teredo in only 4 per cent of the IPv6 connections reaching his measurement server, with failure rates of 1 to 2 per cent against some 13 per cent for 6to4, and 93 per cent of failed Teredo attempts matched by a successful IPv4 connection from the NAT address embedded in the Teredo address. Teredo works because of the NAT, not despite it, so it suffers when the NAT is a provider's: RFC 7021 (September 2013) reports that in 2010 testing behind carrier-grade NAT, both 6to4 and Teredo failed outright or were severely degraded.

Windows and Xbox kept it alive. Microsoft's NetworkTransition module configures it with Set-NetTeredoConfiguration, whose Type accepts Default, Client, Enterpriseclient, Natawareclient, Server, Relay, Automatic and Disabled; Microsoft's documentation says the default state is client, and Enterpriseclient skips the managed network detection that the ordinary client performs. ServerName points the client at a Teredo server, and ClientPort fixes the local UDP port, otherwise chosen by the operating system; netsh interface teredo is the older equivalent, and the DisabledComponents registry value has a bit that turns Teredo interfaces off, although Microsoft recommends the 0x20 bit, which prefers IPv4, over disabling IPv6. In May 2015 Microsoft's Darrin Veit and Christopher Palmer told operators that Xbox One multiplayer used Teredo for NAT traversal and IPsec (Internet Protocol Security) for protection, that Xbox experiences on Windows 10 would do the same while preferring to source traffic from the IANA-registered port 3074, that around 20 per cent of Xbox One devices had native IPv6, and that carrier-grade NAT was steadily degrading peer-to-peer connectivity over IPv4.

Security. A tunnel over UDP is invisible to anything that inspects only the outer IP (Internet Protocol) and UDP headers. RFC 6169 (April 2011) uses Teredo as its example: an unaware security device regulates the outer packet and never sees the inner IPv6 one, and addresses inside the tunnel escape ingress and egress filtering. A Teredo client is, in effect, a host with a global IPv6 address reachable through the perimeter's NAT, so a network that has no IPv6 policy may still have IPv6 traffic. The simple control RFC 6169 gives is to block outbound UDP to port 3544, which stops the client from reaching any Teredo server; on managed Windows fleets the same result comes from Set-NetTeredoConfiguration -Type Disabled or Group Policy. Python's ipaddress module decodes the server and client addresses of any 2001::/32 address through its teredo property, which is the quickest way to tell from a log which NAT a Teredo source sits behind; the IPv6 Toolkit, by contrast, does not recognize the prefix and reports a Teredo address as ordinary global unicast. The numbers worth keeping are 2001::/32, UDP 3544, next header 59 for bubbles, 1,280 bytes, precedence 5, 12 random flag bits, and RFCs 4380, 5991 and 6081.

stun.def: A protocol that lets a host behind NAT ask a server which public address and port its packets arrived from.
stun.context: Session Traversal Utilities for NAT (RFC 8489) serves voice, video and peer-to-peer applications: it reports the mapping a NAT created, checks connectivity between endpoints and keeps mappings alive. It is not a NAT traversal solution by itself, but a tool that such solutions use.
stun.depth:
A client sends a Binding request, by default to port 3478 over UDP or TCP, or 5349 over TLS or DTLS. The server copies the source address and port it sees, the reflexive transport address created by the NAT nearest the server, into an XOR-MAPPED-ADDRESS attribute in the response.

The XOR is a defence against middleboxes. Some NATs rewrote any binary field holding their public address, a misguided generic ALG that broke STUN and its integrity check, so the port is XORed with the top 16 bits of the magic cookie 0x2112A442 and an IPv4 address with the whole cookie. A mapping of 203.0.113.1:51234 travels as port 0xE930 and address 0xEA12D543.

What STUN learns is useful only if the NAT reuses the mapping for every destination: RFC 4787 makes endpoint-independent mapping a MUST so that such methods work, and UDP hole punching depends on it. Older texts sort NATs with STUN's original cone and symmetric names, which RFC 4787 retired as a source of confusion. RFC 8489 obsoletes RFC 5389.

nat-alg.def: Code in a NAT that reads and rewrites addresses inside an application's payload, so protocols such as FTP survive translation.
nat-alg.context: NAT rewrites headers, but protocols such as FTP, SIP and H.323 also write addresses into their payloads. An Application Level Gateway (RFC 2663) repairs those one protocol at a time; the same meddling breaks protected or NAT-aware traffic, which is why RFC 4787 wants UDP ALGs turned off.
nat-alg.depth:
FTP is the model, and RFC 3022 calls it the most popular ALG on NAT devices. The PORT command and the PASV reply carry an address and port in ASCII, so the ALG rewrites them and creates the mapping for the data connection they announce. Rewriting can change the length: with port 51234 written 200,34, the string 10,0,0,10,200,34 has 16 characters and 203,0,113,1,200,34 has 18, so the ALG must also shift TCP sequence numbers for the rest of the session. On Linux these are conntrack helpers, which create expectations, and the data connection is RELATED.

Every ALG is a protocol-specific workaround, and it fails wherever payloads are protected. An encoded payload disables it unless it holds the key; a DNS-ALG that rewrites answers breaks DNSSEC signatures; and NATs that rewrote any field holding their public address broke STUN until STUN XORed its addresses. RFC 4787 says NAT ALGs for UDP should be turned off, and RFC 5382 recommends disabling every TCP ALG except FTP by default.

Behind carrier-grade NAT, subscribers get only the ALGs their provider runs, and RFC 6333 notes that no AFTR can implement every current and future one.

dns-rcode.def: Response code (RCODE): the status field in the header of every Domain Name System (DNS) response, such as NOERROR (0, no error), SERVFAIL (2, server failure), NXDOMAIN (3, the name does not exist) or REFUSED (5).
dns-rcode.context: dig prints it as status on its HEADER line, and nslookup as the reason it can't find a name. It is the first thing to read in a failed Domain Name System (DNS) lookup, because each value of the response code (RCODE) points at a different culprit: the name itself, the server that answered, or a policy that turned the question away.
dns-rcode.depth:
The response code (RCODE) is a four-bit field in the header of every Domain Name System (DNS) message, the last four bits of the 16-bit flags word that follows the message identifier, and it is set only in responses. Request for Comments (RFC) 1035, written by Paul Mockapetris in November 1987, defined six values: 0 no error condition; 1 format error, the server could not interpret the query; 2 server failure, the server could not process the query because of a problem with the name server; 3 name error, the domain name in the query does not exist, a code the RFC calls meaningful only in responses from an authoritative server; 4 not implemented, the server does not support that kind of query; and 5 refused, the server declines for policy reasons, with a zone transfer as the example. Values 6 to 15 were left in reserve. The shorthand names came later: RFC 9499 lists NOERROR, FORMERR, SERVFAIL, NXDOMAIN, NOTIMP and REFUSED, records that RFC 2308 established NXDOMAIN (non-existent domain) as a synonym for name error, and observes that the registry of the Internet Assigned Numbers Authority (IANA) writes them in mixed case (NoError, ServFail, NXDomain) while most documents use capitals.

Sixteen values did not last. Dynamic update (RFC 2136, April 1997) took 6 to 10: YXDOMAIN and YXRRSET for a name or a record set that exists when it should not, NXRRSET for a record set that should exist and does not, NOTAUTH and NOTZONE. DNS Stateful Operations (RFC 8490) took 11, DSOTYPENI, and 12 to 15 are still unassigned. The Extension Mechanisms for DNS (EDNS) widened the field instead: the OPT pseudo-record of RFC 6891 carries an extended RCODE of eight bits that forms the upper part of a 12-bit code, zero meaning that an ordinary four-bit value is in use. That is where BADVERS (16, bad OPT version) and BADCOOKIE (23, bad or missing server cookie, RFC 7873 of May 2016) live, and dig prints the combined value. A server that answers without an OPT record cannot express anything above 15. The records that authenticate transactions with a shared secret go further: TSIG (Transaction Signature, RFC 8945) and TKEY (Transaction Key, RFC 2930) have a 16-bit error field of their own, holding BADSIG (16), BADKEY (17), BADTIME (18), BADMODE (19), BADNAME (20), BADALG (21) and BADTRUNC (22).

RFC 6895 (April 2013), the document that sets IANA's rules for the DNS, states that all three places share one number space, with two exceptions it could only document. Code 16 means BADVERS in an OPT record and BADSIG in a TSIG record, a duplicate assignment the RFC calls accidental; code 9, NOTAUTH, means not authoritative in a plain response and not authorized when a TSIG record with a non-zero error accompanies it. As of 9 November 2026 the registry leaves 24 to 3,840 unassigned and keeps 3,841 to 4,095 for private use, and a new code requires review by the Internet Engineering Task Force (IETF).

The first split to make is between an answer that says no and the absence of an answer. RFC 9520 is explicit that NXDOMAIN and NOERROR with no data are useful responses, not failures, and both are cached for as long as the zone's Start of Authority (SOA) record allows. NXDOMAIN denies the name and, since RFC 8020, everything beneath it. SERVFAIL is the vaguest code: an authoritative server returns it when it has no valid data for a zone, as when a secondary cannot refresh from its primary, and a recursive resolver returns it for many conditions, among them unreachable servers, delegation loops and a failed validation under the DNS Security Extensions (DNSSEC), where RFC 4035 requires RCODE 2 unless the query set the CD (checking disabled) bit. REFUSED usually comes from an authoritative server asked about a zone it does not serve, or from a resolver whose access list excludes the client. FORMERR is often about EDNS, returned by a server that does not implement it or that received malformed option fields, and NOTIMP means the kind of query itself is unsupported.

Failures are cached too, but briefly. RFC 9520 (December 2023), by Duane Wessels, William Carroll and Matthew Thomas of Verisign, requires a resolver to cache a resolution failure for at least one second and no more than five minutes, recommends backing off while the failure persists, and limits a query to three attempts at a given server address over a given transport. The reasons were measured. In 2021 Verisign researchers saw queries for one botnet domain rise from about 50 a second to 60,000 a second when its authoritative servers were made to answer SERVFAIL, and during the six-hour Facebook outage of 4 October 2021 query traffic at the .com and .net servers went from 7,000 to 900,000 a second. That outage is also a lesson in reading the code. Cloudflare opened its incident at 15:51 UTC (Coordinated Universal Time) under the title Facebook DNS lookup returning SERVFAIL, suspecting its own resolver, when the cause was Facebook's withdrawal of its Border Gateway Protocol (BGP) routes, which left every resolver unable to reach the name servers. SERVFAIL names a symptom, not a cause. BIND (Berkeley Internet Name Domain) 9 caches a SERVFAIL for one second by default and never for more than thirty (the servfail-ttl option).

Two readings mislead more than any others. NOERROR does not mean an answer arrived: with an empty answer section it is NODATA, which has no code of its own, and a signed zone that uses compact denial of existence (RFC 9824) answers even a nonexistent name that way. And the exit status of a tool is not the RCODE: dig exits with 0 for any response it receives, NXDOMAIN included, and with 9 only when no server replied, so a script must read the status word on the header line; BIND's nslookup prints two asterisks, server can't find, the name and the name of the code. Two cautions follow from the protocol itself. The header is not covered by DNSSEC signatures, so the RCODE cannot be authenticated, as RFC 9824 points out, and the proof that a name does not exist lives in the signed records of the authority section. And a code can be a policy decision: a response policy zone (RPZ) can turn a real answer into NXDOMAIN, and on an F5 BIG-IP the DNS profile's unhandled-query-action (allow by default, or drop, hint, noerror, reject) and the last action of Rapid Response (drop by default, or allow, noerror, nxdomain, refuse, truncate) decide what a query gets back when it matches neither a name handled by global server load balancing (GSLB) nor a DNS Express zone.

Because one code covers so many causes, RFC 8914 (October 2020) added Extended DNS Errors, an EDNS option with code 15 that carries a 16-bit INFO-CODE and optional text. It was created primarily to explain SERVFAIL and, by its own definition, does not change how the RCODE is processed. The registry held 36 codes on 9 November 2026, numbered 0 to 35, among them 6 DNSSEC Bogus, 7 Signature Expired, 9 DNSKEY Missing, 15 Blocked, 16 Censored, 17 Filtered, 18 Prohibited, 22 No Reachable Authority and 23 Network Error. A SERVFAIL that arrives with code 7 is a signing problem in the zone; the same SERVFAIL with code 22 is a reachability problem, and the RCODE alone would never tell them apart.

The numbers worth keeping are few. Four bits in the header, twelve with EDNS, sixteen inside TSIG. Codes 0, 2, 3 and 5 for almost every case met in daily work. One second to five minutes for a cached failure, against the SOA's negative TTL (time to live) for a cached NXDOMAIN. Sixteen for two unrelated errors. In a packet capture the field is the low four bits of the fourth byte of the DNS message, straight after the RA (recursion available) flag and the reserved bits.

nodata.def: A negative Domain Name System (DNS) answer meaning that the name exists but holds no record of the type asked: the response code is NOERROR (no error) and the answer section is empty.
nodata.context: NODATA has no response code (RCODE) of its own, so it hides behind a status that reads as success. It matters whenever a Domain Name System (DNS) lookup works and still returns nothing: what is missing is a record of that type at that name, not the name itself, which is what an NXDOMAIN (non-existent domain) would have said. The commonest case is harmless: a query for type AAAA, the IPv6 (Internet Protocol version 6) address record, at a name that only has IPv4 (Internet Protocol version 4) addresses.
nodata.depth:
Request for Comments (RFC) 2308, written by Mark Andrews in March 1998, defines NODATA as a pseudo RCODE (response code): the name is valid for the given class, but there are no records of the given type. The Domain Name System (DNS) header has no value for it, so the condition has to be inferred from the message: the RCODE is NOERROR (no error, value 0), the answer section holds no relevant records, and the authority section either contains the zone's Start of Authority (SOA) record or contains no name server (NS) records. NXDOMAIN (non-existent domain, RCODE 3, the name error) denies the name for every type; NODATA denies one type at a name that exists. RFC 9499, the DNS terminology document of March 2024, keeps this definition and adds a warning: NXRRSET is sometimes used as a synonym, and that is a mistake, because NXRRSET is RCODE 8 of dynamic update (RFC 2136) and means something else.

RFC 2308 sorts NODATA responses into three types by what the authority section carries. Type 1 has the SOA and the NS records of the zone, with the servers' addresses in the additional section; type 2 has the SOA alone; type 3 has nothing at all. A referral looks dangerously similar, since it is also NOERROR with an empty answer, but its authority section has NS records and no SOA, and that is the test RFC 2308 gives for telling the two apart. Because some resolvers of the time took a type 1 response for a referral, the RFC recommends that authoritative servers send only type 2. Aliases add one wrinkle: canonical name (CNAME) records may sit in the answer section, and the NODATA then applies to the last name in the chain, not to the name that was asked.

A negative answer has no record to carry a time to live (TTL), so the SOA in the authority section carries it. An authoritative server must include that SOA, with its TTL set to the smaller of the SOA's MINIMUM field and the SOA's own TTL, and that value is how long a resolver may cache the answer; RFC 2308 is the document that redefined MINIMUM as this negative TTL. A NODATA is cached for the exact name, type and class, whereas an NXDOMAIN is cached for the name and class and, since RFC 8020 (November 2016), may be applied to every name beneath it. A response without an SOA, the type 3 form, should not be cached at all. Resolvers cap the value: RFC 2308 reports that limits of one to three hours work well and that more than a day causes trouble, BIND (Berkeley Internet Name Domain) 9 defaults max-ncache-ttl to 10,800 seconds and silently truncates anything above seven days, and Unbound defaults cache-max-negative-ttl to 3,600 seconds. The practical effect is familiar: a record added after someone has already asked for it stays invisible behind that resolver until the negative TTL runs out.

Most NODATA answers are healthy. The commonest is a query for type AAAA, the IPv6 (Internet Protocol version 6) address record, at a name that only has IPv4 (Internet Protocol version 4) addresses. RFC 4074 (May 2005) describes the expected behaviour, RCODE 0 with an empty answer section, which tells the stub resolver to go and look for A (address) records, and lists what broken authoritative servers did instead: ignored the query, answered Not Implemented or Server Failure, or answered Name Error, the worst case, because the cached NXDOMAIN then suppressed the A lookup as well. The second source is the empty non-terminal (ENT), a name that owns no records but has descendants that do; RFC 9499's example is _tcp.example.com sitting above _sip._tcp.example.com. RFC 8020 states that the correct response for an ENT is NODATA and that servers answering NXDOMAIN there are wrong and always have been, which matters now that resolvers such as Unbound (option harden-below-nxdomain) treat an NXDOMAIN as covering the whole subtree. The third is policy: a response policy zone (RPZ) in BIND can rewrite an answer to NODATA, encoded as a CNAME whose target is the wildcard top-level name, an asterisk followed by a dot, where a CNAME to the root encodes NXDOMAIN.

In a zone signed with the DNS Security Extensions (DNSSEC) the absence has to be proved. With NSEC (Next Secure) records, RFC 4035 has the server return the NSEC record owned by the query name together with its RRSIG (Resource Record Signature); the type bitmap in that record lists every type present at the name, the type asked for is not among them, and because the name exists no wildcard needs to be ruled out, so a single signed record is enough. With NSEC3, RFC 5155 requires the record matching the hashed name, with neither the queried type nor CNAME set in its bitmap. An NXDOMAIN proof is heavier, up to two NSEC or three NSEC3 records. RFC 9077 (July 2021) fixed the TTL of these records to the same negative TTL as the SOA, and RFC 8198 (July 2017) lets a validating resolver that holds a suitable NSEC in its cache synthesize a NODATA without asking anyone.

That difference in cost is why RFC 9824 (September 2025), by Shumon Huque, Christian Elmerot and Olafur Gudmundsson, made NODATA far more common. A signed zone using compact denial of existence answers a query for a nonexistent name with NODATA instead of NXDOMAIN: it generates and signs, on the spot, one NSEC record at the query name whose bitmap holds RRSIG, NSEC and the synthetic type NXNAME, number 128, while a genuine ENT gets only RRSIG and NSEC. The technique began at Cloudflare, which described it in June 2016 under the name black lies and reported negative answers of about 300 bytes; the RFC credits the proposal to Filippo Valsorda and Gudmundsson and lists Cloudflare, NS1, Amazon Route 53 and the online signing module of Knot DNS as implementations, with code 128 in use since September 2024. An optional flag in the Extension Mechanisms for DNS (EDNS), CO for Compact Answers OK, lets a resolver ask for the NXDOMAIN code to be restored. The RFC is frank about the costs: security tools that watch the RCODE lose sight of nonexistent names, resolvers can no longer synthesize NXDOMAIN from cached proofs, a lookup function may send an A query that an NXDOMAIN to the AAAA query would have saved, and floods of random subdomains reach the authoritative servers undiluted.

The effect is visible on a name every engineer uses for tests. Observed on 18 October 2026 and again on 12 November 2026, example.com answered a made-up name this way: through Google Public DNS and through Cloudflare's resolver the status was 0, the answer was empty, the SOA came with a TTL of 1,800 seconds, and the NSEC record at the invented name listed RRSIG, NSEC and NXNAME (printed as TYPE128 by Google). A test that needs a real NXDOMAIN should therefore use a name under .invalid, which RFC 6761 lets users assume will always return NXDOMAIN; on the same day the root zone answered such a name with status 3.

Tools report NODATA in their own dialects. dig shows status: NOERROR and ANSWER: 0 in its header lines and the SOA under the authority section; the nslookup shipped with BIND prints a line that starts with three asterisks and reads Can't find, the name, then No answer; the classic resolver library sets h_errno to NO_DATA, documented as a valid name that does not have an address, with NO_ADDRESS as a synonym, as opposed to HOST_NOT_FOUND. dig exits with code 0 for any response it receives, so a script that checks only the exit code or the status word will read NODATA as success, and the count of answer records is the thing to test. When a NODATA is unexpected the questions are few: was the right type asked, is the name an empty non-terminal or the target of a CNAME, was the record created after a resolver cached its absence, and is a policy zone or a compact-denial server answering in place of an NXDOMAIN.

dns-referral.def: A Domain Name System (DNS) response in which a server that cannot answer authoritatively gives no answer itself but names the servers of a zone closer to the name that was asked.
dns-referral.context: Authoritative servers return referrals for names delegated below them, and a recursive resolver follows them from the root down; dig +trace prints each step. Reading one as a failed lookup is a common mistake: a response with status NOERROR, an empty answer section and name server (NS) records in the authority section is a pointer to where the answer lives, not a denial that it exists.
dns-referral.depth:
Request for Comments (RFC) 9499, the Domain Name System (DNS) terminology of March 2024, defines a referral as a response in which a server, signalling that it is not (completely) authoritative for an answer, gives the querying resolver an alternative place to send its query. It arises only when the server is not performing recursive service. RFC 1034 (November 1987) sets out the split: a server answering a non-recursive query, one with the RD (Recursion Desired) bit clear, returns an error, the answer or a referral to a server closer to the answer, and all name servers must support that mode; a server acting recursively returns the answer or an error, but never referrals. A pure referral has a response code (RCODE) of NOERROR, an empty answer section, the name server (NS) records of the child zone in the authority section, possibly their addresses in the additional section, and the AA (Authoritative Answer) bit clear, since RFC 1035 defines that bit as saying the responder is an authority for the name in the question.

The referral is produced in step 3(b) of the server algorithm in section 4.3.2 of RFC 1034: while matching the query name label by label down its zone, the server reaches a node with NS records that mark a cut at the bottom of the zone, copies those records into the authority section, puts whatever addresses it has into the additional section and stops. RFC 1034's own worked example is a query for BRL.MIL sent to C.ISI.EDU, which answered with an empty answer, the two servers for MIL with a time to live (TTL) of 86,400 seconds, and their addresses. The resolver side is step 4(b) of section 5.3.3: a response that contains a better delegation is cached, and the resolver goes back to choosing servers, now one level further down. The root zone shows what a typical delegation looks like: in the root zone file with serial 2026111200, com is delegated to the thirteen servers a.gtld-servers.net to m.gtld-servers.net with a TTL of 172,800 seconds (two days), with glue such as 192.5.6.30 and 2001:503:a83e::2:30 for a.gtld-servers.net and a DS (Delegation Signer) record, key tag 19718 and algorithm 13, that a validating resolver needs to go on trusting the chain.

RFC 9499 separates two kinds. A downward referral, sometimes called a delegation response, comes from a server that is authoritative for some part of the query name and points at the zone cut below it; the bare word referral always means this kind. An upward or root referral comes from a server that holds nothing for the name and points back at the root; no server is required to send one, many people regard it as a sign of misconfiguration, and it is never called simply a referral. Microsoft's DNS team explained in September 2015 that Windows DNS servers up to Windows Server 2012 R2, with recursion disabled, answered names outside their zones with exactly this, a list of the root servers in the additional section, and that attackers could send random queries to get an amplified response; Windows Server 2016 answers SERVFAIL (server failure) instead by default, and on older versions the advice was to delete the root hints file, cache.dns. There is also a mixed form, the partial answer and referral: when the query name is an alias whose target lies in a zone delegated below the server, the response carries the authoritative canonical name (CNAME) record in the answer section, with AA set, and the referral for the target in the authority section. A common F5 BIG-IP DNS design produces exactly that: F5's implementation guide has the existing DNS server hold a CNAME from each application name to a load-balanced name in a subzone, an NS record delegating that subzone to the BIG-IP DNS systems and an address (A) record for each of them, with listeners for both UDP (User Datagram Protocol) and TCP (Transmission Control Protocol) on IPv4 and IPv6 (Internet Protocol versions 4 and 6).

The addresses in the additional section are glue when the name servers sit inside the zone being delegated. RFC 1034 explains why they exist: without them, the NS records would say that to learn the server's address the resolver must ask the server at the address it is trying to learn. RFC 9499 sorts name servers into in-domain (ns.example.org for example.org), sibling domain (inside the parent but outside the child, such as a.gtld-servers.net for com, which sits under net) and unrelated. RFC 9471 (September 2023, by Mark Andrews, Shumon Huque, Paul Wouters and Duane Wessels) updated RFC 1034 to remove the old "whatever addresses are available" vagueness: a referral must include all available glue for in-domain servers or set the TC (Truncated) bit so the resolver retries over TCP, and should include sibling glue, with TC optional when that does not fit. The authors found in late 2021 that 222 of about 209 million delegations depended only on sibling servers in a cycle, which fail when the sibling glue is left out, and cite a referral observed in June 2020 that left out all its glue without setting TC. The sizes matter: they put UDP responses at between 1,232 and 4,096 bytes, depending on the EDNS (Extension Mechanisms for DNS) buffer size the client advertises, and TCP responses at up to 65,535.

Under the DNS Security Extensions (DNSSEC) the referral grows. RFC 4035 has a security-aware server, when the query sets the DO (DNSSEC OK) bit, add to the authority section either the DS record set of the child with its RRSIG (Resource Record Signature) or, for an unsigned child, the NSEC (Next Secure) record proving that there is no DS, placed after the NS records; if those records do not fit, the server must set TC, and they may push the glue out. What is not signed matters as much: the NS records at a delegation point and the glue must not be signed, because they are the parent's copy of data that belongs to the child, and only the child's apex NS set carries a signature. RFC 9499 makes the same point when it notes that parent-side NS records are not authoritative data, and RFC 2181 (July 1997) ranks data from the authority section of a non-authoritative answer and additional information at the bottom of its trust order, below an authoritative answer from the child, and says such data should never be returned as an answer. That is why the NS set and TTL that a resolver ends up using may come from the child rather than from the referral.

A referral is easy to confuse with a negative answer, because all three forms carry NOERROR or a negative code with an empty answer section. RFC 2308 (March 1998) gives the tests. An NXDOMAIN (non-existent domain) is recognized by its RCODE whatever the authority section holds. A NODATA is recognized by an SOA (Start of Authority) record in the authority section or by the absence of NS records there; only NS records with no SOA make a referral. The same RFC records that some resolvers took negative responses carrying both SOA and NS records for referrals, which is why it recommends that authoritative servers send the SOA alone, and it asks that answers served from a cache carry an implicit referral, NS records that point the resolver towards an authoritative source.

Query name minimization changed what referrals reveal. RFC 9156 (November 2021, by Stéphane Bortzmeyer, Ralph Dolmans and Paul Hoffman, replacing RFC 7816) has the resolver send each server only one label more than the zone it already knows, so the root sees com rather than the full name; Paul Mockapetris had explained to one of the authors that sending the full name was a tradition for efficiency, not a protocol requirement. The parent side of a delegation answers with a referral whatever the query type, so the RFC recommends the A or AAAA types for the minimized query; when a label has no zone cut the resolver gets a non-referral answer and adds the next label, and it must cap the work, with recommended limits of 10 iterations and 4 single-label steps.

Referrals are also where DNS cache poisoning did its worst damage. CERT Coordination Center (CERT/CC) Vulnerability Note VU#800113, released on 8 July 2008, explained that a 16-bit transaction identifier needs on average 32,768 attempts to guess, that per-query source port randomization adds about 16 bits, and that network and port address translation (NAT and PAT) devices can strip that randomness again. The technique Dan Kaminsky had found, as an illustrated guide published on 7 August 2008 describes it, was aimed not at the answer but at the referral data: it asked for random, uncached subdomains and raced forged replies whose authority section carried NS records for the whole target domain and whose additional section carried the glue, so a winning race made the resolver cache the attacker's servers as authoritative for the domain. The defence is in RFC 1034's early warning that clients should know whom they trust before accepting referrals, in RFC 2181's ranking, in acceptance rules that ignore records outside the zone the server was asked about (the in-bailiwick and out-of-bailiwick check, terms RFC 9499 now calls historic), and ultimately in DNSSEC. RFC 9499 also retires lame delegation, the old name for a server listed in a delegation that does not answer authoritatively, does not answer at all or cannot be reached, because the term no longer has an agreed meaning.

In practice, dig @server name +norecurse asks one server only what it holds; from a parent zone server the reply shows status NOERROR, flags without aa, ANSWER: 0 and a non-zero AUTHORITY count, which is a referral. The +recurse option toggles the RD bit, which dig sets by default, and +trace turns recursion off and follows referrals from the root servers, printing the answer of each server it used; with +trace, a server named with @ is used only for the initial query for the root name servers. When a trace stops at a referral that leads nowhere, the questions are the usual ones: do the parent's NS records match the child's, is the in-domain glue present and current at the registry, does every listed server answer authoritatively over both UDP and TCP, and, for a signed child, does the DS in the referral match a key the child publishes.

aa-flag.def: The Authoritative Answer bit a DNS server sets when it answers from a zone it serves, printed as aa by dig.
aa-flag.context: Its absence is what nslookup reports as Non-authoritative answer. The line alarms people for no reason: a resolver answering from its cache, or fetching the answer on your behalf, leaves the bit clear, and that is how an ordinary recursive lookup is meant to work.
aa-flag.depth:
RFC 1035 says AA is valid in responses and means the responding server is an authority for the name in the question section. When the answer follows an alias, it covers only the first name: RFC 2181 warns that the other records may have come from the server's cache. A clear bit says only that the server is not an authority, so a cache hit, a freshly fetched recursive answer and a referral all look alike.

To see an authoritative answer, ask one of the zone's name servers directly with recursion off, for example dig @ns.example.com example.com +norecurse, and look for aa on the flags line. The TTL is then the zone's constant value, where a cached copy counts down on every repeat.

AA records where the data came from, not whether it is right. RFC 9499 counts a server that answers without the authoritative bit for a zone delegated to it among the flaws called lame delegation. And RFC 6604 notes that DNSSEC does not protect the AA bit, so only validation authenticates the data.

dns-header-flags.def: The one-bit fields of a DNS (Domain Name System) message header, qr, aa, tc, rd, ra, ad and cd, that dig prints on its flags line, plus the reserved Z bit that must be zero.
dns-header-flags.context: Together they say what kind of message it is and how it was handled: question or response, from an authority or not, cut short or complete, resolved recursively or not, validated or not. They share one 16-bit word of the Domain Name System (DNS) header with the four-bit opcode and the four-bit response code, and most diagnoses of a dig answer start by reading them.
dns-header-flags.depth:
Where they sit. Every DNS (Domain Name System) message begins with a 12-octet header: a 16-bit ID (identifier), one 16-bit word of flags and codes, and four 16-bit counts for the question, answer, authority and additional sections. The second 16-bit word of the 12-byte header holds QR (0 for a query, 1 for a response), a four-bit opcode, AA, TC, RD, RA, a reserved Z bit, AD, CD and the four-bit RCODE (response code). RFC (Request for Comments) 1035 drew a three-bit Z field there in 1987; AD and CD were taken from the old three-bit Z field for DNSSEC (the DNS Security Extensions), the one reserved bit left must be zero, and dig reports it apart as MBZ, printing ; MBZ: 0x4 after the flags when that bit is set. IANA (the Internet Assigned Numbers Authority) numbers the bits from the most significant end in its DNS Header Flags registry: AA is bit 5, TC 6, RD 7, RA 8, bit 9 is reserved, AD is 10 and CD 11.

Reading them in hex. Capture tools often show the word as a hexadecimal number, and the masks follow from that layout: QR 0x8000, the opcode 0x7800, AA 0x0400, TC 0x0200, RD 0x0100, RA 0x0080, the reserved bit 0x0040, AD 0x0020, CD 0x0010 and RCODE 0x000F. An ordinary recursive query is therefore 0x0100, rd alone; the usual answer from a recursive resolver is 0x8180, qr rd ra with RCODE 0; a validated answer adds AD for 0x81A0; and an authoritative answer to a non-recursive query is 0x8400, qr aa. dig prints the same information in words, the opcode and status on its ->>HEADER<<- line and the set flags on the next.

QR and the opcode. QR is set by whoever answers. The opcode is chosen by the originator and copied into the response: 0 is an ordinary QUERY, 1 the inverse query IQUERY, now obsolete (RFC 3425), 2 STATUS, 4 NOTIFY (RFC 1996), with which a primary tells its secondaries a zone has changed, 5 UPDATE (RFC 2136) for dynamic updates, and 6 DSO, DNS Stateful Operations (RFC 8490); 3 and 7 to 15 are unassigned.

AA. The authoritative-answer bit is meaningful only in responses: it says that the responding server is an authority for the name in the question section. Because an answer may hold several owner names when aliases are followed, RFC 1035 ties AA to the name that matches the query name, or the first owner name in the answer section. An answer served from a recursive resolver's cache does not carry aa, which is the quickest way to tell from dig output whether you reached the zone's own servers.

RD and RA. RD is the client's request for recursion and is copied into the response; RA is the server's offer, set or cleared in every response, and RFC 1034 says rd and ra together show recursion was used, adding that RA signals availability rather than use and that a server should never recurse unless asked through RD. A reply with rd but no ra means this server will not recurse for you, and dig prints a warning, recursion requested but not available; that is the normal answer from an authoritative server, not a fault. dig sets RD by default, and +norecurse clears it, which is how to query an authoritative server or walk a delegation by hand. dig can also set aa, ad, cd, ra, tc and the reserved bit in a query, the last three only for testing, since a server ignores RA and TC in a QUERY.

TC. TC means a required record set did not fit: RFC 2181 says to set it only when an RRset (resource record set) the response needs could not be included whole, not because optional extra data was left out, and tells the client to ignore the answer and ask again over a transport such as TCP (Transmission Control Protocol). dig does that by default; +ignore keeps the truncated UDP (User Datagram Protocol) answer instead. Since RFC 7766 (March 2016) every general-purpose DNS implementation MUST support both UDP and TCP, so a firewall that blocks TCP port 53 breaks exactly the large answers, DNSSEC ones above all, that set TC. How large is large has moved: RFC 4035 required DNSSEC servers to support messages of at least 1,220 octets, DNS Flag Day 2020 proposed fitting UDP answers into 1,232 octets (the minimum MTU, maximum transmission unit, of IPv6, Internet Protocol version 6, which is 1,280, less 48 for the headers), and RFC 9715 (January 2025) recommends a maximum UDP payload of 1,400 and leaves the meaning of TC unchanged. Response Policy Zones even use TC on purpose, in their TCP-only action against reflection attacks.

AD and CD. AD claims the answer was validated; CD asks the resolver not to validate. Under RFC 4035 a validating resolver MUST NOT set AD unless it considers every record set in the answer and authority sections authentic, and with CD set it returns the data and leaves validation to the requester. RFC 4035 tells a resolver to disregard both in a response unless it came over a secure channel or the resolver is configured to trust them, so ad is worth as much as the resolver and the path to it. RFC 6840 (February 2013) refined the rules: a validating resolver SHOULD set AD only when the query carried AD or the DO (DNSSEC OK) bit, a client may set AD in a query simply to say it understands the bit, and a validating resolver SHOULD set CD on every upstream query. DO itself is not a header flag: RFC 3225 puts it in the first bit of the EDNS(0) (Extension Mechanisms for DNS) OPT record's flags, where IANA now also lists CO, Compact Answers OK, from RFC 9824. In the same way the header's four-bit RCODE grows to 12 bits with eight more in the OPT record (RFC 6891).

The CD test, live. A SERVFAIL that turns into data when the query sets cd points at a DNSSEC validation failure; ISC (Internet Systems Consortium) puts it as a rule in its DNSSEC guide, and its example domain dnssec-failed.org is signed to fail on purpose. On 12 November 2026 Google Public DNS answered it with status 2, SERVFAIL, rd and ra set, ad clear and the comment DNSSEC validation failure; asked again with cd set, it returned NOERROR, cd set, ad clear and the address record 96.99.227.255. The bits tell the whole story: recursion worked, validation failed, and switching validation off for one query proved where the fault lay. Numbers worth remembering: 0x0100 for a recursive query, 0x8180 for a plain recursive answer, 0x81A0 with ad, bit 0x0040 must be zero, and 1,232 or 1,400 octets as the UDP sizes above which TC and TCP take over.

dhcp-relay-agent.def: A router or host that passes DHCP messages between clients on one subnet and a DHCP server on another.
dhcp-relay-agent.context: A client with no address yet starts with a broadcast, and RFC 2131 says relay agents remove the need for a DHCP server on every network segment. The relay also tells the server which subnet the client is on, which decides the pool its address comes from. Microsoft calls them IP Helpers.
dhcp-relay-agent.depth:
When a relay forwards a client's request it writes the address of the interface the request arrived on into the giaddr field, if that field is still zero, and increments hops. RFC 1542 says the destination it relays to MUST be configurable, and that a request whose hops exceed 16 is silently discarded. The server picks the address from the subnet named in giaddr and sends its replies to the DHCP server port, 67, on the relay, which delivers them on the client's own link.

RFC 1542 calls giaddr rather poorly named: it is never a router for the client to use. A zero giaddr tells the server the client is on its own subnet, so a DHCPNAK is broadcast; otherwise the NAK goes to the relay, which forwards it to the client's hardware address even if the client has moved to a new network.

When one subnet gets no leases while others do, Microsoft's DHCP checklist asks whether the routers or VLAN switches are configured with relay agents, next to whether the scope for that subnet still has addresses. Both failures look the same from the client, because a DHCP server is not required to answer every message it receives.

dhcp-option-43.def: The DHCP option that carries vendor-specific information, such as the controller address a wireless access point needs.
dhcp-option-43.context: RFC 2132 leaves its contents to the vendor named in option 60, so one option number carries several incompatible formats. That is why an access point can get an address, a gateway and DNS servers from DHCP and still never find its controller.
dhcp-option-43.depth:
Option 43 is an opaque object of at least one octet, interpreted by vendor-specific code; RFC 2132 recommends, without requiring, that several items be encoded as sub-options in the same code, length and value form as DHCP options themselves. The vendor is the one named in option 60, the vendor class identifier, and RFC 3925 points out that option 43 itself carries no vendor identifier.

Vendors chose differently. RUCKUS spells the controller address in ASCII under sub-option 6 or 3, Extreme puts a text list in sub-option 1, other vendors document four-byte binary addresses, and FortiAP reads option 138 by default. The same bytes are a valid answer in one format and nonsense in another, and RFC 2132 tells servers to ignore what they cannot interpret and clients to try to carry on without it, so the failure is silent.

RFC 2131 returns class-specific options only on an exact match of the client's vendor class identifier, and the client asks for option 43 in its parameter request list. Options 124 and 125 name the vendor with an IANA enterprise number, and option 138 is a plain list of CAPWAP controller addresses. RFC 5417 adds that the DHCP exchange is usually neither integrity protected nor authenticated, so in security-sensitive networks it should not be the only way an access point picks its controller.

gratuitous-arp.def: An unsolicited ARP packet in which a host announces its own IP address and MAC address to everyone on the link.
gratuitous-arp.context: Hosts send it when they start using an address, and first-hop redundancy sends it at failover so the hosts and switches on the link learn where the gateway address now lives. RFC 5227 calls the same packet an ARP Announcement.
gratuitous-arp.depth:
RFC 5227 defines the ARP Announcement as an ARP request, broadcast on the local link, in which both the sender and the target IP address fields carry the address being announced. Its purpose is to make sure other hosts do not keep stale cache entries left by a host that used the address before. A host following RFC 5227 first probes, then sends two announcements two seconds apart.

It is a request rather than a reply for history and pragmatism: Stevens documented it that way, BSD, Windows and Mac OS all send requests, and some ARP implementations ignore replies nobody asked for. HSRP's RFC 2281 differs and broadcasts an ARP response with the virtual MAC address. When a VRRP router becomes the Active Router, RFC 9568 has it broadcast a gratuitous ARP for each virtual IPv4 address, carrying the virtual MAC address, so the change reaches every cache on the link at once.

RFC 5227 is blunt about one misconception: a single gratuitous ARP is not duplicate address detection. The existing holder logs an error, the newcomer carries on, and both then fail to work properly. Detecting a conflict takes the probes before the announcement and the defence of the address that continues for as long as it is in use.

ping-command.def: The tool that sends ICMP (Internet Control Message Protocol) Echo Requests and times the Echo Replies: the first test of whether a host is reachable.
ping-command.context: Every IP (Internet Protocol) host must answer an Echo Request, which makes ping the universal first check. A reply proves that both directions work and that the responder is alive; silence proves much less, because a filter, a rate limit and a host told to ignore echoes all look the same.
ping-command.depth:
Where it came from. Mike Muuss wrote ping for 4.2a BSD (Berkeley Software Distribution) UNIX at the US Army's Ballistic Research Laboratory (BRL) in December 1983, chasing some odd behaviour on the laboratory's network. The idea came from a remark Dave Mills had made that July about timing ICMP (Internet Control Message Protocol) Echo packets on his Fuzzball systems to measure path latency, and the name came from sonar. In Muuss's own account it was a little thousand-line hack written in an evening, the kernel had no support for raw ICMP sockets so he wrote that too before sunrise, and Berkeley took both into BSD UNIX, from where ping spread to every system including Windows 95 and NT. It is not an acronym; Packet InterNet Grouper is a later backronym, which Muuss heard second-hand that Mills had offered.

The messages. Request for Comments (RFC) 792 (September 1981) defines Echo as type 8 and Echo Reply as type 0, both with code 0, followed by a 16-bit identifier and a 16-bit sequence number that come back unchanged so each reply can be matched to its request; the responder builds its reply by swapping the addresses, setting the type to 0 and recomputing the checksum. ICMPv6, RFC 4443 (March 2006), uses types 128 and 129. The obligations are explicit: RFC 1122 (October 1989) says every host MUST implement an Echo server, that the data in a request MUST be returned entirely in the reply, and that the reply's source address must be the address the request was sent to; RFC 4443 says every IPv6 node MUST implement an Echo responder. RFC 1122 also lets a host silently discard Echo Requests sent to a broadcast or multicast address, a neutral provision it records as the outcome of a passionate debate between diagnostic value and packet storms.

Reading Linux output. The iputils ping sends 56 data bytes by default; with the 8-byte ICMP header and a 20-byte IP (Internet Protocol) header without options, that is the 56(84) on its first line. When the data space is at least the size of a timeval structure, ping writes a timestamp at its start and uses it to compute the round trip, which is why a very small -s gives no times. Each reply line shows icmp_seq, the TTL (time to live) of the reply and the time; the summary gives minimum, average, maximum and mdev, a population standard deviation of the round-trip times. ping exits with 1 when no reply arrives at all, or when a count and a deadline are both set and fewer replies than the count arrive in time, with 2 on other errors and 0 otherwise, which scripts use as a liveness test.

What the TTL says. The TTL in a reply hints at distance only if you know the value the responder started from. The man page gives 255 as the maximum and 64 as the recommended initial value, and lists the variants: Berkeley systems before 4.3BSD Tahoe left the TTL unchanged, so the reply showed 255 minus the routers on the whole round trip; later ones set 255, so it shows 255 minus the routers on the return path; and some systems use 30 or 60, or wilder values. 128 and 255 are also common starting points, so a reply with TTL 124, as in Microsoft's own example, most likely left a host at 128 four routers away.

Options that matter. On Linux, -c sets the count, -s the data size and -t the outgoing TTL, so ping -t 1 becomes a one-hop probe that the first router answers with Time Exceeded. -M do sets the Don't Fragment (DF) bit and lets the kernel reject packets larger than the known path MTU (maximum transmission unit), while -M probe sets DF and skips that check, which is how ping -M probe -s 1472 tests a 1,500-byte path (1,472 plus 8 plus 20). Intervals below 2 ms are for the super-user only. Windows differs in every default: 4 requests (/n), 32 data bytes (/l, up to 65,500), a 4,000 ms reply timeout (/w), /t to run until interrupted, /i for the TTL up to 255 and /f for DF, which Microsoft documents as the path MTU troubleshooting switch. On a FortiGate the parameters are set first with execute ping-options, among them data-size (0 to 65507), df-bit, repeat-count, source, ttl and use-sdwan, checked with execute ping-options view-settings, and then used by execute ping.

Silence has many causes. Routers may be configured to ignore echo requests; Linux has the icmp_echo_ignore_all sysctl, off by default; firewalls drop echoes; and Linux ignores Echo and Timestamp requests sent to broadcast or multicast addresses by default through icmp_echo_ignore_broadcasts. That default is part of the defence against the smurf attack, in which echoes sent to a directed broadcast address turn a whole subnet into an amplifier; RFC 2644 (August 1999, Best Current Practice 34) reversed the old router requirement and made forwarding and receiving directed broadcasts disabled by default. On the sending side, Linux restricts unprivileged ICMP datagram sockets through ping_group_range, whose kernel default of "1 0" lets nobody create them.

Numbers worth remembering: types 8 and 0, or 128 and 129 for IPv6; 56 data bytes on Linux and 32 on Windows; 28 bytes of IPv4 and ICMP header, hence 1,472 for a 1,500-byte MTU test; 64 as the recommended initial TTL and 255 as the maximum; and exit code 1 for no reply.

traceroute.def: A diagnostic tool that lists the routers on the path to a destination by sending probes with a rising time to live (TTL), 1, 2, 3 and upward, and reading the Internet Control Message Protocol (ICMP) Time Exceeded error that each router returns when it discards one.
traceroute.context: It turns a rule every router follows into a map: a router that reduces a packet's time to live (TTL) to zero must discard it and send an Internet Control Message Protocol (ICMP) Time Exceeded message back to the source, and the source address of that message names a router on the way. The output shows where along a path the answers stop and how the round-trip time grows hop by hop. It shows nothing of the return path, and it is easy to read more into it than it says.
traceroute.depth:
What it measures, and what it does not. Every router that forwards an Internet Protocol (IP) version 4 packet, IPv4, must reduce its time to live (TTL), an 8-bit field, by at least one, and Request for Comments (RFC) 1812 (Requirements for IP Version 4 Routers, June 1995) makes the consequence mandatory: a packet whose TTL reaches zero is discarded and, unless it was sent to a multicast address, the router must send the source an Internet Control Message Protocol (ICMP) Time Exceeded message, code 0, TTL exceeded in transit. RFC 792 (September 1981) defined that message as type 11, with code 1 kept for fragment reassembly timeouts, and had it carry the original IP header plus the first 64 bits of the datagram that caused it. In IPv6 (Internet Protocol version 6) the field is the Hop Limit and the message is ICMPv6 Time Exceeded, type 3, code 0 (RFC 4443). RFC 1812 is blunt about why the error survives in every router: Time Exceeded messages are required because the traceroute diagnostic tool depends on them. Traceroute sends probes with TTL 1, 2, 3 and upward and prints who complains at each distance. The result is a list of the devices that decremented the TTL and answered on the forward path, with round-trip times; it does not trace the return path, and it says nothing about how ordinary traffic is treated by the routers it names.

Where it came from. Van Jacobson wrote the original at Lawrence Berkeley Laboratory (LBL) while chasing a routing problem. His comment in the source says the code sort of popped out after 48 hours without sleep, that he took the idea from Steve Deering, and that he later learned Guy Almes and Matt Mathis had proposed it too; the oldest copies in circulation are signed 20 December 1988, with a README of 27 December 1988, and a GÉANT wiki page dates the program to December 1988 and its announcement to the end2end-interest mailing list. It needed root and a kernel modification, because no kernel then available from Berkeley let a raw IP socket send a datagram the user had built in full. The odd port arithmetic comes from RFC 792: an ICMP error quoted only eight bytes of the original payload, exactly the size of a User Datagram Protocol (UDP) header, so everything needed to match a reply to its probe had to live in that header. Jacobson used the process identifier, with its high bit set, as the source port and incremented the destination port for every probe; current implementations start at 33434. RFC 1812 later asked routers to quote as much of the original datagram as fits in a 576-byte ICMP message.

How a run looks. The original defaults have barely moved: three probes per TTL, a maximum of 30 hops and a 5-second wait, one line per TTL with the address that answered and the round-trip time (RTT) of each probe, and several addresses on one line when the answers came from different routers. The trace ends when the destination itself answers: an ICMP Port Unreachable for UDP probes, an Echo Reply for ICMP ones, a reset or a SYN-ACK (synchronize and acknowledge, SYN and ACK) for Transmission Control Protocol (TCP) ones. Annotations after the time report other ICMP errors: !H, !N and !P for host, network and protocol unreachable, !F for fragmentation needed, !X for communication administratively prohibited. Traceroute for Linux 2.1.6 adds methods for networks that filter the unlikely UDP ports: -I sends ICMP Echo; -T sends a TCP SYN to one constant port, 80 by default, with the half-open technique, answering a SYN-ACK with a reset so that the application never sees a connection; -U sends UDP to port 53; -D uses Datagram Congestion Control Protocol (DCCP) requests; -P sends bare IP datagrams of a chosen protocol, 253 by default. It sends 16 probes at once (-N), uses 60-byte probes for IPv4 and 80-byte ones for IPv6, and shortens its wait from answers it has already seen, which is why -N 1 with a fixed -w 5 gives a slower but steadier trace.

Windows and routers. Windows tracert always sends ICMP Echo Requests, ICMPv6 for IPv6 targets, up to 30 hops by default (/h), waiting 4,000 milliseconds for each answer (/w); /d skips name resolution, usually the slowest part of a run; /j adds an IPv4 loose source route of up to nine addresses; /R uses the IPv6 Routing header to send the probe through the destination and back, testing the reverse route. Microsoft's page describes each line as the near-side interface of a router, the one closest to the sender; that is the simple case, not a rule, as the next paragraph shows. For loss per hop over time Microsoft points to pathping. RFC 1812 also says a router should be able to initiate a traceroute itself, and that the facility should be restricted to authorized users.

Which address a line shows. RFC 1812, section 4.3.2.4, requires the source address of a router's ICMP message to be an address of the interface the message is sent from, not the one the probe arrived on. RFC 5837 (April 2010) spells out the consequence: the two coincide only when the error leaves by the same numbered interface, and an asymmetric return path, parallel links or Equal-Cost Multi-Path (ECMP) routing make them differ. Its extension lets a router name the incoming interface explicitly, by interface index, address, name and maximum transmission unit (MTU), inside the multi-part ICMP format of RFC 4884. Linux traceroute -e prints these extensions, including the label stack of a Multiprotocol Label Switching (MPLS) core in the RFC 4950 format, and -A looks each address up in the routing registries to print its autonomous system (AS) path.

Asterisks and silent hops. An asterisk means no answer arrived within the wait. Jacobson's own sample traces show the classic causes: gateways running code that never sent Time Exceeded, and a 4.x Berkeley Software Distribution (BSD) bug that sent the error with the TTL left in the expired datagram, zero, so it could never come back. Today the usual causes are policy. RFC 1812 says a router should be able to limit the rate of its ICMP errors, and RFC 4443 makes that a must for IPv6, recommending a token bucket and advising against limiters that cannot cope with bursty traffic such as traceroute's; the Linux manual suggests -z for spacing and -N 1 when answers go missing. Filters that drop the unlikely UDP ports or ICMP Echo stop the trace at the firewall, and a trace that ends there in asterisks says nothing about the hosts behind it. Silent hops followed by answering ones are a quiet middle, not an end. One of Jacobson's traces even lost exactly the last half of its hops because the destination, a Sun running SunOS 3.5, reused the arriving TTL for its reply, so answers only came back once the probe TTL was at least twice the path length.

Load balancing and Paris traceroute. Routers that spread traffic per flow hash on header fields, and the Paris traceroute team found that they use the classic five-tuple plus the IP Type of Service (TOS), the ICMP code and the ICMP checksum. Classic traceroute changes the UDP destination port, or the ICMP sequence number and so the checksum, on every probe, which makes every probe a different flow. Across a balanced hop the probes then take different branches: some routers are never seen, and consecutive answers from different branches suggest links that do not exist. Brice Augustin, Timur Friedman, Renata Teixeira and colleagues presented Paris traceroute at the Internet Measurement Conference in October 2006. It keeps the fields the balancers hash constant and identifies probes by fields they ignore: the UDP checksum, made to vary by adjusting the payload; the TCP sequence number; or the ICMP identifier and sequence chosen together so that the checksum stays fixed. Per-packet balancing still defeats any single trace, and the tool flags where that is happening.

Reading the numbers. Each RTT includes the return path, which traceroute never sees; Vern Paxson reported in 1995 that 30 per cent of the Internet routes he measured were asymmetric. Linux --back guesses how many hops a reply travelled, assuming the answering router started its TTL at 64, 128 or 255. Latency or loss that appears at one hop and does not persist at the hops after it belongs to that router's handling of its own ICMP, not to the path: the mtr documentation warns that apparent loss at an intermediate hop does not always mean forwarded traffic is being lost there, and that some routers give ICMP Echo a lower priority than other traffic. Only a change that carries through to the destination is a property of the path. A TCP trace that reaches its destination impossibly early is worth a second look, since any proxy or full-proxy load balancer in the path completes the handshake on the server's behalf.

mtr. Written by Matt Kimball and maintained by Roger Wolff of BitWizard, mtr combines traceroute and ping: it keeps probing every hop and prints running statistics, loss percentage, last, average, best and worst RTT and standard deviation. It uses ICMP Echo by default, UDP with -u, TCP SYN with -T and Stream Control Transmission Protocol (SCTP) with -S, port 80 unless set; -r produces a report after the number of cycles set by -c, -w a wide report with full names, and up to eight ECMP paths per hop are displayed by default. It is distributed under the GNU General Public License (GPL) version 2, and its manual warns that each running instance generates a significant amount of traffic.

What else was tried. RFC 1393 (January 1993) proposed an IP option that made each router report itself in a dedicated ICMP Traceroute message, to send fewer packets and finish sooner; it stayed Experimental, is now Historic and was obsoleted by RFC 6814, which formally deprecated a set of IPv4 options. Source routing fared no better: Jacobson called his round-trip version almost worthless because so many gateways botched source routing, and the Linux manual notes that most routers have disabled it. When every method fails, ping -R records the route for the nearest 8 hops only. The FreeBSD manual adds the operational caution: because of the load it can impose, traceroute is unwise in normal operations or automated scripts. The numbers to remember are TTL 1 upward, three probes, 30 hops, port 33434, ICMP type 11 code 0 for IPv4 and type 3 code 0 for IPv6.

recursive-resolver.def: A Domain Name System (DNS) server that answers on a client's behalf, from its cache or by querying authoritative servers until it has the answer.
recursive-resolver.context: The stub resolver in every laptop and phone hands its Domain Name System (DNS) questions to one, usually the address that the Dynamic Host Configuration Protocol (DHCP) supplied or a public service. It sees the names its clients look up, and what it caches, filters or validates is what they get.
recursive-resolver.depth:
Request for Comments (RFC) 9499 defines a recursive resolver as a resolver acting in recursive mode: it answers from its local cache or sends queries to other servers until it has the final answer, and RFC 1034 adds that in this mode a server returns the answer or an error, never a referral. It has two sides, a name server side that takes the client's question and a resolver side that goes and finds out. It is expected to cache, which makes it what RFC 1123 calls a full-service resolver, though some do not; RFC 1123 requires such a resolver to keep a local cache, to time its contents out and to be configurable with several root servers. Recursive server means the same; the manual of BIND (Berkeley Internet Name Domain) counts caching name server among its many names, and RFC 9499 discourages full resolver, a term RFC 1035 uses without defining it. Three neighbours are not the same thing. A stub resolver, in the Domain Name System (DNS) library of an operating system, cannot resolve by itself and depends on a recursive one. An authoritative server answers from the zones it holds and asks nobody. A forwarder passes queries, with recursion requested, to another server to resolve, and in current use usually stands between stubs and a real recursive resolver.

It needs the address of at least one root server, learnt by priming from a root hints list, often built into the software. RFC 9609 (February 2025, replacing RFC 8109) describes the priming query: a request for the name server (NS) records of the root, sent to one of the configured addresses with recursion not requested and with the Extension Mechanisms for DNS (EDNS) advertising at least 1,024 octets, because the full answer no longer fits in 512. The hints file published by InterNIC, dated 3 November 2026, lists thirteen names, A to M under root-servers.net, each with an IPv4 (Internet Protocol version 4) and an IPv6 (version 6) address; the RFC counts 13 operators and more than 1,500 instances behind them.

For a name it has not cached, the resolver follows the four steps of RFC 1034. It looks in local information; it finds the best servers to ask, starting from the closest name servers it knows for the name, then its parent, and the root at worst; it sends them non-recursive queries until one answers; and it analyses the answer.
