Data or a name error is cached and returned. A better delegation is cached and the search continues one level down. A canonical name (CNAME) record restarts the search for the new name. A server failure removes that server from the list and the next one is tried. The result goes to the client and into the cache for at most its time to live (TTL). The +trace option of dig runs the same iteration from the client, starting at the root and showing the answer of each server used.

The cache is where the engineering has gone since 1987. Negative answers are cached under the rules of RFC 2308 and resolution failures for between one second and five minutes (RFC 9520). Serve-stale (RFC 8767, March 2020) lets a resolver answer with expired data when the authoritative servers cannot be reached, with a recommended TTL of 30 seconds on the stale records, a wait of 1.8 seconds before falling back to them and a cap of seven days. Query name minimization (RFC 9156, November 2021) stops the resolver from sending the full name and type to every server on the way down, and RFC 8806 (June 2020) lets it keep a copy of the whole root zone locally. Defaults differ by product: Unbound ships with minimization and aggressive use of signed denial records enabled and serving of expired data off, and BIND 9 uses the relaxed form of minimization.

A reply with both the RD (recursion desired) and RA (recursion available) flags set shows the server worked recursively. A validating resolver, one that checks the signatures of the DNS Security Extensions (DNSSEC), answers SERVFAIL (server failure) when validation fails, unless the query set the CD (checking disabled) flag, and its AD (authentic data) flag can be relied on only over a secure path to a trusted server. Validation is also work an attacker can demand: KeyTrap, CVE-2023-50387 in the Common Vulnerabilities and Exposures list, published on 14 February 2024 with a severity score of 7.5, used responses with many keys and signatures to consume a validator's processor.

The security history of the recursive resolver is mostly about its cache and its openness. In July 2008 Dan Kaminsky of IOActive showed that the 16-bit query identifier was too easy a target for forged answers (CVE-2008-1447); the patches issued on 8 July 2008 widened the range of UDP (User Datagram Protocol) source ports, RFC 5452 (January 2009) wrote the measure down, an unpredictable port being worth up to 16 more bits, and the advisory of the Internet Systems Consortium (ISC) called DNSSEC the only definitive solution. Openness is the other problem. RFC 9499 calls a resolver that serves any client an open resolver, or a public resolver when that is intended, and says most open ones are probably misconfigured; RFC 5358 (October 2008, Best Current Practice 140) explains the danger, queries with a forged source address reflected at a victim with an amplification factor of around 80, and the remedy, recursion only for the intended clients. BIND's allow-recursion defaults to local networks and the local host for that reason.

Whoever runs the resolver sees every name its clients ask for and decides what they get back; RFC 9499 has a term, policy-implementing resolver, for one that changes answers to block malware or unwanted content. The public services differ on exactly these points: Google Public DNS answers on the anycast addresses 8.8.8.8 and 8.8.4.4, Cloudflare launched 1.1.1.1 on 1 April 2018 on addresses held by the research group of the Asia-Pacific registry (APNIC), and Quad9 offers 9.9.9.9 with malware blocking, 9.9.9.10 without it and 9.9.9.11 with Client Subnet, all of them validating. The path from stub to resolver can be encrypted with DNS over TLS (Transport Layer Security; RFC 7858, May 2016, port 853 of the Transmission Control Protocol, TCP), DNS over HTTPS (Hypertext Transfer Protocol Secure; RFC 8484, October 2018) or DNS over QUIC (RFC 9250, May 2022). The EDNS Client Subnet option (ECS, RFC 7871, May 2016) goes the other way and tells authoritative servers part of the client's network, which helps traffic steering and, as the RFC itself admits, has privacy shortcomings.

On network equipment the name on the menu may not mean what the RFCs mean. An F5 BIG-IP licensed for DNS Services has three caches: transparent, which forwards to external resolvers and caches what they return; resolver, which resolves by itself; and validating resolver, which adds DNSSEC validation. F5 advises against using the BIND that ships on the system as the resolver, because it is slower, and calls the resolver a client uses its local DNS (LDNS). On a FortiGate with FortiOS 7.6.0 the DNS server mode called Recursive looks in the local database and then forwards to the system DNS server, which makes it a forwarder; the mode that iterates from the root, new in that release, is called Resolver (set mode resolver), and it knows the 13 default root servers, of which two at most can be given priority. For anything that answers by location, the practical consequence is the same everywhere: the authoritative side sees the address of the recursive resolver, not of the user behind it.

dora.def: Shorthand for the four messages of a first DHCP lease: DHCPDISCOVER, DHCPOFFER, DHCPREQUEST and DHCPACK.
dora.context: The word comes from Microsoft's DHCP troubleshooting guides; RFC 2131 only names the messages. A diagnosis starts with it: capture on the client and check that all four arrive, because the server commits the address only when it sends the DHCPACK.
dora.depth:
The client broadcasts DHCPDISCOVER from source address 0 to 255.255.255.255 and UDP port 67. Each server may answer with a DHCPOFFER carrying an address in yiaddr; the choice among offers is left to the implementation, and ISC dhclient takes the first. The client then broadcasts a DHCPREQUEST naming the chosen server in the server identifier option and the offered address in the requested IP address option, which implicitly declines the other offers. That server commits the binding and answers DHCPACK with the lease time.

Option 53 tells the four apart, with values 1, 2, 3 and 5, and one transaction ID runs through them: the offer copies it from the discover and the request repeats it. Microsoft calls the exchange broadcast-based, but RFC 2131 broadcasts the offer and the acknowledgement only when the client sets the broadcast bit; otherwise the server unicasts them to the client's hardware address and the offered address.

Not every DHCPREQUEST is part of it: the same message confirms an address after a reboot and, at T1, half the lease by default, renews it by unicast to the server. A server that cannot satisfy a request answers DHCPNAK and the client starts again. In Wireshark the display filter dhcp shows the exchange, and dhcp.id with the transaction ID isolates one client.

time-exceeded.def: The ICMP error (type 11, type 3 in ICMPv6) sent when a packet's TTL runs out in transit or its fragments miss reassembly.
time-exceeded.context: Traceroute is built on it, and in RFC 4443's words it indicates either a routing loop or too small an initial hop limit. When a router does not send it, a trace shows asterisks, and a filter, a rate limit and a router configured to stay silent all look the same.
time-exceeded.depth:
RFC 792 defines two codes: 0, time to live exceeded in transit, which may come from a gateway, and 1, fragment reassembly time exceeded, which may come from a host that gave up reassembling a datagram and need not be sent at all if fragment zero never arrived. ICMPv6 keeps both under type 3, code 0 reading hop limit exceeded in transit.

RFC 792 left it optional: a gateway may notify the source. RFC 1812 makes it a MUST for a router that discards a packet for an expired TTL, unless the destination is multicast, because traceroute depends on it, and allows a per-interface option to stop it that must default to sending. Routers should be able to rate-limit it, and IPv6 nodes must, by a method that copes with traceroute's bursts.

Like every ICMP error it quotes the packet that caused it: the IP header and at least 8 data bytes, and from routers as much as fits in 576 bytes, so the sender can match it to a probe by ports or sequence number. tcpdump prints ICMP time exceeded in-transit, and the ICMP bytes start 0b 00, type 11 and code 0. RFC 4890 puts ICMPv6 Time Exceeded code 0, and only code 0, among the messages a firewall must not drop.

pxe.def: PXE (Preboot Execution Environment) is the firmware convention, published by Intel in 1999, for booting a machine over the network: a DHCP (Dynamic Host Configuration Protocol) exchange that identifies the client and names a boot program, then a TFTP (Trivial File Transfer Protocol) download of that program, which the firmware runs.
pxe.context: RFC (Request for Comments) 5970 describes the aim: serve every boot and configuration file from one central server when there are many machines to maintain. A PXE (Preboot Execution Environment) boot is a DHCP (Dynamic Host Configuration Protocol) exchange followed by a download, so a failed one is read in the capture: the architecture the client announced in option 93, the file it was offered and the server named for it. Its weakness is the same simplicity: nothing in classic PXE authenticates the offer or the file, so Secure Boot, signed images or HTTPS (HTTP over TLS, Transport Layer Security) have to supply the trust.
pxe.depth:
Where it came from. The Preboot Execution Environment (PXE) specification, version 2.1, was published by Intel Corporation, with contributions from SystemSoft, on 20 September 1999, as part of Intel's Wired for Management programme (its baseline 2.0 is dated 23 December 1998). It standardized what network cards' boot ROMs (read-only memories) had been doing in incompatible ways: the card's firmware gets an address and a boot file name by DHCP (Dynamic Host Configuration Protocol), downloads a network bootstrap program (NBP) by TFTP (Trivial File Transfer Protocol, defined in Request for Comments 1350) and executes it. The specification also defined a Universal Network Device Interface (UNDI), so that one bootstrap program could drive any compliant card, and boot server discovery: after the address exchange, the client may contact a boot server by broadcast to UDP (User Datagram Protocol) port 67, or by multicast or unicast to port 4011. A separate proxyDHCP service can answer only the PXE part of the conversation, which is how a deployment server can live beside a DHCP server it does not control.

The client identifies itself in its DHCP messages. RFC (Request for Comments) 4578 (2006), which recorded Intel's options for the IETF (Internet Engineering Task Force), defines option 93, client system architecture (16-bit types), option 94, network interface identifier (type 1, the Universal Network Device Interface, and its version), and option 97, client machine identifier (a 16-octet GUID, globally unique identifier), each of which MUST be present in every DHCP and PXE packet a compliant client or server sends. The UEFI (Unified Extensible Firmware Interface) specification adds option 60, a case-sensitive class identifier beginning PXEClient that embeds the architecture and interface version, in the form PXEClient:Arch:xxxxx:UNDI:yyyzzz. The PXE 2.1 client retries its Discover four times, after timeouts of 4, 8, 16 and 32 seconds, and if the only offer it gets lacks the PXEClient tag in option 60 it keeps trying on the 4 and 8 second timeouts for a PXE answer, which is the pause seen when a PXE server is down or unreachable.

The reply names the file and the server: RFC 2131 gives the DHCP header a 128-octet file field for the boot file name and siaddr for the next server in the bootstrap, and RFC 2132 adds option 66 (TFTP server name) and option 67 (bootfile name) for when those header fields are used for options. The client fetches that network bootstrap program by TFTP and runs it, and the architecture decides which file fits: RFC 4578 lists type 0 as Intel x86PC, and the UEFI specification calls 64-bit UEFI type 0x07, a value RFC 4578's own table printed against EFI BC. That misprint was corrected by erratum 4624, verified in March 2016, which swapped EFI BC and EFI x86-64, and the Internet Assigned Numbers Authority's (IANA) Processor Architecture Types registry now reads 0 x86 BIOS (Basic Input/Output System), 6 x86 UEFI, 7 x64 UEFI, 0x0A and 0x0B 32-bit and 64-bit ARM UEFI, and continues through RISC-V and LoongArch. A DHCP server that serves both firmware types therefore matches on option 93 and hands a BIOS client a BIOS bootstrap and a UEFI client a UEFI one; a bootstrap built for the wrong architecture downloads and then cannot run.

RFC 5970 (2010) carried the idea to DHCPv6 (Dynamic Host Configuration Protocol for IPv6): the boot file becomes a URL (uniform resource locator) in option 59, option 60 carries boot file parameters, options 61 and 62 mirror 93 and 94, and HTTP (Hypertext Transfer Protocol) is strongly recommended, superseding for IPv6 the old advice to use TFTP. The UEFI specification describes IPv6 PXE with a Proxy DHCP6 service listening on UDP port 4011. UEFI HTTP Boot, in the specification's words a higher-performance replacement for TFTP-based PXE, announces type 0x0F or 0x10 and the class HTTPClient, and IANA's registry lists those types as x86 and x64 UEFI boot from HTTP. iPXE, the open-source boot firmware, is often chainloaded from classic PXE for the same reason: a small undionly.kpxe arrives by TFTP and then fetches everything else by faster protocols, and because iPXE issues a fresh DHCP request, the DHCP server must hand out iPXE only for the first request, or the machine loops forever.

In enterprise networks. PXE broadcasts, so a client on one subnet reaches a server on another only through the router's DHCP relay, an IP (Internet Protocol) helper address pointing at both the DHCP server and the deployment server. Microsoft's Configuration Manager documentation says so plainly: when one PXE-enabled distribution point serves several subnets, DHCP options are not supported and IP helpers must be configured on the routers; a PXE responder installed on the DHCP server itself needs DoNotListenOnDhcpPort set and DHCP option 60 set to PXEClient; and option 82 works with its PXE responder but not with WDS (Windows Deployment Services). Options 66 and 67 still work for a single subnet and one architecture, which is why they appear in so many quick guides and fail as soon as BIOS and UEFI machines share a VLAN (virtual local area network).

What goes wrong, and the security record. A failed PXE boot is read in the capture: the Discover with options 60, 93 and 94; the Offer, and whether it carries a file and next server; the TFTP request, and whether it gets a file or an error. Causes documented by the sources above include a missing IP helper, an architecture mismatch, and a TFTP block or window size too large for the network, which Microsoft notes can make the boot image download fail with a time-out. The protocol itself has no authentication. RFC 5970 warns that a rogue DHCPv6 server could hand out the URL of a malicious image, and recommends HTTPS (Hypertext Transfer Protocol Secure) or signed boot images; on IPv4 the same rogue offer is what DHCP snooping exists to stop, and UEFI Secure Boot is what refuses an unsigned bootstrap. The firmware's network stack is attack surface too. In January 2024 Quarkslab disclosed PixieFail, nine vulnerabilities (CVE-2023-45229 to CVE-2023-45237) in the IPv6 network stack of TianoCore's EDK II, the open-source UEFI code many vendors build on, including overflows in DHCPv6 Advertise parsing reachable during a PXE boot; CERT/CC's (CERT Coordination Center) note VU#132380 lists disabling PXE where it is not used and isolating the pre-boot network among the workarounds. On 22 October 2026 TianoCore published GHSA-99cj-7hg9-mp4m (CVE-2026-97631, Critical, 9.5): ICMP (Internet Control Message Protocol) error handling in the EDK II PXE driver can overflow a buffer during PXE boot over IPv4 or IPv6, before Secure Boot has verified any operating system component, with no patched release at publication. The numbers to remember are options 60, 66, 67, 93, 94 and 97, DHCPv6 options 59 to 62, UDP ports 67, 68, 69 and 4011, architecture types 0, 7 and 0x10, and the 128-octet file field.

troy-hunt.def: The Australian security researcher who launched Have I Been Pwned on 4 December 2013, the free service that tells anyone whether their email address has appeared in a known data breach, and who writes about breaches at troyhunt.com.
troy-hunt.context: Hunt built the service after the Adobe breach, at the time the largest single breach of customer accounts, because he kept finding the same accounts exposed over and over, often with the same passwords. Its companion, Pwned Passwords, checks whether a password has already been exposed, and law enforcement agencies including the Federal Bureau of Investigation (FBI) and Europol contribute credentials found in their investigations. Before going independent he spent fourteen years at Pfizer, and from 2013 he wrote 47 security courses for an online training company; in 2017 he testified before the US House Committee on Energy and Commerce on proving identity once so much identity data has already leaked. He holds Microsoft's Regional Director title, which he describes as a recognition rather than a job.
troy-hunt.depth:
Troy Hunt has written software for the web since the mid-1990s. He spent fourteen years at Pfizer, the last seven responsible for application architecture in the Asia-Pacific region, and the Australian Broadcasting Corporation (ABC), the public broadcaster, dates his departure from corporate work to 2015. From 2013 he wrote 47 courses, mostly on information security, for an online training company; that work, more than 100 hours of it, paid for his independence, and in 2018 he moved to Have I Been Pwned (HIBP) and public speaking full time. He has been part of Microsoft's award programmes since 2011 and holds the Regional Director title, which he describes as a recognition, not employment. He works from the Gold Coast in Australia; Charlotte Hunt, his wife, joined HIBP in 2021 and runs its operations, and Stefán Jökull Sigurðsson has maintained code and cloud infrastructure part-time from Iceland since 2023.

The service came out of the Adobe breach of November 2013, which the ABC puts at 152 million customer records and which was then the largest single breach of customer accounts. Doing post-breach analysis, Hunt kept finding the same accounts exposed again and again, often with the same passwords, which put the victims' other accounts at risk. He launched HIBP by tweet on 4 December 2013, expecting it to fade like his other side projects; the name was partly a matter of which .com domains were still free. The next day he blogged about making a search across 154 million records fast, the first of 185 posts about building and running the service by its tenth birthday.

The model is simple and the restrictions are where the thought went. Anyone can search one email address at a time. Breaches whose mere membership could harm someone are classed as sensitive and shown only to the verified owner of the address, after a sign-in by email. An organization can list every breached address on its domain only after proving control of it through a DNS record, an email to a predefined address, an uploaded file or a meta tag. Beyond breaches, the index holds pastes, spam lists and stealer logs, the credentials that information-stealing malware collects from infected machines, stored against the website domains they were typed into. When the ABC profiled him in 2023 he kept only email addresses, phone numbers and passwords from a breach, encrypted, discarding names, postal addresses and bank details, and contacted the breached organization first so that it could tell its own users. On 12 November 2026 the home page counted 1,051 breached sites and 17,858,196,501 records (labelled pwned addresses); Hunt's own page describes more than 6 billion unique email addresses, more than 400,000 monitored domains, including more than half the Fortune 500, and dozens of national governments using it free of charge.

Pwned Passwords, launched on 3 August 2017 with 306 million breached passwords anyone could download, answers a different question: not whose account leaked, but whether a password has ever been seen in a breach, so that a site can refuse it. Version 2, on 22 February 2018, held 501,636,842 unique passwords drawn from 3,033,858,815 occurrences and introduced the range search Hunt designed with Junade Ali of Cloudflare. A client hashes the password locally with SHA-1 (Secure Hash Algorithm 1) or NTLM (the NT LAN Manager hash), sends only the first five hexadecimal characters to api.pwnedpasswords.com/range, receives every suffix that shares the prefix with a count of appearances, and finishes the comparison itself, so the service never learns the password or its full hash; an Add-Padding request header pads every response to between 800 and 1,000 entries so that response size does not betray the prefix. The API needs no key, and the service reports more than 18 billion requests a month, a cache hit ratio above 99.9 per cent and delivery from 335 Cloudflare edge locations in more than 125 countries. Its reason to exist is now written into standards: the 2025 revision of the National Institute of Standards and Technology (NIST) authentication guideline, SP 800-63B-4, requires verifiers to compare a new password against a blocklist that may include passwords from previous breach corpuses. On 28 May 2021 Pwned Passwords became open source under the .NET Foundation, with the Federal Bureau of Investigation (FBI) feeding in compromised passwords found in its investigations.

Scale arrives in single events. On 17 January 2019 Hunt loaded Collection #1, 2,692,818,238 rows of email addresses and passwords aggregated from thousands of sources, which reduced to 1,160,253,228 unique combinations, 772,904,991 unique email addresses (the largest breach ever loaded into HIBP to that date) and 21,222,975 unique passwords. In 2023 the FBI used HIBP to notify victims after seizing credentials for 80 million accounts in the takedown of the Genesis Market, according to the ABC.

On 30 November 2017 he appeared before the Subcommittee on Oversight and Investigations of the US House Committee on Energy and Commerce at the hearing Identity Verification in a Post-Breach World. His written statement made nine points: breaches happen through attacks, misconfiguration and products that expose data by design; years can pass before anyone learns of one; cheap cloud services and the Internet of Things have created a perfect storm for exposure; services practise data maximization and keep data for ever; there is little accountability, so organizations repeat their peers' mistakes; breaches are traded and collected as a hobby; much exposed personal data can never be changed or scrubbed; people publish a great deal themselves on social media; and so knowledge-based authentication (KBA), which assumes that only you know your personal details, no longer works.

Running a critical service as an individual brought its own arguments. On 11 June 2019 Hunt announced Project Svalbard, a search for a new owner run with the mergers and acquisitions practice of an accounting firm; on 3 March 2020 he announced that HIBP would stay independent, because after 11 months the party expected to buy it had changed its business model and the deal had become infeasible. The ABC counted 141 parties that had expressed interest, and his friend Scott Helme recalled that many people were angry, accusing him of selling out. On 7 August 2020 he announced that he would open source the code base. The ABC also recorded the criticism directly: Jane Andrew of the University of Sydney said that he is not a company that is audited, just a dude on the web, and that a critical global service resting on one person's goodwill is a critical global risk; a government officer said Hunt had over-egged the nature of their relationship. Hunt's answer is transparency, publishing how he handles data, including the code that encrypts what agencies share with him, on the principle that if you are public about all of it there are no skeletons in the closet. On 20 May 2025 a rebuilt HIBP website went live, dropping username search (added in 2014 for the Snapchat incident) and phone number search (added in 2021 for the Facebook incident).

On 25 March 2025 Hunt himself was phished, and his account of it is a lesson in why one-time passwords are not enough. Jet-lagged in London, he entered his Mailchimp credentials and one-time password (OTP) on a look-alike domain, noting afterwards that his password manager had not offered to fill them in; within minutes an automated attacker had logged in from New York and exported his blog's mailing list of about 16,000 records, including people who had unsubscribed. He concluded that OTP-based two-factor authentication is useless against an automated phishing site that relays the code as soon as it is entered, and pointed to passkeys, which he had been discussing with the UK's National Cyber Security Centre (NCSC) the day before, as the phishing-resistant answer. Following his own advice to breached companies, he disclosed the incident within the hour and loaded the list into HIBP, notifying 6.6 thousand subscribers and 2.4 thousand monitored domains.

pwned-passwords.def: Have I Been Pwned's corpus of passwords exposed in data breaches, with a free API that tells you whether a password is in it without the password or its full hash leaving your device.
pwned-passwords.context: Sites use it at registration and at password change to refuse passwords criminals already hold, the defence credential stuffing calls for. The lookup is a range search: the client sends the first five characters of the password's SHA-1 hash and compares the returned suffixes itself.
pwned-passwords.depth:
Pwned Passwords launched on 3 August 2017 with 306 million passwords from breaches, released for download so that any system could check new passwords against them. Version 2, on 22 February 2018, held 501,636,842 unique passwords that had appeared 3,033,858,815 times across breaches, and added the range search designed with Junade Ali of Cloudflare.

The search applies k-anonymity. The client hashes the candidate password, sends only the first five hexadecimal characters of the hash, and receives every suffix in the corpus that shares that prefix, each with the number of times it has been seen; the match, if any, is found on the client, so the service never learns which password or hash was checked. The API accepts the prefix of a SHA-1 or an NTLM hash, needs no authorization, and can pad each response with a random number of extra entries whose count is zero, so that an observer of the encrypted traffic cannot infer the prefix from the response size. The whole corpus can also be downloaded with an open source tool and run offline.

On 28 May 2021 Pwned Passwords became open source under the .NET Foundation, and the FBI began feeding it compromised passwords found in its investigations. Cloudflare provides the infrastructure that serves it.

kev.def: CISA's public catalogue of vulnerabilities known to have been exploited, each with the date it was added and a due date for the action CISA requires.
kev.context: A CVSS (Common Vulnerability Scoring System) score says how bad a flaw could be; a KEV (Known Exploited Vulnerabilities) entry says attackers are already using it, which is why many teams patch KEV entries first whatever their score. Each entry in the feed carries the CVE (Common Vulnerabilities and Exposures) identifier, the vendor and product, the date added, the required action, the due date and whether use in ransomware campaigns is known. CISA (the Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency) added the two PHP2Shell CVEs on 26 October 2026, five days after the fixes shipped and with a due date three days later.
kev.depth:
The Known Exploited Vulnerabilities (KEV) catalogue is a list kept by CISA, the Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency of the United States, of vulnerabilities for which there is reliable evidence of exploitation in the wild. Three conditions put a flaw on it: the vulnerability has an assigned CVE (Common Vulnerabilities and Exposures) identifier, there is reliable evidence that it has been actively exploited, and there is a clear remediation action, such as a vendor update. CISA defines active exploitation as reliable evidence that malicious code was executed by an actor on a system without the owner's permission, and counts attempted exploitation, such as code that fails against a honeypot, as long as the attacker meant to succeed. Scanning, security research on an exploit and a proof of concept do not count. KEV is therefore not a severity list, not a list of everything with public exploit code and not a prediction; it is a record of what has already happened.

The catalogue began as the instrument of a directive. Its first entries carry the date 3 November 2021, when 287 vulnerabilities were added at once, and that day's due dates show the two deadlines of Binding Operational Directive (BOD) 22-01, Reducing the Significant Risk of Known Exploited Vulnerabilities: most CVEs from 2021 were due in 14 days, most older ones in 181 days, the six months the directive gave for older flaws. The directive bound the federal civilian executive branch agencies, but the catalogue was public from the start and became a prioritization signal far beyond them. The oldest identifier in it is CVE-2002-0367; on 10 November 2026 it held 1,779 entries.

The data are published as a JSON (JavaScript Object Notation) feed whose version is the date of its release, 2026.11.10 at the time of reading, and each entry has the same fields: cveID, vendorProject, product, vulnerabilityName, dateAdded, shortDescription, requiredAction, dueDate, knownRansomwareCampaignUse, forensicTriage, notes and cwes. The required action is usually short, apply updates per vendor instructions, or apply mitigations or discontinue use of the product; the notes link to the vendor advisory and, where relevant, to an emergency directive; the CWE (Common Weakness Enumeration) list names the weakness types. Across the whole catalogue the commonest interval between dateAdded and dueDate is 21 days, which applies to 1,025 entries. knownRansomwareCampaignUse reads Known for 361 entries and Unknown for the rest, which means not known, not known to be absent. The same data reach the National Vulnerability Database (NVD), where cisaExploitAdd, cisaActionDue, cisaRequiredAction and cisaVulnerabilityName appear in the CVE record, and on 12 November 2026 the NVD's hasKev filter returned exactly 1,779 records.

In June 2026 the rules that give the due dates their meaning changed. On 10 June CISA issued BOD 26-04, Prioritizing Security Updates Based on Risk, which revokes and replaces BOD 22-01 and also BOD 19-02, the 2019 directive on internet-accessible systems. Instead of one deadline for every KEV entry, it weighs four yes-or-no questions: whether the asset is publicly exposed, whether the CVE is in the KEV, whether an adversary can automate exploitation, and whether exploitation gives total technical control. The sixteen combinations fall into five tiers, as Tenable's summary of the directive sets them out: three days with forensic triage, required whenever a KEV vulnerability yields total control; three days without it for certain other high-risk combinations, even outside the KEV; 14 days for most KEV entries; 60 days for lower-risk combinations; and fix on system upgrade when none of the four criteria applies. Forensic triage means checking whether the system was already compromised before the patch, because a fix rarely evicts an intruder. CISA publishes the answers to three of the four questions through its Vulnrichment programme; only public exposure has to be determined by each agency. Agencies were given 180 days, to about 7 December 2026, before the timelines apply in every case, and in one agency CISA's initial analysis put 1 per cent of vulnerability instances in the three-day tier and over 60 per cent in the deferral tier.

The feed shows the change. Of the 162 entries added from 11 June 2026, 126 were due three days after being added and 36 after 14 days, and 103 carry forensicTriage set to Yes, a field that did not exist under the old directive. PHP2Shell is a typical case: CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619, memory corruption in PHP, were added on 26 October 2026, five days after the coordinated release of the fixes at 14:00 UTC on 21 October, with a due date of 29 October and a required action that cites BOD 26-04 and its forensics triage requirements.

For anyone outside the federal government the catalogue is a free, curated signal of what attackers are actually using, and the vendors on it look like the edge of a network. Microsoft leads with 391 entries, followed by Cisco with 103, Apple with 96, Adobe with 83 and Google with 77; among network and security vendors Ivanti has 38, Fortinet 32, Citrix 27, SonicWall 20, Palo Alto Networks 16 and F5 8, including CVE-2020-5902 and CVE-2022-1388 in BIG-IP. The practical use is a join: match the KEV feed against an asset inventory and every match is a vulnerability that has been used somewhere, on a product the organization runs.

What KEV does not say matters as much. It is not complete: an entry needs evidence that CISA accepts, so exploitation that nobody reported, or that happened only outside CISA's view, is absent, and absence from the list is not evidence of safety. It is not a forecast either: a public proof of concept does not qualify, and Mandiant found that 72 per cent of the 2023 vulnerabilities with at least one public PoC or exploit were not known to be exploited in the wild. For the vulnerabilities that are not yet on the list, EPSS (the Exploit Prediction Scoring System) of FIRST estimates the probability that a published CVE will be exploited in the next 30 days, and the SSVC (Stakeholder-Specific Vulnerability Categorization) decision points that CISA publishes add automatability and technical impact. KEV, EPSS, SSVC and the asset's exposure answer different questions; a CVSS Base score answers none of them on its own.

The neighbours are easy to place. CVE names the flaw; CVSS rates its severity; the NVD enriches the record; EPSS estimates the chance of exploitation; KEV records exploitation that has happened; BOD 26-04 turns those signals into federal deadlines. The numbers worth remembering are three admission criteria; 3 November 2021 and 287 first entries; 14 days and six months under BOD 22-01; 10 June 2026 for BOD 26-04 and its tiers of three, 14 and 60 days; 1,779 entries and 361 with known ransomware use on 10 November 2026; and three days for PHP2Shell, added on 26 October and due on 29 October 2026.

virtual-patching.def: Blocking attempts to exploit a known flaw in the traffic in front of a system, without changing the vulnerable software, until it can be patched.
virtual-patching.context: It is done with a WAF (web application firewall) or IPS (intrusion prevention system) rule, a signature or a policy written for one flaw, and its value is time: during PHP2Shell in October 2026 several vendors had rules out before disclosure or within a day of it. Its limits are as consistent as its uses. It covers only the exploit shapes the rule knows, the device must see the traffic in clear, the rule must block rather than log or sit in staging, and it never removes the flaw. Every vendor that shipped rules for PHP2Shell also told customers to update PHP.

backport.def: Taking a fix from a newer release of a program and applying it to an older version that a vendor still ships.
backport.context: Distributions do it so customers can stay on a version whose behaviour they know; Red Hat's own explanation uses PHP 5.3 as its example. The side effect is that version numbers stop saying whether a system is vulnerable. In October 2026 Ubuntu's fixed PHP for 24.04 was numbered 8.3.6 and CloudLinux's fixed alt-php85 was 8.5.11, both below the upstream fixed releases, so a scanner reading the version string flags them as vulnerable. The evidence is the package changelog naming the CVE.

cna.def: CVE Numbering Authority: an organization authorized by the Common Vulnerabilities and Exposures (CVE) Program to assign CVE identifiers to vulnerabilities within its declared scope and to publish the CVE records for them, usually as part of the first public disclosure.
cna.context: Many software projects and vendors are their own CNA (CVE Numbering Authority), so the first record of a flaw often comes from the people who fixed it: the PHP project published the records for the two PHP2Shell flaws itself in October 2026, with the description, weaknesses, affected versions and a CVSS (Common Vulnerability Scoring System) v4.0 score. Others add to a record without replacing it, in separate containers: the Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency (CISA) added its decision points and the record's entry in its Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalogue. The National Vulnerability Database (NVD) keeps its own analysis beside the record and gave the same flaw its own CVSS v3.1 score, which is why one CVE can carry several scores and an engineer should read whose score is being quoted.
cna.depth:
What it is. Under the CVE Program's CNA Operational Rules, version 4.2.1, effective 20 October 2026, a CNA (CVE Numbering Authority) is an organization authorized to assign CVE (Common Vulnerabilities and Exposures) identifiers and to publish CVE records, ideally as part of the initial public disclosure of a vulnerability. Being one gives two advantages: a CNA can disclose with an identifier already assigned, and it gets the first opportunity to assign identifiers for vulnerabilities inside its scope definition. Many CNAs are suppliers numbering flaws in their own products, typically through a PSIRT (product security incident response team); the rules also list open source projects and foundations, service providers, vulnerability researchers, national CSIRTs (computer security incident response teams), coordinators, vulnerability databases and bug bounty providers. A CNA is not the National Vulnerability Database (NVD), which analyses and scores records after they are published; it is not a certification; and in older networking usage the same three letters name a Novell certification, Certified Novell Administrator, a different sense altogether.

Where it sits. The program is federated. CNAs sit under Roots, Roots under Top-Level Roots, and the program's own partner list shows two Top-Level Roots: MITRE, which is also the Secretariat and a CNA of Last Resort (CNA-LR), and the Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency (CISA), which is also an Authorized Data Publisher (ADP). Roots in the list include JPCERT/CC, Spain's INCIBE, Germany's CERT@VDE, the EU Agency for Cybersecurity (ENISA), Google, Red Hat, Thales and CISA's industrial control systems team; CNA-LRs take the cases no other CNA covers, and MITRE's own description says it does not handle matters within another Top-Level Root's scope. The vendors network engineers deal with every day are CNAs in their own right, each with a scope written in one line: Cisco for all Cisco products and some third-party research, Palo Alto Networks for its products, Fortinet for "Fortinet issues only", Extreme Networks and Netskope for their products and services, and the PHP Group for code in the php-src repository. Brazilian CNAs on the list include FULL INTERNET and senhasegura. Changes to the rules and exceptions to them are approved by the program's executive committee.

How assignment works. The rules follow a right of first refusal: the CNA with the most appropriate scope, very often the supplier, must be contacted first. For a vulnerability already public, if that CNA declares it will not assign, or does not answer within 72 hours, a Root must make the vulnerability determination and, if it finds one, direct a CNA-LR or another CNA to assign no later than 72 hours after the first refusal. A CNA that is not the supplier should make a good-faith effort to notify the supplier, and a CNA that assigns an identifier to a reported flaw must give it to the reporter. Assigning commits the CNA to disclosure: the vulnerability must become public or the identifier must be rejected, and a CNA must not assign identifiers to flaws it does not intend to disclose. The type of technology, cloud, on-premises or artificial intelligence, may not be the sole reason to assign or refuse.

How many identifiers. The counting rules are where most arguments start. Version 4.2.1 turned two recommendations into obligations: separate vulnerabilities must get separate identifiers, and different, independently fixable vulnerabilities must get different identifiers; when a CNA is unsure whether two issues are independently fixable it should assign one. If several products are vulnerable because they share the same vulnerable code, they must share one identifier; if they do not share code, they should get different ones. Interdependent conditions are one vulnerability: the rules' own example is a buffer overflow that happens only when an integer overflow happens, which gets one identifier, not two.

Publishing and content. A CNA should publish the CVE record within 24 hours of disclosing an identifier it assigned and must do so within 72 hours, after which its Root may have a CNA-LR publish instead; it should also publish within 72 hours of learning that someone else has disclosed one of its identifiers. The record must identify at least one affected product, by supplier, product, versions and dates, with at least one product marked affected or unknown and never only unaffected ones; it should give fixed versions; it must state the type or cause of the vulnerability, preferably as a CWE (Common Weakness Enumeration) entry, a requirement that version 4.2.0 relaxed to allow it to be supplied later; it must contain a prose description and at least one public reference that is not the CVE record itself; and a vulnerability that exists only in a fully hosted service carries the exclusively-hosted-service tag. Disagreements go through the program's dispute procedure, and a disputed record must say so with the disputed tag.

One record, read closely. CVE-2026-109618, the first PHP2Shell flaw, shows the layers. The PHP Group's CNA reserved it on 12 October 2026 and published it on 21 October, in record format 5.2, with the title, the description, weaknesses CWE-416 (use after free) and CWE-755 (improper handling of exceptional conditions), affected ranges per supported branch, such as 8.2 before 8.2.35, and a CVSS (Common Vulnerability Scoring System) v4.0 score of 9.2 with attack complexity High. CISA's ADP container, Vulnrichment, then added SSVC (Stakeholder-Specific Vulnerability Categorization) decision points, exploitation active, automatable no, technical impact total, and the date the flaw entered the KEV (Known Exploited Vulnerabilities) catalogue, 26 October; a CVE Program container and a Siemens container followed. The NVD, which analyses the record in its own database, shows the CNA's 9.2 as secondary and its own CVSS v3.1 score of 9.8 as primary, with attack complexity Low. The two numbers disagree on one input, and a triage policy written as patch everything above 9.0 behaves differently depending on which one it reads.

Scope gaps and end of life. A CNA's scope can stop where support stops. F5's scope covers all F5 products and services, including acquired brands such as NGINX, that have not reached End of Technical Support, and states that F5 does not issue CVEs for products no longer supported. The rules allow that, but version 4.1.0, effective 14 May 2025, added that end of life is not by itself a sufficient reason not to assign, and when a CNA declares it does not assign for end-of-life products, other CNAs with appropriate scope may; to avoid duplicates, CNAs should defer to their Root, and Roots should direct a CNA-LR. For an engineer running an old release this means that silence from the vendor's advisory page is not evidence of safety: the identifier, if one exists, may come from someone else.

A program under strain. The rules are young in their current form: version 4.0 took effect on 8 August 2024, 4.1.0 on 14 May 2025, 4.2.0 was dated 25 August 2026 and 4.2.1 took effect on 20 October 2026. The institution behind them had a close call: MITRE told the CVE Board that its contract with the United States Department of Homeland Security would lapse on 16 April 2025, CISA exercised an option hours before it expired to extend funding by about eleven months, and board members launched the CVE Foundation to reduce dependence on a single sponsor. In September 2026 CISA announced a quality-era framework focused on the reliability and usability of CVE data, with more than 67,000 CVEs published by 18 September that year, while ENISA had grown from a single Root to managing 20 CNAs. The numbers worth remembering: 72 hours for a refusal to escalate and for a record to be published, 24 hours as the target, one identifier per independently fixable flaw, and version 4.2.1 of the rules.

embargo.def: The agreed period during which a vulnerability and its fix are known to a few parties who have promised not to disclose them before a set date and time.
embargo.context: It exists so that vendors and distributions can have fixes ready at the moment of disclosure. The rules of the Openwall distros mailing lists cap it at 14 days, prefer fewer than 7, and forbid sharing outside the distribution's own team, even in the form of an undocumented fix. An embargo is only as strong as its weakest participant: in October 2026 the PHP2Shell identifiers leaked a day early, PHP moved its release forward, and the PHP Foundation says one distributor published fixed images more than six hours before the agreed time.
embargo.depth:
What it is, and what it is not. In coordinated vulnerability disclosure an embargo is the confidentiality agreement that covers the gap between private notification and public release: the reporter, the maintainer and the downstream parties who must ship the fix agree on a date and time, usually written in UTC (Coordinated Universal Time), and promise not to reveal the issue before then. The Openwall rules end it at the agreed date and time or when the information has been substantially published by others, whichever comes first. It is narrower than a disclosure deadline. Deadlines are the finder's terms to a vendor: Google Project Zero gives 90 days to ship a patch and publishes details 30 days after the patch, the Zero Day Initiative gives 120 days once the vendor has responded, and the CERT Coordination Center (CERT/CC) discloses 45 days after the initial report whether or not a patch exists. The embargo is the shorter, multi-party secrecy period that usually sits at the end of that process, when many organizations know the fix and none may say so. The word is also used for trade sanctions, an unrelated sense.

The open source rules, in numbers. The Openwall distros and linux-distros lists, through which distributions such as Debian, Red Hat, SUSE, Ubuntu and FreeBSD receive advance notice, accept only issues that are not yet public but will be very soon; the maximum acceptable embargo is 14 days, fewer than 7 is preferred, and the reasonable minimum is one day, although in extreme cases even a few hours of notice can help. A fix already in a public repository makes the issue public by the list's reckoning, with narrow exceptions granted for the Linux kernel and for curl issues of low or medium severity. Members may share the information only with people in their own distribution's team who need it to fix the issue, never with the rest of their company, their customers or clients, and not in any derived form, not even an undocumented fix; in the terms of the Traffic Light Protocol (TLP) the information is TLP:AMBER under those limits during the embargo and TLP:WHITE afterwards. A member who leaks must tell the reporter and the list at once, investigate and report the extent.

The kernel and Xen. The Linux kernel security team releases fixes for publicly known bugs immediately; for undisclosed bugs it will postpone publication at the request of the reporter or an affected party for at most 7 calendar days from the start of the release process, with an exceptional extension to 14, and the only valid reason it accepts is the logistics of QA (quality assurance) and large rollouts. Everything sent to the security list stays confidential even after the embargo ends. Hardware flaws such as Meltdown, Spectre and L1TF go to a separate hardware security team, because they need coordination across operating system vendors, silicon vendors and integrators; its rules ask for the minimum embargo needed, warn against extending one to meet a conference talk, and publish mitigations to everyone at the same moment with no pre-notification. The Xen Project's usual starting point is one working week from report to an advisory for its predisclosure list and two working weeks from there to publication. List members may tell their users only that an issue exists, its advisory number and the planned date; they may deploy fixed versions during the embargo only with the security team's permission, a rule that matters to the cloud providers on the list; since version 2.2 of the policy, 25 June 2014, they may no longer share the CVE (Common Vulnerabilities and Exposures) number. If the flaw is exploited in the wild, Xen releases at once and expects others to do the same.

Why embargoes leak. The CERT/CC's guide puts it as arithmetic. If each party has a one-in-a-thousand chance of leaking, ten parties keep the secret about 99 per cent of the time, a hundred about 90 per cent, and a thousand only about 37 per cent; the Log4j case, VU#930724, involved notifying 1,643 vendors. The guide's conclusion is to keep embargoes as short as the work allows, because the risk grows with time as well as with the number of people, and to think about fairness when deciding which service providers get advance notice. Project Zero's own deadlines bend the same way: when a flaw is exploited in the wild, its 90-day policy becomes 7 days, and the 14-day grace period becomes 3.

Two embargoes that broke. The speculative execution flaws later named Meltdown and Spectre were reported by Project Zero to Intel, AMD and ARM on 1 June 2017, assigned CVE-2017-5753, CVE-2017-5715 and CVE-2017-5754, and scheduled for coordinated disclosure on 9 January 2018. Google published on 3 January instead, citing existing public reports and growing speculation in the press and the research community: seven months of secrecy ended six days early. PHP2Shell, in October 2026, broke faster. The two identifiers began circulating on forums and social media at about 15:00 UTC on 20 October, with a wrong release time and a wrong CVSS (Common Vulnerability Scoring System) score of 10.0 instead of 9.2, although no technical details leaked. PHP published its pre-announcement at 19:30 UTC and moved the release from 22 October to 21 October at 14:00 UTC, because distributors were still packaging the fix. One of the reporting firms then published a video of its proof of concept by mistake, and at 07:41 UTC on 21 October a distributor published built images containing the fix, which the PHP Foundation describes as unilaterally breaking the embargo more than six hours before the coordinated release.

The fix is the leak. The last example shows why the Openwall rules ban even undocumented fixes. As the PHP Foundation put it, once those images were out any attacker could study the fix in binary form while every other user was still waiting for the release. A patch is a description of the vulnerability for anyone who compares the old binary with the new one, so an embargo protects the fix as much as the advisory, and quietly deploying a fixed build to customers is a disclosure in everything but name. That is also why the Xen policy treats deployment during an embargo as something the security team must allow and may restrict to avoid exposing technical details.

What it means for an operator. Most engineers meet an embargo only at its end, as a release at a fixed hour, so the practical skills are knowing when the clock stops and being ready for it. A release at 14:00 UTC, as PHP's was, has to be translated into every operations team's local shift; a fix published by a distribution is a diff that attackers start reading at the same moment the defenders do; and early notice, where it exists, comes through programmes like the Xen predisclosure list, which carry obligations rather than favours. The numbers worth remembering: 14 days as the Openwall maximum and fewer than 7 preferred; 7 calendar days, or exceptionally 14, for the kernel; one plus two working weeks for Xen; 90+30 for Project Zero, 120 days for the Zero Day Initiative and 45 for CERT/CC as disclosure deadlines rather than embargoes.

proof-of-concept.def: A minimal demonstration that a vulnerability can actually be triggered or exploited, as opposed to a claim that it might be.
proof-of-concept.context: Researchers send one to the vendor so the flaw can be confirmed: Calif shared a working remote code execution (RCE) proof of concept with PHP on 14 August 2026, and PHP confirmed it the next day. Once proofs of concept are public, the distance to attacks shortens: Amazon reported several for PHP2Shell from the night after the identifiers leaked and more within hours of the release, although the PHP Foundation found no functional exploit among those circulating at the time of release. That is why a public PoC (proof of concept) is treated as the start of a countdown rather than a curiosity.
proof-of-concept.depth:
A proof of concept (PoC) answers one question, whether the flaw is real, and answers it with the smallest artefact that can: a request, a crafted file, a short program or a recorded demonstration that makes the vulnerable code misbehave in the way the report claims. It is deliberately less than an exploit. The Common Vulnerability Scoring System (CVSS) version 3.1, published by FIRST (the Forum of Incident Response and Security Teams), draws the line in its Exploit Code Maturity metric: proof-of-concept code is available, or an attack demonstration is not practical for most systems, and the code or technique is not functional in all situations and may require substantial modification by a skilled attacker. Above it sit Functional, code that works in most situations where the vulnerability exists, and High, reliable, widely available and easy-to-use automated tools; below it, Unproven. A weaponized exploit, packaged for reliable use and usually carrying a payload, is a different object, and the distance between the two is often where defenders find their time. The same words also name a trial deployment in projects and sales; this is the vulnerability sense.

Researchers build one first for the vendor. A report with a working demonstration removes the argument about whether a theoretical weakness is reachable, lets the vendor reproduce it on its own systems, and settles severity faster: Calif shared a working remote code execution (RCE) proof of concept with PHP on 14 August 2026 and PHP confirmed it the next day. Reproducibility is the scarce commodity in a security inbox. The PHP Foundation wrote in October 2026 that since 1 July its team had worked through more than 100 reports that turned out to be invalid, duplicates or not reproducible, which is the cost a reliable PoC spares both sides.

The scoring systems treat public PoC code as a distinct state between nothing and attacks. CVSS version 4.0 moved the idea into its Threat metrics as Exploit Maturity, with the values Attacked, Proof-of-Concept, Unreported and Not Defined, the last treated as Attacked when the score is calculated, on the worst-case assumption. Proof-of-Concept there means that each of three things is true: proof-of-concept exploit code is publicly available, there is no knowledge of reported attempts to exploit the vulnerability, and there is no knowledge of public tools that simplify those attempts. The specification describes the usual progression: exploitation is at first only theoretical, then proof-of-concept code, functional code or enough technical detail is published, and the code may progress from a demonstration to something that succeeds consistently, in severe cases delivered by a worm. SSVC (Stakeholder-Specific Vulnerability Categorization), the decision model of CERT/CC and CISA, has an Exploitation decision point with three values: None; Public PoC, when a typical PoC exists in sources such as Metasploit or ExploitDB or the method of exploitation is well known; and Active, shared, observable and reliable evidence of use in the wild.

A proof of concept is not evidence of attack, and the catalogue that tracks attacks says so. CISA (the Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency) adds a vulnerability to its Known Exploited Vulnerabilities (KEV) catalogue only with reliable evidence of active exploitation in the wild, attempted exploitation against a honeypot included, and lists scanning, security research of an exploit and a proof of concept among the things that do not count; in its words, the public availability of a PoC does not automatically indicate that the vulnerability has been or will be exploited.

The data agree that the relationship is loose. Mandiant's analysis of 138 vulnerabilities disclosed in 2023 and exploited, by Casey Charrier and Robert Weiner (15 October 2024), found no correlation between exploit availability and exploitation timelines. Where an exploit was public before exploitation, the medians were 7 days from disclosure to the first public exploit, 30 more days to the first known exploitation and 43 days in all; where exploitation came first, it began a median 15 days after disclosure and a public exploit followed 4 days later. Of the 2023 vulnerabilities with at least one public PoC or exploit, 72 per cent were not known to be exploited in the wild. Two cases show why. CVE-2023-28121, in the WooCommerce Payments plugin for WordPress, was disclosed on 23 March 2023, received its first technical write-up and PoC on 3 July and a Metasploit module on 4 July, yet exploitation began only on 14 July, after a weaponized exploit appeared on 11 July and an upgraded one on 13 July; it needed a single HTTP header to exploit. CVE-2023-27997, the heap overflow in the SSL VPN (Secure Sockets Layer virtual private network) of Fortinet FortiOS known as XORtigate, was disclosed on 11 June 2023 with an advisory on 12 June, had PoCs in blog posts on 13 June and PoC code, scanners and weaponized code public by 16 June, but Mandiant first saw exploitation on 12 September, in limited and targeted campaigns. Ease and reliability decide more than publication does.

PHP2Shell, in October 2026, showed the other side: a demonstration can leak before any code does. The two CVE identifiers began circulating on forums and social media at about 15:00 UTC on 20 October, two days before the planned release, with a wrong release time and a wrong CVSS score of 10.0 instead of 9.2; PHP brought its pre-announcement forward to 19:30 UTC and moved the release to 14:00 UTC on 21 October. Around 20:00 UTC one of the reporting firms published by mistake a video of its proof of concept working against several targets; copies circulated after it was deleted, and the PHP Foundation says the video contributed to accelerated development of various PoCs, although it found no functional exploit among them at release. Amazon Threat Intelligence, writing on 21 October, found an exploitation attempt in its MadPot honeypot telemetry dated 17 October, four days before disclosure, multiple proofs of concept from about 02:00 UTC on 21 October, and more within hours of the embargo lifting, used against its sensors almost immediately; at 07:41 UTC that day a distributor had already published fixed images more than six hours early, putting the patch itself in attackers' hands.

Amazon drew a lesson that changes how a public PoC should be read. In the past, it wrote, most exploitation it observed came after a public proof of concept, because a few capable actors built exploits and everyone else waited for them; that dependency is weakening because AI-assisted analysis makes it cheaper to turn a patch diff or an advisory into a working exploit. Its advice was to measure patch and mitigation timelines for critical internet-facing systems in hours, and to start investigations from the earliest known exploitation rather than from the disclosure date. A public PoC is therefore the start of a countdown rather than a curiosity, and its absence is no longer a reason to wait.

Defenders use proofs of concept too, carefully. A PoC confirms that a patch or a mitigation works, gives detection engineers real traffic to write signatures and virtual patches against, and lets a red team show impact. It is also untrusted code. A study of GitHub repositories offering PoCs for vulnerabilities from 2017 to 2021, by Soufian El Yadmani, Robin The and Olga Gadyatskaya, found some that exfiltrated data, installed malware or contained hard-coded reverse shells, and flagged 899 of the 47,285 repositories it checked, 1.9 per cent, as showing malicious intent. The professional habit follows: run a PoC only with authorization, in an isolated laboratory, after reading it, never against systems one does not own or have permission to test.

Publication remains a policy choice. Disclosure deadlines shape when details become public: Google's Project Zero gives a vendor 90 days to make a patch available and publishes the details 30 days after the patch, or at day 90 if there is none, and coordinated disclosure generally asks reporters to hold demonstrations until users can update. The neighbours are close: an exploit is a working attack, a PoC a minimal demonstration; a zero-day is unknown to the vendor, whether or not a PoC exists; a Metasploit module is a packaged exploit; a KEV entry records attacks, not demonstrations. The numbers worth remembering are the four CVSS v3.1 maturity levels and the three v4.0 values; SSVC's None, Public PoC and Active; Mandiant's 72 per cent and its 7, 30 and 43-day medians; 1.9 per cent malicious PoC repositories; and for PHP2Shell, 14 August, 17 October, and 02:00 and 14:00 UTC on 21 October 2026.

out-of-memory.def: The condition in which a program cannot get the memory it asks for, from the operating system or from a limit it sets on itself.
out-of-memory.context: How a program handles it decides whether running out of memory is only an outage. PHP sets its own ceiling per script, memory_limit, 128M by default, and has handled crossing it by abandoning the request. CVE-2026-109618 was the case where that abandonment left half-built request data for the cleanup to trust, turning an out-of-memory error into remote code execution. The October 2026 fixes made memory_limit a soft limit, backed by a hard limit set with the new memory_hard_limit_percent directive.

php.def: The open-source scripting language that runs on the web server and produces the page the browser receives; it runs most of the websites whose server-side language can be identified from outside.
php.context: PHP (PHP: Hypertext Preprocessor) began in 1994 as Rasmus Lerdorf's Personal Home Page Tools, was rebuilt from 1997 by Andi Gutmans and Zeev Suraski, and now runs on the Zend Engine, reaching the network through a server API (SAPI): PHP-FPM (FastCGI Process Manager) behind NGINX or Apache, the Apache module, CGI (Common Gateway Interface) or the command line. W3Techs counted it on 68.8% of the websites whose server-side language it could identify on 12 November 2026.
php.depth:
What it is. The PHP manual defines PHP, a recursive acronym for PHP: Hypertext Preprocessor, as a widely used open-source general-purpose scripting language especially suited to web development and able to be embedded in HTML (HyperText Markup Language). It is mainly used for server-side scripting, generating a page for each request, and also runs scripts from the command line. The language is executed by the Zend Engine and reaches the web through a server API (SAPI): the FastCGI Process Manager (PHP-FPM) behind NGINX or Apache, the Apache module mod_php, plain CGI, or servers such as LiteSpeed and FrankenPHP. Which SAPI is in use matters operationally, because it decides how a request crosses from the web server into PHP, and that boundary is where several of PHP's worst vulnerabilities have lived.

From tools to a language. Rasmus Lerdorf created the first version in 1994 as a set of CGI binaries written in C to track visits to his online résumé, and called it Personal Home Page Tools. He released the source in June 1995; in September 1995 it briefly became FI, for Forms Interpreter, with Perl-like variables and code embedded in HTML comments; in October 1995 a complete rewrite returned as the Personal Home Page Construction Kit, deliberately C-like; and in April 1996 the names merged into PHP/FI, which gained database support, cookies and user functions. PHP/FI 2.0 had only one full release, leaving beta in November 1997, and a Netcraft survey in May 1998 found nearly 60,000 domains reporting PHP, about 1 per cent of the internet's domains.

The rewrites. Andi Gutmans and Zeev Suraski in Tel Aviv began rewriting the parser in 1997 for a university e-commerce project, joined forces with Lerdorf, and renamed the result simply PHP, now the recursive acronym, dropping the personal-use sense of the old name. PHP 3.0 was announced in June 1998, was on more than 70,000 domains at release, and at its peak ran on about 10 per cent of the internet's web servers; its extensibility drew dozens of module authors. Gutmans and Suraski then rebuilt the core as the Zend Engine, named from Zeev and Andi, introduced in mid-1999, and PHP 4.0 shipped on it in May 2000 with HTTP (Hypertext Transfer Protocol) sessions and output buffering. PHP 5, in July 2004, brought Zend Engine 2.0 and a new object model. PHP 6, planned around deep Unicode support, was abandoned, its other features going into 5.3 (namespaces) and 5.4 (traits and the short array syntax). PHP 7.0 in 2015 brought Zend Engine 3.0, up to twice as fast as PHP 5.6, with consistent 64-bit support and the null coalescing operator; PHP 8.0 in 2020 added named arguments, union types, attributes, match expressions, the nullsafe operator and an optimizing JIT (just-in-time) compiler, followed by enumerations and the Fiber class (full-stack, interruptible functions, in the PHP manual's words) in 8.1, readonly classes in 8.2 and typed class constants in 8.3. PHP 8.5 was released on 20 November 2025, and 8.6.0 reached its fourth release candidate on 21 October 2026.

The support clock. Each branch gets two years of active support, with regular bug and security releases, and then two more years of critical security fixes only, released as needed; support ends on 31 December. On 12 November 2026 php.net listed 8.2 to 8.5 as supported: 8.2, first released on 8 December 2022, receives security fixes until 31 December 2026; 8.3 until 31 December 2027; 8.4 until 31 December 2028; 8.5 until 31 December 2029. Everything older is end of life: 8.1 since 31 December 2025, last release 8.1.34; 8.0 since 26 November 2023 (8.0.30); 7.4 since 28 November 2022 (7.4.33); 5.6 since 31 December 2018 (5.6.40).

How much of the web runs it, and on what. W3Techs counted PHP on 68.8 per cent of the websites whose server-side language it could identify on 12 November 2026. Its version breakdown put 67.0 per cent of PHP sites on PHP 8, 25.5 per cent on 7, 7.5 per cent on 5 and 0.1 per cent on 4, and within PHP 8 the shares were 35.2 per cent for 8.3, 26.3 for 8.2, 13.8 for 8.1, 12.8 for 8.4, 6.5 for 8.5 and 5.3 for 8.0. Combining the two tables, roughly 46 per cent of the PHP sites in that breakdown ran a branch that no longer receives security fixes, and when 8.2's support ends on 31 December 2026 the figure rises past 60 per cent unless those sites move. WordPress, on 39.2 per cent of all websites by W3Techs' count, recommends PHP 8.3 or later but still documents that it works on PHP 7.4 in legacy environments, noting that those versions are past end of life.

A security history at the boundary. Three of the best-known PHP vulnerabilities sit exactly where the web server hands a request to PHP, each tracked by a Common Vulnerabilities and Exposures (CVE) identifier. CVE-2012-1823: php-cgi before 5.3.12 and 5.4.2 treated a query string without an equals sign as command-line options, so a URL (uniform resource locator) could switch PHP's own settings and run code; the US Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency (CISA) added it to its Known Exploited Vulnerabilities (KEV) catalogue on 25 March 2022. CVE-2019-11043: in certain PHP-FPM configurations behind a web server, 7.1, 7.2 and 7.3 before 7.1.33, 7.2.24 and 7.3.11 could be made to write past their buffers into FastCGI protocol data, again remote code execution, scored 9.8 by NVD (National Vulnerability Database) and 8.7 by PHP itself, in KEV from the same day. CVE-2024-4577: with Apache and PHP-CGI on Windows, the Best-Fit replacement of characters in certain code pages let characters in the command line be read as PHP options, affecting 8.1, 8.2 and 8.3 before 8.1.29, 8.2.20 and 8.3.8, scored 9.8 and added to KEV on 12 June 2024.

October 2026. On 21 October 2026 PHP published 8.5.12, 8.4.27, 8.3.36 and 8.2.35 with an advisory headed critical remote code execution, update now, for two flaws in the engine itself. CVE-2026-109618 arises because PHP abandons a request with longjmp() on an out-of-memory error, which can leave request memory uninitialized for the cleanup that follows; CVE-2026-109619 arises because global state that points into one request's memory can outlive that memory and be used by a later request on the same worker. PHP scored both 9.2 in CVSS (Common Vulnerability Scoring System) 4.0, NVD scored them 9.8 and 8.1 in CVSS 3.1, and CISA added both to KEV on 26 October 2026. The advisory put every installation that serves web requests at risk, PHP-FPM, mod_php, php-cgi, FrankenPHP and LiteSpeed alike, and the risk highest for mod_php, where a demonstrated exploit triggers before any application code runs; its interim measures, such as memory_limit=-1 set where applications cannot override it, smaller post_max_size values and session.upload_progress.enabled=0, narrow specific paths without making an installation safe. Only supported branches received fixed releases.

Operating it. PHP has two update streams that fail independently: the runtime, from php.net or from the operating system's packages (distributions and long-term-support vendors received the October 2026 patches in advance), and the application's libraries, which Composer installs per project into a vendor directory and which composer audit checks against published security advisories. The other rule is about the FastCGI listener. The manual's warning is blunt: an exposed FastCGI endpoint allows arbitrary code execution. On the same host a Unix socket should be preferred; with a TCP (Transmission Control Protocol) socket, listen.allowed_clients must list the permitted web servers because it is unset by default and then accepts any address; in containers the FPM port should not be published on the host; and FPM pools are not a security boundary, since they share one OPcache. A FastCGI port reachable from an untrusted network is a remote shell waiting for a client.

zend-engine.def: The compiler and virtual machine at the core of PHP, which turns each script into bytecode and executes it.
zend-engine.context: Andi Gutmans and Zeev Suraski named it after their first names, Zeev and Andi. It first appeared in mid-1999 and has carried PHP since 4.0 in May 2000; Zend Engine 2.0 brought PHP 5's object model and 3.0 the speed-up of PHP 7. OPcache and the JIT compiler both work on its bytecode.
zend-engine.depth:
The engine is separate from the server APIs that connect PHP to a web server or a terminal; the manual's page on the command line lists what changes from one SAPI to another, such as headers, the working directory and a few overridden settings, while the engine underneath stays the same.

Without a cache the engine compiles every script on every request; OPcache stores the compiled bytecode in shared memory so the work happens once, and the JIT added in PHP 8.0 can compile hot code further into machine code. At the end of a request PHP can leave the freeing of the request's variables to the Zend Engine's memory manager, en masse, a fast-shutdown sequence that was an OPcache option until PHP 7.2 and is now built into PHP and used where possible.

sapi.def: Server API: the layer that connects PHP to whatever started it, a web server, a FastCGI process manager or a terminal.
sapi.context: The function php_sapi_name() reports it: cli for the command line, fpm-fcgi for PHP-FPM, apache2handler for the Apache module, cgi-fcgi for php-cgi, among others. The SAPI decides when php.ini is read, which per-directory files apply and which processes hold PHP between requests, so it is the first thing to establish about any PHP server.
sapi.depth:
The PHP manual documents four in detail. The CLI is for shell scripts and cron jobs and lifts the max_execution_time limit; its built-in web server is for development only and should not be used on a public network. PHP-FPM is a FastCGI process manager with pools of workers. The Apache module embeds PHP in every httpd worker, and the manual now says not to use it for new installations. CGI starts an interpreter for each request.

Under FPM and the Apache module one parent coordinates children that each serve one request at a time and many requests over their lives, so anything a worker deliberately keeps, such as a persistent database connection, outlives the request that opened it. The Server API line of phpinfo() shows which SAPI answered a web request.

php-fpm.def: PHP's FastCGI Process Manager: a master process and pools of PHP workers that a web server reaches over FastCGI.
php-fpm.context: It is how NGINX runs PHP, and what the PHP manual now recommends behind Apache httpd's mod_proxy_fcgi instead of mod_php. Each pool has its own user, listen address and settings, and each worker serves one request at a time, so pm.max_children is the pool's concurrency limit. The manual warns that php-fpm must not be reachable from an untrusted network.
php-fpm.depth:
The process manager runs in one of three modes: static, a fixed number of workers; dynamic, a range of idle spares under a ceiling; ondemand, workers started when requests arrive and stopped when idle. pm.max_requests recycles a worker after a number of requests, and the status page (pm.status_path) shows the listen queue, the active and idle workers and whether the ceiling was ever reached.

The listen directive takes a TCP address or a Unix socket. The manual's warning on it is blunt: an exposed FastCGI endpoint allows arbitrary code execution, because a client that can open a FastCGI connection controls the configuration used for the request. On the same host it prefers a Unix socket; over TCP it calls for listen.allowed_clients, which accepts any address when unset. It also says pools are not a security mechanism, since all of them share one OPcache instance.

fastcgi.def: A binary protocol between a web server and long-lived application processes, specified by Open Market in 1996 as an open extension to CGI.
fastcgi.context: Where CGI starts a process for every request, a FastCGI application keeps running and accepts connections on a listening socket. Each request travels as typed records over that connection: parameters, request body, output and errors in separate streams. PHP-FPM speaks it; NGINX speaks it through fastcgi_pass and Apache httpd through mod_proxy_fcgi.
fastcgi.depth:
Mark R. Brown's specification, version 1.0 of 29 April 1996, defines an eight-byte record header (version, type, request ID, a content length of up to 65,535 bytes, a padding length) and eleven record types, from FCGI_BEGIN_REQUEST and FCGI_PARAMS to FCGI_STDOUT and FCGI_END_REQUEST. The request ID lets one connection carry several requests, and the FCGI_KEEP_CONN flag decides whether the application closes the connection after answering or leaves it to the web server.

Applications play roles: Responder, the CGI-like role PHP plays, Authorizer and Filter. fastcgi.com, where the specification was published, is offline, and the text survives in the community FastCGI Archives. Because the parameters a web server sends can carry PHP settings, an exposed FastCGI port is a route to running code, which is why the PHP manual insists that php-fpm stay off untrusted networks.

cgi.def: Common Gateway Interface: the convention, documented as CGI/1.1 in RFC 3875, by which a web server runs an external program for a request and returns what it prints.
cgi.context: The server passes the request as environment variables such as REQUEST_METHOD, SCRIPT_NAME, PATH_INFO and QUERY_STRING and the body on standard input; the program writes headers and a body to standard output. Conventional CGI starts a process per request, the cost FastCGI was designed to remove. PHP began in 1994 as a set of CGI binaries.
cgi.depth:
RFC 3875, published in October 2004 by D. Robinson and K. Coar of the Apache Software Foundation as an Informational document, records the "current practice" of the CGI/1.1 interface developed at NCSA and in use on the web since 1993. It leaves the mapping from a request URI to a script to the server, and defines PATH_INFO as the part of the path that follows the part identifying the script.

That split between the script and the path information is what PHP's cgi.fix_pathinfo setting and the web servers' path-splitting directives deal with, and the PHP manual's NGINX guide sets cgi.fix_pathinfo to 0 as its way of keeping requests for files that do not exist from reaching PHP-FPM. PHP still ships a CGI binary, php-cgi, and its manual calls cgi.force_redirect necessary for security when PHP runs as a CGI under most web servers.

opcache.def: PHP's bytecode cache, which keeps compiled scripts in shared memory so PHP does not parse and compile them on every request.
opcache.context: Bundled since PHP 5.5 and always built in and loaded since 8.5, it is shared by every worker and every PHP-FPM pool on a server. With opcache.validate_timestamps off, new code takes effect only after opcache_reset(), opcache_invalidate() or a restart, so a deployment that skips all three keeps serving the old scripts.
opcache.depth:
Its shared memory segment, sized by opcache.memory_consumption, also holds the buffer of the JIT compiler PHP 8.0 added, which compiles hot code into machine code. PHP's 8.0 release page reported about three times the performance on synthetic benchmarks but typical application performance on par with PHP 7.4, and since PHP 8.4 the JIT is disabled by default.
