Because one OPcache instance serves all pools, the PHP manual says FPM pools are not a security mechanism. The opcache.restrict_api setting limits which scripts may call the cache's management functions; its default is no restriction.

composer.def: The dependency manager for PHP: a project declares its libraries in composer.json, and Composer resolves, locks and installs them into the project's vendor directory.
composer.context: It manages dependencies per project rather than system-wide, writes the exact versions to composer.lock, which its documentation says to commit so every machine installs the same code, and generates the autoloader the application includes. composer audit checks the installed packages against security advisories, abandoned packages and packages flagged as malware.
composer.depth:
Composer resolves version constraints such as 2.0.* against repositories, Packagist by default, and treats PHP itself and its extensions as platform packages (php, ext-name) that a project can require but Composer cannot install. Its documentation names npm and Ruby's bundler as its inspiration. The current release needs PHP 7.2.5, and a long-term-support line, 2.2.x, still runs on PHP 5.3.2 and later.

For an operator it is the second update stream on a PHP server: patching the PHP runtime changes nothing in vendor/, and updating a library changes nothing in the runtime. The lock file is the inventory of that second stream.

packagist.def: The default package repository for Composer, where public PHP libraries are published and from which Composer downloads them.
packagist.context: A package is named vendor/project, and a vendor name is protected once a package under it has been published. Packagist reads versions from the tags of the package's repository. On 27 October 2026 its statistics listed 476,229 packages, 5,986,130 versions and 208,477,133,221 installs since 13 April 2012.
packagist.depth:
Composer falls back to Packagist whenever a project names no other repository, which puts Packagist in the supply chain of almost every modern PHP application. The composer audit command checks installed packages against security advisories through the Packagist API by default, and the Packagist site credits a sponsor for malware detection alongside those for hosting and bandwidth.

Private code goes elsewhere: Packagist's own page points to Private Packagist for packages that should not be public, and Composer can read other repositories listed in composer.json.

php-ini.def: PHP's main configuration file, read when PHP starts: once, at web-server start, for a server module, and on every invocation for CGI and the command line.
php-ini.context: PHP finds it through the SAPI's own setting (PHPIniDir in Apache, -c on the command line), the PHPRC variable, the working directory, the executable's directory and a compiled-in path, preferring php-SAPI.ini over php.ini, then reads extra .ini files from PHP_INI_SCAN_DIR. Each directive has a mode that says where else it may be changed.
php-ini.depth:
The modes are INI_SYSTEM (php.ini or httpd.conf), INI_PERDIR (also .htaccess and .user.ini), INI_USER and INI_ALL (also ini_set() in a script). Under the Apache module php_admin_value fixes a setting so that neither .htaccess nor ini_set() can change it; under CGI and FastCGI PHP reads .user.ini files from the script's directory up to the document root; PHP-FPM pools take php_value and php_admin_value, and a web server can pass PHP_VALUE in the FastCGI parameters.

Two of its directives are often taken for isolation and are not, in the manual's own words: open_basedir is an extra safety net that cannot be relied upon when security is needed, and disable_functions can be circumvented and is not sufficient for shared hosting. expose_php decides whether PHP announces its version in an X-Powered-By header.

pecl.def: PHP Extension Community Library: the repository of compiled PHP extensions, now deprecated in favour of PIE, the PHP Installer for Extensions.
pecl.context: PECL hosted extensions written in C and distributed them with the packaging system of its sister project, PEAR; the pecl command installed them and an extension directive in php.ini loaded them. Both the PHP manual and the PECL site now say that PECL is deprecated and recommend PIE.
pecl.depth:
The difference from Composer matters on a server: Composer installs PHP code into one project, while PECL and PIE install compiled extensions into the PHP runtime itself, shared by every application on it. An extension installed that way has its own version to track.

PEAR, the PHP Extension and Application Repository, was born at the PHP Developers' Meeting in Tel Aviv in January 2000 and created by Stig S. Bakken, the PHP manual's history records. OPcache itself was distributed through PECL for PHP 5.2 to 5.4 before it was bundled with PHP 5.5.

dodekalogue.def: The common name for the twelve rules in Tcl's Tcl(n) manual page that define the whole syntax of the language.
dodekalogue.context: Tcl has no grammar beyond these rules: commands and separators, evaluation, words, double quotes, argument expansion, braces, command substitution, variable substitution, backslash substitution, comments, the order of substitution and word boundaries. Before '{*}' argument expansion became rule 5 there were eleven, the Endekalogue. Most surprises in an Expect script or an iRule that are not about the command itself are one of these rules: braces that keep a \r as two characters, double quotes that run a bracket as a command, a value that is never substituted twice. The twelve rules are the same in Tcl 8.6 and Tcl 9, apart from a few words.

expect-out.def: The array in which Expect leaves what its last expect command matched: the match, up to nine regular-expression groups, and the output read up to the end of the match.
expect-out.context: expect_out(0,string) holds the matched text, expect_out(1,string) to expect_out(9,string) the groups of a -re pattern, and expect_out(buffer) everything from the start of the unmatched output to the end of the match; what follows stays in Expect's buffer for the next expect. Two habits avoid wrong readings: a group that took no part in a match keeps the value of an earlier one, so clear the array before reading groups, and inside a procedure the array is local unless it is declared global.
expect-out.depth:
Expect, the Tcl (Tool Command Language) extension that Don Libes wrote at the United States National Institute of Standards and Technology (NIST) to automate interactive programs such as telnet, ftp and passwd, waits for output with its expect command and reports what it found through a Tcl array named expect_out. The manual for release 5.45.4 sets the rule: upon matching a pattern, or on eof or full_buffer, any matching and previously unmatched output is saved in expect_out(buffer), the text that matched the whole pattern in expect_out(0,string), and up to nine regular-expression substring matches in expect_out(1,string) to expect_out(9,string). With the -indices flag before a pattern, the start and end of each of those strings are added as expect_out(X,start) and expect_out(X,end), character positions counted from 0 with the end inclusive. The spawn id the output came from is stored in expect_out(spawn_id), which matters when one expect watches several processes.

The manual's two worked examples are the clearest definition. If a process has printed abcdefgh followed by a newline, expect "cd" behaves as if expect_out(0,string) had been set to cd and expect_out(buffer) to abcd, and efgh with its newline stays in Expect's internal buffer for the next expect. If it printed abbbcabkkkka and a newline, expect -indices -re "b(b*).*(k+)" sets expect_out(0,string) to bbbcabkkkk at positions 1 to 10, expect_out(1,string) to bb at 2 to 3, expect_out(2,string) to k at 10, and expect_out(buffer) to abbbcabkkkk, leaving a and the newline. Two consequences follow. The buffer element includes the match, so the text before the match is the buffer with the match removed from its end. And the part after the match is not lost, only deferred, unless the pattern was * or -re ".*", which the manual notes flush the whole buffer without reading more. The -notransfer flag leaves even the matched text in the internal buffer, which helps when experimenting.

Python's pexpect, which copied the model, splits the same information differently, and the difference trips people who move between them: after each expect(), pexpect's before holds the text up to the pattern, without it, after holds the text the pattern matched, and match holds the regular expression's match object. Expect's buffer element is pexpect's before and after joined.

The group elements are where scripts go wrong, and the source code shows why. In expect.c of release 5.45.4, after a regular expression matches, a loop walks every subexpression Tcl reports, skips any whose start is -1, meaning it took no part in the match, and writes X,string for the rest. A skipped group's element is therefore not cleared: if one expect matched -re "(a)(b)" against ab and the next matched -re "(c)|(d)" against d, expect_out(1,string) still says a. The same loop computes each group's end as the match end minus one, so an empty group at the very start of the buffer gets an end index of -1, and Tcl's own Tcl_GetRange treats a negative last index as the end of the value, returning the whole buffer instead of an empty string. The loop also runs over every subexpression rather than stopping at nine, so the limit of nine is the manual's statement rather than the code's. For glob and exact patterns only element 0 is written. The safe habit is to run array unset expect_out before an expect whose groups will be read, and to read groups only in the body of the pattern that matched.

Events other than a match matter too. The manual names a match, eof and full_buffer as the events that set the array; a timeout is not among them, so after a timeout expect_out still describes the previous match, and a script that reads it there reads stale data. At eof the source still records the spawn id and whatever output was left in expect_out(buffer), which is how a script collects the last lines a program printed before exiting. When more output arrives than match_max allows (the manual's default is 2000 bytes), earlier bytes are forgotten; whether or not a full_buffer pattern is used, the forgotten characters are written to expect_out(buffer), so the element can hold the discarded head of a long answer rather than the part a pattern was looking for. By default remove_nulls strips null bytes before output is matched or stored, so they never appear in the array.

Scope is the second trap. The manual describes Expect's liberal scoping: variables that Expect's own commands read are looked up first in the local scope and then in the global one, but variables written are always local unless a global command has been issued. An expect inside a procedure therefore fills a local expect_out that disappears when the procedure returns; either return the value or declare global expect_out. The source shows the exception: expect_background writes the array with Tcl's global-only flag, because there is no procedure to write into when a background pattern fires. The interact command keeps a parallel array, interact_out, for its own -re patterns.

When a value is not what the script expected, the fastest check is Expect's own diagnostics. exp_internal 1, or running the interpreter with -d, sends to standard error every character received and every attempt to match it against the patterns, and the source logs each assignment as a line naming the element being set, such as set expect_out(0,string) followed by its value, so the exact contents of the buffer at the moment of the match are visible rather than guessed.

Against network devices the array is how output is captured, and terminal behaviour shapes what it contains. A script that sends a show command and then expects the device prompt finds, in expect_out(buffer), the echoed command, the command's output and the prompt itself, all of which the script must trim. Lines arrive with carriage return and linefeed, because, as the manual warns, the terminal driver usually converts newlines into that pair, so a pattern spanning two lines needs \r\n rather than \n. Pagers that pause output behind a More prompt, long outputs that exceed match_max, and prompts that change with the configuration mode each produce a buffer that looks valid and is incomplete, which is why scripts disable paging first and raise match_max before asking for large outputs.

match-max.def: The Expect setting that sizes the buffer an expect command matches against, 2000 characters by default, past which the oldest output is forgotten.
match-max.context: match_max sets it for the current spawn id and match_max -d for those spawned later. The full_buffer keyword is the pattern that fires when output is about to be forgotten, and the forgotten text lands in expect_out(buffer) either way. In Expect 5.45.4 the buffer holds three times match_max and drops its oldest third when two thirds full, so a long answer can lose its beginning without a sign; a script that needs a long answer whole raises match_max before it sends the command.

glob-pattern.def: A wildcard pattern in which * stands for any run of characters, ? for one character and a bracket for a set; the default pattern style of Tcl's string match and of Expect.
glob-pattern.context: Glob patterns come from the Unix shell's file-name matching. In Tcl's string match the pattern must match the whole string; Expect's own glob matcher, used for every expect pattern without -re or -ex, matches anywhere in its buffer, anchors with ^ only as the first character and $ only as the last, and lets * take the longest run it can. A backslash makes the next character ordinary, which is why a braced \r in a glob pattern means the letter r.

exp-continue.def: The Expect command that, run inside the body of a matched pattern, makes the same expect start waiting again instead of returning.
exp-continue.context: It is how Expect loops without a loop: answer a --More-- pager, a progress line or a second login question inside one expect, then keep waiting for the prompt. By default it restarts the timeout timer, so the timeout then means the longest silence between two matches; with -continue_timer the deadline stays where it was, and the timeout bounds the whole exchange. A device that pages forever keeps a plain exp_continue loop alive forever too.

expect-timeout.def: The variable, 10 seconds unless the script sets it, that limits how long each expect waits for a pattern before it gives up.
expect-timeout.context: -1 means no limit, and -timeout N overrides it for one expect. The clock starts when the expect starts and only exp_continue restarts it: output that matches nothing does not. When it runs out, an arm for the timeout keyword runs; with no such arm Expect takes the implicit null action, returns as if nothing had gone wrong, and the script's next line runs, which is the cause of most Expect scripts that fail without saying so. It is unrelated to the timeout pattern of interact, which measures idle time.

expect-interact.def: The Expect command that hands a spawned program to the person at the keyboard, and gives it back to the script when a chosen key sequence or an idle timeout ends it.
expect-interact.context: Scripts use it to log in and then let a person work, or to hand over at the point of failure while debugging. Patterns inside it are what the person types to get the script back, usually with return in the body; its own timeout pattern measures idle time and has nothing to do with the timeout variable of expect. While it runs, Expect shows the session even if log_user was 0, on the reasoning that nobody wants to interact blindly.

autoexpect.def: The program in the Expect distribution that watches you use another program and writes an Expect script that repeats what you did.
autoexpect.context: Its own manual page is the fairest review of it: the script it writes is not guaranteed to work, it records every character, output that changes from run to run included, and it should not be taken as a model of style. As a first draft it saves typing and shows how Tcl wants a string quoted. As the finished script it waits for an exact banner with no timeout, and it stops the first time anything on the other side changes.

pexpect.def: A pure Python module, modelled on Expect, that spawns a program on a pseudo-terminal, waits for patterns in its output and sends it input.
pexpect.context: It brought Expect's model to the language most network automation is now written in, with the same habits and a few traps of its own: a timeout that raises an exception after 30 seconds where Expect carries on after 10, a sendline that ends with a linefeed where a device documents the Enter key, and a $ that its documentation calls useless for finding the end of a line. Ansible's expect module requires it.

netconf.def: The Internet Engineering Task Force (IETF) protocol of RFC (Request for Comments) 6241 for installing, changing and deleting the configuration of network devices through remote procedure calls encoded in XML (Extensible Markup Language), usually carried over SSH (Secure Shell) on port 830 (RFC 6242).
netconf.context: It is what the command line becomes when a program, not a person, is on the other end: requests and replies are structured, an error arrives as an rpc-error element instead of text to recognize, and a device with a candidate datastore lets a change be prepared and then committed. Where a platform offers it for the task, it replaces the screen scraping an Expect script does.
netconf.depth:
What it is, and what it is not. NETCONF (Network Configuration Protocol) is a protocol, not a data model. RFC (Request for Comments) 6241 of June 2011, edited by R. Enns of Juniper Networks, M. Bjorklund of Tail-f Systems, J. Schoenwaelder of Jacobs University and A. Bierman of Brocade, describes it in four layers: a secure transport at the bottom; a messages layer that frames remote procedure calls and notifications; an operations layer of base operations invoked as RPCs (remote procedure calls) with XML (Extensible Markup Language) parameters; and a content layer, the configuration and state data themselves, which the RFC leaves out of scope. That content is described in YANG, the modelling language written for NETCONF, so the protocol says how to read, change and lock a tree and YANG says what the tree contains. RFC 6241 is a Proposed Standard; it obsoleted the first specification, RFC 4741 of December 2006, also edited by Enns, and has itself been updated by RFC 7803 and RFC 8526.

Sessions and messages. NETCONF is connection-oriented: it needs a reliable, sequenced and persistent connection, sessions are long-lived, and anything a session holds, a lock above all, is released automatically when the connection closes. Each side opens by sending a hello message listing its capabilities, identified by URIs (uniform resource identifiers); the base protocol is urn:ietf:params:netconf:base:1.0 or base:1.1, and the version both sides support decides how the session behaves. A request is an rpc element with a mandatory message-id attribute, and the server echoes that value in its rpc-reply so that a client can match answers to questions. A failure comes back as an rpc-error element with a fixed error-tag, such as data-exists, data-missing, in-use or malformed-message, which a program can test instead of parsing prose. Asynchronous events were added in RFC 5277 of July 2008: a client sends create-subscription and the server pushes notifications from an event stream over the same session.

The nine base operations. get-config reads all or part of a configuration datastore; get reads the running configuration together with device state; edit-config changes a datastore; copy-config replaces one datastore with another; delete-config removes one; lock and unlock give a session exclusive write access; close-session ends the session politely and kill-session forces another one to end. The work is done by edit-config. Each element of the data sent can carry an operation attribute: merge, the default, combines it with what is there; replace overwrites only the configuration actually present in the request, unlike copy-config, which replaces the whole target; create fails with data-exists if the node is already there; delete fails with data-missing if it is not; and remove, added in RFC 6241, deletes if present and is silently ignored otherwise. A default-operation parameter sets merge, replace or none for the request, and an error-option decides what happens on a failure: stop-on-error is the default, continue-on-error carries on and reports, and rollback-on-error restores the datastore to its state before the request. The test-option value test-only, also new in RFC 6241, validates a change without applying it. Reads can be narrowed by subtree filtering, or by XPath (XML Path Language) expressions where the server advertises that capability.

Datastores, capabilities and the confirmed commit. The base protocol knows the running datastore; capabilities add the rest. writable-running lets a client edit running directly; candidate adds a scratch configuration that a commit operation copies into running, and because other sessions may share it, the RFC calls it prudent to lock the candidate before modifying it; startup adds a separate boot configuration; validate checks a configuration before use; url and xpath add file locations and XPath filters. The capability engineers learn to value is confirmed-commit. A commit sent with the confirmed parameter is applied but reverted automatically unless a confirming commit follows within the timeout, 600 seconds by default and adjustable with confirm-timeout; the change is also reverted if the session that sent it ends first, unless a persist token was supplied, and if the device reboots. RFC 6241 added persist, persist-id and cancel-commit. In practice this is the safety net for remote changes: an edit that cuts the management path undoes itself ten minutes later. RFC 8526 (March 2019) brought NETCONF into the Network Management Datastore Architecture (NMDA) with get-data and edit-data, which can address any datastore including the operational state datastore.

Transport and framing. Every implementation must support SSH (Secure Shell), as defined in RFC 6242 of June 2011, which obsoleted RFC 4742. The client invokes NETCONF as an SSH subsystem named netconf, and servers must by default offer that subsystem only on the port IANA (Internet Assigned Numbers Authority) assigned, TCP (Transmission Control Protocol) 830, so firewalls can tell management automation from interactive logins; the RFC's own example of opening a session is ssh -s server.example.org -p 830 netconf. Framing changed between versions. NETCONF 1.0 ended every message with the character sequence ]]>]]> on the assumption that it could not occur in well-formed XML, an assumption RFC 6242 admits was wrong, since it can legally appear in attributes, comments and processing instructions. When both peers advertise base:1.1, the session switches after the hello to chunked framing: each chunk is preceded by a line feed, a hash sign and its length in octets, and the message ends with a line feed, two hash signs and a line feed. A client that speaks only one framing hangs on a server that sends the other, which is one of the first things to check when a session opens and then nothing happens. RFC 7589 (June 2015) defines the alternative transport, TLS (Transport Layer Security) with mutual X.509 certificate authentication on TCP port 6513.

Who may do what. The NETCONF Access Control Model, RFC 8341 of March 2018, which obsoleted RFC 6536, decides which authenticated user may read, write or execute which part of the data tree. Its defaults are worth knowing because they surprise people: access control is enabled, reads and operation execution are permitted when no rule matches, and writes are denied when no rule matches, so a new account can often read the entire configuration but cannot change it until a rule allows it. close-session is always allowed, and an implementation may offer a recovery session that bypasses the rules for emergencies. Vendors add their own gate in front: Cisco IOS XE requires privilege level 15 for any NETCONF work.

On real devices. Cisco IOS XE enables the service with the global command netconf-yang, listens on SSH port 830 by default, and needs no netconf legacy if the older pre-standard implementation is enabled. Its candidate datastore is optional, enabled with netconf-yang feature candidate-datastore, and once enabled the running datastore is no longer writable through NETCONF; a NETCONF global lock also blocks changes from the CLI (command-line interface) and from SNMP (Simple Network Management Protocol), and show netconf-yang sessions lists who holds what. Junos enables it with set netconf ssh at the edit system services level; Juniper recommends the default port 830, because the device can then identify and filter NETCONF traffic, and a custom port configured there accepts only NETCONF over SSH. F5 documents the F5OS programmability interface, RESTCONF and NETCONF, as built on OpenConfig YANG models extended with F5 namespaces. In Python the usual client is ncclient, written by Shikar Bhushan and now maintained by Leonidas Poulopoulos and Einar Nilsen-Nygaard, with device handlers for Juniper, several Cisco platforms (among them Nexus, IOS XR and IOS XE), Huawei, H3C and Alcatel-Lucent; its 0.7.1 release is dated 15 March 2026.

Neighbours and pitfalls. RESTCONF carries the same YANG data over HTTPS (Hypertext Transfer Protocol Secure) and implements a subset of NETCONF without locks or a choice of datastore, so NETCONF remains the tool for coordinated multi-step changes; SNMP still serves monitoring better than configuration; and CLI automation with Expect works everywhere but has to recognize text that was written for people. The recurring mistakes are predictable. Assuming the candidate datastore exists, instead of reading the capabilities in the hello, fails on devices that offer only writable-running, and the reverse fails on Cisco with candidate enabled. Forgetting that merge is the default leaves old entries in place when replace was meant. A script that crashes while holding a lock blocks everyone else until the server notices the dead connection or an operator sends kill-session. And the same interface can exist in a native model, a model of the IETF (Internet Engineering Task Force) and an OpenConfig model on one device, with different paths and different behaviour, so the model list the device itself reports is the only reliable starting point.

scripted-monitor.def: A BIG-IP LTM health monitor that plays a file of send and expect lines against a pool member and passes when every expect matches the start of its reply.
scripted-monitor.context: F5 documents the file's rules in a few lines: LF line endings, exactly one space after the keyword, the text running to the end of the line, characters after a closing quotation mark breaking the match, and a match only on a prefix of the response. It looks like Expect and has none of Expect's machinery: no Tcl, no patterns, no search inside the reply, so a check written the way an Expect user would write it often fails on the first line whose text is not where the reply begins.

crlf.def: The two-character line ending, carriage return then line feed (bytes 0D 0A), that SMTP, POP3, IMAP and FTP put at the end of every line.
crlf.context: Windows text files end their lines the same way and Unix files use the line feed alone, and the difference bites wherever a file meets a protocol: RFC 5321 says a conforming SMTP implementation must not recognize any other line terminator, while a BIG-IP Scripted monitor file must use LF alone and writes the protocol's CR LF as the escapes \r\n inside each send.

pty.def: A pseudo-terminal: a pair of virtual devices whose slave end behaves exactly like a terminal and whose master end a program drives, so that what the master writes reaches the other side as if typed.
pty.context: It is how Expect talks to programs written for a person at a keyboard: spawn starts each one on a pty set up like the user's terminal, so passwords, prompts, echo and line editing behave as they would interactively (pty(7); expect(1), spawn).
pty.depth:
What it is, and what it is not. The Linux manual describes a pseudoterminal, usually shortened to pty, as a pair of virtual character devices forming a bidirectional channel. One end is the master, the other the slave. The slave presents exactly the interface of a classical terminal, so a program that expects a terminal can open it and be driven by whatever holds the master: anything written to the master arrives at the slave as typed input, and anything the slave's program writes can be read at the master. Even the special keys work, because the terminal layer interprets them: writing the interrupt character, usually control-C, to the master raises SIGINT in the foreground process group on the slave. Data flows asynchronously, as it would on a physical line, so there can be a small delay between a write on one side and its effect on the other. A pty is not a shell (the shell is just a program that may run on the slave), not a terminal emulator (the emulator is the program on the master side that draws characters), and not a serial line, although it imitates one.

Why programs behave differently on one. The value of a pty is the terminal discipline it brings, set through the termios interface. In canonical mode, the default, input reaches the program a line at a time, after the user has had the chance to edit it with the erase and kill characters; ECHO controls whether typed characters are echoed, which is how a password prompt hides what is typed; ISIG turns the interrupt, quit and suspend characters into signals; and the output flag ONLCR maps a newline to carriage return plus newline, which is why text captured through a pty ends each line in a carriage return and a line feed. Programs also look at whether their input is a terminal and change behaviour: they prompt, they page, they colour, they buffer differently. The Python documentation says of pty.spawn that it is often used to baffle programs which insist on reading from the controlling terminal, and that is the whole reason Expect exists: spawn starts each program on a pty initialized like the user's terminal, so prompts, echo and line editing behave as in an interactive session.

Two interfaces, and how Linux allocates them. Historically there were two pseudoterminal interfaces, from BSD (Berkeley Software Distribution) Unix and from System V. BSD ptys were precreated pairs named /dev/ptyXY for the master and /dev/ttyXY for the slave, X from a 16-letter set such as p to z and a to e and Y a hexadecimal digit, so /dev/ptyp1 pairs with /dev/ttyp1, and a program found a free one by trying to open masters until one succeeded. The first version of the Single UNIX Specification standardized an interface based on System V, which Linux calls UNIX 98 pseudoterminals; BSD-style ptys have been deprecated since Linux 2.6.4, and the option that provides them, CONFIG_LEGACY_PTYS, has been off by default in the mainline kernel since 2.6.30. The modern sequence is posix_openpt, which opens the master clone device /dev/ptmx (character device major 5, minor 2, normally mode 0666 and owned by root), then grantpt and unlockpt on the master, then ptsname to learn the slave's name and open to open it; each open of /dev/ptmx yields an independent master whose slave appears as a numbered file under /dev/pts. The BSD helpers openpty, login_tty and forkpty wrap the same steps, forkpty starting a child whose controlling terminal is the new slave. The number of ptys is limited: up to Linux 2.6.3 at compile time, with a maximum of 2048 and a default of 256; since 2.6.4 through /proc/sys/kernel/pty/max, with /proc/sys/kernel/pty/nr counting those in use. Since kernel 3.4 every mount of the devpts filesystem keeps its own numbering, which is what lets each container have its own /dev/pts, with a global default of kernel.pty.max = 4096 and kernel.pty.reserve = 1024 kept for the initial mount namespace.

Where engineers meet it. The manual lists the users: remote login services such as ssh, rlogin and telnet, terminal emulators such as xterm, and script, screen, tmux, unbuffer and expect. For sshd the master side is the network: data read from the master is sent to a client that has a real terminal or an emulator. The Secure Shell (SSH) connection protocol, Request for Comments (RFC) 4254 of January 2006, makes the allocation an explicit request: a pty-req message on a session channel carries the TERM value (vt100 in the example), the width and height in characters (80 and 24 in the examples) and in pixels, and the encoded terminal modes, and a later window-change message reports a resized window. The OpenSSH client asks for a pty for interactive sessions only when it has a terminal itself; -t forces one, which screen-based programs need, -T disables it, and without a pty the session is transparent and safe for binary data, while the escape characters work only with one. On the server, sshd_config's PermitTTY, yes by default, decides whether pty allocation is allowed at all. Containers repeat the choice: docker container run -t allocates a pseudo-terminal. And script makes a typescript of a terminal session, with timing data that scriptreplay can play back.

In network automation. Most command-line automation of routers, switches and firewalls is pty work. Paramiko's get_pty requests a pseudo-terminal, by default a vt100 of 80 by 24, usually right before invoke_shell opens an interactive shell; its documentation says it is neither necessary nor desirable for a single command run with exec_command. That split explains a familiar set of symptoms. On an interactive channel with a pty, a device behaves as it does for a person: it echoes each command, ends lines with carriage return and line feed, and pages long output at the terminal height until something answers the more prompt, which is why scripts send a command such as terminal length 0 first. On an exec channel without a pty, many devices run the command as a batch and return plain output, and some refuse. Netmiko and Expect are, at bottom, machinery for driving the first case reliably.

What goes wrong: sharing a terminal. A terminal is a channel of authority, and a pty is how privileged sessions avoid sharing one. The TIOCSTI ioctl inserts a byte into a terminal's input queue as if typed. If a command running as another user shares the terminal of the session that started it, as su and sudo historically did, a malicious program can use it to push characters into the parent shell's input, to be executed with the original user's rights once the program exits. The util-linux su manual says plainly that su sharing a terminal with the original session is potentially vulnerable to privilege escalation through TIOCSTI or TIOCLINUX command injection, and offers two defences: su -c, which starts a new session with no controlling terminal, or --pty, which gives the session its own pseudoterminal. The sudoers manual describes the same attack, a program injecting commands into the user's terminal or keeping a background process with access to it after exiting, and the use_pty flag that prevents it by running the command in a new pseudo-terminal; it has been on by default since sudo 1.9.14. The kernel closed the gap from its side as well: since Linux 6.2, TIOCSTI may require the CAP_SYS_ADMIN capability when the dev.tty.legacy_tiocsti sysctl is set to false. Recording has its own edge: script has been able to log input as well as output since version 2.35, and an input log records keystrokes that echo hid, passwords included.

Numbers worth keeping. /dev/ptmx is character device 5,2; a default of 4096 ptys system-wide, 1024 of them reserved for the initial namespace; a classic terminal request of vt100 at 80 by 24; BSD ptys deprecated since Linux 2.6.4; use_pty on by default from sudo 1.9.14; TIOCSTI restricted from Linux 6.2.

expect-spawn.def: The Expect command that starts a program on a pseudo-terminal, connects its input and output to the script, and makes it the current process, the one expect and send talk to.
expect-spawn.context: It sets the variable spawn_id and returns the process id. A program that cannot be executed is reported at the next expect, as if it had printed the error; a spawn inside a procedure needs global spawn_id to be seen outside it (expect(1)).

openssl.def: The open-source toolkit for general-purpose cryptography and secure communication, made of a library and an openssl command whose subcommands, such as s_client and x509, test TLS (Transport Layer Security) servers and read certificates.
openssl.context: Its project calls it a robust, commercial-grade, full-featured toolkit. Releases from 3.0 are under the Apache License 2.0; earlier ones carried the dual OpenSSL and SSLeay licence. A release comes every April and October, and every two years one of them is a long-term-support (LTS) release, supported for at least five years: 3.5 is supported until 8 April 2030, while 3.0, 1.1.1 and 1.0.2 are out of support. Its manual calls s_client a very useful diagnostic tool for SSL (Secure Sockets Layer) servers, and its output is easy to over-read: unless -verify_return_error is given, a failed certificate check does not stop the connection.
openssl.depth:
OpenSSL is two libraries and a command. libcrypto holds the algorithms, libssl holds the Transport Layer Security (TLS), Datagram TLS (DTLS) and QUIC protocol code (the QUIC server side since 3.5), and the openssl program wraps both in subcommands such as s_client, x509, req and verify. The project, developed under the OpenSSL Mission with support from the OpenSSL Foundation and the OpenSSL Corporation, descends from SSLeay: the oldest entries in its change log, for the unreleased 0.9.1b, are credited to Eric A. Young, and the first OpenSSL release, 0.9.1c, is dated 23 December 1998. That ancestry survives in the licence. Every release before 3.0, including the letter updates of 1.1.1 and 1.0.2, carries the dual OpenSSL and SSLeay licence; 3.0 and later use the Apache License 2.0.

Version numbers changed meaning at 3.0. Up to 1.1.1, letter releases such as 1.0.2a carried only bug and security fixes; from 3.0.0 the scheme is MAJOR.MINOR.PATCH, with API and ABI (application programming and binary interface) compatibility kept within a major version. The release strategy, last revised on 7 May 2026, sets the calendar: a release every April and October, a long-term-support (LTS) release every April of an odd-numbered year, supported for at least five years, so that two LTS releases are always fully supported, non-LTS releases after 3.5 fully supported for 13 months, and from 5.0, in October 2027, a major release every two years, six months after each LTS. As of November 2026, 4.1 is supported until 23 November 2027, 4.0 until 14 May 2027 and 3.5, the LTS, until 8 April 2030; 3.0, 1.1.1 and 1.0.2 are out of public support, with paid extended support for security fixes, and 1.1.0 and older get nothing at all.

Three releases mark the modern library. 3.0.0, on 7 September 2021, introduced providers: old ciphers and digests such as Rivest Cipher 4 (RC4), the Data Encryption Standard (DES), CAST5, Blowfish, Message Digest 4 (MD4) and RIPEMD-160 moved to a legacy provider that is not loaded by default, the low-level interfaces for RSA (Rivest-Shamir-Adleman), DSA (Digital Signature Algorithm), DH (Diffie-Hellman) and EC_KEY were deprecated along with the ENGINE interface, and certificates signed with SHA-1 (Secure Hash Algorithm 1) stopped being trusted at the default security level. 3.5.0, on 8 April 2025, became the current LTS and the post-quantum release: it added the NIST (National Institute of Standards and Technology) post-quantum algorithms ML-KEM (Module-Lattice-Based Key-Encapsulation Mechanism), ML-DSA (Module-Lattice-Based Digital Signature Algorithm) and SLH-DSA (Stateless Hash-Based Digital Signature Algorithm), made the default TLS key shares X25519MLKEM768 and X25519 with hybrid groups preferred, added server-side QUIC, and changed the default cipher of the req, cms and smime commands from triple DES to AES-256-CBC, the Advanced Encryption Standard with a 256-bit key in cipher block chaining mode. 4.0.0, on 14 April 2026, cleared out history: SSLv3 (Secure Sockets Layer version 3), deprecated since 2015 and off by default since 1.1.0 in 2016, was removed, along with acceptance of the SSLv2 Client Hello and the whole engine mechanism, replaced by providers; the curves deprecated by RFC (Request for Comments) 8422 are compiled out by default; and Encrypted Client Hello (RFC 9849) arrived.

The name most engineers associate with OpenSSL is Heartbleed. CVE-2014-0160 (a Common Vulnerabilities and Exposures entry), published on 7 April 2014 and found by Neel Mehta, was a missing bounds check in the TLS heartbeat extension that let a connected client or server read up to 64 kB of the other side's memory per request, private keys and session data included when they happened to be there. It affected 1.0.1 up to, but not including, 1.0.1g, and nothing older. The aftermath produced two forks still in use. LibreSSL was forked from OpenSSL in 2014 inside OpenBSD to modernize the code and improve security; BoringSSL is Google's fork, built for Google's own needs, which its maintainers say is not intended for general use and offers no API or ABI stability. Patch cadence is not a historical curiosity: 3.5.9, released on 29 September 2026, fixed more than a dozen CVEs, the most severe rated High.

For engineers the command is the daily tool. openssl s_client -connect www.example.com:443 -servername www.example.com opens a TLS connection and prints the handshake; -connect without a port goes to 4433, and -servername sets SNI (Server Name Indication), which since 1.1.1 defaults to the -connect name when that looks like a DNS (Domain Name System) name. -showcerts prints the certificates exactly as the server sent them, which is not a verified chain and is the fastest way to spot a missing intermediate. -starttls smtp, imap, pop3, ftp, ldap, postgres, mysql and others make it speak the protocol's own upgrade command first. openssl x509 -noout -text, -dates, -subject, -issuer and -checkend read and test a certificate file.

The classic misreading is s_client's verification. The manual says it is a test tool designed to continue the handshake after any certificate verification error and so accepts any chain, trusted or not; unless -verify_return_error is given, the connection never fails because of a server certificate verify failure. A completed handshake therefore proves nothing about trust: the line to read is the verify return code, and 0 (ok) is the only good answer. The manual adds that a non-test application behaving this way would be open to a man-in-the-middle attack, which is exactly the bug when scripts copy s_client habits into production code.

Numbers worth remembering: 23 December 1998 for 0.9.1c, 7 September 2021 for 3.0, 8 April 2025 for 3.5 and 8 April 2030 for its end of support, 14 April 2026 for 4.0, port 4433 as s_client's default, and 64 kB per Heartbleed request.

starttls.def: The command that turns a connection begun in clear text into a TLS one: the client asks, the server agrees, and the TLS handshake runs on the same connection.
starttls.context: SMTP has had it as a verb since RFC 3207 (2002, replacing RFC 2487); RFC 2595 (1999) gave IMAP STARTTLS and POP3 the STLS command, and the equivalent in LDAP (Lightweight Directory Access Protocol) is the StartTLS extended operation of RFC 4511. Because the upgrade follows a clear-text greeting, a TLS client has to speak the protocol first: openssl s_client sends the protocol's own messages when given -starttls and a keyword such as smtp, imap, pop3, ftp or ldap. Between a mail client and its provider, RFC 8314 (2018) recommends Implicit TLS on a port of its own (465, 993 and 995) instead.

trust-anchor.def: The point of trust a certificate check starts from: a public key and a name the verifier already trusts, usually held as a self-signed root certificate authority (CA) certificate in a trust store.
trust-anchor.context: Request for Comments (RFC) 5280 makes it an input to path validation rather than a link in the chain: when it is supplied as a self-signed certificate, that certificate is not part of the path, and which anchors to trust is a matter of policy. That is why the same chain can verify on one machine and fail on another whose store holds different anchors. OpenSSL ships no default set of trust anchors; many Linux distributions point it at a system store, and s_client takes -CAfile, -CApath or -CAstore to name them explicitly.
trust-anchor.depth:
A trust anchor is where verification stops asking questions. RFC 4949 (Request for Comments 4949), the Internet Security Glossary of August 2007, calls it an established point of trust from which a certificate user begins the validation of a certification path, and warns that documents disagree on what the point is: a bare public key, a certificate authority (CA), a certificate, or some combination. The later standards settle on a key plus data. RFC 6024 (October 2010, R. Reddy and C. Wallace) defines a trust anchor as a public key and associated data used by a relying party to validate a signature, where the associated data constrains what the anchor may vouch for, and adds the point that explains most real-world surprises: trust anchors have only local significance. Each relying party, a browser, an operating system, a VPN (virtual private network) client, a resolver, is configured with its own set, and nothing in the certificate itself can make a verifier trust it.

In path validation for X.509, the International Telecommunication Union's certificate standard, RFC 5280 (May 2008) makes the anchor an input, not a certificate in the path. Its section 6.1.1 lists trust anchor information among the inputs to the algorithm: the trusted issuer name, the trusted public key algorithm, the public key, and optionally its parameters. That information may be supplied as a self-signed certificate, in which case the subject name and the subjectPublicKeyInfo are read out of it, but the self-signed certificate is not counted as part of the path, and its signature, expiry and extensions matter only as far as an implementation chooses to honour them. The information is trusted, the RFC says, because it was delivered by some trustworthy out-of-band procedure, and the choice of anchor is a matter of policy: the top CA of a hierarchy, the CA that issued the verifier's own certificate, or any other CA. The validation procedure is the same whichever is chosen, so the same chain can verify on one machine and fail on another simply because their anchors differ.

There was no standard format for that information until RFC 5914, Trust Anchor Format (June 2010, R. Housley, S. Ashmore and C. Wallace). It defines TrustAnchorInfo, an ASN.1 (Abstract Syntax Notation One) structure carrying the public key, a key identifier, an optional title, certification path controls and extensions, and TrustAnchorChoice, which lets an anchor be a full certificate, an unsigned TBSCertificate or a TrustAnchorInfo; a list of anchors can be signed with CMS (Cryptographic Message Syntax). The point of the format is constraint without re-signing: an operator can attach name or policy limits to someone else's root without breaking the root's signature. RFC 6024 explains why that matters. Machines hold several trust anchor stores, often unsynchronized; being in a store usually conveys implicit authorization for every use of that store; and a key installed to verify timestamps can end up validating certificates or OCSP (Online Certificate Status Protocol) responses. Before RFC 5914 the only scoping tool was to put different anchors in different stores.

In practice the anchors for TLS (Transport Layer Security) are root certificates chosen by root programmes. Mozilla's Root Store Policy, version 3.1 effective 1 July 2026, governs the X.509v3 roots shipped in Firefox and Thunderbird and the trust bits that let them anchor TLS server and S/MIME (Secure/Multipurpose Internet Mail Extensions) certificates without asking the user; it removes the websites trust bit once a root's key material is 15 years old, sets an S/MIME distrust date at 18 years, and from 1 July 2026 accepts new roots only if their keys are under five years old. Google launched the Chrome Root Program in 2022; its policy, version 1.8 of 5 February 2026, also removes roots whose key material is more than 15 years old, and Google now runs a separate quantum-resistant root programme built on Merkle Tree Certificates. Microsoft's Trusted Root Program distributes the roots Windows trusts and requires participants to disclose their whole PKI (public key infrastructure) hierarchy every year in the CCADB (Common CA Database). OpenSSL, by contrast, ships no default set at all: its manual notes that many Linux distributions configure a system default, that Mozilla maintains an influential store, and that -CAfile, -CApath and -CAstore name the anchors explicitly. By default OpenSSL treats a certificate as an anchor only if it is in the store and is self-signed, unless -partial_chain lets an intermediate in the store serve as one.

What an anchor can do when it is misused is the DigiNotar story. In 2011 the Dutch CA's systems were compromised and rogue certificates for google.com were issued under roots that every browser trusted; standard path validation succeeded wherever those roots were anchors, because the anchor itself vouched for the certificates, and what first exposed the attack was Chrome's additional pinning check on Google's own certificates. The only remedy was to take the anchor away, which browsers and the Dutch government did within days of the public disclosure. That is the logic behind term limits, Certificate Transparency and the slow removal of old roots: the trust anchor is the single point whose compromise no client-side check can catch.

DNSSEC (DNS Security Extensions) has one anchor for the whole Domain Name System (DNS): the root zone's key signing key (KSK). IANA (the Internet Assigned Numbers Authority) publishes it in root-anchors.xml and describes it plainly as the trust anchor that DNSSEC-aware resolvers are configured with. The first root KSK, KSK-2010, was generated in a key ceremony in Culpeper, Virginia, on 16 June 2010, entered production in El Segundo, California, on 12 July and was first published on 15 July 2010; its entry, key tag 19036, is valid until 11 January 2019. KSK-2017, key tag 20326, was generated on 27 October 2016 and entered production on 2 February 2017, the validFrom date in the file; it signed the root zone from 11 October 2018 until 11 October 2026, and RFC 9718 gives 11 November 2018 as the date its anchor was first published, a date the sources do not reconcile with the others. KSK-2024, key tag 38696, generated on 26 April 2024 and valid from 18 July 2024 in the file, was introduced into the root zone on 11 January 2025 and has signed it since 11 October 2026. KSK-2017 remains a valid trust anchor until its scheduled revocation on 11 January 2027 and removal on 22 March 2027; a KSK-2023 was generated and abandoned. IANA now plans a rollover about every three years, with the next key published for about two years in standby.

Resolvers learn about a new root key in one of two ways: their vendor ships it, or they follow RFC 5011 (September 2007, M. StJohns), Automated Updates of DNSSEC Trust Anchors. Under RFC 5011 a resolver accepts a new key only after seeing it, signed by the current key, for an add hold-down time of 30 days or the original TTL (time to live), whichever is longer, which is why KSK-2024 was expected to be trusted from 10 February 2025, thirty days after its publication; a key is retired by publishing it with bit 8 of the DNSKEY flags, the REVOKE flag, set. RFC 9718 (January 2025, J. Abley, J. Schlyter, G. Bailey and P. Hoffman, obsoleting RFC 7958) defines how IANA publishes the anchors, with a detached signature that can be checked against the ICANN (Internet Corporation for Assigned Names and Numbers) CA bundle. The lesson is the same as in the web PKI: a validator that cannot update its anchors will fail closed the day the old one stops signing, whatever the quality of everything below it.

xml.def: The World Wide Web Consortium (W3C) markup language for structured documents, a subset of SGML (Standard Generalized Markup Language) in which elements nest properly inside a single root element.
xml.context: The current edition of XML (Extensible Markup Language) 1.0 is the fifth, a World Wide Web Consortium (W3C) Recommendation of 26 November 2008. It separates two levels: a data object is an XML document only if it is well-formed, and it is valid only if it also has a document type declaration and meets the constraints expressed in it. Breaking a well-formedness rule is a fatal error, after which a conforming processor must stop processing the document normally, which is why one unescaped & or < outside markup can stop a whole import. The DOCTYPE, where entities are declared, is also where XXE (XML external entity) attacks begin.
xml.depth:
Where it came from. XML (Extensible Markup Language) was written by a working group formed under the World Wide Web Consortium (W3C) in 1996, first called the SGML Editorial Review Board, chaired by Jon Bosak of Sun Microsystems with Dan Connolly as the W3C's contact. Its goal was to let generic SGML (Standard Generalized Markup Language, ISO 8879:1986) be served, received and processed on the web the way HTML (HyperText Markup Language) already was, so XML is defined as a subset of SGML that the specification describes completely. The first Recommendation is dated 10 February 1998; the fifth edition of 26 November 2008, edited by Tim Bray, Jean Paoli, C. M. Sperberg-McQueen, Eve Maler and François Yergeau, is the current one. Two of its ten design goals explain a lot of later practice: the number of optional features should be kept to the absolute minimum, ideally zero, and terseness in markup is of minimal importance.

Well-formed versus valid. Well-formedness is the grammar every XML processor must enforce. There is exactly one root element, also called the document element, and every other element nests properly inside it; the name in an end-tag must match the name in its start-tag; an attribute name may appear only once in the same tag; and the ampersand and the left angle bracket must not appear literally except as markup delimiters or inside a comment, a processing instruction or a CDATA section. Elsewhere they are written as entity or character references, and XML predefines five entities for that purpose: amp, lt, gt, apos and quot. Validity is the further level: a document type declaration (DOCTYPE) and a document that satisfies the constraints declared in it. Every processor must accept the UTF-8 and UTF-16 encodings of Unicode.

Fatal means fatal. The specification calls a violation of well-formedness a fatal error: the processor must detect and report it, may keep scanning to report further errors, but must not continue normal processing, which means it must not keep passing character data and structure to the application as usual. That rule is deliberate, so a single stray ampersand in a value exported from a database, or a truncated file, makes the whole document unusable rather than slightly wrong.

The versions around it. XML 1.1, whose second edition dates from 16 August 2006, exists mainly for line ends and control characters: it adds NEL (#x85), the line end of IBM mainframe conventions, and the Unicode line separator #x2028; allows character references to the control characters #x1 to #x1F; requires #x7F to #x9F to appear only as references; and still forbids #x0. Namespaces in XML 1.0, in its third edition of 8 December 2009, is the separate recommendation that lets one document mix vocabularies. Request for Comments (RFC) 7303 (July 2014) registers application/xml, keeps text/xml as an alias and standardizes the +xml suffix for other XML-based media types.

Where engineers meet it. The Network Configuration Protocol (NETCONF), RFC 6241 of June 2011, encodes both configuration data and protocol messages in XML and carries its operations as remote procedure calls, so XML is what a router or switch exchanges with an automation system that speaks NETCONF. SAML (Security Assertion Markup Language) 2.0 messages are XML documents, deflated and Base64-encoded into a Uniform Resource Locator (URL) in the Redirect binding or Base64-encoded into a form in the POST binding, which is why single sign-on troubleshooting starts with a decoder.

The DOCTYPE is the attack surface. Entities declared in a DOCTYPE can point outside the document, and the OWASP (Open Worldwide Application Security Project) cheat sheet defines XML external entity (XXE) injection as a processor resolving such an entity from untrusted input, which can expose local files, cause server-side request forgery (SSRF) or exhaust resources. MITRE's Common Weakness Enumeration entry CWE-611 gives the classic payloads: a file:// Uniform Resource Identifier (URI) that reads /etc/passwd back into the response, and an http:// URI that makes the server fetch from hosts the attacker cannot reach, bypassing firewalls or hiding a port scan. Entity expansion is the other half: the billion laughs attack nests entities that each reference the previous one several times until a few hundred bytes expand into gigabytes, and the quadratic blowup repeats one large entity to slip under limits on nesting. Defaults have improved, unevenly: OWASP notes that libxml2 disabled XXE by default from version 2.9, and the Python documentation says Expat neither reads local files nor opens connections by default but that versions before 2.7.2 may still be vulnerable to billion laughs and quadratic blowup. The safe rule in every language is the same: disable document type definitions (DTDs) entirely or reject any DOCTYPE, keep XInclude off, and remember that blocking XXE does not by itself stop every XML denial of service.

Numbers worth remembering: 1998 for the first Recommendation and 26 November 2008 for the fifth edition; one root element; five predefined entities; UTF-8 and UTF-16 mandatory for every processor; and XML 1.1's #x85 and #x2028 as the only new line ends.

pcre.def: A C library of regular-expression functions with Perl's syntax and semantics, now in its second API, PCRE2, and the engine behind the regular expressions of NGINX, PHP and many other programs.
pcre.context: Philip Hazel wrote it at the University of Cambridge's computing service. PCRE2 is the revised API, forked from PCRE1, and the old library is obsolete and no longer maintained. NGINX needs it for regular expressions in location blocks and the rewrite module, and since 1.21.5 uses PCRE2 unless built with --without-pcre2. Its default dialect follows Perl 5, with options that come closer to JavaScript or Python, so a pattern tested in a browser can behave differently once it is in an NGINX location.

wcag.def: The W3C's guidelines for making web content accessible to people with disabilities, written as testable success criteria at three levels, A, AA and AAA.
wcag.context: The current version, WCAG 2.2, was first published as a W3C Recommendation on 5 October 2023, and the text in force is dated 12 December 2024; content that conforms to it also conforms to 2.0 and 2.1. Three criteria decide how code and terminal output should be shown: 1.1.1 asks for a text alternative that serves the equivalent purpose for any non-text content, 1.4.3 for a contrast of at least 4.5:1 for text and images of text (3:1 for large-scale text), and 1.4.5 for text rather than images of text wherever the technology can present it.

python.def: A general-purpose programming language that its own FAQ (frequently asked questions) describes as interpreted, interactive and object-oriented, whose standard library and packages cover most network and security scripting.
python.context: Guido van Rossum started it at CWI (Centrum Wiskunde & Informatica) in the Netherlands during the 1989 Christmas holidays and posted it to USENET in February 1991. A feature release ships every October; from 3.13 on, each gets two years of bug fixes and three more of security fixes, and there is no long-term-support release beyond that. On 11 November 2026 the supported branches were 3.11 to 3.15, with 3.15.2 the newest release. The language is defined by its reference manual; the interpreter nearly everyone runs is CPython.
python.depth:
What it is. The Python FAQ (frequently asked questions) calls it an interpreted, interactive, object-oriented programming language with modules, exceptions, dynamic typing, very high-level dynamic data types and classes; it also supports procedural and functional styles and can be extended in C or C++. The language is defined by its reference manual. The implementation almost everyone runs is CPython, which the documentation calls the canonical implementation, distributed on python.org, as distinct from others such as Jython or IronPython. Interpreted is shorthand: CPython compiles source to bytecode, caches it in .pyc files and executes it on a virtual machine. Its global interpreter lock (GIL) lets only one thread execute Python bytecode at a time, which keeps the object model simple at the expense of multi-core parallelism, a trade the project is now unwinding.

Where it came from. Van Rossum had worked at CWI (Centrum Wiskunde & Informatica), the Dutch national research institute for mathematics and computer science, in the group that built the ABC language, which gave Python its indentation for statement grouping and its very high-level data types; exceptions came from Modula-3. He then joined the group building the Amoeba distributed operating system, which needed a better way to do system administration than C programs or Bourne shell scripts, and decided that an Amoeba-only language would be foolish: it had to be generally extensible. He began during the 1989 Christmas holidays and, after just over a year of work, posted it to USENET in February 1991. The first article about it, by van Rossum and Jelke de Boer in the CWI Quarterly of December 1991, was titled Interactively Testing Remote Servers Using the Python Programming Language, so testing things across a network is one of its oldest jobs. The name comes from Monty Python's Flying Circus, the BBC (British Broadcasting Corporation) comedy whose scripts he was reading; he wanted something short, unique and slightly mysterious.

From 2 to 3, and who decides. Python 3.0 was released on 3 December 2008 as a version incompatible with the 2.x line: the language was mostly the same, but built-in objects such as strings and dictionaries changed considerably, and text versus bytes is the change engineers still trip over. The developers announced in 2008 that Python 2 would end in 2015, extended that in 2014 to 2020, and sunset it on 1 January 2020, with no further fixes even for security problems; 2.7.18, released in April 2020, only bundled what had been fixed before that date. The Python Software Foundation (PSF), an independent non-profit, holds the copyright on versions 2.1 and newer. Van Rossum was Benevolent Dictator for Life (BDFL) until he stepped down in July 2018; the core developers then chose the steering council model of Python Enhancement Proposal (PEP) 8016, now codified in PEP 13, and the 2026 council is Barry Warsaw, Donghee Na, Pablo Galindo Salgado, Savannah Ostrowski and Thomas Wouters. Changes are proposed and recorded as PEPs, design documents that carry a specification and a rationale.

The release calendar. PEP 602, in force since Python 3.9, puts a feature release every twelve months, in October, after about 17 months of development. Each feature version then gets bugfix releases with installers roughly every other month, for two years from 3.13 on (18 months before), followed by source-only security releases until five years after its first release; long-term support releases were considered and rejected. Versions are numbered major.minor.micro, and the micro number counts bugfix releases. On 11 November 2026 the Developer's Guide listed 3.15 and 3.14 in bugfix, 3.13, 3.12 and 3.11 in security-only, and main as the future 3.16, due on 6 October 2027. Python 3.15.0 came out on 9 October 2026 with Hugo van Kemenade as release manager and is supported until about October 2031; 3.15.2 and 3.14.10 followed on 25 October 2026; and 3.10 reached end of life on 1 October 2026, which matters for any appliance or jump host still shipping it.

What changed lately. PEP 703 made the GIL optional in three phases: a free-threaded build arrived as experimental in 3.13 and became officially supported, though not the default, in 3.14 under PEP 779. Python 3.14 also brought template string literals, deferred evaluation of annotations, subinterpreters in the standard library and Zstandard compression. Python 3.15 added explicit lazy imports for faster start-up, frozendict and sentinel built-ins, unpacking in comprehensions, a stable ABI (application binary interface) for free-threaded builds and the Tachyon sampling profiler, and, under PEP 686, made UTF-8 (the 8-bit Unicode Transformation Format) the default encoding for files, standard streams and pipes. Most Unix systems already used UTF-8, so the change mostly affects Windows, where code that silently relied on the locale's encoding can now raise UnicodeError or produce mojibake.

Why engineers meet it. The standard library covers internet protocols such as HTTP (Hypertext Transfer Protocol), SMTP (Simple Mail Transfer Protocol) and IMAP (Internet Message Access Protocol), TCP/IP (Transmission Control Protocol and Internet Protocol) sockets and system calls, and the ipaddress module, added in 3.3, parses and computes IPv4 and IPv6 addresses and networks. Beyond it, the Python Package Index (PyPI) listed 939,716 projects and 10,170,044 releases on 11 November 2026, among them Netmiko, which describes itself as a multi-vendor library to simplify CLI (command-line interface) connections to network devices, and Paramiko, a pure-Python implementation of the SSHv2 (Secure Shell version 2) protocol. Packages are installed with pip, ideally into a virtual environment, a cooperatively isolated runtime that keeps one project's packages from disturbing another's. PEP 668 lets an operating system mark its own interpreter with an EXTERNALLY-MANAGED file, which is why pip on a recent Linux distribution refuses to install system-wide and points to a virtual environment instead.

Where it bites. The pickle module is not secure: malicious pickle data can execute arbitrary code while it is being loaded, so it must never read data from an untrusted source. The subprocess module does not call a shell unless asked; with shell=True, quoting whitespace and metacharacters against shell injection becomes the program's responsibility, which is how a hostname or interface description read from a device turns into a command. Dynamic typing defers many errors to run time, so a script that worked against one firmware's output can fail on the next, and dependency pins, a supported interpreter and output parsed into structures rather than matched as screen text are what keep automation alive across upgrades.

cpython.def: The canonical implementation of Python, written in C and distributed on python.org, where new language features generally appear first.
cpython.context: It compiles source code to bytecode, cached in .pyc files and not stable between releases, and runs that bytecode on its virtual machine. Its global interpreter lock lets only one thread run Python bytecode at a time but is always released during input and output (I/O), so threads still help a script that waits on sockets. Python 3.13 added an experimental build without the lock, and 3.14 made that free-threaded build officially supported but optional. The language reference also names PyPy, Jython and IronPython as other implementations.
cpython.depth:
Python is a language described by a reference manual, and CPython is the program that most people mean when they say they ran it. The documentation's glossary calls CPython the canonical implementation of the Python programming language, as distributed on python.org, and says the name is used when it is necessary to distinguish it from others such as Jython or IronPython. The language reference describes it as the original and most-maintained implementation, written in C, where new language features generally appear first, and admits that CPython is the one implementation in widespread use, so its quirks are worth mentioning where it imposes limits. The alternatives the reference lists show the range: Jython is implemented in Java; Python for .NET actually embeds CPython; IronPython, created by Jim Hugunin, who also created Jython, compiles Python to .NET assemblies; and PyPy is written in Python itself and has a just-in-time compiler.

Its history is the history of the language. The documentation's licence page records that Guido van Rossum created Python in the early 1990s at Stichting Mathematisch Centrum (CWI) in the Netherlands as a successor to a language called ABC; in 1995 he continued at the Corporation for National Research Initiatives (CNRI) in Reston, Virginia; in May 2000 the core team moved to BeOpen.com as BeOpen PythonLabs and in October to Digital Creations, later Zope Corporation; and in 2001 the Python Software Foundation (PSF) was formed, a non-profit created to own Python-related intellectual property. Releases 0.9.0 to 1.2, from 1991 to 1995, belonged to CWI. The PSF's copyright notice is part of the licence every release carries; changes to the language and the interpreter are proposed as PEPs (Python Enhancement Proposals), which the Steering Council accepts or rejects; and the Developer's Guide names a release manager for each feature release.

CPython does not interpret source text line by line. It compiles a module to bytecode, which the glossary calls the internal representation of a Python program in the CPython interpreter, caches it in .pyc files so that a second run can skip compilation, and executes it on a virtual machine; the dis module lists the instructions. The glossary is explicit that bytecode is not expected to work between different Python virtual machines, nor to be stable between Python releases, which is why a cache or a virtual environment belongs to one interpreter version. Memory is managed by reference counting: when an object's count drops to zero it is deallocated, sys.getrefcount() shows the number, and since PEP 683 some objects are immortal, their counts never modified, so they live until the interpreter exits. A cyclic garbage collector detects and breaks reference loops, and 3.14 made its collection incremental.

For most of its life CPython was a straightforward interpreter, and the last five years have changed that. PEP 659, written by Mark Shannon in April 2021, introduced a specializing adaptive interpreter, one that speculatively specializes instructions on the types and values it is operating on and adapts when they change, without generating machine code. Python 3.11, the first release with it, was between 10 and 60 per cent faster than 3.10, 1.25 times on average on the standard benchmark suite. PEP 744, by Brandt Bucher and Savannah Ostrowski, added an experimental just-in-time (JIT) compiler in 3.13 built on a technique called copy-and-patch. Python 3.14 added an optional interpreter that uses tail calls between small C functions instead of one large switch statement, 3 to 5 per cent faster with Clang 19 or newer on x86-64 and AArch64, and shipped the experimental JIT in the Windows and macOS binaries. In 3.15 the official Windows 64-bit binaries use the tail-calling interpreter, and the reworked JIT is 7 to 8 per cent faster than the standard interpreter on x86-64 Linux and 11 to 12 per cent faster than the tail-calling one on AArch64 macOS, with individual benchmarks ranging from a 15 per cent slowdown to more than double the speed.

The global interpreter lock (GIL) is the CPython detail with the most practical consequences. In the glossary's words it is the mechanism that assures that only one thread executes Python bytecode at a time; it simplifies the implementation by making the object model, including built-in types such as dict, implicitly safe against concurrent access, at the expense of much of the parallelism of multi-processor machines. Some extension modules release it for computationally intensive work such as compression or hashing, and it is always released during input and output. For network automation this is the decisive fact: a script that spends its time waiting on SSH (Secure Shell) sessions, HTTP (Hypertext Transfer Protocol) requests or SNMP (Simple Network Management Protocol) replies gets real concurrency from threads or asyncio, while a script that parses gigabytes of logs in pure Python does not, and has traditionally reached for multiple processes instead.

PEP 703, by Sam Gross, created in January 2023 and accepted on 24 October 2023, proposed a build of CPython without the GIL, configured with --disable-gil. Removing the lock safely required replacing a great deal of machinery: biased reference counting, immortalization and a limited form of deferred reference counting instead of plain reference counts, a small per-object lock, critical sections in the interpreter, and changes to the mimalloc allocator. The PEP measured an overhead of 5 to 6 per cent for single-threaded programs and 7 to 8 per cent for multi-threaded ones on two processor families, with biased reference counting the largest cost. The Steering Council accepted it with an explicit proviso: a gradual rollout that breaks as little as possible and can be rolled back, entirely if necessary. PEP 779, accepted on 16 June 2025, set the criteria for the second of three phases: phase I, from 3.13, was an explicitly experimental free-threaded build; phase II makes it officially supported but optional, with targets of no more than 15 per cent slower and 20 per cent more memory; phase III, making it the default, is undecided.

Python 3.14, released on 7 October 2025, entered phase II. Its release notes say the PEP 703 implementation was finished, the specializing interpreter was enabled in free-threaded mode, and the single-threaded penalty fell to roughly 5 to 10 per cent depending on platform and compiler; the current free-threading guide gives an average from about 1 per cent on macOS aarch64 to 8 per cent on x86-64 Linux, and warns that memory use is higher. The build announces itself: python -VV and sys.version say free-threading build, and sys._is_gil_enabled() reports whether the lock is actually off, because the GIL can be turned back on with the PYTHON_GIL environment variable or -X gil, and is re-enabled automatically, with a warning, when the process imports a C extension that does not declare support for free threading. Python 3.15, released on 9 October 2026, added a stable application binary interface for free-threaded builds, abi3t, so that extensions built against the stable ABI (application binary interface) can also run on free-threaded builds, and its official macOS binaries now install free-threading support by default.

On 12 November 2026 python.org offered 3.15.2 as the current release, and the Developer's Guide listed 3.15 and 3.14 in their bugfix phase (first released on 9 October 2026 and 7 October 2025), 3.13 and 3.12 in their security phase, with end of life in October 2029 and October 2028, and 3.16 in development for a first release on 6 October 2027. Two habits follow for anyone who runs CPython in production. Check which interpreter and build is really in use, since the installers can put a free-threaded build beside the default one, and an extension that re-enables the GIL removes the benefit with only a warning to show for it. And treat the interpreter like any other dependency with a support window: bytecode caches, virtual environments and compiled wheels are tied to a version, and a branch past its end of life gets no further fixes from CPython's developers.

pep.def: Python Enhancement Proposal: a design document that proposes a new feature or process for Python, or gives the community information, with a concise technical specification and its rationale.
pep.context: Python Enhancement Proposals (PEPs) are the main way large changes are proposed, discussed and recorded. PEP 602 set the annual release cycle, PEP 440 the version scheme, PEP 668 the marker that makes pip refuse to install into a distribution's Python. Once a feature ships, its living specification can move elsewhere, as the packaging PEPs did to the Python Packaging User Guide, and the release notes warn that PEPs usually are not kept up to date after implementation.
pep.depth:
What it is, and what it is not. A Python Enhancement Proposal (PEP) is defined by the first of them, PEP 1, created on 13 June 2000 and still Active, as a design document providing information to the Python community or describing a new feature for Python, its processes or its environment, with a concise technical specification and a rationale. It sets three purposes: the primary mechanism for proposing major new features, for collecting community input on an issue, and for documenting the design decisions that went into Python. The author must build consensus and record dissenting opinions, and because PEPs are kept as text files in a versioned repository, their revision history is the historical record of the proposal. The closest analogy for network engineers is the Request for Comments (RFC) series, with the difference that a PEP is decided by Python's own governance rather than by a standards body. The same three letters mean something else entirely in security architecture: in access control and zero trust, a PEP is a policy enforcement point, the component that actually enforces a policy decision on a request, as the glossary of the National Institute of Standards and Technology (NIST) records from several of its publications. Context decides which one is meant.

Three types. Standards Track PEPs describe a new feature or implementation, or an interoperability standard supported outside the standard library before a later PEP brings it in. Informational PEPs describe a design issue or give guidelines without proposing a feature, and users are free to ignore them; the best known is PEP 20, the Zen of Python (2004), in which Tim Peters wrote down 19 of 20 aphorisms and which import this prints, while PEP 8, the style guide of 2001, reads like guidance but is filed as a Process PEP. Process PEPs change a procedure around Python rather than the language, and, unlike Informational ones, are not optional. On 12 November 2026 the index listed 748 PEPs: 589 Standards Track, 106 Informational and 53 Process.
