Numbers are assigned by the PEP editors and some ranges have meaning: PEP 0 is the index, the 3000 series belonged to the Python 3000 project (PEP 3000 dates from April 2006), the 8000 series to governance, and the 8100 series records each steering council election.

How a PEP moves. An idea is first aired on the Python Discourse, often in a specialized category for typing or packaging, to find out whether it is new and wanted. It then needs a sponsor, for example a member of the core team, the PEP editors or the Typing Council, and is submitted as a pull request to the PEP repository in reStructuredText, using PEP 12 as the template; the editors check structure and formatting, not correctness. Discussion happens on one canonical public thread, and the decision belongs to the Steering Council or a PEP-Delegate it appoints. The states are Draft, Accepted, Provisional (accepted into the reference implementation but still open to change, rejection or withdrawal), Final, Deferred, Rejected, Withdrawn, Superseded, and Active for documents that are never finished, such as PEP 1 itself. The index on 12 November 2026 counted 375 Final, 132 Rejected, 74 Withdrawn, 57 Draft, 38 Active, 35 Deferred, 25 Superseded, 11 Accepted and 1 Provisional, which says as much about the process as any rule: nearly a third of all proposals were rejected, withdrawn or deferred. PEP 1 adds that a proposal must be pythonic to be accepted, and admits that the term is defined as whatever the Steering Council accepts, a circularity it calls intentional.

Who decides, and how that changed. For most of the PEP era design authority came from Guido van Rossum, Python's creator, as Benevolent Dictator for Life (BDFL) until he stepped down in July 2018. The core developers then wrote competing governance models as PEPs 8010 to 8016, surveyed other projects in PEP 8002, and chose by the vote described in PEP 8001: the Steering Council model of PEP 8016 was accepted on 17 December 2018, with the stated aim of being boring and using well-tested processes. PEP 13, created on 16 December 2018, is now the governing document: a five-person council elected by the core team after each feature release, the 2026 council being Barry Warsaw, Donghee Na, Pablo Galindo Salgado, Savannah Ostrowski and Thomas Wouters, elected under PEP 8107. The old title BDFL-Delegate became PEP-Delegate. Specialized bodies followed for areas outside the core language: the Typing Council under PEP 729 (2023) and the Python Packaging Council under PEP 772, created in January 2025 and accepted on 16 April 2026, with broad authority over packaging standards, tools and implementations.

PEPs and the release calendar. PEP 602, created in June 2019 and in force since Python 3.9, puts a feature release every October after about 17 months of development: five unversioned months overlapping the previous release's betas, seven months of alphas, three months of four betas and two months of release candidates, followed by two years of full support and three more of security fixes. Each release is in practice a bundle of accepted PEPs; the What's New page for Python 3.15 opens with PEP 810 (explicit lazy imports), PEP 814 (a frozendict built-in) and PEP 661 (sentinel values). Language milestones are remembered by number: PEP 484 (type hints, 3.5), PEP 572 (assignment expressions, 3.8), PEP 634 (structural pattern matching, 3.10), PEP 703 (making the global interpreter lock optional, 3.13). Rejection is as informative: PEP 2026, which proposed calendar versioning for Python in 2024, was rejected.

Where the specification lives afterwards. PEP 1 is explicit that once a PEP reaches Accepted, Final, Rejected or Superseded it is a historical document, not a living specification; the behaviour is documented elsewhere, in the Language Reference for core features, the Library Reference for the standard library, or, in its words, the PyPA Specifications for packaging, a list the Python Packaging User Guide now publishes as the Python Packaging Specifications, maintained, it says, by the Python Packaging Council. The What's New pages repeat the warning: read the PEP for the design rationale, but PEPs usually are not kept up to date once a feature has been fully implemented. Packaging shows the pattern most clearly. PEP 440 (2013) defined version identifiers and dependency specifiers, PEP 517 (2015) build-system independence, PEP 621 (2020) project metadata in pyproject.toml, and PEP 668 (2021) the EXTERNALLY-MANAGED marker that makes pip refuse to install into a distribution's own Python; the current, maintained versions are the interoperability specifications in the Python Packaging User Guide, now kept by the Packaging Council. The practical rule is to cite the specification for how something behaves today and the PEP for why it was designed that way.

Why engineers outside Python's core meet them. Network and security engineers rarely read PEPs for pleasure, but they cite them to explain behaviour that surprises them: PEP 668 when pip refuses to install on a jump host, PEP 657 when a traceback underlines the failing expression, PEP 3151 (Python 3.3) for the OSError subclasses such as ConnectionRefusedError that network scripts catch, PEP 578 (Python 3.8) for the runtime audit hooks that let a security tool observe what a Python process does, and PEP 740 for digital attestations on the Python Package Index. A Draft PEP is a proposal, not a promise; only Accepted, Provisional and Final ones describe Python as it is or will be.

repl.def: Read-eval-print loop: an interactive prompt that reads an expression or statement, runs it, prints the result and waits for the next; in Python, the interpreter started without a script.
repl.context: Python's prompts are >>> and ... for continuation lines, and the value of an expression typed there is printed, so it works as a calculator with the whole standard library one import away. python -i script.py opens it after a script has run. Python 3.13 replaced it with a new shell based on PyPy's code, with multi-line editing, colour, F1 for help, F2 for history and F3 for a paste mode; setting PYTHON_BASIC_REPL brings back the old one.

virtual-environment.def: A directory with its own set of Python packages, built on top of a base Python installation and isolated by default from the base's packages and from other environments.
virtual-environment.context: python -m venv .venv creates one: a pyvenv.cfg file naming the base interpreter, a bin directory (Scripts on Windows) and its own site-packages, with pip bootstrapped inside. A script can tell it runs in one because sys.prefix differs from sys.base_prefix. The documentation calls an environment disposable and not movable or copyable, since installed commands point at its interpreter by absolute path. Activation is optional: calling the environment's python by full path is enough, which is the form for cron jobs and services.
virtual-environment.depth:
A virtual environment answers a packaging conflict, not a security one. The Python tutorial states the case: if application A needs version 1.0 of a module and application B needs version 2.0, one installation cannot satisfy both, so each application gets a directory tree with its own packages. PEP (Python Enhancement Proposal) 405, which put the mechanism into the language, defines it as a lightweight environment with its own site directories and its own Python binary that shares the standard library with the base installation. That last clause says what it is not. virtualenv's documentation puts it plainly: virtual environments are not self-contained, they are lightweight shells that borrow most of their content from the system Python and hold only what is needed to redirect its behaviour. Only the set of importable packages is separated. Nothing in the mechanism, a configuration file and a search path, confines what the code can do, so an environment is neither a container nor a virtual machine.

The mechanism is a change to how the interpreter finds its prefix at startup. Before looking for the standard library, Python checks for a file named pyvenv.cfg next to its executable or one directory above it, without dereferencing a symbolic link. If the file has a home key, the binary belongs to a virtual environment, and home is the directory of the Python that created it. The interpreter then sets sys.base_prefix to the base installation and sys.prefix to the directory that holds pyvenv.cfg; the standard library and the header files are found relative to the first, the site-packages directories relative to the second. PEP 405 concludes that an environment in its simplest form is nothing more than a copy or symlink of the Python binary, a pyvenv.cfg file and a site-packages directory. Since Python 3.14 the prefixes are set during path initialization and no longer by the site module, so they hold even when the interpreter is started with -S.

Isolation is the default, and one key relaxes it. Created with --system-site-packages, an environment has include-system-site-packages set to true in pyvenv.cfg, and the site module adds the system site directories to sys.path after the environment's own: system packages can be imported, but a package of the same name installed in the environment takes precedence. Without it, the per-user site-packages directory is not searched either, because PEP 405 counts user-level packages as part of the system's. This is the first thing to check when an environment imports something that was never installed into it.

The venv module, in the standard library since Python 3.3, builds the directory when run as python -m venv followed by a path: the configuration file, a bin directory holding a copy or symlink of the interpreter, and lib/pythonX.Y/site-packages (on Windows, Scripts, and site-packages under Lib). Unless --without-pip is given, ensurepip bootstraps pip into it. The other options are few: --symlinks and --copies choose how the interpreter is placed, --clear empties an existing directory first, --upgrade adapts the environment after Python has been upgraded in place, --upgrade-deps updates pip to the latest release on the Python Package Index (PyPI), and --prompt sets the name shown in the shell. Since 3.13 venv also writes a .gitignore file, because an environment is not meant to be checked into source control. On Windows the documentation advises against symlinks, since double-clicking python.exe resolves the link and ignores the environment. The tutorial explains the usual name, .venv: it stays hidden in a shell listing, says what the directory is for, and does not clash with the .env files in which some tools keep environment variables.

Activation changes the shell, not the environment. The activate script for bash and zsh (activate.fish, activate.csh and Activate.ps1 are its siblings, with activate.bat for cmd.exe) prepends the environment's bin directory to PATH and sets the VIRTUAL_ENV variable; deactivate undoes it. On Windows, PowerShell may refuse to run Activate.ps1 until the user's execution policy allows it, and the documentation gives the command: Set-ExecutionPolicy with RemoteSigned and the CurrentUser scope. Because nothing requires activation, VIRTUAL_ENV cannot be relied on to tell whether an environment is in use; comparing the two prefixes is the test. Commands installed into an environment run without activation because their first line, the shebang, names the environment's interpreter, and that line is why the documentation calls environments inherently non-portable: after moving or renaming the directory, or a parent of it, the environment has to be recreated, typically from a requirements file.

The idea is older than the module. PEP 405, written by Carl Meyer and created on 13 June 2011, credits the popularity of third-party tools, primarily Ian Bicking's virtualenv, and explains why they needed help from the interpreter: virtualenv had to copy the Python binary, duplicate much of the site module and link an ever-changing set of standard-library modules into each environment, while the only built-in alternative, the PYTHONHOME variable, meant copying or linking the entire standard library. The PEP is Final and shipped in Python 3.3 together with a pyvenv script, the recommended tool for 3.3 and 3.4, deprecated in 3.6 and removed in 3.8 in favour of running the module directly. Python 3.4 began installing pip by default, 3.9 added --upgrade-deps, and since 3.12 setuptools is no longer installed alongside pip.

virtualenv did not go away. Its documentation, with a copyright line that starts in 2007, says a subset of it was integrated into the standard library as venv, and compares the two with uv, a newer tool written in Rust. By its account venv is the slowest of the three because it spawns pip as a subprocess to seed the environment, has no plugin system and creates environments only for the Python version it runs under; virtualenv caches its seed packages, can target any installed interpreter and offers the programmatic interface that tox, poetry and pipx build on; uv venv is the fastest and does not install pip into the environment by default. uv's own documentation adds that it creates .venv when no path is given, can download a requested Python version and, unlike pip, requires a virtual environment by default. pipx applies the same idea to command-line applications: a separate environment for each application, with its commands exposed on PATH.

Linux distributions turned the convention into a rule. PEP 668, created on 18 May 2021 and approved in June 2022 as the Externally Managed Environments specification, lets a distributor place a marker file named EXTERNALLY-MANAGED in the standard-library directory. Before installing, a tool such as pip checks two things: whether it is running outside a virtual environment (sys.prefix equal to sys.base_prefix) and whether the marker exists. If both are true it exits with an error, using the message the file supplies, unless the user passes an override that the PEP wants to sound risky, --break-system-packages. pip has read the marker since release 23.0 of 30 January 2023 and gained the override in 23.0.1 on 17 February 2023. Debian 12 (bookworm) marks its python3.11 and pypy3 interpreters this way, and its release notes name the alternatives: pipx for an application, and for a library a virtual environment made with the venv module, which Debian ships in the python3-venv package, or with virtualenv.

Most trouble follows from three properties. An environment is tied to its base: pyvenv.cfg points at one Python installation, which is why venv has an --upgrade option for the case where that Python is upgraded in place. It carries its own copy of pip, bootstrapped when the environment was created, so pip is updated per environment, with --upgrade-deps or with python -m pip install --upgrade pip run by the environment's interpreter. And it is addressed by path: pip's user guide recommends python -m pip because that form runs pip with exactly the interpreter named, and a scheduled job or a service should name the environment's interpreter in full. pip can enforce the habit itself: with --require-virtualenv, or the PIP_REQUIRE_VIRTUALENV environment variable, it exits with an error when run outside a virtual environment. The documentation's closing advice is the rule for any automation host: always keep a simple means of recreating an environment, such as a requirements file.

pip.def: The package installer for Python, which installs packages from the Python Package Index and other indexes into the environment of the interpreter that runs it.
pip.context: Run it as python -m pip, so that the interpreter, and with it the environment, is explicit. Each virtual environment gets its own copy, bootstrapped by ensurepip, so updating Python does not update the pip inside environments that already exist; the Python 3.13.17 release notes of October 2026 asked users to upgrade pip in every existing environment for that reason. pip's documentation warns that by default it does not protect against remote tampering and runs code from distributions; --require-hashes and --only-binary :all: change that.
pip.depth:
The name is its own description. On 28 October 2008 Ian Bicking announced that he had finished renaming his installer pyinstall to pip, and explained the new name as an acronym and a declaration: pip installs packages. The project's documentation still opens with the same sentence in other words, the package installer for Python, used to install from the Python Package Index (PyPI) and other indexes. That scope is the first thing to get right. pip installs, removes and lists distributions in one Python environment; it does not create environments (venv does), does not install or select Python versions, and by its own account does not verify what it installs unless told to.

pip is not part of the standard library, yet almost every Python has it. PEP (Python Enhancement Proposal) 453, written by Donald Stufft and Alyssa Coghlan and created on 10 August 2013, made pip the officially recommended installer and had Python 3.4 provide it by default, preferring it to its predecessor easy_install, whose design problems could not be fixed without breaking compatibility. The mechanism is the ensurepip module: each maintenance and feature release of CPython bundles the latest stable pip as a private copy, and ensurepip installs that copy into an installation or a new virtual environment without accessing the internet. The PEP is explicit that pip stays external to CPython, maintained by the Python Packaging Authority (PyPA). Two things follow. The pip in an environment is as old as the Python that created the environment, and python -m pip install --upgrade pip is the normal way to refresh it. And a pip problem can force a Python release: 3.13.17, of 21 October 2026, was a special security release whose purpose was to raise the embedded pip to 26.2.2, because that pip carries a newer copy of the certifi root-certificate bundle, after a certificate authority incident.

Versions follow the calendar. A version number has the form YY.N, where the first number is the year and the second identifies the quarter, with releases planned for January, April, July and October and a deprecation period of at least six months for documented behaviour. Version 1.0 dates from 4 April 2011; support for Python 2 ended with pip 21.0; pip 26.1 dropped Python 3.9; and the changelog read on 12 November 2026 ends at 26.3, released on 2 November 2026.

An install is a search, a resolution and an unpacking. pip looks for candidates on PyPI, or on the index given with --index-url (the default is https://pypi.org/simple), in local directories, and in any location added with --find-links or --extra-index-url; there is no priority among these places, and the best match by version wins. It then resolves dependencies, which it can only learn by downloading distribution files; since version 20.3 the resolver backtracks when an earlier choice turns out to be incompatible, which is why a long install sometimes shows several versions of the same package being fetched. A wheel is unpacked into site-packages; a source distribution is first built into a wheel by the project's build system, on the installing machine. Two caches, on by default since 6.0, shorten the next run: one for HTTP (Hypertext Transfer Protocol) responses, which behaves like a browser cache, and one for wheels built locally. Everything lands in the environment of the interpreter that runs pip, which is why the user guide spells the command as python -m pip (py -m pip on Windows): the interpreter named is the one that receives the packages.

The command set is small. install, uninstall, list, show, freeze, check and inspect manage and describe an environment; download, wheel and hash handle distribution files; index and search query an index; cache, config and debug concern pip itself; lock, still experimental, writes the standard pylock.toml lock file. A requirements file passed with -r lists what to install, and a constraints file passed with -c only limits versions: naming a package there does not install it, which makes one constraints file usable across an organization. pip freeze prints the environment in requirements format, but PyPI's own incident guidance points out that this is not a lock file, because a lock must carry the hashes of the archives.

Behaviour can be set in three places: on the command line, in environment variables (each option has one, formed with the PIP_ prefix) and in configuration files in INI format at three levels, global (/etc/pip.conf), per user (pip.conf under .config/pip in the home directory) and per environment (pip.conf at the root of the virtual environment), named pip.ini on Windows. The network options are the ones an operations team ends up reading. --proxy takes a proxy URL (Uniform Resource Locator) with optional credentials; --timeout defaults to 15 seconds and --retries to 5. pip has verified HTTPS certificates by default since version 1.3. --cert, or PIP_CERT, points it at a bundle of certificate authority certificates, and since 24.2 pip also trusts the operating system's certificate store, in addition to its bundled certifi list, through the truststore library. That change is what lets pip work behind a proxy that inspects TLS (Transport Layer Security) and re-signs traffic with a private authority the machine already trusts; before it, the authority had to be passed to pip explicitly. --trusted-host does the opposite of all this, accepting a host without valid HTTPS, and belongs in no permanent configuration.

The security defaults are stated without comfort in pip's documentation: by default pip does not perform any checks to protect against remote tampering, and installing involves running arbitrary code from distributions. Hash-checking mode, available since 8.0, answers the first half. A requirement line carries one or more --hash values, and once any line has one the mode is on for all: every requirement and every dependency must be pinned with == and hashed, sha256 being the recommended algorithm, while md5, sha1 and sha224 are refused. The hash an index puts in a download URL does not count, since it comes from the same remote source and only detects a corrupted download. --only-binary :all: answers the second half by refusing source distributions, so that no build code runs, although the 26.3 changelog adds that pip has never considered installing untrusted wheels safe, because Python's import system is dynamic (release 25.0 had fixed a bug that let a crafted wheel execute code during installation). Two more options address the index. pip's documentation calls --extra-index-url unsafe for private packages, the dependency confusion case, and --uploaded-prior-to, added in 26.0 and accepting durations such as P3D since 26.1, ignores releases newer than a given age on indexes that publish upload times.

pip also refuses on purpose. Since 23.0 it reads the EXTERNALLY-MANAGED marker that PEP 668 lets a Linux distribution place in its Python, and outside a virtual environment it stops with an error unless --break-system-packages is given (added in 23.0.1); --require-virtualenv makes the same refusal a local policy. Its neighbours cover what it leaves out: pipx installs command-line applications, each in its own virtual environment, where pip installs into whatever environment is active with no isolation; uv, which like PDM and Poetry also uses PyPI by default, requires a virtual environment unless told otherwise. And pip reports little about its user: it collects no telemetry, but each request tells the index the Python version and operating system in use.

pypi.def: Python Package Index: the default package index for the Python community, at pypi.org, where any Python developer can publish distributions and from which pip installs.
pypi.context: The Packaging User Guide records that the pypi.org domain replaced the legacy pypi.python.org in 2017. pip installs from it unless pointed at another index. Because it is open to all developers and, in its own documentation's words, does not pre-screen or review projects before they are published, a project's name alone says nothing about who published a file or what the file does; pinning versions and hashes is how a deployment fixes exactly what it installs.
pypi.depth:
PyPI (Python Package Index), pronounced pie-pea-eye so that it is not confused with the PyPy interpreter, describes itself as a repository of software for the Python programming language and is the default source for pip, PDM, Poetry and uv. Its content has three levels: a project is a named collection of releases, a release is one version of the project, and a release consists of one or more files, each a source archive or a wheel built for some platform. As read on 12 November 2026 the front page counted 939,906 projects, 10,173,118 releases, 22,837,935 files and 1,141,478 users, and the statistics page put the sum of all release files at 51.2 TB (terabytes). What it is not is a curated catalogue. Its documentation says that anyone can upload projects of any quality, that PyPI does not pre-screen or review projects before they are published, and that anything on a project page not explicitly labelled as PyPI data or as verified should be assumed to be unverified text supplied by the author.

The index began as PEP (Python Enhancement Proposal) 301, written by Richard Jones, created on 24 October 2002 and implemented for Python 2.3. It proposed a central index server, a register command for Distutils and Trove classifiers in the metadata, and it deliberately left out two things that now define the service: package dependencies, and the storage and download of the packages themselves. Jones wanted the index hosted under python.org to give it an air of legitimacy that earlier catalogue efforts lacked, and for years its address was pypi.python.org. The present service runs on a rewritten codebase called Warehouse. A beta at pypi.org was announced on 26 March 2018, and on 16 April 2018 the new site became the canonical index, with browser traffic and pip install calls redirected from the old address and the legacy codebase due to be shut down on 30 April. The Packaging User Guide's glossary dates the replacement of the domain name itself to 2017.

Warehouse is open source, developed under the Python Packaging Authority (PyPA) and supported by the Packaging Working Group of the Python Software Foundation (PSF), which operates the infrastructure. The scale explains the architecture. In August 2026 the PSF's director of engineering wrote that PyPI takes more than six billion requests a day, about thirteen billion counting file downloads, with package egress of around 10 petabytes a day, and that Fastly's content delivery network (CDN) answers almost all of it at a cache hit ratio just under 99 per cent, so that only about one request in seventy reaches the origin, which runs on Amazon Web Services (AWS) with a PostgreSQL database behind the application. For 2025 PyPI reported 2.56 trillion requests, an average of 81,000 a second, 1.92 exabytes transferred, more than 3.9 million new files and more than 130,000 new projects. The August post also counted the people: one and a half full-time employees for development, security reports and maintenance, and one for support requests. Two consequences matter to whoever writes the firewall or proxy rule: files are downloaded from files.pythonhosted.org, not from pypi.org, and because all traffic is routed through the CDN, the list of PyPI's addresses is Fastly's published list of public ranges.

Installers do not use the website. They use the index API (application programming interface) under https://pypi.org/simple/, standardized as the Simple Repository API. Its first form, PEP 503 by Donald Stufft (September 2015), is a tree of HTML (Hypertext Markup Language) pages: the root has one anchor per project, each project page has one anchor per file, and each link should carry the file's hash as a URL (Uniform Resource Locator) fragment, the name of the hash function such as sha256 followed by the digest. A JSON (JavaScript Object Notation) form followed in May 2022 with PEP 691, selected through the Accept header with the media type application/vnd.pypi.simple.v1+json, and later PEPs added upload times (700), yanking (592), provenance (740) and project status markers (792). In August 2026 PyPI adopted PEP 833, which freezes the HTML representation; new features go into the JSON form only. Project names are compared in normalized form, lower-cased with every run of full stops, hyphens and underscores replaced by a single hyphen, so a project named HolyGrail is served at /simple/holygrail/. pip's default --index-url is https://pypi.org/simple, and its documentation is explicit about what happens when --extra-index-url adds a second index: there is no priority among the locations, all are checked and the best match by version wins.

A release or a project can change state without disappearing. Pre-releases are skipped by installers unless requested. A yanked release is ignored by an installer unless it is the only one matching an exact pin written with == or ===, and PyPI yanks whole releases, not single files; the maintainer's reason is published through the index API. An archived project accepts no new releases but still installs. A quarantined project or release, suspected of malware, spam or a policy violation, cannot be installed or modified and is left out of search and of the index API until an administrator reviews it. The limits are few, and the recent ones are worth knowing: by default 100 MB per file and 10 GB per project, doubled since 26 October 2026 for projects owned by an organization; version strings of at most 128 characters since October 2026; and, since 22 July 2026, no new files in a release more than 14 days old, so that a stolen token cannot add a poisoned file to a long-stable release (PyPI asks users not to rely on that behaviour until PEP 694 defines it).

On the publishing side the index has been replacing secrets that last with ones that expire. Two-factor authentication (2FA) has been mandatory for every account since 1 January 2024, with a time-based one-time password (TOTP) application or a WebAuthn security device, which PyPI prefers because it resists phishing. Uploads need an API token, which can be scoped to one project, or Trusted Publishing, introduced on 20 April 2023: an automated build job presents an OpenID Connect (OIDC) identity token from its platform and, if the project trusts that workflow, receives an upload token valid for 15 minutes. GitHub Actions, GitLab CI/CD (continuous integration and delivery), Google Cloud and ActiveState are supported. Since 14 November 2024 a file can also carry attestations under PEP 740, signed statements in the in-toto format that bind the file's digest to the identity that published it; PyPI accepts two kinds, its own publish attestation and SLSA (Supply-chain Levels for Software Artifacts) provenance. They took the place of PGP (Pretty Good Privacy) signatures, which PyPI stopped accepting on 23 May 2023 after an audit found that only 36 per cent of the keys used in three years could be meaningfully verified. By the end of 2025 more than 50,000 projects used Trusted Publishing and 17 per cent of uploads included an attestation.

The documentation lists what an open index attracts. Typosquatting registers a misspelling of a popular name, such as pyth0n-dateutil for python-dateutil. PyPI rejects a new name that collides with an existing one after removing separators and treating look-alike characters such as l, i and 1 as identical, or that matches a standard-library module, and admits that these checks do not catch everything; in March 2024 a large typosquatting campaign made it halt new user and project registration for a time. Names invented by a large language model (LLM) can be registered in advance by an attacker, which the documentation calls slopsquatting. Dependency confusion publishes on PyPI a package with the name of a company's private one and relies on the installer choosing it. Account takeover, phishing (one campaign used the look-alike domain pypj.org) and the re-registration of expired email domains aim at maintainers instead. The case that changed policy was a supply-chain compromise: PyPI's incident report of 2 April 2026 describes releases of litellm and telnyx, published after an API token was exposed through an exploited Trivy dependency, that carried credential-harvesting malware which ran on install. The poisoned litellm versions were downloaded more than 119,000 times in the 2 hours 32 minutes between upload and quarantine, and PyPI estimated that 40 to 50 per cent of litellm installs were unpinned, fetching the latest version every time.

The defences on the consuming side follow from that. PyPI publishes SHA-256 (Secure Hash Algorithm 256-bit) and BLAKE2b digests for every file and states their limit: a checksum shows that the file is the one on PyPI's servers, not that the code is safe. pip's hash-checking mode, --require-hashes, refuses anything whose digest is not in the requirements file. A lock file with hashes fixes the whole dependency tree, which the output of pip freeze does not. A dependency cooldown, pip's --uploaded-prior-to, skips releases younger than a few days so that reports and quarantine have time to work; PyPI handled 66 per cent of the malware reports of 2025 within 4 hours and 92 per cent within 24. pip's documentation calls --extra-index-url unsafe for private packages, because the public index may win. And for rehearsing a release there is TestPyPI at test.pypi.org, a separate instance with its own accounts and a database that is pruned from time to time.

wheel.def: Python's built distribution format: a ZIP archive with a .whl extension whose file name carries the project, the version and the Python, ABI and platform tags it runs on.
wheel.context: Installing a wheel means unpacking it into site-packages and recording the files, with no build step, unlike a source distribution, whose build runs code. The name is the distribution, the version, an optional build tag, then the three tags, joined by hyphens: py3-none-any is pure Python for any platform, while cp311-abi3-manylinux_2_34_x86_64 is compiled for CPython's stable ABI on 64-bit Linux with glibc 2.34 or newer. pip prefers the most specific wheel its own list of tags accepts.

traceback.def: The report Python prints when an exception is not handled: the calls that led to it, outermost first, then the exception's type and message on the last line.
traceback.context: Read it from the bottom. The last line names the exception; the frames above it run from the first call down to the innermost, each with its file, line, function and source line, and since Python 3.11 markers under each line point at the expression that failed (Python Enhancement Proposal 657, PEP 657). Chained exceptions print one after another, separated by The above exception was the direct cause of the following exception for raise from, or During handling of the above exception, another exception occurred when a handler fails. Exception groups print as nested, numbered boxes.
traceback.depth:
What it is, and what it is not. A traceback is two things in Python: an object, the chain of frames attached to every exception as its __traceback__ attribute, and the report the interpreter prints from it when the exception reaches the top without being handled. The printing is done by sys.excepthook, which the interpreter calls for any uncaught exception other than SystemExit, writing to standard error. The report opens with the line Traceback (most recent call last), lists one entry per frame, each with the file, the line number, the function and the line of source, and ends with the exception's type and message, which the tutorial calls the line that indicates what happened. The phrase most recent call last is the key to reading it: the first frame is the outermost call, usually the module itself, and the last frame is where the exception was raised. Other languages print the opposite way. Java's Throwable.printStackTrace puts the exception first and then the frames with the innermost method at the top and main at the bottom, so engineers moving between the two learn to look at opposite ends. A traceback is not a log, although it is often logged, and it is not a core dump: it describes Python frames, not machine state.

Reading one, line by line. Start at the last line: the type (ValueError, KeyError, ConnectionRefusedError) says what kind of failure, the message says what exactly. Then read upwards to the last frame that belongs to your own code, because frames below it are inside libraries you called and frames above it are the path that got there. Since Python 3.11, Python Enhancement Proposal (PEP) 657 adds carets and tildes under the source line pointing at the exact expression that failed, so that in a line such as a['x']['y']['z'] the marker shows which subscript was None. The PEP, Final since its creation in May 2021, made this possible by storing, for every bytecode instruction, the end line and the start and end column offsets, two one-byte offsets per instruction, readable through a code object's co_positions method. The extra tables can be dropped, with smaller code objects and .pyc files and no markers, by running with -X no_debug_ranges or setting PYTHONNODEBUGRANGES. Python 3.13 added colour in the terminal by default, controlled by PYTHON_COLORS, which takes precedence over NO_COLOR, which in turn takes precedence over FORCE_COLOR, and a hint when the cause is a script named like a standard module, such as a file called random.py importing itself. Python 3.15 keeps refining the last line: an AttributeError can now suggest a nested attribute ('.inner.area') or the Python name of a method from another language, and a lazily imported module that fails to load raises at first use with a traceback that shows both the use and the original import.

Chains, notes and groups. An exception raised while another is being handled carries the first one in its __context__ attribute, and the default display prints both, joined by the banner During handling of the above exception, another exception occurred. Writing raise new from original sets __cause__ instead, printed with the banner The above exception was the direct cause of the following exception; raise new from None sets __suppress_context__, which hides the original from the display while keeping it in __context__ for anyone debugging. An explicit cause is always shown, an implicit context only when there is no cause and it is not suppressed, and in every case the last line of the traceback is the last exception raised. Since Python 3.11 an exception can also carry notes: add_note appends a string, stored in __notes__, that the standard traceback prints after the exception message, which is the right way to say which device or which line of input was being processed without replacing the exception. Exception groups (PEP 654, also 3.11) bundle several exceptions, for example from polling many devices at once, and print as nested, numbered boxes; the traceback module's TracebackException limits the display to 15 exceptions per group and 10 levels of nesting by default.

Working with tracebacks in code. The traceback module is the standard interface to extract, format and print them. traceback.print_exc() prints the exception being handled; traceback.format_exc() returns the same text as a string, for a log or a ticket; a limit argument keeps only the last entries, or the first ones when negative. TracebackException captures an exception for rendering later, without keeping the frames alive, and can optionally capture local variables. In logging, Logger.exception logs at level ERROR and adds the exception information, and belongs only inside an exception handler. sys.tracebacklimit sets the maximum number of levels printed, 1000 by default; at 0 or less only the type and value are printed. After an uncaught exception in an interactive session, sys.last_exc holds it so that pdb.pm() can open a post-mortem debugger without re-running anything. When the process itself crashes, in a C extension or on a stack overflow, there is no Python exception to print; faulthandler, enabled with PYTHONFAULTHANDLER or -X faulthandler, installs handlers for SIGSEGV, SIGFPE, SIGABRT, SIGBUS and SIGILL and dumps the Python traceback of each thread, using an alternative stack so that it works even when the stack has overflowed.

In network automation. Scripts that drive devices over Secure Shell (SSH) fail in a small set of ways, and the traceback names them. A ConnectionRefusedError, a timeout or an authentication error from a library such as Paramiko or Netmiko says the device or the path refused; a KeyError or ValueError deep in a parser says the device answered with something the code did not expect, often a different software version or a paging prompt left in the output. The useful habit is the one the chaining rules allow: catch the low-level error where it happens, raise a clearer one from it, or add a note naming the device, and let the traceback carry both. A traceback pasted into a ticket is only useful whole, from the first line to the last, with the exact message; the last line alone loses the path, and a screenshot loses the text.

What goes wrong: tracebacks as information disclosure. A traceback shows file paths, function names, lines of source and, in some frameworks, local variables, which is exactly what an attacker probing an application wants. MITRE classifies the weakness as CWE-209, Generation of Error Message Containing Sensitive Information, with the canonical example of an exception printed straight to a web user. Web frameworks are explicit about it. Django's documentation says never to deploy a site into production with DEBUG on, because its debug pages display a detailed traceback with metadata about the environment and the current settings, filtering only names that contain words such as KEY or PASS. Flask's built-in Werkzeug development server shows an interactive traceback in the browser on an unhandled error, and both projects warn that this debugger allows the execution of arbitrary Python code and must never run in production, which is why it is guarded by a code printed on the server's command line; an exposed debugger is remote code execution, not just a leak. The safe pattern is to log the full traceback on the server, with Logger.exception or format_exc, and return a generic error with a correlation identifier to the client. Numbers worth keeping: 1000 levels by default, PEP 657 in 3.11, colour by default from 3.13, and groups shown 15 wide and 10 deep.

code-point.def: A value in the Unicode codespace, an integer from 0 to 10FFFF hexadecimal, written U+0041 and so on; not every code point is assigned to a character.
code-point.context: Encodings turn code points into bytes: UTF-8 (a Unicode transformation format) writes one in one to four bytes, UTF-16 in one or two 16-bit units. The range U+D800 to U+DFFF holds the surrogate code points, reserved for the pairs UTF-16 uses and not characters on their own, which is why UTF-8 never encodes them. A Python str is a sequence of code points, so len() of a text counts code points, not the bytes it will take on the wire.
code-point.depth:
The Unicode Standard defines the term in two lines of its conformance chapter: the Unicode codespace is the range of integers from 0 to 10FFFF hexadecimal (definition D9), and a code point, also called a code position, is any value in that codespace (D10). That makes 1,114,112 code points in all. The usual way to name one is its value in hexadecimal with a U+ prefix, often followed by the character's official name to remove any doubt, as in U+0061 LATIN SMALL LETTER A. A code point is a number, not a character and not a byte: whether it holds a character, and how it is stored, are separate questions answered by the character repertoire and by the encoding form. The glossary keeps a second, older sense as well, a value or position for a character in any coded character set, which is why people speak of code points in ASCII (American Standard Code for Information Interchange) or in a Windows code page.

Every code point belongs to one of seven types (D10a): graphic, format, control, private-use, surrogate, noncharacter and reserved. Only the first four represent abstract characters. Sixty-five code points, U+0000 to U+001F and U+007F to U+009F, are control codes kept for compatibility with the older C0 and C1 control sets. Sixty-six are noncharacters, U+FDD0 to U+FDEF plus every code point whose last four hexadecimal digits are FFFE or FFFF, permanently reserved for internal use such as sentinel values; they are well formed in every encoding form but are not meant for interchange. Private-use code points have meanings agreed privately, with 6,400 of them in the first plane and 131,068 more in planes 15 and 16. Reserved code points are unassigned today and may be assigned in any future version, which is why software should not treat an unassigned code point as an error in itself.

The codespace is a single range, but it is convenient to divide it into 17 planes of 65,536 code points each, numbered 0 to 16: the last four hexadecimal digits give the position inside the plane and the remaining digits give the plane, so U+23456 sits at position 3456 in plane 2. The Basic Multilingual Plane (BMP, plane 0) holds the common-use characters of all modern scripts and the large majority of real text. The Supplementary Multilingual Plane (SMP, plane 1) takes historic scripts, lesser-used contemporary ones, notational systems and pictographic sets, from Gothic and Shavian to Musical Symbols and Domino Tiles. The Supplementary Ideographic Plane (SIP, plane 2) and Tertiary Ideographic Plane (TIP, plane 3) hold additional, mostly rare ideographs; the Supplementary Special-purpose Plane (SSP, plane 14) holds format controls, tag characters and variation selectors; planes 15 and 16 are for private use. Unicode 18.0.0, released on 16 September 2026, added 13,007 characters for a total of 172,808, including three new scripts (Proto-Cuneiform numerals, Jurchen and Seal), so even now well under a fifth of the codespace holds characters.

Surrogates are the code points that exist because of UTF-16. The high-surrogate range is U+D800 to U+DBFF (D71) and the low-surrogate range U+DC00 to U+DFFF (D73), and a Unicode scalar value is defined as any code point except those (D76). The encoding forms are defined over scalar values, not over all code points. UTF-16 (D91) writes each scalar value from U+0000 to U+D7FF and from U+E000 to U+FFFF as a single 16-bit code unit of the same value, and each value from U+10000 to U+10FFFF as a surrogate pair, a high surrogate followed by a low one; the standard's own example encodes U+10302 as D800 followed by DF02. UTF-8 (D92) assigns each scalar value a sequence of one to four bytes, so a surrogate code point has no UTF-8 form at all; a lone surrogate written out in a UTF-8 stream is not a character but an ill-formed sequence, which conformance clause C9 forbids a process to emit and which decoders replace with U+FFFD. The three forms, UTF-8, UTF-16 and UTF-32, are the Unicode transformation formats (UTF), and the code point is what they have in common. The standard's own example is the sequence U+004D, U+0430, U+4E8C, U+10302: in UTF-8 it takes one, two, three and four bytes (4D, D0 B0, E4 BA 8C, F0 90 8C 82), and in UTF-16 three single units and one surrogate pair.

Programming languages expose the distinction in different places. A Python str is an immutable sequence of Unicode code points, so len() counts code points, indexing returns one code point at a time, and the number of bytes on the wire appears only after encode() chooses a format. Languages and platforms built on UTF-16 count 16-bit code units instead, so a character outside the BMP has a length of two there and one in Python; and neither count is what a user perceives as a single character when combining marks or emoji sequences put several code points under one visible glyph. Bugs live in the gaps between those three units: truncating at a byte or code unit boundary that splits a sequence, comparing strings that look identical but differ in code points, or validating one representation and processing another.

The security consequences follow from the size of the repertoire. Unicode Technical Report (UTR) #36 on security considerations, stabilized and unmaintained since its last revision of 19 September 2014 and now partly superseded by Unicode Technical Standards (UTS) #39 and #55 and Unicode Standard Annex (UAX) #31, describes visual spoofing: an email link to citibank.com that is really a different domain because its first letter is a Cyrillic code point drawn exactly like a Latin c. It notes that the problem predates Unicode, since paypaI.com with a capital I fooled people in plain ASCII, but that a repertoire then of over 107,000 characters multiplies the opportunities. Two strings are visually confusable when they differ in code points yet look alike at small sizes on a screen. UTS #39 on security mechanisms, version 18.0.0 of 27 August 2026, gives the mechanical test: compute each string's skeleton by normalizing it, removing default-ignorable code points and replacing every character with its prototype from the confusables data, and two strings are confusable exactly when their skeletons are equal. It separates single-script, mixed-script and whole-script confusables, with paypal against a version using U+0430 CYRILLIC SMALL LETTER A as the mixed case and scope spelled entirely in Cyrillic as the whole-script one, and defines restriction levels, from ASCII-Only through Highly Restrictive to Moderately Restrictive, for deciding which mixtures of scripts an identifier may contain.

Code points can also mislead without looking like anything. Common Vulnerabilities and Exposures (CVE) entry CVE-2021-42574, the Trojan Source issue published on 1 November 2021 with a CVSS (Common Vulnerability Scoring System) 3.1 score of 8.3, describes how the bidirectional control characters let source code be rendered in an order different from the logical order a compiler reads, so that a reviewer approves code that does something else. The Unicode Consortium's own description of the problem points to UTR #36, UTS #39, UAX #31 on identifiers and rule HL4 of UAX #9, the bidirectional algorithm, for mitigations. The working habit that follows is the same for spoofed domains, hidden characters in configuration files and filter evasion: when text matters, inspect it as a list of code points rather than as glyphs, and decide explicitly which code points an identifier, hostname or policy field may contain.

paramiko.def: A Python implementation of the SSHv2 protocol, for clients and servers, on which Netmiko and ncclient are built.
paramiko.context: Its client checks host keys strictly by default: a server whose key is not already known is refused unless the script chooses another policy, while AutoAddPolicy accepts and saves whatever key it is shown. Release 5.0 removed the SHA-1 key exchanges and SHA-1 RSA signatures, and 4.0 removed DSA keys, so a very old device may refuse to talk to a current Paramiko; the changelog's advice for DSA is to stay on 3.x, and the better fix is to update the device.

netmiko.def: A Python library, built on Paramiko, that drives the command lines of many network platforms over SSH, with a driver per device type that knows its prompts, paging and privilege commands.
netmiko.context: It hides the dialogue a script would otherwise write by hand, finding the prompt, turning paging off, answering the enable question, and it can pass output to TextFSM, TTP or Genie for parsing. Two defaults deserve attention: unknown host keys are accepted unless ssh_strict is set, and when no parsing template matches, send_command returns the raw text without complaint unless raise_parsing_error is set.

scrapli.def: A library for driving network devices over telnet, SSH and NETCONF whose core, libscrapli, is written in Zig, with Python and Go bindings and each platform described in a YAML definition.
scrapli.context: Its 2026 releases replaced the original library, which was written in Python: the default transport wraps the OpenSSH client, the Paramiko and asyncssh transports are gone, and the same code is published on PyPI as scrapli, with calendar versions, and as scrapli2, with semantic ones. Its migration notes say strict host-key checking is now off by default and ask users to turn it on.

ncclient.def: A Python library for NETCONF clients that maps the operations of RFC 6241, such as get-config, edit-config, lock and commit, to method calls over SSH.
ncclient.context: It checks the server's host key against ~/.ssh/known_hosts by default, connects to port 830 unless told otherwise, and in its default mode raises an rpc-error from the device as an RPCError exception. Device handlers adapt it to vendor extensions such as Junos, IOS XE and Nexus.

restconf.def: The protocol of RFC (Request for Comments) 8040, built on HTTP (Hypertext Transfer Protocol), that gives programs access to data modelled in YANG, using the datastore concepts of NETCONF (Network Configuration Protocol).
restconf.context: It must run over TLS (Transport Layer Security), finds its root through /.well-known/host-meta, carries data as application/yang-data+json or application/yang-data+xml, and reports errors in a structured ietf-restconf:errors body instead of free text. A plain PATCH merges into an existing resource and refuses to create one that is missing.
restconf.depth:
RESTCONF is what a YANG model looks like through HTTP (Hypertext Transfer Protocol). RFC (Request for Comments) 8040, published in January 2017 by Andy Bierman, Martin Bjorklund and Kent Watsen, defines it as HTTP methods providing create, read, update and delete (CRUD) operations on a conceptual datastore of YANG-defined data, for models written in YANG 1 or 1.1. It is a Proposed Standard, updated by RFC 8527. The specification is careful about what it is not. It is not intended to replace NETCONF (Network Configuration Protocol) but to offer an interface that follows REST (Representational State Transfer) principles and stays compatible with NETCONF's datastore model, implementing a subset of NETCONF and leaving out explicit locking and the choice of datastore. Nor is it a hypermedia API (application programming interface): responses carry no links to follow, because a client that knows the server's YANG modules can derive every resource address and the structure of every request and response from them. That is the practical difference from a vendor's hand-designed REST API, where the paths come from documentation.

Transport is fixed more tightly than in most HTTP APIs. A server must support TLS (Transport Layer Security), and the protocol must not be used over HTTP without it; implementations must support the https scheme, whose default port is 443, and no particular HTTP version is required, although at least HTTP/1.1 is recommended. The server presents an X.509 version 3 certificate, and the client must either validate its path or match it against a certificate obtained by a trusted mechanism, such as a pinned one. The server must authenticate every client: it should require TLS client certificates and may fall back to an HTTP authentication scheme when certificates are not feasible. What an authenticated user may then read or change is governed by the NETCONF access control model, now RFC 8341. The security considerations add that servers should not accept TLS 1.3 early data (0-RTT) at all, even for idempotent requests. NETCONF itself, by comparison, normally runs over SSH (Secure Shell) on TCP port 830.

A client starts by finding the root. It requests /.well-known/host-meta and reads the one link whose relation is restconf; the value, commonly /restconf, is the prefix of every later request. Under the root sit three things: data, the datastore resource that holds all configuration and state; operations, where each rpc defined in a YANG module is invoked with POST; and yang-library-version, which says which revision of the YANG library the server uses to list its modules. Every server must also implement the ietf-restconf-monitoring module, which reports its capabilities and its event streams.

Paths are the model's tree written as a URI (Uniform Resource Identifier). Node names are joined from the top-level node down, and a module name followed by a colon is put in front of a node whenever the node belongs to a different module than its parent, or sits at the top. A list entry is addressed by the list name, an equals sign and the key value, with the values of several keys separated by commas in the order of the YANG key statement, and reserved characters in a value must be percent-encoded. The interface named eth0 in the standard interfaces model is therefore /restconf/data/ietf-interfaces:interfaces/interface=eth0, and an interface whose name contains slashes has each slash written as %2F. Bodies use the media types application/yang-data+json and application/yang-data+xml, with the JSON (JavaScript Object Notation) rules of RFC 7951: module-qualified member names and 64-bit numbers as strings.

Each method has a fixed meaning, which the specification maps to NETCONF operations. GET and HEAD read. POST on a parent creates a child and fails if it already exists; POST on an operation resource invokes it. PUT creates or replaces the target, answering 201 Created or 204 No Content, and PUT on the datastore resource replaces the entire configuration, the most dangerous request in the protocol. A plain PATCH merges its body into the target: it can create or update children but cannot delete them, and if the target itself does not exist the server must not create it. DELETE removes a resource that must exist. For anything finer there is YANG Patch, RFC 8072 of February 2017, a separate media type (application/yang-patch+json or +xml) carrying an ordered list of edits with seven operations, create, delete, insert, merge, move, replace and remove, applied atomically: if the whole patch cannot be completed, nothing changes. A client learns whether a server supports it from the Accept-Patch field in the reply to an OPTIONS request.

Retrieval is shaped by query parameters, each allowed once per request: content selects configuration, non-configuration or all data, depth limits how far down the reply goes, fields picks out part of the target and with-defaults controls whether default values are returned. Two mechanisms prevent one client from overwriting another's change. The server keeps a last-modified timestamp and an entity-tag for the datastore, returned in the Last-Modified and ETag fields, and a client can make an edit conditional with If-Unmodified-Since or If-Match. Failures come back with a 4xx or 5xx status and a structured errors body that reuses NETCONF's error information, with a defined mapping from error-tag to status code: data-exists, data-missing, in-use and lock-denied are 409, access-denied is 401 or 403, malformed-message is 400, and operation-not-supported is 405 or 501.

Where an edit lands depends on the device. If the server supports a writable running datastore, edits go straight to it. If it works through a candidate datastore instead, the candidate must be committed to running immediately after each successful edit, and any edits other sessions had left in the candidate are committed with it. If the device has a separate startup datastore, the server must update it automatically after running changes, so there is no separate save step. A RESTCONF client cannot take or release locks, and an edit against a datastore locked by a NETCONF session fails with 409 Conflict and the error-tag in-use. Each request is its own edit; there is no way to group several requests into one transaction, which is the main reason to keep NETCONF for large coordinated changes. RFC 8527 (March 2019) added resources under ds for the datastores of the newer architecture, so that a client can read ds/ietf-datastores:operational or ds/ietf-datastores:running explicitly.

Notifications are optional. A server that supports them lists its streams in the monitoring module, and a client receives events by opening a stream with the Accept type text/event-stream, the Server-Sent Events (SSE) transport, optionally with the filter, start-time and stop-time parameters.

Implementations differ in the parts the standard leaves open. Cisco's IOS XE guide enables the service with the restconf and ip http secure-server commands, authenticates through AAA (authentication, authorization and accounting) with users at privilege level 15, and serves the root at /restconf. F5 documents that F5OS accepts the same calls on port 8888 under /restconf and on port 443 under /api, requires the Content-Type application/yang-data+json, and issues an X-Auth-Token that lasts fifteen minutes and can be renewed five times. The recurring mistakes are the same everywhere: a missing module prefix, an unencoded key, a PUT that replaced more than was meant, a PATCH sent to a resource that did not exist yet, and a generic JSON content type where the server expects the YANG one.

yang.def: The data modelling language of RFC (Request for Comments) 7950, used to model configuration data, state data, remote procedure calls and notifications for network management protocols.
yang.context: A YANG module defines the tree that NETCONF (Network Configuration Protocol) and RESTCONF read and change: containers, lists keyed by a leaf, and typed leaves. The ietf-interfaces module of RFC (Request for Comments) 8343 is the usual first example; encoded in JSON (JavaScript Object Notation) under RFC 7951, its data carries the module name in front, as in ietf-interfaces:interfaces, so a program knows exactly which model a value belongs to.
yang.depth:
YANG is a schema language, not a protocol and not an encoding. A module is a text file that describes data as a tree in which every node has a name and either a value or a set of child nodes, together with the types, constraints and operations that go with it. What travels on the wire is something else: the same model is carried as XML (Extensible Markup Language) by NETCONF (Network Configuration Protocol) and as XML or JSON (JavaScript Object Notation) by RESTCONF, and the specification notes that other protocols and encodings are possible. Module files are named after the module, optionally followed by an at sign and a revision date, with the extension .yang; an equivalent XML notation called YIN (YANG Independent Notation) exists for tools and loses nothing in translation.

The language answers a complaint operators made in public. An IAB (Internet Architecture Board) workshop held from 4 to 6 June 2002 in Reston, Virginia, recorded in RFC (Request for Comments) 3535, found that SNMP (Simple Network Management Protocol) worked reasonably well for monitoring but that equipment was usually not fully configurable through it, and listed what operators wanted instead: a clear distinction between configuration data, operational state and statistics, the ability to fetch each separately, configuration transactions across devices, and a way to dump and restore a configuration. NETCONF, now RFC 6241, supplied the protocol. YANG supplied the description of the content: version 1 is RFC 6020 of October 2010, edited by Martin Bjorklund, and version 1.1 is RFC 7950 of August 2016, a maintenance release with a small number of backward incompatibilities that expressly does not obsolete RFC 6020, so both versions remain valid and a 1.1 module must say so with a yang-version statement. Both are Proposed Standards; RFC 7950 has been updated by RFC 8342 and RFC 8526, and RFC 6020 by RFC 9890 (October 2025), which revised how IANA (Internet Assigned Numbers Authority) keeps module names unique.

Four kinds of data node do most of the work. A leaf holds one value of one type and has no children; a leaf-list is a sequence of such values; a container groups other nodes; a list is a sequence of entries, each identified by the value of its key leaf or leaves. A container is by default only structure, and can be declared a presence container when its mere existence carries meaning. The config statement marks a subtree as configuration (true) or state (false), which is the distinction the operators asked for in 2002. There are 19 built-in types, among them the signed and unsigned integers from 8 to 64 bits, decimal64, string, boolean, enumeration, bits, binary, empty, union and three kinds of reference: leafref, which points at another leaf, identityref and instance-identifier. A typedef derives a new type by restricting a base type with a range or a pattern, and the common derived types (addresses, counters, dates) are published as modules of their own, since December 2025 in RFC 9911, which obsoleted RFC 6991. Constraints between nodes are written with must and when statements in XPath (XML Path Language) 1.0. Operations are modelled as well: rpc for a procedure on the whole device, action, added in version 1.1, for one tied to a container or list entry, and notification for events.

Modules are built to be extended and to be honest. Each has a namespace, a prefix and dated revision statements; it can import other modules and reuse definitions through grouping and uses. An augment statement lets one module add nodes to the tree of another, which is how a vendor attaches its own leaves to a standard model. A feature marks part of a model as optional. A deviation statement declares where a server does not implement a module faithfully, and the specification says deviations must never be part of a published standard: they exist so that a client can learn how a particular implementation differs. The YANG Library of RFC 8525 (March 2019) completes the picture by having the server list the modules, datastores and schemas it actually uses.

Nobody reads a long module from top to bottom; engineers read its tree diagram, a notation fixed by RFC 8340 (March 2018). Each line shows a node with flags and markers: rw for configuration, ro for state, -x for an rpc or action, -n for a notification, a question mark for an optional node, an asterisk for a list or leaf-list, the keys of a list in square brackets and an exclamation mark for a presence container. The ietf-interfaces module of RFC 8343 reads, in that notation, as a container interfaces holding a list interface keyed by name, with the writable leaves name, description, type and enabled and the read-only oper-status and statistics, whose octet counters are 64 bits wide. pyang, a validator and converter written in Python, prints such trees and checks modules; yanglint, from the libyang toolkit written in C, does the same job.

Encoding rules are where client code goes wrong. In XML, a node belongs to its module's namespace. In JSON, RFC 7951 uses the module name, not the namespace or the prefix: a member name is qualified as module, colon, node at the top level and wherever a child comes from a different module than its parent, and is written bare everywhere else. Values of the 64-bit types int64, uint64 and decimal64 are encoded as JSON strings, because many JSON parsers cannot hold them exactly as numbers, so an interface counter arrives in quotation marks. The empty type is encoded as an array holding a single null. The same precision limit applies inside constraints: XPath 1.0 numbers are double-precision floating point, and RFC 7950 warns that equality comparisons on 64-bit values may yield unexpected results.

Datastores tie the model to a device. The Network Management Datastore Architecture (NMDA) of RFC 8342 (March 2018) names the configuration datastores running, candidate, startup and intended, which share one schema, and a separate operational datastore for the state in use. Before it, models duplicated every tree, one for configuration and one for state; RFC 8343, which obsoleted RFC 7223, deprecates the old interfaces-state subtree for that reason and keeps it only for servers and clients that do not implement NMDA.

Models come from three kinds of author. The IETF (Internet Engineering Task Force) publishes its own in RFCs, under review guidelines that are now RFC 9907 (March 2026). OpenConfig, a group of network operators, maintains vendor-neutral models written in YANG, and its gNMI (gRPC Network Management Interface) protocol is specified on the assumption that it carries data instances of those schemas. Vendors publish native modules for whatever the first two do not cover; the YangModels repository on GitHub collects the modules of the IETF, of other standards bodies and of vendors in one place. F5 documents that the RESTCONF and NETCONF interface of F5OS is based on OpenConfig models extended with F5-specific namespaces, which is why its paths mix openconfig and f5 prefixes.

The practical difficulties follow from that plurality. The same interface or route can exist in an IETF model, an OpenConfig model and a native one, each with different paths and types, and a device may implement any subset of them with features disabled and deviations applied; the list the device itself reports is the only reliable inventory. A client built against one revision of a module can meet another on the device. And a model is not a behaviour: YANG says what the data looks like and what values are legal, while what the device does on a change is decided by the protocol operation and by the implementation.

textfsm.def: A Python module that parses semi-formatted text, such as a device's command output, into a table of records with a template-driven state machine.
textfsm.context: A template names the columns in Value lines, each with a regular expression, and describes states made of rules with actions such as Record and Error. A template that ends with an Error rule for any unexpected line fails loudly instead of quietly dropping text it does not recognize, which is what makes it safe to run unattended.

ntc-templates.def: A community collection of TextFSM templates for network devices, indexed by platform and command, which Netmiko uses when asked to parse with TextFSM.
ntc-templates.context: Its index accepts abbreviated commands, the way the devices do, and each template chooses its own field names and which columns to keep. Code written against it is therefore tied to those names and to the collection's version, which is worth pinning.

ttp-template-text-parser.def: A Python module that parses semi-structured text with templates that look like the text itself, with the variable parts marked between double curly brackets.
ttp-template-text-parser.context: It suits configurations, whose nesting its groups follow, and offers built-in patterns such as IP and ORPHRASE. Templates can carry Python code in macro tags, which TTP loads with exec, so its documentation warns that templates from untrusted sources are unsafe: review a TTP template as you would review code.

pyats.def: Cisco's Python test and automation framework, whose library Genie includes parsers that turn device command output into nested dictionaries.
pyats.context: Its package page says it supports Python 3.10 and later on Linux and macOS, not Windows, and the full library is large. Netmiko can call the Genie parsers on output it has already fetched, and Genie publishes, for each parser, the keys to leave out when two snapshots are compared, such as counters that change between runs.

getaddrinfo.def: The socket API's resolver function: it turns a host name or address and a service name or port into the arguments needed to create and connect a socket, for IPv4 and IPv6 alike.
getaddrinfo.context: RFC 3493 defines it for protocol-independent translation of names and services. It returns a list of entries, each with an address family, a socket type, a protocol and a socket address; most Linux configurations return the list sorted, and a client should try the entries in order until one connects, or in parallel as Happy Eyeballs does. The AI_NUMERICHOST flag forbids name lookups and accepts numeric addresses only. Python's socket.getaddrinfo() wraps the C function and returns 5-tuples (family, type, proto, canonname, sockaddr).

io-multiplexing.def: Watching many sockets or files with one call that reports which of them are ready to read or write, so that one thread can serve many connections.
io-multiplexing.context: The classic call is select(), which the Linux manual limits to descriptors below FD_SETSIZE (1024), advising modern applications to use poll() or epoll() instead; BSD systems offer kqueue(). Python's select module exposes these calls, and its selectors module wraps them behind one interface, with DefaultSelector choosing the most efficient one the platform has (epoll on Linux). With non-blocking sockets it checks hundreds of devices in the time of one timeout, and it is what asyncio's event loop runs underneath.

happy-eyeballs.def: An algorithm for clients on dual-stack hosts that starts connection attempts over IPv6 and IPv4 in a staggered race and keeps the first one that succeeds, so a broken path costs a fraction of a second instead of a timeout.
happy-eyeballs.context: RFC 8305 (Happy Eyeballs Version 2, 2017) replaced the original RFC 6555. It notes that clients "that attempt multiple connections in parallel have a chance of establishing a connection more quickly", and calls the wait before the next attempt the Connection Attempt Delay, with 250 milliseconds as one recommended default. In Python, asyncio's create_connection() and open_connection() take happy_eyeballs_delay and interleave (since 3.8); socket.create_connection() tries the addresses one after another.

ipv4-mapped-address.def: An IPv6 address of the form ::ffff:a.b.c.d that stands for an IPv4 address, so that IPv6 software can name an IPv4 peer.
ipv4-mapped-address.context: RFC 4291 (section 2.5.5.2) defines the layout: 80 zero bits, 16 one bits, then the IPv4 address. RFC 3493 uses it so that AF_INET6 sockets can reach IPv4 nodes, and Python's documentation notes that a dual-stack listener reports an IPv4 client in this form. Python's ipaddress returns the embedded address as ipv4_mapped, IPv4Address.ipv6_mapped goes the other way (3.13), and since 3.13 is_private, is_global and the other properties of a mapped address follow its IPv4 address. Security checks must unwrap it: ::ffff:127.0.0.1 is the loopback address.

zone-index.def: The suffix after % in an IPv6 address such as fe80::1%eth0, which says which link, or other scope zone, a non-global address belongs to.
zone-index.context: RFC 4007 (section 11) defines the text form address%zone_id, which "an implementation SHOULD support", because the same link-local address can exist on every interface of a host; the format "MUST be used only within a node and MUST NOT be sent on the wire unless every node that interprets the format agrees on the semantics". In Python's ipaddress the zone is the scope_id and part of the object, so fe80::1%eth0 and fe80::1%eth1 are different addresses; an AF_INET6 socket address carries it as its fourth element.

netmask.def: A mask with the network bits set to one and the host bits set to zero, written like an address (255.255.255.0) and equivalent to a prefix length (/24).
netmask.context: Request for Comments (RFC) 4632 explains the prefix 172.16.0.0/16 as a mask whose 16 most significant bits are ones and whose 16 least significant bits are zeros, and requires that "the mask must be left contiguous". Its bitwise inverse is the host mask, which access lists call a wildcard. Python's ipaddress accepts all three IPv4 forms after the slash (/24, /255.255.255.0 and /0.0.0.255) and refuses a mask that mixes ones and zeros; for IPv6 it accepts the prefix length only.
netmask.depth:
What it does. A netmask is a 32-bit value that marks which bits of an IPv4 address name the network and which name the host. A host applies it every time it sends a packet: Request for Comments (RFC) 1122 requires it to extract, with the mask, the same bits from the destination address and from its own, and to deliver directly if they match or hand the packet to a gateway if they do not. A router applies the mask of each route in the same way to decide whether the route covers a destination. The mask itself never travels in the Internet Protocol (IP) header; it is local configuration, which is why two hosts on one wire can hold different opinions about who their neighbours are. It has had several names for the same thing: address mask in RFC 950, subnet mask in most configuration screens, network mask or netmask in routing documents.

Where it came from. In the original classful scheme the mask was implied by the first bits of the address: 172.16.0.0, a Class B network, had an implied mask of 255.255.0.0. Subnetting needed something explicit. Jeffrey Mogul proposed it in RFC 917 (October 1984), and RFC 950, by Mogul and Jon Postel (August 1985), made it the standard, choosing a bit mask over four other schemes for marking the subnet field. Because the bits are named by a mask, RFC 950 noted, they need not be adjacent, but it recommended that they be contiguous and the most significant bits of the local part. It also defined two messages of the Internet Control Message Protocol (ICMP), Address Mask Request (type 17) and Address Mask Reply (type 18), so that a booting host could ask for its mask.

How the rule hardened. RFC 1122 (October 1989) still remarked that its notation did not imply contiguous one bits. Classless Inter-Domain Routing (CIDR) ended the tolerance: RFC 1519 (September 1993), and RFC 4632 which replaced it in August 2006, generalize routing to any network number and mask on the single condition that the mask be left contiguous. RFC 1812 (June 1995) says that discontiguous subnet masks are not permitted, because arbitrary masks can make routing ambiguous, with two equally specific routes matching one destination, and it describes the subnet mask as the historical name for what newer protocols express as a prefix length: a contiguous string of ones at the more significant end, a contiguous string of zeros at the other, and nothing in between. The ICMP messages lasted until RFC 6918 (April 2013) formally deprecated them as superseded by the Dynamic Host Configuration Protocol (DHCP), which carries the mask as option 1, four octets, placed before the router option.

The numbers. With contiguity required there are only 33 masks, one for each prefix length from 0 to 32, and each octet of a mask can take only nine values: 0, 128, 192, 224, 240, 248, 252, 254 and 255. RFC 1878 (December 1995) tabulates them all: /16 is 255.255.0.0, /23 is 255.255.254.0 with 512 addresses, /24 is 255.255.255.0 with 256, /27 is 255.255.255.224 with 32, /30 is 255.255.255.252 with 4, and /32, 255.255.255.255, is a single host route. A block holds two to the power of the number of zero bits, and in ordinary subnets two of those addresses, all zeros and all ones in the host part, are the network and the broadcast. That is why a /30 spends four addresses on a link with two ends, and why RFC 3021 (December 2000) allows the 31-bit mask 255.255.255.254 on point-to-point links. At the other extreme the mask 0.0.0.0 matches everything: 0.0.0.0/0 is the default route.
