The same day President Bill Clinton had signed the Communications Decency Act into law; the text itself names the Telecommunications Reform Act. He e-mailed it to about 600 friends and, he said, it was soon copied to tens of thousands of websites. Addressed to the governments of the industrial world, it declares the global social space being built naturally independent of them, offers the Golden Rule as the one law all its cultures would recognize, names China, Germany, France, Russia, Singapore, Italy and the United States as states erecting guard posts at its frontiers, and ends by declaring virtual selves immune to sovereignty even as their owners consent to rule over their bodies. Wired reports that it became part of the EFF campaign that helped overturn parts of the Communications Decency Act on First Amendment grounds.

The argument over it. The Declaration became the standard target for critics of internet libertarianism. Wired's 20th-anniversary piece collected some of them: the French President Nicolas Sarkozy telling technology firms at a Group of Eight (G8) meeting that their universe was not a parallel one free of law; Google's general counsel David Drummond saying that governments had learned to shape the internet; and the Information Technology and Innovation Foundation (ITIF) proposing a 'Declaration of the Interdependence of Cyberspace' and claiming Barlow had backed away from his own text. He had not. In February 2016 he told Wired that the main thing he had declared was that cyberspace is naturally immune to sovereignty and always would be, that he believed it then and believed it still, while conceding that a state can still imprison anyone it finds in the physical world, and he cited encryption, Tor and Signal as evidence. A 2021 assessment in Nieman Lab called the text the ur-document of tech utopianism, exceptionalism and arrogance, noting that the network it described had in fact been built and funded by a national government. In the 1996 interview Barlow himself was candid about the frontier metaphor's limits: he and Kapor had set out to make cyberspace safe for women and children in a 19th-century, Manifest Destiny kind of way, and there had been very few of either when he arrived.

Later work and death. He was a fellow at Harvard's Berkman Center for Internet and Society and vice-chairman of the EFF board, and in 2013 he was inducted into the Internet Hall of Fame. On 17 December 2012 he launched the Freedom of the Press Foundation with Daniel Ellsberg, Trevor Timm and others, with Xeni Jardin, Glenn Greenwald, Laura Poitras, Josh Stearns and John Cusack on its first board; it was a response to the refusal of PayPal, Visa and Mastercard to process donations to WikiLeaks, and Barlow's line at the launch was that financial transactions are speech. Edward Snowden later joined that board. Barlow died in his sleep at home in San Francisco early on 7 February 2018, aged 70. Cindy Cohn, who had worked with him at the EFF for 27 years, wrote that major parts of the internet exist and thrive because of his vision and leadership; Wired had called him the bard of the internet; Weir said he would live on in the songs they wrote.

declaration-of-the-independence-of-cyber.def: John Perry Barlow's sixteen-paragraph address to the governments of the industrial world, dated Davos, Switzerland, 8 February 1996: the best-known statement of the claim that the network is a place beyond any state's sovereignty.
declaration-of-the-independence-of-cyber.context: It opens with the line everyone quotes, "Governments of the Industrial World, you weary giants of flesh and steel", and tells them they have no sovereignty where the network's people gather. Its trigger is named in the text: the United States had that day created a law, the Telecommunications Reform Act, which Barlow said repudiated its own Constitution. The rest declares the writers' virtual selves immune to government sovereignty "even as we continue to consent to your rule over our bodies", and closes by promising a civilization of the mind more humane and fair than the world those governments had made. The EFF (Electronic Frontier Foundation), which Barlow co-founded, hosts the text.
declaration-of-the-independence-of-cyber.depth:
How it is built. The text is an echo of 1776: governments derive their just powers from the consent of the governed, and the people of cyberspace had neither been asked for theirs nor given it. It is not only about Washington. One paragraph names China, Germany, France, Russia, Singapore, Italy and the United States as trying to ward off the virus of liberty with guard posts at the frontiers of cyberspace, and another attacks information industries that would claim to own speech itself, laws that would declare ideas another industrial product, no more noble than pig iron.

What it claims. Read through, the argument has four steps. Cyberspace is a social space that grows by itself, an act of nature, not a public construction project governments could build. Its people have their own culture, ethics and unwritten codes, which already give it more order than any imposition could, and they are forming their own social contract. Government's legal concepts of property, expression, identity, movement and context do not apply there, because they are all based on matter, and there is no matter here; the only law all its cultures would recognize is the Golden Rule. And because all expression, from the debasing to the angelic, is part of one seamless conversation, it cannot be filtered: in the text's own image, we cannot separate the air that chokes from the air upon which wings beat. The concession sits in the last paragraph, where the writers declare their virtual selves immune to government sovereignty while continuing to consent to its rule over their bodies.

The law it answered. The Telecommunications Act of 1996, Public Law 104-104, which the Federal Communications Commission describes as the first major overhaul of telecommunications law in almost 62 years, dates from 8 February 1996, the date the Declaration carries. Its Title V, the Communications Decency Act, made it a crime knowingly to transmit obscene or indecent messages to anyone under 18, and knowingly to send or display to a minor anything patently offensive as measured by contemporary community standards. Those are the provisions the Declaration's charge of repudiating the Constitution was aimed at, and the reason it speaks of parents who entrust their bureaucracies with responsibilities they are too cowardly to confront themselves.

What happened to that law. The indecency provisions did not survive, but not because cyberspace seceded. The American Civil Liberties Union sued, and in Reno v. American Civil Liberties Union, argued on 19 March 1997 and decided on 26 June 1997, the Supreme Court held that the indecent transmission and patently offensive display provisions abridge the freedom of speech protected by the First Amendment. The same title of the same Act also added section 230 to the Communications Act, which says that no provider or user of an interactive computer service shall be treated as the publisher or speaker of information provided by someone else, and declares a policy of preserving a free market for internet services unfettered by federal or state regulation. The part of the law Barlow hated was struck down by a court applying the old Constitution, and the part that survived became the legal foundation of the platforms that came to govern much of online speech: independence, such as it was, arrived by statute and litigation.

How it travelled. Barlow sent it by email to about 600 friends, as Nieman Lab recounted on its 25th anniversary, and it spread from there across the network it addressed. The Electronic Frontier Foundation (EFF) keeps the canonical copy, signed off Davos, Switzerland, on 8 February 1996, and on 8 February 2018, the day after Barlow died, the World Economic Forum republished the full text, introducing it as a call made in Davos.

Its author was not naive about it. In the EFF's obituary, Cindy Cohn quoted Barlow's own later explanation: he predicted utopia hoping to give liberty a running start before the laws of Moore and Metcalfe delivered what Edward Snowden calls turn-key totalitarianism. Read that way, the Declaration is less a forecast than a tactic: say loudly what the network should be, before somebody else decides. Twenty years on he held the line on its central commitment; asked in 2016 whether online speech should have limits, he answered that he did not know a way to limit one form of speech without limiting any form, and that if you cannot defend the expressions that trouble you, you will have a hard time defending your own.

The critique. The objections are as well known as the text. Joshua Benton, writing for Nieman Lab in 2021, called it the ur-document of tech utopianism, tech exceptionalism and tech arrogance, pointed out that the network had in fact been a public construction project, built by a national government, and asked who exactly the we of the Declaration was, since its author could not imagine the technology companies themselves becoming powers. For an engineer the weakest sentence is the one about matter. Every packet crosses cables, exchanges and data centres that sit in some jurisdiction, and that is where governments have exercised the sovereignty the text denied, by compelling the operators of that infrastructure; Room 641A, in a carrier's building in San Francisco, is the best-documented example.

What it kept. Governments went on legislating for the network, starting with the law the Declaration answered, so as a prediction it lost. What it kept is the claim underneath, that the people who build and use a network have standing in how it is governed, and the line it gave a culture: a world that all may enter without privilege or prejudice accorded by race, economic power, military force or station of birth. That is the line the EFF chose to quote when Barlow died.

mitch-kapor.def: The designer of Lotus 1-2-3 who in 1990 co-founded the EFF (Electronic Frontier Foundation) with John Perry Barlow, helped pay for Craig Neidorf's defence in the Phrack trial, and in 2003 became the founding chairman of the Mozilla Foundation.
mitch-kapor.context: He and Barlow were both visited by the FBI (Federal Bureau of Investigation) in the spring of 1990 over the same stolen Macintosh source code, Kapor because a disk of it had been sent to him unasked. After reading Barlow's account on the WELL (Whole Earth 'Lectronic Link) he dropped in on him in Wyoming, and the two spent several hours, in Barlow's words, hatching what became the EFF (Electronic Frontier Foundation); the foundation's own history lists him as the former president of Lotus Development Corporation. In the Phrack case that summer, Bruce Sterling records, Kapor made a generous payment towards Neidorf's defence. He chaired the EFF until 1994, and in July 2003 Mozilla.org named him chairman of the foundation it had just created, with a personal contribution to the project.
mitch-kapor.depth:
Mitchell Kapor was born in Brooklyn on 1 November 1950, grew up on Long Island and took a BA at Yale in 1971 in an interdisciplinary programme of psychology, linguistics and computer science. In the early personal-computer industry he was head of development at VisiCorp, the distributor of the VisiCalc spreadsheet, and sold it his rights to VisiPlot and VisiTrend before leaving. In 1982 he founded Lotus Development with Jonathan Sachs, backed by the venture capitalist Ben Rosen, and on 26 January 1983 Lotus released 1-2-3, named for its three uses as spreadsheet, graphics package and database. The Computer History Museum calls it the killer app that made the IBM Personal Computer ubiquitous in business; Wikipedia records first-year sales of US$53 million against a business plan of US$1 million, making Lotus the third-largest microcomputer software company of 1983. Kapor decided he was not suited to running a large company and left in 1986. The museum made him a Fellow in 1996.

The episode that turned him into a civil-liberties figure began with the FBI. In the spring of 1990 someone calling itself the NuPrometheus League had distributed stolen source code from the Macintosh ROMs, and FBI agents went looking for whoever was behind it. John Perry Barlow, interviewed in Wyoming on 1 May by an agent who knew little about computers, posted an account on the WELL, the Sausalito bulletin board; Kapor, who had been visited too because one of the disks had been mailed to him unasked, read it, and a few days later had his private jet stop in Wyoming on the way to San Francisco. In Barlow's telling, the two spent several hours during a late spring snowstorm hatching what became the Electronic Frontier Foundation. Kapor gave Barlow the number of the lawyer Harvey Silverglate and said he would pay the bills that start to appear whenever you call a lawyer.

The context was a wave of computer-crime enforcement that, in their view, ignored the Bill of Rights. Barlow's history lists the Secret Service's Operation Sundevil, which seized more than 40 computers and 23,000 data disks from teenagers in 14 American cities; the raid on Steve Jackson Games in Austin, whose bulletin-board mail was read and deleted; and the prosecution of Craig Neidorf (Knight Lightning) for publishing a BellSouth document about the emergency 911 system in Phrack, with a possible sentence of 60 years. When the Washington Post ran the story, Barlow recalled that every headline amounted to Lotus founder defends hackers, which he called an irritating misrepresentation; the publicity also brought Steve Wozniak, who offered an unlimited match to Kapor's contributions, and John Gilmore, Sun Microsystems employee number 5, who offered six figures. The foundation was formally launched in July 1990, announcing on its first day that it was representing Steve Jackson Games and several of its bulletin-board users in a lawsuit against the Secret Service. Bruce Sterling's account of the Neidorf trial records Kapor's generous payment towards the defence. Kapor chaired the EFF until 1994.

He argued for design and for openness in the same years. A Software Design Manifesto, delivered at Esther Dyson's PC Forum in 1990 and published in Dr. Dobb's Journal in 1991, asked for a role for the software designer as a champion of the user experience, comparing software to buildings, where architects rather than construction engineers carry overall responsibility, and borrowing Vitruvius's test of firmness, commodity and delight; software design, he wrote, needed to be recognized as a profession in its own right. In Wired in 1993, as the US debated a National Information Infrastructure built by telephone and cable companies, he described the choice as whether networks would be Jeffersonian: open in access, use and content. He pointed out that telephone companies, as common carriers, were required to be open in access while cable operators had no such obligation, and warned that openness is easy to build into networks but difficult to add after the fact.

His money followed the same line into infrastructure. Wikipedia lists him as the founding investor in UUNET, one of the first and largest early internet service providers, in RealNetworks and in Linden Lab, maker of Second Life, and as the founding chair of the Commercial Internet eXchange (CIX). In July 2003, when mozilla.org launched the Mozilla Foundation as an independent California public benefit corporation (mozilla.org had been founded by Netscape), Kapor became its chairman and contributed US$300,000 personally; he was then also chairing the Open Source Applications Foundation, and said that a competitive, standards-compliant browser was vitally important to freedom and innovation on the internet.

His later work centres on who gets to build technology. He founded what became the Kapor Center in 2000, and its venture arm, Kapor Capital, has invested since 2011 in early-stage start-ups that, in its own words, close gaps of access; the Center describes itself as a family of organizations working through research, STEM (science, technology, engineering and mathematics) programmes for students of colour, investment and policy to make the technology sector more inclusive. In 2015 he and his wife, Freada Kapor Klein, announced US$40 million over three years for that purpose.

john-gilmore.def: Sun Microsystems employee number five, co-founder of the EFF (Electronic Frontier Foundation) in 1990 and of the cypherpunks mailing list, credited by the EFF with finding the documents behind Bernstein's code-as-speech case and with leading the build of its DES (Data Encryption Standard) Cracker.
john-gilmore.context: The account the EFF (Electronic Frontier Foundation) gives of his record is specific. In the 1990s he found the government documents that confirmed the First Amendment problem with export controls on encryption and helped initiate the filing of Bernstein v. Department of Justice, which ended in a ruling that source code is protected speech; and he led the effort to design and build the DES (Data Encryption Standard) Cracker, which showed publicly that the cipher then embedded in banking networks could be broken in about a week and catalysed the adoption of AES (Advanced Encryption Standard). He also co-founded Cygnus Solutions, created Usenet's alt.* hierarchy, and is credited with the line that the Net interprets censorship as damage and routes around it. In 2021 the EFF board voted to remove him after disagreements over how to work together, and named him Board Member Emeritus.
john-gilmore.depth:
Engineer first. John Gilmore's activism has always been carried out by building things and by going to court, and he started as a network engineer. In September 1985, as Sun Microsystems' representative, he co-wrote with Bill Croft of Stanford University RFC (Request for Comments) 951, the Bootstrap Protocol (BOOTP): a way for a diskless workstation to discover its own Internet Protocol (IP) address, the address of a server and the name of a boot file, using two reserved User Datagram Protocol (UDP) ports, 67 for the server and 68 for the client, with requests usually broadcast and the file itself fetched by the Trivial File Transfer Protocol (TFTP). The Dynamic Host Configuration Protocol (DHCP), specified in RFC 2131 in March 1997, is based on BOOTP and interoperates with it, which is why every DHCP exchange on a modern network still runs over the ports Croft and Gilmore chose. Sun employee number five, he left the company wealthy enough, Steven Levy wrote in 1993, to fund public causes.

Usenet's alternative. On 7 May 1987, at G.T.'s Sunset Barbecue in Mountain View, Gilmore, Brian Reid and Gordon Moffett of Amdahl set up a distribution that bypassed the Usenet backbone. By Reid's account Gilmore was distressed that the backbone administrators would not create rec.drugs, and Reid that they wanted his recipe group renamed; Gilmore's home machine, hoptoad, linked to Reid's and to Amdahl, and by the end of May alt.test, alt.config, alt.drugs and alt.gourmand were running. Histories of the network describe alt.* as the point where open expression on Usenet began, a reaction against control at the centre.

Free software as a business. Gilmore was the third founder of Cygnus Support, with Michael Tiemann and David Henkel-Wallace; the State of California approved the company on 13 November 1989, with 6,000 dollars of starting capital. Its premise, in Tiemann's later account, was to sell proven technical support for proven free software, under a slogan Tiemann credits to Gilmore: we make free software affordable. In the push to ship version 2.0 of the GNU C Compiler (GCC) and G++, Gilmore took on the GNU Debugger (GDB). Renamed Cygnus Solutions, it was by Tiemann's account in 1999 the first and largest open-source business.

The Electronic Frontier Foundation (EFF) and its money. When Barlow and Mitch Kapor began organizing in 1990, Gilmore e-mailed a six-figure offer of support, and on 9 October 1990 the first formal board meeting elected him a director alongside Stewart Brand and Steve Wozniak. The EFF credits him with financial support critical to its survival over many years and with recruiting Shari Steele, Cindy Cohn and Lee Tien.

Cryptography and secrecy. The cypherpunks held physical meetings in a conference room at Cygnus; Levy, who attended one for Wired in 1993, named Tim May and Eric Hughes as the founders of the meetings and quoted Gilmore preferring PGP (Pretty Good Privacy) to the bureaucracy of Privacy Enhanced Mail. Gilmore's own method was to force documents into the open. He posted on the Net a Xerox cryptographer's paper that the National Security Agency (NSA) had persuaded Xerox not to publish, and when the NSA failed to answer his Freedom of Information Act (FOIA) request for William Friedman's reclassified Military Cryptanalysis manuals, he sued; a friend then found copies in the Virginia Military Institute library and on microfilm at Boston University. The Justice Department warned that distributing them could violate the Espionage Act, with up to ten years in prison; after a San Francisco Examiner story on 25 November 1992, the NSA declassified the texts again two days later. The EFF says he also found the government documents that confirmed the First Amendment problem with encryption export controls and helped start Bernstein v. Department of Justice, whose outcome made it legal in 1999 for software to use the encryption of its choice.

The DES Cracker. The Data Encryption Standard, a federal standard since 1977 with 56-bit keys, was still being defended by officials as impractical to break. Gilmore led the EFF project that built a machine to show otherwise: an ordinary personal computer driving a large array of custom chips, built in under a year for less than 250,000 dollars. In July 1998 it won RSA Laboratories' DES Challenge II-2, searching more than 88 billion keys a second for 56 hours before finding the key; the decrypted message read: it's time for those 128-, 192-, and 256-bit keys. The previous record, set by tens of thousands of networked computers, was 39 days. The full design was published with O'Reilly as Cracking DES, on paper only, because export controls might have made posting it online a crime. The EFF's 2021 summary describes the result as breaking DES in a week for under 350,000 dollars and credits it with catalysing the adoption of the Advanced Encryption Standard (AES); the 1998 release gives the figures above.

Encrypting the Internet, and a phrase. His project for 1996, he wrote in 1999, was to secure five per cent of internet traffic against passive wiretapping with FreeS/WAN, free Linux software for boxes that would sit near a firewall and opportunistically encrypt every packet with Internet Protocol Security (IPsec) whenever the other end supported it, aiming at 20 per cent the following year and 80 per cent the year after; it took longer than he hoped. The sentence most associated with him, that the Net interprets censorship as damage and routes around it, was attributed to him in print by Howard Rheingold in September 1993 and by Time on 6 December 1993.

Courts and the EFF board. On 4 July 2002 he refused to show identification for a Southwest Airlines flight from Oakland to Washington and was not allowed to fly; he challenged a Transportation Security Administration (TSA) identification rule whose text the government would not disclose, and on 26 January 2006 the Ninth Circuit held that neither the policy nor its application to him violated his constitutional rights. In October 2021 the EFF board, saying it had not seen eye to eye with him on how to communicate and work together, voted to remove him as a director and elected him Board Member Emeritus; Cindy Cohn wrote that it was no overstatement to say the EFF would not exist without him.

the-e911-case.def: The 1990 federal prosecution of Craig Neidorf (Knight Lightning), co-editor of the electronic magazine Phrack, for publishing an edited BellSouth document about Enhanced 911 emergency services; the case collapsed on the fourth day of trial.
the-e911-case.context: The document, an internal BellSouth text on administering Enhanced 911 (E911) services, had been copied from a BellSouth computer; in February 1989 Neidorf and Prophet, a member of the Legion of Doom, cut it nearly in half, removing staff phone numbers and the more specific details, and Phrack issue 24 carried it on 25 February under the pseudonym The Eavesdropper. Prosecutors in Chicago chose to treat Phrack, a free amateur publication, as a fraud scheme rather than a magazine, and gave the text a valuation that made it look like a serious theft. At trial in July 1990 the defence, advised by the new EFF (Electronic Frontier Foundation), showed that Bellcore sold detailed E911 documents to anyone who ordered them from a free public catalogue. The government moved to dismiss, the judge declared a mistrial, and in September 1991 the indictment record was expunged and sealed.
the-e911-case.depth:
The case mattered because of what the government had to argue. Neidorf never broke into anything; even the Legion of Doom, Bruce Sterling reports, did not consider him a hacker at all. He published a magazine. Charging him meant treating an electronic magazine as something other than a publication, because admitting that Phrack was a magazine and Neidorf a publisher would have opened, in Sterling's phrase, a Pandora's box of First Amendment issues.

It collapsed on the facts. Under cross-examination the BellSouth witness was shown a free Bellcore catalogue from which anyone with a credit card could order detailed documents on the E911 (Enhanced 911) system, one of which, the defence put to her, held about twice as much detail as Phrack had printed. On Friday 27 July 1990 the prosecution moved to dismiss, citing information not available at the start of the trial. Neidorf was not found innocent; the case was dropped, and he was left owing his lawyers a large sum despite a generous payment from Mitch Kapor.

No court ruled on the First Amendment question, because the case never reached a verdict. But the episode is a founding story of the EFF (Electronic Frontier Foundation), whose own history traces its creation to the Secret Service raids that chased this document, and it gave Bruce Sterling the closing part of The Hacker Crackdown.

the-hacker-crackdown.def: Bruce Sterling's 1992 book on the 1990 crackdown on the American hacker underground, subtitled Law and Disorder on the Electronic Frontier, which its author released as free electronic text on 1 January 1994.
the-hacker-crackdown.context: It is organized in four parts, Crashing the System, The Digital Underground, Law and Order, and The Civil Libertarians, and it runs from the AT&T long-distance crash of 15 January 1990 through the hackers, the police and the prosecutors to the founding of the EFF (Electronic Frontier Foundation) and the trial of Craig Neidorf. Sterling had kept the electronic rights when the print edition went to Bantam, and in his preface to the electronic release he gave them away: the book became literary freeware, free to copy so long as nobody sells it. His reasoning was that a book about information on networks belonged inside one, and Project Gutenberg has carried it as eBook 101 since that same day.

chelsea-manning.def: The US Army intelligence analyst who in 2010, while stationed in Iraq, passed hundreds of thousands of battlefield reports and diplomatic cables to WikiLeaks; convicted at court-martial in 2013 and sentenced to thirty-five years, she was released in 2017 after President Obama commuted the sentence.
chelsea-manning.context: The court-martial convicted her in July 2013 on charges including espionage and acquitted her of aiding the enemy, the most serious count; prosecutors had asked for sixty years. In January 2017 President Obama commuted the sentence to expire on 17 May 2017, and she was released from Fort Leavenworth that day. Two threads tie the case to this field: she had confided in online chat to the hacker Adrian Lamo, whose information reached the Army's investigators, and the material included the video WikiLeaks published in April 2010 as Collateral Murder. In 2019 she was jailed for contempt for refusing to testify before a grand jury investigating WikiLeaks's founder, and was released in March 2020.

bassel-khartabil.def: The Palestinian-Syrian open-source developer who led Creative Commons in Syria and contributed to Wikipedia and Mozilla Firefox; detained in Damascus in March 2012, he was executed in secret in 2015, which his family learned only in 2017.
bassel-khartabil.context: He was taken from a street in Damascus amid a wave of military arrests, held incommunicado for months, and moved to Adra prison in December 2012. A campaign under the #FreeBassel banner ran for years: Mozilla, Wikipedia, the EFF (Electronic Frontier Foundation) and Creative Commons wrote for his release, the MIT (Massachusetts Institute of Technology) Media Lab offered him a research post, Index on Censorship gave him its Digital Freedom Award in 2013, and in 2015 a United Nations working group called his detention arbitrary. On 3 October 2015 he told his family he was being transferred to an undisclosed location, and nothing more was heard; in August 2017 his family announced that he had been killed in 2015 after a secret hearing before a military field court. His last project, #NEWPALMYRA, set out to model the endangered ruins of Palmyra in open 3D.

alexandra-elbakyan.def: The Kazakhstani programmer who in 2011 created Sci-Hub, the shadow library that serves paywalled research papers to anyone free of charge, and who has been at the centre of the fight over access to scholarly literature ever since.
alexandra-elbakyan.context: She has said she started it because she could not afford the papers she needed for her own research, and the site launched on 5 September 2011. Publishers sued in the United States: Elsevier in New York in 2015 and the American Chemical Society in Virginia in 2017. Sci-Hub did not defend either case and lost both by default; when the New York court awarded Elsevier damages in June 2017, Nature reported doubts that the publisher would ever see any money. Elsevier also won an injunction against her, the site has cycled through domain names since, and she has stayed out of reach of the American courts. In 2016 Nature named her one of the ten people who mattered in science that year.

dmitry-sklyarov.def: The Russian programmer arrested by the FBI (Federal Bureau of Investigation) in Las Vegas on 16 July 2001, after speaking at DEF CON about the weaknesses of Adobe's eBook protection, in the first criminal prosecution of software developers under the DMCA (Digital Millennium Copyright Act).
dmitry-sklyarov.context: He worked for the Russian company ElcomSoft, whose Advanced eBook Processor could read encrypted Adobe eBooks in ways the publishers had not intended. The account of the EFF (Electronic Frontier Foundation) is careful about cause: he was charged over the software, not the talk, but had he not come to DEF CON he would probably have stayed outside US jurisdiction. He spent three weeks in custody; Adobe, after meeting the EFF, withdrew its support for the complaint; protests under the slogan Free Dmitry spread; and in December 2001 he was allowed home under an agreement to testify. In December 2002 a federal jury in San Jose found ElcomSoft not guilty on all counts.

bunnie-huang.def: The MIT-trained hardware hacker who, as a graduate student in 2002, extracted the security keys of the original Microsoft Xbox, wrote Hacking the Xbox, and has argued since, in court and in hardware, for the right to open the devices people own.
bunnie-huang.context: His MIT (Massachusetts Institute of Technology) Artificial Intelligence Laboratory memo of May 2002 showed that the Xbox hid a secret boot block inside a system chip and then passed its code to the processor in the clear over a high-speed bus. In the foreword to the free edition he recalls a letter from MIT's lawyers repudiating any association with the work, which left him to face Microsoft on his own. In March 2013, after the death of Aaron Swartz, he and No Starch Press released Hacking the Xbox free in Swartz's honour. In July 2016 he became a plaintiff in Green v. Department of Justice, the challenge the EFF (Electronic Frontier Foundation) brought on First Amendment grounds against the anti-circumvention rules of the DMCA (Digital Millennium Copyright Act); the appeals court for the District of Columbia Circuit ruled in August 2024 and left the law intact.

ed-felten.def: The Princeton computer scientist whose team broke the music industry's SDMI (Secure Digital Music Initiative) watermarking challenge and was threatened under the DMCA (Digital Millennium Copyright Act) when it tried to publish the results in April 2001; later the first chief technologist of the US Federal Trade Commission.
ed-felten.context: The team declined the challenge's prize so as to keep the right to publish, and then received DMCA-grounded legal threat letters from SDMI member companies before the Information Hiding Workshop. In June 2001 the EFF (Electronic Frontier Foundation) sued on its behalf against the RIAA (Recording Industry Association of America), SDMI and the Department of Justice, asking a federal court to declare a First Amendment right to present the work; the paper, Reading Between the Lines: Lessons from the SDMI Challenge, was presented at the USENIX Security Symposium in Washington that August. A New Jersey court dismissed the suit in November 2001, and the team chose not to appeal, citing assurances from the government and the industry that the threats would not be repeated. He went on to serve as chief technologist of the Federal Trade Commission and deputy US chief technology officer, and is now emeritus at Princeton.

diego-aranha.def: The Brazilian cryptographer, now an associate professor at Aarhus University, who led the team that broke ballot secrecy in Brazil's electronic voting machine during the Superior Electoral Court's public security tests of 2012, and returned in 2017 with a team that compromised the integrity of its software.
diego-aranha.context: The tests are run by the TSE (Tribunal Superior Eleitoral, the Superior Electoral Court) under tight rules, with every participant pre-approved and forms to fill in during the test itself. In 2012 his team, working with access to the source code, found that the mechanism meant to shuffle the stored votes, so that their order could not be matched to the order of voting, drew its randomness from the clock, which made the votes recoverable in order; the log that stamps events with the time then made a specific vote recoverable. In 2017 another team he coordinated found that installation media were not properly encrypted and that keys were shared by every machine and written into the source code. He has presented the work at Real World Crypto, at DEF CON's Voting Village and at Black Hat Asia, and it earned him MIT Technology Review's Innovators Under 35 Brazil award.

fisl.def: FISL (Fórum Internacional Software Livre): the free-software conference held in Porto Alegre since May 2000, long counted among the largest of its kind and a meeting point between Brazil's free-software movement and public administration.
fisl.context: The first edition ran on 4 and 5 May 2000 at the UFRGS (Universidade Federal do Rio Grande do Sul), started by activists who had been building free alternatives inside Porto Alegre's municipal administration, among them Marcelo D'Elia Branco, Mario Teza and Ronaldo Lages; it is organized by the ASL (Associação SoftwareLivre.org). Later editions moved to the events centre of the PUCRS (Pontifícia Universidade Católica do Rio Grande do Sul) and drew thousands: 7,217 participants in 2013, when the theme was security and privacy, free software in the fight against espionage, and Richard Stallman spoke at the close. The eighteenth edition ran in July 2018.

ix-br.def: Brasil Internet Exchange, formerly PTTMetro: the programme of the Brazilian Network Information Center (NIC.br) and the Brazilian Internet Steering Committee (CGI.br) that runs Brazil's internet exchanges, the PTTs (pontos de troca de tráfego), forty of them by September 2026, one or more in every state.
ix-br.context: It began in July 2004, when CGI.br approved NIC.br's PTTMetro project for metropolitan São Paulo, and it took in the exchange that the São Paulo Research Foundation (FAPESP) had run since 1998. The main name changed to IX.br in 2015, for international recognition and because PTT has several meanings. Each location is an independent exchange serving one metropolitan area, its points of interconnection (PIXes) in partner data centres under central management; participants peer multilaterally through route servers under the multilateral traffic exchange agreement, or bilaterally over a private virtual local area network (VLAN). By NIC.br's figures of September 2026 more than 3,700 autonomous systems are connected through about 7,250 connections, aggregate traffic peaked at 55 Tbit/s in June 2026, and the São Paulo exchange carries about 65 per cent of the total.
ix-br.depth:
Origins. Brazil's first exchange point was operated by the São Paulo Research Foundation (FAPESP) from 1998, alongside others that academic and private bodies had set up. In July 2004 the Brazilian Internet Steering Committee (CGI.br) approved the PTTMetro project of the Brazilian Network Information Center (NIC.br): exchanges in metropolitan regions of about 60 km radius, consolidating the existing initiatives, standardized and organized, and not interconnected with one another. The model let every participant exchange traffic with every other from the moment it connected, which is what drew content and access providers in. NIC.br counts 96 distinct participants after the first five years and 788 after ten. In 2015 the São Paulo exchange passed 1 Tbit/s, with 1.25 Tbit/s across all locations; NIC.br opened its own São Paulo data centre, with five times the space and nine times the power of the previous site; and the main name became IX.br, because PTT, ponto de troca de tráfego, means several different things and the English name is recognized abroad. São Paulo moved from 10 to 100 Gbit/s ports in 2017, and in 2024 was moving from 100 to 400 Gbit/s.

How it is run. IX.br is a CGI.br project, coordinated by the committee and operated by NIC.br, a private non-profit civil entity that has carried out CGI.br's decisions since 2005. Its own description lists the conditions it is built on: neutrality, meaning independence from commercial providers; efficient exchange; low cost with high availability; and a single regional traffic matrix in each metropolitan area. Each IX.br is a set of points of interconnection, the PIXes, hosted in commercial and academic facilities with high standards of security and infrastructure and joined under central management. The money comes from the .br registry: NIC.br says the revenue from domain registrations is reinvested in the infrastructure. Participants choose how to peer. Under the multilateral agreement (Acordo de Troca de Tráfego Multilateral) a single Border Gateway Protocol (BGP) session with the route servers delivers the routes of every other participant in the agreement, and BGP communities control where an announcement goes; bilateral peering runs over a private virtual local area network (VLAN) inside the exchange; a public looking glass shows the route tables; and services such as IP transit or protection against distributed denial of service (DDoS) attacks can be bought and sold across the same fabric. NIC.br states that IX.br follows the Internet Exchange Federation's definition of an exchange.

Scale, with its dates. All figures are NIC.br's own. In February 2024 the aggregate reached 35 Tbit/s, 23 of them in São Paulo; in April 2025 it passed 40 Tbit/s; in March 2026 it reached 50 Tbit/s, 32 in São Paulo, across 39 metropolitan areas, with about 3,800 autonomous systems and 7,000 connections and more than 2,500 networks connected directly in São Paulo. The record in June 2026, during the football World Cup, was 55 Tbit/s. On 23 September 2026 NIC.br announced the fortieth exchange, in Macapá, due to start operating on 25 September, the seventh in the North region, completing the presence in every state; the same release counts more than 3,700 autonomous systems and about 7,250 connections, and puts São Paulo at about 65 per cent of the traffic. Fortaleza, where many submarine cables land, is the second largest.

Decentralization and OpenCDN. The weight of São Paulo is the programme's main structural issue, and NIC.br's answer is OpenCDN: shared infrastructure that lets content delivery networks (CDNs) place cache servers in partner data centres connected to exchanges outside São Paulo, so that popular content is served in the region. By September 2026 it was present in Salvador, Manaus, Brasília, Belo Horizonte, Recife, Caruaru, Feira de Santana, Belém, Goiânia and Campo Grande, and in April 2026 NIC.br reported OpenCDN traffic passing 1 Tb/s. The beneficiaries are mostly small and regional providers: at the twentieth anniversary the director of Abrint, the association of internet and telecommunications providers, credited IX.br with letting regional providers bring broadband to towns where large operators had little commercial interest.

Its place among the world's exchanges. NIC.br describes IX.br as the largest set of internet exchange points in the world, by number of locations, participants and traffic, and São Paulo as the world leader in traffic and participants; other operators publish their own claims, measured their own way, and the ranking depends on whether bits, networks or sites are counted. The structure is the more unusual fact. Where the London exchange is owned by its members and DE-CIX by an industry association, IX.br is a national programme of a multistakeholder steering committee, operated by that committee's non-profit executive arm and paid for by the country's domain registry, which is how one organization came to run forty separate exchanges, from São Paulo to Macapá, under one set of rules.

metasploit.def: The open-source exploitation framework H. D. Moore started in 2003, rewritten from Perl into Ruby in 2007 and owned by Rapid7 since 2009, which its maintainers call the world's most used penetration testing framework: free as the Metasploit Framework under a BSD (Berkeley Software Distribution) licence, commercial as Metasploit Pro.
metasploit.context: Moore published the first public version, written in Perl, on 6 October 2003; version 2.0 followed in April 2004 and the from-scratch Ruby rewrite, 3.0, on 27 March 2007. In October 2009 Rapid7 acquired the project's rights, trademarks and domains, made Moore its chief security officer and undertook to keep the framework open source under the BSD licence, which it still is. Everything in it is a module: exploits, which use a vulnerability to run code on a target; payloads, the code that then runs; auxiliary modules, which scan and gather without exploiting anything; post modules for work after access is gained; and encoders, no-operation (NOP) generators and evasion modules. Its best-known payload, Meterpreter, has been part of it since 2004. Rapid7's commercial editions came and went around the free core: Express from 2010 and Community from 2011 have both been retired, and Metasploit Pro remains on sale.
metasploit.depth:
Why it was built. Moore described the origin twice. In 2006 he said that 2003 was a doldrum, with many people who had published security information moving on and private companies starting to hoard it, and that Metasploit was about creating a framework for developing new exploits quickly, cutting through the boilerplate. In 2009 he wrote that he had created it to publish security information to those who needed it most, the security professionals in the field; in another interview he recalled that it began as a curses-based network game. The first public release, announced on 6 October 2003 as the Exploit Framework, ran its command-line interface on Unix-like systems and on Windows under ActiveState Perl. Version 2.0, in April 2004, had 18 exploits and 27 payloads, three user interfaces and a multi-stage payload system, still in Perl. Version 3.0, on 27 March 2007, was a from-scratch rewrite in Ruby that took nearly two years and more than 100,000 lines of code, shipping with 177 exploits, 104 payloads, 17 encoders, 3 no-operation (NOP) modules and 30 auxiliary modules. The licence followed the code: the developers assigned their copyrights to Metasploit LLC, versions 3.0 and 3.1 carried a commercial-style end-user licence, and in 2008 Moore relicensed the whole codebase under the three-clause BSD (Berkeley Software Distribution) licence with release 3.2.

How it is put together. The documentation organizes everything as modules. Exploit modules use a vulnerability so that the framework can run arbitrary code on the target; payloads are the code that runs, from opening a shell to creating a user; auxiliary modules do data gathering or administrative tasks without exploiting anything; post modules work on a machine already compromised. Payloads come in three forms. Singles are self-contained, fire and forget. Stagers are small stubs whose only job is to set up a communication channel and hand execution to the next stage, which keeps the first payload small and separates the transport from the final code. Stages can then be as large as needed, and written in a higher-level language such as C. Encoders rewrite a payload so that it avoids the bad characters a particular target will not accept, and the documentation says plainly that encoding is not really meant as a way to evade antivirus. Every exploit module carries a rank, from modules that should never crash the service to ones that are unstable enough to amount to a denial of service, so that a tester can weigh the risk to the target. The work is driven from msfconsole, the tab-completing console; msfvenom, which on 8 June 2015 replaced the older separate payload generator and encoder, builds payloads; and an optional PostgreSQL database records the hosts, services and credentials an engagement turns up.

Meterpreter, as a concept. Meterpreter is the framework's advanced payload, part of it since 2004 and first written in C by Matt Miller, known as skape, with later implementations in PHP, Python and Java. It runs in memory: its core library is loaded as shellcode using the reflective dynamic-link library (DLL) injection technique developed by Stephen Fewer, and extensions add the commands an operator uses. The documentation calls the compromised side the server and the controlling Ruby side the client, whichever way the network connection runs. It became the archetype of the post-exploitation agent, which is also why defensive tooling learned to recognize it so well.

Owners and editions. On 21 October 2009 Moore announced that Rapid7 had acquired Metasploit and that he would become Rapid7's chief security officer and Metasploit's chief architect, with Rapid7 committed to keeping the project open source with no change of licence. The next day he explained what had been bought: his own and the LLC's assets, including the rights to the 3.x code, the trademarks and domains and the training material. Metasploit Express arrived in May 2010 as a commercial product built on exactly the same framework code; Metasploit Community followed in 2011 as a packaged edition. Rapid7 ended Express on 4 June 2019, a year after announcing it, to concentrate on Metasploit Pro, and ended the availability of Community in July 2019, noting that the framework was by then packaged by Kali Linux, Parrot OS and Rapid7's own nightly installers. As read on 8 November 2026, Rapid7 sells Metasploit Pro for vulnerability validation, phishing and social engineering campaigns and post-exploitation, with access to more than 4,000 exploit modules through the framework and integration with its InsightVM vulnerability management product; the Metasploit Framework itself remains open source, described by its site as a collaboration between the open-source community and Rapid7.

Testing, teaching, and the disclosure argument. The 3.0 announcement listed its users: penetration testers, system administrators verifying patch installations, vendors running regression tests and researchers. Moore's own argument was that a firm hired to assess a network should prove its findings are real rather than hand over a list of bugs, and that a tool like Metasploit verifies a finding by showing whether the exploit works; he also warned that employers may forbid such tools. Its documentation tells users to do their homework before running any module: read what the vulnerability is and what its side effects are, since a failed memory-corruption exploit can crash the service, and rehearse against a recreated environment. Kali Linux packages it, and OffSec's free Metasploit Unleashed course is a standard way in. The argument about it has never settled. Moore's policy in 2010 was that any vulnerability in the public domain, meaning exploited in the wild or with details or a patch already published, was fair game for a module, even if no patch existed, because users should be able to test their defences against every public threat; in 2006 he argued that partial disclosure never works, because information given to anybody has to be given to everybody. The other side was put by Microsoft during his Month of Browser Bugs that year: that reporting vulnerabilities directly to the vendor serves everyone's interests. Defenders, meanwhile, use the openness: because the modules and Meterpreter are public and documented, they are easy to detect: the open Emerging Threats rule set for intrusion detection carries dozens of signatures named for Metasploit and Meterpreter, and Moore described in 2010 how Rapid7's own vulnerability scanner used Metasploit's exploit information to prioritize which flaws to fix.

net-neutrality.def: The principle that an internet access provider should treat all traffic alike, without blocking, slowing or selling priority to particular content, applications or senders: a term coined by the legal scholar Tim Wu, and law, in different forms, in the European Union, in Brazil and, intermittently, in the United States.
net-neutrality.context: Wu's paper, 'Network Neutrality, Broadband Discrimination', presented it as a way of preserving a Darwinian competition among every use of the internet; his law school dates the coinage to 2002. The core rules look alike everywhere: no blocking of lawful content, no throttling, no paid prioritization, and an exception for reasonable traffic management that is transparent, proportionate and not commercially motivated. The disputes are about those exceptions and about legal authority. In the United States the Federal Communications Commission (FCC) adopted rules in 2010, 2015 and 2024 and repealed them in 2017; the courts struck down the first set in 2014 and set aside the last in January 2025. The European Union (EU) legislated in Regulation 2015/2120, and Brazil in the Marco Civil da Internet of 2014 and Decreto 8.771 of 2016. Zero-rating, exempting chosen applications from a data allowance, is where much of the argument now lives.
net-neutrality.depth:
The principle and its name. Tim Wu's 'Network Neutrality, Broadband Discrimination' appeared in 2003 in volume 2 of the Journal on Telecommunications and High Technology Law, and his law school credits him with coining the term in 2002. The paper came out of the open access debate over vertical integration between internet service providers and cable operators, and generalized it: promoting network neutrality, Wu argued, is no different from promoting fair competition in any privately owned environment, and aims at preserving a Darwinian competition among every conceivable use of the internet so that only the best survive. The worry is that the company owning the access line can favour its own services, or those that pay it, over everyone else's. The counter-argument was there from the start: the paper's own summary notes that critics saw open access regulation as unnecessary and likely to slow broadband deployment, and the same case, that utility-style rules deter investment, framed the American repeal of 2017.

The United States: four orders and three courts. The Federal Communications Commission (FCC) adopted its first Open Internet order on 21 December 2010 with three rules: transparency for fixed and mobile providers, no blocking of lawful content, applications, services or non-harmful devices, and no unreasonable discrimination by fixed providers. On 14 January 2014 the Court of Appeals for the District of Columbia Circuit, in Verizon v. FCC, vacated the anti-blocking and anti-discrimination rules: having classified broadband in a way that exempted it from common carriage, the Commission could not impose what amounted to common carrier obligations. The FCC answered on 26 February 2015 with bright-line bans on blocking, throttling and paid prioritization, grounded in section 706 of the Telecommunications Act and in Title II of the Communications Act, with forbearance from 27 of Title II's provisions, and the same court upheld that order on 14 June 2016. On 14 December 2017 the Restoring Internet Freedom order returned broadband to its Title I classification as an information service, eliminated the conduct rules and kept a transparency requirement; on 1 October 2019 the court upheld it in Mozilla v. FCC but vacated the part that preempted state rules. On 25 April 2024 the FCC reclassified broadband once more as a telecommunications service and restored the rules. On 2 January 2025 the Court of Appeals for the Sixth Circuit, no longer deferring to the agency after the Supreme Court overruled the Chevron doctrine in Loper Bright, held that broadband providers offer only an information service, that the FCC lacked the authority it claimed, and set the 2024 order aside.

The European Union. Regulation (EU) 2015/2120 of 25 November 2015 made the principle law across the Union. Its Article 3 gives end users the right to access and distribute information and content and to use the applications, services and terminal equipment of their choice, and requires providers to treat all traffic equally, without discrimination, restriction or interference. Reasonable traffic management is allowed only if it is transparent, non-discriminatory and proportionate and based on objectively different technical requirements of categories of traffic, not on commercial considerations; beyond that, providers may block or slow traffic only to comply with the law, to protect the integrity and security of the network, or to deal with exceptional congestion. Specialized services optimized for particular applications are permitted only when capacity allows and never as a substitute for internet access. The Body of European Regulators for Electronic Communications (BEREC) published its implementation guidelines on 30 August 2016, as the regulation required, reviewed them in June 2020 and revised them again in 2022.

Brazil. Article 9 of the Marco Civil da Internet, Law 12.965 of 23 April 2014, obliges whoever is responsible for transmission, switching or routing to treat all data packets alike, without distinction by content, origin and destination, service, terminal or application. Discrimination or degradation may arise only from technical requirements indispensable to providing services properly or from the prioritization of emergency services, to be regulated by presidential decree after hearing the Brazilian Internet Steering Committee (CGI.br) and the national telecommunications agency, Anatel; even then the provider must avoid harming users, act with proportionality and transparency, inform users in advance and offer non-discriminatory commercial terms, and, subject to those exceptions, it may not block, monitor, filter or analyse the content of packets. Decreto 8.771 of 11 May 2016 filled in the detail: the technical requirements are network security, such as limiting spam and controlling denial of service attacks, and exceptional congestion; Anatel supervises them, taking account of CGI.br's guidelines; providers must disclose their management practices; and unilateral conduct or agreements are forbidden that compromise the public and unrestricted character of internet access, that prioritize packets because of commercial arrangements, or that favour the provider's own applications, while commercial offers must preserve a single, open, plural and diverse internet.

Zero-rating. A zero tariff, in the Court of Justice of the European Union's words, applies a free or cheaper rate to the traffic of particular partner applications, which then does not count against the data volume a customer has bought. The Court ruled first on 15 September 2020, in the Telenor Magyarország case, that packages letting chosen applications run on after the data allowance was used, while everything else was blocked or slowed, were incompatible with the regulation. On 2 September 2021, in three cases on German operators, it went further: a zero tariff option draws a distinction within internet traffic on commercial grounds and so fails the general obligation of equal treatment. BEREC's 2022 guidelines draw the consequence that such offers are inadmissible, while leaving room for price differentiation that treats traffic equally. The argument on the other side was put in BEREC's consultation, where some respondents warned that a general ban on zero-rating would strongly limit consumer welfare; the answer of the Court is that the incentive a zero tariff creates is itself the distinction the law forbids. The Telecom Regulatory Authority of India (TRAI) had already chosen an outright rule: on 8 February 2016 it prohibited tariffs for data services that discriminate on the basis of content, preferring certainty to case-by-case review.

tia-568.def: The structured cabling standards of the Telecommunications Industry Association (TIA), first issued in 1991 and now the ANSI/TIA-568 E series: the cabling topology, the copper categories and their channels, the T568A and T568B pin assignments, and the optical fibre components.
tia-568.context: Work began in 1985, and the first edition, ANSI/EIA/TIA-568-1991, was a commercial building wiring standard; technical bulletins added cable and connector specifications for Categories 3, 4 and 5, and 568-A absorbed them in 1995. 568-B (2001) divided the standard into general requirements, balanced twisted-pair components and optical fibre components, and 568-C (2009) turned it into a family under a generic customer premises standard, 568-C.0. The current series is E: ANSI/TIA-568.0-E dates from 2020, amended in 2022, and ANSI/TIA-568.2-E, the balanced twisted-pair standard, from October 2024. It is the North American counterpart of ISO/IEC 11801, and the two name the same grades differently: TIA speaks of categories, ISO/IEC of classes for channels, and some grades exist only on the ISO/IEC side.
tia-568.depth:
What it standardizes. Before it, a building's cabling followed whatever each system vendor demanded. ANSI/EIA/TIA-568-1991, the Commercial Building Telecommunications Wiring Standard, specified a generic system instead, independent of the applications that would run over it, and its later editions filled in what that system has to meet. The early bulletins gave Category 3, 4 and 5 cable and connector descriptions, which 568-A absorbed in 1995; the technical bulletin TSB67 of 1995 defined how installed twisted-pair links are tested in the field; Addendum 5 of 1999 defined Category 5e. 568-B in 2001 added performance specifications for 50/125 micron optical fibre, allowed small form factor fibre connectors alongside the SC, replaced the basic link with the permanent link as the test configuration, and set minimum bend radius and maximum pulling tension for horizontal and backbone cable.

How the family is organized. With 568-C in February 2009 the standard became a set of documents: 568-C.0 for generic telecommunications cabling for customer premises, 568-C.1 for commercial buildings, 568-C.2 for balanced twisted-pair cabling and components, and 568-C.3 for optical fibre components. The E series keeps that shape. ANSI/TIA-568.0-E, the generic standard, was published in 2020 and amended by an addendum in 2022. ANSI/TIA-568.2-E was released on 24 October 2024, and TIA announced it on 5 November 2024 together with an addendum to 568.5 whose scope includes single-pair cable. According to Siemon, 568.2-E incorporated two amendments of 568.2-D, and with them guidance on delivering power over balanced twisted pair, now Annex H, covering cable categories, cable types and operating conditions including pathways and bundling, and direct current (DC) resistance unbalance limits, previously set only for Category 8, extended to Categories 5e, 6 and 6A, with the consequence that links certified to 568.2-D may not comply with 568.2-E.

The pin assignments. The standard defines two ways of assigning the four pairs to the eight positions of a modular jack, T568A and T568B. A cord terminated the same way at both ends is straight-through; one terminated differently at each end is a crossover. The rule that follows, one scheme per site, recorded in the wiring closet, is the most familiar piece of the whole standard.

TIA and ISO/IEC. The two bodies write similar standards by different votes. As Siemon's standards director explained, TIA standards represent a consensus of North American corporate members, one vote per company, while ISO/IEC standards are voted one per member country, which is why ISO/IEC specifies extra shielded options, such as Category 7A and Class FA, that TIA does not. TIA does not recognize Category 7 or 7A at all; its Category 8 corresponds to ISO/IEC Class I, the variant that keeps the RJ45-style connector. On the fibre side the SC connector was the one standardized in 568-A, and the connector intermateability standards that 568 relies on are TIA's FOCIS documents, the TIA-604 series.

iso-iec-11801.def: The international generic cabling standard of the International Organization for Standardization (ISO) and the International Electrotechnical Commission (IEC), since 2017 a multi-part series whose Part 1 grades copper channels by class (D to FA, then I and II) and components by category.
iso-iec-11801.context: The first edition of Part 1, dated November 2017, together with Part 2, cancelled and replaced ISO/IEC 11801:2002 and its amendments of 2008 and 2010, gathering into Part 1 the requirements common to every kind of premises; Parts 2 to 6 cover specific premises. Channels are graded by class and components by category: Class D (built from Category 5e) to 100 MHz, E (Category 6) to 250 MHz, EA (6A) to 500 MHz, F (7) to 600 MHz, FA (7A) to 1000 MHz, and Classes I and II, built from Category 8.1 and 8.2 components, to 2000 MHz over channels of 30 m. The same standard grades optical fibre, adding OM5 and OS1a in 2017, and its informative annex gives the U/UTP-style names for screened cable. Amendment 1 to Part 1 was published in 2025.
iso-iec-11801.depth:
Generic, international, voted by countries. ISO/IEC 11801-1 was prepared by subcommittee 25 of ISO/IEC Joint Technical Committee 1, the body responsible for the interconnection of information technology equipment. It specifies a multi-vendor cabling system for voice, data and video, built from components standardized by IEC technical committees and related to separate standards for planning, installation and testing, such as the ISO/IEC 14763 series. Its annex of supported applications records which network technologies have been analysed against which cabling classes. Like the TIA-568 family in North America, its purpose is that a building's cabling can be specified once and serve whatever runs over it; unlike TIA, it is voted one vote per member country, which, as Siemon's standards director explained, is why it carries shielded options that North America does not.

Classes and categories. ISO/IEC keeps two words that TIA tends to merge. A category describes components, the cable, the connectors, the cords; a class describes the channel or link they make. Class D, built from Category 5e components, is specified to 100 MHz; Class E (Category 6) to 250 MHz; Class EA (6A) to 500 MHz; Class F (Category 7) to 600 MHz; Class FA (7A) to 1000 MHz; and Classes I and II to 2000 MHz. Classes D to FA are specified for channels of 100 m. Classes F and FA require S/FTP cable and use non-RJ45 interfaces of the IEC 61076-3 family, and the Telecommunications Industry Association does not recognize them; Panduit describes them as recognized mainly in Europe, with very limited adoption elsewhere. Class I is built from Category 8.1 components and keeps the IEC 60603-7 modular connector, the RJ45 style; Class II is built from Category 8.2 components and uses non-RJ45 interfaces. Both are characterized to 2 GHz for channels of up to 30 m with no more than two connectors, aimed at server-to-switch links at the edge of the data centre, and TIA's Category 8 corresponds to Class I.

What changed in 2017. The foreword of Part 1 lists the significant technical changes: the standard was restructured around the elements common to all generic cabling; balanced channel and link Classes I and II were added, with a coaxial class; component requirements were added for Categories 8.1 and 8.2; the cabled fibre categories OS1a and OM5 were added; and OM1, OM2 and OS1 fibre cables were moved to an informative annex.

Naming screened cable. An informative annex of the standard, Annex D in Part 1 of 2017 and Annex E in the 2010 edition, gives the designations for balanced cables in the form XX/YZZ: the overall screen, then the screen of each pair, then the element, as in U/UTP, F/UTP, U/FTP and S/FTP. Because the annex is informative, the names are a convention rather than a requirement, and catalogues still mix them with older trade names such as FTP and STP.

fibre-connectors.def: The plugs that join optical fibres: the ST and SC, both on 2.5 mm ferrules; the LC, on a 1.25 mm ferrule, which has become the default; and the MPO array connector, of which MTP is a trade name, carrying rows of 12 or 16 fibres for parallel optics.
fibre-connectors.context: Each holds its fibre in a precision ferrule, usually ceramic in single-fibre designs, and an adapter aligns two ferrules end to end. ST, a bayonet connector and an AT&T trademark, was probably the most popular multimode connector until about 2005; SC, a snap-in push-pull design, was the connector standardized in TIA-568-A; LC, with a ferrule half the size, is the small form factor (SFF) connector that succeeded where others did not; and MPO (multi-position optical) aligns plastic multi-fibre ferrules on pins and holes, for pre-terminated trunks and 40 and 100 Gbit/s multimode links. Colour carries the end-face polish: blue for a flat physical contact (PC) single-mode connector, green for an angled one (APC).
fibre-connectors.depth:
The ferrule is the connector. A fibre core is a few microns to a few tens of microns across, so joining two fibres means holding each in a rigid, precisely bored ferrule and bringing the ferrules together in a sleeve. The Fiber Optic Association traces the modern designs to the ceramic ferrule that appeared in Japan in the mid-1980s, which made alignment precise enough for ferrules to touch, and to convex end faces for physical contact (PC) between them; in the late 1990s small form factor (SFF) connectors arrived, and of those only the LC became a runaway success, in telecom networks and in high-speed local and storage networks alike.

The common types. ST has a bayonet mount, a long cylindrical 2.5 mm ferrule and a spring that has to seat properly. SC is a snap-in connector on the same 2.5 mm ferrule that latches with a push-pull motion and also comes in a duplex form; it was the connector TIA-568-A standardized, and was slow to spread only because it cost twice as much as ST at first. FC, another 2.5 mm design, screws on and was long a favourite for single-mode before SC and LC displaced it. Because ST, SC and FC share the ferrule size, hybrid adapters can mate one to another. LC uses a 1.25 mm ferrule, half the size of the SC, terminates like any ceramic-ferrule connector and is particularly favoured for single-mode; the MU and LX-5 share its ferrule, the LX-5 adding a shutter over the fibre end.

MPO and MTP. MPO, multi-position optical, is an array connector for ribbon fibre: a plastic ferrule holding 12 or 16 fibres in a row, with up to two rows in common use, aligned by pins on one ferrule and holes in the other. It is used for pre-terminated cable assemblies and for parallel optics, where 40 and 100 Gbit/s multimode links send each lane down its own fibre, and it brings its own complications of polarity and testing. MTP is US Conec's registered trade name for its connector of this family.

Standards and colours. The most popular connectors are specified in TIA's connector intermateability standards, the FOCIS documents of the TIA-604 series: FOCIS-2 for ST, 3 for SC, 4 for FC, 10 for LC, 5 for the 12-fibre MPO and 18 for the 16-fibre version. Colour codes tell the plant apart at a glance: aqua cable for laser-optimised 50/125 multimode (OM3 and OM4), lime green for OM5, yellow for single-mode, and, on single-mode connectors, blue for a flat PC polish and green for an angled APC one.

endianness.def: The order in which a processor, a file format or a protocol lays out the bytes of a number wider than one byte: big-endian puts the most significant byte at the lowest address, little-endian the least significant.
endianness.context: Danny Cohen named the two orders in 1980, after the egg war in Gulliver's Travels. Internet headers are big-endian, which RFC 791 states and POSIX calls network byte order; x86-64 and most Arm systems are little-endian; IBM z is big-endian; Power, RISC-V, MIPS and SPARC can run either way, which is called bi-endian. Code converts at every boundary with htonl, ntohs and their relatives, and a missed conversion produces a valid wrong number rather than an error: port 80 written in host order on a little-endian machine is read from the wire as port 20480.
endianness.depth:
What it is. The 32-bit value 0x0A0B0C0D is stored as the bytes 0A 0B 0C 0D on a big-endian machine and 0D 0C 0B 0A on a little-endian one. POSIX defines the two: a little-endian representation has the least significant byte first, with significance increasing as the address increases, and a big-endian one the most significant byte first. Only numbers wider than a byte are affected: single bytes, ASCII text and UTF-8 look the same either way, and the order of bits inside a byte is the link layer's business, not software's (RFC 2469 records that Ethernet maps the first bit of each byte on the wire to its least significant bit, while Token Ring did the opposite).

Where it is fixed. Intel's manual calls Intel 64 and IA-32 processors little endian machines, and IBM's z/Architecture addresses a field by its leftmost, high-order byte. The Power ISA lets the operating system choose the order with one mode bit; RISC-V defines little-endian, big-endian and bi-endian variants but always stores instructions as little-endian parcels; SPARC V9 is big-endian by default with little-endian data accesses; Linux describes MIPS systems as built for one order or the other. Among formats, the Internet headers, PNG, Java class files, XDR (External Data Representation) and CBOR are big-endian; BMP and WebAssembly memory are little-endian; TIFF marks its order with II or MM, ELF with the EI_DATA byte, and UTF-16 text with a byte order mark, without which the Unicode Standard and RFC 2781 read it as big-endian while browsers, following the WHATWG Encoding Standard, take the label utf-16 to mean UTF-16LE.

Converting. The conversions are cheap and named by direction: htonl and ntohl in POSIX, htobe32 and le32toh in its newer endian.h, cpu_to_be32 in the Linux kernel, the ! and the less-than and greater-than prefixes of Python's struct. Processors carry instructions for it: BSWAP and MOVBE on x86, LOAD REVERSED on IBM z, the byte-reverse loads and stores on Power, rev8 in RISC-V's Zbb extension. To find out what a machine is, Python's sys.byteorder answers little or big, and lscpu prints a Byte Order line.

Why it matters. Neither order wins on merit: Cohen's memo lists what serial comparators prefer and what serial adders prefer, and concludes that it is more important to agree upon an order than which order is agreed upon. RISC-V's designers chose little-endian because it dominates commercially, and kept big-endian variants because IP networking works on big-endian data; RFC 4506 admits that XDR's single big-endian order is unfair to little-endian machines, and argues that one order means no protocol is needed to read the data. The real cost is the conversion at each boundary and the bugs when one is missed: a port or an address loaded raw, UTF-16 decoded in the wrong order, a hash taken over raw bytes. The Linux bonding driver hashes raw address bytes, so an x86-64 server and an s390x guest compute different hashes for the same flow, and with three, five, six or seven members they often send it over different links.

dmca.def: The Digital Millennium Copyright Act, the 1998 US law that made it unlawful to circumvent the technical locks guarding copyrighted works or to traffic in tools that do, and that shields online service providers from liability for their users' infringement when they take material down on notice.
dmca.context: Signed on 28 October 1998 to implement two 1996 WIPO (World Intellectual Property Organization) treaties, the DMCA (Digital Millennium Copyright Act) has two halves an engineer meets. Section 1201 bans circumventing access controls and trafficking in circumvention tools, with narrow statutory exceptions and temporary exemptions set every three years, which now cover good-faith security research and repair. Section 512 gives hosting and search providers safe harbours if they register an agent, remove material on a valid notice, restore it on a counter-notice and terminate repeat infringers. The Sklyarov, Felten, DeCSS and Green v. Department of Justice cases were all fought over section 1201.
dmca.depth:
The DMCA (Digital Millennium Copyright Act) was signed by President Clinton on 28 October 1998 as Public Law 105-304. It implements two treaties concluded at the WIPO (World Intellectual Property Organization) in 1996, the WIPO Copyright Treaty and the WIPO Performances and Phonograms Treaty, which require legal remedies against circumventing technological measures such as encryption and against tampering with rights management information. Title I adds section 1201, the anti-circumvention law, to the US Copyright Act; Title II adds the section 512 safe harbours; Title III lets a computer's owner authorize the copy of a program made when the machine is switched on for maintenance or repair.

Section 1201 separates measures that control access to a work from measures that protect a right such as copying. Circumventing an access control, by descrambling, decrypting or otherwise bypassing it without the copyright owner's authority, is prohibited; circumventing a copy control is not, a distinction the Copyright Office explained in 1998 by noting that fair use can justify copying but is no defence to unauthorized access. Two trafficking bans reach anyone who makes, imports or offers a technology, product, service or component that is primarily designed to circumvent either kind of measure, has only limited commercially significant use otherwise, or is marketed for circumvention. Wilful violation for commercial advantage or private financial gain is a crime: up to $500,000 or five years for a first offence.

Three statutory exceptions matter to engineers. Section 1201(f) lets a person lawfully entitled to use a program circumvent to identify and analyse what an independently created program needs to interoperate with it, build tools for that, and share the results solely for that purpose. Section 1201(g) covers good-faith encryption research on a lawfully obtained copy, after a good-faith effort to obtain authorization. Section 1201(j) covers security testing: accessing a computer, system or network solely to test, investigate or correct a flaw in good faith, with the authorization of its owner or operator. None shelters conduct that breaks other laws, and the text names the Computer Fraud and Abuse Act.

On the recommendation of the Register of Copyrights, the Librarian of Congress exempts classes of works from the ban on the act of circumvention, three years at a time; the trafficking bans are beyond the rulemaking's reach. Good-faith security research entered the rule in 2015 for consumer devices, motorized land vehicles and implanted medical devices, over manufacturers' objections that they already authorize research; the 2018 rule dropped the device list, and in 2021 a condition that the research break no other law became a warning that the exemption is no safe harbour from such laws. Vehicle repair was exempted in 2015 at the request of the EFF (Electronic Frontier Foundation); in 2021 device repair was widened to any software-enabled consumer device, and medical devices gained an exemption. The ninth cycle, in force from 28 October 2024, renewed every exemption petitioned for and added retail-level commercial food preparation equipment and owners' access to vehicle operational data. In the tenth, a notice of 28 October 2026 reported 43 renewal petitions and the Register's intention to recommend readopting every exemption but one: medical-device repair met meaningful opposition and is being argued afresh; renewals will run from October 2027 to October 2030.

Section 512, in Title II, offers safe harbours, each barring money damages, for transitory communications, system caching, storage at a user's direction and information location tools. Every provider must adopt, reasonably implement and tell users about a policy of terminating repeat infringers in appropriate circumstances; hosts and location tools must also name an agent on their site and in the Copyright Office's online directory, where a designation lapses after three years unless renewed. A takedown notice to that agent identifies the work and the material, states a good-faith belief that the use is unauthorized and swears, under penalty of perjury, to the sender's authority; the provider must act expeditiously. A counter-notice swears to a good-faith belief that the removal was a mistake or misidentification, and the material returns within 10 to 14 business days unless the claimant reports having sued. In May 2020 the Copyright Office concluded that the balance Congress intended had been tilted askew.

The cases the glossary tells are all section 1201 cases: civil suits over DeCSS and Felten, the EFF noted, and a criminal prosecution of Sklyarov.
