DeCSS, written in 1999 by the Norwegian teenager Jon Johansen and two others, decrypted the CSS (Content Scramble System) on DVDs (digital versatile discs); eight studios sued Eric Corley of 2600 for posting and linking to it, and in 2001 the Second Circuit upheld the injunction as aimed at the code's function, not its speech. Edward Felten's team, threatened in April 2001 over a paper on breaking the SDMI (Secure Digital Music Initiative) watermarks, sued with the EFF as counsel and presented it that August. Dmitry Sklyarov was arrested in Las Vegas in July 2001, after speaking at DEF CON, and charged with trafficking over ElcomSoft's eBook software; a jury acquitted ElcomSoft in December 2002. Green v. Department of Justice, filed in 2016 for Matthew Green and bunnie Huang, attacked the statute itself; in August 2024 the District of Columbia Circuit rejected its facial First Amendment claims.

The EFF's March 2013 report Unintended Consequences: Fifteen Years under the DMCA argued that section 1201 had been invoked less against pirates than against scientists, consumers and competitors, for instance to block aftermarket printer cartridges and garage door openers, and that its exceptions were too narrow; user groups told the Copyright Office that a right to circumvent can mean little without help from technicians, whom no rulemaking can exempt from the trafficking bans. Copyright owners told the same study that the law had worked as Congress intended, underpinning streaming services built on technical protection, and credited the trafficking bans with keeping circumvention tools out of the mainstream; the court in Green called piracy the law's heartland. The Office's June 2017 report kept the framework and called the trafficking bans critical, but asked Congress to consider easing the authorization requirements for security testing and encryption research and making repair, assistive technology and phone unlocking permanent exemptions.

right-to-repair.def: The principle, and the movement behind it, that whoever owns a machine should be able to fix it, or have anyone they choose fix it, with the parts, tools, documentation, diagnostic software and firmware the manufacturer gives its own authorized repairers, on fair terms and without software locks that reject replacement parts.
right-to-repair.context: It began with cars: Massachusetts voters required carmakers to share dealer-level repair information in 2012 and telematics data in 2020. In May 2021 the Federal Trade Commission (FTC) told Congress it had found scant evidence for manufacturers' reasons for restricting repair, and from 2022 New York, Minnesota, California, Colorado and Oregon passed laws for electronics, Oregon and Colorado also curbing parts pairing. The European Union (EU) set repair rules for smartphones from June 2025 and a repair directive that applies from July 2026. Manufacturers cite safety, security and intellectual property; advocates such as iFixit answer that repair monopolies raise prices and waste working devices.
right-to-repair.depth:
What is asked for. Owners, and any repairer they choose, should get the parts, tools, manuals, diagnostic software and firmware the manufacturer gives its own authorized network, on comparable terms; iFixit, a repair-guide and parts company among the loudest advocates, adds the software to reset security locks and pair parts. Parts pairing, which Oregon's law defines as using software to identify component parts through a unique identifier, can leave a working replacement limited, flagged with warnings or refused. The Electronic Frontier Foundation (EFF) adds copyright: people own the device but only license its software, under terms that can forbid reverse engineering, transfer and unauthorized repair.

Cars first. In 2012 Massachusetts voters approved Question 1, requiring carmakers, from model year 2015, to give owners and independent shops the diagnostic and repair information their dealers get; it took almost 86 per cent of the yes and no votes. A second Question 1 took 75 per cent in 2020 and required a standardized open-access platform for telematics data from model year 2022. The carmakers' Alliance for Automotive Innovation sued, lost in February 2025 and, on appeal, argued that the law forces makers to disable the cybersecurity guarding steering and braking; in February 2026 the parties paused the case to discuss a settlement.

Washington. In May 2021 the Federal Trade Commission (FTC) told Congress, in 'Nixing the Fix', that it had found scant evidence for manufacturers' justifications for repair restrictions, and on 21 July 2021 it voted 5 to 0 to make unlawful restrictions an enforcement priority. Executive Order 14036 of 9 July 2021 had encouraged rules against such restrictions, citing farmers; it was revoked in August 2025. Enforcement reached the farm: in January 2025 the FTC, Illinois and Minnesota sued Deere & Company, alleging that only its dealers had the fully functional Service ADVISOR tool, while Deere had argued that independent repairs risked breaching emissions law. A ten-year settlement filed in July 2026, subject to court approval, obliges Deere to offer owners and independent shops, on fair and reasonable terms, the repair resources its dealers get, including fault codes, reprogramming and the pairing of new parts.

Copyright. Section 1201 of the Digital Millennium Copyright Act (DMCA) makes it unlawful to circumvent technological measures that control access to software, even to repair. Every three years the Librarian of Congress, advised by the Register of Copyrights, grants exemptions for the next three. Repair entered in 2015 for land vehicles and widened to smartphones and home appliances in 2018, to any software-enabled device primarily designed for consumers and to medical devices in 2021, and to retail-level commercial food preparation equipment in 2024, when a broader class for commercial and industrial equipment was declined. No exemption may serve as a defence under any other provision, so the bans on trafficking in circumvention tools still apply.

The states. New York's Digital Fair Repair Act, signed on 28 December 2022, was the first state law of its kind for electronics; it covers equipment first made and sold there from 1 July 2023 but excludes cars, medical devices, off-road equipment, home appliances and business-contract sales. Minnesota's act, in force from 1 July 2024, reaches equipment sold since 1 July 2021, file servers included according to iFixit. California's Senate Bill 244, in force from 1 July 2024, requires parts, tools and documentation for three years after a model's last manufacture at a wholesale price of 50 to 99.99 dollars and seven years above that. Colorado covered powered wheelchairs in 2022, farm equipment in 2023 and digital electronics from 1 January 2026. Oregon's Senate Bill 1596, in force from 1 January 2025, forbids, on devices first made and sold from 2025, parts pairing that blocks a working replacement, degrades performance or shows misleading warnings; Colorado's law has a similar clause.

Europe. In the European Union (EU), ecodesign regulations of 2019 set repairability requirements for appliances, displays and servers, and Regulation (EU) 2024/1781 makes repairability an aspect future rules must improve. From 20 June 2025, Regulation (EU) 2023/1670 requires smartphone and tablet makers to supply professional repairers with spare parts for at least seven years after a model leaves the market and to give them the software that serialized parts need, and an energy label grades repairability from A to E. Directive (EU) 2024/1799, applicable from 31 July 2026, obliges manufacturers to repair covered goods free or at a reasonable price, bars techniques that impede repair unless justified by legitimate and objective factors, and adds 12 months to the seller's liability when a consumer opts for repair. France has shown a repairability score out of ten since 2021, replaced in 2025 by a durability index for televisions and washing machines.

The two cases. The FTC grouped manufacturers' objections as intellectual property, safety, cybersecurity, liability and reputation. Apple, which backed California's bill, opposed Oregon's pairing clause, its engineer John Perry testifying that it would undermine the security, safety and privacy of Oregonians by forcing makers to accept parts of unknown origin; the Business Council of New York warned that sensitive technical data would reach almost any repairer who asked. Advocates cite the FTC's finding, iFixit's teardowns, which found more paired parts in the iPhone 15 than in any earlier iPhone, and cost and waste: Consumer Reports says repair rights save money and cut waste, and the EFF that restrictions drive independent shops out of business.

For network and information technology (IT) engineers. Most laws stop short of the equipment room: New York excludes business-contract sales, Oregon covers household equipment only, Colorado excludes routers or all-in-one devices delivering internet, video and voice, and Minnesota exempts IT equipment intended for critical infrastructure, an exemption the group SecuRepairs warned could reach business routers and switches. A 2026 Colorado bill adding that exemption, backed above all by Cisco according to iFixit, failed 7 to 4 in a House committee after a sponsor said repair instructions could help reverse-engineer critical systems and a retired IT repairer answered that a water utility's router is the one retailers use. Licences and firmware add a layer: Cisco's transfer policy lets software rights pass to a new owner only where law requires it, a listed scenario applies or Cisco consents for a fee, while the EU servers regulation keeps firmware available for eight years after a model's last unit, network servers excepted.

psyop.def: Psychological operations: in military doctrine, planned activities that use communication and other means to influence the perceptions, attitudes and behaviour of selected audiences in support of political and military objectives.
psyop.context: PSYOP (psychological operations) names both a military function and, in the United States Army, the units that perform it. NATO (North Atlantic Treaty Organization) doctrine speaks of approved audiences; US doctrine speaks of foreign ones. The US Department of Defense renamed the function MISO (military information support operations) in 2010, citing sensitivities to the old term; Army Special Operations Command gave its units back the PSYOP name in 2017, and a memo signed on 2 December 2025 by Secretary of Defense Pete Hegseth orders the function renamed PSYOP as well, DefenseScoop reported.
psyop.depth:
Psychological operations, written PSYOP in United States usage and PSYOPS in NATO (North Atlantic Treaty Organization) doctrine, are planned activities that use communication and other means to shape what an audience perceives, believes and does. NATO's strategic communications doctrine, AJP-10 (March 2023), defines a psychological operation as planned activities "directed at approved audiences in order to influence perceptions, attitudes and behaviours, affecting the achievement of political and military objectives". The earlier US Department of Defense definition, as quoted by Majors Chaveso Cook and David Cowen in Military Review in 2018, described activities "directed towards foreign countries, organizations, and individuals".

Leaflets, radio broadcasts and loudspeaker messages are the means a Special Operations Command spokesman named when he described the job to the Associated Press in 2010. US joint doctrine recounts one large case from the Persian Gulf War, citing the April 1992 final report to Congress on its conduct: 29 million leaflets carrying 33 different messages were disseminated in the Kuwait theatre of operations, and a coalition radio network, Voice of the Gulf, broadcast 18 hours a day for 40 days.

Truthfulness and attribution are where doctrine meets its critics. NATO's 2014 psychological operations doctrine, AJP-3.10.1, says PSYOPS "must be based on true information" and are generally attributable to NATO or a concurring partner. The British national elements printed in the same publication sort products into white (acknowledged by the sponsor), grey (not revealing their source) and black (appearing to come from a source other than the true one), and say British PSYOPS are predominantly, but not exclusively, white. Christopher Paul of the RAND Corporation wrote in July 2010 that US doctrine then allowed for messages not wholly true or made to appear to come from someone else, and argued for rewriting it to ban both; The Washington Post reported in September 2022 that Pentagon policy discourages falsehoods but has no specific rule requiring truthful information in psychological operations.

The US name has changed twice. The switch to MISO (military information support operations) was approved in mid-June 2010 by Defense Secretary Robert Gates and Admiral Eric Olson, the spokesman Ken McGraw told the Associated Press, citing foreign and domestic sensitivities to the old term; Alfred Paddock, a retired colonel who had been Director for Psychological Operations in the Office of the Secretary of Defense from 1986 to 1988, said the military was giving in to political correctness. Army Special Operations Command restored PSYOP as the name of its units on 27 October 2017, keeping MISO for their function, and the memo Pete Hegseth signed on 2 December 2025, reported by DefenseScoop, tasks the Under Secretary of Defense for Policy with renaming the function PSYOP by the end of fiscal year 2026. US doctrine notes that the 2010 change did not affect non-US terminology.

miso.def: Military information support operations: the United States Department of Defense term, from 2010, for planned operations that convey selected information to foreign audiences to influence their emotions, reasoning and behaviour in the originator's favour; a December 2025 memo restores the older name, psychological operations (PSYOP).
miso.context: MISO (military information support operations) replaced psychological operations as the US name for the function in 2010, and the doctrine that carries it says US MISO will not target US citizens under any circumstances. From 2017 Army units were again called PSYOP (psychological operations) while their function stayed MISO. In September 2022 the Under Secretary of Defense for Policy ordered a review of MISO after social media companies took down fake accounts suspected of being run by the US military, The Washington Post reported. A memo of 2 December 2025 sets the end of fiscal year 2026 for retiring the term.
miso.depth:
MISO (military information support operations) is the United States term for the function NATO (North Atlantic Treaty Organization) calls psychological operations. Joint Publication 3-13.2, as changed in December 2011, defines MISO as "planned operations to convey selected information and indicators to foreign audiences to influence their emotions, motives, objective reasoning, and ultimately the behavior of foreign governments, organizations, groups, and individuals in a manner favorable to the originator's objectives". Among the legal considerations it lists the requirement that US MISO "will not target US citizens at any time, in any location globally, or under any circumstances".

The name dates from a decision approved in mid-June 2010, which a Special Operations Command spokesman attributed to foreign and domestic sensitivities to the term psychological operations. Rosa Brooks, then senior adviser to the Under Secretary of Defense for Policy, wrote in an internal e-mail later quoted by Army Times that it was "just a terminological change, not a substantive change". A Secretary of Defense memo of 3 December 2010 carried MISO into joint doctrine; an Army message of 19 April 2011 confined the change to the function, and on 27 October 2017 Army Special Operations Command gave its units back the PSYOP (psychological operations) name, its spokesman summing up: "PSYOP forces conduct MISO." Writing in Military Review in 2018, Majors Chaveso Cook and David Cowen found no evidence that the new term changed attitudes in the State Department.

Reported operations put the function under review. In August 2022 Graphika and the Stanford Internet Observatory analysed five years of covert pro-Western accounts removed by Twitter and Meta, noting that neither company had attributed them. In September The Washington Post reported that Under Secretary Colin Kahl had ordered a review of MISO; the Pentagon press secretary, Brigadier General Patrick Ryder, said information operations must comply with relevant laws and policies: "We are committed to enforcing those safeguards." In November 2022 Meta said the network was linked to individuals associated with the US military.

In June 2024 Reuters reported a clandestine psychological operation in 2020 and 2021 to discredit Chinese vaccines in the Philippines. The Pentagon spokesman Pete Nguyen said an initial review had found the US military not responsible for the social media content Reuters cited, while a later US message to the Philippine government, reviewed by Reuters, said the Department of Defense "did message Philippines audiences questioning the safety and efficacy of Sinovac" and had "made some missteps".

On 2 December 2025 Secretary of Defense Pete Hegseth signed a memo, reported by DefenseScoop, replacing MISO with PSYOP and giving the Under Secretary of Defense for Policy, Elbridge Colby, until the end of fiscal year 2026 to complete the change. The memo says the 2010 renaming sought to disassociate the activities from "misleading or negative connotations".

propaganda.def: Information, especially of a biased or misleading nature, used to promote a political cause or point of view, as the North Atlantic Treaty Organization defines it; more broadly, systematic effort to win public support for an opinion or a course of action.
propaganda.context: The word goes back to a congregation of cardinals founded in Rome in 1627 to oversee foreign missions, and it took on a sinister sense mainly during the First World War, as Scientific American wrote in a passage Edward Bernays quoted in 1928. George Creel, who chaired the United States Committee on Public Information from 1917, said the committee avoided the word because German use had tied it to deceit. In the Second World War, white propaganda was openly acknowledged by its sponsor, while black propaganda was disguised as coming from the enemy's own side.
propaganda.depth:
NATO (North Atlantic Treaty Organization) defines propaganda as "Information, especially of a biased or misleading nature, used to promote a political cause or point of view", the wording of its glossary AAP-06 (2019 edition) and of its strategic communications doctrine AJP-10 (2023). Edward Bernays, in his 1928 book Propaganda, quoted dictionary senses tracing it to a congregation of cardinals set up in Rome in 1627 to oversee foreign missions, and defined modern propaganda as "a consistent, enduring effort to create or shape events to influence the relations of the public to an enterprise, idea or group". Whether it is good or bad, he argued, depends on the merit of the cause and the correctness of the information.

The word's sinister sense dates mainly from the First World War, according to a Scientific American passage Bernays quoted. President Woodrow Wilson created the Committee on Public Information by Executive Order 2594 on 13 April 1917, with George Creel as its civilian chairman. Creel wrote in 1920: "We did not call it propaganda, for that word, in German hands, had come to be associated with deceit and corruption." He also wrote that the committee was in no degree an agency of censorship, whereas the National Archives' summary of its records says it administered voluntary press censorship. After the war, Bernays asked whether the techniques used on patriotic opinion could be applied to the problems of peace.

The Second World War sorted propaganda by source. The Office of War Information, established by Executive Order 9182 on 13 June 1942, handled white, openly attributed material, while the Office of Strategic Services ran black propaganda made to appear to come from among enemy troops or from the Axis homelands, as a 2017 review in Studies in Intelligence, a journal of the CIA (Central Intelligence Agency), describes. The Voice of America's first German-language broadcast in 1942 told listeners: "The news may be good for us. The news may be bad. But we shall tell you the truth." Even its date is disputed: the station long marked 25 February, and Chris Kern, a former member of its staff, found script numbering that points to 1 February, the date it now gives.

United States law draws a line at home. The Smith-Mundt Act of 1948, as amended in January 2013, provides that no funds appropriated to the Department of State or the Broadcasting Board of Governors "shall be used to influence public opinion in the United States". In research on information disorder the word sits beside newer ones: Ethan Zuckerman, quoted in the Council of Europe's 2017 report by Claire Wardle and Hossein Derakhshan, called propaganda "weaponized speech designed to support one party over another", one of several things he said the label fake news lumps together.

active-measures.def: A literal translation of the Soviet term aktivnyye meropriyatiya: covert or deceptive operations, such as disinformation, front organizations and clandestine radio, run to influence foreign governments and publics in support of Soviet foreign policy; United States investigators applied the term to Russian operations again in 2019.
active-measures.context: A 1987 US State Department report defined active measures as covert or deceptive operations in support of Soviet foreign policy, distinct from espionage and from ordinary diplomacy, and called deception their essence. A case later documented from Soviet-bloc archives is the 1980s campaign claiming that the United States had created AIDS (acquired immune deficiency syndrome); in 1992 the head of Russia's foreign intelligence service confirmed the participation of the KGB (Committee for State Security). In 2019 the US Special Counsel described the Internet Research Agency's social media operations as active measures, a charge the Kremlin rejected.
active-measures.depth:
The US State Department's report Soviet Influence Activities (August 1987) defines active measures, from the Russian aktivnyye meropriyatiya, as "covert or deceptive operations conducted in support of Soviet foreign policy", distinct both from espionage and counterintelligence and from traditional diplomatic and informational activities, and states: "Deception is the essence of active measures." It placed covert active measures with Service A of the First Chief Directorate of the KGB (Committee for State Security). Thomas Boghardt, writing in 2009 in Studies in Intelligence, a journal of the CIA (Central Intelligence Agency), lists media manipulation, written and oral disinformation, front organizations and clandestine radio among them, and cites a 1980 CIA estimate of their annual cost at $3 billion.

A case later documented from Soviet-bloc archives is the campaign claiming that the United States had made AIDS (acquired immune deficiency syndrome). It opened on 17 July 1983 with an anonymous letter in the Indian newspaper Patriot; by late 1987, Boghardt writes, the story had circulated in the media of 80 countries, in over 200 periodicals and 25 languages. A KGB telegram of 7 September 1985 to Bulgarian state security, found in the Sofia archives by the historian Christopher Nehring, gives the goal as creating a favourable opinion abroad that the disease came from secret US biological-weapons experiments. The US government's 1987 tally, compiled by the campaign's target, lists a placement in Rio de Janeiro's Jornal do Brasil on 18 March 1987.

Moscow never publicly acknowledged authorship in the Soviet period, Boghardt writes. After Secretary of State George Shultz told Mikhail Gorbachev on 23 October 1987 that the Soviet Union had peddled "bum dope" on AIDS, the Soviet Academy of Sciences disavowed, through Izvestia, the thesis that AIDS was artificially created, although Sovetskaya Rossiya repeated the claim the same day. In 1992 Yevgeny Primakov, director of the SVR (Russian foreign intelligence), confirmed the KGB's participation, according to Boghardt, who cites the Boston Globe and Izvestiya of 19 March 1992. Details remain disputed: Douglas Selvage and Christopher Nehring wrote in 2019 that the East German Stasi called the operation Denver, not INFEKTION, and Erhard Geissler and Robert Hunt Sprinkle argue that the biologist Jakob Segal promoted the theory independently of any security service.

The term outlived the Soviet Union. The US Special Counsel's report of March 2019 said the Internet Research Agency's social media operations constituted active measures, "a term that typically refers to operations conducted by Russian security services aimed at influencing the course of international affairs". Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov said in April 2019 that the report contained "no proven evidence" of interference; in February 2023 Yevgeny Prigozhin, charged by US prosecutors in 2018 as the agency's funder, told Der Spiegel that he had invented, created and run it.

disinformation.def: False or misleading information created or spread deliberately, to deceive or to cause harm; definitions differ on whether the intent that counts is to harm, to deceive or to gain, and some newer policy terms judge the behaviour around a message rather than its falseness.
disinformation.context: Claire Wardle and Hossein Derakhshan's 2017 report for the Council of Europe defines disinformation as false information deliberately created to harm, beside misinformation (false, shared without intent to harm) and malinformation (genuine, used to harm). The European Commission's 2020 definition turns on an intention to deceive or to secure economic or political gain, and NATO (North Atlantic Treaty Organization) doctrine uses the dictionary sense, information intended to mislead. The Commission said common definitions still needed refining.
disinformation.depth:
Institutional definitions turn on intent and differ on what the intent is. The Council of Europe report Information Disorder (2017), by Claire Wardle and Hossein Derakhshan, defines disinformation as "Information that is false and deliberately created to harm a person, social group, organization or country". The European Commission's European Democracy Action Plan (December 2020) describes "false or misleading content that is spread with an intention to deceive or secure economic or political gain and which may cause public harm", and says in the same document that refined common definitions are still needed. The 2023 strategic communications doctrine of NATO (North Atlantic Treaty Organization) borrows the Concise Oxford English Dictionary: "Information which is intended to mislead."

The word had an earlier official use. The US State Department's 1987 report on Soviet active measures described disinformation as "a deliberate attempt to deceive public or governmental opinion", which can be oral or written, and treated it as one of the instruments of those measures.

Wardle and Derakhshan avoid the label fake news, which they call woefully inadequate and say politicians have appropriated to describe news organizations whose coverage they find disagreeable. They separate the phases of creation, production and distribution, because the agent who creates a message may differ from the one who produces it and from the many who pass it on, each with different motives; their example is the planners of a state campaign and the low-paid trolls who turn its themes into posts. A BBC (British Broadcasting Corporation) World Service survey of eighteen countries in September 2017, cited in their report, found that 79 per cent of respondents worried about what was fake and what was real on the internet, and that Brazilians were the most concerned, at 92 per cent.

Policy has partly moved from content to behaviour. The EEAS (European External Action Service) describes FIMI (foreign information manipulation and interference) as narrower than disinformation, because it covers only foreign actors, and broader, because the information "does not need to be verifiably false or misleading"; the deciding factor is deceptive or manipulative behaviour. Its fourth threat report, of March 2026, analysed 540 incidents detected in 2025, left 65 per cent of them unattributed and says its findings are neither exhaustive nor representative.

misinformation.def: False information shared without the intention of causing harm, often by people who believe it; the counterpart of disinformation, which is false and deliberately harmful, and of malinformation, which is genuine but used to harm.
misinformation.context: The three-way distinction comes from Claire Wardle and Hossein Derakhshan's 2017 report for the Council of Europe, and the European Commission drew a similar line in 2020, adding that the effects of misinformation can still be harmful. Research on why false beliefs persist bears on it directly: repetition makes statements feel truer, and corrections reduce belief without entirely erasing it. The backfire effect, in which a correction strengthens the error, is disputed: a replication with over 10,000 participants did not find it.
misinformation.depth:
In the typology Claire Wardle and Hossein Derakhshan set out for the Council of Europe in 2017, misinformation is "Information that is false, but not created with the intention of causing harm"; disinformation is false and deliberately harmful, and malinformation is genuine information used to harm. The European Commission's European Democracy Action Plan (December 2020) draws the same line, defining misinformation as false or misleading content shared without harmful intent, "though the effects can still be harmful, e.g. when people share false information with friends and family in good faith".

The report's example is the attack on the Champs-Élysées in Paris on 20 April 2017, after which people on social media published rumours, among them that a second policeman had been killed. People sharing such content, the authors write, are rarely trying to cause harm: they are caught up in the moment, trying to be helpful, and fail to inspect what they pass on.

Psychology helps explain why it spreads and sticks. Repeated statements are rated truer than new ones, the illusory truth effect: in a registered report published in 2021, Emma Henderson, Daniel Simons and Dale Barr found it immediately and after a day, a week and a month, shrinking over time, and Lisa Fazio and colleagues reported in 2015 that it occurred "even when participants knew better". Corrections help without finishing the job: Nathan Walter and Riva Tukachinsky's meta-analysis of 32 studies with 6,527 participants (2020) found that correction does not entirely eliminate the effect of misinformation, and works less well when the false claim came from a credible source, had been repeated, or was corrected after a delay. Researchers call the residue the continued influence effect.

The backfire effect, in which a correction strengthens the false belief, is disputed. It was associated with a 2010 study by Brendan Nyhan and Jason Reifler; Thomas Wood and Ethan Porter, testing 52 issues with over 10,000 participants, found no backfire, and Briony Swire-Thompson, Joseph DeGutis and David Lazer concluded in 2020 that backfire effects are "not a robust empirical phenomenon". Nyhan wrote in 2021 that an emerging research consensus finds corrections "typically at least somewhat effective", although their effects often do not last.

malinformation.def: Genuine information used to cause harm, such as private material released to damage someone; the third category, beside misinformation and disinformation, in the typology Claire Wardle and Hossein Derakhshan proposed to the Council of Europe in 2017.
malinformation.context: What sets malinformation apart is that the content is true and the harm lies in how it is used, often by moving information meant to stay private into public view. Wardle and Derakhshan's example is the leak of Emmanuel Macron's campaign e-mails just before the French presidential run-off of May 2017, and they place some hate speech and harassment in the category too. The European Commission's 2020 action plan, by contrast, defines misinformation, disinformation and two kinds of influence activity, with no class for true information used to harm.
malinformation.depth:
Malinformation is the third category in Information Disorder, the report Claire Wardle and Hossein Derakhshan wrote for the Council of Europe in 2017: "Information that is based on reality, used to inflict harm on a person, organization or country". The executive summary describes genuine information shared to cause harm, "often by moving information designed to stay private into the public sphere". The report places it beside disinformation, false and deliberately created to harm, and misinformation, false but not meant to harm; malinformation is the one whose content is true.

The report's example is the leak of Emmanuel Macron's campaign e-mails on the Friday before the French presidential run-off of 7 May 2017. The information in the e-mails was real, the authors write, although the campaign allegedly included false information to diminish the impact of any leak, and releasing private information minutes before the media blackout in France was designed to cause maximum harm to the campaign.

The category also takes in some hate speech and harassment, the authors write, because people are often targeted for their personal history or affiliations, such as their religion, with information that may be accurate but is used strategically to cause harm. They add that hate speech, harassment and leaks raise distinct issues their report does not examine in depth, and that some such messages are illegal, as with recognized hate speech, privacy infringements or harassment, though what is legal differs by jurisdiction.

Not every framework adopted the category. The European Commission's European Democracy Action Plan of December 2020 distinguishes misinformation, disinformation, information influence operations and foreign interference, with no separate class for true information used to harm. The EEAS (European External Action Service) reaches some of the same ground another way: its concept of FIMI (foreign information manipulation and interference) does not require the information to be false, and judges deceptive or manipulative behaviour instead.

coordinated-inauthentic-behavior.def: Meta's policy term for networks of accounts that work together to mislead people about who is behind them and what they are doing, in order to manipulate public debate, with fake accounts central to the operation; enforcement targets the behaviour rather than the content posted.
coordinated-inauthentic-behavior.context: Coined by Facebook, now Meta, CIB (coordinated inauthentic behaviour) became shorthand across the industry for covert influence networks. Meta defines it as coordinated efforts to manipulate public debate for a strategic goal in which fake accounts are central, and has published takedown reports since 2017. Researchers including Camille François and evelyn douek have criticized the category as imprecise and applied differently from platform to platform, and the company itself has said domestic campaigns blur the line between healthy debate and manipulation.
coordinated-inauthentic-behavior.depth:
Coordinated inauthentic behaviour, CIB in Meta's reports, is a platform policy category rather than a legal one. Meta defines it as "coordinated efforts to manipulate public debate for a strategic goal, in which fake accounts are central to the operation", in which people use fake accounts to mislead others about who they are and what they are doing, and says it enforces on behaviour rather than content, whether the operators are foreign or domestic. Its reports of February 2023 and May 2024 add "no matter who's behind them"; the February 2025 report omits those words. Meta dates its public threat reporting to 2017, and in December 2021 it added two related protocols, brigading and mass reporting.

By its own count Meta had disrupted more than 200 networks under the policy by December 2022, from 68 countries and in at least 42 languages; two-thirds focused wholly or partly on domestic audiences, and in Mexico, it wrote, many networks were linked to public relations or marketing firms, one of them supporting two rivals for the same electoral post. The EEAS (European External Action Service) treats CIB as an intuitive example of foreign information manipulation, because the content need not be false: the deception lies in fake accounts making a narrative look more widely supported than it is.

In July 2020 Facebook, now Meta, removed 33 Facebook accounts, 14 Pages, 1 Group and 37 Instagram accounts in Brazil, saying its investigation had found links to individuals associated with the PSL (Partido Social Liberal) and to employees of the offices of Anderson Moraes, Alana Passos, Eduardo Bolsonaro, Flávio Bolsonaro and Jair Bolsonaro. Its head of cybersecurity policy, Nathaniel Gleicher, said the company could see office employees engaged but no evidence about the politicians themselves or about direction from the offices' leadership. A PSL spokesman denied any responsibility; Senator Flávio Bolsonaro said it was impossible to evaluate what had been banned or whether the platform had crossed the limits of censorship; President Jair Bolsonaro challenged the press to point to a hateful text of his or of the people at his side.

Critics question how objective the category is. Camille François and evelyn douek wrote in 2021 that the term has become a generic stand-in although Twitter and Google used other labels with different boundaries, Information Operations and Coordinated Influence Operation Campaigns, and that Facebook's explanation of how it applies the policy gives little clarity. douek had written in 2020: "[D]efining what is coordination and what is inauthentic is far from a value-free judgment call". In the July 2020 announcement that included the Brazilian network, the company itself wrote that domestic campaigns like those it had removed blur "the line between healthy public debate and manipulation".

illusory-truth-effect.def: The finding that people rate a statement as more likely to be true when they have encountered it before, even though repetition adds no evidence.
illusory-truth-effect.context: Research on the effect goes back at least to 1977, and a 2010 meta-analysis pooled 51 studies of it. The usual explanation is processing fluency: a repeated statement is easier to process, and the ease is taken as a sign of truth. It has been reported for statements participants knew to be false and for fake-news headlines seen once, and it shrinks as time passes. Studies disagree on wholly implausible claims: a 2018 study found no effect for them, while a 2019 experiment reported one at every level of plausibility.
illusory-truth-effect.depth:
The illusory truth effect is the tendency to judge repeated statements truer than new ones. A 2021 registered report in the Journal of Cognition by Emma Henderson, Daniel Simons and Dale Barr puts it this way: "Repeated statements are rated as subjectively truer than comparable new statements, even though repetition alone provides no new, probative information". Research on it goes back at least to a 1977 paper by Lynn Hasher, David Goldstein and Thomas Toppino, which Henderson and her co-authors cite among studies in which repetitions came weeks apart, and a 2010 meta-analysis by Alice Dechêne and colleagues pooled 51 studies of what it calls the "repetition-induced truth effect".

The predominant explanation, Henderson and her co-authors write, is fluency: repetition makes a statement easier to process, and that ease is read as a cue to truth. Prior knowledge does not always block it. Lisa Fazio, Nadia Brashier, B. Keith Payne and Elizabeth Marsh reported in 2015 that "illusory truth effects occurred even when participants knew better", a pattern they called knowledge neglect. Gordon Pennycook, Tyrone Cannon and David Rand reported in 2018 that a single earlier exposure to real fake-news headlines, shown as they had appeared on Facebook, raised their perceived accuracy in the same session and a week later, even when the stories were labelled as contested by fact checkers.

How far and how long the effect reaches is still being measured. Testing 567 participants immediately and after a day, a week and a month, Henderson, Simons and Barr found it at every interval but shrinking with delay, from a difference of 0.67 on their rating scale at once to 0.14 after a month, which they note is inconsistent with an earlier meta-analysis. Pennycook and his co-authors found no effect for entirely implausible statements such as "The earth is a perfect square"; a preregistered experiment by Fazio, Rand and Pennycook in 2019 reported instead that repetition raised belief at every level of plausibility, and attributed the smaller effect for implausible items to the psychometric properties of the task. A 2020 review by Briony Swire-Thompson, Joseph DeGutis and David Lazer cites work by Brashier and colleagues in which simply asking participants to rate statements for accuracy wiped the effect out.

Repetition also matters once a correction arrives: Nathan Walter and Riva Tukachinsky's 2020 meta-analysis of the continued influence of misinformation found corrections less effective when the misinformation had been repeated multiple times before it was corrected.

continued-influence-effect.def: The continued reliance on misinformation in people's memory and reasoning after a credible correction has been presented, even when the correction is understood and accepted.
continued-influence-effect.context: The name appears in the title of a 1994 paper by Hollyn Johnson and Colleen Seifert, and the Debunking Handbook 2020 says the effect has been replicated many times. A 2020 meta-analysis of 32 studies by Nathan Walter and Riva Tukachinsky found that corrections reduce but do not entirely eliminate the influence of misinformation, and work less well when the false claim came from a credible source, was repeated, or was corrected after a delay. The Handbook advises replacing the myth with a factual alternative rather than relying on a bare retraction.
continued-influence-effect.depth:
Misinformation, in the words of a 2022 review in Nature Reviews Psychology by Ullrich Ecker and eight co-authors, "exerts a lingering influence on people's reasoning after it has been corrected", and that persistence is the continued influence effect. The name appears in the title of a 1994 paper by Hollyn Johnson and Colleen Seifert on when misinformation in memory affects later inferences. The Debunking Handbook 2020, by Stephan Lewandowsky, John Cook, Ecker and 19 other researchers, says the effect "has been replicated many times" and gives an everyday example: someone who hears that a relative fell ill from food poisoning, then learns the story was wrong and accepts the correction, may still avoid the restaurant allegedly involved. Corrections appear to work when people are asked about the claim directly, the Handbook notes, while the misinformation resurfaces in questions only indirectly related to it.

A 2012 review in Psychological Science in the Public Interest by Lewandowsky, Ecker, Colleen Seifert, Norbert Schwarz and Cook set out to explain "why retractions of misinformation are so ineffective in memory updating", and noted that misinformation "can originate from rumors but also from works of fiction, governments and politicians, and vested interests". The remedy the 2020 Handbook recommends follows from that account: instead of relying on a simple retraction, a correction should offer a factual alternative that fills the causal gap the retracted claim leaves, so that people have something to put in its place.

Nathan Walter and Riva Tukachinsky's meta-analysis in Communication Research (2020), aggregating 32 studies with 6,527 participants, found that on average "correction does not entirely eliminate the effect of misinformation". Corrections did better when they were coherent, consistent with the audience's worldview and delivered by the source of the misinformation itself, and worse when the misinformation had been attributed to a credible source, had been repeated multiple times before correction, or when time had passed between the two.

The 2012 review also warned that efforts to retract misinformation can backfire and increase misbelief. Later work separates the two findings. The 2020 Handbook treats the continued influence effect as replicated and says backfire effects "occur only occasionally", and Brendan Nyhan, co-author with Jason Reifler of the 2010 study a 2020 review calls the landmark paper on backfire, wrote in 2021 that corrections are typically at least somewhat effective but that their effects often decay or are overwhelmed by cues from elites and the media.

backfire-effect.def: The reported outcome in which a correction increases belief in the misinformation it was meant to correct; large replications have not found it as a general effect, and researchers dispute whether and when it occurs.
backfire-effect.context: The landmark report is Brendan Nyhan and Jason Reifler's 2010 study, in which a correction about weapons of mass destruction in Iraq increased the misperception among conservative participants. Thomas Wood and Ethan Porter's experiments with more than 10,000 participants found no backfire on any of 52 corrected issues, and Nyhan wrote in 2021 that later research and media coverage had exaggerated the finding's generality. A 2020 review calls backfire effects not a robust phenomenon and possibly an artefact of measurement error; whether they occur under narrow conditions is unresolved.
backfire-effect.depth:
A backfire effect, as Briony Swire-Thompson, Joseph DeGutis and David Lazer define it in a 2020 review in the Journal of Applied Research in Memory and Cognition, occurs only where a correction "inadvertently increases misinformation belief relative to a precorrection or no-correction baseline"; it has also been called a boomerang effect. They distinguish two versions: a worldview backfire effect, said to occur when a correction challenges a person's belief system and the person is motivated to defend it, and a familiarity backfire effect, presumed to occur when the misinformation is repeated within the correction.

The landmark paper, in their account, is Brendan Nyhan and Jason Reifler's "When Corrections Fail" (Political Behavior, 2010). Its first study, run online in autumn 2005 with undergraduates at a Catholic university in the Midwest, corrected the misperception that Iraq had weapons of mass destruction immediately before the war. In the authors' accepted manuscript, the share of conservatives agreeing that it had them rose from 32% in the control condition to 64% after the correction (n = 33), while among non-conservatives it fell from 22% to 13% (n = 97). A second experiment did not replicate the effect for conservatives as a whole but found it in a subset, Swire-Thompson and her co-authors note. A 2012 review by Stephan Lewandowsky and colleagues likewise warned that efforts to retract misinformation "can even backfire and, ironically, increase misbelief".

Swire-Thompson and her co-authors describe failures to find or replicate backfire effects as widespread. Kathryn Haglin repeated Nyhan and Reifler's 2015 flu-vaccine study in 2017 and did not replicate it. Thomas Wood and Ethan Porter (Political Behavior, 2019) enrolled more than 10,100 subjects in five experiments on 52 issues and "found no corrections capable of triggering backfire, despite testing precisely the kinds of polarized issues where backfire should be expected"; the four researchers later published a joint study of fact-checking. Nyhan wrote in the Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences in 2021 that research and media coverage had "seized on this finding, distorting its generality", and that an emerging consensus finds corrections typically at least somewhat effective, though their effects often decay.

The dispute now turns on whether backfire exists at all. Swire-Thompson and her co-authors list three readings of the failed replications: the effect is hard to elicit at group level, it is specific to particular items, situations or individuals, or it does not exist. Their own view is that backfire effects "are not a robust empirical phenomenon" and could be an artefact of measurement error, and that familiarity backfire rarely, if ever, occurs when a myth is paired with a clear and salient correction, though it remains theoretically possible. The Debunking Handbook 2020, whose 22 authors include Lewandowsky, Reifler, Wood and Porter, says backfire effects "occur only occasionally" and that the risk is lower in most situations than once thought.

advance-fee-fraud.def: A fraud in which the victim is persuaded to pay money, or hand over personal information, in advance of a promised larger benefit that never materializes.
advance-fee-fraud.context: Its best-known form is the Nigerian or 419 scam: a message asks the recipient to help move a large sum out of the country for a share of it, then asks for fees. The number refers to section 419 of Nigeria's Criminal Code, on obtaining goods by false pretences. The Internet Crime Complaint Center of the United States Federal Bureau of Investigation recorded 7,762 advance-fee complaints and about 155.9 million US dollars in reported losses in 2025. Cormac Herley of Microsoft Research argued in 2012 that the implausible story works as a filter that leaves scammers with the most promising targets.
advance-fee-fraud.depth:
The Internet Crime Complaint Center (IC3) of the United States Federal Bureau of Investigation defines the category as a case in which "An individual pays money to someone in anticipation of receiving something of greater value in return but instead receives significantly less than expected or nothing." CERT.br, Brazil's national computer emergency response team, describes the Nigerian version in its 2012 security primer: a message in the name of someone claiming to be from Nigeria asks the recipient to act as intermediary in an international transfer of an absurdly large sum for a percentage of it, says the recipient was recommended as honest, demands secrecy and urgency, and then asks for a large advance payment for lawyers and transfer fees, followed by further demands or silence.

The number comes from Nigerian law. Section 419 of the Criminal Code Act, headed "Obtaining goods by false pretences", makes it a felony to obtain anything capable of being stolen by any false pretence with intent to defraud, punishable by three years' imprisonment, or seven where the value is one thousand naira or more; CERT.br equates it with article 171 of the Brazilian Penal Code, estelionato. Nigeria's Advance Fee Fraud and Other Fraud Related Offences Act, in force from 5 June 2006, punishes obtaining property by false pretence, in Nigeria or any other country, with seven to twenty years' imprisonment without the option of a fine. CERT.br adds that similar cases have originated from, or named, other countries, usually in poor regions or regions going through political, economic or racial conflict.

In "Why do Nigerian Scammers Say They are from Nigeria?", a 2012 paper for the Workshop on the Economics of Information Security, Cormac Herley of Microsoft Research treated the scam as a classification problem. The first email costs almost nothing per recipient, but every reply needs costly follow-up, so the scammer pays for false positives: people who answer and never pay. Where viable victims are rare, he calculated, yield collapses: "a 10× reduction in density can produce a 1000× reduction in the number of victims found." His suggested answer to the title is that an outlandish, easily recognized story repels all but the most gullible, who select themselves; a less outlandish wording would draw more replies but, he argued, lower overall profit. In a catalogue of scam emails he examined, 51% named Nigeria as the source of funds and 34% another West African country. Scam-baiters who waste scammers' time, he noted, add plausible false positives and so lower the density of viable targets.

Herley presents the explanation as what his analysis suggests, and his victim density, perhaps one in 10,000 or fewer, is an assumption. The anthropologist Radu Umbres wrote in 2013 that its weakest point is "the absence of data on success rates", and proposed imitation of successful scammers as an alternative explanation for the persistent format, while granting that Herley's may still be accurate. The IC3 recorded 155,910,852 US dollars in advance-fee losses in 2025, against 102,074,512 in 2024; it counts complaints filed, and calls its statistics an assessment at a point in time, which may change.

pig-butchering.def: A fraud in which scammers cultivate a friendship or romance with a victim and then draw successive deposits into a fake investment platform, usually in cryptocurrency; the United States Treasury says such scams are largely run by criminal organizations based in Southeast Asia that use trafficked labour.
pig-butchering.context: The name translates the Chinese sha zhu pan and, according to the United States Treasury's Financial Crimes Enforcement Network, comes from the scammers' image of fattening a hog before slaughter. INTERPOL (the International Criminal Police Organization) urged in December 2024 that it be replaced by romance baiting, arguing that it shames victims and deters reporting. The United Nations human rights office cites credible estimates of at least 300,000 people working in scam operations across Southeast Asia, with victims trafficked from 66 countries; governments in the region point to raids and bans and reject some criticism.
pig-butchering.depth:
In September 2023 the Financial Crimes Enforcement Network (FinCEN) of the United States Treasury issued an alert on a virtual currency investment scam known as pig butchering. The name, it explained, comes from the practice of fattening a hog before slaughter: scammers call their victims pigs, fatten them with fictitious identities, relationships and storylines, and speak of butchering them once their assets are taken; a footnote gives the Chinese original, sha zhu pan. Contact typically begins with a text or social media message presented as a wrong number or as an attempt to reconnect with an old friend. Brazil's Anuário Brasileiro de Segurança Pública 2026 describes the scheme as one in which criminals build bonds of trust with victims to induce successive fraudulent investments.

INTERPOL (the International Criminal Police Organization) objected to the name on 17 December 2024, saying it "dehumanizes and shames victims" and deters them from seeking help, and proposed romance baiting, a term it says some law enforcement agencies already use. Elisabeth Carter, a criminologist at Kingston University London, said in the same release that research links fraudsters' tactics to domestic abuse and coercive control. United States agencies kept the name in 2025 and 2026 documents, usually as the scam "commonly known as" pig butchering.

The Office of the United Nations High Commissioner for Human Rights (OHCHR) reported in August 2023 credible indications that at least 120,000 people in Myanmar, and at least 100,000 in Cambodia, may be held and forced to carry out online scams; High Commissioner Volker Türk said: "They are victims. They are not criminals." Its February 2026 report, as summarized by UN News, the United Nations news service, cites credible estimates of at least 300,000 people in such operations across Southeast Asia, victims from 66 countries as of March 2025, and allegations of collusion between syndicates and officials. The United Nations Office on Drugs and Crime (UNODC) estimated losses of 18 to 37 billion US dollars to scams targeting East and Southeast Asia in 2023. The Brazilian Anuário sees in cases of Brazilians exploited in Myanmar, Cambodia and Laos "uma nova fronteira do tráfico de pessoas", a new frontier of human trafficking.

Governments named in these reports answer with enforcement figures and rebuttals. Cambodia's spokesman Pen Bona called "exaggerated" an Amnesty International report of June 2025 that accused the government of deliberately ignoring abuses in scam compounds, citing a task force under Prime Minister Hun Manet; in June 2026 Chhay Sinarith, of the Commission for Combating Online Scams, said the masterminds and financial chains lie outside Cambodian jurisdiction. Myanmar's military government raided the KK Park compound in October 2025, said by December that 413 buildings had been demolished, and described the scams as the work of foreign criminal networks in borderlands held by insurgents; the Centre for Information Resilience, analysing imagery of the first wave of demolition, found 31 structures flattened and at least 78 partly damaged, and experts quoted by Agence France-Presse called the raids likely limited and choreographed. Laos's state news agency reported 771 arrests in the Golden Triangle Special Economic Zone in August 2024, and the Philippines ordered offshore gaming operators to close by 31 December 2024, citing crime and exploitation risks.

influence-operation.def: A coordinated effort to influence what a target audience believes or does by deceptive means, such as fake accounts, concealed sponsors or fabricated material, carried out by state or non-state actors, foreign or domestic.
influence-operation.context: The European Commission defined information influence operations in 2020 as coordinated efforts by domestic or foreign actors to influence a target audience by deceptive means. Platforms act against them under their own labels, Meta's coordinated inauthentic behaviour among them, and analysts describe them with frameworks such as ABC (actors, behaviours, content), DISARM (Disinformation Analysis and Risk Management) and kill chains. Meta reported in 2022 that two-thirds of the networks it had removed since 2017 targeted domestic audiences wholly or partly. A study of a Russian campaign on Twitter in 2016 found exposure concentrated among 1% of users and no meaningful link to attitudes or votes.
influence-operation.depth:
The European Commission's European Democracy Action Plan of December 2020 says an "information influence operation refers to coordinated efforts by either domestic or foreign actors to influence a target audience using a range of deceptive means, including suppressing independent information sources in combination with disinformation". Platforms police the activity under different names: Camille François and evelyn douek listed in 2021 "Coordinated Inauthentic Behavior (CIB)" at Facebook, "Information Operations (IO)" at Twitter and "Coordinated Influence Operation Campaigns (CIOC)" at Google, policies aimed at networks of accounts rather than single users or posts. The European Union's diplomatic service uses a category it calls both narrower and broader, FIMI (foreign information manipulation and interference), which covers only foreign actors and does not require the content to be false.

Analysts describe operations with shared vocabularies. Camille François's ABC framework of September 2019 separates "Manipulative actors, deceptive behaviors, harmful content"; James Pamment extended it in 2020 to ABCDE (actor, behaviour, content, degree and effect). DISARM (Disinformation Analysis and Risk Management), maintained by the DISARM Foundation, adapts information security practice and calls itself "a common language for documenting influence operations", and Ben Nimmo and Eric Hutchins of Meta set out a ten-link Online Operations Kill Chain in 2023 on the premise that disrupting one tactic can disrupt an entire operation.

Operators include governments, companies and political actors. Meta said in December 2022 that the more than 200 networks it had removed since 2017 came from 68 countries and worked in at least 42 languages, and that two-thirds focused wholly or partly on domestic audiences. Attributions are contested by those named. The United States Senate intelligence committee found in 2019 that Russia's Internet Research Agency sought to influence the 2016 presidential election at the direction of the Kremlin; of the Special Counsel's report that year, Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov said "As before, we do not accept such charges", while Yevgeny Prigozhin, named in the 2018 indictment, said in 2023 that he had invented and run the agency. In September 2022 The Washington Post reported that the Pentagon had ordered an audit of its clandestine information operations after platforms removed fake accounts suspected of being run by the United States military, and in November Meta said it had found links between one such network and individuals associated with that military; the Pentagon's press secretary said military information operations must comply with relevant laws and policies: "We are committed to enforcing those safeguards".

Effect is a separate question. Ben Nimmo's Breakout Scale rates operations from 1 to 6; OpenAI assessed in May 2024 that none of five operations it had disrupted scored above 2, activity on multiple platforms without breakout to authentic audiences. Gregory Eady and colleagues, using a Twitter-linked survey panel from the 2016 United States election, found in Nature Communications (2023) that "only 1% of users accounted for 70% of exposures" to the Internet Research Agency's campaign and no evidence of a meaningful relationship between exposure and changes in attitudes, polarization or voting; the study did not measure other platforms.

fimi.def: Foreign Information Manipulation and Interference: the European Union's term for a mostly non-illegal pattern of manipulative, intentional and coordinated behaviour by foreign state or non-state actors, or their proxies, that threatens or may harm values, procedures and political processes.
fimi.context: The European External Action Service (EEAS), the European Union's diplomatic service, uses the term to centre on behaviour rather than truth: an incident need not involve false content, but it must come from foreign actors. Its threat reports began in February 2023. The fourth, in March 2026, counted 540 incidents in 2025, 29% attributed to Russia, 6% connected to China and 65% unattributed, and the EEAS said one in four involved artificial intelligence tools. It says its samples are neither exhaustive nor representative.
fimi.depth:
FIMI (foreign information manipulation and interference) is the European Union's category for hostile foreign activity in the information space. The first report of the European External Action Service (EEAS) on FIMI threats, published in February 2023, defines it as "a mostly non-illegal pattern of behaviour that threatens or has the potential to negatively impact values, procedures, and political processes", manipulative in character and conducted intentionally and in a coordinated way by state or non-state actors and their proxies. The notion, the report says, overlaps with disinformation but is narrower, excluding domestic sources, and broader: "The deciding factor for whether something can be considered FIMI is not false or misleading content, but deceptive or manipulative behaviour". Its example is coordinated inauthentic behaviour, in which fake accounts make a narrative look more widely supported than it is. The Strategic Compass adopted by the Council in March 2022 provided for a FIMI toolbox.

That first report analysed a sample of 100 incidents detected between October and December 2022: Russian actors were involved in 88 and Chinese actors in 17, jointly in at least five. It adopted the open-source DISARM (Disinformation Analysis and Risk Management) framework and a kill-chain model to describe tactics, techniques and procedures, and said the sample did not intend to give a comprehensive overview. In the third report, of March 2025, the High Representative, Kaja Kallas, called FIMI "a major security threat", Agence France-Presse reported.

The fourth report, of March 2026, counts 540 incidents in 2025: 29% attributed to Russia, 6% connected to China and 65% unattributed but showing indicators of coordination with assets linked to Russian or Chinese attributed infrastructure. It lists 10,500 social media channels and websites used to produce or amplify FIMI, and the EEAS said one in four incidents involved artificial intelligence tools. The report cautions that its findings "do not claim to be exhaustive or representative of overall FIMI activity and trends by the mentioned actors" and are subject to revision.

Direct replies by Moscow or Beijing to the four threat reports have not been found, but both governments have answered related European reporting. China's mission to the European Union said of an EEAS special report on COVID-19 disinformation in April 2021 that "A disinformation report that has no factual basis is in itself an example of disinformation", and in March 2022 called accusations against China in a European Parliament report on foreign interference baseless. Russia's permanent representative Dmitry Polyanskiy, speaking at a Permanent Council meeting on 11 June 2026, said that under the euphemistic label of fighting foreign information manipulation "an instrument for suppressing dissent is being created". Criticism also comes from inside the field: a May 2025 study for the Swedish Psychological Defence Agency by James Pamment and Darejan Tsurtsumia, based on 3,100 leaked documents of a Russian company it links to the Doppelganger campaign, concluded that the shared picture produced by what it calls the counter-FIMI community "got a lot right, but also a lot wrong".

utcp.def: An open specification, first released in 2025, that lets AI (artificial intelligence) agents call existing tools directly over their own protocols, guided by a published manual, instead of through a wrapper server.
utcp.context: The Universal Tool Calling Protocol (UTCP) describes a tool instead of wrapping it. A provider publishes a manual, a JSON (JavaScript Object Notation) document listing each tool's inputs and a call template saying how to reach it: HTTP (Hypertext Transfer Protocol), a command-line program, a Server-Sent Events stream, a text file or even an existing MCP (Model Context Protocol) server. The agent then calls the tool itself, through the tool's own authentication. It saves a hop and a server, and moves the work, and the risk, onto the client.
utcp.depth:
The Universal Tool Calling Protocol (UTCP) is an open specification that lets AI (artificial intelligence) agents and other applications discover and call tools directly, each over its native protocol. Its draft request for comments, RFC (request for comments) UTCP 1.0.0 by Razvan-Ion Radulescu, presents it as a reaction to the Model Context Protocol (MCP). Wrapping every tool in a server, the RFC argues, imposes a wrapper tax, the overhead of building, deploying and maintaining adapter services for every tool, and MCP introduces what it calls an unnecessary network hop for every tool call, increasing latency. UTCP's answer is a manual: a document that tells the client how to call the tool, after which the protocol steps out of the way.

A UTCP manual carries version information and a list of tool definitions. Each tool has a name, a description, a JSON (JavaScript Object Notation) Schema for its inputs and a tool call template, which names a call template type (HTTP (Hypertext Transfer Protocol), command line, Server-Sent Events, plain text, MCP and others through plugins) and the details that type needs, such as a URL (uniform resource locator) and an HTTP method. Credentials are referenced, not stored: an authentication object inside the call template says, for example, that an API (application programming interface) key travels in a named query parameter, and its value is a placeholder the client fills from its own environment variables or a dotenv file. Discovery can be as simple as a well-known /utcp path on an API server that returns the manual, and a manual can be generated from an existing OpenAPI description. After discovery the agent talks to the tool as any other client would.

The project moved fast. Its Python client was first published on the Python Package Index on 10 July 2025, reached 1.0.0 on 19 August 2025 and 1.1.0 on 29 November 2025, and 1.2.0 followed on 16 September 2026. Version 1.0 restructured the design: the core was split into pluggable components, one package per protocol, and what had been called providers became call templates. The work happens in the universal-tool-calling-protocol organization on GitHub, which publishes software development kits (SDKs) for Python, TypeScript, Go and other languages, the main ones under the Mozilla Public License 2.0, and the documentation site credits its copyright to UTCP Contributors.

With no server in the middle, security lives at both ends. The RFC sets the requirement as no security tax: an agent calling a tool should get the same security as a human calling it, through the tool's existing authentication and authorization, with no central store of credentials. It also states the cost plainly: the primary drawback of UTCP is that it places more responsibility on the client. The project's security guidance warns that variable substitution introduces injection risks, that command-line execution poses significant security risks and belongs in a sandbox with minimal permissions, that clients must use HTTPS (HTTP Secure) or secure WebSockets except towards a loopback address, and that manual endpoints become discovery targets and need authentication. It does not address prompt injection, and the model still reads every tool description and every result, so the "lethal trifecta" Simon Willison described for agents in general applies here too.

Most comparisons are written by one side. UTCP's own comparison page sets its manual against MCP's middleman and claims lower latency and no servers to run, with benchmark figures it does not source. Independent write-ups are more even. Nordic APIs concluded in January 2026 that neither approach is universally superior: MCP generally simplifies the client at the cost of more infrastructure and added latency, UTCP excels where tools already exist and where latency matters, and the core trade-off is operational simplicity against performance and architectural flexibility. An analysis published by Glama in September 2025 credited MCP with providing a single point for enterprise-wide guardrails, security policies and auditing, which a direct-call design gives up by construction.

The two are less exclusive than the framing suggests. UTCP ships an MCP plugin, so a UTCP client can keep calling existing MCP servers during a gradual migration, and Nordic APIs remarked that UTCP does not so much compete with MCP as incorporate it, expecting hybrids in which UTCP-described tools are surfaced through MCP servers. The difference in backing is large: MCP sits in a Linux Foundation fund alongside the major model vendors, while UTCP is a community specification with a much smaller following. Choosing between them is less a verdict on protocols than a decision about where the work and the trust should sit: in a server that every call passes through, or in a client that calls each tool itself.

e-ciber.def: Brazil's National Cybersecurity Strategy, set by Decree No. 12,573 of 4 August 2025: the instrument through which the objectives of the country's National Cybersecurity Policy are to be reached.
e-ciber.context: The Estratégia Nacional de Cibersegurança (E-Ciber) is the middle link of a three-part chain. The National Cybersecurity Policy (Política Nacional de Cibersegurança, PNCiber), set by decree in December 2023, states principles and objectives. The strategy organizes them into four axes: protecting citizens and society and raising their awareness; the security and resilience of essential services and critical infrastructure; cooperation between public and private bodies; and national sovereignty and governance. A National Cybersecurity Plan, proposed by the National Cybersecurity Committee (CNCiber), is to list the specific initiatives, their schedule and who runs them. The 2025 strategy replaced the first one, of February 2020.
e-ciber.depth:
Decree No. 12,573 of 4 August 2025 begins with a vocabulary. Cyber assets (ciberativos) are the hardware, software, networks, devices, applications, services, systems and data used to process, store or transmit information electronically or digitally. A cyber incident is a cyber offence combined with its real or potential effect; a cybercrime is a crime committed against or by means of cyber assets. The decree separates information technology from operational technology, the cyber assets that command and control industrial processes in sectors such as manufacturing, telecommunications, energy, medicine and building management, and it defines cyber defence as actions coordinated by the Ministry of Defence.

The first axis aims to make digital services safe to use, especially for people in vulnerable situations, which the decree lists as children and adolescents, older people and neurodivergent people. Its actions include support services for victims of offences committed online, cybersecurity in curricula at every level of education and training for teachers, guidance for micro and small businesses and startups on managing risk and recovering after incidents, multisector action against cybercrime and digital fraud, publicizing the Convention on Cybercrime (promulgated in Brazil by Decree No. 11,491 of 12 April 2023), and better channels for reporting cybercrime.

The second axis is the one an incident like the attack on the Santos Port Authority in November 2026 tests. It asks the bodies with regulatory powers to promote risk management and incident protection and response in their sectors; calls for regulation, inspection and control mechanisms covering both information and operational technology; and plans a high-risk cybersecurity list to ground sector risk management, minimum security standards for relevant and sensitive data, a national seal certifying a high level of security of cyber assets, cyber insurance for operators of essential services and critical infrastructure, regular sector and multisector exercises, and incentives for Brazilian companies to buy products and services that meet minimum standards.

The third axis covers incident response teams, information sharing and analysis centres and specialized laboratories, a national mechanism for notifying cyber incidents, coordinated disclosure of vulnerabilities and support for the cyber capacity of neighbouring countries. The fourth calls for a national cybersecurity maturity model, training on a scale the country needs, continuous assessment of the security of products and services, national products and technologies, and the reduction of what the decree calls the country's technological debt in emerging and disruptive technologies.

The strategy does not list projects. Its article 11 leaves them to a National Cybersecurity Plan (P-Ciber), proposed by the committee and approved by the minister heading the Institutional Security Cabinet (Gabinete de Segurança Institucional, GSI), with publication conditional on the consent of the fifteen government bodies represented on the committee. The draft annexed to the committee's minutes of March 2026 lists structuring initiatives that include a "Brasil Ciberseguro" seal, national and institutional maturity models, a general cybersecurity law, a governance body, a national certification programme and seal for products and services, a national register of cybersecurity talent and a national resilience exercise. The minutes of 17 June 2026, the latest the cabinet had published by 11 November 2026, record that silence by 10 May had been meant to count as consent, that the Casa Civil's legal office ruled tacit consent inadmissible, and that formal consent was still missing from the telecoms regulator Anatel, the Ministry of Finance, the Chief of Staff's office (Casa Civil) and the Central Bank. The same meeting approved the report of the group that wrote the maturity models, and closed it, before a new group took them to pilot tests; the models are named CIMBRA (a cimbra is the falsework that holds an arch while it is built): CIMBRA-N for the country, drawing on the Oxford Cybersecurity Capacity Maturity Model and the International Telecommunication Union's Global Cybersecurity Index, and CIMBRA-I for institutions, drawing on C2M2 2.1, the NIST Cybersecurity Framework 2.0 and COBIT 2019. Members observed that the committee has no legal power to impose them; only sector regulators could.

That is the strategy's structural limit. The policy and the strategy are decrees, and they bind the federal executive. On 21 October 2026 the Federal Court of Accounts (Tribunal de Contas da União, TCU), in judgment 2,909/2026, informed the Casa Civil of the risk that, without a law, the policy has neither national reach nor a structure with enough authority to coordinate it; it noted that the committee had drafted a bill that had not yet been sent to Congress. The cabinet's first idea, a National Cybersecurity Agency (ANCiber) built over five years with 800 staff and R$ 600 million a year, gave way in October 2025, for lack of budget room, to a proposal that Anatel take the role. In the Senate, bill PL 4,752/2025, filed on 24 September 2025 by Senator Esperidião Amin and four others, would create a Legal Framework for Cybersecurity, a national cybersecurity authority and a National Digital Security and Resilience Programme; the text the Constitution and Justice Committee approved in December 2025 funds the programme with at least 3% of the National Public Security Fund and 2% of fixed-odds betting revenue. When the Senate's data were read on 11 November 2026, the bill was with its rapporteur, Senator Jorge Seif, in the Science and Technology Committee, whose decision is final for the Senate.

Meanwhile, the sector regulators the second axis addresses have acted on their own powers. The Central Bank's rules for technology providers after the attacks on the Pix settlement accounts in 2025, and the port security commissions that raise protection levels under the International Ship and Port Facility Security Code, are the kind of sector action the axis asks for, taken while the plan waits.

pnciber.def: Brazil's National Cybersecurity Policy, instituted by Decree No. 11,856 of 26 December 2023 to guide cybersecurity activity in the country; the same decree created the National Cybersecurity Committee (CNCiber).
