pnciber.context: The Política Nacional de Cibersegurança (PNCiber) sets seven principles, from national sovereignty and fundamental rights (freedom of expression, protection of personal data, privacy and access to information) to the prevention of attacks on critical infrastructure and essential services, cooperation and international technical cooperation, and eleven objectives. Its two instruments are the National Cybersecurity Strategy (E-Ciber) and the National Cybersecurity Plan. The committee it created follows its implementation and proposes updates to all three.
pnciber.depth:
What kind of instrument it is. The PNCiber (Política Nacional de Cibersegurança, National Cybersecurity Policy) is a presidential decree, not a law: Decree No. 11,856 of 26 December 2023 was issued under article 84, item VI, point a, of the Constitution, was signed by President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva and by the minister heading the Institutional Security Cabinet (Gabinete de Segurança Institucional, GSI), and took effect on its publication in the Diário Oficial da União of 27 December 2023 (section 1, page 10). Its article 1 gives the purpose in one line: to guide cybersecurity activity in the country. It creates no obligations for companies by itself; its instruments are a strategy and a plan, and the body it creates proposes, evaluates and monitors. As read in the Senate's legislation database on 12 November 2026, no later decree is recorded as amending it.

The seven principles. Article 2 lists national sovereignty and the prioritization of national interests; the guarantee of fundamental rights, in particular freedom of expression, protection of personal data, protection of privacy and access to information; the prevention of cyber incidents and attacks, in particular those aimed at national critical infrastructure and at essential services provided to society; the resilience of public and private organizations to incidents and attacks; education and technological development in cybersecurity; cooperation between public and private bodies and entities; and international technical cooperation.

The eleven objectives. Article 3 asks for the development of national cybersecurity products, services and technologies; guaranteeing the confidentiality, integrity, authenticity and availability of the solutions and data that process, store and transmit information electronically or digitally; strengthening diligent behaviour in cyberspace, especially among children, adolescents and older people; contributing to the fight against cybercrime and other malicious action in cyberspace; encouraging protective measures and risk management to prevent, avoid, mitigate, reduce and neutralize vulnerabilities, incidents and attacks and their impact; increasing the resilience of public and private organizations; developing education and technical and professional training; fostering scientific research, technological development and innovation; increasing coordination and the exchange of cybersecurity information between the federal government, the states, the Federal District and the municipalities, the executive, legislative and judicial branches, the private sector and society at large; developing mechanisms of regulation, inspection and control to improve national cyber security and resilience; and implementing collaboration strategies for international cooperation.

Instruments, and how they connect. Article 4 names two instruments, the National Cybersecurity Strategy (Estratégia Nacional de Cibersegurança, E-Ciber) and the National Cybersecurity Plan. The strategy now in force is Decree No. 12,573 of 4 August 2025, which states that the policy's objectives are to be reached through it and organizes it in four thematic axes: protection and awareness of citizens and society; security and resilience of essential services and critical infrastructure; cooperation and integration between public and private bodies; and national sovereignty and governance. Its article 11 leaves the projects to the plan, which the committee proposes and the GSI minister approves, and makes its publication conditional on the consent of the fifteen government bodies on the committee. The content of the strategy, the state of the plan and the gap the Federal Court of Accounts found in a policy set by decree rather than by law are in the E-Ciber entry.

Where it came from. Before 2023 cybersecurity sat inside information security. Decree No. 9,637 of 26 December 2018 instituted the National Information Security Policy (Política Nacional de Segurança da Informação, PNSI), whose scope began with cybersecurity, followed by cyber defence, physical security and the protection of organizational data, and whose national strategy was to be built in modules, the first of them on cybersecurity; the first E-Ciber, Decree No. 10,222 of 5 February 2020, was that module. Decree No. 11,856 took cybersecurity out of both lists (its article 15 revoked item I of articles 2 and 6 of the 2018 decree) and gave it a policy and a committee of its own. In August 2025 the two lines were rebuilt the same day: Decree No. 12,572 of 4 August 2025 instituted a new information security policy for the federal public administration and revoked Decree No. 9,637, and Decree No. 12,573 replaced the 2020 strategy and revoked Decree No. 10,222.

The committee and its seats. The National Cybersecurity Committee (Comitê Nacional de Cibersegurança, CNCiber) sits within the Chamber of Foreign Relations and National Defence of the Government Council, to which its deliberations are submitted. It has twenty-five members: one each from fifteen federal bodies (the GSI, which chairs it; the Chief of Staff's office (Casa Civil); the Comptroller General; the ministries of Science, Technology and Innovation, Communications, Defence, Development, Industry, Trade and Services, Education, Finance, Management and Innovation in Public Services, Justice and Public Security, Mines and Energy and Foreign Affairs; the Central Bank; and the telecoms regulator Anatel), one from the Brazilian Internet Steering Committee (Comitê Gestor da Internet no Brasil, CGI.br), appointed by its executive secretary, and three each from civil society organizations working on cybersecurity or digital rights, from scientific, technological and innovation institutions in the field, and from business associations in the sector. Government members are senior officials (executive commissioned posts of level 15 or above, or general officers of the armed forces), every member has an alternate, and the GSI minister designates them all. The non-government members are chosen under the committee's internal rules for three-year terms, renewable once; for the first composition the GSI minister chose them on a temporary basis. The chair may invite others to meetings without a vote.

How it works. The committee's competences are to propose updates to the policy, the strategy and the plan; to evaluate and propose measures to increase cybersecurity in the country; to propose improvements in the prevention, detection, analysis and response to incidents; to propose measures for cybersecurity education; to promote dialogue with the federative entities and society; to propose strategies for international technical cooperation; and to give opinions when the chair of the Chamber of Foreign Relations and National Defence asks. It meets quarterly in ordinary session and at the chair's call in extraordinary session; a quorum is an absolute majority, decisions are by simple majority, and the chair has a casting vote. It may create thematic working groups by its own act, temporary, for no more than a year each and no more than five at a time. Members in the Federal District meet in person or by video, the others by video; participation is unpaid relevant public service; the GSI provides the executive secretariat, which had to submit the internal rules for approval within two ordinary meetings.

What it has done. The first meeting took place at the Planalto Palace on 20 March 2024 and created three thematic working groups: one to update the E-Ciber, coordinated by CGI.br; one to propose a governance body for cybersecurity in Brazil, coordinated jointly by the Ministry of Management and Innovation and Anatel; and one to define the parameters of Brazil's international action, coordinated by the Ministry of Foreign Affairs, the first two for six months, extendable by six more. By 12 November 2026 the GSI had published the minutes of ten ordinary meetings, from 20 March 2024 to 17 June 2026. The working groups have produced the draft National Cybersecurity Plan, national and institutional maturity models and a draft general cybersecurity law; their status is followed in the E-Ciber entry.

Why it matters to practitioners. The policy sets direction, not rules: the controls an engineer actually has to implement come from sector regulators using their own powers, such as the Central Bank's requirements for the technology providers that connect institutions to the financial system's network, and from the federal government's own incident apparatus around CTIR Gov. What the PNCiber adds is a shared vocabulary and a forum in which government, the Internet Steering Committee, academia, civil society and industry sit at the same table, and the two documents, strategy and plan, against which public effort can be measured. The dates worth keeping are 26 December 2018 for the earlier information security policy, 5 February 2020 for the first strategy, 26 December 2023 for this decree, 20 March 2024 for the committee's first meeting and 4 August 2025 for the new strategy and the new information security policy.

ctir-gov.def: CTIR Gov (Centro de Prevenção, Tratamento e Resposta a Incidentes Cibernéticos de Governo) is the Brazilian federal government's computer security incident response team (CSIRT), part of the Department of Cybersecurity of the Secretariat of Information Security and Cybersecurity of the Presidency's Institutional Security Cabinet (GSI).
ctir-gov.context: CTIR Gov coordinates the Federal Cyber Incident Management Network (ReGIC), set up by Decree No. 10,748 of 16 July 2021. Membership is compulsory for the direct, autarchic and foundational federal administration and voluntary for federal state-owned companies, which join by adherence agreement. It receives notifications from the agencies' own response teams, spreads alerts, recommendations and statistics, and the incident counts the Institutional Security Cabinet (Gabinete de Segurança Institucional, GSI) publishes from its data are the main public measure of attacks on federal systems. It is a coordinating team for the government's own networks, not the internet-wide CERT.br (Centro de Estudos, Resposta e Tratamento de Incidentes de Segurança no Brasil), and not a police body.
ctir-gov.depth:
What it is, and what it is not. The centre describes itself as a computer security incident response team (CSIRT), an organization that receives, analyses and responds to notifications and activity related to security incidents for a defined community, and places itself in the category of a CSIRT with national responsibility for coordination: its community is the federal public administration and the members of the federal network. Under Decree No. 11,676 of 30 August 2023, which sets the cabinet's structure, the Department of Cybersecurity of the Secretariat of Information Security and Cybersecurity must maintain the centre, coordinate the Federal Cyber Incident Management Network, and give subsidiary support to operational incident response when a federal body asks for it; a 2025 ordinance, Portaria GSI/PR No. 149 of 15 April 2025, details the duties of the general coordination that runs it. Its stated objectives go beyond handling tickets: preventing, monitoring, analysing and mitigating incidents, scientific and technical exchange, helping set guidelines on incident management, and a threat intelligence process to inform public policy. Its own guidance is explicit about the limits: CTIR Gov does not carry out criminal investigations and is not a police or judicial authority; where there are signs of a crime, the owners of the assets or the victims must go to the police and preserve the chain of custody of the evidence.

Where it came from. The Igarapé Institute's chronology dates the start to May 2004, when the cabinet's Information Security Management Committee set up a working group to create a network incident handling centre, and to the end of that year, when the cabinet's executive secretariat moved people into a team to begin receiving, analysing and responding to incident notifications. CTIR Gov's own presentation to the second Brazilian forum of response teams, in São Paulo on 17 September 2013, gives the original name, Centro de Tratamento de Incidentes de Segurança de Redes de Computadores da Administração Pública Federal, places its creation and consolidation in 2004 and 2005 and the definition of its general coordination's mission in Portaria No. 13 of August 2006, and records the adoption of the Request Tracker ticket system in 2010 and 2011. The Forum of Incident Response and Security Teams (FIRST), of which it is a full member as CTIR Gov-BR, lists its establishment date as 8 May 2006. Two supplementary norms of the cabinet's information security department still frame the agencies' side of the work: Norma Complementar 05 of 14 August 2009 on creating the agencies' response teams and Norma Complementar 08 of 19 August 2010 on how they manage incidents. The name changed with the vocabulary, to the cyber incident form by Decree No. 10,363 of 21 May 2020 and to the present one, with prevention added, in the 2021 decree.

The network. Decree No. 10,748 of 16 July 2021 created the Federal Cyber Incident Management Network (Rede Federal de Gestão de Incidentes Cibernéticos) to keep federal bodies coordinated in preventing, handling and responding to cyber incidents. Its objectives are to publicize prevention and response measures, share alerts about threats and vulnerabilities, publish information about attacks, promote cooperation and speed up response. Every member body must set up and support its own incident response team. Through CTIR Gov, the cabinet coordinates those teams over a dedicated platform, writes and updates the incident management plan for the federal administration (the current one approved by Portaria GSI/PR No. 120 of 21 December 2022), works with its counterparts abroad, seeks international cooperation with an emphasis on sharing information about threats, vulnerabilities and incidents, and spreads alerts, recommendations and statistics to the network and on its website.

Layers and membership. Sector coordination teams, those of the regulatory agencies, the Central Bank and the National Nuclear Energy Commission or of entities they regulate, coordinate their sectors and centralize the incident notifications of the other teams there. For the Ministry of Defence and the armed forces, the sector team is run by the Cyber Defence Command, the central body of the Military Cyber Defence System. Companies outside the federal administration that sign an adherence agreement with the cabinet report to their sector team, or straight to CTIR Gov where there is none, when an incident exceeds their capacity to fix it or when their team judges that a vulnerability could cause an incident on their network or on others'. The network is open to federal state-owned and mixed-capital companies and their subsidiaries and, by invitation, to state, municipal and private entities; joining takes a formally instituted response team, a letter of interest signed by the head of the organization to the cabinet's executive secretary, and the signed adherence agreement. When a serious incident occurs or the cyber risk is high, the cabinet may convene the Chamber of Foreign Relations and National Defence of the Government Council.

How to notify it. The single point of contact for incident notifications is ctir@ctir.gov.br, and the guidance asks for timeliness over completeness: an early first notice, then updates as handling proceeds. The subject line carries a Traffic Light Protocol (TLP) marking, the organization and the type of incident; the centre follows FIRST's TLP 2.0, with the labels CLEAR, GREEN, AMBER, AMBER+STRICT and RED. The body repeats the marking and gives the current status, the Internet Protocol (IP) addresses, organizations, people and services involved, the logs with their timestamps, a chronology and the actions taken; attachments should include server and service logs, email headers, malicious code and screenshots. Sensitive messages can be encrypted to the centre's published Pretty Good Privacy (PGP) key. Every case gets a number in the subject, in the form CTIR Gov BR followed by a hash sign and six digits, which must be kept in every later message. Like most national teams, it publishes a description of itself in the format of Request for Comments (RFC) 2350, Expectations for Computer Security Incident Response (BCP 21, June 1998), in Portuguese and English.

The numbers. The cabinet's counts of incidents in federal systems were 4,903 in 2021, 3,402 in 2022, 4,908 in 2023, 9,806 in 2024, 10,387 in 2025 and 6,774 in 2026 up to early June, about 45 a day, almost all of them in 2026 social engineering (3,307 cases, 48.8 per cent) or abusive content such as spam and deepfakes (3,166, 46.74 per cent); separately it counted about 14,000 vulnerabilities in 2026 by June, against 5,115 in 2024 and 7,705 in 2025. Its home page adds a wider total of notifications, incidents plus vulnerabilities: 15,132 in 2023, 14,921 in 2024, 18,092 in 2025 and 61,378 in 2026 as of 12 November. The counts measure what reaches the centre, not everything that happens: they did not include, for example, the false extreme-event alerts sent through the national Civil Defence system to phones in six state capitals on the night of 19 to 20 June 2026, which the Federal Police were investigating.

Reading the numbers. The cabinet itself warns that the series is not homogeneous. During 2025 it modernized its processes and, through agreements with external partners, gained access to a much larger volume of information about vulnerabilities and incidents; from 1 January 2026 it consumed more threat feeds and replaced the categories it had used until 2025 (website abuse, abuse of the Simple Mail Transfer Protocol (SMTP) mail service, fake pages, phishing, scans, data leaks, vulnerable software, cryptographic weaknesses and services open to distributed reflection denial of service (DRDoS) amplification) with a taxonomy of its own based on guidance from the European Union Agency for Cybersecurity (ENISA). In February 2026 it began re-notifying an organization about the same vulnerability only after 30 days unless the situation demanded otherwise, and for a time sent the findings for universities and other edu.br institutions in one block to CAIS-RNP, the response team of the RNP (Rede Nacional de Ensino e Pesquisa) academic network, before returning in August 2026 to notifying each institution separately. Part of the rise since 2024 is therefore better visibility and changed counting, not only more attacks.

Not CERT.br. CTIR Gov is not CERT.br. CERT.br (Centro de Estudos, Resposta e Tratamento de Incidentes de Segurança no Brasil) describes itself as a national-responsibility CSIRT of last resort, maintained by NIC.br, the private non-profit entity that operates the .br domain and implements the decisions of the Brazilian Internet Steering Committee (CGI.br), and serves networks connected to the internet in Brazil. CTIR Gov serves the federal government's own systems and the organizations that join its network; sector teams such as the academic network's sit between the two.

pix.def: Brazil's instant payment system, created and run by the Central Bank of Brazil, which moves money between accounts in seconds at any hour of any day; it was launched on 16 November 2020.
pix.context: Pix runs on rules the Banco Central do Brasil (BCB) sets for every participant: Resolution BCB No. 1 of 12 August 2020 instituted the Pix arrangement and its regulation, and transactions settle in the Central Bank's Instant Payment System (Sistema de Pagamentos Instantâneos, SPI), between the settlement accounts participants hold there. Its scale is national: the Central Bank counts more than 150 million individuals using Pix in September 2026, more than 7.8 billion transactions that month and a record of 318,116,744 transactions on 4 September 2026.
pix.depth:
Pix is what Brazilian regulation calls a payment arrangement, and the unusual thing about it is that the regulator, the Central Bank of Brazil (Banco Central do Brasil, BCB), also operates it. The resolution that instituted it made participation mandatory for every financial or payment institution with more than 500,000 active customer accounts; the system opened in restricted operation on 3 November 2020 and in full on 16 November. Its regulation defines an instant payment as a transfer in which the order is transmitted and the funds become available to the receiver in real time, in a service available 24 hours a day on every day of the year. Three pieces of infrastructure, all run by the Central Bank, make that possible. The Instant Payment System (Sistema de Pagamentos Instantâneos, SPI) is a centralized infrastructure for real-time gross settlement between participants. Each direct participant holds there an Instant Payments Account (Conta Pagamentos Instantâneos, Conta PI), out of which every Pix it sends is settled. And the Directory of Transactional Account Identifiers (Diretório de Identificadores de Contas Transacionais, DICT), connected to the National Financial System Network (Rede do Sistema Financeiro Nacional, RSFN), turns a Pix key into an account: the key may be a mobile phone number, an email address, the taxpayer number of a person or of a company, or a random string.

Economists at the Bank for International Settlements (BIS) studied the result in March 2022. In little over a year Pix had signed up 67 per cent of Brazilian adults, with free payments between individuals and low charges for merchants, and they named two ingredients: the mandatory participation of the large banks, which started the network effect, and the central bank's double role as provider of the infrastructure and setter of the rules. That double role is also why the security of Pix is, to an unusual degree, a matter of regulation: when something fails, the same institution that settles the payments can change what every participant must do.

Speed is the point of Pix and the reason its security is built in layers around the user. The Central Bank's own timeline lists among its security additions a precautionary block, a Special Return Mechanism (Mecanismo Especial de Devolução, MED) and night-time limits. The first two took effect on 16 November 2021. The precautionary block lets the receiving institution hold the money at the moment it is credited, for at most 72 hours, when it suspects fraud. The MED is the set of rules for returning a Pix where there is well-founded suspicion of fraud or an operational failure at a participant; the receiver's institution starts it on its own initiative or at the request of the payer's institution, sent through the DICT, and it does not cover disputes about the underlying deal or money that has reached a third party in good faith. Those features answer the fraud most people meet, the scam that talks a customer into sending money.

The attacks of 2025 and 2026 went elsewhere: into the settlement accounts that banks and payment institutions keep at the Central Bank, reached through the technology providers that connect smaller institutions to the financial system's network. On 1 July 2025 credentials were used through C&M Software to reach the accounts of at least five institutions; the Federal Police, in an operation with 26 arrest warrants that October, put the loss at more than R$ 813 million. On 29 August 2025 credentials of suppliers of Sinqia were used to send R$ 710 million out of two institutions, R$ 670 million of it from HSBC. Banco do Nordeste suspended Pix after an attack on 26 January 2026 that came through a flaw at a service provider, and BTG Pactual suspended it in March 2026 after money left the account it held at the Central Bank. In the BTG case the Central Bank said its own systems, Pix included, had not been affected. None of these cases has been shown to break Pix itself; what failed was the access around it.

The rules tightened in steps. Resolution BCB No. 429 of 11 November 2024 allowed only institutions authorized by the Central Bank to apply to join from 1 January 2025 and set a minimum capital and net worth of R$ 5 million for every participant from 1 January 2026. On 3 September 2025 the Central Bank's director for financial system organization and resolution wrote, in the vote proposing the next resolution, that the recent cyber attacks had made new adjustments necessary: the authorization schedule was brought forward to May 2026, transactions originated by unauthorized participants and by participants that reach the network through a technology provider were capped at R$ 15,000 each, the cap falling away once the provider meets security criteria in an accreditation, and only institutions in the larger prudential segments, S1 to S4 and not credit cooperatives, may act as responsible participants for unauthorized ones. The same vote estimated 85 authorization cases to examine by the end of May 2026, against 59 payment institutions authorized in all of 2024. After the BTG attack, Resolution BCB No. 554 of 24 March 2026 let institutions set a minimum balance on their Pix settlement account, the Conta PI, below which it is blocked automatically for any settlement in the SPI until someone at the institution unblocks it by hand.

The conditions for lifting that cap are the most technical part of the September 2025 vote and say plainly where the weakness was. Besides using an accredited provider, the participant must show, in an independent auditor's assurance report, that it does not share with the provider the private keys registered at the Central Bank and used to sign Pix messages, that it validates the integrity of each transaction before signing it, that it uses different certificates for test and production environments, and that it keeps separate certificates for signing messages and for establishing the channel. In other words, a signature made with a key that sits at a third party proves only that the third party, or whoever controls it, sent the message.

The regulation keeps moving, and it is worth reading the current text and not a summary. Since Resolution BCB No. 457 of 6 March 2025 a participant may register a key only after the account has been opened with the holder's identity verified, and only for a holder whose taxpayer registration is in regular standing. Resolution BCB No. 597 of 30 September 2026 obliges participants to publicize the MED in their own channels, with attention to vulnerable users, and to block transactions destined for fixed-odds betting lotteries under the terms of a provisional measure of 25 September 2026, except those needed to wind operations down and refund bettors. For an engineer the system has three separate trust boundaries, and the incidents map onto them: the customer's judgement, which fraud by persuasion attacks and the MED partly repairs; the participant's connection to the network, with its keys, certificates and providers, which the 2025 attacks used; and the Central Bank's own infrastructure, which none of the published incidents is reported to have breached.

psti.def: In Brazilian financial regulation, a company accredited by the Central Bank to process data so that banks, payment institutions and other supervised institutions can reach the National Financial System Network (RSFN), the network that carries the financial system's messages, including Pix and TED settlement.
psti.context: A Provedor de Serviços de Tecnologia da Informação (PSTI) is the connection pipe that many small institutions and newcomers rent instead of connecting to the National Financial System Network (Rede do Sistema Financeiro Nacional, RSFN) themselves, which takes money, specialist staff and systems of their own. Two of them, C&M Software and Sinqia, were the doors through which attackers emptied institutions' settlement accounts in 2025, and the Central Bank rewrote their rules within weeks: Resolution BCB No. 498 of 5 September 2025, amended by Resolution BCB No. 547 of 30 January 2026, replaced the 2019 regime with accreditation, R$ 15 million of capital, mandatory security controls and a R$ 15,000 cap per Pix and TED (Transferência Eletrônica Disponível) transfer for clients of providers not yet accredited.
psti.depth:
What it is, in the regulator's words. Resolution BCB No. 498, as amended in January 2026, defines a PSTI (Provedor de Serviços de Tecnologia da Informação, information technology service provider) as an accredited entity able to provide data processing services, for the purpose of access to the RSFN, to financial institutions and the other institutions the Central Bank of Brazil supervises. The RSFN (Rede do Sistema Financeiro Nacional, National Financial System Network) is in turn the data communication structure that carries information for authorized services within the National Financial System and the Brazilian Payments System, the network over which, among other things, Pix and TED (Transferência Eletrônica Disponível, the same-day bank transfer) orders reach the Central Bank. A direct connection to it requires money, specialist staff and systems of one's own, so renting a PSTI has usually been the first choice of newcomers and small institutions. Accreditation is not a licence to carry on the business and does not change the provider's legal or contractual duties to its clients; companies that process data only for institutions of their own economic group are outside the rule, provided they keep operational segregation. Some cannot be accredited at all: the telecommunications operators contracted to run the RSFN, the firms contracted to manage and monitor it, supervised financial institutions themselves, and companies that control them, are controlled by them or share a controller with them.

The regime before 2025. From 2019 the subject sat in Circular No. 3,970 of 28 November 2019, which set general criteria for electronic data communication in the financial system, with security, efficiency, flexibility, availability, privacy protection and neutrality as its principles, and laid down the requirements and prohibitions for PSTIs. C&M Software had been approved by the Central Bank for this role since 2001, and in July 2025 eight other companies held the same approval; the trade press counted nine providers in operation in September 2025. Until the attacks they worked, as one report put it, behind the scenes.

The attacks that changed it. On 1 July 2025 C&M Software, which connects institutions without their own means of connection to the Central Bank's infrastructures, reported an attack, and the Central Bank ordered it to cut the institutions' access to the infrastructures it operated. Money had been diverted from the reserve accounts that institutions keep at the Central Bank, not from customers' accounts. The attackers had used credentials of C&M's clients; São Paulo's civil police arrested an employee of the provider who, they said, confessed to selling his login and password for R$ 5,000 and taking R$ 10,000 more to build a system that allowed the diversions, and they reported that the transfers had run in the early hours of 30 June, were noticed at 04:30 and continued until 07:00. On 29 August 2025 Sinqia, another provider, detected suspicious activity in its Pix environment, isolated it from its other systems and disconnected it from the Central Bank; a report by its controlling company, Evertec, put the diversion at R$ 670 million from HSBC and R$ 40 million from the fintech Artta, R$ 710 million in all, carried out with access credentials of Sinqia's own IT suppliers. In neither case was the Central Bank's own infrastructure reported as breached: the attackers used the provider's legitimate path into it.

The rules of September 2025. On 5 September 2025 the Central Bank published five resolutions, Nos. 494 to 498. Resolution No. 498, in force on publication, created accreditation and set its requirements: adherence to the RSFN's principles and rules, signed with an ICP-Brasil digital certificate; proven technical and operational capacity under the standards of the bank's Information Technology Department (Deinf); directors responsible for information security, cybersecurity, risk management and compliance, and for operational crisis management; fit and proper controllers and administrators; paid-in capital and net worth of at least R$ 15 million, which the bank may raise; corporate governance and risk management; an information security certification in an internationally recognized standard or an independent assurance the bank accepts; an annual independent audit of information security; civil liability and operational risk insurance covering fraud and cyber incidents; and a business continuity plan with periodic contingency tests, proven to the bank every year. The same day, Resolution No. 496 amended the Pix regulation and Resolution No. 497 the TED regulation; the vote behind No. 496 explained the cap that follows as a containment measure against failures in services provided by PSTIs, as observed in recent events.

The amendments of January 2026. Resolution BCB No. 547 of 30 January 2026, published in the official gazette on 2 February, rewrote much of No. 498 in the week Banco do Nordeste suspended Pix after money left a pooled account. Capital is now to be proportional to the volume of operations, the number of clients and the risk profile, and the bank may demand more at any time during monitoring. The certification requirement became a certification in an internationally recognized standard, without the alternative of an assurance the bank accepts, and the bank may require any requirement to be attested by a reasonable-assurance report from an auditor registered with the securities regulator (CVM). The rule now defines controllers, bars investment funds from being controllers, and requires administrators to be resident in Brazil. The separate requirements for a crisis-management director and an annual continuity-plan proof were dropped from the list; the governance chapter, in both versions, already required policies for information and cyber security, business continuity, crisis management, fraud, internal controls and internal audit, reviewed at least annually, and an operational crisis management committee. Existing providers had eight months from the rule's entry into force, instead of four, to apply for accreditation, and a provider that did not apply is de-accredited by the bank and must carry out an orderly exit plan; the bank's own summary adds simpler de-accreditation, wider reporting duties and new grounds for precautionary measures, such as the prolonged absence of a responsible director. Resolution BCB No. 594 of 30 September 2026 set 60 days as the maximum time for the bank to decide on an accreditation.

What a provider must now do, technically. Article 17 lists the minimum content of a provider's information and cyber security policy: encryption, intrusion prevention and detection, leak prevention and malware protection; transaction traceability, with end-to-end audit trails and logs that reveal processing failures or atypical behaviour; backups; vulnerability assessment and correction and regular patching; access control and network protection; segregation of environments with restricted access to production; physical and logical isolation of the Pix and of the Reserve Transfer System (STR) environments from the provider's other systems where it also sells software as a service to participants, with a dedicated, separate instance when a public cloud is used; digital certificate management; controls on electronic interfaces with other parties; and cyber intelligence that monitors the internet, the deep and dark web and private messaging groups for clients' keys, credentials and vulnerabilities. Its first paragraph is the one that answers 2025 directly: the provider must not have access to the private keys used to sign messages in the Central Bank's payment systems. Article 25 adds fraud controls: round-the-clock real-time monitoring for atypical transactions by value, volume and rate, anomaly checks before a transaction is sent to the Central Bank, integrity validation through processing, a mechanism to interrupt the whole flow of transactions on serious suspicion of compromise, and a channel to warn the institutions that could be affected.

The cap. Under Resolution No. 496, a Pix participant that reaches the RSFN through a PSTI may not have per-transaction limits above R$ 15,000, and under No. 497 such an institution may not issue a TED in favour of a customer of R$ 15,000 or more. The cap is lifted only when two conditions hold together: the provider has completed accreditation, and a reasonable-assurance report by a CVM-registered auditor shows that the institution does not share with the provider the private keys registered at the Central Bank for signing its messages, validates the integrity of each transaction before signing it, and uses separate certificates for different environments such as homologation and production; for Pix, also separate certificates for signing messages and for establishing the channel. On request, the bank may waive the cap for 90 days, or until the conditions are met, if the institution documents the guarantees and measures it has already adopted. In other words, the rule moves the signing keys, and with them the ability to move money, back inside the institution.

The market shrank. Finsiders Brasil reported in July 2026 that of nine providers in September 2025 three remained in operation, Gokei, JD and Tivit. Stark Infra and MAPS had their de-accreditation approved in October and December 2025, Topaz, of the Stefanini group, left the activity on 16 July 2026, and the Associação Brasileira de Bancos (ABBC), C&M and Sinqia, now Evertec, were in orderly exit. C&M said its exit was its own strategic decision and not the result of a regulatory impediment; Evertec attributed it to the regulation and announced a migration to an on-premises model in which clients host and operate the software themselves; ABBC said almost all the institutions it served were choosing to connect directly to the payments system, under an exit plan with 180 days to migrate them. A lawyer interviewed by the same publication warned that with so few providers a systemic failure would have a larger impact; a JD executive said the model still makes sense for small institutions and newcomers, and that some institutions, by meeting the regulatory requirements, had the temporary cap lifted until accreditation is complete.

The lesson. It is the classic one of supply chain attacks, with a Brazilian twist: an institution's security is no better than that of the supplier that holds the keys to its account, and in 2025 the keys, the credentials and the network path all sat with the supplier. Agência Brasil's account of January 2026 puts the pattern plainly: since 2025 attacks on outsourced providers have become more frequent because they are a potentially weaker link that lets criminals get around the stronger protection of large banks. The regulator's answer is not to forbid outsourcing but to make the provider meet bank-grade controls and to keep message-signing keys and transaction validation with the institution, which is the same separation of duties a network engineer applies when a managed service provider is given access to a firewall but not to the keys that make its changes authoritative.

isps-code.def: The International Maritime Organization's set of measures for the security of ships and port facilities, adopted in December 2002 under the Safety of Life at Sea Convention and applied since 1 July 2004.
isps-code.context: The International Maritime Organization (IMO) developed the code in response to the perceived threats to ships and port facilities after the attacks of 11 September 2001. It is implemented through chapter XI-2 of the International Convention for the Safety of Life at Sea (SOLAS), has a mandatory and a recommendatory part, and treats security as risk management: each port facility is assessed and runs an approved security plan under a port facility security officer. Its three security levels are what a government raises when the threat rises.
isps-code.depth:
What it covers. The International Ship and Port Facility Security (ISPS) Code entered into force on 1 July 2004 through chapter XI-2 of the International Convention for the Safety of Life at Sea (SOLAS), Special measures to enhance maritime security. The chapter applies to passenger ships and to cargo ships of 500 gross tonnage and upwards, including high-speed craft, to mobile offshore drilling units, and to the port facilities that serve such ships on international voyages. Regulation XI-2/2 gives the code its force; its Part A is mandatory, and Part B is guidance on how to meet Part A. Every company, ship and port facility in scope designates a security officer, the CSO (company security officer), the SSO (ship security officer) and the PFSO (port facility security officer), who assess the risks and prepare and implement the security plans. Regulation XI-2/8 confirms that the master's professional judgement on the ship's security may not be constrained by the company, the charterer or anyone else.

The three levels. The International Maritime Organization (IMO) defines them. Level 1 is normal, the level at which the ship or port facility normally operates, with minimum appropriate protective measures maintained at all times. Level 2 is heightened, applying for as long as there is a heightened risk of a security incident, with additional measures maintained for a period of time. Level 3 is exceptional, for the period when a security incident is probable or imminent, even if the specific target cannot be identified, and setting it should be an exceptional measure based on credible information. Under regulation XI-2/3 the flag state sets the level for its ships, and a ship entering or lying in the port of another contracting government must comply with that government's level when it is higher than the one its own administration has set.

The technical measures that came with it. Regulation XI-2/6 requires every ship in scope to carry a ship security alert system, which sends a ship-to-shore alert to an authority designated by the flag administration, identifying the ship and its position and saying its security is under threat or compromised; it raises no alarm on board, and it must be possible to activate it from the navigation bridge and from at least one other place. The 2002 package also set a new timetable for the Automatic Identification System (AIS): ships other than passenger ships and tankers, of 300 gross tonnage and upwards but under 50,000, had to fit it by the first safety equipment survey after 1 July 2004 or by 31 December 2004, whichever came first, and keep it running at all times except where navigational information must be protected. Ships were required to carry their identification number permanently marked on the hull or superstructure, and a Continuous Synopsis Record, issued by the flag administration, keeps the ship's history of names, flags, owners and registrations on board.

How it is enforced. The code applies the same way to flag states and port states everywhere. The organization keeps no black list of non-compliant countries and imposes no penalties, which it says is not within its remit; it expects market forces to drive compliance. Control is exercised ship by ship, in port, where the other regulations of chapter XI-2 let a contracting government delay or detain a ship, restrict its operations or expel it. The 2002 conference that adopted the code also invited the World Customs Organization to work on the security of cargo units across the supply chain and the International Labour Organization to develop a seafarers' identity document.

How Brazil applies it. Brazil's Congress approved the code through Legislative Decree 645 of 18 September 2009, and it was promulgated by Decree 9.988 of 26 August 2019. Its application is run by a national commission, the Comissão Nacional de Segurança Pública nos Portos, Terminais e Vias Navegáveis (Conportos), under Decree 9.861 of 25 June 2019, and by state commissions (Cesportos), such as Cesportos-SP in São Paulo. Conportos's consolidated rules, Resolution 53 of 4 September 2020, were signed by its president from the Federal Police together with representatives of the Navy, the Foreign Ministry and the national ports secretariat. In its vocabulary each port facility has a risk assessment study (EAR, Estudo de Avaliação de Risco) and a port security plan (PSP, Plano de Segurança Portuária), approved by Conportos through the state commission, and a port security supervisor (SSP, Supervisor de Segurança Portuária), the code's PFSO; only private security organizations accredited by Conportos may prepare the assessments and plans; and the facility issues a Declaration of Security when a ship's security officer requests one. The resolution lists separate measures for levels 1, 2 and 3 covering access, restricted areas, cargo handling, ship stores, unaccompanied baggage and monitoring.

Cyber is separate. The code is about physical and procedural security. The organization's cyber guidance is separate: guidelines on maritime cyber risk management (MSC-FAL.1/Circ.3, now in its fourth revision), and Resolution MSC.428(98), adopted by the Maritime Safety Committee in June 2017, which encourages administrations to make sure cyber risks are addressed in the safety management systems that the International Safety Management (ISM) Code requires, no later than the first annual verification of a company's Document of Compliance after 1 January 2021. The International Association of Ports and Harbors (IAPH) publishes cybersecurity guidelines for ports and port facilities. For ships, the binding detail now comes from classification societies. The International Association of Classification Societies (IACS) Unified Requirement (UR) E26, Cyber resilience of ships, in its first revision of November 2023, applies to ships contracted for construction on or after 1 July 2024, after the 2022 version was withdrawn before it came into force; it is organized under Identify, Protect, Detect, Respond and Recover, the functions familiar from the NIST (National Institute of Standards and Technology) Cybersecurity Framework, and leaves the requirements for individual systems and equipment to UR E27. Its definitions read like a network design brief: a network segment is an OSI (Open Systems Interconnection) layer 2 Ethernet segment, a broadcast domain; segments communicate only through routing at layer 3; and a security zone is a group of computer-based systems with the same security requirements behind interfaces to which an access control policy is applied. On a new ship, VLAN (virtual local area network) and firewall design is part of the class approval.

The two meet at the gate. When the systems of the Santos Port Authority (APS, Autoridade Portuária de Santos), which runs Brazil's largest port, were attacked in November 2026, the trouble surfaced after a power outage that hit its servers on the morning of Friday 6 November; internet and telephone services came back on Monday 9 November after three days, while the port's website and other internal systems were still down on 10 November, when the authority confirmed a cyber attack and said it could not yet determine its extent or whether data had been accessed. The São Paulo state commission for public security in ports, terminals and waterways (Cesportos-SP), coordinated by a Federal Police officer, voted on 8 November to raise the protection of the port's public accesses to level 2: more checks on people and vehicles entering the customs zone and more cargo inspections, with controls carried out by hand. CLM Brasil reported the decision as a response to the cyber vulnerability and to failures detected at the public gates, and the Federal Police opened an inquiry on 10 November. A Navy exercise with about 700 personnel, Operation Tridente III, ran in Santos and Praia Grande from 9 to 12 November, with no operational link shown to the attack. A cyber attack had raised a physical security level. The numbers worth remembering: 1 July 2004, chapter XI-2, 500 gross tonnage, three levels, and 1 July 2024 for the classification rules on ships' cyber resilience.

febraban.def: The Brazilian Federation of Banks (Federação Brasileira de Bancos), a non-profit association of banks with 114 members in November 2026 (108 financial institutions and six sector associations), which has run a cybersecurity laboratory for the financial system since September 2020.
febraban.context: Febraban's Cybersecurity Laboratory (Laboratório de Segurança Cibernética) opened in São Paulo in September 2020 as the first of its kind built for Brazil's financial system, with an initial investment of R$ 6 million. It works on four fronts, training, simulation, intelligence and standardization, the last analysing the suppliers that serve the financial system, with the aim of a good-practice manual setting criteria for them. The federation also runs the Febraban Tech conference and, with Deloitte, the yearly Febraban Banking Technology Survey.
febraban.depth:
Febraban is a trade association, not an authority. Its statute, in the version approved on 5 April 2023, defines it as a non-profit civil association that brings together banking financial institutions operating in Brazil and associations that represent financial institutions, with its seat in the city of São Paulo; among the purposes listed in article 2 are a healthy, ethical and efficient financial system and proposing and defending changes to legislation and to administrative rules. Its membership page counts 114 members, 108 financial institutions and six representative associations, and its own account of itself speaks of more than five decades of activity. The rules that bind a bank come from the Central Bank of Brazil and the National Monetary Council; what Febraban produces are positions, studies, training, self-regulation and technical standards that its members agree to follow.

Those standards are where most engineers meet the name. The Febraban standard layout of 240 positions, which the market calls CNAB 240 and whose version 11.0 is dated 11 September 2026, is the fixed-width file format in which companies and banks exchange payments, collections, statements and direct debits: one file header record (type 0), one or more service lots, each with a lot header (type 1), detail segments (type 3) and a lot trailer (type 5), and one file trailer (type 9); the payments service now covers credit in account, TED (transferência eletrônica disponível) and Pix. The standard for utility and tax collection documents, version 8, in force from 1 June 2026, fixes the bar code as interleaved 2 of 5 with 44 positions of data, printed above it as numeric fields of 11 positions that each end in a check digit calculated modulo 10 or modulo 11, which is the arithmetic every payment gateway in Brazil implements. The boleto itself dates from 7 October 1993, when a Central Bank circular established the electronic clearing of collection documents; the registered-collection platform that modernized it went live in July 2017 for boletos of R$ 50,000 or more and was complete in November 2018; and DDA (Débito Direto Autorizado) is the banks' system for presenting those obligations electronically instead of on paper.

At the opening the federation's president, Isaac Sidney, said the banks invest R$ 2 billion a year in information security. The R$ 6 million paid for the space, equipment, technology infrastructure, attack simulation software and a consultancy, Accenture at launch. The laboratory first served the fourteen banks on the federation's Executive Cybersecurity Commission and opened to more institutions over time.

By the end of January 2022 it had run 40 free training courses with 3,900 enrolments; 72 of the federation's 114 member institutions had taken part, and 14 of the courses included attack exercises between participants. It runs capture the flag (CTF) competitions in controlled, realistic environments, sends the banks a monthly briefing on attacks, threats and possible solutions, and writes technical reports that reconstruct real attacks step by step. Since then it has opened its doors further: the Cyber Academy, a free 40-hour online course for anyone interested in the field, offered 10,000 places for its sixth edition, in July 2026.

The laboratory is one of several instruments. On 23 August 2024 Febraban signed a technical cooperation agreement with the Ministry of Justice and Public Security, at its own headquarters and with the minister visiting the laboratory, to exchange information against fraud, scams and cybercrime and to build a National Financial Security Strategy with other sectors. The result was the National Alliance to Combat Digital Banking Fraud, whose joint action plan the ministry launched on 3 December 2025 with more than 20 initiatives to be carried out over 60 months, from prevention and consumer education through detection and rapid response to repression and the recovery of assets, with the Central Bank, the federal revenue service, the telecommunications regulator Anatel and the Federal Police among the partners. Febraban also awards a fraud prevention seal to members that adopt consistent standards of prevention, detection and response.

The standardization front matters more after 2025 than it did in 2020. The attacks on the Pix settlement accounts entered through technology providers that connect institutions to the financial system, exactly the kind of supplier that front addresses. The Febraban Banking Technology Survey 2026, presented at Febraban Tech in August, puts the banks' total technology budget for 2026 at R$ 50.4 billion, 8% more than the year before; among the 25 banks sampled, cybersecurity was a high priority for 83% and a medium one for the other 17%, and Finsiders Brasil reported that 58% of the banks have at least one cybersecurity specialist on their boards.

The regulator moved on the same weakness. The Central Bank's vote of 3 September 2025 that tightened the rules for information technology service providers (provedores de serviços de tecnologia da informação) says that recent cyberattack events had made the need evident, and until a provider is accredited the institutions that reach the national financial system network through it are limited to R$ 15,000 per Pix or TED transaction. When the Central Bank adjusted those rules again at the end of January 2026, in the week in which Banco do Nordeste suspended Pix after an attack, the state news agency noted that attacks on outsourced providers had become more frequent since 2025 because they are a more vulnerable link than the large banks themselves.

The survey and the conference are the federation's public face in technology. The 2026 survey, carried out by Deloitte, shows the sector's technology budget growing 58% in five years, and counts R$ 19.2 million spent in 2025 on cybersecurity training for bank staff, 12% more than in 2024, with 33,500 people trained in the 15 banks that answered that question. Febraban Tech, the conference and trade fair at which the survey is presented, has its 2027 edition set for 24 to 26 August at Distrito Anhembi in São Paulo, with 358 exhibition areas, all of them reserved at the launch on 3 November 2026. For a vendor or an engineer who sells to Brazilian banks, those three things, the layouts, the laboratory and the fair, are what the name Febraban means in practice.

en-001.def: The language tag for International English: English as it is used across the world rather than in one country, the variant Unicode's locale data keeps "as country neutral as possible".
en-001.context: In a BCP 47 language tag, a region can be two letters from ISO 3166-1 or three digits from the United Nations' M49 standard, where 001 means World; en-001 is English for the world. CLDR (the Unicode Common Locale Data Repository), the data browsers and operating systems format dates, numbers and lists with, makes en_001 the parent of British, Australian, Indian and 83 other English locales, with day-month-year dates and "metre" for the unit. It decides formats, not spelling.
en-001.depth:
RFC 5646, which defines BCP 47 language tags, allows a region subtag of two letters (an ISO 3166-1 country code) or three digits (a UN M49 code). The digits exist for areas no country code covers, such as the macro-geographical regions; in the UN's M49 table 001 is World, 150 is Europe and 419 is Latin America and the Caribbean, so es-419 is Latin American Spanish and en-001 is English for the world.

CLDR, the Unicode Common Locale Data Repository, created en_001 to take the United States' conventions out of the English that does not follow them. Its English Inheritance proposal says en_001 "was intended to remove much of the U.S. specific data that existed in the 'en' locale at the time, and serve as the inheritance point for most English locales that didn't have a direct relationship to the U.S.", and asks to "Make en_001 be as country neutral as possible": day, month and year in that order for long dates, a 12-hour clock, and "metre" rather than "meter", because "the BIPM spelling is 'metre'". The proposal also suggested ISO 8601 for numeric dates; the released data writes short dates as day/month/year instead (dd/MM/y), so the proposal and the data differ there.

The inheritance is real. CLDR's supplemental data lists 86 English locales whose parent is en_001, among them en_GB, en_AU, en_IN, en_IE, en_NZ, en_SG, en_ZA and en_150 (English in Europe). Plain en is the United States' English, and Canada's English (en_CA) still inherits from it.

In practice, on 11 November 2026, Node 24 (ICU 78.3, CLDR 48) and Chromium 141 formatted the same instant this way: en gave "November 11, 2026", "a, b, and c", "10:05 AM" and "5 meters"; en-001 gave "11 November 2026", "a, b and c", "10:05 am" and "5 metres"; en-GB gave what en-001 gave except the clock, "10:05", 24-hour. Numbers were grouped the same way in all three: 1,234,567.891.

CLDR does not decide how prose is spelt: -ise or -ize, colour or color are a house style's choice, not locale data. CLDR's own en_001 data writes the British forms ("Normalised Sorting", "Sort Without Normalisation", "St Kitts & Nevis" without a full stop), and a site writing International English usually keeps British spelling, in one of its two forms. The European Commission writes -ise in EU texts, though its style guide calls both spellings correct; ISO and the United Nations write Oxford spelling, British spelling with the suffix -ize (organize, standardize, but advise, revise, supervise), and both keep -yse in analyse and paralyse.

On the web, en-001 is a valid value for an HTML page's lang attribute, but not for hreflang: Google supports only ISO 639-1 language codes and ISO 3166-1 alpha-2 region codes there, and says that "other codes that aren't listed in those standards, such as es-419, aren't supported". A site in International English therefore declares hreflang "en", which Google reads as English in every region, and Google says it does not use hreflang or the lang attribute to detect a page's language anyway.

xkcd-is-it-worth-the-time.def: The question of whether automating or speeding up a routine task saves more time than the work of doing so costs, named after xkcd comic 1205, "Is It Worth the Time?", which tabulates the break-even point over five years.
xkcd-is-it-worth-the-time.context: Randall Munroe's table, published on 29 April 2013, crosses how often a task is done (from 50 times a day to once a year) with how much time an improvement shaves off (from 1 second to 1 day), and each cell gives the most time worth spending on the improvement across five years. It is the honest counterweight to the engineer's instinct to automate everything, and a close cousin of yak shaving: the arithmetic is simple, and what it leaves out (maintenance, errors avoided, growth, who else runs the task) is where the real decision lies.
xkcd-is-it-worth-the-time.depth:
The comic is xkcd number 1205, "Is It Worth the Time?", published by Randall Munroe on 29 April 2013. Its caption asks how long you can work on making a routine task more efficient before you are spending more time than you save, across five years. The answer is a table. Its columns are how often the task is done: 50 times a day, 5 times a day, daily, weekly, monthly and yearly. Its rows are how much time the improvement shaves off each run: 1 second, 5 seconds, 30 seconds, 1 minute, 5 minutes, 30 minutes, 1 hour, 6 hours and 1 day. Each cell is the most time that can be invested before the investment loses. The title text, the comic's hover joke, adds the recursion: do not forget the time spent finding the chart, reading the reminder, and wondering whether either makes sense.

Every cell is one multiplication: time saved per run, times runs per period, times the horizon. Shaving 1 second off something done 50 times a day saves 50 times 1,825 days, 91,250 seconds, about 25 hours, so the table says 1 day. Saving 5 minutes on a daily task saves 547,500 seconds, about 152 hours, and the cell says 6 days; saving an hour on a weekly task saves 260 hours, 10 days in the table; a whole day saved once a year is worth 5 days. Some cells are left blank as not applicable, the combinations where the saving per run is too large for that frequency to be plausible, such as 30 minutes saved 50 times a day. The chart rounds, and it counts in round-the-clock time: its 6 days are 152 hours, which is 19 eight-hour working days, so in working time every budget in the table is roughly three times larger than it looks. The asymmetry it exposes runs both ways. Tiny savings on very frequent tasks justify surprising effort (5 seconds saved 5 times a day buys 12 hours), while large savings on rare tasks justify very little (1 minute saved once a year buys 5 minutes).

What the arithmetic leaves out is where the judgment lives. The table assumes the improvement costs nothing after it is built, but scripts break when the device, the interface or the vendor's output format changes, and maintenance is paid for as long as the task exists. It counts only time, not errors: a manual change made a hundred times will eventually be made wrongly, and an automated one is made the same way every time, which is often the real return in network operations. It treats frequency as fixed, while operational work in a growing service rises with the number of devices, sites or users. It counts one person's time, while a task run by a whole team multiplies the saving by the team. And it ignores the value of the knowledge built while automating, which may outlast the script.

Munroe drew the counterweight himself. xkcd 1319, "Automation", published on 20 January 2014, shows two graphs. In theory, a burst of work writing code is followed by the work on the original task falling away. In reality, writing code turns into debugging, then rethinking, then ongoing development, and the original task is never reduced, with a label noting there is no time for it anymore. Read together, the two comics are the whole argument: 1205 says how much an improvement may cost, and 1319 says how badly people estimate what it will cost. Hofstadter's law, the ninety-ninety rule and yak shaving describe the same gap from other directions.

Site reliability engineering turned the question into policy. In Google's book Site Reliability Engineering, the chapter on eliminating toil, written by Vivek Rau and edited by Betsy Beyer, defines toil as work tied to running a production service that tends to be manual, repetitive, automatable, tactical, devoid of enduring value, and that scales linearly as the service grows. Google's site reliability organization advertises a goal of keeping toil below 50 per cent of each engineer's time, so that at least half goes to engineering that reduces future toil or adds features; the chapter reports quarterly surveys averaging about 33 per cent, with individuals ranging from 0 to 80 per cent. The linear growth is the point the xkcd table cannot show: a task whose frequency rises with every new device or customer moves to the left of the chart year by year, and an automation that did not pay at first may pay handsomely later.

A different comic, published eleven weeks earlier, is often confused with this one: xkcd 1172, "Workflow" (11 February 2013), about a user who had built his work on a side effect that an update removed, which has its own entry. The two answer opposite questions about the same engineer. This one asks whether a change is worth making for the person who makes it; "Workflow" asks what a change costs the people who had built on the old behaviour. In practice the first is quoted when someone proposes automating a weekly report, and the second when someone proposes changing what that report's output looks like.

certGuides.title: Certification study guides
certGuides.lede: Blueprint-guided study maps for vendor certification exams. Where a blueprint has been mapped, every objective from the published exam blueprint is linked to the articles, tools and official manual pages that teach it, so you study the right things in the right order; the guides still in preparation say so on their cards and on their pages.

certGuides.philosophyBody: The exam blueprint is the spine. Each objective points to deterministic, grounded resources already on this site plus the vendor's own documentation. No filler, and no guessing which topics matter.
certGuides.ethicsBody: These are independent study aids built from the public exam blueprint. They contain no exam questions, answers, or brain dumps, which violate every vendor's certification agreement. They help you learn the material, not shortcut the exam.

Product names, exam codes, and trademarks belong to their owners and are used only to identify the subject being taught. The guides are not affiliated with or endorsed by any vendor named here, including where their author teaches that vendor's courses as an authorized instructor. If you hold rights in material published on this page and believe it should be removed or corrected, please send the exact URL and a short note on the issue through the contact page; requests are reviewed promptly and in good faith.

redEducation.metaTitle: Red Education - the Authorized Training Center where Rodolfo Nützmann teaches
redEducation.metaDescription: Red Education is a global Authorized Training Center for the world's leading network and security vendors, with more than 120,000 learners trained across 132 countries. Rodolfo Nützmann teaches there as a Senior Technical Instructor.
redEducation.title: Red Education
redEducation.lede: A global Authorized Training Center for the world's leading network and security vendors - and the home of Rodolfo Nützmann's classroom since 2021.
redEducation.whoBody1: Founded in 2005, Red Education is a specialist IT and cyber security training company that has trained more than 120,000 learners across 132 countries, holding a 4.9-star average rating from more than 5,000 reviews.
redEducation.whoBody2: Training is delivered by more than 50 instructors, many certified across multiple vendors, in classroom, virtual, and on-site formats across five global regions: the Americas, Australasia, SAARC, ASEAN, and EMEA.
redEducation.visionBody1: We are passionate about empowering every student with the necessary skills and knowledge by providing the ultimate technical training experience.
redEducation.visionBody2: Delivered in an environment that supports quality adoption and understanding.
redEducation.visionBody3: We successfully enable and deploy IT training solutions across our valued customer ecosystems.

values.v3: We show enthusiasm in serving our clients.
values.v5: Harmony, we all share one voice.

redEducation.authIntro: Red Education delivers vendor-accredited training as an authorized partner of the world's leading network and security vendors, including:
redEducation.awardF5: Best F5 ATC Award 2020/21, with a 98% customer satisfaction rating on F5 courses.
redEducation.awardFortinet: Fortinet Training Institute ATC Partner of the Year for APAC (2026 ATC Awards).
redEducation.rodolfoBody: Rodolfo Nützmann has taught through Red Education since 2021, and full-time as a Senior Technical Instructor since 2023. Through Red Education, he delivers authorized instructor-led training for F5, Fortinet, Netskope, and Extreme Networks to students around the world.
redEducation.caseStudyNote: Red Education's own case study on upskilling 43 engineers at a global IT firm names Rodolfo among the instructors who delivered the training.
redEducation.linkTraining: See the courses taught by Rodolfo
redEducation.tribute: I began teaching through Red Education in 2021 and joined full-time as a Senior Instructor in 2023, which turned out to be one of the best professional decisions of my career. Behind every class I deliver stands an operations team spanning five regions that makes complex logistics look effortless, account managers who genuinely care about outcomes, and a standard of quality that pushes me to be better every single session. This page is my public thank-you to the people of Red Education, for trusting me with their classrooms and their students.
redEducation.ctaBody: Courses taught by Rodolfo Nützmann and other authorized instructors can be booked directly at Red Education, worldwide, in classroom, virtual, or on-site formats.
redEducation.aboutLink: Training is delivered through Red Education, a global Authorized Training Center
redEducation.casesIntro: Red Education publishes case studies of work delivered for named industries, and I am named in two of them. Summarized here in my own words, with each original linked - useful if you want to see what a large training engagement actually looks like before you commission one.
redEducation.case1Title: Fortinet at scale, for a global IT services firm
redEducation.case1Body: A multinational IT services company with more than 200,000 staff across sixty countries had won a large deal and did not have the certified Fortinet engineers to deliver it. Forty-three people went through FCP Fundamentals FortiGate Administrator, in mixed-experience groups. The training was the thing standing between a signed contract and a delivery team, which is a different kind of pressure from a scheduled public course.
redEducation.case1Quote: Your expertise, hard work, and commitment played a pivotal role in making this training a success.
redEducation.case1QuoteAttr: the client's project sponsor, writing to Nandagopal Siddegowda and me
redEducation.case2Title: Developing iRules for BIG-IP, across two cities
redEducation.case2Body: A team of engineers split between Singapore and Hong Kong needed to write custom traffic-management logic on their own F5 estate rather than configure around it. Delivered as virtual instructor-led training so both locations sat in one classroom. iRules is the point where BIG-IP stops being a product you configure and becomes one you program, and it rewards being taught by somebody who has had to debug one in production.
redEducation.casesRights: Both case studies are published by Red Education and remain their copyright. The summaries above are written here; the quotation is the client's own words as Red Education published them. Read the originals:

redEducation.cultureTitle: How the company says it works
redEducation.cultureIntro: Red Education publishes a culture statement, and these are the eight things it commits to. Summarized here in my own words; the original is linked below, and it is worth reading if you are considering working with them or for them.
redEducation.cultureMotto: No one said it would be easy. But it can be done
redEducation.cultureMottoAttr: Red Education, on putting the diversity statement into practice
redEducation.cultureLink: Read the culture statement on Red Education

c1.body: Equal access to information, development and opportunity, stated as a business position rather than a policy annex: a company selling training across five regions has to understand the markets it teaches in.

c2.body: Equal-opportunity hiring judged on demonstrable experience and fit for the role, with the argument that a workforce drawn from many countries is what makes an international training business legible to its customers.

c3.body: Promotion on performance, with managers trained in evaluating fairly - the part that decides whether the rest of it is real.

c4.body: Named reporting procedures for discrimination and harassment, follow-up to prevent recurrence, and partnerships with community groups.

c5.body: The claim that a workforce reflecting its customers serves them better, which for a company teaching in Asia Pacific, the Americas, Europe, India and the Middle East is an operational point rather than a sentiment.

c6.body: A committee of champions drawn from every level of the company, responsible for keeping the policy present in day-to-day decisions.

c7.body: Training for all employees, flexible hours, education assistance, employee networks, parental and childcare support, and mentorship.

c8.term: Five ways to act on it.
c8.body: The statement ends with commitments rather than aspirations: integrate it into strategy, set measurable targets with dates, educate senior leadership, communicate it plainly, and make the business case understood throughout the organization.

own.title: Red Education's own courses
own.lede: For more than twenty years Red Education has taught the vendors' own courses under their authorization, with instructors many of whom came from those vendors and from their largest customers. Now those experts write courses of their own. The FastTrack series is original Red Education courseware, designed and delivered by Red Education for people at the start of the work: junior and aspiring engineers, system administrators moving into security, anyone in their first three years. Two FastTrack courses are open, more are planned, and an on-demand video course on Palo Alto Networks sits beside them.
own.allCourses: All of Red Education's own courses
own.schedules: The FastTrack courses run on three regional schedules: Americas, Europe and Singapore time, which also covers Australia and New Zealand, Asia and India. Companies can pay by purchase order, and team bookings can be arranged, depending on the course.
own.alongside: Read beside them on this site: the <materials>open TCP/IP course</materials> takes apart in depth the protocols both FastTrack courses lean on, and <practice>The Practice</practice> describes the triage, evidence and escalation work they train for.
own.readOn: Read on 6 October 2026 from Red Education's course pages, its three course outlines and the answers on its own-courses page.

openNgfw.summary: A first course for engineers new to firewalls and, in Red Education's words, "100% Red Education original IP". Every learner builds, breaks and fixes a live next-generation firewall of their own, and practises the operating method senior engineers rely on: read the ticket, know the blast radius and the rollback before touching anything, troubleshoot from the logs, and escalate with evidence. The skills transfer to any firewall platform.
facts: Half a day, live and instructor-led: two sessions of 120 minutes in one sitting
10 modules and 5 hands-on labs, for 16 learners at most
Your own OPNsense firewall with Zenarmor, and 7 days of lab pod access
Foundational: roughly 0 to 3 years in network or security roles, no firewall experience assumed
A course companion and a student lab guide, a verified digital badge through Credly, and the REDiUP alumni community

networkFundamentals.summary: How a connection actually travels, taught as a method rather than as a list of facts. Learners trace one live connection from the client through name resolution, the gateway, address translation and the firewall to the service; read the evidence that DNS, DHCP, NAT and the firewall's flow logs leave behind; halve the problem until the fault has nowhere left to hide; and finish with a five-line escalation that says where the connection broke and why. Vendor-neutral, on Linux endpoints and a firewall, with faults planted in each learner's own lab.
facts: Two live, instructor-led virtual sessions of two hours
12 modules in two sessions: knowing the path, then the clues failures leave
Your own live network for 7 days, to trace, diagnose and prove
A course companion with every slide and its full notes, and a verified digital badge through Credly

panOnDemand.summary: Four key Palo Alto Networks topics on video, presented by a Palo Alto Networks certified instructor with enterprise experience: Firewall Essentials (EDU-210), Cortex XSIAM, Cortex XDR and preparing for the exam. By Red Education's own description it is a topic overview to build practical understanding, not a complete training course or a certification programme: a way in before the official courses, which Red Education also teaches as a global authorized training partner for Palo Alto Networks.
facts: On-demand video, at your own pace, on a computer, tablet or phone
3 hours in four topics: EDU-210 Firewall Essentials (1 h 15 min), Cortex XSIAM (30 min), Cortex XDR (55 min), exam preparation (32 min)
No Palo Alto Networks experience needed; some networking and security familiarity helps

career.title: Understanding Cyber Security Career Paths
career.body: A free digital booklet from Red Education, sixty pages long, written for people choosing a path in cyber security, climbing one, or changing careers into it. It maps the profession as seven streams (governance, vulnerability testing, security operations, forensics, incident response, threat analysis and security design) that rise from the associate-level security analyst through analyst and manager roles to the chief information security officer. Each of its fourteen roles gets a job description, the technical skills and personal qualities it needs with the proficiency expected at each, and its key functions and tasks.
career.complements: It complements two parts of this site. <roles>The Roles</roles> describes each position from the inside: what it answers for, who it receives from, who it serves and how it is measured. <practice>The Practice</practice> describes how the work itself is done. The booklet adds the ladder: the skills each step needs, and how well. Its streams line up with the security roles in The Roles like this:
