industry.lede: The corporate genealogies of networking and security: who founded each company, what they built, who bought whom, and where every bloodline ended up. Written from primary sources - SEC filings, inquiry reports, and the trade press of each era.
industry.careerNote: Two kinds of company appear here, and the markers tell them apart: the ones I was employed by, and the ones whose technology I worked with directly from the other side of the table. Chronological by first engagement, from 1996.
industry.careerStripNote: In every one of these, employer or vendor, the work was the same shape: facing the end customer, in pre-sales and in post-sales technical support, and very often acting as the technical proxy and enablement facilitator for the partners who had to carry the product themselves. The job was to leave the customer with something that worked better than it did before - an innovation, a solution, an improvement they could keep running after I left. The full telling lives at the career record.

before-the-network.title: Before the network
before-the-network.lede: The telegraph, the telephone, the transistor, the integrated circuit and the modem: the companies founded here predate networking and built the parts it would be made of.

the-packet-and-the-wire.title: The packet and the wire
the-packet-and-the-wire.lede: From the first ARPANET links in 1969 to the day the ARPANET switched to TCP/IP, 1 January 1983: Ethernet, the TCP paper and DNS between them.

routers-switches-and-the-reserve.title: Routers, switches and the reserve
routers-switches-and-the-reserve.lede: The router and switch companies arrive: spanning tree in 1985, SNMP in 1988, the Ethernet switch in 1990; in Brazil the market reserve of 1984 decides who may build.

the-web-and-the-firewall.title: The web and the firewall
the-web-and-the-firewall.lede: The World Wide Web and the first commercial firewall, both 1991, then LDAP and the open signatures of 1998: the internet becomes a market and a threat surface at once.

the-flood-and-the-rental.title: The flood and the rental
the-flood-and-the-rental.lede: From the denial of service of February 2000 to the smartphone of 2007, through utility computing in 2006: scale becomes the problem, and the computer becomes something you rent.

software-takes-the-network.title: Software takes the network
software-takes-the-network.lede: Control separated from forwarding in 2008, Stuxnet in 2010, containers in 2013, free certificates in 2015: the network becomes a program and so does the attack.

platforms-and-the-things.title: Platforms and the things
platforms-and-the-things.lede: From the Mirai botnet of 2016 to the conversational models of 2022 and today: the platform companies, the things on the network, and the machines that answer in prose.

studyGuidesIndex.title: Study guides
studyGuidesIndex.lede: Two ways to study here, and they answer different questions. Curated reading paths follow a technology rather than an exam: read the Learn library in teaching order, with the tools to practise on as you go. Certification study guides live on their own page and do the opposite - they start from a vendor's published exam blueprint and map it objective by objective.
studyGuidesIndex.pathsLede: A path is a syllabus with no exam behind it. Nothing here is organized around a certification blueprint or scored against one: the order is the order the subject makes sense in, chosen so each article earns the next. Read straight through, or stop when you have what you came for. The tools they link compute in your browser, and nothing is paywalled.
studyGuidesIndex.certLede: These are the exam-shaped ones, and they live on the certifications page. Each follows a vendor's own published blueprint objective by objective, tying every objective to the articles that teach it, the tools that exercise it, and the manual pages that remain the source of truth.

bigip-fundamentals.title: F5 BIG-IP end to end
bigip-fundamentals.lede: Everything the earlier 101, 201, 301A, and 301B blueprints listed (F5 has retired 101, limits 201 to candidates who passed 101 before 1 May 2025, and still lists 301A and 301B in its exam catalogue, as read on 25 October 2026), as this site's articles in teaching order: the networking fundamentals the modern track assumes (OSI (Open Systems Interconnection) to VPN (virtual private network)), the full administration arc from interfaces to high availability to the support workflows the new exams dropped, and the LTM (Local Traffic Manager) specialist craft - iRules, analytics, captures, SSL (Secure Sockets Layer) - closing with the two articles that compare those blueprints against the newer ones.
bigip-fundamentals.outcome: you will understand how a BIG-IP carries, secures and reports on application traffic, from the networking floor it assumes through administration and high availability to the LTM craft of iRules, analytics and captures, and how the retired blueprints relate to the current ones.

modern-identity.title: Modern identity, from the token up
modern-identity.lede: The open standards behind single sign-on, in dependency order: the JWT (JSON Web Token) itself, the signatures and JWKS (JSON Web Key Set) that make it verifiable, the OAuth 2.0 and PKCE (Proof Key for Code Exchange) flows that mint it, OIDC (OpenID Connect) on top, and TOTP/HOTP (time-based and HMAC-based one-time passwords) as the second factor.
modern-identity.outcome: you will understand how a login becomes a token, how a signature and a key set make that token verifiable, how OAuth 2.0 with PKCE and OIDC mint and carry it, and where a one-time password enters as the second factor.

tls-from-zero.title: TLS from zero
tls-from-zero.lede: TLS (Transport Layer Security) from the cipher suite string upward: what each part of a suite name means, what TLS 1.3 removed and why, how hybrid post-quantum key exchange works, how TLS 1.2, TLS 1.3, DTLS (Datagram TLS), and QUIC relate as one family, and how to read what openssl s_client says a real server did.
tls-from-zero.outcome: you will understand what each part of a cipher suite name promises, what TLS 1.3 removed and why, how hybrid post-quantum key exchange works, how TLS 1.2, TLS 1.3, DTLS and QUIC belong to one family, and how to check with openssl s_client what a real server negotiated.

http-evolution.title: HTTP, told forward
http-evolution.lede: HTTP (the Hypertext Transfer Protocol) across its five versions - from the one-line GET of 1991 to HTTP/3 on QUIC - then the operational layer: forward and reverse proxies, HSTS (HTTP Strict Transport Security), and curl beyond the browser.
http-evolution.outcome: you will understand what each of HTTP's five versions changed, from the one-line GET of 1991 to HTTP/3 on QUIC, and how proxies, HSTS and curl sit on top of it in daily operation.

regex-mastery.title: Regular expressions, properly
regex-mastery.lede: The craft skill under log analysis and every parser: quantifiers and classes, groups and backreferences, anchors and boundaries, flags and modes - ending on catastrophic backtracking, the failure mode every production regex must avoid.
regex-mastery.outcome: you will understand how a regular expression engine matches, from classes and quantifiers to groups, backreferences, anchors and flags, and how to recognize and avoid the catastrophic backtracking that takes production systems down.

pingfederate-administration.title: PingFederate administration, end to end
pingfederate-administration.lede: The blueprint's assumed fundamentals first - the directory model and the Kerberos ticket machinery - then the ten product articles in teaching order, SCIM beside the provisioning stop, and the SSO flows to close. The reading spine behind the PFP-001 certification guide.
pingfederate-administration.outcome: you will understand the directory and Kerberos fundamentals the product assumes, then PingFederate itself in teaching order, provisioning with SCIM beside it, and the SSO flows that close the PFP-001 blueprint.

zscaler-zero-trust.title: Zscaler Zero Trust Exchange
zscaler-zero-trust.lede: From tunnels and fundamentals to the full policy brain: forwarding, firewall order, TLS inspection, web and file controls, DLP, CASB, and ZPA's segments, policy, and posture - with the three native tools to practice on.
zscaler-zero-trust.outcome: you will understand how traffic reaches the Zero Trust Exchange and how its policy brain is ordered: forwarding, firewall, TLS inspection, web and file controls, DLP and CASB, and ZPA's segments, policy and posture.

netskope-sase.title: Netskope SASE, End to End
netskope-sase.lede: The whole platform in reading order: architecture and NewEdge, every steering method, the client, TLS decryption, the two protection paths, CCI-driven policy, Private Access, Cloud Firewall, and the analytics layer - with the PAC and SAML tools to practice on. Built to walk the accreditation and certification domains from this site.
netskope-sase.outcome: you will understand the Netskope platform in reading order: NewEdge and the architecture, every steering method and the client, TLS decryption, the inline and API protection paths, CCI-driven policy, Private Access, Cloud Firewall and the analytics layer.

ping-identity-platform.title: The Ping Identity Platform
ping-identity-platform.lede: The whole Ping estate in reading order: the PingOne platform map and the ForgeRock lineage first, so every product name resolves; then PingAccess policy, the PingDirectory data platform, and DaVinci orchestration; closing with the PingFederate shelf - the self-managed federation core - in its established teaching order. The companion walk to the Certified Professional guides on the certifications hub.
ping-identity-platform.outcome: you will understand how the Ping estate fits together, from the PingOne map and the ForgeRock lineage that explains the product names to PingAccess policy, the PingDirectory data platform, DaVinci orchestration and the PingFederate core.

checkpoint-security-administration.title: Check Point security administration
checkpoint-security-administration.lede: The platform in the order the CCSA teaches it: the three-tier split first, because nothing else makes sense until you know the management server and the gateway are different machines with different jobs, then the rule base, then the layer semantics that catch everyone.
checkpoint-security-administration.outcome: you will understand the three-tier split of management server, gateway and console, the rule base built on it, and the layer semantics that decide which rule fires, in the order the CCSA teaches them.

nginx-from-config-to-cache.title: NGINX, from configuration to cache
nginx-from-config-to-cache.lede: In the order the confusions actually arrive: the configuration tree, then which location block wins, then what path the backend receives, then what gets cached and served to whom.
nginx-from-config-to-cache.outcome: you will understand how NGINX reads its configuration tree, which location block wins, what path the backend receives, and what is cached and served to whom.

extreme-fabric-and-voss.title: Extreme fabric and the two operating systems
extreme-fabric-and-voss.lede: ExtremeXOS for the configuration model, then why VOSS feels so different (it came from another company entirely), then Fabric Connect built up from IS-IS through I-SIDs to the resilience features.
extreme-fabric-and-voss.outcome: you will understand the ExtremeXOS configuration model, why VOSS is a different operating system from a different company, and how Fabric Connect is built from IS-IS through I-SIDs to its resilience features.

fortinet-fabric-and-operations.title: Fortinet beyond the single firewall
fortinet-fabric-and-operations.lede: What shows up once a FortiGate is not alone: inspection choices, the branch overlay, cloud integration, the SOC, and the operational technology edge.
fortinet-fabric-and-operations.outcome: you will understand what changes once a FortiGate is not alone: the inspection choices, the branch overlay, the cloud integration, the SOC and the operational technology edge.

bigip-monitors-from-expect.title: From Expect to BIG-IP Scripted monitors
bigip-monitors-from-expect.lede: For the operator who already drives devices with Expect: the four verbs, the Tcl underneath, the buffer every pattern is tried against, the three ways a wait ends, and what a device's prompt and pager do to a script; then the pool and the health monitor that decide which members get traffic; and last the BIG-IP's Scripted monitor, a send-and-expect file that looks like Expect and works nothing like it.
bigip-monitors-from-expect.outcome: you will understand how Expect waits for a program and answers it, from Tcl's quoting to the buffer, the timeout, the end of file and a device's prompt, and how a BIG-IP decides that a pool member is up, ending with the Scripted monitor and the ways it differs from Expect.

web-server-php-and-the-waf.title: The web stack: server, PHP and the WAF
web-server-php-and-the-waf.lede: One request from the web server to the code behind it and the firewall in front of it: Apache httpd and the problem NGINX was written against, how NGINX finds the location that handles a request, what PHP is and how PHP-FPM receives a request over FastCGI, the PHP vulnerabilities of October 2026, and the web application firewall, from its history to how BIG-IP Advanced WAF and FortiWeb put a new signature to work.
web-server-php-and-the-waf.outcome: you will understand how a request travels from NGINX or Apache httpd to PHP-FPM over FastCGI, what PHP's configuration can and cannot enforce, what the October 2026 PHP vulnerabilities were and who had to act, and what a WAF signature does, and does not do, while PHP itself is being updated.

netfun-1.title: Network Fundamentals I: from bits to the LAN
netfun-1.lede: Layers 1 and 2, from the units a network counts in to the frame a switch forwards: the layer model and the bodies that write the standards, copper, fibre and radio, the Ethernet frame and its addresses, VLANs, spanning tree and link aggregation, and Wi-Fi as layers 1 and 2.
netfun-1.outcome: you will be able to read a frame, explain what a switch does with it, and say which layer a fault is on.

m1.title: The map and the units
m1.outcome: Place a protocol on the layer model, count in bits and bytes without mixing the two kinds of kilo, and know which body writes which standard.

m2.title: Layer 1, the physical path
m2.outcome: Follow a signal through copper, fibre and radio, from the wiring closet to the last mile and the sea floor, and say what the physical layer can and cannot be blamed for.

m3.title: Layer 2, frames and switching
m3.outcome: Read an Ethernet frame and the addresses in it, say what a switch, a bridge and a router each decide, and explain VLANs, spanning tree and link aggregation.

m4.title: Wireless as layers 1 and 2
m4.outcome: Explain what Wi-Fi changes at the first two layers: its generations, the handshake an attack once broke, and port-based access control with 802.1X.

planned.fibre-basics: Fibre basics: single-mode and multimode, connectors and the optical budget
planned.ethernet-frame: The Ethernet frame, field by field
planned.vlans-and-8021q: VLANs and 802.1Q trunking: tagged, untagged, native and voice
planned.spanning-tree: Spanning tree in one article: why a blocked port is the feature

netfun-2.title: Network Fundamentals II: addressing and routing
netfun-2.lede: Layer 3, from the address on an interface to the path a packet takes across the internet: IPv4 subnetting and summarization, IPv6, how a host gets its address and finds a name with DHCP and DNS, and how routers choose, from the routing table and the longest match to OSPF, IS-IS, BGP and MPLS.
netfun-2.outcome: you will be able to design an address plan, read a routing table, and explain why a packet went where it went.

m1.title: IPv4 addressing
m1.outcome: Subnet any block by hand, size subnets with VLSM, summarize routes, and tell private address space from public.

m2.title: IPv6
m2.outcome: Read and shorten an IPv6 address, plan IPv6 subnets, and explain how a host configures itself and finds its neighbours.

m3.title: Getting an address and a name
m3.outcome: Follow a DHCP lease from discovery to renewal, read a DNS answer field by field, and say which server is authoritative for a name.

m4.title: Routing
m4.outcome: Read a routing table, predict which route wins and why, and explain what OSPF, IS-IS and BGP each decide.

catDistribution.metaDescription: The tracking console for the internet's most reliable logistics network: stray cats assigning themselves to humans. Enter your name; the System does the rest. Consent was never part of the protocol.
catDistribution.title: The Global Cat Distribution System
catDistribution.tagline: You do not choose the cat. The cat has already chosen.
catDistribution.intro: The Cat Distribution System is the internet's name for a well-documented phenomenon: you do not acquire a stray cat, a stray cat acquires you. This console tracks your assignment. Enter your name (city optional, the System knows anyway), press Track and read the delivery manifest. Assignments are deterministic: the same name always receives the same cat. That is not a bug. That is destiny.
catDistribution.emptyHint: Enter a name. The System is patient. The System is always patient.
catDistribution.stampSub: Resistance is not filed under available options. Prepare a warm surface and lower your expectations of furniture.
catDistribution.creditNote: The Cat Distribution System is genuine internet folklore: the observation, popularized in the early 2020s, that stray cats appear precisely when and where they decide to. No cats were algorithmically generated; all cats are real and currently on their way.

importanceMeter.metaDescription: Measures how much of your attention a thing has actually earned. The arithmetic is real.
importanceMeter.title: Importance Meter
importanceMeter.tagline: Measures, to a defensible standard, the importance a topic has actually earned.
importanceMeter.intro: Enter the matter and its circumstances. Each factor is weighted, the weights are shown, and the subtotal is genuinely computed: it will move as you change things, sometimes dramatically. The subtotal is then multiplied by the bearing the matter has on the work you are accountable for. Results are reproducible.
importanceMeter.urgentLabel: URGENT appears in the subject line, in capitals
importanceMeter.ccLabel: People copied who did not need to be
importanceMeter.escalationLabel: How far it has been escalated
importanceMeter.raisedLabel: Raised in a meeting you were not invited to
importanceMeter.movedLabel: The deadline has already moved once
importanceMeter.coefficientNote: This coefficient is a constant. It is not affected by any input above, and it has never been observed to take another value.

remarks.trivial: Nothing here registers. Unusual, and slightly suspicious.
remarks.elevated: Elevated. Somebody has begun using capital letters.
remarks.considerable: Considerable. There is now a recurring meeting about it.
remarks.spectacular: Spectacular. This will be referred to for years as a lesson, by people who were not involved.

importanceMeter.methodBody: The weights above are arbitrary but consistent: identical inputs always produce an identical subtotal, which is the only property this needed. Nothing is rounded to reach the result and nothing is discarded. The subtotal is multiplied by the coefficient and the product is reported exactly. This tool computes rather than guesses, in keeping with the rest of the site. It happens to be computing something whose answer does not vary.
importanceMeter.gaugeAria: Result gauge. The needle rests at zero.
importanceMeter.overrideHint: The coefficient has resisted every attempt to change it through the interface. Whether it can be changed by other means is not documented.
importanceMeter.disclaimerBody: If English is not your first language: “zero fucks given” is a common informal expression meaning complete indifference, the sense that something does not concern you in the slightest. It is vulgar, and it is used humorously far more often than aggressively, usually about bureaucracy, pointless urgency and work theatre rather than about people. The idea is not particular to English. Most European languages have their own idiom for the same shrug, built variously from food, animals, weather or anatomy, and several are a good deal more colourful than the English one. Register matters more than the words: it belongs in casual speech among people who know each other, and not in professional writing, a customer email or anything with your employer’s name on it.
importanceMeter.ogAlt: Importance Meter: a conservative urgency estimate filled to the top, beside a gauge whose needle rests at zero.

vendor.title: Vendors
vendor.intro: Companies that make the product. Most of this timeline is here, because most of the industry's stories are about somebody building a thing and then discovering what it was for.

distributor.title: Distributors
distributor.intro: Two-tier distribution: they sell to resellers rather than to the organizations that use the equipment. An invisible layer to most engineers, and the one that decides which products are practical to buy in a given country.

reseller.title: Resellers and integrators
reseller.intro: The companies that actually install the thing. They carry other people's products, and their skill is in making a portfolio assembled for commercial reasons behave like a system.

services.title: Services and consulting
services.intro: Outsourcing, consulting, managed operations. They sell people and process rather than product, which is a harder thing to explain to a market and a harder thing to scale.

carrier.title: Carriers
carrier.intro: Operators that move somebody else's traffic. The physical substrate everything above them assumes, and the reason several entries here are really about rights of way and undersea cable.

datacentre.title: Data centres and interconnection
datacentre.intro: Colocation, hosting and the places networks meet. Property businesses with network effects, which is a stranger combination than it sounds.

training.title: Training and certification
training.intro: The companies and bodies that decide what competence looks like and who is allowed to claim it. On a site built by an instructor these are not a footnote.

standards.title: Standards, research and protocols
standards.intro: Not companies selling anything, or not only that: the laboratories, foundations and specifications the commercial entries are built on top of.

industryTags.milestonesLink: Before any of these companies: the milestones they were built on
industryTags.learningLink: The companies that teach the industry: training centres, certification bodies, platforms and schools

media.title: Trade press, media and events
media.intro: The magazines, news sites and conferences where the industry describes itself to itself: who bought whom, which integrator changed its name, and which buyers will be in the room. Read as sources, not as verdicts.

milestones.title: Milestones: the ground the industry stands on
milestones.intro: The company timeline begins in the nineteenth century almost by accident. This page is the other history: the physics and engineering that had to exist first, from a stack of zinc and copper discs in 1800 to the first fibre laid across the Atlantic.
milestones.test: The test for inclusion here is narrow and deliberate. Not "important events in science", but: could a network engineer's working day be explained without it? Induction, amplification, Shannon's channel capacity, random access, packet switching. Things upstream of the job rather than beside it. Every entry says why it matters, not only what happened.
milestones.backToCompanies: The companies that were built on top of this

electricity.name: Electricity
electricity.blurb: Making it, moving it, and working out what it is. Five results between 1800 and 1887 that turn a curiosity into a field, ending with the demonstration of waves that had been predicted on paper twenty years earlier.

electronics.name: Electronics
electronics.blurb: Controlling it. The step from conducting a signal to acting on one: rectification, then amplification, then doing both in solid state, then doing it a million times on one piece of silicon.

digital.name: Digital
digital.blurb: Representing information as discrete symbols and reasoning about it rigorously. Three papers, two of them by the same person, that between them define what a computer is, what it cannot do, and how much can be sent down a noisy wire.

storage.name: Storage
storage.blurb: Keeping it. The arc from sequential to addressable to solid-state, each step changing not just capacity but what a system can reasonably assume about how long a read takes.

transfer.name: Transfer
transfer.blurb: Moving it. From the first separation of a message from its messenger to the fibre under the ocean, by way of the two design decisions - packets rather than circuits, and internetworking rather than one network - that produced everything since.

making.name: Making
making.blurb: The five strands above record what was invented. This one records how any of it gets built - the planar process, the foundry, the licensed architecture, the contract factory. A networking vendor today designs a product it does not manufacture, on silicon it does not fabricate, using a processor architecture it licenses rather than owns. Every step of that arrangement was invented by somebody, on a date.

advisory.title: Independent technical judgement for consequential technology decisions.
advisory.lede: Enterprise networking, cybersecurity, application delivery, identity and infrastructure: before you commit to the architecture, the supplier, the platform, the migration or the budget. The deliverable is a written decision analysis that states the assumptions, the trade-offs, the risks, the operational consequences and the questions that still need answers. The technology is the domain expertise. What you are buying is decision quality.
advisory.availabilityBody: This is not a product catalogue. The work below describes the kinds of question I am useful on; the shape of any particular engagement is agreed before it starts. If what you need is close to one of these but not the same, that is usually fine and worth a conversation.
advisory.scopeTitle: What I do not personally provide
advisory.scopeIn: I do not use these engagements as staff augmentation, project implementation, managed operations, round-the-clock escalation or incident-response engineering. The separation is deliberate: the value of the engagement is independent technical judgement before a consequential decision is made, and that value falls the moment the adviser stands to do the work the advice creates.
advisory.offerReviewBody: Reading a proposed design before it is built and paid for: what it assumes, where it will strain, what it will cost to operate rather than to buy, and which of its assumptions are load-bearing. The failures that matter are rarely in the product; they are in what the design took for granted.
advisory.offerSpecBody: Writing what to ask for. A specification or request for proposal that describes the outcome precisely enough to be scored fairly - and closes the gaps a supplier would otherwise be free to interpret in their own favour. Most bad procurement is decided at this stage rather than at the bid.
advisory.offerAssessBody: An independent second reading of a supplier's quotation and diagram, in writing: what is actually being proposed, what it leaves out, what it assumes about the environment it will land in, and which questions to put back before anything is signed.
advisory.offerSelectBody: Stay or move, consolidate or keep two, on-premises or as a service. A defined question, the trade-offs stated in the terms of the organization rather than the vendor's, and a defensible answer with the reasoning attached - so the decision survives the person who made it.
advisory.offerPostmortemBody: Not incident response - the review afterwards, when the fire is out and somebody has to give an honest account of what happened and what would prevent it recurring. Written to be read by people who were not there, and without the search for someone to blame that makes most such documents useless.
advisory.independenceBody:
Independence is a property of the analysis, and it is worth stating precisely rather than broadly.

The analysis is written by me and carries my name. I hold current instructor authorizations across four vendors' platforms, and I do not personally sell or resell the technologies being evaluated: no sales quota, no resale margin, no referral commission and no implementation award attached to the technology the analysis favours. There is no version of this engagement that pays me more if you buy one thing rather than another, and if the honest answer is that your incumbent is right, that is the answer. You can verify each authorization independently, which is the point of naming them.

What is not claimed is commercial independence from every company in the ecosystem. Engagements are contracted and invoiced through Red Education, which sells authorized training and professional services across several vendors' platforms. Where either is a candidate for what follows a decision, the document says so in plain words, and the choice of who does that work stays yours.

Commercial interest does not invalidate expertise. It does change the context in which a recommendation should be evaluated, and knowing exactly what that context is, on both sides of the table, is part of what you are paying for. It also means the review is not a weapon against suppliers: a supplier confident in its proposal can suggest the review itself, because a proposal that holds up under independent scrutiny is easier for its customer to approve, and one that does not is cheaper to fix before deployment than after.
advisory.howStep1: A conversation about the decision you are facing, at no charge, to establish whether I am the right person for it.
advisory.howStep2: A written scope: the question, the deliverable, the dates and the fee. Fixed price per engagement rather than by the hour. For a post-incident review, the scope also says which kind of review it is.
advisory.howStep3: The work, with access to whoever holds the technical detail.
advisory.howStep4: A written answer you can circulate internally, and a call to walk through it. At close-out I ask whether an account of the engagement may be published later, named, anonymized, or reduced to the shape of the decision; a no is a complete answer, and nothing is published without a yes in writing.
advisory.ctaTitle: If there is a decision on your desk
advisory.ctaBody: Write to me directly. The first conversation is with the person who will do the work, not with an account manager. The useful first message says what the decision is, who has to sign it, and when.
advisory.disclaimerBody: I work full time for Red Education. The advisory work described on this page is delivered personally by me <amber>and contracted through</amber> Red Education, which also issues the proposal and the invoice. The one thing I cannot tell you about is pricing: that comes only after a detailed scoping and expectations call, and is provided exclusively by Red Education. What I can tell you is that inside the engagement I am the main advocate for the best possible outcome for you: since 1996 I have consistently argued for what serves the end customer, not necessarily for what served the company I was working for at the time. If you need training, that goes through Red Education too.
advisory.exclusion1Body: I will review what is planned and audit what was built, but I am not the pair of hands that builds it.
advisory.exclusion2Body: I do not sell hours, and I am not a name on a rota or an escalation path. Attendance during a maintenance window is not offered, on site or remotely.
advisory.exclusion3Body: If what is needed is another person on the team, that is a hiring decision rather than an advisory one.
advisory.exclusion4Term: Training and enablement, in any form
advisory.exclusion4Body: I do not sell training as advisory work. I deliver official instructor-led courses under vendor authorization, and that is a separate engagement with its own scheduling and its own terms; ask and I will point you to it. What I offer here is judgement on a decision, not a curriculum.
advisory.exclusion5Body: I do not offer this. Slides, lab guides, speaker notes and assessment are a separate craft, commissioned on its own scope and its own terms, and it is not advisory time. Telling you whether a course should exist is work I will do. Writing the course is not.
advisory.offerSpeakingBody: Conference talks, keynotes, and internal sessions on where this industry came from, what it was like to be in it, and how that compares with now. Prepared talks, and custom subjects by arrangement.
advisory.advisorBody: Thirty years on the supply side of enterprise networking and security, from inside vendors, value-added resellers and distributors, consulting practices, and direct engagements with the customer: implementing, supporting, deploying and teaching what those companies sell, rather than selling it. That is the whole basis of the advice: my job was to make the thing work afterwards, so I have always had to live with the answer. The analysis is mine and it carries my name; how an engagement is contracted is stated plainly further down this page. The credentials, the career record and what past clients and students say are a click away, because a claim you cannot check is not worth making.
advisory.offerEstateBody: An inventory that becomes a map: what is connected, what each thing actually does, what depends on it, and which parts nobody can currently explain. Named a review rather than an audit, because audit carries assurance meaning this does not claim. Most estates contain something load-bearing that no one has looked at in years.
advisory.offersLede: One offer, stated plainly, for the decision that has consequences.
advisory.offerExecutiveTitle: Executive-level technical advisory for mission-critical decisions
advisory.offerExecutiveBody: For the board, the steering committee or the executive who has to commit to a direction on technology adoption, digital transformation, or enabling and improving a service - and who needs the technical reality of that decision stated by someone with no stake in which technology wins. The deliverable is a structured, methodical and independent analysis: the diagnosis, the options with their trade-offs, the cautions, the risks, and what each path would actually take to carry out. Written to be circulated and defended internally, not presented and forgotten. What it does not include is a recommendation shaped by a commission, because there is no commission - I hold authorized instructor status across four platforms and a sales quota on none of them. The impact is for the business to tell.
advisory.recordTitle: Where this comes from, in the client's words
advisory.recordBody: I spent the first twenty-four years of my career, from 1996 to 2020, doing this work for leading organizations across many segments: financial institutions, government agencies, service providers of every sort, large multinational conglomerates in commerce and services, and industry across a wide range. Delivered, been responsible for, overseen, collaborated on, led and taken part in, many times over, from inside vendors, distributors and integrators. These engagements are no longer what I sell. They are what the advice above is made of.
advisory.earnBody: I will not tell you what to do before I understand your situation, and the first conversation exists to establish whether I can be useful at all, including the answer that I cannot, or that the question is better put to someone else. An advisor who is certain before they have listened is selling something. If the honest answer is that your existing supplier is right, that is the answer you will get in writing, and it will be the most valuable sentence in the document.
advisory.problemBody:
Organizations are being asked to make decisions about technology that their own business models did not prepare them to make, at a pace that does not allow the expertise to be hired and grown in-house first. The result is familiar: the decision gets made from the material supplied by the people selling into it, because that is the only material in the room. Much of what reaches the table comes from parties with a commercial interest in the outcome, and every reference is chosen; some of it comes from internal teams, open-source communities and engineers with no transaction attached, and the first job is knowing which is which. Commercial interest does not invalidate expertise. It does change the context in which a recommendation should be evaluated, and the internal team, who may be excellent, is being asked to referee a game where they only see one side's playbook.

That is the gap this practice exists to close, and nothing more. Not to replace the team, not to run the project, and not to become another supplier with a diagram: to put an independent, experienced technical reading in front of the people who have to sign, in time for it to change the decision rather than explain it afterwards.
advisory.positioning: I provide independent technical analysis for infrastructure and security decisions that have not yet been made, at the level where they are taken: the evidence, the assumptions and the trade-offs, written down before the decision.
advisory.metaTitle: Independent technical advisory for network and security decisions · Rodolfo Nützmann
advisory.metaDescription: Independent technical judgement before you commit to an architecture, supplier, platform or budget: a written decision analysis by Rodolfo Nützmann.
advisory.whenTitle: When this tends to be useful
advisory.whenLede: The people who get the most out of an engagement usually arrive in one of five situations.
advisory.when1Body: A CIO, CISO or head of infrastructure with a technically consequential decision, and either too little independent expertise in-house to test it or the wish for a second opinion before signing.
advisory.when2Body: A group that has to turn technical assumptions into defensible business trade-offs, and needs them stated by someone who can be questioned in the room.
advisory.when3Body: Requirements worth asking for, proposals interpreted on their merits, and scoring that suppliers cannot steer.
advisory.when4Body: Data-centre modernization, SASE and SSE, vendor consolidation, a network redesign, application-security architecture, WAN transformation, a firewall refresh, hybrid and cloud connectivity, a major platform migration.
advisory.when5Body: Not the response, which has its own people: the independent reconstruction afterwards, and what the organization should learn from it.
advisory.shapesTitle: One advisory model, applied to several kinds of consequential decision
advisory.shapesLede: These are shapes, not packages. The question, the inputs, the deliverable, the dates and the fee are agreed in writing before the work starts, and an engagement that sits between two shapes is usual rather than a problem.
advisory.shape1Question: Should we approve this architecture, or this proposal?
advisory.shape1Body: An independent second reading of a supplier's quotation and diagram, in writing: what is actually being proposed, what it leaves out, what it assumes about the environment it will land in, and which questions to put back before anything is signed.
advisory.shape2Question: Which of these approaches, or vendors, fits us?
advisory.shape2Body: Stay or move, consolidate or keep two, on-premises or as a service. A defined question, the trade-offs stated in the terms of the organization rather than the vendor's, and a defensible answer with the reasoning attached, so the decision survives the person who made it.
advisory.shape3Question: What are we overlooking before implementation?
advisory.shape3Output: Architecture findings and a risk register.
advisory.shape3Body: Reading a proposed design before it is built and paid for: what it assumes, where it will strain, what it will cost to operate rather than to buy, and which of its assumptions are load-bearing. The failures that matter are rarely in the product; they are in what the design took for granted.
advisory.shape4Question: What should we actually ask suppliers to deliver?
advisory.shape4Body: Writing what to ask for. A specification or request for proposal that describes the outcome precisely enough to be scored fairly, and closes the gaps a supplier would otherwise be free to interpret in their own favour. Most bad procurement is decided at this stage rather than at the bid.
advisory.shape5Question: What do we actually have, and what depends on it?
advisory.shape5Output: A map of the estate, with the parts nobody can explain marked.
advisory.shape5Body: An inventory that becomes a map: what is connected, what each thing actually does, what depends on it, and which parts nobody can currently explain. Named a review rather than an audit, because audit carries assurance meaning this does not claim. Most estates contain something load-bearing that no one has looked at in years.
advisory.shape6Question: What failed, and what should materially change?
advisory.shape6Body: Not incident response: the review afterwards, when the fire is out and somebody has to give an honest account of what happened and what would prevent it recurring. Written to be read by people who were not there, and without the search for someone to blame that makes most such documents useless. The scope is an engineering learning review. It is not a forensic investigation and not a legal or regulatory analysis: where litigation, insurers, regulators or evidence preservation are in play, those need their own specialists, and the written scope says which kind of review this is before it starts.
advisory.shape7Question: We face decisions like these repeatedly.
advisory.shape7Output: Recurring decision support, written each time.
advisory.shape7Body: For the organization where consequential infrastructure and security decisions reach the executive table several times a year. Described below, under the retained arrangement.
advisory.receiveBody: A written answer, made to be circulated and defended internally rather than presented and forgotten, and a call to walk through it. The document follows a fixed structure, so that a reader who was not in the room can follow the reasoning and challenge it.
advisory.receiveNote: The example is fictional, assembled to show the structure and the level of detail. No client document is ever published.
advisory.layersLede: The first is the flagship, and it is what most engagements are. The other two exist for questions that do not fit inside one decision.
advisory.layer1Body: One decision. Defined inputs, a written memorandum, a walkthrough, a fixed fee. The easiest engagement to buy, and the one the rest of this page describes.
advisory.layer2Body: Larger questions that span several decisions: an architecture, a technology roadmap, the vendor landscape, a transition strategy, the risks and the operational consequences. Still scoped, still written, still non-operational.
advisory.layer3Body: For a small number of organizations, access over three, six or twelve months: recurring decision sessions, challenge of architectures and vendor proposals, participation in steering meetings when a decision reaches them, review of important proposals, interpretation of technology risk, and a written brief each time. Access means recurring decision support over the agreed term, with the cadence, the availability and the scope written into the proposal; it is not an open line for whatever comes up. When consequential infrastructure and security decisions reach the executive table, another person on your side of it. What it is not: line management, helpdesk escalation, project management, operational ownership, availability around the clock, or implementation labour.
advisory.evidenceLede: Most of what people say about me publicly concerns teaching, because that is what I have done most visibly since 2020. Below is the older, advisory-shaped part of the record: what clients and partners wrote about design, selection and procurement work, verbatim, each with the engagement it describes stated in one line. The full set, filtered by kind, is on the endorsements page.
advisory.evidence38: Procurement and vendor selection for a financial-sector client, 2008: consulting, technology definition, the RFP and oversight of the commercial negotiation, then the point of contact through implementation and after it.
advisory.evidence63: Design, conception and analysis of a high-availability IP telephony and recording solution for one of Brazil's largest brokerages, 2008, led across several suppliers.
advisory.evidence42: A data-link capacity analysis, 2012, whose depth and presented results the partner credits for the project's outcome.
advisory.evidence28: How the designs were made, in a security specialist's words, 2020: by applying the concept, not by trial and error.
advisory.reasonTitle: Inspect the reasoning before you hire it
advisory.reasonBody: This site shows how I approach technical questions: the evidence I use, the assumptions I make, and how I reach a conclusion. Tools that compute instead of guessing, each with its test vectors and its sources attached; several hundred technical articles that cite the documentation they rest on; a corpus on the discipline of running networks and support; and a history of the industry written from inside it. Read any of it before the first conversation. It is the same reasoning that goes into a decision memorandum.
advisory.psTitle: When the decision leads to implementation
advisory.psBody: My role in these engagements is advisory: I review, challenge, analyse and document the decision, and I do not personally provide the implementation, managed service or operational support that may follow. That does not mean the engagement ends without a practical path forward. Red Education maintains a Professional Services capability, delivered by its vendor-certified engineers: installations, software and hardware upgrades and migrations, health checks, knowledge transfer, resident on-site engineers and consultants on demand. I work for Red Education full time, and where the work that follows a decision is work Red Education does, that is where I will propose it be done: I know the people who do it, and I believe in the company's commitment to quality and to the customer's satisfaction. The choice remains yours, your existing partner, your internal team or another provider included. What does not move is the analysis: where Red Education's professional services are being considered for the downstream work, the engagement says so explicitly, and the document stays on the technical merits, constraints, risks and requirements of the decision rather than on creating implementation work for anyone, Red Education included.

In every case the proposal and the invoice come from Red Education.

practice.title: How the work is actually done.
practice.lede: Networks and security, from the inside: triage, escalation, evidence, handover, the rota. Not how the technology works, which is covered elsewhere on this site, but how the job is done by the people who do it.
practice.howBody: The parts below are in order, and the order is the life of a system: before it breaks, when it breaks, when it will not yield, after it is over, the life around it, and the craft underneath all of it. Read top to bottom and you have been walked through the whole arc.
practice.howSearch: Or arrive holding one question, read one article, and leave. Each entry shows what it argues rather than what it covers, because somebody scanning for the one about escalation is matching a question to an argument.

before.title: I. Before it breaks
before.note: The work that decides how bad the next two years will be, done while nothing is wrong and nobody is watching.

breaks.title: II. When it breaks
breaks.note: The arc of a single incident, from the moment somebody notices to the moment service is restored.

yield.title: III. When it will not yield
yield.note: What happens when the ordinary path fails: escalation, the vendor, the war room, and decisions made without enough information.

after.title: IV. After it is over
after.note: The half of the job that gets skipped, and the reason the same outage comes back.

life.title: V. The life
life.note: The rota, the queue, the pager, the people. The part no runbook covers and every practitioner recognizes.

craft.title: VI. The craft
craft.note: Evidence, capture, tooling, and the honest limits of automation.

practice.provenanceBody:
Thirty years is long enough to have done a great deal and nowhere near long enough to have done everything. What is here is the part I have lived.

I executed and I planned. I audited other people's estates and oversaw work I did not carry out myself. I was the hands on the keyboard, and I was the name on the rota when it failed at night. I trained operations staff - one at a time at a console, and rooms full of them at once. Some of this I did for vendors, some for integrators, most of it was for the end-customer who had to live with the result on Monday.

None of it is theory I have read about, it is what my career taught me.

roles.title: The positions this industry is made of.
roles.lede: A product passes through many hands between the company that builds it and the person who depends on it. Each pair of hands is a job with its own clients, its own suppliers, its own accountability and its own measurement.
roles.metaDescription: The roles of the network and security industry, grouped by the path a product takes: who makes it, moves it, sells it, deploys it, runs it, supports it, defends it and teaches it.

makes.title: Who makes it
makes.lede: Product management, product marketing, engineering and research: the people who decide what the thing is before anyone can buy it.

moves.title: Who moves it
moves.lede: Distribution and the channel. The layer between the company that builds a product and the company that sells it to whoever will run it.

sells.title: Who sells it
sells.lede: Pre-sales, inside and outside sales, account management, business development - and the procurement function on the other side of the table. A transaction has two sides, and both are described here: the technical truth and the commercial promise, carried by people who answer for the same deal from opposite directions.

deploys.title: Who deploys it
deploys.lede: Professional services, integration and consulting. Turning a design into a working thing inside somebody else's network, on their schedule.

runs.title: Who runs it
runs.lede: Managed service providers, in-house operations, the service desk and the network operations centre. The people for whom the product is a Tuesday rather than a project.

supports.title: Who supports it
supports.lede: Field engineering, the technical assistance centre, third-line product support, escalation and named support. The tiers run from the queue a customer reaches to the engineer who hands a reproduced defect to a developer, and the last of those is the boundary between the organization that runs a product and the organization that makes it.

defends.title: Who defends it
defends.lede: Security operations, offensive and defensive practice, research, incident response and crisis management. The work that assumes an adversary.

teaches.title: Who teaches it
teaches.lede: Instruction, enablement and certification. Capability transfer as a product in its own right.

roles.practiceLede: The Practice covers how this work is done - triage, escalation, evidence, handover - across the whole corpus.

levels.metaDescription: Junior, pleno, senior and above: what changes between grades is the size of the question you are handed. Plus the Y moment, where the ladder splits into management and craft.
levels.lede: A grade runs across every role on this path. The same title exists at four of them, and the same four exist in every group, which is why they are described here once rather than multiplied into the roster.
levels.whatChanges: What changes between grades is the size of the question you are handed. The volume of work stays roughly constant across a career; what moves is how much of the problem arrives already decided.

Pleno is the more useful word, because it states the thing directly: full, complete, working unsupervised on known problems.

technical-instructor.title: Technical instructor
technical-instructor.whatItIs: The engineer who teaches the product to the people who will run it. Authorized instruction is delivered against a vendor's own curriculum to a room of practising engineers, which makes the role a teaching job resting on a practitioner's foundation: the questions arrive from real environments and expect answers that hold up in them. The work is also continuous with what came before it - field, consulting and support roles all end with training the customer's staff, and instruction is that final hour of the visit made into the whole job.
technical-instructor.turnsOn: Evaluation scores measure the week and the value shows up months later, in the engineer who diagnoses something alone. The instructor's real leverage is choosing which questions to follow: a class steered towards the mechanisms underneath transfers to problems well beyond the curriculum, and one steered towards the interface teaches this release. Both score well on the day; only one of them is still working a year later.

theDay.0: Delivering a class, live, to engineers in several countries and time zones at once.
theDay.1: Repairing a laboratory environment during a break, so the exercise runs for everybody.
theDay.2: Answering the question that begins with the curriculum and ends somewhere in the student's own network.
theDay.3: Calibrating pace to a room whose experience ranges from a first week to twenty years.
theDay.4: Feeding back into the courseware what the room revealed about it.

accountableFor.0: Every student leaving able to do the thing the course promised.
accountableFor.1: Technical accuracy, including where the curriculum and the current release have diverged.
accountableFor.2: The learning environment functioning for the whole class.

measuredOn.0: Student evaluation scores and the vendor's own quality thresholds.
measuredOn.1: Classes delivered, and utilization across the calendar.
measuredOn.2: Certification pass rates where the course leads to an examination.

stakeholders.0: The students' own customers, who experience the training as fewer incidents.
stakeholders.1: The vendor's certification programme and its integrity.
stakeholders.2: The courseware authors, for whom classroom feedback is field data.

requirements.0: Deep product knowledge combined with the patience to teach its foundations again.
requirements.1: Presence over video for a full working day, which is a physical skill as much as a rhetorical one.
requirements.2: Preparing thoroughly enough to depart from the plan safely when the room needs it.
requirements.3: Comfort saying that a question exceeds the material, and returning with the answer.

0.what: Curriculum, laboratory environments and certification objectives.

1.what: Schedule, students and the commercial arrangement.

2.what: The environments they came from, which are the source of every interesting question.

0.what: Capability that outlasts the week.

1.what: Engineers who can operate what the organization bought.

2.what: A trained population, which is what makes a product adoptable.

field-network-engineer.title: Field network engineer
field-network-engineer.whatItIs: The vendor engineer who goes to where the equipment is. Field engineers install, commission, troubleshoot and repair in the customer's building, on the customer's schedule, with whatever the site turns out to contain. The role sits between support and services: it carries the vendor's name into the room and answers for the product in front of the people who bought it.
field-network-engineer.turnsOn: The dispatch is written as an installation or a fault, and the visit is an audit, a migration, an improvement, a piece of documentation and a training session wrapped around it. The measurement is time to restore, and the lasting value is the record left behind. A visit that fixes the symptom and captures the evidence turns one customer's fault into a defect the vendor can address for everybody; a visit that fixes the symptom alone leaves the same engineer travelling to the same problem at a different address next quarter. The engineers who understand this write their notes as though a stranger will read them, because one will.

theDay.0: Installing and commissioning equipment, which begins with discovering how the site differs from the plan.
theDay.1: Diagnosing a fault with the customer watching, using the evidence available on site.
theDay.2: Replacing hardware and proving the replacement resolved the thing it was sent for.
theDay.3: Auditing what is already installed, because the site is frequently the only accurate record of itself.
theDay.4: Migrating a customer from equipment that works to equipment that works better, inside a window that ends on time.
theDay.5: Improving what was found: the configuration that predates the current design, the thing everyone has learned to live with.
theDay.6: Writing the environment down, so the next engineer arrives informed rather than exploring.
theDay.7: Training the customer's operations staff on what was built, in the room, on their own equipment.
theDay.8: Capturing what happened in a form the support organization can act on later.
theDay.9: Explaining to the customer's staff what occurred, in terms they can repeat to their own management.

accountableFor.0: The equipment working when the visit ends.
accountableFor.1: The evidence trail: what was found, what was changed, and what remains open.
accountableFor.2: Representing the vendor accurately, including about the parts still under investigation.
accountableFor.3: Leaving the customer's own engineers able to operate and troubleshoot what was installed.

measuredOn.0: Time to restore, and visits closed on the first attempt.
measuredOn.1: Customer satisfaction recorded after the visit.
measuredOn.2: Utilization and travel efficiency, which are a scheduling function rather than an engineering one.

stakeholders.0: The account team, for whom every visit is a reference in progress.
stakeholders.1: The customer's management, who experience the fault as downtime.
stakeholders.2: Product engineering, for whom recurring field findings are a defect signal.

requirements.0: Hands and head together: the role is diagnostic and physical in the same hour.
requirements.1: Working alone with authority, since the decision on site is made on site.
requirements.2: Tolerance for travel, and for the schedule that travel imposes on a life.
requirements.3: The composure to be the visible face of a product that is currently failing.
requirements.4: Teaching as a routine part of the visit, because the people who will live with the system learn it from whoever installed it.

0.what: The case, its history, and the reason a person is being sent.

1.what: Parts, which arrive on their own schedule.

2.what: Access, escort, and the account of what happened that they were able to observe.

0.what: A working system and an explanation they can use.

1.what: Ground truth that a remote case cannot produce.

2.what: Field evidence of how the product behaves outside a laboratory.

product-support-engineer.title: Product support engineer
product-support-engineer.whatItIs: Third-line support: the escalation layer between the technical assistance centre and the people who write the firmware. A case reaches this role once the second line has taken it as far as the product's documented behaviour allows, and it leaves either resolved or as a defect with a reproduction attached. The role is the boundary between the organization that runs a product and the organization that makes it.
product-support-engineer.turnsOn: This tier is a gate, and holding it well runs in two directions at once. A case passed upward that a careful hour would have resolved spends developer time the whole customer base is waiting on; a genuine defect held down here becomes a customer living with a workaround for a release cycle. The engineers who thrive here are the ones who make that call quickly and then write the case up so completely that whichever way it went, nobody has to relitigate it.

theDay.0: Taking an escalation from the second line, which arrives with a history and a customer who has already waited.
theDay.1: Reproducing the fault in a laboratory, which is the hardest part of the day and the most persuasive thing the role produces.
theDay.2: Reading code, or reading close enough to it - release notes, defect records, debug output - to form a hypothesis a developer will recognize.
theDay.3: Deciding what genuinely belongs to engineering, which is the gate this role exists to hold.
theDay.4: Building the case file that a developer can act on without repeating the investigation.
theDay.5: Feeding the resolution back down as a workaround, a knowledge article and an explanation the second line can use next time.

accountableFor.0: A reproduction, or a decisive elimination, rather than a plausible narrative.
accountableFor.1: The defect report standing on its own once it reaches a developer.
accountableFor.2: The second line becoming able to resolve the next occurrence without escalating it.

measuredOn.0: Escalations resolved within third line, against those passed to engineering.
measuredOn.1: Time to resolution on cases that reached this tier, where the clock has already been running.
measuredOn.2: Defect reports accepted by engineering rather than returned for more evidence.

stakeholders.0: Every customer running the release, since a defect confirmed here becomes a fix for all of them.
stakeholders.1: The account team, for whom a critical case at this tier is a commercial fact.
stakeholders.2: Product management, for whom escalation patterns are roadmap evidence.

requirements.0: Reading evidence closely while holding a hypothesis loosely.
requirements.1: Enough fluency in how the product is built to talk to a developer in their own terms.
requirements.2: The discipline to reproduce rather than to assume, especially when the assumption is probably right.
requirements.3: The judgement to hold the gate: deciding what deserves a developer's attention, and defending both answers.
requirements.4: Written English precise enough to survive a handover across time zones and job functions.

0.what: The escalated case, its history, and everything already tried.

1.what: Captures, configurations, core files and access to reproduce.

2.what: Defect status, source-level explanations and the release that will carry a fix.

0.what: Resolutions, workarounds and the reasoning that reduces the next escalation.

1.what: A reproducible defect rather than a customer report, which is the difference between a fix and a conversation.

2.what: An answer with enough mechanism attached to be trusted.

knowledge-base-manager.title: Knowledge base manager
knowledge-base-manager.whatItIs: The person who turns what the organization learned into something the next person can use. Every resolved case contains knowledge that exists in one engineer's head and one ticket nobody will read again; this role converts that into articles, keeps them current, and measures whether they are answering anything. It sits across support and engineering because the raw material comes from both.
knowledge-base-manager.turnsOn: The knowledge exists at the moment the case closes and decays from that moment. An engineer asked a week later remembers the fix; asked a month later remembers that there was one. Capturing it inside that window is the whole discipline, and it competes directly with the next case in the queue - which is why the role has to belong to somebody rather than to everybody's good intentions.

theDay.0: Reading closed cases for the ones that will recur, which is a judgement made from pattern rather than from volume.
theDay.1: Turning a resolution into an article somebody can follow without the engineer who wrote it.
theDay.2: Retiring and correcting: an article describing a release nobody runs is worse than an absent one.
theDay.3: Working the taxonomy, since an article that cannot be found has the same value as an article that was never written.
theDay.4: Measuring deflection - which articles answered a question before it became a case - and feeding that back into what gets written next.

accountableFor.0: Articles being accurate at the version they claim to cover.
accountableFor.1: The corpus being findable by somebody using the words they actually have.
accountableFor.2: Currency: the review cycle happening rather than being intended.

measuredOn.0: Case deflection, and self-service resolution rates.
measuredOn.1: Articles published, reviewed and retired.
measuredOn.2: Search success, and the questions that returned nothing.

stakeholders.0: Every customer running the product, most of whom will meet the vendor only through these pages.
stakeholders.1: Product management, for whom the questions people search are demand signal.
stakeholders.2: The engineers whose expertise the corpus either preserves or loses.

requirements.0: Technical depth sufficient to read a case and know what generalizes.
requirements.1: Writing for a stranger under pressure, in their vocabulary rather than the product's.
requirements.2: The persistence to ask busy engineers for the write-up, repeatedly and pleasantly.
requirements.3: Comfort with an output whose success is a case that never opened.

0.what: Resolutions, and the reasoning behind them while it is still fresh.

1.what: Defect explanations, workarounds and the release a fix landed in.

2.what: What people asked for, including everything the corpus failed to answer.

0.what: An answer at the hour they have the question rather than at the hour a queue reaches them.

1.what: The same answer given consistently, and time returned by the cases that stopped arriving.

2.what: The fastest route into how the product behaves in the field.

knowledge-base-manager.provenanceWhere: at a vendor, for its support centre and engineering

high-touch-operations-manager.title: High-touch operations manager
high-touch-operations-manager.whatItIs: A named vendor engineer assigned to one large customer, holding their support relationship end to end. Where standard support answers whoever calls, a high-touch role knows the customer's environment, their change calendar and their people, and carries their cases through the vendor's organization personally. The arrangement exists for customers whose outage is a public event.
high-touch-operations-manager.turnsOn: The visible work is incident response and the durable work is prevention, which produces quiet. A high-touch engagement that succeeds shows fewer escalations, calmer reviews and a customer who stops needing to phone - and every one of those reads as reduced activity. Making the prevented incident visible, in the reporting and in the review, is what keeps the arrangement funded and is as much part of the role as the diagnosis.

theDay.0: Holding the customer's open cases and knowing each one's actual state rather than its recorded state.
theDay.1: Convening the vendor's specialists on a fault that crosses several product areas.
theDay.2: Reviewing planned changes before they happen, which prevents more cases than any diagnostic skill.
theDay.3: Reporting to the customer's management in terms that connect engineering activity to service outcomes.
theDay.4: Carrying the customer's defect and feature positions into the vendor, with the weight the account justifies.

accountableFor.0: The customer's support experience as a whole, across every case and every product line.
accountableFor.1: Escalations reaching the right people at the right severity, early.
accountableFor.2: The accuracy of what the customer's management is told.

measuredOn.0: Availability and incident outcomes on the account.
measuredOn.1: Case ageing and escalation counts.
measuredOn.2: Renewal of the support contract, and the account's willingness to act as a reference.

stakeholders.0: The public, when the customer operates national infrastructure and the outage is felt outside the building.
stakeholders.1: The vendor's executive sponsors of the account.
stakeholders.2: Every engineer inside the vendor whose queue this role reaches into.

requirements.0: Technical credibility across a portfolio, sufficient to convene specialists and follow them.
requirements.1: Organizational navigation: knowing who inside the vendor can actually move a thing.
requirements.2: Communication calibrated to the audience, from packet detail to a board summary in the same day.
requirements.3: The steadiness to hold a relationship through an incident and remain trusted afterwards.

0.what: Case progress, defect status and release plans.

1.what: Change calendars, architecture decisions and early warning of pressure.

2.what: Commercial context that shapes what is possible.

0.what: One person who knows the whole picture.

1.what: Context that turns a generic case into a specific one.

2.what: A large customer's requirements, evidenced.

high-touch-operations-manager.provenanceWhere: at a vendor, on national infrastructure accounts

systems-engineer.title: Systems engineer
systems-engineer.whatItIs: The technical half of a vendor sales team. A systems engineer owns whether the proposed thing will work, while the account manager owns whether it will be bought. The pairing is deliberate and the split is clean: one person carries the commercial relationship and the other carries the technical truth, and both answer for the same deal.
systems-engineer.turnsOn: The role answers for accuracy and is measured on revenue, and those two lists point the same way only while the truth is favourable. The systems engineers who last are the ones who say early and plainly when the product fits the problem partially, because a deal won on an overstated fit becomes a support case, then a renewal risk, then a reference the vendor stops offering. The honest answer is the commercially durable one, and it is worth having that clear before the pressure arrives rather than during it.

theDay.0: Qualifying an opportunity technically: what the customer runs today, what they are trying to reach, and whether the product genuinely gets them there.
theDay.1: Designing the proposed solution and writing it down in a form the customer's engineers will accept and the customer's finance will approve.
theDay.2: Running a proof of concept in the customer's environment, against the customer's traffic, with the customer's people watching.
theDay.3: Answering a request for proposal, which is a written examination with a commercial consequence.
theDay.4: Briefing the account manager on what the technology will genuinely do and what it will not, so that the commercial promise matches the engineering one.

accountableFor.0: The technical accuracy of everything proposed under the account manager's name.
accountableFor.1: The design surviving contact with the customer's environment.
accountableFor.2: The proof of concept demonstrating the thing it claimed to demonstrate.

measuredOn.0: Revenue on the account, shared with the account manager.
measuredOn.1: Opportunities advanced through the technical stages of the pipeline.
measuredOn.2: Proof-of-concept outcomes, and increasingly customer satisfaction after the sale.

stakeholders.0: The customer's procurement and finance functions, whose questions are commercial and whose answers depend on technical facts.
stakeholders.1: The channel partner, when the deal transacts through one.
stakeholders.2: The vendor's support organization, which inherits whatever the design turns out to be.

requirements.0: Depth in the product, and enough breadth in everything around it to be credible about the whole system.
requirements.1: Writing that a stranger can act on, because the design outlives the conversation that produced it.
requirements.2: The judgement to say when the product fits the problem, which protects the account far more than an eager answer does.
requirements.3: Comfort presenting to a room where some people want the project and some people want it to fail.

0.what: The opportunity, the commercial shape, and the deadline.

1.what: Roadmap, positioning, and the honest limits of the current release.

2.what: The environment as it actually is, which frequently differs from the environment as documented.

0.what: A design they can operate, and answers they can verify.

1.what: Technical confidence the commercial position can stand on.

2.what: A design that survives implementation, and a handover that says what was promised.

systems-engineer.provenanceWhere: at two vendors, the second on a carrier account

network-consulting-engineer.title: Network consulting engineer
network-consulting-engineer.whatItIs: The engineer who turns a design into a working thing inside somebody else's network. Consulting engineers arrive after the sale and before the operations team, and they carry the technical responsibility for the transition: planning it, doing it, proving it, and handing over an environment the customer's own staff can run.
network-consulting-engineer.turnsOn: The statement of work says deployment, and the job is an audit, a migration, an improvement, a document and a training course delivered around it. Utilization measures hours booked, and the work that decides whether a project succeeds happens in the hours that are hard to book: reading the environment properly, writing the rollback, sitting with the customer's engineer until they can do it themselves. Consulting engineers who protect that time deliver projects that stay delivered, and the conversation with whoever owns the utilization target is part of the job rather than an interruption to it.

theDay.0: Auditing the environment as it stands, which is the work that makes every later step honest.
theDay.1: Reading an environment that is documented partially and understanding it fully enough to change it safely.
theDay.2: Migrating services off equipment that is leaving, with the business running throughout.
theDay.3: Improving what the audit surfaced, separately from what the project was sold to do, and saying which is which.
theDay.4: Documenting the result to a standard the customer's own staff can maintain.
theDay.5: Training the customer's operations team and the reseller's engineers on what was built.
theDay.6: Writing the method of procedure: the ordered steps, the verification after each, and the way back.
theDay.7: Executing a change inside a maintenance window that ends whether or not the work does.
theDay.8: Proving the outcome with evidence the customer accepts, rather than with an assurance.
theDay.9: Handing over: documentation, a walkthrough, and the knowledge transfer that decides whether the customer calls again next month.

accountableFor.0: The change working, and the environment being restorable when it does otherwise.
accountableFor.1: The evidence that the work met what was sold.
accountableFor.2: A handover that leaves the customer's team able to operate what was built.
accountableFor.3: The written record of the environment, before and after, being true.

measuredOn.0: Utilization: the proportion of time booked to a paying project.
measuredOn.1: Delivery against the statement of work, in scope and in hours.
measuredOn.2: Customer satisfaction, and the follow-on work that satisfaction produces.

stakeholders.0: The customer's business, which experiences the change as availability rather than as engineering.
stakeholders.1: The customer's security and compliance functions, whose approval the change frequently requires.
stakeholders.2: The vendor, whose product is judged by how this deployment behaves.

requirements.0: Technical depth combined with the discipline to work inside someone else's rules.
requirements.1: Writing under time pressure, because the method of procedure is written before the window and read during it.
requirements.2: Composure at three in the morning, when the window is closing and the verification step has failed.
requirements.3: The social skill to be the outsider in a room of people who built the thing you are changing.

0.what: The design, the statement of work, and whatever was promised in the room.

1.what: Access, change windows, and the environment's real history.

2.what: Support cases, escalation and firmware when the product misbehaves.

0.what: A working environment and the ability to run it.

1.what: Progress that is true, including the parts that are behind.

2.what: A delivery good enough to sell the next one.

network-consulting-engineer.provenanceWhere: at integrators, and in 2008 and 2012 through my own company

channel-systems-engineer.title: Channel systems engineer
channel-systems-engineer.whatItIs: A systems engineer whose customers are other engineers. Distribution sits between the vendor and the reseller, and the channel systems engineer is the technical face of that layer: enabling the partner's engineers, sizing and configuring what the partner will sell, and holding the first line of technical help for a whole population of resellers rather than for one end customer. The role is also the technical arm a reseller borrows - running the proof of concept and the proof of value on the partner's behalf - and the channel through which a partner's technical questions reach the vendor and come back answered.
channel-systems-engineer.turnsOn: The output is capability in other companies, and capability is slow, cumulative and hard to attribute. A partner engineer who becomes self-sufficient stops calling, which reads in the numbers as reduced engagement and reads in reality as the job done. The same shape governs the brokering: a question carried accurately between a partner and a vendor leaves both sides believing they simply understood each other. Holding that line - investing in partners who will need less help next year - is the whole discipline of the role, and it asks for a manager who understands the same thing.

theDay.0: Sizing and configuring a bill of materials for a partner's opportunity, frequently for an end customer nobody in the room has met.
theDay.1: Enabling partner engineers: workshops, demonstrations, and the answering of the same foundational question for a dozen different companies.
theDay.2: Enabling partner SALESPEOPLE, which is separate work with a separate vocabulary: what the product is for, which conversation opens the door, and which technical detail belongs in a first meeting.
theDay.3: Running the proof of concept - PoC, showing the thing works - and the proof of value - PoV, showing the thing is worth what it costs - as the partner's technical arm, in front of the partner's customer.
