theDay.4: Making the technical case for a product to engineers who already run something that works and have reasons to keep it, which is persuasion resting on evidence rather than on enthusiasm.
theDay.5: Brokering between the partner and the vendor on technical matters, so that a question asked in one company's vocabulary arrives in the other's and returns in a form the asker can use.
theDay.6: Standing in for the vendor's systems engineer where the deal is too small for the vendor to staff, which is most deals.
theDay.7: Building the demonstration and lab environments a partner borrows rather than buys.
theDay.8: Carrying vendor programme requirements into partners: certifications to hold, thresholds to reach, accreditations to renew.

accountableFor.0: Configurations that are correct, licensable and orderable as quoted.
accountableFor.1: The technical capability of the partner base, which is a slower thing to move than a quarter.
accountableFor.2: Escalating cleanly to the vendor when a question genuinely exceeds distribution's remit.
accountableFor.3: Proofs of concept and value that demonstrate what they claim, carrying the partner's name as well as distribution's.

measuredOn.0: Revenue through the partner base, and its growth against the same period last year.
measuredOn.1: Partner certifications and accreditations achieved.
measuredOn.2: Attach rates on services and renewals, which are distribution's margin rather than the vendor's.

stakeholders.0: The end customer, who is served by the partner and rarely learns that distribution was involved.
stakeholders.1: The vendor's channel account managers, whose programme targets depend on partner capability.
stakeholders.2: Distribution's credit and logistics functions, for whom a technical error becomes a returned shipment.

requirements.0: Breadth across a portfolio rather than depth in one product, because the partner base sells everything on the line card.
requirements.1: Teaching as a daily skill, since capability transfer is the actual output.
requirements.2: Patience with repetition, and the discipline to answer the tenth identical question as carefully as the first.
requirements.3: Commercial literacy: part numbers, licensing metrics, programme tiers and the arithmetic of margin.
requirements.4: Two registers, held separately: the one that persuades an engineer and the one that equips a salesperson.
requirements.5: Standing in front of a partner's customer under the partner's name, with the partner's reputation attached to the answer.

0.what: Product knowledge, programme rules, pricing structures and the current campaign.

1.what: Opportunities described at whatever level of detail the partner happens to have.

2.what: Commercial priorities, stock positions and the accounts that matter this quarter.

0.what: Capability: the ability to design and support the product themselves.

1.what: A quotable, buildable configuration, the technical confidence to propose it, and enablement pitched at a seller rather than at an engineer.

2.what: A proof of concept and a proof of value, delivered under the partner's name.

3.what: Reach into a market too fragmented to serve directly.

security-operations-analyst.title: Security operations analyst
security-operations-analyst.whatItIs: The analyst who watches an environment for the signs of an adversary. The national framework describes the work as analysing data collected from a range of defensive tools to mitigate risks, and the day is built from that: alerts, logs, traffic records and the judgement that turns them into a decision. The role runs in tiers, with triage at the front and investigation and hunting behind it.
security-operations-analyst.turnsOn: Attention is the finite resource, and it is spent by every alert whether the alert earned it or otherwise. A queue tuned so that arriving alerts deserve a look keeps analysts sharp for the one that matters; a queue that floods trains people to close things quickly, and that training holds on the night it should break. Tuning is therefore the defensive work rather than a chore beside it.

theDay.0: Triaging alerts, where the volume means the first skill is deciding what deserves attention.
theDay.1: Investigating what survives triage, across whatever telemetry the organization happens to keep.
theDay.2: Containing an incident and preserving what an investigation will later need.
theDay.3: Hunting: looking for the activity that generated no alert at all.
theDay.4: Tuning the detections, since every false alert spends attention that a real one will need.

accountableFor.0: The alert being handled and the handling being recorded.
accountableFor.1: Evidence preserved in a state that survives scrutiny.
accountableFor.2: Escalation happening at the right moment, which is earlier than it feels.

measuredOn.0: Time to detect and time to respond.
measuredOn.1: Alert volume handled, and the proportion escalated.
measuredOn.2: Detection coverage against a recognized adversary framework.

stakeholders.0: Legal, regulatory and communications functions, whose obligations begin the moment an incident is confirmed.
stakeholders.1: Customers and the public, when the organization holds their data.
stakeholders.2: The insurers and auditors who will read the record afterwards.

requirements.0: Sustained attention across a shift, which is the physical fact of the job.
requirements.1: Enough breadth to recognize ordinary behaviour in systems the analyst has never operated.
requirements.2: Writing that holds up when read later by a lawyer or a regulator.
requirements.3: The judgement to escalate on partial information, which is the only kind available early.

0.what: Telemetry, at whatever fidelity somebody chose to collect it.

1.what: What adversaries are doing elsewhere, and the indicators that follow.

2.what: Context: the change that explains the anomaly.

0.what: The difference between an incident found early and one found by somebody else.

1.what: A characterized event with evidence attached.

2.what: The feedback that turns a noisy rule into a useful one.

incident-responder.title: Incident responder
incident-responder.whatItIs: The person who takes charge once an event is confirmed as an incident. Where the operations analyst watches and triages, the responder investigates, contains, eradicates and recovers, and then writes what happened. The national guidance frames the work as a lifecycle beginning long before the incident, in preparation, and ending after it, in the lessons the organization keeps.
incident-responder.turnsOn: Preparation is the phase that decides the outcome, and it happens on ordinary days. Whether logs exist, whether the asset inventory is current, whether the escalation list has the right mobile numbers on it - all of that is settled months before an incident and determines how well it goes. The responder's most valuable hours are therefore the quiet ones spent making the next response possible, and those hours compete with everything more visible.

theDay.0: Establishing scope: which systems, which accounts, which data, and since when.
theDay.1: Containing, which trades evidence against spread and is a judgement made with partial information.
theDay.2: Eradicating the foothold and recovering service, in an order the business agrees.
theDay.3: Preserving evidence to a standard that survives a regulator, an insurer or a court.
theDay.4: Writing the post-incident account, which is the phase most often abandoned and the one that changes anything.

accountableFor.0: The scope being right, since an underscoped incident recurs the following week.
accountableFor.1: Evidence integrity throughout the response.
accountableFor.2: The written record: timeline, decisions and reasoning.

measuredOn.0: Time to contain and time to recover.
measuredOn.1: Recurrence, which is the honest measure of eradication.
measuredOn.2: Post-incident actions completed rather than merely recommended.

stakeholders.0: Customers and the public, whose data the incident may concern.
stakeholders.1: Regulators and insurers, who read the record afterwards.
stakeholders.2: Every engineer whose system is inside the containment boundary.

requirements.0: Decision-making on partial information under time pressure, repeatedly.
requirements.1: Forensic care, since the containment step decides what evidence remains.
requirements.2: Writing that a lawyer, an auditor and an engineer can each use.
requirements.3: The composure to lead a room of people who are frightened and senior.

0.what: The characterized event and the evidence gathered so far.

1.what: Access, architecture and the changes that explain what is seen.

2.what: The adversary's known behaviour, which shapes where to look next.

0.what: A clear account of what happened and what it means, while it is still happening.

1.what: Facts firm enough to disclose.

2.what: A boundary they can trust between clean and compromised.

vulnerability-analyst.title: Vulnerability analyst
vulnerability-analyst.whatItIs: The analyst who looks for the weaknesses before an adversary does. The national framework describes the work as assessing systems and networks to identify deviations from acceptable configurations, and measuring how well a defence-in-depth architecture holds against known vulnerabilities. The output is a prioritized account of exposure, which somebody else then has to act on.
vulnerability-analyst.turnsOn: The report is easy to produce and the remediation belongs to somebody else, which makes influence the actual skill. An analyst who arrives with two hundred findings ordered by scanner severity hands over a document; one who arrives with the six that are reachable from the internet, with the fixed version named and the window suggested, hands over a plan. The second gets fixed, and the difference is entirely in the preparation.

theDay.0: Running assessments across an estate whose inventory is a moving target.
theDay.1: Separating the findings that matter from the volume that arrives with them, using exposure rather than score alone.
theDay.2: Verifying that a reported weakness is reachable in this environment, since context decides severity.
theDay.3: Retesting after remediation, which is the step that turns a ticket into a fact.
theDay.4: Reporting to the teams who own the systems, in terms that make the fix ownable.

accountableFor.0: Findings that are true, reachable and reproducible.
accountableFor.1: Prioritization that reflects this organization rather than a generic score.
accountableFor.2: The record of what was tested, when, and with what coverage.

measuredOn.0: Coverage of the estate, and the age of the last assessment.
measuredOn.1: Time to remediate, which belongs to other teams and lands on this report.
measuredOn.2: Findings verified as closed rather than marked as closed.

stakeholders.0: Every team whose maintenance window a remediation will occupy.
stakeholders.1: The organization's insurers and regulators.
stakeholders.2: Customers relying on the systems being assessed.

requirements.0: Breadth across operating systems, networks and applications, since the estate contains all of them.
requirements.1: The judgement to rank by reachable exposure rather than by the number a scanner printed.
requirements.2: Diplomacy, because the deliverable is a list of other people's outstanding work.
requirements.3: Persistence through the retest, which is where the value is realized.

0.what: The inventory, at whatever accuracy the organization maintains.

1.what: Which weaknesses are being used, which changes what matters first.

2.what: Advisories, fixed releases and the details that make a finding actionable.

0.who: The teams who own the systems
0.what: A short, ordered list they can act on.

1.what: Exposure expressed as a trend rather than a snapshot.

2.what: Evidence that assessment happens and that findings close.

threat-intelligence-analyst.title: Threat intelligence analyst
threat-intelligence-analyst.whatItIs: The analyst who studies adversaries rather than systems. The framework describes the work as collecting, processing, analysing and disseminating threat assessments, and the last of those verbs carries the role: intelligence that reaches nobody in a form they can act on has been research rather than intelligence.
threat-intelligence-analyst.turnsOn: Intelligence earns its name by changing a decision. A report that arrives, is read, and leaves the defence exactly as it was has cost the organization an analyst's week and delivered news. The analysts who matter work backwards from the decision - which detection, which priority, which hunt - and write towards it, which also makes the work measurable in a way that generic reporting leaves out of reach.

theDay.0: Collecting from sources of varying reliability, and recording which was which.
theDay.1: Assessing what an adversary can do and what they appear to intend, which are separate judgements.
theDay.2: Translating that into something concrete for the people who defend: a detection, a priority, a hunt.
theDay.3: Writing assessments with confidence stated, so that a reader can weigh them.
theDay.4: Tracking whether the assessment held, which is how the sources are calibrated over time.

accountableFor.0: Sourcing that is recorded and weighted, rather than aggregated into a single confident voice.
accountableFor.1: Assessments that state their confidence and what would change it.
accountableFor.2: Relevance: intelligence about this organization's actual exposure.

measuredOn.0: Detections and hunts that originated with the intelligence.
measuredOn.1: Timeliness against events that later mattered.
measuredOn.2: Assessments used in decisions, which is the honest measure and the hardest to count.

stakeholders.0: The sharing communities the organization both draws from and owes to.
stakeholders.1: Legal, since attribution carries consequences beyond the technical.
stakeholders.2: Every defender whose attention this work directs.

requirements.0: Source discipline, and the habit of recording provenance and confidence together.
requirements.1: Analytic writing: a judgement, its basis, and its uncertainty, in that order.
requirements.2: Enough operational grounding to know which findings a defender can use.
requirements.3: Resistance to the compelling narrative, since a good story is the commonest way an assessment goes wrong.

0.who: External feeds, vendors and sharing communities
0.what: Indicators, reporting and the occasional thing that arrives before it is public.

1.what: What is being attempted here, which outranks anything external for relevance.

2.what: What an adversary actually did once inside, which is the highest-quality source available.

0.what: Priorities, and the detections worth building.

1.what: Context about who this appears to be and what they usually do next.

2.what: The threat picture that shapes where the programme spends.

digital-forensics-analyst.title: Digital forensics analyst
digital-forensics-analyst.whatItIs: The analyst who reconstructs what happened from what remains. Where the responder is deciding what to do next, forensics is establishing what already occurred: from disk images, memory, logs and network records, in an order and to a standard that keeps the findings usable afterwards. The framework frames the output as information that supports mitigation, and in practice it also supports the lawyers.
digital-forensics-analyst.turnsOn: The first hour decides the case. Acquisition made in the right order preserves the volatile evidence that answers the interesting questions; the same hour spent restoring service first leaves an investigation working from what survived by luck. Forensics teams earn their standing before an incident, by agreeing with the business in advance which comes first and in which circumstances, because that conversation held during an incident is decided by whoever is most senior in the room.

theDay.0: Acquiring evidence in a way that preserves it, which decides everything that follows.
theDay.1: Building a timeline: what ran, what was written, what was sent, and in which order.
theDay.2: Recovering what somebody attempted to remove, which is frequently where the intent becomes visible.
theDay.3: Separating what the evidence shows from what it suggests, and writing the two differently.
theDay.4: Documenting handling continuously, so that a finding stays admissible as well as true.

accountableFor.0: Evidence integrity from acquisition onward, and the record proving it.
accountableFor.1: Findings that follow from the artefacts, with the inference stated as inference.
accountableFor.2: A timeline that another examiner could reproduce from the same material.

measuredOn.0: Cases completed, and findings that survive review.
measuredOn.1: Time to a defensible answer, since an investigation runs beside a business waiting to restart.
measuredOn.2: Reports accepted by the audiences that requested them, including outside the organization.

stakeholders.0: The individuals whose activity appears in the evidence, whose interests deserve care.
stakeholders.1: Courts, regulators and insurers, for whom the handling record is part of the finding.
stakeholders.2: The organization, whose account of the incident rests on this work.

requirements.0: Method held under pressure, since the shortcuts available early destroy the options available later.
requirements.1: Depth across file systems, memory, operating systems and network records.
requirements.2: Writing that distinguishes observation from inference in every sentence that needs it.
requirements.3: Discretion, because the material routinely includes things unrelated to the investigation.

0.what: Scope, priority, and the systems believed to be involved.

1.what: Images, logs and access to the machines still holding evidence.

2.what: The standard the work has to meet, which is set before the acquisition rather than after.

0.what: What actually happened, which bounds the containment.

1.what: Findings that hold up under examination by people paid to test them.

2.what: The specific weakness that was used, which is the thing worth fixing.

penetration-tester.title: Penetration tester
penetration-tester.whatItIs: The specialist who tests defences by behaving like an attacker, inside an agreement that says exactly what is permitted. The national skills framework places it at the second or third tier, normally reached after several years in security operations, which is worth stating because the role is frequently imagined as an entry point and is in practice an advanced one.
penetration-tester.turnsOn: The technical work is shared with the adversary; the authorization is what makes it a profession. Scope, rules of engagement and the discipline to stay inside them are the whole distinction, and they are also what makes the findings usable - a test conducted where somebody agreed it would be produces a report the organization can act on, while anything obtained outside that boundary creates a problem rather than a finding. The good ones treat the scope document as the first deliverable rather than as paperwork preceding the real work.

theDay.0: Reading the scope and the rules of engagement until both are unambiguous, since everything afterwards depends on them.
theDay.1: Reconnaissance, scanning and enumeration, which is most of the time and produces most of the findings.
theDay.2: Exploiting what was found, to establish impact rather than to demonstrate cleverness.
theDay.3: Documenting as it happens, because a finding reproduced two weeks later from memory is a finding somebody will dispute.
theDay.4: Writing the report, which is the deliverable the client actually buys.

accountableFor.0: Staying inside the authorized scope, at every moment.
accountableFor.1: Findings that are real, reproducible and ranked by what they would cost this organization.
accountableFor.2: A report that the people who have to fix things can act on.

measuredOn.0: Findings of genuine severity, rather than volume.
measuredOn.1: Engagements delivered to the statement of work.
measuredOn.2: Remediation that follows, which belongs to somebody else and reflects the report's quality.

stakeholders.0: Everybody whose systems are in scope, most of whom learn about it afterwards.
stakeholders.1: Legal, since authorization is what separates this work from the offence it resembles.
stakeholders.2: The teams whose weekend a critical finding will occupy.

requirements.0: Depth across systems, networks and applications, and the patience for the unglamorous enumeration that precedes anything interesting.
requirements.1: Precision with scope, held under the temptation of an interesting path leading outside it.
requirements.2: Writing that an engineer can act on and an executive can weigh, in the same document.
requirements.3: Judgement about impact, since a technically real finding with no consequence spends attention a serious one needed.

0.what: Scope, rules of engagement, and the authorization that makes the work lawful.

1.what: Techniques currently in use, which is what makes the simulation realistic.

2.what: What was found last time, and what happened to it.

0.what: Evidence of what an adversary could reach, obtained safely.

1.what: A view of exposure grounded in demonstration rather than in inventory.

2.what: The starting list, which they then carry over time.

it-auditor.title: IT auditor
it-auditor.whatItIs: The person who establishes whether the controls an organization believes it has are actually there and actually working. Audit runs as an engagement - planning, fieldwork, reporting - and produces evidence rather than opinion. The profession has its own framework of standards covering not only method but ethics and expected behaviour, which exists because the value of the finding rests entirely on the independence of whoever produced it.
it-auditor.turnsOn: Independence is the product, and it is spent by helpfulness. An auditor who begins designing the fix becomes an adviser to the thing they will later examine, and the next report carries their own recommendation as its subject - which is why the profession puts ethics and expected behaviour into the same framework as method. The useful position is close enough to understand the estate and separate enough that the finding still means something, and holding it takes deliberate effort in every friendly conversation.

theDay.0: Planning an engagement against objectives that connect to what the organization is actually exposed to.
theDay.1: Fieldwork: sampling, testing, and asking for the evidence rather than the assurance.
theDay.2: Documenting control strengths, weaknesses and gaps, in workpapers another auditor could follow.
theDay.3: Discussing findings with the people they concern, before the report reaches anybody above them.
theDay.4: Reporting, and then following up on what was agreed and what actually changed.

accountableFor.0: Findings supported by evidence that survives being disputed.
accountableFor.1: Workpapers complete enough for a reviewer to reach the same conclusion.
accountableFor.2: Independence, maintained visibly as well as actually.

measuredOn.0: The audit plan delivered, and coverage across the estate.
measuredOn.1: Findings accepted, and remediation completed rather than agreed.
measuredOn.2: Regulatory and external audit outcomes, where internal work is examined by someone else.

stakeholders.0: Regulators and external auditors, who read the same estate afterwards.
stakeholders.1: Customers, whose data the controls exist to protect.
stakeholders.2: Every engineer whose weekend a finding turns into remediation.

requirements.0: Method: sampling, evidence and the discipline to test rather than to accept.
requirements.1: Technical literacy across the estate, sufficient to know what evidence would look like.
requirements.2: Writing that states a finding, its basis and its consequence separately.
requirements.3: The independence to record a finding about a team whose cooperation the next engagement needs.

0.what: Evidence, at whatever completeness their day allows.

1.what: The mandate, and the plan's priorities.

2.what: The obligations the organization is being measured against.

0.what: An independent view of whether the controls described in the reporting exist.

1.what: Findings early enough to fix before somebody external arrives.

2.what: A written basis for the investment they have been requesting.

security-manager.title: Security manager
security-manager.whatItIs: The first rung of the management arm, in security. A security manager runs the people who do the analysis, the response and the assessment: hiring them, developing them, staffing the rota, and turning a leader's direction into work that fits in a week. It is the rung where a career stops being about your own output and starts being about somebody else's.
security-manager.turnsOn: This is the rung the Y moment leads to, and the trade is immediate: the day fills with other people's work and the technical depth that earned the promotion begins to age from the first week. Managers who thrive decide early what they are keeping current and what they are letting go, and say so - because the alternative is a slow drift in which the team stops asking and the manager stops being able to answer.

theDay.0: Staffing: the rota, the on-call, and the arithmetic of covering a queue that runs at all hours.
theDay.1: Developing people, which is the part that compounds and the part most easily postponed.
theDay.2: Turning strategy into a backlog somebody can actually work through.
theDay.3: Standing between the team and the interruptions, so that the analysis has room to happen.
theDay.4: Reporting upward in the terms the tier above uses, and downward in the terms the team uses.

accountableFor.0: The team producing the outcome, with the people in it still there next year.
accountableFor.1: Coverage: the rota being genuinely staffed rather than nominally filled.
accountableFor.2: The accuracy of what is reported upward, including the parts that reflect on the management.

measuredOn.0: Team outcomes: detection, response, assessment coverage.
measuredOn.1: Retention and time to fill a vacancy.
measuredOn.2: Delivery against the programme the tier above set.

stakeholders.0: The families of everybody on a rota, which is a real stakeholder in a role built on shift work.
stakeholders.1: The teams whose incidents this one handles.
stakeholders.2: Finance, for whom headcount is the largest line in the programme.

requirements.0: Technical credibility, because a team that has to explain its work upward twice starts editing it.
requirements.1: Care taken deliberately, since burnout in this function is an operational risk and shows up as attrition.
requirements.2: The willingness to hold a boundary against work the team has no capacity for.
requirements.3: Honesty upward about capacity, which is the same skill the project manager needs and costs the same to use.

0.what: Direction, budget and the risks the organization has decided to prioritize.

1.what: What is actually happening in the queue, which arrives filtered by how safe it feels to say.

2.what: The market reality behind every hiring plan.

0.what: Room to do the work, and a career with somewhere to go.

1.what: Execution, and an accurate picture of capacity.

2.what: A function that runs at three in the morning as well as at ten.

network-operations-specialist.title: Network operations specialist
network-operations-specialist.whatItIs: The engineer who runs the network an organization depends on. The federal work role puts it as planning, implementing and operating network services and systems, and then does something unusually useful: it lists the titles the same work is advertised under - network administrator, network analyst, network designer, network engineer, network systems engineer, telecommunications specialist. One body of work, seven names, which is worth holding on to before comparing two job descriptions.
network-operations-specialist.turnsOn: Every problem in an organization arrives as a network problem until somebody proves otherwise, which makes proving a negative a large part of the job. That proof is the actual craft: a capture, a counter, a timing that shows the request left and the answer came back, offered quickly enough that the investigation moves on to where the fault really is. Engineers who build the habit of producing that evidence in minutes become the person other teams want in the bridge call; those who assert it instead spend the same hours being doubted.

theDay.0: Configuring and optimizing the switches, routers and the protocols running across them.
theDay.1: Diagnosing connectivity, which begins by establishing whether the network is involved at all.
theDay.2: Monitoring capacity and performance, and planning the growth before it arrives as an incident.
theDay.3: Building and testing the contingency and recovery procedures, which are worth exactly what the last test proved.
theDay.4: Implementing the security practices the network is expected to enforce, since the boundary is made of this equipment.

accountableFor.0: The network being available, and being demonstrably available.
accountableFor.1: Changes to it being deliberate, documented and reversible.
accountableFor.2: The design keeping pace with what the organization is asking of it.

measuredOn.0: Availability and incident count, which are the visible numbers.
measuredOn.1: Time to restore, and time to establish where a fault actually sits.
measuredOn.2: Capacity headroom and change success, which are the numbers that prevent the first two.

stakeholders.0: Everyone in the organization, without exception.
stakeholders.1: The application owners whose service levels rest on this one.
stakeholders.2: Auditors, for whom network segmentation is a control rather than a design.

requirements.0: Depth in the protocols, since the network is the layer where guesses are expensive.
requirements.1: Method under pressure, because the pressure is highest when the fault is least understood.
requirements.2: Evidence-gathering as a habit: captures, counters and timings kept rather than described.
requirements.3: Patience with being the first suspect, repeatedly.

0.what: Symptoms, described by people whose vocabulary is their own work.

1.what: Requirements, and the conviction that the network is the cause.

2.what: Designs, firmware and the support path when the equipment misbehaves.

0.what: A foundation they can assume, and evidence when they cannot.

1.what: Connectivity, which is noticed only in its absence.

2.what: Enforcement points, and the visibility that makes detection possible.

systems-administrator.title: Systems administrator
systems-administrator.whatItIs: The person who keeps the systems running. The framework lists the work plainly: installing, configuring and updating hardware and software, managing accounts, overseeing backup and recovery, and implementing the controls that policy requires. It is the most widely held technical role in any organization of size, and the one whose output is measured almost entirely by the absence of events.
systems-administrator.turnsOn: The role accumulates knowledge that lives nowhere else. Fifteen years of small decisions - why that service runs on that host, which job has to finish before that one starts - become the reason the estate works and the reason it cannot be handed over. Administrators who write it down convert personal indispensability into organizational capability, and the trade is real: the documented administrator is easier to replace and far easier to promote.

theDay.0: Patching, updating and renewing the things that expire: certificates, licences, agents, firmware.
theDay.1: Managing accounts and access, which is a security control performed as an administrative task.
theDay.2: Backup and, far more rarely and far more importantly, restore.
theDay.3: Responding to whatever the monitoring or the service desk sends, in among the planned work.
theDay.4: Automating the parts that repeat, in whatever time the unplanned work leaves.

accountableFor.0: The systems being available, current and recoverable.
accountableFor.1: Access being what the policy says it is.
accountableFor.2: Restores actually working, which is knowable only by testing them.

measuredOn.0: Availability and incident count.
measuredOn.1: Patch currency and audit findings.
measuredOn.2: Tickets closed, which measures the interruptions rather than the engineering.

stakeholders.0: Auditors and insurers, whose questions are about this role's routine.
stakeholders.1: Every team whose application sits on these systems.
stakeholders.2: Whoever inherits the estate, and whatever documentation exists by then.

requirements.0: Breadth, because the estate contains whatever the organization bought over fifteen years.
requirements.1: Discipline with routine work whose value shows up only when it was skipped.
requirements.2: Automation as a habit, since the alternative is a career of the same afternoon.
requirements.3: Writing things down, which is the difference between expertise and a dependency.

0.what: What users are experiencing, filtered through first-line triage.

1.what: Patches, advisories and end-of-support dates.

2.what: Controls to implement and findings to close.

0.what: Systems that work, which is noticed mainly in its absence.

1.what: The controls, actually applied to actual machines.

2.what: The ability to recover, which is worth precisely what the last restore test proved.

systems-analyst.title: Systems analyst
systems-analyst.whatItIs: The role that faces two directions at once. The prefix names the subject - network analyst, security analyst, data analyst - and the word analyst names the stance: studying what an organization currently runs and what it currently needs, and describing each to the other. The framework puts it plainly as bringing business and technology together by understanding the needs and limitations of both.
systems-analyst.turnsOn: The analyst holds the only complete picture in the room, and holds it without authority to act on it. That combination is the role: the business knows what it wants, engineering knows what is possible, and the person who knows both is the one who has to make each legible to the other. Influence comes from the description being trusted, which is why accuracy about the current state matters more here than elegance about the future one.

theDay.0: Studying the systems and procedures as they actually operate, which differs from how they were designed and from how they are described.
theDay.1: Gathering requirements from people whose expertise is their own work rather than technology.
theDay.2: Translating those requirements into something an engineer can build, and translating the constraints back into something a business can decide with.
theDay.3: Measuring: usage, capacity, incidents, cost, and whatever else turns an opinion about the estate into a number.
theDay.4: Documenting the current state, which is frequently the only accurate record the organization holds.

accountableFor.0: The description of the current state being true.
accountableFor.1: Requirements that survive contact with the people who have to build against them.
accountableFor.2: Analysis that leads to a decision rather than to a further meeting.

measuredOn.0: Recommendations adopted, and the outcomes they produced.
measuredOn.1: Reporting delivered on the cadence the organization runs on.
measuredOn.2: Requirements accepted without rework by the teams who implement them.

stakeholders.0: Every team whose work the recommendation changes.
stakeholders.1: Finance, since analysis frequently arrives attached to a budget request.
stakeholders.2: Audit and compliance, for whom the documented current state is evidence.

requirements.0: Fluency in two vocabularies, and the patience to move between them all day.
requirements.1: Enough technical depth to be corrected by an engineer and to notice when the correction is wrong.
requirements.2: Writing, since the analysis outlives the meeting that produced it.
requirements.3: Comfort delivering a finding that somebody in the room would prefer stayed unmeasured.

0.what: What they need, expressed in the vocabulary of their own work.

1.what: What the estate can do, and at what cost.

2.what: The measurements, at whatever quality the organization maintains them.

0.what: A picture of the current state accurate enough to act on.

1.what: Requirements with the reasoning attached, so a trade-off can be made rather than guessed.

2.what: Written knowledge of how the estate reached its present shape.

service-desk-analyst.title: Service desk analyst
service-desk-analyst.whatItIs: The single point of contact between an organization and the people who use its technology. The framework defines the service desk as the practice that captures demand for incident resolution and service requests, and the phrase that matters in that definition is single point of contact: a user reports a problem to one place, and the desk works out who owns it.
service-desk-analyst.turnsOn: The desk exists so that the routing knowledge lives in one place rather than in every head in the organization. That makes first-contact resolution the honest measure and volume a misleading one: an analyst who resolves fewer tickets while raising what the team can handle alone has improved the service, and the numbers show it slowly. It also explains the ceiling - a desk kept purely at intake stays a switchboard, and one given time to learn becomes the reason specialists are left alone.

theDay.0: Logging, categorizing and prioritizing whatever arrives, across every channel the organization offers.
theDay.1: Investigating and diagnosing far enough to resolve at first contact, which is where the value concentrates.
theDay.2: Routing what remains to whichever specialist team owns it, which requires knowing the whole organization.
theDay.3: Keeping ownership of the ticket through the routing, so the user has one thread rather than several.
theDay.4: Communicating status, which is most of what a waiting user actually wants.

accountableFor.0: Every contact being recorded, categorized and visible.
accountableFor.1: Ownership through to resolution, including while somebody else does the work.
accountableFor.2: The user knowing where their request stands.

measuredOn.0: First-contact resolution rate.
measuredOn.1: Time to respond and time to resolve against the service level.
measuredOn.2: User satisfaction, and the volume handled per analyst.

stakeholders.0: Department heads whose people are waiting.
stakeholders.1: The teams downstream, whose day is shaped by what the desk routes to them.
stakeholders.2: Vendors and managed providers, where a ticket eventually crosses out of the organization.

requirements.0: Breadth across everything the organization runs, at the depth first contact requires.
requirements.1: Questioning that gets from a described symptom to a usable description.
requirements.2: Written clarity, since the ticket is what every later person reads.
requirements.3: Steadiness with people who are frustrated and whose day this has interrupted.

0.what: The problem as they experience it, described in their own vocabulary.

1.what: Resolutions, workarounds and the knowledge that raises first-contact resolution.

2.what: What is about to happen, which explains tomorrow's call volume.

0.what: One door, so that nobody needs to know which team owns their problem.

1.what: A filtered queue, with the routine handled before it reaches them.

2.what: The clearest available picture of what the organization is struggling with.

change-manager.title: Change manager
change-manager.whatItIs: The person who decides what may be done to production, and when. The framework states the purpose exactly: maximize the number of successful changes by assessing risk properly, authorizing changes to proceed, and managing the schedule. The word in that sentence carrying the most weight is maximize - the practice exists to let changes happen, with the assessment as the means rather than the object.
change-manager.turnsOn: Two numbers pull opposite ways: change success rate and lead time. A practice tuned only for success reviews everything, and the queue becomes the reason teams stop proposing improvements; one tuned only for speed accumulates the incidents that produce the next review board. The resolution is categorical rather than case by case - deciding which classes of change are standard and letting those flow - and the framework is unusually candid that in product-focused organizations this may be daily practice and automation rather than a job at all.

theDay.0: Assessing what is proposed: blast radius, dependencies, the plan to return, and whether the plan has been tried.
theDay.1: Authorizing, at whatever level the risk justifies, which for routine work should be automatic.
theDay.2: Holding the schedule, so that two safe changes stop being one unsafe evening.
theDay.3: Reviewing what happened afterwards, especially the changes that succeeded in ways nobody expected.
theDay.4: Adjusting the standard changes list, which is where most of the value is realized.

accountableFor.0: Risk assessed at a depth proportionate to the change.
accountableFor.1: The schedule reflecting what is genuinely happening.
accountableFor.2: Failed changes being reviewed for their cause rather than for their author.

measuredOn.0: Change success rate, and the impact of the ones that failed.
measuredOn.1: Lead time from request to implementation.
measuredOn.2: The proportion of changes flowing as standard rather than requiring a meeting.

stakeholders.0: Every user of every service inside the change window.
stakeholders.1: Auditors, for whom authorization records are evidence.
stakeholders.2: The on-call engineer who will meet whatever goes wrong.

requirements.0: Technical breadth sufficient to assess risk in systems somebody else built.
requirements.1: The judgement to route routine work through automatically, which requires trusting a category rather than a request.
requirements.2: Nerve to refuse, and the willingness to explain the refusal in terms of the risk rather than of the process.
requirements.3: A blameless instinct in review, since the alternative is accurate proposals becoming optimistic ones.

0.what: The proposal, and the honesty of its risk assessment.

1.what: When the service can be disturbed, and when it certainly cannot.

2.what: The consequences of previous changes, which is the calibration.

0.what: A path to production that is predictable and quick for ordinary work.

1.what: Change happening at the pace it needs, with the stability it assumes.

2.what: A schedule that keeps unrelated changes out of one another's evening.

problem-manager.title: Problem manager
problem-manager.whatItIs: The person who asks why the same incident keeps happening. Incident management restores the service; problem management identifies the cause and manages what follows from it. The framework gives the vocabulary precisely: a problem is a cause, or potential cause, of one or more incidents; a known error is a problem whose cause is understood while a permanent fix is outstanding; a workaround is what people use meanwhile.
problem-manager.turnsOn: The people best at this work are the people incident management needs most, and only one of those two has a clock on it. That is a structural fact rather than a cultural failing: an incident has a customer waiting and a problem has a spreadsheet, so the resource moves towards the incident every time it is asked to choose. Organizations that get value here protect the time explicitly, and treat a documented known error as a delivered outcome rather than as an investigation that stalled.

theDay.0: Reading incident records for the pattern, which is the identification phase and the one most easily skipped.
theDay.1: Investigating causes across systems owned by teams who each see one part.
theDay.2: Documenting a known error, which delivers value even where the fix is far away or uneconomic.
theDay.3: Managing workarounds so the same one is applied the same way by everybody.
theDay.4: Working proactively: looking for the causes of incidents that have yet to occur.

accountableFor.0: Recurring incidents having a record that explains them.
accountableFor.1: Known errors documented with their workarounds, and reachable by the people who need them.
accountableFor.2: Causes pursued to a decision, including the decision to accept one.

measuredOn.0: Recurrence: the same incident arriving fewer times.
measuredOn.1: Known errors documented, and workarounds in use.
measuredOn.2: Problems closed with a permanent fix rather than with a workaround.

stakeholders.0: The teams whose systems a cause turns out to sit in.
stakeholders.1: Vendors, whose defect this frequently becomes.
stakeholders.2: Finance, since a permanent fix competes for budget with new work.

requirements.0: Analysis across boundaries, since a cause rarely respects a team's edges.
requirements.1: Patience with an investigation whose value arrives after it closes.
requirements.2: Writing a known error clearly enough to be usable by somebody under time pressure.
requirements.3: Diplomacy, because the finding usually names a team rather than a machine.

0.who: Incident management and the service desk
0.what: The record, and the pattern hiding inside it.

1.what: The explanation of a defect, and the release that resolves it.

2.what: What was altered, which is where a proportion of causes live.

0.what: Fewer of them, and a documented answer for the ones that remain.

1.what: The interruption that stops arriving every Monday.

2.what: Evidence of which underlying faults are costing the most.

managed-service-provider-engineer.title: Managed service provider engineer
managed-service-provider-engineer.whatItIs: The engineer who runs other companies' infrastructure for a living. A managed service provider takes on the day-to-day operation under a subscription, mostly remotely, and the engineering is shaped by that arrangement: many customers, one set of hands, and a contract that defines what counts as done. The security variant carries the same shape with an adversary added.
managed-service-provider-engineer.turnsOn: Standardization is the margin. Every customer arrives with an environment shaped by their own history and asks, reasonably, to keep it - and each accommodation granted is a permanent tax on every future change. Providers that thrive negotiate the estate towards a pattern they can operate at scale, and the engineer who explains that trade to a customer in terms of their own resilience is doing the commercial work as well as the technical.

theDay.0: Working a queue that spans several customers, each believing they are the only one.
theDay.1: Responding to monitoring alerts against thresholds the provider chose and the customer accepted.
theDay.2: Applying the same change across many estates, which rewards standardization and punishes exceptions.
theDay.3: Reporting against the service levels the contract names, monthly and in writing.
theDay.4: Onboarding a new customer, which begins with an assessment of an environment nobody documented.

accountableFor.0: The service levels in the contract, per customer.
accountableFor.1: The estate staying current: patches, firmware, certificates and the things that expire quietly.
accountableFor.2: Keeping one customer's incident away from another customer's service.

measuredOn.0: Service level attainment and ticket throughput.
measuredOn.1: Margin per customer, which is where standardization shows up commercially.
measuredOn.2: Retention, since the business model is recurring rather than transactional.

stakeholders.0: The customer's auditors and insurers, for whom the provider's practice is part of the customer's posture.
stakeholders.1: Every other customer sharing the provider's tooling and attention.
stakeholders.2: The vendors whose products the provider standardized on.

requirements.0: Breadth, because the queue contains whatever the customer base runs.
requirements.1: Discipline with process, since the same change applied many times is safe only when it is applied the same way.
requirements.2: Writing that serves a monthly report as well as a ticket.
requirements.3: The judgement to hold a standard when a customer asks for an exception that would be simpler to grant.

0.what: Their environment, their change requests, and their definition of urgent.

1.what: Product, support paths and the escalation route when a defect is involved.

2.what: Alerts, inventory and the automation that makes many estates tractable.

0.what: Infrastructure that runs, without the customer employing the people who run it.

1.who: The customer's own IT staff, where they exist
1.what: Capacity for the work only they can do.

2.what: The service record a renewal conversation rests on.

technical-assistance-centre-engineer.title: Technical assistance centre engineer
technical-assistance-centre-engineer.whatItIs: The engineer a customer reaches when they contact the vendor. A technical assistance centre runs a queue against a clock, in tiers, around the world, and the role is the first place a fault becomes somebody's named responsibility. It is the largest single population of engineers most vendors employ, and the one that meets the product most often. This is the second line inside the VENDOR; what it escalates goes to third-line product support, and from there to the developers. The customer has tiers of its own, beginning at their service desk, and a case crosses between the two ladders at the point where the organization running the product asks the organization that made it.
technical-assistance-centre-engineer.turnsOn: The clock measures the case and the handover decides the outcome. A case that moves between three engineers and three time zones resolves at the speed of its notes, which makes writing the most load-bearing skill in the room and the one least represented in how the role is hired for. Engineers who write their case notes for a stranger arriving at three in the morning are the reason a follow-the-sun model works at all.

theDay.0: Taking ownership of a case, which begins by establishing what actually happened rather than what was reported.
theDay.1: Gathering the evidence that distinguishes between the plausible explanations.
theDay.2: Resolving within the tier where possible, since each escalation costs the customer time.
theDay.3: Handing over across time zones so that a case moves while its owner sleeps.
theDay.4: Feeding recurring findings back as knowledge, so a pattern resolves faster next time.

accountableFor.0: The case: its progress, its record and its accuracy.
accountableFor.1: The severity being right, since severity governs who else becomes involved.
accountableFor.2: A handover that lets the next engineer continue rather than restart.

measuredOn.0: Time to first response and time to resolution against the service level.
measuredOn.1: Backlog age and cases resolved within the tier.
measuredOn.2: Customer satisfaction recorded per case.

stakeholders.0: The account team, for whom an open critical case is a commercial fact.
stakeholders.1: Product management, for whom case volume is roadmap evidence.
stakeholders.2: Every customer running the release that produced the case.

requirements.0: Reading evidence closely while a clock runs.
requirements.1: Written English clear enough to survive a handover to another continent.
requirements.2: Steadiness with a caller whose night this also is.
requirements.3: The habit of recording what was tried, since the record is what makes the next shift useful.

0.what: The report, the evidence they gathered, and the urgency as they experience it.

1.what: Defect status, workarounds and the release carrying the fix.

2.what: A case in progress and the notes that make it continuable.

0.what: A resolution, and reasoning they can carry to their own management.

1.what: A case file complete enough to act on, with everything already tried recorded rather than repeated.

2.what: The article that resolves the next occurrence without a person.

account-manager.title: Account manager
account-manager.whatItIs: The commercial half of a vendor sales team, and the person a customer's management calls. An account manager owns the relationship, the forecast and the negotiation, and pairs with a systems engineer who owns the technical truth. The two answer for the same deal from different directions, which is the arrangement's whole design.
account-manager.turnsOn: The forecast is the product. An account manager who calls a deal accurately, including calling it lost early, lets an entire organization plan around the truth; one whose optimism outruns the evidence spends the quarter's final week explaining. The relationships are how the accuracy is obtained, which is why the role looks social and is arithmetical underneath.

theDay.0: Maintaining a forecast that survives contact with the quarter, which means knowing which deals are real.
theDay.1: Building the relationships that give early warning: a budget moving, a competitor invited, a champion leaving.
theDay.2: Negotiating price, terms and the shape of a contract inside whatever discount authority applies.
theDay.3: Coordinating everyone the account touches: pre-sales, professional services, support, channel partners and the vendor's own management.
theDay.4: Carrying the customer's position back into the vendor when the roadmap and the requirement diverge.

accountableFor.0: The forecast being accurate, including the parts that make the number look worse.
accountableFor.1: The commercial relationship, through renewals and through incidents.
accountableFor.2: Everything promised under their name, including the technical parts somebody else wrote.

measuredOn.0: Quota attainment, quarter by quarter.
measuredOn.1: Pipeline coverage and its progression through the stages.
measuredOn.2: Renewal rate and account growth, which arrive later than the quota does.

stakeholders.0: The customer's procurement and finance functions, whose process governs the timeline.
stakeholders.1: Professional services and support, who inherit the commitments.
stakeholders.2: The vendor's finance organization, for whom the forecast is a planning input.

requirements.0: Enough technical literacy to know which questions need the systems engineer in the room.
requirements.1: The discipline to forecast honestly when an optimistic number would be easier this week.
requirements.2: Patience with sales cycles measured in quarters and relationships measured in years.
requirements.3: Composure through the incident that arrives the month before the renewal.

0.what: Leads, campaigns and the reason a customer took the call.

1.what: What the technology will do, in terms that can be promised.

2.what: Quota, territory, discount authority and the current priority.

0.what: One accountable point of contact across everything the vendor sells.

1.what: Revenue, and an accurate picture of what will close.

2.what: Alignment, so that one deal is worked once rather than twice.

channel-account-manager.title: Channel account manager
channel-account-manager.whatItIs: The commercial counterpart to the channel systems engineer, and the person a partner's management deals with. A channel account manager owns a set of partner companies rather than a set of end customers, which changes the work fundamentally: the revenue arrives through somebody else's sales team, so the job is to make that team choose this line card over the others they carry.
channel-account-manager.turnsOn: Partner attention is the scarce thing. A partner carries several vendors and allocates its engineers and sellers to whichever combination of margin, demand and ease returns most - so the account manager competes with the other logos on that partner's wall rather than with the vendor's own competitors. Making the line easy to sell, easy to configure and easy to support wins more capacity than a richer rebate does, which is why this role and the channel systems engineer succeed together or not at all.

theDay.0: Recruiting and onboarding partners, then working out which of them will actually transact.
theDay.1: Running the programme: tiers, targets, rebates, accreditations and the renewals that keep a partner in benefit.
theDay.2: Building joint business plans with a partner's management, and revisiting them when a quarter disagrees.
theDay.3: Resolving channel conflict, where two partners or a partner and a direct team pursue one customer.
theDay.4: Arranging the marketing funds, campaigns and incentives that turn a partner's attention towards one vendor.

accountableFor.0: Revenue through the assigned partner base.
accountableFor.1: The partners understanding the programme they are being measured against.
accountableFor.2: Conflict resolved in a way that leaves both partners still selling.

measuredOn.0: Partner-sourced and partner-influenced revenue.
measuredOn.1: Partner recruitment, activation and the count still transacting a year later.
measuredOn.2: Programme compliance: certifications held, thresholds met, plans in place.

stakeholders.0: The end customer, who buys from the partner and is served by a chain they rarely see.
stakeholders.1: The vendor's direct sales team, whose territory the channel overlaps.
stakeholders.2: Distribution's credit and logistics functions, which carry the transaction.

requirements.0: Commercial fluency in margin, rebate and programme mechanics.
requirements.1: Influence without authority, since a partner is another company with its own priorities.
requirements.2: The judgement to invest in the partners who will grow, which is a slower signal than this quarter.
requirements.3: Even handling of conflict, because a partner who feels displaced remembers it for years.

0.what: Programme rules, margin structures, funds and the current campaign.

1.what: An accurate read of which partners are technically ready.

2.what: Their own plans, their other vendors, and their commercial reality.

0.what: A reason to invest their capacity in this line rather than another.

1.what: Reach, through companies that already hold the customer relationships.

2.what: Programmes, incentives and support that make a deal worth working.

network-software-engineer.title: Network software engineer
network-software-engineer.whatItIs: The engineer who writes the operating system a network runs on. It is software engineering shaped by an unusual set of constraints: the code runs unattended for years on equipment nobody can reach, an upgrade is a maintenance window somebody negotiated weeks earlier, and a defect is discovered by a stranger at three in the morning. The architecture of the platform decides how much of that pressure reaches any individual change.
network-software-engineer.turnsOn: The architecture decides how expensive a mistake is, and the architecture was chosen long before the current engineer arrived. On a platform where every process shares one address space, a defect in one feature reaches everything, so caution is the only available safety mechanism. On a platform where a process can be restarted from a state store, the same defect is contained, and engineering effort moves from avoiding faults to recovering from them. Understanding which platform you are writing for is therefore the first thing to learn about the job.

theDay.0: Writing and reviewing code against a protocol specification that other implementations also read, and read differently.
theDay.1: Working within the platform's architecture, which sets the terms: a shared address space makes one defect everybody's outage, and a state store makes a process restartable.
theDay.2: Testing against hardware, against scale, and against the interoperability cases that only appear when another vendor is on the far end.
theDay.3: Taking a reproduced defect from third-line support and finding what in the code produced it.
theDay.4: Deciding which release carries a fix, which is a conversation about risk rather than about code.

accountableFor.0: Code that behaves correctly at scale and under the failure conditions the platform promises to survive.
accountableFor.1: Interoperability with implementations written by other people from the same specification.
accountableFor.2: The fix arriving in a release, on a schedule support and customers were told about.

measuredOn.0: Defect escape rate, which is what customers experience as quality.
measuredOn.1: Delivery against the release train, which moves for the whole portfolio rather than for one feature.
measuredOn.2: Test coverage and the results of the regression suite.

stakeholders.0: The customers whose networks carry the release, most of whom will never report anything.
stakeholders.1: Support organizations worldwide, whose case volume is downstream of this code.
stakeholders.2: Other vendors, whose implementations have to interoperate with this one.

requirements.0: Systems programming, and the discipline that comes from code running where nobody can attach a debugger.
requirements.1: Reading specifications closely, since interoperability is agreement about ambiguity.
requirements.2: Comfort with a release cadence measured in months and a support lifetime measured in years.
requirements.3: The judgement to weigh a fix against the risk of shipping it, which is a decision about other people's networks.

0.what: Reproduced defects with the evidence attached, which is the difference between a fix and an investigation.

1.what: Requirements, priorities, and the customers behind them.

2.what: The behaviour the code has to agree with.

0.what: Software that behaves as documented, including when something fails.

1.what: Fixes, workarounds and the source-level explanation behind them.

2.what: Changes that respect the constraints the design was built to give.

security-leader.title: Security leader
security-leader.whatItIs: The top of the management arm, in security. The framework describes the work as establishing vision and direction for an organization's cybersecurity operations and resources, with the authority to make decisions that reach the whole organization, approve policy and engage stakeholders. The ladder below it runs manager, then director, then this - and each rung trades proximity to the work for reach across it.
security-leader.turnsOn: The role is accountable for an outcome it produces through other people's budgets and other people's priorities. Authority over policy is real and authority over the engineering that implements it usually belongs to somebody else, so the work is persuasion carried out with a mandate. Leaders who last make the risk legible to the people who hold the budget, and record what the organization decided to accept - because the record is what turns a later incident from a failure of the programme into a consequence of a decision somebody made knowingly.

theDay.0: Setting direction, and holding it while the quarter argues with it.
theDay.1: Acquiring resources: budget, headcount, and the authority to require things of teams elsewhere.
theDay.2: Approving policy, and owning the consequences when it is applied to a business the policy inconveniences.
theDay.3: Advising senior management and the board, in terms of risk to the organization rather than in terms of technology.
theDay.4: Communicating the value of the programme to stakeholders, which is the task the framework names and the one most easily deferred.

accountableFor.0: The organization's security posture, including the parts owned by teams elsewhere.
accountableFor.1: The programme having a strategy that connects to the organization's actual risks.
accountableFor.2: What the board is told, and whether it was accurate at the time.

measuredOn.0: Risk reduction, which resists measurement and is measured anyway.
measuredOn.1: Incidents and their consequences, which are visible and partly outside the role's control.
measuredOn.2: Audit and regulatory outcomes, and programme delivery against plan.

stakeholders.0: Customers and the public, whose data the organization holds.
stakeholders.1: Every team whose work the policy constrains.
stakeholders.2: Insurers, regulators and, after an incident, the courts.

requirements.0: Technical credibility sufficient to be told the truth by the people who have it.
requirements.1: Fluency in risk, budget and the language a board makes decisions in.
requirements.2: The composure to be accountable for outcomes produced by systems and people beyond direct control.
requirements.3: The judgement to say what the organization is choosing to accept, and to have it recorded as a choice.

0.what: What is happening, at the fidelity the tooling allows.

1.what: Where it is going, which decides what has to be protected next.

2.what: Obligations that arrive with dates attached.

0.what: Risk expressed in terms they can decide with.

1.what: Direction, resources, and cover when a decision proves unpopular.

2.what: Policy that can be followed by people whose job is something else.

project-manager.title: Project manager
project-manager.whatItIs: The person accountable for a piece of work arriving: on the agreed scope, inside the agreed time, at the agreed cost. On a technology delivery the role sits between the customer who bought an outcome and the engineers producing it, and its material is dependencies, sequence and the truth about progress.
project-manager.turnsOn: Status reporting is where this role is decided. A project manager who reports the schedule the customer wants to hear buys three comfortable weeks and pays for them at the end, in a conversation nobody can prepare for; one who reports a slip the day it appears spends an uncomfortable hour and keeps the options open. Everything else in the role is technique, and this is the part that decides whether the technique matters.

theDay.0: Holding the plan, and revising it the moment reality disagrees rather than at the next reporting date.
theDay.1: Chasing dependencies, most of which belong to people outside the project and inside somebody else's priorities.
theDay.2: Running the governance: status, risk log, change control, and the decisions that need a name attached.
theDay.3: Escalating early, which is the difference between a recoverable slip and a lost project.
theDay.4: Protecting the engineers from the meetings that produce nothing, and attending those meetings instead.

accountableFor.0: Scope, schedule and cost, and the trade between them being made deliberately.
accountableFor.1: Status reporting that reflects the project rather than the audience.
accountableFor.2: Risks named while there is still time to act on them.

measuredOn.0: Delivery against the baseline, and margin on the engagement.
measuredOn.1: Change requests handled without the project losing its shape.
measuredOn.2: Customer satisfaction at handover.

stakeholders.0: The customer's own project office, whose governance the engagement has to satisfy.
stakeholders.1: Finance on both sides, since schedule and cost are the same conversation.
stakeholders.2: The operations team who will inherit whatever is delivered.

requirements.0: Enough technical understanding to know when an estimate is optimistic.
requirements.1: The nerve to report a slip on the day it becomes visible.
requirements.2: Organization held lightly, since a plan defended past its usefulness becomes the problem.
requirements.3: Diplomacy across two organizations with different incentives and one shared deadline.

0.what: The statement of work, and whatever was promised in the room.

1.what: What is actually happening, at whatever candour the culture allows.

2.what: Access, windows, decisions, and the changes they have decided they also want.

0.what: One person accountable for the whole, so that they deal with a project rather than with a set of engineers.

1.what: A sequence that makes sense, and cover when the plan needs to change.

2.what: A project whose margin survives its own scope.

procurement-specialist.title: Procurement specialist
procurement-specialist.whatItIs: The person on the other side of every sale described in this corpus. Procurement runs the cycle - market analysis, sourcing, negotiation, contracting and supplier management - with the object of acquiring at the right price, quality, quantity and time. The professional body draws a line worth keeping: procurement covers that whole cycle, while purchasing fulfils the transaction.
procurement-specialist.turnsOn: The seller is measured on revenue captured and the buyer on discount obtained, which makes one number the target of two careers pulling opposite ways. The subtlety is in how a saving is counted: a reduction from a known baseline is auditable, while cost avoided is measured against an increase that was proposed and then prevented - a comparison with something that stayed hypothetical. Buyers who explain that distinction to their own finance function get credit for both kinds; those who leave it implicit find the second kind quietly discounted.

theDay.0: Running a tender or a request for proposal, and keeping it defensible while the business argues for the supplier it already chose.
theDay.1: Negotiating price, terms, service levels and the renewal clauses that decide the next three years.
theDay.2: Building the category strategy: what this organization buys, from whom, and what leverage exists.
theDay.3: Managing suppliers after signature, which is where most of the value either arrives or evaporates.
theDay.4: Recording the saving, in a form finance will accept.

accountableFor.0: A process that stands up to audit, including the parts where a preferred supplier lost.
accountableFor.1: Contracts whose obligations are the ones the organization actually needs.
accountableFor.2: The commercial position: price, terms and the exits.

measuredOn.0: Savings delivered against a baseline, and cost avoided against an increase that was proposed.
measuredOn.1: Contract cycle time, and spend brought under managed agreements.
measuredOn.2: Supplier performance against the terms that were signed.

stakeholders.0: The suppliers on the other side, whose account managers are measured on the same transaction.
stakeholders.1: The legal function, which owns what the contract says.
stakeholders.2: Whoever operates the thing afterwards, and lives with the support terms that were negotiated.

requirements.0: Negotiation held over long horizons, since the renewal is part of the first conversation.
requirements.1: Enough technical literacy to tell a requirement from a preference written as one.
requirements.2: Rigour with process, because the defensibility of a decision is part of its value.
requirements.3: The independence to say that the chosen supplier lost on the criteria the organization set.

0.what: A requirement, sometimes written around a product already chosen.

1.what: Budget, and the definition of a saving they will recognize.

2.what: Proposals, and the pricing behaviour that reveals where the flexibility is.

0.what: Value obtained, and risk removed from agreements before it becomes a dispute.

1.what: The thing they asked for, on terms that survive the next renewal.

2.what: A defensible record of how the decision was reached.

product-manager.title: Product manager
product-manager.whatItIs: The person who decides what the product is. The body of knowledge frames the work across a lifecycle - conceive, plan, develop, qualify, launch, deliver, retire - with a decision point between each phase. A product manager owns those decisions and the reasoning behind them, and owns them without commanding any of the teams whose work depends on them.
product-manager.turnsOn: A roadmap is a list of refusals. Every item on it represents many that were declined, and the declining is where the role is actually exercised - most of all at the gate, where stopping something the organization is already committed to costs more socially than continuing it costs commercially. Product managers who can close a gate produce focused products; those who cannot produce long roadmaps and thin releases, and both look like activity from outside.

theDay.0: Talking to customers, and to the people who talk to customers, which is a different and larger population.
theDay.1: Deciding what enters the roadmap, and revisiting it when the evidence moves.
theDay.2: Writing the requirement precisely enough that engineering can build it and loosely enough that they can build it well.
theDay.3: Holding the gate between lifecycle phases, including the decision to stop.
theDay.4: Preparing the launch with marketing, support and training, all of whom need the product before it exists.

accountableFor.0: The product solving a problem somebody has, evidenced rather than assumed.
accountableFor.1: The decisions and their reasoning, in a form that survives the person who made them.
accountableFor.2: Everything the organization promised about the product being true when it ships.

measuredOn.0: Adoption and revenue, which arrive long after the decisions that caused them.
measuredOn.1: Delivery against the roadmap that was committed.
measuredOn.2: Retention and the outcomes customers report.

stakeholders.0: Every team whose plan depends on the roadmap being roughly true.
stakeholders.1: Executives whose commitments were made from an earlier version of it.
stakeholders.2: Customers who bought partly on what was said about the future.

requirements.0: Reading evidence about people, which is harder and less exact than reading evidence about systems.
requirements.1: Enough technical depth to be told the truth by engineers and to know when an estimate is a negotiation.
requirements.2: Writing that leaves engineering room to solve the problem rather than to implement a solution.
requirements.3: The nerve to hold a gate closed.

0.what: Problems, described as requests for features.

1.what: What is possible, at what cost, and what the architecture will resist.

2.what: Evidence of where the product is failing people, which outranks most opinions.

0.what: A clear problem and the reasoning behind its priority.

1.what: Something they can describe accurately.

2.what: A product that changes in the direction of their actual difficulty.

instructional-designer.title: Instructional designer
instructional-designer.whatItIs: The person who builds the course rather than the person who delivers it. An instructional designer starts from what a learner has to be able to do afterwards and works backwards to the material, the exercises and the assessment. The published study of the field finds design, delivery, technology, communication and collaboration named most often in the job itself, which describes a role that builds and frequently also teaches.
instructional-designer.turnsOn: The objective is written before the content, and everything follows from that order. A course built outward from the material teaches what the author knows; one built backward from an objective teaches what the learner has to be able to do, and the two produce identical-looking slide decks with entirely different results in the room. The discipline is holding the order under time pressure, because the fastest way to produce a course is to write down what you know and call the last slide a summary.

theDay.0: Writing objectives first: what somebody will be able to do, stated so that it can be assessed.
theDay.1: Designing backwards from those objectives to the exercises that produce the ability.
theDay.2: Building the laboratory environments the exercises assume, which is engineering work inside a teaching job.
theDay.3: Writing assessment that measures the objective rather than the memory of the slide.
theDay.4: Revising from delivery feedback, since a room finds every ambiguity within an hour.

accountableFor.0: Objectives that describe a capability rather than a topic.
accountableFor.1: Material an instructor other than the author can deliver.
accountableFor.2: Exercises that work in the environment the students actually receive.

measuredOn.0: Assessment results against the stated objectives.
measuredOn.1: Instructor and student evaluation of the material.
measuredOn.2: Courseware delivered on schedule, and revision cycles completed.

stakeholders.0: The employers paying for the training, who are buying an outcome rather than a week.
stakeholders.1: The certification body, where a course leads to an examination.
stakeholders.2: Every future instructor who inherits the material.

requirements.0: Enough subject depth to interrogate an expert and notice what they left out.
requirements.1: Writing for a reader who lacks the context the author has.
requirements.2: Patience with revision, since a course is finished by its third delivery rather than its first.
requirements.3: Comfort designing for a room you will never meet.

0.what: The technical content, in the form an expert holds it rather than the form a beginner needs.

1.what: What the room struggled with, which is the highest-value feedback available.

2.what: Objectives the course has to cover, where an examination follows.

0.what: Material they can teach from, including the parts they would have written differently.

1.what: A route from where they are to what they need to do.

2.what: Capability that scales past the availability of any one expert.

product-marketing-manager.title: Product marketing manager
product-marketing-manager.whatItIs: The counterpart to product management, facing the other way. Where a product manager decides what gets built, product marketing decides how it is understood: who it is for, which problem it is against, and which alternatives a buyer will weigh it beside. The body of knowledge treats the two as one domain with two halves, which is the most accurate description of how they actually work.
product-marketing-manager.turnsOn: Positioning is choosing the competitor set, and that choice decides the argument before it starts. A product placed against the wrong alternative competes on features a buyer has already stopped caring about; placed against the right one, the same product reads as obvious. The work is therefore an act of judgement about the market rather than an act of writing about the product, and it is the part where a good writer with market sense outperforms a better writer without it.

theDay.0: Positioning: choosing the comparison a buyer will make, which is a decision rather than a description.
theDay.1: Writing the messages, and then the artefacts everybody else repeats them from.
theDay.2: Preparing launches, where the product, the sellers, the partners and the support organization have to arrive on the same day saying the same thing.
theDay.3: Equipping the field: the material a seller uses in a room where the product manager is absent.
theDay.4: Studying competitors closely enough to describe them fairly, since a caricature loses the deal it was written for.

accountableFor.0: Positioning that survives contact with a buyer who has alternatives.
accountableFor.1: Claims that the product can support, since support inherits everything overstated.
accountableFor.2: The organization describing the product consistently across every channel it uses.

measuredOn.0: Pipeline influenced, and win rates against named competitors.
measuredOn.1: Launch execution and the adoption that follows.
measuredOn.2: Sales enablement: material produced, and material actually used.

stakeholders.0: Support, who meet every promise afterwards.
