stakeholders.1: The training organization, whose material carries the same claims into a classroom.
stakeholders.2: Partners, who repeat the positioning in markets the vendor never enters.

requirements.0: Writing plainly about a technical thing for a reader who has ten minutes.
requirements.1: Enough depth to be corrected by an engineer and to argue back where the correction is cosmetic.
requirements.2: Judgement about claims, since the cost of an overstated one lands on somebody else.
requirements.3: Comfort with attribution that stays partial, because influence resists measurement.

0.what: What is being built and why, early enough to prepare.

1.what: What buyers actually ask, and where deals are lost.

2.what: The words they use, which outrank the words the company prefers.

0.what: A story that holds up under questioning, and the material to tell it with.

1.what: An accurate account of what the product is for.

2.what: Market evidence, which is the input a roadmap decision is made against.

management-consultant.title: Management consultant
management-consultant.whatItIs: The adviser who is paid for judgement rather than for hands. Where a consulting engineer implements a design, a management consultant is engaged to work out what should be done and to make the case for it. The profession has a competence framework and a certification behind it, structured across three levels of progression, which is a useful reminder that advisory work has a standard even where a client is buying a person.
management-consultant.turnsOn: The most valuable advice frequently ends the engagement, and the measurement rewards the engagement continuing. A consultant who finds that the client already has the capability and needs a decision rather than a programme has done the best available work and produced the smallest available invoice. Firms that survive on reputation make room for that outcome and say so at the outset; the profession's own competence framework puts professional behaviour underneath every technical competence for exactly this reason.

theDay.0: Establishing the actual question, which is frequently adjacent to the one in the brief.
theDay.1: Gathering evidence inside an organization whose people have their own view of what the answer should be.
theDay.2: Analysis, and the discipline of following it where it goes.
theDay.3: Presenting to a room where somebody sponsored the engagement and somebody else is implicated by the finding.
theDay.4: Handing over in a way that leaves the client able to act without the consultant present.

accountableFor.0: Recommendations that follow from the evidence gathered rather than from the engagement that was sold.
accountableFor.1: Independence, which is the entire product.
accountableFor.2: A client left more capable, rather than more dependent.

measuredOn.0: Utilization and fee income.
measuredOn.1: Recommendations adopted, and the outcomes attributed to them.
measuredOn.2: Repeat engagements and referrals, which is where the tension sits.

stakeholders.0: The staff whose work the recommendation changes, who were interviewed and rarely decide.
stakeholders.1: The firm's reputation, which is carried by every engagement.
stakeholders.2: Whoever inherits the recommendation after the sponsor moves on.

requirements.0: Analysis that survives being checked by people who know the domain better.
requirements.1: Writing that separates the finding, the inference and the recommendation.
requirements.2: Composure in a room where the finding is unwelcome to somebody senior.
requirements.3: The independence to say the engagement should end, which is the profession's defining behaviour.

0.what: The brief, the budget and the political shape of the problem.

1.what: How things actually work, offered at whatever candour the situation permits.

2.what: Method, precedent and the people to staff the work.

0.what: A defensible basis for a decision they own.

1.what: A view assembled by somebody with no stake in the current arrangement.

2.what: Reasoning clear enough to act on after the consultant leaves.

talent-development-manager.title: Talent development manager
talent-development-manager.whatItIs: The person who decides what an organization needs to be able to do, and builds the programme that gets it there. The capability model places this in its organizational domain, above the personal and professional ones: designers build courses and instructors deliver them, while this role works out which capability is missing, what it is worth, and how the answer will be recognized when it arrives.
talent-development-manager.turnsOn: Training is measured on completion and valued for capability, and those are different numbers arriving at different times. A programme optimized for the first fills rooms and reports well; one optimized for the second sends fewer people to longer things and looks quieter for two quarters. Managers who hold that line get asked to justify it, so the durable move is to agree the capability measure with the business in advance and report against it from the beginning.

theDay.0: Assessing capability against what the organization is trying to do next, which requires knowing both.
theDay.1: Deciding what to build, what to buy, and what to leave alone.
theDay.2: Running the budget, the calendar and the vendors, since most programmes are assembled rather than authored.
theDay.3: Measuring, and defending the measurement, because the useful numbers arrive later than the reporting cycle.
theDay.4: Persuading managers to release people, which is where most programmes actually succeed or stall.

accountableFor.0: A programme aimed at capability the organization genuinely lacks.
accountableFor.1: Spend that produces something demonstrable.
accountableFor.2: Learning that reaches the people whose work it changes.

measuredOn.0: Completion and attendance, which are easy and shallow.
measuredOn.1: Assessment and certification outcomes.
measuredOn.2: Capability and performance change, which is the point and the hardest number to obtain.

stakeholders.0: Finance, for whom training is a discretionary line and therefore an early candidate for reduction.
stakeholders.1: The instructors and designers whose work the programme commissions.
stakeholders.2: The customers served by whoever was trained.

requirements.0: Reading an organization: what it claims to need against what its incidents suggest.
requirements.1: Commercial argument, since the budget is defended annually against work with faster returns.
requirements.2: Judgement about buy against build, which is mostly a judgement about how specific the need is.
requirements.3: Comfort with evidence that arrives after the decision it justifies.

0.what: Where the organization is going, and what it will need people to do there.

1.what: What is possible to build, and what a room can absorb.

2.what: Where their teams are struggling, described as requests for training.

0.what: A route to capability they can actually take, inside a working week.

1.what: Teams that can do more without additional headcount.

2.what: Capability that outlasts the individuals who happen to hold it now.

customer-success-manager.title: Customer success manager
customer-success-manager.whatItIs: The person who owns the relationship after the sale closes. Customer success grew out of subscription business, where the revenue arrives in instalments and every one of them is a decision the customer makes again. The role guides onboarding, adoption and expansion, and it is separated deliberately from support, which is reactive, and from the account executive, who owns new business.
customer-success-manager.turnsOn: Satisfaction and retention are different measurements, and the distance between them is the job. A customer can be entirely happy and still leave, because their priorities moved and nobody on the vendor side noticed - which makes the useful question whether the customer is achieving outcomes that justify continued investment, rather than whether they are pleased. Managers who ask the first question find the risk in time; those who ask the second find it at the renewal.

theDay.0: Onboarding: getting a customer to their first real outcome, since the time that takes predicts everything afterwards.
theDay.1: Watching adoption across a portfolio, which runs from a handful of strategic accounts to several hundred at the lighter end.
theDay.2: Reading health signals early enough to act, rather than at the renewal conversation.
theDay.3: Connecting product capability to what the customer is actually trying to achieve this year.
theDay.4: Preparing the renewal long before it arrives, so it becomes a formality rather than a negotiation.

accountableFor.0: Customers reaching the outcome they bought the product for.
accountableFor.1: Risk surfaced while there is still time to change it.
accountableFor.2: The account's story being accurate internally, including where it is going badly.

measuredOn.0: Net revenue retention, which combines renewal, expansion, contraction and churn into one number.
measuredOn.1: Gross retention and logo churn.
measuredOn.2: Adoption depth, health score and time to value.

stakeholders.0: The customer's end users, whose experience decides adoption regardless of the sponsor's enthusiasm.
stakeholders.1: Finance on both sides, for whom the renewal is a forecast line.
stakeholders.2: Support and professional services, whose work shapes the health this role reports.

requirements.0: Reading an account: usage, sentiment and the organizational change nobody mentioned.
requirements.1: Enough product depth to advise rather than to schedule a call with somebody who can.
requirements.2: Commercial literacy, since the conversation ends in a renewal whether or not the role closes it.
requirements.3: The candour to record an account as at risk while the relationship still feels warm.

0.what: The account, and whatever expectations were set to win it.

1.what: What the customer actually uses, which is frequently different from what they say.

2.what: The friction, arriving as tickets before it arrives as sentiment.

0.what: Progress towards the outcome they are accountable for internally.

1.what: Retention, which in subscription business is most of the revenue.

2.what: Evidence of where adoption stalls, which is a roadmap input with numbers attached.

sales-development-representative.title: Sales development representative
sales-development-representative.whatItIs: The first human contact between a company and a prospective customer. Sales development sits at the top of the funnel: researching accounts, reaching out, qualifying interest, and handing over a conversation that somebody else will close. The role exists because prospecting and closing reward different temperaments and different hours, and separating them lets each be done properly.
sales-development-representative.turnsOn: Activity and qualification pull against each other. A representative measured purely on meetings books meetings, and the closing seller spends the following month discovering which ones were real; one measured on meetings that progress works slower and hands over conversations worth having. The organizations that get this right define qualification jointly with the sellers who receive the work, which turns a handover into an agreement rather than a transfer.

theDay.0: Researching accounts well enough that the first message is about them rather than about the product.
theDay.1: Outreach at volume, across whichever channels currently reach people.
theDay.2: Qualifying: establishing whether there is a problem, a budget and a reason to act now.
theDay.3: Handing over to the closing seller with enough context that the prospect avoids repeating themselves.
theDay.4: Recording what happened, since the pattern across hundreds of attempts is the useful output.

accountableFor.0: Meetings that are genuinely qualified, rather than meetings that fill a calendar.
accountableFor.1: The record being accurate, since the next person works from it.
accountableFor.2: Representing the company in the first impression it makes.

measuredOn.0: Qualified meetings booked, and the proportion that progress.
measuredOn.1: Activity: attempts, connections, conversations.
measuredOn.2: Pipeline generated, and eventually the revenue attributed to it.

stakeholders.0: Everybody who receives the outreach, most of whom did not ask for it.
stakeholders.1: The brand, which is shaped by how the first contact reads.
stakeholders.2: The forecast, which begins here.

requirements.0: Resilience, since the role is built on a low response rate by design.
requirements.1: Research, because relevance is the whole difference between contact and noise.
requirements.2: Brevity in writing, held under pressure to say more.
requirements.3: Discipline with the record, since the value compounds across attempts rather than within one.

0.what: Leads, campaigns and the reason somebody might already be interested.

1.what: The territory, the target accounts and the current priority.

2.what: What a good meeting looks like, which is learned rather than briefed.

0.what: Conversations with people who have a reason to have them.

1.what: Pipeline, which is the input everything downstream depends on.

2.what: A route to somebody who can answer, at the moment the question is live.

developer-advocate.title: Developer advocate
developer-advocate.whatItIs: The engineer employed by a vendor whose work serves the people who use its technology. Advocacy sits inside developer relations, the broader function covering community, events, experience and content, and the advocate is its technical face: writing sample code, building reference integrations, answering in public channels, and carrying what the community says back into product and engineering.
developer-advocate.turnsOn: The role is paid by one side and useful to the other, and the value depends entirely on the community believing the second part. That belief is built by the unglamorous half: filing the bug, saying plainly where the product falls short, and returning later with what changed. Advocates who do that are trusted and their companies benefit; the internal half of the job is what makes the external half true, which is why measuring only outbound activity produces a function that gradually stops working.

theDay.0: Writing sample code and reference integrations that show the product doing something real.
theDay.1: Answering in public - forums, chat, issues - where the answer stays available to everybody who arrives later.
theDay.2: Speaking and running workshops, which is teaching to a room that chose to attend.
theDay.3: Filing the detailed bug report that a frustrated user would have abandoned.
theDay.4: Internal advocacy: carrying the community's difficulty into the company, in terms product and engineering can act on.

accountableFor.0: Technical accuracy in public, under a company name.
accountableFor.1: The community's difficulties reaching the people who can resolve them.
accountableFor.2: Material that continues to work after the release it was written against.

measuredOn.0: Adoption signals: sign-ups, integrations built, documentation and sample usage.
measuredOn.1: Community activity and sentiment.
measuredOn.2: Product changes traceable to feedback the role carried, which is the honest measure and the hardest to attribute.

stakeholders.0: The wider community, including the people who never post and read everything.
stakeholders.1: Marketing, whose messages the advocate's credibility either supports or contradicts.
stakeholders.2: Engineering, whose backlog receives what the advocate carries.

requirements.0: Engineering ability, since credibility comes from building the thing rather than describing it.
requirements.1: Writing and speaking for an audience that will check the claims.
requirements.2: The willingness to say a product does something partially, in public, on the company's account.
requirements.3: Comfort with a contribution that is visible everywhere and attributable almost nowhere.

0.what: Questions, complaints and the workarounds they invented without being asked.

1.what: What is coming, and the reasoning behind what is already there.

2.what: The recurring case, which is community difficulty already quantified.

0.what: A route to making the product work, and somebody who answers.

1.what: Field evidence with the vocabulary of the people who hit the problem.

2.what: Adoption built on capability rather than on persuasion.

community-manager.title: Community manager
community-manager.whatItIs: The person who tends the space where users of a technology meet each other. Where an advocate teaches and carries feedback, a community manager builds the conditions in which people help one another: the forum, the meetups, the events, the norms, and the recognition that keeps contributors contributing. The output is a group of people who would continue without the company, which is both the goal and the risk.
community-manager.turnsOn: A community succeeds when members answer each other, and that success looks like the company doing less. Every intervention that resolves a question centrally is a question the community stopped needing to answer, so the discipline is restraint: connecting people, recognizing the ones who help, and leaving room for an answer to arrive from somebody with no badge. Managers who hold that line build something that outlasts them, and have to explain the quieter numbers meanwhile.

theDay.0: Moderating, which is mostly invisible and entirely load-bearing.
theDay.1: Recognizing contributors, since attention is the currency a volunteer community actually runs on.
theDay.2: Running events and meetups, online and in person.
theDay.3: Connecting people who have a question to people who solved it, rather than answering everything centrally.
theDay.4: Reporting sentiment inward, including the parts the company finds unwelcome.

accountableFor.0: The space staying usable: on topic, civil and worth returning to.
accountableFor.1: Norms that are applied evenly, including to people the company values commercially.
accountableFor.2: An accurate account of what the community thinks, rather than a comfortable one.

measuredOn.0: Active participation, and the proportion of questions answered by members rather than by staff.
measuredOn.1: Retention of contributors, and new ones arriving.
measuredOn.2: Event attendance and the activity that follows it.

stakeholders.0: Long-standing contributors, whose goodwill is the community's actual capital.
stakeholders.1: Marketing, which frequently wants to use the space for messages.
stakeholders.2: Legal and trust functions, where moderation meets conduct.

requirements.0: Even handling of people, sustained over years rather than campaigns.
requirements.1: Judgement about when to intervene and when to let a thread resolve itself.
requirements.2: Enough technical grounding to tell a substantive disagreement from a personal one.
requirements.3: The standing to tell the company that a plan would damage the trust it depends on.

0.what: Everything, including the parts posted at two in the morning.

1.what: Technical answers, and the recurring questions worth addressing structurally.

2.what: Programmes, budget and whatever it hopes the community will do.

0.what: A place where their question gets a real answer and their contribution is noticed.

1.what: A relationship with its users that survives individual staff and individual releases.

2.what: A path from lurking to contributing.

security-architect.title: Security architect
security-architect.whatItIs: The person who decides how a system will be defended before it exists. An architect works in drawings and decisions rather than in configuration: which trust boundaries the design has, what each one is enforced by, what happens when a component is compromised, and which controls are load-bearing rather than decorative. The output is a design somebody else builds, and a set of arguments for why it is shaped that way.
security-architect.turnsOn: The architect is accountable for decisions made before anyone can prove them wrong. That is the whole difficulty: the work is judged years later, by an incident, against a threat model written when the budget was set.
theDay: Reading a proposed design and finding the boundary that is assumed rather than enforced.
Choosing between controls that overlap, and saying which one the design depends on when both are present.
Writing the pattern down so that ten teams solve the problem the same way rather than ten ways.
Sitting in a review where the honest answer is that the risk is acceptable, and recording why.
Revisiting a decision made two years ago against a threat that did not exist then.
accountableFor: A design whose failure modes were considered before it was built.
Control choices that are justified against a stated threat rather than a product feature.
Patterns that the teams building them can actually implement.
measuredOn: Designs that survive their first real incident without a redesign.
Adoption of the patterns, which is the only proof they were usable.
Exceptions requested, which measures whether the architecture fits the organization it serves.
stakeholders: The teams who will operate the result long after the architect has moved to the next design.
Procurement, whose purchase is constrained by an architectural decision they did not attend.
Whoever inherits the exception register, which is the true record of where the architecture bent.
requirements: Enough depth in networks, identity and platforms to be wrong in front of specialists and recover.
The judgement to accept a risk deliberately rather than escalating everything.
Writing. An architecture that exists only in conversation is not an architecture.
Tolerance for being overruled commercially, and the discipline to record the decision anyway.

0.what: What is being built, and the deadline it is being built against.

1.what: The obligations the design has to satisfy, and their real deadlines.

2.what: What is actually deployable here, as distinct from what is theoretically correct.

0.what: A design specific enough to build without guessing.

1.what: Boundaries and requirements they can implement in their own systems.

2.what: A written rationale that answers why, not only what.

security-engineer.title: Security engineer
security-engineer.whatItIs: The person who builds and runs the controls. Where the architect decides that traffic between two zones must be authenticated and inspected, the engineer is the one who makes that true in a specific product, on a specific night, without breaking the applications that were already working. This is the role that turns a security decision into a running system, and then owns it.
security-engineer.turnsOn: A control that is deployed but untuned is worse than no control: it produces noise that trains everyone to ignore it, and it is counted as coverage by whoever reports upward.
theDay: Implementing a control in the platform that actually exists, rather than the one the design assumed.
Tuning it afterwards, because the first configuration is always either too permissive or in the way.
Automating the deployment so the twentieth instance matches the first.
Being the person the application team argues with when the control blocks something legitimate.
Patching, upgrading and certificate renewal - the unglamorous work that decides whether the control is still real.
accountableFor: Controls that are deployed, functioning and monitored rather than merely purchased.
Changes that do not take production down in the name of securing it.
Knowing which controls are currently degraded, before someone else finds out.
measuredOn: Coverage: how much of the estate the control actually reaches.
False positives, which is the number that decides whether the control survives its first month.
Time to deploy a change, since a control nobody can modify safely becomes a control nobody modifies.
stakeholders: Every team whose traffic passes through something this role configured.
The service desk, whose ticket volume moves with each tuning decision.
Finance, since licence consumption is a consequence of engineering choices.
requirements: Real depth in at least one platform, and enough in the neighbouring ones to integrate them.
Change discipline, because this role breaks production in a uniquely embarrassing way.
The patience to tune rather than to disable.
Scripting, since consistency at scale is not achieved by hand.

0.what: The design and the requirement it satisfies.

1.what: What is not being detected, and what is drowning them.

2.what: Products, and roadmaps that arrive later than promised.

0.what: Telemetry that is complete enough to detect with.

1.what: Controls that let them ship, rather than a queue.

2.what: The ability to contain, which depends on what was built beforehand.

network-security-engineer.title: Network security engineer
network-security-engineer.whatItIs: The role where the two disciplines on this site meet. A network security engineer owns the controls that live in the traffic path - firewalls, segmentation, remote access, inspection, and increasingly the provider edge - and is accountable to two constituencies whose definitions of success differ: the network must stay up and the boundary must hold. Most organizations discover they need this role when a security decision takes an application down.
network-security-engineer.turnsOn: This role is accountable to two teams that measure it oppositely. The network measures uptime and the security function measures containment, and every interesting decision trades one against the other.
theDay: Writing and pruning policy on the devices that stand between one part of the estate and another.
Proving whether a reported problem is the network, the control, or the application, which is three teams and one packet capture.
Segmenting something that was flat, one segment at a time, without an outage.
Maintaining remote access for people whose work stops when it fails.
Deciding what inspection is worth its cost, now that most traffic is encrypted.
accountableFor: Policy that expresses the intended boundary rather than an accumulation of exceptions.
Availability of the controls in the path, which is a network responsibility whatever the org chart says.
Knowing what would actually be blocked, as distinct from what the policy document claims.
measuredOn: Outages attributable to the security path, which is the number this role is judged by unfairly and permanently.
Rule-base hygiene: exceptions with owners and dates rather than accumulated permits.
Time to implement a change safely, since a slow path drives teams around the control.
stakeholders: Every application owner whose traffic crosses a boundary this role controls.
The network team, whose availability numbers absorb this role's mistakes.
The provider, once part of the boundary moved into their edge.
requirements: Genuine networking depth: routing, translation, encryption and the ability to read a capture.
The discipline to keep a rule base clean when nobody is asking for that.
Enough diplomacy to be the person who says no, repeatedly, to colleagues.
Comfort with the fact that success here is invisible and failure is a conference call.

0.what: The boundary to enforce and the reason for it.

1.what: The topology, and the change window.

2.what: Requests that describe a symptom rather than a flow.

0.what: A path that is both open enough to work and closed enough to matter.

1.what: The ability to isolate a segment on demand.

2.what: Evidence that the boundary is what the design says it is.

grc-analyst.title: Governance, risk and compliance analyst
grc-analyst.whatItIs: The role that writes down what the organization has decided to require of itself, and then finds out whether it is true. Governance is the deciding, risk is the accounting for what could go wrong, and compliance is the evidence that the decisions are being followed. The framework literature separates governance from management for a reason: this role serves the people who set direction, not the people who implement it.
grc-analyst.turnsOn: Compliance measures whether a control is documented and operating. Whether it works is a separate question with a separate answer, and a programme that treats the two as one produces certificates and incidents at the same time.
theDay: Turning an obligation written in legal language into a control somebody can actually operate.
Maintaining the risk register, which means chasing owners who did not ask to own anything.
Collecting evidence, and discovering that a control everyone believed in has no record of running.
Answering a customer security questionnaire, honestly, without losing the deal.
Preparing for an audit, which is mostly finding out what will not survive one.
accountableFor: Policy that is specific enough to follow and general enough to survive a product change.
A risk register that reflects the organization rather than a template.
Evidence that exists before it is asked for.
measuredOn: Audit findings, and whether last year's were genuinely closed.
Certification maintained without a crisis in the month before assessment.
Exceptions with owners and expiry dates rather than an unbounded list.
stakeholders: Customers, whose contracts increasingly specify controls this role has to evidence.
Insurers, who now ask the same questions with money attached.
Every team that inherits a requirement written here.
requirements: Enough technical literacy to know when an implementation claim is not true.
Writing that survives being read by a lawyer, an engineer and an auditor.
The stubbornness to keep asking for evidence after being told it exists.
Judgement about proportion, since a control programme that ignores cost is ignored in turn.

0.what: Obligations, with deadlines that do not negotiate.

1.what: What is actually implemented, which is the input compliance most often lacks.

2.what: Appetite for risk, usually stated only after an incident.

0.what: An account of exposure they can act on.

1.what: The answers that unblock an enterprise customer's review.

2.what: Requirements stated once, rather than rediscovered per project.

stats_page.title: What was read, not who read it
stats_page.metaDescription: The aggregate request counts ronutz.com keeps at its own server: pages served, humans versus crawlers by family, referring hosts, countries and languages. Counted without cookies, third-party analytics or visitor identifiers.
stats_page.whatIsCounted: Counted passively at the edge; nothing that could point to a reader is stored or correlated. A request counts as a person only when it came from a browser on a network that is not a cloud or hosting provider - a check that began on 7 September 2026, so people are counted from that day and earlier requests are shown as unverified. A request counts as a page read only when a page was served; requests for addresses that do not exist are listed on their own, at the end. What is counted and what is never written is set out in full on the
stats_page.unconfigured: Statistics are not configured on this deployment. The counting runs at the server; the reading endpoint needs its credentials before these panels can fill.
stats_page.error: The counts could not be read just now. Nothing is wrong with the page; the reporting endpoint did not answer.
stats_page.sampledNote: These figures are sampled and scaled, which is how the underlying store works; they are close rather than exact, and a number without its conditions is not a measurement.
stats_page.referrerNote: Counts requests from people that arrived with a referring site, aggregated to that site's host and grouped by kind. Full addresses are not published: they can carry other people's data. Counted from 7 September 2026, when the datacenter rule took effect; before that a scraper fleet forging a google.com referral dominated the record and is not shown.
stats_page.itemLabel: Read '{n}' times in the last 90 days.
stats_page.sourceNote: The same referrals, grouped by the family of the referring site: a search engine, an AI assistant that linked here, a social network, or something else. Every engine still sends its host, so the family is always known.
stats_page.timelineNote: Counts requests from people, one per page served, grouped by UTC day. People means every request not matched as automation and not arriving from a datacenter network. Counting began on 5 September 2026, and requests count as people from 7 September, when the datacenter check began, so the series starts on 7 September.
stats_page.pagesNote: Counts requests from people, one per page served, for every page read in the window - the same population as the day-by-day series, so the totals agree. Grouped by the language of the page: the panel opens at its first 13 rows, and Expand all lists the fifteen most-read per language.
stats_page.clientsNote: Every request for a page that exists, sorted into people and families of automation: search crawlers, AI crawlers, monitors, link previewers, tools, and clients that could not be verified. A browser arriving from a cloud or hosting provider's network counts as unverified, not as a person; so does every request from before that check existed, which is the 'before-classifier' line. Requests for addresses that do not exist are at the end of the page.
stats_page.countriesNote: Counts requests from people by the country of the connection, as Cloudflare reports it. Nothing finer than the country is recorded.
stats_page.localesNote: Counts requests from people by the language version of the page served.
stats_page.devicesNote: Shares of requests from people by the coarse class of device - phone or tablet, desktop or laptop, other - derived from the browser at the moment of the request and not stored. The class has been recorded since 6 September 2026; earlier requests have none and are not in this panel, so its total is smaller than the others.
stats_page.panelAiShare: AI crawlers, as a share of all automation
stats_page.aiShareNote: For each UTC day, the share of automated requests that came from AI crawlers - the fetchers behind assistants and model training - against every other kind of automation. Requests from people are excluded; requests from datacenter networks count as automation.
stats_page.sectionsNote: Shares of requests from people by section of the site - tools, articles, the industry catalogue, the glossary, and the rest - derived from the path of each page served.
stats_page.tailNote: From every page people read in the window: how many pages were read exactly once, twice or three times, and the twenty-five least-read pages that were read at all. For a catalogue this size, the tail is most of it.
stats_page.panelCoverage: How much of the site was read
stats_page.coverageNote: Distinct pages that people reached in the window, in total and by language, against the requests that reached them.
stats_page.hourNote: Requests from people by hour of the day, in UTC, summed across the window. The shape shows which parts of the world are awake when the site is read.
stats_page.weekdayNote: Requests from people by day of the week, in UTC, summed across the window.
stats_page.pagesTotal: '{requests}' requests across '{pages}' pages in the window
stats_page.listCut: This list stopped at its limit of '{limit}' pages, the most read in the window, so the figures in this panel cover those pages only.

missing.title: Requests for pages that do not exist
missing.note: Every request for an address that does not exist, from people and automation alike, grouped by what it was looking for. Most come from scanners that try the known flaws of WordPress and other software on every site they reach; each gets the not-found page (a 404) and nothing else, and none is counted in the panels above. Each group lists its most requested addresses as recorded (the first 13, and up to 40 with Expand all), with the language added to an address that has none (/wp-json/ arrives as /en/wp-json/), as text and never as links.
missing.count: {requests, plural, one {# request} other {# requests}} for {addresses, plural, one {# address} other {# addresses}}
missing.countCut: {requests, plural, one {# request} other {# requests}} for the {addresses, plural, one {# most requested address} other {# most requested addresses}}; the list stopped at its limit, so the counts cover those only
missing.legacy: Requests counted before each answer's status (200, 404) was recorded are recognized by their address instead, so a few may still sit in the panels above until they leave the window.
missing.error: This panel could not be loaded.

wp-batch.title: WordPress: the wp2shell chain
wp-batch.what: WordPress's REST API batch endpoint, which runs several API calls in one request, is the way into "wp2shell": CVE-2026-63030, a flaw in the batch endpoint, chained with CVE-2026-60137, an SQL injection, lets anyone run code on WordPress 6.9.0 to 6.9.4 and 7.0.0 to 7.0.1. Fixed in 6.9.5 and 7.0.2; disclosed on 17 July 2026, and both flaws have been in CISA's catalogue of exploited vulnerabilities since 21 July. The prefixes look for WordPress installed in a subfolder.

wp-plugin.title: WordPress plugin: Gravity SMTP
wp-plugin.what: CVE-2026-4020: the Gravity SMTP plugin, up to version 2.1.4, answers this address without checking who is asking, and the answer is a system report that can include the API keys and tokens set in the plugin. Fixed in 2.1.5.

wp-rest.title: WordPress: the REST API's index and its pages
wp-rest.what: A WordPress site answers /wp-json/ with its API's routes and /wp-json/wp/v2/pages with its published pages: asking confirms WordPress and lists its content.

wp-core.title: WordPress itself
wp-core.what: WordPress's own folders (wp-admin, wp-includes with the libraries it bundles, wp-content with uploads, plugins and themes), its usual install folders and its feed address. The install folders include site, news, cms and press: on this site's own counts each is asked for bare in step with the same folder followed by /wp-json/, which is how the scanners above look for WordPress installed in a subfolder. Asking confirms WordPress and looks for a folder that lists its files: an open uploads folder hands over everything ever uploaded. Versions 4.7 to 7.1.3 also stage a full core upgrade in predictable, web-accessible paths, which lets anyone run code on the server during the upgrade (CVE-2026-119977, fixed on 28 October 2026 in 7.1.4 and in a new release of every older branch back to 4.7, such as 7.0.8, 6.9.11 and 4.7.39; in CISA's catalogue of exploited vulnerabilities since 3 November).

secrets.title: Secrets and source code in a published folder
secrets.what: Files that belong in a developer's folder and reach the web only when a server publishes the wrong one: a .git folder (the site's source and history, with any password ever committed) and Subversion's .svn folder (its record of every file in a working copy); Mercurial's .hg folder (its requires file and the dirstate of the working directory confirm a repository, and its store holds the history); .git-credentials (passwords Git keeps unencrypted); .env and the backup copy an editor leaves of it, .env~ (an application's secrets); .aws/credentials and .aws/config (AWS access keys and settings); .ssh/id_rsa and its siblings id_ed25519 and id_ecdsa (SSH private keys), with .ssh/authorized_keys (the public keys allowed to sign in to that account); .vault-token (the token the HashiCorp Vault CLI keeps after a sign-in); a kubeconfig, .kube/config (the clusters, users and authentication kubectl uses to reach a Kubernetes cluster's API server); the Azure CLI's folder, .azure, where its configuration file lives; the Antigravity CLI's folder, .gemini/antigravity-cli, where it keeps its settings; /proc/self/environ behind runs of dots (on Linux, the environment the running program started with); shell and interpreter histories (every command typed, passwords on the command line included); a Python site-packages folder (where Python installs third-party libraries, such as lib/python3.12/site-packages; asked for here with SendGrid's mail library, sendgrid/helpers/mail, whose documentation keeps the API key in SENDGRID_API_KEY or a .env file), which would mean a whole Python environment was published with the site; and macOS's .DS_Store, which reveals what a folder holds. Some of these are asked for through /@fs/, the prefix Vite's development server uses to serve files from disk: CVE-2025-30208 and CVE-2025-31125 let anyone read files outside its allow list on a development server exposed to the network, both fixed by Vite 6.2.4, 6.1.3, 6.0.13, 5.4.16 and 4.5.11; the second has been in CISA's catalogue of exploited vulnerabilities since 22 January 2026. The same kind of bypass returned in Vite 6.4.4 (CVE-2026-118662, fixed in 6.4.5).

frameworks.title: Framework endpoints that reveal configuration
frameworks.what: Spring Boot Actuator's env, configprops and mappings (the application's environment, its settings and every request path it handles), under /actuator/ or, in Spring Boot 1, at the root or under a prefix such as /manage, and the Actuator's discovery page, /actuator itself, which links every endpoint it exposes; the Yii 2 debugger (request data, headers, sessions and environment variables, meant for localhost only); Symfony's profiler page /_profiler/phpinfo, which shows PHP's whole configuration and which Symfony's default setup routes only in the dev environment; Magento's version page, which names its version and edition; and the Kubernetes API server's /healthz, deprecated since Kubernetes 1.16 in favour of /livez and /readyz.

platforms.title: Other platforms' folders
platforms.what: Folder names that give away other software: Drupal, Joomla, OpenCart (its admin code folder), Magento, cPanel's sign-in, Next.js's build folder, _next/static, asked for under guessed subfolders (v1, client, frontend), and more. Naming the platform is the first step before trying its known flaws.

backdoors.title: Backdoors someone else may have left
backdoors.what: By their names, hidden ways back in that an intruder leaves behind: a web shell (a page that runs commands on the server) and a remote-code-execution component. The scanner checks whether another attacker got in first. No published advisory names these exact addresses; this reading is the site's own.

logins.title: Admin, sign-in and account pages
logins.what: Any admin or sign-in page to try passwords on, and the pages around one: registration, to open an account, and password reset, to test which addresses have one, plus the dashboard a sign-in usually leads to and the admin sections behind it (users, settings, reports, orders, products).

exposure.title: Folders that should not be public
exposure.what: Common folder names and forgotten copies of a site (staging, new), asked for in the hope that the server lists their files. /.well-known/ is the standard home of a site's metadata (RFC 8615); asking for the folder itself looks for a listing.

ipfs.title: IPFS: looking for an open gateway
ipfs.what: The address form of an IPFS gateway, /ipfs/ followed by a content identifier. Asked of an ordinary website, it finds servers that fetch and serve any IPFS content on request, which IPFS itself calls prone to abuse: the content then appears under the gateway's name.

ai.title: AI services
ai.what: Agents looking for an MCP server, through which an AI assistant uses a site's tools. The specification's example endpoint is /mcp. Its optional discovery extension, Server Cards, has clients look for a site's servers in an AI Catalog at /.well-known/ai-catalog.json and advises against keeping a server's card under /.well-known/mcp; the addresses scanners try, /.well-known/mcp and /.well-known/webmcp, are defined by neither MCP nor WebMCP (a Community Group draft for a JavaScript interface inside the page). Also requests for /v1/models and /models, the call that lists the models of a server speaking OpenAI's API.

crawlers.title: Careers, jobs and shop pages (not attacks)
crawlers.what: Careers and jobs pages, the usual targets of job-board crawlers, and shop and trade sign-up pages, which bots look for to register accounts or post spam. This reading of the names is the site's own.

misses.title: Honest misses
misses.what: Addresses that moved (the old /contribute/tools), pages that never existed, and links mistyped somewhere else on the web.

laravel.title: Laravel and its packages
laravel.what: Default addresses of Laravel applications. Livewire's update endpoint, /livewire/update, which every Livewire 3 component calls, is also tried under prefixes such as /login/ and /admin/login/: in Livewire 3 up to 3.6.3 it lets an unauthenticated attacker run commands on the server in specific setups, through the way component property updates are hydrated (CVE-2025-54068, fixed in 3.6.4; in CISA's catalogue of exploited vulnerabilities since 20 March 2026). Livewire 4 replaced that address with one carrying a hash of the application key, so asking for the old one looks for version 3. The dashboards of Telescope (the requests, exceptions, queries, jobs and mail an application handled), Horizon (queues), Pulse (performance) and Nova (administration) sit at /telescope, /horizon, /pulse and /nova; Telescope, Horizon and Pulse open by default only in the local environment. /two-factor-challenge, /email/verify and /password/reset are routes defined by Laravel's sign-in packages, Fortify and laravel/ui; /user/profile and /user/api-tokens are the profile and API token pages of Jetstream, Laravel's application starter kit.

stats_page.sourceLine: The code that counts is <analytics>worker/analytics.ts</analytics> and the code that serves these panels is <stats>worker/stats.ts</stats>, both in the public repository. Cloudflare's Workers Analytics Engine, where the counts are kept, stores them for three months (<retention>Cloudflare's documentation</retention>, read {date}).
stats_page.interestKindsNote: Counts sent by readers who said yes to the interest counts: tools worked with, rounds started and finished, articles and entries read to the end, shares, searches, links followed to Red Education and items saved to My desk. They show what is used, not how many people there are.
stats_page.interestToolsNote: How often each tool was worked with (the first typing or button press on a visit to its page), among readers who said yes.
stats_page.interestGamesNote: How often a round of each puzzle or game was started, among readers who said yes.
stats_page.interestLine: The last four panels are counted differently: they are the interest counts, sent by the browsers of readers who said yes when the site asked, and by nobody else. <privacy>What a count holds</privacy> is set out on the Privacy page, and the choice can be changed on the <settings>Settings page</settings>.
stats_page.interestSavesNote: How often each item was saved to My desk, among readers who said yes. Only the save itself is counted, once; removing an item, read marks, reading paths and the desk's layout are never counted.
stats_page.funBrowsersNote: How many browsers published at least one round to the /dev/fun scoreboard on each puzzle day, from the board's own public totals. Each browser counts once a day; this is not a count of people: a phone and a laptop count as two, and a private window or cleared site data counts again. Days before the count began show no data.
stats_page.funPerBrowser: Rounds per browser on the days counted: '{n}'

learning_page.title: Where the industry learns
learning_page.metaDescription: The training centres, certification bodies, learning platforms and schools in the industry catalogue, grouped by what kind of institution each one is.
learning_page.lede: Every company in the industry catalogue that exists to teach, certify or credential, pulled out of the timeline and grouped by what it is: a centre that sells a manufacturer's curriculum, a body that certifies a person, a platform that sells a library, a school that grants a degree. The distinction matters because the entries keep drawing it.
learning_page.centresNote: Companies that deliver a manufacturer's own curriculum through instructors the manufacturer has certified.
learning_page.bodiesNote: Organizations whose product is the credential itself, and the companies that administer the examinations.
learning_page.platformsNote: Libraries, marketplaces and lab environments where the instructor, the university or anyone at all supplies the course.
learning_page.schoolsNote: Institutions that grant degrees or run programmes rather than sell courses.
learning_page.restNote: Entries carrying the training tag that the sections above do not name.

geo.pendingNote: Footprint pending research: the headquarters country is shown by default.
geo.pendingShort: footprint pending research, headquarters shown by default
geo.sourcesTitle: Where the headquarters and footprints come from
geo.sourcesNote: Each card's flag is the founding country, as on the industry timeline; the HQ and the activity line come from the pages below, read on the dates given. A dotted footprint with a question mark is a default, the headquarters country standing in until the footprint is researched.

stories.title: Stories the data in this site tells
stories.lede: Most articles here answer a question. A few do something else: they put other articles in an order that argues something none of them says alone. A category list sorts by subject, and these are sorted by argument, so this is the only page where they appear together.
stories.count: {count} of them, grouped by what they argue.
stories.closer: Each one is an ordinary article and can be read on its own. What makes it a story is that it was written to be read after the pieces it points at, or instead of hunting for them.

failure.title: How things break, and what to decide first
failure.lede: The failure cases sorted by where the fault actually lived, the interval between someone knowing and everyone knowing, and the five practices those cases argue for. The first two collect the evidence; the third is what to do about it.

endToEnd.title: One thing, followed end to end
endToEnd.lede: A request, a service, an answer and a format, each traced through articles that were written to stand alone. Read in sequence they describe a path rather than a topic.

people.title: The industry and the country
people.lede: Where the subject is not the technology but the business around it, and the place it was learned in.

urlAnatomy.cannotSegment: This input could not be cut into parts cleanly, so it is shown unmarked rather than highlighted incorrectly.

advisoryMemo.metaDescription: A complete, fictional example of the written decision analysis an advisory engagement produces: the structure, the level of detail and the questions it leaves for the supplier.
advisoryMemo.noticeBody: The organization, the suppliers, the figures and the findings below are invented, assembled only to show the structure and the level of detail of the document an engagement produces. No client document is ever published, and nothing here is advice to any reader. The structure is the same in every engagement; the content is always the client's own.
advisoryMemo.ctaBody: If a decision like this one is on your desk, the first conversation is free and is with the person who would write the document.

earlierSites.title: What the web remembers
earlierSites.lede: Before ronutz.com there were two domains, nutzmann.net and ntz.com.br, and the Internet Archive kept them. {pages, plural, one {{pages} archived page} other {{pages} archived pages}}, read on {date}, were saved in full, printed and catalogued. Here, era by era: what each site was, when, what it offered and what it contained, with a link to every capture so the record can be checked.
earlierSites.metaTitle: The earlier sites: nutzmann.net and ntz.com.br, 2004 to 2021 · Rodolfo Nützmann
earlierSites.metaDescription: What the Internet Archive kept of Rodolfo Nützmann's earlier websites, nutzmann.net from 2004 and ntz.com.br from 2013: dates, characteristics, offerings, contents, and a link to every capture.
earlierSites.ageLine: The first capture is from 25 August 2004, {years, plural, one {{years} year} other {{years} years}} before this page was built. The home page of that day already linked three small tools, a bits-and-bytes calculator, an IP addressing calculator and a network cabling pinout: the oldest ancestors of the tools on this site.
earlierSites.provenanceBody: Every statement on this page was read from the Wayback Machine's captures of the two domains on {date}; nothing is quoted from memory. Each capture was saved as the archive's raw bytes with its images, stylesheets and scripts folded in, rendered offline and printed, and the inventory under each section links to the archive copy, so a reader can open any page as it was. Where the archive never stored an image, the print shows a gap and the catalogue says so. Client names that appear on the old pages are left to the archive; this page describes the work by shape.

nn-2004.title: nutzmann.net, the Nützmann Networks site
nn-2004.nature: The first site of Nützmann Networks Consultoria em Comunicação de Dados e Tecnologia da Informação LTDA., the consultancy constituted in São Paulo in 2003, presented under the brand nützmann.net and written, in Portuguese, in the plural voice of a firm. Its home page claimed thirteen years in the market, its partners page a presence in the field since 1996, and its areas-of-work page a start in 1991, three ways of counting the same path.
nn-2004.characteristics: A Flash intro at the root, which the archive did not keep, then a frameset of header, side menu and content in the manner of 2004: .htm pages, small sans-serif type, a two-column home with a news strip and a mailing-list box, a design credit and a hosting credit in the footer. About thirty pages. Services, success cases, the team page and the reference library carried a notice that the new site was still being finished. First captured on 25 August 2004; the same design was still being served in June 2007.
nn-2004.offerings: Consultancy in networks, telecommunications and information systems: bespoke projects, modular services, management of a vendor's post-sales relationship with strategic clients, service to the network vendors Cabletron, Enterasys and Riverstone and to their clients, network implementation (Internet, branches, LAN, MAN, WAN and wireless) and professional services on installed estates. A mission page argued for technology spend with a return-on-investment formula and a worked example. The areas-of-work page listed the sectors served, public bodies, banks, carriers, industry, media, universities, call centres, and a roster of some forty organizations served by its professionals.
nn-2004.contents: Home, company, mission, areas of work and clients, team, an explainer on communication in networks, solutions (LAN, WAN, wireless, Internet, VPN, voice and video), services, success cases, a reference library planned in eight sections, partners (ten companies, from the vendors it worked with to the host of the site), contact, privacy and terms. And the three tools linked from the home page, of which the archive kept the bits-and-bytes calculator: a full page with the 1998 IEC prefix note, a transfer-time example and a table of connection types.

nn-later.title: nutzmann.net, year by year
nn-later.nature: One capture per year of the home page, to show the domain's successive faces after the 2004 design. By December 2010 a single page titled N T Z had replaced it, under the same legal name, constituted in 2003 in São Paulo. From June 2013 the domain forwarded to ntz.com.br. In December 2013 it carried a WordPress site for a few months, and from March 2014 to at least June 2021 a plain page titled Engenharia de Redes.
nn-later.characteristics: The 2010 page: a logo, five service lines in capitals (consultancy, auditing, specialized services, project design and management, training), the areas of work in one line each, a wall of some thirty vendor and platform logos, a crisis-management block with a 24-hour on-call line, the languages of service (Portuguese, English, German, Spanish) and the places worked (Brazil, California, Germany, Argentina). The 2014 WordPress site had two posts, a mission statement in English and an announcement of the Engenharia de Redes lines. The page that followed was deliberately plain: numbered lines of scope, a list of the vendor technologies the clients could count on, and a note that services were available in four languages and, pre-scheduled, anywhere.
nn-later.offerings: The 2010 page is the clearest statement of the period: Consultoria independente. Não há vínculo a nenhum fornecedor de tecnologia. Independent consultancy, with no tie to any technology vendor, and a declared command of the technologies of the vendors shown. Incident response, troubleshooting of persistent problems, and escalation to vendors' support centres abroad were offered as named services.
nn-later.contents: The 2005, 2006 and 2007 captures, printed with their frames of the same date; the 2010 and 2011 N T Z page; the 2013 forward; the WordPress home and its two posts of 2013 and 2014; the Engenharia de Redes page as captured in 2014, 2015, 2016, 2017 and 2021.

ntz-2013.title: ntz.com.br, the NTZ Tecnologia site
ntz-2013.nature: The site of NTZ Tecnologia, the trading name of the same company: founded in 2003 by Rodolfo Nützmann, constituted in 2003 in the city of São Paulo, working in the technology market since 1995. Consultancy and specialized services in network communications and information security, in Portuguese, with a success-cases page that reads as a dated chronology from the founding year to 2008.
ntz-2013.characteristics: Static HTML with a shared header and footer, a left menu per section, the long keyword titles of the period, a certification strip and social links on the home page. First captured on 18 May 2013 and still served in May 2017; the rebuilt site appears in October 2017. The home page of each year from 2014 to 2017 is in the inventory.
ntz-2013.offerings: Consultancy (definition, management and delivery of projects, supplier selection, comparative analyses), specialized services (project management, preventive and emergency support, installation and configuration, quality of service, service-level definition, site surveys, network assessments, capacity for new applications, addressing and routing design, security and vulnerability audits, upgrades), a portfolio by theme (security, control, operational efficiency, connectivity), and training: three fundamentals courses, modular protocol classes of two to eight hours, and a forty-hour operations and troubleshooting course, taught by Rodolfo Nützmann, a student of network technologies since 1995 and an instructor since 1999. A remote laboratory of real switches, firewalls, routers, IP telephony, wireless equipment and virtual machines, reachable through console servers and VPN, served the courses and proofs of concept, with a free discussion forum beside it. The mission page: an independent services company, free of ties to manufacturers and suppliers. The partners page: not impartial, on the client's side.
ntz-2013.contents: Home, company (with the market segments served, sector by sector), mission and values, areas of work and clients, consultancy, services, portfolio, training, the laboratory with its equipment list, certifications, success cases (from the 2003 founding and the Brasília contract through a vendor's professional services, through the strategic-support years for another vendor's partners, to projects through integrators in 2007 and 2008), partners, an explainer on communications in networks, contact, privacy and terms, the reference library marked as discontinued, and the same three tools as 2004.

ntz-2018.title: ntz.com.br, rebuilt
ntz-2018.nature: A rebuilt site on a hosted site builder, titled NTZ Comunicações e Segurança em Rede, Desde 1995. Five pages, with a public hourly rate card, and the consultancy now openly presented as the services of Rodolfo Nützmann and a link to his professional profile. The only 2024 capture of the domain is an empty response; nothing later was published there.
ntz-2018.characteristics: Builder templates, a header with the brand and the year, a short menu, long single-column pages. Captured from October 2017 to December 2018. The builder's own fonts and scripts were not part of the archive copy, so the prints may differ slightly in type from the original.
ntz-2018.offerings: Consultancy and services (architecture and engineering of communication and security systems; definition, procurement and deployment management with requirement specification, RFP writing and supplier selection; formation of operations teams with a responsibilities matrix; one- to five-day technology workshops; conduct of tests and proofs of concept), training, a competences page by vendor with F5 as the main focus (pre-sales and training, six years through a distributor and a reseller, the certifications held and the ones in progress in 2018), Palo Alto Networks and others, and a Contrate page with a services list, a public hourly rate card in three time bands and remote-first delivery over video with recorded sessions.
ntz-2018.contents: Home, about, consultancy and services, competences, and Contrate. The training page was not captured.

ntz-prev.title: ntz.com.br before NTZ
ntz-prev.nature: Not one of these sites. Before the domain carried NTZ Tecnologia, ntz.com.br belonged to Plásticos NTZ, a plastic-bag maker in the interior of São Paulo state, captured from June 2003 to January 2008. It is in the inventory so that nobody mistakes it for an earlier version of the consultancy.
ntz-prev.characteristics: A small ASP site with a product catalogue; most of its images were never archived, so the prints are sparse.
ntz-prev.offerings: Plastic bags, refuse sacks, butcher rolls and packaging in general, by its own description.
ntz-prev.contents: Home, products, company history, purpose, management, distributors, location and contact.

carried.tools: The three tools. The 2004 home page linked three tools of its own, a bits-and-bytes calculator, an IP addressing calculator and a network cabling pinout; by 2013 only the first was still the site's own page, the other two names pointing to outside pages. Their descendants are here: the bits-and-bytes calculator was rebuilt in 2026 as Bits, bytes and throughput (by ancestry the oldest tool in the catalogue), the IP calculator became the CIDR calculator, and the pinout lives in the structured cabling article. The record of each, capture by capture, is below.
carried.independence: The independence line, unbroken. 2004: an independent company with no exclusivity ties to specific suppliers. 2010: independent consultancy, no tie to any technology vendor. 2013: free of ties to manufacturers and suppliers, and not impartial, on the client's side. The sentence has grown more careful since: the advisory page now states exactly what is claimed and what is not, including how the work is contracted.
carried.teaching: Teaching, never absent. Training and talks were a listed service in 2004; by 2013 there were named courses in a forty-hour format, taught by an instructor since 1999, with a laboratory of real equipment behind them; the 2017 site offered workshops and executive seminars. The authorized vendor training taught today is the same thread.
carried.vendors: The relationship between client and vendor as the object of the work. 2004: management of a vendor's post-sales relationship with strategic clients, pre-sales and post-sales. 2013: optimizing the relations between clients and their suppliers and partners. 2017: RFP writing, supplier selection, proofs of concept. The career record and the advisory shapes describe the same work from where it stands now.
carried.company: One company, four names. Constituted in São Paulo in 2003 as Nützmann Networks Consultoria em Comunicação de Dados e Tecnologia da Informação LTDA., it traded as nützmann.net, then as NTZ Tecnologia, then as NTZ Comunicações e Segurança em Rede, and in English, since 2015, as NTZ Technology. The short form is: founded 2003, trading as NTZ Technology since 2015. The 2004 terms page, the 2010 footer, the 2013 contact page and the 2013 chronology all give the same name and year.

The availability endpoint of the archive answered that it held nothing for either domain; the index proved otherwise, which is why the inventories were built from the index.

earlierSites.recordsLede: What the Internet Archive holds of each of the three tools the 2004 home page linked, read from its index on {date}: a rendering made here from each saved capture, the capture itself at the archive, and the page that carries the idea today.
earlierSites.recordHome2004: The 2004 home page, with the three links

industryMethod.title: How the research is done
industryMethod.metaDescription: What counts as a source in the industry record, how founding and acquisition dates are chosen, what happens when sources disagree, how current status is verified, how corrections arrive, and the build guards that enforce each rule.
industryMethod.lede: The record states facts about several hundred real companies and people: when they began, who bought whom and for how much, whether they still exist. These are the rules every statement follows, with the record's own examples, and the checks that fail the build when a rule is broken.

sources.title: What counts as a source
sources.p1: Primary first. A company's own filings and the press releases filed with them (a Form 8-K exhibit is the company stating the date and the price under its own name), the company registry for a Brazilian company (the CNPJ record, with its constitution date), the vendor's own documentation for a product fact. Then the press of record, dated. Wikipedia is used as a map to primary sources and is cited as what it is, an encyclopaedia, with its infobox read on a given day.
sources.p2: Every entry lists its sources at its foot, with the date each was read, and every founding year on a card is named by one of them. A chat transcript is never a source: the build refuses a citation that points at one, because a conversation with a language model is not evidence of anything about a company.
sources.p3: Where an entry states something about Rodolfo Nützmann's own work with a company, the source is the portfolio: the dated CVs and the LinkedIn record, read in the order they were written, the earliest closest to the fact.

founded.title: Founded, incorporated, and where a story begins
founded.p1: A card's founding year is the year its own named subject was founded, not its earliest ancestor's. Unisys was founded in 1986, even though its lineage reaches Burroughs in 1886; Riverstone in 2000, not Yago Systems in 1996. Three cards were wrong under the older rule and were corrected on 2 October 2026.
founded.p2: Where a card's story begins before its subject, the record says so in a separate field, and the timeline places the card where the story starts: CommScope was founded in 1976, and its card sits at 1961, where Superior Continental's Comm/Scope division begins, with the predecessor named beside the year. On a card that is explicitly a lineage of several companies, the year is the earliest company's and the card says whose it is.
founded.p3: Incorporation is not founding. A company registered in January 2004 may have been trading since 1992 under another legal person; the record keeps both facts and does not pick one.

acquisitions.title: Acquisition dates and prices
acquisitions.p1: An acquisition has at least two dates, announced and completed, and the record prefers the completion date from the filing that reports it, with the price as that filing states it: Plantronics completed Polycom on 2 July 2018 for an enterprise value of 2.0 billion dollars, HP completed Poly on 29 August 2022 at 40 dollars a share, CommScope completed Avaya's Connectivity Solutions effective 31 January 2004 for 250 million dollars in cash and about 1.8 million shares.
acquisitions.p2: Where the sources give two prices, both are recorded and the disagreement is stated: Wikipedia's own citations give Arris at 7.4 and at 4.93 billion dollars. The record does not average, round or choose.

uncertain.title: Uncertain dates
uncertain.p1: When sources disagree about a date, the disagreement is the fact. TDec registers in March 1992 and brands itself established 1993; InLearn was constituted in 2002 and presents itself as teaching since 2008; Tenable's incorporation is given as 16 September 2002 by most sources and 4 October by one. Each entry says so, in those words, rather than picking the tidier year.
uncertain.p2: A date the record cannot source is left out rather than estimated. A founding year with no citation on its own entry fails the build, which is why a few entries carry a declared reason in place of a year.

status.title: Whether a company still exists
status.p1: An entry carries an ending when a sourced event ended the company's independent existence: absorbed, renamed away, or wound up, with the year and a note. Where the sources establish that a company ended but give no single date, as with Nortel, which entered creditor protection in 2009 and then wound down for years, the card says ended, date not recorded, rather than inventing a year. A card says present only when the record has the company's own live website on file. Where that company is owned by another but still trades under its own name, the card says so beside present and names the owner, with the year the acquisition was completed when a source gives it. An owner that is an investment fund is named as the owner too, worded owned by rather than part of, and a state shareholder is named the same way; where the owner holds a majority rather than the whole company, the page states the percentage. A card that tells several companies, or a protocol, as one story has no single status, and says that instead. Every other card without a recorded ending says status not verified: nothing on file says the company ended, and nothing on file shows that it is still trading.
status.p2: These markers are set by review, never by pattern-matching the prose. A first attempt to derive them automatically from the timelines produced roughly thirty wrong answers out of forty-eight, because a sentence cannot be read for direction by a regular expression: a company acquiring and a company acquired look the same to one. The site's source-liveness run re-checks every cited link on a schedule and records what has moved.

corrections.title: Corrections
corrections.p1: A wrong date, a dead source, a company that has since been sold: the contact page has a route for it, and a correction that lands is recorded in the changelog with its source, so the record's history of being wrong is itself on the record.
corrections.p2: The record also corrects itself against its author. Where the portfolio says one date and a badge says another, the portfolio wins and the badge is called what it is, a badge date; the chapters say so where it happened.

guards.title: The checks that enforce the rules
guards.lede: Each rule above is a script that runs before every build and fails it when the rule is broken. Named here so a reader can tell an enforced rule from a stated intention.
guards.check-sources: Every industry entry cites at least one source; the number of uncited entries may only go down, and it is zero.
guards.check-source-hosts: No citation may point at a chat transcript.
guards.check-vendor-founded-sources: Every founding year on a card is named by a citation on that entry, a story that begins before the subject is dated earlier than its founding, and a lineage card says whose year it shows.
guards.check-placeholder-sources: A source label may not be an appeal to ubiquity, a bare 'documented', a field name with a number, or the entry's own name with a year.
guards.check-person-year-sources: Every year on a person's entry is named by a source.
guards.check-partner-duplicates: No two entries share a slug, and every overlap of names is declared with a reason.
guards.check-citation-fields: Every field that can carry a URL is known to the liveness audit, so no link escapes the re-check.

industryMethod.closer: None of this makes the record complete, and it is not meant to: it makes every statement in it traceable to a page somebody can open, on a date somebody wrote down. The chronology, the chapters and the people are built on those terms.
