tcpip-concepts-and-ip-routing.title: TCP/IP: Concepts and IP Routing
tcpip-concepts-and-ip-routing.subtitle: An introductory course in two modules, first taught in 1999 and updated for this 2026 edition, in English and Brazilian Portuguese
tcpip-concepts-and-ip-routing.lede: A complete introductory training on how internetworks work and how IP finds its way across them: from bridges, routers and the routing algorithms, through the TCP/IP stack, addressing, ARP and a packet followed hop by hop, to RIP, EIGRP, OSPF, IS-IS and BGP-4, access lists, IPv6, multicast, MPLS and VRRP. Every one of the {slides} slides carries speaker notes, so the course can be taught from the deck, or learned from it, without anyone else in the room.
tcpip-concepts-and-ip-routing.lineage: Based on a course Rodolfo Nützmann first taught in March 1999, and rebuilt in 2026: 16:9 slides with the diagrams redrawn as native, editable shapes, the content updated to current practice (CIDR in place of address classes, EIGRP in place of IGRP, BGP-4, IPv6 as RFC 8200 defines it, PIM, VRRPv3), and the historical topics kept for their teaching value and marked LEGACY.
tcpip-concepts-and-ip-routing.level: Introductory, from first principles to the routing protocols
tcpip-concepts-and-ip-routing.notesValue: On all {count} slides, in both languages
tcpip-concepts-and-ip-routing.audienceLearners: Learners. Go through the slides in the presenter on this page, or open the PPTX in presenter view and read the notes as the commentary the instructor would give. The objectives at the start of each module and the summaries at the end tell you what you should be able to explain.
tcpip-concepts-and-ip-routing.audienceInstructors: Instructors. The notes are written to be taught from: what to say on each slide, what to ask the class, where the common confusions are, and what changed since 1999. The deck is fully editable, the diagrams included, and the closing slides list the RFCs and sources by topic, so you can prepare yourself before you prepare a class.
tcpip-concepts-and-ip-routing.frame: Slides 1 to 3 open the course (the title, the agenda and the 1999 to 2026 comparison below); slides 176 and 177 list the RFCs and sources by topic; slide 178 closes it.

p1.title: General routing concepts
topics: Heterogeneity and the components of an internetwork
Interconnection devices and the OSI model
Bridges and Layer 2 switches, the broadcast domain and Spanning Tree
Routers: data flow, advantages and limitations
Routable and nonroutable protocols
Network-layer against data-link addressing, and encapsulation
Static and dynamic routing
Distance vector: metrics, count to infinity, split horizon, poison reverse, hold-down and triggered updates, with a worked example
Link state: principles, advantages and the protocols in use
Autonomous systems

p2.title: TCP/IP
topics: Origin and governance of TCP/IP
The stack against the OSI model: application, transport and internet layers
The IPv4 datagram in detail, protocol and port numbers, demultiplexing
Decimal-to-binary conversion and the IPv4 address
Classful addressing (legacy), CIDR and special-purpose addresses
Subnets, the subnet mask and comparison under mask
VLSM, with an addressing plan for a /24

p3.title: Internet Protocol behaviour
topics: Route determination: local or remote, with the AND
Next-hop gateway lookup
ARP (RFC 826) step by step, for a local and a remote host, with the request and reply packets
Proxy ARP, with a worked example
ARP in 2026: gratuitous ARP, the cache, security and IPv6

p4.title: IP in a routed internetwork: a complete example
topics: The topology and the six-step data transfer, hop by hop
Host names: from the hosts file to DNS
Proxy ARP: vendor defaults

p5.title: IP routing protocols
topics: RIP: origin, variants and the RIPv2 message
Administrative distance
From IGRP to EIGRP: the composite metric, DUAL and multipath
Route redistribution and its risks
OSPF: areas, router types, network types, Hello, adjacencies, DR and BDR, LSAs and the LSDB, inter-area and external routes
OSPFv3 and IS-IS
Interior against exterior protocols, EGP, and BGP-4 attributes and best-path selection

p6.title: Controlling IP access
topics: ACLs in the router's processing flow
Standard ACL examples: permit the internal network, deny a host, deny a subnet
ACLs in 2026: extended, named, IPv6 and stateful firewalls

p7.title: Additional IP routing topics
topics: IP broadcast handling and the DHCP problem
DHCP relay and directed broadcast
Secondary addresses
Unnumbered interfaces

p8.title: IPv6: from 'IPng' to the dominant protocol
topics: From 'IPng' (1995) to RFC 8200 (2017)
The differences from IPv4, the header and the extension headers
Addressing: 128 bits, three types, no broadcast; types and scopes
Neighbor Discovery and SLAAC
Routing, flows and traffic class, security
IPv4 and IPv6 transition and coexistence

p9.title: IP multicast
topics: Multicast addresses and their mapping to MAC addresses
IGMP and MLD
Dense against sparse mode and the RPF check
Multicast routing protocols, and PIM-SM: the RP, the shared tree and the SPT
RSVP, and what is left of it

p10.title: MPLS and VRRP
topics: Label switching and its terminology
FIB, LIB and LFIB, with an example
MPLS applications in 2026
VRRP: default gateway redundancy, with a failover example
The Module 2 summary

m1.title: Internetworking vocabulary
m1.body: Recognize the basic internetworking terms and concepts: LAN and WAN links, interconnection devices, broadcast and collision domains.

m1.title: Bridges and switches versus routers
m1.body: Compare the operation of bridges/Layer 2 switches and routers, and understand Layer 2 and Layer 3 switching.

m1.title: Routable protocols
m1.body: Describe the properties of a routable protocol and put nonroutable protocols in historical context.

m1.title: Distance vector
m1.body: Explain the principle of operation, the inherent instability (slow convergence) and the techniques that correct it.

m1.title: Link state
m1.body: Explain SPF (Dijkstra) algorithms, their advantages over distance vector and the protocols that implement them.

m1.title: Autonomous systems
m1.body: Define autonomous system and distinguish interior from exterior routing protocols.

m2.title: Characteristics of TCP/IP
m2.body: Protocol stack, IPv4 datagram, protocol and port numbers, addressing, subnetting and VLSM, host-to-host communication, ARP and Proxy ARP.

m2.title: The IP routing process
m2.body: Describe in detail, step by step, what happens to a packet between the source station and the destination station in a routed internetwork.

m2.title: RIP and EIGRP
m2.body: Recall the fundamentals of RIP (v1, v2, RIPng) and of EIGRP (composite metric, DUAL, multipath) and the role of administrative distance.

m2.title: Redistribution and OSPF
m2.body: Discuss route redistribution between routing processes and recall the principles of OSPF (areas, router types, Hello, DR, LSAs).

m2.title: BGP-4
m2.body: Distinguish interior from exterior protocols and describe the fundamentals of BGP-4 (path vector, eBGP/iBGP, attributes).

m2.title: Access control
m2.body: Recall how access control lists (ACLs) on routers filter IP traffic, and how they evolved into stateful firewalls.

m2.title: Operational topics
m2.body: Broadcast handling (DHCP relay), secondary addresses, unnumbered interfaces, static and default routes.

m2.title: IPv6 and complementary technologies
m2.body: Understand IPv6 (header, addressing, ND/SLAAC, routing, transition), IP multicast (IGMP/MLD, PIM), RSVP, MPLS and VRRP.

thenNow: Ethernet 1G to 400G, Wi-Fi 6/7; Token Ring and FDDI extinct
IP only (IPv4 and IPv6); the rest is legacy
CIDR/VLSM (RFC 4632); IPv4 exhaustion (IANA 2011, LACNIC 2020); NAT and CGNAT
RFC 8200 (2017); > 50% of Google access (Mar 2026); Brazil ≈ 59% (APNIC, Oct 2026)
OSPFv2/v3, IS-IS, EIGRP (RFC 7868); RIP only in small networks
EGP on the way out, BGP-4 arriving
VRRPv3 (RFC 9568) for IPv4 and IPv6; HSRP

lan-switch-operations-and-maintenance.title: LAN Switch Operations and Maintenance
lan-switch-operations-and-maintenance.subtitle: A hands-on course in four modules, first taught in 2007 on Enterasys switches and rebuilt for this 2026 edition with the current CLI of eight vendors, in English and Brazilian Portuguese
lan-switch-operations-and-maintenance.lede: A complete operations course for enterprise LAN switches: access, users and the CLI session; saving, clearing, backing up and upgrading; ports, link aggregation, VLANs and Spanning Tree; IP addressing, ARP and routing; then OSPF, VRRP, ACLs, syslog, SNMPv3, RADIUS and TACACS+, multicast, and a method for troubleshooting and for opening a support case. Every topic is taught on the 2007 Enterasys platform and then, command by command, on eight current CLIs side by side. All {slides} slides carry speaker notes, and every command row cites the vendor document it comes from.
lan-switch-operations-and-maintenance.lineage: Based on the operations and maintenance course Rodolfo Nützmann taught in 2007 for the Enterasys SecureStack and Matrix lines, and rebuilt in 2026: 16:9 slides, the 2007 material kept where it still teaches and marked LEGACY 2007, and beside it MODERN CLI slides for Extreme Switch Engine and Fabric Engine, Cisco IOS XE (17.18.x and 26.1.x), HPE Aruba Networking AOS-CX, Juniper Junos, MikroTik RouterOS, Arista EOS and Huawei VRP, each row checked against the vendor's current documentation.

lan-switch-operations-and-maintenance.notesValue: On all {count} slides, in both languages
lan-switch-operations-and-maintenance.audienceLearners: Learners. Each topic starts with how a 2007 switch did it and ends with the same task on the switches in use today: read the MODERN CLI slide for your vendor, try the commands in a lab, and measure yourself with the assessments at the start and at the end of the course.
lan-switch-operations-and-maintenance.audienceInstructors: Instructors. Extreme Networks completed the Enterasys acquisition in 2013 and the Avaya networking purchase in 2017; HPE completed the Juniper acquisition in 2025
Telnet or SSH; NetSight over SNMP v1, v2c or v3
SSH; Cisco IOS XE 26.1 blocks Telnet, HTTP, TFTP and SNMP v1 and v2c unless system mode insecure is set; cloud dashboards as a second operating model
A simple password of up to eight characters, or MD5
Clear-text communities in v1 and v2c; v3 with HMAC-MD5 or HMAC-SHA and 56-bit DES

m1.title: Access and manage the switches
m1.body: Access, configure and manage the devices from the console and over the network, with users, privileges and a CLI session set up for daily work.

m1.title: Keep the configuration safe
m1.body: Manage configuration files and backups, reset the configuration to factory defaults and recover access to a device whose password is unknown.

m1.title: Upgrade the firmware
m1.body: Upgrade the switch firmware and choose the image it boots.

m1.title: Read any vendor's CLI
m1.body: Recognize the 2007 Enterasys platforms and their current equivalents on eight vendors, and carry what you learn to other CLI families.

m2.title: Ports
m2.body: Configure and verify port parameters: naming and state, speed and duplex, flow control, broadcast suppression, protected ports and mirroring.

m2.title: Link aggregation
m2.body: Build a link aggregation group with LACP and explain how traffic is spread across its members.

m2.title: VLANs
m2.body: Configure 802.1Q VLANs with their egress, PVID, tagged and untagged ports.

m2.title: Spanning Tree
m2.body: Explain root election and port roles in 802.1D and RSTP, and protect the edge against BPDU attacks.

m3.title: Addressing and ARP
m3.body: Work out a host's network with the mask and the bitwise AND, and follow ARP and Proxy-ARP packet by packet.

m3.title: Routing on a switch
m3.body: Configure IP interfaces, loopbacks and static routes, enable RIP and OSPF, and read route precedence and ECMP in the routing table.

m4.title: OSPF
m4.body: Configure and verify OSPFv2 on a Layer 3 switch: cost, authentication and redistribution.

m4.title: VRRP
m4.body: Build gateway redundancy with VRRP: election, priority and preemption.

m4.title: ACLs
m4.body: Protect a VLAN with ACLs and interpret the hit counters.

m4.title: Syslog and SNMPv3
m4.body: Send logs to a syslog server and monitor the switch with SNMPv3.

m4.title: RADIUS and TACACS+
m4.body: Centralize administrative access with RADIUS and TACACS+.

m4.title: Multicast
m4.body: Explain IGMP snooping and PIM-SM and check the multicast groups.

m4.title: Troubleshooting and support
m4.body: Troubleshoot methodically, use a protocol analyser and gather the evidence a vendor's support team needs.

s13.title: From 2007 to 2026: what changed
s13.alt: A timeline from 2007 to 2026: the original course for the Enterasys line (2007), Extreme's Enterasys acquisition (2013) and its Avaya networking purchase (2017), the end of sale of Extreme Management Center, formerly NetSight (2021), VOSS renamed Fabric Engine (2022), the end of service of the S and K chassis (2024), HPE's Juniper acquisition (2025) and this edition (2026).

s40.title: Access, users and CLI session
s40.alt: A MODERN CLI slide for Extreme Switch Engine 33.7.1: ten tasks, from creating a local admin user to disabling paging, each beside its command, and a note that there is no configuration mode, that SSH2 is disabled and Telnet enabled by default, and that the idle timeout defaults to 20 minutes.

s257.title: IEEE 802.1d Spanning Tree
s257.alt: Six bridges in two rows joined by redundant links of equal cost, each labelled with its bridge ID; bridge 1, ID 80-00:1, is marked as the root.

s310.title: Anatomy of an ARP packet
s310.alt: An ARP packet carried in an Ethernet II frame: destination MAC, source MAC, EtherType 0x0806, the ARP data and the FCS, with the ARP fields above it: hardware type, protocol type, the two address lengths, the opcode, and the sender's and the target's hardware and protocol addresses.

s440.title: VRRP: virtual IP, election and preemption
s440.alt: Two switches share the virtual router 10.1.10.1 on VLAN 10: SW-CORE-01 (10.1.10.2, priority 110) is the active router and SW-CORE-02 (10.1.10.3, priority 100) the backup; the hosts below use 10.1.10.1 as their gateway.

s526.title: IGMP snooping: deliver only to those who asked
s526.alt: A switch running IGMP snooping under the querier at 10.1.10.2: the stream for group 239.1.1.1 goes only to ports 1 and 3, whose hosts joined it, and not to port 2.

traffic-diversion.title: Traffic diversion and the man in the middle
traffic-diversion.lede: Every way traffic is steered through somewhere it was not meant to go, from ARP poisoning on a LAN to a BGP hijack across the internet, each with the defence that answers it.

planned.arpPoisoning: ARP poisoning on a switched LAN
planned.macFloodingStp: MAC flooding and STP root takeover
planned.vlanHopping: VLAN hopping: switch spoofing and double tagging
planned.rogueDhcpRa: Rogue DHCP and rogue IPv6 Router Advertisements
planned.icmpLlmnr: ICMP redirects and LLMNR, NBT-NS and mDNS spoofing
planned.evilTwin: The evil twin and the wireless path

formats-in-between.title: The formats in between
formats-in-between.lede: JSON, YAML, XML, text encodings, Base64, URLs, timestamps, identifiers and diffs, read as one skill: putting meaning into characters so that the other end takes out the same meaning.

json.title: JSON, exactly
json.lede: The format as a strict parser reads it: six types and a few rules, then every place where two parsers can honestly disagree about the same document.

yaml.title: YAML and configuration files
yaml.lede: Why pipelines and orchestration are written in YAML, and the three things YAML does that JSON never does: guess types, fold lines and reuse values.

xml.title: XML and its hazards
xml.lede: Reading a document part by part, the rules a parser enforces first, namespaces and the constructs that are not elements, then the entity features that turn a parser into an attack surface.

text.title: Characters, bytes and Unicode
text.lede: Why a character is not a byte: ASCII's table, Unicode's code points, the bytes UTF-8 and UTF-16 lay down, and what goes wrong when two ends read them differently.

two-alphabets.title: The two alphabets
two-alphabets.lede: The Greek letters and Roman numerals every engineer reads without being taught: where each symbol came from, and then the two systems themselves.

base-encodings.title: Base16, Base32, Base64
base-encodings.lede: Writing arbitrary bytes as text: the alphabets, what each costs in size and readability, and where each one turns up.

urls.title: URLs, read exactly
urls.lede: The five parts every URL is built from, how characters are escaped inside them, how a relative link resolves, and the disguises a hostile link wears.

time.title: Time as computers count it
time.lede: One integer since 1970, the units it is written in, the leap seconds it ignores, the year it overflows, the text formats it becomes, and the arithmetic that calendars make hard.

identifiers.title: Identifiers: UUIDs and their kin
identifiers.lede: How a 128-bit identifier stays unique with nobody issuing it, the eight versions, the odds of a collision, what random keys do to a database, and the sortable alternatives.

diff.title: Diffs, merges and Git
diff.lede: What a diff actually computes, how to read one, why it sometimes blames the wrong lines, the third input that makes merging possible, and the tools built on all of it.

regex.title: Regular expressions
regex.lede: What to match and how many, where a match may sit, what parentheses capture and assert, the flags that change everything, and the patterns that never finish.

hashing.title: Hashes and HMAC
hashing.lede: What a cryptographic hash guarantees and why it cannot be reversed, the properties that measure it, which functions are still safe, and how a key turns a hash into proof of who sent a message.

passwords.title: Storing passwords
passwords.lede: Why a fast hash is the wrong tool for passwords: the two ways an attacker reverses a hash, the salt and the arithmetic that answer each, the slow functions built for the job, and the choice to make.

certificates.title: Certificates: the object and its trust
certificates.lede: What a certificate holds and the files it travels in, how it is requested and issued, how a client validates it and builds its chain (and how to read that check in openssl s_client), how it is revoked, and the trust model that has failed in public.

certificate-lifecycle.title: Certificate lifetimes and renewal
certificate-lifecycle.lede: The schedule that takes public TLS certificates from 398 days to 47, the two timestamps that define validity, renewal lead time and ARI, the shrinking reuse of validation, and the automation that makes it bearable.

tls.title: TLS and the cipher suites
tls.lede: One handshake family in four shapes, the key exchange that gives forward secrecy, how to read a cipher suite and which to run, the attacks that pruned the protocol, where a proxy terminates it, and how to read what openssl s_client reports a server did.

post-quantum.title: Post-quantum cryptography
post-quantum.lede: What a quantum computer would break and what it would not, the three standards NIST finalized in 2024, and the hybrid key exchange the web already runs.

fingerprinting.title: Fingerprinting what a client emits
fingerprinting.lede: What a connection announces before any data flows (the TCP SYN, the User-Agent, the order of the headers, the TLS ClientHello) and how JA3 and JA4 turn the handshake into an identity.

web-security-headers.title: The browser's security headers
web-security-headers.lede: The response headers that tell a browser how to protect a page: HTTPS enforcement, cookie flags, the CORS door in the same-origin wall, Content Security Policy, and frame control.

ssrf.title: Server-side request forgery
ssrf.lede: Making a server fetch a destination of the attacker's choosing: the schemes beyond HTTP, the cloud metadata service that is the prize, and the allow-list defence that survives obfuscation.

curl.title: curl, flag by flag
curl.lede: Reading a curl command the way the shell and curl read it: the method it implies, the body and its Content-Type, headers, authentication and cookies, the flags that weaken security, the translation to fetch(), and the 27 protocols beyond HTTP.

nginx.title: NGINX, from configuration to troubleshooting
nginx.lede: The configuration tree and who owns the worker, how a location is chosen, what proxy_pass sends, what the cache stores and serves, how limits really count, how a reload works, and the server NGINX was written against.

dns.title: DNS, read from the answer
dns.lede: One DNS answer read from the top with dig and nslookup: who replied and with what authority, the header and its flags, the records, the errors, and the options, traces and signatures that ask precisely.

dns-infrastructure.title: DNS as infrastructure
dns-infrastructure.lede: How a file maintained during business hours became the internet's naming system, and the ways that system is poisoned, depended on, chosen and used as a control.

ipv4.title: IPv4 addressing and subnetting
ipv4.lede: The 32 bits behind a dotted quad, the prefix that defines a block, subnetting from the basics to a worked VLSM plan, summarization and aggregation, the special ranges, and the NAT that stretched the space.

ipv6.title: IPv6
ipv6.lede: The 128-bit address and how to write it, why a subnet is almost always a /64, how hosts configure themselves, the multicast that replaced ARP, and how IPv6 and IPv4 run side by side.

routing.title: Routing
routing.lede: How a packet picks its next hop, the interior protocols that draw the map, the exterior one that runs the internet and trusts every announcement, labels in the core, fast failure detection, the redundant gateway, and multicast.

tunnels.title: Tunnels and VPNs
tunnels.lede: What a tunnel protects and what it does not, the plain envelope, the negotiated encrypted one, the small one, the byte arithmetic every tunnel owes, and the remote-access VPN being retired.

load-balancing.title: Load balancing and persistence
load-balancing.lede: The four questions every load balancer answers, the virtual server and the layer 4 proxy that carry them, persistence and its failure modes, global load balancing in two tiers, and how the market began.

syslog.title: Syslog
syslog.lede: A syslog message read field by field: the PRI that packs facility and severity, the 24 facilities and 8 severities, the two message formats, the three transports, the defaults network devices choose, and how other systems count log levels.

saml.title: SAML
saml.lede: Browser single sign-on with SAML 2.0: the identity and service providers, the bindings and who starts the flow, what an assertion holds and what is checked, how it is signed, and the proxy that inserts identity into a session.

oauth-oidc.title: OAuth and OpenID Connect
oauth-oidc.lede: Authorization and authentication told apart: the OAuth code flow, client types and PKCE, the three tokens, the grant to choose, then the identity layer OpenID Connect adds, its ID token, its claims and its discovery document.

jwt.title: JWT and JWKS
jwt.lede: The three segments of a token and why decoding is not verifying, the signing algorithms, the keys that sign them and how providers publish and rotate them, the verification sequence, and the mistakes that turn a verifier into a forgery machine.

one-time-codes.title: One-time codes and passkeys
one-time-codes.lede: How a shared secret becomes a short code, how an authenticator is provisioned, what a server must tolerate and refuse when it checks one, and why passkeys resist the phishing that defeats codes.

unix.title: The operator's Unix
unix.lede: The Unix underneath every appliance's management interface: terminal, shell and TTY, file modes, cron, Expect, and the story of Linux, its families, what grew out of it, and the two meanings of free.

zero-trust.title: Zero trust, SSE and the proxy
zero-trust.lede: What zero trust, ZTNA and SASE mean without the marketing, what single-pass means mechanically, how five vendors answer the same question, and the engines inside: the PAC file, user identity on the proxy, browser isolation, sandboxing and DLP.

cvss.title: CVSS
cvss.lede: How a short vector string becomes a severity from 0 to 10: reading the vector, the eight base metrics, the temporal and environmental adjustments, the bands and what the score does not say, and what changed in v4.0.

f5xc.title: F5 Distributed Cloud, one request end to end
f5xc.lede: F5 Distributed Cloud in the order a request meets it: the site joining the fabric, the listener and the route, the origin and its persistence, TLS, the service policy that allows it, the rate limit, the API inventory, the security event, and the configuration hazards.

bigip-self-description.title: What a BIG-IP says about itself
bigip-self-description.lede: The five languages a BIG-IP describes itself in: its configuration grammar, two API address schemes, its licence file, the dates that decide whether it may upgrade, and F5's release calendar.

bigip-versions.title: BIG-IP and F5OS versions and upgrades
bigip-versions.lede: From the first BIG-IP controller to today: why the version numbers jump, upgrade against update, the licence reactivation that rescues a failed upgrade, the newest line's operations and access changes, and the F5OS platform underneath.

bigip-foundations.title: BIG-IP foundations, from interface to pool member
bigip-foundations.lede: The BIG-IP a student meets first: the layer 2 and 3 chain, route domains, the two ways in, the system services, then a connection through the virtual server, its profiles, the pool and its method, health, persistence, the return path, reuse, the protocol profiles, and the cores and guests underneath.

bigip-ha.title: BIG-IP high availability
bigip-ha.lede: Device trust, device groups and traffic groups, then config sync, the failover states and how to force them, and the persistence records a standby must receive before it takes over.

bigip-troubleshooting.title: BIG-IP troubleshooting and operations
bigip-troubleshooting.lede: How a BIG-IP tells you its condition: the status surfaces and statistics, the log files, tcpdump on a box whose interfaces are not NICs, the F5 trailer and what Wireshark makes of it, the support snapshot, hardware diagnostics, backups, alerting and on-box analytics.

bigip-ssl.title: BIG-IP SSL profiles and ciphers
bigip-ssl.lede: Which side of the session each SSL profile owns, the certificate, key and chain it binds, the protocol versions it offers, the cipher string, rules, groups and order, forward secrecy, renegotiation and stapling, mutual TLS, post-quantum key exchange, ACME, and SSL Orchestrator.

bigip-cookies.title: BIG-IP persistence cookies
bigip-cookies.lede: How a BIG-IP persistence cookie gets into a response, what its value encodes byte by byte, what it tells an attacker, and how to encrypt it.

bigip-dns.title: BIG-IP DNS and global load balancing
bigip-dns.lede: Which of seven answering machines replies to a query, how iQuery tells BIG-IP DNS what is up, global load balancing as two decisions with a three-step chain inside, topology records, and the resolver as a policy engine.

bigip-automation.title: The BIG-IP automation toolchain
bigip-automation.lede: Declarations instead of commands: onboarding the device, describing the applications, streaming what it observes, and the templates that came before and after.

bigip-network-security.title: Network security on the BIG-IP
bigip-network-security.lede: The checkpoints a packet passes on a BIG-IP before any application sees it: packet filters, the network firewall's contexts, SYN flood protection, and the policy that decides which connections die when the table fills.

bigip-apm.title: BIG-IP APM
bigip-apm.lede: Where the access policy keeps what it learned, the single sign-on methods and the blast radius of one bad object, and APM as a SAML proxy in both roles.

awaf.title: BIG-IP Advanced WAF
awaf.lede: A web application firewall policy read as a template plus adjustments, then what it enforces and when, how it parses payloads and layers policies, tracks sessions and masks responses, sees through evasion, tells browsers from bots and absorbs application-layer floods, and how to triage a block without poisoning the policy.

irule-events.title: iRules events and the connection lifecycle
irule-events.lede: When an iRule runs: the fixed order of events through a connection, the two sides of the full proxy, what makes an event exist at all, the events a fast path gives up, the TLS handshake events, priority among several rules, and the order of the questions when you write one.

irules-tcl.title: The Tcl inside iRules
irules-tcl.lede: The language an iRule is written in, read through F5's own style guide: comparisons and numbers, strings and the commands that cut them, branching and lookups, loops, procedures, the namespace that keeps every core busy, performance, and iRules LX.

checkpoint.title: Check Point, from the three tiers to the upgrade
checkpoint.lede: The platform that separates where policy is written from where it is enforced: sessions and publishing, the rule base and its layers, address translation and its silent failure, identity, HTTPS inspection, threat prevention, site-to-site tunnels, logging and events, management high availability, clustering and upgrades.

fortigate.title: FortiGate administration
fortigate.lede: A FortiGate from its factory state to its edges: the CLI and its traps, policies, address translation and their order, debug flow and the sniffer, routing and SD-WAN, security profiles and SSL inspection, identity, IPsec, clustering, logging, shaping, DNS, carrier-scale NAT and ACME.

fortinet-secops.title: Fortinet security operations
fortinet-secops.lede: A security operations centre read as questions rather than products: the analyser that stores and reports, the correlation engine and its database, the orchestration platform and its playbooks, endpoint and network detection, deception, and the attack surface seen from outside.

fortimail.title: FortiMail
fortimail.lede: Mail security on FortiMail: the operation mode that decides everything else, the layered policies and antispam, content security, archiving and identity-based encryption, and protecting the cloud mail platforms.

fortimanager.title: FortiManager
fortimanager.lede: Central management where the database is the source of truth: administrative domains and registration, policy packages and their installs, and where to look when a change does not land.

fortiswitch.title: FortiSwitch
fortiswitch.lede: A switch managed by a FortiGate: FortiLink provisioning and topologies, the VLANs, spanning tree, ports and QoS of the daily work, and port security and diagnostics.

fortiap.title: FortiAP
fortiap.lede: Wireless managed by a FortiGate: the integrated controller and the profiles a fleet is built from, authentication and the segment a client lands in, and troubleshooting what users actually report.

pingfederate.title: PingFederate, installed to upgraded
pingfederate.lede: A PingFederate server's life: what it needs before the archive is unpacked, the files that control it, the two port families, who administers it, the data stores, adapters and authentication policies, OGNL expressions, the logs, the operational habits, and the upgrade.

ping-platform.title: The Ping identity platform
ping-platform.lede: What PingOne is behind its product names, identity orchestration on a canvas, the PingAccess policy model, the PingDirectory data platform, and the lineage that gives the catalogue two of everything.

zscaler.title: The Zscaler Zero Trust Exchange
zscaler.lede: A proxy where the perimeter used to be: the tunnels and the Client Connector that reach it, device posture, the cloud access security broker, the experience score, the logs and reports that come out of it, and the scenarios where the platform earns its architecture.

zia.title: Zscaler Internet Access
zia.lede: The cloud proxy for internet traffic: how traffic reaches it, locations, TLS inspection and its bypasses, URL filtering and cloud app control, the firewall's rule order, file type control and the sandbox, data loss prevention, and the log fields investigations are written in.

zpa.title: Zscaler Private Access
zpa.lede: Private applications reached without exposing them: two outbound calls and a broker in the middle, the vocabulary that names applications and earns access to them, and the three suspects when access fails.

netskope.title: Netskope, one platform and two data paths
netskope.lede: A security cloud on a private network, inspecting traffic two ways: steering and the client, inline TLS decryption, real-time against API protection, the cloud firewall for everything that is not web, private access, and the events and analytics that turn traffic into evidence.

extreme-fabric.title: Extreme Fabric Connect, one service edge to edge
extreme-fabric.lede: Extreme's fabric in the order a service comes into existence: the two operating systems and their names, the configuration model, the vocabulary, the fabric itself, the control plane, the service identifier, multicast without configuration, the edge that asks for what it needs, and dual-homing.

http.title: HTTP, from the request line to QUERY
http.lede: One HTTP exchange read from the top: the raw request, the methods, the status codes, the header fields, cookies, where a message ends, the proxies in the path, the five versions, the newest method, and what people hide in the overhead.

family-histories.title: The family histories
family-histories.lede: Twenty-three technologies the network and its security are built from, each told from its first day: the network from the wire up, what runs on it, then security from the mathematics outward.

transport.title: Transport, from TCP to QUIC
transport.lede: One TCP connection from the handshake to the close and how much it can keep in flight, then QUIC's streams, loss detection and migration, the bytes every tunnel takes from a path, and what an application owes when an answer never arrives.

php.title: PHP, from the language to the incident
php.lede: What PHP is and how a request reaches it, the FastCGI conversation between the web server and PHP-FPM, and the vulnerabilities of October 2026.

expect.title: Expect, end to end
expect.lede: Driving interactive programs with Expect: the four verbs, the Tcl underneath, how patterns meet the buffer, timeouts and loops, secrets, debugging, network devices and BIG-IP's Scripted monitors, every command, and when an API is the better tool.

python.title: Python for network and security engineers
python.lede: What Python is and how long each release lives, environments and packaging, bytes and text, errors and logs; then sockets, addresses, SSH, device APIs and parsed CLI output; then hashing, TLS, secure coding, the supply chain and log and packet analysis, each from the documentation of the module or library itself.

psyops.title: Psychological operations
psyops.lede: From the small lie repeated until it feels true to campaigns run by states, companies and criminal networks: the mechanisms, the actors and their stated aims, the digital amplifier, who decides what is harmful, and the defences, each claim with its evidence and every accused party's response.

planned.voiceClones: Voice clones and deepfakes in fraud
planned.brazilMassMessaging: Brazil: mass messaging, the courts and the CPMI
planned.lodgeToNetwork: From the lodge to the network: how reach changed
planned.echoChambers: Echo chambers and filter bubbles: the evidence and the dispute
planned.profiling: Recommendation and profiling: what platforms disclose
planned.theLaw: The law: Section 230, the DSA, the Marco Civil and the rest

learnSeries.indexStats: {series, plural, one {# series} other {# series}} across {subjects, plural, one {# subject} other {# subjects}} and {vendors, plural, one {# vendor} other {# vendors}}; {articles, plural, one {# article} other {# articles}} in reading order.
learnSeries.bySubjectLede: The ground every platform stands on: protocols, cryptography, the web, identity, formats and the operator's tools.
learnSeries.byVendorLede: One vendor's platform at a time: its own model and its own vocabulary, in reading order.
learnSeries.feed: Follow this series in a feed reader

vlan-trunk.title: Follow a frame across the trunk
vlan-trunk.lede: Two switches share one 802.1Q trunk. Choose each host's access VLAN, the VLANs the trunk allows and the native VLAN at each end, and follow one frame from the left host to the right one.
vlan-trunk.nativeLeft: Native VLAN, left end of the trunk
vlan-trunk.nativeRight: Native VLAN, right end of the trunk
vlan-trunk.leftDrop: the trunk does not allow VLAN {vlan}, so the frame never leaves the switch.
vlan-trunk.leftTagged: sends the frame on the trunk with an 802.1Q tag, VID {vid}.
vlan-trunk.leftUntagged: sends the frame on the trunk untagged, because VLAN {vlan} is this end's native VLAN.
vlan-trunk.rightTagged: reads the tag and places the frame in VLAN {vlan}.
vlan-trunk.rightUntagged: sees no tag and places the frame in this end's native VLAN, VLAN {vlan}.
vlan-trunk.rightAccepts: The trunk allows that VLAN, so the frame is accepted.
vlan-trunk.rightDrop: The trunk does not allow VLAN {vlan}, so the frame is dropped.
vlan-trunk.delivered: delivered. The frame is in VLAN {vlan}, the receiver's VLAN.
vlan-trunk.deliveredCrossed: delivered, but in the wrong VLAN: a frame sent in VLAN {from} arrived in VLAN {to}. Two VLANs are joined at layer 2 without a router in between.
vlan-trunk.wrongVlan: not reached. The frame stays in VLAN {vlan} and the receiver is in VLAN {receiver}; traffic between VLANs has to be routed.
vlan-trunk.droppedLeft: not reached: the frame was dropped at the left end of the trunk.
vlan-trunk.droppedRight: not reached: the frame was dropped at the right end of the trunk.
vlan-trunk.mismatchNote: The two ends disagree on the native VLAN (VLAN {left} on the left, VLAN {right} on the right). Tagged frames are not affected; every untagged frame changes VLAN on the way across.
vlan-trunk.scope: tagging the native VLAN, trunk negotiation (DTP), VLAN pruning, spanning tree, and MAC learning and flooding. It follows the VLAN of one frame, not the whole network.

retry-fan-out.title: Count the calls a failing service receives
retry-fan-out.lede: One user action passes through an entry point and two services before it reaches a service that is failing. Set how many attempts each of the first three makes, and count what reaches the bottom when every attempt fails.
retry-fan-out.service1: Attempts by service 1, per call it receives
retry-fan-out.service2: Attempts by service 2, per call it receives
retry-fan-out.colSingle: Calls received with retries only at the entry point
retry-fan-out.verdictNone: No layer retries: one failed action costs the failing service one call, and the failure reaches the user at once.
retry-fan-out.verdictSingle: Retries at a single point: the failing service receives {n} calls for one failed action.
retry-fan-out.verdictMultiply: Retries at {layers} layers multiply: the failing service receives {n} calls for one failed action, {x} times what retrying only at the entry point would send it.
retry-fan-out.note243: Every layer added multiplies again: three attempts at each of five layers reach the bottom of the stack 243 times for one failed request.
retry-fan-out.errorAttempts: Enter a whole number of attempts from {min} to {max} in each field.
retry-fan-out.scope: time: per-attempt timeouts, the deadline that bounds the whole request, backoff and jitter. It assumes every attempt fails, the worst case, and has no retry budget or token bucket to stop the multiplication.

tcp-window-ceiling.title: Find what limits one TCP connection
tcp-window-ceiling.lede: Set the window a sender may have in flight, the round-trip time and the path's rate. The lab works out the most the window allows, the bytes the path needs in flight, and which of the two decides the throughput.
tcp-window-ceiling.windowLine: {kib} KiB is {bytes} bytes the sender may have unacknowledged at once.
tcp-window-ceiling.ceilingLine: at most one window arrives per round trip, so {bytes} bytes every {rtt} ms is at most {v} Mbit/s.
tcp-window-ceiling.pathLine: keeping {rate} Mbit/s busy over a {rtt} ms round trip takes {bdp} bytes in flight, a window of at least {need} KiB.
tcp-window-ceiling.verdictWindow: the window is the limit. The connection reaches {v} Mbit/s, {pct} of the path, however fast the link is.
tcp-window-ceiling.verdictPath: the path is the limit. The window covers the bandwidth-delay product, so the connection can use the full {rate} Mbit/s.
tcp-window-ceiling.noteScaled: A window above 64 KiB exists only with the window scale option, offered in the SYN and answered in the SYN-ACK. Without it, the 16-bit window field stops this connection at 64 KiB.
tcp-window-ceiling.noteNeedsScaling: Filling this path takes more than 64 KiB in flight, which only the window scale option allows.
tcp-window-ceiling.errorWindow: Enter the window as a whole number of KiB from 1 to {max} (1 GiB, the largest window TCP allows).
tcp-window-ceiling.errorRtt: Enter a round-trip time greater than 0 and at most {max} ms.
tcp-window-ceiling.errorRate: Enter a path rate greater than 0 and at most {max} Mbit/s.
tcp-window-ceiling.scope: slow start and congestion avoidance, which keep the congestion window below this one at first; loss and retransmission; header overhead; delayed acknowledgements; and the buffers at either end. It treats the window as fixed and the path as clean.

regex-partitions.title: Count the ways (a+)+ can split a run of a's
regex-partitions.lede: The pattern (a+)+$ meets a run of a's followed by a !, so it can never match. Choose how many a's there are and count the ways the run can be divided among the outer group's repetitions: each is a path the engine tries before it gives up.
regex-partitions.gapsLine: {n, plural, one {a single a has no gap, so there is exactly one way to take it.} other {# a's have {gaps, plural, one {# gap} other {# gaps}} between neighbours, and each gap either separates two repetitions of (a+) or does not.}}
regex-partitions.splitsLine: {gaps, plural, one {two choices at # gap make 2 to the power 1} other {two choices at each of # gaps make 2 to the power #}}, that is {splits} ways.
regex-partitions.verdict: no match. The engine fails only after trying all {splits} ways, and one more a doubles that to {next}.
regex-partitions.verdictOne: no match, after the one way of taking the run; a second a would make it two.
regex-partitions.listHeading: Every split, one pair of parentheses per repetition of (a+):
regex-partitions.noteFix: Remove the outer quantifier, as in a+$, and the run can be taken in only one way: there is nothing left to split.
regex-partitions.errorLength: Enter a whole number of a's from {min} to {max}.
regex-partitions.scope: the engine itself: the count is the number of ways the run can be split, not a measure of time, and real engines differ in the order they try them and in optimizations that can skip some. It counts only the splits of the whole run, not the attempts that stop earlier.

profile-inheritance.title: Edit a parent profile and see who follows
profile-inheritance.lede: A parent TCP profile has two custom children: child A, used by virtual server 1, leaves the idle timeout alone; child B, used by virtual server 2, either inherits it too or carries its own value. Set the parent's timeout before and after an edit and see which value each profile runs with.
profile-inheritance.parentBefore: Parent's idle timeout before the edit (seconds)
profile-inheritance.parentAfter: Parent's idle timeout after the edit (seconds)
profile-inheritance.verdictNoEdit: No edit yet: every profile runs at {value} s. Change the value after the edit to see who follows.
profile-inheritance.verdictOwnNoEdit: No edit yet. Child B runs at its own {b} s while the parent and child A run at {parent} s.
profile-inheritance.verdictFollow: The edit reaches both children: A and B move from {before} s to {after} s with the parent.
profile-inheritance.verdictLookalike: Child B looked inherited at {before} s, but the value was its own: the parent moves to {after} s, child A follows, and child B stays at {b} s.
profile-inheritance.verdictOwn: Child A follows the parent to {after} s; child B keeps its own {b} s.
profile-inheritance.lookalikeNote: Child B shows the same {value} s as the parent, but the value is its own, so it will not follow the next edit. The number alone cannot tell the two cases apart.
profile-inheritance.errorMode: Choose from the list how child B gets its value.
profile-inheritance.scope: other settings and profile types, connections already open when a value changes, and editing a system default profile itself.

payload-byte-offsets.title: Find the byte offset a payload edit needs
payload-byte-offsets.lede: Type a body and a piece of it to find, and set how much an iRule collects on how many connections at once. The lab counts the text in characters and in UTF-8 octets, places the piece both ways, and bounds the memory the collect can hold.
payload-byte-offsets.verdictDiffer: The counts part here: an HTTP::payload replace of this piece needs offset {offset} and length {length}, in bytes. The character figures would cut a character in half.
payload-byte-offsets.verdictAgree: Every character up to and inside the piece is one octet, so offset {offset} and length {length} are the same in characters and in bytes.
payload-byte-offsets.memoryNote: {kib} KiB collected on {connections} connections at once can hold up to {mib} MiB.
payload-byte-offsets.errorTooLong: Keep the body and the piece to find to {max} characters each.
payload-byte-offsets.errorText: The text holds a lone surrogate, which has no UTF-8 encoding.
payload-byte-offsets.errorCollect: Enter a whole number of KiB from 1 to {max}.
payload-byte-offsets.errorConnections: Enter a whole number of connections from 1 to {max}.
payload-byte-offsets.scope: grapheme clusters (a letter and a combining accent count as two characters here), Unicode normalization, chunked and compressed bodies, and how the platform accounts for its own memory.

snat-port-budget.title: Count the source ports towards one busy member
snat-port-budget.lede: Choose whether the virtual server translates the client's source address, where the member's route back to the client goes, how many translation addresses there are and how many source ports you plan with on each, and the peak of concurrent connections to the busiest member.
snat-port-budget.modeNone: None: the member sees the client's address
snat-port-budget.returnPath: Member's route back to the client (matters without SNAT)
snat-port-budget.returnBypass: Around the BIG-IP (its default route points elsewhere)
snat-port-budget.ports: Source ports you plan with per address
snat-port-budget.demand: Peak concurrent connections to the busiest member
snat-port-budget.seesTranslation: a translation address the BIG-IP owns
snat-port-budget.verdictNoSnatOk: Symmetric without SNAT: the member routes its reply back through the BIG-IP, and the client's address reaches the application.
snat-port-budget.verdictBypass: The reply goes around the BIG-IP, so the client receives a response from an address it never sent to and rejects it. Translate the source address, or route the member's replies through the BIG-IP.
snat-port-budget.verdictFits: Fits, with {spare} source ports to spare at the peak.
snat-port-budget.verdictFull: Every source port towards this member is in use at the peak: the next connection to it has none.
snat-port-budget.verdictExceeds: {shortfall} connections at the peak find no source port, and the SNAT cannot process them until ports come free. Add translation addresses to raise the budget.
snat-port-budget.portFindNote: The BIG-IP's own early warning, port-find-threshold-warning, counts attempts to find a free port rather than a share of ports in use, so do not expect it at a fixed percentage.
snat-port-budget.errorAddresses: Enter a whole number of translation addresses from 1 to {max}.
snat-port-budget.errorPorts: Enter a whole number of ports from 1 to {max}.
snat-port-budget.errorDemand: Enter a whole number of connections from 0 to {max}.
snat-port-budget.scope: the platform's own source-port range and how it picks ports, ports held in TIME-WAIT after a close, other members and virtual servers sharing the same translation addresses, and UDP.

cmp-concentration.title: See where one virtual server's work lands across TMMs
cmp-concentration.lede: Set a virtual server's request rate and the number of TMM instances, then choose how its iRule keeps shared state: none, a global variable it modifies, or one session-table subtable. The lab shows the load on the busiest TMM and where the table work goes.
cmp-concentration.pattern: How the iRule keeps shared state
cmp-concentration.patternSpread: No shared mutable state (static:: constants, data groups)
cmp-concentration.patternGlobal: A global variable the iRule modifies
cmp-concentration.kvIdle: TMMs idle for this virtual server
cmp-concentration.verdictSpread: Spread across all {tmms} TMMs: each carries an equal share in this model.
cmp-concentration.verdictDemoted: Demoted: the whole virtual server runs on one TMM, and {idle} of the {tmms} sit idle for its traffic.
cmp-concentration.verdictSubtable: The requests stay spread across {tmms} TMMs, but all {ops} table operations per second land on the one processor that holds the subtable, with its memory.
cmp-concentration.errorRate: Enter a request rate above 0 and up to {max}.
cmp-concentration.errorTmms: Enter a whole number of TMMs from 1 to {max}.
cmp-concentration.errorOps: Enter a whole number of table operations from 0 to {max}.
cmp-concentration.errorPattern: Choose a pattern from the list.
cmp-concentration.scope: real traffic is placed connection by connection and is never exactly even; the cost of a request or a table operation; other virtual servers sharing the same TMMs; and platforms where CMP does not apply.

request-through-layers.title: Follow one HTTPS request down and across
request-through-layers.lede: Client A, 192.0.2.10, sends one HTTPS request to a web server. Put the server on A's LAN, behind a router or behind a reverse proxy, and see on each link which addresses each layer carries and how many connections and TLS sessions the request really uses.
request-through-layers.pathRouted: on another network, behind a router (198.51.100.20)
request-through-layers.pathProxy: behind a reverse proxy that A connects to
request-through-layers.backend: The reverse proxy, towards the server
request-through-layers.l2Single: one link, so one pair of MAC addresses.
request-through-layers.l2Changed: each link has its own pair of MAC addresses; the device in the middle builds a new Ethernet header.
request-through-layers.l3Lan: the IP addresses are A's and the server's, and nothing in between lowers the TTL.
request-through-layers.l3Routed: the router keeps both IP addresses and lowers the TTL from 64 to 63.
request-through-layers.l3Proxy: the proxy sends its own packets: the server sees 198.51.100.100, never A's address, and a fresh TTL of 64.
request-through-layers.verdictEndToEnd: {tcp, plural, one {# TCP connection} other {# TCP connections}} and {tls, plural, one {# TLS session} other {# TLS sessions}}, end to end between A and the server.
request-through-layers.verdictProxy: {tcp, plural, one {# TCP connection} other {# TCP connections}} and {tls, plural, one {# TLS session} other {# TLS sessions}}: the client's ends at the proxy, which opens its own towards the server.
request-through-layers.notePlain: Between the proxy and the server the request travels in clear text: the TLS session protects only the first link.
request-through-layers.noteBackendIgnored: The re-encryption setting applies only when there is a reverse proxy.
request-through-layers.scope: the DNS lookup and ARP before the request, NAT, VLANs, IPv6, HTTP/3 over QUIC, TLS passthrough and transparent proxies, and headers such as Forwarded that pass the client's address on.

ethernet-transfer-budget.title: Put a whole file on the wire
ethernet-transfer-budget.lede: The bits, bytes and throughput calculator applies one efficiency to a whole transfer. This lab cuts one file into packets and frames: full packets, one short last packet, and every frame's header, tag, preamble and gap. Compare the time on the wire with the bare file at the same speed.
ethernet-transfer-budget.perPacket: {n} (the MTU less {ip} of IP header and {l4} of transport header)
ethernet-transfer-budget.packetsWithLast: {n}: {full} full and a last one carrying {last} bytes
ethernet-transfer-budget.verdict: {time} on the wire, of which {pct} % carries the file.
ethernet-transfer-budget.notePad: The last packet is shorter than 46 octets, so {pad} octets of zeros pad its frame.
ethernet-transfer-budget.errorSize: Enter a size above 0 and up to {max}.
ethernet-transfer-budget.errorMtu: Enter an MTU from {min} to {max} octets.
ethernet-transfer-budget.errorIpv6Mtu: IPv6 needs every link to carry packets of at least {min} octets; enter an MTU of {min} or more.
ethernet-transfer-budget.errorChoice: Choose one of the options offered.
ethernet-transfer-budget.scope: acknowledgements, TCP options, the window and the round trip, slow start, loss and retransmission, and anything the application adds.

ethernet-frame-builder.title: Build a frame and measure it
ethernet-frame-builder.lede: Type a destination MAC address, choose a tag, the protocol inside and the packet's size, and see the frame field by field: what the destination's first bits say, how big the frame is, and how many such frames a link can carry each second. Try a 28-octet ARP packet.
ethernet-frame-builder.vPayloadPadded: the {packet}-octet packet and {pad} octets of zeros
ethernet-frame-builder.kvWire: On the wire, with preamble, delimiter and gap
ethernet-frame-builder.kvFps: Most frames per second at this speed
ethernet-frame-builder.kvShare: Packet's share of the wire time
ethernet-frame-builder.notePad: The packet is shorter than the payload field's 46-octet minimum, so {pad} octets of zeros follow it. They are not part of the packet: the receiver finds its end from the packet's own length field.
ethernet-frame-builder.errorMac: Enter a MAC address as twelve hex digits, with or without colons, hyphens or dots.
ethernet-frame-builder.errorVid: Enter a VLAN ID from 1 to 4094.
ethernet-frame-builder.errorPacket: Enter a packet size from 1 to {max} octets.
ethernet-frame-builder.errorChoice: Choose one of the options offered.
ethernet-frame-builder.scope: the value of the FCS itself, jumbo and envelope frames, LLC and SNAP, double tags, the priority and DEI bits, and half duplex.

arp-and-switch-tables.title: Send one packet through two tables
arp-and-switch-tables.lede: Host A, 192.0.2.10 on switch port 1, sends a packet. A's ARP cache turns the next hop's IP address into a MAC address; the switch's MAC address table turns that MAC address into a port. Fill or empty each table and see where the frame goes.
arp-and-switch-tables.targetGateway: 198.51.100.7, off the subnet, through the router {ip}
arp-and-switch-tables.cache: A's ARP cache for the next hop
arp-and-switch-tables.fdb: The switch's table for the next hop's MAC
arp-and-switch-tables.fdbStale: port {old}, where it was before it moved to port {port}
arp-and-switch-tables.evArpRequest: A broadcasts an ARP request: who has {ip}?
arp-and-switch-tables.evLearnA: The switch learns {macA}, A, on port {portA}.
arp-and-switch-tables.evFloodBroadcast: A broadcast goes out of every port except port {portA}.
arp-and-switch-tables.evArpReply: An ARP reply comes back from {name}: {ip} is at {mac}.
arp-and-switch-tables.evLearnNextHop: The switch learns {mac} on port {port}, where the reply came in.
arp-and-switch-tables.evLearnNextHopReplace: The switch learns {mac} on port {port}, where the reply came in, replacing its entry for port {old}.
arp-and-switch-tables.evReplyForwarded: The switch already knows A on port {portA}, so the reply goes only there.
arp-and-switch-tables.evArpSilent: No reply comes. A has no MAC address for {ip}, so the packet is never sent.
arp-and-switch-tables.evDataSent: A puts the packet for {dest} in a frame addressed to {mac}.
arp-and-switch-tables.evFloodUnknown: The switch has no entry for {mac}, so it floods the frame out of every port except port {portA}; {name} receives it on port {port}, and so does every other port.
arp-and-switch-tables.evForwardKnown: The switch's entry says port {port}: the frame goes out there and {name} receives it.
arp-and-switch-tables.evForwardStale: The switch's entry says port {old}: the frame goes out there, but {name} is on port {port} now.
arp-and-switch-tables.verdictDelivered: Delivered to {name}, out of one port only.
arp-and-switch-tables.verdictFlooded: Delivered to {name}, but by flooding: every other port got a copy too.
arp-and-switch-tables.verdictMisdelivered: Not delivered: the frame went to port {old} and {name} never saw it.
arp-and-switch-tables.verdictNoMapping: Not sent: without a MAC address there is no frame to send.
arp-and-switch-tables.noteStale: The entry stays wrong until {name} sends a frame, which the switch learns on port {port}, or until it is forgotten, {seconds} seconds after {name} was last heard on port {old} (the Linux bridge's default ageing time).
arp-and-switch-tables.scope: timers and retries of ARP entries, gratuitous and proxy ARP, VLANs, spanning tree, and the traffic that comes back after the first packet.

stp-root-election.title: Elect a root and break the loops
stp-root-election.lede: Four switches, A to D, joined in a square with one diagonal, B-C. Their MAC addresses rise from A to D and every link runs at 1 Gb/s except B-D. Choose the root on purpose, change B-D's speed or fail a link, and see every port's role.
stp-root-election.noteTie: {name} reaches the root at the same cost through two ports; the lower-numbered one, port {port} towards {via}, becomes the root port.
stp-root-election.verdict: Root {root}: {forward} links forward and {blocked} block, so there is exactly one path between any two switches.
stp-root-election.scope: port priorities, timers and convergence time, the long cost scale, backup ports, MSTP regions and per-VLAN trees, and edge ports.

vlsm-allocation-order.title: Place the blocks in a different order
vlsm-allocation-order.lede: The article's parent, 203.0.113.0/24, and its five requests: two router links, Management, Office and Guest Wi-Fi, in that order of arrival. Change the host counts and the order, and watch where each block lands, what is skipped and what is left.
vlsm-allocation-order.verdictMissing: Not placed: {list}. The next aligned start lies past the end of the parent.
vlsm-allocation-order.errorHosts: Enter each host count as a whole number from 1 to {max}.
vlsm-allocation-order.errorChoice: Choose one of the options offered.
vlsm-allocation-order.scope: growth allowances, going back to fill a gap, any parent other than 203.0.113.0/24, IPv6, and how the routers are configured.
vlsm-allocation-order.noteGap: A gap in the plan is large enough for {list}, but only by going back for it, and going back is where overlaps come from.

ipv6-host-configuration-sources.title: Build a host's IPv6 configuration from its sources
ipv6-host-configuration-sources.lede: A host with its DHCPv6 client running joins a link. Set what the router advertises and what DHCPv6 offers, and see which addresses the host forms, whether it gets a default route, and where its DNS servers come from.
ipv6-host-configuration-sources.prefix: Prefix in the Prefix Information option
ipv6-host-configuration-sources.routeYes: via the router that sent the RA
ipv6-host-configuration-sources.routeLifetimeZero: none: a Router Lifetime of 0 says the sender is not a default router
ipv6-host-configuration-sources.routeNoRa: none: only Router Advertisements configure a default router, and DHCPv6 cannot
ipv6-host-configuration-sources.dnsStateless: from DHCPv6, option 23, through an Information-request; no DHCPv6 address is needed
ipv6-host-configuration-sources.dnsStateful: from DHCPv6, option 23, in the same exchange as the address
ipv6-host-configuration-sources.slaacRan: SLAAC formed a global address: the RA's /64 plus the 64-bit interface identifier makes 128 bits.
ipv6-host-configuration-sources.slaacNoRa: No SLAAC address: without a Router Advertisement there is no prefix to build one from.
ipv6-host-configuration-sources.slaacAFlag: No SLAAC address: the prefix's A flag is clear, so the Prefix Information option is ignored for SLAAC.
ipv6-host-configuration-sources.slaacPrefix: No SLAAC address: a /60 plus a 64-bit interface identifier is not 128 bits, so the Prefix Information option is ignored.
ipv6-host-configuration-sources.noteSlash128: The DHCPv6 address is a /128: it implies no prefix length, and it brings no default route.
ipv6-host-configuration-sources.noteRdnssOverridden: The RA's RDNSS servers are offered too, but DNS information from DHCPv6 takes precedence.
ipv6-host-configuration-sources.reachLinkOnly: Link-local only: the host can talk to its own link and nothing else.
ipv6-host-configuration-sources.reachOnLink: A global address but no default route: nothing off the link is reachable.
ipv6-host-configuration-sources.reachByAddress: Off-link destinations are reachable by address, but names do not resolve: no DNS servers.
ipv6-host-configuration-sources.reachByName: Ready: a global address, a default route and DNS servers, so names off the link resolve and connect.
ipv6-host-configuration-sources.scope: when an operating system decides to start DHCPv6 (the M and O flags only signal), Duplicate Address Detection, temporary and RFC 7217 addresses, lifetimes and their expiry, prefix delegation, and on-link determination.

dhcp-lease-states.title: Follow a lease through its timers
dhcp-lease-states.lede: One client, one DHCP server. Set the lease, how far into it the client is and where the server sits, and see the client's state, what it sends and whether any server hears it. Try a server on another subnet with no relay agent at 60 % and then at 90 %.
dhcp-lease-states.elapsed: Time into the lease (% of the lease)
dhcp-lease-states.serverRelay: on another subnet, with a relay agent
dhcp-lease-states.serverNoRelay: on another subnet, no relay agent
dhcp-lease-states.stateInit: INIT. The client has no address yet.
dhcp-lease-states.stateBound: BOUND. T1 has not arrived, so the lease is simply in use.
dhcp-lease-states.stateRenewing: RENEWING. T1 has passed, so the client asks the server that issued the lease to extend it.
dhcp-lease-states.stateRebinding: REBINDING. T2 has passed, so the client asks any server.
dhcp-lease-states.stateExpired: Lease expired. The client must stop all other network processing and start again from INIT.
dhcp-lease-states.sendsNone: nothing. The next timer is T1, in {time}.
dhcp-lease-states.sendsUnicast: a DHCPREQUEST, unicast to the address of the server that issued the lease; routers forward it like any other packet.
dhcp-lease-states.sendsBroadcast: a DHCPREQUEST, broadcast to 255.255.255.255 for any server.
dhcp-lease-states.reachRelay: A relay agent on the client's subnet carries it to the server.
dhcp-lease-states.reachNoRelay: A limited broadcast is not forwarded and no relay agent is configured, so it never leaves the client's subnet.
dhcp-lease-states.resultBoundQuiet: nothing to do yet: the address is in use and the lease runs on.
dhcp-lease-states.resultLeased: a server answers and the exchange ends in DHCPACK. The client is BOUND with a new lease.
dhcp-lease-states.resultNoOfferNoRelay: no offer: the broadcast never reached a server. The client has no address and keeps sending DHCPDISCOVER.
dhcp-lease-states.resultNoOfferSilent: no offer: the server does not answer. The client has no address and keeps sending DHCPDISCOVER.
dhcp-lease-states.resultRenewed: the server answers with DHCPACK. The lease restarts from this request and the client is BOUND again.
dhcp-lease-states.resultWaitingRenewing: no answer. The client keeps its address, sends again in {retry}, and moves to REBINDING at T2, in {next}.
dhcp-lease-states.resultRebound: a server answers with DHCPACK. The client is BOUND again with an extended lease.
dhcp-lease-states.resultWaitingRebindingNoRelay: no answer, although the server is up: the broadcast never reached it. The client keeps its address, sends again in {retry}, and must stop when the lease expires, in {next}.
dhcp-lease-states.resultWaitingRebindingSilent: no answer. The client keeps its address, sends again in {retry}, and must stop when the lease expires, in {next}.
dhcp-lease-states.noteRelayHidden: The missing relay agent does not show while the lease is renewed by unicast. It shows at T2, when the client has to broadcast, and at once for any client that has no lease yet.
dhcp-lease-states.errorLease: Enter a whole number of seconds from {min} to {max}.
dhcp-lease-states.errorChoice: Choose one of the options offered.
dhcp-lease-states.scope: the random fuzz on T1 and T2, timers the server sets itself, DHCPNAK, DHCPDECLINE and the address probe, several competing servers, the relay agent's own fields, and the retransmission schedule of a client still waiting for an offer.

dns-two-caches.title: Ask the zone and two caches at once
dns-two-caches.lede: Resolver A cached www.example.com at 0 s and resolver B at 20 s; at 30 s the zone changed. Choose the TTL and the moment a client asks, and compare what the zone's own server and each resolver answer. Then take the authority down.
dns-two-caches.timeline: A cached the name at {a} s, B at {b} s, the zone changed at {change} s, and the client asks at {now} s. Nobody asked either resolver in between.
dns-two-caches.whyCache: cache hit: the entry is {age} s old, younger than its TTL
dns-two-caches.whyFetched: the entry expired ({age} s old), so the resolver asked the zone again
dns-two-caches.whyStale: the entry expired and the zone does not answer: the expired record is served stale
dns-two-caches.whyFailed: the entry expired and the zone does not answer: a resolution failure
dns-two-caches.verdictDisagree: Two clients asking now get different answers, depending only on which resolver they use.
dns-two-caches.verdictBehind: Both resolvers agree with each other, but not yet with the zone.
dns-two-caches.verdictNoAuthority: Both resolvers give the same answer, and the zone cannot be asked to confirm it.
dns-two-caches.verdictAgree: Both resolvers give the zone's current answer.
dns-two-caches.errorTtl: Enter a whole number of seconds from 1 to {max}.
dns-two-caches.errorNow: Enter a whole number of seconds from {min}, when B cached the name, to {max}.
dns-two-caches.errorChoice: Choose one of the options offered.
dns-two-caches.scope: prefetching, DNSSEC, resolvers that cap TTLs, caching of the failure itself, the timers of serve-stale, several authoritative servers and any query between the two fills and the moment chosen; the zone's negative TTL is taken to equal the record's TTL.

rib-to-fib.title: Install the routes, then route a packet
rib-to-fib.lede: One router with Cisco's default distances and up to six routes for parts of 203.0.113.0/24. Switch routes on and off, then type a destination: the table shows what is installed and why, and the lookup picks the longest installed match.
rib-to-fib.ospf: OSPF route to 203.0.113.0/24 (two paths, cost 20 and 40)
rib-to-fib.noCandidates: No route is configured or learned.
rib-to-fib.statusLostMetric: no: OSPF keeps its lower-cost path
rib-to-fib.statusLostDistance: no: a source with a lower distance offers the same prefix
rib-to-fib.statusUnresolved: no: its next hop does not resolve
rib-to-fib.stepMatches: Installed routes that contain the destination:
rib-to-fib.verdictForward: {dest} goes to {hop}, by {prefix}, the longest installed match. Distance played no part in this choice.
rib-to-fib.verdictDiscard: {dest} is dropped by the discard route {prefix}, the longest installed match.
rib-to-fib.verdictNoRoute: {dest} matches no installed route, so the packet is discarded and an ICMP destination unreachable goes back to the sender.
rib-to-fib.errorDestination: Enter an IPv4 address as four numbers from 0 to 255 separated by dots.
rib-to-fib.errorChoice: Choose one of the options offered.
rib-to-fib.scope: equal-cost multipath, a next hop resolved through some other route, other vendors' distances, redistribution, and how the routes were learned.

bfd-versus-hellos.title: Race BFD against the routing protocol's own timer
bfd-versus-hellos.lede: The path to a neighbour dies while the local port stays up. Choose what the route depends on, whether BFD runs and whether that protocol asked BFD to watch the path, and the BFD timers, and see who notices first and when the route goes.
bfd-versus-hellos.bfdRegistered: on, and the protocol asked for it
bfd-versus-hellos.bfdUnregistered: on, but the protocol never asked for it
bfd-versus-hellos.portLine: stays up, so the interface reports nothing.
bfd-versus-hellos.bfdLineOff: off. Nothing watches the path in between.
bfd-versus-hellos.bfdLineHeard: after {time} without a packet the session goes Down, and BFD tells {client}, which asked for it.
bfd-versus-hellos.bfdLineUnheard: after {time} the session goes Down, but {client} never asked for BFD, so nothing hears it.
bfd-versus-hellos.protoOspf: OSPF hears no Hello and declares the neighbour dead when its dead interval runs out, after {time}.
bfd-versus-hellos.protoBgp: BGP receives no KEEPALIVE and drops the session when its hold time runs out, after {time}.
bfd-versus-hellos.protoStatic: a static route has no Hello of its own; with its port up, nothing in it notices.
bfd-versus-hellos.verdictBfdFaster: withdrawn after {time}, on BFD's word: {x} times sooner than the protocol's own timer.
bfd-versus-hellos.verdictProtocol: withdrawn after {time}, when the protocol's own timer runs out. Until then traffic goes into a black hole.
bfd-versus-hellos.verdictNever: never withdrawn while the port stays up. Traffic keeps going into a black hole.
bfd-versus-hellos.errorInterval: Enter each interval in milliseconds, above 0 and up to {max}.
bfd-versus-hellos.errorMult: Enter a whole Detect Mult from 1 to {max}.
bfd-versus-hellos.errorChoice: Choose one of the options offered.
bfd-versus-hellos.scope: the jitter on BFD packets, the one-second rate before a session is Up, Echo and demand modes, graceful restart, the time a router then takes to recompute and reprogram its forwarding table, and what the applications do on top.

tls13-handshake-shapes.title: Lay out a TLS 1.3 handshake, flight by flight
tls13-handshake-shapes.lede: Choose what the client offers, whether its key share fits the server's groups, how the server answers a PSK and 0-RTT data, and whether it wants a client certificate. See the flights in order, the keys that protect each message and the round trips before the client's data counts. Numbers in brackets are sections of RFC 9846. Try the Example: 0-RTT data that a HelloRetryRequest throws away.
tls13-handshake-shapes.scope: external PSKs and more than one PSK offered, the cookie and other reasons for a HelloRetryRequest, a client with no certificate to send, middlebox compatibility mode, post-handshake messages (NewSessionTicket, KeyUpdate, post-handshake authentication), and why a server refuses 0-RTT: its anti-replay and freshness checks (section 8). Early data can be replayed, so a client must only send what is safe to replay.
tls13-handshake-shapes.shareMatch: has a share in a group the server accepts
tls13-handshake-shapes.shareRetry: misses, but supported_groups lists a group the server accepts
tls13-handshake-shapes.shareNone: no group in common with the server
tls13-handshake-shapes.earlyAnswer: The server, given 0-RTT data it may accept
tls13-handshake-shapes.clientCert: The server wants a client certificate
tls13-handshake-shapes.optionalTag: (optional: the client is not yet authenticated)
tls13-handshake-shapes.kxFull: no PSK is offered, so this is a full handshake: (EC)DHE for the keys and a certificate to authenticate the server (2, 4.2.1).
tls13-handshake-shapes.kxDeclined: the server declines the PSK and falls back to a full handshake with (EC)DHE and a certificate, which the client's key_share makes possible (2.2).
tls13-handshake-shapes.kxPskDhe: the server accepts the PSK in psk_dhe_ke mode: the PSK plus a fresh (EC)DHE exchange, so its ServerHello carries both pre_shared_key and key_share, and the application data keeps forward secrecy (2.2, 4.3.9).
tls13-handshake-shapes.kxPskOnly: the server accepts the PSK in psk_ke mode: the PSK alone, so its ServerHello carries no key_share, and the application data has no forward secrecy (2.2, 4.3.9).
tls13-handshake-shapes.kxAbort: none is agreed: this handshake needs (EC)DHE, and the two sides have no group in common.
tls13-handshake-shapes.shareUsed: the client sent a share in a group the server accepts, so the server answers with its own share in that group (4.3.8).
tls13-handshake-shapes.shareRetried: every share the client sent is in a group the server will not use, but its supported_groups lists one the server accepts, so the server sends a HelloRetryRequest naming that group and the client sends a second ClientHello with one share for it: one more round trip (2.1, 4.2.4, 4.3.8).
tls13-handshake-shapes.shareNotNeeded: not used: in psk_ke mode the server sends no key_share, so the client's shares do not matter, and even groups with nothing in common are not fatal (4.2.1, 4.3.9).
tls13-handshake-shapes.shareAbort: no group the client supports is one the server supports, and the key exchange needs one, so the server aborts the handshake with a handshake_failure or insufficient_security alert (4.2.1).
tls13-handshake-shapes.earlyAccepted: accepted. The server returns early_data in EncryptedExtensions; the first-flight data is protected under the client early traffic keys, and after the server's Finished the client closes it with EndOfEarlyData under the same keys (2.3, 4.3.10, 4.6).
tls13-handshake-shapes.earlyRetry: rejected by the HelloRetryRequest. Early data is not permitted after one, so the second ClientHello drops early_data and the server skips the encrypted records of the first flight (4.2.2, 4.3.10).
tls13-handshake-shapes.earlyPskDeclined: rejected. To accept early data the server must select the first PSK the client offered, and it selected none, so it discards the records it cannot decrypt with its handshake keys (4.3.10).
tls13-handshake-shapes.earlyRefused: rejected by the server: no early_data in its EncryptedExtensions, and it discards the records it cannot decrypt with its handshake keys (4.3.10).
tls13-handshake-shapes.earlyResend: The application may send that data again once the handshake is complete; TLS should not resend it by itself (4.3.10).
tls13-handshake-shapes.earlyLost: sent, but the handshake fails, so nothing ever reads it.
tls13-handshake-shapes.authCert: the server sends Certificate and CertificateVerify, then Finished (4.5).
tls13-handshake-shapes.authCertClient: the server sends a CertificateRequest right after EncryptedExtensions, then Certificate, CertificateVerify and Finished; the client answers with its own Certificate and CertificateVerify before its Finished (4.4.2, 4.5).
tls13-handshake-shapes.authPsk: the PSK authenticates the server, so it sends no Certificate or CertificateVerify, only Finished (2.2, 4.5.1).
tls13-handshake-shapes.authPskNoClient: the PSK authenticates the server, so it sends no Certificate or CertificateVerify; and a server authenticating with a resumption PSK must not send a CertificateRequest in the main handshake, so the client is not asked for a certificate (2.2, 4.4.2).
tls13-handshake-shapes.verdictAbort: never: the handshake fails before any keys exist.
tls13-handshake-shapes.verdictZero: in the first flight, after 0 round trips, at the price the standard states: early data can be replayed and has no forward secrecy guarantee (2.3, 8).
tls13-handshake-shapes.verdictRtt: after {n, plural, one {# round trip} other {# round trips}}, right behind the client's Finished (4.5.3).
tls13-handshake-shapes.verdictRetry: The HelloRetryRequest cost one of them.
tls13-handshake-shapes.verdictEarlyLost: The 0-RTT data sent at the start was thrown away.
tls13-handshake-shapes.kvRoundTrips: Round trips before the client's data counts
tls13-handshake-shapes.noteKeys: The three kinds of keys come from three secrets: client early traffic keys from client_early_traffic_secret, handshake traffic keys from each side's handshake traffic secret, and application traffic keys from each side's application traffic secret. ClientHello and ServerHello travel in the clear: together they determine the keys (2, 7.1).

f5-monitor-timing.title: Time a BIG-IP monitor's down and up marks
f5-monitor-timing.lede: One BIG-IP LTM health monitor watches one pool member. Set the monitor's Interval, Timeout, Up Interval and Time Until Up, and the seconds at which the server goes silent and answers again, and see every probe and the moments the member is marked down and back up, with the F5 document behind each rule. Try the Example, a Timeout below F5's recommendation, then a Time Until Up of 10 s.
f5-monitor-timing.scope: the exact probe schedule, which F5 does not document: the lab starts probes at second 0 and spaces them evenly with no jitter, a healthy server answers at once, and after a down mark between two Up Interval probes the next probe goes out one Interval later. It also leaves out replies that arrive late, a server that refuses the connection with a reset (marked down at once by tcp and http monitors, per the TMSH Reference v17), Manual Resume, several monitors or a node monitor on the same member, and the load on bigd itself.
f5-monitor-timing.errorInterval: Enter a whole Interval from 1 to {max} seconds.
f5-monitor-timing.errorTimeout: Enter a whole Timeout from 1 to {max} seconds.
f5-monitor-timing.errorTimeoutBelow: A Timeout shorter than the Interval is not accepted: BIG-IP refuses it (K000138395).
f5-monitor-timing.errorUpInterval: Enter a whole Up Interval from 0 (off) to {max} seconds.
f5-monitor-timing.errorTimeUntilUp: Enter a whole Time Until Up from 0 to {max} seconds.
f5-monitor-timing.errorTimeline: Enter whole seconds: the server stops at second 1 or later and answers again after that, by second {max}.
f5-monitor-timing.eventFirstMissed: the first probe goes unanswered. The Timeout starts here: the member must answer by second {deadline} (K350).
f5-monitor-timing.eventDown: {timeout} s have passed since the first missed probe with no correct answer ({missed, plural, one {# probe} other {# probes}} unanswered): the Timeout has run out, so the member is marked down (K350, K11359).
f5-monitor-timing.eventDownTie: The probe due this same second is too late to count: the reason F5 adds one second to three times the Interval (K12531).
f5-monitor-timing.eventRidden: a probe is answered inside the Timeout, so the member stays up: {missed, plural, one {# probe} other {# probes}} missed and no down mark (K350).
f5-monitor-timing.eventUnseen: the next probe is answered. The one before, at second {last}, came before the outage, so no probe ever went unanswered.
