f5-monitor-timing.eventAnswerUp: the first probe after the recovery is answered, and the member is marked up at once: Time Until Up is 0 (BIG-IP 21.1.0 Monitors Concepts).
f5-monitor-timing.eventAnswerPending: the first probe after the recovery is answered, and Time Until Up starts: every answer for the next {tuu} s must be correct (BIG-IP 21.1.0 Monitors Concepts).
f5-monitor-timing.eventUpAfterTuu: Time Until Up has run with every answer correct, so the member is marked up.
f5-monitor-timing.verdictUnseen: never marked down: the {outage}-second outage fell between two probes.
f5-monitor-timing.verdictRidden: never marked down: the member answered within {timeout} s of the first missed probe, so the {outage}-second outage was ridden through.
f5-monitor-timing.verdictDownUp: out of the pool from second {down} to second {up}: marked down {detection} s after the failure, and up {ret} s after the recovery.
f5-monitor-timing.verdictFlap: bounced: marked down at second {down} and up at second {up}, {downFor} s later, for an outage of {outage} s. With F5's recommended Timeout of {rec} s the member would have stayed up (K350, K12531).
f5-monitor-timing.kvWindow: Probes that fit in one Timeout
f5-monitor-timing.downAt: at second {at}, {after} s after the failure
f5-monitor-timing.upAt: at second {at}, {after} s after the recovery
f5-monitor-timing.noteBelow: The Timeout is below F5's recommendation of 3 × Interval + 1 = {rec} s, so only {n, plural, one {# probe fits} other {# probes fit}} before it runs out: the member can be marked down before the last check has gone out (K12531).
f5-monitor-timing.noteOneProbe: Only one probe fits in the Timeout, so a single missed probe marks the member down (K000138395).
f5-monitor-timing.noteMultiple: F5 recommends that the larger of the Interval and the Up Interval be a multiple of the smaller, to spread checks evenly across monitors (BIG-IP 21.1.0 Monitors Settings Reference).

http-freshness.title: Decide whether a cache may reuse a response
http-freshness.lede: A 200 response to a GET sits in a cache. Set its headers, the kind of cache and how long ago the response arrived, and follow the cache's reasoning: may it store the response, how long it stays fresh and why, how old it is now, and whether it may answer without asking the origin. The Example shows s-maxage overruling max-age in a shared cache only; switch the cache to private, then try no-cache.
http-freshness.scope: request directives such as max-stale, Vary and the cache key, requests carrying Authorization, status codes other than 200, the time the request took (the response delay is taken as zero), ETag, must-understand, and extensions such as stale-while-revalidate, which this cache does not recognize and so ignores; the heuristic, when chosen, is 10% of the time between Last-Modified and Date, rounded down.
http-freshness.cacheShared: Shared (a CDN or a reverse proxy)
http-freshness.date: Date: seconds before the cache received it
http-freshness.expires: Expires: seconds after Date (empty for none)
http-freshness.lastModified: Last-Modified: seconds before Date (empty for none)
http-freshness.heuristic: This cache's heuristic when nothing is explicit
http-freshness.errorDate: Enter Date as a whole number of seconds, up to {max} either way (negative when Date is ahead of the cache's clock).
http-freshness.errorAge: Enter Age as a whole number of seconds from 0 to {max}, or leave it empty.
http-freshness.errorExpires: Enter Expires as whole seconds after Date, up to {max} either way (negative for before Date), or leave it empty.
http-freshness.errorLastModified: Enter Last-Modified as whole seconds before Date, from 0 to {max}, or leave it empty: it is never later than Date.
http-freshness.errorReceived: Enter a whole number of seconds from 0 to {max}.
http-freshness.errorCcSyntax: Cache-Control is a comma-separated list of directives, such as max-age=60, must-revalidate.
http-freshness.errorCcDuplicate: {name} appears twice. The specification lets a cache use the first or treat the response as stale; write it once to see the rest.
http-freshness.errorCcSeconds: {name} needs a whole number of seconds. The specification encourages a cache to treat invalid freshness information as stale.
http-freshness.errorCcQualified: {name} with a list of field names is the qualified form, which the lab does not model; write it without the list.
http-freshness.errorChoice: Choose one of the options offered.
http-freshness.storeAllowed: May store it: nothing forbids it, and a 200 is heuristically cacheable, so it needs no directive to be stored.
http-freshness.storeNoStore: May not store it: no-store applies to every cache.
http-freshness.storePrivateShared: May not store it: private forbids a shared cache to store the response.
http-freshness.storePrivatePrivate: May store it: private keeps the response out of shared caches only, and this cache is private.
http-freshness.lifeSMaxage: {s} s, from s-maxage, which a shared cache reads before anything else.
http-freshness.lifeHeuristic: {s} s, from this cache's heuristic: 10% of the {lm} s between Last-Modified and Date, rounded down. The specification names 10% only as a typical setting.
http-freshness.lifeNone: None: nothing explicit and no heuristic in use, so the response is never fresh.
http-freshness.noteSMaxageIgnored: s-maxage is ignored here: it speaks to shared caches only.
http-freshness.noteExpiresIgnored: Expires is ignored because {by} is present.
http-freshness.noteHeuristicBlocked: The heuristic is not used: an explicit expiration is present.
http-freshness.noteHeuristicNoLastModified: The heuristic needs a Last-Modified, and there is none.
http-freshness.noteClamped: A value above {max} is taken as {max} seconds.
http-freshness.ageLine: {current} s: a starting age of {initial} s (the larger of the apparent age, {apparent} s, and Age, {age} s), plus {received} s in this cache.
http-freshness.ageLineNoAge: {current} s: the apparent age, {apparent} s (there is no Age header), plus {received} s in this cache.
http-freshness.freshYes: Fresh: the lifetime, {lifetime} s, is greater than the age, {current} s, with {remaining} s to go.
http-freshness.freshNo: Stale: the age, {current} s, is not below the lifetime, {lifetime} s.
http-freshness.freshNone: Stale: with no freshness lifetime, it cannot be fresh.
http-freshness.onlineServe: Answers from the cache without contacting the origin, sending Age: {age}.
http-freshness.onlineValidateNoCache: Must validate with the origin first, fresh or not: that is what no-cache means.
http-freshness.onlineValidateStaleIms: Must validate with the origin before reusing it, with a conditional request carrying the stored Last-Modified as If-Modified-Since.
http-freshness.onlineValidateStaleNone: Must validate with the origin before reusing it; with no Last-Modified, the request carries no validator from these headers.
http-freshness.offlineServe: Answers from the cache: a fresh response needs no contact.
http-freshness.offlineCannotNoCache: Cannot answer from the cache: no-cache forbids any reuse without validation.
http-freshness.offlineMustRevalidate: Must answer with an error, which should be 504 (Gateway Timeout): must-revalidate forbids serving it stale.
http-freshness.offlineSharedRevalidate: Cannot serve it stale: in a shared cache, {by} forbids reuse until the response is validated.
http-freshness.offlineServeStale: May serve it stale: a disconnected cache may, and nothing here forbids it.
http-freshness.notStored: Nothing to reuse: every request for it goes to the origin.
http-freshness.noteIgnored: Ignored, as a cache ignores directives it does not recognize: {names}.
http-freshness.notePublic: public changes nothing here: the response could be stored without it.

cookie-send-decision.title: Decide whether the browser sends a cookie
cookie-send-decision.lede: A response to https://www.example.com/account/login set the cookie session=abc123. Choose its attributes, type the URL of a later request and say what kind of request it is, and watch the browser's checks in order, with the rule that decides. The Example is a classic loss: a payment provider's page posts the shopper back, and the session cookie stays behind.
cookie-send-decision.scope: working out same-site or cross-site from the two URLs (you say which), the cookie's lifetime, the __Secure- and __Host- prefixes, the public suffix list, the Lax-allowing-unsafe mode (noted, not applied), reload navigations, redirects, the Fetch Standard's credentials mode and third-party cookie policies. The rules are those of RFC 6265 and draft-ietf-httpbis-rfc6265bis-22 (an Internet-Draft, not yet an RFC), not any one browser's.
cookie-send-decision.url: Request URL (for document.cookie, the page's URL)
cookie-send-decision.errorUrl: Enter a URL such as https://www.example.com/account, up to {max} characters.
cookie-send-decision.errorHost: Use a host name or an IPv4 address, with an optional port and no user name.
cookie-send-decision.errorPath: The path cannot contain spaces or control characters.
cookie-send-decision.errorChoice: Choose one of the options offered.
cookie-send-decision.storeDomainMismatch: Ignored: the host that set it, {host}, does not domain-match Domain={domain}, so the browser drops the whole cookie.
cookie-send-decision.storeNoneWithoutSecure: Ignored: SameSite=None without Secure is never stored.
cookie-send-decision.storeHostOnly: Stored as host-only for {domain}, with path {path}.
cookie-send-decision.storeDomain: Stored for {domain} and every host under it, with path {path}.
cookie-send-decision.storeDefaultPath: With no Path, the path is the directory of {setPath}: {path}.
cookie-send-decision.hostIdentical: {host} is identical to the cookie's domain.
cookie-send-decision.hostNotIdentical: {host} is not {domain}, and a host-only cookie goes to that exact host only.
cookie-send-decision.hostDomainMatch: {host} ends in {domain} right after a dot, so it domain-matches.
cookie-send-decision.hostIp: {host} is an IP address, which never domain-matches.
cookie-send-decision.hostNoMatch: {host} neither is {domain} nor ends in it right after a dot.
cookie-send-decision.pathIdentical: {path} is identical to the cookie's path.
cookie-send-decision.pathPrefixSlash: {path} begins with {cookiePath}, which ends in a slash.
cookie-send-decision.pathPrefixBoundary: {path} begins with {cookiePath}, and the next character is a slash.
cookie-send-decision.secureNot: Not a Secure cookie: any scheme will do.
cookie-send-decision.secureOk: Secure, and https is a secure channel.
cookie-send-decision.secureFail: Secure, and http is not a secure channel.
cookie-send-decision.httpOnlyNot: Not HttpOnly: HTTP requests and scripts both get it.
cookie-send-decision.httpOnlyHttp: HttpOnly does not hold back an HTTP request.
cookie-send-decision.httpOnlyScript: HttpOnly: hidden from document.cookie, a non-HTTP API.
cookie-send-decision.sameSiteSameSite: A same-site request: SameSite holds nothing back.
cookie-send-decision.sameSiteTopLevelGet: Cross-site, but a top-level navigation by GET, a safe method: the one exception {mode} allows.
cookie-send-decision.sameSiteStrict: Strict, and the request is cross-site.
cookie-send-decision.sameSiteUnsafe: Cross-site by POST: {mode} allows a cross-site request only as a top-level navigation with a safe method, and POST is not safe.
cookie-send-decision.sameSiteNotTopLevel: Cross-site, and not a top-level navigation: {mode} holds it back.
cookie-send-decision.sameSiteScript: The page is framed by another site, so document.cookie reads cross-site and shows only SameSite=None cookies.
cookie-send-decision.hiddenScript: Not visible to the script. The deciding rule: {rule}.
cookie-send-decision.noteDefault: No SameSite attribute: the draft's Default enforcement, which its retrieval algorithm treats like Lax. The lab follows the draft; whether a given browser applies it is for that browser's documentation to say.
cookie-send-decision.noteLaxAllowingUnsafe: A browser may waive the safe-method condition for a Default cookie created recently (the draft's Lax-allowing-unsafe mode, with two minutes named as a reasonable limit); this POST would then carry it.
cookie-send-decision.noteScriptContext: For document.cookie, cross-site means the page is framed, directly or through other frames, by a page from another site.

tcp-states.title: Step through a TCP connection's states
tcp-states.lede: Pick an opening, a close or an abort and follow it one event at a time: each end's state, the segment that moved it, in RFC 9293's own notation, and the rule. Try the server closing first, then the simultaneous close.
tcp-states.scenarioCloseClient3: Close, client first, ACK and FIN together (three segments)
tcp-states.statesAfter: Now A is {a} and B is {b}.

rule.active-open: {peer}'s application opens the connection actively: {peer} sends {sent}, the SYN taking one sequence number, and moves from {before} to {state} (RFC 9293, section 3.10.1).
rule.listen-syn: {recv} reaches {peer}, which is listening: {peer} answers {sent}, acknowledging the SYN with the number after it, and moves from {before} to {state} (section 3.10.7.2).
rule.synsent-synack: {recv} reaches {peer} and acknowledges its SYN: {peer} answers {sent} and moves from {before} to {state} (section 3.10.7.3).
rule.synrcvd-ack: {recv} reaches {peer} and acknowledges its SYN: {peer} moves from {before} to {state}. The ACK takes no sequence number, so data can start at the same number (sections 3.5 and 3.10.7.4).
rule.close-established: {peer}'s application calls CLOSE: {peer} sends {sent} and moves from {before} to {state}. It sends no more data but can still receive (section 3.10.4).
rule.close-closewait: {peer}'s application calls CLOSE in turn: {peer} sends {sent} and moves from {before} to {state}, waiting for the ACK of its FIN (section 3.10.4).
rule.fin-established: {recv} reaches {peer}: {peer} acknowledges the FIN with {sent} and moves from {before} to {state}. It may go on sending until its own application closes (sections 3.6 and 3.10.7.4).
rule.fin-established-close: {recv} reaches {peer}, whose application closes before a separate ACK goes out: one segment, {sent}, acknowledges the FIN and carries {peer}'s own. {peer} passes through {via} to {state} (sections 3.1 and 3.10.4).
rule.ack-finwait1: {recv} reaches {peer} and acknowledges its FIN: {peer} moves from {before} to {state} and waits for the other end's FIN (section 3.10.7.4).
rule.fin-finwait1: {recv} reaches {peer} before the ACK of its own FIN: {peer} acknowledges it with {sent} and moves from {before} to {state} (section 3.10.7.4).
rule.finack-finwait1: {recv} reaches {peer} with a FIN and the ACK of {peer}'s FIN together: {peer} answers {sent} and goes from {before} through {via} to {state} (section 3.3.2, Figure 5, note 2).
rule.fin-finwait2: {recv} reaches {peer}: {peer} acknowledges it with {sent}, moves from {before} to {state} and starts its 2 × MSL timer (section 3.10.7.4).
rule.ack-closing: {recv} reaches {peer} and acknowledges its FIN: {peer} moves from {before} to {state} and starts its 2 × MSL timer (section 3.10.7.4).
rule.ack-lastack: {recv} reaches {peer} and acknowledges its FIN: {peer} deletes the connection and moves from {before} to {state} at once, with no TIME-WAIT (section 3.10.7.4).
rule.timewait-timeout: 2 × MSL later, {seconds} s with the MSL of {msl} s that RFC 9293 takes, {peer}'s TIME-WAIT timer expires: {peer} deletes the connection and moves to {state} (sections 3.4.2, 3.6.1 and 3.10.8).
rule.abort: {peer}'s application aborts: {peer} sends {sent}, flushes everything queued, deletes the connection and moves from {before} to {state} (section 3.10.5).
rule.rst-received: {recv} reaches {peer} carrying exactly the sequence number it expects, so the reset is valid: {peer} tells its application the connection was reset and moves from {before} to {state} (sections 3.5.3 and 3.10.7.4).

tcp-states.verdictOpen: Three segments and both ends are ESTABLISHED: data can now flow both ways.
tcp-states.verdictCloseClient: The client closed first, so the client is the end that waited in TIME-WAIT, {seconds} s; the server was CLOSED as soon as its FIN was acknowledged.
tcp-states.verdictCloseClient3: Three segments instead of four: the server's FIN carried the ACK, so the client went straight from FIN-WAIT-1 to TIME-WAIT, where it still waited {seconds} s.
tcp-states.verdictCloseServer: The server closed first, so this time the server waited in TIME-WAIT, {seconds} s, as it will for every connection it closes first; the client was CLOSED at the last ACK.
tcp-states.verdictSimultaneous: Both ends closed at once, both went through CLOSING, and both waited in TIME-WAIT, {seconds} s each.
tcp-states.verdictAbort: One RST and both ends are CLOSED: no FIN exchange, nothing still queued is delivered, and no TIME-WAIT in this model.
tcp-states.moreSteps: {left, plural, one {One more step} other {# more steps}} to the end of this scenario.
tcp-states.noteWaitingBoth: Both ends now sit in TIME-WAIT, each for 2 × MSL, {seconds} s, before deleting the connection.
tcp-states.noteWaitingOne: {peer} now sits in TIME-WAIT for 2 × MSL, {seconds} s, before deleting the connection: {peer} is the end that closed first.
tcp-states.noteAbort: RFC 9293 also says, in section 3.5.2, that the side issuing a reset should enter TIME-WAIT to lighten the load on busy servers. The ABORT call's own processing, in section 3.10.5, enters CLOSED, which is what the lab shows.
tcp-states.scope: data and retransmissions, lost segments, the simultaneous open, a RST answering a SYN for a port with no listener, half-duplex closes, RFC 5961's checks, reopening a connection from TIME-WAIT, and the TIME-WAIT each operating system really uses: the lab takes RFC 9293's MSL of 2 minutes, an engineering choice of the specification, not any system's setting.

tcp-congestion-window.title: Follow the congestion window round trip by round trip
tcp-congestion-window.lede: Set the segment size, the initial window, ssthresh and the round trip in which a segment is lost, and watch cwnd grow and fall under RFC 5681's rules. Then let the timer find the same loss instead of three duplicate ACKs.
tcp-congestion-window.iwOne: One segment: the SYN or SYN-ACK was lost
tcp-congestion-window.lossRound: Loss in round trip (0 for none)
tcp-congestion-window.kvLossValue: round trip {round}, in a window of {flight} bytes
tcp-congestion-window.iwLine5681Small: an SMSS of {smss} bytes is 1,095 bytes or less, so RFC 5681 allows at most 4 segments: IW = {iw} bytes, {segs} × SMSS (section 3.1).
tcp-congestion-window.iwLine5681Mid: an SMSS of {smss} bytes is over 1,095 and at most 2,190 bytes, so RFC 5681 allows at most 3 segments: IW = {iw} bytes, {segs} × SMSS (section 3.1).
tcp-congestion-window.iwLine5681Large: an SMSS of {smss} bytes is over 2,190 bytes, so RFC 5681 allows at most 2 segments: IW = {iw} bytes, {segs} × SMSS (section 3.1).
tcp-congestion-window.iwLine6928: RFC 6928 allows min(10 × MSS, max(2 × MSS, 14,600)), read here with the SMSS as the MSS: {iw} bytes, {segs} × SMSS; the lab takes that bound as the window (RFC 6928, section 2, an Experimental RFC).
tcp-congestion-window.iwLineOne: the SYN or the SYN-ACK was lost, so the initial window is one segment: {iw} bytes (RFC 5681, section 3.1).
tcp-congestion-window.ssLineCapped: slow start adds up to one SMSS per ACK, so with an ACK for every segment cwnd doubles each round trip. It reaches ssthresh, {ss} bytes, in round trip {round}: the lab stops the doubling there, and with cwnd at ssthresh it uses congestion avoidance, one SMSS per round trip (section 3.1).
tcp-congestion-window.ssLineNever: slow start adds up to one SMSS per ACK, so with an ACK for every segment cwnd doubles each round trip; here it does not reach ssthresh, {ss} bytes, before the loss or the end of the table (section 3.1).
tcp-congestion-window.ssLineNone: the initial window is already at or above ssthresh, {ss} bytes, so congestion avoidance runs from the first round trip: one SMSS per round trip (section 3.1).
tcp-congestion-window.lossLine: one segment of the {flight}-byte window of round trip {round} is lost. That window is the FlightSize, so ssthresh = max(FlightSize / 2, 2 × SMSS) = max({half}, {two}) = {ss} bytes (RFC 5681, equation 4).
tcp-congestion-window.dupacksLine: in round trip {r1} three duplicate ACKs arrive: the missing segment is resent at once and cwnd = ssthresh + 3 × SMSS = {inflated} bytes, one SMSS more for each further duplicate ACK (section 3.2). In round trip {r2} the ACK for new data deflates cwnd to ssthresh, {ss} bytes, and congestion avoidance goes on.
tcp-congestion-window.timeoutLine: the retransmission timer expires: cwnd falls to the loss window, one segment of {smss} bytes, whatever the initial window was, and slow start runs again from round trip {r1} until ssthresh, {ss} bytes, in round trip {back} (section 3.1).
tcp-congestion-window.verdictDupacks: found by duplicate ACKs, cwnd is back at ssthresh in round trip {back}. Found by the timer, the same loss would restart from one segment and get back only in round trip {otherBack}, {diff, plural, one {one round trip} other {# round trips}} later, after the wait for the timer itself.
tcp-congestion-window.verdictTimeout: found by the timer, cwnd is back at ssthresh only in round trip {back}, and the wait for the timer comes on top. Found by three duplicate ACKs, the same loss would have it back in round trip {otherBack}, {diff, plural, one {one round trip} other {# round trips}} sooner.
tcp-congestion-window.verdictForced: with one segment in flight only the timer can find the loss: cwnd restarts from one segment and is back at ssthresh in round trip {back}.
tcp-congestion-window.verdictNoLoss: no loss: after {rounds} round trips cwnd is {cwnd} bytes.
tcp-congestion-window.noteForced: One segment was in flight, so nothing followed the lost one and no duplicate ACK could come back: a receiver sends one only when a segment arrives (RFC 5681, section 3.2). The timer found this loss.

ev.deflated: ACK for new data: cwnd = ssthresh

tcp-congestion-window.errorSmss: Enter the SMSS as a whole number of bytes from 1 to {max}.
tcp-congestion-window.errorSsthresh: Enter ssthresh as a whole number of bytes from 1 to {max} (1 GiB).
tcp-congestion-window.errorLossRound: Enter the round trip of the loss as a whole number from 0 (no loss) to {max}.
tcp-congestion-window.errorChoice: Choose one of the options offered.
tcp-congestion-window.scope: CUBIC (RFC 9438), which that RFC says the Linux, Windows and Apple stacks use by default, and every other algorithm; the receiver's window; delayed ACKs; the count of inflation steps during fast recovery; limited transmit; more than one loss; SACK; and how long the retransmission timer takes. Each round trip sends a full window and every segment is acknowledged.

nat-pat-table.title: Build a NAPT translation table and test an inbound packet
nat-pat-table.lede: Five UDP flows from three inside hosts leave through one NAPT. Set the public addresses, the outside port range and the mapping and filtering behaviours, then send a packet in from outside. Try a range of three ports, 51234 to 51236, to watch it run out.
nat-pat-table.inbound: Inbound packet to flow 1's outside port
nat-pat-table.kindPreservedOther: new mapping, inside port kept on the second address
nat-pat-table.kindChangedTaken: new mapping, port changed: the inside port is taken
nat-pat-table.kindChangedRange: new mapping, port changed: the inside port is outside the range
nat-pat-table.kindDroppedPaired: refused: its paired address has no free port (RFC 7857, section 4)
nat-pat-table.lookupLine: {from} sends to {to}. The table maps that outside address and port to {inside}.
nat-pat-table.filterLineEif: endpoint-independent filtering forwards any packet sent to a mapped inside endpoint, whoever sent it (RFC 4787, section 5).
nat-pat-table.filterLineAdf: address-dependent filtering forwards it only if {inside} has already sent to {addr}, on any port. It has sent to {sentTo} (RFC 4787, section 5).
nat-pat-table.filterLineApdf: address and port-dependent filtering forwards it only if {inside} has already sent to {from} itself. It has sent to {sentTo} (RFC 4787, section 5).
nat-pat-table.verdictDropped: dropped: the NAT keeps {from} out and {inside} never sees the packet.
nat-pat-table.noteReused: Flows 1 and 4 share one outside port: under endpoint-independent mapping, the address and port a STUN server reports for flow 4 are the ones every destination sees.
nat-pat-table.noteOwnMapping: Flow 4 got an outside port of its own, {port}: the address and port a STUN server reports for it are not the ones the first server sees.
nat-pat-table.notePortChoice: Where a port was changed, the lab took the next free port upward, wrapping round the range: the lab's choice, not a standard. RFC 7857, section 9, asks a NAPT to obfuscate the replacement port instead.
nat-pat-table.errorPort: Enter each port as a whole number from {min} to {max}.
nat-pat-table.errorRange: The first port must not be above the last.
nat-pat-table.errorChoice: Choose one of the options offered.
nat-pat-table.scope: mapping timers and refresh, TCP and ICMP, hairpinning, port parity and contiguity, the port overlapping RFC 7857 allows, random port choice, ALGs and static port forwarding. The five flows leave in a fixed order and every mapping stays alive.

vrrp-master-election.title: Elect the Active Router and time each failover
vrrp-master-election.lede: Two to four routers back up one gateway, 192.0.2.1, with VRRP version 3 (RFC 9568); their own addresses rise from 192.0.2.2 with their numbers. Set their priorities, preemption and advertisement interval, then fail, shut down or start routers, and see who forwards after each event, how long the change took and which rule decided it.
vrrp-master-election.priority: Priority of R{r} (1 to 254; 255 makes it the address owner)
vrrp-master-election.preemptOn: True, the default: a higher-priority Backup takes over
vrrp-master-election.interval: Advertisement_Interval, in centiseconds (100 is one second)
vrrp-master-election.lateRouter: R{r}: it joins when an event starts it
vrrp-master-election.eventShutdown: the Active Router shuts down cleanly (sends priority 0)
vrrp-master-election.startOwner: R{r} has priority 255 and owns 192.0.2.1, so it sends an ADVERTISEMENT and is Active at once; every other router hears priority 255 and stays Backup.
vrrp-master-election.startElected: No router owns the address, so every router starts as Backup and waits for its own Active_Down_Interval. R{r}, at priority {p}, has the shortest, {time}: its timer fires first, it becomes Active, and the others hear its ADVERTISEMENT and stay Backup.
vrrp-master-election.startTie: No router owns the address, so every router starts as Backup and waits for its own Active_Down_Interval: {time} for the top priority.
vrrp-master-election.startAlone: R{r} is the only router running. It starts as Backup, hears no ADVERTISEMENT and becomes Active when its Active_Down_Interval, {time}, runs out.
vrrp-master-election.failover: R{f} fails without a word. The Backups stop hearing ADVERTISEMENTs, and the highest priority has the shortest Active_Down_Interval: R{r}, at priority {p}, becomes Active {time} after the last ADVERTISEMENT it heard.
vrrp-master-election.shutdownHandover: R{f} shuts down and sends an ADVERTISEMENT with priority 0, which sets every Backup's timer to its Skew_Time: R{r}, at priority {p}, becomes Active after {time}.
vrrp-master-election.noneLeft: R{f} stops and no router is left running: nothing answers for 192.0.2.1.
vrrp-master-election.nothingToStop: No router is Active, so there is nothing to stop.
vrrp-master-election.ownerPreempts: R{r} starts. It owns the address, so it becomes Active at once whatever Preempt_Mode says, and R{prev}, hearing priority 255, goes back to Backup.
vrrp-master-election.ownerAlone: R{r} starts. It owns the address and becomes Active at once.
vrrp-master-election.startAloneLater: R{r} starts as Backup. No router is Active, so no ADVERTISEMENT resets its timer: it becomes Active after {time}.
vrrp-master-election.preempts: R{r} starts as Backup at priority {p}, above R{prev}'s {pp}. Preempt_Mode is True, so it discards R{prev}'s ADVERTISEMENTs; its own timer runs out after {time}, it becomes Active, and R{prev}, hearing the higher priority, goes back to Backup.
vrrp-master-election.staysLower: R{r} starts as Backup at priority {p}. R{prev}'s ADVERTISEMENTs carry {pp}, higher than its own, so each one resets its timer: R{prev} stays Active.
vrrp-master-election.staysEqual: R{r} starts as Backup at priority {p}, the same as R{prev}. An ADVERTISEMENT of greater or equal priority resets a Backup's timer, so R{prev} stays Active: the higher address breaks a tie only between two Active Routers.
vrrp-master-election.staysNoPreempt: R{r} starts as Backup at priority {p}, above R{prev}'s {pp}, but Preempt_Mode is False: it accepts R{prev}'s ADVERTISEMENTs and stays Backup, and R{prev} keeps the gateway.
vrrp-master-election.alreadyRunning: R{r} is already running, so nothing changes.
vrrp-master-election.tieLine: {list} share the top priority, {p}: their timers fire together, all of them become Active, and each one that hears an equal priority from a higher primary address steps back, which leaves R{r} ({addr}).
vrrp-master-election.runnerUp: The next in line, R{r} at priority {p}, would have waited {time}.
vrrp-master-election.verdictActive: After the last event R{r}, at priority {p}, is the Active Router and forwards for 192.0.2.1.
vrrp-master-election.verdictKept: After the last event R{r}, at priority {p}, is still the Active Router although R{best}, at priority {bp}, is running: with Preempt_Mode False a higher-priority Backup does not take the role back.
vrrp-master-election.verdictNone: After the last event no router is Active: the hosts have lost their default gateway.
vrrp-master-election.noteTerms: RFC 9568 says Active Router, Active_Adver_Interval and Active_Down_Interval; RFC 5798 said Master, Master_Adver_Interval and Master_Down_Interval, and router output such as FRR's still says Master.
vrrp-master-election.errorPriority: Give R{r} a whole-number priority from 1 to 255; 0 is reserved for an Active Router that is giving up the role.
vrrp-master-election.errorTwoOwners: Only one router can own the address with priority 255; RFC 9568 says a single router on the link should have it.
vrrp-master-election.errorInterval: Give the interval in whole centiseconds, from 1 to {max} (RFC 9568, erratum 8301).
vrrp-master-election.errorOther: These settings do not describe a group the lab can run.
vrrp-master-election.scope: propagation and queueing delay (timers that expire together fire at the same instant here), different intervals on different routers, Accept_Mode, tracking and other vendor features, IPv6, the gratuitous ARP and the switches relearning the virtual MAC address, and HSRP.

lacp-hashing.title: Hash flows onto a bond's members
lacp-hashing.lede: A Linux server, 192.0.2.10, sends over an LACP bond of 1 Gb/s links, choosing each flow's member with the Linux bonding driver's documented transmit hash. Choose how many members, the hash policy and the flows, fail a member, and see where every flow goes and what moves.
lacp-hashing.flowRouted: {id}, {kind}: port {sp} to {ip} port {dp}, {mbps} Mb/s, through the router
lacp-hashing.flowLan: {id}, {kind}: port {sp} to {ip} port {dp}, {mbps} Mb/s, on the same LAN
lacp-hashing.workTitle: How the hash of {id} is worked out under {policy}, as the Linux bonding HOWTO writes it:
lacp-hashing.workMacs: MAC[5] of the server ({s}) XOR MAC[5] of the destination ({d}) XOR the packet type ID, 0x0800 for IPv4 = {v}
lacp-hashing.workPorts: source port {sp} and destination port {dp}, as in the header = {v}
lacp-hashing.workIps: XOR source IP {sip} ({sx}) XOR destination IP {dip} ({dx}) = {v}
lacp-hashing.workModulo: {hash} modulo {n} members = {m}, so the flow uses member {m}
lacp-hashing.workModuloAfter: with member {f} down, {hash} modulo {n} = {i}, and the surviving members, numbered again from 0, make that member {m}
lacp-hashing.afterMoved: {m}, moved although its member is up
lacp-hashing.loadOver: {v} Mb/s, more than the link carries
lacp-hashing.verdictNoFlows: No flow is running: tick at least one.
lacp-hashing.verdictLoad: Member {m} is the busiest, with {load} of the {total} Mb/s offered ({share}); an even spread would give each member {even}.
lacp-hashing.verdictOver: Member {m} is offered {load} of the {total} Mb/s ({share}), more than its {cap} Mb/s, while an even spread would give each member {even}.
lacp-hashing.verdictFailure: With member {f} down, flows that change member: {moved} of {count}; of those, {up} whose own member is still up.
lacp-hashing.noteShared: {ids} share member {m}. The same flows go to: under layer2, {l2}; under layer2+3, {l23}; under layer3+4, {l34}.
lacp-hashing.noteSameHosts: Some of them run between the same two hosts, and a policy that reads only addresses puts all traffic to one peer on one member; only layer3+4, which adds the ports, can separate them.
lacp-hashing.noteGateway: Every flow through the router is addressed to the router's MAC address, so layer2, which reads only MAC addresses, puts all of them on one member.
lacp-hashing.noteMoved: {ids} moved although their own member stayed up: the hash is now reduced modulo {n}, over the surviving members numbered again from 0.
lacp-hashing.scope: the byte-order switch reads the addresses and the ports most significant byte first, as the HOWTO writes its formulas (what a big-endian processor computes), or least significant first, as a little-endian processor loads them; which fields count, the folding, the modulo and the reshuffle after a failure are the same on both. Also left out: IPv6, fragments and non-IP traffic, the encap and vlan+srcmac policies, the switch's own hash for traffic coming back, LACP negotiation and aggregator selection, and flows whose rate changes.
lacp-hashing.orderBig: As the HOWTO writes it (a big-endian processor)
lacp-hashing.orderNote: A 32-bit value takes four bytes: a big-endian processor stores its most significant byte at the lowest address, a little-endian one its least significant. Of the Linux architectures Debian lists, amd64, arm64, ppc64el, riscv64 and loong64 are little-endian; s390x, ppc64, mips and sparc64 are big-endian. The driver XORs the addresses and the ports as raw words loaded from the header, so the two give different hashes for the same flow, and the member can differ only when the member count is not a power of two: Big-endian and little-endian.
lacp-hashing.workTitleLittle: How the hash of {id} is worked out under {policy} on a little-endian processor, which loads each address and the two ports least significant byte first:
lacp-hashing.workPortsLittle: source port {sp} and destination port {dp}, their four header bytes loaded least significant first = {v}
lacp-hashing.workIpsLittle: XOR source IP {sip} ({sx}) XOR destination IP {dip} ({dx}), each loaded least significant byte first = {v}

wifi-airtime.title: Price each client's frames in airtime
wifi-airtime.lede: Up to four clients share one channel, each at its own data rate and frame size. Every frame is priced with the 802.11ac timings HPE Aruba Networking publishes, then each client sends one frame in turn: see how long each frame holds the channel and how much of it a slow client takes.
wifi-airtime.workTitle: The frame of client {n}, part by part ({rate}):
wifi-airtime.workProtection: an RTS of 20 bytes and a CTS of 14 bytes, each after a 20 μs legacy preamble, sent at {ctl} Mb/s and followed by a 16 μs SIFS: {v}
wifi-airtime.workPreambleVht: the 20 μs legacy preamble and the 24 μs VHT preamble, both at 6 Mb/s: {v}
wifi-airtime.workPreambleLegacy: the 20 μs legacy preamble, at 6 Mb/s: {v}
wifi-airtime.workPayloadVht: {bytes} bytes plus the 4-byte A-MPDU delimiter, times 8, divided by {mbps} Mb/s: {v}
wifi-airtime.workBlockAck: a 16 μs SIFS, then a 32-byte Block Ack at {ctl} Mb/s after its own 20 μs legacy preamble: {v}
wifi-airtime.workAck: a 16 μs SIFS, then a 14-byte Ack at {ctl} Mb/s after its own 20 μs legacy preamble: {v}
wifi-airtime.workTotal: {v} on the air, of which the payload is {share}.
wifi-airtime.kvRound: One round (one frame from each client)
wifi-airtime.kvCell: Payload the cell moves per second of airtime
wifi-airtime.verdictAlone: Client {n} alone: each frame holds the channel for {v}, so the cell moves {cell} Mb/s of payload.
wifi-airtime.verdictFair: Client {n} ({rate}) is the slowest and holds {share} of each round; the cell moves {cell} Mb/s of payload, {without} Mb/s without it.
wifi-airtime.verdictHog: Client {n} ({rate}) holds {share} of each round, more than twice an even share: the cell moves {cell} Mb/s of payload, against {without} Mb/s without it.
wifi-airtime.errorBytes: Give client {n} a frame size in whole bytes, from {min} to {max}.
wifi-airtime.errorOther: Choose one of the rates offered.
wifi-airtime.scope: the arbitration before each frame (AIFS and the random contention window), retries, several MPDUs aggregated into one A-MPDU, the service field, padding and tail bits around the payload (drawn in the guide's preamble figure), longer VHT preambles for more spatial streams, control rates other than the 6 Mb/s default, 802.11b clients, whose preamble times the documents read do not give, and 802.11n, 802.11ax and 802.11be clients.

bgp-best-path.title: Walk the BGP best-path decision
bgp-best-path.lede: Your router, in AS 64496, holds two to four paths to one prefix. Edit each path, choose the decision process and follow it step by step: which step removes which path, and which step decides.
bgp-best-path.scope: import policy itself (LOCAL_PREF is typed in, and RFC 8212's rule that an eBGP route with no import policy is ineligible is not applied), AS_SET and confederations, several paths from one peer, multipath, Cisco's step 3 (paths the router originated itself) and knobs such as bgp always-compare-med, and other vendors' orders. The Cisco profile compares MED as with bgp deterministic-med, takes the path that was best before this run to be the oldest, and applies each step to all remaining paths at once, where Cisco compares them in pairs.
bgp-best-path.learnedRr: an iBGP peer, reflected by a route reflector
bgp-best-path.originatorId: ORIGINATOR_ID (the router that originated it in the AS)
bgp-best-path.excludeNone: every NEXT_HOP resolves and no AS_PATH contains AS {as}.
bgp-best-path.excludeOwnAs: {path} (its AS_PATH contains AS {as}, this router's own: a loop)
bgp-best-path.excludeList: {count, plural, one {{list} is excluded.} other {{list} are excluded.}}
bgp-best-path.medGroups: {groups}. MED is compared only within each neighbouring AS.
bgp-best-path.decided: {count, plural, one {Removed: {list}.} other {Removed: {list}.}} Only {best} is left.
bgp-best-path.keepNoPrevious: no path was best before this run, so there is nothing to keep.
bgp-best-path.keepNotInContention: path {path}, the best before this run, is already out, so the rule does not apply.
bgp-best-path.keepNotExternal: the paths left are internal; the rule applies only between external paths.
bgp-best-path.keepWinsAnyway: path {path}, the best before this run, also wins on the steps that follow.
bgp-best-path.keepSameId: the steps that follow would choose {wouldBe}, which shares its BGP Identifier with {path}, so the rule is not applied.
bgp-best-path.keepApplied: the steps that follow would choose {wouldBe}, but {path}, the external path that was best before this run, is kept.
bgp-best-path.ciscoNoPrevious: skipped: there is no current best path.
bgp-best-path.ciscoNotExternal: skipped: the paths left are internal.
bgp-best-path.ciscoSameId: skipped: the paths left come from the same router ID as {path}.
bgp-best-path.ciscoApplied: {path} was received first (the path that was best before this run arrived first, the others in the order A, B, C, D), so it is preferred over the newer external paths.
bgp-best-path.verdictOnly: Best path: {path}, the only path left after the exclusions.
bgp-best-path.verdictNone: No best path: every path was excluded.
bgp-best-path.noteMed: {path} wins with MED {med}, although {count, plural, one {path {others} had a lower one} other {paths {others} had lower ones}}: MED is compared only between paths from the same neighbouring AS (RFC 4271, section 9.1.2.2).
bgp-best-path.noteCisco: Cisco profile: no path here was originated by this router, so step 3 never applies; step 9 (multipath) does not change the best path; MED is compared as with bgp deterministic-med (Cisco document 13759).
bgp-best-path.errorChoice: Choose one of the options offered.
bgp-best-path.errorLocalPref: Path {path}: LOCAL_PREF is a whole number from 0 to 4294967295.
bgp-best-path.errorAsPath: Path {path}: AS_PATH takes AS numbers from 1 to 4294967295, separated by spaces (at most 20 in this lab).
bgp-best-path.errorEbgpEmpty: Path {path}: an eBGP peer always puts its own AS in the AS_PATH, so it cannot be empty.
bgp-best-path.errorMed: Path {path}: MED is empty, or a whole number from 0 to 4294967295.
bgp-best-path.errorCost: Path {path}: enter the IGP cost as a whole number, from 0 to 4294967295 in this lab.
bgp-best-path.errorId: Path {path}: the BGP Identifier is four numbers from 0 to 255 separated by dots, and not 0.0.0.0.
bgp-best-path.errorPeer: Path {path}: the peer address is four numbers from 0 to 255 separated by dots, and not 0.0.0.0.
bgp-best-path.errorOriginator: Path {path}: a reflected path needs an ORIGINATOR_ID, four numbers from 0 to 255 separated by dots, and not 0.0.0.0.
bgp-best-path.errorDuplicatePeer: Path {path}: another path already comes from this peer address. Give each path its own peer.
bgp-best-path.errorCiscoOwnAs: Path {path}: Cisco documents the own-AS check for eBGP paths only, so the lab does not model an iBGP path carrying AS {as}.

ospf-neighbour-and-dr.title: Elect the DR and see who becomes adjacent
ospf-neighbour-and-dr.lede: Three to five routers share one Ethernet segment in one area. Set each router's priority, Router ID and turn to come up, configure one parameter differently on one router, or make the DR fail, and see the election, then which pairs reach Full and which stop at 2-Way.
ospf-neighbour-and-dr.scope: timers and how long each step takes, NBMA and point-to-point networks, the network-LSA and flooding, a failed router that comes back, more than one mismatch at a time, authentication keys (only the type is compared), and vendor behaviour that departs from RFC 2328. Routers that share a turn are taken to come up within one Wait Timer of each other.
ospf-neighbour-and-dr.routersCaption: Each router's priority, Router ID and turn to come up (the same turn: together)
ospf-neighbour-and-dr.mismatchEbit: E-bit (stub area on one side only)
ospf-neighbour-and-dr.whereUp: {n, selectordinal, one {#st} two {#nd} few {#rd} other {#th}} turn:
ospf-neighbour-and-dr.upElect: {routers} {count, plural, one {comes} other {come}} up with no DR declared; when the Wait Timer ends, the eligible routers elect {dr} as DR and {bdr} as BDR.
ospf-neighbour-and-dr.upElectNoBdr: {routers} {count, plural, one {comes} other {come}} up with no DR declared; {dr} is the only eligible router, so it becomes DR and there is no BDR.
ospf-neighbour-and-dr.upNoEligible: {routers} {count, plural, one {comes} other {come}} up; with priority 0, no one is eligible, so there is no DR or BDR.
ospf-neighbour-and-dr.upAccept: {routers} {count, plural, one {comes up and finds} other {come up and find}} DR {dr} and BDR {bdr} already declared in the Hellos, and {count, plural, one {accepts} other {accept}} them.
ospf-neighbour-and-dr.upAcceptNoBdrStill: {routers} {count, plural, one {comes up and finds} other {come up and find}} DR {dr} declared and no BDR; none of the newcomers is eligible, so there is still no BDR.
ospf-neighbour-and-dr.upAcceptFillBdr: {routers} {count, plural, one {comes up and finds} other {come up and find}} DR {dr} declared and no BDR, so the empty seat is filled: {bdr} becomes BDR, and {dr} stays DR.
ospf-neighbour-and-dr.upOutranked: {routers} {count, plural, one {outranks} other {outrank}} {dr} on priority and Router ID, but the election is not pre-emptive.
ospf-neighbour-and-dr.upIsolated: {router} comes up too, but every Hello between it and the others is dropped ({param} differs). It hears no neighbour and, alone when its Wait Timer ends, declares itself DR, with no BDR.
ospf-neighbour-and-dr.upIsolatedIneligible: {router} comes up too, but every Hello between it and the others is dropped ({param} differs). It hears no neighbour, and with priority 0 it cannot even elect itself.
ospf-neighbour-and-dr.failPromote: {dr}, the DR, goes down. BDR {bdr} becomes DR, and only then is a new BDR chosen from the routers left: {newBdr}.
ospf-neighbour-and-dr.failPromoteNoBdr: {dr}, the DR, goes down. BDR {bdr} becomes DR; no router left is eligible, so there is no new BDR.
ospf-neighbour-and-dr.failElect: {dr}, the DR, goes down with no BDR to take over; the routers left elect {newDr} as DR and {newBdr} as BDR.
ospf-neighbour-and-dr.failElectNoBdr: {dr}, the DR, goes down with no BDR to take over; {newDr}, the only eligible router left, becomes DR and there is no BDR.
ospf-neighbour-and-dr.failNoEligible: {dr}, the DR, goes down with no BDR to take over, and no router left is eligible: the segment has no DR and no BDR.
ospf-neighbour-and-dr.roleIsolatedDr: DR of its own, unseen (no neighbours)
ospf-neighbour-and-dr.verdict: {full, plural, =0 {No pair reaches Full} one {One pair reaches Full} other {# pairs reach Full}}; {twoWay, plural, =0 {none stops at 2-Way} one {one stops at 2-Way} other {# stop at 2-Way}}.
ospf-neighbour-and-dr.verdictStuck: {stuck, plural, one {One pair is} other {# pairs are}} stuck before Full.
ospf-neighbour-and-dr.verdictNoNeighbour: {none, plural, one {One pair never becomes} other {# pairs never become}} neighbours.
ospf-neighbour-and-dr.noteTop: {router} ranks highest on the segment (priority {priority}, Router ID {id}) yet is {role}: a declared DR and BDR keep their roles when a router that ranks higher comes up later (RFC 2328, sections 7.3 and 9.4).
ospf-neighbour-and-dr.noteNoDr: With no DR and no BDR, no pair on the segment becomes adjacent (RFC 2328, section 10.4).
ospf-neighbour-and-dr.noteMtu: The MTU is not in the Hello, so the election is untouched. Only pairs that try to become adjacent exchange Database Description packets, and those across the mismatch get no further (RFC 2328, section 10.6).
ospf-neighbour-and-dr.noteTwoDrs: {lone} and {dr} both call themselves DR on one segment, each unaware of the other.
ospf-neighbour-and-dr.errorPriority: {router}: Router Priority is a whole number from 0 to 255.
ospf-neighbour-and-dr.errorRouterId: {router}: enter the Router ID as four numbers from 0 to 255 separated by dots, not 0.0.0.0.
ospf-neighbour-and-dr.errorDuplicate: {router}: another router already uses this Router ID; each router needs its own.
ospf-neighbour-and-dr.errorChoice: Choose one of the options offered.

bigip-vs-precedence.title: Find the virtual server that takes a connection
bigip-vs-precedence.lede: Define three to five BIG-IP virtual servers and one new connection, and see which virtual servers match it and which one takes it: destination first, then source, then port, as F5's K14800 orders them for BIG-IP 11.3.0 and later. Write addresses as address/mask (a host is /32) or * for the wildcard. Try the Example: K14800's own case, where the virtual server with the right port and the client's source loses to a network destination.
bigip-vs-precedence.scope: versions of BIG-IP before 11.3.0, which had no source address and compared the longest destination subnet, then the port (K6459); address lists and port lists, which K14800 refers to without saying how they rank; route domains, which K14800 does not mention; IPv6; the protocol, taken to be the same for every virtual server; the virtual server's type; a disabled virtual server and the tm.continuematching variable (K8009); NATs and SNATs (K9038); and what BIG-IP does with a packet no virtual server takes.
bigip-vs-precedence.virtualsCaption: Each virtual server: destination and source as address/mask or *, port as a number or *
bigip-vs-precedence.candidatesSome: {count, plural, one {# virtual server matches} other {# virtual servers match}} the packet's destination, source and port: {list}.
bigip-vs-precedence.candidatesNone: No virtual server matches the packet's destination, source and port.
bigip-vs-precedence.destinationDecides: {kept} {keptCount, plural, one {has} other {have}} the most specific destination ({best}); {dropped} {droppedCount, plural, one {drops} other {drop}} out.
bigip-vs-precedence.destinationTie: {kept} share the same destination ({best}), so the source decides.
bigip-vs-precedence.sourceDecides: {kept} {keptCount, plural, one {has} other {have}} the most specific source ({best}); {dropped} {droppedCount, plural, one {drops} other {drop}} out.
bigip-vs-precedence.sourceTie: {kept} share the same source ({best}), so the port decides.
bigip-vs-precedence.portDecides: {kept} names port {port}; {dropped} {droppedCount, plural, one {listens} other {listen}} on every port and {droppedCount, plural, one {drops} other {drop}} out.
bigip-vs-precedence.verdictWinner: {vs} takes the packet. K14800 row {row}: destination {dest}, source {src}, port {port}.
bigip-vs-precedence.verdictNone: No virtual server takes the packet, so K14800 has nothing to rank. What BIG-IP then does with it is outside this lab.
bigip-vs-precedence.notePortLoses: {loser} names port {port} and still loses: the destination is compared first and then the source, and the port only breaks a tie that is left. {winner} listens on every port.
bigip-vs-precedence.noteConflict: By K14800's rows alone, {table} (row {tableRow}) would come before {winner} (row {winRow}), because the table counts every network address as one class. The lab compares the masks, as K14800's examples word it (the closest subnet wins) and as K9038 states for destinations (the more specific address and netmask win). F5 publishes no worked example of this case: confirm it on your version.
bigip-vs-precedence.errorDestination: {vs}: write the destination as address/mask (192.168.1.0/24), a single address (a host) or * (the wildcard).
bigip-vs-precedence.errorSource: {vs}: write the source as address/mask (192.168.2.0/24), a single address (a host) or * (the wildcard).
bigip-vs-precedence.errorHostBitsDestination: {vs}: the destination has bits set beyond its mask; write the network address itself (192.168.1.0/24, not 192.168.1.5/24).
bigip-vs-precedence.errorHostBitsSource: {vs}: the source has bits set beyond its mask; write the network address itself (192.168.2.0/24, not 192.168.2.5/24).
bigip-vs-precedence.errorPort: {vs}: the port must be a number from 1 to 65535, or * for every port.
bigip-vs-precedence.errorDuplicate: {vs} has the same destination, source and port as another virtual server; make each one different.
bigip-vs-precedence.errorPacketSource: The packet's source must be a single address, such as 192.168.2.1.
bigip-vs-precedence.errorPacketDestination: The packet's destination must be a single address without a mask, such as 192.168.1.200.
bigip-vs-precedence.errorPacketPort: The packet's port must be a number from 1 to 65535.

fortigate-session-dirty.title: Change a FortiGate policy under a live session
fortigate-session-dirty.lede: A session is flowing through a FortiGate, accepted by one firewall policy, when an administrator changes the policies. Set firewall-session-dirty and the change, and see whether the session is flagged dirty and re-evaluated at its next packet, and dropped if it is no longer allowed, or keeps flowing until it ends, with the FortiOS 7.6 document behind each step. Try the Example: a policy edited to deny under check-new.
fortigate-session-dirty.scope: route changes and other changes that are not policy changes; NGFW policy-based mode, where only check-all is available; strict-dirty-session-check disabled (the lab keeps its default, enabled); another policy lower down that would also accept the traffic; hardware offload; how soon the session's next packet arrives; and how long a blocked session stays in the session table. Under check-policy-option, a new deny policy above the accepting one is a change to another policy, and Fortinet's documents do not say whose option then governs, so the lab does not decide.
fortigate-session-dirty.policy: config firewall policy: firewall-session-dirty on the accepting policy
fortigate-session-dirty.openedBefore: before check-new was set, under check-all
fortigate-session-dirty.changeEditToDeny: edits the policy's action to deny
fortigate-session-dirty.changeNarrow: changes its addresses or services so the session no longer matches
fortigate-session-dirty.changeDenyAbove: adds a deny policy above it that matches the session
fortigate-session-dirty.changeStillMatches: adds an address to it; the session still matches
fortigate-session-dirty.kvFlags: Session marks in diagnose sys session list
fortigate-session-dirty.flagsDirty: may_dirty, then dirty may_dirty after the change
fortigate-session-dirty.flagsNotNamed: not named in Fortinet's documents for this case
fortigate-session-dirty.kvNewSession: A new session with the same addresses and ports
fortigate-session-dirty.beforeGlobalAll: A firewall policy accepted the session's first packet. Under check-all the session carries the may_dirty mark (Technical Tip: Information about firewall-session-dirty).
fortigate-session-dirty.beforeGlobalNew: A firewall policy accepted the session's first packet after check-new was set, so the session is flagged persistent (FortiOS 7.6.0 Best Practices, Policy configuration changes).
fortigate-session-dirty.beforeGlobalNewOlder: The session opened under check-all, before check-new was set. Changing the setting revalidates nothing and does not make older sessions persistent (Technical Tip: Information about firewall-session-dirty; FortiOS 7.6.0 Best Practices).
fortigate-session-dirty.beforePolicy: The VDOM is set to check-policy-option, so the accepting policy's own firewall-session-dirty, {option}, applies to changes to that policy (FortiOS 7.6.6 CLI reference, config firewall policy; Technical Tip: Information about firewall-session-dirty).
fortigate-session-dirty.changeTextEditToDeny: The administrator sets the accepting policy's action to deny.
fortigate-session-dirty.changeTextNarrow: The administrator changes the accepting policy's addresses or services, and the session no longer matches it.
fortigate-session-dirty.changeTextDenyAbove: The administrator adds a new deny policy above the accepting one, and the session's traffic matches it.
fortigate-session-dirty.changeTextStill: The administrator adds an address to the accepting policy, and the session still matches it.
fortigate-session-dirty.effectDirty: The policy change marks the session dirty: its next packet is checked against the policies as they now stand (FortiOS 7.6.0 Best Practices; Technical Tip: 'Dirty' session).
fortigate-session-dirty.effectPersistent: A persistent session is not revalidated against policy changes, which apply to new sessions only (FortiOS 7.6.0 Best Practices).
fortigate-session-dirty.effectPolicyAll: The policy's check-all flushes the sessions it accepted, which must be matched against the policies again (FortiOS 7.6.6 CLI reference, config firewall policy).
fortigate-session-dirty.effectPolicyNew: The policy's check-new continues to allow the sessions it has already accepted (FortiOS 7.6.6 CLI reference, config firewall policy).
fortigate-session-dirty.effectUndocumented: This changes another policy, a new one. The 7.6.6 CLI reference describes a policy's option for changes to that policy's own configuration, and no Fortinet document says whose option governs here.
fortigate-session-dirty.nextAllowed: Re-evaluated, the session still conforms to the policies, so it carries on (FortiOS 7.6.0 Best Practices).
fortigate-session-dirty.nextDeniedEdit: Re-evaluated, the session meets its policy's new deny action: it is flagged as blocked and removed from the session table, and its traffic is dropped (FortiOS 7.6.0 Best Practices).
fortigate-session-dirty.nextDeniedNarrow: Re-evaluated, the session no longer matches the policy that allowed it. strict-dirty-session-check, enabled by default, deletes such a session (FortiOS 7.6.6 CLI reference, config system global), and its traffic is dropped (FortiOS 7.6.0 Best Practices).
fortigate-session-dirty.nextDeniedAbove: Re-evaluated, the session now meets the deny policy first: it no longer matches a valid policy, so it is blocked and its traffic is dropped (FortiOS 7.6.0 Best Practices; Technical Tip: Troubleshooting FortiGate traffic drops caused by dirty session handler and policy 0).
fortigate-session-dirty.nextUnchecked: Not re-evaluated: the session keeps the decision taken at its first packet and flows until it ends.
fortigate-session-dirty.nextUndocumented: Whether this packet is re-evaluated is not documented.
fortigate-session-dirty.verdictDropped: Dropped at its next packet: the policies no longer allow it.
fortigate-session-dirty.verdictRevalidated: Re-evaluated and still allowed: the session carries on.
fortigate-session-dirty.verdictUncheckedDenied: Still flowing, though a new session with the same addresses and ports would now be denied.
fortigate-session-dirty.verdictUncheckedAllowed: Still flowing without a new check; a new session would be allowed too.
fortigate-session-dirty.verdictUndocumented: Not decided: Fortinet's documents do not cover this combination.
fortigate-session-dirty.noteTest: A test that reuses this session says nothing about the change. Test with a new session and read its policy_id in diagnose sys session list.

cors-preflight.title: Follow a cross-origin fetch through the preflight and the CORS checks
cors-preflight.lede: A script on https://app.example calls fetch() on https://api.example/orders. Set the request and the server's answers, and see whether the browser sends a preflight first and why, the preflight it sends, whether each response passes, and what the script can read. Names after # are anchors in the WHATWG Fetch Standard (Last Updated 19 October 2026). Try the Example: a POST with Content-Type: application/json to a server that answers its GET requests correctly.
cors-preflight.scope: the preflight cache across requests (this browser starts with an empty one), the use-CORS-preflight flag (upload listeners, streamed bodies), the request body and the Content-Type a browser adds for it, Range, redirects, a preflight answered with a status other than 200 to 299, Access-Control-Expose-Headers, which cookies include actually sends (cookie attributes and the browser's third-party cookie settings), and any browser's own ceiling on Access-Control-Max-Age: the standard leaves that limit to the browser, and no browser vendor's document was read for this lab. The server sends the same headers on the preflight response and on the actual response.
cors-preflight.xhAcceptLong: Accept: a list of types longer than 128 bytes
cors-preflight.credSameOrigin: same-origin, fetch's default (credentials only to the same origin)
cors-preflight.scriptTypeError: gets a network error: fetch() rejects with a TypeError
cors-preflight.preflightIntro: The preflight the browser sends first, without credentials (#cors-preflight-fetch-0):
cors-preflight.simpleWithHeaders: No preflight: {method} is a CORS-safelisted method and every header the script set is CORS-safelisted (#cors-safelisted-method, #cors-safelisted-request-header).
cors-preflight.simpleNoHeaders: No preflight: {method} is a CORS-safelisted method and the script set no header (#cors-safelisted-method).
cors-preflight.whyMethod: {method} is not a CORS-safelisted method; only GET, HEAD and POST are (#cors-safelisted-method).
cors-preflight.whyTooLong: The value of {name} is {n} bytes, and a safelisted header's value may not exceed 128 (#cors-safelisted-request-header).
cors-preflight.whyUnsafeByte: The value of {name} holds a byte the standard marks CORS-unsafe (#cors-unsafe-request-header-byte).
cors-preflight.whyBadBytes: The value of {name} holds a byte outside the few its safelist allows (#cors-safelisted-request-header).
cors-preflight.whyContentType: Content-Type {essence} is not one of the three safelisted types: application/x-www-form-urlencoded, multipart/form-data and text/plain (#cors-safelisted-request-header).
cors-preflight.whyOverTotal: The safelisted header values add up to more than 1024 bytes, so {name} counts as unsafe too (#cors-unsafe-request-header-names).
cors-preflight.preflightPass: Passes: the response passes the CORS check, the method is allowed, and every header named in Access-Control-Request-Headers is allowed (#cors-preflight-fetch-0).
cors-preflight.maxAgeDefault: No Access-Control-Max-Age: the browser may reuse this result for 5 seconds, the standard's default (#http-responses).
cors-preflight.maxAgeSet: The browser may reuse this result for {n} seconds, or for less if it imposes its own limit, which the standard allows (#cors-preflight-fetch-0).
cors-preflight.preflightFail: Fails: {reason} The actual request is never sent.
cors-preflight.failAcaoMissing: the response has no Access-Control-Allow-Origin, so the CORS check fails (#cors-check).
cors-preflight.failAcaoWildcard: Access-Control-Allow-Origin is *, which the CORS check refuses when the credentials mode is include (#cors-check).
cors-preflight.failAcaoMismatch: Access-Control-Allow-Origin is {value}, not the page's serialized origin, {origin}, and the comparison is exact (#cors-check).
cors-preflight.failAcacMissing: the credentials mode is include and Access-Control-Allow-Credentials is not exactly true (#cors-check).
cors-preflight.failMethod: {method} is neither CORS-safelisted nor listed in Access-Control-Allow-Methods (#cors-preflight-fetch-0).
cors-preflight.failMethodWildcard: Access-Control-Allow-Methods is *, which stands for any method only when the credentials mode is not include, so {method} is not allowed (#cors-preflight-fetch-0).
cors-preflight.failAuthorization: Authorization is not named in Access-Control-Allow-Headers, and * never stands for it (#cors-non-wildcard-request-header-name).
cors-preflight.failHeaderWildcard: Access-Control-Allow-Headers is *, which stands for any header only when the credentials mode is not include, so {header} is not allowed (#cors-preflight-fetch-0).
cors-preflight.actualNotSent: Never sent: a failed preflight is a network error, and nothing else leaves the browser (#cors-preflight-fetch-0, #http-fetch).
cors-preflight.actualSent: The browser sends the {method} request with an Origin header and without credentials.
cors-preflight.actualSentCookies: The browser sends the {method} request with an Origin header and the user's cookies.
cors-preflight.actualPass: Its response passes the CORS check (#cors-check).
cors-preflight.actualFail: Its response fails: {reason} The server has already received the request and may have acted on it (#http-fetch).
cors-preflight.verdictReadable: Reads the status, the body and the safelisted response headers ({headers}); any other header only if Access-Control-Expose-Headers names it (#concept-filtered-response-cors).
cors-preflight.verdictBlockedResponse: A network error: fetch() rejects with a TypeError, after the server has received the request (#fetch-method).
cors-preflight.verdictBlockedPreflight: A network error: fetch() rejects with a TypeError, and the actual request never left the browser (#fetch-method).
cors-preflight.noteServer: CORS decides what a script may read and, through the preflight, what it may send. curl, servers and mobile apps never consult it, and a simple request reaches the server whatever the answer.

kerberos-exchanges.title: Walk the three Kerberos exchanges, key by key
kerberos-exchanges.lede: The user alice reaches HTTP/intranet.example.com through the AS, TGS and AP exchanges. Set the clocks, the acceptable skew, pre-authentication, an expired ticket and where the SPN is registered, and see which key seals each message, what it carries, and the first check that fails, with its RFC 4120 error name. Try the Example: the client and the KDC agree, but the web server's clock runs 7 minutes fast.
kerberos-exchanges.scope: clients that correct their own clock from the KDC's (the optional offset of RFC 4120 section 3.1.5; MIT's kdc_timesync, on by default), the KDC's time check on the TGS request (a client whose clock is off already fails at the AS exchange here), tickets not yet valid, lifetimes and renewal, key version numbers, cross-realm referrals, FAST, PKINIT, encryption types, the SPNEGO messages around the ticket, the PAC and the authorization decision. The KDC's time check on the AS exchange follows Microsoft's documentation for Active Directory, because RFC 4120 does not specify it; when two conditions fail at once, the lab reports the one RFC 4120 describes first.
kerberos-exchanges.clientOffset: Client's clock against the KDC's (minutes, + is ahead)
kerberos-exchanges.skew: Acceptable skew (minutes; 5 by default in Active Directory and in MIT Kerberos)
kerberos-exchanges.preauthSent: the client sends an encrypted timestamp
kerberos-exchanges.ticketsFresh: a fresh logon, then the first visit
kerberos-exchanges.ticketsTgtExpired: the TGT has expired since logon
kerberos-exchanges.ticketsStExpired: the cached service ticket has expired
kerberos-exchanges.spnRegistered: on {account}, whose key is in the service's keytab
kerberos-exchanges.keyService: the long-term key of {account} (in the keytab)
kerberos-exchanges.partApRep: encrypted part (when mutual authentication is asked for)
kerberos-exchanges.carriesAsReqBody: client alice@EXAMPLE.COM, server krbtgt/EXAMPLE.COM, a nonce
kerberos-exchanges.carriesTicket: {key}, the client's name, authtime, start and end times, flags
kerberos-exchanges.carriesRepEnc: {key}, the nonce, the ticket's times, the server's name
kerberos-exchanges.carriesTgsAuthenticator: the client's name, its time (ctime), a checksum of the request body
kerberos-exchanges.carriesApRep: the authenticator's ctime and cusec, sent back
kerberos-exchanges.kvKdcGap: Client and KDC clocks apart by
kerberos-exchanges.kvServiceGap: Client and service clocks apart by
kerberos-exchanges.asOk: The KDC finds alice, decrypts her timestamp with her long-term key and finds it {kdcGap} min from its own clock, within the {skew}-minute skew. It returns the TGT, sealed in the TGS's key so that alice cannot read it, and the TGS session key, sealed in hers (RFC 4120, 3.1.3).
kerberos-exchanges.asPreauth: The account requires pre-authentication and the request carries none: KDC_ERR_PREAUTH_REQUIRED, with METHOD-DATA naming the methods the KDC accepts (RFC 4120, 3.1.3). A client able to pre-authenticate retries with an encrypted timestamp; Microsoft notes that most MIT clients do, and that the error can then be ignored.
kerberos-exchanges.asSkew: The client's timestamp is {kdcGap} min from the KDC's clock, more than the {skew}-minute skew: KRB_AP_ERR_SKEW. RFC 4120 does not specify this check; Microsoft documents it for Active Directory's TGT requests (event 4768).
kerberos-exchanges.tgsOk: The KDC decrypts the TGT with its own key, opens the authenticator with the TGS session key, looks {spn} up and finds it on {account}. It returns a service ticket sealed in the key of {account}, and the service session key sealed in the TGS session key (RFC 4120, 3.3).
kerberos-exchanges.tgsExpired: The TGT is past its end time by more than the skew: KRB_AP_ERR_TKT_EXPIRED. The TGS accepts no expired ticket; the client needs a new AS exchange (RFC 4120, 3.3 and 3.2.3).
kerberos-exchanges.tgsUnknown: No account holds {spn}: KDC_ERR_S_PRINCIPAL_UNKNOWN, Server not found in Kerberos database (RFC 4120, 3.3.3 and 7.5.9). The KDC has no key to seal a ticket in.
kerberos-exchanges.apOk: The service decrypts the ticket with the key of {account} from its keytab, opens the authenticator with the service session key and finds the client's time {serviceGap} min from its own, within the {skew}-minute skew. The user alice is authenticated; an AP-REP proves the service to her if she asked for mutual authentication (RFC 4120, 3.2.3 and 3.2.4).
kerberos-exchanges.apBadIntegrity: The KDC sealed the ticket in the key of {other}; the service tries the key of {account} and decryption fails: KRB_AP_ERR_BAD_INTEGRITY, as RFC 4120 puts it, "chances are good that different keys were used to encrypt and decrypt" (3.2.3).
kerberos-exchanges.apSkew: The time in the authenticator is {serviceGap} min from the service's clock, more than the {skew}-minute skew: KRB_AP_ERR_SKEW (RFC 4120, 3.2.3). The KDC was satisfied; the service is not.
kerberos-exchanges.apExpired: The service ticket is past its end time by more than the skew: KRB_AP_ERR_TKT_EXPIRED (RFC 4120, 3.2.3). The client asks the TGS for a new one.
kerberos-exchanges.verdictOk: Authenticated, with no prompt, and the password never crossed the network.
kerberos-exchanges.verdictRenew: Stopped by {error}; the client recovers with a new {again} exchange.
kerberos-exchanges.noteKeys: Only the KDC holds every long-term key. The client carries tickets it cannot read, and proves itself with authenticators sealed in the session keys those tickets hold.
kerberos-exchanges.errorOffset: Each clock offset must be a whole number of minutes from {lo} to {hi}.
kerberos-exchanges.errorSkew: The acceptable skew must be a whole number of minutes from {lo} to {hi}.
kerberos-exchanges.errorChoice: A setting is outside the values the lab offers.

dnssec-chain.title: Follow a DNSSEC validation from the root's key to the answer
dnssec-chain.lede: A validating resolver asks for www.example.org. A and checks each link from its trust anchor, the root's key, through ., org. and example.org. Break the chain one way at a time and see the state the answer ends in (Secure, Insecure, Bogus or Indeterminate), what the client receives, and the RFC rule that decided. Try the Example: example.org. is signed, but org. has no DS for it.
dnssec-chain.scope: computing any signature or digest (key tags and digests here are labels), negative answers and NSEC or NSEC3 proofs other than the proof that a DS does not exist, a DS RRset with several records or algorithms, several RRSIGs over one RRset (as during a double-signature rollover), the RRSIG over the DS RRset itself, wildcards, CNAMEs, TTLs and caching, RFC 5011 trust anchor updates, and local policy such as negative trust anchors.
dnssec-chain.faultDsMismatch: the DS no longer matches, after a KSK roll
dnssec-chain.faultNoDs: no DS at a delegation (with signed proof)
dnssec-chain.faultUnsupportedAlg: an algorithm the validator does not implement ({alg})
dnssec-chain.faultNoAnchor: the validator has no trust anchor
dnssec-chain.placeTldKeys: over the DNSKEY set of org.
dnssec-chain.placeZoneKeys: over the DNSKEY set of example.org.
dnssec-chain.placeZoneDelegation: the delegation from org. to example.org.
dnssec-chain.anchorNone: The validator has no trust anchor, so nothing tells it that any part of the tree should be signed (RFC 4033, section 5).
dnssec-chain.anchorMatch: The trust anchor, key {tag} (algorithm {alg}), is in the root's DNSKEY set with the Zone Key flag (RFC 4035, section 5); the set holds {keys}.
dnssec-chain.dsMatch: The DS for {zone} in the parent zone, {parent}, authenticated by the parent's key {by}, names key {tag}, algorithm {alg}, with the digest of key {digestOf}; the DNSKEY set of {zone}, which holds {keys}, has that key (RFC 4035, section 5.2).
dnssec-chain.rrsigValid: The RRSIG that key {signer} made over the set is valid in time (RFC 4035, section 5.3.1).
dnssec-chain.rrsigExpired: But the RRSIG that key {signer} made over the set has expired: the validator's time must not be later than its Expiration field (RFC 4035, section 5.3.1).
dnssec-chain.rrsigMissing: But no RRSIG by key {signer} covers the set, so the set cannot be authenticated (RFC 4035, section 5.2, third condition).
dnssec-chain.rrsigMissingRoot: But no RRSIG covers the root's DNSKEY set, so the anchor cannot authenticate it (RFC 4035, section 5).
dnssec-chain.dsMismatch: The DS for {zone} in the parent zone, {parent}, still names key {tag} (algorithm {alg}, digest of key {digestOf}), but after a key roll the DNSKEY set of {zone} holds {keys}: no key matches its key tag, algorithm and digest (RFC 4035, section 5.2, second condition). The delegation says {zone} is signed, and its keys cannot be authenticated.
dnssec-chain.noDs: The parent zone, {parent}, has no DS for {zone} and proves it with an NSEC signed by its key {by}, whose type bitmap has NS but not DS or SOA (RFC 4035, section 5.2; RFC 6840, section 4.4). There is no authentication path into {zone}, whatever keys and signatures it publishes, here {keys}.
dnssec-chain.unsupportedAlg: The DS for {zone} uses algorithm {alg}, which this validator does not implement, as the IANA registry requires (MUST NOT). With no DS left that it can use, it treats {zone} as unsigned (RFC 4035, section 5.2; RFC 6840, section 5.2).
dnssec-chain.answerOk: The A record set carries an RRSIG by key {signer}, a key of the authenticated DNSKEY set of example.org.; it is valid in time and the signature verifies (RFC 4035, sections 5.3.1 and 5.3.3).
dnssec-chain.answerExpired: The RRSIG by key {signer} over the A record set has expired (RFC 4035, section 5.3.1), and no other RRSIG covers it: an RRset is Bogus only when every RRSIG fails (RFC 6840, section 5.4).
dnssec-chain.answerMissing: The A record set arrives without an RRSIG, from a zone the chain says is signed: data that the DNSSEC records say should be there is missing (RFC 4035, section 4.3).
dnssec-chain.belowInsecure: Not validated: it lies below the insecure delegation.
dnssec-chain.belowIndeterminate: Not validated: there is no trust anchor above it.
dnssec-chain.aboveFailed: Not checked: the chain broke above it.
dnssec-chain.clientAd: the answer, with the AD bit
dnssec-chain.clientNoAd: the answer, without the AD bit
dnssec-chain.clientServfail: SERVFAIL (RCODE 2); the data only if the query set CD
dnssec-chain.verdictSecure: Secure: a chain from the trust anchor to the answer, and every signature verified (RFC 4033, section 5). The resolver sets AD.
dnssec-chain.verdictInsecure: Insecure: signed proof that {zone} has no DS the validator can use (RFC 4033, section 5; RFC 4035, section 4.3). The answer comes back without AD: not a failure, and not vouched for either.
dnssec-chain.verdictBogus: Bogus: the chain says the data should be signed, and it does not validate (RFC 4035, section 4.3). The resolver answers SERVFAIL, RCODE 2, and returns the data only to a query with CD set (RFC 4035, section 5.5).
dnssec-chain.verdictIndeterminate: Indeterminate: no trust anchor covers this part of the tree (RFC 4033, section 5). The answer comes back without AD, and a client cannot tell it from Insecure.
dnssec-chain.noteLabels: The root's key tag 38696 is the real anchor, KSK-2024, algorithm 8; every other key tag is an invented label, and a digest is named by the key it was made from. Nothing is computed: the lab models the decisions.

tcl-substitution.title: Read a line the way Tcl reads it
tcl-substitution.lede: Type one line of an Expect script, or pick a case. The lab splits it into words by Tcl's twelve rules and shows what each word becomes, what the command receives, and where Tcl would stop with an error.
tcl-substitution.scope: running commands: a bracket stays in its word as the result of its command, which the lab never runs; the variables are the fixed set shown; one command per line, with what follows a semicolon only named; and \U escapes above U+FFFF, which Tcl 8.6 and Tcl 9 read differently.
tcl-substitution.variables: The variables the line can read

part.cmd: {raw} runs the command {name}; the word holds its result
part.cmdUnknownName: {raw} runs a command whose name is itself substituted

tcl-substitution.empty: Nothing to read: the line is empty.
tcl-substitution.comment: Tcl reads this line as a comment and runs nothing.
tcl-substitution.stopCommand: Tcl stops when it looks the command up.
tcl-substitution.receives: Tcl calls {command} with {count, plural, one {# argument} other {# arguments}}:
tcl-substitution.receivesUnknownCount: Tcl calls {command}; how many arguments it gets depends on what the expanded command returns:
tcl-substitution.receivesFromCommand: Tcl calls the command named by a substitution, with {count, plural, one {# argument} other {# arguments}}:
tcl-substitution.unknownExpansion: the words of the command's result, each one a separate argument

why.missing-quote: A word that starts with a double quote ends at the next double quote, and this one never finds it (rule 4).
why.missing-close-brace: A word that starts with a brace ends at the matching brace, and this one never finds it (rule 6).
why.missing-close-bracket: A command substitution runs to the matching close bracket, and this one never finds it (rule 7).
why.extra-after-quote: After the closing double quote only white space or the end of the command may follow; anything else is an error.
why.extra-after-brace: After the closing brace only white space or the end of the command may follow; anything else is an error.
why.missing-varname-brace: A name written as $'{'name'}' runs to the next close brace, and there is none (rule 8).
why.missing-paren: An array element's index runs to the close parenthesis, and there is none (rule 8).
why.no-such-variable: The name was read by rule 8 and no variable has it. A name stops at the first character that is not a letter, digit or underscore, so check where it ended; $'{'name'}' sets the limit yourself.
why.no-such-element: The array exists but has no element with that index.
why.not-array: The name holds a plain value, so it has no elements: drop the parentheses or write $'{'name'}' to keep them as text.
why.variable-is-array: The name is an array, so it needs an element: $name(index).
why.invalid-command: Tcl looked the command up and found none with that name. Inside double quotes a bracket runs a command: write the word in braces when the brackets belong to a pattern.
why.list-brace-extra: Rule 5 reads the value as a list, and a braced element there is followed by something other than a space.
why.list-quote-extra: Rule 5 reads the value as a list, and a quoted element there is followed by something other than a space.
why.list-unmatched-brace: Rule 5 reads the value as a list, and an open brace in it has no partner.
why.list-unmatched-quote: Rule 5 reads the value as a list, and an open double quote in it has no partner.

note.braced-escape: Word {word} is in braces, so each backslash sequence in it stays two characters: a send would type a backslash and a letter, and a glob pattern would read the letter.
note.braced-dollar: Word {word} is in braces, so its dollar sign stays as written: no variable is read.
note.braced-bracket: Word {word} is in braces, so its brackets reach the command as written: no command runs, and a regular expression keeps its character class.
note.send-ends-cr: The string ends in a carriage return, the \r a line-buffered program waits for.
note.send-ends-backslash-r: The string ends in a backslash and the letter r, not in a carriage return: the program keeps waiting for the end of the line.
