note.send-no-return: The string does not end in \r: a program that reads lines will not act on it yet.
note.expect-one-line-block: This braced block is on one line, so Expect 5.45.4 reads it as one glob pattern, not as patterns and bodies. Start the block with a line break after the opening brace.
note.rest-comment: After the semicolon, the rest of the line is a comment.
note.rest-command: After the semicolon comes another command; the lab reads the first one only.

error.bad-char: Use printable ASCII characters only (a tab is allowed).
error.not-modelled-unicode: A \U escape above U+FFFF is left out: Tcl 8.6 and Tcl 9 read it differently.

expect-buffer-matching.title: Match patterns against Expect's buffer
expect-buffer-matching.lede: Type what a program prints, choose how it arrives, and list up to four patterns in the order an expect command gives them. The lab tries them the way Expect 5.45.4 does and shows which one wins, when, and what expect_out holds.
expect-buffer-matching.scope: the timeout, eof and the other keywords; match_max and full_buffer (the buffer here stays far below 2,000 characters); expect_before and expect_after; -indices and -notransfer; nulls; reads that split the output elsewhere than the three arrival choices; characters outside ASCII; and the -re constructs the lab names when it refuses them.
expect-buffer-matching.arrivalWaiting: Already in the buffer when expect starts
expect-buffer-matching.arrivalOneRead: In one read, after expect starts
expect-buffer-matching.pty: Through a terminal: each line break arrives as \r\n
expect-buffer-matching.patternsCaption: The patterns, in the order the expect command lists them, written as Expect receives them (as if in braces)
expect-buffer-matching.notTried: not tried: an earlier pattern matched
expect-buffer-matching.verdictNone: No pattern matches: expect keeps waiting for more output.
expect-buffer-matching.verdictBefore: Pattern {row} matches before any output has arrived.
expect-buffer-matching.verdictMatch: Pattern {row} matches, with {arrived} of the {total} characters arrived.
expect-buffer-matching.noteBefore: A pattern that can match an empty buffer does not wait. The manual says it of * and -re .*, which flush the buffer without reading more output.
expect-buffer-matching.noteWaiting: Expect now waits for more output. The timeout, the end of the output or a full buffer decide what happens next, and without a timeout arm the script simply carries on.
expect-buffer-matching.noteEmptyAtStart: In Expect 5.45.4 a match or group that is empty and sits at the very start of the buffer reads back as the whole buffer as it stood, although it matched nothing (run on 27/10/2026).
expect-buffer-matching.noteBackslashLetter: Pattern {row} holds \r, \n or \t as a backslash and a letter. Glob reads a backslash as a sign that the next character is ordinary, so the pattern means the letter itself: write it in double quotes in the script, or use -re.
expect-buffer-matching.noteNocaseBracket: Pattern {row} uses a bracket with -nocase. In Expect 5.45.4 the bracket's characters are lowered and the output's are not, so the bracket never matches a capital letter.

error.bad-output-char: Use printable ASCII characters, tabs and line breaks only.
error.bad-pattern-char: Pattern {row} holds a character outside printable ASCII.
error.re-invalid: Tcl refuses pattern {row}: couldn't compile regular expression pattern: {reason}.
error.re-not-modelled: Pattern {row} uses {what}, which Tcl accepts but this lab does not model.
error.too-complex: This combination takes more work than the lab allows: shorten the output or the pattern, or choose another way of arriving.

construct.escape: an escape the lab leaves out
construct.embedded-option: an embedded option such as (?i) (use -nocase instead)
construct.director: a director (a pattern that starts with three asterisks)
construct.literal-brace: a brace that is not a repetition count
construct.quantified-group: a repeated group that captures, or that mixes greedy and non-greedy quantifiers
construct.capture-in-alternation: a capturing group inside one of several | branches
construct.too-many-captures: more than nine capturing groups (Expect keeps nine)

expect-timeout-timeline.title: Watch one expect wait, second by second
expect-timeout-timeline.lede: One expect waits for a device's prompt while the device prints a progress line every few seconds. Choose how the script sets its timeout, what the arm for the progress line does, how the device ends and which keyword arms the expect carries, then follow the timer: when it restarts, when it runs out, and what the script does next. Try the Example: exp_continue -continue_timer and no timeout arm.
expect-timeout-timeline.scope: the clock's fine detail. The lab puts every event on a whole second and counts an event in the very second the timer runs out as too late, where a real run races it; Expect 5.45.4 also keeps its deadline in whole seconds of the clock, so once text has arrived a real wait can end up to a second early or late (expect.c). It leaves out pattern order when several patterns match at once, expect_before and expect_after, full_buffer and match_max, and the time a program takes to start.
expect-timeout-timeline.modeDefault: Not at all: the default, {s} s
expect-timeout-timeline.progressArm: The arm for the progress line
expect-timeout-timeline.armNone: None: the line is just text
expect-timeout-timeline.errorChoice: Choose one of the options offered.
expect-timeout-timeline.errorTimeout: Enter a whole number of seconds from 0 to {max} for set timeout.
expect-timeout-timeline.errorEvery: Enter a whole gap from 1 to {max} seconds between progress lines.
expect-timeout-timeline.errorCount: Enter a whole number of progress lines from 0 to {max}.
expect-timeout-timeline.errorEndTime: Enter a whole second from 1 to {max} for the prompt or the eof.
expect-timeout-timeline.errorEndBefore: The device ends after its progress lines: the prompt or the eof must come after second {last}.
expect-timeout-timeline.codeNoTimeout: # timeout not set: the default is {s} s
expect-timeout-timeline.outcomeShort: {outcome, select, prompt {the prompt's arm} progressArm {the progress arm, which has no exp_continue} timeoutArm {the timeout arm} defaultTimeout {the default arm, on the timeout} timeoutNull {no arm: the implicit null action} eofArm {the eof arm} defaultEof {the default arm, on eof} eofNoArm {no arm: an eof nothing handles} other {nothing: it is still waiting}}
expect-timeout-timeline.linesValue: {matched, plural, =0 {none matched} one {# matched} other {# matched}}; {unmatched, plural, =0 {none ignored} one {# matched no pattern} other {# matched no pattern}}
expect-timeout-timeline.stepStart: the expect starts, and with it the timer: it runs out at second {deadline}.
expect-timeout-timeline.stepStartForever: the expect starts with no time limit.
expect-timeout-timeline.stepUnmatched: a progress line arrives and matches no pattern. It waits in the buffer, and the deadline stays at second {deadline}: text that matches nothing does not restart the timer.
expect-timeout-timeline.stepUnmatchedForever: a progress line arrives and matches no pattern; it waits in the buffer.
expect-timeout-timeline.stepRestart: the progress line matches, and its body ends in exp_continue, which restarts the timer: the new deadline is second {deadline}.
expect-timeout-timeline.stepRestartForever: the progress line matches, and exp_continue keeps the expect going; with no time limit there is no deadline to move.
expect-timeout-timeline.stepKeep: the progress line matches, and exp_continue -continue_timer keeps the expect going without restarting the timer: the deadline stays at second {deadline}.
expect-timeout-timeline.stepKeepForever: the progress line matches, and exp_continue -continue_timer keeps the expect going; there is no deadline.
expect-timeout-timeline.stepReturn: the progress line matches. Its body does not call exp_continue, so the expect returns here, and the script's next line runs while the device is still busy.
expect-timeout-timeline.stepPrompt: the prompt arrives and matches: the expect returns and the script goes on.
expect-timeout-timeline.stepEofArm: the device closes the connection: the eof arm runs.
expect-timeout-timeline.stepDefaultEof: the device closes the connection: the default arm runs, as it would for a timeout.
expect-timeout-timeline.stepEofNoArm: the device closes the connection. No arm handles eof, so the expect returns at once, without waiting for the timer, and the script's next line runs.
expect-timeout-timeline.stepTimeoutArm: the timer runs out: the timeout arm runs.
expect-timeout-timeline.stepDefaultTimeout: the timer runs out: the default arm runs, as it would for eof.
expect-timeout-timeline.stepTimeoutNull: the timer runs out. No arm handles timeout, so expect takes the implicit null action: it returns as if nothing had gone wrong, and the script's next line runs.
expect-timeout-timeline.stepForever: No prompt, no eof and no deadline: with timeout -1 the expect waits forever.
expect-timeout-timeline.verdictProgressArm: The expect returned at second {at}, on the first progress line, before the device was ready.
expect-timeout-timeline.verdictTimeoutArm: No prompt in time: at second {at} an arm noticed, so the script can report the failure and stop.
expect-timeout-timeline.verdictTimeoutNull: The script carries on blind from second {at}: no error and no arm, and its next send goes to a device that never showed its prompt.
expect-timeout-timeline.verdictEofArm: The connection closed at second {at}, and an arm noticed: the script can report it.
expect-timeout-timeline.verdictEofNoArm: The connection closed at second {at} and the script carries on blind: its next send fails with "spawn id not open".
expect-timeout-timeline.verdictForever: The expect never returns: the script hangs, and so does whatever started it.
expect-timeout-timeline.alternative: With {form, select, continue {plain exp_continue} other {exp_continue -continue_timer}} instead, the same device would {outcome, select, prompt {see the prompt matched at second {at}} timeoutArm {end with the timeout arm at second {at}} defaultTimeout {end with the default arm at second {at}} timeoutNull {end with the implicit null action at second {at}} eofArm {end with the eof arm at second {at}} defaultEof {end with the default arm at second {at}} eofNoArm {end with an eof that no arm handles, at second {at}} progressArm {end at second {at}} other {leave the expect waiting forever}}.
expect-timeout-timeline.noteTimeoutNull: After a timeout that no arm handles, expect_out(buffer) is not updated: it still holds the text of the previous match, so a script that reads it now reads the wrong moment.
expect-timeout-timeline.noteEofNoArm: After an eof the spawn id is closed: a send or an expect on it raises an error, and wait collects the program's exit status.

scripted-monitor-dialogue.title: Play a Scripted monitor against a server, line by line
scripted-monitor-dialogue.lede: Pick a protocol, a server and a mistake to make in the script, then follow each line beside the reply it was compared with. Try the IMAP Example, where the expected text is in the reply but not at its start.
scripted-monitor-dialogue.scope: the monitor's timing (Interval and Timeout, which the monitor timing lab models), TLS, logging in, every other command, servers that answer only in part, and everything F5's published rules do not settle, which the lab reports as undetermined rather than guessing.

mistakeOption.two-spaces: two spaces after expect on line 3
mistakeOption.after-quote: text after the closing quote on line 3
mistakeOption.not-prefix: expects text from the middle of a reply
mistakeOption.code-space: expects the reply code and a space
mistakeOption.no-crlf: the first send has no CR LF

outcome.matched: matched: the reply starts with the text

scripted-monitor-dialogue.moreSteps: {shown, plural, one {# line} other {# lines}} of {total} shown; show all lines for the verdict.
scripted-monitor-dialogue.verdictPass: The check passes: every expect matched the start of its reply.
scripted-monitor-dialogue.verdictOpen: The check cannot be decided at line {line}: {why}

reason.not-prefix: the text is in the reply, at character {at}, but F5 matches only a prefix of the response.
reason.mismatch: the reply does not start with the text.
reason.after-quote: F5 says any characters that follow a closing quotation mark will break the match.
reason.crlf-after-quote: the file has CR-LF line endings, so a CR follows the closing quotation mark, and F5 says that breaks the match.
reason.no-reply: no reply arrives, and F5 marks a target that does not respond within the Timeout down.
reason.separator: F5 requires exactly one space after the keyword and does not say what happens otherwise.
reason.other: see the explainer for the reason.

scripted-monitor-dialogue.rulesNone: nothing: the script keeps every rule F5 states.

rule.S1: S1, CR-LF line endings where F5 requires LF.
rule.S2: S2, not exactly one space after the keyword.
rule.S3: S3, characters after a closing quotation mark.
rule.S6: S6, a send with no line ending.
rule.S16: S16, a reply code and a space, which never starts a multi-line reply.

scripted-monitor-dialogue.prefixNote: F5 compares each expect with the start of the response only: no wildcards, no regular expressions, no search inside the reply.
scripted-monitor-dialogue.timingNote: F5 documents no timer inside the script: whether a member is marked down depends on the monitor's Interval and Timeout (by default 10 and 31 seconds for a Scripted monitor).

python-bytes-and-text.title: Send a text through encode and decode
python-bytes-and-text.lede: Type a text, pick the codec and error handler that turn it into bytes and the ones that read the bytes back, and follow it as CPython 3.13 would: the bytes, the text that returns, or the exception with its exact message. Try UTF-8 read as cp1252, or Latin-1 bytes read as UTF-8 with each handler in turn.
python-bytes-and-text.handlerSurrogateescape: surrogateescape: keep each byte as U+DCxx
python-bytes-and-text.stepText: The text, {count, plural, one {# code point} other {# code points}}:
python-bytes-and-text.stepEncoded: Encoded with {codec}, {count, plural, one {# byte} other {# bytes}}:
python-bytes-and-text.stepDecoded: Decoded with {codec}, {count, plural, one {# code point} other {# code points}}:
python-bytes-and-text.stepNotReached: Decoding is never reached: Python stopped at the encoding.
python-bytes-and-text.verdictRoundTrip: Round trip: the same text came back.
python-bytes-and-text.verdictMojibake: Mojibake: both steps worked, but the bytes were read with a codec other than the one that wrote them, so a different text came back.

cv.bioShort: Rodolfo Nützmann is a Senior Technical Instructor at Red Education, teaching official F5, Fortinet, Extreme Networks and Netskope courses to organizations worldwide, in English or Brazilian Portuguese. He has worked in networking and security for thirty years and was named an F5 DevCentral MVP three years running, from 2022 to 2024.
cv.bioMedium: Rodolfo Nützmann is a Senior Technical Instructor at Red Education, teaching official F5, Fortinet, Extreme Networks and Netskope courses to organizations worldwide, in English or Brazilian Portuguese. His career began in 1996 at Cabletron Systems and ran through Riverstone Networks, Cisco, IronPort, Enterasys and Juniper, implementation work for end customers and the F5 channel, before teaching became the whole job in 2020. Half of those thirty years were spent hands-on, in implementation and troubleshooting; the other half went into studying, designing and teaching resilient, secure network communications. He was named an F5 DevCentral MVP from 2022 to 2024, and he writes ronutz.com, a toolbox and record for network and security engineers. He is based in São Paulo, Brazil.
cv.bioLong: Rodolfo Nützmann is a Senior Technical Instructor at Red Education, where he delivers official, certified instructor-led courses on F5, Fortinet, Extreme Networks and Netskope to organizations worldwide, in English or Brazilian Portuguese. Teaching has been part of his work since 1997, in every role he has held: internetworking at Cabletron Systems, routing at Riverstone Networks, switching and network access control at Enterasys, JUNOS at Juniper, and vendor enablement through his years in F5's channel. In 2020 it became the whole job. Half of his thirty years in the field were spent hands-on, in implementation and troubleshooting; the other half went into studying, designing and teaching resilient, secure network communications. He holds instructor authorizations on all four platforms and current certifications from their vendors, was named an F5 DevCentral MVP three years running, from 2022 to 2024, and received Red Education's Captain's Call Award in 2025. He also writes ronutz.com, an open toolbox and record for network and security engineers: calculators that compute instead of guessing, explanations that cite the vendor's own documentation, and a history of the industry that anyone can check. He speaks at conferences and company events about technology and industry change and about the people behind the machines. He is based in São Paulo, Brazil.

tcpdump-filter-explainer.basis: The text you paste is parsed entirely in your browser: nothing is captured, run, resolved or sent. A command line is split into words as a POSIX shell would split it, then read option by option as the getopt_long of tcpdump 4.99.7 reads it. The filter is tokenized and parsed by our own code following libpcap's scanner and grammar, so defaults, the qualifier shorthand, precedence and the errors libpcap would report come out as libpcap produces them, for libpcap 1.10.7 and 1.11.0 alike, and where the two differ the explanation says which does what. Names are not looked up, so what a name resolves to, and what a link-layer type supports, are stated as unknown.

cgn-port-blocks.basis: Integer arithmetic run in your browser over the port field of a shared IPv4 address. Port blocks: the usable range (1024-65535 unless you change it) is cut into blocks and every subscriber's blocks are counted on one address, as RFC 6888's paired pooling requires; the log figures are RFC 7422's per-session numbers divided by the block size, the factor RFC 7768 gives. Deterministic mapping: RFC 7422 algorithm 0 (Sequential), step by step, forward and reverse, with the configuration record of its section 3. MAP: the port field A | PSID | j of RFC 7597 section 5.1, which MAP-T (RFC 7599) uses unchanged. Times are inputs; nothing reads a clock or the network.

bfd-timers.basis: Everything is computed in your browser from the numbers you enter, by the rules of RFC 5880: in each direction the agreed transmit interval is the larger of the sender's Desired Min TX and the receiver's Required Min RX (sections 6.8.2 and 6.8.7), each interval is shortened by a random 0 to 25% (10 to 25% with a Detect Mult of 1), and the receiver's detection time is the sender's Detect Mult times that interval in Asynchronous mode, or its own Detect Mult times its own agreed transmit interval in Demand mode (section 6.8.4). While the session is not Up every Desired Min TX is raised to one second (section 6.8.3). Echo follows section 6.8.9 and RFC 5883 section 3; Common Intervals follow RFC 7419. Implementation floors are reported only where a vendor document states one. The packet decoder reads the RFC 5880 section 4.1 layout and applies the section 6.8.6 receive checks. Behaviour is pinned by 42 golden vectors.

rpki-origin-validation.basis: The validation runs entirely in your browser on the route and the VRP list you supply: nothing is fetched from any RPKI repository, validator or route collector, so the verdict holds for that list only. It applies RFC 6811 section 2 word for word: a VRP covers the route when its prefix length is no longer than the route's and the two agree on every bit of the VRP's length, and matches when it also allows the route's length and names the route's origin; Valid means at least one VRP matches, Invalid that at least one covers and none matches, NotFound that none covers. AS 0 VRPs cover and never match (RFC 6811 section 2, RFC 6483 section 4), a route with origin AS 0 is refused as malformed (RFC 7607 section 2), and every VRP whose maxLength reaches past its own prefix is reported with the number of prefixes it authorizes, the case RFC 9319 asks operators to avoid. Behaviour is pinned by 40 golden vectors.

It is pure date arithmetic with no clock and no network: the version's License Check Date and the service check date are both inputs, so the same inputs always give the same answer.

Behaviour is pinned by 111 golden vectors, whose expected structure was written from the exception objects, not from the parser.

Each finding is an error when the specification says MUST or MUST NOT, a warning for SHOULD, MAY-refuse and deprecations, and a note otherwise. The maths is implemented directly from the FIRST.org CVSS v3.1 specification: the Impact and Exploitability sub-scores, the Base score, and, when those metrics are present, the Temporal and Environmental scores, using the specification's floating-point-safe Roundup. It looks nothing up and fetches nothing. The implementation is validated against officially published reference scores, so a canonical unauthenticated remote code execution scores 9.8, a scope change pushes it to 10.0, and a reflected cross-site scripting vector scores 6.1.

From the parsed request the tool derives both the explanation and every translation. It never sends the request or contacts the host (zero egress). Content-Type is resolved the way curl actually behaves, where -d defaults to application/x-www-form-urlencoded rather than JSON, which is a common source of confusion the tool flags.

cidr.basis: All results are computed locally from the blocks you enter, using standard IPv4 addressing arithmetic: one block's network, mask, host range and counts (a /31 counts two usable hosts, RFC 3021); variable-length subnets carved from a parent, largest block first, with the free space left as blocks; the minimal aggregate and single supernet of a list; and the overlaps and gaps among prefixes. The special-purpose classification compares a block with an embedded copy of the IANA IPv4 Special-Purpose Address Space registry, read on 2026-10-26 and shared with the SSRF URL classifier, plus the multicast range 224.0.0.0/4; nothing is looked up remotely and nothing is sent anywhere. Behaviour is pinned by 26 golden vectors.

Nothing is looked up remotely.

ssrf-url-classifier.basis: The classifier decides purely from the URL string and never touches the network: it does not resolve DNS and never issues the request. It extracts the host from the raw input (not from a normalizing URL parser, which would erase the obfuscation), decodes the inet_aton spellings of an IPv4 address (decimal, octal, hex, short-form), normalizes every IPv6 spelling to its RFC 5952 form, and decodes the IPv4 address carried inside six IPv6 layouts: IPv4-mapped (::ffff:0:0/96), the deprecated IPv4-compatible ::a.b.c.d, NAT64 (64:ff9b::/96 and 64:ff9b:1::/48), 6to4 (2002::/16) and Teredo (2001::/32, whose server address and XOR-obfuscated client address are both shown, the more internal one deciding). Every one of the 25 IPv4 and 25 IPv6 rows of the IANA Special-Purpose Address Space registries (read 2026-10-26; the CIDR calculator reads the same copy of the IPv4 rows) is matched most specific first and rated by its own name and Globally Reachable flag: not globally reachable rates reserved unless the row is loopback, private, link-local or CGNAT; globally reachable rates public but is named, and the anycast service addresses (192.0.0.9, 192.0.0.10, 2001:1::1, 2001:1::2, 2001:1::3, and the 6a44 relay 192.88.99.2) are flagged as such. The cloud metadata addresses (169.254.169.254, metadata.google.internal, fd00:ec2::254, 100.100.100.200) outrank their covering rows. Dangerous non-HTTP schemes (file, gopher, dict, ftp, ldap, and similar) and embedded credentials are flagged. The range definitions come from the IANA registries and the RFCs they cite, the SSRF guidance from the OWASP SSRF prevention cheat sheet; behaviour is pinned by 113 golden vectors.

hash-preimage-finder.basis: The search runs entirely in your browser: candidates are enumerated over the alphabet and length you choose, each one is hashed locally, and the first match is returned. There is no dictionary, no wordlist, and no precomputed table (unlike lookup services such as CrackStation), so nothing is stored and nothing is fetched. The MD5, SHA-1, and SHA-256 implementations are verified against their published test vectors. The keyspace is capped, so the tool only ever recovers trivially weak inputs, which is exactly the point: it demonstrates why fast, unsalted hashes fall for low-entropy secrets and hold for anything with real entropy, and it pairs every result with the defences (salting, slow KDFs, algorithm choice).

arcade.metaDescription: IT-themed arcade games on ronutz.com, built on classic game formulas and played in your browser for as long as you like; several have a daily run that goes to the public scoreboard.
arcade.title: Arcade
arcade.intro: Game formulas everyone knows, each given a theme of its own from networks, security or operations. Play for as long as you like; the games with a daily run are the same for everyone on a day of Coordinated Universal Time (UTC), and a finished run goes to the public scoreboard unless you switch sharing off. Your best scores stay in this browser.
arcade.shelfLink: The daily puzzles and the toys are on the /dev/fun shelf.

learnMethod.title: How this series reports
learnMethod.body: Each part reports what was published elsewhere (court records, official and parliamentary reports, peer-reviewed research, the platforms' own documents and the statements of the parties), cited with the date it was read. It does not declare who is right. Every claim is labelled by what supports it, from established to alleged or denied, and when a party is accused, its published response is given beside the accusation. What is not known is said to be unknown, and conclusions change when the evidence does. Where the evidence leaves something open, the part does not settle it: it leaves the reader questions to think about.

edit.title: Arranging the page
edit.entered: Arranging the page: move, resize, add or remove widgets. Every change is kept at once and can be undone. Press Done when you have finished.
edit.help: Use the buttons on each widget, or focus a widget's frame and use the keys below. Sizes apply on wider screens; a phone shows one column, in this order.
edit.keys: Keys on a focused frame: the arrow keys move it earlier or later, Home and End move it first or last, minus and plus change its size, Delete removes it, and Ctrl+Z (Cmd+Z on a Mac) undoes the last change.
edit.escape: To leave arranging, press Done. Your changes are already kept.

deskData.anotherBody: Your desk, the games' results, the pages you opened last and your settings (theme, language, glossary hints and the like) can follow you to another browser or device, in three ways. The Privacy page lists what moves and what stays with each browser, and why.
deskData.pairTitle: Pair with a QR code or a link
deskData.pairBody: This browser shows a QR code and a link that carry a sync code. Scan the QR code or open the link on the other browser and say yes there: both browsers then keep one copy on this site's server, encrypted here with a key made from the sync code, so the server cannot read it. From then on both sync after each change and when you come back to the tab.
deskData.pairShow: Show the QR code and link
deskData.pairQrLabel: QR code of the pairing link
deskData.pairWarn: The QR code and the link carry your sync code: whoever has them can read and change what you sync. Show them only to your own devices.
deskData.typedBody: The same sync code typed by hand, in groups of four, does what the pairing link does. The code is made in your browser; the site never receives it and cannot recover it, so keep it somewhere safe, such as a password manager.
deskData.settingsLater: Some settings from the other browser take effect on the next page you open.
deskData.serverlessBody: These two ways carry the same things directly from one browser to the other; nothing is sent to the site.
deskData.linkTooLong: This link would be {kb} KB long, more than the {max} KB a link carries reliably. Use the file instead.
deskData.timesTitle: When a setting changed in two browsers
deskData.timesBody: By default the latest change wins. To know which change came last, this browser notes the minute each of your settings (theme, language, shortcuts, an index page's view and the like) last changed here. Those times are kept in this browser and, when you sync, inside the encrypted copy, which only your own browsers can read; the site's server cannot read them.
deskData.timesKeep: Keep this browser's value when both changed (records no change times)
deskData.timesKeepNote: With this on, this browser notes no times, sends none and deletes the ones it kept; a setting changed in both browsers then keeps this browser's value when it syncs, and a browser syncing for the first time takes the other's.
